description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost. Transplant deep — buried stems grow extra roots. Cage or stake early; mulch once soil warms.
name: Tomato

varieties.name: Cherokee Purple
varieties.note: Indeterminate heirloom beefsteak; dusky rose-purple fruit.

varieties.name: Brandywine
varieties.note: Indeterminate heirloom; large pink beefsteak, rich flavor.

varieties.name: Roma
varieties.note: Determinate paste tomato; meaty, few seeds — for sauce.

varieties.name: Sungold
varieties.note: Indeterminate cherry; exceptionally sweet orange fruit.

varieties.name: Early Girl
varieties.note: Indeterminate; one of the earliest slicers.

description: Needs warm soil (75–85°F) to germinate — a heat mat helps a lot. Transplant only after nights stay above 55°F.
name: Pepper (Bell)

varieties.name: California Wonder
varieties.note: Classic blocky bell; green to red.

varieties.name: King of the North
varieties.note: Short-season bell; ripens reliably in cool summers.

description: Super-hots can take 3+ weeks to sprout — be patient. Slight stress (less water) once fruiting boosts heat.
name: Pepper (Hot)

varieties.name: Jalapeño
varieties.note: Medium heat; pick green or let ripen red.

varieties.name: Serrano
varieties.note: Hotter than jalapeño; great for salsa.

varieties.name: Habanero
varieties.note: Very hot; needs a long warm season.

description: Direct-sow after frost; hates transplanting. Trellis to save space and keep fruit straight. Pick often — big cukes slow the vine.
name: Cucumber

varieties.name: Lemon
varieties.note: Round yellow heirloom; mild, never bitter.

description: One plant feeds a neighborhood. Harvest at 6–8 inches; oversized fruit signals the plant to quit.
name: Zucchini

description: Give vines room to roam. Cure harvested fruit in sun 1–2 weeks for thicker skin and sweeter flesh.
name: Winter Squash

varieties.name: Table Queen Acorn
varieties.note: Compact acorn squash for small spaces.

description: Pinch flower buds relentlessly — flowering turns leaves bitter. Harvest from the top to force bushy growth.
name: Basil

varieties.name: Genovese
varieties.note: Classic pesto basil; large tender leaves.

varieties.name: Thai
varieties.note: Anise-clove scent; holds up in heat.

description: Cool-season crop; bolts in heat. Sow every 2 weeks for continuous harvest. Shade cloth extends the season.
name: Lettuce

description: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, again in late summer for fall. Bolts fast once days lengthen.
name: Spinach

description: Sweetens after frost. Harvest outer leaves; the center keeps producing. Watch for cabbage worms.
name: Kale

description: Keep the seedbed evenly moist until sprouts show — a board over the row helps. Thin ruthlessly or roots fork.
name: Carrot

description: Fastest payoff in the garden. Sow with slow carrots to mark the row. Gets pithy if left too long.
name: Radish

description: Each 'seed' is a cluster — thin to one. Greens are edible too. Steady water prevents woody roots.
name: Beet

varieties.name: Detroit Dark Red
varieties.note: Classic globe beet; greens edible too.

description: Direct-sow after frost; seeds rot in cold wet soil. Pick every couple days to keep pods coming.
name: Bean (Bush)

varieties.name: Provider
varieties.note: Early and reliable; tolerates cool soil.

description: Needs a sturdy trellis before sowing. Produces longer than bush types from the same footprint.
name: Bean (Pole)

varieties.name: Kentucky Wonder
varieties.note: Classic pole snap bean; heavy yields.

description: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost. Fades in summer heat — plan a fall round too.
name: Pea

varieties.name: Wando
varieties.note: Shelling pea; tolerates heat better than most.

description: Plant sets pointy-end-up as soon as soil is workable. Stop watering when tops fall over; cure before storing.
name: Onion (from sets)

varieties.name: Walla Walla
varieties.note: Sweet onion; best grown from transplants.

description: Plant cloves in late October, mulch heavily, harvest early summer when lower leaves brown. Hardneck suits cold zones.
name: Garlic

description: Plant certified seed potatoes, eyes up. Hill soil over stems as they grow — light turns tubers green and bitter.
name: Potato

description: Grown from slips, not seeds — plant after soil is warm. Needs a long season; black plastic mulch helps up north.
name: Sweet Potato

description: Plant in blocks, not single rows, for pollination. Heavy feeder — side-dress when knee-high.
name: Corn

description: Loves heat — transplant late, mulch with black plastic. Flea beetles love seedlings; row cover early.
name: Eggplant

description: Soak seeds overnight to speed sprouting. Pick pods at 3–4 inches daily — they go woody fast.
name: Okra

description: Bolts at the first hint of heat. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks; let one plant go to seed for coriander.
name: Cilantro

description: Direct-sow where it will live — taproot hates moving. Self-sows freely; great for beneficial insects.
name: Dill

description: Slow to sprout — pour hot (not boiling) water over the row to hurry it. Biennial; overwinters in mild zones.
name: Parsley

description: Perennial — plant once, snip for years. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. Pretty purple flowers are edible.
name: Chives

description: Perennial that demands sharp drainage — sandy soil or a pot. Shear after flowering to keep it compact.
name: Thyme

description: Perennial; flavor peaks just before flowers open. Spreads — give it its own corner or a container.
name: Oregano

description: Slow from seed — a nursery start saves a season. Overwinters outdoors only in mild zones; otherwise pot it and bring in.
name: Rosemary
'38N' Kkaennip (Namu Farm Korean Perilla)
description: '38N' is a named Korean perilla strain maintained by Namu Farm and selected specifically for branching low from the base into a dense, bushy plant rather than growing as a single tall stalk, which means more growing points and a longer window of continuous leaf harvest than an unselected kkaennip planting. The broad leaves are green on top with a distinctive golden-lilac cast on the underside, and carry the large, thick-textured, strongly aromatic character typical of Korean perilla — used as ssam wraps for grilled meat, pickled into jangajji, and shredded into banchan. Harvest leaves in the cool of early morning for the best flavor and the longest shelf life, snipping from the outside of the plant to keep new growth coming from the base. It self-seeds enthusiastically once established, so deadhead spent flower spikes in gardens where volunteer seedlings would be unwelcome. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: 119-40B Hardy Kiwi (Male Pollinator)
description: 119-40B is a male hardy kiwi selection grown exclusively as a pollen source, since Actinidia arguta is dioecious and female vines set little or no fruit without a nearby male. It produces abundant, well-timed blossoms that overlap the bloom period of widely grown female cultivars, making it a standard pairing for plantings of 'Ananasnaja' and similar selections. The vine itself never fruits, so it can be pruned hard and trained on a modest support rather than a full production trellis. Site it centrally among several female vines for the most even pollination coverage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: 3309 Couderc Grape Rootstock
aliases: Vitis riparia x Vitis rupestris '3309 Couderc'
description: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; 3309 Couderc is grown as a phylloxera-resistant understock, not for its own fruit. A classic French-American hybrid rootstock bred in the nineteenth century from two native North American grape species specifically to resist the root-feeding phylloxera aphid that devastated European wine grape vineyards, it remains one of the most widely planted grape rootstocks worldwide for its reliable phylloxera and some nematode resistance, moderate vigor, and good performance in well-drained, moderately fertile soils. Its long track record and predictable, moderate vigor have made it a benchmark rootstock against which many newer selections are compared, though it is less well suited to very dry or high-lime soils than some other rootstock options. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and provide well-drained soil, since it performs poorly in wet or poorly aerated ground. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Barrackpore Pepper (Smooth-Podded Trinidad Superhot)
description: 7 Pot Barrackpore takes its name from the Barrackpore district of Trinidad and is prized among superhot growers for pods that are less bumpy and wrinkled than most other 7 Pot strains, ripening from green to a glossy orange-red. Its heat arrives with a noticeably smoky, savory edge that Trinidad cooks favor for pepper sauces rather than fresh eating. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and stunted pod set on this variety. Because plants are tall and heavily branched once mature, stake or cage them early to keep the fruit-laden limbs from snapping in wind. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Brain Strain Pepper (Yellow Brain Strain)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the medium warm to encourage the slow-to-sprout chinense seed, then transplant once the soil has warmed well past frost danger. Stake heavily loaded plants and keep watering even to prevent blossom end rot on the convoluted pods. Brain Strain is a 7 Pot type selected for its intensely wrinkled, brain-like fruit surface and sits among the hottest strains within the already fierce 7 Pot family. It is grown in both yellow and red-fruited forms, both intensely pungent. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Bubblegum Pepper (Trinidad Superhot Chile)
description: 7 Pot Bubblegum is a Trinidad-origin selection prized for smooth, slightly bumpy orange pods that ripen from pale green through a distinctive salmon-pink stage before finishing deep orange. Growers favor it for a fruitier, less acrid heat than many 7 Pot strains, with fragrance reminiscent of tropical fruit alongside the scorching capsaicin load. Give plants a long warm season and consistent moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and misshapen pods on this variety. Cage or stake mature plants, as heavy fruit clusters can snap brittle branches in wind. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Douglah Pepper (Chocolate 7 Pot)
description: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since chinense seed can take several weeks to germinate, and pot up seedlings before moving them to the garden once nights are reliably warm. Support the branching stems as fruit accumulates, and reduce watering slightly as pods mature to concentrate flavor. Douglah is a Trinidad 7 Pot strain that ripens to a distinctive dull brown 'chocolate' color rather than red, and it is regarded as one of the hottest of the 7 Pot varieties with a smoky, earthy flavor. Always wear gloves when handling ripe fruit. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Jonah Pepper (Trinidad Superhot Chile)
description: 7 Pot Jonah is a Trinidad-origin strain of the 7 Pot family, producing bumpy, elongated pods that ripen from green to a distinctive pale, almost bone-white to light-yellow or pinkish color rather than the deep red typical of most 7 Pot types. Heat runs from roughly 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville units, placing it firmly among the world's hottest cultivated peppers alongside Douglah and Primo, but it is prized among chileheads for a sweet, fruity flavor that comes through despite the intensity. Plants grow tall and vigorous for a Capsicum chinense, often exceeding three feet, and benefit from staking once heavily laden with fruit. Always wear gloves when harvesting or processing ripe pods, and keep hands away from eyes and face. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Pepper (Seven Pot Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, since the extreme capsaicin content can cause burns even from brief contact. 7 Pot Pepper is a legendary superhot pepper from Trinidad, named for the traditional claim that a single pod is potent enough to season seven pots of stew — a nod to its extreme heat, which commonly measures in the range of 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville heat units, placing it among the hottest peppers ever recorded alongside its close relatives Trinidad Scorpion and Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. The gnarled, bumpy, lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a deep, glossy red and carry a fruity, floral Capsicum chinense aroma beneath the ferocious heat, making it prized by hot sauce makers who want maximum intensity along with genuine habanero-family flavor complexity. A serious specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts only, best grown where its extended season can be accommodated, zone 8–11. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: 7 Pot Primo Pepper
description: Germinate at 85°F on a heat mat for 2–4 weeks; grow under strong lights before transplanting outdoors after all frost risk has passed. 7 Pot Primo was developed by Louisiana hot pepper grower Troy Primeaux (the 'Primo' in the name) as a cross between a Naga Morich and a Trinidad 7 Pot variety; the name '7 Pot' refers to the traditional Trinidadian claim that one pod is hot enough to season 7 pots of food. At 1.0–1.5 million SHU it is among the most intensely hot peppers available to home growers, with a distinctive gnarled, elongated 'tail' that distinguishes it from the rounder Trinidad 7 Pot types. The flavor beneath the heat is described as fruity, earthy, and robust; used in extremely small quantities in hot sauces, fermented hot pepper mash, and as a smoking or drying chile for superhot spice blends. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: 74-49 Hardy Kiwi (Forty-Niner Chico-Selected Kiwiberry)
description: 74-49, sometimes sold as Forty-Niner, is a female Actinidia arguta selection from a California breeding program prized for large, sweet, shiny green-to-reddish fruit that ripens earlier than many other hardy kiwi selections. Like all hardy kiwi, this is a dioecious vine and will not set fruit without a separate male vine planted within pollinating range. Provide a strong permanent trellis, as the twining vine is vigorous and long-lived, and expect several winters of establishment before heavy cropping begins. Vines tolerate cold well into zone 4 once established, though young plants benefit from winter protection. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: A4 Macadamia
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality. One of the classic Hawaiian-selected macadamia cultivars developed for commercial orchards, it produces medium-sized nuts with a high proportion of premium-grade, whole-kernel cracking quality and rich, high oil content prized by processors, making it a benchmark variety in Hawaiian macadamia production for decades. Like other macadamias it needs consistent warmth, protection from frost, and several years of growth before reaching significant bearing age, along with a compatible cross-pollinator variety for the best nut set. Water regularly during nut development, allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest, and provide the same warm, humid, frost-free conditions the species requires throughout the year. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Abashi Bitter Melon
description: An Okinawan heirloom prized for unusually mild bitterness, Abashi produces cylindrical, deep green fruit 8-10 inches long that is popular sliced into stir-fries and Okinawan goya chanpuru. Give it a sturdy trellis and full sun, since this long-season type also performs well in a large container with a stake, provided the container gives roots room to run. Pick fruit while still firm and green for the mildest flavor and best texture; overripe fruit turns orange and splits. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Abata Kola (Kola Nut)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kola nut is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. This West African rainforest tree bears large, star-shaped pods containing caffeine-rich seeds that are chewed fresh across much of West Africa as a stimulant and used ceremonially to welcome guests, and were historically the original flavoring source for early cola soft drinks before synthetic flavorings largely replaced them. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and need consistently warm, humid, partly shaded conditions similar to their native rainforest understory habitat, limiting cultivation outside the tropics to botanical collections and large frost-free properties. Water regularly, especially while young, and provide the dappled shade of taller companion trees where possible to mimic natural forest conditions. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Abate Fetel Pear (Elongated Italian Dessert Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Bred beginning in 1865 by the French abbot Fetel, first at Chessy in the Rhône and later at Charentay, it is instantly recognizable by its long, slender, bottle-like shape and pale green-yellow, lightly russeted skin, with white, fine-grained, very sweet and juicy flesh. It has become the most widely produced and exported pear cultivar in Italy, concentrated in the Emilia-Romagna region under Protected Geographical Indication status, prized for both its elegant form and its long storage life of up to several months under refrigeration. Harvest in September while still firm, then hold in cold storage and ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Abbott Kiwi (Low-Chill New Zealand Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a strong permanent trellis or arbor since the vine becomes heavy and long-lived. Abbott is one of the early New Zealand fuzzy kiwi selections bred alongside Hayward and Allison in the twentieth century, and unlike Hayward it tolerates lower winter chill accumulation, which is why extension sources recommend it for warm-winter, low-chill regions such as southern California, the Gulf Coast, and Florida where Hayward struggles to break dormancy evenly. As a female-only cultivar it never sets fruit on its own and needs a male vine planted within pollinating distance during bloom. Prune annually while dormant to remove old fruiting wood and keep the vigorous canopy manageable, and mulch to conserve soil moisture through hot summers. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Abiu
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; abiu (Pouteria caimito) is a tropical Sapotaceae tree native to the Amazon basin that produces smooth, glossy, bright lemon-yellow fruits with a custardy, translucent white flesh of exceptional sweetness — often described as tasting of caramel, vanilla, or crème brûlée — that clings to a small number of large seeds. The fruit is eaten fresh by scooping out the flesh, taking care to avoid the slightly sticky latex in the skin, which can irritate the lips if left in contact. Abiu is widely grown in Brazil and Queensland, Australia, where its productivity and flavor have made it one of the most popular exotic Sapotaceae fruits among tropical fruit enthusiasts. Trees respond well to regular fertilization with a balanced tropical fruit fertilizer and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development; mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and maintain root health. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Abominable Pumpkin
description: Sow two or three seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. These white-skinned fruits reach 12 to 15 pounds and hold their clean color well after harvest, so give vines plenty of room to sprawl. The strong, sturdy handle makes them ideal for carving and display. Intermediate powdery mildew resistance helps vines stay productive, but water at the base and space plants for airflow to further reduce disease pressure. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Abraham Lincoln Tomato (Classic 1923 Red Beefsteak Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun. Abraham Lincoln is an American heirloom tomato dating to 1923, prized for large, deep-red, meaty beefsteak fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor and good disease tolerance for a variety of its age, which helped it remain popular with home gardeners for decades after its introduction. The vigorous indeterminate vines are strong producers over a long season and benefit from sturdy staking or caging to support the heavy fruit. Water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit is fully colored and yields slightly to gentle pressure for the best flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Abrialii Lavandin (Early French Oil Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and allow generous spacing, since lavandins grow considerably larger than English lavender types. Selected in Provence in the 1930s, 'Abrialii' was one of the first lavandin clones grown commercially for essential oil and remains valued for its narrower, more refined flower spikes and higher linalool content compared to modern high-yield lavandins like 'Grosso'. It forms a large, rounded shrub of silvery foliage with long flowering stems held well above the plant in mid to late summer. Cut back hard in early spring every few years to prevent the woody base that develops in older lavandin plantings. Matures in 100–150 days from transplant.

name: Abundance Blueberry (High-Yield University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil amended generously with pine bark or peat, and mulch deeply to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. Abundance is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for heavy, consistent cropping and a moderate-to-low chill requirement that suits the mild winters of the western Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida alike. The medium-to-large berries are firm and well flavored, holding up well through a home garden's typical multi-week picking window. Though partially self-fruitful, Abundance sets a noticeably heavier crop when interplanted with a second southern highbush cultivar such as Star or Camellia for cross-pollination, and an early-spring feeding with acid-forming fertilizer supports the vigorous new growth the variety is known for. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Acadia Spinach (Semi-Savoy Downy Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Acadia is a semi-savoy spinach hybrid, with leaves that carry moderate crinkle for good texture while staying easier to wash clean than fully savoy types, bred with resistance to an unusually wide range of downy mildew races that helps it stay healthy through the damp, humid conditions common in a Gulf South fall or winter garden. It is well suited to both field and high-tunnel production for a spring or fall crop. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out, and use promptly since fresh spinach quality declines quickly after harvest. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Acai Palm
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; acai palm is a frost-tender floodplain species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse with high humidity. Native to the seasonally flooded várzea forests of the Amazon River basin, this multi-stemmed, clustering palm produces heavy clusters of small, dark purple, antioxidant-rich berries that are pulped fresh into the acai bowls and juices that have become a global health-food phenomenon, though the fruit itself is highly perishable and must be processed within a day of harvest. It thrives in wet, swampy, even periodically flooded soil unlike most palms, reflecting its floodplain origin, and forms multiple clustering trunks over time rather than a single stem. Water generously and consistently, since it does not tolerate drought, and expect several years of growth before the first fruit clusters are produced. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Acco Pomegranate
description: Acco is a compact, early-ripening pomegranate from Israel that reaches harvest well ahead of standard cultivars like Wonderful, making it useful for stretching out a home orchard's pomegranate season. Fruit is medium-sized with ruby-red skin, sweet flavor, and comparatively tender seeds, and the juice content of the arils tends to run higher than many other cultivars. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, since it is naturally suited to dry Mediterranean-type climates and appreciates good airflow in humid Gulf Coast summers to reduce fruit-skin blemishing. Once established it tolerates drought well and needs only occasional deep watering. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ace 55 Bush Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost, keeping the mix at 70 to 85 degrees for quick germination. This 1950s heirloom is a determinate type, so most of its 6 to 8 ounce, low-acid fruits ripen over a concentrated window, making it excellent for canning. Transplant seedlings deeply once nights stay warm, and stake or cage the compact bushes to keep fruit off the ground. Harvest tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft for the best fresh flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Ace 55-VF Tomato
description: Ace 55-VF is a determinate heirloom bearing round, low-acid red fruits of 5-6 inches with thick, juicy flesh, and it carries resistance to verticillium and fusarium wilt. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before your last frost, then harden off and transplant once nights stay above 50F. Give plants a sturdy cage even though the compact vines are self-limiting, and mulch to keep soil moisture even and prevent blossom-end rot. Because it sets much of its crop at once, this variety is well suited to canning and batch preserving. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Ace Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Green Bell Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Ace, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is prized for reaching harvestable size unusually early compared with other bell peppers, producing blocky, thick-walled, mild green fruit that ripens to red if left on the plant longer, all on a compact, sturdy plant that sets fruit reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions. Its early maturity makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting a head start on the pepper harvest or a reliable crop in shorter growing seasons. Harvest at green stage for classic bell pepper use or let fruit ripen to sweeter red for a different flavor, and pick regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Ace Savoy Cabbage
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ace Savoy is a compact, early-maturing savoy cabbage producing small to medium (3–4 pound), round heads with the distinctively crinkled, blistered, dark blue-green leaves that define the savoy type — quite different from the smooth, pale heads of standard green cabbage. Savoy cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. sabauda) has a more complex, refined flavor than standard smooth cabbage: milder, sweeter, more tender, and less pungent, making it the preferred cabbage for fresh preparations where the subtle flavor can be appreciated rather than cooked down to blandness. The crinkled texture and tender leaves hold sauces and dressings differently than smooth cabbage — savoy is the cabbage preferred for upscale coleslaws, stuffed cabbage leaves (the larger, more pliable leaves wrap easily), and any preparation where delicate texture matters. Ace's compact size and rapid maturity (72–82 days) make it practical for fall planting in zone 9 where the cool growing window is relatively short. Matures in 72–82 days from transplant.

name: Acerola (Barbados Cherry)
description: Acerola produces cherry-like fruits with one of the highest natural concentrations of vitamin C of any food plant — up to 65 times that of an orange. The shrubby tree is self-fertile and can bear multiple times per year in truly frost-free climates; it is very sensitive to cold below 30°F and root systems are damaged below 28°F. Plant in well-drained, slightly acid to neutral soil and fertilize lightly with a balanced fertilizer three times per year. Fruit ripens very quickly from green to red and is extremely perishable — harvest when fully red and process (freeze, juice) within 24–48 hours for maximum vitamin C retention. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Acerola Cherry (Barbados Cherry, Highest Vitamin C Natural Tropical Fruit)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting wood. Acerola Cherry (Malpighia emarginata, Barbados Cherry, West Indian Cherry) is a tropical American shrub producing small, bright red, cherry-shaped fruits with the highest Vitamin C content of any commonly cultivated fruit — measured at 1,600–4,700 mg per 100 grams of fresh fruit, compared to 50–90 mg per 100 grams in oranges. This extraordinary Vitamin C concentration — 30–100 times that of citrus — makes acerola one of the most nutritionally significant fruits available to home gardeners in zone 9–11, where the plant is well-adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South. The fruits are small (0.5–1 inch), three-lobed, brilliantly red at ripeness, with soft, juicy, somewhat tart flesh — the tartness masks the sweetness but reflects the very high ascorbic acid content. Acerola fruit has extremely limited commercial availability in North America because the ripe fruits are too soft and perishable for commercial shipping; the best quality fruit is available only to gardeners who can harvest and consume them immediately. Acerola is used for fresh eating, juicing, smoothies, and is commercially important in South America (especially Brazil) for vitamin supplement production from the concentrated juice. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Achachairu (Bolivian Mangosteen)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; achachairu is a Bolivian fruit tree in the same genus as mangosteen (Garcinia) and widely considered the superior subtropical Garcinia for warm temperate gardens — significantly more cold-tolerant than true mangosteen (which requires tropical conditions) while producing excellent fruit. The oval, orange-yellow fruits are 2–3 inches long with a thick, hard rind and sections of white, juicy, translucent flesh with a flavor profile that directly recalls mangosteen: sweet, tropical, slightly acidic, and complex, with an aromatic quality unique in temperate fruits. The tree is dense, dark-green, and attractive as an ornamental, with glossy leaves and a naturally compact, rounded form. Commercially grown in Bolivia, the fruit is popular fresh and in juices, ice creams, and desserts. It grows much faster than mangosteen and begins fruiting in 7–10 years from seed. Australia has embraced it as a commercial orchard crop, and it is increasingly available in subtropical zones 9–11 in the United States. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Achilles Gooseberry
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Achilles is a mildew-resistant red gooseberry developed at England's East Malling Research Station, valued for pairing heavy, reliable cropping with much better resistance to American gooseberry mildew than older varieties like Leveller. The medium-large, smooth berries ripen to a deep pinkish-red with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. Its upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and pick than sprawling heirloom types, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Achira (Edible Canna)
description: Achira is the oldest cultivated plant in South America, grown for thousands of years by Andean civilizations for its large, starchy rhizomes that produce a superior arrowroot starch used in gluten-free cooking and baking — distinct from ornamental cannas (Canna indica and hybrids) because the rhizomes are the primary crop, though the tall plants also produce showy flowers. Rhizomes are harvested 8–10 months after planting when plants begin to die back; they can be cooked like a starchy root vegetable, peeled and steamed, or dried and ground into a fine white starch known as 'canna starch' or 'Queensland arrowroot' that is an excellent thickener for sauces and soups. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, achira grows vigorously as a warm-season perennial that fills in quickly from spring through fall, providing both edible harvest and tropical visual interest; the leaves are also traditionally used to wrap foods for cooking like corn husks. Divide and replant small side rhizomes each spring to maintain a productive colony. Matures in 270–360 days from transplant.

name: Achocha (Wild Cucumber, Stuffing Cucumber)
description: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide strong trellis — achocha is a vigorous climber. Cyclanthera pedata (achocha, wild cucumber, or stuffing cucumber) is an underappreciated Peruvian and Andean cucurbit vine producing distinctive, hollow, pale-green, cucumber-like fruits 3–4 inches long with a pointed beak and soft, edible seeds inside — the hollow interior makes them naturally adapted for stuffing with meat, rice, and cheese (a traditional Andean dish). The flavor of the raw fruit is mild, slightly bitter, and reminiscent of a blend of cucumber and green pepper; they can be eaten raw in salads, stir-fried, or stuffed and baked. The vine is extremely productive and easy to grow, climbing rapidly with coiled tendrils and producing prolific fruits over a long season in cool to warm conditions. In Andean markets, achocha is a common and affordable everyday vegetable; it is essentially unknown in North American supermarkets but straightforward to grow from seed as a specialty home garden vegetable. In zone 9, the fall-to-spring season is ideal; direct sow in September for a fall-through-spring harvest. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Aci Sivri Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aci Sivri (pronounced ah-juh SIV-ree, meaning 'hot sharp' in Turkish) is a Turkish heirloom cayenne-type pepper producing long (4–6 inch), thin, slightly wrinkled, pointed fruits that turn from pale green to deep red when ripe. The heat level ranges from mild when young and green to genuinely hot (15,000–30,000+ Scoville) when fully red-ripe, with the heat increasing significantly as the fruit matures and dries. The thin-walled, aromatic fruits dry quickly and are widely used in Turkish cuisine as a dried spice pepper, ground into flakes or paprika-style powder. Fresh green Aci Sivri is used in Turkish salads and grilled vegetable dishes where its mild-to-medium heat adds flavor without overwhelming. The prolific, heavily-bearing plants are extremely popular in Turkish home gardens and have been grown continuously for centuries. In zone 9 the long warm season allows multiple harvests and the plants often overwinter as perennials, returning larger each year. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Ackee (Aki, Akee Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; avoid planting in frost-prone sites. Blighia sapida (ackee) is a West African tree that became the national fruit of Jamaica, where the arils (fleshy seed coverings) of the opened, ripe fruit are the key ingredient in Jamaica's national dish, ackee and saltfish. The three large, black seeds of each red ackee pod are surrounded by creamy-yellow, buttery, scrambled-egg-textured arils that taste mildly savory and are typically sautéed with salt cod, onions, and peppers. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unripe ackee (pods not fully opened naturally) contains hypoglycin A, a toxin that can cause Jamaican Vomiting Sickness — consume only the fully ripe arils after the pod has opened completely on the tree and seeds have developed fully. The ripe arils are nutritious, high in protein, fat, and niacin. The tree is an attractive, medium-sized evergreen with pinnate leaves and small white flowers. Fresh ackee is available in Jamaican and Caribbean communities in South Florida; canned ackee (already safely processed) is widely available. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Aconcagua Pepper (Argentine Giant Sweet Frying Pepper, 12-Inch Fruits with Mild Flavor)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake plants; harvest green or fully ripe to salmon-red. Aconcagua is an Argentine heirloom sweet frying pepper that produces some of the largest sweet pepper fruits of any variety in home garden cultivation — individual fruits typically measuring 8–12 inches in length and 2–3 inches wide, with a conical to slightly flattened form that tapers to a point. The variety takes its name from Aconcagua, Argentina's (and the Americas') highest mountain, a reference to the pepper's origin in the Andean region of South America where diverse pepper varieties have been cultivated for millennia. The fruit size is genuinely dramatic: Aconcagua peppers dwarf most other sweet peppers in the garden and attract immediate attention at farmers markets and in garden displays where their unusual scale distinguishes them from any standard frying or bell pepper. Despite the imposing size, the walls are moderately thin (thinner than bell peppers, in the frying pepper tradition) and the flavor is mild, sweet, and fruity — the flesh has the pleasant, slightly aromatic quality characteristic of good heirloom frying peppers. The ripening progression of Aconcagua goes from green through light yellow-green to a distinctive salmon-pink to pale red-orange, a color not typical of most peppers and part of the variety's visual distinction. The large individual fruit size makes Aconcagua exceptionally practical for stuffing (the hollow interior accommodates substantial filling) and for roasting whole, where the large peppers yield significant amounts of sweet roasted flesh per fruit. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward from fully ripe fruits. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Acorn Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in compost-enriched hills after soil reaches 65°F, planting 3–4 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Allow vines to spread freely or train onto a sturdy trellis. Leave fruits on the vine until the rind is hard and resists a thumbnail; the stem will also begin to dry and cork over. Cure harvested squash at room temperature for 1–2 weeks to harden the skin before storage. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Adam Kiwi Vine (Male Pollinator Variegated Kolomikta Kiwi)
description: Grow in rich, moist, well-drained, non-calcareous soil with a sturdy trellis or wall support, siting it out of harsh afternoon sun since kolomikta foliage can scorch in full exposure. Adam is a Polish-bred male selection grown strictly as a pollinator for female Arctic Beauty kiwi cultivars such as Eve, and it does not itself produce fruit, but it more than earns its space with striking foliage variegated in shades of pink, cream-white, and green that rivals or exceeds most female selections for ornamental impact. Small, lightly citrus-scented white flowers with yellow stamens open in late spring and are visited readily by bees carrying pollen to nearby female vines. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than typical kolomikta seedlings, so provide winter wind protection in the coldest parts of its range and prune lightly after flowering to maintain a manageable, well-branched framework. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Adams Crabapple (Rose-Red Flowered Disease-Resistant Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Adams produces an abundant spring flush of deep rose-red buds opening to rose-pink flowers, followed by small, glossy, cherry-red fruit about half an inch across that persists into winter and draws robins, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It is a reliably disease-resistant crabapple, showing good resistance to apple scab and cedar-apple rust that plague many older, less-improved cultivars, and its rounded, well-branched form makes it a dependable small flowering shade tree for a home landscape. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Adams Elderberry (Classic High-Yield Large-Cluster American Elderberry Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the oldest and most widely established named elderberry cultivars — selected from wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) populations and long used as the benchmark for comparison in elderberry cultivar trials. It produces large, flat-topped flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — among the largest of named elderberry cultivars — followed by heavy, pendant clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late August–September. Adams is valued not only for its direct productivity but as an exceptionally effective cross-pollinator for other cultivars: planting Adams near Bob Gordon, Nova, or other cultivars consistently boosts overall production across the planting. The heavy, well-formed berry clusters of Adams are well-suited to all standard elderberry processing: elderberry syrup (a popular immune support product), elderberry wine, elderberry jelly, and elderflower preparations from the spring flowers. The large flower clusters are among the most attractive of any elderberry cultivar for elderflower cordials, fritters, and other culinary uses. As with all American elderberry, Adams spreads vigorously by root suckers and can naturalize in favorable moist conditions — manage the suckering to maintain a defined shrub rather than a spreading thicket. In zone 9, elderberry performs best in the slightly cooler, moister areas — near water features or in low spots where soil moisture is consistent. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Adams I Elderberry (Adams No. 1, Original Union Springs American Elderberry)
description: Adams No. 1 was one of two wild American elderberry seedlings selected by grower William Adams near Union Springs, New York in the early 1910s and released together in 1926 after an eleven-year evaluation by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva. For decades it stood alongside its sibling Adams No. 2 as one of the only named elderberry cultivars available to North American growers, valued for its heavy, dependable cropping and vigorous, upright cane growth rather than for the exceptionally large individual berries that made Adams No. 2 more famous. Broad, flat-topped clusters of white flowers open in June and July, maturing into small dark purple-black berries by late summer that, like all elderberry fruit, must be cooked before eating. Plant it near a genetically distinct cultivar such as Adams No. 2, York, or Nova to boost pollination, and remove the oldest canes each winter to keep the planting productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Adams II Elderberry (Adams No. 2, Large-Fruited Union Springs American Elderberry)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Adams No. 2 is one of two wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) selections made by grower William Adams near Union Springs, New York in 1915; the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva trialed the seedling alongside its sibling Adams No. 1 for eleven years before releasing both as named cultivars in 1926. Until improved mid-century releases such as York and Kent arrived, the two Adams selections were essentially the only named elderberry cultivars grown commercially in North America, and Adams No. 2 in particular became known for producing the largest individual berries of any named American elderberry, borne in broad, flat-topped cymes up to six inches across. Flowers open in June–July and the small, dark purple-black berries ripen late, from late August into September, over an extended four-week picking window. As with all elderberry, raw fruit contains cyanogenic glycosides and must be cooked before eating; the ripe berries are used for elderberry syrup, wine, jelly, and juice, and the flower clusters can be battered and fried or steeped for elderflower cordial. Like other American elderberry, it spreads by root suckers and benefits from removing the oldest canes each winter to keep the planting productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Adams Pearmain Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Adams Pearmain is a reliable, easy-to-grow classic English russet apple well suited to a home orchard. An old English variety first recorded in the early nineteenth century, it bears medium, elongated, pearmain-shaped apples with a dull red flush over a russeted yellow ground and dense, crisp, nutty-sweet flesh, ripening in mid-fall as a reliable, well-flavored traditional dessert apple. Its consistent, moderate cropping and good disease tolerance compared to some other classic English varieties have made it a dependable choice for a home orchard wanting an easy-to-grow heirloom russet-type apple. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months for the best rich, nutty dessert flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Adirondack Blue Potato (Cornell High-Anthocyanin Blue Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost in cool weather; hill soil over emerging plants twice as they grow to increase yield and prevent tubers from greening. Adirondack Blue was developed by Dr. Walter De Jong and colleagues at Cornell University's potato breeding program and released in 2003, representing a significant improvement over older blue-flesh potato varieties; it was specifically bred for the uniformly intense blue-purple flesh coloration (without the white marbling or streaking common in older blue varieties), higher anthocyanin content (the pigment responsible for blue and purple coloration and associated health benefits), and better agronomic performance than heirloom blue types. The tubers have blue-purple skin and uniformly vibrant blue-purple flesh that holds its color remarkably well when boiled or steamed; the texture is waxy and the flavor is rich and earthy — similar to high-quality waxy potatoes with an additional visual dimension. The blue color is striking in potato salads, mashed potatoes (turns lavender-blue), and roasted presentations. Mid-season maturity of 70–90 days from planting; produces reliably in most US climates. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Adirondack Crabapple (Narrow Upright Disease-Resistant White Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Adirondack, bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, bears red buds opening to abundant white flowers on a distinctly narrow, upright, vase-shaped tree, considerably more columnar than most crabapples and well suited to street tree plantings, foundation use, or tighter residential lots where a wide-spreading crabapple wouldn't fit. Small orange-red fruit follows the spring bloom and persists into winter, feeding birds. It shows strong resistance to apple scab, fire blight, and cedar-apple rust, making it a reliably low-maintenance choice. Prune in late winter to remove crossing or damaged branches and maintain the narrow form. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Adirondack Red Potato (Cornell Red-Flesh Specialty Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; hill twice as plants grow. Adirondack Red was released in 2004 by Dr. Walter De Jong's Cornell University potato breeding program, one year after Adirondack Blue, specifically developed to provide a red-fleshed complement to the blue-fleshed Adirondack Blue; both share the goal of combining high anthocyanin content, superior visual appeal, and reliable agronomic performance in a named, certified-disease-free variety. The medium-sized, round to oblong tubers have rose-red skin and uniformly pink to red flesh throughout — significantly more uniformly red than older red-flesh varieties like 'Red Gold' which tend to develop red only near the skin. The flavor is excellent — rich, waxy, earthy, and slightly nutty — with flesh that holds its color when boiled or steamed, making it excellent for colorful potato salads, roasted potato platters, and any presentation where the red color adds visual value. Disease resistance, yield, and overall agronomic performance are significantly improved compared to heirloom red-flesh types. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Adjuma Pepper (French Antillean Habanero-Type Chile)
description: Adjuma is a traditional pepper of Guadeloupe and Martinique, prized in Antillean kitchens for a strikingly fruity, floral aroma alongside solid habanero-level heat. Its squat, deeply wrinkled orange-yellow pods form in clusters and are typically used fresh, muddled into vinegar-based hot sauces rather than dried, so plan for repeated light harvests through the season instead of one large drying batch. Like other chinense types it thrives in consistent warmth and humidity, so mulch heavily and water deeply but infrequently to avoid the stress that triggers blossom drop. Choose Adjuma over a standard habanero when the goal is a more perfumed, less sharply citrusy aroma to complement Caribbean-style marinades and condiments. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Admiral Wilkes Jujube (Historic Late-Season Elongated Jujube)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; jujubes are highly drought-tolerant once established and largely untroubled by pests or disease in Gulf Coast conditions. Admiral Wilkes bears elongated, tooth-shaped fruit similar in form to 'Silverhill' but distinguished by very late-season ripening, typically mid-to-late November in most growing regions, useful for extending the jujube harvest well past main-season cultivars like 'Li' and 'Lang'. Fruit skin turns deep reddish-brown at maturity over crisp, juicy, honey-flavored flesh. Historic specimens are noted for exceptional vigor and size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Adriana Lettuce (Fast-Maturing Compact Romaine)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Adriana is a miniature romaine lettuce in the Little Gem tradition, producing small, dense, upright heads with crisp outer leaves and a sweet, tender heart, but bred for notably faster maturity and better heat tolerance than older Little Gem strains, letting gardeners push both the early spring and late fall ends of the lettuce season a bit further. Its compact size makes it well suited to intensive spacing and container growing, and the whole small heads work perfectly as individual salad or Caesar-salad portions without needing to be cut down for a mixed bowl. Harvest the whole head once it feels firm and dense at the base, or begin picking outer leaves earlier for a cut-and-come-again approach. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to delay bolting as temperatures rise. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Adriatic JH Fig (JH Adriatic, Joe Hood Selection)
description: Adriatic JH is a named selection maintained by Texas fig grower Joe Hood of Austin, distinct from White Adriatic and reportedly healthier and more productive than some virus-affected Adriatic clones circulating in the nursery trade. Fruit ripens later in the season than typical White Adriatic and is medium-sized with pale green skin and deep red pulp, with a berry-forward flavor. It bears a modest breba crop followed by a heavier main crop, and its Texas origin and heat tolerance make it a reasonable candidate for Gulf Coast dooryards. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Advance Loquat (Early-Ripening Gulf Coast Orange-Fleshed Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil; Advance loquat ripens earlier than most other varieties, often beginning in January–February in zone 9a, making it the first fresh tree fruit of the year in Gulf Coast gardens; fruits are medium, orange-fleshed, and sweet with moderate acidity; harvest sequentially as individual fruits ripen since this variety does not ripen all at once. Advance is an early-ripening loquat cultivar prized in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens for its ability to bring the first fresh homegrown tree fruit of the year to the table — typically ripening in January or February in zone 9a, 2–3 weeks ahead of the standard loquat season. This early ripening characteristic is agriculturally significant in two ways: it extends the effective loquat season (allowing home growers to plant multiple varieties for a longer fresh-fruit window from January through April), and it potentially reduces frost-damage risk to the developing fruit since early-ripening varieties complete their fruit development before the most severe January-February cold events. The fruits of Advance are medium-sized, rounded, with orange to golden-orange skin and firm, sweet orange flesh that is well-flavored without being as intensely aromatic as some other varieties. The tree is moderately vigorous and productive, and its earlier bloom time (September–October) compared to later-season varieties means some cross-pollination timing considerations when planting alongside other loquat varieties. Advance is a standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want reliable loquat production. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Adzuki Bean
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained soil; adzuki beans are relatively drought-tolerant once established and prefer soil that is not overly rich in nitrogen. Plants produce clusters of small, dark red beans in slender pods; harvest fresh pods at 60–70 days for green shelling beans, or leave pods until they dry and turn tan for the classic small red dried bean. Watch pods closely at maturity as they shatter easily — harvest when most pods are tan but before they split open. The small, sweet beans are famous in East Asian cuisine, particularly for red bean paste in confections. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Ae Ae Banana (Hawaiian Variegated Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade after the last frost, in a spot sheltered from strong wind; Ae Ae is a historic Hawaiian banana cultivar prized above all for its striking variegation, with broad white-and-green striped leaves and fruit that also shows white-and-green striping before ripening to a more solid yellow. It is grown as much as an ornamental tropical foliage specimen as for its sweet, edible fruit, and the variegated leaves are notably more prone to wind tatter and sunscald than solid-green banana cultivars, so a protected courtyard or the shelter of taller plantings improves its appearance. Because variegated plants generally grow more slowly than their all-green counterparts, give Ae Ae rich soil, consistent moisture, and regular feeding to keep it vigorous. Cold tolerance is limited like most ornamental Musa cultivars, so plan on container culture or serious winter protection in zone 9. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Affirmed Watermelon (Seedless High-Yield Triploid Hybrid)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Affirmed is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred as part of a modern commercial series developed for consistent, high-count yields under Southern growing conditions. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set on the vines. It produces medium to large, crisp, sweet, deep red-fleshed fruit with the classic dark green striping. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned, and handle seedless melons gently since their rinds tend to be slightly thinner than seeded types. Matures in 82–90 days from transplant.

name: Afghanistan Pomegranate (Double-Flowered Deep-Red Dual-Purpose Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates handle heavy clay and alkaline conditions better than most fruiting trees once roots are established. Afghanistan is a vigorous, heavy-blooming pomegranate selection grown in home orchards as much for its dense flush of large, ruffled, semi-double red-orange spring flowers as for its fruit, making it one of the more ornamental fruiting cultivars available. The medium fruit ripens to a deep red rind enclosing garnet-colored arils with a rich, wine-like, tart-sweet flavor and firmer seeds than soft-seeded types, suited to juicing as much as fresh eating. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and tend toward a naturally dense, twiggy, multi-stemmed shrub form; prune lightly to open the canopy and remove root suckers, since fruit forms on new growth. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: African Basil (Clove Basil)
description: Root cuttings in warm conditions and transplant to rich, well-drained soil in full sun; African basil is a large, woody, heat-tolerant basil relative native to tropical Africa and widely grown across West Africa, East Africa, and South Asia as a culinary and medicinal herb. The flavor differs substantially from European sweet basil — it has a strong clove-like note, more eucalyptus, and a camphor-like medicinal quality rather than the sweet anise of Italian basil. Used in soups, stews, and pepper sauces across Nigeria, Ghana, and Ethiopia; the dried leaves are an ingredient in berbere spice blend. In hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens it thrives and produces prolifically where annual basil struggles with disease. Small white flowers attract pollinators profusely. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: African Birdseye Pepper (Tiny Very Hot Piri-Piri Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. African Birdseye produces tiny, upright, intensely hot red pods on a compact, heavily branching bush, the traditional source pepper for piri-piri (peri-peri) sauce across southern and East Africa, later carried by Portuguese traders to become a staple flavoring in Mozambican and Angolan cuisine as well. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: African Blue Basil
description: Take 4–6 in stem cuttings, remove lower leaves, and root in moist perlite or water; transplant once a vigorous root system develops. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; in zones below 10, treat as a long-season annual or overwinter rooted cuttings indoors under grow lights. Because this sterile hybrid never sets seed, it flowers continuously throughout the season — a great benefit for pollinators — without the bolting problem common to culinary basil. Harvest stem tips freely; the camphor-scented, dark-veined foliage is used in cooked dishes and infused oils. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: African Breadfruit (African Breadnut, Ize)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; a very large tree requiring considerable space — suitable primarily for large tropical properties in zone 11–12. Treculia africana (African breadfruit or ize) is one of the most ecologically and nutritionally important food trees of West and Central Africa — a massive, buttressed tropical tree native to the humid forests of Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, DRC, and Central Africa, producing the largest fruits of any species in the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae). The enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, weighing 10–65 lbs) erupt directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) and are technically similar to jackfruit or breadfruit in structure, but used very differently: unlike common breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis, where the flesh is eaten) and jackfruit (where the flesh is the food), in African breadfruit, the edible product is the starchy, protein-rich seeds embedded in the fibrous flesh. The seeds are extracted, boiled or roasted, ground into flour, fermented (to make ugba or ukpaka — a traditional condiment in southeastern Nigeria), made into porridge, or pressed for oil. The fermented seed product (ukpaka) is a major flavor ingredient in Igbo cuisine, used similarly to cheese or miso as an aged, complex-flavored condiment. African breadfruit seeds are exceptionally protein-rich (21%) compared to other starchy staples. The tree is too large and slow-growing for most home gardens but represents one of the most important indigenous food forest trees of sub-Saharan Africa. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: African Bush Mango
description: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Dacryodes buettneri requires consistently high rainfall and humidity typical of tropical rainforest conditions — water abundantly during dry spells, mulch heavily, and maintain high organic matter content. Dacryodes buettneri (African Bush Mango, Ozigo, or Arbre à Beurre in French) is a large, emergent to canopy rainforest tree native to Gabon, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, and the Congo Basin forests, a member of the same Burseraceae genus as the widely grown African olive (Dacryodes edulis / Safou). Like safou, D. buettneri produces oblong, oil-rich fruits with thin, waxy skin ripening from green to dark-blue or black-purple, cooked (boiled or roasted) rather than eaten raw — the soft, creamy, rich, butter-like pulp develops a flavor somewhat reminiscent of avocado or a rich olive when heated. The fruits are an important food and oil source for forest-dwelling communities in Gabon and Cameroon, and the extracted fat is used for cooking and traditional personal care. Dacryodes buettneri is a tall-growing, high-humidity, tropical rainforest species best suited to humid equatorial climates in zones 11–12; it does not tolerate drought, salt, or cold and needs rich, moist, forest-type soils to perform well. Matures in 2190–5475 days from transplant.

name: African Cherry
description: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun in cooler climates; Prunus africana requires the cool, moist conditions of montane forest environments — it performs poorly in hot, humid tropical lowlands and is best suited to highland subtropical and warm-temperate climates. Prunus africana (African Cherry, Pygeum, or African Plum) is a large, slow-growing, evergreen tree native to the montane forests of sub-Saharan Africa — occurring on nearly every major mountain range from Mt. Cameroon and the Ruwenzori to the Ethiopian Highlands, Drakensberg, and Kilimanjaro above 1,500m elevation — and listed on CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting of its medicinal bark. The bark contains a rich complex of phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, beta-sitostenone), ferulic acid esters, and n-docosanol with well-documented anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects on prostate tissue — making standardized Pygeum bark extract one of the most widely prescribed botanical medicines in France, Germany, and Italy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms. The annual global trade in Prunus africana bark exceeds 4,000 metric tons, putting wild populations under severe pressure across its range. Cultivating nursery-grown trees (which require 8–15 years to produce harvestable bark) is a sustainable alternative to wild collection. The small, cherry-like, red-to-black fruits are edible but very bitter; primarily a timber and medicinal tree. Matures in 3650–10950 days from transplant.

name: African Cucumber
description: Plant Kedrostis africana seeds or tuber sections in very well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; water sparingly during establishment and infrequently once growing — the large tuberous roots store water for extended dry periods; allow to dry down significantly in winter (the plant may appear dead); new growth emerges from the tuber in spring. African Cucumber is one of the most drought-adapted vines in the Cucurbit family — a member of the extraordinary African flora adapted to seasonal drought — growing from a large, knobby, water-storing tuber (caudex) that can persist underground through months-long dry seasons without any rainfall. Slender, twining vines emerge from the tuber in the wet season and bear small, deeply lobed leaves and clusters of tiny, exquisite, green-and-cream-striped oval fruits that look like perfect miniature watermelons as they develop, then ripen through yellow-orange to bright scarlet-red, splitting to reveal black seeds. In African folklore and traditional medicine, the tuberous roots and fruits of related Kedrostis species have various documented uses; the fruits are eaten by birds and mammals in the wild. The ornamental miniature fruits make it a conversation piece in the dry garden; it is well suited to succulent gardens, xeriscapes, and dry South Africa-inspired plantings in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: African Eggplant (Garden Egg)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 80°F and provide consistent warmth until transplanting. This West African species produces small, rounded fruits in white, green, yellow, or red and is more heat and drought tolerant than common eggplant; it is widely grown as a staple vegetable across sub-Saharan Africa. Harvest fruits while skin is still glossy and firm — they are best eaten cooked in stews, soups, and sauces where their slightly bitter flavor mellows and complements. Plants are perennial in frost-free climates and can be cut back hard after the main season to produce a second flush of fruiting growth. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: African Fan Palm
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, sandy to loamy, alkaline-tolerant soil; Borassus aethiopum is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods of African savanna — water regularly only in the first few years of establishment; growth is very slow initially as the palm develops its extensive root system before vertical growth. Borassus aethiopum (African Fan Palm or African Palmyra) is one of the largest and most ecologically important palms of sub-Saharan Africa — a massive, solitary-trunked fan palm native to the savanna, woodland, and seasonal floodplain ecosystems of tropical and subtropical Africa from Senegal east through Nigeria, Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, and south to Zimbabwe and Mozambique. The closely related Asian Toddy Palm (Borassus flabellifer) is a separate species adapted to South and Southeast Asian monsoon climates. The African Fan Palm reaches impressive dimensions — trunks to 80+ feet topped by a large, rounded crown of enormous, pleated, circular fan fronds up to 10 feet across. The large (4–6 inch), smooth, orange-brown fruits are economically important: the jelly-like germinating seed tissue is eaten by children and livestock; the fleshy mesocarp is eaten raw or cooked; palm sap tapped from the crown is fermented into 'African palm wine.' The hard, extremely dense, durable black palm heartwood is used for construction, tool handles, and musical instruments across its range. A dramatic, long-lived specimen palm for large tropical landscapes in zone 9–12 with patience — first 5–10 years of growth are slow as the root system establishes. Matures in 3650–10950 days from transplant.

name: African Locust Bean (Dawadawa, Nere)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep, sandy-loam to clay-loam soil in full sun; African locust bean is drought-tolerant once established and fixes nitrogen. Parkia biglobosa (African locust bean, dawadawa, or nere) is a massive, wide-canopied leguminous tree from the West African savanna and Sudan zone — one of the most economically and nutritionally important trees across a broad band of West Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia. The tree produces striking, spherical, red to orange pompom flower heads on pendulous stalks — spectacularly ornamental. The fruits are long pods containing seeds embedded in a dry, yellow, powdery, sweet pulp. The sweet pulp (high in sugar, vitamin C, and tannins) is eaten fresh or dissolved in water as a sweet drink. The seeds are the critical product: fermented over several days into dawadawa (called iru in Yoruba, ogiri-nono in Igbo, sumbala in Mande-speaking regions) — an intensely aromatic, deeply umami-flavored condiment with a pungent smell similar to very strong blue cheese or natto. Dawadawa is the essential flavoring in West African soups, stews, and sauces in the same way that fish sauce is essential in Southeast Asia — providing deep umami richness. The tree also fixes atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium symbiosis), improving soil fertility. A supremely important multi-use tree for tropical food forests in zone 10–12. Matures in 2190–5475 days from transplant.

name: African Mango
description: The African mango, or bush mango, is a large tropical tree grown for its mango-like fruit and especially its oil-rich seed kernel, called dika nut. It demands a hot, humid, frost-free climate with abundant moisture and deep, fertile soil. Plant in full sun with plenty of room, as mature trees become tall and broad. Trees are slow to bear from seed, so grafted stock fruits sooner; harvest the fallen fruit and dry the prized kernels. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: African Mangosteen (Imbe)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African mangosteen tolerates brief light frosts to about 28°F when established, making it considerably more cold-hardy than tropical mangosteen and viable in zone 9 sheltered locations. Garcinia livingstonei is an African native shrub or small tree grown for its small (1–2 inch), orange-yellow to orange-red, edible fruits with juicy, sweet-tart, apricot-like flesh and 1–3 large seeds; the flavor is pleasant and described as a combination of apricot and mango, and the fruits are eaten fresh, made into juices, and used to make a fermented beverage in southern Africa. Unlike tropical mangosteen (G. mangostana), which is notoriously difficult to cultivate outside the humid tropics, African mangosteen is adaptable, drought-tolerant when established, and significantly more cold-hardy — an excellent choice for Gulf Coast subtropical gardens in zones 9–11. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: African Nutmeg (Calabash Nutmeg, Ehuru, Airama)
description: Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, humid, wind-protected location; African nutmeg is a mid-sized rainforest tree of West and Central Africa closely related to custard apple, notable for its unusual pendulous, ribbon-like, spiraling flowers followed by large round woody fruits the size of a grapefruit. Inside each fruit, numerous seeds embedded in aromatic pulp are dried and grated much like true nutmeg, imparting a similar warm, slightly bitter, musky-spicy flavor used in West African soups, rice dishes, and traditional remedies. Because seedlings take many years to reach bearing size, it is best suited to permanent agroforestry plantings or large tropical gardens rather than short-term cultivation, and young trees should be shaded and kept consistently moist during establishment. Matures in 1825–3285 days from transplant.

name: African Pride Atemoya (Compact Heavy-Bearing Atemoya)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. African Pride is a popular commercial and home garden atemoya cultivar known for a more compact tree size and heavy, reliable fruit production compared to some other cultivars, making it a practical choice where space is somewhat limited. The rich, sweet, custard-like flesh is classic atemoya quality, and hand pollination in the morning hours, transferring pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set and size. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the skin lightens in color, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for the best eating quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: African Rice
description: Start seeds in shallow flats of moist potting mix at 70-80F, then transplant 6-9-inch seedlings to flooded paddies, water gardens, or large containers filled with heavy garden soil and submerged under 2-4 inches of standing water; African rice tolerates upland, non-flooded cultivation somewhat better than Asian rice, but still performs best with consistent moisture or shallow flooding. Domesticated independently in the Niger River delta region of West Africa thousands of years ago, entirely separately from Asian rice (Oryza sativa), African rice was brought to the Americas by enslaved West Africans and became foundational to the historic Carolina and Gulf Coast lowcountry rice culture, carrying deep agricultural and culinary heritage. It is generally more tolerant of heat, drought, poor soil, and weed competition than Asian rice, though yields tend to run lower and the grain shatters (drops from the panicle) more readily at maturity, so harvest promptly once panicles droop and grains turn golden. Drain standing water three to four weeks before harvest and allow the plant to dry on the stalk before cutting; hand threshing is practical for small home plots. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: African Rosemallow (Cranberry Hibiscus, False Roselle)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after frost; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; cranberry hibiscus grows rapidly in warm conditions and begins producing harvestable leaves within 6–8 weeks of planting. Hibiscus acetosella (cranberry hibiscus or African rosemallow) is a tropical West African edible shrub producing dramatically beautiful, deeply lobed, maple-leaf-shaped, deep burgundy-red to maroon foliage on rapidly growing plants that reach 4–6 feet by summer's end — among the most ornamental of all edible plants. The young leaves are harvested and eaten raw in salads (slightly tart, like sorrel, with a bright red-purple color that bleeds into dressings) or cooked as greens in the same manner as its close relative roselle (H. sabdariffa); the tart, cranberry-like flavor comes from hibiscus acids and anthocyanins. Small, lavender-pink flowers bloom in late summer and are also edible. In zone 9, it grows as an annual (or short-lived perennial) from March through November; in zones 10–12, it persists year-round. The rich leaf color and tropical texture make it as ornamental as it is edible — outstanding as a focal point or screening plant in the vegetable garden. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: African Runner Peanut (Historic Small-Seeded Heirloom Peanut)
description: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods. This small-seeded heirloom peanut traces to peanuts brought to the American South through the transatlantic slave trade and was documented growing at Monticello in Jefferson's own garden notes, making it one of the oldest peanut lines still in American cultivation. Its bushy, low-spreading habit and heavy yield of small, sweet, easy-shelling pods make it well suited to home-scale roasting and boiling, and the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season matches its full maturity window better than most northern gardens can offer. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: African Spiderflower (Spiderwisp, Cat's Whiskers Vegetable, Mchicha wa Pori)
description: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — African Spiderflower germinates rapidly in warm soil and begins producing harvestable leaves within 4–6 weeks. Gynandropsis gynandra (formerly Cleome gynandra) is a fast-growing, warm-season annual native throughout tropical Africa, South and Southeast Asia in the Cleomaceae family, one of the most nutritionally important leafy vegetables in the diets of millions of people throughout sub-Saharan Africa, where it is known by many names including 'mchicha wa pori' (Swahili), 'mbikira' (Uganda), and 'nyanya' (parts of West Africa). The plant produces compound leaves of 3–5 leaflets on upright, slightly sticky, aromatic stems, terminating in elongated clusters of small white to pale purple flowers with prominent, long, spider-like stamens — the spider-flower appearance is characteristic of the Cleomaceae family. The young leaves and shoot tips, harvested before the plant flowers, are boiled or stir-fried as a nutritious cooked vegetable — the flavor is slightly bitter and cabbage-like when raw, becoming mildly pleasant when cooked.
