Nutritional analyses document exceptionally high protein content (the highest of commonly grown leafy vegetables), high iron, calcium, and riboflavin levels — properties that have made G. gynandra the subject of food security research as a nutrient-dense leafy green for hot climates where cool-season greens cannot be grown. Self-seeds prolifically in zone 9-12 gardens once established. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: African Star Apple (Agbalumo, Udara)
description: African star apple is a large, fast-growing rainforest tree of West and Central Africa distinct from the more familiar Caribbean star apple (Chrysophyllum cainito), bearing egg-shaped orange to yellow fruit with sweet, gelatinous, milky pulp around several flattened seeds arranged in a star pattern. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, since seedlings do not tolerate heavy shade; young trees need consistent moisture but established specimens handle brief dry spells once their root system is developed. Trees are naturally very large in the wild but can be kept to a manageable orchard size with regular structural pruning, and seedling trees are slow to bear, often taking many years, so grafted stock is preferable where available. Fruit is harvested when it softens slightly and turns fully orange or yellow, then eaten fresh by squeezing the pulp free of the tough skin, avoiding the sticky white latex in the unripe rind. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: African Walnut (Gaboon Nut, Walnut of the Congo)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in part shade; African walnut is a slow-growing canopy tree for large properties in zone 11–12 humid tropics. Coula edulis (African walnut or Gaboon nut) is a large, slow-growing canopy tree of the humid tropical rainforests of West and Central Africa — native to Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, and the DRC — and one of the most important wild nut-producing trees of the Central African forest zone. The tree produces small (1–1.5 inch), olive-to-cherry-sized, oval to round fruits with a thin, olive-like outer flesh and an extremely hard, woody shell inside (in the Olacaceae family, related to the African walnut group). The single kernel within the hard shell has a distinctly walnut-like flavor — nutty, oily, and rich — and is eaten fresh (raw), roasted in hot ashes, or boiled by forest communities across its range. The nuts are gathered from wild trees and are sold in markets in Cameroon, Gabon, and DRC as an important forest food product and source of income for forest-dependent communities. The high fat content (40–50%) makes the kernels calorie-dense and nutritionally valuable. Coula edulis is listed as a species of conservation concern in parts of its range due to overharvesting of wild nuts and habitat loss. A remarkable and entirely unknown tree outside West Central Africa. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: African White Eggplant (Small Round Ivory Heat-Tolerant Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm soil once nights are reliably above 55F; harvest fruit while still glossy white and firm, since pods age to yellow and then red as they overripen and lose their mild flavor. African White is a tropical African heirloom eggplant that produces abundant clusters of small, round, ivory fruits on a vigorous, glossy-leaved plant that doubles as an attractive ornamental in a mixed vegetable bed. The 2-3 inch fruits have a mild, faintly nutty flavor and few seeds when picked young, making them good for quick sautes, curries, and pickling. Because it hails from hot equatorial growing conditions, African White tolerates the extended heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer better than many standard purple-fruited types, continuing to set fruit through the stretch of the season when cooler-adapted eggplants slow down. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: African Wild Calabash
description: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; African wild calabash produces small, bitter, non-culinary fruit grown mainly for its ornamental or utilitarian gourd rather than eating fresh. A wild relative of the cultivated bottle gourd, this vigorous, fast-climbing African vine bears small, round, hard-shelled fruit that, unlike the sweeter cultivated bottle gourd, is intensely bitter and not eaten fresh, but the dried, hollowed shell is used traditionally as a small container, rattle, or utensil much like other calabash gourds. Its vigorous growth and attractive white, evening-opening flowers make it a fast-covering vine for a trellis or fence in a frost-free warm-season garden, valued more for ornamental screening and traditional craft use of the dried gourds than as a food crop. Harvest fruit once the shell hardens and the vine begins to die back, then dry thoroughly before hollowing and using the shell. Matures in 90–130 days from seed.

name: African Wild Mango (Ogbono, Dika Nut)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African wild mango grows as a large forest tree requiring considerable space in zone 10–12. Irvingia gabonensis (African wild mango, ogbono, or dika nut) is a large, canopy forest tree native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, Ivory Coast, and the Congo Basin — and one of the most economically important non-timber forest trees of the West African rainforest zone. The tree produces round to oval, 2–3 inch fruits that superficially resemble small mangoes externally (hence 'African wild mango') but are unrelated: the fruit flesh (mesocarp) is sweet, yellowish, edible, and pleasant, but it is the large, hard-shelled seeds inside that represent the primary economic and culinary product. The seeds (ogbono nuts or dika nuts) are dried, smoked, or processed into ground ogbono powder — the essential thickening and flavoring agent in Nigerian ogbono soup (also called draw soup for its slimy, mucilaginous texture) and related soups across the forest zone of West Africa. Ground ogbono has a distinctive, complex, slightly bitter, earthy-nutty flavor and contains mucilaginous compounds (similar to okra) that create the characteristic 'draw' texture of the soup. The seeds also yield dika oil (Gaboon chocolate), used in confectionery. The tree gained international attention as a weight-loss supplement ingredient (IGOB131 extract) in the 2000s, with preliminary studies suggesting effects on blood lipids. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: African Wormwood
description: Plant Artemisia afra in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; avoid rich, wet soils which produce lush but less aromatic and medicinally active foliage; prune back hard each spring to maintain compact, bushy form; propagate easily from cuttings in late spring. African Wormwood is the cornerstone of South African traditional herbal medicine — a deeply aromatic, silver-grey-green shrub with finely divided leaves and a characteristic powerful, camphor-dominated fragrance that is instantly recognized across southern Africa. Traditional use includes steaming the crushed leaves in a bowl of hot water for inhalation to relieve cold and flu symptoms; drinking infusions (umhlonyane tea) for fever, malaria, coughs, and stomach complaints; and rubbing the leaves on the body as an insect repellent. The plant is used by practitioners of all major South African healing traditions — Zulu izinyanga, Xhosa izangoma, Cape Malay bonesmiths — and is sold in enormous quantities at traditional medicine markets (muthi shops) throughout the country. Research has confirmed antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic activity of various leaf extracts. The plant is hardy, attractive, and easy to grow in any warm, dry garden position; it makes an excellent border shrub for drought-tolerant Mediterranean-style gardens in zone 8–11. Related to the Northern Hemisphere wormwoods (Artemisia absinthium, A. annua) but distinct and more cold-hardy than expected for an African species. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: African Yam Bean (Haricot Igname)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun after danger of frost has passed; African yam bean is a twining annual legume from West Africa producing seeds with an extremely high protein content (23–29%) — one of the richest protein sources among African grain legumes. The seeds are a major staple and market commodity in Nigeria, Ghana, and surrounding countries, used in a variety of traditional dishes including moi-moi (steamed bean pudding), bean stew, and roasted bean snacks. A notable cooking challenge is the trypsin inhibitors in the raw beans, which require extended cooking or fermentation to neutralize — the seeds cook much more slowly than common beans. The vine is ornamental when trained on a fence or trellis. In zone 9a it grows as a warm-season annual from late spring through fall, producing a reasonable harvest in the long Texas growing season. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Agarita (Agarito, Algerita, Texas Barberry)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; agarita is a classic native Texas evergreen shrub with small, three-lobed, holly-like leaves (each with sharp spines) arranged in a distinctive trifoliate pattern — it looks like a small holly with fierce spines and makes an impenetrable wildlife barrier hedge. In spring it produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant yellow flowers, followed by brilliant red tart berries in late spring that are relished by birds and made by Texas foragers into highly prized jelly. The flavor is tart-sweet, similar to a currant. The berries ripen and fall quickly — traditionally harvested by spreading a tarp under the shrub and shaking the branches. Deer browse it rarely due to the spines. A tough, beautiful, and ecologically valuable native for difficult dry spots in zone 6–9. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Agati (Hummingbird Tree, Vegetable Hummingbird, August Tree)
description: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil after temperatures warm above 70°F; Agati grows equally well in poor, sandy, or clay soils and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility. Sesbania grandiflora is one of the most useful edible trees in tropical and subtropical agroforestry — a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing legume tree native to South and Southeast Asia where its white or red flowers (2–4 inches long, the largest flowers in the Fabaceae), young leaves, and tender seed pods are prized vegetables in Thai, Filipino, Indonesian, and Indian cuisines. The flowers are eaten raw in salads, battered and fried, or cooked in curries and soups; the young leaves are used like spinach or kale; the long, flat seed pods are cooked as a vegetable. The tree is also an important fodder and green manure crop. In zone 9, Sesbania grandiflora grows spectacularly fast — often reaching 20+ feet in a single growing season — and produces beautiful pendant flowers continuously. It is killed to the ground by hard frost but may resprout from the crown in zone 9b. Harvest foliage and flowers regularly to stimulate continuous production and prevent the plant from becoming leggy. The large white or red flowers are highly attractive to hummingbirds and native bees. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Aglandau Olive (Cold-Hardy Provençal Oil Olive)
description: Aglandau is a heritage cultivar from the hill country of Haute-Provence, prized in French groves for producing oil with a bold, green, artichoke-and-almond character, and it is one of the more cold-hardy French olive cultivars, tolerating brief dips into the low teens Fahrenheit better than many Mediterranean selections once established. It is self-sterile, so a compatible second cultivar such as Picholine or Leccino should be planted nearby to ensure a good fruit set. The tree carries narrow, willowy foliage and bears medium, elongated olives that are typically pressed for oil while still green rather than cured as a table fruit. Expect slow establishment in the first few years in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil, followed by strong, reliable production once the tree matures. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Agretti (Monk's Beard)
description: Sow very fresh seed 1/4 inch deep thickly in cool, well-drained soil, as germination rates drop dramatically when seed is more than a few months old — plan to sow thickly and use thinnings. Agretti is an Italian coastal plant related to glasswort, and it thrives in sandy, saline, or alkaline soils where most vegetables struggle; it is very intolerant of waterlogged conditions. Harvest young shoot tips and the grass-like, succulent leaves when 6–8 inches tall by snipping with scissors 1–2 inches above the soil, allowing the plant to regrow once or twice before it goes to seed. The slender, fleshy, bright-green leaves have a mildly salty, slightly mineral flavor outstanding blanched with lemon or served alongside fish and seafood in the Italian spring tradition. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Agrimony (Common Agrimony)
description: Agrimonia eupatoria is a slender, upright, rosette-forming perennial herb native to dry grasslands, hedgerows, and woodland edges throughout Europe and western Asia, producing pinnate, strongly aromatic, slightly rough-hairy leaves and long, slender spikes of small, five-petaled, bright-yellow flowers from early to mid summer, followed by small, hooked bur-fruits that cling to clothing and animal fur for seed dispersal. Direct-sow seeds in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline or calcareous soil in a sunny to partly shaded position; seeds require cold stratification for reliable germination and will germinate in spring after a natural winter cold period. In traditional Western herbalism, the whole above-ground plant is harvested in flower and used as a gentle astringent, anti-inflammatory, and tonic herb with a long history of use for wound healing, sore throats, digestive complaints, and urinary tract support — it was a primary wound herb of medieval European medicine. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and perform best in lean, well-drained soil; avoid rich, wet conditions. The dried herb makes a pleasant, mildly apricot-scented tea. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Ahipa (Andean Yam Bean)
description: A domesticated relative of jicama from the eastern Andean valleys of Bolivia and northern Argentina, ahipa grows as a compact, bushy, semi-erect legume rather than jicama's rampant climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and fits closer garden spacing. Pinch off flower buds as they form throughout the season to keep the plant's energy directed into the turnip-shaped storage roots instead of seed production. As with jicama, only the root is edible; the foliage, pods, and seeds contain rotenone and should not be eaten. Harvest once foliage begins to yellow in fall, typically 5–6 months after sowing. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Aidan Fruit Tree (Prekese)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to West African forests, this legume tree bears distinctive long, dark brown, four-winged (tetrapterous) pods filled with an intensely aromatic pulp used as a seasoning in soups and stews across Ghana and Nigeria, known as prekese, and long valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic properties. A member of the pea family, it fixes nitrogen in the soil like many of its legume relatives, and its distinctive winged seed pods make it an interesting specimen tree for a tropical botanical or ethnobotanical planting in frost-free climates. Water regularly while young, and expect pods to be harvested for seasoning once the tree reaches bearing maturity after several years. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Ailsa Craig Onion
description: Ailsa Craig is a long-day heirloom producing very large, globe-shaped golden bulbs with a mild, sweet flavor, best grown in northern latitudes. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set out seedlings as soon as the soil is workable, spacing 4-6 inches apart. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly watered through bulbing, then taper off water as tops begin to fall. These sweet onions store only a few months, so use the largest bulbs first. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Ailsa Craig Tomato (Classic Scottish Heirloom Slicer)
description: Sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F, staking or caging the vines as they grow. Ailsa Craig was bred in Girvan, Scotland in the early 1900s and quickly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in British gardens and allotments, prized for producing heavy clusters of medium, smooth, bright red fruit with a well-balanced, classic tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark variety in the UK for home growers wanting a dependable, flavorful, mid-sized slicer. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Air Potato (Air Yam, Potato Yam)
description: Plant aerial bulbils (the small, potato-like structures that form along the stems) or underground tubers after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree for support; air potato grows extremely rapidly in warm conditions. IMPORTANT: In Florida and other warm states, Dioscorea bulbifera is listed as invasive and its cultivation is regulated or prohibited — consult USDA and state Department of Agriculture guidelines before planting. Dioscorea bulbifera is a tropical Asian vine grown widely in Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands as a minor food crop — the aerial bulbils (small, edible tubers that develop at the leaf axils) and the underground tubers are both edible after cooking, though many wild or feral populations contain potentially toxic compounds that require thorough boiling in multiple changes of water to render safe; cultivated varieties are generally milder. In markets across West Africa and Asia, edible cultivars are distinguished from bitter, toxic ones by appearance and flavor; seek out named edible cultivars from specialty tropical plant sources. The vine is a remarkably productive food plant in tropical gardens but must be managed aggressively to prevent escape. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Aizumishirazu Persimmon (Seedless Japanese Astringent Kaki for Drying)
description: Aizumishirazu hails from the Aizu region of Fukushima Prefecture and is one of Japan's classic astringent persimmon cultivars grown specifically for drying into anpogaki and hoshigaki, traditional sweet dried persimmon treats made by peeling and air-curing the firm fruit until the sugars concentrate and the tannins mellow. Fruit is medium-sized, conical, and seedless without pollination, with deep orange flesh that turns amber and jammy once fully soft for fresh eating instead of drying. The tree is a reliable, heavy annual bearer and handles the Gulf Coast's mild winters and modest chill hours without difficulty, though its astringency at harvest means growers should plan on either drying racks or a patient windowsill-ripening routine rather than eating fruit straight off the branch. Vivid orange fall foliage and heavily laden bare branches in late autumn make this a strong ornamental as well as a productive fruit tree. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Aji Amarillo Pepper (Fruity Orange-Yellow Peruvian Hot Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aji Amarillo is the foundational hot pepper of Peruvian cuisine — considered one of the essential 'holy trinity' ingredients of Peruvian cooking (with garlic and onion) and the basis for Peru's iconic yellow sauces. The 3–5 inch, elongated-conical, thin-walled fruits ripen from green through orange-yellow to bright yellow-orange, with a distinctive fruity, tropical flavor and significant heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville units) that is entirely different from the neutral burn of jalapeños. The fruity, complex flavor — often described as combining apricot, mango, and passion fruit with a persistent, building heat — makes Aji Amarillo irreplaceable in Peruvian cooking and increasingly prized by chefs worldwide for its unique flavor profile. As a Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean species group distinct from C. annuum and C. chinense), Aji Amarillo requires somewhat warmer germination temperatures and a longer season than standard bell peppers. In zone 9, the long growing season is ideal for the 90–120 day maturity period, and the plants may become quite large (3–4 feet) and productive by mid-summer. Fresh fruits, paste, and dried/powdered form all have distinct culinary applications. The dried, rehydrated paste is the standard form used in traditional Peruvian cooking. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Aji Charapita Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aji Charapita is a wild-type Capsicum chinense pepper from the Peruvian Amazon, producing an extraordinary abundance of tiny pea-sized (3–5 mm) round yellow fruits on a prolific, heavily branching plant. The fruits are one of the most expensive peppers by weight in the world — sold as a specialty ingredient in high-end Peruvian and international cuisine for their unique combination of intense heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville), exceptional fruity citrus-tropical fragrance, and concentrated flavor. Because each fruit is pea-sized, a single productive plant can bear hundreds of fruits simultaneously, covering the plant in an impressive display of tiny yellow peppers. The flavor is described as intensely fruity with citrus, mango, and passion fruit notes beneath the heat — the signature Capsicum chinense fruity aromatic character concentrated into a miniature fruit. In Peru, Aji Charapita is used in ceviche, sauces, and as a table condiment in vinegar brine. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Aji Colorado Pepper (Bolivian-Peruvian Sweet-Hot Aji)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this Bolivian-Peruvian baccatum type needs a long warm season to fully ripen its pendant, 3-5 inch pods. Fruit matures from green through orange to a deep brick-red, carrying a fast-hitting heat (roughly 20,000-30,000 Scoville units) that fades quickly and leaves a sweet, fruity aftertaste. Thin walls make it well suited to drying or blending into fresh aji sauces once red-ripe; harvest continuously to extend production into fall. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Aji Crystal Pepper (Chilean Mild Yellow Baccatum Sweet Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest pale yellow to cream-white fruits for mildest flavor; allow to ripen orange-red for sweeter, more developed flavor. Aji Crystal is a Chilean baccatum pepper from the Capsicum baccatum species — a pepper species distinct from the common C. annuum and characterized by the spotted calyx markings at the base of the flower, a more complex flavor profile, and a heat level that can range from mild to medium-hot. Aji Crystal is at the mild end of the baccatum spectrum, with very low heat (typically under 500 SHU) that makes it essentially a sweet pepper with baccatum's distinctive flavor complexity. The fruits are elongated (4–5 inches), thin-walled, and pale yellow to near-white at the harvest stage — almost translucent in appearance, suggesting the crystal-clear quality for which the variety is named. The flavor is crisp, bright, slightly sweet and tangy with a fruity, aromatic quality distinctive of baccatum peppers — difficult to describe but clearly different from C. annuum sweet peppers and very pleasant raw in salads, stuffed, or used fresh in Peruvian-style preparations where baccatum peppers are traditional. Aji Crystal is popular among pepper enthusiasts and chefs interested in flavors beyond the standard C. annuum palette. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Aji Dulce Pepper (Sweet Habanero, Cachucha Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger; aji dulce is the sweet-fruited strain of the habanero pepper species (Capsicum chinense) — it looks exactly like a miniature habanero with thin, wrinkled skin in green ripening to yellow-orange or red, and has all the distinctive floral, fruity, intensely aromatic habanero fragrance without any heat whatsoever (Scoville 0–500, vs 100,000–350,000 for regular habanero). The aroma and flavor are extraordinary — simultaneously citrusy, floral, fruity, and deeply savory — making aji dulce irreplaceable in Puerto Rican, Dominican, Venezuelan, and Cuban cooking, where it is the backbone of sofrito, the aromatic base paste for countless dishes. In zone 9–12 gardens it often becomes a short-lived perennial shrub. An outstanding unique pepper for gardeners who love the habanero aroma but want zero capsaicin heat. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Aji Fantasy Pepper (Finnish-Bred Translucent Yellow Baccatum)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost; this compact, high-yielding baccatum variety was developed in Finland and matures faster than most aji types, making it a good option for shorter growing seasons. The roughly 2 inch, bonnet-shaped pods ripen to a translucent yellow and deliver a mild-to-medium heat (about 5,000-10,000 Scoville units) with pronounced tropical sweetness. Stake plants as they load up with fruit, and pick continuously to keep the heavily branching bushes producing. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Aji Mango Pepper
description: Aji Mango is a newer selection within the aji (Capsicum baccatum) group, prized for tapered two- to three-inch pods that ripen from green through orange to red and deliver a distinctly sweet, tropical, mango-like fruitiness ahead of a moderate, lingering heat. Grow it exactly as you would other baccatum types: rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and even moisture, since the plants can turn woody and less productive if allowed to dry out repeatedly between waterings. The sprawling, heavily-branched bushes benefit from staking or a tomato cage once loaded with fruit, and picking ripe pods regularly keeps new flowers setting through a long warm season. In frost-free zones the plant can be overwintered and will return as a short-lived perennial, producing an even heavier crop in its second year. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Aji Panca Pepper (Peruvian Brown Pepper)
description: Start seeds on a heat mat at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when soil is warm. Aji Panca is one of the most important and distinctive chiles in Peruvian cuisine, a large (3–4 inch), elongated, deep brownish-red pepper belonging to Capsicum chinense but with very mild heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) and an extraordinary flavor profile: smoky, deeply fruity, berry-like, and slightly sweet with almost no raw pungency — it is more like a richly flavored dried fruit than a typical hot pepper. In Peru it is primarily used dried and pureed as a chile paste (pasta de aji panca) that forms the flavor base of marinades, braises, anticuchos (grilled beef hearts), and the classic preparation aji de gallina. Rarely found outside Latin American grocery stores in the US; growing your own from seed is the only way to access this unique pepper fresh in most American gardens. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Ajo Rojo Garlic (Creole Softneck)
description: Brought to the United States from Spain by way of Nevada growers in the early 1990s, Ajo Rojo is a Creole-type softneck prized for its brilliant purple-streaked clove wrappers and adaptability to hot, arid regions where hardneck garlics struggle. Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up in fall in well-drained soil, mulching lightly over winter in colder zones. The flavor is mild and creamy when roasted but builds into a slow, powerful heat when eaten raw, making it popular with cooks who want garlic with real punch. Harvest when the lower third of leaves has browned, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; Creole types store notably longer than most hardnecks. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Ajwain (Carom Seed, Bishop Weed, Ajowan)
description: Direct sow seeds in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 8–12 inches. Trachyspermum ammi (ajwain or carom seed) is an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to Egypt and the Near East, cultivated extensively in India, Pakistan, and Iran for its small, ribbed seeds with an intensely pungent thyme-like but more piercing aroma and flavor — the dominant compound is thymol, which is also found in thyme, but present in much higher concentrations in ajwain seeds. In Indian cooking, ajwain is used in breads (naan, paratha), lentil dishes (dal), fritters (pakoras), pickles, and dry spice blends where its strong, distinctive flavor contributes essential character that cannot be substituted. The seeds are used whole (dry-roasted to release their oil before adding) or ground; they also have significant traditional medicinal use in South Asian medicine for digestive complaints. The plant resembles a small, upright dill or caraway with feathery, blue-green leaves and compound white flower umbels in spring; harvest when seed heads dry and turn brown. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Akane Apple (Tokyo Rose, Early Scab-Resistant Tart-Sweet Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible early-blooming pollinator. Bred in Japan from a cross of Jonathan and Worcester Pearmain and released in 1970, Akane produces small-to-medium, bright red apples with crisp, juicy, tart-sweet flesh reminiscent of Jonathan but with better resistance to apple scab. It ripens in late summer, ahead of most main-season apples, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early harvest without spraying heavily for disease. Fruit is best used fresh or in sauce shortly after picking, as it does not store as long as later-season varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Akers West Virginia Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Akers West Virginia is an heirloom tomato preserved in the Appalachian tradition of West Virginia seed saving, producing large, meaty, deep red beefsteak-type fruits with a classic, complex, sweet-acidic flavor typical of the best Old World tomato varieties maintained by Appalachian farm families for generations. The large (often 12–24 ounce) fruits have thick, meaty walls with small seed cavities and outstanding fresh-eating flavor — the balanced combination of sweetness and bright acidity makes Akers West Virginia one of the most satisfying large heirloom varieties for fresh slicing. The fruit shows good resistance to cracking despite its size. Like most Appalachian heirlooms, Akers West Virginia developed in a region with variable, challenging weather and has proven adaptability to different growing conditions. In zone 9 the fall crop (planted in August, harvested October–November) often produces exceptionally flavored fruits as cooler temperatures concentrate sugars and acid. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Akizuki Asian Pear (Autumn Moon Pear)
description: Bred in Japan and released as a newer alternative to older russet cultivars, Akizuki produces large, round, brown-gold fruit with a flavor that is notably sweeter and lower in acid than many older Asian pear cultivars. The flesh is crisp and stays firm in storage longer than most nashi types, which has made it popular with growers who want an extended eating window after harvest. It ripens in mid-to-late season, generally after Hosui and Shinseiki but before Korean Giant, and requires cross-pollination to set a full crop. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Al-Sirin-Nar Pomegranate (Turkish Soft-Seeded Deep-Red Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Al-Sirin-Nar, a Turkish cultivar whose name translates roughly to 'sweet pomegranate,' bears large fruit filled with deep-red, notably soft-seeded arils and a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that has made it one of the more sought-after fresh-eating pomegranate cultivars among collectors. Trees are vigorous and productive, ripening fruit in the fall for fresh eating, juicing, or preserving. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Alabama Blackeye Butterbean (Alabama Black Eye Lima Bean)
description: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, training the long twining vines up a tall, sturdy trellis, fence, or row of poles. Alabama Blackeye is a family-passed-down Alabama heirloom baby lima, also known regionally as a butterbean, bearing small, creamy white seeds marked with a distinctive small black eye at the hilum. It is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant and keeps setting pods heavily through the hottest, muggiest stretches of Gulf Coast summer that slow many other lima varieties, making it a reliable choice for zone 9a gardens. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh eating in classic Southern butterbean dishes and succotash, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage; shell beans regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive into fall. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Alabama Blue Collard (Heirloom Blue-Green Collard)
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing once seedlings have several true leaves. Alabama Blue is a Deep South heirloom collard grown for generations for its striking blue-green, slightly savoyed leaves and excellent cold hardiness, surviving hard freezes that damage less hardy greens and developing sweeter, milder flavor after exposure to frost. The tall, upright plants produce abundant leaves over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again style, taking outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best leaf production, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, which can be managed with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Alabama Blue Collards (Southern Heirloom Blue-Green Collard)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard with broad, slightly savoyed, distinctly blue-green leaves, maintained and passed down through generations of Southern home gardeners rather than developed by a commercial breeding program. The flavor is rich and full-bodied even before frost, and like other collards sweetens further after the first light freezes of fall. Plants are tall and vigorous, tolerating both Gulf South summer heat and winter cold well, and the open-pollinated nature means seed can be saved from the best plants each year to maintain the strain in a home garden. Harvest the lower and outer leaves as needed, leaving the growing tip intact so the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the top over a long cool-season harvest window. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Alabama Red Okra
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches in rows 3 feet apart; soak seeds overnight before planting. Alabama Red is a regional heirloom okra from Alabama home gardens, one of the distinct Deep South red-podded okra strains that differs from Red Velvet in being taller, more vigorous, and producing somewhat more slender pods with an intensely dark red to mahogany coloring; the flavor is excellent, with a slightly richer taste than some green varieties, and the pods are harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness. Like other red okras, the pigment is water-soluble and leaches from the pods during cooking unless they are quickly roasted or fried. The tall plants (5–8 feet) with deeply lobed leaves and large yellow-centered flowers make Alabama Red an outstanding ornamental-edible for the Southern food garden. Maintained by seed savers in Alabama and nearby states and representative of the regional diversity in Southern okra cultivation. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Alabaster Celeriac (Pale-Skinned Storage Celery Root)
description: Alabaster is a light-skinned celeriac whose pale flesh discolors noticeably less than many other varieties once peeled or cooked, an advantage for cooks who want a bright white puree or gratin. The globes are typically smaller and more rounded than some maincrop celeriac, with a strong, clean celery flavor and good storage life in a root cellar. Grow exactly as other celeriac: start early indoors given the slow germination, transplant into deep, fertile, constantly moist soil, and remove developing side roots through the season to channel growth into a single dense globe. Harvest in fall after light frost, which improves the flavor. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Alachua Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to maintain productive fruiting wood. Alachua is a University of Florida-released black muscadine bred and selected specifically for the low-chill, high-heat, high-humidity conditions of Florida and the Deep South, where it produces large, high-quality fruit reliably even in areas too warm for many Georgia- and Carolina-bred muscadine cultivars. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, bearing medium-to-large black fruit with good sweetness and flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Its Florida-focused breeding makes it a particularly strong choice for muscadine growers in the warmest parts of the Gulf South, zone 7–10. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Alachua Southern Highbush Blueberry (Florida-Bred Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Amend the planting bed to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and mulch well to conserve moisture around the shallow root zone. Alachua is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for the state's mild winters, producing medium to large, firm, flavorful berries on a vigorous bush that ripens over a solid midseason window. Its very low chilling requirement makes it a dependable choice even after an unusually warm winter along the Gulf Coast, where higher-chill varieties can bloom poorly or fail to set fruit. Plant with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination and yield, fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alamo Turnip (Bolt-Resistant Hybrid Greens Turnip)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a modern hybrid turnip grown for its greens rather than its roots, producing up to 50% higher yield than standard turnip greens varieties along with excellent regrowth after cutting, letting a single planting support several harvests through the cool season. It shows moderate resistance to bolting and tolerates aphids and mosaic virus better than many older turnip greens varieties, useful for stretching a spring planting later into warming weather. Harvest young leaves at 6-10 inches for the most tender greens, cutting to about 4 inches above the crown and allowing regrowth for the next cutting. Because it establishes and regrows quickly, Alamo suits both a fall planting for winter greens and a spring planting for an early crop. Matures in 33–45 days from seed.

name: Alampur Baneshan Mango (Historic Telangana Parent of Pickering)
description: Alampur Baneshan takes its name from the temple town of Alampur in present-day Telangana, where it has been grown for generations across the Deccan Plateau as one of South India's most widely planted commercial mango cultivars. The medium to large fruit ripens to a golden-yellow skin over fiberless, richly aromatic flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor prized for both fresh eating and juicing, and it was later carried to Florida as the parent of the compact dooryard cultivar Pickering. Like many Indian cultivars it tends toward alternate bearing and sets its heaviest crops after a dry, sunny bloom period that limits anthracnose. Shelter young trees from any frost and give the eventual canopy plenty of room, since established trees become large, long-lived specimens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Alano Sapodilla
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor, alkaline-tolerant soil — Alano is one of the few high-quality sapodilla cultivars that sets fruit reliably on South Florida's rocky, calcareous soils. The round to oval fruits have smooth, thin skin and fine-grained, low-grit tan flesh with a rich, malty, brown-sugar sweetness that Florida growers rank among the best-flavored sapodilla selections available, distinct from and often preferred over 'Brown Sugar' for its smoother texture. Trees are self-fertile, wind-tolerant, and extremely drought-hardy once established, needing supplemental water mainly during establishment and dry fruit-set periods. Harvest fruit when it develops a dull, scurfy skin and yields slightly to gentle pressure, then ripen off the tree for several days at room temperature before eating. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Alapaha Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Alapaha is an early-ripening rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia and named for the Alapaha River region of south Georgia, bred to combine early harvest timing with better-than-average tolerance of Septoria and other leaf-spot diseases common in humid Gulf South summers. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and firm with good flavor for an early variety. Fruit set improves noticeably with a second rabbiteye cultivar planted nearby, since Alapaha is only partially self-fruitful. The upright, vigorous bush needs little training beyond removing old unproductive canes each winter. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day to further reduce leaf-spot pressure in humid climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alapaha Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Alapaha is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for exceptional berry quality — the fruit is large, light blue, and has a dessert quality with a sweet-tart balance and crisp texture that earned it high consumer preference ratings in taste trials. Released in 2001, Alapaha is among the newer rabbiteye cultivars with improved fruit quality over the older varieties developed in the mid-20th century. It ripens early in the rabbiteye season (late May to mid-June in zone 8–9), overlapping with Premier and producing well with 300–400 chilling hours. The moderately vigorous, upright-to-spreading shrubs are productive and show reasonable resistance to late-season water stress. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Albariño Wine Grape (Crisp Coastal Spanish White)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Albariño is the signature white grape of Galicia in northwestern Spain, known there as Albariño and just across the border in Portugal as Alvarinho, producing crisp, aromatic wines with bright citrus and stone fruit character and a distinctive faint salinity often attributed to the vineyards' proximity to the Atlantic coast. The grape's notably thick skin gives it real practical resistance to the rot and fungal pressure common in the humid, maritime climate of its home region, a useful trait that also helps it perform well in other humid growing areas where thinner-skinned white varieties struggle. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize good airflow through the canopy, and harvest to preserve the variety's signature bright acidity, since Albariño loses its refreshing character if left to hang too long. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Albemarle Muscadine Grape
description: Albemarle is a self-fertile, black-skinned muscadine named for the Albemarle Sound region of northeastern North Carolina, where it has long been prized as a dependable dooryard and small-vineyard selection. Berries are medium-sized with unusually high sugar content and a dry stem scar that lets fruit be pulled cleanly for fresh eating, juice, or preserves without tearing. It ripens early to midseason and holds up reliably through the humid Carolina and Gulf South growing season. Train vines on a two-wire trellis or arbor and prune hard each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Albiflora Sage (White-Flowered Culinary Sage)
description: Albiflora is ordinary common sage in every respect except flower color: instead of the usual violet-blue spikes, it blooms in pure white in early summer, making it a useful choice for a white or moon garden where the typical purple sage flower would clash. The grey-green pebbled leaves are fully flavored and can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like standard culinary sage. It shares the same drought tolerance, sprawling woody habit, and need for excellent drainage as the species, and old plants benefit from a hard spring pruning to keep them from becoming leggy. Choose it when you want the culinary reliability of common sage without the purple flower color competing with nearby plantings. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Albiflorus White Creeping Thyme (White-Flowered Groundcover Thyme)
description: Albiflorus is a pure white-flowered form of creeping thyme that hugs the ground so tightly it is often grown as a flowering lawn substitute or stepping-stone filler in place of turf. In early summer the fine, light-green mat all but disappears beneath a smothering flush of small white blooms that draw bees in large numbers, a striking contrast to the pink and magenta tones of most other creeping thyme selections. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and is exceptionally cold hardy for a thyme, but still demands sharp drainage and lean soil, since it declines quickly in wet or heavy ground. Mow or shear lightly after flowering if a tidier, more turf-like appearance is wanted. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Albina Vereduna Beet (Non-Bleeding White Heirloom)
description: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 3–4 inches once true leaves appear. Albina Vereduna is an old Dutch heirloom beet that produces round, creamy-white roots with a sweet, mild flavor generally regarded as less earthy than red beets, and because it contains no betalain pigment it can be roasted, pickled, or grated into salads without staining hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients pink. The glossy green tops are also excellent cooked as greens and, lacking red pigment, cook up a cleaner green than the tops of red beet varieties. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at 2–3 inches across for the best texture, since oversized roots can turn woody. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Albino White Beet (White Wonder Beet)
description: Sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep in loose, deep, well-amended soil; thin to 4 inches after seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Albino White Beet is a German heirloom producing smooth, round, pure white-fleshed roots that completely lack the red pigment (betalain) of standard beets. The absence of betalains means Albino White beets do not bleed red — they do not stain cutting boards, hands, clothing, or dishes, solving the primary practical complaint about cooking with beets. Flavor is milder, sweeter, and less earthy than red beets — some tasters describe the flavor as more like a very sweet parsnip than a classic beet. Excellent raw in salads where they won't discolor other ingredients, roasted until caramelized and sweet, or pickled in the traditional manner (they turn slightly golden-pink when pickled in wine vinegar). The greens are pale green and mild, also excellent cooked. White beets are often grown alongside red and golden beets for a colorful root vegetable display. In zone 9, fall-planted white beets mature beautifully through mild winters. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Albion Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral with Premium Flavor and Firm Flesh)
description: Plant crowns at soil level in full sun, well-amended soil. Pick fully red for best flavor. Albion Strawberry was released by the University of California Davis in 2006 (Plant Patent PP16172) by breeder Douglas Shaw and colleagues, and rapidly became one of the most commercially significant day-neutral strawberry varieties in North American production — widely planted in California's Watsonville and Salinas Valley commercial strawberry regions and increasingly adopted by home gardeners seeking premium-flavored everbearing varieties. The Albion name honors the historic English name for Great Britain, though the variety is entirely a California development. Albion's reputation among strawberry enthusiasts centers on its flavor: the combination of high sugar content, balanced acidity, and pronounced strawberry aroma places Albion consistently at or near the top in flavor comparisons among day-neutral varieties — closer to the flavor profile of heirloom or wild strawberries than most commercial types. The fruit is conical to long-conical in shape, medium to large, with uniformly bright red skin and firm, fully red flesh without the white center that characterizes lower-quality commercial strawberries. The firmness — significantly firmer than older varieties like Seascape — gives Albion good shipping quality for commercial growers and several days of excellent quality after harvest for home gardeners. Disease resistance is good: Albion shows strong resistance to Verticillium wilt and crown rot (Phytophthora cactorum), two of the most economically damaging strawberry diseases in California production systems. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Albus Rosemary (White-Flowered Culinary Rosemary)
description: Albus is an upright culinary rosemary selected for pure white flowers rather than the usual blue-violet, giving it the same needle-like aromatic foliage and classic pine-and-citrus flavor as standard rosemary but a distinct look in the garden. Plant it in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, since it is just as intolerant of wet feet as other rosemary types. It flowers most heavily on wood from the previous season, so prune lightly right after bloom rather than in fall to avoid removing next year's flower buds. Because it is somewhat less cold-hardy than upright green-flowered types, protect it or grow it in a container where winters regularly dip below the mid-teens. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Albus Southern Highbush Blueberry (Firm Extended-Harvest Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Albus is a 2022 University of Florida southern highbush release notable for holding firm fruit quality from the start of harvest all the way through the end of the picking season, rather than declining as many cultivars do late in the cycle. Its low chill requirement fits it for the mildest Gulf Coast winters, and it is typically grown under the evergreen (leaf-retaining) production system. Plant in raised, well-drained acidic beds and pair with another low-chill southern highbush cultivar for cross-pollination and fuller berry set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alcosa Savoy Cabbage
description: Alcosa forms dense, medium-sized heads wrapped in deeply blistered, blue-green savoyed leaves that hold their crinkled texture well into cold weather. Its compact frame allows tighter in-row spacing than standard round cabbages, making it a good fit for smaller beds or intensive succession planting. The heavily textured leaves are notably tender for a savoy type and hold up in the garden without splitting for an extended harvest window. Choose Alcosa when you want the classic savoy crinkle and cold tolerance in a shorter-season, space-efficient package. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Alden Grape (Large Blue Table Grape)
description: Released from the Geneva, New York breeding program, Alden produces very large, sweet, blue-black berries with a mild, distinctly non-foxy flavor prized by home growers who find Concord's flavor too strong. Clusters ripen in mid-season and the berries cling well, tolerating light delays in harvest. The vine is moderately vigorous and benefits from cluster thinning to maximize the impressive berry size it is known for. It withstands cold winters well and performs reliably as a dessert grape in northern home orchards. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alderman Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Alderman (also known as Tall Telephone) is a large-vine heirloom shelling pea producing very large, dark green pods of 4–5 inches, each containing 7–9 fat, sweet, dark green peas — the largest peas of any standard shelling type. It has been grown in American gardens since the 1880s and remains a benchmark for flavor and production among home garden peas. The large, starchy-sweet peas are particularly good for freezing because their size and firm texture hold up better than smaller-seeded varieties. The tall vines (4–5 feet) require stout support but reward with heavy production when trellised properly. Alderman is specifically adapted to the heavy production that makes the short cool-season window economically worthwhile for home gardeners and market growers — the high pod count and large pod size maximize yield from the brief growing window in zone 9. Do not fertilize heavily with nitrogen; peas fix their own and excess nitrogen promotes foliage over fruit. Matures in 68–74 days from seed.

name: Aleppo Pepper (Halaby Pepper, Syrian Dried Spice Chile with Fruity Mild Heat)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest when fully red; dry and crush for spice. Aleppo Pepper (also known as Halaby pepper, from Halab, the Arabic name for Aleppo) is a Capsicum annuum variety from Aleppo, Syria — a historic spice and trading city in northern Syria that gave its name to the region's most important spice pepper. Aleppo pepper occupies a unique position in global spice use: with a Scoville rating of approximately 10,000 units, it provides mild to moderate heat (significantly less than cayenne at 30,000–50,000 SHU) combined with a complex, distinctive flavor profile — fruity and slightly sweet, with undertones of cumin and salt, and a characteristic oiliness and depth unlike any other commonly used dried pepper spice. The pepper's distinctive quality comes from the drying and processing method: fruits are split, seeds are removed (seeds are slightly bitter), and the halved peppers are dried partially before being crushed into coarse, slightly moist flakes with a characteristic dark red color and shiny surface from the natural oils retained through partial drying. This traditional processing is quite different from completely desiccated paprika or cayenne, producing a spice with a unique fresh-dried quality. The Syrian civil war that began in 2011 severely disrupted Aleppo pepper production, causing supply shortages and price spikes in global markets; production has since been supplemented by Turkish-grown peppers of similar varieties and by growers in North America who have adopted the variety. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Alexanders
description: Smyrnium olusatrum, known as alexanders, is one of the oldest cultivated European pot herbs, widely grown by the Romans throughout their empire as a celery substitute and still naturalized along coastal cliffs, roadsides, and hedgebanks in mild, maritime regions of Europe from the Azores to the British Isles; it is a robust, biennial or short-lived perennial with bright, glossy, three-lobed leaves, hollow celery-scented stems, and distinctive rounded heads of small, greenish-yellow flowers followed by large, ridged, black seeds. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade, particularly in mild coastal gardens where it performs best; it is frost-hardy but prefers mild, maritime climates and does not thrive in hot, continental summers. All parts of the plant were used in Roman and medieval cooking as a celery substitute before celery (Apium graveolens) was cultivated: the young shoots and leaves are eaten as a potherb, the blanched stems as a vegetable, the flower buds in salads, and the roots and seeds as flavoring — the flavor is a distinctive, aromatic blend of celery and black pepper. Alexanders largely fell from culinary use after the widespread adoption of cultivated celery in the 17th century but is undergoing a revival among foragers, chefs interested in historical European cuisines, and those growing heritage kitchen garden crops. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Alexandria Alpine Strawberry (Heavy-Bearing Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)
description: Start Alexandria's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since germination depends on light exposure and steady moisture at room temperature, then transplant the young clumps into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, making it one of the more shade-adaptable strawberries for tucking beneath taller vegetables, shrubs, or fruit trees where full-sun beds are unavailable. Alexandria is valued among seed-grown alpine strawberries for its unusually heavy, extended production of small, intensely sweet, aromatic red berries with true wild-strawberry perfume. Because the runnerless plants stay in a tidy clump, they also work well as a low edible edging along a partly shaded path or border. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Alexandrian Laurel (Tamanu, Beauty Leaf, Beautyleaf, Kamani)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky coastal soils — Alexandrian Laurel is one of the most salt-tolerant large trees available for tropical coastal gardens and is an outstanding choice for beachfront and coastal landscapes in zone 10-11. Calophyllum inophyllum is a large, slow-to-moderately growing evergreen tree native to coastal environments from East Africa through South and Southeast Asia to Australia and the Pacific Islands — one of the few tree species with a genuinely pan-tropical coastal distribution, adapted to sandy, saline soils and salt-laden coastal winds. The tree produces a broad, spreading, dense canopy of large (4–8 inch), glossy, dark-green, oval leaves with distinctive parallel lateral veins that converge at both the midrib and leaf edge — a leaf venation pattern so distinctive that it is diagnostic for the genus Calophyllum. In spring and summer, the tree produces small clusters of intensely fragrant, white, 4-petaled flowers with prominent yellow stamens — the fragrance is sweet, fresh, and carries on the breeze. The round, green fruits (1–1.5 inches) contain a nut that is pressed to yield tamanu oil — a thick, nutty, golden-green fixed oil traditionally used throughout Polynesia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands for wound healing, skin care, and as a muscle pain remedy, and now widely used as a premium ingredient in natural cosmetics. The wood has been used for traditional outrigger canoes and structural timber throughout the Pacific. Matures in 1095–3650 days from transplant.

name: Alexandrian Senna
description: CAUTION: for short-term use only, contraindicated in pregnancy and intestinal obstruction; can cause cramping or electrolyte imbalance with overuse. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before starting indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost, then transplant into full sun and sandy, fast-draining soil once nights stay warm. Leaves and pods contain sennosides and are dried for the classic short-term stimulant laxative used in traditional and modern medicine alike. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Alfalfa Microgreens
description: Sow the small seed densely across a moist tray or shallow container of medium, indoors year-round. Keep evenly moist and provide bright, indirect light once the shoots emerge and green up. Harvest the tender, nutty micro shoots with scissors in about a week when the first leaves appear. Rinse and eat fresh in salads and sandwiches; no thinning or spacing is needed for this quick indoor crop. Matures in 7–10 days from seed.

name: Ali Baba Watermelon
description: Plant in hills spaced 6–8 feet apart in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; Ali Baba is an heirloom watermelon landrace from Iraq, where it has been cultivated for centuries in the intense heat and aridity of the Tigris-Euphrates region. The large (20–30 pound), pale green, blocky-oval fruits have vibrant red, exceptionally sweet and flavorful flesh with small seeds. What sets Ali Baba apart for Gulf Coast and zone 9 gardeners is its remarkable adaptation to heat: it continues setting fruit and maintains its characteristic sweetness through temperatures that stress modern commercial varieties, making it one of the best heirlooms for hot, dry or hot-humid summer conditions. It is also notably drought-tolerant compared to most watermelons once established. Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds introduced it to American growers and it has gained a devoted following among gardeners who prize heat tolerance and excellent flavor. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit dries and the skin lightens; the yellow ground spot also intensifies as fruit ripens. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Alicante Tomato (British Garden and Greenhouse Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once temperatures are reliably warm, providing a stake or cage for the indeterminate vines. Alicante is a long-established open-pollinated British variety known for consistent early cropping and smooth, medium-sized, deep red fruit with a well-rounded, sweet-tart flavor that holds up in cooler, shorter growing seasons. It has been a staple recommendation of UK seed catalogs and gardening programs for decades as a reliable outdoor and unheated-greenhouse tomato. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Aliceblue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Early-Season Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Aliceblue was released in 1978 by the University of Florida IFAS to give North and Central Florida growers a rabbiteye that fruits reliably across both high- and low-chill winters, and it remains one of the earliest-flowering, earliest-ripening rabbiteye selections available. Berries are medium-sized and sweet on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers very early, site it with good air drainage to reduce frost risk to blooms during a late cold snap, and pair it with a pollinizer other than Beckyblue due to known cross-incompatibility between the two. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain productive new fruiting canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: All American Parsnip
description: Sow fresh seed 1/2 inch deep directly in loose, stone-free soil, since parsnips do not transplant well and seed is short-lived. Germination is slow, often two to four weeks, so keep the bed evenly moist and mark the row. This variety thickens early, maturing in as little as 95 days, producing tender white roots with a sweet, distinctive flavor. Flavor sweetens further after a fall frost, so leave roots in the ground and harvest as needed through cold weather. Matures in 95–120 days from seed.

name: All Blue Potato (Purple Potato)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, loose, well-drained soil; All Blue (also called All Purple) is a heritage variety with Andean ancestry, producing medium-sized, oblong tubers with deep blue-purple skin and intensely blue-purple flesh throughout — the color does not fade with cooking, making brilliant blue-purple mashed potatoes, blue potato salad, and striking roasted wedges. The color is produced by anthocyanins — the same pigments in blueberries — that are potent antioxidants. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty, pleasant but not as rich as Yukon Gold or fingerlings. All Blue has relatively firm, waxy flesh that holds its shape when boiled or roasted. The plants are vigorous and productive. In zone 9, the unusual color makes them a conversation-starting crop at the farmers' market or dinner table; they are consistently one of the most visually dramatic vegetables in the garden when cut open. Plant alongside Red LaSoda for a striking red, white, and blue potato planting. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: All Gold Lemon Balm (Bright Golden-Yellow Foliage Lemon Balm)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; some morning sun deepens the golden foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch and leaf burn in hot climates. All Gold bears strikingly bright, uniform golden-yellow leaves rather than the plain green of the species, carrying the same fresh, lemony scent and flavor prized for teas, sachets, and culinary use, and its bright color makes it a strong foliage accent in a partly shaded herb bed even when not being harvested. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh, brightly colored new growth and to reduce self-seeding, since Melissa officinalis can spread aggressively from seed. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: All Purple Sweet Potato (Whole-Root Purple-Skin Purple-Flesh Heirloom)
description: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since overly rich soil favors vine growth over root formation. All Purple is a heirloom sweet potato selection distributed by small specialty growers as its own distinct cultivar alongside other named purple types like Molokai Purple and Purple Passion, producing roots with purple skin over dense, uniformly deep-purple flesh from center to edge. The texture is drier and firmer than orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, with an earthy, mildly sweet flavor that holds its color well when roasted or steamed, though it fades somewhat when boiled in acidic water. Sprawling vines with purple-tinged, deeply lobed leaves make it a dual-purpose plant, since the young leaves and shoot tips are also edible and commonly cooked as greens. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure in warm, humid conditions for a week or two to develop full sweetness and improve storage life. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: All The Year Round Lettuce
description: This adaptable heirloom lettuce forms crisp, mild green heads and resists bolting better than most, letting you harvest across spring, summer, and fall. Sow seed shallowly, barely covering it, since light aids germination, and thin plants to 8-12 inches for full heads. Succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply, and provide afternoon shade during hot spells to keep leaves sweet. It also performs well in containers and hydroponic setups. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: All-in-One Almond (Self-Fertile Genetic Dwarf Almond)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, since almonds are highly intolerant of wet feet and poorly drained sites lead to root rot. All-in-One is a genetic dwarf almond selected in California for reliable self-fertility, so unlike most almond varieties it does not need a separate pollinizer tree to set a crop, making it a practical choice for smaller home gardens with room for only one tree. The compact, naturally semi-dwarf habit stays smaller than standard almond trees while still producing a full-size, sweet, flavorful kernel. Very early spring bloom is both a strength and a risk: it allows an early start to the growing season but also exposes flowers to occasional late frost damage, so avoid planting in frost pockets. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the outer hulls split open, then dry nuts thoroughly before storing. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Allegheny Blackberry
description: Allegheny Blackberry is one of the most productive and widely distributed wild blackberries of eastern North America, growing in open fields, roadsides, forest edges, and disturbed ground from Nova Scotia south to Georgia. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing plants 4 to 6 feet apart; plants spread rapidly by root sprouts and will form dense, wildlife-supporting thickets if not managed. White flowers appear in spring on stout, heavily prickled, arching second-year canes, followed by large, firm, sweet black drupes from June through July that rank among the finest-flavored of any native blackberry. After harvest, cut spent floricanes to the ground to encourage strong new primocanes; very cold-hardy plants will begin reliable production in their second full year. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Allegheny Chinkapin (Eastern Chinkapin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; the Allegheny chinkapin is the smaller native cousin of the American chestnut and is fully resistant to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) — making it an irreplaceable food plant in regions where the American chestnut was eliminated. It produces small but richly flavored sweet nuts enclosed in a spiny bur, just one nut per bur (unlike 2–3 per bur in true chestnuts); they are superb eaten raw or roasted. Forms a thicket-like shrub to small tree via root-sprouting and is heavily used by deer, turkeys, and squirrels as mast. Best performance is on well-drained, acidic upland soils; heavy or wet soils cause decline. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Allegheny Pawpaw (Large-Fruited Peterson Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to more sun as the tree matures; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from decades of evaluation work aimed at identifying the largest, best-flavored, and most productive pawpaw seedlings for named release. It produces good-sized fruit with the rich, complex banana-mango-custard flavor pawpaw enthusiasts prize, on a vigorous, dependable tree. As with all pawpaws, Allegheny is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar such as Susquehanna or Shenandoah planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set — pawpaw flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so hand-pollinating with a small brush between two open flowers of different cultivars can meaningfully improve yield in a home planting. In zone 9, site trees where they get afternoon shade in the hottest years and expect best performance toward the cooler end of the zone. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Allegheny Plum (Porter's Plum)
description: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in fall or spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Allegheny plum spreads by root suckers and forms thickets over time, useful for naturalizing on a slope or bank. Clouds of white flowers cover the thicket-forming branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by small, dark purple, tart plums historically gathered by Appalachian settlers for jams and preserves, ripening in late summer on a small, suckering native tree found on dry ridges and rocky slopes of the central Appalachian region. Its suckering, thicket-forming habit makes it useful for stabilizing an eroding bank or naturalizing a difficult dry slope where its dense thicket provides wildlife cover as well as fruit. Water during establishment, then rely on natural rainfall, and allow it to sucker and spread if a naturalized thicket is the goal, or remove suckers to maintain a single specimen. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Allegheny Serviceberry
description: Divide root suckers or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade; Allegheny serviceberry is a native eastern North American multi-stemmed small tree of exceptional four-season ornamental value — in early spring (March–April), before the leaves emerge, the smooth gray-barked stems become covered with clusters of delicate, drooping, pure-white, star-shaped flowers that are among the first tree flowers of the year; the bronze-red emerging leaves turn green in summer; round, sweet, dark-purple, blueberry-like fruits ripen in June (hence an alternative common name 'Juneberry') and are edible, sweet, and excellent fresh, in pies, jams, and for drying like raisins; and the foliage turns vivid orange-red to burgundy in autumn. As a native understory tree that grows naturally at forest edges and in open woodlands, Allegheny serviceberry is one of the most shade-tolerant fruiting trees available and will produce a useful fruit crop in partial shade conditions where no other small fruit tree would bear productively. The ripe berries are eagerly sought by at least 35 species of birds. Excellent combined with witch hazels and native azaleas in a naturalistic woodland edible garden. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Alleppey Turmeric (High-Curcumin Kerala Turmeric for Gulf South Gardens)
description: Plant rhizome pieces 2–4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Alleppey turmeric is a high-curcumin selection named for the Alleppey (Alappuzha) region of Kerala, India — one of the primary commercial turmeric production areas — where this variety is selected for the deep orange-yellow color and high curcumin content that make it particularly valuable for culinary and medicinal uses. Curcumin is the bioactive compound responsible for turmeric's anti-inflammatory properties and vivid yellow-orange color; Alleppey selections typically contain 5–7% curcumin by dry weight versus 2–3% in ordinary turmeric. The turmeric plant itself is ornamentally beautiful in Gulf South tropical gardens: broad, paddle-shaped leaves (similar to canna) on upright stems reaching 3–4 feet, with occasional cream-and-pale-purple flower spikes that emerge from the leaf bases in summer. In zone 9, turmeric grows as a perennial if mulched heavily during winter, or the rhizomes can be stored frost-free and replanted each spring. Harvest fresh turmeric rhizomes in fall for immediate use — the fresh rhizome flavor is brighter and more complex than dried powder — or cure, dry, and powder for long-term storage. The plant grows best in the same conditions as its ginger relatives: warm, humid, partially shaded, with consistent moisture. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Alliance Bell Pepper (Multi-Virus and Bacterial Spot-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Alliance is a bell pepper hybrid bred for resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot along with tolerance to an unusually wide range of viruses, giving it strong protection against both the bacterial and viral diseases that spread readily through humid Gulf South gardens via rain splash and aphid activity. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good flavor if left on the plant. Because viral diseases have no cure once a plant is infected, Alliance's broad tolerance package helps prevent the stunting, mottled foliage, and reduced yield that viruses cause in more susceptible varieties. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued fruit set. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Alligator Pepper (Hepper Pepper, Mbongo Spice)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in tropical conditions; alligator pepper is a West African spice plant in the ginger family producing large ridged pods (resembling a small alligator's head, hence the name) packed with numerous seeds that have a complex, resinous, cardamom-like flavor with black pepper heat and citrus overtones. An important ceremonial and culinary spice in Nigeria, Cameroon, and other West African nations, used to season soups, stews, and meat dishes, and traditionally presented to guests as a mark of respect. Related to and used similarly to grains of paradise (Aframomum melegueta) but with a more complex flavor profile. Rare in Western cultivation but rewarding for adventurous tropical gardeners. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Alligator Root (Renealmia, Vanilla-Leaf Ginger, Wild Ginger Lily)
description: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Renealmia alpinia thrives in the shaded, moist conditions of a tropical understory garden and wilts and declines in exposed, dry, or overly sunny positions. Renealmia alpinia is a clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to the Caribbean Islands, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the family Zingiberaceae (the ginger family), related to Alpinia and Zingiber. The plant produces tall (4–8 foot), cane-like, leafy stems clothed in large, lance-shaped to oblong, dark-green leaves that, when crushed, release a pleasant fragrance combining vanilla, ginger, and green herbs — a quality that has led to the plant's use in traditional folk medicine and cooking throughout its native range, where the aromatic leaves, rhizomes, and berries flavor foods and beverages.
