The inflorescences emerge near the base of the plant on short separate stems — a basal inflorescence style common in Renealmia — bearing showy clusters of orange-red to red flowers followed by decorative, bright red to scarlet berries (capsules) that are genuinely ornamental. The berries are used medicinally and as a condiment in parts of Colombia and Venezuela. An unusual and attractive shade-garden ginger relative for zone 10-11 tropical gardens. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Allison Kiwi (New Zealand Fuzzy Kiwifruit Selection)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and give the vine a sturdy, permanent trellis, since fuzzy kiwi vines grow large and live for decades. Allison is one of the historic New Zealand fuzzy kiwi cultivars developed in the early twentieth century alongside Hayward, named for nurseryman Alexander Allison, and it remains a female-only selection that will not fruit without a nearby male vine, with a common pollination guideline of about one male for every eight to ten female vines. Fruit quality is good and comparable to other classic New Zealand selections, though Hayward remains the dominant commercial standard worldwide. Prune during winter dormancy to thin overcrowded canes and expose fruiting wood to light, and water deeply and regularly through the growing season since kiwi vines have relatively shallow roots and dislike drying out. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Allred Plum (Red-Purple-Leaved Ornamental-Edible Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible plum cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set. Allred is a hybrid plum valued as much for its landscape impact as its harvest, holding rich red-purple foliage color through the growing season that rivals purpleleaf ornamental plums, while still producing sweet-tart, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit good for fresh eating and preserves. Its dual-purpose nature makes it a good choice for a home orchard that also wants ornamental structure in the landscape. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that improves airflow and fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Allspice (Jamaica Pepper)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — allspice is a tropical Caribbean tree native to Jamaica and Central America, the source of the spice whose dried unripe berries combine the flavors of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg in a single berry (hence 'allspice'). The large, glossy, aromatic leaves also contain significant allspice flavor (used to wrap jerk meats in Jamaica). The tree is medium-sized (30–40 feet at maturity) with attractive smooth, exfoliating bark and fragrant white flowers. Allspice is a dioecious tree — both male and female plants are needed for fruit production, though the leaves of either sex can be harvested for culinary use. In South Florida it grows well outdoors in zone 10–11; in zone 9 it requires a container that can be moved to frost protection. An extraordinary ornamental, aromatic, and culinary tree for warm gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Allstar Strawberry (Mid-Late June-Bearing, High-Yield Disease-Resistant)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring; Allstar produces very large berries (among the largest of any June-bearer) with good flavor; the plants are vigorous and send out abundant runners; remove runners the first year to encourage crown establishment; plant Allstar alongside Earliglow to extend the June-bearing strawberry season by 1–2 weeks. Allstar is a USDA-bred June-bearing strawberry variety (released 1981) that has become one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden strawberries in the eastern United States, valued for its combination of high yields, large fruit size, and exceptional disease resistance. The berries are large — often significantly larger than Earliglow and most other June-bearers — with a conical shape, good firmness, and attractive glossy red color that makes them particularly well-suited for fresh market sales, U-pick operations, and home garden display. The flavor is sweet with moderate acidity — generally considered slightly less intensely flavored than Earliglow but still excellent for fresh eating, preserves, and pies. Allstar's greatest strength is its extremely broad disease resistance profile: it shows good to excellent resistance to red stele root rot, Verticillium wilt, and powdery mildew, making it a reliable producer even in challenging conditions. The combination of Earliglow (early) and Allstar (mid-late) is a classic recommendation from northeastern extension services for home gardeners who want a 2–3 week strawberry harvest window instead of a single concentrated crop. Vigorous runner production makes Allstar easy to propagate and maintain. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Allsweet Watermelon (Striped Oblong Southern Heirloom Watermelon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds (thin to 2 plants) or individual transplants after soil warms; provide ample space (6–10 feet in all directions) for vigorous vines; stop irrigation when fruits are nearly ripe to concentrate sugars; test ripeness by thumping (dull thud), checking the ground spot (turning yellow), or pressing on the vine end of the fruit. Allsweet is a large, oblong, open-pollinated watermelon developed and marketed by Dessert Seed Company that became one of the most widely grown home garden and commercial watermelons in the Southern states during the latter decades of the 20th century. The classic appearance — elongated oval fruits averaging 25–35 pounds with dark green skin boldly marked by lighter green stripes, bright red flesh, and black seeds in the traditional style — made Allsweet the archetypical 'picnic watermelon' of the American South. The flavor lives up to the name: exceptionally sweet (Brix 12–14), with the characteristic deep red color and firm, crisp texture that distinguished traditional open-pollinated watermelons from modern seedless varieties. Allsweet produces fruits with good keeping quality after harvest — they hold well in cool storage for 2–3 weeks — and the vines are productive and disease-tolerant under Gulf Coast and Deep South summer conditions. A standard comparison point against which other traditional watermelons are measured in Southern gardens, and an important landmark in the history of American watermelon breeding. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Alltop Turnip (Bulbless Cut-and-Come-Again Greens Turnip)
description: Direct sow thickly in fertile, well-drained soil, in full sun for the fastest growth or partial shade in warmer weather; Alltop is a Southern-bred turnip selected purely for its tops and produces no usable bulb at all, channeling its energy instead into a heavy, upright flush of smooth, dark, mild-flavored leaves. It is markedly more heat- and bolt-tolerant than dual-purpose turnip varieties, which lets it be sown earlier in late summer and later into spring than most turnip greens, and it regrows vigorously after cutting for repeated cut-and-come-again harvests through fall and winter. Because there is no root to size up, plants can be spaced tightly and simply mowed or sheared back by a third to a half whenever leaves reach eating size, making it an efficient, high-yield choice for gardeners who grow turnips strictly for potlikker and greens rather than roots. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Alma Fig
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Alma is a Texas-bred fig developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1974, bred specifically for the alkaline, calcareous soils and hot, humid summers of Texas. It is the most widely planted fig variety in Texas home gardens because of its exceptional adaptability to Texas soils, heat, and moderate drought tolerance. The fruit is small to medium, golden-tan to amber when ripe, with very sweet, rich, amber-colored flesh and a distinctive honey flavor superior to most brown-skinned varieties. Alma produces a very heavy main crop in August–October in zone 9. Skin is thin and the fruits are best eaten fresh or for preserves; they do not ship well, which is why Alma remains primarily a home and farmers' market variety. The tree produces few to no Breba (first-crop) figs but compensates with tremendous main-crop productivity. Trees are slightly cold-sensitive below 10°F; in zone 8, protect with mulch around the base in winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alma Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Round Paprika for Drying and Grinding)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and harvest when fully red for drying. Alma Paprika Pepper is a Hungarian heirloom variety prized by home paprika makers for its compact, round fruits that dry easily and produce an aromatic, sweet paprika powder with far more complexity than commercially available dried paprika. The variety belongs to the traditional Hungarian paprika pepper classifications — distinguished from the longer 'szegedi' or 'kalocsal' types by its apple-like round shape — and is named 'Alma' (Hungarian for 'apple') in direct reference to this distinctive fruit form. The flavor progression through ripening stages is one of this variety's most interesting characteristics: at the creamy-white stage the fruit is mildly sweet and slightly starchy, similar to a mild Italian frying pepper; at yellow it develops a fruitier, slightly citrusy edge; at full red ripeness the paprika sweetness is fully expressed with a rich, slightly smoky underlying note. Gardeners can use Alma Paprika at any ripe stage for fresh eating — it performs well in salads, stuffed preparations, and light sautés — but its primary use is drying. Halved and laid cut-side-down on screens in warm sun or placed in a food dehydrator at 120–130°F, the fruits dry thoroughly within 3–5 days and grind to a vivid orange-red powder. Compact plant size makes Alma Paprika one of the most productive paprika types per square foot of garden space. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Almond
description: Almonds bloom earlier than almost any other tree fruit and are severely damaged by late spring frosts, which is why commercial production is limited to Mediterranean-type climates. Most varieties require a cross-pollinator — plant at least two compatible cultivars (Non-Pareil with Carmel or Price, for example). Trees thrive in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soils and are drought-tolerant once established. Harvest when the hulls split open and the shells dry and harden, typically in late summer; spread nuts to dry for two weeks before storing. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Aloe Vera (True Aloe)
description: Plant offsets in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — aloe vera is one of the oldest cultivated plants in human history, grown for millennia in tropical and subtropical climates as the premier first-aid plant for minor burns, sunburns, cuts, insect bites, and skin irritation; the clear gel inside the thick, fleshy leaves contains anti-inflammatory and wound-healing compounds including polysaccharides, vitamins, and amino acids. Break off a lower leaf and apply the clear gel directly to burns for immediate cooling relief. In zone 9–12 it grows as an outdoor landscape succulent, tolerating drought, poor soil, reflected heat, and neglect with remarkable resilience; it produces dramatic yellow to orange tubular flower spikes in late winter on established plants. It spreads prolifically by offsets (pups) that form around the base — remove and replant pups to create new plants. Every household and kitchen garden should have one within reach. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Alphonso Mango (Hapus Mango, Indian Royal Mango)
description: Widely regarded as India's most prized mango and grown historically along the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, Alphonso bears medium fruit with smooth, deep-orange, fiberless flesh and an intensely fragrant aroma often described as saffron, coconut, and citrus layered together. It is sweeter and less tangy than the Florida-bred commercial cultivars in this collection, but its thin skin and short shelf life make it a specialty dooryard tree rather than a shipping variety outside its native growing region. Fruit ripens mid-season on a vigorous, upright tree, and quality drops noticeably in cooler or more humid climates than its native subtropical range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Alpine Bearberry (Black Bearberry)
description: Alpine bearberry is a low, mat-forming, deciduous dwarf shrub of arctic and alpine tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, with small, deeply veined leaves that turn brilliant red in autumn before dropping. It spreads slowly by trailing woody stems that root as they touch the ground, forming a dense evergreen-textured carpet well suited to rock gardens and cold-climate shaded groundcover plantings. Small urn-shaped white to pink flowers in late spring are followed by juicy black berries that ripen through red before turning glossy black; the fruit is edible raw but rather bitter and improves with cooking, and has traditionally been eaten by northern peoples with fat or fish. Site it in acidic, well-drained soil with some shade from hot afternoon sun, since it is adapted to short, cool growing seasons and struggles in warm, humid climates. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alpine Currant (Mountain Currant)
description: Alpine currant is an extremely tough, compact, mound-forming shrub long used for shade hedging in cold climates where few other woody plants tolerate dense shade and dry soil so well. Plant in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil; it is not particular about soil pH or fertility and shrugs off urban pollution and road salt. Inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in spring, and female plants (this species is dioecious, so both sexes are needed for fruit) set small, glossy red currants in midsummer that are edible but tart and bland, used mainly by birds or for jelly rather than fresh eating. Prune after flowering to maintain a formal hedge shape, since it tolerates shearing extremely well and rarely needs spraying for pests. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alpine Lovage (Mountain Lovage)
description: Alpine lovage is a true high-mountain relative of garden lovage native to the Alps, Pyrenees, and other European mountain ranges, forming a much smaller clump of finely divided, aromatic leaves that carry a milder, more herbaceous version of lovage's celery flavor. Unlike garden lovage, it thrives in cool, humus-rich, well-drained mountain soils and struggles in hot, humid lowland summers, making it best suited to alpine troughs, rock gardens, and cool-summer climates. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall so it experiences natural winter chilling, since seed loses viability quickly and often germinates unevenly the following spring. Young leaves can be used fresh as a celery-like potherb or dried for tea, and the whole plant has a long history of traditional culinary and medicinal use in Alpine farming communities. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Alpine Regina Strawberry
description: Alpine Regina is an everbearing woodland strawberry that produces small, intensely aromatic berries all season on tidy, runnerless clumps. Surface-sow the tiny seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, pressing them onto moist mix without covering, since light aids germination; a few weeks of cold stratification improves the sprouting rate. Transplant seedlings 8-12 inches apart in rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and some afternoon shade. Plants make an excellent edible border or container crop and often fruit the first year. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Alpine Strawberry
description: Alpine strawberries are compact, clumping, runner-free plants that produce small but intensely fragrant and flavored berries continuously from early summer through fall frost. Seeds are tiny and require light for germination — surface sow in trays and do not cover; keep moist at 65–75°F. Unlike garden strawberries, alpines form clumps rather than runners and are best propagated by division every 3–4 years or from seed. They are more shade-tolerant than hybrid strawberries, making them excellent for edging partially shaded paths. Harvest individual berries when fully red and aromatic. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Alpine Woundwort / Limestone Woundwort
description: Sow seeds directly in fall onto the surface of prepared soil in a lightly shaded, calcareous or neutral spot, covering them with a thin layer of fine grit or soil; the cold of winter breaks dormancy and promotes reliable germination the following spring. Plants establish slowly in their first season, focusing energy on root development, so expect the tall, woolly-leafed stems and whorled purple flower spikes in the second year. Choose a site with good drainage and moderate moisture — Alpine Woundwort tolerates partial shade under open tree canopy where it would naturally occur in mountain scrub and woodland edges. Leave spent flower stems standing through winter to provide structure and overwintering habitat for beneficial insects, then cut back to the base in early spring before new growth emerges. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Alstonville Finger Lime (Commercial Australian Caviar Lime Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Alstonville is the leading commercial finger lime cultivar in Australia, selected for vigorous upright growth, heavier yields, and consistent production of glossy green, cylindrical fruit filled with pale green caviar-like pulp vesicles. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than most finger lime seedlings when grown on grafted rootstock. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the tangy pulp fresh as a garnish since it does not store well once opened. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Altaglow Saskatoon (White-Fruited Columnar Prairie Serviceberry)
description: Selected from wild stock in Alberta and released through the Brooks Horticultural Research Station, Altaglow is an erect, narrow, multi-stemmed saskatoon grown chiefly as a hardy prairie ornamental rather than a commercial fruit crop. Its most distinctive feature is fruit that ripens ivory to pale yellow-white instead of the usual blue-black, turning brown if left to dry on the shrub; because it is self-sterile, plant it alongside a standard blue-fruited saskatoon to ensure pollination and any fruit set at all. Clusters of white spring flowers precede foliage that turns gold, red, and deep purple in a long-lasting fall display, and the columnar habit suits narrow screens, windbreak rows, or foundation plantings on the northern prairies. It tolerates severe cold, wind, and a wide range of soils once established. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Altus Muscadine Grape
description: Altus (selection AM-77) was released alongside Mighty Fine in fall 2025 by the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, co-developed by enologist Renee Threlfall specifically for wine and juice production rather than fresh eating. It is a smaller-berried, black-skinned, seeded muscadine, and in consumer trials the pressed juice outscored the long-standard wine cultivar Noble for flavor, sourness balance, and overall impression. Like Mighty Fine, it was bred with an emphasis on cold hardiness that should let growers push muscadine culture into cooler zones than traditional Gulf South and Deep South selections tolerate. Being a brand-new release, expect limited nursery availability and thin long-term field data for the next few seasons. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Alubia de Tolosa Bean (Tolosa Black Bean, Basque Heirloom)
description: Alubia de Tolosa is a small, matte-black dry bean grown under a protected designation of origin around Tolosa in Spain's Basque Country, where it is the star of the traditional autumn alubiada bean feast served with cabbage, chorizo, and pork. The beans cook to an intensely creamy, almost velvety texture with an earthy, faintly smoky flavor that Basque cooks prize above other black bean types. Bush plants stay compact and productive without support; allow pods to dry fully and rattle before harvesting, then shell and cure before storage. It performs best where summers are mild to moderately warm rather than scorching, echoing its native Atlantic-coast climate. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Amager Cabbage
description: Amager is a Danish heirloom bred for the cold, damp climate of its namesake island, producing extremely dense, round heads that keep in a root cellar longer than most cabbage varieties. The tight internal packing that makes it a slow, late-season grower is the same trait that gives it exceptional storage life, often into late winter under proper conditions. Its heavy cold tolerance lets it stay in the field later into fall than earlier-maturing cabbages, concentrating sugars and improving flavor after frost. Plant Amager specifically for long-haul winter storage rather than fresh summer eating. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Amana Orange Tomato (Very Large Sweet Low-Acid Orange Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Amana Orange is one of the finest very-large orange beefsteak heirloom tomatoes — producing massive (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, deeply orange-colored fruits with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid flesh that creates the most mild, sweet, non-acidic fresh tomato experience available from any heirloom type. The very large fruit size and characteristic sweet, almost candy-like low-acid flavor make Amana Orange one of the most distinctive eating experiences among heirloom tomatoes. The brilliant, uniform deep-orange color — consistent across the exterior and interior flesh without the bicolor patterns of Pineapple or Big Rainbow — provides a vivid single-color presentation that is striking in its own right. The meaty, dense orange flesh has relatively few seeds and an exceptionally high flesh-to-gel ratio that maximizes the edible portion. As an open-pollinated heirloom from the Amana Colonies of Iowa, the variety carries cultural significance alongside its outstanding eating quality. Amana Orange plants are large, vigorous indeterminate vines requiring sturdy 6-foot support. The long growing season (80–95 days) means zone 9 gardeners should start seeds as early as possible to ensure fruit development before summer heat. An outstanding choice for anyone who finds standard tomatoes too acid. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Amanus Oregano (Trailing Pink-Flowered Alpine Oregano)
description: Native to the Amanus Mountains of southern Turkey, this species forms a dense, low, wiry-stemmed mat of small aromatic leaves that stays only a few inches tall, in contrast to the papery hop-like bracts of Kent Beauty; instead it produces open, funnel-shaped, bright rose-pink flowers held just above the foliage from summer into fall. Its diminutive scale and tolerance for poor, gritty soil make it a natural for troughs, raised alpine beds, and rock garden crevices rather than the open border. Winter wet, not cold, is the main threat, so a raised, sharply drained planting site with alkaline soil is essential for it to persist. Trim lightly after the main flush of bloom to keep the mat compact and encourage rebloom. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Amara Mustard (Ethiopian Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow shallowly into fertile soil and thin seedlings as they grow, cutting outer leaves for continuous harvest or letting plants reach full size. This traditional Ethiopian selection produces large, smooth, paddle-shaped blue-green leaves with a sharper, more pungent bite than common mustard greens, and it is a staple ingredient in Ethiopian gomen dishes. It tolerates both heat and cool weather better than many mustards, giving it a longer harvest window through the season. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Amaranth (Callaloo)
description: Scatter tiny seeds on the soil surface or press in no deeper than 1/8 inch, and keep moist until germination; thin to 6–12 inches once seedlings are established. Vegetable amaranth thrives in heat and is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, making it a reliable summer green when spinach has bolted. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips continuously from 30 days onward; regular harvesting delays flowering and extends the harvest window. Leaves are best cooked briefly — sautéed, steamed, or simmered in soups — and are rich in iron and calcium. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Amarillo Hops
description: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability. Discovered as a chance seedling in Washington's Yakima Valley in the 1990s and named for its bright golden-orange color, this widely used American aroma hop delivers pronounced orange citrus and floral notes that became a defining character of American pale ale and IPA styles through the 2000s and remains a brewer favorite for its distinctive, bright citrus aromatics. Its exact genetic parentage was kept proprietary for years, and while cuttings are now more widely available to home growers, tracking down true, correctly identified Amarillo rhizomes can still be more difficult than sourcing more common commercial hop varieties. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and provide full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Amazel Basil (Sterile Downy-Mildew-Resistant Basil)
description: Transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun only after all frost danger passes. Amazel was bred specifically to resist downy mildew, a fungal disease that can wipe out a planting of traditional Genovese basil in a single humid season, and because the plant is sterile it never flowers or goes to seed, channeling all of its energy into continuous, vigorous leaf growth all season long. The flavor is classic sweet basil, well suited to pesto and general cooking, and the plant's disease resistance and non-flowering habit make it especially valuable for humid Gulf South gardens where downy mildew is a persistent problem. Because it is propagated from cuttings rather than seed, plants are typically purchased as starts. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Amazing Cauliflower (Self-Blanching Fall Cauliflower)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 24-36 inches between rows, and feed generously since Amazing needs vigorous leaf growth to protect its curd. This variety is valued for its self-blanching habit: large, upright wrapper leaves naturally curl in over the developing curd, shielding it from sun and weather so it stays creamy white without the hand-tying required by older cauliflower varieties. Amazing's extended, somewhat uneven maturity window is actually an asset for home gardeners, since plants in the same bed don't all come ready at once, spreading a single planting's harvest out over several weeks instead of demanding it all be used or preserved immediately. It is widely regarded as one of the more forgiving fall cauliflowers for gardeners still learning to time brassica plantings against the first frost. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Amazon Grape (Uva Caimarona)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the western Amazon basin, this fast-growing relative of cecropia trees bears grape-like clusters of purple, thin-skinned fruit with sweet, translucent, juicy pulp eaten fresh, unusual among tropical fruit trees for reaching bearing age within just a few years of planting rather than a decade or more. Its palmate, cecropia-like leaves and relatively quick growth to fruiting make it an appealing option for a tropical fruit collector wanting faster results than many slower Amazonian species, though it still needs consistent warmth and humidity to thrive. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and expect the first fruit clusters within three to five years under good growing conditions. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Amazonian Yam Bean (Chuin, Jicáma de Árbol)
description: Native to the Amazon basin and cultivated across lowland tropical South America, this vigorous twining vine produces the largest storage roots of the cultivated yam beans, sometimes exceeding several pounds under good conditions, with flesh that is starchier and less sweet than jicama's. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence, since the vine climbs aggressively and can smother nearby plants if left unsupported. Remove flower buds as they appear to keep the plant's energy focused on root bulking rather than seed set. As with its relatives, only the cooked or raw root is edible; the leaves, pods, and seeds contain rotenone and are toxic. Matures in 240–300 days from seed.

name: Ambarella
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Spondias cytherea is fast-growing and drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently in subtropical conditions; excellent performance in South Florida's calcareous soils and in Gulf Coast sandy soils. Spondias cytherea (Ambarella, Golden Apple, or June Plum) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous tropical tree native to the Society Islands of French Polynesia, spread throughout tropical Polynesia by Polynesian voyagers and later widely planted across tropical Asia, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and tropical West Africa. The oval, 2–3 inch, golden-yellow fruits have crisp, fibrous, firm, juicy, tart-sweet, aromatic flesh with flavors of unripe mango, pineapple, and apple — remarkably refreshing as a fresh fruit when ripe (golden-yellow), and extensively used green (firm, crunchy, very tart) as a condiment, relish, chutney base, and snack with salt, fish sauce, and chili across South and Southeast Asia. In the Caribbean (Jamaica) it is 'June Plum,' in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia 'Ambarella.' Trees are fast-growing — fruiting in 3–4 years from cuttings — and highly productive, dropping fruit that must be gathered regularly. One of the easiest tropical fruit trees to establish in zone 9b–12; an outstanding choice for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates where it naturalizes readily. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Ambarella (June Plum, Golden Apple, Otaheite Apple)
description: Plant in very well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; ambarella is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree native to Melanesia and widely cultivated throughout the Pacific islands, Caribbean, and Southeast Asia for its versatile fruit. The oval, golden-yellow to orange fruits are eaten at all stages: the crisp, acidic green fruit is popular in Southeast Asian salads, slaws, and pickles with a tart mango-apple flavor, while fully ripe fruits are sweeter and eaten fresh. The fibrous pit germinates reliably in a few weeks. Ambarella is one of the faster-fruiting tropical trees, often bearing within 2–3 years from air-layers. It drops leaves briefly in dry season. In zone 9a it grows in a large container (25+ gallon) and must be moved indoors or into a greenhouse before the first frost; in zone 10+ it is an outstanding productive landscape tree. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Amber Cup Squash (Small Red-Orange Buttercup-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow seed in hills after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow the moderately vigorous vines room to run. Amber Cup produces small, 2 to 4 pound, deep red-orange fruit with the flattened, ridged shape typical of buttercup-type squash, and the flesh is exceptionally dry, dense, and sweet, making it well suited to steaming, roasting, and inclusion in Japanese and Korean dishes where kabocha-type squash is traditional. Its compact fruit size makes it convenient for a single household meal without leftovers, unlike larger winter squash. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the vine begins to decline, and cure for a week or two in a warm spot before moving to cool storage. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Amber Globe Turnip
description: A yellow-fleshed heirloom turnip documented since before 1840, grown for smooth globe roots with fine-grained, sweet flesh unlike the sharper white-fleshed types. Best picked around 3 inches across for peak sweetness and tenderness, though roots can size up to 6 inches for winter storage. Sturdy tops also cook well as greens, giving two harvests from one planting. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Ambercup Squash (Golden Orange Compact Kabocha-Style Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil; vines are moderate in length (6–8 feet), more manageable than butternut or hubbard types; harvest when the skin is a uniform deep golden-amber and resists fingernail denting; cure for 2–3 weeks after harvest to maximize sweetness and storage life. Ambercup is an heirloom-type open-pollinated winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species — the same species as kabocha, Red Kuri, Blue Hubbard, and Buttercup — that produces compact, round to slightly flattened fruits with smooth, glossy, deep golden-orange skin and a very small indented cavity at the blossom end. The flesh is the dry, dense, intensely orange, and very sweet type characteristic of the best maxima squashes, making Ambercup one of the most flavorful winter squashes for baking, roasting, and soup-making. The golden-amber skin is distinctive and attractive — warmer in color than the grey-green of standard kabocha, lighter than Buttercup's dark green, and different from Red Kuri's red-orange — making it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. Ambercup performs reliably across a wide range of climates from zone 3 to zone 9 and stores exceptionally well under cool, dry conditions — quality often improves with 1–2 months of storage as the starches convert to sugars. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Ambercup should be direct-sown in late March or early April to allow the full season before summer heat arrives. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Ambersweet Orange (Cold-Hardy Early Hybrid Sweet Orange)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun; Ambersweet tolerates more cold than most sweet oranges and ripens very early, from October, extending the citrus season in areas at the cooler edge of the Gulf Coast citrus belt. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ambition Shallot (F1 Red-Violet European Shallot)
description: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 bulbs; keep consistently moist during establishment and in spring; reduce watering as leaves begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when tops fall and bulb skins are dry and papery, then cure for 2–3 weeks before storage. Ambition is a European F1 hybrid shallot produced by commercial seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, where the commercial shallot industry has been refined over centuries into highly productive, uniform varieties for both professional kitchen use and home garden production. The Ambition variety produces medium-sized, uniformly shaped, oval to pear-shaped bulbs with red-violet to copper-mahogany skin and purplish-pink inner flesh; each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 distinct bulbs, the characteristic growth habit that distinguishes shallots from onions (which produce a single bulb from a set). The flavor is the classic shallot character — more subtle, sweet, and complex than onions, with a slightly garlicky undertone that distinguishes shallots as the preferred allium in French haute cuisine for vinaigrettes, pan sauces, and dishes where onion flavor would be too harsh. Storage life is excellent — 6–9 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark). The F1 hybrid nature of Ambition means it does not come true from saved seed, but sets (bulbs) from the previous year's crop can be replanted successfully. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Ambrosia Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ambrosia requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. Discovered as a chance seedling in a British Columbia orchard in the 1980s, likely a natural cross of Golden Delicious and Jonagold, it produces large, blushed pink-and-gold fruit with exceptionally low acidity, a honeyed sweetness, and fine, crisp, low-tannin flesh that resists browning better than many apples once cut. The tree is precocious and productive, often bearing at a young age, and the fruit's mild, sweet flavor and attractive coloring have made it a fast-growing favorite in both commercial orchards and home gardens since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background skin color shifts from green to yellow beneath the pink blush. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ambrosia Cantaloupe
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — melons require warm soil, abundant sun, and good air circulation; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning cantaloupe (muskmelon) that earned recognition for its exceptionally sweet, deeply aromatic, thick-fleshed, orange interior — with sugar content and fragrance significantly exceeding most commercial cantaloupe varieties bred for shipping durability. The medium-sized, rounded fruits with heavily netted tan rind and the unmistakable, intensely musky-sweet fragrance that announces ripeness from several feet away represent the classic cantaloupe eating experience at its best. Most commercial cantaloupes are harvested before full-slip (when they still cling to the vine) to withstand shipping without bruising — the result is fruit that is often underripe, bland, and lacking the musky sweetness that a vine-ripened cantaloupe develops. A homegrown Ambrosia harvested at true full-slip ripeness is fundamentally different from any commercial cantaloupe — genuinely aromatic, extremely sweet, and with a perfumed complexity that makes tasting it for the first time a revelation about what cantaloupe actually tastes like. Powdery mildew resistance makes Ambrosia reliable in the humid conditions of zone 9 summer. Matures in 84–90 days from transplant.

name: Ambrosia Pomegranate (Giant-Fruited Mild Sweet Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate clay, sand, and alkaline soils better than most fruiting trees once established. Ambrosia is a French heirloom pomegranate selected for its exceptionally large fruit, sometimes approaching softball size and well over a pound, with pale pink-blushed skin and mild, low-acid, sweet arils that are gentler and less tart than Wonderful. The large fruit size makes Ambrosia a favorite for fresh eating and for show, though the thinner-flavored juice is less concentrated than smaller, more intensely flavored cultivars. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and benefit from thinning excess fruit to prevent limb breakage and splitting from the sheer weight of the oversized crop; prune lightly each year to encourage new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ambrosia Sweet Corn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning bicolor sweet corn recognized in 1982 for its outstanding combination of sweetness, tenderness, and one of the best flavor profiles of any bicolor sweet corn variety. The sugary-enhanced (SE) genetics give Ambrosia a higher sugar content and better post-harvest sugar retention than traditional open-pollinated sweet corn — the ears remain sweet and tender for several days after harvest rather than converting sugars to starch rapidly as standard sweet corn does. The bicolor ears with alternating white and yellow kernels have been the classic American sweet corn appearance for backyard gardens since the 1980s, and Ambrosia set the standard for bicolor flavor that later varieties aimed to match. The slender, well-filled ears (7–8 inches) have a fine kernel texture, tender pericarp (no toughness in the kernel skin), and outstanding raw flavor for eating directly off the cob without cooking. Ambrosia remains one of the most widely grown and recommended bicolor sweet corn varieties for home gardens. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Ambrosia Sweet Corn
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good pollination. This bicolor sugar-enhanced hybrid produces 8-inch ears of tender, creamy kernels and offers early vigor plus strong disease resistance. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when silks brown and kernels release a milky juice when punctured, and refrigerate quickly to preserve sweetness. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Ambulo Blanc Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
description: Released by UC Davis in 2019 as one of the first Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes bred through marker-assisted selection, Ambulo Blanc carries resistance from the wild Southwestern species Vitis arizonica while remaining predominantly Vitis vinifera. The resulting wine is described as similar to Sauvignon Blanc, offering a genuine vinifera-style white option for regions where Pierce's disease has long ruled out European varieties. Texas Gulf Coast vineyards facing high sharpshooter pressure are among the early adopters trialing the variety. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun; supply through licensed nurseries remains limited while multiplication continues. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Amelia Tomato (Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicing Tomato with Broad Southeast-Adapted Resistance Package)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when uniformly deep red. Amelia Tomato is a commercially developed F1 hybrid slicing tomato specifically designed for production in the humid southeastern United States, where the combination of warm temperatures, high humidity, and disease inoculum in garden soils creates challenging conditions for standard tomato varieties. The variety's VFFNTAs resistance code represents one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a single tomato variety: resistance to Verticillium wilt (a soilborne fungal disease that colonizes the xylem and causes progressive wilting), two races of Fusarium wilt (a related soilborne pathogen with multiple strains that can overcome single-race resistance), root-knot nematodes (a serious pest in the warm, sandy soils of the Gulf Coast), tobacco mosaic virus (a seed- and contact-transmitted virus), and Alternaria stem canker (a foliar and stem fungal pathogen that can cause significant early-season damage in humid conditions). This combination of resistances directly addresses the primary disease challenges in zone 9 tomato production: nematode pressure is extremely common in the sandy soils of the Gulf Coast plain; Fusarium and Verticillium are endemic in soils with previous tomato production history; Alternaria stem canker increases in severity during warm, wet weather. For gardeners who have experienced repeated tomato crop failures in zone 9 from disease without knowing the specific cause, Amelia's broad resistance package provides protection across the most likely disease scenarios. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Ameliore Dandelion (Thick-Leaved French Dandelion)
description: Direct sow Ameliore Dandelion seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; thin seedlings to 6–10 inches apart and keep evenly watered for fast, tender growth. Unlike lawn dandelion, this French culinary selection produces a dense rosette of broad, deeply notched, dark-green leaves that stay comparatively mild and non-bitter, especially when harvested young or blanched by covering the crown for 1–2 weeks before cutting. Leaves are cooked like a hearty green or used raw in salads for their distinctive earthy, slightly bitter edge that mellows with cooler weather; the taproot can also be dug, roasted, and ground as a caffeine-free coffee substitute. A cut-and-come-again crop, it regrows readily after repeated harvest and tolerates light frost, making it useful for extending the salad-green season into early spring and late fall. Matures in 60–95 days from seed.

name: Amelonado Cacao
description: The classic lower-Amazon Forastero-type variety introduced to West Africa in the nineteenth century, Amelonado remains the genetic backbone of cacao production in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, the world's two largest cacao-producing countries. It takes its name from its smooth, rounded, melon-shaped pods, distinct from the warty, ridged pods of Criollo. Genetically narrow and largely self-compatible, it produces dependable but modest harvests of solid bulk cacao rather than the fine-flavor beans associated with Criollo or Nacional, and it has served as the foundation for most West African cacao breeding programs. Grow it under filtered shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil like other heirloom cacao types. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: America Grape (T.V. Munson-Bred Pierce's Disease-Resistant Texas Heirloom)
description: Bred in the late 1800s by T.V. Munson of Denison, Texas, America was selected specifically because its wild American parentage kept it healthy where European and labrusca-type vines succumbed to Pierce's disease and major fungal diseases. The blue-black berries are tart and better suited to juice, jelly, and home winemaking than fresh eating, and the vigorous vine still survives today largely through heirloom grape collections and Texas viticulture history programs rather than commercial vineyards. Grow on a strong trellis in full sun and prune hard each winter, since the vine can be quite vigorous once established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: America Spinach
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in cool soil in early spring or late summer, thinning seedlings to give each plant room. This 1952 All-America Selections winner has thick, savoyed leaves and unusual tolerance to both heat and drought, extending the harvest window. It performs well in the ground or in containers, so it suits small gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed, or cut the whole plant before it bolts in warm weather. Matures in 42–50 days from seed.

name: American Barberry
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is a thorny, deciduous Appalachian native shrub with small, spine-tipped leaves, drooping clusters of small yellow flowers in late spring, and bright red, elongated berries that ripen in fall and persist into winter, providing food for birds when little else is available. It is a genuinely native, non-invasive alternative for gardeners who want the ornamental berry and thorny-hedge qualities of barberry without planting the widely naturalized and ecologically disruptive Japanese barberry. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for wheat stem rust, avoid planting it in large numbers near commercial grain fields, a precaution that led to historic eradication programs targeting common barberry in agricultural regions. Otherwise easy to grow and largely trouble-free, it works well as an informal barrier hedge, wildlife planting, or specimen in a naturalistic border. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: American Basil (Spice Basil, Hoary Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after soil warms in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinch regularly to prevent bolting and encourage bushy growth; more heat and drought tolerant than sweet basil. Ocimum americanum (American basil, spice basil, or hoary basil) is a distinct basil species with a somewhat confusing common name — it originated in Africa and Asia, not the Americas, though it has become naturalized in tropical regions worldwide including the Americas. It differs from sweet basil (O. basilicum) in several ways: the leaves are smaller and lighter green, often with a slightly hairy (hoary) surface texture; the flavor is lighter, more lemony-citrus, with less of the clove-richness of sweet basil and a more herbal, slightly resinous character. O. americanum is widely used in West African cooking (particularly in Nigeria, Ghana, and Cameroon, where it is known as 'efirin' and is a common soup herb), East African cuisine, and in parts of South and Southeast Asia where it grows wild. It is significantly more drought-tolerant and heat-resistant than cultivated sweet basil, making it a good choice for hot, dry gardens where O. basilicum struggles. Several cultivated basil varieties are hybrids between O. americanum and O. basilicum, including lemon basil cultivars. The plant produces attractive white flower spikes and is a good pollinator plant. Matures in 50–75 days from seed.

name: American Beauty Dragon Fruit
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil — dragon fruit is an epiphytic cactus requiring extremely well-drained soil and excellent air circulation; American Beauty is one of the most popular self-fertile dragon fruit cultivars, producing large (0.5–2 pound), oval fruits with vivid pink-red skin, prominent green-tipped scales, and brilliant magenta-red flesh with small, soft black seeds — one of the most visually stunning and nutritionally distinctive tropical fruits available. The intense magenta-red color of the flesh is caused by betacyanin pigments (similar to those in beets) that transfer vivid color to smoothies, drinks, yogurt, and desserts that incorporate the fruit, creating a dramatically colored culinary presentation that has made dragon fruit one of the most popular colorful ingredients in contemporary food photography and high-end food service. As an epiphytic cactus, dragon fruit requires a different cultural approach from conventional fruit trees — treating it more like a succulent with periodic deep watering rather than regular irrigation, and providing structural support for the long, three-ribbed, succulent stems that climb by aerial roots. Zone 9 gardeners in the warmest, most frost-free locations can grow dragon fruit successfully in the ground; others should use large containers that can be moved to frost-free locations during cold spells. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: American Beech (Beechnut)
description: American beech is monoecious and wind-pollinated, but nut production is highly variable and irregular — large mast crops occur every 2–5 years, driven by weather patterns; at least two trees (ideally a grove) dramatically improves mast yield in any given year. The triangular beechnuts are sweet and nutritious, high in fat and protein, and valued by both wildlife and people; they are best eaten raw or lightly roasted and are traditionally used for oil extraction. Beech is extremely sensitive to soil compaction and grade changes around the root zone — construction damage is the primary killer of mature trees in urban settings. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained, acidic soil away from construction zones and plan for very long-term production: significant nut crops typically begin 10+ years after planting. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: American Black Currant (Wild Black Currant)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to full shade; American black currant is a native fruiting shrub found in moist woodlands and streambanks from Nova Scotia to Virginia and west to the Rockies, producing clusters of small, round, black-purple currants in July–August that are excellent for jams, jellies, juice, and wine. The fruit flavor is similar to European black currant but milder, without the strong 'cassis' musk of Ribes nigrum, making it more palatable to those who find European black currant too strong. Most importantly, it is one of very few fruiting shrubs that produces in deep shade, making it irreplaceable for woodland edible gardens where blueberries and most other fruit shrubs fail. The fragrant, small, white to yellowish tubular flowers in spring are attractive to hummingbirds and native bees. The foliage is attractively lobed and resinous-scented when brushed. American black currant is alternate host for white pine blister rust and should not be planted within 900 feet of white pines in susceptible regions — check with local extension before planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: American Black Nightshade
description: Direct sow onto the soil surface after last frost in partial shade to full sun; seeds need light and warmth to germinate and will often self-sow where established. This widely distributed native annual bears small white star-shaped flowers followed by clusters of small berries that turn fully black when ripe in late summer and fall. CAUTION: green and unripe berries and all other plant parts are toxic and must never be consumed; only correctly identified, fully black, ripe berries have a history of use cooked (never raw) in certain African, Southeast Asian, and indigenous North American culinary traditions. Plants naturalize readily in gardens and disturbed open ground, requiring little care once established. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: American Brooklime
description: American brooklime is a sprawling native North American relative of watercress that roots naturally along the shaded, mucky margins of springs, seeps, and slow streams, making it a good match for a boggy, partly shaded corner of a Gulf Coast garden that stays wet through summer. Snip the thick, glossy, paired leaves and tender stem tips year-round in mild climates for a crisp, peppery, watercress-like green used raw in salads or wilted briefly into soups. Keep the roots constantly saturated or standing in an inch or two of water, since the plant declines quickly if the soil is allowed to dry out between waterings. Established patches spread steadily by rooting stems and can be divided and replanted at almost any time during the growing season. Matures in 45–60 days from transplant.

name: American Bugleweed (Water Horehound)
description: Plant in moist to wet, fertile to average soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, stream banks, and wet meadow margins; American bugleweed is a native mint-family herb of North American riparian habitats, closely related to European gypsywort (Lycopus europaeus). The plant has a long history of use in American herbal medicine, particularly for reducing elevated thyroid function (hyperthyroidism) — a traditional application supported by modern research showing that lycopus extracts inhibit thyroid hormone activity. The small, white tubular flowers are inconspicuous but attract numerous small native bees and hoverflies. The plant is valuable in rain gardens, bioswales, and wet garden edges where its preference for saturated soil makes it naturally suited. Note: persons with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare provider before using medicinally. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: American Chestnut
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun — the American chestnut was once the dominant tree of the eastern forest, comprising 25% of all trees from New England to the Deep South and providing the primary mast crop sustaining deer, turkeys, bears, and passenger pigeons across millions of acres. The introduction of chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) from Asia in the early 1900s killed an estimated 4 billion trees within 50 years in the most catastrophic ecological disaster in American history. The root system of most trees survives and sends up shoots that grow to 10–20 feet before dying of blight — these sprouts can produce a small crop of nuts. The American Chestnut Foundation has developed blight-tolerant hybrid trees (about 94% American chestnut genetics) and restoration planting is actively underway. Planting American chestnut seedlings or blight-resistant hybrids is a meaningful conservation act; the trees grow fast, produce sweet nuts, and support 125 species of caterpillars. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: American Elderberry
description: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun, planting two different cultivars for cross-pollination; American elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of floodplains and woodland edges that produces large, flat-topped clusters of tiny, white, fragrant flowers in early summer followed by hanging clusters of small, dark-purple to black berries in late summer that are among the most nutritious and medicinally valued native fruits in North America — the basis of elderberry syrup, wine, pies, jams, and traditional immune-support preparations. Never eat raw elderberries in quantity (mildly toxic); cooking destroys the problematic compounds. The flowers are also edible and delicious battered and fried or infused into cordials. Excellent wildlife plant, supporting over 50 bird species. Named varieties 'Bob Gordon', 'Adams', and 'Nova' have larger berries and heavier yields. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: American Flag Leek
description: American Flag is a cold-hardy heirloom leek with long white shanks, blue-green leaves, and a mild, sweet onion flavor that holds in the garden through fall and into winter. Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into holes 6 inches deep to blanch the stems white. Hill soil up around the shanks as they grow to lengthen the tender white portion. Harvest as needed once shanks reach an inch across; the plants tolerate hard frost and can be dug even after snow. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: American Germander (Wood Sage)
description: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — American germander is a native perennial of moist woodland edges, wet meadows, roadsides, and stream margins throughout eastern North America, producing spikes of rose-pink to lavender tubular flowers with exserted stamens in summer that are excellent for native bees, bumble bees, and hummingbirds. The aromatic foliage has a sage-like scent when crushed (giving rise to the common name 'wood sage') and was used medicinally by indigenous peoples and early American herbalists. It spreads by stolons to form colonies in moist, shaded conditions — excellent for naturalizing along shaded stream banks, wet meadow edges, and the shaded margins of rain gardens. A relative of culinary germander (T. chamaedrys) and a historically used bitter herb for digestive complaints. Very adaptable and requires essentially no care once established in appropriate moist-to-moderate-moisture soil. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: American Ginseng
description: Purchase properly stratified seed and sow 1–2 in deep in a shaded, forested bed with well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; do not expect germination until the following spring at the earliest. Ginseng requires 60–75% canopy shade and the deep, crumbly forest soil of its native Appalachian habitat — it will not thrive in open garden conditions. Plants must grow for a minimum of 5–7 years before roots reach marketable size, making patience the primary gardening virtue here. Harvest roots in autumn by carefully digging to preserve the branched root shape; roots are dried slowly at low heat and used in adaptogenic teas, tinctures, and traditional Chinese medicine preparations. Matures in 1825–2920 days from seed.

name: American Gooseberry (Northern Gooseberry)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun — American gooseberry is the native gooseberry of the northeastern US and Canada, one of the most productive edible native shrubs for cool-climate food gardens. The tart-sweet berries (ripening from green to reddish-purple in midsummer) are excellent for pies, jams, preserves, and fresh eating when fully ripe. The shrub tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting shrubs and produces reliably in conditions too shaded for currants and jostaberries. The stems bear short, sharp spines at the nodes; wear gloves when harvesting. American gooseberry is more resistant to powdery mildew than European gooseberry (R. uva-crispa), making it easier to grow in humid climates. Best in zones 3–7; does not perform well in hot, humid summers of zone 8 and south. Check state regulations on Ribes planting before ordering. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: American Groundnut
description: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; provide a trellis or other structure for the vining stems to climb. Apios americana is a native North American twining vine in the legume family that produces chains of small, starchy, potato-like tubers in the soil that were a major food staple for dozens of indigenous tribes throughout eastern North America and reportedly sustained the Pilgrims through their first harsh New England winter; the tubers can be boiled, roasted, or mashed like potatoes with a sweeter, nuttier flavor. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility while producing food. The vine also produces attractive, fragrant, dark-rose to reddish-brown flower clusters in late summer that are excellent for native bees; it thrives in moist, partially shaded woodland edges, streambanks, and open forest understories. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: American Hazelnut
description: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; American hazelnut tolerates a wide range of soil conditions but produces the most nuts in full sun; it spreads by root suckers and should be allowed to form thickets for best wildlife habitat value. Corylus americana is a vigorous, multi-stemmed native shrub of eastern North American woodlands and thickets, producing small, round hazelnuts similar in flavor to European hazelnuts (C. avellana) enclosed in distinctive, toothed, leaf-like husks from August through October; the nuts are eagerly consumed by squirrels, blue jays, turkeys, and other wildlife. Long yellow-green male catkins appear very early in spring (February–March), providing one of the first pollen sources for emerging native bees, and the rounded, hairy leaves turn bright orange-yellow in fall. It is native, low-maintenance, and excellent for naturalizing into wildlife hedgerows and edible landscaping. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: American Highbush Cranberry
description: American highbush cranberry is a native Viburnum — not a true cranberry — bearing clusters of bright red, tart berries in fall that persist on the shrub into winter, providing critical food for wildlife during cold months. The berries have a distinct musky aroma when raw that largely disappears with cooking; they are high in pectin and excellent for jellies, sauces, and syrups as a cranberry substitute. Do not confuse with the European cranberrybush (V. opulus), which produces lower-quality, more bitter fruit. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and an open, multi-stemmed form. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: American Highbush Cranberry
description: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, planting at least two shrubs to ensure cross-pollination; American highbush cranberry is not a true cranberry but a native viburnum that produces bright red, translucent, cranberry-sized berries in clusters from fall through winter that birds love and that can be made into preserves, sauces, and jellies with a flavor resembling true cranberries. The lacy white flower clusters in late spring are attractive, and the three-lobed leaves turn brilliant red-purple in fall. Plants are also important wildlife habitat shrubs for nesting birds. The native var. americanum is preferred over the European V. opulus (which escaped and has naturalized invasively in some areas). Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: American Licorice (Wild Licorice)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; American licorice is the native North American relative of the commercial licorice plant (Glycyrrhiza glabra), native to the Great Plains and western prairies where it grows along stream banks, roadsides, and moist prairie edges. The thick, deep roots have a genuine licorice flavor from glycyrrhizin compounds (the same compound as commercial licorice) and were used extensively by Native American nations as a food and medicine — chewed fresh, dried as candy, brewed as tea, and used to treat sore throats, toothaches, and stomach complaints. The pinnate compound leaves and small white to pale violet flowers are attractive; the bur-like bristly seed pods cling to fur and clothing. A nitrogen-fixing prairie legume, it improves soil fertility. Spreads by rhizome; contain in smaller gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: American Lotus (Yellow Lotus)
description: Plant tubers in heavy clay-loam soil (not potting mix, which will float) in containers placed in 12–24 inches of water in full sun; the massive circular leaves and huge pale-yellow flowers up to 10 inches across are among the most spectacular sights in water gardening. All parts of this native aquatic plant are edible — the starchy rhizomes are eaten like potatoes, the seeds like nuts, and the young leaves and flower petals as vegetables. The large, sculptural seed heads remain on the plant through winter and are popular in dried floral arrangements. In a natural pond, the rhizomes can spread aggressively; use containers to control spread in small water features. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: American Lovage
description: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates significantly, and established plants will self-sow once the colony matures. Ligusticum canadense is a robust native carrot-family herb of rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests across the central and southern Appalachians and adjacent piedmont, growing 2 to 4 feet tall with large, finely divided, celery-scented leaves and broad, flat-topped white umbel flowers in late spring and early summer that are among the most effective native plants for attracting small native bees, parasitoid wasps, and syrphid flies. The aromatic roots and foliage were used extensively in food and medicine by many Indigenous peoples throughout the plant's range, and the plant serves as a larval host for the black swallowtail butterfly. It is an excellent structural plant for the back of shaded borders and native woodland gardens where height and late-season structure are needed. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: American Mountain Ash
description: Collect seeds in autumn as soon as the berries ripen and sow immediately in a prepared bed or seed flat at a depth of about 1/4 inch, then allow winter temperatures to provide the necessary stratification sequence. Seeds will germinate in spring once soil warms; transplant seedlings to a permanent site in their second year when they have developed a robust root system. Choose a cool, moist site with well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, reflecting this tree's preference for northern forests and high-elevation ridges. Consistent moisture during establishment is critical, as young trees are drought-sensitive; once established, they are exceptionally cold-hardy and low-maintenance. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: American Pennyroyal
description: Direct sow in lean, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; American pennyroyal is a small, aromatic native annual in the mint family, distinct from the European pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) but similarly pungently mint-scented with a sharp, camphor-like quality. Indigenous peoples throughout eastern North America used the plant extensively as an insect repellent (rubbing the leaves on skin to repel mosquitoes and flies), a medicinal herb for colds and fevers, and a culinary flavoring. The plant self-sows freely in dry, lean, open, sandy conditions and can be left to naturalize in appropriate sandy garden areas. Caution: do not use medicinally in large amounts, especially during pregnancy, as concentrated pulegone-containing plants can be toxic in excess. For fragrance and insect-repellent purposes, moderate use is traditional and appropriate. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: American Pennywort
description: American Pennywort is a native semi-aquatic groundcover of eastern North American forest seeps, springheads, and streambanks, forming a low carpet of small, round, glossy leaves on slender creeping stems. Plant in constantly moist to saturated, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; it will not tolerate drought or dry conditions even briefly. The leaves are edible in small quantities, with a mild, slightly peppery flavor similar to other pennyworts, and have a long history of use as a trail nibble or minor salad green. Use it as a living mulch beneath moisture-loving ferns and native wildflowers in rain gardens or along shaded pond margins. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: American Persimmon
description: Plant in deep, well-drained to average soil in full sun to partial shade; American persimmon is a tough native tree with striking blocky, alligator-hide bark and excellent fall color that produces small, intensely sweet, apricot-flavored fruits after the first hard frost when they become fully ripe and astringency disappears. The fruits are outstanding for puddings, breads, and fresh eating and are highly attractive to deer, foxes, opossums, and birds. Trees are quite drought-tolerant once established and will grow in poor, rocky, or clay soil where few fruit trees survive. Named female cultivars (Meader, Szukis, Yates, Pieper) with improved fruit size are grafted onto seedling rootstock — grow these for reliable, large-fruited production. Allow fruits to fall naturally after frost and collect from the ground before wildlife does. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: American Plum (Wild Plum, Osage Plum)
description: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; American plum is drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes readily in hedgerows and woodland edges. Prunus americana (American wild plum) is a native small tree or large shrub found across much of the eastern and central United States, producing clusters of fragrant white flowers in March–April before leaf emergence (a spectacular early-spring display that attracts native bees, especially mining bees and andrenid bees) followed by abundant 3/4-inch, red to orange-yellow plums in July–August. The fruits are quite tart when fully ripe but develop excellent plum flavor when fully ripe and dead-ripe, and are highly prized for jams, jellies, wines, and preserves; they were a staple food of many Native American peoples and European settlers. American plum spreads by root suckers to form thickets valuable for wildlife (providing dense nesting cover for songbirds and food for over 70 bird species), and has been extensively used as rootstock for grafting hybrid plum cultivars. It is among the most cold-hardy, drought-tolerant, and disease-resistant of all plums. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: American Purple Top Rutabaga
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in loose, fertile soil about three months before your first fall frost, thinning to 6 inches apart. Roots grow 4 to 6 inches long with sweet, mellow yellow flesh that mashes like potatoes or adds body to soups and stews. The tender tops are also edible as sauteed greens. Rutabagas develop the best flavor in cool weather, so leave them in the ground until after a light frost before harvesting. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: American Sea Rocket
description: Direct sow into loose, well-drained beach or dune-type sand in full sun; American sea rocket is a fleshy-leaved, mustard-family annual that colonizes the upper beach and foredune along both Atlantic and Pacific coasts, tolerating salt spray, sand burial, and drought that would kill nearly any conventional vegetable. The succulent, deeply lobed leaves and young seed pods have a sharp, peppery, radish-like bite and are eaten fresh in salads or as a pungent garnish, much like a wild, salt-tolerant arugula. Small four-petaled pale lavender to white flowers appear over a long season, followed by distinctive two-segmented, corky seed pods that float and disperse on tides and currents. It self-sows readily in loose sand and is best grown in a sandy raised bed or true beach-adjacent garden rather than ordinary rich soil, where it becomes leggy and short-lived. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: American Silverberry (Wolf Willow)
description: Set out rooted suckers or container plants in spring on poor, sandy, or saline ground where its vigorous, nitrogen-fixing roots and suckering habit can be left to spread without crowding cultivated beds. This silvery-leaved North American native tolerates conditions few other fruiting shrubs can, needing no supplemental fertility once established. Small, fragrant yellow flowers in early summer give way to silvery, mealy berries that ripen in fall and are used for jam, drying, and winter forage for birds. Unlike the related autumn olive and Russian olive, American silverberry is a true native across most of its range and behaves far less aggressively, making it a sound choice for windbreaks, erosion control, and reclamation plantings. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: American Wild Plum
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; American wild plum is a rugged native shrub or small thicket-forming tree that produces fragrant white flower clusters in early spring before the leaves emerge, then bright red or yellow-orange tart plums 3/4–1 inch in diameter in July through August. The thickets provide excellent wildlife cover and nesting sites. Wild plum suckers heavily and can naturalize into large hedgerows — a valuable feature in permaculture designs. The tart fruits are excellent for jams, jellies, sauces, and fruit leathers; deer, foxes, raccoons, and dozens of bird species rely on them. Tolerates drought, clay, alkaline soils, and extreme cold once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: American Wintergreen (Round-leaved Pyrola)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained, undisturbed forest soil in deep to partial shade; American wintergreen is a native evergreen herb of cool, moist, acidic woodland floors in the northern hardwood and mixed conifer forests of eastern North America. The rounded, leathery, glossy dark-green leaves form attractive low rosettes that persist through winter. The raceme of nodding, waxy white flowers in summer resembles a miniature lily-of-the-valley flower stalk. Like its relatives in the family Pyrolaceae (now Ericaceae), it depends on mycorrhizal fungi and resists conventional cultivation — it is best appreciated in its natural habitat or in undisturbed, established woodland gardens with intact acidic duff. The plant has a long history of herbal use in traditional medicine, with the leaves containing substances similar to aspirin. Collect only nursery-propagated stock; do not disturb wild populations. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Amethyst Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Purple Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the deepest, most uniform purple leaf color. Amethyst is an All-America Selections winner bred for consistent, richly saturated purple foliage from seedling stage onward, along with improved resistance to premature bolting compared with older purple basil types, keeping the compact plant productive and attractive for a longer stretch of the growing season. Its uniform color and tidy habit make it useful as an ornamental edible in containers and border plantings as well as a culinary and vinegar-infusing basil. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and encourage bushier growth, and harvest leaves often to keep new growth coming. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Amethyst Cauliflower
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before transplanting, then set out sturdy seedlings in rich, evenly moist soil. This variety forms striking purple, domed heads that mature early and reliably in spring or fall and hold color best with steady moisture. Vigorous plants tolerate a range of climates and perform especially well in the Eastern US. Harvest heads while the curds are still tight, and enjoy the tender, flavorful florets steamed or roasted. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Amethyst Falls Oregano (Trailing Pink Hop-Flowered Ornamental Oregano)
description: Amethyst Falls is an ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its cascading clusters of overlapping, papery, rose-pink bracts that resemble small hanging hops, held above rounded, gray-green, aromatic leaves on trailing stems. Like its close relative Kent Beauty, it is grown chiefly for its ornamental flower display rather than culinary use, and its trailing habit shows best spilling from a raised bed, rock garden pocket, or hanging container where the pendant flowers can be appreciated up close. Give it lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since excess moisture and humidity quickly lead to rot, and expect a shorter garden life than culinary oregano, particularly in hot, humid summers.
