Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Amethyst Passionflower (Deep Purple Fringed Flower Vigorous Vine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils. Amethyst bears deep, rich purple flowers with a fine, densely fringed filament corona, an intensely colored bloom that has made it a popular hybrid for gardeners seeking a bolder purple than the paler blue-lavender of the straight species. It flowers heavily through summer and draws pollinators readily. In zones at the cooler edge of its range it dies back to the ground in winter and regrows strongly from deep roots in spring; mulch the crown heavily where marginal. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Amethyst Radish (Bright Purple Uniform Spring Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Amethyst is a modern spring radish bred for uniform, smooth, round roots with bright, consistent purple skin and crisp white interior, offering reliable color and shape for gardeners and market growers who want a purple radish that performs predictably. Flavor is mild and clean, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types, without the excess pepperiness that develops in some varieties left too long in the ground. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, and succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Amfissa Olive (Greek Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)
description: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Amfissa, also known as Conservolia, is grown around the Greek town of Amfissa near Delphi and is one of Greece's most important dual-purpose olive varieties, producing large, round, mild-flavored fruit used both as a popular table olive, typically cured black and glossy, and pressed for good-quality oil when the crop or market calls for it. The tree is reliably productive and well adapted to traditional Greek Mediterranean growing conditions, and the fruit's large size and mild flavor have made it a familiar sight in Greek markets and export products. As with all olives, harvested fruit must be properly cured before eating, since fresh olives straight off the tree are intensely, unpalatably bitter regardless of variety. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Amigo F1 Florence Fennel
description: Direct sow shallowly into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to final spacing rather than transplanting, since fennel seedlings dislike root disturbance. Amigo is an F1 bulbing fennel that produces flattened, broad white bulbs with dense, crisp flesh and reliably resists the premature bolting that ruins many Florence fennel plantings in variable weather. Its flattened bulb shape and tight leaf base make it well suited to close spacing and mechanical harvest in market-garden rows. Hill soil around the developing bulb to keep it blanched and tender, and harvest once the bulb reaches full size but before any central flower stalk begins to elongate. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Amish Butter Popcorn
description: Maintained for generations among Pennsylvania Dutch growers, Amish Butter is a pre-1885 heirloom popcorn that produces tall, dark-green stalks topped with two conical ears carrying a mix of rice- and pearl-shaped ivory-white kernels. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, or finish drying them indoors on their husks, until kernels rattle loosely in the cob before shelling and storing in a breathable container. Because the kernels are soft enough to also grind for flour, hominy, or polenta, gardeners get a genuinely dual-purpose corn from a single planting rather than a popcorn-only crop. The fluffy white pop and rich, naturally buttery flavor are the main reasons collectors keep this variety in circulation. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Amish Deer Tongue Lettuce (Heirloom Pointed-Leaf Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Amish Deer Tongue is a longtime Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom named for its distinctive triangular, pointed leaves that resemble a deer's tongue, forming loose, upright rosettes of thick, crisp, richly flavored green leaves. It is notably more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many other loose-leaf lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the lettuce harvest into warmer weather in Gulf South spring gardens. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette at the base once it fills out. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Amish Melon (Heirloom Amish-Grown Cantaloupe)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to the strongest seedlings once established. Amish Melon is an open-pollinated heirloom muskmelon preserved and passed down through generations of Amish farming families, producing medium to large, netted, orange-fleshed cantaloupe-type fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor typical of well-grown heirloom melons. The vigorous, productive vines are known for reliable fruit set and good flavor even in less-than-ideal seasons, a hallmark of many Amish-preserved garden varieties bred for dependable performance in working farm gardens rather than showy uniformity. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind color has turned from green to tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Amish Paste Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, keeping the mix warm for even germination. This indeterminate heirloom produces meaty, acorn-shaped red fruits of 8 to 12 ounces with few seeds, excellent for rich sauce and paste but also good for slicing. Provide a tall stake or trellis and prune suckers to manage the vigorous vines. Water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and pick fruit as it colors fully. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Amish Paste Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Amish Paste is an heirloom paste tomato from Wisconsin Amish communities, producing large (6–8 ounce) ox-heart to plum-shaped fruits with very few seeds, thick meaty flesh, low water content, and rich concentrated flavor that makes it outstanding for sauces, pastes, and canning. It far outperforms Roma for sauce production due to its greater size while retaining the low acidity and meatiness needed for good paste. Also excellent sliced fresh. An indeterminate vine with a long season; in short-summer climates, start early and use season-extension techniques. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Amish Paste Tomato
description: Amish Paste is a vigorous indeterminate heirloom yielding large, plum-to-oxheart-shaped fruits of 8-12 ounces with dense, richly flavored flesh ideal for sauce and canning. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights are reliably warm. Provide tall stakes or a strong trellis and prune suckers to improve air flow, since the sprawling vines produce all season. Keep watering even and mulch well to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot on the heavy fruit. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Amish Pie Pumpkin (Heirloom Sweet Baking Pumpkin)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run, or trellis smaller fruit for a large vertical crop. Amish Pie is a heritage pumpkin passed down through Plain communities for its large, ribbed, deep-orange fruit and thick, dense, notably sweet flesh, considered by many bakers superior to jack-o'-lantern pumpkins, which tend to be stringy and watery by comparison. Fruits commonly run 10-20 pounds and store well into winter in a cool, dry spot, making it practical to bake from a single pumpkin over several months. Keep vines well watered as fruit sizes up and reduce watering as the rind hardens and colors fully in fall, then cure harvested pumpkins for a week or two before storage to concentrate sweetness and toughen the skin. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Amish Rocambole Garlic (Hardneck)
description: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in well-drained, compost-enriched soil and mulch for winter insulation in cold regions. Snap off the coiling scape as it appears to send more energy into the developing bulb, and cure bulbs in a shaded, breezy spot before trimming roots and tops for storage. Amish Rocambole is a long-grown American heirloom hardneck strain passed down through Pennsylvania Dutch farming communities, admired for its rich, robust garlic flavor, easy-peeling cloves, and classic rocambole scapes once used fresh in early-summer cooking. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Amish Snap Pea (Amish Snap)
description: Amish Snap is a tall heirloom snap pea passed down through Amish and Mennonite farm families in Pennsylvania and the Midwest and preserved by seed savers rather than commercial breeding programs. Vigorous vines climb readily on a trellis and set heavy quantities of sweet, plump, stringless pods that hold their quality well in variable spring weather. Because the vines are unusually tall, plan on netting or a fence at least five to six feet high and harvest every couple of days once pods fill out to keep the plants productive. The pods are good eaten fresh off the vine, lightly steamed, or stir-fried. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Amity Raspberry (Large Fall-Bearing Oregon Red Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, providing support for canes as they fill in. Amity was bred at Oregon State University as a fall-bearing (primocane) red raspberry, producing large, firm, richly flavored berries on the current season's new canes from late summer through fall, well after most summer-bearing varieties have finished. Because primocane types fruit on new growth, the entire planting can be mowed or cut to the ground each winter, radically simplifying pruning compared to summer-bearing varieties that require selective cane removal. This makes Amity a particularly low-maintenance choice for home gardeners wanting a single, reliable, high-quality fall raspberry crop without the more involved care summer-bearing brambles need. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Amla (Indian Gooseberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; amla is a deciduous small tree native to South and Southeast Asia, grown for its round, pale green, translucent fruits that are extremely high in vitamin C and intensely sour and astringent when fresh. The tree tolerates poor, rocky soils and considerable drought once established, and produces feathery, fine-textured foliage that drops in the dry season. Fruits ripen in fall to early winter and are typically pickled, candied, dried, or processed into juice, chutney, and the Ayurvedic preserve chyawanprash rather than eaten out of hand. Trees are usually grafted onto seedling rootstock for faster, more reliable bearing and are sensitive to hard freezes, restricting outdoor culture to the warmest parts of zones 9-11 or container growing elsewhere. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Amling Pecan (Scab-Resistant Type I Pecan)
description: Plant a grafted tree in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it plenty of room to reach its mature size and pairing it with a Type II pollinator cultivar for a good nut set. Amling is a Gulf South pecan cultivar valued for strong resistance to pecan scab, the humid-climate fungal disease that is the single biggest challenge to growing pecans without a heavy fungicide spray program in the Southeast, making it a lower-maintenance choice than older scab-susceptible standards. It bears a good crop of medium-sized, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality on a vigorous, productive tree. Young trees take several years to bear their first nuts and reach full production only after ten years or more; water deeply and regularly during establishment and through nut fill in late summer, since drought stress during fill reduces kernel quality. Provide deep, infrequent irrigation rather than frequent shallow watering to encourage a deep root system. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Amsoi Mustard (Filipino Broadleaf Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; Amsoi is a broadleaf mustard type long grown in Filipino home gardens and widely used in Filipino cooking, particularly in noodle dishes and sauteed vegetable sides. The smooth, glossy, dark green leaves are broader and less deeply lobed than curled mustard types, with a flavor that is noticeably milder and less sharply pungent than Southern mustard greens, making it approachable for cooks who find typical mustard heat too strong. Because it prefers steady moisture and moderate temperatures, it performs best as a cool-season crop and tends to turn bitter and bolt quickly once hot weather sets in. Harvest by cutting outer leaves or the whole young plant, since regrowth from the cut stem is reliable during the cool months. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Amsterdam Forcing Carrot (Fast Early Dutch Baby Carrot)
description: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the surface evenly damp until the slow-to-emerge seedlings appear, then thin to about 2 inches apart. Amsterdam Forcing is a classic Dutch heirloom bred specifically for speed, producing slender, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots with a fine, sweet flavor and almost no core, ready to pull well before slower main-crop carrots. Its small size and rapid growth make it an excellent choice for containers, cold frames, and tight succession sowings every few weeks through the cool season. Harvest young, at finger to baby-carrot size, for the best texture and sweetness, since roots left in the ground too long lose the tenderness that defines the type. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Amy Chinese Chestnut (Extremely Cold-Hardy Ohio-Bred Selection)
description: Amy is a Greg Miller selection (numbered 72-400) chosen from a 1972 planting of Chinese chestnut seedlings grown from Ackerman Nursery stock in Carrollton, Ohio, the same planting that produced the Gideon and Peach cultivars. It stands out for exceptional cold hardiness, reliably surviving winters at least to USDA zone 5b, well beyond the comfort range of many Chinese chestnut selections, while still budding out early and cropping heavily and consistently once established. Nuts are small to medium and shrink somewhat further as the tree matures, but carry excellent flavor and peel cleanly, and like other Chinese chestnuts Amy carries the species' natural resistance to chestnut blight that eliminated American chestnut from eastern forests. Because chestnuts are self-incompatible, plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set, and site trees in deep, well-drained soil since Amy can be prone to blossom-end nut disorders in poorly drained ground. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anacafe 14 Coffee
description: Anacafe 14 originated as a chance cross between Catimor and Pacamara discovered by a Guatemalan farmer and was released commercially by ANACAFE, the country's national coffee association. It inherits coffee leaf rust resistance and drought tolerance from its Catimor parent while retaining more of the Pacamara side's large bean size and cup complexity than most rust-resistant hybrids manage. Grown at higher Guatemalan elevations it can produce a surprisingly structured, sweet cup, helping shift the reputation of rust-resistant varieties away from flat or woody flavors. It grows as a vigorous, moderately sized tree and appreciates the same rich volcanic soil, partial shade, and consistent moisture as other Guatemalan highland arabicas. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Anacua (Sandpaper Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; anacua is a native south Texas and Mexico tree of the Rio Grande Plains and Gulf Coast, valued for its multi-season ornamental interest: fragrant white flowers in spring, followed by clusters of small orange-yellow fruits (edible, slightly sweet) in late spring and early summer that attract numerous birds. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves give the tree its secondary common name. The fruit is eaten by numerous bird species, particularly golden-fronted woodpeckers, white-tipped doves, and mockingbirds. Semi-evergreen in mild winters in zone 9a; may lose some leaves in hard freezes but re-leafs readily from the base or branch tips. An excellent, underused native tree for south and central Texas gardens providing year-round interest, wildlife value, and adapting well to the alkaline soils of the Edwards Plateau and lower Rio Grande valley. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Anaheim Chili Pepper
description: Anaheim, also called New Mexico chile, is a mild heirloom pepper producing long, tapered fruits with a smoky flavor prized for roasting, stuffing, and grilling. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using bottom heat, since the seeds need warm soil to sprout. Transplant only after nights stay above 55F, spacing plants about 18-24 inches apart in full sun. Harvest green for chiles rellenos or leave fruit to ripen red for a sweeter, deeper flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Anaheim Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm mix at 80°F and provide bright light once germinated to prevent leggy growth; transplant after frost danger has completely passed. Anaheim peppers are mildly hot (500–2,500 Scoville units), long and tapered, and the classic pepper for green chile and chiles rellenos. Harvest green at 75 days for mild flavor, or allow pods to ripen to red for a sweeter, slightly hotter pepper that can be dried and ground into pure chile powder. Consistent watering and a light fertilizer application when flowers begin to set helps prevent blossom drop in heat. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Ananas Melon (Pineapple Melon)
description: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in deeply enriched, well-drained soil; Ananas is a large-fruited type needing 6–8 feet of row space or a very strong trellis with hammock-style fruit supports. Ananas melon (ananas is French and many Mediterranean languages for pineapple) is a widely grown Middle Eastern, Israeli, and Mediterranean heirloom producing large, oval to round, netted fruits (3–7 lb) with a sweet, spicy, intensely aromatic fragrance when ripe that has been compared to pineapple, vanilla, and spiced honey. The flesh can be white (in the traditional Israeli 'Ananas Yokneam' type) or orange, always with a distinctive rich, complex fragrance that perfumes a room when a ripe fruit is present. Several regional strains exist: French Ananas (yellow netted, orange flesh), Israeli Yokneam (white smooth skin, white flesh), and American strains. Generally large-fruited and somewhat heat-sensitive; best grown in dry conditions as wet weather can dilute flavor. Considered by some the finest-flavored muskmelon type in existence. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Ananasnaja Kiwi (Pineapple-Flavored Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Ananasnaja (sometimes sold as Ananasnaya) is a heavy-bearing Russian-bred hardy kiwiberry selection valued for grape-sized, smooth-skinned fruit with a distinctive pineapple-tinged sweetness. Vines are extremely vigorous twining climbers that require a strong permanent trellis or arbor and yearly winter pruning to control growth and encourage fruiting wood renewal. As a female clone it must be planted within about 30 to 50 feet of a compatible male arguta vine for pollination and fruit set. Fruit ripens in early to mid fall and is typically harvested by taste-testing a few berries, since the smooth green skin gives little visual ripeness cue. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Anasazi Bean
description: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, thinning to 4–6 inches apart; Anasazi beans are an ancient Southwest Native American dry bean with distinctive burgundy-and-white speckled seeds that cook faster than most dry beans due to thinner seed coats and produce a sweet, rich, mealy flavor. Unlike many heirloom dry beans, they are reputed to cause less flatulence because their lower oligosaccharide levels. Harvest pods when they are fully dry and yellow-brown before rainfall can cause mold. In humid climates, pull whole plants and hang to finish drying in a sheltered location. Seeds remain viable for 3–5 years when stored in cool, dry conditions. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Anatoki Feijoa
description: Anatoki takes its name from the Anatoki River valley in New Zealand's Golden Bay region, an area known for feijoa breeding, and produces medium to large, rounded fruit with thin skin and rich, sweet, aromatic flesh typical of the newer wave of dessert-quality New Zealand selections. The shrub grows with a naturally rounded, well-filled habit that needs less corrective pruning than older, leggier feijoa cultivars to look good as either a specimen or an informal hedge. Its spring flowers are abundant and showy, drawing pollinators for the fruit set as well as offering sweet, edible petals as an incidental garden snack. As with all feijoas, give it full sun, well-drained soil on the acidic side, and steady moisture through summer for the best fruit size, and expect it to shrug off Gulf Coast heat and humidity that would stress less heat-tolerant fruiting shrubs. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anatolian Oregano (Sharp-Toothed Oil Oregano)
description: Native to the mountains of central and eastern Anatolia in Turkey, this species is one of several wild oreganos harvested regionally for the dried-herb trade known locally as kekik, valued for its notably high concentration of aromatic oils compared to many garden oregano species. Its narrow, pointed leaves and pale pink to white summer flower spikes are smaller and more delicate-looking than common Greek oregano, but the dried leaf carries a robust, resinous, peppery bite. Grow in lean, rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun, mimicking its native hillside habitat, and avoid rich, moisture-retentive beds that dilute flavor and invite root rot. Harvest just before flowering for the most concentrated essential-oil content, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Ancho/Poblano Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the mix at 75 to 90 degrees since peppers germinate slowly in cool soil. Transplant into warm, well-drained soil after nights are reliably above 55 degrees. The 3 to 6 inch green poblano is excellent stuffed for chiles rellenos, while the dried, reddish-brown ancho anchors sauces like mole poblano, with mild heat around 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units. Harvest green for fresh use or leave fruit to ripen red for drying. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Andaliman (Batak Pepper, Sumatran Sichuan Pepper)
description: Andaliman is the signature spice of Batak cuisine from the highlands of North Sumatra, prized for its bright, citrusy aroma and the same tongue-numbing sanshool compounds found in Sichuan pepper, but with a fresher, more limey character than its Chinese relatives. Unripe green berries are harvested and used fresh or dried, most famously in the fish and pork dishes arsik and saksang. Because it naturally grows as an understory shrub in cool, humid highland forest, it prefers filtered light and consistently moist, rich soil rather than full sun and is intolerant of any frost, limiting outdoor culture to the warmest, nearly frost-free gardens or large containers overwintered under cover elsewhere. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, so more than one specimen is needed for a fruit harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Andover Parsnip (Canker-Resistant Award-Winning Hybrid)
description: Andover is a British-bred parsnip widely recognized for combining strong field resistance to canker with the smooth, well-shaped, medium-length roots gardeners expect from older heirlooms. It has become a standard recommendation in cool, damp growing regions where canker-prone varieties like Hollow Crown often develop the disfiguring rust-brown shoulder rot that ruins a crop. Sow shallowly and keep the seedbed evenly moist through the slow, uneven germination typical of parsnip, marking rows carefully since seedlings emerge slowly and are easy to lose to weeding. As with all parsnips, flavor sweetens dramatically after the roots experience several weeks of near-freezing temperatures, so delay harvest until after hard frost for the best eating quality. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Andovy Hamburg Root Parsley
description: Andovy is a Hamburg-type root parsley grown for its smooth, parsnip-like white taproot rather than its foliage, with a mild, earthy, parsley-scented flavor that works well roasted, mashed, or added to stocks. It produces uniform, straight, slow-to-fork roots when grown in loose soil, along with edible flat leaves that can be harvested lightly through the season without harming root development. As a hardy biennial root, it can be left in the ground and harvested through fall and into early winter after light frosts, which sweetens the flavor. Gardeners grow Andovy as a dual-purpose crop, choosing it over standard leaf parsley when a storable root vegetable is the goal. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Andrews American Highbush Cranberry
description: Andrews is a named selection of American highbush cranberry chosen by northern breeders for producing larger, less bitter fruit than typical wild seedlings, making the tart red berries more pleasant for fresh sauces and jelly without as much of the musky flavor common to the species. Like the straight species it is a true Viburnum rather than a cranberry, blooming with flat white lacecap clusters in late spring before setting heavy fruit clusters that ripen in fall and persist on the shrub well into winter as valuable cold-season wildlife food. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating northern Great Plains and prairie winters that few fruiting shrubs survive, and grows best in consistently moist, well-drained soil. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the multi-stemmed shrub vigorous and productive. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Angel Hair Winter Spaghetti Squash
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, spacing hills to give vines room to run. Prolific plants yield up to fifteen uniform fruits weighing 1.5 to 2 pounds each, sized perfectly for serving on the half-shell. When cooked, the flesh forks away in tender spaghetti-like strands. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot for a week or two to improve storage life, and keep on the vine until the rind hardens. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Angel Red Pomegranate (Soft-Seeded Sweet Red Fresh-Eating Pomegranate)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Angel Red is a soft-seeded pomegranate variety — one of the most important distinctions in pomegranate selection for fresh eating. Standard pomegranate varieties (including Wonderful) contain hard, woody seeds at the center of each aril that some people find unpleasant to eat; soft-seeded varieties like Angel Red have soft, barely-noticeable seeds that allow the entire aril to be eaten without extraction, fundamentally changing the fresh-eating experience. Angel Red produces large, bright-red fruits with deep-red, juicy arils and rich pomegranate flavor — somewhat sweeter and less astringent than Wonderful at peak ripeness. The soft-seeded quality makes Angel Red excellent for fresh eating out of hand (where hard seeds are an obstacle), salads (where whole arils are used as a garnish), and for fresh juice where the softer seeds blend or press more easily. Like all pomegranates, Angel Red is self-fruitful, drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, and ornamentally attractive with showy orange-red flowers in summer and richly colored fall fruit. In zone 9, Angel Red ripens in October–November at essentially the same time as Wonderful — the harvest timing is similar but the eating experience is distinctly more accessible for fresh consumption. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Angeleno Plum (Very Late-Season California Japanese Plum)
description: Angeleno is a late-season Japanese plum developed in California and prized for extending the harvest into September, well after Santa Rosa and most other Japanese types have finished. The deep purple-black skin encloses meaty amber-yellow freestone flesh that holds up unusually well in storage and shipping compared to earlier-season Japanese plums. Because it blooms in mid-season, plant Angeleno with another mid-blooming Japanese plum such as Santa Rosa or Burgundy within about fifty feet to ensure a full crop. Thin fruit early to four to six inches apart so the remaining plums size up properly on this heavy-setting tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Angelica
description: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest or purchase in autumn, pressing 1/4 in deep into moist soil; stored or old seed germinates poorly. Angelica is a short-lived perennial or biennial that requires deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil and partial shade — its ideal habitat is moist woodland edge. Removing the flower head in the second year prolongs the plant's life, while allowing it to set seed means the plant dies after seeding but self-sown seedlings will follow. Harvest young leaf stems and petioles in spring for candying; collect seeds when ripe for use in gin and liqueur flavoring. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Angelique Fig (Early Yellow French Heirloom Fig)
description: Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom fig, historically grown around Paris and known there as Angelique or Melette, that Thomas Jefferson brought to Monticello after seeing it cultivated abroad. It bears medium to large fruit with pale greenish-yellow, subtly striped skin and sweet, cream-colored flesh, ripening notably early in the season and extending the fig harvest before later-season cultivars come in. As a common-type fig it is self-fertile and produces without pollination, and its long history of wide cultivation across France attests to its adaptability across a range of soils and climates. In the Gulf South, Angelique's early ripening window helps growers bring in a crop ahead of the peak summer humidity that promotes fruit souring and splitting in later-maturing varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Angled Luffa (Ridge Gourd)
description: Grow on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; angled luffa (turiya in Gujarati, turai in Hindi) is a staple vegetable in South Asian cuisine, prized for its delicate, slightly bitter flavor and ability to hold up in cooked dishes. Unlike the smooth luffa used for sponges, the angled luffa has prominent longitudinal ridges and must be harvested young at 6–10 inches while the flesh is tender and the ridges peel off easily; older fruits become fibrous and bitter. The plant grows vigorously in summer heat and humidity, producing heavily if given consistent moisture and regular fertilization. Harvest every 2–3 days to prevent fruits from maturing on the vine. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Anise
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in their final location in rich, well-drained soil; anise develops a taproot that transplants poorly. Thin to 6–12 in apart once seedlings are established, and stake plants in exposed sites as they can be top-heavy when in flower. Anise needs a long, frost-free season to set seed—at least 120 days—so start as early as possible in cool climates. Harvest umbels when seeds begin to turn gray-green, cutting whole heads into paper bags to catch seeds as they ripen. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Anise Basil (Licorice Basil, Thai Anise Basil)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger has passed, since basil is quickly killed by cold. Anise Basil, sometimes called licorice basil, is a classic heirloom type with dark purple stems, purple-flushed leaf veins, and tall spikes of pinkish-purple flowers that make it as ornamental as it is useful in the kitchen, where its bold anise-licorice flavor is prized in Vietnamese and Persian cooking and pairs well with fruit, fish, and Asian-style dishes that sweet basil can't match. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive through the season, though leaving a few spikes to bloom brings in a steady stream of pollinators. It tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer as well as most basils and will grow in a large container with the same care as sweet basil. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Anise Hyssop
description: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; anise hyssop is a native prairie perennial with strongly anise-scented leaves and stems that produces upright spikes of densely packed lavender-blue flowers from midsummer through fall — arguably the single most attractive plant for native bumblebees in the temperate garden, hosting extraordinary numbers of pollinators at peak bloom. The leaves make an excellent herbal tea with a pleasant, sweet anise flavor and can be used fresh in salads and fruit dishes. Plants are short-lived perennials or biennials that self-sow reliably to maintain a colony. Deadhead half the spent spikes to extend bloom; leave the rest for self-seeding and winter finch food. Very drought-tolerant. 'Blue Fortune' (robust, long-blooming hybrid) is the most widely grown cultivar. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Anise Root (Long-Styled Sweet Cicely)
description: Anise root is a native woodland perennial of moist, rich, shaded forests across the eastern United States and Canada — every part of the plant, from root to leaf to seed, is intensely fragrant with a sweet, anise-licorice scent that is among the most pleasant of any native wildflower. The thick, fleshy, white taproots are edible raw or cooked and taste strongly of anise; the seeds are used as a spice similar to caraway or anise; and the leaves are used fresh as an anise-flavored garnish and in teas. It is one of the finest shade-garden herbs available, thriving in deep, moist woodland conditions under hardwood canopy where most culinary herbs fail, and it attracts a wide variety of native pollinators to its small white flower umbels in late spring. Sow seeds immediately after ripening in fall — seeds lose viability rapidly if dried and stored; once established, it spreads by self-seeding to form a pleasant aromatic colony in the woodland garden. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Aniseed Myrtle
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring in compost-enriched, consistently moist, well-drained soil, sited with protection from cold wind and, ideally, afternoon shade in hotter climates. Native to subtropical rainforest gullies of coastal New South Wales and southeast Queensland, this glossy-leaved tree contains one of the highest natural concentrations of anethole of any plant, giving the dried, ground leaf an intensely sweet licorice-anise flavor. Use the dried leaf in baking, fruit desserts, herbal tea blends, and as a striking substitute anywhere star anise or fennel seed is called for; it can be clipped and kept as a large shrub in gardens where space is limited. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Anji Baicha Tea (Baiye 1, White Leaf No. 1)
description: Discovered as a chance mutation on a wild tea bush in Anji County, Zhejiang, China, and propagated as the clonal cultivar Baiye 1, this cultivar produces new spring leaves that emerge pale ivory to jade-white because cool temperatures temporarily suppress chlorophyll development, greening up again as the weather warms. That temporary pigment deficiency concentrates unusually high levels of amino acids in the young leaf, giving the resulting green tea, marketed as Anji Baicha, an exceptionally sweet, brothy, umami-rich character prized in the Chinese specialty tea market. Grow it in the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil as other tea cultivars, harvesting quickly once the pale spring flush appears since the white-leaf window is brief. It performs best where cool early-spring nights are followed by a gradual warm-up. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anna Apple (Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Anna is a low-chill apple cultivar developed in Israel and introduced to the United States in the 1960s, requiring only 200–400 chill hours (hours below 45°F). This low chill requirement makes it the most successful apple in Florida, south Texas, and the Gulf Coast South where winter temperatures rarely accumulate the 800+ hours needed by most apple varieties. The medium-large fruits are greenish-yellow with a red blush, similar in appearance to Golden Delicious, with crisp, juicy flesh and a pleasant sweet-tart flavor. Anna is an early-season apple ripening in May–June in zone 9 — remarkably early, making fresh Gulf Coast apples available in late spring when no other apple is in season. Cross-pollination with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer significantly improves yields; plant them within 50 feet. For the finest flavor, allow fruit to ripen fully on the tree until it lifts easily from the branch. Anna is susceptible to apple scab and fire blight — maintain good air circulation and remove infected wood promptly. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anna Hardy Kiwi
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, with a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor structure in place before planting. Anna is one of the most widely planted female hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivars in North America, valued for its heavy, reliable production of smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit that can be eaten whole, skin and all, unlike fuzzy supermarket kiwifruit. The fruit ripens in early fall with sweet, richly flavored, bright green flesh, and the vigorous vine is notably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below what damages standard fuzzy kiwi (Actinidia deliciosa). As a dioecious cultivar, Anna requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine planted nearby for pollination — without one, the vine will grow and flower but set little to no fruit. A vigorous, productive choice for a well-supported arbor or fence line in zone 4–8. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anna Kiwi (Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Anna is a widely grown, reliably productive hardy kiwiberry cultivar valued for good vigor and heavy fruit set once a compatible male is nearby. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet, bright green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. As with all kiwiberry vines, plants take a few years to reach full bearing size but then produce heavily and reliably for decades. Prune hard each winter on a permanent framework of cordons to control the very vigorous twining growth and keep the fruiting wood renewed and productive, and install a sturdy trellis or pergola from the start, since mature vines and their fruit load become quite heavy. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Anna Russian Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to well-prepared, deeply amended soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the heart-shaped fruits. Anna Russian is a Ukrainian/Russian oxheart-type heirloom with distinctive heart-shaped, pink-red fruits up to 12 ounces that are extremely fleshy, nearly seedless, and have a rich, sweet, mild flavor making them outstanding for eating fresh; it is one of the earlier-maturing large heirloom types at 68–80 days, which makes it especially valuable for growers who want to harvest ahead of the worst summer heat. The indeterminate vines set fruit in loose clusters of 2–3 and continue producing through the season if heat stress does not prevent fruit set; in the South, plant early for spring harvest. Matures in 68–80 days from transplant.

name: Annapolis Strawberry
description: Annapolis was bred at the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and released in 1984 as an Earliglow-derived selection resistant to red stele root rot, giving northern growers an early cultivar for sites with a history of root disease. Fruit is medium-large, light red, and mildly sweet, ripening ahead of most other hardy June-bearers and extending the start of the home harvest season. The vigorous, freely runnering plants tolerate winters to zone 3 with only modest straw mulch protection. Because it fruits early, protect open blossoms from late spring frosts with row cover when a cold snap is forecast. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Annatto (Achiote, Lipstick Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; annatto (achiote) is a tropical American shrub known worldwide as the natural source of the orange-red pigment used to color cheese, butter, smoked fish, and countless processed foods — the intensely colored seeds inside the spiny red seed pods are ground or infused in oil to make the widely used Latin American spice paste. The seeds color and flavor rice, tamales, soups, and sauces in Latin American and Filipino cuisine. The attractive plant also produces large pink-lavender flowers similar to single roses followed by striking, bristly bright-red seed pods in clusters. A striking ornamental and useful spice shrub for zone 10–12 gardens; in zone 9a it may be grown in a large container and protected from frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Anne Arundel Melon
description: Anne Arundel is a colonial Maryland heirloom traced to Anne Arundel County, where it was grown by a small circle of local farmers for well over a century. Its nutmeg-shaped fruit ripens to a golden-yellow rind over sweet, pale green flesh with a flavor often compared to honeydew. The strain nearly vanished before being preserved through much of the twentieth century by a Maryland family, and it now circulates through Seed Savers Exchange membership. Give vines full sun and steady moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons approach ripeness to concentrate their sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Anne Golden Raspberry
description: 'Anne' produces exceptionally large, pale-yellow fall-bearing berries with a sweet, apricot-like flavor. Grow in rich, moisture-retentive soil and support the tall canes with a two-wire trellis to keep fruit off the ground. As a primocane variety it can be mown down each winter for a single autumn crop, simplifying pruning. The soft golden fruit does not ship well, making it an ideal home-garden and fresh-eating selection. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Anne Raspberry (Yellow Primocane Fall-Bearing Raspberry)
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil and irrigate consistently during fruit development. Anne is a large-fruited, primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry notable for its pale golden-yellow fruit, an unusual color among raspberries, with a rich, sweet flavor often described as more complex than standard red types. As a primocane variety it fruits on the current season's new canes, so the simplest pruning method is to cut all canes to the ground in late winter, sacrificing an early summer crop in exchange for one large, heavy fall harvest and eliminating the need to sort live from dead canes. It benefits from afternoon shade and consistent moisture in hot climates, since raspberries generally struggle with intense summer heat. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Annie Oakley II Okra
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Annie Oakley II is a hybrid, spineless, compact okra developed as an improved successor to the original Annie Oakley hybrid — the 1988 AAS Award-winning variety that introduced the compact, spineless, early-maturing concept that transformed home garden okra production. Annie Oakley II improves on the original with earlier maturity (48 versus 56 days), heavier production, improved disease resistance, and better heat tolerance for extended season production. The compact, 3–5 foot plant produces straight, uniform, deep green, 5-ribbed pods with excellent tenderness when harvested at 3–4 inches. The thornless, compact habit makes Annie Oakley II the best choice for gardeners with limited space, raised beds, and those who find full-size okra plants too large to manage easily. In zone 9 the compact habit is advantageous because plants fit more naturally into intensive garden beds without overwhelming neighboring crops. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Annie Oakley Okra
description: Direct sow after soil warms to 65°F in full sun; Annie Oakley is a spineless, compact hybrid okra that produces early (52 days) and prolifically on plants 3–4 feet tall — smaller than most standard okra and suitable for smaller gardens or containers. The smooth, straight, dark-green pods are 5-ridged and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for maximum tenderness; pods become fibrous and woody if left beyond 5–6 inches. The spineless habit makes harvest comfortable without gloves; hand-pick every 2–3 days in summer heat. An AAS Award winner, Annie Oakley has proven reliable across the South and performs especially well in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Anouk Spanish Lavender (Compact Butterfly Lavender)
description: This Spanish lavender selection produces dense, plump flower cones topped with tall, showy purple bracts that resemble rabbit ears or butterfly wings, blooming earlier and more repeatedly through the season than many other stoechas types on a naturally compact, rounded plant. It is less cold-hardy than English lavenders and struggles in humid summers or heavy soils, so gardeners outside its comfort zone often grow it in pots that can be moved to shelter for winter. Give it full sun, lean soil, and minimal supplemental water once established, and deadhead spent spikes regularly to keep the repeat bloom coming. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Antigua Bush Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent transplanting and rot in cold ground. This vigorous variety produces 5 to 5.5 inch pods that stay tender and crisp even as the season heats up. Sturdy, upright plants hold pods off the soil for clean, easy picking and do well in containers. Harvest frequently while pods are young and snap crisply to keep plants producing over a long window. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Antigua Eggplant (Antigua F1)
description: Start seed indoors under warm conditions and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay above 55F, since this hybrid performs best with steady heat. Provide even moisture and support for the upright plants as fruit clusters develop. Antigua is a modern Italian-type hybrid bred for a compact plant habit and heavy early set of glossy, dark purple, oval fruit, making it a reliable choice for market growers and small gardens alike. Its relatively quick maturity suits gardeners in cooler regions who want classic eggplant flavor without a long growing season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Antiquorum Taro (Imperial Taro, Small Taro, Dasheen)
description: Plant corms in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained to wet soil — Antiquorum Taro grows vigorously in the warm, moist conditions of Gulf Coast zone 8b-12 and produces harvestable corms through a long growing season. Colocasia antiquorum is a tuberous, rhizomatous perennial aroid in the Araceae family — botanically, the name C. antiquorum has been applied to the smaller-corm types of taro grown throughout Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean that differ from the larger-corm 'dasheen' forms of C. esculenta in corm size, corm flesh color (often with a distinct purple center), and the number of cormels (small side corms). The plant is a core food staple throughout the Pacific Islands, the Caribbean, West Africa, and parts of Asia where taro is a traditional staple crop — the corms are peeled and cooked (boiled, steamed, baked, or fried) to neutralize the calcium oxalate crystals present in all raw Colocasia, and the cooked flesh has a distinctive mildly sweet, somewhat starchy, earthy flavor similar to potato. The large, distinctly peltate (shield-shaped, with the petiole attached in the center of the blade rather than at the edge), arrow-shaped leaves are ornamentally attractive and can reach 24–36 inches. In zone 8b-12, the plants grow through the warm months, die back to the corms in cold winters, and resprout in spring. The corms are harvested in fall before frost. Multiple smaller cormels form around the central corm and can be replanted. CAUTION: cook thoroughly before eating. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Antohi Romanian Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Antohi Romanian is notably earlier than most sweet peppers and can be productive even in short-season gardens. Antohi Romanian pepper arrived in North American heirloom seed circles through Romanian dissident Silviu Antohi, who escaped Romania during the Communist period and brought pepper seeds with him that he shared with gardeners and seed savers in Canada; the variety entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1990s and has since become widely appreciated for its exceptional earliness and high quality. The medium-sized (3–4 inch), blocky to elongated-oval, pale yellow to orange fruits have thin walls and an exceptionally sweet, fruity flavor with virtually no bitterness; they are among the earliest sweet peppers to begin producing, with plants in production 60–72 days from transplant — significantly earlier than most sweet bell types. Outstanding fresh, roasted, or pickled; the thin walls cook down quickly and the fruits need no peeling when roasted. A highly productive plant for short-season gardens and an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast early-season plantings. Matures in 60–72 days from transplant.

name: Antonovka Apple (Cold-Hardy Seedling Rootstock)
description: Plant bare-root seedlings in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Antonovka is grown chiefly as an extremely cold-hardy rootstock or grafting understock rather than for its own fruit. A historic Russian apple selection prized above nearly all other apple rootstocks for exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating winter temperatures that kill or severely damage most other apple rootstocks, making it the standard understock for grafting desired apple varieties in the coldest northern growing regions of North America. Trees grown from Antonovka seed produce full-sized, vigorous trees rather than the dwarfing habit of modern clonal rootstocks, and the fruit itself, while edible, is tart and primarily used for cooking and processing rather than fresh eating. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young Antonovka seedlings in late winter or early spring for a cold-hardy, long-lived, full-sized tree well suited to harsh northern climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Anuenue Lettuce (Heat-Tolerant Hawaiian Iceberg-Type Lettuce)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest as a full head once the center fills in. Anuenue was released by the University of Hawaii in 1987 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates, forming a small, crisp, iceberg-type head with bright green outer leaves and a well-packed pale heart, but with seed and heat tolerance far beyond typical crisphead lettuce. It is one of the few lettuce varieties whose seed will germinate reliably in hot soil rather than going dormant, and the plant resists developing the bitterness that ruins most lettuce as summer heat builds. For Gulf Coast gardeners this makes Anuenue a valuable bridge variety, extending fresh salad lettuce production later into late spring and earlier into late summer than standard cool-season types allow. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Aoshima Satsuma (Late-Season Wase Mandarin Strain)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and water and feed regularly through the growing season to size up the crop. Aoshima ripens later than standard Owari, typically in December, with seedless, easy-peeling mandarins that are slightly larger and deeper orange than the base variety, holding well on the tree without excessive puffiness. Mature, dormant trees tolerate brief drops to roughly 15-20F, making Aoshima suitable for zone 8b-9a dooryard citrus, though young trees should be covered during hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Apache Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Apache is a thornless erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas as part of their world-leading blackberry breeding program. It produces very large, firm, sweet-tart, jet-black berries — among the largest of any thornless blackberry variety at 1–1.5 inch length and 8–12 grams per berry. The erect habit allows Apache to be grown without trellis support, though light support improves the crop. The exceptional fruit size and good flavor make Apache a top choice for fresh eating, farmers' markets, and home preserving. In zone 9 Apache performs well and is resistant to the orange rust fungus that can devastate susceptible blackberry varieties in the humid Gulf South. The thornless canes make harvest much more pleasant and efficient than thorny types, and the erect habit means berries are not dragged through the mud on trailing varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Apache Blackberry (Thornless Erect Arkansas Blackberry)
description: Plant rooted canes or tissue-culture transplants in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil; prune floricanes to the ground after harvest to maintain plant vigor. Apache is a 2003 release from the University of Arkansas blackberry breeding program (the same program that produced Arapaho, Navaho, Kiowa, and Ouachita) and produces some of the largest blackberry fruits in commercial production — individual berries averaging 14–17 grams (roughly 3–4 times the size of a typical wild blackberry), with an excellent balance of sweetness and mild acidity that makes them outstanding for fresh eating. The thornless, erect canes (4–6 feet tall) require no support structures and are easy and pleasant to harvest without the scratches common to thorny types. Apache ripens in late July in Arkansas (later than Arapaho and Navaho), extending the fresh blackberry season into peak summer. The large, firm berries hold their quality well after harvest, giving Apache better shipping and shelf life than softer varieties — an advantage for market growers and home gardeners who want berries for preserving. Very productive when properly established, and the thornless, self-supporting habit makes it the most garden-friendly of the Arkansas blackberry releases. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Apache Bunching Onion (Purple-Tipped Scallion)
description: Apache is a fast-growing open-pollinated scallion selected for shanks that flush from rosy purple to a deeper wine color as the plant matures, set off nicely against slender blue-green tops. Sow thickly in shallow drills and thin as needed, since it is typically pulled young for salads, garnishes, and quick pickles rather than grown to full onion size. Flavor is mild and sweet compared with many bunching types, making it popular raw. Because it germinates and bulks up quickly in cool conditions, succession sowing every two to three weeks keeps a steady harvest through spring and fall. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Apalachee Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Early-Season Small-Nut Pecan)
description: Apalachee was released by the USDA-ARS Pecan Breeding Program in 2009 from a cross of Moore and Schley made in Brownwood, Texas. It is highly resistant to pecan scab (Fusicladosporium effusum), the dominant disease constraint on Gulf South pecan production, making it a strong low-spray option for home orchards. Nuts are small, roughly 84 per pound, but well filled, with about 54% kernel, and ripen early, about three weeks after Pawnee. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it with a Type II cultivar for full nut set, and expect a moderate tendency toward alternate bearing common to most early-ripening pecans. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Aphrodite Cantaloupe (Fusarium-Resistant Eastern Shipper Type)
description: Aphrodite is a widely grown commercial Eastern shipper-type cantaloupe bred with resistance to fusarium wilt and tolerance to several common vine and foliar diseases, traits that also make it a dependable performer in home gardens with a history of melon problems. It produces uniform, heavily netted, oval fruit averaging 5-6 pounds with firm, deep orange flesh and a small seed cavity, and vines hold up well and keep setting fruit through extended harvest periods. Ripe fruit develops a full slip, separating cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a shift to a more golden background color under the netting and a sweet aroma at the blossom end. Its vigorous, disease-tolerant vines and consistent fruit size make it a good choice for gardeners who want reliable yields without babying a finicky heirloom melon. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Apollo Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Supermale Hybrid)
description: Apollo is one of the original Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus releases, developed alongside Atlas and Eros before the breeding program's later Jersey-series introductions. Its all-male genetics mean plants never set the small red berries typical of female asparagus, so beds stay cleaner and free of the crowded volunteer seedlings that reduce spear size over time. Apollo produces a heavy early flush of medium-thick spears and shows good resistance to rust in humid regions. Wait until the third spring after crown planting to begin a full harvest season, cutting spears at soil level every one to two days during the peak flush. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Apollo Feijoa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Apollo is a New Zealand-selected feijoa (pineapple guava) cultivar prized for producing very large, oval fruits with exceptionally smooth skin and outstanding flavor — rated by New Zealand feijoa growers as one of the best-flavored cultivars, with a rich, complex tropical aroma combining pineapple, guava, strawberry, and mint notes. The thick-skinned, moderately large fruits (3–6 ounces) have a balance of sweetness and acidity that appeals to a wide range of palates. Apollo is among the earlier-ripening feijoa varieties, beginning to drop fruit in October in zone 9 — ahead of the main feijoa season — and providing a longer total harvest window when planted alongside mid-to-late ripening varieties. Like all feijoa, Apollo's spring flowers with white petals and edible bright red stamens are ornamental and can be eaten fresh as a sweet-tart floral treat. The silvery-green evergreen foliage and attractive compact shrub form make Apollo an excellent edible landscape plant for year-round interest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Apollo Mahonia (Low Spreading Heavy-Flowering Oregon Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding exposed sites with harsh winter wind and afternoon sun; Apollo is a low, dense, spreading selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 2 feet tall while slowly forming a broad colony by suckering. It is prized for an unusually profuse spring flower display — dense clusters of brilliant yellow flowers smother the branch tips in early spring, noticeably heavier than the species — followed by the same dusty-blue, tart, edible berries and spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns bronze-purple in cold weather. Its low, spreading habit and heavy bloom make Apollo a strong choice for a flowering groundcover under high shade or as a foreground planting in a shaded shrub border. Prune only to remove dead or leggy canes at ground level, since its naturally low, suckering habit needs little other maintenance. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Appalachian Mountain Mint (Narrowleaf Mountain Mint)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian mountain mint is a spreading native perennial of the eastern US with narrowly linear, intensely minty-scented leaves and flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers with purple spots from July through September that are exceptional pollinator magnets — research has found that mountain mint species attract more species of native bees per plant than virtually any other wildflower, making this one of the highest-value pollinator plants for the eastern garden. It spreads by rhizomes to form colonies but is not aggressively invasive and can be controlled by edging; cut plants to the ground in fall. The crushed foliage repels insects and can be used as a natural mint flavoring. A workhorse plant for native meadows, rain gardens, and sunny to lightly shaded borders. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Appalachian Wild Ginger (Variable-leaf Wild Ginger)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; Appalachian wild ginger is a variable-leaved native evergreen groundcover of the central and southern Appalachians, one of several closely related Hexastylis species with overlapping ranges in the mountain and foothill forests of the Southeast. The heterophylla species name (variable-leaved) refers to the tendency to produce leaves of varying shapes on the same plant or population. Like all Hexastylis, it produces the characteristic leathery, heart-shaped, dark evergreen leaves and the odd, urn-shaped, brownish-maroon flowers at ground level in spring, pollinated by ground beetles. A low, slow-spreading, extremely shade-tolerant groundcover that is virtually maintenance-free once established in appropriate forest conditions. Best combined with other evergreen groundcovers like wild ginger, green-and-gold (Chrysogonum), and Christmas fern for a natural mountain forest floor planting. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Appaloosa Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; direct seeding is preferred as beans do not transplant well. Appaloosa bean is an heirloom dry bean named for its dramatic black and white spotted coloring that closely resembles the distinctive coat pattern of the Appaloosa horse breed; the irregular black speckles and splashes on creamy white background make each bean unique and the dried beans are among the most visually striking of all heirloom bean varieties, remaining attractive even after cooking. The flavor is rich and earthy with a creamy texture similar to pinto beans but with more character; they are excellent for baked beans, bean soups, and slow-cooked dishes. Can be eaten as a snap bean when pods are young and tender; most commonly grown for dry use at 85–100 days to full maturity. Drought-tolerant once established; performs well in Gulf Coast spring planting with harvest before summer heat peaks. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Apple
description: Plant bare-root stock in well-drained soil, spreading roots carefully; stake dwarf trees for the first two seasons. Most varieties require a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination — check chill-hour requirements to match your climate (600–1200 hours for standard types, under 400 for low-chill selections). Prune annually in late dormancy to an open-center or central-leader form to improve light penetration and air flow. Harvest when fruit separates with a gentle upward twist and seeds have turned brown, 2–5 years after planting. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Apple Blossom Swiss Chard Blend
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin lightly, or broadcast densely for a cut-and-come-again baby-greens crop. This chard blend produces colorful young leaves ideal in salads or steamed, stir-fried, and added to soups, omelets, and lasagna. It can be grown indoors any time of year for a fresh winter harvest. Snip outer leaves when a few inches tall and the plants will regrow for repeated cuttings. Matures in 25–55 days from seed.

name: Apple Geranium
description: Root Apple Geranium cuttings in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; water moderately and allow to dry between waterings — it is susceptible to root rot in wet conditions; pinch stems to encourage compact growth; bring indoors as a houseplant in winter in zone 8 and colder. Apple Geranium is the most apple-scented of all the scented pelargoniums — the round, soft, velvety leaves have a pure, sweet, green apple scent with a slight minty freshness that is immediately recognizable and universally appealing. The plant has a low, spreading, trailing habit quite different from the upright rose geranium, making it excellent for container edges, hanging baskets, ground cover in sunny borders, and spilling over walls. In the kitchen, the apple-scented leaves are used to flavor jellies and jams, infused in cream or sugar for desserts, floated in cocktails and lemonade, and used to scent and flavor herbal teas. The small white flowers with pink-purple veining are charming though the plant is grown primarily for the scented foliage. Native to the southwestern Cape of South Africa in sandy, rocky, fynbos-adjacent soils, it is adapted to lean, well-drained, slightly dry conditions — performing best without heavy fertilization or overwatering. One of the most useful and fragrant herbs for the container herb garden. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Apple Mint (Woolly Mint)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; apple mint is more drought-tolerant and adaptable than peppermint or spearmint and tolerates poorer, drier soils. Mentha suaveolens is a densely woolly-leaved European mint producing large, round, velvety, gray-green leaves with a pleasant, fruity mint flavor with mild apple overtones; it is especially valued for making mint jelly, apple-mint sorbet, fruit salads, and flavored vinegars, and is an attractive, textural contrast to smooth-leaved herbs in the garden. The variegated cultivar 'Variegata' (pineapple mint) has cream-edged leaves and is one of the most ornamental of all mints, excellent in containers. Apple mint is more heat-tolerant than most mints and performs well in the Gulf South if given afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Apple Serviceberry (Apple Shadblow)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; apple serviceberry is the most widely planted Amelanchier hybrid — a cross between A. arborea and A. laevis producing larger flowers and larger, juicier berries than either parent. In early to mid-spring, before or just as the leaves emerge, it produces a spectacular display of pure-white flowers in drooping clusters that are among the first flowers of the season for early native bees, mining bees, and other spring pollinators that emerge before many plants are flowering. The blueberry-like fruits that ripen in June are sweet, purple-black, and edible fresh, in pies, jams, and wine — they are exceptionally rich in antioxidants and have a pleasant flavor combining blueberry and mild almond notes. The fruits are intensely attractive to birds. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and occasionally yellow, providing a final season of interest. Multi-season value: spring flowers, summer edible fruit, fall color, ornamental winter silhouette. Tolerates part shade and is among the most wildlife-valuable small trees available. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Applegreen Eggplant (AAS-Winning Round Green Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Applegreen is an All-America Selections winner grown for its smooth, round, apple-sized fruit with pale to medium green skin, mild flavor, and tender, virtually seedless flesh that resists browning better than many purple eggplants once cut. Plants are compact and heavily productive, setting fruit steadily over a long season and performing well in raised beds or large containers where space is limited. Harvest fruit while still glossy and firm, roughly the size of a baseball, since overripe fruit dulls in color and develops tougher skin and more seeds. Its mild flavor and quick cooking time make it a versatile choice for grilling, roasting, and stir-fries. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Apricot
description: Most apricot varieties are self-fertile, which simplifies home-orchard planting, but two trees will increase yields. The key limiting factor in temperate climates is the tree's early bloom time — a hard frost after bud break will eliminate the crop, so choose a sheltered north-facing or slightly elevated site to delay bloom, or select late-blooming cultivars. Prune in early summer rather than winter to reduce risk of cytospora canker infection. Harvest when the fruit is fully orange, fragrant, and gives slightly to the touch. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: April Cross Daikon
description: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked, stone-free soil, thinning to a wide final spacing so the smooth white Minowase-type roots can size up without forking. April Cross is prized among daikon growers for its unusually strong resistance to bolting, which lets it be sown earlier in spring than most daikon types without running to seed. Roots stay tender, mild, and non-pithy even when left in the ground to reach full size, making them well suited to fresh eating, pickling, and simmered dishes. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Aprium
description: An aprium is an apricot-dominant hybrid with the sweetness of apricot and a hint of plum, often bearing a faint fuzz. Plant in full sun on light, well-drained soil in a frost-protected spot, since apricot-type blooms open very early. Many apriums are self-fruitful but crop more heavily with an apricot pollinator nearby. Prune in dry summer weather to limit disease and thin the fruit for good size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Aquadulce Claudia Fava Bean (Broad Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep directly in the garden while soil is still cool, spacing plants closely in blocks so they can support each other or provide staking for tall stems. This classic English heirloom is prized for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating hard frosts that would kill other legumes, making it a favorite for autumn sowing in mild climates or the earliest possible spring planting elsewhere. Pods grow long and fleshy, typically holding six to eight large, buttery-flavored beans that are excellent shelled fresh, dried for storage, or used in traditional Mediterranean and British dishes. Pinch out the growing tips once the first pods set to discourage aphids and encourage the plant to channel energy into pod development. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Arapaho Blackberry
description: 'Arapaho' is an early-ripening erect thornless blackberry with medium-large berries containing small, unobtrusive seeds. Its self-supporting canes need minimal trellising, making it well suited to compact plantings and home gardens. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and provide even moisture during the fruiting period for best size and flavor. Remove floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to five or six vigorous shoots per plant. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Arapaho Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Arapaho was the first thornless erect blackberry ever released, developed by the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program in 1993 — a significant milestone in blackberry cultivation that eliminated the primary obstacle to home garden blackberry growing for many people who found thorned blackberries impractical to pick and manage. The erect, self-supporting canes reach 5–7 feet and require only tipping (not a full trellis system) to remain manageable. The large, glossy, firm-yet-juicy berries with excellent sweet-tart flavor ripen in early June in zone 9, among the earliest erect blackberries. The firm texture allows berries to be picked and stored for several days without softening — an advantage for home gardeners who harvest on a schedule. Arapaho was succeeded by later thornless varieties (Apache, Natchez) with larger berries, but remains widely planted for its early ripening, good flavor, and reliable performance in zone 6–9. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Arbequina Olive (World's Most Popular Home Garden Olive, Compact Spanish Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Arbequina is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually produces better oil quality under moderate stress — do not over-fertilize or over-water; harvest olives in November–December when shifting from green to purple-black for oil; for table olives, harvest green in October–November and cure in brine for 6–12 months. Arbequina olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world and by a large margin the most popular olive for home garden use globally — a small Spanish variety from the town of Arbeca in Catalonia that was historically confined to a small region of northeastern Spain before becoming a worldwide standard through its adoption in super-high-density olive plantations in California, Australia, Chile, and Argentina. The variety's global success derives from a combination of characteristics ideally suited to modern olive production: extremely compact habit (10–15 feet versus the 25–30 feet of traditional olive varieties), heavy and precocious bearing (producing significant crops in year 3–4 rather than the 7–10 years of traditional varieties on standard spacing), self-fertility (producing good crops as a single tree), low chill requirement (300–400 hours, allowing successful growing in zones 7–10), and excellent high-quality oil — mild, fruity, golden-colored oil with low acidity that is considered among the finest olive oils. For home gardeners, Arbequina's compact size makes it suitable for large containers, small gardens, and courtyard plantings where standard olive trees would be too large. The small, round olives (1–2g each) can also be table-cured in brine though the size is small by table olive standards. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Arbosana Olive (Compact Cold-Hardy High-Density Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid over-fertilizing or over-watering, since moderate stress improves oil quality. Arbosana is another small Spanish olive variety, alongside Arbequina, widely adopted in modern super-high-density olive orchards for its compact habit, precocious and heavy bearing, and good cold hardiness relative to larger traditional olive cultivars. The small fruit yields a well-regarded, balanced, mildly fruity oil, and the tree's naturally smaller size makes it practical for large containers and compact home landscapes, similar in scale to Arbequina but noted for handling occasional colder winter dips slightly better. Harvest olives as they shift from green to purple-black for oil production in late fall to early winter, or pick green and cure in brine for table olives. Established trees are drought-tolerant and need minimal fertilization. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Arcadia Blueberry (Early-Leafing Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Amend planting rows with generous pine bark or peat to hold pH near 4.5-5.2, and set dormant bushes in late winter with the crown slightly above grade for good drainage. Arcadia is a University of Florida southern highbush selection bred for reliable production under the reduced winter chill typical of the Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida, combining an early bloom period with good natural leafing so plants aren't left bare and unproductive after a warm winter. Fruit is medium-sized, firm, and well flavored, borne on a moderately vigorous, spreading bush that benefits from a nearby southern highbush pollinizer for a heavier set. Water deeply during dry spells and bud swell, since the fibrous, shallow blueberry root system draws most of its moisture from the top foot of soil. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Arcadia Broccoli (Cold-Tolerant Hybrid Fall Broccoli)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with pH 6.0–7.0. Arcadia is an F1 hybrid broccoli that has become a benchmark variety for fall and overwintering broccoli production in zones 6–8 — valued specifically for the combination of excellent cold tolerance, uniformly dark blue-green head color, and disease resistance. Most broccoli varieties produce their best heads in the narrow temperature range of 60–65°F and deteriorate rapidly when exposed to hard frosts — heads yellow, open up, or develop loose, poor-quality florets. Arcadia was selected specifically for the ability to hold tight, well-formed heads through significantly colder temperatures, allowing gardeners and growers in the mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest to harvest marketable broccoli after hard frosts in October and November that would compromise most other varieties.
