The deep blue-green color of Arcadia heads is exceptionally attractive — darker and more uniform than many broccoli varieties — and holds through the cold exposure. Disease resistance includes downy mildew, black rot, and clubroot, which are important fall disease concerns in humid climates. Arcadia is a top recommendation from Johnny's Selected Seeds for fall production and has a loyal following among market gardeners who rely on fall broccoli as a key late-season crop. Matures in 63–70 days from transplant.

name: Archer's Gold Thyme (Golden Creeping Groundcover Thyme)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Archer's Gold is a low, spreading thyme selection valued as much for its bright, glowing golden-yellow foliage, which holds its color through the growing season, as for its mild, lemon-tinged thyme flavor and fragrance. It forms a dense, low mat well suited to edging a path, filling gaps between paving stones, or spilling over a rock garden wall, and small lavender-pink flowers appear in summer, drawing bees. Like other thymes it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, quickly declining in heavy, wet soil, and a light shearing after flowering keeps the mat dense and encourages fresh new growth. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Kolomikta Kiwi, Kiwiberry)
description: Plant male and female vines (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; prune heavily each winter to manage size. Actinidia kolomikta (Arctic beauty kiwi or kolomikta kiwi) is an East Asian kiwi vine native to the cold, humid forests of Siberia, northern China, Korea, and Japan — the hardiest of all Actinidia species, surviving temperatures to -40°F (USDA zone 3) with no winter protection. It produces abundant, smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits (no need to peel) with green flesh, a flavor similar to full-sized kiwi fruit, and a slightly sweeter, more complex character — excellent fresh or in fruit salads, smoothies, and preserves. The vine is dioecious — plant at least one male per 6-8 female vines for pollination and fruit set. What makes Arctic beauty kiwi especially garden-worthy is the extraordinary variegated foliage of the male plants: in late spring and early summer, the new leaves emerge with spectacular patches and splashes of bright pink, cream-white, and green — rivaling any ornamental vine in beauty. Female vines are solid green but highly productive. A superb ornamental-edible vine for cold-climate gardens where fuzzy kiwi (A. deliciosa) cannot survive. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Arctic Frost Satsuma (Ultra-Cold-Hardy Seedless Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting in the warmest available microclimate for the first few winters. Arctic Frost is a satsuma mandarin selection bred for improved cold hardiness beyond standard satsuma cultivars, allowing mature trees to tolerate brief drops into the low 20s or upper teens Fahrenheit with only minor wood damage, when standard citrus of similar fruit quality would be killed to the ground. Fruit is sweet, low-acid, essentially seedless, and easy to peel, with the loose, glossy rind typical of satsumas, ripening in fall to early winter. Young trees need cold protection for the first two to three winters until established, but mature wood is notably tougher than most edible citrus. Like other satsumas, it is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, and it tends to bear well even as a young tree. Protect the trunk and graft union with mulch or wrap in the coldest years, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization in late summer, which can push tender new growth that is more vulnerable to an early freeze. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Arctic Kiwi / Kolomikta Kiwi
description: Actinidia kolomikta is the hardiest kiwi species, tolerating temperatures to -40°F in zone 3, and is grown for its small (1 in), sweet, smooth-skinned fruits that ripen in late summer. The vine is ornamentally striking due to pink-and-white variegated foliage on male plants. It is dioecious and requires both male and female plants — one male per 4–6 females. Cats are intensely attracted to the plants and will damage young vines, so protect new plantings with wire cages. Prune each dormant season to maintain a framework of lateral arms on a sturdy arbor or fence. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Argelino Loquat (Algerie Loquat, Spain's Leading Commercial Loquat)
description: Also known as Algerie after its origin as an introduction from Algeria, Argelino has long been the dominant loquat cultivar of the Callosa d'en Sarria growing district in Alicante, Spain, where it and its bud-mutation offshoots account for the great majority of Spanish commercial loquat production. It ripens very early in the loquat season, bearing orange fruit that is notably high in sugar but carries enough tang to keep the flavor from tasting flat or one-dimensional. Several distinct bud sports have arisen from Argelino over the decades and are grown regionally under their own names, a testament to how widely the original selection has been propagated. In a home orchard it performs much like other Eriobotrya japonica cultivars, self-fertile and reliable, but is worth seeking out specifically for its early ripening and well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Argentata Swiss Chard (Silver Ribbed Italian Heirloom Chard)
description: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have a couple of true leaves, and keep beds evenly watered through summer heat. This old Italian type produces broad, dull green savoyed leaves atop wide, flat, silvery-white ribs that many cooks prize for braising separately from the greens. It is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt, allowing continuous cut-and-come-again harvest well into the warm months. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Argenteuil Purple Asparagus
description: Argenteuil is an award-winning French heirloom asparagus with tender, sweet purple-and-green spears tipped in pink, valued for early, heavy yields. Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, soaking seed first to speed the slow germination, then transplant seedlings to a deeply prepared permanent bed. Wait until the third spring to begin cutting spears so the crowns can build strong roots, and let ferns grow all summer to feed the plants. A well-tended bed remains productive for 15 to 20 years. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Arikara Yellow Bean (Ree Bean, Northern Plains Native American Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Arikara Yellow is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in poor to moderately fertile soils without supplemental irrigation in all but the driest conditions; harvest dry pods before fall rains can induce mold on the dried pods. Arikara Yellow Bean is a traditional heirloom dry bean of the Arikara people (also called the Ree), a Caddoan-speaking people who lived in permanent earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River in present-day North Dakota and South Dakota, where they practiced intensive agriculture including cultivation of corn, squash, sunflowers, and beans for centuries before European contact. The Arikara were important traders in the Missouri River trade network, and their agricultural products — including seeds — were traded widely, distributing their bean varieties to neighboring peoples and eventually to European and American settlers and traders. Arikara Yellow is characterized by small to medium-sized, oval, pale yellow to light tan seeds with a mild, earthy, somewhat buttery flavor that is excellent in soups, stews, and as a baked bean. The variety's most distinctive horticultural characteristic is its extremely short maturity for a dry bean — 80–95 days — which allows it to be grown and harvested in the short frost-free season of zones 3–4 where most dry beans cannot ripen before fall frost. This same short-season adaptation makes Arikara Yellow valuable for gardeners in any region who want a reliable dry bean with insurance against early fall frosts or a compressed summer schedule. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Aristocrat Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Compact Green Zucchini)
description: Aristocrat won an AAS award in 1973 for combining a compact, space-saving bush habit with the kind of dark green fruit color and shape consistency that open-pollinated zucchini of the era could not match. Plants stay under two feet tall, making this a practical choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots where vining winter squash would take over. Water deeply every few days rather than a light daily sprinkle to keep production steady through hot spells, and harvest fruit at 6-7 inches before the skin toughens. Decades after its release it remains available from mainstream seed catalogs, a testament to its enduring garden performance. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Aristotle Basil (Compact Downy Mildew-Resistant Genovese-Type Basil)
description: Transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, spacing plants to keep air moving through the dense, compact canopy. Aristotle is a modern Genovese-type basil bred specifically for resistance to downy mildew, the fungal disease that turns older sweet basil varieties yellow and defoliated within weeks in hot, humid climates, making it a far more reliable choice for Gulf Coast summers than heirloom Genovese types. The tight, uniform, mounding habit produces an abundance of medium-sized, classic sweet-basil-flavored leaves that hold quality well in containers and small beds. Harvest by pinching stem tips regularly, which delays flowering and keeps the compact plant producing tender new leaves through the entire growing season. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Aristotle Bell Pepper (Bacterial Spot-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aristotle is a widely grown commercial and home-garden bell pepper hybrid bred specifically for resistance to three races of bacterial leaf spot, a disease that thrives in the warm, humid, rain-prone conditions common across the Gulf South and can otherwise strip a pepper plant of foliage and ruin fruit quality. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red if left on the plant, on a compact, well-branched plant that holds up well to heat. Because it keeps its leaf canopy healthier than more disease-susceptible varieties, Aristotle tends to shade and protect its own developing fruit from sunscald better through the peak of summer. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Arizona Walnut (Texas Walnut, Little Walnut)
description: Plant young trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, rocky to sandy soil in spring; Arizona walnut (Juglans major) is a native walnut of the Desert Southwest, growing along canyon bottoms and mountain slopes in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and northern Mexico. The small, round, thick-shelled nuts are labor-intensive to crack but have excellent, rich flavor comparable to eastern black walnut — and have been a valued food of indigenous peoples of the Southwest (Apache, Navajo, Pueblo peoples) for centuries. More heat and drought tolerant than eastern walnuts, the tree is the dominant native walnut of the semi-arid West and an outstanding choice for dry-climate food-forest systems. It is also an important wildlife tree and rootstock for grafting cultivated walnuts in desert climates. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Arkansas Black Apple (Ozark Heirloom Dark-Skinned Keeper Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator variety. This late-1800s Ozark heirloom is famous for skin that darkens from deep red to nearly black in full sun, and for fruit that is rock-hard and tart at harvest but mellows into a dense, sweet, aromatic apple after two to three months in storage. Because of this, growers pick it in October and cellar it rather than eating it fresh off the tree. The thick skin and firm flesh make it an outstanding long-keeping cider and baking apple that was once a major shipping variety before modern refrigeration existed. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Arkansas Blackeye #1 Cowpea (Early Commercial Blackeye Southern Pea)
description: Arkansas Blackeye #1 was the first blackeye-type southern pea released specifically for commercial production in Arkansas, developed through the University of Arkansas cowpea breeding program. It forms a medium-sized bush, 20-26 inches tall with no basal runners, suited to conventional or narrow-row planting. Seeds carry a distinct, medium-sized black eye similar to California Blackeye No. 5, and the variety matures a few days earlier than Coronet or Pinkeye Purple Hull-BVR, typically 60-70 days from sowing. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Arkansas Traveler Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in warm (70–85°F) starting mix; transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Arkansas Traveler is the quintessential heat-tolerant Southern heirloom, developed at the University of Arkansas and introduced around 1939 as a reliable producer through the oppressive midsummer heat of the South and Gulf Coast that causes most other tomatoes to drop blossoms and go dormant. The indeterminate vines produce medium to large (6–8 oz) pink, globe-shaped fruits with mild, low-acid flavor, thin skin, and very good crack resistance — exactly the qualities that make it a top recommendation for zone 8–10 gardeners frustrated by summer tomato failure. The meaty, juicy flesh has classic sweet tomato flavor without sharp acidity. A dependable heirloom for hot climates: one of the best-adapted tomatoes for gardens where summer heat is the limiting factor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Arkin Carambola
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Arkin is the leading commercial carambola cultivar in Florida, selected by the University of Florida for its combination of large fruit size, sweet flavor, and attractive appearance — the five-lobed, waxy, golden-yellow fruits are the classic star-fruit appearance when sliced crosswise, producing the familiar star-shaped cross-sections used to garnish drinks, fruit platters, and Asian dishes. Unlike the sour Malaysian varieties (planted for processing), Arkin is a sweet variety with a balanced sweet-tart flavor suitable for fresh eating, juicing, and garnishing. The self-fertile tree is moderately productive even as a single plant, producing 200–400 pounds annually in good conditions. Carambola is high in vitamin C and very low in sugar compared to most tropical fruits, making it popular in health-conscious cuisines. In zone 9 the tree requires careful siting to avoid frost damage — plant against south-facing structures for maximum cold protection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Armenian Cucumber (Snake Cucumber, Yard-Long Cucumber)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; provide trellis for best fruit shape; harvest at 12–18 inches for best texture. Cucumis melo var. flexuosus (Armenian cucumber or snake cucumber) is one of the most unusual cucurbits in cultivation — despite being called a 'cucumber,' it is botanically a muskmelon, not a true cucumber. The distinction matters in practice: Armenian cucumber is significantly more heat-tolerant and better-adapted to Gulf Coast summers than true cucumbers (Cucumis sativus), continuing to produce prolifically in summer heat that stresses and collapses standard cucumber vines. The extraordinarily long fruits (reaching 12–36 inches) are pale sage-green, lightly ridged, with a very thin, edible skin and white flesh that has a mild, slightly melon-scented cucumber flavor without bitterness. The seeds are nearly absent in young fruits, only becoming prominent in overripe specimens. Armenian cucumber does not need peeling, has no bitterness (the cucurbitacins that cause cucumber bitterness are absent), and is excellent fresh, in Middle Eastern salads (fattoush, tabbouleh), and in tzatziki. A standard fixture in Middle Eastern, Armenian, and Persian home gardens, it deserves much wider use in Southern gardens where true cucumbers struggle in summer. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Armenian Pale Green Cucumber
description: Armenian Pale Green is actually a heat-tolerant melon grown like a cucumber, producing long, ribbed, pale-skinned fruits that stay crisp and mild without bitterness. Direct-sow after the soil warms to at least 70F, planting seeds about an inch deep, and thin or transplant to 12-18 inches apart. Grow on a trellis to keep the long fruits straight and clean, harvesting at 12-18 inches while the skin is still tender. Because the thin skin needs no peeling, these are excellent for fresh salads and quick pickles. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Armking Nectarine
description: A California-bred medium-chill nectarine long grown across the Deep South for its large, semi-freestone fruit with olive-green skin blushed deep red and richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in early-to-mid June. It sets fruit heavily and shows good tolerance to bacterial spot, but nectarines as a group are more prone to brown rot than peaches in humid Gulf climates, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through ripening. Choose an inland or upland Gulf South planting site over the immediate coast to ensure it receives adequate winter chilling for consistent bloom and fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Armstrong Satsuma (Armstrong Early Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas. A bud-sport selection of Owari satsuma found in the Gulf South, it produces the same sweet, easy-peeling, nearly seedless fruit but ripens two to three weeks earlier, letting growers harvest ahead of the season's first hard freeze in marginal citrus climates. The compact, glossy-leaved, thornless tree is heavily productive and, like other satsumas, hardier to cold than most other mandarins, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit once mature. Mulch the root zone and wrap or cover young trees during hard freezes, and pick fruit as soon as it colors since satsumas hold poorly on the tree once ripe. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aroma 2 Basil (Highly Aromatic Disease-Tolerant Genovese-Type Hybrid Basil)
description: Sow indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. This vigorous hybrid Genovese-type basil was bred for exceptionally strong, sweet basil aroma and flavor along with improved vigor and tolerance to common basil diseases compared to open-pollinated Genovese strains. Large, glossy dark-green leaves hold up well through the season for continuous cutting; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep plants leafy and productive for pesto and fresh use. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Aromas Strawberry (Vigorous UC Davis Day-Neutral Strawberry)
description: Plant crowns at proper depth (crown at soil surface, roots fully buried) in raised, well-drained beds in full sun, spacing plants to allow good air movement around the dense foliage. Aromas is a day-neutral strawberry released by the University of California, Davis strawberry breeding program, valued for its large, firm, aromatic berries and strong, vigorous plant habit that tolerates heat better than many older day-neutral varieties. Like other day-neutral types it flowers independent of day length, so in zone 8-9 a fall planting yields a long winter-into-spring picking season rather than the single flush typical of June-bearing strawberries. Mulch with straw to keep fruit clean and off the soil, and thin runners regularly since Aromas's extra foliage vigor can otherwise divert energy away from fruit production. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Aromata Summer Savory
description: Aromata is a German (Erfurt-bred) seed strain of summer savory selected for a bushier, more branched habit and a notably higher essential-oil content in the leaf than common summer savory, giving a more concentrated peppery bite from the same amount of fresh or dried herb. It is grown exactly like ordinary summer savory, direct-sown after the last frost into full sun and lean, well-drained soil, then thinned and pinched to encourage branching. Because the oil content is higher, cooks can generally use it more sparingly than standard summer savory in the bean, lentil, and sausage dishes where the herb is traditional. Cut whole stems for drying just as the first flower buds appear, when oil concentration peaks. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Aromatnaya Kolomikta Kiwi (Sweet Aromatic Arctic Beauty Kiwi)
description: Aromatnaya is a Russian-bred female Actinidia kolomikta selection producing medium-sized, very sweet, fragrant fruit on a vigorous and exceptionally productive vine, typically ripening in mid-August. Spring foliage on vigorous shoots shows the green, white, and pink variegation characteristic of the species, adding ornamental interest alongside the fruit crop. As with all kolomikta kiwi, this is a dioecious selection and requires a separate male vine planted within range for reliable pollination and fruit set. The species is exceptionally cold hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below zero, making it a good choice for far northern gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aromatnaya Quince (Russian Quince Edible Fresh Without Cooking)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Aromatnaya is a Russian quince cultivar notable among quince types for fruit that is mild and pleasant enough to eat fresh, unlike most quince varieties that require cooking to be palatable due to their hard, astringent flesh. The pineapple-yellow fruit is intensely fragrant and still excellent for cooking into preserves and quince paste, but its unusually mild, less astringent flavor when fully ripe has made it popular with gardeners who want a more versatile quince. The tree is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and otherwise managed like other quince cultivars, benefiting from good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Aromatto Basil (Purple Leaf Genovese-Type Basil)
description: Transplant into full sun after the last frost and pinch flower spikes regularly to prolong leaf production through summer. Aromatto is an All-America Selections winner bred to combine deep, glossy purple foliage with the robust, spicy-sweet flavor of a true Genovese-type basil, filling a gap left by most purple basils, which tend toward milder, clove-like flavor. Its vigorous upright habit and strong aroma make it useful both as a culinary basil for pesto and vinegars and as an ornamental accent in the herb bed. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Aron Black Chokeberry
description: Aron is a Danish-origin black chokeberry selection that became the dominant cultivar in Eastern European commercial aronia orchards, prized for its upright vigor, heavy and consistent fruit set, and berries that hold well on the bush for mechanical or hand harvest. It grows taller and more upright than compact cultivars like Nero, tolerates poor and periodically wet soils, and produces little suckering compared to the wild species. Its high-anthocyanin berries are typically processed into juice, syrup, or dried snacks rather than eaten fresh due to their astringency; harvest in late summer once berries turn from red to glossy black. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aronia / Chokeberry
description: Aronia is exceptionally hardy and tolerates wet, poorly drained soils, making it suitable for rain gardens. It is self-fruitful and rarely needs a pollinator, though yields improve with a second plant nearby. Prune by removing the oldest, thickest canes at the base every 3–4 years to encourage vigorous new growth and better light penetration. Harvest clusters in late summer when berries are very dark purple-black; the astringent flavor mellows after a light frost or processing. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Arp Rosemary (Extra Cold-Hardy Upright Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Arp was discovered growing outdoors through winter in Arp, Texas, and remains one of the most reliably cold-hardy rosemary selections for gardeners north of the mild-winter regions where most rosemary is grown, surviving temperatures that kill standard culinary rosemary outright. Its upright, shrubby habit and lighter, grayer-green needle-like leaves have a milder flavor than some other culinary types, but it is still fully usable in cooking, and the plant produces pale blue flowers in spring. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a full, bushy shape, and avoid heavy, wet, or poorly drained soil, which is a far greater threat to rosemary survival than cold in most gardens. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Arracacha (White Carrot, Peruvian Parsnip)
description: Plant stem cuttings in spring in deeply cultivated, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; arracacha is one of the most important root crops of the South American Andes and is gaining attention among adventurous food gardeners in mild climates for its exceptional flavor — the white to cream-colored roots have a starchy texture and a flavor that combines the best qualities of celery, carrot, and parsnip with a slightly sweet, buttery richness. The roots are boiled, roasted, fried, or used in soups; they do not store well after harvest and are best consumed within a few days. The plant resembles a flat-leafed parsley or celery relative with compound leaves and naturally produces multiple offsets from the crown that can be replanted as cuttings to propagate. It thrives in the cool, humid conditions of zones 8–10 coastal areas and mild highlands where temperatures remain moderate — it is not well suited to the extreme summer heat of the Gulf Coast interior but performs in coastal areas and in partial shade. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Arrowhead (Wapato, Duck Potato)
description: Plant tubers or divisions in shallow water (1–6 inches deep) or in saturated soil at a pond or stream margin in full to partial sun; arrowhead is a native aquatic perennial with distinctive arrow-shaped leaves, three-petaled white flowers in midsummer, and underwater starchy tubers (called wapato or katniss) that were a critically important food source for many Native American peoples across North America, harvested by wading and loosening the tubers with the feet in fall when starches are concentrated. The tubers are nutritious and delicious when boiled or roasted like small potatoes. The plant also provides outstanding wetland habitat — frogs shelter in the leaves, diving ducks (especially mallards and teals) eat the tubers, and shorebirds and herons hunt at its margins. In favorable conditions it spreads aggressively; contain in submerged containers if space is limited. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Arrowroot
description: True arrowroot is a tropical perennial native to the Caribbean and northern South America, cultivated for its slender, white rhizomes that produce the purest, most digestible starch of any root crop — genuine arrowroot starch is almost flavorless, dissolves crystal-clear in cooking (unlike cornstarch which turns cloudy), and is prized in gluten-free baking and as a thickener for delicate sauces, jellies, and gravies. In Gulf Coast gardens, it grows vigorously as a shade-tolerant understory crop under fruit trees and along the edges of covered patios — one of the few starchy root vegetables that thrives in partial shade, making it ideal for interplanting beneath taller tropical crops. Harvest slender, finger-like rhizomes 10–12 months after planting when the leafy tops begin to yellow; the rhizomes can be eaten boiled or baked, or processed into starch by grinding, washing, and drying. Start rhizome sections each spring; in frost-free areas it grows as a true perennial, expanding into spreading clumps. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Arthur Menzies Mahonia (Extra-Hardy Winter-Flowering Oregon Grape Hybrid)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, siting it where its bold, spiny, holly-textured pinnate leaves and stiff, upright habit have room to develop into a large architectural evergreen. Raised at San Francisco's Strybing Arboretum and prized above other Mahonia x media selections for its outstanding cold tolerance and vigor, it produces dense, upright racemes of fragrant bright yellow flowers in late fall to early winter, an unusually early and generous show that feeds overwintering pollinators, followed by powdery blue-black berries that birds strip through late winter. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and dry shade beneath trees once rooted in, needing only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or overly leggy canes, cutting them back near ground level to encourage fresh basal growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Artichoke Garlic (Softneck Garlic)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Artichoke garlic (named for its overlapping layers of cloves resembling an artichoke) is the most widely grown garlic group in the world and the standard garlic of commercial production. The large, white to purple-streaked bulbs contain multiple layers of cloves (10–20 per head) with a mild to moderately pungent flavor that is the familiar 'standard' garlic taste of commerce. Artichoke types are softneck garlics (no central flower stalk), making them the type used for braiding and one of the longer-storing types. In zone 9, Artichoke types perform better than most Hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe) because they require somewhat less cold vernalization. Named Artichoke varieties recommended for the South include 'Inchelium Red' (already in the dataset), 'California Early,' 'Red Toch,' and 'Lorz Italian.' Plant in fall, fertilize in late winter with high-nitrogen fertilizer, and harvest in April–May when lower leaves are dry but 4–5 green leaves remain. Cure in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 3–4 weeks. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Artisan Bumble Bee Blend Pole Cherry Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This blend combines Pink, Purple, and Sunrise Bumble Bee cherry tomatoes, each striped and no two alike, sweet and tangy right off the vine. The indeterminate plants grow large and yield heavily, so provide sturdy support and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly to reduce cracking, and harvest fruit as it colors fully throughout the season. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Artwork Broccoli (AAS-Winning Heat-Tolerant Stem Broccoli)
description: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Artwork is an AAS-winning stem broccoli, closer in style to broccolini than a traditional single-head broccoli, forming a modest central head that is quickly followed by a long, heavy, extended flush of slender, tender side shoots that can be harvested continuously for weeks — total yield per plant far exceeds a standard main-head variety. It is notably more heat tolerant than most broccoli, holding quality and continuing to produce shoots even as warm weather sets in, which makes it a good choice for stretching the harvest later into a Gulf South spring than most broccoli allows. Harvest shoots with 4-6 inches of stem while the small flower buds are still tight; regular picking encourages more side shoots to form. Keep soil consistently moist and side-dress with compost partway through the harvest period to sustain the long production window. Matures in 60–100 days from transplant.

name: Arugula
description: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season green with a bold, peppery bite that is delicious in salads, on pizza, and lightly wilted. Direct-sow shallowly every two to three weeks from early spring through fall for a steady supply of tender leaves. Harvest young outer leaves cut-and-come-again, and cut the whole plant before hot weather triggers bolting and a sharper flavor. In warm regions grow it in partial shade or indoors to extend the harvest window. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Arugula
description: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil and press lightly without covering; arugula is one of the fastest-maturing and easiest-to-grow leafy vegetables, germinating within 5–7 days in cool conditions and ready to harvest as baby greens in 3 weeks or full-size leaves in 4–6 weeks. The peppery, nutty, mustardy flavor is most mild and complex in cool weather; leaves become intensely bitter and peppery in hot weather. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous supply; cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting 1 inch above soil) extends each planting significantly. Both flowers and leaves are edible; the white flowers with purple veins are excellent salad garnishes. Fall-planted arugula has superior flavor to spring plantings in most climates. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Arugula Baby Greens
description: Broadcast seed thickly about 1/4 inch deep for a dense baby-greens crop, sowing every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Peppery leaves are rich in vitamin C and potassium and taste great with balsamic and Parmesan. This crop grows quickly in cool weather and can be raised indoors year-round for fresh winter greens. Cut leaves when 2 to 3 inches tall and the bed will often regrow for a second harvest. Matures in 20–30 days from seed.

name: Arugula Microgreens
description: Broadcast the tiny seeds thickly and evenly across a moist tray of soil or a microgreen mat, then keep covered for the first two days to speed germination. Sprouts appear within a few days and grow best in bright indirect light at room temperature. Mist gently to keep the surface moist without waterlogging, and harvest with scissors once the first true leaves show, usually around a week to ten days. The peppery, mustard-like bite is at its best when cut young and eaten fresh. Matures in 7–12 days from seed.

name: Arugula/Rocket
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool weather and thin for full-size plants, or leave dense for baby greens ready in about 20 days. The peppery, mustardy leaves brighten salads and are also good steamed or on pizza. Grow in full sun to part shade and keep soil moist to slow bolting, which turns leaves bitter and hot in heat. Succession sow every two to three weeks in spring and fall for a continuous harvest. Matures in 20–40 days from seed.

name: Arugula/Wild Rocket
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil; wild rocket grows more slowly than common arugula but offers a stronger, more complex peppery flavor. Harvest as baby greens or let plants reach full size for salads, pizza, or pesto. It grows well in containers and tolerates part shade, and the deeply lobed leaves regrow after cutting. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest regularly to keep leaves tender and slow flowering. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Arum-Leaf Arrowhead (Wapato)
description: Arum-leaf arrowhead ranges farther north than any other North American Sagittaria, growing wild in shallow ponds, marsh edges, and slow streams from Alaska and the Yukon south through the Rocky Mountains and Great Lakes to New Mexico. It is smaller and daintier than broadleaf arrowhead, with narrower, more triangular leaf blades that taper to a rounded arum-like base rather than the sharp basal lobes typical of the genus. The starchy corms, known as wapato, were an essential root vegetable for many Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and northern Plains, traditionally gathered by wading barefoot through the mud to loosen corms so they floated free. Its extreme cold tolerance and ability to persist under ice make it a good choice for northern water gardens, and the corms and foliage provide food for waterfowl, muskrats, and beaver. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Asafoetida (Hing, Devil's Dung, Ferula)
description: Sow fresh seed in fall in deep, perfectly drained, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; asafoetida is a tall, carrot-family perennial (Ferula assa-foetida) native to the dry steppes and mountains of Iran and Afghanistan, grown for the pungent resinous sap (hing) tapped from the roots of mature 4–5 year old plants — used as a cooking spice in South Asian, Middle Eastern, and ancient Roman cuisine that imparts an onion-garlic flavor when cooked in oil despite its famously unpleasant raw odor. The plant requires full sun, perfectly dry, well-drained alkaline soil and is very intolerant of summer humidity and wet conditions, making it challenging to grow outside arid regions. Primarily of interest to specialty herb growers; commercial hing is tapped from plants growing wild in Central Asia. Matures in 1825–2555 days from seed.

name: Asakura Sansho (Thornless Japanese Pepper)
description: Asakura Sansho is a long-cultivated, essentially thornless selection of Japanese sansho pepper (Zanthoxylum piperitum), prized in Japan for producing an abundant crop of aromatic young leaves (kinome) in spring and green, citrusy-hot berries in summer that are ground into the classic sansho spice used on eel, tempura, and miso dishes. Unlike wild sansho and most other Zanthoxylum, the near-absence of thorns makes hand-harvesting the leaves and unripe fruit clusters far more pleasant. It grows best with some afternoon shade and consistent moisture, especially in hotter climates, and appreciates a woodland-edge type site rather than full baking sun. Both male and female plants are needed for fruit set since sansho is typically dioecious, though male plants alone are still valuable for their prized kinome leaf harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Asam Gelugur (Sour Garcinia)
description: Grow asam gelugur in full sun to light shade on deep, moist, well-drained tropical soil, giving it plenty of room since wild trees exceed 60 feet and even cultivated specimens become substantial shade trees over time. This dioecious species, native from the eastern Himalayas through Myanmar, Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and Sumatra, needs both a male and a female tree present to set fruit, producing large, round, bright orange-yellow fruit 7 to 10 centimeters across at the branch tips. The intensely sour pulp is rarely eaten fresh; instead it is sliced and sun-dried into 'asam keping,' a traditional souring ingredient used throughout Malaysian and Thai curries, fish dishes, and pickles. Give young trees consistent moisture and complete protection from cold, since the species has no frost tolerance and is strictly limited to humid, frost-free tropical gardens. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Ascolano Olive (Large Mild Table and Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Ascolano is an Italian-origin olive cultivar long grown in California for its large, thin-skinned, mild-flavored fruit — one of the highest-quality table olives available, with less bitterness before curing than most cultivars and flesh that separates easily from the pit. Its thin skin bruises more readily than firmer-skinned table olives such as Manzanillo or Sevillano, so fruit is best hand-harvested carefully rather than shaken or mechanically picked. Ascolano can be cured green or ripe black and also produces good-quality oil, though its lower oil content and thinner skin make it less common in commercial oil orchards. Trees are moderately vigorous and only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and overall yield. As with other olives, established Ascolano trees are notably drought-tolerant and adapt well to the alkaline, low-fertility soils common across much of the Gulf Coast and Texas. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ashanti Pepper (West African Black Pepper, Uziza)
description: Train cuttings up a post, tree trunk, or trellis in fertile, well-drained soil with light shade, especially while young; Ashanti pepper is a woody perennial climber native to the West and Central African rainforest that is prized for two distinct products from the same plant. The young, peppery-aromatic leaves, known as uziza leaf in Nigeria, are chopped fresh into pepper soups and stews, while the dried unripe fruit, uziza seed, is ground as a pungent, more intensely hot substitute for true black pepper. Harvest leaves lightly and repeatedly once the vine is established; fruit clusters ripen from green to red over several years as the plant matures. Mulch well and water during dry spells, since the species comes from consistently humid forest conditions. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ashitaba (Tomorrow's Leaf, Japanese Angelica, Longevity Herb)
description: Surface sow fresh seed in a partially shaded, moist, humus-rich location; ashitaba prefers morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates — in zone 9a it is best grown in a site with dappled shade or east-facing exposure to protect from summer afternoon heat; harvest young stems and leaves regularly to promote continuous new growth; the yellow sap of the cut stems is edible but bitter. Ashitaba (Angelica keiskei, meaning 'Angel Herb of Keiske') is a remarkable culinary and medicinal herb native to the Izu Islands of Japan — a subtropical island chain stretching south from the Izu Peninsula, where the inhabitants are noted for their exceptional longevity and good health, which traditional Japanese culture attributes in part to regular consumption of ashitaba. The plant is a tall, hollow-stemmed member of the carrot family (Apiaceae) with large, glossy, deeply divided leaves and the characteristic umbellate flower clusters of the family; unlike most Apiaceae herbs which are harvested for seeds or roots, ashitaba is grown for its young leaves and tender stems. The common name 'Tomorrow's Leaf' (ashita = tomorrow, ba = leaf) reflects the plant's extraordinary regrowth rate — young leaves emerge with such speed that a stem cut today is visibly growing another leaf by the following morning, an exceptional characteristic even among fast-growing herbs. The leaves are somewhat bitter, celery-like in flavor, and rich in flavonoids — particularly chalcones and xanthoangelol — that are the subject of extensive research in Japan for potential health benefits. The stems and leaves are used in Japanese cooking in tempura, salads, juices, and tea. The distinctive yellow sap that oozes from cut stems is a characteristic feature of the species. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Ashley Cucumber (Clemson Heat-Tolerant Slicer)
description: Ashley was released in 1956 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station's Truck Experiment Station in Charleston, bred to hold up under the humidity and downy mildew pressure typical of Lowcountry and Gulf Coast summers. Vines are vigorous and medium-length, producing dark green, slightly tapered slicers 7-9 inches long with a mild, sweet flavor. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sufficient summer slicer rather than a hybrid. Provide a trellis or let vines sprawl, and pick regularly to keep production going through peak heat. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Ashmead's Kernel Apple (English Heirloom Sharp-Flavored Russet Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Raised from seed around 1700 by Dr. William Ashmead of Gloucester, England, this is one of the oldest russet apples still grown and is treasured by cider makers and flavor enthusiasts for its intense, sharp, pear-drop sweetness balanced against high acidity. The medium, dull green-gold fruit is entirely covered in rough russet skin and looks unassuming, but the dense, dry, richly flavored flesh has made it a favorite of English apple connoisseurs for centuries. It ripens in mid-fall and its flavor improves somewhat with a few weeks of storage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ashwagandha (Indian Ginseng, Winter Cherry)
description: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 24 inches; harvest roots when berries form on the plant and begin to dry. Withania somnifera (ashwagandha or Indian ginseng) is one of the most important medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine — a short-lived perennial shrub native to the dry regions of India, North Africa, and the Mediterranean, producing an extensive root system with thick, fleshy, woody roots that are the primary medicinal product. The roots contain withanolides, a class of steroidal lactones that are the subject of extensive clinical research showing adaptogenic, stress-reducing, anti-inflammatory, and potential cognitive-protective effects. Ashwagandha root powder and extracts are among the most widely sold herbal supplements globally, used for stress management, anxiety reduction, athletic performance enhancement, and cognitive support. The plant itself is an attractive, somewhat felty-leaved, branching shrub with small, inconspicuous flowers and small, tomato-like red berries enclosed in paper lantern-like calyces. Harvest roots 5–6 months after transplanting. The plant is in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) — the berries are mildly toxic. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Ashwagandha / Indian Winter Cherry
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix and keep consistently warm at 70–80°F until germination; transplant after last frost into sandy or loamy, well-drained soil. Ashwagandha thrives in hot, dry conditions similar to its native Indian range — avoid overwatering and boggy soil. The fleshy taproot is the primary medicinal part and is harvested after the plant's first autumn, when the small lantern-like berries begin to turn red. Wash, slice, and dry the roots for use in adaptogenic powders and decoctions; yields improve substantially if plants are grown through a full growing season. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Asian Ginseng (Korean Ginseng, True Ginseng)
description: Plant pre-stratified seeds or 2-year rootlets in fall in moist, deeply humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil under 70–80% shade from deciduous trees; ginseng is extremely slow and demanding, needing years of careful growing before harvest. Asian ginseng is one of the most prized medicinal herbs in East Asian traditional medicine, used for thousands of years as a general tonic and adaptogen; commercially grown in Korea and China where demand far exceeds supply from wild populations. Home cultivation requires patience — seeds need 18 months of stratification, plants take 5–7 years to produce marketable roots, and they are highly susceptible to damping-off, voles, and deer. Excellent drainage is critical; plant in raised woodland beds with 50% shade cloth or under deciduous trees on a north-facing slope. Consult a qualified herbalist before medicinal use of the root. Matures in 1825–2190 days from seed.

name: Asian Hazel (Siberian Hazelnut)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing the shrub to form its natural dense, multi-stemmed thicket. Asian hazel is native to Siberia, Korea, northern China, and Japan and is exceptionally cold hardy compared with the European hazelnut, tolerating harsh continental winters that would damage most commercial filbert cultivars. It produces small nuts in short, bristly husks and is widely used by breeders working to develop cold-hardy, blight-resistant hazelnut cultivars for the northern United States and Canada by crossing it with European hazelnut. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Asian Pear
description: Asian pears ripen on the tree — unlike European pears they do not need post-harvest ripening — so taste-test for sweetness before picking. Most varieties are self-unfruitful and yield best with a second Asian pear or even a compatible European variety nearby. Chill requirements are moderate (450–700 hours), making many selections suitable for zones 5–9. Annual thinning of fruit clusters to one per spur prevents limb breakage and encourages larger, better-flavored fruit. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Asian Persimmon
description: Asian persimmons come in astringent types (such as Hachiya, best eaten when jelly-soft) and non-astringent types (such as Fuyu, eaten firm like an apple). Most cultivars are self-fertile and produce well as single trees. Trees need very little pruning — maintain a central leader and remove inward-growing branches to open the canopy. In cooler parts of zone 7, choose hardier varieties and site against a south-facing wall; in zones 9–10, low-chill cultivars perform best. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Asian Tempest Garlic (Asiatic Hardneck)
description: Asian Tempest is an Asiatic-type hardneck garlic that came to American growers through an Oregon gardener who obtained it from South Korea, and it has since become known for its vigorous growth and heavy bulbil production on the scape. Cloves are fewer but plump, and the flavor starts mellow when cooked but turns notably sharp and intense when eaten raw. Grow it like other hardnecks, removing the curling scape in late spring to redirect energy into bulb size, and harvest once the lower leaves begin to brown. It stores only moderately well compared to Porcelain types, so plan to use it earlier in the season. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Askola Sea Buckthorn (High-Vitamin German Seaberry)
description: Askola was selected in former East Germany and is prized among small-scale growers for exceptionally high vitamin C and E content in its late-August-ripening orange fruit, along with some of the strongest, most vigorous shoot growth of any commonly grown sea buckthorn cultivar. That vigor means it benefits from an annual thinning cut to remove crowded interior wood and keep the thorny canopy manageable for hand or branch harvest. Like all sea buckthorn, its nitrogen-fixing root system tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils that would stunt most other fruiting shrubs, but it dislikes waterlogged ground. Being dioecious, it requires a male plant nearby to set any fruit at all. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Aspabroc Broccolini
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out sturdy transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. This hybrid combines the mild, sweet flavor of broccoli with tender, asparagus-like stems and matures quickly. After the first central shoots, plants keep producing slender side shoots for multiple harvests. Cut stems when buds are still tight and harvest often to encourage continued production; steam or stir-fry the whole tender stem. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Asparagus
description: Set one-year crowns in 8-in-deep trenches with roots spread over a ridge of compost, then gradually backfill as growth emerges. Do not harvest any spears in the first year and harvest lightly in year two to let the root system build strength. Beginning in year three, cut or snap spears at soil level when they are 6–8 in tall and before the tips begin to feather open. Stop harvesting after 4–6 weeks to allow ferns to grow and replenish the crown for the next season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Asparagus Pea (Winged Pea, Asparagus Vetch)
description: Sow 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; the asparagus pea is a Mediterranean annual legume with attractive brick-red flowers and uniquely four-winged seed pods. Pods must be harvested when they are tiny — no more than 1 inch long — because they become woody and inedible extremely quickly. At the correct size they have a mild flavor reminiscent of asparagus, delicious lightly steamed, stir-fried, or pickled. The plant fixes atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil for subsequent crops. It is low-growing and sprawling rather than climbing, often used as a flowering groundcover in cool-season borders in addition to its edible value. The deep red flowers attract pollinators. In mild-winter climates sow in fall and harvest through winter. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Asparagus Yard-Long Bean
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with sturdy trellis support; Asparagus Yard-Long Bean is a traditional variety of the Chinese long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis), producing impressively long (18–24 inch), slender, pale green to light-colored pods that hang in pairs from the vines, resembling bundles of very long, thin asparagus spears in their pendant arrangement. The flavor of Asparagus yard-long beans is distinctly different from common snap beans — denser, less watery, slightly nutty, with a pleasant asparagus-like quality that explains the variety name. The texture holds up well to stir-frying and high-heat cooking that would make common snap beans too soft, making yard-long beans the preferred bean for stir-fries, curries, and Asian vegetable preparations where snap beans would become unpleasantly mushy. As a heat-adapted legume related to black-eyed peas rather than to common beans (Phaseolus), yard-long beans genuinely thrive in zone 9's summer conditions — producing abundantly in temperatures that stop snap bean production — making them one of the most practical fresh-bean crops for the Gulf South summer garden. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Asparagus Yardlong Bean
description: This heat-loving Asian cowpea is a vigorous pole bean that produces slender pods up to a meter long, best picked young at 12-18 inches for tender eating. Direct-sow after the soil has thoroughly warmed to 70F or more, planting an inch deep at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis. The climbing vines thrive in hot, humid weather where common beans struggle and keep producing with regular harvest. Pick pods frequently while still smooth and firm to encourage continued set. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Aspen Pumpkin (F1 Semi-Bush Storage Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, spacing hills three to four feet apart to suit the semi-bush growth habit, which takes up markedly less room than sprawling field-pumpkin types. Aspen finishes quickly at around 95 days, producing large, solidly fleshed fruit with a rich orange rind, a thick stem, and handles that hold up well through harvest handling and shipping. Its dense flesh and sturdy rind translate into good post-harvest storage and shipping quality, useful for growers who need fruit to hold up in warm regional markets. Cut fruit with several inches of stem once fully colored and firm, cure in a warm, airy spot, then move to cool, dry storage. Matures in 90–95 days from seed.

name: Assam Indigo (Indigo Bush, Japanese Indigo Strobilanthes)
description: Plant in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Strobilanthes cusia performs best in dappled shade and will wilt or scorch in full afternoon sun in zone 9. Strobilanthes cusia (Assam Indigo or Indigo Strobilanthes) is a subtropical shrub native to the hill country of Assam (India) and southern China that has been cultivated for centuries as the primary source of natural indigo dye in Japan, where it is called 'Ryukyu-ai' and used to produce the distinctive deep blue of traditional Japanese katazome (paste-resist dyeing) and aizome (indigo dyeing). The leaves contain the indigo precursor indican, which when fermented produces indigotin — the same deep blue pigment as in Indigofera tinctoria (true indigo), though the two plants are from different families. In zone 8–10 Gulf Coast and Southeast gardens, Strobilanthes cusia is a striking shade plant: large, dark-green, quilted leaves form a bold textural mass in shaded beds, and in fall (September–December) the plant produces compact clusters of small, violet-blue, snapdragon-like flowers. An excellent shade shrub with historical textile craft significance. The leaves can be processed into a paste indigo vat for natural dyeing wool, silk, and cotton. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Assam Tea (Broad-Leaved Tropical Tea Variety)
description: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Assam tea is the large-leaved, tropical botanical variety of the tea plant, native to the hot, humid Assam region of northeastern India, and is the source of the malty, full-bodied character prized in classic Assam and many English breakfast-style black teas. Compared to the small-leaved China variety (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) more commonly grown in cooler climates, Assam tea grows faster, produces larger leaves, and tolerates heat and humidity better, but it is noticeably less cold-hardy, making it a better fit for the warm, humid Gulf South than for northern tea gardens. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once plants are three to four years old and well established; frequent light plucking encourages a dense, bushy, more productive shape. Provide consistent moisture, since tea plants are sensitive to drought stress, and mulch well to keep roots cool and the acidic soil moist. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Astia Zucchini (Compact French Container Zucchini)
description: Astia is a French-bred bush zucchini selected specifically for container growing and tight garden spaces, with silvery, deeply lobed foliage that makes the compact plant almost as ornamental as it is productive. Fruit sets close to the base of the plant, which keeps harvest easy even in a large pot on a patio, and the smooth, glossy green zucchini are best cut at about 5 inches for peak tenderness. Because it stays under 30 inches across, Astia suits Gulf Coast gardeners who want fresh zucchini without dedicating a full bed to a sprawling vine, and frequent picking keeps the early, prolific plants setting new fruit. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Astragalus (Huang Qi, Milkvetch Root)
description: Astragalus is a long-lived perennial legume grown for its pale, fibrous taproot, dried and sliced into the flat, tongue-depressor-shaped root known in traditional Chinese herbalism as huang qi, one of the most widely used tonic herbs in that tradition. The plant itself is an airy, pea-family perennial with ferny, pinnately compound leaves and small pale-yellow flowers in early summer, useful as a low-key border filler and pollinator plant as it slowly builds root mass over three or more growing seasons before harvest. It prefers lean, deep, well-drained soil and full sun and, like most deep-rooted legumes, is very drought-tolerant once established but does poorly in heavy, poorly drained clay. Roots are traditionally harvested in fall after the third or fourth year of growth, once they have reached pencil-to-finger thickness. Matures in 1095–1460 days from seed.

name: Astragalus (Huang Qi, Milkvetch)
description: Sow scarified seeds in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; astragalus (huang qi, huang qi root) is one of the most important medicinal plants in Chinese medicine — used for over 2,000 years as a primary tonic herb for immune system support, energy, and longevity. The dried, sliced root (huang qi) appears in countless traditional Chinese medicine formulas and is increasingly studied in Western medicine for its immunomodulatory, adaptogenic, and antioxidant properties, including possible effects on telomerase activation. The plant itself is an attractive legume producing pinnate leaves on erect stems and small, pale-yellow pea flowers in spring. The root (used medicinally) is harvested in year 3–4 and dried into the characteristic yellow sticks sold in Chinese herb shops. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen and tolerates poor, dry soils. Now increasingly grown as a medicinal garden plant in North America as interest in traditional Chinese herbs grows. Matures in 365–1095 days from seed.

name: Astro Arugula/Rocket
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil and thin for full plants or leave dense for baby greens ready in about a month. This variety has wider leaves and is slower to bolt than other arugulas, giving more leaf per harvest and a milder, peppery flavor. Keep soil moist and grow in part shade during warm spells to delay bolting. Cut outer leaves regularly, and succession sow for a steady supply through spring and fall. Matures in 21–38 days from seed.

name: Aswad Eggplant (Iraqi Black Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors with steady warmth and transplant into full sun after the soil has warmed, since this heirloom thrives in hot climates and resents cool, wet soil. Keep watering consistent to avoid stress that can toughen the skin. Aswad, whose name means "black" in Arabic, is an Iraqi heirloom prized for its small, round, near-black fruit and dense, creamy flesh that holds up well in stews and grilling. It is a favorite among growers seeking heat-tolerant regional varieties adapted to arid conditions. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Atago Asian Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Atago is a Japanese heirloom Asian pear prized for producing some of the largest fruit of any pear cultivar, commonly reaching a pound or more with light tan, lightly russeted skin and crisp, very juicy flesh. It is a late-season variety, ripening from late September into October, well after most other Asian pears have finished, and unlike some heat-loving Asian pear cultivars it develops good sweetness even where summers run cooler. Atago is not self-fruitful and needs cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar blooming at the same time to set a full crop. The upright, spreading tree is a vigorous, heavy producer, so thin young fruit to prevent limb breakage under the weight of a full crop. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ataulfo Mango (Honey Mango, Champagne Mango)
description: Selected in Chiapas, Mexico and now sold commercially as 'Honey' or 'Champagne' mango, Ataulfo produces small, kidney-shaped fruit that ripens to a deep golden yellow with an unusually thin, flattened seed that leaves far more edible flesh per fruit than firmer Florida cultivars like Haden or Kent. The flesh itself is soft, buttery, and virtually fiberless, with an intensely sweet, low-acid, almost custardy flavor and peach-like aroma once fully ripe. Trees are early-to-midseason bearers and stay noticeably more compact and manageable than large seedling-type mangoes, making Ataulfo a good dooryard choice where space is limited. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Atemoya
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 9–11; atemoya is a hybrid between the cherimoya (Annona cherimola) and the sugar apple (Annona squamosa), combining the better qualities of both parents — the large size and richly flavored flesh of cherimoya with the tropical heat tolerance of sugar apple. Atemoya is widely considered one of the finest-flavored fruits in the world, with a rich, creamy white flesh tasting of vanilla custard with notes of pineapple and coconut. It requires hand pollination in most US gardens — transfer pollen from flowers in the male stage to flowers in the female stage in the morning using a small brush. Plant grafted trees for faster fruiting (typically 2–3 years) rather than seedlings. Popular cultivars include 'Gefner' (nearly self-fruitful) and 'African Pride'. An outstanding subtropical fruit for South Florida and Gulf Coast gardens where winter temperatures stay above 28°F. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Athena Cantaloupe (Eastern US Commercial Standard, AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Hybrid Melon)
description: Direct sow in warm soil; thin to 2 plants per hill, 3–4 feet between hills. Harvest when skin shows cream-yellow color under netting and fruit is fragrant. Athena Cantaloupe is an F1 hybrid melon developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds for commercial production in the humid, warm conditions of the eastern United States — particularly the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast commercial melon-producing regions. Athena received All-America Selections recognition for its outstanding disease resistance, productivity, and flavor in eastern growing conditions, and became one of the dominant commercial cantaloupe varieties in the eastern US melon industry after its release. The eastern US commercial melon market has distinct requirements from California production: the combination of high summer humidity, heavy disease pressure (particularly powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria leaf blight), and earlier harvest requirements create conditions where California-bred varieties with limited disease resistance often underperform. Athena's development specifically addressed the eastern market's disease challenges, with strong powdery mildew resistance and tolerance to the other major eastern melon pathogens. The fruit quality is excellent for a hybrid: large, round melons with thick, deeply netted tan skin, firm orange flesh with good Brix (10–12 typical) and genuine cantaloupe flavor, and a shelf life after harvest of 10–14 days — significantly better than most heirloom types. For zone 9 Gulf Coast gardeners, Athena's disease resistance is particularly valuable: the Gulf South's combination of warm temperatures and high humidity creates ideal conditions for foliar diseases that terminate melon plantings before maximum fruit production. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Athens Blue Spires Rosemary (Extra Cold-Hardy Upright Georgia Gem Selection)
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Athens Blue Spires was selected at the University of Georgia Horticulture Department trial gardens in Athens as one of Allen Armitage's Georgia Gems, chosen for an upright, extensively self-branching habit, extremely narrow needle-like leaves, and light blue flowers produced heavily from winter into spring. It is among the most cold-hardy rosemary selections available, tolerating winter lows well below what damages standard culinary rosemary, which makes it a reliable choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of rosemary's range. Prune after the main flowering flush to maintain a dense, upright form, and avoid heavy or poorly drained soil, which threatens rosemary far more than cold does in most gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Athens Cantaloupe (University of Georgia Heat-Tolerant Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and fruit set, then reduce irrigation as fruits approach full size to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip (fruit pulls free from vine with light pressure). Athens is a cantaloupe variety developed by the University of Georgia (named for the city of Athens, Georgia, home of the university) specifically for performance in the hot, humid Southeast — a regional adaptation that addresses the specific challenges of cantaloupe production in the Gulf South and mid-Atlantic coastal plain where high humidity, heat, and disease pressure reduce quality and yield in the Western-adapted muskmelon types that dominate commercial production in California and Arizona. Athens produces medium-sized (4–5 lb), round, well-netted fruits with the orange flesh, small seed cavity, and aromatic sweetness that define quality cantaloupe; it has good disease resistance to Fusarium wilt and Alternaria leaf blight. The flavor is consistently excellent even under the humid, warm conditions that cause quality to drop in less-adapted varieties. Athens is the most commonly recommended cantaloupe for home gardens in the southeastern states, where the combination of heat tolerance, disease resistance, and consistent eating quality under Gulf South growing conditions makes it the appropriate regional choice over the Western-adapted varieties that dominate seed catalogs. Matures in 79–86 days from seed.

name: Atlantic Giant Pumpkin
description: Atlantic Giant is the classic record-breaking pumpkin, capable of producing fruits weighing hundreds of pounds under ideal care. Sow seed after all frost danger in deeply amended, compost-rich soil, giving each plant sprawling room of 10 feet or more. For the largest fruit, allow only one or two pumpkins per vine and remove the rest, then feed and water generously all season. Support the growing fruit on sand or a board to prevent rot, and protect the tender vines from any late frost. Matures in 115–130 days from seed.

name: Atlas Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Supermale Hybrid)
description: Atlas was among the earlier Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids released before the later Jersey series, bred by crossing selected male parents to eliminate female seed-bearing plants and the volunteer seedling weediness they cause in a bed. Because no energy is spent on berry and seed production, Atlas channels more resources into spear number and thickness than open-pollinated heirlooms, and it carries improved tolerance to Fusarium crown rot compared to older strains. Skip harvest entirely the first year and take only a light cutting the second spring, letting the ferny top growth run all summer to recharge the crown. Established beds can remain productive for well over a decade with an annual fall topdressing of compost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Atlas Pistachio / Terebinth
description: Cold-stratify seeds in damp sand in the refrigerator for four to six weeks before sowing in spring into deep pots to encourage taproot development before transplanting. Move seedlings to their permanent site while still young and small, choosing a spot in full sun with rocky, sandy, or otherwise fast-draining soil. Once established this tree is exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-lived, requiring no supplemental irrigation in Mediterranean or dry climates. Plant at least one male and one female tree to ensure fruit production, as this species is dioecious. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Atomic Red Carrot
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil free of rocks and compaction; Atomic Red is a red-exterior, red-interior carrot variety producing the color from lycopene — the same antioxidant carotenoid that makes tomatoes and watermelon red — rather than the beta-carotene that makes standard orange carrots orange. This makes Atomic Red carrots a rare lycopene-containing vegetable that is not a tomato, with research suggesting that lycopene from carrots has similar bioavailability to tomato lycopene. The flavor of Atomic Red is less sweet than orange carrots and has a slightly more complex, herbal quality — different from, not inferior to, standard orange. The intense red color makes Atomic Red striking in mixed-carrot salads and vegetable platters alongside yellow, white, purple, and orange carrots. Like all colored carrots, the unique color is the primary appeal for market gardeners and home cooks interested in visual diversity in vegetable cooking. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Atomic Red Carrot
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the bed evenly moist until the slow seedlings emerge. This imperator-type carrot grows 8 to 10 inches long with a brilliant deep-red exterior and orange core, and roasting or steaming intensifies the color contrast. Thin seedlings to 2 to 3 inches so roots size up well. Sow successive crops every three weeks for a continuous supply of these colorful, sweet, crisp carrots. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Atreano Fig
description: Atreano is a Portuguese fig notable for its pale yellow-green skin that stays light even when the fruit is fully ripe, which makes judging harvest timing by color alone unreliable; instead check for softening and a slight neck droop. The amber flesh is mild, honeyed, and low in seediness, making it a favorite for fresh eating among growers who find darker figs too intensely flavored. It is a vigorous, heavy-bearing tree well suited to warm Mediterranean-type and humid subtropical climates alike. Give it full sun, good drainage, and room to spread, since it can become a large, dense specimen if left unpruned. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Atria Pawpaw (Low-Seed Red Fern Farm Selection)
description: Atria is a pawpaw selection introduced by Red Fern Farm, the Iowa permaculture nursery known for its cold-climate fruit and nut selections. It bears large fruit with excellent flavor and a notably low seed count for the species, ripening mid-season. Like other pawpaws, Atria requires a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination to set a reliable crop. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Atropurpurea Oregon Grape (Purple Winter-Foliage Selection)
description: Grow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade, giving it enough open sky to color well without the scorching that full sun can cause on hot summer afternoons. Atropurpurea carries the same glossy, spiny-toothed, holly-like leaflets and dense clusters of fragrant yellow spring flowers as typical Oregon grape, but its foliage consistently deepens to a rich plum-purple through the cold months, a trait more pronounced and dependable on this selection than on unnamed seedlings. Dusty blue-black berries follow the flowers and are readily eaten by birds. It suckers gently to form a tidy colony useful for a shaded shrub border or woodland edge, and old or leggy canes can be cut to the ground periodically to keep the planting dense and renew winter color. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Attar of Roses Geranium (Classic Rose-Scented Pelargonium)
description: Root cuttings in lean, well-drained soil and grow in full sun to partial shade with light, infrequent watering, allowing soil to dry between waterings; overly rich soil or heavy shade will dull the fragrance. Pinch stems regularly to maintain a full, shrubby shape; the deeply cut, velvety grey-green leaves release an intense, sweet rose fragrance at the lightest touch, among the strongest of any rose-scented pelargonium, while small lavender-pink flowers appear in loose clusters but are secondary to the foliage's aromatic value. The leaves are used fresh or dried to flavor sugar, baked goods, jellies, and teas, or historically distilled for rose-scented oil. Bring indoors well before first frost as a houseplant, since it has no cold hardiness. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Attika Cherry (Early-Season Firm Dark Sweet Cherry)
description: Attika is a German-bred sweet cherry from the same breeding program that produced Regina, ripening in the early-to-midseason window at about the same time as Bing. Its large, near-black fruit is very firm with good crack tolerance, holding up well on the tree through occasional rain before harvest. It is self-unfruitful, so plant a compatible early-blooming pollinizer nearby for a reliable crop. Grow in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water evenly during fruit development, and prune each winter to maintain an open, productive canopy. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Au Amber Plum (Auburn University Amber-Skinned Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator within 50 feet. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches. Harvest when amber-yellow skin has fully developed and flesh gives slightly. Au Amber Plum is one of the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station's series of Japanese-American plum hybrids bearing the 'Au' prefix — a family of Gulf South-adapted plum varieties developed by crossing Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) with American plum (Prunus americana) to combine quality fruit with regional disease and humidity tolerance. The 'Amber' designation refers to the fruit's distinctive amber-yellow to golden skin, which sets it apart from the red and rose-colored Au-series varieties (Au Rosa, Au Rubrum) within the same breeding program and from the predominantly red-skinned Japanese plum varieties available in American nurseries. The amber-yellow coloring of the ripe fruit is unusual among commonly available plums — most market plums are red, purple, or dark-skinned — making Au Amber visually distinctive both in the garden and at market or farmers markets where consumers are accustomed to seeing darker plum colors. The flesh is yellow-amber, juicy, and sweet with mild plum flavor appropriate for fresh eating, jams, and jellies. The relatively high chilling requirement within the Au-series makes Au Amber better suited to zone 8 and the cooler parts of zone 9 than the lower-chill Au Rosa, providing a range of options across the Gulf South's varied climate zones. Auburn University developed the Au series specifically based on performance trials in Alabama, and the varieties' continued presence in extension service recommendations decades after their introduction reflects their practical suitability to the region. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: AU Buck IV Chestnut (Auburn University Annual-Bearing Chinese Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck IV is part of a numbered series (AU Buck I through V) of Chinese chestnut selections patented by Auburn University from open-pollinated seedlings of the AU-Cropper cultivar, chosen for blight resistance, precocious bearing, and dependable annual cropping rather than the alternate-bearing pattern common in seedling chestnut trees. It sets a medium to heavy crop of large nuts most years once established, and like other Auburn chestnut releases it is bred specifically to perform under the heat, humidity, and soilborne disease pressure of the Deep South. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar nearby, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful.
