Harvest nuts from the ground in September-October as the spiny burrs split open, and refrigerate cured nuts to sweeten the starches before eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: AU Gobbler I Chestnut (Auburn University Wildlife Food-Plot Chinese Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Gobbler I was the original release in Auburn University's Gobbler line of Chinese chestnut selections, bred under the same heat-, humidity-, and disease-pressure conditions of the Deep South as the university's other chestnut releases and later followed by the extended-drop AU Gobbler II. It was selected for dependable annual nut drop timed to coincide with fall wildlife food-plot season, making it a favorite of hunters and land managers as well as home orchardists who want a blight-resistant, low-input nut tree. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a good crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: AU Gobbler II Chinese Chestnut (Early Extended-Drop Auburn University Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Gobbler II, developed through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the Deep South, was selected for its early and unusually extended nut drop, beginning around the first week of September and continuing over four to five weeks, spreading the harvest window and the wildlife forage value well beyond that of single-flush cultivars, and complements the related earlier-released AU Gobbler I. Its smaller nuts (roughly 5.7 grams) are typical of trees bred with wildlife food-plot use in mind, though it is equally suited to home orchard planting for its reliable annual bearing and blight resistance. Space trees widely for their broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: AU Golden Dragon Kiwi (Auburn University Low-Chill Golden Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, training the vigorous vine onto a permanent overhead arbor or T-bar trellis from the start. AU Golden Dragon was an earlier golden-kiwi release from Auburn University's low-chill breeding program, predating and paving the way for the later AU Golden Sunshine selection, which ripens roughly three weeks after it; both were bred specifically to fruit reliably under the mild, low-chill winters of the Deep South rather than requiring the colder winters standard green-fleshed 'Hayward' kiwi needs. Fruit is smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic golden flesh and high sugar content, best harvested firm and ripened at room temperature. Because gold-fleshed Actinidia chinensis types are more prone to bacterial canker (Psa) than green-fleshed A. deliciosa, avoid overhead irrigation, prune annually to keep the canopy open, and disinfect pruning tools between plants. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: AU Golden Sunshine Kiwi
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training onto an overhead arbor or T-bar trellis strong enough to support a mature vine for decades. AU Golden Sunshine was patented by Auburn University from Chinese golden-kiwi breeding stock and selected specifically for its low winter-chill requirement and early fruit maturity, ripening about 20 days after fellow Auburn release AU Golden Dragon, making it far better suited to the mild winters of the Deep South than standard green-fleshed 'Hayward'. Fruit is cylindrical and smooth-skinned with sweet, non-acidic golden flesh, high soluble solids, and excellent flavor. Gold-fleshed kiwi types are generally more prone to bacterial canker (Psa) than green kiwi, so avoid overhead irrigation and prune to keep the canopy open for airflow. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Au Producer Plum (Auburn University High-Yielding Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Upper Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, since Prunus species decline quickly with wet feet. Au Producer was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station in 1977 as a high-yielding early-season plum, part of the Auburn 'Au' series of Japanese-American hybrids bred to combine the disease tolerance of native American plum with the fruit quality of Japanese plum for the humid Southeast. The clingstone fruit has purple skin and sweet, juicy red flesh good for fresh eating and canning, and the tree carries strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial leaf spot, and bacterial canker, diseases that trouble many plum varieties in Gulf South humidity. Because its moderate chill requirement is higher than the ultra-low-chill 'Gulf' series plums, Au Producer performs most reliably in zone 8 gardens and should be evaluated cautiously in the warmest parts of zone 9. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Au Rosa Plum (Auburn University Low-Chill Japanese-American Plum for Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters when marble-sized. Harvest when skin shows full rose color and fruit gives slightly. Au Rosa Plum is one of the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station's series of Japanese-American plum hybrids developed specifically for the Gulf South — an ongoing breeding program at Auburn that produced a family of plum varieties (the 'Au' prefix indicating Auburn University origin) adapted to the unique challenges of plum production in the humid southeastern coastal plain. The Au series hybrids combine genetics from Japanese plum (Prunus salicina, a high-quality fruiting species requiring adequate cross-pollination and moderate chill) with American plum (Prunus americana, a native North American species with significant humidity and disease tolerance) to produce varieties that retain good fruit quality while performing more reliably in the humid, relatively mild-winter conditions of the Gulf South than either parent species performs alone. Au Rosa produces medium-sized fruits with rose-pink to dark red skin and yellow flesh — the distinctive pinkish-red blush of the 'rosa' name. The flesh has good sweetness and plum flavor, appropriate for fresh eating, jams, and jellies. Au Rosa was one of the earlier Auburn releases and established the pattern of named, region-specific plum varieties that Gulf South extension services could recommend with confidence based on local trial performance rather than relying on variety data from California or Pacific Northwest conditions that may not translate to Gulf Coast performance. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: AU-Cherry Plum (Auburn Disease-Resistant Southern Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second plum cultivar nearby to boost fruit set even though AU-Cherry is largely self-fruitful. Released from Auburn University's fruit breeding program, AU-Cherry was selected specifically for the disease pressures of the humid Southeast, showing strong resistance to bacterial leaf spot and plum leaf scald that limit many older plum cultivars in the region. The small, dark red, cherry-like fruit ripens about two weeks after Methley with a sweet, juicy flavor good for fresh eating. Trees are noted for staying vigorous and productive for many years, making AU-Cherry a dependable long-term choice for Southern home orchards. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: AU-Cropper Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper is a Chinese chestnut selection released through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program, developed specifically for reliable, precocious production under the heat, humidity, and disease pressure typical of Alabama and the broader Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting rather than the decade or more required by seedling trees. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in September–October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy and to maintain the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid Southern summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: AU-Homeside Plum (Disease-Resistant Auburn University Gulf South Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and plant a second, compatible plum cultivar nearby for pollination and reliable fruit set. AU-Homeside, part of Auburn University's plum breeding program alongside AU-Rosa, AU-Amber, AU-Producer, and AU-Cherry, was developed specifically for strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial canker, and leaf scald, the trio of fungal and bacterial diseases that most limit plum production under the humid, disease-favoring conditions of the Deep South. It bears a solid mid-summer crop of flavorful fruit on a tree that requires substantially less fungicide input than susceptible standard plum cultivars to stay productive and healthy. As with the rest of the AU series, it is well matched to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure, making it a lower-maintenance choice for home orchards in the region. Prune to an open center for good air circulation, which further reduces disease pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: AU-Homestead Chestnut (Auburn University Southeastern Chinese Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead is a Chinese chestnut cultivar developed through Auburn University's chestnut improvement program as a companion release to AU-Cropper, selected for good nut quality and disease tolerance under the heat, humidity, and soil conditions typical of Alabama and the wider Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it inherits strong resistance to chestnut blight, the introduced fungal disease that historically devastated American chestnut, and begins cropping within a few years of planting on a grafted tree. Space trees widely to accommodate the broad, spreading mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut, and interplant with a second, unrelated named cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts require cross-pollination for a full nut set. Harvest nuts from the ground in September–October as burrs split and drop, and store cured nuts refrigerated for the sweetest flavor, since chestnut starches convert to sugar during cold storage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: AU-Leader Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU-Leader is a Chinese chestnut selection from Auburn University's chestnut improvement program, drawn from the same precocious, blight-resistant seedling population that also produced AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead, and was chosen for a strongly upright, single-leader growth habit that makes it easier to train and maintain than the sprawling form typical of many chestnut selections. Like its sibling releases it inherits good resistance to chestnut blight and begins bearing at a young age on a grafted tree. Nuts run large for a Chinese chestnut, averaging roughly a dozen grams each, and mature and drop free of the split burr in early-to-mid September, ahead of many other Southern-adapted cultivars. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy, and interplant with a second unrelated chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: AU-Roadside Plum (Auburn University Dark Red Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Gulf South)
aliases: Prunus salicina x Prunus americana 'Au Roadside'
description: AU-Roadside was developed by the Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station at Auburn University from a cross of 'Ozark Premier' and 'Methley,' combining the fruit size of the former with the reliable Gulf South adaptation of the latter, and it outperforms Ozark Premier itself in Southern growing conditions. Fruit is large and round with striking red skin and juicy amber-yellow flesh; while capable of some self-fruitfulness, yields improve substantially with a second Japanese or Japanese-American plum planted nearby for cross-pollination. The cultivar was bred for strong resistance to bacterial canker, bacterial leaf and fruit spot, and plum leaf scald, traits that made it a favored choice for home and roadside-stand plantings across Alabama and neighboring Gulf Coast states. It ripens early in the season, extending the harvest window for home orchards that also grow later Au-series plums. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: AU-Rubrum Plum (Auburn University Early-Season Dark Red Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Gulf South)
aliases: Prunus salicina x Prunus americana 'Au Rubrum'
description: AU-Rubrum was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station as an early-ripening selection within its Japanese-American 'Au' plum breeding line, arising as a sport of the earlier Auburn release 'Crimson.' Trees are self-fruitful but set noticeably heavier crops when a second Japanese or Japanese-American plum such as Methley or another Au-series variety is planted within pollinating range. Fruit ripens mid-to-late June, well ahead of most Japanese plums, and is notably large with very dark red skin and sweet red flesh suited to fresh eating, canning, and preserves. Like the rest of the Au series, it was bred specifically for resistance to bacterial canker, bacterial leaf spot, and black knot, giving it an edge over older plum varieties under humid Southeastern growing conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Aunt Ada's Italian Bean
description: Sow seed an inch deep and provide a tall pole or trellis, since this vigorous climber produces over a long season. Aunt Ada's Italian is a family heirloom pole bean brought from Italy to Colorado around the turn of the twentieth century, prized for its dual usefulness: the flat, tender pods make excellent snap beans when picked young, while pods left to mature and dry yield a flavorful soup bean. Its productivity and reliability across a long harvest window made it a treasured keeper variety passed down within one family for generations before wider seed-saver distribution. Pick regularly for fresh eating to keep vines producing, or let the last flush dry fully on the vine for winter storage beans. Matures in 55–85 days from seed.

name: Aunt Gertie's Gold Tomato
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost has passed and provide staking or caging for the tall, indeterminate vines. Aunt Gertie's Gold is a Virginia heirloom reportedly traced to a Virginia woman named Aunt Gertie; it produces very large, golden-orange, oblate to slightly irregular fruits that can weigh 1–2 pounds, with sweet, rich, complex flavor that is noticeably lower in acid than red tomatoes — making it a preferred choice for people who find red tomatoes too acidic. The color is beautiful ranging from deep gold to orange-gold, and the fruits are meaty with dense flesh and few seeds. An outstanding fresh-eating tomato; the low-acid flesh is also excellent for sauces and drying. Grow as a standard indeterminate in full sun with consistent moisture and fertility. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Aunt Hettie's Red Okra (Tennessee Heirloom)
description: Soak seeds overnight before direct sowing 1 inch deep after the last frost, thinning plants to 12-18 inches apart. Aunt Hettie's Red traces back to a Tennessee home garden, where it was kept true for generations before seed-saving groups began sharing it more widely, and it is now grown as far south as the Gulf Coast. Compared with taller red heirlooms, its plants stay a manageable 4-5 feet with deep red stems and leaf veins, setting plump, meaty burgundy pods that should be cut before they exceed 4 inches to keep them tender. In blind tasting panels among dozens of okra varieties it has repeatedly placed among the most flavorful reds, making it worth growing for the table as much as for its ornamental color. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Aunt Mary's Sweet Corn (Ohio Heirloom White Corn)
description: Stewarded by an Ohio farm family since before 1850, this open-pollinated white corn was once marketed as one of the finest white sweet corns available. Stalks reach 6-8 feet and typically carry one to two ears with eight to twelve rows of large, deep kernels that turn rich and creamy when cooked, with sweetness varying somewhat ear to ear. Because it needs a full season to fill out, give it consistent moisture and nitrogen through tasseling, and plant in blocks rather than single rows for full ears. Its Midwestern farmhouse pedigree makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow and save a genuinely old regional corn. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Aunt Molly's Ground Cherry (Polish Heirloom Sweet Pineapple-Vanilla Husk Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest when the papery husk has browned and dried; ripe fruits drop to the ground. Aunt Molly's Ground Cherry is a Polish heirloom Physalis pruinosa — a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) in the same genus as cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana) but distinct in plant size (Physalis pruinosa is smaller and more compact than the large cape gooseberry) and fruit flavor profile. According to Seed Savers Exchange lore, the variety was brought from Poland by a gardener known as 'Aunt Molly' and preserved in American seed-saving collections, where it has been distributed and maintained as one of the finest flavored ground cherry varieties available. The fruits are small (0.5–0.75 inch), round, yellow-orange when ripe, enclosed in a papery tan husk (the inflated calyx) that the plant uses to enclose and protect the developing fruit. The flavor is the defining characteristic of Aunt Molly's and the reason it consistently receives the highest flavor ratings among ground cherry varieties in trial evaluations: a complex, intensely sweet flavor with distinct notes of pineapple, vanilla, and tropical fruit, sometimes described as tasting like a sweet tomato crossed with a pineapple. This flavor is more complex and concentrated than most Physalis pruinosa types. In zone 9, ground cherries thrive in the warm climate, producing prodigiously through summer and fall; established plants may behave almost as short-lived perennials in the mildest zone 9 locations, and self-seeding creates a supply of volunteer plants in subsequent seasons. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Aunt Ruby's German Green Tomato
description: Aunt Ruby's German Green is an indeterminate heirloom beefsteak that ripens to a green-and-amber blush and offers a sweet, slightly spicy, well-balanced flavor. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once the weather is settled and warm. Cage or stake the tall vines and prune suckers for airflow, since the large fruits can reach a pound each. Judge ripeness by a slight softening and yellow-green color rather than by red, harvesting before the fruit becomes overly soft. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Aunt Ruby's German Green Tomato (Large Sweet Green-When-Ripe Heirloom)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aunt Ruby's German Green is one of the most famous and beloved green-when-ripe heirloom tomatoes — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped beefsteak type that retains a bright, chartreuse-green to apple-green exterior color even at full ripeness, producing green flesh with amber-yellow internal marbling that makes it unique among ripe tomatoes. The flavor is exceptional: sweet, rich, spicy, and complex with a distinctive quality often described as 'herbal' or 'spicy-sweet' — quite different from the fruity sweetness of yellow types or the savory depth of purple/dark varieties. This variety is named for Ruby Arnold of Greeneville, Tennessee, who saved the seed from German origins and preserved it for decades. The green color at full ripeness challenges harvest timing: rather than using color change as a ripeness indicator, judge by gentle pressure (ripe fruits yield slightly, like a ripe peach), by the subtle yellowing of the blossom-end shoulder, and by cutting a sample fruit to check for amber-green flesh and developed seeds. Aunt Ruby's German Green is outstanding in fresh preparations where the unusual green color and spicy-sweet flavor create memorable flavor combinations with standard red and yellow tomatoes. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Aurea Golden-Leaved Cornelian Cherry (Yellow-Foliage Cornus mas Selection)
description: Aurea is an older golden-leaved sport of cornelian cherry, opening chartreuse-yellow new growth each spring that softens toward yellow-green as summer heat advances, giving the shrub a bright, sunlit presence long after its late-winter yellow flower display has faded. It sets the species' typical tart, cherry-like red drupes when a compatible pollinator is nearby, and shares the same excellent cold hardiness, drought tolerance once established, and adaptability to a wide range of soils and urban sites. Foliage color is strongest with morning sun and some afternoon relief in warmer zones; deep shade will cause the leaves to revert toward plain green. Use it as a season-long color accent or informal screen where a golden-foliage large shrub is wanted. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Aureomarginata Elderberry (Gold-Margined Black Elderberry)
description: Aureomarginata is a long-cultivated heirloom elder valued for its crisp green leaves edged in bright gold, giving a brighter, more finely detailed look than solid golden-leaved forms. Flat clusters of creamy white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small black berries, though the shrub is grown primarily for season-long foliage interest rather than fruit. Provide partial shade or morning sun with afternoon protection in hot climates to keep the gold margins from bleaching or scorching, and cut back older stems in late winter to encourage fresh, well-marked new growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aureum Crispum Oregano (Curly Golden Culinary Oregano)
description: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; strong light keeps the foliage a bright gold rather than fading toward green. Aureum Crispum is a low, mat-forming golden oregano distinguished from the smooth-leaved Golden Oregano by its tightly crinkled, crimped leaf texture, giving the mound a ruffled, almost mossy appearance. The leaves carry a milder oregano flavor than green culinary types but are still usable fresh in small amounts. Shear back after flowering to renew the compact habit and refresh leaf color for the following season. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Auroch Spinach (Upright Smooth-Leaf Hybrid)
description: Direct sow into cool, fertile soil and keep consistently moist; Auroch produces large, oval, smooth, dark green leaves on an upright plant with long, sturdy stems, a habit that resists leaf damage and soil-splash from heavy rain better than more sprawling spinach types. It can be picked at any stage from baby leaf through full bunching size, giving flexibility for both quick salad greens and larger cooking leaves, and it shows strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races. It performs best as a fall, winter, or early spring crop and tolerates moderate winter cold with light protection. Cut whole plants at the base or harvest outer leaves individually to extend the picking window. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Aurora Blueberry (Very Late Season Northern Highbush Blueberry, Season-Extender Blueberry)
description: Plant in very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; maintain pH 4.5–5.2 with acid fertilizer; mulch with pine bark; Aurora ripens very late (late August through September) producing large, firm, light blue berries with outstanding flavor — considered by MSU researchers to have among the best flavor of any northern highbush variety; plant early-season varieties (Duke, Bluecrop) alongside for cross-pollination and a full-season harvest. Aurora blueberry is a Michigan State University-released variety (2003) that has become highly regarded among serious home blueberry growers and specialty producers for its combination of very late ripening season and exceptional berry quality. The variety was specifically developed as part of MSU's late-season breeding program aimed at extending the Michigan commercial blueberry season into September, reducing market glut during the peak July–August production and commanding higher prices for September-ripening fruit. Aurora ripens the latest of any major highbush blueberry variety — typically 4–6 weeks after early-season varieties like Duke and 2–3 weeks after Jersey (itself a late variety), making September fresh blueberries possible in zones 4–6 where frost would otherwise end the season. The berries are large to very large, firm (excellent handling and shelf life for a highbush variety), and have a notably good flavor — sweet, aromatic, and complex — that is consistently rated among the best of all highbush varieties in blind flavor tastings. The very firm texture also makes Aurora berries excellent for fresh eating (they snap satisfyingly rather than bursting), baking, and freezing. An excellent choice for home orchardists wanting to extend fresh blueberry season as late as possible into autumn. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aurora Honeyberry (Late-Season University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Aurora is self-infertile. Aurora was released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the leading haskap breeding program in North America, and is valued for its large, elongated berries with a sweet, well-balanced flavor closer to blueberry than the tart, sometimes bitter flavor of earlier haskap introductions. It blooms and ripens later than earlier-generation cultivars like 'Borealis', which helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, and the fruit holds on the bush longer without dropping, extending the harvest window. Like other haskaps, Aurora is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F and flowers that survive down to about -8F, but it is poorly suited to hot, humid climates and performs best in short-season, cold-winter regions. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Aurore Grape (Early-Ripening French-American White Wine Grape)
description: One of the earliest-ripening French-American hybrids, Aurore was for decades a workhorse variety in eastern American vineyards, valued for its reliable heavy crops of pale golden-green berries used in light, fruity white wines. Its early ripening lets it succeed in regions with shorter frost-free seasons where later-maturing grapes struggle to fully develop. The vine is vigorous and productive, so cluster thinning helps concentrate flavor and prevent overcropping from weakening the plant. It tolerates cold winters well and is best trained to a cane-pruned system. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Austin Blueberry
description: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Austin is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected as an early-to-midseason ripening variety that fills the harvest window alongside Climax, extending the picking season before the midseason varieties come on. Berries are medium-large, light blue, and firm with good flavor, borne on vigorous, upright, productive bushes that establish quickly. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Austin is not self-fruitful and should be planted with at least one other compatible variety within about 50 feet for cross-pollination and full crops. Remove flower buds the first year or two after planting to direct the plant's energy into root and cane development rather than fruit; full production typically begins by year four. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and irrigate consistently during fruit swell, since rabbiteye blueberries have shallow, fibrous roots that dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Austin Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Austin is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens just after Climax in the early part of the season, producing medium-to-large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It extends the early harvest window when planted alongside Climax and Premier, and its dependable, heavy cropping habit combined with good disease tolerance has made it a standard early-season choice for Gulf South home orchards and u-pick plantings. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Australe Butterhead Lettuce
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. This easy variety forms bright green leaves dusted with iridescent bronze tips and combines the buttery texture of a butterhead with the upright habit of a mini romaine. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head once it fills out. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Australian Blood Lime (Red-Fleshed Finger Lime-Mandarin Hybrid)
aliases: Citrus australasica x Citrus reticulata 'Australian Blood Lime'
description: This Australian hybrid crosses the red finger lime with an Ellendale mandarin to produce egg-shaped, burgundy-skinned fruit filled with tangy, ruby-red vesicles resembling citrus caviar. It bears a resemblance to finger lime in leaf and habit but flowers and fruits on a somewhat sturdier framework. Fruit ripens in winter and is prized by chefs for garnishing seafood and cocktails or for pressing into a striking pink-red juice. Give it full sun, well-drained soil, and frost protection, since it is hardy only to around 25-30F and best suited to warm, essentially frost-free gardens or a container that can be moved under cover. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Australian Brown Onion (Heirloom Storage Onion)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant hardened-off seedlings into loose, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, spacing plants to give bulbs room to expand. Water consistently during bulb development, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and fall, curing bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storage. Australian Brown is an old open-pollinated storage onion prized for its exceptionally firm, small-to-medium copper-brown bulbs and pungent flavor that mellows in cooking, and it has a long-standing reputation among heirloom growers for keeping longer in storage than many modern hybrids. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Australian Butter Squash
description: Australian Butter is an uncommon heirloom maxima squash producing large, pale peach-orange fruit with a hard rind and dry, deep-orange flesh that bakes up dense and sweet. It needs a long, warm season and generous spacing since a single vine can cover significant ground while setting several 15-pound fruits. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to die back, then cure in a warm, airy location for one to two weeks before storing. It appeals to gardeners hunting for lesser-known maxima types with outstanding dessert-quality flesh and long winter storage life. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Australian Desert Lime
description: Native to the semi-arid interior of Australia, this small-fruited citrus relative is among the most cold-hardy true citrus species available, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established, which makes it a worthwhile dooryard planting for zone 9a gardeners where standard limes struggle. The pea-to-marble-sized round fruits have a tart, intensely aromatic lime flavor and are used in marmalades, cordials, and as a lime substitute; the species is also valued by citrus breeders as rootstock and hybrid parent material for cold tolerance. Give it excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, since it is adapted to low-rainfall conditions and resents wet feet more than most citrus. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Australian Finger Lime
description: The Australian finger lime bears elongated fruit packed with juicy, caviar-like vesicles that burst with tart citrus flavor, making it a chef's favorite. Native to rugged coastal Australia, this compact, thorny citrus is tough and adapts well to container culture. Grow from a potted tree in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and protect it from frost by moving it indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season and water steadily without letting roots sit wet. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Australian Native Ginger (Rainforest Ginger)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; Australian Native Ginger is endemic to the coastal and sub-coastal rainforests of eastern Australia, ranging from the Gosford district of New South Wales north through Queensland to Cape York and the Torres Strait islands. It forms tall, arching, cane-like clumps under the rainforest canopy, with broad, glossy, alternately arranged leaves reaching well over a foot long. Unlike most gingers grown for the rhizome, the traditional bush-food harvest here is the tender white flesh at the base of the young stems, which has a mild ginger flavor, along with the bright blue, globose fruits that ripen through much of the year and were traditionally eaten fresh by Aboriginal Australians. As a true rainforest understory plant it is intolerant of dry soil, strong sun, or frost, and performs best in a consistently moist, sheltered, shaded position in zones 9b-11 or as a container specimen brought under cover in winter elsewhere. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Australian Rosemary (Coastal Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Australian rosemary is a coastal Australian native shrub from the mint family that closely resembles culinary rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis) in appearance — with narrow, whorled, needle-like leaves, a similar upright to spreading habit, and small tubular flowers — but is not used as a culinary herb and is generally more drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable than true rosemary. The flowers are white to pale lavender, produced nearly continuously through the year in mild coastal climates, providing a steady nectar source. It is one of the most reliable evergreen flowering shrubs for hot, dry, coastal zones 8–11, tolerating conditions of salt spray, poor soil, and extended drought that defeat most ornamentals. Widely planted in California coastal landscaping as a rosemary substitute where salt exposure makes true rosemary struggle. The cultivar 'Wynyabbie Gem' has more consistent lavender-mauve flowers; 'Morning Light' has cream-variegated foliage. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Australian Round Lime (Dooja, Native Round Lime)
description: Known to Aboriginal Australians as dooja, this rainforest-margin native from subtropical Queensland is the largest of the wild Australian citrus, forming a substantial shrub or small tree with glossy dark-green leaves and pinkish-white spring flowers. Its knobbly-skinned, spherical fruit ripens greenish-yellow from early to mid-winter and carries a thick, edible, aromatic peel traditionally candied or ground into a spicy paste similar to kaffir lime zest. It tolerates light frost and drought once established but grows best with full sun, rich well-drained soil, and regular water through the warmer months. Because of its eventual size it makes a better large hedge, screen, or open-ground specimen than a container plant, though young trees can be kept compact for some years in a large pot. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Australian Yellowleaf Lettuce
description: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up for extended cut-and-come-again production. An Australian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tall, crinkled, chartreuse-yellow leaves and notable heat tolerance, it is a reliable performer where many lettuces bolt or turn bitter in warm weather. It has been preserved largely through heirloom seed exchanges as a distinct warm-climate alternative to common green and red leaf types. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Austrian Crescent Potato (Nutty Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom Fingerling)
description: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Austrian Crescent is a classic heirloom fingerling potato with tan-gold skin and yellow, waxy flesh, prized for its rich, buttery, nutty flavor that many consider among the best-tasting of the fingerling types. Tubers grow in a distinctive curved, crescent shape, and the plant is a reliable, moderately high-yielding producer. As with other fingerlings, the low-starch, waxy texture holds its shape well through boiling, roasting, and potato salad preparations rather than becoming mealy or falling apart. Because it is a later-maturing variety, allow it a longer season than early potatoes; harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait for full maturity and vine dieback for larger tubers with better storage life. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Autumn Beauty Jujube (Qiyuexian, Early-Ripening Crisp Fresh-Eating Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established. Autumn Beauty, also sold as Qiyuexian, needs only about 400 chill hours and stays compact at 8 to 10 feet tall, with attractive zigzag branching and glossy foliage that turns yellow in fall. The apple-crisp, subtly spicy fruit is prized for fresh eating when harvested at the crunchy green-to-tan stage, ripening earlier than many other Chinese jujube selections. Its low chill requirement and tolerance for hot, humid summers make it a good complement to Gulf Coast-adapted jujube selections like Li and Sherwood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Bliss Raspberry
description: Plant dormant canes in full sun in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, and cut all canes to the ground in late winter since fruit forms on the current season's growth. Bred at East Malling Research in England, Autumn Bliss was one of the first widely planted primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry cultivars and remains valued for ripening its crop earlier in the season than most other fall types, which is a real advantage in shorter-season gardens. The medium-to-large, dark red, conical berries have good flavor and hold reasonably well after picking, and the compact, sturdy canes often need little or no trellising. It can be more susceptible to certain cane diseases than newer primocane releases, so good air circulation and sanitation help keep it productive. Matures in 110–140 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry (Brilliant Fall Color Multi-Season Native Tree)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Autumn Brilliance is one of the most widely planted serviceberry cultivars for its exceptional multi-season interest: clouds of white flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge, sweet, blueberry-like edible fruit in early summer that birds also relish, and some of the most reliable, brilliant orange-red fall foliage color of any small flowering tree. It works well as a single or multi-trunked small specimen tree, a large shrub border, or a naturalized planting, and tolerates a range of soil conditions with minimal care once established. The berries can be harvested for fresh eating, baking, and preserves if picked before birds strip the tree, or left entirely for wildlife. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Crown Squash
description: Autumn Crown is a modern interspecific F1 hybrid bred by crossing a Crown Prince-type maxima with a butternut moschata to combine butternut's sweet, dense flesh with earlier ripening and better cool-weather set. Its more compact vines and shorter days to maturity make it a good option for gardeners in cooler or shorter-season regions where standard butternuts often fail to fully ripen. Fruit develops a classic buff-tan skin and a small seed cavity, giving high usable flesh yield per squash. Grow it as you would any butternut, but expect a slightly earlier harvest window and more reliable ripening under marginal heat conditions. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Autumn Giant Leek
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; sow 1/4 inch deep in trays at 65–70°F; transplant when seedlings are pencil-thick, 6–8 inches tall, in late spring. Autumn Giant (sometimes listed as 'Autumn Giant Carentan' in older European catalogs) is a traditional European heirloom leek developed specifically for the production of very large, thick-shafted leeks harvested in autumn — it consistently produces some of the most substantial, heavy-yielding individual leek plants of any variety, with shanks that can exceed 2–3 inches in diameter and 8–10 inches of usable white shank. The name refers to both the size (genuinely giant compared to most leek varieties) and the harvest timing: Autumn Giant is best harvested from September through December, before the coldest winter weather arrives, as it does not have the extreme winter hardiness of specifically bred winter leeks like Bleu de Solaise or Musselburgh. Plant deeply in a trench or use a dibble to create 6-inch planting holes to encourage long, blanched shanks; the rich, mild, sweet flavor is excellent for any leek preparation. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Glo Apricot (Very Low-Chill Late-Ripening Apricot)
description: Autumn Glo is a Zaiger Genetics apricot bred specifically for mild-winter regions, combining a very low chill requirement with an unusually late ripening window that stretches the apricot season well past the early-summer finish of most low-chill types. Fruit is medium-sized with attractive orange-blushed skin and sweet, aromatic flesh. The tree is self-fruitful and does not need a separate pollinator. Because it still blooms earlier than most other fruit trees even with its later harvest, site it away from frost pockets, and thin fruit if it sets heavily to keep fruit size and quality up. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Glory Apple (Caramel-Flavored Very Late Keeper Apple)
description: Autumn Glory was discovered and developed by Broetje Orchards in Washington State and is notable for a distinctive caramel and cinnamon-spice flavor unlike most dessert apples, layered over a sweet, dense, crisp bite. It is one of the last apples to ripen each season, typically harvested in late October, and its firm flesh keeps in cold storage for many months without losing quality. The tree bears reliably once established and colors to a deep red over most of the fruit surface. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Gold Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Early-Turning Orange Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; fertilize generously and maintain consistent moisture. Autumn Gold is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning pumpkin that earned recognition for addressing one of the most practically important challenges in pumpkin production: the timing gap between Halloween (when orange pumpkins are in peak demand) and most pumpkin varieties' natural maturity schedule. Standard pumpkin varieties like Connecticut Field and Jack-O-Lantern reach their mature orange color in late September to October — sometimes too close to Halloween to allow adequate display time and recovery from any early-season shortfalls. Autumn Gold was bred to turn orange earlier than standard varieties while still maintaining an acceptable carving-type form, giving growers 2–3 extra weeks of salable orange pumpkins in the critical mid-September to early October market window. The fruits are medium-large (10–15 lbs), round to slightly flat, with bright orange skin and a good handle-stem; the flesh is moderately thick and adequate for cooking in addition to decorative use. Autumn Gold's earlier orange color development is driven by genetics that accelerate chlorophyll breakdown in the skin — the fruits reach full orange color when they are still in the immature stage compared to standard varieties. A consistently valuable variety for pumpkin patch operators and farm stand growers who want to extend the salable orange pumpkin window into early fall. Matures in 88–95 days from seed.

name: Autumn King Carrot (Berlikum-Type Large Storage Carrot)
description: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in very deep, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; thin to 3–4 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches. Autumn King (also sold as 'Autumn King 2') is a Berlikum/Flakkee-type heirloom carrot that represents the large-rooted tradition of European storage carrot breeding — producing very large, long (10–12 inch), broad-shouldered, tapered roots with dark orange skin and rich orange flesh that are built for cold storage and extended winter use. The Berlikum/Flakkee type was developed in the Netherlands for large-scale commercial storage carrot production and is characterized by the widest shoulders and largest root volume of any carrot type, with correspondingly excellent storage characteristics: properly cured Autumn King roots keep 4–6 months in cold storage (32–38°F, high humidity) without significant quality loss. The flavor is rich, sweet, and distinctly carrot-forward — more concentrated and traditional in character than some modern sweet hybrids, with a satisfying density and substance that makes these carrots outstanding for soups, stews, roasting, and winter cooking generally. Autumn King is the standard large storage carrot in British gardens (where it has been grown since the 1950s) and is valued throughout northern Europe for its combination of large yield per plant, excellent storage, and authentic robust carrot flavor. An excellent choice for home gardeners who want to store carrots through winter. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Autumn Magic Aronia (Compact Ornamental Black Chokeberry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Magic is a compact black chokeberry cultivar selected primarily for landscape use, staying notably smaller and more rounded than seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa while still producing a good crop of glossy black, antioxidant-rich berries. The shrub is a genuine multi-season landscape plant: clusters of white flowers in spring, clean dark green summer foliage, and some of the most vivid red-purple fall color of any Aronia selection, making it a strong choice for a foundation planting or mixed border that also happens to produce useful fruit. Berries are highly astringent eaten raw and are best processed into juice, syrup, or dried additions to baked goods and trail mixes. The self-fertile, adaptable shrub tolerates wet or dry soils and both full sun and considerable shade, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems to stay dense and well-shaped. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Mammoth Leek (Giant of Elbeuf Heirloom)
description: Also known historically as the Giant of Elbeuf, this Normandy heirloom is grown for its exceptionally thick, short shanks rather than height, with broad light-green fans of foliage instead of the blue-tinted leaves typical of winter types. Start seed early indoors since this is one of the longest-season leeks available, then transplant into deep holes or trenches and hill soil progressively around the stems as they thicken to maximize blanched length. It tolerates hard frost and can remain in the ground into early winter without losing quality. The mild, completely fiber-free white flesh is especially prized for braising and gratins. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Olive
description: Autumn olive is a nitrogen-fixing Asian shrub with extremely high yields of small red-speckled berries that are rich in lycopene and have a sweet-tart flavor; it is among the most productive fruiting shrubs per acre in temperate climates. However, it is considered an invasive species across much of the eastern U.S. and is prohibited or discouraged in many states — verify legal status in your jurisdiction before planting. Named fruit-producing selections such as 'Garnet' or 'Red Wing' are more compact and productive than seedlings. Harvest by hand-stripping clusters in fall when berries are fully red; fruit quality improves after light frost. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Royal Grape
description: Bred by USDA researcher David Ramming and released in 1996, Autumn Royal produces very large, elongated, jet-black seedless berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large clusters that ripen quite late in the season. It extends the black seedless grape harvest well into fall, after most other black varieties have finished. Vines are vigorous and heavy-bearing, benefiting from cluster thinning and a strong permanent cordon system to support the oversized bunches. A long, warm growing season is needed to fully ripen this late-hanging variety. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Autumn Wings Gourd (Winged Ornamental Gourd)
description: This heirloom ornamental gourd produces small to medium fruit ringed by five or six pronounced double fins or 'wings' running from a bulbous base to a slender curved or straight neck, in cream, yellow, and green tones with occasional warting. Grow on a trellis or arbor to let the necks hang straight and the wings develop evenly, watering consistently until the vines set fruit and then tapering off as the shells begin to harden. Leave fruit on the vine until the stem browns and dries, then cure gourds in a warm, airy space for several weeks until the shell is rock-hard and lightweight. Handle cured gourds gently, since the delicate wing ridges can chip or break if bumped. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: AV2 Tea (Darjeeling Muscatel Clone)
description: Selected as a clonal cultivar for the Darjeeling tea gardens of West Bengal, India, AV2 has become one of the most sought-after cultivars in the region for its ability to produce a pronounced 'muscatel' character, a distinctive grape-like, wine-like aroma most famous in premium second-flush Darjeeling black tea. It is a China-type, small-leaved selection that adapts well to the steep, cool, high-elevation slopes typical of Darjeeling estates, though it can also perform respectably at somewhat lower elevations. Plant it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and expect a more delicate, slower-establishing plant than robust Assam-type cultivars. Careful withering and oxidation during processing are essential to bring out its signature aromatic profile. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Avalanche Beet (AAS-Winning Pure-White Non-Bleeding Beet)
description: Direct sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have their first true leaves. Avalanche is an AAS-winning beet with pure-white roots and a sweet, clean flavor without the earthy or bitter aftertaste that some gardeners and children dislike in standard red beets. Because it produces no red pigment, it does not stain hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients when cooked or pickled — a genuine kitchen convenience, particularly useful for gardeners who want to combine beets with other vegetables without turning everything pink. The greens are tender and edible as well, cooked the same way as other beet tops. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly sized roots, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture; oversized roots can become woody. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Avalon Pecan (Modern UGA Scab-Resistant Large-Nut Pecan, Type II)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible Type I pollinator nearby for a good nut set. Avalon is a modern cultivar released by the University of Georgia pecan breeding program in Tifton, carrying the scab-resistant Gloria Grande in its parentage, and it combines large, high-quality nuts with disease resistance that university scab trials have found superior to most other cultivars of similar size — a rare pairing, since many large-nut pecans are scab-prone. Nuts run 46-54 per pound with a strong 53-54% kernel percentage, and the tree bears precociously, reaching far heavier yields by its sixth to eighth year than older standards like Desirable. Because it is a recent release, Avalon has a shorter Gulf South track record than heirloom cultivars, but its combination of size, quality, and scab resistance makes it a promising choice for home orchards willing to plant a newer variety. Water deeply through nut fill and apply a spring foliar zinc spray as with any pecan. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Avanti Southern Highbush Blueberry (Firm Very-Low-Chill Small-Scar Blueberry)
description: Avanti is a 2015 University of Florida southern highbush release valued for firm, high-quality fruit with a small, dry picking scar that resists juice leakage after harvest. Its very low chill requirement makes it one of the better choices for the warmest Gulf Coast winters, though the bush can be more susceptible to Botrytis fruit rot in wet, humid conditions, so good air circulation and a preventive fungicide program during bloom are worthwhile. Plant in raised, sulfur-amended beds with excellent drainage and pair with another very-low-chill cultivar for fuller pollination. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Averre Sweet Potato
description: Averre was released by North Carolina State University's sweetpotato breeding program and named for plant nematologist Kenneth R. Averre, reflecting its strong resistance to root-knot nematode, a major limiting pest in sandy Southern soils. It produces moist, orange flesh and rose-copper skin similar in eating quality to Jewel and Beauregard, with smooth, uniform, fusiform roots well suited to fresh-market and home use. Averre performs reliably in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast growing season and is a good rotation option for gardeners working nematode-infested ground. Cure roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for about a week after harvest to develop full sweetness and improve storage life. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Avocado
description: Avocados bear Type A flowers (open as female in the morning) and Type B flowers (open as female in the afternoon); planting one of each type near each other ensures pollen is available throughout the day and greatly increases fruit set. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years; seedlings may take 8–10 years. Avocados are sensitive to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soils — plant on a mound or raised bed and irrigate deeply but infrequently. Fruit does not ripen on the tree; pick when full-sized and let ripen at room temperature for 3–8 days. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Avonblue Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early Florida-Bred Blueberry)
description: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in winter into acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) heavily amended with pine bark or peat moss, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Avonblue is one of the older University of Florida southern highbush releases and remains valued for its dependable early ripening, largely self-fruitful flowers, and tolerance of Florida's sandy, warm-winter growing conditions. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and mildly tart, produced on a moderately compact, rounded bush well suited to smaller home garden plantings. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Avonresister Parsnip
description: Bred at England's National Vegetable Research Station specifically for strong resistance to parsnip canker, a fungal disease that disfigures roots of many older varieties in humid climates. Roots are shorter and more bulbous than exhibition types, trading some length for reliability and more uniform shape. Its disease tolerance makes it a practical choice in warm, humid growing regions where canker pressure is high. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Avoyelles Sweet Potato (Early-Maturing LSU AgCenter 2024 Release)
description: Avoyelles has light rose-to-copper, mostly smooth skin over uniformly deep orange flesh that bakes to a bright color, and was bred for southern root-knot nematode resistance. It was the top-ranked variety for total and U.S. No. 1 yield across LSU AgCenter multi-state trials leading up to its release. Its early 90-day maturity makes it a good fit for Gulf Coast gardeners who want to free up bed space sooner than Beauregard or Covington allow. As the first new LSU sweet potato variety released in over a decade, it represents the current state of the breeding program's disease-resistance work. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: Ayers Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ayers is a mid-to-late season pear developed at the Tennessee Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1939. It is valued in the mid-South and upper Gulf Coast (zone 7–8b) for producing excellent-quality, Bartlett-like pears with moderate fire blight resistance in climates where Bartlett itself succumbs to disease. The medium-large, yellow, bell-shaped fruits have sweet, juicy, white flesh with a smooth texture and excellent Bartlett-like aroma and flavor — considerably better quality than Kieffer for fresh eating. Ayers is widely considered the best-flavored Southern pear for zones 7–8b and is recommended by extension services across Tennessee, Alabama, and Georgia for home orchards. Harvest when green-yellow color appears and the fruit begins to soften at the neck; ripen at room temperature for 3–5 days for best flavor. Fire blight susceptibility requires vigilant pruning and copper spray during bloom in wet springs. Not recommended for zone 9a where insufficient chill accumulation is likely. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ayocote Blanco Bean (White Mexican Runner Bean)
description: Ayocote Blanco is the white-seeded member of Mexico's ayocote runner bean group, grown alongside its better-known black (ayocote negro) and purple (ayocote morado) siblings in highland milpa plots from central to southern Mexico. The large, plump white seeds cook to a dense, mealy texture with a mild, earthy flavor, traditionally simmered slowly with epazote and used in regional bean stews and moles. Like other ayocote beans, plants are vigorous climbers that benefit from tall, sturdy support and consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before harvesting, then shell and cure the beans before sealing for storage. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Ayocote Morado Bean
description: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support with a long season of striking scarlet-purple flowers that draw hummingbirds. Ayocote beans have been cultivated in the highlands of central and southern Mexico since long before European contact, and the deep purple-black seeds of this particular landrace are prized in Oaxacan and other regional cuisines for their dense, meaty texture and earthy flavor once cooked. Like other runner beans, it sets pods best when nights stay cool, so growers in hot-summer regions may see reduced yields in high summer. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before shelling for the best storage-quality dry bean. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Ayocote Negro Bean (Black Mexican Runner Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous vines to climb. Ayocote Negro bears large, glossy black seeds inside long runner bean pods, a traditional Mexican dry bean valued for its meaty texture and rich, earthy flavor in stews and slow-cooked dishes, distinct from the smaller common bean species most Americans grow. As a runner bean it produces attractive clusters of flowers that also draw hummingbirds before setting pods, making it ornamental as well as productive. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine before shelling for storage. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Azacca Hops
description: Azacca is a trademarked dual-purpose American cultivar whose cones give off a distinctive mango and tropical citrus aroma alongside enough alpha acid to serve as a bittering addition when needed. The bine grows vigorously and produces heavy cone sets, so a tall, sturdy trellis and generous spacing pay off in yield. It tolerates full sun and average garden soil well, though like most hops it rewards consistent moisture during the summer growth push. Harvest promptly once cones dry and become papery to lock in its tropical fruit character before it fades. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Azarole (Mediterranean Hawthorn)
description: Plant grafted trees or container-grown saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; azarole is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the dry, hot summers of the Mediterranean basin and similar climates in the American South and West. Crataegus azarolus is a large shrub or small tree native to southern Europe and western Asia cultivated for millennia for its edible fruits — unusually large for a hawthorn (up to 3/4 inch across), round to oblong, and ripening yellow, orange, or red depending on selection, with sweet to slightly tart, apple-like flesh used fresh, in jams, jellies, liqueurs, and preserves throughout Italy, Spain, and the Middle East. The profuse white spring flowers and ornamental fruits make it as attractive as it is useful; it is well adapted to alkaline, dry, rocky soils. The Arabic name for this species, "za'rour" or "azaroul," is the origin of the English name. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Azores Laurel (Til)
description: Plant Azores laurel in humus-rich, reliably moist, well-drained soil in a sheltered site with full sun to partial shade, choosing the warmest microclimate available since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than Mediterranean bay laurel. Endemic to the Azores and Canary Islands, this Macaronesian laurel-forest tree forms one of the dominant canopy species of the ancient til woodlands and can eventually reach substantial size, with downy young twigs and much larger leaves than common bay laurel. Crushed foliage releases the same warm, aromatic bay fragrance and has traditionally been used interchangeably with Laurus nobilis in regional cooking, though in cultivation outside its native range it is grown mainly as a rare specimen tree for large gardens and conservatories in mild climates. Because it is dioecious, only female trees produce the small blue-black fruit that follows the pale greenish-yellow spring flowers; site young plants away from cold, exposed positions and mulch well to conserve soil moisture. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Azores Thyme (Tufted Thyme)
description: Native to the Azores, Madeira, and the northwest Iberian coast, this diminutive species forms a very low, dense tuft of narrow, spatula-shaped leaves that carry a resinous, almost pine-like fragrance distinct from the thymol scent of common thyme. In early summer it disappears under a haze of small bright-pink flowers that draw bees heavily. The tiny leaves can substitute for lemon thyme in the kitchen, but most gardeners grow it as a choice rock-garden or trough plant, where its compact tufted habit and unusual scent set it apart from sprawling creeping thyme cultivars. Give it gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or consistently damp ground, which quickly rots the crown. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Azoychka Tomato (Russian Yellow Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained, deeply prepared soil; provide staking or caging as plants grow 4–6 feet tall. Azoychka is a Russian heirloom yellow tomato brought to American seed preservation networks from Moscow in the early 1990s and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange; its exact origins are unclear, but it is believed to be a traditional Russian variety grown in home gardens for generations before reaching Western gardeners. The medium-sized (4–8 oz), flattened to slightly oblate, lemon-yellow to pale golden-orange fruits are distinguished from other yellow heirloom tomatoes by their flavor profile — Azoychka has a bright, tangy, citrusy complexity rarely found in yellow tomatoes, which typically run sweet and mild; the flavor has been compared to a lemon-spiked yellow tomato with good acid balance for a yellow-fruited type. The combination of mild sweetness and tanginess makes Azoychka outstanding for fresh slicing, tomato salads where both color and flavor stand out, and gazpacho. An indeterminate variety of moderate size and good productivity; excellent for any region with a long warm season. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Aztec Half Runner Bean (Black-and-White Heirloom Half-Runner)
description: Aztec is a Southern heirloom half-runner dry bean, producing seeds boldly patterned in black and white that stand out in storage jars and seed-saving collections alike. Plants split the difference between bush and pole habit, sending out short runners that benefit from a low trellis or a few stakes but do not require the tall support of true pole beans. The dense, meaty beans hold their shape through long simmering, making them well suited to soups and slow-cooked bean pots in the Appalachian and Southern dry-bean tradition. Let pods dry fully on the vine, harvesting once they rattle, then shell and cure before storage. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Aztec Red Flour Corn (Heirloom Red-Kerneled Soft Corn)
description: Aztec Red is a Mexican heirloom flour corn grown for medium-sized ears densely packed with glossy, deep-red kernels that grind into a soft, faintly rose-tinted flour used for cornbread, atole, and tortillas. Like other flour corns, its soft, starchy kernels lack the hard glassy layer of flint or dent types, so ears should be harvested promptly once husks dry and finished drying indoors before storage to avoid weather damage and storage mold. It can be eaten fresh in the milk stage as a novelty sweet-adjacent corn, but its real value is as a dry grinding corn once fully mature and cured. Isolate plantings from other corn types by distance or timing if saving pure seed, since open-pollinated corn readily cross-pollinates with neighboring varieties. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Aztec Sweet Herb
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; aztec sweet herb (hierba dulce, Mexican candy herb, honeyherb) is a Mexican native tropical herb that contains hernandulcin, a natural sesquiterpene sweetener approximately 1,000 times sweeter than sucrose by weight — placing a single small leaf on the tongue immediately produces an intensely sweet, slightly anise-flavored sweetness that lasts for several minutes. The plant has been used in traditional Mexican medicine and as a sweetening herb since pre-Columbian times. It grows as a low, spreading, stoloniferous herb with small, oval, hairy, wrinkled leaves and small white flower clusters, and functions as a low groundcover in tropical garden settings. Current medical interest focuses on hernandulcin's potential as a natural low-calorie sweetener. Tea made from the fresh or dried leaves is pleasantly and intensely sweet with subtle herbal notes. In zones 9–12 it grows as a perennial groundcover; in cooler climates it is grown in containers brought indoors in autumn. Matures in 45–75 days from transplant.

name: Azufrado Bean (Frijol Azufrado, Sulphur-Yellow Mexican Dry Bean)
description: Azufrado, Spanish for sulphur-colored, is a pale yellow Mexican dry bean market class especially associated with Sinaloa and other northwestern growing regions, prized for its thin skin, quick cooking time, and mild flavor that made it a major commercial bean class alongside Peruano and Flor de Mayo types. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, since common beans germinate poorly in cold ground. The upright bush plants require no staking and set a concentrated crop of small, oval, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that dry down uniformly for storage. Cooked azufrado beans turn a soft cream color and are valued in Mexican cooking for refried beans and soups where a smooth, quick-cooking texture is desired. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: B-17 Acerola (Barbados Cherry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; B-17 is a selected acerola cultivar developed in Puerto Rico for larger fruit size and heavier yields than seedling acerola, while retaining the species' famously high vitamin C content, among the highest of any fruit. The small, bright-red, cherry-like fruits are thin-skinned, juicy, and tart, best used fresh in juice, syrups, and preserves rather than fresh eating alone since the flavor is quite acidic. The dense, rounded shrub can be maintained as a hedge or specimen and bears repeatedly through the warm months, making it one of the most productive fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast home gardens. Fruit is highly perishable once ripe and should be harvested promptly and processed or refrigerated within a day or two. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bababerry Raspberry (Low-Chill Everbearing Southern Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, organically rich soil in full sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool, since raspberries are naturally adapted to cooler regions and struggle with Gulf South summer heat. Bred in Louisiana specifically to fruit in low-chill, high-heat conditions where almost no other raspberry succeeds, Bababerry is an everbearing cultivar producing two crops a year — a smaller early-summer crop on floricanes and a heavier fall crop on primocanes — with medium red berries of good flavor. It represents one of the only realistic raspberry options for Gulf South gardeners determined to grow this normally cool-climate fruit, though yields and vigor remain modest compared to raspberries grown in their preferred cooler range. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after their early summer crop and manage primocanes for the fall crop, keeping the planting well watered and mulched through the hottest months. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Babaco (Mountain Papaya Hybrid)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; babaco is a naturally occurring hybrid of two Andean Vasconcellea species, selected and cultivated in Ecuador for its large, distinctively five-angled, torpedo-shaped fruits that are entirely seedless — a parthenocarpic trait that makes it the only papaya relative that does not require cross-pollination for fruit set. The flavor is refreshing and tropical, combining papaya with pineapple and strawberry notes, with lower enzyme activity than mountain papaya so the fruit can be eaten fresh. The tree stays compact at 6–10 feet and fruits prolifically in zone 9. In zone 9a, provide frost protection below 28°F or grow in large containers moved indoors in winter. A novelty fruit tree that produces a steady supply of unusual, edible fruit without the gender complications of other Vasconcellea species. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Babcock Peach (White-Fleshed Low-Chill California Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Babcock is a heritage California peach dating to the late 1800s, valued for its low chill requirement and its white, sweet, low-acid, freestone flesh, quite different in character from the more common yellow-fleshed commercial peaches. The medium-sized fruit has a red-blushed, creamy-white skin and delicate, aromatic, honey-sweet flavor that is prized for fresh eating, though the tender white flesh bruises more easily than firmer yellow peaches and is less suited to shipping. Its low chill requirement makes it one of the more reliable white peaches for warm, mild-winter climates where standard high-chill peach varieties struggle to break dormancy properly. Thin fruit early to improve size and prevent limb breakage, and pick at full ripeness for the best flavor, since white peaches do not ripen further once picked. Matures in 65–90 days from transplant.

name: Babington's Leek (Perennial Leek)
description: Plant bulbils or transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Babington's leek is a wild, perennial form of the cultivated leek native to the Atlantic coasts of western Europe, where it naturalizes on cliffs and hedgerows. Unlike annual leeks, it forms a persistent clump that produces new leaves each season, dies back in summer heat, then regrows vigorously in fall — making it particularly well-adapted to Mediterranean-climate and zone 9 gardens where annual leeks struggle in summer. Harvest leaves, stems, and green tops throughout the cool season much like walking onions. In late summer it produces a tall umbel of flowers plus abundant aerial bulbils — collect these and replant to expand your patch. The flavor is mild and leek-like, less pungent than multiplying onions. A classic cottage garden perennial allium valued in permaculture systems for its low maintenance once established. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Baby Bay Dwarf Bay Laurel
description: Baby Bay is a plant-breeders'-rights-protected selection of common bay laurel valued for its naturally rounded, dense growth habit, which holds a neat ball or standard shape with far less clipping than seed-grown bay requires. Its small, glossy, aromatic leaves are used in cooking exactly like ordinary bay laurel, making it a dual-purpose choice for growers who also want a tidy topiary specimen. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil and let it dry out somewhat between waterings, since it dislikes wet feet. In cold climates keep it as a container plant and move it to a sheltered spot before hard frost arrives. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Baby Bear Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Small Hull-Less-Seed Pie Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin, producing round, deep-orange fruit around 1.5 pounds each with sweet, fine-grained, good-baking flesh well suited to pies, soups, and purees, and small enough to make an attractive miniature carving or decorative pumpkin as well. Its standout feature is hull-less (naked) seeds — unlike most pumpkins, the seeds lack the tough outer hull, so they can be roasted and eaten whole with no shelling required, making Baby Bear a favorite for gardeners who want a dual-purpose crop of both good-eating flesh and easy snacking seeds from the same fruit. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or storage. Matures in 100–105 days from seed.

name: Baby Blue Eucalyptus
description: Start the fine seed indoors well before the last frost, surface-sowing it into a well-drained mix and keeping it warm, as germination is slow and uneven. Grow this florist's silver dollar eucalyptus in full sun with lean, well-drained soil once transplanted; it is frost tender and grown as an annual in cold regions. Harvest the long stems of rounded, dusty blue-green leaves for fresh or dried arrangements, where they hold up well and carry a menthol-like fragrance. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Baby Blue Hubbard Squash (Little Gem Hubbard, Compact Blue Hubbard)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Baby Blue Hubbard produces compact vines of 4–6 feet, more manageable in home gardens than full-sized Hubbard; harvest when the teardrop-shaped fruits are fully blue-gray and the skin resists fingernail penetration; cure for 2–3 weeks and store up to 6 months in a cool, dry location. Baby Blue Hubbard is a compact selection from the classic Blue Hubbard squash (Cucurbita maxima 'Hubbard') — one of the premier American heirloom winter squash varieties, famous for its distinctive blue-gray, bumpy, teardrop-shaped fruits and its extraordinarily sweet, dry, richly flavored flesh. The standard Blue Hubbard can produce fruits of 15–25 lbs or more — too large for most modern households to use in one or even several meals, requiring the awkward step of cutting up a huge squash and storing the remainder.
