Baby Blue Hubbard addresses this practical limitation by producing fruits of 4–8 lbs with the same culinary qualities as the full-sized type: the thick, deeply orange, dry, intensely sweet flesh that has made Hubbard squash the gold standard of American winter squash for over a century. The skin is the same distinctive blue-gray, somewhat bumpy, teardrop-shaped form of the parent variety, recognizable at a glance, and equally hard to cut open (a mallet or drop from a height is the traditional method). The flavor after curing is superb — often described as the richest, most complex flavor of any winter squash, combining sweetness with an earthy, slightly nutty character. Stores exceptionally well for 4–6 months. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Baby Boo Pumpkin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Baby Boo is a white-skinned miniature pumpkin producing small (2–3 inch), perfectly round, deeply ribbed fruits of pure creamy white — the white color makes it the natural complement to the orange Jack Be Little in autumn decorating, where the two varieties together provide the classic orange-and-white color combination of fall décor. The white skin remains crisp and ornamental for 3–4 months after harvest, making Baby Boo extremely long-lasting in decorative arrangements compared to fresh-cut flowers. Like all miniature pumpkins, Baby Boo is edible — the small amounts of sweet, dense flesh inside the tiny fruits can be scooped out after roasting in the oven. The pure white skin is unusual among Cucurbita pepo varieties and results from absence of the carotenoid pigments that give most pumpkins their orange color. Baby Boo plants are productive, often generating 8–15 fruits per plant from compact vines. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Baby Bubba Okra (AAS-Winning Dwarf Compact Okra)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Baby Bubba is a compact, dwarf okra cultivar bred specifically for smaller gardens and container growing, staying considerably shorter than standard okra varieties while still producing a good crop of tender, dark green, ribbed pods over a long summer season. Its shorter stature also makes harvesting easier, without needing a ladder or long reach for pods higher up on a tall plant. As with all okra, pick pods young, at two to four inches, and harvest every day or two during peak production to keep the compact plant setting new pods rather than diverting energy into maturing tough, oversized ones. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Baby Choi Bok Choy
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool, fertile soil and thin to about 5 inches apart, or grow in containers. This Asian green, also called pak choi, is ready in about 35 days when harvested at 5 to 6 inches tall for tender baby choi. It resists bolting and makes an attractive addition to mixed containers. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent bolting, and harvest whole heads or outer stalks for stir-fries and marinated salads. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Baby Kale Garden Blend
description: Sow this blend of curly, flat-leaf, and oak-leaf kales thickly in a band for baby-leaf harvests, or thin to 6 inches for full-size plants. Direct-seed 1/4 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Cut outer leaves at 3-4 inches for tender salad greens, harvesting cut-and-come-again over several weeks. Cold weather and light frost sweeten the leaves, so this mix carries well into winter in mild zones. Matures in 25–60 days from seed.

name: Baby Milk Bok Choy
description: Direct sow thickly and thin gradually, using early thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants size up into small, palm-sized heads. Baby Milk forms neat, compact rosettes of ivory-white stems and dark green leaves that mature quickly enough to fit into tight rotations between other crops, and its small footprint and tolerance of a partly shaded spot make it well suited to container culture on a porch or balcony. Because heads reach usable size in about a month, it is an efficient way to work fresh bok choy into partially shaded beds that would leave slower crops undersized. Harvest whole heads at the base as soon as they feel firm, since older plants lose their tender, single-serving texture. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Baby Pak Choi
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; baby pak choi matures much faster than full-size bok choy and is harvested as a complete, tender plant rather than by removing individual leaves. The entire head — including the thick, juicy white or light green stems and soft jade leaves — is cut at soil level when 4–6 inches tall. Mild, sweet, and slightly mustardy in flavor, it needs only a very brief stir-fry or a quick blanch. Baby pak choi is excellent for cut-and-come-again growing: cut above the growing crown and plants will resprout several times before bolting. Consistent moisture is essential; drought stress causes premature bolting. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Baby Pam Pumpkin (Small Sweet Pie Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seed in warm, rich soil in full sun after the last frost, planting in hills with ample space for the vines to spread. Baby Pam is a widely grown pie pumpkin hybrid producing small, uniformly round, deep-orange fruit around 4 to 6 pounds, prized for dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh with less watery fiber than large carving pumpkins, making it excellent for pies, purees, and soups. It sets fruit reliably and uniformly across the vine, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated pie pumpkin varieties, and its handsome, deeply ribbed miniature form also works well for small-scale fall decorating. Harvest once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Backlim Asparagus (Dutch Green Hybrid)
description: Backlim comes from the same Dutch breeding program that produced Gijnlim, part of a family of hybrids bred in the Netherlands for uniform, high-yielding green asparagus grown both for fresh market and for forced early production under tunnels. It sends up thick, straight, deep-green spears with dense, tightly closed tips that hold their quality well during the flush of a heavy spring harvest. Like other modern Dutch hybrids, Backlim shows good vigor and reasonably even emergence, which simplifies daily cutting on a productive bed. Give the crowns at least two seasons to establish before harvesting, and maintain full fern growth after cutting ends each year to recharge the root system for the following spring. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Baco Noir Grape (French-American Hybrid Red Wine Grape)
description: Bred in France from a Folle Blanche x Vitis riparia cross, this hybrid produces small dark berries that make a deeply colored, earthy red wine and has long been favored in cool-climate wine regions for its reliable ripening in cool seasons. It shows strong resistance to downy mildew and better cold tolerance than most vinifera, though it can be vigorous and needs regular canopy management to prevent overcrowding. The wine has a distinctive herbal, smoky character that mellows with age. Vines typically reach full bearing by their fourth year. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: Bacon Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mild Avocado, Type B Winter Avocado, Zone 8b Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with frost protection on the coldest nights; Bacon benefits from a Type A companion for maximum fruit set; harvest November through March when fruit is fully sized and softens slightly when gently squeezed; Bacon's mild flavor makes it versatile for cooking, guacamole, and fresh eating for those who prefer less rich avocado. Bacon avocado was developed by James Bacon in Buena Park, California, and introduced in 1954 — it became valued primarily for its cold-hardiness among avocado varieties, with documented survival at temperatures below 26°F that would damage Hass and below 22°F in some trials, making it one of the most cold-tolerant commercial avocado varieties available and the most commonly recommended cold-hardy variety for zone 8b home orchards. The variety's cold-hardiness derives from its pure Mexican race genetics (Persea americana var. drymifolia lineage), which evolved in the highlands of Mexico at elevations where frost occurs regularly — an origin that also confers anise-scented leaves and a distinctive flavor to the fruit. Bacon produces medium-sized, oval to pear-shaped avocados with smooth, thin, deep green skin that does not change color appreciably as it ripens; the flesh is pale yellow-green, creamy, and mild in flavor — significantly less rich in oil content than Hass or Fuerte, giving it a lighter taste that some consumers prefer. Bacon ripens winter to early spring (November–March in California). A good choice for zone 8b–9 gardens in the Gulf South, Texas, and similar climates where the extra cold-hardiness margin matters. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bacopa (Brahmi, Water Hyssop)
description: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; brahmi (bacopa) is a small, creeping, succulent-looking wetland herb native to tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, widely used in Ayurvedic medicine for over 3,000 years as a brain tonic and cognitive enhancer — modern clinical research has substantiated its traditional use for improving memory, reducing anxiety, and supporting neurological function. The small, rounded, fleshy leaves have a mild, slightly bitter flavor and are eaten fresh in salads or cooked in the coastal cuisines of India and Southeast Asia. In the garden it forms a low mat in consistently wet or boggy conditions, producing tiny white five-petaled flowers nearly continuously in warm weather that attract small native bees. It is one of the few edible herbs that thrives in the partially shaded margins of water gardens and boggy low spots. In zone 8–9 it may die back after hard freezes but regrows from the roots; in zone 10–11 it is evergreen year-round. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bacupari (Madruno, Madroño)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; bacupari is slow-growing and may take 8–10 years to fruit from seed. Garcinia madruno (bacupari or madruno) is a Colombian and South American tropical fruit tree in the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae/Guttiferae) — related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) and native to the cloud forests and tropical lowlands of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. It produces small (1–2 inch), oval, bright-yellow to orange fruits when ripe, with thin, slightly resinous skin and white, juicy pulp with 1–3 seeds — the flavor is sweet-tart with floral-citrus notes similar to mangosteen but somewhat less complex. The tree is adapted to partial shade as an understory species in its native cloud forest habitat, making it one of the few tropical fruit trees that can be grown productively in partial shade. Bacupari/madruno is virtually unknown outside of Colombia and the Andean region where it is grown as a local specialty fruit. For zone 11–12 tropical gardeners seeking the most unusual and rare edible collectors' plants. Extremely rare in commercial availability. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Bacuri
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the Amazon and Brazilian cerrado regions, this large forest tree produces a thick-shelled, yellow fruit containing creamy, tangy-sweet white pulp considered one of the finest-flavored fruits of the Amazon, used fresh and in ice creams, juices, and preserves across northern Brazil, though the tree is notoriously slow to reach fruiting age. A relative of mangosteen in the same plant family, it shares that group's exacting climate requirements and very long juvenile period, often a decade or more before first fruiting, making it a specialty tree for dedicated tropical fruit collectors and botanical gardens rather than a quick home orchard planting. Water regularly during the long establishment period, and provide the warm, humid, consistently frost-free conditions the tree requires to eventually bear fruit. Matures in 2920–4380 days from transplant.

name: BadaBing! Tomato (AAS-Winning Crack-Resistant Large Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the vine to support fruit clusters. BadaBing! is an AAS-winning large cherry, nearly cocktail-sized tomato, bearing juicy, bright red, roughly 1.5 to 2 inch fruit with excellent flavor and strong resistance to cracking even after rain. It carries notable resistance to septoria leaf spot, early blight, and late blight, which helps keep foliage healthier through a humid season. Despite an indeterminate growth habit, the plant stays relatively compact, making it a good fit for large containers as well as garden beds; pick fruit as it fully colors for the best flavor and to keep the vigorous plant setting more. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Badger Flame Beet (Sweet Low-Earthiness Orange Beet)
description: Direct sow seed clusters a half-inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once they emerge, since each beet seed cluster produces several sprouts. Badger Flame was bred through a collaboration between Row 7 Seed Company and University of Wisconsin plant breeders specifically to reduce the earthy geosmin compound responsible for the polarizing 'dirt' flavor many people associate with beets, resulting in roots with a notably sweet, mild flavor and a distinctive flame-like pattern of yellow and red rings when sliced. Its mild sweetness holds up well eaten raw, shaved thin, or roasted, appealing to cooks and diners who normally avoid beets. Keep soil consistently moist for even root development, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Bael (Bengal Quince)
description: Bael is a spiny citrus relative (family Rutaceae) highly revered in South Asian horticulture and medicine that tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and brief frosts to about 25°F once the trunk is mature — among the hardiest of the true tropical fruit trees. Trees are self-fertile and pollinated by insects; a single specimen fruits reliably. The hard-shelled, woody fruit takes 9–12 months to ripen on the tree; harvest when the skin turns from green to yellowish-green and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. The sticky, aromatic flesh is scooped out and eaten fresh with sugar, blended into a popular cooling drink (bael sherbet), or dried; dried slices brew into a medicinal tisane with mild anti-diarrheal properties. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Bahamian Goat Pepper (Small Elongated Very Hot Bahamian Pepper)
description: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Bahamian Goat bears small, elongated, tapering pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange, carrying intense habanero-relative heat and a bright, fruity aroma, and is the traditional pepper behind Bahamian goat pepper sauce, a fiery condiment served throughout the islands with seafood and conch dishes. The compact, productive plants bear heavily over a long warm-season harvest. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly to keep new flowers setting. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Baheda
description: Plant Terminalia bellirica in deep, well-drained, fertile, moderately moist soil in full sun; the tree grows large and needs space to develop its wide-spreading crown; water during establishment and in dry periods, though mature trees are somewhat drought-tolerant. Baheda (vibhitaki in Sanskrit — meaning 'that which removes disease') is one of the three foundational plants in Triphala (Sanskrit: 'three fruits'), the cornerstone polyherbal formula of Ayurvedic medicine used for thousands of years across India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. Triphala — consisting of equal parts Amla (Phyllanthus emblica), Haritaki (Terminalia chebula), and Baheda (Terminalia bellirica) — is the most widely used compound herb in Ayurveda, prescribed as a rejuvenating tonic, digestive aid, gentle laxative, and general health formula. The dried rind of Baheda fruits is particularly high in tannins (gallic acid, ellagic acid, chebulagic acid) with demonstrated antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective activity in research studies. Baheda's traditional Ayurvedic indications include respiratory conditions (bronchitis, asthma, cough), hair loss, eye diseases, and digestive disorders. The tree is also valuable for its hard, durable timber and as a shade and avenue tree in India; it produces inconspicuous cream-white flower spikes and later the characteristic ridged, oval grey-green fruits. An important tree for gardens serving South Asian communities in zone 10–12. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Bai Jiguan Tea (White Cockscomb)
description: Bai Jiguan, meaning "White Cockscomb," is named for its distinctive pale yellow-green new growth, which emerges noticeably lighter than the surrounding foliage and curls somewhat like a rooster's comb — the palest-leaved of the four historic Wuyi Si Da Ming Cong cultivars grown alongside Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, and Shui Jin Gui. Its naturally lower chlorophyll content in young leaves is said to give the finished oolong a lighter, more delicate character than the deeper, more heavily roasted styles typical of other Wuyi rock teas. Grow it in the same mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soil and partial shade favored by other Wuyi cultivars, and expect a somewhat less vigorous, slower-growing bush than its siblings. Traditional processing uses a lighter roast than Da Hong Pao to preserve its comparatively delicate aromatics. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bai Zhu (White Atractylodes)
description: Sow in a loose, humus-rich, well-drained bed in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun, as this thistle-like aster relative resents soggy or heavy clay soil. Foliage is coarse and somewhat ornamental with purplish thistle-type flower heads in late summer, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its aromatic, camphor-scented rhizome, dug in fall of the second or third year for traditional use in Chinese herbal preparations. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and divide or replant offsets in early spring to keep a patch productive. Because it is slow to establish from seed, many gardeners start with purchased rhizome divisions instead. Matures in 545–730 days from seed.

name: Baidum Longan (Black-Leaf Longan)
description: Baidum, meaning 'black leaf' in Thai, is named for its distinctively dark, near-black young foliage and has become one of the most widely planted longan cultivars in Thailand, prized for consistently sweet, exceptionally aromatic white flesh and reliable heavy cropping. Fruit typically ripens in midsummer with a thin, tan-brown shell that peels away cleanly from a large, sweet aril. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during fruit development but allowing a drier, cooler rest period in winter to promote flower induction. Baidum trees are vigorous and benefit from annual pruning after harvest to maintain a manageable, well-lit canopy for the next season's crop. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Balaton Cherry (Hungarian Sour Cherry, Dark Sour Cherry, Sweet-Tart Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Balaton is self-fertile; it ripens 7–10 days after Montmorency (late June to mid-July in Michigan and the northeastern states), producing large, dark red to mahogany-red fruits with dark red flesh and juice — unlike Montmorency's lighter flesh — with a distinctly sweeter and milder flavor that can be enjoyed fresh as well as used for processing. Balaton sour cherry is a Hungarian variety (from the Balaton region of Hungary, named for Lake Balaton) introduced to North American production through Michigan State University's cherry breeding and evaluation program in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming the most important new sour cherry variety introduced to the American market since Montmorency dominated the category throughout the 20th century. The primary distinction of Balaton from Montmorency is the fruit character: Balaton produces large (slightly larger than Montmorency), very dark red to nearly black fruits with dark red flesh and intensely colored juice, in contrast to Montmorency's lighter pink-red skin and clear to pale yellow flesh. This dark flesh and sweet-tart balance gives Balaton a distinct advantage for certain uses: the fruit can be eaten fresh (it is significantly sweeter and less acidic than Montmorency, approaching the level of fresh-eating quality), the juice is intensely pigmented for concentrated cherry products, and the fruit makes darker, richer-colored preserves and pies. MSU Extension has actively promoted Balaton as an alternative to Montmorency for Michigan commercial producers and home orchardists, particularly for growers wanting a second variety to extend the harvest window and access specialty markets. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Baldmoney (Meu, Bear Root)
description: Direct sow fresh seed in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, cool, moderately fertile soil; fresh seed germinates best — old seed has very poor germination. Meum athamanticum (baldmoney or meu) is a rare and unusual European mountain herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae), native to the highlands of Scotland, Wales, and the Alps, where it grows on moist, acidic mountain meadows and rocky slopes at high elevations. The intensely aromatic, finely cut, ferny, bright-green foliage has a distinctive, complex fragrance and flavor combining anise, caraway, dill, celery, and lovage — more aromatic and complex than any of those herbs individually. The roots (called 'bear root' — bears reportedly seek out and dig the roots in spring) are also aromatic and have been used in alpine herbal medicine and liqueur production. In Scottish Gaelic folk medicine and cooking, the leaves were used to flavor soups and stews in the Highlands where few other herbs grew. The plant produces white umbel flowers in early summer, resembling a small cow parsley. As a garden plant, baldmoney requires cool, moist, acidic conditions found in zone 4–7 mountain and cool-temperate climates — it does not tolerate summer heat and is genuinely rare in cultivation, making it a prized collector's plant for cool-climate herb enthusiasts. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Baldwin Apple (Dominant 19th-Century New England Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Baldwin originated in Massachusetts in the late 1700s and went on to become the single dominant commercial apple across New England through most of the 1800s and into the early 1900s, prized for large, firm, red-blushed fruit with crisp, juicy, slightly tart flesh that stores exceptionally well and holds up beautifully for baking, sauce, and hard cider alike. Baldwin's commercial dominance ended abruptly after the catastrophic winter of 1933-34, when extreme cold killed a huge share of New England's Baldwin trees, prompting growers to replant with hardier varieties like McIntosh; the apple never fully regained its former commercial standing, though it remains treasured by heirloom orchardists and cider makers. Harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and expect flavor to improve somewhat with a few weeks of cold storage, a classic trait of many old New England keeper apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Baldwin Fig (Florida-Bred Souring-Resistant Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soils better than most fruit trees and do well in raised beds or large containers where restricted roots encourage fruiting over rampant growth. Baldwin was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected specifically for resistance to souring, a common problem in the Gulf South and Florida where warm, humid weather during ripening lets yeasts and bacteria enter the open eye of the fruit and spoil it before harvest. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, pink-amber flesh and a closed eye that helps keep out rain and insects, giving Baldwin an edge over open-eyed varieties in humid climates. It produces a reliable main crop in late summer without needing a pollinator, and benefits from a thick mulch layer and occasional deep watering during dry spells. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Baldwin Pear (Louisiana Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baldwin is a Louisiana-origin pear valued by Gulf South growers for its adaptability to the region's heat, humidity, and disease pressure, showing good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many higher-chill European pear cultivars in the Deep South. Like other regionally adapted low-chill pears it produces reliably even after a mild winter and pairs well with a second locally adapted pear cultivar for improved pollination and fruit set. Prune to an open, airy framework to reduce disease pressure, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well below visible damage into clean wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Baldwin Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Firm-Fruited Blueberry)
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive conditions rabbiteye blueberries need. Baldwin is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening quite late in the season, extending the blueberry harvest well past earlier cultivars, with small to medium, firm, dark blue berries that hold their shape and flavor well, making them useful for fresh eating, freezing, and machine harvest alike. The plant is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the acidic, sandy soils typical of the Gulf South, requiring a second compatible rabbiteye variety nearby for good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Balegal Pomegranate
description: Balegal is a California pomegranate selected in San Diego, grown for large, round fruit with pale pink skin and deep red, juicy arils that are distinctly sweet with soft flesh surrounding the seeds. It produces noticeably larger fruit than the related Fleishman selection while carrying similarly dark-colored arils, making it a favorite among warm-climate collector orchards. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; established plants are drought-tolerant, though deep, even watering as fruit sizes up in late summer reduces splitting. Prune lightly each dormant season to remove root suckers and open the canopy for better airflow in humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ball's Double White Feverfew
description: Ball's Double White is an old heirloom feverfew strain prized for its abundant, fully double, snowball-like white flowers held above finely divided, aromatic foliage on stems somewhat taller than most modern dwarf selections. It performs best in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and benefits from consistent moisture during bud formation for the fullest blooms. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, and deadhead spent flowers continually through summer to prolong bloom and limit self-seeding, since seedlings often revert to single flowers. Like the species, the foliage is the medicinal part of the plant and can be harvested fresh for tea or tincture, though gloves are recommended when handling large quantities. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Ballerina Serviceberry
description: Ballerina is a vase-shaped hybrid serviceberry that blooms and fruits about a week later than most cultivars, extending the harvest window for its sweet, blue-black berries. Bronze-red spring foliage matures to green, then turns orange and purple in autumn, giving strong three-season interest. It shows good resistance to fireblight, a common concern in the rose family, and adapts to a wide range of soils as long as drainage is decent. Grow in full sun to light shade and net the ripening fruit if birds are a problem, since they find it just as appealing as gardeners do. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ballerina Spanish Lavender
description: Ballerina produces plump purple flower cones topped with long-lasting bracts that open white and slowly fade through pink to purple as they age, giving each spike a two-tone, aging-in-place look over several weeks. The aromatic silvery foliage and rounded habit make it a good match for mass plantings, low informal hedges, and containers. Plant in full sun in well-drained, on the leaner side of average soil, and let the soil dry between waterings once the plant is established, since overwatering is the most common cause of failure. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong the mid-spring through late-summer bloom period. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Balsam Apple (African Bitter Melon)
description: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun; balsam apple is the African species of the bitter gourd group — a climbing vine with deeply lobed, attractive leaves and small, oval, prominently warty orange-yellow fruits (smaller and rounder than bitter melon) that split dramatically when ripe to reveal bright scarlet-coated seeds in a striking display. Native to tropical and subtropical Africa and widely naturalized across Africa, South Asia, and northern Australia. The leaves, young shoots, and unripe fruits are eaten as cooked vegetables across Africa, where it is an important pot herb and relish ingredient in many regional cuisines. The ripe fruit is ornamental and was traditionally used medicinally as a topical treatment for skin conditions (the name 'balsam' refers to the resinous, aromatic properties historically attributed to the fruit). More compact and less bitter than bitter melon (M. charantia). The red-seeded, splitting fruit display is striking and ornamental in the garden. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Balsamic Blooms Basil (Texas Superstar Edible-Flower Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Balsamic Blooms is a Texas Superstar-designated basil bred to solve a problem common to every other basil variety — once basil flowers, the leaves typically turn bitter and the plant's culinary usefulness declines — by keeping leaf flavor mild and pleasant even as it flowers continuously, so the whole plant, showy purple flower spikes included, stays harvestable and edible all season. This lets it double as both a productive culinary herb and an ornamental, pollinator-friendly bedding plant without the usual tradeoff of pinching off every flower to preserve leaf quality. Harvest leaves and flower spikes together for salads, garnishes, and infused vinegars. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier plant, though unlike most basil, letting it flower freely does not ruin its usefulness in the kitchen. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Bambara Groundnut (Ground Bean, Njugo Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost in loose, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun; bambara groundnut is a West African staple legume that forms its nutritious pods underground after pollination — a fascinating growth habit that requires loose, easily penetrated soil for the gynophore (pod peg) to bury itself. The seeds contain 19–21% protein and 40–65% carbohydrate with a nutty, slightly sweet flavor; they are boiled fresh or dried for storage, ground into flour, or fermented into condiments. Among the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant legumes in cultivation, outperforming cowpeas and soybeans on poor dry soils where other legumes fail while fixing nitrogen and improving soil structure. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Bambi Romaine Lettuce (Mini Heat-Tolerant Romaine)
description: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning or transplanting to close spacing since mature heads stay compact. Bambi is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true miniature romaine, forming dense, upright 6-inch heads with sweet, crisp leaves in about half the space and time of standard romaine, and it holds quality and resists bolting notably longer as temperatures rise. Its small size also makes it well suited to container growing and to serving as an individual single-portion salad head. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Bambina Feijoa (Dwarf Patio/Container Selection)
description: Bambina is a genuinely dwarf feijoa selection bred for patios and containers, staying only a few feet tall and wide at maturity compared to the 8-12 foot bushes typical of full-sized cultivars, while still flowering and fruiting on the same schedule as its larger relatives. Fruit is smaller than that of standard cultivars but carries the same sweet, aromatic flavor, and the compact form makes hand-pollinating or netting against birds far more practical than on a full-height shrub. Because of its small size, Bambina is an excellent option for Gulf Coast gardeners who want to grow feijoa in a container that can be moved to a protected spot during an unusual hard freeze, or tucked into a small-space edible landscape where a standard feijoa would not fit. Give it full sun, a large pot or well-drained garden soil, and regular summer water for the best fruit set on this space-saving selection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bambino Eggplant (Dwarf Container Mini Purple-Black Eggplant)
description: Bambino is a true dwarf eggplant, growing only 12-20 inches tall on plants with dark stems and lavender flowers, yet it sets heavy clusters of one to three small purple-black fruits at nearly every node. Its small stature and shallow root system make it a strong performer in containers, where its compact form fits tight patios and balconies as easily as a garden row. It begins fruiting earlier than most standard-sized eggplants and keeps producing steadily once established. Pick the egg-sized fruit while still glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds inside begin to harden. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Banana (Edible Banana, Dessert Banana)
description: Plant pups in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; banana is the most-consumed fruit on earth and one of the most productive food plants for Gulf Coast zone 8–11 gardens, where established clumps produce a nearly continuous succession of hands. Each pseudostem flowers once and fruits once, then should be cut to the ground after harvest, allowing the pups already pushing up around it to take over. In zone 8–9 the top growth dies back in hard freezes but established root mats resprout reliably in spring; heavy mulching protects the rhizomes. Popular zone-8-hardy varieties include 'Orinoco,' 'Lady Finger,' 'Dwarf Cavendish,' and the ultra-cold-hardy ornamental/edible 'Basjoo' hybrid. The large, exotic leaves make banana a spectacular tropical accent plant even in years when the winter prevents fruiting. Matures in 270–450 days from transplant.

name: Banana Legs Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with stake or cage support; Banana Legs is a yellow paste tomato producing clusters of elongated, banana-shaped fruits (4–5 inches long, 1–1.5 inches across) with pale golden-yellow skin that deepens to a richer yellow at full ripeness. The low-acid, sweet, mild flavor of yellow paste tomatoes like Banana Legs fills a different culinary niche than standard red paste tomatoes — the mildness and sweetness make Banana Legs outstanding for golden tomato sauces, sun-dried yellow tomatoes, and fresh eating as a snack tomato, where the sweet, non-acidic character appeals to people who find standard red tomatoes too sharp. The thick walls and small seed cavities are characteristic of paste tomatoes, making Banana Legs efficient to process for sauce and giving it a meaty, dense texture when eaten fresh. Unlike many paste tomatoes that are primarily functional, Banana Legs produces well-flavored fruits suitable for both cooking and fresh eating. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Banana Melon (Heirloom Elongated Yellow Melon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart, or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Banana Melon is a 19th-century American heirloom named for its distinctive shape — long, cylindrical fruit up to 20 inches that closely resembles an oversized banana — with smooth yellow skin and pale salmon-pink flesh that is sweet and aromatic when fully ripe. As a winter (inodorus) melon type, the fruit has little external fragrance even when ripe, so gardeners should judge readiness by the skin turning fully yellow and the blossom end softening slightly to the touch. Its long, heat-loving growing season makes it well suited to Gulf South summers with a long, warm stretch to fully mature and sweeten. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Banana Mint
description: Start banana mint from divisions or cuttings, as it will not reproduce true from seed. Its soft fuzzy leaves carry a sweet fruity aroma prized for desserts and beverages. Grow in consistently moist, fertile soil in dappled sun, keeping roots contained to stop rampant spreading. Water generously in hot weather and cut plants back hard mid-season to renew tender foliage. Lift and divide crowded clumps every couple of years. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Banana Passion Fruit (Curuba, Tumbo, Taxo)
description: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with trellis or fence support; banana passion fruit produces elongated pale yellow-green fruits 2–4 inches long with a strong passion fruit flavor and abundant aromatic juice used in drinks and ice cream throughout the Colombian highlands, where it is called curuba. The soft-hairy three-lobed leaves and pendant pink tubular flowers attract hummingbirds and are highly ornamental; the vine tolerates light frost better than most passion fruits and grows best in mild, humid conditions rather than the hot lowland tropics. It has escaped cultivation in Hawaii and New Zealand where it is invasive — deadhead spent fruits to prevent self-seeding when grown in mild climates. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Banana Passionflower (Curuba)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; banana passionflower is more cold-tolerant than most passionflowers, surviving brief frosts to about 27°F when established, and has been successfully grown in sheltered spots in zone 8b and even zone 8a. Passiflora mollissima is an Andean native cultivated throughout the Andes from Colombia to Bolivia for its edible, banana-shaped, yellow, oblong fruits (curuba) 3–5 inches long with juicy, bright-orange, passion-fruit-flavored pulp used in juices, ice cream, and desserts; it is one of the most commercially important passionfruit species in South America. The flowers are beautiful — long-tubed, rose-pink to coral-pink, with a reduced corona — and are pollinated by hummingbirds. It grows vigorously and is considered invasive in warm, humid climates outside its native range (especially Hawaii, New Zealand, and South Africa); confirm it is legal to grow in your area. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Banana Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and keep at 75–80°F until sprouts appear. Transplant to the garden after last frost and water evenly to maintain steady growth and prevent fruit splitting. Banana peppers are mild and productive; pick fruits at 4–6 inches long when pale yellow for the mildest flavor. Leaving fruits to mature to orange or red increases both sweetness and slight heat. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Banana Shallot
description: A large elongated shallot combining the size of an onion with a shallot's refined flavor. Plant individual sets in early spring with the tip barely showing, spacing them 6 inches apart. Unlike clustering shallots, banana shallots often size up as a single large bulb, so give each room. Keep weeded and evenly watered until tops begin to yellow in midsummer. Lift, cure thoroughly, and store the papery bulbs in a cool dry place for months. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Banana Squash (Pink Banana Squash)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows; Banana squash requires a long season (105–120 days) and is best suited to zones 5–11 with warm summers; in short-season areas, start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting. Banana squash is a Cucurbita maxima type producing some of the longest and heaviest fruits of any winter squash, with cylindrical, slightly curved, banana-shaped fruits typically 18–36 inches long and weighing 10–35 lbs; the distinctive pale pink-salmon to peachy-orange skin makes it instantly recognizable and it is commonly sold in cut wedges at Western US grocery stores and farmers' markets where the whole fruit would be too large for most households. The flesh is dense, smooth-textured, golden-orange with excellent sweetness and a rich, slightly nutty flavor excellent for roasting, soups, and pies. A vigorous, sprawling vine requiring considerable space (at least 8 feet in each direction); store harvested fruits in a cool, dry location where they keep for 3–6 months. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Banana Yucca (Datil Yucca)
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; banana yucca forms a dense, largely stemless or low-trunked clump of thick, rigid, blue-green leaves and is notable among yuccas for producing a large, fleshy, banana-shaped fruit rather than the typical dry, papery capsule of most yucca species. A stout flower stalk of creamy white to purple-tinged bell-shaped blooms appears in late spring, followed by heavy green fruit that ripens to brown by late summer and was a significant traditional food source for Native American peoples of the Southwest, eaten fresh, dried, or baked once fully ripe and soft. It spreads slowly into a substantial multi-headed clump over the years and is exceptionally drought and cold tolerant, thriving in the same lean, rocky soils used by mountain mahogany and other tough Southwestern natives. Harvest fruit once it softens and begins to turn brown, and wear gloves when working near the sharp, rigid leaf tips. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bandera Purple Spanish Lavender
description: Bandera Purple was bred as one of the first Spanish lavenders reliably grown from seed, producing a uniform, compact mound topped with dense flower cones in deep purple crowned by showy purple flag bracts. Sow indoors and grow on cool and bright to avoid legginess, then transplant into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Its dwarf, tidy habit suits containers and small-garden borders better than larger stoechas types, and it tends to flower earlier in its first season than cutting-grown cultivars. Water only when the soil has dried and avoid rich soil or heavy mulch, both of which invite root rot in this drought-adapted plant. Matures in 90–130 days from seed.

name: Bandit Leek
description: Bandit is an open-pollinated late-season leek bred for standing through hard freezes without splitting or losing quality, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fresh leeks well into winter rather than a single fall harvest. Trench or hill soil around the dark blue-green shanks as they grow to lengthen and blanch the edible white portion, since this variety produces very little natural bulbing and stays uniformly thick and straight. Keep plants weeded and evenly watered through summer so the stalks bulk up before cold weather triggers the hardiness that lets Bandit sit in the garden, unharvested, through repeated freezes. Choose Bandit over early-season leeks when the goal is a reliable, cold-tolerant crop to pull as needed from November through late winter. Matures in 120–140 days from transplant.

name: Banyan Tree (Bengal Fig, Indian Banyan, Strangler Fig)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, well-drained soil with ample space — Banyan Tree is one of the largest living organisms on Earth and requires consideration before planting in any developed landscape. Ficus benghalensis is a massive evergreen fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal), sacred in Hinduism and one of the national trees of India. The Banyan Tree has produced the largest tree canopy of any living plant species: the famous Great Banyan Tree in the Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden near Kolkata, India covers more than 4 acres with approximately 3,500 aerial prop roots and a canopy circumference of more than 1,500 feet. The tree's extraordinary growth mechanism — aerial roots that descend from the branches, root in the soil, and gradually thicken into secondary trunks capable of supporting additional branches — allows an individual tree to expand laterally without limit, progressively creating a multi-trunked 'forest' from a single genetic individual. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Banyan Trees are major landscape and street trees. Small specimens are excellent as container bonsai or large indoor specimens in zone 9. The milky sap is irritating to skin. The small figs are eaten by birds but are not palatable to humans. Matures in 1095–7300 days from transplant.

name: Baobab
description: Plant Baobab in deep, freely draining, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; they are highly drought-tolerant once established and dislike any root waterlogging — excellent drainage is non-negotiable; water moderately during summer active growth and reduce or stop watering in winter when deciduous; container-grown Baobabs make striking bonsai or patio specimens for decades before size becomes an issue. Baobab is one of the most extraordinary trees on Earth — capable of living 2,000–5,000+ years (and possibly far longer), storing thousands of liters of water in its massive, spongy, swollen trunk, and providing food, medicine, fiber, and shelter for both people and wildlife across its native sub-Saharan Africa range. The large, white, bat-pollinated flowers open at night and are strongly fragrant; they are followed by the football-sized, hard, hanging fruits — known commercially as 'baobab fruit' or 'monkey bread' — containing dry, chalky-white pulp naturally rich in Vitamin C (6x more than oranges per weight), calcium, potassium, and antioxidants. The pulp, leaves, seeds, bark, and roots all have documented food and medicinal uses across Africa; commercial baobab fruit powder has grown into a global superfood industry. In zone 10–12, it makes a spectacular, extraordinarily long-lived specimen tree; young plants grow slowly but rewards patient gardeners with one of the planet's most remarkable organisms. Matures in 3650–36500 days from seed.

name: Barbados Cherry
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; barbados cherry (acerola, West Indian cherry) is a subtropical shrub or small tree that produces cherry-sized, three-lobed, bright red to orange-red fruits containing the highest natural concentration of Vitamin C of any food crop — approximately 65 times the Vitamin C of orange juice by weight. In south Florida, Texas Gulf Coast, and zone 9–11 climates, established plants produce three to four fruiting cycles annually, yielding heavy crops of sweet-tart, highly perishable fruits that must be processed immediately (fresh eating, juice, smoothies, frozen puree) as they deteriorate within hours of harvest. The plant is an attractive, dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with small, pink, orchid-like flowers and is often grown as a fruiting hedge or informal screen. Productive and relatively pest-free in tropical and subtropical climates. 'B-17', 'Manoa Sweet', and 'Florida Sweet' are improved selections with larger, sweeter fruit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Barbados Gooseberry (Lemon Vine, Leaf Cactus)
description: Root cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Barbados gooseberry is one of the most botanically fascinating of all edible plants — a primitive cactus (family Cactaceae) that retains true persistent leaves unlike all other cacti, making it a living link between leafy plants and the succulent cacti. The woody, thorny scrambling vine can reach 30 feet when climbing, with oval, slightly succulent leaves and masses of fragrant white to pale pink flowers in fall. The yellow to orange fruits ripen to 0.75 inches with multiple seeds embedded in pulp with a pleasant acid-sweet, citrus-like flavor — used fresh, in jams, and as a vegetable cooked with rice in the Caribbean. The young leaves are edible as a potherb. In South America the leaves are consumed as 'ora-pro-nobis,' valued for their exceptionally high protein content (25% dry weight). An unusual and productive edible vine for frost-free gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Barbara Tingey Ornamental Oregano
description: Barbara Tingey is a hardy ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its cascading clusters of overlapping chartreuse-green bracts that blush dusky pink-purple as they mature, resembling small dangling hops held above aromatic gray-green foliage. Compared with the similar but more tender Kent Beauty, this selection is generally considered more vigorous and better able to shrug off winter wet in temperate gardens. It suits a raised bed, dry stone wall, or container where its trailing stems can spill over an edge and be viewed from below. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid heavy, waterlogged ground, which quickly causes crown rot in humid or wet winters. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Barbara's Blush American Persimmon (WS8-10)
description: Barbara's Blush, also sold under its breeding number WS8-10, was developed by Indiana breeder Jerry Lehman and named for his wife. The fruit develops an attractive pinkish-red blush that extends into the flesh and carries an intensely sweet, honey-like flavor with a smooth, melting texture. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; this selection has shown good disease resistance in home orchard trials. As with all American persimmons, wait for full softening after color break before harvesting to avoid puckering astringency. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Barbecue Rosemary (Stiff Upright-Stemmed Culinary Rosemary Grown for Skewers)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, and avoid overwatering since rosemary is far more likely to fail from soggy roots than from drought. Barbecue is an upright culinary rosemary selected for unusually long, straight, rigid stems that hold together well enough to thread meat and vegetables directly onto for grilling, imparting a subtle piney rosemary flavor as the skewer chars. Its needle-like leaves have the same robust, resinous culinary flavor as other upright rosemary types and are equally good stripped fresh for roasting and seasoning. Established plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in the Gulf South once past their first season, though in zones below 8 they should be grown as a container plant and brought in over winter, since rosemary's hardiness varies considerably by selection. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Barbeque Rosemary (Upright Skewer-Stem Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; rosemary tolerates poor, rocky, sandy soils far better than rich garden soil, which promotes lush but frost-tender growth. Barbeque is an upright, vigorous rosemary cultivar selected specifically for producing long, strong, straight woody stems, prized by cooks for stripping the needles and using the stem itself as an aromatic skewer for grilling meat, seafood, or vegetables, infusing the food with rosemary flavor as it cooks. Beyond its skewer use, it is a fully capable culinary rosemary with the classic piney, resinous fragrance and flavor, and its upright, well-branched habit also makes an attractive hedge or specimen shrub. Like other rosemary cultivars, it thrives on relative neglect once established, needing little water or fertilizer, and is more prone to root rot from overwatering than from drought. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a tidy shape and to harvest a fresh supply of long, straight stems for skewers. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Barbera Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Barbera is a red wine grape native to the Piedmont region of northern Italy, historically the everyday table wine of the region before a wave of quality-focused winemaking in the late 20th century elevated it to serious status, prized for naturally high acidity paired with relatively low tannin, producing fresh, juicy, food-friendly red wines with bright cherry and berry flavors. The vine is notably vigorous and productive, more forgiving and adaptable to a range of growing conditions than many of the finicky, low-yielding grapes used for premium wine, which has made it a popular choice both in its native Italy and increasingly in New World regions including California. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor and crop load through canopy work and thinning to avoid diluted flavor from overcropping, and harvest once sugars are adequate, since Barbera's naturally high acidity gives some flexibility in exact picking date. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Barcelona Hazelnut (Barcelona Filbert, Pacific Northwest Commercial Filbert Standard)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barcelona requires a companion pollenizer variety; the catkins (male flowers) shed pollen in late winter before the tiny female flowers emerge; nuts ripen in September–October and fall naturally when ripe — sweep them from the ground daily for best quality before mold develops. Barcelona hazelnut is the dominant commercial hazelnut (filbert) variety in the Willamette Valley of Oregon, which produces approximately 99% of the American commercial hazelnut crop and is the third-largest hazelnut production region in the world after Turkey and Italy. The variety was introduced from Spain (where it was a standard filbert cultivar) to the Oregon hazelnut industry in the late 1800s and quickly became the commercial standard because of its productive, consistent cropping, large nut size for the era, and good kernel quality. For over a century, Barcelona dominated Oregon hazelnut production so completely that the Oregon hazelnut industry and Barcelona hazelnut were essentially synonymous. The primary limitation of Barcelona — and the reason it has begun to be replaced by newer OSU-released varieties — is its extreme susceptibility to Eastern Filbert Blight (EFB), a canker disease caused by the native American fungus Anisogramma anomala that is devastating in the eastern United States where it is endemic but historically absent from Pacific Coast orchards. EFB reached Oregon in the 1990s, and its spread has prompted the Oregon hazelnut industry to shift toward the new EFB-resistant OSU varieties (Jefferson, Yamhill, others). Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Barhi Date Palm
description: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Barhi needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates. An Iraqi soft date variety highly prized for being one of the very few dates good to eat fresh at the crisp, yellow, apple-like khalal stage rather than only after fully drying to the traditional wrinkled brown tamr stage, giving it a uniquely refreshing, crunchy-sweet quality unlike most commercial dried dates. Once fully ripened to the soft, caramel-brown stage it becomes exceptionally sweet and soft with a rich, almost butterscotch flavor, making it a favorite among date connoisseurs for both fresh and fully cured eating. Like all date palms it demands a long, hot, dry growing season to ripen properly, needs a male pollinator tree or hand pollination for fruit set, and requires many years of growth before reaching bearing maturity. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Barker's Hot New Mexico Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Barker's Hot is a New Mexico State University-developed hot New Mexico-type chile with significantly higher heat (10,000–15,000 SHU) than standard Hatch and New Mexico No. 9 varieties, making it the choice for gardeners who want traditional New Mexico flavor with serious heat. The long, 7–8 inch fruits are produced in abundance on large, productive plants and are harvested green for roasting or left to ripen and dry red for red chile powder and ristras. Roasting mellows the heat while concentrating the flavor; roasted Barker's Hot chiles freeze well for year-round use. This variety is particularly well-suited to hot, dry climates but also performs in the humidity of zone 9 Gulf Coast with good air circulation. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Barland Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Barland is an exceptionally slow tree to reach bearing age, sometimes taking well over a decade. A classic Herefordshire perry pear long prized for producing exceptionally high-tannin, astringent juice that gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, it is considered one of the finest true perry pears despite, or because of, fruit far too harsh and bitter for fresh eating. Its notoriously slow growth to first bearing has always made it a tree planted for a future generation rather than quick reward, a tradition reflected in the old West Country saying about planting pears for one's heirs. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and mellow, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Barnea Olive (Self-Fertile Heat-Tolerant Israeli Oil Olive)
description: Barnea is a modern Israeli olive cultivar bred for productivity, self-fertility, and adaptability to hot climates, which has made it a favorite among home growers experimenting with olives outside the classic Mediterranean growing zones. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil; because Barnea is self-fertile it will crop reliably as a single tree, though yields improve further with a second variety nearby. It tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many older European cultivars and produces good-quality oil with a robust, peppery flavor. Harvest in late fall as fruit color darkens, and prune annually to maintain an open center that improves fruit quality and reduces disease pressure in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Baron Solemacher Alpine Strawberry (Runnerless German Heirloom)
description: Baron Solemacher is a nineteenth-century German heirloom alpine strawberry prized for forming tidy, runnerless clumps rather than spreading by stolons, which makes it well suited to edging, containers, and small raised beds. Surface-sow the tiny seeds indoors and keep them consistently moist at 60-75F, since germination can be slow and uneven over several weeks. Transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade after the danger of frost has passed, and expect a light crop the first year with fuller production from year two onward. Plants bear small, intensely aromatic red berries from early summer into fall and are best increased by division every few years once established. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Barossa Fest Tomato (Bicolor Red-and-Black Australian Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Barossa Fest bears medium fruit blending red and dusky purple-black tones in a distinctive bicolor pattern, combining the rich, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes with the compact habit of a Dwarf Tomato Project plant, developed through the program's Australian breeding collaboration and named for the country's famous Barossa Valley wine region. Its manageable size suits raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Bartlett Pear (Williams' Bon Chrétien Pear, Williams Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Bartlett (Williams' Bon Chrétien in Europe) is the most widely grown pear in North America and the world's most commercially important pear cultivar — the classic yellow, buttery, bell-shaped fruit that defines the word 'pear' in popular culture. The large, sweet, aromatic fruit with fine-grained, melting flesh ripens from late summer to early fall and is excellent fresh, canned, dried, and used in pies and preserves. Trees are moderately susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), which can cause significant damage in warm, humid climates; planting on well-drained sites and applying copper during bloom reduces risk. Bartlett needs 600–800 chill hours and is best suited to zones 5–7 where winters reliably provide sufficient cold. For warmer zones 8–9, low-chill pears like 'Hood', 'Flordahome', and 'Orient' are more appropriate than Bartlett. Trees bear at 3–5 years and live for decades. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bartram's Serviceberry
description: Collect ripe blue-black berries in midsummer and sow seeds fresh in fall, pressing them lightly into moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered outdoor bed or cold frame. Unlike most serviceberries that bear fruits in long clusters, Bartram's Serviceberry ripens single fruits or small groups of 2–4, making hand-harvest easy. This cold-hardy species thrives in cool, moist conditions resembling its native boreal and subalpine habitat; avoid planting in heavy clay or hot, dry sites. Established shrubs are trouble-free and begin producing their first meaningful berry crops within 2–5 years of transplanting. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Basket of Fire Pepper (Texas Superstar Hanging-Basket Hot Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, large container, or garden bed in full sun. Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental-edible pepper bred for a compact, naturally trailing habit that shows off its abundant small, upright-then-cascading fruit especially well in a hanging basket, unlike most hot peppers, which grow upright. The fruit carries substantial heat, around 80,000 Scoville units, well into cayenne-and-above territory, ripening from green through yellow and orange to red, so a single plant often displays several fruit colors at once. It thrives in the heat and lower humidity of a Texas summer and continues producing heavily through the hottest months when many other peppers slow down. Harvest continuously to keep new fruit setting, and water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Bassano Beet
description: An Italian heirloom documented in 19th-century European seed catalogs, grown for its flattened roots with distinctive pink-and-white concentric rings when sliced, milder and less earthy than solid red beets. It matures quickly, making it well suited to early spring sowings ahead of summer heat or a late-summer succession crop. Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops, which can also be cooked as greens. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Bassett Beach Plum (Bassett's American, Earliest Named Beach Plum)
description: Grow in sandy, well-drained, salt-exposed soil in full sun and site a second beach plum cultivar nearby to ensure fruit set. Known historically as Bassett's American, this New Jersey selection was recognized as one of only a couple of named beach plum cultivars documented by pomologist U.P. Hedrick in his 1911 survey of American plums, making it among the earliest fruit-improved selections of the species on record. It was chosen for producing noticeably larger fruit than typical wild seedling beach plum stands, harvested in late summer for jams, jellies, and preserves. As a true coastal dune native, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and it needs only light pruning after bloom to remain productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bastard Cardamom (Chinese Cardamom, Villous Amomum)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this understory ginger relative needs the warm, humid, sheltered conditions of a tropical forest floor and is not frost-tolerant. A clumping, cane-forming member of the ginger family native to the forest understories of southern China and Southeast Asia, it produces small flowers low on the rhizomes near the soil surface, followed by reddish-brown, spiny-husked seed capsules that are dried and used as a substitute for true cardamom in traditional Chinese medicine and cooking, with a similar but more camphorous, less refined aroma. Its broad, glossy, tropical foliage and shade tolerance make it a useful textural understory plant in a warm, humid shade garden even where the spice itself is not harvested. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and maintain vigor, and protect from any temperature below the mid-40s Fahrenheit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bates Cereal Rye (Early-Maturing Winter-Hardy Grazing and Cover Crop Rye)
description: Broadcast or drill seed in fall into well-drained, average soil in full sun; cereal rye tolerates poor, sandy, or compacted ground better than almost any other cover crop grain. Bates is an early-maturing cereal rye selection noted for rapid, vigorous fall establishment and good tolerance to grazing or repeated mowing, making it a practical dual-purpose choice for gardeners or small farms wanting both winter forage and spring soil-building biomass. Its dense, fibrous root system scavenges leftover soil nitrogen, prevents winter erosion, and suppresses weeds, while the extensive root mass and above-ground residue break up compacted soil and add substantial organic matter when terminated by mowing, rolling, or tillage in spring, generally two to three weeks before the following crop is planted to allow allelopathic residues to break down. Cereal rye is among the most cold-hardy of all cover crop grains and will continue growing through cold snaps that stop other winter cover crops. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Bath's Cos Lettuce
description: Sow directly in cool soil; one of the oldest documented cos lettuces, dating to eighteenth-century England and named for the city of Bath, it produces compact, upright, small-to-medium heads with sweet, buttery, self-blanching hearts. Its small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture, and it was historically valued for delivering a fine cos lettuce in a smaller garden footprint than larger romaines. Heirloom seed savers maintain it as a variety predating most commercial romaine breeding. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Batian Coffee
description: Released in 2010 by Kenya's Coffee Research Institute as the successor to Ruiru 11, Batian retains resistance to both coffee berry disease and leaf rust but was specifically selected to close the cup-quality gap with heirloom Kenyan cultivars such as SL28 and SL34. It grows into a taller, more open shrub than the very compact Ruiru 11 and comes into bearing faster, giving growers an earlier return on establishment costs. Kenyan producers value it as a disease-resistant option that still produces the bright, complex cup quality Kenyan coffee is known for. Cultivate it under the same filtered shade and rich, well-drained acidic soil conditions as other Arabica selections. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Battaglia Green Fig
description: Battaglia Green traces to cuttings an Italian immigrant family brought to Virginia Beach, Virginia, where it was propagated and named by grower Sandy Battaglia; it is an Adriatic-type fig, distinct from both White Adriatic and Adriatic JH. Medium-sized fruit keeps its bright green skin even at full ripeness, hiding a jammy, strawberry-red interior with an intensely fruity flavor. It is notably cold-hardy and early-ripening, producing both a breba and a main crop, and shows good resistance to splitting in humid weather even though it prefers a drier climate overall. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bauer Lettuce (AAS-Winning Heat-Tolerant Oakleaf)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently, or start transplants indoors for an earlier crop; germinate at 50-70F. Bauer is an AAS-winning oakleaf lettuce recognized for outstanding heat tolerance and slow bolting compared to older oakleaf varieties, producing a loose, deeply lobed rosette of tender, mild green leaves that hold their quality and texture well into warmer weather. It is well suited to both cut-and-come-again harvesting of outer leaves and a single whole-head cut. In zone 9, use it as an early-spring or fall crop and provide afternoon shade during any unseasonably warm stretch to delay bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender leaves. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Bavay's Green Gage (Reine Claude de Bavay, Late-Season European Gage Plum)
description: Bavay's Green Gage is a nineteenth-century Belgian selection from the greengage family, ripening several weeks later than the classic Reine Claude and holding its fruit on the tree longer without dropping. The medium, round fruit has yellow-green skin and very sweet, richly flavored flesh considered among the finest of the late gages for fresh eating. It is largely self-fertile but crops more heavily with another European plum nearby for cross-pollination. Prune to an open center after harvest and thin fruit if the set is heavy, since gages tend toward small fruit size when overcropped. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bay Junior Dwarf Bay Laurel
description: Bay Junior is a naturally dwarf, slow-growing bay laurel cultivar with smaller, more delicate leaves than the species, bred for patio and container culture rather than for eventual tree size. It tolerates colder winters better than plain bay laurel and needs only a light annual trim to keep its neat, rounded head. Grow it in well-drained soil in a sunny, sheltered position, or in a pot that can be brought into an unheated porch or garage during severe cold. The small aromatic leaves can be picked and used fresh or dried exactly like standard bay leaf, though a mature plant yields a modest harvest given its diminutive size. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bay Laurel
description: Take semi-ripe stem cuttings in summer, dip in rooting hormone, and insert into gritty propagating mix; expect rooting in 6–9 weeks. Plant in well-drained soil in a sheltered, sunny site; in zones 7 and colder, grow in containers that can be moved indoors before hard frost. Clip the canopy to shape annually and remove any reverted plain shoots from variegated forms. Harvest individual leaves as needed once the plant is established; leaves are most pungent when dried for 1–2 weeks. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bay Rum Tree (West Indian Bay, Bay Laurel of the Caribbean)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; the leaves can be harvested year-round for culinary and aromatic use. Pimenta racemosa (bay rum tree or West Indian bay) is a small to medium-sized aromatic evergreen tree native to the Caribbean islands — particularly Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles, and the Virgin Islands — in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), closely related to allspice (P. dioica). The glossy, elliptic, leathery leaves of P. racemosa are extraordinarily aromatic when crushed or steam-distilled — yielding 'bay oil' or 'bay rum oil,' a complex essential oil rich in eugenol (clove-scented), myrcene, and chavicol, with warm, spicy, clove-bay character. Bay rum oil is the defining ingredient in traditional West Indian bay rum — a classic men's aftershave, hair tonic, and skin care product used throughout the Caribbean since the mid-19th century and still produced in the Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico today. The same leaves can be used as a culinary herb: dried or fresh leaves add a warmer, more complex, clove-tinged bay flavor to Caribbean stews, soups, and marinades compared to Mediterranean bay laurel. Small, white, fragrant flowers are produced in panicles, followed by small, black, spice-flavored berries. An outstanding aromatic tree for zone 10–12 gardens that combines culinary, aromatic, and cultural heritage. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bay Starvine (Wild Sarsaparilla Vine)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade at forest edges and woodland understory positions; bay starvine is the native North American member of the Schisandraceae — the same family as the famous five-flavor berry (S. chinensis) of Chinese medicine. It grows in the moist, shaded ravines, stream bottoms, and rich forest understory of the southern Appalachians and adjacent lowlands, producing small red flowers in spring that require cross-pollination between male and female plants. The fruits, clustered like a miniature bunch of grapes on an elongated stalk, ripen red in late summer. The plant tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines, filling a valuable niche in shaded woodland garden designs. Though less medicinally celebrated than the Asian species, the native bay starvine has similar phytochemical constituents. A rare and beautiful native vine deserving wider use in woodland shade gardens. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bayhorse Gold Squash (Short-Season Idaho Heirloom Buttercup-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give the vines moderate room to spread. Bayhorse Gold is a golden-orange buttercup-type squash selected by a home gardener at high elevation in Idaho, prized for setting a reliable crop of 3 to 5 pound fruit even where summers are cool and the frost-free window is short. The dense, dry, sweet flesh is well suited to baking and pureeing, matching the quality of better-known buttercup strains while maturing faster. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the vine begins to die back, then cure for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Bayo Bean (Frijol Bayo, Traditional Mexican Tan Dry Bean)
description: Bayo, meaning tan or bay-colored in Spanish, is one of the principal traditional dry bean market classes of Mexico, especially common in the northern and central highland states, where its small, oval, tan seeds are a household staple distinct from the pinto, flor de mayo, and peruano classes often grown alongside it. Direct sow seed into warm soil after all frost danger has passed, since like other common beans it germinates poorly in cold, wet ground. The compact bush plants need no staking and produce a concentrated harvest well suited to home drying. Cooked bayo beans have a mild, earthy flavor and a slightly mealy, tender texture that holds together well in soups, stews, and refried preparations. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Bayou Belle Sweet Potato
description: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Bayou Belle is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release bred to combine the deep-orange, sweet flesh Gulf South consumers expect with improved resistance to soil rot and other soil-borne diseases that build up in continuously cropped sweet potato ground. Roots are smooth-skinned, uniform, and size up reliably in Louisiana's long warm season. As with all sweet potatoes, cure freshly dug roots at 85-90F and high humidity for about a week to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars before storing or eating; uncured roots taste starchy rather than sweet. Start with certified, virus-indexed slips rather than sprouting grocery-store roots, since accumulated viral disease is the main long-term yield killer in home sweet potato patches. Rotate planting beds year to year to keep soil-borne disease pressure low. Matures in 95–115 days from transplant.

name: Bays Cherimoya
description: Bays cherimoya is grown like other named Annona cherimola selections: set out a grafted tree in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and hand-pollinate morning-opened flowers with a small brush, since cherimoya flowers change sex through the day and rarely self-pollinate. Selected by grower James Bays in Ventura, California around 1920, this cultivar produces medium-sized, round, light green fruit marked with a distinctive fingerprint-like ('impressa') skin pattern and sweet, smooth flesh carrying the classic pineapple-banana flavor of good cherimoya. Trees are moderate growers, typically reaching only about 20 feet, which makes Bays a manageable choice for a compact home orchard compared with larger-growing selections. Protect young trees from frost and water consistently through bloom and fruit development, since cherimoya, native to cooler Andean valleys, dislikes prolonged heat and humidity nearly as much as it dislikes freezing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.
