name: Beach Plum
description: Beach plum is a native Atlantic coastal shrub that thrives in sandy, salt-spray-exposed sites where few other fruits survive, making it invaluable for coastal and xeric gardens. The small (0.5–1 in), round fruits range from red to purple to blue at maturity in late summer and are traditionally used for preserves and jams on Cape Cod and Long Island. Plant at least two named cultivars such as 'Autumn' and 'Premier' for adequate cross-pollination, as seedlings are variable and often infertile. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape; heavy pruning reduces fruiting the following year. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beach Strawberry (Chilean Strawberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy, infertile to average soil in full sun to light shade; beach strawberry is one of the two wild strawberry species that were crossed by French botanists in the 18th century to create the modern garden strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) — the other parent being the Virginian strawberry (F. virginiana). It is native to the Pacific coast of the Americas from Alaska to Chile, naturally growing on sandy bluffs, dunes, and coastal prairies where it tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil. The fruits are small by commercial standards but deeply aromatic and richly flavored compared to grocery store strawberries. The leathery, blue-green leaves are distinctly more salt- and drought-tolerant than those of garden strawberries. An excellent low-maintenance groundcover for sunny, dry, or coastal sites; spreads by runners to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Beaked Hazelnut
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; beaked hazelnut is distinguished from American hazelnut (Corylus americana) by the long, tubular, beak-like husk that encloses each nut — the 'beak' can be twice the length of the nut itself. The nuts ripen in late summer and are enthusiastically gathered by squirrels, chipmunks, turkeys, woodpeckers, and grouse; you must act quickly to harvest any for yourself. Plant two or more seedlings for reliable cross-pollination since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and often self-infertile. The catkins that appear in late winter before the leaves are an early source of pollen for native bees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Beall Fig (Heirloom Gulf South Bronze Fig)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate a wide range of soils but produce their best fruit with consistent moisture during ripening. Beall is a long-passed-down heirloom fig from the Gulf South, maintained by home orchardists and fig collectors rather than through commercial nursery release, producing medium bronze-brown fruit with sweet, richly flavored, pink-to-amber flesh. Like most Gulf Coast heirloom figs, it is valued for its vigor and reliability under regional heat and humidity, ripening over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to control size and remove winter dieback, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system; established Beall trees tolerate the occasional hard freeze common to zone 8-9 winters, resprouting from the base if top growth is killed back. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Beam's Yellow Pear Tomato (Heirloom Strain)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beam's Yellow Pear is a named heirloom strain of the classic yellow pear cherry tomato, kept distinct from the generic commercial Yellow Pear seed line by seed savers who selected it over many generations for productivity and reliable pear-shaped fruit. The small, teardrop-shaped fruits ripen to a bright, glossy yellow and carry the same mild, low-acid, sweet flavor the type is known for, making them a favorite for salads and snacking as well as for gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes. The indeterminate vine is vigorous and needs sturdy staking or caging, setting fruit in long, heavy clusters over a long season. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom strain, seed can be saved true-to-type from the healthiest, most productive plants for future seasons. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Bear Huckleberry
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; bear huckleberry is a deciduous native shrub of the high-elevation Appalachian forests from North Carolina to Tennessee, naturally growing in the understory beneath oaks, hemlocks, and rhododendrons. The shiny black berries ripen in late summer and are eaten by bears (which explains the common name), black bears being primary dispersers in its mountain habitat. The berries are edible by humans as well — sweet and flavorful, similar to blueberries but with a distinctive tang. Like all huckleberries, the plant is challenging to cultivate outside its specific acidic, woodland conditions; it does not tolerate alkaline soil, dry soil, or full sun. Excellent for native woodland gardens in the southern mountains. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bearberry
description: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or gravelly, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade; bearberry (kinnikinnick) is a native, circumboreal evergreen groundcover that forms a tight, mat-forming carpet of small, shiny, paddle-shaped leaves with pink urn-shaped flowers in spring followed by bright red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter, providing critical food for bears, grouse, foxes, deer, and songbirds. It is specifically adapted to barren, acid, infertile soils — adding fertilizer or organic matter kills it. Excellent for stabilizing slopes, covering dry banks under conifers, and in rock gardens. The berries are edible but mealy and very astringent when raw; historically used for medicinal tea and food in harsh conditions. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bearberry / Kinnikinnick
description: Bearberry is a prostrate, evergreen groundcover native to circumpolar regions, widely used in northern and mountain landscapes for erosion control on dry, acidic, sandy slopes. The small red berries ripen in fall and persist through winter, providing important wildlife food for bears, grouse, and other species; they are mealy and bland fresh but edible when cooked or dried. Bearberry is best propagated from rooted stem cuttings as seed germination is notoriously slow and difficult. Once established, the plant is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free; avoid fertilizing or overwatering, which quickly kills it. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beatrice Eggplant
description: Sow indoors with warm soil temperatures and transplant into full sun after frost danger has passed, keeping plants evenly watered so the tender skin does not toughen. Mulching helps retain the consistent moisture this heirloom prefers. Beatrice is an Italian heirloom similar in type to Rosa Bianca, producing rounded to oval fruit blushed rose-pink over creamy white, with dense, mild, and notably low-bitterness flesh. It is often grown for its striking market appearance as well as its tender texture when roasted or grilled. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Beaumont Macadamia
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars. A hybrid between the two main macadamia species, this Australian-bred cultivar is widely planted for home gardens and smaller orchards because it begins bearing noticeably earlier than many other macadamia selections, often within three to four years, and produces large clusters of good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous tree. Its relatively quick time to first bearing makes it a popular choice for home growers wanting a faster return than the decade-plus wait typical of some macadamia cultivars, though like all macadamias it needs consistent warmth and is easily damaged by frost. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and harvest nuts as they fall naturally from the tree when fully mature, since immature nuts do not ripen further once picked. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Beauregard Sweet Potato (Louisiana-Developed Leading Commercial Orange Sweet Potato)
description: Plant certified sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Beauregard is the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States — developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1987 to address both production efficiency and consumer preference for the deep-orange-fleshed sweet potato that now defines the American market standard. The deep orange-copper skin over vivid orange flesh, consistently uniform tuber shape, and high sugar content that develops fully after curing represent the qualities LSU breeders targeted: a variety that performs reliably in the humid Gulf South climate while producing the attractive, sweet, deeply colored roots that American consumers prefer. Beauregard matures in 90–110 days from slip transplanting, making it one of the faster-maturing sweet potato varieties and allowing good production within the Gulf South warm season. Sweet potatoes require curing to develop their characteristic sweetness — newly harvested tubers are starchy and less sweet than properly cured ones. Cure at 85–90°F with high humidity (85–90%) for 5–7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars. Plant certified virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery store sweet potatoes to avoid introducing sweet potato virus diseases that reduce yield. As a Gulf South native crop commercially centered in Louisiana, Beauregard performs with particular reliability in zone 8-10 humid conditions. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Beauty Plum (Red-Skinned Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Beauty is one of the earliest-ripening Japanese plum cultivars, producing medium-sized, bright scarlet-red to crimson fruit with red-streaked yellow flesh in late spring — often the first plum available from the orchard in a given season. The flesh is sweet and juicy with good flavor for fresh eating, canning, and jam production. Beauty is partially self-fertile but produces best crops with a pollinizer nearby (Santa Rosa, Methley, or other Japanese plums). Its low chill requirement (approximately 250–400 hours) makes it well-adapted to zone 7–9, where it performs more reliably than higher-chill European plum cultivars. Trees are moderately vigorous and somewhat susceptible to brown rot, which can be managed with timely fungicide applications and prompt removal of infected fruit. Beauty ripens over an extended period of 2–3 weeks, reducing harvest pressure compared to plums that ripen all at once. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Beaver Dam Pepper (Wisconsin Hungarian Heirloom Mild Hot Pepper)
description: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nighttime temperatures stay above 55F, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Beaver Dam is a Hungarian-American heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, by immigrant Joe Hussli in 1912 and is still celebrated there with an annual pepper festival; it is also listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste. Fruits are large, horn-shaped, and mildly hot, roughly comparable to a pimento in heat, ripening from lime green to a deep reddish-orange and reaching 6-9 inches long on tall, vigorous plants. Harvest green for milder flavor or let fruits ripen fully red for sweeter, more intense flavor; plants are heavy yielding and adapt well to a range of climates. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Beck's Big Buck Okra (Texas Heirloom Giant-Pod Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight and direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom prized for pods that stay tender and stringless even when allowed to grow well past the 4-inch mark where most okra varieties turn fibrous, making it far more forgiving for gardeners who cannot check the patch daily during peak summer production. Plants are tall and vigorous, often topping 6 feet by late summer, and keep setting pods heavily through the worst of the Gulf South's heat once regular blackeyed-pea-type production varieties have slowed. Harvest pods at 4–8 inches for the best balance of size and tenderness, and keep picking to encourage continued flowering; a single well-fed row easily supplies a household through the summer for gumbo, frying, and pickling. Matures in 58–68 days from seed.

name: Beckyblue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Early-Season Florida Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Beckyblue is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry bred specifically for the low winter chill of the Deep South and Florida, ripening among the earliest of the rabbiteye cultivars and giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the blueberry season. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and pleasantly mild-flavored, borne on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers early, plant it in a site with reasonable air drainage to reduce frost risk to the blooms in years with a late cold snap. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well to conserve moisture, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong early yields. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beddome's Nutmeg (Wild Nutmeg, Bitter Nutmeg)
description: Plant seedling trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil under the partial shade of taller forest canopy, matching the wet evergreen forest understory of the Western Ghats where this species is endemic. Unlike true nutmeg, Beddome's nutmeg is grown almost exclusively as rootstock in South Indian nurseries, since seedlings establish more vigorously and produce a stronger root system than Myristica fragrans seedlings, onto which scions of true nutmeg are later grafted; the tree's own seed and aril are bitter and not marketed as a spice. The smooth, blackish-green bark bleeds a distinctive deep-red exudate when cut or blazed, a useful identification feature in the nursery or garden. Grown as an ornamental or nurse tree, it also provides dense shade valuable to other understory spice plantings. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Bedfordshire Champion Onion
description: Bedfordshire Champion is a Victorian-era English heirloom maincrop onion, introduced in the 1860s-70s and still valued for its large, well-shaped, straw-yellow globes and reliable heavy cropping. Sow indoors in late winter or set out sets after the ground has warmed, spacing plants to let bulbs size up fully, and keep weeds down since onions compete poorly with neighboring growth. It is prized among long-day storage onions for holding firm for many months when cured properly, making it a staple for root-cellar keeping. Lift once the foliage has fallen over and dried, then cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded location before trimming and storing. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Bee Balm
description: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; bee balm is an eastern North American native herb with shaggy, whorled, scarlet or pink flower heads from midsummer through early fall that are the preferred nectar source of ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern gardens. The leaves and flowers have a bergamot-orange flavor and aroma, making them valuable for brewing Oswego tea (historically used by the Oswego nation and early American colonists), garnishing salads, and flavoring jellies. Powdery mildew is a persistent issue in humid climates — choose resistant cultivars like 'Jacob Cline', 'Raspberry Wine', or 'Gardenview Scarlet'. Divide overcrowded clumps every 2–3 years in spring; replant vigorous outer portions and discard the worn-out center. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Beedy's Camden Kale (Maine Heirloom Overwintering Curly Kale)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or space plants 12-18 inches apart and harvest outer leaves as needed. Beedy's Camden traces to a single kale plant that gardener Beedy Parker noticed overwintering in her Camden, Maine garden in the 1980s; she saved and shared its seed for years before Fedco Seeds arranged commercial production, introducing it more widely in 2009. The semi-savoyed, ruffled, medium-green leaves are notably more tender than the true Siberian types it resembles, staying pleasant through summer heat while also surviving hard New England winters, and the flavor turns markedly sweeter after several fall frosts. Its ready self-seeding habit and strong regional pedigree have made it a favorite among Northeast market growers and seed savers looking for a genuinely open-pollinated, locally adapted alternative to hybrid curly kales. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Beefmaster Tomato (Large-Fruited Hybrid Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beefmaster is one of the most popular extra-large slicing tomato hybrids in American home gardens — an indeterminate hybrid producing truly giant fruits averaging 16–32 ounces (1–2 pounds) or more per fruit, with the classic beefsteak form: large, meaty, low-seed, deep-red flesh with rich, balanced tomato flavor that makes it the premier choice for thick-sliced tomatoes for sandwiches and BLTs. The extremely heavy fruit size requires robust support — the vines need strong cages or stakes and should have the heaviest fruit clusters supported or tied as they develop to prevent stem breakage. Beefmaster was developed to combine maximum fruit size with disease resistance (V, F, N, T, A resistance package) that most older beefsteak heirlooms lack, making it significantly more reliable in warm, humid Gulf South climates. In zone 9, Beefmaster performs best in the spring window (February–May transplanting) when temperatures allow the large fruits to develop without excessive heat during fruit set — temperatures above 95°F can cause blossom drop and inhibit fruit development on large-fruited varieties. Consistent, deep watering reduces blossom-end rot, which can affect the large-fruited types more than small-fruited varieties. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Beefsteak Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even sprouting. This century-old indeterminate heirloom produces thick, meaty slices prized for sandwiches and any dish wanting rich tomato flavor. Vines are extremely vigorous, reaching 6 feet or more, so provide a sturdy cage or wire support and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and harvest fruit fully colored. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Beefsteak Tomato
description: Start seeds 1/4 inch deep indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F and transplant in full sun in deeply cultivated, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; beefsteak tomatoes produce the largest fruits of any tomato type, with individual fruits commonly weighing 1–2 pounds and sometimes exceeding 3 pounds in favored varieties. They are indeterminate and long-season (78–95 days to first harvest), requiring heavy-duty caging or staking and consistent, deep watering throughout the season. Prune to one or two main stems for the largest individual fruits; allowing multiple stems produces more but smaller fruits. The unrivaled flavor and meaty, low-seed flesh make beefsteaks the top choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and sandwiches. Popular heirloom varieties include 'Brandywine' (pink), 'Cherokee Purple', and 'German Johnson'. Matures in 78–95 days from transplant.

name: Beefy Purple Bush Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This determinate type delivers a rich, umami-packed flavor that finishes with smoky, fire-roasted notes, ripening most of its crop over a concentrated window. Stake or cage the compact bushes to keep fruit clean and support the yield. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Beema Bamboo (Giant Thorny Bamboo)
description: Beema bamboo forms massive, densely packed clumps of thick-walled culms armed with short thorny branches near the base, and it is among the fastest-growing bamboos in the world under warm, humid conditions. It is grown throughout South Asia for timber, construction poles, paper pulp, and biomass, and the young shoots are also harvested and cooked as a vegetable in parts of its native range. Because it is strictly tropical and frost sensitive, it is only appropriate for USDA zone 9b and warmer, and young plants should be protected from any cold snap during establishment. Give it generous space, deep fertile soil, and steady moisture, since mature clumps become extremely large and heavy over time. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Beer Friend Edamame
description: A popular Japanese edamame cultivar named for its traditional role as a beer-hall snack, Beer Friend produces sturdy, upright plants that concentrate their pod set for an unusually uniform, once-over harvest. Pods are plump, hold 3 to 4 large light-green beans each, and mature earlier than many edamame types, making this a good choice for shorter-season gardens. Harvest whole plants or individual clusters when pods are fully filled but still bright green, then blanch briefly and serve pods lightly salted for snacking straight from the pod. Because the crop ripens together rather than trickling in over weeks, it is well suited to a single big harvest for freezing or serving fresh. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Beet Microgreens
description: Presoak the multigerm seed balls for several hours so they sprout more evenly, then sow them densely across a moist tray. Beet microgreens germinate a little slower than brassicas, so keep them covered and warm until shoots emerge, then move to bright light to develop their deep red stems. Water carefully from below or with a fine mist to avoid crushing the delicate seedlings. Harvest the striking crimson-stemmed greens at the cotyledon or first-true-leaf stage for their mild, earthy sweetness. Matures in 10–18 days from seed.

name: Beit Alpha Cucumber
description: Beit Alpha is a burpless, thin-skinned heirloom cucumber that is parthenocarpic, setting smooth, mild fruit without pollination and free of bitterness. Direct-sow after the soil warms to 70F, or start indoors three weeks early, and grow up a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest at 4-6 inches while the skin is deep green and tender, picking often to keep the vines producing. Because no peeling is needed, these cucumbers are ideal for fresh salads and snacking. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Beit Alpha Cucumber
description: Trellis for best results; sow 3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thinning to the strongest when 3 inches tall. Beit Alpha is the classic Middle Eastern cucumber type — short (4–6 inches), thin-skinned, virtually seedless, and extremely crisp and sweet, with no bitterness even at room temperature. It is parthenocarpic, meaning it sets fruit without pollinator visits, and gynoecious (predominantly female flowers), resulting in extremely heavy production from compact vines. The thin skin requires no peeling and wilts less in high summer heat than standard American slicing cucumbers. Harvest frequently — the fruits reach ideal eating size within 24–48 hours in zone 9's summer heat and become puffy if left too long. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Belaruskaja Black Currant (Floral-Flavored Sweet Black Currant)
description: Belaruskaja is a black currant cultivar bred in Belarus, selected for berries with an unusually rich, floral aroma and enough sugar to be enjoyed fresh rather than only cooked. It shows good resistance to white pine blister rust, the disease that once led many U.S. states to restrict Ribes planting, making it a lower-risk choice where local rules require rust-resistant cultivars. The plant is self-fertile and ripens in mid- to late summer, but like other black currants it needs a substantial winter chill to set a full crop, so it is best suited to cold-winter gardens rather than the Gulf South. Plant in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and renew the bush by removing the oldest canes each dormant season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bele (Aibika, Edible Hibiscus)
description: Root cuttings and plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; bele (aibika) is a large-leafed tropical relative of okra grown widely across Papua New Guinea, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia as one of the most important leafy vegetables — the large, soft, mucilaginous leaves are harvested young and eaten as a cooked green vegetable, used to thicken soups and stews, or wrapped around other foods before cooking, exactly as collard or banana leaves are used. The mucilage thickens soups in the same way okra does. The large, showy yellow hibiscus flowers with dark centers are ornamental and also edible. Bele is heat-tolerant, productive, and thrive in Gulf Coast zone 9 summers when other leafy greens bolt and fail. It grows as a perennial shrub in frost-free conditions and can be harvested continuously. Rich in protein relative to most leafy vegetables. Matures in 45–75 days from transplant.

name: Belgian Endive (Witloof Chicory)
description: Sow seeds thinly in rows 12–18 in apart in late spring; thin to 8–10 in spacing when seedlings reach 2–3 in tall. Grow the plants through summer, then in fall dig the roots (which resemble fat parsnips), trim tops to 1 in, and store in a cool, dark, humid place. To force the distinctive tight pale chicons (the white-leaved heads sold in stores), pack roots vertically in a box of moist sand, cover to exclude all light, and keep at 50–60°F for 3–4 weeks — the blanched white chicons emerge from the root tops. The bitter, tender chicons are excellent braised, roasted, or eaten raw. Never allow light to reach the forcing roots or the chicons will turn green and bitter. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Belgian White Carrot (White Belgian Carrot)
description: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, stone-free soil, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear so roots have room to size up. Belgian White is a long, tapered, white-skinned and white-fleshed heirloom carrot historically grown across Europe as a large, productive dual-purpose root for both the table and livestock feed. The roots often push up out of the soil as they mature, developing a green shoulder where exposed to light, and can grow considerably larger than typical orange table carrots while staying reasonably tender. Its mild, less sweet flavor compared to orange carrots and unusual coloring make it a distinctive choice for gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Nantes and Danvers types already common in home gardens. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Bell Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix; peppers germinate best when soil stays above 75°F. Harden off transplants over 7–10 days before planting, and wait until soil temperature reaches at least 65°F. Keep moisture consistent to prevent fruit drop, and apply a balanced fertilizer once flowering begins. Pick green for mild flavor or leave on the plant to ripen to red, yellow, or orange for maximum sweetness. Matures in 65–85 days from transplant.

name: Bell's Seedling Chilean Pernettya (Self-Fertile Prickly Heath)
description: Bell's Seedling is a UK-raised, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of Chilean pernettya notable for being a rare hermaphrodite form of an otherwise dioecious species, so it fruits reliably as a single plant rather than needing a separate male shrub nearby. It still sets an even heavier crop of berries when a male Gaultheria mucronata is grown within bee range, so gardeners assembling a mixed planting can pair it with a male selection for maximum yield. The berries are a bright, deep red and ripen in autumn, persisting on the low, needle-leaved evergreen mounds well into winter. Give it the same acidic, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland conditions as other ericaceous shrubs, and use it as a groundcover-scale edging plant beneath taller acid-loving shrubs. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Bella Rosa Tomato (Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid tomato developed for disease resistance and heat adaptation in humid Southern gardens, an AAS (All-America Selections) winner that earned recognition for reliable production in difficult growing conditions. The medium-large (8–12 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have excellent flavor — more complex and acidic than purely mild hybrids but not harsh — with thick walls and small seed cavity that make them suitable for slicing, sandwiches, and fresh preparations. The broad disease resistance package (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot) addresses the main failure modes of standard tomatoes in humid Gulf South gardens where disease pressure is severe. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for gardeners who want a concentrated harvest for preserving, sauce-making, or sharing with neighbors. An excellent choice for zone 9 spring and fall tomato seasons where disease resistance is more important than variety novelty. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Belle de Boskoop Apple (Large Tart Dutch Heirloom Cooking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a strong compatible pollinizer variety nearby, since this apple's own pollen is of poor quality and it benefits from a robust partner variety. Belle de Boskoop was discovered in the Dutch town of Boskoop in 1856 and became one of the most important cooking and baking apples in continental Europe, prized for large, rough-skinned, red-and-russet fruit with dense, notably tart, aromatic flesh that holds its shape beautifully under heat, making it outstanding for pies, tarte tatin, and applesauce. The tree is vigorous and long-lived, and the fruit stores exceptionally well, often keeping well into winter and even improving somewhat in flavor with a few weeks of storage. Its sharp, assertive tartness sets it apart from milder modern eating apples, making it a favorite specifically among European-style baking enthusiasts. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Belle Epine Chestnut (French Late-Ripening European Chestnut Pollinizer)
description: Belle Epine (clone CA 114) is a traditional French Castanea sativa cultivar registered under the French CTPS certification system, producing medium-sized nuts around 14 grams each with a moderate flavor. It flowers and ripens late in the season and sheds pollen at a useful time for cross-pollinating other late-blooming French and European x Japanese hybrid chestnuts, making it a valued pollinizer tree as much as a nut producer in its own right. As a straight European chestnut, it lacks the strong blight resistance of Chinese-chestnut-derived hybrids, so it is best suited to regions with lower blight pressure or grown alongside more resistant cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Belle of Georgia Peach (Classic White Freestone Heirloom Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Belle of Georgia is a self-fruitful peach requiring no cross-pollinator; thin fruit to 6–8 inches after petal fall; harvest when fruit is fully colored and gives slightly to pressure — white-fleshed peaches like Belle of Georgia lose the green background and develop a creamy-white blush at full ripeness. Belle of Georgia is one of the great classic American peach varieties, an heirloom white-fleshed freestone that has been grown in Southern home orchards for over 150 years, originating in Georgia before 1870 from a cross believed to involve Chinese Cling and other Southern peach stock. The variety demonstrates a characteristic that distinguishes white-fleshed peaches from the more common yellow-fleshed types: the flesh is pure white to blush-pink, with a flavor that is typically sweeter and less acidic than yellow peaches, with floral aromatic notes that many peach connoisseurs consider more complex and refined than yellow varieties. The flavor at peak ripeness — juicy, very sweet, almost honeyed, with a delicate fragrance — is exceptional for fresh eating and traditional Southern preserves. The skin is creamy white to pale pink with a bright red blush over much of the surface, making the ripened fruit visually distinctive. Belle of Georgia is a mid-season variety that ripens in late June to mid-July in most of the South, producing large, fully freestone fruits that separate cleanly from the pit at full ripeness. The trees are vigorous and consistent producers with reasonable disease tolerance under good management. A genuine heirloom variety that has earned its continuous popularity over more than a century of Southern home orchard growing. Matures in 95–115 days from transplant.

name: Bellevue Sweet Potato (Copper-Skinned Disease-Resistant Louisiana Release)
description: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Bellevue is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (trial line LA06-52) prized for its smooth copper skin with few surface indentations, bright orange flesh, and moist, sweet texture that holds a consistent shape and quality from field to plate. It carries good resistance to southern root-knot nematode along with the major fungal diseases Fusarium wilt and Streptomyces soil rot, all common problems in warm, sandy Gulf Coast garden soil that can cripple less resistant varieties. Bellevue also stores exceptionally well after curing, keeping its eating quality for months longer than many other varieties, which suits Gulf South gardeners who dig a large fall crop and want it to last through winter. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before moving them to cool, dry storage. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Belstar Broccoli
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Selected for heat tolerance, this variety suits both spring and late-summer sowings and forms large, 6 to 8 inch, tightly packed blue-green heads. After the main head is cut, many smaller side shoots follow for continued harvests, and it grows well through winter in mild climates. Cut the central head while buds are tight, then keep harvesting side shoots. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Ben Alder Black Currant
description: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil, and prune out any wood older than three years each winter. Ben Alder is a late-season black currant from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's Ben breeding program, the same lineage that produced Ben Lomond, Ben Sarek, and Ben Nevis. It extends the black currant harvest window later into summer than most other Ben-series cultivars, bearing large, richly flavored berries on a vigorous, upright, cold-tolerant bush. Its late flowering helps it dodge spring frost damage that can cut yields in earlier-blooming currants, a useful trait in frost-prone regions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ben Connan Black Currant
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, setting the crown a couple of inches deeper than it sat in the pot to promote vigorous basal shoots. Bred in Scotland, Ben Connan is a compact black currant selection prized for combining a smaller, more garden-friendly bush size with very heavy yields of large, richly flavored berries, making it a popular choice where space is limited. It ripens earlier than many other black currant cultivars, giving a head start on the harvest season, and its dense, tidy growth habit needs less room between plants than older, larger currant varieties. Prune in the dormant season by removing about a quarter to a third of the oldest wood each year, since the best fruit forms on one- and two-year-old stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ben Davis Apple (Mortgage Lifter Apple, New York Pippin)
description: Ben Davis tolerates less-than-ideal soil and irregular watering better than most apples, making it forgiving for beginning orchardists or marginal sites. Introduced in the early 1800s and possibly of Kentucky or Tennessee origin, it became one of the most widely planted commercial apples in 19th-century America, prized for its precocious, heavy, reliable annual crops and its exceptional storage life rather than for outstanding fresh flavor, which is mild and somewhat bland compared to dessert apples. It remains of interest to homesteaders and heirloom growers today mainly for its toughness, productivity, and long keeping quality in cold storage. Matures in 160–180 days from transplant.

name: Ben Lear Cranberry
description: Ben Lear is an older, widely grown cranberry cultivar selected from a Wisconsin bog in the early 20th century, valued for its early ripening, large dark-red berries, and vigorous, easy-to-establish vines that make it a good choice for home bog beds where an early harvest is wanted. Flavor and color develop earlier in the season than in later-ripening cultivars like Stevens, though total yield per vine tends to run somewhat lower than the most productive modern releases. It requires the same demanding conditions as all cranberries: strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), constant moisture, and a sandy-peat substrate that mimics its native bog habitat, along with a sand mulch layer to suppress weeds and support proper rooting. Vines take several years to establish before cropping heavily, but then perform reliably for decades. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once berries color fully and bounce when dropped, ahead of the main-season harvest of later cultivars. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ben Lomond Black Currant
description: 'Ben Lomond' is a heavy-cropping Scottish black currant with large, aromatic berries high in vitamin C, ideal for cordials and preserves. It flowers slightly late, giving some protection from spring frosts, and tolerates a range of soils if kept moist. Plant deeply, burying the crown a couple of inches, to encourage strong shoots from the base. Prune in late winter by removing about a third of the oldest wood, since fruit is borne best on one- and two-year-old stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ben More Black Currant (Late-Flowering Large-Fruited Black Currant)
description: Ben More is a black currant from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's 'Ben' breeding series, selected for very late flowering that lets it dodge spring frosts and for unusually large fruit borne in heavy strings on a vigorous, strong-branched bush. Its mid-late ripening window follows earlier Ben-series cultivars such as Ben Sarek and Ben Lomond, so growers who plant several Ben currants can stretch out the picking season. Like other black currants, it needs a substantial winter chill to flower and fruit well, so it performs best in cold-winter regions and is not a realistic choice for the mild winters of USDA zone 8-9. Grow it in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ben Nevis Black Currant (Heavy-Cropping Scottish Cultivar)
description: Plant dormant bare-root Ben Nevis bushes in early spring, several inches deeper than they grew in the nursery row to encourage a multi-stemmed base, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in part shade to full sun. This Scottish-bred cultivar is prized on commercial currant farms for its heavy, reliable yields of large, glossy black berries that ripen a little later than older Ben-series varieties, which helps spread out the harvest window. The berries carry black currant's intense, tart, aromatic flavor and high vitamin C content, and are traditionally cooked into jams, cordials, and the French liqueur cassis rather than eaten fresh off the bush. Like other currants, Ben Nevis fruits well with several hours of daily shade, making it one of the more shade-tolerant fruiting shrubs for a partly wooded garden edge. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ben Sarek Black Currant
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Ben Sarek is a compact black currant cultivar from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's 'Ben' series — the same breeding program that produced Ben Lomond and Ben Tirran. Ben Sarek is the most compact of the Ben series, growing only 3–4 feet tall while producing very heavy crops of large, dark, richly flavored black currant berries in July. The combination of compact size and exceptionally high productivity makes Ben Sarek the best choice for small gardens and urban growing situations where standard currant shrubs are too large. Black currants have a distinctive, intensely aromatic, bittersweet flavor — the basis for cassis liqueur and blackcurrant jam — that is unlike any other common fruit. The very high vitamin C content (more per ounce than almost any other fruit) and exceptionally high anthocyanin levels have made black currant products popular in European functional food and nutraceutical markets. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ben Sarek Currant (Compact High-Yield Black Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Ben Sarek is a Scottish Crop Research Institute black currant bred for a naturally compact, dense habit that stays notably smaller than older black currant cultivars while still producing very heavy crops of large, richly flavored berries. Its compact size makes it one of the better black currant choices for small gardens and large containers, where a full-sized black currant bush would quickly outgrow the space. Berries are strongly aromatic and tart, best cooked into jam, syrup, cordial, and baked goods. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so remove the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the compact bush renewing itself with vigorous young growth. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ben Tirran Black Currant (Late-Flowering Frost-Avoiding Scottish Black Currant)
description: Ben Tirran is a late-flowering, late-season release from the James Hutton Institute's black currant breeding program, bred so its blossoms open after the usual late-frost window, sharply cutting the risk of frost-damaged crops compared with earlier Ben-series currants. It forms a vigorous, compact bush carrying large, glossy black berries that ripen in late July into heavy, mechanically harvestable clusters with good resistance to powdery mildew and other common currant diseases. Because it needs a substantial cold winter chill to flower and fruit well, Ben Tirran is best suited to cold-winter regions and is unlikely to perform reliably in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens; northern growers should plant it with another black currant for cross-pollination. Harvest full clusters once berries turn glossy black and prune out about a third of the oldest wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Benenden Blue Rosemary (Narrow-Leaf Vivid Deep-Blue-Flowered Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Benenden Blue, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder, bears narrow, dark green needle-like leaves and an especially vivid, saturated deep-blue flower display in spring, among the showiest flowering of any commonly grown rosemary cultivar. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden, and its fragrant, flavorful foliage is fully usable in the kitchen in addition to its strong ornamental value. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Bengal Lychee
description: Bengal produces some of the largest fruit of any lychee cultivar, with bright red, bumpy skin drawn out to a distinct pointed tip and sweet, juicy, mildly floral white flesh with a favorable ratio of flesh to seed. Despite its excellent eating quality, the tree bears irregularly from year to year and has never become a Florida commercial mainstay the way Brewster or Mauritius have, making it more of a connoisseur's dooryard selection than a dependable orchard cultivar. It is grown commercially in parts of Australia and southern Africa and is believed to trace back to a seedling with a West Bengal, India parent. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Beni Shogun Fuji Apple (Low-Chill Early-Ripening Pink-Blushed Fuji Sport)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Beni Shogun Fuji, a pink-blushed sport of standard Fuji, needs roughly 500 chill hours rather than the 550 to 600 hours true Fuji requires, letting it flower and fruit more reliably in gardens at the warmer edge of apple-growing range where standard Fuji sets an uneven crop. It ripens about a month earlier than standard Fuji, with the same sweet, crisp, juicy flesh but a slightly deeper pink blush over the yellow skin. Thin fruit to one per cluster in late spring to improve size, and pick when fully colored for the best sweetness. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Beniazuma Sweet Potato (Classic Japanese Purplish-Red-Skin, Yellow-Flesh Satsumaimo)
description: Beniazuma is a Japanese satsumaimo (sweet potato) cultivar first produced in Ibaraki Prefecture in the 1980s, with purplish-red skin, firm yellow flesh, and a drier, flakier texture than typical American orange-fleshed types. Its mild sweetness and dense texture make it well suited to Japanese preparations such as yaki-imo (stone- or oven-roasted sweet potato), tempura, and sweet potato desserts. It remains widely grown in Japan's Kanto region, though acreage there has been overtaken in recent years by the sweeter Beniharuka. Curing after harvest improves both sweetness and storage life. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Benicia Strawberry (California-Bred Short-Day Cultivar for Gulf South Winter Production)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Benicia was developed by the University of California strawberry breeding program as a short-day type suited to fall planting for winter and spring fruiting in mild subtropical climates. Though bred in California, it was trialed and recommended by the LSU AgCenter as one of the top-performing varieties — alongside Festival and Sweet Ann — for Louisiana home garden and Gulf South production, where its fall-set winter annual habit fits the same short-day plasticulture system used throughout the region. Plants are slightly more compact than Ventana but produce individual-plant yields greater than Camarosa, with larger, higher-quality fruit than Ventana at a comparable fruit count per plant. As with other short-day strawberries grown as annuals in zone 9, replace crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds and harvest from winter through spring before summer heat ends production. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Benifuuki Tea
description: Released by Japan's national tea research program and bred in part from Assam-type stock, Benifuuki was originally developed for black tea production but is now grown mainly for green tea and matcha because its leaves are unusually rich in methylated catechins, compounds studied for their anti-allergy properties. Its Assam ancestry gives it larger leaves and faster growth than classic small-leaved Japanese cultivars like Yabukita, but also leaves it noticeably less cold-hardy, so plants need reliable winter protection outside the warmest zones. Grow in acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with consistent moisture, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Begin light plucking of the top two leaves and a bud once bushes are three to four years old and well established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Beniharuka Sweet Potato (Japan's Top-Grown Ultra-Sweet Purple-Skin Satsumaimo)
description: Beniharuka was bred from a cross of Beniazuma and Kyushu No. 30 in the early 1990s and registered as a cultivar in March 2010 by Japan's Kyushu Okinawa Agricultural Research Center. It has reddish-purple skin and pale yellow flesh that turns almost melt-in-the-mouth soft and intensely sweet when baked, and by 2022 it had become the top-acreage sweet potato variety in Japan, prized by growers for high yield and by consumers for its rich sweetness and moist, sticky texture after curing and long storage. It is popular for yaki-imo roasted sweet potatoes and other dessert-style preparations. Curing and extended storage continue to raise its sugar content, so it benefits from patience after harvest. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Benlehr Loquat (Compact Self-Fruitful Gulf Coast Loquat)
description: Benlehr is valued among Gulf Coast growers for staying noticeably smaller and more compact than standard loquat seedlings, topping out around 6 to 12 feet rather than the 15 to 25 feet many loquat trees eventually reach, which keeps the whole canopy within reach for pruning and harvest. It is self-fruitful, so an isolated dooryard tree still produces a reliable crop, though yields can improve slightly with a second cultivar such as Premier or Champagne planted nearby for cross-pollination. Fruit ripens over winter into early spring following the loquat's characteristic fall bloom, and like other loquat cultivars it should be thinned in heavy-set years to improve fruit size. Its smaller stature also makes Benlehr a practical choice for espalier training against a warm south-facing wall in the cooler parts of zone 8. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Benne (Historic African Heirloom Sesame)
description: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once the danger of frost has passed and soil has thoroughly warmed. Benne is the historic name for sesame brought to the South Carolina Lowcountry by enslaved West Africans, who carried both the seed and the West African Bantu word 'benne' for it, and who used it in traditional dishes and confections that remain part of Lowcountry foodways today, most famously benne wafers and benne brittle. The tall, branching plants produce small tubular flowers followed by seed pods that split open when fully dry, releasing the small, flavorful seeds prized both toasted for cooking and pressed for oil. Benne is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in conditions that stress many other summer crops, and needs relatively little care beyond weeding while young. Harvest whole seed stalks once the lower pods begin to split, and finish drying upside down in a paper bag to catch seed as pods open. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Benning's Green Tint Scallop Squash (Pale Silvery-Green Heirloom Pattypan)
description: Direct sow after soil has warmed in spring, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in full sun; this early-20th-century heirloom produces flattened, scalloped fruit in a pale, silvery-green that sets it apart from the more common yellow and white pattypan types. It was popular in home gardens well before many modern hybrid scallop squash were developed, valued for its fine-grained, nutty flavor when picked young. Harvest the scallop-shaped fruit at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, since older fruit becomes seedy and less tender. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Benton Harbor Chestnut (Michigan State University Chinese Chestnut Selection)
description: Benton Harbor is a Chinese chestnut seedling selection from Michigan State University's Benton Harbor, Michigan research station, valued for its cold hardiness and high, dependable yields, growers in Michigan have reported 70 to 90 pounds of nuts per mature tree. It produces dark red-purple nuts that peel well and are largely free of the double embryos and splits that reduce quality in some other selections, and it tends to bear earlier in the season than many Chinese chestnut selections. Field observations note good resistance to chestnut blight, though performance can vary by site. Plant with a genetically distinct second chestnut cultivar for reliable cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bereczki Quince (High-Yielding Hungarian Heirloom Quince)
description: Bereczki is a nineteenth-century Hungarian quince named for pomologist Mate Bereczki and still ranked among that country's best cultivars for its heavy, dependable crops of large, pear-shaped fruit. The juicy, sweet-tart yellow flesh turns a distinctive reddish hue once cooked, making it a favorite for jelly, paste, and preserves where color as well as flavor matters. Trees grow into a somewhat larger, vigorous framework than many quince selections, so give it a bit more room and prune in winter to maintain an open, airy canopy that discourages fire blight. Harvest in late September as fruit turns deep gold and fragrant; picked fruit stores in a cool space for several weeks before it needs to be cooked down. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bergamot Mint (Eau de Cologne Mint)
description: Divide runners and plant in moist, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; bergamot mint is a peppermint relative with a distinctive, complex fragrance of bergamot orange, lavender, and lemon — caused by the predominance of linalool and linalool acetate rather than the menthol characteristic of peppermint. The scent is sometimes described as eau de cologne, hence the alternate name. The flavor is equally distinctive and less sharply mentholous than peppermint, making it preferred for herb teas, lemonade, cocktails, and delicate desserts where a floral-citrus mint quality is desired. The leaves are rounded, dark-green to slightly bronze-tinged, and the plant produces small, pale-lavender flower spikes in summer that attract pollinators. Several named cultivars exist including Chocolate Mint (with a chocolate-menthol scent), Orange Mint (with a stronger orange character), and Grapefruit Mint (grapefruit-citrus overtones) — all are selections of this same botanical grouping. Grows identically to spearmint or peppermint in its need for consistent moisture and tendency to spread. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bergamot Orange
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; bergamot orange is a small citrus tree grown almost exclusively in Calabria, Italy, for the essential oil extracted from the peel — the aromatic compound that gives Earl Grey tea its distinctive floral-citrus character. The fruit is yellow-green when ripe, roughly lemon-sized, and inedible raw due to intense bitterness. The peel oil is also used extensively in high-end perfumery, providing the top notes to Chanel No. 5 and countless other classic fragrances. In the garden it is an ornamental conversation piece; harvest peels from ripe fruit and dry them, or make a simple extract by steeping fresh peel in vodka. A reliable performer in zone 9–11 with minimal maintenance beyond regular citrus feeding. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Berggarten Sage
description: Root 3–4 in semi-ripe cuttings in moist perlite in late summer; Berggarten sage rarely flowers and is almost exclusively vegetatively propagated. Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; the exceptionally large, rounded, gray-green leaves make it one of the most productive and ornamental culinary sages. Because it does not bolt to flower, the plant concentrates energy into leaf production and remains more compact and tidy than the species. Harvest large leaves throughout the season, cutting back the plant by one-third in spring to remove any winter-killed wood and encourage fresh basal growth. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Bergman Cranberry (Wisconsin Native Bog Selection)
description: Bergman is one of the 'native' Wisconsin cranberry selections, a naturally occurring bog vine identified and propagated directly from wild stock rather than produced through deliberate hybridization, in the same category as Searles and McFarlin among the varieties that predate the mid-century breeding programs. It has long been grown on older Wisconsin marshes for its reliable production and adaptability to local bog conditions, though its berries run smaller and less uniform than those of modern hybrid cultivars like Stevens, and it has been progressively replaced by higher-yielding hybrids on newly planted acreage. Culture is identical to other cranberries: strongly acidic (pH 4.0-5.0), constantly saturated, sandy-peat bog soil in full sun, with a sand top-dressing every few years to suppress weeds and refresh rooting surface for the spreading vines. Because it is a genuine cold-bog native selection, it needs a sustained winter dormancy and is not a candidate for warm-winter or Gulf Coast plantings. It remains of interest mainly to heirloom growers and Wisconsin cranberry marsh operations maintaining legacy plantings. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Berkeley Blueberry
description: Grow in full sun on well-drained, acidic soil and mulch with pine bark or sawdust to hold moisture around the shallow, fibrous root system. Berkeley is an older, widely planted mid-season highbush cultivar valued for large, firm, pale sky-blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good resistance to cracking. Its spreading, vigorous bushes are heavy and reliable producers over a long lifespan, and the plant also offers attractive orange-red fall foliage. Because it dislikes waterlogged soil, raised beds or amended rows are worthwhile on heavier ground. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato (Multicolor Striped Modern Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern specialty tomato bred for its vividly striped fruit, splashed with purple, green, red, and orange in a swirled, painterly pattern that makes it one of the most visually striking tomatoes a gardener can grow, with rich, complex, sweet-tart flesh to match its looks. It is a strong, productive indeterminate vine that sets clusters of medium-to-large fruit over a long season. Stake or cage plants securely for the heavy fruit load, water evenly to reduce cracking, and pick once the stripes have fully developed and fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Bernicker Black Sapote (Chocolate Pudding Fruit)
description: Bernicker is a widely grown grafted selection prized for near-spherical, medium-to-large fruit that carries only one or two seeds, easier to eat and process than seedy seedling trees. It bears heavily and reliably, with fruit maturing over an extended fall-into-winter window, later than most other Gulf Coast tree fruits. Grow it in full sun to light shade in well-drained fertile soil, with patience, since the glossy evergreen tree needs several years to bear after planting. Pick fruit firm and green and let it fully soften at room temperature for a week or more before spooning out the dark, custard-textured flesh. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Berrettina Piacentina Squash (Italian Heirloom Turban Squash)
description: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build the dense flesh this variety is known for. Named for its distinctive tan, beret-like elongated turban shape, this traditional squash from the Piacenza province of Emilia-Romagna has long been grown for the region's celebrated tortelli di zucca, a pumpkin-filled pasta requiring dry, intensely sweet flesh. Its knobby, ridged rind and rich orange interior set it apart from rounder turban types, and it stores well through winter when cured properly. Regional seed houses in northern Italy have kept the variety in circulation for home and market gardeners alike. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Berries and Cream Mint
description: Berries and Cream is a variegated mint cultivar with cream-splashed leaves and a sweet, fruity fragrance reminiscent of mixed berries, making it a favorite for iced drinks and dessert garnishes. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part sun, and always contain the roots since it spreads as vigorously as other mints. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth bushy and to delay flowering, which can reduce leaf flavor. Divide congested clumps every couple of years to maintain vigor and strong variegation. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Berry Blue Honeyberry
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Berry Blue is not reliably self-fertile. This is one of the earlier commercially available honeyberry cultivars in North America, forming a compact, tidy bush well suited to small gardens and mixed borders, with round-to-oval berries that ripen a bit later than the earliest University of Saskatchewan releases, helping spread out the harvest window when several cultivars are planted together. Flavor is tart with a mild blueberry-like undertone, better suited to jam, syrup, and baking than to fresh eating for most palates, though fully ripe fruit sweetens considerably. Berry Blue is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winters well below -30F, but struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is a poor match for zone 8-10 gardens. As with other haskaps, avoid heavy pruning in the first several years and then renew the oldest wood periodically to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Berry Hill Elderberry (Lewis Hill Vermont Alkaline-Soil-Tolerant American Elderberry)
description: Berry Hill was developed in Vermont by nurseryman and author Lewis Hill and is among the most vigorous and cold-hardy of the named American elderberries, ripening its large, deep-red berries early and uniformly across the cluster. Its spreading, decumbent flower cymes are held lower and more horizontally than upright cultivars, which some growers find offers a degree of natural protection from bird predation. Berry Hill is notably the most alkaline-soil-tolerant Sambucus canadensis selection commonly available, making it a good choice on neutral-to-limey garden soils where other elderberry cultivars struggle. It pairs well with its Vermont-bred companion cultivar Coomer for cross-pollination and a staggered but still early harvest window. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: BerryBux Dwarf Blueberry (Boxwood-Like Self-Pollinating Container Blueberry, 'ZF08-095')
description: BerryBux is a patented dwarf blueberry from Fall Creek Farm and Nursery's Bushel and Berry collection, bred for a dense, rounded, boxwood-like habit with small, glossy, evergreen-in-mild-climates foliage that holds its shape and color year-round, making it as much a formal hedge or edging plant as a fruit crop. It is self-pollinating, so a single plant will produce a crop of deep-blue, nearly black berries with an intensely aromatic, wild-blueberry-style flavor, though a second nearby blueberry cultivar can improve fruit set. Grow in an acidic, well-drained mix in a container or raised bed, and water consistently since its compact root system dries out faster than a full-sized bush. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bertram Anderson Thyme (Golden Lemon Thyme)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Bertram Anderson is a golden-leaved lemon thyme cultivar prized as much for its bright chartreuse-yellow foliage, which deepens toward green in summer heat, as for its citrus-scented culinary use, making it a useful low, spreading edger that lights up a sunny herb bed or path edge. The lemon-thyme flavor and fragrance are shared with green-leaved lemon thyme and work well in the same fish, poultry, and tea preparations. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the low mat tidy and encourage fresh, brightly colored new growth, and ensure sharp drainage year-round, since wet feet in humid climates are the most common cause of failure. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bessell Brown Loquat (Compact Large-Fruited Loquat Grafted on Quince Rootstock)
description: Bessell Brown is a large-fruited loquat cultivar typically grafted onto quince rootstock to produce a compact, small tree suited to smaller Gulf Coast gardens. The fruit has thick, bruise-resistant orange skin and firm, golden flesh with a mild flavor reminiscent of pear, apricot, and pineapple. Because it is grafted onto quince, the tree stays notably smaller than seedling loquats while still producing full-sized fruit, though the dwarfing rootstock does not change the plant's fundamental cold sensitivity during its fall-to-winter bloom period. A hard freeze while Bessell Brown is in flower or setting fruit can still reduce or eliminate that season's harvest. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Betel Pepper (Betel Vine, Paan Leaf, Sirih)
description: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a support for climbing — Betel Pepper grows most luxuriantly in the warm, moist, shaded understory conditions similar to its native habitat and will languish in full sun or dry soil. Piper betle is a perennial, climbing vine in the Piperaceae family native to South and Southeast Asia — the same genus as black pepper (P. nigrum) — and one of the most culturally and economically significant plants in the traditional medicine and daily life of South and Southeast Asia. The plant produces heart-shaped, glossy, smooth, dark-green leaves on a climbing, node-rooting vine that ascends trees and structures by adhesive root pads. The leaves are the harvest product: fresh betel leaves (called 'paan' in South Asian tradition) are harvested and used in the preparation of the traditional South Asian chewing combination of areca nut (from Areca catechu), slaked lime, and betel leaf — a preparation with mild stimulant effects consumed by hundreds of millions of people across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia. Beyond this traditional use, fresh betel leaves are used as a cooking wrapper, an herbal digestive, and in various ethnobotanical and Ayurvedic applications throughout the Asian traditional medicine systems. The leaves contain chavicol, eugenol, and other phenolic compounds that contribute their distinctive flavor and mild bioactivity. Grown in zone 10-12 as a permanent perennial shade vine, or as an annual-treated container plant in zone 9. Non-toxic in culinary amounts. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Betony (Wood Betony)
description: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 weeks in the refrigerator before sowing 1/4 in deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Betony (Betonica officinalis, synonym Stachys betonica) has a long history in European herbal medicine as a nervine tonic and digestive herb; the leaves are dried for tea. Grow in partial shade with moisture-retentive soil; plants are long-lived once established and require little attention beyond dividing crowded clumps every 3–4 years. Harvest leaves and flowering tops in early summer when the rosy-pink flower spikes are just opening, then dry thoroughly in a well-ventilated space. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Better Boy Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–75°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Better Boy is a Petoseed Company introduction from the 1960s that became one of the best-selling tomato varieties in US history, consistently appearing in Guinness World Records lists for the heaviest yields from a single plant — a Better Boy at the Chattanooga Times Free Press Demo Garden reportedly produced 342 pounds of fruit from a single plant. The large (8–16 oz), smooth, deep-red fruits are meaty with thick walls, excellent rich-sweet tomato flavor, and few seeds — the archetype of what many American gardeners consider an ideal home garden tomato. Indeterminate vines continue growing and producing until frost, requiring substantial staking or a heavy-duty cage. Disease resistance covers Fusarium wilt (race 1) and Verticillium wilt. Better Boy's long production season, large fruit size, and excellent flavor have kept it among the top five best-selling tomato varieties in the US for over 50 years. In zone 9, it thrives as a spring crop and can resume production in fall after summer heat subsides. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Better Bush Tomato (Compact Semi-Determinate Container Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Better Bush is one of the finest compact tomatoes for container gardening and small-space production — a semi-determinate hybrid that naturally stays 3–4 feet tall with sturdy, stocky stems that are largely self-supporting (minimal or no staking required), compact enough for large containers, and productive enough to provide a meaningful harvest without the sprawling, aggressive growth of indeterminate types. The medium-sized (8–10 oz), round, globe-shaped, bright-red fruits have good flavor and firm texture appropriate for fresh eating and all standard culinary uses. Better Bush carries disease resistance to V, F, and N — a standard Gulf South disease package. The compact size, self-supporting habit, and container suitability make Better Bush the first recommendation for zone 9 gardeners growing tomatoes on patios, balconies, or in raised beds where space is limited. For best container production, use containers of at least 15 gallons with premium potting mix and consistent watering and fertilization — container-grown tomatoes require more frequent irrigation and feeding than in-ground plants. Two plants per patio can provide significant summer tomato production with only 30–40 square feet of container space. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Betternut 401 Squash (Semi-Bush Hybrid Butternut)
description: Betternut 401 is a commercial hybrid butternut bred by Rupp Seeds for growers who want the uniform tan fruit and deep-orange flesh of classic butternut squash without the full sprawl of open-pollinated vining types. Its semi-bush growth habit keeps vines shorter and more manageable, allowing tighter spacing and easier harvest while still producing well-shaped, roughly two to three pound fruit with a small seed cavity. The variety carries tolerance to powdery mildew and better resistance to fruit cracking than many older butternut lines, both of which support cleaner, more uniform fresh-market packouts. Cure fruit in a warm location for one to two weeks after harvest to firm the skin and concentrate sugars before storing. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Betty Wirt Pawpaw
description: Betty Wirt originated in Wirt County, West Virginia and is documented in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar table among the named regional selections gathered from historic pawpaw literature. Fruit can weigh up to a pound at its largest, though typical specimens run closer to 6 ounces, in line with other good wild-origin Appalachian selections of its era. Like most of the West Virginia and Ohio Valley selections cataloged alongside it, it never went through modern multi-state trials or wide commercial release, so treat it as a regionally adapted heirloom valued for genetic diversity and Appalachian provenance in a home orchard rather than a guaranteed top performer. Give young trees consistent moisture and partial shade, moving them into fuller sun as they approach bearing age. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Betty's Blue Compact English Lavender
description: Plant in full sun in lean, gritty, well-drained soil, since this compact cultivar is no more tolerant of wet feet than any other English lavender. Selected in New Zealand, 'Betty's Blue' forms a neat, rounded mound of fine gray-green foliage and produces abundant deep blue-violet flower spikes over a long summer season, with a tendency to rebloom if deadheaded promptly. Its compact, uniform habit makes it a reliable choice for low hedges and mass edging plantings. Cut back the spent flower stems and shear lightly after the main bloom to keep the plant dense and prevent it from splaying open with age. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Beurre Hardy Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard. A classic French dessert pear introduced in the early nineteenth century, its name meaning roughly buttery and hardy, it bears attractive bronze-russeted, greenish fruit with exceptionally juicy, melting, sweet flesh carrying a distinctive light rosewater aroma prized by pear connoisseurs, on a notably vigorous, reliably productive, and disease-tolerant tree. Its combination of rich flavor, vigorous growth, and good disease resistance compared to some other classic European pears has kept it in cultivation as a favorite home orchard variety for two centuries. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer to early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure near the stem. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beurré Diel Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. Found around 1800 as a wilding near Vilvoorde, Belgium by Meuris, head gardener to the famed pomologist Van Mons, and named for the German pomologist Diel, it bears medium to large, round-to-oval fruit with dull yellowish-green, slightly rough skin marked with russet patches, and creamy white, juicy, melting flesh with an excellent sweet flavor when properly ripened. Because it is a triploid it cannot pollinate other pears and requires two other varieties planted nearby. Harvest in fall while still firm, then ripen at room temperature for a week or more until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beurré Giffard Pear (Early-Ripening French Summer Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Beurré Giffard is a French heirloom from the 1820s prized for ripening remarkably early, among the very first quality European pears of the summer, well ahead of the classic fall and winter storage pears most gardeners grow. The medium, greenish-yellow fruit blushed with red has soft, juicy, melting, richly flavored flesh in the classic 'buttery' (beurré) style, but the tradeoff for its buttery texture and early ripening is a very short window of peak quality — the fruit must be picked at just the right moment and eaten promptly, since it goes from underripe to overripe quickly with little margin. For gardeners willing to watch the crop closely, it rewards with some of the season's first fresh pears. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beurré Superfin Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site with a compatible pollinizer. Raised near Angers, France in 1837, it ripens in late September, bearing round-conical fruit that turns from green to yellow with light brown russet as it matures, with creamy yellow, melting flesh considered among the finest-flavored of the classic French dessert pears. A high-quality variety, it rewards a warm, sheltered planting site with excellent buttery, aromatic fruit, though it performs poorly in cool or exposed locations. Harvest in late September while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Beverly Hills Apple (Very Low-Chill California-Bred Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible low-chill pollinator such as Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer. Beverly Hills was discovered as a chance seedling in Beverly Hills, California and remains valued today as one of the lowest-chill apples available, needing only around 300 chill hours, which lets it set fruit reliably even after the mild winters typical of the Gulf South where most standard apple varieties bloom poorly or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized, red-striped, with tart, crisp flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in mid to late summer. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good airflow and fruit quality in humid conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bhagwa Pomegranate (Phule Bhagwa Pomegranate)
description: Bhagwa is the dominant commercial pomegranate cultivar of Maharashtra, India, prized for a vivid saffron-red rind, deep red glossy arils, and soft, easily chewed seeds that make it a favorite for both fresh eating and export markets. It was formally released as 'Phule Bhagwa' by an Indian agricultural university breeding program and performs best with a hot, dry ripening period, so in the humid Gulf South it benefits from wider plant spacing, good airflow, and prompt removal of any cracked or fungal-affected fruit. Trees are self-fertile and productive but tend toward heavier disease pressure than drier-climate selections when grown in high-humidity gardens. Give full sun and sharp drainage, and expect the first meaningful crop three to five years after planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bhagya Moringa (KDM-1, Semi-Dwarf Long-Lived Drumstick Tree)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; drought-tolerant once established.
