Bhagya is a semi-dwarf moringa selection that can be maintained at a manageable height with pruning and training, making it more manageable for home gardens than seedling moringa, which often reaches 20-30 feet. Unlike some high-yield annual selections meant to be replanted every year or two, Bhagya is bred for a long productive lifespan, reportedly remaining in production for many years under good management. It flowers roughly 100-110 days from sowing with first harvest around 160-180 days, producing pods averaging about two feet long. In zone 9, expect frost to kill top growth each winter, with vigorous resprouting from the root base in spring; the compact habit makes it easier to net or protect than larger seedling trees during marginal winters. Matures in 160–240 days from seed.

name: BHN 589 Tomato
description: BHN 589 is a widely grown Southeastern hybrid valued by market growers and home gardeners for combining excellent flavor with a strong resistance package to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium wilt, and tobacco mosaic virus. Semi-determinate vines set heavy clusters of crack-resistant 8-10 ounce fruit that hold shelf life well after picking. Stake or cage for support and maintain even soil moisture to minimize splitting during the humid summer fruit set. Choose this variety where disease pressure is high but you still want dependable, large-fruited flavor rather than a purely commercial round tomato. Matures in 72–78 days from transplant.

name: BHN 602 Tomato (Heat-Set Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging to support the compact determinate vines. BHN 602 is a Florida-bred hybrid slicing tomato carrying a strong disease package — resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus — that holds up well against the soilborne and thrips-vectored diseases common in humid Gulf South gardens. The plants produce large, firm, deep-red, globe-shaped fruit averaging 10-12 ounces with good flavor for a hybrid of its size. It is widely recommended by Gulf South extension services as a reliable heat-set variety for both spring and fall planting windows, continuing to set fruit at temperatures that cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in less heat-adapted tomatoes. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: BHN 968 Tomato (Heat-Tolerant Disease-Resistant Hybrid Cherry Tomato)
description: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the compact determinate plants to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. BHN 968 produces abundant clusters of small, shiny, deep-red cherry tomatoes prized for being notably sweeter and better textured than most determinate cherry types, backed by broad resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes. Its combination of compact habit, disease resistance, and standout heat tolerance makes it a dependable producer through the peak of Gulf Coast summer, when many indeterminate cherry varieties slow down or drop blossoms. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production through the warm season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Bianca Riccia Endive
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bianca Riccia (White Curly) is an Italian fine-cut curly endive producing a loose, open rosette of very finely divided, heavily frizzy white-to-cream leaves — naturally self-blanching at the center without the tying required by some other frisee types. The fine cutting and natural pale color of the interior make Bianca Riccia one of the most elegant frisee types for Italian insalata recipes and for the French frisee au lardons preparation where the delicate pale center is the centerpiece. The outer leaves, being more exposed, are darker green and more bitter; the pale interior heart is the culinary prize with its mild, slightly bitter, elegant flavor. Unlike darker-centered frisee varieties, Bianca Riccia requires little or no artificial blanching because the dense, overlapping outer leaves naturally shade the center as the head matures. In zone 9 fall planting produces heads of excellent quality through November and December. Matures in 55–75 days from transplant.

name: Bibb Lettuce (Limestone Bibb)
description: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil; thin to 9–12 inches and harvest the whole head when the center begins to feel firm. Bibb lettuce was developed by amateur horticulturist Jack Bibb of Frankfort, Kentucky around 1865 and was distributed to neighbors and friends for decades before entering commercial seed trade; it is a butterhead-type lettuce producing small, loose, semi-cupped heads of exceptionally tender, silky, buttery leaves with a mild, sweet, distinctive flavor that many consider the finest of any lettuce for raw salads. The original Limestone Bibb (named for the limestone water of Kentucky) is more delicate and refined than commercial butterhead varieties but slightly slower and less uniform; it is the 'real' Bibb for flavor purists. Modern hybrid butterhead varieties ('Boston,' 'Summer Bibb,' etc.) are improvements in yield and bolt-resistance but lack some of the exceptional flavor of the true heritage Bibb. Matures in 57–70 days from seed.

name: Bicentennial Peach
description: An early-season Southern peach named for the 1976 US bicentennial, producing attractive medium-to-large freestone fruit with yellow flesh streaked red and good eating quality for an early ripener. It is a solid choice for growers in the cooler, higher-chill pockets of the Deep South who still want an early harvest, complementing very-low-chill coastal types on properties that span a range of microclimates. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, prune annually to an open-center form, and thin fruit in spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage from heavy crop loads. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bicolor Pear Gourd (Pear Bi-Color Ornamental Gourd)
description: This classic heirloom gourd bears abundant small pear-shaped fruit, typically 2-3 inches long, with a green lower half and yellow upper half divided by cream streaking. Vines are vigorous and productive, so plan on a trellis or fence for cleaner fruit and easier harvest. Water regularly through bloom and fruit set, then reduce moisture as fruit approach full size to encourage the rind to toughen. Harvest once the shell resists denting, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for two to three weeks until lightweight and hard, ready for autumn display or craft use. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Biew Kiew Longan (Thai Longan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Biew Kiew is a highly regarded Thai longan cultivar prized for large, thin-skinned fruit with a small seed and exceptionally sweet, faintly floral, translucent flesh often described as richer than Kohala. It ripens later in the season than Kohala, typically late summer into early fall, which helps spread out the harvest window for growers who plant both. Like all longans it needs a period of cool, relatively dry winter weather to set flower buds, making zone 9 climates with real winter chill better suited to consistent bearing than frost-free zone 10-11 sites. Trees are vigorous and can bear heavily once established, usually beginning by their fourth or fifth year from a grafted or air-layered start. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Big Beef Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines, which can reach 6 feet or more. Big Beef was introduced by Seminis Vegetable Seeds and won the All-America Selections award in 1994 — it has since become one of the best-selling tomato varieties in the United States, valued for combining the large size and exceptional flavor of old-fashioned beefsteak types with outstanding disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt, nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus) that makes it more reliable across a wide range of climates and conditions. Fruits are large (8–12 oz or more), round to slightly oblate, meaty with few seeds and small blossom scars, and richly flavored — among the best-tasting large hybrid tomatoes available. Widely adaptable from cool northern gardens to Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: Big Bertha Bell Pepper (Giant Extra-Large Sweet Bell Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Bertha is one of the largest bell pepper varieties in general cultivation — producing extra-large, four-lobed fruits 7 inches long and 3.5–4 inches wide with very thick, crunchy walls and excellent sweet flavor. The enormous fruit size makes Big Bertha outstanding for stuffed pepper preparations where the cavity size determines how much filling can be used, and for slicing use where individual slices are large, substantial, and visually impressive. Big Bertha is a hybrid variety with disease resistance that includes tolerance to tobacco mosaic virus — an important practical quality in zone 9 gardens where virus pressure is a consistent challenge for sweet peppers. Fruits ripen from green to red, with the sweet flavor deepening and vitamin C content increasing significantly as the pepper fully ripens red. However, the thick-walled green stage is also excellent for fresh use. Big Bertha plants are vigorous and produce prolifically through the long Gulf South pepper growing season. The combination of extra-large fruit, good disease tolerance, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Big Bertha one of the most popular large-fruited bell pepper varieties in American home gardening. Support plants with a stake or cage as the heavy fruits can cause branches to break. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Big Boy Tomato (Classic Large Beefsteak Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost; Big Boy is one of the most historically important and widely grown large-fruited tomato cultivars in American home gardens — introduced by Burpee in 1949 and still one of the most recognizable tomato names in American horticulture. The large beefsteak-type fruits typically weigh 1–1.5 pounds with deep red, meaty, flavorful flesh and the classic balanced tomato flavor — rich, full, and aromatic without the extreme acidity of some heirloom beefsteaks. Big Boy is an indeterminate, vining cultivar that continues to grow, flower, and fruit until killed by frost — it requires a strong cage or staking support to manage its vigorous 4–7 foot growth. The large fruit production and classic flavor made Big Boy the standard large-fruited tomato in American garden catalogs for decades. In zone 9, tomatoes should be transplanted in mid-February for the spring window, with the goal of harvesting as much as possible before temperatures consistently exceed 95°F (at which point pollen viability fails and fruit set stops). A second planting in late August captures the fall window. Prevent blossom end rot with consistent irrigation and calcium-balanced fertilization. Better Boy is the improved hybrid successor with added disease resistance — both are widely grown. Matures in 78–82 days from transplant.

name: Big Brandy Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even germination. This hybrid crosses Big Dwarf with Brandywine to yield dark pink, ribbed fruits of 12 to 15 ounces with rich flavor and productive, nearly blemish-free yields. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Big Girl Tomato (Classic Large Red Hybrid Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vine for support. Big Girl produces large, smooth, deep red slicing tomatoes with classic rich tomato flavor on a productive plant bred with improved disease resistance over older open-pollinated slicers, making it a dependable choice for home gardeners wanting big, reliable beefsteak-style fruit for sandwiches and slicing. It sets fruit over a long season from early summer through fall in the Gulf South's extended growing window. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking, and feed regularly through the season to sustain the heavy fruit load on the vigorous vine. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Big Jim Loquat (Large-Fruited Orange Loquat, Jim's Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil; thin fruit clusters heavily (3–4 per cluster) to achieve the maximum individual fruit size that Big Jim is capable of; harvest when fruit is fully golden-orange and gives slightly to pressure; consume quickly as loquats have short shelf life (2–3 days at room temperature, 2 weeks refrigerated). Big Jim is a large-fruited loquat variety selected for the home garden market for its impressive individual fruit size — one of the largest-fruited loquat varieties available to home gardeners in the United States. The fruits are elongated, pear-shaped to oblong, with a warm orange skin and deep orange flesh that is sweet-tart and richly flavored — the classic loquat flavor in a package that provides more edible flesh per fruit than smaller varieties. Because loquats have large central seeds relative to their flesh, fruit size matters considerably in terms of eating efficiency: a large loquat like Big Jim offers a much better flesh-to-seed ratio than a small-fruited variety. The tree is moderately vigorous with an upright to spreading habit reaching 15–20 feet at maturity, blooming in fall (October–December in the Gulf South) with fragrant white flower clusters and ripening fruits from late winter through spring. Big Jim performs well in zones 8–10 and has been popular in Gulf Coast and California home gardens for generations. Heavy fruit thinning (to 3–4 fruits per cluster) is particularly important with Big Jim to achieve the maximum individual fruit size. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Big Lifeberry Goji (Large-Fruited Compact Patio Goji)
description: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Big Lifeberry is a modern breeding-program goji selection producing notably larger berries than seed-grown goji, on a more compact, better-branched plant that fruits at a younger age and fits large containers as well as garden beds. Its bushier, less sprawling habit than wild-type goji makes it easier to manage without the loose, arching growth typical of the species. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals; harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling on the fruit directly, since the sap can stain. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Big Mama Lima Bean (Large-Podded Creamy Pole Lima)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis for the climbing vine. Big Mama is a pole lima bean bred for large, broad, flat pods carrying big, creamy-textured seeds, giving a substantial harvest per pod compared to smaller-seeded lima types and making shelling more efficient for a given volume of beans. The rich, buttery flavor and dense, satisfying texture have made it a popular choice for Southern home gardeners who want generously sized lima beans for classic Southern succotash, butter bean dishes, and freezing for winter use. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled for the best flavor and texture, and pick regularly to keep the productive vine setting new pods through the season. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Big Mama Tomato
description: Big Mama produces oversized plum-shaped fruit up to five inches long, far larger than a typical Roma or San Marzano, while keeping the dense, low-seed flesh needed for thick sauce and paste. The indeterminate vines need sturdy staking and steady watering to support the heavy fruit load without splitting. Its meaty walls and easy-peel skin make it a favorite for home canners who want fewer tomatoes to process a given volume of sauce. Pick this cultivar when you want paste-tomato texture in a fruit large enough to slice and eat fresh as well. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Big Max Pumpkin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with ample room for the extensive vines; Big Max is the standard large pumpkin variety for home gardeners seeking impressively large fruits — a Cucurbita maxima (not the common Cucurbita pepo pie/carving pumpkin) that can reach 100 pounds or more under ideal growing conditions, though typical well-grown specimens are 50–80 pounds. The large, round, ribbed, salmon-pink to orange fruits with thick orange flesh are primarily grown for fall display and competition rather than culinary use — the flesh is edible and has a sweeter, less stringy character than standard carving pumpkins, but the enormous size and thick shell make kitchen preparation challenging. The fascination with growing large pumpkins — a pursuit that becomes genuinely competitive at county fairs and pumpkin festivals across North America — has made Big Max and its descendants the gateway variety for the hobby of giant pumpkin growing, which extends through increasingly specialized varieties into fruits exceeding 2,000 pounds. For zone 9 gardeners, Big Max must be started in time to mature before the most intense summer heat — a March planting targets a July–August harvest that avoids both late spring cold and late summer heat extremes. Matures in 120–130 days from seed.

name: Big Max Pumpkin
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, richly amended soil and give each vine ample space to run. This heirloom is a favorite of giant-pumpkin growers, producing round fruits with smooth, light-orange skin well suited to Halloween carving and decorating. For maximum size, grow one pumpkin per vine and water and feed generously through the season. Leave fruit on the vine until the rind hardens, then cut with a length of stem attached. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Big Moon Pumpkin (Giant Orange Exhibition Pumpkin)
description: Get a jump on the season by starting seeds indoors, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil with generous spacing once frost danger has passed, watering deeply and consistently as fruit develops. Big Moon is an open-pollinated giant pumpkin variety, registered in the USDA germplasm collection, capable of producing single fruits weighing up to around 200 pounds under good growing conditions. Its smooth orange rind and classic rounded form have made it a long-standing choice for both giant pumpkin hobbyists and fall carving displays. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Big Orange Candy Roaster (Large Bright-Orange Appalachian Heritage Squash)
description: Big Orange Candy Roaster is an Appalachian candy roaster strain selected for larger fruit size and a solid, bright orange rind, setting it apart at a glance from the salmon-pink North Georgia type and the tan-bronze Tennessee type within the same regionally diverse candy roaster group. Fruits are elongated to slightly bulbous with a curved neck, commonly reaching 15-25 pounds or more under good growing conditions, and the thick, dense, deep-orange flesh shares the group's signature high sugar content that intensifies dramatically when roasted low and slow. Give the exceptionally long, vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with steady moisture through flowering and fruit development to size the large fruit fully. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the stem has dried and corked, then cure two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before moving to cool storage, where the flesh continues to sweeten for months. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Big Rainbow Tomato (Very Large Bicolor Gold-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Rainbow is one of the most spectacular large bicolor heirloom tomatoes — a giant beefsteak type producing very large (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, heavily ribbed fruits with a stunning golden-yellow to orange base skin suffused, streaked, and marbled with bold crimson-red blushing, creating a vivid yellow-and-red bicolor display on the exterior that is dramatically beautiful when the massive fruits are displayed sliced. The cut interior reveals the full character of the variety: a yellow-gold to orange flesh with red sectors and mottling arranged in irregular patterns — each fruit slightly different in its specific bicolor expression but consistently vivid and visually remarkable. The flavor is excellent: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a tropical, complex quality comparable to the Pineapple tomato in style but with a distinctly different appearance — Big Rainbow's background color tends toward deeper gold-orange while Pineapple's is more lemon-yellow. Big Rainbow is a Minnesota heirloom variety believed to have been maintained by northern seed savers. The very large fruit size requires the full spring growing season in zone 9 (February–June) to develop properly before summer heat diminishes fruit quality. As with all large bicolor heirlooms, Big Rainbow plants require sturdy cage or stake support and benefit from consistent moisture and fertility for maximum fruit development. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Big Red Bell Pepper
description: Big Red is a sweet heirloom bell pepper with thick walls and large, blocky three-to-four-lobed fruits that ripen from green to deep red and grow sweeter as they color. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, and transplant only after nights stay above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun and stake taller plants to keep the heavy fruit off the ground. Pick green for a crisp, mild flavor or leave on the plant to ripen fully red for maximum sweetness. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Big Red Mayhaw
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil — mayhaw is a wetland native that actually thrives in poorly drained areas where most fruit trees would fail; Big Red is an improved cultivar of native mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis), the regional fruit of the Gulf South that has been gathered wild for generations and more recently cultivated for commercial jelly production. The small (grape to crabapple sized), round, bright red berries are borne in clusters and ripen in May — giving the tree its common name — with a tart, mildly astringent, aromatic flavor that makes exceptional jelly and is used in sauces, wines, and sweet preparations throughout southern Louisiana, Mississippi, and east Texas where mayhaw culture is a regional food tradition. Mayhaw jelly is the Gulf South equivalent of beach plum jelly in New England — a hyperlocal, regionally specific preserve made from a native fruit with no close cultural equivalent elsewhere in the United States. Big Red was selected for larger-than-average fruit size and high productivity compared to wild-collected mayhaw. The tree's unusual preference for wet, acidic, swampy conditions makes it one of the few commercially valuable fruit trees suitable for low-lying zone 9 sites that would be unsuitable for conventional orchards. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Big Red Ripper Cowpea (Heirloom Dual-Purpose Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; Big Red Ripper is a heirloom Southern cowpea grown for its large, dark brownish-red seeds and rangy, vigorous vines that produce heavily even in poor, dry soil where other legumes struggle. It serves double duty as both a dry-shell eating pea, with a rich, earthy flavor good in soups and stews, and as a soil-building summer cover crop or wildlife food plot planting, since the sprawling vines fix nitrogen and suppress weeds while the abundant seed feeds deer, quail, and dove. Let pods dry fully on the vine for shell-bean storage, or harvest young green pods for fresh shelling if a more tender pea is preferred. Because vines ramble extensively, either trellis plants for easier picking or allow them to sprawl as a living mulch between wider-spaced garden rows. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it needs little irrigation through a Gulf Coast summer. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Big Seeded Mache (Corn Salad)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil in late summer or fall, since mache germinates best in cool conditions. This big-seeded variety tolerates heat better than others without turning bitter and is also very cold-hardy, often surviving to about 10 degrees. Enjoy the tender rosettes alone as a salad, mixed with other greens, or lightly cooked like spinach. Harvest whole rosettes at the base as needed through cool and cold weather. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Big Stem Gai Lan (Chinese Broccoli)
description: An open-pollinated heirloom Chinese broccoli selected for unusually thick, crisp main stalks alongside large, deep-green leaves, giving more edible stem per plant than standard gai lan types. Harvest the main stalk when it reaches 12-18 inches tall and 2-3 flower buds are just about to open, then peel any tough outer fiber before slicing for stir-fries, where its dense, succulent texture holds up well to high heat. Side shoots regrow readily after the main stalk is cut, extending the harvest window. Its heavier stems make it a favorite for gardeners who prize the stalk over the leaf in classic garlic and oyster-sauce preparations. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Big Time Blue Lavender (Compact Deep Blue English Lavender)
description: Big Time Blue is a dwarf English lavender bred for pot and edging use, forming a tight, rounded mound of narrow silvery foliage topped with unusually large, dark blue-purple flower spikes for its small size. It blooms earlier than many standard-height English lavenders and tends to repeat if lightly sheared after the first flush. Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since like all lavenders it is intolerant of wet feet and rich, heavy soils that promote root rot and floppy growth. Its compact habit makes it a strong choice for patio containers, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny border where larger lavender cultivars would overwhelm the space. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Big Top Bitter Melon
description: Big Top produces unusually large, softball-sized bitter melon with a rounded, heart-shaped profile and thick, bumpy dark green skin that ships and stores better than slender types. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun and warm, fertile soil, harvesting fruit while it is still firm and bright green, since fruit left to yellow becomes markedly more bitter and eventually splits to release red-coated seeds. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine setting new fruit through the summer. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Big V Mayhaw (Selected Western Mayhaw Cultivar)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a native wetland tree that thrives in the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most fruit trees fail. Big V is a named selection of western mayhaw grown by Gulf South orchardists for its good fruit size and productive habit, bearing clusters of small, tart, aromatic red fruit that ripen in May and are gathered for the region's traditional mayhaw jelly. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby to ensure strong cross-pollination and fruit set, and expect the young tree to begin bearing within three to five years, with production increasing steadily as it matures over the following decade. Mayhaw needs little care once established beyond occasional pruning to remove crossing or damaged limbs. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Big Zac Tomato (Giant Competition-Class Beefsteak Hybrid)
description: Big Zac is a hybrid beefsteak bred specifically for producing enormous fruit, regularly topping 2-3 pounds and capable of exceeding 5 pounds under heavy feeding and aggressive pruning to a few fruit per plant, making it a favorite at state fair giant-tomato competitions. The pinkish-red, ribbed, meaty fruit has a mild flavor and relatively low seed count typical of very large-fruited types, and is best used fresh since the huge slices don't fit standard sandwiches. Feed heavily and consistently through the season, remove most side shoots and excess flowers to concentrate the plant's energy into fewer, larger fruit, and support developing tomatoes with fabric slings tied to a heavy-duty stake or cage. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Bigflower Pawpaw
description: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; bigflower pawpaw is adapted to Florida scrub and sandhill habitat and requires sharp drainage, performing poorly in heavy or poorly drained soils. Asimina obovata is a Florida-endemic shrub or small tree grown for its large, showy, creamy-white, three-petaled flowers with a sweet fragrance in spring, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit smaller than the common pawpaw but edible fresh. Its thick, leathery, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen leaves and drought tolerance make it a distinctive addition to a sandy-soil food forest or native pollinator garden in the Deep South, where it serves as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies just as its northern relative does. It needs excellent drainage and full sun to partial shade, tolerates poor, infertile sand, and should never be irrigated on a schedule suited to typical garden shrubs. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bignay (Bugnay, Chinese Laurel)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — bignay is a medium-sized tropical tree of Southeast Asia and the Pacific, producing spectacular long (12–18 inch) pendulous clusters of small (pea-sized) berries that ripen from green through red to deep purple-black in sequence on the same cluster, creating a striking multi-colored effect. The berries have a pleasant tart-sweet flavor with some astringency and are eaten fresh, made into wine, juice, and jam; in the Philippines bignay wine is a traditional fermented beverage. The tree is dioecious and shade-tolerant, growing naturally as an understory tree in mixed tropical forests. The polished, reddish-brown seeds (resembling small nutmegs) are made into decorative necklaces in the Philippines. An outstanding ornamental fruiting tree for zone 9b–12 gardens offering shade tolerance and dramatic fruiting clusters. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Biker Billy Jalapeño Pepper (AAS-Winning Long Mild Jalapeño)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Biker Billy, named for a television chili-pepper personality, was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for producing notably long, slender jalapeño fruits, up to 5-6 inches, considerably longer than standard jalapeño varieties, along with earlier maturity and heavier overall yield. Heat is milder and more consistent than many jalapeño varieties, which can vary widely in spiciness depending on growing conditions, making Biker Billy a more predictable choice for recipes needing reliable, moderate jalapeño heat. Fruits ripen from dark green to red and can be harvested at either stage, with red fruit slightly sweeter. Its high productivity and vigorous, disease-resistant plants make it a dependable choice for home gardens and market growers alike. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Biker Leek (F1 Hybrid)
description: Biker is an F1 hybrid leek with upright, tidy foliage and shanks that bulk up quickly through the mid-early season, resisting bulbing and staying easy to clean at harvest. Set pencil-thick transplants 4-6 inches apart in fertile soil with a pH of 6.2-6.8, and hill or trench soil around the stems two or three times as they grow to lengthen the blanched white shank. It holds good eating quality even at a large size and shows intermediate resistance to common rust, purple blotch, and white tip. Harvest through summer and fall and store several weeks near freezing in a humid cooler. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Bilberry
description: Bilberry is a low-growing European relative of blueberry that differs in producing berries singly rather than in clusters; the deep purple-red flesh (unlike blueberry's white flesh) stains heavily and has an intense, slightly tart flavor. It demands strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) with high organic matter and cool, moist conditions, making it challenging to grow in most American gardens but worth attempting in zones 3–7 under high shade or at elevation. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants lightly every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Harvest in mid- to late summer when berries are fully dark blue-black and tender. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bilberry Cactus (Blue Candle, Garambulla)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty soil in full sun; water sparingly — once every 2–3 weeks in summer, almost none in winter. Myrtillocactus geometrizans (bilberry cactus or garambulla) is a striking Mexican columnar cactus forming a large, candelabra-like tree cactus with multiple blue-green columnar branches — the blue-grey waxy coating on the branches gives it an extraordinary, almost artificial blue-steel color that makes it one of the most ornamentally distinctive columnar cacti for full-sun landscaping in warm, dry climates. The columns have 6 prominent ribs with clusters of short spines. The plant produces abundant small, grape-sized, dark-purple to blue-black fruits called garambullos in Mexico — they are sweet, mildly flavored, and eaten fresh or made into aguas frescas; they are among the most economically important wild cactus fruits in Mexico. The flowers are small, white, and produced in spring. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and cold-hardy to about 25°F. An outstanding specimen or hedge cactus for dry, alkaline, sunny gardens in zone 9–12. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Bilimbi (Cucumber Tree)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or air-layered trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bilimbi is more shade-tolerant than its close relative starfruit and is a good choice for partially shaded spots in tropical gardens, though it fruits best in full sun. Averrhoa bilimbi is a relative of carambola producing clusters of small (2–4 inch), cucumber-shaped, intensely sour, pale-green to yellow fruits that grow directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) in a bizarre but highly productive display; the extremely tart fruit is rarely eaten fresh but is valued in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cuisine for its acidity in curries, preserves, pickles, and beverages, substituting for tamarind or lime. Trees fruit heavily multiple times per year in frost-free climates (zones 10–12) and can be grown in large containers moved indoors in zone 9; the pinnate leaves and clustered trunk fruits make it an ornamental specimen even when not fruiting. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bilko Napa Cabbage (Clubroot-Resistant Long-Storage Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer for a fall harvest, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Bilko is a napa (Chinese) cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to clubroot and Fusarium yellows, two persistent soil-borne diseases that can build up in garden soil where brassicas are grown repeatedly and have no cure once established. It forms tall, dense, barrel-shaped heads with crisp, sweet, pale green and white leaves well suited to stir-fries, kimchi, and salads. Beyond its disease resistance, Bilko is noted for holding well in cold storage after harvest, letting a fall crop stretch well into winter use. Cut heads when firm and full-sized, and keep soil consistently moist through head formation for the best texture. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Bill Archer Borage (Variegated Cream-Splashed Borage)
description: Direct sow a quarter inch deep where plants are to grow, since borage resents transplanting once its taproot forms. Bill Archer is a variegated strain of common borage, its fuzzy leaves irregularly splashed with cream, while the star-shaped flowers remain the familiar brilliant blue of the species. Leaf variegation varies from plant to plant and even shifts with temperature and season, so cull any seedlings that emerge solid green to keep the planting showy. Harvest young leaves and flowers for their mild cucumber flavor, and let a few plants stand to self-sow for next year's patch. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Bill Baker Oregano (Tall Pink-Flowered Ornamental Oregano)
description: Bill Baker is a selection of common oregano grown mainly for its display rather than the kitchen, standing noticeably taller than typical wild oregano and topped from midsummer into fall with dense, soft pink flower clusters that pollinators visit heavily. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; like other oreganos, rich or overly wet soil produces floppy, weak-stemmed growth. Its height makes it useful toward the middle of a border or herb garden rather than as an edging plant, and the airy flower heads hold up well when cut fresh or dried. Shear plants back hard in late winter or early spring to keep the clump from becoming woody and sparse at the base. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Biloxi Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Biloxi is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by USDA and Mississippi State University, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — among the lowest chilling requirements of any productive blueberry and making it suitable for the warmest areas of zone 9 and parts of zone 10. The medium-sized, light blue, firm berries ripen in April–May in zone 9 — among the earliest-ripening blueberries of the season — with a mild, sweet, and slightly tart flavor. The early ripening window allows Biloxi to produce before summer heat stresses the plant and before peak blueberry pressure from insects and birds. The vigorous, upright plant habit is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions. Biloxi was tested and released as a variety specifically suited to the Gulf South and Florida, giving it a track record of success in the climate conditions that characterize zone 9a and 9b. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bing Cherry (Dark Sweet Cherry, American Commercial Cherry Standard)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bing must be paired with a compatible pollinizer (Rainier, Lapins, or Black Tartarian) — Bing cannot cross-pollinate Stella, Lambert, or Napoleon; protect ripening fruit from birds using netting; avoid planting in poorly drained sites or low spots where frost collects; Bing ripens in late June to early July in the Pacific Northwest, the timing that has made it the dominant commercial cherry. Bing cherry is the most widely grown commercial sweet cherry variety in the United States — the cherry that defines what most Americans mean when they say 'sweet cherry' — a dark mahogany-red to nearly black, large, firm, heart-shaped variety with exceptionally sweet, complex flavor developed in Oregon in 1875 by Seth Lewelling on his fruit farm near Milwaukie, Oregon. Lewelling named the variety after his Chinese foreman, Ah Bing, in recognition of his contributions to the orchard — an unusual act of recognition for a Chinese immigrant worker in that era. The variety quickly spread from Oregon throughout the Pacific Coast commercial cherry-growing regions (the Columbia Basin of Oregon and Washington State, the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys of California) because its combination of large size, dark color, firm flesh, excellent sweetness, and good shipping characteristics made it ideal for the developing rail-shipped fresh fruit trade. Today, Bing accounts for more than 90% of the sweet cherry production in the Pacific Northwest and a major share of all American commercial sweet cherries. The characteristic Bing appearance — large, round to heart-shaped, very dark mahogany-red to black — is so iconic that 'a bag of Bings' has become synonymous with sweet cherries in American culture, and fresh Bing cherries in early summer represent one of the quintessential seasonal fruits of the American marketplace. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bingo Hardy Kiwi (WULS Poland Red-Blushed Kiwiberry Hybrid)
description: Bingo is a female hardy kiwi cultivar bred at Warsaw University of Life Sciences in Poland from a cross of Actinidia purpurea Purpurna Sadova and A. arguta, with fruit and vine characteristics dominated by its arguta parentage. The elliptical, laterally flattened fruit has smooth yellow-green skin with a strong rose-red blush and is rich in vitamin C with well-regarded flavor. As a dioecious vine, Bingo will not fruit without a compatible male hardy kiwi planted within pollinating range. Its Polish breeding origin gives it reliable cold hardiness for northern gardens on a sturdy, permanent trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bingo Mandarin (Early-Season Seedless Easy-Peel HLB-Tolerant Florida Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and bring container-grown trees under cover or protect in place during hard freezes, since Bingo is a true mandarin without the added cold tolerance of trifoliate-hybrid citrus. Bingo, released by the University of Florida, was bred primarily for improved field tolerance to huanglongbing (citrus greening), the bacterial disease that has devastated citrus groves across Florida and the Gulf South, while still delivering good fresh-market quality: an easy-peel, essentially seedless mandarin with sweet, richly flavored flesh ripening early in the season, from October into November, ahead of many other mandarin selections. It suits the milder, more coastal parts of the Gulf South citrus range where standard mandarins are already grown, rather than the colder inland areas where cold-hardy hybrids are needed. Fertilize according to standard citrus nutrition programs and monitor for greening symptoms even on resistant selections, since tolerance reduces but does not eliminate disease impact. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Binjai Rambutan
description: Binjai is a popular Indonesian rambutan cultivar renowned for exceptionally heavy yields and attractive, spherical, red-skinned fruit covered in soft red spines. The aril is comparatively firm and less juicy than other cultivars, with high sugar content that makes it a favorite for fresh eating, and fruit holds its quality for a few days after harvest better than many softer-fleshed rambutan selections. Grow grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with wind protection, providing steady moisture through bloom and fruit set to maximize the cultivar's naturally high productivity. As with all rambutan, Binjai has no frost tolerance and requires warm, humid, essentially tropical conditions year-round, restricting it to the warmest microclimates of zone 10b and above. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Bintje Potato (Classic Dutch All-Purpose Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow. Bintje is a classic Dutch potato bred in 1904 and, for much of the 20th century, one of the most widely grown potato varieties in Europe, prized for its pale yellow, moderately starchy flesh, excellent all-purpose cooking qualities, and reliable, heavy yields. It is especially well regarded for frying — Bintje is a traditional choice for Belgian and French fries — while also performing well boiled, mashed, or roasted, making it one of the more versatile heirloom varieties available. Tubers have smooth, light tan skin and store reasonably well after curing. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let vines die back fully for mature tubers with the best storage life and frying quality. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Bird Cherry
description: Clean seeds from ripe black fruits in late summer and sow immediately to take advantage of the warm-soil period before winter cold sets in; this two-phase stratification requirement is essential and skipping either phase will delay germination by a full year. Plant in moist, fertile soil near a stream bank or in a woodland clearing, reflecting its natural preference for riparian and marginal woodland habitats throughout northern Eurasia. Bird cherry grows vigorously once established and will naturalize readily, so site it where suckering can be managed or is welcome as a thicket for wildlife. Expect the first flower racemes by year four to six, filling the garden with a heavy almond-like fragrance in mid to late spring before the leaves fully expand. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Bird Grape (Munson's Wild Grape)
description: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large shrub in well-drained sandy soil in full sun. Bird grape is a slender, thin-barked native vine of Florida hammocks, pinelands, and Gulf Coast scrub, distinguished from the related muscadine by its smaller leaves and less shaggy bark, and it climbs readily by tendrils once given support. Its small, sweet black grapes ripen over a long season and are eaten avidly by songbirds, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife hedge or fence line rather than a fruit crop for the table. It tolerates the heat, humidity, sandy soils, and periodic drought of the Gulf Coast better than most grape species, needing only occasional pruning to keep it in bounds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Biriba (Wild Sweetsop, Rollinia, Lemon Meringue Fruit)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil; Biriba grows rapidly in zone 10–11 humid conditions and benefits from regular irrigation and fertilization to produce its heavy crops of large, distinctive fruits. Rollinia deliciosa (often treated as a synonym within the soursop genus: Annona mucosa) is a tropical fruit tree from the Amazon basin of Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, prized by tropical fruit enthusiasts for producing one of the most extraordinarily flavored and unusual-looking fruits in the Annona family. The fruits are large (4–8 inches), covered in soft, flexible, yellowish-green to golden spines or fingerlike projections that soften completely when ripe, and contain white, extremely juicy, sweet-tart flesh described as tasting like a combination of lemon meringue, vanilla custard, and banana — some connoisseurs consider it the finest-flavored of all the Annona relatives, surpassing cherimoya and soursop. The fruits ripen very rapidly (within 1–2 days of picking) and bruise at the slightest touch, making commercial distribution virtually impossible and confining the fruit almost entirely to home gardens and local markets in tropical growing regions. In zone 10–11 South Florida, Biriba is increasingly grown by rare-fruit enthusiasts and community gardens as a fast-growing, productive tree that rewards the patient gardener with extraordinary fruits unavailable in any market. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bishop Crown Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Bishop Crown is a South American aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) with an extraordinary, immediately recognizable shape — a round, slightly flattened main body like a small bell pepper, with 3 or 4 small, prominent, finger-like lobes hanging from the bottom equator like a bishop's miter or crown. This unusual shape (also sold as 'Chapeau de Frade' or 'Balloon Pepper') is unique among peppers and makes it instantly identifiable at markets and in the garden. The flavor is fruity, slightly sweet, and aromatic — mild to medium-hot (5,000–10,000 Scoville) with the distinctive citrusy, tropical fruitiness characteristic of Capsicum baccatum. The thick, crisp walls make it excellent for fresh eating and stuffing — the hollow interior and large body are well-suited to filling with cheese, meat, or grains. The bright red color at full ripeness is vivid and attractive. In zone 9 the perennial habit allows Bishop Crown plants to develop into productive multi-year specimens. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Bishop Crown Pepper (Balloon Pepper, Three-Lobed Ornamental South American Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost. Harvest green for mild use or red for maximum flavor. Bishop Crown (also called Balloon Pepper, Christmas Bell, or Joker's Hat) is a Capsicum baccatum variety named for the distinctive three-pointed crown shape of the fruit — which resembles a bishop's mitre hat from above, or a three-winged balloon when viewed from the side. The fruit has three prominent shoulder lobes that extend outward with a small pendant point below, creating a completely unique silhouette among commonly grown peppers. This shape is genetically characteristic of the Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean peppers, including the ají varieties of South America), where several related varieties share the winged crown form under different names. Bishop Crown fruits measure 2–3 inches in diameter and 1–2 inches in length — small but with a visually complex three-dimensional shape. The walls are thin and crisp, the interior is hollow with minimal placental tissue, and the heat level is mild to moderate (5,000–15,000 Scoville units) — substantially less hot than habanero types but with a fruity, slightly acidic flavor characteristic of the baccatum species. The visual novelty of Bishop Crown makes it one of the most attention-getting peppers in garden displays and at farmers markets, and its mild heat makes it accessible to gardeners who want interesting pepper shapes and flavors without extreme heat levels. Matures in 75–95 days from transplant.

name: Bishop's Crown Pepper (Christmas Bell Pepper, Joker's Hat, Capsicum UFO)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun, well-drained soil, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart. Bishop's Crown is one of the most visually distinctive peppers available to home gardeners — a South American Capsicum baccatum variety that produces fruits with an unmistakable three-lobed shape resembling a bishop's crown or mitre when viewed from above, or an upside-down hat when viewed from the side. The fruits are typically 2–3 inches wide and 1.5–2 inches tall — flat, wide, and three-winged with a central pointed lobe — and they ripen from green through yellow and orange to deep red. The three-winged shape is unique among commercially available peppers and makes each fruit instantly recognizable. Beyond the striking visual character, Bishop's Crown delivers the distinctive fruity, citrusy flavor characteristic of Capsicum baccatum varieties — sweeter and more tropical-fruity than C. annuum types with a pleasant heat in the mild-to-medium range (approximately 5,000–20,000 SHU, varying with growing conditions) that builds gradually rather than hitting all at once. The thin walls make the fruits excellent for fresh eating, stuffing with soft cheeses, or quick-pickled as a garnish. The unusual shape makes every bite a conversation starter and the fruits are genuinely beautiful sliced or whole in salads. Very productive and beautiful in the garden as an ornamental-edible plant. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Bitter Kola
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; bitter kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the humid rainforests of West and Central Africa, this understory to mid-canopy tree bears a fruit whose bitter, astringent seeds are widely chewed fresh across West Africa, valued both as a traditional stimulant, similar in cultural role to true kola nut, and as an important item in traditional hospitality and ceremony. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and require the warm, humid, shaded forest conditions of their native range to thrive, making this a specialty planting for tropical botanical collections, ethnobotanical gardens, or large frost-free properties rather than a typical home garden tree. Water regularly, especially while young, and protect from any exposure to direct hot afternoon sun, which the shade-adapted seedlings do not tolerate well. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Bitter Leaf
description: Root Gymnanthemum amygdalinum (Bitter Leaf) stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plants establish quickly and grow vigorously in warm climates — prune regularly to maintain a compact, shrubby form and encourage dense, tender leaf production; older stems become woody and less productive. Bitter Leaf (formerly Vernonia amygdalina) is arguably the most important vegetable shrub in West and Central African cuisine — a fast-growing, multi-purpose plant grown in every kitchen garden from Nigeria to the DRC, valued equally as a culinary ingredient, medicinal herb, and forage plant. The leaves contain bitter sesquiterpene lactones (vernodalin, vernomygdin) that give the plant its distinctive medicinal and flavor properties; for culinary use, fresh leaves are washed thoroughly, squeezed and kneaded repeatedly in water, and the liquid pressed out to reduce bitterness to a palatable level before adding to soups, stews, and sauces. The squeezed leaves add a distinctive savory, slightly bitter depth to Ofe Onugbu (Igbo bitter leaf soup with cocoyam and assorted meats) and other traditional dishes. In tropical Africa, the plant is also used to treat malaria, diabetes, fever, and intestinal parasites; research has identified antihelminthic and hypoglycemic compounds. In zone 9–12, Bitter Leaf grows as a perennial shrub reaching 4–8 feet; in cooler areas it can be grown as an annual in a large container. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Bitter Leaf
description: Root stem cuttings in moist soil at 75°F; bitter leaf establishes quickly from cuttings in warm weather and begins producing harvestable leaves within a few months. The large, dark green leaves have an intensely bitter flavor that is fundamental to West African cooking — particularly egusi soup, ofe akwu (palm nut soup), and a wide range of Nigerian, Cameroonian, and Ghanaian stews. Fresh leaves are squeezed and rinsed repeatedly in water to reduce bitterness before cooking; or bitter leaf powder (dried, ground leaves) is used in smaller quantities. The bitterness decreases with cooking. The plant is used medicinally throughout sub-Saharan Africa for treating fever, malaria, and hypertension. In Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a large semi-woody perennial. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Bitter Melon (Bitter Gourd, Karela)
description: Nick seeds and sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a trellis or fence; keep soil consistently moist. Momordica charantia (bitter melon, bitter gourd, or karela) is one of the most widely consumed vegetables across South and Southeast Asia, East Africa, and the Caribbean — a fast-growing tropical vine producing distinctive, warty, oblong to tapered green fruits 3–10 inches long that contain a bold, intensely bitter flavor considered an acquired taste but essential in dozens of traditional Asian dishes: Indian karela sabzi (stir-fried bitter melon with onions and spices), Chinese stir-fries with black bean sauce, Filipino ginisang ampalaya, Japanese goya champuru (the classic Okinawan dish). The bitterness decreases substantially when seeds are scooped out and the flesh is salted and rinsed; parboiling further reduces bitterness. Bitter melon has significant traditional medicinal use for blood sugar regulation and is the subject of ongoing pharmaceutical research for antidiabetic compounds. In zone 9, it thrives in summer heat and produces abundantly from June through October; harvest fruits when fully green and before yellowing begins. Matures in 55–85 days from seed.

name: Bitter Yam (Cluster Yam, Bitter Yam)
description: Plant tuber pieces in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun; bitter yam is a tropical African species of yam that produces clusters of small to medium tubers with intensely bitter flavor from toxic alkaloids — these require thorough processing (peeling, boiling in multiple changes of water, and prolonged soaking) to make safe for consumption. Despite this challenge, it is an important food crop in West Africa during food shortages and is also grown for its edible aerial tubers (bulbils) that have lower toxin levels and require less processing. Primarily of interest to gardeners interested in West African food plants, ethnobotany, or food security crops; properly prepared, the tubers have an earthy, slightly sweet flavor similar to other yams. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Bitternut Hickory
description: Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy or clay soil in full sun; bitternut hickory is the most widely distributed hickory in eastern North America and one of the fastest growing, making it valuable as a canopy tree where time to a large shade tree is a priority. The nuts are notably bitter and unpalatable to humans (hence the common name), being too high in tannins for human consumption even after shelling — unlike the sweet-nutted shagbark and shellbark hickories. However, they are consumed by squirrels, deer, and wood ducks after additional caching and processing. The distinctive butter-yellow winter buds are an important winter identification trait. The golden-yellow fall color is attractive, and the tree provides superb canopy for native plant understories. One of the most moisture-tolerant hickories. Matures in 2555–3650 days from seed.

name: Bixby Hazelnut (Gellatly Hybrid Filbert)
description: Bixby is one of the original hybrid hazelnut selections bred in British Columbia by J.U. Gellatly from crosses of the cold-hardy American hazelnut with the larger-nutted European hazelnut, combining winter hardiness with improved nut size over the pure American species. It has served for decades as important parent material in subsequent hybrid hazelnut breeding programs aimed at bringing commercial-scale hazelnut production into cold-winter regions where European hazelnut alone struggles. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a genetically distinct pollenizer, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible. Expect a large, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunk tree, and prune out old wood periodically to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Amber Plum (Early-Season California Japanese Plum)
description: Black Amber (also sold as Blackamber) is an early-summer Japanese plum bred in California that has long been one of the most widely planted commercial plum varieties in the state. The nearly black skin covers firm amber flesh with a pleasant balance of sweetness and tartness, similar in appearance to the later-ripening Friar but ready weeks earlier in late June. The tree is vigorous and productive but needs a different mid-season-blooming Japanese plum nearby, such as Santa Rosa, for reliable pollination and fruit set. Its relatively low chilling requirement makes it a workable choice for warmer zone 8 and 9 gardens where many European plums fail to set fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Aztec Corn (Black Mexican Sweet Corn)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows once soil has warmed, since wind pollination in isolated single rows gives poor ear fill. Black Aztec dates to at least the 1860s in Mexico and the American Southwest and was long grown as a dual-purpose corn: pick the ears for fresh eating while the kernels are still pale cream and milky-sweet, or leave them on the stalk to dry, when the kernels darken dramatically to a glossy blue-black prized for cornmeal and corn flour. Its old-fashioned, richly sweet flavor at the milk stage made it a garden favorite before modern sugary hybrids replaced open-pollinated sweet corns, and the jet-black dried ears remain popular for autumn decoration as well as grinding. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Black Beauty Eggplant
description: Black Beauty is the classic heirloom eggplant, producing large, glossy deep-purple fruits with tender, mild flesh perfect for grilling and roasting. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, and transplant only after nights reliably stay above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun and stake them to support the weight of the fruit. Harvest while the skin is firm and glossy, cutting rather than pulling; picking regularly keeps the plants productive. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Black Beauty Mulberry (Large Sweet Black Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant. Black Beauty is a black mulberry selection prized for producing unusually large, elongated berries with the rich, intensely sweet-tart, wine-like flavor characteristic of true black mulberry (Morus nigra), widely regarded among mulberry enthusiasts as having the finest flavor of any mulberry species — deeper, more complex, and more balanced between sweet and tart than the milder white or red mulberries. The large fruit size makes hand harvest more efficient than picking the smaller berries of many other mulberry types. Because ripe mulberries drop as they mature and stain heavily, plant away from patios, walkways, and parking areas, or spread a sheet beneath the canopy at harvest time to catch fruit. Trees need only light annual pruning to maintain shape and size. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Beauty Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Black Beauty is a University of Arkansas release bred specifically for fresh-market eating, producing very large, glossy black berries with a tender skin and mild, sweet flavor that is less musky than many older muscadine varieties. It is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though nearby vines improve fruit set. Vigor is strong and disease resistance is good across the humid Gulf South. Because berries ripen unevenly over several weeks rather than all at once, plan on repeated picking passes through the harvest season for the best quality fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Beauty Plum (Dark-Skinned Amber-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Black Beauty is a Japanese-type plum grown for its striking dark purple-black skin, which encloses firm, amber-yellow flesh with a sweet, well-balanced flavor and good, meaty texture that holds up well to handling and eating fresh out of hand. The vigorous tree is a reliable commercial and home-orchard producer in California-style plum growing regions, valued for combining attractive dark color with genuinely good flavor rather than color alone. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and has developed full dark color, since plums ripen further off the tree but develop the best flavor with some vine-ripening first. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Beauty Summer Squash
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest plants per hill. This highly productive bush-type zucchini from the 1920s takes little space and yields dark green, glossy fruits with tender skin. Harvest fruit young, around 6 to 8 inches, for the best texture and to keep plants producing. Pick every day or two at peak season, as fruit sizes up fast and overgrown squash slows further set. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Black Beauty Zucchini
description: Black Beauty is a dependable, prolific heirloom zucchini bearing glossy dark-green fruit on compact, bushy plants. Direct-sow two or three seeds per hill after the soil warms to 70F, then thin to the strongest seedling, spacing hills two to three feet apart. Harvest zucchini young at 6-8 inches for the best texture, and pick every day or two at peak season to keep the plant producing. Water evenly at the base and mulch to reduce disease and keep fruit clean. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Black Beauty Zucchini (Classic Dark Zucchini, Italian Squash)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Black Beauty is the classic standard-setting zucchini cultivar — the benchmark dark-green zucchini against which other varieties are measured, widely grown since the mid-twentieth century and still the most recognizable and most-planted zucchini in American home gardens. The compact, bush-habit plant (non-vining, unlike winter squash) produces very dark green, slightly speckled, tender-skinned fruits with mild, slightly sweet flavor and excellent firm texture. Harvest at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality — zucchini left on the plant more than a day or two at peak size rapidly grows into oversized clubs with tough skin and poor flavor. Check plants daily during peak production. Black Beauty is remarkably productive for its compact habit, typically producing more fruit per plant than the garden can reasonably consume during the peak summer weeks. In zone 9, plant in late February to March for the spring window before summer heat triggers powdery mildew and reduces production; a fall planting in late August extends the season. Squash vine borers can devastate plants — check the base of stems for entry holes and use row covers to exclude the moth. Powdery mildew appears in summer heat; newer disease-resistant cultivars extend the productive season where mildew is persistent. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Black Beluga Lentil
description: Sow directly in cool spring soil a few weeks before last frost, taking advantage of this lentil's tolerance for light frost and cool growing conditions. Black Beluga produces small, glossy, jet-black lentils that resemble caviar once cooked, a resemblance that has made it a favorite of chefs and market growers looking to diversify beyond the common brown lentil. The low, wiry plants need minimal input and thrive in lean soil, since excess fertility encourages foliage over pod set. Harvest the whole plant once the majority of pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Black Brandywine Tomato (Dark Potato-Leaf Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage the vine early to support the heavy fruit clusters. Black Brandywine belongs to the celebrated Brandywine family of potato-leaf heirloom beefsteaks, distinguished from the classic pink Brandywine by fruit that ripens to a deep purplish-brown to brick-red color with dark green shoulders, carrying the smoky, rich, complex, almost wine-like flavor that 'black' tomatoes are prized for. The large, somewhat irregular fruit can run smaller and less uniform than standard pink Brandywine, a common trait of this style of dark heirloom tomato, but the depth of flavor more than compensates for growers seeking something beyond a standard slicer. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and pick as soon as color and give indicate ripeness, since the dark skin can make judging ripeness by color alone trickier than with red tomatoes. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Butte Blackberry (Oregon State Extra-Large-Fruited Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a trellis, pruning out fruited floricanes each year after harvest to keep new primocanes productive. Black Butte was released by the Oregon State University blackberry breeding program in the 1980s and is best known among Pacific Northwest growers for producing exceptionally large fruit, with individual berries often noticeably bigger than those of Marionberry or most other trailing types. The berries ripen early in the trailing-blackberry season, are glossy black with good flavor, and their large size makes hand-picking notably faster than with smaller-fruited varieties. Because the canes are thorny and quite vigorous, Black Butte requires the same sturdy trellising and winter pruning used for other trailing blackberries grown in maritime climates. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Black Calabash (Black Gourd Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average tropical soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 10–12; black calabash is a tropical tree of the Bignoniaceae family (the same family as trumpet creeper and catalpa) native to Central American and Caribbean coastal forests, producing unusual, large, round-to-oblong, gourd-like fruits with extremely hard, black shells when mature. The hard shells are used throughout Central America and the Caribbean to make maracas, rattles, cups, bowls, and other traditional crafts and musical instruments — the same traditional use as the unrelated calabash gourd (Lagenaria). The fleshy inner pulp is eaten by bats and birds, which disperse the seeds. The flowers, which appear directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), are interesting botanical curiosities. Adapted to partial shade of tropical forest edges and hammocks. A rare conversation piece for south Florida collectors and native plant enthusiasts. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Black Cardamom
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained but consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in deep to partial shade; Black Cardamom thrives in cool, moist conditions resembling its native Himalayan forest understory — mulch heavily, maintain consistent moisture, and protect from hot afternoon sun and frost. Amomum subulatum (Black Cardamom, Large Cardamom, or Nepal Cardamom) is a large, clumping, ginger-family rhizomatous perennial native to the cool, misty, shaded montane forests of Sikkim (India), Nepal, Bhutan, and adjacent mountain regions, where it grows wild at elevations of 3,000–5,000 feet in dense forest understory along streams and in humid ravines. The plant is cultivated extensively under Alnus nepalensis alder trees in the traditional 'Sikkim Cardamom' agroforestry system, which provides the required dense shade, consistent moisture, and forest microclimate. The seed pods — harvested and kiln-dried or traditionally fire-dried over bamboo smoke — are large (1–1.5 inch), dark brown, wrinkled, and distinctively smoky-camphor-menthol in aroma and flavor, completely different from green cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum). Black cardamom is a fundamental spice in North Indian biryani, dal makhani, garam masala blends, and many Nepali and Tibetan dishes; it is also used medicinally in Ayurvedic, Tibetan, and Chinese traditional medicine. A superb shade-garden spice plant for warm, humid zone 8–10 climates; the large, banana-like foliage is ornamentally attractive even when not in pod. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Cardamom / Greater Cardamom
description: Choose a partially shaded site with deep, rich, constantly moist soil and plant divisions at least 3-5 feet apart, as established clumps spread broadly through underground rhizomes. Water frequently and generously throughout the growing season, as Black Cardamom requires high moisture levels to produce its characteristic large, aromatic pods. Feed with a balanced organic fertilizer in spring and a potassium-rich fertilizer in summer to encourage flower and pod formation, which typically begins in the second or third year. Harvest the mature seed pods at the base of the plant by hand when they turn deep reddish-brown, traditionally before smoke-drying to develop their distinctive camphor-like flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Cherry (Wild Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; black cherry is arguably the most ecologically important fruiting tree in eastern North America, supporting the larvae of over 400 species of moths and butterflies (more than almost any other tree genus), providing early-spring nectar in its white flower racemes, and producing thousands of small black cherries in summer that are consumed by over 70 species of birds — robins, waxwings, thrushes, catbirds, woodpeckers — as well as bears, foxes, and raccoons. The small black cherries are edible and intensely flavorful, traditionally used for cherry wine, jelly, and syrups. The wilted leaves and seeds contain prussic acid and are toxic to livestock. The bark has traditional medicinal use as a cough suppressant. A fast-growing native tree (2–3 feet per year) that can seed prolifically. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Cherry Tomato
description: Black Cherry is an indeterminate heirloom producing clusters of round, dark mahogany cherry tomatoes with a sweet, rich, and complex flavor. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant sturdy seedlings once nights stay above 50F, setting them deep. Give the vigorous vines a tall cage or trellis and prune suckers for airflow, since they can top six feet. Harvest when fruit turns deep purple-brown and gives slightly to the touch; frequent picking keeps the clusters coming all season. Matures in 64–75 days from transplant.

name: Black Cherry Tomato (Dark Purple-Red Cherry Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Black Cherry is one of the most unusual and striking cherry tomato varieties — an heirloom producing small (1-inch), round fruits in a deep mahogany-purple to almost black color with brick-red flesh, offering a distinctly rich, complex, wine-like flavor with chocolate-tomato undertones that is remarkably different from standard red or yellow cherry tomatoes. The dark color comes from high anthocyanin content in the skin — the same antioxidant pigments responsible for the dark color of blueberries and black raspberries — giving Black Cherry a distinctive nutritional profile alongside its unusual flavor. The complex, slightly smoky, wine-tomato flavor makes Black Cherry outstanding in raw preparations where the flavor stands alone: fresh from the vine, in caprese-style salads with mozzarella and basil, or in mixed cherry tomato platters where its dark color contrasts dramatically with red Sun Gold and yellow pear tomatoes. The indeterminate vine produces prolific clusters from transplanting through the end of the warm season. As an open-pollinated heirloom, true seed can be saved from season to season. Resistance to cracking (a weakness of many dark-colored tomatoes) is better than many purple/black tomato varieties. Matures in 64–70 days from transplant.

name: Black Chia (Standard Dark-Seeded Chia)
description: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. Black Chia is the standard, most widely grown dark-seeded chia strain, producing the small, deep-brown-to-black seeds most familiar from commercial chia products, on whorled flower spikes of small purple blooms that appear in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris. Matures in 120–160 days from seed.

name: Black Chokeberry
description: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil — moist or dry, acidic or neutral, clay or sand — in partial shade to full sun; black chokeberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, thriving under conditions that defeat most other fruiting shrubs. Aronia melanocarpa produces stunning clusters of small white flowers with prominent pink anthers in May, glossy, dark-green summer foliage, and massive clusters of small, dark-purple to near-black berries in August and September that persist into winter; the berries are extremely high in anthocyanins and antioxidants — among the highest recorded for any fruit — with an astringent, tart flavor excellent for juices, syrups, and wine. Fall foliage is a brilliant scarlet-red. The plant is essentially bulletproof once established, tolerating wet soils, clay, drought, and partial shade; it spreads by root suckers into dense thickets over time. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Coat Runner Bean (1600s Heirloom Black-Seeded Runner)
description: Black Coat is among the oldest documented runner beans still in cultivation, with references to it in European botanical writing dating back to the 1600s, long before most modern runner bean cultivars existed. Its flowers range from deep orange to cherry-red and are heavily visited by hummingbirds, while young pods can be picked for snap use in the same way as other runner beans. Left to mature, the pods yield glossy black seeds that dry well for winter storage and cooking, giving the variety a genuine dual purpose. Because of its age and rarity, it is grown today mostly by heirloom seed savers and gardeners interested in historic bean varieties. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Black Coco Bean (French Dwarf Dry and Shell Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing dwarf bush plants 4-6 inches apart; no trellising is needed.
