Black Coco is a French heirloom valued for its versatility, with dark lilac flowers giving way to slender pods that are tender and crisp if picked young, meaty and flavorful as fresh shell beans about ten days later, and rich and nutty once fully dried. Harvest pods for shelling when seeds have filled but pods are still green, or leave plants standing until pods dry and rattle for storage as dry beans. This variety tolerates both drought and cooler conditions better than many bush beans, making it a dependable choice across a range of climates. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Black Cumin
description: Black cumin is an easy, drought-tolerant annual with delicate blue flowers followed by seed pods full of pungent black seeds used in cooking and traditional wellness. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, as it dislikes root disturbance. The ornamental flowers attract pollinators before giving way to inflated seed capsules. Let pods dry on the plant, then crush them to release the peppery, aromatic seeds. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Black Cumin (Kala Jeera, Shahi Jeera)
description: Direct sow in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 6 inches; harvest seed heads when fully mature and dry. Bunium persicum (black cumin, kala jeera, or shahi jeera — literally 'royal cumin' in Urdu) is a wild carrot family (Apiaceae) plant from the mountain steppes and alpine meadows of Central Asia — particularly Kashmir, Iran, Afghanistan, and the Hindu Kush range — and represents the genuine botanical source of the highly aromatic spice sold in Indian specialty markets as 'kala jeera' or 'shahi jeera.' It is frequently confused with two other spices sharing the common name 'black cumin': Nigella sativa (black seed or black caraway, an entirely different plant) and regular cumin (Cuminum cyminum). Bunium persicum has a uniquely complex, intense, earthy-herbal-thyme-like aroma with bitter-sweet warmth — dramatically different in character from common cumin, more aromatic and complex, with additional notes reminiscent of dried thyme and warm spice. In Kashmiri cooking, kala jeera is the defining spice of pulao rice (the famous Kashmiri mutton pulao), yakhni lamb broth, and korma dishes. In Persian cuisine, it flavors traditional breads, rice dishes, and pickles. The plant grows as a delicate, feathery-leaved annual resembling miniature Queen Anne's lace, producing small umbel flowers followed by the narrow, ridged, black-brown aromatic seeds. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Black Currant
description: Black currants fruit most heavily on one-year-old wood, so annual renewal pruning is critical: remove one-third of the oldest canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new shoots. The berries have a strong, tannic flavor prized for jams and juices; harvest when the entire strig has turned glossy black. Choose blister-rust-resistant cultivars such as 'Consort' or 'Titania' where regulations permit. Verify local restrictions before planting. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Currant (Ben Hope)
description: Ben Hope is a Scottish-bred black currant selected for resistance to gall mite (big bud) and leaf spot, giving it lower maintenance needs than older black currant cultivars. Its late flowering habit helps buds escape frosts that damage earlier-blooming currants. Bushes grow upright and vigorous, setting heavy clusters of tart, aromatic black berries suited to jams, syrups, and cordials. This cultivar needs cold winters to thrive and is not recommended for the Gulf Coast or other low-chill regions. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Diamond Blackberry
description: Black Diamond is a Washington State University thornless trailing blackberry developed as a machine-harvestable processing cultivar, prized for large, firm, jet-black berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good post-harvest storage compared to older trailing types. Vigorous, long canes require a sturdy multi-wire trellis; fan-train fruiting canes along the wires and cut them to the ground immediately after harvest, tying in the new season's primocanes to bear the following year's crop. Like other Pacific Northwest trailing blackberries, Black Diamond is bred for cool, dry summers and is more disease-prone in hot, humid climates, so growers in the Gulf South should give it full sun, excellent air drainage, and a well-drained raised bed to reduce fungal pressure. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Black Diamond Watermelon
description: Sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, warm soil after last frost; Black Diamond needs full sun and warm nights — it performs best in zones 7–11 and Gulf Coast gardens where the long, hot summers allow the large fruits to fully develop. Black Diamond was one of the most important commercial watermelon varieties of mid-20th century America, grown throughout the South for roadside stands, truck farming, and local markets; the very large (30–50+ lbs), round to oblong fruits have an unusually dark, blue-green skin that approaches black in color and firm, bright red flesh with excellent, classic sweet watermelon flavor. The tough skin and firm flesh gave Black Diamond reasonable shipping quality in an era before refrigerated transport was universal. Now prized as an heirloom variety for gardeners wanting the authentic large-fruited Southern watermelon experience. Days to maturity of 85–90 make it best for long-season Southern and Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Black Elderberry (European Elderberry, Elder)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; prune hard in late winter to maintain shape and vigor. Sambucus nigra (black elderberry or European elder) is the classic European elder — a fast-growing, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree long cultivated for its remarkable botanical generosity: in late spring it produces large, flat-topped, highly fragrant clusters (corymbs) of tiny, cream-white flowers with a distinctive musky-lychee-pear elderflower fragrance; by late summer these transform into heavy, drooping clusters of small (1/4-inch), jet-black, glistening berries. Both flowers and berries are culinary staples in English and Scandinavian cooking: elderflower cordial (steeped flowers, sugar, lemon, citric acid) is one of England's most beloved summer drinks; elderflower 'champagne' (a lightly fermented drink) and elderflower fritters are summer traditions. The berries are made into elderberry syrup (rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C, widely sold as an immune-support supplement), elderberry wine, elderberry jam, and in Scandinavian juices (hyldebær saft). CAUTION: Raw flowers and berries contain mild cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries before eating in quantity; flower clusters are generally safe raw in cordials and wine but not in large raw amounts. The cultivar 'Sambuco' and 'Haschberg' are selected for large berry yields; 'Black Beauty' and 'Black Lace' are ornamental dark-leaved forms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Fonio (Iburu)
description: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; black fonio thrives on poor, marginal soils and needs no fertilizer, but requires consistently warm weather to mature its tiny grain. A close relative of the more widely known white fonio, this ancient West African cereal grass produces tiny, nutrient-dense grains on slender seed heads, traditionally grown in Togo, Benin, and Nigeria on poor soils where few other grain crops perform well, and prized for a quick cooking time and fine, couscous-like texture once hulled. It is one of the most drought- and poor-soil-tolerant of all cultivated cereals, requiring essentially no soil amendment to produce a harvestable crop, though its very small seed size makes hand-processing and hulling labor-intensive at home scale. Hand-harvest seed heads once they dry and turn tan on the plant, and thresh and winnow to separate the tiny grains before cooking or storage. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Black From Tula Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, planting deeply and staking firmly. Black From Tula is a Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato from the Tula region south of Moscow, producing large 8–16 ounce fruits with very dark brownish-purple skin and deep reddish-brown flesh similar to Black Krim but with slightly more robust structure and a complex, smoky, earthy-sweet flavor; it is among the finest of the Russian black-type heirlooms and is particularly well adapted to conditions where hot days are followed by cool nights, which intensifies the dark pigmentation. Harvest when the blossom end yields to gentle pressure and the dark color has fully developed around the equator of the fruit. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Fry Muscadine Grape (Dark-Skinned Sport of Classic Fry)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible self-fertile pollinizer variety nearby. Black Fry is a dark-skinned sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine, retaining the same large fruit size and sweet flavor as its well-known parent while offering the deep black-purple skin some growers and markets specifically prefer over the bronze color. As with the original Fry, individual berries are notably large for a muscadine, and the vine is a strong, productive grower once established. Because it is not self-fertile, ensure a compatible pollinizer variety is planted within pollination range, and harvest as berries fully darken and detach easily with a gentle tug over an extended late-summer harvest window. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Futsu Squash (Japanese Heirloom Kabocha-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing plenty of room for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash valued for its striking appearance — small, flattened, deeply ribbed fruit covered in a warty, near-black rind when first harvested, which fades over several weeks of storage to a warm tan-orange with a slight bloom, a color transformation that also signals improving flavor and sweetness. The dense, dry, deep orange flesh has a rich, sweet, chestnut-like flavor considered among the best of any winter squash by many chefs, excellent roasted, pureed into soup, or used anywhere a rich kabocha-type squash is called for. Vines are vigorous and productive, typically setting several fruit per plant, each running 2-3 pounds, a manageable size for a single meal without excess storage bulk. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before eating — Black Futsu's flavor and sweetness improve markedly with curing and continue to develop in storage over the following months. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Black Galingale / Thai Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in a partially shaded spot with loose, well-draining, humus-rich soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart. Keep the soil consistently moist throughout the active growing season, then reduce watering as the foliage dies back in autumn to allow the rhizomes to cure. Harvest rhizomes in late fall once the tops have yellowed, or leave them in the ground in frost-free climates to naturalize over time. For the best development of the characteristic dark purple flesh, ensure plants receive warm temperatures (above 65 degrees F) through the entire growing season. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Black Gem Blackberry (APF-205T Thornless Primocane University of Arkansas Release)
description: Bred by John R. Clark at the University of Arkansas as selection APF-205T, patented and introduced in 2017 and later marketed as Stark Black Gem, this thornless, upright blackberry fruits on both second-year floricanes and current-season primocanes. Berries are notably sweet, with 11-12% soluble solids and lower acidity than most blackberries, giving it a dessert-quality flavor, and mature plants have been reported to yield 11-15 pounds of fruit per season. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and provide a simple trellis for the vigorous canes. Prune spent floricanes to the ground after the early crop and tip primocanes in midsummer to encourage lateral branching for the fall harvest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Genoa Fig
description: Black Genoa is a widely grown Italian heirloom producing purplish-black skinned fruit with deep amber-pink flesh and a rich, sweet flavor that many growers rank among the best dark-skinned figs for fresh eating. It is a reliably heavy producer of both an early breba crop on overwintered wood and a larger main crop on new growth, giving an extended summer-into-fall harvest in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune in winter to control size, since trees can become quite large and dense without management. Long popular in California and Australian home orchards, it performs well in Mediterranean and humid subtropical climates alike. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Giant Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Large-Fruited Georgia Selection)
description: Plant dormant bushes into raised, well-drained beds amended to a strongly acidic pH, spacing generously since this cultivar builds an especially large, spreading frame over time. Black Giant dates to the same mid-20th-century Georgia rabbiteye breeding program that produced Homebell and Ethel, and it earned its name from unusually large, deep-blue-black berries with a firm skin that holds up well to handling. It is a vigorous, long-lived bush but ripens its crop somewhat unevenly compared to modern cultivars, so home growers should expect to pick over several weeks rather than in one concentrated flush. Keep it mulched with pine bark and prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to maintain fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Gilliflower Apple (Elongated Deep Purple-Red New England Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Black Gilliflower, also historically known as Sheepnose for its distinctive elongated, conical shape said to resemble a sheep's nose, is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s prized for skin that darkens to a deep, dusky purple-red so intense it appears nearly black, one of the most visually striking older American apple varieties. The dry, mildly sweet, somewhat coarse flesh is not as juicy as many modern apples but was historically valued for baking whole and for its distinctive appearance in mixed heirloom displays. The tree is a dependable, long-lived bearer typical of old New England farmstead varieties; harvest in fall once fruit fully darkens, and expect moderate storage life typical of the era's cooking apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions just 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled light; Kaempferia parviflora is compact and low-growing — dies completely back to dormant rhizomes in winter and re-emerges in spring; mulch in zone 8–9 to protect rhizomes from hard frost. Kaempferia parviflora (Black Ginger, Krachai Dam, or Thai Ginseng) is a compact, deciduous, rhizomatous perennial native to Laos and northern Thailand, traditionally cultivated at altitude in the Chiang Mai and Mae Hong Son highlands, and one of the most important medicinal plants in Thai and Lao traditional herbal medicine. The small, dark-purple to nearly black rhizomes (distinctive in color compared to all other Kaempferia species) contain a unique array of methoxyflavones — particularly 5,7-dimethoxyflavone and 3,5,7,3',4'-pentamethoxyflavone — that have been extensively researched for anti-fatigue, adaptogenic, vasodilatory, and exercise-performance properties. Black Ginger is now marketed internationally as a sports supplement and traditional herbal tonic. Small, pale-purple, orchid-like flowers are held just above the ground among attractive, broad, ground-level leaves from spring through summer. An excellent partial-shade novelty herb for zone 8–11 gardens; the compact size makes it ideal for container growing in cooler climates. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Black Gold Jackfruit
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — jackfruit is intolerant of waterlogged soil and will decline rapidly if the root zone remains saturated; Black Gold Jackfruit is a named, semi-dwarf cultivar of Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), the world's largest tree-borne fruit, selected for compact tree size and superior fruit quality — sweet, aromatic, deep yellow flesh with lower latex content than seedling trees, making the fruit more pleasant to prepare and eat. Jackfruit is one of the most nutritionally complete and calorie-dense tropical fruits: the ripe, sweet arils (seed pods) are eaten fresh and have a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and mango; the unripe green fruit, with its fibrous, neutral, meat-like texture, has become internationally popular as a plant-based meat substitute in pulled pork, tacos, curries, and other savory dishes. The combination of edible ripe fruit and valuable unripe culinary use gives jackfruit two entirely different roles in the kitchen — one as a sweet tropical fruit and one as a versatile vegetable protein. In the warmest zone 9 microclimates and zone 10 the semi-dwarf Black Gold produces a manageable ornamental and productive fruit tree that brings one of the most unique and globally significant tropical fruits into the home garden. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Gram (Urad Dal, Urid Bean, Black Lentil)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile to poor soil in full sun; black gram (urad dal) is one of the most important legumes in South Asian cuisine — the small, shiny black pods and seeds are the basis of dal makhani, idli, dosa, pappadams, and dozens of other dishes in Indian, Sri Lankan, and Southeast Asian cooking. The mature dried seeds are split (urad dal) for cooking or used whole; young green pods can also be eaten fresh like snap beans. Unlike many legumes, black gram fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in hot, dry conditions where other beans struggle. An outstanding heat-tolerant food-garden legume for the South and Southwest. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Black Grape Tomato (Dark Purple-Black Grape Cluster Tomato with Complex Rich Flavor)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake. Harvest when fruits are uniformly deep purple-black throughout the cluster. Black Grape Tomato is a compact indeterminate variety producing clusters of small, oval to elongated-grape-shaped fruits that ripen to a very dark purple-black color — one of the darkest small-fruited tomato varieties commercially available. The dark coloration results from high anthocyanin content in the skin (the same class of pigments responsible for the color of blueberries, eggplant, and purple cabbage) combined with the lycopene that gives tomatoes their characteristic red color. When anthocyanins are expressed strongly in tomato skin and lycopene is present in the flesh, the result is a dark fruit that appears almost black in good light. This anthocyanin content has nutritional significance — anthocyanins are potent antioxidants, and dark-fruited tomatoes contain higher concentrations than red or yellow types. The flavor of Black Grape combines the sweetness of a cherry tomato with additional complexity and depth — a rich, almost wine-like quality that distinguishes dark tomatoes from standard red types. The texture is firm and the grape shape (elongated, 1–1.5 inch) makes Black Grape practical for packing and transporting without the splitting that affects rounder cherry types. This firmness combined with the dramatically dark color makes Black Grape particularly popular at farmers markets and in restaurant settings where visual distinction is valued. The variety's compact growth habit relative to Sweet 100 and similar indeterminate cherry types makes it easier to manage in average-sized garden spaces. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Black Hawthorn (Douglas Hawthorn)
description: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; black hawthorn is a widespread native of western North America from Alaska to California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing distinctive shiny black fruits (rather than the red of most hawthorns) that ripen in late summer. The blackish-purple haws are sweet and flavorful, traditionally eaten fresh and dried by Pacific Northwest Native peoples including the Klallam, Nlaka'pamux, and many others. The thorny thickets provide exceptional nesting habitat for songbirds. White spring flowers attract numerous pollinators. The fruit is also made into jam, jelly, and wine. More tolerant of wet soils than most hawthorns and common along stream banks in its native range. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Black Hickory
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, rocky, or red clay soils in full sun; black hickory is the most drought-tolerant hickory native to Texas and the Coastal Plain, naturally inhabiting dry sandy uplands, rocky ridges, and sandstone hills where other hickories fail. The nuts are small and have thick shells relative to their edible kernel, but are consumed by squirrels, deer, wild turkeys, and other wildlife that provide the ecological services of seed dispersal. The dark, rough, blocky bark becomes increasingly distinctive with age. Like all hickories, black hickory is very slow to establish (most growth goes underground in early years as the taproot develops) but eventually becomes a long-lived, tough, low-maintenance tree well-suited to the challenging dry sandy soils of east Texas and Oklahoma. Important wildlife food tree for dry upland woodland habitats. Matures in 2555–3650 days from seed.

name: Black Highbush Blueberry
description: Black highbush blueberry is a wetland-loving native shrub of the eastern United States, ranging south into the Florida panhandle, closely related to and often confused with Vaccinium corymbosum but distinguished by its blackish young twigs and shiny black berries that lack the pale waxy bloom of common highbush blueberry. It naturally colonizes swamp edges, bogs, and pond margins, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and consistently moist, acidic sites where standard highbush blueberry cultivars often struggle. Plants sucker gently to form loose thickets over time and provide the same white urn-shaped spring flowers and valuable wildlife fruit as their more widely cultivated relative, with good red fall color as a bonus. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Highbush Blueberry
description: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; black highbush blueberry is native to wet coastal-plain woodlands and pocosins and tolerates wetter soil than most cultivated blueberries. Vaccinium fuscatum is a tall, southeastern coastal-plain native blueberry with small, urn-shaped white to pink flowers in spring followed by sweet, dark purple-black berries in summer that are edible and attractive to wildlife, growing naturally in the moist, acidic soils of pocosins, bay forests, and wet flatwoods from the Carolinas to the Gulf Coast. Its tolerance for consistently damp soil and light shade makes it a good choice for a rain garden, pond margin, or the moist, partly shaded portion of a mixed berry planting where standard rabbiteye or southern highbush blueberries would struggle. It benefits from a second blueberry species or cultivar nearby for improved pollination and fruit set, following the same acidic-soil culture as other Vaccinium. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Horehound
description: Avoid during pregnancy, as this herb has a traditional history of use as a uterine stimulant. Direct-sow around the last frost into average, well-drained soil; this coarse, strong-smelling mint-family perennial naturalizes easily and self-seeds once established. Traditionally the flowering tops are dried for tea used to settle nausea and mild anxiety, distinct from white horehound (Marrubium vulgare), which is used mainly for coughs. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Black Huckleberry
description: Black huckleberry (Gaylussacia baccata) is a native eastern North American shrub distinct from Vaccinium huckleberries, bearing shiny blue-black berries in summer that differ from blueberries in having 10 large, hard seeds rather than many tiny seeds. Plants form slow-spreading colonies via rhizomes in dry, acidic soils (pH 4.0–5.0) and are extremely fire-adapted and long-lived. The berries have a rich, complex flavor prized for pies and preserves — often considered superior to blueberries by foragers. Difficult to cultivate commercially; best suited to naturalistic plantings in appropriate native habitat. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Ischia Fig
description: Black Ischia is a small-to-medium fig with near-black, purple-black skin that lacks a pronounced neck, opening to reveal strawberry-pink to red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor. Long grown on the Mediterranean island of Ischia and popularized in American gardens through heirloom fruit exchanges, it typically bears both a light early breba crop and a heavier main crop in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune lightly in winter to maintain an open, easily harvested framework, since the thin skin bruises readily. It is valued by home growers for its rich flavor rather than shipping quality, making it best suited to dooryard planting rather than commercial production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Jack Fig (Compact Semi-Dwarf Dark-Fruited Container Fig)
description: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to maintain size and shape. Black Jack is a compact, semi-dwarf fig tree — a sport or selection from the Brown Turkey class producing somewhat smaller stature (8–12 feet rather than the 15–25 feet of standard fig trees) while bearing large, richly flavored dark purple-black fruits. The moderate compact habit makes Black Jack one of the most practical fig varieties for residential gardens and particularly well-suited to large containers (20–25 gallon) for small spaces, patios, and areas where a standard-sized fig would be too large. The fruits are medium to large, elongated, with dark purple-black to near-black skin and deep strawberry-red flesh — a visually dramatic appearance that makes the fruits ornamentally attractive at the harvest stage. The flavor is rich, very sweet, and fig-like with deep, complex, sweet notes that improve when fruits are allowed to fully ripen on the tree (they should feel soft and droop slightly at the neck before harvest). Black Jack produces reliably in zone 7–11 with proper cold protection when young. In zone 9, the long, warm growing season allows excellent main crop development and often a bonus early-season breba crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Jack Zucchini (Classic High-Yielding Dark Green Zucchini)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Black Jack is a classic open-pollinated dark green zucchini grown for its vigorous, upright bush habit and dependable, heavy yields of glossy, cylindrical, deep green fruit with tender, mild-flavored flesh. It has long served as a dependable garden standard for gardeners wanting a straightforward, reliable zucchini without the complexity of some newer hybrid disease-resistance packages, performing well across a wide range of soils and conditions. Pick fruit at six to eight inches long for the best flavor and texture, and harvest every day or two once the plant starts producing, since zucchini left on the vine even briefly can balloon rapidly into oversized, seedy, less flavorful fruit. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Black Kabuli Chickpea (Dark-Seeded Heirloom Garbanzo Bean)
description: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, giving plants full sun and lean-to-average fertility, since overly rich soil favors foliage over pod set. Black Kabuli produces the same bushy, drought-tolerant growth habit as other chickpeas, but each pod holds one or two dark brown to near-black seeds that keep their striking color when dried, making them a favorite for gardeners who like to grow and cook heirloom bean and legume varieties not found in stores. Flavor is often described as earthier and nuttier than standard tan Kabuli chickpeas, and the dried seeds hold their shape well in long-simmered stews. Handle mature plants carefully, since the foliage and pods carry the same sticky, irritating hairs typical of the species; harvest once most pods have dried and turned brittle, then thresh and store the seed somewhere cool and dry. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Black Kat Pumpkin
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil once frost danger has passed, giving vines room to sprawl. These dramatic, deeply ribbed pumpkins darken as they mature until nearly black and weigh only 1 to 2 pounds, making tidy personal-sized decorations. Group several together for striking fall displays. Leave fruit on the vine until the rind hardens and color fully develops, then cut with a bit of stem attached for the best keeping quality. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Black Knight Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Black Knight is a purple passionfruit cultivar distinguished by its deep, nearly black rind at full ripeness and dense, richly aromatic, sweet-tart pulp that many growers rate among the most flavorful of the purple types. Like other purple passionfruit, it fruits within the first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant and drops ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to pick. The vine is vigorous and needs sturdy support along with periodic tip-pruning to keep growth directed toward fruiting wood. In zone 9, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily before winter, since it shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit types and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Black Knight Tatsoi
description: Black Knight tatsoi is a heirloom Asian green forming tidy rosettes of dark, spoon-shaped leaves with a sweet, mild mustard flavor. Direct-sow shallowly in early spring and again in late summer, thinning plants to 6-10 inches for full rosettes or leaving them close for baby greens. Harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut the whole rosette; the plant tolerates hard frost and sweetens in cold weather. It grows quickly and does well in containers and cold frames for winter harvests. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Black Krim Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This Russian heirloom produces baseball-sized, 10 to 12 ounce fruits with reddish-brown flesh and a rich, slightly salty flavor, and it sets fruit well in heat. Provide a sturdy stake or cage for the indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly to reduce cracking, and harvest when shoulders take on their characteristic dusky color. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Black Krim Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost risk passes into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Krim is a heirloom beefsteak tomato originating from Crimea (the Black Sea region of Ukraine), producing medium-to-large fruits with a distinctive deep brownish-red to almost black skin with green shoulders, and dark red marbled flesh with a rich, complex flavor that is earthy, smoky, and slightly sweet. One of the most striking and flavorful of the dark or 'black' tomato types. Fruits show their best color in warm weather with cool nights; in hot climates the colors may be less dramatic but flavor remains outstanding. Harvest when the skin darkens significantly and gives slightly to pressure. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Krim Tomato
description: Black Krim is a Crimean heirloom beefsteak bearing large, dark purple-brown fruits with a rich, full-bodied, faintly smoky and salty flavor. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights are reliably warm. Support the indeterminate vines with a strong cage or stake and prune suckers for air movement to reduce cracking in the shoulders. Harvest when the fruit develops its dark color and gives slightly; the color deepens in hot weather and sun. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Limbertwig Apple (Slow Food Ark of Taste Southern Cider Limbertwig)
description: Black Limbertwig is a Slow Food USA Ark of Taste-listed heirloom, one of the darkest-skinned of the many Southern Limbertwig strains, with red fruit deepening over a green background as it ripens in October. The yellow flesh is juicy with a distinctive smoky, musky tang layered over a deep sweet base, a flavor profile Southern heirloom orchardists rate among the best of the Limbertwig family for cider and apple butter. Like its relatives it takes its name from limber, drooping twigs that bend rather than snap under a heavy crop. It is not self-fruitful and should be planted with another apple cultivar for cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Madeira Fig (Prized Dark-Skinned Strawberry-Red Fleshed Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Madeira, of Portuguese origin, is prized among serious fig growers as one of the finest-flavored dark fig varieties available, producing deep purple-black skinned fruit that opens to reveal dense, richly colored strawberry-red flesh with an intensely sweet, complex flavor that has earned it a devoted following among fig collectors and specialty growers. The tree has moderate vigor compared to some more rampant fig varieties and performs best with a long, warm growing season to fully ripen its crop and develop peak flavor. Given its more particular growing requirements and somewhat lower yields than workhorse varieties, it is often grown as a specialty or connoisseur's fig alongside more prolific everyday varieties rather than as a primary production tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Mission Fig
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Black Mission fig is the most widely grown commercial fig in California, introduced by Spanish Franciscan missionaries in the 1700s and now the cornerstone of the California fig industry. It produces two crops yearly in favorable climates — a breba crop on last year's wood in early summer, and a main crop in late summer to fall. The large, purplish-black figs have pink to reddish flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet-jammy flavor that is among the finest of all fig varieties. Excellent fresh, dried, or made into preserves. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and is relatively drought-tolerant once established. In humid climates, fruit splitting and souring can be problematic; select LSU Purple or Celeste for the Southeast. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Mitcham Peppermint
description: Black Mitcham is the historic English-origin peppermint strain that became the backbone of American commercial peppermint oil production in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its exceptionally high menthol content and clean, intense peppermint flavor. Stems and leaf undersides carry a distinctive dark bronze-red flush that darkens further in cool weather, making the plant easy to distinguish from ordinary green peppermint at a glance. Grow it in a contained bed or sunken pot in consistently moist, rich soil, since like all mints it spreads aggressively by rhizome and will overrun neighboring plants if left unchecked. Choose this cultivar over generic peppermint when you want the strongest, most classic peppermint flavor for tea, extracts, or candy-making. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Monukka Grape
description: Introduced to the United States from Central Asia in the early 20th century, Black Monukka bears small to medium, elongated, reddish-black seedless berries with a distinctly sweet, honeyed flavor on medium, loose clusters that ripen mid-season. It is one of the oldest seedless grape varieties grown in American home gardens and is well suited to both fresh eating and drying into raisins. Vines are vigorous and productive, tolerating a wider range of climates than many other vinifera table grapes, though annual dormant pruning to a permanent cordon system keeps fruiting wood renewed and clusters well formed. It benefits from a long, warm season but is somewhat more forgiving of cooler summers than late-ripening varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Mulberry
description: The black mulberry is a slow-growing, long-lived tree bearing intensely flavored dark fruit far superior to that of white or red mulberries. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a spot sheltered from cold winds. It is self-fertile, so one tree crops well, though the staining fruit is best sited away from paving. Prune only lightly in winter, as mulberries bleed heavily from large cuts. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Black Mustard
description: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in early fall where winters are mild; black mustard grows quickly into a tall, branching plant with small, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers in loose clusters, followed by slender seed pods that shatter readily when fully ripe. It produces the pungent, sharply flavored small brown-black seeds traditionally used to make true Dijon-style prepared mustard and are also used whole in Indian and other South Asian tempering and pickling, delivering more heat and complexity than the milder white mustard seed. Because ripe pods shatter and drop seed the moment they dry, harvest whole seed heads into a paper bag as soon as pods begin to turn from green to brown, then finish drying and threshing indoors to avoid losing the crop to shattering in the field. Rotate away from other brassica family crops each season to reduce pest and disease buildup, and expect volunteer seedlings the following year from any seed that drops before harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Black Nebula Carrot (Deep Purple Skin and Flesh)
description: Black Nebula is a specialty carrot bred for pigment that runs all the way through the root rather than surrounding an orange core, giving nearly black-purple skin and a deep purple interior with only a faint lighter center. Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and keep the row consistently moist until germination, which is slower and less even than with standard orange carrots. The intense anthocyanin coloring holds up well in raw preparations, quick pickles, and shaved salads, though like other purple carrots it fades toward gray-brown if simmered without an acid. Thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart for well-formed roots and harvest at 70-80 days for full flavor and color development. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Black Nightshade (Garden Nightshade)
description: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; black nightshade is a widespread, weedy annual cosmopolitan plant whose cultural significance varies dramatically by geography — considered an undesirable toxic weed in Europe and North America, but an important traditional vegetable food plant across Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, where the young leaves and fully ripe berries are eaten after cooking (boiling, sautéing, or stewing). The leaves are cooked as a pot herb (like spinach) across many African countries where it is called 'mnavu' (Swahili) or 'imboga' (various East African languages). The fully ripe, jet-black berries (glossy, round, about 1/4 inch) are cooked into sauces and stews or made into jam. IMPORTANT: unripe green berries contain toxic solanine and must never be eaten raw or unripe — only fully ripe (jet-black), well-cooked berries are safe. Young leaves are also cooked, not eaten raw. Self-sows readily in disturbed, rich soil. Tolerates partial shade. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Black Opal Tomato
description: Black Opal is a modern English open-pollinated selection bred from Black Cherry for a firmer texture and sweeter flavor than its parent, ripening to a deep chocolate-black skin over dusky red flesh. Indeterminate vines are early and heavy-yielding, producing clusters of half-to-one-ounce fruit through the season on a slightly more compact growth habit than many dark cherry types. Regular even watering and full sun bring out the complex, well-balanced sweetness the variety is known for. Select this cultivar for gardeners who want the dark cherry-tomato flavor profile with improved earliness and cracking resistance. Matures in 60–68 days from transplant.

name: Black Oxford Apple (Maine Heirloom Long-Keeping Purple-Black Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Black Oxford originated in Paris, Maine in the 1790s and takes its name from its remarkably dark skin — deep purple, nearly black, and covered with a dusty blue-gray bloom — one of the most visually striking apples in American horticulture. Fresh off the tree in fall the dense, firm flesh is sharply tart, but Black Oxford is famous for its extraordinary keeping ability, mellowing and sweetening in cold storage over months and often holding excellent quality clear into spring, longer than almost any other apple variety. This long storage life made it historically valuable in northern New England before mechanical refrigeration, and it remains prized today by cider makers and heirloom orchardists both for its keeping quality and its distinctive appearance. Harvest in mid to late fall and store cool for the best results, tasting periodically since the flavor genuinely improves with age. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Pearl Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Processing Cultivar)
description: Black Pearl is a thornless, trailing blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University, one of three thornless trailing cultivars (alongside 'Black Diamond' and 'Nightfall') developed to give the processing industry machine-harvestable alternatives to the thorny standard 'Marion'. Trials found its fruit quality, once frozen and processed, comparable to Marion, making it attractive for jam, juice, and bakery use in addition to fresh eating. Train the long, sprawling canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since like other trailing blackberries they need full support and generous row spacing. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and tie in the current season's primocanes for next year's crop, and site the planting for excellent air movement to limit fungal disease in humid climates. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Black Pearl Ornamental Pepper (Near-Black Foliage Award-Winning Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Pearl won the All-America Selections award in 2006 for its dramatic, glossy, near-black foliage and abundant small, round, pearl-like fruit that emerges black and ripens through deep red, creating a striking, ever-changing color display on a single compact plant that works as well in a decorative container or mixed bed as it does in a vegetable garden. The fruit carries substantial heat, comparable to a cayenne pepper, and while edible it is grown mainly for ornamental impact rather than as a culinary crop. Its dark foliage provides dramatic color contrast against silver or chartreuse companion plants, and the compact, well-branched habit needs no staking or special care beyond routine watering and feeding. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Black Pearl Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Black Pearl is an All-America Selections award-winning ornamental pepper notable for its intensely dark, shiny, almost black foliage throughout the growing season — one of the darkest-leaved edible plants available for ornamental garden use. The small, round, pea-sized fruits emerge shiny black, gradually transitioning through red-black to a final vivid red as they mature, so that at any moment the plant displays all three colors simultaneously against the near-black foliage — creating a dramatically ornamental display that performs equally well as a container specimen and in ornamental borders. The fruits are genuinely hot (approximately 10,000–30,000 Scoville) and fully edible — suitable for hot sauces, dried chiles, and as a garnish for dishes where both heat and visual drama are desired. The compact size and outstanding ornamental value make Black Pearl one of the most popular choices for edible ornamental garden design. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Black Pearl Wax Apple
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with steady moisture, since wax apple fruit quality and size drop sharply under drought stress. Black Pearl is one of the most sought-after wax apple selections grown in Taiwan, prized for fruit that ripens to a deep purplish-red, almost black skin, noticeably darker than standard pink or red wax apple types, enclosing crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh with the characteristic hollow, rose-scented core. Compared to seedling wax apple trees, Black Pearl grows in a shorter, more compact form that is easier to net against birds and harvest without a ladder. Pick fruit by hand as soon as the skin reaches full color, since ripe wax apple does not continue to sweeten after picking and bruises easily, and keep young trees well mulched and watered through their first two dry seasons to establish a strong root system. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with a support structure or trellis — black pepper is the world's most traded spice and a shade-tolerant climbing vine native to India's Malabar Coast, where it grows as a climbing epiphyte in the forest understory. In tropical gardens (zone 10–12) the vine climbs 10–30 feet up a tree or post, producing clusters of peppercorns that start green, turn red when fully ripe, and are picked at different stages to produce green pepper (fresh), black pepper (dried unripe), red pepper (ripe), and white pepper (ripe, hull removed). The vine requires warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture. As a container plant in zone 8–9 gardens, it makes an attractive tropical accent vine moved indoors for winter. A genuinely rewarding home-grown spice for warm-climate gardeners. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Peppermint (Strong Peppermint)
description: Plant divisions in moderately moist, fertile soil in partial to full sun and contain spreading runners with buried barriers or grow in submerged pots; black peppermint (Mentha x piperita f. piperita) is distinguished from white peppermint by its dark purple-tinged stems and leaf margins, deeper green leaves, and significantly higher menthol content — the form prized for peppermint tea, essential oil production, and confections where strong clean menthol flavor is essential. Harvest stems just before flowering for maximum oil content, cutting back to 2–3 inches above ground to promote bushy regrowth; a second flush will come before frost. Divide every 2–3 years as older plants lose vigor. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Black Plum
description: Plant Vitex doniana in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established; prune young trees to develop good branching structure; the tree grows slowly at first then more vigorously once the root system is established. Black Plum is one of the most important multi-purpose trees of the African sahel and Sudan savanna zone — spread across a vast belt from Senegal and Gambia through Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, and east to Sudan, Uganda, and Kenya. The sweet, date-like, purple-black fruits are eaten fresh throughout the region, made into local beverages, and dried for storage; the nutritional profile includes iron, calcium, and vitamins. Young leaves are cooked and eaten as a vegetable (especially important during the 'hungry season' before the harvest) and the leaves are also used medicinally for fever and rheumatism. The dense, golden-yellow heartwood is highly prized for furniture, carvings, drums, and mortars; a single tree can be worth significant sums in local markets. In the Sahel agroforestry system, Black Plum is a valued component of parkland farming systems (farmer-managed natural regeneration) where it provides food, shade for crops, fodder, and materials. An outstanding drought-tolerant shade tree for zone 10–12 dry tropical gardens. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Black Plum Tomato (Russian Heirloom Dark-Red Paste Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong cage or stake support and consistent, even moisture. Black Plum is a Russian or Eastern European heirloom paste-type cherry tomato that has become one of the most appreciated 'dark' tomato varieties in American heirloom tomato culture — producing small (1.5–2 inch), plum-shaped fruits with an extraordinarily dark skin color ranging from deep mahogany-red to near-black-purple on the sun-exposed surface and shoulders. The dark color comes from high levels of chlorophyll that breaks down to brownish-red tones in the skin, combined with the fruit's deep red flesh, creating an intensely rich, almost chocolatey appearance that makes Black Plum one of the most visually distinctive cherry/paste types. The flavor is equally distinctive: rich, complex, and deeply sweet with more winey, umami-forward notes than typical sweet red cherry types — a sophisticated flavor more commonly associated with large beefsteak types than small tomatoes. Black Plum produces in abundant clusters throughout the season and is excellent fresh in salads, halved on cheese plates, dried whole, or roasted — the meaty, paste-type interior with relatively few seeds makes it particularly good for drying and roasting. One of the most beautiful and flavorful of all dark tomato varieties. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Black Prince Tomato (Russian Black Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Black Prince performs exceptionally well in cool climates due to its Siberian origin and can be transplanted earlier than most heat-requiring varieties. Black Prince is a Russian heirloom tomato from Siberia, where it was developed to produce ripe fruits under cool growing conditions with a shorter summer season than most tomato-growing regions — a characteristic that makes it one of the earliest-maturing of the 'dark tomato' class, which typically run late. The medium (3–6 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits develop dark red-purple to near-black pigmentation in sun-exposed areas of the skin (from anthocyanin development under UV exposure), while shaded areas remain deep burgundy-red; the interior flesh is dark red to mahogany with dense, meaty texture and a distinctively complex flavor profile — sweet and rich with earthy, slightly smoky undertones and good acid balance. Black Prince is an excellent introduction to the 'dark tomato' flavor category for gardeners unfamiliar with the type; it is earlier, more compact, and more productive than larger dark varieties like Cherokee Purple or Paul Robeson, making it particularly suitable for containers, short seasons, and cooler gardens. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Black Quinoa (Deep Black-Seeded Grain Quinoa)
description: Black quinoa produces tall seed spikes densely packed with small, glossy jet-black seed, a distinct type from the more familiar tan, red, or bicolor quinoa strains and one that takes noticeably longer to fully ripen. Its dark, tightly closed seed coat sheds moisture well, which can help it stand up to a wetter harvest window better than paler quinoa types. Grow it exactly as other quinoa: direct sow into cool spring soil, keep watering light once established since quinoa dislikes soggy roots, and stake or support plantings in windy sites given their height. Harvest whole seed heads once thoroughly dry and shattering starts, then thresh and rinse well before cooking, as the seed coat still carries the typical bitter saponin layer. Matures in 110–140 days from seed.

name: Black Radish
description: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in loose, deeply prepared, fertile soil in late summer for fall harvest; thin seedlings to 6–8 inches to allow the large roots to develop fully. Black radish is an ancient European winter storage root with rough, jet-black skin and crisp, pungent white flesh — significantly hotter than spring radishes and reminiscent of strong horseradish. Harvest after light frost, which mellows the intense pungency; roots can reach 3–4 inches in diameter and 4–6 inches long. The robust flavor is best appreciated when the flesh is grated raw into salads with sour cream, pickled in brine, or cooked in soups where the heat moderates pleasantly. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Black Radish (Spanish Black Radish, Winter Radish)
description: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in deeply cultivated, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 4–6 inches for large root development. Raphanus sativus 'Black Spanish' (black radish or Spanish black radish) is a large, ancient European winter radish producing round to turnip-shaped roots with jet-black, rough, firm skin and strikingly white, dense, extremely pungent flesh — the flavor is intensely sharp, mustard-hot, and horseradish-like when raw, making it far more assertive than common spring radishes. Black radish is one of the oldest cultivated radish types — documented in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome — and remains popular in Eastern Europe, Germany, and France as a traditional winter vegetable. Raw, it is grated and dressed with salt, sour cream, or vinegar as a condiment (German Schwarzer Rettich); cooked, the pungency mellows considerably and the radish becomes milder and sweet. The roots store exceptionally well in cool conditions for weeks to months — a genuine winter storage vegetable unlike spring radishes, which must be used immediately. Black radish is also highly valued in naturopathic medicine for liver-supportive and digestive-stimulating properties attributed to high glucosinolate content. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Black Raspberry (Black Cap, Thimbleberry)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; black raspberry is a native eastern North American cane fruit with intensely flavored, deep purple-black fruits that are prized above all other raspberries for their rich, complex flavor — more aromatic and concentrated than red or purple types. The canes are biennial, growing vegetatively the first year (primocanes) and fruiting in summer of the second year (floricanes), after which they die and should be cut out. New primocanes arise from the base annually. Unlike red raspberry, black raspberry spreads by tip-rooting: when the arching cane tips touch the ground in late summer, they root and form new plants. Harvest the hollow-centered fruits when they turn fully black — they release easily from the core. Excellent fresh, in preserves, syrup, and wine; also dried. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Black Raspberry (Niwot)
description: Niwot is a primocane-fruiting black raspberry from Colorado State University's breeding program, notable for producing fruit on current-season canes in addition to the traditional floricane crop, which extends harvest into late summer and fall. Berries are firm, glossy black, and carry the rich, classic black raspberry flavor prized for preserves and baking. The upright canes are vigorous and more manageable than many older black raspberry selections. Black raspberries generally struggle in hot, humid summer climates, so Niwot performs best in cooler-summer regions rather than the Deep South. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Sage (Honey Sage)
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; black sage is one of the dominant shrubs of California coastal sage scrub — a white-flowered, strongly aromatic native sage with dark green, wrinkled, very fragrant leaves that produce a characteristic camphor-sage scent that perfumes the California coastal air on warm days. The clusters of small, white to pale lavender flowers in spring are exceptionally attractive to native bees — black sage is one of the most important native bee plants in California, producing abundant nectar and pollen particularly for bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many solitary native bees. The dried seed capsules (nutlets) are eaten by seed-eating birds and small mammals. Completely drought-tolerant once established, requiring no summer irrigation in coastal California gardens. The aromatic leaves can be used as a culinary sage substitute, with a flavor described as a blend of culinary sage and camphor. An essential native for California habitat gardens. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Black Sapote
description: Black sapote is a relative of the Asian persimmon; when ripe its flesh turns chocolate-brown and has a rich, pudding-like flavor often described as chocolate mousse. Trees are dioecious or polygamous — plant at least two seedlings or a grafted female with a male nearby for reliable fruiting. They prefer well-drained, fertile soils with a pH near 6.5 and are sensitive to frost, waterlogging, and salt winds. Harvest when the skin turns from bright olive-green to olive-yellow-green and the fruit gives to very gentle pressure; leave at room temperature 5–7 days until the inside is completely dark and custardy. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Black Sapote (Chocolate Pudding Fruit)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; black sapote produces tomato-sized fruits with thin green skin that turns olive-yellow at full ripeness, concealing soft black pulp with a rich, sweet, chocolate-like flavor that famously resembles chocolate pudding — often eaten directly from the skin with a spoon. A relative of persimmons, it must be completely soft before eating; hard fruits are extremely astringent. Excellent used in smoothies, ice cream, mousses, and as a low-fat substitute for chocolate in baked goods. Trees are moderately fast-growing and begin bearing 3–5 years from transplant; an outstanding conversation piece and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 10–12 gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Satin Blackberry (Classic Thornless Semi-Erect Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the sprawling semi-erect canes onto a sturdy two-wire trellis. One of the earliest widely available thornless blackberry cultivars, introduced in the 1970s, Black Satin remains valued for its reliable, heavy production of large, glossy, firm black fruit with good flavor, ripening over a fairly long midsummer season. The semi-erect canes need more support and tying than fully upright modern cultivars, but the plant is vigorous, dependable, and tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting productive and make room for new fruiting canes. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Black Sea Man Tomato (Compact Russian Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger passes. Black Sea Man is a Russian heirloom with distinctive potato-leaf foliage and a naturally compact habit that makes it a good choice for smaller gardens or large containers where full-sized indeterminate vines would be unwieldy. The mahogany-brown fruit has olive-green shoulders and deep, marbled flesh with a rich, smoky-sweet flavor. Modest staking is usually enough to support the shorter, sturdier plants through their production window. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Black Sea Tea (Georgian Coastal Cold-Hardy Cultivar)
description: Black Sea Tea traces to former Soviet-era tea research plantings on the Georgian coast of the Black Sea, a growing region with a climate more similar to the American mid-South than to tea's native subtropical range. Like its close relative Sochi, it was selected primarily for cold tolerance and vigorous, reliable growth rather than for any single specialized tea style, producing narrow, roughly 4 to 5 inch leaves on a broad, multi-stemmed shrub. Home growers value it for pushing tea cultivation into cooler zones than typical China-type selections tolerate. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias, and begin harvesting once plants are three to four years old. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Black Seed (Black Cumin)
description: Broadcast or direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun; black seed (Nigella sativa) is the source of one of the oldest and most significant medicinal spices in the world, used continuously for 3,000 years in Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African medicine. It is entirely distinct from love-in-a-mist (Nigella damascena), though both share the same feathery foliage and ornamental seed capsules. The peppery, slightly bitter, toasted seeds are used to top breads in Egypt and Turkey, are a key component of Indian panch phoron spice blend, and flavored Ethiopian berbere. Allow seed capsules to fully ripen and dry on the plant before harvesting, then shake seeds into a bag. Plants self-sow reliably in suitable climates. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Black Seeded Simpson Leaf Lettuce
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate in cool soil. A garden favorite since 1850, this loose-leaf variety yields full-sized, frilly leaves in just over a month and baby greens in about three weeks. It withstands hot, dry conditions and light frosts better than many other lettuces. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again supply, or cut the whole plant before it bolts in heat. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Black Seeded Simpson Lettuce
description: Black Seeded Simpson is a fast, reliable heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tender, light-green ruffled leaves and a mild, crisp flavor. Direct-sow shallowly, barely covering the seed since light aids germination, and thin plants to 6-10 inches apart. Harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again for a prolonged supply, and succession-sow every two weeks from early spring through fall. Provide afternoon shade in hot weather to delay bolting; it also grows well in containers and hydroponics. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Black Sesame
description: Direct sow thinly in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; black sesame is a color variant of common sesame producing jet-black seeds with a distinctly richer, nuttier, and more complex flavor than the pale white sesame seeds familiar from Western cooking — the higher pigment content is associated with higher concentrations of antioxidant sesamin, sesamolin, and lignans. Black sesame is the standard seed for traditional East and Southeast Asian preparations including black sesame paste (used in tang yuan rice balls and Asian pastries), black sesame ice cream, Japanese gomashio (sesame salt), Korean jook (sesame rice porridge), and black sesame halva. Toasted black sesame seeds have an almost smoky, deep nutty profile that white sesame cannot replicate. The slender, upright, ornamental plants with white-to-pink tubular flowers are attractive in the garden. Harvest by cutting and hanging entire plants over a cloth when pods begin to ripen — mature pods open at the top and shed seeds readily. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Black Spanish Grape (Lenoir Grape, Jacques Grape, Historic Gulf Coast Red Grape)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Black Spanish is notably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the thin, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country; train on cordon system; prune in late winter; fruit ripens in July–August in the Gulf South; the small, dark blue-black berries are very juicy with moderate tannins and produce a robust, full-bodied red wine and excellent red grape juice. Black Spanish (also called Lenoir, after a French viticulturalist named Lenoir who promoted it, or 'Jacques' after a French settler who may have introduced it) is a historic American hybrid grape variety that has been cultivated in Louisiana, Texas, and the broader Gulf South since before the Civil War — one of the earliest wine grapes to be grown commercially in Texas. Its precise parentage is disputed (likely a complex hybrid of Vitis aestivalis or Vitis berlandieri with other American species, possibly with some vinifera ancestry from early French colonial plantings), but its performance characteristics are well-established: Black Spanish is exceptionally tolerant of Pierce's disease, heat, and drought. In the 19th century, when European settlers attempted to establish vineyards in the South with vinifera varieties, virtually all of these plantings failed within a few years due to Pierce's disease — but varieties like Black Spanish, which incorporated native American species with natural resistance, survived and produced fruit year after year. This made Black Spanish the cornerstone of the early Texas and Louisiana wine industries, and it remained the dominant red grape in Texas through much of the early 20th century. The wine produced is dark, deeply colored, with robust tannins and an earthy, slightly rustic character that is quite different from European reds but has its own distinctive appeal. Modern Gulf Coast winemakers continue to work with Black Spanish as a component of blended wines. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Spanish Radish
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches in loose, deep, well-prepared soil in full sun; Black Spanish Radish is an ancient winter storage radish documented in cultivation since at least the 1500s and widely grown in France, Germany, and Eastern Europe as a cold-season storage crop. The round to slightly elongated roots are 3–4 inches across with striking jet-black skin and brilliant white, very firm, pungent flesh inside — the flavor is substantially stronger and more peppery than spring radishes, with a dry, dense texture and a sharp spicy bite that is characteristic of all large winter radish types. The traditional preparation is sliced paper-thin and eaten with butter and salt as a crudité, or grated raw into salads where the pungency is diluted by other ingredients. Black Spanish radish stores for 2–3 months in cold storage with the greens removed, making it a genuine cold-pantry root crop unlike the quick-to-deteriorate spring radish types. The distinctive black skin and white interior create dramatic visual contrast in raw preparations. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Black Summer Bok Choy
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to allow the glossy dark-green leaves and tender white stems to fill out into a compact, slow-bolting head. Black Summer was bred as a heat-tolerant companion to white-stemmed types like Joi Choi, so it can be planted through the warmer parts of the growing season with far less risk of premature flowering. Harvest at 8-10 inches tall for a sweet, crisp bok choy suited to stir-fries, soups, and fresh use. Matures in 35–50 days from seed.

name: Black Surinam Cherry (Dark-Fruited Pitanga)
description: The dark-fruited (black or near-black) form of Surinam cherry is a distinct selection prized by fruit growers for milder, sweeter flavor and reduced resinous aftertaste compared to the common orange-red form, though both share the same ribbed, lantern-shaped fruit and dense, glossy-leaved habit. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, watering regularly during flowering and fruit set; established plants tolerate brief light frost and some drought once mature. The shrub flushes into fragrant white bloom followed by ripening fruit several times per year in warm climates, and responds very well to shearing, making it a popular formal or informal fruiting hedge in South Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes. Harvest fruit only when fully dark and slightly soft, as underripe fruit is strongly astringent and resinous even in this improved form. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Tartarian Cherry (Black Tartar Cherry)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Black Tartarian is one of the oldest and most reliable sweet cherry cultivars in cultivation — an early-season cherry with large, dark mahogany-red to nearly black, heart-shaped fruit with sweet, rich, dark-red flesh. It ripens 1–2 weeks before Bing and is one of the first sweet cherries to mature in a given location. The fruit is softer than Bing or Rainier and does not store or ship as well, making it particularly suited to home garden production and immediate fresh consumption. Black Tartarian also serves as an excellent pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties. It was imported from Russia in the early 1800s and is one of the oldest sweet cherry cultivars still in commercial and home garden production. Trees are vigorous, relatively disease-resistant, and productive. Require 900+ chill hours; best suited to zones 5–8 in areas with reliable cold winters. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black Thorn Durian (D200)
description: Black Thorn (clone D200), named for the dark bases of its thorny husk spines, is a premium Malaysian durian cultivar that rivals Musang King in price and reputation, prized for an unusually small seed, thick flesh, and a rich, dense, custardy texture with a distinct bittersweet, almost boozy depth of flavor. It is a relatively slow, low-yielding cultivar compared to older commercial clones, which contributes to its scarcity and high value. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with consistently high humidity and warm temperatures, and protect flowering periods from pesticide disturbance since pollination depends on nocturnal bats. As with all durian, allow the heavy spined fruit to fall naturally, and plant only in genuinely frost-free, humid tropical conditions. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Black Tower Elderberry (Columnar Dark-Purple-Leaved Ornamental Elder)
description: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil and give afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the near-black foliage from scorching. Prune out about a third of the oldest canes each late winter to keep the columnar form dense and encourage new flowering wood. Pair with a genetically distinct elderberry cultivar nearby to improve pollination and berry set, since the dark leaf color is the main draw but the pink-white flower clusters still ripen into small edible (cooked-only) black fruit. Expect a slower, more restrained growth habit than green-leaved elderberry types. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Black Turmeric (Blue Ginger, Kali Haldi)
description: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in enriched, loose, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade once soil temperatures reach 65°F; black turmeric is a rare curcuma species from northeastern India with striking blue-gray to nearly black interior flesh in contrast to the familiar orange of common turmeric — the color derives from anthocyanins rather than curcuminoids. Prized primarily in Ayurvedic medicine and traditional tribal use in Odisha and Bengal as an anti-inflammatory and pain reliever; it is less a culinary spice than an important medicinal plant. The attractive large leaves with a dark maroon central midrib stripe make it highly ornamental as a shade garden subject. Lift rhizomes after foliage dies back in fall; store dry above 50°F. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Black Turtle Bean (Black Bean)
description: Sow 1–2 inches deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; black turtle beans are the standard black bean of Latin American, Caribbean, and American cuisine — the dense, shiny black seeds are rich in protein (15g per cup) and antioxidant anthocyanins, used in black bean soup, rice and beans, burritos, tacos, and countless other dishes. Both bush and pole varieties are available; the most common home-garden varieties include 'Black Valentine' (bush) and 'Black Coco' (bush). Allow pods to dry completely on the plant for dry bean harvest — seeds should rattle in the pod. Thresh by spreading dried plants on a tarp and walking on them, then winnow. In zone 9a, plant in spring for a late-summer dry bean harvest; the plants fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil for subsequent crops. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Black Valentine Bush Bean (Heirloom 1897 Bush Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long and still tender before seeds swell. Black Valentine is one of the oldest continuously maintained snap bean varieties in American cultivation, introduced around 1897 — a bush snap bean with more than 125 years of documented garden history, making it one of the few surviving American snap bean varieties from the pre-hybrid, pre-modern-breeding era. The black seed (from which the name derives) is the seed coat color at the dry stage: the seeds are jet black when fully dried, producing a useful dry black bean with excellent flavor for soups and stews. As a snap bean, Black Valentine produces dark green, round to slightly flat pods of good length (5.5–6.5 inches) on compact, bushy 18–22 inch plants. The flavor is richer and more complex than most modern bush snap bean hybrids — characteristic of traditional open-pollinated varieties that were selected for eating quality over the decades of their use. Black Valentine shows good tolerance for cool soil germination (as low as 55°F, versus the 60–65°F requirement of most snap beans), which allowed earlier planting in the pre-modern gardening era when it was a primary garden staple. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Black Velvet Gooseberry (Purple-Black Dessert Gooseberry, Blueberry-Flavored Hybrid)
description: Black Velvet is a hybrid dessert gooseberry combining European Ribes uva-crispa fruit quality with the vigor and disease resistance of American Ribes hirtellum parentage, selected for its commercial and home-garden potential as a fresh-eating fruit. Ripe berries turn from green through burgundy to a deep purple-black, with a sweet, mild flavor many tasters compare to blueberries rather than the tart bite typical of green or red gooseberries, making it excellent for fresh eating off the bush as well as pies, jams, and desserts. The bush is notably vigorous and disease-resistant, showing good tolerance of powdery mildew and leaf spot compared with older European cultivars, and it is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating temperatures to -40F once dormant. Like other Ribes, it prefers cool summers and consistently moist soil, and benefits from afternoon shade and mulch to keep roots cool in warmer parts of its range; expect reduced vigor and fruit quality in hot, humid summer climates. Prune out the oldest third of canes each winter to renew fruiting wood and improve air circulation through the thorny growth. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Black Walnut
description: Black walnut is a native North American species grown primarily for its richly flavored nuts and valuable timber. It produces high concentrations of juglone in its roots, leaves, and hulls, which is toxic to many garden plants including tomatoes, peppers, apples, and blueberries; maintain a 50–80 foot buffer from sensitive plants. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but cross well with a second tree. Hulls stain skin and clothing an indelible dark brown; wear gloves when husking. Nuts are ready when hulls are yellow-green to black and dent when pressed; cure for 2–3 weeks after husking. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Black Worcester Pear (Historic English Culinary Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. One of England's oldest named pear cultivars, dating back for centuries and long associated with the city of Worcester, whose coat of arms depicts three of its distinctive dark fruits, it bears hard, dense pears covered in a dull, purplish, near-black skin that sets it apart from nearly every other pear variety. The dense, gritty flesh is unsuitable for fresh eating but excellent baked, poached, or stewed, and the fruit keeps exceptionally well in storage over winter. Harvest in mid-autumn once mature, store cool, and cook whole or sliced until the flesh softens and turns tender. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Black-Eyed Pea
description: Black-eyed peas are a heat-tolerant cowpea grown for their nutritious seeds and their ability to fix nitrogen and improve soil. Direct-sow after the soil warms to 70F, planting an inch deep and thinning to 3-6 inches apart, since the plants dislike transplanting. They tolerate heat and drought well, so water moderately and avoid overly rich soil, which favors foliage over pods. Harvest young pods for fresh snap peas or leave them to dry on the plant for shelling and storage. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Black-Seeded Simpson Lettuce
