description: Broadcast or direct sow seed on the soil surface (light aids germination — do not cover) in early spring, thinning to 8–12 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall; Black-Seeded Simpson is the most widely grown American heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, documented since at least 1850 and still one of the best choices for the home garden due to its excellent heat tolerance (bolts much more slowly than most head lettuces), fast maturity (45–50 days), light green crinkled leaves with a pleasant, mild flavor, and the heavy yields of a cut-and-come-again plant. Harvest outer leaves when plants are 6–8 inches tall, leaving the center growing point to continue producing. Self-shades the soil and benefits from afternoon shade in warm climates. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Blackberry
description: Blackberries fruit on second-year floricanes; remove all fruited canes at the base after harvest and thin new primocanes to 4–6 per hill. Erect types can be tip-pruned at 3–4 ft in midsummer to encourage lateral branching and larger yields. Harvest when berries are fully black, slightly soft, and the white core is not visible — they do not ripen further off the plant. Trailing cultivars require a T-trellis; thornless varieties are easier to manage but may be less cold-hardy. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Blackcap (Western Raspberry)
description: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; blackcap fruits on second-year canes, so tip-prune first-year primocanes in summer to encourage branching and next year's crop. Rubus leucodermis is a western North American native bramble with arching, prickly canes coated in a whitish, waxy bloom, producing small white flowers in spring followed by dark purple-black, dome-shaped berries in early to midsummer that are tart, seedy, and excellent for jam, syrup, and baking. It tolerates lighter, drier soils and more shade than most cultivated raspberries, and its thicket-forming habit makes it useful for naturalized plantings, wildlife hedgerows, and erosion control on slopes as well as a home fruit patch. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting each year to keep the planting productive and manage its spreading habit. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Blackhawk Black Raspberry (Cold-Hardy Iowa State Black Raspberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in full sun in well-drained soil, giving each hill enough room for air to move freely through the canes. Blackhawk was bred at Iowa State University and released in 1955 at a time when Midwest black raspberry plantings were routinely losing canes to hard winters and to anthracnose, a fungal cane disease that thrives in wet springs, and it remains one of the hardiest and most disease-tolerant blackcap cultivars available for northern gardens today. Plants are self-fertile and set a full crop from a single planting, producing medium to large glossy black fruit with good flavor on vigorous, upright canes. Tip-prune new primocanes in summer to promote branching, and remove old floricanes immediately after harvest to keep the planting open and reduce disease pressure through the following winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blacktail Mountain Watermelon
description: Direct sow in hills or rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blacktail Mountain is an early-maturing open-pollinated watermelon developed by Glenn Drowns of Seed Savers Exchange to produce reliably sweet, ripe melons in the short summers of northern Idaho and the northern Plains. The small to medium round fruits (8–12 pounds) have a strikingly dark — almost black-green — rind that distinguishes them instantly from most other watermelon varieties. The bright red, sweet, juicy flesh is comparable to the best commercial watermelons in flavor, with a thin rind and few seeds. In zone 9 the early maturity (70–80 days from direct sow) means it finishes before the most brutal August heat and is particularly useful for succession-planted summer crops that bridge the gap between spring and fall production. The dark rind warms faster in cool spring soil, giving Blacktail Mountain an advantage early in the season when soil temperatures are marginal. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Bladder Campion (Maidenstears)
description: Direct sow in early spring or fall in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained, preferably neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; bladder campion is a European native naturalized throughout North America that has long been eaten in Mediterranean countries — particularly Italy and Spain — where the young spring shoots and leaves are gathered and cooked like asparagus or used raw in salads, with a flavor often described as fresh, pea-like, and slightly peppery. The inflated silvery-white balloon-like calyx is highly ornamental, and white five-petaled deeply notched flowers appear from late spring through fall with an evening fragrance. Naturalizes readily in dry meadows and borders and is fully drought-tolerant once established. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Blake Kiwi (Compact Self-Fertile California Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor. Blake was bred in California as a self-fertile fuzzy kiwifruit with a somewhat more compact, manageable growth habit than the very vigorous Hayward, making it a practical choice for home gardeners with limited space who still want to grow classic fuzzy-skinned kiwifruit without dedicating room to a separate non-fruiting male vine. Fruit is smaller than Hayward but has good flavor, and the self-fertile trait means a single plant can produce a crop, though yields improve somewhat with a nearby pollinizer if space allows. Prune annually during dormancy to manage vine growth and maintain productive fruiting wood, and provide sturdy, long-term support, since kiwi vines are heavy and long-lived. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Blake's Pride Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing trees to allow good air circulation through the canopy to further limit blight pressure. Blake's Pride was released by USDA breeders working out of the Appalachian Fruit Research Station in West Virginia specifically to combine strong fire blight resistance with genuinely good dessert quality, producing a Seckel-type fruit that is sweeter and larger than old Seckel itself. Plant it alongside another mid-season European pear such as Moonglow or Magness for reliable cross-pollination. Pick the fruit while still firm in late summer and let it finish ripening indoors at room temperature for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blakeney Red Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Blakeney Red is a vigorous, self-fertile perry pear, but still crops more heavily with a second variety for cross-pollination. One of the most widely planted traditional English perry pears, originating in the Forest of Dean area of Gloucestershire, it produces a heavy, reliable crop of small, red-blushed pears on a large, vigorous, long-lived tree, valued by perry makers for moderate tannin and good juice yield that blends well in traditional West Country perry production. Unlike many perry pears, it is self-fertile, making it a more forgiving choice for an orchard with limited space for a dedicated pollinator tree, though a second variety still improves cropping. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, and let it sweat in a pile for a few days before milling and pressing. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Blanc du Bois Grape (Gulf Coast Pierce's-Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
description: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun; prune in late winter; Blanc du Bois ripens in June–July in the Gulf South, much earlier than northern grapes; the fruit is white-green to golden at maturity and produces crisp, fruity white wine with notes of melon, citrus, and tropical fruit; fruit can also be eaten fresh or made into juice. Blanc du Bois is the most important Gulf Coast white wine grape variety, bred by Dr. John Mortensen at the University of Florida's Levin College of Law agricultural breeding program (USDA-ARS Fort Pierce) specifically for the hot, humid climate of the American Southeast and Gulf South where European vinifera varieties cannot survive. The critical factor in Gulf Coast viticulture is Pierce's disease — a bacterial infection caused by Xylella fastidiosa spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter leafhopper (Homalodisca vitripennis) — which kills European vinifera varieties (Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, etc.) within 1–5 years throughout the Gulf South. Blanc du Bois was developed as a complex hybrid incorporating Vitis champinii (heat-tolerant wild Texas grape) and other native American species to provide Pierce's disease resistance, while retaining enough vinifera quality characteristics to produce high-quality white wine comparable to European-style dry whites. The resulting wine is crisp, fruity, and aromatic with Muscat-like floral notes and good acidity — genuinely world-class for a Pierce's disease-resistant variety and the backbone of the emerging Gulf Coast wine industry. Blanc du Bois grapes ripen unusually early — in June to early July in zone 9a, compared to September ripening in northern vineyards — which allows harvest before the peak summer heat and humidity. Several Texas and Florida wineries produce award-winning Blanc du Bois wines that have helped establish the variety's reputation nationally. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blanka White Currant
description: 'Blanka' is a heavy-yielding white currant producing long trusses of large, translucent, mild-sweet berries that are less tart than red types. It is a robust, healthy bush that crops later in the season and holds its fruit well on the plant. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with partial shade in warm areas to avoid scorching the pale fruit. Prune to an open framework in winter and mulch annually to conserve moisture and feed the shallow roots. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Blauhilde Pole Bean (Deep Purple German Heirloom Snap Bean)
description: Blauhilde is a German heirloom pole bean prized for its striking deep purple pods, which grow long and wide yet stay tender and stringless, set off nicely against rose-purple blossoms. The pods turn green when cooked but hold their purple color when lightly steamed, making raw and blanched harvests fun to tell apart in the kitchen. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines bear over a long window when picked at 6-8 inches, and the plant's dramatic coloring makes it a popular choice for growers who want both a productive snap bean and an ornamental accent on the trellis. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Blauwschokker Pea (Purple Podded Dutch Soup Pea, Capucijner)
description: Blauwschokker is a centuries-old Dutch heirloom prized for its bicolor purple-and-white flowers and deep violet pods, making it as ornamental as it is useful in the vegetable garden. Pods can be picked young and shelled fresh like a standard garden pea, or left on the vine until they dry to a papery tan for storage as a marbled grey-green soup pea, traditionally used in Dutch pea soup. The vigorous climbing vines benefit from a trellis and produce over a long picking window in cool weather. This variety is a good choice for gardeners who want a dual-purpose pea that also adds color to a spring garden. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Blenheim Apricot (Royal Blenheim, California Standard Apricot, Santa Clara Valley Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blenheim is self-fertile and drought-tolerant once established; thin to 3–4 inches after June drop; harvest when fruits are deep golden-orange and begin to soften — Blenheim must be harvested and eaten within days of peak ripeness, as the aromatic, intensely flavored flesh does not hold. Blenheim (sold commercially as 'Royal Blenheim' to distinguish it from Moorpark, with which it shares British origins) was the commercial apricot standard of California for over a century, dominating the Santa Clara Valley apricot industry that made California's 'Apricot Capital' from the 1880s through the mid-20th century before urban development replaced the orchards. The variety's characteristics — low chill requirement, self-fertility, reliable production in California's mild winters, and exceptional flavor — made it ideal for the Central Valley and Bay Area climates where it had no commercial equal. The fruits are medium-sized, golden-orange with a red blush, with rich, highly aromatic, intensely flavored flesh that is considered by many apricot enthusiasts to be the most complex-flavored of any commercial apricot variety — a concentrated sweetness with floral, honeyed notes and classic apricot fragrance at peak ripeness that far surpasses the flavor of supermarket apricots harvested underripe for shipping. Blenheim's low chill requirement (400–600 hours) makes it a good choice for zone 7–9 gardeners where higher-chill varieties like Moorpark and Harcot may not receive adequate winter cold. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blenheim Orange Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby. An old English variety dating to the eighteenth century, it bears large, handsome, orange-red-flushed apples with dry, nutty, richly flavored flesh good for both fresh eating once fully ripe and for cooking, one of the classic dual-purpose apples that bridges the line between dessert and culinary use. As a triploid, it produces sterile pollen and requires two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination of itself and each other, a detail worth planning for before planting, and it makes a large, vigorous, long-lived tree. Harvest in mid-fall and let the fruit mellow in storage for a few weeks before eating fresh, since the flesh is at its best after a short period off the tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blessed Thistle
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun; blessed thistle thrives in lean conditions and declines in rich, moist soil. As a cool-season annual it bolts in summer heat, so early spring or late summer sowing provides the best leaf harvest. Harvest the young leaves and leafy stems before the spiny flower heads fully open, wearing gloves to protect against the prickles. Dried aerial parts are used in traditional bitter digestive tinctures, teas for stimulating appetite, and historical preparations reputed to support lactation. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Bleu de Solaise Leek (Blue of Solaise)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost date; sow 1/4 inch deep in flats or cell trays at 60–70°F. Bleu de Solaise is a traditional French winter leek from the Rhône valley region near Lyon, classified as a winter-type leek because it is sown in late winter or early spring, transplanted in late spring, and harvested from autumn through the following spring — the main harvesting season runs from November through February in most climates. The most distinctive characteristic of Bleu de Solaise is its dramatic foliage color: the leaves develop an intense steel-blue to blue-violet pigmentation in response to cold temperatures through the anthocyanin response, making each plant increasingly vibrant and beautiful as winter progresses; in hard frosts the blue becomes almost purple-blue. Transplant seedlings in late spring when 6–8 inches tall, planting deeply in a trench or dibbling holes 6 inches deep to blanch the shanks and develop long, tender white stems; the thick shanks (6–8 inches long) have a sweet, mild, sophisticated flavor that intensifies rather than diminishes in cold weather. One of the most cold-tolerant of all leeks, surviving temperatures well below 0°F when established. Matures in 105–130 days from transplant.

name: Blinks (Water Chickweed)
description: Broadcast seeds across the surface of very moist, even waterlogged soil beside a spring, seep, stream edge, or perpetually wet bed, and do not cover them as they need light for germination; blinks is an inconspicuous but historically valued wild potherb of cool, wet habitats across Europe, Asia, and North America, producing mats of tiny, fleshy, bright-green leaves with a clean, mild, slightly succulent flavor reminiscent of purslane. Gather the young shoots and leaves by the handful for use raw in salads or cooked briefly as a light pot herb alongside other spring greens. Blinks is seldom deliberately cultivated and is far more commonly encountered as a volunteer in damp garden corners, irrigation runnels, and beside water features; the gardener's role is more to encourage and harvest it than to manage it as a conventional crop. It self-sows abundantly in suitable wet conditions and will naturalize into a permanent spring presence in any reliably wet microhabitat in the garden. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Blond Psyllium
description: Psyllium must always be taken with plenty of water, since swallowing it dry can cause choking or intestinal blockage. Direct-sow shallowly after frost danger passes into hot, dry, well-drained soil, since this low rosette-forming annual is prone to rot in humid or overwatered conditions. The mature seed husks, threshed and cleaned once seed heads dry, are the source of psyllium fiber, traditionally and medically used as a bulk-forming laxative and to support healthy cholesterol levels. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Blonde de Lyon Sorrel
description: Blonde de Lyon is the classic French market strain of garden sorrel, selected for extra-large, tender leaves that are milder and less acidic than wild sorrel and much slower to bolt. Grow it in rich, moisture-retentive soil with some afternoon shade, since consistent moisture keeps the leaves succulent and prevents premature flowering. Harvest outer leaves continuously through the cool season, and shear the whole clump back if a flower stalk appears to redirect energy into fresh leaf growth. As a hardy perennial it dies back in winter and resprouts reliably from the crown each spring for years. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Blondkopfchen Tomato (Little Blonde Girl German Heirloom Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with a sturdy cage or tall stake. Blondkopfchen (German for 'little blonde girl' or 'little blondie') is a German heirloom cherry tomato that produces one of the most spectacular fruiting displays of any tomato variety — extremely long, drooping clusters of 30–50 or more tiny (0.5–0.75 inch), round, clear golden-yellow to light lemon-yellow fruits that cascade like bunches of golden grapes from indeterminate vines growing 6+ feet. The fruits are uniformly pale golden-yellow, translucent-skinned, and have an exceptionally sweet, mild, almost honey-sweet flavor with very low acidity — a delicate sweetness that is quite different from the richer red cherry types and makes Blondkopfchen appealing to those who find red cherry tomatoes too tart. The combination of the fruit's pale golden color, the translucent skin through which the interior is visible, and the long hanging clusters makes Blondkopfchen one of the most beautiful tomato plants in the garden — genuinely ornamental as well as productive and delicious. Very popular in European heirloom gardens and increasingly appreciated in the US by tomato collectors who value both visual character and eating quality. Seed Savers Exchange and specialty seed companies carry this variety as an example of German heirloom tomato excellence. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Blondy Okra (AAS-Winning Compact Cream-Podded Okra)
description: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest cream-colored pods every 2–3 days at 2–5 inches. Blondy is a 1986 All-America Selections-winning okra that earned recognition for two distinguishing traits: compact plant size and distinctive cream-white to pale chartreuse pod color. Standard okra varieties like Clemson Spineless and Emerald are tall plants (5–7 feet) that require staking and become difficult to harvest at the top as the season progresses; Blondy stays compact at 3–4 feet, keeping all pods within easy reach throughout the harvest season. The pale cream-colored pods are the most visually distinctive feature — where standard okra is dark forest green, Blondy's pods are almost white-green to cream-yellow, giving a noticeably different appearance both in the garden and on the table. Beyond the visual novelty, the pale pods have a slight cooking advantage: they do not contribute the dark green color that sometimes bleeds into dishes, making them preferable for light-colored preparations like cream soups, gumbo with light roux, or pickled okra where visual clarity is desired. The pods remain tender at larger sizes than dark-green types, providing a more forgiving harvest window. Blondy produces heavily on its compact plants, making it particularly well-suited to small gardens and raised beds. Matures in 48–56 days from seed.

name: Blood Orange
description: Blood orange cultivars (Moro, Tarocco, Sanguinello) develop their signature ruby-red flesh and juice through the accumulation of anthocyanins, a pigment triggered by cool nights during fruit development — temperatures between 40 and 50°F for several weeks from late autumn through midwinter produce the deepest coloring. In frost-free tropical climates the flesh remains orange with little anthocyanin. Trees are self-fertile, medium-sized, and managed identically to other sweet oranges: plant in well-drained soil, fertilize with a citrus blend three times per year, and irrigate deeply but infrequently. Harvest from late winter through early spring when the flesh has developed full color and the fruit is sweet. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Blood Orange (Moro Blood Orange)
description: Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; fertilize with citrus formula in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × sinensis 'Moro' (Moro blood orange) is the most intensely red-fleshed blood orange variety — a Sicilian mutation of sweet orange in which the flesh, juice, and sometimes the rind develop stunning deep-red to near-purple color from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to cool autumn nights. The 'Moro' cultivar produces the deepest, most intensely colored blood-red flesh and dramatic dark-red juice of any blood orange, with a distinctive flavor that combines sweet orange with a raspberry-berry overtone from the anthocyanins. In zone 9, the cool fall and winter nights (below 60°F) trigger the red pigment development; in warmer climates the color development is minimal. Blood orange juice makes extraordinary cocktails, salad dressings, and sauces. The 'Tarocco' variety (less cold-hardy, zone 10) produces the best flavor; 'Sanguinelli' is another reliable variety. Blood oranges ripen December through March in zone 9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Blood-Veined Sorrel (Red-Veined Ornamental Edible Sorrel)
description: Sow direct or plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; a little afternoon shade helps the striking foliage color hold up better in hot summer weather. Blood-Veined Sorrel bears bright green leaves dramatically marked with deep red-purple veins, an ornamental pattern striking enough to earn it a spot in shade borders and mixed containers as well as the herb garden, while the young leaves carry the same tart, lemony flavor typical of sorrel and are edible raw in small amounts or cooked into soups and sauces. It tolerates more shade than most edible greens, making it a useful dual-purpose plant for a partly shaded kitchen garden bed. Remove flower stalks as they appear to prolong leaf quality and reduce self-seeding, and harvest young leaves continuously for the best flavor and most vivid color. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Bloody Butcher Corn (Red Dent Corn)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows to ensure cross-pollination; plant in fertile, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during pollination and kernel fill. Bloody Butcher is a tall, vigorous Appalachian heirloom dent corn documented in Virginia and the Appalachian region since at least the 1840s; the plants are impressive, reaching 10–12 feet, and produce 2–4 ears per stalk of medium-length (10–14 inch) ears with kernels that are dramatic deep blood-red to red-brick with darker red cob — the most vividly colored of the traditional red dent corns. Dried, the kernels are ground into deeply flavored, reddish-tinged cornmeal with a rich, earthy, sweet corn taste that is distinct from modern yellow dent meal. Also used for hominy, grits, masa, and heritage whiskey distilling. At the milk stage (80–90 days) the ears can be eaten as roasting ears; for grain and meal, allow to dry on the stalk or cure indoors. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Bloody Dock (Red-veined Sorrel)
description: Direct sow in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; thin to 12 inches. Rumex sanguineus (bloody dock or red-veined sorrel) is a European perennial dock producing some of the most visually striking leaves of any vegetable — glossy, lance-shaped, medium-green leaves dramatically marked with vivid crimson-red veins and midribs, creating a graphic color contrast that makes this plant as ornamental as it is edible. Young leaves are harvested like sorrel and used raw in salads, where the mild, slightly acidic flavor adds interest; older leaves become more strongly acidic (from oxalic acid) and are best cooked briefly like spinach or used sparingly as a flavoring. Unlike common garden sorrel, the leaf flavor is milder and the visual interest much greater. Plants are long-lived perennials that die back in hard winters and regrow in spring; in zone 9, they may persist semi-evergreen through mild winters. The tall, reddish flower stalks should be removed as they develop to keep plants producing leaves rather than going to seed. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Bloody Dock Sorrel
description: Direct-sow in early spring in cool, moist soil, covering seed lightly and thinning to a hand's width. The striking red-veined leaves add tangy lemon flavor and ornamental color to salads. Grow in partial shade with steady moisture to keep leaves tender and slow bolting. Remove flower stalks to prolong leaf harvest and prevent aggressive self-seeding. Cut leaves young for the best texture and divide crowns every few years. Matures in 55–80 days from seed.

name: Bloomsdale Long Standing Spinach (Heirloom Savoy Spinach)
description: Direct sow seed a half inch deep into cool, moist soil as soon as the ground can be worked, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear. This selection is one of the oldest named spinach types still grown today, prized for its heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves and slower tendency to bolt compared with smooth-leaf types. It tolerates light frost and often tastes sweetest after a cold snap, making it a dependable choice for both early spring and fall sowings. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Bloomsdale Spinach
description: Bloomsdale is a cold-hardy heirloom spinach with heavily crinkled, deep-green leaves and a sweet, mild flavor that stands up well in cool weather. Direct-sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked and again in late summer, since seed germinates poorly in warm soil. Thin plants to 4-6 inches apart and harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut whole plants before hot weather triggers bolting. In mild zones a fall planting under cover can overwinter for an early spring harvest. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Bloomsweet Grapefruit (Cold-Hardy Grapefruit Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bloomsweet is a grapefruit-like hybrid selected for cold hardiness beyond that of standard grapefruit cultivars, producing pale yellow, thin-skinned, juicy fruit with a mild, less bitter flavor than classic grapefruit and only a light blush of the typical grapefruit tang. The tree's improved cold tolerance, credited to its mixed parentage, has made it a popular choice for gardeners in the cooler parts of the Gulf Coast citrus belt who want grapefruit-style fruit without the cold sensitivity of true Citrus x paradisi selections. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree, sweetening further if left to hang after coloring fully. Give young trees winter protection for their first several years in zone 8, since even improved hardiness has limits; mature trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s F with minimal damage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blossom Hardneck Garlic
description: Separate bulbs into cloves at planting and set each clove pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes. This Turban-type hardneck forms large, plump bulbs with violet-streaked wrappers and 8 to 10 easy-peel cloves. Mulch after planting to protect roots over winter, and cut off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place before storing. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Blue Ballet Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, composted soil; Blue Ballet is a compact vine type needing 4–6 feet of space, much more manageable than giant Hubbard types while retaining the same outstanding eating quality. Blue Ballet is a small, 2–4 pound, blue-grey teardrop-shaped winter squash in the Cucurbita maxima (Hubbard) family, with dense, smooth, bright orange flesh that is extraordinarily dry, sweet, and nutty — essentially the same outstanding Hubbard flavor in a size perfect for a single serving or small family portion that eliminates the wrestling match of cutting a 15-pound Blue Hubbard. Excellent for roasting halved in the oven with butter and maple syrup; the small size also makes it practical for stuffing. Cure for 10 days and store for 3–4 months. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Blue Bean Shrub (Dead Man's Fingers)
description: Give this large, coarse-leaved shrub a sheltered spot with dappled or half-day shade and consistently moist, rich soil, mimicking the Himalayan and Chinese forest margins it comes from. By autumn, established plants hang thick with startling metallic-blue, finger-like seed pods several inches long; split one open to reach the sweet, translucent, gelatinous pulp inside, which tastes something like watermelon or lychee, though the numerous black seeds must be spit out. It needs a male and female plant, or a self-fertile seedling, to set the curious pods reliably. Few other fruiting shrubs offer both genuine shade tolerance and such a conversation-starting harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Blue Bean Shrub (Dead Man's Fingers)
description: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; blue bean shrub needs a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for reliable pod set and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh drying wind. Decaisnea insignis is a striking, large, multi-stemmed shrub from the Himalaya and western China with big, compound, tropical-looking leaves and drooping clusters of small yellow-green flowers in late spring, followed by the plant's signature feature — dangling, metallic blue, sausage-shaped seed pods in fall that give rise to its unsettling common name. The pods split open to reveal a translucent, gelatinous, mildly sweet pulp around black seeds that can be eaten fresh, similar in texture and flavor to a mild melon, though it is grown mostly as a conversation-piece ornamental rather than a serious food crop. It prefers a woodland-edge setting with shelter from wind and consistent moisture, and its architectural form and unusual fruit make it a standout specimen in a shaded border. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Blue Belle Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Belle is self-infertile. Blue Belle was one of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Bird, and Blue Moon) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that brought large-fruited modern haskaps into wide North American cultivation. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening two to three weeks ahead of standard blueberries in most climates. Like other haskaps, Blue Belle is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving winter temperatures to -40F with flowers tolerating brief dips to about -8F, but it is not well suited to hot, humid summers and performs best in cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the shrub productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Bird Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Blue Bird was part of the founding quartet of University of Saskatchewan haskap releases, alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Moon, selected from the same early breeding population for its rounder, more compact berries and dependable, heavy fruit set. Like its siblings it flowers very early in spring and is self-infertile, so plant it with a compatible cultivar that blooms at the same time to ensure a full crop. The fruit carries the classic sweet-tart, blueberry-raspberry flavor of early-generation haskaps, though later University of Saskatchewan introductions have since surpassed it in fruit size and flavor, leaving Blue Bird grown today mostly in heritage collections and as a pollen source for its still-popular siblings. Give it the same well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun as other haskaps, and limit pruning to dead or crossing wood for the first several years while the shrub's framework establishes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Boy Rosemary
description: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil; Blue Boy is a dwarf, compact, mounding rosemary that forms a tight hemisphere of small, fine-textured, intensely aromatic needlelike leaves — the most compact of the named rosemary cultivars and the best choice for container growing, small herb gardens, edging, and topiary. Unlike the large, sprawling upright rosemary types that reach 3–6 feet, Blue Boy stays under 18–24 inches with a mounding, naturally rounded habit that requires little pruning to maintain its shape. The flavor and fragrance are identical to full-sized rosemary — strongly resinous, piney, and aromatic — and the fine leaves are actually preferred for delicate uses where coarser standard rosemary leaves are too large. Blue Boy blooms prolifically in late winter and early spring, covering the mound in tiny blue flowers that are excellent for bees. In zone 9 the compact habit and lean soil requirements make it ideal for containers on patios and decks, where the intensely aromatic foliage is accessible for kitchen harvest. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Blue Boy Rue (Compact Blue-Foliage Rue)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid wet or highly fertile soils. CAUTION: handle with gloves, since rue contains furanocoumarins that can cause skin blistering after contact and subsequent sun exposure. Blue Boy is a compact selection of rue with especially vivid blue-gray, finely divided foliage on a tidy, low-mounding plant, smaller and more richly colored than the species, making it a favorite for herb garden edging and formal knot gardens where its striking foliage color is the main attraction. Small yellow flowers appear in summer but the plant is grown primarily for foliage. It serves as a larval host plant for Giant Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, and its strong scent is reputed to repel a number of garden pests. Cut back after flowering to keep the plant compact and encourage fresh foliage growth. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Blue Chip Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Blue Chip is a low-chill-hour dwarf southern highbush blueberry selected for compact growth habit — typically reaching only 3–4 feet tall and wide, making it the most container-appropriate blueberry variety and an excellent choice for small gardens, patios, and raised beds where standard blueberries are too large. The moderate-sized, sweet, firm berries ripen in May–June in zone 9 with good flavor and production relative to the small plant size. Blue Chip's dwarf habit is not a compromise in productivity — the plant concentrates its energy into fruit production rather than excessive vegetative growth, and a mature container-grown Blue Chip in a large pot can produce 2–4 pounds of fruit annually. The ornamental value is also high: the spring white flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, and brilliant orange-to-red fall color make Blue Chip a true four-season specimen for containers and small gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blue Coco Pole Bean (French Heirloom Snap, Shell, and Dry Bean)
description: Blue Coco is a dual- to triple-purpose French heirloom pole bean bearing slender, bluish-purple pods on vines with purple-tinged leaves and lavender flowers, an attractive plant as much at home on an ornamental trellis as in the vegetable rows. Young pods snap tender with a mild, sweet flavor, while pods left to fill out yield plump beans with rich chocolate-brown seed coats that shell fresh or dry down for winter soup beans. Its origins are debated, with some tracing the name to Central America rather than France, but it has circulated in French seed trade and heirloom collections for generations. Provide a tall, sturdy support, since the vigorous vines climb readily and produce over a long season when picked regularly. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Blue Curled Scotch Kale (Classic Tightly-Curled Dwarf Blue Kale)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Blue Curled Scotch'
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun or partial shade. Blue Curled Scotch (also called Dwarf Blue Curled Scotch or Blue Curled Dwarf) is one of the oldest and most recognized curly kale varieties in American cultivation — a compact, very tightly-curled kale with deeply blue-green, intensely frilled and crinkled leaves on a low, spreading, dwarf plant. The very dense curling of Blue Curled Scotch is the most extreme in the curly kale category — each leaf is curled and recurled into a compact, almost cabbage-like head of texture that is visually striking and creates distinctive culinary behavior when cooked (the very curly leaves trap oils and seasonings in their folds). The tightly frilled leaves also create the most decorative appearance among common kale varieties, making Blue Curled Scotch useful in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings where visual appeal is important. The dwarf habit (12–18 inches) is practical in raised beds and containers. Like all curly kales, flavor improves dramatically after frost — the sweetness increases and the bitterness decreases as cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, making fall and winter the optimal harvest window. Matures in 55–70 days from transplant.

name: Blue Cushion Lavender (Dwarf Mounding English Lavender)
description: Blue Cushion forms an exceptionally dense, low, rounded mound of fine silvery-green foliage, living up to its name as one of the tightest-growing English lavender cultivars available. Slender deep violet-blue flower spikes rise just above the foliage in a tidy, uniform flush, making this a favorite for edging, knot gardens, and mass plantings where a neat, consistent shape matters. Plant in full sun in gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid overwatering or fertile soil, both of which loosen the naturally tight habit and invite root rot. Shear lightly right after bloom to preserve the cushion form and encourage dense new growth for the following season. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Blue Elderberry (Blue Elder, Western Elderberry)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; blue elderberry is the western counterpart to eastern black elderberry, native from British Columbia to New Mexico, producing large flat-topped clusters (corymbs) of tiny white flowers followed by abundant powder-blue to nearly black fruits with a distinctive waxy blue bloom. The berries are somewhat sweeter and milder than eastern elderberry and were a major food plant for over 50 indigenous nations of the Pacific Coast and interior West — eaten fresh (ripe only), dried, made into jam, syrup, wine, and elderflower cordial. Like eastern elderberry, unripe or raw berries can cause nausea; cook before eating in quantity. An exceptional wildlife plant and one of the most productive native fruiting shrubs. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blue Elderberry (Blueberry Elder)
description: Plant in any moist to well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — blue elderberry is the western North American native elderberry, native from British Columbia to Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing large, flat-topped clusters of dark blue to blue-black berries with a distinctive waxy, blue-gray bloom (giving both plant and fruit their names). The berries are slightly sweeter than American elderberry (S. canadensis) and are used the same way — in jellies, juices, wines, elderflower cordial, and traditional medicine. Blue elderberry is significantly more drought-tolerant than American elderberry, adapts to alkaline soils, and grows in the dry, sunny conditions of western landscapes where the eastern species struggles. It is an important food and medicine plant in the traditions of dozens of western Native American nations. Plant where spreading by suckers is acceptable. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Blue Fenugreek (Sweet Trefoil, Blue Melilot)
description: Direct sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; harvest seed heads when yellow-brown and dry seeds thoroughly. Trigonella caerulea (blue fenugreek or sweet trefoil) is a Mediterranean and Central Asian annual herb in the legume family — the specific herb used to flavor Schabziger, a distinctive small, green, very hard Swiss cheese also known as 'green cheese' or 'sap sago.' The ground seeds of T. caerulea are the source of the unique flavor of Schabziger — a warm, herbaceous, slightly fenugreek-coumarin aroma with hay-like notes, distinctly milder and less bitter than common fenugreek (T. foenum-graecum). The seeds contain coumarin and are also used to flavor breads, crackers, and Alpine herb mixtures in Austria, Switzerland, and Germany. The plant produces distinctive blue-purple flower heads somewhat resembling clover (hence 'blue fenugreek') and trifoliate clover-like leaves. The dried, ground seeds are available in specialty stores as 'Trigonella' or under the name 'blue fenugreek powder.' The fresh leaves are also edible — mildly herb-scented, usable as a green in salads and cooked dishes. Rarely grown in North American gardens but easily cultivated as a spring annual where fenugreek grows. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Blue Globe Onion
description: Sow seed or plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since this Siberian steppe native colors up best when protected from the harshest midday heat. Flower buds nod distinctively as they emerge before straightening into dense, rounded pink-purple umbels in mid to late summer, well after most other alliums have finished. Both the blue-green strap leaves and the flowers are edible with a clean onion flavor, and the clumps are useful for filling gaps in partly shaded herb borders. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant but perform best with even moisture during active growth. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Blue Hopi Corn
description: Sow seeds about 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good wind pollination. This Hopi heirloom tolerates dry, hot conditions better than most corn, so avoid overwatering once established. Allow the ears to dry fully on the stalk before harvesting the deep-blue kernels for grinding into flour or cornmeal. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Blue Hubbard Squash (Large Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Blue Hubbard is a classic, large-fruited heirloom winter squash producing enormous, blue-gray, warty, thick-skinned fruits typically weighing 15–35 pounds — the quintessential large storage squash that has fed families through winter for generations in American kitchen gardens. The flesh is deep orange, very dry and dense, richly flavored, and exceptional for pies, soups, and roasting — the flavor is often described as richer and more complex than the more commonly grown butternut squash. The thick, warty, blue-gray skin provides outstanding storage capacity — well-cured Blue Hubbard fruits store at room temperature for 6 months or longer. The vine is vigorous and space-demanding, spreading 8–15 feet — provide ample space and consider training the vine to maximize space efficiency. In zone 9, plant in late July for fall harvest (counting back 100–110 days from the average first frost date). Harvest after the skin hardens and turns fully blue-gray; cure in a warm location for 10–14 days before storage to harden the skin and improve sweetness. The large fruits are sometimes sold cut into sections at farm stands — cut pieces must be refrigerated and used within a week. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Blue Jade Sweet Corn (Dwarf Blue Sweet Corn, Container Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for pollination — even dwarf corn requires block planting; thin to 6–9 inches; Blue Jade can be grown in large containers (15+ gallons) for patio gardens; harvest when kernels exude milky liquid when punctured; Blue Jade silk is blue and the husk has blue streaks; eat immediately for best sweetness as the sugars convert rapidly. Blue Jade is the most practical sweet corn for small gardens and containers — a genuinely dwarf sweet corn variety (plants only 3–4 feet tall) that was selected specifically for its compact habit, making it the rare sweet corn that can be grown in large containers, small raised beds, or urban gardens where standard corn's height and space requirements are prohibitive. The kernels are a vivid blue-purple when raw, turning a distinctive slate-blue when cooked — a color unlike any other common sweet corn, derived from the same anthocyanin pigments found in blue tortilla corn, blueberries, and purple cabbage. Despite the striking color, the flavor at the perfect milky stage is sweet and tender, comparable to standard sweet corn, though with a slightly more complex, starchy background flavor reflecting the corn's partial flint heritage. Blue Jade is classified as a sugary-enhanced (se) type sweet corn — not as sugary as supersweet (sh2) types but sweeter than old su types, with a longer window between milk and dough stages than original open-pollinated sweet corns. The entire plant is attractive: blue silk, blue-streaked husks, and blue-purple stalk coloring make Blue Jade an ornamental as well as productive corn. Excellent for children's gardens for its manageable size and dramatic appearance. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Blue Jarrahdale Pumpkin
description: Plant seeds an inch deep in hills once the soil is thoroughly warm, thinning to the two strongest vines per hill. Give these sprawling plants plenty of room and a steady supply of water and compost to size up the deeply ribbed fruits. Cure the blue-gray pumpkins in a warm, dry spot after harvest for long winter storage and sweet, dense flesh. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Blue Java Banana (Ice Cream Banana)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Java banana is a cold-hardy hybrid distinguished by its striking silvery-blue unripe fruit that turns pale yellow when ripe and by the remarkably creamy, vanilla-like flavor of the flesh — so reminiscent of vanilla ice cream that it is commonly called the ice cream banana. The silver-blue color of the unripe fruit is caused by a natural wax coating on the skin. It is one of the hardiest bananas available, tolerating temperatures to 22°F without damage when established, which expands its range significantly compared to Cavendish and plantain types. The fruits are eaten fresh (with a scoopable ice cream-like texture) or frozen for a natural one-ingredient ice cream. A single pup planted in spring will produce a full bunch within 18 months in zone 9+. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Blue Lake 274 Bush Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans dislike transplanting and rot in cold ground. This variety produces a very large concentrated crop of round, 6 inch pods on 16 to 18 inch bushy, disease-resistant plants. Because it crops all at once, sow in successions two weeks apart for a steady supply. Harvest pods while young and tender before the seeds swell, and pick frequently to encourage more pods. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Blue Lake FM-1K Pole Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or pole in warm soil once frost danger has passed. Vigorous 5 to 8 foot vines are high-yielding and produce a bounty of 5 to 7 inch, white-seeded pods excellent fresh, canned, or frozen. Provide strong support before the vines begin to climb. Harvest pods while young and tender, picking every few days to keep the vines producing over a long season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Blue Lake Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Purple Dooryard Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing good airflow through the canopy. Blue Lake is a purple Florida bunch grape carrying strong resistance to Pierce's disease, one of a small group of University of Florida-recommended cultivars able to shrug off the bacterial infection that limits most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South. Unlike several of its Florida-bred counterparts, it typically grows well on its own roots and does not need grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in alkaline soils, simplifying establishment for home growers. Its purple berries are used both for fresh dooryard eating and for juice and jelly making, ripening in midsummer shortly after the earlier 'Stover' cultivar. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and maintain a preventive fungicide program to control the fungal fruit rots that are the main remaining disease threat in Florida's hot, humid summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Lake Pole Bean (Classic Climbing Standard Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost near trellis support; harvest pods at 5–6 inches length for best eating quality. Pick every 2–3 days to encourage continued production. Blue Lake Pole is the climbing, vining form of the Blue Lake bean family — the standard against which all green snap beans are measured in American vegetable gardening. The Blue Lake name comes from Blue Lake, California, where commercial snap bean growers in the Humboldt County area developed and refined the variety for the canning industry in the early 20th century. The Blue Lake type (both bush and pole forms) became the dominant American snap bean because it set the standard for straight, dark green, round pods with excellent tenderness, stringlessness, and flavor — characteristics that made it both the go-to home garden bean and the standard for the commercial canning and frozen bean industry. Blue Lake Pole's climbing habit (6–8 feet) gives it significant advantages over the bush form: the vine continues producing over a longer season (12–16 weeks vs. 6–8 weeks for bush), the elevated flowers and pods are slightly cooler and better-ventilated in humid conditions, and the vertical growth makes efficient use of small garden space with a supporting trellis. The beans are indistinguishable in flavor from the bush form — round, meaty, stringless, medium-dark green, with excellent eating quality fresh, frozen, or canned. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Blue Max Collards (Large Upright High-Yield Smooth-Leaf Collard Hybrid)
description: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Max is a hybrid collard variety valued for its large, smooth, blue-green, broadly rounded leaves and high-yield production — producing some of the largest, most productive collard plants available for home garden and small-farm production. The large leaf size (leaves reaching 18–24 inches across on well-fed plants) and tall, upright habit produce an impressive harvest volume from each plant. As a hybrid variety, Blue Max produces uniform, vigorous plants with excellent disease tolerance and the high-yield characteristics that result from hybrid vigor. The smooth, thick, waxy leaf surface holds up well in cooking and has good culinary quality in traditional preparations — braised with smoked meats, in Southern-style stewed greens, and in other long-cooked preparations where the thick leaves benefit from extended cooking time. Blue Max is cold-hardy and continues producing through Gulf South winters, sweetening after frost exposure as starches convert to sugars — the post-frost harvest typically produces the finest-flavored greens. In zone 9, plant in August–September for fall/winter production and harvest outer leaves progressively through November–February. The very large leaves and tall plants provide ample harvest from relatively few plants in a garden bed. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Blue Moon Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Moon is self-infertile. Blue Moon was part of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Bird) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that established large-fruited modern haskaps in North American gardens and orchards. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often described as a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening well ahead of standard blueberries and giving cold-climate gardeners one of the first fresh berry harvests of the season. Like other haskaps, Blue Moon is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F with flowers surviving brief dips to about -8F, but it performs poorly in hot, humid summers and is best suited to cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first three to four years to removing dead or crossing branches, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Passionflower (Hardy Passionflower)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils; blue passionflower is the most cold-hardy of the fruiting passion vines, tolerating brief dips to 10–15°F when established roots are protected by mulch. The intricate blue, white, and purple flowers with their alien-looking filament corona rank among the most striking summer blooms of any garden vine, followed by oval orange-yellow fruits that are edible but bland compared to commercial passion fruit — grow it primarily for the spectacular flowers and cold hardiness. Dies to the ground in zones 7–8 but regrows strongly from deep roots; do not remove dormant crowns too early in spring. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Blue Ridge Southern Highbush Blueberry (Large-Fruited NC State Release)
description: Establish dormant, container-grown plants in winter in raised, acid-amended beds, keeping the shallow root zone mulched with pine bark year-round. Blue Ridge is a North Carolina State University southern highbush release bred primarily for large berry size and rich flavor rather than for the very lowest chill requirements, so it rewards growers in the cooler, more inland pockets of the Gulf South with fewer, larger-scale flushes of fruit than the deep-South low-chill cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush holds fruit well without excessive splitting during summer rains. Renewal-prune the oldest canes each winter and pair it with another midseason highbush cultivar to extend the harvest window. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Rose Rice (Historic Louisiana Short-Grain, Sol Wright's Red-Rice-Resistant Selection)
description: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Blue Rose is one of the most historically important American rice varieties: Louisiana breeder S.L. (Sol) Wright selected it in 1907 from Japanese rice grown near Jennings, Louisiana, specifically to resist the red rice contamination that was devastating the milled quality of the era's crop, and released it commercially in 1911. Blue Rose went on to dominate American rice production for more than 25 years — by 1934, roughly three-quarters of all rice grown in the United States traced to Wright's Blue Rose breeding work, and Louisiana State Rice Milling sold it as its flagship short-grain product under the Water Maid brand. The short-to-medium grain mills cleanly and cooks up tender, making it well suited to jambalaya, dirty rice, and other Cajun and Creole one-pot dishes that favor a softer grain. The historic site of Wright's original selection in Crowley is preserved today at Crystal Rice Heritage Farm. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling. Matures in 100–125 days from seed.

name: Blue Sausage Vine
description: Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage, since this evergreen twiner from central China resents waterlogging even though it tolerates low light well. Small, fragrant purple-and-white flowers open in spring and are followed in a good year by sausage-shaped purple fruits with sweet, translucent pulp, though fruiting improves markedly when two plants are grown together. Its leathery, trifoliate evergreen leaves make it a valuable year-round screen for shaded boundaries where deciduous vines would leave a winter gap. Prune after flowering to control its vigorous twining growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blue Spice Basil (Compact Mild Anise-Flavored Basil with Lavender Flower Bracts)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F or direct sow after last frost. Pinch growing tips frequently to encourage bushy growth. Harvest leaves before flowers fully open. Blue Spice Basil is a compact sweet basil variety selected for its distinctive lavender-blue flower bracts and mild anise-sweet flavor profile, which is lighter and less intensely clove-like than standard Genovese basil. The variety produces small, bright green oval leaves on compact bushy plants with a tidy, mounding habit that makes it well-suited to container and edging use, as well as herb gardens where a more compact, ornamental basil is preferred over the large-leafed Italian varieties. The 'Blue Spice' name reflects the plant's most distinctive feature: the flower spikes develop conspicuously blue-lavender bracts (the small leaves associated with each flower) that give the blooming plant a distinctly blue-tinted appearance unusual in the basil family. This blue coloration makes Blue Spice one of the most ornamental of the sweet basil group, bridging the gap between standard culinary basil and the more intensely colored Thai basils. The flavor is in the mild, sweet end of the basil spectrum — less intense than Genovese, with a gentle anise note and sweet basil fragrance — making it appropriate for fresh use in salads, as a garnish, and in preparations where a subtle basil flavor is preferred over the intensity of full-strength Italian types. The flowers and bracts are edible with the same flavor as the leaves and make an attractive edible garnish. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Blue Spires Rosemary
description: Blue Spires forms a narrow, upright column of needle-like foliage topped with vivid deep-blue flower spikes in spring, making it a striking accent as well as a culinary rosemary. Grow in lean, gritty soil with excellent drainage, since wet roots in winter are the most common cause of loss. Once established, water only during extended dry spells and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which softens growth and reduces cold hardiness. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the upright habit dense and tidy. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Blue Taro (Purple Taro, Violet-Stemmed Taro, Black Taro)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil — Blue Taro grows vigorously in a range of light conditions and is notably more shade-tolerant than many edible root crops, making it a valuable choice for partially shaded food gardens in zone 8b-12. Xanthosoma violaceum is a large, corm-forming, rhizomatous perennial aroid native to the Caribbean and tropical Americas in the Araceae family — closely related to the Dasheen/Taro group (Colocasia) but in the distinct genus Xanthosoma, which tends to have larger, lighter-colored leaf undersides and edible corms with a different starch profile. The plant is most immediately distinguished by its spectacular petioles (leaf stems) in very deep purple-violet to almost black — a color so intense it verges on the appearance of metal or wood rather than a plant part. The large, sagittate (arrowhead-shaped) leaf blades are blue-green with a slightly waxy, glaucous surface. The overall effect is of a large, bold-textured tropical plant of great ornamental impact. The corms (and young leaves, when properly prepared) are used throughout the Caribbean, West Africa, and Pacific Islands as a starchy vegetable similar to taro. Both the corms and young leaves must be thoroughly cooked to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals. The plant provides excellent large-scale ground cover in shaded areas and combines dramatically with lighter-textured shade plants. CAUTION: toxic if eaten raw; cook thoroughly. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Blue Vantage Cabbage (Fusarium-Resistant Field-Holding Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Blue Vantage is a cabbage hybrid bred for resistance to Fusarium yellows race 1, a persistent soil-borne disease, combined with unusually good tolerance for excess soil moisture and tip burn compared to most cabbage varieties. It forms dense, round, blue-green heads that hold well in the field without splitting even after reaching full maturity, giving gardeners flexibility in harvest timing. Because it handles wet soil better than many cabbage types, it is a strong choice for the heavy spring rains common across the Gulf South. Cut heads once firm and full-sized, and use promptly or store in a cool spot for best quality. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Blue Winter Savory
description: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, cutting the woody stems back hard in early spring to keep growth dense. Blue Winter Savory is a selection of common winter savory grown as much for its show of pale violet-blue flower spikes in summer as for the kitchen, with the same narrow, hairy-edged, strongly aromatic green leaves and upright bushy habit as the species. The leaves carry the familiar robust, resinous, peppery winter savory flavor and can be used interchangeably with the plain species in bean and slow-cooked meat dishes. Protect the crown from standing winter moisture, since like other winter savory selections it is far more tolerant of cold and drought than of wet feet. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Bluebelle Rabbiteye Blueberry (Classic 1985 Florida-USDA Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Bluebelle, released in 1985 through a joint Florida-USDA breeding effort, requires a moderate 450 to 500 chill hours and bears a long, productive mid-to-late-season crop stretching from mid-June through late July, extending the rabbiteye harvest window when planted alongside earlier cultivars. It is a vigorous, reliable, well-established variety with a long track record in Southern home orchards and commercial plantings alike. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Blueberry (Blueray)
description: Blueray was one of the original USDA-New Jersey highbush releases alongside Bluecrop and Coville, prized for its very large, light-blue, firm berries with excellent dessert flavor. The upright bush is exceptionally cold-hardy and reliably productive once established, ripening in midseason. It remains a benchmark backyard variety across the northern and mid-Atlantic blueberry-growing regions. Because of its high chill requirement, it is a poor fit for the low-chill conditions of the Gulf Coast or Deep South. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Blueberry (Cooper)
description: Cooper is a low-chill southern highbush blueberry developed for Deep South growing conditions, valued for tolerating somewhat heavier and less acidic soils than many southern highbush types demand. It ripens early to midseason with medium-sized, well-flavored berries on a compact, manageable bush. Its modest chill requirement lets it set a reliable crop where colder-climate highbush cultivars often bloom poorly. Cooper fruits best when planted alongside another southern highbush cultivar to improve pollination and berry size. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Blueberry (Coville)
description: Coville is a late-season USDA-New Jersey highbush blueberry, named for pioneering blueberry breeder Frederick Coville, producing large, light-blue berries on a vigorous, spreading bush. Fruit holds well on the plant, extending the harvest window after earlier cultivars finish, though berries need to fully color before losing their tartness. It makes a reliable pollinizer partner for other midseason highbush types in home plantings. Like most northern highbush selections, it needs cold winters and is not appropriate for low-chill southern gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Blueberry Ash
description: Plant Elaeocarpus reticulatus in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and in dry periods; mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity; grows well in coastal gardens with some protection from strong wind. Blueberry Ash is one of the most ornamentally multi-season of all Australian native trees — providing year-round interest through its attractive, elliptical, fine-toothed leaves; the exquisite spring flowers (white or blush-pink, tiny fringed bells hanging in clusters, earning the nickname 'Fairy Petticoats'); and the persistent, brilliant cobalt-blue to blue-violet, blueberry-sized drupes that can be present on the tree year-round and are avidly consumed by parrots, doves, and other birds. The blue fruits are technically edible for humans but very astringent and are not eaten except in famine conditions; birds have no such reservation. Elaeocarpus reticulatus is a small to medium rainforest tree (20–40 feet in the wild) that adapts well to cultivation in garden situations, particularly in the humid, subtropical Gulf Coast climate. It makes an outstanding specimen, street tree, or privacy screen for zone 9–11 gardens; the year-round blue berries make it perhaps the most effective bird-attracting tree available for subtropical plantings. Matures in 1095–2920 days from transplant.

name: Blueberry Buckle (Self-Fertile Evergreen-Foliage Container Blueberry, 'Corablue')
description: Blueberry Buckle traces back to a chance seedling found near Hawthorne, Florida, apparently a natural cross between native shiny blueberry (Vaccinium myrsinites) and highbush blueberry, patented as Corablue and sold under the Bushel and Berry brand. It forms a compact, rounded shrub with small, glossy, semi-evergreen leaves that give it ornamental value beyond its fruit, making it a good fit for patio containers as well as garden beds. It is self-fertile and will set some fruit alone, but yields and berry size improve noticeably with a compatible blueberry cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bluecrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Fleshed University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended generously with pine bark or peat, keeping the shallow root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. Bluecrisp was bred by the University of Florida for an unusually firm, crisp bite that holds up well through shipping, on a vigorous, semi-upright bush with a low chilling requirement suited to mild Gulf Coast winters. It shows useful field tolerance to Phytophthora root rot and Botryosphaeria stem blight, two diseases that limit many older highbush selections in the Southeast, though it is only partially self-fruitful and yields best with a different southern highbush cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and renew the planting each winter by removing the oldest, least productive canes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bluecrop Blueberry
description: Bluecrop is a dependable northern highbush blueberry that yields large, mild, juicy berries in mid-season. Plant in acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending with peat or pine bark if needed, and mulch heavily to keep the shallow roots cool and moist. Give it full sun and consistent water, especially during fruit development. Prune out old canes each late winter to keep the bush productive, and plant a second highbush variety nearby to improve pollination and yields. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bluecrop Highbush Blueberry (Standard Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Bluecrop is the gold-standard northern highbush blueberry cultivar — developed by the USDA at Beltsville, Maryland, and introduced in 1952, it remains the most widely planted highbush blueberry in commercial production worldwide and the benchmark against which other northern highbush cultivars are measured. The very large, firm, light-blue, mildly flavored berries are produced in long, loose clusters in mid-season (July in zone 6–7) and hold exceptionally well on the bush without dropping or softening. The fruit quality combines large berry size, excellent flavor, distinctive whitish bloom, and good resistance to cracking in rain that makes Bluecrop outstanding for both fresh eating and freezing. The vigorous, upright shrub grows 4–6 feet tall with attractive white urn-shaped flowers in spring, bright-blue fruit in summer, and outstanding red-orange to crimson fall color. Bluecrop requires 800–1000 chill hours and is best suited to zone 4–7; in zone 8 and warmer, southern highbush cultivars (Vaccinium corymbosum hybrids with V. darrowi) requiring only 200–400 chill hours are more appropriate. Plant with another mid-season highbush cultivar such as Blueray or Legacy for cross-pollination. Maintain strict soil pH below 5.5 using elemental sulfur and acidic fertilizers — pH above 6.0 causes severe iron chlorosis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bluefre Plum (Late-Season European Prune Plum)
description: Bluefre is a European prune-type plum, a cross of President and Stanley developed to ripen later in the season than either parent. The fruit is large for a prune plum, with dark blue skin, firm greenish-amber flesh, and a rich, sweet flavor good for fresh eating, canning, and drying. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will bear, though yields improve with a second European plum nearby. Prune to an open center in late winter and thin fruit if the crop sets heavily to keep fruit size up and limbs from breaking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bluegem Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Low-Chill Florida Selection)
description: Set dormant plants into raised, sulfur-amended beds if the native soil isn't already strongly acidic, and mulch heavily with pine bark to buffer root temperatures through long Gulf Coast summers. Bluegem was among the earliest named rabbiteye selections released by University of Florida breeders in the 1950s, prized for setting a full fruit crop even in unusually warm, low-chill winters that leave many later rabbiteye cultivars with erratic bloom. The medium, light-blue berries have a firm skin and mild flavor, ripening over a fairly long midseason window. Plant it alongside a second rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, and renewal-prune the oldest canes out each winter to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bluegold Blueberry (Compact Midseason Michigan Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Bluegold was bred at Michigan State University for a compact, dense, cold-hardy growth habit that fits well into smaller home garden beds and large containers where full-sized highbush varieties would quickly outgrow the space, while still producing a solid midseason crop of sweet, firm, light-blue berries. The naturally tidy shape needs less aggressive pruning to keep in bounds than many vigorous highbush cultivars, making it a practical choice for gardeners with limited room or those growing blueberries primarily as an ornamental edible landscape plant. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bluejay Blueberry (Cold-Hardy Michigan Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Bluejay was bred at Michigan State University for reliable cold hardiness and good resistance to several diseases that affect blueberries in humid climates, including some tolerance of mummy berry, producing firm, light-blue, mildly sweet berries in early to midseason on a vigorous, upright bush. The bush's tolerance for cold and its dependable, consistent production have made it a long-standing favorite for northern home orchards and commercial plantings alike, even as newer releases have entered the market. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Blumenthal White Sapote (Hawaii-Origin Selection for Humid Subtropics)
description: Blumenthal was imported from the Kona region of Hawaii and stands out among white sapote cultivars for its strong performance in wet, humid subtropical climates that cause fungal and fruit-set problems for cultivars bred in California's drier conditions — a trait Gulf Coast growers should find directly relevant. Because its flowers are functionally female only, a Blumenthal tree will not set a useful crop on its own and needs a cross-pollinating cultivar with viable pollen, such as Pike or Vernon, planted within bee range. Fruit is a typical ovoid white sapote with thin green-to-yellow skin and smooth, custard-textured flesh. Growers in humid subtropical regions outside the mainland US, including northern New South Wales, Australia, have reported it among their best-performing cultivars, which is a useful data point for Gulf Coast gardeners weighing white sapote selections against the region's high humidity and rainfall. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Blunt-leaved Waterleaf
description: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade to partial shade; blunt-leaved waterleaf is a native woodland ephemeral-like perennial of rich forest floors across eastern North America, valued as an early spring edible — the young, furled leaves before flowering are among the most easily harvested native spring greens, with a mild flavor suitable for salads, soups, and sautéing as a pot herb. Unlike Virginia waterleaf (H. virginianum) which has sharply pointed leaflets, this species has distinctly rounded, blunt leaflet tips. The white to pale lavender flowers in spring attract specialist native bees. The plant dies back in summer heat, so it pairs naturally with summer-active ferns and hostas that fill in as it goes dormant. An excellent deep-shade groundcover for moist, woodland gardens that doubles as a spring salad green. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Blushing Beauty Pepper
