description: Blushing Beauty was named an All-America Selections winner for a fruit that skips green entirely, opening ivory and then blushing through light pink, orange-red, and finally deep scarlet as it ripens, often showing several colors on the plant at once. The thick-walled, blocky fruit is sweet and usable at any color stage, giving gardeners flexibility in when to harvest. Its compact, disease-resistant plants perform well in containers on a patio as well as in a garden bed, and the multicolored fruit display makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Pick some fruit at the pale stage to encourage continued setting through the season. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Bob Gordon Elderberry (Kansas State University Very Large Fruit Elderberry)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Bob Gordon was selected by James Millican from a wild elderberry population in Kansas and released through Kansas State University — it produces some of the largest individual berries of any American elderberry cultivar, with berry diameter significantly exceeding the standard wild-type, and heavy, pendant clusters of dark purple-black berries that ripen in late summer. American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) is a vigorously suckering native shrub producing flat-topped, white flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — large, fragrant, and excellent for elderflower cordials, vinegars, and baked goods — followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in August–September used for elderberry syrup, wine, jelly, and juice. 'Bob Gordon' performs well in the humid heat of Gulf South zone 8-9 conditions, though elderberries prefer the slightly cooler and more reliably moist soils of zone 7-8 for maximum production. In zone 9, provide consistent moisture and afternoon shade protection to maintain health through summer. The very large berry size and heavy production make Bob Gordon one of the top choices for home and commercial elderberry production in the eastern US. Plants spread by suckers to form colonies — remove suckers regularly to maintain a well-defined shrub form. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bocking 14 Comfrey (Sterile Russian Comfrey for Permaculture Green Mulch and Fertilizer)
description: Plant root cuttings 2–4 inches deep, 24–36 inches apart; the cutting can be placed horizontally. Cut leaves to the ground 3–4 times per season when the plant reaches 2 feet and use as mulch. Bocking 14 is a sterile cultivar of Russian comfrey (Symphytum × uplandicum, the hybrid between S. asperum and S. officinale) selected by Lawrence D. Hills at the Bocking research station in Essex, UK during the 1950s-60s under the auspices of the Henry Doubleday Research Association (now Garden Organic) — the British organic horticulture organization Hills founded and named for the Victorian market gardener who first championed comfrey's agricultural value. Hills's systematic variety trials of Russian comfrey selected Bocking 14 as the best cultivar for productive leaf yield, high mineral content (particularly potassium, which is 2–3× higher than in most organic mulch materials), and sterility — ensuring that once planted, Bocking 14 would not become an invasive weed spreading by seed across the garden. The sterility that makes Bocking 14 the preferred permaculture comfrey is also the reason it must be purchased as root cuttings rather than seed: no viable seed is produced. The deep taproot (reaching 6+ feet in established plants) functions as a dynamic accumulator — mining calcium, phosphorus, and especially potassium from deep in the soil and concentrating these nutrients in the rapidly-growing leaves. These nutrient-rich leaves, laid around fruiting plants as mulch, break down quickly to release plant-available nutrition, making Bocking 14 a valued fertility tool in organic and low-input garden systems. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bodacious Sweet Corn
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination. This sugar-enhanced hybrid produces 8-inch ears packed with 16 rows of juicy golden kernels that hold their sweetness well after harvest. Sturdy stalks carry a strong disease package for consistent yields. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks brown and kernels are plump and milky. Matures in 75–82 days from seed.

name: Bodacious Sweet Corn (Early Yellow Supersweet Hybrid)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in blocks for good pollination, keeping it isolated from other corn types to protect its supersweet genetics. Bodacious is a widely planted early yellow supersweet hybrid known for large, well-filled ears, dependable vigorous performance across a range of conditions, and excellent sweetness that holds up well for several days after harvest thanks to its sh2 supersweet trait. Its relatively early maturity makes it a good choice for a first planting of the season or for shorter growing windows, and it has long been a standard variety in home garden and market trials. Harvest once silks brown and kernels are plump and milky when tested, and refrigerate promptly to preserve peak sweetness. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Bodegold German Chamomile
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-moderate soil — chamomile prefers lean soil and self-seeds most productively when not over-fertilized; Bodegold is a German-selected high-yield commercial chamomile cultivar developed for maximum essential oil production — the flowers contain 2–3 times the essential oil of wild-type chamomile plants, with particularly high chamazulene (the anti-inflammatory blue compound responsible for chamomile oil's characteristic deep blue color when steam-distilled). This variety is widely grown in Germany, Hungary, and Eastern Europe for pharmaceutical and cosmetic chamomile production where standardized high-oil content is required. For home herbal use, Bodegold provides substantially stronger tea and extract from the same weight of dried flowers compared to ordinary chamomile. The apple-scented white flowers with yellow centers are used fresh or dried for chamomile tea, herbal baths, hair rinses, and digestive tinctures. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Bog Bilberry (Bog Blueberry)
description: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; bog bilberry absolutely requires constantly moist to wet, strongly acidic, poorly drained peaty or boggy soil and will not succeed in drier, neutral conditions. Vaccinium uliginosum is a circumboreal subarctic and subalpine species found in bogs, tundra, and moist mountain heaths across North America, Europe, and Asia — the hardiest of all Vaccinium, surviving temperatures to -60°F; it produces small, round, blue-black berries with a sweet, mild flavor and exceptionally high antioxidant content (higher than commercial blueberries). The berries are an important subsistence food for northern indigenous peoples and are used in jams, pies, and fresh eating. Best suited to cold, wet, acidic sites in zones 1–6 where it is invaluable for bog gardens and moist native plantings. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bog Myrtle (Sweet Gale, Meadow Fern)
description: Plant in moist to wet, peaty, slightly acidic to neutral, poor, boggy soil in full sun to part shade; bog myrtle requires consistently moist to wet conditions and does not tolerate drought; fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis. Myrica gale (bog myrtle or sweet gale) is a deciduous aromatic shrub native to the peat bogs, wet heathlands, and lakeshores of northern North America, northern Europe, and northern Asia — found from Labrador and Maine across Canada to Alaska, and from Ireland and Scotland east through Scandinavia and Russia. The small, lance-shaped, blue-green leaves are intensely aromatic when crushed — a warm, sweet, resinous, herbal fragrance combining elements of bay, eucalyptus, and spice — that has been exploited for culinary and brewing purposes for thousands of years. Before hops (Humulus lupulus) became the universal bittering agent in European beer in the late Middle Ages, bog myrtle (along with other herbs in the 'gruit' mixture) was the primary flavoring of European ale — recorded in historical documents as far back as the 5th century CE. Gruit ale is currently experiencing a major revival in craft brewing, with bog myrtle used in traditional Scottish, Scandinavian, and craft brewery gruit beers. The leaves are also used to flavor Scandinavian aquavit, Scottish whisky cocktails, and gin botanicals. The plant naturally spreads by rhizomes in wet soils and fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. A unique and historically significant herb plant for pond edges and bog gardens in zone 1–6. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bogatyr Garlic (Russian Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Plant large cloves pointed end up about 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil, mulching after planting for winter protection in colder zones. Remove the woody scape once it forms a loop to concentrate the plant's energy into bulb sizing, and cure bulbs in a warm, shaded, ventilated space before storage. Bogatyr, whose name means "hero" or "warrior" in Russian, is a vigorous porcelain-type hardneck valued for its very large bulbs, few but hefty cloves, and pronounced hot, pungent flavor that mellows somewhat with cooking. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Bok Choy
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing 6–12 inches apart; bok choy (pak choi) is the most widely grown Chinese vegetable outside of Asia, producing compact plants with crisp, white-ribbed stalks and dark-green, spoon-shaped leaves used in stir-fries, soups, braises, and salads. It grows rapidly in cool weather and is one of the best fall vegetables for zone 5–11, tolerating light frosts and continuing to produce into early winter in mild climates. Harvest either the entire plant when mature or individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Baby bok choy varieties (Shanghai, Toy Choy) mature in 30–40 days and are ideal for tender whole-plant harvest. Keep evenly moist to prevent premature bolting. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Bok Choy Choko
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to about 4 inches apart, or grow in containers. This baby bok choy tolerates heat, so you can sow it through summer, harvesting at about 4 inches tall for delicate, crisp, mild-flavored leaves. The uniform green plants are an indispensable stir-fry ingredient and also good fresh or marinated. Keep soil evenly moist to keep growth tender, and harvest whole heads while young for the best texture. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Boldo
description: Boldo is a slow-growing, aromatic evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean-climate scrublands of central Chile, where its thick, leathery, sandpapery leaves release a strong camphor-eucalyptus fragrance when crushed. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer, since seed is slow and erratic to germinate, and set young plants in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade with protection from hard freezes. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well but need winter protection or container culture outside zone 9, and in the ground it takes several years to reach a size worth harvesting. The dried leaves, rich in the alkaloid boldine, are steeped as a traditional after-meal digestive tea throughout Chile and are also used to flavor some South American liqueurs. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Boldog Hungarian Spice Paprika Pepper (Heirloom Drying Paprika)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and set plants out once the soil has warmed thoroughly. Boldog Hungarian Spice takes its name from the Hungarian town of Boldog, a historic center of paprika production, and produces compact plants loaded with small, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen to a deep brick red. Bred specifically for drying and grinding, the pods carry sweet, richly aromatic flesh with no heat, and their thin walls dry quickly once strung into ristras or dehydrated. The heavy, early fruit set makes it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting to produce their own homemade sweet paprika powder in a single season. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Boldor Golden Beet (Deep-Gold Bejo F1 Hybrid Non-Bleeding Yellow Beet)
description: Direct sow seed clusters 0.5 inch deep; thin to 3–4 inches. Harvest roots at 2–3 inches diameter for best texture; harvest greens at any size. Boldor is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid golden beet developed specifically to maximize the golden-yellow pigmentation of the root while maintaining the culinary qualities — tender, sweet, earthy — of the best red beet types. Golden beets (yellow beet varieties) differ from standard red beets in their pigmentation: instead of betacyanin (the red-purple betacyanin of standard beets), golden beets produce betaxanthin — a yellow-orange pigment in the same betacyanin family but in the yellow portion of the spectrum. This difference creates the visually striking golden color and the important culinary advantage of significantly reduced bleeding: while red beets stain everything they contact an intense crimson, golden beets' yellow betaxanthin pigment migrates far less during cutting and cooking, making golden beets practical for preparations where color bleeding would be problematic (roasted vegetable mixes, salads with white cheese, light-colored sauces). Boldor consistently achieves the most saturated, vivid golden color of any commonly available golden beet variety — the deep gold interior is visually striking when roasted and served as golden rounds, and the Bejo breeding produces more uniform root sizing than many open-pollinated golden beet types. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Bolero Carrot
description: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall to allow roots to develop fully. Bolero is an outstanding Nantes-type hybrid carrot developed for exceptional disease resistance, particularly to alternaria leaf blight and carrot fly, with excellent tolerance to heat and humidity that makes it one of the most reliable carrots for gardens in zone 7–11 where summer heat normally makes carrot culture difficult. The 6–8 inch, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange, smooth-skinned, and have a sweet, mild flavor with good core-to-cortex ratio and excellent storage quality — they can be left in the ground for weeks without going woody. In zone 8–9, sow in late winter for spring harvest and again in late summer for fall harvest. Matures in 72–80 days from seed.

name: Bolita Bean (New Mexico Traditional Round Pueblo Indian Dry Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when pods are completely dry and papery; beans are round, cream to pinkish-tan. Shell and store in airtight containers. Bolita Bean is the traditional dry bean of New Mexico and the Pueblo cultures of the American Southwest — a variety with documented cultivation in New Mexico and Pueblo Indian communities for centuries, predating European contact and representing one of the most important food plants of southwestern Indigenous agriculture. The name 'bolita' (little ball in Spanish) describes the characteristic round, rotund shape of the dried seed, distinctly rounder than most common beans and immediately recognizable in any collection of dried bean varieties. The dried seeds are cream to pinkish-tan with a slightly glossy surface — a modest appearance that belies the exceptional culinary quality Bolita is known for among Southwest cooks and food historians. The flavor is earthy, slightly sweet, and deeply savory when slow-cooked — Bolita makes extraordinary refried beans (frijoles refritos): the beans cook to a very creamy, smooth texture when mashed and fried, with a richness that commercial pinto beans rarely achieve. Bolita is the traditional bean of New Mexican red and green chile preparations, cooked simply with onion, garlic, and salt or with rendered lard in the traditional method. Seed Savers Exchange and Native Seeds/SEARCH maintain diverse traditional Bolita strains. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Bolivian Coriander (Quilquina, Papalo Quelite)
description: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest tender young leaves frequently. Porophyllum ruderale (Bolivian coriander or quilquiña) is a fast-growing, erect annual herb from South America in the daisy family (Asteraceae) — notable for the distinctive oil glands visible as dark dots on the leaves when held to light. The leaves have an intensely aromatic flavor that is often described as combining cilantro (coriander) with rue and black pepper — pungent, citrus-herbal, with a slightly sharp, medicinal undertone. In Bolivia, the herb is called 'quilquiña' and is used fresh (never cooked — heat destroys the volatile oils) as a condiment for salteñas, silpancho, and sauces; in Peru and Colombia it is called 'papalo quelite' and used in ceviches, guacamole, and fresh salsas. The herb is especially valued in regions where cilantro bolts rapidly in summer heat — Porophyllum is more heat-tolerant and continues producing leaves through summer when cilantro fails. A closely related species, P. macrocephalum (also called papalo), is grown in Mexico and the southwestern US. The leaves must be used fresh and sparingly — the flavor is roughly 4-5 times more intense than cilantro. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Bolivian Giant Achocha (Caigua, Stuffing Cucumber)
description: Bolivian Giant is a large-fruited achocha selection popularized by UK seed savers, bearing smooth to lightly spined, hollow fruit noticeably bigger than the standard species type and well suited to stuffing whole. The vigorous, tendril-climbing vine easily covers 10 to 12 feet of trellis or fence in a single season and produces heavily even in cooler summers where cucumbers struggle. Harvest fruit while still young and tender, before the interior seeds harden and blacken, for the best crisp, mild, cucumber-like flavor. Because the plant self-seeds readily and can naturalize in mild climates, remove spent vines at season's end if volunteer seedlings are unwanted. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Bolivian Rainbow Pepper (Ornamental-Edible Multicolor Hot Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; Bolivian Rainbow is one of the most visually spectacular ornamental-edible peppers available — a compact plant that simultaneously displays fruits at multiple stages of ripening, cycling through purple, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, creating a stunning multicolored display that earns it a place in ornamental borders and container arrangements as much as in vegetable gardens. The plants are dense, attractive, and heavily loaded with small (1–1.5 inch), upward-pointing conical fruits; the visual effect of dozens of multicolored fruits pointing upward from the dark green foliage is genuinely striking and unlike any other common garden plant. The fruits are very hot (50,000–100,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat appropriate for hot sauce, spicy condiments, or any preparation where decorative whole dried peppers provide both heat and visual interest. The purple stage is particularly ornamental (purple pigmentation rarely seen in fruiting stage of other varieties) and fades to yellow, then orange, then the final red as the fruit matures. In zone 9+, established plants often behave as perennials, developing increasingly thick, woody stems and producing heavier crops each successive season. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Boltardy Beet (Bolt-Resistant Early Beetroot)
description: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Boltardy is a Dutch-bred Detroit-type beet that has become one of the most widely grown home garden beets in Britain because it resists bolting to seed when exposed to the cold snaps and temperature swings of an early spring sowing, letting gardeners start the crop weeks ahead of standard varieties. It produces smooth-skinned, deep burgundy, globe-shaped roots with minimal internal ringing and a sweet, tender flavor well suited to boiling, roasting, or pickling. Keep the soil consistently moist for even root development and pull roots at two to three inches across for the best texture. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Bonanza Apricot (Genetic Dwarf Patio Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Bonanza is a genetic dwarf apricot that naturally stays under six feet tall while still producing normal-sized, sweet, orange-fleshed fruit, making it one of the few apricots practical for a large container or a very small yard. Like most apricots it blooms quite early in spring, so a sheltered site away from low-lying frost pockets improves the odds of a good fruit set. The dense, compact form needs little pruning to maintain shape beyond removing crossing branches, and the tree is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator variety. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bonanza Patio Peach
description: Bonanza is a genetic dwarf peach that fits easily on a patio yet produces full-size, sweet, rosy fruit. Its naturally compact habit and showy pink spring blossoms make it as ornamental as it is productive, ideal for containers and small yards. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and provide a large pot or a spot with room for the roots. Thin the young fruit for better size, prune in late winter to shape, and water consistently while fruit is developing. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bonbon Squash (AAS-Winning Sweet Early Buttercup-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bonbon is an AAS-winning improvement on the classic buttercup winter squash, ripening earlier and growing on a more compact vine than standard buttercup types while producing the same dark-green, turban-shaped fruit with a distinctive gray-blue button on the blossom end. The dense, deep-orange flesh is notably sweet and dry-textured, excellent baked, mashed, or used in place of pumpkin in pies and soups. Its earlier maturity is a real advantage in areas with a shorter warm season or where gardeners want to fit squash into a tighter succession-planting schedule. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry and corky; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Bonfire Patio Peach
description: Bonfire is a compact ornamental peach grown chiefly for its striking deep-crimson foliage and pink spring flowers, though it can set small edible fruit. Its fiery color and dwarf size make it a dramatic focal point for patios and small gardens. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil in a large container or bed. Prune after flowering to maintain its tidy form, water regularly during the growing season, and expect the best leaf color in full sun. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Boniato (White Sweet Potato, Cuban Sweet Potato, Batata)
description: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam, enriched ridges in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; boniato is the traditional sweet potato of Cuban, Caribbean, and Latin American cuisine, prized for its dry, fluffy, white to pale cream flesh that is less sweet, less moist, and more starchy than orange sweet potatoes — more similar in texture to a russet potato and much preferred in savory preparations. The skin is irregularly shaped, pinkish to light brown, and the plants are slightly more drought-tolerant than standard sweet potatoes. Excellent roasted, mashed, or fried; does not have the cloying sweetness that makes American orange sweet potatoes unsuitable for some savory applications. Stores well in a cool, dry location. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Bonita Peach (Award-Winning Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. A California-bred freestone needing under 400 chill hours, Bonita performs well in zone 8-9 winters too mild for standard high-chill peaches. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed with a red blush, and has repeatedly scored among the top varieties in formal taste trials for its sweet, subacid flavor. It ripens in mid to late summer, later than most low-chill Gulf selections, which helps extend the home orchard's peach season. Self-fruitful and vigorous, a single tree sets a full crop without a pollinizer. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bonita Rabbiteye Blueberry (Early-Season Florida-Bred Blueberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil, incorporating pine bark fines to boost organic matter and moisture retention. Released by the University of Florida in 1985, Bonita is one of the earliest-ripening rabbiteye cultivars available, typically flowering and fruiting several weeks ahead of midseason types like Tifblue. It requires a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Beckyblue blooming at the same time to set a good crop, and while modern mid- and late-season rabbiteyes have generally surpassed it in overall yield, Bonita remains a useful choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible rabbiteye harvest. The vigorous, spreading bush performs well across the humid Gulf South once established in properly acidified soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bonita Sweet Potato
description: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to sandy-loam soil — sweet potatoes do not tolerate waterlogged or compacted soil; Bonita is a white-fleshed sweet potato released by the Louisiana State University AgCenter specifically for Gulf Coast production conditions, selected for its firm, dry, mildly sweet flesh that is used as a staple starchy vegetable rather than as a dessert-sweet orange-fleshed type. The large, oblong, tan-skinned tubers have creamy white flesh with a dry, starchy texture more similar to a dry-type white potato than to the moist, orange Beauregard type — making Bonita suitable for soups, stews, fried preparations, and the Latin American-style cooking (boniato) where a dry, non-sweet white sweet potato is traditional. The vine shows good heat and humidity tolerance and is specifically tested for performance in the Gulf South's challenging summer conditions. Bonita is popular in Louisiana and Gulf Coast markets catering to Caribbean and Latin American culinary traditions. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Bonnie Best Tomato (Early 1900s Heirloom Slicing Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed. Introduced around 1908 and long a staple of American home and market gardens, Bonnie Best produces smooth, deep red, medium-sized fruit with excellent classic tomato flavor and good production over a long season, having served for decades as a standard against which other tomato varieties were measured before modern hybrids became dominant. Its old-fashioned, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and reliable performance make it a satisfying choice for gardeners seeking a historically significant slicing tomato with genuine heirloom character rather than a specialty color or shape. Harvest when fruit is fully red and yields to gentle pressure, and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vines producing. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Bonnie Brae Lemon (California Heirloom Slender Lemon)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site, giving this vigorous, somewhat thorny tree room to spread. Water consistently during establishment and avoid waterlogged soil, which quickly stresses lemon roots. Bonnie Brae produces distinctively long, slender, thin-skinned lemons with abundant tart juice and few seeds, and it can flower and fruit nearly year-round in mild climates. Once grown commercially in Southern California, it remains a sought-after heirloom for home growers who prize its exceptionally juicy fruit over its irregular, less market-friendly shape. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bonnotte Potato (Early French Island New Potato)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained, sandy soil; Bonnotte is an early-maturing variety best harvested young as a thin-skinned new potato rather than left to mature fully. Bonnotte is celebrated in France as one of the earliest and most prized new potatoes, traditionally hand-harvested on the sandy, salt-influenced soils of the Île de Noirmoutier off the Atlantic coast, prized for delicate, thin skin and sweet, buttery flesh that needs little more than a quick steam and butter to shine. Harvest young, while the skin still rubs off easily, for the best texture and flavor, and use promptly since new potatoes do not store as long as mature ones. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Bonny Best Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Bonny Best performs well with or without staking — it is an indeterminate but moderately compact type compared to most indeterminate heirlooms. Bonny Best was introduced in 1908 (previously distributed as 'John Baer') and rapidly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in early 20th century America, prized for reliable, heavy production of attractive, round to slightly oblate, medium to large (6–10 oz), uniformly red fruits with a classic balanced sweet-acid flavor that home gardeners and canners found superior to the watery commercial varieties of the era. Bonny Best's particular virtues are its productivity, disease resilience, and flavor — a reliable old-fashioned tomato that consistently produces good crops without fuss. By midcentury it was eclipsed in commerce by hybrid varieties but remained in home garden cultivation; it is now maintained by seed savers and available from heritage seed companies as one of the historically important American tomato varieties. Good canning and fresh-eating tomato. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Boone County White Corn (Historic Midwestern White Dent Corn)
description: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in blocks of at least four rows, and give this long-season dent corn a full growing season with consistent moisture through pollination for best ear fill. Boone County White originated in Indiana and Illinois in the late 1800s and became one of the most widely grown white dent corns of the pre-hybrid Corn Belt, valued for tall, productive stalks and large, well-filled ears of smooth white dent kernels. It was historically important both as a table and livestock feed corn and as breeding stock, and it still produces excellent white cornmeal and hominy for gardeners wanting to grow a piece of Midwestern agricultural history. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Booth 7 Avocado (Florida Guatemalan-West Indian Hybrid)
description: Booth 7 is a Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid bred in the historic Homestead, Florida avocado district, valued for combining better cold tolerance and richer flavor than pure West Indian cultivars with reasonably good adaptation to Florida's wet, humid summers. Fruit is medium-sized, pear-shaped, with moderately high oil content and a nutty flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. It is a somewhat more compact, precocious tree than the old West Indian heritage cultivars, making it a practical choice for dooryard growers wanting improved flavor without excessive tree size. Provide full sun and sharply drained soil, and avoid heavy irrigation once fruit begins to mature. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Booth 8 Avocado (Florida Guatemalan-West Indian Hybrid)
description: Booth 8 shares its Guatemalan x West Indian parentage with Booth 7 and was selected from the same Homestead, Florida breeding program, but it ripens somewhat later in the fall and holds well on the tree once mature. The medium, pear-shaped fruit has thicker skin than many Florida cultivars, which makes it more forgiving to handle and ship, along with moderately rich, nutty flesh. It combines better disease tolerance in humid conditions than pure Guatemalan cultivars with more cold hardiness than pure West Indian types, making it a solid dual-purpose dooryard choice. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage and avoid letting the root zone stay wet for extended periods. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Booth Cherimoya
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Booth is a long-established Florida cherimoya selection prized for reliable production and good-sized, conical, mildly ribbed fruit with rich, sweet, custardy white flesh and the classic tropical flavor blend of pineapple, banana, and vanilla. It has a reputation as one of the more dependable croppers among named cherimoya cultivars in Florida's warm, humid subtropical conditions, which can otherwise be a challenging environment for a species that prefers the cooler, drier climate of its Andean homeland. As with all cherimoya, hand-pollinate by transferring pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers with a small brush in the morning hours, since the flowers' protogynous timing makes natural self-pollination unreliable. Grafted trees bear within two to four years; protect young trees from frost and give them consistent moisture during fruit development. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Boothby Blonde Cucumber
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Boothby Blonde is a Maine heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family of Livermore Falls and introduced to the broader seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange. The small, oval fruits are ivory-to-pale-yellow with black or white spines — the pale color is the key distinguishing feature that makes identification by color a reliable harvest guide. Harvest when the fruits are still ivory-white at 3–5 inches; yellowing indicates over-maturity. The flesh is exceptionally crisp, mild, and sweet with thin skin that does not require peeling — the flavor is more delicate than standard green cucumbers, with less bitterness and a refreshing, clean taste ideal for fresh eating, simple salads, and sliced into yogurt or dressings. The unusual pale exterior makes it a novelty in the garden and at farmers' markets. Heat tolerance is adequate for zone 9 spring crops, but fall production is best. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Boothby's Blonde Cucumber (Maine Heirloom Cream-Yellow Oval Cucumber, Seed Savers Classic)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when cream-yellow and firm. Boothby's Blonde is a Maine family heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family from Livermore Falls, Maine, and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange — the network through which most American home-saved heirloom vegetable varieties have been maintained and distributed since the organization's founding in 1975. The cucumber is immediately distinguishable from every other commonly grown variety by its fruit color: the skin is creamy white to pale yellow at harvest maturity, oval to oblong in shape (3–4 inches long), with black spines on the surface ribs rather than the white spines of European or Asian cucumber types. This combination of cream-yellow skin and black spines produces a visual character unlike any other cucumber commonly available — the pale fruit with dark spines stands out dramatically in the garden and on the plate. The eating quality is excellent: thin skin (no peeling needed), crisp and juicy flesh, mild sweet flavor with no bitterness, and a good seed cavity for a traditional cucumber type. Boothby's Blonde exemplifies the category of heirloom vegetables that persist not because of exceptional yield or disease resistance but because of unique visual and flavor qualities unavailable in commercial varieties — preserved specifically because gardeners valued those qualities enough to maintain the seed across generations. Matures in 56–65 days from seed.

name: Borage
description: Sow seeds 1/2 in deep directly in their permanent position; borage has a taproot that is easily damaged and transplants poorly. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil—even poor, dry soil suits it. Once established it self-seeds readily, so remove unwanted seedlings while they are small. The star-shaped blue flowers are edible with a cool cucumber flavor; harvest them when newly opened for garnishing salads and drinks. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Bordelon Banana (Cold-Hardy Fruiting Gulf South Banana)
description: Bordelon is a fruiting banana selection that circulated among Gulf South banana growers for its unusual combination of an exceptionally cold-hardy rhizome and the ability to still set an edible bunch within a single Gulf Coast growing season. Like Orinoco, the pseudostem is killed back by hard freezes, but the underground rhizome survives winters into the upper teens Fahrenheit and resprouts vigorously each spring, giving gardeners in zone 8b-9 a realistic shot at homegrown bananas most years rather than only in true zone 10-11 climates. The medium-sized fruit is sweet and best eaten fresh once fully ripe, and the large paddle-shaped leaves supply the same bold tropical look as more tender banana cultivars. Full sun, heavy irrigation, and monthly feeding through the growing season push it toward flowering before the first fall cold snap. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Boreal Beast Honeyberry (University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with at least one other overlapping-bloom haskap cultivar nearby, since Boreal Beast will not set fruit on its own. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program alongside Boreal Beauty and Boreal Blizzard, Boreal Beast is prized for its large, elongated fruit and vigorous, upright bush that holds its berries well without excessive drop as they ripen in mid-to-late season. Like other haskaps it tolerates winter cold to roughly -40F but struggles in hot, humid summer regions, making it best suited to short-season, cold-winter gardens. Avoid heavy pruning for the first three to four years beyond removing dead or crossing wood, since fruit forms on second-year and older growth, then begin light renewal pruning of the oldest canes to sustain production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Boreal Beauty Honeyberry (Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Boreal Beauty needs cross-pollination from another haskap cultivar to crop well. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program as part of its 'Boreal' series, Boreal Beauty ripens later than the earliest haskap introductions and produces firm, elongated, deep-blue berries bred to hold well on the bush without dropping, making it well suited to mechanical or delayed hand harvest. Like other haskaps, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in short, cool-summer growing seasons, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid climates. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then shift to renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Boreal Blizzard Honeyberry (Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, as Boreal Blizzard will not set a meaningful crop without a compatible pollinizer nearby. Part of the University of Saskatchewan's 'Boreal' haskap series, Boreal Blizzard produces a heavy crop of good-flavored blue berries and blooms at a time that makes it an effective pollen source for several other Saskatchewan-bred cultivars, so it is commonly planted in pairs specifically to boost yields in a mixed haskap planting. The upright, vigorous shrub is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating deep winter cold typical of the Canadian prairies, but struggles in hot, humid summer regions. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood while the bush is young, then begin renewal pruning of older canes once the planting is established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Borealis Honeyberry (Large-Fruited University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Borealis is self-infertile and needs cross-pollination to set fruit. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, Borealis produces some of the largest berries of any haskap cultivar, with a sweet-tart flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, and ripens in late spring, about two to three weeks before strawberries in most climates, making it one of the earliest fresh fruits of the season. Flowers open very early and tolerate temperatures down to about -8F, but a hard late freeze can still reduce fruit set, so plant in a site that avoids obvious frost pockets. Like other haskaps, Borealis is bred for cold-winter regions and struggles with root and crown health in hot, humid summers, so it is a poor fit for the Gulf Coast and performs best in short-season northern gardens. Minimal pruning is needed for the first four to five years beyond removing dead wood; thereafter remove one or two of the oldest, thickest canes annually to keep the shrub renewing itself. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Borettana Cipollini Onion (Flat Golden Italian Onion)
description: Direct sow or set transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This Italian heirloom produces distinctively flat, disc-shaped bulbs with coppery-gold skin and sweet, mild flesh, and is the classic cipollini used in Italian agrodolce (sweet-and-sour) roasted onion dishes as well as pickling, since the flat shape cooks evenly and looks attractive whole on the plate. It matures relatively quickly for an onion and the small-to-medium bulbs cure and store reasonably well for a sweet type. Space plants a bit closer than standard globe onions, since the flattened bulbs take up less lateral room, and reduce watering as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over near harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Boro Beet (Blight-Resistant Bolt-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Boro is a hybrid beet whose tops resist common foliar blights that can weaken plants in humid, wet weather, while the roots show strong resistance to bolting and hold good quality in storage after harvest longer than many varieties. It produces smooth, round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and healthy dark green tops good for cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across; Boro's good storage quality makes it a solid choice for gardeners who want to hold part of the crop rather than using it all immediately. Matures in 55–62 days from seed.

name: Borojó
description: Grow this understory shrub from the Colombian Chocó rainforest in a large pot of rich, moisture-retentive potting mix, since it wants filtered light and constant humidity rather than harsh full sun. It produces large, dense, brown fruits packed with a thick, tart pulp that is almost always processed into juice or preserves rather than eaten fresh. Because it is one of the most cold-sensitive fruiting plants grown by tropical fruit collectors, Gulf Coast and Florida growers keep it strictly as a greenhouse or sunroom container specimen and never leave it outside once temperatures dip toward 50°F. Consistent watering and high humidity are more important to fruit set than any particular soil type. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bosc Pear (Beurré Bosc, Kaiser Pear)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil; amend with compost before planting; Bosc pear requires a cross-pollinator within 100 feet — plant with Bartlett, Anjou, or Comice for best fruit set. Bosc pear (Beurré Bosc, also marketed as Kaiser in Europe) is a Belgian heirloom originating in the early 1800s and named for Louis Bosc, a French diplomat and naturalist; it is immediately distinguished from other pears by its elongated shape, long graceful neck tapering to a slender stem, and russeted skin ranging from golden-yellow to russet-brown — unlike the smooth, green or yellow skin of Bartlett and Anjou types. The flesh is white to cream, dense, crisp and aromatic when just harvested but quickly transitions to the typical soft, buttery, juicy pear texture; the flavor is spicy-sweet with hints of vanilla, cinnamon, and honey — considered by many pear enthusiasts among the most complex and interesting flavors of the major commercial pear varieties. Bosc ripens mid to late season (September–November depending on location), later than Bartlett; it is the superior pear for cooking, baking, and poaching because it holds its shape under heat better than soft-fleshed types, while also excellent for fresh eating at peak ripeness. Requires 600–900 chill hours; zones 5–8. Matures in 130–150 days from transplant.

name: Boskoop Giant Black Currant (Historic Dutch Black Currant)
description: Boskoop Giant is one of the oldest black currant cultivars still commercially available, originating from the Dutch nursery town of Boskoop around the turn of the twentieth century and prized for its vigorous growth and unusually large, aromatic berries borne on long strigs. Because Ribes nigrum is a highly effective alternate host for white pine blister rust, confirm this cultivar is legal to plant in your state or county before ordering, since several eastern and midwestern jurisdictions restrict or ban black currants outright. Give plants rich, evenly moist soil and full sun to light shade, and renew the bush each dormant season by removing wood older than three years, since Boskoop Giant fruits most heavily on one- and two-year-old canes. The intensely flavored fruit is better suited to jam, syrup, and cassis production than fresh eating, and the bush's older, less disease-resistant genetics mean it benefits from good air circulation to limit leaf spot and mildew. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bossa Nova Squash (Mottled Caserta-Type Virus-Resistant Zucchini)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Bossa Nova is a distinctive Caserta-type zucchini with striking dark and light green mottled skin, bred with intermediate resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus and watermelon mosaic virus, two viruses spread by aphids that commonly shorten a summer squash season in humid Gulf Coast gardens. It is also noted for an unusually extended harvest window compared to most zucchini, continuing to produce good-quality fruit later into the season. Pick fruit at 6-8 inches for the best texture and flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since squash left on the vine quickly grows oversized and seedy. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Boston Marrow Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, enriched soil, spacing hills 4–6 feet apart and thinning to 2 plants per hill; Boston Marrow requires 90–100 days of warm weather, so plant promptly after last frost. Boston Marrow is one of the oldest American heirloom winter squashes, offered by commercial seedsmen in New England since the 1830s; it produces round to pear-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with spectacular, deep orange-red skin and extremely sweet, fine-grained, nearly stringless flesh of exceptional quality — it was reportedly the standard squash for pies before Hubbard types became popular. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin is fully colored; cure for 10 days and store in a cool, dry place for 2–3 months. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Boston Pickling Cucumber
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Boston Pickling is a fast-maturing (55–65 days) pickling type that produces very early and keeps producing well if harvested at 2–3 inch length for small dill pickles or 3–4 inch length for whole dill pickles. Boston Pickling is an American heirloom documented since the 1870s, producing short, blocky, light-to-medium green fruits with slightly ridged skin, crisp white flesh, and a small seed cavity that gives pickles an excellent bite; the skin absorbs brine beautifully, producing crunchy pickles that store for months. Harvest at least every two days when production peaks to keep the vine producing; fruits left to yellow dramatically slow new production. Both vine-type and bush selections exist. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Boston Red Sunchoke (Heirloom Red-Skinned Jerusalem Artichoke)
description: Boston Red is a long-grown New England heirloom sunchoke selected for its striking maroon-red tuber skin, which contrasts sharply with the white flesh beneath and makes it a favorite of seed savers maintaining regionally distinct strains. Like other Jerusalem artichokes it grows into a coarse, sunflower-like stand 6-10 feet tall, topped with small yellow flowers in late summer, and tolerates poor soil and neglect once established. Dig tubers after the tops are killed by frost and continue harvesting through winter and into early spring as needed, leaving some tubers in the ground each year to regenerate the patch. Its flavor is the same nutty, sweet-earthy inulin-rich profile typical of the species, and it sweetens further after tubers experience a hard freeze. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Bottle Gourd (Calabash)
description: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in warm mix or directly in warm soil; nick the seed coat or soak overnight to speed germination. Bottle gourd is a vigorous, tropical vine that requires a sturdy trellis or fence and very warm conditions to thrive. Harvest immature fruits when they are 6–8 inches long (or the desired shape depending on variety) for vegetable use — they are delicate and best cooked; allow fruits to mature fully and dry on the vine if growing for use as a gourd vessel. Pollination requires both male and female flowers to be open simultaneously; hand-pollinate in the morning if fruit set is poor. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Bouche de Betizac Chestnut (Large-Nutted Blight-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator chestnut within range for the best nut production, since yields improve substantially with cross-pollination even in partially self-fertile cultivars. Bouche de Betizac is a French-bred hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut species, combining the large, sweet, high-quality nuts prized in European chestnut cookery with meaningful resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that devastated native American chestnut populations and continues to threaten susceptible European chestnut plantings. It bears precociously, often producing a first crop within just a few years of planting, and continues with heavy, reliable yields of large, easy-to-peel nuts on a vigorous, productive tree. Its blight resistance and large nut size have made it a popular choice for both commercial and home chestnut orchards seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant alternative to susceptible pure European chestnut cultivars. Harvest nuts as burs split and drop in fall, collecting promptly to avoid rodent and insect loss. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Boufu (Japanese Hamaboufuu, Coastal Hog Fennel)
description: Direct sow into sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; boufu is a coastal Japanese and Okinawan perennial in the carrot family, grown for its tender young shoots and finely divided, aromatic leaves, which are harvested in spring and used in Okinawan cooking much like a cross between celery and parsley — lightly blanched, added to tempura, or used fresh in salads. It forms a low mound of blue-green, feathery foliage and produces flat clusters of small white flowers on taller stalks if allowed to bolt in its second year. In its native coastal habitat it tolerates sandy soil, salt spray, and part shade from adjacent dune vegetation, making it a good choice for a lean, well-drained herb bed that doesn't stay wet. Harvest young leaves and shoots regularly to keep the plant productive and delay flowering, which coarsens the texture. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Boulder Raspberry (Delicious Raspberry)
description: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; boulder raspberry is one of the most beautiful ornamental native shrubs of the Rocky Mountain foothills — an entirely thornless, arching shrub with attractive, deeply lobed, maplelike leaves and stunning large (up to 2.5 inch), pure white, rose-like flowers in late spring. The species name 'deliciosus' was reportedly given because the flowers are so delightful, though the fruit (small, dry, sparse drupelets) is technically edible but far from impressive compared to other raspberries. The magnificent white flowers in May and June make boulder raspberry outstanding as a flowering ornamental in dry, rocky garden situations in zones 4–8. Completely thornless — unlike virtually all other Rubus — making it safe for high-traffic areas of the garden. The state flower of Colorado (not officially, but very emblematic of the Front Range foothills). Drought tolerant once established, appropriate for xeriscape plantings in the Rocky Mountain West. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Boule d'Or Melon (Golden Ball Muskmelon)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after frost danger has passed, thinning to 2 strong plants per hill; mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds around the sprawling vines. Harvest when the golden-yellow rind fully colors and the fruit releases a musky-sweet fragrance at the stem end, usually with a slight give when pressed. Boule d'Or ('Golden Ball') is a French heirloom cantaloupe-type melon dating to the late 1800s, bearing round, 2–3 lb fruit with a distinctive smooth, deep-gold rind faintly ribbed rather than netted, enclosing firm, pale orange flesh with a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. Unlike most cantaloupes, Boule d'Or keeps for several weeks after picking without losing flavor, making it valued by market gardeners for extending the melon season. Vines are moderately vigorous and benefit from trellising in smaller gardens if fruit weight is supported in slings. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Bounty Strawberry (Historic Ottawa-Bred Vigorous Strawberry)
description: Bounty was bred at Agriculture Canada's Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa and released for its vigorous, heavy-yielding plants and good general disease tolerance, making it a dependable mid-season strawberry for the cooler strawberry-growing regions of Canada and the northern United States. Plant bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, giving the vigorous runners plenty of room to fill in a matted row over the first season. Its firm, bright red berries hold up well for local sale and home preserving, though flavor is considered solid rather than exceptional next to modern dessert-type cultivars. Bounty's vigor and hardiness made it valuable parent stock for later Canadian strawberry breeding, including the widely grown cold-hardy cultivar Glooscap. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bouquet de Fleurs Sour Orange (Fragrant Dwarf Ornamental Orange)
description: Bouquet de Fleurs is an old Florida sour orange selection grown chiefly for its exceptionally heavy, powerfully fragrant flush of white spring blossoms, historically harvested for neroli-scented orange flower water and perfumery. The naturally compact, low, spreading tree tops out around 6 to 8 feet, fitting large containers or small dooryard plantings better than standard sour orange seedlings. Like other sour oranges, it carries the same cold hardiness that made Citrus aurantium the traditional rootstock and hedge citrus of the Gulf South, shrugging off brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit once established. The tart, seedy, puckering fruit hangs on the tree for months and makes excellent marmalade or liqueur flavoring, though it is not meant for fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bouquet Dill
description: Direct sow seed where the plants are to grow, since dill has a taproot and resents being transplanted; make succession sowings for a steady supply. This variety is especially good for pickling thanks to its early, abundant seed heads, while the aromatic foliage is delicious on potatoes, fish, and vegetables. Let some plants flower to attract pollinators and support swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, for which dill is an important host plant. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Bourbon Coffee
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Named for the former French colonial name of Réunion Island, where it was first cultivated after being introduced from Yemen, this historic Arabica coffee variety is one of the parent lines behind many modern specialty coffee cultivars and is still prized by growers and roasters for producing sweet, well-balanced, complex cups, though its lower yield compared to newer hybrid varieties has made it less common in large-scale commercial production. Like other Arabica coffees it grows best in the dappled shade of taller companion trees, mimicking its native highland forest understory habitat, and needs consistent warmth and moisture without ever standing in wet, waterlogged soil. Water regularly but ensure good drainage, provide filtered shade, and expect the first coffee cherry harvest after three to four years of growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bourgeault Quince (Le Bourgeault, French Heirloom Culinary Quince)
description: Bourgeault, also known as Le Bourgeault, is an old French culinary quince introduced into the United States around 1885 and still propagated today by heirloom fruit specialists. It forms a vigorous, self-fertile tree bearing medium-sized fruit with juicy yellow flesh and good cooking flavor. As with other true quince, the raw fruit is hard and astringent and is not eaten fresh; instead it is prized for jelly, paste, and baked preserves, turning a warm rose color as it cooks down. Grow in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest in fall once the downy skin turns fully golden and gives off the characteristic strong quince fragrance. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bourjasotte Noire Fig (Noire de Barbentane, Black Bourjasotte)
description: Grown around the western Mediterranean for centuries under names like Brogiotto Nero and Noire de Barbentane, this dark purple-to-black fig is a separate old cultivar from the paler Bourjassotte Grise. Fruit is large and broad-based with a blue-purple bloom over near-black skin, enclosing dense, glossy dark red flesh with a honeyed, faintly tart, berry-and-melon flavor. Its notably firm, thicker skin gives it better resistance to rain-cracking and splitting than many other dark-fleshed figs of similar quality. Expect a single generous main crop rather than a significant breba flush. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bourjassotte Grise Fig (Grise de Bourjassotte)
description: A classic fig of Provence, Bourjassotte Grise bears medium-sized fruit with a distinctive grayish-brown to violet-tinted skin covering deep strawberry-red flesh with a rich, sweet, complex flavor long prized in French markets. The tree is moderately vigorous and reliably productive once established, generally favoring a single strong main crop over a heavy breba crop. Plant in full sun with good air circulation, since the thin skin is prone to splitting after heavy rain near harvest. It is best suited to long, warm-summer climates where the late-season fruit has time to fully ripen before cool weather arrives. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bournette Chestnut (French Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Bournette is a French European x Japanese hybrid chestnut cultivar developed alongside Marigoule and Bouche de Betizac, selected for good nut size and the blight and ink disease tolerance typical of this hybrid group. It is grown mainly in French orchards for the fresh and processed chestnut trade, where its reliable production complements earlier- and later-ripening sibling cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a distinct pollenizer nearby, since chestnuts will not set a full crop from a single tree. Space trees widely to accommodate their eventual broad canopy. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Bowles Mint (Bowles' Apple Mint)
description: Grow in consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Bowles Mint tolerates more shade than most culinary mints and holds up better under it, making it a reliable choice for a herb bed that only gets morning sun. Its rounded, softly downy, bright-green leaves carry a mild, sweet flavor that blends spearmint and apple-mint notes without the sharper edge of peppermint, and it is the classic choice for traditional English mint sauce. Compared with plain apple mint, this selection is noted for better rust resistance and slightly less rampant spreading, though it should still be grown in a container or behind a root barrier to keep it in bounds. Shear plants back after flowering to renew tender growth for harvest through fall. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bowling Red Okra
description: Sow directly into warm garden soil after frost danger has passed, since okra grows poorly if started indoors and transplanted. Pick the deep red pods small and often to keep plants productive through the heat of summer. Bowling Red is a Kentucky heirloom valued for its striking burgundy-red pods and reddish stems, which add ornamental interest to the vegetable garden as well as color to the harvest basket. The pods darken to a rich maroon-green when cooked but retain their tender texture if picked young. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Box Car Willie Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Box Car Willie is an American heirloom red beefsteak tomato named with Old West flair and popular for its reliable productivity, large 8–14 ounce fruits with smooth, meaty red flesh and excellent balanced sweet-acid flavor, and its relative disease resistance compared to many other heirlooms — it typically outproduces more famous heirlooms like Brandywine under variable conditions. The vigorous, indeterminate vines need staking or caging; fruits are round to slightly flattened with smooth, crack-resistant skin. A solid everyday heirloom choice for gardeners who want large, flavorful tomatoes without the fussiness of some heritage types. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Box Huckleberry (Long-Lived Evergreen Creeping Shade Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, and mulch with pine needles or leaf litter to maintain acidity and moisture. Box Huckleberry is a rare, low, evergreen, boxwood-like shrub native to scattered sites in the eastern United States, forming slow-spreading clonal colonies that are among the longest-lived plant clones known, with some wild colonies estimated at over a thousand years old. Small, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves cover the low, dense mat of stems, and it bears small pink, bell-shaped spring flowers followed by sparse but edible, sweet, dark blue berries in summer, similar in flavor to other huckleberries though the plant fruits lightly in cultivation. Because it tolerates deep shade and stays low and evergreen year-round, it makes a distinctive, slow-growing woodland groundcover for shaded native gardens where few other fruiting shrubs will grow; give it consistent moisture and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizome mat once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Boxcar Willie Tomato (Reliable Red Beefsteak Heirloom)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and stake early to support the productive vine. Boxcar Willie is a widely grown red beefsteak heirloom, said to be named after country singer Boxcar Willie, prized among home gardeners for combining classic large, meaty, smooth, round-oblate red fruit with a more reliable, heavier yield and better disease tolerance than many older large-fruited heirlooms. The mild, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor and consistent fruit set make it a good gateway heirloom for gardeners moving beyond hybrid slicers, and the regular-leaf indeterminate vines keep producing steadily over a long season. Water evenly and feed regularly through fruit set, and stake generously, since the productive vine sets a heavy load of good-sized fruit. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Boxwood Basil (Dense Globe-Shaped Dwarf Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Boxwood basil forms an unusually dense, tightly rounded mound of small, aromatic leaves that closely mimics the look of a miniature clipped boxwood shrub, making it a favorite for formal-looking edible edging, knot gardens, and containers where a tidy, structural basil is wanted alongside its classic sweet basil flavor. Its slow-to-bolt, compact habit needs little shaping beyond occasional light trimming to keep the globe form neat, and regular harvesting for the kitchen doubles as maintenance pruning. Keep soil evenly moist and pick leaves regularly through the season to encourage continued dense, bushy growth. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Boyne Raspberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Manitoba Red Raspberry)
description: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and provide a simple wire trellis for support. Developed at the Morden Research Station in Manitoba, Boyne is prized in the coldest raspberry-growing regions of North America for surviving harsh prairie winters with minimal cane dieback while still producing an early, heavy crop of medium-sized, firm, richly flavored red berries. As a floricane-fruiting cultivar it bears on second-year wood, so cut spent canes to the ground immediately after harvest and thin the following year's primocanes to keep the row open and productive. Its combination of hardiness and early ripening has made it a long-standing standard for home gardeners across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Boysenberry
description: Boysenberries are vigorous trailing hybrids (blackberry x raspberry x loganberry lineage) that must be trained to a two- or three-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft. Cut all fruited canes to the ground after the summer harvest and tie new canes along the wires for next year's crop. Harvest when berries turn deep maroon-purple and have a rich, winey aroma. In zone 5–6 winters, remove canes from wires and lay them on the ground under mulch for protection. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Bradenton Loquat (Vigorous Large-Fruited Tropical Florida Loquat)
description: Give Bradenton a warm, sheltered site with excellent drainage, since it is one of the more tropical-leaning loquat selections and reacts poorly to hard freezes compared to older Florida cultivars. The stout, bushy tree bears at a young age and produces large, roughly two-inch, sweet fruit with good flavor, ripening late in the loquat season into April. In frost-free microclimates it can flush repeated small crops through the year rather than a single spring harvest, a trait growers sometimes call 'everbearing.' Thin dense fruit clusters to improve fruit size, and prune lightly after harvest to keep this naturally compact tree manageable in a small Gulf Coast yard. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Bradford Watermelon
description: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Bradford Watermelon is a South Carolina heirloom dating to the 1840s, developed by the Bradford family of Sumter County and grown continuously within the family for over 170 years before nurseryman Nat Bradford reintroduced it commercially in the 2010s. Large oblong fruits (often 25–40 pounds) have a distinctive soft, thin rind and exceptionally sweet, deep red flesh — historically prized enough that the whole melon, rind included, was cooked down into watermelon rind preserves and syrup. That same soft rind made it too fragile for the rail-shipping trade of the early 20th century, which nearly drove the variety extinct as tougher-rinded shipping melons took over the commercial market; it survived only because the Bradford family kept saving and replanting seed on their own land. A true living-history heirloom for the home garden, where a thin, easily bruised rind is no obstacle, in zone 4–11. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Bradley Atemoya (Late-Season Florida-Bred Atemoya)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bradley is a Florida-developed atemoya cultivar valued for ripening later in the season than Gefner, extending the atemoya harvest window into late fall and helping spread out the crop for home growers with more than one tree. Like other atemoya cultivars it produces rich, custardy, sweet flesh with tropical vanilla and pineapple notes, and benefits from hand pollination for the most reliable and largest fruit set. Harvest when fruit begins to soften slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bradley Okra
description: Bradley is a widely grown Deep South home-garden hybrid prized for smooth, spineless, dark green pods that stay tender well past the 3-4 inch stage, forgiving gardeners who miss a picking day or two in peak summer heat. Plants stay a manageable, well-branched height compared to rangy heirloom types, which makes hand-harvesting easier and keeps pods within easy reach all season. It sets pods heavily and continuously through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many other vegetables shut down, and responds well to a side-dressing of nitrogen once plants begin flowering. Pick every day or two once pods start forming, since Bradley pods can pass tenderness quickly in hot weather. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Bradley Tomato (Arkansas Pink Heirloom Slicer)
description: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Bradley is a pink-fruited slicing tomato released by the University of Arkansas and grown widely across the Mid-South and Gulf South for decades as a reliable home-garden standard. The large, smooth, globe-shaped fruits have the mild, sweet, low-acid flavor typical of pink tomatoes, with meaty flesh and few seeds that make them excellent for fresh slicing and sandwiches. Plants are vigorous and produce well through the first flush of Southern summer heat, though yields taper once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s like most standard hybrids. Stake or cage plants early and keep watering even to prevent cracking and blossom end rot through the swings between Gulf South downpours and dry spells. A good companion to a heat-set variety like Neptune or Phoenix for a longer harvest window into peak summer. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Bradshaw Plum (Large Purple Heirloom European Plum)
description: Bradshaw is a long-cultivated European plum dating to the early nineteenth century, prized for its large, oval, reddish-purple fruit and juicy, yellow, freestone flesh. It is mostly self-fertile but crops more heavily with a second European plum nearby. The tree is vigorous and productive, with fruit that is good fresh, canned, or cooked into jam, though it needs substantially more winter chill than Japanese plum types and struggles in mild-winter climates. Thin fruit if the crop is heavy and prune in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and airflow. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Braeburn Apple (Crisp Aromatic New Zealand Sweet-Tart Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and provide a cross-pollinator, since Braeburn is not reliably self-fruitful. Discovered as a chance seedling near Motueka, New Zealand in 1952, it quickly became one of the most widely exported dessert apples of the late 20th century for its dense, crisp flesh and layered sweet-tart flavor with a faint spice note. Fruit ripens late in the season and colors in streaky red over a green-gold background; it keeps exceptionally well in cold storage, often holding good eating quality for months. Thin heavy fruit sets in early summer to improve size and prevent biennial bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bramley's Seedling Apple (Bramley Cooking Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space. Grown from a pip planted in Nottinghamshire, England around 1809, this is the definitive British culinary apple, producing very large, bright green, sharply tart fruit that cooks down into a smooth, fluffy puree prized above nearly all other apples for pies, sauces, and traditional English cooking, though it is far too acidic and firm-fleshed for most people's taste eaten fresh off the tree. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for cross-pollination, and it makes a notably large, vigorous, long-lived tree that benefits from ample permanent space and a sturdy semi-standard or standard rootstock. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fully ripe, and the acidic fruit stores exceptionally well through winter when kept cool, making it a valued keeper for a home cook's cooking apple supply. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brandy Boy Tomato (Hybrid Brandywine-Type Pink Beefsteak)
description: Brandy Boy was bred by Burpee to reproduce the rich, complex flavor of the beloved heirloom Brandywine on a modern F1 hybrid frame that sets fruit far more reliably. The rosy-pink, deeply flattened beefsteak fruit runs 10-16 ounces with the dense, low-acid, old-fashioned flavor Brandywine fans expect, but the hybrid vigor and improved disease tolerance mean noticeably higher yields per plant than the open-pollinated original. Give the tall indeterminate vine a sturdy 6-foot cage or stake, prune lower suckers for airflow, and pick fruit at full color for the best flavor. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Brandywine Pink Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This classic heirloom, thought to date to the late 1800s, has distinctive potato-leaf foliage and produces massive 16 to 24 ounce pink fruits with rich, old-fashioned flavor. The indeterminate vines need a tall, sturdy stake or trellis and benefit from suckering for airflow. Water evenly at the base to reduce cracking, and harvest fruit when fully colored and slightly soft. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Brandywine Red & Yellow Blend Pole Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This blend pairs Red Brandywine, with its rich, well-balanced flavor, and golden Yellow Brandywine, which is sweet-tart, both producing large fruits often near a pound and sometimes close to two. The indeterminate vines need a tall, sturdy support and benefit from pruning for airflow. Water evenly to prevent cracking, and harvest each color when fully ripe and slightly soft. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Brandywine Sudduth's Strain Tomato (Authenticated Original Pink Brandywine)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and provide strong staking, since this vigorous, long-season Brandywine strain produces very heavy fruit over an extended harvest. This is the specific pink Brandywine strain traced to the Sudduth family of Tennessee and distributed to the wider heirloom seed-saving community by collector Ben Quisenberry in the 1980s, and it is widely regarded among heirloom tomato growers as the strain most faithful to the original 19th-century Brandywine. The large, rosy-pink, potato-leaf beefsteak fruit carries the rich, sweet, well-balanced, classically 'old-fashioned' tomato flavor that made Brandywine famous, though yields can run lower and the season longer than modern hybrids. Water consistently and feed moderately through the season, since Brandywine strains are notably more sensitive to inconsistent care than modern disease-resistant hybrids. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Brandywine Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant after frost risk passes, burying the stem deeply to encourage rooting; Brandywine is arguably the most celebrated American heirloom tomato, a large pink-red beefsteak type with potato-leaved foliage and 1–2 pound fruits that ripen slowly but reward the patient gardener with extraordinarily rich, complex, sweet-acidic flavor widely considered the gold standard of tomato taste. Stake or cage firmly — the vigorous indeterminate vines grow to 6 feet and heavy fruits weigh branches down without support. Days to maturity are long, making it best suited to long-season gardens; in the south, plant early for spring harvest before summer heat sets in. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.
