name: Brandywine Viburnum (Blue-Berried Smooth Witherod Viburnum)
description: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a second, genetically distinct viburnum nudum nearby to ensure heavy fruit set, since this species needs a compatible cross-pollinator. Brandywine is a Southeastern native shrub selected for its extraordinary berry display: clusters of pink berries that ripen through shades of rose and blue to a deep, glossy blue-black, often showing several colors on the same cluster at once, held above glossy, dark-green, disease-resistant foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall. It tolerates consistently wet soil better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and low, poorly drained spots where many shrubs struggle. The berries are an excellent food source for songbirds, who typically strip them soon after they ripen. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bravo Cabbage (Crack-Resistant Blue-Green Hybrid Cabbage)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, using tighter 12-inch spacing for smaller fresh-market heads or 18-24 inches for larger heads and kraut production. Bravo is a Bejo-bred hybrid valued for uniform, solid, blue-green round heads with good resistance to head cracking and to black rot and fusarium yellows, two disease pressures that build up quickly in warm, humid fall gardens. It has a reputation among market growers for performing well across a wide range of climates, from Deep South winter production to northern summer crops, which makes it a dependable second cabbage choice alongside more region-specific varieties. Feed consistently through head formation, since Bravo's large frame needs steady fertility to fill out its heads before a hard freeze. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Bravour Parsley (RHS Award-Winning Curled)
description: Bravour is a European moss-curled parsley that earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its dense, tightly ruffled, dark green foliage and reliable garden performance. Its compact, uniform habit and exceptional cold tolerance make it a dependable choice for spring, summer, and overwintered plantings alike. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep the tight rosette producing tender new growth, and expect it to hold color and flavor through several hard frosts before finally succumbing to deep winter cold. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Brazil Nut
description: Plant Brazil Nut trees in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with adequate space for their ultimate enormous size; they require mycorrhizal fungi associations established in forest soil for optimal growth; fruiting does not begin until trees are 10–15 years old and requires the presence of orchid bees (Eulaema spp.) for pollination of their complex flowers — making commercial fruiting difficult outside the Amazon Basin. Brazil Nut trees are among the most ecologically important trees in the Amazon — their hard, 4-inch woody seed pods (cocos) fall from the canopy with enough force to be fatal, making harvesting genuinely dangerous; they are collected by harvesters who enter the forest after the natural fall season. The seeds (nuts) are extraordinarily rich in selenium — a single Brazil nut provides the recommended daily allowance — and are one of the world's most nutritionally dense foods. Brazil Nut is also an indicator of primary forest health: the trees only reproduce successfully in intact, undisturbed Amazonian rainforest where their Euglossine bee pollinators (attracted exclusively by certain orchid species) and agouti seed dispersers are both present. This extraordinary ecological dependency makes Brazil Nuts one of the best arguments for conservation of intact Amazonian forest, as deforestation eliminates both the trees and their irreplaceable ecosystem partners. Matures in 3650–10950 days from seed.

name: Brazil Nut Tree (Para Nut, Castanheiro do Para)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, moist to wet tropical soil; Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) is one of the largest trees of the Amazon rainforest, reaching 150 feet tall, and requires 10–20 years from seed to first fruiting in optimal conditions. The pods (actually large, woody capsules weighing up to 5 lbs) each contain 8–24 seeds (the 'nuts') and fall from height, posing a safety hazard — harvest sites require protective gear. The Brazil nut ecosystem depends entirely on the orchid bee (Eulaema sp.) for pollination and the agouti (a large rodent) for seed dispersal, making it nearly impossible to grow commercially outside its native ecosystem. Trees in south Florida and Hawaii produce limited fruit but are grown primarily as impressive specimen trees; the heavy, dense, rot-resistant wood is also extremely valuable. Matures in 3650–5475 days from transplant.

name: Brazilian Guava (Cas)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in zones 9–11; Brazilian guava (also called cas in Costa Rica) is a small to medium-sized tree native to tropical America that produces heavy crops of small, round fruits with white, aromatic, pleasantly sour flesh — highly prized throughout Latin America for fresh-squeezed juice, fruit nectars, jellies, fermented beverages, and agua fresca. Unlike common guava, it shows considerable resistance to the devastating guava wilt fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii) and is more tolerant of occasional frosts, making it a practical choice for gardeners at the cool edge of the tropical fruit range in zones 9–10. Trees begin producing in 3–6 years from transplant and fruit prolifically once established, often producing two crops per year in warm climates. Fruits drop quickly when ripe and should be harvested promptly or they will be taken by wildlife. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Brazilian Pepper Tree (Pink Peppercorn)
description: This fast-growing evergreen tree, native to Brazil, Paraguay, and Argentina, produces the small, bright red-pink drupes sold commercially as pink peppercorns, though botanically unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Harvest ripe berry clusters in late fall to winter once fully colored, then dry them whole for use as a mild, sweet-peppery spice or steep the dried berries in vinegar or brine. The tree is dioecious, so only female trees bear the ornamental red fruit clusters, and a nearby male is required for pollination. It tolerates poor soil, salt, and drought once established, but note that it is cashew-family (Anacardiaceae) and can trigger contact reactions in people sensitive to poison ivy or cashews, and is aggressively invasive in Florida and other subtropical regions where its cultivation is now restricted. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Brazilian Spinach
description: Plant cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; this low-growing groundcover from Brazil spreads to fill in bare areas beneath shrubs and fruit trees, providing a living mulch while yielding edible leaves. The slightly succulent, wavy-edged leaves are harvested young and used raw in salads or briefly cooked like spinach, with a mild, pleasant flavor free of bitterness. It is extremely productive in the subtropics, rooting wherever stems contact moist soil. Take cuttings in early fall to overwinter indoors in a sunny window, or treat as an annual in zone 8 with fresh transplants each spring. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Brazilian Starfish Pepper
description: Brazilian Starfish is a Peruvian aji type domesticated in Brazil and grown chiefly for its unusual flattened, deeply-lobed pods that flare out into a five- or six-pointed star shape as they mature from green to red. The flavor is floral and fruity with a medium heat in the 15,000-20,000 Scoville range, similar in punch to a serrano but with the tropical fruitiness typical of Capsicum baccatum. Plants have a lax, weeping, almost vine-like habit rather than the upright form of most peppers, so light staking or a small cage keeps the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Sliced starfish-shaped pods are a striking addition to pickle jars, salsas, and salads; consistent moisture and rich soil produce the heaviest pod set over a long warm season. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Brazos Best Avocado (Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters. Brazos Best is a Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado prized alongside cultivars like Joey and Lila for cold hardiness well beyond that of standard Guatemalan or West Indian avocado types, allowing it to survive brief hard freezes that would kill most avocado trees. It produces small to medium, thin-skinned, purple-black fruit with rich, nutty-flavored flesh typical of Mexican-race avocados, ripening in late summer through fall. Its combination of cold tolerance and dependable fruiting makes it one of the more practical avocado choices for in-ground planting in the milder parts of the Gulf Coast and coastal Texas, where standard avocado cultivars are too tender. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Brazos Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil in full sun; Brazos is a thorned, semi-erect blackberry developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1959 — for many decades it was the dominant commercial blackberry variety in Texas and the Gulf Coast South. Though newer thornless varieties have largely replaced it commercially, Brazos remains prized by home gardeners and farmers' market growers for its exceptional heat adaptation, flavor, and productivity on the alkaline soils that characterize much of central and south Texas. Berries are large, elongated, and very flavorful, ripening from late April through June in zone 9 — among the earliest major varieties. Unlike the University of Arkansas thornless releases (Natchez, Ouachita), Brazos tolerates alkaline soil pH (7.0–7.5) and calcareous caliche significantly better, making it the variety of choice for gardens on tight, rocky Hill Country soils or coastal prairie clay. Canes require trellising due to vigorous, semi-trailing growth. Wear heavy gloves when pruning. Remove fruited canes after harvest and select 4–5 of the strongest new canes per plant. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Breadfruit
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis) is a Polynesian staple food tree that has been cultivated throughout the Pacific and Caribbean for centuries, prized for its large, starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled, fried, or dried into flour — providing a remarkably complete carbohydrate staple that sustained entire island civilizations. A single mature tree can produce 50–200 or more large fruits per year, yielding hundreds of pounds of nutritious food with minimal inputs. Most improved varieties are seedless triploids propagated from root suckers or cuttings; plant these for the fastest fruiting and best productivity. Trees are highly sensitive to frost and cold winds, but once established in a frost-free tropical location they are vigorous, long-lived, and capable of producing fruit within 3–5 years of planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Breadnut (Seeded Breadfruit, Ma Afalo)
description: Plant in rich, deep, well-drained, moist, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; in south Florida, protect young trees from the rare hard freeze. Artocarpus camansi (breadnut) is the seeded ancestor of the seedless breadfruit (A. altilis) and produces large, spiny, oblong to round fruits 8–12 inches long containing 20–50 large, protein-rich seeds embedded in creamy, starchy, edible flesh; both the seeds and flesh are eaten. The seeds (when boiled, roasted, or ground into flour) are the primary food value of breadnut, tasting somewhat like chestnuts or macadamia nuts — they are a traditional protein-rich staple in the Pacific Islands and Philippines (where the tree is called 'kulo'). The flesh (ripe) is sweet and may be eaten similarly to breadfruit. The large, deeply lobed, tropical leaves and rapid growth rate make breadnut an impressive specimen tree in tropical gardens. Breadnut is native to New Guinea and the Philippines and widely naturalized in tropical America; it is closely related to jackfruit, durian, and the edible fig within the family Moraceae. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Breda Giant Medlar
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Breda Giant is a classic Dutch medlar selection prized for producing unusually large, russeted brown fruit on a small, gnarled, ornamental tree with showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is rock-hard and inedible at harvest in late fall and must be 'bletted' — stored in a cool place for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens and browns internally to a soft, spiced, wine-like custard texture before eating fresh or making jelly and butter. The tree is very cold-hardy, tolerates poor soils, and is largely pest- and disease-free, making it an easy, low-maintenance addition to a home orchard once its unusual harvest-and-ripen routine is understood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brentwood Leaf Lettuce
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate in cool soil. This variety holds its pretty leaves high above the core for easy cutting and forms compact heads that yield well in a small space. Strong bolt resistance extends the harvest, and it resists downy mildew, lettuce leaf aphid, and Fusarium wilt. Keep soil evenly moist, provide afternoon shade in warm weather, and harvest outer leaves or the whole head as needed. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Brew-Tea-Ful Tea (Compact Container Tea Selection)
description: Brew-Tea-Ful is a compact tea camellia bred specifically for container growing, with a naturally dense, well-branched form that requires minimal shaping compared to more open, leggy tea selections. It produces respectable green or black tea from the same harvested flush, making it a practical option for patio or small-space tea gardens rather than field-scale production. Keep it in a large container of acidic, well-drained potting mix, water consistently, and site it in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once the plant is well established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Brewster Lychee
description: The Brewster lychee is a classic favorite bearing sweet, juicy fruit encased in a glossy red shell over fragrant white flesh. This subtropical evergreen prefers hot, humid summers and needs a brief cool period to trigger flowering. Grow a grafted or air-layered tree in full sun with acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and shelter it fully from frost. Keep the root zone consistently moist, mulch heavily, and protect young trees from wind while they establish. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Brianna Grape (Aromatic Cold-Hardy White Wine Grape)
description: Developed by Elmer Swenson, this cold-hardy white hybrid produces medium clusters of golden-green berries with a distinctive tropical, pineapple-like aroma that carries into its wine, setting it apart from most other cold-climate whites. It ripens relatively late for a hardy hybrid but withstands harsh northern winters with minimal cane damage. The vine is vigorous and productive, often needing shoot positioning and crop thinning to maintain fruit quality and avoid overcropping. It has become a popular blending or single-varietal choice among small wineries across the upper Midwest. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: Bride Eggplant (White and Purple-Streaked Asian Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Bride is a Chinese-derived hybrid eggplant with slender, cylindrical fruit that emerges ivory-white and develops soft purple-lavender streaking as it fills out, topped by a distinctive green calyx. Fruit is best picked around 6-8 inches long and 1.5 inches thick, while the streaking is still light and the flesh is at its most tender and mild. The compact, branching plants set fruit in small clusters rather than singly, giving a steady succession of harvests through the hot part of the season. Because the thin skin bruises easily, handle fruit gently and cook it soon after picking in stir-fries or on the grill. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Bright Lights Swiss Chard (AAS-Winning Rainbow Multi-Color Stem Swiss Chard)
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; each chard 'seed' is actually a seed cluster that may produce 2–3 seedlings — thin to the strongest. Harvest outer leaves at any size; plants continue producing from the center. Bright Lights is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning Swiss chard — a variety selection that produces the same flavor and productivity as standard chard while dramatically expanding the visual appeal of the garden. Each individual plant in a Bright Lights planting develops stems of a single color, but a planting from any seed packet includes plants with yellow, orange, red, pink, white, lavender, and purple stems, with the blade of each leaf complementarily colored against the bright stem. Photographed in morning light, a mature Bright Lights planting is among the most colorful edible garden plantings available in any vegetable category. The flavor is identical to standard Swiss chard — the young leaves are mild and spinach-like for raw salads; the mature leaves are substantial and slightly earthy-sweet when cooked. The colored stems and midribs hold their color reasonably well through cooking (yellow and white stems hold best; red and pink stems bleed somewhat). Bright Lights is valued in both edible gardens and ornamental-edible plantings where it provides extended color through the cooler months. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Bright Lights Swiss Chard (Rainbow Chard)
description: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6–9 inches; chard seed is a cluster (multigerm) so thinning is essential. Bright Lights is an All-America Selections winner rainbow chard that transformed chard's reputation from a workmanlike spinach substitute to a showstopping ornamental-edible. The plants produce stems in a vivid spectrum of yellow, orange, red, pink, purple, and white — a single bed creates extraordinary visual impact in the garden. Leaves are tender, mild, and slightly earthy, superior to red chard for flavor; stems are crisp and colorful even when cooked, with a mildly sweet, earthy flavor that stands up to sautéing, braising, and pasta dishes. For zone 9 fall gardens, Bright Lights is one of the most reliable cool-season crops: it germinates quickly in September warmth, grows through October–November, survives light freezes, and can continue producing into January–February. Harvest outer leaves regularly for continuous production; plants can produce for months. Tolerates partial shade in hot weather, which extends the harvest season significantly. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Bright Yellow Swiss Chard (Golden-Stemmed Chard)
description: Sow directly and thin plants to stand several inches apart, keeping soil evenly moist to encourage broad, tender leaves. Unlike multicolor chard blends, this selection breeds true for solid golden-yellow stalks and veins beneath crumpled dark green leaves, giving a uniform look for market bunching. Its flavor is mild and slightly sweeter than red-stemmed types, and it holds up well as both a baby green and a mature cooking chard. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Brightest Brilliant Rainbow Quinoa
description: Quinoa is an ancient, nutritious South American grain, and this rainbow blend adds striking seed-head colors of hot pink, burgundy, red, orange, yellow, white, and green. Direct sow in early spring in cool soil, in full sun and well-drained ground. The tender young leaves can be cooked like spinach, while the protein-rich seeds are harvested when the plants dry down. Rinse the harvested seeds well to remove the naturally bitter saponin coating before cooking. Give the tall plants room, as they can reach 4 to 6 feet. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Brightwell Blueberry
description: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Brightwell is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1983 that became the dominant commercial rabbiteye variety in the southeastern US for its outstanding combination of yield, adaptability, and suitability for mechanical harvesting on u-pick and commercial farms. Mid-season ripening (late June to July in zone 8–9) follows the early-ripening Climax and Premier, extending the harvest window. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, with a dry scar and mild, sweet flavor that improves with heat — they tend to sweeten noticeably as they ripen fully over 2–3 weeks, making daily picking rewarding. The upright, vigorous plants are productive and show good disease tolerance under Gulf Coast conditions. As with all rabbiteye blueberries, plant at least two compatible varieties for cross-pollination. Mulch deeply with pine bark or wood chips; never use fresh hardwood mulch as it raises pH. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Brightwell Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Brightwell is the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the southeastern United States, valued for its consistent mid-season production, outstanding flavor, and broad adaptability across zone 6–9. The medium to large, light blue berries ripen in June–July in most Gulf Coast plantings and hold well on the bush, extending the harvest window over 4–6 weeks. Brightwell's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) suits it perfectly to zone 8–9 conditions where high-chill northern varieties fail. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through summer, and fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) at bloom and again after harvest. Avoid lime applications, which raise soil pH above the acceptable range. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brigitta Blueberry (Late-Season Firm Australian Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Brigitta was bred in Australia and became internationally popular for its exceptionally firm, large, late-ripening berries with outstanding shelf life, holding quality in storage and transit better than most highbush varieties, a trait that has made it a favorite for both commercial growers and home gardeners wanting fruit that keeps well after picking. Ripening late in the season, it extends the harvest window when planted alongside earlier varieties, and the vigorous, upright bush is a reliable, heavy producer once established. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Brilliant Celeriac (Smooth-Rooted European Celery Root)
description: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into deep, fertile, evenly moist soil, since celeriac's long development window punishes any lapse in watering with cracked or hollow roots. Brilliant is grown for its notably smooth-skinned, low-knobbed globes, which peel far more cleanly than older, rougher celeriac types while keeping the same concentrated celery flavor. Remove side shoots and surface roots from the developing globe through the season to channel growth into the main root, and harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing crop that holds well in a root cellar. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Brilliantissima Red Chokeberry
description: Plant in average garden soil that stays reliably moist and prune out a few of the oldest canes each year to keep the upright, suckering shrub full and vigorous. Brilliantissima is a selection of native red chokeberry prized for its glossy, dark green summer foliage that turns brilliant scarlet in fall, paired with clusters of small white spring flowers and abundant bright red berries that persist into winter. The astringent fruit is not usually eaten fresh but is popular for jams, syrups, and wildlife forage, since birds tend to leave it until late in the season. It tolerates wet soil, drought, and a wide range of conditions, making it a tough, low-maintenance hedge or naturalized planting choice. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Brimmer Tomato (Wood's Famous 1907 Virginia Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to bear the weight of the fruit. Developed in the early 1900s by a Richmond, Virginia seed company, Brimmer, marketed historically as Wood's Famous Brimmer, won a Grand Prize in 1907 for its large, round, pink-to-purple fruit that is thick-skinned, meaty, and low-acid, often exceeding a pound at full size. The variety fell out of commercial favor by the mid-1960s but has since been preserved and revived by regional seed savers, including Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Brison Blackberry (Texas A&M Blackland-Clay Thorny Blackberry)
description: Brison is a thorny, erect-to-semi-erect blackberry released by Texas A&M University in 1977 and long favored across the western Gulf South for its reliable performance on heavy blackland clay soils where many other cultivars struggle. Fruit is firmer and sweeter than the older Texas standard Brazos, and plants are early-bearing and consistently productive. Its main drawback is susceptibility to rosette (double blossom), so prune out any distorted, witches'-broom-like growth promptly and keep plantings open and well-ventilated. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto a simple trellis for easier picking around the thorns. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Bristly Dewberry (Swamp Dewberry)
description: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; bristly dewberry is a trailing native bramble of moist, shaded, acidic habitats — sphagnum bog margins, moist pine flatwoods, wet woodland edges, and streambanks — producing small, rounded, black berries with a pleasant, mildly tart flavor. The semi-evergreen leaves have a distinctive leathery texture and glossy appearance. The plant is armed with tiny, bristle-like prickles (hence 'bristly') rather than the stout thorns of most blackberries. An important understory plant for moist, shaded, acidic native gardens where it provides both wildlife fruit value and ground cover function. Thrives in conditions too wet and shaded for most other fruiting plants. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Bristly Sarsaparilla
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or rocky acidic soil in open woodland, clearings, or partial shade at a woodland edge; unlike its shade-loving relatives, bristly sarsaparilla thrives in leaner, more open sites and tolerates dry, infertile ground poorly suited to most other Aralia. The lower stem is distinctively armed with fine bristles rather than stout spines, and plants form low colonial patches topped by rounded clusters of small white flowers in summer, followed by dark purple-black berries used by birds and historically by foragers alongside the related wild sarsaparilla. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is well suited to naturalizing a sandy barren, pine clearing, or rock garden edge rather than a moist shade bed. Division in spring is the reliable way to propagate named colonies, since seed germination is slow and erratic. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Bristol Black Raspberry (Cornell Standard Black Raspberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and tip-prune vigorous new canes in midsummer to encourage the lateral branching that carries next year's crop. Bristol was released by Cornell University in 1934 and quickly became a garden standard for its large, glossy-black, firm berries with rich, classic black raspberry flavor, produced in heavy clusters on strong, upright canes that need less support than sprawling types. It ripens in a concentrated midsummer window that makes for an efficient single harvest push, and the vigorous habit means a modest planting fills in and produces well within its second season. Watch for anthracnose in humid climates and provide good air circulation between hills; remove spent floricanes immediately after harvest to reduce disease pressure on the new canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Briteblue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic 1969 Georgia Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Briteblue, released in Georgia in 1969, is a sister selection to the well-known Delite and Bluebelle rabbiteye cultivars, valued for large, light-blue, firm berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush, and has remained in cultivation for over half a century as a dependable mid-to-late-season producer for Southern home orchards. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Britewell Rabbiteye Blueberry (High-Yield UGA Blueberry)
description: Plant dormant or container bushes in winter in raised, sulfur-acidified beds where native soil is not already acidic, and keep a permanent layer of pine bark mulch over the root zone. Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye selection valued by growers for consistently heavy, reliable cropping of firm, medium-blue berries with good flavor on a moderately vigorous, upright-spreading bush, ripening in the mid-season window alongside cultivars like Tifblue. Plant with a second mid-season rabbiteye for cross-pollination and fuller berry set, and feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest. Renewal-prune the oldest wood out each winter to keep young, productive canes coming and sustain the heavy yields the variety is known for. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Britton Perilla (Bicolor Heirloom Shiso)
description: Britton is an old heirloom strain of perilla distinguished from ordinary green or red shiso by two-tone frilled foliage, splashed with maroon-purple over a green base rather than solid-colored leaves. It carries the same anise-mint-cinnamon flavor complex prized in Japanese and Korean kitchens, but its striking variegated look also earns it a spot in ornamental beds and containers. Grow it as you would any culinary shiso: pinch young plants to encourage bushiness, harvest leaves continuously through summer, and let a few plants flower and drop seed at season's end for a self-sustaining patch the following year. It performs best with a little afternoon shade in hot climates, which also helps preserve the crispness of the leaf edges. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Broad-Leaf Batavian Endive
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Broad-Leaf Batavian Endive is the flat-leafed, large-headed escarole-type endive — distinct from frizzy curly endive in having broad, wavy, slightly ruffled leaves rather than finely cut, frilly ones. The large, open heads weigh 1–2 pounds with pale green to cream-white interior leaves (if blanched) and a mild, slightly bitter flavor that is more approachable than radicchio or frisee. Broad-Leaf Batavian endive is extensively used in Italian cooking — sautéed with garlic and olive oil, incorporated into soups and braised bean dishes, and used as a pizza or pasta topping where its mild bitterness counterbalances richer ingredients. It is also used raw in salads when blanched to a creamy interior. The large, substantial leaves hold up better to cooking than frisee or standard lettuces. In zone 9 it is a reliable fall crop that matures through November and December for harvest into January. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Broad-Leaf Thyme (Large Wild Thyme)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; broad-leaf thyme is a more robust and cold-hardy thyme species than the common culinary thyme (Thymus vulgaris), producing larger, broader, oval leaves with a strong, sweet thyme fragrance and flavor used interchangeably with common thyme in cooking. Native to limestone hills and rocky grasslands of central and western Europe, it forms a semi-shrubby, spreading mound of woody stems with soft, gray-green to dark-green, aromatic leaves and clusters of pink-purple flowers in summer that are magnets for bees — particularly bumblebees and honeybees. The culinary quality of the leaves is excellent and often considered superior to common thyme in flavor intensity. It is more tolerant of heavier soils and colder winters than Thymus vulgaris, making it a better choice for gardens in zones 4–5 where common thyme may winterkill. Several cultivars exist including 'Foxley' (silver-variegated), 'Kurt' (very compact), and 'Oregano-Scented' (with marjoram-like notes). Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Broad-Leaved Bulbine (Cattle Bulbine)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; broad-leaved bulbine is a larger South African species than the orange-flowered B. frutescens — producing broader, more succulent, aloe-like strap leaves in rosettes and in spring through summer, tall, branching scapes of small, yellow, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers with distinctive, fluffy, bearded yellow stamens that give each individual flower a charming, hairy-bearded appearance. The multiple scapes on an established clump produce a fine, airy cloud of small yellow flowers over the striking succulent foliage for an extended period. In South African traditional medicine, the clear, viscous gel from the leaves is used topically for burns, itching, and skin irritations, similarly to aloe vera but with a more watery, less viscous consistency. As a garden plant it is a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant succulent perennial for hot, dry, sunny positions, combining well with other South African succulent plants — kniphofia, bulbinella, agapanthus, and ornamental grasses — in water-wise subtropical plantings. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Broad-Leaved Thyme (Mother of Thyme)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thyme is intolerant of wet, heavy soils and will rot quickly in poorly drained ground. Thymus pulegioides is the broad-leaved thyme of European meadows and hedgerows, producing larger, broader leaves than common thyme (T. vulgaris) with a pungent, highly aromatic thymol fragrance that is considered by many herb growers to be the most intensely flavored thyme species for cooking; the broader leaves also dry and crumble more easily than narrow-leaved types. The sprawling, somewhat woody stems root where they touch the soil, making it an effective aromatic path-side groundcover, and the pink to lilac flowers in summer are heavily visited by bees. Harvest before full bloom for the most concentrated flavor; cut stems back by half after flowering to keep plants compact. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Broadleaf Arrowhead / Duck Potato
description: Plant corms in heavy aquatic soil in saturated mud or standing water 2–12 inches deep in full sun; broadleaf arrowhead thrives in freshwater marshes, pond edges, slow streams, and ditches across most of North America and is both a highly ornamental aquatic perennial and a traditional Indigenous food plant. Sagittaria latifolia produces bold, arrowhead-shaped leaves on long petioles rising 1–4 feet above the water surface, and attractive whorled racemes of bright-white, three-petaled flowers with yellow stamens from midsummer through early fall — providing valuable nectar for native bees. The starchy, potato-like corms produced at the tips of underground stolons were a critical food source for many Native American and First Nations peoples and were gathered in enormous quantities, especially by Plains tribes — Meriwether Lewis and William Clark documented their use extensively; the corms can be baked, boiled, roasted, or dried and ground into flour. Outstanding for naturalizing pond margins and rain gardens while providing important food and cover for ducks (hence 'duck potato'), muskrats, and other wetland wildlife. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Broadleaf Czech Garlic (Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Set cloves 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fertile, well-worked soil, then mulch heavily for winter insulation in cold climates. Trim the tough central scape once it curls to push more energy into bulb development, and cure harvested bulbs in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks. Broadleaf Czech is a robust porcelain-type hardneck grown widely across the Czech Republic and imported to North America by garlic collectors, valued for its large, easy-to-peel cloves, strong hot flavor, and reliable cold hardiness in northern gardens. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Broadleaf Sage
description: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart. This drought-tolerant, hardy perennial has bold, assertive, savory flavor valued for seasoning rich foods like pork, poultry, and cheese, plus stuffing, soups, and stews. It also bears edible purple-blue flowers that draw pollinators; cut plants back in spring to keep them bushy and productive year after year. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Broadleaf Silverberry (Bigleaf Elaeagnus)
description: Broadleaf silverberry is an evergreen shrub native to the coastal cliffs and dunes of Japan and Korea, notable for unusually large, rounded, leathery leaves with a bright silver-scaled underside that catches light dramatically in a breeze. Small, intensely fragrant, creamy white flowers open in autumn and are followed by orange-red, silver-speckled fruits that ripen in spring and are edible with a tart, astringent flavor similar to its relatives. It is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, wind, and poor coastal soils, making it a strong choice for seaside windbreaks and screening, and it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules like other Elaeagnus. It is the seed parent of the widely planted hybrid E. x ebbingei and shares that hybrid's toughness, but the true species is less commonly offered in the nursery trade and worth seeking out for its bolder foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Broadview Walnut (Cold-Hardy Canadian English Walnut)
description: Broadview is a Canadian-selected English walnut valued in cold-winter regions for hardiness well beyond that of typical Carpathian strains, tolerating winter lows reported near -30F once established. It is protandrous, partially self-fertile, and notably precocious, often bearing a light crop within its first few years from planting, though a second distinct cultivar improves nut set. Its mid-to-late leafing habit helps young growth escape damaging late spring frosts, an important trait for northern growers. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and give it room to reach the large mature size typical of English walnuts, harvesting nuts in mid-to-late season once hulls begin to split. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Broccoli
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in starter mix and keep at 70–75°F until germination, then grow on in bright light to prevent leggy transplants. Set out 2–4 weeks before last frost and fertilize with a nitrogen-rich feed at planting and again when heads begin to form. Harvest the central head while florets are still tight and dark green, before any yellow shows. Cut with a few inches of stem to encourage side-shoot production after the main head is removed. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Broccoli Microgreens
description: Broadcast broccoli seed thickly across an evenly moist tray and cover for the first couple of days to encourage strong, uniform germination. Once shoots stand up, uncover and give them bright light so the stems stay short and sturdy. Keep the medium consistently moist and provide gentle airflow to prevent damping-off. Harvest the crisp, mild greens at the cotyledon stage in about a week for the sweetest flavor and best texture. Matures in 7–10 days from seed.

name: Broccoli Raab (Rapini)
description: Direct sow seed 1/4 in deep and thin to 4–6 in; rapini grows quickly and is best as a cool-season crop because heat intensifies bitterness and accelerates bolting. Side-dress with nitrogen once plants are established to encourage the leafy shoot growth that is the primary harvest. Harvest when flower buds are visible but before they open fully, cutting the top 6–8 in of the shoot with leaves included. Repeated cuts extend the harvest, as side shoots continue to develop after the main stem is removed. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Broccoli Sprouts
description: Rinse seeds and soak overnight, then drain and spread in a sprouting jar or tray kept out of direct sun. Rinse and drain two to three times daily to keep sprouts moist but never standing in water. Harvest tangy, nutrient-dense sprouts in four to six days once the first true leaves show and greening begins. Refrigerate harvested sprouts and use within a week for the best crunch and peppery bite. Matures in 4–6 days from seed.

name: Brock's Imperial Asparagus
description: Brock's Imperial is an old open-pollinated English heirloom asparagus valued for producing exceptionally thick, well-flavored spears on vigorous, long-lived crowns. Because it is not an all-male hybrid, plants include both sexes, so expect some volunteer seedlings from the red berries that female plants set in late summer. Gardeners who favor traditional, seed-saveable strains over modern hybrids often choose it to keep an older lineage of asparagus in circulation. Allow a full two seasons of foliage growth before the first light harvest to build a strong root system. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Brogdon Avocado
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — root rot in heavy wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable; Brogdon is a Florida-developed avocado cultivar prized as one of the most cold-hardy named avocado varieties, making it the top choice for gardeners in zone 9a and the warmer parts of zone 8b who want to grow avocados at the northern edge of their hardiness range. The medium-to-large fruits develop deep purple-black skin when ripe — the color change from green to dark purple indicates increasing maturity, but fruits may be harvested slightly early and ripened indoors. The flesh is creamy, rich, and flavorful with excellent avocado oil content. Brogdon has Guatemalan race genetics that contribute its cold hardiness — Guatemalan race avocados are considerably more cold-tolerant than West Indian race types and can survive light frosts. In zone 9 Brogdon is one of the few avocado varieties that can survive the occasional subfreezing nights that occur during cold winters, making it the recommended variety for the most frost-challenged avocado planting sites. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bronco Bush Bean (BCMV-Resistant Commercial Standard)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Bronco is a widely grown commercial bush snap bean valued for excellent resistance to bean common mosaic virus, an aphid-spread disease that can stunt and discolor susceptible bean plantings, along with good heat tolerance and strong pod quality under summer growing conditions. It produces glossy, dark green, straight pods on an upright, high-yielding bush that needs no staking. Harvest pods young and tender, before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall, and pick every couple of days to keep plants setting new flowers. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for a continuous harvest. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Bronvaux Medlar (Hawthorn-Medlar Bigeneric Hybrid)
description: This unusual small tree originated in Bronvaux, France in the 1890s as a graft chimera or bud sport between hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) and medlar (Mespilus germanica), and it displays traits of both parents on the same plant, sometimes even on the same branch. Leaves range from lobed, hawthorn-like foliage to broader medlar-type leaves, and the tree bears an abundance of small white spring flowers followed by a mix of small hawthorn-like haws and larger, true medlar fruits that require bletting (soft ripening after frost) before eating. It tolerates poor, chalky, or heavy soils better than plain medlar and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, making it a low-maintenance curiosity for collectors of unusual fruiting trees rather than a productive orchard crop. Because it is a graft hybrid rather than a stable botanical species, named specimens are propagated by grafting onto hawthorn or quince rootstock. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Bronze Arrow Lettuce
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to a foot apart for full heads or leaving plants closer together for repeated baby-leaf cuts. Bronze Arrow forms an upright, loose, romaine-like rosette of narrow, pointed leaves that emerge green at the base and deepen to a rich bronze-red at the tips and edges, especially in cool weather and strong sun. It is notably slow to bolt and holds good quality longer into warm weather than many heirloom lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the spring lettuce season. The arrow-shaped leaves and striking two-tone coloring also make it a popular addition to mixed salad plantings for looks as well as flavor. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Bronze Fennel
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in their final position; bronze fennel resents root disturbance and transplants poorly. Grow in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil and deadhead spent flower heads to limit self-seeding, which can become excessive. Plant away from dill, coriander, and most vegetables as fennel is allelopathic to many garden neighbors. Harvest the feathery bronze fronds as needed; flavor is best before flowering. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Bronze Loquat
description: The bronze loquat is grown both for its striking coppery new foliage and small, tart edible fruit. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered position, as the flowers and young growth are frost-sensitive. Water regularly while establishing, then only during dry spells once mature. Prune after fruiting to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged tips. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bronze Mignonette Lettuce
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil — lettuce requires steady moisture and cool temperatures; Bronze Mignonette is a miniature French heirloom butterhead lettuce forming small, compact, dense heads with deeply bronze-tinged outer leaves grading to butter-yellow in the blanched interior — the same color pattern as a large butterhead but scaled down to a single-serving head of 3–5 inches across. The Mignonette name (French for 'small and delicate') describes both the size and the tender, buttery character of these compact heads, which provide the soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth texture of butterhead lettuce in a size perfectly proportioned for a single-person salad. Unlike large butterhead varieties where a single head may be too much for one meal, Bronze Mignonette heads can be harvested and eaten in one serving — a practical advantage for small households and container growers who want variety without waste. The bronze outer leaves and buttery-sweet interior flavor make Bronze Mignonette one of the most attractive and best-tasting small lettuces for kitchen garden edging, window boxes, and mixed salad plantings. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Broom Girl Gooseberry (Large Pale-Yellow Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Broom Girl is an older English gooseberry cultivar grown for its large, pale yellow dessert fruit, ripening in mid- to late June, later than early cultivars such as Early Sulphur. It belongs to Ribes uva-crispa var. reclinatum, the trailing-stemmed European gooseberry group prized for large-fruited dessert types. As with other European gooseberries, it needs cold winters to flower and crop reliably, making it a better fit for cold-winter regions than the mild Gulf South. Plant in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center to reduce mildew pressure. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Broomcorn
description: Broomcorn is a specialty sorghum grown not for its small, mostly inedible seed but for its 'brush' — the long, wiry, fibrous seed-head branches that were the traditional raw material for handmade brooms. It is field-grown like grain sorghum but harvested differently: stalks are cut or bent over ('tabled') just as the brush straightens and seed begins to color, since waiting too long lets the fiber lose its flexibility and turn brittle. After cutting, the brush is stripped from the stalk, tied into small hands, and hung or laid out to cure and dry for one to two weeks before the individual straws are cleaned of seed and sorted by length for weaving into hand brooms or whisks. Distinguishing traits from grain, syrup, and forage sorghum types already grown for cereal, sweet cane, or livestock feed: broomcorn's seed head is a loose, elongated panicle of long straight fibers rather than a dense compact grain head, bred over centuries specifically for that structural fiber quality. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Brown Crowder Southern Pea (Heirloom Drying Crowder Pea)
description: Direct sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil, allowing extra room for the semi-vining growth habit to sprawl. Brown Crowder is a traditional Southern heirloom named for the way its brown-hulled peas pack tightly, or 'crowd,' against one another inside the pod, developing the rich, earthy flavor and quick-cooking texture prized in old-fashioned Southern pea dishes. Vigorous vines produce heavily even in the poor, sandy soils and intense heat that stall many other legumes, and the plants show good general tolerance to common cowpea pests and diseases. Like other cowpeas, Brown Crowder fixes nitrogen through its root nodules, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods green for fresh shelling once well filled, or let them dry fully on the vine for classic dried crowder peas. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Brown Dutch Lettuce (Historic Dutch Heirloom Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: One of the oldest documented lettuce names in cultivation, Brown Dutch appears in print as early as the 1740s in English gardening manuals and was carried by American colonial and nineteenth-century gardeners as a reliable cool-season green. It forms a loose, nonheading rosette of large, floppy, deep lime-green leaves with ruffled edges that take on a bronzy pink-brown tinge in cool weather or bright sun, making it as ornamental as it is edible. The old-fashioned, tender leaves have a mild flavor and hold up reasonably well to light frost and summer heat compared with tighter heading types. Because it is open-pollinated and easy to save, it remains a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow a genuinely centuries-old lettuce. Matures in 48–60 days from seed.

name: Brown Flax (Traditional Oilseed and Fiber Flax)
description: Broadcast seed onto a firm, fine seedbed and rake in lightly to about 1/4 inch deep, sowing thickly so plants support each other against wind and rain. Brown flax is the older, more widely grown oilseed color type worldwide, with a stronger, earthier flavor than golden flax and a long history of use for both pressed oil and fiber where stands are allowed to grow taller and thinner. Harvest by pulling or cutting whole plants once the lower third of the stem has yellowed and most seed capsules have turned brown and dry, then shock the bundles upright to finish curing for about two weeks. Thresh over a tarp or inside a barrel and screen the seed carefully, since brown flaxseed is oily and can clump if stored before it is fully dry. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Brown Select Satsuma (Premier Gulf Coast Satsuma Mandarin, Louisiana Commercial Standard)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with full sun. Protect from frost below 28°F by covering young trees. Harvest October–November when fully orange. Brown Select Satsuma is a mandarin orange selection developed and popularized in Louisiana, where Satsuma mandarins have been grown commercially and in home gardens along the Gulf Coast since Japanese immigrants introduced the variety to Louisiana in the late 19th century. Satsuma mandarins (Citrus reticulata, specifically the 'Unshiu' or 'Satsuma' group) became an integral part of Gulf Coast culture — Louisiana's St. Bernard Parish and adjacent areas were once a significant commercial Satsuma production center, and Satsuma season (October–December) remains a beloved Gulf South annual event with home trees producing for family and community distribution. The name Satsuma comes from the Satsuma Province of Japan, where the variety was cultivated for centuries before reaching the United States. Brown Select's primary distinction from the more widely distributed Owari Satsuma is earlier ripening (Brown Select ripens 2–3 weeks earlier, in October rather than November) and what many Gulf Coast growers consider superior juice quality — slightly richer, sweeter, and with more complex flavor than Owari in typical Gulf Coast growing conditions. The tree is vigorous and productive under good culture, reliably producing heavy crops of 2-inch flattened-round fruits with loose, easy-peel skin, seedless flesh (typically zero to few seeds per fruit), and intensely sweet, juicy mandarin character. For zone 9 gardeners seeking a productive citrus tree, Brown Select Satsuma is often the first recommendation — earlier than most other mandarins, reliably productive, cold-tolerant enough for zone 9, and producing fruit of exceptional quality. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Brown Select Satsuma Mandarin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Brown Select is a distinctly early-ripening Satsuma mandarin developed and selected in Louisiana as an improvement on Owari Satsuma in terms of harvest timing — the trees produce ripe, full-flavored, easy-peeling mandarins in late September to October, making Brown Select the first commonly grown citrus to ripen in the Gulf South citrus season. The flavor at peak ripeness is comparable to Owari — sweet, aromatic, with the characteristic Satsuma complexity — but the earlier timing extends the homegrown citrus season by 3–4 weeks before Owari becomes ready. Brown Select carries the same exceptional cold hardiness as Owari (among the hardiest of all citrus to freezing temperatures) and the same practical advantage of loose, easily peeled skin and nearly seedless, juicy flesh. The combination of extreme cold hardiness, high productivity, and early ripening makes Brown Select specifically important to Gulf South citrus culture in the zones where winter cold is a genuine risk factor for citrus growing, and where starting the fresh fruit season as early as possible is valuable. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brown Snout Apple (Herefordshire Bittersweet Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends. A traditional Herefordshire, England cider apple named for the distinctive russeted, elongated end of its small, dull orange-brown fruit, it is a well-regarded bittersweet variety contributing good tannin structure and moderate sugar to a blended cider, and it remains a component of some well-known commercial English cider blends. It ripens late in the season, later than many other classic cider varieties, and stores reasonably well after harvest before milling, giving cider makers some flexibility in scheduling the press. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press once fully ripe, since the astringent fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brown Sugar Sapodilla
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil — sapodilla is one of the few tropical fruits that tolerates the alkaline, rocky soils of South Florida; Brown Sugar is a Florida-selected sapodilla cultivar named for its extraordinary sweetness and distinctive brown-sugar-molasses flavor that sets it apart from standard sapodilla varieties. The medium-sized, round to slightly oval, brown-skinned fruits have grainy, sandy-textured, translucent tan flesh that is so sweet it rivals candy — one of the sweetest fruits grown in North America, with a caramel-brown-sugar-molasses flavor that is universally appreciated even by people unfamiliar with the species. Sapodilla latex in the flesh (chicle, historically the base of chewing gum) gives the texture a slightly sticky, granular quality that is distinctive. Brown Sugar is considered the finest-flavored sapodilla cultivar for fresh eating and is the recommended variety for home orchards in zone 10 South Florida. The evergreen, windproof tree is also extremely drought-tolerant once established. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Brown Teff (Traditional Ethiopian Red-Brown Teff)
description: Blend the minuscule seed with dry sand or fine compost before broadcasting onto a firm, well-prepared bed, then roll or tamp lightly instead of covering with soil. Brown teff carries the deeper reddish-brown seed coat and stronger, tangier flavor traditionally used for classic sour injera, and is generally the hardier, more widely adapted seed class for home growers experimenting with teff outside its native highlands. Its fine tillers form an airy stand that should be cut at the base once the majority of seed heads have dried to a rusty brown, well before a hard rain can shatter the crop. Dry the cut bundles under cover for a week or more, then thresh by gentle flailing and winnow in a light, steady breeze to separate the small heavy seed from the chaff. Matures in 75–120 days from seed.

name: Brown Turkey Fig
description: This cold-hardy fig tolerates temperatures near 10 degrees F, making it a good choice for cooler regions where most figs struggle. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and provide consistent moisture while fruit is developing for deep burgundy fruit with a pink center. In borderline zones, mulch heavily around the base or grow in a pot to overwinter in a protected spot. Prune in late winter to keep the tree at a manageable height and encourage a strong branching structure. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Browne's Savory (Swamp Savory, Florida Pennyroyal, Creeping Savory)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet soil — Browne's Savory is uniquely among aromatic herbs in tolerating and preferring consistently moist, even seasonally wet, conditions that would rot most culinary herbs. Clinopodium brownei is a low-growing, mat-forming, rhizomatous aromatic herb native to the coastal plain of the southeastern United States (peninsular Florida north through coastal Georgia), the Caribbean islands, Mexico, and Central and South America in the Lamiaceae (mint family). The plant grows as a trailing, spreading groundcover with small, oval to round, bright-green, somewhat succulent leaves that, when brushed or crushed, release a pleasant, distinctly pennyroyal-like to savory-like aroma — a clean, slightly minty, herbal fragrance that makes Browne's Savory attractive as a groundcover in garden areas where foot traffic will release the scent. Tiny, pale lavender to white, two-lipped flowers are produced in clusters throughout the warm months, attractive to native bees and small pollinators. The plant spreads by stolons (horizontal runners) to form a low, dense, aromatic groundcover over moist soil areas. Browne's Savory is a native Florida plant of high ecological value — it serves as a larval host plant for the Florida-native hairy-footed flower bee and supports numerous native pollinator species. Excellent for rain gardens, pond margins, and consistently moist landscape areas in zone 8-11 where a fragrant, low-growing native groundcover is needed. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Bruce Plum (Gulf Coast Japanese Plum)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Bruce is a classic Gulf Coast Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) developed by B.W. Stone at the Texas A&M Experiment Station in the early twentieth century and released in 1952 — one of the first specifically developed low-chill plum varieties adapted to the warm winters of the Gulf South. Bruce requires only 250–400 chill hours and ripens in late May to early June in zone 9, producing heavy crops of medium to large, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed plums with sweet, juicy, pleasant flavor that makes it excellent for fresh eating, jams, and preserves. The tree is vigorous, productive, and fairly disease-resistant under Gulf South conditions — it handles the humid climate better than many other plum varieties. Bruce is partially self-fertile but benefits significantly from cross-pollination: planting with Methley or another low-chill Japanese plum reliably doubles production. Prune annually in late winter to maintain open-center structure at 10–12 feet; thinning fruit to 3–4 inches after June drop produces full-sized, high-quality plums. Brown rot is the primary disease challenge for plums in humid climates; preventive fungicide applications during bloom and as fruit develops reduce losses significantly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Brune d'Hiver Lettuce
description: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop, since it is also reasonably slow to bolt. This French heirloom butterhead, whose name translates to brown of winter, forms compact rosettes of bronze-tinged green leaves and ranks among the most cold-hardy lettuces in cultivation, often overwintering under row cover or in a cold frame. Its history traces to at least the nineteenth century in France, where it kept kitchen gardens supplied with greens through the cold months. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Bruni Dragon Fruit (Green-Skinned Hybrid Pitaya)
description: Provide a sturdy post or arbor in full sun with sharply drained soil; Bruni is a hybrid pitaya bred by a German hobbyist, distinguished from ordinary dragon fruit by neon pink-purple stem tips and smaller, prolific green-skinned fruit with sweet white flesh. Because it carries stenopterus parentage it is self-sterile and needs a compatible undatus-type pollinator planted nearby or hand pollination with foreign pollen for fruit to set. The triangular stems are more slender and tender than standard undatus, so protect from wind and hard freezes below 35F. Its flowers, like other pitayas, open for one night only and are most reliably pollinated by hand in the evening. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bruno Kiwi (Early-Ripening Cylindrical Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a sturdy arbor or T-bar trellis built to carry decades of heavy vine growth. Bruno was one of the earliest fuzzy kiwifruit selections planted commercially in California alongside Hayward, Abbott, Allison, and Monty, and it is distinguished by its narrower, more cylindrical fruit and an earlier harvest window than Hayward. Because kiwi vines are dioecious, a female Bruno vine will not set fruit without a compatible male pollinizer flowering at the same time, and only one male vine is needed to pollinate several females. Prune hard during winter dormancy to control rampant cane growth, thin overcrowded shoots in summer, and expect several years of establishment before the vine reaches full bearing size. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Brunswick Cabbage
description: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in summer for a fall crop. This heirloom forms dense, flattened drumhead heads that tolerate hard frosts and store well. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed with nitrogen to build large heads, and harvest after cool weather sweetens the leaves. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Brunswick Fig (Magnolia Fig, Madonna Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Brunswick is a common fig type requiring no pollinator and one of the most widely grown figs in the American South under various regional names. Brunswick (known throughout the southeastern United States as 'Magnolia fig' and occasionally as 'Madonna fig') is an old European fig variety that has been grown in Southern gardens for at least 150 years, widely distributed through cuttings exchanged between generations of gardeners in the Gulf Coast states; the very large (3–5 oz), pear-shaped to oblong fruits have thin, pale yellowish-green to bronze-green skin, prominent ribs, and dark amber to brownish-strawberry interior flesh with moderately sweet flavor and good quality. A vigorous, large-growing tree that tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many European fig varieties. Excellent for preserves, fresh eating, and drying. Because of widespread cutting-sharing over generations, plants sold or shared under the name 'Magnolia fig' may vary somewhat; most are similar to or identical with Brunswick. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Brush Cherry (Magenta Brush Cherry, Australian Cherry)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; shape with hedge shears for formal use or allow to grow naturally as a specimen. Syzygium paniculatum (brush cherry or magenta brush cherry) is an Australian native tree or large shrub in the rose apple family (Myrtaceae) — closely related to rose apple (S. jambos) and other Syzygium fruit trees — that has become one of the most widely planted evergreen hedge, screen, and topiary plants in zone 9–12 landscapes in Florida, California, and the Gulf Coast. The plant produces glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green new growth that flushes copper-red to bronze-red as it emerges — making it attractive year-round — and responds well to shearing into formal hedge shapes. It produces abundant, 1/2-inch, bright magenta-pink fruits in summer that are edible but primarily astringent and mild, with a rose-water and mild apple flavor; they are eaten fresh in small quantities, made into jams, or used in drinks. The flowers are fluffy, cream-white, and produced in clusters; they attract bees and butterflies. As a hedge plant, brush cherry is outstanding: it maintains dense, dark-green foliage, responds well to clipping, and is salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established. More widely available in the nursery trade in Florida and California than most other Syzygium species. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Brussels Sprouts
description: Sow 1/4 in deep indoors under bright lights; transplant into deeply prepared soil and stake tall plants against wind. When sprouts at the base reach marble size, remove the growing tip (topping) to concentrate energy and speed maturation of the remaining sprouts. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward once they are 1–2 in across and tight. Flavor peaks after exposure to a hard frost. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Brussels Winter Chervil (Cold-Hardy Heirloom Anise Herb)
description: Direct-sow Brussels Winter chervil seed shallowly into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in late summer or early fall, since this old cold-hardy strain thrives on a fall-to-spring schedule and resents the heat that makes most chervil bolt. Give it a partly shaded spot with dappled light, where its fern-like foliage stays tender and productive right through cold snaps that would finish off less hardy sowings. The leaves carry chervil's signature mild anise-parsley flavor, best used fresh and added at the end of cooking to season eggs, soups, and delicate sauces. Because it holds quality in cold, shaded conditions better than standard chervil, Brussels Winter is a reliable way to keep a fresh culinary herb coming from a shady bed through the off-season. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Bryan Apricot (Texas Heat-Tolerant Home Orchard Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bryan is self-fertile so a single tree can produce fruit without a pollinizer. A found seedling selection promoted by Texas A&M for its ability to bear fruit in the state's difficult apricot climate, Bryan is considered one of the more dependable apricots for Texas gardeners even though, like all apricots grown there, it does not crop every single year because of erratic late-winter warm spells followed by hard freezes. Fruit is medium-sized with the classic sweet-tart apricot flavor, good for fresh eating, preserves, and drying. Choose a site on a slope or high ground with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to the early spring blooms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Buartnut (Butternut-Heartnut Hybrid)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting two or more trees for reliable pollination. Buartnut is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between butternut (Juglans cinerea) and Japanese walnut or heartnut (Juglans ailantifolia), combining some of butternut's rich, oily flavor with heartnut's heavier and more reliable nut production. Because true butternut has been decimated across its range by butternut canker disease, buartnut is grown by nut enthusiasts in colder climates as a hardier, often more disease-tolerant alternative that still carries much of the butternut flavor profile. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Bubba Blue Ginger
description: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in dappled shade to part sun; keep evenly moist through the growing season. 'Bubba Blue' is a named culinary ginger cultivar grown in university variety trials alongside other named strains for rhizome yield and quality comparison, notable for the distinctive blue-purple blush at the base of its stems and buds, which distinguishes it visually from plain commercial ginger while producing rhizomes of comparable culinary quality. Harvest young 'baby' ginger in 4-5 months for a milder, less fibrous root, or allow foliage to yellow and die back for a fully mature, more pungent harvest. In zone 8-9, mulch heavily or lift and store rhizomes over winter. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Bubblegum Toka Plum
description: This cold-hardy hybrid plum produces juicy reddish-purple fruit with a distinctive sweet, spicy flavor often compared to bubblegum. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and include a compatible pollinizer nearby since Toka also serves as an excellent pollinator for other plums. Water consistently during fruit set and thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune in late winter to an open-center form for good light penetration and air flow. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Buccaneer Walnut (Dutch Blight-Resistant Self-Fertile Persian Walnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Buccaneer is self-fertile and produces heavy yields of high-quality nuts from a relatively young age (typically 4-5 years); its late-leafing habit protects the developing catkins and foliage from late spring frost damage, and it shows excellent resistance to walnut blight, a bacterial disease that can be serious in cooler, damper walnut-growing regions such as the UK and parts of northern Europe. Buccaneer originated in the Netherlands as a robust, disease-resistant Persian walnut selection bred for reliability outside the classic Mediterranean and Californian walnut belts, forming a broad-canopied tree valued both for nut production and wildlife value. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Buchu (Round-Leaf Buchu)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; buchu is one of the most important medicinal plants of the South African Cape fynbos and one of the few Cape plants to have achieved significant international commercial significance as a herbal supplement. The small, oval, dark-green leaves are powerfully aromatic — the fresh or dried leaf releasing a strong, distinctive, somewhat blackcurrant-minty-spicy scent from oil glands visible as transparent dots in the leaf surface. In traditional San and Khoikhoi medicine, and later in European colonial medicine, buchu was used primarily for urinary tract and kidney complaints, and dried buchu leaf extract is still sold today as a supplement for urinary health and anti-inflammatory purposes. As a garden plant it is a neat, bushy, heather-textured small shrub of the fynbos type — small, oval, aromatic leaves on fine stems — that produces in spring small, white, five-petaled flowers in moderate quantity. The aromatic foliage is the primary ornamental and practical value. Excellent for a dedicated medicinal herb garden or Cape fynbos planting in zones 8–11 where its drainage and lean-soil requirements are met. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Buckingham Apple (Sweet-Tart Southern Heirloom, Byers)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Buckingham, also historically known as Byers, is a large Southern heirloom apple with red-striped skin over a yellow-green background, carrying juicy, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh that made it a favorite for fresh eating, cooking, and cider across the mid-Atlantic and upper South for generations. The tree is well adapted to warmer Southern growing conditions than many Northern-bred heirlooms tolerate comfortably, making it a good option for gardeners in the middle latitudes of apple-growing range wanting a genuine historic Southern variety. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect reasonably good, though not exceptional, storage life in cool conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Buckingham Tayberry
description: Buckingham is a thornless Scottish-bred tayberry selection, carrying the same long, conical, deep purple-red berries and rich, sweet-tart raspberry-blackberry flavor as the original tayberry but on spineless canes that are much more pleasant to train, prune, and hand-pick. Fan-train the long trailing canes along wires, keeping the current season's primocanes separated from the fruiting floricanes to simplify post-harvest cleanup. Cut fruited canes to the ground immediately after harvest and tie the new canes onto the wires for next year's crop. In the cooler part of its range, detach canes from the trellis after leaf drop and cover with straw mulch or row cover for winter protection; in the humid Gulf South, prioritize good air circulation and a well-drained, elevated bed to reduce cane and fruit rot pressure. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Buckland Mahonia (Graceful Arching Winter-Flowering Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Buckland, like 'Charity' and 'Lionel Fortescue' a selection from the original Mahonia japonica x M. lomariifolia seedlings raised at The Garden House in Buckland Monachorum, Devon, is notable for a looser, more gracefully arching habit than its stiffly upright siblings, carrying long, fragrant yellow flower racemes in early to midwinter above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by tart blue-black berries. Its softer form suits an informal shaded border or woodland-edge planting where a less architectural silhouette than 'Charity' is wanted. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Buckland Ornamental Oregano (Dusty Pink Hop-Flowered Trailing Oregano)
description: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Buckland is a low, spreading ornamental oregano with small, rounded, blue-green aromatic leaves, blooming all summer with whorls of pendulous, dusty-pink, hop-like bracts that half-conceal tiny orchid-pink flowers, giving it a softer, more subdued look than brighter hop-flowered oreganos. The foliage is aromatic but not grown for the kitchen, since flavor and oil content are much lower than culinary Greek oregano. It works well trailing over the front of a sunny border, in containers, hanging baskets, or window boxes, and the persistent flower bracts can be cut for dried arrangements. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep growth compact and encourage rebloom. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Buckler Sorrel (French Sorrel, Shield-Leaf Sorrel)
description: Sow directly in spring or fall in any well-drained soil; buckler sorrel is drought-tolerant when established and tolerates light shade, making it useful under taller plants; harvest young leaves by cutting 2–3 inches above the crown; remove flowering stalks to encourage continued leaf production; plants are perennial and will regrow from the crown each spring.
