Buckler sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is a European perennial herb closely related to but distinct from common garden sorrel (Rumex acetosa) — the differences are important for culinary use: where common sorrel has large, elongated arrow-shaped leaves with a strong, pungent, distinctly acidic flavor, buckler sorrel has small, rounded, shield-shaped (scutate — hence 'scutatus') leaves with a more delicate, lemony-tart flavor that is fresh and citrusy without the harsh tang of the larger-leaved species. The name 'buckler' refers to the small round medieval shield (a buckler) that the leaf shape resembles. Buckler sorrel is considered the superior culinary sorrel in French cooking: it is used in the classic potage à l'oseille (cream of sorrel soup), as a chiffonade in salads where the milder flavor is more versatile, in sauce oseille served with fish and eggs, and as an herbal flavoring in vinaigrettes where lemon-acid flavors are desired without citrus. The leaves are high in oxalic acid (as is common sorrel), so large quantities should not be eaten regularly, but culinary use in normal amounts is entirely safe. Once established, buckler sorrel is a tough, long-lived perennial that self-sows readily and can spread if not managed. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Buckler-Leaf Sorrel
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained soil with moderate fertility; thin to 12 in apart once seedlings reach 2 in. Buckler-leaf sorrel has small, shield-shaped silvery-green leaves with a clean, bright lemon-acid flavor that is preferred over common sorrel in French cuisine for sorrel soup and sauces. Remove flowering stalks as they appear to redirect energy into leaf production; divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Harvest the small leaves regularly while they are fresh and tender, as flavor intensifies in older foliage to the point of bitterness. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Buckman Pawpaw (White-Fleshed Heirloom Selection)
description: Buckman is an older named pawpaw selection distinguished by unusually pale, white-toned flesh rather than the yellow-orange color typical of most cultivars, paired with a mild flavor. It is a late to very-late ripening selection, extending the harvest window for growers who also plant earlier cultivars. Buckman survives today mainly in historical cultivar records rather than wide commercial distribution, and like other pawpaws it requires a genetically distinct second tree for cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Buckthorn Bumelia (Buckthorn Bully)
description: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in woodland garden settings; buckthorn bumelia is a native thorny shrub of the eastern Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing naturally in moist, mixed woodlands and forest edges from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the more drought-adapted gum bumelia, this species prefers moist woodland soils and grows in shade-adapted situations at woodland margins and in the forest understory. The small, black fruits in fall are eaten by numerous species of birds and the thorny branches provide valuable nesting habitat. A useful shrub for creating dense, bird-friendly hedgerows at the edge of native woodland garden designs in zones 6–9. The small white flowers in summer attract pollinators. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Buckwheat Microgreens
description: Soak the unhulled buckwheat seed overnight and rinse it before spreading it densely on a moist tray. Cover for a few days while the heart-shaped cotyledons push up, then expose to bright light and mist as needed. Keep an eye out for seed hulls clinging to the leaves and mist them off before harvest. Cut the tender, lightly nutty greens once the cotyledons have fully opened, generally around a week to ten days. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Bud 9 Apple Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Bud 9 is grown as a fully dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit. Bred in Russia and among the most cold-hardy of the fully dwarfing apple rootstocks available, it produces a small, highly precocious tree roughly a quarter to a third the size of a full seedling tree, bearing fruit remarkably early, often within two to three years of grafting. Its combination of extreme size control and superior winter hardiness compared to similarly dwarfing rootstocks like M9 has made it a favorite for high-density home and commercial orchards in cold-winter regions. Provide permanent staking or trellising, since its small root system anchors poorly without support, and expect a compact, easy-to-harvest and easy-to-spray tree well suited to a small home orchard. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Budai Torpe Tomato (Hungarian Heirloom Dwarf Tomato)
description: Budai Torpe, whose Hungarian name translates roughly to 'Buda dwarf,' is a compact, potato-leaf heirloom tomato from Hungary grown for generations before it entered wider international seed exchange. Its thick, rugose foliage and short, self-supporting stems are typical of old-world dwarf tomato lines, and it bears medium-sized red fruit with a brisk, well-balanced flavor. Along with other historic dwarf varieties, it was folded into the founding gene pool of the modern Dwarf Tomato Project, most notably crossed with Black From Tula to produce the early-maturing Dwarf Arctic Rose. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine. Matures in 72–85 days from transplant.

name: Buddha's Hand Citron
description: Buddha's hand is a citron variety bearing distinctive finger-like lobes that contain only aromatic peel with no juice or pulp; it is valued entirely for its intensely fragrant zest used in baking, cocktails, and as a natural air freshener. Trees are self-fertile and small enough to grow in 15–20 gallon containers, making them suitable for patios and sunrooms in colder climates; bring indoors before temperatures fall below 32°F. Fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year and maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop. Harvest when the fingers have turned fully yellow and the fragrance is intense; fruit can be stored at room temperature for 1–2 weeks. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Buena Mulata Pepper
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Buena Mulata is a treasured African-American heirloom pepper with roots in Philadelphia's Black community, saved for generations and brought to wider attention through Seed Savers Exchange; it produces thin, cayenne-shaped pods 4–5 inches long that pass through a remarkable spectrum of colors as they ripen — pale cream to lavender-purple to orange to red — making the plant highly ornamental at every stage. The flavor is moderately hot (about 30,000 SHU) with a distinctive spicy, slightly fruity complexity; use fresh at any stage or dry to a rich red powder. This is a historically significant cultivar that deserves preservation and wider growing. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Buena Vista English Lavender (Twice-Blooming Deep Blue Lavender)
description: Bred in Oregon, Buena Vista is a hard-to-find twice-blooming English lavender, producing its first flush of elongated, bi-colored spikes, dark blue-violet calyxes with lighter blue corollas, in late spring, then reblooming in late summer into fall. Deadhead spent spikes by midsummer to encourage the second flush, and shear the whole plant back by about a third after the final bloom to keep growth compact and woody. Give it excellent drainage and avoid summer irrigation once established, since wet feet are the most common cause of failure. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Buffalo Gourd (Wild Gourd, Missouri Gourd)
description: Direct sow in spring after last frost in any well-drained, dry to moderately moist, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — buffalo gourd is one of the most extraordinarily drought-tolerant plants native to North America, a perennial-rooted annual vine of dry prairies, roadsides, and desert washes from Nebraska to California, extending its large, rough-textured, gray-green leaves on trailing stems up to 30 feet in a single season. The plant has a distinctly unpleasant, musky-fetid odor when handled (hence the species name 'foetidissima' — most stinking). Round, striped, baseball-sized gourds develop in summer that are toxic and extremely bitter when raw (cucurbitacins); these were used by indigenous peoples after processing to remove bitterness, and the seeds are oil-rich and nutritious. The massive taproot (potentially hundreds of pounds on mature plants) stores enormous water reserves. Most appropriate for large-scale wildlife habitat plantings, erosion control on dry slopes, and arid restoration projects rather than conventional garden settings. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Buffaloberry
description: Silver buffaloberry is an extremely cold-hardy nitrogen-fixing shrub native to the Great Plains, valued for its bright red, tart berries that have historically been used by Indigenous peoples of North America for pemmican and sauces. It is dioecious and wind-pollinated, requiring male and female plants; purchase sexed plants, as seedlings cannot be sexed until flowering at 3–5 years. The thorny, silver-leaved plants thrive in alkaline, dry, or infertile soils where other fruits fail. Harvest by spreading a tarp and gently shaking or beating branches after a light frost, which softens the bitterness; berries are very tart raw but excellent cooked. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Bugle Butternut Squash (Compact Powdery Mildew-Resistant Butternut)
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Bugle is a butternut squash bred at Cornell University with strong resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically coats squash foliage in a white film and shuts down photosynthesis well before fruit has finished sizing and curing in humid Southern gardens. Because the leaf canopy stays healthier longer, Bugle tends to fill out a fuller crop of the classic tan, elongated-neck fruit with dense, sweet orange flesh than mildew-susceptible butternut varieties planted in the same conditions. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks; properly cured fruit stores for several months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Bulb Onion
description: Press sets or transplants 1 in deep with the pointed tip facing up in rich, well-drained, loose soil. Onion bulb size is determined by the number of leaves at the time of bulbing: each leaf corresponds to a ring, so healthy top growth is essential throughout spring. Reduce watering once the necks begin to soften and tops start to fall over naturally. Cure harvested bulbs in a warm, airy spot for 2–3 weeks before moving to dry, cool storage. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Bulgarian Carrot Pepper
description: Start seed at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in a moist starting mix and pot up once the first true leaves appear; transplant after frost danger passes and begin fertilizing with a low-nitrogen, high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage fruit set. Bulgarian Carrot is an eastern European heirloom producing vivid orange, carrot-shaped fruits 3–4 inches long with thin, crispy walls and a surprising fruity, almost apricot-like sweetness that precedes a sharp, clean, medium heat (5,000 SHU). It is exceptionally productive, with dozens of fruits per plant, and is highly ornamental as fruits turn from yellow to brilliant orange at maturity. Use fresh in salsas and relishes where the fruity flavor is showcased, or pickle whole for a pantry staple. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Bulgarian Triumph Tomato (Meaty Bulgarian Heirloom Paste Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional heirloom from Bulgaria, bearing medium-sized red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh well suited to sauce and paste, a style of tomato long favored in Eastern European home gardens for preserving. Its productive, reliable vines yield a heavy crop over the growing season in gardens with a long, warm summer. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture in cooked preparations. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Bulida Apricot (Spanish Heirloom Golden-Orange Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bulida, a long-cultivated Spanish heirloom apricot, bears large, golden-orange, sweet and juicy fruit on a rustic, adaptable tree with a history of reliable performance across variable climates. Its chill requirement, while not the lowest among apricots, is manageable in much of zone 8, and its tough, forgiving nature has kept it in cultivation for generations. As with other apricots, early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap, so good air drainage at the planting site helps protect the flowers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Bull Nose Pepper (Historic Jefferson-Era American Sweet Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented sweet pepper varieties in American gardens, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and preserved by seed savers as a living link to early American kitchen gardens, producing blocky, mild, thick-walled fruit that matures from green to red. It performs reliably through the long, hot Gulf South growing season on compact, productive plants well suited to garden beds or large containers. Harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage continued fruit set through summer. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Bull's Blood Beet
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, deeply worked, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil; soak seeds overnight to improve germination and thin to 3–4 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet first listed in Burpee's catalog in the 1840s, grown for 175+ years for its spectacular deep burgundy-red to near-purple foliage that is among the most vivid of any vegetable; the young leaves and stems are intensely colored and are prized as a microgreen, baby salad leaf, and ornamental edging plant. The roots are also deep red, sweet, and excellent at any size from marble (35–40 days) to mature golf ball (55–60 days). The dramatic foliage remains strongly colored through the season and is highly heat-tolerant for a beet. An outstanding dual-purpose ornamental-vegetable for edible landscaping, container growing, and intensive salad gardens. Matures in 35–58 days from seed.

name: Bulltongue Arrowhead (Lanceleaf Arrowhead, Duck Potato, Wapato)
description: Plant in shallow water, saturated soil, or the wet margins of ponds and rain gardens in full sun to partial shade; Bulltongue Arrowhead is a native Gulf Coast emergent aquatic plant that provides outstanding wildlife habitat, water quality improvement, and ornamental interest in naturalistic water features. Sagittaria lancifolia is one of the most common native aquatic plants of the Gulf Coast from Texas through Florida, growing in freshwater marshes, ditches, bayous, pond edges, and slow-moving streams where it forms dense, productive stands of bold, lance-shaped, upright leaves. The three-petaled white flowers with yellow centers appear throughout summer on tall stalks above the foliage and attract native pollinators including specialist bees that rely on aquatic pollen sources. The small, acorn-sized, starchy tubers or corms produced at the tips of underground runners ('duck potatoes') are an important food source for ducks, geese, muskrats, and other waterbirds — and are edible for humans when cooked like a potato or roasted in coals: mild, slightly nutty, and starchy, they were a staple food for southeastern indigenous peoples. In water gardens and rain garden plantings, Bulltongue Arrowhead is a native alternative to non-native aquatic plants, providing the same bold vertical accent while supporting native wildlife. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Bun Long Taro
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in rich, moist to wet soil — Bun Long thrives at pond margins and in consistently waterlogged conditions that would kill most vegetables; Bun Long is a Hawaiian-adapted wetland taro cultivar used as the primary taro for poi production in Hawaii, producing large starchy corms with a distinctive pale lavender-purple flesh that turns light gray-purple when cooked and pounded. The large corms (often 2–5 pounds each) are a primary poi taro precisely because of their excellent starch content and texture when cooked and pounded or processed. The leaves and stems are also edible when thoroughly cooked — the tender young leaves (luau leaves in Hawaiian cuisine) are used in laulau, stew, and other dishes. In zone 9 Bun Long taro is an outstanding productive crop for the long, hot, humid growing season and thrives in the wet spots and poorly drained areas of Gulf Coast gardens where other vegetables struggle. The handsome large leaves with their distinctive pale purple veins provide ornamental value as well. Matures in 200–365 days from transplant.

name: Bunch Porto Rico Sweet Potato (Compact Vintage Heirloom)
description: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Bunch Porto Rico is an early-20th-century American selection from the old Porto Rico sweet potato line, valued for a more compact, semi-bush vining habit that spreads far less aggressively than standard long-vine heirlooms, making it practical for gardeners short on space. It produces copper-skinned tubers with moist, deep-orange, sweet flesh similar in eating quality to its Porto Rico parent, and its shorter vines are easier to manage, hill, and keep out of walkways through the growing season. Dig tubers once the vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts and concentrate sweetness before storage. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Bunch Purple Hull Cowpea (Compact Bush-Type Purple Hull Southern Pea)
description: Bunch Purple Hull is a compact, upright, bush-habit selection within the purple hull class of Southern peas, bred to concentrate pods near the top of self-supporting plants rather than the sprawling growth habit of older purple hull field types. Direct sow into warm, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, spacing plants a few inches apart in rows. The cream-colored peas marked with a purple-pink eye retain the classic mild, slightly sweet purple hull flavor prized in Southern cooking, and pods can be picked at the green-shell stage for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage. Bunch Purple Hull has served as parent breeding stock for later disease-resistant purple hull and blackeye releases, including Mississippi State University's Magnolia Blackeye. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Bunching Onion (Welsh Onion)
description: Direct sow thinly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in fall or late winter; thin to 3–4 inches as seedlings grow, using thinnings as your first scallion harvest. Unlike common onions, bunching onions never form a bulb — the entire plant from leaf tip to root is used, and cutting stems back to 1–2 inches above soil level promotes regrowth for a cut-and-come-again harvest cycle. Clumps can be divided every year or two to rejuvenate growth; older clumps become crowded and produce thinner stalks. In zone 9 they overwinter reliably and often survive light freezes, making them a year-round perennial green-onion source. Matures in 60–120 days from seed.

name: Bunya Nut (Bunya Pine)
description: Sow fresh seed straight from a fallen cone into a deep container, since the large nut and long taproot make this towering Australian conifer resent transplanting once it is well rooted. Bunya pine takes many years to reach flowering and cone-bearing size but rewards patient growers with basketball-sized cones containing dozens of large, chestnut-flavored nuts that are traditionally roasted or boiled. Give it a wide, open site well away from structures, parking, and foot traffic, because mature cones can weigh more than twenty pounds and drop from a great height without warning. Young trees tolerate a light frost but need full protection for their first several winters in the coolest parts of their growable range. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Bupleurum (Chai Hu, Thorowax)
description: Bupleurum chinense is an upright, clump-forming perennial in the carrot family grown in traditional Chinese medicine gardens for its slender taproot, known as chai hu, one of the most frequently prescribed herbs in Chinese herbal formulas. Direct sow scarified or cold-stratified seed in early spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven, so overseed generously and be patient. The narrow, willow-like leaves and small yellow umbel flowers resemble a fine-textured fennel or dill and make an attractive, airy addition to an herb border while the root develops below ground. Roots are traditionally left undisturbed for two to three growing seasons before being dug in autumn, cleaned, and dried for use in tea and decoction. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Burbank Plum (Luther Burbank's Japanese Plum, Red Plum Classic)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit in spring to 4–6 inches apart; plant with a companion Japanese plum for reliable fruiting; Burbank produces medium to large round, dark red to mahogany-red fruits in mid-July to early August with amber-yellow flesh; the flavor is very sweet with tropical-fruity notes and low acidity — one of the best fresh-eating Japanese plums. Burbank plum is Luther Burbank's most famous and historically significant Japanese plum variety, released by the legendary plant breeder in the 1880s from his Santa Rosa, California plant breeding operations where he created an extraordinary number of new fruit varieties through deliberate hybridization and selection from germplasm imported from Japan. Burbank introduced Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) to American horticulture, obtaining seeds directly from Japan through the USDA and developing multiple varieties — but 'Burbank' became the most widely planted and commercially important of these, establishing the Japanese plum as a standard American backyard fruit and farm market crop throughout zones 5–9. The fruits are medium to large, round, with a distinctive deep red to mahogany skin and amber-yellow flesh that is firm, juicy, and very sweet with characteristic Japanese plum flavor — a somewhat tropical, stone-fruit sweetness with lower acidity than European plums. The combination of low chill requirement (approximately 600–700 hours), broad adaptability from zone 5 to zone 9, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Burbank one of the most successful home garden stone fruits of the 20th century. Santa Rosa plum (also by Luther Burbank) is considered the superior variety by many modern tasters, but Burbank predates it and remains widely planted and recommended. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Burbank Spineless Prickly Pear
description: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Burbank Spineless is propagated only from pads, never seed, and pads root readily after callusing for a week or two in a dry, shaded spot before planting. Bred by Luther Burbank in the early twentieth century, this classic selection produces broad, paddle-shaped pads that are nearly free of the large spines typical of prickly pear, though fine, easily irritating glochids remain and gloves are still recommended when harvesting. Both the tender young pads (nopales) and the sweet, magenta-fleshed fruit (tunas) are edible, giving the plant dual value as a low-water vegetable and fruit crop for hot, dry gardens. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs little more than occasional pad thinning to control its spreading, architectural form. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Burdock (Gobo)
description: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in soil loosened to at least 18 inches; raised beds filled with light, compost-rich mix make harvest far easier than attempting to dig clay or compacted soil. Thin to 4–6 inches once seedlings are established. Gobo roots are harvested at 18–24 inches long and about 3/4 inch in diameter, typically 120 days after sowing; use a spading fork to loosen the soil alongside the root before pulling to prevent breakage. Scrub roots and slice thinly for kinpira and stir-fries; soaking cut pieces in acidulated water prevents browning. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Burdock Root (Gobo)
description: Burdock, also called gobo, is a vigorous biennial grown for its long, slender edible roots and traditional herbal uses. Sow directly in deep, loose, stone-free soil so the roots can grow straight and long. Harvest the tender first-year roots in fall before they turn woody in the second year. Keep the bed weeded and evenly watered to encourage crisp, mild-flavored roots. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Burgess Buttercup Squash (1932 Heirloom Dark Green Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits at warm temperature for 10 days to harden skin. Burgess Buttercup is an heirloom winter squash introduced by the Burgess Seed and Plant Company in 1932 — the original 'buttercup' type squash from which the entire buttercup squash class takes its name. The distinctive physical characteristic of Burgess Buttercup is the prominent gray-green button or cup on the blossom end — a flat, circular, gray-green protrusion that sits like a cap on the bottom of the round, turbaned, dark green-and-striped fruit. The fruits are medium-sized (3–5 lbs), round and flattened, with dark forest green skin and narrow lighter stripes. The flesh is very deep orange-yellow, extremely dry and dense with a fine, smooth grain — a floury, potato-like texture (similar to kabocha, to which it is related) rather than the moist, stringy texture of acorn or some other winter squash types. The flavor is intensely sweet and rich, widely considered among the finest-flavored of all winter squashes — sweeter than butternut, drier and more concentrated than acorn. Burgess Buttercup improved on by the sweet, slightly dry, concentrated squash flavor that has made the buttercup/kabocha class the most highly-rated squash type in culinary comparison. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Burgundy Broccoli
description: This purple sprouting type forms a modest central head, then rewards patient growers with abundant tender side shoots. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and set transplants eighteen to twenty-four inches apart in rich, consistently moist soil. Purple broccolis can be finicky, so keep them well fed and cool for the best flavor and antioxidant-rich color. Harvest the main head first to encourage a long flush of flavorful, tender side shoots. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Burgundy Okra (Ornamental AAS-Winning Deep-Red Pod and Stem Okra)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Burgundy is an All-America Selections award-winning okra cultivar with outstanding dual ornamental and culinary value — producing deep burgundy-red to crimson-red pods, stems, leaf veins, and flowers that make it one of the most visually spectacular edible garden plants available. The crimson coloration extends through virtually every part of the plant: the pods are deep red-burgundy rather than the standard green, the main stems carry the same red coloring, leaf veins are crimson, and the large (3–4 inch), yellow hibiscus-like flowers have a red center. The dramatic color creates an outstanding ornamental display in the summer garden that standard okra varieties cannot approach. The pods are edible and flavorful when harvested young (2–3 inches) — tender and mild, with the typical okra character. A critical practical note: the dramatic burgundy pod color disappears when cooked — the pods turn green when heated, which surprises first-time Burgundy okra growers. For the best ornamental and culinary effect, harvest pods at 2–3 inches (they toughen very quickly after 3–4 inches on this variety). In zone 9, Burgundy okra thrives through the brutal Gulf South summer when most other vegetables struggle, and produces prolifically from May through October with regular harvest. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Burgundy Plum (Small Dark-Red Japanese Plum for Zone 9, Very Low Chill Requirement)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches when marble-sized. Harvest when deep burgundy-red and slightly soft. Burgundy Plum is a Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) variety originating in California that has become one of the most valued low-chill plum varieties for gardeners in zones 8–10 where the winter chilling hours required by standard plum varieties are inconsistently accumulated. The variety takes its name from the fruit's distinctive deep red to burgundy-purple skin color — one of the darkest red Japanese plum varieties — which covers a sweet, amber-yellow flesh with good sweetness and mild plum flavor. The fruit is smaller than most Japanese plum types (typically 1.5–2 inches) but produced prolifically in good crop years, and the deep color makes Burgundy one of the most visually attractive plums when displayed at market or in fresh fruit arrangements. California agriculture recognized the low-chill potential of Burgundy and similar varieties in the warm Central Valley and southern coastal regions, leading to its adoption as a commercial variety in some California districts and its recommendation by cooperative extension services in low-chill regions nationwide. For Gulf Coast and Gulf South gardeners in zone 9, Burgundy represents one of the few plum varieties that can be grown reliably without the risk of insufficient chilling — a real advantage in an area where most stone fruit production is challenging. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Burgundy Sweet Potato (LA 04-175, Disease-Resistant Red-Skin LSU Release)
description: Burgundy is a red-skinned, orange-fleshed, high-yielding sweet potato developed by the LSU AgCenter, valued for resistance to Streptomyces soil rot, Fusarium wilt (stem rot), and southern root-knot nematode. It matures on roughly the same schedule as Beauregard, making it a straightforward substitute for growers wanting improved disease tolerance without a longer season. Flesh color and eating quality are similar to other standard orange-fleshed Louisiana releases, cooking moist and sweet after curing. Its multi-pathogen resistance package is particularly useful in Gulf Coast gardens with a history of nematode or soil rot pressure. Matures in 85–105 days from transplant.

name: Buriti Palm (Moriche Palm)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently wet soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; buriti palm is a frost-tender wetland species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11 and grows naturally standing in shallow water. One of the most iconic palms of the Amazon basin and Venezuelan and Colombian llanos wetlands, it forms dense stands, called buritizais, in permanently waterlogged swamp forest, its tall, solitary trunk topped with a crown of large fan-shaped fronds and heavy clusters of reddish-brown, scaly-skinned fruit prized fresh or processed into juice, oil, and traditional foods across the Amazon region. It is an exceptionally slow-growing, long-lived palm that needs many years, often a decade or more, before reaching fruiting maturity, and its dependence on permanently wet or flooded soil makes it unsuitable for anything but a wetland or pond-margin planting. Provide constant moisture or standing water at the roots and full sun, and be prepared for a very long wait before any fruit harvest. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Burkett Pecan (Large-Nutted West Texas Commercial Pecan)
description: Discovered around 1912 as a chance seedling near San Saba, Texas, Burkett became one of the signature commercial pecan cultivars of the arid irrigated orchards of West Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. It produces a large, attractive, well-filled nut with excellent cracking quality that made it a favorite for retail and gift-pack sales under the Texas pecan label. Burkett performs best where humidity stays low, since it is notably more susceptible to pecan scab than modern disease-resistant cultivars and struggles in the humid Gulf South without an aggressive fungicide program. Give it full sun, deep soil, and reliable irrigation through nut fill, along with a compatible pollinator, for consistent large-nut production. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Burmese Grape
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Baccaurea ramiflora benefits from consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from strong drying winds — mulch heavily and water regularly throughout the growing season. Baccaurea ramiflora (Burmese Grape, Latka, or Mafai) is an evergreen to semi-deciduous tree of the Phyllanthaceae family native to Bangladesh, Myanmar, Bhutan, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and south into the Malay Peninsula, where it is cultivated and semi-wild in forest edges, village gardens, and homestead agroforestry systems. The tree exhibits cauliflory — fruiting directly on the trunk and large branches in dense, pendulous racemes — producing small (1–2 inch), round to slightly oval, yellow-to-pinkish-red, thin-skinned fruits with translucent, white, sweet-sour, mucilaginous pulp around large seeds. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, made into jams, pickles, and fermented drinks, and are an important local market fruit in Bangladesh (where it is called Lotkon), Thailand (Mafai thet), and Myanmar. The tree is dioecious — male and female trees are separate — so plant at least one male with every 4–6 female trees. Baccaurea ramiflora is related to rambai (B. motleyana) and shares the genus's characteristic trunk-borne fruiting and acid-sweet flavor profile popular across Southeast Asian tropical fruit markets. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Burmese Okra (Vigorous Long-Podded Heirloom Okra)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burmese is a vigorous heirloom okra producing long, tender, ribbed green pods on tall, productive plants that continue bearing heavily through the hottest part of summer, a season when many other vegetables slow down. It has a reputation among heirloom seed savers for strong yields and reliable performance across a range of Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods every day or two once production begins, picking at three to four inches for the most tender texture, since pods left too long on the plant quickly become tough and fibrous. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Burpee Butterbush Squash (Compact Bush Butternut)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced 2-3 feet apart, or start indoors and transplant after the danger of frost has passed. Burpee Butterbush was bred to solve the space problem that keeps many gardeners from growing butternut squash — standard butternut vines sprawl 10-15 feet and can overrun a small garden — by combining a compact, bush-type growth habit that stays within a 3-4 foot footprint with fruit that is essentially identical in size, shape, and sweet, nutty flavor to full-sized vining butternut varieties. This makes it one of the few butternut options practical for raised beds, small gardens, and even large containers. Vines still produce a running habit to a modest degree as the season progresses, but nowhere near the sprawl of standard butternut, and yield per plant is comparable to vining types when given full sun and consistent water. Harvest when the tan rind is hard enough to resist a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and corky, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storage to concentrate sugars and toughen the skin for long keeping. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Burpee Hybrid Cantaloupe (Classic Reliable American Muskmelon)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burpee Hybrid is a long-standing American cantaloupe standard, producing medium-large, heavily netted, orange-fleshed melons with sweet, aromatic flavor and reliable, heavy production that made it a home garden mainstay for decades. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably under a wide range of growing conditions, and the variety's decades-long track record reflects genuinely good, consistent performance rather than novelty. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind has turned from green to golden-tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Burpless Beauty Cucumber (Mild Non-Bitter Slicing Cucumber)
description: Direct sow seeds an inch deep into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis to keep fruit straight and reduce disease pressure. Burpless Beauty produces long, slender, dark-green fruit with thin, tender skin that can be eaten unpeeled, and it was bred specifically to be milder and easier to digest than standard slicing cucumbers, a trait long marketed as burpless. Vines are vigorous and productive over a long summer harvest window when picked regularly. Harvest fruit at 8-10 inches while still glossy and firm; letting cucumbers oversize on the vine slows further production and can make the skin tougher and more bitter. Matures in 60–62 days from seed.

name: Burr Gherkin (West Indian Gherkin, Maroon Cucumber)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; burr gherkin is a West Indian species distinct from common cucumber (Cucumis sativus), producing 2–3 inch oval fruits densely covered with short spines or warts — it has been grown in the Caribbean and Gulf South for centuries and is extremely heat and drought tolerant compared to regular cucumbers. The fruits are harvested young for pickling or sliced fresh with a flavor somewhere between cucumber and zucchini; mature fruits become bitter and dry. Excellent for hot-summer gardens in zones 8–12 where standard cucumbers decline in midsummer heat; the vines are vigorous, prolific, and resistant to cucumber mosaic virus and most diseases that afflict common cucumbers. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Burro Banana (Chunky Banana, Horse Banana)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Burro banana (also called 'Chunky Banana', 'Horse Banana', or 'Bluggoe') is a distinctive ABB genome banana producing uniquely short, thick, blocky fruits (4–6 inches long but very broad and nearly square in cross-section with squared-off ridges) that stand out visually from the typical elongated banana shape. The fruits ripen from green to yellow and develop a characteristic tangy, lemon-tinged sweetness with a slightly chewy texture when fully ripe (skin may be greenish-yellow outside but flesh is cream-colored and sweet); when eaten green-ripe or cooked, the starchy texture is similar to plantain, making Burro a dual-purpose banana suited to both fresh eating when ripe and cooking applications when green. The trees are medium-large (10–14 feet) and vigorous in tropical to subtropical conditions, producing large bunches with up to 8 hands. Burro is well adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat in zones 9b–11 and is particularly popular in Mexican and Central American households for its unique dual-use character. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Burton Hican (Pecan-Hickory Hybrid)
description: Burton is a historic natural shagbark hickory x pecan hybrid discovered near Owensboro, Kentucky, in the late 1800s and long kept alive mainly through Northern Nut Growers Association members and university nut collections rather than commercial nurseries. Like other hicans it combines pecan-style productivity with hickory cold hardiness, producing a large, richly flavored nut, though kernel fill and seed germination rates can be inconsistent from year to year the way they often are in this hybrid group. Give it the same deep, well-drained planting site and cross-pollination planning you would use for pecan, and expect a long juvenile period before first nuts. It is best suited to collectors and diversified nut orchards rather than growers wanting a predictable annual harvest. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Bush Delicata Squash (Compact Vine Delicata for Small Beds)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart since the compact bush habit needs far less room than a standard vining delicata. Bush Delicata produces the same sweet, creamy, striped-skinned fruit prized in classic delicata squash, but on a tidy, short-vined plant that stays contained rather than rambling 6 to 10 feet like the traditional vining type, making it a good fit for raised beds, small gardens, or anywhere space is at a premium. Provide steady, even moisture through flowering and fruit set, and mulch around the base to conserve water and suppress weeds. Harvest once the rind hardens and the cream-and-green stripes deepen in color, then cure fruits in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to concentrate their sweetness and extend keeping quality. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Bush Early Girl Tomato (Compact Container Slicer)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 50F, or grow directly in an 18-24 inch container. Bush Early Girl is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true determinate, space-saving counterpart to the classic indeterminate Early Girl, staying under 30 inches tall while still producing full-flavored, 6-8 ounce red slicing tomatoes only a few days later than its parent. Its short, sturdy frame makes it a favorite for patios, raised beds, and small gardens where staking a full-size vine is impractical, and it carries verticillium and fusarium wilt resistance for reliable production. Matures in 54–65 days from transplant.

name: Bush Okra (Wild Jute, Krin Krin)
description: Sow seed directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost and keep evenly moist until germination, which is fast in hot weather. Bush okra is a fast-growing annual jute relative widely eaten across West Africa and Sudan, where the young leaves and shoots, known locally as krin krin, kraan kraan, or bush okra, are chopped and simmered into a slippery, okra-like soup base rich in vitamins and minerals. It is closely related to tossa jute (Corchorus olitorius) but tends to be more low-growing and branching, tolerating poorer soils and shorter, drier growing seasons. Harvest by pinching tender shoot tips every couple of weeks, which encourages continued branching and delays the onset of tough, fibrous stems and flowering. Matures in 35–60 days from seed.

name: Bush Pickle Cucumber (Compact Pickling Cucumber for Small Gardens)
description: Sow directly 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; no trellis required for the compact bush plants; harvest pickling cucumbers at 3–4 inches for small gherkin-style pickles or 4–5 inches for standard dill pickle size; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production. Bush Pickle is a compact, determinate (bush-habit) pickling cucumber developed specifically for small-space gardening — raised beds, containers, urban gardens, and patios where growing the standard trailing pickling cucumber vines (Boston Pickling, National Pickling, Calypso) is impractical due to their 4–6 foot spread. The compact plants (18–24 inches wide) produce a dense cluster of uniform, blocky, 3–5 inch pickling cucumbers with the classic pickling cucumber characteristics: firm, crisp flesh; thin skin; minimal hollow seeds; and a blocky, multi-bumped exterior that is traditional for dill pickles. Production is somewhat concentrated in a shorter harvest window compared to vining types — Bush Pickle tends to set most of its fruit within 2–3 weeks of first harvest, then declines, making succession planting (a second sowing 3–4 weeks after the first) useful for extended pickle production. Still holds well under warm summer conditions for Gulf Coast gardeners growing in small raised beds. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Bush Tea (Zulu Tea Bush)
description: Athrixia phylicoides is a wiry, heath-like shrub of South African grassland margins and forest fringes, long harvested by Zulu and other southern African communities for its narrow, resinous, silver-backed leaves, which are dried and steeped into a mild, reddish, slightly astringent herbal tea traditionally valued for soothing coughs and settling digestion. Clusters of small, daisy-like, mauve-pink flowers with yellow centers appear from late summer into autumn, giving the plant ornamental interest beyond its use as a tea herb. It responds well to light, regular tipping to keep growth dense and to encourage the fine new leaf growth preferred for harvest. Give it open, airy placement rather than dense shade, since crowding encourages dieback in humid climates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Bushel Gourd
description: Soak seeds overnight and sow an inch deep once frost danger is well past, giving this long-season gourd every warm day it can get. Provide a very sturdy trellis or let vines run on the ground with straw beneath the developing fruit. The enormous round gourds can reach three to five feet in circumference and dry into durable containers and craft shells. Matures in 120–140 days from seed.

name: Bushy Lippia (White Lippia, Lemon Verbena Relative)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established. Lippia alba (bushy lippia or cidreira in Brazil) is a sprawling, aromatic, semi-woody perennial shrub from South America and the Caribbean, native from Mexico south to Argentina, that has become one of the most widely used and important medicinal herb teas throughout Latin America. The leaves have a pleasant, complex aroma ranging from lemon-mint to spearmint-citrus to slightly camphor-herbaceous depending on the chemotype (several distinct essential oil chemotypes exist: carvone-type, linalool-type, and citral-type, each with different scent profiles). In Brazil, where it is called 'erva-cidreira' or 'falsa melissa,' it is the most popular folk remedy for anxiety, nervous tension, insomnia, and digestive upset — sold fresh in markets and as a prepared tea in pharmacies. Throughout South and Central America, the leaves are used as a flavoring herb for desserts, drinks, and savory dishes. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Lippia alba is ornamental, drought-tolerant, and virtually pest-free. The small, pale-lavender to white flowers attract pollinators. It is distinct from lemon verbena (Aloysia citrodora, formerly Lippia citriodora) but closely related and in the same family (Verbenaceae). Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Bustic (False Mastic)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic (false mastic) is a medium to large evergreen tree native to the tropical hammocks and rockland forests of south Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dense, spreading canopy of large, glossy, leathery leaves. The small, white, fragrant flowers are produced throughout the year in clusters, followed by small, yellow to orange edible fruits with a sweet, apricot-mango-like flavor. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, gray catbirds, and numerous other birds as a critical food source in the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is extremely hard and durable — historically used for railroad ties and boat building. A superb shade tree for south Florida native landscapes, providing an evergreen canopy, wildlife food, and attractive flowers. One of the characteristic dominant trees of the endangered Miami rock ridge hammock ecosystem. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and handle fruits with protective gloves; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion was recognized as the world's hottest pepper by the Guinness World Records in 2011 (since surpassed by the Carolina Reaper), measuring over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units in official testing — placing it among the most intensely hot peppers ever documented. The variety was developed by Troy Primeaux ('Butch T') in Louisiana from Trinidad Moruga Scorpion genetics. The small to medium, wrinkled, deeply colored red-orange fruits have the distinctive scorpion tail-like protrusion at the tip that gives the Trinidad Scorpion type its name. The extreme heat is accompanied by a pronounced fruity, tropical Capsicum chinense flavor beneath the intense burn. Used in tiny quantities in hot sauce production, powders, and as a daring culinary challenge. In zone 9 the long warm season and perennial habit allow Butch T plants to develop into large, extremely productive multi-year shrubs. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper (Former World's Hottest Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Butch T Trinidad Scorpion, a selection developed by grower Butch Taylor, held the Guinness World Record for the world's hottest pepper in 2011, testing over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units, among the most extreme heat levels achievable in a pepper. The small, wrinkled, scorpion-tail-shaped fruits ripen from green to a deep red and carry the fruity, slightly sweet undertone typical of superhot Capsicum chinense peppers beneath the overwhelming heat. Always wear gloves when handling fresh or dried fruit and avoid touching the face, since the capsaicin can cause serious skin and eye irritation; use in tiny quantities, typically a single pepper diluted into a large batch of hot sauce or infused oil. Plants are moderately productive and benefit from a long, warm growing season and consistent moisture. This is a specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts and hot sauce makers, not general culinary use. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Butler Hazelnut (Historic Willamette Valley Filbert)
description: Butler is a 1970s-era Oregon State University release that was widely planted in the Willamette Valley before Eastern Filbert Blight reshaped the industry toward resistant cultivars, and it remains a good-flavored, large-nutted choice for home orchards outside blight-endemic areas. Set it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and give it a compatible pollenizer, since hazelnuts shed and receive pollen on catkins through the winter months while otherwise dormant. In regions where Eastern Filbert Blight is present, inspect canes each dormant season and prune out cankers well below any visible infection to slow disease spread, since Butler lacks the resistance bred into newer OSU releases. It rewards attentive orchard sanitation with a dependable fall harvest of easily cracked, richly flavored nuts. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Butte Almond
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer variety planted nearby, since Butte is not self-fertile. Butte is a mid-to-late blooming California commercial almond noted for its heavy, consistent bearing, semi-hard shell, and small, plump kernel, and it is frequently interplanted with Nonpareil as a reliable cross-pollinating partner. Its later bloom compared with Nonpareil reduces exposure to early spring frost damage in many California growing regions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Butter and Sugar Sweet Corn
description: This long-popular bicolor normal-sugary (SU) hybrid produces two ears per stalk with kernels randomly mixed between golden yellow and creamy white, giving each cob a distinctive speckled look on the plate. Because it is a standard SU type rather than a supersweet, it does not need to be isolated from other sugary corns and holds its eating quality on the stalk for several days past peak, giving gardeners a wider harvest window. Keep plants well watered from tasseling through ear fill, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poorly filled tips. It remains a favorite roadside-stand and home-garden choice for gardeners who want classic old-fashioned corn flavor rather than the extra crunch of newer sh2 hybrids. Matures in 73–78 days from seed.

name: Butter Lamp Squash (AAS-Winning Mini Butternut-Type Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Butter Lamp is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a mini, pumpkin-shaped fruit weighing about 1 to 2 pounds, with rich yellow, smooth, sweet and nutty flesh and strong resistance to powdery mildew, heat, and insect pressure. The short-vined plant needs notably less garden space than traditional butternut squash and can be grown as a trellised hanging fruit or left to sprawl on the ground. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail scratch; fruit stores exceptionally well into winter when cured in a warm, dry spot for a week or two first. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Butterbaby Squash (Mini Butternut Squash)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Butterbaby's semi-compact vines can be left to sprawl or trained up a trellis to save garden space. Butterbaby is a hybrid mini butternut bred for uniform, single-portion fruits weighing about a half to one and a half pounds, with the same tan skin and rich, nutty-sweet, deep orange flesh as full-size butternuts but scaled down for one or two servings. Plants set fruit heavily and consistently, making them well suited to succession harvests through the fall. Harvest when the rind has hardened and turned fully tan, cure for a week or two, and store in a cool, dry spot for several months. Matures in 100–105 days from seed.

name: Butterbeans Edamame (Edamame Soybean)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in rows or wide bands, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria if soybeans have not been grown in that bed before to boost nitrogen fixation and yields. Harvest whole pods while still bright green and plump but before the beans inside turn hard and yellow, usually indicated by pods filling out fully along the stem. This variety produces unusually large, sweet-flavored beans on tall, productive plants, making it a favorite among home gardeners who want bigger portions per pod than typical edamame types. Blanch or steam the harvested pods briefly and pop the beans free of the fuzzy pod before eating as a snack or adding to salads and stir-fries. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Buttercrunch Butterhead Lettuce
description: A vigorous butterhead beloved since 1963 for its buttery flavor and melt-in-your-mouth texture around a creamy yellow heart. Sow seed shallowly, barely covering it, since lettuce needs light to germinate well. Its compact heads are ideal for containers and single-serve salads, and tolerate a bit more heat than most butterheads. Keep soil evenly moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting and bitterness. Matures in 48–65 days from seed.

name: Buttercrunch Lettuce
description: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, and keep the surface moist during cool spring or fall weather. This Bibb-style butterhead forms loose rosettes with a tender, sweet yellow heart and holds up better to heat than most lettuces. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head, and succession sow every few weeks for a steady supply. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Buttercup Squash
description: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost when soil is above 65°F; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow 5–8 feet between hills. Buttercup squash was introduced by Harris Seeds of Rochester, New York in 1932 and became the gold standard for winter squash flavor for much of the twentieth century; a Cucurbita maxima type with a distinctive flattened-round shape, dark green skin with grayish-green stripes, a small, warty 'button' (the remnant of the blossom end), and dense, dry, sweet, deep-orange flesh that is exceptionally dry and rich — much less watery than kabocha or acorn types. The sweet, nutty, slightly dry flesh is outstanding for mashing, baking, and pies; it stores for 2–3 months. The modern 'kabocha' squash type is very similar in form and is often confused with Buttercup; true Buttercup is larger and has the distinctive button. Cure for 10 days at room temperature before storage. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Butterhead Lettuce
description: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun and thin to 8–12 inches apart; butterhead (Boston/Bibb) lettuce forms a loose, soft, irregular head with velvety-tender, mild-flavored leaves that are more delicate and buttery-textured than the crisp crunchiness of romaine or crisphead types. It is more heat-sensitive than loose-leaf types and should be grown as a spring or fall crop in most climates — high heat causes rapid bolting and bitterness. Harvest the entire head when formed and compact, or harvest outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach. Excellent in simple green salads dressed with vinaigrette; the cupped leaves are also ideal for individual salad presentations. 'Bibb', 'Tom Thumb', 'Buttercrunch', and 'Boston' are classic varieties. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Butternut
description: Butternut, or white walnut, produces rich, oily nuts with a milder, sweeter flavor than black walnut and is native to eastern North America. The species is severely threatened by Sirococcus clavigignenti-juglandacearum (butternut canker), so seek out canker-resistant cultivars or hybrids (butternut x heartnut crosses, or selections from university breeding programs) rather than straight-species seedlings. Like other walnuts, butternut is monoecious and partially self-fertile but benefits from a second tree nearby; it also produces juglone that can inhibit nearby sensitive plants. Harvest when the sticky, hairy green hulls begin to soften and turn yellow-brown in early to mid-fall; hull promptly and dry nuts for 2–3 weeks before cracking or storing. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Butternut Squash
description: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest vine. Butternut is a long-season crop, so calculate the days to maturity against your first fall frost date before planting. The vines spread widely; allow 8–10 feet of run per plant. Harvest when the skin has turned uniformly tan and the stem dries out fully; cure for 10–14 days in a warm location before storing. Matures in 85–110 days from seed.

name: Butterscotch Squash (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Butternut Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Butterscotch is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a compact, semi-bush vine and small, personal-size fruit — about a pound each, roughly half the size of standard butternut squash — making it easy to fit multiple plants into a smaller garden and giving perfectly portioned single-serving squash for roasting or stuffing without leftovers. The tan-skinned, elongated fruit has dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh with the classic butternut flavor, and its smaller size means faster cooking too. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep tan color; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest to improve flavor and storage life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems on all winter squash in the Gulf South. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Butterstick Hybrid Squash (Golden-Yellow Straightneck Summer Squash)
description: Butterstick is a straightneck-type hybrid that carries the zucchini plant's productive, single-stem habit but sets bright golden-yellow, straight-necked fruit instead of green cylinders. Its smooth skin and creamy flesh stay tender at a generous 7-8 inches, giving a bit more forgiveness than crookneck types if a fruit is missed during a hot Gulf Coast picking cycle. Plants bear over a long season with a steady, single-stem habit rather than sprawling widely, so regular spacing in a sunny bed keeps air moving through the foliage. Consistent moisture and twice-weekly harvest keep the plant setting new fruit rather than bottlenecking on a few oversized squash. Matures in 48–53 days from seed.

name: Byadgi Chilli (Byadagi Hot Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Byadgi Chilli takes its name from the town of Byadagi in Karnataka, India, and carries Geographical Indication protection for its distinctive deep red, wrinkled pods. Unlike most chiles grown for pungency, Byadgi is prized above all for color: the slender 2–3 inch pods have a thin, oily skin packed with red pigment but comparatively mild-to-moderate heat, generally cited around 5,000–15,000 Scoville units with a faintly sweet, smoky flavor. Pods are harvested fully red, sun-dried, and used whole or ground to give curries, rasam, and chili powder blends a vivid red color without overwhelming heat. A reliable, productive plant for gardeners who want a true chili flavor and color without intense fire. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Byrongold Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Yellow-Fleshed Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination and best fruit set. Byrongold was released in 1985 by the USDA-ARS research station in Byron, Georgia, from Ozark Premier breeding lines, selected specifically to hold up better against the disease pressure common in humid Southeastern orchards while producing round, yellow-fleshed fruit with good eating quality. Its Southeastern breeding background makes it a solid choice for Gulf South home orchards facing the fungal and bacterial diseases that trouble many plum cultivars developed for drier climates. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that promotes airflow and reduces disease pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: C-100 American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Low-Speck Claypool Selection)
description: C-100 is a named American persimmon selection bred by the late James Claypool, valued by growers because its fruit contains few or no of the black flecks in the pulp that mar many seedling persimmons, an important quality trait for fresh and processed fruit alike. Its orange-red fruit resembles the well-known Morris Burton cultivar in appearance and flavor but runs larger, with excellent sweetness once fully soft-ripe; like all American persimmons it is astringent and inedible until then. Beyond fruit quality, C-100 offers strong landscape value, with dark green summer foliage that turns vivid red and yellow in autumn. The tree is cold-hardy and easily grown in full sun on a wide range of soils. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: CA 538 INTA Yerba Mate
description: CA 538 INTA is a commercial yerba mate cultivar developed over decades of breeding by Argentina's INTA research station at Cerro Azul, Misiones, and registered with Argentina's national seed registry (INASE) in 2016. It has become a standard high-yield reference cultivar across the Paraguay-Argentina-Brazil mate-growing region, valued for medium-sized leaves, abundant and uniform new-growth flushes, and strong vigor compared with unselected seedling plantings. In gardens it grows and is harvested the same way as species yerba mate, a large, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree yielding leaf for the traditional roasted, grassy infusion, but with more consistent, heavier production. Give it moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and partial shade to protect against summer leaf scorch. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cabbage
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors and harden seedlings off gradually before setting out into cool soil. Feed transplants with a balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when heads begin to size. Keep soil moisture consistent, as uneven watering causes heads to split. Harvest when the head feels firm and solid when squeezed; a light frost sweetens the flavor. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Cabeludinha
description: Plant Cabeludinha in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water consistently; maintain high organic matter; protect from hard frost below 28°F; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Myrciaria glazioviana is one of the lesser-known but highly regarded wild fruits of Brazil's endangered Atlantic Forest — a small to medium-sized tree whose golden, hairy fruits are prized locally though almost unknown internationally. The fruits (roughly 0.5–1 inch diameter) are covered in short, fine hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy appearance, unlike the smooth skin of the closely related jaboticaba (Myrciaria cauliflora). The pulp is translucent, juicy, sweet-tart, and grape-like in texture — excellent eaten fresh directly from the tree and used for juices, fruit wines, and liqueurs in the same tradition as jaboticaba. Unlike jaboticaba, Cabeludinha produces its fruits on the branch tips rather than cauliflorous directly on the trunk, giving a different fruiting habit. Growing naturally in the understory to mid-canopy of Atlantic Forest remnants, it tolerates partial shade better than full-sun species. Part of the rich Myrtaceae fruit tree diversity from Brazil that includes Cambuci (Campomanesia phaea), Grumixama (Eugenia brasiliensis), and Araçá (Psidium cattleianum), representing an extraordinary regional flora of underexploited edible berries. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Cabernet Eggplant (AAS-Winning Glossy Purple-Black Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Cabernet, a 2006 All-America Selections winner, produces glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit on a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid plant that holds up well to the heat and disease pressure of a long Gulf South growing season. Its strong vigor and heavy fruit set make it a reliable choice compared with some older open-pollinated eggplant varieties that struggle in extended summer heat. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and taut, before seeds inside begin to harden, and pick regularly to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season. Matures in 60–68 days from transplant.

name: Cabernet Franc Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Cabernet Franc is a red Bordeaux grape historically important as one of the two parent varieties of Cabernet Sauvignon (along with Sauvignon Blanc), and it remains widely grown both as a blending grape and as a distinctive varietal wine in its own right, particularly in the Loire Valley of France. Wines are generally lighter in body and tannin than Cabernet Sauvignon, with a distinctive aromatic profile often described as bell pepper, violet, and red berry, and the grape's earlier ripening window and better cold tolerance make it more reliably productive than Cabernet Sauvignon in cooler or shorter-season growing regions. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for good sun exposure on developing clusters to soften the variety's herbaceous, green-pepper character, and harvest once tannins are fully ripe rather than relying on sugar level alone. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cabernet Onion (Red Long-Day Storage Onion)
description: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after hardening off, and space 4-6 inches apart. Cabernet is a long-day hybrid red onion producing large, globe-shaped bulbs with deep wine-red skin and firm, moderately pungent flesh with good color that holds up well through cooking, giving dishes an attractive red tint. It stores notably well for a red onion, holding firm in a cool, dry, well-ventilated location for several months after curing. As a long-day type, it needs the 14 or more hours of summer daylight found north of about the 35th parallel to bulb properly, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the Gulf South. Harvest when the tops fall over and begin to yellow, then cure for two to three weeks before trimming and storing. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Cabernet Sauvignon Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Cabernet Sauvignon is the world's most widely planted premium red wine grape, a natural cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc first identified in 17th-century Bordeaux, prized for small, thick-skinned, deeply pigmented berries that yield full-bodied, tannic red wines with characteristic blackcurrant and cassis notes and strong aging potential. The thick skin that defines the variety also gives it better resistance to fruit rot than many thinner-skinned grapes, a real advantage in humid climates, though the late ripening window still means the vine needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature fruit before fall. Train young vines to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for good sun exposure and air movement around developing clusters, and harvest based on sugar and acid balance rather than a fixed date, since ripening timing varies by site and season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cabot Strawberry
description: Cabot was released in 1998 from the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and is grown for its unusually large, pale-red, glossy berries produced over a mid-season harvest window. Plants carry relatively few blossoms per crown but compensate with fruit size, and the cultivar shows good resistance to red stele root rot, a soilborne disease common in cool, humid strawberry ground. Its cold hardiness and vigor have made it popular with home growers throughout the Canadian Maritimes and the New England states. Thin runners regularly to keep berry size from declining as matted rows fill in. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Cabrillo Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral Everbearing Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Cabrillo is a day-neutral strawberry from the University of California, Davis breeding program, bred as an improvement on the widely grown Albion and Monterey cultivars, producing large, uniform berries with strong yield across multiple planting seasons rather than a single concentrated harvest. Because it is day-neutral, it can flower and fruit throughout the growing season rather than only during short winter days, giving Gulf South gardeners a longer strawberry season if grown as a spring-planted crop rather than the typical fall-planted short-day type. Maintain consistent drip irrigation, raised beds, and regular removal of runners to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Cacao (Chocolate Tree)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cacao is the source of chocolate, one of the world's most important food crops, and is an understory tree of the tropical rainforest that grows naturally in partial to deep shade. The unusual cauliflorous flowering habit (flowers and fruits growing directly from the main trunk and large branches rather than at branch tips) produces football-shaped pods in vivid yellow, orange, red, or purple at maturity, each containing 30–50 seeds (cocoa beans) embedded in sweet white pulp. The pulp is eaten fresh in cacao-growing regions; the seeds are fermented, dried, and processed to produce cocoa powder and chocolate. In South Florida and tropical zones, small cacao trees fruit in as little as 3–4 years and produce two crops per year. An exceptional specimen plant for the tropical garden that actually prefers shade over full sun. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Caddo Blackberry (Compact Early-Season Thornless Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Caddo is a more recent University of Arkansas thornless blackberry release, bred for a compact, upright plant habit that is noticeably shorter and tidier than older erect thornless cultivars, making it well suited to smaller home gardens and even large containers. It ripens early in the season, ahead of many other thornless varieties, with large, firm, glossy black, well-flavored berries. The compact habit reduces the need for trellising and makes hand harvest easier. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Caddo Pecan (Scab-Resistant Productive Mid-Season Pecan, Type II Gulf South Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile soil in full sun; Caddo is consistently high-yielding and somewhat more scab-resistant than varieties like Desirable and Wichita in humid conditions; nuts are medium-sized (50–55 per pound) with excellent filling and flavor; a good choice for home orchards in the humid Gulf South where scab management is a primary concern. Caddo pecan is a USDA-released variety that has become an important recommended variety for the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, particularly valued for its combination of reliable productivity, above-average scab resistance, and good nut quality in the hot, humid growing conditions of the Gulf South. In the humid pecan-growing regions of Louisiana, Mississippi, and coastal Texas, pecan scab disease (caused by the fungal pathogen Fusicladium effusum) is the primary limiting factor in pecan production — attacking leaves, shoots, and developing nuts in wet spring and summer conditions, reducing kernel quality and yield. Varieties with good scab resistance are substantially more forgiving for home orchardists who cannot maintain the intensive fungicide spray programs used by commercial producers. Caddo's above-average scab tolerance compared to Desirable (which is quite scab-susceptible in humid conditions) makes it a more practical choice for many Gulf South home orchards. The nuts are medium-sized with an attractive appearance, good kernel percentage (57–60%), and solid, sweet pecan flavor. Caddo is also considered a relatively good cross-pollinator as a Type II variety paired with Type I varieties in mixed plantings. Louisiana State University's AgCenter has included Caddo as a recommended variety for Louisiana pecan production for many years. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Caigua (Stuffing Cucumber)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and provide a trellis; caigua is an Andean climbing cucurbit that produces hollow, oblong fruits 3–4 inches long with a soft interior cavity perfect for stuffing — the hollow fruits are filled with meat, cheese, or vegetable mixtures and baked in Peruvian cuisine. The flavor is mild and crisp, similar to cucumber or chayote. Fruits are harvested when young and still tender; if left on the vine they develop soft, black seeds. The plant climbs vigorously and produces prolifically in hot summer conditions in zones 8–11. In traditional Andean medicine the plant has a long history of use for managing blood sugar and cholesterol. An unusual and conversation-starting vegetable for adventurous gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cailletier Olive (Niçoise Olive, Cold-Tolerant French Dual-Purpose Olive)
description: Cailletier is the classic small black olive of Nice, brine-cured to produce the true Niçoise olive used in the region's namesake salad, and it also presses into a delicately flavored, high-quality oil. Unlike many French cultivars it is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit reliably, though planting a second cultivar nearby increases yield. The tree grows large with an erect habit and gracefully weeping outer branches, and it is considered one of the more cold-tolerant table-olive selections, handling short freezes into the low teens Fahrenheit once well established. Harvest fruit at the deep purple-black stage for traditional Niçoise-style curing, or leave it slightly longer for oil pressing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cajun Belle Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Sweet Pepper for Hot-Humid Gardens)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red. Cajun Belle is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning pepper variety recognized for its consistent performance across diverse North American growing conditions, including the hot-humid southeastern United States where standard large bell pepper varieties often underperform due to blossom drop during heat peaks. The variety produces compact plants (18–24 inches) bearing abundantly on the small, blocky 3-inch bell-shaped fruits — smaller than the standard 4-lobed market bell but produced in much greater abundance per plant, especially in conditions that cause larger-fruited varieties to set poorly.
