The fruit profile of Cajun Belle differs from standard market bell peppers not only in size but in flavor: the smaller, thinner-walled fruits ripen fully and develop sweetness more quickly in the garden than large bells, which can take additional weeks to reach full red-ripe stage in the garden. Cajun Belle can be harvested green (mild, slightly sweet, similar to grocery-store green bell peppers) or allowed to ripen to red (sweeter, more complex, with the characteristic sweetness of fully ripe sweet peppers). The flavor is genuinely sweet — comparable to the best large red bell peppers — with none of the bitterness associated with unripe green bell peppers. The variety's most important attribute for zone 9 gardeners is heat tolerance: Cajun Belle continues setting fruit during warm periods that cause standard bells to drop their blossoms, providing reliable production through more of the Gulf Coast growing season. Matures in 57–70 days from transplant.

name: Cajun Delight Okra (AAS-Winning Compact Early Hybrid Okra)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Cajun Delight is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning compact hybrid okra developed for Southern garden production — selected specifically for early production (55–60 days, versus the 65–80+ days typical of older varieties), compact plant habit (4–5 feet vs. the 6–8 feet of full-size types), and exceptional pod quality. The dark green, straight, smooth-ridged, spineless pods are harvested at 2–4 inches for best tenderness and flavor; at this size they are non-fibrous, mild-flavored, and have the classic okra texture that makes them outstanding for gumbo, fried okra, and all Southern okra preparations. The compact habit makes Cajun Delight ideal for smaller plots, raised beds, and gardens where the full-height traditional types would be difficult to manage, and the early production date extends the productive season at both ends. Recognized as one of the best commercial and home-garden okra varieties for the Gulf South, where early establishment before peak summer heat is advantageous. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Cajun Jewel Okra
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Cajun Jewel was developed by LSU AgCenter plant breeders as a compact, dwarf-type okra specifically adapted to Gulf Coast conditions, producing spineless, dark-green, tender pods on 4–5 foot plants that are more manageable in home garden beds than the 6–8 foot giants of traditional varieties. The pods are ready to harvest at 2–4 inches long and have excellent flavor and tenderness; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants producing — pods left too long become fibrous and woody in days in Gulf Coast heat. The compact size makes it easier to pick, the spineless pods reduce irritation from the fine hairs on standard varieties, and the improved disease package helps the plants maintain production through the summer. Outstanding for zone 7–10 gulf coast gardens. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Cal Sweet Bush Watermelon (Compact Bush-Habit AAS Winner)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Cal Sweet Bush is a genuine dwarf-vine watermelon, growing on compact 14-18 inch vines instead of the sprawling 8-10 foot vines of standard varieties, so it fits in a small raised bed or even a large container without taking over the garden. It still produces good-sized, 8-10 pound, round melons with sweet red flesh and the classic striped rind. Because the compact vines carry fewer leaves to shade developing fruit, keep an eye on ripening melons in intense heat to prevent sunscald. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Calabash Tree (Gourd Tree, Huacal, Totumo)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil — Calabash Tree grows most vigorously with full sun and regular water during establishment, then tolerates periods of drought in sandy and rocky soils once established. Crescentia cujete is a medium-sized tropical tree native to Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America, widely distributed by pre-Columbian peoples throughout tropical America as a utilitarian and sacred plant — the large, round, hard-shelled fruits of the calabash have been among the most widely used natural containers, bowls, cups, ladles, and musical instrument bodies across all cultures of the tropical Americas for thousands of years. The tree is immediately recognizable by its phenomenon of 'cauliflory' — flowers and fruits borne directly on the trunk and major branches rather than on the growing tips, a strategy that attracts bat pollinators that can access the flowers and fruits by hovering next to the trunk. The greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers open at night for bat pollination, and the mature fruits are perfectly round to slightly ovoid, 4–14 inches in diameter, hanging directly from the bark on short stalks. The fruit shell is extraordinarily hard when dried — traditionally cut in half for bowls, carved and decorated as art objects, or used as maracas. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes, the Calabash Tree is a distinctive tropical ornamental valued for its unusual fruiting display. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Calabaza
description: Direct sow 3–4 seeds per hill 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning each hill to the 2 strongest plants; calabaza (also called West Indian pumpkin or Cuban squash) is the quintessential winter squash of the Caribbean and Gulf South, producing large, round to pear-shaped fruits with mottled green-to-tan skin and deep-orange, sweet, dry flesh that rivals butternut squash in flavor. Plants are notably more heat-tolerant and disease-resistant than other Cucurbita species and produce well through hot, humid Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when the skin is hard and the stem corky-dry; fruits store for 2–5 months in a cool, dry location. Excellent for soup, stews, and tamales. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Calabrian Peperoncino (Calabrian Hot Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Calabrian peperoncino benefits from a long, hot growing season and thrives in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens where it often behaves as a perennial in zone 9–11. Calabrian peperoncino (piccante calabrese, diavolicchio) is the defining hot chile of Calabria in southern Italy, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary heat element of the local cuisine; the small (1–2 inch), round to conical, bright red fruits (at 25,000–40,000 Scoville) are moderately hot with a fruity, complex flavor that distinguishes them from the clean heat of cayenne or the fruity intensity of habanero. Calabrian peperoncino is most commonly used dried — strung in traditional pepper braids (sporte di peperoncini) to air-dry in the Mediterranean sun — and is used throughout Italian cuisine as 'nduja filling (the spreadable Calabrian salumi), peperoncino in olio (chiles preserved in olive oil), as crushed dried flakes on pizza, pasta, and grilled meats, and as chili paste. The plants are highly productive and the small fruits dry readily on the vine or indoors. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Calafate (Magellan Barberry)
description: Calafate is a spiny, semi-evergreen Patagonian shrub bearing small, golden-yellow spring flowers followed by dusky blue-black berries with a tart, slightly sweet, faintly spicy flavor traditionally gathered by Mapuche and Patagonian settler communities for jams, syrups, and a regional liqueur. Folklore holds that anyone who eats a calafate berry is destined to return to Patagonia. Plant in full sun to light part shade on a well-drained slope or bank; established shrubs tolerate wind, drought, and poor stony soil far better than richer garden ground. Prune lightly after fruiting only to remove dead wood, since flowers and fruit form on older growth and heavy pruning reduces the next season's crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Calamansi (Philippine Lime, Calamondin)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; calamansi is self-fruitful and produces small, round fruits year-round in warm climates. Citrofortunella microcarpa (calamansi, calamondin, Philippine lime) is a kumquat-tangerine hybrid that is the most important souring citrus in Filipino cuisine and widely used in Southeast Asian cooking generally; the tiny (1–1.5 inch), round, orange-rinded fruits with intensely tart, aromatic green to orange juice are used in Philippine cooking the way lemons and limes are used in Western cuisine — squeezed over virtually every savory dish, mixed with soy sauce as the ubiquitous sawsawan dipping sauce, squeezed over grilled meats, noodles, soups, and rice. The distinctive, intensely floral-tart flavor is quite different from standard lime or lemon. Bears fruit almost continuously in warm climates; highly ornamental with glossy foliage. Outstanding as a large container citrus that can be moved indoors in colder zones. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Calamint
description: Surface-sow seeds on well-drained seed-starting mix and lightly press in; germination is steady within two to three weeks in warm conditions. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; calamint thrives in rocky or gravelly sites and is highly drought-tolerant once established. The small, aromatic leaves have a flavor that blends pennyroyal-mint with oregano, making it a traditional Italian seasoning for mushrooms and bean dishes. Cut back by half after the first flush of lavender flowers in midsummer to encourage a second bloom and fresh, tender growth for harvesting. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Calamint
description: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; calamint (nepitella) is a Mediterranean and European herb with small, rounded, intensely minty-oregano-scented leaves and a sustained cloud of tiny, lavender-blue to white tubular flowers from midsummer through frost that attract bees in extraordinary numbers — few plants are visited more intensely or continuously by native bees at peak bloom. The plant forms a neat, mounding, drought-resistant groundcover that is virtually pest-free. Used in Italian cooking as a substitute for mint in pasta and bean dishes (the leaves are more savory and less sweet than true mint). Self-sows moderately in suitable conditions. Excellent for edging, rock gardens, and sunny herb borders. 'Blue Cloud' (compact, intense blue) is a widely grown cultivar. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Calamondin
description: Calamondin is a hybrid between a kumquat and a mandarin orange, producing prolific small, sour-sweet fruits that are eaten whole like kumquats or used as a lime substitute in Southeast Asian cooking. The tree is self-fertile, nearly thornless, highly ornamental with fragrant white flowers, and among the easiest citrus to grow in containers — it tolerates indoor conditions better than most citrus. It tolerates brief dips to about 20°F when established. Fruit ripens from late autumn through spring; harvest when fully orange for best flavor, though the rind remains sweet while the flesh is tart even at the green-orange stage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Calamondin Orange
description: This ornamental citrus, a kumquat-mandarin cross, bears a heavy crop of small, round, tart fruit prized for marmalades and drinks. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In non-tropical climates keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot before frost. Fragrant white blossoms and glossy evergreen leaves make it as decorative as it is productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Calhoun Crowder Pea (Wilt- and Nematode-Resistant Louisiana Heirloom Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Calhoun Crowder, developed in 1949 at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana, bears speckled crowder-type peas packed tightly in the pod, bred specifically for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematodes, two pressures that limit cowpea production in the heavy, humid soils of the Deep South. Its disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardens where cowpeas have struggled in the past, without sacrificing the rich, hearty crowder-pea flavor Southern cooks favor. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Calhoun Gray Watermelon (Disease-Resistant Louisiana Heirloom)
description: Released in 1965 from the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station as a cross involving Calhoun Sweet and Charleston Gray, this variety was bred specifically to bring stronger disease resistance to the classic gray-rind Southern watermelon type. It produces 25-30 pound oblong fruits with light gray-green rind and sweet red flesh, and it holds up better against fungal wilts than its Charleston Gray parent, letting it succeed as far north as Massachusetts with proper season length. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruits near maturity. It's a solid choice for gardeners who want old-style picnic-watermelon size and flavor with fewer disease headaches than older heirlooms. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Calico Crowder Pea (Heirloom Multi-Color Seed Crowder Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Calico Crowder is an heirloom Southern pea producing the characteristic multi-colored seeds that give it its calico name — tan, brown, black, and cream mottled seeds with a distinctive pattern that creates a beautiful, rustic visual when dried and stored, distinguishing this traditional variety from the uniform-colored modern selections. Crowder peas are named for their growing habit: the seeds are so tightly packed in the pod that they are 'crowded' and develop flattened sides where they press against each other — this crowding is a defining type characteristic that distinguishes them from black-eyed peas and cream peas. The crowder texture — denser, starchier, and more potato-like than cream peas — produces a hearty, substantial broth when slow-cooked, which is the traditional cooking method for old-field varieties like Calico. As a vining-type crowder, Calico produces well on a trellis or fence and can be managed in a smaller space than sprawling bush types. The heirloom seeds can be saved year after year from the dried pods. In zone 9, Calico Crowder can be planted from April through August for multiple successive crops through the long warm season — Southern peas are uniquely suited to Gulf South heat that stops most other legumes. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Calico Lima Bean
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calico lima bean is a large, pole-type heirloom producing spectacular seeds splashed with deep red-purple and cream in an irregular speckled pattern — each seed is uniquely marked, no two alike, and the visual drama makes them among the most beautiful beans in the garden and at harvest. The large seeds are best used as fresh-shell or dry beans; the meaty, starchy texture and rich, buttery lima flavor are excellent. Fresh-shell calico limas cook faster than dried and have a creamier texture. Despite the striking appearance of the dried seeds, the calico pattern largely disappears when cooked as the pigments are water-soluble. The vigorous pole vines need substantial support and are highly productive through the long Gulf Coast growing season. Heat tolerance is excellent, and the plants continue to set pods when green beans have long since quit in summer heat. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: California 500 Asparagus (West Coast Open-Pollinated Standard)
description: California 500 is a widely grown open-pollinated selection developed for the mild-winter, low-chill growing conditions of California's commercial asparagus districts, where it has long served as a dependable field standard. It produces vigorous, uniform, medium-green spears with good tip retention over an extended cutting season in regions too warm for northern selections to go fully dormant. Because plants are not all-male, expect a mix of male and female asparagus and remove any weak or overly seedy female plants over the years to keep the stand productive. It performs best where winters are too mild for deep dormancy but summers still bring enough heat to fuel strong fern growth after the harvest window closes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: California Barberry (Shinyleaf Oregon Grape)
description: Site beneath open tree canopy in well-drained soil, giving California barberry the dappled or filtered light of its native oak-woodland and mixed-forest understory from the California Coast Ranges and Sierra foothills. Its finely divided, glossy leaflets are more numerous and slender than those of the related Mahonia aquifolium, giving the shrub a lighter, lacier texture, and bright yellow flower clusters open in early to mid spring ahead of powder blue-black berries favored by birds. Once established it needs little supplemental water and tolerates the dry summer shade typical of California gardens, making it a useful evergreen structural shrub for a low-water woodland planting. Cut back older, leggy canes at ground level occasionally to keep the clump renewing itself. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: California Bay Laurel (Pepperwood)
description: Native to the coastal forests and canyons of California and southern Oregon, this aromatic evergreen tree produces leathery leaves that are used fresh or dried as a bay leaf substitute in cooking, though its flavor and essential oil content are considerably more intense than Mediterranean bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) and a single leaf usually suffices per dish. Harvest individual leaves as needed year-round; crushing fresh leaves releases a pungent camphor-like aroma that has earned the tree the nickname "headache tree" among some foragers sensitive to its volatile oils. It tolerates a wide range of soils, from streamside to dry slopes, and can be kept pruned as a large shrub or hedge for easier leaf harvest rather than allowed to reach its full forest stature. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: California Black Walnut (Southern California Black Walnut)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; California black walnut is a multi-trunked, drought-adapted tree native to the coastal ranges and foothills of Southern and Central California, historically an important food source for indigenous peoples and still valued by native plant and wildlife gardeners for its small, thick-shelled, richly flavored nuts. It is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than eastern black walnut and has long been used as rootstock for grafting English walnut in California orchards because of its vigor and disease resistance. Trees are slow-growing and produce nuts within a juglone-rich root zone, so keep sensitive plants at a distance. Given its wild, spreading habit and long lifespan, it suits large properties, hedgerows, and wildlife plantings more than small home gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: California Blackberry (Pacific Blackberry)
description: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; California blackberry is the native blackberry of the Pacific Coast — and one of the most historically significant berry plants in horticultural history, because it is one of the parent species of some of the world's most important hybrid blackberry cultivars. Rubus ursinus is a parent of the boysenberry (R. ursinus × loganberry), the loganberry (R. ursinus × red raspberry), and the marionberry (a complex hybrid involving R. ursinus) — three of the Pacific Northwest's most important blackberry cultivars. The small, intensely flavorful native blackberries (smaller than commercial blackberries but more aromatic and complex in flavor) are highly prized for fresh eating and making jams, pies, and wine. The plant is a sprawling, slender-caned, moderately thorny shrub that tolerates considerable shade — growing naturally in the moist shade of Douglas-fir forests and redwood groves along the Pacific Coast. The deeply lobed, compound leaves are attractive. An excellent native for wildlife gardens, edible landscapes, and shaded moist woodland edges in the Pacific Coast states. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: California Blackeye 5 Cowpea (Nematode-Resistant Improved Blackeye)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye 5 is an improved release from the University of California, Davis, bred from a cross of California Blackeye and the nematode-resistant Iron cowpea to combine the classic black-eyed pea's mild, earthy flavor with real genetic resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt, two soil-borne problems that persist for years in garden soil and are especially common in sandy Gulf Coast ground. The semi-bush plants are more compact and manageable than old-fashioned vining types and need no staking. Harvest the fresh green pods as snap beans, pick the shelled green peas for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for the classic dried black-eyed peas of Southern cooking. Like other Southern peas, it fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: California Blackeye Cowpea (Classic Commercial Black-Eyed Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which promotes foliage at the expense of pod set. California Blackeye is an upright, semi-bush cowpea developed by University of California breeding programs and grown extensively as the standard commercial black-eyed pea, valued for its concentrated pod set that ripens fairly uniformly for efficient once-over harvest, along with good disease resistance and dependable yields. The classic cream-colored pea with its signature black eye has excellent flavor whether cooked fresh, dried for storage, or prepared in the traditional Southern black-eyed pea dishes served for New Year's luck. Like all cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil and thrives in hot summer weather that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: California Blackeye Pea (California Blackeye Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye is the most commercially significant blackeye pea cultivar — the variety responsible for most of the blackeye peas sold in American grocery stores. The distinctive black-eyed, cream-colored dry beans cook quickly, have a mild, earthy, slightly sweet flavor, and a mealy texture that makes them a staple of Southern cooking — particularly the iconic Southern New Year's Day dish of hoppin' john (black-eyed peas and rice), eaten for good luck. California Blackeye is a semi-bush type that is more compact and less sprawling than old-fashioned vine types, making it manageable in typical garden beds without staking. The fresh green pods are eaten as snap beans or the fresh shelled green peas are eaten before the seeds dry; the dried seeds are the standard black-eyed peas of commerce. In zone 9, California Blackeye thrives in the long hot season, producing crops from June through September with successive plantings. Southern peas fix nitrogen in the soil through symbiotic bacteria and actually improve soil fertility — one of the few warm-season vegetables that enriches rather than depletes garden soil. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: California Dreaming Che (Large-Fruited Upright Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Grow like other che selections: full sun and unfussy, well-drained soil, with tolerance for poor, dry, or alkaline conditions that few other fruiting trees can match. California Dreaming is valued among che growers for larger-than-typical fruit and a more upright, tree-like habit that is easier to manage and harvest than sprawling seedling che. As with most che cultivars other than seedless female selections, California Dreaming is generally grown with a male pollinator nearby for reliable fruit set. Fruits ripen in late summer to fall to a maroon-red, bumpy-skinned berry with sweet, melon-like flavor. Young plants can be thorny; formative pruning improves shape and eases harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: California Early Garlic (Classic Commercial Silverskin Softneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil; in mild-winter zones like the Gulf Coast, planting in October-November gives roots time to establish before the brief winter chill. California Early is the classic commercial silverskin softneck grown across California's Central Valley and is prized for its adaptability to warm-winter regions, low chilling requirement, and tight, easy-to-braid skins. Bulbs are medium-sized with 12-16 cloves in white to faintly purple-blushed wrappers and a flavor that is strong raw but mellows well when cooked. As the name suggests, it matures earlier than most other varieties, often ready for harvest by late spring, which helps it dodge the fungal pressure that builds in humid Gulf Coast soil as summer heat arrives. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store; well-cured bulbs keep 6-8 months. Matures in 200–240 days from transplant.

name: California Honey Mandarin
description: This compact mandarin produces sweet, juicy, easy-peeling fruit and stays small enough for patios or sunny indoor rooms. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and water deeply but allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season and protect from frost, moving containers indoors when temperatures drop. Light pruning after harvest keeps the canopy open and the tree productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: California Late Garlic (Long-Storing Commercial Silverskin Softneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. California Late is the other pillar of California's commercial silverskin garlic industry alongside California Early, grown for its higher yield, larger bulb size, and notably long storage life of up to 10-12 months when well cured — among the best of any garlic type. Bulbs typically hold 16-20 cloves in tight white wrappers arranged in the overlapping layers characteristic of true silverskins, with a flavor that is sharp raw and mellow when roasted. Its low chilling requirement makes it as well suited to warm-winter Gulf Coast gardens as California Early, though it needs several additional weeks in the ground to fully size before harvest. Harvest once the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed and browned, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, airy location for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store somewhere cool and dry. Matures in 230–270 days from transplant.

name: California Poppy Herb
description: Direct-sow in early spring onto lean, sandy soil, as the taproot dislikes disturbance and transplanting. The whole plant is used in traditional herbalism as a mild sedative and sleep aid. Give it full sun and minimal water, since rich, moist ground produces weak, floppy growth. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and let some flowers set seed for reliable self-sowing. Harvest the aerial parts when in bloom and dry them for tea or tincture. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: California Wild Grape
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil along a strong support; California wild grape is a vigorous, deciduous native vine of streambanks and canyons from Oregon to Baja California, grown both as a fast-growing ornamental shade vine and for its small, tart, blue-black grapes that ripen in early fall. Fruit is seedy and sharply acidic, used mainly for jelly, juice, and wine rather than fresh eating, and is an important wildlife food. The species is a parent of the widely planted, purple-leaved ornamental cultivars 'Roger's Red' and 'Rogers Red', and its rootstock has been used in grape breeding for drought and Pierce's disease tolerance. Once established, the deep-rooted vine is remarkably drought-tolerant and requires only annual dormant-season pruning to control its vigorous growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: California Wonder Bell Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep them warm for even germination. Transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm, spacing plants so air moves freely between them. The thick-walled, blocky fruits ripen from green to sweet deep red; harvest at either stage and support heavily laden plants if needed. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: California Wonder Bell Pepper (Classic Red/Green Bell Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; California Wonder is the standard classic bell pepper — introduced in 1928 and for most of the twentieth century THE bell pepper grown in American home gardens and produced commercially. The large, blocky, thick-walled, four-lobed fruits are harvested green when mature (70–80 days after transplant) or allowed to ripen to deep red for sweeter, fully ripe peppers. The thick, crisp walls and mild, sweet, distinctly 'bell pepper' flavor are the benchmarks against which other bell peppers are measured. California Wonder is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast growing conditions — tolerant of heat and humidity better than some northern-bred bell peppers. In zone 9, bell peppers can produce from February transplants through June and then resume production in September–October after the worst summer heat passes — temperatures above 90°F during flowering cause blossom drop. Apply calcium-containing fertilizer (or side-dress with gypsum) to prevent blossom end rot, which is common in bell peppers during irregular watering. The plants are technically short-lived perennials in frost-free zone 9 and can be carried over winter for a second year of production in protected locations. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: California Wonder Sweet Pepper
description: A classic bell pepper since 1928, valued for its large, blocky, uniform fruits that are perfect for stuffing. Start seed indoors eight weeks before the last frost and keep soil warm for reliable germination. Transplant after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants eighteen to twenty-four inches apart. Green peppers left on the plant ripen to sweet red with even higher vitamin C, so harvest at whatever stage you prefer. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Calimyrna Fig (Smyrna-Type Caprified Fig)
description: Calimyrna is the California-grown descendant of the ancient Lob Injir fig of Smyrna (modern Izmir), Turkey, brought into the San Joaquin Valley in the late 1800s and still the backbone of California's dried-fig and fig-paste industry. Its large, golden-green fruit ripens to a distinctive nutty, honeyed flavor with a thin skin and an interior packed with edible, crunchy seeds, considered by many growers to have the richest flavor of any commercial fig. Unlike common figs, Calimyrna requires true caprification: a caprifig tree carrying the fig wasp Blastophaga psenes must be planted nearby, or the flowers drop unfertilized and the crop fails, which makes home cultivation far more demanding than self-fertile common-type figs and largely limits it to hot, arid growing regions where the wasp's short breeding window lines up with bloom. In humid Gulf South climates the wasp is absent and caprification is impractical, so Calimyrna is a poor choice outside California's Central Valley and similar dry-summer regions. Where it can be grown, it wants the same deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and minimal winter pruning as other figs, with irrigation timed to avoid splitting as the main crop ripens in late summer. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Callaloo
description: Direct sow on the soil surface in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; callaloo is the name given in the Caribbean to green amaranth (Amaranthus viridis), a self-sowing annual leafy green that thrives in tropical heat and humidity and is one of the most important summer vegetables in the Caribbean and West Africa. The young leaves, shoot tips, and tender stems are harvested continuously and cooked like spinach — the most famous preparation is callaloo soup, a velvety Caribbean dish made with coconut milk, crab or salt fish, and okra. The plant tolerates poor soil, drought, and intense heat, and is one of the few summer greens that genuinely thrives in zone 9's most challenging months. Flavor is mild and slightly earthy; texture softens quickly when cooked. Plants self-sow freely and will return each summer without replanting once established. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Callaway Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Callaway was released around 1970 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station, from the same breeding effort that produced Briteblue and Delite. It needs about 400 chill hours below 45 degrees F and ripens midseason, from mid-to-late June in zone 7-9, with medium-to-large berries of good light-blue color and better flavor than the older Homebell and Gardenblue selections. The bush is vigorous and upright with solid production, though it has been largely overshadowed commercially by later, higher-yielding introductions and today is found mostly in older home orchards and heritage plantings across the Gulf South. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil heavily amended with pine bark or peat, mulch to conserve moisture, and pair it with a second midseason rabbiteye for reliable fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Calliope Eggplant (Compact Globe Magenta-White Striped Italian Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 2–3 inches diameter when firm and glossy. Calliope is a compact F1 hybrid eggplant bred for small-fruit production with an Italian-type rounded form and striking bicolor fruit appearance. The fruits are globe to slightly pear-shaped, 2–3 inches in diameter, with a distinctive pattern of deep magenta-purple on the upper half and creamy white on the lower half — a color distribution that differs from the vertical striping of varieties like Fairy Tale or Listada de Gandia. The bicolor magenta-white pattern makes Calliope one of the most visually distinctive eggplants in garden displays and farmers market presentations. As a culinary variety, Calliope's small globe form is practical for preparations requiring the whole fruit: the 2–3 inch fruits are ideal for stuffing (halved or hollowed), for roasting whole, for grilling cut in half, or for slicing into rounds for layered preparations. The flesh is tender and sweet at harvest size, with minimal seed development and no bitterness — a consistent characteristic of modern F1 hybrid eggplant varieties. The compact plant habit and prolific fruiting make Calliope one of the best eggplant choices for container gardens where standard varieties would be impractically large and less productive per square foot. Matures in 65–72 days from transplant.

name: Calloose Grape (Florida Grape, Leatherleaf Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade against a fence or into the edge of a pineland or hammock planting; calloose grape is a compact, heat-tolerant native vine of central and south Florida pinelands and hammocks, easily told apart from the sprawling muscadine by its pointed leaves with dense, woolly, gray-white undersides and forked (rather than simple) tendrils. It stays smaller and more manageable than most wild grapes, reaching roughly 15 to 20 feet, which makes it a practical choice for a modest trellis or wildlife screen in a native Florida garden. The dark red to purple-black grapes ripen over summer and are eagerly taken by mockingbirds, cardinals, raccoons, and other wildlife, while the small spring flowers offer an early nectar source for native bees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Caloro Pepper (Yellow Wax Hot Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Caloro is a yellow wax-type hot pepper developed in California in the mid-twentieth century and widely grown in commercial agriculture as the standard pickled yellow hot pepper of California; the conical, medium-sized fruits (3–4 inches long) emerge green, ripen to bright yellow (the commercial harvest stage for pickling), and eventually turn orange-red at full maturity. Heat level is moderate at 5,000–10,000 SHU — noticeably hot but not extreme — with a waxy, crisp texture ideal for pickled pepper rings, banana pepper-style pickles, roasting, and fresh eating. Highly productive and disease-resistant; particularly well-suited to warm California, Gulf Coast, and Southwestern climates. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Calville Blanc d'Hiver Apple (French Culinary Heirloom Apple)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Documented in France since the 1500s, Calville Blanc d'Hiver is one of the oldest named apple cultivars still grown and became the classic dessert and pastry apple of French cuisine, famously used in tarte Tatin and other traditional preparations. The irregularly ribbed, pale greenish-yellow fruit has a distinctive, complex, almost pineapple-like flavor and unusually high vitamin C content for an apple. It ripens quite late in the season and improves with several weeks of storage, but the tree can be a light or biennial bearer and benefits from a warm site and careful thinning. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Calypso Bean (Yin Yang Bean, Oreo Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calypso is a bush dry bean with a striking black and white two-toned pattern — each seed is precisely half black, half white — that has earned it nicknames such as 'yin yang bean' and 'oreo bean' for the dramatic visual contrast. The pattern fades somewhat on cooking but the bean retains excellent earthy, full-bodied flavor with a smooth creamy texture when fully cooked. Among the fastest dry beans to reach maturity, making it suitable for short-season gardens; the compact bush habit produces a concentrated flush excellent for preserving. Color fades on drying — store in a dark, cool location to preserve seed appearance. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Calypso Cilantro (F1 Hybrid Bolt-Resistant Cilantro with Extended Leaf Production Season)
description: Direct sow in cool soil; thin to 6 inches. Harvest outer leaves continuously; Calypso's extended bolt resistance allows repeated harvests well into warming spring weather. Calypso is an F1 hybrid cilantro variety developed and released by Johnny's Selected Seeds, the Maine-based seed company known for developing and trialing specialty vegetable varieties for commercial and home garden use. The variety represents the current apex of bolt-resistance breeding in cilantro — the characteristic that most limits cilantro's usefulness in spring and fall gardens, where temperatures inevitably warm and trigger the plant's transition from vegetative leaf production to reproductive flowering and seed set. In university and industry trials comparing cilantro varieties for bolt resistance, Calypso consistently produces the most leaf material and maintains quality leaf production the longest under warming conditions. The mechanism of Calypso's extended bolt resistance involves both the genetic selection for delayed photoperiod and temperature sensitivity in triggering the flowering response, and the F1 hybrid vigor that produces more robust vegetative growth generally. Calypso plants are somewhat taller and more vigorous than many open-pollinated varieties, producing more leaf material per plant in addition to bolting more slowly. The flavor is standard cilantro — the same characteristic aromatic profile from the volatile oils common to all Coriandrum sativum — with no meaningful flavor difference from other cilantro varieties. For zone 9 spring gardens where the cilantro harvest window is compressed by rapid warming, Calypso is the most productive choice among commonly available varieties; in the fall-winter planting season (October–March in zone 9), when temperatures are consistently cool, the bolt-resistance advantage is less important and open-pollinated varieties perform nearly as well. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Calypso Cucumber (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straighter fruits and improved air circulation. Calypso is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning pickling cucumber that earned recognition for its exceptional disease resistance package and concentrated production — bred to perform reliably in a wide range of climates and conditions where fungal and viral diseases limit cucumber yields. Calypso carries resistance to angular leaf spot, cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, papaya ringspot virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and zucchini yellow mosaic virus, plus tolerance to powdery mildew — one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a pickling cucumber. The dark green, warted, blocky fruits (3–4 inches for fresh pickle use, 1.5–2 inches for whole baby pickles) have thick, crisp walls and excellent pickle texture that holds up to both quick-process and long-fermented pickle methods. The gynoecious (all-female) breeding concentrates fruit set into a shorter, more predictable harvest window — convenient for processing large pickle batches. An outstanding choice for home pickle-makers, zone 9 summer gardens where disease pressure is high, and any gardener wanting maximum yields with minimum disease management input. Matures in 50–56 days from seed.

name: Camak's Sweet Apple (Rediscovered Carolina-Georgia Heirloom Sweet Apple)
description: Camak's Sweet is a medium-to-large, round apple with smooth, matte-yellow skin blushed red on the sun-exposed side and marked with abundant, slightly raised tan russet lenticels. The yellowish flesh is fine-grained, firm, and juicy, with a distinctly sweet, aromatic flavor rather than the tart profile typical of most Old Southern cider and cooking apples. It is a very late-season variety and an excellent keeper, historically valued for fresh winter eating once tarter apples had been used up. Considered extinct for decades until its 1997 rediscovery, it is now maintained by a handful of Southern heirloom orchards preserving Lee Calhoun-documented cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Camaro PMR Pumpkin (Powdery Mildew Resistant Hybrid Jack-O-Lantern)
description: Direct sow in hills after danger of frost has passed, giving the reduced-vine plants a bit less room than sprawling heirloom types but still allowing air circulation between hills. Camaro PMR carries genetic resistance to powdery mildew, keeping foliage photosynthesizing later into the season so that fruit reaches its full 20-22 pound, near-round, lightly ribbed potential even under heavy disease pressure. The strong handles and deep orange rind make it a reliable choice for growers selling carving pumpkins, and the shorter vine habit suits smaller Gulf Coast garden plots better than old-line field pumpkin types. Watch soil moisture during fruit set, since consistent watering paired with the plant's disease tolerance produces the most uniform, market-ready fruit. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Camarosa Strawberry
description: Plant dormant crowns with crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Camarosa is a large-fruited, early-season strawberry developed by the University of California at Davis and released in 1992. For nearly a decade it was the most widely planted commercial strawberry in California and dominated early-season Florida production as well. The large, conical berries are dark red, very firm, and mildly sweet — excellent for shipping and processing but slightly less intensely flavored fresh than Sweet Charlie or Festival. Camarosa's principal strengths are its very high productivity, large and attractive berry appearance, and exceptional firmness that makes it the preferred variety for growers who need to ship or sell at farmers' markets where berries must look their best. In zone 9, Camarosa is planted October–November and harvested primarily in January–March. The plants are vigorous and productive but susceptible to powdery mildew and some soil-borne diseases — plant in raised beds with fresh soil or strawberry-specific fumigation. Maintain consistent drip irrigation to reduce disease and ensure uniform berry sizing. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Cambodian Green Giant Eggplant (Southeast Asian Heirloom Striped Round Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay warm; harvest fruit while pale green with dark green stripes and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds enlarge. Cambodian Green Giant is a Southeast Asian heirloom producing large, round, slightly flattened fruit striped in pale and dark green on compact 2-3 foot plants, giving strong yields relative to the space the plant occupies. The dense, full-bodied flesh holds its texture well on the grill or in a wok, a quality suited to the quick high-heat cooking common in Southeast Asian cuisine. Because it is bred for tropical growing conditions, it handles the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer with ease and produces most heavily from midsummer into fall, right as many spring-planted eggplants begin to decline. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Cambridge Favourite Strawberry (Classic English Garden Standard)
description: Cambridge Favourite was released in the 1950s from a strawberry breeding program in Cambridge, England, and went on to become one of the most widely grown garden strawberries in the United Kingdom for the remainder of the twentieth century. It is valued less for exceptional flavor than for its dependable, heavy mid-season cropping, reasonable tolerance of mildew, and adaptability to a wide range of garden soils and situations. The medium-sized, bright orange-red berries are firm enough to hold up well to freezing and preserving as well as fresh eating. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing off old foliage and thinning runners to keep plantings vigorous for several years. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Cambridge Gage Plum (Small Sweet English Gage-Type Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Cambridge Gage is an English selection from the historic gage family of European plums descended from the original Reine Claude, producing small, round, greenish-gold fruit with the same rich, exceptionally sweet, honeyed flavor that made the original Green Gage famous, in a somewhat more reliably productive tree than some other gage selections. The delicate skin and juicy, tender flesh make it best suited to fresh eating and preserves rather than heavy handling or long-distance shipping, since fruit bruises easily once ripe. Harvest when fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and the green skin has softened toward gold, and use promptly, since gage-type plums typically have a short window of peak ripeness. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cambucá
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full sun in zones 10–11; cambucá is a rare Atlantic Forest gem in the Myrtaceae family (closely related to jaboticaba) that produces large, round, yellow-green fruits directly on its trunk and major branches — a phenomenon known as cauliflory that makes the tree a striking spectacle when loaded with fruit. The thick-skinned fruits hold exceptionally sweet, white, juicy flesh with a fragrant, complex flavor described as a blend of mango and passion fruit, and are eaten fresh or made into artisanal jams and wines in the Brazilian coastal states where it is native. Cambucá prefers the high humidity and warm temperatures of its coastal rainforest home and performs best with regular deep watering and organic mulch kept away from the trunk. Seed must be planted fresh — sow immediately after extraction from ripe fruit, as viability falls dramatically within two to three weeks. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Camelina (False Flax)
description: Surface-sow tiny seed at 5–8 lb/acre and tamp firmly; camelina requires light for good germination and should not be buried more than 1/4 in deep. It matures in under 100 days and tolerates drought and cold better than any other oilseed crop, making it a fine spring or overwintered autumn oilseed in short-season gardens. Harvest when 80% of the pods are golden and dry — thresh by beating bundled stalks into a bucket, then winnow. The oil is exceptionally high in omega-3 fatty acids and has a pleasant nutty flavor for culinary use. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Camellia Southern Highbush Blueberry (Mild-Flavored Productive Blueberry)
description: Amend planting beds to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and keep roots consistently moist with a thick mulch layer since southern highbush blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems. Camellia is a University of Florida release known for very high, consistent yields of medium to large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, low-acid flavor that many home growers find especially easy-eating fresh off the bush. The upright, vigorous plant tends to hold its crop well without excessive splitting in Gulf Coast humidity. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and fertilize lightly with an acid-forming blueberry fertilizer split between early spring and shortly after harvest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Camelot Shallot
description: Camelot is a round-bulbed shallot cultivar grown for its coppery-brown skin, dense clove-free flesh, and consistently heavy yields from each planted set. Set bulbs shallowly in loose, fertile, well-drained soil and keep the row weeded, since shallots have a shallow, easily shaded root system. Each bulb divides into a cluster of several new bulbs over the growing season, ready to lift once the foliage yellows and falls over in midsummer. Cure the whole cluster in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks before separating the bulbs for storage or replanting a portion for next year's crop. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Cameo Apple (Modern Crisp Sweet-Tart Washington Discovery)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Cameo was discovered as a chance seedling in a Washington State orchard in the late 1980s, believed likely to be a cross involving Red Delicious, and quickly rose to commercial prominence through the 1990s and 2000s for its exceptional eating quality. The medium-to-large fruit has a distinctive appearance, with soft red stripes over a cream to pale yellow background, and the dense, crisp, juicy flesh delivers a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up impressively well in cold storage, often improving in flavor after a few weeks. Cameo is a strong all-purpose apple, equally good fresh, in salads, or baked, and its firm texture and good keeping quality make it a satisfying choice for home orchards wanting a reliable modern variety alongside older heirlooms. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cameo Flowering Quince (Double Peach-Pink Flowering Quince)
description: Cameo carries fully double, soft peachy-pink flowers, a gentler pastel departure from the hot reds and oranges typical of most flowering quince cultivars, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage. Its compact, rounded, largely thornless growth habit makes it easier to work around than older, thornier quince cultivars, and small yellow-green fruit follows the bloom, usable for jelly and preserves though not typically eaten fresh. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid cutting off next season's flower buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Caminante Blanc Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
description: Caminante Blanc was released in late 2019 as the fifth of UC Davis's Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes, bred by Dr. Andy Walker with resistance from Vitis arizonica introgressed into a mostly Vitis vinifera vine. The wine shows characteristics of both Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, giving growers in high-disease-pressure areas a vinifera-quality white option that can survive where traditional varieties fail. Gulf South and Texas vineyards contending with severe glassy-winged sharpshooter and Pierce's disease pressure are among those beginning to plant it. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun; because it is a recent, patent-pending release, nursery stock remains limited. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Camino Real Strawberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil with high organic matter; Camino Real is a University of California Davis-developed short-day strawberry cultivar selected for warm-winter California production and widely adapted to Gulf Coast and subtropical conditions. The large, firm, conical, deep red berries have outstanding fresh-eating flavor — a combination of sweetness, bright strawberry aroma, and moderate acidity that consistently ranks among the top cultivars in taste evaluations for warm-climate production. Firm berries have good shelf life after harvest (important for home gardeners who may not harvest daily), retaining quality for 3–5 days refrigerated without softening or loss of flavor. The plant shows good tolerance for common strawberry diseases including Phytophthora crown rot, which is important in humid Gulf Coast conditions where soil moisture management can be challenging. The variety performs best when planted in fall as a fresh transplant, fruiting through the cool season in zone 9 and producing its best-quality fruit in the cool winter months. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Camminare Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)
description: Released by UC Davis in 2019, Camminare Noir carries Pierce's disease resistance from the wild Southwestern species Vitis arizonica bred back into a mostly Vitis vinifera vine, giving growers in high-PD-pressure regions like the Texas Gulf Coast a red wine grape with far better survival odds than traditional European varieties. The wine has been compared to a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Petite Sirah, with good color and structure, and it has already been planted experimentally in several Texas vineyards battling severe sharpshooter-driven Pierce's disease pressure. Train on a cordon trellis and prune in late winter; because the variety is still new to commercial production, availability through licensed nurseries remains limited. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Camouflage Sweet Potato
description: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil amended with sand or compost in full sun; Camouflage is an ornamental-edible sweet potato selected for striking purple-and-cream streaked or mottled flesh that creates a dramatic presentation when sliced — the irregular pattern of cream and purple pigmentation resembles military camouflage when cut crosswise. The flavor is mild and moderately sweet, suitable for roasting, baking, and mashing where the color pattern is partially preserved; water-boiling dulls the visual effect. The exterior skin has a similar mottled purple-green or purple-tan coloring that makes the roots attractive at harvest and at market. Flavor quality is secondary to the ornamental value of the flesh pattern — for pure eating quality, standard colored varieties outperform Camouflage, but for presentations and table drama it is unmatched among commonly grown sweet potatoes. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and high humidity for 7–10 days to develop sweetness. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Campbell CW3 Heartnut (Cold-Hardy Ontario-Selected Heartnut)
description: Campbell CW3 was selected by Ontario nut breeder Doug Campbell from superior heartnut seedlings and remains a parent behind several later Grimo Nut Nursery introductions, valued for staying more compact than seedling heartnut trees while still producing good crops of heart-shaped nuts. Kernels typically crack out in halves or whole pieces with a mild, sweet flavor much less oily than black walnut. Because it produces pollen early relative to when its own flowers are receptive, planting a second heartnut selection nearby improves fruit set even though some self-pollination can occur. Grow in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest in early autumn once the husks soften and nuts drop free of the hull. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Camphor Basil (African Basil, East African Basil)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; camphor basil is a species from East Africa (particularly the slopes of Kilimanjaro, as the name suggests) with a strong, sharp, camphor-eucalyptus fragrance unlike any other basil. The essential oil is composed primarily of camphor and 1,8-cineole rather than the linalool or estragole that characterize most familiar culinary basils. In East Africa, the plant is used medicinally for respiratory conditions (inhaling the vapors), as an insect repellent, and as a flavoring ingredient in certain traditional foods. It has been used as a parent in breeding disease-resistant basil hybrids, contributing resistance to Fusarium wilt. A larger, woodier, more shrubby plant than culinary sweet basil, it makes an impressive ornamental with a strong fragrance when brushed. Bees and butterflies are attracted to the white flower spikes. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Camphor Tree (Camphor Laurel)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; camphor tree is a majestic, aromatic evergreen tree from China and Japan, the source of natural camphor extracted from the wood and leaves. Every part of the tree contains camphor and 1,8-cineole, giving the foliage a powerful medicinal scent when crushed. It is an important timber, medicinal, and aromatic tree in traditional Asian culture. In the American South (particularly Texas and California), it is a common large shade tree planted for its ornamental value and fragrant foliage. NOTE: Camphor tree is classified as invasive in Florida and should not be planted there; it is suitable for other Gulf Coast states. The berries are consumed by birds but the plant as a whole is toxic to humans. Provides exceptional shade and is remarkably drought tolerant once established. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Camu Camu (Cacari, Camocamo)
description: Plant in moist, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; camu camu (Myrciaria dubia) is a shrubby Amazonian Myrtaceae producing small, cherry-like, reddish-purple fruits with a powerfully acidic, cranberry-passion-fruit flavor that are virtually inedible raw due to their extreme sourness but are valued as one of the highest natural sources of vitamin C on earth — 20–60 times more vitamin C per 100g than oranges. The fruit is processed into powders, juices, and health supplements widely sold in health food stores; home production is possible in south Florida and Hawaii with specimens growing in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil or at pond edges. An outstanding addition to a food-forest understory in zone 10+, where it also provides white, fragrant flowers and attractive foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Camus de Bretagne Artichoke (Large Round Breton Artichoke)
aliases: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Camus de Bretagne'
description: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, working in plenty of compost before planting. Camus de Bretagne produces very large, rounded, tightly closed globe artichokes with a pale green color and tender, meaty heart, the classic variety grown in Brittany, France, where it holds Protected Geographical Indication status and accounts for the majority of French artichoke production. Like other globe artichokes it is a true perennial in mild-winter climates, though it can be grown as an annual from an early start in colder zones. Harvest buds while still tightly closed, before the scales begin to loosen, for the best eating quality. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Camus de Bretagne Leek (Classic French Winter Leek)
aliases: Allium ampeloprasum var. porrum 'Camus de Bretagne'
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or sow in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Camus de Bretagne, a classic French heirloom leek from Brittany, is prized for exceptionally thick, short, sturdy stalks with a mild, sweet flavor and good cold tolerance that allows it to stand in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, it can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Canada Crookneck Squash (Pre-1820 Heirloom Squash)
description: Canada Crookneck traces to the Iroquois Nations and was first offered commercially in the 1830s, making it one of the oldest named squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. The bottle-shaped, curved-neck fruits are relatively small, typically 2-4 lbs, with a warty tan rind and sweet, fine-grained orange flesh. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving for its history and flavor. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has notably better resistance to squash vine borer than C. pepo or C. maxima types. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Canada Plum
description: Plant grafted trees or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Canada plum is the most cold-hardy of the native North American plums, surviving temperatures to -40°F and producing fruit reliably in zones 2–6 where most stone fruit trees would be killed by winter cold. Prunus nigra is a native small tree or large shrub of eastern and central Canada and the northern US producing prolific white flowers in early spring (before leaves) and medium-sized, oval plums ripening yellow to red to deep purple in late summer with a tart, wild-plum flavor excellent for jams, jellies, and sauce. Cross-pollinate with American plum (P. americana) or another Canada plum seedling for best fruit set; it also attracts wildlife heavily — the fruit is avidly eaten by bears, raccoons, foxes, and many bird species. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Canada Red Chokecherry (Schubert Chokecherry)
description: Plant in average, well-drained soil and stake young trees for their first year or two, since they establish quickly and grow at a moderate to fast rate. Canada Red is a selection of the native chokecherry whose new leaves emerge green in spring and gradually deepen to a rich burgundy-purple by summer, providing strong seasonal color alongside white spring flower clusters. It bears heavy clusters of small, tart, dark red-to-black cherries that are astringent fresh but make excellent jelly, syrup, and wine once cooked with sugar. Extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, it is a popular multi-purpose shelterbelt and specimen tree across the northern Plains and prairie provinces. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Canada Red Rhubarb (Cold-Hardy Sweet Red Rhubarb)
description: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Canada Red is a cold-hardy rhubarb cultivar prized for its uniformly deep red stalks that stay red all the way through the flesh, not just the skin, along with a sweeter, milder flavor than many tart green-stalked rhubarb varieties, meaning less sugar is needed when cooking. It performs best in climates with cold winters that satisfy its chilling requirement for strong spring growth, making it less reliable in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, and always discard the leaves, which are toxic and should never be eaten. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Canada Wild Lettuce
description: Direct sow in spring, surface-sown since seed needs light to germinate, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Canada wild lettuce self-sows readily, so allow it room to naturalize or deadhead before seed matures if volunteers are unwanted. Lactuca canadensis is a tall, biennial-to-short-lived-perennial North American native related to cultivated lettuce, forming a basal rosette of deeply lobed leaves the first year and a towering flowering stalk topped with numerous small, pale yellow, dandelion-like flowers in late summer that draw bees, small butterflies, and seed-eating songbirds. Young spring leaves are edible and were traditionally eaten like garden lettuce, though they turn increasingly bitter as the plant matures and bolts toward flowering. It tolerates partial shade and a wide range of soils, making it a low-maintenance native for a woodland edge, pollinator meadow, or informal naturalized planting, though its height and reseeding habit suit an informal setting better than a tidy border. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Canadian Blackberry (Smooth Blackberry)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Canadian blackberry is an Appalachian and northeastern native distinguished from most wild brambles by canes that are nearly or entirely without prickles, making harvest and pruning far more pleasant than with typical thorny wild blackberries. White flowers in late spring give way to large, sweet, juicy black fruit ripening in mid- to late summer, well suited to fresh eating, baking, and preserves. It tolerates more shade than many fruiting brambles, performing well at woodland edges and in partially shaded hedgerows where full-sun brambles struggle. Manage its spread by root suckers with an annual perimeter mowing or trenching, and remove spent floricanes after harvest each year to keep the patch productive and open. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Canadian Burnet
description: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Canadian burnet is a magnificent tall native of wet meadows and moist openings, producing elegant, pinnate compound leaves and distinctive bottlebrush flower heads — pure white 'poker' shapes on tall, airy stems — in late summer and fall. The flowers are among the most important late-season pollen sources for native bees, attracting sweat bees, bumblebees, and specialist pollen foragers to their elongated catkin-like heads. In the garden, Canadian burnet provides distinctive architectural interest when paired with tall ornamental grasses and late asters in moist borders or rain gardens. Unlike European sanguisorbas often found in nurseries, this native species naturally colonizes moist, shaded bottomlands and moist meadow edges throughout eastern North America. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Canadice Grape (Cornell-Bred Red Seedless Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Canadice was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is a dependable, heavily productive red seedless table grape, bearing compact clusters of small, sweet, mildly Labrusca-flavored berries on a vigorous, cold-hardy vine. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning early in the season to improve berry size and quality. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Canary Island Date Palm
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Canary Island date palm is the most majestic and widely planted ornamental palm in the world — a massive, slow-growing palm with an immense crown of arching, dark green, pinnate fronds each up to 18 feet long, creating a fountain-like canopy of extraordinary scale and beauty. The pineapple-like patterned trunk develops from years of old frond bases and becomes a powerful architectural statement in landscapes. Native to the Canary Islands, it has been planted throughout the Mediterranean, California, Florida, and worldwide tropical and subtropical climates. The orange-yellow fruits produced in massive pendant clusters are date-like and technically edible but too astringent for pleasant eating. Mature trees create the grandest scale of any landscape palm — worth every inch of space. Widely used as street trees in California, Spain, Portugal, and Florida. Fusarium wilt disease (Fusarium oxysporum) is a serious and fatal threat; purchase only certified disease-free specimens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Canary Melon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during fruit development; Canary Melon (also called Spanish Melon or Yellow Melon) is an Inodorus-group muskmelon producing large (5–7 pound), oval to oblong fruits with a distinctive, intense, brilliant chrome-yellow skin at full ripeness — one of the most visually striking melons available, with the vivid yellow color making ripe fruits immediately identifiable in the garden and market. The flesh is white to pale ivory, very sweet, very juicy, with a mild, clean, faintly musky flavor that differs from cantaloupe's complex aromatic sweetness — canary melon's flavor is cleaner, lighter, and more delicate, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too intense. The Inodorus (winter melon) classification means canary melons have firmer flesh and longer shelf life than cantaloupes — they don't 'slip' from the vine at ripeness, can be kept at room temperature for up to two weeks, and ship better than soft-fleshed types. Zone 9's extended warm season and summer heat are ideal for canary melon production, providing the long, hot growing period these melons need for full sugar development. Matures in 78–90 days from seed.

name: Canary Melon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Canary Melon (also called Juan Canary or amarillo melon) is an oblong to football-shaped melon with dramatically vivid, glossy, bright canary-yellow skin that makes it one of the most visually striking melons in the market or garden — the name describes the intense yellow of a canary bird's plumage. The creamy white to very pale green flesh is smooth, firm-crisp rather than soft, mildly sweet, and extremely mild-flavored with a delicate freshness completely different from the musky richness of cantaloupe — the flavor is subtle and refreshing, with a light sweetness and almost no aroma. This delicate flavor profile is characteristic of Spanish-type melons (inodorus group), which are also notable for their thick rind and long post-harvest shelf life. Canary Melon is widely grown in Spain and is a standard melon type in Spanish and Latin American markets. In zone 9 the long, warm summer produces the full sweetness that Canary Melon develops best in extended heat. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Canary Melon (Juan Canario, Yellow Melon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart; Canary melon is an inodorus type that stores well on the vine and post-harvest — harvest when skin turns deep canary yellow and the blossom end yields to gentle pressure. Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Canary' (Juan Canario, Yellow Canary melon) is a winter melon type grown extensively in Spain, Latin America, and the Middle East and sold widely in American Hispanic grocery markets; the medium to large (5–10 lb), elongated oval fruits have a striking, smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and white to pale green flesh with a delicate, honey-sweet flavor that is milder and less aromatic than muskmelon or cantaloupe types but refreshingly sweet and very appealing. The inodorus type means the ripe fruit has little fragrance from the exterior — you must taste to judge ripeness; the flesh is crisp at the center and creamy near the rind. An excellent heat-tolerant melon for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that maintains flavor even in high temperatures; stores well at room temperature for 2–4 weeks after harvest. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Cancer Bush (Sutherlandia)
description: Lessertia frutescens (long known as Sutherlandia frutescens) is a fast-growing, silver-grey-leaved legume shrub from the dry interior of South Africa, prized in Khoisan and Cape traditional medicine as a general tonic and immune-supporting herb; the dried leaf is still sold today as a popular southern African herbal supplement. Showy, brilliant orange-red, pea-shaped flowers appear over a long season and are followed by distinctive, inflated, papery, balloon-like seed pods that give the plant strong ornamental appeal beyond its medicinal use. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same lean, sharply drained conditions favored by most Cape fynbos and Karoo herbs. Prune lightly after flowering to keep growth compact, and expect a relatively short-lived shrub of three to five years that is easily renewed from fresh seed. Matures in 150–240 days from seed.

name: Candle Bush
description: Direct sow Senna alata seeds (scarify or nick seed coat before sowing to improve germination) in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; plants grow very rapidly in warm conditions and can reach 4–8 feet in a single season; deadhead spent spikes to prolong blooming and cut back hard in late winter to prevent woodiness. Candle Bush is one of the most dramatic flowering shrubs of the tropics and subtropics — its upright, glowing flower spikes are truly candle-like before the bright-yellow, butterfly-shaped individual flowers open, giving the plant an almost magical quality in the garden. It is a pan-tropical species now naturalized throughout the tropics worldwide, spread from its likely South American origin. In traditional medicine across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, a leaf paste or extract is applied topically to treat ringworm, athlete's foot, and other fungal skin infections — giving rise to the common name 'Ringworm Bush'; the antifungal compound chrysophanol has been isolated from the leaves. The plant is also an important butterfly host plant, particularly for sulphur butterflies (Catopsilia spp.) whose caterpillars feed on the leaves. In zone 9, it self-sows readily and may re-establish from seed each year after frost kills the tops; in zone 10–12, it grows as a woody perennial shrub. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Candle Fire Okra (AAS-Winning Red Round-Podded Okra)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost into warm soil in full sun; thin to 18-24 inches apart. Candle Fire is an AAS-winning okra selected for round (not sharply ribbed), deep-red pods that resist the rapid fiber buildup common in older red okra varieties, so pods stay tender for harvest over a longer size range and a more forgiving picking schedule — useful in the Gulf South's fast summer growth, when okra can go from tender to woody within a day or two. The tall, upright plants are heavy producers with attractive maroon-tinted foliage and pale yellow, red-throated flowers that make the whole plant a good-looking addition to the summer vegetable garden. Like other red okra, the color is water-soluble and fades during cooking unless pods are quickly grilled, roasted, or fried rather than boiled. Harvest every day or two once pods start forming to keep the plant productive. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Candlenut (Kukui Nut, Kemiri, Buah Keras)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; candlenut (Aleurites moluccanus, kukui in Hawaiian) is an extremely versatile tree native to tropical Asia and the Pacific Islands, widely cultivated for its large, oily nuts that are a critical ingredient in Indonesian (kemiri), Malaysian, and Hawaiian cuisine — the roasted kernels are ground into pastes, sauces, and curries. Caution: raw candlenuts are toxic and mildly purgative due to saponins; always roast or cook before eating. The nuts have the highest oil content of any edible nut and burn like candles, giving the tree its common name; the oil was traditionally used for lighting, wood finishing, and skin care. The Hawaii state tree (kukui), with distinctive silvery-green foliage visible from a distance. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Candy Cane Chocolate Cherry Sweet Pepper
