description: An ornamental edible with variegated foliage and striped fruit that ripens from green-and-white to chocolate-red and cream. Start seed indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep warm to encourage germination. Its compact, showy habit makes it a standout in patio containers and balcony gardens. Harvest peppers green for a crisp bite or let them fully stripe and color up for sweeter flavor. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Candy Corn Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is compact enough for containers and makes an eye-catching patio or border plant. Bred for its ornamental-edible dual purpose, Candy Corn produces upright clusters of small, tapered fruit that ripen through a sequence from pale yellow at the base through orange to a bright red tip while still on the plant, closely mimicking the look of the classic Halloween candy for which it is named. Fruits carry moderate heat, milder than a typical cayenne but with real chile flavor, and are fully usable fresh, dried, or in hot sauce at any color stage, though flavor and heat both increase slightly as fruit ripens toward red. The compact, well-branched plant holds its colorful fruit upright above the foliage for maximum visual display, making it as valuable in a mixed ornamental border or container planting as in a dedicated vegetable bed. Harvest fruit continuously through the season to encourage more flowering and fruit set. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Candy Onion (AAS Winner Intermediate-Day Sweet Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost (onion transplants tolerate light frost); set 4–6 inches apart with the bulb base at soil level; keep consistently moist through bulb formation; reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest and cure 2–3 weeks before storage. Candy is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning hybrid onion developed specifically for its exceptional sweetness and adaptability as an intermediate-day variety capable of producing high-quality bulbs across a wider latitudinal range than either long-day or short-day types. Intermediate-day onions (requiring 12–13 hours of daylight to trigger bulbing) are particularly valuable in zones 5–8 — the mid-latitude transition zone where long-day varieties (14+ hours required) often form small bulbs in the shorter days of the mid-latitudes and short-day varieties (10–12 hours) often bolt prematurely in the longer summer days further north. The result is that Candy succeeds in climates from Maine to Georgia where the 'wrong type' onion is a common gardening mistake. The large, round to slightly flattened, white-skinned bulbs have extraordinarily sweet, mild flesh with low pyruvate content — the same characteristic that makes Vidalia and other famous sweet onions nearly non-pungent; Candy onions can be eaten raw like a mild apple, used in salads without overwhelming other flavors, or caramelized into an intensely sweet onion jam. Yields are excellent for a sweet onion type. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Candy Pecan (USDA-Released Precocious Heavy-Bearing Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Candy is valued for bearing precociously, often producing a crop within a few years of planting, well ahead of many older commercial cultivars. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and a well-filled, attractive shell, and the tree tends to crop reliably from a young age rather than needing a long establishment period before its first real harvest. As with other pecans, supplement with zinc on alkaline soils and monitor for scab disease pressure in humid climates. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Candy Roaster Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in a prepared hill of well-composted soil after last frost, planting 3 seeds and thinning to the strongest; Candy Roaster needs a long season of 90–110 days, so in zone 9–11 plant in late winter for a spring harvest or late summer for fall. Candy Roaster is a Southern Appalachian heirloom producing large, elongated, banana-shaped fruits 12–20 inches long with pinkish-tan to salmon-orange skin often tipped with blue-green at the stem end, and sweet, orange, dry-textured flesh that roasts to a concentrated, candy-like sweetness the name describes perfectly. Fruits can reach 15–30 pounds; cure for 2 weeks in warm, dry conditions and store for 3–5 months. An essential heirloom for gardeners who want an authentic piece of Appalachian foodway heritage. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Candy Stevia
description: Start seed indoors with warmth and transplant the bushy plants out only after the danger of frost has passed. Stevia, also called sweetleaf, produces leaves up to 300 times sweeter than sugar, giving a calorie-free, low-glycemic sweetener with a faint anise aftertaste. Grow it in full sun and pinch the tips to encourage branching; harvest leaves before flowering for peak sweetness and dry them for storage, or overwinter potted plants indoors in cold climates. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Candyland Red Tomato (AAS-Winning Currant Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine for support. Candyland Red, a 2020 All-America Selections winner, is a currant-type tomato producing an enormous quantity of tiny, intensely sweet, deep red fruit in loose clusters continuously from midsummer until frost, offering some of the highest sugar content of any tomato type for snacking straight off the vine. The vigorous vine benefits from regular watering and feeding to sustain its heavy, continuous fruit set through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest clusters as fruit ripens to full red color, and expect the plant to keep producing right up until cold weather ends the season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Candystick Dessert Delicata Squash
description: Candystick Dessert is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by independent plant breeders Carol Deppe and Nate France in Corvallis, Oregon, and released through the Open Source Seed Initiative to keep it permanently free of patent restriction. Fruits are tan with green stripes and notably larger than standard delicata, averaging 2-3 lbs, with thick flesh and a smaller seed cavity. The dense flesh has an intensely sweet, dessert-like flavor that many compare to Medjool dates, and it holds its sweetness in storage longer than most delicata types. It is widely adapted, grown successfully from the Pacific Northwest to the Southeast and Northeast. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Canesi Squash (Italian Giant Butternut-Type Heirloom)
description: Canesi is an Italian heirloom in the butternut group, grown historically for producing unusually large, pale tan fruit that can dwarf standard butternut in size while keeping the same sweet, dense, deep-orange flesh. Vines are exceptionally vigorous and productive, so plants benefit from generous spacing or a strong support structure to keep the heavy fruit from resting directly on wet soil. Harvest once the rind has turned mostly tan with only faint traces of green remaining, since fruit picked too early lacks the full sweetness the variety is known for. Like other moschata squash, cured Canesi fruit stores well through winter in a cool, dry location. Matures in 85–110 days from seed.

name: Caney Fork Limbertwig Apple (Cumberland Mountains Heirloom Keeper)
description: Caney Fork Limbertwig takes its name from the Caney Fork area of Kentucky's Cumberland Mountains, and produces medium-to-large, round, symmetrical fruit with dull yellow skin mostly covered by a bright red flush and prominent white dots. The crisp, juicy, yellowish flesh has a sweet, spicy, fruity flavor and a firm, moderately breaking texture that makes it equally good for fresh eating and for cooking. It ripens in early October and is an excellent long keeper, a trait shared with most of the Limbertwig family. As with other Limbertwig strains it is not self-fruitful and needs a compatible apple cultivar nearby for cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Canistel (Egg Fruit)
description: Canistel is an evergreen tropical tree that produces smooth, orange-yellow fruit with dense, dry, egg-yolk-colored flesh — hence the common name egg fruit. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings; seedlings may take 5–7 years to fruit and show variable quality, while grafted plants can begin bearing in 2–3 years. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and tolerates a range of well-drained soils but is damaged by temperatures below 32°F even briefly. Harvest when the skin turns fully golden-yellow and yields firmly to pressure; ripen indoors at room temperature for 3–5 days until completely soft and sweet. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Cannellini Bean (White Kidney Bean, Fazolia Bean)
description: Sow seeds 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; cannellini is the classic Italian white kidney bean — an heirloom variety of the white kidney bean with large, plump, white seeds and a distinctly creamy, mild, earthy flavor that absorbs olive oil, garlic, rosemary, and sage beautifully. It is the essential bean of Tuscany: the foundation of ribollita and pasta e fagioli, the bean that defines Florentine cuisine, and arguably the finest-flavored dry bean for Italian cooking. The seeds are harvested dry for storage or 'semi-dried' (fresh-shelled and briefly cured) for a fresh-eating texture that is superior to fully dried beans. Bush-type plants produce pods that are allowed to dry on the vine before harvest; the dry seeds store indefinitely in cool, dry conditions. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Cannonball Tree (Nagalingam, Sala Tree, Shivalinga Tree)
description: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil — Cannonball Tree grows most rapidly and blooms most prolifically in full sun with regular watering, becoming a dramatic, multi-season ornamental after 5–10 years. Couroupita guianensis is a large tropical tree native to tropical South America (Guiana, Venezuela, Peru, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), famous for two simultaneous ornamental spectacles occurring directly on its trunk and branches. The flowers are produced year-round on long, pendant cauliflorous racemes (flower stalks) that hang directly from the trunk and major branches — each fragrant, complex, waxy flower 3–4 inches across with large, creamy-white to pale pink petals surrounding a modified stamen structure in pink, orange, and yellow that creates an exotic, orchid-like appearance. Simultaneously, the tree bears the previous season's fruits: enormous, perfectly spherical, hard-shelled, rust-brown fruits 6–12 inches in diameter (the 'cannonballs') that are attached in clusters to the same trunk racemes as the flowers — so the tree often displays flowers and fruits simultaneously. The fruits fall explosively when ripe, with a loud impact that explains the 'Cannonball Tree' name. In Hindu and Buddhist temple gardens throughout South and Southeast Asia (where the tree is sacred as the 'Shivalinga Tree' and 'Sala Tree'), the trunk-borne flowers and spherical fruits have profound religious symbolism. Matures in 1095–3650 days from transplant.

name: Cantaloupe
description: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost when soil exceeds 70°F; cantaloupe requires consistently warm temperatures (over 70°F days and over 60°F nights) for fruit to develop maximum sugar content — cool, cloudy summers produce watery, bland melons. Reduce watering significantly about 1 week before harvest to concentrate the sugars; overwatering near maturity is the most common cause of bland, watery flavor. Harvest when the stem slips easily from the vine ('full slip') and the blossom end gives slightly to pressure with a sweet, musky fragrance; these indicators are more reliable than days-to-maturity. The cultivar 'Hales Best Jumbo', 'Ambrosia', and 'Athena' are standard slippage-type cantaloupes. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Cantaloupe / Muskmelon
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4–5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars in the flesh. Ripe cantaloupes emit a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure; this is called full-slip harvest. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause splitting. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Cantaloupe Pawpaw (Large Freestone Melon-Flavored Kentucky Pawpaw)
description: Cantaloupe is one of three named freestone pawpaw selections discovered on a late-1800s orchard in Richmond, Kentucky, alongside Honeydew and Marshmallow, and released by pawpaw enthusiast Woody Walker through England's Orchard. It is the largest-fruited of the three, with a tropical, melon-like flavor carrying a trace of banana that gives the cultivar its name. Because it lacks a fibrous seed sack, the seeds lift out cleanly, making Cantaloupe especially easy to process for fresh eating or freezing, and the fruit freezes exceptionally well for out-of-season use. As with all pawpaws, plant at least two genetically distinct named cultivars for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set, and site young trees in partial shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil, moving them into full sun once established. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Cantare Bush Bean
description: A high-yielding French filet-style bush bean producing dark green, stringless pods five to six inches long with excellent flavor. Sow seed directly one inch deep after the soil warms, since beans resent cold, wet ground. Its strong disease resistance and productivity make it a reliable succession crop for a long harvest window. Pick pods regularly while young and slender to keep the plants producing. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Canton White Stem Pak Choi
description: Sow seeds shallowly in cool spring or late summer weather, as heat and stress push this brassica to bolt. Thin plants to give each room to form crisp white stems and tender green leaves. Keep the soil consistently moist for fast, mild growth and harvest whole heads when they reach full size, ideal for stir-fries and soups. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Canyon Grape (Arizona Grape)
description: Canyon grape climbs by tendrils into cottonwoods, willows, and mesquite along desert washes and canyon bottoms from Arizona and New Mexico south into northern Mexico, tolerating both flash flooding and long dry spells. Its deeply lobed leaves and small, dark purple-black grapes were historically gathered by Southwestern Native American peoples for fresh eating and drying, though the tart, seedy fruit is more often used today for jelly or wine after sweetening. The species is best known in modern viticulture as a wild source of genes for Pierce's disease resistance, nematode resistance, and drought tolerance, and it has been extensively used in university grape breeding and rootstock programs in California and Arizona. In a home landscape it makes a rugged, low-water vine for a large arbor in hot, dry climates where other grapes struggle. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cape Aloe (Bitter Aloe, Red Aloe)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Cape aloe is a magnificent large aloe from South Africa that develops a single upright trunk over time, crowned by a rosette of large, glaucous, spiny-toothed leaves that may develop reddish or copper tints in strong sun. It produces tall (4–5 foot) candelabra-like flower spikes in winter and spring bearing dense clusters of orange-red to orange tubular flowers that attract sunbirds in South Africa and hummingbirds in cultivation. The plant is one of the primary sources of commercial aloe latex (used in laxative preparations and cosmetics) — distinct from aloe gel — produced as a dark, bitter exudate from the cut leaves. The botanical name 'ferox' (meaning fierce) refers to the prominent spines on the leaf margins and surfaces, which are more numerous than in aloe vera. As a landscape plant it is outstanding for large, bold, architectural effect in zone 8–11 gardens, developing impressive specimens over decades. The commercial production of Aloe ferox bitter is centered in the Eastern Cape of South Africa. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Cape Elderberry (Bourtree, Southern Elder, Yellow Elderberry)
description: Root stem cuttings in spring or autumn in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plant in partial shade to full sun; cape elderberry (Sambucus australasica) is an Australian species native to Queensland and New South Wales rainforest edges and creek margins, producing large clusters of small, bright yellow berries (distinct from the dark purple-black of northern elderberries) that ripen in summer. The berries are edible when fully ripe and can be used in the same applications as European elderberries — jams, jellies, syrups, and wines — though they are reportedly less intensely flavored. The flowers are also edible as elderflower tea and fritters. An attractive subtropical alternative to common elderberry for zone 9–11 gardens, with similar wildlife value and similar requirements for moist, moderately fertile soil. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cape Fear Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Cape Fear is a southern highbush blueberry released by North Carolina State University and selected for an early ripening window combined with a comparatively low chill requirement, which lets it set a full crop even after mild Gulf South winters that shortchange higher-chill northern highbush types. Fruit is medium-large, light blue, and firm with good classic highbush flavor. Cape Fear is only partially self-fruitful, so plant a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar nearby to improve fruit set and berry size. Because southern highbush types have shallower, less drought-tolerant roots than rabbiteye, keep a thick layer of pine bark or pine straw mulch over the root zone and irrigate through dry spells, especially in the first two years after planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cape Fear Pecan (Mid-Atlantic Southeastern Pecan, Type I Reliable Cross-Pollinator)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun; Cape Fear is a reliable medium-to-large nut producer with moderate scab resistance; it is widely adapted throughout the southeastern states from coastal North Carolina through the Gulf South; trees are vigorous and come into production in 5–7 years; supplement with zinc spray in spring. Cape Fear pecan is a variety developed by the USDA Pecan Breeding Program and named for the Cape Fear River valley of North Carolina, where the variety demonstrated particularly reliable production under the moderately humid coastal plain conditions of the mid-Atlantic South. The variety has proven broadly adapted throughout the southeastern states from eastern North Carolina through the Gulf Coast, performing reliably under a range of humidity levels and soil types typical of the coastal plain and river bottom land of the region. Cape Fear produces medium-to-large nuts (45–52 per pound) with good kernel percentage (57–61%) and solid pecan flavor — not the exceptional nut quality of Desirable or Wichita but consistent, reliable, and commercially acceptable. The variety's primary contribution to many home orchard designs is as the Type I cross-pollinator for the more challenging-to-fruit Type II varieties: since pecan varieties are strongly cross-pollinated (most nut set requires pollen from a different variety), placing Cape Fear alongside Type II varieties like Desirable, Wichita, Elliott, or Stuart ensures reliable pollination and heavier crops on both trees. Cape Fear is also the companion pollinator recommended in many pecan extension publications for home gardeners planting the newer precocious varieties like Pawnee. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Cape Gooseberry (Husk Cherry, Golden Berry)
description: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; cape gooseberry is a South American relative of tomatillo with intensely flavorful, tangy-sweet golden berries enclosed in papery brown husks — the same fruit sold as 'golden berries' or 'physalis' in supermarkets and restaurants worldwide. The distinctive papery husks enclose 3/4-inch golden-orange berries at maturity; berries are eaten fresh, dried, in salsa, preserves, and baked goods. Each plant produces hundreds of berries over a long season from midsummer to frost. In zone 9–11 it overwinters as a perennial and becomes a shrubby plant 3–5 feet tall producing fruit year-round. It self-sows generously in warm climates and can naturalize. An outstanding fruit crop for the Gulf Coast garden. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Cape Snow Bush (African Rosemary, Wild Rosemary)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape. Eriocephalus africanus (Cape snow bush or African rosemary) is a native South African fynbos shrub with needle-like, silver-grey, intensely aromatic leaves — the leaves have a fresh, camphor-pine aroma similar to rosemary but with distinctly South African floral-herbal notes. The plant is used in Cape Malay traditional cooking and South African herbal medicine as a seasoning and medicinal herb: the dried leaves flavor lamb stews, braai (barbecue) marinades, and herbal teas; the essential oil is used in aromatherapy for respiratory conditions. Common name 'Cape snow bush' derives from the small, fluffy, white seed heads that cover the plant in late summer, giving a snow-dusted appearance. As a landscape plant, Eriocephalus africanus is outstanding for hot, dry, lean, well-drained soils where European rosemary often struggles with root rot — it has superior drought tolerance and performance in alkaline coastal soils. The cultivar 'Silver Beads' is grown as an ornamental for its exceptionally silvery foliage. An excellent substitute for rosemary in challenging dry garden conditions. Matures in 120–240 days from transplant.

name: Cape Sorrel (Bermuda Buttercup)
description: Plant small bulbils in fall in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, sandy soil; cape sorrel is a Mediterranean import that has naturalized across California, the Gulf Coast, and many mild-winter regions as a winter-growing edible. The clover-like leaves and bright yellow flowers are both edible — the leaves have a pleasantly tart, lemony flavor from oxalic acid and can be used in salads, stir-fries, or as a garnish in the same way as garden sorrel. The bright yellow flowers are also edible and attractive as a garnish. Note that like all oxalis, cape sorrel should be consumed in moderation as oxalic acid can interfere with calcium absorption in large quantities. Plants die down completely in summer heat and re-emerge from dormant corms in fall. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Caper Bush
description: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established. Sprawling, spiny stems carry rounded, fleshy, blue-green leaves and large, showy, white-to-pink flowers with a prominent burst of long purple stamens, opening for just a single day each but produced continuously through the hot summer months. The edible product is the unopened flower bud, hand-picked daily at pea size and brine- or salt-cured into the tangy, briny capers used in Mediterranean cooking; unpicked buds open into flowers and later develop into a caper-berry fruit that can also be pickled. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, it is well suited to a rock wall, dry slope, or container where poor soil and reflected heat are assets rather than liabilities, and it dies back to the root in hard freezes, resprouting the following spring in marginal zones. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Captivator Gooseberry
description: 'Captivator' is a nearly thornless American-type gooseberry producing sweet, teardrop-shaped reddish-purple berries that are pleasant for fresh eating. Its low thorn count and good mildew resistance make it one of the most user-friendly varieties for home gardeners. Grow in full sun to light shade in cool, moist, well-drained soil with a thick organic mulch. Prune lightly in winter to remove old and crowded wood, keeping the bush open and productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cara Cara Orange
description: The Cara Cara is a sweet, low-acid navel orange distinguished by its rosy-pink flesh and berry-like flavor. This adaptable citrus performs well in the ground in mild regions or in a large container that can be moved indoors where winters are cold. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed it a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Water deeply but allow the top of the soil to dry between waterings, and protect it from frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Caraflex Cabbage
description: A compact, pointed cabbage weighing just one and a half to two pounds, ideal for small households and small gardens. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and transplant twelve to eighteen inches apart. Its tightly wrapped, ornamental conical heads shrug off weather and pests while protecting the tender interior. Keep evenly watered and harvest when heads feel firm and full for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Carambola (Starfruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; carambola is sensitive to flooding and cold below 27°F even briefly, limiting outdoor cultivation to frost-free zones. The tree blooms multiple times per year and produces fruits along the trunk and main branches — a trait called cauliflory — so hang fruit-protection bags in commercial settings to prevent blemishes. Harvest when the ribs have turned fully yellow and the fruit has slight give; overripe fruit browns quickly at the tips. Fertilize with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer 3–4 times per year to sustain heavy bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Caraway (Meridian Fennel, Persian Cumin)
description: Direct sow seeds in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; caraway does not transplant well — sow in place. Carum carvi (caraway) is a biennial or short-lived annual herb producing the anise-flavored, ribbed, crescent-shaped seeds indispensable in German and Central European rye bread, sauerkraut, cheese (Havarti caraway), and liqueurs (aquavit, Kümmel); the seeds are also a traditional flavoring for sausages, pickles, and roasted vegetables across northern and eastern European cuisines. The fresh leaves and roots are also edible (roots somewhat parsnip-like) and used in Scandinavian and German cooking. In the first year, caraway forms a low rosette of finely divided, feathery, carrot-like leaves; in the second year (or the same spring after fall sowing in mild climates), it sends up 1.5-to-2-foot stems topped with compound white flower umbels, setting seed in May–June. Harvest seed heads when they turn brown and before they shatter; thresh out seeds and dry fully before storing. In zone 9, treat as a fall-sown winter annual for best results. Matures in 365–550 days from seed.

name: Caraway Thyme (Sardinian Thyme)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean soil — excellent in rock gardens, paving cracks, and dry stone walls where other thymes excel; caraway thyme gets its distinctive name from the strong caraway-like aroma of its leaves, which contain carvone (the same compound that gives caraway seed its character), producing an anise-caraway fragrance quite unlike common thyme. This low-growing prostrate thyme from the mountains of Sardinia and Corsica forms a tight mat of tiny dark green leaves covered in small pink to pale lavender flowers in summer that are excellent for bees and other pollinators. Use fresh or dried in the same applications as caraway seed: potato dishes, sauerkraut, braised meats, and bread. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Carbon Pole Tomato
description: An award-winning heirloom slicer with ten to twelve ounce fruits that are purplish-brown outside and brick-red within. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant after nights warm. As an indeterminate vine it needs a tall stake or cage and regular pruning of suckers for airflow. Water deeply and evenly to prevent cracking, and let the fruit fully color for its rich, complex flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Cardamom (True Cardamom)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade — cardamom naturally grows as an understory plant in the humid rainforests of southern India and is one of the world's most valuable spices after vanilla and saffron. The large, aromatic leaves are beautiful throughout the growing season; fragrant flowers are produced on separate ground-level stems and develop into the prized seed pods. Cardamom is only reliably hardy in zone 10–12 but makes an outstanding container plant in zone 8–9 that overwinters indoors. It requires high humidity, consistent moisture, and shade from afternoon sun — an excellent fit for the shaded, humid conditions of South Florida and the Gulf Coast. Harvest pods when they are pale green before they open. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cardava Banana (Cardaba, Philippine Cooking Banana)
description: Cardava, also spelled Cardaba, is one of the most economically important banana cultivars of the Philippines, closely related to and often confused with Saba but classified as its own distinct ABB-group selection. It is grown primarily as a starchy cooking banana, harvested green and fried, boiled, or processed into chips, though it can also be eaten ripe. The tough, weather-resistant ABB foliage handles wind and drought better than dessert-type bananas, and the plant forms a large, vigorous clump over time. Give it full sun, deep rich soil, and heavy irrigation through the growing season, and expect over a year to first harvest. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Cardinal Basil
description: Start seed indoors and transplant out after all danger of frost, or direct sow once the soil is warm, spacing plants about a foot apart. This dual-purpose basil combines robust culinary flavor with large, richly colored maroon flower heads that make it a striking accent in mixed containers and bouquets. Pinch the plants often to keep them bushy; its strong aroma means a little goes a long way in cooking, and it can be grown indoors on a sunny sill. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Cardinal Grape
description: A USDA cross of Flame Tokay and Ribier released in 1939, Cardinal is prized for very early ripening large, round, deep-red berries in loose, well-filled clusters with a mild, sweet flavor. Train vines onto a permanent cordon system and prune hard each dormant season, since fruit forms on one-year-old canes. It sets heavy crops and colors up reliably in hot-summer regions but tends toward loose, uneven clusters and thin skin that bruises easily, so it is best suited to home gardens rather than long-distance shipping. Like most vinifera grapes it needs a long, warm growing season and struggles with fungal disease in humid climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cardinal Persimmon (Non-Astringent Korean Persimmon, syn. 'Jo Choo')
description: Cardinal, grown under the cultivar name Jo Choo in its native Korea, is a non-astringent Asian persimmon that can be eaten firm and crisp straight off the tree, without the softening required by astringent types like Hachiya or Eureka. The compact tree produces large, sweet, orange fruit that ripens early in the season, and its naturally smaller stature makes it a good fit for home gardens with limited space. Vivid orange-red fall foliage adds ornamental value after the fruit is harvested. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, and expect the tree to perform well in the mild winters typical of zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cardinal Royal Mountain Ash (Michred European Mountain Ash)
description: Cardinal Royal, patented under the name Michred by Michigan State University, is a European mountain ash selection prized for a tighter, more symmetrical oval crown than seedling-grown Sorbus aucuparia and for berries that ripen a deeper, brighter red rather than the species' typical orange. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, and the compound, fern-like leaves turn shades of orange and red in fall alongside the heavy berry clusters that persist into winter and draw waxwings and other fruit-eating birds. The tart berries can be cooked into jelly once softened by frost. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; like other mountain ash, it performs best in cool-summer climates and struggles with borers and fire blight in hot, humid regions, so it is best suited to the northern tier of its hardiness range. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Cardinal Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Season NC State Release)
description: Plant into raised beds of very acidic, well-drained soil and mulch thickly with pine bark to protect the fibrous, shallow root system. Cardinal is an early-ripening southern highbush cultivar released by North Carolina State University, valued for producing a concentrated flush of firm, light-blue, well-flavored berries near the start of the harvest season, ahead of most rabbiteye cultivars. Because its chill requirement runs a bit higher than true low-chill Florida-bred selections, it performs best in the cooler, more inland parts of zone 9a rather than immediately along the Gulf. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and prune out the oldest wood each winter to keep new fruiting canes coming. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cardinale Radicchio
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinale is an Italian radicchio variety producing medium-sized, round to slightly elongated heads with deep garnet-red to cardinal-red leaves and white midribs — the color is consistently deeper and more saturated than many other radicchio varieties, which gives it its name. The bitter-sweet, complex radicchio flavor is characteristic of the Cichorium intybus species, with the bitterness mellowing appropriately after cold exposure. Cardinale is valued by market growers for its reliable head formation in variable fall weather and its consistent deep color that holds through the harvest and storage period. In Italian cooking, Cardinale works in all standard radicchio preparations — grilled, braised, in risotto, in pasta, or raw in salads where its deep color provides dramatic visual contrast. In zone 9 the fall-winter-early spring season produces the most deeply colored and best-flavored heads, with improvement after the first frosts. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Cardoon
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deep, rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun after all frost risk has passed, spacing 3–5 feet apart as cardoon is a very large plant. Cynara cardunculus is the wild ancestor of the globe artichoke and a spectacular ornamental-cum-culinary plant; unlike artichoke (grown for flower buds), cardoon is grown for its thick, silvery-gray, thistle-like leaf stalks (blanched in fall by wrapping plants in burlap or paper for 3–4 weeks to remove bitterness), which are then braised, gratinéed, or served in the Italian-French Christmas tradition. The plant reaches 4–7 feet tall with dramatic, silver-arching, deeply cut leaves and produces purple, artichoke-like flower heads in its second year that are exceptionally attractive to bees and beautiful as cut or dried flowers. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Cardy Cardoon (Self-Blanching Cardoon)
description: Sow indoors and transplant into deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun with steady moisture through the growing season. Cardy is a modern cardoon selection bred to naturally pale and mellow its leaf ribs as the plant matures, largely eliminating the traditional multi-week job of bundling and wrapping stalks in cardboard or straw to exclude light. The tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage still makes an imposing ornamental clump even where it is not harvested, and a light earthing-up of the base in the final weeks before cutting can further improve rib color and tenderness. Harvest the thick leaf stalks in autumn once they have filled out, trimming away the spiny leaf blades before cooking. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Careless Gooseberry
description: Plant dormant, thorny bushes in fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with cool root conditions, mulching to conserve moisture and prune to an open framework to make harvest through the spines easier. Careless is a traditional English culinary gooseberry long grown for its heavy, reliable crops of large, pale green, thin-skinned berries that are quite tart when picked early for cooking but sweeten as they ripen toward translucent pale yellow-green, making it equally suited to pies, fools, and preserves or later fresh eating. The vigorous, somewhat spreading bush is one of the most widely planted gooseberry cultivars in British gardens and allotments. Prune in the dormant season to an open, airy shape to improve light penetration and reduce mildew pressure on the ripening fruit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Carenero Superior Cacao
description: Carenero Superior takes its name from the small Venezuelan port on the Barlovento coast east of Caracas, where Trinitario trees carrying a strong strain of native Criollo blood have been grown for centuries. The fermented beans are prized by fine chocolate makers for a rounded, mellow chocolate base layered with notes of caramel, dried fruit, and light florals, with less astringency than many other Trinitario-type cacaos. Trees are typically grown in the humid, shaded coastal lowlands under taller shade canopy, following the same cultivation needs as other Venezuelan fine-flavor cacao. It is traded and blended as a distinct regional bean type rather than propagated under a single registered clone name, so seed and budwood sources vary by farm. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cargamanto Bean (Cargamanto Rojo, Colombian Cranberry Bean)
description: Cargamanto is the iconic cranberry-mottled dry bean of the Antioquia region of Colombia, grown up cornstalks or poles in Andean smallholder plots and central to dishes such as frijoles antioqueños and bandeja paisa. The mottled cream-and-maroon seeds resemble North American cranberry beans but tend to be larger and starchier, softening to a dense, creamy texture that holds together well in slow-simmered pots. Let pods dry fully and rattle on the vine before picking, then shell and cure the beans another week or two indoors before sealing them for storage. Because it is a true pole type, give plants sturdy 8-foot supports and consistent moisture while pods are filling out. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Caribbean Red Habanero (Extremely Hot Red Habanero Type with Fruity Heat)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Caribbean Red is a habanero-type pepper (Capsicum chinense) producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits that ripen from green to bright scarlet-red — one of the hottest commercially available habanero types, typically measuring 400,000–500,000 Scoville heat units compared to the 100,000–350,000 SHU of standard orange habaneros, making it roughly 2–4 times hotter than standard habanero by Scoville measurement. The heat is the intense, building, lingering habanero burn style — not the immediate sharp heat of cayenne — accompanied by the same characteristic fruity, tropical, citrus-floral aroma that makes habanero-type peppers uniquely valuable in hot sauces, salsas, Caribbean jerk seasonings, and mango-habanero condiments. The red color produces a visually different (and often considered more attractive) hot sauce than the orange of standard habanero, making Caribbean Red popular with home hot sauce makers. The large, productive plants grow well in zone 9's long warm season, often continuing to fruit into November after a spring transplant. In zone 9b and warmer, the plants may overwinter and become large perennial pepper shrubs producing for multiple seasons. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Caribe Potato
description: Caribe is an early-season potato notable for its striking purple-pink skin over pure white flesh, and for tolerating warmer soil temperatures better than many other potato varieties, which has made it a long-time favorite among Southern gardeners. The moist, waxy flesh holds its shape well after cooking, making Caribe well suited to potato salad and roasting. Its quick maturity and heat tolerance are especially useful in zone 9, where potatoes must be planted early and harvested before the ground becomes too warm for good tuber set. Plant seed pieces as early as the soil can be worked in late winter and hill regularly as the vigorous vines grow. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Carlin Pea
description: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps. Carlin Pea is a survivor of a once-widespread English tradition of eating dried, soaked, and pan-fried peas on Carlin Sunday in the weeks before Easter, and it remained a staple crop in northern England long after most gardeners moved on to modern shelling peas. Give the vining plants light twiggy brush or netting for support, and either pick pods young for shelling green or let them dry fully on the vine for the traditional parched preparation. The plants tolerate poor soil and are notably resilient compared with modern pea cultivars. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Carlos Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Carlos is a bronze-skinned muscadine developed by North Carolina State University and released in 1970, and remains one of the two or three most widely planted muscadines in the southeastern US because of its exceptional adaptability, consistent yields, and suitability for both fresh-eating and bronze muscadine wine production. The medium-sized, bronze-gold berries ripen uniformly in mid-season and have a mild, sweet musky flavor that is less pronounced than Scuppernong — making Carlos wines and juice more accessible to people new to muscadine flavors. Self-fertile, so it produces well as a single plant, though yields improve with a black muscadine variety nearby. Carlos is resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and other diseases that devastate European wine grapes in the humid South — no spray program is needed in most home garden settings. Prune in late winter, leaving only short spurs on permanent cordons. Harvest when berries slip from the cluster at a gentle tug. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Carlos Muscadine Grape (Classic Bronze Self-Fertile Wine-Quality Gulf South Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Carlos is the benchmark bronze muscadine cultivar — one of the most widely planted and historically important Gulf South muscadines, valued equally for fresh eating quality and as the primary variety for muscadine wine production in the Southeast. The medium to large, round grapes ripen to bronze-tan to bronze-gold color with thick skin and sweet, aromatic, musky flesh typical of the muscadine type; the flavor profile is somewhat more refined and balanced in acidity than many other muscadine cultivars, which is why Carlos is the preferred variety for wine production and has long been the standard against which other muscadines are evaluated. Muscadine wine from Carlos has a characteristic sweet, floral, musky quality — distinctively Southern and quite unlike any European wine style — with enough natural acidity to provide balance. Carlos is self-fertile with perfect flowers and is an outstanding cross-pollinator for female-flowered cultivars including Fry, Higgins, and others. The vines are vigorous and productive, disease-resistant to the fungal diseases (black rot, downy mildew, powdery mildew) that make growing European grapes nearly impossible in Gulf South conditions, and adapted to the heat, humidity, and long growing season of zones 6–10. Grapes ripen in August through September, with individual grapes in each cluster ripening sequentially. Excellent for fresh eating, juice, muscadine wine, jelly, and preserves. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Carmel Almond (Reliable California Pollenizer Almond, High-Production Soft-Shell Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained fertile soil in full sun; Carmel is primarily planted as a companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil in commercial orchards but also produces its own crop of soft-shell almonds with good flavor; it ripens slightly after Nonpareil (mid-August); kernels are slightly smaller than Nonpareil but of good quality for snacking and roasting. Carmel almond is a UC Davis release developed specifically to serve as the ideal companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil — the two are now the most common planting pair in California commercial almond orchards, with the standard three-variety system often being Nonpareil + Carmel + Mission or Butte. Carmel's most important attribute in commercial production is pollination efficiency: its bloom time coincides precisely with Nonpareil, it produces abundant viable pollen, and it bears its own crop reliably and heavily — making it productive as both a pollinator and a production variety rather than just a sterile companion tree. The variety was developed at UC Davis by Floyd Zaiger and William Sims and has been important in the rapid expansion of California almond acreage since the 1970s because its reliable early bearing and high productivity complemented Nonpareil's commercial requirements. Carmel produces soft-shell almonds of moderate size with a sweet, mild almond flavor somewhat similar to Nonpareil — entirely acceptable for all uses including direct consumption, roasting, and confectionery — while its primary role remains as the preferred pollinator in the world's most important almond-producing region. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Carmelo Walnut (UC Davis Late-Leafing Persian Walnut)
description: Carmelo is a University of California walnut release valued for its very large, well-filled nuts and light kernel color, harvesting slightly later than Chandler on a vigorous, spreading tree. Like other UC Davis Persian walnut selections, it leafs out relatively late in spring, which helps the developing catkins and pistillate flowers avoid damage from late frosts common in interior valley orchard sites. Plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and expect the first meaningful nut crop several years after grafted trees are established. Space trees widely, since mature Persian walnuts develop broad canopies that shade out understory plantings. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Carmen Pepper (AAS-Winning Italian Frying Pepper, Early-Producing and Heat-Tolerant)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red for best flavor. Carmen pepper is an F1 hybrid Italian frying pepper that received the All-America Selections recognition in 2006 for its consistent performance across varied North American growing conditions — specifically for its combination of earliness (reaching harvest stage significantly sooner than traditional Corno di Toro types), productivity (high fruit set per plant), and fruit quality. The All-America Selections program evaluates new vegetable and flower varieties across multiple trial locations nationwide, and a 2006 AAS designation reflects verified performance advantages over competing varieties at the time of release. Carmen's fruits are medium-large (4–6 inches long, 2 inches wide), with a form intermediate between a large Cubanelle and a Corno di Toro: longer and more pointed than a Cubanelle, but somewhat less dramatically curved and elongated than a classic Corno di Toro. The flesh is thick enough to provide substance for roasting and stuffing but still thinner-walled and more flavorful at full ripeness than standard bell peppers. The ripening process in Carmen goes through green to light orange to fully red — a complete color change that signals maximum sweetness and vitamin C content. Carmen's Italian frying pepper lineage gives it the characteristic sweetness and frying quality that makes this pepper type so valued in Mediterranean cooking: roasted Carmen peppers develop a silky, caramelized richness that is genuinely different from roasted bell peppers. For zone 9 gardeners, the early-producing quality of Carmen means productive harvests before midsummer heat stress limits continued flower and fruit production. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Carmen Sweet Pepper (AAS Winner Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Carmen peppers ripen from green to vivid red about 2 weeks earlier than most bell peppers, making them excellent for northern gardens; harvest at any stage from green (mild, slightly tangy) to full red (sweet, rich, complex flavor). Carmen is a top-performing Italian-style sweet frying pepper that won the All-America Selections award in 2006 — one of the most widely grown sweet pepper varieties to emerge from recent AAS trials, valued for combining the Italian frying pepper form (long, tapered, thin-walled, easy to peel) with exceptional earliness and garden productivity. The peppers are long (5–7 inches), tapered, and horn-shaped in the classic Italian style, maturing from pale green through deep red in about 70–80 days from transplant — significantly earlier than standard bell peppers (85–95 days) and most sweet Italian types. The flavor at full red maturity is distinctively sweet, rich, and complex in a way that sets Italian frying peppers apart from bell peppers: the thin walls cook faster and more evenly, caramelize beautifully in a hot pan, and develop a sweeter, more concentrated flavor than the thick-walled bell. Carmen is the go-to recommendation from most seed companies and extension services for gardeners who want a reliable sweet Italian frying pepper that performs consistently across a wide range of climates from zones 3 to 11. Excellent raw in salads, roasted, sautéed, or used for Italian-American pepper-and-egg preparations. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Carmine Jewel Cherry (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Bush Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Carmine Jewel tolerates a wide range of soils and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Carmine Jewel is a University of Saskatchewan-bred dwarf sour cherry hybrid, part of a breeding program aimed at producing extremely cold-hardy, compact cherry shrubs for the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, where standard sweet and tart cherry trees cannot survive. The dense, shrubby plant stays under 8 feet tall, bears dark red, sweet-tart fruit good for fresh eating, baking, and preserves, and is self-fertile, bearing reliably without a second pollinator. Because of its extreme cold hardiness (surviving winter lows well below -40°F), it is grown mainly in northern climates outside the Gulf South's typical range, but is included here as a distinctive, easy-care option for gardeners in colder zones who want cherries without the size and chill-hour demands of standard cherry trees. Prune only lightly, removing dead or crossing wood, since the shrub form needs little training. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Carmine Splendor Okra (Red F1 Hybrid Okra with Edible Pink Flowers)
description: Sow seed 1/2 to 1 inch deep in full sun after soil has warmed; stalky, upright plants stay manageable while producing heavily. Carmine Splendor is a modern F1 hybrid bred for uniform, stout, five-pointed pods that emerge deep red and soften to a lighter red-pink as they enlarge, giving a longer tender-harvest window than many older red okra types. The pale yellow, red-throated flowers are edible and often used fresh as a garnish or lightly battered and fried, in addition to the pods themselves. Harvest pods at 3-4 inches every day or two during peak summer heat, since red okra fibers up quickly once pods exceed that size. Matures in 51–58 days from seed.

name: Carménère Wine Grape (Chile's Rediscovered Bordeaux Red)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Carménère is one of the original six red grapes of Bordeaux, nearly wiped out in France by the phylloxera epidemic of the late 1800s and long presumed extinct until it was recognized, decades later, growing widely in Chile under vines mistakenly identified and sold as Merlot — a discovery that has since made Carménère something of Chile's signature red grape. Wines are deeply colored with distinctive dark fruit and characteristic green, herbal, bell-pepper notes when not fully ripe, softening into riper black fruit and spice character when the grape achieves full physiological ripeness, which requires a long, warm growing season and late harvest. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize sites with a long frost-free season, and be prepared to leave fruit hanging later than most other red varieties to avoid the unripe vegetal character the grape is prone to. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Carnes Pear (North Florida Grit-Free Low-Chill Pear)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of any texture; Carnes is a North Florida heirloom European pear selected for producing exceptionally sweet, buttery, completely grit-free flesh — a notable improvement in eating quality over grittier Deep South standbys like Kieffer and LeConte. It requires very little winter chill and shows good resistance to both fire blight and powdery mildew, making it well suited to the low-chill, high-humidity conditions of coastal zones 8 and 9 from the Florida Panhandle through the Gulf Coast. Trees bloom in late March and typically begin bearing within three years, with medium-sized yellowish-green fruit ripening by July. Fruit is excellent for fresh eating straight off the tree as well as for preserves; harvest when the fruit begins to soften at the neck and give slightly to pressure, then finish ripening at room temperature for best flavor. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Carnival Blend Carrot
description: A colorful mix of red, purple, yellow, and orange carrots, each carrying its own nutrients and sweet flavor. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination. Thin seedlings to two to three inches so roots can size up evenly. Harvest young for baby carrots or at full size, and note that colors sweeten with a light frost. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Carnival Squash
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Carnival is an All-America Selections award-winning acorn-type winter squash that produces medium-sized (1–2 lb), acorn-shaped fruits in an extraordinarily variable pattern of cream, orange, yellow, and green — no two Carnival squash are identical in coloration, with each fruit displaying a unique combination of the variety's characteristic colors in an irregular patterned display. The diversity of color on each individual squash and across the harvest makes Carnival as ornamental as it is edible, used for autumn fall displays, Thanksgiving centerpieces, and decorative arrangements alongside pumpkins. The flesh is orange, mildly sweet, and nutty — essentially the same eating quality as high-quality acorn squash, with a dry, dense texture that accepts butter, brown sugar, or maple syrup preparations well. Carnival is extremely productive and compact for an acorn-type, making it practical for backyard gardens with limited space. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Carnival Squash (Festival Squash)
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with ample compost; carnival squash is a hybrid acorn-type winter squash with uniquely multicolored skin — a striking mosaic of orange, yellow, cream, and green that deepens and brightens as the season cools. The compact, semi-bush vines fit smaller gardens better than most winter squash. Individual fruits weigh 1–2 pounds and have sweet, dense, orange-yellow flesh with good nutty flavor for roasting, baking, or steaming in halves. Fruits that have been exposed to light frost tend to develop richer color and sweeter flavor. Cure for 7–10 days at room temperature and store up to 3 months in a cool, dry location. The colorful fruits make excellent decorative gourds through autumn and into winter. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Carob
description: Carob is a slow-growing evergreen legume tree that fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils where few other fruits survive; it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Trees are dioecious — plant one male for every 8–10 female trees, or choose hermaphroditic cultivars such as Santa Fe and Clifford that produce fruit without a separate male. The long, dark-brown seed pods ripen in late summer and fall and are left on the tree to dry and sweeten; they are harvested when fully brown, dry, and the seeds rattle inside. Carob pods are sweet and chocolatey and used ground as a cocoa substitute or in stock feed. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Carola Potato (German Waxy Yellow All-Purpose Potato)
description: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Carola is a German-bred potato valued for its smooth, thin, light tan skin and dense, waxy, deep yellow flesh with rich, buttery flavor, performing well boiled, roasted, and in potato salads where a firm texture that holds together is wanted. It is a reliable, heavy-yielding variety with good resistance to common potato diseases and stores reasonably well after curing. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge, and harvest for storage after the vines have died back naturally. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Carolina Black Peanut
description: Sow raw, unroasted seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since the pegs that carry developing pods underground need soft ground to penetrate easily. Carolina Black is a rare African-heritage heirloom, distinguished from ordinary tan-skinned peanuts by its jet-black seed coat and a sweet, rich flavor that is prized by preservationist growers and heirloom seed keepers in the Carolinas and across the Deep South. Pods typically hold two kernels and are slightly larger than a Spanish peanut, so plants respond well to light hilling of loose soil around the base once yellow blooms appear. Because the variety is scarce commercially, growers often treat a first planting as seed increase, saving pods for replanting the following season. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Carolina Broadleaf Mustard (Disease-Resistant Southern Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season. USDA Agricultural Research Service breeders released Carolina Broadleaf in the mid-2010s as a deliberate improvement on the beloved old Florida Broadleaf mustard, developed specifically to resist a strain of bacterial leaf blight that had begun devastating Florida Broadleaf plantings across the South. It keeps the same large, crinkled, deep-green leaves and classic peppery mustard-green flavor gardeners expect, so it substitutes directly into traditional Southern cooking, but its added disease resistance makes it a more dependable choice where blight has become a recurring problem. Harvest young leaves for salads or let plants mature for the bolder-flavored cooking greens central to Southern braises. Matures in 42–50 days from seed.

name: Carolina Bunch Sweet Potato (Compact Bush-Type for Small Gardens)
description: Carolina Bunch was developed at North Carolina State University specifically for small-space growers, with a tight, semi-bush habit that stays under 3 feet of spread instead of sprawling 6-8 feet like standard vining sweet potatoes. Despite the compact vines, it is a solid producer of light copper-skinned, dark orange-fleshed roots that store and bake well. Because the plants don't sprawl and cover ground the way most sweet potatoes do, keep the bed mulched to suppress weeds and maintain even soil moisture. This is a practical choice for raised beds or anywhere a gardener wants sweet potatoes without letting vines take over the whole plot. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Carolina Cayenne Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Compact Cayenne)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Carolina Cayenne was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining classic cayenne heat and flavor with notably earlier maturity and a more compact, well-branched plant habit than older cayenne varieties, making it a reliable choice for gardeners with a shorter growing season or limited space. Fruits are thin, curved, and about 5-6 inches long, ripening from green to bright red with the sharp, straightforward heat cayenne is known for, well suited to drying, grinding into cayenne powder, or using fresh in cooking. The compact plants are heavily productive relative to their size, and the early maturity allows for a longer overall harvest window within the growing season. Harvest regularly, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on or off the plant for storage as dried cayenne. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Carolina Cross #183 Watermelon (Giant Exhibition Watermelon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in a heavily amended hill after last frost, allowing at least 8-10 feet in every direction per vine since this variety produces exceptionally long, vigorous runners. Carolina Cross #183 is an oblong striped hybrid bred specifically for maximum fruit size rather than eating quality, and it has been the variety of choice for generations of giant-watermelon growers at county fairs and record competitions, with individual fruits commonly reaching 100-200 lbs and record specimens well over 200 lbs. To grow oversized fruit, limit each vine to one or two developing melons, feed heavily throughout the season, and water deeply and consistently since the huge fruit places large demands on the root system. Flesh is red and reasonably sweet, but the plant's primary appeal is spectacle and competition rather than refined flavor. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Carolina Crowder Southern Pea (Disease-Resistant Heirloom Crowder Cowpea)
description: Carolina Crowder is a classic Southern crowder pea selected and maintained by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, updated over time for broader Fusarium wilt resistance while keeping its old-fashioned flavor. Pods are straw colored with a purple tint, 7-9 inches long, and packed tightly with light-brown crowder-type seeds that shell out easily. Large, prolific, bushy plants make it a reliable choice for a big drying-pea harvest, ready in about 61 days to first picking. Matures in 61–70 days from seed.

name: Carolina Gold Rice
description: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Carolina Gold is America's most historically significant rice variety, the first variety commercially grown in colonial South Carolina and Georgia during the 18th century, and the foundation of lowcountry cuisine including pilau, perloo, and hoppin' john. It is a long-grained, gold-hulled, aromatic variety with exceptional flavor — nutty, fragrant, and creamy when cooked — that is the standard against which all Southern rice is measured. The variety nearly disappeared after the Civil War but was revived by dedicated seed savers and is now grown by specialty mills in the Carolinas. Home gardeners can grow it in consistently moist beds without true paddies; simply keep soil saturated throughout the growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain has turned golden, then thresh and process as whole-grain brown rice or hull fully. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Carolina Reaper Pepper
description: Start seeds at 85–90°F soil temperature with bottom heat — germination is erratic and may take 3–4 weeks; transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay above 60°F. Carolina Reaper was certified by Guinness World Records as the world's hottest pepper in 2013, averaging 1.57 million Scoville Heat Units (SHU) with peak measurements above 2.2 million SHU — roughly 200 times hotter than a jalapeño and significantly more potent than habaneros. It was bred by Ed Curlin (PuckerButt Pepper Company) in Rock Hill, South Carolina, by crossing a Pakistani Naga with a Red Habanero. The distinctive wrinkled, red-orange fruits are small (1–2 inches) with a characteristic scorpion-tail sting at the tip and a fruity, complex flavor underneath the extreme heat. Handle with nitrile gloves and eye protection — touching eyes or face after handling can cause serious irritation. Used in hot sauces, salsas, and challenge eating. The plants are attractive and productive in warm climates. In zone 9, treat as a long-season annual or overwinter as a perennial in zone 9b. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Carolina Red June Apple (Early-Ripening Southern Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Carolina Red June is a Southern heirloom apple documented since at least the early 1800s and grown widely across the antebellum South, valued above all for its extremely early ripening, often ready to pick in June, weeks ahead of nearly every other apple variety and giving Southern growers fresh apples at a time of year when no other apple is available. Fruit is small to medium, deep red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating, sauce, and early-season pies. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the variety's relatively low chill requirement makes it one of the more Gulf-South-adapted heirloom apples compared with higher-chill Northern varieties. Because it ripens so early and doesn't store particularly long, plan to use or process the crop promptly rather than relying on it for winter storage. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Carolina Ruby Sweet Potato (Early Deep-Red-Skin Orange Sweet Potato)
description: Carolina Ruby was bred at North Carolina State University and released in the late 1990s as an earlier-maturing companion to Beauregard, with striking deep red-purple skin and moist orange flesh. It bulks up quickly and can be dug a couple of weeks ahead of most other orange sweet potatoes, which is a real advantage for beating fall's first frost in a home garden. Vines are thin and trailing rather than bushy, so give them room to ramble or trellis them along a fence. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch and avoid heavy irrigation in the final weeks. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Carolina White Rice (Historic Lowcountry Sister to Carolina Gold)
description: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Carolina White was the pale-hulled sister landrace grown alongside gold-hulled Carolina Gold throughout the antebellum South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry, part of the same rice culture built on enslaved West African agricultural expertise that made Charleston one of the wealthiest colonial ports. Like Carolina Gold, Carolina White nearly vanished after the Civil War and through the collapse of Lowcountry rice culture in the early 20th century; the two landraces are close kin, and rice geneticists working with the Carolina Gold Rice Foundation and Anson Mills have noted that recovered Carolina Gold populations can express Carolina White characteristics. Grow it exactly as Carolina Gold — in a saturated bed or shallow paddy — and expect a tall, long-grained rice with a milder, less golden husk color but similar exceptional cooking quality. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling. Matures in 110–135 days from seed.

name: Carolina Wonder Sweet Pepper (NCSU Disease-Resistant Sweet Bell)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Carolina Wonder's disease resistance package makes it superior to susceptible commercial bell varieties in humid climates where Phytophthora blight and bacterial leaf spot cause mid-season collapse of unprotected plants. Carolina Wonder was developed at North Carolina State University's pepper breeding program to address the specific disease challenges of Southeastern sweet bell pepper production — the combination of summer heat, humidity, rainfall, and the disease complex it creates (Phytophthora capsici root and crown rot, bacterial leaf spot caused by Xanthomonas, tobacco etch virus) creates extremely difficult conditions for standard sweet bell varieties that lack specific resistance genes. Carolina Wonder combines resistance to multiple diseases with excellent sweet bell quality: the large (4-lobed, blocky, 3.5–4 inch), thick-walled fruits are green-to-red with crisp, sweet flesh typical of the best sweet bells. The disease resistance package — particularly the Phytophthora crown and root rot resistance — gives Carolina Wonder dramatically better survival in wet years and poorly drained soils compared to susceptible varieties. Carolina Wonder is sometimes paired with Charleston Belle (which adds nematode resistance not included in Carolina Wonder) in gardens where both nematodes and Phytophthora are concerns; together they address the full disease complex of Gulf South pepper production. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Caroline Raspberry
description: 'Caroline' is a vigorous fall-bearing red raspberry prized for large, intensely flavored fruit with high antioxidant content. Plant in full sun in fertile, slightly acidic soil and irrigate consistently during fruit development. Prune as a primocane type by cutting canes to the ground in late winter for one large fall harvest. Its heat tolerance makes it a strong choice for warmer parts of its range, though it benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Carouby de Maussane Snow Pea (French Provence Heirloom Large Flat Edible-Pod Pea)
aliases: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Carouby de Maussane'
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep along a trellis or fence; thin to 3–4 inches. Provide 4–5 foot support. Harvest pods flat before seeds bulge. Carouby de Maussane is a French Provençal heirloom snow pea — a mangetout (French for 'eat all,' referring to the edible pod) variety from the village of Maussane-les-Alpilles in the Alpilles region of Provence that has been grown continuously in the gardens and small farms of that region for generations. The variety is distinguished by unusually large flat pods (3–5 inches long) that are visually unlike standard snow peas: broader, larger, and often tinged with purple at the shoulders when young — and by the ornamental beauty of the plant itself, which produces the bi-colored purple-and-white flowers of the original pea species (most modern pea varieties have been selected for white-only flowers) against dark green foliage on 4–5 foot vines. The pods have the flat, wide, meaty snow pea character at optimal harvest — tender, crisp, and sweetly flavored without the starchy density of fully-podded shelling peas. Carouby de Maussane is a cold-hardy, vigorous variety well-suited to fall planting in zone 8–9 where it can grow through the mild winter and produce the spring snap-pod harvest before summer heat arrives. The variety is maintained by seed savers and heirloom seed companies as an example of the genetic and culinary diversity that existed in traditional European peasant food gardens. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Carpathian Garlic (Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Set cloves 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil and mulch heavily through winter, especially in northern climates, removing mulch gradually in spring. Cut the scape once it curls to direct the plant's energy into bulb formation, then cure bulbs for several weeks in a dry, shaded, well-ventilated space. Carpathian is a cold-hardy porcelain-type hardneck originating in the Carpathian Mountains of Eastern Europe, grown for its large white bulbs, thick papery wrappers, and strong, long-lasting garlic flavor well suited to harsh winter climates. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Carpathian Walnut (Cold-Hardy English Walnut Strain)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, away from vegetable gardens and other sensitive plants since walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Carpathian refers to a cold-hardy strain of the common English (Persian) walnut originating in the mountainous Carpathian region of Poland, introduced to North America in the mid-20th century specifically because it tolerates far colder winters than typical English walnut selections from milder climates. The thin-shelled, easily cracked nuts have the classic mild, rich English walnut flavor, and the trees are large, long-lived, and productive once mature, typically beginning to bear within five to seven years of planting. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Carrick Pear (University of Tennessee Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Carrick was released alongside its companion selection Morgan from the University of Tennessee's dedicated 1950s fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program, developed specifically to give Southern home orchardists pear options that could withstand the fire blight pressure of humid summers without heavy spraying. Fruit has the firm, reliable qualities typical of Southern-bred pears, suited to fresh eating once ripened off the tree as well as canning and preserving. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions typical of home orchard management. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Carrie Mango
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Carrie mango is prized for its compact size and rich flavor, making it a favorite dooryard tree in frost-free and marginal citrus climates. A Florida-bred seedling selection, it produces small to medium, fiberless fruit with deep orange flesh and an intensely rich, sweet, complex, almost spicy flavor that many home growers rate among the best-tasting mangoes available, though the skin stays mostly green even when ripe. The tree is naturally more compact and precocious than many mango cultivars, bearing at a young age and staying manageable in a home orchard or large container. Water deeply during fruit development and reduce irrigation as fruit nears harvest to concentrate sweetness; protect young trees from any frost, since mango is damaged by temperatures near freezing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Carrion Flower
description: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Unlike its thorny greenbrier relatives, this species is unarmed and herbaceous, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring. Young emerging shoots are harvested and cooked like asparagus in early spring before the tendrils toughen, while the small, unshowy flowers give off a carrion-like scent that draws fly pollinators later in the season. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Carrizo Citrange Rootstock
description: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired orange, grapefruit, or other citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Carrizo is grown as an understock, not for its own fruit. A citrange hybrid between sweet orange and trifoliate orange developed in California, it is among the most widely planted citrus rootstocks worldwide for its strong resistance to citrus tristeza virus, good cold hardiness compared to purely tropical rootstocks, and production of high-quality, well-anchored, moderately vigorous trees compatible with most scion varieties. Its combination of disease resistance and adaptability to a range of soil types has made it a standard commercial rootstock choice, though it is sensitive to high-pH, calcareous soils where iron chlorosis can become a problem. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and provide winter protection in the coldest parts of its recommended range, since the trifoliate parentage improves but does not eliminate cold sensitivity of the resulting tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Carter's Blue Apple (Alabama Heirloom Purple-Blushed Apple)
