description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and plant a second apple cultivar nearby for pollination, since Carter's Blue is not reliably self-fruitful. An old Alabama heirloom, Carter's Blue is named for its striking skin — a deep red so dark it takes on a distinct purple-blue bloom, especially when coated in the natural waxy blush that develops on the fruit — surrounding crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart white flesh good for fresh eating and cooking alike. Its long history in Deep South orchards and relatively low chill requirement have kept it in cultivation among heirloom fruit collectors seeking apples suited to warm-winter climates where many Northern cultivars fail to fruit reliably. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall; harvest when the color deepens fully and the fruit releases easily from the spur. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Casaba Melon (Golden Beauty Casaba)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Casaba needs dry conditions at harvest to prevent splitting and rind cracking — reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Casaba melon takes its name from Kasaba (now called Turgutlu), a city in western Turkey from which seeds were brought to the United States in the late 19th century; it is an inodorus winter-type melon with no surface netting and little external fragrance when ripe, unusual among American melons. The large (8–14 lb), round to slightly pointed-at-one-end fruits have deeply furrowed, wrinkled, golden-yellow skin and creamy-white to pale yellow flesh with mild, sweet, cucumber-like flavor that is less intensely aromatic than cantaloupe but refreshing and distinct. Casaba's extraordinary keeping quality (3–5 months at cool room temperature without refrigeration) made it historically important as a late-season melon available well after other varieties were finished; harvested in October it could remain in good condition through December. Excellent for dry summer climates (California, Arizona, Gulf Coast with good drainage); susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Cascabel Pepper (Rattle Chile)
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to the garden in warm soil after all frost risk has passed. Cascabel — named for the rattle the seeds make inside the dried pod — is a round, 1.5-inch, deep red-brown dried Mexican chile with mild to moderate heat (1,500–2,500 Scoville), a uniquely nutty, slightly smoky, woody flavor with an earthy depth that is used in traditional Mexican moles, salsas, and braised meats; it is harvested fully red on the plant and dried for 2–3 weeks in a warm, airy location. Plants are compact and bushy, producing round pods in clusters; the fully dried pods have a distinctive rattling sound from the loose seeds inside, making them easy to identify in a pantry. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture to maximize fruit set. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Cascade Delight Raspberry
description: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile soil and support the vigorous canes on a trellis, removing spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year. Released by Washington State University as an improvement on older Pacific Northwest cultivars like Meeker, Cascade Delight was specifically bred for resistance to Phytophthora root rot, a major limitation in wetter or heavier soils, while still producing large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor. It ripens slightly later than Meeker, extending the summer harvest window, and its firmer fruit holds up well for both fresh eating and shipping. Its improved disease resistance makes it a more forgiving choice than many older varieties for gardeners with imperfectly drained soil. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Cascade Glaze Collard (Oregon Re-Selection of Heirloom Green Glaze)
description: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24-30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cascade Glaze was bred as a careful re-selection of the classic 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze collard, retaining the same smooth, glossy, waxy leaf surface that sheds cabbage worm eggs and deters other leaf-eating pests better than fuzzier-leaved collard varieties, while offering improved uniformity from the breeding work. The open, non-heading rosette produces tender, mild-flavored leaves that hold up well to both heat and light frost, making it productive across a long Gulf South growing season. Harvest outer leaves continuously as the plant grows, and expect sweeter flavor after the first light frosts convert starches to sugars. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Cascade Hops (Iconic Citrus-Floral American Aroma Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Cascade, released by Oregon State University in 1972, is the single most influential American hop cultivar, prized for its distinctive grapefruit-citrus and floral aroma that came to define the American craft beer movement and remains the signature hop of classic West Coast pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; soft green cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and slightly sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Performs best in cool-summer climates with long day length; struggles with the persistent heat and humidity of zone 8-9 Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, best-ventilated site available and expect reduced cone yield compared with Pacific Northwest production. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Cascadia Snap Pea (Disease-Resistant Oregon State-Bred Snap Pea)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing light support such as netting or twiggy brush for the vines. Cascadia was bred at Oregon State University and is valued for good resistance to powdery mildew and other common pea diseases, along with sweet, crisp, edible pods on compact, easy-to-support vines that produce reliably even in less-than-ideal spring weather. Its snap-pea type pods are eaten whole, pod and all, once they fill out but before the peas inside become starchy. Harvest regularly once pods reach full size to encourage continued production through the relatively short Gulf South pea season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Cascara Sagrada
description: WARNING: bark must be harvested only from mature (8+ year old) trees and aged at least a year before use — fresh, unaged bark causes severe cramping and should never be used directly off the tree, and long-term laxative use is discouraged due to dependency and electrolyte loss risk. Transplant dormant bare-root or potted stock in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of an understory site, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest forest habitat. This slow-growing native tree is the traditional source of cascara bark, a classic stimulant laxative once aged properly. Matures in 2920–3650 days from transplant.

name: Case Knife Bean
description: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick young for snap beans, at the shelly stage for a creamy fresh bean, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Case Knife is an old Southern heirloom pole bean named for its long, flat, slightly curved pods, which resemble the folding blade of a case knife (a traditional pocketknife). The vigorous vines climb readily to 6–8 feet and bear heavily over a long summer season, producing broad, tender pods best picked young for snap use before the beans inside swell; left to mature, the pods yield plump, cream-white beans that shell out easily and cook to a smooth, buttery texture, or can be dried fully for winter storage. Valued in old Southern gardens for its dependable heat tolerance and heavy yield from a small footprint of trellis space, making it a practical choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens where many bush beans falter in midsummer heat. Matures in 65–95 days from seed.

name: Caserta Italian Zucchini
description: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Caserta is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom Italian zucchini with distinctive gray-green striped skin and creamy interior, different in appearance and texture from the solid dark-green standard zucchini. The cylindrical, 6–8 inch fruits have firmer, denser, less watery flesh than most hybrid zucchini — excellent for grilling, sautéing, and stuffing where a firmer texture is preferred. The compact, AAS-winning bush plant produces abundantly in both spring and fall crops in zone 9; summer production may slow during peak heat. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — oversized fruits become seedy and pithy. The attractive, striped fruits are ornamental as well as useful. Matures in 53–60 days from seed.

name: Cash Flow Hybrid Zucchini (High-Yield Market Zucchini)
description: Cash Flow was bred as a market-grower's zucchini, prized for setting an unusually high number of straight, uniform dark-green fruit in quick succession from an open, easy-to-harvest plant. Pick fruit small, at 6-8 inches, for the best texture and to keep the vigorous plant cranking out more; a single well-fed plant can produce for weeks with regular harvest. The open habit makes fruit easy to spot under the leaves, cutting down on the oversized zucchini that hide until harvest day. A dependable choice for gardeners who want a steady, heavy zucchini harvest without much fuss. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Cashew
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic to neutral, infertile to average soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; cashew is native to northeastern Brazil and now cultivated throughout the tropics as one of the world's most important nut crops. The 'nut' is actually a large seed attached to the outside of a swollen, fleshy, pear-shaped 'cashew apple' (pseudofruit) which is edible fresh, juiced, or fermented into cashew wine. The seed shell contains urushiol — the same irritating compound in poison ivy — and must never be handled or roasted without protection. Commercial cashews are processed to remove this compound before the familiar pale nut is edible. The cashew apple, rarely seen in North America, is highly perishable and consumed fresh throughout tropical regions as a vitamin-C-rich refreshing fruit. In zone 9, treat as a container specimen moved indoors in winter. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Cashmere Hops
description: Plant rhizomes in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy 12-20 foot trellis, pole, or string for the twining bines to climb; Cashmere was released by Washington State University's hop breeding program as a descendant of Cascade, developed to offer a similar mild, floral-citrus aroma profile with improved yield and a more manageable, less vigorous growth habit than its parent. Cones are used mainly for aroma and flavor additions in craft brewing, contributing notes of citrus, melon, and mild spice. Hops are perennial bines that die back to the crown each winter and regrow vigorously each spring, needing several years to reach full production. Water consistently during the growing season, especially as cones develop in mid-to-late summer, and harvest when cones feel dry and papery and release a strong aromatic, slightly sticky lupulin scent when rubbed. Hops generally prefer a period of winter chill and struggle with the mild winters and intense summer humidity of the Deep South, performing best in cooler, drier climates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Casper Eggplant (White Heirloom Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest, sweetest flavor and fewest seeds. Casper is a classic heirloom eggplant producing smooth, pure ivory-white, oblong fruit with tender skin that needs no peeling, and notably mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh that browns less than purple varieties once cut — a practical advantage for dishes where appearance matters, like gratins or stuffed preparations. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season and are less prone to the bitterness that can develop in some eggplant varieties under stress. Its striking white color and mild flavor make it a favorite for gardeners wanting a visually distinctive eggplant with excellent kitchen versatility, zone 4–12. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Casper Pumpkin
description: Plant seeds an inch deep in warm soil in hills, thinning to the two best vines each. Give the plants space and steady moisture to develop the smooth, ghostly white rinds and sweet orange flesh. Harvest when the stems harden and cure in the sun to firm the skin for both fall displays and baking. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Casper White Eggplant (Italian Ivory White Heirloom Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest when fruits are 5–7 inches and solid creamy white before yellowing. Casper is an Italian-style white eggplant — a medium-sized, oval-to-elongated variety producing distinctive ivory-white to cream-white fruits in the 4–7 inch range. White eggplant varieties have a long tradition in Italian cooking, where they are considered particularly well-suited to oven-roasted preparations and eggplant parmesan, as the white skin and flesh remain visually lighter during cooking compared to the purple-flesh types that can discolor. The flavor of Casper white eggplant is noticeably different from standard purple varieties: consistently milder, creamier, with significantly less bitterness — white-skinned eggplants in general tend toward less bitterness than dark-skinned types, though the reason may be as much cultural (bred and selected for mild flavor in the white-eggplant tradition) as biological. The flesh is very creamy and smooth-textured, making Casper an excellent choice for dips, spreads, baba ganoush-style preparations, and dishes where a mild, creamy eggplant flavor is desired without the assertiveness of purple types. The ivory-white skin also makes Casper a visually interesting garden plant and conversation piece at farmers markets. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Casperita Pumpkin
description: A petite ornamental pumpkin producing pure-white fruits four to four and a half inches across, perfect for painting and displays. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm, or start indoors briefly in short-season climates. Give the vines room to run and keep soil evenly moist while fruit sizes up. Harvest when the skin is hard and the stem corks, leaving a length of stem attached for longer storage. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Caspian Pink Tomato (Russian Heirloom Low-Acid Beefsteak Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, deeply prepared soil. Stake securely — the large, heavy fruits can pull down unsupported vines. Caspian Pink is a Ukrainian-Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato introduced to the United States by Marianna Kezenberger, an immigrant from the Caspian Sea region of the former Soviet Union — the name references both the geographic origin and the distinctive color. The variety is a large-fruited, low-acid pink-skinned beefsteak type: fruits weigh 8–14 oz or more, with the flattened, slightly irregular, shouldered shape characteristic of traditional beefsteaks. The skin is thin, smooth, and a clear rose-pink rather than true red, indicating the absence of the yellow skin gene — a characteristic associated with lower perceived acidity and sweeter flavor in tomatoes. The flavor profile is rich, complex, and less sharp than red-skinned beefsteaks — noticeably sweeter at the same sugar content because lower acid allows sweetness to predominate. Caspian Pink is consistently rated among the best-tasting pink heirloom beefsteaks in comparative tastings, often mentioned in the same conversation as Brandywine and Cherokee Purple as a top-tier beefsteak for eating quality. Matures in 80–88 days from transplant.

name: Cassabanana / Sikana
description: Start seeds indoors in warm, moist potting mix at least 4–6 weeks before the last expected frost, as cassabanana needs a very long growing season to produce its large, fragrant fruits. Provide a strong trellis, arbor, or fence — this vigorous vine can easily reach 20–30 feet in a single season. Water consistently and fertilize every few weeks with a balanced fertilizer; reduce watering once fruits begin to color and fill out. In frost-free zones (USDA 10–11) the vine is perennial and will produce fruit year after year from the same root system. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Cassava (Yuca / Manioc)
description: Plant stem cuttings (stakes) horizontally 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; cassava is drought tolerant once established and produces in poor soils where other root crops fail, making it one of the world's most important calorie crops. All varieties contain some cyanogenic glycosides — sweet varieties are low enough for safe eating after cooking, while bitter varieties require extensive washing and fermentation to detoxify. Never eat raw cassava. Harvest tubers when 8–18 months old by digging carefully to avoid breaking the fragile roots; they must be used within a few days of harvest or frozen, as they deteriorate rapidly. In zone 9, the above-ground plant freezes back but roots may survive with heavy mulch. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Casselman Plum (Dark Red-Skinned California Japanese Plum)
description: Casselman emerged from the same mid-twentieth-century California breeding effort that produced Santa Rosa, Friar, and Laroda, and it shares their combination of vigorous growth and heavy, reliable cropping. The medium-to-large fruit ripens to a deep red skin over firm, juicy, amber flesh with a sweet flavor and mild acidity, and it hangs well on the tree without softening quickly, which is useful in humid climates where fruit rot pressure is high. Plant a second compatible plum within about 50 feet for pollination and thin the crop early if it sets heavily, since Casselman is a prolific bearer that can overproduce small fruit. Harvest when the skin colors fully but the flesh still gives slightly to thumb pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cassumunar Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Zingiber montanum dies back in winter in zone 8–9 — mulch the root zone heavily after frost and the plant will re-emerge reliably from the persistent rhizome in late spring. Zingiber montanum (Cassumunar Ginger, Plai, or Bengal Root) is a medium-sized rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to South Asia (India, Bangladesh) and Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam, Indonesia), where its aromatic, yellow-fleshed rhizomes are the source of one of the most important herbal medicines in Thai traditional medicine — 'Plai' or 'Phlai.' The essential oil distilled from the rhizomes is rich in terpinen-4-ol and sabinene, giving it strong anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antispasmodic properties extensively documented in Thai traditional medicine for joint pain, sprains, bruises, and postpartum care. Plai oil is a standard ingredient in Thai massage therapy liniments and is now internationally distributed as a sports and pain-relief product. The plant is ornamentally neat — compact, clumping, with attractive narrow lanceolate leaves — and the aromatic rhizomes are easy to harvest by simply digging, taking what is needed, and replanting the remainder. An outstanding and under-grown medicinal spice for warm-climate herb gardens in zone 8–11. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Castelfranco Radicchio
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in summer, thinning to 12–14 inches apart; Castelfranco is sometimes called the 'Flower of the Veneto' for its extraordinarily beautiful, loosely ruffled heads that open like a rose, with creamy white or pale yellow leaves splashed and spotted with deep wine-red markings — no two heads are alike. The flavor is distinctly milder and more buttery than the sharply bitter Chioggia or Treviso types, making it accessible to diners who find radicchio too harsh. Cool autumn temperatures intensify the color development — heads grown in warm weather are primarily green. Use individual leaves as edible cups for salads or hors d'oeuvres; the visual presentation is stunning. In the South, this is an ideal late-fall and winter salad green for gardens in zones 8–9. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Castillo Coffee
description: Released in 2005 by Colombia's Cenicáfe research center, Castillo was bred to replace the aging, increasingly rust-susceptible Colombia variety while preserving comparable cup quality, and it is now the dominant cultivar on Colombian farms. It combines solid resistance to coffee leaf rust with a compact, productive habit suited to the country's steep, densely planted hillside farms. Growers value its dependable yields and disease tolerance, while roasters generally find its cup quality good, if slightly more variable regionally than older heirloom Colombian selections. Grow it as for other Arabicas, in filtered shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Castlebrite Apricot (Self-Fruitful Blushed-Red Reliable Early Bearer)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Castlebrite is self-fruitful and bears bright orange fruit blushed with red, semi-sweet in flavor, on a tree noted for reliably early and consistent bearing once established. Its chill requirement of roughly 500 hours suits it to the milder parts of zone 8 as well as zone 7. As with other apricots, early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap, so good air drainage at the planting site helps protect the flowers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cat Thyme (Marum, Germander Catmint)
description: Propagate from stem cuttings or sow seeds in well-drained, poor, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cat thyme is a compact, woody Mediterranean subshrub (despite the name, not a true thyme) with small, oval, intensely aromatic leaves and small pink-purple flowers that attract bees; the plants have a strong, pungent, resinous, slightly camphor-like scent distinct from culinary thyme. As its common name suggests, it attracts cats intensely, similar to catnip but stronger in effect — cats will roll on the plants and sometimes destroy them, so caging or placing them in pots on high shelves is advisable in gardens with cats. Used in traditional herbal medicine and as a garden plant for rocky banks, walls, and Mediterranean-themed plantings. Excellent drainage is non-negotiable. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Cat's Whiskers (Java Tea, Kidney Tea Plant)
description: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; cat's whiskers is one of the most striking tropical herbs for zone 9–11 shade gardens, producing distinctive white or lavender flower spikes with extraordinarily long stamens that project like cat's whiskers beyond the petals — an unusual, eye-catching floral structure that attracts bees and butterflies. The plant is widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia as a medicinal herb — Orthosiphon leaves are dried to make Java tea, a traditional remedy for kidney and urinary tract conditions. In the Gulf Coast garden it is an outstanding tender perennial for partial shade where it blooms almost continuously from late spring through frost in frost-free climates. The fresh or dried leaves make a mild, pleasant-tasting herbal infusion. Harvest leaves and young stems by pinching before they flower to encourage bushy growth and maximize leaf yield. Propagate easily from tip cuttings placed in moist soil in a warm, humid location. In zone 9 it dies back to the roots in frost but recovers vigorously in spring. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Catalina Plum (Dark Red-Purple California Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Catalina is a California Japanese plum producing dark red to purple-skinned fruit with sweet, juicy, amber flesh, ripening in mid-season and valued for reliable, heavy production alongside good eating quality. The vigorous tree performs well under standard commercial plum-growing conditions and has remained a solid choice for home orchardists wanting a dependable, attractive dark plum without the more particular care some specialty varieties demand. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and reaches full color for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Catalina Spinach (Heat-Tolerant Flat-Leaf Fall Spinach Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing for full-sized leaves or leave more densely sown for baby spinach harvest. Catalina is a flat-leaf hybrid spinach from Johnny's Selected Seeds selected specifically for fall and winter production in a wide range of climates — a smooth, flat-leaved type (as opposed to the crinkled savoy and semi-savoy types) that is preferred for salad mixes, commercial baby spinach production, and any application where the spinach will be eaten raw rather than cooked. The flat-leaf type is easier to wash than savoy types because soil and debris don't get trapped in the leaf crevices, making Catalina a practical choice for cut-and-wash baby greens. Catalina carries good resistance to multiple races of downy mildew, extending its productive life in humid fall conditions. The leaves are medium-large, oval to lance-shaped, dark green, and have the clean, mild spinach flavor that works well in all raw applications. Its performance in fall and winter production makes Catalina particularly valuable for the Gulf South zone 8–10 garden where fall and winter are the primary growing seasons for spinach — direct-seeding in September and October establishes plants that grow slowly through winter and provide steady leaf harvests. Matures in 42–50 days from seed.

name: Catalogna Chicory
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalogna Chicory (Cicoria di Catalogna, also called Asparagus Chicory or Puntarelle in its bolted form) is the traditional Italian cut-leaf chicory of Lazio and Apulia, producing elongated, deeply toothed, dandelion-shaped leaves with a pleasantly bitter, refreshing flavor that is considerably milder than radicchio. In Italy the outer leaves are eaten braised or in soups, while the inner pale stems are prized as the luxury green 'puntarelle' — the hollow, pale, crunchy stem shoots that emerge when the plant begins to bolt, traditionally served raw in Rome with an anchovy-garlic-lemon dressing. Catalogna is one of the most widely eaten cooking greens in southern Italy and is slowly gaining recognition in North American specialty markets. In zone 9 it provides a productive cut-and-come-again winter green harvest from fall sowings, and the mild temperatures allow it to slowly develop the inner stem shoots (puntarelle) that make it exceptional. Harvest outer leaves throughout winter and allow the center to develop stem shoots in late winter for puntarelle. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Catawba Grape (Historic American Pink Wine and Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Catawba is one of the oldest named American grape varieties, discovered in North Carolina in the early 1800s and once the most widely planted wine grape in the country, producing distinctive coppery-pink to reddish-purple berries with the characteristic musky, richly sweet Labrusca 'foxy' flavor, used historically for sparkling and still wine as well as fresh eating and juice. It is self-fruitful and ripens in mid to late season. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease pressure and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers do better with muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Catawissa Onion (Heirloom Perennial Tree Onion)
description: Plant topset bulbils 1-2 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall or early spring; established clumps are extremely low-maintenance and benefit from dividing every few years to maintain vigor. Catawissa is a historic American heirloom perennial onion, first documented in Pennsylvania in the 1800s, that produces clusters of small aerial bulbils atop tall seed stalks; as the topsets mature and become heavy, the stalk arches over and the bulbils root wherever they touch soil, letting the planting slowly spread, or 'walk', across the bed on its own. Compared with the more commonly sold Egyptian walking onion, Catawissa's topset clusters are looser and sometimes mixed with small true flowers, and some gardeners find its flavor slightly milder. Harvest green tops through the season like scallions, or dig the underground bulbs once foliage begins to die back; the aerial bulbils themselves can be pickled or used as new planting stock. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Catbird Grape (Red Grape)
description: Plant along a moist streambank, low woodland edge, or wet fence line in full sun to part shade; catbird grape is a striking native vine of the Mississippi Valley and Gulf South wetlands, named for its bright red young stems and deeply palmate, hand-shaped leaves that set it apart from every other native grape at a glance. It thrives in soggy, seasonally flooded ground where few other fruiting vines survive, making it a useful choice for rain gardens and low, wet corners of the landscape. The small, tart black grapes ripen in late summer and are quickly stripped by catbirds, thrashers, and other fruit-eating songbirds, while the inconspicuous spring flowers still provide an early nectar source for native bees. Give it a tall support and expect vigorous growth once the roots find consistent moisture. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Catillac Pear (Historic French Culinary and Perry Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. A historic French pear grown in the gardens of Louis XIV at Versailles and first described in 1665, it bears large, hard fruit with slightly gritty flesh that turns an attractive pink when cooked, and greenish-yellow skin with a dull red blush at maturity. Suitable only for very slow cooking rather than fresh eating, it is a long-established culinary pear of high quality that can also be pressed for perry, and the vigorous, reliable, hardy tree produces fruit that keeps exceptionally well after a mid-autumn harvest. Harvest in mid-autumn once firm and mature, store cool, and cook slowly whole or in pieces until the flesh turns pink and tender. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Catimor Coffee
description: Bred in Portugal in the 1950s by crossing the dwarf Caturra with the naturally rust-resistant Hybrido de Timor, Catimor introduced leaf rust resistance into commercial Arabica production for the first time and has since become one of the most widely planted cultivars across Central America, South Asia, and parts of Africa. Its compact, dwarf habit and early, heavy bearing make it attractive for smallholders and high-density plantings, though cup quality is generally considered a step below heirloom lines like Bourbon or Typica unless carefully processed. Give it the same warm, filtered-shade conditions and consistently moist, well-drained soil that other Arabicas need, and expect the first harvest within three years of transplanting. Matures in 1095–1400 days from transplant.

name: Catnip
description: Nepeta cataria is a bushy, square-stemmed perennial in the mint family with distinctive soft, gray-green, heart-shaped to triangular leaves with a strong, distinctive musky-minty scent, and dense spikes of small, white to pale lavender, purple-spotted flowers from June through September that are excellent bee plants; the nepetalactone compound in the foliage produces the well-known euphoric response in domestic cats, and the plant is used to stuff cat toys and promote play. As an herbal tea, catnip has mild sedative and digestive properties; it has a long history of use for insomnia, anxiety, and infant colic. Cut back hard after the first bloom flush to promote fresh growth and a second flowering. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cats Claw
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with a large, strong support structure — trellis, pergola, or tree — for the vine to ascend; Uncaria tomentosa is a vigorous grower in tropical conditions and requires annual pruning to manage size and direct growth. Uncaria tomentosa (Cat's Claw or Uña de Gato) is a large, woody liana in the Rubiaceae (coffee) family native to the humid tropical rainforests of the Amazon Basin, particularly Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, and Ecuador, where it climbs to the forest canopy using distinctive, recurved, claw-like thorns at the leaf nodes — the feature giving it its common name. The thorned inner bark and root bark are the primary medicinal parts, containing a unique array of pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids (mitraphylline, isomitraphylline, rhynchophylline) with well-documented anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immune-modulating activities. Cat's Claw has been used for centuries by Peruvian Asháninka and other Amazonian peoples to treat arthritis, gastrointestinal inflammation, infections, and cancer — and is now one of the top-selling botanical supplements in the United States and Europe for arthritis and joint pain. Bark is harvested sustainably by removing sections of outer bark without felling the vine. In the garden, it is an ornamental, fast-growing tropical vine with attractive, paired opposite leaves and small, tubular, white flowers. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Catskill Brussels Sprouts
description: Start seeds indoors and set out sturdy transplants so the long season finishes as cool fall weather arrives. This 1940s heirloom forms compact, dwarf stalks packed with large, tightly wrapped sprouts. Keep the plants well fed and watered, and wait to harvest until a few frosts have sweetened the sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Catuai Coffee
description: Bred in Brazil by crossing Mundo Novo with the dwarf Caturra, Catuai combines a compact, sturdy frame with heavy, reliable production, and its strong branch attachment keeps ripe cherries from dropping in wind and rain far better than taller heirloom varieties. It is sold in both red-fruited and yellow-fruited forms, both equally productive, and its short stature and early bearing have made it one of the most widely planted commercial cultivars across Latin America. Home growers appreciate that it stays manageable in a large pot yet still produces a respectable home harvest within a few years. Provide the same dappled shade, steady moisture, and rich, well-drained acidic soil that other Arabica coffees need. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Catucaí Coffee
description: Bred in Brazil beginning in the 1980s from a cross of Catuaí and Icatu, Catucaí combines the compact, manageable stature and heavy productivity of Catuaí with genetic material from the taller, more disease-tolerant Icatu (itself an old Typica x Bourbon x robusta-derived line), producing a vigorous, high-yielding, fairly compact Arabica selection favored on Brazilian smallholdings for its productivity and adaptability across a range of elevations. Several numbered Catucaí sub-selections exist, differing slightly in vigor, bean size, and cup profile, but all share the parent cross's combination of good yield and manageable size. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica coffees, feed regularly to sustain heavy bearing on a compact frame, and expect the first cherries after three to four years. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Caturra Coffee
description: This naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon was first found on a Brazilian farm and quickly caught on because its short, compact, densely branched habit allows far tighter spacing than lanky heirloom Arabica types. Its shrubbier form makes it a good choice for patio containers or small greenhouses where a full-size coffee tree would be unwieldy, though the same compact vigor means it depletes soil nutrients faster and rewards regular feeding. Cup quality is very good, similar to its Bourbon parent, though heavier bearing can dilute flavor if the plant is not fed and watered consistently. Give it the same warm, humid, filtered-light understory conditions as other Arabica coffees and expect the first cherries after three to four years. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Caucasian Spinach (Hablitzia)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade against a wall, fence, or trellis; Caucasian spinach is a remarkable perennial climbing green from the Caucasus mountains and one of the very few shade-tolerant vining vegetables, making it invaluable in north-facing or deeply shaded spots. The young leaves and shoot tips are harvested throughout spring and summer exactly like spinach — steamed, sautéed, or eaten fresh — with a mild, pleasant flavor similar to New Zealand spinach. The plant dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges reliably from its rootstock in spring, climbing vigorously to 6–12 feet when given support. In zone 9, provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture to prevent summer decline; the plant often goes partially dormant in peak heat and recovers for fall harvests. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Cauliflower
description: Sow 1/4 in deep in well-drained starter mix 6–8 weeks before transplanting; cauliflower is sensitive to temperature swings and nutrient deficiencies. When the developing curd is about the size of a golf ball, gather outer leaves over it and secure with a rubber band to blanch for white varieties. Harvest when the head is firm, tight, and 6–8 in across before the curds begin to separate. Consistent soil moisture and boron-sufficient soil prevent hollow stem and poor curd formation. Matures in 55–80 days from transplant.

name: Cavolo Nero Kale
description: Also known as Tuscan or lacinato kale, this Italian heirloom bears puckered blue-black strap leaves used in soups and braises. Start indoors and transplant, or direct sow, spacing plants 15 inches apart in fertile soil. Harvest lower leaves first, working upward and leaving the growing crown intact for continuous production. Cold weather concentrates sugars, so the best-flavored leaves come after the first hard frosts. Watch for cabbage worms in warm spells and cover with row fabric if needed. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Cawood Delight Rhubarb
description: Cawood Delight is a modern English rhubarb, raised in Yorkshire and selected for stout, glossy, deep red stalks colored through to the flesh rather than only on the skin, giving pies and sauces a rich color without added dye. Stalks are noticeably thick for a garden cultivar, and the plant holds its color and firmness well into the main season rather than fading to green. It is a sturdy, cold-hardy grower well suited to northern gardens but can struggle through prolonged summer heat, so give it a site with some afternoon shade in warmer regions. Harvest by pulling stalks from the outside of the crown once established, and always discard the toxic leaves. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cayenne Blend Chile Pepper
description: A prolific blend of pencil-thin cayenne peppers used fresh, dried, ground, or strung into a decorative ristra. Start seed indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep warm for good germination. Transplant after nights stay above 55 degrees and support heavily laden plants if needed. Let fruits ripen to red for full heat, and dry them whole or grind for homemade red pepper flakes. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Cayenne Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix, maintaining soil temperature above 75°F for prompt sprouting. Set transplants out once the garden is fully warm and side-dress with a balanced fertilizer once plants begin flowering. Thin-walled cayenne fruits dry exceptionally well; allow them to redden fully on the plant before harvesting for drying. String harvested peppers in a warm, airy location or use a dehydrator to preserve them. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Cayennetta Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact No-Stake Cayenne)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cayennetta is an AAS-winning cayenne-type pepper bred for a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant that holds its heavy load of slender, upward-pointing red fruit without staking, unlike tall traditional cayenne varieties that tend to flop under the fruit's weight. The heat is noticeably milder than classic cayenne — moderate rather than fiery — making it more versatile for cooks who want cayenne flavor and color without maximum heat. Fruits can be picked green or left to ripen to full red for the best flavor and heat development, and the tidy plant size suits containers as well as garden beds. Harvest continuously to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Cayuga White Grape (Cornell-Bred Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
description: Released by Cornell's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in 1972 from a Seyval x Schuyler cross, this hybrid combines good winter hardiness with strong resistance to black rot and mildew, making it a reliable choice for home vineyards in humid eastern climates. Clusters of pale green-white grapes work well for both fresh eating and light, fruity white wine. Vines are moderately vigorous and benefit from cluster thinning to avoid overcropping, which can delay ripening. It buds out relatively late in spring, giving some protection from late frosts. Matures in 150–160 days from transplant.

name: CCN-51 Cacao
description: Bred in Ecuador in the 1960s by cacao researcher Homero Castro and named for the Colección Castro Naranjal breeding program, CCN-51 was developed for high yield and strong resistance to witches-broom and monilia pod rot, problems that devastated many older Ecuadorian cacao plantings. Unlike shade-loving heirloom types such as Criollo, it tolerates considerably more direct sun and bears earlier and more heavily, which has made it popular with commercial growers even though its beans need careful, extended fermentation to develop good chocolate flavor and avoid the acidic, astringent notes it is sometimes criticized for. Give it rich, moist, well-drained soil, consistent warmth and humidity, and protection from wind while young. Expect a vigorous, relatively fast-bearing tree that reaches production in as little as three years under good conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cedar Bay Cherry (Beach Cherry, Reinwardtiana Berry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; excellent salt and wind tolerance makes it outstanding for coastal gardens. Eugenia reinwardtiana (cedar bay cherry or beach cherry) is an Australian native Eugenia shrub or small tree from the tropical beaches, coastal scrub, and dry vine thickets of far north Queensland and the Northern Territory — one of the few Eugenia species native to Australia (most Eugenia, including the commercial Brazilian cherry group, are from the Americas). The plant bears small (1/2-inch), round, bright orange-red to scarlet fruits in clusters along the branches — similar in size and color to Surinam cherry (Eugenia uniflora) but with a different, distinctly sweet-acid, pleasant flavor without the resinous undertone characteristic of Surinam cherry. The fruits are eaten fresh as a snack and used in jams and beverages. Cedar bay cherry is especially valued in coastal tropical gardens for its outstanding tolerance of salt spray, wind, sandy soils, and coastal drought — growing naturally on exposed beaches and coastal headlands. The plant can be grown as a low shrub or allowed to develop into a small tree; it responds well to pruning for hedge use. The attractive, glossy, oval leaves and prolific berry production make it ornamentally pleasing. Very rare in cultivation outside tropical Queensland and the Pacific Islands. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Celebration Runner Bean (Salmon-Pink Flowered Ornamental-Edible Runner)
description: Celebration is a British-bred runner bean, an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner grown as much for its fragrant, salmon-pink flowers as for its harvest. The blossoms are a gentler color than the typical scarlet runner bean bloom, making the plant a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want an ornamental flowering vine that also produces a real crop of pods. Long, smooth, nearly stringless pods form heavily and stay tender when picked young, and the variety shows good tolerance to rust compared with older runner bean types. Its early cropping habit and rust tolerance have made it a reliable choice in cooler, damper climates where runner beans are a garden staple. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Celebration Swiss Chard
description: A rainbow-stemmed chard in red, magenta, orange, pink, yellow, and white beneath glossy dark green leaves. Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to six to twelve inches apart. It tolerates both light frost and summer heat, making it productive from spring through fall. Harvest outer leaves regularly and the plant keeps generating new growth from the center all season. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Celebrity Plus Tomato (Improved Anthracnose-Resistant Selection)
description: Celebrity Plus builds on the original 1984 AAS-winning Celebrity by adding resistance to anthracnose fruit rot, a fungal disease that causes sunken, discolored spots on ripening fruit in warm, humid, rain-prone regions. It keeps the same reliable determinate habit, uniform 7-8 ounce red globes, and broad resistance to Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, nematodes, and tobacco mosaic virus that made the original a garden standard. Stake or cage the compact plants, water at the soil line to keep foliage dry, and pick promptly at full color since the added anthracnose resistance still benefits from good sanitation practices. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Celebrity Tomato
description: Start seeds at 70–80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F; Celebrity is the most widely sold tomato variety in the United States, an All-America Selections winner from 1984 that became ubiquitous in home gardens because of its extraordinary disease resistance, consistent production, and reliable flavor across a wide range of climates. The medium-large (7–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits ripen uniformly and have classic tomato flavor — not exceptional, but reliably good and much better than supermarket tomatoes. The determinate, semi-bushy plants (3–4 feet tall) resist nearly every major tomato disease: Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), Verticillium wilt, nematodes, Alternaria, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot — the VFFNTASt on the label. This combination of compact size, disease resistance, and reliability makes Celebrity the recommended first tomato for new gardeners and the backup choice for experienced growers in difficult disease environments. In zone 9, it performs well in the spring window (transplanted February–March for May–June harvest) and in fall (transplanted late August for October–November harvest). Matures in 70–79 days from transplant.

name: Celeriac
description: Sow seeds on the surface of moist starting mix — they need light to germinate — and barely cover with vermiculite; seedling growth is extremely slow for the first 6 weeks. Transplant into rich, consistently moist soil and remove the lower side shoots throughout summer to encourage bulb development. Celeriac bulbs are at their best after light autumn frosts, which deepen the nutty flavor. Harvest before the ground freezes hard; trim roots and leaves and store in slightly moist sand in a cold root cellar. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Celery
description: Surface-sow or barely cover tiny seed with 1/8 in of moist mix; celery germinates slowly and needs consistent warmth and bright light from the start. Transplant into deeply prepared, rich soil and provide consistent, abundant moisture throughout the season, as drought quickly causes tough, stringy stalks. Hill soil around the base or use collars to blanch stalks to a paler color and milder flavor if desired. Harvest entire plants by cutting at soil level when stalks are 12–18 in tall and firm. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Celeste Fig
description: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; Celeste is the most popular and cold-hardy fig in the Deep South, producing small to medium, violet-brown figs with a honey-sweet, rose-pink interior that ripen mid-July through August. It is the standard home garden fig from Virginia to Texas and is considered by many to have the best flavor of any common fig variety. Figs fruit on second-year wood and on new growth late in the season — do not prune heavily in winter. Mulch roots in zone 7 to prevent root freeze-kill. Trees rarely need fertilizer and will produce heavy crops with minimal care once established. Other excellent Gulf Coast cultivars include 'Brown Turkey', 'LSU Purple', and 'LSU Gold'. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Celestial Blackberry (Heat-Tolerant Thornless Semi-Erect USDA Release)
description: Celestial, patented in 2023, is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry from the USDA-ARS/Oregon State cooperative program, bred from a cross between the thornless Eclipse and a thorny breeding selection carrying wild and cultivated Rubus germplasm from the southeastern United States. That Southeastern parentage gives Celestial noticeably better heat tolerance than most Oregon-bred blackberries. It yields heavily over a long mid-to-late-season harvest window, with small-to-medium, glossy, low-defect berries of excellent flavor. Canes are largely self-supporting but crop better on a simple trellis; remove fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and train in new primocanes for next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Celestial Radish (China White Winter Radish)
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked soil and thin early to prevent forked roots, since mature roots can reach 6-8 inches long and 2-3 inches thick. Celestial, also sold as China White, is a large all-white winter radish predating most modern daikon strains in Western seed trade, producing dense, crisp flesh that stores well in a root cellar or in the ground under mulch through early winter. Its flavor is milder and sweeter than black winter radishes but firmer and more substantial than spring salad types, making it well suited to braising, roasting, and long-keeping pickles. Harvest after a light frost for the best texture and flavor concentration. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Celtuce (Stem Lettuce)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or start indoors and transplant at 4–5 weeks; celtuce is grown primarily for its swollen, asparagus-like central stalk rather than its leaves, though young leaves are also edible. The stalk is ready when it is 1–1.5 inches in diameter and 12–15 inches tall; peel away the outer layer to reveal the crisp, mild interior. Keep soil consistently moist and rich in nitrogen for the fastest stalk development. Harvest before the plant bolts, as heat causes bitterness and pithy texture in the stalk. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cempedak (Champedak)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; cempedak tolerates partial shade better than jackfruit — useful in the middle canopy of tropical food forests. Artocarpus integer (cempedak or champedak) is a Southeast Asian fruit tree in the breadfruit family (Moraceae) — a close relative of jackfruit (A. heterophyllus) native to the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, and Sumatra. Like jackfruit, cempedak produces large composite fruits on the trunk and branches through cauliflory, but the fruits are smaller than jackfruit (typically 6–15 inches long, 4–6 inches diameter), cylindrical, and covered in small, soft, hexagonal-patterned protrusions with a yellow to orange-green exterior. The interior fruit segments are rich, sweet, aromatic, and exceptionally good — widely considered by Malaysian and Indonesian fruit lovers to be superior in flavor to jackfruit, with a denser, creamier, more strongly tropical-fruit character combining mango, banana, and custard apple notes. Cempedak is particularly popular in Malaysia fried: the individual fruit segments are battered and deep-fried as a street food (exactly like a tropical doughnut), which is a major culinary tradition. The seeds are edible when roasted or boiled. Cempedak is more shade-tolerant than jackfruit, making it useful as a middle-canopy tree in multi-story agroforestry systems. Requires genuinely tropical conditions (zone 11–12) without frost. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Centennial Hops (Super Cascade, Balanced Citrus-Floral Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Centennial is a Washington State-bred hop, often nicknamed 'Super Cascade' for its higher alpha acid content and similar but more intense citrus and floral aroma compared with Cascade, making it a versatile dual-purpose hop used for both bittering and aroma in American pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dried promptly. Like other Humulus lupulus cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a smaller harvest than in traditional hop-growing regions. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Centennial Sweet Potato (LSU 1966 Orange Gulf Coast Standard)
description: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in rows 3–4 feet apart in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost; avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes excessive vining and reduces root yield. Centennial was developed and released in 1966 by the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center, named to commemorate the 100th anniversary of LSU's establishment, and rapidly became the standard commercial sweet potato in Louisiana and throughout the Gulf South; it held that position for nearly two decades before Beauregard displaced it commercially in the late 1980s. Centennial produces medium to large, elongated, smooth, red-orange-skinned roots with deep orange, moist, sweet flesh of excellent quality; it was specifically selected for resistance to Fusarium wilt and other soilborne diseases persistent in Gulf Coast sweet potato production. Now maintained by seed savers and specialty nurseries as an important historical variety of Louisiana and Gulf South agriculture; excellent for home garden use with low inputs. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: Centennial Variegated Kumquat (Variegated-Leaf Ornamental Sweet Kumquat)
description: Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the best combination of foliage variegation and fruit color, since strong light intensifies both. This sport of a sweet round kumquat is grown as much for ornamental appeal as for fruit, with cream-and-green variegated leaves and young fruit that displays green-and-yellow stripes before ripening to solid orange, sweet-skinned fruit similar in flavor to Meiwa. It is self-fertile and well suited to large containers, where its compact size and eye-catching foliage make it a striking patio specimen. Bring container plants into a bright, cool indoor spot before hard frost in colder zones. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Centroamericano Coffee
description: Developed through a regional breeding collaboration led by World Coffee Research and PROMECAFE, Centroamericano is an F1 hybrid bred specifically for Central American smallholders, combining leaf rust resistance with yields substantially higher than long-standing regional standards like Caturra and Catuai. As an F1 hybrid its full vigor and yield benefits are only expressed in the first hybrid generation, so growers must obtain fresh hybrid seed from licensed nurseries rather than save their own. Field trials across the region have reported strong performance under real smallholder conditions rather than just experiment-station settings. Cultivate it under filtered shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil as with other Arabica cultivars. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Centurion Blueberry
description: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Centurion is a USDA-ARS-released rabbiteye blueberry prized as one of the latest-ripening varieties available, extending the harvest well past Tifblue into late July and into August in zone 8–9 and stretching the fresh-picking season for home growers and u-pick operations alike. It is also among the more cold-hardy rabbiteye selections, tolerating winter temperatures further north than many older varieties. Berries are small to medium, dark blue, firm, and flavorful, holding well on the bush without softening even in late-season heat. Plant with an early- or midseason variety such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, since rabbiteye blueberries including Centurion set little fruit without a compatible partner nearby. Established Centurion bushes are vigorous and heavy-bearing; renew a portion of the oldest canes each winter by cutting them to the ground to keep the bush productive and to encourage fresh, high-yielding new wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Centurion Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Centurion is a late-season rabbiteye blueberry that ripens in July in zone 8–9, extending the pick-your-own season after mid-season varieties like Brightwell have finished. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor and shipping quality, and the upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet at maturity. Centurion requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, making it suitable for zone 7–8b but less reliable in the mildest parts of zone 9a where chilling accumulation can be inconsistent. Plant as part of a multi-variety planting to achieve full-season harvest from late May through mid-July. The firm, large berries are particularly well-suited to fresh markets and U-pick operations where shelf life matters. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cerignola Olive (Large Mild Italian Table Olive)
description: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Cerignola takes its name from the town of Cerignola in the Puglia region of southern Italy and is grown for some of the largest table olives commonly available, producing plump, glossy fruit sold cured in both green and black stages with a mild, pleasant flavor and satisfyingly meaty texture that makes each olive feel substantial. The tree is vigorous and productive, well suited to warm Mediterranean-climate regions, and the large fruit size makes hand-harvesting and processing somewhat easier per volume of usable olive compared to smaller-fruited varieties. Harvest at the desired ripeness stage for green or black-cured olives, and cure appropriately, since fresh-picked olives of any variety are far too bitter to eat without proper processing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ceriman (Swiss Cheese Plant)
description: Root cuttings in moist mix and transplant to rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Monstera deliciosa (ceriman, Mexican breadfruit) is the beloved houseplant grown everywhere, but in frost-free zones 10–11 it grows outdoors as a vigorous climbing vine with its characteristic enormous, deeply split and hole-perforated leaves reaching 3 feet across, producing exotic 6–8 inch cone-shaped edible fruits that taste like a combination of banana, pineapple, and vanilla. The fruit takes over a year to ripen from flower to harvest — it ripens from the base upward as the hexagonal scale-like sections of the outer husk lift and fall away, revealing the white, creamy, flesh underneath. Unripe fruit contains oxalate crystals that cause severe mouth irritation; only fully ripe sections should be eaten. The flavor of ripe ceriman is exceptional and unlike any common fruit. It climbs vigorously by aerial roots and makes a dramatic specimen in tropical landscapes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ceylon Gooseberry (Kitambilla, Dovyalis)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; plant both male and female trees for fruit production. Dovyalis hebecarpa (Ceylon gooseberry or kitambilla) is a Sri Lankan thorny shrub or small tree producing small, 1-to-1.5-inch, velvety, dark-purple to maroon fruits with an intensely tart, acidic flavor somewhat resembling a sour cranberry or gooseberry crossed with tamarind — extremely sour fresh but outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups when sweetened. The plant is densely armed with sharp thorns and can be grown as an impenetrable security hedge while also producing edible fruit — a combination making it practically useful as a barrier plant in tropical gardens. In Sri Lanka, the fruits are made into a traditional preserve and the juice is used as a refreshing tart drink. The tree tolerates moderate drought and poor soils once established and can be used as a rootstock for grafting related Dovyalis species. It is dioecious — plant both male and female plants for fruiting. The compact form and spiny character make it useful as a living fence. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ceylon Spinach (Red Malabar Spinach)
description: Direct sow or transplant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade with a support to climb; Ceylon spinach is the red-stemmed form of Malabar spinach, producing striking bright-red vining stems, dark green to purplish leaves, and decorative dark reddish-purple berries. Like green Malabar spinach (B. alba), the leaves are thick, succulent, and mild-flavored when young, used fresh in salads or cooked as a spinach substitute in stir-fries, soups, and curries throughout tropical Asia. The red-stemmed form is highly ornamental — it can be used as a colorful edible trellis plant or allowed to cascade over a fence. It thrives in heat that wilts true spinach and is particularly productive in Gulf Coast summer gardens. In zone 9–11 it overwinters as a short-lived perennial. Tolerates partial shade better than most summer leafy greens. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Cha-Cha Kabocha Squash (Sweet Dry-Fleshed Japanese Squash)
description: Direct sow seed in warm, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in hills with room for the moderately compact vines. Cha-Cha is a Japanese-bred kabocha-type squash that won recognition as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally sweet, dry, dense orange flesh and reliable, early, high-yielding production compared to older kabocha types. The dark green, lightly ribbed rind covers flesh that develops a rich, nutty-sweet flavor similar to roasted chestnut once cured, making it a favorite for soups, roasting, and tempura in Japanese cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage to concentrate sugars. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Chadwick Cherry Pole Tomato
description: An heirloom indeterminate cherry tomato named for horticulturist Alan Chadwick, bearing heavy trusses of sweet, crack-resistant one to two ounce fruits. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Provide a tall trellis or cage and prune suckers to keep the vigorous vines manageable. Water evenly and pick the glossy red fruits regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Chadwick Cherry Tomato (Vigorous Heirloom Red Cherry)
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, providing tall, sturdy support for the exceptionally vigorous vines. Chadwick Cherry is a heirloom cherry tomato associated with biodynamic gardening pioneer Alan Chadwick, grown for its large, sprawling vines and heavy production of medium-sized, deep red, richly flavored cherry fruit with classic old-fashioned tomato taste. The plants are notably larger and more vigorous than many cherry tomato varieties, often reaching well over 8 feet if left unpruned, so give them generous space and a tall cage or trellis system. Harvest regularly once fruit turns fully red for the best flavor, and prune selectively to improve air circulation, since the dense vine growth can encourage fungal disease in humid climates. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Chambourcin Grape (Disease-Resistant French-American Red Wine Grape)
description: Chambourcin is a French-American hybrid bred by Joannes Seyve that has become a signature red wine grape of Missouri, Pennsylvania, and other humid eastern growing regions because of its strong natural resistance to downy and powdery mildew. It is a late-ripening variety that needs a fairly long, warm growing season to fully mature, so it is less suited to the shortest-season northern climates than Minnesota-bred hybrids. The wine is deeply colored with soft tannins and fruity black-cherry and berry character, and can be produced in styles ranging from light and fruity to full-bodied and oak-aged. Canopy management to expose fruit clusters helps color and ripeness given its late harvest window. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chamburo
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil; Vasconcellea candicans is adapted to dry inter-Andean valley conditions and is considerably more drought tolerant than common papaya — water moderately and avoid overwatering or waterlogged soils. Vasconcellea candicans (Chamburo or White-flowering Papaya) is a small tree in the Caricaceae family native to the dry inter-Andean valleys and hillside scrub of Ecuador and northern Peru at elevations of 200 to 2,800 meters — adapted to significantly drier conditions than most Vasconcellea species, which are predominantly cloud-forest plants. The white-flowered trees (the species name 'candicans' means 'becoming white' in reference to the flowers) produce clusters of elongated, oval, pale-yellow to white-green, fragrant fruits about the size of a large egg, with soft, white, papaya-textured flesh and a mild, sweet-sour, papaya-lemon-vanilla aromatic flavor. Chamburo fruits are traditionally cooked in Ecuadorian highland cuisine — used in the classic dish cuy al horno (roasted guinea pig with vegetable accompaniments) and in fruit preserves and juices. The plant tolerates dry conditions, shallow soils, and light frost considerably better than common papaya, making it potentially useful for drier zone 8b–10 gardens in the southwestern United States and similar Mediterranean climates. Dioecious; plant male and female trees. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chameleon Plant (Variegated Houttuynia)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally inside a buried barrier or large container; Chameleon plant spreads aggressively by rhizome and can quickly overrun a bed if planted directly in the ground without containment. Houttuynia cordata 'Chameleon' is a colorful variegated sport of the East Asian herb prized in Vietnamese and Chinese cooking for its citrus-and-fish-scented leaves, with heart-shaped foliage splashed in red, cream, yellow, and green and small white flower bracts in summer. The leaves are edible with the same distinctive pungent, coriander-and-citrus flavor as the plain green species and are used fresh in salads and wraps, but the cultivar is grown mainly as a striking, tough groundcover for wet shade, pond margins, and rain gardens where its color and vigor are assets rather than liabilities. Because it spreads so readily by rhizome and is difficult to fully eradicate once established, confine it firmly to containers or barrier-lined beds away from more delicate neighbors. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Chamomile (German)
description: Surface-sow the tiny seeds by pressing them onto moist soil without covering; they require light to germinate. Thin seedlings to 6–9 in apart in well-drained, moderately poor soil—rich soil encourages lush stems that flop easily. German chamomile self-seeds reliably and will naturalize in a sunny spot with minimal care. Harvest flower heads just as the white petals begin to reflex downward, which indicates peak essential oil content for tea. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Champagne Fig (Light-Skinned Heat-Tolerant Texas Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Champagne is a light greenish-yellow fig long grown in Texas dooryards, prized for its thin skin, amber-pink pulp, and very sweet, honeyed flavor that many gardeners rank above darker-skinned figs for fresh eating. It fruits on both old and new wood, giving a small early-summer breba crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer. Trees tolerate heat and humidity well and need little fertilizer once established, though a summer mulch layer helps even out soil moisture during fruit ripening. Protect young trees during hard freezes in the cooler end of its range; established plants regrow readily from the base after cold damage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Champagne Loquat (White-Fleshed California Loquat, Golden Yellow Loquat)
description: Plant grafted tree in well-drained soil in full sun; loquats tolerate poor soils and occasional drought once established but produce much better fruit with regular moisture; thin fruit clusters to 3–5 per cluster for larger individual fruits; harvest when fruit is fully colored and slightly soft to pressure — loquats do not ripen further after picking. Champagne is the premier commercial loquat variety of the American Pacific Coast — the standard variety grown in California's loquat orchards and the type most commonly available in specialty markets and Asian grocery stores on the West Coast. The fruits are medium to large (1.5–2.5 inches), pear-shaped to rounded with a pale yellow to warm golden-yellow skin, and the flesh inside is distinctively cream-white to very pale yellow — unlike the deeper orange flesh of most loquat varieties. The white-fleshed characteristic is associated with a milder, more delicate, slightly acidic-sweet flavor profile that many tasters consider the finest among loquats, with a subtle fragrance sometimes compared to mild apricot or very ripe melon. The 'Champagne' name captures this refinement of flavor. Trees are vigorous and productive, blooming in fall-winter and fruiting in late winter to spring — one of the earliest fruit trees to ripen in the year, providing fresh fruit in February to April when little else is available. In zone 9a and the Gulf Coast, Champagne loquat reliably crops when winter temperatures stay above 26°F; the developing fruits are the most frost-sensitive part of the plant. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Champanel Grape (Extremely Vigorous Pierce's Disease-Resistant Grape)
description: Plant in average to poorly drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis able to support very vigorous growth. Bred by Texas grape pioneer T. V. Munson in the late 1800s from a cross of the wild Vitis champinii with an American labrusca-type grape, Champanel is renowned for tolerating conditions that kill most grape vines outright, including heavy soil, occasional flooding, and Pierce's disease, a bacterial illness common in the humid South. The large, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, better suited to juice and jelly than fresh eating, but the vine's toughness makes it a dependable arbor and shade grape where other varieties fail. Prune to a permanent framework each winter to manage its rampant growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Champion Collard Greens
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Champion is an open-pollinated Southern collard variety developed as a disease-resistant improvement over traditional Georgia Southern — the same large-leafed, upright, non-heading collard type of traditional Southern cuisine but with improved resistance to downy mildew (Peronospora brassicae) that affects other varieties in warm, humid growing conditions typical of the Gulf South. The large, smooth, dark green to blue-green leaves with a prominent pale midrib are slightly more uniform in size and more upright in growth habit than Georgia Southern, making Champion a preferred choice for growers seeking both culinary quality and consistent appearance. The classic slow-simmered Southern preparation — cooking collard leaves for hours with smoked pork until deeply tender — works identically with Champion; the mild, rich flavor and large leaf size produce the same deeply satisfying braised greens associated with Southern food culture. Disease resistance makes Champion the practical choice for fall production in the Gulf South where humidity and warmth encourage fungal disease in more susceptible varieties. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Champion Collards (Upright Heat-Adapted Medium-Leaf Gulf South Collard)
description: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Champion is a widely recommended collard variety for Gulf South home gardens — producing upright plants with medium to large, waxy, blue-green leaves that are somewhat more compact and manageable than old-fashioned large-leaf types. Champion is valued for its combination of good heat tolerance in the planting period (August–September establishment in zone 9 requires tolerance of remaining summer heat), productive fall and winter yields, and excellent flavor quality that improves after frost exposure — the cold sweetens collard leaves by converting starches to sugars, a phenomenon well-known to Gulf South gardeners who prefer the post-frost harvest for their finest-flavored greens. The waxy leaf surface of Champion reduces water loss and contributes to the heat-establishment tolerance. In zone 9, collards are grown as a cool-season crop planted in August–September and harvested through November–February; the mild Gulf South winter allows continuous harvest from established plants without the repeated freeze damage that ends collard production in northern climates. Harvest outer leaves progressively (leaving the growing tip intact) for extended production from each plant. Champion has been recommended by southern cooperative extension services for decades as a reliable, productive, good-quality collard for both home garden and small-farm production. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Champion of England Pea
description: Sow directly in cool soil several weeks before the last frost, since this tall Victorian heirloom needs a long, cool season to reach its full six-foot height. Introduced in England in 1843, Champion of England quickly became renowned among market gardeners and exhibitors for the exceptionally sweet flavor of its plump pods, a reputation that has kept it in cultivation among heirloom growers ever since. Set stakes, netting, or brush at planting time, as the tall vines will topple without sturdy support. Pick pods regularly once they fill out to keep the vines productive and to catch the peas at their sweetest before starches develop. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Champion Quince (Large Late-Blooming American Heirloom Quince)
description: Champion is a nineteenth-century American quince selection valued for large, smooth, golden-yellow fruit and heavy, reliable production on a compact, self-fruitful tree. Its late bloom period helps flowers escape the late frosts that can wipe out a quince crop in colder springs, and the mild, less astringent flesh cooks down into fragrant preserves, paste, and baked dishes with less added sugar than sharper quince cultivars need. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune lightly in winter to maintain an open framework and good air circulation, which reduces fire blight risk. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic floral aroma. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Champion Radish
description: Sow seeds a half inch deep directly in the garden and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. These fast radishes are ready in under a month, producing round, cherry-red roots with crisp, mild white flesh. Keep the soil evenly moist to avoid pithiness and pungency, and sow in succession during the cool ends of the season. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Chanca Piedra (Stone Breaker, Shatterstone)
description: Direct sow in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; thin to 12 inches; harvest whole aerial plant before seeding for herbal use.
