Phyllanthus niruri (chanca piedra or stone breaker) is a small, unassuming tropical annual from the spurge family — widely distributed across the humid tropics of South America, Asia, and Africa — that has become one of the most studied herbal remedies for kidney stones, liver health, and hepatitis B. The common name 'chanca piedra' (Spanish: 'stone breaker') and 'shatterstone' reflect the plant's traditional Amazonian use for dissolving kidney and gallstones, a use with some clinical support in published research. The plant contains phyllanthin, hypophyllanthin, and other compounds with documented effects on calcium oxalate crystal formation (the primary component of kidney stones). As a garden plant, it is a neat, small annual with tiny, oval, alternate leaves arranged on graceful, feathery branches resembling a miniature fern — it volunteers readily in warm, moist gardens and self-seeds prolifically once established. Harvest the entire aerial plant when it begins to flower; dry for use in tea or tincture. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Chancellor Grape (Historic French-American Red Wine Grape)
description: Chancellor, originally bred in France as Seibel 7053, was one of the most widely planted French-American red hybrids in the eastern United States through the mid-20th century, prized for its reliable productivity and moderate winter hardiness. The grape ripens midseason into loose clusters of blue-black berries that yield a soft, fruity red wine, historically used both as a varietal and as a blending grape to add color and body. It is more susceptible to bunch rot in wet years than the newer Minnesota-bred hybrids, so growers should prioritize good air circulation and timely fungicide applications during fruit set. Cane- or cordon-train on a vertical trellis and moderate crop loads to concentrate flavor in the smaller clusters. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chandler Blueberry (Giant Blueberry)
description: Site bushes in full sun on acidic soil amended with peat or pine bark and mulch heavily to keep shallow roots cool and moist. Chandler is famous for producing some of the largest berries of any highbush blueberry, often nickel- to quarter-sized, with a mild, sweet flavor and a very long harvest window since ripe fruit holds well on the bush. Its extended ripening period spreads picking over several weeks rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Vigorous, upright canes benefit from a second pollinator variety nearby to improve fruit set and size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chandler Pomelo
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun in a warm, sheltered site; Chandler is a University of California Riverside pomelo selection prized for its very large fruit (often 4-6 pounds), thick pink-blushed rind, and sweet, low-acid pink flesh with relatively little of the bitterness found in some other pomelo types. The huge fruit takes a long season to mature, typically ripening in late fall to winter, and the tree needs a warm, essentially frost-free site to size and sweeten the crop properly, making it best suited to zone 9b-10 in sheltered microclimates or container culture that can be moved under cover for winter. The thick rind makes the fruit easy to peel and section by hand once cut open, and segments hold their shape well for fresh eating, salads, and citrus platters. Give young trees consistent moisture and wind protection, and expect the first meaningful crop several years after planting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chandler Strawberry
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-amended, raised beds or hill-and-furrow systems with good drainage; Chandler was released jointly by the California Strawberry Advisory Board and the USDA in 1983 and rapidly became the most widely planted commercial strawberry in the world. In California's Central Coast, it produces the majority of fresh market strawberries sold in the United States. In Florida and the Gulf Coast, it is the standard commercial season variety, planted October–November for harvest December–April. Chandler produces very large (1–2 oz), firm, bright red, conical berries with excellent sweet-acid flavor that remains consistent over an extended harvest season. The early-season production (December–January in zone 9) and large berry size made it the commercial benchmark. For home growers in zone 9, plant in raised beds with plastic mulch and drip irrigation; Chandler's vigor and large size reward careful management. Fruits can develop poorly in extreme heat — Chandler's season ends as temperatures rise above 80°F. Remove runners to keep plants productive. In zone 9, treat as an annual. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Chandler Walnut (California Commercial Standard Walnut, UC Davis Walnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Chandler benefits from cross-pollination though it will produce some crop alone; the large, thin-shelled nuts ripen in September–October and are harvested by mechanical knock-down or hand-collection when hulls begin to split; allow nuts to dry at 100°F for several days after harvest to reduce moisture content for storage. Chandler walnut is the most widely planted commercial English (Persian) walnut variety in California and among the most important walnut varieties in the world — released by UC Davis in 1979 from the UC Walnut Improvement Program as a selection with exceptional combination of large nut size, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (above 50%), and excellent kernel color and quality. California produces approximately 75% of the world's English walnut supply, and Chandler accounts for more than half of that production — making Chandler the single most economically important walnut variety on earth. The variety produces very large (28–30 mm), well-shaped nuts with a thin shell that cracks easily and yields plump, light-colored halves with mild, sweet walnut flavor and high oil content typical of premium English walnuts. The light kernel color (essential for premium market pricing, where darker kernels command lower prices) and consistent quality in the drying and processing process made Chandler the preferred commercial variety over the older standards (Franquette, Hartley, Serr). For home orchards in zones 6–9, Chandler delivers premium walnut quality with good productivity. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chanee Durian (D123)
description: Chanee (registered in Malaysia as D123 and grown widely in Thailand as well) is one of the earliest-fruiting and most productive durian cultivars, popular with growers for its precocious bearing, consistent annual cropping, and moderately sweet, fiber-free flesh. Because it fruits reliably at a younger tree age than many other cultivars, Chanee is often recommended as a starter or trial cultivar in new durian plantings. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with high humidity and steady warm temperatures, protecting flowers from pesticide disturbance since durian relies on nocturnal bat pollination. Allow the spiny husks to drop naturally rather than cutting them, both for safety and because the fruit continues to develop sugars right up to natural fall. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chang Bai Hardy Kiwi (Chinese Changbai Mountain Kiwiberry)
description: Chang Bai is a female hardy kiwi selected near the Changbai Mountain region on the China-North Korea border, valued for productive, sweetly flavored, unusually apple- or heart-shaped green fruit. Originating from a cold, mountainous native range, it carries strong winter hardiness typical of Actinidia arguta selections from northern China. As a dioecious vine it will not fruit without a compatible male hardy kiwi planted nearby, and its late flowering allows pollination from either hardy arguta males or early-blooming fuzzy-kiwi males. Provide a sturdy permanent trellis for the vigorous twining growth habit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Changsha Tangerine (Cold-Hardy Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, sheltered from cold north winds; mulch well and protect young trees through their first few winters until established. Changsha is a small-fruited mandarin native to Hunan Province, China, valued above nearly all other citrus for its exceptional cold hardiness — mature trees have survived and fruited after temperatures well below 10°F, making it one of the few true mandarins that can be grown outdoors, unprotected, in the Gulf South and even into the coastal Southeast beyond typical citrus range. The small, flattened, deep orange fruits are intensely sweet with a rich, aromatic mandarin flavor, though they are notably seedy, which has historically limited commercial interest despite the outstanding flavor and hardiness. Changsha is widely used by cold-hardy citrus breeders and hobbyists both as a garden fruit tree in its own right and as breeding stock for hardier hybrid mandarins. A rewarding choice for Gulf South gardeners who want the flavor of a true mandarin from a tree that can survive outdoors through a hard winter, zone 8–10. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chantenay Carrot (Red Cored Chantenay)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Chantenay is the ideal carrot for difficult clay or stony soils where standard longer varieties fork and struggle — the squat, broad-shouldered, 4–6 inch roots with wide tops and tapered tips develop fully in heavy or shallow soils that prevent the growth of Nantes or Imperator types. Despite being originally bred for difficult soils, Chantenay has excellent rich flavor and high sugar content, with crisp orange flesh and a traditional carrot taste. Perfect for canning, juicing, and storage; the broad shoulders and high shoulder content also make it efficient to harvest. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Chantenay Royal Carrot
description: Sow seeds shallowly in loose soil and keep the surface consistently moist through the slow germination period. This stocky, tapered variety about four to five inches long tolerates heavier and clay soils better than long carrots. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and harvest as needed, storing the sweet, red-cored roots in a cool place for winter use. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Chaotian Pepper (Facing Heaven Chili)
description: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chaotian bears clusters of small, conical, very hot red chilis that point upward toward the sky as they ripen, giving the pepper its Chinese name, and is a staple in Sichuan and Guizhou cooking, used both fresh and dried in chili oil, hot pots, and spice blends. The compact, heavily fruiting plants produce abundant small pods over a long summer harvest. Harvest continuously to encourage more flowering, or leave pods to dry on the plant for storage. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Chapalote Corn (Ancient Mexican Popcorn-Type Flint Corn)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Chapalote is one of the oldest documented corn varieties still cultivated in the Americas, a tall, dark-kerneled flint corn from the coastal state of Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico with a distinctive popcorn-like kernel texture that connects it to some of the earliest domesticated maize lineages. It is used both for pinole (roasted, ground corn) and as a genuinely popping corn, reflecting its ancient, less fully domesticated kernel structure. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Chaparral Sage (Purple Sage)
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; chaparral sage (purple sage) is a large, aromatic California native shrub of the southern Coast Ranges, producing distinctive white-woolly (leucophylla = white-leaved) leaves that reflect harsh summer sunlight and reduce water loss — an adaptation to the extreme summer heat and drought of California chaparral. The lavender-purple flowers in late spring to early summer are striking and produce abundant nectar for native bees and hummingbirds. One of the 'allelopathic' California sages — the plant releases volatile chemicals that inhibit the germination of competing plants around it, creating a distinctive bare zone between the sage canopy and the surrounding grassland. The famous 'elfin forest' scent of California chaparral comes largely from this species and coast sage (S. apiana). Essential for authentic California coastal sage scrub plantings. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Chaparral Weeping Mulberry (Fruitless Ornamental Weeping Mulberry)
description: Chaparral is a fruitless male selection of white mulberry grown strictly as an ornamental, valued for cascading, gracefully weeping branches clothed in glossy, deeply cut emerald-green leaves that arch to the ground when left untrimmed. Because it produces only small, inconspicuous male catkins and sets no fruit, it is a favorite patio and small-yard tree in Gulf Coast landscapes where homeowners want mulberry foliage texture without the mess of dropped berries. It tolerates heat, drought, urban pollution, and salt spray better than most flowering ornamentals, making it useful along coastal streets and parking areas. Prune annually just above the graft union to shape the weeping canopy and remove any upright shoots that revert toward the rootstock's growth habit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Charapita Pepper (Wild Peruvian Pepper)
description: Start seeds at 80–85°F with bottom heat and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nights are reliably above 60°F; charapita is a tiny wild Capsicum chinense from the Peruvian Amazon, producing hundreds of pea-sized (4–5mm), perfectly round yellow to orange fruits on sprawling, branchy plants. Despite their diminutive size, charapita peppers are among the hottest available (50,000–100,000 Scoville) with an extraordinary fruity, citrusy, aromatic complexity that has made them the world's most expensive pepper by weight in specialty markets — a single small jar of charapita paste can command premium prices in European cuisine. The flavor is uniquely fruity and intensely floral, unlike the purely sharp heat of most hot peppers. Plants are prolific producers if given warmth and consistent moisture, loaded with dozens of tiny fruits that ripen from green to yellow to orange over several months. In zone 9, treat as an annual or overwinter indoors; in zone 10–12, plants can become productive multi-year shrubs. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Chardonnay Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Chardonnay needs a long, warm growing season and consistent trellising and pruning to ripen fruit and produce quality wine grapes. The most widely planted white wine grape in the world, it produces tight clusters of small, thin-skinned green-gold grapes that adapt to a remarkably wide range of climates and winemaking styles, from crisp, mineral, unoaked wines in cool regions to rich, buttery, oak-aged wines in warmer ones. Vigorous and relatively easy to grow compared to some finicky wine varieties, it still requires careful canopy management, disease monitoring, and a well-drained site to reach commercial fruit quality, and benefits from professional pruning guidance for home vineyard growers new to viticulture. Train young vines to a permanent trellis system, thin fruit clusters if overcropping occurs, and harvest based on sugar and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date, since ripeness timing varies significantly by site and season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Charentais Cantaloupe Melon
description: A true French cantaloupe too fragile to ship commercially, with smooth skin, light green stripes, and intensely fragrant creamy-orange flesh. Start seed indoors in peat pots two to three weeks before setting out, or direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm. Give vines full sun, warmth, and steady moisture while fruit develops. Harvest at full slip when the fruit detaches easily from the stem and the aroma turns rich and sweet. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Charentais Melon
description: This intensely fragrant French melon has smooth gray-green skin and deep orange, aromatic flesh. Start seed indoors three weeks before transplanting to gain a head start in short-season areas, handling the sensitive roots gently. Grow on black plastic mulch with row cover early to trap warmth, removing cover at flowering for pollinators. Reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit turns yellowish, smells sweet, and slips easily from the vine. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Charisma PMR Pumpkin (Cornell-Bred Powdery Mildew Resistant Jack-O-Lantern)
description: Sow directly in hills after the soil has warmed, spacing hills three to four and a half feet apart to give the reduced-length vines room to develop without crowding. Charisma PMR emerged from a joint Cornell University and Johnny's Selected Seeds breeding program and matures a bit later and lighter orange than earlier types like Racer, filling out to 14-18 pounds with a blocky, slightly russeted rind and a slender but sturdy handle. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew keeps leaves functional longer into the season, which matters most in regions where warm, humid nights favor the disease. Let fruit color fully and the rind harden before cutting from the vine, leaving several inches of stem attached to prolong storage life. Matures in 100–105 days from seed.

name: Charity Mahonia (Upright Fragrant Winter Flower Spikes)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Charity, a classic Slieve Donard nursery hybrid of Mahonia japonica and Mahonia lonicera, bears tall, upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers in late fall into winter, held above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by tart blue-black berries usable for jelly or wine. Its architectural form and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Charleston Belle Sweet Pepper (USDA Nematode-Resistant Sweet Bell)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Charleston Belle is particularly important for Gulf South gardeners with heavy, sandy soils where root-knot nematodes are endemic — standard sweet bell varieties often show severe stunting and yield loss in nematode-infested soils where Charleston Belle performs normally. Charleston Belle was developed by USDA-ARS researchers at the U.S. Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina specifically to address one of the most significant problems in Southern pepper production: root-knot nematodes (primarily Meloidogyne incognita and M. arenaria), soil-dwelling parasites that infest the roots of peppers and virtually every other vegetable grown in the sandy soils of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, causing severe root galling, stunted growth, and dramatically reduced yields. Most commercial sweet bell pepper varieties are highly susceptible to these nematodes; Charleston Belle incorporates strong resistance derived from Capsicum chinense sources, allowing normal growth and fruit production in soils that would cripple susceptible varieties. The bell-shaped fruits are medium to large (3–4 lobes, 3–4 inches in diameter) and ripen from pale cream-yellow to red; they are crisp, sweet, and of excellent quality comparable to standard commercial bell varieties. Charleston Belle is an invaluable vegetable for Gulf South gardeners (zones 8–10) gardening in sandy or loamy soils where nematodes are a documented problem. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Charleston Gold Rice
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; keep the bed consistently saturated through the growing season, whether in a true flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Charleston Gold was bred at Clemson University by crossing historic Carolina Gold rice with a semi-dwarf Southeast Asian variety to combine Carolina Gold's prized nutty, aromatic flavor with sturdier, shorter stalks that resist lodging and a shorter season to maturity. The gold-hulled, long grain cooks up fragrant and tender, much like its Carolina Gold parent, but the more compact plants stand up better to wind and rain and free up the bed several weeks earlier. Harvest when seed heads droop and the grain has turned golden-brown, then thresh and dry before hulling. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Charleston Gray Watermelon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, fertile soil — watermelons are especially productive in sandy soils common to the Gulf South and Southeast; Charleston Gray is a 1954 All-America Selections award winner developed by the USDA in Charleston, South Carolina, and for several decades it was the dominant commercial and home-garden watermelon variety in the American South. The large, oblong fruits with distinctive pale gray-green skin and bright red, sweet, crisp flesh are resistant to anthracnose and fusarium wilt — the two most destructive watermelon diseases in the humid Southeast — which made Charleston Gray vastly superior to earlier varieties in southern garden conditions. The extra-thick rind (up to 1 inch) also gave exceptional shipping durability, which drove its commercial adoption. The sweetness and texture of Charleston Gray flesh represent the classic Southern watermelon flavor profile: intensely sweet, very juicy, with a fine-grained, melting texture that differs from modern seedless types. In zone 9 the heat and long growing season bring out the best flavor and maximum size. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Charleston Gray Watermelon
description: A classic oblong watermelon with greenish-gray rind and sweet red flesh, bred by the USDA for disease resistance to Fusarium wilt and anthracnose. Start seed indoors in peat pots or direct sow once soil is warm, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room. Water consistently while fruit sizes up, then ease off as melons approach ripeness to concentrate sweetness. Harvest when the ground spot turns creamy yellow and the tendril nearest the fruit dries. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Charleston Hot Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Charleston Hot is a Clemson University-developed cayenne-type hot pepper (70,000–100,000 SHU) bred specifically for production in the hot, humid South. An All-America Selections winner, it produces abundantly on compact, upright plants and carries strong disease resistance to tobacco etch virus and tobacco mosaic virus, which is valuable in zone 8–9 where solanaceous virus pressure is high. The slim, tapered, 3–4 inch fruits ripen from yellow-green through yellow-orange to red; they are used fresh, dried, or ground into hot sauce and cayenne powder. The heavy yield of small-fruited plants makes this variety excellent for hot sauce production — a single mature plant can yield hundreds of pods per season. Dry fully ripe red fruits in a dehydrator or oven for ground cayenne. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Charleston Long Speckled Butterpea
description: Set a sturdy 6- to 8-foot trellis or pole at planting time, since this old South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom is a rampant climber that will not perform as a bush type. The small, flattened seeds are handsomely mottled brown-on-tan, giving the variety its name, and cook down tender with the rich, mild, buttery flavor Charleston cooks prize in a proper pot of butterbeans and rice. It sets pods steadily through the hottest, most humid weeks of a Gulf Coast summer when many snap beans have stalled, and because it flowers over a long season, regular picking at the green-shell stage keeps vines productive into fall. Save seed by letting some pods dry fully on the vine, since this open-pollinated heirloom breeds true. Matures in 78–90 days from seed.

name: Charleston Wakefield Cabbage
description: Set transplants 15–18 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered as heads size up to avoid splitting. Charleston Wakefield was selected in South Carolina from Early Jersey Wakefield stock as a slightly larger, slightly later-maturing improvement, retaining the same distinctive pointed, conical head shape while producing bigger 3–4 pound heads with a bit more heat tolerance for Southern spring gardens. It became a standard commercial and home-garden variety across the South in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, valued for uniform heads, good tip-burn resistance, and dependable performance under the variable spring weather of the Gulf Coast and Southeast. The sweet, tender, finely textured heads are excellent fresh, in slaw, or braised. A dependable regional heirloom for zone 4–10 gardens. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Charlotte Swiss Chard (AAS-Winning Compact Red Chard)
description: Direct sow or transplant into rich soil and keep evenly watered, since this compact hybrid rewards close, container-friendly spacing. Named an All-America Selections winner, it produces bright cherry-red stalks and veins beneath glossy, deeply savoyed dark green leaves on a notably uniform, tidy plant. Its shorter stature and vigorous regrowth after cutting make it well suited to raised beds and pots as well as open garden rows. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Chater Pomegranate (Camarillo Mottled-Skin Pomegranate)
description: Chater originated in Camarillo, California, selected for large fruit, typically four to five inches across, with an unusual mottled red-green rind that stays noticeably lighter than the deep red of Wonderful even at full ripeness. The flavor is sweet, though the seeds run harder than in soft-seeded modern selections, and the shrub has a reputation as a comparatively shy bearer that rewards patience with a smaller but distinctive crop. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune to an open form since airier canopies help the mottled fruit ripen evenly. Its unusual coloring makes it a conversation piece in a mixed pomegranate planting even where yield takes a back seat to more productive cultivars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chattooga Blackberry (Early-Ripening Erect Thornless Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Chattooga is a University of Arkansas erect thornless blackberry release valued for ripening earlier in the season than most other thornless cultivars, extending the harvest window at the front end. It produces medium to large, firm, glossy black berries with good flavor on vigorous, upright canes that need only modest trellising support. Its early ripening makes it a useful companion to later-season thornless cultivars for a longer overall blackberry harvest. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Chaucer Blueberry (Rabbiteye Blueberry)
description: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5-5.0 with pine bark, peat, or sulfur before planting; Chaucer is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Florida in 1985 and named for the English poet, ripening mid-season a bit after Climax and around the same time as Woodard. The bushes are vigorous and distinctly spreading in habit, throwing out wide lateral canes that benefit from an every-other-year thinning of old wood to keep the canopy open and productive. Berries are medium-sized with a somewhat wet picking scar, so they are best suited to home use, farmers-market sales, or u-pick harvest rather than mechanical picking or long-distance shipping, since the moist scar shortens shelf life. Heavy yields and reliable mid-season ripening make Chaucer a solid gap-filler between earlier and later rabbiteye varieties in a Gulf Coast planting; mulch deeply with pine bark and irrigate through fruit swell, as the shallow, fibrous roots dry out quickly in sandy coastal soils. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chautauqua Gooseberry (Large Sweet English-Type Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, siting for good air circulation, and prune annually to an open center. Chautauqua is a large-fruited English-type dessert gooseberry, producing pale yellow-green berries considerably larger than most American-type varieties, with a rich, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating out of hand rather than only cooking, a genuine treat among gooseberries where many varieties lean more tart. Because it descends primarily from European Ribes uva-crispa stock rather than the mildew-resistant American Ribes hirtellum lineage, it is more susceptible to American gooseberry mildew and benefits from a well-ventilated planting site and attentive pruning to reduce disease pressure. Harvest when berries reach full color and soften slightly for the sweetest dessert-quality fruit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chaya (Tree Spinach)
description: Plant stem cuttings in well-drained to sandy soil in full sun; chaya is a vigorous, heat-tolerant tropical shrub native to the Yucatan that produces enormous crops of large, spinach-like leaves year-round in frost-free climates. The leaves are exceptionally nutritious — very high in protein, calcium, iron, and carotenoids — but must be cooked for at least 5 minutes before eating, as raw leaves contain hydrocyanic glycosides that dissipate completely with cooking. Once cooked, leaves taste like a mild, slightly earthy spinach and can substitute in any cooked greens recipe. Chaya is extraordinarily productive: a single mature bush can yield over 10 pounds of leaves per week in warm weather. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and neglect better than almost any other vegetable. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Chaya (Tree Spinach, Mayan Spinach, Cnidoscolus)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Chaya is extremely drought-tolerant once established and adapts to poor, sandy, or clay soils with minimal fertilizer. Cnidoscolus chayamansa is a spinach tree native to the Yucatan Peninsula and Central America where it has been cultivated as a staple cooked green by the Maya civilization for over a millennium. The leaves are exceptionally nutritious — with higher concentrations of protein, calcium, iron, vitamin C, and beta-carotene than most leafy vegetables including kale and spinach — and Chaya has become a widely promoted food security crop in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The plant is an incredibly productive cut-and-come-again perennial: harvest the top 6–10 inches of stem tips continuously through the warm season and the plant regrows rapidly. The large, dark-green, deeply-lobed, maple-like leaves are strikingly ornamental. CRITICAL SAFETY NOTE: Never eat Chaya raw — the fresh leaves contain hydrocyanic glycosides that can cause poisoning. Cook for a minimum of 5 minutes (boiling, steaming, or sautéing) to neutralize the toxins. Once cooked, the greens are safe and delicious, tasting like a mild spinach-collard cross. In zone 9, Chaya is one of the most productive warm-season leafy greens available, producing from May through November even in summer heat that wilts conventional spinach. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Chaya Tree Spinach
description: IMPORTANT: Cook leaves for 20 minutes before eating — raw chaya contains toxic hydrocyanic acid glycosides; also do not cook in aluminum cookware as the reaction can cause illness. Plant cuttings in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained, fertile soil; Cnidoscolus chayamansa grows vigorously in warm climates, producing abundant leaves for harvest within 90 days of planting. Cnidoscolus chayamansa (Chaya, Tree Spinach, or Mayan Spinach) is a vigorous, semi-succulent, fast-growing shrub in the Euphorbiaceae family native to the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico and cultivated throughout Mesoamerica, the Caribbean, and increasingly in warm-climate gardens worldwide as one of the most productive and nutritious perennial leafy greens available for subtropical and tropical climates. The Maya civilization used chaya as a primary vegetable crop for thousands of years — and modern nutritional analysis confirms it is extraordinarily nutrient-dense: the leaves contain 2–3 times more protein, iron, calcium, and vitamin C than spinach (Spinacia oleracea), and are among the highest vitamin-K-containing vegetables known. Chaya is propagated exclusively from stem cuttings (it rarely sets seed in cultivation) and grows into a large, productive bush that can be harvested continuously throughout the year in warm climates — making it potentially the most productive perennial leafy green per square foot available for Gulf Coast, Florida, and subtropical gardens. CRITICAL WARNING: raw chaya leaves contain hydrocyanic acid glycosides that cause serious illness if eaten raw or undercooked — leaves must be boiled (not steamed or microwaved) for a minimum of 20 minutes and the cooking water discarded before eating. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Chayote
description: Plant the whole fruit (it is the seed) on its side with the broad end slightly angled down, barely covered with moist soil; sprouting begins from the narrow end. Provide a very strong trellis as a single mature vine can reach 30 feet and produce dozens to hundreds of fruits per season. Harvest fruits when they are 3–6 inches long and the skin is still smooth and light green; older fruits become pithy and hard. In Zones 9–11, chayote is perennial and will produce an edible tuberous root as well as fruits; in cooler zones, grow as an annual by starting fresh each spring. Matures in 80–120 days from transplant.

name: Che Fruit
description: Che, sometimes called the Chinese mulberry, produces round, red, fig-like fruit with a mild, melon-melon flavor. It is drought-tolerant and adaptable once established, growing well in full sun on well-drained soil. Seedling trees can be thorny and slow to bear, so plant a grafted, female cultivar for earlier crops; a male tree nearby can improve set. Prune to keep it manageable and net the sweet fruit against birds as it ripens in autumn. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cheddar Cauliflower (Yellow-Orange Beta-Carotene Cauliflower)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; set out transplants in rich, moist, well-drained soil 18–24 inches apart; keep consistently moist; in warm climates (zones 7–10) plant for fall harvest from summer transplants for best head development; harvest when heads are tight and before the curds begin to separate. Cheddar is a yellow-orange cauliflower that gets its remarkable color from high concentrations of beta-carotene — the same orange pigment found in carrots, sweet potatoes, and winter squash — resulting in orange cauliflower heads that retain and even intensify their color when cooked (unlike red cabbage, which loses color to cooking liquid). The orange coloring signals significantly higher nutritional value than white cauliflower: approximately 25 times more beta-carotene per serving, providing provitamin A activity that white cauliflower lacks. The flavor is slightly sweeter and nuttier than standard white varieties, and the heads hold their color well through roasting, steaming, and cauliflower 'steaks' — making Cheddar cauliflower one of the most visually dramatic and nutritionally enriched brassicas for the home garden. The AAS award-winning orange/yellow Cheddar type was developed by Cornell University researchers and initially commercialized by Bejo Seeds; it performs best as a fall crop in warm climates where summer transplants mature into cooler fall temperatures that favor head development. Matures in 68–80 days from transplant.

name: Cheers Cabbage (Crack-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Cheers is a cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to Fusarium yellows and intermediate resistance to black rot, two diseases that can persist in garden soil and spread through wet conditions. It is especially valued for resisting head-splitting even when hit by high heat or a sudden heavy rain after a dry spell, a common cause of wasted cabbage crops in changeable Gulf South weather. The round, dense, blue-green heads have good storage quality once harvested. Cut heads once firm and fully sized, and keep soil evenly moist through head formation for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Chef's Choice Bicolor Tomato (AAS-Winning Gold-and-Pink Beefsteak)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Bicolor is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato producing large fruit with a striking golden-yellow background streaked and blushed with rose-pink, giving each slice a marbled, sunset-like appearance on the plate as well as sweet, low-acid, heirloom-style flavor with far less of the tanginess of standard red tomatoes. It shares the reliable size, productivity, and disease resistance of the wider Chef's Choice series. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Chef's Choice Black Tomato (AAS-Winning Dark Beefsteak)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Black is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato bringing the dense, complex, almost smoky-sweet flavor associated with heirloom black tomatoes into a modern hybrid, with large, dusky mahogany-red-brown fruit and a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing. It joins the wider Chef's Choice color series — the fruit color changes but the reliable size, disease resistance, and productivity of the line carry through. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Chef's Choice Orange Tomato (AAS-Winning Orange Beefsteak)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Orange is an AAS National Winner bred from the beloved heirloom Amana Orange, keeping its rich, sweet, low-acid flavor and bright orange beefsteak-size fruit while adding the disease resistance and productivity of a modern hybrid. Fruits regularly reach a pound or more, with a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing, and the vivid orange color makes a striking addition to a mixed tomato platter or salad. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Chef's Choice Pink Tomato (AAS-Winning Large Pink Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines and pruning to a few main leaders for the largest fruit. Chef's Choice Pink is an AAS-winning member of the Chef's Choice series of large-fruited, richly colored heirloom-type beefsteaks bred for exceptional flavor alongside modern disease resistance, producing smooth, deep rosy-pink 10–12 ounce fruit with the low-acid, sweet, complex flavor prized in classic pink heirlooms like Brandywine but on sturdier, more productive plants. Consistent watering and monthly feeding through the season support the heavy fruit load these large-fruited types carry, and mulching helps prevent blossom end rot during dry spells. The rich pink color and superior flavor make it a favorite for fresh eating and slicing, holding up well in Gulf South heat better than many thin-skinned pink heirlooms. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Chefini Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Dark-Skinned Zucchini)
description: Chefini was bred by Petoseed and released in 1965 as one of the first hybrid zucchinis to win an AAS award, valued for fruit so deeply dark green it reads almost black under garden light. The vigorous vines spread more than many modern compact hybrids, so give plants extra room or plan on a wider bed than typical bush-type zucchini. Harvest young at 6-8 inches for the most tender skin and flavor, and keep picking every couple of days since the sprawling growth habit hides fruit under the foliage. In Gulf Coast gardens, its early maturity lets gardeners get a harvest in before summer heat and squash vine borer pressure peak. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Chehalem Blackberry
description: Chehalem is a USDA-ARS trailing blackberry bred and released in Oregon, historically significant chiefly as one of the two parent cultivars — together with Olallie — used in the 1945 cross that produced the modern benchmark cultivar Marion. Like Marion, it carries long, thorny trailing canes and ripens firm, richly flavored fruit, though it has been almost entirely eclipsed in commercial plantings by its more celebrated offspring and by later thornless USDA-ARS releases. Plant dormant canes in early spring against a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since the sprawling growth habit will not support itself. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and train the current season's primocanes onto the wires to bear next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Chelan Cherry (Early-Season Dark Sweet Cherry)
description: Chelan was developed by a Washington State tree fruit breeding program and is grown commercially for its dark red, firm fruit that ripens roughly a week to ten days ahead of Bing, making it one of the earliest good-quality dark sweet cherries available. It is self-unfruitful and needs a pollinizer such as Black Tartarian or Index that blooms at the same time. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and protect the early blossoms from late frosts, since early bloom is both its advantage and its main risk. Water consistently as fruit sizes to reduce cracking, and thin overloaded branches to keep fruit size up. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chelois Grape (French-American Hybrid Red Wine Grape)
description: A Seibel-bred French-American hybrid, Chelois produces medium clusters of dark blue berries that yield soft, fruity red wines often compared in style to light Burgundies. It ripens reliably in mid-season and has a long history in eastern American vineyards for both varietal and blending wines. The vine performs best on a cane-pruned trellis and appreciates cluster thinning to concentrate flavor in cooler years. It shows good resistance to winter injury but benefits from fungicide attention in humid climates due to moderate mildew susceptibility. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chemlali Olive (Heat-Tolerant Tunisian Dual-Purpose Olive)
description: Chemlali is Tunisia's dominant olive variety, prized for exceptional heat and drought tolerance and dual use for both oil and cured table olives. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility soil, where it will tolerate the intense summer heat of the Gulf Coast better than many cooler-climate Mediterranean cultivars. It is only partially self-fertile, so plant a second cultivar such as Arbequina or Koroneiki nearby to ensure good fruit set. Harvest green for brine-cured table olives in early fall, or allow fruit to darken into November for oil pressing. Established Chemlali trees need very little supplemental irrigation once their deep root system is in place. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chempedak
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; chempedak is a close relative of jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), native to Southeast Asia from Indonesia to Thailand, producing large, barrel-shaped compound fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches like jackfruit but typically smaller and sweeter. The fruits have a strongly aromatic, intensely sweet, almost fermented flavor that is more pronounced than jackfruit — considered by many Southeast Asian aficionados to be superior to jackfruit for fresh eating. The soft, yellow-orange arils surrounding the seeds are eaten fresh, fried in batter (a popular street food in Malaysia), or incorporated into desserts. The seeds are roasted or boiled and eaten. More tolerant of wet, poorly drained soils than jackfruit, making it suitable for sites that jackfruit would struggle in. An outstanding choice for tropical South Florida gardens seeking an alternative to the more common jackfruit. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chenango Strawberry Apple (Delicate Strawberry-Scented New York Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Chenango Strawberry originated in Chenango County, New York in the early 1800s, prized for its distinctive elongated, conical shape and delicate strawberry-like aroma and flavor note that gives it its evocative name — a subtlety not found in most other apple varieties. The thin, red-striped skin covers pale, tender, juicy flesh that is best appreciated fresh, since the delicate texture and short storage life make it poorly suited to long keeping or heavy cooking. Grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors for its unusual character and history rather than commercial reliability, it rewards patient home growers with a genuinely distinctive eating experience unlike common modern apples. Harvest in late summer to early fall and use fairly promptly, since the fruit softens quickly off the tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cheniere Rice
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cheniere is a very early-maturing, semi-dwarf long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter and named for the wooded ridges (cheniers) of coastal Louisiana, bred to reach harvest several days sooner than standard varieties like Cocodrie while keeping good milling quality and yield. The early maturity is useful for a second (ratoon) crop from the same plants after the first harvest, a practice common in the Gulf South where the long warm season allows regrowth from cut stubble to produce a smaller second harvest in fall. Keep the bed continuously saturated through the growing season for best results, and harvest the first crop when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan. After cutting the first crop high (leaving several inches of stubble), keep the field flooded and fertilized lightly to encourage ratoon regrowth for gardeners who want to try the extended Gulf South rice-growing technique. Matures in 100–125 days from seed.

name: Chenin Blanc Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Chenin Blanc originated in the Loire Valley of France and stands out among fine wine grapes for its remarkable versatility, capable of producing bone-dry still wines, off-dry and sweet dessert wines, and high-quality sparkling wines all from the same naturally high-acid, honey-and-quince-flavored fruit, depending on when it is picked and how it is vinified. The vigorous, productive vine is more heat-tolerant and adaptable than many classic white wine varieties, giving it a genuine practical advantage in warmer growing regions where more delicate cool-climate grapes struggle to retain acidity. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor through canopy work and crop thinning since the variety can overproduce if left unchecked, and choose harvest timing deliberately based on the intended wine style, since Chenin Blanc's high natural acidity gives growers real flexibility in when to pick. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cheongyang Pepper (Korean Hot Green Chile)
description: Cultivate in full sun with consistent watering, staking taller plants once heavily laden with fruit. Bred in South Korea in the early 1980s as a cross between a Thai chile and a Korean landrace pepper, Cheongyang delivers notably more heat than standard Korean green chiles while keeping their thin walls and grassy flavor. Slice fresh into stews like jjigae, dip raw into ssamjang, or dry and grind for a fiery version of gochugaru. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Cherapu
description: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Garcinia prainiana requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from wind and cold — mulch well and water regularly throughout the growing season. Garcinia prainiana (Cherapu or Button Mangosteen) is an evergreen fruit tree endemic to the lowland and hill forests of Peninsular Malaysia and southern Thailand, member of the Garcinia family (Clusiaceae) and closely related to the famous Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana). The fruits are distinctive: small (1.5–2 inch), round, with thin, orange to mandarin-colored skin (not the thick, purple rind of mangosteen) that peels easily to reveal 4–5 segments of soft, sweet-sour, orange-to-white, juicy, aromatic pulp with a complex tropical flavor — often described as a blend of sweet orange, lychee, and tangy passion fruit. The tree is compact and ornamental with glossy, dark-green, opposite leaves, and suits smaller tropical gardens better than the slower-growing mangosteen. Like all Garcinia species, G. prainiana is slow-growing and requires patience — typically 5–8 years from grafted stock to first fruit. A prized and rarely exported tropical fruit tree for serious tropical fruit collectors in zone 10–12. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Cherimoya (Custard Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; cherimoya (Annona cherimola) was famously described by Mark Twain as "the most delicious fruit known to men," and it remains one of the most sought-after fruits in the world among tropical fruit enthusiasts, producing heart-shaped, scaly green fruits with a snow-white, custardy flesh of extraordinary sweetness and complexity — with flavors of pineapple, banana, vanilla, and cream all at once. Native to the Andean highlands of Ecuador and Peru, cherimoya prefers a mild, subtropical rather than hot tropical climate and performs best where summers are warm but not brutally hot, and winters are cool but frost-free. Hand-pollination is essential in cultivation: transfer pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers using a small brush or cotton swab in the morning for reliable fruit set. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Lisa,' 'Booth,' and 'McPherson' begin bearing in 2–4 years and produce superior fruit size and flavor compared to seedling trees. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Blackberry (Classic Thornless Erect Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5); Cherokee is one of the earliest University of Arkansas thornless blackberry releases, introduced in the early 1970s and long a standard against which newer thornless varieties are measured. Canes are erect and self-supporting, requiring only light trellising, and produce medium-to-large, firm, well-flavored black berries in a concentrated early-to-mid season harvest. Because it is an older release, Cherokee is generally less productive and somewhat more disease-prone than modern Arkansas thornless cultivars like Natchez or Ouachita, but its cold hardiness and long track record still make it a dependable choice. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to keep the planting productive. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Carbon Pole Tomato
description: A cross of the heirlooms Cherokee Purple and Carbon that delivers rich purple-beefsteak flavor earlier, with more fruit and fewer cracks. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. The indeterminate vines need a tall cage or stake and periodic pruning for airflow. Water deeply and evenly, and harvest the ten to twelve ounce fruits when fully colored and slightly soft for peak flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Carbon Tomato (Deep-Dark Rich-Flavored Hybrid of Cherokee Purple)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Cherokee Carbon is a hybrid cross between two celebrated dark tomatoes — Cherokee Purple and Carbon — that combines the outstanding flavor profile of Cherokee Purple (one of the most beloved dark heirloom tomatoes) with improved productivity, crack resistance, and disease resistance contributed by the Carbon parent. The result is a medium-large (8–12 oz), deep mahogany-to-near-black-brown tomato with characteristic green shoulders and the dense, complex, rich, earthy-sweet flavor that makes dark tomatoes so compelling — a flavor often described as having depth, smokiness, and wine-like complexity quite unlike standard red tomatoes. Cherokee Carbon achieves the flavor combination of its heirloom parent varieties while outperforming both in garden productivity: the plants set more fruit, crack less in wet weather, and show better resistance to soilborne diseases than the pure-heirloom parents. For Gulf South gardeners who have been frustrated by the relatively low productivity and disease susceptibility of pure heirloom dark varieties in the hot, humid zone 9 climate, Cherokee Carbon provides the dark tomato flavor experience with practical garden performance. The deep color results from anthocyanin accumulation in the skin enhanced by sun exposure. In zone 9, grow as a spring crop (February–June) for best fruit development before summer heat. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Chocolate Tomato
description: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, rich soil after all frost risk has passed; bury the stem deeply to develop a robust root system. Cherokee Chocolate is a sport or selection from Cherokee Purple with even darker, mahogany-brown skin and deep chocolate-red flesh, yielding large 10–16 ounce beefsteak fruits with an outstandingly rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor prized by growers who love the dark-fruited heirlooms. Harvest when fruit softens slightly at the blossom end since the unusual dark coloring makes it difficult to judge ripeness by color alone; shoulder color transitions from green to brownish rather than the typical red flush. Excellent raw or in salads where the dramatic interior color makes a striking visual impact. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Collard (Heirloom Purple-Tinged Collard)
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning or transplanting seedlings to final spacing once they have a few true leaves. Cherokee is a Southeastern heirloom collard carried for generations by seed savers, notable for its blue-green leaves brushed with a purple tinge that deepens with cool weather, along with excellent cold hardiness and a mild, sweet flavor that improves further after frost. Harvest cut-and-come-again by picking the lower, outer leaves while the growing point continues to produce new leaves through fall and winter. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer to sustain steady leaf production, and monitor for cabbage worms and aphids, controlling with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide as needed. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Gold Tomato (Golden-Orange Beefsteak, Cherokee Series)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Cherokee Gold belongs to the celebrated Cherokee family of heirloom beefsteaks alongside Cherokee Purple and Cherokee Chocolate, distinguished by large, smooth, golden-orange fruit with the same rich, complex, low-acid flavor and meaty texture that made the original Cherokee Purple a modern heirloom classic. The bright, sunny color makes it a favorite for mixed heirloom tomato platters and salads alongside its darker-fruited siblings, and the indeterminate vine produces reliably over a long season. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking on the smooth skin, and harvest once color deepens to full gold for the sweetest, most complex flavor. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Green Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once the soil warms. This indeterminate heirloom, bred from the Cherokee Purple lineage, produces large fruits that ripen green with an amber blush and firm, juicy flesh. Stake or cage the tall vines, water evenly to prevent cracking, and judge ripeness by a slight softening since the color stays green. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Long Ear Popcorn (Colorful Long-Eared Heirloom Popcorn)
aliases: Zea mays var. everta 'Cherokee Long Ear'
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for reliable wind pollination; let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure an additional few weeks indoors before shelling and popping. Cherokee Long Ear is an heirloom popcorn grown for its distinctively long, slender ears — noticeably longer than most popcorn types — filled with small kernels in a mix of colors including reds, browns, and yellows on the same ear, giving each harvest a naturally varied, decorative look. It pops into small, tender, flavorful popcorn once fully dried and cured. The tall, vigorous stalks and long ears also make it a popular choice for fall decoration and dried-corn displays in addition to eating. Harvest when husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, and test-pop a small handful before committing the full harvest to storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Long Ear Small Popcorn (Heirloom Native Popcorn)
description: Plant in blocks in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherokee Long Ear Small is a slender-eared heirloom popcorn preserved through Cherokee seed-saving tradition and maintained today by heritage seed savers, notable for its small stature and small, narrow ears carrying rows of hard, glossy kernels in mixed colors from white through red and blue. Plants are shorter and the ears smaller than modern hybrid popcorn, but the strain is valued for its resilience, drought tolerance, and the deep cultural history tied to Southeastern Native American foodways. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are hard before harvesting; cure further indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing. Kernels pop reliably once fully cured, with a notably tender hull compared to many commercial popcorn hybrids. Save the best ears for the following year's seed to keep the strain vigorous and true. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Long Greasy Bean (Shiny-Podded Appalachian Heirloom Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Cherokee Long Greasy is one of many named greasy bean varieties preserved within Cherokee communities of the Southern Appalachians, its pods smooth and shiny rather than fuzzy, a trait that gives the whole greasy bean class its name, with tender, flavorful pods good for snapping and flavorful seeds that also dry well for winter storage. It reflects a long tradition of bean cultivation and seed saving among Cherokee gardeners in the mountains of western North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia. Harvest young for snap beans or let pods dry fully on the vine for a dry bean crop. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Purple Pole Tomato
description: A century-old heirloom said to trace to the Cherokee people, prized for dusky purple-red fruits balancing sweetness with a hint of smoke. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. This indeterminate vine needs sturdy support and regular pruning to keep it productive from summer to fall. Water consistently to reduce cracking and harvest when the shoulders stay dusky and the fruit yields slightly. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Purple Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant after all frost risk has passed into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherokee Purple is a large beefsteak heirloom tomato with a striking dusky rose to purple-maroon skin, deep reddish flesh with purple-green shoulders, and a rich, complex, smoky-sweet flavor that makes it a standout at the table and at farmers' markets. Harvest when fruits soften slightly at the blossom end and shoulders lose their green tinge, as the unusual coloring can make standard ripeness indicators unreliable. An outstanding variety for cooler summers; in zone 9 plant early for spring harvest. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Purple Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and set transplants deeply once nights are warm. This indeterminate heirloom yields large, dusky rose-purple beefsteaks with dense, meaty flesh and a rich, smoky-sweet flavor. Provide strong support and even watering, and harvest when the shoulders take on their characteristic dusky hue and the fruit yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Cherokee Tan Pumpkin
description: This Cherokee heirloom from the North Carolina and North Georgia mountains produces medium-sized, buff-tan skinned fruit with dense, deep orange, sweet-nutty flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries the family's excellent resistance to squash vine borer and better tolerance of humid, disease-pressured Southern summers than most Cucurbita pepo pumpkins. Let vines sprawl generously, since a single plant can cover a large area and set several fruit; harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail and stems have begun to dry and corky. Cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a reliable keeper crop for fall and winter kitchens. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Trail of Tears Bean (Black Snap Pole Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost at the base of poles, trellis, or fence 6–8 feet tall; provide support immediately as vines grow rapidly; thin to 4–6 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Cherokee Trail of Tears bean is one of the most historically significant heirloom varieties in American cultivation — a pole bean carried as seeds by members of the Cherokee Nation during the forced removal from their homelands in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to what is now Oklahoma in 1838–1839, the journey now known as the Trail of Tears in which more than 4,000 Cherokee people died. The black-seeded, purple-streaked pod variety was maintained by Cherokee families after their arrival in Indian Territory and has been preserved as a living memorial to this history, entering mainstream heirloom seed preservation networks through the Seed Savers Exchange in the 20th century. The vigorous vines produce long, slender pods with deep purple to black markings at the snap bean stage; fully mature dry seeds are glossy black and excellent for cooking as a dry bean. The dual snap-and-dry utility, vigorous productivity, and deep cultural history make Cherokee Trail of Tears one of the most important heirloom beans available. Matures in 60–100 days from seed.

name: Cherokee Wax Bush Bean (Heirloom Yellow Wax Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost; harvest when pods are 5–6 inches long and bright golden-yellow before pods begin to become stringy. Cherokee Wax is a traditional open-pollinated yellow wax bush bean that has been grown in American gardens since at least the early 20th century — one of the oldest continuously maintained wax bean varieties in American seed commerce. Unlike modern hybrid wax beans selected for mechanical harvest uniformity, Cherokee Wax represents the traditional wax bean type: productive, reliable, with good flavor, and completely open-pollinated so seed can be saved from season to season. The pods are bright golden-yellow, fairly straight, moderately thick-podded, with the characteristic waxy skin that gives the wax bean type its name. The eating quality is excellent — the thick walls provide a satisfying snap and the mild, slightly sweet wax bean flavor is cleaner and lighter than green bean types. Cherokee Wax has a loyal following among seed-saving gardeners and those who prefer open-pollinated varieties for independence from commercial seed sources. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Cherokee White Eagle Corn (Native American Flint-Dent White Corn)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for pollination; allow ears to fully dry on the stalk before harvest for the best grain quality; Cherokee White Eagle makes excellent hominy (nixtamalized corn), grits, and cornbread; select seed from ears showing the traditional dark-kernel eagle pattern to maintain the variety's distinctive characteristic. Cherokee White Eagle is a corn variety maintained and revered by the Cherokee people, one of the Five Civilized Tribes of the American Southeast (originally from the mountains of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia), who grew multiple varieties of corn as a primary food staple for centuries before European contact. The corn takes its name from the visual pattern that occasionally appears on a cob: most kernels are white, but scattered dark blue-black or red-black kernels create a pattern that, when viewed on the ear, suggests the spread wings of an eagle — a symbol of great importance in Cherokee culture. The proportion and distribution of dark kernels varies among individual ears, and Cherokee tradition holds that cobs with the most pronounced eagle pattern should be selected for seed saving to perpetuate both the variety and its spiritual significance. As a grain, Cherokee White Eagle is a flour/dent-type corn producing large, soft, white kernels that grind into fine, flavorful cornmeal and are excellent for making hominy (the traditional Indigenous preparation where corn is nixtamalized with alkali — wood ash or lime — to improve nutritional availability). The variety adapts well to the heat and humidity of the southeastern United States where it was developed. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Cherriette Radish
description: Cherriette is an F1 hybrid improvement on the classic Cherry Belle type, bred for extra uniformity and unusual resistance to pithiness even if roots are left in the ground past ideal size. Sow seed shallowly in loose, stone-free soil and thin early so roots have room to size up into smooth, bright cherry-red globes with dense, crisp white flesh. Its speed and evenness make it a favorite for market growers who need a reliable, uniform crop, while home gardeners appreciate that a missed harvest window rarely ruins the eating quality. Matures in 21–25 days from seed.

name: Cherry Belle Radish
description: A fast, easy Holland heirloom producing round, bright-red radishes with mild, crisp white flesh in about a month. Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. Keep soil evenly moist and grow in cool weather to avoid pithy, overly pungent roots. Harvest promptly when roots reach about an inch across, since they turn woody if left in the ground too long. Matures in 22–30 days from seed.

name: Cherry Bomb Pepper (Cherry Hot Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cherry Bomb is an All-America Selections winning pepper producing compact, globe-shaped, 1.5–2 inch fruits that resemble large cherries; at 2,500–5,000 SHU (mild-to-medium heat) it is significantly hotter than banana peppers but much milder than jalapeños, with thick, juicy, crunchy walls and excellent sweet pepper flavor with a moderate bite. Fruits ripen from green to brilliant red and are prized for stuffing whole (the round shape makes perfect stuffed cherry peppers), pickling in oil and vinegar in the Italian style, and fresh slicing. Compact, bush-type plants are highly productive and perform well in containers. Widely available in the Italian-American food tradition as pickled cherry peppers in antipasto. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Cherry Falls Bush Cherry Tomato
description: A compact, cascading cherry tomato bred for containers and hanging baskets, spilling clusters of bright red one-and-a-half-inch fruits. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Its trailing habit is ornamental and needs little staking, making it ideal for balconies and patios. Keep container soil evenly moist and harvest the abundant fruit throughout the season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Cherry of the Rio Grande
description: Plant Eugenia involucrata in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; once established it tolerates moderate drought, alkaline soils, and light frost to about 25°F; harvest fruits as they deepen to dark red-purple and become fully soft, as they drop quickly when ripe. Cherry of the Rio Grande is one of the most rewarding subtropical fruiting plants for Gulf Coast and South Texas gardens — it produces an early-season crop (April–June) of small, round to pear-shaped, dark red to almost black fruits on a handsome, densely branching shrub or small tree. The fruits have a sweet, rich, aromatic flavor with a pleasant cherry-like tang; they are eaten fresh, made into jams and jellies, or fermented into wine. A close relative of the more commonly known Pitanga (Surinam Cherry, Eugenia uniflora), but with a more refined, less resinous flavor. Hardy to about 25°F (zone 8 with some protection in zone 8a), and remarkably adaptable to the alkaline, often caliche soils of South Texas where many Eugenia species fail. Plants fruit at a young age and can bear two crops per year in warm climates. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape; the dense branching also makes it suitable as an informal hedge or screen. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cherry of the Rio Grande
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; cherry of the Rio Grande is a Brazilian Eugenia species prized by subtropical fruit enthusiasts for its exceptional flavor — the dark red to purple, oblong, cherry-sized fruits have a rich, complex flavor that blends cherry, wine, and grape notes with a slight aromatic complexity that is unique in the subtropical fruit world. It is one of the most sought-after specialty fruits for zone 9 food gardens. The dense, glossy, evergreen foliage is attractive year-round and the showy white flowers appear in spring. It grows as a medium shrub or small tree and tolerates partial shade well, making it suitable as an understory specimen in the food forest. The fruit ripens from May through June on the Gulf Coast and must be harvested promptly as it ferments rapidly after picking. In zone 9a it may need frost protection in hard winters; established plants recover readily. One of the top five subtropical fruits for Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cherry Plum (Myrobalan, Flowering Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; self-fertile but produces better with a second tree for cross-pollination; cherry plum is extremely adaptable and flowers early. Prunus cerasifera (cherry plum or myrobalan) is a small deciduous tree native to Western Asia and southeastern Europe — one of the earliest flowering Prunus species in spring, often opening white or pale-pink blossoms in late winter or very early spring even before peaches or almonds, creating a spectacular early-season display. The cherry-sized (3/4–1 inch) fruits ripen in summer in a range of colors from bright yellow to red to dark purple-black depending on variety, with sweet to sweet-tart, plum-like flesh that can be eaten fresh, cooked into jam, preserved as conserves, or fermented into wine or vinegar. Cherry plum is enormously important horticulturally as one of the primary rootstocks onto which commercial plum, apricot, and nectarine varieties are grafted. Several ornamental purple-leaved forms (particularly 'Atropurpurea' and the popular 'Thundercloud' and 'Purple Pony') are among the most commonly planted street and specimen trees in zone 5–9 landscapes for their deep maroon-purple spring foliage and masses of pink flowers. The species naturalizes readily and has escaped into the wild in parts of North America and Europe. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cherry Tomato
description: Start seeds 1/4 inch deep indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F and transplant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil after nights consistently stay above 50°F; cherry tomatoes are the most prolific and carefree of all tomato types, producing hundreds of small, intensely sweet fruits per plant from midsummer through frost with minimal attention. Most cherry types are indeterminate (continue growing and fruiting all season) and need a tall cage or stake; compact determinate cherry types like 'Tumbling Tom' and 'Tumbler' are ideal for containers. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking; irregular watering causes cherry tomatoes to split their skins. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and come off the vine easily with gentle pressure. Outstanding for container growing, children's gardens, and fresh snacking. Matures in 55–75 days from transplant.

name: Cherry Vanilla Quinoa (Deep Cherry-Red and Cream Bicolor Quinoa)
description: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; quinoa performs best in cool weather and can struggle through extended hot, humid summers. Cherry Vanilla bears striking bicolor seed heads combining deep cherry-red and creamy vanilla-white tones on the same plant, one of the most visually dramatic quinoa selections available and prized as much for its ornamental cut-flower value as for its edible seed. The tall, colorful seed-head spikes make an eye-catching addition to a cutting garden as well as a productive grain crop. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Chervil
description: Scatter seeds on the soil surface and press them in lightly, or cover with 1/8 in of fine soil; chervil prefers cool, partly shaded conditions and bolts quickly in heat. Direct sow rather than transplanting, as the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Keep the soil consistently moist during germination and throughout the cool season. Harvest delicate, fern-like leaves when plants are 6–8 in tall, before any flower stalks emerge, to capture the mild anise flavor. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Chesnok Red Garlic (Purple Stripe Hardneck, Prized for Roasting)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Chesnok Red, originally from the Republic of Georgia, is a purple stripe hardneck consistently rated by garlic growers as one of the best varieties for roasting and baking, since it stays mild and creamy rather than overpowering when cooked, while still carrying good pungency raw. Bulbs are medium-sized with striking purple-streaked skin over eight to ten easy-to-peel cloves. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus energy into the bulb; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, and expect good but not exceptional storage life, typically four to six months. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Chesnok Red Hardneck Garlic
description: A hardneck heirloom from the Republic of Georgia with purple-streaked bulbs and nine to ten easy-to-peel cloves of rich, mellow flavor. Plant individual cloves pointed end up about two inches deep in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, and mulch for winter protection. Snap off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb formation. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place before storage. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Chester Thornless Blackberry (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Chester is one of the most widely planted thornless blackberry cultivars in North America, valued for a rare combination of good cold hardiness, strong resistance to cane blight and other diseases, and reliable production of large, firm, mild-flavored fruit that ripens later in summer than most cultivars, extending the blackberry harvest season. Its tolerance of colder winters than many thornless blackberries has made it a standard choice well beyond the Gulf South, though it performs well there too given adequate summer water. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for the next season's fruiting canes. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Chestnut
