description: Chestnuts require cross-pollination between at least two different cultivars or seedlings — plant them within 50 feet of each other for reliable nut set. American chestnut was devastated by blight, so choose blight-resistant Chinese, European, or hybrid selections (such as Dunstan Chestnuts). Trees strongly prefer acidic soils (pH 4.5–6.5) and perform poorly in alkaline or wet conditions. Harvest in fall when burs open and nuts fall; collect daily as nuts on the ground deteriorate quickly. Fresh chestnuts are perishable — refrigerate promptly and use or freeze within a month. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chestnut White Sapote
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind, since white sapote wood is somewhat brittle. Chestnut is a vigorous, heavy-cropping California selection that produces round, yellow-green fruit with smooth, custard-textured flesh recalling banana and caramel once fully ripe, though the skin itself carries a persistent bitterness and should not be eaten. Its firmer flesh holds up to handling and shipping better than many softer-fleshed sapote selections, making it a good choice for growers who want fruit that survives a trip from the yard to the kitchen intact. Allow harvested fruit to soften fully at room temperature for several days before eating, and prune young trees to a strong scaffold framework, since mature trees can become large and top-heavy without early shaping. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cheyenne Blackberry (Vigorous Early-Season Thorny Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and provide a two-wire trellis to support the vigorous, thorny canes. Cheyenne is an erect University of Arkansas blackberry released in 1977, prized for its early-to-midseason ripening and consistently high yields, making it a longtime favorite for pick-your-own plantings. Berries are large, sweet, and firm with a distinctive hint of raspberry flavor, ripening ahead of most other Arkansas-bred thorny cultivars. Because it retains thorns, plant it where hand-harvesting around the canes is acceptable in exchange for its productivity and fruit quality. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to maintain vigor and berry size in subsequent years. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Cheyenne Pecan (Early-Bearing Compact High-Quality Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA breeding program, Cheyenne is notable for its smaller, more compact tree size compared to many pecan cultivars, along with excellent kernel quality and a high percentage of kernel to shell. It tends to bear at a younger age than older heirloom cultivars, giving growers an earlier return on a new planting, though it is more susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and benefits from good spacing and airflow. Its compact habit makes it a reasonable option where space is more limited than a full commercial pecan grove requires. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Cheyenne Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Upright Cayenne)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Cheyenne is a long-established All-America Selections winning cayenne cultivar bred for a compact, upright plant that holds its thin, curved, hot red pods well above the foliage rather than letting them dangle near the soil, keeping fruit cleaner and easier to spot and harvest. The classic sharp cayenne heat and flavor make it well suited to drying and grinding into cayenne powder, pickling, or fresh use in cooking. Its compact size makes it a good choice for containers and smaller garden beds where a sprawling pepper plant would be impractical. Harvest regularly for fresh use, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on the plant for storage as dried cayenne. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Chia
description: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18–24 in once seedlings emerge. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. The plant flowers in autumn as day length shortens and produces whorled spikes of small purple flowers followed by seed-filled calyces; harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed. Place harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris; seeds are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, calcium, and fiber. Matures in 120–160 days from seed.

name: Chia Tsao Tea (Taiwan Mountain Oolong Selection)
description: Chia Tsao originates from tea gardens in the mountain village of the same name in Taiwan, and is grown chiefly for the unusually fragrant oolong tea its small, narrow leaves produce when processed with partial oxidation. The plant has a more open, spreading habit than typical China-type tea camellias, rather than the dense upright form of many named selections. Growers have reported it tolerating brief drops into the mid-20s Fahrenheit without injury, suggesting reasonable cold tolerance for the humid Southeast. Provide the standard acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias, and process the harvested flush as oolong to showcase its signature aroma. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chiba Green Soybean (Edamame)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in warm soil after frost, as soybeans dislike transplanting. The compact, bushy plants set clusters of plump pods that fill with large, sweet green beans. Harvest the whole plant when most pods are full but still bright green, then boil the pods briefly and pop out the tender edamame. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Chicago Hardy Fig
description: One of the hardiest figs available, Chicago Hardy can be grown down to Zone 5, where the tops may freeze back but resprout from the roots to fruit on new wood. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and mulch heavily over winter in colder regions to protect the crown. Water steadily while fruit develops for the best sweetness. In the coldest zones, grow it in a container that can overwinter in a garage or basement. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chicago Pickling Cucumber (1888 Heirloom Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Chicago Pickling dates to the late 1880s and was long a mainstay of Midwestern commercial pickle production, producing an abundant crop of medium-green, black-spined fruit that holds its blocky shape well through brining and fermentation. Pick fruit small, at around 2-4 inches, for classic dill and bread-and-butter pickles, and harvest frequently to keep the vigorous vines setting new fruit. Because it is open-pollinated, gardeners can save seed season to season, continuing a variety with over a century of documented use in American home and commercial pickling. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Chicago Warted Hubbard Squash (1894 Heirloom Winter Storage Squash)
description: Chicago Warted Hubbard is an 1894 heirloom winter squash introduced by a Chicago seed house and it remains one of the more heavily warted, thick-shelled Hubbard-type squashes still grown today. The dusky olive-green, deeply wrinkled rind protects finely textured, sweet orange flesh that keeps exceptionally well in a cool, dry location, often lasting well into spring. Its dense flesh and excellent storage life made it a favorite for canning and pies in the era before mechanical refrigeration was common. The vigorous vines need significant space and a long, warm season to fully size and cure their large fruit. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Chickadee Blueberry (Very Early Large Low-Acid University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Chickadee is a University of Florida southern highbush release combining a very low chill requirement with unusually large, sweet, low-acid fruit, an appealing combination for fresh eating that also ripens very early in the season, giving Gulf South growers a jump on the blueberry harvest before summer heat and pest pressure build. As a southern highbush type it needs consistently moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil rather than the more forgiving conditions rabbiteye types tolerate. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to maintain vigor and berry size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chickasaw Blackberry (Vigorous Erect Thorny Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun and trellis the vigorous, thorny canes for support and easier harvest. Chickasaw is an older University of Arkansas blackberry release valued for its very large fruit size and vigorous, productive canes, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the season. Unlike the newer thornless Arkansas releases, Chickasaw retains thorns, so plant it where hand-picking around thorny canes is acceptable in exchange for its exceptionally large, firm, flavorful berries. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain vigor and berry size in subsequent years. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Chickasaw Plum (Sand Plum, Mountain Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chickasaw plum thrives on neglect and is essentially care-free once established. Prunus angustifolia (Chickasaw plum or sand plum) is one of the most important native fruit plants of the Gulf Coastal Plain, East Texas, and Piedmont Southeast — a tough, fast-growing, suckering shrub or small tree producing abundant 1/2-to-3/4-inch, bright-red to orange-red or yellow plums in May–June that are tart-sweet and excellent for jellies, preserves, wines, and eating out of hand. The tree is one of the earliest flowering native plants of the Southeast, producing dense clusters of small white flowers in February–March (before the leaves emerge) that provide extremely valuable early nectar for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Chickasaw plum forms thickets by root suckers, creating dense, thorny hedgerows that provide outstanding nesting cover and food for a wide range of wildlife. It is self-fertile (though cross-pollination improves yields) and one of the most heat, drought, and disease-resistant of all stone fruits for southeastern gardens. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chickpea (Garbanzo Bean)
description: Sow chickpeas 2 in deep in light, well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH; they perform poorly in heavy, waterlogged ground. The plants produce distinctive sticky, glandular hairs on stems and pods that can cause a mild skin reaction in sensitive individuals, so harvest with gloves. Pick pods when they are green and plump for fresh eating, or leave plants to dry fully in place and harvest entire plants when 90% of pods have turned tan. Shell and sun-dry for a day before long-term storage. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Chickweed (Common Chickweed, Stellaria)
description: Scatter seed on the surface of moist, fertile soil in partial shade in fall; chickweed is one of the most nutritious and widely available wild edibles in the world — a cool-season annual that appears in gardens, lawns, and disturbed areas throughout winter, producing mats of small, oval-leaved stems with tiny, deeply notched white petals that look like stars (the genus name Stellaria means 'star'). The tender shoots and leaves are rich in vitamins C, B-complex, iron, and calcium, used fresh in salads, smoothies, and as a potherb (briefly cooked like spinach). The flavor is mild and pleasant, reminiscent of corn silk. In zone 9a it grows vigorously from November through March and self-sows prolifically, providing free winter salad greens in any garden patch where temperatures stay below 70°F. A traditional forage food eaten across Europe and Asia for centuries and by many indigenous North American peoples. Matures in 35–60 days from seed.

name: Chicle Tree (Chicozapote)
description: Manilkara chicle is the classic wild chicle tree of the lowland rain forests of Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala, historically tapped by chicleros for its milky latex, which was the original base ingredient of natural chewing gum before synthetic substitutes took over the industry. It is closely related to sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) and produces similar small, brown-skinned, sweet fruit with grainy, malty-flavored flesh, though it is grown far more often as a massive forest timber and latex tree than as a dooryard fruit crop. In cultivation it wants full sun and deep, well-drained, fertile soil, and rewards patience with a very long-lived, wind-firm, drought-tolerant canopy tree once established. Because of its eventual great size, it is best suited to large properties or naturalistic plantings rather than small home gardens, and young trees need frost protection in any zone cooler than the tropical range they evolved in. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chico Jujube (USDA Chico Station Fresh-Eating Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and neglect far better than most fruit trees once it is established, which suits the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season well. Chico originated at the USDA's Chico Plant Introduction Station in California as an open-pollinated seedling of the older 'So' (Contorted) jujube, and was released for its medium-to-large, flattened round fruit with a fine, crisp texture. Unlike many jujube cultivars that taste purely sweet, Chico carries a noticeable tang alongside its sweetness, giving it a more balanced flavor that many fresh-eating fans prefer. It is partly self-fruitful, ripens over a long midseason harvest window, and needs only routine pruning to remove root suckers and keep its naturally upright, thorny growth in bounds. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chicory
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in deep, well-drained soil; chicory develops a long taproot that makes it drought-tolerant once established but resists transplanting. Young leaves provide a pleasantly bitter addition to salads and are most palatable before the plant flowers; blanching the developing crown under an upturned pot for 2–3 weeks produces creamy, milder forced leaves in late winter. The thick taproot is roasted and ground as a coffee substitute or additive, harvested in the plant's second autumn. Bright blue flowers open and close with the sun daily, attracting bees through summer. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Chieftain Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Chieftain is a red-skinned, white-fleshed round potato released from a USDA and North Dakota State University breeding program in the 1960s for the Upper Midwest fresh market. The smooth, deep red skin holds its color well in storage, and the moist, moderately waxy flesh boils cleanly without excessive breakdown, making it a dependable variety for potato salad and general table use. It has a strong reputation among northern growers for consistent yields and good storage quality compared to older red cultivars of its era. Choose it over Red Norland or Red Pontiac when a slightly later, higher-yielding red round is wanted for storage rather than earliest harvest. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Chieftain Savoy Cabbage (1938 AAS-Winning Heirloom Savoy)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost, or in early-to-midsummer for a fall crop, since Chieftain reaches full size only in cool weather and its flavor improves markedly after light frost. Chieftain Savoy is a 1938 All-America Selections winner bred by Ferry-Morse, producing large, nearly round, densely savoyed dark green heads averaging four to six pounds with a tender, sweet crunch that distinguishes savoy types from smooth-leaved cabbage. It is notably cold hardy and holds well in the garden into late fall and early winter, making it a dependable choice for extending the cabbage harvest well past the first frosts. Space plants generously to allow the broad, crinkled outer leaves to develop fully, and side-dress with nitrogen midseason to support the long growing period to a full-sized head. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Chiffon Summer Squash
description: An early, heavy-yielding summer squash on upright, compact two-foot bushes with moderate powdery mildew resistance. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm and settled. The open, upright habit makes harvesting easy and improves airflow around the plants. Pick fruit young and tender, checking daily at peak season since squash size up quickly. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Chikusui Asian Pear
description: Chikusui produces orange-russeted fruit with yellowish-white flesh that is soft-crisp and juicy, with a firmness close to Kosui and slightly higher than Hosui, eaten fresh rather than stored to soften. It was developed specifically to improve on the productivity problems of the earlier Shinsui cultivar while keeping a similarly early harvest window. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and shares the general fire blight susceptibility common to nashi pears. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chilacayote Squash (Fig-Leaf Gourd, Malabar Gourd)
description: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed near a trellis or open ground where its vigorous, fig-shaped-leaved vines can climb or sprawl, watering regularly during establishment. Distinct from other Cucurbita species, this cool-tolerant Andean and Mesoamerican heirloom produces watermelon-striped fruit with black seeds and stringy white flesh traditionally candied into the Mexican sweet cabello de ángel or brewed into a folk remedy. Its unusual cold hardiness for a squash and ability to fruit at higher elevations made it a long-season staple crop from Mexico through the Andes. Fruit stores exceptionally well, often lasting a year or more in cool, dry conditions. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Chile de Agua (Fresh Oaxacan Valley Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chile de Agua produces medium-to-large, tapered, pale to medium green pods with mild-to-moderate heat, a defining fresh chile of Oaxaca's central valleys used widely for roasted rajas (strips) and stuffed chile dishes in Oaxacan cuisine. The productive plants perform well over a long warm season, and pods are typically harvested and used green rather than allowed to ripen to red. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production through the summer. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Chile de Arbol
description: Start indoors and transplant to warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; chile de arbol (tree chili) is a tall, upright-growing Mexican pepper variety that produces prolific clusters of slender, 2–3 inch pointed red fruits that ripen from green through red and are both the primary flavor base of traditional Mexican table salsas and one of the most frequently used chilis in Mexican restaurant kitchens. The heat level is substantial (15,000–30,000 SHU) with a clean, slightly smoky, grassy flavor. They are dried and toasted whole for use in salsas de chile de arbol or ground into powder. The plant's name comes from its tree-like growth habit — stems become woody and the plant can produce prolifically for years in frost-free zones 9–11. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Chile Puya (Mexican Dried Chile, Guajillo's Fiery Cousin)
description: Grow as a standard warm-season pepper in full sun with well-drained soil, watering deeply but infrequently once established. Chile Puya produces slender pods closely resembling guajillo but shorter, narrower, and notably hotter, typically left on the plant to ripen fully to deep red before drying. Dried pods are toasted and rehydrated for robust red salsas, adobos, and marinades across central and western Mexico, often blended alongside guajillo and ancho for layered heat and flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Chilean Guava
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chilean guava is a compact, evergreen shrub with small, dark-green, aromatic leaves that produces masses of tiny, deep-pink to red berries with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor reminiscent of strawberries and vanilla — reportedly Queen Victoria's favorite jam fruit. The plant makes an excellent evergreen hedge or foundation shrub in mild climates and tolerates light frost to about 12–15°F once established. Harvest berries in fall when they are fully ripe and very dark pink-red. Excellent for jams, jellies, and fresh eating. The closely related Ugni candollei (Chilean strawberry guava) is very similar with slightly different flavors. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chilean Hazelnut (Avellano, Gevuin Nut)
description: Native to the temperate rainforests of Chile and adjacent Argentina, this evergreen Proteaceae relative of macadamia produces clusters of small, round, orange-red nuts with a mild flavor often compared to a cross between hazelnut and macadamia, prized locally for pressing into a light culinary oil as well as for out-of-hand eating. It prefers cool, humid, mild-winter climates with consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil, performing best in Pacific coastal regions and struggling in areas with intense summer heat, drought, or hard freezes below the mid-teens Fahrenheit. Plant in filtered sun to partial shade in warmer climates to protect foliage from scorch, and expect several years of establishment before the tree begins bearing its distinctive fern-like, glossy compound leaves and drooping nut clusters. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chilean Myrtle
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Luma apiculata is adapted to the cool, moist, oceanic climate of Chilean Patagonia and performs best in mild, humid, coastal climates — avoid extreme summer heat and drought; mulch to maintain cool, moist root conditions. Luma apiculata (Chilean Myrtle, Arrayán, or Temu) is an evergreen shrub or small to medium tree native to the temperate rainforests of southern Chile (Araucania, Los Ríos, Los Lagos) and adjacent Neuquén in Argentina, growing in moist, sheltered valleys, forest edges, and riparian zones as an abundant component of the remarkable Southern Beech forests. The outstanding ornamental feature is the strikingly beautiful bark — smooth, exfoliating in large, irregular patches to reveal layers of cinnamon-orange, cream, and gray, producing a mottled, jewel-like trunk surface of extraordinary beauty, particularly on mature multi-stemmed specimens. Dense masses of small, white, 4-petaled flowers cover the plant in summer, followed by round, 1/4–1/3 inch, blackish-purple, aromatic, sweet, edible berries — the 'arrayán' fruit eaten by Chilean indigenous peoples and used for jams and fermented beverages. Luma apiculata is one of the most ornamentally desirable trees for mild-winter, cool-summer coastal gardens in zones 8b–10 and is widely planted in UK, Ireland, and the Pacific Northwest for its bark beauty. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chilean Pernettya (Prickly Heath)
description: Chilean pernettya is a low, spreading, needle-leaved evergreen shrub from the temperate rainforest understory of Chile and Argentina, producing marble-sized berries in shades of white, pink, magenta, or deep purple that persist on the plant from autumn well into winter. The mild, faintly sweet berries are edible fresh, though they are grown mainly as a striking woodland-garden ornamental with genuinely edible fruit rather than a production crop. Like other ericaceous shrubs it requires acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and is happiest in the dappled shade of taller shrubs or trees, where it colonizes slowly by suckering to form a dense groundcover. The species is dioecious, so a male pollinator plant must be grown nearby for the showier female selections to fruit heavily. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Chilean Wine Palm (Coquito Palm, Honey Palm)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; exceedingly drought-tolerant once established. Jubaea chilensis (Chilean wine palm or coquito palm) is the world's most cold-hardy large-growing palm species — native to the central Chilean Andes coastal valleys where it experiences occasional frost and cold winters — and the most massive palm in terms of trunk girth, with a single trunk reaching 3–5 feet in diameter at maturity. It tolerates temperatures briefly to approximately 18–20°F (zone 8) — making it growable outdoors in zone 8 or warmer, far colder than any other large pinnate palm. The 'wine' in the common name refers to the traditional Chilean practice of felling mature trees to tap the sap as it flows from the cut stump — producing large quantities of sweet sap boiled to 'miel de palma' (palm honey, a thick, dark, amber, molasses-like sweetener), or fermented to palm wine ('chicha de palma'). CAUTION: The traditional sap harvest requires killing the tree. The small fruits ('coquitos,' little coconuts) contain a sweet, coconut-flavored seed that is sold commercially as a snack in Chilean markets. Jubaea is critically endangered in the wild due to centuries of sap-tapping and habitat loss; it is protected in Chilean national reserves. An extraordinary garden palm for warm-temperate climates where most large palms fail. Matures in 5475–14600 days from transplant.

name: Chilgoza Pine (Neoza Pine, Gerard's Pine)
description: Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky soil in full sun on a site that mimics its native semi-arid mountain slopes of the northwestern Himalaya. Chilgoza pine is a slow-growing, long-lived five-needle pine with distinctive flaking, patchwork bark and is cultivated commercially in its native range for its large, thin-shelled, richly flavored pine nuts, among the most prized pine nuts in South and Central Asian cuisine. It requires cold winter dormancy and sharp drainage, and takes many years from planting to first significant cone production. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Chilhuacle Negro Pepper (Black Chilhuacle, Oaxacan Black Mole Chile)
description: Start indoors in a warm seedling tray 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after all frost danger passes; chilhuacle plants are large and productive but slow-maturing — plan the long growing season carefully; harvest when fruits turn fully dark reddish-black to black and the skin begins to feel slightly leathery; dry thoroughly on screens in a single layer. Chilhuacle Negro is one of the most important and irreplaceable chiles in Oaxacan cuisine — the primary chile in mole negro, one of the canonical seven moles of Oaxaca and arguably the most complex mole sauce in Mexican gastronomy. The fresh chile is a medium-large (2–3 inch wide, 3–5 inch long), slightly squat, triangular to shoulder-shaped fruit with thick, dark green walls that transitions through red to a very deep reddish-black at full maturity — the darkened color indicating the presence of additional flavor compounds that develop in the fully mature and dried state. The dried chilhuacle negro is unique among Mexican dried chiles for its distinctive flavor: deeply complex, somewhat fruity, mildly earthy with a chocolate-like depth, moderately hot (2,500–5,000 Scoville units), and with a characteristic thick skin that retains more texture when rehydrated than thinner-skinned chiles. Only three types of chilhuacle exist: negro (black), rojo (red), and amarillo (yellow) — all grown in the Cañada region of the northern Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, particularly around the town of Huajuapan de León and the Mixteca Alta, where the specific combination of altitude, temperature, and local soil conditions produces chiles with flavor characteristics impossible to replicate elsewhere. A critical ingredient for cooks interested in authentic Oaxacan cuisine. Matures in 110–130 days from transplant.

name: Chilhuacle Rojo Pepper (Red Chilhuacle, Oaxacan Red Chile)
description: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest at full red maturity for drying; dry on screens in a single layer in a warm, airy location until leathery-crisp; store dried chiles in airtight containers away from light. Chilhuacle Rojo is the red form of the chilhuacle chile, one of the three varieties grown specifically in the Cañada district of Oaxaca state in Mexico. While the chilhuacle negro (black) is the defining ingredient of mole negro, the chilhuacle rojo plays the lead role in Oaxacan mole coloradito — a complex red mole that, while less dark and mysterious than mole negro, is equally complex and represents one of the pillars of Oaxacan cooking. The dried rojo chile is a vivid brick-red to deep red color with moderately thick walls that rehydrate to a smooth, velvety texture. The flavor is distinctively fruity and somewhat tart-sweet, with moderate heat (3,000–6,000 Scoville units), and a characteristic sweetness that distinguishes it from the guajillo and other red dried chiles with which it is sometimes confused. The shoulder-shaped, somewhat flattened form (wider near the stem, tapering to the tip) is characteristic of all three chilhuacle varieties and distinguishes them from other Oaxacan chiles like the negro or costeño. In Mexican markets, chilhuacle rojo is sometimes substituted with a blend of ancho and guajillo chiles, but genuine chilhuacle rojo has a unique flavor profile that the blend does not replicate. Increasingly available from specialty seed companies as interest in authentic regional Mexican cuisine grows among American gardeners and home cooks. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Chilly Chili Pepper (Heatless Kid-Friendly Ornamental Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Chilly Chili won an All-America Selections award as the first heatless ornamental pepper, bred to eliminate capsaicin entirely so its abundant small, slender, upright fruit — which ripens through a colorful progression of purple, yellow, orange, and red, often several colors present on the plant at once — can be safely tasted by curious children without any burning heat. Its compact, tidy habit and long-lasting, weather-resistant fruit display make it an excellent choice for children's gardens, containers, and edging where the bright, changing fruit color provides months of interest from summer through fall. Because the fruit holds its color and shape well after ripening, plants often remain colorful and attractive right up until frost. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Chiltepin Pepper (Chile Tepin, Bird Pepper)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; the chiltepin is the only wild chile pepper native to the United States, growing in rocky canyon bottoms and shaded washes from Texas through Arizona and south into Mexico. The tiny round to oval fruits — barely the size of a pea — ripen from green to vivid red and pack an intense, clean heat (50,000–100,000 Scoville) that fades quickly unlike cultivated chiles. Birds disperse the seeds and are unaffected by capsaicin, making this a superb wildlife plant as well as a culinary one. In mild winter zones (8b+) plants are truly perennial and can reach shrub size over several seasons; in colder climates grow as an annual started indoors. Harvest fruits as they redden or allow birds to disperse naturally for a self-seeding colony. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Chimayó Chile
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chimayó Chile is a true landrace pepper grown for at least three centuries by Pueblo and Hispanic farming families in the village of Chimayó, in the foothills of New Mexico's Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The thin-walled, 4–6 inch tapered pods ripen from green to deep red and carry a moderate, warming heat (roughly 4,000–6,000 Scoville units) alongside a complex, sweet, smoky flavor that distinguishes it from other New Mexico-type chiles. Pods are traditionally strung into ristras and air-dried, then ground into the red chile powder used for New Mexican posole, carne adovada, and red chile sauce. Because it developed in an isolated, arid high-desert valley, seed-grown plants stay relatively compact and thrive with less humidity and lower water than Gulf Coast or Southeastern pepper varieties. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: China Express Napa Cabbage
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil timed for a fall harvest, since this fast-growing hybrid is bred for slow bolting and reliably forms dense, barrel-shaped heads even under variable weather. Thin plants to their full spacing early so uniform, well-wrapped heads can develop without stress cracking. The crisp, mildly sweet leaves are well suited to fresh salads, quick stir-fries, and kimchi, and mature heads store well in a cold, humid location for several weeks. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: China Rose Radish (Rose China Winter Radish)
description: Sow seeds directly a half-inch deep and thin seedlings to a few inches apart, since crowded roots stay thin and pithy. Unlike fast-maturing spring radishes, this nineteenth-century heirloom is grown as a fall crop and left in the ground longer, forming a smooth, tapered root five to six inches long with rose-pink skin and crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably more pungent than spring salad radishes, and its roots hold their quality in the ground or in cold storage well into winter, making it a traditional keeper variety for root cellars. Cool fall temperatures improve both texture and flavor, so avoid sowing it for a hot-weather harvest. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: China Rose Radish Sprouts
description: Rose-colored radish sprouts deliver a spicy bite popular in Chinese and Japanese cooking, from raw salads to sushi. Soak seed briefly, then drain and spread in a sprouting jar or tray out of direct sun. Rinse and drain two to three times daily until the sprouts stand an inch or two tall with open leaves. Harvest in four to six days and refrigerate, using within a week for the freshest peppery flavor. Matures in 4–6 days from seed.

name: China S-1 Satsuma (Hubei-Origin Cold-Hardy Satsuma Selection)
description: China S-1 is one of a numbered series of satsuma selections collected from Chinese orchards after a catastrophic freeze wiped out less hardy trees, chosen because the parent tree survived and kept producing decent fruit under conditions that killed neighboring satsumas. It has become a reference variety in cold-hardy citrus trial collections for comparing hardiness against Gulf Coast standards like Owari and Brown Select, offering solid, easy-peel, seedless mandarin fruit with slightly more modest eating quality than the top Gulf Coast selections but a meaningful edge in wood hardiness. Grow it as a hedge against a hard winter loss in a mixed satsuma planting rather than as your only tree, since its main strength is survival rather than superior flavor. Protect young trees for their first two winters and expect full hardiness benefits only once the tree is well established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: China S-9 Satsuma (Smooth-Peel Hubei-Origin Cold-Hardy Satsuma Selection)
description: China S-9 was selected from the same freeze-survivor orchards in Hubei and Sichuan Provinces as other numbered China satsuma lines, prized by cold-hardy citrus collectors for pairing good winter hardiness with a smoother, glossier peel than typical satsumas, which some growers find easier to hand-peel. Fruit quality and vigor are rated acceptable rather than exceptional, placing it a notch below flagship Gulf Coast satsumas like Brown Select or Owari in eating quality, but its cold tolerance makes it a useful backup planting in the coldest parts of zone 8. Give it full sun and excellent drainage, and treat it as part of a diversified home citrus planting rather than a single specimen, since its selection criteria prioritized survival over peak flavor. As with other satsuma types, expect full production and best fruit quality only after the tree is several years established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: China Yellow Bean (Sulphur Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the danger of frost; the low, compact bushes need no support and mature quickly compared with most dry beans. China Yellow, also called the Sulphur Bean, is a New England heirloom documented before 1870, valued for its small, plump, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that cook down quickly to a soft, creamy consistency ideal for stewing and baking. Despite the name, it has no connection to China; the name simply describes its distinctive pale yellow color. Let pods dry fully on the plant, then thresh and store the beans in an airtight container. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: China-Type Tea (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis)
description: Var. sinensis is the small-leaved, shrubby, cold-hardy botanical variety of the tea plant, native to the mountains of southwestern China, and is the parent stock behind most of the world's named green, white, and oolong tea cultivars. Its narrow, finely serrated leaves and slow, dense branching habit make it far more tolerant of winter cold than the tropical var. assamica, and it is the type most reliably grown outside the humid subtropics. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil required by all tea camellias, with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates. Named regional selections of this variety span from Japanese sencha cultivars to Chinese oolong mother trees. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chinebuli Persimmon (Early-Ripening Georgian Non-Astringent Persimmon)
description: Chinebuli is a non-astringent (PCNA) Asian persimmon of commercial importance in the subtropical persimmon-growing regions of Georgia (the country), where it is valued for losing its astringency while still on the tree, allowing fruit to be picked and eaten firm without waiting for it to soften. It ripens from early October, notably earlier than cultivars that finish at the end of October, which lets it reliably produce a high-quality crop even where the growing season runs short. The fruit is medium-sized, oval and somewhat flattened, with a crisp texture and sweet, pleasantly aromatic flavor when picked ready-to-eat. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil; like other non-astringent kaki types, Chinebuli is self-fruitful and does not require a second tree for pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Apricot
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil on a gently sloping site to encourage cold air drainage away from spring blossoms; Chinese Apricot (also known as 'Chinese Sweet' or 'Mormon Apricot') is an heirloom apricot variety valued for its early and reliable fruiting in warm-climate zones, exceptional ornamental spring bloom of pure white blossoms (among the most beautiful of any stone fruit), and large, orange-blushed fruits with rich, sweet, classic apricot flavor. The self-fertile habit — rare among apricots, which are often incompatible — makes Chinese Apricot practical for small gardens with space for only a single tree. The primary challenge in zone 9 for any apricot is that the early bloom (January–February) may be damaged by late frost; selecting a well-drained site with good cold air movement significantly reduces frost-damaged crop losses. Chinese Apricot has demonstrated better heat tolerance in warm-summer climates than most European apricot selections, contributing to its success in the South and Southwest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Artichoke (Crosnes, Knotroot)
description: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese artichoke produces the most visually distinctive tubers in the vegetable garden — small (1–2 inch), cream-white, segmented underground stems that resemble tiny white caterpillars or coiled seashells. Known in French cuisine as 'crosnes' (from the French town where they were introduced in the late 19th century), they have a crisp, sweet, delicate flavor similar to water chestnuts, used raw in salads, lightly stir-fried, or pickled. The plant is in the mint family and spreads by tubers — contain it or plan for its spread. Harvest in fall after frost kills the tops, when the tubers are at their crisp best. The tubers discolor quickly after harvesting; use immediately. Tolerates partial shade, making it useful in a shaded food garden where few vegetables thrive. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Bayberry
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Chinese bayberry (yang mei, yumberry) is one of China's most celebrated fruits — a small, deep red to purplish, lychee-like berry on a large, shade-tolerant evergreen tree that is almost unknown in American gardens despite growing well in zone 7–9. The fruits, borne in June–July, are intensely flavored with a sweet-tart taste similar to a cross between pomegranate and raspberry, with a slightly grainy texture around a central pit. Chinese bayberry is rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C. The tree is dioecious — female trees bear fruit when pollinated by a male; most nurseries sell sexed trees. It grows slowly to 25–35 feet but can be kept smaller with pruning. The dark, glossy, evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Box Orange (Boxthorn)
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese box orange tolerates poor, sandy, and salt-affected soils and is commonly grown as a dense, thorny hedge in coastal and southern landscapes. This slow-growing, densely branched citrus relative carries small, glossy, boxwood-like leaves on stiff, thorny stems, with tiny, fragrant white flowers followed by small, dark, olive-black berries that are not palatable but are eaten by birds. Its dense, twiggy, thorn-armed growth makes it an outstanding impenetrable barrier hedge or foundation screen, and it shears well to a formal shape, tolerating heat, drought, and salt spray once established far better than most true citrus. Prune after the main spring flush to maintain a tight hedge form and remove any wayward growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Broccoli (Gai Lan)
description: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun during the cool season; Chinese broccoli is more heat-tolerant than heading broccoli but still performs best between 50–70°F. Harvest the central flower head and 6–8 inches of stem just as the first buds show color but before flowers open; side shoots continue to develop for weeks of successive harvest. The stems are sweet and tender when young — the entire harvested shoot including leaves and stem is eaten, typically stir-fried with oyster sauce in Cantonese cuisine. Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool; consistent watering prevents the stems from becoming fibrous. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Chinese Broccoli Kailaan
description: Also called gai lan, this Asian green offers tender flowering stems, juicy stalks, and leaves with a sweet, slightly bitter flavor. Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to six to ten inches apart. It is more heat tolerant than regular broccoli, so it can be sown across a longer season. Harvest the whole plant or cut the main stem to encourage tender side shoots before the flower buds fully open. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Chinese Celery
description: Start the tiny seeds indoors, pressing them into the surface since they need light to germinate, and keep them evenly moist. Transplant into rich, damp soil and grow through the cooler parts of the season. This variety forms slender, hollow, intensely aromatic stalks used more as a seasoning than a raw snack, so cut stalks as needed for stir-fries and soups. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Celery
description: Sow tiny seeds on the surface of moist starting mix and press lightly without covering; seeds need light to germinate and are very slow — allow 2–3 weeks. Chinese celery produces slender, hollow stems and abundant leaves with intense celery flavor far more pungent than Western stalk celery; it is used primarily as an herb and flavoring rather than eaten in large quantities raw. Transplant into moisture-retentive, fertile soil and keep evenly moist throughout the season, as drought causes bitterness and premature bolting. Harvest outer stalks continuously once plants are established; the leaves are the most intensely flavored part. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Chestnut
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Chinese chestnut is the blight-resistant alternative to the devastated American chestnut, producing sweet, edible nuts very similar to the native species. It grows naturally in China where it evolved resistance to the fungal blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that destroyed American chestnuts, and is now the primary species used in chestnut restoration hybrids and in commercial chestnut orchards throughout the eastern US. The tree is medium-sized (30–50 feet), requires two or more trees for cross-pollination, and begins producing nuts within 3–5 years from a grafted tree. The burr-enclosed nuts ripen in fall and are harvested fresh for roasting, boiling, grinding into flour, and use in stuffings and desserts. Chinese chestnut wood is also blight-resistant and durable. An important and practical nut tree for the food forest and home orchard in zone 4–9. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Chinkapin (Henry's Chestnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, giving the tree room to develop its narrower, more elongated leaves than other chestnut species. Native to central and southern China, Chinese chinkapin is a distinct chestnut species from Castanea mollissima, bearing small burs that typically enclose a single sweet nut rather than the two or three found in most chestnuts. It has been used by breeders exploring additional sources of blight tolerance and is planted both as a nut producer and as an ornamental shade tree in its native range. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Cinnamon (Cassia Cinnamon)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 8b–11; Chinese cinnamon is the source of most commercial cinnamon sold in the United States — the cassia bark sold in grocery stores as 'cinnamon' is typically the bark of this or related Cinnamomum species rather than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The inner bark is harvested by stripping the outer bark from young shoots and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills. Chinese cassia has a stronger, more pungent flavor with higher coumarin content than the mild, sweet Ceylon cinnamon — a trait that limits consumption quantities but makes it the preferred spice for strongly-flavored applications. In zone 9 gardens, this attractive evergreen tree or large shrub provides handsome, dark green, three-veined leaves and an aromatic quality throughout the year. Harvest bark from branches 2–3 years old for optimal flavor concentration. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Cling Peach (Historic Clingstone Peach, Foundational Elberta Parent)
description: Chinese Cling is one of the most historically important peaches in American horticulture, imported from southern China to Charleston, South Carolina around 1850 and quickly distributed through the Southern nursery trade for its large size, vigorous growth, and adaptability to warm climates. It bears large, round, downy-skinned fruit with white, richly flavored, strongly clingstone flesh streaked with red near the pit — a distinctly Old World peach character quite different from the freestone yellow peaches that later came to dominate American orchards. Its greatest legacy is genetic: Samuel Rumph of Marshallville, Georgia crossed Chinese Cling with Early Crawford in 1875 to produce Elberta, the freestone peach that became the backbone of the Southern peach industry for a century, and Chinese Cling parentage runs through many other historic Southern cultivars as well. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart after petal fall, prune annually to an open-vase form, and maintain a preventive fungicide and dormant-oil spray program, since like most heirloom clingstone types it has only modest resistance to brown rot and peach leaf curl. Matures in 110–130 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Cucumber (Tian Hua Fen, Gua Lou)
description: Unlike its tropical cousins snake gourd and pointed gourd, Chinese cucumber is a temperate-climate vine native to China, Korea, and Japan that dies back to a large tuberous root each winter and can survive outdoors as far north as zone 8. Its claim to fame is not the bitter, inedible fruit but the plant's use in traditional Chinese medicine: the dried root (tian hua fen), the ripe fruit rind and pulp (gua lou), and the seeds (gua lou ren) are all harvested as distinct medicinal preparations, the root typically dug in autumn once vines are several years established. The vine itself is also a striking ornamental for a sunny trellis or arbor, producing intricately lace-fringed white flowers that open at dusk and are followed by round to oval fruit that ripens from green to bright orange-red. Grow it in full sun on rich, well-drained soil with a sturdy support, and be patient, since the root needs two to three seasons to bulk up to a size worth harvesting. Matures in 100–150 days from seed.

name: Chinese Eggplant
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F soil temperature 8–10 weeks before last frost, then transplant into warm, deeply tilled, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nighttime temperatures stay above 55°F; Chinese eggplant varieties produce long, slender, lavender to deep purple fruits that are less bitter, have thinner skin, and contain fewer seeds than standard Italian-type eggplants, making them ideal for stir-frying, grilling, and steaming. Plants are highly productive in hot, humid climates and are better adapted to the Gulf South than globe types. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch heavily to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature. Support plants with stakes if fruit load causes stem breakage. Matures in 55–80 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Five-Color Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Chinese Five-Color is a compact ornamental hot pepper prized for producing small, upward-facing fruit in purple, cream, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, since individual peppers ripen through this color sequence at slightly different rates, creating a constantly shifting, jewel-like display against the plant's purple-tinged green foliage and purple flowers. The small, tapered fruit carries real heat in the cayenne range and is fully edible, useful in hot sauces or pickling, though most growers treat the plant primarily as a container or bedding ornamental. The compact, well-branched habit needs no staking and performs equally well in the ground or in a decorative pot on a sunny patio; harvest fruit at any color stage once past the initial pale coloring. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Flowering Kale (Yod Fah, Flowering Gai Lan)
description: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin seedlings to allow strong flowering stalks to develop. Known in Thai and Southeast Asian markets as yod fah ('flower tip'), Chinese flowering kale is a gai lan (Chinese broccoli) type grown specifically for its tender, slightly sweet flowering stems, harvested with the small buds still tightly closed or just beginning to open, rather than for leaves or heads as with most brassicas. Stems, leaves, and unopened flower buds are all edible with a mild, cabbage-broccoli flavor and pleasant crunch, commonly stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce. Harvest the main flowering stalk when buds are plump but unopened, which encourages side shoots to develop for a continued harvest over several weeks; plants that are allowed to fully flower and set seed turn tough and bitter. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Chinese Giant Pepper (Extra-Large Thick-Walled Heirloom Bell)
description: Chinese Giant is a pre-1900s heirloom sweet pepper prized for its nearly square, extra-large, thick-walled fruit that can reach 4-6 inches long and wide, ripening from dark green to a bright cherry red with mild, sweet, fruity flavor. The compact, 2 to 2.5 foot plants stay relatively short despite the outsized fruit, so working compost into the planting hole and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers to their full potential without stressing the plant. Its thick flesh and generous cavity make it an outstanding stuffing pepper, and the large flat surfaces also suit it well to slicing for salads or grilling. Support heavily loaded branches with light staking in windy sites, since the fruit's weight can snap stems on an otherwise sturdy plant. Matures in 73–90 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Groundcover Mahonia
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to deep partial shade beneath trees, where Mahonia confusa spreads slowly by suckers into a low, broad, ground-covering colony rather than growing as a single upright shrub like most of its relatives. Its narrow, glossy, sparsely spined leaflets give it a softer, less prickly look than Mahonia aquifolium, making it easier to work around at the front of a bed. Slender racemes of small yellow flowers appear in late summer to autumn, an unusually late season for the genus, followed by blue-black berries. Once established it tolerates dry shade and root competition well and needs only occasional deep watering during prolonged drought; thin out old canes at the base periodically to keep the colony from becoming congested. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Hawthorn (Mountain Hawthorn)
description: Plant grafted trees or container saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese hawthorn is extremely cold-hardy, surviving temperatures to -30°F, and is one of the most productive and large-fruited hawthorns available for northern gardeners. Crataegus pinnatifida is the most commercially important hawthorn in China where it is grown in extensive orchards for its unusually large (up to 1 inch across), bright-red, shiny fruits with white-speckled skin; the tart, apple-like fruits are eaten fresh, candied (as Chinese candied hawthorn skewers — tanghulu), made into jams, dried, and used extensively in traditional Chinese medicine for digestive health. The tree is heavily thorned, produces profuse white spring flowers, and has attractive, deeply lobed leaves with good fall color. It adapts readily to a wide range of soils and climates in zones 3–8. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Keys / Fingerroot
description: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in moist, well-draining soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in a partially shaded bed or in a large container with excellent drainage. Water regularly to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer during the active growing season to support lush foliage and rhizome development. The distinctive clusters of finger-like yellow rhizomes are ready to harvest when the foliage begins to yellow and die back in autumn, typically 6-10 months after planting. In cooler climates (zone 8-9), dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter in slightly damp peat or coconut coir at 55-65 degrees F, replanting the following spring. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Leek Flower
description: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost, sowing in clusters and keeping soil around 65F. This garlic chive selection is grown especially for its tender edible flower stalks used in stir-fries. Transplant clumps to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly watered. Harvest the round flower buds and stems just before they open for the mildest flavor. Divide the perennial clumps every few years and cut back foliage after frost. Matures in 80–120 days from seed.

name: Chinese Licorice (Gan Cao)
description: Chinese licorice is a rhizomatous perennial legume native to the steppes of northern China, Mongolia, and Siberia, cultivated for its sweet, fibrous root, known as gan cao, one of the most frequently used herbs in traditional Chinese medicine formulas, prized for harmonizing other herbs in a blend. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing in spring into deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; as a nitrogen-fixing legume it tolerates poor, sandy soils but struggles in heavy, waterlogged clay. The plant spreads steadily by underground rhizomes and can become assertive in loose soil over time, so give it room or a root barrier in smaller gardens. Roots are traditionally left in the ground for three to four years to bulk up before being dug in autumn, then sliced and dried; this species is distinct from the Mediterranean licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra) more commonly grown in Western herb gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from seed.

name: Chinese Mallow (Cluster Mallow, Whorled Mallow)
description: Direct sow in early spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; harvest young leaves frequently to promote continuous leaf production; very easy and fast-growing. Malva verticillata (Chinese mallow, cluster mallow, or dong kui) is a tall, fast-growing cool-season annual or biennial in the mallow family (Malvaceae) — widely grown as a vegetable and medicinal plant in China, Korea, and Japan, but largely unknown in Western vegetable gardens despite being exceptionally easy to grow. The plant produces large, round, slightly lobed, bright-green leaves arranged in whorls up tall stems, with tiny, pale-pink to white flowers clustered tightly in the leaf axils (verticillate = whorled) — the common name 'cluster mallow' refers to this tight clustering of flowers. The young leaves are mild, slightly mucilaginous (like okra, a mallow family relative), tender, and nutritious — eaten raw in salads when small, or cooked like spinach, added to soups, or stir-fried. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the seeds (dong kui zi — 'mallow seeds') are used as a urinary tonic and to promote milk flow in nursing mothers. The plant is exceptionally productive and self-sows readily; in mild climates it functions as a perennial, re-growing from the base. The curly-leafed form (var. crispa) is especially popular as a leaf vegetable. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Chinese Motherwort (Yi Mu Cao)
description: Its uterine-stimulant action means it should be avoided in pregnancy except under professional postpartum guidance. Direct-sow after the last frost into full sun and average garden soil, where this tall, bitter mint-family plant grows quickly and self-seeds much like its Western relative, common motherwort. The flowering tops are dried for TCM decoctions traditionally used to invigorate blood flow, ease menstrual discomfort, and support postpartum recovery. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Chinese Mugwort (Ai Ye)
description: Artemisia argyi is the specific mugwort species (known in Chinese as ai ye) that supplies the compressed floss burned in moxibustion, a cornerstone practice of traditional Chinese medicine distinct from the more general culinary and craft uses of European mugwort or Japanese yomogi. The deeply lobed leaves have a dense, silvery-white wooly underside that is processed and aged before being rolled into moxa sticks or cones. Cut foliage in mid-summer just before flowering, when the aromatic oil content is highest, and dry bundled stems in a shaded, airy location. The plant spreads vigorously by rhizome and self-sows in favorable sites, so confine it with a root barrier or grow it in a dedicated bed away from cultivated borders. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Olive (Canary Tree, White Olive)
description: This large subtropical tree, widely cultivated across southern China and Southeast Asia, produces olive-shaped drupes with an edible oily, nut-like kernel inside fibrous flesh that is traditionally pickled, candied, or cooked rather than eaten raw off the tree. It is unrelated to the Mediterranean olive but fills a similar culinary role in Chinese cuisine, where preserved and salted fruits are a common snack. Because it is only reliably hardy to around 25-28°F, treat it as an experimental planting for the warmest, most sheltered Gulf Coast sites, and expect a long juvenile period of many years before first fruiting from seed-grown trees. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Pink Garlic (Early Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Chinese Pink is a Porcelain-type hardneck known for finishing about two weeks ahead of most other hardneck garlics, making it useful for gardeners wanting an early harvest or a hedge against unpredictable weather. Bulbs are smaller, typically holding just 4 to 6 plump cloves wrapped in blush pink-tinged wrappers, with a flavor many describe as gentler and easier on the stomach than sharper varieties. Grow and cure it like other hardnecks: plant in fall, remove the scape once it curls, and harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown. Its mild character makes it a good entry point for cooks who find stronger hardneck garlics overpowering raw. Matures in 220–250 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Prickly Ash (Flatspine Prickly Ash, Sichuan Pepper Relative)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; wear thick gloves when harvesting or pruning due to sharp thorns. Zanthoxylum simulans (Chinese prickly ash or flatspine prickly ash) is a thorny deciduous shrub from eastern and central China — one of several Zanthoxylum species used as sources of the Sichuan pepper-type spice in Chinese cooking, alongside the more commonly cultivated Z. bungeanum (Sichuan pepper) and Z. piperitum (Japanese sansho). Like its famous relatives, Z. simulans produces small, red, split-open seed husks (pericarps) after the black seed falls out; these husks contain hydroxy-alpha-sanshool and related sanshool compounds that cause the unique 'ma' (numbing-tingling) sensation of Sichuan cooking — a distinctive electric, oscillating numbness of the tongue and lips, combined with floral, citrus, and spicy aromatic notes. Z. simulans is more cold-hardy than the primary Sichuan pepper (Z. bungeanum) and is one of the species sometimes sold as 'Sichuan pepper' in the US market. The fresh husks, dried husks, and sometimes the young leaves are all used as aromatic seasonings. As a garden plant, it is an attractive, fast-growing thorny shrub with fragrant compound leaves that provides hedging function while producing a useful spice crop. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Quince (Chinese Flowering Quince)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Chinese quince (Pseudocydonia sinensis) is a small ornamental tree related to quince and pear but in its own monotypic genus, producing magnificent exfoliating bark (flaking in irregular puzzle-piece patches of green, cream, and tan like a camouflage pattern), beautiful pale pink spring flowers, and large, 6-inch, yellow, pear-shaped fruits in autumn with a powerful quince-like fragrance that fills a room. The fruits are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, paste (membrillo), and syrup; the trees are also spectacular in fall when the leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and yellow. One of the most ornamentally distinguished small trees available for zones 5–9, combining beautiful bark, flowers, fruit, and fall color in a single specimen. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Red Ripper Cowpea (Small-Seeded Bushy Red Ripper Type)
description: Chinese Red Ripper, also sold as Chinese Red, is a smaller-seeded, bushier selection of the classic Red Ripper cowpea. It is highly heat tolerant, blooms and sets pods early, and produces long 12-14 inch pods holding 18-21 seeds each, making it a heavy producer for a bush-type pea. It works equally well as a fresh green-shelled pea, a dried storage pea, or a summer cover crop and wildlife forage planting. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Chinese Skullcap
description: Chinese skullcap, or Huang Qin, is a hardy perennial with violet-blue tubular flowers, long valued in traditional East Asian herbalism. Sow seed after a period of cold stratification into well-drained soil in full sun. Roots are typically harvested from plants three or more years old, after the tops die back. Keep soil moderately moist and avoid waterlogging, which can rot the crown. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Chinese Taro (Chinese Elf Ear)
description: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moist soil in partial to full shade in zones 8–11; Chinese taro is the most cold-hardy member of Alocasia and one of the few genuinely shade-tolerant large-leaved tropical plants, making it extraordinarily valuable for filling shaded spaces in zone 8–11 gardens with bold, architectural foliage. The waxy, medium-green, upright-pointing leaves on sturdy petioles have a distinctive hooded appearance (cucullata means 'hooded' in Latin). In Buddhist traditions across Southeast Asia, this plant is kept in temple gardens as a sacred plant and is associated with good fortune. In zone 9, it grows as a reliable outdoor perennial in shade, dying back in hard freezes and re-emerging from the corm in spring. The corms are technically edible after thorough cooking (raw alocasia contains calcium oxalate crystals), but this species is primarily ornamental rather than a food crop. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Toon (Toona, Chinese Cedar)
description: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in full sun; Chinese toon is one of the most unusual food plants in world horticulture — a large, fast-growing deciduous tree whose young leaves and shoot tips are a prized traditional vegetable in Chinese cuisine ('xiang chun' in Mandarin), with a distinctive, complex, slightly onion-garlicky, savory, slightly resinous flavor unlike any other leaf vegetable. The young spring shoots — harvested when the leaves are emerging, brilliantly colored in red-bronze to burgundy — are stir-fried, used in tofu dishes, scrambled eggs, and pancakes, or eaten raw as a garnish. The harvest window is narrow (only the youngest, most tender growth is palatable; older leaves become tough and more bitter). Coppicing the tree in late winter each year keeps it shrub-sized (4–8 feet) and maximizes the production of young, tender shoots. One of the very few trees in the world cultivated specifically for its edible leaves. An extraordinary permaculture and forest garden plant for zones 6–9. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Water Chestnut
description: Plant corms in large containers or pond margins filled with fertile soil kept saturated or covered with 2–4 inches of standing water; Chinese water chestnuts are aquatic sedges that produce sweet, crisp, walnut-sized brown corms in fall after the above-ground foliage dies back. Start corms in pots indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, keep them sitting in shallow water in a warm, sunny spot, then move containers outdoors after last frost. In October or November when the hollow cylindrical foliage yellows and collapses, drain the container and harvest corms by rummaging through the mud. Fresh-harvested corms are intensely sweet and crunchy — a completely different experience from the bland canned version. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Chinese White Mulberry (Silkworm Mulberry, King White Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mulberry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions once established. Morus multicaulis (Chinese white mulberry or silkworm mulberry) is the mulberry species most important to global sericulture (silk production) — the leaves are the sole or preferred food source for the silkworm (Bombyx mori), whose cocoons are processed into silk thread. The species is a distinct subspecies or variety within the Morus alba complex, selected over millennia in China, Japan, and Korea for large, tender, nutritious leaves with high silkworm productivity. It produces sweet, large, white-to-pale-lavender to white-pink fruits that ripen in early summer — slightly milder and sweeter than red mulberry, excellent fresh, in pies, jams, syrups, and wine. The tree is fast-growing and quite large, eventually reaching 20–30 feet with a spreading canopy that provides excellent summer shade. In zone 9, the large, sweet fruits ripen in May–June; the tree is deciduous and provides summer shade then winters interest with a distinctive, broadly spreading branch structure. An underused fruit tree for Gulf Coast food gardens where its heat and drought tolerance are genuine assets. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Wolfberry (Barbary Wolfberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade — Chinese wolfberry is similar to goji berry (L. barbarum) but more cold-hardy and shade-tolerant, producing red-orange elongated berries with the same sweet-astringent, tart-sweet flavor. In traditional Chinese medicine, the leaves (often cooked as a vegetable), young shoots, and berries are all used. The dried berries (gou qi zi) are a fundamental ingredient in Chinese tonic soups and herbal preparations, used for eye health and as a general tonic for centuries. Fresh berries are also edible and pleasant. The arching, thornless-to-spiny stems produce attractive light purple flowers in summer before the berries. Remarkably adaptable to difficult soils including alkaline, clay, and dry soils, and more shade-tolerant than most full-sun fruiting shrubs. Note that it spreads by roots and seeds; manage accordingly. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Yam (Asiatic Yam, Sweet Yam, Lesser Yam, Intoxicating Yam)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil with a tall climbing support — Chinese Yam produces a vigorous twining vine that requires sturdy vertical support and rewards deep soil preparation with a generous yield of multiple smaller tubers around the central plant. Dioscorea esculenta is a tuberous, climbing vine native to Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia through Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines) and widely cultivated across the Pacific Islands and tropical world in the Dioscoreaceae family. Unlike the large, single-tuber yam species (D. rotundata, D. cayennensis), D. esculenta produces clusters of multiple smaller, ovoid to elongated tubers 2–6 inches long, smooth to slightly warty, with white flesh and a naturally sweet, pleasant starchy flavor — one of the most palatable raw-flavor yam species and one that can be eaten simply baked, boiled, or roasted with a sweet, potato-like quality. The vines are typically spined at the base (small spines on the lower stems), climbing vigorously 10–15 feet per season. D. esculenta is the most widely grown yam species in the Pacific Islands and southern Asia, where it is valued both for its edible tubers and for the medicinal compounds in the leaves and skin. In zone 9-12 Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, it provides a productive, tropical root vegetable harvest from fall plantings or spring starts, with harvest occurring before the first frost in zone 9 or when the vine dies back naturally in zone 10-12. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Yam (Cinnamon Vine)
description: Plant tuber sections or aerial bulbils (small potato-like growths that form in the leaf axils) 2–3 inches deep in deep, loose, stone-free soil; the main tuber can grow 3 feet straight down, so deep, well-prepared beds are essential. Provide a trellis or fence immediately as this vigorous twining vine can reach 15 feet in a season. Harvest main tubers in late fall after the vine dies back, being careful to dig deeply and extract the entire tuber without breaking; the secondary bulbils can also be harvested and eaten or saved for replanting. The raw tuber is one of the few yams that can be eaten uncooked and grated — called nagaimo in Japanese cuisine — where its distinctive gluey texture is prized. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Chinese Yellow Ginger
description: Chinese Yellow is the large-rhizome, mild-flavored ginger type most commonly sold fresh in American and Asian grocery markets, distinguished from Hawaiian Yellow and Bubba Blue strains by its paler, less fibrous flesh and lower pungency. Plant rhizome pieces 2-3 inches deep in loose, rich, well-drained soil after the soil has warmed in spring. Provide dappled shade during the hottest afternoon hours and consistent moisture through the long 8-10 month growing season; mature rhizomes are ready to dig once the foliage yellows and dies back in fall. In zone 9a, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter or heavily mulch in a well-protected bed, since prolonged soil temperatures below the upper 40s Fahrenheit will rot the rhizome. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Ching Chiang Bok Choy
description: Ching Chiang is a semi-dwarf Taiwanese bok choy with smooth, medium-green leaves and pale green petioles, bred to reach usable baby-bok-choy size quickly while still holding quality if left to mature further. It shrugs off the weather swings of shoulder-season planting better than many bok choy types, tolerating both a late cold snap and an early warm spell without much bolting or damage. Harvest whole plants at about five inches tall for the most tender baby heads, or let them grow another week or two for a larger stir-fry-sized crop. Matures in 40–45 days from seed.

name: Ching-Chiang Pak Choi
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to a close final spacing, since Ching-Chiang forms a compact, vase-shaped baby Shanghai-type plant with pale-green, spoon-shaped petioles and medium-green leaves. This variety is notably tolerant of heat, rain, cold, and dampness, which makes it more forgiving than many pak choi types for both early spring and late summer sowings. Harvest whole plants at about 6 inches tall for tender stir-fry and soup greens with a mild, sweet flavor. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Chinkapin (Golden Chinquapin)
description: Chinkapin (Castanopsis chrysophylla, also called golden chinquapin) is a large Pacific Coast evergreen related to chestnuts and oaks, bearing small, intensely sweet nuts in spiny burs — often considered the finest-flavored nut native to the Pacific Northwest. Unlike American chestnut it is not susceptible to chestnut blight, making it a valuable blight-free nut tree for western gardeners. Trees are monoecious but require cross-pollination between at least two seedlings or distinct cultivars for reliable nut production; wind and insects both carry pollen. Burs take two years to mature and split open in autumn — collect nuts promptly before squirrels and jays claim the entire crop, and consume or freeze within a month as the small nuts dry out quickly. Matures in 2190–4380 days from transplant.

name: Chinkapin Oak (Chinquapin Oak)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, calcareous or acidic soil in full sun; chinkapin oak is among the most drought-tolerant native oaks and the only species that thrives naturally on dry limestone outcrops and bluffs — a trait that makes it excellent for rocky, alkaline soils where most oaks fail. The toothed, chestnut-like leaves are distinctive and turn attractive gold and brown in fall. The sweet, small acorns are among the least bitter of any oak, maturing in a single season and consumed immediately by deer, turkeys, squirrels, and wood ducks. The tree adapts to a wide range of soils including limestone-derived clays, shallow rocky hillsides, and deep loams, making it one of the most landscapeable native oaks for challenging sites. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Chinook Hops (Piney Spicy Dual-Purpose Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Chinook, released by the USDA in 1985, is a high-alpha dual-purpose hop valued for strong bittering power paired with a distinctive piney, spicy, slightly grapefruit aroma, widely used in American IPAs and pale ales that call for assertive hop character. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet on a trellis; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect reduced yield compared with traditional hop-growing regions. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Chinook Leek (F1 Hybrid Summer Leek)
description: Chinook is a fast-growing, adaptable F1 leek bred for reliable summer production, reaching harvest size faster than most fall and winter types. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil at pH 6.0-7.0, spacing plants 4-5 inches apart in rows 12-18 inches apart.
