Despite its quick summer maturity it is frost-hardy, and in mild climates can be left in the ground and harvested through winter or stored in the ground until the soil freezes. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Chinotto (Myrtle-Leaf Sour Orange)
description: Chinotto is a compact, thornless, slow-growing citrus historically cultivated on the Italian and French Riviera, prized for its small, dense, myrtle-like foliage and long-held crop of small round bitter oranges. The fruit is the traditional flavoring source for chinotto soda and is also candied whole, much like miniature Seville oranges. Its tidy habit and fragrant white spring flowers make it an outstanding container or patio specimen even where fruit is not harvested. Grow in full sun with rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and protect from hard freezes, since it tolerates only brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chioggia Beet
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, loose, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Chioggia is an 1840s Italian heirloom beet from the town of Chioggia near Venice, producing medium-sized, round roots with distinctive alternating concentric rings of deep rose-red and white when sliced — resembling a bulls-eye or candy cane pattern that makes the cross-section one of the most visually striking of any vegetable. The candy-stripe pattern is most vivid in raw beets; cooking softens the color contrast. Chioggia has a notably milder, sweeter, less earthy flavor than standard red beet varieties — the 'dirt' or 'earthiness' commonly associated with beets is less pronounced in Chioggia, making it preferred by people who enjoy the sweetness of beets but find the strong earthy undertone of red beets off-putting. Raw Chioggia slices are excellent in salads and cheese boards where the color pattern can be appreciated, and they don't stain hands and cutting boards with the deep red juice of standard beets. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Chioggia Beet
description: This Italian heirloom reveals concentric pink-and-white rings when sliced, and the rings show best when eaten raw or lightly cooked. Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3 inches once true leaves appear. Keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody, zoned roots and to encourage tender growth. Harvest when roots reach 1.5 to 2 inches across for the sweetest flavor. The greens are also edible and can be cooked like chard. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Chipilin
description: Scarify and sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost; chipilin is a traditional leafy vegetable and nitrogen-fixing shrub-legume of Central America and southern Mexico, where the young leaves, shoots, and tender pods are eaten as a cooked green vegetable with a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor. It is a dietary staple in Chiapas, Guatemala, and El Salvador, added to soups, tamales, and rice. The plant is a prolific nitrogen fixer that can improve soil fertility significantly over a few seasons. Young growth is harvested continuously — cutting the stem tips promotes bushy, tender new growth. The yellow flowers are also edible and attract pollinators. In Gulf Coast zones 9–11 it grows as a multi-year perennial subshrub. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Chippewa Blueberry (Early-Season Half-High Cold-Hardy Blueberry)
description: Chippewa is a later University of Minnesota half-high release valued for combining a compact, 2- to 3-foot habit with unusually large berries for a half-high type and an early-to-midseason ripening window. It tolerates winter lows to roughly -30°F and performs reliably in zones where standard highbush blueberries suffer dieback, while still producing fruit with good sweetness and firm texture. Like other half-high cultivars it needs highly acidic soil, so growers should test pH and amend with elemental sulfur before planting if needed. Cross-pollinate with a second half-high or highbush cultivar to maximize berry size and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chirimen Squash (Japanese Yokohama-Type Winter Squash)
description: Chirimen is an old Japanese squash of the Yokohama group, named for its deeply ribbed, warty rind reminiscent of crinkled chirimen crepe fabric. Fruit starts dark green and ripens to a mottled bronze-orange, enclosing thick, moist, deep-yellow flesh with a sweetness similar to kabocha or butternut. The vines are extremely productive, often setting eight to twelve flattened, globe-shaped fruit weighing five to eleven pounds apiece over a season. Popular in Japan since the Edo period, it is well suited to simmering in broth, roasting, or tempura once fully cured, and stores for months when kept cool and dry after harvest. Matures in 95–120 days from seed.

name: Chivers Delight Apple (English Late-Season Cox-Type Dessert Apple)
description: Chivers Delight was raised in Cambridgeshire, England, by fruit grower Stewart Chivers and selected for its rich, aromatic, Cox-like flavor in a more reliably productive tree than Cox's Orange Pippin itself. The yellow-green, red-striped fruit ripens late in the season and develops a dense, sweet, complex flavor that improves after several weeks in storage. It is a good option for gardeners who love Cox's flavor profile but want a hardier, more consistent cropper. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Beauty Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep them warm for good germination. Transplant into full sun once nights stay warm, and allow the blocky fruits to ripen fully from green to glossy chocolate brown for the sweetest flavor and thickest walls. Support laden plants and harvest regularly to keep new fruit setting. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Chocolate Ghost Pepper)
description: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia is a dark-podded strain of the classic ghost pepper, ripening through green and reddish-brown before settling into a deep, glossy chocolate color. It carries the same wrinkled pod texture and formidable heat as red bhut jolokia, with a slightly earthier, roasted undertone favored by hot sauce makers. Because the fruit colors up slowly, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture to extend the ripening window. Keep soil evenly moist and handle harvested pods with gloves. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Bhutlah Pepper (Ghost x Trinidad Scorpion Superhot Hybrid)
description: Bhutlah, sometimes sold as Chocolate Bhutlah, is a deliberate cross of bhut jolokia (ghost pepper) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, producing small, extremely gnarled dark-brown pods that rank among the most searing chiles grown by home superhot enthusiasts. Because the fruit is slow to size up and slower still to fully color from green to chocolate-brown, gardeners in short-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture so plants can be moved to protect them from early frost. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since chinense superhots are prone to root stress that shows up as blossom drop weeks later. Handle harvested pods with gloves, as oleoresin transfer from Bhutlah is unusually persistent even after washing. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Cherry Pole Cherry Tomato
description: A prolific indeterminate cherry tomato bearing one-inch purplish-red fruits that add sweetness to salads and pastas. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. The vigorous vines set long trusses of six to eight crack-resistant fruits, so give them a tall trellis and prune for airflow. Water evenly and harvest when the fruit turns dusky red for the fullest flavor. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Cherry Tomato (Brownish-Red Heirloom Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support their vigorous, indeterminate vines. Chocolate Cherry is an heirloom cherry tomato bearing clusters of round, one-inch fruit in an unusual dusky brownish-red color reminiscent of the larger Cherokee Purple, carrying the same rich, complex, sweet-and-smoky flavor in a bite-sized package rather than a full beefsteak-size fruit. Its productive, long-season vines yield heavily from midsummer through frost, making it a favorite for snacking, salads, and roasting where its deep color and complex flavor stand out from ordinary red cherry tomatoes. Harvest when fruits soften slightly and the color deepens fully, as the dusky skin tone makes visual ripeness cues subtler than on standard red tomatoes. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Habanero Pepper (Congo Black Habanero)
description: Start seeds on a heat mat at 85°F for reliable germination 10–21 days; transplant after last frost when nighttime temperatures stay above 60°F. Chocolate Habanero (also called Congo Black or Dark Habanero) is a Capsicum chinense variety that ripens to a deep chocolate brown color rather than the typical orange, with heat levels of 300,000–400,000 Scoville units — significantly hotter than standard orange habaneros and with a distinctive earthy, smoky-sweet flavor that many hot pepper enthusiasts consider more complex and interesting. Originally from Jamaica and Trinidad, it is prized by hot sauce makers for its unique color and flavor profile; the pods are slightly larger than standard habaneros, with thick walls and a rich, fruity aroma. Grow in full sun with warm nights for the best fruit set; perennial in zone 9–12, often producing for multiple years as a shrubby plant. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Mint
description: Plant divisions in rich, consistently moist soil and confine the roots with a buried barrier or container, as this mint spreads aggressively like all peppermint cultivars. Provide consistent moisture and partial shade in hot climates to prevent the dark-stemmed foliage from scorching. Harvest stems just before flowers open for the most pronounced menthol-and-chocolate aroma; the leaves are prized for their distinctive scent in desserts, hot chocolate, and after-dinner teas. Cut plants back to 2–3 in above ground after each main harvest to stimulate a flush of fragrant new growth. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Mint Geranium
description: Root Chocolate Mint Geranium cuttings in well-drained, lean soil; grow in full sun to partial shade and let the soil dry between waterings, as it is prone to root rot when kept wet. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the somewhat sprawling habit compact and bushy. The bold, velvety leaves — bright green edged in a broad chocolate-brown central patch — carry a soft, mild mint fragrance when brushed or crushed, making the plant a striking foliage accent in containers as much as a kitchen herb. Use the leaves sparingly to flavor cream, sugar, and iced tea, or simply grow it for its ornamental two-tone foliage among a scented-geranium collection; bring indoors as a houseplant before first fall frost since it has no cold tolerance. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Persimmon (Brown-Fleshed Sweet Pollination-Variant Persimmon)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chocolate is a PVNA (Pollination Variant Non-Astringent) Japanese persimmon — a type that produces sweet, non-astringent, crunchy-when-firm fruit with distinctive brown ('chocolate') flesh when pollinated and seeds are present, but remains astringent if no seeds develop from lack of pollination. The presence of a pollinator tree (Gailey, Maru, or another male or seeded cultivar) within 50 feet allows Chocolate to develop its characteristic dark brown, sweet, crunchy flesh that can be eaten firm at the orange-yellow stage — unlike astringent types that must be soft. This firm-eating non-astringent quality (shared by Fuyu) makes Chocolate outstanding for fresh use, salads, and eating out of hand. The unusual brown flesh color — resulting from tannin-anthocyanin reactions stimulated by seeds — is distinctive and has no direct equivalent among common temperate fruits. With a pollinator nearby, Chocolate produces medium-large, flat to slightly rounded, orange fruits with brown flesh that are ready from late September through November in zone 9. Without a pollinator, fruits are astringent and must ripen soft (similar to Hachiya) before eating. For maximum enjoyment, plant Chocolate near another persimmon variety for cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Sprinkles Pole Cherry Tomato
description: An extraordinarily productive cherry tomato with elongated, deep-red fruits striped in green and brown and a rich, sweet flavor. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Provide a tall cage or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water consistently and keep picking, as the fruit keeps coming all season long. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Stripes Tomato (Mahogany-Striped Beefsteak Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Chocolate Stripes is a dark-fruited heirloom beefsteak tomato with dusky mahogany-brown skin overlaid with darker green-brown stripes radiating from the stem, and rich, complex, slightly smoky-sweet flesh characteristic of the best dark-colored heirloom tomatoes. Fruit runs large for slicing and sandwiches, and the deep coloring makes it a striking addition to a mixed heirloom tomato platter. Stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine well, water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure and the shoulders have darkened fully. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Chocolate Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
description: Chocolate Trinidad Scorpion produces the same tailed, stinger-tipped pods as the classic red scorpion strains, but ripens to a rich mahogany brown with a deeper, more smoky flavor beneath the intense heat. It is a separate color strain from Butch T and Moruga lines, grown by superhot collectors for hot sauce and extract use. Provide a long warm season, steady moisture, and staking once fruit clusters get heavy, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under water stress. Handle ripe pods with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Choctaw Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, acidic soil; Choctaw is an erect, thorny blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in 1980, one of the earliest-ripening blackberry varieties available and long valued in the mid-South and Gulf Coast for extending the harvest season ahead of later thornless varieties. The medium-sized berries are glossy black, firm, and exceptionally sweet with small seeds and outstanding flavor, considered by many Southern growers among the best-tasting of the University of Arkansas blackberry releases even decades after its introduction. The erect canes are self-supporting and highly productive, though the thorns require more careful handling at harvest and pruning than newer thornless varieties. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; tip primocanes at about 36 inches in summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry the following year's crop. An excellent early-season partner for later-ripening varieties like Ouachita or Natchez to extend the blackberry harvest across the whole season. Zone 6–9. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Choctaw Pecan (Large-Nut Premium Gulf South Pecan, Type II Late-Season Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Choctaw is a late-season variety ripening in October–November, later than most other pecans; supplement with zinc spray in spring; Choctaw is somewhat susceptible to pecan scab in very humid coastal conditions and benefits from fungicide applications in wet years; best in zones 7–9 with adequate growing season length. Choctaw pecan is a USDA-ARS variety (released 1959) known primarily for producing some of the largest individual nuts of any commercial pecan variety, with nut counts typically running 35–40 per pound compared to the 50–60 nuts per pound typical of smaller varieties — in pecan marketing, where size commands premium prices, Choctaw's exceptionally large nuts give it distinct commercial value. The nuts are well-filled, with 60–64% kernel percentage, and the kernel quality is excellent — bright golden color, plump halves, and a rich, sweet buttery flavor. Choctaw has broader adaptation through the Gulf South than some varieties, performing reasonably well in the humid coastal plain from eastern Texas through the Florida Panhandle, though like most pecans it requires fungicide management for scab control in high-humidity years. The trees are vigorous and upright-growing, ultimately becoming very large specimens, and are somewhat slow to come into production compared to precocious varieties like Pawnee. The late ripening season (October–November) is an advantage in areas prone to early fall wet weather — the nuts are harvested and on the ground before the worst scab-spreading conditions of mid-fall. A prestige variety for home orchards and direct-market operations where extra-large nut size commands attention. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Chojuro Asian Pear (Brown Russet Japanese Pear, Butterscotch Asian Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chojuro requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in late August to mid-September when the skin color transitions from greenish-brown to warm brown-russet; Chojuro stores well under refrigeration (2–3 months) longer than many other Asian pears; flavor improves slightly with 2–4 weeks of cold storage after harvest. Chojuro is one of the oldest named Asian pear varieties in continuous cultivation, developed in Japan from a cross of two traditional Japanese pear varieties in the late 1800s and widely grown there for well over a century before introduction to North American home orchards. The variety's distinguishing characteristic is a unique flavor profile — described as butterscotch, caramel, or anise-like by different tasters — that is completely unlike any other Asian pear variety and arguably more complex than the straightforward crisp sweetness of varieties like Shinseiki and Hosui. The nuts are medium to large, round to oblate, with a rich brown-russet skin that is slightly rough in texture, and crisp, dense, white flesh with the characteristic refreshing juiciness of Asian pears combined with the distinctive butterscotch flavor undertone. Chojuro has become popular among specialty Asian pear growers and farmers' market vendors precisely because its unusual flavor creates a point of differentiation from the more neutral-flavored standard varieties — customers who taste it for the first time often find the flavor complex and memorable. Good fire blight resistance compared to some other varieties. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Chokecherry
description: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; chokecherry is one of North America’s most cold-hardy and adaptable native fruiting shrubs, ranging from Alaska to Tennessee and coast to coast. Fragrant white flower racemes appear in spring followed by clusters of small dark red to purple-black fruits in mid-summer. The astringent, very tart fruits are too acidic to eat raw in quantity but cook into outstanding jams, syrups, and wines with a flavor reminiscent of Concord grape; the juice has been used by indigenous peoples for centuries as a food, dye, and medicine. It suckers freely to form thickets, providing excellent wildlife habitat. Cultivars 'Schubert' and 'Canada Red' have striking purple summer foliage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Choppee Okra (South Carolina Lowcountry Heirloom Okra)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Choppee is an heirloom okra passed down among South Carolina Lowcountry gardening families near the Choppee community in Georgetown County, valued for producing tender, nearly spineless, slightly ridged green pods with a reddish tinge at the base earlier in the season than many other Southern heirlooms. The plants are productive and well adapted to the humid, hot conditions of the coastal Southeast, and pods should be picked at 3-5 inches for the best table quality. Like most heirloom okras it is open-pollinated and easily saved from year to year, helping preserve a piece of Lowcountry foodways history. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Choquette Avocado (Late-Season Florida Avocado)
description: A West Indian x Guatemalan hybrid bred in Florida, Choquette is known for producing some of the largest avocados grown in home gardens, with individual fruit often exceeding three pounds. The thin, glossy green skin encloses mild, buttery, relatively low-oil flesh typical of West Indian-influenced cultivars. Its late harvest window, generally October through December, extends the backyard avocado season well past most other Florida cultivars, but the tree's ultimate size calls for a spacious planting site away from structures. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chowan Muscadine Grape (Bronze Female Cultivar)
description: Chowan is an early bronze-fruited muscadine released in the 1960s and long grown across the North Carolina and Virginia coastal plain, prized for its golden-bronze skin and classic musky-sweet muscadine flavor. Because Chowan carries only female flowers, plant it within 10-15 feet of a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to ensure a full fruit set each season. The vigorous vine performs best trained onto a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis, where the loose clusters ripen through late summer and are picked individually as berries soften and detach easily. Like other muscadines, Chowan shrugs off the heat, humidity, and Pierce's disease pressure of the Gulf Coast that limit bunch-grape production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Choy Sum
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows, thinning to 6–10 inches; plants can be sown more densely and thinned progressively, using the thinnings as greens. Harvest the central flower stalk when buds are just beginning to show yellow but before flowers open, cutting 6 inches down to leave side shoots. The stems, leaves, and flower buds are all edible; successive harvesting keeps production going for several weeks. Even soil moisture and cool temperatures produce the sweetest, most tender stalks. Matures in 35–55 days from seed.

name: Christ's Thorn Jujube / Sidr
description: Remove the seed from its hard stone before sowing, then plant 1 inch deep in sandy, well-drained soil in a warm, sunny location once all frost risk has passed. This tree demands heat and full sun and will not tolerate waterlogged or heavy clay soils; raised beds or slopes with excellent drainage are ideal in marginal climates. Protect young trees from frost in zones 8 and 9 during their first few winters until the trunk thickens and cold hardiness improves. Fruit production begins within three to five years of transplanting and increases substantially as the tree matures. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Christine's Choice Tea (Cold-Hardy Southeast Tea Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal, especially in hot Gulf South summers; Christine's Choice is a tea cultivar selected and named by Camellia Forest Nursery in North Carolina from Southeast-grown seedling stock, chosen specifically for vigorous, reliable growth and good leaf quality in the humid, hot-summer conditions of the American Southeast rather than for the extreme cold tolerance bred into Sochi-type selections. It is a popular choice for home tea growers from the Carolinas through the Gulf Coast who want a productive plant adapted to regional humidity and disease pressure rather than one optimized for northern cold snaps. Leaves and growth habit are typical of small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch well to protect the acid-loving root system. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Christmas Basil (Compact Heat-Tolerant Clove-Scented Hybrid Basil for Extended Season)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost in warm soil. Pinch flower buds to extend leaf production. Harvest continuously. Christmas Basil is a hybrid basil variety that represents a key development in warm-climate basil breeding: the combining of sweet basil's mild, widely-appealing flavor with the improved heat tolerance and disease resistance of Asian basil species, particularly Thai basil (Ocimum × citriodorum). Standard Genovese-type sweet basil, while ideal for Italian cooking and widely preferred for pesto, has two significant limitations in zone 9 and other hot-humid climates: it is susceptible to Fusarium wilt (a soilborne fungal disease that wilts and kills plants) and downy mildew (an airborne pathogen that devastates basil foliage in warm-humid conditions), and it performs poorly in sustained heat, often bolting and declining during the Gulf Coast summer. Christmas Basil's hybrid origin provides significantly better tolerance to both heat and these pathogens — plants remain productive and healthy through conditions that would collapse standard Genovese types. The flavor of Christmas Basil occupies an intermediate position between sweet basil and Thai basil: more complex and spicy than plain Genovese, with distinct clove and anise notes from the Thai parentage, but milder than full-strength Thai basil. This flavor profile is versatile — appropriate for Italian applications (especially where some aromatic complexity is desired), for Southeast Asian-inspired dishes, and as a general culinary herb where the assertive clove character of straight Thai basil would be too dominant. The compact, mounding growth habit (12–20 inches) keeps plants tidy and manageable in containers and herb beds. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Christmas Lima Bean (Speckled Lima, Chestnut Lima)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost at the base of a sturdy trellis, fence, or poles in full sun, in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Christmas Lima is a striking heirloom pole lima with large seeds dramatically streaked and mottled in red-maroon and cream — the colors fade somewhat on cooking but the flavor more than compensates, often described as chestnut-like with a rich, buttery texture superior to common limas. A long-season variety that rewards gardeners in warm climates; in zone 9–10, the extended growing season produces heavy yields late into fall. Dry the seeds for storage as beautiful speckled beans that are prized for soups, stews, and succotash. Requires cross-pollination and benefits from hand removal of diseased pods. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Christmas Loquat (Very Early-Ripening Florida Loquat)
description: Site Christmas loquat in full sun on well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, and protect the fall bloom from hard freezes since flower and young-fruit damage below the mid-20s F is the main limit on cropping in zone 8b-9. This cultivar was selected in Florida for a markedly early ripening window, often filling the gap before the main January-March loquat harvest that most other cultivars occupy. Fruits are medium-sized with orange flesh and a bright, tangy-sweet flavor typical of Florida-bred selections rather than the milder Californian white-fleshed types. Thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage, and pick fruit only after full color develops since loquats do not ripen further once removed from the tree. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Chuan Xiong (Sichuan Lovage)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chuan Xiong is a cool-climate herb traditionally grown at higher elevation in Sichuan and prefers cooler summer conditions than the Gulf South provides. Finely divided, celery-like aromatic foliage and small umbels of white flowers grow from a knobby, strongly aromatic rhizome that is the part harvested and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, where it has long been valued for supporting healthy circulation. Historically cultivated at elevation in Sichuan province, it performs best where summers stay relatively mild and struggles with prolonged heat and humidity, making it a better fit for a cooler mountain or northern garden than a hot, humid Gulf Coast bed. Harvest and dry the rhizomes in fall after the foliage dies back, typically after one to two seasons of growth. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Chufa (Tiger Nut)
description: Plant soaked tubers of the cultivated variety (var. sativus) 1–2 inches deep in loose, moist soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing 6–12 inches apart; this is the domesticated food crop, not the invasive weed form. Keep soil continuously moist to encourage dense networks of underground stolons tipped with nutty, sweet tubers that mature in 90–120 days. Harvest after foliage yellows in early autumn by loosening the soil deeply with a fork and sifting through to collect the small, wrinkled tubers; yield can reach several pounds per plant under ideal conditions. Dried tubers keep for months and are eaten raw as a snack, soaked and blended into the Spanish drink horchata de chufa, or ground into gluten-free flour. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Chul Ri Che (Precocious Korean Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Chul Ri is a fast-growing, precocious female che selection from Korea that can set a light crop in its first year and reaches full production quickly thereafter. Left unpruned it becomes a large multi-stemmed tree, but it responds well to training as a smaller standard; growers commonly graft che onto Osage orange rootstock to encourage tree form over shrubby growth. Requires full sun and consistently moist soil through the heat of summer for best fruit set; like most che other than seedless selections, plant a male pollinator nearby for a reliable crop. Fruits are maroon-red, bumpy-skinned, and sweet with a fig-and-melon flavor. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Chullpi Quinoa (Andean Sweet Corn Quinoa)
description: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather. A traditional Andean landrace distinct from the more familiar white, red, and black quinoa sold commercially, this variety is prized in its native Peru and Bolivia for translucent, pale golden seed with a naturally sweet flavor reminiscent of corn, traditionally toasted and eaten as a snack rather than cooked as a grain like standard quinoa. It grows on tall, colorful seed-head spikes typical of quinoa and is naturally low in the bitter seed coating (saponin) found on many quinoa varieties, requiring less rinsing before cooking or toasting. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before storing or toasting. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Chun Yeon Gold Napa Cabbage
aliases: Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis 'Chun Yeon Gold'
description: Chun Yeon Gold is a modern Korean napa cabbage bred for the tight, cylindrical, uniform heads and bright golden-yellow interior leaves that Korean cooks favor for kimchi, wrapped around deep green outer leaves. It is notably slow to bolt, which makes it more forgiving of an early spring sowing than older napa types, and it carries resistance to downy mildew and soft rot that helps it hold up in humid conditions. Keep the soil consistently moist as heads fill out, since drought stress toughens the ribs and encourages tip burn. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, then use fresh in kimchi, soups, or braises, or store whole heads in a cold, humid space for several weeks. Matures in 60–68 days from seed.

name: Churchill Brussels Sprout (Mid-Season F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before the first fall frost and transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil; stake tall plants to keep them upright as sprouts fill in. Churchill is a dependable mid-season Brussels sprout hybrid known for setting a heavy, closely spaced column of smooth, dark green sprouts along a sturdy stalk, and for standing well in the garden without the stems toppling or the sprouts loosening. Its moderate cold tolerance lets it carry a harvest through the first hard frosts, which sweetens the sprouts. Pick from the bottom of the stalk upward once sprouts firm to about an inch across, and remove yellowing lower leaves as you go to improve air circulation. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Chuyskaya Sea Buckthorn (Star of Altai, Russian Low-Thorn Seaberry)
description: Chuyskaya, also marketed as Star of Altai, is a widely grown Russian sea buckthorn cultivar selected at breeding stations in the Altai region for noticeably fewer thorns than wild seaberry, which makes hand harvest considerably easier. It bears heavy clusters of bright orange, mildly tangy berries prized for juice, preserves, and vitamin-rich health products, and is counted among the sweeter and earlier-ripening seaberry selections available. Like all sea buckthorn it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root system and thrives in poor, sandy, or coastal soils that would stunt most other fruiting shrubs, but it dislikes waterlogged ground. Being dioecious, it requires a male sea buckthorn nearby to set any fruit at all. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Chwinamul (Korean Starwort, Japanese Aster)
description: Plant chwinamul in cool, humus-rich soil under the broken light of deciduous trees, where the broad basal leaves stay tender longer than they do in open sun. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips repeatedly through spring; a quick blanch mellows their mild, herbal, faintly sesame-like flavor before they are tossed with sesame oil, garlic, and soy for the classic Korean namul side dish. It is one of the most widely grown wild greens in Korean home gardens precisely because it tolerates the shady, moist corners where lettuce and other sun-loving greens struggle. Left unharvested in late summer it produces small white daisy-like flowers that draw pollinators to the shade garden. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Ciao Bella Basil Blend Microgreens
description: A fragrant basil blend grown as microgreens for a milder, nutrient-rich basil flavor any time of year. Sow seed densely on the surface of a shallow tray of moist growing mix and keep warm and evenly moist. Provide bright light once the seedlings emerge, since basil microgreens grow best warm. Harvest with scissors at the first true leaf stage, about two to three weeks after sowing, and use fresh. Matures in 16–25 days from seed.

name: Cilantro
description: This open-pollinated cilantro produces lush leafy greens and, when it bolts, aromatic coriander seed. Sow directly in cool weather since it bolts quickly once temperatures climb. Make small successive sowings every two to three weeks for a steady leaf harvest. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed to collect coriander or let them self-sow for the next round. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Cilantro Microgreens
description: Cilantro is one of the slower microgreens, so gently crack or presoak the split coriander seed to encourage faster, more even sprouting. Sow densely on a moist tray and keep it covered and warm for up to a week while germination gets underway. Once shoots appear, move to bright light and water carefully to avoid mold on the extended growing surface. Harvest the aromatic, citrus-scented greens after two to three weeks when the first true leaves emerge. Matures in 14–25 days from seed.

name: Cimarron Lettuce (Heat-Tolerant Bronze-Red Romaine Lettuce)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.125 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 8–12 inches for full-sized heads. Cimarron is a heat-tolerant romaine-type (cos) lettuce with beautiful bronze-red outer leaves that fade to green-red at the interior — a coloring that is visually distinctive from standard green romaine types while maintaining the characteristic romaine form: tall, upright, with a slightly folded, elongated head and the crisp, crunchy mid-rib texture that makes romaine the preferred lettuce for Caesar salad. The red pigmentation in Cimarron is not as deep or uniform as fully red romaines, but the attractive mottled bronze-red appearance combined with the green interior gives a bicolor effect that is especially attractive when heads are cut crosswise to reveal the color contrast. Cimarron's standout characteristic is its heat tolerance — while standard romaine types bolt (send up a seed stalk and become bitter) at sustained temperatures above 75–80°F, Cimarron holds its quality better at higher temperatures, extending the productive window by 2–3 weeks in warm spring conditions. This heat tolerance makes Cimarron particularly valuable in zone 8–10 gardens where spring temperatures rise quickly and the window for lettuce production is narrow. Named for the Cimarron Territory of the historic Southwest. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Cimmaron Romaine
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Cimmaron is a large, full-headed red romaine lettuce from the American Southwest — its name evokes the Cimarron River of the Oklahoma-Kansas plains country. It produces tall, upright, well-formed romaine heads with bronze-red to mahogany-red outer leaves and a pale green-to-cream interior heart, combining the classic romaine flavor and crunch with deep red coloration. The large, mature heads at 58–68 days are suitable for Caesar salad in the traditional whole-leaf format, where the combination of romaine structure and visual color impact makes Cimmaron stands out among red romaine options. Cimmaron is slower-bolting than most red looseleaf types and holds quality in the garden longer as a planted head. The flavor is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet — traditional romaine quality with no bitterness. In zone 9 fall planting produces the most satisfying heads; spring-planted Cimmaron benefits from light shade cloth in late spring to delay bolting. Matures in 58–68 days from seed.

name: Cincinnati Market Radish (Long Red Heirloom Radish)
description: Sow seed a half-inch deep directly in loose, well-worked soil, and thin seedlings early to a couple of inches apart so roots have room to elongate without forking. Cincinnati Market is an old market-garden heirloom prized for its long, cylindrical, bright scarlet-red roots with crisp, mild-flavored white flesh that stays tender without turning pithy or overly hot if harvested promptly at full size. It matures quickly, making it a reliable choice for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady radish supply, and its uniform, attractive shape made it a historic favorite for market bunching. Keep the soil consistently moist as roots size up, since inconsistent watering causes cracking and harsh flavor, and harvest promptly once roots reach full size, since radishes left too long in warm soil quickly turn woody and overly pungent. Matures in 28–35 days from seed.

name: Cinderella Pumpkin
description: The French heirloom Rouge Vif d'Etampes, a deeply ridged, flattened pumpkin twelve to twenty-four inches across weighing fifteen to twenty pounds. Sow seed directly one inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines ample room to sprawl. Keep soil evenly moist while fruit develops and set ripening fruit on a board to prevent rot. Harvest when the rind hardens to a vivid red-orange and the stem begins to cork. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Hybrid Flat Heirloom-Type Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vines ample room to spread. Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid take on the classic Cinderella-type pumpkin — the flattened, deeply ribbed, deep-orange-red fruit famously associated with the Rouge Vif d'Etampes heirloom — bred to add meaningful powdery mildew resistance and more consistent, higher yields than the older open-pollinated version, while keeping the same striking flattened silhouette prized for fall display. Fruit reaches 15-25 pounds with dense, good-flavored flesh usable for cooking as well as decoration. Because it is naturally more disease-resistant than the heirloom, the vines tend to stay productive and healthy later into the season in humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens and color deepens fully, cutting the stem rather than pulling to avoid damaging the fruit, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Cinnamon Basil
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in fertile, moist seed-starting mix held above 65°F, and transplant outdoors once night temperatures stay above 50°F. Cinnamon basil has reddish stems and pink-purple flowers; it contains methyl cinnamate, which gives the foliage a distinct warm spice note alongside the usual basil flavor. Pinch out flower stalks as they appear to maintain leaf production, and harvest by cutting stems back to a set of lower leaves. Use fresh or dried in fruit dishes, desserts, teas, and anywhere a subtle cinnamon note complements the basil flavor. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Cinnamon Girl Squash (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Butternut Hybrid)
description: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing. Named an All-America Selections winner in 2018, this hybrid butternut produces uniform, single-serving fruit around a pound each with deep tan skin and dense, sweet, richly colored flesh well suited to roasting whole. Bred for strong disease tolerance and heavy yields of personal-portion squash, it fits neatly into small households and market growers wanting consistent, easy-to-handle fruit. Cure harvested squash in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage life and sweetness. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Cinnamon Tree
description: This tropical evergreen yields true cinnamon, harvested from the fragrant inner bark of young stems. Grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil kept consistently moist but never soggy. Outside frost-free regions, keep it potted and bring it into a warm, bright room before temperatures drop, since it is very frost-sensitive. Coppice mature stems to encourage the tender shoots that produce the best bark for harvesting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cinsaut Grape (Cinsault, Historic Southern French and South African Red)
description: Cinsaut, also spelled Cinsault and grown in South Africa for generations under the name Hermitage, is a historic red wine grape of southern France's Languedoc and Provence regions, valued for large, loose clusters of thin-skinned berries that produce soft, lightly colored, fruity wine most often used in blends and rosé rather than bottled alone. Its vigor, heat tolerance, and reliable heavy cropping made it one of the most widely planted red grapes in the south of France for much of the twentieth century, prized by growers even as its soft tannins and pale color kept it out of the great varietal reds. Cinsaut carries outsized historical importance as one of the two parent grapes, crossed with Pinot Noir in 1925, of South Africa's signature Pinotage variety. Old, dry-farmed Cinsaut vines are increasingly sought after today for characterful, juicy varietal reds and natural wine blends. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the vigorous canopy for airflow to limit bunch rot in the loosely packed but still humidity-sensitive clusters, and thin crop in wet years to concentrate flavor, since Cinsaut left to overcrop produces thin, diluted wine. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cipollini Onion
description: These flat, disc-shaped Italian onions are prized for roasting whole and caramelizing due to their high sugar content. Start seed indoors ten weeks before last frost and transplant seedlings when pencil-thick. Keep beds weed-free since onions compete poorly, and water steadily until tops begin to fall. Stop watering once necks soften and leaves yellow, then lift and cure in a dry airy place. Well-cured bulbs store for several months in a cool spot. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Citation Rootstock (Dwarfing Stone Fruit Rootstock)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Citation is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit. A California-bred interspecific hybrid rootstock valued for producing a semi-dwarf tree roughly two-thirds the size of a standard seedling tree across a wide range of stone fruit species, including peaches, nectarines, plums, and apricots, offering rare cross-species versatility compared to most rootstocks bred for a single fruit type. Its size control makes for an easier-to-manage, easier-to-spray, and easier-to-harvest home orchard tree than a full-sized seedling rootstock, while still tolerating heavier soils better than some other dwarfing stone fruit rootstocks. Graft a desired named stone fruit variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide moderate staking support while the semi-dwarf root system establishes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Citra Hops
description: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2007 and quickly becoming one of the most sought-after and widely used hop varieties in modern craft brewing, this vigorous climbing bine produces resinous, aromatic cones with a distinctive tropical fruit, citrus, and gooseberry character that helped define the juicy, hazy IPA styles that have dominated craft beer for over a decade. Like other hops it is a perennial vine that dies back to the ground each winter and regrows vigorously each spring, needing a sturdy tall support and full sun to reach its full trellis height and cone production. Train young bines up the support as they grow, harvest cones in late summer when they feel dry and papery and spring back after being squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for the best cone development. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Citron
description: Citron is an ancient citrus grown mainly for its thick, fragrant rind, which is candied or used in preserves. It is among the most frost-tender citrus, so grow it in full sun in the warmest possible spot or in a container to move under cover. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, feeding regularly during growth. Prune to remove the plant's stout thorns and dead wood, and harvest the large fruit when fully colored. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Citronella Grass
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free or frost-protected conditions; citronella grass is a large, clumping, tropical grass native to Sri Lanka that is the primary commercial source of Ceylon citronella oil — the essential oil used in mosquito-repellent candles, torches, sprays, and lotions worldwide. The essential oil from the leaves and stems contains citronellol, geraniol, and related terpenes that mosquitoes find repellent. The plant itself, when its leaves are crushed or bruised, releases a strong, complex citrus-rose fragrance. Growing it in the garden is an attractive proposition — the blue-green, arching grass clumps are handsome and the repellent effect is modest when the plant is growing undisturbed, but crushing a few leaves releases the fragrance. It is completely distinct from lemon grass (C. citratus), which is grown for cooking rather than insect repellency and has a different chemical profile dominated by citral rather than citronellol. In zones 10-12 it is a reliable perennial ornamental grass; in zones 9 it often overwinters with protection. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Citronella Lemon Balm
description: Citronella is a selected strain of lemon balm bred for an especially strong lemon-citronella scent, valued both as a culinary tea herb and as a natural mosquito-deterrent planted near patios and doorways. Give it moist, humus-rich soil and afternoon shade in hot climates, since leaves scorch and lose fragrance in dry heat. Shear plants back hard after flowering to prevent excessive self-seeding and to force a flush of fresh, more fragrant new growth for harvest. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and to control its naturally spreading habit. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Citronella Scented Geranium
description: This fast-growing scented geranium has citrus-fragrant foliage and pretty pink blooms, thriving in hot, sunny gardens and patio pots. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and let the top of the soil dry slightly between waterings. Pinch stems to keep it bushy and take cuttings easily to make more plants. It is frost-tender, so bring containers indoors to a bright window before the first freeze. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Clammy Ground Cherry
description: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; clammy ground cherry is one of the most common and widespread native ground cherries of the eastern and central US — a perennial, rhizomatous plant producing the typical Physalis papery husk (the inflated calyx) surrounding a small, round, yellow berry when ripe. Named 'clammy' for the sticky, viscid glandular hairs covering the stems and leaves. The ripe yellow berries inside the papery husks have a pleasant, sweet-tart, slightly tropical flavor and are eaten fresh, used in jams, preserves, and pies, or dried like raisins. The fruits are ripe when the papery husk has turned tan and papery and the berry inside has turned from green to yellow. Like all Physalis, only the ripe berries are edible — unripe berries and all other plant parts contain toxic alkaloids. A weedy but edible native for natural gardens and food forests. Spreads aggressively by rhizomes. Tolerates partial shade — more shade-tolerant than tomatillo. Matures in 80–120 days from seed.

name: Clancy Potato
description: A rare potato grown from true botanical seed, producing a diverse mix of round and fingerling tubers in rose-gold and red shades. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings after hardening off. Hill soil or mulch around the stems as they grow to keep developing tubers covered and prevent greening. Harvest once the tops die back and cure the small, flavorful tubers before storage. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Clapp's Favorite Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Clapp's Favorite ripens quickly once picked and bruises easily, so harvest and handle it gently. Bred in Massachusetts in the 1860s, it bears large, pale yellow-green pears blushed with red, similar in shape and flavor to Bartlett but ripening about two weeks earlier, with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that made it a widely planted early-season dessert pear in American orchards for well over a century. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's fresh pear season ahead of the main Bartlett crop, though the fruit softens and turns mealy very quickly once ripe and bruises easily, so it needs prompt picking and careful handling compared to firmer, better-keeping pear varieties. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer, then ripen indoors at room temperature and eat promptly once the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Clapper Chestnut (USDA Blight-Resistant Trihybrid Chestnut)
aliases: Castanea dentata x mollissima x crenata 'Clapper'
description: Clapper is a mid-twentieth-century USDA release combining American, Chinese, and Japanese chestnut ancestry in an effort to pair the tall, timber-like form of American chestnut with the blight resistance of its Asian relatives. It grows straighter and taller than pure Chinese chestnut orchard types, making it of interest for both nut production and reforestation plantings in blight-affected eastern woodlands. Site it in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and plant a second unrelated chestnut cultivar nearby for pollination, since chestnuts set poorly without cross-pollination. Harvest burrs as they split and yellow in early autumn, and store cured nuts cold and slightly moist to preserve sweetness. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Clara Eggplant (Italian White Oval Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Clara is an Italian hybrid eggplant grown for its striking, brilliantly white, oval fruit set off by a bright green calyx, giving it strong visual appeal at market and in the garden alike. The dense white flesh is mild and free of the bitterness that can affect some white-skinned types, holding its color well when cut and cooking down smoothly for baked and roasted preparations. Clara shows good tolerance to common eggplant diseases and sets fruit heavily and early relative to many other Italian-type hybrids, extending the productive harvest window in a single season. Harvest fruit at 6 to 7 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white eggplant dulls and toughens quickly once past its prime. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Clarion Grape (Cold-Hardy Low-Vigor White Wine Grape)
description: Clarion is the University of Minnesota's sixth cold-hardy wine grape release, introduced in 2021 after roughly two decades of breeding work, and shares the aromatic, low-acid style of its sibling Itasca. Compared with older Minnesota-bred hybrids, Clarion grows with noticeably less vigor and produces looser clusters, which eases canopy management and lowers bunch-rot and insect pressure in humid summers. The white wine shows citrus, pear, melon, apricot, and chamomile character, and the vine has demonstrated good resistance to downy mildew in university trials. While bred for Zone 4 cold tolerance, early plantings have performed most consistently in Zone 5 conditions such as Iowa and Wisconsin, so growers in the coldest sites should still watch for winter injury. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Clark Gooseberry (High-Yielding Mildew-Resistant Canadian Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Clark is a Canadian-bred gooseberry hybrid selected for genuinely heavy, reliable production combined with good resistance to American gooseberry mildew, producing medium to large, red-pink berries with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. The vigorous, productive bush has made it a favorite among home orchardists in colder regions who want dependable yields without the mildew management headaches that plague more disease-susceptible European heirloom varieties. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for the sweetest fresh eating, or pick a touch earlier and firmer for pies, jams, and fools where a tarter flavor is preferred. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Clary Sage
description: Salvia sclarea is a majestic biennial sage with large, wrinkled, woolly, gray-green leaves and tall (4-5 foot), airy panicles of pale lavender-blue and white flowers with large, colorful bracts in early summer of the second year that are spectacular in the garden and highly attractive to bumblebees; it is one of the most valuable aromatic plants for the perfume industry (used in Eau Sauvage and Chanel No. 19), for aromatherapy (clary sage essential oil), and as a culinary herb for flavoring wines and beers. The large leaves can be dipped in batter and fried as a traditional Italian dish; the essential oil is considered antispasmodic and is used in herbal medicine. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Classic Eggplant
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, spacing plants far enough apart for good air circulation. Classic is a widely grown commercial hybrid bred for a heavy, uniform set of large, glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a productive, disease-tolerant plant, and it has become something of a benchmark against which other standard American-type eggplants are compared. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, matte skin signals over-mature fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Consistent watering during fruit set is important, since moisture swings can trigger blossom drop and misshapen fruit. Matures in 73–80 days from transplant.

name: Claypool American Persimmon (Productive Midwestern Native Persimmon)
description: Claypool is an old Indiana-origin named selection of native American persimmon recognized for heavy, reliable annual production and good fruit size compared to typical seedling trees found in the wild. Fruit ripens in fall to a deep orange, soft, jelly-like texture with rich, honeyed sweetness once fully ripe, but remains harshly astringent while firm, so let fruit soften fully or wait for it to drop before eating. As with most native persimmons, Claypool grows a deep taproot and tolerates heat, drought, and marginal soils far better than typical orchard fruit trees once established, making it well suited to low-input food-forest plantings. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon cultivar nearby for pollination and heavier fruit set, and thin root suckers to keep the tree from spreading into a thicket. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Clayton's Sweet Cicely
description: Direct sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds have complex dormancy requirements (double dormancy requiring one warm then one cold period) and germinate in the second spring after sowing — purchasing nursery transplants is faster. Clayton's sweet cicely is a native woodland herb of eastern North American deciduous forests that is nearly identical in appearance and use to Osmorhiza longistylis and O. berteroi; it produces large, feathery, compound leaves with a strong, sweet anise-licorice fragrance when crushed, and small, white, flat-topped flower clusters (umbels) in spring that are excellent for native bees and beneficial insects. The roots and leaves are edible with a mild anise flavor, historically used by Native Americans; it is an excellent, fragrant, deep-shade groundcover that naturalizes quietly under deciduous trees. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Clearwater Jerusalem Artichoke (Sweet Smooth-Skinned Sunchoke)
description: Plant tuber sections 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil around the last frost date. Clearwater is a Maine-origin Jerusalem artichoke selection valued among sunchoke growers for two traits that set it apart from most named varieties: tubers that form smooth, rounded, potato-like shapes rather than the knobby, eye-covered lumps typical of the species, and a notably mild, sweet, nutty flavor that lacks the faint piney or resinous aftertaste some people notice in standard sunchoke stock. Plants are tall even by Jerusalem artichoke standards, often topping 11-12 feet by late summer, and are crowned with the same small yellow sunflower blooms typical of the species, which are also edible. Clearwater spreads by underground tubers less aggressively than many sunchoke varieties, producing fewer long runners, though it should still be given a dedicated bed since any missed tuber will resprout. Dig tubers after fall frost kills the foliage and continue harvesting through winter into early spring; cold exposure sweetens the flavor further by converting stored inulin to sugar. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Cleavers (Goosegrass, Sticky Willie)
description: Harvest young plants in early spring from moist, shaded garden beds and hedgerow edges before they become too large and stringy; cleavers are primarily encountered as a scrambling annual weed notable for the tiny hook-covered stems and leaves that cling to clothing and pet fur. In herbal medicine traditions across Europe and North America, the fresh plant has been used as a lymphatic tonic, diuretic, and spring cleansing herb — the young shoots are the most active medicinally and are harvested in early spring. The young tips can be eaten as a pot herb or juiced; the roasted seeds have been used as a coffee substitute. Note that cleavers is different from sweet woodruff (Galium odoratum), which is grown as a shade groundcover. As a medicinal herb, cleavers is best used fresh rather than dried. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Clementine
description: Clementines are sweet, seedless, easy-peeling mandarins that ripen in early winter. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, sheltered from frost, or in a large pot to overwinter under glass in cool climates. Some cultivars fruit more reliably without a cross-pollinator, which keeps them seedless. Feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season and harvest as soon as the fruit colors, since it holds only briefly on the tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Clementine Mandarin
description: Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; water deeply and infrequently once established; fertilize with citrus-formulated fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × clementina (clementine mandarin) is the small, seedless, thin-skinned, intensely sweet mandarin orange known worldwide as the holiday tangerine — a hybrid of mandarin and sweet orange discovered in Algeria around 1900 by Brother Clément Rodier (for whom it is named). The clementine is distinguished from ordinary mandarins by its typically seedless fruits (in isolated plantings without cross-pollination), deep-orange, extremely glossy, smooth peel that peels effortlessly, and exceptional sweet flavor with minimal tartness. In zone 9, clementines ripen from November through January — the ideal cool-season ripening period that concentrates sugars. Trees are moderately compact and more cold-tolerant than many citrus types, surviving brief drops to 28°F when established. Plant only grafted trees (not seedlings) for true-to-type fruit and quicker bearing; trees typically bear first fruit 2–3 years after planting. A reliable, productive choice for Gulf Coast home orchards. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Clementine Mandarin (Clementine Tangerine, Clementine Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Clementine is the most widely grown and beloved easy-peel mandarin orange in the world — the source of the small, bright-orange, seedless (when grown without cross-pollination) tangerines marketed as 'Cuties' and 'Halos' in American grocery stores. The fruit is small (2–2.5 inches diameter), very easy to peel with virtually no pith, with 8–14 segments of rich, sweet, complex mandarin flavor and distinctive floral aroma. The thin, glossy, bright-orange rind peels effortlessly, making Clementines the most practical fresh-eating citrus for children and adults who want convenient, mess-free citrus. Fruit ripens in November through January in zone 9 — the holiday season — making it one of the most seasonal and eagerly anticipated citrus fruits. The tree is compact, well-shaped, and attractive, with glossy dark-green foliage and fragrant white spring flowers. Clementines can produce seeds if cross-pollinated by other mandarin or sweet orange varieties growing nearby — for seedless fruit, avoid planting near other mandarins, or select a seedless clementine variety. In zone 9, Clementines should be sited in warm, protected locations and protected from temperatures below 28°F. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually: February, May, and September. Matures in 270–330 days from transplant.

name: Clemson Spineless 80 Okra
description: An improved 1980 selection of the classic Clemson okra, bearing dark green, grooved, straight, spineless pods with full-bodied flavor. Soak seed overnight and sow directly one inch deep once the soil is warm, since okra sulks in cold ground. The tall, hollyhock-related plants bear hibiscus-like blooms and thrive in summer heat. Pick pods young at two to four inches every day or two, as they toughen quickly if left on the plant. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Clemson Spineless Okra
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — okra thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that challenge most other vegetables; Clemson Spineless is the most widely grown okra variety in the United States, a 1980 All-America Selections winner and the standard against which all other okras are measured — smooth, bright green, spineless pods in the classic okra shape eliminate the spine irritation that makes harvesting traditional okra varieties uncomfortable. The spineless pods (technically very few small, soft spines compared to original okra types) can be harvested without gloves, a significant practical improvement over older varieties. Clemson Spineless produces straight, uniform 5-ribbed pods with the mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that defines okra — the mucilage (a natural thickener) is the basis for gumbo's characteristic body-giving quality that makes real gumbo unmistakably different from any other soup. In zone 9 okra is among the most productive and reliable summer vegetables available — it is native to Africa and genuinely thrives in the same conditions (intense heat, humidity, heat soil) that defeat cool-season crops and stress many warm-season vegetables. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Clemson Spineless Okra
description: Soak seeds overnight and sow an inch deep only after the soil is truly warm, since okra sulks in cold ground. This 1939 AAS winner grows into tall, productive plants that set spineless pods over a long season. Pick the pods young at about three inches every couple of days, as they toughen quickly and frequent harvest keeps the plants producing. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Cleopatra Mandarin Rootstock
description: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired mandarin, orange, or other citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Cleopatra mandarin is grown as a salt-tolerant understock, not for its own fruit. A small-fruited, seedy mandarin of little value for fresh eating, it is instead prized as a citrus rootstock for its outstanding tolerance of saline and poorly drained soils, good compatibility with mandarin and mandarin hybrid scion varieties in particular, and production of high-quality fruit on the grafted variety, though it is notably slow to bring young trees into full production compared to faster rootstocks like trifoliate orange hybrids. Its salt tolerance has made it a valued rootstock choice in coastal and irrigation-salinity-prone citrus growing regions where other common rootstocks struggle. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and be patient with the extended juvenile period before the tree reaches full bearing compared to more precocious rootstock choices. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cliff Date Palm
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Phoenix rupicola is among the more shade-tolerant date palms — adapting to filtered light beneath taller trees — and tolerates moderate drought when established; water deeply but infrequently in subtropical and Mediterranean conditions. Phoenix rupicola (Cliff Date Palm or Rupicola Date Palm) is one of the most elegantly formed and ornamentally refined of all Phoenix date palm species, native to the rocky escarpments, cliff faces, and hill forests of the eastern Himalayan foothills — Sikkim, Bhutan, Assam, and Meghalaya in northeast India, and Bangladesh. The common name 'Cliff Date Palm' accurately describes its native habitat: the palm naturally grows in rock crevices and on steep, exposed cliff faces at elevations of 1,500–5,000 feet. The fronds are the defining ornamental feature: extraordinarily graceful, arching, and soft-textured — lacking the stiff, rigid quality of many Phoenix palms — with a deep, rich green color and a naturally weeping, 'fountain' form that makes the plant immediately distinctive in a landscape setting. Phoenix rupicola shows more shade tolerance than most date palms due to its cliff-forest habitat and is one of the better date palms for partially shaded landscape positions. The small, orange, date-like fruits are eaten locally. Among the best date palms for compact landscapes, courtyard gardens, and partial-shade positions in zones 8–11. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Climax Blueberry
description: Amend soil with peat moss, pine bark, or sulfur to achieve pH 4.5–5.5 before planting; rabbiteye blueberries like Climax will not thrive in neutral or alkaline soils. Climax is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium ashei) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1974 and remains one of the most widely grown rabbiteye varieties in the Deep South because of its early season (it ripens in late May to early June in zone 8–9, the earliest of the major rabbiteye varieties), consistent productivity, and excellent fruit quality. Berries are medium-sized, light blue with a mild, sweet flavor and small dry scar. Plant in groups of 2–3 varieties for cross-pollination (rabbiteye blueberries are not self-fruitful). Remove flowers the first 2 years to direct energy into root establishment; full crops develop by year 3–4. Mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or wood chips to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Climax is notably upright in growth habit and tolerates the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Climax Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Climax is one of the original rabbiteye blueberry cultivars released by the USDA and University of Georgia, selected for very early ripening — typically the first rabbiteye to color in a planting, beginning to ripen in late May in zone 8–9. The medium-sized, firm, light blue berries have good flavor but a somewhat thicker skin than later-season varieties; this firmness improves shipping quality. Climax's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) ensures reliable bloom in zone 8–9 without risk of late-season freeze damage. The upright, vigorous shrubs are productive and long-lived. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain acid fertilization with ammonium sulfate, and keep soil consistently moist through the production season. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Clivia Apple (German Breeding Parent of Pinova)
description: Clivia was bred at the Institute for Fruit Research in Dresden-Pillnitz, Germany, from a cross involving Golden Delicious and the cold-hardy Duchess of Oldenburg, combining a measure of Oldenburg's hardiness with Golden Delicious-style sweetness. It is grown today chiefly as a historical curiosity and breeding parent rather than a widely marketed dessert apple, most notably contributing to the German cultivar Pinova when crossed again with Golden Delicious. The medium, red-flushed fruit over a green-yellow ground color has crisp, juicy, mildly aromatic flesh good for fresh eating. The tree is moderately vigorous and reasonably disease-tolerant for a mid-20th-century German release, making it an interesting addition for collectors tracing the parentage of modern club apples. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cloud Nine Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Cloud Nine is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing very large (often 1–2 pound) fruits with ivory-white to pale cream skin and nearly white flesh — one of the few tomato varieties that is genuinely white rather than pale yellow or cream-colored at full ripeness. Like other white tomatoes, Cloud Nine lacks the red lycopene pigment that colors standard tomatoes, instead producing a nearly colorless fruit with very low acid content. The flavor is exceptionally mild, honey-sweet, and rich without the sharpness of red varieties — often described as having a complex sweetness that is difficult to describe as 'tomato-like' in the traditional sense, more like eating a sweet, meaty fruit with subtle complexity. Cloud Nine is preferred for fresh eating and mild preparations where the low-acid, ultra-sweet character can be fully appreciated — it is less well-suited to cooking where the delicate pale color and mild flavor are lost. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Cloudberry
description: Cloudberry is a low-growing, rhizomatous Arctic-boreal species that requires cold winters, strongly acidic peat or sphagnum-rich soil (pH 3.5–5.0), and consistent moisture — it is exceptionally difficult to cultivate outside its native subarctic habitat. It is dioecious, so both male and female plants must be planted in proximity for fruit to set. The amber-golden berries are among the most highly prized wild fruits in Scandinavia and are used in traditional preserves; ripe berries are extremely soft and must be processed immediately. Not suited to continental climates south of USDA zone 5. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Clove Basil
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface-pressing it and keeping flats near 78F. This African and Asian shrubby basil carries a warm clove-like scent used medicinally and in cooking. Transplant to warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost, giving each plant ample room to bush out. Pinch flowering tips to prolong leaf production and improve branching. In cool climates grow it as a container plant that can overwinter indoors. Matures in 80–110 days from transplant.

name: Clove Currant
description: Clove currant (Ribes odoratum, syn. R. aureum) is a tough, drought-tolerant native prairie shrub with intensely clove-spice-scented yellow spring flowers and glossy black berries in mid-summer. It tolerates alkaline, clay, or droughty soils far better than European currants, making it the best Ribes choice for the Great Plains and intermountain West. The berries range from mild to somewhat astringent depending on selection; look for named fruit-producing cultivars such as 'Crandall'. Prune by removing the oldest canes at the base every few years; the plant suckers moderately and can form a thicket if not managed. Verify state restrictions before planting. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Clove Tree
description: Plant Syzygium aromaticum (Clove Tree) in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic, deep loamy soil in full sun; requires consistent moisture year-round and high humidity; protect from all frost and cold winds; harvest flower buds (cloves) when they turn from green to light pink but before they open — dried immediately after harvest to the familiar dark-brown clove. Clove is one of the most historically significant spice plants on Earth — the dried, unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, native exclusively to the North Maluku (Spice Islands) of Indonesia, were so extraordinarily valuable in the medieval spice trade that they were literally worth their weight in gold in European markets. The trade in cloves drove European exploration and colonialism throughout the 15th–17th centuries; the Banda Sea spice islands' control by the Dutch VOC was among the most economically significant monopolies in history. Today, Zanzibar (Tanzania), Indonesia, and Madagascar are the primary producers. The essential oil eugenol (80–90% of clove bud oil) is the source of clove's characteristic powerful aroma; it is used in dentistry as a topical analgesic, in perfumery, and as a food flavoring. The whole spice is used in biryani, mulled wine, pumpkin spice blends, pickling, and traditional medicine worldwide. A large, handsome, aromatic evergreen tree with attractive red-flushed young growth and cream-white flower clusters when not harvested. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Clove Vine (Cipo Cravo, Cipó Cravo, Panama Clove Vine)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with strong climbing support — Clove Vine grows vigorously and its stems will clothe a fence, trellis, or tree in dense, attractive foliage once established. Tynanthus panurensis is a woody, liana-climbing vine native to the Amazonian regions of Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, and Ecuador in the Bignoniaceae family, known not primarily for its flowers (small, tubular, cream to white, produced in axillary clusters) but for one of the most remarkable aromatic properties of any tropical climbing plant: the bark, stems, and wood of the vine smell powerfully, precisely, and unmistakably of cloves — the familiar spice from Syzygium aromaticum — when cut, scraped, or bruised. The fragrant compound responsible is eugenol, the same aromatic phenol that gives true cloves their characteristic fragrance, occurring in Tynanthus panurensis as a convergent natural chemistry that produces an olfactory experience nearly identical to the spice.
