Throughout the Amazon Basin, the bark of T. panurensis is harvested and macerated in spirits (rum, cachaça, or aguardiente) to create 'licor de cipó cravo' (clove vine liqueur) — a traditional tonic drink used medicinally and consumed recreationally with an unmistakable clove-spice flavor. A genuinely unique aromatic plant for zone 10-12 tropical garden enthusiasts interested in useful and ethnobotanically significant plants. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cluster Bean (Guar)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, warm soil after last frost; cluster bean (guar) is a summer-annual legume with clusters of small pods along the stems that are harvested young as a vegetable — particularly popular in Indian cooking, where the tender young pods (called gawar phalli) are stir-fried with spices. Mature seeds are the source of guar gum, a key industrial thickener used worldwide in food production, oil drilling, and manufacturing. The plant is a nitrogen-fixing cover crop adapted to hot, dry conditions and marginal soils. In South Asia it is grown over millions of acres. In the home garden it provides an unusual, prolific summer vegetable with minimal water requirements, excellent for Gulf Coast and arid Southwest climates. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cluster Hops (Oldest American Hop Cultivar)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Cluster is the oldest surviving American hop cultivar, an heirloom variety of unclear original parentage that dominated US hop production for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries before newer aroma hops took over, and it remains valued today for its clean, mild, slightly spicy and floral character and reliable, disease-resistant vigor. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; harvest the soft green cones in late summer when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dry promptly for brewing or storage. Like other hops, Cluster performs best in cool-summer climates with long day length, and struggles with the sustained heat and humidity of zone 8-9 Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, best-ventilated site available and expect a lighter cone yield than in traditional hop-growing regions. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Cluster Ridge Luffa
description: This ridged luffa sets several fruits together at each node rather than singly, giving a concentrated flush of harvest when the small orb-shaped young gourds are ready to pick for stir-fries, curries, and soups. Left on the vine through its long 110-130 day season, the fruit dries into the familiar fibrous sponge once the skin turns brown and papery. Train the vigorous vines up a tall trellis in full sun to keep the ridged fruit straight and improve airflow, and keep soil consistently moist and mulched through the hot months it needs to finish. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Coastal Dewberry (Rubus trivialis)
description: Plant rooted tip cuttings in moist, well-drained sandy loam in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry is a low, trailing Gulf Coast and Southeastern native bramble that hugs the ground rather than growing upright, with slender, prickly canes that root wherever the tips touch soil. It is among the earliest brambles to flower, opening white blooms as early as late winter in the Deep South, followed by glossy black, sweet-tart drupes ready to pick weeks ahead of upright blackberries. Because canes trail and root freely, give it room to spread or confine it with a mowed border, and expect it to naturalize readily in sunny, sandy fields, roadsides, and open pine woods edges. After fruiting, cut back spent floricanes to tidy the patch and encourage vigorous new primocane growth for next year's crop. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Coastal Groundcherry
description: Plant into loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, where its tuberous roots and underground stolons let it persist through drought and sandy, nutrient-poor conditions typical of Gulf Coast dunes and coastal scrub. The nodding yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers give way to small yellow fruits enclosed in a papery lantern husk, similar in form to a garden ground cherry but produced by a true native of Gulf shoreline habitat from Texas to Florida. It dies back in cooler winters further inland but stays evergreen in the mildest coastal zones, resprouting reliably each spring to take advantage of the long, hot growing season. Use it in a naturalized coastal bed or dune-edge planting where its sprawling habit and light fruit set are more curiosity than crop, though the ripe fruit is edible. Matures in 80–120 days from seed.

name: Coastal Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Georgia Selection)
description: Set out dormant plants in winter into sulfur-amended, well-drained beds, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through hot Gulf South summers. Coastal is one of the original named rabbiteye releases from the Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station's 1950s breeding program, sharing parentage with Homebell and Menditoo, both already grown across the Deep South. Its medium blue berries have a pleasant, mild flavor, and the bush itself is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, reflecting its native Coastal Plain selection. Because it is not self-fruitful, interplant with another rabbiteye cultivar and prune out the oldest canes each winter to sustain vigorous new growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Coastal Star Lettuce (Heat-Tolerant Full-Size Romaine)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Coastal Star is a dark green romaine bred for heat tolerance and slow bolting, producing full-size, dense, heavy hearts even as temperatures climb toward the point where most romaine varieties turn bitter and send up a seed stalk. The upright heads have crisp, sweet leaves with excellent texture through to the crunchy heart. Provide afternoon shade during the hottest stretches of a Gulf Coast spring to further extend the harvest window, and keep soil consistently moist, since drought stress accelerates bolting even in heat-tolerant varieties. Harvest whole heads once hearts have filled out, or pick outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Cobham Improved Marrow Parsnip
description: A classic English heirloom developed from the older Marrow parsnip type and long favored by British allotment gardeners for its short neck and broad shoulders that taper to a blunt, well-filled root. It shows better resistance to canker than many older parsnip lines, an important trait in the damp, heavy soils common in British gardens. Direct sow thinly in deeply worked ground, thin seedlings to a few inches apart, and harvest after frost for the sweetest flavor; it has long held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Cochineal Nopal
description: Root a dried Nopalea cochenillifera pad cutting (allow cut end to callus for 1–2 weeks before planting) in dry, coarse sandy soil in full sun; plant only 2–3 inches deep; water sparingly until established, then infrequently; the plant is highly drought-tolerant once established and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Cochineal Nopal is the cactus at the center of one of the most remarkable stories in natural dye history — the basis of carmine (E120), the brilliant scarlet-red dye that became one of the most valuable trade commodities between the Americas and Europe after Spanish conquest, worth more than silver by weight in 16th-century Spain. The cactus is the host of the cochineal insect (Dactylopius coccus), tiny scale insects that feed on the cactus pads and produce carminic acid as a defense compound — the source of intense, colorfast red dye. Pre-Columbian Aztec and Mixtec civilizations had cultivated cochineal production for centuries before European contact; after conquest, the Spanish maintained it as a closely guarded trade secret for two centuries. Carmine remains important today in natural food coloring, cosmetics (lipstick, rouge), and textiles; it is the red in many 'natural' food colorings. The pads (nopales) are edible like other Opuntia species and can be harvested as young, tender pads for cooking; small red fruits also edible. A large, dramatic, sculptural cactus for hot, dry gardens. Matures in 90–365 days from transplant.

name: Cocke's Prolific Corn (Colonial Virginia Multi-Ear Dent Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks for good wind pollination and give plants extra room, since Cocke's Prolific grows tall and leafy and puts its energy into multiple smaller ears rather than one big one. This Virginia heirloom dent corn has been passed down since the 1700s and was long valued by small farmers precisely because a prolific, multi-eared plant hedges against a poor pollination year better than a single-ear hybrid does. Ears are white to pale yellow dent kernels good for cornmeal and grits once fully dried on the stalk, and the tall, leafy plants also produce useful fodder. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it by distance or timing from other corn varieties to keep the seed line true for saving. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Cockspur Prickly Pear (Sand Prickly Pear)
description: Plant a callused joint shallowly in loose, fast-draining sand in full sun and let it sprawl; cockspur prickly pear is a low, mat-forming cactus of coastal dunes, sandhills, and pine flatwoods along the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from the Carolinas through Florida and west into Texas. Its small, easily detached, somewhat cylindrical joints break off at the slightest touch and root wherever they land, an adaptation that lets the plant spread quickly across bare, shifting sand. Pale yellow flowers open in early summer, followed by small reddish fruit, and the dense clusters of fine glochids make this species notorious for hitchhiking on bare feet and shoes along beach trails. It is an excellent, tough choice for stabilizing loose, sandy, full-sun sites where little else will grow. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cocktail Semi-Dwarf Grapefruit
description: This semi-dwarf grapefruit-pomelo hybrid produces juicy, sweet-tart, low-acid fruit on a compact tree ideal for patios or small yards. Grow in full sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and water deeply while letting the surface dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season for good fruit development. Move container trees to a bright indoor location before frost, as grapefruit is cold-sensitive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Coco de Paimpol Bean
description: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit near the cool, damp Brittany coast where it was traditionally grown. Coco de Paimpol earned its own French protected designation for a distinctive fresh-shelling bean — plump, cream-colored seeds lightly speckled with rose, picked while the pods are still green rather than left to fully dry. Harvest pods when the seeds inside have filled out but the pods remain supple, then shell immediately for the tender, buttery texture the variety is prized for. It can also be left to dry fully on the vine for storage as a soup bean, though the fresh-shell stage is when its flavor is best known. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Coco Jujube
description: Coco is notable among jujube cultivars for a fruit flavor many growers describe as distinctly coconut-like once the small, golden-brown fruit fully ripens, setting it apart from the more straightforwardly apple- or date-flavored cultivars in wider circulation. The zigzagging branch pattern gives the tree ornamental interest through the leafless winter months, and like most jujube it develops a deep taproot that makes it notably drought-tolerant once established. Trees typically begin bearing in their second or third year and are partially self-fertile, though fruit set and size improve with a second cultivar such as Autumn Beauty planted nearby for cross-pollination. Harvest when the skin turns golden-brown for the best expression of the variety's distinctive flavor, or let fruit fully wrinkle for a chewier, date-like texture. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Coco Plum (Icaco, Paradise Plum)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained to seasonally wet, sandy, alkaline, or coastal soil; coco plum is a versatile South Florida and Caribbean native that ranges from a 3-foot groundcover to a 15-foot shrub depending on the cultivar and site conditions. The round to oval fruits ripen to white, red, or dark purple depending on variety and are eaten fresh when ripe — they have starchy, mildly sweet, coconut-flavored flesh around a large seed — or made into jam and jelly. The seed kernel contains a fat that is extracted for cosmetics in South America. Coco plum is both a valuable wildlife plant, supporting many birds and butterflies, and one of the few edible natives for South Florida's challenging alkaline, salty, and wet conditions. Tolerates periodic flooding and salt spray better than almost any other fruiting plant. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cocodrie Rice
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cocodrie is a semi-dwarf, long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter in 1998 and named for Louisiana's Bayou Cocodrie, quickly becoming the dominant commercial rice variety across the Gulf South rice belt because of its early maturity, high milling yield, and reliable performance under both flooded and continuously moist conditions. Home gardeners can grow it in beds kept saturated through the season rather than in true paddies, though yields are highest with standing water for at least part of the cycle. The semi-dwarf, sturdy stalks resist lodging (falling over) better than older tall varieties, which matters most in wet, windy Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when the seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry and hull. As a widely proven Louisiana-bred variety, Cocodrie is an accessible entry point for gardeners curious about growing their own rice in zone 8-10 conditions. Matures in 105–130 days from seed.

name: Cocona (Orinoco Apple, Peach Tomato)
description: Start seeds in warm, moist mix at 75–85°F indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moist soil after soil warms; cocona (Solanum sessiliflorum) is a tomato relative from the Amazon basin of Colombia, Peru, and Brazil, producing 2–4 inch yellow to orange fruits that resemble a slightly fuzzy tomato with a pleasant, acidic, tomato-citrus flavor widely used in Amazonian cuisine for juices, jams, and salsas. The plants are large-leafed and fast-growing, producing fruit 6–9 months after transplanting in suitable tropical conditions. Rich in iron and an important component of the diet of indigenous Amazonian peoples; increasingly available as a specialty crop in Florida and Hawaii. Thrives in humid tropical conditions with good rainfall or irrigation. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Coconut Palm
description: Plant container-grown seedlings in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; coconut palm is the most widely cultivated and economically important palm tree in the world — a single tree provides coconut fruit (with meat, milk, water, and oil), fibrous husk (coir), palm fronds (for thatching and weaving), and palm heart, making it one of the most useful food trees in human history. In zone 10–12 Florida, Hawaii, and tropical coastal areas it grows to 30–60 feet with a gracefully curving trunk and a spreading canopy of long, feathery fronds. Trees begin producing coconuts 6–10 years after planting and can remain productive for 70–80 years. Excellent salt tolerance makes it one of the best trees for coastal landscapes. 'Malayan Dwarf' cultivars are shorter, earlier fruiting, and moderately hurricane-resistant. Growth is faster in deep, moist, sandy soil with access to groundwater. Extremely frost-sensitive — any freezing temperature causes permanent damage; restricted to southernmost Florida and Hawaii in the US. Matures in 2920–3650 days from transplant.

name: Coconut Thyme (Trailing Fruity-Scented Ornamental Thyme)
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since this low, mat-forming thyme is intolerant of wet or heavy soil and thrives on genuine neglect once established. Coconut Thyme is grown primarily as an ornamental ground cover for its dense, glossy, dark green foliage and — true to its name — a distinctly sweet, coconut-like fragrance released when leaves are brushed or crushed, an unusual scent profile among thymes that are more typically savory or lemony. Small pink flowers appear in early summer and are attractive to bees, and the tight, trailing mat is well suited to cascading over rock walls, edging pathways, or filling gaps between pavers. Avoid overhead watering and rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which encourage root and crown rot in this drought-adapted plant. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Cocoplum
description: Cocoplum is an extremely adaptable native Florida and Caribbean shrub-tree that tolerates salt spray, periodic flooding, alkaline soils, and full sun — one of the toughest edible landscape plants for coastal south Florida. Plants are self-fertile and fruit reliably as hedges or specimens; the white, pink, or purple oval drupes ripen sporadically through the warm months. The sweet, mildly flavored flesh is eaten fresh or made into jams and jellies; the large oily seed is edible and has a coconut-like flavor when roasted. Harvest when fruit has reached its full color (cream, pink, or deep purple depending on ecotype) and is soft to the touch. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cocoyam (Tannia, Malanga)
description: Plant corm divisions or small cormels 4–6 inches deep in deep, rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost risk has passed and the soil has warmed to 70°F; tannia requires a long hot growing season of 6–9 months to produce well-developed corms. Xanthosoma sagittifolium is a large, dramatic tropical plant grown throughout the Caribbean, West Africa, and Latin America for its starchy, edible corms (harvested at 7–10 months when leaves begin to yellow) and young leaves, which are used as a spinach substitute after thorough cooking to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals. Unlike taro (Colocasia esculenta), tannia corms are generally less mucilaginous and somewhat easier to peel; they are boiled, mashed, fried, or pureed and have a nutty, earthy flavor. In frost-prone climates, lift corms before the first frost and store in a cool, dry, frost-free location. Matures in 180–300 days from transplant.

name: Cocozelle Summer Squash
description: An Italian heirloom zucchini with long, cylindrical dark-green fruit striped in lighter green, best picked around eight inches. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm and settled. The bush-type plants are productive, so harvest fruit young and often before they grow seedy past twelve inches. Keep soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs and vine borers common to summer squash. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Cocozelle Zucchini
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm soil, planting a few per hill and thinning to the strongest. This compact Italian bush type produces slender, ribbed fruits striped in light and dark green with firm, flavorful flesh. Harvest zucchini young at six to eight inches and pick often, since a single missed fruit quickly grows into a marrow and slows the plant. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Coe's Golden Drop Plum
description: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Coe's Golden Drop needs a compatible European plum or gage pollinator and blooms late, helping it dodge some spring frosts. An English gage-type dessert plum bred in Suffolk in the late eighteenth century, it is celebrated by connoisseurs for exceptionally rich, honeyed, sweet flesh inside a translucent golden-yellow skin often blushed pink in full sun, generally considered one of the finest-flavored dessert plums grown, though the tree is a notoriously shy and unreliable bearer compared to workhorse varieties like Victoria. Its late bloom period helps it escape some late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering plums, but it still benefits from a warm, sheltered site to ripen its sugars fully and from a compatible pollinator, since it does not reliably self-pollinate. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and be patient with its lighter, less predictable crops in exchange for exceptional dessert flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Coffee (Arabian Coffee)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade — coffee is an attractive, glossy-leaved tropical shrub or small tree native to the forest understory of Ethiopia, grown worldwide in tropical highlands for the seeds (coffee beans) contained inside the red or yellow 'cherry' fruits, which ripen 9–12 months after the heavily fragrant white flowers bloom. As an ornamental plant it is outstandingly handsome: the dark green, glossy, waxy leaves are beautiful year-round; the clusters of jasmine-scented white flowers in spring are intensely fragrant; and the red coffee cherries are decorative and visually striking in fall and winter. Coffee is a genuine shade plant, preferring filtered light under taller trees rather than full sun, which scorches the leaves and stresses the plant in warm climates. In zone 10–11 it can be grown outdoors permanently; in cooler zones it is a remarkable large container plant for bright indoor spaces or protected outdoor areas in summer. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Coffee Plum (Indian Plum, Rhoea Plum, Puneala Plum)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in frost-free tropical conditions; coffee plum (also known as Indian plum or Puneala plum in India and Sri Lanka) is a Southeast Asian Flacourtia related to governor's plum but distinctly different — producing attractive clusters of small red to deep red-purple fruits with a sweet-acidic, slightly astringent flavor reminiscent of sour plum combined with cherry. The name 'coffee plum' is used in southern India where it is made into jams and pickles and eaten fresh when fully ripe. Often hermaphroditic and self-fertile, making it easier to grow than most Flacourtia species. An attractive thorny shrub with glossy leaves, useful as a security hedge in subtropical gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Coffeecake Persimmon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Coffeecake is a PVA (pollination-variant astringent) Japanese persimmon selected for its distinctive deep cinnamon-brown flesh coloration and extraordinary flavor when cross-pollinated — the richly colored flesh has a complex, spiced sweetness reminiscent of warm cinnamon and brown sugar that gives the variety its distinctive name. The medium to large, flat-round, orange-skinned fruits develop their characteristic dark interior progressively as pollination stimulates dark flesh development, and fully pollinated fruits may have almost entirely dark, non-astringent, sweet, dense flesh while still firm enough to slice. The flavor of cross-pollinated Coffeecake is considered among the finest of any persimmon type — complex, sweet, and aromatic with none of the astringency that makes unripe persimmons inedible. In zone 9 Coffeecake ripens in late October–November and the tree is vigorous and productive with attractive form and good fall leaf color. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cogshall Mango
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Cogshall mango's naturally dwarf habit makes it one of the best mango cultivars for small yards and container culture. A compact Florida seedling selection related to Carrie, it bears small to medium fruit with fiberless, deep orange, richly sweet flesh and a distinctive flavor often compared to butterscotch, borne heavily on a tree that stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars even at maturity. Its dwarf habit and heavy, reliable bearing make it a favorite for gardeners with limited space who still want full-sized mango flavor, and it responds well to being kept pruned and compact in a large container. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches harvest to concentrate flavor, and protect young trees from any frost or freeze. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Col de Dame Blanc Fig (Neck of the Lady Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to average soil in full sun; Col de Dame Blanc performs best with reflected heat from south or west-facing walls and requires genuine summer heat to ripen its fruit fully — not recommended for cool-summer Pacific Northwest climates. Col de Dame (literally 'neck of the lady' in Catalan, for the fruit's distinctive elongated, graceful neck) is a group of heirloom Spanish figs from the Catalonia region particularly associated with the town of Sitges; the Blanc (white) form produces elongated, pear-necked, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with exceptionally thin skin and almost liqueur-like white interior flesh with a concentrated honey sweetness and complex figgy aroma that experienced fig growers frequently describe as among the finest flavors of any variety. A common fig type requiring no pollinator. Less cold-hardy and less vigorous than many commercial varieties but the extraordinary flavor rewards the extra attention; increasingly popular among American fig collectors and now more readily available from specialty nurseries than a decade ago. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Col de Dame Grise Fig (Grey Neck of the Lady Fig)
description: This French heirloom is one of the gray-skinned members of the historic Col de Dame family, distinct from the pale Col de Dame Blanc and near-black Col de Dame Noir. Fruit is medium-to-large and pear-shaped with thick greenish-purple skin that develops a grayish bloom and fine surface cracking at full ripeness, surrounding dense, dark red, jam-textured flesh. Unlike many dual-cropping figs, it produces only a single late main crop with no breba, so patience is rewarded with an unusually rich, wine-like sweetness in early fall. The tree is a vigorous, heavy-cropping grower once established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Col de Dame Noir Fig (Coll de Dama Negra)
description: Col de Dame Noir is a black-skinned counterpart to the more widely known Col de Dame Blanc, sharing the same elongated, narrow-necked fruit shape said to resemble an old French collar or necklace. The dense, deep-red flesh inside near-black skin is exceptionally sweet and rich, prized by fig collectors for drying as well as fresh eating. As a late-season fig it demands a long, warm growing season, ripening well into fall in climates with mild autumns. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Colby Black Walnut (Cold-Hardy Wisconsin Black Walnut)
description: Colby is a named black walnut selection identified in Wisconsin and valued by northern nut growers for combining good cold hardiness with respectable kernel quality in a region at the edge of the species' reliable range. Grafted trees bear sooner and more predictably than seedling black walnuts and produce a nut with fair cracking characteristics for the species. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from vegetable gardens and juglone-sensitive plants, and give it the wide mature spacing typical of black walnut. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Colby Pecan (Far-Northern Large-Nut Native Pecan)
description: Colby is a native selection out of Illinois, introduced in 1957 and long used as a benchmark far-northern pecan cultivar for growers well outside the traditional Gulf South range. It produces a medium-large, oval nut, around 60 per pound, roughly 45% kernel, that is notably large for an ultra-northern-adapted variety, though its thicker shell gives a lower kernel percentage than Gulf South standards. Colby is scab susceptible and benefits from a fungicide program where humidity is high; it has also served as a parent of other cold-hardy cultivars such as NC-4. As a Type II pollen shedder, plant it with a Type I pollinator nearby for reliable nut set. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Cold Hardy Red Pomegranate
description: This cold-tolerant pomegranate bears vibrant red-fruited crops and handsome orange-red flowers on a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it thrives in heat and tolerates drought once established. Water deeply but infrequently, easing off as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In the colder end of its range, site it against a warm south wall and mulch the base for winter protection. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cole's Early Watermelon (Short-Season Iowa Heirloom)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by A.B. Cole in Iowa in 1908, this heirloom was developed specifically to bring reliable, sweet watermelon to gardeners in short-season Northern climates where later-maturing Southern varieties often failed to ripen before fall frost. It bears medium-sized, oval, dark green striped melons with crisp, sweet red flesh on vigorous, productive vines. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned and the underside spot has turned from white to cream-yellow, reliable signs of ripeness in a short-season melon bred for gardens with a narrow window to work with. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Colette Pear (Compact Self-Fertile Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Colette's naturally compact, upright growth habit makes it a practical choice for a small yard or large container where a full-size pear tree would not fit. Bred in France with an emphasis on tolerance to common pear diseases as well as self-fertility, it will set a crop as a single tree, though fruiting is heavier with another European pear blooming nearby. The fruit is medium-sized with the classic sweet, juicy dessert flavor typical of French pear breeding programs. Prune lightly in winter mainly to keep the naturally tidy form open to light and air. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Collard Greens
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun 10–12 weeks before first fall frost; collard greens are the signature leafy vegetable of the American South, producing large, broad, blue-green, somewhat waxy leaves with a mild, slightly bitter, cabbage-like flavor that mellows considerably after frost or slow cooking. More heat-tolerant than most brassicas, collards can grow year-round in zone 8–11 and are the most cold-hardy of all the non-kale brassica greens. The traditional Southern preparation is slow-braising with smoked pork, but the leaves are also excellent blanched, stir-fried, and used as a low-carbohydrate wrap. Harvest outer leaves continuously; well-maintained plants can produce for a full year or more in mild climates. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Collective Farm Woman Melon (Kolkhoznitsa)
description: Sow 3–4 seeds per hill after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 strongest plants per hill; direct vines along rows or up a strong trellis. Collective Farm Woman (Russian: Kolkhoznitsa) is a Ukrainian/Russian heirloom muskmelon introduced in 1930 that became the standard garden melon across the Soviet Union and is still the most widely grown open-pollinated melon in Russia and Ukraine; the small (1–2 lb) round to oval fruits ripen to creamy-white to yellow with thin, smooth skin and extremely aromatic, sweet, creamy-white flesh that has an exceptional honey-floral fragrance when perfectly ripe. Despite its short ripening window once mature, the flavor is outstanding — rich, sweet, and intensely perfumed. One of the earliest-maturing muskmelons (75–85 days from transplant), making it excellent for short-season northern gardens and for early production in the South and Gulf Coast. Harvest when skin turns creamy-yellow and the blossom end softens slightly. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Collier Mulberry (Early-Ripening Large-Fruited Red Mulberry Hybrid)
description: Collier is a natural hybrid selection between red mulberry (Morus rubra) and white mulberry (Morus alba), chosen for its large fruit — up to two and a half inches long — and heavy, reliable production. It closely resembles the popular 'Illinois Everbearing' mulberry but ripens about two weeks earlier and concentrates its fruit set into a shorter, more manageable harvest window rather than trickling in over many weeks. Collier is markedly cold-hardy, tolerating winters well into the northern half of the country, which also gives it plenty of margin for the mild winters and long, hot growing season of Gulf Coast gardens. As with other mulberries, site female-fruiting trees away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended period and stain hard surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Collingwood Ingram Rosemary
description: Named for the English plantsman Collingwood Ingram, this cultivar produces long, arching stems studded with pale lavender-blue flowers in late winter and spring, and works equally well cascading over a wall or as a loose groundcover. It prefers poor to average, sharply drained soil and resents both soggy roots and heavy shade. Harvest sprigs regularly for cooking, which also helps keep the sprawling growth in bounds. In borderline climates, site it against a warm wall to boost winter survival. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Colobel Grape (Teinturier French-American Hybrid Wine Grape)
description: Another Seibel-bred teinturier hybrid closely related to Rougeon, Colobel carries deeply pigmented flesh that makes it valuable for adding color and body to blended red wines and juice rather than for varietal bottling on its own. It crops heavily and ripens reliably even in cool northeastern and Canadian growing regions, where it has traditionally been used to reinforce lighter-colored hybrid reds. The vine is vigorous and cold-hardy, and needs cluster thinning in productive years to keep the crop from overwhelming the plant. Train to a cane-pruned system for best results. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Colombia Coffee Variety (Cenicafé Rust-Resistant Caturra Selection)
description: Released in 1980 by Colombia's national coffee research center, Cenicafé, the Colombia variety was bred to combine durable resistance to coffee leaf rust with the large bean size, high productivity, and good cup quality growers expect from a Caturra-type plant. Its rust resistance traces back to the naturally occurring Timor Hybrid, an interspecific cross between arabica and robusta that was, at the time, the only known reliable source of resistance genes for arabica breeding programs. The variety keeps a compact, short-statured growth habit similar to Caturra, allowing dense planting and straightforward hand-harvesting. It became a cornerstone of Colombian coffee agriculture for two decades before newer rust-resistant releases such as Castillo largely superseded it. Cultivate it with the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and filtered shade recommended for other compact arabica types. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Colorado Red Rhubarb
description: Colorado Red is a widely sold American heirloom selection prized for thick, deeply pigmented red stalks and the vigorous, cold-hardy habit that made it a staple in high-plains and mountain-region kitchen gardens. It tends to produce especially large, robust plants once established, with broad crinkled leaves shading a productive clump of stalks each spring. As with all rhubarb, only the stalks are eaten — the leaves contain concentrated oxalic acid and should always be removed and composted rather than consumed. Harvest by pulling stalks with a twisting motion rather than cutting, and stop picking by midsummer to let the plant rebuild energy reserves for next year. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Colorado Star Artichoke (Cold-Tolerant Purple AAS Winner)
description: Start seed indoors and set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes; Colorado Star is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid bred for reliable first-year flowering across a wide range of climates, including regions with cooler or shorter growing seasons than traditional artichoke territory. Buds are medium-sized with an attractive purple-tinged blush over green, tender at a smaller size than many varieties, and produced in good quantity on a plant more compact than older perennial types, making it a reasonable choice for smaller gardens. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its ease of first-year production from seed. Water regularly and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat, and harvest buds promptly while tightly closed for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Colossal Chestnut (European-Japanese Hybrid Chestnut, California Large Chestnut, Giant Chestnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Colossal requires cross-pollination; harvest nuts in October when burrs open and nuts fall naturally; collect promptly from ground; Colossal chestnuts are among the largest available — single nuts can reach 30+ grams, comparable to the best Italian and French chestnuts — with sweet, creamy flesh excellent for roasting, marrons glacés, and fresh cooking. Colossal chestnut is a hybrid of European sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) and Japanese chestnut (Castanea crenata) developed in California in the late 1800s by Felix Gillet, a French-born nurseryman who operated the Nevada City Nursery in northern California and imported and trialed numerous European and Asian chestnut varieties and crosses. The variety became the standard commercial chestnut in California and the Pacific Northwest, where it grows vigorously in the mild, well-drained soils of the region and produces exceptionally large individual nuts — among the largest of any named chestnut variety, comparable to the finest Italian and French chestnuts in size and flavor. The large nut size (a single nut can weigh an ounce or more) and good flavor — sweet, starchy, and rich — make Colossal the variety of choice for specialty fresh-market chestnut sales, marron glacé (candied whole chestnuts), and roasting. It has been widely planted in California's chestnut-growing regions (Nevada County, the Sierra Nevada foothills) and in Oregon and Washington for commercial and home production. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Colossus 80 Pea (High-Yield Mechanical-Harvest Purple Hull Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods once they color up to a deep purple. Colossus 80 is a widely grown purple hull cowpea developed for commercial production, bred for a concentrated fruit set that ripens in a narrow window well suited to a single mechanical or hand harvest, along with high yield and vigorous, productive vines. Its purple-hulled pods contrast clearly against the foliage, making ripe peas easy to spot for hand-picking home gardeners as well. Like other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the fresh shelling stage for the best flavor, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for long-term dry storage. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Colossus Blueberry (Large-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in raised beds or mounded rows of acidic, pine-bark-amended soil in full sun, spacing bushes generously to accommodate Colossus's vigorous, upright growth. Released by the University of Florida breeding program alongside the earlier Optimus, Colossus was selected chiefly for its unusually large berry size and firm texture, both of which make it a standout for fresh-market and home use where big, easy-to-pick fruit is prized. It carries a low-to-moderate chill requirement well suited to zone 8-10 winters and shows good field vigor, though cross-pollination with another southern highbush cultivar improves fruit set and berry size further. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter and fertilize lightly with an acid-forming blend in early spring to sustain the large fruit size over successive seasons. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Colossus Southern Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Colossus is a vigorous, bush-type Southern pea selected for exceptionally large seeds and long, productive pods — the big, cream-colored seeds with the characteristic black eye shell out more quickly than the smaller-seeded varieties, making it a practical choice for preserving and cooking in large quantities. Like all cowpeas, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers when most other legumes fail. The high yield per plant and large seed size make Colossus a commercial and home-garden standard in the Gulf Coast South, particularly for fresh-shell operations. Harvest when pods are fully plump and light green, before the hull begins to dry and yellow. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Colt Cherry Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Colt is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit. Bred in England from a cross of sweet cherry and Chinese sour cherry, it produces a semi-vigorous tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a standard seedling cherry tree, offering meaningful size control along with good compatibility across most sweet and sour cherry varieties and better tolerance of wetter soils than many other cherry rootstocks. Its moderate size control without the brittleness and disease susceptibility issues of some fully dwarfing cherry rootstocks made it a long-standing standard choice before newer Gisela-series rootstocks became widely available. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide well-drained soil despite its improved wet-soil tolerance relative to other cherry rootstocks. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Columbia Star Blackberry
description: Columbia Star is a USDA-Oregon State University thornless trailing blackberry bred for very large, firm, glossy-black berries with excellent, well-balanced sweet flavor, developed as a fresh-market improvement over older Pacific Northwest trailing cultivars like Marion. Canes are extremely vigorous and need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous plant spacing to manage their length. Train fruiting canes along the wires and remove them at ground level right after harvest, tying in the current season's new primocanes to bear next year's crop. Trailing blackberries of this type are bred primarily for the cool, dry summers of the Pacific Northwest and can struggle with fungal disease pressure in humid climates, so in the Gulf South prioritize excellent air circulation, full sun, and well-drained raised beds. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Columbus Hops (Tomahawk)
description: A high-alpha American bittering workhorse, prized for pungent, dank, black-pepper aromatics alongside heavy resin production, and sold under both the Columbus and Tomahawk trade names depending on the grower. It is exceptionally vigorous, throwing long laterals that benefit from a wide, tall support structure and generous spacing. Full sun and rich, well-drained soil produce the heaviest cone set, and the plant tends to shrug off many diseases that trouble older bittering cultivars. Harvest once cones feel dry and papery, since delayed picking dulls the sharp resinous character brewers prize it for. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Columbus Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Large-Fruited Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Columbus is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens late in the Southern blueberry season, extending fresh harvest well past most mid-season cultivars while still producing large, flavorful fruit on vigorous, productive bushes. Pairing Columbus with earlier-ripening cultivars like Austin, Alapaha, or Premier gives a Southern blueberry planting a long, staggered harvest from late spring through midsummer. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Columbus requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Comanche Blackberry (Vigorous Erect Thorny Processing Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and trellis the strong, moderately thorny canes for easier harvest. Comanche is an erect University of Arkansas blackberry originating from a 1965 cross of Darrow and Brazos, a sister seedling of Cherokee, and long valued for consistently outyielding older varieties like Brazos. Berries are firm and well-flavored, and the vigorous, upright canes hold up well to mechanical harvesting, making Comanche a reliable choice for both processing plantings and home gardens across the Gulf South. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain yield and cane vigor in following years. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Comanche Leek (F1 Hybrid Summer-Fall Leek)
description: Comanche is a high-yielding, adaptable F1 leek especially favored in Pacific Northwest gardens for its clean, upright habit and long, thick white shanks under dark blue-green flags. It performs well as both a summer and fall crop, and gradually filling the planting trench with soil as the plants grow lengthens the blanched shank for a milder, more tender base. Harvest young at finger size for a mild flavor or let stems reach a half-inch or more in diameter for fuller texture. It tolerates frost well and holds in the garden into the fall harvest window. Matures in 95–105 days from transplant.

name: Comballe Chestnut (French Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Comballe is a French hybrid chestnut cultivar noted for vigorous growth comparable to Bouche de Betizac and Marsol, grown in orchards across southern France for its productive, disease-tolerant habit and good nut quality. As with related hybrid chestnut selections, it combines the eating quality and size associated with European chestnut with the blight resistance contributed by its Japanese chestnut parentage. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a distinct pollenizer for reliable nut set, and harvest fallen burs promptly in autumn before wildlife or ground moisture damage the nuts. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Comfrey
description: Propagate from 2–4 in root cuttings planted horizontally 2–3 in deep; plants grow vigorously and are nearly impossible to eradicate once established, so site them permanently. Mulch heavily around plants and cut back to the ground two or three times per growing season to harvest the biomass-rich leaves as a liquid fertilizer or compost activator. Leaves can also be processed into poultice form for topical soothing use on bruises and minor sprains. Note that internal use is not recommended due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid content. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Comice Pear (Doyenné du Comice, Christmas Pear)
description: Plant in full sun in rich, deep, well-drained soil with pH 6.0–6.5; Comice is the most demanding major pear variety for soil quality, climate precision, and careful management — thin fruits to 1–2 per cluster for maximum quality; pick before full ripeness and ripen indoors at room temperature. Comice (full name Doyenné du Comice, 'Doyenne of the Show') was raised by the Comice Horticole d'Angers agricultural society of Angers, France in 1849 and rapidly gained recognition as the finest dessert pear in the world — a reputation it has maintained for 175 years among pear enthusiasts and chefs. The large (8–16 oz), roundish-oval to slightly pear-shaped fruits have greenish-yellow skin with slight red blush and are the pears most associated with luxury gift boxes, cheese pairings, and the finest fresh-eating experience: the flesh is extraordinarily buttery, creamy-smooth, and dripping with juice, with an intense pear fragrance and honey-sweet flavor with vanilla and floral overtones that is unmatched by any other pear variety. Oregon's Rogue Valley is the primary American commercial production area for Comice, where the specific valley climate — hot days, cool nights, volcanic soil — allows the fruit to reach a quality level rarely achieved elsewhere. Ripens late (October–November); requires careful storage and monitoring for peak ripeness. Matures in 140–160 days from transplant.

name: Common Banana (Cavendish Banana)
description: Plant rooted suckers (pups) in moist, well-drained, richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; common banana is the species underlying the world's most important fruit crop — the seedless, triploid Cavendish and related commercial cultivars that supply the global banana market, all derived from the diploid wild species Musa acuminata native to tropical Southeast Asia. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, selected cultivars including 'Dwarf Cavendish' (6–8 feet), 'Grand Nain' (the commercial Cavendish, 8–12 feet), and 'Goldfinger' produce genuine, edible, sweet bananas from plants grown in-ground as perennials. Each pseudostem (the apparent trunk, composed of tightly overlapping leaf-base sheaths) grows for 10–14 months, then produces a pendant inflorescence from which the banana bunch develops — the large, pendulous, purple-red flower bract opening to reveal successive 'hands' of bananas along the central axis. After fruiting, the fruited pseudostem dies and is cut to the ground; the continuously produced suckers (pups) at the base replace it, maintaining the clump and producing the next generation of fruiting pseudostems. The plant requires consistently rich, moist soil and heavy feeding with high-potassium fertilizer during the growing season for optimum fruit production. In zone 9a the pseudostems may be killed back to the ground by hard freezes but the rhizome resprouts in spring; however, this resets the 10–14 month fruiting clock, often preventing fruit set before the next winter. In zone 9b and 10 the pseudostems persist year-round and fruit reliably. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Common Barberry (European Barberry)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean, alkaline to slightly acidic soil in full sun; common barberry is drought-tolerant and adaptable to poor soils but is an alternate host for wheat stem rust (Puccinia graminis) and is prohibited in many wheat-growing states — confirm legality before planting. Berberis vulgaris is a thorny, deciduous European shrub producing clusters of small, oval, bright-red berries (barberries) in fall with an intensely tart, citrusy, slightly astringent flavor rich in vitamin C; they are used in Persian cooking (zereshk polo — barberry rice pilaf) where they are a quintessential flavoring, and for making barberry jam, juice, wine, and candy throughout Europe and western Asia. The bright-yellow wood and bark contain berberine, a traditional medicinal compound. The berries are also an important food source for birds in winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Common Carrionflower (Blue Ridge Carrion Flower)
description: Plant root divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Common carrionflower is a thornless, herbaceous Smilax found from the Appalachians west across the prairie states and into the Rockies foothills, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring, much like its more eastern relative Smilax herbacea. Young emerging shoots and tendril tips are harvested and cooked much like asparagus before the vine toughens, while the small, globe-shaped clusters of greenish flowers give off a mild carrion scent in late spring to draw in fly pollinators, followed by dark blue-black berries relished by birds. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established at a woodland or prairie-edge planting. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Common Cattail (Broadleaf Cattail)
description: Plant rhizome divisions or seeds in saturated soil or up to 12 inches of standing water in full sun; common cattail is one of the most comprehensively edible native plants in North America, with nearly every part edible at different seasons: the tender white shoots in spring are eaten like asparagus, the immature green female flower spikes can be boiled and eaten like corn on the cob in late spring, the golden pollen is collected in early summer and used as a flour supplement, and the starchy rhizomes can be processed into flour year-round. The familiar brown hotdog-shaped seed heads are iconic in wetland and rain gardens. Spreads aggressively by rhizome — grow in contained pond pockets or regularly remove rhizomes from the margins to prevent dominance. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Common Centaury
description: Should be avoided by anyone with active peptic ulcers given its intense bitterness. Surface-sow the dust-fine seed directly in early spring, since it germinates best with light exposure and resents root disturbance from transplanting. The whole flowering plant is cut and dried at bloom time to make a classic bitter tea, taken in small amounts before meals in traditional European herbalism to stimulate appetite and digestion. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Common Chervil (Classic French Fines Herbes Anise Herb)
description: Direct sow fresh seed on or near the soil surface in cool weather; do not cover deeply — chervil needs some light. Do not transplant. Chervil (Anthriscus cerefolium) is one of the four classic herbs of the French fines herbes blend (with parsley, chives, and French tarragon) — a cool-season, shade-tolerant herb with delicate, lacy, bright green leaves resembling a more refined parsley, and a distinctive flavor that combines mild parsley with a clean anise note. The anise quality distinguishes chervil from all other common culinary herbs — it is present but not dominant, providing a refined freshness that enhances eggs, fish, chicken, and light cream sauces without overwhelming the primary ingredients. Chervil is the most perishable of the major culinary herbs: the delicate flavor dissipates rapidly when dried (dried chervil has almost no culinary value), when cooked at high heat (add at the end of cooking), or when refrigerated for more than 2–3 days. These perishability characteristics mean chervil is essentially only available to gardeners — it is rarely found fresh in American markets. Chervil bolt rapidly (runs to seed) in heat, making it strictly a cool-season herb for zone 8–9 gardeners, but the fall-through-spring window in zone 9 provides several months of harvest from a fall planting. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Common Chicory (Witloof)
description: Sow direct in spring for leaf chicory or late spring for forcing types; for witloof (Belgian endive) production, sow in May–June, lift roots in fall, and force in a dark, warm (55–65°F) location in moist sand to produce the tender, pale, bullet-shaped chicons used as winter salad. Cichorium intybus is a remarkably versatile species encompassing leaf chicories (radicchio, puntarelle), forcing chicories (witloof/Belgian endive), and the roasted-root coffee substitute; all types are naturally bitter, a quality that can be reduced by blanching or frost exposure. The wild roadside plant with brilliant blue flowers is also the same species and is strikingly beautiful in naturalized plantings; the flowers are edible and the roasted root is a caffeine-free coffee substitute. Perennial in the garden but usually grown as an annual for leaf and root crops. Matures in 85–120 days from seed.

name: Common Chive
description: Common chives are a hardy perennial allium forming grassy clumps with a mild onion flavor and edible lavender-pink flowers. Sow seed in clusters and thin lightly, since chives grow happily in tight bunches. Snip leaves from the outside of the clump throughout the season and they will regrow. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep them vigorous and productive. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Common Chives
description: Sow seed indoors or direct sow in clusters, since chives grow best planted in small clumps rather than single plants. This easy, low-maintenance perennial tolerates drought and returns year after year, offering hollow foliage with a mild onion flavor for salads, potatoes, and eggs. The edible lavender flowers attract bees, make a flavorful chive vinegar, and dry well for arrangements; snip the leaves regularly to keep fresh growth coming. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Common Dandelion
description: Scatter seed on the surface and press it in lightly, as dandelion needs light to germinate. This tough perennial thrives in a wide range of soils and will naturalize if flowers are allowed to set their puffball seed heads. Harvest young leaves before flowering for the mildest greens, use the blooms fresh, and dig the taproots in fall for roasting. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Common Guava
description: Guava is self-fertile and productive as a single tree; grafted selections of known cultivars (Ruby Supreme, Thai White) are superior to seedlings for flavor and bearing consistency. Trees tolerate a wide range of soils but are sensitive to standing water and prolonged frost — temperatures below 28°F damage foliage and below 24°F kill established trunks. Prune annually to 10–12 ft to simplify harvest and improve light penetration; guava bears on new growth so heading-back encourages productivity. Harvest when the skin softens, the color shifts from green to yellow or pink, and the fruit is intensely fragrant. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Common Hawthorn
description: Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; common hawthorn is an exceptionally tough small tree or large shrub valued for its dense thorny habit providing excellent wildlife cover, profuse white spring flowers, and abundant red berries (haws) that feed birds through winter. The haws are edible — mildly flavored, slightly mealy, and high in antioxidant flavonoids — and are used to make jellies, wines, and medicinal syrups with a long history in European herbal medicine. Tolerates urban pollution, heavy clay, coastal exposure, and severe pruning. For hedging, plant 18 inches apart and shear twice yearly; the dense spiny habit makes a stock-proof barrier within a few years. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Common Juniper (Ground Juniper)
description: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; common juniper has the largest natural distribution of any woody plant in the world — native to and present across the entire Northern Hemisphere from the Arctic Circle to the mountains of Mexico, Morocco, and the Himalayas. The small, blue-black, resinous berry-like seed cones (juniper berries) are the essential flavoring of gin — virtually all gin production worldwide uses common juniper berries to achieve the characteristic piney, resinous flavor. The berries also flavor sauerkraut, game dishes, and aquavit across Scandinavia and central Europe. The needled, prickly foliage creates excellent wildlife habitat — the berries feed waxwings, thrushes, and other birds through winter. Garden forms range from prostrate, low-growing groundcover types to loose, upright shrubs. The species is dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production. Matures in 730–1825 days from seed.

name: Common Lady's Mantle
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; common lady's mantle is one of the most beloved cottage garden perennials, treasured for the exquisite way its rounded, softly pleated, velvety leaves catch and hold water droplets and dew in perfect spherical beads that roll around the leaf surface. The frothy sprays of tiny, chartreuse-yellow flowers in early summer are superb as a foil for pink and lavender flowers and effective cut fresh or dried. In traditional European herbal medicine, Alchemilla was used as a wound herb and for women's health conditions — the genus name references medieval alchemists who collected the dew from the leaves. Self-sows reliably to naturalize in cool, moist, shaded garden areas. Best in cool-summer climates; in the South, plant in shade and ensure consistent moisture. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Common Mallow
description: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; common mallow is a biennial or short-lived perennial edible herb of European origin that has been used as food and medicine for thousands of years — the young leaves, fresh or cooked, have a mild, slightly mucilaginous, pleasantly neutral flavor and can be used in salads, cooked as a pot herb (substitute for spinach), or simmered in soups and stews. The leaves, stems, seeds (called 'cheeses' for their round shape), and flowers are all edible. The plant has long been valued in herbal medicine for its mucilaginous properties, which soothe irritated tissues of the throat, digestive tract, and urinary system. The attractive, pale to deep-pink or purple flowers with darker veining are produced throughout the growing season and are excellent in salads. The ornamental cultivar 'Zebrina' with striped purple-and-white flowers and 'Brave Heart' are grown primarily for their striking flowers. Tolerates partial shade, poor soil, and drought once established. Self-seeds freely to maintain persistent garden colonies. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Common Mallow
description: Sow seeds directly in spring around the last frost date, pressing them a quarter-inch into the soil in a sunny location with average, well-drained ground — this adaptable plant thrives in poor soils with minimal fertility and water. Thin seedlings to 12–18 inches apart and begin harvesting the mild, slightly mucilaginous young leaves once plants reach 6 inches tall, using them raw in salads or cooked as a spinach substitute. The round, segmented fruits known as 'cheeses' are also edible and have a mild, slightly starchy flavor when harvested young and green. Plants will self-sow readily and may persist as short-lived perennials in warmer zones, so deadhead spent flowers if you wish to limit volunteer seedlings. Matures in 45–90 days from seed.

name: Common Manzanita
description: Plant rooted cuttings in fall in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; manzanita absolutely requires excellent drainage and summer drought — it will not survive in humid climates or wet soils and is best suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens in California and similar dry-summer climates. Arctostaphylos manzanita is a large, beautiful, evergreen California native shrub or small tree with signature smooth, mahogany-red bark that peels to reveal bright, polished inner bark; it produces masses of urn-shaped, pink-white flowers beloved by hummingbirds and native bees in late winter through early spring, followed by small (1/3 inch), round, apple-like fruits (manzanita means "little apple" in Spanish) that ripen red to dark burgundy in summer. The edible fruits are tart and mealy, used by California Native Americans for making a refreshing cider-like beverage by soaking in water, and for making pinole (ground dried fruit). The exfoliating bark is one of the most beautiful features of any native western shrub. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Common Mint
description: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings out, ideally into a buried pot or contained bed, since mint spreads aggressively by runners. Grow it in moist soil and partial to full sun; the aromatic leaves enhance iced tea, mixed drinks, and savory dishes like meats, stews, and vegetable fritters. Cut plants back regularly to encourage tender new growth, and let some tiny flowers bloom to feed the bees. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Common Mugwort
description: Artemisia vulgaris is one of the most widespread and ancient medicinal herbs in the world, used across Europe, Asia, and the Americas for digestive complaints, menstrual regulation, and as a flavoring in traditional European and Korean cuisine; the leaves have a distinctive aromatic, slightly bitter flavor and are traditionally used to stuff roast goose or used in moxibustion in traditional Chinese medicine. The silver-backed, deeply dissected foliage is attractive, and the plant is highly drought-tolerant once established; however, it is potentially invasive and should be managed carefully. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Common Mullein
description: Scatter tiny seeds on bare, disturbed soil and do not cover — they need light to germinate; thin to 18–24 in apart once seedlings are established. As a biennial, mullein forms a large, velvety rosette of leaves in the first year before sending up a tall flower spike in its second season. First-year leaves are harvested and dried for use in respiratory-support teas and smoking blends; flowers are gathered as they open along the stalk, often infused into olive oil for ear-drop preparations. Allow the towering flower spike to set seed for reliable self-sowing in subsequent years. Matures in 365–548 days from seed.

name: Common Myrtle
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; common myrtle is one of the oldest cultivated plants in human history — sacred to Aphrodite, woven into Roman bridal wreaths, and mentioned in the Old Testament — a Mediterranean evergreen shrub with small, intensely aromatic leaves (releasing a fresh, clean, camphor-like fragrance when brushed), white flowers with prominent yellow stamens in summer, and small, round, blue-black berries in autumn. All parts of the plant are aromatic and culinary: the leaves are used to flavor meats and poultry in Sardinian and Corsican cuisine (similar to bay leaves), the berries are edible with a resinous, slightly gin-like flavor and are used to flavor liqueurs and as a spice in traditional Mediterranean cooking. The plant is compact and shapeable into hedges, topiary, and formal geometric shapes. Both leaves and berries are used in myrtle liqueur, particularly the Sardinian Mirto. It grows well in zone 8–10 with dry summers and is an excellent plant for Gulf Coast and California gardens with mild winters. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Common Oregano
description: Start the tiny seed indoors, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into full sun and well-drained soil. This common oregano, also called wild marjoram, has a milder flavor than the pungent Greek type and is the traditional variety for medicinal use. It is a hardy perennial with pretty pink to lavender flowers that draw pollinators; harvest leaves before flowering for the strongest flavor, fresh or dried. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Common Plantain
description: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering, since it germinates best with light. This resilient broadleaf perennial establishes even in compacted or disturbed ground where little else grows. Harvest the young leaves for fresh or dried herbal use, and let a few plants set seed to maintain the patch year after year. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Common Purslane
description: Direct sow seeds on the surface of poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil — do not bury them, as they require light to germinate. Purslane is one of the most nutritious leafy greens available, with the highest plant-based omega-3 fatty acid (alpha-linolenic acid) content of any vegetable, plus high levels of vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, and glutathione. Harvest the succulent stem tips and young leaves when plants are 3–4 inches tall; the plants regrow vigorously after cutting. The mild, slightly lemony flavor works raw in salads (a staple in Turkish cacik and Middle Eastern fattoush), cooked in stews, or pickled. Remove plants before they set seed if you don't want them naturalizing throughout the garden. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Common Rue (Herb-of-Grace, Rue)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; avoid wet or highly fertile soils. CAUTION: Handle with gloves — rue contains furanocoumarins that cause photodermatitis (severe skin blisters on contact followed by sun exposure). Ruta graveolens (rue or herb-of-grace) is one of the oldest cultivated herbs in Western horticulture, used since antiquity as a culinary, medicinal, and ritual plant; in the kitchen it is used very sparingly as a seasoning in Mediterranean cuisines (especially in Southern Italian and Ethiopian cooking), where a few leaves are added to salads, cheeses, grappa, and meat dishes for its intensely bitter, aromatic, slightly citrusy, and resinous flavor — the bitterness is powerful, and it should be used in very small quantities by those not accustomed to it. The attractive blue-green, finely divided foliage and small yellow flowers make rue an ornamental herb-garden plant; it is also reputed to repel many insects including aphids, Japanese beetles, and cats, making it useful as a companion plant. It is the larval host plant for Giant Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, adding wildlife value. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Common Sage
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix; germination is reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and prune plants hard in spring to remove winter-killed tips and promote bushy growth from the base. Harvest leafy stems before flowering for culinary and medicinal use; the volatile oils are most concentrated on sunny mornings before flowering. Dried sage leaves and bundles are used in cooking, traditional salubrious teas, and as smudge sticks in ceremonial contexts. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Common Sorrel
description: A hardy perennial green whose lemony, tangy leaves brighten salads, soups, and sauces in the French tradition. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep and thin plants to eight to twelve inches apart. Harvest young spring leaves for the mildest flavor, cutting outer leaves so the plant keeps producing. Remove flower stalks to prolong leaf production, and divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Common Sow-thistle (Hare's Lettuce)
description: Common sow-thistle appears spontaneously in garden beds, compost areas, and disturbed ground across virtually all of North America — a Eurasian annual naturalized worldwide. The leaves are edible at all stages but mildest and most pleasant when harvested young (before the plant bolts), tasting somewhat like a milder, less bitter version of dandelion greens. Young rosette leaves are excellent in salads, stir-fries, or as a cooked pot herb — used in this way throughout the Mediterranean, China, and Africa as a common food plant. Despite the name and resemblance, it is in the Asteraceae family and not related to true thistles. The milky sap is harmless. Hares and rabbits eat the leaves avidly (hence 'hare's lettuce'). Recognized as a valuable foraging green in many food traditions. The daisy-like yellow flowers attract small native bees. Best harvested regularly as it appears in the garden, rather than deliberately cultivated in good beds where it would compete with food crops. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Common Tansy
description: Tanacetum vulgare is a vigorous, aromatic perennial producing deeply divided, fern-like, dark-green leaves with an intensely camphor-like scent and flat-topped clusters of bright, button-yellow flower heads in late summer that were historically planted near doorways to repel flies, ants, and fleas; the dried flowers hold their color well and are valuable for dried arrangements. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested in significant quantities; it contains thujone, a neurotoxic compound, and should not be consumed internally. Do not grow near vegetables or edible crops as the allelopathic compounds can inhibit germination. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Common Thyme
description: Surface-sow seeds or cover to 1/8 in in warm, well-drained starting mix; seedlings are small and slow to establish so start early indoors. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun — like other Mediterranean herbs, thyme deteriorates in fertile, moist conditions. Trim plants lightly after each harvest to prevent woodiness; replace plants every 3–4 years when the center becomes unproductive. Harvest leafy stem tips before or during flowering for the highest thymol content, using fresh or dried in culinary preparations and traditional antiseptic and cough-relief remedies. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Common Thyme / Garden Thyme
description: Thymus vulgaris is the primary culinary thyme of European and world cuisine — a low, bushy, semi-woody perennial with tiny, aromatic, gray-green leaves containing thymol and carvacrol, the essential oil compounds responsible for its powerful, distinctive fragrance. It is the definitive herb of French, Italian, Spanish, and Middle Eastern cooking; an essential component of bouquet garni and herbes de Provence; and one of the most important medicinal herbs in Western herbalism, used for respiratory infections, coughs, and as an antimicrobial. The tiny, pale-lavender flowers in late spring are outstanding for honeybees and are the source of highly prized thyme honey. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Common Vervain
description: Verbena officinalis is an ancient medicinal herb with one of the longest recorded histories of use in European and Near Eastern herbal tradition, valued from classical antiquity through the Middle Ages as a nervine tonic, digestive bitter, and sacred ritual plant; it is a slender, upright perennial with deeply lobed, rough-textured gray-green leaves and long, wiry spikes of tiny, pale lilac to white flowers throughout summer that are visited enthusiastically by small native bees and hoverflies. Direct-sow seeds in a dry, sunny, well-drained position — common vervain is a plant of waste ground, roadsides, dry grasslands, and disturbed soils and thrives in lean, free-draining, neutral to alkaline conditions where more vigorous herbs might be out-competed; it will decline in rich, moist, or shaded sites. Harvest the leafy, flowering tops during full bloom for use fresh or dried in traditional herbal preparations; the bitter iridoid glycosides (particularly verbenalin) give the plant its characteristic medicinal properties valued by herbalists for supporting the nervous system and digestion. Common vervain self-sows reliably and naturalizes easily in gravel gardens, dry banks, and cottage herb gardens, where it adds an airy, wild-flower quality while maintaining its important role as a medicinal herb and pollinator plant. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Compact Dill
description: This dwarf dill stays short and bushy, making it ideal for containers, raised beds, and small gardens while delivering classic dill flavor. Sow directly where it will grow, as dill resents root disturbance. Harvest the ferny foliage as needed and let some plants flower for pickling heads and seed. Make successive sowings for a continuous supply of fresh leaves through the season. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Compacta Sage (Dwarf Compact Culinary Sage)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Compacta packs the same robust, savory flavor of standard garden sage into a tidy, dense little shrub that rarely needs staking or hard pruning to stay in bounds. Its small gray-green leaves and violet-blue early-summer flowers make it as useful in a mixed container or edging planting as it is in the kitchen, and its compact size means a single plant is often enough for a household's fresh sage needs. Harvest leaves lightly throughout the growing season and trim the whole plant back by about a third in spring to remove any winter-damaged growth and keep it dense. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but resents wet feet, so make sure drainage is sharp. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Compactum Oregano (Dwarf Culinary Ornamental Oregano)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where the plant develops its strongest flavor. Compactum is a dwarf oregano selection that stays low and dense, only 4–8 inches tall, forming a tidy mound rather than the looser, more upright growth of standard oregano, making it useful as a fragrant edging plant or rock garden filler in addition to a culinary herb. It carries the same bold, aromatic flavor as standard oregano in a more compact package suited to smaller herb gardens and containers. Harvest sprigs regularly and shear plants back after flowering to keep growth dense and productive for years. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Compactum Oregon Grape (Dwarf Mahonia)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, and avoid the hottest afternoon sun, which can scorch the glossy, holly-like leaflets.
