Compactum is a dwarf selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — roughly half the size of the species — while still producing the same fragrant, bright yellow spring flower clusters followed by dusty-blue, edible (if tart) berries beloved by songbirds, and the same spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns purple-bronze in winter cold. Its smaller stature suits it to foundation plantings and shaded borders where full-size Oregon grape would eventually crowd the space. Prune only lightly, if at all, since its naturally compact habit needs little maintenance to stay tidy. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Compactum Sweet Marjoram (Dwarf Culinary Marjoram)
description: Compactum is a dwarf selection of sweet marjoram, staying in a tight, low mound well under the 12-18 inches typical of the species while carrying the same sweet, floral, mildly resinous flavor prized in Mediterranean cooking. Its small scale and neat habit make it well suited to window boxes, edging, and container culture where standard sweet marjoram would grow loose and sprawling. Like the species it is a tender perennial grown as an annual outside USDA zone 9-11, though potted plants can be brought indoors for winter. Pinch tips regularly to keep the mound dense and to delay flowering, which is when leaf flavor is at its peak just before buds open. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Compactum Thyme (Dense Non-Flowering Culinary Edging Thyme)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; thyme performs poorly and can rot in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil. Compactum is a dense, mounding form of common culinary thyme that stays low and tidy without the sprawling, woody growth typical of standard thyme, and flowers only sparingly, keeping its energy focused on producing tender, flavorful leaves rather than seed. Its neat habit makes it a popular choice for edging garden beds and paths, filling gaps between stepping stones, or growing in containers. Trim lightly after any bloom and shear back by about a third in early spring to keep the mound dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody over time. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Compactus Thyme
description: Compactus is a naturally dwarf, dense form of common culinary thyme, forming a tight mound of small aromatic leaves without the woody sprawl of the species. Grow in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, since crowded, damp conditions promote rot in the tight center of the plant. Because of its small stature, light and frequent harvesting is preferable to hard pruning. It is well suited to pots, window boxes, and the front of an herb border. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Compassion Seedless Grape (Crisp White Table Grape, formerly 'Passion')
description: Compassion is a University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture seedless table grape, first released in 2017 under the name Passion and renamed in 2018 to avoid confusion with an unrelated fruit variety of that name. Its white-green berries combine the crisp, thin-skinned bite typical of California table grapes with the richer, fruitier flavor common to eastern American hybrids, a texture combination the breeding program specifically targeted. Vines show good general disease resistance and vine health for the humid South, and fruit is non-slipskin with resistance to cracking after summer rain. As with other Arkansas releases, it is best suited to home gardens and local-market sales rather than long-distance shipping, since fruit softens quickly after harvest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Conadria Fig
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Conadria is a common fig type (no pollinator needed) and one of the most productive figs per tree, bearing heavily in its second and third years. Conadria was released in 1955 by USDA fig breeder Ira J. Condit from the Riverside California station after decades of fig selection work; it was selected for exceptional fruit quality combined with high yields, producing large (3–5 oz), turbinate, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with strawberry-pink interior flesh and very sweet, rich flavor comparable to the finest White Adriatic and Calimyrna types. Outstanding for fresh eating and particularly excellent for drying, producing firm, sweet dried figs with good shelf life. A vigorous, upright, productive tree that performs exceptionally in hot, dry Western climates (Central Valley California, Arizona, Texas, Gulf Coast) and ripens reliably in the main crop (August–October). Somewhat more heat-tolerant than many high-quality white figs. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Concerto Artichoke (First-Year Flowering Hybrid Artichoke)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give young seedlings a period of cool temperatures once they have several true leaves to encourage first-year bud formation. Transplant outdoors after frost danger has passed into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest buds while the scales are still tightly closed. Concerto is a compact F1 hybrid bred to reliably flower and produce full-sized rounded green buds in its very first season, making globe artichoke growing practical in shorter-season gardens that could not otherwise ripen a traditional perennial variety in time. Where winters are mild it can also be left in the ground to behave as a genuine short-lived perennial, cropping again in subsequent years. Matures in 100–140 days from transplant.

name: Concord Grape (American Blue Grape, Slip-Skin Grape, New England Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter — Concord is cane-pruned, leaving 2 strong canes per vine; fruit ripens in September in most zones; Concord is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator; the berries slip easily from their skins ('slip-skin'), which facilitates juice making but means they are not firm enough for shipping. Concord grape is the foundational American table and juice grape, developed in 1849 by Ephraim Wales Bull in Concord, Massachusetts, from a chance seedling of Vitis labrusca — the native American 'fox grape' species of the northeastern forests. Bull spent six years selecting seedlings for fruit quality from a wild Labrusca vine growing on his property before exhibiting the named variety at the Massachusetts Horticultural Society in 1853, where it immediately attracted attention and within decades became the most widely planted grape in the United States. The Concord grape flavor — simultaneously musky, sweet-tart, and intensely 'grapey' in a way that European vinifera grapes are not — became the defining American grape taste through Welch's grape juice (first produced in 1869 to provide an unfermented communion grape drink by Dr. Thomas Welch) and the ubiquitous grape jelly that made the PB&J sandwich a cultural icon. The flavor compound primarily responsible for the characteristic Concord aroma is methyl anthranilate, a naturally occurring ester found at high concentrations in Labrusca-type grapes and essentially absent from European vinifera varieties. Concord is a seeded grape (seeds are a minor inconvenience for fresh eating but irrelevant for juicing and jelly making) producing large, round, blue-black berries in substantial clusters in mid-to-late September. The vines are cold-hardy to -20°F and require 100–150 chill hours, which are met in zones 4–8 but rarely in zones 9+. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Concord Seedless Grape
description: Grow this cold-hardy American grape on a two- or four-arm kniffin trellis, pruning heavily each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and clusters well spaced. It produces the same deep blue-black, musky-sweet slip-skin berries prized in classic Concord grape juice and jelly, but without the seeds that fill traditional Concord fruit, making it far more pleasant for fresh eating. The vines share Concord's toughness and reliable heavy cropping in short-season northern climates, though clusters are typically a bit smaller and looser than the seeded parent. It is self-fruitful and widely adapted to home gardens outside hot, humid grape-growing regions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Concorde Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Concorde benefits from a compatible pollinizer such as Conference or Comice for best fruit set. Bred in England from a cross of Conference and the richly flavored Doyenne du Comice, it combines the best traits of both parents, producing long, slender, Conference-shaped fruit with the sweeter, more aromatic dessert flavor of Comice, on a tree that is notably more compact and easier to manage in a home garden than either parent. Its excellent flavor, attractive fruit shape, and good storage life have made it an increasingly popular modern addition to home orchards, particularly where garden space favors a smaller, more manageable tree. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature, since pears ripen best off the tree rather than left to soften on the branch. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Condo Mango (Extreme Dwarf Container Mango)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a container that can be moved under cover before frost. Condo is one of the smallest mango cultivars in cultivation, bred specifically for balcony and patio container growing, staying under 6 feet even at maturity while still producing full-sized, flavorful fruit. Its extreme dwarf habit makes it the most practical mango option for gardeners with very limited space or those who need to bring the tree indoors or into a greenhouse for winter protection in zone 9 and cooler areas. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect the tree from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Conehead Thyme (Spanish Oregano, Persian Hyssop)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant; the most flavorful and intense of all thyme-related herbs. Thymbra capitata (conehead thyme, also known as Coridothymus capitatus or sold as Thymus capitatus) is a compact, thorny-based, perennial aromatic subshrub from the dry Mediterranean hillsides of Spain, Portugal, the Balearic Islands, and extending east through the Mediterranean basin. It is one of the most intensely aromatic herbs in the Mediterranean flora — the small, crowded, stiff leaves and pink flower heads (arranged in the characteristic rounded 'cone' clusters that give the plant its name) contain very high concentrations of carvacrol and thymol, the same aromatic compounds found in both thyme and oregano, but at higher concentrations than either cultivated thyme or Greek oregano. The flavor is powerfully savory, hot, and intensely aromatic — making it highly valued as a culinary herb (used as a substitute for oregano in Spanish cooking), as one of the traditional components of Mediterranean za'atar blends, and as a source of essential oil. In Israel and the Levant, dried conehead thyme is an important za'atar component. The plant requires perfectly drained, lean, alkaline, sun-baked conditions — overwatering or clay soil will kill it. In zone 8–10 Mediterranean-climate gardens, it is long-lived, decorative, and worth growing as a specimen culinary herb. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Conehead Thyme / Spanish Oregano
description: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; this subshrub suffers in heavy clay or waterlogged ground and thrives on neglect. Shear lightly after the distinctive cone-shaped flowers fade to maintain a compact mound and encourage fresh aromatic growth. Avoid overhead watering and do not fertilize heavily, as rich soil dulls the intensely oregano-like fragrance that makes this herb prized in Greek and Middle Eastern cuisines. In zones 7–8, mulch the crown lightly before hard freezes; in zones 9–10 it grows virtually year-round with minimal care. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Confection Squash (AAS-Winning Sweet Acorn-Type Hybrid)
description: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form and ripen to deep orange. Recognized as an All-America Selections winner in 2017, this hybrid was bred for markedly sweeter, less fibrous flesh than typical acorn squash along with strong resistance to powdery mildew that keeps foliage productive later into the season. Its semi-compact vines produce a heavy, uniform set of small fruit ideal for roasting or stuffing whole. Harvest once rinds are fully colored and hardened, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry space. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Conference Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Conference sets a reasonable crop on its own but yields much better with a compatible pollinizer such as Comice or Bartlett. The single most widely grown pear in the United Kingdom and one of the most recognizable European pears, it bears reliable, heavy crops of long, tapered, bronze-russeted fruit with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that stores and ships notably well compared to more delicate dessert pear varieties. Its partial self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and good disease tolerance compared to some other European pears have made it a standard, forgiving choice for a home orchard, though a second variety nearby still meaningfully boosts yield. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the characteristic sweet, juicy texture, since pears ripen from the inside out and are best picked underripe from the tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Confetti Cilantro (Fine-Leaf Feathery Cilantro)
description: Sow seed directly into well-drained soil a quarter inch deep and thin to a few inches apart, since cilantro's taproot makes it a poor candidate for transplanting. Confetti is a fine-cut ornamental-leaf selection producing lacy, thread-like foliage instead of the broad lower leaves of standard cilantro, while keeping the same citrusy coriander flavor. Its dissected leaves make it a favorite for garnishing and for gardeners who want a distinct texture from a typical cilantro planting. Succession sow every few weeks in cool weather since, like all cilantro, it bolts quickly once temperatures climb into the 80s. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Congo Pepper (Trinidad Superhot Chile Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors well ahead of the season, since Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and need a long, hot growing season to fully ripen; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Congo Pepper is a traditional Trinidad and Tobago chile closely related to the island's famous Trinidad Scorpion and Moruga Scorpion lines, producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally deep red, carrying extreme superhot heat well beyond a habanero. Beneath the heat is a distinctly fruity, almost tropical flavor that makes it prized in Trinidadian pepper sauces and hot sauce blends despite its intensity. Handle ripe fruit with gloves, since the capsaicin level is high enough to cause skin irritation, and harvest as pods fully color for the best flavor and heat development. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Congo Trinidad Pepper (Wrinkled Orange-Red Very Hot Habanero-Type)
description: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Congo Trinidad bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through orange to red, carrying intense heat well into superhot territory along with the characteristic fruity habanero aroma, a traditional variety long grown in home gardens across Trinidad. It is prized for hot sauce and pepper sauce making, where its heat and fruity depth of flavor come through strongly. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; handle ripe pods with gloves. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Congo Watermelon (Southern Picnic Watermelon)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Congo requires plenty of space (hills or rows 6–8 feet apart) for its vigorous, spreading vines and very large fruits. Congo is a classic Southern summer watermelon of the 'picnic' or 'family' type, producing very large, elongated-oblong fruits (35–50+ lbs) with dark green skin patterned with lighter green stripes and solid deep red flesh with excellent sweetness and rich melon flavor; Congo-type watermelons were an important part of Gulf Coast and Deep South truck farming and summer culture in the first half of the 20th century, when enormous watermelons were hauled to market and sold by the slice from wagons and stands. The very large size makes Congo impractical for modern small households (a single fruit can feed 30 people) but it remains grown by enthusiasts of traditional Southern garden culture and heirloom melon growers. Best suited to long-season Southern gardens (zones 7–11) where 85–95 day maturity can be fully achieved. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Conilon Coffee (Brazilian Robusta, Kouilou)
description: Conilon, also called Kouilou, is the principal cultivated form of Coffea canephora in Brazil, where it accounts for the great majority of the country's robusta production, concentrated in the state of Espírito Santo. Compared with wild-type robusta populations it grows as a smaller, more manageable shrub, tolerates drought and heat better than most coffee types, and thrives at lower elevations than arabica requires, but it remains considerably more susceptible to coffee leaf rust than other canephora selections. Beans are valued mainly for blends, instant coffee, and the crema they add to espresso rather than for delicate cup complexity. Because it tolerates more direct sun than arabica, it can be grown with less overhead shading, though afternoon shade is still helpful in the hottest climates. Give it warm, humid conditions, fertile well-drained soil, and steady moisture through the growing season. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Connecticut Field Pumpkin (New England Field Pumpkin, Classic Carving Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in full sun; provide ample space for vigorous vines and fertilize generously with balanced fertilizer or compost. Connecticut Field Pumpkin is the traditional American carving and field pumpkin — an open-pollinated heirloom that has been the archetypal 'pumpkin' in American agriculture and home gardens for well over a century, serving as the standard from which Halloween carving pumpkins, field decoration pumpkins, and processing pumpkins have all descended. The deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits typically weigh 15–25 pounds, develop a deep, saturated orange color at maturity, and have thick, firm walls that support carving without collapsing — the defining characteristics for jack-o-lantern use. Connecticut Field has a very long cultivation history in New England and the mid-Atlantic states where it was grown both for decorative autumn use and as a livestock feed crop; the tough, fibrous flesh is not considered prime for pie (Long Island Cheese, Small Sugar, and Winter Luxury pie pumpkins have been favored for baking), but it is edible and was historically used for pumpkin butter and pie. One of the most iconic American vegetables with strong cultural associations to autumn, harvest season, and Americana — a variety that connects any garden to a centuries-long tradition of pumpkin growing in the Eastern United States. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Connover's Colossal Asparagus (Classic Victorian Heirloom Asparagus)
description: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring into a trench 6-8 inches deep with a ridge of loosened, compost-enriched soil, spreading the roots over the ridge before backfilling. Let all spears grow into fern the first year and delay harvest until the third spring to build strong root reserves. Connover's Colossal is a nineteenth-century English heirloom, one of the oldest named asparagus varieties still commercially available, originally selected for its unusually thick, early spears at a time when most asparagus was thin and slow to establish. It is an open-pollinated, non-hybrid variety, so it comes true enough from seed for home seed-saving, and it remains popular with heirloom vegetable growers for its historic pedigree and dependable, tender spears. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Conquistador Grape (Disease-Resistant Black Juice and Jelly Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Developed from breeding lines descended from T. V. Munson's disease-resistant Texas grape stock, Conquistador produces vigorous vines with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and other conditions that limit grape growing in hot, humid regions. The medium-sized black berries are tart and well suited to juice, jelly, and homemade wine rather than fresh eating out of hand. Because vines are vigorous and productive, prune firmly each winter to a permanent set of cordons and thin fruit clusters if growth becomes crowded, which improves air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Consort Black Currant
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Consort is a Canadian Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada black currant cultivar bred specifically for resistance to white pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) — a fungal disease that historically devastated currant and gooseberry plantings throughout much of North America and led to federal and state bans on Ribes species in the early 20th century. Consort's white pine blister rust resistance is an important practical attribute in regions where susceptible Ribes cultivars are still regulated or adjacent to white pine forests. The medium-sized, glossy, dark black berries ripen in July with the characteristic intensely aromatic, bittersweet black currant flavor valued for jams, cassis, juice, and wine. Consort grows as a vigorous, upright, productive shrub that is among the more cold-hardy black currant varieties, performing well throughout the northern US and Canada. The rust resistance trait means it can be grown where standard black currant cultivars are prohibited. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Consort Currant (Blister-Rust-Resistant Black Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Consort is a Canadian-bred black currant developed specifically for resistance to white pine blister rust, a disease black currants can host and spread to nearby white pines, which historically got the crop restricted or banned in parts of North America. This resistance makes Consort a legal, low-risk choice for gardeners in areas where white pines grow nearby. Berries are the classic strong, aromatic black currant flavor, best used cooked into jam, syrup, and baked goods rather than eaten fresh, since raw black currants are quite tart and intense. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so prune out the oldest, least productive canes each dormant season and encourage a steady supply of vigorous young growth from the base. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Constance Eliott Passionflower (Fragrant Pure White Hardy Passion Vine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils; Constance Eliott shares the exceptional cold hardiness of its parent species, blue passionflower, tolerating brief dips to 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit when established roots are protected by mulch. It bears creamy pure-white flowers with a soft, sweet fragrance, a cleaner, more subtle color than the blue-and-purple typical of the species, followed by oval orange-yellow fruits that are edible but mild-flavored. Dies to the ground in zones 7-8 but regrows strongly from deep roots; do not remove dormant crowns too early in spring. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Containers Choice Red Bush Tomato
description: A compact determinate hybrid bred for containers, producing red beefsteak-style tomatoes of six to eight ounces in about seventy days. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant into large pots or grow bags after nights warm. Its tidy habit needs only light support and suits small spaces and balconies. Keep container soil evenly moist and feed regularly, since potted tomatoes are heavy feeders. Matures in 68–72 days from transplant.

name: Contender Bush Bean
description: Sow seeds about an inch deep directly in the garden after the last frost, as beans dislike root disturbance. This early, adaptable variety sets heavy crops of crisp, flavorful pods and tolerates both cooler and warmer conditions than many bush beans. Harvest the tender pods young and pick frequently to keep the plants productive over several weeks. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Contender Bush Bean (Popular Early Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Contender is a longtime favorite early bush snap bean, valued for reaching harvest size faster than most other bush beans and tolerating somewhat cooler soil at planting than many varieties, giving Gulf South gardeners an early start on the bean season. Its round, meaty, stringless pods have good flavor and hold quality well for a short window before toughening, making regular harvest important. Because the whole crop tends to mature at once, Contender is an excellent choice for succession sowing every two to three weeks to maintain a steady bean harvest through summer, and for canning or freezing a full batch at one time. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Contender Bush Green Bean
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Contender is a classic open-pollinated bush snap bean introduced by Asgrow Seed Company in 1949 and one of the most reliable and widely grown snap beans in the southeastern US. It is valued particularly for its heat tolerance — Contender sets pods at higher temperatures than most bush beans and continues producing when Blue Lake and other popular varieties quit in early summer heat. The straight, round, 6–7 inch pods are tender, stringless, and have excellent classic green bean flavor with no fibrous texture. Contender produces a heavy concentrated crop that is ideal for large-scale fresh picking, canning, and freezing. It was the standard commercial and home canning bean for decades in the South and still recommended by extension services across the region. In zone 9, Contender's heat tolerance makes it the go-to bush snap bean for the spring garden; successive plantings starting in late February through April can yield beans from April through early June before summer heat becomes too intense for fruit set. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Contender Peach
description: Contender is a disease-resistant, cold-hardy, self-pollinating peach that produces abundant medium-to-large juicy freestone fruit across many climates. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently during fruit development. Thin young fruit to about 6 inches apart to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape for light penetration, and apply dormant sprays as needed to manage common peach diseases. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Contorta Flowering Quince (Twisted-Branch Corkscrew Quince)
description: 'Contorta' is a slow-growing, compact flowering quince selection prized for its dense, twisted, corkscrew-like dark brown branches, which provide sculptural winter interest long after the leaves have dropped. In early spring, pale peach-pink flowers fading toward white open directly on the contorted stems ahead of the curled, twisted foliage that follows, giving the shrub a strikingly gnarled silhouette all season. Small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom, usable for jelly and preserves. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, only right after flowering to preserve next year's buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Contorta Jujube (Dragon Jujube, Contorted Twisted-Branch Jujube)
description: Contorta, sometimes sold as Dragon Jujube, is an ornamental selection of the common Chinese jujube prized for its exaggerated, tightly zigzagging and twisted branch structure, which gives even young trees striking winter architectural interest reminiscent of a corkscrew hazel. Like all jujubes it tolerates heat, drought, and poor or alkaline soils far better than most fruit trees once established, and it thrives in the long, hot summers of the Gulf Coast. Fruit is edible and has the typical apple-crisp texture and sweetness of jujube when harvested at the tan-mottled stage, though yields and fruit size are generally smaller than on fruiting-focused cultivars like Li or Sherwood since Contorta is grown primarily for its ornamental branch form. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; a second jujube cultivar nearby improves fruit set, though established trees will still produce some fruit on their own. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Convis Pawpaw (Large Yellow-Fleshed Michigan Pawpaw)
description: Convis was selected from the same Michigan fields kept by fruit collector Corwin Davis that produced the well-known 'Davis' pawpaw, and it stands out for very large fruit that can approach a pound each, with rich yellow flesh and a mild, sweet flavor. As with all pawpaws, it is self-incompatible and needs a genetically distinct second cultivar planted nearby to set a full crop. It prefers deep, fertile, evenly moist soil and benefits from partial shade while young before converting to full sun as a mature tree. Harvest when the fruit yields to gentle pressure and separates easily from the branch, usually over several weeks in early to mid fall. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Cooke's Jumbo Quince (Giant California Paste-and-Preserving Quince)
description: Cooke's Jumbo was discovered as a chance seedling near Dinuba, California, likely related to the old Turkish cultivar Smyrna, and was introduced commercially by the L. E. Cooke Company nursery in 1972 specifically for its outsized fruit. It produces pear-shaped quinces that run notably larger than standard cultivars, often 15 to 20 cm across, with downy yellow-green skin ripening to gold and firm white flesh. Like all true quince, the hard, astringent fruit is not eaten raw; it is prized for quince paste (membrillo), preserves, jelly, and baking, and its large size means fewer fruits are needed to fill a batch. The tree is self-fertile, blooms with pale pink flowers in mid-spring, and ripens fruit in mid to late fall (September to October, varying by region). Its low chill requirement of about 100 hours suits warm-winter and Mediterranean climates as well as traditional quince country, and established trees are low-maintenance, tolerating a range of soils with good drainage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cooking Plantain
description: Plant corms or rooted pups in deep, rich, well-drained soil amended heavily with compost; cooking plantains require consistent moisture, warmth, and fertility to produce heavy fruit bunches. Unlike dessert bananas, plantains are starchy and low in sugar when unripe, requiring cooking at all stages — green plantains are fried (tostones), boiled, or baked; yellow-ripe plantains are sweet-fried (maduros). Each pseudostem produces one bunch of 100–200 fruits over 12–18 months, then dies back — remove it at the base and allow suckers to replace it. Mulch heavily in zones 8–9 where tops may freeze back to the rhizome; established rhizomes often survive to 20°F. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer high in potassium. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Coolidge Feijoa
description: Coolidge is a self-fertile pineapple guava selection, useful where only one plant can be grown. Set it in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently through the fruiting season for the best crop. It tolerates coastal conditions and light frost once established, and can be grown as a shrub or clipped hedge. Fruit is ripe when it drops naturally, so gather it daily from the ground beneath the plant. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Coomer Elderberry (Lewis Hill Vermont Large-Fruited American Elderberry)
description: Coomer is one of two elderberry cultivars developed in Vermont by Lewis Hill, distinguished from its companion release Berry Hill by a more upright growth habit and large, deep-purple-black berries borne in showy clusters. Coomer and Berry Hill were selected to flower and fruit on a similar schedule, making the pair a practical combination for growers who want simultaneous, easy-to-manage harvests along with reliable cross-pollination. As with all American elderberry, cook the berries before eating and expect vigorous root suckering that should be thinned annually to keep the shrub in a defined form. Coomer performs well in the cooler, moist growing conditions of the northern United States and tolerates the partial shade of a woodland edge. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Copan Mamey Sapote
description: Copan is a Cuban-origin selection producing medium fruit with deep red flesh of outstanding quality and typically only one large seed, making it easier to prepare than seedier cultivars. It bears more lightly than heavy producers like 'Pantin' or 'Magana', so it suits a home dessert planting rather than a commercial block. Culture matches other named mamey sapote selections: deep, fertile, well-drained soil, full sun, and generous space for a tall, long-lived tree that needs several years after planting before its first crop. Protect young trees from frost and wind, and harvest fruit firm, ripening it indoors at room temperature. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Copenhagen Market Cabbage
description: A Danish heirloom from 1909 that became the standard for round, early cabbages, forming tight six-to-eight-inch heads of three to four pounds. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and transplant twelve to eighteen inches apart. Its uniform, quick-maturing heads sit compactly on short stems, saving garden space. Keep evenly watered and harvest when heads feel solid to avoid splitting. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Copia Tomato (Bicolor Yellow-Red Speckled Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun. Copia is a striking modern heirloom, named for the American food and wine culture center in Napa where it was introduced, prized for its large, meaty fruit that ripens to a warm golden-yellow background overlaid with red marbling and streaks radiating from the blossom end. The flesh is sweet with balanced acidity and holds its shape well for slicing, making the fruit as good on a cheese board as in a sandwich. Provide sturdy staking or caging for the tall indeterminate vine, water evenly to reduce cracking, and pick fruit once fully colored for the best sweetness. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Copra Onion (F1 Hybrid Long-Storage Brown Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; set transplants 3–5 inches apart in rows 12 inches apart. Cure harvested bulbs with tops intact in warm, airy conditions for 2–3 weeks before storage. Copra is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid onion that has earned a reputation as one of the best long-keeping onions available — consistently ranking among the top storage onions in variety trials for its combination of high solids content (which concentrates flavor and extends keeping time), thin, tight-fitting brown outer scales, and small, tight-necked tops that dry down cleanly. The 'copra' connection (the dried coconut meat used in oil production) suggests the dried, concentrated character of the bulbs — high in solids, relatively low in water — which gives Copra good pungency but exceptional storage quality (6–9 months in proper conditions versus the 1–3 months of most sweet onions). Copra produces medium-sized (2.5–3 inch), globe-shaped, uniformly brown-skinned bulbs of consistently good quality. The pungency makes Copra most appropriate for cooking (caramelized onions, soups, braises) rather than raw eating, but the storage capability means gardeners can harvest a crop in late summer and have homegrown onions through the following spring. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Coquille de Louviers Mâche (Corn Salad)
description: Direct sow shallowly into cool, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist through germination, which is slow and improved by a period of cold stratification if sowing in late summer heat. Coquille de Louviers is a traditional French heirloom named for its cupped, shell-like leaves, which form dense, slightly domed rosettes distinct from flatter mâche types. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving hard freezes under light mulch or row cover to provide fresh greens deep into winter. Harvest whole rosettes at the base and use raw in salads for its mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Coralburst Crabapple (Dwarf Double-Flowered Coral-Pink Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Coralburst is a true dwarf crabapple, staying compact enough for small residential landscapes and courtyard plantings, bearing an especially heavy flush of fully double, coral-pink flowers each spring that give the tree an almost solid-pink appearance at peak bloom. It sets little to no fruit, since the doubled flower form is largely sterile, meaning less litter to clean up compared to heavy-fruiting crabapple cultivars. Its small mature size and dense, rounded canopy make it a popular choice as a specimen tree or for planting in a large container. Prune in late winter, if needed, to shape and remove crossing branches. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Coratina Olive (High-Polyphenol Southern Italian Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Coratina is a Southern Italian olive cultivar from Puglia prized for producing intensely robust, bitter, peppery oil with exceptionally high polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown olive cultivar — making it a favorite for growers and consumers seeking a bold, health-forward oil rather than a mild table experience. The tree is vigorous, heat-tolerant, and productive, and has performed well in warm-climate US oil-olive trials outside its native Mediterranean range, including in parts of the Southeast. Harvest early, while fruit is still green to just turning color, for the most intensely peppery, high-polyphenol oil; later harvest mellows the flavor but reduces polyphenol content. Coratina is largely self-fruitful, though yields improve with a second compatible cultivar nearby. Established trees are drought-tolerant and, like most olives, thrive on benign neglect once past the first two establishment years, needing supplemental water mainly during prolonged dry spells at fruit set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Corbaci Pepper (Turkish Long Sweet Frying Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest green at 8–10 inches or allow to ripen red. Corbaci Pepper is a long-standing Turkish heirloom sweet frying pepper that has gained significant popularity among American specialty growers and seed-savers for its combination of outstanding productivity, heat tolerance, and distinctive flavor profile. Unlike standard bell peppers, which develop thick walls that can flag in extreme heat, Corbaci's thin-walled, elongated fruits tolerate zone 9 summer temperatures without developing bitter off-flavors or collapsing at the blossom end — a common issue with large-fruited sweet peppers in the Deep South. The fruits ripen from lime green through yellow to vivid red; all stages are usable, but the fully red fruit develops a richer, slightly sweeter flavor with a soft, tender texture ideal for roasting, grilling, or raw eating. Corbaci is particularly well-suited to frying in olive oil (a classic Turkish preparation called 'körbacı biber tava'), where the thin walls soften quickly and the skin blisters attractively without the need for extended cooking time. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type each season. The plants are vigorous and upright with good leaf cover that provides some protection to the pendant fruits in intense afternoon sun. Corbaci performs best with consistent moisture but tolerates brief drought better than bell types due to its smaller fruit size and lower water demand per fruit. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Corbarino Tomato (Small Campanian Plum-Cherry Preserving Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Corbarino bears small, oval, bright red fruit in loose clusters, a traditional variety of the Corbara area near Naples valued for concentrated, sweet-tart flavor and thick flesh that holds up well to preserving whole in jars or drying, a regional specialty product in its home area. Its compact fruit size and productive habit make it a good choice for a home preserving garden. Harvest clusters as fruit fully colors for the best flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Cordner Sweet Potato (Louisiana Heirloom Baking Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun, and hill soil up over the row as vines run to keep developing roots covered. Cordner is a Louisiana dooryard heirloom with pinkish-purple-blushed skin and moist, deep-orange flesh that bakes up sweet and soft, grown by Gulf South home gardeners for generations before modern commercial varieties took over most production. The vigorous, sprawling vines tolerate the heat and humidity of a Louisiana summer with ease and provide good ground cover that shades out weeds once established. Dig roots once vines begin to yellow in fall and before frost threatens, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin and sweeten the flesh before storing in a cool, dry place. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Corinto Cucumber (Parthenocarpic Mini Seedless Slicer)
description: Sow directly 1 inch deep and provide a trellis for vertical growing; Corinto is parthenocarpic and sets fruit without pollination, making it more reliable in cool springs or greenhouses where bees are absent; harvest frequently (every 2–3 days) at 5–6 inches for the sweetest quality. Corinto is an F1 parthenocarpic (self-pollinating) cucumber from Seminis/Monsanto Seeds specifically bred for high tunnel and greenhouse production but equally excellent in open garden conditions — the key 'parthenocarpic' characteristic means the plant sets fruit without requiring pollinating bees, an advantage in enclosed structures, in cool early spring conditions when bees are inactive, or in suburban gardens with limited pollinator activity. The fruits are small to medium (5–6 inches), cylindrical, dark green, and nearly seedless with very thin, tender skin that doesn't require peeling — the 'mini seedless cucumber' style increasingly available in grocery stores. The thin skin and near-absence of seeds gives Corinto a different texture from seeded slicing cucumbers — more uniformly crisp and mild throughout without the slightly bitter jelly surrounding seeds. The flavor is mild, sweet, and clean; Corinto stays mild and non-bitter even when slightly over-mature (unlike seeded types which become more bitter as they yellow). Excellent for fresh eating, salads, and pickling whole. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Cork Oak
description: Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; cork oak is the source of virtually all wine and champagne cork in the world — the extraordinarily thick, spongy, deeply furrowed outer bark is harvested every 9–12 years from mature trees (a process called 'cork stripping') that does not harm the tree, as the bark regenerates completely. Portugal and Spain produce about 80% of the world's cork. The tree is an evergreen with a broad, spreading canopy and small, evergreen, slightly holly-like leaves. First cork harvest is typically at age 25 years; subsequent harvests every 9–12 years for the remaining 150–200 years of the tree's life. In California, cork oaks have been grown for over a century as ornamentals and heritage trees, thriving in the Mediterranean climate. An interesting tree with historical and economic significance for home gardeners in zones 7–10. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Corn Mint
description: Plant rooted divisions in moist soil in partial shade to full sun, containing the plant in a buried pot or raised bed to limit rhizome spread; corn mint is the most widely distributed of all mints and the primary commercial source of natural menthol, producing a strong, clean, true peppermint-like fragrance and flavor that makes it excellent for tea, beverages, cooking, and distillation. Harvest stems for fresh use throughout the growing season, cutting plants back by half monthly to promote fresh, tender growth and delay flowering. The plant tolerates wetter, shadier, and more challenging conditions than many other mints. Dry harvested stems in bundles for winter use. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Corn Salad
description: Direct sow thinly in late summer or early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, barely covering seeds with fine soil; corn salad (mâche) produces rosettes of tender, spoon-shaped, dark-green leaves with a mild, slightly nutty flavor that is sweeter and less assertive than arugula or watercress. It grows through frost and even light snow — the foliage sweetens with cold — making it one of the most valuable winter salad crops in zones 5–9. In the Gulf South sow in fall for winter and early spring harvest; it will struggle in summer heat. Self-sows freely and can naturalize as a seasonal gap-filler in kitchen gardens. Cut individual outer leaves or harvest whole rosettes as needed. Matures in 40–65 days from seed.

name: Corn Salad Verte de Cambrai (Mache)
description: Sow seeds shallowly in cool soil in late summer or fall, since this green germinates poorly in heat. The small, spoon-shaped leaves form tight rosettes that shrug off hard frosts and can be harvested through winter under a light cover. Cut whole rosettes at the base for their mild, nutty flavor, and let the very cold-hardy plants stand in the garden as a living winter salad supply. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Corne de Bélier Snow Pea (Ram's Horn Pea)
aliases: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Corne de Bélier'
description: Corne de Bélier, French for ram's horn, is a classic French heirloom snow pea named for its long, curved, flattened pods. The vigorous climbing vines produce attractive bicolor flowers followed by an abundant set of stringless, tender pods best harvested while young and flat for stir-fries, salads, and quick sautés. It is a long-standing favorite in French market gardens and heirloom seed collections both for its culinary use and for its ornamental flowers. Provide a trellis and pick frequently to keep pods tender and encourage continued production. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Corne de Cerf Chicory (Stag Horn Chicory)
description: Direct sow into well-drained garden soil in full sun and thin young plants to give room for the sprawling rosette to develop. Corne de Cerf is an old French cutting chicory documented in nineteenth-century seed catalogs, prized for its long, narrow leaves cut into sharp, irregular lobes reminiscent of deer antlers, giving the variety its name. The leaves are eaten young as a pleasantly bitter salad green or cooked briefly like other chicories to mellow the flavor. It is closely related to the Catalogna and asparagus chicory group and, like them, can be allowed to bolt in late winter for tender, blanched inner shoots. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Cornelian Cherry
description: Cornelian cherry is one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small yellow flowers appear in late winter before the leaves — and the small, olive-shaped drupes ripen in late summer to a rich ruby red. Plant at least two seedlings or cultivars for best fruit set, as it is partially self-fertile but cross-pollination greatly improves yields. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban pollution once established. Harvest when fruit is fully dark red and slightly soft; it is too tart to eat out of hand but makes outstanding preserves, syrups, and fruit leather. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Cornelian Cherry Dogwood (Cornelian Cherry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions. Cornus mas (cornelian cherry dogwood) is a large, multi-stemmed European and Asian shrub or small tree producing one of the very earliest spring flower displays of any hardy plant — tiny, bright-yellow flowers clustered in small, button-like heads that cover the bare branches in February–March (often while snow still falls) before any other spring-blooming shrub. The flowers are followed by oval, cherry-like fruits that ripen to deep scarlet-red in August, tasting like a tart-sweet cranberry crossed with a sour cherry — used in jams, jellies, liqueurs (the Georgian chacha), and sauces throughout Eastern Europe and the Caucasus, where the sour flavor is prized in cooking much like tamarind. The tree is also fall-ornamental with excellent red-pink fall foliage and attractive peeling bark. 'Golden Glory' and 'Redstone' are widely grown cultivars. At the warm edge of its range (zone 8), it grows best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture; it is marginal in zone 9 and does best in the cooler northern parts of zone 8. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Cornell Bush Delicata Squash (Compact Non-Vining Delicata)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to allow the compact bush to fill in without crowding. Cornell Bush Delicata was bred at Cornell University to bring the sweet, nutty, edible-skinned delicata squash into a compact, non-vining bush habit that takes up a fraction of the space of standard vining delicata varieties, making winter squash growing practical in small gardens and raised beds. The oblong, cream-colored fruit striped with green matures with the same rich, sweet, dense orange flesh delicata is prized for, excellent roasted with the thin skin left on. Harvest once the rind has hardened and stripes have deepened in color, and cure fruit in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve keeping quality. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Cornito Giallo Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Yellow Mini Frying Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container on a sunny patio. Cornito Giallo is an AAS-winning miniature Italian frying pepper, a scaled-down version of the classic Corno di Toro type, producing an abundance of small, slender, sweet yellow fruits on a compact plant well suited to container culture. Fruits can be picked young and green-yellow for a milder flavor or left to fully color for peak sweetness; the thin walls cook down quickly when sautéed whole. The heavy, continuous fruit set on a relatively small plant makes it one of the more productive choices for patio and small-space pepper growing. Harvest regularly to keep new flowers and fruit coming. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Cornito Rosso Pepper (Sweet Red Mini Snack Pepper)
description: Transplant into full sun after the soil has warmed, staking lightly if the compact plant becomes heavy with fruit. Cornito Rosso is the red-ripening companion to the yellow Cornito Giallo, an elongated, tapered mini pepper bred for sweet, thin-walled flesh that is equally good eaten fresh as a snack or quickly pan-fried whole. Fruits ripen to a glossy deep red about a week later than the yellow type and hold well on the plant for a long harvest window. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Corno di Toro Giallo Pepper (Yellow-Ripening Italian Bull's Horn Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55F, staking or caging plants since the long, heavy pods can bend lighter branches. Corno di Toro Giallo is the yellow-ripening strain of the classic Italian bull's horn frying pepper, maturing from green to a bright golden yellow rather than the red of the standard Rosso strain, though both share the same tapering, curved eight-inch pods and thin, sweet flesh prized for roasting. The pale color develops fully only with extra time on the plant, so gardeners wanting peak sweetness should let fruit ripen past the green stage rather than harvesting early for yield. Roast or grill whole until the skin blisters and slips off easily, then dress the silky flesh with olive oil and garlic in the Italian antipasto tradition. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Corno di Toro Pepper (Bull's Horn Italian Frying Pepper, Sweet and Thin-Walled for Roasting)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully ripe. Corno di Toro (Bull's Horn Pepper) is one of Italy's most beloved culinary peppers — a sweet, thin-walled frying and roasting pepper grown throughout southern and central Italy and named for the long, tapering, curved shape of the ripe fruit that resembles a bull's horn. The typical fruit is 6–10 inches long, 1.5–2 inches wide at the shoulder, tapering to a point, with a slight irregular curve along the length — distinctly different in shape from both the blocky bell pepper and the narrow frying types like Jimmy Nardello. Red-ripening ('Corno di Toro Rosso') and yellow-ripening ('Corno di Toro Giallo') strains are both traditional in Italy and both produce sweet, mild fruit with no heat. The thin walls are the key culinary property: Corno di Toro lacks the thick, watery flesh of bell peppers and has instead a thinner, more concentrated flesh layer that caramelizes deeply and quickly under high cooking heat — roasted in a hot oven or over open flame, the peppers char and soften to a silky, intensely sweet texture that is quite different from the same cooking treatment applied to thick-walled bell peppers. In Italian antipasto tradition, roasted Corno di Toro peppers are dressed with olive oil, garlic, and capers, or sautéed in olive oil until very soft and served as a condiment with grilled meat. The variety has been grown by Italian-American gardeners in the United States for generations and has become more widely available through specialty seed companies. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Corno di Toro Rosso Pepper (Red-Ripening Italian Bull's Horn Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost, spacing plants far enough apart for good airflow around the tall, productive stems. Corno di Toro Rosso is the traditional red-ripening strain of Italy's bull's horn frying pepper, its long, twisted, tapering pods turning from green to a deep brick-red as they mature and sweeten. The thin walls caramelize quickly under high heat, so roasting or charring over an open flame brings out a smoky sweetness that a thick-walled bell pepper cannot match. Harvest continually through summer to encourage further fruit set, picking some pods green for a milder flavor and letting others ripen fully red for the most intense sweetness. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Coronet Black Currant (Blister-Rust-Resistant Early-Ripening Black Currant)
description: Coronet was bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva alongside 'Consort' and 'Crusader' to carry resistance to white pine blister rust, the fungal disease that led many US states to restrict or ban Ribes cultivation for much of the 20th century. It ripens its medium-sized, glossy black berries earlier than many other rust-resistant cultivars, and while the flavor is a touch more bitter than dessert-type European black currants, it processes well into jam, syrup, and cassis. Plants are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 10 to 20 pounds of fruit once established. Prune out canes older than three years each dormant season, since black currants fruit mainly on one- and two-year-old wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Coronet Southern Pea (Nematode-Resistant Cream Cowpea)
description: Coronet was developed through a Southern land-grant university breeding program as a compact, semi-bush cream-type southern pea selected for resistance to root-knot nematodes and Fusarium wilt, two soil-borne problems that plague many older cowpea varieties in the Deep South. It holds its pods well above the foliage, making hand-picking easier than with sprawling types. Like other cowpeas, it thrives in hot, humid summer weather that stresses most other vegetable crops and fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules, benefiting whatever is planted after it. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage for fresh cream peas or allow them to dry fully on the vine for storage. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Corot Noir Grape (Cornell-Bred Cold-Hardy Red Wine Grape)
description: Released by Cornell's Geneva breeding program alongside Noiret and Corot Noir's other 'NY' hybrid siblings, this variety produces deeply colored, medium clusters that yield full-bodied red wines with good tannin structure, unusual for a cold-hardy hybrid. It ripens in mid to late season and has become popular with Finger Lakes and other northeastern wineries seeking vinifera-quality reds from hardier vines. Prune to a cane or cordon system and manage vigor through shoot positioning to expose fruit to adequate sunlight for full color and tannin development. It tolerates winter cold considerably better than the vinifera reds it is often compared to. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Correnta Spinach (Upright Smooth-Leaf Bolt-Tolerant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow shallowly into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings as they develop, harvesting the upright, easy-to-clean leaves individually or as whole plants. This hybrid forms a distinctly vertical rosette of smooth, dark green leaves that stay cleaner and easier to bunch than sprawling types, while its strong resistance to bolting extends the practical harvest window. Extension programs in warm-winter regions have recommended it for both fall and late-winter plantings where standard spinach would bolt too quickly. Matures in 38–45 days from seed.

name: Corsican Blue Rosemary (Vigorous Semi-Prostrate Deep-Blue-Flowered Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun. Corsican Blue is a dense, semi-prostrate rosemary selection, part of the narrow-leaved Angustifolia Group, prized as one of the most intensely aromatic rosemary cultivars available along with small tubular deep blue flowers borne over a long spring-into-summer season. Its sprawling, cascading habit suits raised beds, banks, and the tops of retaining walls where the stems can spill downward, and the finely textured, dark green needle-like foliage remains ornamental year-round in mild climates. Harvest sprigs regularly for cooking to keep growth dense, and site in sharply drained soil, since wet feet are the most common cause of failure. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Corsican Mint
description: Plant small divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded spot; Corsican mint forms a moss-like carpet of tiny peppermint-scented leaves just 1–3 in tall and is ideal between stepping stones or at the edge of a cool, moist path. Unlike most mints, it dislikes hot, dry conditions and should never be allowed to dry out completely. The plant releases a powerful peppermint fragrance when lightly stepped on, making it a sensory ground cover. In zones 6–7 it may die back in hard winters but typically returns from the root; mulch lightly in late autumn to protect the shallow root system. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Corsican White Chives (Dwarf White-Flowered Selection)
description: Corsican White is a very dwarf, fine-textured chive selection originally collected as wild seed from Corsica and later named for its distinctive pure white flower globes, a color break from the usual lilac-pink of common chives. Its narrow leaves and slender stems are noticeably sparser and shorter than standard chives, making it better suited to small edging, rock garden, or container plantings than to bulk culinary harvest. Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, since the compact habit is prone to being overwhelmed by competing foliage in rich, damp beds. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the tight, tidy mound from thinning out, and shear off spent flower heads to tidy the display once bloom fades. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cortland Apple (McIntosh × Ben Davis Cross, Non-Browning Salad Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cortland is an excellent cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties including McIntosh; ripens mid-season (September–October); the non-browning flesh makes it uniquely valuable for salads, charcuterie boards, and fresh-cut preparations where apples must remain attractive for hours without discoloring. Cortland apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1915 from a cross of McIntosh and Ben Davis — two of the most important apple varieties of the early 20th century. Cortland inherits McIntosh's aromatic, sweet-tart flavor character in a larger, firmer fruit with significantly better keeping quality than McIntosh. However, Cortland's most famous and unique characteristic is the slow-browning tendency of its flesh when cut: while most apple varieties brown rapidly after cutting due to enzymatic oxidation, Cortland flesh is notably slower to brown, making cut pieces remain white and attractive for much longer than most varieties. This property makes Cortland uniquely valuable for fresh preparations where apple slices need to remain appealing: fresh fruit platters, salads, charcuterie boards, and school lunch boxes where the apples won't be eaten immediately after cutting. The fruit is large, round, red over greenish-yellow skin with very white, juicy, tender flesh and the characteristic McIntosh aromatic quality. It is an excellent cross-pollinator for most other apple varieties due to its abundant, viable pollen. A classic in northeastern U.S. home orchards. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Corvair Spinach (Downy Mildew-Resistant Smooth-Leaf Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Corvair is a smooth-leaf hybrid spinach bred with resistance to numerous races of downy mildew, the fungal disease that most commonly cuts a spinach planting short in humid or damp conditions, and it holds an upright habit that keeps leaves cleaner and easier to harvest than sprawling types. Its slow-bolting habit extends the productive window into warmer weather better than many older varieties, useful for stretching a Gulf Coast spring or fall spinach crop. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Coscia Pear (Ercolini, Ancient Italian Summer Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. An ancient Italian landrace also known as Ercolini, it bears small, elongated fruit with green skin that turns yellow as it ripens, with white, juicy, sweet flesh carrying a faint spicy note, ripening in late summer ahead of most other European dessert pears. The tree is vigorous and highly productive, especially in the warmer growing regions of central and southern Italy, and while partially self-fertile it sets a heavier crop with a second pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Harvest as soon as the skin begins to yellow and eat promptly, since the fruit ripens and softens quickly off the tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cosford Hazelnut (Thin-Shelled English Pollenizer Cobnut)
description: Cosford is a long-cultivated English cultivar prized both for its own oblong, very thin-shelled, sweet-kernelled nuts and for its value as a dependable pollenizer, since its bright yellow catkins shed pollen abundantly over a long bloom window. It is a hardy, reliable grower across a wide range of soils and produces fewer root suckers than many other hazel cultivars, making it easier to keep tidy. Plant it within an orchard or mixed hedgerow alongside Kentish Cob or other named cultivars so its early, generous pollen shed overlaps with their receptive female flowers. Harvest in late September when the thin, light-brown shells loosen from the husk. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cosmic Crisp Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cosmic Crisp requires a substantial chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A cross between Honeycrisp and Enterprise developed by Washington State University and released commercially in 2019 after two decades of breeding and testing, it combines Honeycrisp's exceptionally crisp, juicy texture with dramatically better storage life, keeping fresh in refrigeration for up to a year without the bruising and softening problems that plague its Honeycrisp parent. Large, deep red fruit with a name inspired by the pale lenticel dots scattered across the skin like stars against a dark sky, it has rapidly become one of the most sought-after new apple varieties for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting Honeycrisp's texture without its notorious storage and growing difficulties. Thin fruit in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and harvest based on color and taste rather than a fixed date, since ripening time varies by climate. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cosmic Purple Carrot
description: A striking carrot with bright purple skin and orange interior, reviving a color grown for over a thousand years. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface moist through the slow germination. Thin seedlings to two to three inches so the roots can size up evenly. Harvest when roots reach full size and enjoy the sweet flavor and extra antioxidants in the purple skin. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Cosmonaut Volkoff Tomato (Russian Red Beefsteak Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Cosmonaut Volkoff bears medium-to-large, deep red, round beefsteak-type fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor on vigorous, productive indeterminate vines, a Russian heirloom that has become a steady favorite among tomato collectors for combining classic flavor with reliable yields. It performs well across a range of climates and continues fruiting over a long summer season. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Cossack Pineapple Ground Cherry
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cossack Pineapple is a well-regarded heirloom ground cherry variety that produces larger fruits than most ground cherry types — up to 3/4 inch — with an intense, complex flavor combining pineapple, vanilla, and a citrus-caramel sweetness that makes it one of the most acclaimed varieties in Seed Savers Exchange evaluations. Like other ground cherries, the fruits are enclosed in papery husks (calyces) that dry and tan as the fruit ripens, and the fruit drops naturally when ripe; collect from the ground and remove the papery husk before eating. Delicious fresh, in pies (ground cherry pie has been popular in the Midwest and Appalachia for generations), in preserves, and dried. Self-sows readily and can naturalize in the garden if left to drop seed. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Costa Rica 95 Coffee (CR95)
description: Developed through pedigree selection by the Instituto del Cafe de Costa Rica (ICAFE) from a cross between Hibrido de Timor and Caturra, Costa Rica 95 is a compact, conical-shaped tree with short branches, reddish-bronze new growth, and red ripe fruit. It was bred primarily for high productivity rather than lasting disease immunity, and field evaluations have shown its early rust resistance can decline over time in some growing regions, so growers still need an active disease-management program. The dwarf habit allows dense planting and it responds strongly to fertilizer inputs, rewarding well-managed farms with heavy yields. Grow it like other Central American dwarf arabica hybrids, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with partial shade. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Costa Rican Guava
description: Plant Psidium friedrichsthalianum in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; tolerates some frost once established but best in zone 10–12; harvest fruits when they turn fully yellow and give slightly under gentle pressure. Costa Rican Guava ('cas' in local parlance — a word so fundamental it has no direct English translation outside of the botanical name) occupies a unique place in Costa Rican culture — the guava-sized, white-fleshed, intensely tart fruits are the basis of agua fresca de cas (the most popular fresh juice in the country), used in refresco mixtures, ice creams, jams, and as a souring agent in cooking. The flavor is bracingly tart and intensely guava-fragrant, with significantly more acidity than the common tropical guava (Psidium guajava) — more similar to a tart lemon guava in flavor profile. The tree is somewhat smaller and more cold-tolerant than the common guava, performing well in humid subtropical conditions. In zone 10–12 Gulf Coast gardens and Florida, it fruits reliably and heavily with minimal care. The fruit's high pectin content makes it excellent for jams and jellies without needing commercial pectin. For Costa Rican immigrants and lovers of Central American cuisine, this tree represents home in a way that the common guava cannot replicate. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Costa Rican Mint Bush (Jamaican Mint Bush, Minty Savory)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pinch regularly to maintain bushy form and encourage leaf production; propagate by stem cuttings. Satureja viminea (Costa Rican mint bush or Jamaican mint bush, also known as Clinopodium vimineum) is a tropical perennial shrubby herb from the mountainous regions of Jamaica, Costa Rica, and Central America — notable for producing one of the most intensely and cleanly 'minty' fragrances of any plant in the Lamiaceae (mint) family, far exceeding true peppermint (Mentha x piperita) in the purity and strength of the mint-eucalyptus aroma. The aromatic compound profile is dominated by pulegone and other menthane-family compounds that create the characteristic cool, clean mint sensation. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Costa Rican mint bush grows as an upright, multi-branched, woody-based shrub with small, oval, intensely aromatic leaves and small white to lavender flowers attractive to bees and butterflies. The leaves are used as a fresh mint substitute for teas, cocktails (authentic mojito-style drinks in parts of Central America), and culinary uses wherever fresh mint flavor is desired. The plant tolerates light shade and thrives with regular trimming in tropical and subtropical gardens. Hardy to about 28–30°F; useful in containers in zone 8. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Costata Persimmon (Ribbed Seedless European-Grown Astringent Kaki)
description: Costata is a vigorous astringent-type persimmon cultivar widely grown in European orchards, producing distinctively ribbed, seedless orange fruit. The flesh is tender and melting once fully ripe, losing its astringency completely as the fruit softens, but is puckery and unpleasant if eaten while still firm. Fruit ripens in October and is considered an early-season cultivar among astringent kaki types. The tree is a strong, reliable grower and, like most Diospyros kaki, is self-fertile and productive without a pollinator. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Costata Romanesco Summer Squash
description: This Italian heirloom zucchini bears ribbed, mottled fruit with a firm texture and rich, nutty flavor. Harvest young at 4 to 8 inches for the best tenderness, or let fruit reach up to 18 inches for cooking. Pick often to keep the compact plants producing all season. The abundant male blossoms are also excellent stuffed or fried. Water evenly and give plants room for good airflow to reduce powdery mildew. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Costata Romanesco Zucchini
description: This ribbed Italian heirloom zucchini has firm, richly flavored flesh and produces attractive star-shaped slices. Direct sow in warm, fertile soil and give the large, somewhat sprawling plants plenty of room. It yields fewer fruit than hybrids but each has superior nutty flavor and holds up well when grilled. Its abundant male blossoms are excellent for stuffing and frying. Harvest fruit young at 6 to 8 inches for the best texture and to keep production going. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Costeño Amarillo Pepper (Yellow Coastal Oaxacan Chile)
description: Start indoors and transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost; harvest at full golden-yellow to orange maturity for drying or fresh use; costeño amarillo is one of the hotter Oaxacan chiles (5,000–15,000 Scoville units) and can be used fresh at the yellow stage or dried to a papery, wrinkled yellow-orange state; the dried chile keeps well for 1–2 years. Costeño Amarillo is a distinctive Mexican landrace chile native to the southern coast of Oaxaca state — particularly the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and the Pacific coastal plain of the Costa Chica region — where it grows in the hot, humid tropical climate and is the defining chile of coastal (costeño) Oaxacan cuisine as distinct from the highland Sierra Norte tradition that uses chilhuacle negro and rojo. The name means simply 'coastal yellow chile' — named for its place of origin and its golden-yellow to orange color when ripe. The fresh and dried chile is distinctive: thin-skinned, elongated (3–4 inches), tapering to a point, and at full maturity a vivid golden-yellow to orange-yellow color that produces the characteristic bright golden color in authentic mole amarillo and the yellow-orange sauces of Tehuantepec cooking. The flavor is moderately hot (5,000–15,000 Scoville units), with a fruity-citrusy quality and a pleasant tartness distinct from the earthier highland varieties. Costeño amarillo is the chile for authentic yellow mole — the sauce for which Oaxacan 'Zapotec-style' tamales are famous — and cannot be genuinely replicated with any other dried chile variety. A critical piece of the Oaxacan chile puzzle for gardeners interested in authentic regional Mexican cooking. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Costmary (Bible Leaf)
description: Divide the clumping rhizome in early spring, replanting sections 2–3 in deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; costmary tolerates partial shade but becomes straggly and produces fewer of the large, minty-balsamic leaves. The broad, silver-green leaves were historically placed in Bibles and hymnals as bookmarks because the pleasant fragrance helped keep the reader awake during long services — hence the common name. Harvest large, mature leaves at any point during the growing season for use as a herb in ales and meat dishes, for sachets in linen, or as a flavoring in salads and teas. Cut plants back hard after flowering to rejuvenate the foliage and prevent excessive spread. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Costoluto Fiorentino Tomato (Ribbed Florentine Heirloom Slicer)
description: Costoluto Fiorentino is a classic Italian heirloom from the countryside around Florence, known for its deeply lobed, ribbed, flattened fruit that looks almost like a squash blossom in cross-section. The bright red fruit has a bold, tangy, old-fashioned tomato flavor prized in Tuscan cooking for sauces and fresh sliced dishes, and the strong ribbing means fruit is often cut into wedges rather than round slices. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vine well, since the irregular fruit shape can make individual tomatoes heavier and more awkward on the stem than a smooth round variety, and expect some cracking around the ribs in wet weather. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Costoluto Genovese Pole Tomato
description: A classic Italian heirloom, this indeterminate variety produces deeply ribbed, rich-red fruit of 6 to 8 ounces with an intense, old-world flavor balancing sweetness and acidity. The thick, meaty walls make it ideal for sauces and paste. Provide sturdy staking or a tall cage since vines grow long and heavy. Prune suckers for larger fruit and better airflow. Feed and water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Costoluto Genovese Tomato
