description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant deeply after all frost risk has passed; Costoluto Genovese is a centuries-old Italian heirloom widely grown around Genoa and throughout the Mediterranean, recognizable by its distinctive deeply ribbed, lobed, oblate-flattened fruits with rugged, almost corrugated red skin and intensely flavored, somewhat acidic, meaty flesh that makes it arguably the finest sauce and paste tomato in the heirloom world. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; fruits weigh 6–10 ounces and are best used cooked, as the complex, tart flavor concentrates beautifully in sauces and soups. Stake or cage firmly and harvest when fully red and slightly soft; in warm climates this variety often produces two flushes — early spring and again in fall. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Cot-N-Candy Aprium (Fuzzy-Skinned Apricot-Plum Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator flowering at the same time, since Cot-N-Candy sets fruit poorly on its own. This Zaiger Genetics aprium, an apricot-plum interspecific hybrid weighted mostly toward apricot, looks much like a fuzzy-skinned apricot but carries noticeably sweeter, richer, more aromatic flesh thanks to its plum parentage. It ripens early in the stone fruit season, giving a jump on the summer harvest, and is generally grown and pruned like a standard apricot, with an open-center form and moderate annual pruning to renew fruiting wood. Because apricots and apriums bloom very early, plant in a site protected from the latest spring frosts, which can damage the flowers before fruit ever sets. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cotton Candy Mango (Dwarf Sweet Container Mango)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover before frost. Cotton Candy is a dwarf mango bred for a small, manageable size and exceptionally sweet, nearly fiberless flesh with a soft, dessert-like flavor that has made it a popular choice among home growers seeking a compact tree without sacrificing fruit quality. Its small stature suits container growing in zone 9, where in-ground plantings risk winter damage, allowing the tree to be sheltered during freezes. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect the tree from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cotton Lavender (Gray Santolina)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cotton lavender requires superb drainage — it will rot in wet or waterlogged soil and performs poorly in humid climates without excellent drainage. Santolina chamaecyparissus is a low, aromatic, silvery-gray, evergreen Mediterranean subshrub with dense, coral-like, deeply cut foliage that emits a strong, somewhat pungent, herbal scent when brushed; it produces small, button-like, bright-yellow flower heads on long, slender stems in mid-summer. In the traditional European herb garden, it was used as a low hedging plant in knot gardens and formal herb borders (the silver foliage contrasting beautifully with the green of boxwood and rosemary), and the dried leaves were used as a moth repellent for linen closets. Shear after flowering to maintain a neat, compact shape and prevent woodiness; takes well to clipping. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Countess Parsnip (Canker-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Countess is a modern F1 hybrid parsnip bred for strong resistance to canker, the fungal disease that causes unsightly brown-black shoulder rot in many older open-pollinated varieties. It produces long, smooth, uniform roots with a sweet, refined flavor and a notably high percentage of usable roots even in less-than-ideal soil. Because it is an F1 hybrid, seed should be purchased fresh each season rather than saved, and parsnip seed in general loses viability quickly regardless of source. Choose Countess over heirloom types like Hollow Crown where canker has historically been a problem in the garden. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Country Cream Variegated Oregano
description: Plant in well-drained, preferably alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Country Cream' is a bushy, semi-woody culinary oregano selected for its small aromatic leaves edged in creamy white, giving it strong ornamental value as an edging or container plant alongside its usual kitchen uses. Loose sprays of tiny pink flowers appear from summer into early autumn and are attractive to pollinators. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but resents prolonged high humidity around the crown, so give it sharp drainage and good air circulation. Propagate by cuttings of non-flowering shoots in midsummer or by division in spring or fall to maintain the cream variegation, since seedlings revert to plain green. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Country Gentleman Sweet Corn (Shoepeg Corn)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; isolate from other corn by 250–400 feet or by planting to mature 14 days apart to prevent cross-pollination. Country Gentleman sweet corn dates to 1890 and is a distinctive old SU (standard sugary) type characterized by its 'shoepeg' kernel arrangement — the narrow, elongated, irregular-spaced white kernels are packed so closely they fill the space between rows and lack the defined row pattern of normal corn, a characteristic shared with Stowell's Evergreen and a handful of other white heirloom corns. This unique kernel arrangement has been prized by cooks for generations because the irregular corn can be packed more densely into cans and jars; Country Gentleman shoepeg corn canned at home was a Southern kitchen staple for much of the 20th century. The flavor is rich, complex, and exceptionally sweet for an old-type corn. The variety is a late-season type (88–95 days) suited to long-season gardens; the tall plants (6–8 feet) are vigorous and productive. Matures in 88–95 days from seed.

name: County Fair Cucumber (Bacterial Wilt-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed; County Fair is a compact, gynoecious pickling cucumber notable among cucumber varieties for carrying real genetic resistance to bacterial wilt, a serious disease spread by cucumber beetle feeding that quickly wilts and kills susceptible vines with no cure once infected. It also shows tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus, powdery mildew, angular leaf spot, and anthracnose, giving it an unusually broad disease package for a pickling type. Fruit is blocky and uniformly sized, ideal for dill or bread-and-butter pickles when picked at 3-5 inches. Because cucumber beetles and the wilt they spread are a persistent problem in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens, County Fair is a strong choice where bacterial wilt has wiped out other cucumber plantings in the past. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Court Pendu Gris Apple (Ancient Late-Blooming Frost-Avoidant Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Court Pendu Gris is one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation, with a history some trace back to Roman times and documented in France and England for centuries, prized above all for blooming remarkably late in spring, well after most other apple varieties, which gives it outstanding natural resistance to the late frosts that damage or destroy the crop of earlier-flowering trees. The small, flattened, gray-russeted fruit has firm, dense, sharply flavored flesh that mellows and sweetens with storage, and the variety is an exceptional keeper, often holding good quality into late winter or even spring. Its low, spreading, naturally compact growth habit and remarkable frost avoidance have kept it valued by heirloom orchardists for centuries despite its modest fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cousa Squash (Middle Eastern Zucchini)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost; cousa squash is a compact bush type that produces prolifically even in hot weather, making it well-suited to the Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 summer conditions where European zucchini often fails under humidity and heat stress. Cousa is a traditional Middle Eastern summer squash with fat, club-shaped to slightly bulging, light-green to pale-grey-green fruits harvested at 4–6 inches for the classic Levantine stuffed squash dish (mahshi kousa), where the flesh is hollowed out, filled with seasoned rice and meat, and braised in tomato broth; the compact interior, firm flesh, and mild, sweet flavor make it superior to standard zucchini for stuffing as it holds its shape better. Also excellent sliced and sautéed or grilled. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Couve Manteiga (Portuguese Butter Collard)
description: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to a loose, non-heading rosette habit rather than the upright single stalk typical of Southern collard types. The broad, smooth, pale-to-medium green leaves are notably thinner and more tender than typical American collards, cooking down faster and with a milder, almost cabbage-like flavor that suits quick sautes as readily as long-simmered pots. This is the collard type traditionally used in Portuguese caldo verde soup, where leaves are shredded into fine ribbons, so gardeners growing it for that purpose should prioritize leaf tenderness over plant size when harvesting. Because the plant does not form a strong central stalk, it is more prone to sprawling in heavy rain or wind and benefits from a bit more spacing than compact collard hybrids. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Covington Sweet Potato (NCSU-Developed Leading Eastern US Commercial Sweet Potato)
description: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Covington was developed by North Carolina State University and released in 2005 — and has rapidly become the dominant commercial sweet potato variety across the Eastern United States, particularly in North Carolina (the leading sweet potato production state) and throughout the Gulf South. The combination of outstanding tuber uniformity (straight, symmetrical, consistent-sized roots), excellent deep-orange flesh color, good sweetness, exceptional storage quality, and broad adaptability drove Covington's rapid adoption over the previously dominant Beauregard. The copper-orange skin over vivid orange flesh produces the familiar market sweet potato appearance, but the distinctive Covington quality is the remarkable uniformity — roots are notably more consistent in size and shape than Beauregard or older varieties, reducing culled roots and improving marketable yield. The eating quality is excellent: moist, sweet, flavorful orange flesh with good texture after baking, boiling, or roasting. Covington is resistant to Fusarium wilt and several other sweet potato pathogens important in southeastern production. Cure harvested tubers for 5–7 days at 85–90°F with high humidity to convert starches to sugars and develop maximum sweetness. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: Cow Horn Okra (Long-Podded Southern Heirloom Okra)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 70°F, soaking seeds overnight to improve germination; harvest pods at 4–6 inches length before they become fibrous. Cow Horn is a distinctive heirloom okra producing very long, slender, slightly curved pods that visually resemble a cow's horn when mature — one of the more unusual and visually interesting okra types in the Southern heritage seed tradition, with pods that can reach 10–14 inches at full maturity but should be harvested young for eating quality. The curved, ribbed, light-green pods are tender and excellent when harvested young, with the mild okra flavor and characteristic mucilaginous texture that thickens gumbo and gives fried okra its character. Cow Horn plants are tall and vigorous (5–7 feet), producing abundantly through the Southern summer heat season; the large plant size requires adequate spacing and is well-suited to garden rows where height is not a constraint. The variety has been passed down through Southern seed-saving traditions, particularly in the Deep South where heirloom okra varieties have been maintained for generations. The extended pod length also makes Cow Horn excellent for pickled whole okra, where the elongated pods are visually striking in the jar. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Cow Parsley (Wild Chervil, Queen Anne's Lace Look-alike)
description: Sow seed in fall for natural stratification in moist, fertile soil at woodland edges, shaded borders, or hedgerow margins in partial shade; cow parsley is a widespread European biennial or short-lived perennial with frothy white umbel flowers that naturalize readily in hedgerows and woodland margins. Young stems and leaves have a pleasant, mild parsley-carrot flavor and have been eaten in Britain and Europe as a spring potherb, in salads, and cooked as a vegetable. Despite its culinary history, extreme caution is warranted: cow parsley closely resembles the deadly poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) and water hemlock (Cicuta species); even experienced foragers have been poisoned by misidentification. Learn positive identification from multiple authoritative sources before ever considering consumption. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cow Parsnip (American Cow Parsnip)
description: Grow in moist to average, humus-rich soil in partial shade or at woodland edges and stream margins; cow parsnip is the largest native North American member of the carrot family, with enormous palmate leaves and flat-topped white flower umbels up to 12 inches across that serve as insect landing pads for hundreds of pollinator species. The young peeled shoots and leaf stems have been eaten by Indigenous peoples across North America — cooked, the flavor resembles a mild celery-like vegetable. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: The sap of cow parsnip contains furanocoumarins that cause severe photodermatitis — blisters and burns when sap-exposed skin is hit by sunlight. Always wear gloves and long sleeves when harvesting or handling, and wash hands thoroughly afterward. Do not confuse with the invasive and more toxic giant hogweed (H. mantegazzianum), which is larger with a purple-blotched stem. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Cowart Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cowart is an early-ripening black muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (now UGA) and released in 1974. It is widely valued as a dual-purpose black muscadine: the large, jet-black berries (larger than Noble) are excellent for fresh eating with a rich, sweet, full-flavored muscadine taste, and also produce outstanding dark wine, juice, and jam. As one of the earliest-ripening black muscadines, Cowart extends the beginning of the black muscadine season and is frequently paired with Noble and other later-ripening varieties to spread harvest over a longer window. The thick skin makes berries more durable and longer-lasting after harvest than most muscadines. Cowart is self-fertile and requires no pollinizer, though yields increase with nearby compatible varieties. Disease resistance is excellent across the humid Gulf South. Harvest in late August when berries are fully black and slip freely from the stem with gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cowhorn Okra (Long-Pod Southern Heirloom Okra)
description: Soak seeds 8–12 hours in warm water before planting to improve germination; direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun, well-drained soil, 12–18 inches apart; harvest pods at 6–8 inches for tender eating quality — Cowhorn pods remain tender longer than standard varieties at larger sizes. Cowhorn Okra is a traditional Southern heirloom variety whose long, pale green, slightly curved pods inspired the name — resembling the curved horn of a cow — and it has been grown throughout the Gulf South and Deep South for generations as the preferred okra of gardeners who want large pods for pickling and traditional okra dishes. The plants are vigorous and tall (4–6 feet), producing prolifically through the summer heat of zone 9 and the Gulf South, and the pods remain tender at longer lengths (6–8 inches) compared to modern commercial varieties that become fibrous past 3–4 inches. This extended tenderness window makes Cowhorn particularly valued for whole-pod pickling, where large uniform pods are cut to fit mason jars, and for large-format gumbo preparations where longer pod segments are preferred. Cowhorn is a classic open-pollinated heirloom that can be saved seed from year to year; the plants also reseed readily in warm climates if any pods are left to mature. An important ecological note: okra in general is adapted to the same climate as cotton (to which it is related in the Malvaceae family) and handles the heat, humidity, and occasional drought of Gulf Coast summers better than almost any other food crop. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Cowpea (Black-Eyed Pea)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep into any well-drained soil, including poor sandy or clay soils — cowpeas fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility without added fertilizer. They are exceptionally heat and drought tolerant once established, making them the premier summer legume for the Gulf Coast and similar hot, humid climates. Harvest green-shell peas when pods are plump but skins are still soft, or leave pods to dry on the vine for dry beans. Bush types need no support; vining or half-runner types benefit from a simple trellis. Inoculate seeds with cowpea rhizobia if growing in new ground for maximum nitrogen fixation. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cox's Orange Pippin Apple (World's Finest Eating Apple, English Dessert Apple Standard)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with good air movement; Cox's Orange Pippin is highly susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew in humid climates — a preventive spray program or planting in the dry Pacific Northwest is strongly recommended; it requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in October when fully colored and giving slightly to pressure, then store 4–6 weeks to allow flavor to fully develop. Cox's Orange Pippin is the variety most consistently named by apple connoisseurs worldwide as the finest-flavored dessert apple in existence — a small to medium English heirloom discovered as a seedling by retired brewer Richard Cox in his garden at Colnbrook Lawn in Slough, Berkshire, England around 1825, and distributed commercially from 1850 onward. The flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinarily complex and rich by apple standards: intense, spicy-sweet, aromatic, with distinct notes of pear, mango, honey, and fresh nuts that no other apple variety precisely replicates — and which Cox's defenders argue no modern commercial variety (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) can equal in flavor depth and complexity. Cox's became the dominant apple of British gardens and orchards for 150 years and remains the benchmark of the English fresh-eating apple tradition. In the United States, Cox's is most successfully grown in the maritime Pacific Northwest (Oregon and Washington's western valleys, similar in climate to England) where the cool, moist summers allow the apple to develop its characteristic complex flavor without disease pressure overwhelming the susceptible trees. In the humid eastern states, disease resistance is a significant challenge that requires diligent management. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Coyote Mint
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; coyote mint is a low, mounding California native with soft, gray-green, strongly aromatic foliage carrying a fragrance somewhere between mint and oregano, released readily when the leaves are brushed. Dense, rounded clusters of pale lavender-pink flowers cover the plant from summer into fall, drawing large numbers of native bees and butterflies, including numerous specialist pollinators adapted to the mint family. It is well suited to dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and low-water borders once established, needing little more than good drainage and occasional deep watering during the longest dry spells. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep growth compact and encourage a second, lighter bloom later in the season. Matures in 120–240 days from transplant.

name: CP 65-357 Sugarcane (Historic Louisiana Commercial Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. CP 65-357 (the CP designation stands for Canal Point, Florida, the site of the joint USDA-University of Florida sugarcane breeding program) was one of the standard commercial sugarcane varieties grown across the Louisiana sugar belt for many years, valued for reliable tonnage and sugar content under Gulf South growing conditions. While it was developed for large-scale sugar production rather than dooryard syrup-making, home growers can use it the same way as heirloom syrup canes: harvest in late fall after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, strip the leaves, crush the stalks, and cook the juice down into syrup, or simply chew the sweet stalks fresh. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Crabapple
description: Crabapples bear small, tart fruit excellent for jelly and serve as reliable pollinizers for dessert apples. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing disease-resistant selections to limit scab and rust. They are extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soils. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy, and harvest the high-pectin fruit after the first firm color develops. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cracoviensis Lettuce
description: Sow directly in early spring; a Polish heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, named for Kraków, with deeply notched, savoyed red-bronze leaves and a fast cut-and-come-again habit. It matures quickly from an early spring sowing and can be harvested leaf by leaf or cut whole, often regrowing a second flush in cool conditions. Central European seed keepers have maintained it for generations as a colorful, reliable early salad green. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Cranberry
description: Cranberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), consistent moisture, and sandy-peat substrate — conditions that closely mimic their native bog habitat. A 3–4 in layer of coarse sand mulch helps suppress weeds and maintains the proper surface environment. The vines are slow to establish and typically take 3–4 years to produce a meaningful crop. Harvest in fall when berries turn deep red and bounce when dropped; home growers pick by hand rather than flooding. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cranberry Bean (Borlotti Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; cranberry beans can be grown as a bush or pole type depending on variety. Harvest at the fresh shell stage when pods are colorfully streaked with red and cream and beans inside are plump but not yet dry — this is the classic fresh borlotti stage prized in Italian cooking. For dried beans, leave pods on the plant until they are papery and rattle when shaken, then pull entire plants and cure under cover before threshing. Regular watering during pod fill prevents shriveled beans. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Cranberry Hibiscus (African Rosemallow)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after soil warms to 70°F; the deep burgundy-red, deeply lobed foliage is ornamental throughout the season, making this one of the most attractive edible plants for a zone 9–11 garden. The young leaves have a tart, cranberry-sorrel flavor excellent in salads, wraps, and as a garnish; the fuchsia flowers are also edible and make a vivid cranberry-colored tea. In zone 9–11 it grows as a perennial but blooms only in short days, producing flowers in late fall; in cooler zones treat as a warm-season annual for leaf harvest. Cut back by half in late summer to promote fresh tender growth. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Crandall Clove Currant (Heat-Tolerant Fragrant-Flowered Currant)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Crandall is a selection of clove currant, a North American native species distinct from and considerably more heat- and drought-tolerant than the European black and red currants that struggle in hot summers, making it one of the more workable currant options for warmer zones. In spring it produces abundant, intensely spice-clove-scented yellow flowers that perfume the surrounding garden before setting large, sweet-tart black currants used fresh or in preserves. It is generally self-fertile though yields improve with a second plant nearby, and needs only routine removal of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the shrub vigorous and productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crandall Currant (Heat-Tolerant Clove Currant)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Crandall is a selection of the American clove currant, native to the central United States and far more tolerant of heat and humidity than the European black and red currants that generally struggle south of zone 7. In spring, the bush covers itself in small, bright yellow flowers with an intense clove fragrance that perfumes the whole garden and draws early pollinators, followed in summer by large, sweet-tart black currants excellent for fresh eating as well as jam and preserves. Because it genuinely performs in warm climates, Crandall is one of the few currants a Gulf South gardener can grow successfully without fighting the plant's preference for cool summers. The naturally spreading, suckering habit forms an attractive informal hedge over time; prune out the oldest canes periodically to keep the planting vigorous and productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Crane Melon (California Heirloom Sonoma County Specialty Melon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; reduce irrigation as fruits near maturity. Harvest when the skin turns from green to cream-white to pale gold and a sweet, complex aroma is detectable at the stem end. Crane melon is a California heirloom developed by Oliver Crane in Santa Rosa, Sonoma County, California in the 1920s–1930s — a melon variety born from the crossing of several melon types over multiple generations that became a regional specialty deeply associated with its place of origin, to the point that authentic Crane melons are considered a Slow Food Ark of Taste variety. The fruits are large (5–10 lbs or more), irregularly shaped — often lopsided, elongated, or vaguely oblong with uneven shoulders — with cream-white to pale tan, slightly netted or smooth skin that looks nothing like the standard cantaloupe. The appearance is rustic and non-commercial, which partly explains why the Crane melon never became a commercial crop despite extraordinary flavor. The white to pale cream-colored flesh is extremely sweet and aromatic, with a complex vanilla-floral character that many tasters describe as the best-flavored melon they have ever tasted — a flavor profile unlike any other commonly available melon type. Crane melons are a California heirloom of significant regional importance and represent the type of locally-adapted, place-specific vegetable variety that defines the Slow Food movement's preservation work. Matures in 88–100 days from seed.

name: Cranz Black Walnut
description: Cranz is a named black walnut cultivar long favored by nut growers for combining vigorous, upright growth with heavy, consistent nut set once the tree reaches bearing age. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun, and keep it well clear of gardens and orchards, since black walnut roots and fallen leaves release juglone that suppresses many other plants. A second seedling or grafted black walnut nearby improves pollination and fill, though established Cranz trees crop reliably on their own. Gather nuts promptly after they drop and remove hulls quickly to prevent staining and mold before curing kernels for storage. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Crapaudine Beet
description: Considered one of the oldest documented beet varieties still in cultivation, tracing back to at least the 1600s in France, where its name (French for toad) refers to the rough, dark gray-brown bark-like skin that develops as the root matures. Sow directly into loose, deep soil once the ground can be worked, and expect a slower bulking rate than modern hybrid beets, so allow a long season for full-size roots. The deep garnet flesh stays firm and sweet, making Crapaudine one of the best-keeping beets for winter root cellar storage. Light frost before harvest improves its already rich, earthy sweetness. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Craquerelle du Midi Lettuce
description: Sow directly in the cool season; this heirloom Batavia lettuce from southern France, its name loosely translating to crunchy one of the Midi, produces elongated, savoyed, crisp heads bred to withstand the hot, dry summers of Provence. It is notably slow to bolt, making it well suited to late-spring and early-summer sowings when many other lettuces would turn bitter. Heirloom seed houses reintroduced it to American gardeners as a heat-season alternative to iceberg. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Crawford Turnip (Southern Heirloom Greens Turnip)
description: Direct sow into well-worked, fertile soil in full sun; Crawford is a regionally maintained Southern heirloom kept in circulation primarily by seed savers and small seed houses rather than large commercial catalogs, valued for producing abundant, tender leaves ahead of a usable root. The leaves are typically harvested young and often cooked alongside the thinnings, since the strain was selected on Southern farms as a dependable greens crop rather than for uniform root size or shape. Because it is an open-pollinated landrace-style variety rather than a modern hybrid, expect some natural variation in leaf shape and root form from plant to plant. Flavor improves with cool weather and light frost, following the same pattern as other greens-type turnips grown in Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Cream Crowder Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun, without pre-soaking or inoculation unless growing in new ground. Cream crowder peas take their name from the cream-colored seeds that pack (crowd) tightly into the pods, producing a high yield per pod. The large, plump seeds are preferred for fresh shelling over black-eye or purple hull types in much of Louisiana and Mississippi, where cream peas have been a kitchen garden tradition for generations. The mild, starchy flavor cooks smoothly into soups and side dishes; combine with hog jowl and rice for the classic Louisiana New Year's Day luck dish. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and thrive in the summer heat that ends most other legumes. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Cream of Saskatchewan Watermelon
description: This heirloom watermelon produces round, 6 to 11 pound fruit about 10 inches across with sweet, creamy pale-white flesh under a thin, delicate rind. Its relatively short season makes it a good choice for northern gardens, especially with a black plastic mulch to warm the soil. Handle the fragile rind gently at harvest. Water deeply but reduce moisture as fruit ripens to concentrate sweetness. Give vines ample space to sprawl. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Cream of the Crop Acorn Squash (White Bush Acorn Squash)
description: Direct sow into warm soil once frost risk has passed, spacing plants for their compact bush habit which suits smaller garden beds. Cream of the Crop was named an All-America Selections winner in 1990 for its productive bush vines and creamy white-skinned acorn-type fruit with golden, nutty-flavored flesh. Its space-saving growth habit made it notable among winter squash of its time, since most acorn squash varieties before it required significantly more sprawling room. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Cream Sausage Bush Tomato
description: This determinate variety bears cylindrical, cream to pale-yellow fruit best picked at about 3 inches when they resemble small sausages. The smooth, buttery, mild flavor is excellent eaten fresh or simmered into pale sauces. The compact bush habit suits containers and small beds and needs little staking. Because it sets fruit over a concentrated window, it is well suited to canning batches. Keep watering steady to avoid cracking. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Creek Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Precocious Type I Pecan for the Southeast)
description: Creek is a USDA-ARS release (1996) valued for exceptionally precocious bearing, often producing a crop within five years of planting, and for moderate-to-good resistance to pecan scab that makes it more forgiving in the humid Gulf Coast than older susceptible cultivars. Nuts are long, narrow, and elliptical, running about 54 per pound with good flavor and filling. As a Type I pollen shedder, Creek needs a Type II cultivar planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination. Its tolerance of partial shade and closer spacing makes it a flexible choice for smaller Gulf Coast home orchards. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Creek Plum
description: Creek Plum is a native shrubby plum of stream banks, creek margins, woodland edges, and disturbed open lands across Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states, producing clusters of small, bright red to yellow plums in mid-summer that are sweet, tart, and excellent fresh or for jams, jellies, and preserves. The profuse clusters of white flowers that cover the branches in early spring before leaf emergence are as ornamentally striking as any cultivated ornamental plum, making Creek Plum a multi-season landscape value as well as an edible landscape plant for zone 6–9 gardens. Spreads readily by root sprouts to form dense, multi-stemmed thickets that provide valuable wildlife habitat — nesting cover for mockingbirds and other birds, and the plums are consumed by mockingbirds, thrashers, raccoons, and white-tailed deer. Plant in full sun in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil; Creek Plum tolerates heat, periodic drought, and moderate clay once established. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Creel Crowder Southern Pea (Alabama Family Heirloom Crowder Cowpea)
description: Creel Crowder is a family heirloom traced to R.E. Creel, a truck farmer in Warrior, Alabama in the 1930s, and preserved through Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Its semi-vining plants produce curved 6-inch pods that turn golden yellow as they dry, filled with large brown crowder seeds. Very productive for a heritage variety, it reaches first harvest around 61 days and is well suited to both fresh shelling and dry storage. Matures in 61–70 days from seed.

name: Creeping Blueberry
description: Plant container stock in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping blueberry is native to the southeastern coastal plain and needs consistently acidic soil, so avoid liming or planting near concrete foundations. Vaccinium crassifolium is a trailing, mat-forming evergreen blueberry native to sandy pinelands and coastal areas of the Carolinas, with small, glossy, leathery leaves that take on bronze-red tones in cooler weather, pale pink urn-shaped flowers in spring, and small, sweet, edible blue-black berries in summer that both people and birds enjoy. It roots as it spreads to form a dense, low, evergreen carpet well suited to acidic-soil groundcover plantings, slopes, and the front of a native shrub border in Gulf South and coastal Southeast landscapes. Mulch with pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture, and avoid overhead irrigation with hard, alkaline water, which can gradually raise soil pH and reduce vigor. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Borage (Prostrate Borage)
description: Creeping borage is a low, sprawling perennial relative of common borage, native to Corsica, Sardinia, and the nearby island of Capraia, forming loose rosettes of hairy, oval leaves topped by airy sprays of pale blue, bell-shaped flowers from late spring into autumn. Unlike annual borage it persists for a few seasons as a woody-based perennial and tolerates dry, lean, gravelly ground better than its taprooted cousin. Grow it in full sun in sharply drained soil, where it works well as a front-of-border filler, in dry gravel gardens, or trailing over a low wall. The edible flowers can be used as a cucumber-flavored garnish just as with common borage, and the plant self-sows lightly in favorable spots without becoming aggressive. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Creeping Bramble (Chinese Bramble)
description: Native to woodland understories in western China, this low, evergreen, mat-forming bramble is grown mainly as a tough groundcover for dry or dappled shade under trees, where it roots at every node to knit together a dense, weed-suppressing carpet. Small white flowers in late spring give way to red, raspberry-like drupelets that are edible fresh but mild and somewhat seedy, making them more a curiosity snack for gardeners and wildlife than a serious crop. Stems are covered in soft reddish bristles rather than hooked thorns, so it is far easier to handle than typical brambles, though its vigorous spread means it needs a contained bed or a hard edge to stay in bounds. Cut back hard every few years to renew growth and prevent the mat from building up excessive old, woody stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Comfrey (Dwarf Comfrey)
description: Plant in moist to average, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creeping comfrey is the most refined and garden-worthy of the comfreys for shade groundcover use, forming a low, dense mat of hairy, elliptical leaves with pale cream to yellow tubular flowers in spring that attract bumblebees. Unlike the vigorous and sometimes invasive S. x uplandicum (Russian comfrey) and S. officinale, creeping comfrey stays low to 12-14 inches and spreads at a moderate pace rather than becoming aggressively weedy. The leaves are mineral-rich and can be cut repeatedly and used as mulch or compost accelerator, as with other comfreys, but this species is primarily grown as an ornamental shade groundcover. Excellent for suppressing weeds under trees and shrubs where little else grows. The semi-evergreen foliage provides year-round weed suppression in mild winters. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Cucumber / Guadeloupe Cucumber
description: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, well-amended soil in a partly shaded location after the last frost date. This delicate, tendriling vine climbs readily through neighboring shrubs, fences, or trellises and requires little care beyond consistent moisture. Harvest the tiny, striped-green fruits while they are still firm and cucumber-green — they are mild and crisp eaten fresh or pickled; never eat fruits that have turned black, as ripe fruits have a strong laxative effect. The plant often self-seeds generously, so allow a few mature fruits to drop if you want it to return next season. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Creeping Oregon Grape
description: Creeping Oregon grape is a low-growing, mat-forming relative of upright Oregon grape, native to dry mountain forests and plains of western North America and exceptionally hardy once established. It spreads slowly by underground stems to form weed-suppressing colonies bearing clusters of blue-purple berries in summer that are sour but edible and rich in vitamin C. Like its taller relative, the berries are best used in jellies and syrups with added sweetener rather than eaten fresh. The plant requires no fertilizer and very little irrigation once established in appropriate rocky or sandy soil; excess moisture and fertility promote root rot. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Raspberry (Emerald Carpet)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping raspberry roots as it spreads along the ground and knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat within one to two growing seasons. Rubus rolfei (long sold as Rubus calycinoides) is a low, mat-forming evergreen groundcover from Taiwan with small, crinkled, maple-like leaves that bronze in cool weather, tiny white flowers, and sparse, dull orange-red raspberry-like fruit that is edible but mild and seedy rather than flavorful. It is grown primarily as a tough, fast-spreading ornamental groundcover for slopes, walls, and container edges rather than for fruit production, tolerating foot traffic, heat, and a range of light conditions from partial shade to full sun. Shear back hard in late winter if growth becomes leggy, and take tip cuttings in summer to propagate new plants. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Raspberry (Taiwanese Bramble Groundcover)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, spacing plants to knit together into a solid groundcover; established plantings tolerate light foot traffic and need only occasional shearing to keep them tidy. Creeping Raspberry is a low, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen trailing bramble native to Taiwan, grown chiefly as an ornamental groundcover for its glossy, crinkled, bronze-tinged leaves, small white flowers, and small orange-red, raspberry-like fruits produced in late summer that are edible, if mild and seedy, and readily eaten by birds. Its dense, mounding, self-rooting habit makes it useful for covering slopes, edging shaded beds, or spilling over walls in areas too shady for turfgrass, and unlike upright brambles it stays low and thornless-feeling underfoot. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to renew growth and prevent the center of the planting from thinning out. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Red Thyme (Magenta-Flowered Groundcover Thyme)
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun. Creeping Red Thyme forms a very low, dense mat of tiny, dark green leaves that disappears almost entirely beneath a vivid carpet of magenta-crimson flowers in late spring and early summer, among the showiest bloom displays of any low-growing groundcover thyme and a strong draw for bees. It tolerates light foot traffic once established, making it useful between stepping stones, along the edges of dry paths, and cascading over rock walls, and it spreads steadily to fill gaps without becoming aggressive or weedy. Like other creeping thymes, it is grown primarily for ornamental groundcover use and pollinator value rather than culinary purposes, and it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, sun-baked conditions that stress most other groundcovers, making it valuable for hot, dry sites such as gravel gardens and rock gardens. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh new growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Savory (Caucasian Savory)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, gravelly or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; creeping savory spreads by runners to form a low aromatic mat — excellent for stone paths and rock gardens. Satureja spicigera (creeping savory or Caucasian savory) is a low-growing, spreading perennial from the dry hillsides, steppe meadows, and rocky outcrops of the Caucasus region (Turkey, Georgia, Armenia) — one of the most useful and underplanted creeping herbs for Mediterranean-style gardens. The plant spreads by prostrate stems to form a dense, aromatic mat (2–4 inches tall, 18–36 inches wide) of tiny, needle-like, intensely aromatic leaves with a flavor more persistently savory-peppery than summer savory (S. hortensis), containing high concentrations of carvacrol and thymol. As a culinary herb, creeping savory is used like summer and winter savory — for beans, lamb, poultry, marinades, and herb vinegars. It produces abundant small white-to-pale-lilac flowers in late summer that attract bees and beneficial insects. The mat-forming habit makes creeping savory outstanding for ground-cover use between stepping stones, in herb spirals, and in rock garden crevices where no other herbs would thrive. More cold-hardy than winter savory (S. montana) and consistently more flavorful than annual summer savory. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Snowberry (Maidenhair Berry)
description: Plant in very moist, highly acidic, peaty or sphagnum-based, humus-rich soil in full shade in cool, humid climates zones 2–6; creeping snowberry is a delicate, thread-like native evergreen groundcover of boreal bogs, mossy conifer forests, and cool, acid swamps across Canada and the northern United States. The tiny, rounded, glossy evergreen leaves form a fine mat just 1–3 inches tall, and the tiny white berries that form in late summer are pure white, edible, and have the characteristic wintergreen flavor of the Gaultheria genus. They were collected and eaten by indigenous peoples and early settlers as a minor food source. Like all Gaultheria, the leaves contain methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) and have been used as a flavoring. This species requires very specific, cool and perpetually moist conditions and is not appropriate for most garden settings, but excellent for recreating boreal bog gardens in the northern states and Canada. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Thyme
description: Surface-sow tiny seeds on well-drained seed-starting mix and press in without covering; germination is slow and irregular over 2–4 weeks. Plant in dry, gritty soil in full sun; creeping thyme thrives in rock gardens, between stepping stones, and on sunny slopes where it forms a fragrant, flowering mat. Avoid heavy clay and excessive moisture, which rot the shallow roots quickly. Harvest sprigs as needed for cooking — the flavor is milder than upright thyme but usable; the primary garden value is as a low, aromatic, bee-friendly ground cover. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Creeping Thyme
description: Creeping thyme forms a low, fragrant evergreen mat covered in purple-lavender blooms that draw bees and butterflies. Surface sow the tiny seed and press it into the soil without covering, since it needs light to germinate. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil and tolerates foot traffic, making it excellent between pavers and in rock gardens. Trim after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Creme Brulee Shallot Onion
description: This award-winning eschalion produces oblong, 4 to 5 inch bulbs with coppery-pink skin and rosy-purple inner rings, combining the fruity sweetness of shallots with the easy peeling of onions. Start seed indoors early since it needs a long season to size up. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Keep beds weed-free and evenly watered until tops begin to fall, then cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot. Stored properly they keep for months. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Crenshaw Melon
description: Plant in hills of 3–4 seeds in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; Crenshaw (also spelled Cranshaw) is an old American hybrid between Casaba and Persian melon types, producing very large (8–10 pound), distinctively shaped fruits — pointed at the stem end, rounded at the blossom end, with smooth, pale green-yellow skin that turns golden-yellow at maturity. The flesh is thick, deep salmon-orange, nearly seed-free in the center, very juicy, extremely sweet and fragrant with a complex flavor combining the rich sweetness of cantaloupe with the floral aromatics of a Persian melon — widely considered among the finest-flavored melons available. Crenshaw requires intense heat to develop its characteristic sweetness, making zone 9's long summer ideal. Harvest when the blossom end yields to gentle thumb pressure and the skin turns golden and waxy; a fully ripe Crenshaw has a heavenly, heady fragrance. They do not keep long after picking — eat within a few days. For years they were a fixture at high-end produce markets and disappearing from supply chains has made them a garden treasure. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Creole Garlic
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Creole garlic (Allium sativum subsp. sativum) is a group of softneck garlic varieties historically cultivated in the hot, humid regions of southern Spain and the Americas, and the only garlic group that performs consistently well in zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions. While northern hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Purple Stripe, Porcelain) require 6–8 weeks of cold below 40°F for proper bulb formation, Creole types bulb reliably in zone 9 mild winters without pre-chilling. Named varieties include 'Ajo Rojo,' 'Burgundy,' 'Creole Red,' and 'Pescadero Red.' The bulbs are medium to large with 8–12 purple-streaked cloves per head; flavor is complex, rich, and moderately hot with a lingering sweet aftertaste distinctly different from commercial Chinese garlic. Creole garlic also stores significantly longer than most hardneck types — up to 9–12 months in a cool, dry location. For zone 9 gardeners who struggle to grow garlic successfully, switching to Creole types is transformative. Harvest when lower leaves die and 4–5 green leaves remain; cure for 3–4 weeks in a shaded, airy location. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Creole Red Hardneck Garlic
description: This heat-tolerant Creole-type garlic has bright pinkish-red wrappers and yields the largest bulbs in mild-winter regions, with a distinctive shallot-like flavor. Plant single cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, in fall in loose, fertile, well-drained soil. Mulch after planting, keep evenly watered in spring, and stop watering as the lower leaves brown. Harvest when several lower leaves have died back, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: Creole Rose Garlic (Warm-Climate Softneck Garlic for Gulf South Gardens)
description: Plant individual cloves 1–2 inches deep, pointed end up, 4–6 inches apart in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Creole Rose is a Creole-type garlic — one of the most important garlic types for Gulf South gardeners because it forms full, large bulbs without the cold-vernalization requirement that makes most northern hardneck garlic types unreliable in zone 8-10. While Rocambole, Purple Stripe, and Porcelain hardneck garlics require many weeks of cold temperatures below 40°F to form proper bulbs, Creole garlics originated in warm-climate regions of Spain and the American South and thrive with the mild winters of zone 8-10. 'Creole Rose' produces attractive bulbs with rose-pink to rosy-purple outer wrappers and large, flavorful, ivory cloves with a rich, complex, moderately sharp garlic flavor — excellent for roasting, where the flavor becomes sweet and nutty, and for raw preparations where its full-bodied character is distinctive. Plant in fall for spring harvest: in zone 9, plant October through December for a late March–May harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown and fall over. Allow at least two weeks of drying in a warm, airy location after harvest before storage. The scape (central flower stalk) of softneck types is not produced, unlike the decorative and edible scapes of hardneck types. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Creole Tomato
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent moisture prevents blossom end rot and cracking in humid conditions. Creole is an indeterminate tomato developed by the LSU AgCenter specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the lower Mississippi River valley, and it gave its name to the famous 'Creole tomatoes' grown in the rich alluvial soil of Louisiana's river parishes and sold at the long-running French Market in New Orleans. It sets fruit reliably even through the hot, muggy stretches of a Gulf South summer that cause many other tomatoes to drop blossoms, and carries useful resistance to fusarium wilt and other soilborne diseases common in southern gardens. The medium-large, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have the rich, well-balanced sweet-acid flavor that built the Creole tomato's regional reputation, celebrated every June at the New Orleans French Market Creole Tomato Festival. A dependable, disease-resistant choice for zone 4–11 gardeners who want a genuinely Deep South tomato. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Crespo Squash (Andean Zapallo Heirloom)
description: Crespo is one of the traditional zapallo squash of the Andes, grown in Peru and Bolivia and sold widely in local markets there before being introduced to North American gardeners through Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. As a Cucurbita maxima type it produces large fruits valued for their dense, sweet, gourmet-quality flesh, well suited to roasting, soups, and traditional Andean dishes. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the stem has browned, then cure for improved storage and flavor. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Cresthaven Peach (Michigan-Bred Freestone Canning Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall to size fruit properly. Cresthaven was released by Michigan State University in the 1960s and became one of the standard late-midseason freestone peaches across the Midwest and Northeast, valued for firm, richly flavored, yellow flesh that holds up exceptionally well to canning, freezing, and other preservation, in addition to excellent fresh eating quality. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a peach, tolerating harsher winters than many Southern-bred varieties, but that same trait means it needs a real winter chill to fruit well and is not well suited to the mild winters of the Deep South. Prune annually to an open-vase form for good light penetration and fruit quality, and maintain a regular fungicide and dormant-oil spray program, since brown rot and peach leaf curl affect Cresthaven as they do most peach cultivars. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Crimson and Gold Flowering Quince (Red Quince with Golden Stamens)
description: Crimson and Gold is a compact flowering quince selection named for its striking bicolor blooms — deep crimson-red petals surrounding a bold cluster of bright golden-yellow stamens, a sharper color contrast than the softer stamens of most red quince cultivars. Flowers open directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter into early spring, well ahead of the foliage, and small yellow-green fruit follows in fall, usable for jelly and preserves though rarely eaten fresh. Its low, spreading habit stays more compact than the larger species types, suiting foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a smaller-scale quince is wanted. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established; prune only immediately after flowering, since it blooms on old wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Flowered Fava Bean
description: This English heritage broad bean dates to at least the early 1800s and was nearly lost before a handful of seeds were rescued and redistributed by heirloom seed preservationists, making it as much a conservation story as a garden vegetable. Unlike the white blossoms of most fava beans, Crimson Flowered produces clusters of deep magenta-crimson flowers that make the plant genuinely ornamental as well as productive, followed by shorter, upright pods holding 3 to 4 beans each. Grow it exactly as any fava, sowing directly into cool, fertile soil and pinching growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Shell the beans young and tender for the best flavor, or let a portion of the crop dry fully for storage and traditional slow-cooked dishes. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Crimson Forest Bunching Onion (Red-Stalked Scallion)
description: Crimson Forest is a Japanese-type bunching onion whose slender, non-bulbing stalks stain a deep garnet-red at the base, holding that color well even after cooking, which sets it apart visually from standard green scallions. It clumps and regrows from a fibrous root system rather than forming a bulb, so a single sowing can be cut repeatedly as new shoots emerge. Flavor is crisp and mildly pungent, good raw in salads or as a colorful garnish, and it holds up reasonably well through short cold snaps. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart for straight, uniform stalks and keep beds evenly moist for tender texture. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Crimson Giant Radish
description: This large spring radish reaches 1 to 2 inches across with a crisp white interior and a mild flavor perfect for salads and sandwiches. It grows fast, making it a great choice for children and impatient gardeners. Sow directly in cool weather since heat causes it to bolt and turn pithy. Thin seedlings early to give roots room to swell. Keep soil evenly moist for tender, uncracked roots. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Crimson Glory Manuka (Double Maroon-Red New Zealand Tea Tree)
description: Crimson Glory produces densely packed, fully double flowers in a deep, dusky maroon-red that reads almost purple in certain light, one of the darkest flower colors available among manuka cultivars and a striking companion to the pinks and reds of other Leptospermum selections in a mixed shrub border. Foliage is the typical tiny, needle-like, aromatic manuka leaf on an upright, medium-sized evergreen shrub. Grow in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; manuka cultivars are markedly more drought-tolerant than moisture-tolerant, and root rot in heavy, poorly drained soil is the leading cause of decline. Light shearing after the spring flush keeps the shrub dense and well-shaped; avoid hard pruning into old bare wood, from which manuka regenerates poorly. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Glory Vine
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun on a strong, large-scale support, since this East Asian ornamental grape climbs vigorously by tendrils and can quickly cover an arbor, pergola, or old tree. It is grown chiefly for its huge, heart-shaped, deeply veined leaves, which can reach 10 inches or more across and turn spectacular shades of crimson, scarlet, and purple in autumn, rivaling any deciduous tree for fall color. Small, fragrant flowers in late spring are followed by clusters of small, dark purple grapes that are edible but seedy, tart, and generally considered better for jelly or wildlife forage than fresh eating. Because of its exceptional vigor, Crimson Glory Vine needs a sturdy, generously sized structure and room to run, and benefits from hard annual pruning in late winter to control size and encourage the largest, most colorful leaves the following season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Mayhaw (Improved Western Mayhaw for Gulf South Jelly Production)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, taking advantage of mayhaw's unusual tolerance for the poorly drained, low-lying bottomland where most other fruit trees decline. Crimson is a named western mayhaw selection grown alongside cultivars such as Texas Star and Super Berry by Gulf South orchardists seeking improved, more consistent fruit production than wild-collected mayhaw offers, bearing clusters of small, tart, aromatic red berries that ripen in May. As with all mayhaw selections, fruit is gathered from the ground or shaken onto tarps and processed quickly into the region's traditional mayhaw jelly, since the berries are too tart and dry for fresh eating. Plant a second, genetically distinct mayhaw cultivar within range for the best cross-pollination and yield, and expect three to five years to first bearing with production increasing steadily over the following decade. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Passion Cherry (Sweet Romance Series Dwarf Bush Cherry)
description: Crimson Passion is a University of Saskatchewan Romance series bush cherry bred as a sweeter-eating counterpart to Carmine Jewel, with dark red-black fruit that leans closer to dessert-sweet than tart. The dense, rounded shrub is extremely cold hardy and stays small enough for foundation plantings or edible hedges. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils but yield best with regular water while fruit is sizing. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes out every few years to keep the bush vigorous and productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Plum (Auburn University Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Gulf South)
description: Crimson was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station as one of the earlier selections in its Japanese-American 'Au' plum breeding line, later giving rise to the darker-fruited sport AU-Rubrum. Trees are self-fruitful but set noticeably heavier crops when a second Japanese or Japanese-American plum, such as Methley or another Au-series variety, is planted within pollinating range. Fruit ripens in late spring to early summer with dark red skin and sweet, juicy red flesh well suited to fresh eating and preserves. Like the rest of the Au series, it was bred specifically for resistance to bacterial canker, bacterial leaf spot, and black knot, giving it a real advantage over older plum varieties under the humid, disease-prone growing conditions of the Southeast. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Queen Cranberry (Rutgers High-Color Processing Cultivar)
description: Crimson Queen was bred at the Rutgers P.E. Marucci Center for Blueberry and Cranberry Research in Chatsworth, New Jersey, part of a modern breeding program aimed at combining high yield with exceptionally deep, uniform red color for the juice and processing market. Its berries carry unusually high anthocyanin content even before full ripening, which makes it attractive to processors who value color extraction over fresh-market appearance, and vines are noted for vigorous growth and heavy fruit set on established beds. Like other cranberries it demands strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), a sandy-peat bog substrate, and constant moisture, along with periodic sand top-dressing to control weeds and encourage new rooting along runners. Home growers in cold-winter regions with the acidic, poorly drained ground cranberries require can grow it as a novelty high-pigment selection, though it is planted almost exclusively in commercial New Jersey, Wisconsin, and Quebec bogs supplying the processed cranberry market. It is unsuited to the Gulf Coast and other regions without a sustained cold winter dormancy period. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Red Rhubarb
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with good organic matter; Crimson Red is a named rhubarb variety selected for deep red stalk color throughout the length of the stalk — many rhubarb varieties, including the popular Victoria, produce stalks that are primarily green with only a reddish blush at the base, while Crimson Red maintains the desirable deep red color from base to tip. The red color has no effect on flavor (rhubarb's characteristic tart-sour character comes from oxalic and malic acids regardless of color) but makes the stalks more visually appealing in fresh preparations and strawberry-rhubarb pies where the vivid red shows through the filling. The flavor is the same bright, intense rhubarb tartness that defines the species. Crimson Red is also grown as an ornamental vegetable — the large, dramatic dark red stalks and enormous ribbed leaves create a striking architectural effect in the garden before harvest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Seedless Grape
description: Train young vines onto a permanent support system and prune annually in dormancy, since fruit forms on the current season's growth from one-year-old canes. Crimson Seedless bears elongated, crisp, pink-to-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen late in the season. It is a late-season companion to earlier seedless grapes, extending the fresh-eating harvest into fall, and tends to color best where nights cool down as the fruit matures. Like most vinifera grapes it prefers a long, warm growing season and struggles in areas with high humidity and fungal disease pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crimson Sweet Watermelon
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in hills only after the soil is thoroughly hot, since watermelons demand warmth. Give the long vines ample room and steady water while the fruits size up, then ease off watering as they near ripeness to concentrate sugars. The 20 to 25 pound striped melons are ripe when the ground spot turns creamy yellow and the tendril nearest the fruit dries. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Crimson Sweet Watermelon (Standard Oblong Watermelon)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil warms; Crimson Sweet is the most widely planted home-garden slicing watermelon in American horticulture — an open-pollinated variety introduced in 1964 that set the standard for the modern round-to-oblong, striped watermelon with deep crimson flesh and excellent crisp texture. The light green fruits with dark green stripes grow to 15–25 pounds with a hard rind, making them good keepers and suited for roadside stands and home storage. The deep crimson, firm-textured flesh has excellent flavor — very sweet with the quintessential watermelon aroma. Crimson Sweet introduced the high lycopene, disease-resistant genetics that are the foundation of modern watermelon breeding programs. In zone 9, watermelon is a warm-season crop that thrives in the heat — plant after the last frost in late March or April for summer harvest in July–August. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, abundant space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill causes small fruit and hollow heart. Determine ripeness by the ground spot yellowing from white to yellow, the curling of the tendril nearest the fruit, and a hollow 'thump' sound when knocked. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Crimson Tide Watermelon (Fusarium-Resistant Crimson Sweet Type Hybrid)
description: Crimson Tide is a Crimson Sweet-type F1 hybrid bred for growers who need reliable Fusarium wilt resistance without giving up the classic bright red, crisp-fleshed eating quality that made Crimson Sweet famous. Fruits run large, around 20-25 pounds, semi-elongated in shape, with a slightly darker green stripe pattern than standard Crimson Sweet. Because seed-borne and soil-borne wilts can build up in beds planted to melons repeatedly, this hybrid is a practical option for gardeners rotating crops on limited space where full rotation isn't always possible. Manage it like any full-size vining watermelon: full sun, warm soil, steady moisture through fruit fill, and a dry-down period before harvest to maximize sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: CrimsonCrisp Apple (Scab-Immune Crisp Red Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. CrimsonCrisp comes from the same Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program that produced GoldRush and Enterprise, carrying genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to cedar-apple rust and fire blight, making it a strong low-spray choice for home orchards in humid climates where scab is a constant pressure on susceptible varieties. The medium-size fruit has deep crimson-red skin over crisp, dense, juicy flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, ripening in early-to-mid fall — earlier than the late-season GoldRush and Enterprise, giving a staggered harvest when planted alongside them. It stores reasonably well under cool conditions, though not as long as the latest-ripening disease-resistant selections. Thin fruit clusters to one apple per cluster in late spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Criollo Cacao
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Considered the finest-flavored and rarest of the three main cacao varieties, Criollo (Spanish for 'native' or 'creole') produces pale, thin-shelled pods with mild, complex, low-bitterness flavor prized by fine chocolate makers, but the tree is notably more susceptible to disease and lower-yielding than the hardier Forastero variety that dominates most commercial cacao production worldwide. It requires the warm, humid, sheltered understory conditions of a tropical rainforest, ideally grown beneath taller shade trees, and demands more careful disease management than more robust cacao types, making it a specialty planting for dedicated chocolate enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors rather than an easy home crop. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cripps Pink Apple (Pink Lady, Late-Season Low-Chill Sweet-Tart Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a cross of Golden Delicious and Lady Williams, it is marketed commercially as Pink Lady and is among the latest-ripening apples grown, often left on the tree into late autumn to fully develop its rosy-pink blush and dense, crisp, sweet-tart flesh. Its lower chill requirement compared to classic northern apples makes it one of the more workable dessert apples for warmer growing regions. Fruit stores exceptionally well and resists browning better than many varieties once cut. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crista Tomato (Disease-Resistant Southeastern Hybrid)
description: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Crista is a determinate hybrid slicing tomato bred as part of the North Carolina State University Southeastern tomato improvement program, which targets the combination of diseases (Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, and gray leaf spot chief among them) that most often cut short a tomato season in the humid Southeast. Fruits are medium-large, round, and firm with reliable, well-rounded flavor rather than novelty sweetness, making Crista a workhorse slicer for the kitchen rather than a specialty variety. The compact determinate plants concentrate their harvest over a few weeks, which suits gardeners who want a predictable crop for canning or sharing. Stake or cage for support and clean fruit, and keep watering consistent through fruit set to avoid blossom end rot in the Gulf South's swings between downpours and dry spells. Matures in 72–82 days from transplant.

name: Croatan Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Croatan is a historic North Carolina State University highbush blueberry release from the 1950s, bred specifically to bring highbush fruit quality to areas with milder winters than the traditional northern highbush belt, and it remains one of the lower-chill highbush options that can crop reasonably well in zone 8-9. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, and sweet with the classic highbush flavor that many gardeners prefer over rabbiteye. Croatan is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier, larger-berried crops with a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar blooming nearby. The compact, rounded bush needs consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil to perform well in Gulf South clay, so raised beds or heavily amended planting holes give the best results. Prune out the oldest wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Croisic Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Croisic is a French fig variety named for the coastal commune of Le Croisic in Brittany, notable primarily for its prolific breba crop — the early-season figs produced on previous year's wood that ripen in late May to early June in zone 9, weeks ahead of the main crop figs on most other varieties. The early-ripening breba figs are medium to large, with a yellow-green to yellow skin and amber to orange-tinged flesh with a mild, honey-sweet flavor. In zone 9 the Croisic fig provides the earliest fresh fig harvest of the season and is particularly valued by gardeners who want to extend the fig-eating season by starting early. The main crop figs on new wood ripen in August–September and are similar in quality to the breba crop. In zone 9 the mild winters and long growing season allow Croisic to produce heavy breba crops — the consistently warm temperatures maintain the tree's vigor for prolific breba production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crosby's Egyptian Beet (Flat-Root Heirloom Early Beet)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, fertile soil with consistent moisture; thin to 4–5 inch spacing after germination for root development. Crosby's Egyptian is an American heirloom beet dating to before 1869, developed by Josiah Crosby of Massachusetts from the older Egyptian type and named for both its creator and the flat-topped root shape associated with Egyptian-type beets — a distinctly different root form from the round globe shape of Detroit-type beets and the cylindrical shape of Cylindra and Formanova. The flat-topped, medium-sized roots have very dark, nearly black-red skin, deep red flesh with excellent texture, and a rich, sweet, earthy flavor that beet enthusiasts often consider superior to modern round types — more complex and less sweet without being harsh. Crosby's Egyptian is one of the earlier-maturing beet varieties (55–65 days) and was particularly valued in New England gardens for its early productivity when other beets were still sizing up. The slightly flattened shape makes the beets easy to peel evenly after boiling and gives them a distinctive appearance in pickled or roasted presentations. Widely grown in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, Crosby's Egyptian represents the heirloom beet tradition at its finest and remains a deserving choice for gardeners who want historical authenticity alongside excellent eating quality. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Crosne (Chinese Artichoke)
description: Plant small knobbly tubers 2–3 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost; crosne has a straggly growth habit with square stems and small lavender flowers typical of the mint family. The tops die back in fall, signaling that tubers have reached full size — harvest by digging carefully, as the small spiral tubers break easily. Leave some tubers in the ground for next season’s planting stock. Tubers are eaten unpeeled; the thin ivory skin is too delicate and intricate to remove. Steam or sauté briefly — the texture is crunchy like a water chestnut with a mild, slightly nutty flavor. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Crow Garlic (Wild Garlic)
description: Plant small bulbs or bulbils 2 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; crow garlic is extremely adaptable and cold-hardy, naturalizing in lawns, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout much of North America — control by harvesting the bulbils before they disperse if you want to limit its spread. Allium vineale is a European native now widely naturalized in North America, producing slender, hollow, cylindrical, dark-green leaves in late fall through spring and tall scapes bearing umbels of bulbils (and sometimes pinkish flowers) in early summer; it is the "wild garlic" most commonly encountered as a lawn weed in the eastern US. All parts are strongly garlic-flavored and fully edible; the leaves can be harvested in fall through spring and used like garlic chives, and the small bulbs are edible as a substitute for garlic. It is best harvested as a forage plant rather than deliberately cultivated due to its weedy nature. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Crowberry
description: Crowberry is a low, mat-forming evergreen shrub of arctic and subarctic bogs, heathlands, and tundra, requiring strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and cool summer temperatures to thrive. The glossy black berries ripen in late summer and persist into winter under snow, remaining palatable after freezing — they are a critical subsistence food for northern Indigenous peoples and a major food source for migratory birds. Propagate by semi-hardwood cuttings taken in mid-summer; the plant rarely sets fruit in warm, humid climates. Minimal maintenance is needed once established as a groundcover in appropriate cold, northern gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crowder Pea (Iron and Clay, Mississippi Purple)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; crowder peas get their name because the seeds are crowded so tightly in the pod that they press against each other and develop flat sides. They are a cornerstone of Southern cuisine — shelled fresh and cooked with pot likker and fatback, or dried for winter storage — and also a superb summer cover crop that fixes atmospheric nitrogen at high rates in hot weather. Bush-type plants need no support and mature quickly even in poor, sandy soils. Pick pods when they have turned fully colored (purple, tan, or buff depending on variety) and the seeds feel firm but not hard for fresh-shell use; allow pods to dry completely on the vine for dry peas. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Crowley Cranberry (Processing Cranberry Hybrid)
