description: Crowley is a 1961 cross of McFarlin and Prolific developed as part of mid-twentieth-century efforts to breed cranberries better suited to processing rather than the fresh market. It produces medium-sized, dark red berries with good color development, making it valued for juice and sauce production rather than for fresh whole-berry sales. Vines show the vigor typical of McFarlin parentage while ripening somewhat more uniformly, and they respond well to the same bog culture, winter flooding, and sanding practices used for other cranberry cultivars. It remains a minor but historically notable selection in breeding programs tracing the development of modern processing cranberries. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Crown of Thorns Gourd (Shenot Crown of Thorns Ornamental Gourd)
aliases: Cucurbita pepo var. ovifera 'Crown of Thorns'
description: Named for the ring of curved, thorn-like points that circle the blossom end of each rounded fruit, this multicolored ornamental gourd ripens in shades of orange, cream, yellow, and dark green on the same vine. Plants are heavy producers, often setting more than a dozen fruit per vine, so give them room to spread or a trellis strong enough to support the ripening gourds. Keep soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit set, then withhold water as the rind hardens and the crown-like points fully form. Cut fruit with a short stem once fully colored and cure in a dry, ventilated spot for several weeks before use in fall displays or crafts. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Crown Prince Squash (Steel-Blue Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thin to 2 plants) after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; harvest when the stem begins to cork and dry and the skin is completely firm. Crown Prince is a Cucurbita maxima winter squash of Japanese origin that became a dominant market squash in the United Kingdom and Australia and has grown in popularity in the US — producing medium-large (6–12 lb) flat-lobed fruits with an unusual and striking steel-blue to silver-grey skin color that makes them one of the most distinctive vegetables in the fall garden. The skin color is unlike any other commonly grown squash and makes Crown Prince exceptional as both a culinary and ornamental squash. The flesh is deep orange, dense, smooth-textured, and richly sweet with a complex, almost butterscotch-like flavor profile that many tasters consider among the best of any squash; it lacks the wateriness of less concentrated types and has a low seed cavity relative to flesh volume. Crown Prince keeps exceptionally well (6–12 months in proper cool, dry storage) and the long storage window makes it valuable for extended autumn and winter cooking. In zone 9, direct sow in March–April for a July–August harvest, or in August for a November harvest if the growing season allows. An excellent choice for serious squash growers wanting a variety with both superior flavor and visual impact. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Cruiser Cilantro (Bolt-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Cruiser is a commercial hybrid cilantro bred for uniform, upright plants with broad, dark green leaves and a pronounced resistance to premature bolting under warm conditions. Its vigor and even stand make it a dependable choice for growers who need a predictable, heavy leaf harvest over a longer cutting window than standard varieties provide. The strong aromatic flavor is typical of full-size cilantro, making it suitable for fresh market bunching as well as home harvest. As with all cilantro, expect the plant to eventually flower and set coriander seed once day length and temperature rise, even on a slow-bolt selection like this one. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Crusader Black Currant
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, since black currants are shallow-rooted and dislike drying out. Crusader was bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva alongside 'Consort' and 'Coronet' specifically to carry resistance to white pine blister rust, the fungal disease that led many US states to restrict or ban Ribes cultivation for decades. Its parentage from resistant wild currant stock gives it a slightly more assertive, tart flavor than European dessert-type black currants, so fruit is best suited to jams, syrups, cassis, and baking rather than fresh eating. Crusader needs real winter chill and struggles in hot-summer climates; prune out canes older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, since fruit forms mainly on one- and two-year-old wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Crystal Apple Cucumber (White Apple Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm soil; Crystal Apple can sprawl on the ground or be trellised — vertical growing keeps fruits cleaner and makes them easier to find. Crystal Apple is a New Zealand heirloom cucumber producing distinctively rounded to oval fruits about the size and shape of a small apple, ripening from green to creamy-white to ivory-yellow; the fruits are tender-skinned with no bitterness at any stage, with exceptionally mild, refreshing, sweet flavor even when large. They are best harvested at the white-to-pale-ivory stage before turning yellow, when the interior is crisp and seeds are still small. An outstanding cucumber for warm-climate gardens: more heat-tolerant than most slicing types, with less bitterness in hot conditions; highly productive and self-trellising if grown on a support. Popular at farmers markets for the unusual appearance and superior flavor. Matures in 63–70 days from seed.

name: Crystal Hops
description: Crystal is an American aroma cultivar released through USDA-ARS breeding trials, carrying Hallertauer-descended parentage that gives it a mild, floral, and spicy aroma reminiscent of German noble hops. Its lower alpha acid content makes it best suited to aroma and finishing additions rather than bittering. Compared with true European landraces it establishes and yields more reliably in home gardens, tolerating a wider range of soils and climates. Provide full sun, a tall support structure, and even moisture through summer to keep cone production and aroma quality consistent. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Crystal Lemon Cucumber (Lemon Cucumber, Crystal Apple)
description: Direct sow or transplant to well-drained, warm, enriched soil in full sun after last frost; Crystal Lemon cucumber (sometimes called Crystal Apple) produces round to oval fruits roughly the size and color of a lemon at harvest — pale ivory to pale yellow, 2–3 inches in diameter, with a very mild, sweet, almost non-existent bitterness and a thin skin that does not need peeling. One of the most productive and heat-tolerant cucumbers available, and excellent for gardeners who find regular cucumbers too bitter or those who want a conversation-starting variety. Fruits should be harvested while still pale ivory-yellow; fully yellow fruits are over-ripe and seedy. Very popular with children for its unusual round shape. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Crystal White Wax Onion (Heirloom Pickling and Sweet Onion)
description: Sow seed thickly for baby pickling-size bulbs or space more widely for larger fresh-eating onions, transplanting into loose, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Harvest small bulbs young for pickling once they reach the desired size, or allow later sowings to size up further for fresh use, since this variety does not store well long-term. Crystal White Wax is a historic short-day southern heirloom whose small, flattened, pure-white bulbs and mild flavor made it the classic choice for cocktail onions and pickled onions, and it was among the parent stock used to develop the modern Vidalia sweet onion. Matures in 60–95 days from transplant.

name: Cuban Mint (Mojito Mint, Large-Leaf Heat-Tolerant Gulf South Spearmint)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Cuban Mint (also called Mojito Mint or Apple Mint hybrid) is Mentha x villosa — a hybrid mint between spearmint (M. spicata) and apple mint (M. suaveolens) that produces the distinctive large, crinkled, soft-textured, heavily aromatic leaves most closely associated with the traditional Cuban mojito cocktail. The broad, deeply textured leaves have a strong, clean spearmint fragrance with a sweeter, fruitier quality than standard spearmint — a flavor complexity that is particularly well-suited to the classic mojito (fresh Cuban Mint + lime + rum + sugar + soda) and makes excellent fresh herb tea. Cuban Mint's practical advantage over standard spearmint and peppermint for Gulf South gardeners is substantially better heat and humidity tolerance — where peppermint and even spearmint often melt out in the intense summer heat of zone 9, Cuban Mint produces reliably through Gulf South summers with consistent moisture and partial shade protection from afternoon sun. The large, broad leaves are easy to pick and produce abundantly. Spreads by vigorous underground runners in the mint family manner — grow in containers or with buried root barriers to keep contained. In zone 9, Cuban Mint may be semi-evergreen through mild winters or die back and return vigorously in spring. An indispensable herb for Gulf South gardeners who want fresh mint for mojitos, tea, and culinary use during the summer months. Matures in 30–60 days from transplant.

name: Cuban Oregano (Broad-Leaf Thyme)
description: Propagate from stem cuttings 4–6 in long; cuttings root in 1–2 weeks in moist perlite or a glass of water and are far more reliable than seed. Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun to bright partial shade; Cuban oregano tolerates heat, humidity, and dry spells far better than Mediterranean oregano. The thick, succulent leaves have a pungent, oregano-like aroma intensified by thyme — use fresh in Caribbean, Indian, and Southeast Asian cooking. Remove flower spikes to keep the plant in vigorous vegetative growth; take a few cuttings before the first frost if growing as an annual. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Cuban Queen Watermelon (Historic Large American Shipping Heirloom)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills spaced 7–10 feet apart once soil is reliably warm. Cuban Queen was introduced by W. Atlee Burpee & Co. in 1881 and quickly became one of the leading commercial shipping watermelons of the late 19th century, its round-to-oblong fruit distinguished by a pale, whitish-green rind overlaid with irregular dark green stripes and its image reproduced on countless Victorian-era seed company advertising cards. Period accounts describe exceptionally large fruit under the field conditions of the time, though gardeners today should expect a more modest, still substantial melon from home-garden care. Judge ripeness by the classic combination of a drying tendril at the fruit stem, a ground spot that has turned from white to creamy yellow, and a dull, hollow sound when thumped. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Cuban Seedless Sugar Apple
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this compact-growing selection room to branch out into a small, rounded tree. Unlike typical seedy sugar apples, this cultivar sets fruit that are largely seedless or nearly so, with the same custardy, sweet, segmented flesh that makes the species popular across south Florida dooryards. It defoliates in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor sheltered south-facing walls or grow young trees in containers that can be moved into a garage during freezes. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning often improves fruit set, since natural pollinators can be scarce in home gardens. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cubanelle Pepper (Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and maintain soil at 80°F for best germination; grow seedlings in bright light to prevent stretching. The cubanelle produces thin-walled, tapered fruits 4–6 inches long that ripen from pale yellowish-green to red; they are nearly sweet with very mild heat and excellent for frying, stuffing, and fresh eating. Harvest green fruits at 65 days or leave on the plant to ripen red for sweeter flavor. Plants are prolific producers; side-dress with a balanced fertilizer midseason to maintain yield. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Cubeb Pepper (Tailed Pepper, Java Pepper)
description: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and grow in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade in tropical or subtropical gardens; cubeb is a spice pepper from Indonesia (primarily Java), its dried unripe fruits distinguished by a distinct 'tail' (the dried stalk) that gives it the alternative name 'tailed pepper.' The flavor is complex — peppery, slightly bitter, with eucalyptus, camphor, and allspice overtones distinctly different from black pepper. A major spice in medieval European and Arab cuisines and still used in Moroccan ras el hanout and in Indonesian, East African, and West African cooking. The unique flavor profile is winning new culinary attention as chefs explore historical spice traditions. Matures in 240–365 days from transplant.

name: Cucamelon (Mouse Melon)
description: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm mix indoors and pot on without disturbing the root ball when transplanting; cucamelon develops a large tuberous root that can overwinter in frost-free climates. Train the delicate vines up a trellis or netting and keep soil consistently moist for best fruit set. Harvest the grape-sized fruits when they look like tiny watermelons and feel firm — they become seedy and bitter if left too long. The flavor is a pleasant combination of cucumber and lime; pick frequently to maintain heavy production. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Cuccio White Sapote
description: Cuccio is a light-green-skinned white sapote selection prized for its rich, complex flavor, often described as a blend of peach, pear, banana, caramel, and vanilla, and for holding well on the tree after ripening rather than dropping and bruising immediately. It comes into bearing earlier than many other named white sapote cultivars, making it a good choice for gardeners who want fruit sooner. Plant in deep, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind, since sapote wood is somewhat brittle, and let harvested fruit finish softening at room temperature for several days before eating. A second white sapote cultivar nearby can improve fruit set, though established trees will produce alone. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cucuzza (Italian Edible Gourd, Sicilian Snake Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, and give the sprawling vine a sturdy arbor or fence so the long, pale-green fruit can hang straight rather than curl on the ground. Cucuzza is a long-season Italian-American heirloom bottle gourd grown throughout Louisiana's historically Sicilian communities, where the immature fruit is peeled and cooked like a mild summer squash in soups, stews, and sautés. Left on the vine past the edible stage, the mature shell dries into a hard, lightweight gourd useful for crafts. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and, like other bottle gourds, benefits from hand-pollination in the evening since its flowers open at night for moth pollinators. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cue Ball Squash (Round Pale Green Hybrid Summer Squash)
description: Cue Ball is a round-fruited hybrid squash bred as a paler, milder companion to the dark-skinned Eight Ball type, producing pale green fruit mottled with white on an open, upright bush that keeps the golf-ball to billiard-ball-sized squash easy to spot. Harvest at around 3 inches in diameter for the best texture, since the round shape can hide inside the foliage and size up quickly in hot weather. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is a real advantage in humid Gulf Coast summers where aphid-spread viruses build up on cucurbits. The compact plant works well in raised beds where a standard vining summer squash would be too sprawling. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Culantro (Recao)
description: Sow seeds on the soil surface and press in lightly; germination can be slow and erratic, so sow generously and keep soil consistently moist and warm. Culantro thrives in partial shade and high humidity, performing well in spots too hot and bright for cilantro; its strap-like, serrated leaves have a much more intense cilantro flavor and hold up better in cooking. Thin seedlings to 9–12 in apart and keep soil moderately moist; the plant bolts to flower in dry or cool conditions. Harvest individual outer leaves at any time; one or two leaves substitute for a much larger amount of cilantro in sofrito, chutneys, and Caribbean stews. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Culinary Ginger (Common Ginger)
description: Plant fresh, plump rhizome sections with viable buds in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade, keeping the rhizome section just below soil surface level; culinary ginger is the universal spice plant — one of humanity's most ancient, most widely used, and most globally traded spice and medicinal plants, native to tropical Asia (probably India or coastal southern China) but cultivated throughout the tropics for at least 3,000 years and now grown in tropical and subtropical regions of every continent. The rhizome (underground stem) is the harvested, used portion: the knobby, multi-branched, pale-tan to buff-tan fresh rhizome with its characteristic pungent-hot, warm-spicy, aromatic flavor and scent comes from the volatile oil compounds (primarily gingerol, shogaol, and zingerone) that also provide the medicinal properties (anti-nausea, anti-inflammatory, digestive). In the garden, it is a handsome, substantial plant reaching 3–4 feet — erect, reed-like stems with alternating, glossy, lance-shaped, aromatic leaves of deep green — with an attractively tropical, lush appearance. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a reliable perennial, the aerial stems dying back in winter and rhizomes resprouting each spring. Young (green) ginger can be harvested after 4–5 months (mild, juicy, less fiber); mature ginger after the leaves die back naturally (8–10 months, full pungency). One of the most rewarding home-garden edibles for partial-shade plots in zones 8–11. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: Culinary Sage
description: Culinary sage is a woody perennial with dusty gray-green leaves and a savory, aromatic flavor essential in the kitchen. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil, watering sparingly once established since it dislikes wet feet. Harvest leaves lightly the first year and more freely in following seasons. Prune in spring to remove dead wood and keep the plant compact and productive. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Culinary Sumac
description: Plant in well-drained, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun; culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) is the source of the brilliant deep-red, intensely tart spice used throughout Middle Eastern cooking as the primary acidifying agent before lemons became available. The dried, ground berries coat kebabs, top hummus, season fattoush salad, and form the backbone of za'atar spice blend. Harvest berry clusters (drupes) in late summer when fully red and dark but before rain softens them; dry completely before grinding. This species is distinct from the ornamental staghorn sumac (Rhus typhina) of North American gardens — culinary sumac is a Mediterranean species grown specifically for its tart, lemony fruit. The shrub is extremely drought-adapted and well-suited to zone 7–10 gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Culver's Physic
description: Surface-sow the dust-fine seed in fall, leaving it uncovered so cold and light can trigger germination. This tall native perennial was used by Indigenous peoples and early settlers as a liver remedy. Grow it in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade where the white flower spires shine in summer. Keep the roots evenly moist, as dry soil causes lower leaves to scorch. Harvest roots from established plants in autumn and dry for at least a year before use. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Cumari do Pará Pepper (Brazilian Wild Hot Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 7-9 weeks before the last frost with gentle bottom heat, since this small-fruited chinense type is slow to establish, and transplant once nights stay warm. The bushy plants benefit from routine picking, which encourages continuous flowering and fruit set through the season. Cumari do Pará comes from the Pará region of Brazil and produces tiny, round to oval berry-like fruits on long thin stems that belie an intense, sharp heat, and it is traditionally used fresh, pickled in vinegar, or as a garnish. Its diminutive size makes it a good candidate for container growing despite the plant's habanero-relative heat level. Matures in 85–110 days from transplant.

name: Cumberland Black Raspberry (Classic Heirloom Black Raspberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and give the tall, arching canes a simple wire support or tip-prune them at knee height in summer to keep the planting manageable. Cumberland is one of the oldest black raspberry cultivars still in commerce, long valued for unusually large, firm, deep-black berries with an intense, old-fashioned flavor well suited to jam, pie, and syrup making. The vigorous canes root at the tips wherever they touch soil, which is a fast way to propagate new plants but also means unchecked plantings will spread beyond their bed if canes aren't tipped back or trained. Remove spent floricanes after the midsummer harvest and thin to the sturdiest canes each spring for the best fruit size the following year. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Cumberland Rosemary
description: Propagate from stem cuttings taken in late spring or summer rather than from seed, as germination is erratic and slow; root cuttings in clean sand and transplant rooted starts in spring into dry, lean, sandy, slightly acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun. Avoid clay, enriched, or moisture-retentive soils, as the species is endemic to sandy and gravelly river bars along the Big South Fork and upper Cumberland River system in Tennessee and Kentucky, where it is federally listed as threatened. Dense mats of wiry, upright stems bear tiny, needle-like, intensely rosemary-scented leaves and masses of small, pale pink to lavender, 2-lipped mint flowers in spring; the entire plant releases a strong fragrance when brushed. An outstanding native aromatic subshrub for rock gardens and sandy borders in zones 5-8 where its narrow habitat requirements of sharp drainage, lean soil, and full sun can be met. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Cumin (Cumin Herb, Jeera)
description: Direct sow seeds thinly in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in fall or early spring; thin to 6 inches. Cuminum cyminum (cumin) is the annual herb whose seeds are the third most-consumed spice in the world after salt and black pepper — the warm, earthy, aromatic, slightly bitter cumin flavor is foundational to the spice profiles of Indian, Mexican, Middle Eastern, North African, and Turkish cuisines, appearing in curry powders, garam masala, chili powder, taco seasoning, hummus, and countless spice blends. The small (6–18 inch), slender, feathery-leaved annual herb native to Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean is rarely grown in North American home gardens, yet it is straightforward to grow in well-drained, dry, infertile soil in full sun in climates with warm, dry summers or cool, dry springs. In zone 9, fall planting produces spring harvest before summer humidity arrives. Harvest when seed heads turn brown and dry; cut stalks and hang to dry in paper bags, then thresh out seeds. Growing your own cumin produces seeds with fresher, more intense aroma than store-bought. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Cuostralee Tomato (French Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the heavy fruit. Cuostralee is an old French family heirloom obtained from a grower in Hellimer, France in 1992 by American tomato collectors Craig LeHoullier and Carolyn Male, who helped introduce it to North American gardeners. Its deeply ribbed, pink-red fruit can top a pound or more per tomato and is known for dense, meaty flesh and a rich, old-fashioned sweet flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Cupid's Shaving Brush (Ebolo, Yoruba Tassel Flower)
description: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cupid's shaving brush self-sows readily in warm, humid climates and is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again warm-season green. Known as ebolo in West African cooking, this fast-growing, weedy annual produces tender, slightly bitter, mineral-rich leaves used cooked in soups and stews much like a spinach substitute, along with small, tufted, magenta-pink brush-like flower heads that give the plant its whimsical common name. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and light shade of a Gulf South summer better than most temperate greens, continuing to produce through the hottest months when lettuce and spinach have long since bolted. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips regularly to keep plants productive and delay flowering, and expect volunteer seedlings the following season once it is established in a bed. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Cupuassu (Cupuassu Tree)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part to full shade; cupuassu requires consistent moisture and high humidity and will not tolerate any frost or prolonged dry periods. Theobroma grandiflorum (cupuassu) is a Brazilian Amazon rainforest relative of cacao (T. cacao) producing large, 8-to-12-inch, oblong, woody fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflorous), each containing 20–50 seeds surrounded by a thick, creamy-white, intensely fragrant pulp with a flavor combining chocolate, pineapple, banana, and guava — considered by many food scientists to be one of the most complex and delicious tropical flavors in the world. The pulp is used to make juices, ice creams, yogurts, and confectioneries throughout Brazil, where it is the second most important Amazonian fruit after açaí. The seeds can be fermented and processed into a chocolate-like product ('cupuaçu butter') and are the basis of a proprietary chocolate-substitute trademarked as 'cupulate.' Growing cupuassu outside zones 11–12 requires a greenhouse; at the frontier of zone 10b, protected microclimates may support growth. A rare and extraordinary specialty fruit for true tropical enthusiasts. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Curled Chervil
description: Curled chervil, sometimes called French parsley, is a delicate cool-season herb with lacy leaves and a subtle anise flavor. Sow directly in cool weather and part shade, as it bolts rapidly in summer heat. Make successive sowings in spring and again in late summer for fall harvests. Snip the tender leaves young and use them fresh, since their flavor fades when dried or cooked long. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Curled Cress Microgreens
description: Sow curled cress seed dry and densely on a moist tray, since it forms a gel coat that makes presoaking impractical. It germinates almost overnight, so uncover early and give it bright light to keep growth compact. Mist frequently to keep the fine seedlings hydrated without drowning them. Snip the fast-growing, peppery peppergrass greens within a week to ten days for a bold, spicy garnish. Matures in 7–12 days from seed.

name: Curled Mustard (Osaka Purple Mustard)
description: Scatter seeds thinly in rows 12 inches apart and cover lightly with 1/4 inch of fine soil; curled mustard germinates rapidly and can be thinned progressively, using the thinnings as baby salad greens while allowing remaining plants to develop full size. Young leaves are mild and work well fresh in salads or as a peppery sandwich green, while more mature leaves develop significant heat and are best wilted briefly in a hot pan or added to soups and stir-fries. The frilly, often purple-tinged foliage is among the most ornamental of the edible brassicas and lends visual appeal to the kitchen garden through the cool months. Avoid overhead watering late in the day, and pull plants promptly when they begin to bolt, as the leaves become very pungent and tough once the flower stalk elongates. Matures in 21–45 days from seed.

name: Curly Cress (Curled Garden Cress)
description: Curly cress is the finely ruffled, deeply frilled-leaf type of garden cress most familiar from grocery-store cress punnets, its tight curled leaf margins distinguishing it from smooth-leaved garden cress and giving each cutting a decorative, parsley-like texture. It grows fast enough to be cut as tender baby greens within a few weeks of sowing, or left a little longer for a fuller, more mustard-forward peppery bite. Direct sow thickly and shallowly into moist, cool soil, since the mucilage-coated seed needs to stay damp to germinate evenly. Succession sow every two weeks through the cool season and provide light afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting and keep the ruffled leaves tender. Matures in 21–35 days from seed.

name: Curly Dock (Yellow Dock, Sour Dock)
description: Plant in a controlled bed or harvest wild populations growing in moist, disturbed soils; the young spring leaves of curly dock are one of the first edible wild greens available in early spring, with a pleasantly tart, lemony flavor from the oxalic acid content. They are excellent raw in small quantities in salads, or cooked briefly to reduce the oxalates in soups, stews, and egg dishes. Larger, older leaves are tougher and more strongly flavored — cook with one change of water to moderate the sourness. The seeds, which form on tall russet-colored stalks in summer, can be winnowed, ground into meal, and added to flatbread or porridge. The thick yellow taproot (yellow dock) has a long history of use in herbal medicine as a digestive bitter. Moderately invasive in the garden; contain by removing seed stalks before they mature. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Curly Girl Rue (Ruffled Curly-Leaf Rue)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid wet or highly fertile soils. CAUTION: handle with gloves, since rue contains furanocoumarins that can cause skin blistering after contact and subsequent sun exposure. Curly Girl bears distinctively ruffled, tightly curled blue-green foliage on a compact plant, an unusual textural novelty among rue cultivars that makes it a conversation piece in an herb garden or formal edging planting. Like other rue, it is grown mainly as an ornamental and companion plant rather than for culinary use in quantity, since the flavor is intensely bitter. It serves as a larval host plant for Giant Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, and its strong scent is reputed to repel several garden pests. Cut back after flowering to maintain a tidy, compact form. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Curly Kale
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last spring frost; curly kale is one of the most cold-hardy and nutritious leafy vegetables available, withstanding temperatures well below freezing and actually improving dramatically in sweetness and flavor after repeated light frosts convert the leaf starches to sugars. Harvest outer leaves continuously from midsummer or fall onward, leaving the growing center intact — plants will continue producing through winter in zone 7–11 and into early spring in colder zones. Rich in vitamins K, A, and C as well as minerals; the tightly curled, dark-green to blue-green leaves are widely used raw in salads, massaged in dressings, and cooked in soups, stir-fries, and braised dishes. Excellent companion to short-day cover crops and a staple of the fall-to-spring kitchen garden. Matures in 55–70 days from transplant.

name: Curly Mint (Tightly Ruffled Crinkled-Leaf Spearmint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Curly Mint bears distinctively tightly ruffled, crinkled leaves that give it strong ornamental and textural interest in an herb garden beyond its milder, softer spearmint flavor compared to plain spearmint, useful for garnishing where a decorative leaf shape is wanted. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Curly Parsley
description: Curly parsley is a hardy biennial grown as an annual for its bright green, frilled leaves used as garnish and seasoning. Germination is slow, so soak seed overnight and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest outer stems first and the plant will keep producing from the center. In milder zones it overwinters and flowers the second year, at which point flavor declines. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Currant Tomato (Wild-Species Ancestor Tomato with Intensely Complex Flavor, Tiny Fruits)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost; provide large cage or trellis. Harvest clusters when red throughout. Solanum pimpinellifolium, the currant tomato, is the wild progenitor species of modern cultivated tomatoes — one of the wild species native to western South America (Ecuador and Peru) from which Solanum lycopersicum was domesticated thousands of years ago by indigenous peoples of the Americas. The currant tomato has been preserved as a distinct variety in seed collections and home gardens and represents a connection to the pre-domestication history of the tomato: the tiny fruits (roughly the size of a pea or large currant, giving the species its common name) look nothing like modern beefsteak or even cherry tomatoes, but they represent the ancestral form before artificial selection increased fruit size dramatically over millennia. Despite or because of this wild ancestry, the flavor of currant tomatoes is frequently described as intense, complex, and distinctly more flavorful than larger cultivated varieties — a small amount of wild material containing concentrated flavor compounds produces a dramatically different eating experience from a standard cherry tomato. The flavor is balanced sweet-acid with herbal, almost earthy notes that have led food writers to describe currant tomatoes as tasting 'more like a real tomato' than most cultivated varieties. The species is also significantly more heat, drought, and disease tolerant than cultivated tomatoes — traits expected from a wild plant that survived without human irrigation or disease management. In zone 9, S. pimpinellifolium plants perform exceptionally well through the full summer growing season and can sometimes persist as short-lived perennials in the mildest locations. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Curry Leaf
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; curry leaf shrubs grow slowly at first but accelerate once established in a warm zone 9–11 site. Fresh leaves are essential to South Indian cooking and release their aroma only when heated in oil — dried leaves are a poor substitute, so growing your own is worthwhile. Harvest by snipping young branch tips regularly, which encourages dense new growth; remove flower clusters as they appear if you prefer to maximize leaf production. Mulch heavily through zone 9 winters and wrap the trunk if temperatures below 28°F are expected for more than a night or two. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Curry Plant
description: Take 3–4 in softwood cuttings in late spring, strip lower leaves, and insert into sharp-draining propagating mix; roots develop in 3–4 weeks. The silver-needle foliage has a striking curry-like aroma but this herb is primarily used for its fragrance rather than as a true culinary spice — a leaf or two can be added to braises or soups but should be removed before serving. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; it is native to Mediterranean coastal cliffs and thrives under hot, dry conditions. Trim lightly after the yellow button flowers fade to keep the plant tidy; in zone 7 mulch over winter or take cuttings as insurance against hard freezes. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Curtis Pecan (Cold-Hardy Small-Nut Florida Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Curtis is an old, Florida Panhandle-origin pecan cultivar valued for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab and other humid-climate fungal diseases, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for Deep South home orchards. The nuts are smaller than many modern commercial cultivars but well filled, with good flavor, and the tree bears consistently and precociously once established. Because of its disease tolerance and long track record along the Gulf Coast, Curtis is frequently recommended as a dependable, low-maintenance pollinator and production tree for home growers who do not want to run a fungicide spray program. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Cush Cush Yam (Mapuey, Indian Yam)
description: Plant small tubers in loose, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide trellis for the climbing vine. Dioscorea trifida (cush cush yam or mapuey) is the only major cultivated yam native to the Americas — all other important yams (D. alata, D. cayenensis, D. rotundata) originate from Asia or Africa. Native to the Caribbean, Central America, and the Amazon Basin, where it was cultivated as an important food crop by indigenous peoples before European contact, cush cush yam produces distinctive tubers — often three-lobed (hence 'trifida' and the name 'cush cush') — with high-quality flesh ranging from white to cream to purple-violet, depending on variety. The flesh is notably smooth and non-mucilaginous (unlike many Asian yams), with a mildly sweet, earthy, chestnut-like flavor. Cush cush yam is considered one of the finest-flavored yams in terms of culinary quality: the texture cooks to a smooth, dry, mealy consistency similar to the best potatoes. Purple-fleshed varieties have high anthocyanin content and a spectacular color. The vine is ornamental — the deeply three-lobed, arrowhead-shaped leaves are distinctive and attractive. One of the most overlooked Native American food crops, now rare even in its home region. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Cushaw Squash
description: This heirloom winter squash bears large crook-necked fruit with sweet flesh traditional in Southern pies. Direct sow several seeds per hill in warm soil, thinning to the two strongest plants. Give the vigorous vines ample room to ramble, as they can run 12 feet or more. Cushaws show useful resistance to squash vine borers compared with pumpkin types. Harvest when the rind hardens and the vine dies back, then cure in a warm spot to sweeten and improve storage. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Cushaw White Squash (White Cushaw)
description: Plant seeds directly outdoors once soil has warmed after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage strong root development. A colonial-era American heirloom closely related to Green Striped Cushaw, this variety bears crookneck-shaped fruit with smooth cream-white rind and pale flesh that is drier and less sweet, making it especially favored for savory cooking and livestock feed. Its resistance to squash vine borer and adaptability to hot, humid conditions kept it popular across the South long before modern butternut types became dominant. Store cured fruit in a cool, dry space where it will keep for several months. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Custard Apple (Bull's Heart)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; custard apple is a deciduous to semi-evergreen Annona tree producing round to heart-shaped yellow-green to brownish fruits 3–4 inches in diameter with a reticulated (net-patterned) skin. The creamy white flesh inside is sweeter and softer than sugar apple, with a custard-like texture and a mild, slightly musky flavor. It is the Annona most widely grown across tropical Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where it is known variously as bull's heart, corazon, nona, and anon. Hand-pollinate flowers using a small brush in the morning to transfer pollen between flowers on the same tree; like other Annona species, the stigma and anther are not receptive at the same time. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Cut-leaved Selfheal
description: Broadcast seeds onto short, closely mown grass or lightly raked bare soil in fall, pressing them into good contact without covering; winter cold stratifies the seed naturally so that germination occurs reliably the following spring. Cut-leaved Selfheal thrives in dry, calcareous grassland conditions — once established it is drought-tolerant and competes well among low meadow plants, making it an excellent candidate for wildflower turf or lawn alternatives. Allow flower heads to mature and set seed before mowing so the colony can spread and self-sow; mow no lower than three inches to protect the low rosettes. Where it co-occurs with common selfheal (Prunella vulgaris), expect natural hybridization producing intermediate flower colors ranging from white to pale lilac. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Cutleaf Ground Cherry
description: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; cutleaf ground cherry is a tropical annual widely distributed throughout warm regions of the Americas, distinguished from other ground cherries by its more deeply lobed, angular leaves that give the plant a distinctive, fernlike texture among the lantern-papery husked physalis clan. The small yellow berries with papery, lantern-shaped husks ripen inside the husk from green to yellow and have a sweet, tropical flavor suitable for eating raw, making jam, or drying. Widely used as a traditional food plant in Mexico and Central America, where it grows as a weed of agricultural fields and gardens. Very drought-tolerant once established and naturalistic in garden settings where it self-sows to maintain a permanent colony. Distinguished from the toxic black nightshade (Solanum) relatives by the distinctive papery husk enclosing each fruit. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cutting Celery
description: Surface-sow indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, keeping the fine seed moist and lightly covered. This leafy celery is grown for its strongly flavored foliage rather than thick stalks. Transplant to rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade and never let it dry out. Harvest outer stems and leaves as needed, and the plant will keep producing all season. In mild winters it survives to provide an early spring cut, and it stores well dried. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Cyclone Strawberry
description: Cyclone is a June-bearing strawberry noted for reliable survival to zone 3, making it a long-time favorite for home gardens across Minnesota, the Dakotas, and other regions with severe winters. Its concentrated harvest window is short compared to many cultivars, typically lasting about ten days, so plan for prompt picking and processing once the medium-to-large, bright red berries begin to ripen. Flavor is sweet and full-bodied, suiting fresh eating as well as freezing and preserving. Because the bulk of the crop ripens quickly, staggering plantings of an earlier and later cultivar alongside Cyclone can extend the overall harvest season. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Cydora Robusta Quince (Disease-Resistant European Fruiting and Rootstock Selection)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. A German-bred selection valued for its climatic robustness, it shows good tolerance of fire blight and resistance to mildew and leaf spot disease, with fruit that resists the internal browning that troubles some other quince cultivars. It bears large, pear-shaped, bright yellow, slightly hairy fruit with medium-firm, creamy yellow pulp and an intense quince aroma, produced in heavy crops in October on a hardy, upright, slow-growing tree well suited to smaller gardens. Its fragrant pink spring blossom attracts pollinators even though the tree needs none for fruit set. Harvest in October once golden and fragrant, and use for jams, jellies, pastes, and compotes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Cylindra Beet
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of compaction and stones; Cylindra (also known as Formanova) is a Danish heirloom beet producing an unusual elongated, cylindrical root shape — 4–6 inches long and 1.5–2 inches across — completely different from the familiar round beet shape. The cylindrical form was developed specifically for sliced beet production: when cut crosswise, Cylindra produces perfectly uniform, consistently sized circular slices from the entire length of the root, making it the preferred variety for home canning, pickled beet slices, and any preparation requiring uniform beet rounds. A round beet produces irregularly sized slices (small at the shoulders, large in the middle, small at the base), while every slice from Cylindra is the same diameter. The dark red flesh and rich, classic beet flavor are typical of traditional red beet varieties. Cylindra is also highly productive per square foot of garden space because the elongated root utilizes vertical growing space rather than lateral. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Cylindra Beet
description: This Danish heirloom produces long cylindrical roots that yield uniform slices, ideal for pickling and canning. Sow seed half an inch deep in loose, stone-free soil so the elongated roots can develop straight. Thin to 3 inches and keep the beds evenly moist to prevent zoning and cracking. As roots push upward, draw a little soil over exposed shoulders to prevent greening. Harvest when roots reach about 6 inches long and 2 inches thick. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Cypress Rice (Semi-Dwarf High-Yield Louisiana Long-Grain Rice)
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cypress is a semi-dwarf, sturdy-strawed long-grain rice bred by the LSU AgCenter that was, for years, one of the most widely planted commercial rice varieties in Louisiana thanks to its high yield, good milling quality, and resistance to lodging (falling over) compared to older tall rice varieties. Keep the bed continuously flooded or saturated through the growing season, since rice is a wetland crop that depends on standing water to suppress weeds and support steady growth. Harvest when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry the grain thoroughly before hulling and storing. Its shorter, stiffer straw makes it easier to manage in a home rice paddy than older tall heirloom rice varieties, which are more prone to lodging in wind and rain. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Czar Plum
description: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums. An English culinary plum introduced in the 1870s, it bears heavy, reliable crops of dark purple-black, medium-sized fruit ripening notably earlier in the season than most other European plums, with tart, firm flesh that holds together well for cooking, canning, and jam-making even though it is somewhat less sweet than a fresh-eating dessert plum. Its self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and early ripening have made it a longstanding favorite for a productive, low-maintenance home orchard plum, particularly where an early culinary crop is wanted ahead of the main plum season. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for better size, since it often sets a very heavy crop. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Czar Runner Bean
description: Czar is a British heritage runner bean distinguished by pure white flowers rather than the scarlet blooms of most runner beans, and by its dual use as both a fresh snap bean and a dry shelling bean. Young pods are broad, fleshy, and stringless when picked at 8 to 10 inches, while pods left to mature yield plump, pure-white seeds prized for drying and cooking like butter beans. Give plants a tall, sturdy trellis or bean poles and consistent moisture, since runner beans are shallow-rooted and stop setting pods readily in dry or very hot conditions. This heirloom performs especially well in cooler summer climates where heat can otherwise cause runner beans to drop blossoms. Matures in 70–95 days from seed.

name: D'Anjou Pear
description: D'Anjou is a vigorous, productive European pear yielding sweet, juicy fruit excellent for fresh eating, baking, and canning. Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and include a different pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Water consistently during fruit development and prune in late winter to a central-leader form. Harvest the fruit while still firm and ripen it off the tree in cool storage for the best texture. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: D'Arcy Spice Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer. A rare old English apple originating in Essex in the late eighteenth century, it bears small, dull green-brown, unassuming-looking russeted apples that belie a uniquely rich, warm, nutmeg-and-spice-like flavor unlike any other apple, prized by heirloom enthusiasts and considered one of the most distinctively flavored traditional English dessert apples. It is a late-ripening, long-keeping variety that develops its best spiced flavor only after a period of storage, but the tree can be an unreliable, biennial bearer and needs a warm, sheltered site to ripen and flavor the fruit well, making it better suited to a favorable microclimate than an exposed site. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a month or more before eating, since the distinctive spiced flavor develops and intensifies in storage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: D'Etampes Mâche (Corn Salad)
description: Sow seed shallowly and thinly into cool, moist soil, since germination slows dramatically once soil warms past the mid-60s. D'Etampes is an old French heirloom mâche with dark green, spoon-shaped leaves that stand up to hard freezes and light snow better than most other named selections, making it a reliable choice for winter harvest under row cover or cold frame. The rosettes have the classic mild, nutty flavor typical of mâche and are ready to cut whole or picked leaf by leaf. Succession sow into early fall for a continuous supply through the coldest months. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: D24 Durian (Sultan)
description: D24, also marketed as Sultan, is one of Malaysia's oldest and most widely recommended commercial durian clones, valued for a distinctive bitter-sweet flavor balance, creamy pale-yellow flesh, and consistently good yields that made it an industry benchmark before Musang King's rise in popularity. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with abundant humidity and stable warm temperatures; flowering occurs at night and pollination depends heavily on bats, so avoid disturbing nocturnal pollinators with pesticides near dusk. Fruit matures roughly 3-5 months after flowering and should be allowed to fall naturally, since the heavy spined husk makes hand-cutting hazardous and premature harvest results in poor flavor development. D24 remains a common choice for growers wanting a well-documented, reliable cultivar alongside newer premium selections. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Da Cheong Chae Pak Choi
aliases: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Da Cheong Chae'
description: A vigorous Korean-style F1 hybrid pak choi with dark green, upright leaves and thick, crunchy pale-green petioles, distinct from the flatter, whiter-stemmed Chinese pak choi types most familiar to American gardeners. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, non-fibrous stems, and harvest whole heads or individual outer leaves as needed. Its upright, semi-savoyed leaf habit and good bolt tolerance make it well suited to Korean-style kimchi and soups as well as general stir-frying, and it can be succession sown through spring and again in fall for a steady supply. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Da Hong Pao Tea (Big Red Robe)
description: Descended from mother bushes rooted in a rock crevice on Jiulongke cliff in the Wuyi Mountains of Fujian, China, Da Hong Pao is the most storied of the Wuyi rock (yancha) oolong cultivars and today's commercial plantings are cutting-propagated clones of those original plants rather than seedlings. It rewards the mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils of its native terrain with a deep, roasted character locals call yan yun, or 'rock rhyme,' though growers outside Wuyi can still get a respectable approximation in acidic, humus-rich beds. Give it partial shade and steady moisture, and expect a heavier, slower-growing shrub than the milder green-tea cultivars. Traditional processing involves multiple rounds of charcoal roasting, so leaf destined for this style is usually picked slightly more mature than tea grown for green or white styles. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Da Vinci Melon (Sweet Disease-Resistant Galia-Type Hybrid)
description: Da Vinci is a Galia-type hybrid melon bred by Rijk Zwaan that has become a favorite among home gardeners and market growers for pairing intensely sweet, aromatic green-to-orange flesh with strong resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that often cuts melon harvests short in humid climates. The round, lightly netted fruit ripens with the fragrant, floral perfume characteristic of Galia and Charentais-type melons rather than the heavier musk of standard American cantaloupe. Give the vigorous vine full sun and generously amended, well-drained soil, keeping moisture even through flowering and fruit development before tapering off as the fruit nears harvest to concentrate sugars. Judge ripeness by a shift in background color toward gold beneath the netting, a strong sweet aroma at the blossom end, and a clean slip from the vine with light pressure. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Dabinett Apple (Bittersweet Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Dabinett is reliably productive and a good choice for a first cider-apple planting. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, red-flushed apple is one of the most widely planted bittersweet cider apples in both traditional English cider and the modern American craft cider industry, valued for contributing soft, rounded tannin and moderate sugar that blends smoothly with sharper or more acidic varieties. Unlike the temperamental Kingston Black, it is a reliable, consistent, heavy-bearing tree that ripens late in the season and tolerates a range of growing conditions reasonably well, making it a popular starting point for home cider orchardists. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the small, tannic fruit is grown exclusively for cider rather than fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dade Okra (Florida-Bred Disease-Tolerant Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F. Dade was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected for improved tolerance of the fusarium wilt and virus pressure that build up in hot, humid gardens over a long growing season, making it a dependable choice for the Gulf South's extended okra harvest. Plants stay a bit more compact than rangy heirloom types, setting smooth, tapered, medium-green pods that stay tender well past the usual 3-inch mark. Harvest every one to two days once pods start forming to keep plants productive, and remove any pods that slip past picking size, since leaving them on the plant slows new flowering. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Dade Pole Bean (University of Florida Heat-Tolerant Snap Bean)
description: Dade was introduced by the University of Florida in 1962 as a vigorous, leafy pole bean bred for the state's heat, humidity, and disease pressure. Pods are straight, flattened, and about 7 inches long, staying stringless and tender well past the point most snap beans turn tough, giving a wider harvest window before quality drops. The variety carries resistance to rust and several mosaic viruses and tolerates brief waterlogging better than most snap beans, a useful trait during Gulf Coast summer downpours. Set a sturdy 6-foot pole or trellis at planting, since Dade is a true climbing type that will keep producing later into the season than bush varieties. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Dade White Sapote (Compact Early-Bearing Self-Fertile Florida Selection)
description: Dade was bred in Florida in the 1930s specifically to target the humidity tolerance that many California-bred white sapote cultivars lack, and it remains one of the more reliable choices for Gulf Coast conditions as a result. The tree is comparatively compact for the genus and comes into bearing quickly after grafting, an advantage over slower-maturing seedling trees. Fruit stays green even when fully ripe rather than yellowing, has excellent sweet flavor, and holds well on the tree for an extended harvest window rather than dropping and bruising quickly. Although Dade produces mostly non-functional pollen, it has proven highly self-fertile in practice, making it one of the few white sapote cultivars that reliably sets a crop as a stand-alone tree — a real convenience for gardeners without room for a second tree as pollinator. Stake young trees and shelter from wind, since white sapote wood is notably brittle and prone to limb breakage in storms. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dah Pon Carambola
description: Dah Pon is a Taiwanese-origin carambola cultivar grown for large, chunky, deeply five-ribbed fruit that is sweeter and less acidic than many older selections, making it popular for fresh slicing without the tartness some carambola varieties need time to lose. Trees are moderately vigorous and productive, flowering on new flushes several times a year in frost-free climates. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, maintaining even soil moisture through flowering and fruit fill to reduce fruit drop, and thin heavy fruit clusters if branches begin to bend excessively under the load. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Daikon Radish
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6 inches apart in deep, loose, stone-free, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; daikon is a large, long-rooted Japanese radish that develops roots 12–18 inches long and 2–4 inches wide with mild, crisp, slightly peppery white flesh that is essential in Japanese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cuisines for pickling (takuan), salads (daikon salad), braising (oden), and grated as a fresh condiment (oroshi daikon) for tempura and sashimi. Fall planting (8–10 weeks before first frost) avoids the premature bolting that ruins spring-planted crops. In cover-cropping applications, 'tillage radish' varieties (deep-rooting daikon types) are grown as cover crops to break up compacted soil and capture nitrogen; the large roots freeze and decompose over winter, creating channels for water infiltration. Harvest when roots reach full size but before they become pithy. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Daisui Li Asian Pear
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Daisui Li was bred at UC Davis by Ben T. Iwakiri from a cross of the Japanese Kikusui and Chinese Tse Li pears and patented in the mid-1980s, combining Asian pear crispness with unusually large fruit size. Individual fruits can approach a pound apiece, with juicy, sweet, yellowish-green flesh, and the tree ripens its crop in mid-to-late September, after Bartlett and Shinko have finished. The tree shows good resistance to fire blight, an important trait for Gulf Coast gardens where humid spring weather favors the disease, but it requires cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar to fruit well. Thin developing fruit clusters to one pear each so the tree can support the variety's characteristically oversized crop. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dakota Black Popcorn (Deep Purple-Black Heirloom Popcorn with White Pop)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for pollination; let ears dry completely on the stalk, then harvest and cure an additional 3–4 weeks indoors before popping. Dakota Black is an heirloom popcorn variety with some of the most visually striking dried ears available in home-grown popcorn — the kernels are very deep purple-black, almost jet black, creating ears that are dramatically different from the pale yellow, red, or multicolored ears of other popcorn types. The deep coloration comes from a very high concentration of anthocyanins in the kernel pericarp — the same class of pigments found in black rice, black beans, and blueberries, associated with antioxidant properties. Like all colored popcorn types, Dakota Black pops white (the dark pigment is in the outer pericarp layer, not the starchy endosperm that expands during popping), producing attractive, white, tender-crisp popcorn with good flavor. Dakota Black has a place in the Native American Great Plains agricultural tradition where black, dark purple, and multicolored corns were cultivated alongside white and yellow types — the variety's association with Dakota peoples and plains agriculture gives it cultural significance beyond its ornamental appeal. The dried ears are as valuable for ornamental use (fall decoration, wreaths, dried corn displays) as for eating, making Dakota Black one of the most versatile specialty corns for home gardeners. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Dale Sorghum (Southern Syrup Sorghum)
description: Sow seed about an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once the danger of frost has passed, thinning stands to their final spacing to encourage thick, juice-heavy stalks. Dale grows upright on medium stalks covered with a waxy bloom and stands well through late-season winds, resisting anthracnose, red rot, and maize dwarf mosaic better than many older Southern syrup cultivars. Cut canes for pressing once seed heads reach the hard-dough stage, then mill and boil the juice promptly, since the mild, amber, good-bodied syrup Dale is prized for depends on getting cut stalks to the evaporator before their sugar content drops. Leftover bagasse and grain heads can be fed to livestock or left standing for birds after the cane harvest. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Damiana
description: Take 3–4 in stem cuttings in spring or summer and root in gritty, barely moist medium; damiana is easier and faster from cuttings than from the slow-germinating seed. Plant in sharply drained, sandy or rocky, poor soil in full sun — damiana is native to the dry shrublands of Mexico and the Caribbean and rots in moist, fertile conditions. In zones below 9, grow in containers and overwinter in a frost-free, bright location, watering sparingly. Harvest leafy stems and the small yellow flowers throughout the growing season, drying them for use in traditional Mexican tonic teas and liqueur preparations. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Damson Plum
description: The damson is a hardy, self-fertile culinary plum whose tart, astringent fruit shines in jams, gins, and preserves. It thrives even on heavier soils and in exposed positions where dessert plums struggle. Plant in full sun to partial shade and keep young trees weed-free and mulched. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in summer; expect reliable heavy crops after three to four years. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Damson Plum (Blue Damson, Shropshire Damson)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; prune to open center form after harvest. Prunus domestica 'Damson' (Damson plum or Blue Damson) is an ancient, small-fruited European plum type — distinct from both Japanese plums (P. salicina) and common European plums in being smaller, more astringent, and more intensely flavored when raw, but superb when cooked or preserved. The small (1-inch), oval, blue-purple to nearly black fruits ripen in late summer through fall with a rich, complex, winelike, slightly tannic flavor that becomes sweet and luscious when cooked with sugar. Damson plum is the traditional fruit of English damson jam, damson cheese (a firm fruit paste), damson gin (sloe-gin equivalent made with damsons rather than sloes), and damson wine. The Shropshire Damson is the most celebrated English variety; Merryweather is the largest-fruited commercial type. Damson trees are notably hardy, long-lived, disease-resistant, and productive — often naturalizing at hedgerow edges across England — and require less winter chill than Japanese plums. Generally self-fertile or partially self-fertile; a pollination partner improves yields. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Damson Plum (Bullace)
description: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson is more self-fertile than most plums and often sets good crops without a pollinator, though cropping improves with cross-pollination from another plum. Prunus instititia is the wild source of the cultivated damson, a small tree or large shrub producing small, oval, blue-black to purple plums in late summer with dense, richly flavored, astringent flesh quite distinct in character from the sweet, fresh-eating Japanese plums; damsons are the traditional plum for cooking, being too astringent to eat in quantity raw but transforming into superb jam (damson jam is one of Britain's most prized traditional preserves), jelly, cheese, wine, and gin. The tree is extremely long-lived, hardy, and productive even in cold, exposed, and acid soils where other plums fail. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dan Shen (Chinese Red Sage)
description: Start transplants indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and set out in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Shen is grown chiefly for its distinctive brick-red roots, harvested after the plant has grown for at least one full season. Soft, hairy, deeply veined leaves and spikes of violet-blue, two-lipped flowers typical of the sage family top a clumping perennial whose real value lies underground, in thick, branching roots with a distinctive brick-red exterior that is a cornerstone herb of traditional Chinese medicine, long used to support healthy circulation. It is easy to grow in ordinary garden conditions much like culinary sage relatives, tolerating a range of soils, and the showy flowers are an added bonus for pollinators even where the roots are not harvested. Dig roots for use in fall after two or more years of growth, when they have reached a useful size, and cut back spent flower stalks after bloom to keep the clump tidy. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Dana's Hovey Pear (Small Exceptionally Rich-Flavored Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Raised by Francis Dana of Massachusetts in 1854, this heirloom bears small, yellow, lightly russeted pears that are widely considered among the richest and most refined-flavored of all American-bred pears, with dense, buttery, aromatic flesh that rewards patient ripening despite the fruit's unassuming size. Its late-season timing extends the home orchard's pear harvest well into the cooler months. Harvest while still firm in fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure; the fruit stores and keeps notably well for a dessert pear. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dancy Tangerine (Classic Florida Zipper-Skin Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted nursery trees in full sun, well-drained soil; fertilize with a citrus fertilizer 3 times per year (February, May, September). Dancy is the original American tangerine — named for Col. George L. Dancy of Orange Mills, Florida, who cultivated this variety beginning around 1867, making it one of the oldest named tangerine cultivars in the United States. For over a century, 'Dancy tangerine' was synonymous with 'tangerine' for most Americans — it was the predominant commercial tangerine grown in Florida and the citrus most commonly associated with Christmas stocking traditions, the holiday season timing of its December–January ripening. The fruits are medium-small, oblate, and deep orange-red at maturity with a distinctively loose, easily peeled 'zipper-skin' — the loose skin peels away from the flesh with minimal effort, releasing the fruit in clean, separate segments. The flavor is the classic tangerine profile: tart, sweet, aromatic, and intensely citrus with the characteristic spicy-sweet note that distinguishes tangerines from oranges. Dancy has substantial seeds (8–15 per fruit), which reduces its appeal compared to modern seedless mandarin hybrids; however, the intense traditional tangerine flavor is considered by many to be unmatched by the sweeter but blander modern seedless types. Trees are productive and long-lived in zone 9–11. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dandelion
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in deep, loose, well-drained soil; cultivated broad-leafed varieties produce larger, more tender leaves than typical lawn weeds. Blanch developing rosettes under a cover for 1–2 weeks in spring to produce milder, less bitter leaves for salads. All plant parts are useful: young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, flowers are made into wine or fritters, and the taproot is roasted as a coffee substitute or used fresh in bitter-tonic preparations. Harvest roots in autumn of the second year when they are largest and most concentrated in the liver-supportive compound taraxacin. Matures in 60–95 days from seed.

name: Dang Shen (Poor Man's Ginseng)
description: Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with a trellis or fence to climb; dang shen is one of the most important tonic herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine, used as an energy-building adaptogen and substitute for the more expensive Panax ginseng. The twining, climbing vine produces pale greenish-yellow bell-shaped flowers with purple-veined interiors in summer. The thick, fleshy taproot is harvested after 3-5 years and used in soups, teas, and tonic preparations throughout China, Korea, and Japan. Modern research confirms adaptogenic compounds in the root that support energy and immune function. The plant dies back in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Grow in a position where the deep taproot will not be disturbed. Matures in 365–1095 days from seed.

name: Dangleberry (Blue Huckleberry, Dwarf Huckleberry)
description: Plant in acidic, moist, sandy or organic soil in partial to full shade; Dangleberry tolerates and indeed thrives under open pine forest canopies where acid soil and dappled light create its native habitat. Gaylussacia frondosa is a native deciduous shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, found in longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and sandy pine-oak barrens from Maine to the Gulf Coast — a classic component of the native understory throughout zone 7–9. The small blue-black berries, ripe July–August, are sweet, distinctly resinous in flavor, and historically among the most prized wild fruits gathered by indigenous peoples and early settlers throughout the Southeast — often preferred over blueberries for their more complex flavor when made into jams, pies, and preserves. Dangleberry is closely related to the Black Huckleberry (G. baccata) but tends to be taller, more open in habit, and more shade-tolerant. The plant spreads by underground stolons to form loose colonies that provide excellent wildlife habitat — birds, black bears, and small mammals rely heavily on huckleberry fruits. In zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes with acidic, sandy soil, it is an outstanding native understory berry for shaded woodland gardens where blueberries struggle in too much shade. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dangshan Su Li Asian Pear (Chinese White Pear)
description: Dangshan Su Li is one of China's most widely grown white pear cultivars, native to Dangshan County, a region long known for large-scale pear production. Its smooth golden-yellow skin covers crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh eaten fresh at harvest, unlike the soft-ripening habit of European pears. As a Pyrus bretschneideri cultivar it needs a compatible cross-pollinator and, like most Asian pear species, has limited natural resistance to fire blight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Daniecki Che (Male Pollinator for Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Che is normally dioecious, and Daniecki is the named male selection most commonly planted to pollinate seedless female cultivars like Darrow and Norris, which otherwise set only a partial or unreliable crop without a compatible pollen source nearby. Its own flowers form small, pollen-bearing structures rather than edible fruit, so it is planted for function rather than harvest, typically one male for a small orchard block of female trees. Like other che selections it carries little winter chilling requirement and tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees, while young wood is thorny and benefits from early training to an open form. Plant within reasonable bee-flight distance of female che trees for best fruit set on the females. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Danish Ballhead Cabbage (Large Late-Season Storage Cabbage for Sauerkraut)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Danish Ballhead is a classic large-headed fall/storage cabbage from the Scandinavian and Northern European tradition — one of the primary heirloom cabbages for sauerkraut production, coleslaw for large quantities, and long-term cold storage. The very large (5–8 lb), perfectly round, extremely dense, blue-green heads form tight, compact, hard balls — the firmness that gives Ballhead its name means the heads have a very high leaf-to-air-space ratio, ideal for shredding into sauerkraut. Danish Ballhead has been the reference variety for Scandinavian sauerkraut production for generations — Scandinavian food traditions rely heavily on fermented cabbage through the winter months, and the large, dense, sweet heads of late-season cabbage like Danish Ballhead are the ideal base. The variety keeps very well after harvest — 3–4 months in proper cold storage (near 32°F with high humidity) — providing fresh cabbage through winter. Excellent for coleslaw, braised preparations, and fresh use. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Danube Cherry (Hungarian Duke-Type Sweet-Tart Cherry for Zone 9)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, choosing a site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the early flowers. Danube, a Hungarian duke-type cherry combining sweet and sour cherry parentage, was introduced to American growers by cherry breeder Amy Iezzoni and needs only about 450 chill hours, unusually low for a cherry, making it one of the very few named cherry cultivars explicitly marketed as workable at the northern edge of zone 9. It is partially self-fertile and ripens in early July, with balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of duke cherries. As with other low-chill stone fruit at the edge of their range, true performance under Gulf Coast humidity and disease pressure is less proven than in drier low-desert climates, so treat as a promising trial selection. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Danvers 126 Carrot
description: This late-19th-century heirloom offers strong color, high yield, and uniform, tapered roots that perform well even in heavy soils thanks to their vigorous tops. Sow seed thinly directly in the garden and keep the surface consistently moist until the slow seeds sprout. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and forked roots. It interplants nicely with onions. Loosen and deeply cultivate the bed before sowing for the straightest roots. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Danvers Carrot
description: Danvers 126 is a dependable heirloom that produces tapered, deep-orange roots even in heavier or imperfect soils. Loosen the bed deeply and remove stones so roots stay uniform, then sow seed thinly about a quarter inch deep. Keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination period, and thin seedlings to a couple inches apart once they establish. Harvest at roughly 70 to 80 days when shoulders reach three-quarters of an inch, and hold roots in cool storage for winter use. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Dapple Dandy Pluot (Dinosaur Egg Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible plum or pluot pollinator such as Santa Rosa or Flavor Supreme, since Dapple Dandy is not reliably self-fruitful. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this pluot, an interspecific plum-apricot hybrid weighted mostly toward its plum parentage, is instantly recognizable by its greenish-yellow skin dappled with maroon-red splotches, which gave rise to its Dinosaur Egg nickname, and by the vivid magenta-red flesh inside that is exceptionally sweet with a rich, complex flavor many tasters rate among the best of the pluot varieties.
