Fruit ripens over a fairly long midsummer window, giving a spread-out harvest rather than one concentrated picking, and the tree is otherwise managed much like a standard plum, with dormant pruning to an open center and thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve size. Its moderate chill requirement fits mild-winter Southern gardens better than many traditional European plums. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dapple Fire Pluot (Dramatic Dappled Red-Green Skin, Red-Fleshed)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Dapple Fire is a Zaiger Genetics pluot notable for its striking appearance, with dark green skin splashed and streaked with fiery red dapples that intensify as the fruit ripens, opening to reveal firm, deep red flesh with a rich, sweet-tart flavor and good, dense texture. The visual drama of the skin pattern makes it a favorite at farmers markets and among home orchardists who enjoy growing something visually distinctive alongside more conventionally colored stone fruit. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure, since the dappled skin can make judging ripeness by color alone trickier than with solid-colored varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dark Jade Bitter Melon
description: An Indian-type F1 hybrid bitter melon bred for high yield and noticeably reduced bitterness compared with older open-pollinated Indian types, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to the crop. Fruit is slender and spindle-shaped, 8-10 inches long, with dark green, densely bumpy skin and roughly half a pound in weight. Both immature fruit and tender young shoots are edible, and the fruit holds well on the vine without rapidly yellowing, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom types. Provide a strong trellis in full sun and rich, well-drained soil for best production through the hot summer months. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Dark Opal Basil
description: Sow indoors 4-6 weeks ahead of the last frost and keep flats warm and bright to preserve rich color. This deep-purple basil adds dramatic color to vinegars, salads, and garnishes. Transplant after frost into full sun, where strong light intensifies the burgundy pigment. Pinch regularly to build a dense plant and prevent early flowering. Harvest young leaves for the most vivid color and infuse them into oils or vinegars. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Dark Star Zucchini (Near-Black Dark-Striped Hybrid Zucchini with Superior Heat Tolerance)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 6–8 inches when skin is uniformly very dark green. Dark Star Zucchini is an F1 hybrid summer squash variety developed for its dramatically dark fruit color, vigor, and heat performance in warm-summer conditions — qualities that make it particularly appropriate for Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens where summer zucchini production is challenging due to the combination of heat, powdery mildew pressure, and vine borer activity. Standard zucchini typically produces well in spring (March–May in zone 9) and again in fall (August–October) but struggles during the July–August peak summer period. Dark Star's improved heat tolerance extends the productive period somewhat beyond what standard green zucchini varieties manage, though no summer squash is fully tolerant of zone 9 peak summer conditions. The fruit's near-black to very dark green color (produced by high concentrations of chlorophyll and other pigments in the skin) is the variety's most immediately distinctive characteristic — a mature Dark Star fruit at 6–8 inches harvest size is substantially darker than a standard green zucchini, with a glossy, nearly black-green skin that stands out dramatically when displayed with lighter-colored vegetables. The flesh is standard zucchini quality — white, mild, with good flavor at proper harvest size — with no meaningful flavor difference from standard green varieties. The AAS recognition for Dark Star reflected consistent performance advantages in vine health, production duration, and uniformity across trial locations including warmer growing regions. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Darki Parsley (Dark Green Triple-Curled)
description: Darki is a French heirloom triple-curled parsley prized for its very dark green, densely ruffled leaves and heavy, repeat-cutting productivity through a long season. It holds up unusually well to cold, tolerating hard frosts and light freezes that flatten less hardy curly types, which makes it a favorite for late-fall harvest and overwintering in milder gardens. The compact, uniform plants stay attractive and upright rather than sprawling, so they work well massed as an edging or container planting. Cut outer leaves regularly to keep new growth coming and to delay the plant's second-year bolt into flower. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Darkibor Kale (Dark Blue-Green Curly Hybrid Kale)
description: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Darkibor is a vigorous hybrid curly kale producing densely ruffled, dark blue-green leaves on a productive, uniform plant, valued commercially and by home gardeners alike for reliable yields and good cold tolerance that lets it stand in the garden well into winter in many climates. The tightly curled leaf texture holds up well to cooking methods like sauteing and braising, and the dark color signals a good concentration of nutrients typical of kale. Harvest outer leaves as needed, working from the bottom up, and expect improved sweetness after the plant experiences a light frost. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Darlene Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Darlene is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) bronze muscadine released by the University of Georgia for home garden and commercial production, valued for combining good fresh-eating fruit quality with the self-fertility that allows a single vine to produce a full crop. The medium to large, bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, mild, pleasant muscadine flavor with less of the strong musky note that some consumers find overpowering in older varieties. The tender skin and mild, sweet flavor make Darlene one of the more approachable fresh-eating muscadines for people new to the variety. The self-fertile habit is particularly valuable for home gardeners who have space for only one vine; unlike female-flowered varieties that require a separate pollinator, Darlene sets fruit reliably on its own. In zone 9 the vigorous vine grows readily in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and produces consistently. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Darlington Oak (Laurel Oak)
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; Darlington oak is a medium-sized semi-evergreen oak of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, often confused with the closely related laurel oak (Q. laurifolia) that grows in moister soils. The elliptical leaves are semi-evergreen to evergreen in the deep South, making this an excellent year-round shade and wildlife tree for zone 8–10 landscapes. Like most oaks, it produces abundant small acorns that provide essential food for wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and white-tailed deer. It is one of the most commonly encountered oaks in dry upland portions of the Florida peninsula and the Gulf Coastal Plain, thriving in the kind of deep, dry, infertile white sand that challenges most trees. An excellent canopy tree for naturalistic landscapes in the coastal Southeast where heat, drought, and sandy soils limit tree choices. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Darrow Blackberry (USDA Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and train the vigorous, self-supporting canes onto a wire trellis to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. Darrow was developed by USDA breeders and released in the late 1950s, named in honor of the noted small-fruit breeder George M. Darrow, and it was bred specifically for cold hardiness beyond what most erect blackberries of the era could tolerate. The berries are large, firm, glossy black, and tart-sweet, produced in heavy clusters over a mid-to-late season harvest window that extends the bramble season after earlier varieties finish. Its thorny, upright canes and strong winter hardiness have kept it in cultivation as a dependable choice for northern growers who need a blackberry that survives cold winters without cane dieback. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Darrow Blueberry (Evergreen Blueberry, Native Florida Blueberry)
description: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich, sandy to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun; amend with peat moss or pine bark to increase acidity; mulch heavily with pine straw. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow blueberry or evergreen blueberry) is a native Florida and southeast Georgia blueberry species — one of several native blueberries of the southeastern coastal plain — producing small, 1/4-inch, intensely flavored, blue-black berries in April–May with an extraordinarily rich, sweet-tart blueberry flavor that many consider superior to commercial cultivars. The small, semi-evergreen to evergreen, blue-green leaves are among the smallest of any blueberry species; the white, urn-shaped flowers in February–March are especially important for native bee pollinators emerging early. This species is a parent of several southern highbush blueberry cultivars (including 'Sharpblue,' 'Gulf Coast,' and 'O'Neal') bred for low-chill southern climates. Darrow blueberry is extremely low-maintenance in native soils — requiring no supplemental irrigation once established and producing reliably in the conditions of the coastal plain with minimal care. It is rarely available commercially but is outstanding as a native wildlife plant — birds and small mammals consume the berries eagerly. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Darrow Che (Seedless Self-Fertile Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Che is a close relative of mulberry and Osage orange grown for its mulberry-shaped, maroon-red fruit that tastes something like a cross between fig and watermelon; the species is normally dioecious, but Darrow is a female selection propagated from a tree grown by USDA breeder George Darrow that reliably sets a full, seedless crop with no male pollinator required. It carries essentially no winter chilling requirement, so it flowers and fruits without the cold-dormancy failures that limit many temperate fruits in mild Gulf Coast winters, while the tree itself tolerates temperatures well below what its heat tolerance would suggest. Expect a large shrub or small tree that can be kept compact with annual pruning; young wood is thorny, so training to an open, easily harvested form early pays off later. Fruit ripens over an extended late-summer to fall window and is best picked when fully soft. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Darselect Strawberry (French Large-Fruited Dessert Strawberry)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring at soil level in fertile, well-drained ground, and mulch with straw to keep the large fruit clean and off the soil surface. Darselect was bred in France in the 1990s and quickly became a leading commercial and market-garden variety across western Europe before gaining a following among Mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest growers in North America. The berries are notably large, elongated-conical, and deep glossy red, with dense, firm flesh and a rich, well-balanced sweet flavor that holds up better in storage than many other June-bearing types. It ripens midseason and is often favored by growers who sell at farmers markets because the fruit's size and firmness make for an especially attractive display basket. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Darto Kale (Very Dark Blue-Black Lacinato-Type Kale)
description: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Darto is a striking Lacinato-type (dinosaur kale) selection with unusually dark, almost blue-black, deeply savoyed leaves, even darker than standard Lacinato kale, giving it strong ornamental value in addition to its classic sweet, nutty flavor prized in Tuscan cooking. The long, narrow, crinkled leaves hold their quality well in cool weather and are excellent massaged raw into salads, sauteed, or added to soups. Harvest outer leaves as needed, allowing the central growing point to continue producing new leaves over a long season, and expect the flavor to sweeten further after light frost. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Daruma Wasabi (Cold-Hardy Commercial Wasabi Cultivar)
description: Establish Daruma wasabi by planting healthy rhizome divisions or crowns in spring into cool, constantly moist, richly organic soil kept below about 70F, ideally alongside a shaded stream bank or in a heavily mulched bog bed fed by clean, moving water. Daruma is the cultivar most commonly grown by commercial wasabi farms in North America because of its vigorous growth and comparatively good tolerance of temperature swings, though it still demands full to partial shade and unfailing moisture to avoid rot or stunting. After 18 to 24 months the thick rhizome is ready to harvest and grate fresh, releasing the same clean, sinus-clearing heat that fades within minutes, a world apart from the horseradish-and-dye paste sold as wasabi in most restaurants. Its dense, heart-shaped leaves also make an attractive textural groundcover for a deeply shaded, moisture-rich corner of the garden. Matures in 540–730 days from transplant.

name: Dasher II Cucumber (Disease-Resistant Gynoecious Slicer)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Dasher II is a gynoecious hybrid slicing cucumber that has been one of the most consistently recommended disease-resistant slicing cucumber varieties since its release — carrying resistance to cucumber mosaic virus, scab, angular leaf spot, powdery mildew, and anthracnose, providing protection against the most common disease failures in cucumber production across a wide range of climates. The dark green, 7–8 inch, slightly tapered fruits have a smooth, attractive appearance with small, even bumps and white spines; the flesh is crisp, mild, and refreshing with very low bitterness (very low cucurbitacin content), making Dasher II distinctly more palatable than older cucumber varieties that could be quite bitter. The gynoecious character concentrates fruit set into a more uniform harvest window than open-pollinated types. In humid Gulf South conditions where cucumber diseases (especially powdery mildew and angular leaf spot) severely limit cucumber production in summer, Dasher II's comprehensive disease resistance is particularly valuable, allowing productive summer growing that standard varieties cannot sustain. An excellent backbone slicer for any home garden or market garden where disease pressure is a concern. Matures in 55–62 days from seed.

name: Date Palm
description: Dates are dioecious — you need a male tree to pollinate female trees, with one male sufficient for up to 50 females; commercial growers hand-pollinate by shaking male flower strands over female inflorescences in spring. Ripe dates require extremely hot, dry summers (110°F daytime heat preferred) with very low humidity during the ripening period — this limits quality fruit production in the continental U.S. almost entirely to the Coachella Valley and low desert Arizona. Offshoots from the base of female palms are the preferred planting material as they preserve the sex and fruit type of the parent; seed-grown palms yield 50% males and highly variable fruit. Harvest in fall when fruit reaches the desired stage: khalal (crisp, astringent), rutab (partly soft, sweet), or tamr (fully dried). Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Date Plum (Caucasian Persimmon)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; date plum is a medium to large tree native from the Caucasus and Mediterranean to eastern Asia, producing small (1/2–1 inch) yellow to blue-black persimmon fruits in October–November that resemble tiny plums and have a sweet, date-like flavor — hence 'date plum.' The fruit contains high tannin levels when unripe (astringent like American persimmon) but becomes sweet after frost or extended hanging on the tree. Historical records suggest the fruit may be the legendary 'lotus fruit' of Homer's Odyssey that made Odysseus's sailors forget their homes. The tree is highly ornamental with glossy, dark-green leaves that turn yellow and red in fall, interesting orange bark on mature specimens, and small, attractive cream-colored flowers. More cold-hardy than Asian persimmon and easier to establish in temperate gardens, it is used as a rootstock for kaki persimmons. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Datil Pepper
description: Start seeds at 80–85°F soil temperature; germination is slow and benefits from bottom heat. Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Datil peppers are a habanero-type (Capsicum chinense) variety historically grown in and around St. Augustine, Florida, for at least 200 years — their exact origin is debated but they are deeply embedded in Minorcan and northeast Florida food culture. The small, wrinkled, yellow-orange fruits are fiercely hot (100,000–300,000 Scoville) with a distinctive fruity, citrusy sweetness that sets them apart from pure heat bombs. They are the defining ingredient in St. Augustine's datil pepper sauce tradition, used in chowders, seafood dishes, and condiments. Plants thrive in Florida's humid summers and can be treated as perennials in zone 9b–11 when protected from frost. Mulch heavily, water consistently, and side-dress with compost mid-season to sustain productivity. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Dattock (Sweet Detar, Tallow Tree)
description: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock is a forest tree that benefits from some shade protection when young. Detarium senegalense (dattock or sweet detar) is a tall leguminous tree from the coastal forests, gallery forests, and moist woodland savannas of West Africa — native across Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Nigeria. The tree produces round to slightly flattened, 1–1.5 inch, thin-shelled fruits containing large, flat, hard seeds embedded in sweet, brown, fibrous, edible mesocarp with a distinctive sweet-acid, almost tamarind-like flavor. The fruits are exceptionally rich in vitamin C (up to 100 mg per 100g — roughly twice that of orange juice), and are eaten fresh as a pleasant sweet-sour snack across rural West Africa. The hard seeds contain a starchy meal used in traditional foods. The tree yields a useful timber and a resin used in traditional medicine. In Senegal, the sweet detar fruits are particularly popular and are sold in local markets. Sweet detar (D. senegalense) is the sweet-fruited species, distinguished from bitter detar (D. microcarpum), which has similar fruits but with an unpleasantly bitter taste — an important distinction for edibility. A largely unknown and underexplored fruit tree outside West Africa. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Daubenton's Kale (Perennial Kale)
description: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Daubenton's kale is one of the oldest known perennial brassicas, grown continuously as a cutting-propagated vegetable in European kitchen gardens since at least the 18th century — named after the French naturalist and physician Louis Jean-Marie Daubenton (1716–1800). The plant never (or rarely) sets seed, remaining in a perpetual vegetative state and producing edible, tender, kale-like leaves throughout the growing season year after year. In zones 7–10, plants survive winter outdoors and return each spring with renewed vigor. Flavor is mild and pleasant, similar to curly kale but without the toughness of mature kale leaves. Harvest by cutting young side shoots and leaves regularly. An excellent plant for low-maintenance, productive food forests and permaculture gardens where a perennial harvest of leafy greens is desired. Propagate from 6-inch stem cuttings at any time. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Dauphine Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Dauphine is a French fig variety named for the Dauphiné region of southeastern France, producing large, round to flattened fruits with violet to brown-purple skin and pink to reddish-amber flesh with a rich, sweet, mild flavor. The large fruit size (2–3 inches) is among the biggest in the fig world and makes Dauphine figs particularly impressive for fresh eating and market presentation. The vigorous, productive tree performs well in zone 9 heat and provides abundant harvests of the large, handsome fruits from August through September. Dauphine figs are best eaten fresh at peak ripeness; the large size can lead to cracking if late-season rains arrive during ripening. The French Dauphiné region has a tradition of fig cultivation in its milder southern valleys, and Dauphine represents the large-fruited table fig tradition of this region. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast conditions closely approximate the warm, humid conditions of the Dauphiné valleys. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dave's Fave Tea (Dark-Leaved Hedge-Form Cultivar)
description: Dave's Fave was selected by a camellia nursery breeder for its exceptionally dark, glossy, rounded leaves and short spacing between leaf nodes, producing a naturally dense, well-shaped shrub that needs little corrective pruning to serve as a tea hedge. Its sturdy, woody stems hold up well under repeated harvesting. Trial processing has shown it yields a cup broadly comparable to the cold-hardy Sochi selection, though it was chosen for form rather than winter hardiness specifically. Grow it in the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other China-type tea camellias, and begin light plucking once plants are established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Daviana Hazelnut (Historic English Pollinizer Filbert)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Daviana is planted primarily as a companion pollenizer rather than for nut production, since its own nut quality is considered mediocre; its catkins shed pollen later in the season than most commercial cultivars, making it a useful match for cultivars with a later-receptive bloom window. Daviana originated in England and became, historically, the most widely planted pollenizer in 'Barcelona' hazelnut orchards in the Pacific Northwest and Europe. Its high susceptibility to Eastern Filbert Blight and unremarkable nut quality have caused it to be steadily replaced by EFB-resistant pollenizers in modern commercial plantings, though it remains of interest to home orchardists in EFB-free regions. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: David Bowie Dragon Fruit
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil, giving the epiphytic cactus a sturdy post or trellis to climb rather than the regular watering a typical fruit vine would need. David Bowie is a self-pollinating white-fleshed pitaya cultivar prized for its mildly sweet, distinctly lemony flavor, often described as a cross between kiwi and pear, wrapped in vivid pink-red skin edged with green triangular bracts. Flowers open only after dark and close by morning; because the vine is self-fertile, a single plant can set fruit, though hand-pollinating at night with a small brush improves fruit set in cool or humid weather. In zone 9, keep it in a container that can be moved under cover whenever frost threatens, since even brief cold exposure damages the succulent stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: David Pear (Cold-Hardy Ussurian-Bartlett Hybrid Pear)
description: David is a cross between the classic European Bartlett pear and the extremely cold-hardy Ussurian pear (Pyrus ussuriensis), bred to survive prairie and northern winters where standard European pears fail outright, and reported to tolerate temperatures of -50F or colder once established. Like other Ussurian-type hybrids, the medium-to-small, round, golden fruit is powerfully astringent, especially if picked underripe, and is best used for cooking, hard cider, and perry blends rather than fresh eating unless left to fully ripen and soften. Plant with a second cold-hardy pear such as Ure or Rescue nearby for cross-pollination, and expect a vigorous, disease-resistant tree well suited to zone 2-3 gardens where fruit tree choices are otherwise limited. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Davidson's Plum (Ooray, Queensland Davidson's Plum)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum grows naturally as a rainforest understory tree and requires protection from direct hot afternoon sun. Davidsonia pruriens (Davidson's plum or ooray) is a rainforest understory tree native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia — one of the most commercially important fruits in the Australian native food industry. The tree is notable for its highly unusual growth habit: the large (1.5–2.5 inch), dark-purple to burgundy-black, plum-like fruits grow directly from the trunk and main branches in dense clusters (cauliflory), similar to cacao and jaboticaba. The fruits are intensely, mouth-puckeringly tart — far too sour to eat fresh in quantity without processing — but with extraordinary depth of flavor that has made them the darling of Australian native food chefs and product makers. Davidson's plum jam, Davidson's plum sauce (excellent with game, lamb, and dark meats), Davidson's plum sorbet, Davidson's plum wine and gin, and Davidson's plum dried food products are among the most celebrated products of the native food movement. The fruits are extremely rich in antioxidants — anthocyanins, ellagic acid, vitamin C — with a deep, complex, sour-fruity character that processing and sweetening reveals as intensely flavorful. Hardy to light frost in zone 9, Davidson's plum is increasingly available from Australian specialty nurseries. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Davis Elderberry (California-Selected American Elderberry)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant at least one other named elderberry cultivar nearby, since elderberries set a far heavier crop with cross-pollination than they do alone. Davis is a selected American elderberry cultivar grown for its broad, flat clusters of small white flowers in early summer, useful for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer that are cooked into syrup, jelly, and wine rather than eaten raw. Like other American elderberry cultivars it spreads by root suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket if left unmanaged, so remove unwanted suckers each season to keep the planting to a defined shrub. Elderberry prefers consistently moist soil and performs best in a low spot or near a downspout where it won't dry out during summer heat; prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the shrub vigorous and productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Davis Pawpaw (Reliable Historic Michigan Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Davis is one of the oldest widely propagated named pawpaw cultivars, selected by Michigan pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis in the mid-20th century from wild seedling trees and long valued for its consistent, reliable production and good flavor. Fruits are medium-sized with smooth, pale yellow, fiber-free flesh and a rich, sweet, banana-custard flavor, though the seeds are somewhat larger in proportion to flesh than in some newer cultivars. Davis ripens in the early-to-mid part of the pawpaw season and, alongside cultivars like Sunflower and Taytwo, played a foundational role in the mid-20th-century revival of interest in pawpaw as a cultivated fruit. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, since pawpaw's natural pollinators (flies and beetles, drawn to the maroon flowers' faint carrion scent) are often scarce in home gardens. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Day Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican Avocado)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with excellent drainage; Day is one of the most cold-hardy avocado cultivars available, an important trait for Gulf South growers pushing avocado culture north of the traditional Florida and California ranges. A Mexican-race avocado selected in the mid-Atlantic for cold tolerance, it bears small, thin-skinned, rich, high-oil fruit with the anise-scented foliage typical of Mexican-race avocados, ripening in late summer to early fall on a tree reported to tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit once well established. Like all avocados it demands sharp drainage and will not tolerate wet feet, so plant on a mound or raised bed in heavy Gulf Coast soils, and protect young trees with frost cloth during their first several winters. Its cold hardiness makes it one of the more realistic avocado choices for gardeners in zone 8b who want to attempt the crop outside the classic Florida-Texas-California avocado belt. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Daytona Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Pink Dooryard Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy. Daytona was released in the early 1980s from the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program and is grown chiefly as a home dooryard grape, valued for its pink-blushed fruit and for standing up to Pierce's disease and downy mildew far better than European wine grapes in Florida's hot, humid climate. It does remain somewhat susceptible to anthracnose, ripe rot, black rot, and powdery mildew, so an ongoing fungicide program through the growing season is worthwhile even on a resistant cultivar like this one. Fruit is best suited to fresh eating off the vine rather than commercial wine or juice production. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce disease pressure in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Dazzling Blue Kale
description: This extra-cold-hardy lacinato-type kale features striking purple midribs against blue-green, savoyed leaves that deepen in color during cool fall weather. It withstands frost better than most dinosaur kales, and flavor sweetens after a light freeze. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, moist soil. Harvest outer leaves as needed to keep plants producing. It overwinters well in mild regions for early spring greens. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: De 18 Jours Radish (Classic French Ultra-Fast Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. De 18 Jours, French for 'of 18 days,' is a classic heirloom radish named for its exceptionally fast maturity, historically prized by French market gardeners for getting a crop to harvest faster than almost any other vegetable. Roots are small, round to oval, bright red, and crisp, with a clean, mild flavor typical of quick spring radishes when harvested promptly at the right size. Because it matures so quickly, it is well suited to intercropping between slower-growing vegetables or squeezing in an extra succession planting in a short cool window. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows, and succession sowing every two weeks keeps a steady supply coming. Matures in 18–25 days from seed.

name: De Barbentane Eggplant (Violette Longue de Barbentane, French Heirloom)
description: De Barbentane is a French heirloom dating to the early 1800s from the Provence region, prized for its shiny dark-purple, cylindrical fruit and firm, sweetly fragrant flesh with little of the bitterness common in older eggplant types. Vigorous plants routinely carry eight to ten fruits at once, each 6-8 inches long, making it one of the more heavily fruiting heirloom eggplants once established. Its early finish and cool-summer breeding background mean it sets fruit reliably even in a season that starts on the cool side. Harvest while the skin is still taut and glossy for the best flavor in ratatouille or grilled preparations. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: De Belleville Sorrel
description: De Belleville is reputedly the oldest cultivated sorrel strain, selected in France around 1730 for its large, productive, low-acid leaves that hold up well through a long summer harvest. Plant in rich, evenly moist soil with light afternoon shade in warmer climates, since drought stress makes the leaves bitter and speeds bolting. Pick outer leaves continually to keep the plant producing tender new growth, and remove any flower stalks promptly to prolong the harvest. This vigorous perennial forms a long-lived clump that benefits from division every three to four years to maintain leaf quality. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: De Bourbonne Cucumber (French Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, providing a trellis or light support to keep fruit clean and straight. De Bourbonne is a traditional French heirloom from the Burgundy region bred specifically for pickling, producing short, blocky, black-spined fruit typically harvested at two to four inches long for classic French-style cornichons and gherkins. The vigorous vines set fruit prolifically over a long season, and frequent picking is essential since the cucumbers mature quickly and turn seedy and bitter if left too long on the vine. Its small size and firm, crisp texture make it well suited to whole-fruit pickling rather than fresh slicing. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: De Chaunac Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American Red Wine Grape)
description: Named for the Canadian winemaker who popularized it, this hybrid was once one of the most widely planted French-American varieties in the Finger Lakes and Ontario before newer hybrids surpassed it, but it remains a dependable, productive vine for home growers wanting a cold-hardy red. It produces heavy crops of small blue-black berries that yield a soft, fruity red wine and needs cluster thinning to avoid overbearing and delayed ripening. The vine tolerates winter cold better than vinifera and resists downy mildew reasonably well but can be susceptible to bunch rot in wet autumns. Prune moderately hard each dormant season to balance vigor and fruit quality. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: De Cicco Broccoli
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant when daytime temperatures are below 75°F and after hardening off. De Cicco is one of America's oldest and most beloved heirloom broccolis, introduced to the US from the Lazio region of Italy and appearing in seed catalogs since at least 1890; unlike modern large-headed hybrids, De Cicco produces a smaller, open, bluish-green central head (4–6 inches) that is best harvested before flowers open, then rebounds with a prolific and sustained harvest of tender, slender sideshoots that are more delicate and sweet-flavored than the central head — this sideshot harvest can continue for weeks in cool weather, making De Cicco arguably more productive than single-heading types over the full season. The tender sideshoots (broccoletti) are the classic vegetable of Italian cooking braised with olive oil and garlic. An outstanding variety for Gulf Coast fall and winter production and for cool-climate spring gardens. Matures in 48–60 days from transplant.

name: De Croissy Turnip
description: Named for Croissy-sur-Seine, a historic market-gardening town near Paris, this French heirloom produces slightly curved, cylindrical white roots that were traditionally bunched and sold young for their tender, sweet flesh. It matures faster than globe-type turnips, making it well suited to close spring and late-summer sowings where a quick, mild crop is wanted before or after the main season. Its half-long, tapered shape and old-market-garden history distinguish it from the round purple-top types that dominate most American gardens. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: De Milpa Tomatillo
description: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants generously since De Milpa sprawls more loosely than domesticated tomatillo strains. This is an old, semi-wild landrace type still gathered from milpa (cornfield) plantings in central and southern Mexico rather than a modern breeding selection, so fruit size and husk color vary noticeably plant to plant, ranging from green to purple-blushed. The small, marble-sized fruits fill their husks completely and have a sharper, more acidic bite than commercial green tomatillos, making them prized by cooks seeking a rustic, old-style salsa verde. Because tomatillos are self-incompatible, grow at least two plants for reliable fruit set; harvest once husks split or turn papery and fruit fills the husk. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: De Soto Plum (Historic Iowa Heirloom American Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and site a second seedling or cultivar of American plum nearby, since De Soto is not reliably self-fruitful. Selected from a wild seedling near Lansing, Iowa and distributed by nurseryman Elisha Hale beginning in 1864, De Soto became one of the most widely planted named selections of native American plum during the 19th-century prairie plum boom, prized enough that it was carried on the American Pomological Society's recommended fruit list on and off for decades. It bears clusters of red to reddish-orange, thick-skinned, clingstone fruit with a rich, tangy-sweet flavor that many growers still rate above the wild species for jams, jellies, and preserves. The tree suckers readily to form a small thicket if left unpruned, so remove root sprouts to maintain a single-trunk form, and expect it to shrug off drought, cold, and poor soil once established far better than any modern hybrid plum. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Deadon Cabbage (Dark Red Savoy-Type Winter Cabbage)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into well-amended, firm soil in full sun, giving plants room for a dense, round head. Deadon is a modern British-bred winter cabbage prized for producing solid, deep red-purple heads with excellent flavor and remarkably long field-holding ability, standing in good condition through hard frosts and well into winter without splitting or losing quality. Its rich color, cold hardiness, and dense, slow-to-bolt heads make it a favorite for extending the fresh cabbage harvest deep into the cold season, and the color deepens further after frost. Firm transplants in well to prevent wind-rock, protect young plants from cabbage worms and aphids, and harvest as needed through winter, since mature heads hold in the garden far longer than most summer cabbages. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Deanna Fig (UC Davis Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Fig)
description: Deanna was developed through University of California, Davis fig breeding work as a cold-hardier, crack-resistant alternative to Calimyrna-type figs, which need caprification and are prone to splitting. Fruit is exceptionally large, often exceeding 100 grams, with green-yellow skin that ripens toward yellow and sweet amber-to-strawberry flesh with a pronounced honey flavor. It bears a substantial breba crop in addition to a significant main crop and tolerates winter cold well beyond what most Gulf Coast winters require, giving a wide safety margin against the occasional hard freeze. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Deep Purple Bunching Onion (Purple-Shanked Scallion)
description: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart for straight, uniform stalks. Deep Purple is a non-bulbing bunching onion selected for shanks that flush a striking violet-purple, especially in cool weather, contrasting with its blue-green tops; the color makes it a standout in salads, garnishes, and pickles compared with standard green scallions. Flavor is typical mild-to-sharp onion, good raw or cooked, and the plant is otherwise grown exactly like any other bunching onion. Harvest at scallion size for the best color and tenderness, or let a portion mature further for thicker stalks; successive small sowings keep a continuous supply. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Deer Magnet American Persimmon (Heavy Annual Fruit-Drop Native Persimmon)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot native persimmons develop early in life. Deer Magnet is a named American persimmon selection prized above all for the sheer volume and reliability of its annual fruit drop, a trait that made it a favorite among wildlife food-plot growers before its excellent eating qualities also drew fresh-eating enthusiasts, producing abundant deep-orange, soft, honey-sweet fruit through fall once fully ripened. Like other native persimmons, the fruit is harshly astringent while firm and must be allowed to soften fully, or be picked up once it drops, before eating. The tree develops a deep taproot and tolerates heat, drought, and marginal soils far better than typical orchard fruit trees once established, and as a native species it is right at home in the Gulf South's heat and humidity. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon cultivar nearby for pollination and heavier fruit set. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Deer Tongue Lettuce (Matchless Lettuce)
description: Scatter seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full rosettes or 6 inches for cut-and-come-again harvest. Deer Tongue (also known as Matchless) is one of America's oldest heirloom lettuces, documented in seed catalogs since at least 1740 and recorded in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden journals; the distinctive tongue-shaped, elongated, slightly pointed, wavy-edged leaves form loose, open rosettes with a crisp-yet-buttery texture and mild, sweet flavor. A green variety ('Green Deer Tongue') and a bronze or red variant ('Bronze Deer Tongue') exist; both are more heat-tolerant than most lettuce types, slower to bolt in warm conditions, and excellent for spring and fall production in warm climates. The elongated leaf shape is immediately distinctive and visually striking in the garden; makes beautiful salad contributions for the unusual leaf form. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Deerberry
description: Deerberry is a native eastern North American Vaccinium species bearing clusters of small, blue-green to purple berries that ripen in midsummer with a flavor ranging from tart to mildly sweet depending on provenance and growing conditions. Unlike most blueberries, the flowers have exserted stamens (protruding well beyond the petals), giving them a distinctive open, star-shaped appearance that attracts native bees. The plant is very drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes well in dry, acidic woodland margins. Berries are edible fresh or cooked but have variable palatability; select superior-tasting wild ecotypes or named cultivars when available. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Defiant PhR Tomato (Late Blight-Resistant Slicer)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, and cage or stake the semi-determinate plants; Defiant PhR was bred by Dr. Randy Gardner at North Carolina State University to give home and organic growers a reliably productive slicing tomato that resists late blight, the fast-moving fungal disease capable of destroying an entire planting within days in wet, humid weather. It bears a heavy crop of medium to large (6-8 oz), round, deep red fruit with solid, meaty flesh and good classic tomato flavor, ripening early enough to get well ahead of peak disease season in many climates. Because it also shows good tolerance to early blight and septoria leaf spot, it tends to hold healthy foliage later into the season than most slicing tomatoes grown in the humid Gulf South, keeping plants productive longer. Harvest as fruit ripens to full red color and keep picking regularly to encourage continued fruit set. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Deglet Noor Date Palm
description: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Deglet Noor needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates. Known as the 'light of the date' for its translucent amber color when held to the light, this semi-dry cultivar is the most widely grown commercial date variety in the United States, historically the backbone of California's Coachella Valley date industry after being introduced from Algeria in the early twentieth century, prized for a firm, chewy texture and balanced, not-too-sweet flavor that holds up well in baking and storage. Like all date palms it requires an extremely long, hot, arid growing season to properly cure and sweeten its fruit on the tree, making it poorly suited to humid climates where fruit is prone to souring or fermenting before it fully ripens. Female trees need a nearby male date palm or hand-pollination to produce fruit, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Del Rio Avocado (Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Del Rio is a Mexican-race avocado cultivar selected for cold hardiness in South and West Texas, where hard freezes regularly test the limits of what avocado trees can survive, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. It represents the ongoing regional effort among Texas home orchardists to identify and propagate avocado selections tough enough for zone 8b-9a gardens. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Delaware Grape (Historic Small-Berried American Pink Wine Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Delaware is a historic American grape dating to the mid-1800s, producing small, tightly clustered, pink-red berries with notably high sugar content and a delicate, sweet, wine-quality flavor considered superior to many other Labrusca-type grapes of its era, and it remains valued today for both fresh eating and wine and juice production. It is self-fruitful and matures in midseason. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Delbarestivale Apple (Early-Season French Red-Striped Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Delbarestivale was bred by the Delbard nursery in France and released for ripening notably early in the season, giving gardeners fresh apples well ahead of the main fall harvest window most varieties occupy. The medium, bright red-striped fruit over a yellow-green background has crisp, juicy, sweet flesh with good, well-balanced flavor for such an early-season apple, since many early apples sacrifice flavor complexity for speed. The tree is productive and reliable; harvest in mid to late summer once fruit fully colors, and use fairly promptly, since early-season apples typically do not store as long as fall and winter varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Delfino Cilantro (Feathery Fernlike-Leaf Cilantro Variety for Ornamental and Culinary Use)
description: Direct sow thinly in cool soil; thin to 6 inches. Harvest young leaves before bolting for best flavor; allow some plants to flower for seed production. Delfino Cilantro is a named selection of Coriandrum sativum distinguished by its unusual leaf morphology: while standard cilantro produces broad, somewhat lobed leaves resembling flat-leaf parsley at the base, Delfino produces very finely divided, thread-like foliage that resembles dill or fennel fronds far more than it resembles conventional cilantro. This leaf form is caused by a genetic trait affecting leaf development — Delfino consistently produces only the finely dissected leaf form throughout its growth, never the broad lower leaves typical of standard cilantro. The flavor and aroma are identical to standard cilantro: the same distinctive volatile compounds (primarily linalool and various aldehydes) that give cilantro its characteristic citrusy, herbaceous, and for some people soap-like quality are present in the same proportion in Delfino as in standard types. The feathery foliage has several culinary advantages: the very fine texture integrates easily into salads and garnishes, the delicate fronds are visually striking on finished dishes, and the fine cut of the leaves releases aromatic compounds easily when torn or chopped. For zone 9 gardeners growing cilantro in fall and early spring gardens, Delfino provides a visually distinctive alternative to standard varieties with the same flavor and culture requirements. Like all cilantro, Delfino is a host plant for black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed on cilantro, dill, fennel, and related Apiaceae plants. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Delica Kabocha Squash
description: Delica is the dark green, deeply lobed kabocha type most widely sold as fresh kabocha in North American grocery stores, prized for its dry, deep-orange flesh with a dense, chestnut-like sweetness. Vines are vigorous and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set, tapering off as the rind hardens near harvest. Cure fruit for one to two weeks in a warm spot to concentrate sugars before moving to cool storage, where it keeps for two to three months. Choose Delica when you want the classic Japanese squash experience for tempura, soups, and roasting rather than a sweeter American-bred kabocha hybrid. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Delicacy Purple Kohlrabi
description: Delicacy Purple forms a smooth, deep violet globe above the soil line while the interior flesh stays crisp white, giving a striking contrast when sliced for a vegetable tray. Its bulb stays tender and mild even as it sizes up, resisting the woodiness that affects many kohlrabi types if harvest is delayed slightly. Fast to mature and compact in the row, it works well tucked into small spaces or grown in quick succession through spring and fall. Choose Delicacy Purple for its ornamental color and reliably sweet, crunchy texture in both raw and cooked preparations. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Delicata Winter Squash
description: This 1894 heirloom develops oblong fruits with hard cream skin striped in green and sweet, tender flesh. Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil, spacing plants generously to give the semi-vining habit room to run. Provide steady moisture through fruit set and mulch to conserve water and suppress weeds. Harvest when the skin hardens and the stripes deepen, then cure fruits in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage and flavor. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Delicata Winter Squash (Sweet Dumpling Squash, Carnival Squash)
description: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Delicata is a compact, heirloom winter squash producing cylindrical, cream-colored to pale yellow fruits with distinctive green and orange-tan longitudinal stripes — an exceptionally attractive squash with outstanding flavor quality. The flesh is deep orange, very sweet, very dry, and intensely flavored — widely considered one of the finest-flavored winter squash cultivars, with a sweet, almost chestnut-like richness that needs little added fat or sugar when roasted or baked. The thin skin is completely edible after roasting — one of the few winter squash varieties where peeling is unnecessary. The manageable fruit size (6–9 inches long, 3–4 lbs) is practical for single-meal preparation. Delicata vines are more compact than most winter squash — the semi-bush to short-vine habit reaches 4–6 feet — making it more manageable in smaller garden spaces. In zone 9, the summer planting (late July–early August) for fall harvest generally works better than spring planting, as the hottest summer temperatures tend to prevent adequate fruit set. The fruit stores well at room temperature for 2–3 months. Squash vine borers and squash bugs are the primary pests; row covers at planting and prompt removal of egg masses help manage populations. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Delicious 51 Cantaloupe (Classic 1951 USDA Commercial Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Delicious 51, released by the USDA in 1951, was a standard commercial cantaloupe variety for decades, prized for well-netted rind, thick, sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh, and good disease tolerance for its era, and it remains a solid, reliable open-pollinated choice for home gardeners today. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Delicious Muscadine Grape
description: Delicious is a self-fertile, black-fruited muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross between a bronze parent and a large-fruited self-fertile black selection, released in the late 2000s. The oval berries color to a deep purple-black at full ripeness and the vine ripens its crop earlier than many older black cultivars, making it a useful bridge between early and midseason harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-resistant, and heavy-bearing, holding up well to the fungal pressure typical of humid Gulf Coast summers. Grow on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, pruning hard each winter to renew fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Delicious Tomato
description: Delicious is an old Burpee introduction famous for producing some of the largest tomato fruit of any variety, including the fruit that held the Guinness World Record for heaviest tomato for nearly three decades. Stake or cage plants heavily and prune to a few main leaders so the vigorous indeterminate vines can channel energy into fewer, larger scarlet-red beefsteak fruits. Consistent deep watering and calcium availability help reduce cracking and blossom end rot on fruit that can exceed a pound. Choose this variety when garden bragging rights and classic rich tomato flavor matter more than earliness or disease-package breadth. Matures in 77–90 days from transplant.

name: Delight Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Delight is a long-established North Carolina State University bronze muscadine cultivar known for consistent production of medium-sized, sweet, thin-skinned bronze berries with good flavor for fresh eating, well ahead of the peak-season bronze varieties like Fry. Vines are vigorous and reliably productive, and the early-to-mid-season ripening window makes Delight useful for extending the start of the bronze muscadine harvest when paired with later cultivars. It is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinizer, though yield improves with additional muscadine varieties nearby. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that limit bunch grape production in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input once established. Harvest as berries color fully and detach easily from the stem; train vines to a sturdy two-wire trellis and prune annually in winter to keep fruiting wood renewed. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Delikat Dill
description: Delikat is a European leaf-type dill selected for dense, bushy growth and heavy foliage yield rather than for seed production, making it a good choice for gardeners who mainly want fresh dill weed. Its compact stature compared to tall seed-strain dills also suits container growing and small raised beds. Harvest leaves regularly by snipping outer stems, which encourages the bushy plant to keep pushing new growth before it eventually bolts to flower. Like other dill, it self-sows readily if a few plants are allowed to set seed, and its ferny foliage supports black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Delite Blend Sweet Snacking Pepper
description: This blend of mini sweet snack peppers ripens to red, yellow, and orange, all prized for crunchy, juicy texture and vibrant color. Start seed indoors early since peppers need a long warm season. Harden off carefully and transplant only after soil and nights are reliably warm. Plants are productive and well suited to containers and small beds. Pick regularly once fruit colors up to encourage continued set. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Delite Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur well before planting; Delite is a USDA-ARS rabbiteye blueberry released from the small fruit research station at Poplarville, Mississippi, and prized among Gulf South gardeners for having the sweetest, lowest-acid flavor of the classic mid-century rabbiteye releases. Berries are medium-sized, dull blue, and ripen over a fairly long mid-to-late season window, making Delite a good choice for spreading out the fresh-eating harvest rather than a single heavy flush. Plants are vigorous and productive but need a compatible rabbiteye pollinator within about 50 feet, since Delite sets poorly on its own. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system from Gulf Coast summer heat, and avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizers that blueberries tolerate poorly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Delite Rabbiteye Blueberry (Extra-Sweet Midseason Southern Blueberry)
description: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly. Delite is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for producing some of the sweetest fruit of any rabbiteye cultivar, with medium to large, light blue berries that ripen midseason. Like other rabbiteyes it needs cross-pollination from a second rabbiteye variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop, and its moderate chill requirement fits well within the zone 7-9 range common along the northern Gulf Coast. The upright, moderately vigorous bushes are long-lived and low-maintenance once established in properly acidified soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Delizz Strawberry (F1 Seed-Grown Everbearing Patio Strawberry)
description: Delizz is an F1 hybrid strawberry bred specifically to be raised from seed and fruit reliably in its first year, unlike most garden strawberry cultivars, which are propagated vegetatively from runners or crowns to preserve hybrid vigor. Surface-sow the fine seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping it warm and consistently moist until germination, then transplant seedlings into full sun after frost danger passes. Plants stay compact and mounding, making Delizz a popular choice for hanging baskets, window boxes, and patio containers as well as small beds. It is day-neutral and everbearing, producing a steady succession of small to medium, sweet, aromatic red berries from summer through the first frosts rather than a single flush. Keep soil evenly moist while fruiting and deadhead spent trusses to encourage continued flowering; in cold climates it is commonly grown as an annual, though plants can overwinter with protection in milder zones. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Della Rice (Louisiana Aromatic Long-Grain Rice)
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated through the growing season whether in a flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Released by the LSU AgCenter in the 1970s, Della was one of the first American-bred aromatic long-grain rices, developed by crossing domestic rice lines with basmati-type genetics to produce a fragrant, popcorn-scented grain that helped establish Louisiana's aromatic rice industry and became a parent behind several later Southern aromatic varieties. The tall plants yield well in the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season, and the cooked grain carries a distinctive nutty, toasted-popcorn aroma prized in Cajun and Creole cooking. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain turns golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before storage or milling. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Den's Choice Feijoa (Australian Selection)
description: Den's Choice is an Australian feijoa selection valued by home orchardists for consistently large, well-flavored fruit on a vigorous, heavy-cropping bush, making it a favorite in warm-climate feijoa plantings outside its native New Zealand breeding grounds. Fruit is oval to oblong with smooth skin and sweet, aromatic, moderately seeded flesh, ripening in the typical autumn window for the species. The shrub grows upright and dense with the characteristic gray-green, silver-backed evergreen foliage, and takes well to being clipped into a productive hedge or left more open as a specimen shrub. As with other feijoa cultivars, expect the best fruit set and size when a second, genetically distinct cultivar is planted within pollinator range, though established plants will still set some fruit on their own in a good season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Denniston's Superb Plum (Cold-Hardy American Gage-Type Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, though a nearby pollinizer can improve yields. Denniston's Superb is an early 1800s American gage-type plum bred for cold hardiness and reliable self-fertility, two practical advantages over many European gage selections that need cross-pollination and struggle in harsher climates. The medium, round, greenish-yellow fruit has dense, sweet, richly flavored flesh in the classic gage tradition, good for both fresh eating and preserves. The vigorous, hardy tree bears reliably once established, making it a solid choice for northern home orchardists who want good gage-type flavor without the fussier pollination and hardiness requirements of some European varieties. Harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Densuke Watermelon (Black-Rind Hokkaido Watermelon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, spacing vines 3-6 feet apart in rows with ample room to sprawl. Densuke is distinguished from typical striped watermelons by a rind that ripens to an almost uniform matte black rather than developing stripes, enclosing crisp, sweet red flesh; the fruit was originally developed and marketed by a small growers' cooperative in Toma, Hokkaido, where the cooler northern Japanese summers and volcanic soil were credited with its intense sweetness. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest by checking the dulling of the ground spot and the drying of the tendril nearest the fruit stem, since the solid dark rind makes the classic thump test and stripe patterns unreliable ripeness cues. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Dente di Cavallo Pomegranate (Italian Horse's-Tooth Heirloom Pomegranate)
description: Dente di Cavallo, literally 'horse's tooth,' takes its name from the elongated, angular shape of the fruit's crown, and is one of the traditional heirloom pomegranates grown across Italy for centuries for its dependable, heavy cropping. The medium-to-large fruit has greenish skin blushed with red and encloses sweet, delicately flavored ruby arils that store well after harvest. Plant on well-drained soil in full sun; the variety is noted for tolerating a broad range of soil conditions and for consistent yields even in less-than-ideal ground, making it a forgiving choice for a first Gulf Coast pomegranate planting. Light annual thinning of crowded or crossing branches keeps the canopy open and encourages new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Deodeok (Bonnet Bellflower)
description: Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb; deodeok, known as sha shen in Chinese medicine, is a twining East Asian vine grown for its thick, aromatic, ginseng-scented taproot, which is a well-known ingredient in Korean cuisine, roasted, grilled, or pounded and seasoned as a savory side dish (deodeok-gui and related preparations) and also used in traditional herbal tonics. The vine climbs by twining stems clothed in soft blue-green leaves and produces distinctive bell-shaped flowers, greenish outside and dramatically mottled maroon-purple within, that hang facing downward through mid to late summer. Unlike its close relative dang shen (Codonopsis pilosula), deodeok's root has a stronger, more resinous, distinctly aromatic flavor that intensifies with the plant's age, and roots are traditionally harvested at three years or older for the best culinary and medicinal quality. Grow it where the deep root can develop undisturbed, and provide support for the twining vine to climb. Matures in 365–1095 days from seed.

name: Derby Bush Bean (Derby Green Bean)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in the garden after soil has warmed, spacing plants close together in rows since compact bushy plants need little support. This dependable bush bean produces long, straight, round pods about five to six inches long that stay tender and stringless even when picked slightly larger than average. Vigorous, heavy-yielding plants tend to hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, which keeps them cleaner and makes for faster picking. It has long been a standard choice for home gardeners wanting a reliable, high-quality green bean for fresh eating, freezing, or canning. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Des Vertus Savoy Cabbage (French Heirloom Drumhead Savoy)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost for a summer harvest, or sow in early summer for transplanting out for a fall crop, since Des Vertus develops its full flavor and holds especially well after cool autumn weather sets in. Des Vertus Savoy, also known as Large Drumhead Savoy, is a French heirloom cabbage dating to the early 1800s that produces large, rounded, medium-green heads of four to six pounds with deeply crinkled, blistered savoy-type leaves. Its flavor is notably mild, sweet, and tender compared to smooth-leaved cabbage, and the crinkled leaves make it a traditional choice for stuffed cabbage preparations across French and other European cuisines. It is more cold-tolerant than many cabbages, standing well into fall and even overwintering in mild climates, and offers moderate storage life once harvested. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Desert Agave (Mescal Agave, Shaw's Agave)
description: Plant offset pups or young container specimens in full sun in gravelly, sandy, extremely well-drained desert soil with no summer irrigation once established; desert agave (Agave deserti) is the agave of the Sonoran and Mojave Deserts, historically one of the most important food plants for desert-dwelling indigenous peoples of California, Arizona, and Mexico — the Cahuilla, Kumeyaay, and Coahuilla people harvested the immature flower stalks (quiote) and the heart of the plant (piña) before flowering, roasting them in earth ovens to produce a sweet, molasses-like food that sustained desert communities. Plants live 10–20 years before producing a single tall flower stalk, then dying, leaving behind pup offsets. The leaf tips are sharp and require care during placement. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: Desert Date (Heglig, Soap Berry Tree)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available — tolerates 3–6 months of complete drought once established. Balanites aegyptiaca (desert date, heglig, or soap berry tree) is a thorny, slow-growing tree native to the arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, and the Middle East — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important trees of the African drylands, found from Senegal and Mauritania east through Sudan and Ethiopia and into the Arabian Peninsula. The tree produces oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown to dark-brown fruits (drupes) with fleshy, oily mesocarp that is sweet-bitter with a date-like character; the fruits are eaten fresh, used to flavor traditional porridges, fermented into beer, and pressed for oil. The seed kernel yields an edible oil used in cooking and as a skin preparation. The bark, leaves, and fruit rind contain saponins traditionally used as soap — hence 'soap berry tree' — and in traditional fish stunning for fishing (the saponins narcotize fish). The tree has extensive traditional medicinal applications across Africa (treatment of malaria, diabetes, skin conditions) and is increasingly studied for bioactive compounds. One of the premier trees for the dryland agroforestry systems of the Sahel, where it withstands extreme drought, poor soils, and degraded conditions that defeat most other trees. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Desert Gold Peach (Early Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Introduced from Fresno, California in 1969 for about 250 chill hours, Desert Gold opens peach growing to the mildest winters of zone 8-9 where standard varieties will not set fruit. It is among the earliest peaches to ripen, often by late April to May, with medium semi-freestone fruit, yellow flesh, red-blushed skin, and a sweet, slightly tart flavor. Because it blooms early, a site sheltered from late cold snaps helps protect the blossoms from frost damage. Self-fruitful and heat-tolerant, it remains a long-standing standard recommendation for warm-winter home orchards. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Desert King Fig
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun against a south-facing wall in cooler climates to maximize heat accumulation; Desert King is a San Pedro type that requires no pollinator for its reliable breba crop but benefits from caprification for main crop development in warm climates. Desert King is the dominant fig cultivar in Pacific Northwest gardens (Oregon, Washington, British Columbia) where it excels for its large, spectacular breba crop (early summer, June–July) that ripens reliably without the extended heat required by most other figs; the very large (3–6 oz), flattened-turbinate fruits have thick, green to greenish-yellow ribbed skin and dark strawberry to amber-red interior flesh with rich, sweet flavor. In warm climates (California, Gulf Coast) it also produces a substantial main crop in August–October. Among the most cold-hardy of all quality fig varieties, surviving to about 10–12°F when established and dormant. A vigorous, large tree that requires space; well-suited to training as an espalier against south-facing masonry walls. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Desertnyi Pomegranate (Levin Selection Sweet-Tart Pomegranate)
description: Desertnyi comes from famed Turkmen pomegranate breeder Gregory Levin's collection and is maintained in the USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, notable in cultivar comparison trials for having among the highest sugar content of the varieties tested, giving it an intensely sweet, citrusy flavor balanced with some tartness. Fruit has a light orange rind over dark red, soft-seeded flesh, and the plant is relatively compact, reaching around ten feet, with reports of bearing within one to two years of planting and yields of twenty pounds or more once mature. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it needs only a modest chilling period to set fruit well, which suits the mild winters of zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens. Established plants are drought-tolerant, though even moisture as fruit ripens helps prevent splitting given how juicy and thin-skinned the fruit becomes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Desi Chickpea (Small Dark-Seeded Garbanzo Bean)
description: Direct sow seed an inch or so deep into well-drained soil once hard frost danger has passed, since chickpeas of any type quickly rot in cold, waterlogged ground. Desi types form a bushier, more branching plant than Kabuli chickpeas and set smaller, angular, thick-coated seeds ranging from tan and speckled to brown or near-black, borne one or two per small pod. The thicker seed coat makes Desi chickpeas notably more drought-tolerant in the field and is traditionally removed by splitting the dried seed into chana dal, though whole seeds can also be cooked as a firmer, earthier-flavored garbanzo bean. Let the crop dry down fully in place, harvesting once most pods have turned brittle and tan, then thresh and store the seed somewhere cool and dry. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Desirable Pecan
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun; Desirable is the most widely planted named pecan cultivar in the United States and the benchmark against which other commercial varieties are measured. Developed by the USDA and released in 1940, it produces large, well-filled nuts (50–55 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and superb flavor — considered by many pecan growers to be the highest-quality commercial pecan available. It is a consistent, reliable producer in zone 7–9 and well-adapted to the Gulf Coast South from Texas to Georgia. The principal challenge is susceptibility to pecan scab disease (Fusicladium effusum) in humid climates — in very humid areas like coastal Louisiana and Mississippi, it may require fungicide protection in wet years. Space trees widely: pecans ultimately become very large trees (60–80 feet tall, 40–60 feet wide) that shade out everything below. Supplement with zinc spray in spring; pecan is notorious for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Desiree Pea
description: This early Dutch heirloom shelling pea charms with pink blooms and vivid purple pods on compact, productive vines. Sow seed an inch deep as soon as the soil is workable, since peas thrive in cool spring weather. Provide a short trellis or brushy support to keep the vines tidy and the pods clean. Harvest the purple pods while plump and shell out the sweet green peas promptly, as flavor is best right after picking. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Desiree Potato (Classic Red-Skinned Yellow-Flesh Potato)
description: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Desiree is a widely grown Dutch-bred potato with smooth, rosy-red skin and pale yellow, moderately waxy flesh that holds its shape well when boiled, making it a versatile choice for roasting, salads, and general cooking. It is a vigorous, heavy-yielding variety with good tolerance for a range of soil conditions and reasonably good drought tolerance compared to some other cultivars. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to prevent tubers from greening in the sun, and harvest for storage once the vines have died back naturally. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Dester Tomato (French Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant deeply into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, then stake or cage the vine early. Dester is a French heirloom beefsteak prized for its smooth, rounded, deep pink-red fruit that runs unusually free of the cracking and catfacing that plague many large heirloom slicers, often reaching a pound or more with very few seeds and a thin, tender skin. The flesh is dense, low in acid, and richly sweet, making it a favorite among heirloom growers for fresh eating despite the plant's somewhat unassuming, ordinary-looking foliage. Water evenly and mulch well through fruit set, since the smooth skin is still thin enough to split under drought-then-deluge conditions; the vigorous, disease-tolerant vine keeps setting fruit steadily through a long Gulf Coast season. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Detroit Dark Red Beet
description: Detroit Dark Red is a classic heirloom prized for deep crimson roots, tender texture, and sweet flavor that holds up for canning and storage. Sow seed about half an inch deep in loose, well-drained soil, keeping the bed evenly moist to aid the multi-seeded clusters. Thin seedlings to three or four inches apart so roots size up well, and use the thinnings as tender greens. Pull roots at two to three inches for the best eating quality, and hold larger roots in cool, damp storage over winter. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Detroit Golden Beet
description: A beloved heirloom with sweet, non-bleeding orange roots and nutritious edible greens that stay mild whether raw or cooked.
