Direct sow seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping moisture steady during germination. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart and remove weeds so roots can swell evenly. Harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for tender eating, and cure larger roots for cool storage. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Devil's Claw (Unicorn Plant)
description: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; devil's claw sprawls widely and needs plenty of room, and its sticky, glandular foliage can irritate sensitive skin. Large, sprawling, sticky-hairy leaves and showy, orchid-like, pale pink to lavender flowers give way to the plant's real claim to fame: long, curved, green seed pods that, when young and tender, are pickled or cooked like okra, and when mature dry to a woody, split, two-pronged 'claw' historically gathered by Indigenous peoples of the Southwest and used as a black fiber in basketry. Native to the central and southwestern United States, it grows easily from seed in ordinary garden soil and self-sows readily once established, sometimes appearing as a volunteer weed in disturbed garden soil in following years. Harvest pods young and tender (a few inches long) for pickling and eating, or let some mature and dry fully on the plant to collect the distinctive woody claws for craft use or seed saving. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Devil's Club
description: Site in deep, consistently moist shade beneath conifers, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest old-growth understory habitat. Wear gloves when handling, as stems and leaf undersides bear dense sharp spines. Bark and root bark are traditionally harvested from mature stems in fall for medicinal preparations, similar in use to Panax ginseng. Grows slowly and spreads by layering sprawling stems that root where they touch moist duff; leave leaf litter in place as mulch rather than clearing it away. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Devil's Tongue Lettuce (Red-Splashed Cos)
description: Sow seed shallowly in cool, fertile soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches once they have several true leaves. Devil's Tongue is a small upright cos-type lettuce whose older outer leaves flush dramatically from light green to deep wine-red at the margins while new growth stays a contrasting fresh green, giving each head a striking mottled two-tone look. The heads stay relatively compact at 6-7 inches, so it works well in small beds or containers, and the crisp ribs and mild sweet flavor hold up better than many red lettuces as temperatures warm. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pick outer leaves individually for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest window. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Devil's Tongue Pepper (Caribbean Habanero-Type Superhot)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat to improve germination, then transplant into well-drained, fertile soil once the weather is reliably warm. Feed lightly and keep moisture consistent, since chinense peppers are prone to blossom drop under heat stress or drought. Devil's Tongue produces distinctively wrinkled, tapering pods and is closely related to habanero types, with heat that reaches well into the habanero-to-superhot range along with a fruity flavor. It is grown in shades ranging from pale yellow to deep red depending on the strain. Matures in 90–115 days from transplant.

name: Devils Claw
description: Direct sow in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, low-fertility soil in full sun; Harpagophytum procumbens is a dryland plant that requires excellent drainage and tolerates severe drought — overwatering or clay soils cause root rot; grow in raised beds or sandy garden beds with no supplemental fertilizer. Harpagophytum procumbens (Devil's Claw, Grapple Plant, or Duiwelsklauw) is a low-growing, trailing, tender perennial in the Pedaliaceae family native to the Kalahari Desert, Namibian desert, and Karoo drylands of Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa — an extraordinarily specialized dryland plant adapted to survival in some of the harshest desert soils in the world. The plant is named for its grotesque, claw-covered, woody seed pods — each pod festooned with multiple long, hooked claws designed to attach to the hooves and legs of large mammals (springbok, wildebeest, zebra) for long-distance dispersal across the desert. The secondary storage tubers (secondary roots) are the medicinal part — harvested commercially in Namibia and Botswana — containing harpagoside, 8-p-coumaroylharpagide, and related iridoid glycosides with well-documented anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. Devil's Claw root extract is one of the top three best-selling botanical medicines in Germany and France, prescribed for osteoarthritis, lower back pain, and musculoskeletal inflammation. Wild harvesting is regulated; cultivated production increasingly supplies European pharmaceutical markets. Matures in 730–1825 days from seed.

name: Devotion Basil (Downy Mildew-Tolerant Genovese Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Devotion is one of the Rutgers University downy-mildew-tolerant Genovese basil releases, bred specifically to resist Peronospora belbahrii, the airborne fungal pathogen that causes basil downy mildew and can wipe out an entire planting of standard Genovese basil within days during warm, humid, or rainy weather — a near-annual problem for basil grown along the Gulf Coast. It retains the classic large, glossy, sweetly aromatic Genovese leaf and flavor prized for pesto and Italian cooking, without sacrificing disease resistance for flavor. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive all season; harvest leaves anytime once the plant is established, picking in the morning for the best essential oil content. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Di Cicco Broccoli (Italian Sprouting Broccoli, Continuous-Harvest Broccoli)
description: Set out transplants in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun during cool seasons; Di Cicco is a classic Italian heirloom sprouting broccoli dating to the nineteenth century — producing smaller, blue-green central heads followed by prolific side shoots (sideshoots) that continue producing edible florets for weeks or months after the central head is harvested. Unlike compact heading broccoli (Calabrese, Marathon) that produces one large head and then is done, Di Cicco is a continuous-harvest type — the plant continues to produce side shoot clusters for 6–10 weeks after the main head is cut, giving each plant a much longer productive season. In zone 9, Di Cicco is best planted in September–October for fall production, with continued harvest through the winter months. The open, branching plant habit and the loose, smaller head size of Di Cicco give it a more old-fashioned, informal appearance compared to tight-headed modern cultivars — but the flavor and the extended harvest period make it an excellent choice for the Gulf Coast kitchen garden where a long, productive cool-season broccoli is needed. Cold-tolerant to light freezes; protect from temperatures below 26°F. Matures in 48–68 days from transplant.

name: Di Huang (Chinese Foxglove, Rehmannia)
description: Grow in loose, deeply worked, fertile soil so the thick tuberous roots can expand without obstruction, and site in full sun to light afternoon shade in hotter climates. The plant forms a low rosette of hairy, wrinkled leaves and sends up spikes of tubular reddish-purple flowers reminiscent of foxglove, its distant relative. Fresh root or steamed, dried root is the part used in traditional Chinese herbalism, and mature roots are typically harvested in autumn after two full growing seasons. Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and mulch in colder zones since the crown can be marginally hardy where winters are severe. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Di Sicilia Viola Cauliflower (Sicilian Purple Heritage Cauliflower)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. botrytis 'Di Sicilia Viola'
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before planned fall transplanting date; set out in rich, fertile, moist soil; Di Sicilia Viola matures later than modern hybrids (85–100 days) but produces heads of exceptional flavor — considered by Italian cooks to be superior to any hybrid purple cauliflower. Di Sicilia Viola (Sicilian Violet) is a traditional heirloom purple cauliflower from Sicily, where purple and violet cauliflower varieties have been grown for centuries as an important winter vegetable in Sicilian cuisine. The Sicilian purple types are the oldest cultivated purple cauliflowers in the world and are quite distinct from modern purple hybrids like Graffiti — they mature later (85–100 days versus 70–80 for hybrids), produce looser, less uniformly round heads, and have a distinctly different flavor: richer, more complex, and sweeter than modern varieties, with a particular quality when braised or roasted that traditional Sicilian cooks consider superior to any modern hybrid. In Sicily, Di Sicilia Viola is used in pasta con i cavolfiori alla palermitana (pasta with cauliflower, olives, pine nuts, raisins, and saffron — one of the signature dishes of Palermo), roasted with olive oil and capers, and in arancini (Sicilian rice balls). The longer maturity makes it best suited as a fall crop in zones 5–9, where it matures into cool fall weather that intensifies the purple color and sweetens the flavor. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Di Sicilia Violetto Purple Cauliflower
description: This rare Italian heirloom forms striking violet-purple curds with a tender texture and mild, subtly nutty flavor. Start seed indoors about six weeks before setting out, then transplant into rich, evenly moist soil for steady, uninterrupted growth. Feed regularly and keep water consistent, since stress can cause loose or bitter heads. Cut heads while the curds are firm and richly colored, knowing the purple may soften toward green when cooked. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Diablo Brussels Sprout (Disease-Resistant Frost-Sweetened F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Diablo is a hybrid Brussels sprout bred with strong overall disease resistance, including tolerance to white blister and ring spot, two fungal diseases that can disfigure sprouts in humid, wet conditions. Its sprouts sweeten after exposure to frost, so a Gulf Coast fall planting that carries into the region's cool but mild winter can produce a long, steadily improving harvest. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Diamant Celeriac
description: A German-bred open-pollinated celeriac long favored by market growers for producing round, relatively smooth globes with fewer fibrous rootlets than older celeriac types, which makes peeling and trimming considerably easier. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out only once nights stay reliably above freezing. Keep the bed evenly and constantly moist through the long growing season, and periodically strip away side shoots and surface roots to concentrate growth into a dense, clean-skinned globe that stores well into winter. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Diamante Citron (Classic Italian Candying Citron)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate. Diamante is the classic Italian citron cultivar, named for the coastal Calabrian town where it has been cultivated for centuries, grown almost entirely for its extraordinarily thick, sweet, aromatic white rind, which is the traditional source of candied citron peel used in panettone, fruitcake, and other European confections. The fruit itself is large, bumpy, and pale yellow, with relatively little pulp or juice compared to the mass of rind, and the whole fruit is typically processed rather than eaten fresh. Like other citrons it is quite cold-sensitive and benefits from a sheltered, frost-free site or container culture that can be moved to protection during freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Diamond Eggplant (Classic Large Globe Purple Eggplant)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Diamond is a classic open-pollinated eggplant variety of Eastern European origin — an old, reliable, large-fruited cultivar producing oval to slightly pear-shaped, deep purple-black fruits with a glossy, smooth skin and white, firm, mild-flavored flesh with minimal bitterness. The fruits reach 4–6 inches long and 3–4 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — large, substantial fruits with good wall thickness and flavor. Diamond is one of the most commonly grown open-pollinated eggplant varieties in American home gardens for its combination of large fruit size, classic flavor, outstanding productivity, and the practical advantage of being a true open-pollinated variety from which seeds can be saved true to type season after season. The compact, upright plants (24–36 inches) produce prolifically from transplanting through the first killing frost. The key to quality eggplant is harvesting before the seeds fully develop: pick when the skin is shiny and fruits yield slightly to gentle pressure — dull skin indicates over-ripeness and bitter, seedy flesh. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables and produce reliably from a spring planting through early summer, with a fall crop from an August transplanting that often outlasts the tomatoes. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Diamond Grape (Moore's Diamond, Historic White American Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Diamond, also known as Moore's Diamond, is a white American grape introduced in the 1880s, producing greenish-yellow berries in compact clusters with a mild, sweet flavor much less pronounced in the musky 'foxy' Labrusca character than many other American grapes, making it a pleasant fresh-eating and juice grape as well as a wine grape valued for delicate white wines. It is self-fruitful and ripens in early to midseason with good vigor and disease resistance for its type. As a high-chill Labrusca-derived grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Diamond River Longan
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Diamond River is a Florida-selected longan valued for combining good fruit quality with markedly better cold tolerance than 'Kohala' and other tropical longan selections, allowing it to be grown successfully in zone 9 areas of the Gulf South where longan was historically considered too tender to fruit reliably. Clusters of thin-shelled, tan-brown fruit ripen in mid-to-late summer, with sweet, juicy, translucent flesh similar in flavor to lychee but more floral and less acidic. Prune young trees to an open, low-branched form for wind resistance and ease of frost-cloth coverage during establishment; mature trees need protection only in unusually severe freezes. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Diane Sweet Potato (Heavy-Yielding Louisiana Copper-Skin Type)
description: Diane was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a high-yielding sweet potato with smooth copper skin and deep orange flesh, developed to out-produce older Louisiana standards of its era. It shows useful tolerance to soil pox and resistance to white grubs, though like many older cultivars it is susceptible to root-knot nematode, so rotate beds or choose a nematode-resistant companion cultivar if that pest is a known problem in the garden. The vigorous vines and heavy root set reward rich, deeply worked soil and consistent moisture during the bulking stage in mid-to-late summer. Its dependable heavy yield made it a longtime favorite among Gulf Coast home growers before newer LSU releases like Beauregard and Evangeline became more widely available. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Dickinson Pumpkin (Kentucky Field Pumpkin, Libby's Select)
description: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, giving vines ample room to sprawl, and let fruit fully mature on the vine until the rind hardens and dulls in color. Traced to early nineteenth-century Kentucky and carried to central Illinois by farmer Elijah Dickinson, this tan, oblong pumpkin is more closely related botanically to butternut squash than to typical jack-o'-lantern types. Libby's acquired rights to the strain in 1929, and the Dickinson pumpkin remains the primary variety grown for canned pumpkin in the United States today, prized for its dense, smooth-textured, deep orange flesh. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Dimpled Brown Crowder Pea (Bush-Type Flattened Crowder Cowpea)
description: Dimpled Brown Crowder is a bush-type southern pea whose seeds are packed so tightly in the pod that they take on a flattened, dimpled shape, the classic crowder trait. Large pods each hold 12-15 seeds, and plants are prolific yielders good for freezing, canning, or drying. Fresh green-shell shellies can be picked well before the roughly 80 days needed for fully dry pods, giving a long harvest window from one planting. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Diplomat Broccoli (Downy Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil; Diplomat is a broccoli hybrid bred with resistance to downy mildew, a fungal disease that thrives in the cool, damp weather typical of a Gulf South winter broccoli crop and can otherwise blemish and stunt developing heads. It forms dense, uniform, blue-green heads on a plant that tolerates both heat during establishment and cold during head development, giving it flexibility across spring and fall plantings. After the central head is cut, side shoots continue to develop, extending the harvest for several more weeks. Cut the main head while the buds are still tight and before any yellow petals show, then keep harvesting side shoots as they reach a similar tight-bud stage. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Diplomat Dill (Slow-Bolt European)
description: Diplomat is a European-bred dill developed for commercial fresh-cut dill weed production, valued for tall, sturdy plants that resist lodging and a leafy stage that persists well before the plant switches to flowering. The blue-green foliage is finely cut and aromatic, holding good quality for bunching and fresh cutting over an extended harvest period. Its slower transition to bloom compared with older field varieties gives gardeners more flexibility in timing successive sowings through the cool part of the season. Allow a portion of the planting to flower and set seed heads if dill seed is also wanted for pickling. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Dipper Gourd
description: This heirloom hardshell gourd produces distinctive long-handled fruits reaching up to two feet, useful for ladles, birdhouses, and crafts. Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines a sturdy trellis so the handles hang straight. Water steadily through the long season and let fruits fully mature on the vine. Harvest after the stems dry and cure the gourds in a dry, airy space for several weeks until the shells harden and rattle. Matures in 120–140 days from seed.

name: Dirani Summer Squash
description: This pale, tender squash is ideal for the Middle Eastern stuffed dish koosa, thanks to its firm flesh and hollow-friendly shape. The compact plants produce continuously all summer, and large leaves shade and protect developing fruit. Harvest young and often to keep production going. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Provide steady moisture and good airflow to limit mildew. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Discovery Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Discovery is one of the earliest apples of the season and does not store for long once picked. Bred in Essex, England in the mid-twentieth century, this bright red, crisp early-season apple is prized for being one of the first dessert apples ready to eat each year, typically harvested in late summer well ahead of most other varieties, with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart white flesh that occasionally shows an attractive pink-tinged blush just under the skin. Its early ripening and reliable, moderate cropping have made it a popular home garden choice for gardeners eager for the first fresh apple of the season, though the fruit is best eaten within a few weeks of picking rather than stored long-term. Harvest in mid-to-late summer as soon as fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Disharoon Apple (Rediscovered Georgia Heirloom Dessert Apple)
description: Named for the north Georgia grower on whose land it was found in the mid-1850s, Disharoon produces medium, roundish fruit flattened at the ends, with green skin taking on a yellowish-gold hue on the sunny side and numerous obscure greenish, russet-centered dots. The pale yellow flesh is tender, moderately juicy, crisp, and sweet, making it a well-regarded dessert apple rather than primarily a cooking or cider type. Fruit ripens in September to October, fitting into the early-fall harvest window for Deep South orchards. Long believed extinct, it survives today only in a few Southern heirloom collections working from Lee Calhoun's documentation of Georgia's old apple varieties. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dittany of Crete (Hop Marjoram)
description: Plant in sharply drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; dittany of Crete is one of the most distinctive and ornamental of all Mediterranean herbs — a native of the rocky hillsides of Crete and the eastern Aegean producing small, rounded, densely woolly, silver-gray leaves so thickly covered with white hairs that the plant appears to be made of pale velvet or silver felt, with a warm, spicy aromatic scent when brushed. In summer it produces nodding clusters of small pink to purple flowers surrounded by overlapping, hop-like, purple-green bracts in elegant dangling clusters — both the foliage and flowers being remarkably ornamental. It has been valued since antiquity: Aristotle described wild goats eating it to remove arrows from wounds; it appears in Virgil and Pliny as a wound herb; and it is still used in Cretan herbal tea and liqueur (Cretan digestif). Outstanding as a trailing container plant where the woolly, nodding flower clusters can cascade over the pot edge. Related to culinary oregano but much more ornamental than culinary. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Diva Cucumber (Seedless Thin-Skinned Cucumber)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Diva is an All-America Selections Award winner (2002) and one of the most acclaimed cucumbers introduced in the past quarter century — a parthenocarpic (self-fruitful, seedless) cucumber that produces extremely uniform, smooth-skinned, 6–8 inch fruits with thin, tender, never-bitter skin that requires no peeling and no bitterness removal. Unlike most cucumbers that require cross-pollination by insects for reliable fruit set, Diva is parthenocarpic — each flower sets fruit without pollination, ensuring consistent production regardless of pollinator activity. The fruit is reliably seedless or nearly so, with crisp, mild, sweet flesh and completely absent the bitterness that affects some cucumbers. Diva's thin skin, which requires no peeling, and its mild, sweet, never-bitter flavor make it outstanding for fresh eating, salads, and children's snacking. The vigorous, prolific vines produce heavily over a long season — harvest fruits at 6–8 inches before seeds begin to develop for the best eating quality. In zone 9, Diva performs well in the spring and fall growing windows and is among the most heat-tolerant, productive cucumbers for the Gulf South. Matures in 54–60 days from seed.

name: Divergent Melon (Fusarium-Resistant Galia-Cantaloupe Hybrid)
description: Direct sow in warm soil, thinning to 2 plants per hill spaced 3-4 feet apart; Divergent is a galia-type melon crossed with cantaloupe genetics, bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt (a soil-borne fungal disease that can persist in garden soil for years) along with intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, making it a resilient choice for gardens where melons have struggled with disease in the past. The smaller, aromatic fruit has the sweet, floral flavor typical of galia melons with the familiar netted rind of a cantaloupe, ripening earlier than many standard cantaloupe varieties. Harvest when the skin turns from green to golden-tan under the netting and the fruit slips easily from the vine with a fragrant aroma at the stem end. Because it is an organic-bred hybrid popular with market growers, it performs well under lower-input, disease-conscious growing conditions. Matures in 68–78 days from seed.

name: Dixie Butterpea (Compact Bush Southern Lima)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Dixie Butterpea is a compact bush-type lima bean, sparing gardeners the trellising that pole lima varieties require while still delivering the classic small, mild-flavored, buttery-textured seeds Southern cooks know as butterpeas or butter beans. The bush habit concentrates its harvest into a shorter window than pole types, making it convenient for a single large batch of shelling and canning or freezing, and the plant's heat tolerance suits it well to Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled for classic butterpea flavor, and succession sow every few weeks through summer for a more continuous supply if desired. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Dixie Crimson Clover (Long-Season Gulf South Winter Annual Cover Crop Clover)
description: Broadcast or drill seed in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is the preferred crimson clover variety for Gulf South cover crop use — selected specifically for the warmer winter conditions of the Deep South where it outperforms northern varieties by remaining vegetative longer before bolting to flower, providing a longer window of ground cover, weed suppression, and nitrogen fixation. Crimson clover is the most widely used winter annual legume cover crop in the Gulf South, seeded after the main crop harvest in October–November, establishing through the cool months, fixing atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, then terminated by mowing, rolling, or light tillage in spring before planting warm-season vegetables. A well-established stand of crimson clover can fix 50–100 pounds of nitrogen per acre — equivalent to a significant fertilizer application — while also improving soil organic matter, preventing winter erosion, and suppressing winter weeds. The 'Dixie' variety's later bolting (compared to 'Autauga' and other early varieties) is its primary advantage in zone 9: it maintains active vegetative growth through February and into March in most years, providing several extra weeks of weed suppression and soil coverage before initiating the red, conical flower heads that signal the end of the vegetative growth period. The showy crimson flower heads that precede termination are also excellent for early-spring pollinators. Inoculate seed with legume inoculant when planting in fields with no history of crimson clover. Matures in 180–240 days from seed.

name: Dixie Golden Giant Tomato (Very Large Golden-Yellow Southern Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Dixie Golden Giant is a southern heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (1–2+ lb), round to slightly flattened fruits in a golden-yellow to deep-yellow color with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid, meaty flesh that is characteristic of the finest golden beefsteak types. The very large size and golden-yellow color combine to make Dixie Golden Giant one of the most visually impressive golden tomatoes — the large yellow fruits sliced on a plate have a beautiful, rich golden color and the thick, dense flesh produces substantial slices without excess seeding or gel. The flavor is typical of the best large yellow heirlooms: very sweet, very mild, fruity, and low in acid — appealing to those who find standard red tomatoes too sharp or acidic. As a southern-adapted heirloom that has been selected and maintained in Gulf South gardens, Dixie Golden Giant may show somewhat better adaptation to zone 9 conditions than northern golden beefsteak types — though all very large beefsteak tomatoes are challenging to grow through Gulf South summer heat and produce best in the spring growing season (February–June). An open-pollinated variety with saveable seed that grows true-to-type from season to season. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Dixie Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is a large, dark-skinned muscadine released by the University of Georgia, producing very large, round, dark purple to black berries with a sweet, rich flavor and thin, relatively tender skin that makes fresh eating more comfortable than older tough-skinned muscadine varieties. As a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) cultivar, Dixie sets heavy crops reliably without a pollinator vine — a significant practical advantage for home gardeners. The late-season ripening (September–October in zone 9) extends the fresh muscadine harvest into fall when most other fresh fruit has finished. The vigorous vines are productive once established and show good resistance to the common muscadine diseases including black rot and angular leaf spot that can be problems in the humid Gulf South. Dixie pairs well with Triumph (bronze) for a complementary planting that provides both dark and bronze-skinned muscadines from the same trellis system. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dixie Queen Watermelon (Round Striped Southern Heirloom)
description: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Dixie Queen is a classic Southern heirloom watermelon dating to the early 20th century, producing round-to-oval fruit with light and dark green striping and sweet, bright red flesh with good old-fashioned watermelon flavor. It was once a popular commercial variety before being largely displaced by modern hybrids bred for tougher rinds and shipping durability, but it remains a favorite among heirloom growers for its reliable production and classic taste in the home garden. Vines are vigorous and productive over a moderate-length season, and fruits typically run in the 15-25 pound range, a manageable size for home use. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Dixie Speckled Butterpea (Red-Speckled Southern Bush Lima)
description: Direct sow into warm, light, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants close in rows about two feet apart since this variety stays compact and needs no support. This old Southern bush butterpea produces heavily branched plants that keep flowering and setting pods through the hottest, driest stretches of summer when many bean types shut down. Pods run about four inches long and typically hold three or four small, rounded seeds boldly mottled maroon-on-pink, a color pattern that sets it apart from plain cream-seeded butterpea types. Pick at the green-shell stage for classic buttery flavor, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage and seed saving. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Dixieland Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Bronze Cultivar)
description: Dixieland is a self-fertile bronze muscadine with medium-large berries, medium-tough skin, and excellent sweet flavor, making it a reliable choice where space allows for only one vine. It holds a notable place in muscadine breeding history as the pollen parent crossed with the black female cultivar Black Fry to produce the popular commercial cultivar Supreme. Yields can be somewhat uneven from year to year compared to the most productive modern releases, but fruit quality for fresh eating remains excellent. Train vines onto a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun and well-drained soil, and prune hard each winter to renew the fruiting wood for the following season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Dixielee Southern Pea (Disease-Resistant Cream Pea)
description: Direct sow in full sun into warm, well-drained soil, choosing this variety over other cream peas if root-knot nematode or fusarium wilt has been a problem in the bed. Dixielee was released by the University of Georgia specifically for its combined resistance to root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, and southern pea mosaic virus, packaged into a productive, semi-vining plant that yields extra-large cream-colored peas with excellent fresh and canning quality. Pods are borne well above the foliage for easy picking and hold their quality over a longer harvest window than many older cream-type varieties. As with other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods once they fill out and begin to yellow for fresh shelling, or leave to dry fully for storage. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Djena Lee's Golden Girl Tomato (Sweet Low-Acid Yellow Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Djena Lee's Golden Girl is an American heirloom yellow beefsteak tomato producing large, smooth, deep-golden fruit with sweet, mild, notably low-acid flesh that is easy on sensitive stomachs and a favorite for gardeners who find red tomatoes too sharp. It is a heavy, dependable producer for an heirloom, setting good yields of large fruit over a long season on a vigorous indeterminate vine. Stake or cage plants for support, water evenly to prevent cracking and blossom end rot, and pick fruit once the skin turns fully golden-yellow and gives slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Doe Hill Pepper (Doe Hill Golden Bell, Pre-1900 Virginia Heirloom Sweet Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperatures, then transplant into the garden once nights stay reliably above 55F and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Doe Hill is a pre-1900 Appalachian family heirloom named for the small town in Highland County, Virginia, prized for its small, flattened, deeply lobed bells that mature quickly from green to bright orange. The thick flesh and sweet, multidimensional flavor are notably good for such a small fruit, and its early, dependable production makes it an excellent choice for short-season gardens. Plants are compact and disease tolerant; harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or wait for full orange color and maximum sweetness. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Doerfler's Thyme
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Doerfler's thyme forms a dense, mat-forming carpet of small, gray-green, softly hairy leaves that give the foliage a silvery, felted appearance distinct from smoother-leaved culinary thymes. Clusters of small, rich pink to rose-lilac flowers cover the mat in late spring to early summer, drawing bees heavily and creating a striking two-toned effect against the silvery foliage. Like other creeping thymes, it tolerates light foot traffic and is well suited to planting between stepping stones, along path edges, or cascading over a low rock wall, releasing a mild aromatic scent when brushed or stepped on. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which shortens its life. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Dog Ridge Grape Rootstock (Vigorous Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Texas Understock)
description: Dog Ridge (sometimes written Dogridge) is a wild Vitis champinii selection first collected near Dog Ridge, Texas, prized as one of the most vigorous and deep-rooted grape rootstocks available, giving grafted vines excellent drought tolerance and the ability to thrive in poor, sandy, or infertile soils where own-rooted bunch grapes struggle. Like the related Tampa rootstock, it confers meaningful tolerance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by glassy-winged sharpshooters and other leafhoppers, and it also carries useful resistance to root-knot nematodes and phylloxera. Florida, Texas, and Gulf South growers choose between Dog Ridge and Tampa largely based on vigor and soil-type compatibility, since Dog Ridge tends to be the more vigorous of the two and is often favored on the poorest, driest sites. Bench-graft or bud a named bunch grape or muscadine cultivar onto young Dog Ridge rootstock in late winter or spring; left ungrafted, the vine is extremely rampant and produces only small, seedy black fruit of little culinary interest, so it is grown almost exclusively as an understock rather than for its own fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Dogridge Grape Rootstock
description: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; Dogridge is a highly vigorous, nematode-resistant understock bred for sandy Southern soils. Selected from a wild Texas grape species adapted to the sandy, nematode-prone soils of the Gulf South and Southern Plains, it is among the most vigorous grape rootstocks available, imparting strong nematode and Pierce's disease tolerance along with drought resistance once established, making it a favored choice for vineyards planted on marginal, sandy, or previously grape-planted soils in the warm-summer South. Its exceptional vigor can be excessive on rich soils, where it tends to promote overly vegetative growth at the expense of fruit quality unless managed with appropriate canopy and irrigation control. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and reserve it for sandy, low-fertility, or nematode-prone sites where its vigor and resistance traits are most valuable rather than a liability. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Dokwal (Korean Angelica, Manchurian Aralia)
description: This robust herbaceous perennial dies back to a woody crown each winter and pushes up thick new shoots in spring that are harvested young, before the huge compound leaves fully expand, in the same manner as Japanese angelica tree shoots. Peel and blanch the shoots to soften a mild, resinous bitterness, then stir-fry or season with sesame oil for a classic Korean spring vegetable known as dokwallamul. The root has a long history in Korean herbal medicine as well, though it is the tender shoots that make it worth growing in a shaded vegetable bed. Give it deep, rich soil and generous moisture and it will return reliably for many years from the same crown. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dolce Fresca Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Genovese Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container on a sunny patio. Dolce Fresca is an AAS-winning Genovese-type basil bred for a naturally compact, dense, dome-shaped habit and slower bolting than standard Genovese basil, so it holds its productive shape and classic sweet, clove-and-anise basil flavor for a longer stretch of the season without becoming leggy or rushing to flower. Its tidy size makes it especially well suited to containers, window boxes, and small kitchen gardens where a full-size Genovese plant would sprawl. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove any flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and delay bolting further; harvest leaves anytime once the plant is established, picking in the morning for the best flavor. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Dolgo Crabapple (Cold-Hardy Jelly Crabapple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, watering deeply through establishment and pruning in late winter to open the canopy for good air circulation. Dolgo was introduced from Russia in the early 1900s and became one of the most widely planted crabapples in cold-climate North America for its extreme hardiness, heavy fragrant white spring bloom, and abundant crop of oblong, bright red fruit up to an inch and a half long. The tart, high-pectin fruit sets bright red jelly and cider without added pectin and ripens in late summer, well ahead of most crabapples, so it is often harvested before other apples are even ready. Because it blooms early and profusely over a long window, Dolgo is also planted purely as a pollinizer tree in orchards of standard apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dolly Basil (High-Yield Field Genovese Basil)
description: Dolly is a high-yielding Genovese-type basil bred for field production, with large, cupped leaves up to 4 inches long that are somewhat lighter green than standard Genovese and lightly serrated at the margin. Plants are notably uniform in habit and leaf shape while remaining somewhat compact for the leaf size, giving good yield per square foot for market growers and home gardeners alike. Flavor is classic sweet basil, suited to pesto, Caprese salads, and general Italian cooking. Pinch out flower spikes to prolong leaf harvest, and cut whole stem tips regularly to keep plants bushy and productive through the season. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Dollywood American Persimmon
description: Dollywood was introduced by Illinois breeder James Claypool and is grown for its remarkably large, exceptionally sweet fruit on a spreading, productive tree. Full astringency until fully soft-ripe is typical of American persimmon, so let fruit color deeply and soften on the tree before harvest. It tolerates poor and compacted soils once established and needs little supplemental water in most regions. Because most American persimmons are dioecious, plant a male pollinator nearby unless the cultivar is confirmed self-fertile. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Donald Wyman Crabapple (Persistent Red-Fruited Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Named for the noted Arnold Arboretum horticulturist, Donald Wyman produces a heavy spring flush of white flowers from pink buds, followed by small, bright red fruit that persists on the branches well into winter, often until the following spring, providing months of ornamental interest and emergency food for birds during lean winter weeks. It is a vigorous, wide-spreading, disease-resistant crabapple with good resistance to apple scab, making it a dependable, low-maintenance flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, giving it room to reach its considerable mature spread. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dong Quai (Chinese Angelica, Female Ginseng)
description: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; dong quai is one of the most important herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine and ranks among the top-selling botanical supplements globally. The fleshy taproot, harvested in the fall of the third year of growth, has been used for over 2000 years in Chinese medicine primarily for women's reproductive health — regulating menstruation, easing menopausal symptoms, and treating anemia — earning the common name 'female ginseng.' Modern research confirms phytoestrogenic and blood-moving compounds in the root. Use only under guidance of a healthcare professional as it interacts with blood-thinning medications. The plant is a biennial to short-lived perennial that dies after flowering; remove flower stalks as they appear to extend the life of the root. Partial shade and consistent moisture are essential. Matures in 365–1095 days from seed.

name: Dongzao Jujube (Winter Jujube, Late-Season Honey-Sweet Chinese Jujube)
description: Dongzao, meaning 'winter jujube,' produces large fruit (roughly 25-30 grams) with an exceptionally crisp, juicy, almost melting texture and sugar content that can reach 25-30 Brix at full maturity, distinguishing it from crisper but less sweet Chinese selections already grown here. The tree is extremely cold-hardy in dormancy but is a late-maturing cultivar that needs a long, warm growing season to fully convert its sugars, which makes the extended Gulf Coast summer and fall an asset rather than a limitation. Fruit should be left on the tree until it colors fully to maximize sweetness, since Dongzao picked early is markedly less flavorful than fully ripened fruit. As with other jujubes, trees tolerate poor, alkaline, or compacted soil and need little irrigation once established, but appreciate full sun and good drainage to avoid root issues in Gulf Coast clay during wet winters. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Doon Major Rutabaga
description: Also sold under the name Major Dunne, this Scottish-origin swede was once a commercial variety in the British Isles before falling out of the seed trade and being preserved by seed-saving networks. Roots are more elongated than a typical rutabaga, with smooth golden-tan skin and purple shoulders, standing tall above the soil with vigorous leafy tops. It retains good texture and mild, sweet flavor even when roots are allowed to grow quite large. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Doone Valley Thyme (Gold-Variegated Lemon-Scented Creeping Thyme)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Doone Valley thyme is a low, mounding, spreading lemon thyme cultivar with dark green leaves speckled and edged in gold that flush deep bronze-red in cool fall and winter weather, giving it strong multi-season ornamental interest beyond its culinary use. The foliage carries a distinct lemony fragrance and flavor, milder and more citrusy than common thyme, and is good for teas, poultry and fish dishes, and infused oils and vinegars. Small pale lilac flowers appear in early summer and attract bees. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh new growth, and avoid heavy, wet soils, which lead to crown rot. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Doreen Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Doreen is a bronze muscadine released by Mississippi State University in 1979 and named for a long-serving clerical employee at the university's experiment station. It is the most widely used late-season bronze muscadine, valued by commercial growers and home winemakers for extending the harvest season past Carlos and Scuppernong into late September and October. Yields are among the highest of any self-fertile bronze variety, making Doreen important for commercial production where volume matters. Berries are medium-sized, bronze-tan at maturity with a pleasant, mild muscadine flavor and good sugar content that makes excellent late-season wine. The plants are very vigorous and productive with strong disease resistance. Doreen is often planted in combination with Carlos to extend the bronze muscadine season from mid-August through October and to provide a range of flavors for blending. Prune heavily each winter; leave only short spurs on permanent cordon arms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Doretta Klaber Thyme (Tight Miniature Mat-Forming Thyme)
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun. Doretta Klaber is a miniature thyme cultivar with minute, fuzzy gray-green leaves that form an exceptionally tight, ground-hugging mat, among the tightest-growing forms in the genus, so dense that few weeds can compete once it is established. Tufts of deep lavender-pink flowers cover the mat in early summer, and the foliage takes on mahogany tones in cold weather for extra seasonal interest. Its diminutive scale suits troughs, stone walls, staircases, and the cracks between paving stones far better than open groundcover use. Shear lightly after bloom to keep growth dense, and avoid heavy or wet soil, which quickly rots the shallow roots. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Doric Brussels Sprout (RHS AGM Early Season F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant firmly into rich, well-drained soil and firm the base of each plant well since Doric's strength is its short, sturdy stem rather than height; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward as they firm and tighten. Doric is a widely grown F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, prized for its strong, compact, wind-resistant stems and heavy yields of smooth, bright, tightly rounded sprouts with good resistance to fusarium and useful tolerance of white blister and mildew. Because the plants stay shorter and stockier than many hybrids, staking needs are minimal even in exposed sites, and the whole stalk can be cut and stood in a cool spot to extend the usable harvest well past when the sprouts would otherwise be picked. Doric's long cropping window, from late autumn through midwinter, and its dependable disease tolerance make it a practical workhorse choice for a sustained home sprout harvest. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Dorman Red Raspberry (Heat-Tolerant Deep South Trailing Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun and trellis the long, trailing canes on a two-wire support, since this variety sprawls rather than growing upright. Selected in the Deep South specifically to withstand summer heat that kills most raspberry cultivars outright, Dorman Red is one of the few raspberries that reliably fruits in zone 8-9 gardens where standard northern types decline within a year or two. It produces a single crop in late spring on second-year canes, with medium-sized, tart-sweet red berries that are excellent for preserves as well as fresh eating. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest to make room for the current season's new growth, and keep roots mulched to buffer summer soil heat. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Dorris Hazelnut (Blight-Resistant Oregon Filbert)
description: Dorris was released by the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program with strong resistance to eastern filbert blight, the disease that devastated older European cultivars across the Pacific Northwest. It bears large, round, high-quality kernels on a vigorous, upright tree and ripens in the midseason window alongside cultivars like Jefferson. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible blight-resistant pollinizer nearby, since hazelnuts will not set a crop alone. Harvest begins once nuts drop free of the husk in early fall; gather promptly from the ground to beat squirrels and reduce mold risk. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dorset Golden Apple (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf Coast Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Dorset Golden is one of the two or three apple cultivars with the lowest chill requirements that can be reliably grown in Gulf South zone 9 gardens — requiring only 100–200 chilling hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break and fruit set. This ultra-low chill requirement makes Dorset Golden one of the very few apples that can be grown productively in the Gulf South where total winter chill hours range from 200–600 hours in zone 9, often falling short of the 700–1,000+ hours required by standard northern apple varieties. Dorset Golden originated as a chance seedling in the Bahamas — an unexpected confirmation that apples with very low chill requirements can produce high-quality fruit in tropical and subtropical climates. The fruit is medium to large, golden-yellow with a light blush, and has a firm, crisp texture with a good balance of sweetness and mild acidity — far superior in flavor to most other low-chill apple varieties. In zone 9, Dorset Golden ripens in June — exceptionally early for a full-sized apple. It is partially self-fertile but produces larger crops when cross-pollinated with Anna (another ultra-low-chill variety). For Gulf South apple growing, pair Dorset Golden with Anna for reliable cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Dorset Naga Pepper (UK-Bred Superhot Capsicum chinense)
description: Give Dorset Naga a long, warm season indoors before transplanting, since it needs more heat units than a standard habanero to fully ripen its fruit to deep red. This English-developed selection was bred from Bangladeshi naga stock and yields smoother, more elongated pods than typical wrinkled bhut jolokia types, with fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Stake plants once fruit load builds, and pick some pods slightly early if frost threatens since later flushes often fail to color up in short seasons. It is best suited to collectors in long, hot-summer regions or to greenhouse culture where a longer ripening window can be guaranteed. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Dorsett Golden Apple
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dorsett Golden originated as a chance seedling discovered in the Bahamas by Irene Dorsett in the 1950s, thriving in a climate with almost no winter chill. It requires only 100–200 chill hours — the lowest of any significant apple cultivar — and produces reliable crops in zone 9b–10a where even Anna struggles. The medium-large, golden-yellow fruits resemble Golden Delicious in appearance but ripen 2–3 weeks before Anna (April–May in zone 9), making it the first ripe apple of the season in the deep South. Flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasant with moderately crisp flesh. Dorsett Golden is partially self-fertile but sets significantly heavier crops when cross-pollinated with Anna or Ein Shemer. In zone 10, this trio of low-chill apple varieties (Anna, Dorsett Golden, Ein Shemer) makes apple growing possible where it would have been considered impossible a generation ago. Fire blight can be a problem — avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes lush growth susceptible to infection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dotted Hawthorn
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along forest edges, stream banks, or open lowlands; dotted hawthorn is among the showiest of the eastern native hawthorns, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of white flowers in spring that are excellent pollinator forage, followed by heavy crops of round, dull-red to yellow haws distinctively spotted with pale lenticels — the 'dots' that give the species its name. The persistent haws are eagerly consumed by cedar waxwings, robins, grouse, and foxes through fall and early winter, making this one of the most productive wildlife trees in its native range. It forms a dense, thorny canopy well suited to wildlife hedgerows or naturalized areas where its formidable spines can serve as a living fence. Seeds require double dormancy and may take two full seasons to germinate; container-grown transplants establish most reliably. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Dotted Horsemint (Spotted Beebalm)
description: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established and one of the best late-summer nectar plants for a huge diversity of native bees and wasps. Monarda punctata (dotted horsemint, or spotted beebalm) is a striking native mint-family perennial with an unusual bloom structure quite different from typical bee balm: pale creamy-yellow flowers marked with fine purple spots are packed into tight whorls stacked in tiers up the stem, each whorl subtended by showy, pale pink to lavender bracts that provide much of the plant's ornamental color and persist attractively after the small flowers fade. The strongly aromatic, thymol-scented foliage was traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and early American settlers as a source of thyme-like oil and as a folk remedy. In late summer, the plant becomes a genuine pollinator magnet, attracting an exceptional diversity of native bees, wasps, and other beneficial insects, more so than almost any other native perennial. An outstanding, easy-care choice for a dry, sunny pollinator garden or sandy coastal planting, zone 4–9. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Double Delight Nectarine (Showy Double-Flowering Ornamental Fruiting Nectarine)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Double Delight is grown as much for its spectacular spring floral display as for its fruit, opening large, fully double, deep pink blossoms that rival an ornamental flowering peach or cherry before setting a genuinely good crop of sweet, white-fleshed, freestone nectarines in summer. This dual-purpose ornamental-and-edible quality makes it a popular choice for home landscapes wanting a fruit tree that earns its space as a spring showpiece as well as a producer. Like other nectarines, the smooth skin makes it more susceptible to brown rot and other fungal issues than fuzzy-skinned peaches, so a dormant-season spray program helps protect both the spectacular bloom and the eventual fruit crop. Thin fruit after natural drop for the best size and flavor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Double G Mayhaw (Heavy-Bearing Texas Star x Royal Star Hybrid Mayhaw)
description: Double G is a cross between the Texas Star and Royal Star mayhaw selections, chosen for dark red fruit with distinctive strawberry-colored pulp and for combining heavy production with some of the best fire blight resistance of any named mayhaw. Like Maxine, it develops a naturally open, upside-down-umbrella canopy that needs little pruning to fruit well. It blooms relatively late, which helps it avoid spring frost damage, and Louisiana growers report some of the heaviest yields among named mayhaw selections from this cultivar. Grow it on wet to moist, acidic soil in full sun with a second cultivar nearby for pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Double Greater Celandine (Flore Pleno Tetterwort)
description: Flore Pleno is a double-flowered heirloom selection of greater celandine, replacing the wild species' simple four-petaled blooms with small, pompom-like clusters of golden-yellow petals held above the same lobed, blue-gray foliage. Because the doubled flowers set little to no viable seed, this cultivar spreads far more slowly than the free-seeding wild type, making it a better-behaved choice for cottage and woodland borders. Grow it in the same dry shade and disturbed soil the species tolerates, dividing congested clumps in fall to increase stock. Handle broken stems with care, since the bright orange latex sap is caustic and can irritate skin, exactly as in the straight species. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Double Mahoi Banana (Dwarf Hawaiian Double-Bunching Banana)
description: Double Mahoi is a Hawaiian-origin sport of Dwarf Cavendish notable for an unusual trait: a single pseudostem can push out two flowering heads and mature two full bunches instead of the normal one, a rare habit in edible bananas. The fruit is a sweet, creamy Cavendish-type dessert banana, and the plant's compact stature makes it well suited to patios and large containers. It has no meaningful cold hardiness, so the pseudostem must be protected from frost, and it is best treated as a container specimen moved under cover before temperatures drop into the 40s. Give it full sun, rich soil, and heavy summer feeding to support its doubled fruit load. Matures in 270–450 days from transplant.

name: Double Roman Chamomile (Flore Pleno)
description: Plant divisions into well-drained soil and water them in well, then let the low, apple-scented foliage knit into a dense mat over the season. Unlike the single-flowered species, 'Flore Pleno' produces fully double, button-like white blooms that are especially prized for drying into chamomile tea and for scenting chamomile lawns and garden seats. It tolerates light foot traffic and releases a sweet, fruity fragrance when brushed or mown, but it flowers less heavily in deep shade or overly rich soil. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Double Standard Sweet Corn (Bicolor SE Hybrid Corn)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row, since corn is wind-pollinated and needs neighbors on all sides for full ears. Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced bicolor hybrid that carries the classic tender-creamy texture of older SE types rather than the crisper, sometimes tough texture of supersweet (sh2) hybrids, and it germinates dependably in soil a bit cooler than most supersweets tolerate, which suits an early planting. Ears fill out with a mix of white and yellow kernels and hold good eating quality in the garden for several days past peak without turning starchy as fast as older open-pollinated types. Succession-sow every two to three weeks through early summer for a extended harvest, and pick when silks have browned and a punctured kernel weeps milky juice. Matures in 68–70 days from seed.

name: Double Take Orange Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Quince)
description: Double Take Orange carries fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in bright orange, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, and was specifically bred to be thornless, unlike the sharply spined branches of traditional flowering quince. Because the flowers are fully double and largely sterile, the shrub produces little to no fruit, putting its energy entirely into the showy bloom display rather than fruit set, and making it easier to handle for pruning, cutting for arrangements, or planting near a walkway. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next season's flower buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Double Take Pink Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Quince)
description: Double Take Pink bears fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in soft pink, opening directly on bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, and like its Double Take series siblings was bred to be thornless, unlike the sharply spined branches of traditional flowering quince. Because the flowers are fully double and largely sterile, the shrub sets little to no fruit, putting its energy into the showy bloom display and making it easier to handle for pruning or cutting for arrangements without the scratches typical of older quince cultivars. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next season's flower buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Double Take Scarlet Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Red Quince)
description: Double Take Scarlet produces fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in a rich, saturated red, opening on bare stems in late winter into early spring before the foliage emerges, giving one of the boldest early-season color displays of any hardy shrub. Bred thornless like its Double Take series siblings, it lacks the sharp spines that make older flowering quince cultivars unpleasant to prune or work around, and its largely sterile double flowers mean little to no fruit forms, concentrating the plant's energy into bloom. It tolerates poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and needs very little care beyond pruning right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning at other times removes the coming season's flowers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Double Yield Cucumber
description: Introduced in 1924, this prolific heirloom bears slender, dark-green fruit 4 to 6 inches long, ideal for pickling or fresh slicing. Frequent picking spurs even heavier production, living up to the name. Grow on a trellis to save space and keep fruit clean and straight. Sow into warm, rich soil and water consistently to avoid bitterness. Keep vines evenly moist during flowering and fruiting. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Douglas #1A Chestnut (Blight-Resistant Chinese Chestnut Hybrid Selection)
description: Douglas #1A is a Chinese chestnut hybrid selected by breeder E. Douglas and carries recorded resistance to chestnut blight. Nuts are modest in size, around 8 grams, and ripen early, typically from the first to the third week of September, making it a useful early-season selection in a mixed chestnut planting. Like most chestnuts, it will not self-pollinate reliably and should be planted with a distinct, overlapping-bloom cultivar nearby. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Douglas Pear (Fire-Blight-Tolerant Texas Home Orchard Pear)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Douglas is grouped with Kieffer, Orient, and Garber as a moderately fire-blight-resistant Southern pear recommended for Texas home orchards by the Texas Plant Disease Handbook, tolerating the humid conditions that make European dessert pears difficult to grow without heavy spraying. Fruit has the firm, somewhat gritty texture typical of Southern-adapted pears, well suited to canning and preserving as well as fresh eating once fully ripened off the tree. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature for the best texture. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Doum Palm
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, alkaline, lean, arid soil; Hyphaene thebaica is adapted to extreme desert and semi-arid conditions — drought tolerant, heat tolerant, alkaline-soil adapted, and saline-tolerant; avoid clay or wet soils. Hyphaene thebaica (Doum Palm, Gingerbread Palm, or Egyptian Doum) is a large, majestic, fan palm native to the Nile Valley, northeastern Africa, and the dry savannas and deserts of sub-Saharan Africa from Egypt and Sudan through East Africa to South Africa — one of the most distinctive and botanically remarkable palms in the world because of its naturally dichotomously branching trunk. Unlike virtually all other true palms (which are monocots and cannot branch), Hyphaene thebaica produces true dichotomous bifurcation at each growing point, creating a naturally multi-headed, tree-like branching architecture that makes it instantly recognizable and utterly unlike any other palm. The large (2–4 inch), smooth, orange-brown fruits have a hard, starchy, dry, reddish inner mesocarp with a flavor and texture remarkably similar to gingerbread — giving the common name 'Gingerbread Palm.' The fruits were a significant food source in ancient Egypt — doum fruit has been found in Egyptian tombs dating to 3200 BCE and is depicted in reliefs at Luxor and Karnak. The hard endosperm ('vegetable ivory') is carved into buttons and small ornaments. Excellent accent palm for hot, dry, alkaline-soil landscapes in zone 8–11. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Doux d'Espagne Pepper (Sweet of Spain Frying Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off seedlings, and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Harvest elongated fruit green for a mild, grassy flavor or let them ripen fully to red for a sweeter, richer taste well suited to roasting and frying. Doux d'Espagne ('Sweet of Spain') is a 19th-century French heirloom frying pepper producing long, tapered, blocky-shouldered fruit up to 6–8 inches that are thin-walled and entirely sweet with no heat, similar in use to Italian frying types but with a distinctively rich, old-world flavor. Plants are productive and tolerate a range of soils, making this a dependable choice for gardeners wanting a classic European sweet pepper for skillet cooking rather than fresh salad use. Fruit is best picked while walls are still tender, since older peppers can develop a slightly tougher skin. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Doux Long des Landes Pepper (French Heirloom Sweet Frying Pepper)
description: Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Doux Long des Landes is a traditional French sweet pepper named for the Landes region of southwestern France, producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen from pale green to red with a mild, sweet flavor and virtually no heat. Its thin flesh makes it well suited to quick pan-frying in oil in the French country style, or to roasting whole until the skin blisters and slips off easily. The plants are productive over a long season and tolerate the warm, humid summers common in the Gulf South. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Downing Gooseberry (Classic American Heirloom Gooseberry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Downing is a nineteenth-century American gooseberry, a Houghton seedling introduced in the 1850s and still one of the most widely planted heirloom gooseberries because of its reliable production, vigorous growth, and good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many European gooseberry cultivars. Berries are medium-sized, pale green, and tart, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, picked slightly underripe for cooking or left to fully ripen for a milder, sweeter fresh-eating berry. The self-fertile bush needs no separate pollinator and bears reliably from a young age. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the thorny bush productive and open enough for easy harvest, and site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Downing Mulberry (Historic American Sweet Black-Fruited Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Downing was selected in the mid-1800s from the mulberry plantings established during the era of American silk-culture experiments and became the first widely distributed named mulberry cultivar in the United States, prized above seedling trees for its consistently excellent flavor. The tree bears an abundance of long, cylindrical, glossy black fruit over a several-week summer harvest window, with a rich, sweet, low-acid flavor good for fresh eating, preserves, and drying. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and adaptable to a wide range of soils, tolerating heat and some drought once established, though it lacks the extreme cold hardiness of the later alba-rubra hybrid selections bred for northern climates. Site away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the juicy ripe fruit drops steadily and stains hard surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Downy Ground Cherry (Husk Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors in individual cells 6-8 weeks before the last frost date, transplanting to the garden once soils are reliably warm and settled; downy ground cherry is a more compact, earlier-maturing species than the common tomatillo, and its small yellow fruits — each wrapped in a papery tan husk — carry a distinctive sweetness with vanilla and citrus undertones that makes them exceptional for jams, pies, salsas, and fresh eating. Fruits are ready to harvest when they fall from the plant or when the husk turns papery-tan and the fruit fills it completely. Like its relatives, this Physalis will self-sow freely in warm climates, often returning year after year from fallen fruits. Space plants generously and stake or cage them as they develop a somewhat sprawling, branching habit under productive conditions. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Downy Hawthorn (Large-Fruited Hawthorn, Red Haw)
description: Plant in full sun to light shade in any fertile, well-drained to moist soil; downy hawthorn (Crataegus mollis) is among the largest-fruited native hawthorns in the eastern United States, producing abundant clusters of large, red-orange fruits (haws) nearly 3/4 to 1 inch across in late summer — far more substantial than most hawthorn species — that are suitable for making jelly, jam, and fruit leather with a pleasant, apple-like flavor. The tree itself is large and spreading with downy (hairy) leaves and branchlets and spectacular white flowers in spring. An outstanding wildlife tree providing critical food for over 100 species of birds and mammals, and exceptional browse habitat for deer and rabbits. The thorny branches also provide nesting protection for songbirds. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Downy Serviceberry (Shadblow)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the colonial serviceberry (A. canadensis), this species develops a single trunk to form a graceful multi-season small tree with spectacular clouds of white flowers in early spring, blueberry-like fruit in June, and brilliant orange-red fall foliage. The sweet berries ripen all at once in early summer and are excellent fresh, dried like raisins, or used in pies and jams; birds compete fiercely for the crop. Prune to remove crossing branches in late winter; do not top the tree. Cedar-apple rust and fire blight are potential problems in humid climates — ensure good air circulation around the canopy. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Downy Wood Mint (Ohio Horsemint)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; downy wood mint is a drought-tolerant native mint relative of dry, rocky, open woodlands, slopes, and wood margins across the eastern US, more tolerant of dry conditions than hairy wood mint and naturally at home on thin, rocky soils over limestone or sandstone. The whorled clusters of small, lavender to pale purple flowers with purple spotting are produced in midsummer and attract numerous small native bees, bumblebees, and clearwing sphinx moths. The leaves are fragrant with an oregano-mint scent and can be used as a culinary herb or brewed as tea. Spreads modestly by self-sowing in appropriate dry, rocky, shaded conditions. A refined, low-maintenance native herb for dry shade gardens, rocky woodland edges, and naturalistic settings in zones 4–8. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Downy Woundwort / German Woundwort
description: Sow seeds directly into their final position in early spring, 2 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost, in a sunny site with well-drained, lean, preferably alkaline or neutral soil; cover seeds very lightly and thin seedlings to 18 to 24 inches apart once they are large enough to handle. Downy Woundwort demands excellent drainage and suffers in heavy, wet soils — raised beds, gravel gardens, and south-facing slopes suit it well and show off the intensely felted, silver-white foliage to its best advantage. Plants flower in their second year, sending up stems of pale pink, whorled flowers that attract bees; leave a portion of the flower heads to ripen for self-sowing. Cut back dead stems in late winter and apply a grit mulch rather than organic material to keep the base dry and prevent crown rot during wet winters. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Doyle's Thornless Blackberry (Vigorous Trailing Thornless Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, trailing, thornless canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since this cultivar's vigor can overwhelm a light support structure within a couple of seasons. Doyle's Thornless was developed and patented by an amateur grower in Illinois and marketed directly to home gardeners rather than released through a university breeding program, and it became known for extremely heavy per-plant yields once established, with growers regularly reporting a single mature plant can produce many gallons of fruit. The berries are medium-to-large, sweet-tart, and hold their shape well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserving, ripening over an extended midseason window. It is self-fertile, though many growers plant more than one to maximize the already generous yields typical of the variety. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Dr. Martin Lima Bean (Giant-Podded Heirloom Pole Lima)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-worked soil once all frost danger has passed, training vines up a tall, sturdy trellis or pole from the start since this variety climbs far higher than most garden limas. Dr. Martin is a pre-1900 heirloom pole lima known for its enormous vigor and outsized flat pods, each holding three to four quarter-sized beans, borne on vines that can top ten feet in a long, hot season. Pick pods at the plump green-shell stage for the best flavor and tenderness, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for storage beans; consistent picking keeps the vines setting new flowers through summer heat. Because the vines invest heavily in height before bearing, give plants a long, warm season and avoid crowding so pods lower on the trellis still get good airflow and light. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Dr. Potter Pawpaw (Reliable Late-Season Indiana Selection)
description: Dr. Potter is a wild-tree selection documented from Julietta, Indiana, and cataloged among Kentucky State University's historic pawpaw cultivar records. The fruit runs on the small side with rich, deep-yellow flesh and a mild, gently sweet flavor, and it holds up well after picking compared to many softer-fleshed pawpaws.
