It ripens late in the season and, like all pawpaws, needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination and fruit set. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Dr. Wyche's Orange Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost, transplant into fertile, well-draining soil in full sun, and bury the stem deeply for a stronger root system. Dr. Wyche's Orange honors Dr. John Wyche, a Cherokee chief and circus impresario from Hugo, Oklahoma, who grew tomatoes fertilized with circus animal manure and shared his seeds with Seed Savers Exchange; the variety produces large, up to 2-pound, brilliant orange beefsteak fruits with very meaty, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that appeals especially to those who find red tomatoes too acidic. Stake or cage plants solidly as the vines are vigorous and the fruits are heavy; consistent watering prevents cracking. Harvest when fully orange and slightly soft at the blossom end. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Dr. Wyche's Yellow Tomato (Oklahoma Heirloom Large Orange-Yellow Beefsteak Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly orange-gold and slightly soft. Dr. Wyche's Yellow is a large-fruited heirloom tomato from an extraordinary source: Dr. John Wyche, a circus man from Hugo, Oklahoma, who operated King Brothers Circus and simultaneously maintained an extensive collection of heirloom seeds that he distributed to seed savers and gardeners over many years. Dr. Wyche reportedly used manure from the circus animals (elephants, big cats, and other exotic animals) to fertilize his prodigious garden at his Hugo farm, giving his tomatoes — which he claimed grew unusually large and vigorous — the colorful story of being 'circus-fertilized.' The tomatoes that bear his name are large beefsteak-type fruits ripening to a warm orange-gold to orange-yellow, with a complex, rich flavor that many tasters describe as fruity, sweet, and low-acid with more depth than typical yellow tomatoes. The fruits are large (often 12–16 oz or more under ideal conditions) and meaty — the solid orange-yellow flesh is dense and flavorful with relatively few seed cavities for a beefsteak type. Dr. Wyche's Yellow has been distributed by Seed Savers Exchange and other heirloom seed sources and has gained a devoted following among heirloom tomato enthusiasts who value the combination of large size, distinctive warm orange-gold color, and excellent flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Dragon Carrot (Deep Purple-Red Heirloom Carrot)
description: Direct sow in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dragon is a distinctive heirloom carrot producing long, tapered roots with deep red-purple to maroon skin — an unusually vivid exterior color caused by high anthocyanin content — and orange interior flesh with a reddish core that bleeds red-orange color when cut. The flavor is excellent: sweet, slightly spicy, and more complex than standard orange carrots, with the characteristic flavor depth often associated with high-anthocyanin vegetables. Raw Dragon carrots turn a stunning deep red-orange when sliced, making them visually dramatic in fresh salads, crudité platters, and fresh presentations — the color contrast of the purple-red exterior against the orange-red interior is striking and unique. When cooked, the anthocyanin pigments partially convert to blue-gray tones (as with all purple vegetables cooked without acid), so Dragon carrots are best appreciated raw, lightly pickled in vinegar, or roasted at high heat for caramelized flavor development. The excellent flavor and extraordinary color make Dragon an outstanding choice for market gardeners and home gardeners who value both flavor and visual interest. In zone 9, sow in August through September for a fall/winter crop — the cool temperatures intensify both the purple skin color and the sweetness of the flesh. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Dragon Egg Cucumber
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines on a trellis or fence to make harvesting easier and keep fruits off the ground. Dragon Egg is a Croatian heirloom cucumber with a charming and unusual appearance — the fruits are oval to distinctly egg-shaped, smooth-skinned, and creamy-white to pale yellow when ripe, with a delicate internal structure of mild, sweet flesh and small seeds. They are harvested when fully white-to-cream colored (before they turn orange, which indicates over-maturity and seedy, bitter flesh); at the right stage the flavor is mild, refreshing, and virtually non-bitter even in hot conditions. The plants are extremely productive in warm weather and the fruits hang in clusters, making them easy to spot and harvest. Outstanding for hot summer gardens where standard cucumbers become bitter; one of the most reliably productive white-fruited novelty cucumbers. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Dragon Fennel
description: Direct sow seed where it is to grow, since fennel forms a taproot and dislikes being transplanted; keep the soil evenly moist. This bulbing fennel is easy to grow and slow to bolt, producing big, sweet, succulent bulbs that are excellent raw, added to soups and pasta, or charred on the grill. Hill soil around the swelling bases to keep them tender and white, and let the feathery fronds attract pollinators. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Dragon Fruit
description: Dragon fruit is a climbing, white-fleshed cactus that produces dramatic sculptural stems and sweet fruit following its large night-blooming flowers. Grow it in fast-draining cactus soil and provide a sturdy trellis or post for the heavy vining stems to climb. Water only when the soil dries out, since the plant stores moisture and is prone to rot if kept wet. It needs warmth above 40 degrees, so grow it in a container to move indoors where frost occurs. Hand-pollinate the evening flowers for reliable fruit set. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dragon Fruit (Pitaya, Pitahaya)
description: Root cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy or amended cactus soil in full sun; dragon fruit is a climbing cactus native to Central America that produces spectacular night-blooming white flowers 12 inches across, followed by the familiar large, brightly colored fruit with its distinctive pink-magenta or yellow skin and speckled white or red flesh. Plants take 1–2 years from cuttings to first fruit, then produce prolifically. The vine-like stems climb via aerial roots and require a sturdy post or trellis. In zone 9a, protect from hard freezes with frost cloth — stems will die back at 28°F but established plants often resprout from the base. Fruit ripens 30–50 days after flowering; harvest when the pink color fully develops and the wings begin to wilt. Multiple varieties exist including red-fleshed 'American Beauty' and yellow-skinned Selenicereus megalanthus. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dragon Tongue Bean
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Dragon Tongue is a Dutch heirloom wax bean producing flat, wide, golden-yellow pods dramatically streaked and splashed with deep purple markings — one of the most visually striking beans in the garden and the most eye-catching bean at farmers markets and in kitchen displays. The pods are harvested as a wax bean (snap bean without strings) in the flat stage before seeds swell, when the crisp, flat pods have a buttery, mild wax bean flavor noticeably different from standard round snap beans. The purple streaking serves no flavor function but makes the pods immediately recognizable and appealing; the color vanishes completely during cooking. Dragon Tongue also works as a shellout bean if pods are allowed to mature fully, with cream-colored seeds streaked with black-purple markings. The bush habit and early maturity (55–60 days) make Dragon Tongue productive in relatively short growing seasons, and the ornamental pods add visual interest to the vegetable garden beyond what most productive bush beans offer. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Dragon Tongue Bean
description: This Dutch heirloom wax bean produces buttery yellow pods streaked with purple that fade when cooked. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil, spacing seeds 4 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart. Harvest as a snap bean at 5-6 inches or leave to mature for a fine shell bean. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young, so gather every few days. Avoid working among wet plants to reduce spread of bacterial blight. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Dragon Tongue Mustard (Colorful Streaked Chinese Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 30 days or cut the whole plant at 40–45 days. Dragon Tongue Mustard is a visually striking Asian mustard green with broad, frilly, bright green leaves overlaid with vivid red-purple veining and midribs — the colorful contrasting veination giving the leaves a dramatic appearance unlike any other mustard type and making Dragon Tongue one of the most ornamental edible greens in the winter garden. The name describes the leaf form: long, broad, and pointed like a tongue, with the red-purple coloring suggesting the fieriness appropriate to a dragon. The flavor is spicy, sharp, and pungent in the characteristic Asian mustard style — more aggressive than mild Asian greens like tatsoi or pak choi, but that pungency mellows significantly with cooking. Raw leaves are assertive and best used in small quantities as a spicy accent in salad mixes; cooked leaves (sautéed, steamed, or braised) are excellent alongside other winter vegetables and complement pork, sausage, and beans. Dragon Tongue grows rapidly in cool weather and is one of the most productive and visually interesting additions to a fall and winter garden in the Gulf South. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Dragon's Breath Pepper (Extreme Ornamental Superhot Chile)
description: Dragon's Breath was bred in Wales through a collaborative trial investigating the essential oil's potential as a topical anesthetic, and it produces small, wrinkled, roughly one-inch fruits on a compact, well-branched plant that suits container growing as easily as garden beds. Independent lab testing reported an extraordinary capsaicin concentration around 2.48 million Scoville units, though this figure has not been formally certified, so treat it as a claimed rather than official record. Because of its almost unmanageable heat, growers treat the fruit as a novelty or oil-extraction crop rather than a table pepper, and any handling should be done with gloves, eye protection, and excellent ventilation. Give plants the same warm, sunny, well-drained conditions used for habaneros, and expect a long season since fruit set and full ripening take considerably longer than most annuum peppers. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Dragon's Tongue Cucumber (Dragon Tongue, Dutch Yellow Cucumber)
description: Direct sow or transplant to well-amended, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Dragon's Tongue is a strikingly beautiful Dutch heirloom cucumber producing medium-sized (5–6 inch) cucumbers with creamy-white skin dramatically streaked and splashed with purple-violet, resulting in an ornamental appearance unlike any standard green cucumber. Harvest when fruits are creamy-white with purple markings and firm to the touch — as they continue to mature they turn yellow then bitter. The flavor when harvested at prime ripeness is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet, excellent for fresh eating and pickling. A productive and prolific vining type that does not require trellis but benefits from it. Matures in 60–65 days from transplant.

name: Draper Blueberry (Firm Long-Shelf-Life Michigan Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Draper was released by Michigan State University in the 2000s and quickly became popular for producing exceptionally firm, crack-resistant, light-blue berries that hold their quality remarkably well after picking, a trait originally valued for mechanical harvesting but equally useful for home gardeners who want berries that keep well in the refrigerator. Ripening early to midseason on a vigorous, upright, productive bush, Draper combines good flavor with the kind of fruit durability that makes picking and storing a whole harvest far more forgiving than with softer-fruited varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Drilea Nanking Cherry (Historic Upright Annual-Bearing Bush Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Drilea, a historic named Nanking cherry selection documented in USDA and nursery literature, bears firm, sweet, round red fruit on an upright-spreading, reliably annual-bearing shrub, ripening in mid-July, later than many other Nanking cherry selections. It offers a genuinely heat-tolerant bush-cherry alternative to true sweet and sour cherries, which generally fail in the Deep South's mild winters and humid summers, though it is now rarely commercially available and best sourced from specialty or heritage fruit nurseries. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain an open, productive form, since Nanking cherry blooms and fruits on one-year-old wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Drummond's False Pennyroyal
description: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Drummond's false pennyroyal is a small, wiry, intensely aromatic native mint relative found on dry limestone slopes and prairies from Texas through the Southwest, releasing a strong, minty-camphor scent when the foliage is brushed or crushed. Tiny, tubular, pale lavender to pink flowers appear in the leaf axils from spring through fall, adding subtle color to a dry rock garden or xeriscape planting rather than serving as a showy bedding flower. Historically used in folk medicine as a tea and traditional remedy, it is grown today mostly for its fragrance, drought tolerance, and value as a low, textural filler among rocks and gravel mulch. It is short-lived but self-sows readily in loose, undisturbed soil, so allow some plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-renewing population. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is an Italian heirloom looseleaf lettuce with one of the most whimsical names in the vegetable kingdom — a literal translation of the Italian 'Ubriaca della Testa Frizzy' — producing large, loosely-headed plants with heavily frilled, ruffled, wavy leaves in a mix of red-bronze tones on green, giving the plant an exuberant, disheveled appearance that the name aptly describes. The large, floppy, curly leaves have a mild, tender, slightly buttery flavor with the red-bronze pigmentation adding a slight edge of complexity over standard green looseleaf. The decorative appearance makes it a standout in the garden and at market, where the dramatic frilly form catches the eye among more uniform types. Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is notably slow to bolt and holds in the garden longer than many other looseleaf types, a quality valued in warm climates. The large leaf size makes it easy to harvest by stripping outer leaves for a continuous cut-and-come-again operation. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Druzba Tomato (Bulgarian Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed. Druzba is a Bulgarian heirloom whose name means 'friendship,' prized for combining an unusually early harvest window with the deep, balanced flavor more typical of longer-season tomatoes. The smooth, red, slightly flattened globes resist cracking better than many heirlooms and the vigorous indeterminate vines stay productive over a long season. Stake or cage securely and pinch suckers lightly to keep the sprawling growth manageable. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Dryland Blueberry (Hillside Blueberry)
description: Plant in dry to well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in partial shade or dappled woodland light; dryland blueberry is a compact native Vaccinium of eastern US woodlands and acidic ridge tops that earns its common name from its exceptional tolerance of dry, lean, acidic conditions — it is among the most drought-tolerant blueberries in cultivation. The white to pink bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, intensely sweet blue-black berries in midsummer that are prized for fresh eating and bird fodder. Excellent fall color in shades of orange, red, and burgundy. Unlike highbush cultivars, no irrigation or supplemental fertilizer is needed once established in appropriate soil. Plant several individuals for cross-pollination and heavier berry crops. An underused native for dry, shaded slopes and woodland gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Duarte Plum (Historic California Red-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Duarte is an early 20th-century California heirloom Japanese plum notable for red flesh streaked through the fruit's interior rather than the more common amber or yellow flesh of most Japanese plums, a striking trait when the fruit is cut open, paired with dark red skin and a rich, tangy-sweet flavor. Historically significant in early California plum breeding, it remains grown today by heirloom fruit enthusiasts and specialty orchards valuing its distinctive red-fleshed character and genuine history. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and develops full color for the best flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Duborskian Rice (Cold-Tolerant Paddy Rice)
description: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into rich, heavy soil kept flooded with 1-2 inches of water through the growing season in full sun; Duborskian rice is a short-season, cold-adapted paddy variety that can mature even in cool-summer northern climates. Bred in Russia for a much shorter and more cold-tolerant growing season than typical rice, it is one of the few rice varieties that home gardeners in temperate, non-tropical climates can realistically bring to harvest, maturing in around 100 days compared to 150 or more for most tropical rice. Grow it in a lined kiddie pool, stock tank, or purpose-built paddy bed that can hold standing water, keeping the bed flooded through most of the growing season and draining it as the grain heads mature and dry down in late summer. Hand-harvest by cutting whole seed heads once grains have hardened and the plant has yellowed, then dry, thresh, and hull before cooking. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Duchess of Oldenburg Apple (Cold-Hardy Russian Cooking Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Duchess of Oldenburg is a Russian heirloom apple brought to the United States in the 1830s and 40s, valued from the start for extreme cold hardiness that let orchardists in the harshest northern climates grow quality apples for the first time, and it became an important parent in the breeding of many later cold-hardy varieties. The medium-sized fruit has red-striped skin over a yellow background, and the crisp, juicy, notably tart flesh is prized above all for cooking, making exceptionally flavorful applesauce and pies, though it can be eaten fresh by those who enjoy a sharply tart apple. Fruit ripens in mid to late summer, earlier than most storage apples, and does not keep long, so plan to use or process it within a few weeks of harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Duchesse d'Angoulême Pear (Enormous Knobby French Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Duchesse d'Angoulême is a French heirloom from the early 1800s grown for one of the largest, most irregularly knobby and lopsided fruit shapes of any common pear, a genuinely striking apple-defying form that can make individual pears weigh over a pound. Beneath the rough, uneven skin, the flesh is buttery, juicy, and richly flavored, excellent for fresh eating once fully ripe and equally good poached or baked given its substantial size. The tree is a reliable, moderately vigorous producer; harvest while still firm and green, since like most European pears it should be picked underripe and finished ripening indoors at room temperature for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Duck Potato (Broadleaf Arrowhead, Wapato)
description: Plant in shallow standing water or saturated soil at a pond, ditch, or rain garden margin in full sun to partial shade; requires permanently wet to submerged conditions and will not persist in soil that dries out. Sagittaria latifolia (duck potato, broadleaf arrowhead, or wapato) is a native wetland perennial named for its distinctive arrow-shaped leaves rising above the water's surface, and for the starchy, walnut-sized tubers it produces at the tips of its underwater rhizomes — a food source of major historical importance to Indigenous peoples across North America, who harvested the tubers by wading into shallow water and dislodging them with bare feet so they floated free for collection. The tubers have a mild, potato-like flavor and can be boiled, roasted, or fried much like a small potato, while the plant's white, three-petaled summer flowers and bold foliage also make it a valuable ornamental and wildlife plant, providing food for waterfowl (hence 'duck potato') and habitat for aquatic insects. An excellent dual-purpose edible and ornamental for a pond margin or rain garden in zone 4–10. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Duganski Garlic (Spicy Russian Purple Stripe Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck garlic originally from Russia, valued for its notably strong, hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, robust taste when roasted or cooked, making it a favorite among gardeners who want an assertive, full-flavored garlic. Bulbs have deep reddish-purple streaked skin over 8-10 tightly packed cloves. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Duganski also stores somewhat better than many other purple stripe types, often holding for 6-8 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming. Matures in 230–260 days from transplant.

name: Dukat Dill (High-Oil European Dill Variety with Superior Foliage Flavor)
description: Direct sow thinly in early spring or fall; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest leaves before flowering for best flavor. Dukat Dill is a Danish dill variety (Dukat is a Danish word for a coin or ducat) developed and selected for high essential oil content in the leaves — the characteristic that translates to superior flavor intensity in dill weed, the fresh or dried feathery leaf material used in cooking rather than the seeds. All dill contains aromatic volatile oils (primarily carvone and limonene), but the proportion and intensity of these oils varies substantially among varieties, with Dukat consistently showing higher leaf oil content than standard American dill varieties in comparative trials. This difference is directly perceptible in the kitchen: Dukat dill weed has a stronger, more clearly identifiable dill aroma and flavor than standard varieties harvested at the same stage, making it preferable for recipes where dill flavor should be distinct without using large quantities of herb. The plants are tall (3–4 feet) with the characteristic ferny, blue-green dill foliage and produce yellow flower umbels at maturity. Dukat has also been noted for slightly more vigorous early leaf growth than standard varieties, giving it a head start on production. Like all dill, it is a favorite host plant for black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed on dill, fennel, parsley, and related Apiaceae members — planting dill in zone 9 gardens supports local butterfly populations while providing a culinary herb. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Duke 7 Avocado (Cold-Hardy Phytophthora-Tolerant Mexican-Race Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding low or poorly drained spots; Duke 7 is a Mexican-race avocado selection out of California best known as a Phytophthora root rot-tolerant rootstock, but it is also grown and fruited directly in cold-marginal plantings for the same cold-hardiness that characterizes Mexican-race avocados generally, tolerating brief exposure to around 18°F once well established. Fruit is smaller than commercial Guatemalan or hybrid types like Hass, with thin, often edible skin and rich, high-oil flesh typical of the Mexican race. Because root rot caused by Phytophthora cinnamomi is one of the most serious problems in wet or heavy soils, Duke 7's tolerance is a genuine practical advantage for gardeners without ideal, fast-draining soil — even so, plant on a slight mound or berm and avoid overwatering, since good drainage remains important for avocado health generally. Plant with a Type B pollinator such as Fuerte or Zutano nearby to improve fruit set, and expect a compact, cold-tolerant tree well suited to marginal avocado climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Duke Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and shield young trees for their first few winters with frost cloth or a temporary structure. Duke is an old Mexican-race avocado selection notable for its cold hardiness, historically used both as a fruiting variety in marginal climates and as rootstock material for grafting less cold-tolerant scions in colder parts of the avocado-growing range. Fruit is small, thin-skinned, and rich-flavored, with the anise-scented leaves typical of the Mexican race, ripening in late summer to fall. Because avocados set fruit more reliably with a cross-pollinator, plant Duke alongside a complementary flowering-type cultivar where space allows. Established Duke trees are among the more cold-hardy avocados available, tolerating brief drops into the low 20s Fahrenheit, though a hard freeze during bloom can still eliminate a season's crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Duke Blueberry
description: 'Duke' is a highly reliable early-season northern highbush blueberry with firm, mild-flavored berries that ripen over a concentrated window. It blooms late but ripens early, helping it dodge spring frosts while still producing an early harvest. Plant in full sun in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, amending heavily with peat moss and mulching with pine bark. Provide consistent moisture, avoid lime, and prune out weak twiggy growth each late winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dulcet Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Dulcet is one of the black-fruited selections to emerge from the University of Georgia's early twentieth-century muscadine breeding program, prized for generations of Southern growers for its rich, sweet flavor and productive vigor. Because it carries only female flowers, it produces no pollen of its own and needs a nearby self-fertile black or bronze cultivar to ensure a full fruit set every season. Like other muscadines, it shrugs off Pierce's disease, black rot, and the humid-summer fungal pressure that limits bunch grapes in the Gulf South, and it needs no fungicide spray program in most home gardens. Prune hard each winter back to short spurs on permanent cordons to keep the vigorous vine productive and manageable. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Dumbarton Oaks Hardy Kiwi (Historic Vigorous Kiwiberry Vine)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, with a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor in place before planting; Dumbarton Oaks is one of the older named hardy kiwi selections in American cultivation, long associated with the historic ornamental gardens of the Dumbarton Oaks estate in Washington, D.C., and maintained since among hardy fruit collectors and specialty nurseries as a vigorous, reliably productive female vine. Like other Actinidia arguta cultivars it produces smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit that is eaten whole without peeling, with a sweet, complex flavor often compared to a cross between kiwi and green grape. As a dioecious cultivar it requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine planted nearby for pollination, since it will flower but set little fruit on its own. The vine is notably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below what damages fuzzy kiwi, and grows vigorously once established, so provide a very sturdy, permanent support structure from the start. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Duncan Grapefruit (Oldest Named Grapefruit Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Traced to a tree found growing on Florida's Gulf Coast in the 1830s and later propagated commercially in 1892 by A. L. Duncan, this is the oldest named grapefruit cultivar still grown today and the ancestor of most modern seedless grapefruit varieties. The pale yellow, white-fleshed fruit is notably seedy by modern standards, but its tart, deeply flavored juice is prized by grapefruit enthusiasts and is still used in breeding programs for flavor quality. The tree is vigorous, productive, and among the more cold-tolerant grapefruit selections, making it a reasonable choice at the cooler edge of the grapefruit-growing range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dunja Zucchini (Organic Multi-Virus-Resistant Green Summer Squash)
description: Sow seeds directly in warm soil 1-2 weeks after the last spring frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for short-season climates. Dunja was bred specifically for organic growers and shows strong resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and papaya ringspot virus, making it dependable where aphid-transmitted viruses commonly cut a squash planting short. The medium-green, cylindrical fruit forms on an open, easy-to-harvest plant; picking regularly at 6-8 inches keeps vigorous plants producing all season. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Dunstan Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Chestnut Hybrid, Food Forest Nut Tree)
description: Plant two or more trees for cross-pollination; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split and nuts fall naturally. Dunstan Chestnut is a hybrid between American chestnut (Castanea dentata) and Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima) that was developed by plant breeder Robert Dunstan beginning in the 1950s after he obtained blight-resistant American chestnut seedlings identified by plant pathologist Arthur Graves. Dunstan crossed these blight-resistant American chestnut trees (which retained their blight resistance while displaying more American-type tree form) with Chinese chestnut to create offspring that combined the superior nut quality, upright tree form, and improved blight resistance of the selected parent material. The Dunstan Chestnut is commercially distributed by Chestnut Hill Nursery in Alachua, Florida — itself a significant note, as Alachua/Gainesville, Florida is in zone 9, confirming that Dunstan Chestnut grows in zone 9 conditions. The nuts are large to very large (often 1 inch diameter), sweet, richly flavored — closer to American chestnut quality than Chinese chestnut — and produced in large quantities in well-established trees. Chestnuts have significant nutritional value: high in complex carbohydrates (unusual among tree nuts, which are typically high in fats), relatively low in fat, and with a flavor and texture that makes them excellent roasted, boiled, pureed into soups and stuffings, or ground into flour for baked goods. Chestnut trees are also long-lived, productive wildlife food trees: the nuts are consumed by deer, turkey, squirrel, and many other wildlife species, making Dunstan Chestnut valuable for food forest and wildlife habitat plantings in the Gulf South. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Dunstan Citrumelo (Sweetest Least-Resinous Cold-Hardy Citrumelo Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and protect young trees during their first winter or two while cold hardiness develops. Dunstan is a citrumelo, a hybrid of grapefruit and trifoliate orange, and among citrumelo selections it stands out for having noticeably better fresh-eating quality than most, with sweeter juice and less of the bitter, resinous flavor that limits many trifoliate hybrids to juice or marmalade use only. Established trees tolerate temperatures down to around 10 degrees Fahrenheit, considerably colder than standard grapefruit or orange, making it one of the more cold-hardy citrus options for the northern edge of the Gulf South citrus range. Fruit ripens from fall into winter, with flavor improving the longer it hangs on the tree in mild weather. As with other trifoliate-derived hybrids, expect a semi-deciduous habit and light thorns in colder winters. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut (American-Chinese Hybrid Chestnut, Blight-Resistant Eastern Chestnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy loam or loamy soil in full sun; Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut is self-fertile; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split open and chestnuts fall; gather from ground promptly as ground moisture causes rapid spoilage; refrigerate fresh nuts within days of harvest since they are perishable. Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut represents one of the most important advances in American chestnut restoration, developed by Dr. Robert Dunstan of Greensboro, North Carolina in the 1950s and 1960s after discovering a surviving American chestnut tree in Ohio (the Graves tree) that appeared to have some natural resistance to the chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that wiped out approximately 4 billion American chestnut trees from the eastern forest between 1904 and 1950. Dunstan crossed this apparently blight-resistant American chestnut with Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima), which has co-evolved with the blight fungus in Asia and carries true genetic resistance, to produce a hybrid combining the large size and straight timber form approaching American chestnut with the blight resistance of the Chinese parent. The Dunstan Hybrid produced nuts with excellent size and sweet flavor — closer to American chestnut sweetness than to the less-flavorful Chinese chestnut — while demonstrating substantially better blight resistance than standard American chestnut. Dunstan Hybrids have been widely planted in the southeastern and Mid-Atlantic states for orchard nut production, wildlife habitat (deer, turkey, and squirrels relish chestnuts), and as a productive native-type chestnut for home orchards where the formerly dominant American chestnut once grew. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Duplex Scorzonera (Slow-Bolting Continental Black Salsify)
description: Duplex is a long-cultivated Continental European scorzonera selected for heavy, uniform yields of long, black-skinned, white-fleshed roots and for notable resistance to bolting compared with older strains. Direct sow into deeply loosened soil, since the taproot resents disturbance and will fork in compacted or stony ground, and thin seedlings early to give roots room to size up straight. The cooked root has a sweet, mild, faintly oyster-like flavor similar to salsify, and is traditionally peeled, cut into pieces, and steamed or simmered before finishing with a sauce. Roots can be left in the ground over winter in most climates and lifted through the cold months, with flavor improving after frost. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Durango Mirasol Guajillo Chile Pepper
description: This dual-purpose chile is used mirasol-style when fresh with a fruity, mild-to-medium heat around 2,500 to 5,000 Scoville units, then becomes guajillo when dried into deep-burgundy pods. Vigorous plants yield tapered fruit of 6.5 to 8 inches with good dry weight for sauces, rubs, and powders. Start seed indoors early for a long warm season. Transplant into full sun after frost danger passes. Harvest fully ripe pods and dry them in a warm, airy place. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Durian
description: Durian demands deep, fertile, well-drained soil, high humidity, and temperatures between 75°F and 95°F year-round; it is the most climate-specific of the major tropical fruits and can only be grown outdoors in the most tropical parts of the continental United States (extreme south Florida). Flowers open at night and are primarily bat-pollinated, so maintain nearby native habitat and avoid pesticide applications at dusk; hand-pollination improves set in enclosed settings. Fruit develops over 3–5 months and the spiny husk is potentially dangerous — trees should be netted and fruit harvested from the ground after it falls naturally. The ripe flesh has a rich custard flavor with a pungent sulfurous aroma that intensifies rapidly after harvest; consume or freeze within 24–48 hours. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Durum Wheat (Pasta Wheat)
description: Durum is the hard, amber-grained wheat relative behind the world's pasta, couscous, and semolina, distinct from common bread wheat in the same way emmer and einkorn are distinct, and it fills a market-class gap that no bread-wheat cultivar can substitute for. It carries deep roots in the Fertile Crescent and is well adapted to semi-arid growing conditions, tolerating dry spells better than many bread wheats once established. Sow in early spring into well-drained soil in full sun; the plant grows a stiff, upright stand with prominent awned heads that dry down to a distinctive amber color at harvest. Home millers mostly grind the very hard kernels for semolina or coarse pasta flour rather than standard loaf bread, since durum's gluten behaves differently than that of hexaploid bread wheat. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Dusa Avocado Rootstock
description: Plant container-grown clonal rootstock liners after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired avocado variety onto the young rootstock; Dusa is a Phytophthora-tolerant clonal understock, not grown for its own fruit. A South African clonal avocado rootstock selection bred specifically for strong tolerance of Phytophthora root rot, one of the most economically damaging avocado diseases worldwide, while also imparting good vigor, high yields, and reasonably good tolerance of some soil salinity to the grafted variety. Its clonal propagation gives far more uniform performance across an orchard than older seedling avocado rootstocks, whose disease tolerance and vigor vary unpredictably from tree to tree. Graft a desired named avocado variety onto young rootstock, provide excellent drainage despite the improved Phytophthora tolerance, since no avocado rootstock is fully immune, and expect vigorous, productive growth in warm, frost-free climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Dusky Eggplant (Early Disease-Resistant Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dusky is a compact hybrid eggplant that became a home-garden standard for its combination of early maturity, good disease resistance, and heavy sets of deep purple, glossy, oval-to-teardrop fruit. Fruits reach a full 8 to 9 inches while still maturing notably faster than many older large-fruited eggplants, which lets gardeners in shorter-season regions get a reliable harvest before fall cooling slows production. The dense, disease-tolerant bush habit performs well in raised beds and large containers as well as open garden rows. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm and the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit left to overripen turns dull, seedy, and bitter. Matures in 60–65 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Arctic Rose Tomato (Early Pink Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the thick, rugose-leafed stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Arctic Rose bears round to oblate pink fruit with smooth shoulders and clear skin over red flesh, offering well-balanced flavor on one of the earliest-maturing plants in the Dwarf Tomato Project lineup, sometimes ready weeks ahead of other dwarf releases. It was bred from a 2005 cross of Budai Torpe and Black from Tula made by Patrina Nuske Small, with selection work carried out largely by Alaska-based growers well-suited to short seasons. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 65–78 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Blue Curled Kale
description: This hardy 1800s variety forms compact, deeply curled blue-green leaves and overwinters in all but the coldest climates. It grows best in cool weather but tolerates some heat, and flavor sweetens after frost. The nutrient-dense leaves are low in calories and rich in vitamins. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep the plant producing. Grow in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist soil. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Blue Scotch Kale (Blue-Green Curly Dwarf Kale)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Dwarf Blue Scotch'
description: Sow directly 1/2 inch deep in cool weather and thin to 12–18 inches apart; Dwarf Blue Scotch is very compact and can be planted more closely than full-size curly kales; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again; the plants tolerate temperatures well below 0°F and produce through winter in zones 5–7 without protection. Dwarf Blue Scotch is an old heirloom curly kale variety that combines three notable characteristics: exceptional cold hardiness, compact plant habit, and an attractive, intensely blue-gray-green leaf color that gives it its name. The plants grow only 12–18 inches tall with tightly packed, finely curled and ruffled leaves of a distinctive blue-green color — sometimes described as 'glaucous' or 'sea blue' — that deepens and intensifies after cold exposure, making Dwarf Blue Scotch one of the most visually attractive kales in the winter garden. The flavor is traditional curly kale — somewhat peppery and earthy raw, becoming sweet and mellow after frost exposure, with the classic kale character that mellows beautifully with cooking in soups, stews, sautés, and traditional Scottish 'kail' preparations. The 'Scotch' name reflects the deep Scottish culinary tradition of kale (kail in Scots dialect), where kale was so central to the diet that the kitchen garden was historically called the 'kailyard' and kale broth (kail brose) was a daily staple. The dwarf habit makes it ideal for raised beds, intensive planting, and smaller gardens where space is limited. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Brazilian Banana (Santa Catarina Prata)
description: Dwarf Brazilian is a naturally occurring dwarf mutant of the Brazilian (Santa Catarina Prata) banana, imported to the United States in the late 1970s and valued for combining good cold and wind tolerance with a much shorter, sturdier pseudostem than its parent. It produces smaller but still sweet, good-flavored fruit, and the compact habit and strong wind resistance make it a practical choice for exposed Gulf Coast sites where taller cultivars are prone to leaf shredding or toppling. It tolerates cooler conditions better than tender dessert-type Cavendish bananas, though the pseudostem is still killed by a hard freeze and regrows from the rhizome in spring. Grow in full sun with rich, moist soil and heavy summer feeding. Matures in 300–455 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Cavendish Banana Tree
description: Dwarf Cavendish is a compact banana cultivar that fruits at a manageable height, making it well suited to containers and small spaces. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, feeding heavily through the warm season since bananas are gross feeders. Keep the soil consistently moist and shelter the large leaves from strong wind that can shred them. Where temperatures drop below the mid-50s, move the plant indoors to a bright, warm spot for winter. Each stem fruits once, after which it is cut down and replaced by new pups from the base. Matures in 270–540 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Champion Tomato (19th-Century Potato-Leaf Dwarf Heirloom)
description: Dwarf Champion is a 19th-century American heirloom notable as one of the earliest true dwarf, potato-leaf tomato varieties grown in home gardens, predating both the modern Dwarf Tomato Project and its own later yellow-fruited sport, Golden Dwarf Champion, by roughly a century. Plants stay short and stocky with thick, rugose foliage and need little to no staking, setting round to slightly oblate, medium-sized pink-red fruit with mild, old-fashioned tomato flavor. Its compact, self-supporting genetics made it valuable breeding stock for later short-statured tomato lines long before dwarf habit became a deliberate modern breeding goal. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, harvesting as fruit fully colors and softens slightly at the blossom end. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Emerald Giant Tomato (Green Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)
description: Dwarf Emerald Giant produces large beefsteak-type fruit that ripens from deep green to a green-gold color with an amber blush at the blossom end, revealing translucent lime-green flesh with a rich, spicy-sweet flavor reminiscent of full-size green heirloom beefsteaks. The compact, dwarf-indeterminate plant packs that big-fruit heirloom character onto a manageable 2-4 foot frame suited to raised beds and large containers. It is a release of the Dwarf Tomato Project, the volunteer breeding collaboration begun in 2005 by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small to combine heirloom flavor and color diversity with compact plant habit. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Everbearing Mulberry (Compact Container Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact size is a real advantage. Dwarf Everbearing is a naturally small mulberry, reaching only a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees while still producing a long, extended harvest of sweet, dark berries over many weeks rather than the shorter few-week fruiting window of many fruit trees. Its small size makes it one of the few mulberries practical for a small urban yard, patio, or large container, and it can even be grown as a modest specimen shrub rather than needing the space of a full-sized shade tree. It fruits at a young age and requires only routine pruning to control size and shape. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Ginseng (Groundnut Ginseng)
description: Plant tubers or divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, cool, humus-rich, loamy woodland soil in full to partial shade; dwarf ginseng is the smallest and least-known member of the ginseng family (Araliaceae) — a tiny, ephemeral woodland wildflower of cool, moist eastern deciduous forests from Nova Scotia and Quebec south to the Appalachians. Unlike its much larger relative American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius), dwarf ginseng produces a small, round, tuber-like root (rather than the large, spindle-shaped ginseng root). The small plant emerges early in spring, produces a tiny umbel of white flowers, sets seed, and dies back to the ground by midsummer — a spring ephemeral that completes its entire above-ground life cycle in just a few weeks. The small, peppery-tasting root was eaten raw by Cherokee, Iroquois, and other Indigenous peoples. An excellent, highly ephemeral native wildflower for naturalizing in deeply shaded, moist, acidic woodland gardens where it grows with hepatica, bloodroot, trout lily, and spring beauty. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Glasswort (Annual Sea Bean)
description: Direct sow into wet, saline mud or sand at the tidal margin in full sun; dwarf glasswort is a true halophyte adapted to regular tidal flooding with salt water and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone. Leafless, jointed, bright green succulent stems form dense colonies along salt marsh and tidal flat margins, turning red as they mature in fall, and the crisp, salty, juicy young stem tips are harvested and eaten raw or lightly cooked as a gourmet vegetable known variously as sea bean, sea asparagus, or samphire greens. Unlike the perennial glassworts, this annual species completes its life cycle in a single season, germinating on bare tidal mud in spring and setting seed by fall, making it useful both as a foraged coastal vegetable and as a candidate crop for experimental saline agriculture research irrigated with seawater. It requires the specific conditions of a real tidal or brackish marsh edge to thrive and is not a candidate for a typical home garden setting away from the coast. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Golden Gypsy Tomato (Yellow Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, potato-leaf stems lightly for support. Dwarf Golden Gypsy bears medium to large oblate yellow fruit with pale yellow flesh and an intense, sprightly, refreshingly tangy flavor rated among the best of the newer dwarf releases. It began as a Golden Dwarf Champion x Elbe cross made by Patrina Nuske Small, was selected and renamed by Wendy Montanez, and stabilized over multiple generations by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers before its 2015 release as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for best flavor. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Green Long Pod Okra
description: Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost, soaking seed overnight to promote even germination, then thin to give plants adequate spacing for good air circulation. Harvest the ribbed, tapering pods young and often to keep the compact plants producing steadily. Dwarf Green Long Pod is a long-standing heirloom selected for its shorter, bushier habit compared to older tall okra types, making it easier to harvest while still delivering abundant, tender green pods. Its manageable size has kept it a staple in home gardens with limited space. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Grey Sugar Pea (Snow Pea, Grey Sugar)
description: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in early spring (up to 8 weeks before last frost) in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dwarf Grey Sugar is an old heirloom snow pea, documented since at least the 1800s, distinguished by its unusually attractive purple-tinged vines and flowers against blue-grey foliage — the purplish cast coming from anthocyanins that also make the young tendrils and pods slightly reddish before the pods mature to green. Compact habit (24–30 inches) makes it ideal for small gardens and containers. An early and productive snow pea; harvest pods frequently when flat and young before seeds swell. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Hannah's Prize Tomato (Orange-Gold Dwarf Beefsteak)
description: Dwarf Hannah's Prize bears medium-to-large orange-gold beefsteak fruit with the mild, fruity sweetness and creamy texture typical of gold-fruited heirloom tomatoes. Named for a member of the LeHoullier family, it grows as a sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate plant reaching just 2-4 feet, concentrating heirloom-quality fruit onto a footprint well suited to containers and small gardens. It is one of the many named releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, the volunteer-driven breeding collaboration coordinated by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small since 2005. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Hawthorn / One-flowered Hawthorn
description: Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), infertile soil in full sun; dwarf hawthorn is one of the few native woody plants genuinely adapted to the challenging conditions of pine barrens and sandhills, where richer soils and supplemental moisture will actually harm it by promoting overly lush growth susceptible to disease. Unlike all other native hawthorns, which bear flowers in corymbs, this species bears a single white flower at each thorn tip in spring — an unusual and botanically distinctive habit. The small, round red haws that follow are an important food source for songbirds in the dry-woods habitats where little else fruits abundantly. Its thicket-forming habit makes it useful as a wildlife brush pile and nesting cover in naturalized dry-soil gardens and restorations. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Huckleberry (Bush Huckleberry)
description: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf huckleberry is a low-growing, colony-forming native shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain longleaf pine ecosystem, spreading by rhizomes across the forest floor of dry, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats. The small, black to deep blue-black berries are edible and flavorful — similar in taste to other huckleberries but produced on a very low-growing plant. The sticky, gland-dotted leaves are a distinctive feature. In the garden, it makes an excellent low, spreading ground cover for dry, sandy, sunny, acidic sites in zone 9a where few plants thrive. It is fire-adapted and rebounds strongly after prescribed burns in its natural habitat. An underused native ground cover for longleaf pine ecosystem restoration and dry, acidic, native plant gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Jade Beauty Tomato (Green-When-Ripe Dwarf Tomato)
description: Dwarf Jade Beauty produces medium round fruit that ripens to a translucent jade-green with an amber blush at the blossom end, offering the sweet-tart, slightly spicy complexity typical of green-when-ripe tomatoes. The plant keeps a compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet, making it a practical choice for gardeners with limited space who still want an unusual green-fleshed heirloom. It emerged from the Dwarf Tomato Project, the international volunteer breeding effort founded by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small in 2005 to pair dwarf growth habit with heirloom flavor and color diversity. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Kelly Green Tomato (Green-Fleshed Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the thick, rugose-leafed stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Kelly Green bears medium, round fruit that stays green with a translucent amber-tinged skin even at full ripeness, offering the tangy, well-rounded flavor typical of green-fleshed tomatoes. It came from the same 2005 Golden Dwarf Champion x Green Giant cross that produced Dwarf Sweet Sue, stabilized through the Dwarf Tomato Project and named for Australian bushranger Ned Kelly. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone will not signal ripeness. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Liz Birt Tomato (Pink Dwarf Beefsteak)
description: Dwarf Liz Birt produces medium-to-large pink beefsteak fruit with the balanced sweet-tart flavor and meaty texture prized in pink heirloom tomatoes. Named in honor of a longtime Dwarf Tomato Project volunteer, the plant keeps a compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet that suits raised beds and large containers. It is one of dozens of named cultivars to come out of the Dwarf Tomato Project since its founding in 2005 by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Moonglow Tomato (Golden-Orange Dwarf Tomato)
description: Dwarf Moonglow bears medium round fruit in a glowing golden-orange color with a mild, sweet flavor and low acidity typical of orange-fruited tomatoes. It grows as a compact, dwarf-indeterminate plant reaching 2-4 feet, making it a good choice for patio containers and small-space vegetable gardens. The variety is a release of the Dwarf Tomato Project, the collaborative volunteer breeding effort that has produced well over 100 named dwarf-growth-habit tomato varieties since 2005. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Namwah Banana (Compact Pisang Awak Selection)
description: Dwarf Namwah is a compact selection of the Pisang Awak (Namwah) group, retaining the parent cultivar's sweet, creamy, slightly tangy fruit and good cold and disease tolerance while topping out at a much more manageable height. Like standard Namwah, the ABB genome contributes resilience against common Gulf South banana diseases and better cold tolerance than pure dessert-type Cavendish cultivars, with the pseudostem dying back in hard freezes and regrowing reliably from the rhizome. Its shorter size makes it easier to protect fully during winter and a better fit for smaller yards or large patio containers. Feed heavily and water consistently through the growing season for best bunch fill. Matures in 300–455 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Nasturtium (Tom Thumb Nasturtium)
description: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; dwarf nasturtium is a compact, bushy form of nasturtium that stays under 14 inches — ideal for containers, edging, and small gardens where the larger trailing species would overrun the space. All parts are edible: the peppery, watercress-flavored leaves are used in salads, the bright flowers as garnish and salad decoration, and the young seed pods pickled as a caper substitute. Unlike many edible flowers, nasturtiums are genuinely flavorful rather than merely decorative. The abundant flowers are rich in nectar and attract hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. The plants prefer lean soil — rich, highly fertilized soils produce lush leaves at the expense of flowers. In zone 9a, grow as a winter annual sown in October for winter and spring display. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Orinoco Banana
description: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil with high organic matter; Dwarf Orinoco is a compact, cold-hardy edible banana producing medium-sized, angular, somewhat starchy fruits that can be eaten fresh when fully ripe (developing a rich, sweet-tart flavor) or cooked as a plantain when green. The Orinoco type bananas (also called 'Horse Banana') are among the most cold-hardy fruiting bananas in cultivation, with Dwarf Orinoco selected for a shorter stature (6–10 feet) that is more manageable in home gardens and more wind-resistant than tall-growing types. In zone 9 Dwarf Orinoco regularly produces edible fruit clusters on pseudostems that survive mild winters without die-back, making it one of the most reliably productive edible banana choices for the Gulf South. Feed generously with high-potassium fertilizer during the growing season to support fruit development. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Pawpaw (Small-flower Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade — small-flower pawpaw is the native pawpaw of the southeastern coastal plain, growing in the dry understory of longleaf pine flatwoods and open, sandy woodlands from Virginia to Florida and west to Louisiana. It is more shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant than the common pawpaw (A. triloba) and produces smaller but similarly flavored fruits — small oblong yellow-green pawpaws 1–2 inches long with the characteristic sweet, custard-like tropical flavor of the familiar large pawpaw. Like all Asimina species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which depends entirely on Asimina for its caterpillars. The small maroon flowers in early spring resemble the larger common pawpaw flowers. A valuable native plant for the shaded, dry woodland garden in the Southeast, supporting both edible fruit production and butterfly habitat. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Red Banana
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Dwarf Red is a compact banana cultivar that stays a manageable 6-8 feet tall, considerably shorter than most fruiting bananas, with maroon-red pseudostems and leaf undersides that add ornamental color even before fruiting. The fruit itself has reddish-purple skin and a rich, dense, sweet flesh, ripening on a smaller bunch than standard dessert bananas but with good flavor for fresh eating. The compact size is the main practical advantage for zone 9 growers, since a Dwarf Red planted in a large container is much easier to move to shelter or wrap for winter protection than an 12-15 foot tropical banana. Give it rich soil, consistent moisture, and regular feeding through the growing season, and protect the rhizome from hard freezes, since like most Musa acuminata types it has limited cold tolerance compared to Orinoco or Musa basjoo. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Sarah's Delight Tomato (Apricot-Orange Dwarf Tomato)
description: Dwarf Sarah's Delight bears small-to-medium round fruit in a warm apricot-orange hue with a sweet, mild flavor good for fresh eating and salads. The plant grows as a sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate bush 2-4 feet tall, concentrating heirloom-quality fruit onto a footprint well suited to containers and small raised beds. It was released through the Dwarf Tomato Project, the breeding collaboration founded by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small to pair dwarf growth habit with heirloom flavor and color diversity. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Serviceberry
description: Sow seeds in fall directly into a prepared bed with lean, well-drained soil, pressing them just below the surface and allowing winter cold to provide the stratification needed for spring germination. Dwarf Serviceberry spreads aggressively by root sprouts and will form dense thickets over time, so site it where naturalized spread is welcome rather than in manicured borders. The profuse white spring flowers provide early nectar for pollinators, and the sweet blue-black berries that follow are among the first wild fruits to ripen each summer. Established colonies are highly drought-tolerant and require virtually no maintenance, making this shrub an outstanding choice for habitat restoration, erosion control, or low-maintenance edible landscaping. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Siberian Kale
description: This compact heirloom kale grows low and wide with finely curled green leaves that stay sweet and mild, and it tolerates both cold and heat. Sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep in fertile soil, thinning to give plants room to spread. Harvest outer leaves for baby greens or let plants size up for cut-and-come-again picking. Cold weather and light frost improve the flavor, making it ideal for containers, raised beds, and small-space fall gardens. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Dwarf Sunray Jerusalem Artichoke (Early Dwarf Sunchoke)
description: Dwarf Sunray was selected long ago as a shorter, tidier alternative to towering standard sunchoke varieties, topping out around 4-5 feet instead of the 8-10 feet common to most Helianthus tuberosus strains, which makes it far less prone to toppling in wind or shading neighboring crops. It concentrates its white-skinned tubers in a tight cluster close to the base of the stem rather than scattering them widely underground, so harvest is quicker and the planting is easier to contain within a bed. Foliage dies back with the first hard frosts, at which point tubers can be dug as needed through fall and winter, with flavor sweetening after cold exposure converts stored inulin to sugar. As with all sunchokes, leave a few tubers in the ground each season to regenerate next year's crop, and dig thoroughly at bed's end if you want to remove the planting entirely. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Sweet Sue Tomato (Golden-Yellow Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, potato-leaf stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Sweet Sue bears round to oblate golden-yellow fruit, often blushed pink at the blossom end when fully ripe, with a rich, well-balanced, notably sweet flavor for a yellow tomato. It was bred from a 2005 cross of Golden Dwarf Champion and Green Giant by Patrina Nuske Small and named by Craig LeHoullier for his wife, one of the earlier stabilized releases of the international Dwarf Tomato Project. Harvest as fruit colors fully and softens slightly for peak sweetness. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Wild Fred Tomato (Compact Red Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, stout stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Wild Fred bears clusters of medium red fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact, potato-leaf plant that stays under 4 feet, one of the early releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, an international collaboration of home breeders working to create full-flavored heirloom-quality tomatoes on space-saving dwarf plants. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where sprawling indeterminate tomatoes would be impractical. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Dwarf Winter Savory (Creeping Winter Savory)
description: This naturally compact sport of common winter savory forms a dense, low mat of narrow, glossy dark-green leaves rather than the upright woody shrublet of the species, making it well suited to edging paths, tumbling over container rims, and filling gaps between paving stones. The flavor is slightly milder and less resinous than standard winter savory but is used the same way, especially with beans, lentils, and slow-cooked meats. Shear lightly after the small white-to-lilac summer flowers fade to keep the mat tight and prevent bare, woody centers from developing. Because true dwarf plants must be propagated from cuttings or divisions to hold their compact form, start new plants vegetatively rather than from seed. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Dyer's Alkanet (Alkanna)
description: Dyer's alkanet is a low, bristly-leaved Mediterranean perennial in the borage family, distinct from the common bugloss and borage grown for their edible flowers, valued instead for its thick, dark-skinned taproot. The root bark contains alkannin, a red-purple pigment historically used to color wax, wood stains, cosmetic rouges, and oils, and still sought by natural-dye and soap-making hobbyists today. Small blue, forget-me-not-like flowers appear over a low rosette of hairy gray-green leaves in late spring. Roots are traditionally lifted in autumn of the second year, when pigment concentration peaks, then cleaned and dried whole for later dye extraction. Give it the leanest, driest, sunniest spot available; rich or damp soil produces lush foliage but weak, thin, poorly colored roots. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Dyer's Chamomile (Golden Marguerite)
description: Anthemis tinctoria is an upright, bushy perennial or biennial native to Europe and western Asia, producing deeply divided, fernlike, aromatic foliage and an exceptionally long succession of bright, golden-yellow, 1.5-inch daisy flowers from early summer through early fall; it is one of the most prolific and long-blooming of all yellow-flowered perennial herbs. Direct-sow seeds in early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in a warm, sunny position; it performs best in poor, gritty, or stony soil and will decline in rich, moist conditions — lean soil extends plant longevity and promotes maximum flowering. The whole plant, especially the flowers, yields a clear, warm, golden-yellow dye when used with an alum mordant; it has been used as a natural textile dye throughout Europe and the Middle East for centuries and was a primary source of yellow for wool dyeing. Deadhead or shear plants after the first main flush of bloom to stimulate continued flowering; short-lived plants are easily renewed from self-sown seedlings. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Dyer's Greenweed (Dyer's Broom)
description: Dyer's greenweed is a low, mounding, nitrogen-fixing legume shrub of European heaths and dry meadows, covered in bright golden pea-like flowers along its wiry stems from early to mid-summer. For centuries the flowering tops were cut and boiled to yield a strong yellow dye for wool and linen, which was traditionally over-dyed with woad or indigo to produce the deep green historically known as Kendal Green. The plant thrives on neglect in poor, lean, unamended soil and sulks or sprawls loosely if given rich ground or extra water. Cut back lightly after flowering to keep the low mound dense and to collect flowering tops at their peak dye potency; established plants are long-lived and need no routine feeding thanks to their own nitrogen fixation. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Eagle Pass Okra (South Texas Heirloom Okra)
description: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is thoroughly warm, since this variety germinates poorly in cool soil; space plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Eagle Pass is a Texas heirloom okra originating from the border region around Eagle Pass, Texas, selected over generations for tolerance of extreme heat and limited water, making it a strong performer in South Texas and other arid warm-climate gardens where many other okra varieties struggle. Plants grow tall and produce ribbed green pods that should be harvested young, at around 3-4 inches, for best tenderness. It remains a favorite among regional seed savers for its resilience and reliable yields under harsh summer conditions. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Earlibrite Strawberry (UF/IFAS Early-Season Gulf-Latitude Cultivar)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Earlibrite was released by the UF/IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center in Balm, Florida, bred specifically to ripen its first flush of fruit earlier in the winter production window than the older industry-standard cultivars of its era, giving Gulf Coast growers marketable strawberries before the main season gets underway. As with other short-day cultivars grown in the Deep South annual plasticulture system, set out fresh crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds and treat the planting strictly as a winter annual, since plants decline once summer heat arrives. Earlibrite was later used as a parent (crossed with 'Florida Radiance' in 2005) in the breeding of the UF release 'Winterstar', reflecting its value as an early-fruiting genetic source even after newer cultivars surpassed it commercially. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Earlidew Honeydew Melon (Early Northern-Adapted Honeydew)
description: Earlidew was developed to bring honeydew melon within reach of gardeners in shorter, cooler growing seasons where standard honeydew varieties often fail to ripen before fall. It produces smooth, pale green-white rinds around sweet, light green flesh on vines noticeably more compact than typical honeydew types. Because honeydew does not slip from the vine at maturity the way cantaloupe does, watch for the blossom end to soften slightly and the rind to take on a faint yellow cast as ripeness cues. Its earlier maturity window makes it one of the more practical honeydew choices for northern vegetable gardens. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Earliglow Strawberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil with excellent moisture retention — strawberries are shallow-rooted and require consistent moisture; Earliglow is widely regarded by strawberry enthusiasts as one of the finest-flavored June-bearing varieties available, producing medium-sized, conical, deep-red berries with intense, aromatic, old-fashioned strawberry flavor uncommon in modern commercial varieties bred for shipping durability rather than taste. Earliglow is the earliest of all June-bearing strawberries — the first variety to ripen each season, typically one to two weeks ahead of mid-season types — and the red color extends through the flesh to the center (no white core), reflecting the full flavor development. The intense, sweet-tart, richly aromatic flavor is most comparable to wild strawberries and old heirloom varieties rather than the large but bland commercial berries in grocery stores. Earliglow produces most reliably in zones 3–8 where winter chilling is adequate; gardeners in the Gulf South should choose day-neutral types instead. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Earliglow Strawberry (Early June-Bearing, Disease-Resistant Eastern Strawberry)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in early spring in full sun in well-prepared, well-drained soil; Earliglow is a June-bearing type (single concentrated crop in late spring) that produces abundant runners for establishing new beds; remove blossoms in the first year to encourage plant establishment for a heavier crop in year 2; mulch with straw over winter. Earliglow is a USDA-developed June-bearing strawberry variety released in 1975 that became one of the most important and widely planted commercial and home garden strawberries in the eastern United States for its combination of early ripening, excellent flavor, and disease resistance. The early ripening characteristic is particularly valuable in northeastern gardens (zones 4–7) where late spring frosts are a constant concern for berry production — Earliglow matures and is harvested before most other varieties even turn red, providing insurance against frost damage to developing fruits. The berries are medium-sized, glossy red, with a characteristic conical shape and excellent fresh flavor — consistently rated among the best-tasting June-bearing varieties by university extension trials for their balance of sweetness and acidity. Earliglow has exceptional disease resistance compared to many older varieties, showing good resistance to red stele root rot (Phytophthora fragariae) and Verticillium wilt — two of the most damaging strawberry diseases in cool, wet eastern growing conditions. The combination of early harvest, great flavor, and disease resistance made Earliglow the dominant strawberry variety in the Mid-Atlantic states for decades, and it remains one of the most-planted varieties in the region. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Earligold Apricot (One of the Earliest-Ripening Low-Chill Apricots)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Earligold, needing only roughly 250 to 400 chill hours, is among the earliest-ripening apricot cultivars available, well suited to climates with minimal winter cold accumulation, giving gardeners the first fresh apricots of the season in a favorable year. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Earligrande Peach (Early Very-Low-Chill Yellow Clingstone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Earligrande needs only about 275 chill hours, making it a dependable early peach for zone 8-9 gardens along the Gulf Coast where higher-chill varieties fail to break dormancy evenly. Fruit ripens very early, usually mid to late April, with yellow, semi-clingstone flesh under mostly red-blushed skin. Trees are vigorous and heavy-bearing, so consistent hand thinning is needed to size the fruit and avoid limb stress. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Early Acre Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Early Acre is a compact, early-maturing bush cowpea that completes its fresh-shell harvest in just 55–65 days, among the earliest of any southern pea type. The small, cream-colored seeds with a small eye have a mild, slightly sweet flavor preferred by many over the stronger-flavored crowder and black-eye types. This variety is well-adapted to the Gulf Coast's brief spring and fall shoulder seasons, fitting in a productive crop before summer extremes take hold or closing out the season after summer heat breaks. The drought tolerance of cowpeas generally extends to Early Acre, which needs minimal irrigation once established. Harvest pods while the hulls are firm and the seeds have fully plumped but before the hull begins to dry. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Early Alaska Pea
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; in zone 6+ this means January–February; in zone 3–5, as soon as soil thaws. Early Alaska is one of the oldest and most cold-tolerant pea varieties, germinating in soils as cold as 38–40°F and maturing in 55–60 days from seed — making it one of the fastest peas available. The smooth-seeded peas are not as sweet as wrinkled-seed types but have traditional pea flavor and historically represent the 'early pea' of American kitchen gardens. Short (24–30 inch), self-supporting plants produce cylindrical pods with 5–7 peas; smooth seeds tolerate cold, wet soil better than wrinkled types that can rot. In Gulf Coast and Southern gardens (zones 8–10), Early Alaska planted in January finishes before March heat ends the pea season. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Early Amber Peach (Extra-Early Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)
