description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape to admit light and air into the canopy. Early Amber is a very low-chill selection bred for mild-winter growing regions, requiring roughly 300-350 hours below 45 degrees F, which lets it flower and fruit consistently on the Gulf Coast even in warm winters that leave many standard peach cultivars barren. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will produce a crop without a pollinator partner nearby, and it ripens extremely early, typically by late May in the Deep South. The medium-sized, semi-freestone fruit has yellow skin with a red blush and juicy, richly flavored yellow flesh; thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart when marble-sized to encourage larger, better-flavored peaches. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Early Black Cranberry
description: Early Black is one of the oldest named cranberry cultivars still in cultivation, first selected from wild New England bogs in the mid-1800s and long favored in Massachusetts cranberry growing for its small, very dark, deeply colored fruit and dependable early ripening. Its early harvest window makes it useful in shorter-season northern locations where later-ripening cultivars like Pilgrim may not fully color before frost. Vines are relatively compact and cold hardy, tolerating the harsh winter conditions of traditional New England bogs with proper winter flooding or sanding. As with all cranberries, success depends on maintaining strongly acidic soil, a continuous water source, and a sandy-peat rooting layer. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Early Blood Turnip Beet
description: One of the earliest American beet varieties on record, grown widely since the early 1800s and named for its flattened, turnip-like shape rather than any relation to actual turnips. It was the dominant garden beet in the United States for much of the 19th century before newer selections like Detroit Dark Red largely replaced it commercially. Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; the deep red roots have dense, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and pickling, and the plant can be resown for a fall crop as well. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Early Butternut PMR Squash (Powdery Mildew-Resistant Early Butternut)
description: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give vines moderate room to spread. Early Butternut PMR was bred to bring the classic tan-skinned, orange-fleshed butternut squash to gardeners in shorter growing seasons, reaching harvest well before standard Waltham-type strains while carrying built-in resistance to powdery mildew, a common late-season problem on butternut vines. Fruit averages 2 to 3 pounds, a convenient size for single-meal use, with the same dense, sweet, nutty flesh gardeners expect from butternut squash. Harvest once the rind has turned uniformly tan and hardened, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm spot to improve storage life and sweetness. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Early Crawford Peach (Crawford's Early, Historic 19th-Century Freestone Peach)
description: Early Crawford, also sold as Crawford's Early, was discovered around 1815-1820 by William Crawford of Middletown, New Jersey, and went on to become one of the most widely planted peaches in 19th-century America, prized for its large, showy, yellow-skinned, red-blushed fruit and rich, yellow, freestone flesh. Its combination of size, color, and flavor made it the commercial standard of its era and the parent stock behind many later cultivars, most notably crossed with Chinese Cling by Samuel Rumph in 1875 to produce Elberta, the freestone peach that eventually eclipsed it in Southern orchards. Trees are vigorous and productive but the fruit buds are only moderately cold-hardy and the ripening fruit is prone to brown rot in humid weather, so growers should thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart after petal fall, prune to an open-vase form for airflow, and maintain a fungicide program through the ripening period. It remains worth growing today chiefly for its historical significance and its rich, old-fashioned peach flavor, which many heirloom fruit growers consider superior to modern shipping-bred cultivars. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Early Curled Simpson Lettuce (Silesia, Historic Overwintering Loose-Leaf)
description: Descended from the French heirloom Silesia and known by several names over the years, including Curled Silesia and White-Seeded Simpson, this loose-leaf lettuce came into wider American use in the 1850s as a quicker-maturing alternative to older sorts. It forms a tight, quick-growing bunch of light green, crumpled leaves about a foot across, without ever forming a true head. Exceptionally cold-hardy, it was traditionally the lettuce of choice for overwintering in cold frames or under straw mulch, shrugging off hard freezes that would kill tenderer types. Its speed and hardiness make it a good pick for the earliest spring salads or a late fall planting pushed into winter. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Early Elberta Peach (Earlier-Ripening Elberta Sport)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun. Early Elberta is a sport selection of the legendary Elberta peach, the single most historically important commercial peach variety in American horticulture, chosen specifically for ripening one to two weeks ahead of standard Elberta while retaining the same large size, rich yellow freestone flesh, and full, well-balanced classic peach flavor that made the parent variety dominant across the South for a century. The earlier ripening window is a genuine practical advantage for gardeners wanting to beat the peak-summer disease and pest pressure that builds through a long peach season, without giving up the flavor Elberta is famous for. Thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall for good size, prune annually to an open-vase form, and maintain a dormant-season spray program for peach leaf curl and brown rot. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Early Fortune Cucumber
description: Early Fortune was selected by a Michigan grower from the older Davis Perfect cucumber and introduced commercially around 1910 as an early, dependable white-spine slicer, quickly becoming one of the most widely planted cucumbers in the country. Fruits reach 7-8 inches with smooth, deep green skin and crisp, mild white flesh, and the vines begin bearing notably faster than many other open-pollinated slicers of similar type. It is a traditional monoecious variety needing insect pollination between separate male and female blossoms, so plant in blocks rather than single rows for reliable fruit set. Its short time to harvest and long production history make it a forgiving choice for gardeners wanting a classic slicing cucumber without relying on modern hybrid seed. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Early Fry Muscadine Grape (Early-Ripening Sport of Classic Fry)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible self-fertile pollinizer variety nearby. Early Fry is a sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine selected specifically for ripening earlier in the season than the standard variety, giving growers a jump on the muscadine harvest while retaining the same large fruit size and rich, sweet flavor that made the original Fry so popular across the South. The earlier ripening window can also help the crop finish before the heaviest late-summer pest and disease pressure builds, a practical advantage in humid Gulf Coast growing conditions. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily from the stem with a gentle tug, and expect the harvest window to open somewhat ahead of standard Fry plantings. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Early Girl Tomato (Classic Early-Season Slicing Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Early Girl is one of the most popular home garden tomato varieties in American history — a determinate-to-indeterminate hybrid introduced by Petoseed in 1975 that produces medium-sized (4–6 oz), globe-shaped, deep-red slicing tomatoes 50–60 days from transplant, weeks before most main-season varieties ripen. The combination of early maturity, classic tomato flavor, reliable production, and adaptability to a wide range of climates made Early Girl the best-selling tomato variety in many US markets for decades. In zone 9, Early Girl performs best in the spring window (February–June transplanting), producing the first ripe tomatoes well ahead of main-season varieties while temperatures are still moderate. The plant is a compact to medium-sized indeterminate that requires staking but is less vigorous than large-vined cherry tomatoes — a cage of 48–60 inches is usually sufficient. The classic red, round, full-flavored fruits are excellent for fresh slicing, sandwiches, and summer salads where a moderately sized, well-flavored tomato is preferred over giant beefsteak types. Good disease resistance package makes it dependable in humid Gulf South conditions. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Early Golden American Persimmon (Classic Early-Ripening Native Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, siting the tree carefully since American persimmon forms a deep taproot and resents being moved once established. Early Golden is one of the oldest and most widely planted named selections of native American persimmon, valued for ripening earlier in the fall than most other cultivars and for its rich, honey-sweet flavor once fruit is fully soft-ripe. It has served as an important parent in later persimmon breeding programs and remains a dependable choice for home orchards across its hardiness range. Never eat the golden-orange fruit while still firm, since unripe American persimmon is strongly astringent; wait until it softens fully or falls from the tree. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and needs little maintenance beyond removing root suckers each year. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Early Golden Summer Crookneck Squash (Colonial-Era Yellow Crookneck)
description: Direct sow in hills in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed. Early Golden Summer Crookneck is one of the oldest documented American squash varieties, first offered commercially by Thorburn's seed catalog in 1828 and grown in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden, producing bright golden-yellow, warty-skinned fruit with the classic curved neck of crookneck squash. Its early, prolific bearing and compact bush habit make it a reliable, fast-producing choice for a home vegetable garden. Harvest young, four to six inches long, for the best tenderness and flavor, picking every day or two during peak production to keep the plant setting new fruit. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Early Harvest Apple (Classic Early-Season American Heirloom)
description: One of the oldest named apples grown in American gardens, Early Harvest was prized in colonial and 19th-century orchards for ripening well before almost any other cultivar, often in midsummer. The pale yellow-green skin and tender, tart flesh cook down quickly into sauce and are best picked and used within days, since the fruit bruises easily and does not store. Because the whole crop does not ripen at once, expect several light pickings over a couple of weeks rather than one harvest. Grow it as a nostalgia piece or for the earliest homemade applesauce of the season, not as a keeper apple. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Early Hegari Grain Sorghum
description: Early Hegari is an open-pollinated grain sorghum released in 1940 and valued for combining a short growing season with a compact, broad-leafed plant only 3 to 4 feet tall, making it easy to manage in a home garden bed rather than a field. Its open heads carry white grain with a pink blush, and the plant is notably drought-tolerant and tolerant of poor soils, producing sweet, juicy stalks along the way. Because it matures faster than most grain sorghums, it is a good option for gardeners with shorter summers or those wanting to fit a grain crop into a succession planting. Harvest heads once grain has reached hard dough stage and dried down, then thresh and store the seed for flour, cereal, or poultry feed. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Early Jade Gai Lan (Chinese Broccoli)
description: A fast, uniform hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for reliable slow-bolting performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings. Dark green, tender leaves and thick, juicy stalks top out with small clusters of edible white buds that taste milder and sweeter than standard broccoli. Cut the main stalk once it reaches pencil thickness and buds are just starting to open, then keep harvesting side shoots for several more weeks of production. Its speed and dependable bolt resistance make it a good choice for gardeners who want repeated gai lan harvests through an entire growing season rather than a single spring or fall flush. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Early Jalapeno Chile Pepper
description: This jalapeno bears bold flavor in a compact 3 inch pepper and is better adapted to cooler climates than most jalapenos, making it a good choice for short-season gardens. Enjoy pods green for a mild-to-medium kick or let them ripen red for added sweetness. Start seed indoors early and transplant into full sun after the soil warms. Pick regularly to encourage continued production. Fruit sets best with warm days and consistent moisture. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Early Jersey Wakefield Cabbage
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Early Jersey Wakefield'
description: Set transplants 12–15 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the tight spacing and quick maturity make this variety well suited to succession planting and small-space gardens. Early Jersey Wakefield is one of the oldest cabbage varieties still in cultivation, introduced to American gardens from England in the 1840s and named for Wakefield, England, where it was developed. It forms small, dense, distinctively cone-shaped (pointed) heads of 2–3 pounds that mature earlier than nearly any other cabbage, historically prized for beating both the spring heat and cabbage-worm buildup that plague later varieties. The compact plants and short row-space needs make it a classic choice for small kitchen gardens, and its speed makes it valuable for a quick spring crop ahead of summer vegetables, or a fast fall crop in mild-winter climates. A true living heirloom with over 180 years of continuous garden use, in zone 3–9. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Early Jewel Persimmon (H-118 Claypool Early-Ripening Selection)
description: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and prune annually if you want to keep the naturally vigorous tree contained to 20-25 feet rather than letting it grow to full native persimmon height. Also sold under its original breeding designation H-118, Early Jewel came out of the late James Claypool's Indiana persimmon breeding program and stands out for ripening its large, reddish-orange fruit in early September, weeks ahead of standard cultivars like Early Golden and Prok, which stretches the harvest season for home growers. The soft, fully ripe fruit carries a distinctive rich butterscotch-and-rum flavor that fans of native persimmon prize highly. It is a strong, reliable annual bearer that comes into production at a relatively young age for the species, and like all American persimmon needs full sun and deep soil to perform its best. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Early Laxton Plum (Early-Ripening English Gage-Type Plum)
description: Early Laxton was raised by the English fruit-breeding firm Laxton Brothers and is valued for ripening well ahead of most other European plums, filling the gap before the main dessert-plum season begins. The medium, yellow fruit is flushed with red and has a rich, gage-like sweetness when fully ripe. It is self-fertile, so a lone tree will crop, though yields are fuller with a second plum nearby. Because it ripens early and the blossom appears early too, site it away from frost pockets to protect the flowers from late cold snaps, and thin fruit if the set is heavy to improve size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Early Long Purple Eggplant
description: Sow indoors under warm conditions and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, since this heirloom is sensitive to cold snaps. Space plants generously and water evenly to keep the slender fruit from developing a bitter edge. Early Long Purple is a traditional Italian variety valued for producing its slim, curved, deep-purple fruit earlier than many other eggplant types, making it a useful choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions. Its thin skin and few seeds make it popular for frying and grilling whole. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Early Prolific Straightneck Squash (Classic American Yellow Summer Squash)
description: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Early Prolific Straightneck is the classic American yellow summer squash — the standard straightneck type that has defined the yellow summer squash category in American home gardens and commercial production for decades. The smooth, straight, medium-yellow to golden-yellow squash (6–8 inches at ideal harvest) has the classic straight-neck shape (no bulge or curve at the blossom end) that distinguishes straightneck from crookneck types. The tender, mild-flavored flesh is excellent sautéed, grilled, steamed, stuffed, and in casseroles — the standard all-purpose yellow summer squash for every culinary application. An All-America Selections winner recognized for its exceptional productive performance and consistent quality. Harvest squash when small to medium (6–8 inches) for best flavor and tenderness — oversized squash develop tough skin, large hard seeds, and coarse, watery flesh. In zone 9, summer squash is best grown in spring (February–April) and fall (August–October) — the summer heat accelerates production to the point of difficulty managing harvests. The squash vine borer is the primary pest challenge in zone 9; fall planting (August) often escapes the peak infestation period. Extremely productive — a few plants provide more squash than most families can use during peak season; succession planting at 2–3 week intervals provides more manageable quantities. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Early Prolific Straightneck Summer Squash
description: This award-winning yellow straightneck squash yields thick, firm, fine-grained fruit in as little as 45 days. Versatile in the kitchen, it can be eaten raw, pickled, cooked, or baked into sweet breads. Harvest young, around 4 to 6 inches, for the best texture and to keep plants producing. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Keep evenly watered and pick frequently. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Early Purple Sprouting Broccoli
description: Unlike single-head types, this cold-hardy heirloom produces a flush of deep purple florets on many side shoots for an extended harvest. Start seed in summer and set robust transplants into rich soil so they establish before winter. Plants overwinter in mild climates and reward growers with tender sprouts in late winter and early spring. Pick shoots regularly while the buds are tight to keep new sprouts coming; a brief cook preserves the color. Matures in 200–220 days from transplant.

name: Early Red Loquat (Very Early-Ripening California Loquat)
description: Early Red is grown specifically to bring loquat harvest forward, with fruit commonly ripening as early as February in mild-winter climates, well ahead of standard-season cultivars such as Champagne or Premier. This early timing lets Gulf Coast and California growers plant it alongside a mid- or late-season cultivar to stretch the loquat harvest across several months rather than concentrating it into a few spring weeks. Because its fruit finishes developing during the coldest part of winter, Early Red is somewhat more exposed to freeze damage than later-ripening cultivars, so a warm microclimate against a south-facing wall improves consistency. Like other loquat cultivars it is self-fertile and benefits from thinning after a heavy bloom to improve fruit size. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Early Richmond Cherry (Classic American Heirloom Sour Cherry)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Early Richmond is a classic 19th-century American sour cherry, one of the most widely planted tart cherries before Montmorency largely replaced it commercially, prized for producing the earliest sour cherry crop of the season, ripening ahead of Montmorency and most other pie cherries. The medium-sized, bright red fruit has tender, juicy, acidic flesh that is outstanding for pies, preserves, and baking, and the self-fertile tree needs no separate pollinizer, making it a practical single-tree choice for home orchards. The tree is smaller and more manageable than most sweet cherries, cold-hardy, and reliably productive; net against birds as fruit ripens, since sour cherries are just as attractive to birds as sweet ones despite their tartness. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Early Round Dutch Cabbage
description: This 19th-century heirloom produces compact, round green heads with a mild flavor and dependable cold tolerance. Start seed indoors about five to six weeks before transplanting into firm, fertile soil. Keep watering even and steady, since fluctuations can split maturing heads. Harvest once heads feel solid and firm, cutting cleanly at the base; it performs well in both spring and fall plantings. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Early Scarlet Globe Radish (Classic Fast Spring Radish)
description: Sow in thin rows 1/4 inch deep; no need to thin closely if sown sparsely; harvest when roots are 3/4 to 1 inch across; Early Scarlet Globe holds slightly better in the ground than some varieties without becoming immediately pithy — useful for succession plantings where exact harvest timing is impractical. Early Scarlet Globe is a foundational heirloom spring radish that has appeared continuously in American seed catalogs since the 19th century and remains one of the most widely recognized and consistently reliable spring radish varieties for home garden use. The name describes it precisely: the variety matures early, produces globe-shaped (round, not oval or elongated) roots, and has the classic bright scarlet skin color of traditional spring radishes. The roots are smooth and round, typically reaching 3/4 to 1 inch in diameter at the ideal harvest stage, with bright white, crisp, mildly peppery flesh that is refreshing and clean-flavored. Early Scarlet Globe is somewhat more forgiving than some spring radish varieties — it maintains quality for a few extra days in the ground after reaching harvest size before becoming pithy or hollow — a useful characteristic when garden timing is imprecise. Its very fast maturity (22–28 days) makes it one of the quickest-maturing vegetables a gardener can grow and ideal for teaching children about gardening: almost immediate gratification. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Early Scarlet Globe thrives in the short cool season windows of January–March and October–November before heat forces bolting. Matures in 22–28 days from seed.

name: Early Select Kkaennip (Short-Season Korean Perilla)
description: Early Select is a regionally adapted kkaennip strain developed by growers at roughly 44°N latitude who noticed that ordinary Korean perilla, being highly sensitive to daylength, often failed to finish and dry viable seed before fall frost that far north. This selection was chosen over several seasons for plants that reliably complete their seed cycle in a shorter window, while still producing the large, strongly mint-and-basil-scented green leaves used fresh in wraps, pickled into kimchi, or pressed for their seed oil. Starting seed indoors well ahead of the last frost gives plants the extra weeks they need, and transplanting into a full-sun to partial-shade bed keeps growth vigorous through summer. Because it was bred as a dependable seed-saving strain, allow at least a few plants to flower and fully dry their seed heads at season's end to keep the line going. Matures in 70–120 days from seed.

name: Early Snowball Cauliflower (Classic Compact Heirloom White Cauliflower)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant sturdy seedlings into rich, evenly moist soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants 15-20 inches apart; Early Snowball is a compact, open-pollinated heirloom that has stayed popular for well over a century because it forms tight, pure-white 5-6 inch heads faster and more dependably than many modern hybrids. Tie the outer leaves loosely over the developing curd once it reaches golf-ball size to shield it from sun and keep the head bright white, checking every few days since this variety heads up quickly once it starts. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from healthy plants that are isolated from other Brassica oleracea varieties in bloom. Harvest as soon as heads reach full size and are still tight and smooth, since Early Snowball's curds loosen and turn ricey faster than slower-maturing types if left too long in the field. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Early Spanish Peanut (Bunch-Type Boiling and Roasting Peanut)
description: Sow shelled seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since the flower stalks (pegs) must push down into the soil after pollination to form pods underground. Early Spanish is a small-seeded, upright bunch-type peanut with a single kernel per pod more often than the two-seeded Virginia types, and it reaches maturity noticeably faster, which suits it to gardens outside the Deep South's longest growing seasons as well as within them. Mound soil gently around the base of the plants once flowering begins so pegs have an easy path into loose earth, and keep the bed evenly moist through flowering and pegging since drought at that stage sharply cuts yield. Dig the whole plant once the foliage begins to yellow, then cure the pods in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before shelling, boiling, or roasting. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Early St. Ann Satsuma (Early-Maturing LSU AgCenter Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Early St. Ann came out of the LSU AgCenter's fresh-market citrus improvement program and was released as an early-maturing satsuma bred to outperform the older Armstrong selection in fruit size, yield, and eating quality. Fruit is oblate, medium-to-large, thin-skinned with a light leathery rind and deep orange, richly flavored flesh, ripening from early September into mid-October. Trees are productive and manageable in size, making this a good choice where gardeners want fruit ahead of the main satsuma season. It shares the general cold tolerance of other satsuma mandarins but still benefits from trunk wraps or covers during hard freeze events in zone 8 plantings. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Early Sulphur Gooseberry (Historic Very-Early Yellow Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Early Sulphur is one of the oldest English dessert gooseberry cultivars still in commerce, possibly identical to the 'Yellow Lion of Ward' introduced in 1825, and it remains valued for ripening earlier than almost any other gooseberry. Its primrose-yellow, hairy berries are prized for excellent flavor, equally suited to fresh eating and jam, and the bush grows in a strong, upright habit. Because gooseberries need a real winter chill to perform well, Early Sulphur is best grown in cold-winter climates rather than the mild-winter Gulf South. Plant in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, and prune to an open center each dormant season to improve airflow and reduce mildew. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Early Sunglow Sweet Corn (Ultra-Early Yellow Short-Vine Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Early Sunglow is the gold standard of early-maturing sweet corn for home gardeners who want corn on the table as soon as possible in the season — a yellow su (standard sugary) hybrid that ripens in just 62–68 days from planting, providing corn approximately 3–4 weeks before mid-season varieties like Silver Queen. The compact (4–4.5 foot) stalks are one of Early Sunglow's most practical attributes for home gardens: shorter plants are less susceptible to lodging in wind or storms and fit better in smaller garden plots where standard 6–7 foot corn would be too tall. Early Sunglow's germination in cooler soils (down to about 55°F) also allows planting 1–2 weeks earlier in spring before soils warm fully, extending the effective growing season at the front end. The ears are smaller than mid-season varieties (6–7 inches, 12–14 rows) but are well-filled with tender, sweet, yellow kernels with the classic su corn flavor — pleasantly sweet without the overwhelming intensity of sh2 supersweet types. For gardeners in zones 4–6 with short seasons, Early Sunglow may be the only way to reliably produce sweet corn before fall frosts; in zones 7–10, it provides the season's earliest fresh corn while later varieties are still maturing. Matures in 62–68 days from seed.

name: Early White Bush Scallop Squash (Classic White Patty Pan Squash)
description: This is one of the oldest American summer squash types, grown by colonial gardeners well before it was formally selected and named in the 19th century, producing the classic ivory-white, scallop-edged flying-saucer fruit. Harvest at 2-3 inches across while the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail; older fruit turns starchy and tough quickly. The compact bush habit suits small beds and containers better than vining winter squash, and steady picking every couple of days keeps the plant setting new fruit through the season. Its pale color and mild, delicate flavor make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a change from the more common yellow and green scallop types. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Early White Vienna Kohlrabi
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes 'Early White Vienna'
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Early White Vienna is the standard open-pollinated kohlrabi variety — the pale green, globe-shaped swollen stem that has defined kohlrabi's appearance in seed catalogs and markets for more than a century. Kohlrabi is among the most distinctive of all vegetables because the edible part is neither a root nor a leaf but a dramatically swollen, above-ground stem that balloons into a globe shape at the base of the plant with the leaves attached at the sides — a growth habit that surprises gardeners encountering kohlrabi for the first time. The crisp, juicy white flesh beneath the thin pale-green skin has a flavor often described as a mild, sweet, slightly broccoli-stem-flavored apple — kohlrabi is excellent eaten raw like an apple, cut into sticks for snacking and dipping, shredded into slaws, or cooked in stir-fries and soups where it retains some crunch even when heated. The flavor is far milder and sweeter than most brassicas, making kohlrabi one of the most approachable and snackable vegetables directly from the garden, particularly attractive to children who enjoy the mild sweetness and the theatrical process of peeling and eating the unusual globe. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Early Wonder Beet
description: Grown since the early 1900s, this early variety delivers abundant, tasty greens up to 18 inches tall along with flavorful roots, and is ideal where multiple crops fit the season. The leaves are high in vitamins A and C, iron, and potassium. Since each seed is a cluster, thin seedlings for well-shaped roots. Sow in cool weather and keep soil evenly moist. Harvest roots young and tender or let them size up. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Earth Pea (Tuberous Pea, Fyfield Pea)
description: Plant tubers in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun, giving the climbing stems support from a trellis, fence, or neighboring plants; earth pea is a remarkable perennial legume from central Europe that forms small, chestnut-flavored starchy tubers along its root system — the edible reward in addition to the ornamental rose-pink flowers. The tubers can be eaten raw, boiled, or roasted and have a pleasant, sweet, slightly floury flavor. Historically the plant was gathered as a famine food across rural Europe and was cultivated as a minor food crop in the Netherlands and France. Like other legumes, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and gradually improves soil fertility. The vine is vigorous and twining, to about 3–6 feet, and the fragrant flowers attract bumblebees. An unusual, under-exploited edible perennial for food forest and permaculture plantings. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: East Indian Lemon Grass (Tall Aromatic Culinary Lemon Grass for Tea and Cooking)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; East Indian Lemon Grass (Cymbopogon flexuosus) is a tall, strongly aromatic grass from India and Sri Lanka — the primary source of lemongrass essential oil in commercial production worldwide and an excellent culinary and medicinal herb for Gulf South gardens where it grows as a warm-season perennial. The flavor and aroma are distinctly similar to but slightly different from West Indian Lemon Grass (C. citratus): both produce the characteristic bright, clean, citrus-lemon fragrance from the essential oil citral, but East Indian Lemon Grass is considered more intensely aromatic and is the preferred species for essential oil distillation. For culinary use, both species are suitable for Thai cooking, Vietnamese soups, herbal teas, and marinades — the inner stalks harvested and used the same way as standard lemongrass. East Indian Lemon Grass grows taller and more slenderly than C. citratus, reaching 4–6 feet with a more open, arching habit rather than the dense clumping habit of West Indian Lemon Grass — the differences in habit and aroma make it worth growing alongside the common species for comparison. In Gulf South zone 9, it grows as a warm-season perennial, potentially surviving mild winters with mulch protection but requiring replanting if hard freezes kill the crown. Fresh lemongrass harvested from the garden has a brighter, more vivid flavor than dried or frozen commercial lemongrass — a strong argument for growing your own in the Gulf South kitchen garden. Matures in 75–120 days from transplant.

name: East Indian Lemongrass
description: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost in warm, moist flats and keep soil at 75-85F for reliable sprouting. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil once nights stay above 50F, spacing clumps well apart to allow fanning growth. Water consistently through the season and feed monthly with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer for lush stalks. In zones colder than 9, dig and pot up a division to overwinter indoors in a bright window. Harvest by twisting off outer stalks at the base once they reach pencil thickness. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: East Kent Golding Hops
description: One of the oldest named English hop varieties, treasured for its delicate honeyed, earthy-floral aroma that defines classic English bitters and pale ales. It is somewhat lower-yielding and more susceptible to verticillium wilt and downy mildew than newer cultivars, so give it good air circulation and avoid overhead watering. Home growers in cooler, humid climates similar to Kent, England tend to have the best luck. Harvest cones when they feel dry and papery and spring back after a gentle squeeze. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Easter Beurré Pear (Doyenné d'Hiver)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Originating around 1823 at the Capucin Monastery at Louvain, Belgium, where monks knew it as Pastorale de Louvain, it is also known in France as Doyenné d'Hiver. The obovate-pyriform fruit has yellow skin marked with conspicuous russet dots and patches, often with a dull brownish-red blush, and yellow-tinged, tender, melting, buttery flesh with a rich, aromatic, sweet flavor. The tree is medium-sized, vigorous, upright-spreading, and slow-growing; historically its very long keeping quality made it valuable for extending the fresh pear season into late winter and spring. Harvest quite late in fall while very hard, store cool for many weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Easter Egg Blend Radish
description: This colorful mix produces red, white, rose-pink, purple, and bicolor spring radishes for a rainbow at harvest, making it a fun crop for kids. As a spring type it grows best in the cool periods of spring and fall and turns pithy in summer heat. Sow directly and thin seedlings early for well-formed roots. Keep soil evenly moist for crisp, mild radishes. Eat fresh in salads or as a crunchy snack. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Easter Egg Radish Blend
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and 1 inch apart, thinning to 2–3 inches after germination; Easter Egg is a blend of radish varieties producing a cheerful mix of purple, red, white, and pink round radishes (all similar in size to a chicken egg) in the same row — the variety gets its name from the surprise of digging mixed-color 'eggs' from the soil. Individual plants in the blend mature at slightly different rates over 2–3 weeks, naturally extending the harvest window. The crisp, mild, slightly spicy roots are excellent raw in salads, on veggie platters, or sliced and eaten with butter and salt in the classic French crudités style. This mixed-color planting is particularly popular in children's gardens for its surprise-reveal at harvest. In zone 9, fall and winter plantings (October–January) produce the crispest, mildest roots — spring radishes bolt quickly as temperatures rise. Harvest promptly when roots reach egg size; leaving them too long makes them hollow and pithy. One of the fastest and most satisfying crops for impatient gardeners. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Eastern Prickly Gooseberry (Dogberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; eastern prickly gooseberry is a native woodland shrub found scattered through rocky, deciduous forest understory from the Appalachians west to the Great Plains, distinguished from cultivated gooseberries by its densely bristly, spine-covered fruit and its genuine tolerance of significant shade, making it one of the few fruiting shrubs suited to a true woodland edible garden. Small, greenish, bell-shaped flowers in spring give way by midsummer to round, purplish-brown berries covered in soft prickly bristles that are removed by rubbing before eating; the tart-sweet pulp is used in preserves and pies much like other gooseberries once the spines are dealt with. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose thicket at a woodland edge, providing cover and fruit for wildlife as well as the gardener, and needs little care beyond removing the oldest canes every few years to keep new growth productive. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Eastern Prickly Pear (Devil's Tongue)
description: Plant callused pad sections in very well-drained, dry, sandy to rocky soil in full sun — eastern prickly pear is the most cold-hardy prickly pear cactus in North America, native from New England to the Gulf Coast and surviving zone 4 winters without damage. The flattened pads (2–4 inches across) grow close to the ground in a spreading mat; large, showy yellow flowers with numerous prominent orange stamens appear in May–June and are followed by barrel-shaped, red to purple-red edible fruits (tunas) that persist through winter. Both the young pads (nopales) and the fruits are traditional foods: young pads are peeled of their glochids and eaten as a vegetable; fruits are juiced, made into jelly, candy, and syrup. The glochids (tiny barbed hair-spines) on the fruits require careful handling — burn or scrub them off before consuming. An outstanding, zero-care native groundcover for dry, rocky, sandy, full-sun spots where lawn and conventional plants would fail. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Eastern Prince Schisandra
description: Plant in partial shade with morning sun in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Eastern Prince is a self-fertile cultivar of Schisandra chinensis, the 'five-flavor berry' used for centuries in Chinese and Russian herbal medicine and prized in its native forests for fruit and foliage said to combine sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and pungent notes in one berry. The twining vine bears small, waxy white flowers in spring followed by long, pendant clusters of glossy red berries in late summer, best used for juice, tinctures, syrup, and jam rather than fresh eating due to their intense tartness. Because it is perfect-flowered rather than dioecious, Eastern Prince fruits reliably without a separate pollinator vine, making it far more practical for small gardens than seed-grown schisandra. Provide sturdy support and consistent moisture, and mulch to keep roots cool. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Eastham Beach Plum (Named Cape Cod Beach Plum Selection)
description: Plant in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun, siting near another named beach plum cultivar since seedlings and single clones set fruit poorly on their own. Eastham is one of the older Massachusetts-selected beach plum cultivars, chosen for large, well-flavored fruit and heavy, dependable cropping compared with typical wild seedling stands. Its purple-red fruit is prized for jams, jellies, and the traditional New England beach plum preserves that built the species' local reputation. Being a true coastal native, it tolerates salt spray, drought, and lean sandy soil that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, making it as useful for dune stabilization as for harvest. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove dead or crossing wood, since heavy pruning reduces the following year's crop. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eaton Chinese Chestnut
description: Eaton is a Chinese chestnut selection valued for consistently large, sweet, easy-to-peel nuts on a productive, comparatively fast-bearing tree. Like other Chinese chestnuts it carries strong resistance to chestnut blight, letting it thrive in regions where the related American chestnut has vanished. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and plant a genetically distinct pollinizer within a hundred feet or so for a full crop. Harvest burs as they split open and drop in early fall, and gather promptly since fallen nuts spoil quickly and attract wildlife. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ebenezer Onion (Old Dutch Yellow Storage Heirloom)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free through bulb development. Ebenezer is a classic Dutch-derived heirloom onion, long grown in American gardens both from seed and from sets, producing firm, globe-to-slightly-flattened yellow-brown bulbs with pungent flesh and outstanding storage life compared to sweeter modern hybrids. It is one of the parent lines behind several later commercial yellow storage onions and remains popular with gardeners who want an old-fashioned, strong-flavored keeper for cooking rather than fresh eating. Stop watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for a few weeks, and store in a cool, dry place where it will keep considerably longer than sweet onion types. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Ebisu Kabocha Squash
description: A traditional Japanese kabocha type especially popular around Tokyo, prized for its dry, deep-yellow, chestnut-flavored flesh. Sow directly after frost danger passes, or start indoors for an earlier crop in cool climates. Vines set three to four uniform, squat globe-shaped fruits with dark green skin and faint white speckling. Harvest once the skin dulls and resists puncture, then cure in a warm location for a week or two; curing converts starches to sugars and noticeably improves flavor. Stores well for several months in a cool, dry spot. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Ebolo (Redflower Ragleaf)
description: Sow or transplant into moist, fertile soil in partial shade; ebolo is a fast-growing, soft-stemmed leafy green widely eaten across West and Central Africa and parts of Southeast Asia, where the tender young leaves and shoot tips have a distinctive bitter-savory, slightly peppery flavor often compared to a cross between spinach and arugula. It performs best with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which keeps leaves tender and delays the small, brush-like reddish-orange flowers that signal the plant is turning bitter and going to seed. Pinch shoot tips regularly for continuous harvest and to keep plants bushy and productive; in frost-free areas it behaves as a short-lived perennial and self-sows freely, while gardeners farther north grow it as a warm-season annual. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Ebony Acorn Squash (Black-Skinned Bush Acorn Squash)
description: Ebony Acorn is an All-America Selections winner from the 1960s bred for its deep, glossy black-green rind and compact bush vines that need far less garden space than sprawling acorn types. Fruit develops the classic deeply ribbed acorn shape and matures to a dense, dry, sweet orange flesh well suited to baking or stuffing. Because the bush habit concentrates fruit near the crown, side-dress with compost partway through the season to sustain the shorter root run, and harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before long-term storage to improve flavor and shelf life. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Ebony King Dewberry (Heirloom Self-Fruitful Southern Dewberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a low wire trellis to keep fruit clean and easy to pick. Ebony King is an early twentieth-century Southern dewberry selection once popular from Texas through the Gulf South for its dependable, self-fruitful cropping and glossy black, firm, sweet-tart berries that ripen ahead of blackberry season. It largely fell out of commercial favor as upright, easier-to-manage blackberry cultivars became available, but it remains a hardy, low-input option for gardeners wanting the distinctive early-season flavor of a true dewberry. Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for the following year's crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Echinacea / Purple Coneflower
description: Sow seed on the surface or just 1/8 in deep; cold stratification for 4–8 weeks significantly improves germination rates, especially for fresh seed. Plant in well-drained soil and avoid overwatering once established, as echinacea tolerates drought well. Roots are the primary medicinal part and are harvested in fall of the third or fourth year; flowers and leaves can be harvested earlier for teas and tinctures. Allow some seed heads to remain for self-seeding and to feed overwintering birds. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Eclipse Blackberry (Semi-Erect Thornless USDA Release)
description: Eclipse is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University, notable along with its sibling release 'Galaxy' for being among the first cultivars to combine germplasm from both the eastern and western North American blackberry breeding pools. It produces uniformly shaped, medium-sized berries on vigorous, largely self-supporting canes. A simple trellis is still worthwhile to keep fruiting laterals upright and organized for picking, especially in a home planting where rows are short. As with other floricane-fruiting blackberries, remove spent canes to the ground immediately after harvest and train the new season's primocanes in their place for next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: ECOS Beach Plum (Named Beach Plum Selection for Improved Fruit)
description: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun with a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species is only partially self-fertile and sets fruit poorly on its own. ECOS is one of a small group of named beach plum clones, alongside Jersey Gem and Resigno, selected for producing larger, better-flavored fruit than typical unimproved wild seedling stands, whose fruit quality is notoriously inconsistent from bush to bush. Its drupes ripen in late summer to red, purple, or blue-black and are traditionally used for jams, jellies, and preserves along the Atlantic coast from Cape Cod to the mid-Atlantic. As a true dune-adapted native shrub, it withstands salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress or kill most other fruiting plants, and needs only light pruning after bloom to stay productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Edamame (Soybean)
description: Sow seeds 1 to 1.5 in deep in rows 18–24 in apart; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium for best nitrogen fixation. Edamame is self-supporting but benefits from well-drained, fertile soil with only modest added nitrogen. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and the seeds fill the pod but the shell has not yet begun to yellow. To harvest, pull the entire plant and strip pods at once; blanch immediately for best flavor and color. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Eddo Taro
description: Plant cormels in moist, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; Eddo (eddoe, eddo taro) is the small-corm type of Colocasia esculenta widely grown in the Caribbean, West Africa, and Southeast Asia for its edible corms and cormels — small, round to ovoid corms 1–2 inches across with hairy brown skin and white-to-purple-tinged starchy flesh. Unlike the large dasheen-type taro that produces a single massive central corm, eddo produces numerous small cormels clustered around a small central corm, making harvest easy — simply pull the plant and break apart the cormel cluster. The flesh is starchy and mild, with a slightly mucilaginous, creamier texture than dasheen, and is used in soups, stews, boiled as a side dish, and fried into chips throughout the African and Caribbean diaspora. The oxalic acid in raw taro requires thorough cooking; always boil or roast before eating. Eddo tolerates partial shade and moist soils and thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Edelweiss Grape (Cold-Hardy White Wine and Table Grape)
description: Bred by Elmer Swenson and released by the University of Minnesota in 1980 from a complex labrusca-vinifera-riparia parentage, this early-ripening hybrid tolerates winters well below zero with minimal cane damage, making it a mainstay for northern growers who cannot overwinter vinifera. Clusters of pale green-gold berries carry a mild, foxy labrusca flavor and work equally well for fresh eating, juice, or a light, fruity white wine. It ripens very early in the season, one of the first hardy hybrids to mature, which suits short-season gardens. The vine is vigorous and productive, so cluster thinning in the early years helps avoid overcropping and improves fruit quality. Matures in 130–145 days from transplant.

name: Edelweiss White Lavandin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil, spacing plants generously to accommodate its broad, mounding growth. 'Edelweiss' is the standard white-flowered lavandin, a sport of the classic lavandin type bred for buds that emerge blushed pale pink before opening to pure snowy-white spikes on long, straight stems, making it one of the most popular lavenders for cut flowers, bouquets, and wedding work. Like other lavandins it inherits vigor and heat tolerance from its spike lavender parentage, blooming later in summer than English lavender with a longer, more robust flower stem well suited to drying and fresh arrangements. Shear back hard after flowering to maintain a dense, rounded shape and prevent the woody base from splitting open. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Eden's Gem Melon (Rocky Ford Green-Flesh Muskmelon)
description: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, spacing hills to let the compact vines spread, and water evenly while fruit is sizing. Developed at Rocky Ford, Colorado and introduced in 1905 as a descendant of the older Green Nutmeg melon, Eden's Gem produces softball-sized, heavily netted fruit with green flesh and a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor. Its early maturity made it a popular shipping melon in the early twentieth century, and it remains prized by heirloom growers for its complex flavor in a compact package. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Edgar's Baby Dragon Fruit
description: Edgar's Baby is a compact dragon fruit, a climbing epiphytic cactus that rewards growers with sweet, vividly colored fruit on a manageable plant. It produces large, fragrant night-blooming flowers followed by fruit and thrives with warmth and strong support to climb. Grow from a rooted cutting in full sun and fast-draining, sandy soil, watering only when the mix dries since the cactus rots in soggy conditions. Provide a trellis or post, feed lightly, and shelter it from any frost. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Edible Amaranth (Joseph's Coat Amaranth, Tampala)
description: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; harvest outer leaves from 30 days; pull entire plant at 50–60 days before flowering. Amaranthus tricolor (edible amaranth or tampala) is a South and Southeast Asian edible leafy vegetable that is one of the most important leaf vegetables in tropical Asian cooking — the primary amaranth grown for its edible leaves (as distinct from grain amaranths like A. cruentus). The plant produces large, oval, slightly crinkled leaves in spectacular color combinations ranging from solid green or red-tinged green to dramatic tricolor varieties with patches and blotches of red, gold, and green or entirely deep crimson to magenta — the basis for the ornamental varieties sold as 'Joseph's Coat' in Western gardens. The leaves are nutritionally outstanding: very high in protein (15–20% on a dry-weight basis), iron, calcium, and vitamins A and C — one of the most nutrient-dense leafy vegetables. In Chinese cooking (where it is called 'xian cai'), the leaves are stir-fried with garlic; in Indian cooking (used as 'chaulai' in Hindi), the leaves are sauteed with spices; throughout Southeast Asia, it is used in soups and curries as a heat-tolerant spinach substitute. The heat tolerance of tampala — thriving in temperatures that cause spinach and other cool-season greens to bolt — makes it especially valuable in Gulf Coast and tropical summer gardens. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Edible Amaranth (Spleen Amaranth, Caribbean Amaranth)
description: Scatter seed thinly on the soil surface and press in gently — amaranth seeds need light to germinate and should not be buried more than 1/8 inch deep; thin to 6–12 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Amaranthus dubius is the primary edible-leaf amaranth of the Caribbean and tropical Africa, where it is known as callaloo, bhaji, or Chinese spinach and harvested as a highly nutritious leafy green with more than twice the iron, calcium, and protein of spinach per serving; it is one of the few leafy vegetables that produces abundantly through Gulf Coast and tropical zone summers when temperatures exceed 95°F and humidity is high. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips from the time plants are 6 inches tall; regular cutting encourages bushy growth and delays flowering. The entire young plant can be cooked like spinach in soups, stews, and sautés. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Edible Canna (Achira, Queensland Arrowroot, Tous-les-Mois)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately wet soil; Edible Canna produces its largest, most nutritious rhizomes in rich, consistently moist conditions with full sun, but tolerates partial shade in hot zone 9 summers. Canna indica (the species form, as opposed to modern ornamental Canna hybrids) is an edible perennial from tropical and subtropical America that has been cultivated as a food crop in the Andes, Central America, and the Caribbean for over 4,500 years — rhizomes found at archaeological sites in coastal Peru date to 2500 BCE. The starchy rhizomes — large, horizontal, thick, and up to 2 feet long in well-grown plants — are processed like arrowroot: washed, peeled, grated, pressed to extract starch, dried, and used as a thickener and flour substitute called 'Queensland Arrowroot' (in Australia) or 'Tous-les-Mois' (in the French Caribbean). The fresh rhizomes can also be cooked and eaten like potatoes or dried and ground into a fine, easily digestible starch valuable for people with wheat sensitivities. The plant produces small orange-red flowers (much less showy than ornamental Canna hybrids) and bold, paddle-shaped tropical leaves. In zone 9, it overwinters in the ground and regrows rapidly each spring. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Edible Hibiscus (Sunset Muskmallow, Aibika)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; edible hibiscus grows rapidly and may be harvested as a cut-and-come-again leafy green from 6 weeks. Abelmoschus manihot (edible hibiscus, aibika, or sunset muskmallow) is a large, fast-growing, tropical Asian shrub that produces an edible leaf crop as important as spinach across much of Melanesia, Papua New Guinea, and the Pacific Islands — the large, lobed, maple-leaf-like leaves (4–8 inches wide) are harvested young and cooked as a spinach substitute in stews, stir-fries, and soups; the young leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous (okra-like) texture and are highly nutritious, rich in protein, calcium, and vitamins A and C. The plant also produces very large, 4-to-6-inch, sulfur-yellow hibiscus flowers with a dark-purple eye that are strikingly ornamental; the flowers are also edible (used in salads and desserts). In zone 9, edible hibiscus grows as a fast annual or short-lived perennial, easily reaching 6–8 feet in a single season. The plants are closely related to okra (A. esculentus) and share its preference for heat, humidity, and well-drained, fertile soil; they cross readily with ornamental hibiscus but not with roselle (H. sabdariffa). Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Edible Landscaping Seedless Che (Self-Fertile Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Introduced and long propagated by Edible Landscaping nursery in Virginia, this selection is a self-fertile female che that reliably sets a full, seedless crop of maroon-red, mulberry-shaped fruit on its own, with no male tree required. The fig-and-watermelon-flavored fruit ripens over an extended late-summer-to-fall window and is best picked once fully soft, since underripe fruit is unpleasantly astringent. Grafted onto Osage orange rootstock, as is standard practice for che, the tree grows quickly into a large shrub or small standard tree that tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees and needs little winter chill to flower reliably. Young wood carries small thorns that diminish with age, so training to an open form early makes later harvest easier. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Edible Red Leaf Amaranth
description: This heat-loving green offers nutritious, colorful foliage with a hearty spinach flavor that is sweet and slightly tangy. It thrives when spring greens bolt in warm weather and is drought tolerant once established. Use it fresh in salads or steamed, stir-fried, or added to soups. Sow directly into warm soil in full sun. Harvest young leaves regularly to keep plants tender and productive. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Edisto 47 Cantaloupe
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun, well-drained sandy soil, 1–2 weeks after last frost; Edisto 47 is a Clemson University (South Carolina) heirloom cantaloupe developed in 1953 specifically for the humid, disease-pressure conditions of the Deep South where most cantaloupe varieties fail to powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria blight. It produces medium-sized (3–5 lb), oval, heavily netted fruits with thick, salmon-orange flesh of very good, rich cantaloupe flavor. The 'Edisto' name honors the Edisto Research and Education Center in Blackville, SC, and '47' the year development began. For over 50 years it was the cantaloupe of choice for Deep South gardeners because no other variety could reliably produce through summer humidity — even as newer hybrids have been developed, Edisto 47 remains a benchmark for disease resistance and regional adaptation. Matures in 88–95 days from seed.

name: Edward Bowles Santolina (Pale Primrose-Yellow Rosemary-Leaved Lavender Cotton)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty soil in a sunny, sheltered position; 'Edward Bowles' carries long, finely cut, rosemary-like gray-green leaves that are more feathery and open in texture than gray santolina's coral-like foliage, and it produces masses of pale, primrose-yellow button flowers in summer. Its taller, looser habit makes it a good textural foil for both silver and green Mediterranean subshrubs in a gravel garden or mixed dry border. Shear hard after flowering to maintain a rounded shape, since unpruned plants become open and leggy at the base within a few seasons. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Edward Mango (Rich-Flavored Florida Heirloom Mango)
description: Edward is a mid-twentieth-century Florida-origin mango cultivar valued by home gardeners for producing rich, sweet, nearly fiberless flesh considered by many to rank among the best-tasting Florida mangoes, though it has never been grown commercially at the scale of Tommy Atkins or Kent. Fruit is medium-sized with yellow-green skin lightly blushed with red, and it ripens in mid-summer. The tree is moderately vigorous and benefits from a warm, sunny, well-drained site and occasional pruning after harvest to maintain a manageable size. Protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is damaged by even brief cold exposure. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: EET 400 Cacao
description: Bred by Ecuador's INIAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Agropecuarias) at its Pichilingue Experiment Station, EET 400 was selected from Nacional-type parentage specifically to combine the prized floral 'Arriba' fine-flavor aroma with better yield and disease tolerance than unimproved heirloom Nacional trees. It is grown commercially in Ecuador alongside high-yield hybrids like CCN-51 by producers who want to retain access to fine-flavor cacao price premiums rather than switch entirely to bulk cacao. Growth habit and vigor fall between the very heavy-bearing CCN-51 and the more delicate heirloom Nacional. Cultivate it with the same filtered shade and rich, well-drained soil other Nacional-lineage cacao needs. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Egg Fruit
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pouteria campechiana benefits from regular water during fruiting but tolerates brief drought once established — maintain good drainage and avoid standing water around the root zone. Pouteria campechiana (Egg Fruit, Canistel, or Tiesa) is an evergreen or briefly deciduous tree native to the tropical forests of Central America — Guatemala, Belize, Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula — and introduced throughout the Caribbean, South Florida, the Philippines, Southeast Asia, and tropical West Africa. The fruit is one of the most distinctive of the sapote family: ovoid to pear-shaped, 2–4 inches long, with smooth, waxy, vivid orange to golden-yellow skin, and dense, dry, smooth, richly sweet orange-yellow flesh with a starchy texture remarkably similar to a hard-boiled egg yolk — sometimes described as sweet potato crossed with pumpkin pie. The flesh is eaten fresh, made into egg fruit nog, smoothies, ice cream, jam, and pies; it is particularly popular in Cuba, the Philippines, and South Florida ethnic markets. Trees require grafted or air-layered specimens to fruit true-to-type and within 3–5 years; seedling trees may take 6–8 years to fruit. A productive and adaptable tropical fruit tree for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Egoma (Deulkkae) Oilseed Perilla
description: Egoma, called deulkkae in Korean and egoma in Japanese, is the oilseed variety of Perilla frutescens, distinct from the leafy shiso and kkaennip types grown as var. crispa and var. japonica. Its plain, non-wrinkled green leaves and stronger, more resinous perilla-ketone aroma make it less refined as a fresh table herb, but it is prized for its plump seeds, which are toasted and ground into the nutty seasoning deulkkae-garu or cold-pressed into deulgireum (perilla oil), a staple finishing oil in Korean cooking. Like other perilla, flowering is triggered by shortening daylength in late summer, so full-season growth in a sunny bed is needed to bring the seed heads to maturity before frost. Cut whole seed stalks once the lower seed pods begin to dry and rattle, then finish drying upside down in a paper bag to catch the shattering seed. Matures in 70–110 days from seed.

name: Egremont Russet Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Egremont Russet is partially self-fertile but crops best with a compatible pollinator, and it is one of the more reliably disease-resistant older English apples. The most widely grown and best-known russet apple in Britain, dating to the nineteenth century, it bears medium, dull golden-brown, rough-skinned fruit with dense, crisp, distinctively nutty, slightly sweet flesh that is prized by connoisseurs and pairs especially well with cheese. Its good resistance to scab and canker compared to many other classic English apples has kept it a popular, relatively trouble-free choice for a home orchard wanting a true old-fashioned russet apple. Harvest in early-to-mid fall and eat fresh from the tree or after a short period of storage, since russet apples generally do not keep as long as some smooth-skinned dessert varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Egusi Melon (West African Oilseed Melon)
description: Sow in hills of warm, well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing vines to sprawl across at least 6 feet of row; egusi is a distinct culinary melon from dessert watermelon, grown throughout West Africa for its flat, oil-rich seeds that are dried, ground, and used to thicken egusi soup and stews. The round, pale green fruit has bland, unpalatably bitter to fibrous flesh that is discarded — do not harvest young for eating like watermelon. Leave fruit on the vine well past the point a watermelon would be picked, until the rind dulls and the vine begins to dry back, then split fruits open and ferment or wash the pulp away to recover the flat white seeds for drying. Rotate away from other cucurbits each year to limit vine borer and powdery mildew buildup. Matures in 85–110 days from seed.

name: Egyptian Mint
description: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian Mint is a large, vigorous mint with soft, rounded, gray-green woolly leaves closely related to apple mint but taller and more robust, reaching up to 3 ft with spikes of pale lavender flowers in late summer. Its flavor is notably milder and sweeter than spearmint or peppermint, with none of the sharp menthol bite of Mentha x piperita cultivars, making it the traditional mint of choice in Middle Eastern cooking for tabbouleh, yogurt sauces, and mint tea where a subtle, gentle mint note is preferred over an assertive one. The soft, fuzzy leaf texture and pale green-gray color also distinguish it visually from smoother-leaved spearmint types already in cultivation. Harvest leaves regularly through the season; the plant tolerates heat well for a mint and holds flavor even in warm weather. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Egyptian Walking Onion (Tree Onion)
description: Plant the small topset bulbils 1–2 inches deep in fall or early spring, pressing firmly into well-drained soil; established clumps need dividing every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Egyptian walking onions produce clusters of small bulbils at the top of the flower stalk; as these become heavy the stalk bends and the bulbils root where they land, effectively 'walking' across the garden. Harvest underground bulbs in early summer after the foliage begins to die back, or harvest green tops continuously throughout the growing season like scallions. The topset bulbils can be harvested for pickling or used as transplants. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Egyptian Walking Onion (Tree Onion)
description: Plant aerial bulblets 1–2 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian walking onion is a perennial onion cross that 'walks' itself across the garden by producing clusters of small bulblets at the top of its flowering stalks — when the bulblets become heavy enough, the stalk bends to the ground and the bulblets root where they touch soil, establishing a new cluster a foot away. The entire plant is edible year-round: the underground bulbs are used like small onions, the hollow green tops are used like green onions or chives, and the aerial bulblets are pickled or used as pearl onions. Varieties with particularly fine bulblet clusters and flavor include 'Zebrune' and 'Catawissa'. Essentially zero-maintenance once established — just harvest and leave the rest to multiply. An outstanding permanent edible for the low-maintenance food garden. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Egyptian Wheat (Tall Forage Sorghum Biomass and Screening Cover Crop)
description: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, and thin or drill to a moderate stand since plants grow extremely tall and can shade neighboring rows. Egyptian Wheat is a tall, robust forage sorghum, despite the common name it is not a true wheat, prized for reaching 8 to 12 feet with thick, sturdy stalks and broad leaves that produce heavy summer biomass, build organic matter, and outcompete summer weeds. Its height and density make it a popular seasonal screen, windbreak, or living privacy hedge in addition to its cover-crop role, and the seed heads that follow provide valuable food for doves, quail, and songbirds through fall and winter. Mow, roll, or cut and drop the stalks at the end of the season to return biomass to the soil, or leave standing for winter wildlife cover; it is killed outright by the first hard freeze. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Eight Ball Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Near-Black Pomegranate)
description: Eight Ball was selected from cold-tolerant dwarf pomegranate seedlings for its unusually dark, nearly black fruit skin loaded with anthocyanins, and for a compact, densely twiggy habit that suits hedgerows or large containers as easily as open ground. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; once established the shrub tolerates drought and Gulf Coast heat with minimal irrigation, and the deep red interior arils ripen to a sweet flavor with softer seeds than many standard-sized pomegranates. Because growth is naturally dense and twiggy, remove crowded interior wood and root suckers each dormant season to keep light reaching developing fruit and to reduce fungal issues in humid weather. Ripe fruit can be left on the plant for a period after coloring without much splitting, giving some slack in harvest scheduling. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eight Ball Squash (Round Dark Green Zucchini, Compact Summer Squash for Stuffing)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter when skin is dark green and glossy. Eight Ball is a compact, round-fruited zucchini variety that produces unusually shaped globose fruits — perfectly spherical when harvested at optimal size — on upright, compact bush plants significantly smaller than standard elongated zucchini types. The name 'Eight Ball' references the eight-ball billiards ball — a solid black sphere — which the dark green, round squash resembles at small harvest size. The round form is the primary distinctive quality: while standard zucchini is selected for elongated cylindrical shape that makes it easy to slice into uniform rounds, Eight Ball's round form creates a naturally shaped container ideal for hollowing and stuffing. For stuffed squash preparations, Eight Ball provides several practical advantages: the round form creates a stable base for baking without additional support, the natural cavity when the top is removed is more generous relative to fruit size than elongated squash, and individual fruits at optimal 3–4 inch harvest size provide a single-serving portion that is visually appealing when presented whole. The flavor is typical mild zucchini with slightly denser flesh than elongated types at comparable harvest sizes — the round form concentrates more flesh relative to surface area than a cylinder of comparable diameter. Eight Ball was developed and released by Park Seed, with the AAS award confirming performance across diverse North American trial conditions. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Eight Ball Zucchini
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained, enriched soil; Eight Ball is a compact bush type that needs 2–3 feet of space but no support. Eight Ball is an All-America Selections award-winning round zucchini producing compact, perfectly spherical, dark green fruits 2–4 inches in diameter — essentially billiard ball-shaped summer squash with the same mild, tender, slightly sweet flavor as regular zucchini but in a form perfect for stuffing whole. Hollow them out (a melon baller works perfectly), fill with cheese, rice, meat, and herbs, and bake for a complete stuffed vegetable presentation; they hold their round shape beautifully when baked. Harvest at 2–3 inches for perfect stuffing size; larger fruits become seedy and tougher. Highly productive on compact, bushy plants; good for small-space and container gardens. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Eight-Row Flint Corn (New England Flint, Rhode Island Flint)
description: Sow in blocks of 4+ rows after last frost; Eight-Row Flint is earlier-maturing than most heritage corns and well-suited to shorter northern seasons. Eight-Row Flint (also called New England Flint, Rhode Island Flint, and Narragansett Flint) is the traditional corn of the Algonquian peoples of the northeastern United States — the corn that sustained the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Mohegan, and neighboring peoples for centuries before European contact, and the corn that taught early colonists of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay how to survive in New England. It bears exactly eight rows of hard, flinty, small kernels in orange-red, white, or multi-colored patterns on slender 7–9 inch ears; the flint kernel type (hard, glass-like outer layer rather than dented) grinds into a fine, sweet, dense cornmeal. This is the corn of traditional New England johnnycakes, the grain type tested by Narragansett Flint Corn restoration projects. A critical piece of American agricultural heritage. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Ein Shemer Apple (Very Low-Chill Gulf South Apple for Zone 8-9)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most apples, Ein Shemer was selected in Israel specifically for regions with mild, short winters and thrives where classic high-chill apples like Red Delicious or Fuji fail to break dormancy properly. The medium, yellow-green fruit is mild and sweet with a soft, quick-to-ripen texture, best eaten soon after picking rather than stored long term. It ripens early in the season, generally ahead of most other low-chill apples, and its abundant, well-timed bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator in a mixed low-chill apple planting. This is one of the more dependable apple choices for zone 9a gardens along the Gulf Coast. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Einkorn Wheat
description: Sow seed 1 in deep in fall at 80–100 lb per acre (about 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft); einkorn is an ancient hulled wheat that outperforms modern wheats on poor, low-fertility soils and has exceptional drought tolerance. It overwinters, then bolts in spring to reach harvest in early summer, about 2 weeks earlier than modern winter wheat. Harvest when the grain is in the hard dough stage — the straw turns yellow but the heads have not yet shattered — by cutting and binding into sheaves left to dry for a week before threshing. Einkorn retains a tough hull after threshing that requires dehulling before milling; the flour is notably nutty and golden from higher carotenoid content. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Einset Seedless Grape (Strawberry-Flavored Cornell Red Table Grape)
description: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Einset Seedless was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York research station, producing small to medium, pink-red, seedless berries with a distinctive, delicately fruity flavor often described as reminiscent of strawberry, an unusual and pleasant trait that sets it apart from more neutrally flavored table grapes. The vine is cold-hardy and ripens relatively early in the season, giving gardeners in shorter-season regions a good chance at a full seedless grape harvest before fall frost. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if the vine sets a heavy crop, since concentrated clusters develop better size and flavor than overcrowded ones. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ekmek Quince (Turkish Bread Quince)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun.
