A Turkish cultivar whose name means "bread" in Turkish, it bears large, golden, slightly fuzzy, intensely fragrant fruit with crisp flesh that carries enough natural sugar to be eaten fresh off the tree, unlike most quince, though it is more commonly gently roasted or poached, or processed into jam, candy, compote, or custard. Brought to the United States from Turkey in 1986 and released from USDA quarantine in 1991, it has since been highly rated by American pomologists for its flavor and disease resistance. The tree is productive and hardy, blooming with pale pink spring flowers before fruit ripens in fall. Harvest in fall once fragrant and fully colored, and use fresh or in cooked preparations. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: El Dorado Hops
description: El Dorado is a trademarked dual-purpose cultivar from the Yakima Valley whose cones deliver an unusually candy-sweet aroma of watermelon, pear, and stone fruit rather than the sharper citrus or resin notes typical of many American hops. Its moderate alpha acid content lets brewers use it for both late aroma additions and light bittering. The bine is moderately vigorous and benefits from a tall trellis and consistent watering during cone set, since drought stress can mute its fruit-forward character. Pick cones as soon as they feel light and papery to preserve the delicate aromatics. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: El Dorado Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Low-Chill Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, El Dorado is a genetic dwarf nectarine that naturally grows to only six to eight feet, a fraction of a standard tree's size, while still producing full-sized, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit. Its low chill requirement of around 300 hours lets it fruit reliably in mild-winter regions like the Gulf South where standard nectarines often fail to break dormancy evenly. The compact size makes it an excellent choice for large containers or small yards, though the dense, naturally rounded canopy still benefits from light annual thinning to let light into the interior. Fruit ripens in early summer and is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Elah Apple (Israeli Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Elah is one of several Israeli-bred low-chill cultivars evaluated by University of Florida researchers as mid-season alternatives to Anna and Dorsett Golden, needing about 450 chill hours to break dormancy reliably. It ripens in mid-summer with smaller, round-to-oblique fruit of medium texture and good eating quality rather than the largest fruit size in the low-chill group. Its value on the Gulf Coast is chiefly as a pollination and harvest-window companion rather than a standalone dessert apple, since it fills the gap between the earliest low-chill ripeners and the later-season Israeli selections. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Elberta Peach (Classic Southern Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Elberta is the single most historically significant peach cultivar in American horticulture — developed in 1875 by Samuel Henry Rumph of Marshallville, Georgia, from a cross of Chinese Cling × Early Crawford, and for a century it was the standard commercial and home-garden freestone peach across the South. The large, yellow-fleshed, freestone fruit has a rich, full peach flavor with the balanced sweetness and acidity that defines the classic Southern peach flavor profile. Despite the development of countless newer peach cultivars with improved disease resistance and self-fertility, Elberta remains widely grown for its outstanding flavor quality, large fruit size, and proven production in zone 9 with sufficient chill hours. Elberta requires approximately 800 chill hours (hours below 45°F), which accumulates reliably in zone 9a and most of zone 9 during normal winters, though borderline years may occur. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart after petal fall to achieve maximum fruit size. Prune annually to an open-vase form to maintain production. Peach leaf curl, brown rot, and oriental fruit moth are common pests; a preventive fungicide and dormant oil spray program beginning at bud swell is essential for disease management. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Elderberry
description: Elderberries are fast-growing shrubs that fruit on current-season wood arising from two-year-old stems; cut one-third of the oldest canes to the ground each late winter to keep the planting vigorous. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination — solo plantings produce far fewer berries. Harvest entire umbels (flat-topped clusters) in late summer when at least 95% of berries in a cluster are dark purple-black. Raw berries and green plant parts contain cyanogenic glycosides; always cook berries before eating. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Eldorado Blackberry (Historic Cold-Hardy Heirloom Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and cut new canes back after their first season to encourage strong lateral branching for the following year's crop. Eldorado was discovered as a chance seedling in Ohio in the early twentieth century and went on to become one of the most widely planted home-garden blackberries in the eastern and midwestern United States for much of the century, valued above all for its reliable cold hardiness and productivity without needing a second variety for pollination. The berries are medium-sized, glossy black, sweet, and nearly seedless-tasting compared to many older thorny types, ripening over a fairly long midseason picking window. Eldorado's erect, self-supporting thorny canes tolerate harsh winters better than many later thornless introductions, which is why it persisted in northern gardens long after flashier commercial varieties came and went. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Elecampane
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep indoors after a brief cold stratification period; plants grow into impressive clumps by their second year, eventually reaching 6–8 feet tall. Plant in moist, deep, fertile soil as this large plant develops an extensive root system that benefits from ample space. Harvest the thick, inulin-rich roots in autumn of the second or third year, washing and slicing them before drying for respiratory-supportive preparations. The yellow daisy-like flowers appear in midsummer of the second year and are attractive to pollinators. Matures in 540–730 days from seed.

name: Electric Onion (Overwintering Red Onion)
description: Electric is a popular overwintering red onion prized for combining the deep reddish-purple skin of a standard red onion with the earlier harvest timing of autumn-planted sets. Push sets into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving the tip exposed, and provide light winter protection only in the coldest parts of its range. Growth resumes quickly as spring days lengthen, and bulbs color up well even under the shorter, cooler growing period overwintering onions experience. Because overwintered red onions tend to be milder and slightly less firm than maincrop reds, plan to use the harvest within a few months of the early-summer lift. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Elegant Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Elegant is a named cornelian cherry cultivar selected for larger, glossy red fruit than typical seedling Cornus mas, with a tart cherry-like flavor suited to preserves and syrups once fully ripe and slightly soft. Trees bloom on bare branches in very early spring with small yellow flowers that are among the first nectar sources for pollinators after winter. Fruit set improves with a genetically distinct second tree nearby, since seedling-grown Cornus mas is only partially self-fertile. The species is tough and adaptable, tolerating urban conditions, drought once established, and a range of soil types. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Elegantissima Tricolor Cornelian Cherry (Pink-and-White Variegated Cornus mas)
description: Elegantissima, also sold as Aureoelegantissima, is the showiest of the variegated cornelian cherry cultivars, with leaves splashed yellow and cream and flushed pink to rose along the margins, an effect that intensifies in cooler spring and fall weather. It flowers on bare branches in late winter like the species and can produce the typical tart red drupes when cross-pollinated, though it is grown primarily as a specimen foliage shrub rather than for fruit. Because strong variegation reduces overall vigor, growth is slower and more compact than green-leaved cornelian cherry, and plants benefit from some shelter from harsh afternoon sun and wind to keep leaf color from scorching. Otherwise it is as cold-hardy and adaptable as the species, tolerating a range of soils once established. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Elephant Dill
description: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so mature plants have room for their tall, sturdy stems. Elephant is a large, late-flowering dill selection that stays in vigorous leaf production noticeably longer than standard varieties before bolting to flower, giving a wider window for harvesting fresh dill weed. Its height and productivity also make it a strong choice for gardeners who want abundant seed heads later in the season for pickling brine and spice use. Because it delays bolting, Elephant tolerates a broader range of sowing dates through spring and early summer without immediately running to seed. Stake or plant in a sheltered spot if wind is a concern, since the tall stems can lean once heavy with seed heads. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Elephant Foot Yam (Whitespot Giant Arum, Suran)
description: Plant corm sections in well-drained, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade in spring after soil warms; lift corms before first frost in zone 9. Amorphophallus paeoniifolius (elephant foot yam or suran) is a tropical Asian aroid producing a single, enormous, deeply divided, umbrella-like leaf (resembling a tropical fern frond writ large) on a mottled green-and-grey petiole, and a massive underground corm that can reach 20–30 lbs in a single season. The corm is an important starchy food crop throughout South and Southeast Asia — particularly in India and Sri Lanka, where it is cooked as a curry vegetable, fried in oil, and made into a popular Bengal-region dish. The flesh is white, somewhat mucilaginous (like taro), with a mild, slightly bitter flavor that is neutralized by cooking with acidic ingredients like tamarind. Like all amorphophallus species, the occasional flower is an extraordinary, though briefly malodorous structure — a large, purple-maroon spathe and spadix with the characteristic carrion-flower smell that attracts pollinators. The plant is entirely ornamental in terms of foliage, with a single dramatic leaf reaching 4–6 feet across. Must be cooked thoroughly before eating — raw corms contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals. Matures in 210–300 days from transplant.

name: Elephant Garlic
description: Plant individual cloves 2–4 inches deep pointed end up in well-drained, fertile soil in fall, with the flat base downward. Elephant garlic is technically a leek relative (Allium ampeloprasum) rather than a true garlic; its flavor is much milder and sweeter than hardneck garlic, lacking the pungent bite, and the huge cloves are easy to peel. Remove flower scapes (curling stems) in early summer to redirect energy into bulb development, just as with true garlic. Harvest when the lower third of the leaves has browned, dig carefully, and cure in a warm, ventilated location for 3–4 weeks before storing or braiding. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Elephant Hardneck Garlic
description: More closely related to leeks than true garlic, elephant garlic produces very large bulbs of 1 to 6 mild, tan cloves that are superb roasted. Plant individual cloves in fall, pointed end up, in fertile, well-drained soil and mulch for winter protection. Remove the edible scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place. Space plants generously since they grow tall and wide. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: Elephant Heart Plum
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires cross-pollination with Santa Rosa, Shiro, Satsuma, or another Japanese plum. Elephant Heart is a Luther Burbank plum introduced around 1929 and named for the large, heart-shaped fruits that can weigh 4–6 oz each — unusually large even among Japanese plums. The dark red to near-black skin encloses blood-red to deep crimson flesh with intensely rich, sweet-tart, wine-complex flavor that many consider the most interesting and complex of the Japanese plum flavors; it is notably more flavorful and less mild than Shiro or Santa Rosa when eaten at peak ripeness (late August to September, relatively late for Japanese plums). The depth of pigmentation (both in skin and flesh) makes Elephant Heart particularly striking and flavorful for fresh eating, jam, and preserves. Chill requirement is approximately 400–500 hours. The distinctive, intense flavor comes through even when cooked; a justly famous heirloom plum maintained by Slow Food and heirloom orchardists. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Eleuthero (Siberian Ginseng, Devil's Shrub)
description: Plant root divisions or hardwood cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; eleuthero is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and tolerates drought once established. Eleutherococcus senticosus (commonly marketed as Siberian Ginseng, though not a true Panax ginseng) is a thorny, deciduous shrub of northeastern Asia that is one of the most studied adaptogenic medicinal plants; its root bark is used in clinical herbalism as a tonic to improve stress resilience, physical endurance, and immune function, with hundreds of published studies supporting its use in Russian and Chinese traditional medicine. The dried root bark is made into tea or tincture; harvest bark from roots of 3–5 year old plants in autumn. The plant is fully hardy, grows readily in cool northern climates, and is far easier to cultivate than true ginseng. Note: consult a qualified herbalist before medicinal use. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Elfin Thyme (Miniature Mat-Forming Groundcover Thyme)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Elfin is among the smallest and slowest-growing thyme cultivars available, forming a dense, tightly cushioned mat of tiny leaves only an inch or two tall, far more compact than standard creeping thyme, which makes it a favorite for miniature gardens, trough plantings, and tucking between small paving stones where a larger thyme would quickly overwhelm the space. Small pale pink flowers appear in a light early-summer bloom above the foliage mat, drawing bees. Like other thymes it demands sharp drainage and resents wet feet, especially in winter; light foot traffic is fine on an established planting, releasing a mild fragrance when stepped on. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Elizabeth Passionflower (Purple-and-White Vigorous Hybrid Passion Vine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils. Elizabeth bears large, intricately structured flowers combining deep purple filaments with white and lavender petals, a striking hybrid passionflower display on a fast-growing, heavily blooming vine. It draws pollinators readily during its long summer bloom season, and while it can produce fruit, it is grown chiefly for its exceptional flower display. In zones at the cooler edge of its range it dies back to the ground in winter and regrows strongly from deep roots in spring; mulch the crown heavily where marginal. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Ella Dill
description: Direct sow thickly into cool, moist soil in full sun, or broadcast into trays or pots for a dedicated cut-and-regrow crop. Ella is a compact, dark-green dill bred specifically for container growing and baby-leaf production, staying shorter and denser than field dill types like Bouquet or Mammoth while still delivering strong, classic dill flavor. Its tight, upright habit lets growers pack more plants into a small footprint and harvest repeated cuttings of tender young foliage before the plants have a chance to bolt. Shear whole plantings back to an inch or two of growth for a quick regrowth cycle, and resow every few weeks through the cool months for a steady supply of fresh dill weed. Matures in 25–40 days from seed.

name: Ellagance Purple English Lavender (Seed-Grown Dark Purple-Blue Lavender)
description: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination, and transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil after frost danger has passed. Ellagance Purple produces long, strong stems topped with large, dense, fragrant flower spikes, dark purple buds opening to rich purple-blue blooms, over compact, spreading mounds of grey-green foliage, and it was bred for excellent uniformity, earliness, and spike quality compared to older seed strains. It is winter-hardy and blooms reliably the first year from an early sowing, making it useful for both bedding displays and permanent perennial plantings. Keep water low once established, since drainage matters more than fertility to long-term survival. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Ellagance Snow English Lavender (Seed-Grown White Lavender)
description: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination; Ellagance Snow germinates without cold stratification but needs consistent warmth and bright light. Transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil after frost danger has passed. It bears pure white flower spikes on strong, long stems above silvery-green foliage, standing out as an accent among purple-flowered lavenders in mixed plantings or as a monochrome display on its own. Like other Ellagance series lavenders it is compact, uniform, and winter-hardy, blooming reliably in its first year from an early sowing. Keep water low once established and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils that shorten its lifespan. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Ellen Felton Dark Collard (North Carolina Family Heirloom Collard)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ellen Felton Dark'
description: This slightly-heading collard traces to at least 1935 in Beaufort County, North Carolina, where a family seed saver grew and passed it down before it was shared with a USDA heirloom-collecting effort and later added to the Seed Savers Exchange catalog. The elliptic, wavy-to-toothed green leaves form a loosely gathered rather than open habit, distinguishing it from fully open Southern collards like Georgia Southern. Cooked leaves carry a notably sweet, faintly fruity flavor compared to more assertive collard types, and the plant handles hard cold well into the low 20s Fahrenheit. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Ellen Marker Loquat (Modern Florida Seedling Selection with Creamy White Flesh)
description: Ellen Marker is a modern Florida seedling selection introduced in 2020 by fruit explorer Craig Hepworth, chosen for its large, pear-shaped fruit and complex flavor. The creamy white flesh combines classic loquat peach-apricot notes with a brighter, almost grape-like tartness when fruit is left to fully color to yellow-orange before picking. As with other loquats, its fall-to-winter bloom period leaves flowers and young fruit vulnerable to hard freezes, an important consideration for Gulf Coast growers when choosing a planting site. Being a relatively new selection, its performance and self-fruitfulness outside Florida are still being documented by home growers. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Elliot Pecan
description: Plant in full sun in deep (6+ feet), well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — pecans are deep-rooted trees that require deep, fertile bottomland or well-amended upland soil for maximum production; Elliot is one of the most important pecan cultivars for the Gulf South, selected specifically for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab (Venturia effusa) — the most damaging fungal disease of pecans in the humid Gulf Coast climate where without resistance, pecan production requires intensive fungicide programs that make orchard production impractical. Elliot's scab resistance means it can produce quality nuts in the humid Gulf South with minimal or no fungicide applications — a fundamental practical advantage for home orchard growers. The small-to-medium, ovate nuts have thin shells and a high kernel percentage (approximately 52%), with the sweet, rich, buttery, distinctively pecan flavor that makes Gulf South-grown pecans the gold standard among nut crops. Elliot's consistent production, excellent kernel quality, and scab resistance make it the recommended home orchard pecan for Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Texas Gulf Coast — the regions where pecan is culturally important and where Elliot's disease resistance matters most. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Elliott Blueberry (Very Late-Season Extended-Harvest Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Elliott is prized above all for ripening later than almost any other highbush blueberry, extending the home harvest well into fall after earlier varieties have finished, with firm, small to medium, light-blue berries that start out fairly tart and develop better sweetness the longer they are left to fully color on the bush. The very late ripening window also means the crop largely escapes the peak pressure of many early-season pests and diseases. The vigorous, upright bush stores its fruit well both on the plant and after picking, making Elliott a valuable addition alongside early- and midseason varieties for gardeners wanting the longest possible blueberry season. Give full sun and consistent moisture, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety for best pollination. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Elliott Pecan
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Elliott is a Florida-origin pecan variety selected for commercial production in the humid Gulf Coast Southeast because of its outstanding resistance to pecan scab disease — the most economically damaging disease of pecans in the humid South. While Stuart and Desirable require protection in rainy years, Elliott produces consistent yields without fungicide programs in most Gulf Coast locations, making it the variety of choice for low-spray and organic home orchards in zone 8–9. Nuts are smaller than Desirable or Stuart (60–70 per pound) but kernel quality is excellent — thin shells, high kernel fill (55–60%), and very good flavor. Elliott is a late-season variety, maturing in October–November after most other varieties. Its smaller stature (60–70 feet mature) compared to some pecan giants also makes it slightly more manageable. An excellent choice for humid coastal and transitional zone 9 gardens where disease pressure is high. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Elliott's Blueberry
description: Elliott's Blueberry is one of the most valuable native blueberries for the warm, humid southeastern coastal plain, native to the moist to dry, acidic, sandy soils of pocosins, pine flatwoods, bay swamp edges, and woodland margins from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it grows in association with other ericaceous plants on acidic, well-drained soils. A vigorous, upright to arching shrub that can reach 8–12 feet in favorable conditions, it produces an abundance of small, sweet, dark blue berries in spring (April–May, depending on location) that ripen earlier than most highbush blueberries and are highly palatable to wildlife and humans alike. One of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the native blueberries, it is an excellent choice for the Gulf Coast region where northern highbush varieties struggle; it requires consistently acidic, well-drained soil and benefits from cross-pollination with other Vaccinium species. Plant multiple shrubs for cross-pollination and heavier fruiting; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ellis Pecan (Consistent Annual-Bearing Georgia Heritage Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, and plant a compatible pollinator cultivar of the opposite pollen type nearby. Ellis is a chance-seedling selection out of Georgia that has earned a lasting place among Southern pecan growers for its unusually consistent annual bearing, avoiding the alternate-bearing boom-and-bust cycle that troubles many pecan cultivars, along with medium resistance to pecan scab and heat and drought tolerance comparable to well-regarded Gulf South standards like Cape Fear and Sumner. Medium-sized nuts of good flavor and kernel percentage mature and drop free of the shuck around October. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and provide the deep, loose, well-drained soil pecans need for healthy taproot development. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Ellison's Orange Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ellison's Orange ripens in late summer to early fall and is best eaten within a few weeks of harvest. Bred in Lincolnshire, England from Cox's Orange Pippin parentage, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red and carrying rich, aromatic flesh with a distinctive light aniseed note layered over classic Cox-like sweetness, a flavor combination that has made it a favorite among English apple enthusiasts seeking something a bit different from the standard dessert apple. It ripens earlier in the season than its famous Cox parent and is a somewhat easier, more forgiving tree to grow well, making Cox-like flavor accessible to gardeners without ideal conditions for true Cox's Orange Pippin. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks for the best distinctive aromatic flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Elmer Myers Black Walnut
description: Elmer Myers is a Pennsylvania-origin black walnut selection valued above most seedling trees for its unusually easy cracking and high proportion of whole kernel halves, a trait that matters more for black walnut than almost any other quality since wild-type nuts are notoriously hard to pick clean. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil with full sun exposure and generous spacing, since mature trees form a broad, heavy canopy. Because black walnut is wind-pollinated and only partially self-fruitful, siting a second cultivar or seedling within range improves nut set. Harvest as hulls soften and darken, hull promptly, and cure kernels in a dry, ventilated spot for a few weeks before eating or storing. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Elmo American Persimmon (Large Spot-Free Claypool Selection)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and site a second American persimmon nearby, since Elmo is not self-fertile and needs cross-pollination to bear a reliable crop — only self-fertile selections such as Meader or Yates can be grown alone. Developed as a hand-pollinated cross of Golden Supreme and Garretson and originally released under the breeding designation Claypool A-118, Elmo was chosen for its large, richly flavored orange fruit that stays notably free of the black surface spotting that can mar other American persimmon selections. Fruit ripens October into November and, like all American persimmons, must fully soften after a hard frost before the astringency disappears and the deep, honeyed sweetness comes through. Elmo is a consistently heavy bearer once established and tolerates the heat, humidity, and clay soils typical of zone 7-9 Southern gardens with little more than watering during its first two seasons. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Elmwood Fuzzy Kiwi
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy arbor or trellis system. Elmwood is widely regarded as one of the best low-chill fuzzy kiwi selections available, needing only around 400-700 hours of winter chill compared to the much higher requirement of classic 'Hayward', which makes it a realistic choice for the mild winters of Gulf South gardens. Large, showy, fragrant white spring blossoms make the vine ornamental even before fruiting begins, and mature fruit is unusually large for a fuzzy kiwi, up to 10 ounces, with typical brown, hairy skin and green flesh. As with all kiwifruit, expect several years of vine establishment before the first meaningful harvest, and prune annually in the dormant season to keep fruiting wood productive and manageable. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Elsanta Strawberry (Netherlands-Bred European Commercial Standard)
description: Elsanta was bred in the Netherlands and released in the early 1980s, quickly becoming the dominant commercial and garden strawberry across the UK, Netherlands, Belgium, and much of Western Europe, a position it still holds in many regions decades later. It produces large, glossy, conical, bright red berries with a classic sweet-tart flavor when allowed to ripen fully on the plant, though fruit picked underripe can taste comparatively bland. Plants are vigorous and heavy-yielding but relatively susceptible to crown rot and red core (Phytophthora) in poorly drained soil, so raised beds and good drainage are important for a healthy planting. Renovate beds after harvest by removing old foliage and excess runners to keep plantings productive for several seasons. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Elstar Apple (Popular Crisp Aromatic Dutch Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Elstar was bred in the Netherlands from a cross of Golden Delicious and Ingrid Marie and has become one of the most widely planted apples across Europe, prized for crisp, juicy, aromatic flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that has broad appeal for fresh eating, and it also performs well in baking, holding its shape reasonably well under heat. The medium, red-blushed fruit over a yellow-green background ripens in early to mid fall, and the productive, reliable tree has made it a commercial and home-orchard standard throughout its native growing region. Harvest once fruit fully colors, and store cool for good, though not exceptionally long, keeping quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Elvira Grape (Historic American Hybrid White Wine Grape)
description: Bred in Missouri in the 1860s, Elvira was once a mainstay of Midwestern wine production, prized for its heavy yields of small, pale green-white berries and its tolerance of humid, disease-prone conditions that challenge finer vinifera types. The wine produced is light, tart, and historically valued more for volume and reliability than refinement. The vine is exceptionally vigorous and cold-hardy, needing firm pruning and cluster thinning to prevent overcropping and to keep berry quality acceptable. It remains of interest today for its own-rooted resilience and its place in American viticultural history. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Emanuel Loquat (Early-Ripening Israeli-Origin Orange-Fleshed Loquat)
description: Emanuel is an Israeli-origin loquat cultivar valued for its early ripening season, with medium-sized fruit typically ready in February through March in warm climates like the Gulf Coast. The thin-skinned, dark yellow-to-orange fruit encloses juicy, mildly sweet flesh with two to three seeds. Like all loquats, Emanuel blooms in fall and winter, so a hard freeze during bloom or early fruit set can wipe out the crop for that year, making a sheltered planting site valuable in zone 9a. Grafted trees begin bearing within a couple of years of transplanting. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Emek Pomegranate
description: Emek is a vigorous, self-fertile Israeli pomegranate bred specifically for very early ripening, reaching harvest roughly six weeks before the widely grown Wonderful cultivar. Fruit is medium to large with an attractive dark pink to red skin and sweet, juicy red arils of good eating quality. Because it fruits so early, it can help a Gulf Coast garden get a jump on pomegranate season before summer humidity and fruit-splitting rains set in later on. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune to an open vase shape to maximize airflow and light penetration into the fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Emerald Artichoke (Spineless Annual Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, richly amended soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Emerald is a spineless, dark green annual hybrid bred as a seed-grown alternative to older perennial artichoke types, forming a slightly more compact plant than some annual comparisons while still setting a good number of medium, tightly furled buds in its first season. It shares the same need for a brief cool spell after transplanting to trigger uniform first-year flowering, and it holds up well to the heat of long, dry summers once established. Keep the soil evenly moist and fertile through the growing season and harvest buds while the scales are still closed tight for the best texture. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Emerald Blueberry (UF Southern Highbush Excellent-Flavor Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Emerald is a University of Florida IFAS southern highbush blueberry introduction recognized as one of the finest-flavored and most productive low-chill blueberry varieties for Gulf South gardens — producing large, round, sky-blue to medium-blue berries with a desirable balance of sweetness and mild acidity, firm texture, small dry scar, and excellent fresh-eating quality that compares favorably with the best northern highbush varieties. Emerald requires only approximately 200 chill hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break and reliable annual fruit production — far fewer than the 700–1,000+ hours required by northern highbush varieties, making it fully adapted to zone 9 winters where chill accumulation frequently falls in the 200–400 hour range. The early to mid-season ripening (March–May in zone 9) provides fresh local blueberries before summer heat arrives. Soil pH management is the most critical cultural requirement: blueberries in general, and southern highbush especially, require very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) — outside this range, nutrients become unavailable regardless of fertilization, causing slow growth, yellowing foliage, and poor production. Amend soil with sulfur well before planting to lower pH; maintain with acidifying fertilizer (azalea/camellia formulas) and pine bark mulch. For maximum production, plant Emerald with at least one other southern highbush variety for cross-pollination. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Emerald Bush Buttercup Squash
description: Emerald Bush Buttercup is a compact, short-vined strain selected from classic Buttercup squash, holding the same turban shape and small blossom-end button but on a plant that stays within a few feet rather than running eight feet or more. Give it consistent moisture and full sun; because the foliage is dense and close together, watch for powdery mildew in humid climates and space plants for airflow. Fruit averages about four to five pounds with nearly black-green skin and dry, sweet, deep orange-yellow flesh well suited to baking and mashing. Cure harvested fruit at room temperature for a week or two before moving it to cool, dry storage. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Emerald Delight Summer Squash
description: This zucchini was bred with a more compact, open habit so fruit is easier to spot and harvest before it grows oversized. Plants produce reliably all summer, yielding versatile dark-green squash for countless dishes. Harvest young at 6 to 8 inches and pick often to keep production high. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water consistently and allow airflow to reduce mildew. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Emerald Drop Pluot (Green-Skinned Low-Chill Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible pollinizer within 50 feet since Emerald Drop sets little fruit on its own. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this upright, heavy-cropping tree produces medium-to-large fruit with green skin that can be picked firm and sweet in mid-summer or left to hang until it turns honey-yellow with amber flesh and a richer, more complex flavor. The long harvest window from mid-July into late August is useful for extending the pluot season in warm-winter gardens. Thin fruit early to 4–5 inches apart to prevent limb breakage under a heavy crop, and prune annually to an open center to keep the dense canopy productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Emerald Gem Melon (1886 Heirloom Cantaloupe)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three plants per hill. Emerald Gem produces small, globe-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with smooth, dark emerald-green skin that conceals thick, richly flavored, pale orange flesh often described as having a distinctive spicy sweetness beyond typical cantaloupe. Discovered as a chance seedling in the Michigan garden of William G. Voorhees, it was purchased and introduced commercially by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886 and quickly became a benchmark variety praised for combining fine flavor with dependable, uniform type. Because the fruit is compact and matures relatively quickly for a melon, it suits shorter-season gardens; keep soil evenly moist through fruit set and harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the vine. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Emerald Giant Sweet Pepper (Very Large Thick-Walled Green Bell Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; Emerald Giant is one of the standard large-fruited bell pepper varieties for American home and commercial gardens — producing very large (4–5 inch long, 3–4 inch wide), blocky, 4-lobed, thick-walled green bell peppers with the classic sweet bell pepper flavor and firm, crunchy flesh that defines the standard bell pepper for American cooking. The name reflects both the large fruit size ('Giant') and the deep green color at the typical fresh-market harvest stage — the brilliant, deep-green, shiny-skinned fruits are the archetypal green bell pepper form. Left to ripen fully, Emerald Giant turns red, producing a sweeter, more complex flavor than the green stage. The thick walls (3/8–1/2 inch) provide more usable pepper flesh per fruit than thin-walled types, better heat retention in cooking preparations, and superior durability at harvest. In zone 9, bell peppers produce best in the spring season (March–June) and a brief fall window (September–October) — the extended summer heat reduces fruit set and causes sunscald on exposed fruits. The large, heavy fruits on 'Emerald Giant' require staking or caging to prevent branch breakage when the plant is heavily loaded. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Emerald Okra
description: This heirloom okra is prized for smooth, rich green pods that stay tender even when they grow larger than usual, over a long harvest window. Sow seed about an inch deep in warm soil, soaking overnight first to hasten sprouting. Give plants full sun and steady moisture, and they will grow tall and productive through the heat of summer. Pick pods every day or two while young to keep the plants setting; frequent harvest greatly increases total yield. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Emerite Filet Bean (French Haricot Vert Pole Bean for Thin Tender Pods)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide trellis or pole support to 6 feet and harvest every 1–2 days when pods reach 4–5 inches and are no thicker than a pencil. Emerite Filet Bean is a French-bred pole-type haricot vert that delivers the classic thin-podded, tender filet bean quality of French cuisine on a vigorous climbing plant that produces heavily over months rather than the 2–3-week harvest window of bush filet types. The haricot vert category — defined by pod diameter under 6mm and harvest at pencil-thin stage before any internal seed development is visible — requires frequent harvesting to maintain pod quality; pods left on the plant for even an extra day begin to develop seeds and shift from the tender, fine-textured filet bean to a coarser snap bean. This harvesting discipline rewards with pods of extraordinary tenderness: lightly steamed for 3–4 minutes, Emerite haricots verts have a delicate, slightly squeaky texture and refined mild flavor that is categorically different from mature-harvested snap beans. Pole-type filet beans like Emerite provide a practical advantage over bush types for home production: a single planting in spring can continue producing through fall in zone 9 (with a brief mid-summer slowdown during peak heat), whereas bush filet varieties exhaust themselves within 2–3 weeks and require successive plantings every 3 weeks to maintain a continuous harvest. The climbing habit also improves air circulation around pods in the humid Gulf Coast environment, reducing the fungal disease pressure that can limit bush bean production in midsummer heat and humidity. Blanch harvested pods in salted boiling water for 2–3 minutes, shock in ice water to set the bright green color, then serve simply with butter, lemon, and salt to showcase the delicate flavor. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: EMLA 26 Apple Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; EMLA 26 is a virus-free selection of M26 with the same semi-dwarfing size and staking needs. Developed through the joint East Malling and Long Ashton research stations' virus-indexing program in England, this is a heat-treated, virus-free selection of the classic M26 semi-dwarfing rootstock, offering the same 40-50 percent size reduction, cold hardiness, and precocious early fruiting as standard M26 but with improved vigor and productivity thanks to the elimination of latent viruses that historically reduced older rootstock stock's performance. Its virus-free status has made the EMLA-prefixed rootstock selections the preferred commercial source for M-series rootstocks in North America since their introduction. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, stake for the first few years as with standard M26, and expect a compact, vigorous, productive semi-dwarf tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Emma K Black Walnut
description: Emma K is a widely propagated named black walnut selection valued by home nut growers for its comparatively thin shell and high percentage of easily removed kernel meat relative to typical wild seedling trees. Grafted trees bear considerably sooner and more consistently than seedling-grown black walnuts. Give it wide open spacing away from vegetable gardens and susceptible landscape plants due to juglone sensitivity in nearby soil. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Empeltre Olive (Cold-Hardy Spanish Sweet Oil Olive)
description: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Empeltre originates in the Aragon region of northern Spain, where it has adapted to somewhat cooler conditions than many Mediterranean olive varieties tolerate, giving it a useful edge in cold hardiness for growers at the margins of olive-growing climate. The medium, dark purple-black fruit produces a mild, sweet, fruity oil low in bitterness, prized in traditional Spanish and Balearic Islands cooking, and the fruit can also be cured as a sweet, mild table olive. The tree is self-fertile and reliably productive, a practical choice for smaller home orchards wanting a single olive tree without needing a separate pollinizer variety. Cure harvested fruit properly before eating, since raw olives are far too bitter to consume fresh. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Emperor Francis Cherry (Light-Skinned Sweet Cherry, Royal Ann Type)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Emperor Francis is a light-skinned sweet cherry in the same Royal Ann-Napoleon family, valued for its yellow skin blushed with red, firm, sweet flesh, and reliably heavy production, and it has historically been grown both for fresh eating and for the same maraschino and light-cherry processing markets as Royal Ann. Compared to some light sweet cherries, Emperor Francis is noted for its firmness and good resistance to cracking after rain, making it a somewhat more forgiving choice for growers in less-than-ideal dry climates. The tree is vigorous and productive; harvest once fruit reaches full blush color and sweetness, since light-skinned cherries do not continue to ripen or sweeten after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Emperor Grape
description: A historic California table grape grown commercially since the early 1900s, Emperor produces large, round to oval, pale pinkish-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor and notably firm flesh that keeps in cold storage longer than most table grapes. It ripens very late in the season and was long the standard variety for holiday-season fresh grapes before newer red seedless types largely replaced it commercially. Vines are vigorous and long-lived, so an established permanent cordon system and annual dormant pruning keep fruiting wood renewed. It needs a long, warm season to fully ripen its late-hanging clusters. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Emperor Lychee
description: Plant an air-layered or grafted tree in acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a sunny site protected from strong wind. This cultivar is grown for its unusually large, thin-shelled fruit with sweet, juicy flesh and a smaller seed than many other lychee selections. Established trees handle brief dips into the upper 20s better than young trees but still benefit from overhead frost protection or covering during hard freezes on the Gulf Coast. Lychees need a period of cool, dry weather to initiate flowering, which makes fruiting inconsistent in the humid Gulf South even though the trees themselves can be grown successfully. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Empire Apple (McIntosh × Red Delicious, Cornell Commercial Release Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Empire requires a cross-pollinator; fruits ripen in September–October with medium to large, deep red to nearly all-red skin and crisp, firm, creamy-white flesh; Empire stores significantly better than McIntosh — refrigerated fruits hold quality for 3–5 months — making it preferable for wholesale and storage. Empire apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1945 from a deliberate cross of McIntosh and Red Delicious, and released for commercial planting in 1966 — named for 'The Empire State' of New York to honor the variety's state of origin. The cross combined the aromatic, sweet-tart character and eating quality of McIntosh with the firmer flesh and better keeping quality of Red Delicious, achieving an apple that outperformed both parents in commercial viability: Empire is significantly firmer than McIntosh (which quickly becomes soft and mealy after harvest), stores considerably longer under refrigeration, and maintains its crispness and good flavor for months. Today Empire is one of the most important commercial apple varieties in New York State — which produces the second-largest apple crop in the United States — and is widely planted throughout the northeastern states and eastern Canada. For home gardeners, Empire's earlier bearing age (compared to Northern Spy), reliable productivity, and superior storage compared to McIntosh make it an excellent choice for the home orchard where both fresh-eating and winter storage apples are desired. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Empress Plum (Large Late-Season Purple European Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Empress is an English European plum grown for very large, deep purple fruit with firm, sweet, richly flavored flesh, ripening late in the season alongside President and extending a home orchard's plum harvest well past the peak of earlier varieties. The substantial fruit size and firm texture make Empress a good all-purpose plum, equally suited to fresh eating, baking, and preserving, and the tree is a dependable, consistent bearer once established. Thin fruit if the tree sets an especially heavy crop, since overloaded branches can break under the weight of large plums, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and has fully colored for the best flavor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Enano Gigante Banana (Giant Dwarf Cavendish)
description: Enano Gigante, or 'Giant Dwarf,' is a Cavendish subgroup selection long grown in the Canary Islands and other Cavendish-producing regions for its stockier, wind-firm pseudostem compared to taller Cavendish clones like Valery. Its whimsically contradictory name reflects a plant that is taller and more vigorous than true Dwarf Cavendish but still shorter and less prone to wind lodging than the tallest Cavendish selections. Grow it in full sun with deep, fertile, well-drained soil, heavy summer watering, and regular feeding to size up its bunches. It carries the same cold sensitivity as other Cavendish types, so in zone 9a it is best grown in a container or heavily wind-sheltered bed with winter protection. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Encore Mandarin (Very Late-Season UC Riverside Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Encore, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, is prized above all for ripening extremely late, holding excellent eating quality on the tree well into spring at a point when nearly every other mandarin variety has finished, giving growers fresh mandarins for months longer than a standard planting would otherwise allow. The rich, deeply flavored, sweet-tart fruit contains noticeable seeds, unlike many modern seedless mandarins, but the flavor intensity and remarkably extended season have made it a favorite among citrus collectors and home growers who value variety over convenience. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Encore Raspberry
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Encore is a Cornell University late-season summer raspberry producing very large, conical, firm, dark red berries in the last 2–3 weeks of the summer raspberry season — ripening after most other summer varieties have finished, significantly extending the fresh raspberry harvest into mid-to-late summer. The very large berry size (larger than most summer varieties) and excellent sweet-tart flavor with complex aromatic notes make Encore the highest-quality of the late-season summer raspberry types. In zone 9 summer raspberries face significant challenges from heat — raspberries are most productive in zones 6–7 with cool summers — but in the cooler parts of zone 9a, along the coast, or at modest elevation, Encore can produce a satisfying late-season crop. The late-season ripening of Encore avoids the hottest weeks of summer, giving it better zone 9 performance than earlier varieties. Provide consistent irrigation and mulching to maintain the cool root zone conditions raspberries require. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Endive (Escarole)
description: Sow direct in late summer (8–10 weeks before first fall frost) or in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in the Gulf South (zones 8–10), sow from September through January for a fall through spring season. Cichorium endivia encompasses two main types: curly endive (frisée) with very finely cut, curly, frilly leaves and a pronounced bitter flavor, and escarole (broad-leaved endive) with flat, broader, less curly leaves and a milder flavor; both can be blanched by tying outer leaves over the heart for 1–2 weeks to reduce bitterness and produce the pale, creamy heart used in bistro salads. Endive is an outstanding fall and winter salad plant in the Gulf South, tolerating light frost and performing through the cool season. The bitter compounds are reduced by cold temperatures. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Endura Blueberry (Late-Season Firm-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Endura is a low-chill southern highbush blueberry released by the University of Florida in 2015, bred to extend the Gulf Coast harvest window into the late season. Its berries are notably large and firm with an excellent, persistent blue color that holds up well to handling and short-term storage, making it a strong choice for growers who want fruit that survives the walk from bush to kitchen. The upright, vigorous bush carries a somewhat higher chilling requirement than the earliest-ripening Florida releases, so it performs best where winters reliably deliver at least a moderate chill accumulation. Grow alongside another late-season southern highbush cultivar for best cross-pollination and berry size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Endurance Lablab (Perennial Forage Hyacinth Bean)
description: Endurance was bred by crossing the widely grown forage cultivar Rongai with a vigorous wild perennial accession from Zimbabwe (CPI 24973), then released as a weakly perennial lablab selection for tropical and subtropical forage systems. Unlike standard annual lablab cultivars, established Endurance stands can regrow from the crown into a second and even third growing season after grazing, mowing, or cutting, provided winters stay mild, making it a candidate for reduced-replanting cover cropping in zone 9 and warmer. It climbs and sprawls vigorously, fixes nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis, and produces heavy biomass valued for grazing, green manure, or trellised summer cover in the Gulf South. Because true commercial seed supply is limited compared to Rongai or Highworth, gardeners wanting Endurance may need to source it through tropical forage seed banks or university research collections. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Engelmann Prickly Pear
description: Plant paddles vertically with the cut end 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann prickly pear is the most widespread cactus of the American Southwest, ranging from Texas to California and into Mexico, and the principal source of edible tunas (fruits) and nopales (young pads) used in Mexican and Southwestern cooking. The large, red-purple tunas that ripen in late summer are exceptionally sweet with a flavor reminiscent of watermelon and bubblegum, high in antioxidants and vitamin C — they are eaten fresh, juiced into agua fresca and syrups, or made into jelly and candy. Harvest fruits with tongs and singe off glochids over a flame or scrub under running water before eating. This native cactus requires essentially zero maintenance once established in appropriate soil and will not tolerate standing water or clay soil. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Engelmann's Prickly Pear
description: Root Engelmann's Prickly Pear pad cuttings by allowing the cut surface to callus for 1–2 weeks before placing upright in dry, sandy soil; water sparingly; once established, this cactus thrives on neglect and natural rainfall in zone 5–11. Opuntia engelmannii is the quintessential Texas prickly pear — a large, sprawling native cactus forming dense clumps to 3–6 feet tall with round to oval, blue-green pads armed with clusters of stiff white to yellow spines. In spring the cheerful, waxy yellow flowers (2–3 inches across) open in profusion, attracting native bees and providing critical early-season pollen; by midsummer the flowers give way to deep reddish-purple tunas (prickly pear fruits) 1.5–2.5 inches long and sweet-tart with a distinctive watermelon-like flavor. Both the fruits and the young, spine-free green pads (nopales) are important traditional foods throughout Texas, Mexico, and the Southwest: fruits are eaten fresh, made into juices, jellies, syrups, and candy; nopales are sliced and grilled, sautéed with eggs (nopalitos), or pickled. Handle pads and fruits with tongs — both the large spines and tiny hair-like glochids cause intense skin irritation. Exceptional drought tolerance, native wildlife value, and dual culinary uses make this a natural choice for xeriscape gardens in zone 7–11. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: English Broadleaf Thyme
description: English Broadleaf is a selection of common thyme with notably wider, larger, darker-green leaves than standard French or common thyme, giving a milder, less pungent, slightly sweeter flavor than narrow-leaved types. The broader foliage also makes it faster to harvest and easier to strip from the stem for kitchen use. It is somewhat less cold-hardy and less drought-tolerant than French thyme, preferring slightly richer soil and more consistent moisture, and it tends toward a more sprawling, less compact habit that benefits from a light shearing after flowering to keep it from opening up in the center. Popular as a robust, easy-care culinary thyme for cooks who want ample leaf volume without the intensity of narrow-leaved cultivars. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: English Hawthorn (Midland Hawthorn)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; English hawthorn is the traditional hedgerow hawthorn of Britain and Europe, historically used to create stockproof field boundaries and now cultivated primarily for its spectacular late-spring flower display. The popular double-flowered cultivar 'Paul's Scarlet' (Crimson Cloud in North America) produces vivid deep pink to red double flowers that smother the thorny branches before the leaves fully emerge. The small red fruits (haws) ripen in fall and are consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and numerous other birds. The thorny dense habit makes it one of the most effective wildlife-friendly hedging plants for gardens. More susceptible to leaf blight diseases than native American hawthorns in humid summer climates. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: English Lavender
description: Surface-sow seeds and keep barely moist; germination is slow and uneven, so starting from cuttings or divisions is often more reliable. Plant in fast-draining, lean soil — rich or wet conditions promote rot and weak growth. Prune plants back by about one-third after the first flush of blooms to keep growth compact and encourage a second flowering. Harvest flower spikes just as the buds begin to open, bundling and hanging upside down in a warm, airy space to dry for sachets, culinary use, and aromatherapy. Matures in 90–200 days from transplant.

name: English Tall Vera Lavender
description: This tall, old-fashioned English lavender is intensely fragrant and prized for sachets, potpourri, and cut or dried arrangements. Start seed indoors in a light, well-drained mix, as germination is slow and benefits from a few weeks of cold stratification before sowing. Give plants full sun and sharp drainage; lavender resents wet feet and thrives in lean, alkaline soil. Space transplants well for air circulation and shear lightly after bloom to keep plants compact and productive. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: English Thyme
description: English thyme offers a subtle, woodsy flavor that suits a wide range of dishes and is a key component of bouquet garni. Start seed indoors and barely cover, since the seed is fine and needs some light to sprout; transplant to a sunny, well-drained bed after frost. This drought-tolerant perennial forms a low, spreading mat with small leaves and edible flowers that draw pollinators. Harvest sprigs regularly to encourage bushy growth and avoid overwatering, which can rot the crown. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: English Walnut
description: English walnuts are monoecious — male (catkins) and female flowers occur on the same tree — and most cultivars are partially self-fertile, though a second tree improves yields. The tree produces juglone, a chemical that inhibits growth of many plants beneath its canopy; avoid planting near vegetables, berries, or sensitive ornamentals. Grafted Carpathian-strain trees are more cold-hardy and begin fruiting in 4–7 years; seedling trees may take 10+ years. Harvest in fall when hulls begin to crack and turn dark; remove husks promptly and cure nuts for 2–3 weeks before storing. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Ennis American Persimmon (Seedless Tetraploid Selection)
description: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and give the tree room to develop its taproot undisturbed, since American persimmon resents transplanting once established. Ennis is one of only a handful of known tetraploid selections of native persimmon, distinguished from the more common hexaploid cultivars by its ability to reliably produce seedless, orange fruit roughly 1-2 inches across. Because of its genetics, Ennis has also been used as breeding stock in programs working toward seedless persimmon cultivars. Let the fruit soften fully on the tree or after a light frost before eating, as unripe fruit is intensely astringent, and expect this tough native tree to tolerate heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care once it is established. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ennis Hazelnut
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region. A classic Oregon hazelnut cultivar prized for producing exceptionally large, high-quality kernels favored by the fresh-eating and confectionery trade, it has long been a benchmark large-nut variety even as newer blight-resistant cultivars have gained ground in commercial orchards. Like older Pacific Northwest hazelnut cultivars bred before eastern filbert blight resistance was a priority, it is quite susceptible to that serious fungal disease and performs best in the relatively dry summer climate of western Oregon, struggling with disease pressure in humid eastern growing regions. Plant a compatible pollinator variety within range for good nut set, and monitor closely for filbert blight cankers, pruning out infected wood promptly if the disease appears. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Enorma Runner Bean (British Exhibition Scarlet Runner)
description: Enorma is a long-established British exhibition runner bean, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized by show growers for its extremely long, smooth, slender pods that can reach 20 inches under good conditions. Bright scarlet flowers cover the vigorous vines early and heavily, drawing hummingbirds and bumblebees and setting an abundant crop over a long season. Pods are best picked well before they reach exhibition length for eating quality, since very long pods used for showing tend to be tougher and more fibrous. Give it a tall, sturdy support, since well-fed plants can climb well over 8 feet. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Enormity Loquat (Extra-Large Late-Blooming Golden-Yellow Loquat)
description: Enormity is a large-fruited loquat selection with extra-large, oval, golden-yellow to orange fruit and juicy, sweet flesh carrying apricot and pineapple notes. It flowers about a month later than most standard cultivars, which extends the loquat harvest season and can offer some protection from the earliest winter freezes that damage the blossoms of earlier-flowering varieties. Even so, because loquats bloom in the cooler months, a hard freeze during Enormity's later fall-to-winter bloom period can still reduce fruit set. The tree is vigorous and needs a few years to reach bearing size after transplanting. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Enterprise Apple (Disease-Resistant Crisp Late-Season Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and released in the early 1990s, Enterprise is immune to apple scab and resists fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards. The medium-large, dark red fruit is crisp, firm, and sweet-tart with flavor that holds up well and even improves somewhat in storage. It ripens late in the season and keeps for several months under cool conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Enterprise Squash (Broad-Spectrum Virus-Resistant Zucchini)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Enterprise is a hybrid zucchini bred for resistance to a broad spectrum of the mosaic viruses that commonly spread through squash plantings via aphids, keeping foliage healthier and fruit better colored later into a humid Gulf South summer than more virus-susceptible varieties. The compact, open bush habit produces uniform, dark green cylindrical fruit that is easy to spot and harvest as the plant fills in. Pick fruit at 6-8 inches for the best texture and flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized and tough if missed for even a couple of days. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Envy Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Envy requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Braeburn and Royal Gala, it produces large, brilliantly two-toned red-and-pink fruit with dense, sweet, exceptionally slow-to-brown flesh that stays fresh-looking far longer than most apples once cut, making it a favorite for lunchboxes, fruit trays, and salads. The tree is vigorous and productive with good disease resistance for a modern apple, and the fruit's slow browning and long storage life have made it an increasingly popular commercial and home-orchard variety since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer to improve size and annual bearing, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background color shifts from green to yellow-green beneath the red blush. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Envy Edamame (Extra-Early Cold-Tolerant Edamame)
description: Sow seed 1 to 1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Envy is a widely grown edamame cultivar valued for its notably early maturity — among the fastest edamame varieties to reach harvest — and for better cold-soil tolerance at planting than many other edamame types, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible edamame crop or a second planting for fall harvest. Plants are compact and productive, with pods clustering densely on relatively short, sturdy bushes. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and fully filled but before the shell begins to yellow — sample a pod for tenderness and flavor to judge exact timing. For the classic preparation, boil or steam whole pods briefly in well-salted water, then squeeze the beans directly from the pod to eat; pods themselves are fibrous and not eaten. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Epazote
description: Surface-sow the tiny seeds by pressing them gently into soil without covering, as they require light for germination; thin to 12–18 in. Epazote is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean, well-drained soil; rich, moist conditions encourage excessive growth. Deadhead regularly to control self-seeding, which can be invasive in warm climates. Harvest young stem tips throughout the season; the pungent, resinous flavor mellows somewhat with cooking. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Epic Eggplant (Virus-Resistant Classic Black-Skinned Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Epic is a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid eggplant carrying resistance to tobacco mosaic virus and is specifically recommended by Southern extension programs for Florida and Texas growing conditions. It produces large, classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, well-branched plant that holds up well to summer heat. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure — dull skin and hard flesh signal overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep picking regularly through the season to encourage continued flowering and fruit set, and provide consistent moisture, since eggplant grown under drought stress tends to develop tougher skin and more bitterness. Matures in 62–70 days from transplant.

name: Epicure Tarragon
description: Set out rooted cuttings or rhizome divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, since this tetraploid tarragon selection almost never flowers normally and never produces viable seed. Epicure is a smooth-leaved, strongly aromatic tarragon clone whose essential oil is dominated by methyl chavicol, giving it a cleaner, more concentrated anise-licorice flavor than many run-of-the-mill nursery tarragon starts sold simply as 'French tarragon.' Harvest by snipping young stem tips through the growing season and expect the top growth to die back completely over winter, re-emerging from the crown once soil warms in spring. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and multiply stock, since seed propagation is not an option. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Erbette Chard (Ribless Italian Leaf Chard)
description: Broadcast or row sow seed clusters thickly and shallowly, since this type is grown for its abundant tender leaves rather than for large stalks. This unusual Italian chard lacks the thick, wide ribs of standard Swiss chard, instead producing slender stems and smooth, spinach-like leaves that regrow quickly after cutting. Favored by cooks for its mild flavor and quick-cooking texture, it tolerates both cool weather and mild heat better than many leafy greens, making it useful for extended cutting through a Gulf Coast winter. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Erlene's Green Cotton (Heirloom Naturally Green Cotton)
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Erlene's Green is a Southern heirloom naturally colored cotton, maintained and passed down by home seed savers, that produces sage-green lint instead of the usual white -- part of the same tradition of naturally pigmented cottons that inspired the modern Foxfibre breeding work reviving colored cotton for eco-conscious textile spinning. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, and bolls split open at maturity to reveal soft green fiber that is prized by hand-spinners and fiber artists for producing yarn and cloth that needs no dye. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality can both fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Erntesegen Lingonberry (German Heavy-Cropping Lingonberry)
description: Grow in partial shade to full sun in very acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, the same conditions favored by blueberries and other ericaceous shrubs. Erntesegen, German for 'harvest blessing', is a long-established European lingonberry cultivar bred specifically for unusually heavy, dependable fruit set, producing abundant clusters of small, tart, bright-red berries on a dense, low, evergreen mat. Its glossy foliage doubles as an attractive year-round groundcover, and its shade tolerance relative to most fruiting shrubs makes it a good underplanting for blueberries or acid-loving conifers. Shear plantings back lightly every few years to renew growth and keep the mat dense and productive, and harvest the fall crop after the berries deepen to full red for the best flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eros Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Supermale Hybrid)
description: Eros rounds out the trio of early Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids bred from crosses with the 'Rutgers Beacon' and related male lines, predating the better-known Jersey series. Like its siblings Atlas and Apollo, it directs all of its energy into spear production rather than seed set, giving heavier early yields than older open-pollinated Mary Washington-type strains. Give the crowns two full seasons to build a root system before any harvest, then cut spears daily during the flush to keep the plant signaling new growth. A well-maintained Eros bed rewards gardeners with a productive asparagus patch for fifteen years or more. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Errante Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)
description: Errante Noir is one of the UC Davis Pierce's disease-resistant wine grape releases from Dr. Andy Walker's breeding program, which used marker-assisted selection to introgress resistance from the wild Vitis arizonica while keeping the vine predominantly Vitis vinifera. The wine has been compared most closely to Cabernet Sauvignon in style. Because the resistance trait allows the vine to tolerate the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa spread by sharpshooters, it is of particular interest to Gulf Coast and Texas growers where Pierce's disease historically eliminates most European wine grapes. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun and expect limited nursery supply as commercial propagation ramps up. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eru (Okazi, Fumbua, African Jointfir Vine)
description: Establish rooted cuttings in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil at the base of a tree, pole, or trellis, since this dioecious woody liana climbs by twining and will scramble many feet into a support if left unchecked. Eru is a slow-growing rainforest understory vine from Central and West Africa whose thick, glossy, leathery leaves are shredded fine and cooked into the beloved eru and okazi soups of Cameroon, Nigeria, and the Congo Basin, usually simmered with palm oil, meat or fish, and other greens. Because wild populations have been heavily overharvested, cultivating a few vines on a shaded fence or living trellis provides a sustainable home supply once the plant is established, after which stems can be selectively cut back for repeated leaf harvest for many years. Keep roots shaded and evenly moist and mulch heavily, as the plant resents drought and full, hot sun. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Escamillo Pepper (AAS-Winning Golden Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Escamillo is an AAS-winning Italian frying-type sweet pepper producing long, tapered, elegantly curved fruits that ripen unusually early from green to a rich golden yellow, giving a full harvest of fully ripe, sweetest-stage peppers well before many other sweet pepper varieties finish coloring. Fruits are thin-walled and sweet, excellent sautéed or grilled as well as eaten fresh, and the plant is productive and reasonably compact for a frying-pepper type. Stake plants loosely if fruit load bends the branches, and harvest continuously once fruits reach full gold color to keep new peppers setting. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Escarole
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-amended soil; escarole forms broad, flat rosettes with broad wavy leaves that are less bitter than curly endive. Blanch by gathering outer leaves and tying them over the center for 10–14 days before harvest to produce a creamy, tender heart. Harvest the full rosette by cutting at the soil line when heads are 12–14 in across. Escarole holds well in the garden through light frosts, which improve its mellow, slightly bitter flavor. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Esmee Arugula (Ruffled Oakleaf Rocket)
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist to slow bolting; Esmee is a fast, cold-tolerant arugula with deeply lobed, rounded oakleaf-shaped foliage that is fluffier and more ruffled than standard salad arugula, giving noticeably more visual loft in a mixed salad bowl. Its flavor leans nutty and mild rather than sharply peppery, making it approachable for gardeners and eaters who find standard rocket too pungent. Harvest baby leaves as early as three weeks for salad mixes, or let plants grow on for a fuller-size cutting at about six weeks. Like all arugula it bolts quickly in heat, so it performs best as an early spring or fall crop. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Esopus Spitzenburg Apple (Thomas Jefferson's Favorite Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating in Esopus, New York in the 1700s, this heirloom became famous as the reported favorite eating apple of Thomas Jefferson, who planted it at Monticello.
