The bright red-orange fruit, dotted with pale russet, has firm, yellow, intensely rich and spicy-sweet flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all apples, though the tree can be a shy, uneven bearer compared to modern commercial varieties. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well in cold storage, developing more complexity over several weeks. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Espadín Agave (Mezcal Agave, Tobaziche)
description: Plant in full sun in rocky, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil with minimal irrigation once established; espadín agave (Agave angustifolia) is the workhorse of the mezcal industry in Oaxaca, Mexico — accounting for approximately 90% of mezcal production globally — and is the most planted agave for spirits production due to its vigorous growth, prolific offsetting, and the distinctive smoky, earthy mezcal flavor its roasted piña produces. The plant produces numerous offsets ('hijuelos') around the base that are used to propagate new plants; after 7–15 years the plant flowers and dies. The young flower stalks are edible when roasted and a significant food source in Oaxacan villages. An attractive, medium-sized agave for warm, dry gardens and a living connection to the ancient mezcal tradition of Mexico. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Espanola Improved Chile (Short-Season High-Altitude New Mexico Red Chile)
description: Espanola Improved was released by New Mexico State University in 1984 as an early-maturing red chile bred for the shorter growing season and higher elevation of the Espanola Valley north of Santa Fe, where standard New Mexico chiles often fail to reach full red maturity before fall frost. The medium-length, tapered pods carry mild-to-medium heat and are traditionally harvested green for roasting or left on the plant to ripen fully red for the dried red chile ristras the region is known for. Compared to longer-season New Mexico cultivars, Espanola Improved sets fruit earlier and matures its red crop reliably even where the frost-free window is tight, making it a good choice for gardeners at altitude or in northern climates who still want authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Provide full sun, even moisture, and a warm start, since fruit set benefits from getting plants established as early as safely possible after the last frost. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Espelette Pepper (Piment d'Espelette)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed. Piment d'Espelette is the unique chile pepper of the Espelette commune and neighboring villages in the Pays Basque region of southwest France and northern Spain, where it holds PDO (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) status — meaning the authentic product can only come from that specific area. The elongated, 3–5 inch, initially green peppers ripen to brilliant red and are traditionally strung in long chains and dried in the mountain air; the resulting dried, ground powder has a distinctive mild-to-medium heat (1,500–4,000 SHU), sweet pepper aroma, and earthy-fruity flavor that is unlike any other pepper spice. Used to season virtually all savory foods in Basque cooking in place of black pepper — on eggs, fish, piperade, axoa (veal stew), chicken basquaise, and fromage de brebis (Basque sheep cheese). Grow in any warm garden; the fresh peppers have excellent flavor even without the Basque drying climate. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Essex Hybrid Squash
description: Essex Hybrid dates to an 1880s New England seed catalog description as a natural cross between a turban squash and a Hubbard, combining the turban's rounded shape with the Hubbard's tough, heavily warted rind in a bright orange-red skin. Once a popular fall display squash in the Northeast, it faded from commerce and now survives mainly through small heirloom seed savers, so seed can be harder to source than mainstream Hubbard types. Grow it exactly as you would any vining Cucurbita maxima, giving the sprawling plant six to eight feet of room and steady moisture through fruit set. The dense, sweet flesh cooks well for pies and mashing, and the thick, warty rind makes it an excellent long-term keeper once cured. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Estamino Rootstock Tomato
description: This vigorous interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite tomato scion variety rather than eaten itself, valued for a somewhat more moderate, better-balanced vigor than the extremely aggressive Maxifort rootstock, making it a popular choice where growers want the disease resistance and yield benefits of grafting without excessive vegetative growth crowding out fruit production. It carries strong resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts, corky root rot, and nematodes, and its more restrained root vigor compared to Maxifort suits closer plant spacing or shorter growing seasons where overly rampant rootstock growth would be a liability. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Eston Green Lentil (Small Green Culinary Lentil)
description: Released by the University of Saskatchewan's Crop Development Centre and long grown across the Canadian and northern U.S. prairies, Eston is the classic small, green-seeded lentil behind most grocery-store green lentils sold in North America. The low, wiry, bushy plants need lean soil and minimal fertility, since excess nitrogen pushes foliage at the expense of pods, and they hold up well to the light frosts common during early spring establishment. The small round seeds keep a firm bite and hold their shape better than red lentils when simmered, making them well suited to soups, pilafs, and salads. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Eta Hazelnut (EFB-Resistant Pollenizer)
description: Eta is a pollenizer selection from the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program, released to supply reliable, compatible pollen for eastern filbert blight-resistant orchards planted to cultivars such as Jefferson and Yamhill. It carries strong resistance to eastern filbert blight and sheds pollen over an extended window, improving nut set in commercial and home plantings alike. Because it is grown for catkins rather than a marketable nut crop, prune lightly to maintain an open habit with abundant flowering wood and site it upwind of the cultivars it is meant to pollinate. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ethel Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Georgia Selection)
description: Amend planting beds to a strongly acidic pH before setting out dormant plants, and mulch with pine straw or pine bark to keep the shallow, fibrous root system cool and moist. Ethel is a foundational rabbiteye selection released by the Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station in the 1950s, part of the same breeding cohort as Homebell, Menditoo, and Callaway, though it has been largely superseded commercially by later, higher-yielding cultivars like Tifblue and Climax. It still produces vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes with medium-sized, mild-flavored berries and is grown today mainly by heritage-variety collectors and small Southern homesteads. Prune out the oldest wood each winter and plant with a compatible rabbiteye pollinator for a full fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ethiopian Kale (Gomen, Abyssinian Mustard)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 12-18 inches apart, thinning to 6-12 inches for full-sized plants or leaving dense for cut-and-come-again baby greens. Ethiopian Kale, known as gomen in its native highlands, is a vigorous leafy brassica long grown as a staple green across Ethiopia and Eritrea, valued for its notable resistance to flea beetles and other brassica pests as well as its unusual heat tolerance, which lets it keep producing tender leaves through early summer heat that would send most kales and collards straight to bolting. Leaves are broad, slightly savoyed, and blue-green, with a flavor milder than collards but more assertive than standard kale, excellent braised, sauteed, or added to stews. Harvest outer leaves starting around 30 days for baby greens or let the plant mature and harvest the whole head; regular picking of outer leaves encourages continued production from the center. Because it shares pests and diseases with other brassicas, rotate away from beds that recently grew cabbage-family crops. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Ethiopian Moringa (Cabbage Tree, African Moringa)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; coppice every few months to maintain leaf production. Moringa stenopetala (Ethiopian moringa or cabbage tree) is the second commercially important moringa species after M. oleifera — native to the semi-arid highland areas of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, particularly the Konso region of the Omo Valley, where it has been cultivated and consumed as a major vegetable crop for an estimated 2,000+ years, far longer than M. oleifera in most of Africa. The tree is sometimes called 'cabbage tree' because the large, oval, blue-green leaves (much larger than M. oleifera's tiny leaflets) are eaten cooked in large quantities like cabbage — chopped and boiled or sautéed as a staple vegetable, often cooked with sorghum paste (injera dough), and also added to bean stews. The flavor is milder and less bitter than M. oleifera leaves. Like its more famous relative, M. stenopetala has exceptional nutritional density — high in protein, iron, calcium, vitamins A and C. The seeds produce a high-quality oil (ben oil) used for cooking. M. stenopetala is more adapted to cooler, higher-elevation tropical conditions than M. oleifera, and may perform better in humid tropical highland climates. Both can be grown in zone 10–12 lowland tropical gardens. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Etna Runner Bean (Black-Seeded Dual-Purpose Runner Bean)
description: Etna is an Italian heirloom runner bean grown for its solid, glossy black-seeded pods, a striking departure from the mottled reds and pinks typical of most runner bean varieties. Grown as a dual-purpose bean, young pods can be picked and cooked like a broad snap bean while the surface is still tender, or left on the vine to mature into fully dried black shelling beans with a rich, dense flavor suited to long-simmered pots. As with other runner beans, give the vigorous climbing vines tall support and steady moisture, since pod set falters in hot, dry conditions. Allow pods intended for drying to turn brown and papery on the vine before harvest. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Etrog Citron (Esrog, Hebrew Citron)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate; Etrog citron (Citrus medica 'Etrog', also spelled 'Esrog') is the specific cultivar of citron used for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles), where it serves as one of the Four Species (arba minim) central to the religious observance — a use with over 2,000 years of continuous documented history, making it one of the oldest cultivated citrus varieties still grown for a specific purpose. The fruits are very large (4–8 inches long), yellow, highly aromatic, with a very thick, white-fleshed rind and very little juice; the entire fruit, including the extraordinarily thick, sweet, resinous peel, is the primary edible product, commonly candied, used in liqueurs and confections, or made into jam. The strongly ribbed, warty, irregular shape and intense, complex citrus-resin fragrance make etrog citron immediately distinctive. Ritual-quality etrogs (used for Sukkot) must meet specific halachic requirements — fully yellow, unblemished, with the pitam (style/stigma) intact at the blossom end — and command very high prices. Etrog trees are quite ornamental, with large leaves and dramatic fruit, but are tender and need winter protection in most of zone 9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Eudora Muscadine Grape (Fresh-Market Female Cultivar)
description: Eudora is a female-flowered muscadine released by the University of Florida in 2006, bred for the fresh market and notable for its purple, oval berries that form in unusually tight clusters rather than the loose, few-berried sets typical of older cultivars. Each berry carries high sugar content and good eating texture, and the semi-recumbent vines show strong resistance to Pierce's disease and many of the fruit rots that plague muscadines in humid climates. Fruit ripens in midseason, typically late August along the Gulf Coast. Because Eudora carries only female flowers, plant it within 10-15 feet of a self-fertile cultivar such as Southern Jewel or Delicious to ensure good pollination and a full crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Eugenioides Coffee (Highland Low-Caffeine Wild Coffee)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Coffea eugenioides is a small understory tree native to the montane forests of the African Great Lakes region (Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, eastern DR Congo), where it grows at higher, cooler elevations than either of the two dominant commercial species. It holds a special place in coffee genetics as one of the two wild parent species — alongside C. canephora (robusta) — whose ancient natural hybridization produced C. arabica; as such it carries genetic interest for breeders working on climate resilience and novel flavor profiles. Its beans are notably small and its leaves narrow and glossy, and the species is distinguished by unusually low caffeine content (roughly a quarter that of typical arabica), making it a subject of recent specialty-coffee interest in naturally low-caffeine coffee breeding. Rarely offered outside botanical collections and specialty coffee research nurseries, it is grown by collectors and rare-fruit enthusiasts in zone 10-12 tropical gardens under the same filtered-shade, humid conditions as other coffee species, with tolerance for slightly cooler nights than lowland types. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Eureka Lemon (Standard Lemon Tree, Four-Season Lemon)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka is the standard lemon cultivar in American commercial production and one of the most widely grown home-orchard lemons in zone 9–11 — a vigorous, nearly thornless tree that is truly everbearing, producing lemons year-round with peak crops in winter and spring. The classic medium-to-large, yellow lemons have thin, smooth skin, high juice content, classic lemon acidity, and excellent fragrance — the gold standard of lemon flavor for culinary use. The everbearing production habit means there is nearly always some fruit on the tree in zone 9, even if the heaviest crops come in winter and early spring. The tree reaches 8–15 feet with glossy, aromatic leaves and fragrant white flowers that bloom repeatedly throughout the year. Eureka is slightly more cold-sensitive than Lisbon lemon and significantly more cold-sensitive than mandarins or kumquats; temperatures below 28°F for more than 4 hours can cause fruit and leaf damage. In cooler parts of zone 9, Lisbon lemon (more cold-tolerant) or Meyer lemon (much more cold-tolerant) may be better choices. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually; iron and zinc deficiencies are common in alkaline soils and should be corrected with chelated micronutrient sprays. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Eureka Persimmon (Classic American Astringent Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Eureka is a long-established Southern astringent persimmon valued for its reliable heavy production and good cold tolerance compared to many Asian cultivars. The medium, flattened, deep orange-red fruit must fully soften after ripening before eating, since the tannins in unripe flesh are strongly puckering, but once jelly-soft it turns richly sweet and custardy, excellent fresh or baked into puddings and breads. Trees are self-fruitful, precocious, and tend to bear reliably once established, with fruit typically ripening from October into November after color develops fully. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eureka Pomegranate (Classic American Red-Fleshed Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Eureka is a long-cultivated American pomegranate valued for its compact, more shrubby growth habit compared to larger cultivars, making it a good fit for smaller yards or container culture, and for producing small to medium, bright red fruit with tender, tart-sweet, deep-red arils over a long harvest season. Its attractive orange-red spring flowers also make it useful as a flowering ornamental in addition to fruit production. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: European Hackberry (Nettle Tree)
description: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in any well-drained, alkaline to acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; European hackberry is remarkably adaptable to poor, dry, rocky soils, alkaline conditions, and urban pollution. Celtis australis is a long-lived (500+ year), medium to large tree of the Mediterranean basin and southern Europe, producing small (1/3 inch), round fruits that turn from yellow to orange to dark-purple-black when fully ripe in autumn, with a sweet, date-like flavor and a single large seed; the fruits were widely eaten by Mediterranean peoples since antiquity (the "lotus" fruit referenced by Homer that caused forgetfulness, though the identity of Homer's lotus is debated). The tree's beautiful, long-petioled, rough-textured leaves, tolerance of drought and heat, and picturesque form make it an excellent ornamental in zones 7–11; it is one of the best shade trees for very hot, dry, alkaline landscapes. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: European Hazel, Cobnut
description: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts. Corylus avellana is the hazel of European woodlands and hedgerows, grown for millennia for its nutritious hazelnuts (cobnuts and filberts in commerce); flexible, coppiced stems have been used for furniture, wattling, and charcoal production since prehistoric times; and the soft, round catkins that dangle from every bare stem in February and March are one of the earliest and most important pollen sources of spring for emerging native bees, including queen bumblebees and early Andrena mining bees. The large, rounded leaves turn golden-yellow in fall; the twisted cultivar 'Contorta' (Harry Lauder's Walking Stick) is a popular ornamental selection. Plant two different cultivars for best nut yield. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: European Mountain Ash
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; European mountain ash is a graceful ornamental tree with pinnate, ash-like leaves that delivers three seasons of interest — clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring, abundant bright orange-red berry clusters from late summer through winter, and orange-red fall foliage. The profuse berries are eaten by waxwings, robins, thrushes, and other songbirds so eagerly that trees can be stripped within days of peak ripeness. The berries are edible to humans but contain parasorbic acid when raw (causing nausea) and must be cooked or frozen to destroy this compound; cooked berries make excellent jelly with a tart, cranberry-like flavor. Prefers cool, moist climates and does not perform well south of zone 6. Matures in 730–2190 days from transplant.

name: European Serviceberry (Snowy Mespilus)
description: European serviceberry is a compact, multi-stemmed shrub native to the mountains and limestone hills of central and southern Europe, producing clouds of star-shaped white flowers in April followed by small, sweet, blue-black berries in midsummer that ripen a few weeks after the flowers fade. The fruit is traditionally eaten fresh, dried like currants, or made into preserves in Alpine and Mediterranean regions, with a mild flavor similar to a mellow blueberry. It thrives on thin, stony, alkaline soils where richer-feeding shrubs struggle, and tolerates part shade along a woodland edge as well as full sun. Established plants need only occasional thinning of old wood to keep the shrub open and productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Eustis Limequat (Cold-Hardy Lime-Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a lime-flavored citrus, tolerating temperatures that would kill true Key lime and Persian lime trees outright. Eustis limequat was developed in Eustis, Florida, in 1909 by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle as a cross between Key lime and kumquat, aiming to combine the tart, aromatic lime flavor with the cold hardiness of kumquat, one of the toughest edible citrus species. The resulting small, oval, yellow-gold fruit has a genuinely lime-like tart flavor along with an edible, sweet-tart rind in the kumquat tradition, making the whole fruit usable — sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved in marmalade — without peeling. The compact tree bears prolifically and tolerates cold that would damage or kill a true lime, making it one of the few practical ways to grow lime-flavored citrus in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 outside the true lime-growing range. Protect young trees through their first few winters; mature wood handles cold considerably better. Harvest fruit once it colors up gold, and use promptly, as limequats do not store as long as some other citrus. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Eva Purple Ball Tomato (German Black Forest Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking the indeterminate vines as they grow. Eva Purple Ball traces to Germany's Black Forest region in the late 1800s and was carried to New Jersey by the Bratka family, producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of five to seven ounces with a sweet, well-balanced flavor. Gardeners in hot, humid regions especially value it for staying productive and relatively blemish-free when many other heirlooms struggle with disease pressure. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Evangeline Sweet Potato (LSU Crack-Resistant Orange Gulf Coast Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost; Evangeline is an LSU AgCenter release named for the Cajun heroine of Longfellow's poem and bred to match Beauregard's rich orange flesh and copper skin while ripening slightly earlier and resisting the growth cracking that Beauregard develops in wet Louisiana clay. Vines are moderately compact, and roots are uniform, smooth-skinned, and store well. Flavor is sweet and moist, excellent baked, mashed, or roasted. Because it matures a week or two earlier than Beauregard, Evangeline is a good choice for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest window or extra insurance against fall frost. Cure roots at 80-85F and high humidity for about a week after digging to heal skins and concentrate sugars, then store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated spot. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Evelyn American Persimmon (Early-Ripening Native Persimmon)
description: Evelyn is a named native persimmon selection prized chiefly for ripening its crop earlier than most American persimmon cultivars, letting growers in shorter-season areas harvest a full crop of soft, sweet fruit before hard frost cuts the season short. Fruit is medium-sized and richly sweet once fully soft-ripe, but like all American persimmons is intensely astringent while firm and must be left to ripen fully on the tree or after dropping. The tree shares the species' deep taproot, drought tolerance, and adaptability to poor or marginal soils, asking little beyond routine watering while young and occasional sucker removal. Pair Evelyn with a second, genetically distinct persimmon selection nearby to improve pollination and fruit set. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Even' Star Ice-Bred Collards (Cold-Hardy Landrace Collard)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. viridis 'Even' Star Ice-Bred'
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow air movement through the dense winter canopy. This is a farmer-bred landrace rather than a fixed variety, so individual plants show some variation in leaf shape and color, a trait intentionally preserved because it broadens genetic resistance to hard freezes. Repeated exposure to temperatures well below freezing triggers a marked increase in sweetness as the plant converts stored starches to sugars for cold protection, so flavor peaks after the first several freeze events rather than at first harvest. Because the strain was selected under working-farm winter conditions rather than in a breeding trial, gardeners should expect a rougher, more variable-looking plant than commercial hybrids in exchange for exceptional cold survival. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Everbearing / Fall Raspberry
description: Primocane-fruiting (everbearing) raspberries bear on the top portion of first-year canes in fall, then on lower portions the following summer if left. For the simplest management, mow all canes to the ground each late winter and enjoy a single fall crop on new primocanes — this eliminates disease buildup and minimizes pruning. Harvest from late summer through first frost when berries release easily from the plug. Consistent moisture during fruit development prevents crumbling. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Everbearing Mulberry Tree
description: This everbearing mulberry yields sweet, plump berries over a long season on a compact, shrubby tree that is easy to manage. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates a range of conditions and is quite drought resistant once established. Prune in winter to keep it at a pickable height and to open the canopy. The fruit ripens over many weeks, so harvest regularly and expect birds to compete for the crop. Note that ripe berries stain, so site it away from patios and walkways. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Everbearing Strawberry
description: This everbearing 'Delizz' strawberry produces flushes of fruit from summer through the first frost rather than a single early crop. Plant crowns so the growing point sits right at the soil line, since burying it invites rot and planting too high dries out the roots. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist while berries are forming. It performs well in containers, hanging baskets, and beds. Pinch off early flowers on new plants to build strong roots before letting them fruit. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: EverCrisp Apple (Honeycrisp x Fuji, Long-Storing Modern Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; EverCrisp requires a substantial chill period similar to its Fuji parent and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. Bred by Ohio orchardist Bill Dodd through the Midwest Apple Improvement Association from a cross of Honeycrisp and Fuji, it was selected specifically to capture Honeycrisp's famously crackling, juicy texture while solving that parent's notorious storage weaknesses and inconsistent bearing. The large, red-blushed fruit ripens later than Honeycrisp, typically in October, and keeps its crisp texture and sweet-tart flavor in cold storage for many months longer than Honeycrisp, with far less bruising and breakdown. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and harvest once the background color shifts and fruit separates easily from the spur. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Everglades Tomato (Wild Tomato)
description: Transplant into any well-drained soil in full sun; the Everglades tomato is the wild currant tomato (Solanum pimpinellifolium) as it naturalized and adapted to South Florida's extreme subtropical heat, humidity, and occasional drought over generations. It is the most heat-tolerant of all cultivated tomatoes — it reliably sets fruit at temperatures above 95°F and through humidity levels that shut down every commercial variety. The tiny (marble-sized, 1/2 inch) red fruits grow in long clusters of 20–40 and have an intensely rich, sweet-acidic tomato flavor disproportionate to their size — considered by many to have the purest tomato taste of any variety. The vines sprawl and climb enthusiastically (6–8 feet) and are extremely drought-tolerant once established. In South Florida, Everglades tomatoes produce year-round and naturalize along roadsides and garden fences. In zone 9a, they perform as a long-season annual. Seeds are collected easily and the plant passes selected characteristics to offspring, making it an important parent in breeding heat-tolerant tomatoes. Highly recommended for hot, humid, low-maintenance gardens. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Evergreen Blueberry (Darrow's Blueberry, Lowbush Evergreen Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy or amended soil in full sun to partial shade; in hot zone 9 climates, afternoon shade improves fruit quality. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow's Blueberry or Evergreen Blueberry) is a native, low-growing blueberry species from the coastal plain flatwoods and sandhills of the Southeast, ranging from South Carolina through Florida to Louisiana. It is unique among native blueberries for being semi-evergreen to fully evergreen — retaining most of its small, bluish-gray leaves through mild winters — and for requiring very few chill hours (100–200 hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable blueberries for warm zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where the commonly-planted Rabbiteye types (Vaccinium ashei) may not receive enough cold in mild years. Vaccinium darrowii is also an important breeding parent used by blueberry breeders at the University of Florida and USDA to develop the Southern Highbush blueberry series — its drought tolerance, evergreen foliage, and minimal chill requirement were bred into commercial cultivars. The wild species produces small but sweet, intensely flavored berries that are beloved by wildlife. It tolerates the high heat, humidity, and wet-dry cycles of Gulf Coast flatwoods better than most northern blueberry species. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Evergreen Cutleaf Blackberry (Thorny Parent of Oregon Thornless Blackberry)
description: Evergreen is a vigorous, heavily thorned blackberry cultivar named for its deeply cut, fern-like leaflets that hold their glossy dark green color later into fall and winter than typical blackberry foliage. It is best known today as the parent from which the widely grown thornless sport 'Oregon Thornless' was selected, but the thorny original is still grown where its notably firm, small-seeded, long-shelf-life berries are valued for processing and jam-making. Train the long, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis each season, tying in first-year primocanes that will fruit the following summer, and remove spent floricanes after harvest to make room for new growth. Its dense, thorny habit also makes it useful as an impenetrable barrier hedge in addition to its fruiting value. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Evergreen Hardy White Bunching Onion (Cold-Hardy Perennial Scallion)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike bulbing onions, this classic bunching onion (Welsh onion type) never forms a true bulb, instead producing clusters of straight, white-shanked scallions with mild, tender green tops. Its exceptional cold hardiness lets it overwinter in the ground in many climates, providing an extra-early harvest the following spring, and it can be cut back repeatedly through the growing season for a continuous supply. Because it multiplies by division at the base, an established clump can be divided every year or two to keep plantings vigorous and productive. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Evergreen Huckleberry
description: Evergreen huckleberry is a slow-growing Pacific Coast native prized both as an ornamental evergreen shrub and as a source of small, sweet-tart black berries that ripen from October through January — one of the few edible fruits to ripen in the Pacific Northwest winter. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 with pine bark or sawdust mulch. The plant is extremely slow to establish from container stock and may take 5–7 years for significant fruit production. Florists prize the glossy foliage as a cut green; pruning for floral use also serves to shape the shrub. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Evergreen Sumac (Tobacco Sumac)
description: Plant in well-drained, rocky or gravelly, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen sumac is one of the finest drought-tolerant evergreen shrubs for dry Southwest and Texas Hill Country landscapes, holding its glossy, leathery dark-green leaves through winter and providing year-round structure. Small creamy-white flowers bloom in late summer and attract bees and other pollinators, followed by dense clusters of deep-red, slightly sticky fruits that are documented as a food source for over 100 bird species including mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and Montezuma quail. It thrives on neglect once established and is an excellent choice for wildlife gardens, slopes, or as a large screening hedge. Avoid overwatering and heavy soils, which are the primary causes of decline. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Everleaf Emerald Towers Basil
description: This columnar basil grows into an upright herbal tower of deep, glossy emerald leaves, making it as ornamental as it is useful. It delays flowering up to twelve weeks longer than standard types, so plants keep producing tender leaves without the flavor decline that comes with bolting. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil has thoroughly warmed. Its compact, non-branching habit suits patio pots and small beds; harvest leaves often and provide steady moisture and full sun. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Everleaf Genovese Basil (Non-Flowering Extended-Harvest Genovese Basil)
description: The original release in the Everleaf breeding series that later added Everleaf Thai Towers and Everleaf Emerald Towers, this classic Genovese-flavored basil is bred for a sterile, non-flowering habit so plants keep channeling energy into leaf production instead of seed set. The upright, well-branched plants hold sweet, glossy dark-green leaves in classic pesto flavor for weeks longer than standard Genovese types before quality declines. Harvest by cutting stem tips regularly to encourage continued branching. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Everleaf Thai Basil (Non-Flowering Extended-Harvest Thai Basil)
description: Start seed indoors or transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Part of the Everleaf breeding series that also produced Everleaf Emerald Towers, this Thai-type basil carries the classic anise-clove flavor and purple-tinged stems and flower bracts of traditional Thai basil, but its non-flowering habit means the plant keeps producing fresh, flavorful leaves for weeks longer than seed-setting types before quality declines. The upright, columnar growth habit also makes it a good choice for narrow spaces and containers. Harvest by cutting whole stem tips, which encourages continued branching and leaf production through the season. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Eversweet Pomegranate (White-Juiced Seedless Sweet Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Eversweet is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant once established, requiring little irrigation in most Gulf Coast settings after the first year; harvest when fruits are fully colored (rosy-orange to red skin) and sound hollow when tapped; fruits are sweet enough to be eaten with minimal mess. Eversweet is a distinctive pomegranate variety unlike any other in its combination of extreme sweetness, very soft (almost absent) seeds, and clear non-staining juice. Most pomegranates have deep red to crimson arils producing intensely colored red juice — the juice stains are notorious and pomegranate processing indoors is typically done over the kitchen sink with care to avoid contact with clothing. Eversweet breaks this rule: the arils are a soft rose-pink rather than deep red, and the juice they produce is clear to very light pink rather than the deep crimson of standard pomegranates, and crucially, it does not stain permanently. This characteristic makes Eversweet a more family-friendly choice for fresh eating, especially with children, and allows pomegranate eating and juicing without the usual mess concerns. The flavor is very sweet with low acidity — milder and less complex than Parfianka or Wonderful, but consistently rated among the sweetest pomegranates available. The seeds are extremely soft and virtually undetectable when eating the arils fresh. The exterior of the fruit is more orange-pink than red, making it visually distinct from other varieties at harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Eversweet Strawberry (Day-Neutral Everbearing Strawberry)
description: Plant crowns in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing about a foot apart in raised beds or containers, and keep evenly moist with drip irrigation and a straw mulch to keep developing berries clean. Eversweet is a day-neutral strawberry bred for a longer, more consistently sweet fruiting season than many other everbearing types, producing a steady supply of medium, richly flavored berries from late spring through fall rather than concentrating fruit into one or two flushes. Pinch off the first flush of blossoms for a few weeks after planting to help young plants establish a strong root system before letting them fruit continuously. Renew the planting every two to three years as yields decline, and watch for the same pests and diseases common to other strawberries, including spider mites and gray mold in humid weather. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Evertender Okra (Long-Season Spineless Hybrid Okra)
description: Evertender is a spineless hybrid okra bred for pods that stay tender and stringless days longer than most varieties, reducing the pressure to pick every single day to avoid tough, fibrous pods. The smooth, spineless pods and foliage also make harvest far more comfortable, since typical okra plants are covered in fine irritating spines. Direct sow after the soil has warmed, since okra germinates poorly in cool, wet ground, and pick pods at 3-4 inches for the most tender eating. Its extended tenderness window makes Evertender a practical choice for gardeners who can only harvest okra every few days rather than daily. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Everthornless Blackberry (Non-Reverting Thornless Cutleaf Trailing Blackberry)
description: Everthornless, developed at the University of Illinois as an ex vitro somaclonal variant of the classic cutleaf Thornless Evergreen blackberry, was bred to fix a longstanding flaw in its parent: because Thornless Evergreen's thornlessness comes from a chimeral mutation confined to the outer cell layer, its root suckers frequently revert to thorny growth as plantings age. Everthornless carries the thornless trait through all cell layers, so its root suckers stay thornless too, making it a lower-maintenance option for replanting old Thornless Evergreen patches. It keeps the same deeply cut, fern-like foliage and produces good yields of well-flavored, mildly tart berries late in the season. Train the vigorous trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, prune hard after harvest, and keep cane tips off the soil to prevent unwanted rooting. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Excalibur Pecan (University of Georgia Scab-Resistant Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, siting a compatible Type I pollinator within range since pecans are wind-pollinated and set poorly from a single cultivar. Excalibur was released from the University of Georgia pecan breeding program at Tifton, selected primarily for its strong resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most consistent yield losses for home and commercial growers across the humid Gulf South, letting it produce a reliable crop with far less fungicide input than older scab-susceptible standards. Nuts are large with good kernel quality and a bright, attractive shell. Supplement with an annual zinc sulfate foliar spray, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and harvest once the shucks split open in October and November. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Excel Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur several months before planting; Excel is an early-season rabbiteye blueberry from the University of Georgia breeding program, selected to open the harvest window ahead of standard mid-season varieties while still carrying good rabbiteye vigor and heat tolerance. Berries are medium to large, light blue, and firm, with a mild sweet-tart flavor typical of early rabbiteyes. Excel's relatively low chill requirement makes it reliable in zone 8-9 Gulf South winters that sometimes shortchange higher-chill northern varieties. It is not self-fruitful, so interplant with Climax or another early-blooming rabbiteye within about 50 feet for good fruit set and larger berries. Mulch with pine bark to keep roots cool and moist, and skip lime and phosphorus fertilizers, which blueberries handle poorly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Excel Fig
description: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage; Excel is an LSU (Louisiana State University) AgCenter-developed fig cultivar released specifically for Gulf South production, selected for its large, distinctively yellow-skinned fruit with rich amber flesh and the high resistance to fruit souring that is a serious problem for figs in the humid Gulf Coast climate. While traditional Southern figs like Celeste and Brown Turkey are prone to splitting and souring in rainy, humid conditions at harvest time, Excel was specifically bred for improved resistance to these problems — producing firmer skin that resists splitting and reduces the entry of yeasts that cause souring. The large, sweet fruits have an extremely rich, complex, honey-fig flavor that is the archetypal fresh fig experience — one of the most sophisticated and complex flavors of any temperate fruit. Figs are the quintessential Gulf South home fruit tree: tolerant of heat, humidity, and occasional drought once established, self-fruitful (no cross-pollination required), highly productive, and producing fruit of exceptional quality that cannot be found in stores (fresh figs ship and store very poorly, making the homegrown experience irreplaceable). Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Excel Pecan (Scab-Resistant Louisiana Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Excel is a modern Louisiana-bred pecan cultivar selected for strong resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the humid-climate fungal disease that plagues many older commercial cultivars along the Gulf Coast, reducing or eliminating the need for fungicide sprays in home plantings. It produces large, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality and ripens relatively early, helping it escape late-season disease and weather pressure. Because of its disease tolerance, Excel is increasingly recommended for Gulf South home orchards where spray programs are impractical. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and watch for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils, correcting with a foliar zinc spray in spring. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Excel Sweet Potato (High-Yield NCSU Copper-Skin Orange Sweet Potato)
description: Excel has light copper skin over orange flesh and is noted for out-yielding Jewel by roughly 15% in North Carolina State University trials. It carries strong resistance to southern root-knot nematode, stem rot (Fusarium wilt), and internal cork, making it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of these problems. Baking and canning quality are considered excellent, and roots store well after curing. Flavor and texture are comparable to other classic moist, orange-fleshed dessert-type sweet potatoes. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Excelsior Plum (Heirloom Low-Chill Japanese-American Hybrid Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and site a compatible plum cultivar such as Methley or Bruce within pollinating distance, since Excelsior needs a partner to set fruit reliably. Introduced from Florida nurseries over a century ago as one of the early hybrids between the Japanese plum and native American plum species, Excelsior has persisted as a heirloom home-orchard favorite in the Deep South thanks to a modest chill requirement of roughly 400 hours that suits mild Gulf Coast winters. Fruit ripens mid-season with deep wine-red skin and juicy yellow flesh, offering a good balance of sweetness and tartness for fresh eating. Give the upright tree room to spread and thin the crop if it sets heavily, since Excelsior can overbear on young trees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Exclamation Watermelon (Full-Season Disease-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Exclamation is a full-season seedless watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, along with reduced tendency toward hollow heart, a cracking defect that can hollow out the center of large seedless melons grown under Southern heat stress. Because triploid seedless varieties need a seeded pollenizer nearby for fruit set, plant a compatible pollenizer variety in the same bed. It produces large, blocky, crimson-fleshed fruit with excellent sweetness and firm texture. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 85–92 days from transplant.

name: Explosive Ember Pepper (Purple-Foliage Ornamental Hot Pepper)
description: Explosive Ember is an ornamental pepper bred as a companion to the popular Black Pearl variety, distinguished by bright purple young foliage and white-and-purple flowers rather than Black Pearl's near-black leaves. Its slender, upright, conical fruit emerges a vivid neon purple and ripens through orange to red, often showing all three colors in the same cluster for a long-lasting, ever-changing display. The fruit carries genuine heat in the tabasco-to-cayenne range, roughly 30,000 Scoville units, and while technically edible it is grown almost entirely for ornamental impact in beds, containers, and hanging baskets. Plants stay compact and well-branched without pinching, tolerate summer heat well, and continue setting new fruit clusters over a long season with routine watering and light monthly feeding. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Extra Curled Dwarf Parsley (Compact Heirloom Curly Parsley)
description: Extra Curled Dwarf is a French heirloom curly parsley selected for a low, dense, tightly compact habit and finely ruffled, deep-green leaves, making it noticeably shorter and more uniform in the row than taller curly types like Triple Curled or Paramount. Its neat, mounded form suits edging, window boxes, and container plantings where a tall parsley would look leggy, while retaining the same mild, clean parsley flavor prized for garnish and fresh chopping. As a biennial it forms an edible rosette the first year and will bolt to flower and seed in its second season if overwintered in mild climates. Harvest outer leaves continuously to keep the compact rosette productive. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Extra Dwarf Pak Choi
description: Direct-sow seed thinly and shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, in fertile soil, since this miniature pak choi matures in as little as 30 days and can be grown at very tight spacing for dense baby-green production. Its curled, glossy dark-green leaves sit atop short, thick white petioles, giving each plant a compact, rounded form even smaller than standard baby bok choy. Because it thrives across a wide range of temperatures, it can be succession-sown nearly year-round in mild climates for continuous harvests of whole tender plants used raw, steamed, or stir-fried. Matures in 30–35 days from seed.

name: Extra Early Blackeye Cowpea (Fast-Maturing Blackeye Southern Pea)
description: Extra Early Blackeye is a fast-maturing selection within the classic blackeye cowpea group, historically valued for reaching harvest noticeably sooner than standard blackeye types, an advantage for gardeners working within a short frost-free window or wanting an early flush of black-eyed peas. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, since cowpeas germinate poorly in cold ground. Plants carry the familiar cream-white, black-eyed seed in slender pods on compact, semi-bush vines that need little to no staking. Extra Early Blackeye has been used as breeding stock in university cowpea improvement programs, including as one of the parent lines of the disease-resistant Magnolia Blackeye released by Mississippi State University. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Extra Long Handled Dipper Gourd
description: This selection of Lagenaria siceraria is bred specifically for exceptionally long, slender necks that can stretch two to three feet, far exceeding the handle length of a typical dipper gourd. Provide an overhead arbor or fence at least eight feet tall so the developing handle hangs straight down under its own weight instead of curling on the ground. The large white flowers open in early evening and are pollinated mainly by moths, so hand-pollinating with a soft brush at dusk improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Let fruit remain on the vine until the stem shrivels and the shell turns hard, then cure the gourds in a warm, airy space for one to several months until they feel light and the seeds rattle before cleaning and finishing them as dippers or ladles. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto Fava Bean (Italian Violet-Seeded Broad Bean)
aliases: Vicia faba 'Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto'
description: Long grown in home gardens across Liguria and Tuscany, this heirloom takes its name from its dark violet-to-near-black seed coat and its notably early maturity compared to standard English broad beans. Sow directly into cool, fertile soil in blocks so the sturdy stems support one another, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to slow aphid buildup. Pods can be picked young for fresh shelling, but many Italian cooks let a portion dry fully on the plant, since the violet seed coat holds its color and the beans store and cook well for soups and purees. Because it matures earlier than most fava strains, it suits gardeners with a short cool season or those looking to free the bed for a following summer crop. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Extrakta Oregano (High-Oil Concentrated-Flavor Culinary Oregano)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; oregano flavor intensity is strongest when grown a bit lean rather than heavily fertilized. Extrakta was selected for an unusually high concentration of essential oils in its leaves, giving a bolder, more pungent, more robustly flavored oregano than many ordinary culinary strains, prized by cooks who want maximum flavor impact from a smaller amount of fresh or dried herb. The compact, mounding perennial forms a tidy clump well suited to an herb garden border or container. Harvest leaves and stems regularly through the growing season, and for the most concentrated flavor for drying, cut just before the plant flowers, when essential oil content peaks. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Extrakta Sage (High-Oil Culinary Sage)
description: Extrakta was selected as a commercial oil strain and carries a noticeably higher essential-oil content in its leaves than ordinary garden sage, translating into a bolder, more pungent flavor from the same amount of fresh or dried leaf. The narrow, upright green leaves are less broad than common culinary sage, and the plant sends up generous spikes of lilac-purple flowers in early to midsummer that draw bees well before most other kitchen herbs bloom. Because the flavor is more concentrated, cooks can use noticeably less of it per dish than standard sage, making it a good choice for drying and storage. Harvest leaves anytime through the season but cut for drying just before flowering, when oil content peaks. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Eye of the Goat Bean (Ojo de Cabra)
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in warm, well-drained to dry soil; Eye of the Goat is adapted to dry conditions and does well with minimal supplemental irrigation in zones 7–11 once established. Eye of the Goat (Ojo de Cabra) is a traditional Mexican heirloom dry bean with large, oval, cream-to-beige seeds marked with a distinct tan 'eye' or ring surrounding a dark hilum — resembling, as the name suggests, the eye of a goat. This bean has been grown in Mexico and the American Southwest for generations and is particularly heat- and drought-tolerant, making it valuable in hot, dry climates. When cooked, the seeds have a rich, earthy, slightly sweet flavor with a creamy texture that holds its shape well; excellent in soups, stews, and as refried beans in traditional Mexican cooking. An outstanding heirloom for Gulf Coast and Southwest gardeners who need a reliable dry bean in hot, occasionally dry summers. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Ezrilla Leaf Lettuce
description: This uniform, short-headed leaf lettuce has little core, so a single cut above the base releases evenly sized leaves for easy salad prep. It is slow to bolt for a long harvest and offers resistance to downy mildew and lettuce aphid. Grow in full sun to partial shade in cool weather, providing afternoon shade in heat. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, sweet leaves. Succession sow every couple of weeks for a continuous supply. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Faassen's Catmint
description: Because Faassen's Catmint is a sterile hybrid, propagate it by dividing established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, or take stem cuttings in late spring; replant divisions promptly in well-drained soil in full sun. Site in average to lean, dry soil — fertile or overly moist conditions produce floppy, open growth rather than the neat mounding habit this plant is prized for. Shear the entire plant back by half immediately after the first heavy flush of bloom in late spring to promote a dense second flush of lavender-blue flower spikes through summer and into fall. Divide clumps every three to four years to keep them vigorous, as the center of older plants can die out over time. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Facing Heaven Pepper (Chao Tian Jiao, Upward-Pointing Chinese Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; Facing Heaven pepper (朝天椒, Cháo Tiān Jiāo, meaning 'facing heaven pepper') is one of the foundational chili pepper varieties of Chinese cuisine — a small to medium-sized (1.5–2.5 inch), bright red, upward-pointing hot pepper produced in prolific clusters where each plant can carry 50–100 fruits simultaneously, the upward orientation giving the variety its evocative name as the fruits point skyward like tiny flaming torches. The peppers are hot (30,000–70,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat and a characteristic bright, slightly fruity flavor that is distinct from Mexican or Caribbean chiles — a flavor that has made this pepper type essential in the cooking of Sichuan, Hunan, Yunnan, and Guizhou provinces, where it appears in red oil (hóng yóu), chili pastes, dried whole peppers for stir-fries, and fermented condiments like dòubànjiàng. The dried bright red fruits maintain excellent color and retain their heat well; they are often dry-roasted in oil with Sichuan peppercorns as the starting point for the characteristic ma-la (numbing-hot) flavor profile of Sichuan cooking. Very productive in the Gulf South's warm climate, producing abundantly from midsummer through fall. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Faerie Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Rind Personal Watermelon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks earlier for a head start in cooler climates; vines are notably more restrained than most watermelons, spreading to roughly 10-11 feet rather than sprawling widely. Faerie was bred by Taiwan's Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its distinctive creamy yellow rind marked with thin light stripes, enclosing crisp, high-sugar pink-red flesh, and for producing a heavy set of personal-size, 4-6 lb oval fruit on a comparatively space-efficient plant. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruit set, then ease back as melons near maturity. Harvest by watching the ground spot shift from white to creamy yellow and the nearby tendril dry and brown, since the pale rind makes color-based ripeness cues less obvious than on dark-skinned watermelons. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Fagiolo di Controne Bean (Controne Bean, No-Soak Campania Heirloom)
description: Controne bean is a small, ivory-white heirloom grown for centuries on the terraced slopes around Controne in Campania and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium variety. Its defining trait is an exceptionally thin, delicate skin that lets the beans cook through in well under an hour without an overnight soak, softening to a smooth, buttery interior. Provide poles or a trellis for the climbing vines and consistent moisture while pods fill, then let pods dry fully before shelling. Because the thin skin bruises and splits more easily than thicker-skinned beans, handle dried pods gently during threshing and winnowing. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Fagiolo di Lamon Bean (Lamon Bean, Italian PGI Borlotto)
description: Fagiolo di Lamon carries Protected Geographical Indication status for the mountain valleys around Lamon in Italy's Belluno province, where cool nights and mineral-rich alluvial soils are credited with the bean's thin skin and rich, nutty flavor. The plump borlotto-type seeds are cream colored with deep maroon streaking, nearly indistinguishable in appearance from cranberry beans but noted by Italian cooks for cooking down into an especially creamy, unified texture rather than staying distinctly bean-shaped. Harvest pods once fully dry and papery, then shell and finish curing indoors for a week before storing airtight. Give vines full sun and a tall support, since plants can reach 8 feet in a long warm season. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Fagiolo di Sorana Bean (Sorana Bean, Tuscan Flat White Shell Bean)
description: Sorana bean is a Slow Food Presidium variety grown in the sandy river-bottom soils near Pescia in Tuscany, prized for a seed coat so thin it seems to dissolve into the cooking liquid, leaving a velvety, almost skinless texture. The flattened, kidney-shaped white seeds are smaller and more delicate than typical cannellini types, and growers traditionally avoid heavy clay soils that thicken the skin. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine, since the thin-skinned seeds are more prone to splitting if picked while still damp, then cure indoors before storage. A well-drained, sandy raised bed is a reasonable substitute for the variety's native river-valley soil. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Fair Ellen Oak-Leaf Geranium (Deep-Cut Scented Pelargonium)
description: Fair Ellen is a selection of oak-leaf geranium prized for foliage cut even more deeply and finely than the species, giving the sticky, aromatic leaves a lacy, almost fern-like outline while keeping the same pungent bitter-almond to balsamic fragrance when brushed. It grows into a noticeably more compact, denser shrub than seedling oak-leaf geranium, making it easier to manage in pots and mixed scented-herb plantings. Root stem cuttings in a lean, fast-draining mix and grow in full sun with light, infrequent watering, since rich soil or excess moisture produces soft, less fragrant growth. It has no cold tolerance and must be overwintered as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside the warmest zones. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Fairchild Canistel
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to sandy soil; Fairchild is a long-established Florida canistel selection known for smooth-textured, deep golden-orange flesh with the dense, dry, custard-like texture that gives the fruit its common name, 'egg fruit.' The flavor is sweet and mealy, often likened to a baked sweet potato or boiled egg yolk sweetened with brown sugar, and the flesh is popular blended into shakes, flans, and baked desserts throughout South Florida and the Caribbean. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate a range of soils and are relatively wind-firm. Pick fruit when the skin turns fully glossy orange-yellow and let it finish softening at room temperature for several days before eating, as canistel is only palatable when fully ripe and soft. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Fairchild Mango (Compact Panama Dooryard Mango)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Fairchild is a Panama-origin mango named for plant explorer David Fairchild and grown widely in South Florida dooryards for its small, dense, naturally dwarf-tending habit that suits small yards and container culture better than most mango cultivars. Fruit is small to medium with mild, sweet, fiberless flesh and a gentle flavor that is a good introduction to mango for those used to only supermarket varieties. The tree's compact growth and tolerance for hedging or pruning make it especially practical for zone 9 gardeners who want to keep a container specimen small enough to move indoors or into a greenhouse before winter cold arrives. Reduce irrigation as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold exposure. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fairchild Pawpaw (Early-Ripening Ketter Seedling)
description: Fairchild is a named seedling selection of the Ohio cultivar Ketter, sharing some of that parent's rich flavor while ripening earlier in the season. It is documented in Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records among the many named selections that arose from open-pollinated Ketter seed. As with all pawpaws, Fairchild needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination, since it will not reliably set fruit on its own. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Fairchild Tangerine (Clementine x Orlando Hybrid)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine is a Clementine x Orlando tangelo hybrid developed by USDA breeders in 1964, producing deep reddish-orange, medium-sized (2.5–3 inch) fruits with rich, sweet-tart, spicy-aromatic tangerine flavor — one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available. The skin is thin, slightly rough, and adheres somewhat to the flesh (tighter than most loose-skinned mandarins but peels relatively easily by hand); fruits typically contain 6–12 seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor. Fairchild is one of the earlier-ripening mandarins in the California/Gulf South season, ripening November through December, and is an excellent choice for gardeners who want full-size mandarin flavor earlier in the season than the late-ripening Honey or Murcott types. The tree is medium-sized (8–14 feet), well-branched, and productive under good conditions with a cross-pollinator present. Trees in zone 9 should be sited in the warmest available microclimate as Fairchild is somewhat cold-sensitive; it tolerates brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established but young trees need frost protection in the first 2–3 years. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fairfax Wax Myrtle (Dense Upright Southern Bayberry Selection)
description: Fairfax is a selected, more compact and densely upright form of the Gulf Coast native southern wax myrtle, retaining the species' aromatic, glossy, blue-green foliage and tolerance of drought, salt spray, and poor sandy soils while staying tidier and better proportioned for hedges and mixed screens than seedling-grown plants. As with the species, it is a nitrogen-fixing, wildlife-friendly evergreen whose female plants produce waxy gray-blue berries valued by overwintering songbirds. Grow in full sun for the densest habit, though it also performs well with afternoon shade in hot climates; established plants need little supplemental water and respond well to light shearing to maintain a formal hedge line. Avoid heavy, poorly drained clay soils, which can shorten its lifespan compared with sandy or loamy sites. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fairhope Select Tea (Gulf Coast Alabama Heritage Selection)
description: Fairhope Select is a Gulf Coast heirloom tea selection with a direct link to Lipton's mid-20th-century Fairhope, Alabama tea research plantation; when that project was abandoned, a handful of surviving plants were rescued and propagated into the selections sold today. It carries small to medium, heavily serrated green leaves, tolerates more direct sun than many China-type tea plants, and flowers and sets seed prolifically. Vigorous shoot production makes it a productive choice for growers wanting green or black tea from the same plant. Give it the standard acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil tea camellias require, and expect solid performance across the humid Gulf South. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fairy Tale Eggplant (AAS 2005 Miniature Lavender-White Striped Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost when nights are consistently above 55°F. Harvest fruits at 3–4 inches before they fully mature. Fairy Tale is a Sakata Seed F1 hybrid eggplant that earned All-America Selections recognition in 2005 for its exceptional productivity, compact plant habit, and near-elimination of the bitterness and seedy texture that can make standard large eggplants unpalatable to some cooks. The fruits are distinctively beautiful: elongated-oval, 3–4 inches long, with an eye-catching pattern of alternating lavender-purple and creamy white vertical stripes — a color combination different from any other commonly grown eggplant type. The white striping on mature fruits is genetically stable and does not fade with cooking, making Fairy Tale attractive in stir-fries, roasted vegetable mixes, and fresh preparations where the color contrast remains visible. The key culinary advantage of Fairy Tale over standard large eggplant varieties (Black Beauty, Diamond) is the dramatically lower seed count and virtually absent bitterness: Fairy Tale fruits have fewer, smaller seeds than large types, and the flesh requires no salting or pressing to remove bitterness before cooking. A single established plant can produce 30–50 fruits over a long season in zone 9's warm climate — significantly more than a comparable large-fruited variety — making Fairy Tale an exceptionally productive choice for gardeners who want consistent eggplant supply through summer. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Fairytale Pumpkin
description: Also called Musquee de Provence, this heirloom produces deeply lobed pumpkins that ripen from green to warm chestnut-brown with rich, flavorful flesh favored by cooks. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give the long vines plenty of room to sprawl. Water consistently and side-dress with compost as fruits swell. Let pumpkins ripen fully to their bronze color, then cure in a warm spot to deepen flavor and extend storage. Matures in 105–125 days from seed.

name: Faith Mahonia (Slieve Donard Winter-Flowering Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Faith is a sister seedling of the classic 'Charity', raised at Windsor Great Park from open-pollinated 'Charity' seed and named alongside its sibling 'Hope', leaning closer to Mahonia lomariifolia in habit and foliage than 'Charity' does, with softly colored, fragrant yellow flower spikes held above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage in late fall and winter, followed by tart blue-black berries. Its architectural form and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Faith Seedless Grape (Early Blue Table Grape)
description: Faith is a blue-skinned seedless table grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program, one of a quartet released together with Gratitude, Hope, and Joy for local-market growers. It is the earliest-ripening of the four, typically ready in late July to early August, with semi-crisp flesh and a mild, faintly fruity flavor. Like its siblings, the fruit is non-slipskin with good skin quality and resistance to cracking after rain, and the vine has shown solid winter hardiness and general vine health in Arkansas trials. Because berries soften after picking, Faith performs best in dooryard plantings or short local supply chains rather than for extended storage or shipping. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Falcon Southern Highbush Blueberry (Jumbo Very-Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
description: Falcon is a 2023 University of Florida southern highbush release bred for jumbo-sized, sweet-flavored berries that ripen early in the season, giving Deep South growers an entry into the earliest and most profitable picking window. It performs best under the evergreen production system common to Florida's low-chill growing regions, where leaves are retained through winter rather than defoliated by cold. Plant in raised, sulfur-acidified beds with excellent drainage, and pair with a second early-season southern highbush cultivar to improve pollination and berry size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fall Gold Raspberry
description: 'Fall Gold' is an extra-hardy everbearing yellow raspberry that produces very sweet amber berries on both first- and second-year canes. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil amended with organic matter and keep evenly moist. It bears a summer crop on overwintered canes and a fall crop on new primocanes; leave floricanes standing for two harvests or mow for one large fall picking. Suckers freely, so contain the planting with regular removal of wandering shoots. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Fallglo Mandarin (Early-Season Large Easy-Peel Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Fallglo was bred by USDA researchers in Florida from a cross involving Bower citrus and Temple orange, producing large, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with rich, sweet flavor that ripens notably early in the citrus season, often ready to harvest by early fall well ahead of most other mandarins — the trait that gives the variety its name. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the early ripening window makes Fallglo a good choice for growers wanting to open their mandarin harvest as soon as possible each year. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit size and quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: False Daisy (Bhringraj)
description: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, near a pond edge, rain garden, or regularly irrigated bed; false daisy, known as bhringraj in Ayurvedic and Southeast Asian herbal traditions, is a sprawling, low-growing annual with small white daisy-like flowers, traditionally harvested for its leaves and juice, which are infused into hair oils and used in folk remedies for hair and scalp health, liver support, and minor wound care. It grows as an opportunistic weed of damp ditches, rice paddy margins, and pond edges throughout the warm regions of the world, which translates in the garden to a plant that thrives with regular moisture and spreads readily by both trailing stems that root at the nodes and abundant self-seeding. Harvest leaves and stems as needed through the growing season; the plant regrows quickly after cutting. Because it seeds around freely in consistently damp soil, site it where volunteer seedlings are easy to manage or grow it in a container to keep it contained. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: False Jaboticaba (Blue Grape Tree)
description: Site False Jaboticaba in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil, and keep it out of cold wind since it bruises easily in temperatures much below 40°F even though established plants can shrug off a brief light frost. Native to roadside thickets and forest edges in Costa Rica, Panama, and Venezuela, this slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree carries glossy foliage year-round and produces small, dark purple to nearly black, plum-scented berries about an inch across, distinctly bigger and thicker-skinned than fruit of true jaboticaba (Myrciaria/Plinia cauliflora). The thin, juicy, sweet-tart pulp surrounding one or two large seeds tastes grape-like but can run resinous, and the tough skin and seeds are not eaten, so most growers treat it as a fresh snacking or juicing fruit rather than a dessert-quality selection. A single well-established plant can set a heavy crop of fruit clustered along the branches, and its compact, ornamental habit makes it workable in large containers as well as in the ground for collectors wanting jaboticaba-adjacent species beyond the more common cauliflorous types. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: False Pennyroyal (Rough False Pennyroyal)
description: Direct sow in dry, sandy or rocky, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; false pennyroyal is a small, hairy (hispid — reflecting the species name) annual of dry, sandy, and rocky prairies and open areas across the central US, closely related to American pennyroyal (H. pulegioides). The plant has a similar pungent, camphor-mint aroma when crushed and has been used in similar ways as a mild insect repellent and flavoring herb. The small, lavender-blue, tubular flowers are produced throughout summer and are visited by small native bees. Like American pennyroyal, the plant self-sows freely in appropriate dry, lean, sandy conditions and can be left to naturalize in a dry wildflower or prairie garden. More common in the Great Plains and Midwest than eastern pennyroyal, occupying similar dry, disturbed, sandy-soil habitats. Matures in 45–90 days from seed.

name: False Rosemary (Coastalplain Conradina)
description: Plant in sandy, well-drained, dry, acidic soil in full sun; false rosemary is a stunning native shrublet of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coastal Plain that looks remarkably like culinary rosemary but is a separate genus in the mint family. The needle-like foliage has a pleasant resinous-minty fragrance when crushed, and the plant produces masses of lavender-pink flowers in spring. In its native Florida scrub habitat, it grows on the most droughty, infertile white sand where almost nothing else survives. It is a critically rare and threatened species in the wild due to habitat loss from development. Growing false rosemary in Gulf Coast gardens both provides an ornamental plant suited to the region's sandy soils and supports the conservation of a plant under severe pressure in the wild. Needs excellent drainage above all else — no standing water ever. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: False Sesame (African Sesame, Wild Sesame)
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed directly into warm, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, then thin seedlings as young leaves are harvested. False sesame is a fast-growing annual widely gathered and cultivated across West and Southern Africa's savanna zones as a leafy relish vegetable; its tender, mucilaginous leaves are cooked much like okra to thicken soups and stews and are valued as a nutritious, drought-tolerant green in the dry season. The plant produces small tubular pink to lilac flowers similar to true sesame and its close relative, followed by seed capsules that yield an edible oil in some traditions, though leaf harvest is the primary use. Repeated cutting of the growing tips encourages bushy regrowth and extends the harvest window through the warm season. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Falstaff Apple (English James Grieve x Golden Delicious Apple)
description: Falstaff was bred at England's East Malling Research Station from a cross of James Grieve and Golden Delicious, producing a compact, reliably cropping tree well suited to smaller home gardens. The fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with crisp, juicy flesh and a balanced sweet-sharp flavor milder than Golden Delicious but brighter than most dessert apples. It is a dependable, easy-care variety that tolerates a range of soils and needs relatively little disease management compared with older English heirlooms.
