Harvest when the greenish-yellow skin develops a light orange-red flush and fruit separates easily from the spur. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Falstaff Brussels Sprout (Deep Red-Purple Anthocyanin-Rich F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil; Falstaff needs consistently cool fall temperatures to develop its deepest purple color — color intensifies dramatically after frost; harvest when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Falstaff is the premier purple Brussels sprout for home gardeners and is named for the colorful, exuberant Shakespearean character Sir John Falstaff — the name suggests something robust, larger-than-life, and visually dramatic, which the deep red-purple sprouts certainly are. The intense color comes from very high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments distributed throughout the outer leaves and (to a lesser degree) the interior of each sprout; the color deepens dramatically with cold temperatures, making late-season fall-harvested Falstaff significantly more deeply purple than sprouts harvested in early fall before hard frost. The purple color fades to an unappetizing grayish-green if overcooked in water, but holds better with roasting, steaming, or quick stir-frying — and the raw purple sprouts are spectacularly visual in slaws and salads where the color impact is undiminished. The flavor is equivalent to standard green Brussels sprout varieties: nutty, slightly bitter, sweet — some gardeners find the flavor of purple types slightly milder than green types, possibly because the anthocyanin pigmentation is linked to somewhat lower glucosinolate levels. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Fameuse Apple (Snow Apple, French-Canadian Heirloom with Pure White Flesh)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Fameuse, commonly called the Snow Apple for its strikingly pure white flesh, traces back to French settlers in what is now Quebec in the 1600s, making it one of the oldest apple varieties associated with North American cultivation, and it is widely believed to be a parent of the famous McIntosh. The small to medium fruit has deep red, sometimes nearly crimson skin over snow-white flesh that is tender, juicy, and aromatic with a mild, sweet-tart flavor, best enjoyed fresh rather than cooked, since the delicate flesh breaks down quickly with heat. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, reflecting its origins in the harsh climate of early Quebec, and fruit ripens in fall but does not keep especially long, so it is best used within a couple of months of harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fan-Stil Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Fan-Stil was bred by Fanick Nursery of San Antonio as an improvement on the old LeConte pear, keeping LeConte's low chill requirement (roughly 150–300 hours) while adding markedly stronger fire blight resistance, a major advantage in the humid Gulf Coast growing season. The semi-dwarf, upright tree tops out around 10–15 feet, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards, and it bears bell-shaped, pale yellow fruit blushed red that ripens in late August to September. Unlike many hybrid pears, Fan-Stil is self-fruitful and will set a crop on its own, though yields increase with a nearby cross-pollinator. Watch new growth for fire blight strikes after wet spring weather and prune out any infected shoots well below the visible damage. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fang Feng (Siler Root)
description: Fang Feng is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant Apiaceae grown in northern China for its aromatic taproot, a staple ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries. It produces finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat umbels of small white flowers typical of the carrot family, followed by ribbed seed that loses viability quickly and should be sown fresh. Deep, loose, unobstructed soil is essential for straight root development, and the plant resents heavy clay, waterlogging, or salty soils. Roots are traditionally dug in the second year of growth after the foliage has died back, then dried for storage. Matures in 545–730 days from seed.

name: Fantasia Nectarine (Large-Fruited California Standard Nectarine, Freestone Commercial Nectarine)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Fantasia is self-fertile; thin to 5–6 inches in spring for maximum fruit size; Fantasia ripens mid-to-late season (late July to mid-August in California) producing very large, red to yellow-red blushed freestone nectarines with firm, yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor; outstanding for fresh eating and fruit stands. Fantasia nectarine is one of the most widely planted mid-season nectarine varieties for commercial and home production in California and the warmer western states, developed by Zaiger Genetics and released in the 1970s as part of the wave of nectarine variety improvement that transformed nectarine from a specialty fruit to a mainstream commercial crop in California's San Joaquin Valley. The variety's primary attributes — very large fruit size (among the largest freestone nectarines available), excellent red skin color with bright yellow background, firm flesh for shipping and handling, and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor — made it ideal for the fresh market where visual appeal and size command premium prices. Fantasia consistently produces one of the largest individual fruits of any nectarine variety, with well-colored red-over-yellow skin that is visually very attractive, and the freestone flesh separates cleanly from the pit at full maturity — a practical advantage for home eating and cooking. The variety's moderate chill requirement (400–500 hours) makes it reliable in zone 7–9 climates beyond California, including the Pacific Northwest and some parts of the Southeast. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fantastic Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or temporary cover. Fantastic is a Mexican-race avocado selected for cold hardiness and dependable fruiting, grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists alongside sister selections like Joey and Lila as part of the small pool of avocado cultivars that can be planted in-ground north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium with thin, edible-adjacent skin typical of Mexican-race avocados and rich, high-oil-content flesh with a pronounced anise note in the foliage and fruit. Fruit set improves with a complementary Type A or Type B flowering cultivar planted nearby. Mature, well-established trees can shrug off brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit, though reliable fruiting still depends on avoiding a hard freeze during bloom. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fantasy Seedless Grape (Black Seedless Table Grape)
description: A University of California release, Fantasy Seedless produces large, elongated clusters of sweet, crisp, black-skinned berries popular in warm-summer table grape regions. As a pure vinifera selection it lacks the cold hardiness of American hybrids and performs best where winters stay mild and summers are long and hot. The vine is vigorous, so shoot positioning and cluster thinning are needed to keep berry size and quality consistent across a heavy crop. Growers in marginal zones should provide winter protection or choose a sheltered planting site. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Far North Melon
description: Far North is a compact, extra-early heirloom muskmelon bred specifically for gardeners in short-season and far-northern climates, ripening its small, lightly netted fruit in as little as two months from direct seeding. It trades the larger fruit size and richer sugars of long-season eastern cantaloupes for the reliability of actually finishing before fall frost arrives, making it a practical fallback where standard cantaloupe varieties routinely fail to ripen. Vines stay relatively compact compared with vigorous heirloom types, so they fit reasonably well in smaller garden beds. Today the variety is kept in circulation mainly through small regional seed-preservation growers rather than mainstream catalogs. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Farao Cabbage (Early Tip Burn-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Farao is one of the earliest-maturing fresh-market cabbage hybrids available, forming compact, round, 2-3 lb heads that size up quickly, an advantage for Gulf Coast gardeners racing to finish a spring cabbage crop before summer heat sets in. It is bred for resistance to tip burn, a physiological disorder that browns and damages inner leaves under fluctuating moisture and heat, and holds well in the field for a week or more past maturity without splitting. The mild, tender heads work well fresh in slaw or lightly cooked. Because of its early maturity, Farao is also a good choice for a second, fall planting timed to mature before the first hard freeze. Matures in 62–68 days from transplant.

name: Farkleberry (Sparkleberry, Tree Huckleberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established, requiring no irrigation in the Southeast. Vaccinium arboreum (farkleberry or sparkleberry) is the largest native Vaccinium in the southeastern United States — a multi-stemmed, deciduous to semi-evergreen large shrub or small tree reaching 6–15 feet with smooth, reddish-brown exfoliating bark that is ornamentally attractive year-round. It is native to the dry, acidic soils of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, piedmont, and lower Appalachians, tolerating drought, sandy soils, and poor fertility far better than cultivated highbush blueberries. The small (1/4 inch), dark blue-black berries are technically edible, but are mealy, seedy, and quite astringent when eaten fresh — quite different from cultivated blueberries. They are far better suited to drying (they were used extensively by southeastern Native Americans as a dried fruit), cooking into jams and pies, or fermenting. Birds and wildlife consume the abundant fruit crops enthusiastically. As a garden plant, farkleberry is an underused native with beautiful four-season interest: white urn-shaped flowers in spring, glossy foliage in summer, brilliant red-orange fall color, and attractive bark in winter. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Faroka Hazelnut (Gellatly Hybrid Filbert)
description: Faroka is another of J.U. Gellatly's mid-twentieth-century hybrid hazelnut selections, bred in British Columbia to combine the cold hardiness of American hazelnut with better nut size and quality from European hazelnut parentage. Along with sibling selections such as Bixby and Potomac, it has been used repeatedly as breeding stock in later hybrid hazelnut programs targeting the cold-winter Upper Midwest and eastern United States. Grow as a multi-stemmed shrub in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and plant with a compatible pollenizer since hazelnuts do not self-pollinate reliably. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Farthing Southern Highbush Blueberry (High-Yield Midseason Blueberry)
description: Plant container-grown or dormant bare-root bushes in winter into raised, sulfur-amended beds if native soil is not already strongly acidic, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through summer heat. Farthing is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued by Gulf Coast growers for its exceptionally heavy, reliable yields of medium-large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, well-balanced flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It ripens over a fairly long midseason window, which spreads out the harvest and makes it a strong choice for home orchards wanting an extended picking period. Feed lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and renewal-prune out the oldest wood each winter to sustain the heavy fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fascination Watermelon (Seedless Disease-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Fascination is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, two diseases that can build up quickly in warm, humid Gulf Coast soil. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen of their own, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set. It produces large, crisp, sweet red-fleshed fruit with excellent post-harvest holding quality, staying in good eating condition longer after picking than many other seedless types. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 82–90 days from transplant.

name: Fat Baby Achocha (Slipper Gourd)
description: Fat Baby is a compact, early-fruiting achocha selection with softer spines and smaller, rounder fruit than the typical Cyclanthera brachystachya type, reaching harvestable size in as little as two months from transplanting. Its quicker maturity and gentler spines make it one of the easier achocha types for short-season or cool-summer gardens. Train the twining vine onto netting or a trellis, where it climbs vigorously by tendrils and sets fruit continuously if picked young and often. Slice or stuff the immature, hollow fruit as a mild, crunchy cucumber substitute; older fruit toughens and its black seeds become bitter. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Fatalii Pepper (Yellow Fatalii)
description: Germinate seeds at 85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Fatalii is a Capsicum chinense variety originating in central Africa — most likely from the Central African Republic or surrounding region — that has been grown by chileheads and pepper enthusiasts for decades as an outstanding 'extreme fruity heat' pepper; at 125,000–400,000 SHU it surpasses most habaneros in heat while delivering a distinctive, intensely citrusy, almost lemon-lime fruity aroma that makes it popular in hot sauces and fruity salsas where both extreme heat and complex flavor are desired. The fruits are elongated, pointed, and wrinkled at maturity, ripening to a brilliant golden yellow. Highly productive in warm climates; the plants are vigorous and tall for a Capsicum chinense, often reaching 3–3.5 feet. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Fathead Spanish Lavender (Extra-Large-Headed French Lavender)
description: Fathead earns its name from its unusually large, plump flower cones, noticeably oversized compared with most Spanish lavender cultivars, crowned with showy upright purple bracts above aromatic silvery-green foliage. It flowers heavily from mid-spring into summer and often reblooms if deadheaded promptly after the first flush fades. Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since it shares the family's low tolerance for wet feet, humidity, and heavy clay. Its well-branched, rounded habit and bold flower heads make it a strong container or border-front specimen where its oversized blooms can be appreciated up close. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Fava Bean
description: Sow seeds 2 in deep in cool, moist soil; they germinate well even near freezing and are damaged by summer heat. Pinch out the top few inches of growth once the first pods begin to set to discourage black bean aphids, which congregate on tender new shoots. Harvest young pods when about 3 in long for eating whole, or let them fill out for shelling; seeds toughen quickly once they lighten in color. Support tall varieties with stakes and twine as plants approach flowering. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Favorite Grape (Pierce's-Disease-Tolerant Black Spanish Seedling)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, providing good air circulation to reduce fungal disease pressure. Favorite is a seedling selection of Black Spanish (Lenoir), one of the historic Gulf Coast grape varieties long grown for its exceptional tolerance to Pierce's disease, a bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes within a few years in the warm, humid South. It produces blue-black, juicy berries used for both fresh eating and home winemaking, ripening reliably where Vitis vinifera varieties fail. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and airflow through the canopy. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Feaster Family Heirloom Mustard (Florida Family Mustard Green)
description: This family heirloom was grown and saved by generations of a family in rural Marion County, Florida, with stewardship reportedly reaching back to the Civil War era, before being shared with Seed Savers Exchange. The plant produces smooth green leaves that cook up milder and slightly sweeter than many Southern mustards, making it a gentler entry point for gardeners who find sharper types like Southern Giant Curled too pungent. Its fast maturity and mild flavor place it well alongside collard and turnip greens in a traditional fall Gulf Coast greens patch. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Federle Tomato
description: Federle, also called Federle's Italian Paste, is an heirloom preserved through Seed Savers Exchange that produces unusually long, slender paste fruit up to seven inches, distinct from the more common blocky Roma shape. Indeterminate vines are highly productive and keep setting fruit steadily through the season, so gardeners canning or making salsa get an extended harvest window rather than one heavy flush. The dense, nearly seedless flesh cooks down quickly with little waste, and the deep red color holds well in finished sauce. Grow this variety when you want an open-pollinated, seed-saveable paste tomato with a distinctive elongated shape for home preserving. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Fedora 17 Hemp (Dual-Purpose Fiber and Grain Cultivar)
description: Drill seed about 3/4 inch deep at a dense rate to encourage tall, straight stalks with reduced branching, since crowding improves both fiber quality and lodging resistance; 'Fedora 17' is one of the most widely certified industrial hemp cultivars in Europe and appears on many US state-approved variety lists because its THC content reliably stays under the 0.3% compliance threshold. Being monoecious, every plant in the stand can be left to mature and set seed, simplifying dual-purpose harvest compared with dioecious cultivars that separate male and female plants. Cut stalks for fiber once flowering finishes and the lower leaves begin to yellow, or wait longer for the grain harvest if seed is the primary goal, though delaying reduces fiber quality as stems coarsen. A license from the appropriate state hemp program or the USDA is required before planting, and growers must submit to pre-harvest THC testing in most jurisdictions. Matures in 110–140 days from seed.

name: Feher Ozon Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Heirloom Sweet Paprika)
description: Feher Ozon is a Hungarian heirloom whose name translates roughly to 'white torrent,' referring to the ivory-white color of its immature pods before they ripen through orange to red. Compact, upright plants stay productive under garden conditions and set heavy clusters of thick-walled, tapering pods around five inches long, with a mild, fruity sweetness and essentially no heat. It belongs to the classic family of Hungarian paprika peppers grown specifically to be dried and ground into homemade sweet paprika, though the fresh pods are equally good sliced raw, roasted, or stuffed. Its dwarf, self-supporting habit makes it easier to manage in small gardens than taller Hungarian paprika types. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Feijoa (Pineapple Guava)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; established feijoas tolerate drought but produce better fruit with regular moisture during flowering and fruit development. Acca sellowiana (feijoa or pineapple guava) is a South American evergreen shrub native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and northern Argentina, producing exceptionally ornamental flowers in May — petals of white and crimson with red stamens that are edible and sweet, often harvested from the ground — and unique oval fruits in fall that have an intensely aromatic, tropical, pineapple-guava flavor unlike any other temperate-climate fruit. The silvery-green leaves with white undersides are attractive year-round; the plant is exceptionally cold-hardy for a subtropical fruiting plant, tolerating 12–15°F and making it viable throughout the Gulf Coast, the Southeast, and mild West Coast gardens. Most selections require two plants for cross-pollination, though self-fertile cultivars like 'Coolidge' and 'Pineapple Gem' are available. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Fennel (Common Fennel, Sweet Fennel)
description: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean, full-sun soil; does not transplant well due to taproot — sow in place; in zone 7+, often self-sows prolifically. Foeniculum vulgare (fennel or sweet fennel) is one of the most versatile and widely used culinary herbs in the world — a perennial (often treated as a biennial) Mediterranean herb producing delicate, feathery, bright-green to bronze-purple fronds, hollow stems, and golden-yellow flat-topped flower umbels followed by aromatic oval seeds. The distinctive, sweet-anise, warm-licorice flavor of fennel fronds, seeds, flowers, and the swollen stem base pervades cuisines worldwide: Italian sausage, Provençal bouillabaisse, Indian chai spice, Bengali panch phoron (five-spice), Indian paan, Middle Eastern bread, German sauerkraut, and Scandinavian aquavit all rely on fennel. Florence fennel (var. azoricum) produces the fat, crisp, sweet, anise-flavored stem base eaten as a vegetable across Mediterranean Europe. The dried seeds are one of the most important spices in Italian cuisine and make a classic digestive tea. COMPANION PLANTING CAUTION: Fennel produces allelopathic compounds from its roots that stunt the growth of tomatoes, peppers, kohlrabi, and many other vegetables — plant it in a separate herb bed away from the vegetable garden or at the garden perimeter. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Fenugreek
description: Soak seeds overnight to speed germination, then sow 1/2 in deep in rows and thin to 6 in apart; fenugreek prefers cool conditions and will bolt quickly in summer heat. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Days to maturity listed is for young leaf harvest; allow 3–5 months for seed pods to develop and dry if growing for seed spice. Harvest leaves at any time for use as a slightly bitter herb, and collect seed pods once they turn tan and feel firm. Matures in 20–30 days from seed.

name: Fenugreek Sprouts
description: Fenugreek sprouts are easy to grow indoors and rich in vitamins A, B6, and C along with iron and potassium. Rinse seeds and soak overnight, then drain and rinse two to three times daily in a sprouting jar or tray. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun and harvest in about four to seven days when small shoots appear. Enjoy the mildly bitter, nutty sprouts fresh in salads and sandwiches. Refrigerate after harvest to keep them crisp. Matures in 4–7 days from seed.

name: Fernleaf Dill (Dwarf Dill)
description: Scatter seeds thinly and press in lightly on the soil surface in full sun; Fernleaf is an All-America Selections winner dwarf dill variety that grows to only 18–24 inches (versus 4–5 feet for standard dill) with fine, feathery, dark blue-green foliage. The compact size makes it ideal for container growing, small herb gardens, and raised beds where standard dill would overwhelm its neighbors. It is also notably slower to bolt than standard varieties — where standard dill races to flower within 6 weeks, Fernleaf holds its leafy form for 8–10 weeks before setting flower heads. For zone 9 gardeners, this bolt resistance is particularly valuable since the cool season is short and every extra week of foliage harvest matters. Harvest the feathery leaves ('dill weed') regularly — cutting the tips encourages branching and delays bolting. Dill weed is used fresh in tzatziki, salmon dishes, deviled eggs, potato salad, and dressings; dried dill weed loses much of its fresh flavor. A second sowing in September provides fall dill. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Fernleaf Lavender (Egyptian Lavender, Cut-Leaf Lavender, Warm-Climate Lavender Species)
description: Start seeds indoors or take cuttings; transplant to full sun, very well-drained soil. Cut back lightly after flowering. Fernleaf Lavender (Lavandula multifida), also known as Egyptian Lavender or Cut-Leaf Lavender, is a Mediterranean lavender species native to North Africa and southern Europe that differs from the familiar English lavender (L. angustifolia) in both appearance and adaptability. The most distinctive visual characteristic is the foliage: instead of the narrow, smooth gray-green leaves of English lavender, Fernleaf Lavender has deeply cut, ferny, bipinnate leaves that create a lacy, delicate appearance quite unlike other lavender species. The leaf texture is more reminiscent of carrot foliage than conventional lavender, and the overall plant has a lighter, airier appearance that makes it attractive as a foliage plant even when not in bloom. The flowers are produced on branched spikes (unlike the simple single spikes of English lavender) in the characteristic lavender-purple color, and the plant blooms repeatedly through the warm season when deadheaded regularly. The fragrance is lighter and less intense than English lavender — closer to rosemary than the heavy camphor-lavender scent of L. angustifolia — which some gardeners prefer as a more delicate aromatic quality. For zone 9 gardeners, Fernleaf Lavender fills an important niche: it provides the lavender aesthetic (gray-green aromatic foliage, purple flowers, bee attraction) in a form that tolerates warm summers and mild winters better than the standard English lavender types that often decline in zone 9's summer heat and humidity. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Fernor Walnut (French Late-Leafing Hybrid Persian Walnut)
description: Fernor is a French walnut selection bred from a Franquette-line cross for late leafing, heavy precocious bearing, and good disease tolerance suited to modern orchard spacing. Its late spring growth start helps flowers escape frost while its lateral-bearing habit, unusual among traditional French cultivars, lets trees crop earlier and more densely than old standards like Franquette. Grow in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and expect a heavier, more consistent nut set than older late-leafing French cultivars once trees reach bearing age. Matures in 1460–3285 days from transplant.

name: Ferris Wheel Tomato (1894 Salzer's Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared soil once all frost risk has passed. Ferris Wheel is an 1894 commercial release from the John A. Salzer Seed Company of Wisconsin that nearly vanished before being rediscovered and reintroduced by heirloom tomato researchers in the 1990s. It produces large, slightly flattened pink beefsteak fruit with colorful shoulders that blush attractively as they ripen, and the flesh is juicy, mild, and slightly sweet. Provide sturdy staking for the tall, regular-leaf indeterminate vines, which can exceed six feet over a 90-day season. Matures in 85–90 days from transplant.

name: Festival Strawberry
description: Plant dormant crowns or plugs with crown at soil level in well-drained, raised beds or hills in full sun; Festival is a mid-to-late-season short-day strawberry released cooperatively by the USDA and University of Florida in 2000 that has become the dominant commercial strawberry variety in Florida's Hillsborough County, the largest strawberry-producing county east of the Mississippi River. Festival was developed to balance production timing with Chandler and extend the Gulf Coast season; it begins producing 2–3 weeks after Sweet Charlie and Chandler and continues fruiting longer into the spring. Berries are medium to large, very attractive, firm, bright red, with good sweet flavor and an excellent fresh appearance that makes them the standard for appearance at retail and export markets. Festival's disease resistance to anthracnose (Colletotrichum acutatum) is significantly better than Chandler, making it more reliable in warm, humid conditions where anthracnose crown rot can devastate the crop. An excellent choice for Gulf Coast home gardens and commercial growers where the extended season and disease tolerance are priorities. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Feverfew
description: Seeds are tiny and require light for germination — press them gently onto moist starting mix without covering. Once established, plants are quite drought-tolerant and spread readily by self-seeding. Shear plants back by half after flowering to maintain a tidy mound and encourage fresh foliage. The leaves are the medicinal part; harvest fresh leaves for tea or tincture — wear gloves as some people experience skin irritation from the foliage. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Few-Flowered Garlic
description: Set small bulbs or bulbil offsets 2 inches deep in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in early autumn, where they will naturalize alongside bluebells and other spring ephemerals. Because flower heads produce clusters of tiny bulbils instead of true seed, colonies spread quickly and can become assertive groundcover in favorable shaded sites, so site it where spreading is welcome. The mild, garlicky strap-shaped leaves emerge in late winter and are harvested young for salads or as a ramp substitute before the plant goes dormant in summer. Give it consistent moisture through spring growth and let beds go dry once foliage yellows. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: FHIA-03 Banana
description: FHIA-03 is a tetraploid hybrid banana bred by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf spot and Panama disease, the pathogens that most limit backyard banana growing in the humid Gulf South. Unlike its sibling Goldfinger (FHIA-01), FHIA-03 produces a starchier, dual-purpose fruit that can be eaten cooked when green or sweet when fully ripe, giving gardeners flexibility similar to a plantain. The plant regrows readily from the rhizome after a freeze knocks back the pseudostem, making it a practical choice where winter dieback is expected most years. Give it heavy summer feeding and constant soil moisture to reach fruiting size within a single warm season. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: FHIA-18 Banana (Disease-Resistant Apple-Flavored Hybrid)
description: FHIA-18 is a hybrid banana bred by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research (FHIA), derived in part from the cold- and wind-tolerant Dwarf Brazilian cultivar, and selected for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf spot and Fusarium wilt (Panama disease). The fruit ripens naturally to yellow with a sweet, mild apple-like flavor reminiscent of its Gros Michel-type ancestry, but with a softer texture. It is a semi-dwarf, productive, disease-tolerant option for gardeners in humid Gulf South climates where Sigatoka pressure limits older commercial cultivars. Give it full sun, rich soil, and heavy summer feeding and irrigation to support a full bunch within one growing season. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Field Corn (Dent Corn)
description: Field corn (dent corn) is the primary grain corn of American agriculture and the most versatile of all corn types for the home garden and homestead — used as dried grain, cornmeal, animal feed, and the raw material for bourbon whiskey, the kernel's characteristic 'dent' or indentation forms as the starchy center dries and shrinks. For home gardeners, dent corn varieties like 'Hopi Blue', 'Reid's Yellow Dent', or 'Bloody Butcher' are grown to full dry-grain maturity (husks dry and papery, kernels hard), then shelled and ground in a stone mill for the most flavorful, nutritious cornmeal and polenta. In the Gulf South, excellent heat-tolerant open-pollinated varieties can be grown spring and fall, with adequate irrigation during tasseling and pollination being critical for good ear fill; dent corn has been a cornerstone of Gulf Coast homestead gardens since colonial times. Harvest when kernels are completely dry and hard — typically 90–120 days from planting — then shell and store in cool, dry conditions for grinding throughout the year. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Field Horsetail (Common Horsetail, Scouring Rush Cousin)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, sandy, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun; field horsetail (Equisetum arvense) is an ancient, primitive, spore-bearing plant (a living fossil) in the same lineage as 300-million-year-old coal forest horsetails, identifiable by its distinctive jointed, whorled, branched stems. The dried sterile stems are used medicinally as one of the highest-silica herbal remedies available — traditional use includes strengthening nails, hair, and connective tissue; teas made from dried stems are used for urinary tract support and bone health. Young fertile fronds (the brown, non-branched spring shoots) were historically eaten by Native American peoples. Caution: horsetail contains thiaminase and can cause thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in livestock and humans if consumed in large quantities; use medicinally in moderate amounts only. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Fiero Radicchio
description: This elongated, torpedo-shaped F1 hybrid resembles the classic heirloom Treviso radicchios but matures in a much shorter 50 to 60 days and colors reliably without the traditional post-cutback forcing that old-style Tardivo types need. Leaves are deep wine-red with prominent white midribs, held in slim, upright, self-blanching heads that stay tender as they size up. 'Fiero' tolerates a wider sowing window than most chicories, performing well from both an early sowing and a late-summer sowing for fall harvest. Its quicker cycle and forgiving nature make it a practical way to get Treviso's elegant shape without the long season or hands-on forcing older varieties require. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Fiery Costus (Insulin Plant, Spiral Ginger)
description: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; fiery costus is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Fleshy, spirally arranged leaves wind distinctively up thick, jointed stems in the characteristic 'spiral ginger' habit, with small yellow-orange flowers emerging from cone-like bracts at the stem tips through the warm season. Native to Mexico and Central America, its fresh leaves are chewed or brewed as a folk remedy for blood sugar management in traditional Latin American and South Asian herbal medicine, earning it the common name insulin plant, though this use has not been established by rigorous clinical evidence and it should not replace medical treatment. Grown primarily for its striking spiraled foliage in a humid, shaded container or greenhouse setting, it propagates readily from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist soil. Matures in 120–200 days from transplant.

name: Fiesta Apple (Red Pippin, English Cox's Orange Pippin Successor)
description: Fiesta, also marketed as Red Pippin, was bred at England's East Malling Research Station from a cross of Cox's Orange Pippin and Idared, aiming to capture some of Cox's celebrated complex flavor in a hardier, more dependable tree. The red-flushed fruit ripens in mid-to-late fall with crisp, juicy flesh and a balanced sweet-sharp flavor milder than Golden Delicious but brighter than most dessert apples. It bears more consistently and resists disease better than Cox's Orange Pippin, making it a practical choice for home gardeners who want Cox-like flavor without Cox's finicky reputation. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fiesta White Sapote
description: Selected in Yorba Linda, California in 1973, Fiesta is valued more for dependable, heavy annual cropping than for exceptional size, since its fruit runs noticeably smaller than most other white sapote cultivars at only one to two inches across. It ripens very late in the season, which makes it a useful companion to earlier-fruiting selections like Chestnut or McDill for stretching out the sapote harvest. The tree can set fruit on its own, but planting a second white sapote cultivar nearby generally improves yield and fruit quality. Give it full sun, wind shelter, and well-drained soil, and allow fruit to soften at room temperature after picking before eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fife Creek Cowhorn Okra
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, soaking seed overnight to speed germination, then thin seedlings to allow room for these towering plants to spread. Harvest curved pods every day or two while young and tender, since they toughen quickly once mature. Fife Creek Cowhorn is a Southern heirloom known for its exceptionally tall growth, often reaching well over six feet, and its long, curved, rib-free pods reminiscent of a cow's horn. Gardeners who grow it out for seed appreciate its reliable productivity in hot, humid summers. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Fig
description: Common figs (the type grown in most gardens) are parthenocarpic and self-fertile — no pollinator or fig wasp is needed. In zones 6–7 protect the trunk and lower branches over winter by wrapping with burlap or mounding mulch; established roots often resprout even after top-kill. Figs bear two crops on some cultivars: a small breba crop on old wood in early summer and a main crop on new growth in late summer. Harvest when the neck droops, the skin splits slightly, and the fruit is soft and fragrant; a drop of syrup at the eye signals perfect ripeness. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Figleaf Gourd (Malabar Gourd)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis; figleaf gourd is one of the most unusual cucurbits in cultivation — an Andean species producing large, distinctive fruits with white-striped, dark-green skin resembling a watermelon but with the elongated form of a large pumpkin, reaching 10–15 pounds. The most remarkable characteristic of this species is the extraordinary keeping quality of its mature fruits: when harvested fully mature, figleaf gourds can keep at room temperature for five or more years without refrigeration, decomposition, or significant quality loss — a storage capability unique among cucurbits and practical in the Andean communities of origin where refrigeration was unavailable. The white, fibrous flesh is used in traditional South American cooking — shredded in sweets, soups, and as a pasta filling — and has an interesting, neutral flavor. The seeds are edible roasted. The vine is large and requires substantial support. More cold-tolerant than many tropical cucurbits and thrives across zones 8–11 where seasons are long. A fascinating and genuinely different crop for the vegetable garden, particularly in Gulf Coast climates. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Fignomenal Fig
description: Fignomenal is a true dwarf fig reaching only 2 to 3 feet, making it ideal for containers and small patios while still producing full-sized sweet fruit. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently, easing off as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor. Its compact size makes it easy to move indoors to a cool bright space for winter in colder regions. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove weak wood. Feed during the growing season for steady production of its self-fertile crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Figwort
description: Because related Scrophularia species contain cardioactive compounds, internal use should be approached cautiously and avoided by anyone with heart conditions without professional guidance. Sow or divide established clumps into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring, since this woodland-edge perennial prefers damp ground similar to a stream bank or ditch. The whole flowering plant, despite its strong odor, is traditionally made into a poultice or wash applied topically for minor skin irritations and historically taken to support lymphatic health. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Filbert (Giant Filbert, Lambert's Filbert)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing at least 10–15 feet from other plants to allow for the naturally wide-spreading form; filbert (Corylus maxima) is the large-fruited European hazelnut, distinguished from Corylus avellana by its longer tubular husk that completely encloses the nut, and is the parent of many named cultivars including 'Butler', 'Ennis', and 'Tonda di Giffoni'. A multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that bears pollen-heavy catkins in late winter while fully dormant — one of the earliest signs of spring — with small red pistillate flowers that require wind cross-pollination from a second genetically distinct plant to set nuts. Harvest when husks begin to brown and nuts release easily; dry in a single layer before storage to prevent mold. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Filderkraut Cabbage
description: Filderkraut is a traditional German conical cabbage from the Filder plain near Stuttgart, prized for tall, dense, pointed heads that can weigh several pounds each. The tapered shape and tightly wrapped leaves pack unusually well for shredding, making this heirloom the historic variety of choice for large-batch sauerkraut production. It tends to tolerate warm spells better than round-headed cabbages while still standing up to fall frost, giving it a wide harvest window. Grow Filderkraut where a heavy-yielding, storage-friendly cabbage with genuine heirloom pedigree is wanted for preserving. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Filius Blue Ornamental Pepper (Color-Changing Compact Chile)
description: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings into pots or beds once nights are warm, since this compact annuum is often grown as a patio or container ornamental. Keep it evenly watered and in full sun for the heaviest, most colorful fruit display. Filius Blue is bred for its dense, upright habit and small purple-flushed leaves, with round fruits that ripen through purple and cream shades before finishing bright red, making the plant look multicolored all at once. The pods carry real heat and are edible, though the plant is grown mainly for its ornamental fruit color. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Finger Lime (Caviar Lime)
description: Finger lime is an Australian rainforest citrus producing cylindrical finger-length fruits filled with spherical pulp vesicles that burst on the palate like caviar — highly prized in fine dining as a garnish. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings, which are slow to fruit and thorny; grafted plants begin fruiting in 2–3 years and are more manageable in size. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator; it performs well in containers and espalier forms. Fruit ripens in late autumn through winter; harvest when the skin (green, yellow, red, or black depending on variety) is fully colored and the fruit releases easily with gentle pressure — avoid overripening, as the vesicles lose their pop. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Finger Millet (Ragi)
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 6–9 in when plants are 4 in tall; finger millet produces distinctive finger-like seed head rays that are diagnostic and easy to recognize at harvest. The seed turns dark reddish-brown when ripe and the heads curve inward; harvest before birds strip them by cutting the heads at early dough stage and finishing the dry-down on a tarp in the sun. Rub heads between palms to release the very small seeds, which need no hulling; grind into flour (ragi flour) or soak and ferment for traditional beverages. The crop is notably high in calcium and iron compared to other small grains. Matures in 90–130 days from seed.

name: Fingerroot
description: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fingerroot (Chinese ginger, Chinese keys, krachai) is a Southeast Asian tropical ginger widely used in Thai, Cambodian, and Indonesian cuisine, where the elongated, finger-like rhizomes (resembling a bunch of small, yellowish fingers, hence the common name) have a distinctive, slightly bitter-pungent, gingery-citrus flavor and aroma used to season curries, seafood dishes, stir-fries, and medicinal preparations. The rhizomes are harvested 4–6 months after planting, with a cluster of 6–12 finger-like secondary rhizomes branching from the central rhizome. The above-ground plant produces a compact rosette of attractive, oval, dark-green leaves with ornamental silver and green feathering similar to Kaempferia, and periodically produces small, pale-pink to white, orchid-like flowers at the leaf base. Fingerroot is medicinally important in traditional Southeast Asian medicine and is the subject of modern pharmaceutical research for its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties. More shade-tolerant than most culinary gingers. In zone 10–12 it is a year-round perennial; elsewhere lift and store the rhizomes in winter. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Fino de Jete Cherimoya (Self-Fertile Spanish Coastal Cherimoya)
description: Fino de Jete was selected in the late 19th century in the town of Jete along Spain's Rio Verde valley and today accounts for the great majority of cherimoyas grown on the Costa Tropical of Granada and Málaga, a region protected under Spain's Denominación de Origen system. Its light green, only lightly indented skin and rich, sweet-tart flesh carry tropical notes of pineapple, banana, and strawberry, and fruit typically weighs from about 200 to 500 grams. Growers particularly value it for being rustic, high-yielding, and unusually self-fertile compared with most cherimoya cultivars, which typically require laborious hand pollination to set a worthwhile crop — a real time-saver for home growers. It also tends to ripen earlier and tolerate cooler conditions somewhat better than other cherimoya selections, though Gulf Coast humidity remains a bigger obstacle to this species than cold, so a well-ventilated, well-drained site is essential to limit anthracnose and fruit rot. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fino Verde Basil
description: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Fino Verde is the classic Italian Greek-style dwarf basil used throughout southern Italy as a border herb, pot herb, and fresh seasoning for Caprese and Neapolitan-style dishes — producing a dense, compact mound of tiny, intensely fragrant leaves with a strong, clove-spicy basil aroma more concentrated than large-leafed sweet basil varieties. The extremely small, oval leaves (roughly the size of a fingernail) are traditionally used whole, directly stripped from the stem, and scattered over sliced tomatoes and mozzarella, into pasta, or onto pizza immediately before serving — the tiny leaf size means no chopping is needed. Fino Verde is the correct basil for traditional Neapolitan pizza making, where the small leaves are placed on the cooked pizza whole. The naturally compact, self-branching mound habit needs minimal pinching and forms a tidy, ornamental rounded shape in containers or along garden borders. The flavor intensity is noticeably higher per leaf than in large-leafed sweet basil. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Fino Verde Basil
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Fino Verde is the classic compact Ligurian basil from the Italian Riviera, where the small, dark green, rounded leaves are the traditional variety used in authentic Genovese pesto. The tiny leaves (less than 1 inch) are more aromatic per unit area than large-leafed varieties — the essential oil concentration is higher in the smaller leaves — and the resulting pesto has a brighter, more complex flavor than pesto made with Genovese or large-leaf types. The compact, tidy, 12–18 inch plants are ideal for container growing and rarely need staking. Regular pinching maintains bushiness and dramatically delays bolting in summer heat. In zone 9 the small leaf size also makes it more heat-tolerant than large-leafed types in peak summer. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Fino Verde Basil
description: Sow indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the seed and keeping flats around 75F. This tiny-leaved Italian basil naturally forms a dense round bush without much pinching. Transplant after all danger of frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water evenly and harvest by clipping whole stems just above a leaf pair to keep growth bushy. Remove flower buds promptly to extend the productive leafy season. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Finocchio Fennel
description: Florence fennel forms a swollen, anise-flavored bulb that can be eaten raw, sauteed, or added to soups and pasta, while its feathery leaves garnish fish. Direct sow into rich, moist soil since transplanting can stress plants and cause premature bolting. Keep the bed evenly watered and blanch the bulb by mounding soil around its base as it swells. Grow it as a cool-season crop, timing plantings for spring or fall to avoid the summer heat that pushes it to seed. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Fire Cherry
description: Fire Cherry — also called Pin Cherry — is a fast-growing native pioneer tree of disturbed forest openings, clear-cuts, burned areas, and roadsides across the northern United States and Canada, where it is usually the first woody species to colonize forest gaps and recently disturbed sites, earning the name 'fire cherry' for its rapid colonization of burned forest. The clusters of bright red, pea-sized cherries ripen in summer and are among the most important late-season wildlife fruits in northern forest ecosystems, heavily consumed by American robins, cedar waxwings, grosbeaks, ruffed grouse, bears, and deer during the late summer fattening period before winter. Short-lived by nature — typically 15–30 years in the wild — Fire Cherry grows extremely fast for a native cherry, reaching 20 feet in just a few years and serving as a pioneer nurse species that modifies the site for longer-lived forest trees to follow. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Fire Cherry thrives in open, disturbed conditions and makes an excellent fast-growing wildlife planting for northern gardens, fields, and woodland restoration projects. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fire Crystal Persimmon (Compact Self-Fertile Asian Persimmon)
description: Fire Crystal is an Asian persimmon selected near Xi'an in central China and prized in cultivation for its tidy, tight growth habit compared to other kaki cultivars, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards. It bears abundant crops of bright orange fruit that must soften fully before eating; once ripe, the flesh is very sweet with a smooth, custardy texture. The tree reaches 12-15 feet with regular pruning, or up to 20 feet if left unpruned, and carries large, glossy leaves that turn vivid colors in fall before dropping to reveal the ripening fruit. Fire Crystal is self-fertile and does not need a second tree for pollination, is hardy to at least 0°F once dormant, and ripens its crop late in the season from late October into November. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fire N Ice Radish
description: An improved French Breakfast-type radish bred for a striking two-tone root: bright scarlet shoulders fading cleanly to white at the tip. The elongated roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even as they size up, resisting the pithiness that hits many spring radishes in warm soil. Direct-sow in cool weather and harvest young for the best color contrast and snap; excellent sliced raw for its visual appeal on a relish tray. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: First Lady Tomato (Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicing Tomato, Classic Backyard Producer)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red and gives to slight pressure. First Lady Tomato is an F1 hybrid indeterminate slicing tomato developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds (now Bayer Vegetable Seeds) with a comprehensive disease resistance package that has made it one of the most reliably productive backyard tomato varieties in the humid southeastern United States. The 'VFFNTAs' resistance package (Verticillium wilt, two races of Fusarium wilt, Nematodes, Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Alternaria) addresses virtually every major soil-borne and airborne pathogen that limits tomato production in the Gulf South — in humid zone 9 conditions where tomato plants commonly succumb to one or more of these diseases before the season ends, First Lady's resistance allows plants to remain productive through the summer. The variety's profile — medium-sized (8–10 oz) red tomatoes on vigorous indeterminate plants with the comprehensive disease package — represents a classic template for southeastern home garden tomato production that prioritizes plant health and extended production over extreme fruit size or complex flavor. First Lady was marketed and sold through retail garden center channels for decades and became one of the most recognized tomato variety names in southeastern garden retail, appearing consistently on transplant packs in spring garden center displays across the Gulf South. For zone 9 gardeners dealing with nematode pressure (very common in sandy Gulf Coast soils) or Fusarium wilt (endemic in soils with tomato production history), First Lady's 'N' and 'F' resistances provide practical protection that keeps plants alive and producing when susceptible varieties decline. Matures in 66–75 days from transplant.

name: First Prize Pumpkin (F1 Giant Pumpkin Hybrid)
description: Start indoors 2-3 weeks before last frost or direct sow into hills of heavily composted soil, allowing at least 15-20 feet of space per plant since a single vine can spread over several hundred square feet. First Prize is a hybrid giant pumpkin bred for competitive growers, capable of producing fruit up to 300 pounds under intensive management, though most home-garden fruit lands well under that with less aggressive pruning and feeding. For maximum size, growers typically remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine and pinch side shoots to direct the plant's energy into the remaining pumpkins. Heavy, consistent watering and monthly feeding through the growing season are essential; harvest before hard frost once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry. Matures in 120–130 days from seed.

name: Fish Mint
description: Plant rooted divisions in moist to boggy soil in spring, ideally in a sunken container to curb its aggressive rhizomes. This Southeast Asian herb carries a distinctive tangy, fishy-citrus aroma used raw in Vietnamese and Chinese cooking. It thrives in partial shade with constant moisture and even tolerates shallow standing water. Cut back runaway runners to keep it from overtaking a bed. Harvest young leaves and tender shoots through the growing season, and mulch crowns in colder zones. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Fish Pepper (African American Heirloom Striped Hot Pepper with Variegated Foliage)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Fish Pepper is an African American heirloom pepper with a unique history — the variety was maintained in the Black community of Baltimore and the Chesapeake Bay region through the 19th and early 20th centuries, where the unripe green-striped fruits were used to season fish and shellfish dishes without the red coloring that would be visible in pale-sauced seafood preparations. Rediscovered by artist and food historian William Woys Weaver through Seed Savers Exchange, Fish Pepper is now recognized as one of the most historically significant African American food heritage vegetables. The ornamental impact is extraordinary: the plant produces dramatically variegated, cream-and-dark-green streaked foliage unlike any other pepper variety, and the immature fruits are striped in cream and pale green, ripening through orange-and-cream striped stages to solid deep red at full maturity. The range of stripe patterns and color stages at different ripeness levels creates a constantly changing visual display. The heat level is medium-hot (comparable to cayenne, 30,000–50,000 SHU) — appropriate for seasoning fish sauces, seafood dishes, and hot sauces. The ornamental quality of both foliage and fruit at all stages makes Fish Pepper an outstanding choice for kitchen garden beds and container growing on patios. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Five Color Silverbeet Swiss Chard
description: This colorful chard mix produces stems and veins in shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white on tender, nutritious leaves. Enjoy baby greens in as little as 20 days or let leaves mature for cooking. It is as ornamental as it is edible and looks at home in vegetable beds, flower borders, and containers. Sow directly and thin seedlings, since each seed is a cluster. Harvest outer leaves regularly and it will keep producing into fall. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Five Flavor Berry (Schisandra)
description: Schisandra chinensis is a vigorous deciduous twining vine native to northeastern China and Russia, bearing pendant clusters of small, brilliant red berries in late summer whose juice is famously described as simultaneously sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent — hence the common name wu wei zi ('five flavor fruit'). The plant is predominantly dioecious, so plant at least one male and one female vine for fruit production, though some cultivars bear perfect flowers. Train on a trellis, pergola, or fence with afternoon shade; the vine prefers cool, moist, slightly acidic woodland conditions. Prune to control size after fruiting; berries are used medicinally and in herbal preparations worldwide. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Five-Leaved Bramble (Strawberryleaf Raspberry)
description: Grow as a low trailing groundcover in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil under dense conifer or mixed forest shade, replicating its native old-growth Pacific Northwest habitat. Thin trailing stems root at the nodes and spread slowly across mossy duff, bearing small three-to-five-lobed strawberry-like leaves. Solitary white flowers give way to small raspberry-red aggregate fruits prized by foragers but rarely produced in cultivation outside cool, humid coastal climates. Avoid heat, drought, and disturbed or compacted soil, which the species will not tolerate. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Flageolet Bean (French Haricot Chevrier)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; flageolet is harvested at the shell bean stage — when pods are plump and seeds are well-developed but still pale green, before the pods begin to yellow and dry. Flageolet (from the Latin 'flagellum' referring to the flute or pipe shape) is a uniquely French bean variety that occupies the role of the 'shell bean' par excellence in French cuisine — it is neither a fresh snap bean nor a fully dried bean, but is harvested at the intermediate shell-bean stage when the kidney-shaped, pale green to white seeds have developed fully in size and shape but retain their characteristic pale green color and fresh, delicate flavor. The distinctive color persists through cooking when properly prepared (not overcooked), making the finished beans a beautiful pale sage green on the plate — dramatically different from the drab gray-white of common dried beans. Flageolet is most famously the traditional accompaniment to gigot d'agneau (roast leg of lamb) in classic French cuisine, where the delicate flavor of the beans perfectly complements the rich lamb; it is also an important ingredient in traditional cassoulet and flageolets au gratin. Seeds can also be allowed to dry fully for storage and reconstituted, though the characteristic green color is then lost. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Flakkee Carrot
description: Named for the Flakkee polder region of Zeeland in the Netherlands, this sturdy Dutch heirloom produces broad-shouldered, blunt-tapered roots up to 8-9 inches long with strong tops that hold up well for bunching. It is a true maincrop storage carrot, best sown from mid-spring through early summer for a fall harvest that keeps exceptionally well in a root cellar or clamp. Flakkee's productivity and keeping ability made it foundational breeding stock behind many of today's Imperator and Autumn King-type carrots. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Flambeau Chilean Guava (Variegated Ornamental-Fruiting Ugni)
description: Flambeau is a variegated sport of Chilean guava grown as much for its ornamental foliage as its fruit, with cream, green, and soft pink leaf coloring that stands out year-round in a border or container. It produces the same small, aromatic, red berries with a strawberry-vanilla flavor as the species, though typically in lighter quantity than green-leaved selections since variegated growth is somewhat less vigorous. It ripens earlier in the season than many Chilean guava plantings, extending the harvest window when grown alongside standard green forms. Give it a sheltered spot in partial shade to full sun and protect it from hard frost, since variegated foliage is generally less cold tolerant than the straight species. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flame Grapefruit (Seedless Deep-Red Texas Grapefruit)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected and released by Texas A&M's citrus breeding program in 1987 from the Rio Red lineage, Flame produces medium-large, seedless fruit with intensely red-pigmented flesh and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. It is one of the reddest-fleshed grapefruit cultivars commercially grown and holds its color reliably even in warmer winters that can wash out the blush in older red grapefruit types. Fruit matures from late fall through winter and holds well on the tree, allowing a long, flexible harvest window. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Flame Red Seedless Grape
description: Flame Red Seedless is a vigorous grape producing sweet, juicy, ruby-red seedless berries in large clusters. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis or arbor to support the heavy vining growth. Train a permanent trunk and cordons the first years, then prune hard every dormant season to a few productive spurs or canes, as grapes fruit on the current year's growth. Water steadily while fruit swells but reduce moisture as harvest approaches for sweeter grapes. Good air circulation helps prevent mildew. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flame Seedless Grape
description: Released by the USDA in 1973, Flame Seedless is the most widely planted red seedless grape in the United States, valued for crisp, round, bright-red berries with a sweet, mildly fruity flavor on medium, well-filled clusters that ripen mid-season. Vines are vigorous and productive, and thinning clusters and berries early in the season improves size and air circulation. It performs best with a long, hot growing season and reliably colors well even in warm-night climates where many red grapes struggle to develop color. Prune to a permanent cordon system in dormancy and renew fruiting spurs each winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flame Star Cauliflower (Heat-Tolerant Orange Cauliflower)
description: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Flame Star produces smooth, well-domed heads in a vivid, natural, sunny orange, colored throughout the curd (not just the surface) by a higher-than-normal beta-carotene content, so the color holds through cooking rather than fading like some orange cauliflower selections. It is notably more heat tolerant during head formation than white cauliflower varieties, making it a more forgiving choice for a Gulf South spring crop that runs into early-summer warmth before harvest. Blanching is unnecessary since sun exposure does not bleach or damage the orange curd the way it can discolor white types. Harvest heads while curds are still tight and firm, before the individual florets begin to separate and loosen. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Flame Tokay Grape (Historic Lodi Red Table Grape)
description: Flame Tokay, usually sold simply as Tokay, is the historic red-skinned table grape that made Lodi, California the self-proclaimed 'Tokay Capital of the World' for much of the twentieth century, complete with an annual Tokay harvest festival once the region's signature civic event. The large, oval, crimson-pink berries form loose, well-filled clusters with crisp, mild, sweet flesh and substantial seeds, eaten fresh off the vine and once shipped nationwide as a fall specialty grape before seedless varieties reshaped the table-grape market. Vines are vigorous and productive but need a long, hot growing season to fully color the thick-skinned berries, and the loose cluster habit helps reduce bunch rot in years with late-season moisture compared with tighter-clustered varieties. Train to a permanent cordon system and prune hard each winter, thinning crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size, and harvest by taste rather than color alone since Tokay can look ripe before its sugar fully develops. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flaming Flare Pepper (Ornamental-Edible Color-Changing Pepper)
description: Transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed, growing it as either a landscape edging plant or a container specimen. Flaming Flare is an All-America Selections winner grown as much for its upright, torch-like clusters of small fruit that shift from purple to yellow to orange to red as it matures as for its edible use, giving a single compact plant several color stages at once. The fruit carries mild-to-moderate heat and can be harvested for cooking at any color stage, making the plant genuinely dual-purpose in the garden. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Flamingo Chinese Toon (Pink Spring Shoot Toona)
description: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun. Keep the root zone evenly moist while the tree establishes, and prune hard each late winter to keep the plant at a manageable shrubby size that resprouts with an even heavier flush of the prized pink shoots. The blush-colored young leaves and shoot tips share the same onion-garlic, slightly resinous flavor as the green-leaved species and are harvested the same way, stir-fried or folded into egg dishes while still tender. Because the pink coloring is most vivid in filtered light, 'Flamingo' doubles as a striking foliage accent for a partly shaded edible garden bed. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Flamingo Water Celery (Variegated Japanese Parsley)
description: 'Flamingo' is a compact, boldly variegated sport of water celery, its narrow leaves splashed in pink, cream, and green rather than the plain green of the wild species, making it a dual-purpose plant for the edge of a shaded pond or rain garden bed. The tender young stems and leaves carry the same crisp, mild parsley-celery flavor used fresh in Korean and Japanese cooking and can be snipped regularly for salads, garnishes, and cold noodle dishes. Because the color is brightest in cooler weather and with some direct morning sun, site it where it gets a few hours of light before afternoon shade takes over in a hot Gulf Coast summer. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to maintain vigorous color and prevent the planting from reverting toward plain green foliage. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Flanders Fig
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the more cold-hardy fig cultivars available, reliably resprouting from the roots after winters that kill back the top growth of less hardy varieties. Flanders is an old Belgian fig cultivar long grown in home gardens and small orchards for its dependable production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber flesh and good flavor, and for its resilience in marginal fig-growing climates where winter cold is a limiting factor. It typically produces a modest breba (early summer) crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and the fruit holds reasonably well against splitting in humid weather. Its cold tolerance makes it a valuable choice for gardeners at the northern edge of the fig range, or in a Gulf South garden where an occasional hard freeze is a risk, zone 6–10. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Flash Collards (Fast-Maturing Tender Smooth-Leaf Collard Hybrid)
description: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Flash is a fast-maturing collard hybrid reaching harvest in only 55–65 days from sowing — significantly faster than traditional open-pollinated collard varieties (70–90 days), making Flash particularly valuable for late-season zone 9 plantings where the window for establishing slow-maturing varieties has closed. The smooth, dark-green leaves are more tender and less coarse than the thick leaves of older collard varieties — the faster maturity corresponds with a younger, more tender leaf stage at harvest, making Flash better suited to raw preparations and quick sautés where tenderness is important. Flash has the same excellent cold-hardiness as other collards — exposure to light frost sweetens the leaves by converting starches to sugars, improving flavor quality through the Gulf South winter. As a hybrid variety, Flash cannot be saved for seed but produces reliable, vigorous, uniform plants each season from purchased seed. The faster maturity also allows two consecutive collard plantings within a Gulf South fall season — a first planting in mid-August for October–November harvest and a second planting in late September for December–January harvest. Excellent disease tolerance reduces the need for preventive fungicide applications in the humid Gulf South fall garden. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Flashy Trout Back Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Flashy Trout Back (Forellen or Forellenschluss variant) is an Austrian heirloom romaine-type lettuce producing upright, semi-cos heads with large, spoon-shaped, bright green leaves heavily spotted with wine-red to maroon splashes and streaks — the pattern resembles the speckled back of a brown trout, giving the lettuce its evocative name. The combination of romaine structure (crisp, upright leaves with a prominent midrib) with the unique spotted coloring makes Flashy Trout Back one of the most visually distinctive lettuces for mixed plantings and specialty salad mixes. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — typical romaine quality without bitterness. The Austrian origin indicates good cold hardiness and a slow-to-bolt character that extends the harvest window in zone 9's warm springs. The dramatic spotted pattern on each leaf makes every head unique and immediately recognizable in market displays; it is one of the most frequently photographed heirloom lettuce varieties. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Flat of Italy Cipollini Onion
description: This Italian heirloom, grown since the late 1800s, forms wine-colored, flattened globes about 1 inch tall and 2 to 3 inches across with a sweet flavor perfect for roasting and grilled kebabs. Start seed indoors early since onions need a long season. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Keep beds weeded and evenly watered until tops flop over, then cure bulbs in a dry, airy place. Choose day-length appropriate types for your latitude for best bulbing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Flat White Boer Pumpkin
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced widely apart once soil is reliably warm, as this variety resents any lingering chill. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so give them ample room or train them along a fence. The flattened, pale ivory fruit develops slight ribbing and deep orange flesh as it matures, and it is ready to harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail. Cure fruit in a warm spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flat shape makes stacking easy through winter. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Flatwoods Plum (Hog Plum, Sloe Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — flatwoods plum is a spectacular native small tree of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf Coast pine flatwoods, producing masses of pure white five-petaled flowers on bare branches in February–March, among the earliest and most profuse of all native spring-blooming trees and a critical early nectar source for native bees before other flowers open. The small round fruits (3/4 inch) ripen in July to purple-black with a blue bloom; they are tart to sweet depending on the tree, used for preserves, jellies, wine, and as wildlife food for deer, foxes, and dozens of bird species. An excellent candidate for wildlife food plots and naturalistic plantings in the pine flatwoods region. Many individual trees have superior fruit; select superior-fruiting trees to propagate for orchard use. Drought tolerant once established in adapted sandy soils. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Flava Yellow Cornelian Cherry (Golden-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Flava is the classic yellow-fruited form of cornelian cherry dogwood, producing translucent golden-amber fruit instead of the species' typical cherry red. The fruit is generally milder and less tart than red-fruited seedlings, making it more pleasant to eat fresh off the tree in addition to its use in preserves and syrups. Like other cornelian cherries it flowers on bare stems in late winter to earliest spring, tolerates a wide range of soils and urban conditions, and is largely trouble-free once established. Because its fruit color makes it stand out clearly against foliage, Flava also doubles as a distinctive landscape and hedgerow specimen alongside red-fruited cultivars. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Delight Aprium (Early-Season Apricot-Plum Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and site it away from the latest spring frost pockets, since aprium flowers open very early and are vulnerable to late cold snaps. Flavor Delight was among the first apriums released by Zaiger Genetics, and it remains valued for ripening earlier than almost any other stone fruit hybrid, giving gardeners a fresh, sweet, apricot-flavored fruit well ahead of the main summer harvest. The reddish-blushed, apricot-like skin covers dense, aromatic, low-acid flesh, and a compatible pollinator, such as an early-flowering plum, pluot, or aprium, is needed nearby since it is not reliably self-fruitful. Prune and thin as for a standard apricot, removing crossing interior branches in the dormant season and thinning heavy fruit sets in spring to improve final size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Finale Pluot (Amber-Red Complex-Flavored Late-Season Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Flavor Finale (originally trialed as selection 5Z366, U.S. Plant Patent 16590) is a Zaiger Genetics plum-apricot hybrid noted for consistently topping Dave Wilson Nursery's in-house taste trials. Medium-to-large fruit has purplish-red skin over juicy amber-red flesh with a notably complex, layered flavor, and it holds on the tree from the second week of September well into October, making it one of the latest-ripening pluot selections. With a relatively low chill requirement of around 500 hours, it performs well in milder winter climates. The tree is not self-fertile and needs a pollinizer such as Santa Rosa or Burgundy plum, or Flavor Grenade pluot; the upright habit sets heavy crops that benefit from spring thinning for fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Grenade Pluot (Firm Late-Season Green Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a second plum or pluot variety nearby for pollination, since Flavor Grenade sets fruit poorly on its own. Another of the Zaiger Genetics pluot introductions, Flavor Grenade keeps its green skin even at full ripeness, which can make judging harvest timing tricky for gardeners used to color-based cues, but the crisp, exceptionally firm, deep red-streaked flesh holds its sugary, tangy-sweet flavor for days after picking better than most stone fruit, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fruit that doesn't turn to mush a day after ripening. It ripens later in the season than most pluots, extending stone fruit harvest into late summer, and the moderately vigorous tree is managed and pruned much like a standard plum. Thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Heart Pluot (Heart-Shaped Dark Red Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Flavor Heart is a Zaiger Genetics pluot notable for its distinctive elongated, heart-like fruit shape, with dark red to nearly maroon skin covering rich, sweet, deeply flavored red-tinged flesh characteristic of the best pluot varieties. The unusual fruit shape sets it apart visually from the more typically round or oval pluots, making it a conversation piece as well as a good-eating specialty stone fruit for home orchards.
