Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored, since pluots generally do not continue to ripen significantly after picking. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor King Pluot (Reddish-Purple Sweet Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator, since Flavor King is not self-fruitful. This Zaiger Genetics pluot ripens to a deep reddish-purple skin over intensely sweet, dark red flesh with very little tartness, making it one of the sweeter pluot selections and a favorite for fresh eating out of hand. It ripens in mid-to-late summer, after earlier pluots like Flavor Supreme have finished, extending the harvest window for gardeners growing more than one pluot variety. As with other pluots, thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final size and quality, and prune in the dormant season to an open center to let light into the canopy. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Queen Pluot (Sweet Yellow-Skinned Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Flavor Queen is a Zaiger Genetics pluot, an interspecific hybrid combining plum and apricot parentage weighted toward plum, producing golden-yellow skinned fruit with sweet, richly flavored, apricot-tinged yellow flesh that ripens in mid to late summer. Like other pluot varieties, it delivers intensely concentrated, complex sweetness that many growers find surpasses either parent species on its own, a hallmark of the entire pluot breeding program. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and reaches full color, since pluots do not continue ripening much once picked, unlike some other stone fruit. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavor Supreme Pluot (Original Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a compatible plum or pluot pollinator nearby, since Flavor Supreme does not set a reliable crop on its own. Bred by Floyd Zaiger and one of the earliest pluot introductions, Flavor Supreme is still considered by many fruit growers to have the finest flavor of the whole pluot group, with mottled dark red-and-green skin over intensely sweet, richly flavored, deep red flesh that drips juice when fully ripe. It ripens early in the pluot season, and fruit left to color fully on the tree develops noticeably better flavor than fruit picked while still firm and greenish. Thin the heavy early fruit set to improve final size, and manage the tree with the same dormant pruning to an open center used for standard plums. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavorburst Bell Pepper (Color-Changing Purple-to-Orange Sweet Bell Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Flavorburst is a blocky bell-type sweet pepper bred for its unusual ripening sequence, with fruit passing from green through deep purple to yellow before finishing at bright orange, giving multiple colorful harvest stages from a single planting. The thick, crisp walls carry a sweet, mild flavor at every color stage, though sweetness increases as the fruit reaches its final orange color. Because the color changes track ripeness, gardeners can pick fruit at whichever stage suits their taste rather than waiting solely for full color change. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Flavorfall Pluot (Extra-Large Maroon-Skinned Late-Season Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Flavorfall is a Zaiger Genetics interspecific plum-apricot hybrid (U.S. Plant Patent 11990, now expired) bred to extend the pluot harvest into the fall, ripening in late September to early October after most other stone fruit has finished. Fruit is extra-large with smooth maroon skin and golden flesh, with a crisp, sweet bite (around 17 Brix), and it holds well on the tree for several weeks without softening. The tree needs roughly 800 chill hours and is not self-fertile, so plant a compatible pollinizer such as Dapple Fire pluot or Honey Punch nectaplum nearby; thin the heavy fruit set in late spring for best size, and prune to an open center in the dormant season. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavorfest Strawberry (USDA High-Flavor June-Bearer)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown right at soil level in full sun in well-drained, well-prepared soil, and remove the first flush of blossoms in a spring-planted bed's first weeks to push energy into establishment. Flavorfest was released by the USDA in the mid-2010s from the Beltsville breeding program specifically to combine excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor with good resistance to common foliar diseases and better tolerance of a range of soil conditions than many older June-bearing varieties. The large, firm, glossy red berries ripen in a mid-to-late June-bearing window and hold their flavor and size well through the peak of the harvest rather than tapering off in smaller, less flavorful late fruit. Renovate the bed after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to maintain a productive planting for several years, and mulch with straw over winter in colder parts of its range. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Flavorich Pluot (Dark Purple Late-Summer Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Flavorich is a Zaiger Genetics interspecific hybrid originating from a cross of Friar plum with an unnamed pluot selection, producing large, dark purple-skinned fruit with firm, very sweet yellow-orange flesh. It ripens in late August to early September, roughly two to three weeks after Flavor King pluot, giving growers a mid-to-late-season option with a vigorous, upright growth habit. Trees need about 800 chill hours and are not self-fruitful, so pair Flavorich with a pollinizer such as Dapple Dandy or Flavor King pluot, or a Japanese plum like Santa Rosa or Late Santa Rosa. Thin fruit clusters in spring to improve final size, and prune annually to maintain an open canopy for good light penetration. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavorite Pluot (Sweet Red-Skinned Summer Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Flavorite is a Zaiger Genetics interspecific plum-apricot hybrid bred for exceptional sweetness, testing among the highest-Brix pluot selections at around 20 degrees Brix. Fruit is medium-to-large with red skin, and it ripens early, typically in the first two weeks of August, filling a gap between the earliest pluots and the mid-season varieties. The vigorous, semi-spreading tree needs roughly 700 chill hours and is not self-fertile, requiring a compatible pollinizer such as Flavorfall pluot planted nearby for reliable fruit set. As with other pluots, thin the fruit set in late spring to concentrate sugars and improve final fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavorosa Pluot (Early Purple-Skinned Low-Chill Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible early-blooming pollinizer nearby, since fruit set depends on cross-pollination. Flavorosa is one of the earliest-ripening Zaiger pluots, bearing medium-sized fruit with dark purple skin and juicy red flesh that carries a concentrated, plum-forward sweetness well above average brix. The moderately vigorous, spreading tree bears reliably where winter chill is on the lower end, making it a candidate for warm Gulf gardens that struggle with higher-chill plums. Thin fruit clusters to a single fruit every 4–5 inches once set to improve size, and prune to an open vase form each winter to keep the spreading habit manageable and fruit within easy reach. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flavortop Nectarine Tree
description: Flavortop is a fast-growing nectarine producing large, juicy, well-balanced freestone fruit that ripens in mid to late summer. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, avoiding low frost pockets that harm early bloom. It is self-fruitful, so one tree will bear without a partner. Prune yearly in late winter to an open-center form for light and airflow, and thin developing fruit to boost size and prevent limb breakage. Provide steady water while fruit develops, and manage peach leaf curl with dormant sprays if needed. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flax (Oilseed / Linseed)
description: Broadcast seed at 25–30 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 40 sq ft) and rake to 1/4 in depth on a firm, weed-free seedbed; flax produces delicate sky-blue flowers that last only a morning and then forms round seed capsules (bolls) that rattle when dry. Harvest entire plants when half the bolls have turned brown and the stems are yellowing, cutting at the base and bundling into sheaves; finish drying upside-down for 10–14 days over a tarp. Thresh by beating sheaves inside a barrel, then winnow and screen; the small, oval, brown or golden seeds store for 1–2 years and are rich in omega-3 fatty acids. Grind seeds just before use for maximum nutrition, as whole seeds pass largely undigested. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Flemish Beauty Pear (Cold-Hardy Belgian Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Flemish Beauty originated in Belgium around 1810 and became historically important in North American pear growing for its outstanding cold hardiness, allowing pear cultivation in regions too harsh for many other European varieties. The large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with russet has sweet, aromatic, juicy flesh with real depth of flavor when picked and ripened properly. The tree's biggest weakness is susceptibility to fire blight and pear scab, which can be a real challenge in humid, disease-prone climates, so it benefits from good air circulation and, where scab pressure is high, a basic fungicide program. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best texture. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fleshy Hawthorn
description: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fleshy hawthorn tolerates a range of soils and is thorny, so site away from foot traffic. Clusters of white spring flowers cover this thorny native small tree, followed by unusually large, juicy, bright red fruit for a hawthorn, historically gathered and eaten fresh or made into preserves by Indigenous peoples and early settlers across its native range in the northern and central United States and Canada. Like other hawthorns it provides valuable dense, thorny cover for nesting birds and small wildlife, along with fall fruit that persists into winter as a food source when little else remains available. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune to remove crossing or damaged branches while avoiding the sharp thorns. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fletcher White Loquat (White-Fleshed Mild-Flavored Loquat)
description: Grow Fletcher White in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving it room to reach its mature rounded canopy. It belongs to the white-fleshed group of loquat cultivars, alongside Champagne and Vista White, prized for a delicate, low-acid, almost pear-like sweetness rather than the tangier orange-fleshed types. The medium to large fruits ripen in a tight cluster in late winter to early spring and are best harvested by hand as each fruit colors fully, since uneven ripening within a cluster is common. Provide supplemental irrigation during fruit swell for larger, juicier fruit, and thin crowded clusters to reduce disease pressure in humid Gulf Coast summers following harvest. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Flicker Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Season Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
description: Flicker is a 2009 University of Florida southern highbush release bred for early-season harvest potential in low-chill climates, part of the same UF breeding cycle that produced Kestrel, Chickadee, and Meadowlark. Growers should watch for anthracnose fruit rot in wet spring weather, as this cultivar can be more prone to the disease than some newer releases, so a preventive fungicide program through bloom and fruit set is recommended. Plant in raised, sulfur-acidified beds with excellent drainage, and provide a second early-blooming southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flint Corn (Indian Corn)
description: Flint corn is among the oldest cultivated corn types — the 'Indian corn' of the Americas, developed by indigenous peoples across North and South America over thousands of years in varieties of brilliant, diverse colors ranging from deep purple and blue-black to red, orange, yellow, cream, and multi-colored — and is both the most ornamental and among the most nutritious of all corn types for human consumption. The hard, glassy (flint-like) kernels have no dent when dry because they are mostly dense, hard starch rather than the soft floury starch of dent corn; this dense endosperm produces superior polenta and grits with more complex flavor than modern hybrid dent corn. Classic open-pollinated varieties like 'Glass Gem', 'Bloody Butcher', and 'Hopi Blue' are primarily flint types celebrated both for their ornamental dried-ear beauty and their exceptional culinary quality when ground into stone-milled cornmeal. Grow to full dry-grain maturity by allowing husks to dry completely on the stalk before harvest; cured ears can be used as autumn decorations, then shelled for grinding or replanting. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Flor de Durazno Bean (Peach Blossom Bean, Mexican Heirloom)
description: Flor de Durazno takes its name, 'peach blossom,' from the soft pink-and-cream mottling on its seed coat, a color pattern reminiscent of peach flowers rather than the bolder maroon speckling of many other Mexican dry beans. This bush-type heirloom produces a heavy set of pods on compact plants, yielding beans with a smooth, buttery texture and mild flavor once cooked, well suited to simple pot beans, soups, and refried preparations. Allow pods to dry completely and turn tan on the vine before harvest, then shell and cure the beans for another week or two indoors before sealing for storage. Its moderate days-to-maturity make it a good option for gardeners without a long, hot growing season. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Flor de Mayo Bean (Mexican May Flower Bean, Flor de Mayo Brillante)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Flor de Mayo is well-adapted to semi-dry, warm conditions and performs particularly well in the hot, dry growing season of zone 7–10 areas with low humidity; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery. Flor de Mayo (Spanish for 'May Flower') is one of the oldest and most culturally significant dry bean varieties in Mexico, where it has been grown for centuries as a primary food staple — ranking among the most commercially important beans in the Mexican market alongside Bayo, Peruano/Canario, and Azufrado varieties. The fresh seeds are distinctively beautiful: oval, slightly plump, and marked with magenta, rose-pink, and cream-white in a speckled and streaked pattern reminiscent of the flowers it was named for; the pattern and color intensify at the fresh-shell stage and fade to a more subdued cream-and-tan speckled pattern when fully dried. When cooked, the beans become uniformly pale tan-brown, but the texture and flavor are the key appeal: Flor de Mayo cooks to a mild, slightly sweet, creamy texture with thin skins that are almost imperceptible — making them one of the quickest-cooking dry beans and one of the smoothest for refried beans where texture matters. In Mexican home cooking, Flor de Mayo is the bean that many home cooks from Jalisco, Nayarit, and Michoacán states grew up eating; it is available in Mexican markets under this name and under regional names including 'Flor de Mayo Brillante' and 'Crema'. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Floradade Tomato (Heat-Adapted Open-Pollinated Gulf South Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Floradade is a University of Florida open-pollinated tomato variety developed specifically for Florida and Gulf South production — one of the older heat-tolerant open-pollinated varieties that has served as a reliable standard for Gulf South home garden production since its introduction. As an open-pollinated variety with good heat tolerance, Floradade produces medium-large (6–8 oz), round, firm, deep-red fruits with excellent fresh-eating and processing quality on a determinate plant that requires minimal staking. The disease resistance package includes Fusarium wilt race 1 — the most common race affecting Gulf South gardens. The primary practical advantage of Floradade over hybrid varieties is the ability to save seeds: since Floradade is open-pollinated, seeds saved from the best fruits grow true to type, allowing Gulf South gardeners to maintain a self-sufficient seed supply without annual seed purchases. This seed-saving advantage is significant for Gulf South gardeners who find locally-adapted, open-pollinated varieties often outperform northern hybrids in their specific climate. In zone 9, Floradade performs well in both spring and fall planting windows. The combination of local adaptation, open-pollination, heat tolerance, and reliable production has kept Floradade in production and recommendation by Gulf South cooperative extensions for decades. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Floragold Apricot (Early-Ripening Reliable Low-Chill Backyard Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Floragold was bred specifically as a dependable low-chill backyard apricot, needing roughly 400 chill hours or less and ripening two to three weeks ahead of the classic Blenheim, with all-purpose freestone fruit good for fresh eating and preserving. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flordabest Peach (Early Large-Fruited University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Developed by the University of Florida for about 250 chill units, Flordabest is well matched to zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and peninsular Florida. It ripens very early, about a week to ten days ahead of TropicBeauty, with large, firm yellow melting flesh under 90-100 percent bright red skin. Trees are self-fertile, moderately vigorous, and semi-upright, setting heavy annual crops that need early thinning to size the fruit well. A strong pick for gardeners who want an early low-chill peach with above-average fruit size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordablue Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Flordablue is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — one of the standard blueberry varieties for zone 9 and zone 10 gardens where inadequate winter chilling prevents northern varieties from producing. The medium-sized, firm, dark blue berries ripen in March–May in zone 9, among the very earliest blueberries of the season. Flordablue produces reliably in the mild winters of north-central and north Florida and the Gulf Coast, where more northerly varieties like Bluecrop or Blueray would fail to receive adequate winter chill. The flavor is mild, sweet, and pleasant — not as intensely flavorful as northern highbush varieties grown in their optimal cool climates, but very acceptable for fresh eating and processing. As a University of Florida release, it has an extensive track record of performance in Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordacrest Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, since peach roots are quickly damaged by standing water. Flordacrest is a low-chill freestone peach from the University of Florida breeding program, bred to extend the low-chill peach harvest window with medium to large fruit, attractive red-blushed yellow skin, and firm, good-flavored yellow flesh that holds up well for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and does not require a second tree for pollination, though planting a second early-blooming low-chill peach nearby can improve fruit set in a light bloom year. Thin fruit clusters to 6-8 inches apart when fruit reaches marble size to improve final size, and expect ripening in late spring to early summer, consistent with other low-chill Florida-bred peaches. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordadawn Peach (Early University of Florida Low-Chill Peach for North Florida)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred by the University of Florida for roughly 350 chill hours, Flordadawn suits the milder end of zone 8 through 9 where standard peaches often set little or no fruit. It ripens in the early season with melting, semi-clingstone flesh and the mild sweet flavor typical of Florida's low-chill breeding lines. Like most Gulf South peaches it benefits from a dormant fungicide application and open-center pruning to manage the fungal pressure that comes with humid winters and springs. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordaglo Nectarine (University of Florida Very Low-Chill Yellow Nectarine for Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root tree in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart. Harvest when fully yellow-orange and gives slightly to pressure. Flordaglo Nectarine was released by the University of Florida IFAS as part of the same low-chill stone fruit breeding program that produced Flordaking, Flordaprince, and other Gulf South-adapted peach and nectarine varieties. Nectarines (smooth-skinned peaches, genetically a single-gene variant of the standard fuzzy peach) are typically even more demanding in their chill hour requirements than their peach counterparts, making the development of a reliable very low-chill nectarine a significant achievement. With approximately 150–200 chilling hours required, Flordaglo can be grown in most of Florida and the Gulf Coast — conditions under which virtually all standard nectarine varieties fail to bloom and set properly. The fruit is medium-sized, with a yellow-red skin and yellow freestone flesh — the smooth nectarine skin distinguishing it visually from the closely related fuzzy peaches. The flavor is typically sweeter and slightly more aromatic than many standard low-chill peaches, with the characteristic nectarine quality that growers in cool climates take for granted but that gardeners in zone 9 rarely get to experience from home-grown fruit. For zone 9 home orchardists who want to grow nectarines — generally considered nearly impossible in the Gulf South — Flordaglo is one of the very few varieties with a realistic chance of success. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordagrand Blackberry (Low-Chill Central Florida Trailing Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, sandy soil and train the long, thorny, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since this cultivar sprawls rather than growing upright on its own. Flordagrand was released by the University of Florida in the 1950s specifically for the low-chill conditions of Central Florida and the Gulf Coast, where its evergreen canes need only a fraction of the winter chilling hours that Northern blackberries require. The berries are large and flavorful, ripening in April and May, but the plant is largely self-unfruitful and must be interplanted with its University of Florida companion release 'Oklawaha' to set a full crop. Because of its sprawling, thorny canes it never became a commercial crop, but it remains a dependable heirloom choice for gardeners in the Deep South who need a blackberry that thrives with minimal winter cold. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: FlordaGrande Peach (Ultra-Low-Chill University of Florida Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. FlordaGrande requires fewer than 100 chill hours, among the lowest of any named peach, so it sets fruit reliably even where winters barely dip below 60°F. It ripens very early, typically late April into May, on medium to large freestone fruit with orange-red skin and sweet, melting yellow flesh. Self-fertile and vigorous, it benefits from a hard summer prune to keep growth compact and from fruit thinning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy set. This is the standard recommendation for growers at the extreme low-chill end of zone 9-11 where even other Florida-bred peaches may fall short. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordaguard Peach (Ultra-Low-Chill Nematode-Resistant Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Flordaguard is a University of Florida release with an exceptionally low chill requirement of roughly 150 hours, making it one of the few peaches that reliably flowers and fruits in the mildest winters of the Gulf South and peninsular Florida, and it is separately valued in the nursery trade as a root-knot nematode-resistant rootstock for grafting less-hardy peach cultivars. Its own fruit is small to medium, clingstone, and mainly ornamental to fair-eating quality, with showy pink spring flowers that make it attractive even where fruit quality is secondary. Thin fruit if a heavier crop sets than the tree can properly size, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordahome Peach (Early University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first year or two to establish a strong, light-filled framework. Flordahome is one of the University of Florida's early low-chill peach releases, bred alongside Flordaking to give Gulf Coast and Florida growers a dependable option where standard high-chill peaches bloom erratically or fail to set fruit after mild winters. It bears medium, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with a red-blushed skin and pleasant, mild flavor for a low-chill selection, ripening in late spring before the worst of the summer heat. The tree is self-fertile and productive, though a late-season freeze after unusually early bloom can still reduce a crop, so avoid planting in frost-prone low spots. Thin developing fruit to 6-8 inches apart and fertilize lightly each spring to sustain consistent annual production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordahome Pear (Low-Chill Florida Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome is a University of Florida-developed pear cultivar requiring only 150–200 chill hours — the lowest chill requirement of any commonly available pear cultivar, making it the primary choice for zone 9b, zone 10, and any warm-winter location where standard pear varieties (which require 600–1000+ chill hours) consistently fail to bloom and fruit adequately. Flordahome produces medium-sized, yellow-green, round fruits with mild, sweet flesh that ripens in early summer — often in June in zone 9 — earlier than most other pear varieties. The fruit quality is pleasant but not as buttery or complex as high-chill European pears; it is best enjoyed fresh at peak ripeness or processed into preserves and sauces. Plant with Hood or Orient pear for cross-pollination — Flordahome is not self-fertile and requires a pollinizer. Fire blight resistance is moderate; preventive copper sprays at bloom reduce fire blight incidence in humid Gulf South climates. Flordahome trees grow vigorously in zone 9 and may need pruning to maintain manageable size — prune annually during dormancy to develop and maintain an open-center structure. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Flordaking Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Early Freestone Peach for Zone 9)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; prune to an open-vase shape in year 1. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches between fruits when marble-sized. Flordaking Peach was released by the University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center (then Florida Agricultural Experiment Station) in 1957 as one of the pioneering low-chill peach varieties specifically bred for Florida and Gulf Coast conditions. The development of low-chill peach varieties began in earnest at the University of Florida under the leadership of George Lyrene and others who recognized that the warm-winter climate of Florida and the Gulf Coast made it impossible to grow standard peach varieties requiring 600–800+ chilling hours. Flordaking became one of the landmark early low-chill releases: a freestone variety (the pit separates easily from the flesh at full ripeness) with medium-large fruit, yellow skin blushed with red, and yellow flesh of good eating quality for a low-chill variety. The variety's reputation for reliability in low-chill conditions — producing consistent crops when other peach varieties bloom prematurely or fail to set properly in zone 9's mild winters — established Flordaking as a foundation variety in Gulf Coast peach production, and it remains planted and recommended decades after its introduction. For zone 9 gardeners, Flordaking represents one of the most accessible routes to growing tree-ripe peaches at home in a climate where most stone fruits are impractical. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordaprince Peach
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Flordaprince is a very-low-chill peach released by the University of Florida's fruit breeding program in 1982, bred specifically for the Gulf Coast and central Florida where most standard peach varieties fail to fruit because winters are too mild to accumulate sufficient chill hours. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Flordaprince blooms and sets fruit consistently across zone 9. The fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone, with a pleasant mild peach flavor ripening in mid-April to early May — remarkably early compared to northern varieties. Trees grow vigorously and require annual pruning to an open-center form to maintain size and fruit quality. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart in April for large fruit size. Protect blooms from late cold snaps in zone 8b; blooms appear in January–February and can be damaged by freezes below 28°F. Fire blight can be a problem — remove affected wood promptly. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Flordaqueen Peach
description: An early University of Florida low-chill introduction bearing firm, juicy yellow-fleshed fruit with an attractive light red blush and a fairly long shelf life for a low-chill peach. It ripens earlier than most standard peaches, giving Gulf Coast gardeners fresh fruit well ahead of the general peach season. Grow in full sun with well-drained, slightly acidic soil, thin heavy fruit set for larger peaches, and monitor for bacterial spot, which can be more troublesome on early-blooming, low-chill types in wet springs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Florea Fig (Early-Ripening Self-Pollinating Cold-Hardy Fig)
description: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Florea is prized for ripening its light amber-brown, honey-flavored fruit notably earlier in the season than most named fig cultivars, often starting well before the peak summer humidity that brings on souring and splitting in later-ripening types. It is self-fertile like all common figs, needs no pollinator, and tends toward a smaller, more compact tree than vigorous types like Celeste or Brown Turkey, making it a reasonable choice for a large container or a tight garden spot. Fruit quality is best picked fully ripe and soft, since it can taste bland if harvested early. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and control size; heavy pruning sacrifices the following season's breba crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Florence Fennel
description: Also known as finocchio, this cool-season crop forms a rounded bulb of swollen leaf stems topped with feathery, dill-like foliage. Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil, and thin so bulbs have room to swell. Keep water steady and consider mounding soil around the base to blanch and sweeten the bulbs. Harvest before summer heat triggers bolting; both the bulb and the anise-scented fronds are useful in the kitchen. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Florence Fennel
description: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in spring 4 weeks before last frost or in late summer for fall harvest, thinning to 6–12 inches apart; Florence fennel (finocchio) forms a crisp, anise-flavored bulb at the base of overlapping leaf sheaths and should be harvested when the bulb reaches 3–4 inches in diameter before it bolts in heat. Hill soil up around the bulb base 2–3 weeks before harvest to blanch it to a sweeter, more tender white. Succession-sow every 3 weeks for an extended harvest. Keep fennel away from tomatoes, peppers, and most garden vegetables as it produces allelochemicals that inhibit their growth — plant it at the garden edge or in its own dedicated bed. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Floriana Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Pierce's-Disease-Resistant Red Wine Muscadine)
description: Plant self-fertile vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Floriana, bred by Florida A&M University, was developed specifically to fill a gap in muscadine wine production: while most muscadine wine cultivars produce white or bronze fruit, Floriana bears deep red berries suited to producing genuine red muscadine wine, combined with strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that devastates traditional bunch grapes across the Gulf South and much of Florida. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a pollinator. Fruit ripens in August and September. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity and vine health. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Floriani Red Flint Corn (Italian Polenta Corn, Mais Rosso della Val di Fiemme)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks; allow ears to dry fully on the stalks until the husks are completely papery before harvest; dry further at low heat (under 100°F) to bring moisture content below 12% before milling; stone-grind for the finest polenta texture; the distinctive deep red-orange color of the meal is unique among American corns. Floriani Red Flint is widely considered one of the finest polenta corns in the world — an Italian heirloom from the Fiemme Valley (Val di Fiemme) of Trentino, in the northeastern Italian Alps, where this particular strain of red flint corn has been grown by mountain farmers for centuries and is deeply embedded in the local food culture. The name 'Floriani' commemorates the Floriani family who maintained and preserved this specific strain. The corn produces large, deeply pigmented red-orange to brick-red flint kernels with a very hard, glassy endosperm characteristic of flint corn — the same endosperm structure that gives flint corns their superior milling quality and longer shelf life compared to dent corns. When stone-ground, the flour from Floriani Red Flint is a rich deep gold-orange color with a complex, nutty, slightly sweet fragrance quite unlike the pale, bland commercial cornmeal most American cooks know. Cooked polenta from this corn has a dense, complex flavor with depth that fully justifies the artisan price of stone-ground Italian polenta. Chefs at farm-to-table restaurants have sought out this variety specifically for its polenta quality. American growers in zones with a full summer can produce the authentic Italian-quality polenta grain that was formerly available only through import. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Florida 47 Tomato (South Florida Commercial Hybrid)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Florida 47 is a University of Florida-developed determinate hybrid tomato bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid Florida and Gulf Coast environment — part of a long series of Florida-bred tomatoes (including Florida 91, Floradade, and Solar Set) developed by UF's tomato breeding program to address the unique challenges of Southern tomato production. The large (8–12 oz), globe to slightly flattened, firm, bright red fruits have the thick walls, uniform shape, and long shelf life that commercial producers require, but perform equally well for home gardens; the flavor is balanced and pleasant without the blandness of many commercial types. Excellent disease resistance including Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, and tobacco mosaic virus — the full-package resistance crucial for reliable performance in disease-prone Southern soils. Florida 47 is widely planted commercially in the Immokalee, Florida production region during the fall and spring seasons and performs similarly well for home gardeners across zone 8b–11. Matures in 75–82 days from transplant.

name: Florida 91 Tomato (Disease-Resistant Heat-Adapted Gulf South Hybrid Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Florida 91 is a University of Florida hybrid tomato developed specifically for Gulf South production, representing one of the most disease-resistant commercially available tomato varieties — carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, Alternaria stem canker, and leaf mold (V, F1, F2, N, A, L), providing broad-spectrum protection against the primary soilborne and foliar diseases that devastate less protected varieties in the humid Gulf South climate. The large (6–8 oz), round, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have excellent fresh-eating and processing quality with good shelf life compared to softer varieties. Florida 91 is determinate (bush-type), maturing its crop in a compressed 4–6 week window and requiring minimal staking — a practical advantage for gardeners who prefer a defined harvest period over the continuous production of indeterminate types. In zone 9, Florida 91 is outstanding for both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The comprehensive disease resistance package makes Florida 91 particularly valuable for gardeners who have experienced soilborne disease problems in their garden soil — the resistance package allows production in locations where unprotected varieties fail repeatedly. A primary recommendation from University of Florida and Louisiana State University extension services for Gulf South home garden tomato production. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Florida Basket Tomato (Dwarf Hanging-Basket Saladette)
description: Florida Basket is a compact, determinate dwarf tomato bred at the University of Florida for hanging baskets and patio containers, needing no staking or caging as its short, self-supporting stems spill gently over the container rim. It sets clusters of small, red, plum-shaped saladette fruit around 2 inches long with good flavor for a container type, ripening over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of determinate dwarf tomatoes. Because container soil dries out quickly, water consistently and feed every couple of weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to keep the shallow root system productive through the season. Florida Basket later became scientifically significant as one of the two parent cultivars, alongside Ohio 4013-3, used to breed Micro-Tom, the ultra-dwarf tomato now used worldwide as a model organism in plant genetics research. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Florida Beauty Strawberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with high organic matter content; Florida Beauty is a University of Florida-developed day-neutral strawberry cultivar specifically bred for warm-winter production in zones 8–10, where traditional June-bearing strawberries from northern breeding programs produce poorly or fail entirely. The 'day-neutral' characteristic allows Florida Beauty to initiate flower buds and set fruit based on temperature rather than day length, enabling continuous fruit production throughout zone 9's cool season (November–April) regardless of the photoperiod. The medium-to-large, glossy, red fruits have excellent flavor — sweet with the bright strawberry character that distinguishes the best fresh-market strawberries from commercial long-distance shipping varieties. Florida Beauty was developed for performance in Florida, Gulf Coast, and similar warm-winter climates where most northern strawberry varieties fail to produce adequate fruit, making it one of the most appropriate strawberry choices for zone 9 home gardens. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Florida Beauty Strawberry (Day-Neutral Gulf Coast Strawberry)
description: Transplant plugs or bare-root plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, sandy loam in full sun; Florida Beauty is a University of Florida IFAS strawberry introduction developed specifically for Gulf Coast production — a day-neutral cultivar adapted to the warm winters and mild springs of zone 8–10 where standard June-bearing northern varieties (Chandler, Camarosa) perform unreliably in recent warmer winters. Day-neutral strawberries are not dependent on day length for flower initiation — they flower and fruit based on temperature rather than photoperiod, making them more reliably productive across a range of winter weather patterns in the Gulf South. Florida Beauty produces attractive, large (medium-to-large), bright red, excellent-flavored fruits with firm texture and good fresh-eating quality. In zone 9, transplant in October–November for a production window from January through April — the peak of Gulf South strawberry season when temperatures are ideal for fruit development and quality. The plants are treated as annuals in commercial production (removed after the spring harvest) but can be maintained as short-lived perennials in home garden beds. Florida Beauty represents the most recent generation of Gulf South strawberry breeding that addresses the challenges of warm-winter climate change on traditional day-length-sensitive cultivar performance. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Florida Betony
description: Florida Betony is a native perennial herb of moist, disturbed habitats, roadsides, and open areas across Florida and the southeastern coastal plain, best known for its white, segmented, rattlesnake-rattle-shaped underground tubers — earning it the folk name 'rattlesnake weed' — that are crisp, sweet, and edible raw or cooked with a flavor reminiscent of water chestnuts. The small pink flowers produced in spring attract native bees and are mildly ornamental, though the plant is primarily known as a prolific lawn weed throughout the Southeast due to its ability to spread rapidly from fragments of its segmented tubers. As a cultivated edible herb, the tubers are harvested in late fall through early spring when the plant is dormant or growing slowly, cleaned, and eaten raw in salads, pickled, or stir-fried. Plant in contained beds to prevent uncontrolled spreading — once established in a garden, Florida Betony is virtually impossible to eradicate without repeated effort. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Florida Brilliance Strawberry (Early High-Yield UF/IFAS Winter Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun. Florida Brilliance was bred at the University of Florida's Gulf Coast Research and Education Center to ripen earlier in the season than the older Florida Radiance and Festival releases it has largely replaced in commercial Gulf-latitude production, with conical fruit that is a deep, glossy red both inside and out and holds excellent flavor even in the warm early-season conditions typical of Gulf Coast fall plantings. As with other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, setting out fresh crowns each fall for harvest from winter through spring rather than expecting the planting to persist as a true perennial. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce fruit rot in humid conditions. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Florida Broadleaf Mustard (Southern Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Florida Broadleaf is the classic Southern mustard green — the most widely grown mustard green cultivar in the Gulf South for generations, with large, flat, broad, smooth, dark-green leaves with a pungent, spicy mustard flavor that is a cornerstone of traditional Southern cooking. Unlike curled mustard varieties (Southern Giant Curled, Green Wave) that have ruffled, frilly leaves, Florida Broadleaf has smooth, flat leaves that are easier to wash and which have a slightly more robust, bold flavor. Florida Broadleaf is grown in zone 9 gardens from September through April — the cool-season growing window when mustard greens develop the best flavor and avoid the extreme bitterness and quick bolting that heat causes. Young leaves are mild enough for salads; mature leaves are best cooked, typically braised with smoked meat (ham hock, smoked turkey) and seasoned vinegar in the traditional Southern style. Frost improves mustard green flavor — the conversion of starches to sugars after cold nights produces a richer, more complex, slightly sweeter flavor. Harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the entire plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Florida Conch Pea, Bush (Small White-Seeded North Florida Heirloom)
description: Florida Conch is a now-rare southern pea that arrived in north Florida in the late 1800s, likely from the West Indies, and became prized for its tiny white seeds, delicate texture, and short cooking time. The original conch pea was a vining plant, and a vining strain still exists, but this bush-type selection was developed later as vining peas fell out of favor for home gardens. Green-shell shellies are ready in about 63 days, with fully dry peas following around 70 days, and the mild, delicate flavor sets it apart from heartier crowder and blackeye types. Matures in 63–70 days from seed.

name: Florida Cranberry Roselle
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Florida Cranberry is a named roselle cultivar selected specifically for very large, fleshy, deeply colored calyces — the thick, star-shaped, burgundy-red sepals that encircle each seed pod after the flower drops and are the edible product of roselle cultivation. The deep cranberry-red calyces have an intensely tart, cranberry-like flavor with hibiscus floral notes, used to make a vivid crimson tea (agua de Jamaica), jam, syrup, sauce, and desserts. The exceptional calyx size and deep color of Florida Cranberry make it the standard named cultivar for calyx production in the Gulf South. In zone 9 the short-day flowering response means calyces set abundantly in October–November when temperatures are cooling — a natural alignment with the Thanksgiving and holiday season when cranberry-flavored products are in demand. Harvest calyces before the seed pod matures for best flavor; the calyces are easily separated from the seed capsule by hand. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Florida Ember Strawberry (UF/IFAS Neopestalotiopsis-Resistant Organic-Adapted Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun, ideally set out October 1–15; Florida Ember is a 2024 release from the University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center bred as an early, disease-resistant companion to Florida Brilliance. It carries the strongest disease resistance package of the current UF short-day lineup, including the lowest susceptibility to Neopestalotiopsis fruit and leaf spot of any UF cultivar, along with moderate resistance to anthracnose, charcoal rot, crown rot, and botrytis — traits that make it especially well suited to humid Gulf South conditions and to organic production, where it performs best in open fields rather than high tunnels. The robust, compact plants carry medium-to-large, uniform conic berries with bright red skin and a light red to nearly white interior, low acid, and high Brix sweetness comparable to Florida Medallion, along with unusually good rain resistance for a short-day cultivar. Treat as a winter annual, replacing crowns each fall. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Florida Encore Strawberry (UF/IFAS High-Yield Firm-Fleshed Shipping Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun, ideally set out October 12–22; Florida Encore is a 2024 release from the University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center bred as an improvement on Florida Brilliance. The vigorous plants produce a heavy first inflorescence that drives high early yields from mid-October plantings and continues into steady winter and spring harvests. Fruit is large, glossy, and evenly red both outside and in, with moderate acid and Brix and notably firm flesh that gives Encore excellent shelf life and shipping quality compared to most short-day Florida cultivars. It is moderately resistant to anthracnose fruit rot and phytophthora crown rot but moderately susceptible to Colletotrichum crown rot and charcoal rot, so maintain good bed drainage and avoid planting into fields with a history of soilborne disease. Treat as a winter annual, replacing crowns each fall. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Florida Giant Watermelon (Southern Heirloom Picnic Watermelon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F, planting 4–5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2 plants; harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and the ground spot has turned from white to cream-yellow. Florida Giant is a classic large-fruited Southern heirloom watermelon producing enormous fruits (30–60 pounds or more) with light green to dark green striped skin and deep red, sweet flesh — the quintessential 'picnic' or 'table' watermelon of the Gulf South where the long, hot summer provides adequate heat units for the 85–100 day maturation period. The very large fruits are challenging to transport single-handed but are impressive in the garden and at the table, providing abundant fresh fruit for summer gatherings. Florida Giant performs excellently under Gulf Coast hot humid summer conditions, showing reasonable tolerance of the fungal diseases (Fusarium wilt, anthracnose) common in humid climates, and is well-adapted to the sandy, fertile, moderately acid soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast region. The traditional size and flavor make it a regional staple and a nostalgic choice for gardeners who remember the giant watermelons of summer cookouts. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Florida Grande Peach
description: Bred by the University of Florida stone fruit program for the state's subtropical climate, this very-low-chill freestone peach produces medium red-skinned fruit with soft, melting yellow flesh and good flavor for such an early-ripening variety. Because it blooms extremely early, protect flowers from occasional cold snaps and avoid planting in low-lying frost pockets. Keep trees pruned to an open, low-vase form for easy harvest and better airflow, which helps limit fungal disease in humid Gulf Coast springs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Florida Green Chayote
description: Florida Green is the standard smooth, light-green, pear-shaped chayote cultivar recommended by University of Florida IFAS Extension for home gardens across the state, prized for consistent fruit set even through the region's oppressive summer humidity. Fruits run six ounces to a pound and are lightly grooved but essentially spineless, making them easier to handle and peel than heirloom spiny types. Give the sprawling vine a very sturdy arbor or fence, since a single well-sited plant can cover several hundred square feet and yield dozens of fruit from late summer into the first hard freeze. Along the Gulf Coast the rootstock often survives mild winters and resprouts, so mulching the crown heavily after dieback can save a year of establishment. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Florida High Bush Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once the soil and nights are warm; Florida High Bush is an old Southern heirloom eggplant bred for reliable production through the intense heat and humidity of a Deep South summer, when many standard eggplant varieties stall or drop blossoms. Plants grow tall and vigorous — notably taller than most eggplant cultivars, as the name suggests — and bear a heavy, extended crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval to pear-shaped fruit with classic mild, creamy flesh. Because the bushes get large and top-heavy once loaded with fruit, stake or cage plants at transplanting to prevent wind and fruit-weight damage. Harvest fruit at about two-thirds of full size, while the skin is still glossy and taut — dull skin signals over-mature, seedier flesh. Regular harvesting encourages continued flowering and keeps plants productive from early summer through the first fall frost in zone 8–9. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Florida King Peach (Large Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Florida King is one of the premier low-chill peach cultivars for the Gulf South — a large-fruited, yellow-fleshed, freestone peach that produces high-quality fruit with approximately 450–500 chill hours of cold requirement, making it adapted to the winter climate of zone 8–9a where higher-chill northern peach varieties fail to break dormancy properly. The large fruits (2.5–3 inches diameter) have golden-yellow skin with an attractive red blush, yellow-orange flesh, small pit (freestone type), and excellent sweet peach flavor. Florida King ripens in May in zone 9 — one of the earliest major peach harvests, ahead of the intense summer heat that can reduce quality in later-ripening cultivars. Like all peaches, Florida King must be thinned aggressively after set: thin to one fruit every 6–8 inches on each branch to allow the remaining fruits to develop to full size — unthinned trees produce large numbers of small, inferior fruits. Prune annually in late winter (February in zone 9) to maintain tree size at 10–12 feet, promote new wood development on which next season's crop will form, and open the canopy to air circulation that reduces disease pressure. Peach leaf curl and brown rot are the primary disease challenges in the humid Gulf South — preventive dormant sprays with copper fungicide are standard practice. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Florida Market Eggplant
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture and warm soil temperatures; Florida Market is an open-pollinated eggplant variety developed specifically for production in hot, humid, disease-prone Gulf Coast and Florida conditions — it shows markedly better performance in zone 8b–11 than northern varieties selected for cool, short-season growing conditions. The large, oval to cylindrical fruits are 6–8 inches long with smooth, glossy deep purple skin and dense, firm white flesh with relatively few seeds — the classic eggplant form ideal for slicing, grilling, roasting, baba ghanoush, moussaka, and Parmesan preparations. The superior heat tolerance allows Florida Market to continue flowering and setting fruit through Gulf Coast summers when temperatures regularly exceed 95°F — a period when many northern varieties drop their flowers. Consistent irrigation is more critical than for most vegetables, as uneven moisture causes fruit development problems and bitter flesh. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Florida Medallion Strawberry (UF/IFAS Sweet Aromatic Winter Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Florida Medallion was released in 2020 by the University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center and has become a steadily more widely planted alternative to Florida Brilliance and Sensation in commercial Gulf-latitude short-day production. The robust, medium-vigor plants carry medium-to-large, uniform conic fruit with bright red skin and a light red to nearly white interior; low acid and high Brix give it a sweet, intensely fruity, aromatic flavor that stands out among subtropical short-day cultivars, making it popular with growers selling direct to consumers as well as through wholesale channels. As with other short-day strawberries in the Deep South annual system, treat it strictly as a winter annual, setting out fresh crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds for harvest from winter into spring. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Florida Mountain Mint
description: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; Florida mountain mint is an endemic species of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, adapted to the subtropical growing conditions of zone 8–10 where more northern mountain mints fail in summer heat and humidity. Like all Pycnanthemum species, it produces small white flowers with purple speckling in dense, flat-topped clusters in summer — an absolute magnet for native bees, especially small sweat bees and Halictid bees that are specialist mountain mint pollinators. The crushed foliage is intensely minty-aromatic, similar to wild mint but more pungent. Mountain mints are among the top-ranked native plants for native bee diversity in scientific studies. This Gulf-adapted species fills the role of mountain mint in zones 8–10 where slender mountain mint (P. tenuifolium) is the most common alternative. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Florida Onyx Muscadine Grape (Large-Cluster Black Fresh-Market Muscadine)
description: Plant vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Florida Onyx, released by Florida A&M University's muscadine breeding program for the fresh market, is notable for forming unusually dense, tight clusters of 8 to 15 large, deep black-red berries, far more than the loose groups of three to five berries typical of most muscadine cultivars, giving it a bunch-grape-like cluster appearance while retaining the thick skin, disease resistance, and heat tolerance of true muscadine. The berries also hold their quality unusually well after harvest, extending shelf life for fresh sales or home storage. It shows good resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits bunch grape production across the Gulf South. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Florida Pearl Strawberry (UF/IFAS White-Fruited Pineberry Release)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Florida Pearl is the University of Florida IFAS strawberry breeding program's first white-fruited 'pineberry' release, developed by crossing descendants of Japanese white strawberries with red Florida short-day breeding lines for yield, disease resistance, and adaptation to Gulf-latitude winter production. Fruit is pure white internally with a white-to-pink-blushed exterior, red achenes, moderate gloss, and a distinctive low-acid flavor with aromatic notes of pineapple or apricot; the plant is denser and shorter-stemmed than Florida Brilliance. Because pineberries are low in self-fertility, interplant with a standard red-fruiting short-day cultivar such as Florida Brilliance or Sweet Charlie to ensure adequate pollination and fruit set; expect yields roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of a standard red cultivar. Treat strictly as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Florida Prince Peach (Low-Chill Gulf South Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Florida Prince is the standard low-chill peach cultivar for Gulf Coast zone 9–10 production — requiring only approximately 150 chill hours (hours below 45°F), compared to 800–1000 hours required by standard northern peach cultivars. This dramatically low chill requirement allows reliable peach production in coastal Louisiana, southern Texas, central Florida, and other warm winter areas where standard peach cultivars receive inadequate chilling to bloom and set fruit properly. Florida Prince produces medium-sized, round, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone to clingstone fruit with a red blush on the sunny side — quality is good for fresh eating and suitable for canning and preserves, though not equal to the finest high-chill peach cultivars in flavor complexity. Fruit ripens in late April through May in zone 9 — very early in the season — which helps avoid much of the summer disease pressure that affects later cultivars. The tree is vigorous, productive, and well-adapted to the clay and sandy loam soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain. Thin fruit heavily (6–8 inches between remaining fruits) after natural June drop to develop full-sized fruits. Annual pruning to maintain an open-vase form is essential for air circulation and disease management in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Florida Radiance Strawberry (UF/IFAS Gulf-Latitude Short-Day Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida Radiance is a University of Florida IFAS-bred short-day strawberry that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in Florida and similar Gulf-latitude winter production regions, prized for its combination of early, high yield and good flavor in warm winter climates unsuited to many Northern-bred strawberry varieties. The bright red, well-formed berries perform reliably through a Gulf South winter growing season. As with other short-day strawberries in zone 9, plant fresh crowns each fall and treat as a winter annual, harvesting from winter into spring before the plants decline in summer heat. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure common in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Florida Rose Rabbiteye Blueberry (Pink-Fruited Novelty Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Florida Rose is a University of Florida rabbiteye selection bred by Paul Lyrene and notable for large, sweet, low-acid berries that stay pink on the sun-exposed side and pale on the shaded side at full ripeness, rather than the typical blue-black rabbiteye color. Its roughly 300-hour chill requirement is unusually low for a rabbiteye cultivar, letting it fruit reliably in the mildest Deep South gardens where standard rabbiteyes may underperform. As with all rabbiteye blueberries, it is not self-fertile and needs a different rabbiteye cultivar blooming at the same time for good pollination and full-sized berries. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Florida Serviceberry
description: Florida Serviceberry is a native shrub of moist to wet, sandy coastal plain habitats from Virginia south to Florida, producing clusters of small white flowers in late winter to early spring — among the first native flowers to open each year — that provide a critical early nectar and pollen source for emerging native bees and butterflies at a time when little else is blooming. The sweet, dark blue-purple berries that follow in late spring and early summer have a mild flavor reminiscent of blueberries and are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, Baltimore orioles, cedar waxwings, and over 40 other bird species during the critical spring migration feeding period. The smaller, more compact stature compared to the familiar Downy Serviceberry makes Florida Serviceberry well suited to smaller gardens and naturalized plantings in the coastal plain Southeast. Plant in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Florida Serviceberry tolerates the wet, sandy, coastal plain soils that can challenge other native fruit shrubs. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Florida Soapberry
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Florida soapberry is a native tree of the Florida Peninsula, growing naturally in upland sandy forests, sandhills, and dry flatwoods. Like its relative western soapberry (S. drummondii), it produces fleshy, translucent, amber fruits high in saponins that lather in water and have been used as natural soap. The pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall. Florida soapberry tends to be smaller and more restricted in distribution than western soapberry, naturally adapted to the sandy, acid, well-drained soils of Florida's uplands rather than the calcareous plains soils of the central US. The fruits are eaten by mockingbirds and robins. An underused drought-tolerant native for sandy, dry garden conditions in Florida and adjacent Gulf States where its multiple seasons of interest — spring flowers, fall color, and persistent amber fruits — make it a useful ornamental native. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Florida Speckled Lima Bean (Heat-Tolerant Southern Pole Lima)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a trellis or pole for the climbing vine. Florida Speckled is a Southern heirloom pole lima bean grown for its handsome maroon-and-white speckled seeds and, more importantly, for genuine heat tolerance that lets it set pods reliably through the hot, humid conditions of a Deep South summer that cause many lima varieties to drop blossoms and stop producing. The vigorous vine climbs readily and produces well over an extended season once established. Harvest pods at the green shell stage for the classic buttery lima flavor, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for a dry bean harvest that stores well through winter. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Florida Strangler Fig
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is the only native fig species of the continental United States (excluding Hawaii), naturally occurring in the subtropical hammocks and rockland of south Florida and the Keys. In nature it begins as an epiphyte — a seed dropped by a bird into a tree crotch germinates and sends aerial roots down to the soil that eventually engulf and 'strangle' the host tree. As a free-standing garden tree it simply grows as a magnificent, large-canopy evergreen. The small yellow-orange figs are eaten by an extraordinary variety of wildlife — dozens of bird species, Florida panthers, and raccoons — making the strangler fig one of the most ecologically productive trees in south Florida. The dense canopy provides important nesting habitat for raptors. A keystone species of the south Florida hammock ecosystem. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Florida Sweet Acerola (Barbados Cherry)
description: Florida Sweet is a named acerola selection developed for a milder, less tart flavor than typical seedling-grown Barbados cherry, making the fresh fruit more palatable for out-of-hand eating while retaining exceptionally high vitamin C content. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, watering regularly during establishment and fruit set but allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings once mature. Expect several flowering and fruiting flushes per year in warm weather, with bright red fruit that must be picked and used within a day or two since it does not store or ship well. Light, regular pruning after each fruiting flush keeps the dense, twiggy shrub attractive and encourages continued cropping; protect plants from temperatures below the high 20s F, especially when young. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Florida127 Strawberry (Sweet Sensation, UF/IFAS Winter Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida127, sold under the brand name Sweet Sensation, was bred at the University of Florida's Gulf Coast Research and Education Center specifically for the mild winters of Central Florida and similar Gulf-latitude climates. It produces larger fruit and higher yield than the earlier Florida Radiance release, along with a longer shelf life and sweeter flavor that has made it popular with both commercial growers and home gardeners in the region. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Flour Corn (Soft Corn)
description: Flour corn is the ancient soft-starch corn type developed by indigenous peoples of the Americas for grinding into fine cornmeal and masa — its kernels, composed almost entirely of soft, starchy endosperm without the hard, glassy outer layer of flint corn, grind into an exceptionally fine, silky flour with a mild, sweet flavor superior for baking cornbread, making hominy, and preparing traditional tortillas and tamales. Classic open-pollinated varieties like 'Hopi Blue' (a flour-type despite sometimes being called flint), 'Bloody Butcher', and 'Aztec Red' flour corns were grown for centuries by Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest, where soft corn was the staple grain; in the Gulf South, flour corns adapted to humid climates perform well as spring and fall crops. The soft kernels are more susceptible to corn earworm and storage fungi than hard flint or dent types — harvest promptly when husks dry, dry completely before storage, and store in sealed containers with desiccant in a cool, dry location. The beautifully colored ears of traditional flour corn varieties make outstanding autumn decorations before grinding. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Flowering Quince
description: Plant in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; flowering quince is one of the earliest-blooming ornamental shrubs of the temperate garden — producing brilliant flowers in red, scarlet, orange, salmon, pink, or white directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter and very early spring (February–March in the mid-South), often through snow. The dense, interlocking thorny growth makes it an impenetrable barrier hedge as well as an ornamental specimen. After the flowers, the shrub produces hard, green to yellow-green quincelike fruits 2–3 inches across that are not particularly palatable raw but make excellent jelly, preserves, and liqueurs — a quality long exploited in Japanese and Chinese cuisine. The fruits are high in pectin, which makes them particularly valuable for preserving, and have an intense quince fragrance when ripe. Extremely cold-hardy, drought-tolerant once established, and adaptable to a wide range of soils. The many named cultivars span the full color range from pure white ('Jet Trail') to deepest blood-red ('Crimson and Gold'). Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Flowers Muscadine Grape (Historic Black Female Cultivar)
description: Flowers is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still passed down in Southern gardens, historically grouped with early favorites like James and Thomas for its vigor, reliability, and dessert-quality fruit well before formal university breeding programs began. The medium-to-large berries ripen black with the deep, musky-sweet flavor prized in traditional muscadine cookery, fresh eating, and homemade wine. Because Flowers produces only female flowers, it sets little or no fruit without a nearby self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to provide pollen. This tough, long-lived heirloom vine tolerates the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the Gulf South with minimal spraying once established on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fluted Gourd
description: Sow Telfairia occidentalis seeds directly in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a strong trellis or fence for the vigorous vine; harvest young, tender leaves and shoot tips continuously from 4–6 weeks after planting for use as a cooked green vegetable; harvest mature gourds for seed when the skin turns yellow-green. Fluted Gourd (known as 'ugu' in Igbo) is arguably the single most important leafy vegetable in southern Nigeria — a vine plant that is grown in virtually every family plot and kitchen garden throughout Igboland and beyond. The large, prominently ribbed leaves (resembling pumpkin leaves but more tender and palatable) are harvested in volume and sliced into fine strips before being added to soups and stews at the end of cooking to preserve their vivid green color. The leaves are especially important in Egusi soup (with ground melon seeds), Ofe Onugbu, and Ofe Owerri. The enormous, ribbed, green-striped gourds can weigh 10–30 kg and contain large, flat, oval seeds rich in oil and protein; the seeds are dried, shelled, and eaten as a protein source or pressed for cooking oil (fluted pumpkin seed oil). Unlike most gourds, Telfairia occidentalis has separate male and female plants; female plants bear the gourds while male plants are grown primarily for continuous leaf harvest. In zone 9–12 it grows as a perennial vine. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Fluted Pumpkin (Ugu, Climbing Okra)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a very sturdy trellis; fluted pumpkin (ugu) is one of the most important leafy vegetables in West and Central Africa, particularly Nigeria, where the tender shoots and leaves are harvested continuously for soups, stews, and cooked greens rich in iron, zinc, and protein. The flesh of the huge ribbed fruits is also eaten, and the seeds are pressed for cooking oil. In the US it is grown as a perennial vine in zones 10-12 and as an annual in frost-free areas where the season is long enough. Harvest leaves and shoot tips regularly when vines are actively growing; the fresh leaves wilt quickly and are best used the same day they are harvested. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Flying Dragon Hardy Orange
description: Flying Dragon is a dwarf, contorted selection of trifoliate orange with curved thorns and twisting stems, valued both ornamentally and as a size-controlling rootstock. It bears the same small, aromatic fruit and shares the species' extreme cold hardiness. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where its sculptural winter silhouette is a feature. Prune minimally to preserve the natural twisting form, and use the tart autumn fruit for preserves. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fo-Ti (He Shou Wu, Chinese Knotweed)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil against a strong trellis, fence, or arbor, since this vigorous twining vine can climb 20 feet or more in a season once mature. The tuberous roots, harvested at three to four years or older, are the part traditionally processed and used in Chinese herbalism, most often after steaming with black beans; fresh raw root is generally considered unsuitable for casual use. Grown ornamentally for its glossy heart-shaped leaves and airy sprays of small white flowers in late summer, it tolerates a range of soils but appreciates consistent moisture while establishing. Cut back hard in late winter to control size, as unmanaged vines can become congested and woody at the base. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Folgate Lavender (Early English Lavender)
description: One of the earliest English lavenders to flower each season, this compact heirloom cultivar produces slender, deep violet-blue spikes with an exceptionally sweet, classic lavender scent on narrow silvery foliage. Its early bloom window and neat, rounded habit make it a favorite for edging paths and low hedges, and the flowers dry especially well for sachets and culinary use. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, since wet feet in winter are the most common cause of failure, and shear back by about a third right after flowering to keep the plant compact and woody growth in check. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Fonio (Acha)
description: Broadcast seed densely onto a fine, firm seedbed after last frost in full sun; fonio (acha) is one of Africa's oldest cultivated grains, grown for at least 5,000 years across the Sahel and West Africa in the semi-arid regions of Senegal, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Nigeria, where it is the first grain to be harvested each season and a critical food security crop. The grain is tiny — resembling a grain of sand — but nutritionally remarkable: gluten-free, high in essential amino acids methionine and cystine that are deficient in most other grains, and with a pleasant, slightly nutty, delicate flavor that is different from any familiar grain. Cooked fonio is fluffy and lighter than couscous. It is increasingly available in US natural food stores and is experiencing a culinary renaissance promoted by West African chefs. As a crop, it thrives in hot, dry, marginal conditions and completes its cycle in just 70–90 days, making it exceptionally productive per day of growing season in difficult conditions. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Football Black Walnut
