description: Football is a long-cultivated named black walnut selection valued for its distinctly elongated, football-shaped nuts, which are noticeably larger than typical wild seedling nuts and crack out in good-sized kernel pieces. It has circulated through nut grower collections and variety trials for decades as a reliable producer once established on grafted rootstock. Give it wide open spacing in full sun and deep soil, and keep it away from vegetable gardens, fruit trees, and other juglone-sensitive plantings. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Forastero Cacao
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Forastero cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. The hardiest, highest-yielding, and by far the most widely grown of the main cacao varieties, accounting for the large majority of the world's chocolate supply, it produces thick-shelled pods with a stronger, more straightforwardly bitter and less nuanced flavor than the rarer Criollo type, but far better disease resistance and productivity that make it the backbone of commercial cacao farming across West Africa and Brazil. Easier to grow than Criollo, it still requires the same warm, humid, shaded rainforest understory conditions typical of all cacao, ideally interplanted beneath taller banana or other shade trees as is traditional in cacao agroforestry systems. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity and its first pod harvest. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fordhook 242 Lima Bean
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — lima beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil quality for subsequent crops; Fordhook 242 is the standard large-seeded bush lima bean — an All-America Selections award-winning variety from the Burpee Fordhook line that has defined the Fordhook (large, flat, meaty-seeded) type of lima bean in American horticulture for nearly a century. The large, flat, creamy-green seeds are the classic 'butter bean' of Southern cooking — much larger and meatier than baby lima beans, with a rich, starchy, almost buttery flavor and firm-yet-creamy texture that makes them one of the most satisfying of all shelling beans. Lima beans are often unfairly associated with canned or frozen product quality that gives no sense of their fresh garden character — freshly shelled and immediately cooked Fordhook lima beans have a completely different, far superior flavor to processed versions, with genuine sweetness and a rich, filling character. The large seeds also dry well for winter use, expanding culinary possibilities beyond the fresh-shelled season. Matures in 70–78 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Fancy Mustard (Curled Heirloom Mustard Green)
description: Direct sow shallowly and thin seedlings to stand several inches apart, harvesting outer leaves regularly to keep the plant productive. This old American selection, once distributed under the Fordhook name, forms dense rosettes of tightly curled, ruffled bright green leaves with a peppery mustard bite that mellows when cooked. Its frilly texture makes it a distinctive addition to mixed braising greens, and it tends to hold in the garden a bit longer than plain-leaf mustards before bolting. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Giant Chard
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Fordhook Giant is the classic white-stalked Swiss chard — one of the oldest and most productive chard varieties in American seed catalogs, developed by the Burpee seed company and named for Burpee's Fordhook Farm in Pennsylvania where it was trialed and selected. The very large, heavily blistered, dark green leaves with thick, pure white, celery-like stalks represent the classic Swiss chard appearance and deliver maximum productivity per square foot — the substantial white stalks are among the meatiest and most impressive of any chard variety, making Fordhook Giant the preferred choice in preparations where stalks are eaten separately from the leaves. The thick stalks can be prepared raw like celery, steamed and buttered like asparagus, or braised for their mild, slightly sweet, beet-adjacent flavor; the large leaves cook down like spinach with a mild, earthy, slightly mineral character. Individual plants in good conditions can produce leaves exceeding 2 feet long, making the garden presence of Fordhook Giant among the most dramatically large of any leafy vegetable. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the best vegetables for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun exposure. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Giant Swiss Chard
description: This classic heirloom chard produces broad, glossy green leaves with thick white stems and a mild, tender flavor for fresh or cooked dishes. Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to give each plant room to bush out. Harvest outer leaves regularly for cut-and-come-again production while the center keeps growing. Unusually heat and cold tolerant, it yields continuously from late spring well into fall with steady moisture. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Giant Swiss Chard
description: This old favorite features broad, crinkled leaves and wide white stems packed with vitamins and minerals. A vigorous grower with a long season, it provides fresh greens from early summer into fall and year-round in mild climates. White-stemmed types are generally sweeter and milder than colored varieties. Sow directly, thin seedlings since seeds are clusters, and harvest outer leaves regularly. Keep evenly watered for continuous, tender growth. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Lima Bean
description: This All-America Selections bush lima is valued for resilience, drought tolerance, and heavy crops of large, buttery beans. Sow seed an inch to an inch and a half deep only once the soil has warmed, since limas rot in cold, wet ground. Grow in full sun with even moisture through flowering and pod fill. Pick pods when they feel plump and full for fresh shelling, or leave them to dry on the bush for storage beans. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Fordhook Zucchini
description: Fordhook Zucchini was bred at Burpee's historic Fordhook Farm trial grounds in Pennsylvania and became an early All-America Selections winner, predating most of the modern hybrid zucchini lines still sold today. It forms a compact, upright bush rather than a sprawling vine, producing straight to slightly curved, smooth dark-green fruit best picked young at 6-8 inches for the most tender, seedless texture. Because it sets fruit heavily and quickly, plants benefit from daily harvesting during peak summer heat to prevent oversized, seedy squash and to keep new blossoms coming. Its open-pollinated seed can be saved true from year to year, unlike the many F1 hybrids that have largely replaced it in seed catalogs. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Forelle Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Forelle is a smaller, ornamental-looking pear well suited to a home orchard with limited space. An old German heirloom pear whose name means trout in German, a reference to the distinctive red speckles that cover its bright yellow skin as it ripens, giving the fruit a striking, ornamental appearance quite different from most solid-colored pears, with crisp, sweet, juicy flesh good for fresh eating. Its small, attractive, speckled fruit and moderate tree size have made it a popular choice for a home orchard wanting an ornamentally distinctive dessert pear alongside its good eating quality. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow in early-to-mid fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly near the stem. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Forellenschluss Lettuce (Flashy Trout's Back, Speckled Trout)
description: Sow seed on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; Forellenschluss is a legendary Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce — the name means 'trout's back' in German for its distinctive pattern of bright red-bronze speckles scattered across brilliantly green leaves, giving each leaf the dappled appearance of a brook trout. Considered one of the most beautiful and best-flavored lettuces in the world, with butter-soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth leaves. Also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back' in the United States. Suitable for both spring and fall, it is less tolerant of summer heat than loose-leaf types; harvest heads when full but before bolting. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Foremanii Skimmia (Heavy-Berrying Female Evergreen Shrub)
description: Foremanii is a long-grown, robust female skimmia valued for its exceptionally heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter once a nearby male plant provides pollen. It builds a broader, denser mound than some of the newer compact female selections, with glossy evergreen leaves that show off clusters of ripe fruit particularly well against the dark foliage. Small white spring flowers precede the berries and add mild fragrance to the shaded border, though the fruit display is the main event on this cultivar. Grow it in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade, and avoid pruning after midsummer so as not to remove the wood that carries the coming winter's berry crop. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Forest Green Curly Parsley
description: Forest Green is a tightly curled parsley selected for its dark, glossy foliage and dense, upright habit that holds its color and vigor later into the season than older curly strains. The deeply ruffled leaves are excellent for garnish work while still offering good fresh-eating flavor, milder than flat-leaf types. It performs well in containers and edging plantings thanks to its compact, uniform growth. Gardeners pick Forest Green when they want a curly parsley with richer color and better heat tolerance than standard moss-curled selections. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Forestburg Saskatoon (Serviceberry)
description: Forestburg is a prairie-bred saskatoon cultivar developed for the harsh growing conditions of the northern Great Plains and Canadian prairies, ripening among the earlier-maturing cultivars in comparative trials. It produces good yields of sweet, almond-flavored, blueberry-like fruit prized for jams, pies, and fresh eating. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and expect it to sucker over time, forming a productive hedgerow if not controlled. It tolerates extreme cold and drought once established, making it a reliable choice where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Forkert Pecan (Papershell Mississippi Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Forkert is a classic Mississippi pecan cultivar valued for its thin, papery shell that cracks out easily in large, whole kernel halves, along with rich flavor and good kernel percentage. It bears precociously and produces consistent crops in the Gulf South, though like many older cultivars it benefits from a fungicide program in wet years to manage pecan scab. Forkert is commonly recommended alongside scab-resistant cultivars in home orchard plantings to diversify harvest timing and pollination. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring on alkaline soils. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Formosana Banana (GCTCV-218, Fusarium Wilt-Resistant Cavendish Somaclone)
description: Formosana, registered from the research line GCTCV-218, is a Giant Cavendish somaclonal variant selected by the Taiwan Banana Research Institute after a farmer noticed it surviving in Fusarium wilt (Panama disease)-infested soil that killed neighboring plants. It has since been adopted in Taiwan, the Philippines, and Mozambique as a Cavendish-type replacement in ground contaminated with the aggressive tropical race 4 strain of the fungus. The fruit is a standard sweet, mild Cavendish-type dessert banana, and the plant otherwise behaves like other AAA Cavendish types, with no particular cold hardiness and susceptibility to pseudostem freeze damage. Its main value for a home garden is peace of mind in soil with a history of banana wilt problems; grow it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and heavy feeding. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Forono Beet (Italian Cylindrical Slicing Beet)
description: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots. Forono is an Italian heirloom beet distinguished by its long, cylindrical, carrot-like shape rather than the typical round beet form, an advantage in the kitchen because its uniform diameter yields evenly sized slices from end to end with almost no waste, and a single root often provides several servings. The deep red flesh is sweet, tender, and free of the pale internal rings some other beets show, and because the roots grow mostly upward out of the soil rather than swelling wide, more roots can be grown in the same row space. Harvest at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, and the tops are also good cooked as greens. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Forskohlii (Indian Coleus)
description: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; forskohlii is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. A relative of ornamental coleus and culinary sage, this fleshy-rooted perennial produces soft, aromatic, gray-green leaves and small blue-purple flowers, but is grown chiefly for its thick, tuberous roots, the source of the compound forskolin studied in traditional Ayurvedic medicine and modern dietary supplements. It tolerates poor, dry, sandy soil and drought better than ornamental coleus relatives, reflecting its native habitat on dry, rocky hillsides in India, and is easy to propagate from stem cuttings or root divisions. Harvest roots for use after the plant has grown for at least one full season, and protect from any frost, since both foliage and roots are damaged by freezing temperatures. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Fort Laramie Strawberry
description: Fort Laramie was bred at the University of Wyoming for extreme winter hardiness and continues to be one of the most cold-tolerant everbearing strawberry cultivars available, surviving open winters in zone 3 with minimal mulch protection. Plants produce a moderate spring flush followed by a lighter but steady crop through summer and into fall, with medium, firm, bright-red berries of good dessert quality. Because it tolerates cold so well, it is a reliable choice for northern Plains and mountain-region gardeners where many everbearing varieties struggle to overwinter. Remove blossoms for the first several weeks after spring planting to encourage strong root and crown establishment before fruiting begins. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Fortamino Rootstock Tomato
description: This vigorous rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite heirloom or hybrid scion to boost its performance, offering better leaf cover to reduce sunscald, more flowers and fruit weight, and improved resistance to soil stresses and diseases. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, then graft when stems are pencil-thick. Keep grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber to heal before hardening off. Transplant after frost into full sun. Support the vigorous vines with sturdy stakes or cages. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Fortex Pole Bean (Extra-Long French Filet Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; provide a sturdy trellis or support structure before planting and harvest regularly while pods are still slender and young. Fortex is considered by many gardeners and chefs to be the finest French filet (haricot vert) style pole bean available — a European heirloom that produces extraordinarily long (10–12 inch), very slender, round-podded, deep green beans with exceptional tenderness and refined flavor that places it far above standard snap beans for fresh eating and French-style preparations. Unlike flat, wide snap beans, Fortex pods are round, very slender (filet-style), and remain tender and flavorful well beyond the size at which most beans become tough — they can be harvested at any point from finger-thin to full pencil thickness and maintain excellent quality. The flavor is genuinely superior, with a rich green bean taste and very fine texture that makes Fortex the preferred bean for blanching, sautéing with garlic and butter, and all preparations where bean quality is the focus. Very productive vines climb 7–9 feet and bear continuously when picked frequently. An outstanding bean for serious vegetable gardeners and those who want restaurant-quality produce from their home garden. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Foster Grapefruit (Historic First Pink-Fleshed Grapefruit)
description: Plant grafted trees in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and mulch to conserve moisture through the long Gulf Coast summer. Foster arose in Florida in the early 1900s as a limb sport on a Walters grapefruit tree, making it one of the earliest pink-fleshed grapefruit ever found and a direct ancestor in the pigmented-grapefruit lineage that later produced Thompson, Ruby Red, and Star Ruby. Its flesh coloring is lighter and less consistent than those later red-fleshed selections, and the fruit still carries a modest number of seeds, but the tree is vigorous, cold-tolerant for a grapefruit, and appeals to gardeners who want a piece of citrus history rather than a modern seedless hybrid. Fruit matures in winter and, like most grapefruit, holds well on the tree and sweetens the longer it hangs. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fourth of July Tomato (Ultra-Early Hybrid Slicing Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Fourth of July is an indeterminate hybrid tomato that holds the distinction of being one of the earliest-producing standard-sized tomatoes available to home gardeners — producing its first ripe fruits approximately 49–55 days after transplanting, roughly the same time that slower varieties are just beginning to set fruit. The name references the plant's ability to provide ripe tomatoes by or before the Fourth of July holiday in northern gardens when planted on schedule. The medium-small (4–6 oz), round, bright red fruits have good sweet-tart tomato flavor for an early variety — notably better than most extremely early types, which often sacrifice flavor for speed. The indeterminate vines continue producing throughout the summer and fall after early harvests, unlike determinates that produce one concentrated crop. Fourth of July is outstanding for gardeners in any climate who want fresh home-grown tomatoes as early as possible, and particularly valuable in Gulf South gardens where early production before summer heat peak extends the harvest season significantly. A practical, reliable early variety that should be in every serious tomato garden alongside a mid-season variety. Matures in 49–55 days from transplant.

name: Fowble Black Walnut
description: Fowble is a named black walnut selection recognized in nut-grower variety trials for a favorable shell-to-kernel ratio that makes cracking noticeably easier than typical wild seedling trees. Grafted trees bear at a younger age and with more consistent annual yield than seedling stock. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and generous spacing clear of juglone-sensitive garden plants. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Fowler Chestnut (UC Davis Large-Nutted European Hybrid Selection)
description: Fowler (UCD 92-359-1) is a European chestnut hybrid selected by K. Ryugo in the University of California, Davis chestnut breeding program and is notable for large nuts, roughly 22 to 25 grams each, with a thin pellicle that peels away easily. Nuts drop free of the bur without the internal shell-invagination problems that trouble some other large-nutted selections. Fowler is pollen-sterile, so it must be interplanted with a compatible, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar to produce a crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fox Grape
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full to partial sun; provide a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence from the start, as fox grape is a vigorous vine that can reach 30 feet and requires strong support to realize its full fruit production potential. Vitis labrusca is the native northeastern grape species that gave rise to the Concord, Catawba, and Niagara cultivated varieties; it produces large, round, purple to amber grape clusters with the characteristic musky, distinctly "foxy" flavor in September and October, beloved by wildlife and humans alike. The dense summer canopy provides excellent nesting habitat and cover for songbirds, and the ripe fruit draws foxes, raccoons, deer, turkeys, and a wide array of frugivorous birds including mockingbirds, catbirds, and thrushes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Foxfibre Cotton (Sally Fox's Naturally Colored Organic Cotton)
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Foxfibre is the trademarked line of naturally colored, organically grown upland cotton developed by California breeder Sally Fox beginning in the 1980s from a chance discovery of brown, pest-resistant cotton seed; through years of selection and crossing with long-staple and Pima lines, Fox produced the first naturally colored cotton fiber strong and long enough to be spun on modern commercial machinery. Foxfibre bolls open in shades of camel, tan, rust-brown, and soft sage green that need no dye, and the plants show useful natural pest resistance. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Foxley Thyme (Cream-Variegated Broadleaf Thyme)
description: Plant in well-drained soil with average fertility in partial shade to full sun; Foxley's broad, rounded leaves are irregularly edged in cream and take on a soft pink blush in cool weather, giving the low mat visual interest well beyond its short spikes of lilac-pink summer flowers. It has a milder, slightly less camphorous flavor than common English thyme, making it a pleasant everyday cooking thyme as well as a groundcover along a shaded path or between shady stepping stones. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and prevent the center from opening up and going woody, and avoid heavy mulch or soggy soil, which this thyme tolerates less well than drought. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Foxtail Rosemary (Dense Congested Bottlebrush-Foliage Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Foxtail bears unusually dense, tightly congested foliage packed along each stem, giving it a distinctive bottlebrush or fox-tail silhouette unlike the more open, spreading branch habit of most rosemary cultivars, making it a novelty specimen for collectors and a striking textural accent in the landscape. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container or raised bed where its unusual form can be appreciated up close. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense new growth. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Foxwhelp Apple (Historic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Foxwhelp is an old, variable seedling-origin variety, so named-clone stock is preferable to seed-grown trees for predictable fruit quality. One of the oldest documented English cider apples, traced back to seventeenth-century Herefordshire, it is a classic bittersharp valued for high acidity balanced with substantial tannin, producing a sharp, vigorous, long-keeping cider prized by traditional cider makers for its aging potential. Its long history has led to several slightly different clonal strains circulating under the same name, so sourcing named, virus-indexed nursery stock rather than seedlings gives the most reliable fruit quality. Harvest in early-to-mid fall, notably earlier than many other classic cider apples, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fragrant-Flowered Garlic (Sweet Garlic Chive)
description: Sow seed or plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this East Asian species closely resembles garlic chives in flavor and use, its flat, garlic-scented leaves harvested fresh for the same culinary purposes, but its white, star-shaped flower umbels carry a notably sweeter fragrance that makes it a worthwhile addition to a pollinator or cutting bed as well as the herb garden. It spreads slowly by offsets into a dense clump and self-sows modestly in favorable conditions. Cut leaves at the base as needed through the growing season, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep plants vigorous. Matures in 75–110 days from seed.

name: Franklim Asparagus (Dutch All-Male Hybrid)
description: Franklim was bred in the Netherlands from a supermale line derived from self-pollinated 'Ruhm von Braunschweig,' making it one of the earliest all-male asparagus hybrids widely grown in Europe. Because every plant is male, beds put no energy into seed production and never develop the volunteer seedling problem common to older open-pollinated strains, so spear production stays concentrated and beds keep a tidy, even stand for years. Spears emerge thick, straight, and closely spaced along the crown, tolerating both traditional green cropping and mounded cultivation for blanched white spears. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and avoid cutting for the first two years so crowns can build the reserves needed for a long productive life. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Franklin Cranberry (Massachusetts Heirloom Hybrid Cranberry)
description: Franklin is a hybrid cranberry developed in the mid-twentieth century at the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station's Cranberry Station in East Wareham, part of the same breeding effort on Cape Cod that produced Stevens and Pilgrim, at a time when growers needed hybrid vines with better vigor and disease tolerance than the old wild bog selections like Early Black and Howes. It bears small-to-medium, round, dark-red berries in modest but dependable yields, and while it was largely superseded commercially by the higher-yielding Stevens, it persists in heirloom bog collections and older Massachusetts marshes for its historical role in the state's cranberry breeding program. Grow it like any cranberry, in strongly acidic (pH 4.0-5.0), constantly moist, sandy-peat bog soil topped with a sand mulch layer to control weeds and encourage rooting along the runners. Vines need several years to establish a full crop but then persist and produce for decades with minimal care beyond steady moisture and acidic fertility. It is a cold-climate plant through and through, requiring a genuine winter dormancy and unsuited to Gulf Coast or other mild-winter regions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Franquette Walnut (Late-Leafing French Walnut, Frost-Safe Walnut, Isère Valley Walnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Franquette requires cross-pollination; the late leafing habit means the catkins emerge significantly later than standard varieties — reducing spring frost damage that can eliminate the entire nut crop in frost-prone sites; Franquette ripens late (October–November), producing medium to large nuts with moderately thin shells and good flavor. Franquette walnut is a French variety with origins in the Isère department of southeastern France, where it was grown as a commercial production variety long before California walnut production began, and was one of the first named walnut varieties introduced to the Pacific Coast of North America in the 1870s and 1880s when California's walnut industry was developing. The variety's most important attribute is its late-leafing phenology — Franquette emerges from dormancy 3–4 weeks later in spring than most other walnut varieties, including Chandler, Hartley, and Serr. This late emergence is critically important in frost-prone regions: walnut catkins (male flowers) and developing leaves are extremely frost-sensitive, and an unexpected late spring frost at the critical bloom period can eliminate the entire nut crop for the season — a problem that Franquette largely avoids due to its delayed bud break. This characteristic made Franquette the variety of choice for sites at higher elevations, more northerly latitudes, or valleys prone to late spring frosts where earlier varieties fail too frequently. Franquette also serves as an important cross-pollinator for Chandler and other protogynous varieties in commercial orchards. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Frantoio Olive
description: Frantoio is a renowned Italian olive prized for producing high-quality oil and rich, dark fruit that ripens mid-season. This evergreen brings old-world Mediterranean character to the garden and tolerates heat and drought once established. Grow a young tree in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, watering sparingly since olives dislike wet roots. Prune to an open framework for light and air, and in marginal climates grow it in a container to shelter from hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Freckles Lettuce (Forellenschluss Romaine, Trout's Back Lettuce)
description: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Freckles lettuce (Austrian name: 'Forellenschluss', meaning 'Trout's Back', also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back') is a traditional Austrian/Central European heirloom romaine-type lettuce with one of the most distinctive and beautiful appearances in the lettuce world — pale green, slightly upright loose-romaine leaves dramatically spotted and splashed with burgundy-red markings in irregular patterns that genuinely resemble the markings of a brook trout's back. Despite its ornamental appearance, Freckles is an excellent eating lettuce with the substantial, crisp, slightly crunchy texture of romaine and mild, sweet, pleasant flavor without bitterness. The visual impact makes it outstanding for decorative vegetable gardens and for using fresh as a centerpiece lettuce. Freckles is moderately heat-tolerant for a lettuce and somewhat slow to bolt, extending the spring harvest window. An outstanding conversation-piece heirloom lettuce that combines genuine beauty with excellent eating quality. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Freckles Romaine Lettuce
description: This 1793 European heirloom romaine has bright green, crisp leaves dappled with striking red freckles and a vase-like habit. The flavor is mildly bitter with a clean finish, and it tolerates heat better than many romaines, resisting bolting. Grow in full sun to partial shade in cool, moist soil, offering afternoon shade in warm spells. Harvest whole heads or pick outer leaves as needed. Succession sow for a steady supply. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Fred Boutin Lavender (Vigorous Silver-Leaved Lavandin)
description: Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, in lean soil amended with coarse grit if the site tends to hold moisture; Fred Boutin is a lavandin hybrid, originally selected in California, prized for its exceptionally broad, dense, silvery-gray foliage mound and reliable production of long, richly fragrant purple-blue flower spikes in early summer. It is one of the more heat- and humidity-tolerant lavandins, making it a workable choice for Gulf South gardeners who have struggled with English lavender, and its large, uniform habit suits mass plantings and low hedges as well as single specimens. Shear the plant back by about a third right after flowering to keep growth compact and prevent the woody, sparse center that develops in unpruned lavenders over time. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Frederick Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Frederick is a vigorous purple-fruited passionfruit cultivar valued for heavy production of aromatic, tart-sweet fruit on fast-growing vines. Like other purple passionfruit types it fruits within the first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant, considerably faster than seed-grown vines, and ripe fruit drops naturally from the vine when ready to pick. Vines are vigorous climbers and need sturdy support along with regular tip-pruning to keep growth directed and manageable rather than sprawling. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily going into winter, since purple passionfruit types are more cold-sensitive than the hardier Possum Purple selection and a hard freeze can kill the vine to the ground or outright. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Fredonia Gooseberry (American-Type Dark Red Disease-Resistant Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Fredonia is an American-type gooseberry, bred from the same disease-resistant Ribes hirtellum lineage used in many modern hardy gooseberry releases, producing dark red, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and much better tolerance of American gooseberry mildew than older European heirloom varieties. The compact, manageable bush fits well into smaller home gardens, and its reliable, moderate productivity makes it a practical choice for growers who want a straightforward, low-fuss gooseberry without extensive mildew management. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for fresh eating, or pick a bit earlier for cooking and preserving, since gooseberries hold well on the bush at multiple ripeness stages. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Fredonia Grape (Early Blue Concord-Type Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system, leaving a couple of strong canes per vine. Fredonia was bred at the Geneva, New York agricultural research station specifically to ripen earlier than Concord, giving gardeners in shorter-season climates a reliable blue slip-skin grape with the same rich, musky-sweet 'foxy' Labrusca flavor prized in grape juice and jelly. It is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator, producing large clusters of blue-black berries in late summer to early fall. Because it is a high-chill Labrusca type, it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease-tolerant muscadines or hybrid bunch grapes are more reliable choices. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Freedom Apple (Scab-Immune Cornell Disease-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Freedom was released by Cornell University's Geneva breeding program and is field-immune to apple scab, one of the most damaging fungal diseases of apple in humid climates, while also showing high resistance to cedar apple rust and powdery mildew. The medium-large, red-striped fruit is crisp and juicy with a tart, tangy flavor good for fresh eating and cooking, and it stores reasonably well for a few months under cool conditions. Because it needs so little disease-management spraying, Freedom is a strong choice for a low-input or organic home orchard. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety for good fruit set, and harvest once fruit has developed full color and comes away easily from the spur with a gentle twist. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fremont Cauliflower (Self-Blanching Summer Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil. Fremont is a self-blanching hybrid whose upright inner leaves curl naturally over the forming curd, shielding it from sunlight and keeping the head bright white without the usual step of tying leaves up by hand. It performs reliably through the warmer, less predictable conditions of a summer planting, forming smooth, dense, well-domed heads. Harvest as soon as the curd is tight and fully formed, since cauliflower heads can quickly become ricey or loose if left too long once mature. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: French Breakfast Radish
description: This elegant heirloom produces elongated roots with bright crimson tops and clean white tips, offering a tender, mildly peppery bite. Direct sow seed a half inch deep and keep the bed consistently moist for quick, uniform roots. Thin promptly so each radish has room, and succession sow every week or two for continuous harvest. Pull the roots young while crisp, as radishes left too long turn pithy and sharp; they excel in cool spring and fall weather. Matures in 23–30 days from seed.

name: French Breakfast Radish (Elongated Red-and-White Radish)
description: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; French Breakfast is a classic European heirloom radish with a history dating to the early nineteenth century — producing oblong-to-cylindrical, 3–4 inch roots with a distinctive two-tone color pattern: brilliant scarlet-red over the upper two-thirds grading to crisp white at the tip. The elongated, elegant shape is distinctly different from the standard round red radish and makes French Breakfast instantly recognizable in the garden and at market. The flavor is mild and crisp — somewhat milder than globe radishes when harvested young, with a light, clean pepper-radish flavor that becomes stronger and more pungent if roots are left in the ground too long or grown during warm weather. Traditional French usage was to eat them dipped in butter with a pinch of salt at breakfast — hence the name. In zone 9, French Breakfast radishes are a cool-season crop performing best September through April; they bolt and become pungent in the summer heat. Succession sow every 2 weeks for continuous harvest. Thin to 2–3 inches for the best root development. Harvest when roots reach 3/4–1 inch diameter for the mildest flavor. Matures in 23–30 days from seed.

name: French Filet Bush Bean
description: These slender French filet beans, or haricots verts, are pencil-thin at about a quarter inch across and 4 inches long, with exceptional tenderness. Pick them young and often for the best texture and to keep the compact bush plants producing. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, since seeds rot in cold, wet ground. Water at the base to keep foliage dry and reduce disease. Steam or saute lightly to preserve their delicate flavor. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: French Fingerling Potato (Pink-Skinned Fingerling with Rose-Marbled Flesh)
description: Plant seed potato pieces 3–4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest when vines begin to die back. French Fingerling is valued primarily for its visual distinction and culinary versatility: the combination of rose-pink skin and cream-yellow flesh with distinctive pink marbling through the interior makes French Fingerling one of the most visually striking fingerling varieties when halved or sliced — the pink marbling pattern within the creamy flesh is unique and makes the roasted or halved potato distinctly attractive in presentations. The texture is waxy and firm — a characteristic of fingerling potato varieties that have lower starch content than baking types (Russet Burbank) and retain their shape well through cooking. This waxy texture makes fingerlings the preferred choice for roasting whole (they develop a crispy exterior while staying firm inside), for potato salads (they don't become mushy when dressed), and for sautéed preparations where pieces need to hold their shape. French Fingerling's flavor is described as nutty, sweet, and complex — more interesting than the relatively neutral flavor of standard Russet types, with a richness that farmers market customers and restaurant chefs find particularly valuable. The variety performs well for small-scale and home garden production, producing enough tubers per plant for household use without requiring the large-scale inputs (cool storage, extensive land) of commercial Russet production. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: French Gray Shallot
description: Plant small bulbs (sets) pointy-end up, 1 inch deep and 6–9 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in early spring or fall; the true French gray shallot (échalote grise) is considered the premier shallot of French haute cuisine, with a distinctive grayish-purple skin, elongated teardrop shape, and more complex, less harsh flavor than common shallots. Each planted bulb divides into a cluster of 8–12 daughter bulbs by harvest time in midsummer when the tops fall over. Lift, clean, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 2–3 weeks before storing. Save the smallest bulbs as next year's planting sets. Do not overwater — shallots are prone to rot in wet soils. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: French Green Lentil (Puy Lentil)
description: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in. This variety takes its name from the volcanic plateau around Le Puy-en-Velay in France's Auvergne region, where a legally protected growing area produces small, marbled slate-green lentils famous for holding their shape and delivering a peppery, mineral flavor after cooking. Skip heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods, and let the sparse, wiry plants lean on light twiggy brush if needed. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have turned tan and papery, then dry and thresh before storing the seed. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: French Lace Lemon Geranium (Cream-Variegated Compact Scented Pelargonium)
description: French Lace pairs the same crinkled, fan-shaped, lemon-scented foliage typical of lemon geranium with a striking creamy-white leaf margin that gives the small, dense plant an eye-catching, frosted look even when not in bloom, making it as much a foliage accent for mixed containers as a culinary herb. Its more compact, restrained growth compared to larger green-leaved lemon geranium cultivars suits it well to smaller pots, window boxes, and the front of an herb garden bed. Root stem cuttings in a well-drained mix and grow in partial shade to full sun; variegated pelargoniums generally hold their leaf pattern best with a little protection from the most intense midday sun, which can scorch the pale leaf margins. In zones 9-11 grow as a perennial sub-shrub outdoors; elsewhere overwinter as a container plant in a bright, cool indoor spot, watering sparingly through winter dormancy. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: French Lavender (Fringed Lavender)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; French lavender is a distinctly different lavender species from English lavender, immediately recognizable by its linear, gray-green leaves with serrated, tooth-like margins along their length — the dentata name refers directly to these toothed leaf edges. The oblong flower spikes are topped with small, pale-purple, feathery bracts and produce a strong, somewhat medicinal-aromatic scent. In zones 8-11, it blooms nearly year-round — producing flowers in almost every month — making it by far the longest-blooming lavender species and an invaluable year-round pollinator plant in mild climates. Native to rocky Mediterranean hillsides and the Canary Islands, it thrives in the heat, drought, and alkaline soils of Gulf Coast and California gardens where English lavender can struggle with summer humidity. An excellent choice for low hedges, herb gardens, and companion planting in drought-tolerant borders where a near-perpetual lavender bloom is desired. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: French Mission Coffee
description: Brought from Ethiopia to the Congo basin and the Great Lakes region of East Africa in the early twentieth century by French Catholic missionaries, this Typica-type landrace became the genetic foundation for much of the Arabica coffee still grown today in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, and Burundi. It shares the tall, open, willowy growth habit typical of unimproved Typica-derived lines, along with a sweet, clean cup and only modest resistance to leaf rust and berry disease. Cultivate it with the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, dappled shade, and consistent warmth other heirloom Arabica types require, and allow extra headroom since it grows larger than compact modern hybrids. Because seed lots are less standardized than named commercial hybrids, expect some natural variability in vigor and cup character between individual plants. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: French Prune Plum (Prune d'Agen, Classic Drying Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, though a nearby pollinator can increase yields. French Prune, known in its native France as Prune d'Agen, is the historic variety behind essentially the entire California and worldwide dried-prune industry, prized for exceptionally high natural sugar content that allows the small to medium, deep purple-blue oval fruit to be dried whole, pit and all, into the classic wrinkled prune without added sugar or elaborate processing. Fresh off the tree the rich, sweet, dense flesh is also excellent for eating out of hand, baking, and preserves, though the variety's fame rests on its drying quality. Harvest when fruit is fully ripe and soft, since sugar content peaks at full ripeness; for drying, halve or leave whole and dehydrate at low heat until leathery and shelf-stable. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: French Red Shallot (Copper-Red Skinned True Shallot)
description: Plant individual bulbs pointed-end-up, just below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 6-8 inches apart to allow each bulb to multiply into a cluster. French Red produces clusters of small, round-to-oval bulbs with distinctive coppery-red skin and pale purple-tinged flesh, carrying the rich, complex, mild-pungent flavor that distinguishes true shallots from ordinary onions and makes them prized in French cooking. Grow much like garlic, keeping soil evenly moist through bulb development and reducing water as the tops begin to yellow and fall over. Harvest when most of the foliage has died back, cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks, then store in a cool, dry location; shallots typically store longer than onions of similar size. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: French Slenderette Bush Bean
description: This compact haricot vert produces slender, stringless pods with fine flavor on tidy dwarf bush plants ideal for small spaces and containers. Sow seed about an inch deep directly in warm soil, as beans dislike transplanting. Keep moisture even through flowering and pod set, and avoid handling wet foliage to reduce disease. Harvest the pencil-thin pods often while young and tender to keep the plants producing over several weeks. Matures in 53–60 days from seed.

name: French Sorrel (Buckler-Leaved Sorrel)
description: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; French sorrel is more drought-tolerant than garden sorrel and thrives in poor, well-drained soils — rich, moist soil produces rank growth with coarser flavor. Rumex scutatus is a low-growing, somewhat sprawling European perennial herb with small, distinctive, shield-shaped or hastate (arrowhead-shaped) leaves that have a milder, more refined, less harsh acid flavor than the common garden sorrel (R. acetosa) and are preferred by many chefs for their superior taste — it is the traditional sorrel used in fine French cuisine and is sometimes called "true French sorrel." It is an excellent perennial groundcover in the kitchen garden, spilling attractively over path edges and walls; unlike R. acetosa it tolerates dry, rocky conditions. Harvest the small leaves continuously and remove flower stalks to prevent self-seeding. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: French Tarragon
description: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; French tarragon is one of the defining herbs of classical French cuisine, with long, narrow, glossy dark-green leaves that carry an intense, distinctive anise-like flavor irreplaceable in béarnaise sauce, fines herbes blends, tarragon vinegar, and chicken dishes. It does not produce viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively — any plant sold as 'tarragon' from seed is the inferior Russian tarragon (A. dracunculus) with little flavor. Harvest by snipping stem tips regularly from spring through fall; the plant dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges from the roots in spring. Divide established clumps every 2–3 years in spring, replanting vigorous outer portions to maintain flavor intensity. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: French Thyme (Narrow-Leaf Culinary Thyme)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens the plant's life and dilutes flavor. French Thyme is a narrow, gray-green-leaved culinary thyme selection, distinguished from broader-leaved common thyme by its more delicate texture and milder, sweeter flavor, making it a favorite of classically trained cooks for bouquet garni, herbes de Provence blends, and dishes where a subtler thyme flavor is desired. The small, upright, woody-based subshrub bears tiny pale lavender-pink flowers in early summer that attract bees, and the foliage can be harvested year-round in mild climates, though flavor is best just before flowering. Shear lightly after flowering and again in late summer to keep the plant compact and prevent it from becoming leggy and woody; replace plants every 3-4 years, as thyme naturally declines with age. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Frenzy Frisee Endive
description: 'Frenzy' is a fast, uniform frisee-type endive with finely dissected, frizzy leaves and improved bolt resistance that lets it be direct sown in spring as well as in the late-summer window most curly endives need. Heads self-blanch as the deeply cut outer leaves arch over the pale, feathery heart, though tying the outer leaves closed for the last week or two before harvest produces a larger blanched center. Its quicker 45 to 55 day cycle and heat tolerance make it more forgiving of an early sowing than older frisee varieties. Harvest whole heads at the base once the centers are tight, or pick individual outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop while the heart keeps developing. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Fresno Pepper
description: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm mix at 80°F and pot up once seedlings have two true leaves; transplant to the garden after last frost. Fresno peppers resemble jalapeños but are slightly thinner-walled, fruitier in flavor, and ripen from green to bright red, with heat increasing as they mature (2,500–10,000 Scoville units). Harvest green fruits at 70 days for a jalapeño substitute, or ripen fully to red for a sweeter, hotter pepper that is excellent in hot sauces and salsas. Consistent deep watering (rather than frequent shallow watering) produces the best quality fruit and reduces stress-induced heat spikes. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Friar Plum (Dark-Skinned California Japanese Plum with Mild Sweet Amber Flesh)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit to 4–5 inches. Harvest when skin is fully dark purple-black and fruit gives slightly under firm pressure. Friar Plum is a California-developed Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) released by the University of California Cooperative Extension in the 1960s as part of a systematic program of plum variety evaluation and selection for California commercial production — a program that produced several varieties (Santa Rosa, Friar, Laroda, Casselman) that became mainstays of California plum production and eventually found their way into home garden cultivation throughout the United States. Friar is distinguished by its very dark, near-black skin — the dark purple-black coloring that covers the entire fruit surface at maturity — contrasting with the amber-yellow flesh beneath, which creates a dramatic visual contrast when the fruit is cut. The skin color of Friar is among the darkest of any common Japanese plum variety. The flesh is firm, sweet, and mildly flavored with moderate acidity — less acid than Santa Rosa — creating a mild, sweet eating character that appeals to consumers who prefer less tangy plum flavor. The fruit is large (often 2–2.5 inches), globe-shaped, and produced in good quantity on a moderately vigorous tree. Friar's late ripening (July in California, slightly earlier in the humid South due to the longer season) helps extend the Japanese plum harvest season beyond the earlier-ripening varieties, providing fresh market plums during a period when earlier types have finished. In zone 9, Friar benefits from the long growing season but requires adequate chill to set reliably. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Friariello Pepper (Neapolitan Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Friariello is a traditional Neapolitan frying pepper whose name derives from the Italian verb for frying, reflecting centuries of use in southern Italian home kitchens. Tall, vigorous plants bear small, tri-lobed, thin-walled pods only a few inches long that mature from green to bright red, with a sweet flavor and no measurable heat. The classic preparation fries the whole pepper, seeds and skin included, in olive oil with garlic until blistered, then finishes it with tomato and fresh basil. Because the plants grow taller and set a heavier fruit load than many bell-type sweet peppers, staking or caging helps keep the brittle branches from snapping under the weight. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Frisee Endive
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Frisee is the fine-leaved, deeply curled, frizzy form of curly endive — a classic French bistro salad ingredient produced by its pale, blanched interior heart surrounded by a halo of fine, frizzy dark-green outer leaves. The pale interior (the blanched portion) has a mild, gently bitter, nutty flavor that is the defining taste of the classic frisee salad with lardons and a warm poached egg — one of the most recognizable French bistro dishes. The dark green outer leaves are more bitter and are usually removed or used for cooking. Frisee blanches naturally when the outer leaves overlap and shade the center, but deliberate blanching (tying the outer leaves for 1–2 weeks before harvest) produces a larger, more uniform pale center. In zone 9 frisee is a fall-through-winter crop that produces its characteristic delicate, pale center in the cool, short-day conditions from November through February. Matures in 55–70 days from transplant.

name: Frisée (Curly Endive, Fine Curled Endive)
description: Direct sow or transplant into moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; frisée (curly endive or fine curled endive) is the distinctive French salad green with deeply cut, finely fringed, pale green to yellowish leaves that create a loose, finely textured head with a pleasantly bitter flavor — one of the defining ingredients of classic French and Belgian cuisine. Unlike its flat-leaved cousin escarole, frisée has intensely ruffled, narrow, spiky-looking leaves that form a sprawling head; the outer leaves are dark green and quite bitter, while the interior (naturally or artificially blanched by excluding light from the heart for 7–10 days) turns pale yellow and becomes substantially more tender and mild. Frisée is the traditional green in salade lyonnaise (the classic Lyon salad with poached egg, lardons, and mustard vinaigrette) and in the Belgian warm salad tradition. The moderately bitter flavor pairs beautifully with rich dressings, warm bacon vinaigrettes, and strong cheeses. In zone 9, frisée is grown as a fall-through-winter crop when cool temperatures bring out its best flavor; summer production results in extremely bitter, loose plants that quickly bolt. Extremely cold-hardy once established, tolerating frosts to about 22°F. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Frontenac Grape (Cold-Hardy Riparia-Derived Red Wine Grape)
description: Frontenac was released by the University of Minnesota from a Landot 4511 by Vitis riparia cross, and its riparia parentage gives it exceptional hardiness to roughly -35°F, making it a mainstay for upper-Midwest and Canadian vineyards. The vine is vigorous, productive, and reliably winter-hardy without hilling, but the fruit carries very high natural acidity that typically needs to be balanced through deacidification or blending during winemaking. Berries are small, black, and produce a deep ruby wine with cherry and dried-cranberry character; the foliage also colors attractively red-purple in autumn. Prune to a bilateral cordon or cane system and thin fruit clusters in high-vigor years to concentrate flavor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Frontenac Gris Grape (Cold-Hardy Gray-Skinned White Wine Grape)
description: This gray-skinned bud sport of Frontenac was released by the University of Minnesota and shares its parent's exceptional riparia-derived cold hardiness while producing an aromatic white wine with notes of apricot and citrus rather than Frontenac's deep red. It buds and ripens on a similar schedule to standard Frontenac and shows the same strong resistance to fungal disease and winter injury. Fruit can develop high sugar levels for late-harvest or dessert-style wines if left on the vine, though growers should watch for excessive acid drop in warm years. Like its parent, it benefits from cluster thinning to balance yield against flavor concentration. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: Fronteras Strawberry (Crown Rot and Mildew-Resistant Short-Day Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Fronteras is a short-day strawberry from the University of California, Davis breeding program with a documented, unusually broad disease-resistance package, including resistance to Macrophomina crown rot, an emerging soil-borne disease that has become a significant problem in strawberry production, plus moderate resistance to powdery mildew, Verticillium wilt, and Phytophthora crown rot. This combination of resistances makes it a strong choice for gardeners whose beds have struggled with soil-borne disease in previous strawberry plantings. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds for the best results. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Frost Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Early-Ripening Variegated Kolomikta Kiwi)
description: Frost is a female Actinidia kolomikta selection notable for bearing fruit unusually early after planting and ripening earlier in the season than most other kolomikta cultivars, typically in early to mid-August. It produces good crops of medium to large, bright green, very sweet fruit high in vitamin C, alongside foliage with distinct pink-edged variegation for ornamental appeal. As a dioecious vine it needs a separate male kolomikta selection, such as Pasha, planted within range for cross-pollination and fruit set. Like other kolomikta selections, it is exceptionally cold hardy, tolerating winter lows to around -40F. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Frost Owari Satsuma (Nucellar Cold-Hardy Owari Strain)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and water deeply and regularly during the growing season while allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings. Selected from seedling Owari trees for improved vigor and slightly larger fruit, Frost Owari bears the same seedless, loose-skinned, richly sweet mandarins from October into December on a small, spreading tree well suited to containers. Mature, dormant trees are among the most cold-tolerant of all edible citrus, shrugging off brief dips to roughly 15-20F, though trees under three years old should still be covered or lighted during hard freezes. Its reliability and wide availability through mainstream citrus nurseries have made it one of the most commonly planted satsuma strains for zone 8b-9a home orchards. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Frost Peach Tree
description: Frost is a hardy peach bred for cooler climates, offering sweet, juicy fruit and notable resistance to peach leaf curl. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and it tolerates spring frosts better than many varieties. It is self-fruitful, producing a crop from a single tree. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape and thin the young fruit to improve size. Water deeply during fruit development for the best harvest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Frostproof Guava (Cold-Hardy Guava)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Frostproof is a compact, shrubby guava cultivar selected for better cold tolerance than standard tropical guava types, making it one of the more realistic guava choices for in-ground planting at the cooler edge of guava-growing range. Fruit is smaller than many named guava cultivars but still sweet and fragrant, with pink-blushed flesh good for fresh eating and preserves. Because it stays more compact than most guavas even at maturity, Frostproof also works well trained as a large container specimen that can be moved under cover during a hard freeze. As with other guavas, root hardiness exceeds top-growth hardiness, so established plants generally resprout from the base after a freeze that kills the canopy; mulch the root zone heavily each winter and prune out dead wood once new growth confirms which stems survived. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Frotscher Pecan (Frotscher's Egg Shell, Historic 1840s Louisiana Pecan)
description: Frotscher, sometimes recorded historically as Frotscher's Egg Shell, was selected and propagated near New Orleans in the 1840s, making it one of the earliest pecan cultivars ever given a name and grafted for orchard use, decades before most of today's commercial cultivars existed. It produces a notably large, thin-shelled nut with a high kernel percentage typical of the old Louisiana river-bottom selections that first drew commercial attention to pecans as an orchard crop. Give it deep, moist bottomland-type soil and full sun, and expect a large, spreading tree that needs a compatible pollinator for consistent nut set. Because of its age and rarity today, Frotscher is grown mostly by pecan-history enthusiasts and heritage orchards rather than commercial growers, who favor newer scab-resistant selections. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Frugana Sea Buckthorn (Ornamental-Fruiting Seaberry)
description: Frugana is a vigorous, heavy-cropping female sea buckthorn valued as much for its ornamental show as for its harvest, with graceful gray-green foliage that turns silvery beneath and branches that become laden with bright orange berries by early September. It is one of the larger-growing named selections, forming a substantial multi-stemmed shrub or small tree over time, so give it room compared with more compact cultivars. As with all sea buckthorn it is dioecious and needs a male plant nearby to set fruit, and its nitrogen-fixing roots make it well suited to poor, sandy, or windswept sites. Because ripe berries cling tightly to the stem, most growers harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches to strip or freeze rather than picking by hand. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fruitless Mulberry (Non-Fruiting Male Shade Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, siting away from walks and drives since the wide-spreading surface roots can heave paving as the tree matures. Fruitless is a male clone of white mulberry selected specifically because it produces no berries, giving gardeners the dense, fast-growing shade canopy and glossy foliage of mulberry without the mess of dropped, staining fruit that plagues fruiting seedling trees. It grows rapidly into a broad, rounded shade tree that tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban pollution once established, making it a popular low-maintenance choice for patios, driveways, and parking areas where fruiting trees would be a nuisance. Prune while young to establish strong scaffold branching, since mature wood can be brittle in storms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fry Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun alongside a self-fertile pollinizer variety; Fry is a bronze muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station and released in 1972, consistently regarded as the best fresh-eating muscadine available — the benchmark for table-quality muscadine grapes. The berries are extraordinarily large (up to 1.5 inches in diameter, one of the largest of any muscadine), bronze-gold at maturity with a beautiful appearance, excellent mild-sweet flavor, and thinner skin than most muscadines, making fresh eating more pleasant. Fry's principal limitation is its lack of self-fertility: it will produce essentially no fruit without a compatible self-fertile pollinizer planted within range. This has made it less popular commercially where single-variety plantings are common, but in home gardens where a pollinator is easily added, Fry is unmatched for fresh table quality. The vines are vigorous, productive once pollinated, and disease-resistant. Harvest when berries are fully bronze-gold and yield to gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fry Seedless Muscadine Grape (Seedless Sport of Classic Fry)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun. Fry Seedless is a seedless sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine, retaining the same large size and sweet, richly flavored fruit that made the original Fry a Southern favorite, but without the large seeds most muscadines carry, making it more convenient for fresh eating. As is typical of seedless muscadine selections, individual berries run somewhat smaller than the seeded parent variety, a common tradeoff in muscadine breeding, but the flavor and eating quality remain excellent. Unlike seeded Fry, which requires a separate pollinizer, Fry Seedless is self-fertile, simplifying planting for gardeners who want just one or two vines. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily with a gentle tug, typically over an extended late-summer season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Fuding Dabaicha Tea (Fuding Da Bai Cha)
description: Originating in Fuding, Fujian Province, China, Fuding Dabaicha ('Fuding Large White Tea') is the primary cultivar behind China's most prized white teas, including Silver Needle and White Peony, thanks to unusually large, plump, downy silver-tipped buds that give white tea its signature fuzzy appearance and delicate sweetness. It is also processed into green tea in the same region. Vigorous and productive compared to many fine Chinese cultivars, it responds well to careful hand plucking of only the youngest bud and adjacent leaf for top-grade white tea, with coarser plucking used for green tea production. Grow it with the same acidic, humus-rich soil and partial shade favored by other tea cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fuerte Avocado (Former Commercial Standard Avocado, Type B Large Green Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Fuerte performs best with a Type A companion (Hass, Mexicola) for maximum fruit set; mulch heavily over roots; apply balanced citrus/avocado fertilizer in spring; Fuerte ripens from November through March in California, producing large, pear-shaped, dark green fruits that remain green (do not darken) when ripe — test ripeness by cutting, as the skin color is not a reliable indicator. Fuerte avocado was the dominant commercial avocado variety in California and globally from the 1920s through the 1950s, named for the Spanish word 'strong' after the tree demonstrated remarkable cold-hardiness during a destructive California frost in 1913, surviving when other avocado varieties died — leading to its commercial selection and widespread planting. For three decades, Fuerte was the avocado that most Americans encountered in markets, setting the standard for avocado flavor and quality. It was gradually displaced by Hass after Hass's commercial introduction, primarily because Hass's pebbled skin turns black when ripe (providing a reliable harvest indicator that Fuerte's green skin lacks) and Hass handles shipping better. The Fuerte fruit itself is large, pear-shaped with smooth, thin, bright green skin and rich, creamy, pale green flesh with a moderately nutty, rich flavor — many avocado connoisseurs consider its flavor superior to Hass, with a richer oil content and more complex character, though the harvest timing challenge (no color change at ripeness) makes it less practical for commercial sales. A winter-ripening variety (November–March in California), it extends fresh avocado season when Hass is between crops. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fuggle Hops (Classic English Aroma Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Fuggle is a classic English hop cultivar dating to the late 19th century, long the backbone of traditional English bitters and other cask ales, prized for its mild, earthy, woody, and slightly minty aroma that defines the classic English hop character as distinctly as Cascade defines American craft brewing. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring, climbing 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; cones ripen in late summer and should be picked when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for use. Fuggle prefers a cool, temperate, long-day growing season and struggles with the intense heat and humidity of Gulf South summers, so site it in the coolest, most open-air spot available and expect reduced yield and cone quality compared to traditional English or Pacific Northwest production. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Fuji Apple
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil in the best-drained location available; Fuji was developed in Japan in the 1930s and released in 1962 as a cross between Red Delicious and Ralls Janet — it has become one of the most popular apple varieties in the world and is now the leading apple in Japan, China, and a major variety in American specialty markets. The large, firm, round fruits with distinctive pink-red and yellow-green streaked skin contain exceptionally crisp, dense, very sweet flesh with a high sugar content (typically 15–18 brix) and mild, pleasant apple flavor that has made Fuji the preferred apple for fresh eating in Asian markets and increasingly in mainstream American grocery stores. The flavor is distinctly sweeter than Gala or Honeycrisp with low acidity. In zone 9 Fuji is a marginal but feasible apple choice in areas that receive adequate winter chilling — inland areas and northern parts of zone 9 typically accumulate more chill hours than coastal areas. Low-chill Fuji selections ('Fuji Babe', 'Low-Chill Fuji') have been developed for warmer climates. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Fuji Apple Tree
description: Fuji is a Japanese-bred apple beloved for its exceptionally sweet flavor and crisp, dense texture that stores well. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide a compatible pollinating apple nearby since Fuji is not self-fertile. Prune each dormant season to a central-leader or open form for light and air, and thin fruit clusters to improve size. Water consistently during establishment and dry spells. Fuji ripens late in the season, so allow ample time on the tree for full sweetness. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fukushu Kumquat Tree
description: Fukushu is a compact kumquat producing small oval citrus with an edible sweet rind and tart flesh, well suited to container growing. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and water when the top inch dries, avoiding both drought stress and soggy roots. In climates with frost, keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot for winter. Feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Full Heart Escarole
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Full Heart Batavian is the classic escarole for Italian home cooking — a broad-leaved chicory endive forming a large, dense head with a characteristic self-blanching, creamy-yellow interior heart surrounded by darker outer leaves. The center heart has the mildest, most tender flavor of any escarole or endive type; the outer leaves are more bitter and are often removed or reserved for long-cooked soups and braises. Full Heart Batavian is the standard escarole used in Italian-American cooking — the primary green in Italian wedding soup (minestra maritata), in braised escarole with white beans and garlic, and as a pizza topping. The dense, substantial head stores well for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator after harvest, making escarole one of the most practical winter greens for home cooks. In zone 9 the fall growing season from August transplants produces excellent heads by November; the plants are cold-hardy and withstand light frosts that improve flavor. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Full Moon Pumpkin (Giant White Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in heavily composted soil, spacing hills at least 8-10 feet apart to accommodate the large-fruited vines. Full Moon is a giant white pumpkin producing smooth, lightly sutured fruit that commonly reaches 60-90 pounds and stands roughly 3 feet tall by 2 feet wide under good growing conditions, with a long 120-day-plus season needed to size up fully. The pale rind is retained best when fruit is left to mature fully on the vine rather than harvested early, and consistent deep watering through fruit set is important to avoid rind cracking on such large specimens. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has hardened completely, and handle carefully since the size and weight make the fruit prone to bruising and stem breakage. Matures in 120–130 days from seed.

name: Fuller's Teasel (Dyer's Teasel)
description: Fuller's teasel is grown not for fiber or pigment itself but as the traditional tool used to process fiber: its dense, egg-shaped seed heads are ringed with stiff, backward-hooking spines that were historically mounted on frames or wheels ('teasel gigs') and dragged across woven woolen cloth to raise a soft nap before shearing it smooth, a step still done by hand by small-scale fiber artisans and hand-weavers today. It grows as a coarse biennial rosette the first year, then sends up a tall, spiny-stemmed flower stalk topped with cone-like flower heads in its second summer; cut the mature seed heads once they have dried to a stiff tan-brown color and their small purple flowers have fully finished, then hang them to finish curing before use. This cultivated form is selected for firmer, straighter, more strongly recurved bracts than its weedy relative, common or wild teasel (Dipsacus fullonum), whose softer, straighter spines make it far less useful for napping cloth. Because the species can self-sow aggressively, cut and remove spent seed heads promptly if naturalizing beyond a contained bed is a concern. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Fuseau Jerusalem Artichoke (Classic French Smooth-Skinned Sunchoke)
description: Plant whole or cut seed tubers, each with at least one or two eyes, about 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once the soil can be worked in spring. Because sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground, choose a bed where the planting can be permanently contained or is not a problem to leave in place. Fuseau is a long-established French heirloom named for its elongated, relatively smooth, club-shaped tubers, which are far easier to scrub and peel than the knobby, eye-covered tubers typical of unnamed Jerusalem artichoke stock. Its tall late-summer sunflower-like blooms are followed by a fall and winter tuber harvest that continues after light frosts, and the tubers themselves have the same nutty, sweet flavor common to the species, sweetening further after cold exposure. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Futo Spindle Bitter Melon
description: A traditional Japanese heirloom bitter melon prized for exceptional heat tolerance and vigorous, dense vining growth. The long, spindle-shaped fruit has deeply ridged, heavily warted dark-green skin and can reach 7-12 inches, ripening to orange-yellow if left unpicked. Harvest while still firm and green for the classic assertively bitter flavor used in goya champuru and other Okinawan stir-fries, or let a few fruit fully color for milder, sweeter eating. Its climbing habit and heat tolerance make it a good choice for a hot, humid summer trellis planting where other bitter melon types struggle. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Futura 75 Hemp (Fiber-Type Industrial Hemp)
