description: Drill seed at a high density of roughly 25-30 lb per acre to force tall, slender, largely unbranched stalks, since crowded stands are essential to good fiber quality in this cultivar. 'Futura 75' was bred in France for bast fiber production and has been used in several US university trials, including early Kentucky industrial hemp research plots, as a benchmark fiber-type cultivar because of its reliable low-THC compliance and strong stalk yield. Plants can reach 10 to 13 feet in a full season under good conditions, considerably taller than dual-purpose or grain cultivars, and stems become increasingly coarse and woody as flowering finishes. Harvest for fiber at the onset of flowering, when bast fiber content and quality peak, then ret and process the stalks as with any bast fiber crop; a hemp growing license and pre-harvest THC testing are required in nearly all US jurisdictions. Matures in 130–150 days from seed.

name: Fuyu Persimmon (Non-Astringent Flat Asian Persimmon for Gulf Coast)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuyu is the most popular non-astringent Asian persimmon for home garden production — producing flat, tomato-shaped, medium-large (4–6 oz), deep-orange fruits that can be eaten while still firm, like an apple, without the intense mouth-puckering astringency that makes other persimmons (including Hachiya) inedible until fully soft. The flat shape, firm texture when ripe, sweet flavor, and brilliant orange color make Fuyu the most practical and versatile fresh-eating persimmon. Fuyu ripens in October–November in zone 9, producing fruit after the summer growing season has ended and providing sweet, colorful fresh fruit at a time when few other locally grown fruits are available. The attractive deciduous tree puts on a spectacular fall display of orange to red fall foliage as the persimmons ripen — a visual combination that is outstanding in the autumn landscape. Fuyu is self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator tree) and produces reliable annual crops on mature trees with minimal pest and disease pressure. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and require minimal fertilizer input — excessive nitrogen encourages vegetative growth at the expense of fruit production. Japanese persimmons (D. kaki) require approximately 100–200 chill hours — readily accumulated in Gulf South winters — making Fuyu well-adapted to zone 9 production. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Fuyu Persimmon Tree
description: Fuyu is a non-astringent persimmon whose sweet, firm fruit can be eaten crisp like an apple while still firm. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit develops, then it tolerates some drought. Prune in dormancy to build a strong framework, since heavy fruit can break branches. The fruit ripens in fall and holds on the tree well after the leaves drop, creating an ornamental display. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Fuzzy Gourd (Hairy Melon, Mo Qua)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist soil in full sun, and grow on a sturdy trellis to keep the fuzzy fruit clean and straight. Fuzzy gourd is a smaller, fast-maturing variety group of the same species as winter melon, but it is harvested young while the cylindrical fruit is still tender, pale green, and covered in the soft fuzz that gives it its name, rather than being left to mature into the large, waxy-coated winter melon. It is a staple vegetable in Cantonese and Southeast Asian cooking, prized for its mild flavor and tender texture in soups, stir-fries, and braises, where it readily absorbs the flavors of broth, meat, and aromatics. Harvest fruits at 6-10 inches long while the skin fuzz is still soft, since older fruit develops a tougher, less palatable rind; frequent picking encourages continued production through the hot summer months that this heat-loving vine relishes. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Fuzzy Kiwi
description: Fuzzy kiwi (the standard grocery-store kiwifruit) requires a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days. Like hardy kiwi, it is dioecious and requires male and female plants — one male pollinates up to 8 females. Train vines on a T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each dormant season to manage the vigorous growth. Harvest in late fall before hard frost when the seeds have turned black and the flesh is tender; fruit ripens off the vine. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Fwang Tung Carambola (Starfruit)
description: Plant a grafted specimen in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a warm, sheltered site out of harsh drying winds since young leaves are sensitive to cold snaps. This widely grown Thai-origin selection produces heavy clusters of sweet, low-acid, deeply ribbed fruit and tends to bear more prolifically than seedling carambola trees. Because established wood can suffer damage below the upper 20s, Gulf Coast growers plant it in the warmest microclimate on the property or keep smaller trees in containers that can be moved under cover during freezes. Regular irrigation through fruit development produces juicier, less fibrous fruit. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: GA-866 Jujube (USDA Chico Sweet Crisp Jujube)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season. GA-866 originated at the USDA Plant Introduction Station in Chico, California, from an unrecorded cross evaluated during the agency's mid-1900s jujube trials, and was never given a formal cultivar name before the breeding program was discontinued — growers and nurseries have since propagated and sold it simply under its USDA accession number. The fruit is elongated and plump, ripening to a shiny reddish-brown skin with dense, crisp, apple-like flesh and a concentrated sweetness that many growers rate among the best-flavored jujubes for fresh eating. Compared with the more common Li and Lang cultivars it remains relatively rare in commerce, but it is valued for strong drought and cold tolerance, high yields, and good disease resistance. Space trees to allow for their naturally upright, somewhat thorny, suckering growth habit, and remove root suckers as needed to keep the planting in bounds. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gac Fruit
description: Gac is a vigorous, tuberous-rooted perennial vine in the cucumber family that regrows each year from a starchy tuber in zones 9–11 and can be grown as an annual elsewhere; it requires a sturdy trellis or fence. Plants are dioecious, so grow at least one male and several female plants together; bees transfer pollen between the separate male and female flowers. The football-sized, brilliant orange-red fruit is among the richest known sources of lycopene and beta-carotene; the red aril surrounding the seeds is the edible portion, traditionally mixed into Vietnamese sticky rice (xôi gấc). Harvest when the skin is fully orange-red and the surface texture softens from spiny to smooth; fruit is mature approximately 4–5 months after planting. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Gafford Pecan (Scab-Resistant Type-1 Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible Type-2 pollinator such as Zinner nearby for good nut fill, since pecans are wind-pollinated and most cultivars set a much heavier crop with a cross-pollinator. Gafford is a Type-1 pecan valued by Gulf South growers for its notably strong resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most consistent yield losses for pecan growers in humid regions and drives the need for regular fungicide spraying on susceptible cultivars. Its disease resistance makes it a lower-maintenance choice for home orchards without a commercial spray program. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the tree to take several years to reach bearing age before producing consistent annual crops. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Gai Choy (Swollen-stem Mustard, Zhacai Mustard)
description: Direct sow in late summer for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; gai choy (swollen-stem mustard, zhacai type) is the Chinese mustard grown for its enlarged, knobby, swollen basal stem that forms a distinctive corm-like structure — salted, dried, and fermented with chili and Sichuan pepper to produce 'zhacai' (榨菜), the pickled Sichuan preserved vegetable that flavors noodle soups, fried rice, and countless Chinese dishes. The peppery, pungent young leaves are also edible as cooking greens. Growing your own allows fresh stem harvest for home pickling or fresh use. Requires a long, cool growing season for the stem to swell to usable size — an autumn crop planted 10–12 weeks before frost in zones 7–9 works best. A fascinating vegetable for those interested in Asian fermentation and pickling traditions. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Gai Choy Mustard
description: This pungent Chinese mustard, also called Indian mustard or Swatow mustard, forms curled leaves and wide, crunchy stems favored in Chinese, Korean, and Japanese cooking and pickling. The flavor is milder when young and grows sharper with maturity and heat. Grow in cool weather in full sun to partial shade, sowing in spring and fall. Keep soil evenly moist to slow bolting and keep flavor mild. Harvest whole heads or outer leaves as needed. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Gai Lan (Chinese Broccoli, Chinese Kale)
description: Direct sow in early spring or late summer in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 9–12 inches for best results. Gai lan (also written kai-lan or gai laan) is the Chinese broccoli or Chinese kale of Cantonese cuisine, a leafy brassica producing thick, succulent stems, broad blue-green leaves, and small clusters of white flower buds that are harvested together as the edible vegetable; unlike Italian broccoli where the heads are the prize, gai lan is prized for its juicy, thick stems with a clean, mild, slightly bitter flavor that takes well to the intense heat of a wok and oyster sauce. Harvest when the first buds are just beginning to open for peak flavor and tenderness; the plants regrow from the base for additional cuts. More heat-tolerant than most brassicas and an excellent vegetable for Gulf Coast fall and spring seasons when traditional broccoli bolts quickly. Essential in Chinese restaurant cooking — the vegetable in classic 'Chinese broccoli with oyster sauce.' Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Gailey Persimmon (Male Pollinator Asian Persimmon)
description: Gailey is grown less for its own small, seedy fruit than for the abundant male flowers it produces, making it the standard pollinator variety planted alongside pollination-variant Asian persimmons such as Chocolate and other PVA/PVNA types that only develop their best flavor, texture, and dark flesh color when fertilized. One Gailey tree can supply pollen for several seed-dependent persimmons within about 50 feet, letting a home orchard grow a wider range of specialty non-astringent persimmons than seedless cultivars alone would allow. The tree itself is tough, low-maintenance, and drought-tolerant once established, needing little beyond routine pruning to keep it manageable near the trees it pollinates. Because most persimmon cultivars in trade are self-fruitful, Gailey is a specialty planting for gardeners specifically chasing pollination-variant fruit quality rather than a first persimmon tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gala Apple
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — apples require excellent drainage and are not adapted to clay-heavy sites; Gala is a New Zealand-developed apple variety (Golden Delicious x Kidds Orange Red) released in 1934 that has become one of the top-selling apple varieties in the world and the most planted apple in the United States as of the 2010s. The medium-sized, striped red-and-gold fruits have a distinctive mild, sweet, honey-like flavor with very low acidity that makes them exceptionally popular for fresh eating across all age groups — the approachable, sweet flavor profile has made Gala the preferred apple in school lunch programs, grocery stores, and fresh snacking applications. The crisp, fine-grained texture holds up well for several weeks in refrigerator storage. Numerous Gala strains and sports ('Royal Gala', 'Regal Prince', 'Galaxy') offer improved color or earlier ripening but share the same flavor profile. The early-to-mid season ripening (August in warm climates) makes Gala one of the first fresh apples available each year. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gala Apple Tree
description: Gala is a widely grown apple with a sweet, mild flavor and firm, crisp flesh that suits fresh eating and cooking alike. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and include a compatible pollinating apple nearby, as Gala benefits from cross-pollination. Prune every dormant season for structure and light, and thin fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Water steadily during establishment and dry periods. Gala ripens in late summer to early fall, earlier than many other apples. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gala Mâche (Corn Salad)
description: Sow seed about 1/4 inch deep and keep the bed consistently moist and weeded, since Gala develops slowly and germinates over a long, uneven window even in ideal cool conditions. This heirloom French selection is valued for good mildew resistance and a rich, buttery texture, forming neat, fist-sized rosettes of oval leaves with a mild, nutty flavor. It tolerates light frost well and holds in the garden through cold snaps better than many quick-maturing salad greens. Harvest whole rosettes by cutting them at the base once they reach full size. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Galahad Tomato (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicer)
description: Galahad was named an AAS Edible-Vegetable Winner for combining large, meaty beefsteak-type fruit with a shorter, more compact, well-branched plant that needs less space than a typical vining slicer. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, and tobacco mosaic virus, and sets its 8-12 ounce fruit earlier in the season than most large-fruited hybrids. Cage or stake the plant even though it stays relatively compact, since the heavy fruit load can still bend unsupported stems, and keep up regular watering to reduce blossom end rot on the big first fruits. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Galangal
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; kaempferia galanga is a small, ground-hugging tropical herb with flat, round, beautifully marked leaves and white flowers with a violet center that bloom at soil level; the aromatic rhizomes are a key flavoring ingredient in Indonesian, Thai, and Malaysian cuisine (known as kencur, cekur, or pro hom) and have a distinctive, camphor-pine-earthy aroma quite unlike other galangals. It can be grown in containers and brought indoors in zones below 9; in zone 9–10 it thrives in partial to deep shade under tropical canopy and goes dormant in winter. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Galangal (Greater Galangal)
description: Plant rhizome sections with at least one growing bud 2–4 in deep in rich, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade; galangal needs consistent moisture and high humidity to thrive. Unlike ginger, galangal has a distinctly peppery, piney, medicinal flavor with less sweetness, and is a foundational ingredient in Thai, Indonesian, and Malay cuisines. In zones below 9, grow in large containers that can be moved indoors before frost; the rhizomes are frost-sensitive but the plant can be stored dormant above 50°F in winter. Harvest rhizomes after 10–12 months when the foliage begins to yellow in fall, digging with care to take only what is needed while leaving part of the clump to regrow. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Galaxy Blackberry (Semi-Erect Thornless USDA Release)
description: Galaxy is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry from the USDA-ARS breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, bred from a cross of the unpatented selection 'ORUS 1393-1' with the thornless 'Triple Crown'. Its medium-large, dark, firm berries ripen early within the semi-erect fruiting season, and like its sibling release 'Eclipse' it draws on both eastern and western North American blackberry germplasm for improved vigor and fruit quality. Canes are largely self-supporting but produce heavier, more manageable harvests when tied to a simple two-wire trellis. Remove fruited floricanes at ground level right after harvest and train in the new primocanes to bear the following season's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Galaxy Hops
description: Galaxy is an Australian aroma cultivar, released by Hop Products Australia from Perle-descended breeding stock, whose cones carry an intense passionfruit, citrus, and peach character that has made it one of the most sought-after hops in modern craft brewing. It performs best with a long, warm growing season and abundant sunshine, conditions that concentrate its essential oils. The bine is vigorous and cone-heavy, so plan on a very tall, sturdy trellis and rich, well-drained soil. Because its aroma is so concentrated, even modest late-addition or dry-hop rates produce a pronounced tropical fruit character in the finished beer. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Galena Hops
description: A high-alpha American bittering hop bred at USDA-Idaho, valued by home brewers for heavy, reliable cone production and clean grapefruit-citrus bittering character. It stores well and resists many common hop diseases better than older bittering varieties, making it a low-maintenance choice. Provide rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and generous vertical space, since Galena regularly produces the heaviest cone yields of any widely grown home-garden hop. Harvest promptly once cones dry and papery to preserve alpha acid content. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Galeux d'Eysines Pumpkin
description: This French heirloom, nicknamed peanut pumpkin for the sugar-crystal warts on its peach-colored skin, is prized for its supremely sweet, velvety orange flesh in soups and sauces. Fruit weighs 10 to 15 pounds and needs a long warm season to mature fully. Sow into rich, well-drained soil in full sun and give vines ample room to sprawl. Water deeply and feed for best size. Harvest when the rind hardens and cure in a warm, dry place before storage. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Galia Melon (Israeli Hybrid Netted Green-Flesh Muskmelon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns yellow-gold and a sweet tropical aroma is detectable at the stem end. Galia is an Israeli hybrid muskmelon type developed in the 1970s at the Newe Ya'ar Research Center by Dr. Zvi Karchi, named for his daughter — an F1 hybrid that combines the netted, aromatic skin characteristics of cantaloupe/muskmelon with the pale green, spicy-sweet flesh of honeydew, creating a novel flavor profile found in no other commonly available melon type. The round to slightly oval fruits (3–5 lb) have heavily netted, yellow-green to yellow-gold skin at maturity (the skin begins green and transitions to yellow-gold as the melon ripens — a useful visual harvest cue not present in cantaloupe types that stay tan). The flesh is pale green to cream-green, aromatic, and extremely sweet with a distinctive tropical character — floral, spicy, and complex, distinctly different from both orange-fleshed cantaloupe and the blander honeydew. Galia melons are widely grown and marketed throughout Europe, Israel, and Central America and have become increasingly available in American specialty markets, where they are often sold under the name 'Israeli melon.' The flavor is among the most complex and interesting of any melon type, making Galia a top choice for gardeners who want to explore beyond standard cantaloupe. Matures in 78–88 days from seed.

name: Galicjanka Aronia (Polish Commercial Black Chokeberry)
description: Galicjanka is a Polish-bred black chokeberry that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in Central Europe's commercial aronia industry, chosen for consistently heavy fruit set and berries with very high anthocyanin and polyphenol content, a trait studied extensively in food-science literature on aronia juice and supplements. The upright, vigorous shrub produces abundant white spring flowers followed by dense clusters of glossy black fruit that ripen in late summer, with astringent raw flavor that is better suited to juice, syrup, and jam than fresh eating. It adapts to a wide range of soils, including damp or heavy ground where many other fruiting shrubs struggle, though it performs poorly in shallow, chalky soils unless amended. Little pruning is required beyond removing the oldest canes every few years to keep the planting productive, and fall color turns a vivid red-orange before leaf drop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Galina's Tomato (Siberian Yellow Cherry Tomato)
description: A Siberian heirloom with soft, blue-green potato-leaf foliage that sets abundant clusters of translucent, pale-yellow, one-inch cherry tomatoes with a rich, sweet flavor. Bred for a short, cool growing season, Galina's sets fruit reliably in cooler spring and fall conditions that cause many other cherry tomatoes to drop blossoms, making it a strong choice for a Gulf South fall tomato planting timed to ripen as temperatures moderate. The prolific, early-bearing vines need only routine staking and produce continuously from first ripe fruit until frost. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Galine Eggplant
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after danger of frost has passed. Galine is a French-bred hybrid eggplant valued for its notably early maturity and reliable fruit set even in cooler summers, producing slender, cylindrical, glossy near-black fruit on a compact, manageable plant. The thin skin and few seeds make it well suited to quick-cooking preparations like grilling and stir-frying without the bitterness that can develop in larger, later-maturing types. Harvest at about two-thirds full size while the skin is taut and glossy for the mildest flavor and tenderest texture. Matures in 62–68 days from transplant.

name: Galip Nut
description: Plant Galip Nut in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water regularly during establishment; large trees are fairly drought-tolerant when established; harvest nut clusters when the outer drupes turn dark purple-black. Canarium indicum produces clusters of dark purple, almond-sized drupes resembling large olives, each enclosing a very hard, triangular-ridged shell containing a single cream-colored kernel of exceptional quality. The kernels are rich (approximately 70% fat) with a sweet, mild, buttery flavor reminiscent of a combination of almonds and macadamia nuts — widely considered among the finest edible nuts of the Pacific region. They are eaten fresh directly from the shell, roasted over fire, and processed into oil for cooking and for use in traditional body oil preparations. Galip nuts are the single most important indigenous tree nut of Papua New Guinea, traded widely in coastal markets, and of growing international interest as a specialty nut crop. The large trees (reaching 60–80 feet in their native forest habitat) are also highly valued for their straight-grained, durable timber. Closely related to the Pili Nut (Canarium ovatum) of the Philippines, which is also commercially grown; both species deserve wider cultivation in tropical Pacific and Caribbean gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Galletta Strawberry (NC State Day-Neutral Strawberry)
description: Plant on raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first several weeks of flowers on spring-set plants to build a stronger root system before letting the crop set. Galletta is a day-neutral strawberry from the North Carolina State University breeding program, selected to keep flowering and fruiting through summer heat rather than pausing like traditional June-bearers, which gives a longer, more spread-out harvest from spring through fall in the Southeast. Berries are firm, glossy, and well flavored, holding up better to summer warmth than many older day-neutral varieties bred for cooler California conditions. Keep plants consistently watered through hot spells, since day-neutral types are actively fruiting during the stress of summer, and refresh the planting every year or two as vigor declines. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Gambooge (Malabar Tamarind, Brindleberry)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; plant multiple trees for cross-pollination as the species is polygamous. Garcinia cambogia (gambooge or Malabar tamarind) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malabar Coast of India and Sri Lanka, producing small (2–3 inch), distinctively pumpkin-ribbed, yellow-orange, extremely sour fruits. The fresh fruit pulp is too acidic to eat raw, but the dried rind (kokum or kodampuli, depending on region) is an essential souring agent in Kerala, Konkani, and Sri Lankan coastal cooking — adding a fruity-tart, slightly sweet tartness to fish curries, sambars, and the famous Goan sol kadhi coconut drink. The dried rind is also used in Sri Lankan fish preparations and as a food preservative in traditional coastal cuisine. The fruit rind gained enormous international attention in the 1990s–2010s as a weight-loss supplement ingredient: it is the primary natural source of hydroxycitric acid (HCA), which was heavily marketed as a fat-burning compound — though clinical evidence for significant weight loss has been mixed. The tree is also the source of gamboge resin (from incisions in the bark), a yellow pigment historically used as a watercolor pigment. The tree needs multiple trees for fruiting as it is polygamous (different trees have different flower types). Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gamma Hazelnut (EFB-Resistant Pollenizer)
description: Gamma is another eastern filbert blight-resistant pollenizer from the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program, developed to keep pollen supply reliable as growers replaced blight-susceptible pollenizers like Daviana in modern EFB-resistant orchards. Its bloom period is timed to overlap with widely planted cultivars, and its resistance means it will not become a disease reservoir the way older susceptible pollenizers could. Like other pollenizer selections, its own nuts are secondary; focus management on maintaining vigorous flowering wood rather than nut size or cluster count. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gamthi Curry Leaf (Dwarf Aromatic Indian Strain)
description: Gamthi is a regional Indian strain of curry leaf, most associated with Gujarat, prized by cooks and gardeners for thicker, darker, more intensely aromatic leaves than the fast-growing commercial curry leaf commonly sold in nurseries. It grows noticeably slower and stays more compact, which makes it a better fit for long-term container culture on a patio or in a sunroom outside zones 9-11. Give it the same warm, sunny, well-drained conditions as standard curry leaf, and expect a few years of patience before harvests become generous. Snip branch tips regularly once established to keep growth dense and to encourage the flush of new aromatic leaves used fresh in South Indian tempering. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Gandaria (Plum Mango, Marian Plum)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; gandaria prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Bouea macrophylla (gandaria or Marian plum) is a Thai, Malay, and Indonesian tropical fruit tree in the mango family (Anacardiaceae) — closely related to mango (Mangifera) and producing small (1–1.5 inch), oval, egg-shaped fruits with a thin, smooth skin progressing from bright green through yellow-orange to golden when fully ripe, surrounding a large seed. The fruit's flavor profile is remarkably mango-like — fragrant, sweet-tart, resinous — but in miniature form; the flesh is juicy, fibrous, and intensely aromatic. Unripe fruits are highly acidic (like green mango) and are used as a souring agent in Thai and Malay curries, fish dishes, and the Thai-Malay salad-style dish 'rujak.' Ripe fruits are sweet enough to eat fresh. The tree is dense, compact compared to true mango, with large, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small cream flowers. Gandaria is extremely popular in rural and home gardens of Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand but is almost completely unknown in Western horticulture. For tropical zone 11–12 gardeners seeking unusual, genuine Southeast Asian fruits. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Ganesh Pomegranate
description: Selected near Pune, India in the mid-20th century, Ganesh was for decades the leading pomegranate cultivar in Indian home orchards and retail markets before being partly displaced by later selections such as Bhagwa and Mridula. Fruit is medium-sized with a pink-blushed skin and soft, sweet-tart pink arils, and the tree bears dependably once established, making it a good dooryard choice for growers who want a well-proven heirloom rather than a newer commercial release. Like other Indian selections, quality and fruit-skin condition are best where the ripening period stays hot and relatively dry, so thin overcrowded branches to maximize airflow in humid Gulf Coast plantings. It remains widely available through fruit-tree specialty nurseries as an older, still-respected cultivar. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ganjyu Bitter Melon
description: Known in Okinawa as a 'longevity' vegetable, Ganjyu is an extra-large, light green type with deeply ridged skin and notably milder bitterness than typical dark green bitter melons. Set plants slightly closer than most bitter melon at 12-18 inches and provide a sturdy trellis at planting time, since the fast-growing vines need vertical support from early on. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruiting, and encourage bee activity or hand-pollinate to ensure good fruit set on the long ridged fruit. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Garbanzo Bean Sprouts
description: Garbanzo bean sprouts are easy to grow indoors and rich in vitamins and protein for snacking or adding to many dishes. Rinse and soak the seeds overnight, then drain and rinse two to three times a day in a sprouting jar or tray. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun and harvest in just a few days when short sprouts appear. Cook lightly or eat the crisp sprouts fresh. Refrigerate promptly after harvest to keep them fresh. Matures in 2–4 days from seed.

name: Garber Pear
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Garber is an old American hybrid pear selected around 1880 in Florida and one of the most fire-blight resistant pear varieties known — it is sometimes used as a rootstock for other pears specifically for its superior adaptability to Southern soils and resistance to the fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) that devastates European pear varieties in humid climates. The large, roundish-pear-shaped fruits are yellow to golden at maturity with crisp, gritty, mildly sweet flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. Garber ripens mid-season (August–September) and is widely planted in the Gulf South as a dual-purpose tree: ornamental landscape specimen with beautiful spring bloom and reliable production under low-spray conditions that would be impossible for Bartlett or d'Anjou. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades in zone 7–9. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end; Garber pears ripen better when picked slightly underripe and allowed to ripen at room temperature. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Garden Angelica (Wild Celery)
description: Sow fresh seeds in late summer or fall in moist, humus-rich, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; seeds lose viability quickly — sow immediately after harvest. Angelica archangelica (garden angelica) is a magnificent biennial herb of Scandinavian origin — one of the most architecturally impressive herbs in cultivation, reaching 5–8 feet in its flowering year with hollow, bright-green, purple-tinged stems as thick as a wrist and enormous, compound umbrella-flower heads (3–6 inches across) of tiny yellow-green flowers beloved by beneficial insects, especially predatory wasps and hoverflies. The stems, leaves, roots, and seeds are all used in European cuisine and confectionery: the young stems are candied (crystallized angelica) as a traditional cake and pastry decoration; the leaves and seeds flavor aquavit, vermouth, Chartreuse, Bénédictine, and Cointreau liqueurs; the roots have been used medicinally for centuries in Scandinavian and central European folk medicine. The plant prefers cool, moist, shaded conditions and struggles in hot, humid southern summers — in zone 9, a shaded, moist spot with afternoon protection is essential. CAUTION: sap can cause phototoxic skin reactions. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Garden Annie Apricot (Self-Fertile Low-Chill Genetic Dwarf Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil on a site with good cold-air drainage to protect the early pale-pink bloom from late frost, the main risk for any apricot in the Gulf South. Garden Annie is a genetic dwarf reaching only 8–10 feet at maturity, making it practical for smaller lots or large containers while still producing full-sized, firm, bright-yellow semi-freestone fruit that holds well on the tree through June without softening. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree will crop reliably, though hand-thinning green fruit to about 3 inches apart improves final size on this compact, densely branched tree. Watch for the shorter chill requirement to trigger occasional off-season bloom during warm winter spells, and delay heavy nitrogen feeding until after fruit set to avoid excess vegetative growth on the small frame. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Garden Cress
description: Direct-sow thickly in cool weather, barely covering the seed, which sprouts within days. This peppery quick crop is harvested young as a spicy microgreen or baby salad green. Sow in succession every couple of weeks and keep the soil evenly moist to slow bolting. Provide partial shade in warm spells to extend the harvest window. Snip seedlings with scissors just above the soil once they reach a few inches tall. Matures in 15–30 days from seed.

name: Garden Gold Miniature Peach Tree
description: This genetic dwarf peach tops out around 4-6 feet, making it ideal for large containers or tight yards while still yielding full-size, sweet yellow freestone fruit. Site it in full sun with well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through the growing season. Thin the young fruit to about 6 inches apart so remaining peaches size up well. Prune lightly in late winter to keep an open, vase-shaped canopy, and expect a harvest beginning two to three years after planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Garden Huckleberry (Sunberry, Wonderberry)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; garden huckleberry is an African cultivated nightshade that produces abundant clusters of small, round, glossy black fruits about the size of a large pea. Unlike its wild nightshade relatives, the ripe fruits are edible but ONLY when fully cooked — raw berries contain solasodine alkaloids that cause digestive upset. When properly cooked, they lose their bitterness and make good pies, jams, and preserves with an earthy, slightly tart flavor. Harvest only fully black, ripe berries. The plant is extremely productive in warm climates and tolerates partial shade, making it useful for lightly shaded food gardens. It is distinct from the true huckleberry (Gaylussacia species) and true blueberry, and should not be eaten raw under any circumstances. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Garden Peach Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is an indeterminate, moderately sized variety requiring staking or caging; it is quite productive and continues bearing through the season. Garden Peach tomato is a remarkable heirloom curiosity that mimics a real peach in appearance with unusual fidelity — the small (2–3 oz), round fruits have pale cream to blush-yellow skin covered in tiny dense hairs (trichomes) that create a distinctly fuzzy, velvet-textured surface virtually identical to peach fuzz; when held in the hand, a ripe Garden Peach tomato is nearly indistinguishable from a small peach by touch alone. The flavor is sweet and mild with a hint of fruity peach character, very low acidity, and soft, juicy texture — appealing to those who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The novelty factor is considerable: Garden Peach tomatoes generate immediate curiosity and conversation, and children in particular are captivated by the peach resemblance; they are excellent for farm stands and markets as well as home garden curiosity. The fuzzy skin, unlike most tomatoes, does not split in rain or overhead irrigation. A productive and reliable variety for any garden where the growing season exceeds 70 days. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Garden Sorrel
description: Sow direct in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; garden sorrel is one of the easiest and most productive perennial vegetables — once established, remove flowering stalks to maintain leaf production and divide clumps every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Rumex acetosa is a European native perennial herb grown for its large, arrow-shaped leaves with a distinctive, bright, lemony-sour flavor from oxalic acid that is the defining ingredient in classic French sorrel soup, sorrel sauce (excellent with fish), and sorrel-cream pasta; the leaves can be used fresh in salads when young and small, or cooked and pureed when larger, though they turn an unappetizing khaki color on cooking. The plant is extremely cold-hardy, re-emerging reliably in early spring, and is one of the first fresh greens available in the spring garden; harvest leaves continuously from the outside of the clump. Consume in moderation due to oxalic acid content. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Gardenblue Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Gardenblue was released in 1955 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton alongside Homebell and Tifblue, making it one of the earliest formally named rabbiteye cultivars. It needs roughly 400-450 chill hours below 45 degrees F and ripens midseason, typically mid-to-late June in zone 7-9, several weeks behind Climax or Premier. The medium-sized berries are a good light blue with fair flavor and were prized in their era mainly for the plant's vigor and heavy production rather than dessert quality, and the cultivar was widely planted commercially through the 1960s before being replaced by higher-quality introductions like Tifblue and Brightwell. It remains an option for gardeners wanting a tough, reliably productive heritage rabbiteye; set in acidic, pine-bark-amended soil and pair with a second midseason cultivar since it will not self-pollinate. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gardener's Delight Pole Cherry Tomato
description: This 1950s German heirloom is often praised as one of the best cherry tomatoes, with extra-sweet, flavor-packed fruit borne in clusters of 6 to 12 all summer until frost. The vigorous indeterminate vines easily reach 6 feet or more. Provide tall, sturdy support and prune suckers for airflow and larger clusters. Start seed indoors early and transplant into full sun after frost. Water consistently to prevent cracking and pick often to keep vines producing. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Gargoyle Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Warty Bicolor Ornamental Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines room to sprawl and set their oddly textured fruit. Gargoyle earned its All-America Selections award for an unmistakable look: dense, bumpy warts cover the entire orange-and-dark-green rind, giving each pumpkin a rugged, almost reptilian surface unlike smooth carving types. The tough, thick rind holds up well through a full season of fall display without softening, making it a durable choice for porch and entryway arrangements. Harvest before hard frost once color and warting have fully developed, and expect several fruits per vine across the season. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Garlic Chive
description: Garlic chives are a hardy perennial allium with flat, grass-like leaves that carry a mild garlic flavor, plus fragrant edible white flowers late in the season. Sow seed in clumps and harvest leaves by snipping from the outside as needed. The star-shaped blooms attract pollinators but self-sow prolifically, so deadhead if you want to limit spread. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep them vigorous. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Garlic Chives
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep and keep soil moist; germination is similar to common chives but the flat, grass-like leaves have a distinct mild garlic flavor. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil and divide clumps every 2–3 years to prevent overcrowding and maintain productivity. Deadhead flowers promptly, as garlic chives self-seed prolifically and can become weedy. Harvest flat leaves at any height; older leaves become slightly tough but remain useful cooked. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Garlic Chives / Chinese Chives
description: Allium tuberosum, commonly known as garlic chives or Chinese chives, is a vigorous, clump-forming perennial allium native to eastern Asia and widely cultivated throughout China, Japan, and Southeast Asia as both a culinary herb and a vegetable; unlike common chives, its flat, strap-like leaves carry a mild but distinct garlic flavor, and its star-shaped white flowers borne on upright scapes in late summer are both ornamental and edible. Direct-sow seeds in early spring in moderately fertile, consistently moist but well-drained soil in full sun; plants are more drought-tolerant than common chives once established but produce the most flavorful and abundant foliage with consistent moisture. Harvest leaves by cutting to within 1-2 inches of the ground, repeating every few weeks throughout the season; garlic chives are also commonly grown in the dark to produce blanched, yellow-etiolated leaves (jiu huang) prized in Chinese cooking for their tenderer texture and milder flavor. Deadhead the attractive white flower clusters before seeds ripen, as garlic chives self-sow prolifically and can become invasive in favorable garden conditions; established clumps benefit from division every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Garlic Mustard
description: Garlic mustard is a biennial woodland-edge herb whose first-year rosette of scalloped, dark-green leaves carries a distinctive garlic-and-mustard bite that makes it a useful, unusually shade-tolerant flavoring green for a food forest understory. Harvest the mild, tender first-year leaves for pesto, chopped salads, and sauteed greens, then gather the young second-year flower shoots in spring before the small white flowers open, when they can be cooked like a peppery broccoli raab. Because it self-sows aggressively and is classified as invasive in much of eastern North America, grow it only in a contained raised bed or large container and remove flowering stalks before seed set to keep it from escaping into nearby woodland. A single planting in a partly shaded bed typically self-perpetuates for years with no further sowing needed. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Garnet Sweet Potato (Red Garnet Moist-Flesh Orange Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose soil; do not overwater or over-fertilize with nitrogen (promotes vine over root). Cure harvested roots before storage. Garnet Sweet Potato (also sold as 'Red Garnet') is one of the most widely grown and commercially important sweet potato varieties in the United States, recognizable to millions of shoppers as the 'yam' with reddish-purple to copper-red skin and brilliant orange flesh sold in most American supermarkets. The confusion between true yams (Dioscorea species, tropical tubers with starchy white flesh) and sweet potatoes is a historical American marketing accident: in the mid-20th century, Louisiana farmers and marketers began calling their orange-fleshed sweet potatoes 'yams' to distinguish them from the paler-fleshed Northern sweet potato types, and the term 'yam' became permanently associated with moist, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes in American grocery retail. Garnet's moist orange flesh has the classic American sweet potato eating character: very sweet, soft when baked, and vibrantly orange — characteristics that come from a high beta-carotene content (beta-carotene is the pigment in carrots, orange squash, and other orange vegetables that converts to Vitamin A in the body). The roasted Garnet sweet potato is one of the most nutritionally dense foods in regular American cooking: high in complex carbohydrates, very high in beta-carotene (Vitamin A precursor), and a good source of potassium, fiber, and Vitamin C. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Garretson American Persimmon (Early Golden Seedling Selection)
description: Garretson is a named selection of the native American persimmon, raised as a seedling of the well-known 'Early Golden' cultivar and valued for its large, deep-orange, richly sweet fruit. Like most American persimmon selections it is primarily pistillate (female), so fruit set is heaviest when a seedling or named male tree is planted within pollinating range, though occasional male flowers on some branches can allow limited fruit set on their own. Fruit ripens in early October and, like all American persimmons, needs to fully soften after frost before it loses its mouth-puckering astringency and becomes honey-sweet. Garretson is cold-hardy into zone 4 and, thanks to the species' deep taproot and tolerance of heat, humidity, and poor soils, also thrives through the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gaviota Plum (Early-Season Dark-Skinned California Japanese Plum)
description: Gaviota is a University of California-bred Japanese plum valued for ripening well ahead of Santa Rosa while still delivering good size and flavor. The medium-to-large fruit has dark red-black skin over firm, amber-yellow flesh with a rich sweet-tart balance. Plant with another early to mid-season Japanese plum for cross-pollination, and thin fruit clusters to a hand's width apart to encourage larger size and reduce limb stress. Because it ripens early, it is a useful choice for extending the fresh plum harvest window before later varieties like Friar or Elephant Heart come in. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gaviota Strawberry (Early, Sweet California Short-Day Heirloom)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Gaviota is a short-day strawberry from the University of California breeding program, prized among home gardeners and farmers-market growers for exceptionally sweet, aromatic flavor that many tasters rank above more widely shipped commercial cultivars. Its dark red, glossy berries ripen earlier in the season than many other short-day types but are softer and less shelf-stable, making it better suited to home use and local sales than long-distance shipping. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual. Pick promptly since the soft ripe fruit is more prone to rot in humid conditions than firmer cultivars. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Gaziantep Jujube (Turkish Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Gaziantep is a Turkish jujube selection prized for very large fruit and performs well anywhere Chinese jujube cultivars thrive. Named for the jujube-growing region of southeastern Turkey, this selection produces unusually large, oblong fruit with crisp, sweet, apple-flavored flesh at the green-mature stage, among the biggest fruit sizes seen in jujube collector plantings, sweetening and wrinkling further if left to ripen to full brown maturity. The tree shares the toughness typical of the species — tolerant of heat, drought, poor soil, and light frost once dormant — and bears at a young age with minimal care once established. Harvest fruit in successive pickings from the crisp green-mature stage through the fully wrinkled, date-like brown stage depending on preferred texture and sweetness, and prune lightly in winter to control the tree's naturally twiggy, zigzag growth habit. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gbanja Kola (Commercial Kola Nut)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gbanja kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. The more widely commercially cultivated of the two main kola species, this West African rainforest tree produces large pods of caffeine-rich seeds that are the primary source of kola nuts in international trade, chewed fresh as a stimulant and once used as a flavoring base for early cola beverages before synthetic flavorings took over. Like its relative Cola acuminata, it requires many years of warm, humid, partly shaded growing conditions to reach bearing age, restricting realistic cultivation outside the tropics to specialty botanical or ethnobotanical plantings. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and provide filtered shade to replicate the tree's native rainforest understory habitat. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Gboma Eggplant (African Garden Egg)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun; gboma eggplant is one of the most important vegetable plants of tropical West and Central Africa — a large, robust eggplant species (distinct from the common eggplant Solanum melongena) with large, lobed, hairy leaves and rounded to oblong, whitish-green to purple-streaked fruits. The leaves, young shoots, and immature fruits are all cooked and eaten as vegetables in West African cuisine — the leaves are particularly important as a cooked vegetable eaten with fufu (pounded starchy staples) and soups across Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, and neighboring countries. An important traditional African food plant adapted to hot, humid tropical conditions where standard eggplant varieties may struggle. The fruits can also be used like conventional eggplant in curries and stews. More robust and heat-tolerant than standard eggplant cultivars. A valuable addition to home gardens in zone 9–12 where traditional West African vegetables are of interest. Matures in 80–120 days from transplant.

name: Gefner Atemoya (Nearly Self-Fruitful Popular Home Garden Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Gefner is the most widely planted atemoya cultivar for home gardens, valued for setting a reasonable crop with less hand pollination effort than most other cultivars, since it is considered nearly self-fruitful under good conditions, though hand pollination still improves fruit set and size. The rich, creamy white flesh has the classic atemoya flavor of custard, vanilla, and tropical fruit notes, and the tree bears at a relatively young age once grafted. Fruit ripens in fall and should be picked when it just begins to soften and change from green to a slightly yellow-green color, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature indoors. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Geisha Coffee (Gesha)
description: Originally an Ethiopian forest landrace named for the Gesha district near where it was collected, this variety languished as an obscure, low-yielding curiosity in Central America for decades until a Panamanian lot won international acclaim in 2004 for its unusually intense floral, jasmine, and stone-fruit cup character. Its tall, willowy growth habit, sparse branching, and light bearing make it a poor economic choice for large-scale production but an appealing specimen for collectors chasing an exceptional home-grown cup. It is fussier than sturdier hybrids, generally wanting slightly cooler nights and consistent filtered light to develop its best flavor. Expect a taller, more open plant than Bourbon or Typica and the same three-to-four-year wait before the first harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Geisha Garlic Chives (AAS-Winning Late-Flowering Garlic Chives)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and keep soil moist; germination is similar to common chives, but Geisha produces noticeably wider, more vigorous, flat, grass-like leaves with the same mild garlic flavor as standard garlic chives. Its key improvement, and the reason for its AAS award, is delayed flowering — by blooming later in the season than common garlic chives, it produces far fewer of the seed heads responsible for the prolific, sometimes weedy self-seeding that gives standard garlic chives a reputation for spreading where unwanted. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and divide clumps every 2-3 years to prevent overcrowding and keep production vigorous. Harvest the flat leaves at any height for kitchen use; older leaves become slightly tough but remain useful cooked into dishes. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Geisha Girl Flowering Quince (Apricot-Pink Double Late-Blooming Quince)
description: 'Geisha Girl' is a later-blooming, more compact flowering quince selection bearing semi-double, soft apricot-pink flowers accented by prominent yellow stamens, opening on the bare branches in mid-to-late spring after many other quince cultivars have finished. A UK Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit winner, it forms a dense, rounded, spiny shrub with glossy dark green foliage and small, aromatic yellow-green fruit useful for preserves though too tart to eat fresh. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing the next season's buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gelber Englischer Pattypan Squash
description: This German heirloom pattypan bears vibrant yellow, scalloped fruit with creamy yellow and light-green striping. For the best flavor and texture, harvest squash starting at about 2 inches wide up to 4 inches. Pick young and often to keep the plants producing all season. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water consistently and allow good airflow to limit powdery mildew. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Gem Squash (South African Baby Round Squash, Bush Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Gem squash grows as a compact bush (unlike most squash vines) and is excellent for small gardens and containers; harvest when fruits reach 3–4 inches (tennis-ball to softball size) with dark green skin — do not allow to mature to yellow or tan as flavor and texture degrade; cook whole (boiled, steamed, or baked) until just tender. Gem squash is a South African heirloom variety with deep roots in the home gardens of South Africa, where it is so culturally central that it appears in traditional Afrikaner recipes, South African school cookbooks, and family food traditions going back to the early colonial period. The small, round, dark green fruits are harvested at a much smaller stage than American summer squash — when they are about the size of a tennis ball to softball, with soft seeds and tender flesh — and are traditionally cooked whole rather than sliced. The most common preparation in South Africa involves boiling or steaming the whole small squash in salted water until tender, then halving and scooping out the seeded core, filling the cavity with butter, cream cheese, or condensed milk (a classic dessert preparation), and serving the squash halves on the plate. The flavor of properly young Gem squash is milder and sweeter than zucchini, with a delicate texture that makes it very versatile. The bush-type plant (not a vine) is exceptionally productive, producing many small fruits from a compact plant, making it practical for small raised-bed gardens. Increasingly available in American specialty and heirloom seed catalogs as gardeners discover this productive, compact, and culturally interesting vegetable. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Gemini Feijoa (Compact Dessert Selection)
description: Gemini is a compact-growing feijoa selection popular with home orchardists working in smaller garden spaces or large containers, staying noticeably more restrained in height and spread than rangier older cultivars while still producing good-quality, sweet, aromatic fruit. Fruit is medium-sized and egg-shaped with smooth skin and juicy, low-grit flesh, ripening in the typical mid-to-late season window shared by most feijoa cultivars. Its dense, naturally rounded evergreen habit makes it a strong choice for hedging or foundation planting where a full-sized feijoa would eventually crowd its neighbors, and the sweet, showy spring flowers are as much an ornamental draw as the autumn fruit crop. Give it full sun, consistent summer moisture, and a light annual prune to keep the canopy open and fruit accessible for harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Geneva 41 Apple Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Geneva 41 is grown as a dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit. Developed by the Cornell University and USDA apple rootstock breeding program at Geneva, New York, this modern dwarfing rootstock produces a small, highly productive tree roughly 40-50 percent the size of a full-sized seedling tree, with outstanding resistance to fire blight and Phytophthora root rot, two of the most serious diseases limiting older rootstocks like M9 and M26. Its combination of size control, disease resistance, and precocious early fruiting has made it one of the most widely adopted modern dwarfing apple rootstocks in commercial and high-density home orchards. Provide permanent staking or trellising, since the small, brittle root system does not anchor well without support, and graft a desired named variety onto young rootstock in late winter for best results. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Geneva Hardy Kiwi
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a permanent, sturdy support structure. Geneva is a female hardy kiwi cultivar selected and released by Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural research station, bred for excellent fruit quality, good productivity, and reliable cold hardiness suited to northern growing conditions. The smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit ripens in fall with sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi, eaten whole without peeling, and the vine's Cornell breeding gives it dependable performance and disease tolerance in the humid Northeast, translating well to other regions with cold winters. As with all Actinidia arguta, Geneva is dioecious and needs a separate male vine planted nearby to ensure pollination and fruit set. A well-vetted, university-tested choice for a hardy kiwi arbor in zone 4–8. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Geneva Kiwi (Cornell-Selected Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Geneva is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar selected at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station, part of a long-running kiwiberry breeding and evaluation program aimed at improving fruit size, flavor, and reliability for cold-climate growers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good classic kiwi flavor. As a university-trialed selection, Geneva offers more consistency in fruit quality and vine performance than many seedling-grown kiwiberry vines sold without named cultivar status. Prune hard each winter on a permanent cordon framework to control the vigorous twining growth, provide sturdy trellising from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for good fruit set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Geneva Red American Persimmon
description: Geneva Red was bred by George Slate at the Geneva, New York experiment station and is valued as one of the earliest-ripening, sweetest American persimmons suited to short, cool growing seasons. It sets fruit reliably even where summers are marginal for other native persimmon selections. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, which promotes vegetative growth at the expense of fruit. Allow fruit to fully soften after coloring, as unripe flesh remains strongly astringent. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Genoa Lemon Tree
description: Introduced from Genoa, Italy, this productive lemon bears juicy, tangy fruit much like Eureka. Give it at least 8 hours of sun, fast-draining slightly acidic soil, and a dedicated citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9 grow it in a container and move it indoors near a bright window before frost. Water deeply but let the top inch of soil dry between waterings to avoid root rot. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Genovese Basil
description: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, covering lightly and keeping soil near 75F. This large-leaved Italian classic is the standard for pesto and Mediterranean cooking. Transplant into warm, rich soil in full sun only after all frost danger passes. Pinch out the growing tips at six leaves to force a bushy, high-yielding plant. Harvest whole stems above a leaf node and remove flower buds promptly to keep leaves tender and sweet. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Genovese Basil
description: Genovese basil is the classic Italian pesto basil, prized for its large, tender, deeply fragrant green leaves. Sow once soil is warm and keep plants well watered in full sun. Pinch the growing tips regularly and remove flower buds to encourage bushy growth and prevent the leaves from turning bitter. Harvest often, as frequent picking keeps the plant producing until frost. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Genovese Compact, Improved Basil (Uniform Container Pesto Basil)
description: Genovese Compact, Improved carries the same cupped, dark-green, 2-3 inch pesto-type leaves and classic sweet Genovese flavor as standard Genovese basil, but on shorter, more uniform 16-18 inch plants bred for even germination and consistent habit in container and retail production. That compactness and uniformity also make it a reliable choice for home gardeners who want a tidy, productive basil in a pot on a patio or windowsill rather than the taller, more sprawling standard Genovese. Pinch flower spikes regularly to keep leaf production going and delay the flavor decline that comes with flowering. Harvest by cutting stem tips just above a leaf node to encourage bushy regrowth through the season. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Gentry Crookneck Squash (Disease-Tolerant Hybrid Yellow Crookneck)
description: Gentry is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash selected for improved disease tolerance and heavy, uniform production of smooth, warty-skinned, classically curved fruit, giving Southern gardeners a more resilient alternative to older open-pollinated crookneck lines that decline quickly once powdery mildew takes hold. The compact, open bush habit keeps fruit visible and easy to pick, and plants continue setting well through the heart of summer heat if harvested regularly. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed; pick fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak season since oversized fruit quickly turns tough, seedy, and signals the plant to slow production. As with all summer squash, consistent moisture and a thick mulch layer help maintain steady yields through hot, humid Gulf South summers. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Genuine Cornfield Bean
description: Sow at the base of standing corn or a sturdy pole in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a true climbing type, it needs tall support to perform well. Genuine Cornfield Bean is an old-time American heirloom pole bean, so named because it was traditionally grown climbing up living corn stalks in the cornfield rather than on a dedicated trellis — a direct descendant of the indigenous 'three sisters' companion-planting tradition of interplanting corn, beans, and squash, in which the bean's nitrogen-fixing roots benefit the heavy-feeding corn while the cornstalk provides the bean a ready-made climbing pole. The vigorous vines produce a heavy crop of medium green pods good for snap use when young, or left to mature and dry for a flavorful winter soup bean. A practical, space-efficient heirloom for gardeners who want to grow beans and corn together in the traditional way, zone 4–10. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Genuwine Tomato (Brandywine x German Johnson Cross Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage early to support the heavy fruit load. Genuwine is a modern open-pollinated selection bred by crossing Brandywine and German Johnson to combine the rich, complex flavor of Brandywine with German Johnson's smoother skin, more regular fruit shape, and improved productivity. The large, pink-red beefsteak fruit, often exceeding a pound, has a meaty, low-seed interior and a sweet, deep flavor that heirloom-tomato fans compare favorably to Brandywine itself while avoiding some of its notoriously erratic, lower-yielding habit. Feed and water consistently through fruit set, and pick as soon as fruit colors fully to avoid splitting during Gulf Coast summer rain. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Geo Pride Pluot (Early Red-Skinned Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a compatible plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set. Geo Pride is one of the earlier-ripening pluots from Zaiger Genetics, opening the pluot harvest with attractive bright red skin over firm, juicy, sweet-tart flesh that holds up well to picking and handling. Its early season makes it a useful complement to later pluot varieties like Flavor King or Flavor Grenade in a garden with room for more than one, spreading pluot harvest over a longer stretch of summer. Manage the tree as a standard plum, with dormant-season pruning to an open center and spring thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve final size and sweetness. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Basil (Southeastern Calamint)
description: Sow seeds in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Georgia basil is a small, aromatic, mint-family native wildflower of the southeastern Piedmont and coastal plain, native to Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina, and northern Florida, growing in pine flatwoods, open roadsides, and dry woodland edges. It produces slender stems with small, oval, hairy, basil-scented leaves and bears clouds of small, two-lipped, pink to lavender-pink flowers throughout summer into fall that attract small native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies. As a genuine southeastern native, it is superbly adapted to the hot, humid summers, periodic drought, and acid sandy soils of the Deep South where non-native mints often struggle. The strong basil-like fragrance from the crushed leaves is pleasant and distinctive. An excellent plant for native gardens, pollinator borders, and naturalized areas in zones 6-9 where it provides season-long bloom with minimal care once established. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Georgia Belle Peach (Classic Southern White Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile heirloom needs no second tree to set fruit. A 19th-century Georgia heirloom still prized today, Georgia Belle bears large, mostly white-fleshed freestone fruit blushed with red over a creamy background, with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor that many old-time Southern gardeners consider unmatched by modern yellow-fleshed commercial peaches. The tree ripens in mid to late summer and bears reliably where its moderate chill requirement is met, though the soft, thin-skinned fruit bruises easily and does not ship well, which is part of why it remains mostly a dooryard and farmstand variety rather than a supermarket peach. Thin fruit to one per 6-8 inches of branch in late spring to improve size, and pick when the background color turns from green to creamy white or yellow and the fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Blue Stem Collard (Pre-1900 Southern Heirloom Collard)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Georgia Blue Stem'
description: Documented under the names Blue Stem and Georgia Blue Stem in American seed literature predating 1900, this large heirloom was preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange member network before returning to wider circulation. Its obovate leaves are blue-green with prominent white midribs and a rounded, toothed margin, carried on a big, open plant with narrow petioles. It is prized among older Southern collard types for a notably sweet, juicy eating quality once cooked, distinct from the coarser bite of some other heirloom strains. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Dawn Blueberry (Very-Early-Season University of Georgia Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to buffer soil temperature and moisture through the Gulf Coast growing season. Bred by the University of Georgia from a cross of 'Star' and a southern highbush selection, Georgia Dawn is grown chiefly for its very early ripening, flavor, and good berry color, scar, and firmness that let growers reach market ahead of most other cultivars. Its flowers open very early in the season, so sites prone to late-winter cold snaps need frost or freeze protection during bloom to avoid crop loss. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and again lightly post-harvest, and thin out old canes each dormant season to keep young, fruitful wood coming. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Flame Pepper
description: Georgia Flame is an old heirloom pepper from the country of Georgia in the Caucasus, not the American state, passed down as a dual-purpose sweet-to-mild roasting pepper for generations there. Plants set an abundance of long, tapered, conical pods that ripen from green to a deep, glossy red, with thick walls and a fruity flavor that sits right at the sweet-hot border, roughly on par with a mild jalapeno. Because the pods hold their shape and thick flesh under high heat, they are especially well suited to open-flame roasting, grilling, and salsa, and the plants are vigorous, heavy producers once established in warm soil. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Green Peanut
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, calcium-rich soil — peanuts require loose, deep, well-drained soil for the pegs to penetrate easily and the pods to develop properly; Georgia Green is the leading commercial and home garden Virginia-type peanut variety in the United States, released by the North Carolina State University breeding program and immediately adopted across the peanut belt for its superior resistance to late leaf spot (Cercosporidium personatum) and Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) — the two most economically important peanut diseases in the Southeast. The Virginia type produces larger kernels than Spanish or Valencia peanuts, with the characteristic elongated, two-kernel pods and excellent roasted flavor that make Virginia peanuts the preferred type for in-shell roasting, boiling, and gourmet peanut products. Georgia Green has maintained commercial adoption for over 25 years — an unusual longevity for a field crop variety — because the disease resistance package continues to provide practical advantages over older and newer alternatives under Gulf South conditions. In zone 9 the long, hot growing season (110–130 days) and sandy coastal plain soils are ideal for peanut production, making Georgia Green one of the most naturally adapted and rewarding warm-season food crops available for Gulf South gardens. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Georgia Jet Sweet Potato
description: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; Georgia Jet is a productive open-pollinated sweet potato variety that reaches harvest in 90 days — one of the earliest-maturing sweet potatoes available, making it a reliable choice for shorter growing seasons and for gardeners in zones 5–7 who need a variety that matures before fall frost. In zone 9 it is equally useful as an early-maturing variety that can be planted as a second crop after spring vegetables finish. The deep reddish-purple skin and vivid orange flesh are very attractive; the flavor is sweet, moist, and rich — considered excellent for baking, steaming, and as a dessert sweet potato. An outstanding heirloom variety that produces well without synthetic fertilizers and stores reliably. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Rattlesnake Watermelon
description: This Southern heirloom from the 1830s produces oblong, green-striped fruits of 25 to 35 pounds with sweet, rosy-red flesh. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines abundant space. Water consistently while fruits swell, then ease off as they near ripeness to concentrate sweetness. Look for a curled, dry tendril near the stem and a creamy ground spot as ripeness cues before cutting the melon. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Georgia Red Sugarcane (Heirloom Red-Stalked Chewing Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Georgia Red is an heirloom chewing cane with deep red to maroon, slender stalks, softer-rinded and juicier than syrup types, whose fibers stick together in a wad rather than shredding apart when chewed — the trait that defines a true chewing cane. It was traditionally bundled and sold fresh at farm stands, country stores, and gas stations across Georgia and the Gulf South each fall as a hand-peeled snack, gnawed in short sections for the sweet juice, though the stalks can also be pressed or cooked into syrup like any other cane. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy stalks before hard frost, bed them in a shaded, well-drained trench under a heavy mulch of soil or pine straw to keep them dormant without freezing, and replant the sets in spring once the soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh eating can begin once stalks reach full size in September, but flavor and sweetness improve markedly after the first cool nights of fall concentrate the sugars in the stalk. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Southern Collard Greens
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Georgia Southern is the original Southern heirloom collard variety — one of the oldest and most historically significant vegetables in American Southern cooking, with documented continuous cultivation in the southeastern United States for well over a century. The large, smooth, blue-green leaves with a prominent pale midrib are the defining collard green appearance in traditional Southern cuisine — different from the crinkled leaves of kale and the heading structure of cabbage, collards are a non-heading form of Brassica oleracea that produces large individual leaves harvest continuously from the outer portions of the plant. The slow-cooked Southern preparation — simmering collards with smoked pork (ham hock, fatback, or smoked turkey) for hours with salt and vinegar until tender — transforms the tough, slightly bitter raw leaves into silky, rich, deeply flavorful cooked greens that are a cornerstone of Southern food culture. Georgia Southern is particularly valued for its mild flavor, large leaf size, and exceptional heat tolerance that allows spring and fall production in zone 9. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Georgia Southern Collard Greens
description: This time-tested Southern heirloom yields large, tender, blue-green leaves with a rich, traditional flavor and strong vigor. Sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep and thin plants so the broad leaves have room to develop. Harvest lower leaves as needed for cut-and-come-again picking, leaving the growing tip intact. Highly cold hardy, the greens sweeten noticeably after fall frost and produce reliably in both spring and fall gardens. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Georgia Southern Collards (Classic Old-Fashioned Southern Heirloom Collard)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil. Georgia Southern (also simply 'Georgia Collards' or 'Old Georgia') is the foundational heirloom collard variety of the American South — an open-pollinated type with a continuous documented growing history in Southern gardens spanning well over a century, representing the traditional collard before the development of modern compact hybrids. Plants grow 3–4 feet tall and 2–3 feet wide, producing large, broad, blue-green, relatively smooth leaves with a somewhat open, non-heading habit.
