The flavor is the classic Southern collard character: substantial, slightly bitter when raw, sweet and savory when cooked slowly with salt pork, ham hocks, or smoked turkey — the traditional pot-likker preparation where the cooking liquid becomes as important as the greens themselves. Georgia Southern is notably heat-tolerant for a brassica, surviving Gulf South summers better than most collard varieties, and produces some of the most vigorous growth in the warm, humid conditions of zone 8–10 fall and winter gardens. Its open-pollinated nature allows seed saving from the most productive plants year after year. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Streak Tomato (Southern Heirloom Bicolor Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines early. Georgia Streak is a Southern heirloom beefsteak in the same bicolor family as Pineapple and Hillbilly, producing large, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red through the flesh as well as the skin, so each slice shows the same vivid marbling as the exterior. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity, characteristic of yellow-red bicolor heirlooms, and the fruit's soft shoulders and juicy flesh make it a fresh-eating and slicing tomato rather than one suited to canning or long storage. In the Deep South it performs best in the spring crop before peak summer heat interferes with fruit set, so get transplants in as early as the weather allows and mulch well to keep roots cool. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true from year to year with basic isolation from other tomato varieties. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Georgia Sweet Onion (Yellow Granex-Type Short-Day Sweet Onion)
description: Set transplants or sets 4 to 6 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping weeds down early since onions compete poorly with weeds while bulbs are sizing up. Georgia Sweet is a Yellow Granex-type short-day onion grown throughout the Vidalia region of southeast Georgia, where the area's naturally low-sulfur soils contribute to the same mild, sweet flavor that makes true Vidalia onions famous, even though only onions grown within the legally defined Vidalia district may carry that trademarked name. The flattened globe bulbs have thin, pale yellow skin and mild, juicy flesh best eaten fresh, since the low pungency that makes sweet onions so pleasant raw also shortens their storage life compared to pungent keeping onions. Reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over, then cure bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks before moving them to storage. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Georgiagem Rabbiteye Blueberry (1986 Georgia Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Georgiagem, released by the University of Georgia in 1986, produces a vigorous, productive bush bearing medium-to-large, well-flavored berries on a plant that has proven well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Deep South growing season. It fills a useful spot in the rabbiteye ripening sequence for growers building an extended harvest by combining early, mid, and late cultivars. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Georgian Crystal Garlic (Large-Clove Mild Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Crystal is a porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating in the country of Georgia, valued for its large, glossy white bulbs with just 4-6 very large cloves that are quick and easy to peel, along with a mild-to-medium, clean garlic flavor that works well both raw and cooked. It is a vigorous, reliable producer that adapts well across a range of cold-winter climates. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct energy into bulb growth; scapes are excellent sautéed or made into pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; storage life is moderate, typically 5-7 months in a cool, dry location. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Georgian Fire Garlic (Spicy Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Fire, originating from the Republic of Georgia, is a porcelain hardneck garlic valued for notably hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, savory sweetness when roasted, along with large bulbs of four to six big, easy-to-peel cloves under smooth white skin typical of porcelain types. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; porcelain types like Georgian Fire generally offer good storage life of six months or more under proper conditions. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Georgian Fire Hardneck Garlic (Spicy Porcelain Heirloom)
description: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Georgian Fire is a porcelain-type hardneck heirloom, also brought out of the Republic of Georgia, producing large bulbs with just four to six plump, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white wrappers, and it is prized among heirloom garlic growers for a noticeably hotter, more pungent bite than milder porcelain varieties like Georgian Crystal or Music. Cut the curling scapes in early summer once they appear to push more energy into bulb development, and cure harvested bulbs in a warm, dry, airy spot for several weeks before trimming and storing. Porcelain types store considerably longer than Rocamboles, generally holding good quality for six months or more under cool, dry conditions. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Gerardi Dwarf Mulberry (Compact Full-Size-Fruit Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Gerardi Dwarf is a naturally compact mulberry selection that stays a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees — often kept as low as 3–6 feet with pruning — while still producing full-sized, sweet, juicy dark berries typical of good mulberry cultivars, making it one of the few mulberries genuinely practical for a small yard, large container, or spot under bird netting. It is self-fertile, so a single plant fruits without a pollinator, and its small stature allows the whole canopy to be netted against birds, which is otherwise the biggest challenge in mulberry growing since ripening fruit is intensely attractive to them. Prune annually in late winter to maintain the compact form and to encourage a flush of new fruiting wood, since mulberries fruit on both old and new growth. Harvest by gently shaking ripe branches over a sheet or tarp, since ripe mulberries detach easily and bruise if hand-picked one at a time; fruit ripens over several weeks rather than all at once, extending the harvest season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: German Butterball Potato (Rich Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; German Butterball is a late-mid-season variety (70–90 days) that produces medium-large, round to slightly oval, netted-skin, golden-fleshed tubers. German Butterball is a traditional German heirloom potato that entered American heirloom potato circles through the Rodale Institute and seed saver networks in the 1980s; it is consistently rated among the finest-flavored potato varieties by tasting panels — the rich, buttery, dense golden-yellow flesh has a flavor intensity that significantly exceeds Yukon Gold (the most popular yellow potato commercially) and makes German Butterball a benchmark for those seeking the very best potato flavor. The tubers have thin, netted tan-gold skin and deep golden-yellow flesh with a texture that is semi-waxy when young and becomes more floury when mature, making it excellent for all cooking purposes: baked, roasted, mashed, boiled, or fried. The exceptional flavor when simply roasted or baked with olive oil is what defines German Butterball's reputation — no other potato consistently delivers this depth of rich, buttery potato flavor without any embellishment. One of the most sought-after varieties in the specialty potato market. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: German Chamomile
description: German chamomile bears masses of small, daisy-like flowers whose apple-scented petals make a soothing tea and lend themselves to dried arrangements and crafts. Sow seed on the soil surface and press in lightly, since it needs light to germinate; it establishes easily and often self-sows for future seasons. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil and modest water. Harvest the open flower heads regularly to keep the plant blooming and to build up a supply for drying. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: German Extra Hardy Garlic (Robust Cold-Climate Porcelain Hardneck)
aliases: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'German Extra Hardy'
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. German Extra Hardy is one of the most popular and reliable porcelain hardneck garlics for cold-climate gardeners, prized for its outstanding winter hardiness and consistent production of large bulbs with 4-5 big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, sometimes with faint purple streaking. Flavor is strong and full-bodied raw, mellowing to a rich, savory sweetness when roasted. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location, then trim and store; German Extra Hardy has only moderate storage life, typically 4-6 months, so use it earlier in the year relative to longer-storing softneck types. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: German Garlic
description: Direct sow or set divisions in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed in spring, spacing clumps to allow the twisting, chive-like foliage room to fan outward. It tolerates light woodland-edge shade far better than most culinary onions and forms a tidy, long-lived edging clump rather than spreading aggressively. Leaves and the late-summer lilac-pink flower heads are both edible with a mild, chive-like bite, making it useful as both a garnish plant and a low border feature. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep vigor up. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: German Giant Radish
description: This aptly named radish can be pulled small at quarter size or left to grow as large as a tennis ball while staying crisp and flavorful. It is crack-resistant and holds its texture without turning woody or spongy as it matures. Sow directly in cool weather and thin seedlings to give the large roots room. Keep soil evenly moist for the best flavor. Grows well in spring and fall in full sun to partial shade. Matures in 28–35 days from seed.

name: German Head Tomato (Large Meaty German Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking or caging early to support the heavy fruit. German Head is a German heirloom beefsteak grown for enormous, smooth, pink-red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh and a rich, sweet, well-balanced flavor typical of the great German pink beefsteak tradition that also produced varieties like German Johnson and German Pink. Individual fruit regularly tops a pound, making it an excellent slicing tomato for sandwiches and fresh eating, and the indeterminate vine remains productive over a long season when given consistent water and feeding. Provide sturdy support for the heavy fruit clusters, and water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking on the large, smooth-skinned fruit. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: German Johnson Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. German Johnson is a large-fruited, indeterminate, pink-fleshed heirloom long popular throughout the American South and Mid-Atlantic states — it is considered a parent variety of the famous Mortgage Lifter, crossed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia to produce that legendary tomato; the fruits themselves are large, slightly irregular, meaty, and deeply flavored with a rich, slightly acidic, classic old-fashioned tomato taste and minimal gel content. The plants are vigorous and highly productive, with good resistance to common foliar diseases in hot, humid Southern conditions. Excellent for slicing, sandwiches, and home canning. Matures in 79–85 days from transplant.

name: German Pink Tomato (Bavarian Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm soil, staking or caging the sprawling vines. German Pink descends from seed brought from Bavaria to Iowa in 1883 by the family of Seed Savers Exchange co-founder Diane Ott Whealy, and it produces huge, meaty, nearly seedless pink-skinned fruit with a mild, sweet flavor well suited to slicing and canning alike. It remains one of the founding heirloom varieties associated with the Seed Savers Exchange movement. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: German Red Hardneck Garlic (Rocambole Type Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart, in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch with 4–6 inches of straw after ground cools; keep consistently moist in spring and remove scapes when they curl to redirect energy to bulbs; stop watering as lower leaves yellow and harvest in early to midsummer. German Red is a Rocambole-type hardneck garlic with origins in Germany, gaining wide recognition in North America through garlic enthusiast and seed-saver networks in the Pacific Northwest and through specialist growers like Filaree Garlic Farm — Rocambole types are considered by many garlic connoisseurs to produce the finest flavor of all garlic types, and German Red is consistently ranked among the best Rocamboles for its deep, rich, complex, slightly spicy flavor and the full-bodied pungency that distinguishes well-grown Rocambole from milder softneck types. The bulbs produce 8–12 large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer, with brownish-purple outer skin typical of Rocamboles; the cloves are rounded-edged and notably easy to peel (another Rocambole characteristic). The flavor is excellent when raw but truly reveals its complexity when roasted, sautéed, or used in slow-cooked dishes. The main limitation of Rocambole types including German Red is storage life — typically only 3–5 months under good conditions, compared to 10–12 months for softneck types; grow what you will use by midwinter and source next season's seed before that. Matures in 220–250 days from transplant.

name: German Red Strawberry Tomato (Heart-Shaped German Oxheart Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking well as vines can reach 5-7 feet. German Red Strawberry is a German oxheart heirloom prized for its large, strawberry- or heart-shaped fruit, typically 3-4 inches long and 10-16 ounces, that ripens to a deep red with smooth shoulders and thick, meaty, relatively low-seed flesh. The flavor is rich and well-balanced with classic old-fashioned sweetness, making it popular for slicing as well as sauce, though fruit shape can be somewhat variable from plant to plant. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: German Stripe Tomato (Old German Bicolor)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil; provide substantial staking or caging as plants reach 5–8 feet. German Stripe (also sometimes called 'Old German' or 'Old German Stripe') is a large Mennonite heirloom beefsteak tomato of the bicolor class — producing very large (12–28 oz), flattened to slightly lobed fruits that are visually unremarkable from the outside (reddish-gold exterior) but stunning when sliced: the interior flesh is dramatically streaked and marbled with alternating crimson red and golden yellow in bold, irregular patterns radiating from the blossom scar, making each cross-section unique and visually captivating. The flavor matches the dramatic appearance — exceptionally sweet and rich with a honey-complexity that is one of the hallmarks of the best bicolor heirlooms; the sweetness from the golden areas contrasts with the more acid-forward richness of the red portions to create a layered, complex taste. One of the finest beefsteak heirlooms for fresh eating, tomato salads, and caprese where the bicolor slices can be displayed to advantage. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: German White Stiffneck Hardneck Garlic
description: This porcelain hardneck garlic, also sold as German Extra-Hardy, forms impressive 2 inch or larger bulbs with 4 to 7 fat, easy-peeling cloves and a strong, robust flavor. Plant individual cloves in fall, pointed end up, in fertile, well-drained soil, then mulch for winter protection. Cut the scapes in early summer to channel energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown and cure in a dry, airy place. It stores well and is very cold-hardy. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: German Wine Rhubarb (Heirloom Deep-Red Rhubarb)
description: Set out crown divisions in early spring in full sun and deeply worked, fertile soil, positioning the crown bud just below the surface. Keep the planting bed weed-free and consistently moist through the first growing season while the perennial root system develops. German Wine is an old European heirloom prized for stalks that are colored a deep wine-red from skin to core, a trait that produces especially rich, richly colored sauces, pies, and the traditional home-brewed rhubarb wine that gave the cultivar its name. It is a moderately vigorous grower with good cold hardiness, making it a dependable choice for northern kitchen gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: German Winter Thyme
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or gritty, lean soil — thyme rots in wet, heavy soils; German Winter is a named thyme cultivar selected for maximum cold hardiness among culinary thymes while retaining excellent flavor — the selection criterion being survival in harsh northern winters without the flavor reduction that sometimes accompanies cold-hardy breeding in other thyme types. The narrow, dark green, intensely aromatic leaves have a classic culinary thyme flavor — warm, slightly sweet, slightly piney, with clove-like notes — that is considered superior to many named thyme cultivars for cooking. German Winter forms a tidy, compact mound and remains evergreen in mild climates. It is the preferred culinary thyme for zone 4–7 gardeners where standard English thyme may winterkill. In zone 9 German Winter performs as a reliable perennial through its first several years before the heat-stressed plants may need replacement; fall planting ensures the best establishment. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Gernika Pepper (Basque Pimiento de Gernika Frying Pepper)
description: Gernika (Gernikako Piperra) is a slender, thin-walled sweet frying pepper protected under Spain's Denominacion de Origen Protegida in the Basque Country, where it is a signature tapas ingredient traditionally flash-fried whole in olive oil and finished with coarse salt. Pods are harvested small and immature, typically 2.5 to 3.5 inches long, while still green, since the variety is never grown to full ripeness for market; frequent harvesting at this young stage also keeps the compact plants setting new fruit continuously through summer. The thin flesh cooks in under a minute in hot oil, blistering the skin while the interior stays tender, with a flavor that is mild and sweet with only an occasional peppery bite from scattered hotter individual fruits, similar to Spain's Padron pepper but generally milder and more consistent. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and a support stake or cage for the heavily branched, fruit-laden plants. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Gete Okosomin Squash (Ancient Native American 'Get Big' Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, sprawling vines generous room. Gete Okosomin — an Anishinaabemowin name often translated as 'big old squash' or 'cool old squash' — is an heirloom traced to seed recovered from a centuries-old clay pot in an archaeological context associated with Native peoples of the Great Lakes region, and subsequently grown out, verified, and shared by Miami Nation seed keepers and Native seed-saving networks, making it one of the oldest documented squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. Fruits are large, often 10-15 pounds, striped in shades of green, orange, and cream on a somewhat elongated, ribbed form, with dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and pies. As a Cucurbita maxima type, it needs a long, warm growing season and ample space for its long vines, along with consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Beyond its culinary value, growing Gete Okosomin is a way for gardeners to participate directly in the ongoing revival of an Indigenous foodway; seed saved from open-pollinated fruit can be replanted, continuing a lineage that stretches back many generations. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and the stem has dried, then cure for two to three weeks before storing in a cool, dry location. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Gewürztraminer Wine Grape (Aromatic Pink-Skinned Variety)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Gewürztraminer, a pink-to-russet-skinned variety most closely associated with Alsace, France and Germany, is grown for intensely aromatic wines carrying strong floral, lychee, rose, and warm spice notes unlike almost any other white grape, a character so distinctive that the German word 'gewürz,' meaning spiced, was appended to the older Traminer name to describe it. The vine is only moderately vigorous and can be somewhat inconsistent in fruit set, and it performs best in cooler climates with a wide gap between warm days and cool nights, which helps preserve the delicate aromatics that define good Gewürztraminer wine. Train to a permanent trellis, thin crop if fruit set is heavy to concentrate flavor, and harvest based on aromatic development as much as sugar level, since the variety's signature perfume can be lost if fruit hangs too long in hot conditions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ghost Bhut Jolokia Chile Pepper
description: One of the hottest peppers on earth at over one million Scoville units, so wear gloves when handling ripe fruit. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and provide bottom heat around 85F for reliable germination. Transplant into the warmest spot in the garden after nights stay above 55F. Fruits ripen slowly from green to fiery red; dehydrate and grind them into flakes for a fruity, intense heat. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Ghost Pepper (Bhut Jolokia)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and maintain a constant soil temperature of 85–90°F; germination is slow and irregular, so start more seeds than needed and be patient. Transplant to a sheltered, heat-retaining bed after all frost danger has passed, and protect young plants from cool nights with row cover. Fruits turn from green to red (or yellow in some strains) at full maturity; wear gloves and avoid touching the face when harvesting, as the heat exceeds one million Scoville units. The extremely long growing season makes this pepper best suited to zones 9–12 or greenhouse culture in cooler regions. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Ghostbuster Eggplant (Glossy White Oval Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Ghostbuster is a compact, early hybrid eggplant that produces smooth, glossy, pure-white oval fruit with creamy flesh and notably fewer seeds than many heirloom white varieties. Its hybrid vigor and disease resistance make it more forgiving for beginners than older open-pollinated white eggplants, which can be slower and less productive. Harvest fruit at 4-5 inches while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white types can develop a yellow tinge and bitter flavor if left too long on the plant. Choose Ghostbuster when you want the striking look of a white eggplant on a plant with the reliability and earliness of a modern hybrid. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Giant Anise Hyssop (Sunset Hyssop)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sunset hyssop is a southwestern Agastache with unusually bright orange to flame-red flowers — the most vivid color in the genus, quite different from the lavender and purple typical of most anise hyssops. The nectar-rich, tubular flowers are magnetically attractive to hummingbirds and the flowers and leaves have a fruity, licorice-mint fragrance used in herbal teas. Several popular garden cultivars including 'Apricot Sunrise', 'Peachie Keen', and 'Sunset Hyssop' derive from this species. Drought tolerant once established; prefers lean soil over rich, organic beds where it tends to be short-lived. In zone 9, the combination of heat tolerance, hummingbird attraction, and fragrant foliage makes it an excellent late-summer nectar plant. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Giant Bamboo (Dragon Bamboo, Rough Bamboo)
description: Plant in deep, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide deep, consistent irrigation — giant bamboo is a water-demanding tropical plant. Dendrocalamus asper (giant bamboo or dragon bamboo) is one of the largest bamboo species in the world — a clumping (not running, not invasive) tropical giant native to Southeast Asia producing massive culms (stems) that can reach 20–40 meters tall and up to 20 cm in diameter in tropical climates, although in zone 9 conditions it is somewhat smaller (20–30 feet) and more manageable. The young shoots are among the most commercially important bamboo shoots in Southeast Asia — extraordinarily large, thick, and mild-flavored, sold fresh and canned throughout the region. Unlike running bamboo (Phyllostachys and others), Dendrocalamus asper forms a tightly clumped, slowly expanding clump and does not send runners underground to colonize surrounding areas — making it vastly more manageable in a garden setting. The mature culms are used for structural bamboo construction, furniture, crafts, and musical instruments. In zone 9, the clump will be killed to the ground by hard freezes but may resprout from the base if the root zone is well-mulched. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Giant Belgium Pink Tomato (Belgian Giant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Belgium Pink (also called Belgian Giant) is an indeterminate heirloom tomato with large, flattened, sometimes deeply lobed, pink to pinkish-red beefsteak fruits that frequently weigh 1–2+ lbs, rivaling Brandywine in size and beauty; the flesh is dense, meaty, sweet, and low-acid with a rich complexity suited for fresh slicing and sandwich use. The fruits share the large-pink-beefsteak class with Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter, providing an additional option with slightly different flavor character for gardeners who prize this class of tomato. Indeterminate; stake or cage as plants reach 5–8 feet; productivity is good for a giant beefsteak but individual fruits require time to develop fully. Outstanding for Gulf Coast spring tomato production planted February through March for May–June harvest. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Giant Cane (Native Bamboo)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; giant cane is the only bamboo native to North America, once forming vast canebrakes across the South and Mississippi Valley that were critical habitat for the now-extinct Carolina parakeet and Bachman's warbler, as well as important forage for Swainson's warbler. The young shoots in spring are edible, similar to commercial bamboo shoots, and were an important food source for Native American peoples. The mature canes were used for tools, weapons, and construction. As a landscape plant it provides fast-growing subtropical screening and naturalistic structure. It spreads aggressively by rhizome and should be managed; use underground root barriers to contain it in smaller spaces. The plant supports several rare specialist moth species. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Giant Carentan Leek
description: Sow seeds indoors in flats or trays well ahead of the last frost, then transplant seedlings into holes or shallow trenches several inches deep so soil can be gradually mounded up around the stems to blanch them white as they grow. This classic French heirloom is known for its thick, broad blue-green leaves and unusually wide, well-blanched shaft, making it one of the largest and most substantial leeks commonly grown in home gardens. It has good cold tolerance and can often stay in the ground for a late fall or early winter harvest in milder climates, developing a mild, sweet flavor after light frost. Hill soil around the stems every few weeks through the growing season for the longest, whitest shafts. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Giant Chives
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Giant Chives ('Forescate') is a selected cultivar of common chives that produces hollow stems 18–24 inches tall — significantly taller and more robust than standard chive types — with a more pronounced, buttery onion flavor particularly valued for garnishing soups and baked potatoes where the extra visual impact of longer stems improves presentation. The larger stems are also more practical for fine chopping in large quantities. The lavender-pink globe flowers are identical to standard chives but borne on longer stems, making them excellent cut flowers and attractive to pollinators. 'Forescate' is the French market cultivar selected for consistent large size and rapid regrowth after cutting. Like all chives, it dies to the ground in severe winters but re-emerges reliably in spring; in zone 9 it remains partially green through mild winters. Divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Giant Fennel (Common Giant Fennel)
description: Sow fresh seeds in fall in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; giant fennel does not transplant well — sow in place. Ferula communis (giant fennel) is an imposing, large-scale Mediterranean perennial herb — related to but very different from common fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) — that spends its first several years as a large, dramatic, knee-to-waist-high rosette of finely divided, blue-green, intensely ferny foliage before producing a towering, 6-to-10-foot flower stalk bearing large, golden-yellow umbels of flowers in late spring. The plant is monocarpic, meaning it flowers once, sets seed, then dies; it must be grown from seed and takes 3–7 years to reach flowering size. In Greek mythology, the giant fennel (narthex) was used as the staff by which Prometheus carried fire from the gods — the pithy, slow-burning stems were historically used as torches and fire-carriers across the Mediterranean. NOTE: Unlike culinary fennel (which is edible), giant fennel contains sesquiterpene coumarins that can cause skin photosensitivity and is toxic to livestock (especially sheep); it is grown as an ornamental structural plant, not a food plant. Seeds lose viability quickly; sow within weeks of harvest. Matures in 730–1825 days from seed.

name: Giant Fuyu Persimmon
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; persimmons are drought-tolerant once established but benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development. Giant Fuyu is a large-fruited, non-astringent Japanese persimmon cultivar, an improved selection from the standard 'Fuyu' producing much larger fruits (often 8–16 oz per fruit, compared to 4–6 oz for standard Fuyu) while retaining the outstanding non-astringent quality of the Fuyu type — meaning the fruits can be eaten firm and crisp right off the tree when fully orange without any astringency, like eating a sweet, spiced apple. An excellent choice for Gulf Coast, California, and mild-climate gardens where it ripens in October–November; trees are self-fruitful, moderate in vigor, and begin producing in 3–5 years from grafted trees. The fruit has beautiful fall color and the bare orange fruits persisting on leafless branches in late fall are ornamentally striking. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Giant Granadilla (Badea, Giant Passion Fruit)
description: Plant in deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun with an extremely sturdy support capable of handling 8-pound fruits; giant granadilla produces the world's largest passion fruits — 6 to 12 inches long and weighing up to 8 pounds — with whitish-yellow skin, a thick edible rind used as a vegetable, and seedy interior pulp that makes refreshing juice and drinks popular across tropical Latin America. The vine is extraordinarily vigorous, growing 30–50 feet annually, and requires rigorous pruning after harvest. Flowers measure 4–5 inches across with a remarkable corona of purple, white, and pink filaments. In Central America, the unripe fruit rind is cooked as a vegetable in soups and stews; the ripe pulp is eaten fresh or juiced. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Giant Japanese Butterbur (Giganteus Fuki)
description: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant them into consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants generously since 'Giganteus' is the larger-leaved, more dramatic form of Japanese butterbur commonly offered by nurseries. Its rounded leaves can exceed three feet across on stout petioles, creating a bold, almost tropical look in a shaded, damp corner of the garden where few other food plants would thrive. The thick petioles are harvested in early spring before the leaves fully unfurl and prepared the traditional Japanese way, peeled, blanched, and simmered in dashi or miso as fuki. Because the rhizomes spread aggressively in wet shade, confine 'Giganteus' with a buried barrier or dedicate it to a naturally moist, shaded low spot where its size and vigor become an asset rather than a nuisance. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Giant Leek
description: This AAS-winning heirloom leek produces thick, mild, onion-flavored stalks that store well through cold weather. Start seed indoors about ten weeks before the last frost, then transplant the pencil-thick seedlings into deep dibbled holes to blanch the lower stems. Water steadily and hill soil around the shafts as they grow to lengthen the tender white portion. Harvest as needed through fall and winter, since the hardy plants tolerate hard freezes. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Giant Marconi Sweet Pepper (AAS-Winning Italian Roasting Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Marconi is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning Italian sweet frying/roasting pepper that produces some of the largest and most productive sweet non-bell peppers available to home gardeners — long (7–10 inch), slightly tapered, blocky-shouldered fruits with very thick flesh and virtually no heat. The distinctive form is characteristic of Italian frying peppers: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a ridged, slightly irregular exterior and a meaty, thick-walled interior with surprisingly few seeds relative to total volume. The large, thick-walled fruits are extraordinary for roasting and grilling — the thick flesh holds its structure as the skin blisters and chars, and after peeling, the roasted flesh is silky, sweet, and rich with concentrated pepper flavor. Giant Marconi is the ideal choice for Italian peperonata (braised peppers with olive oil and garlic), stuffed peppers, antipasto, and any application calling for large quantities of roasted sweet pepper. The plants are tall and productive, often requiring staking when heavily loaded; they produce heavily from midsummer through fall in zone 9. The very sweet, mild flavor at the red-ripe stage is excellent raw in salads and on cheese boards where the visual impact of the large, vivid red fruits is attractive. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Giant Noble Spinach
description: This classic heirloom spinach forms large, deep-green leaves with a mild, tender flavor, spreading widely as it grows. Direct sow seed half an inch deep in cool, fertile soil as early as it can be worked, since spinach bolts quickly in heat. Keep moisture even and thin plants so leaves size up fully. Harvest outer leaves or cut whole plants young, and sow again in late summer for a productive, cold-tolerant fall crop. Matures in 43–50 days from seed.

name: Giant of Italy Parsley
description: Giant of Italy is a vigorous flat-leaf Italian parsley with large, aromatic dark green leaves and a robust, authentic flavor. Germination is slow, so soak seed overnight and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest outer stems first and the plant keeps producing from the center all season. This hardy biennial often overwinters in milder zones, flowering and setting seed in its second year. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Giant of Naples Celery (Sedano Gigante di Napoli, Italian Heirloom Braising Celery)
aliases: Apium graveolens var. dulce 'Giant of Naples'
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil that stays consistently moist, since celery's shallow roots suffer quickly in dry spells and stress produces tough, stringy, bitter stalks. Giant of Naples is a classic heirloom from the Campania region of Italy, grown less often as a raw salad celery and more as a cooking celery, since its thick, pale-green ribs soften into a rich, mellow flavor that anchors soffritto, braises, and long-simmered sauces. The stalks are notably broad and fleshy compared to standard American celery, and the plant tends to be more heat-tolerant and less prone to bolting than delicate salad types. Harvest by cutting individual outer stalks as needed through the season, or dig the whole plant once it reaches full size; a light frost sweetens the flavor rather than damaging the crop. Matures in 105–120 days from transplant.

name: Giant Pascal Celery (Classic French Heirloom Winter Celery)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Giant Pascal, also sold as Giant Golden Pascal, is a French-derived heirloom celery documented in American seed catalogs since the late nineteenth century and long regarded as the standard for winter keeping. Its stalks grow notably thick and full-bodied, with a rich, nutty flavor that many gardeners find fuller than modern hybrid celery, and the ribs stay crisp and remarkably tolerant of cool fall and winter conditions. Blanch by tying the outer stalks together and mounding soil or wrapping paper around the base of the plant for two to three weeks before harvest, which lightens the green color to gold and softens any bitterness. Because it stores and holds in the garden well into winter, Giant Pascal has traditionally been the go-to celery for late-season harvest and root-cellar storage. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Giant Poha Berry (Hawaiian Cape Gooseberry)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since Giant Poha Berry needs a long season to reach its notably larger fruit size compared to standard cape gooseberry. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants generously to accommodate their sprawling, half-woody habit, and stake or cage the sturdy branches to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. This selection, popularized in Hawaii, produces papery husks enclosing golden-orange berries roughly twice the diameter of the wild-type poha berry, with a rich, tropical sweet-tart flavor prized fresh, dried, or cooked into jams and sauces. In zones 9-11 plants can persist as short-lived perennials and will self-seed readily in warm garden soil. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Giant Prague Celeriac
description: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — celeriac demands high fertility and absolutely consistent moisture throughout its long development; Giant Prague is the standard open-pollinated celeriac variety — celery root — one of the most important and widely grown vegetables in European cuisine that remains dramatically underutilized in American cooking despite its extraordinary culinary versatility. The edible part of celeriac is not a root but a swollen hypocotyl (the base of the stem) that develops into a large, round, rough-surfaced globe of dense, white flesh with an intense, concentrated celery flavor — pure celery essence without the stringy fiber or water content of celery stalks. Celeriac's culinary applications are among the most diverse of any European vegetable: raw in the classic French preparation celeriac rémoulade (grated raw celeriac in mustardy mayonnaise), pureed into silky soups and mashes as a potato alternative, roasted, braised, or added to stocks for their distinctive aromatic depth. The dense, concentrated flavor means a small amount of celeriac adds substantial impact — a quarter of a root can flavor an entire pot of soup that whole bunches of celery stalks would struggle to match. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Giant Red Celery
description: Giant Red is a 19th-century English heirloom celery valued for its tough, deep pink-to-red stalks and pronounced, old-fashioned celery flavor that is stronger and more concentrated than modern green types. Traditionally grown in trenches and earthed up to blanch and sweeten the ribs, it can also be left unblanched for a more intense, almost peppery flavor better suited to cooked dishes than raw eating. It tolerates cool fall weather better than many stalk celeries, holding quality after light frost. Gardeners grow it for its striking color in soups and braises and as a genetic link to celery grown before uniform green hybrids became standard. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Giant Red Mustard Greens
description: This heirloom mustard combines ornamental burgundy-red leaves brushed with green and a bold, spicy flavor that mellows with cooking. Direct sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep and thin for baby leaves or fuller plants. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in salads or let them mature for cooking greens. Grow in cool spring and fall weather with steady moisture, since heat pushes plants to bolt and turns the flavor sharp. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Giant Taro (Upright Elephant Ear)
description: Plant in deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in bright indirect light or dappled shade; unlike Colocasia (which faces its leaves downward and outward), Alocasia macrorrhiza holds its enormous leaves facing up and skyward on stout, upright petioles, creating a dramatic architectural effect in tropical gardens. The stems and corms are edible after extensive cooking in many Pacific Island and Asian cuisines, but all parts contain high levels of calcium oxalate and must be boiled for at least 45 minutes to neutralize the crystals. Water generously during the growing season and reduce irrigation in cooler months; the large leaves transpire heavily and wilting is the first sign of drought stress. Clumps spread slowly by offsets that can be separated and replanted. Matures in 240–365 days from transplant.

name: Giant Timber Bamboo
description: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Bambusa oldhamii is a clumping bamboo that does not run — the rhizomes are pachymorph (tightly clumping), so it stays where you plant it and never invades neighbors; water deeply and regularly in establishment and during summer heat. Bambusa oldhamii (Giant Timber Bamboo, Oldham Bamboo, or Eating Bamboo) is a large, fast-growing, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to Taiwan and adjacent southeastern China, and the most widely planted timber bamboo in California, Florida, and the Gulf Coast states due to its massive size, non-running growth habit, and cold hardiness to zone 7b. The culms (canes) grow rapidly to 50–65 feet tall and 3–5 inches in diameter, straight-walled and deep green when young, maturing to yellow-green or golden. The shoots produced in spring are among the largest, most palatable, and best-tasting of any bamboo available in the United States — harvested when 6–12 inches tall, boiled to remove bitterness, and used in Asian cooking exactly like commercial canned bamboo shoots. Giant Timber Bamboo also produces outstanding landscape screening, windbreak, and carbon-sequestration value — fully grown culms can be harvested every 3–5 years as timber for furniture, flooring, fencing, and structural poles. Excellent Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 privacy screen, grove specimen, and food-producing landscape plant. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Giant Winter Spinach (Cold-Hardy Heirloom Savoy Spinach)
description: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to four to six inches apart once true leaves appear. Giant Winter is an old European heirloom selected for exceptional cold hardiness and large, heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves that hold quality through hard freezes and short winter days far better than most spinach varieties, making it a strong choice for a Gulf Coast fall-through-winter planting. The extra-large, thick leaves are slower to bolt in cool weather and develop a sweeter, richer flavor after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette once plants reach full size. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Gideon Chinese Chestnut
description: Gideon is a Chinese chestnut selection notable for its cold hardiness well beyond the range where most Chinese chestnut cultivars perform reliably, making it a favored parent tree and orchard choice in colder northern climates. It bears a good crop of medium nuts with the sweet, easy-peeling qualities typical of Chinese chestnut. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant at least two unrelated seedlings or cultivars within pollination range for consistent nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gigante di Romagna Cardoon (Italian Large Nearly-Spineless Cardoon)
description: Start seed indoors and set transplants into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous space for its large mature footprint; Gigante di Romagna is a heirloom Italian cardoon from the Romagna region prized for producing unusually thick, wide, nearly spineless leaf ribs that are easier and less prickly to handle at harvest than most other cardoon strains. As with other cardoons, the coarse, bitter raw ribs are transformed by blanching, achieved by wrapping the mature plant in cardboard, burlap, or straw for three to four weeks before harvest to exclude light and mellow the flavor. The blanched ribs are classically braised, breaded and fried, or baked into a gratin, and the plant's tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage and thistle-like purple flower heads make it a dramatic architectural presence in the garden even where it is not harvested. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Gigante Tomatillo
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gigante (also called Grande) tomatillo is a large-fruited Mexican selection producing fruits 2–3 inches in diameter, substantially larger than the standard tomatillo — each fruit can weigh 3–4 ounces, compared to 1–2 ounces for standard types. The large fruit size dramatically reduces the number of fruits needed per batch of salsa verde and makes individual-fruit processing (husking, cleaning) more efficient. The flavor is bright, mildly tart, and herbal — characteristic of the tomatillo — without the papery, husked fruit becoming bitter at full size. Harvest when husks begin to split and feel papery but before they yellow significantly. Plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination, which is essential for good fruit set. Plants sprawl widely and may benefit from staking or support. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Gijnlim Asparagus
description: Gijnlim is a Dutch all-male hybrid developed for the European white and green asparagus trade, prized for spearing very early in spring and producing an unusually concentrated first flush of thick, straight spears. Growers who mound soil over the crowns get pale, tender spears for traditional white asparagus, while unmounded beds yield classic green spears just as reliably. Its early emergence means it can beat frost-sensitive varieties to market by a week or more in cool climates. Established beds reward deep, fertile, well-drained soil and a thick mulch layer to suppress weeds between rows. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gilfeather Turnip (Vermont State Vegetable, Heirloom Turnip-Rutabaga Cross)
description: Direct sow seeds thinly in well-tilled, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, thinning to 8–12 inches when plants are 3 inches tall; harvest in late fall after light frosts have sweetened the roots. Gilfeather turnip is one of the most historically significant and culinarily distinctive heirloom vegetables in New England — the Vermont state vegetable, named for John Gilfeather of Wardsboro, Vermont, who reportedly kept this variety secret by cutting off the tops and bottoms of roots before selling or trading them to prevent others from saving seed, maintaining a monopoly on his exceptional variety for decades in the early 20th century. The Gilfeather is not a standard turnip but appears to be a cross between turnip (Brassica rapa) and rutabaga (Brassica napobrassica), inheriting characteristics of both — the roots are large (up to 5 lbs), elongated to round with a distinctive greenish-white skin, and the white flesh is significantly sweeter, milder, and less peppery than standard turnips, with a creamy texture when cooked that many tasters prefer to either parent species. The flavor is sweet, rich, and substantial — excellent mashed, roasted, or in soups and stews — without the sharpness that can make standard turnips polarizing. A unique and genuinely outstanding heirloom vegetable with an authentic piece of New England agricultural heritage behind it; a excellent fall/winter root vegetable for zone 9 production. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Gill's Golden Pippin Acorn Squash (Heirloom Golden-Skinned Acorn Squash)
description: Sow seed directly in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to give the semi-vining plants room without the sprawl of a full-size squash vine. This heirloom stands apart from the ubiquitous dark green acorn squash by ripening to a bright golden-orange rind, and its dry, fine-grained flesh has a milder, sweeter flavor that many gardeners prefer for baking and stuffing. Harvest once fruit reaches full color and the stem has begun to dry and cork over, since acorn types do not continue to ripen off the vine. It stores for two to three months in a cool, dry spot, making it a good keeper for a squash that matures relatively early in the season. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Gilpin Apple (Little Red Romanite, Exceptional Long-Keeping Appalachian Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Gilpin, also called Little Red Romanite, is a Virginia and Appalachian heirloom famous historically for its extraordinary keeping ability, remaining crisp and usable in cold storage for many months longer than nearly any other common apple variety, a trait that made it invaluable for pre-refrigeration households needing fresh fruit through the depths of winter. The small, deep red fruit has firm, dense, notably tart flesh, sharp fresh off the tree but mellowing somewhat with extended storage, and it was historically prized as a cider apple as much as for eating and cooking. The productive, hardy tree suits mountain and upland Appalachian growing conditions well; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for exceptional long-term keeping. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ginger
description: Break fresh ginger rhizomes into 1–2 in pieces each with a visible growth bud and pre-sprout them in a warm, moist environment for 2–3 weeks before planting 2 in deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil. Ginger thrives in dappled shade and resents direct afternoon sun in hot climates. Keep soil consistently moist and avoid letting it dry out. Harvest young ginger in as little as 4–5 months for milder flavor, or leave in the ground until foliage yellows for full-size, more pungent roots. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Ginger Gold Apple (First-of-the-Season Crisp Yellow-Green Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Fuji. Found as a chance seedling near a Golden Delicious orchard in Nelson County, Virginia after Hurricane Camille in 1969, the tree was named for the discoverer's wife, Ginger Harvey. It is prized as one of the very first apples ready to harvest each year, well before Gala, with crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh that resists browning after slicing. The pale yellow-green skin sometimes develops a light pink blush in full sun. Because the fruit softens quickly once ripe, it is best picked promptly and used within a few weeks rather than stored long term. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ginger Mint
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Ginger Mint (Mentha x gracilis) is a naturally occurring hybrid mint producing slender, red-stemmed plants with smooth, bright green to slightly variegated leaves that carry a distinctive ginger-mint aroma — a warm, spicy, gingery note overlaid on the base mint freshness, quite unlike spearmint or peppermint. The flavor is used in teas, cold drinks, fruit salads, and Southeast Asian cooking where ginger notes complement the mint. Some variegated selections ('Variegata') display gold-streaked leaves that add ornamental interest. Like all culinary mints, Ginger Mint spreads by underground runners and should be contained to prevent it from colonizing adjacent plantings. The red stems are distinctive and make Ginger Mint identifiable even at a distance. In zone 9 it grows vigorously in spring and fall and benefits from afternoon shade to prevent leaf scorch in summer. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Ginkgo (Maidenhair Tree)
description: Ginkgo is dioecious — only female trees produce the edible nut, but a male is needed nearby for pollination; purchase named female cultivars (Tit, Megi, Oishi) or graft known female wood to avoid planting only males, which cannot be sexed until first flower at 20+ years. The outer fleshy seed coat (sarcotesta) smells powerfully of rancid butter when ripe and contains urushiol-related compounds — wear gloves when handling and process outdoors; the inner cream-colored nut inside the hard shell is the edible portion. Harvest when the fleshy coating has turned yellow-orange and fallen from the tree in autumn; clean immediately, dry the shells, and roast or steam before eating. Do not eat ginkgo nuts raw or in excessive quantities — they contain 4-O-methylpyridoxine, which is toxic in large amounts. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Ginseng Orange Sweet Potato (Orange-Fleshed Sport of Ginseng Red)
description: Ginseng Orange is a color-sport selection derived from the Virginia heirloom Ginseng Red, retaining the same early maturity, semi-bush vine habit, and cut, lobed leaf, but with orange skin and orange flesh in place of Ginseng Red's pinkish-red skin and light orange flesh. Its compact, semi-bush growth is well suited to smaller garden beds where a fully sprawling vine variety would be unwelcome. Set slips in full sun in loose, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, keeping the row lightly hilled as vines fill in to protect developing roots from sun exposure and cracking. Growers note this variety produces reliably above-average yields for an heirloom type; cure roots for about a week in warm, humid conditions after digging to firm the skin and improve storage life before moving them to cooler, drier long-term storage. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Ginseng Red Sweet Potato (Virginia Heirloom)
description: Ginseng Red is a semi-bush heirloom sweet potato with a distinctive cut, lobed leaf and pinkish-red skin over light orange flesh, an early-maturing variety long grown by a Virginia farm family before it entered wider seed-saver circulation. Its more restrained, semi-bush vine habit takes up less garden space than sprawling standard sweet potato varieties, making it a reasonable choice for smaller plots. Plant slips in full sun in loose, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, and hill soil lightly around the base as vines establish to encourage even root development. After harvest, cure roots for about a week at warm temperatures and high humidity, then continue storing them for several additional weeks, since growers report the flavor and sweetness of Ginseng Red noticeably improve the longer it is kept in storage. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Giombo Persimmon (Large Elongated Astringent Asian Persimmon)
description: Giombo is a Japanese astringent-type Asian persimmon, long grown commercially in Italy's Romagna region and increasingly offered by US specialty nurseries, prized for very large, elongated fruit up to 5 inches long with a tapered tip similar in shape to Hachiya. The smooth-textured flesh is typically seedless and, once fully soft-ripe, becomes deeply sweet and honey-like with flavor notes drawing comparisons to ripe apricot and mango; like all astringent kaki types it must soften completely before eating or it will pucker the mouth. The medium-sized tree reaches roughly 15 feet and ripens its crop late in the season, making it a good choice for extending the persimmon harvest window in the Gulf South. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect Giombo to be self-fruitful like most kaki cultivars, producing reliably without a second tree nearby. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Girkanets Pomegranate
description: Girkanets is a Central Asian pomegranate cultivar originating from the Caucasus and Turkmenistan region, valued in germplasm and breeding collections for its outstanding cold tolerance among fruiting pomegranates. It bears medium-sized, dark-red-skinned fruit with tart-sweet, juicy ruby arils that suit juicing and cooking more than fresh eating. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; established trees are extremely drought-tolerant and, like other cold-hardy Central Asian selections, can survive winter lows that would kill less hardy varieties such as Wonderful. It is a useful choice for gardeners at the colder edge of pomegranate-growing range who want insurance against occasional hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gisela 6 Cherry Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Gisela 6 is a semi-dwarfing, precocious understock, not grown for its own fruit. Developed at Justus Liebig University in Giessen, Germany, this member of the widely adopted Gisela rootstock series produces a semi-dwarf tree roughly 70-80 percent the size of a Mazzard seedling tree, combining meaningful size control with earlier, heavier fruit production and good tolerance of a range of soil types compared to more fully dwarfing rootstocks in the same series. Its combination of moderate size control, precocious early bearing, and good vigor and anchorage without requiring permanent staking has made it one of the most popular modern cherry rootstocks for both commercial and home orchards. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect fruiting within two to three years, notably earlier than on a seedling Mazzard rootstock. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Glacier Bush Tomato
description: A cold-tolerant bush tomato that sets fruit in cooler temperatures than most, giving you some of the earliest ripe tomatoes of summer and a long fall harvest. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and harden off before transplanting. The compact 30-inch plants stay tidy and do well in containers, though a small cage helps. Pick the 2-inch flavorful slicers as they color up to keep production going. Matures in 55–60 days from transplant.

name: Glacier Tomato (Early Cold-Tolerant Slicing Tomato)
description: Transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; Glacier is a determinate to semi-determinate variety that does not require extensive staking; it produces most of its fruit in a compressed season (excellent for northern and coastal climates) and can be grown without pruning. Glacier is an open-pollinated early-season slicing tomato specifically suited to cool-summer and short-season climates: it sets fruit at nighttime temperatures as low as 45–50°F, a capability that distinguishes it from most standard tomato varieties (which require consistent nighttime temperatures above 55°F for pollen viability and fruit set). This cold-setting ability makes Glacier valuable for Pacific Northwest coastal gardens where summer temperatures rarely exceed 75°F, high-altitude Rocky Mountain gardens with cool nights, and short-season northern gardens (zones 3–5) where the growing season is compressed. The medium-small (3–4 oz), round to slightly oblate, red fruits ripen early (55–65 days from transplant) and have good flavor for an early variety — pleasantly sweet-acidic balance with classic fresh tomato character; the flavor intensifies if warm conditions prevail at harvest time. The determinate to semi-determinate plants (36–48 inches) do not require the extensive staking that indeterminate varieties need, making them convenient for short-season production in smaller garden spaces. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Gladiator Parsnip
description: The first F1 hybrid parsnip bred in Britain, combining vigor with smooth, blemish-free skin and strong canker resistance. Roots are wide-shouldered and taper to a short body, staying tender and free of a woody core even at large sizes. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is popular with both home gardeners and show growers for its consistency. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Gladiator Pumpkin (F1 Powdery Mildew Tolerant Jack-O-Lantern)
description: Sow seeds directly in hills after frost danger has passed, spacing hills widely since Gladiator carries a full, sprawling vine that needs room to support its large fruit load. Fruit grows round to slightly ribbed, deep orange, and sizeable at 20-25 pounds, with a thick, well-anchored handle that stands up to hauling and display without snapping off. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew keeps the canopy productive later into the season than older open-pollinated field types, which matters most where warm, humid nights push disease pressure hard in late summer. Cut fruit from the vine with several inches of stem once the rind has hardened and colored fully, then cure before storing in a cool, dry, well-ventilated space. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Gladstone Onion
description: An intermediate-day onion that forms clean, crisp white bulbs 4 to 5 inches across with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh use. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings once the soil can be worked. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist, tapering off water as the tops fall over near harvest. Cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Glaskin's Perpetual Rhubarb
description: Glaskin's Perpetual is a seed-grown heirloom rhubarb bred to bolt (flower) far less readily than most seed strains, so stalk production stays steady all season instead of stalling after the plant runs to seed. Its notably low oxalic acid content lets gardeners take a light first-year harvest, a rarity among rhubarbs that normally need a full year or two to establish before cropping. Stalks are medium-thick and pink-green rather than deep red, with a mild, less astringent flavor suited to lighter sweetening. It remains popular with gardeners who want a reliable, true-breeding rhubarb they can start cheaply from seed rather than buying divisions. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Glass Gem Corn (Rainbow Jewel-Toned Ornamental Flour Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows after last frost; harvest ears 3–4 weeks after the husks become fully dry and papery. Peel back husks and hang in a dry, well-ventilated place for additional drying before storage or decorative use. Glass Gem is a visually extraordinary ornamental flour corn that became an internet sensation in 2012 when photographs of its polychrome, jewel-toned ears went viral — sparking massive interest in heirloom and decorative corn that had not previously existed in the gardening public. The corn was developed by Carl Barnes, a half-Cherokee seed saver from Oklahoma, who spent decades crossing and back-crossing different traditional Cherokee corn varieties to create a flour corn capable of producing kernels in any color of the rainbow — deep red, crimson, burgundy, purple, violet, blue, aqua, green, gold, orange, pink, cream, and white, often on the same ear in translucent, jewel-like forms. Barnes shared seed with fellow seed saver Greg Schoen, who further developed and distributed the variety through Native Seeds/SEARCH. Each ear is unique — no two are identical — and the translucency of the kernels in bright light has no equivalent in any other corn or vegetable. While Glass Gem can be ground into flour (it is a genuine flour corn with functional starch composition), its primary use is ornamental — for corn arrangements, wreaths, and displays where the extraordinary color variation is the attraction. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Glass Gem Flint Corn
description: A stunning ornamental flint corn with kaleidoscopic, translucent rainbow kernels that can also be dried for cornmeal, flour, or popcorn. Direct sow after the last frost in blocks of at least four short rows so wind pollination fills out the ears. Give steady water during tasseling and silking for well-filled cobs. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure indoors before shelling or displaying. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Glenn Mango (Compact Florida Dooryard Mango)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, protecting young trees from any frost since mangoes have no cold tolerance. Glenn is a Florida-bred mango cultivar prized for its comparatively compact, semi-dwarf growth habit and precocious bearing, producing medium-to-large fruit with yellow-blushed skin and smooth, fiberless, sweet flesh with a mild, non-resinous flavor that makes it broadly popular for fresh eating. Its smaller stature compared to many mango cultivars suits large containers or smaller yards where a full-size mango tree would be impractical. Reduce watering as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate flavor, and harvest when fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure and develops full color. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Globe Artichoke
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors and expose young plants to 2 weeks of 50°F nights to vernalize them for first-year bud production. Transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil in a permanent location, as plants are long-lived when winters are mild enough. Harvest the central bud first, while bracts are tight and the stem snaps cleanly, then side buds as they develop. In zones 7–9, cut plants back to 12 in after harvest and mulch heavily for overwintering; divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Glohaven Peach (Classic Large Commercial Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall. Glohaven was developed by Michigan State University and became one of the most widely planted commercial freestone peaches in the Midwest and Northeast for decades, prized for very large, firm, attractive fruit with yellow flesh, a red-blushed skin, and a well-balanced, classic peach flavor that holds up well both fresh and processed. The tree is vigorous and reliably productive, with better resistance to bacterial spot than many older varieties of its era, which helped cement its reputation as a dependable commercial standard. Prune to an open-vase form for good light and air circulation, and maintain a regular dormant-oil and fungicide program to manage peach leaf curl and brown rot, common problems across most peach cultivars. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Gloire des Sablons Pink Currant
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; this cultivar performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity. Gloire des Sablons is a distinctive French heirloom currant whose berries ripen with a marbled pink-and-cream streaked skin, midway in both color and sweetness between typical red and white currants. It is grown as much for its unusual coloring as for its genuinely good eating quality, being milder and less acidic than most red-fruited types. The self-fertile bush is vigorous, producing long, well-filled strigs in midsummer, and responds well to the same renewal pruning favored by other Ribes rubrum cultivars. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Glooscap Strawberry
description: Glooscap is a 1983 release from the Kentville breeding program in Nova Scotia, bred from a cross of Micmac and Bounty, and remains valued decades later for its exceptional winter hardiness and heavy mid-season yields. The medium-sized berries separate cleanly from the cap at harvest, a trait that makes hulling for jam and preserves noticeably faster than with many dessert-type cultivars. Its toughness has made it a long-standing recommendation for cold-climate gardens from Newfoundland to the northern Plains. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to sustain productivity in following years. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Gloria Grande Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Shade-and-Nut Pecan)
description: Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Gloria Grande was selected specifically for outstanding resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that devastates susceptible cultivars in the humid Southeast. It forms an unusually large, vigorous, long-lived tree, which has made it popular as a dual-purpose shade-and-nut planting for home landscapes and parks as well as orchards in high-scab-pressure regions. The nut itself is medium in size and only fair to good in kernel quality compared with top commercial dessert cultivars, so Gloria Grande is chosen more for reliability and low spray input than for exceptional eating quality. Plant it in full sun with deep soil and a compatible pollinator, and expect a tree that shades a wide area at maturity, so allow generous spacing from structures and other trees. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Glory of Enkhuizen Cabbage
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Glory of Enkhuizen'
description: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the round, dense heads benefit from consistent moisture to avoid splitting as they finish sizing up. Glory of Enkhuizen is a classic Dutch heirloom cabbage introduced in the late 19th century from the seed-growing town of Enkhuizen in the Netherlands, long one of Europe's most important vegetable-seed production centers. It forms medium-large, round to slightly flattened, blue-green heads with a tender, sweet, finely grained interior that holds its quality well both fresh and cooked, and it has a good reputation for splitting resistance and reasonable storage life for a mid-season type. Widely grown across Europe and North America through the 20th century as a dependable, high-yielding main-crop cabbage, it remains a favorite heirloom for gardeners wanting classic round-head cabbage with proven, old-world reliability, in zone 3–9. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Glou Morceau Pear (Beurré d'Hardenpont)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Raised around 1750 by the Abbé Hardenpont of Mons, Belgium and also known as Beurré d'Hardenpont, it was introduced to Britain in 1820 and became immensely popular in Victorian England before nearly disappearing from modern markets. The medium-to-large, pyriform fruit has semi-smooth, pale olive-green skin covered in brown russet patches and specks, with ivory to off-white flesh that is moist, soft, fine-grained, and melting, sweet with a delicate sugary flavor; its name translates as "delicious morsel." Harvest in fall while still firm, store cool for several weeks, then ripen at room temperature until the buttery flesh softens before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Go Big Okra (Burpee Hybrid with Extra-Large Tender Pods)
description: Go Big is a modern hybrid bred to produce noticeably thick, dark green pods that hold their tenderness at a larger size than most standard okra. Plants grow tall and wide over the season, so give them room to branch and check pods every day or two once production ramps up in midsummer heat. Because the pods stay fry- and stew-worthy even when picked slightly larger, Go Big forgives a missed harvest day better than finer-podded heirlooms. Consistent moisture and full sun keep this vigorous hybrid setting new pods until temperatures cool in fall. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: Goat Horn Pepper
description: Goat Horn is a long, tapered cayenne-type Capsicum annuum whose curved, horn-shaped four- to six-inch pods ripen from green to a deep orange-red and carry a robust 20,000-50,000 Scoville heat with a bright, fruity edge. Despite its popularity in Sichuan and other Southeast Asian cooking, the variety traces to the Caribbean and grows vigorously in any warm-season garden with full sun and well-drained, fertile soil. Plants are heavy bearers of thin-walled pods that dry quickly on or off the plant, making Goat Horn a good choice for home-ground chili flakes, infused oils, and the toasted whole dried chiles used in stir-fries. Space plants to allow good airflow and stake tall specimens, since a fully loaded plant can carry dozens of pods at once. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Gobbo di Nizza Cardoon (Piedmontese Heirloom Blanching Cardoon)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gobbo di Nizza Monferrato is a heritage Piedmontese cardoon, listed by Slow Food's Ark of Taste, grown for its broad, fleshy, greeny-gray leaf ribs that carry relatively few strings and spines compared with wild cardoon. In late fall growers traditionally dig a shallow trench, lay the whole plant over into it, and bury the stalks in soil for several weeks, which both blanches the ribs pale and forces them into the curved, hunchbacked form that gives the variety its name. Blanched stalks are braised, fried, added to gratins, or eaten raw dipped in olive oil, and the fleshy root is edible as well, prepared much like a parsnip. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Goji Berry
description: Goji berries are highly adaptable, tolerating poor, alkaline soils where other fruits fail, but perform best in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0. The arching, slightly thorny canes can be left as a shrub or trained to a central leader with a stake. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers — ripe fruits are bright red-orange, soft, and drop easily (avoid touching them, as the sap stains). Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Gold Coast Okra (Dwarf Drought- and Nematode-Tolerant Heirloom Okra)
description: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep after soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart; Gold Coast was developed at the LSU AgCenter and selected for a compact, heavily branched habit with long petioles that make hand-harvesting easier than on tall heirloom types. The spineless, light green pods stay tender to about 6 inches and hold up well to canning and freezing. Its strong root system gives Gold Coast above-average tolerance of both drought and root-knot nematodes, two of the most common stresses on okra grown in the sandy soils of the Deep South. Because pods are slower to fiber up than many varieties, Gold Coast forgives an occasional missed picking day better than fast-maturing hybrids. Matures in 56–70 days from seed.

name: Gold Delight Muscadine Grape (Ga. 6-1-269)
description: Gold Delight is a recent University of Georgia release, selected from a cross of Early Fry and Tara, that combines self-fertility with unusually large bronze berries for an early-to-midseason cultivar.
