In UGA trials it showed better resistance to fruit rot than older bronze standards and lost less moisture in cold storage, giving it noticeably better shelf life than many bronze muscadines sold fresh. The vigorous, self-fertile vines need no separate pollinator and bear heavily once established, making this a strong choice where growers want the large-berried, high-sugar eating quality of Fry-type muscadines with improved rot tolerance in humid weather. Train on a sturdy arbor or two-wire trellis in full sun and well-drained soil. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gold Dust Rosemary (Variegated Golden Culinary Rosemary)
description: Gold Dust is an upright, branching rosemary whose needle-like leaves carry a bright gold edge around a deep green center, giving the whole shrub a variegated glow that holds its color through the growing season better than most golden-leaf herbs. Despite the ornamental foliage it is fully culinary, with the same piney, resinous flavor as green-leaved rosemary, and it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity notably well for a variegated selection. Site it in full sun for the best gold coloration, since shade fades the variegation toward plain green, and give it the same lean, sharply drained soil that all rosemary needs to avoid root and crown rot. Use it as a specimen or low hedge where its color can be appreciated, and harvest sprigs for the kitchen just as you would any culinary rosemary. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Gold Kist Apricot (Low-Chill Southern Apricot, Gulf South Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gold Kist is self-fertile and drought-tolerant once established; thin fruits to 3–4 inches after natural fruit drop; Gold Kist ripens early (May in the Gulf South and central Texas), one of the earliest-ripening apricots; harvest when fully orange and beginning to soften for best flavor. Gold Kist apricot was developed by Zaiger Genetics in California and released in the mid-1980s specifically to address the near-absence of suitable apricot varieties for mild-winter regions — the Gulf South, South Texas, the lower San Joaquin Valley, and other areas where winter temperatures rarely accumulate the 700+ chill hours required by standard apricot varieties. With a chill requirement of approximately 300 hours, Gold Kist dramatically expanded the geographic range of apricot production in the United States, particularly through the deep South and the Gulf Coast where no practical apricot had previously been available. The fruits are medium-sized, golden-orange to light orange at full ripeness, with good sweet-tart apricot flavor — somewhat milder than the finest California varieties like Blenheim but very acceptable for fresh eating and preserves. The early ripening season (May in zone 8–9) is an important characteristic: Gold Kist delivers fresh apricots weeks before any other stone fruit of comparable quality, giving it a clear market window at farmers' markets and roadside stands. It remains the primary recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Louisiana State University's AgCenter for home garden apricot production in the Gulf South. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gold Medal Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Gold Medal (also known as B&L's Gold Medal) is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing spectacular bicolor fruits with bright golden-yellow skin blushed with red and dramatically marbled interior flesh — when sliced, the cross-section reveals a swirled pattern of deep red-orange and golden-yellow that makes Gold Medal arguably the most beautiful heirloom tomato variety for fresh-cut presentations and tomato salads. The flavor combines the mild, low-acid sweetness characteristic of yellow tomatoes with the rich, complex notes of a large beefsteak type, producing a fruit that is simultaneously sweet and substantial in flavor without the sharp acidity of most large red heirlooms. The low-acid, sweet character makes Gold Medal appealing for people who enjoy the fresh sweetness of yellow tomatoes but want a larger, meatier fruit. Large fruits commonly reach 1–2 pounds and have meaty walls with small seed cavities, making them outstanding for fresh slicing. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Gold Medallion Squash (Hybrid Buttercup-Type Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since vines run vigorously across the season. Gold Medallion is a hybrid buttercup-type squash that sets a heavy crop of uniform, 3 to 4 pound, deep-orange fruit with the characteristic small button at the blossom end, and its dense, dry, sweet flesh cooks up well for baking and pureeing. Growers value it for setting fruit reliably even under variable weather, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated buttercup strains. Harvest when the rind has hardened and the vine begins to decline, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm space before moving to cool storage to concentrate the sugars. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Gold Nugget Loquat (Yellow-Fleshed Small-Seeded California Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Gold Nugget produces abundant crops of small to medium golden fruits from February through April in California and similarly timed in the Gulf Coast; the small seed size is a significant advantage for fresh eating and processing; no thinning is generally necessary due to the naturally smaller fruit size. Gold Nugget is a California loquat selection noted primarily for two characteristics: the unusually small seeds relative to fruit size, and the deep golden-yellow to amber flesh color that gives the variety its name. While most loquat varieties have relatively large seeds that reduce the proportion of edible flesh in each fruit, Gold Nugget produces a seed that is noticeably smaller than average, leaving more of the interior as eating flesh — a practical advantage for fresh eating and for any processing application (jams, preserves, sauces). The flesh color is a rich golden-yellow rather than the white of Champagne or the orange of Premier and Big Jim, and the flavor is sweet, richly aromatic, and quite juicy at peak ripeness. The tree is moderately vigorous and productive, and the smaller fruit size (typically 1–1.5 inches) means higher fruit counts per cluster compared to large-fruited varieties. In the Gulf Coast zone 9a, Gold Nugget blooms in fall and ripens in late winter to spring alongside other loquat varieties. An excellent choice for gardeners who want to maximize edible yield and minimize the frustration of handling large seeds. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Gold Nugget Mandarin (Late-Season Seedless UC Riverside Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Gold Nugget, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, produces small, bumpy-skinned, essentially seedless mandarins with rich, sweet flavor, notable for ripening later in the season than most mandarins, which extends fresh citrus availability into late winter and early spring. The medium-sized tree is well suited to container culture in areas cooler than its hardiness range. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gold Nugget Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Buttercup-Type Squash)
description: Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since this variety's bush habit needs far less room than sprawling buttercup types. Bred at North Dakota State University for the region's short, cool growing season and named an All-America Selections winner in 1966, it produces small, round, deep-orange fruit with sweet, fine-grained flesh similar to buttercup squash but ready weeks earlier. Its compact, non-vining plants make it a practical choice for northern gardens and small plots where space and season length are limited. Harvest once the rind resists thumbnail pressure, then cure briefly to concentrate sugars before storage. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Gold Rush Bush Bean
description: A golden-yellow wax bean whose bright pods stand out against green foliage, making picking quick and easy. Direct sow after the soil warms past 65F, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows. This compact, disease-resistant bush type does well in containers and holds quality both on the plant and after harvest. Pick pods young and often to encourage continued production. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Gold Rush Potato (Golden-Flesh Russet-Type Baking Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gold Rush is a North Dakota State University russet-type potato introduction combining the classic russet potato appearance (oblong, netted-brown skin) with the bright golden-yellow flesh of yellow-flesh varieties — providing a visually distinctive combination of the familiar russet form with surprisingly vivid yellow-gold interior color. The golden-yellow flesh — darker than standard Russet Burbank white flesh and more intense than the pale yellow of Yukon Gold — creates an attractive visual quality in baked, mashed, and roasted preparations where the golden color adds visual appeal to the finished dish. Gold Rush has the high-starch, dry, fluffy interior texture of classic russet-type potatoes — ideal for baking (fluffy, dry-textured baked potato), French fries (crispy exterior, dry interior), and mashed potatoes where a light, dry texture is desired. The russet skin type and long oblong shape produce the classic large baked potato form. In zone 9, Gold Rush's longer season (90–100 days) requires early planting (January) to ensure harvest before summer heat ends the cool potato growing season. Plant deeper than most varieties (6–8 inches) and hill aggressively to promote maximum tuber development in the long cool season before heat forces harvest. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Gold Rush Wax Bean (Bright Yellow Stringless Bush Wax Bean with Straight Pods)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest when pods reach 5–6 inches before seeds swell noticeably inside. Gold Rush Wax Bean is a high-yielding yellow wax bush bean developed by Burpee for home garden production, distinguished by the uniformity and straightness of its bright golden pods and its concentrated harvest set that makes it one of the most productive yellow wax types per planting. The wax bean category — yellow-podded varieties that lack the green chlorophyll of standard snap beans — developed historically as a distinct preference in European-American cooking traditions where the pale color was associated with tenderness and delicacy; wax beans are botanically identical to green snap beans, with the yellow coloration resulting from the absence of chlorophyll development in the pod walls, allowing carotenoid pigments (which would normally be masked by green) to express visibly. Gold Rush's pods are straight and uniform (an advantage for commercial packing but also convenient for home preparation), stringless from the earliest edible stage through full harvest size, and have a mild flavor with a slightly more buttery taste than equivalent green snap varieties — a characteristic that many cooks attribute to the different pigment chemistry of wax pods, though the underlying flavor compounds are essentially the same. The compact bush plant reaches 18–24 inches with an erect, self-supporting habit that keeps pods above soil contact and makes one-pass harvesting efficient. For highest yield and quality, harvest every 2–3 days throughout the peak bearing period and do not allow pods to yellow beyond the characteristic bright gold; overripe pods become pale, stringy, and starchy. Matures in 54–58 days from seed.

name: Gold Rush Yellow Wax Bean (AAS-Winning Straightpod Wax Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 4–6 inches long and still tender. Gold Rush is a 1980 All-America Selections-winning yellow wax bush bean that earned recognition for producing exceptionally straight, slim, uniformly golden-yellow pods in a well-concentrated set ideal for both fresh market and home canning. Yellow wax beans are a distinct culinary category from green snap beans — the pale golden-yellow color (which remains after cooking), slightly creamier texture, and subtle flavor difference (milder, slightly less grassy than green beans) make wax beans a favorite in German and Eastern European cooking and preferred by many home gardeners for pickled beans and canned beans. Gold Rush produces pods of exceptional straightness and uniformity — the 5–6 inch pods are nearly pencil-straight, a quality attribute for both visual appeal at the table and ease of packing for canning. The plants are compact, upright, and productive, concentrating the pod set over a 7–10 day harvest window suitable for once-over mechanical harvest or home garden batch picking. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Gold Rush Zucchini (AAS-Winning Yellow-Skinned Summer Squash)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gold Rush is an All-America Selections-winning yellow zucchini hybrid — producing the classic straight, cylindrical zucchini form (6–8 inches at optimal harvest) in brilliant golden-yellow skin rather than the standard dark-green of typical zucchini. The golden-yellow skin is visually striking and creates attractive contrast with standard green zucchini in market displays, mixed vegetable dishes, and grilled presentations — the same tender, mild, slightly sweet flesh as green zucchini in a color that makes it immediately distinguishable. Gold Rush is a compact bush-type plant reaching 18–24 inches with a moderate 3–4 foot spread — appropriate for typical garden spacing without the sprawling habit of some summer squash. The AAS recognition reflects exceptional performance across multiple growing regions and conditions. In zone 9, Gold Rush is best grown as a spring crop (February–March planting for April–May harvest) or fall crop (August planting for September–October harvest) — summer heat causes powdery mildew and reduced production. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and tenderness; oversized fruits become seedy and tough. Squash vine borers are the primary pest challenge in zone 9; monitoring and early action against eggs is essential for spring production. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Goldcot Apricot (Cold-Hardy Reliable Northern Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Developed at Michigan State University for reliable cropping in colder apricot-growing regions where most cultivars bloom too early and lose their crop to frost, Goldcot combines good winter hardiness with a comparatively later bloom time that improves the odds of a successful harvest. The medium, deep orange, firm-fleshed fruit is sweet and well flavored, suitable for fresh eating, canning, and drying, and ripens in mid-summer. The tree is self-fruitful and productive, making it a dependable choice for northern home orchards that struggle with more tender apricot varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Abundance Mahonia (Wagner's Hybrid Oregon Grape)
description: Grow in well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh midday sun, which can bleach the foliage of this Mahonia aquifolium x Mahonia pinnata hybrid raised in Washington state. Golden Abundance lives up to its name with an exceptionally dense, heavy display of bright egg-yolk-yellow flower clusters in late winter to early spring, well beyond the bloom of an ordinary Oregon grape, followed by blue-black berries that draw birds. New spring foliage emerges with a bronze-red flush before settling to glossy dark green, adding a second season of color ahead of flowering. It is a tough, low-maintenance evergreen for a mixed shrub border or foundation planting; water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Golden Acre Cabbage
description: This early heirloom produces compact, round green heads quickly, making it a good fit for small gardens and short seasons. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before transplanting into firm, fertile soil. Water evenly and consistently, as swings in moisture can crack the maturing heads. Harvest as soon as heads feel solid, since the early type is prone to splitting if left too long; it succeeds in both spring and fall. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Golden Ball Feverfew (Double Yellow Button Feverfew)
description: Golden Ball is a compact, dwarf feverfew selection bearing small, fully double, golden-yellow button flowers with no visible ray petals, quite distinct from the typical white daisy of the species. Its short, tidy habit suits front-of-border plantings and pots better than the taller straight species. Grow it in average, well-drained soil in full sun with even moisture for the heaviest bloom; established plants tolerate short dry spells but flower less freely under stress. Shear back after the first flush to encourage rebloom and remove spent flowerheads regularly to keep the compact form from becoming leggy. The button flowers dry well for everlasting arrangements while still being usable medicinally like other feverfew forms. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Golden Ball Turnip (Yellow-Fleshed Sweet Heirloom Fall Turnip)
description: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches as plants establish. Golden Ball (also known as Robertson's Golden Ball and Amber Globe) is a Victorian-era heirloom turnip with a strikingly different appearance from the standard purple-top white-fleshed types that dominate American turnip culture: the round, smooth roots are golden-yellow skinned with deep golden-yellow flesh, rather than the white flesh of standard types. The yellow flesh color indicates a different carotenoid profile and, notably, a distinct flavor: Golden Ball is considered one of the sweetest, mildest turnips available — the yellow-fleshed types tend toward greater sweetness and less sulfur-pungency than white-fleshed types when grown in the same conditions. This mild, sweet quality makes Golden Ball excellent for eating raw (rare for turnips), roasted whole (the golden color makes an attractive presentation), and in preparations where the sulfur bite of standard turnips would be unwelcome. Golden Ball has been grown in British kitchen gardens since at least the 1850s and represents the traditional European approach to turnip cultivation that emphasized flavor diversity across multiple colors and flesh types rather than the American focus on the single purple-top type. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Golden Bantam Sweet Corn
description: This historic open-pollinated heirloom brought sweet yellow corn to the home table and still delivers rich, old-fashioned flavor. Sow seed an inch to an inch and a half deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows so wind pollination fills the ears. Provide plenty of water and nitrogen through tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when the silks brown and kernels are plump and milky, and cook or preserve promptly for the best flavor. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Golden Bantam Sweet Corn
description: Sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in blocks rather than single rows to ensure adequate pollen distribution to every silk. Golden Bantam is perhaps the most historically important sweet corn variety in American garden history. Introduced in 1902 by W. Atlee Burpee Company from a selection by E.L. Coy of New York, it was the first widely successful yellow sweet corn at a time when white corn was considered superior — Golden Bantam changed American tastes permanently and proved that yellow sweet corn could surpass white in flavor. The short (6–7 foot), early-season plants produce 6–7 inch ears with 8 rows of deep golden-yellow kernels with a distinctive rich, full sweet corn flavor different from modern supersweeet hybrids — a milk-and-sugar intensity that is the archetype of 'real corn flavor.' Still one of the best open-pollinated sweet corns and superior to any hybrid for seed saving. Harvest at milk stage (silk brown, kernel milky when pierced) and cook or freeze immediately — sugar converts to starch within hours of picking. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Golden Bay Laurel
description: Plant Golden Bay in well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest gold color, or partial shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch; water moderately and protect from harsh winter wind, which can damage foliage below the high 10s °F. Give it more shelter and shade than plain green bay, since the golden foliage is more prone to sunburn in intense heat. Prune to shape and to harvest leaves — the aromatic, leathery gold-and-green leaves are dried and used exactly like ordinary bay laurel in soups, stews, braises, and stocks, with identical flavor to the green form. Grown as much for its bright, formal, topiary-friendly foliage as for cooking, it is a popular container specimen for patios and entryways in cooler climates where it can be moved indoors over winter. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Beet
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and hard pan; Golden Beet produces roots with bright golden-yellow skin and deep orange-gold flesh that stands out dramatically from red beet varieties — the color results from betaxanthin pigments rather than the betacyanin (red-purple) pigments of standard beets. The most important practical difference from red beets is that Golden Beet does not bleed or stain hands, cutting boards, or other foods with the intense crimson juice of red beets — a major advantage in salads and prepared dishes where red beet juice can dominate the visual presentation. The flavor of Golden Beet is also distinctly sweeter and milder than most red beet varieties, with less of the earthy 'dirty' undertone that some people find off-putting in red beets. The combination of non-staining, mild sweetness, and attractive golden color makes Golden Beet the preferred choice for beet salads, roasted vegetable medleys, and restaurant presentations. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Golden Beet
description: Golden beets offer a mild, sweet flavor without the earthy note of red types and do not bleed when cut. Because germination is often spotty, presoak seed for a few hours and sow slightly denser than usual. Thin ruthlessly to 3 inches so roots can size up without crowding. Keep beds weed-free and evenly watered to avoid tough, cracked roots. Harvest young for salads or at full size for roasting. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Boy Beet
description: A golden-orange fleshed beet with sweet, mild flavor that won't stain like red types, plus tender edible greens. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked, and thin seedlings to about 3 inches since each seed cluster produces several plants. Keep soil evenly moist for smooth, uniform globes and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots. The strong upright stems make for attractive bunches. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Boy Pear (North Florida Low-Chill Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)
aliases: Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia 'Golden Boy'
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Golden Boy originated in Wakulla County, Florida and is believed to be an improved seedling or bud sport of LeConte, sharing that cultivar's Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia hybrid vigor. It is prized in the Deep South and Gulf Coast for a very low chill requirement and outstanding fire blight resistance, tolerating the humid, high-disease-pressure conditions of north Florida, south Georgia, and coastal Alabama and Mississippi with minimal spray intervention. Trees are precocious, often bearing within three to four years of planting. Fruit is best used for canning, preserving, and cooking rather than fresh eating, similar to LeConte and Kieffer, since the flesh can retain some grit if picked too late; harvest while still firm and green with a slight color break, then ripen indoors. Early bloom makes it vulnerable to occasional late-winter freezes in zone 7 plantings, so site it with some frost protection where possible. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Bush Scallop Squash (Golden Custard Squash)
description: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest fruit young, at 2–3 inches across, for the sweetest, most tender flesh and thinnest skin, and pick every couple of days to keep the compact bush producing all summer. Golden Bush Scallop is a classic American heirloom summer squash producing the traditional flying-saucer-shaped 'patty pan' fruit in a bright, buttery golden-yellow, with a scalloped edge and creamy, mild, slightly nutty flesh when harvested young. The compact, non-vining bush habit keeps the plant tidy and productive in a relatively small footprint compared to sprawling vine squash, making it a good choice for smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds. Like all summer squash, frequent harvest at a small size is the key to extended production — fruit left to grow large quickly turns tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow down. A cheerful, productive, old-fashioned squash for zone 3–11 gardens. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Cal Wonder Sweet Pepper
description: A blocky sweet bell that starts green and ripens to a sunburst yellow blushed with orange, excellent stuffed, grilled, or stir-fried. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, then transplant after the soil and nights have warmed. Mulch to keep roots evenly moist and side-dress once fruit sets. Peppers freeze well, so harvest generously as they color up. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Golden California Wonder Pepper (Gold-Ripening Open-Pollinated Bell Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Golden California Wonder is the gold-maturing selection from the California Wonder bell pepper family — producing the same blocky, four-lobed, large, thick-walled bell pepper fruit as standard California Wonder but ripening to a golden-yellow color rather than red. The fruits begin green and ripen to a warm, rich golden-yellow at full maturity — a color stage with sweeter, more mellow flavor than the green stage and a different flavor profile from fully red bell peppers. Golden bell peppers are noticeably sweeter and lower in Scoville units than green bell peppers — the color change from green to gold/yellow reflects the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids and the simultaneous conversion of starches to sugars. As an open-pollinated variety, Golden California Wonder seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The golden fruits create visual contrast in mixed salads, stir-fries, and grilled vegetable platters where the gold color pairs beautifully with red and orange companions. The same thick walls and blocky form as California Wonder make Golden California Wonder outstanding for stuffed peppers. In zone 9, plant in spring (February–March) for a spring crop and in August for a fall crop. Matures in 72–82 days from transplant.

name: Golden Chia (Columbine-leaf Sage)
description: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, lean soil in full sun; golden chia is the native California and Southwest counterpart of the commercial chia (Salvia hispanica), producing a similar small, nutritious, edible seed in dense whorls on a single upright stem — the seeds were a staple food of Chumash, Diegueno, and other California Native peoples, eaten dry, mixed with water as a drink, or ground into a flour. The gelatinous coating of wet golden chia seeds, like commercial chia, creates a mucilaginous texture used in traditional beverages. The deep blue to violet flower whorls are attractive and pollinated by native bees. An important cultural and ecological plant of the California landscape — the name 'chia' refers to this native California species in traditional California usage, predating the commercial use of S. hispanica. Grows as a quick winter annual in the California climate cycle. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Golden Crookneck Summer Squash
description: This classic yellow summer squash offers buttery flavor and tender texture on compact, bush-style plants that suit home gardens. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil, spacing plants for good air movement. Keep moisture steady and harvest fruits young, while the curved necks are still small and the skin is tender. Frequent picking keeps the plants producing heavily, since mature fruits left on the plant slow new set. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Cross Bantam Sweet Corn
aliases: Zea mays var. saccharata 'Golden Cross Bantam'
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in blocks rather than single long rows to ensure reliable pollination, and side-dress with nitrogen once plants reach knee height. Introduced in the 1930s as one of the first widely grown hybrid sweet corns, this variety became a benchmark standard for decades thanks to its resistance to Stewart's wilt and its dependable yields of seven-inch ears filled with tender, golden-yellow kernels. Its classic old-fashioned sweet corn flavor, rather than the ultra-sugary taste of modern supersweet hybrids, still appeals to gardeners who remember it from earlier generations of home gardens. Harvest when kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pierced. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Golden Crown Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Rind Icebox Watermelon)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox-type watermelon with an unusual and genuinely useful feature — the rind ripens from green to a distinctive solid golden-yellow at full maturity, giving gardeners a clear, unmistakable visual cue for ripeness instead of relying only on the ground-spot color, tendril drying, and thump-sound methods needed for green-rind watermelons. Inside, the flesh is sweet and red, with a compact plant habit and fast maturity that suit smaller gardens and shorter growing seasons well. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development for the best size and flavor; ease off watering slightly as fruit nears full color to help concentrate sugars. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Golden Currant (Clove Currant)
description: Plant in moist to moderately dry, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; golden currant is a broadly adaptable native shrub of western and central North America producing intensely fragrant yellow flowers in spring — fragrant with a spicy clove-like scent that carries in the air, giving rise to the alternate common name 'clove currant' — that are followed in summer by round currants ripening from red to black-purple, sweet-tart and edible fresh or made into jelly, jam, and wine. The spring floral fragrance is among the most remarkable of any native shrub, detectable at a distance on warm spring days. The attractive foliage turns red and orange in fall. Unlike European black currant (Ribes nigrum), golden currant has no unpleasant 'catty' flavor and produces a pleasant, gently flavored fruit. It is one of the most important nectar sources for early hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees in the western states. Drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to part shade, and much more garden-friendly than many currant species. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Delicious Apple (Self-Fertile West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Countless Modern Apples)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike most apple varieties, Golden Delicious is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator, though its long, generous bloom period makes it one of the most valuable universal pollinizers for other apple cultivars planted nearby. Discovered as a chance seedling on the Mullins family farm in Clay County, West Virginia in the 1890s, likely a cross involving Grimes Golden, it was introduced commercially by Stark Bro's Nursery in 1914 and went on to become one of the single most important parent varieties in modern apple breeding, contributing to Gala, Jonagold, Mutsu, Pinova, Elstar, Spigold, Rubinette, Opal, and Ambrosia, among many others. The medium to large fruit ripens from green to a smooth golden yellow with light russeting around the stem, and the crisp, juicy flesh carries a mellow, honeyed sweetness with little tartness, excellent fresh, in salads, sauces, and baking. The thin skin bruises easily and the fruit softens faster in storage than firmer modern varieties, so handle gently and use within a few months of harvest; ripens midseason, typically in September. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Golden Delicious Squash
description: Golden Delicious is a 1920s Oregon-bred heirloom, a cross of Delicious and Boston Marrow, grown for its top-shaped, red-orange fruit and thick, fine-grained flesh originally favored for commercial baby food production. Give the long vines plenty of room and consistent moisture through fruit development, then let fruit finish on the vine until the rind resists a thumbnail. It stores exceptionally well for a maxima squash, often holding good eating quality into winter without special curing conditions. Gardeners choose it today for its old-fashioned sweetness in pies and its reliability as a dependable keeper compared to showier modern hybrids. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Golden Detroit Beet (Non-Bleeding Yellow Heirloom Beet)
description: Sow the multigerm seed clusters about half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil in full sun, and thin seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Golden Detroit is a yellow-fleshed sport of the classic Detroit type, producing round, orange-skinned roots that cook down to a warm mustard-gold color instead of bleeding red, so it can be roasted, pickled, or shaved raw into salads without staining hands or other ingredients. The flavor is sweet and mild, generally considered gentler and less earthy than red beet varieties, and the tender tops are excellent cooked as greens. Harvest at two to three inches across for the best texture, and keep the soil evenly moist throughout to prevent tough, fibrous roots. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Dwarf Champion Tomato (Heirloom Yellow Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)
description: Golden Dwarf Champion is a yellow-fruited sport of the 19th-century heirloom Dwarf Champion tomato, one of the earliest true dwarf, potato-leaf tomato lines grown in American gardens. Plants stay short and self-supporting while producing round to oblate golden-yellow fruit with a mild, sweet flavor typical of yellow heirloom tomatoes. Along with other old dwarf lines, it was preserved by seed savers into the era of the modern Dwarf Tomato Project, where its compact genetics have been bred into newer releases such as Dwarf Sweet Sue, crossed with Green Giant. Harvest as fruit turns fully golden and softens slightly for peak sweetness. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Golden Elderberry 'Aurea' (Golden-Leaved American Elderberry)
description: This long-grown ornamental sport of American elderberry is grown chiefly for its bright chartreuse-to-gold foliage, which lights up a partly shaded border far more than the plain green leaves of the wild species. Wide, flat-topped clusters of white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small red berries rather than the typical dark purple-black fruit of most Sambucus canadensis selections. In hot Gulf Coast gardens, afternoon shade is important to keep the gold color from scorching to a dull tan by midsummer. Cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth with the best foliage color, and remove root suckers regularly to keep the planting from spreading into a colony. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Golden Feverfew
description: Golden Feverfew is grown as much for its chartreuse-to-gold, finely cut foliage as for its small daisy-like flowers, making it a popular edging and container plant in addition to a medicinal herb. The bright leaf color is most vivid in cool spring weather and with light afternoon shade; intense summer sun can bleach or scorch the foliage in hotter regions. Shear plants back hard after the main bloom flush to refresh the color and habit, and remove spent flowerheads to reduce volunteer seedlings, since this form can revert toward green foliage from self-sown seed. As with the species, harvest the aromatic leaves fresh for tea or tincture, and handle with gloves since the foliage can irritate sensitive skin. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Golden Flax (Yellow-Seeded Oilseed and Culinary Flax)
description: Broadcast seed thickly over a firm, weed-free bed and rake in to about 1/4 inch, since golden flax relies on dense stands to keep its slender stems from lodging. This yellow-seeded type is grown specifically for the table — the mild, nutty flaxseed is favored for grinding into meal for baking and smoothies over the more assertive brown-seeded types. Watch the sky-blue flowers give way to round seed capsules, and cut whole plants at the base once most capsules have dried to a tan color and rattle when shaken. Dry the cut bundles under cover for one to two weeks before threshing by flailing or treading, then winnow thoroughly, as golden seed shows any chaff more readily than brown flax. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Golden Frill Mustard (Yellow-Green Frilly Mustard)
description: Broadcast or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches; for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the whole plant 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; milder than red frills types at the same growth stage. Golden Frill is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with the same fine, lacey, frilly leaf form as Ruby Streaks but with chartreuse to bright yellow-green coloring — a deliberate complement to red frills types in mesclun mixes and specialty salad production. The deeply incised, pinnately cut leaves (resembling an extremely large, pungent parsley) are the characteristic form of the 'frills' mustard group, but Golden Frill's bright color is distinctive and valuable in ornamental kitchen garden plantings where the yellow-green foliage contrasts dramatically with red-leaved varieties, dark green kales, and purple cabbages. The flavor is mustard-sharp but somewhat milder than red-leaved mustard varieties at the same stage of maturity — mild enough to use raw in quantity in salads at the baby leaf stage, with more heat developing in mature leaves. Golden Frill is a standard component of mesclun and Asian salad mixes alongside Ruby Streaks, mizuna, and tatsoi; the combination of all four creates dramatic visual contrast (red, chartreuse, dark green, and pale green) with complementary flavors. Extremely fast-growing in cool weather — baby leaves in 21 days, full plants in 35–40 days. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Golden Frills Mustard (Frilled Gold Salad Green)
description: Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop, since Golden Frills grows best in the cool temperatures of spring and autumn and can suffer flea beetle damage in warm weather. Golden Frills is a strikingly ornamental mustard green with finely dissected, deeply lobed, chartreuse-gold leaves that add texture and bright color to salad mixes and cut-and-come-again plantings. Its flavor is sweet and aromatic with a mustard bite that is milder than many mustard greens, and mature plants sometimes develop a crisp, edible root reflecting a mustard-turnip heritage in its lineage. Harvest young for baby leaf salads at around three weeks, or allow plants to grow to full size for a spicier, more robust cooking green. Matures in 21–50 days from seed.

name: Golden Giant Amaranth (Tall Golden-Yellow Grain and Cut-Flower Amaranth)
description: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covered, in warm soil after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks early. Golden Giant produces tall, dense, upright golden-yellow flower plumes on vigorous, sturdy stems, grown both for its abundant edible grain and as a dramatic fresh or dried cut flower for fall arrangements. Heat-tolerant and low-maintenance, it thrives in full sun and average soil, producing heavy yields of small, protein-rich seed by the time the plumes fully color and dry. Harvest seed heads once they rattle and the seed sheds easily when rubbed, then thresh and winnow; cut plumes for drying just as they color for the best cut-flower use, and expect self-sowing if seed heads are left in place. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Golden Ginger Mint
description: Golden Ginger Mint is a variegated selection of the naturally occurring spearmint x corn mint hybrid, its narrow, slightly wrinkled leaves streaked and edged in bright gold against dark green, giving it strong ornamental value beyond its warm, spicy-gingery aroma. The red-tinted stems and gold-splashed foliage make it easy to identify in a mixed herb bed even before you brush a leaf to release its scent. Grow it in part shade to prevent the variegation from scorching in hot afternoon sun, and confine the roots in a buried container since it spreads by runners just as vigorously as any other mint. Use the leaves fresh in iced tea, fruit salads, or Southeast Asian-style dishes where a ginger note complements mint's natural coolness. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Golden Girl Ginkgo (Female Nut-Producing Maidenhair Tree with Golden Fall Color)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, watering regularly through establishment; mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough, tolerating heat, drought, pollution, and compacted urban soils. Golden Girl is a female cultivar selected for its exceptionally reliable, uniform golden-yellow fall color, a trait less consistent in many seed-grown female ginkgo trees. As a female clone it requires a nearby male pollinator, such as Autumn Gold, Princeton Sentry, or a wild male seedling, to produce fruit; once fertilized, the fleshy, apricot-colored seed coat that develops in autumn is notoriously foul-smelling and messy as it drops and decomposes, so site Golden Girl away from walkways, patios, and parking areas. Beneath that odorous flesh, however, each seed contains an edible kernel (ginkgo nut, or ginnan) that is a prized ingredient in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean cuisine, roasted or simmered in dishes like chawanmushi and used in soups and stir-fries; harvesters typically collect fallen seeds while wearing gloves, since the fleshy coating can cause skin irritation, and cure the cleaned seeds before cooking. Ginkgo is essentially free of serious pests and disease, and little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing branches while young. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Golden Globe Pomegranate (Yellow-Skinned Sweet Pomegranate)
description: Golden Globe is a large-fruited pomegranate cultivar with a golden-yellow rind blushed pink, enclosing sweet, juicy, pink arils with notably soft seeds well suited to fresh eating. It is generally recommended for regions with milder summer heat, so in Gulf Coast plantings it benefits from light afternoon shade during the most intense mid-summer weeks and consistent moisture to avoid stress-related fruit drop. Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, and expect a strikingly different-looking harvest than the red-skinned cultivars typically grown alongside it. Because it can rival some of the largest pomegranate cultivars in fruit size, establish sturdy branch structure through early pruning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Globe Turnip (Classic Sweet Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom Turnip)
description: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3–4 inches apart once seedlings have their first true leaves, using the thinnings as tender salad greens. Golden Globe is a 19th-century English heirloom valued for its smooth, golden-skinned, yellow-fleshed roots, which are noticeably sweeter and milder than white-fleshed turnips and hold good texture even when they size up past baseball size. It bulks up quickly from a compact top, making it a good choice for close spacing and succession sowing, and the mild flavor suits it equally well to roasting, mashing, or eating raw and thinly sliced. Keep soil evenly moist for fast, uninterrupted growth, since checks from drought or heat toughen the roots and sharpen their flavor. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Golden Glory Cornelian Cherry (Upright Heavy-Flowering Cornus mas Cultivar)
description: Golden Glory is a selection of cornelian cherry prized for its unusually dense, heavy display of small yellow flowers along bare branches in very early spring, well ahead of forsythia, making it one of the first woody plants to bloom each year. Its habit is more upright and uniform than seedling-grown Cornus mas, so it is often planted as a screen or informal hedge as well as a specimen tree. Like other cornelian cherries, it produces oblong, cherry-red, tart edible fruit in summer that can be gathered for syrup, jam, and traditional Eastern European preserves once fully soft-ripe. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils, drought once established, and urban conditions with very few pest or disease problems. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Golden Gopher Melon
description: Golden Gopher was released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s from a cross thought to include honeydew parentage, giving it unusually high sugar content and useful resistance to fusarium wilt for a melon of its era, though it remains susceptible to powdery mildew. The lightly ribbed, sparsely netted, roughly two-and-a-half-pound fruits carry deep orange flesh of excellent eating quality and are known among growers as 'pop open' melons for how they sometimes split at the blossom end when fully ripe. Its compact vine and dependable production have kept it in circulation with small seed stewardship organizations long after most other university-bred melons of its generation disappeared from commerce. Watch fruit closely as it nears maturity and harvest promptly once it slips or begins to crack to avoid loss to splitting. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Golden Gourmet Shallot (Dutch Yellow Shallot, Banana Shallot)
description: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 bulbs; maintain consistent moisture during spring growth; reduce watering when tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when bulb skins are dry and golden, then cure 2–3 weeks in a warm, dry location before storage. Golden Gourmet is a Dutch-type yellow shallot produced by seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, the global center of commercial shallot breeding and production; the variety represents the classic 'Dutch shallot' style — elongated-oval (sometimes banana-shaped), golden to copper-amber skinned bulbs with very pale yellow to white inner flesh, as opposed to the red-violet type represented by Ambition and Zebrune. The flavor profile is mild, sweet, and delicately onion-like with the characteristic shallot complexity — somewhat different from red-type shallots, with a cleaner, lighter character that particularly suits cream sauces, light vinaigrettes, and dishes where the golden color and mild flavor complement pale or delicate ingredients. Each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 uniform bulbs that cure to a beautiful, uniform golden-amber appearance — the classic appearance of the shallots found in upscale grocery stores and restaurant supply. Stores 8–10 months under good conditions, outlasting most red-type shallots. Can be replanted from the previous year's sets. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Golden Hills Pistachio
description: Golden Hills is a female pistachio cultivar developed by the University of California, Davis, and released in the early 2000s to give California growers an alternative to the industry-standard Kerman. It leafs out and blooms roughly one to two weeks earlier than Kerman, which lets it pair with earlier-flowering male pollinators and helps spread orchard harvest timing, and it is noted for bearing more consistently from year to year with less pronounced alternate bearing. Like all pistachio, it needs the same demanding regime of 700-1000 winter chill hours and long, hot, dry summers to fill and split its shells, so it performs poorly in humid climates even where winters are cold enough. Grow it in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, and expect several years of establishment before the tree reaches significant nut production. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Golden Hubbard Squash
description: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 1–2 plants once true leaves appear and keep hills evenly moist through fruit set. Golden Hubbard was introduced around 1898 as a smaller, easier-to-handle alternative to the large blue Hubbard types, producing teardrop-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with vivid orange-red, bumpy skin and dense, sweet, yellow-orange flesh with excellent dry texture ideal for baking and puréeing. Harvest after the first light frost has killed the vines and the rind resists puncture with a fingernail; cure in a 70–85°F location for 10–14 days then store at 50–60°F for up to 4 months. The relatively manageable fruit size makes it more practical for home cooks than the 15–20 pound Blue Hubbard. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Golden Isles Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Golden Isles was released in 1987 by University of Georgia grape breeder Ron Lane from a cross of Fry with a Creek-derived selection, and was specifically chosen for juice and wine use because its thin-skinned, pink-bronze berries have a much softer, less 'foxy' muscadine aroma than standard cultivars, making it approachable for people new to muscadine flavor. Self-fertile, it sets a reliable crop on its own and needs no companion pollinator vine. It carries the same strong native resistance to Pierce's disease and humid-climate fungal pressure that makes muscadines nearly maintenance-free in Gulf Coast gardens. Prune heavily each winter, leaving only short renewal spurs along permanent cordons, and thin dense clusters in early summer to improve airflow and fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Jenny Melon (Miniature Golden-Skinned Muskmelon)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three seedlings per hill; the compact vines and small fruit size make this a good candidate for raised beds or smaller vegetable plots. Golden Jenny produces round, one to two pound fruits with smooth golden-yellow skin and juicy, aromatic, orange-gold flesh, and was developed from the classic 19th-century Jenny Lind muskmelon, retaining that heirloom's sweetness and old-fashioned melon aroma in a smaller, quicker-maturing package. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then let it dry slightly as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure and the fruit releases a strong, sweet fragrance at the blossom end. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Golden Jubilee Anise Hyssop (Golden-Leaved Licorice-Scented Herb)
description: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; good drainage matters more than fertility, since wet winter soil is the most common cause of loss. Golden Jubilee is an All-America Selections-winning form of anise hyssop grown as much for its bright, licorice-scented chartreuse-to-gold foliage, which holds its color from spring through fall, as for its lavender-blue flower spikes that appear from midsummer into fall and draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in steady numbers. The aromatic leaves can be used fresh or dried for tea and as an anise-flavored culinary herb, much like the green-leaved species. It self-seeds modestly in favorable conditions, tolerates drought well once established, and needs little more than a spring cutback of old growth and an occasional deadheading to tidy the plant and extend bloom. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Golden Jubilee Tomato (Classic Low-Acid Golden Heirloom)
description: Golden Jubilee is a classic open-pollinated slicing tomato introduced by Burpee in 1943, producing smooth, globe-shaped, deep golden-orange fruit with a mild, notably low-acid flavor that has made it a long-standing favorite for gardeners who find red tomatoes too tart or acidic. The 6-8 ounce fruit holds its shape well for slicing and has a pleasant, sweet flavor without the intensity of tangier heirlooms, giving it a reputation as an easygoing, family-friendly garden tomato. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vine well, and because the fruit ripens to a lighter color than red tomatoes, judge readiness by gentle give at the shoulders as much as by color alone. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Golden Kiwi (Yellow Kiwifruit, Gold Kiwi)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; provide a very sturdy trellis or pergola — mature vines are extremely vigorous and heavy; one male plant pollinates up to 8 female plants. Actinidia chinensis (golden kiwi or yellow kiwifruit) is a separate species from the common fuzzy kiwifruit (A. deliciosa), native to the forests of central and eastern China — though the two species are closely related and sometimes hybridized commercially. The golden kiwi is distinguished from fuzzy kiwifruit by its smooth, thin, golden-yellow to bronze skin (no fuzzy brown hairs), golden-yellow to bright-orange-yellow flesh, and distinctly sweeter, tropical, less acidic flavor profile with notes of mango, papaya, and vanilla in addition to the classic kiwifruit taste. Golden kiwis are now among the most commercially valuable kiwifruit worldwide; the New Zealand-bred 'Zespri SunGold' variety (patented) dominates the premium market, but non-patented gold kiwi cultivars are available to home growers. Like fuzzy kiwifruit, A. chinensis is a vigorous deciduous vine requiring a substantial support structure, annual dormant pruning, and separate male and female plants (dioecious). It is somewhat less cold-hardy than A. deliciosa and requires mild winters without late spring frosts to protect the early-emerging shoots. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Golden Lemon Balm (Gold Variegated Lemon Balm)
description: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; golden lemon balm requires shade protection — full sun bleaches and scorches the golden leaves; divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Melissa officinalis 'Aurea' (golden lemon balm) is a variegated cultivar of common lemon balm distinguished by its striking foliage: bright golden-yellow to gold-spashed-green leaves that glow in dappled shade conditions, creating a luminous effect in the shaded herb garden. Unlike the green-leafed species, which tolerates full sun well, 'Aurea' requires partial to dappled shade — the golden pigmentation means it lacks the green chlorophyll needed to handle direct sun exposure, causing the leaves to scorch and bleach in bright direct sunlight. This makes 'Aurea' uniquely valuable as the best lemon balm choice for shaded herb gardens, woodland herb borders, and partially shaded areas where the standard green form becomes stressed. The culinary properties and lemon-mint flavor of the golden form are identical to the green species — the fresh or dried leaves make the same pleasant lemon-herbal tea, the same addition to salads and garnishes, and the same aromatic edging plant. The golden foliage makes 'Aurea' outstanding for purely ornamental use in shade gardens even when not harvested for culinary purposes. Does not come true from seed — must be propagated from divisions of the parent plant. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Golden Lemon Thyme (Gold-Leafed Ornamental Lemon-Scented Thyme, Aureus Thyme)
description: Plant cuttings or divisions in well-drained gritty soil; harvest lightly without removing more than a third of the plant. Golden Lemon Thyme (Thymus × citriodorus 'Aureus') is a hybrid thyme cultivar — a cross between common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) and a lemon-scented thyme species — selected for its variegated gold-and-green foliage pattern, which gives it significant ornamental value beyond the culinary use shared with all thyme varieties. The 'Aureus' (meaning golden in Latin) name describes the characteristic yellow-gold coloration of the leaf margins and tips, which contrasts with the green center of each small oval leaf and creates a bright, luminous appearance in garden plantings. This golden variegation is consistent throughout the growing season, making Golden Lemon Thyme one of the most visually distinctive ground cover herbs available for sunny, dry garden situations. The fragrance is the combination of thyme's characteristic aromatics with a distinct lemon overlay — lighter and more citrus-like than standard cooking thyme, which has a more herbaceous, almost medicinal scent. This lemon-thyme fragrance makes Golden Lemon Thyme particularly useful in cooking applications where the pungency of standard thyme would be too dominant: it pairs well with fish, chicken, vegetables, and in preparations where a lighter herbal-citrus note is wanted. The plants bloom in late spring with clusters of tiny lavender to pale pink flowers that attract bees and other pollinators — the combination of gold-green foliage and lavender flowers at bloom time is particularly attractive in rock gardens and herb beds. In zone 9, Golden Lemon Thyme performs well in cool months and requires excellent drainage year-round to survive summer heat and humidity. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Golden Marjoram
description: Golden marjoram is a foliage sport of sweet marjoram selected for chartreuse-to-gold leaves that hold their brightest color in full sun and fade toward green in shade, while carrying the same mild, sweet, floral flavor as ordinary sweet marjoram. Its low, spreading habit and bright foliage make it as popular for edging and container plantings as it is for the kitchen, softening the look of an herb bed while remaining fully usable at the stove. Like the species it is frost-tender and grown as an annual outside zones 9-11, though potted plants can be overwintered indoors on a sunny windowsill. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep plants bushy and to delay the flower spikes that mark a drop in leaf flavor. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Golden Midget Sweet Corn (Extra-Dwarf Heirloom Sweet Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers, since its compact stature makes it one of the few sweet corns genuinely practical for small gardens, raised beds, and pots. Golden Midget was bred at a New Hampshire agricultural research station in the mid-1900s specifically to give home gardeners a fast, space-saving sweet corn, reaching only two to three feet tall while still producing petite four-inch ears of golden-yellow kernels. Its short season and small footprint have kept it a favorite heirloom for northern gardeners and anyone growing corn in limited space, and it remains a genuinely useful, if lesser-known, member of the open-pollinated sweet corn family. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Golden Midget Watermelon (Compact Early Watermelon with Unique Golden-Yellow Ripeness Indicator)
description: Direct sow after soil warms; space 4–5 feet apart. Harvest when skin turns solid golden-yellow. Golden Midget Watermelon was developed and introduced by Elwyn Meader and Albert Yeager at the University of New Hampshire in the 1950s, specifically targeting short-season northern gardens where standard large watermelons require more summer heat than is available. The breeding goals — early maturity (70–75 days), compact vine, and small fruit — made Golden Midget one of the pioneering compact watermelon varieties for home garden production. The most distinctive characteristic is the skin color change at ripeness: unlike any other standard watermelon variety, Golden Midget's skin transitions from striped green to solid golden-yellow as the fruit reaches full maturity inside, providing the clearest possible visual harvest cue. Standard watermelon ripeness indicators (dried stem tendril, ground spot color change, sound when thumped) require interpretation and experience; Golden Midget's golden skin change is unambiguous and visible from across the garden. The fruit size (6–8 lbs, fits in a refrigerator shelf whole) suits modern households that cannot easily consume a 25-pound watermelon and want a seedless or small-fruited option. The flesh is pink to red with conventional watermelon sweetness — appropriate for fresh eating, salads, and summer use — without the extraordinary flavor intensity of the best large heirloom varieties, but reliable and consistent in flavor quality across the growing season. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Golden Mombin (Ambarella)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; golden mombin is fast-growing and may produce fruit within 3–4 years from cuttings. Spondias dulcis (golden mombin, ambarella, or June plum) is a Polynesian and Melanesian tropical fruit tree — widely cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and tropical Americas — producing oblong, golden-yellow, 2-to-4-inch fruits that ripen to orange-yellow with a fibrous central pit and flesh with a flavor combining mango, pineapple, and tart apple. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, or green (unripe) as a crisp, tart, mango-like condiment in curries, chutneys, and salads across Southeast Asian cuisines — particularly popular in Vietnam and Cambodia where unripe ambarella is eaten with salt, chili, and sugar. The tree is fast-growing and highly productive once mature, often requiring thinning of the heavy crop to prevent limb breakage; it is semi-deciduous in seasonal climates. The leaves are also edible as a vegetable in some Pacific Island cuisines. In zone 9, grow as a container plant or in the most frost-protected locations, bringing indoors or covering when frost threatens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Muscat Grape (Historic American Hybrid Table and Wine Grape)
description: Bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a Diamond and Muscat Hamburg cross, Golden Muscat combines labrusca cold-hardiness with a pronounced muscat aroma more typical of finer vinifera grapes. Its large, loose clusters of amber-gold berries are enjoyed fresh, made into juice, or fermented into aromatic wine. The vine ripens late in the season, so it performs best where autumns are long and mild, and benefits from cluster thinning to hasten ripening. It is vigorous and productive once established on a cane-pruned trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Nugget Loquat (Large-Fruited Sweet Named Loquat Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Golden Nugget is one of the best-fruiting named loquat cultivars for Gulf South gardens — producing larger, sweeter, better-quality fruits than seedling loquats with the same outstanding adaptability to Gulf Coast conditions that makes loquat one of the most reliable subtropical fruit trees for zone 8b–9. The round to oval, deep golden-orange fruits are substantially larger than typical seedling loquat (1.5–2 inches diameter compared to 1–1.5 inches for seedlings) and have excellent sweet flavor with a mild, tropical quality. Loquats bloom in fall and winter (November–January in zone 9) and ripen fruit in early spring (February–March) — providing fresh tree fruit at a time when virtually no other locally grown fruit is available. The winter flowering is the primary limitation of loquat production in zone 9: the flowers and young fruit are frost-sensitive, and a hard freeze during the fruit development period can eliminate the entire crop. In years without hard freezes, Golden Nugget produces heavy crops of high-quality fruit. The evergreen tree is attractive year-round with large, bold, dark-green leaves and is suitable for use as a landscape tree as well as a fruit producer. Loquat tolerates a wide range of soils, partial shade when necessary, and is highly adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Orach
description: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves, since older leaves and stems toughen as plants approach flowering. This golden-yellow-leaved form of mountain spinach has been grown as a spinach substitute since antiquity and tolerates heat and poor soil far better than true spinach, eventually bolting to tall, ornamental seed spikes in summer. Its bright color makes it a popular contrast alongside the more familiar red and green orach forms in mixed salad plantings. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Golden Oregano (Gold-Leafed Italian Oregano)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; Golden oregano is an attractive, low-growing, spreading oregano cultivar with bright golden-yellow foliage that functions simultaneously as a culinary herb and a decorative ground cover — the vivid chartreuse to golden leaf color brightens sunny herb gardens, rock gardens, and container compositions while the leaves retain the characteristic Mediterranean oregano flavor for culinary use. The low, mat-forming habit (6–12 inches tall, spreading indefinitely) makes it useful as a ground cover on dry, sunny slopes and as a fragrant edging plant along paths. In summer, small pink to purple flowers appear in clusters, attracting bees and butterflies. Golden oregano's flavor is milder than standard Greek or Italian oregano — the ornamental leaf color comes at some cost to the pungent oil concentration that gives oregano its intense flavor. For the most flavorful culinary herbs, grow standard green oregano varieties alongside Golden oregano. Like all Mediterranean herbs, Golden oregano is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually develops the most concentrated flavor in lean, dry soil with limited irrigation. Perfect drainage is essential — waterlogged roots cause rapid crown rot, particularly in hot, humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Golden Passionflower (Citrus-Yellow Passion Vine)
description: Golden passionflower produces small, star-shaped, citrus-yellow flowers that appear in flushes nearly year-round in frost-free climates, drawing hummingbirds and bees to the garden. Unlike many tropical passionflowers, it tolerates a range of light from full sun to fairly bright shade and stays comparatively compact and easy to manage on a small trellis, obelisk, or large container. It roots readily from cuttings and is self-fertile, so a single plant reliably sets its small, elongated yellow fruits without needing a second vine nearby. In climates colder than zone 9 it has little cold tolerance, so grow it in a container and bring it into a bright, frost-free location for winter. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Golden Pillow Jackfruit (Mong Thong Jackfruit)
description: A compact Thai cultivar known locally as Mong Thong, Golden Pillow tops out at only 8 to 10 feet, far more manageable than standard jackfruit trees that can reach 40 to 70 feet. Fruit is also modest for the species at 8 to 10 pounds, with thick, golden, crunchy flesh carrying a mild sweetness and a distinctive musky aftertaste as the fleshy skin spines flatten and separate at ripeness. Its small stature and moderate fruit size make it far better suited to container culture or a small suburban lot than full-sized cultivars like Black Gold or NS1. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Purslane
description: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun — purslane thrives in the heat and poor soils that discourage other vegetables; Golden Purslane is a cultivated, golden-yellow-stemmed selection of the common wild purslane (Portulaca oleracea), developed for the edible vegetable trade and producing larger, more succulent stems and leaves than the weedy wild type. The thick, fleshy, yellow-green leaves and golden stems have a mild, slightly lemony, succulent flavor with a mucilaginous texture when raw and a spinach-like softness when cooked. Purslane is one of the highest plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids and contains significant amounts of vitamins A, C, and E — nutritionally rich in a plant that requires almost no inputs and grows vigorously in the heat that exhausts other summer vegetables. In zone 9 it is one of the most productive summer greens from May through October when the heat prevents all other leafy green production. The golden color distinguishes it from the wild weedy type and makes it more attractive in salads. Harvest young stem tips and leaves continuously; older stems become woody. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Golden Purslane (Claytonia Purslane, Culinary Purslane)
description: Scatter seeds on warm, bare soil and press in lightly — seeds need some light to germinate; thin to 4–6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Portulaca oleracea sativa (culinary or golden purslane) is the large-leaved, succulent, upright or spreading culinary form of the common purslane weed, distinguished from the weed by larger, more succulent, often golden-yellow to golden-green leaves and a more upright, less spreading habit. It is one of the most nutritious and heat-tolerant summer vegetables — extraordinarily high in omega-3 fatty acids (the highest of any leafy vegetable), vitamin C, and beta-carotene — with a mildly tart, slightly mucilaginous, fleshy texture and pleasant sour flavor used raw in salads, stir-fried, or added to soups and stews throughout Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Mexican cuisines. In zone 9, culinary purslane can be grown from April through October, thriving in summer heat and drought when all other salad plants fail — it is the definitive summer salad green for hot, dry gardens. Common golden purslane cultivars include 'Goldberg' (large, golden-yellow leaves) and 'Gruner' (green leaves, more upright). Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Queen Tomato (Livingston's 1882 Smooth Yellow Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the vigorous vines to support fruit. Released by Livingston Seed Company in 1882, Golden Queen was long marketed as the finest smooth yellow tomato available, producing large, 8-12 ounce, waxy golden-yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed with pink at the blossom end, with meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor that made it a favorite among 19th- and early 20th-century home gardeners seeking a low-acid alternative to red slicers. Matures in 75–82 days from transplant.

name: Golden Rain Rosemary (Gold-Splashed Variegated Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Golden Rain bears needle-like green foliage irregularly splashed with bright gold-yellow variegation, an ornamental departure from the plain green of most culinary rosemary cultivars, grown as much for its bright, eye-catching color in the landscape as for cooking. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden where its variegated foliage provides color contrast against darker-leaved companions. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Golden Raspberry
description: Golden raspberries are yellow-fruited mutations of red raspberry cultivars, most commonly primocane-fruiting (everbearing) types such as 'Anne' or 'Fall Gold', with exceptionally sweet, mild flavor and low acidity. Manage as you would a primocane-fruiting red raspberry: for the simplest system, mow all canes to the ground each late winter and allow new primocanes to grow and fruit in fall. For a two-crop system, retain canes over winter to produce a summer crop on floricanes. Harvest when berries turn fully golden-yellow and release easily; they are more fragile than red types and should be processed quickly. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Golden Russet Apple (American Heirloom Dessert and Cider Russet)
description: This 19th-century American heirloom is distinct from the English russets already common in orchards, carrying some of the highest natural sugar content of any apple, which cidermakers prize for producing high-alcohol, well-balanced ferments. The small to medium fruit has a rough golden-bronze skin over crisp, honeyed flesh that is equally good eaten fresh once fully ripe in fall. The tree tends toward biennial bearing and benefits from thinning in a heavy year to even out production. Plant it for a dual-purpose tree that serves both the cider press and the fresh fruit bowl. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Sage (Golden-Variegated Culinary Sage)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; sage rots readily in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil, so good drainage is essential, especially through humid Gulf South summers. Golden Sage bears the same savory, aromatic culinary flavor as common garden sage in leaves brightly variegated with golden-yellow margins, providing ornamental color to an herb garden or border in addition to a full culinary harvest. It flowers in early summer with small blue-violet blooms attractive to bees, and the plant develops a woody, shrubby base over time like other garden sages. Harvest leaves as needed through the growing season, and prune lightly after flowering and again in early spring to keep the plant compact and prevent it from becoming leggy and woody in the center. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Golden Self-Blanching Celery (1883 Naturally-Blanching Heirloom Celery)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, spacing plants closely in a block rather than a single row; Golden Self-Blanching Celery was introduced in the United States in the early 1880s and became one of the most widely grown home garden celeries of its era because it needs no earthing up or wrapping to pale its stalks. Grown tightly together, the inner stalks naturally shade one another and turn a soft golden-green by fall, staying crisp and largely stringless with a clean, mild celery flavor. It matures somewhat faster than many older celery types, making it a practical choice for gardeners without a long, reliably cool season to spare. Water evenly and consistently throughout the growing period, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of stringy, bitter stalks in any celery. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Golden Sentinel Columnar Apple (Yellow Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Golden Sentinel is one of the original Ballerina-series columnar apples developed in England in the 1980s, growing as a single narrow, upright trunk clothed directly in short fruiting spurs rather than wide lateral branches, thanks to a natural genetic dwarfing mutation rather than grafting or pruning tricks. It bears attractive yellow-gold, crisp, sweet fruit similar in flavor to Golden Delicious, ripening in early to mid fall. The extremely narrow footprint makes it a practical choice for a large patio container, a tight side-yard planting, or a productive row spaced just 2–3 feet apart, where a standard apple tree would never fit. As with other columnar apples, plant a second compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since a single columnar apple alone sets little fruit. Prune only lightly, removing any rare side shoots that try to form, and thin crowded spurs occasionally to keep fruit size good. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Shadows Pagoda Dogwood (Variegated Rainbow Pagoda Dogwood)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows is a variegated sport of native pagoda dogwood selected for leaves edged in bright golden-yellow around a green center, a combination that brightens through the season and glows in the dappled light of a woodland-edge planting. It retains the species' distinctive tiered, horizontal branching habit — the source of its 'pagoda' name — along with small, flat-topped clusters of white spring flowers and blue-black summer berries relished by songbirds, but it stays noticeably smaller and shrubbier than the green species, usually 8-12 feet tall. Like the species it is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker, so avoid trunk injuries, provide good air circulation, and keep it out of hot, reflected-sun locations where the variegated leaf margins scorch. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Spice Pear (Cold-Hardy Canning and Preserving Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Golden Spice was bred in Minnesota for extreme cold hardiness and reliable production even in short northern growing seasons, producing small to medium, yellow-skinned pears with a distinctively spicy-sweet flavor that makes them outstanding for canning, spiced preserves, and pear butter, more than for out-of-hand fresh eating. The tree is notably productive and resistant to fire blight, bearing heavily and consistently once established, which has made it a long-standing favorite among northern home orchardists focused on putting up preserves rather than fresh market fruit.
