Harvest while still firm in early to mid fall and process promptly, or ripen briefly at room temperature if fresh eating is preferred, keeping in mind that the flavor truly shines once cooked with sugar and spice. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Golden Star Carambola
description: Golden Star was released from the University of Florida's Tropical Research and Education Center in the 1960s and remains grown for its large, deeply lobed fruit with an intense gold-orange color at full ripeness. Compared to the sweeter Arkin, Golden Star carries more acidity when picked early, so allow fruit to color fully on the tree before harvest to mellow the tartness into a balanced sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and juicing. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and irrigate consistently through bloom and fruit set, since irregular watering increases fruit drop and cracking. The tree bears on new growth flushes and can produce two overlapping crops per year in warm zones. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Summer Crookneck Summer Squash
description: A classic yellow crookneck producing bright, tender fruits best picked at 6 to 8 inches long on compact bushy plants. Direct sow two or three seeds per hill once soil warms past 70F, then thin to the strongest. Keep well watered and harvest every day or two, since regular picking keeps the plants productive all season. The bushy 2-foot habit and 2 to 4 foot spread make it manageable in smaller beds. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Supreme American Persimmon (Heavy-Cropping Parent of Elmo)
description: Golden Supreme is an older American persimmon clone of garden origin, grown for its bright orange, round fruit and consistently heavy annual cropping on a female tree. Ripening around mid-October, the fruit must fully soften after frost before its astringency fades, and while some growers rate its flavor as merely good rather than exceptional compared with named selections like Early Golden or Yates, its dependable yield has kept it in cultivation. Golden Supreme carries lasting breeding significance as one of the two parents, hand-pollinated with Garretson by Illinois hobbyist Jim Claypool, of the well-regarded modern selection Elmo. Give it the same deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and minimal care that other American persimmons need, and expect the tree's deep taproot to make it drought-tolerant once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Golden Sweet Pea (Yellow Snow Pea)
description: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost with trellis support; Golden Sweet is a distinctive heirloom snow pea from India with vivid lemon-yellow pods against deep green foliage and attractive purple flowers — one of the most ornamental edible peas available. The flavor of the bright yellow flat pods is sweet and delicate with a slightly more tender texture than green snow peas; they make a visually striking addition to salads and stir-fries. Harvest pods when fully yellow and flat before seeds begin to swell for best quality. The yellow color provides an interesting contrast to green and purple-podded pea varieties grown together. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Golden Sweet Snow Pea
description: A striking heirloom snow pea with bicolor purple blossoms and flat, lemon-yellow pods that are tender raw, steamed, or stir-fried. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost as soon as the soil is workable, and set up a tall trellis for the 6 to 8 foot vines. Keep the soil cool and moist with mulch, and harvest pods young while flat and crisp. Frequent picking extends the productive window before summer heat. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Golden Treat Apple Tree
description: This columnar Fruit Snacks apple grows tall and narrow, producing sweet snack-size fruit in as little as 2 feet of width, perfect for patios and small gardens. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and provide a compatible apple pollinator blooming at the same time. Water regularly the first two seasons while roots establish. Its naturally slim habit needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Golden Udo (Sun King, Chartreuse-Leaved Edible-Shoot Ornamental)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in a few hours of morning sun with shade during the hottest part of the day, and the leaves turn lime-green rather than scorching in fuller shade. Golden Udo, named the 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a dramatic ornamental sport of the Japanese vegetable udo, producing huge, bold, compound leaves in a luminous chartreuse-gold that light up a shaded border from spring through fall, while retaining the parent species' edible young shoots, which can be blanched and harvested in spring and prepared much like asparagus. It dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges vigorously in spring, forming a large, architectural clump within a couple of seasons. Divide congested clumps in early spring, and provide consistent moisture, since the large leaves wilt readily in dry soil. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Golden Wax Bush Bean
description: This productive yellow wax bean produces bright, stringless pods with tender texture on compact 15 to 20 inch bush plants. Sow seed about an inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent root disturbance. Keep moisture even during flowering and pod set, and avoid working among wet plants to limit disease. Pick pods often while young and slender for fresh eating or preserving, which keeps the plants setting new pods. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Golden Zucchini
description: This heirloom, open-pollinated variety produces bright yellow, cylindrical fruits with classic zucchini flavor on compact bush plants. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give each plant room for air circulation. Water consistently at the base and harvest fruits young, around six to eight inches, for the best texture. Pick every day or two during peak season, since fruits enlarge fast and steady harvest keeps production high. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Golden Zucchini Summer Squash
description: A 1973 heirloom zucchini with vivid yellow fruit and creamy-white flesh, most tender when picked at 8 inches or less. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, planting in hills and thinning to the strongest seedlings. Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom-end rot, and harvest frequently to keep the plant producing. Excellent roasted, grilled, sauteed, or baked. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Goldenseal
description: Plant small rhizome pieces 1–2 in deep in autumn in deep, shaded woodland soil rich in leaf mold; rhizome division is far more reliable than growing from seed. Goldenseal requires 70–80% shade and the moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic conditions of mature eastern North American forests — raised beds under deciduous trees work well. This is a slow-growing, at-risk native species; growing your own reduces pressure on wild populations, but expect 4–6 years before roots are substantial enough to harvest. Harvest small portions of the golden rhizome in autumn of the fourth or fifth year, leaving the majority of the root system intact for continued growth. Matures in 1460–2190 days from seed.

name: Goldfinger Banana (FHIA-01)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Goldfinger banana (FHIA-01) is a tetraploid hybrid developed by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research (FHIA) in the 1980s, bred specifically for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf disease, Fusarium wilt (Panama disease), and moko bacterial wilt — the three most destructive banana pathogens — making it a significant improvement over susceptible Cavendish varieties for home gardeners in humid subtropical climates. The fruit clusters are large, with medium-sized, slightly angular fruits ripening yellow that have sweet, full banana flavor with a hint of apple when fully ripe; texture is firmer than Cavendish and the fruits resist bruising and handle well. Goldfinger is productive (producing 40–70 pounds of fruit per pseudostem) and regrows quickly from the rhizome after freeze dieback in zone 8b–9, typically reaching fruiting size within 12–18 months of resprouting. An excellent choice for Gulf South food gardens where disease pressure is high and cold resilience is valued. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Goldie Ground Cherry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Goldie is a named ground cherry cultivar specifically selected for larger-than-average fruit size and superior sweetness compared to standard ground cherry selections — the distinctive golden-yellow to pale orange fruits inside their papery lantern-like husks are significantly larger and sweeter than wild-type plants, with a complex tropical flavor combining vanilla, pineapple, and tomatillo notes with a sweet-tart finish unlike any other common garden fruit. Ground cherries (Physalis pruinosa) are closely related to tomatillos but used as a sweet fruit rather than a savory vegetable — excellent eaten fresh, baked into pies and cobblers, or made into jam with a natural pectin content that produces a firm set. The plant grows as a sprawling, somewhat sticky annual related to tomatoes, producing continuously from midsummer until frost. In zone 9 Goldie ground cherries produce abundantly and the plants often self-sow from fallen fruits. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Goldilocks Acorn Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Acorn Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously even though the semi-bush habit takes noticeably less room than traditional sprawling acorn squash vines. Goldilocks is an AAS-winning acorn squash producing golden-orange, deeply ribbed fruit with sweet, fine-textured, deep-orange flesh, on a plant compact enough for smaller gardens while still yielding a full crop of 4-6 fruits per plant. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the color deepens to a solid gold-orange, typically as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which are common problems for all Cucurbita pepo squash in the Gulf South. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Goldkrone Dill (High-Yield German)
description: Goldkrone (German for 'golden crown') is a German dill selection bred for heavy foliage production and a strong, classic dill aroma, with feathery blue-green leaves borne on upright, well-branched plants. It is grown primarily for fresh and dried dill weed rather than seed, producing a full flush of cutting-quality foliage before bolting to flower. The variety performs reliably in the cool conditions dill favors and responds well to regular harvesting, which encourages continued leafy growth. As with other dill, plant it away from fennel to avoid cross-pollination if you intend to save seed. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Goldmine Nectarine (White-Fleshed Sweet Nectarine, New Zealand White Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; Goldmine is self-fertile; thin to 5–6 inches; Goldmine ripens mid-season (late June to mid-July in California) producing medium-sized, reddish-white to pale red blushed nectarines with cream-white flesh and a very sweet, low-acid flavor with floral aromatic notes — quite different from yellow-fleshed varieties and appealing to those who find standard nectarines too tart. Goldmine nectarine is a New Zealand variety that became widely grown in California and Australia as the premier white-fleshed nectarine for home orchards — belonging to the white-fleshed stone fruit category that is vastly more popular in Asia (Japan, China, Korea) and is now gaining appreciation among Western fruit connoisseurs for its distinctly different flavor profile: lower acidity, higher sugar concentration, and floral aromatic notes that distinguish white nectarines from the familiar sweet-tart profile of yellow-fleshed varieties. White nectarines like Goldmine are at their best consumed very ripe — the flesh is tender and can bruise easily, making them poorly suited to commercial shipping but excellent for home-grown fresh consumption. At peak ripeness, Goldmine is exceptionally sweet and fragrant with honeyed floral notes, and the white flesh is tender, melting, and extraordinarily juicy — a texture and flavor profile that many white-flesh enthusiasts consider superior for fresh eating to even the best yellow nectarines. Best in zone 7–9 climates with warm, dry summers for ripening. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: GoldRush Apple (Late-Season Disease-Immune Long-Keeping Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released in 1994 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program, GoldRush carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with strong resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it one of the most reliable choices for growers who want to avoid a heavy fungicide program. The yellow-green, russeted fruit is quite tart and firm at harvest in October but mellows over weeks of cold storage into a dense, complex, honey-sweet apple that keeps for months, rivaling many classic long-keeping heirlooms. Pick late and store cool for the best eating quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Goldstream Creeping Thyme (Gold-and-Green Variegated Groundcover Thyme)
description: Goldstream is a prostrate creeping thyme whose small leaves are mottled and margined in yellow, green, and cream, giving the mat a warm, variegated glow that is distinct from the plain-green species. Mauve flowers appear in whorls along the trailing stems in summer, drawing bees, and the foliage releases a lemony thyme scent whenever it is brushed or lightly stepped on. Its extremely low, dense habit suits paving crevices, gravel paths, and between stepping stones, where the color and fragrance can be appreciated close to the ground. Divide congested mats in spring to renew vigor and to propagate new plants for filling in bare patches. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Gomchwi (Fischer's Ligularia, Korean Mountain Vegetable)
description: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, watering during dry spells since this clumping woodland species does not tolerate drought. Gomchwi is a large-leaved perennial from the mountains of Korea, northern China, and the Russian Far East, prized in Korean cuisine as one of the most sought-after wild spring greens (sannamul); the young, mildly aromatic leaves are picked in early spring and eaten as a fresh wrap green, blanched, or preserved as pickled jangajji. Unlike its ornamental Ligularia relatives, it is grown primarily for repeated leaf harvest rather than for its tall late-summer spikes of yellow daisy-like flowers, though the flower stalks are also ornamental if left to bloom. Harvest outer leaves regularly through spring and early summer to encourage a continuous flush of tender new growth from the crown. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Gonzales Baby Cabbage (Compact Small-Head Cabbage for Small Space Gardens)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Harvest when heads feel firm and solid. Gonzales is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid green cabbage designed specifically for closer plant spacing, smaller garden plots, and the restaurant/market garden demand for mini or baby vegetable formats — a market segment that has grown substantially with the trend toward smaller household sizes and the restaurant emphasis on individual-portion vegetables. The heads average 3–4 pounds (compared to 5–8 lbs for full-sized standard green cabbage types) but form a properly tight, round, firm head with the same dense, crinkle-free outer leaves and pale, crisp interior of larger standard types — not a soft or immature head, but a fully developed compact head. Gonzales's early maturity (66–75 days from transplant vs. 80–110 days for full-sized storage types) combined with its compact size makes it particularly practical in zone 9's fall garden where planting time from mid-summer is limited. The flavor is classic mild, sweet, crisp green cabbage — excellent for coleslaw, stir-fries, braises, and fresh salads. The small size is practical for household use where a standard large cabbage requires several meals to consume before it deteriorates. Matures in 66–75 days from transplant.

name: Good King Henry
description: Cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for 2–4 weeks before sowing to improve germination rates; sow 1/4 in deep in moisture-retentive, fertile soil. This old European cottage garden vegetable-herb was once widely grown for its young shoots (used like asparagus), leaves (used like spinach), and flower buds (used like broccoli). Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; plants are long-lived perennials once established and require little care. Harvest young shoots in spring, leaves throughout the season, and flower buds before they open; do not harvest heavily in the first year to allow the plant to establish. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Good King Henry
description: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in moist, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Good King Henry is a European perennial edible plant of the goosefoot family (Chenopodiaceae, now Amaranthaceae) that was widely cultivated as a potherb and vegetable in medieval and early modern Europe but has been largely replaced by spinach and other modern leafy vegetables — leaving it as a largely forgotten but highly useful perennial edible for the shade garden. The large, arrow-shaped, dark-green leaves are produced abundantly from an expanding perennial crown that persists for many years; in spring, the young leaves and shoot tips are eaten raw or cooked (with a mild, spinach-like flavor), and the young flowering shoots are eaten like asparagus when they first emerge, blanched and steamed. The flowers themselves are used as a condiment. The primary advantage over annual spinach is permanence — once established, Good King Henry returns year after year with progressively larger harvests from an increasingly robust perennial crown, requiring virtually no replanting. It performs acceptably in partial shade, making it one of the few perennial vegetables useful in the shade vegetable garden. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Good Mother Stallard Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil against a tall trellis; do not soak beans before planting as it can cause the seed coat to split. Good Mother Stallard is an heirloom pole bean introduced through Seed Savers Exchange with beautiful, plum-purple and white mottled pods and seeds that develop into a creamy, meaty dry bean with a remarkably rich, complex, steak-like flavor when cooked — widely considered one of the best-flavored dry beans available to home gardeners. Allow pods to mature and dry completely on the vine before harvesting; if frost threatens, pull the entire vine and hang in a protected location to finish drying. Store shelled dry beans in a cool, airtight container for up to a year. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Goodbarn Elderberry (Elwyn Meader New Hampshire Chance-Seedling American Elderberry)
description: Goodbarn originated as a chance seedling discovered growing under the barn eaves of noted plant breeder Elwyn Meader in Rochester, New Hampshire, and was later named and introduced for its unusual hardiness and vigor. It is among the smallest and shortest-statured named American elderberry cultivars, making it a good option for smaller home gardens, and blooms heavily to set large, evenly ripening annual crops of smaller berries. Goodbarn is notably cold-hardy, tolerating conditions as far north as USDA zone 3, and appears self-fertile, though interplanting with another cultivar is still recommended for maximum fruit set. Cook the berries before eating, as with all elderberry. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Goodwin Creek Lavender (Heat-and-Humidity-Tolerant Southern Lavender)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, ideally on a raised bed, berm, or slope to keep roots from sitting in wet soil, especially through humid Gulf South summers. Goodwin Creek Lavender is a hybrid (Lavandula x ginginsii) prized as one of the most reliable lavenders for hot, humid climates where classic English lavender types typically struggle with root and crown rot; it bears silvery, deeply toothed foliage and long-blooming purple-blue flower spikes over an extended season. It tolerates heat and humidity noticeably better than most lavender types, though it is somewhat less cold-hardy, so mulch lightly and avoid heavy winter wet in colder zones within its range. Prune after flowering to maintain a compact, woody shape and avoid the leggy, splayed-open form lavender develops if left unpruned for several years. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Gooseberry
description: Gooseberries tolerate partial shade better than most fruits and prefer cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, removing canes older than 3 years and any crossing branches to reduce disease pressure. Pick berries early for cooking (when green and firm) or allow them to ripen to red, yellow, or white for fresh eating. Note: check local regulations, as Ribes species are restricted in some U.S. states due to white pine blister rust. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Gooseberry (Hawthorn Gooseberry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide consistent moisture during fruit development. Ribes hirtellum (hawthorn gooseberry or Appalachian gooseberry) is a native North American gooseberry species found naturally in cool, moist woodlands, bog margins, and rocky slopes from Labrador to Missouri — the most widespread of the native American gooseberries and a parent of many modern gooseberry cultivars. The shrubs are compact and moderately thorny, producing clusters of small, 1/2-inch, green to red-purple, translucent fruits in June–July with the characteristic sweet-tart gooseberry flavor excellent for preserves, pies, fools, wines, and chutneys. Unlike European gooseberry cultivars (Ribes uva-crispa), which often struggle with mildew in humid eastern North American summers, R. hirtellum and its native cultivar hybrids have better disease resistance in humid climates. An important distinction: Ribes species (gooseberries and currants) can serve as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust; planting within 1,000 feet of white pine stands is regulated or prohibited in some states — check local regulations. In zone 9, gooseberry requires deep mulching and consistent moisture and is marginal at the southern edge of its range; best in cooler climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gooseberry (Red Jacket)
description: Red Jacket is an American-type gooseberry bred for nearly thornless canes and strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for gooseberries in humid climates. Berries start green and ripen to a translucent deep red with a sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and preserves alike. The spreading, productive bush is easier to hand-harvest than thornier European cultivars. It tolerates warmer, more humid summers better than many gooseberries, though it still prefers cooler nights than true Gulf Coast conditions provide. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Goosebumps Pumpkin (Hybrid Warty Jack-O-Lantern Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills widely to accommodate vigorous 15 to 20 pound fruit. Goosebumps produces an orange jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin covered in fine, dense bumps rather than the larger, sparser warts seen on some novelty pumpkins, giving it a distinctively pebbled texture that has made it popular with retail growers and fall-festival displays. The heavy warting develops progressively as the fruit matures, so color and texture continue to intensify right up to harvest. Pick before hard frost once the rind has hardened and the bumpy texture has fully developed, and expect the thick rind to hold up well through weeks of autumn display. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Gopher Apple (Ground Oak)
description: Plant in very well-drained, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun — gopher apple is native to the xeric scrub and dry pinelands of the southeastern coastal plain and is exceptionally drought-tolerant, thriving on soils too poor and dry for most plants. The small, low-growing shrub produces white apple-like edible fruits about 1 inch long that are sweet and mild when fully ripe, eaten by gopher tortoises (for which the plant is named), bears, deer, and other wildlife. A critically important food source for gopher tortoises in Florida. Spreads slowly via an extensive root system; once established, this tough native is essentially maintenance-free. Excellent for butterfly gardens and native scrub restorations in the deep South. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gordon Apple (California Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Gordon arose as a chance seedling discovered on a Whittier, California property and was patented in 1976 for its unusually reliable fruiting in mild-winter climates. It needs only about 400 chill hours and is fully self-fruitful, so a single tree can be planted where cross-pollination options are limited. Fruit ripens late August into September, with firm, crisp, aqueous white flesh under yellow-green skin washed and striped with dark red, good for fresh eating and cooking alike. In Gulf Coast plantings it pairs well with Anna or Dorsett Golden as an extended-season companion. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gorham Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Raised in 1910 by Richard Wellington at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a cross of Williams Bon Chrétien (Bartlett) and Josephine de Malines, it was introduced to Britain in 1923 and received a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. The small-to-medium fruit has pale green skin turning pale yellow, sometimes entirely covered in light brown russet, with fine, juicy, cream-colored flesh carrying a sweet, musky flavor reminiscent of its Bartlett parent. It shows high resistance to scab and good resistance to mildew, making it a reliable, low-fuss choice for a home orchard. Harvest in early-to-mid fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gorizia Rosemary (Large-Leaf Italian Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Gorizia is an heirloom Italian rosemary cultivar, named for the city in northeastern Italy, valued for producing notably larger leaves than standard rosemary along with a milder, sweeter, less resinous flavor that many cooks find more versatile in the kitchen since it is less likely to overpower a dish. It grows into a large, vigorous, upright shrub, often taller and more substantial than typical rosemary cultivars, making it a good choice as a specimen shrub, informal hedge, or the backbone of a culinary herb bed where its size and productivity provide a generous, continuous harvest. Like other rosemary, it thrives in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and struggles in heavy clay or soil that stays wet, so raised beds or berms are useful in areas with poor drainage. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than selections like Arp and performs best in zone 8-10, where it can remain evergreen and productive year-round. Prune after flowering to maintain shape and encourage bushy new growth for continued harvest. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Gotu Kola
description: Propagate from stolons (creeping stems with nodes), which root readily in moist potting mix or at the edges of ponds; plant in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade, as gotu kola thrives in the margins of water bodies in its native tropical Asian habitat. In zones below 9, grow in containers that can be overwintered on a warm, bright windowsill with consistently moist soil. Harvest the small, fan-shaped leaves regularly once the plant is established; the fresh leaves are eaten in salads in Sri Lankan cuisine and used in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine as a cognitive tonic and wound-healing herb. Harvest leaf material by snipping stems without uprooting the plant to allow continued production. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Goumi
description: Goumi is a nitrogen-fixing shrub from East Asia that produces abundant small, cherry-red, speckled fruits with a sweet-tart flavor reminiscent of cherry. It is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, making it a valued plant in permaculture systems. Prune lightly after fruiting to shape the plant and encourage denser branching; heavy pruning stimulates excessive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit. Harvest when berries are fully red and slightly soft — ripe fruits have little to no astringency and taste excellent fresh or dried. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Goumi Berry (Cherry Silverberry, Natsugumi)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; extremely adaptable — drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and fixes nitrogen. Elaeagnus multiflora (goumi berry or natsugumi) is a deciduous shrub from China and Japan producing one of the earliest ripening berry crops in the edible landscape — the elongated, cherry-red, silver-speckled fruits ripen in late May to June (in zone 6–7), several weeks before blueberries or raspberries, filling a gap in the fresh fruit calendar. The fruits are tart-sweet, somewhat astringent when slightly underripe, with a pleasant fresh berry flavor when fully red; they are rich in lycopene (higher concentration than tomatoes), vitamins A, C, and E, and flavonoids. Unlike its aggressive invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), goumi is not considered invasive in most regions — it produces less seed, spreads less aggressively, and is widely grown in permaculture and food forest systems. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis, making goumi a valuable soil-building companion plant in the food forest understory layer. The attractive silvery-green foliage and small, fragrant, creamy-yellow flowers in spring are also ornamentally pleasing. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Gourmet Blend Beet
description: A colorful mix of beet varieties including deep-red Detroit Dark Red and candy-striped Chioggia, offering a rainbow of roots and tasty greens. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked and thin each seed cluster to a single plant about 3 inches apart. Keep evenly moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size. The assorted colors make a beautiful bunch and a striking roasted medley. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Governor Simcoe Strawberry (Ontario-Bred Cold-Hardy June-Bearer)
description: Governor Simcoe was bred at the Vineland research station in Ontario, Canada, and became a widely grown June-bearing cultivar across Canadian and northern U.S. home gardens for decades after its release, valued for large, firm, richly flavored berries on vigorous, winter-hardy plants. It produces a concentrated mid-season harvest and holds up well both for fresh eating and preserving, a combination that kept it in wide cultivation long after many contemporaries from the same era fell out of favor. Its cold hardiness suits it to prairie and northern climates where many modern patented cultivars struggle to overwinter reliably. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to sustain productivity in following years. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Governor's Plum (Ramontchi, Madagascar Plum)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil — tolerates drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions once established; governor's plum is a thorny tropical small tree or large shrub from Africa and Asia producing prolific clusters of small (1/2–1 inch) dark red to purple-black fruits with a flavor blending cherry and plum with pleasant tartness. One of the most reliable and productive tropical fruit plants for the subtropical home garden, fruiting heavily from a young age with minimal care beyond adequate drainage. The spiny branching habit makes it a formidable security hedge. Fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe, made into jams, jellies, and juices, or fermented into alcoholic beverages in East Africa. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Governors Plum
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia indica is drought tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types including lateritic and calcareous soils, and grows vigorously with minimal care — prune to shape after fruiting and to maintain desired height. Flacourtia indica (Governor's Plum, Ramontchi, or Madagascar Plum) is a thorny, fast-growing, many-branched shrub or small tree native to tropical and subtropical Africa and South Asia from Madagascar, the East African coast, and sub-Saharan Africa east through India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia to the Philippines. The small (0.5–1 inch), round to slightly flattened fruits ripen from green through red to deep red-purple or nearly black, with tart-sweet, juicy, dark-red flesh eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, syrups, and fermented into wine across its broad native range. The flesh is astringent when underripe but richly sweet-tart and plum-like when fully ripe. Governor's Plum is a tough, adaptable, undemanding fruiting plant tolerant of poor soils, drought, alkalinity, and partial neglect — an excellent productive hedgerow plant or edible security hedge plant for zone 8–11. The plants are dioecious (separate male and female trees required for fruit set). Naturalized and sometimes invasive in tropical regions outside its range. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Graffiti Cauliflower (Vivid Purple Cauliflower)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; transplant into rich, moist, fertile soil with consistent watering; fall crops typically produce the most vivid purple color as cool temperatures intensify the anthocyanin pigmentation; harvest when heads are tight. Graffiti is a vivid purple cauliflower developed by Syngenta Seeds, with intensely purple heads caused by very high anthocyanin concentrations — the same pigments responsible for the colors of red cabbage, blueberries, blackberries, and purple sweet potatoes, and associated with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory health properties. Unlike the orange beta-carotene in Cheddar cauliflower, the purple anthocyanins in Graffiti are water-soluble and somewhat heat-sensitive: the vivid purple color turns gray-blue or fades when the vegetable is boiled or steamed, though the color remains more stable with roasting or stir-frying. For maximum visual impact, Graffiti is best used raw — in crudités platters, purple cauliflower hummus, raw salads, and grain bowls where the intense purple provides a visual anchor. The flavor is typically cauliflower — slightly nutty, mild, sweet — with no unusual taste despite the dramatic color. Cool temperatures intensify the purple color, making fall-grown Graffiti more vividly colored than spring crops. An excellent conversation piece and visual anchor for vegetable gardens. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Graffiti Eggplant
description: This Italian type bears glossy fruit striped in purple and white that fades to solid purple as it matures. Start seed indoors eight weeks before the last frost and transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60 F. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and stake plants that become top-heavy with fruit. Harvest while the skin is still glossy for the mildest, least seedy flesh. Consistent picking encourages the plant to keep flowering and fruiting. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Grain Amaranth (Kiwicha, Inca Wheat, Prince's Feather)
description: Scatter seeds thinly on firm, moist, weed-free soil and press gently without covering — seeds are tiny and need light to germinate well; thin seedlings to 12–18 inches when they reach 3 inches tall. Grain amaranth is a tall, drought-resistant warm-season annual producing enormous plume-like flower heads packed with thousands of tiny seeds that are 13–16% complete protein and rich in lysine, an amino acid deficient in most grains. The seeds pop like popcorn, cook into porridge, or grind into gluten-free flour. Young leaves are edible as a potherb. Harvest when the seed heads begin to dry but before rain can cause mold — cut the stalks and dry in a ventilated space, then thresh by rubbing between hands or rolling in a cloth sack. One plant can produce several pounds of grain in a good season. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Grain Sorghum (Milo, Kafir Corn)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil in full sun in rows 30–36 inches apart; grain sorghum is one of the most drought-tolerant of all cereal grains, adapted to hot, dry conditions that would devastate corn. In the South it is called 'milo' and is traditionally grown as a feed grain for livestock, but the grain is also edible for humans — it can be popped like popcorn, ground into gluten-free flour for flatbreads and porridges, cooked as a rice-like grain, or fermented into traditional African and South American beverages. White and tan grain varieties are milder-flavored than red varieties for human consumption. The upright plants top out with a dense grain head; harvest when seeds are hard and the heads have dried on the plant. Sorghum's deep root system makes it exceptionally drought-resistant once established, and it responds well to brief dry spells that would reduce corn yields. Matures in 75–110 days from seed.

name: Grains of Paradise
description: Plant rhizomes in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; grains of paradise is a West African ginger relative producing striking orchid-like pink to purple flowers at the base of the plant, followed by red oval fruits each containing 60–100 small brown seeds. The seeds have a complex, layered flavor combining warm pepper heat, floral cardamom, and citrus — used historically in European medieval cooking as a pepper substitute and today experiencing a culinary revival in craft brewing, gin production, and spice-forward cooking. In Ghana it is known as efom wisa and is used in traditional stews and spice blends. The ornamental foliage and unusual basal flowers make this a beautiful specimen plant for warm-climate shade gardens. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Gran Nain Banana
description: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil with abundant organic matter; Gran Nain is the world's most commercially important banana — the standard Cavendish-type export banana sold under the Chiquita and Dole brands. The medium to large, curved, smooth-skinned, sweet, mild-flavored fruits are the archetype of the supermarket banana and are grown on multi-stem mats that require minimal specialized knowledge. Gran Nain grows 8–12 feet tall — moderately tall for a Cavendish type — and produces large, heavy bunches of 7–9 hands when given full sun, abundant water, and high nitrogen and potassium fertilization throughout the growing season. In zone 9 the long, hot growing season produces excellent banana development; the main challenge is protecting pseudostems from the occasional hard freeze. Zone 9 gardeners who can grow Gran Nain successfully typically achieve production equivalent to small commercial planting density. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Grand Duke Kohlrabi
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Grand Duke is the 1979 All-America Selections-winning kohlrabi cultivar and remains the standard cool-season kohlrabi for home gardens. The pale green, smooth-skinned swollen stem enlarges more uniformly and remains tender longer than older varieties — it can be harvested at 2–3 inches and still be mild and crisp, even as other varieties turn woody and pungent. The flavor is mild, sweet, and slightly turnip-like — excellent raw, sliced thin in salads, or stir-fried. In zone 9 kohlrabi is a fall-through-winter vegetable, transplanted in September–October for harvest from November through February. The plants are relatively frost-hardy and will survive most zone 9 winters without protection. Pull the entire plant at harvest; the leaves are also edible when young and cooked like kale. Matures in 45–55 days from transplant.

name: Grand Frost Lemon (Cold-Hardy Zone 8b Culinary Lemon)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing a warm, sheltered spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter protection. Grand Frost is a University of Georgia release bred for improved cold tolerance, extending reliable in-ground lemon culture into zone 8b gardens where standard lemon varieties struggle to survive most winters. It bears bright yellow, classically tart, aromatic fruit typical of a good culinary lemon, ripening over an extended season on a vigorous, thorny tree. For Gulf Coast gardeners in the cooler parts of the region, Grand Frost offers a realistic path to growing lemons outdoors with only modest winter protection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Grand Nain Banana (Commercial Cavendish-Type Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Grand Nain is the commercial Cavendish-type banana grown worldwide for fresh export and the variety most home gardeners already know from the grocery store. Fruit is medium-sized, thin-skinned, and sweet with the familiar mild banana flavor, produced on a comparatively shorter, sturdier pseudostem than many tropical banana cultivars, which helps it stand up better to wind. Unlike Gulf South stalwarts such as Orinoco, Grand Nain has little cold tolerance and the rhizome can be killed outright by a hard freeze rather than simply resprouting, so zone 9 gardeners should grow it in a large container that can be moved to shelter for winter, or commit to heavy mulching and wrapping in a protected microclimate. Full sun, high heat, consistent moisture, and rich soil with regular feeding all speed the roughly 12-15 months it takes from planting to a full bunch of fruit. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Grand Rapids Lettuce (Historic American Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Grand Rapids is a historic American loose-leaf lettuce introduced in the late 1800s that became the standard commercial greenhouse lettuce variety across the United States for much of the early 20th century, prized for its light green, deeply frilled, crinkled leaves and fast, dependable growth. It does not form a true head, instead producing a loose rosette that can be harvested leaf by leaf for a cut-and-come-again crop or cut whole at the base once full size is reached. Grand Rapids is more heat- and cold-tolerant than many lettuce varieties, extending the usable harvest window on either end of the cool season, though very hot weather will still eventually push it to bolt and turn bitter. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Grand Traverse Hazelnut (Cold-Climate Trihybrid Filbert)
description: Grand Traverse was selected in Michigan by breeder Cecil Farris from a cross tracing back to Turkish tree hazel, giving it exceptional cold hardiness and good tolerance of eastern filbert blight compared with pure European filbert cultivars. Nuts are thin-shelled, fiber-free, and well flavored, borne on a vigorous tree that handles harsh continental winters better than Pacific Northwest hazelnut selections. Because it carries mixed parentage, plant it alongside an unrelated pollenizer such as a wild American hazelnut for reliable nut set, and space trees generously to accommodate its eventual tree-like habit. Harvest in early autumn as husks dry and nuts drop free; gather promptly from the ground to stay ahead of squirrels. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Grandad's Favourite Rhubarb
description: Grandad's Favourite is a traditional English heirloom passed down through generations of allotment growers and prized for its reliably sweet flavor and tender texture even in stalks left to grow a bit larger than usual. It forces well for an early, pale pink forced crop when covered with a forcing pot in late winter, then produces a second flush of deep red, more strongly flavored stalks in open growth through spring. Established clumps are notably vigorous and long-lived, often remaining productive in the same spot for well over a decade with minimal care beyond an annual mulch. As with other rhubarb, discard the leaves and harvest only the stalks, pulling rather than cutting them from the crown. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Grande Rio Verde Tomatillo
description: A compact tomatillo about 24 inches tall that yields husked green fruit nearly all at once, ideal for canning or freezing salsa verde. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather warms. Plant at least two, since tomatillos need cross-pollination to set fruit well. Harvest when the papery husks fill out and split, and stake plants if they get top-heavy. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Grandma Nellie's Yellow Mushroom Bean
description: This family heirloom pole bean traces to seed a Russian immigrant gave to Nellie Chernoff, who grew it for decades before it was passed down and eventually shared with seed preservationists. Pick pods at about 4 to 5 inches while still tender for fresh eating; cooked pods develop a distinctive savory, umami-like richness that sets this variety apart from typical green beans. Provide sturdy 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis, as the vines are vigorous climbers that bear over a long harvest window. Keep pods picked regularly to keep the plant productive through the season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Grandpa Admire's Lettuce
description: Sow seed shallowly in cool, moist soil and thin plants as they grow to give each head room to fill out. Grandpa Admire's is an Ozark family heirloom lettuce preserved and distributed by Seed Savers Exchange, forming a loose, semi-heading rosette that bridges the gap between a butterhead and a romaine in both leaf shape and texture. The pale green leaves are tender and mild-flavored with a buttery crunch, and the variety is valued for holding in the garden without turning bitter longer than many spring lettuces. As a passed-down heirloom with a documented family origin, it is a good choice for gardeners interested in preserving lesser-known regional lettuce lines. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Granex Sweet Onion (Vidalia-Type Short-Day Onion)
description: Transplant onion sets or starts in November through January in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Granex is the foundational sweet onion cultivar behind the famous Vidalia onion — a short-day, mild, sweet onion variety grown in the Vidalia, Georgia, area since the 1940s that became the basis for the legally protected Vidalia Onion designation. The Granex onion (and closely related Granex 33 and similar cultivars) produces round to slightly flattened, large, sweet, mild bulbs with high sugar content and low pyruvic acid — a combination that creates the characteristic sweetness and lack of pungency that makes Vidalia-type onions so prized for fresh eating. Granex is a short-day onion (bulbs when day length reaches 12 hours or less), making it the correct onion type for Gulf South gardens where the short winter days trigger bulbing in March through May. Long-day onion varieties (grown in the northern US) will not bulb in the Gulf South — short-day varieties (Granex, Texas 1015, Red Creole) are essential for zone 9 production. In zone 9, transplant November through January and harvest when the tops begin to fall over (May–June), indicating full bulb development. The mild, sweet Granex onion is outstanding for fresh salads, burgers, and raw applications where a sweet onion is desired. Matures in 95–120 days from transplant.

name: Granny Franklin Okra (Alabama Heirloom Frying Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once the soil is warm; pick pods every 1-2 days at 3-4 inches for the most tender texture. Granny Franklin is an Alabama family heirloom, kept going for generations by home gardeners specifically for its heavy, consistent yield of classic green pods and its reputation as an outstanding frying okra. The tall, vigorous plants shrug off the intense heat and humidity that stress many other vegetables through a Deep South summer, continuing to set pods reliably as long as they are harvested regularly. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saved from healthy plants breeds true, letting Gulf Coast gardeners maintain their own line of this regional variety year after year. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Granny Smith Apple Tree
description: The iconic tart green Granny Smith is prized for baking and long storage as well as fresh eating. It needs a long, warm season to fully ripen and a second apple variety nearby for pollination. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water consistently while the tree establishes. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy that ripens fruit evenly and improves air circulation. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Granny Val Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Granny Val is a Mississippi State University muscadine release bred for exceptionally large, glossy black berries with a good balance of sweetness and the classic musky muscadine flavor, ranking among the largest-fruited black muscadine cultivars available for home gardens. The large berry size makes it a favorite for fresh eating and an eye-catching addition to a mixed muscadine planting, and vines are vigorous and reliably productive once established on a sturdy trellis. Granny Val is self-fertile and does not need a separate pollinizer, though nearby compatible varieties tend to improve overall yield. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that make bunch grapes difficult to grow in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem, and prune annually each winter to renew fruiting wood and keep the vigorous vine in bounds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Grantham's Royal Fig
description: Grantham's Royal is a San Pedro-type fig, meaning it reliably produces a large breba (first) crop on the previous year's wood but needs fig wasp pollination for a true second main crop, which rarely occurs outside the Mediterranean's native range. The large, deep-purple fruit has jammy, richly flavored red flesh with berry and peach notes that collectors rank among the best-tasting of all fig varieties. It is hardy to roughly 0-5°F, tolerating cooler summers better than many Mediterranean fig cultivars, making it a favorite among Pacific Northwest and coastal California growers. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Grape Honeysuckle (Kinnikinnick Honeysuckle)
description: Plant in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade, providing a sturdy trellis, fence, or shrub for support; Grape Honeysuckle is a non-invasive native alternative to the notorious Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) that offers nearly all the same wildlife value — tubular yellow flowers for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees in June–July, followed by clusters of red berries consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and other songbirds in fall — without any of the aggressive, smothering growth habit that makes Japanese honeysuckle a serious ecological threat. One of its most distinctive features is its perfoliate leaves, where paired leaves fuse at the base so the stem appears to pass directly through a single disk-shaped leaf, giving the foliage a sculptural, unusual appearance. It is substantially more cold-hardy than most ornamental honeysuckle vines, thriving in zones 3–8, and is well-suited to the upper Midwest and Great Plains where few ornamental vines are fully reliable. Established vines are drought-tolerant once rooted. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Grape Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.8) with consistent moisture; grape tomatoes are distinguished by their small, elongated, thick-walled fruits — typically 1–2 inches long and grape-shaped — with a sweeter, less acidic flavor and firmer texture than cherry tomatoes, making them excellent for eating fresh, roasting, and salads. Most varieties are indeterminate and highly productive, setting fruit prolifically in large pendant clusters throughout the growing season. The thick skin resists cracking even when watering is inconsistent, a significant advantage over round cherry types. Provide a sturdy cage or stake early, keep soil evenly moist to prevent blossom-end rot, and side-dress with balanced fertilizer when the first flowers open. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Grape-Leaved Passionflower (Scarlet Passionflower)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in a frost-free location; in zone 9 and cooler, grow in large containers that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse in winter. Passiflora vitifolia is a spectacular tropical passionflower vine native to Central and South America producing three-lobed, grape-like leaves (giving the species its name) and the showiest flowers in the genus — brilliant scarlet-red, 4-inch flowers with a striking corona of white-tipped, red filaments in the center; it blooms nearly continuously in tropical climates. The edible fruits are small, oblong, and yellow-green when ripe with a sweet-tart, grape-like flavor. It is one of the finest tropical passionflowers for greenhouse culture and large patio containers, with some of the most intensely colored and beautiful flowers in the genus; it requires warm temperatures year-round. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Grapefruit
description: Grapefruit is self-fertile and produces best in the warmest citrus climates — the prolonged heat of south Texas and southern California delivers better sugar development than coastal or inland zones 9. Trees are large and vigorous; allow 20–25 feet between them and avoid overcrowding with other trees. Ruby Red and Flame are popular pink-fleshed varieties with good cold tolerance for zone 9. Fruit takes 12–18 months from bloom to full ripeness; taste-test from late autumn onward — the peel may remain slightly greenish even when the juice is sweet. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Grapefruit Mint (Citrus-Scented Mint Cultivar)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Grapefruit mint is one of the citrus-scented mint cultivars, prized for its bright, tangy grapefruit-like aroma and flavor that comes through clearly in iced tea, fruit salads, and cocktails, distinct from the sharper menthol notes of peppermint or spearmint. Like other mints it grows vigorously and spreads by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it in a container or a firmly edged bed. Water generously through hot weather to prevent wilting, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut the whole planting back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage for the rest of the growing season. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Grappenhall Lavandin (Vigorous Tall Grey-Leaved Lavandin)
description: Grappenhall is a large, vigorous lavandin prized for its broad mound of long, wide grey-green leaves and tall, gracefully arching stems topped with pale lavender-blue flower spikes among the longest of any lavandin cultivar. Like other lavandins it inherits improved heat and humidity tolerance from its spike lavender parentage, making it more forgiving than pure English lavender in hot, muggy climates. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained to dry soil, spacing generously to allow its broad, billowing form to develop without crowding. Shear back hard after flowering to keep the substantial size in check and prevent the woody, splayed-open habit lavenders develop with age. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Grass Pea
description: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun, 4–6 weeks before last frost; grass pea is one of the most ancient cultivated grain legumes, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent and still grown today across South Asia, Ethiopia, and the Mediterranean as a drought-resistant crop that produces nutritious, starchy seeds used whole, split, or ground into flour. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen and performs remarkably well in thin, poor, drought-stressed soils where other legumes fail — making it a resilient choice for dry-summer gardens and marginal land. Provide light support for the scrambling stems and harvest pods when fully dry on the vine. Important safety note: prolonged consumption of large quantities of grass pea seeds as a dietary staple without adequate protein diversity can cause lathyrism, a neurological condition — consume in normal dietary variety and not as a sole food source. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Gratitude Seedless Grape (Crisp Green Table Grape)
description: Gratitude is a green-skinned seedless table grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program, released alongside its siblings Faith, Hope, and Joy for home garden and local-market use. It stands out among the four for its notably crisp flesh and mild, neutral flavor, and it ripens later than Faith, typically in late August. The berries are non-slipskin with good resistance to cracking, and the vines have shown reliable winter hardiness and general disease tolerance in Arkansas Division of Agriculture trials. Because it was bred for regional and dooryard production rather than commercial shipping, expect smaller clusters and more variable seed remnants than typical grocery-store seedless grapes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gravenstein Apple (Historic Early-Season Sauce and Baking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring two different compatible pollinizer varieties are planted nearby, since Gravenstein is a triploid and cannot pollinize itself or other trees. Gravenstein traces to northern Europe in the 1600s and became world-famous after its introduction to Sonoma County, California in the 1820s, where the region's climate proved so ideal that Gravenstein orchards once dominated the local economy and gave the apple lasting fame as a California heritage crop. The fruit ripens unusually early, in mid to late summer well ahead of most storage apples, with crisp, juicy, aromatic flesh balancing bright tartness and real sweetness that is outstanding for fresh eating, and especially prized for applesauce and baking, where its flavor is considered exceptional. Gravenstein is not a long keeper and bruises easily, so it is best picked and used promptly rather than stored, which is part of why it remains more popular with home gardeners and local markets than large-scale commercial shipping operations. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gray Alder
description: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil along streambanks, pond edges, or other consistently moist sites in full to partial sun; gray alder establishes vigorously in wet conditions and should be sited where roots will have reliable access to subsurface moisture or periodic flooding. Alnus incana is a fast-growing native tree of northern North America, prized for its ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Frankia bacteria and to stabilize eroding streambanks with its dense, fibrous root system; male catkins emerge in early spring before the leaves, providing an important pollen source for early-flying native bees. The persistent small woody cones that remain through winter supply seeds to goldfinches, siskins, and redpolls, and the bark and foliage support a rich diversity of Lepidoptera larvae including many specialist moth species of northern forests. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Gray Pine (Digger Pine, Foothill Pine)
description: Plant in dry, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid summer irrigation once established, since this California foothill native is adapted to long, hot, dry summers and thin, mineral soils. Gray pine has an open, sparse, gray-green crown and produces very large, heavy cones armed with hooked spines that contain large, oily, edible seeds long harvested by California Indigenous peoples as a staple food. It is one of the most drought-tolerant pines suitable for a nut crop and grows slowly but steadily on marginal sites unsuited to most other nut trees. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Greasy Back Bean (Appalachian Heirloom Cornfield Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a trellis or tall support in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Greasy Back belongs to a distinctive family of Appalachian heirloom 'greasy bean' varieties named for pods that lack the fine fuzz found on most bean pods, giving them a smooth, shiny, almost oiled appearance that is unmistakable at a glance. Traditionally grown climbing up corn stalks in mountain garden plots, the vigorous vines produce tender, flavorful pods that can be picked young as snap beans, allowed to mature further for flavorful fresh shell beans, or left to dry fully for a rich, hearty dry bean prized in Appalachian cooking. Pick regularly to keep vines productive over a long season, and let the last flush of pods dry on the vine if a dry bean harvest is wanted. Matures in 65–95 days from seed.

name: Greasy Bean (Appalachian Cutshort Pole Bean)
description: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young for snap beans or let pods mature for a rich, flavorful shelly or dry bean. Greasy Bean is a distinctive category of heirloom Appalachian pole bean named for the unusual smooth, glossy, almost oil-slicked appearance of the pods, which lack the fuzzy surface texture of most common beans — a trait that has made these beans prized heirlooms passed down through generations of mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and West Virginia, with many distinct named strains maintained within individual families. The tender, stringless pods have excellent flavor as snap beans when young, and the plump, flavorful seeds shell out well for cooking as a traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous, productive vines reward a sturdy support and reliable moisture through the growing season. A true regional heirloom treasure for gardeners interested in Appalachian foodways, zone 4–10. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Greasy Cutshort Bean (Tightly-Packed Appalachian Heirloom Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Greasy Cutshort combines two classic Appalachian heirloom bean traits in one variety: smooth, shiny, fuzz-free 'greasy' pods, and seeds packed so densely inside each pod that the tip is squared off rather than tapered, the 'cutshort' trait long selected for by mountain gardeners saving their own seed. The tender pods are good for snapping young, and the beans shell out well for a flavorful dry bean later in the season. Allow some pods to dry fully on the vine each year to save seed and maintain the strain. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Greasy Grits Bean (Appalachian Heirloom Cutshort)
description: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy trellis, pole, or teepee for the vigorous climbing vines; Greasy Grits is one of the many named strains of Appalachian greasy bean, so called for the smooth, shiny, almost oil-slick sheen on the pod surface caused by a lack of the fine fuzz found on most snap beans. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young for snapping, with a rich, savory flavor prized in traditional mountain cooking, and the plant can also be left to mature for shelling as a dry bean. Like other greasy beans it is a genuine landrace maintained by generations of Appalachian seed savers rather than a modern breeding-program release, so some variation between seed lots is normal and part of its heirloom character. Provide consistent moisture through pod set and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive over a long summer harvest window. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Great Burdock (Gobo)
description: Arctium lappa (great burdock, gobo) is a large, vigorous biennial native to temperate Asia and Europe, prized in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese cuisine for its long, slender, sweet, earthy taproot (gobo) which can reach 3 feet or more in depth; roots are best harvested in the first year of growth (before the plant flowers and sets seed in the second year) when they are most tender and flavorful. Direct-sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in early spring in deeply dug, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; the soil must be worked to at least 18 inches depth to allow the taproot to develop without forking — closely spaced rows of 6–8 inches produce slender, straight roots ideal for the table. In traditional Western herbalism, the root is used as a blood-purifying and liver-supportive tonic, and both the root and seed have a long history of use in treating skin conditions; the immature flower stalks can also be peeled and eaten like celery in spring of the second year. Do not allow plants to set seed and self-sow freely as burdock can become weedy in disturbed soils; harvest all roots before the plant flowers in the second year. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Great Lakes 118 Crisphead Lettuce
description: A crisp iceberg-type lettuce, this 1960s improvement over the original Great Lakes is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt. Direct sow in cool soil and thin to about 12 inches so heads can fill out fully. Keep consistently watered to avoid bitterness and tip burn, since even moisture builds those firm, crunchy heads. Harvest when heads feel solid, and enjoy the cool crunch in salads and on sandwiches. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Great Lakes Iceberg Lettuce (AAS-Winning Original American Crisphead Lettuce)
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to cool-season bed. Harvest when head is firm and compact. Great Lakes is the original American crisphead (iceberg) lettuce — developed by W.D. Blystone at the Michigan Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1941 (awarded All-America Selections in 1944), Great Lakes defined the iceberg lettuce type that became the dominant American commercial and restaurant lettuce through the mid-20th century. Before Great Lakes, commercial head lettuce was dominated by softer butterhead types; Great Lakes demonstrated that crisp, tight-heading lettuce could be grown reliably across a wider range of conditions and shipped the long distances needed for national distribution — characteristics that made it the foundation of the California iceberg lettuce industry that supplied American consumers coast-to-coast. The 'iceberg' name comes from the practice of shipping these firm-headed lettuces packed in ice during rail transport — an innovation in food distribution that made fresh lettuce available nationally for the first time. Great Lakes produces large (1.5–2 lb), very firm, round, pale-green to white-interior heads with the extreme crispness and mild flavor of the classic iceberg type. While largely replaced in commercial production by more uniform hybrid iceberg varieties, Great Lakes remains the reference open-pollinated iceberg for home garden and seed-saving use. Matures in 82–90 days from transplant.

name: Great Northern Bean
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Great Northern is the most widely grown white dry bean in the United States, a medium-large, oval, white-seeded bush-type bean with mild, creamy flavor and a tender skin that cooks quickly — the standard white bean for baked beans, soups, and casseroles in American cooking. Developed in the northern Great Plains, it matures in 70–85 days and stores indefinitely as a dry bean. More delicate in flavor than navy beans and larger in size, making it the preferred choice for premium baked bean recipes and New England-style preparations where the bean is the star. Harvest by pulling entire plants when most pods are dry and golden; dry in a warm, airy location and thresh to remove seeds. Great Northern beans are nutritionally excellent, high in protein and fiber. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Great Pignut (Earth Chestnut, Ground Chestnut)
description: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, chalky or loamy soil in full sun; harvest tubers in autumn when the feathery tops die back; difficult to cultivate commercially but rewarding in wild-style gardens. Bunium bulbocastanum (great pignut, earth chestnut, or ground chestnut) is a perennial carrot-family (Apiaceae) plant native to the chalk downs, limestone grasslands, and open woodland edges of southern and central Europe — from England and France south to the Mediterranean basin and Turkey. The plant produces feathery, finely-cut, carrot-like leaves above ground and a remarkable underground structure: a round, swollen tuber (1–2 inches diameter) with a thin brown skin and white, crisp, starchy flesh. The flavor is one of the most pleasant of any wild edible root: sweet, mild, and distinctly reminiscent of a blend of chestnut and hazelnut, with a crisp, juicy texture when fresh — eaten raw, cooked in stews, or roasted. 'Earth chestnut' and 'ground chestnut' both describe the remarkable resemblance of the flavor to chestnuts. In European wild food foraging, great pignut is one of the most highly regarded finds; in cultivation, it is challenging because it dislikes transplanting and requires lean, calcareous, well-drained soils. Distinct from Bunium persicum (black cumin, kala jeera), which is valued for its seeds rather than roots. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Great Wall Persimmon (Hardy Astringent Asian Persimmon)
description: Great Wall got its name when plant geographer J. Russell Smith spotted a superior tree growing near the Great Wall of China in the 1920s and brought scionwood back to the United States, and it remains one of the hardiest and most productive astringent-type Asian persimmons available. The medium-sized, squarish fruit is firm and puckery until fully soft, at which point the flesh turns a rich cinnamon-orange and sweet with none of the astringency remaining, so plan to let it ripen on a windowsill or in the fridge until it gives completely to gentle pressure. The tree stays compact at around 20 feet, is upright and long-lived, bears heavily once established, and colors up with strong red fall foliage that makes it a genuine landscape asset as well as a fruit tree. It tolerates a wider range of soils than most fruiting trees but still performs best with good drainage and full sun. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Great White Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy cage or stake support; Great White is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing fruits that ripen to an unusual cream-white to pale ivory-yellow color — one of the most distinctive-appearing heirloom tomatoes in any garden collection. The color difference from standard red tomatoes stems from the absence of normal red lycopene pigments: Great White produces primarily colorless carotenoids that result in the pale white-cream skin and flesh. The flavor is extraordinarily mild, sweet, and very low in acid — often described as honey-sweet with almost no tartness, making it popular for people who find acidic tomatoes hard to digest. The thick, very meaty flesh with small seed cavities makes Great White outstanding for fresh eating and mild salsas where a lower-acid tomato flavor is preferred. The pale color also makes it a striking visual contrast element in colorful heirloom tomato salads alongside red, purple, orange, and yellow varieties. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Great White Tomato
description: This rare heirloom beefsteak produces creamy pale fruits of one to two pounds with sweet, low-acid, almost tropical flavor. Start seed indoors about six weeks before transplanting, then set hardened plants deep into rich, warm soil. As an indeterminate vine, it benefits from sturdy staking or caging and consistent watering to prevent cracking. Harvest when the pale fruits take on a faint blush and yield slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Greater Celandine (Tetterwort)
description: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade to part shade; greater celandine is a European and western Asian member of the poppy family that has naturalized extensively in North America in disturbed, shaded situations — old walls, woodland edges, shaded garden corners, and waste ground — where it grows as a short-lived, freely self-sowing perennial producing pale-blue-gray, deeply lobed, softly hairy foliage and small, four-petaled, cheerful-yellow flowers from spring through summer in a nearly continuous display. When the stems or leaves are broken, they exude a bright, intense orange-yellow latex sap that has been used since antiquity to treat skin conditions, particularly warts (the name tetterwort refers to its historical use for skin eruptions). The sap is caustic and can irritate skin and is toxic if ingested. In the garden it is best used as a shade-tolerant naturalizing plant under trees and shrubs where its self-sowing habit creates a tapestry of bluish foliage and yellow flowers without requiring care. The double-flowered cultivar 'Flore Pleno' has attractive pompom-like flowers and is somewhat less freely self-sowing than the species. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Greater Galangal (Thai Galangal)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; greater galangal is the essential culinary rhizome of Southeast Asian cooking — a large, handsome ginger-family plant native to coastal Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand) that provides the distinctive aromatic flavoring in Thai tom kha soup, Thai curry pastes, Indonesian rendang, Cambodian dishes, and numerous other Southeast Asian preparations where it is as fundamental an ingredient as garlic or lemongrass. The flavor of galangal rhizome is completely distinct from culinary ginger (Zingiber officinale): sharper, more medicinal and piney, with strong citrus-pepper notes and a resinous, camphor-like quality that is immediately recognizable in the cuisines that use it — the characteristic flavor that makes tom kha soup taste like tom kha and nothing else. The rhizome is distinguished visually from ginger by its dense, concentric-ringed, smooth skin with distinctive rose-pink to red-tinged growing points (unlike the warty tan skin of ginger). In the garden it is a very handsome, bold, tropical plant — a large, upright clump of robust stems with broad, dark-green, somewhat glossy, lance-shaped leaves reaching 4–8 feet, with attractive white-and-maroon-striped flowers occasionally in summer. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a reliable perennial in sheltered positions with consistent moisture. Once established, rhizomes can be harvested year-round as needed by carefully digging at the clump margin. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Greek Basil
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm, moist seed-starting mix and thin seedlings to avoid crowding once they have two true leaves. Greek basil forms a naturally compact, globe-shaped mound with tiny, intensely aromatic leaves — no pinching required to maintain shape, though removing flower buds prolongs leaf harvest. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the petite habit makes it an excellent edging plant or container herb. Harvest by snipping small stem tips; the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of the small leaves delivers concentrated flavor. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Greek Mountain Tea (Sideritis)
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in well-drained, alkaline starting mix and keep warm at 68–72°F until germination; use gritty, mineral-rich mix to mimic its rocky Mediterranean mountain habitat. Plant out in the poorest, most well-drained spot in the garden — excess moisture and rich soil are the primary causes of failure. The silver-felted stems and leaves are harvested in full bloom in summer when the yellow flowers are visible; cut entire stems and hang in bundles to dry in a warm, airy space. Brew the whole dried stems as an herbal tea by simmering 5–10 minutes; the resulting infusion has a mild, honey-and-herb flavor and is traditionally consumed throughout Greece for immune support and as an everyday tonic. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Greek Oregano
description: Surface-sow seeds by pressing them into barely moist, well-drained seed-starting mix without covering, as they need light to germinate. Greek oregano (also called Italian or true oregano) is the pungent, white-flowered subspecies prized in Mediterranean cooking; it has far stronger flavor than common Origanum vulgare. Plant in lean, gritty, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun — excessive fertility dilutes the essential oils that give it its distinctive bite.
