Cut plants back by one-third after flowering each year to keep them compact; harvest just as buds begin to open for peak aroma. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Greek Oregano Kaliteri
description: Plant in full sun in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — avoid overwatering and rich fertilization; Greek Oregano Kaliteri is a select strain of true Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) chosen for exceptionally high essential oil content and intense, pungent flavor — the variety name means 'the best' in Greek. The aromatic, white-woolly leaves are strongly pungent with the hot, spicy, complex oregano fragrance that defines Mediterranean cooking from Greek salads to Neapolitan pizza to Spanish sofrito. Most oregano sold at grocery stores is mild and nearly flavorless compared to properly grown Greek oregano subsp. hirtum; Kaliteri represents a selected high-oil strain of an already superior subspecies. The small, compact mound of woolly gray-green leaves is attractive in the herb garden and the white summer flowers are valuable to bees. In zone 9 the plant grows vigorously in fall, winter, and spring but may become semi-dormant in peak summer heat. Soil drainage is more critical than fertility — soggy soil kills Greek oregano quickly. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Greek Sage (Three-Lobed Sage, Cretan Sage)
description: Root stem cuttings or sow seeds in well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Greek sage (Salvia fruticosa) is the wild sage of the eastern Mediterranean islands — the primary sage of Greek, Cypriot, and Turkish cuisine and the sage used in dried herb mixes sold as 'mountain tea' throughout Greece and the Middle East. The flavor is fuller, more complex, and somewhat milder than common garden sage, with distinctive 3-lobed leaves (giving it the name 'three-lobed sage') and lavender-pink flowers. More heat tolerant and longer-lived than common sage in hot-summer climates, making it an excellent culinary sage for zones 8–11 where Salvia officinalis tends to decline. Used fresh or dried in Greek lamb dishes, lemon-sage teas, and Mediterranean marinades. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Green and Red Shiso Perilla
description: Also called Japanese basil or beefsteak plant, shiso carries a complex flavor blending cinnamon, mint, and clove with hints of cumin, and this mix offers both green and red-leaved plants. Surface-sow seed indoors as it needs light to sprout, and set out only after the soil has warmed. Heat- and drought-tolerant, it makes a handsome bedding plant that attracts pollinators. Pinch growing tips to encourage branching and harvest young leaves for wraps, pickles, and garnishes. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Green Arrow Shelling Pea
description: A productive heirloom shelling pea whose sweet green peas fill pods set in pairs atop compact 28-inch plants for easy harvesting. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost as soon as the soil is workable, and give the vines a short trellis or netting. Keep the soil cool and moist and pick pods when plump but still bright green. Excellent for fresh eating and freezing. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Green Bean
description: Direct-sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F — inoculating seeds with rhizobium bacteria before planting improves nitrogen fixation and yields in soils where beans have not grown before; beans rot in cold, wet soil so waiting for warmth is essential. Bush beans form compact plants and produce all at once (60 days) while pole beans require a trellis and produce continuously over a longer season (65–80 days). Harvest green beans when pods are firm, snap crisply, and seeds inside are just beginning to swell — overmature pods become tough and stringy. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks for a steady supply throughout summer. Avoid working in the bean patch when plants are wet to prevent spreading bacterial diseases. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Green Boy Komatsuna (Cold-Tolerant Hybrid Japanese Mustard Spinach)
description: Green Boy is a modern komatsuna hybrid selected for compact, glossy, deep green leaves on pale, tender petioles, with a flavor that sits between spinach and mild mustard. It stands out among komatsuna types for its cold tolerance, continuing to produce usable leaves well into cool weather when other Asian greens have stalled or bolted, which extends the harvest window in fall and early winter. Direct sow and harvest young for salad-size baby leaves or let plants develop further for bunching greens suited to stir-fries and quick braises. Succession sow every few weeks in the cooler shoulder seasons for a steady supply. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Green Cabbage Microgreens
description: Spread cabbage seed thickly over a moist tray and cover for the first two or three days to draw the seedlings up evenly. Uncover once the stems have lengthened and give bright light to keep them stocky and green. Maintain steady moisture and light airflow to fend off damping-off. Harvest the crisp, mildly sweet shoots at the cotyledon stage in eight to ten days. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Green Comet Broccoli (AAS Early Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting transplants into fertile, evenly moist soil, spacing plants closer than later-maturing types since this hybrid stays compact. Green Comet earned an All-America Selections award for its speed, forming a tight, uniformly domed blue-green head only about eight weeks after transplanting, which makes it a reliable choice for short-season gardens or an early jump on the spring harvest before summer heat arrives. Side shoots follow the main head, though they are smaller and less numerous than in later hybrids. Cut the central head promptly once buds are tight, since this variety runs to flower quickly in warm weather. Matures in 55–60 days from transplant.

name: Green Curled Ruffec Endive
description: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather, or sow in early spring for a summer crop. A French heirloom frisée-type endive named for the town of Ruffec, it is prized for its finely dissected, deeply curled dark-green leaves and notable cold hardiness compared to other curly endives. Traditionally the outer leaves are gathered and tied to blanch the heart, producing the pale, tender center prized in French bistro salads. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Green Delicious Squash (1903 Heirloom, Parent of Golden Delicious)
description: Green Delicious was introduced in 1903 by James J.H. Gregory and Sons of Marblehead, Massachusetts, and was described in the historical reference The Vegetables of New York as among the finest-flavored of all squash. Its thick, hard green rind protects dense, orange, fine-grained flesh with an exceptionally sweet, dry texture prized for pies and baking. It later served as a parent, crossed with Boston Marrow, in the 1926 development of the now much more widely grown Golden Delicious squash by Gill Brothers Seed Company. Green Delicious survives today mainly through heirloom seed preservationists. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Green Dragon Arum / Crow Dipper
description: Pinellia ternata is a small Asian aroid grown in traditional Chinese medicine gardens for its tubers (ban xia), which are used dried and processed as an anti-nausea and antiemetic herb — the raw tubers are toxic and cause intense oral irritation and burning; always handle with care. The plant produces trifoliate leaves on long petioles and a slender, hooded spathe in late spring, followed by a spike of tiny orange-red berries; it grows happily in the deep shade of trees where few other plants thrive and makes a useful, if spreading, shade groundcover in Asian herb gardens. In zone 9, it may behave as a cool-season annual. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Green Express Cabbage
description: A quick-growing miniature cabbage forming 5 to 6 inch heads of 2 to 3 pounds, ready in as little as 50 days. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out, then transplant while temperatures remain cool. The small heads suit container and raised-bed gardens; space them a bit tighter than full-size cabbage. Keep evenly watered and harvest promptly once heads firm up to avoid splitting. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Green Gage Plum (Reine Claude, Historic French Fine-Flavored Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Green Gage, known in France as Reine Claude, is an ancient European plum predating the 1500s that was named in England after Sir William Gage, who introduced it there in the 1720s, and it has been prized ever since as one of the finest-flavored plums grown, favored by chefs and preserve-makers above almost any other variety. The small to medium round fruit ripens to a yellow-green, sometimes lightly blushed with red, and the golden, freestone flesh carries an extraordinarily rich, sweet, honeyed flavor with none of the tartness common in many other plums. Harvest when fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and the skin's green tone has softened toward amber-yellow, since underripe Green Gage lacks the sugar concentration that makes the variety famous; use promptly, since the delicate, thin-skinned fruit bruises easily and does not store long. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Green German Sugarcane (Heirloom Gulf South Syrup Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Green German is an old dooryard heirloom, unstriped and solid deep green-stalked, that UF/IFAS Extension lists alongside Louisiana Ribbon as one of the traditional syrup-type canes: its juice carries a lower sucrose-to-total-sugars ratio than crystal (refining-grade) cane, which resists graining up in the kettle and cooks down into a smooth, pourable table syrup rather than crystallized sugar. Because sugarcane rarely sets viable seed true-to-type in Gulf South conditions, growers propagate it entirely from stalk sets: in fall, before the first hard freeze, the healthiest, disease-free stalks are cut, laid horizontally in a shaded trench or covered cane bed, and mulched heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic sheeting to keep them dormant but unfrozen through winter. Harvest for syrup runs from the first light frosts in late October through December, when cool nights have converted starches to sugar; stalks are stripped of leaves, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked in an open kettle or pan evaporator into dark, mild-flavored cane syrup. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Green Giant Tomato (Large Green-When-Ripe Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Green Giant is a large-fruited, green-when-ripe heirloom beefsteak tomato grown for its sweet, richly flavored amber-green flesh rather than the red color most gardeners expect at harvest. Because the skin stays green to yellow-green even at full ripeness, judge readiness by a slight give under gentle thumb pressure and a faint softening or blush at the blossom end rather than by color change alone. It is best known in tomato-breeding circles as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Golden Dwarf Champion, crossed in 2005 to create the compact, gold-fruited Dwarf Sweet Sue for the Dwarf Tomato Project. Grow the sprawling indeterminate vines on a sturdy cage or stake in full sun, and pick fruit promptly once it softens, since overripe green tomatoes are easy to mistake for underripe ones and can spoil on the vine if left too long. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Green Ginger Rosemary (Ginger-Scented Upright Rosemary)
description: Green Ginger is a bushy, upright rosemary cultivar with narrow, dark green needle-like leaves that release a distinctive ginger note alongside the typical resinous rosemary scent when crushed, making it a novelty choice for cooks who want a warmer, spicier undertone in rosemary dishes. It bears clusters of pale blue-and-white, two-lipped flowers in the leaf axils from mid-spring through summer, often repeating sporadically into autumn. Among the hardiest rosemary selections available, it tolerates winter cold well below what damages many other cultivars and has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for garden-worthiness. Grow it in poor to average, sharply drained soil in a sunny, sheltered spot; like all rosemary it resents heavy, wet soil far more than it minds cold, so drainage is the key to long-term success. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Green Glaze Collard (Waxy Insect-Resistant Heirloom Collard)
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard, prized among organic growers for its thick, glossy, cabbage-like leaf surface that gives noticeably better natural resistance to cabbage worms, loopers, and flea beetles than standard collard varieties, reducing the need for pest control sprays. The tall, vigorous plants produce large, tender leaves with good flavor over a long cut-and-come-again harvest season, and cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, as with other collards. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season, and although the glossy leaves offer real pest resistance, monitor young transplants closely, since seedlings are more vulnerable before the waxy cuticle fully develops. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Green Glaze Collards (Pest-Resistant Waxy-Leaf Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard distinguished by unusually smooth, thick, glossy, jade-green leaves with a waxy cuticle that makes it noticeably more resistant to cabbage worms, cabbage loopers, and other leaf-chewing pests than standard fuzzy-leaved collard varieties, an especially useful trait for organic growers. The flavor is mild and sweet for a collard, and the smooth leaf texture that deters pests also makes the leaves pleasant for fresh use in wraps as well as traditional slow-cooked greens. Like other collards it tolerates both summer heat and considerable cold, with flavor sweetening noticeably after the first light frosts of fall. Harvest outer leaves as needed and the plant continues producing new growth from the top through a long cool-season harvest window. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Green Globe Artichoke
description: This heirloom perennial grows into a bold 4 to 6 foot plant producing large green buds tipped with light purple. Start seed indoors early and give young plants a cool period, which helps them form buds in the first season. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture and ample space for the architectural foliage. Harvest buds while tight and firm before the scales open; in mild zones the plants return and yield for several years. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Green Globe Improved Artichoke
aliases: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Green Globe Improved'
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Globe Improved is the primary commercial artichoke variety grown in California's Monterey County — the heart of American artichoke production — and the selection standard against which most other artichoke varieties are measured. The large, globe-shaped, tightly-closed heads of deep green overlapping bracts contain the edible fleshy bract bases and the prize, the meaty, tender artichoke heart at the center. The 'Improved' designation indicates a more consistent, uniform selection with better vigor than the original Green Globe. In zone 9, artichoke is particularly well-adapted — the mild winters provide the natural vernalization required to initiate bud production, and the plants can persist for 5–8 years as perennial specimens if given adequate space and annual fertilization. Zone 9's long growing season supports two harvesting periods: the main spring crop (February–May) and a secondary fall crop (September–October) after the summer regrowth period. Matures in 85–150 days from transplant.

name: Green Globe Improved Artichoke
description: An improved Green Globe with more uniform plants, fewer spines, and better production, allowing artichokes even in northern gardens grown as an annual. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, and expose young plants to a few weeks of cool temperatures to trigger budding. Give each plant plenty of room and rich, well-drained soil. Expect 3 to 5 tender buds per plant; harvest while the scales are still tight. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Green Goliath Broccoli (Large-Head Side-Shooting Heirloom Broccoli)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with good calcium availability. Harvest the central head while florets are still tight and before the head begins to open or yellow; side shoots will continue for 4–6 weeks. Green Goliath is an open-pollinated broccoli that produces large central heads — typically 8–10 inches across and 1–2 lbs — with the classic well-domed, dark green form that represents the traditional ideal of quality broccoli. The 'goliath' name refers to the head size: substantially larger central heads than many modern hybrid varieties that have been bred for smaller, more uniform heads suited to commercial harvest. After the central head is harvested, Green Goliath produces abundant and persistent side shoots — small 2–4 inch heads — that continue for 4–6 weeks, extending the productive season significantly beyond a single harvest. The side-shooting characteristic makes Green Goliath particularly valuable for home gardeners who want an extended harvest rather than a single concentrated yield. The open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from year to year, making it a popular choice for seed savers and those interested in maintaining productive self-sustaining vegetable gardens. Very good flavor at both the head and side-shoot stages. Matures in 58–68 days from transplant.

name: Green Grape Tomato (Sweet Amber-Green Cherry Tomato that Ripens Green)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and show a slight translucent amber-green glow rather than the opaque dark green of unripe fruit. Green Grape Tomato is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety that remains green at full maturity — a characteristic that surprises first-time growers accustomed to using color change as the primary ripeness cue. The variety was developed by Tim Peters of Peters Seed and Research in Oregon and introduced in the 1990s as part of a wave of interest in non-standard-colored tomatoes that offered novel flavors and visual interest compared to standard red types. Green Grape fruits are approximately 1 inch in diameter with a round to slightly oval shape and thin green skin that ripens to a yellow-green or amber-green with characteristic translucency at peak ripeness; experienced growers learn to identify this translucency as the reliable ripeness indicator. The flavor is notably sweet with a complex, slightly tropical undertone — a combination that many tasters find more interesting than the straightforward sweetness of yellow or red cherry types. The green color is not from chlorophyll retained past ripening but from specific chloroplast development patterns that persist through the normal ripening process; the fruit is fully ripe when the color reaches amber-green, not when it turns red. Fruits cluster in medium-sized trusses of 8–12 and tend to hold well on the vine for several days after reaching peak ripeness without cracking, which is an advantage for gardeners who can't harvest daily. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Green Hawthorn (Winter King Hawthorn)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; green hawthorn — especially the cultivar 'Winter King' — is one of the finest native small trees for four-season ornamental value and wildlife habitat. In spring the tree is covered with small white flowers that are excellent bee forage; in fall the foliage turns burgundy-orange; and in winter the persistent glossy orange-red berries shine against bare branches well into February, providing critical food for cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes. The tree has a vase-shaped form with slightly pendulous branches and is relatively free of the fireblight and cedar-apple rust that plague many hawthorns. The thorns are formidable — plant away from walkways. Excellent as a wildlife garden specimen or fall/winter focal point. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Green Hubbard Squash (True Green Improved Hubbard)
description: Green Hubbard, sometimes offered as True Green Improved Hubbard, is regarded by many seed historians as the original Hubbard type from which the more familiar blue- and orange-skinned Hubbard squashes were later selected. It bears large, teardrop-shaped fruit with a hard, dark green rind that is smoother and less warted than the later Chicago Warted strain, protecting dense, dry, golden-orange flesh with a rich, sweet flavor well suited to soups and purees. Like other Hubbard types, well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a genuine long-season keeper squash. It needs generous vine space and a full warm season to size up and fully mature before harvest. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Green Ice Loose-Leaf Lettuce (Crinkled Glossy Heat-Tolerant Loose-Leaf Variety)
description: Scatter seeds 0.25 inch deep; thin to 6–9 inches for full plants or leave dense for baby leaf cut-and-come-again. Harvest outer leaves, leaving 4–5 inner leaves to continue growing. Green Ice is a loose-leaf lettuce with a distinctive appearance that sets it apart from other common loose-leaf varieties: the leaves are deeply frilled and crinkled — more so than standard looseleaf types — and have an unusual, almost waxy glossiness on the upper leaf surface that gives the fresh leaves a bright, polished look unlike any other commonly grown lettuce. The deep green color is vibrant and consistent, making Green Ice one of the most visually striking lettuces in garden displays, cut flower and produce market presentations, and harvested salad mixes. The flavor is mild, clean, and slightly sweet — typical of loose-leaf types, without the bitterness of romaine or the grassiness of some outer head leaves. Green Ice's combination of heat tolerance (better than most loose-leaf types), productivity in cut-and-come-again harvest systems, glossy visual appeal, and excellent shelf life after harvest has made it a popular variety with market gardeners and home growers seeking a reliable, attractive loose-leaf for continuous harvest through the cool seasons of zone 8–10. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Green in the Snow Mustard (Xue Li Hong)
description: This traditional Chinese mustard, known as xue li hong, meaning red amid the snow, is grown specifically for its ability to keep producing tender, deeply toothed serrated leaves through hard frosts and light snow cover. Direct sow into fertile soil in late summer for the best cold-season crop, harvesting leaves continually as a cut-and-come-again green. Leaves develop a purplish tinge and a distinctive sharp, mustardy tang in cold weather, and are traditionally salted or lightly fermented as a pickle as well as used fresh in soups and stir-fries. Its extreme hardiness makes it one of the last leafy greens standing in an unheated winter garden. Matures in 21–45 days from seed.

name: Green Ischia Fig (Ischia Verde)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Green Ischia is a common fig type (no pollinator required) and typically produces both a reliable breba crop and a main crop. Green Ischia (also called Ischia Verde or simply 'Ischia') is one of the oldest continuously documented fig cultivars in European cultivation, with recorded references going back to at least the 16th century — one of the ancient Italian figs associated with the island of Ischia in the Bay of Naples. The small to medium, round to pear-shaped fruits have greenish-yellow skin that turns to golden-yellow when fully ripe; the interior flesh is pale amber to strawberry-amber with excellent sweetness and mild, delicate fig flavor with a gentle honey note. A two-crop variety that typically produces a moderate breba crop in early summer and a more abundant main crop in August–September. The small tree size (usually 8–15 feet with mature girth) makes Green Ischia more manageable than large fig varieties and an excellent choice for container culture in zones north of 7 where frost protection is needed. Outstanding fresh and dried. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Green Lance Gai Lan
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to stand so the thick, tender flowering stalks can develop; Green Lance is a hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for better heat tolerance than older gai lan strains, letting it be sown over a longer window without bolting prematurely. Harvest the central stalk with its small cluster of unopened flower buds once it reaches pencil thickness, then continue cutting side shoots for several more weeks. The mildly bitter, broccoli-like stems and leaves are classically blanched and stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Green Light Cucumber (Seedless Snacking Cucumber, AAS Winner)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the danger of frost has passed, or set out transplants, providing a small trellis or cage for the compact vines. Green Light was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining parthenocarpic (seedless, self-fruitful) fruit set with a compact plant habit and outstanding yield of crisp, thin-skinned, 4-5 inch mini cucumbers ideal for snacking whole or slicing. Because the plant sets fruit without pollination, it performs reliably even when bee activity is low and produces cucumbers with essentially no seed cavity or bitterness, with skin tender enough that peeling is unnecessary. The compact vines are well suited to small raised beds, large containers, and gardens with limited trellis space, and the plant's dense productivity means frequent picking — every one to two days once fruiting begins — keeps cucumbers at the ideal small size and encourages continued production through the season. Consistent watering during fruit development prevents bitterness and misshapen fruit. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Green Lightning Pattypan Squash (AAS-Winning Striped Scallop Summer Squash)
description: Direct sow seed after the danger of frost has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Lightning is an AAS-winning pattypan summer squash with a compact bush habit and glossy, scalloped fruit striped in dark green over a lighter green background, giving it a more vivid, eye-catching look than typical solid-colored pattypans. A small seed cavity keeps more of the fruit as tender, edible flesh compared to older scallop types. Harvest young, at about 3-5 inches across, for the best texture and flavor, and pick every day or two once plants start producing to keep the vigorous bush setting new fruit. Matures in 40–52 days from seed.

name: Green Macerata Cauliflower
description: This rare Italian heirloom forms vivid green curds with a mild, buttery flavor and reliable performance across seasons. Start seed indoors about six weeks ahead, then transplant into rich, evenly moist soil for uninterrupted growth. Consistent feeding and watering prevent stress that leads to loose or off-flavored heads. Cut heads while the green curds are still tight and firm for the best eating quality. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Green Machine Zucchini (High-Yield Virus-Tolerant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Green Machine is a vigorous hybrid zucchini widely grown by market farmers for its exceptionally heavy, sustained yield and improved tolerance to common summer squash viruses, which spread fast via aphids in humid conditions and can quickly stunt and discolor fruit on less tolerant varieties. It produces uniform, dark green, cylindrical fruit on an open, upright bush habit that makes harvesting easy even as the plant fills out. Because it keeps producing healthy, well-colored fruit later into the season than many older zucchini varieties, it is a strong choice for gardeners who have struggled with virus or mildew cutting squash harvests short. Pick fruit at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality, checking plants daily during peak production since zucchini left on the plant quickly grows oversized and tough. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Green Magic Broccoli
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Magic is an F1 hybrid broccoli producing well-domed, tightly beaded, medium-green central heads with excellent side-shoot production after the main head is harvested — extending the productive harvest period significantly beyond varieties that produce only a central head. The hybrid vigor produces uniformly sized plants and large, dense heads that reach harvest size in 60–70 days from transplant. Broccoli flavor is at its absolute best when grown to maturity in cool weather — the combination of cool nights (below 50°F) and cool days in fall and winter concentrates the sulfur-containing compounds responsible for broccoli's characteristic flavor while reducing the bitterness that heat stress introduces. Green Magic's F1 hybrid status provides disease resistance and uniformity that open-pollinated varieties often lack, making it one of the most reliable fall broccoli varieties for humid Gulf South conditions. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Green Malabar Spinach
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Green Malabar Spinach is the all-green form of Basella alba, producing the same climbing vine, thick succulent leaves, and heat-tolerant growth habit as the red-stemmed form but with completely green stems, petioles, and developing berries. The green form is less ornamental than the red-stemmed type but produces the same culinary product — thick, glossy, succulent leaves with a mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that makes an excellent heat-season substitute for true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) during zone 9's summers when cool-season spinach is impossible to grow. The green form's less distinctive appearance makes it blend more naturally into vegetable garden beds without the ornamental statement of the red-stemmed variety — a practical choice for gardeners who want the culinary benefit without the color drama. The slight mucilage in the leaves and stems — the same compound that gives okra its characteristic texture — naturally thickens soups, stews, and green smoothies and contributes a smooth, slightly viscous mouthfeel to cooked preparations. In zone 9's summer heat and humidity, Malabar spinach (both forms) is one of the most productive leafy green crops available. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Green Meat Radish (Green-Skinned, Green-Fleshed Asian Radish)
description: Direct sow about half an inch deep in loose, well-worked soil, thinning seedlings to 4-6 inches apart; because the roots grow larger than a typical spring radish, deep, stone-free soil helps them develop a smooth, well-formed shape. Green Meat is prized in Chinese cuisine for its bright green skin and vivid green-and-white interior flesh, a striking contrast to the familiar red-skinned, white-fleshed Western radishes. It has a milder, sweeter flavor than most spring radishes and holds its crisp texture well, making it good raw in salads or lightly cooked. For the best size and flavor it is often grown as a late-summer to fall crop like daikon, though early spring sowing also works. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Green Noodle Yardlong Bean (Green Asparagus Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a tall trellis once the soil is warm, since yardlong beans germinate poorly and grow slowly in cool soil compared to bush snap beans. Green Noodle produces the classic slender, pale to medium-green pods of 18-24 inches typical of the yardlong bean group, and unlike red-podded forms it keeps its color through cooking, making it a versatile stand-in for standard green beans in stir-fries and braises. The vines thrive in the hottest, most humid part of summer when many Phaseolus beans stop setting pods, so plan for continuous harvest from midsummer through early fall in the Gulf South. Pick pods while still slender and before the seeds inside swell noticeably, since older pods turn fibrous quickly; frequent picking also keeps the vines producing new flowers. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Green Nutmeg Melon (Nutmeg Muskmelon)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in enriched, well-drained hills spaced a yard apart, keeping soil evenly moist until vines establish and then easing off water as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Green Nutmeg is a 19th-century American heirloom muskmelon named for its ribbed, netted rind, which resembles the wrinkled shell of a nutmeg seed and sets it apart from smoother-skinned melon types of the same era. The pale green flesh is notably sweet and aromatic for an old variety, ripening to a musky perfume that signals harvest readiness alongside the classic full slip from the vine. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting an old American melon type distinct from the many French and Charentais heirlooms already common in seed catalogs. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Green Onion (Scallion)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in bands 3–4 in wide rather than single rows to maximize bed productivity. Thin seedlings to 1–2 in apart; the thinnings are already usable as tiny scallions. Water steadily to keep growth rapid and tender; drought causes tough, hot-tasting stems. Pull bunching types when stems reach pencil width, or cut leaves an inch above the base and allow them to regrow for a second harvest. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Green Perilla Shiso
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Green Perilla Shiso (the green-leaved form of Perilla frutescens var. crispa) is the standard Japanese culinary shiso used extensively in Japanese cuisine — the large, ruffled, bright green leaves with their distinctive complex fragrance combining mint, anise, cinnamon, and citrus are served with sashimi, used to wrap sushi, sliced into cold noodle dishes, tempura-battered and fried, and used as a garnish for countless Japanese preparations. Green shiso is the preferred type for fresh-leaf use, having a brighter, more delicate flavor than red shiso (which is primarily used for coloring and flavoring pickled umeboshi plums). The large, attractive, deeply ruffled leaves have an impressive appearance for a kitchen herb, growing to 4–5 inches across on robust plants that do not require much care. Green shiso thrives in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf South and tolerates some shade, making it practical for partially shaded kitchen herb gardens. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Green River Belle Pawpaw
description: Green River Belle was found growing wild near the Green River in Hart County, Kentucky, and selected in 1998 for its large fruit and subtle cinnamon-tinged flavor. It shows good resistance to Phyllosticta leaf spot, a common pawpaw fungal issue in humid climates, making it a lower-maintenance choice for home growers. Site it in rich, slightly acidic soil with reliable moisture and cross-pollinate with a genetically unrelated pawpaw. Protect young trees from rabbits and deer, which will browse the bark and foliage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Green Ruffles Basil (Frilled Lettuce-Leaf Ornamental-Culinary Basil)
description: Sow indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. The green-leaved companion to Purple Ruffles basil, this heirloom-type ornamental basil produces large, deeply crinkled and fringed lettuce-leaf-shaped foliage with sweet, mild classic basil flavor good for salads and pesto. Its dramatic ruffled texture also makes it a popular edible-ornamental for borders and containers; pinch flower spikes to prolong leaf production. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Green Salad Bowl Lettuce
description: This AAS award-winning oakleaf-type lettuce produces frilly green leaves that stay sweet and tender even in warm weather. Direct sow seed shallowly and press lightly into moist soil, since lettuce needs light to germinate. Thin plants for full heads or harvest as loose-leaf, cut-and-come-again greens. More heat tolerant and slow to bolt than many lettuces, it extends the salad season with steady moisture and light afternoon shade in summer. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Green Santolina (Holy Flax)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; green santolina requires the same excellent drainage and sunny, dry conditions as gray santolina but has slightly more tolerance of humidity and moisture. Santolina rosmarinifolia (syn. S. viridis) is a green-leaved counterpart to the familiar gray cotton lavender; it produces feathery, bright-green, rosemary-like foliage with a similar strong, herbal, camphor-like scent and equally bright-yellow button flowers in summer. The contrasting use of gray (S. chamaecyparissus) and green (S. rosmarinifolia) santolinas is a classic technique in traditional knot garden design; the green species' brighter, more vivid foliage makes it excellent as a companion to silver or purple-leaved plants in formal herb plantings. Shear after flowering to maintain shape. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Green Sapote (Mamey Verde)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; green sapote is a Central American relative of the mamey sapote, producing large, round fruits with an olive-green skin and a rich, caramel-flavored orange flesh that is eaten fresh, in milkshakes, and in ice cream. It is less commonly cultivated than mamey sapote but produces equally delicious fruit and is somewhat more cold-hardy — able to tolerate brief dips to 28°F with some defoliation but surviving in protected locations in zone 9b. The fruits ripen in winter, providing fresh tropical fruit at a time when most trees are bare. In zone 9a, plant against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available and protect from frost when young. Grafted trees from named selections begin fruiting in 3–5 years. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Green Sausage Tomato (Striped Green-and-Yellow Paste Tomato)
description: Green Sausage is an open-pollinated paste tomato bred by Wild Boar Farms, producing elongated, sausage-shaped fruit striped in yellow-green over a base of deeper green that ripens to a translucent chartreuse-yellow rather than red. The firm, meaty flesh with a bright, tangy flavor holds up well when sliced fresh, fried green, or made into a distinctively colored salsa verde or sauce. Judge ripeness by softening and color shift toward gold-green rather than by looking for red, since this variety never turns the classic tomato red, and stake the indeterminate vine for season-long support. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Green Shiso (Japanese Culinary Herb for Sushi and Tempura)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Shiso (Perilla frutescens var. viridis) is the standard culinary form of Japanese perilla — the bright green, deeply toothed, wrinkled leaves with their distinctive aroma (a complex combination of mint, cinnamon, anise, and citrus that is unique and difficult to compare to other herbs) are an essential ingredient in Japanese cuisine. The large leaves (2–4 inches) are used as wrappers for grilled meats and fish, shredded as a garnish for sashimi and sushi, fried as tempura, pickled (shiso pickles), and used in a range of salads and rice dishes throughout Japanese cooking. The aroma and flavor are entirely distinct from red shiso (var. crispa) used primarily for coloring umeboshi and other preserved items — green shiso has a brighter, more herbal, slightly minty quality versus the more intensely aromatic and slightly sharper red shiso. Green shiso grows vigorously in Gulf South summer heat, reaching 2–3 feet and self-sowing prolifically at the end of the season. The ornamental quality is significant — the large, bright-green, textured leaves with purple tinges on the undersides and pink flower spikes in late summer are decorative in both herb and ornamental gardens. Regular harvest of the growing tips delays bolting and maintains leafy production through summer. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Green Sprouting Calabrese Broccoli
description: This traditional Italian heirloom is the familiar garden broccoli, producing large blue-green central heads followed by abundant side shoots. Start seed indoors about six weeks before transplanting into rich, firm soil. Keep water and nutrients steady, since stress can cause premature buttoning. Cut the main head while the buds are still tight, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks of continued production. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Green Star Apple (Caimito)
description: The green-skinned form of star apple ripens to a pale yellow-green rather than turning purple, with thinner skin and a softer, juicier interior than the purple type, though the flavor of the two color forms is essentially identical -- a mild, sweet, milky sweetness. Because the ripe green fruit shows little color change, growers judge ripeness mainly by a slight softening and a faint waxy bloom on the skin rather than by color shift. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and handle ripe fruit gently since the thinner skin bruises more readily than the purple form. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within 3-5 years and produce over a long summer harvest window. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Green Star Okra (High-Yield Compact Hybrid Okra for Commercial and Home Production)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches every 2–3 days. Green Star is an F1 hybrid okra variety selected for compact plant habit, high productivity per plant, and good pod quality — attributes that make it one of the more practical hybrid okra varieties for small-scale and home garden production in the Gulf South. The hybrid vigor of F1 varieties (first-generation crosses between distinct parental lines) typically produces improved uniformity, vigor, and productivity compared to open-pollinated varieties, and Green Star's compact growth habit — reaching 4–5 feet rather than the 6–10 feet of some tall heirloom types — makes it easier to harvest without a ladder and fits better in standard garden plots. The pods are dark green, slightly ridged in the standard okra style, spineless to low-spine (important for comfort in harvesting), and tender and good-flavored at the 3–4 inch harvest stage. Green Star's earliness — first harvest approximately 50–55 days from direct seeding — is competitive with the fastest-maturing okra varieties and allows harvest to begin before the peak of Gulf Coast summer heat. Okra is one of the most important and culturally significant vegetables in Gulf South cooking: a staple of gumbo (where it serves as a natural thickener via its mucilaginous properties), fried okra (a Southern culinary tradition), pickled okra, and fresh vegetable side dishes. Zone 9 is ideal for okra production — the combination of heat and humidity that limits most cool-season vegetables is precisely what okra requires to thrive. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Green Strawberry (Pineapple Strawberry)
description: Plant rooted runners or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; green strawberry spreads much more slowly than wood strawberry (F. vesca) and forms compact, slowly spreading clumps rather than long-running stolons. Fragaria viridis is a European native wild strawberry distinguished from the more common F. vesca by its fruits, which remain green even when fully ripe (turning creamy-white to slightly pinkish), and by its distinctively sweet, pineapple-like aroma that some find even more delicious than common wild strawberries. The berries are small (under 1/2 inch) but pack an extraordinary fragrance and flavor; they do not separate cleanly from the calyx when picked (unlike F. vesca) and are best eaten fresh directly from the plant. An excellent collector's plant and conversation piece in the fruit garden, though not productive enough for large-scale harvest. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Green Striped Cushaw (Heat-Tolerant Southern Cushaw Pumpkin, Gulf Coast Staple Squash)
description: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart after soil is warm; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin pattern develops full color and stem begins to dry. Green Striped Cushaw is the classic variety of Cucurbita argyrosperma — the cushaw species native to Mexico and Central America — that has been grown in the American South for centuries as one of the most heat-tolerant large squash available. The 'cushaw' name is of Native American origin and has been applied to this distinctive squash type in the South since colonial times. The Green Striped Cushaw produces large fruits (10–20 lbs) with a distinctive form: a rounded to oblong base swelling to a thick, curved neck — quite different from the globular or flattened form of most Cucurbita maxima pumpkins. The skin is cream-white with longitudinal green stripes that fade to tan-green at full maturity. The flesh is cream-yellow to pale orange, mild and sweet, with less of the rich pumpkin flavor of darker-fleshed types but with an important practical advantage: it is the squash that can be grown in zone 9's summer heat when virtually all other squash species have died. Cucurbita argyrosperma's heat and humidity tolerance is substantially greater than C. maxima, C. pepo, or C. moschata, and in the historical Gulf South kitchen, cushaw was the standard large winter-storage squash precisely because it produced reliably in the climate where other species failed. Cushaw's mild flesh is used in pies (a Southern tradition), as a cooked vegetable, and in Mexican and Central American cuisines where the species originated. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Green Thai Eggplant
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with warm soil temperatures; Green Thai Eggplant produces small, round to oval, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits in bright green to greenish-white with striping or mottling, harvested young at marble to golf ball size for the best flavor and texture. The flesh is firmer, drier, and significantly more bitter than standard globe eggplant — the characteristic bitterness and firm texture are intentional qualities in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking, where the small green eggplants are sliced and added raw to green curry pastes or braised whole in red curry. They absorb coconut milk and spice sauces without becoming mushy, maintaining their distinctive firm bite even in extended cooking. Unlike the standard Italian or Japanese eggplants where bitterness is considered a defect, the natural bitterness of green Thai eggplant is a flavor feature that rounds and deepens the overall taste of Thai curries. In zone 9 the plants are extremely heat-tolerant and productive through the hottest months. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Green Tomatillo (Standard Heirloom Tomatillo)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil; stake or cage plants as they sprawl. Green tomatillo is the standard culinary tomatillo of Mexican cuisine — not a green tomato but a distinct species (Physalis ixocarpa) with a characteristic papery husk that expands around the developing fruit; fruits are harvested when the husk splits and the fruit fills it completely, at a bright green to yellow-green stage with a tangy, tart, citrus-herbal flavor that is distinctly different from any tomato flavor. The tart flavor of the fresh tomatillo is the foundation of salsa verde, a primary sauce in Mexican cooking alongside salsa roja; tomatillos are also used in mole verde, enchiladas verdes, chile verde, and canned as salsa. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; does extremely well in Gulf Coast and Southwestern gardens. Two or more plants are needed for pollination — a single plant produces little to no fruit. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Green Velvet Okra
description: Sow seed directly in the garden after all frost danger has passed, soaking it overnight to speed germination in warm soil. Pick pods every day or two once they begin forming, since Green Velvet quickly grows past its tender stage. This long-cultivated variety produces smooth, spineless, dark green pods on a vigorous, productive plant, and it has been a dependable garden staple for generations of Southern cooks who value its mild flavor in gumbo and frying. Its smooth pod surface also makes it easier to handle at harvest than spinier heirloom types. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Green Wave Mustard Green
description: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–18 inches; Green Wave is an AAS winner mustard green producing large, beautifully ruffled, deep green leaves with a distinctive curled and frilled edge that gives it strong ornamental value as well as excellent eating quality. Flavor is pungent and spicy like Southern Giant Curled but with finer leaf texture and more cold-hardiness. Green Wave is the recommended mustard green for raw use in salads (young leaves) and sautés where texture is prized; the intricate ruffling and curling increases leaf surface area, creating both a decorative appearance in the garden and a textural interest on the plate. In zone 9, fall-planted Green Wave produces beautifully through winter, the cold sweetening and mellowing its characteristic spicy bite — the finest mustard green eating comes after temperatures drop below 40°F. Harvest outer leaves regularly; the plant regrows vigorously. An excellent substitute for kale or collards in anyone who wants a faster-maturing, more flavorful cooking green. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Green Zebra Pole Tomato
description: A gourmet indeterminate tomato bearing smooth, crack-free 2 to 3 inch fruits striped golden green and forest green, with a slight amber blush when ripe. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply after the weather warms. Stake or cage the vigorous 6-foot-plus vines and prune suckers for airflow. Judge ripeness by softness and blush rather than color, since the fruit stays green when ready. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Green Zebra Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to deeply prepared, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Green Zebra is a modern heirloom tomato developed by Tom Wagner in 1983, producing attractive 2–3 inch fruits with distinctive lime-green skin and dark green stripes that warm to yellow-green stripes against chartreuse skin when ripe, with a bright, tangy, acidic flesh that is a refreshing counterpoint to sweeter tomatoes. Excellent sliced fresh in salads, as a garnish, or for green salsa — one of the most visually striking tomatoes available. An indeterminate vine, it tends toward compact growth relative to larger beefsteak heirlooms. Yields prolifically over a long season. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Greenfinch Gooseberry
description: Greenfinch was bred at England's East Malling Research Station specifically to combine strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew with a tidy, semi-upright bush that is far easier to pick than sprawling older varieties. Because it is a Ribes species, check local regulations before planting, as gooseberries can be restricted in areas managing white pine blister rust. The medium-sized, smooth pale green berries hold their tart flavor well and are excellent for pies, sauces, and preserves, though they also sweeten enough for fresh eating if left to fully ripen. Keep roots cool with mulch and prune out the oldest third of the wood each winter to maintain the open framework that keeps this compact cultivar productive and easy to harvest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Greengage Plum
description: Greengage is an old European dessert plum prized for its honeyed, amber-green fruit. Give it a warm, sheltered site with fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil to ripen its sugars fully. Many greengage selections benefit from a compatible European plum pollinator planted within about 50 feet. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for best size and sweetness. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Greenleaf Desmodium (Mat-Forming Nitrogen-Fixing Tropical Forage Legume)
description: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade, inoculating seed with an appropriate Rhizobium inoculant for best nodulation on new ground. Greenleaf Desmodium is a sprawling, mat-forming tropical legume long used across the tropics as a soil-building cover crop and high-protein grazing forage, spreading vigorously by trailing stems that root at the nodes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover while fixing substantial atmospheric nitrogen. It is also a key component of push-pull intercropping systems, where its scent helps repel stem-boring pests from adjacent food crops while trapping and disrupting their reproduction, making it useful in integrated pest management as well as soil building. In the Gulf South it behaves as a warm-season annual, killed by the first hard frost, so plant after the soil has warmed and mow or till the residue under before fall planting to release its nitrogen back to the soil. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Greensleeves Apple (English Self-Fertile Garden Apple)
description: Greensleeves was bred at East Malling Research Station in England from the same James Grieve and Golden Delicious cross that produced Falstaff, and it was selected for its dependable, heavy cropping and self-fertility, meaning a single tree can set fruit without a separate pollinator nearby. The pale green-yellow fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking. Because it bears young and abundantly, thin fruit clusters in early summer to prevent overcropping and biennial bearing. It has become one of the most widely recommended apples for small English gardens for exactly these easy-care traits. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gregori's Altai Tomato (Early Siberian Red Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably mild, staking the moderately vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows. Gregori's Altai is a Siberian heirloom from the Altai Mountains region prized for setting medium-large, four-inch, deep red fruit with a faint golden blush at the shoulders unusually early and even in the cool, fluctuating spring temperatures that stall most other beefsteaks. The rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor rivals much larger, later-maturing heirlooms, and the plant's tolerance for cool nights makes it an excellent first-wave spring tomato for Gulf Coast gardens that need to beat the arrival of intense summer heat. Keep watering even as fruit sizes up to avoid cracking on the thin, tender skin. Matures in 67–75 days from transplant.

name: Grenache Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis or head-trained system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grenache is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant, well suited to hot, dry growing climates. One of the most widely planted red wine grapes in the world, it produces high sugar levels even in scorching heat, yielding fruity, medium-to-full-bodied red wines and, when picked earlier or pressed gently, some of the world's finest dry rosés, particularly from southern France's Rhône Valley and Spain, where it is also known as Garnacha. Its thin skin and upright growth habit make it well suited to traditional bush-vine (head-trained, unstaked) cultivation in hot, arid climates, requiring minimal irrigation once its deep root system is established. Consider head-training rather than a full trellis system in very hot, dry climates for traditional bush-vine culture, and monitor sugar levels closely since it can ripen quickly and lose acidity if left too long in hot weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Grenada Pomegranate (Texas Heirloom Pomegranate)
description: Plant in well-drained soil of almost any pH in full sun; Grenada is a long-cultivated heirloom pomegranate variety passed down through Central Texas homesteads and nurseries, valued for combining good cold hardiness with the classic sweet-tart flavor and deep-red arils of a fully flavored pomegranate, unlike some ultra-hardy selections bred mainly for toughness over taste. Plants bear as a multi-stemmed large shrub or can be trained to a small single-trunk tree, produce showy orange-red trumpet flowers over a long season that attract hummingbirds, and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, needing little supplemental water beyond the first year or two. Fruit ripens in September and October, signaled by a hollow sound when the fruit is tapped and skin that has taken on full color; harvest promptly once ripe, since fruit left too long on the plant is prone to splitting after rain. Prune out root suckers to maintain a tidy shape and remove crossing interior branches each winter to keep the canopy open for good fruit coloring and air circulation. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gretel Eggplant (AAS-Winning White Mini Eggplant, Tender Bitter-Free Companion to Hansel)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches while skin is pure white; yellowing indicates overripeness. Gretel Eggplant won the All-America Selections award in 2009, one year after its companion Hansel (purple mini eggplant), both from the same PanAmerican Seed breeding program and sharing the same compact plant habit, prolific cluster fruiting, early maturity, and exceptional eating quality. Gretel's white fruit color distinguishes it visually and culinarily from standard purple eggplants: the white coloration (caused by the absence of the anthocyanin and chlorogenic acid pigments present in purple eggplant skin) correlates with a fundamentally different flavor profile — white eggplants, including Gretel, are consistently sweeter, milder, and less bitter than purple varieties because they lack the phenolic compounds that contribute bitterness. This means white eggplant varieties like Gretel can be used raw in preparations where purple eggplant's bitterness would require salting to draw out (a traditional technique for reducing eggplant bitterness before cooking): Gretel's naturally sweet, mild flesh is pleasant raw in thin slices or cubed in salads. The AAS recognition of Gretel in consecutive years with Hansel highlighted the appeal of offering home gardeners a white-fruited alternative to the standard purple that combined the same outstanding productivity and compact habit with meaningfully different flavor characteristics. For zone 9 gardeners growing multiple eggplant varieties for culinary diversity, Gretel and Hansel planted together provide a visually striking paired harvest of white and purple mini eggplants from compact, easily managed plants. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Grey Zucchini
description: This heat-tolerant heirloom produces smooth, straight fruits with mottled silver-grey skin on compact, heavy-yielding bush plants. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and space plants for good airflow. Water at the base to keep foliage dry and harvest fruits young, around six to eight inches, for tender flesh. Pick frequently during the peak of summer, as fruits size up quickly and steady harvest sustains production. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Grimes Golden Apple (West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Golden Delicious)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Discovered as a chance seedling on Thomas Grimes' farm in Brooke County, West Virginia in the early 1800s, this heirloom is historically significant as the presumed parent of Golden Delicious, one of the most commercially important apples of the 20th century. The medium, deep yellow fruit has dense, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh with a wine-like richness that many old-apple enthusiasts consider superior to its more famous offspring. It ripens in early-to-mid fall and was historically valued both fresh and for cider, keeping reasonably well in a cool cellar. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Grise de Saint-Jean Fig
description: An old, robust and productive French fig traced to the collection of grower M. Baud, Grise de Saint-Jean is distinct from the other gray-skinned figs in the collection such as Bourjassotte Grise and Col de Dame Grise. Fruit is large and pear-shaped with thin, hazy gray-purple-and-green skin and pinkish-brown flesh that often has a pool of honey at the eye. It is a two-crop variety whose breba flush is especially well regarded, since it can ripen reliably even in seasons too cool or short for the late main crop to fully mature. Vigorous and productive once established, it needs the same easy care as any common fig. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Griselle Shallot (French Grey Shallot, True Shallot)
description: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer. Griselle is regarded by French cooks as the only true shallot, a distinct species from common onion-derived shallots, forming small, teardrop-shaped bulbs under a papery grey-brown skin around pinkish flesh with fine purple veining and an intensely complex, refined flavor prized raw in vinaigrettes and salads. Reduce watering once the tops yellow and topple over, then lift the cluster and cure it in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks. Because Griselle does not keep as long as red or Dutch yellow shallots, plan to use the harvest within a few months or replant a portion of the smaller bulbs the following season. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Groff Lychee
description: Raised in Hawaii from a Hak Ip seedling and named for horticulturist George Weidman Groff, this late-season cultivar ripens after Brewster and most other lychee in cultivation have already finished, extending the harvest window for growers who have earlier cultivars established. Fruit is smaller than Brewster with dull-red, rough skin and a notably small seed, and the firm white flesh turns sweetly aromatic once it reaches full ripeness, though it can taste acidic if harvested early. Its main value is as a late-ripening companion tree rather than a primary crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Grolau Chives (Broad-Leaf)
description: Grolau is a German-bred chive selection prized for unusually broad, thick, dark green foliage that stays tender even as clumps mature, making it a favorite for continuous cutting and for forcing indoors during winter months. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep leaf production vigorous and to prevent the center from thinning out. The plant sends up abundant lilac-pink flower heads in late spring, which pollinators favor and which can be removed to redirect energy into leaf growth. Because the leaves are noticeably thicker than standard chives, Grolau holds up well to freezing or drying for winter storage. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Groninger Blue Kale (Dutch Heirloom Feathery Kale)
description: Direct sow in mid-summer and thin to wide final spacing so plants can develop their large, sprawling frames before winter sets in. This traditional Dutch farmhouse kale, long grown around the province of Groningen, produces finely divided, feathery blue-green leaves on tall stems and was historically a winter storage vegetable harvested straight from the frozen garden. Repeated frost exposure noticeably mellows its flavor, and the plant continues producing new leaves from the top through much of the winter. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Gros Michel Banana (Big Mike, Original Commercial Banana)
description: Gros Michel was the dominant export banana worldwide until Fusarium wilt (Panama disease) devastated commercial plantations by the mid-twentieth century, prompting the industry-wide switch to Cavendish types. Home gardeners still seek it out for its richer, more intensely banana-flavored fruit and thicker, sturdier peel compared to modern supermarket bananas. The tall, vigorous pseudostem needs a wind-sheltered spot and heavy irrigation and feeding through the growing season; avoid planting in soil where bananas have previously declined, since the Fusarium pathogen persists indefinitely once established. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Gros Vert de Laon Artichoke (Large French Green Artichoke)
aliases: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Gros Vert de Laon'
description: Gros Vert de Laon is a hardy French heirloom grown for its very large, rounded, tightly scaled green heads with fleshy, delicately flavored bracts, produced on a bold, silvery-leaved plant substantial enough to anchor a bed on its own. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many Mediterranean artichoke cultivars, a legacy of its long cultivation in the cooler climate of northern France. Cut the terminal bud while still firm and tightly closed for the best eating quality, which encourages the plant to push out smaller side buds afterward. Divide and replant offsets every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous and productive. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Grosso Lavandin (Commercial Fragrance Lavender, Provence Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Grosso grows larger than English lavenders and needs 24–36 inches of space; shear spent flower stalks after bloom to prevent woody sprawling; in zones 8–10 where summer humidity is high, Grosso performs better than English lavender due to the L. latifolia parentage contributing some heat tolerance. Grosso is the world's dominant commercial lavender variety — it covers the rolling purple fields of the Provence and Drôme regions of France that define the iconic 'lavender landscape' image of southern France, and it is the primary source of lavender oil in the global fragrance and cosmetics industry. As a lavandin hybrid (a sterile cross between English lavender, L. angustifolia, and spike lavender, L. latifolia), Grosso inherits characteristics of both parents: the floral-sweet fragrance of English lavender combined with the higher camphor content, larger plant size, and greater heat tolerance of spike lavender. This combination makes the Grosso essential oil slightly different from pure English lavender oil — with a more complex, slightly camphor-accented fragrance that is valuable in perfumery but considered less pure for culinary use. For garden use, Grosso produces the longest, most striking flower spikes of any commonly grown lavender — up to 12–16 inches — in a dense, voluminous display that is far more dramatic than any English lavender. Harvested just before fully open for maximum essential oil content; used in sachets, potpourri, culinary (in small amounts), and craft arrangements. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Ground Cherry
description: This heirloom Physalis produces small golden fruits inside papery, lantern-like husks with a sweet pineapple-vanilla flavor. Start seeds indoors six to eight weeks before your last frost and set out sprawling plants once nights stay warm. Fruits are ripe when the husks turn tan and drop naturally to the ground, so harvest from the soil below the plant. Let them cure a few days in their husks to develop full sweetness for fresh eating or preserves. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Ground Cherry (Strawberry Tomato, Husk Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; ground cherry is an often-overlooked member of the Physalis family closely related to the tomatillo, producing small, marble-sized golden-yellow fruit enclosed in papery tan husks like a miniature tomatillo. The flavor is remarkable — simultaneously sweet, tropical, and slightly vanilla-like, unlike any other common garden vegetable. The plants are bushy and sprawling, reaching 2–3 feet high, and produce prodigiously once established. Fruit drops to the ground when ripe (hence the name), where it can be left in its husk for several weeks without deteriorating. Eat fresh, bake in desserts, make preserves, or dry for extended storage. In zone 9, treat as a cool-season annual planted in fall for winter through spring production. The husk protects the fruit from pests and makes storage easy. Self-seeds prolifically in warm soils and will naturalize in suitable areas. Not to be confused with the cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana), though they are closely related. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Ground Cherry / Cape Gooseberry
description: Ground cherries are grown as warm-season annuals in most climates; start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed. The bushy plants produce prolific small fruits enclosed in papery husks and often sprawl without support — a tomato cage or light staking helps. Harvest when the papery husk has dried to tan-brown and the golden berry inside detaches easily. Fallen fruits left in their husks on the ground remain fresh for several weeks. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Ground Elder (Goutweed, Bishop's Weed, Herb Gerard)
description: Plant only in buried containers with solid bottoms, or in walled raised beds with no soil contact — ground elder spreads by deeply rooted, tenacious rhizomes that regenerate from small fragments and are nearly impossible to eradicate once established in open soil. Despite this invasive tendency, it is a genuinely useful shade edible: young spring leaves have a pleasant, lightly celery-like, slightly peppery flavor and have been eaten across Europe and Asia since medieval times, used in salads, soups, and as a potherb. The variegated form 'Variegatum' with cream-edged leaves is less vigorous and a better garden choice. For foragers, it is easily identified in spring before any other look-alikes emerge. Matures in 30–60 days from transplant.

name: Ground Hug Aronia (Dwarf Groundcover Black Chokeberry)
description: Ground Hug is a University of Connecticut-bred dwarf selection of black chokeberry, part of the Proven Winners Low Scape series, prized for a mat-forming habit under 14 inches tall that spreads gently rather than suckering aggressively into thickets like the wild species. It carries the same white spring flower clusters and small glossy black berries as full-size Aronia melanocarpa, plus vivid red-orange fall foliage, all on a scale suited to groundcover use. The shrub tolerates wet, dry, clay, and salt-affected soils with ease, making it a practical choice for parking-lot islands, slopes, and mass plantings where mowing is impractical. Beyond an occasional light shearing to keep the mat even, it needs no routine pruning. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ground Ivy (Gill-over-the-Ground, Alehoof)
description: Plant in partial to full shade in any reasonably moist soil; ground ivy is a creeping, mat-forming member of the mint family with distinctively kidney-shaped, scallop-edged leaves that release a pleasantly pungent, minty-medicinal aroma when crushed — small purple to blue flowers appear in whorls along the stems from spring through early summer. The young leaves and shoots are edible: they were used in medieval Europe to clarify and bitter ale before hops (earning the name 'alehoof'), and are used today in small amounts as a bitter herb in salads, soups, and herbal teas. Medicinally, ground ivy has a long tradition in European herbal medicine as an anti-inflammatory and respiratory herb. It is one of very few plants that will produce a dense, attractive groundcover in deep, dry shade under trees — a condition that defeats almost everything else. Can be invasive in favorable, moist conditions; contain with edging where needed. Matures in 30–60 days from transplant.

name: Ground Plum (Prairie Milkvetch)
description: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — ground plum is a native sprawling legume of the southern Great Plains and central prairies, historically one of the most important native edible plants of the southern prairie, producing clusters of purple to reddish-purple pea flowers in April–May followed by the remarkable, plum-like fruit pods — green when young, reddish when ripe — that gave the plant its common name. The young, unripe pods have a mild, slightly sweet, pea-like flavor and were eaten raw by Plains peoples as a seasonal vegetable and green snack food on the prairie. The pods are edible raw when fully green and firm, but become papery when ripe. An important nitrogen-fixing prairie legume that improves soil for neighboring plants. Outstanding for prairie restoration plantings in well-drained, alkaline, or rocky soils in zone 3–9. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Groundnut (Hopniss)
description: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near a support for the twining stems; this native leguminous vine was a staple food for many Indigenous nations and early European settlers and was considered for commercial cultivation before potatoes became dominant. Harvest the small, walnut-shaped tubers strung along underground rhizomes in fall after frost kills the vines; they taste like a richer, nuttier potato and can be boiled, baked, or roasted. The fragrant reddish-purple flowers in midsummer fix atmospheric nitrogen. Tubers are small in the first year but grow larger each subsequent year — the plant becomes more productive the longer it is left undisturbed. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Grumichama (Brazil Cherry)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — grumichama is a beautiful small-to-medium Brazilian Eugenia producing glossy, deep burgundy-to-black cherries (3/4 inch) with sweet, soft, slightly acidic flesh and 1–3 seeds, eaten fresh, made into preserves, or used in beverages. The trees are ornamental year-round with attractive smooth, pinkish-brown peeling bark, handsome dark glossy leaves, and masses of white flowers before fruiting. Unlike many tropical fruits it tolerates partial shade and moist conditions and has some cold hardiness to about 28°F. The fruits are produced in late spring and are consumed enthusiastically by birds. Closely related to jaboticaba and surinam cherry, the grumichama is one of the finest but least known of the Brazilian Eugenia fruits, producing a fruit that resembles a cherry in size and sweetness. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Grumolo Verde Chicory
description: Sow seeds in late summer and allow plants to grow through autumn; after hard frosts, the tops die back and the plant enters semi-dormancy before the root drives up a tight, flat rosette of dark green leaves in late winter or early spring — a delicacy treasured in northern Italy as a salad green when little else is available. The name 'grumolo' means 'little cluster' in Italian, describing the compressed button-rosette form. Grumolo verde is exceptionally cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free through winter. The bitter, nutty flavor is characteristic of chicory; young spring leaves are the most tender and least bitter. In warm-winter climates like zones 8–9, the plants may not go fully dormant but still produce acceptable rosettes in winter. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Grygleski #1 Cranberry (Wisconsin Grower-Selected Hybrid)
description: Grygleski #1 is a numbered hybrid selection that arose and was propagated within Wisconsin's cranberry marsh country, named for the Grygleski family, longtime Wisconsin cranberry growers and vine suppliers who identified and increased it for regional planting. It is grown almost exclusively on Wisconsin marshes rather than distributed as a national commercial release, valued locally for its vigor and productivity under the state's marsh soil and flood-management practices. Like other cranberries it must have strongly acidic, sandy-peat bog soil (pH 4.0-5.0) that stays constantly moist, full sun, and a periodic sand top-dressing to keep weeds down and encourage new rooting along the spreading vines. Establishing plantings takes several years before a full crop develops, after which vines can produce for decades with steady moisture and acidic fertility as the main ongoing inputs. As with all cranberries, it requires a real winter chill period and will not perform in warm-winter or Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Guaba (Inga Vera)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; guaba is a frost-tender rainforest and riverbank tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Closely related to and grown much like the more familiar ice cream bean, this fast-growing tropical legume tree produces long, ribbed pods containing seeds wrapped in the same soft, sweet, cotton-candy-like white pulp eaten fresh straight from the pod across Central and South America, though its pods and pulp are typically somewhat smaller than its larger relative. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it enriches surrounding soil and is commonly used as a fast-growing shade tree in coffee and cacao agroforestry systems throughout its native range. Water regularly, especially while young, and expect a few years of growth before the tree reaches significant pod production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Guabiyú (Uruguayan Guabiju, Black Cherry of the Forest)
