description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; guabiyú (Myrcianthes pungens) is a subtropical rainforest tree of southern South America producing small, round, deep purple to black berries in clusters, with a sweet, aromatic, cherry-like flavor and a pleasant Myrtaceae fragrance — consumed fresh, in jams, juices, and liqueurs throughout its native range. The tree is more cold-hardy than most Myrtaceae relatives, tolerating temperatures down to 25°F (-4°C) when established, making it potentially the most cold-tolerant South American Myrtaceae and an excellent candidate for zone 9 Gulf Coast fruit gardens. The attractive, reddish-barked tree also provides ornamental value year-round with glossy leaves. A growing interest among Gulf Coast gardeners and subtropical fruit collectors. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Guadalupe Palm (Guadalupe Island Palm)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained soil; Guadalupe Palm requires excellent drainage and is highly drought-tolerant once established — it will not tolerate poorly-drained or consistently moist soils. Brahea edulis is a single-trunk fan palm endemic to Guadalupe Island, a remote volcanic island 150 miles off the Baja California coast of Mexico, where it survived in harsh, wind-scoured, fog-desert conditions for millennia. In cultivation it has proven to be among the most drought-tolerant and cold-hardy fan palms available for zone 9 Gulf Coast and California gardens — surviving brief dips to 20°F and thriving in the extreme summer heat and drought of zone 9. The crown of large, fan-shaped, bright mid-green fronds has a full, lush appearance that contrasts beautifully with the more compact, gray-green look of Mexican Blue Palm (Brahea armata). Guadalupe Palm produces edible dates — round, black, cherry-sized fruits with sweet, date-like flesh that was an important food for the indigenous people of Guadalupe Island and is still eaten fresh or dried. The species is rare in its native habitat due to feral goat browsing and is considered vulnerable in the wild. In zone 9 landscapes, it is a prized specimen palm for dry gardens and xeriscape plantings. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Guajillo Pepper
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost, harden transplants thoroughly, and plant into warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil after all frost risk has passed. Guajillo is one of the most commonly used dried chiles in traditional Mexican cooking, the dried form of the Mirasol pepper, producing long (3–5 inch), tapered, shiny red fruits with smooth, thin skin that dries to a deep red-brown; heat is mild to medium (2,500–5,000 SHU). The distinctive sweet, tangy, slightly fruity flavor with mild heat makes guajillo an indispensable base for authentic red enchilada sauce, pozole rojo, and adobo marinades. Harvest fully red and dry slowly on the plant or by hanging in a warm, ventilated space; dried guajillos store for 6–12 months. Matures in 85–105 days from transplant.

name: Guarana
description: Guarana is an Amazonian climbing shrub cultivated in Brazil for its seed capsules, which contain a notably high concentration of caffeine and are roasted and ground into a traditional stimulant paste. It tolerates poor, acidic, aluminum-rich soils in its native range but requires consistent warmth, high humidity, and a strong support structure to climb as it matures. Seed must be started fresh because it loses viability within days of ripening, and germination itself can take several months. Once established, expect years of vegetative growth before the vine produces its first clusters of red, seed-bearing capsules. Matures in 1095–1825 days from seed.

name: Guardian Strawberry
description: Guardian was developed through the Rutgers-USDA strawberry breeding program and was widely planted across the eastern United States for its strong resistance to red stele and verticillium wilt, two soilborne diseases that historically limited strawberry production in humid climates. Plants are vigorous with a spreading habit, producing large, firm, conical berries with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving. Guardian remains a useful choice for gardeners in older strawberry ground or areas with a history of root disease pressure. Mulch with straw over winter in colder zones and renew beds every three to four years as yields decline with plant age. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Guardsman Bunching Onion (Extra-Hardy Overwintering Scallion)
description: Guardsman resulted from breeding between bunching and bulb onion types, combining a vigorous root system and thicker, milder shank with the non-bulbing habit of a scallion. It was bred specifically to survive cold winters when sown in late summer, resuming growth early the following spring ahead of most other bunching cultivars. The larger tops and root vigor also make it a strong performer for a standard spring or summer sowing. Because it is milder than many bunching onions, it suits fresh eating as well as light cooking, and clumps can be divided to extend a planting. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Guatemalan Blue Banana Squash (Slate-Blue Elongated Heirloom Winter Squash)
description: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has thoroughly warmed, since this Guatemalan heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill out its elongated, club-shaped fruit. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous room or train them up a strong trellis to keep the two-to-three-foot fruits off wet ground. The thin, slate-blue to gray-blue rind hides deep orange, dense, sweet flesh that is excellent baked, and well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot. Cure harvested squash in a warm location for one to two weeks before moving to long-term storage to firm the rind and concentrate sweetness. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Guava
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; guava tolerates a wide range of soil types including sand and clay but performs poorly with standing water. Young trees are frost-sensitive — provide frost cloth when temperatures threaten to drop below 28°F; mature trees can survive brief dips to 24°F but may lose production for a season. Prune after each fruiting flush to control size and encourage new wood, which bears the heaviest crop; a light annual fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer maintains vigor. Harvest fruit when the skin transitions from bright green to pale yellow-green and the aroma becomes noticeable — guavas ripen rapidly off the tree in 2–5 days. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Guayusa
description: Establish rooted cuttings in spring under the dappled shade of taller trees, since this caffeinated Amazonian holly is naturally an understory species requiring humid, warm, tropical conditions with well-drained but consistently moist soil. Traditionally grown alongside cacao and coffee in Kichwa agroforestry plots of Ecuador, guayusa produces glossy, elongated leaves that are harvested young, lightly toasted or sun-dried, and steeped into a stimulating morning tea richer in caffeine than yerba mate. Light harvesting can begin about a year after planting, with full annual yields developing as the tree matures over roughly five years. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Guduchi (Heart-leaved Moonseed, Giloy)
description: Plant stem cuttings 6–8 inches long directly in moist, moderately fertile soil in spring; provide trellis or tree support — guduchi is a vigorous climber. Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi or giloy) is one of the three most revered medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine (the others being ashwagandha and shatavari) — a tropical Indian climbing vine that has been used continuously in Ayurvedic medical practice for over 3,000 years. Modern research has identified numerous bioactive compounds including tinosporin, berberine, and various alkaloids and glycosides with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antipyretic, and hepatoprotective properties. The stem is the primary medicinal part — consumed as a decoction, powder, or extract. The plant is a vigorous, twining vine with broad, heart-shaped, bright-green leaves resembling a large morning glory vine in appearance. In India, a respected folk tradition holds that guduchi plants growing on neem trees (Azadirachta indica) — absorbing constituents from the host — have enhanced medicinal potency. The plant naturalizes readily in tropical and humid subtropical climates; it spreads vigorously and may require management to prevent overgrowth in frost-free zones. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Guelph Millennium Asparagus (High-Yield Cold-Hardy All-Male Hybrid)
description: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared, well-drained trench in full sun, and resist harvesting at all during the first year to let the fern grow and build root reserves. Guelph Millennium is an all-male hybrid developed at the University of Guelph in Ontario and has become the standard replacement for the older Jersey series across much of North America, valued for exceptionally high, concentrated spear yield, uniform smooth green spears with tight tips, and a root system that establishes unusually quickly for a full-sized harvest by year three. Its later spring emergence than most varieties is an advantage in regions with unpredictable late frosts, since fewer emerging spears are lost to cold snaps. Harvest lightly in year two, moderately in year three, and the full six-to-eight-week season from year four onward, snapping or cutting spears at soil level once they reach 6–8 inches. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Guernsey Parsnip
description: An old Channel Islands and northern French heirloom parsnip valued for its shorter, broad-shouldered roots, a useful trait in shallow or stony soils where long-rooted parsnip types tend to fork or stall. Sow directly as early as the ground can be worked, using fresh seed since parsnip germination declines quickly with seed age. The dense white flesh has the classic sweet, nutty parsnip character and improves further after exposure to autumn frost, making it best left in the ground and dug through fall and early winter. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Guggul (Indian Bdellium)
description: Guggul is a slow-growing, thorny, drought-adapted shrub of the arid scrublands of Rajasthan and Gujarat, tapped for the fragrant oleo-gum-resin exuded from its bark, a resin central to Ayurvedic medicine for millennia. Because seed germination is slow and unreliable, most growers propagate it from hardwood stem cuttings rooted under warm, dry nursery conditions. It demands intense heat, full sun, and gritty, sharply draining soil, and will not tolerate frost, prolonged wet feet, or humid climates. Wild populations are now conservation-threatened from overharvesting, so cultivated stock is preferred wherever it can be sourced. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Guincho Purple Elderberry
description: Guincho Purple, originally found near Guincho, Portugal and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, opens with near-black spring foliage that softens to a deep purple-green through summer, setting off pink-tinged flower heads followed by shiny black berries and rich purple-red fall color. It is grown chiefly as an ornamental foliage and flowering shrub rather than for fruit production, and responds well to an annual hard prune to keep a compact, richly colored shrub instead of a lanky tree form. Site it where afternoon light can shine through the dark leaves for best effect, and give it the same moist, fertile soil favored by wild elderberry. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Guinea Hen Weed (Anamu)
description: Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; guinea hen weed is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, upright stems carry narrow leaves with a distinctive strong garlic-like smell when crushed or bruised, topped with thin spikes of small white flowers, and the whole plant, known as anamu across the Caribbean and tropical Latin America, is widely used in traditional folk medicine for a range of purported benefits, though rigorous clinical evidence remains limited. Easy to grow in warm, humid climates, it spreads readily by both seed and root suckers once established, sometimes naturalizing in disturbed ground in frost-free regions. Harvest leaves and roots for traditional preparations as needed, but consult a healthcare provider before using medicinally, since it has documented interactions and safety concerns, particularly during pregnancy. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Guinea Millet (Hungry Rice)
description: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Guinea millet thrives on poor, marginal soils and matures quickly, traditionally valued as a fast emergency crop during lean growing seasons. Grown across the West African savanna, this small-grained cereal grass produces edible seed on slender panicles in a remarkably short season, earning it the common name 'hungry rice' for its traditional role as a fast-maturing food source that could be harvested before other slower crops during periods of food scarcity. It tolerates poor, sandy soils and limited rainfall better than most cereal grains, making it valuable in marginal growing conditions where more demanding crops fail, though the small grain size means threshing and hulling by hand is labor-intensive. Hand-harvest seed heads once dry, and thresh and winnow to separate the small grains before cooking as a rice or couscous substitute. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Gulf Annual Ryegrass (Fast-Establishing Gulf Coast-Bred Italian Ryegrass)
description: Broadcast seed onto well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall, raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Gulf is a fast-germinating, vigorous annual ryegrass cultivar developed for the humid, mild-winter conditions of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, where it is widely used to overseed dormant bermudagrass and bahiagrass lawns and pastures for winter green cover, as well as as a general-purpose erosion-control and biomass cover crop on bare fall ground. Its fibrous, shallow root system germinates and establishes faster than most other cool-season cover crops, quickly stabilizing loose or eroding soil and suppressing winter weeds, then dies back naturally with warming spring temperatures or can be mowed and turned under to add organic matter ahead of spring planting. It tolerates close, repeated mowing better than cereal grains, making it a good choice where winter foot traffic or turf appearance matters. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Gulf Coast Blueberry
description: Prepare acidic soil to pH 4.5–5.0 before planting; Gulf Coast is a Southern highbush blueberry developed jointly by the USDA and the University of Florida and released in 1987, specifically bred for the lower-chill coastal regions of the Gulf South including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle. It requires 200–300 chill hours and produces reliable crops where northern highbush varieties fail to fruit. Berries are medium-large, blue, firm, with a dry scar and good sweet flavor that develops best with warm, sunny ripening conditions. The plant has a naturally spreading habit and is fairly tolerant of the heavy clay soils found in coastal areas if drainage is adequate — raised beds work excellently. Gulf Coast is also noted for tolerance of the wet winters common on the Gulf Coast, as long as roots are not waterlogged for extended periods. An excellent variety to pair with Climax rabbiteye blueberry to extend season: Gulf Coast ripens 2–3 weeks before Climax begins. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gulf Crimson Peach (UF IFAS Low-Chill Freestone Peach for the Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; stake young trees and train to an open-center form. Thin fruit aggressively in the first weeks of fruit set for maximum size. Gulf Crimson is one of the University of Florida IFAS releases from the peach breeding program that has made commercial and home peach production possible throughout the Gulf South — a region where most standard peach varieties fail because they require 700–1,200 chilling hours that the mild Gulf South winters cannot provide. Gulf Crimson's low chill requirement (300–350 hours) means that even in the warmest parts of zone 8–9, the tree accumulates adequate winter dormancy to bloom and set fruit reliably each year. The fruit is medium to large-sized, with attractively red-blushed skin over a yellow-green ground color, and yellow flesh that is sweet, aromatic, and freestone — the pit separates cleanly from the flesh at ripeness. Gulf Crimson's early ripening (late April to May in zone 9) means the harvest precedes the peak summer heat that stresses trees and reduces fruit quality in later-season varieties. The University of Florida peach breeding program (which also produced Gulf Gold, Gulf King, and Gulfrose) developed Gulf Crimson specifically for the low-chill peach market across zone 7–9 of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coastal Plain. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulf Gold Peach (Low-Chill Early Yellow Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Gulf Gold is a low-chill peach cultivar developed by the University of Florida — requiring only 150 chill hours (hours below 45°F) to break dormancy reliably, making it one of the most dependable peach varieties for the Gulf Coast where chill hours are consistently limited. The fruit is medium-sized with yellow flesh, excellent eating quality, and very good flavor for a low-chill peach variety — ripening in late May to early June in zone 9, well ahead of standard-chill peaches that struggle to fruit in the Gulf South. Gulf Gold is a white-flowering, self-fertile peach that does not require a pollinizer, though planting two low-chill varieties together improves yield. Prune annually after harvest to maintain an open-center tree structure at 10–12 feet — reducing disease pressure and making fruit easier to harvest. Peach leaf curl, brown rot, and bacterial spot are the primary disease challenges in humid Gulf South climates; copper fungicide applied at dormant bud swell and follow-up fungicide applications through bloom are essential for reliable production. Thin fruit to 6 inches apart after natural fruit drop (June drop) for full-sized, high-quality peaches. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Gulf King Peach (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and thin developing fruit to 6–8 inches apart once they reach marble size to improve final fruit quality. Gulf King is one of a series of low-chill peach cultivars bred for Gulf Coast growing conditions, sharing the Gulf-series naming with siblings like Gulfprince and Gulfcrest, producing medium to large, firm, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with attractive red-blushed skin in early to mid season. Its moderate-low chill requirement provides reliable bloom and fruit set through the region's variable, often too-warm winters, giving Gulf South gardeners a dependable option among the several regionally bred low-chill peach releases. Prune annually to an open-vase form for good light penetration, and protect the shallow, rot-prone root system with sharply drained soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: GulfAtlas Peach
description: GulfAtlas is the latest-ripening member of the Gulf series of peaches jointly released by the University of Florida, University of Georgia, and USDA-ARS Byron program, reaching harvest about three weeks after its sibling Gulfcrimson in mid-June. It bears very large, round, non-melting clingstone fruit with bright yellow flesh and heavy red blush over yellow ground color, giving growers a way to extend the low-chill peach harvest later into the season than most Gulf Coast cultivars. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect a moderate chill requirement of around 400 hours, higher than the earliest Gulf series releases but still workable in much of the Gulf Coast. Thin fruit to improve size and prune annually to an open vase form for good light penetration into the fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfbeauty Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil. Gulfbeauty is one of the University of Florida's 'Gulf' series of Japanese-type plums bred with resistance to bacterial spot and plum leaf scald, two disease pressures that are common in the humid Gulf South and that can devastate plums selected for drier western growing regions. The 1.5-2 inch fruit has red skin and good eating quality, and the tree typically ripens its crop in May, roughly two weeks ahead of plums grown farther north. Thin developing fruit to a few inches apart once set to improve final size, and plant a second Gulf-series plum nearby to raise yields, since cross-pollination improves fruit set even on trees described as self-fruitful. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfblaze Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, away from low spots where cold air and moisture pool. Gulfblaze is part of the University of Florida's 'Gulf' series of low-chill Japanese plums, bred alongside Gulfbeauty and Gulfrose with resistance to bacterial spot and plum leaf scald, both significant problems for plum growers in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Fruit has bright red skin and ripens in the same early-to-late May window as its Gulf-series siblings, giving Gulf Coast gardeners fresh plums well ahead of the general plum season. Thin fruit to a few inches apart once set, and interplant with a second Gulf-series plum to improve pollination and overall yield. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfcoast Southern Highbush Blueberry (Original Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
description: Plant in raised beds or native soil amended to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines, setting out dormant bushes in winter and mulching well to protect the shallow root system from summer heat. Gulfcoast was among the first University of Florida southern highbush releases bred specifically for the state's mild winters, and it remains a reliable, vigorous producer of medium, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on an upright, spreading bush. Its very low chilling requirement makes it dependable even after unusually warm winters along the Gulf Coast, where many northern blueberry varieties fail to set fruit. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water during dry spells to support fruit sizing, and prune out old wood each winter to keep the planting productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Gulfcrest Peach (University of Florida Release, 450-Chill Gulf South Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches. Harvest when skin is yellow with red blush and fruit gives slightly to firm pressure. Gulfcrest Peach was released by the University of Florida IFAS (then Florida Agricultural Experiment Station) in 1978 as part of a series of Gulf South-adapted peach releases that included Flordaking, Flordaprince, and other low-to-moderate chill varieties developed specifically for Florida and Gulf Coast conditions. The UF peach breeding program, which began producing named releases in the 1950s and accelerated in subsequent decades, addressed the fundamental challenge of growing peaches in warm-winter climates: standard commercial peach varieties requiring 700–900+ chilling hours bloom prematurely, fail to set adequate fruit, or produce poor-quality fruit in zone 8–9 where winter temperatures inconsistently meet chill requirements. Gulfcrest occupies a specific niche in the low-to-moderate chill continuum — with approximately 450 hours required, it demands more winter cold than very low-chill varieties like Flordaking (250–350 hours) but considerably less than standard northern varieties. This positions Gulfcrest as a practical option for the transition zone between the lowest-chill Gulf Coast locations and the higher-chill interior areas, providing good fruit quality in locations where the very lowest-chill varieties may over-bloom or produce poor quality in warmer-than-average years. The fruit has yellow skin with good red blush, yellow freestone flesh, and adequate flavor quality for fresh eating and preservation. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfcrimson Peach (Low-Chill Gulf South Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; Gulfcrimson is a low-chill freestone peach bred for the same mild-winter Gulf Coast conditions as its better-known siblings Gulfking and Gulfcrest, resistant to bacterial leaf spot, a disease that can defoliate susceptible peach varieties in the humid South. Fruit is medium-to-large, firm, and yellow-fleshed with attractive crimson-blushed skin and good classic peach flavor, ripening in late spring. Trees are vigorous and self-fertile, setting a full crop without a second variety nearby. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart in spring to size the remaining crop properly, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop each winter to maintain good light penetration and airflow, which helps control brown rot and other fungal problems common in humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfgold Plum (Very Low-Chill Yellow-Fleshed University of Florida Plum)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam with good air drainage to reduce spring frost damage to blossoms. Requiring only about 150-200 chill hours, Gulfgold is among the lowest-chill plums in the University of Florida's Gulf series, suited to the mildest winters found in zone 8 through 10. Fruit ripens from late May to mid-June, with yellow skin that develops a red blush and sweet yellow flesh with a faint greenish tinge that clings lightly to a small pit when fully soft-ripe. Its susceptibility to certain fungal and bacterial problems means it benefits from the same disease-conscious pruning and spray program used for Gulfbeauty and Gulfblaze. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfking Peach (Texas A&M Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; Gulfking is a freestone peach developed by Texas A&M AgriLife as part of its low-chill 'Gulf' series (alongside Gulfprince and Gulfcrest) bred specifically for the mild-winter Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast. With a chill requirement of roughly 400 hours, it sets a reliable crop in zone 8b-9 areas where standard peach varieties bloom erratically or fail from insufficient winter chilling. Fruit is medium-large, yellow-fleshed, and fully freestone with good classic peach flavor, ripening in late May to early June. Trees are vigorous and self-fertile. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart in April to size the crop properly, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop to maintain good light penetration and airflow in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfprince Peach (Texas A&M Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; Gulfprince is a freestone peach from the Texas A&M AgriLife low-chill 'Gulf' series, bred alongside Gulfking and Gulfcrest for the mild-winter Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast where standard peach varieties fail to accumulate enough winter chilling. It requires about 400 chill hours and ripens slightly earlier than Gulfking, giving Gulf Coast growers a way to extend the harvest window when the two are planted together. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good flavor for a low-chill selection, ripening in mid-to-late May. Trees are vigorous and self-fertile. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart in April, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop to maintain airflow and reduce brown rot pressure in humid conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfrose Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Blood-Red Japanese Plum)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam in full sun. A University of Florida Japanese plum release needing about 275 chill hours, Gulfrose extends the low-chill Gulf series into zone 8-10 gardens from the Florida Panhandle through the warmer Gulf Coast. It ripens roughly a week after its sibling Gulfblaze, with a fruit development period near 95 days, yielding round, semi-freestone fruit with dark reddish-purple skin and striking blood-red flesh. It was selected alongside Gulfbeauty and Gulfblaze for resistance to plum leaf scald and bacterial spot. Plant it with another low-chill Japanese plum such as Gulfbeauty for reliable cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfruby Plum (Earliest-Ripening University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam in full sun. The earliest-ripening member of the University of Florida's Gulf series of low-chill Japanese plums, Gulfruby needs only about 225 chill hours and ripens seven to ten days ahead of Gulfblaze. Fruit develops full red skin color a few days before it is ready to pick, with the sweet, juicy character typical of the Gulf breeding line. It is more susceptible to bacterial canker than its Gulf series relatives, so growers in humid zone 8-10 climates should watch for cankers and defoliation and remove infected wood promptly. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gulfsnow Peach (Low-Chill White-Fleshed Gulf Series Peach)
description: Gulfsnow was developed through a joint USDA Agricultural Research Service, University of Georgia, and University of Florida breeding effort as part of the low-chill Gulf series of peaches, sized for growers whose winters are too mild for standard commercial varieties. It carries firm, non-melting, white flesh under skin that blushes red over a pale ground color, and it ripens in early June at trial sites in the Deep South, cropping more reliably from year to year than older low-chill selections. Being self-fertile, a single tree will set a full crop, though thinning young fruit to about 6 inches apart along the branch improves final size and quality. Its non-melting flesh holds up unusually well for fresh eating and processing compared to most low-chill peaches, which tend to soften quickly after ripening. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gum Bumelia (Chittamwood, Gum Elastic)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun; gum bumelia is a thorny native small tree or large shrub of dry uplands, rocky hillsides, and dry woodlands across the south-central US from Kansas to Florida. The small, black, olive-like fruits are edible and mildly sweet — consumed by numerous birds including mockingbirds, thrushes, and cedar waxwings — making it an outstanding wildlife plant for dry, sunny, naturalistic landscapes. The thick, spiny branches provide secure nesting habitat for mockingbirds and other cavity-nesters and the dense crown offers excellent cover. The milky sap was historically chewed as gum by Indigenous peoples (hence 'gum elastic' and 'gum bumelia'). Extremely drought tolerant and long-lived. The thorny habit makes it effective as an impenetrable wildlife hedge or barrier plant. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Gumi (Cherry Elaeagnus, Goumi Berry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of any fertility — gumi fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria, improving the surrounding soil and feeding itself even in infertile, sandy, or rocky ground. The shrub produces silvery-speckled dark red to cherry-red fruits in early summer that are sweet-tart with a slight astringency that some compare to a tangy cherry; they are excellent eaten fresh, dried, or made into preserves and juice. The fragrant creamy-yellow flowers in spring attract pollinators. Unlike its invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), gumi is a well-behaved garden shrub that doesn't spread aggressively. It makes an excellent companion plant in food forests and permaculture systems, enriching the soil for neighboring fruit trees and shrubs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Guntur Chilli (Guntur Sannam Hot Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Guntur Chilli is a landrace grown for generations in the Guntur and Prakasam districts of Andhra Pradesh, India, where the Guntur Sannam (S4) type has earned Geographical Indication status and become one of the most heavily traded chili types in the world. Plants bear slender, crimson, thick-skinned pods 2–5 inches long with fierce, wine-red pungency, typically cited in the 35,000–75,000 Scoville range depending on strain and growing conditions. Grown almost exclusively as a drying chile, pods are left to fully redden on the plant, then sun-dried and ground into the vivid, pungent chili powder that underlies much of South Indian cooking. A heavy-yielding, heat-loving plant well suited to long, hot growing seasons. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Guthrie Chickasaw Plum (North Florida Large-Fruited Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to light shade; Guthrie tolerates drought and neglect once its roots are established. Guthrie is a north Florida selection of Chickasaw plum chosen for unusually large, tangy-sweet, red-blushed yellow fruit approaching an inch and a half across, noticeably bigger than the typical wild Chickasaw plum crop, ripening in early to mid-summer and excellent fresh or cooked into jelly. The shrubby small tree forms a dense, thicketing, round-headed crown and, like the species, blooms very early in spring before leaf-out, providing one of the season's first nectar sources for native bees. It is fast growing, self-pollinating, and essentially carefree, asking only for good drainage and occasional removal of root suckers if a single-trunk form is wanted. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Gwang Yang Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Korean Persimmon)
description: Gwang Yang, named for the persimmon-growing region of Gwangyang in South Korea, is a compact, dwarf-habit Asian persimmon that comes into bearing earlier than most kaki cultivars and carries better cold tolerance than typical Japanese-bred types, reflecting its Korean origin. Fruit is non-astringent, bright orange, seedless, and large for the tree size at roughly 6 ounces, ripening late in the season from October through mid-November. Its naturally small stature makes Gwang Yang a good option for growers with limited space or for container culture, while its cold hardiness broadens the range of gardens where a non-astringent persimmon can be grown reliably. Plant in full sun with good drainage; like most kaki cultivars it is self-fruitful and does not require a pollinator tree. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Gwen Avocado
description: Bred at UC Riverside as a compact, slow-growing descendant of Hass, Gwen stays small enough to prune easily while yielding roughly twice the fruit per acre of standard Hass trees on the same footprint. Fruit is oval and slightly larger than Hass, with thick, pebbled green skin that dulls rather than blackens at ripeness, surrounding creamy gold-green flesh and a small-to-medium seed. Its extended harvest season and naturally compact habit make it useful for growers who want Hass-like flavor without the eventual size of a full standard Hass tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Gymnema (Sugar Destroyer, Gurmar, Cowplant)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; provide a trellis or support structure; propagate by stem cuttings. Gymnema sylvestre (gymnema, sugar destroyer, or gurmar — Hindi for 'destroyer of sugar') is a woody climbing vine native to the tropical dry forests of central and southern India and Sri Lanka, famous in both traditional medicine and modern nutritional science for one of the most remarkable food interactions known in botany. The fresh leaves of gymnema contain gymnemic acids — triterpene saponins that temporarily bind to and block the sweet taste receptors on the tongue — causing a complete, reversible suppression of the ability to taste sweetness for 1–2 hours after the leaves are chewed. After chewing gymnema leaf, eating sugar tastes like sand, honey tastes like nothing, chocolate loses all sweetness, and sweet fruits taste only of their sour or astringent components — a dramatic, repeatable, pharmacological food interaction. This property has given gymnema both its ancient role in Ayurvedic medicine (used for 2,000+ years for 'sweet urine' — now understood as diabetes) and modern research interest: clinical studies suggest gymnemic acids may reduce sugar absorption in the intestine and support healthy blood glucose management. Gymnema is now one of the most widely sold botanical supplements for blood sugar support worldwide. In zone 9–12, it grows as an ornamental vine with elliptical leaves and small, yellow, tubular flowers. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Gypsy Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Gypsy is a widely grown hybrid selected for adaptability across a broad sowing window, holding quality through the heat and inconsistent weather of a summer planting better than many broccoli varieties, which makes it a dependable choice for closing the gap between an early spring crop and a fall one. It forms medium-large, tightly beaded blue-green heads and continues producing a generous flush of side shoots after the main head is harvested. Cut the central head while the buds are firm and tightly closed, then keep picking side shoots as they reach the same stage. Matures in 58–65 days from transplant.

name: Gypsy Pepper (All-America Sweet Elongated Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Gypsy is an All-America Selections winner (1981) — a sweet, elongated, tapering pepper that produces medium-sized (4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), semi-thick-walled fruits that ripen through a distinctive color progression from pale creamy-yellow, through orange, to bright red, with excellent flavor at every stage. The early maturity (60–70 days) gives Gypsy a head start on the sweet pepper season compared to larger bell types, and the disease resistance package includes tobacco mosaic virus tolerance — a significant advantage. Gypsy is a semi-sweet, elongated type rather than a classic blocky bell — closer to an Italian frying pepper shape but with thicker walls and a sweeter, less pungent flavor than traditional frying types. The elongated fruits are outstanding for fresh eating, stuffing (the tapering shape holds stuffings differently than blocks), grilling, and roasting. The color progression from pale yellow through orange to red creates an attractive multi-colored harvest display when fruits at different maturity stages are present on the plant simultaneously. Plants are productive, compact, and well-suited to both spring and fall production in zone 9. An outstanding early-maturing sweet pepper for home garden use. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: H-63A American Persimmon (Claypool Caramel-Flavored Native Persimmon)
description: H-63A is a named selection from the late James Claypool's extensive Indiana persimmon breeding program, distributed today mainly through collector nurseries and Northern Nut Growers Association members. It is prized among American persimmon enthusiasts for a distinctive rum- and caramelized-sugar-like flavor note layered over the typical rich, honeyed sweetness of a fully ripe native persimmon, making it a favorite for puddings, pies, and fruit leather. Fruit is medium-sized and deep orange, and like all Diospyros virginiana selections it remains firm and strongly astringent until fully soft-ripened by cool fall weather, after which the flesh turns custardy and sweet. The tree has a notably upright, narrow growth habit compared to many seedling persimmons, which can make it easier to site in smaller home orchards. It tolerates heat, drought, and a range of soils once established, and benefits from thinning of root suckers to prevent thicket formation. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ha'Ogen Melon (Israeli Green-Fleshed Muskmelon)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and fruit set, then taper watering in the final week to concentrate sugars, and harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with a full, sweet aroma at the blossom end. Ha'Ogen is a kibbutz-bred Israeli heirloom named for Kibbutz HaOgen, prized for its compact 2–3 lb round fruit with lightly netted, gold-green rind that streaks orange as it ripens, enclosing pale green flesh with an intensely sweet, spicy-floral flavor reminiscent of Charentais melons. Because it slips clean from the vine at peak ripeness rather than holding firm like shipping cantaloupes, it is best suited to home gardens and farmers markets rather than long-distance transport. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines produce heavily over a relatively short window, so successive plantings extend the harvest. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Habanada Pepper (Heatless Habanero-Flavor Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Habanada was bred at Cornell University and further developed by Row 7 Seed Company by selecting for the characteristic fruity, floral, tropical habanero flavor and aroma while breeding out the capsaicin that gives habaneros their intense heat, resulting in a pepper that tastes like a habanero but can be eaten fresh in quantity without any burn. Small, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green to a bright golden-orange, and the plant is productive over a long season much like a standard habanero. It is excellent fresh in salsas, salads, and sauces where habanero flavor is wanted without the heat. Harvest at the fully ripe orange stage for the strongest flavor, and expect steady production through summer into fall. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Habanero Chile Pepper
description: An intensely hot pepper prized for its fruity aroma as much as its fire, said to be many times hotter than a jalapeno. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost with warmth around 85F for even germination. Transplant into a warm, sunny spot after nights stay above 55F, and mulch to keep roots evenly moist. Wear gloves when picking and processing the ripe orange fruit. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Habanero Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and maintain soil temperature at 85–90°F to achieve reliable germination, as Capsicum chinense species are notably slow to sprout. Transplant into the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden once conditions are fully settled. Consistent feeding with a potassium-rich fertilizer during fruiting will maximize yields. Harvest when fruits reach their characteristic orange or red color and feel firm; handle with gloves due to extreme capsaicin levels. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Habego Sea Buckthorn (Certified German Seaberry)
description: Habego is a German-bred female sea buckthorn certified for commercial propagation alongside the cultivar 'Sirola' in the mid-2000s, and it shares the strong, upright shoot growth typical of the modern German breeding line, though it generally yields somewhat less fruit per bush than older selections like 'Hergo' or 'Askola'. Its orange berries ripen in late summer in tight clusters along second-year wood and are best harvested by cutting whole fruiting branches, since the tart fruit clings tightly and bruises if picked by hand. Grow it in poor, sandy, or rocky soil in full sun, where its nitrogen-fixing roots give it a real advantage over less tolerant fruiting shrubs, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay. Prune only to remove crossing or dead wood, since flower buds form on the previous season's growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hachiya Persimmon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Hachiya is the classic large acorn-shaped astringent Japanese persimmon, with deeply orange 6–12 oz fruits harvested in late October and November that must fully soften (bleten) to jelly-like consistency before eating — frozen overnight or left on the counter for 1–3 weeks achieves this, producing a rich honeyed, spiced flavor. Excellent for making Japanese dried persimmon (hoshigaki), baked goods, puddings, and purées. Trees are remarkably drought-tolerant once established, require minimal spraying, and bear reliably in warm temperate to subtropical gardens — one of the most rewarding and lowest-maintenance fruit trees for zones 7–10. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hackberry (Common Hackberry)
description: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; hackberry is among the most adaptable native trees, thriving in urban heat, clay soils, drought, flooding, and alkaline conditions that defeat many other species. The small dark-purple berries that ripen in September–October have a sweet, date-like flavor and are edible directly from the tree; the thin skin is nutritious and the sweet pulp surrounds a hard seed. The berries are a critical fall food source for over 50 bird species, including cedar waxwings, robins, bluebirds, and many migrating warblers. The distinctive corky bark warty growths are a natural feature, not a disease. Excellent choice for difficult urban sites or as a wildlife anchor tree. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Hackensack Melon
description: Sow several seeds per hill an inch deep in well-amended soil once the ground has warmed, thinning to the strongest two plants and giving the sprawling vines several feet of room in each direction. Hackensack is an old American heirloom muskmelon named for the New Jersey town where it was popularized in the late 1800s, prized in home gardens of the era for its large, round, deeply ribbed and heavily netted fruit and its thick, sweet green flesh. Keep soil evenly moist through vining and fruit set, then let it dry out slightly as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Judge ripeness by a shift to full slip, where the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a strong musky aroma at the blossom end. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Haden Mango (Historic Florida Mango)
description: Haden was grown from a seed of the Indian cultivar Mulgoba in Coconut Grove, Florida, in the early twentieth century and became the parent or grandparent of many of the mango cultivars grown in Florida today. It bears medium to large fruit with a striking yellow skin heavily blushed crimson-red, and juicy, moderately fibrous flesh with a rich, aromatic flavor when fully ripe. The tree tends toward alternate bearing and is more susceptible to anthracnose in humid weather than newer commercial cultivars, so good air circulation and a dry bloom period improve fruit set. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate sugars, and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is easily damaged by cold. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hahs American Highbush Cranberry (Largest-Fruited Selection)
description: Hahs is a named selection of American highbush cranberry prized above other cultivars for producing the largest fruit of any highbush cranberry, borne in heavy, drooping clusters that ripen bright red in fall and hang on well into winter. The berries carry high pectin content, making them especially well suited to homemade jam and jelly without added pectin, and their tart, cranberry-like flavor mellows after the first hard frost. Unlike many highbush cranberry selections, Hahs is self-fertile and will set a good fruit crop on its own, though a second plant nearby increases yield further. It is not fussy about soil and tolerates full sun to partial shade, forming a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub more compact than the wild species. Extremely cold-hardy, it thrives through northern Great Plains and upper Midwest winters that few other fruiting shrubs survive; prune out the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep it vigorous and productive. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Hairy Beggartick (Black Jack, Spanish Needles)
description: Sow seeds or allow to self-seed in any well-drained, moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; harvest young leaves and shoots for culinary use before flowering. Bidens pilosa (hairy beggartick or black jack) is one of the world's most widespread tropical annual herbs — a common 'weed' of disturbed soils throughout the tropical and subtropical world that is simultaneously one of the most widely used edible and medicinal plants in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. In many African countries (particularly Kenya, Zimbabwe, and Central Africa), the young shoots and leaves are a major leafy vegetable cooked in stews and soups; in Asia, it is cooked like spinach; in Brazil and the Caribbean, it is used as a medicinal tea. The plant is a prolific producer of small, black seed-needles with two barbed prongs (the 'beggar ticks' or 'Spanish needles' that attach to clothing and animal fur). Despite its weedy character in gardens, the small, white, daisy-like flowers with yellow centers are important nectar sources for native bees and butterflies. Young leaves are mildly flavored and nutritious, used in many cultures as a green vegetable. A genuinely dual-use plant — volunteer edible and medicinal herb. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Hairy Bittercress
description: Harvest young plants from shaded garden beds and pathways in late winter through early spring when they appear as small rosettes; hairy bittercress is a widespread annual or overwintering weed of gardens, nurseries, and cultivated ground throughout North America that is almost universally underappreciated as food. The small, watercress-like leaves have a pleasant, sharp, peppery flavor exactly like watercress and can be eaten raw in salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a garnish — ideally harvested before the white flowers open when flavor is best. The spring-loaded seed capsules shatter explosively when ripe, scattering seeds widely; harvesting before flowering prevents this and gives you both the greens and a cleaner garden. An excellent early-spring foraged green requiring no cultivation whatsoever. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Hairy Mountain Mint (Pilose Mountain Mint)
description: Plant divisions or transplants in full sun to light shade in average, dry to moist, well-drained soil; hairy mountain mint (Pycnanthemum pilosum) is a native prairie and woodland-edge mint of the central and eastern United States with strongly aromatic foliage — the intense spearmint-oregano fragrance is released when leaves are brushed — and masses of small white flowers with purple spots that are exceptionally attractive to native bees, butterflies, and wasps from July through September, making it one of the highest-rated native plants for pollinator gardens. The dried leaves can be used as a mild mint tea or herb. Unlike invasive common mint (Mentha), mountain mints spread slowly and politely. An outstanding native herb for the meadow garden, pollinator strip, and naturalizing in dry to average soils. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Hairy Sweet Cicely
description: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; seed must not be allowed to dry out before sowing, as viability drops sharply with desiccation. Osmorhiza claytonii is one of the earliest-blooming native herbs in eastern deciduous forests, producing soft, fernlike, anise-scented foliage in early spring and flat-topped white umbels that serve as critical early nectar sources for small native bees and beneficial insects before most woodland flowers open. The plant naturalizes readily by self-seeding in moist shaded areas and is a useful addition to native woodland gardens, forest edges, and streamside plantings. Roots and young leaves carry a mild, pleasant anise flavor and have a long history of food and medicinal use by Indigenous peoples of eastern North America. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Hairy Wood Mint
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in woodland gardens, shaded borders, and moist shaded areas; hairy wood mint is a little-known native perennial of the mint family (Lamiaceae) with distinctively hairy stems and leaves and whorled clusters of small, two-lipped, white to pale lavender flowers with purple spotting in midsummer. The minty-aromatic foliage is pleasantly fragrant. An outstanding native for the challenging combination of shade and adequate moisture — one of the few mint-family plants truly adapted to woodland understory conditions. The flowers are visited extensively by small native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies. The leaves can be brewed as a mild mint tea with a pleasant oregano-mint blend flavor. Self-sows modestly in appropriate conditions to naturalize in the shade garden. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Hak Ip Lychee (Haak Yip, Black Leaf Lychee)
description: Named for its dark, glossy foliage, this mid-season Chinese cultivar is valued for consistent bearing in humid subtropical climates where many other lychee cultivars fruit erratically. The medium-size fruit has thin, bumpy, rose-red skin over sweet, aromatic, juicy flesh wrapped around a small seed. Like other lychees it needs several weeks of cool, dry nights in winter to set flower buds, so withhold irrigation during that stretch rather than watering on a fixed schedule; ripening falls in late spring to early summer and fruit should be picked promptly, as birds and squirrels find it just as appealing as people do. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Haku-Botan Pomegranate (White Pomegranate)
description: A Japanese heirloom cultivar, Haku-Botan is grown for its showy double white flowers with a faint yellow blush as much as for its fruit, and it stays notably more compact than standard orchard pomegranates. Unlike the strictly ornamental dwarf 'Nana' type, Haku-Botan reliably produces medium fruit with pale greenish-yellow skin and white to pale pink arils carrying a mild, low-acid flavor. It bears at a young age, often within one to two years, and its small stature suits patio containers or tight garden beds where a full-sized pomegranate would outgrow the space. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect both a longer ornamental bloom season and a lighter, milder-tasting harvest than heavier-bearing commercial cultivars. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hakuho Asian Pear
description: Hakuho is an older mid-20th-century Japanese cultivar distinguished from Hosui and Niitaka by its smooth, pale yellow-green skin rather than a russeted brown finish. The large fruit is very juicy with mild, well-balanced sweetness and less of the aromatic intensity of newer cultivars, but it ripens earlier in the season, typically in late July to early August in warm climates. It has historically been used by Japanese breeders as parent stock for several later-introduced pear cultivars valued for earliness. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hakurei Turnip (Japanese Salad Turnip)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-prepared, loosened soil and thin to 3–4 inches apart; crowding produces forked or stunted roots. Hakurei is a Japanese F1 hybrid turnip bred to be eaten raw: the pure-white, smooth globe roots (2–3 inches in diameter at harvest) are remarkably sweet, mild, and almost fruity — nothing like the sharp, peppery flavor of conventional turnip varieties. Unlike storage turnips, Hakurei is best harvested small and young; roots toughen and lose their fresh crispness if left past 2 inches. The greens are also tender and mild and excellent raw or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, fall-sown Hakurei seeded in October is often the finest salad turnip in the cool-season garden, maturing just before the holidays. A favorite for farmers' market growers because of its eye-catching appearance and reliably sweet flavor. Matures in 38–45 days from seed.

name: Hale's Best Cantaloupe (Classic California Heirloom, Sweet Orange-Flesh Standard Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when slip from vine and fragrant. Hale's Best is the quintessential American heirloom cantaloupe — a variety that defined the flavor standard of what a good cantaloupe should taste like for generations of American home gardeners and market growers. The variety was developed in the early 20th century by Paul Halladay of Turlock, California, from melon seed brought from Japan, and selected specifically for shipping quality, flavor, and thick, deeply netted skin. The resulting variety — medium to large, round to slightly oval, covered in a thick network of raised tan netting over a gray-green background, with a heavily perfumed blossom end and deeply orange, very sweet flesh — became so widely grown in California's San Joaquin Valley melon production region that 'Hale's Best' essentially defined the commercial cantaloupe market in mid-20th-century America. The flesh is thick, dense, and intensely orange — higher in beta-carotene than pale-fleshed cantaloupe varieties — with genuine sweetness and the rich, complex melon aroma that distinguishes a truly good cantaloupe from a bland one. The Brix (sugar content) of properly grown, vine-ripened Hale's Best in warm conditions can reach 14–16, producing sweetness comparable to the best modern hybrid melons. Several numbered strains of Hale's Best were selected for regional performance: Hale's Best #36 and Hale's Best Jumbo are among the subvarieties that have remained in commerce through heirloom seed preservation. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Hale's Best Jumbo Cantaloupe
description: A classic heirloom muskmelon with exceptionally sweet, thick-walled flesh and a small seed cavity, in 3 to 5 pound fruits. Direct sow two or three seeds per hill once soil warms past 70F and thin to the strongest plant. Water deeply while vines grow and fruit sizes up, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and smells fragrant. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Hale's Best Melon
description: Hale's Best is a classic heirloom cantaloupe prized for exceptional sweetness, tender juicy flesh, and a small seed cavity that yields more edible fruit. Sow seeds in warm soil once frost has passed, giving vines several feet to sprawl. Water consistently while fruit develops, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the melon separates cleanly from the vine with a light pull. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Half-High Blueberry
description: Half-high blueberries are crosses between highbush and lowbush species, combining the large-berry quality of highbush with the extreme cold hardiness of lowbush — cultivars such as 'Northblue', 'Northcountry', and 'Polaris' survive to -35°F when snow-covered. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.0 and mulch heavily with pine bark or sawdust. Cross-pollination between two compatible cultivars improves berry size and total yield. Pruning is minimal for the first five years; thereafter remove the thickest, oldest canes each late winter to encourage fresh productive wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hall Avocado (Florida Midseason Commercial Avocado)
description: Hall is a Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid that has long been one of the more widely planted commercial and dooryard avocados in South Florida, valued for a productive, fairly reliable bearing habit. Fruit is medium to large and pear-shaped with somewhat rough, dark green skin and rich, nutty flesh with moderate oil content, ripening in fall. The tree tolerates Florida's humid summer rains better than pure Guatemalan cultivars while carrying noticeably better flavor than the older pure West Indian selections. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, and thin overly heavy fruit loads if limbs show signs of breaking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hall Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Bronze Muscadine)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun. Hall is a self-fertile bronze muscadine producing medium to large, sweet, flavorful fruit on a vigorous, productive vine with good disease resistance, making it a practical, low-fuss choice for home gardeners who want reliable production from a single vine without needing to plant a separate pollinizer. The self-fertile trait, shared by a growing number of modern muscadine releases, has made varieties like Hall increasingly popular for smaller home gardens where space for multiple vines is limited. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily from the stem with a gentle tug, typically over an extended ripening window from late summer into early fall. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hall's Hardy Almond (Cold-Hardy Almond, Northern Almond, Zones 5-8 Almond)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, deep soil in full sun on a protected slope or elevated site to reduce late spring frost damage to blossoms; Hall's Hardy blooms later than standard almonds, reducing but not eliminating frost risk to flowers; harvest nuts in September when hulls split; the small to medium kernels have a mild almond flavor but thicker shells than California varieties — crack-in-shell type. Hall's Hardy almond occupies a unique market niche as essentially the only widely available almond variety for cold-climate gardeners in zones 5–8 of the northeastern and Midwestern United States, where the low temperatures that standard California almonds cannot survive and the late spring frosts that kill the early-blooming California almond flowers make standard almond production impractical or impossible. Hall's Hardy is believed by many pomologists to be a hybrid between Prunus dulcis (almond) and Prunus persica (peach) rather than a pure almond — it demonstrates characteristics of both parents, including cold-hardiness exceeding pure almond by a substantial margin, later bloom time, and nuts with a thick shell and moderate almond flavor. These characteristics — while reducing the quality compared to premium California almonds — allow Hall's Hardy to produce viable almond-type nuts in zone 5–8 climates where no standard almond variety will survive reliably. The nuts are smaller and have a thicker shell than Nonpareil or Mission, with a mild but acceptable almond flavor that is usable for cooking, baking, and direct consumption. For cold-climate home orchardists interested in growing their own almonds, Hall's Hardy is essentially the only viable option. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hallertau Hops (Hallertauer Mittelfruh)
description: The archetypal noble aroma hop, mild and spicy-herbal, that defines authentic German lagers and pilsners. It is a low-yielding, slow-to-establish landrace variety that is genetically susceptible to Verticillium wilt, so home growers should source certified disease-free rhizomes and rotate planting sites if problems appear. Full sun and steady moisture during the summer bine-growth push are essential for reasonable cone set. Because true Hallertau is finicky, many home brewers substitute Mount Hood or Liberty, but growing the genuine article is a rewarding project for patient gardeners. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Halley's Comet Dragon Fruit
description: Propagate from mature stem cuttings and train the sprawling, three-angled stems onto a stout trellis in full sun with sharply draining soil, since standing water quickly rots the succulent growth. This white-fleshed cultivar is prized among collectors for consistently sweet, well-balanced flavor compared with many bland commercial dragon fruit. Gulf Coast growers keep it in large pots so it can be wheeled under cover whenever temperatures threaten to drop into the 30s, since the stems are more cold-tender than typical landscape cactus. Hand-pollination in the evening, when the large white flowers open, improves fruit set for home growers. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Halona Cantaloupe (AAS-Winning Hybrid Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Halona is a 2015 All-America Selections Gold Medal winner cantaloupe — one of the most highly awarded AAS winners in recent years — developed for exceptional eating quality combined with early maturation and disease resistance. Halona produces medium-sized (4–5 pound), deeply netted, tan-skinned fruits with dense, deep orange flesh and exceptional sweetness (Brix 14–17°, very high for an open-pollinated type) with complex, honey-like flavor that compares to the finest specialty melons. The fruit set is consistent and the plants show resistance to powdery mildew — a significant disease in humid climates. Halona's early maturation (73–80 days) and compact vine habit make it suitable for small gardens and shorter growing seasons; two plants produce more than enough for a family. The small seed cavity and thick, firm flesh give excellent eating quality with no watery texture. Halona is the recommended first melon for new growers due to its reliable production, disease resistance, and superior flavor — and one of the best choices for zone 9 spring production where a short fruiting window requires a reliable early variety. Matures in 73–80 days from seed.

name: Halvin's Sidewinder Pawpaw (Cold-Hardy Wild-Selected Iowa Pawpaw)
description: Plant a container-grown tree in early spring in rich, well-drained soil with some shade for the first year or two, then let full sun take over as the canopy fills in; a second, unrelated pawpaw cultivar is required nearby for pollination, since Halvin's Sidewinder cannot set fruit with its own pollen. Found growing wild in southwestern Iowa by Tyler and Danae Halvin, this selection stood out for exceptional cold hardiness and reliably early ripening, qualities that also translate into vigorous, trouble-free growth through the long hot summers of zone 7-9 gardens. Fruits run 8 to 14 ounces with smooth, sweet flesh carrying a distinct hint of pineapple and none of the bitter aftertaste some wild pawpaws show. The tree stays a manageable 15 to 20 feet tall and wide, making it easier to net or hand-thin than some larger-growing named cultivars. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Hamburg Parsley (Root Parsley)
description: Soak seeds in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination; sow 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, stone-free soil in rows, as seeds germinate slowly and unevenly over 2–4 weeks. Thin seedlings to 6–8 inches apart once established; the flat-leaf parsley-like foliage is edible throughout the season as an herb. The ivory-white, parsnip-like root develops slowly all season and tastes like a concentrated, slightly sweet parsley-parsnip hybrid — exceptional in Central European soups and stews. Harvest in fall after light frost improves sweetness; roots left in the ground over winter in milder climates will re-sprout in spring but roots lose quality as the plant prepares to bolt. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Hamese Asian Pear
description: Hamese bears medium-size, yellow-skinned fruit that is the first Asian pear to ripen in many home orchards, with crisp, crunchy, very juicy flesh and a refreshingly sweet, mild flavor unlike the soft, buttery texture of European pears. Because it is not self-fertile, plant it near a different Asian pear cultivar with overlapping bloom for reliable fruit set, and watch for fire blight, to which most nashi cultivars remain susceptible. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hamlin Orange (Early Cold-Hardy Sweet Orange, Standard Florida Juice Orange)
description: Plant grafted tree in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost in zone 9 when young. Fruit in October–December. Hamlin Orange is the most commercially important sweet orange in Florida — the variety that produces the majority of Florida's fresh-squeezed and not-from-concentrate orange juice, and the dominant early-season orange in Florida commercial groves. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling in Glenwood, Florida in 1879 by A.G. Hamlin, who recognized its value and began propagating it; the combination of very early ripening (October–December harvest, months ahead of navel oranges), excellent cold hardiness for a sweet orange, prolific bearing, and high-quality juice made Hamlin rapidly popular among Florida citrus growers. The fruit is medium-sized, round, smooth-skinned, thin-skinned, with pale orange-yellow to bright orange exterior. The flesh is tender, very juicy, with excellent sweet-acid balance and nearly seedless character (typically 1–3 seeds per fruit) — qualities that make Hamlin ideal for juicing, where seed count affects yield and flavor extraction. Hamlin's cold hardiness is one of its most significant practical attributes for zone 9 gardeners: it is more reliably cold-hardy than navel orange, Valencia, or most other sweet orange varieties, making it the recommended choice for zone 9a plantings where severe freezes are possible. Established trees in good health can survive temperatures to 26°F briefly without significant damage, though young trees and flowers are more sensitive. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hancock Beach Plum (Fort Hancock Named Beach Plum Selection)
description: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun with a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species sets fruit poorly without cross-pollination. Hancock was selected near Fort Hancock, New Jersey, during the early-to-mid 20th-century push to develop beach plum into a viable commercial fruit crop for coastal growers, and it is valued for its early ripening and blue-skinned fruit. The fruit is well suited to jellies, jams, and syrups, ripening earlier than many other named beach plum selections, which can help extend a home harvest season when grown alongside later cultivars. Being a true dune shrub, it thrives in poor sandy soil and salt-laden wind that would damage most other fruiting plants, and it needs only light post-bloom pruning to stay productive and shapely. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Handa Vanilla (Disease-Resistant, Non-Splitting Pod Selection)
description: Handa was bred by CIRAD, the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, on Réunion Island from a self-pollinated seedling selected for disease resistance and improved agronomic performance rather than as an ornamental novelty. It shows useful resistance to Fusarium oxysporum root and stem rot, a soil-borne disease that has damaged vanilla plantations worldwide, and produces thicker, darker green leaves along with heavier, rounder pods than standard planifolia stock. Unlike ordinary vanilla, its pods stay closed at maturity instead of splitting open, which reduces harvest losses and makes curing easier, even though vanillin content per pod runs somewhat lower than traditional stock, a tradeoff offset by higher overall yield per vine. Like all cultivated vanilla it is a climbing hemi-epiphytic orchid that must be trained up a support tree, pole, or trellis and pollinated by hand within hours of each flower opening, since its natural pollinator is absent outside Mesoamerica. Grow it in bright, filtered light and high humidity, in a loose, fast-draining orchid or bark-based medium, with warmth above 60°F year-round. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hannah Sweet Potato (White-Fleshed Dry-Type NCSU Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips after last frost when soil is above 65°F, setting each slip 3–4 inches deep with the crown at or just above soil level; Hannah is a white-fleshed, cream-to-tan skinned sweet potato developed by North Carolina State University that has become one of the most popular white-fleshed varieties in US production — offering a substantially different culinary experience than the familiar orange-fleshed types. The flesh is cream to pale ivory, firm, and notably dry (less moist than orange varieties), with a mild, subtly sweet flavor that reads more like a russet potato than a typical sweet potato — making Hannah uniquely versatile for preparations like roasted potato dishes, gratins, soups, and anywhere a firm, dry-textured potato is preferred. The dry, non-gummy texture means it mashes cleanly, holds together in casseroles, and is excellent when baked whole with a crisp skin. Hannah produces smooth-skinned, uniform tubers in a standard 90–100 day window and yields reliably in Southern and Gulf Coast production areas. For gardeners familiar only with orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, Hannah represents a practical bridge variety that can replace russet potatoes in the garden while still being a true sweet potato culturally and agronomically. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Hannibal Leek (Early Heavy-Cropping Leek)
description: Hannibal is a reliable, heavy-cropping leek that matures early and heavily, producing long, thick white shafts under dark green leaves from midsummer well into fall. It can be grown at closer spacing and pulled young as an excellent baby leek, or left to size up for a standard harvest. With soil mounded around the base and a layer of mulch, Hannibal tolerates cold well and can overwinter in the ground for a late harvest in mild climates. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Hanover Salad Green (Colonial-Era Southern Heirloom Salad Green)
description: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves. Hanover Salad is a colonial-era Southern heirloom green in the same species as rutabaga, prized historically in Virginia and Gulf South gardens for its mild, cabbage-like flavor eaten raw as salad greens when young or cooked like collards once mature. It tolerates both cold snaps and the on-and-off warmth of a Gulf Coast fall and winter better than many mustards, holding quality in the garden for extended picking rather than bolting at the first warm spell. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Hansel Eggplant (AAS-Winning Slender Mini Purple Eggplant, Prolific and Early Cluster Producer)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches when skin is glossy deep purple. Hansel Eggplant was developed by PanAmerican Seed and won the All-America Selections award in 2008, one of a pair of complementary mini eggplant varieties (Hansel purple, Gretel white) from the same breeding program that were recognized in consecutive years for their outstanding performance in AAS trials. The Hansel and Gretel naming reflects the paired nature of the complementary varieties and their petite, fairy-tale proportions compared to standard full-sized eggplants. Hansel's outstanding AAS trial performance was attributed to several factors that distinguish it from both standard large eggplant varieties and other small-fruited eggplants: the combination of extremely early production (55–60 days from transplant, compared to 70–80+ days for large varieties), prolific cluster fruiting (multiple fruits per node vs. one to two for standard types), compact plant size (20–24 inches, easily managed in containers), and excellent eating quality (tender skin with no bitterness, minimal seed content, clean white flesh) created a variety with compelling advantages in every direction. For zone 9 gardeners, Hansel's short days-to-maturity is particularly valuable: zone 9 eggplant production spans March–October, but the most productive and high-quality harvest period is before the peak summer heat (June–July); Hansel's early maturity allows significant harvest before conditions become stressful. Matures in 55–60 days from transplant.

name: Hansen's Bush Cherry
description: Hansen's Bush Cherry is the classic named strain of western sandcherry selected and distributed by South Dakota State plant breeder N.E. Hansen in the early 1900s specifically for fruit quality, chosen out of wild seedling populations for larger, sweeter, purple-black cherries than the straight species typically bears. It remains one of the most reliable fruiting shrubs for the Northern Great Plains and prairie provinces, tolerating extreme winter cold, drought, and alkaline soils that eliminate most other stone fruits. Plants bloom with abundant white flowers in early spring and ripen fruit in mid- to late summer, useful fresh, dried, or cooked into jam, syrup, and wine, though flavor and astringency vary somewhat from seedling to seedling since it is propagated as an open-pollinated strain rather than a single clone. Prune out the oldest stems at ground level every few years to renew fruiting wood on this low, spreading shrub. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hanson Lettuce (Historic Maryland Heirloom Crisphead)
description: According to family tradition, this lettuce was grown for generations by a Maryland farm family before a Philadelphia seed house introduced it commercially around 1870. It forms a large, light green head of curly, fringed leaves around a crisp white heart, giving it the crunch of a crisphead with more cold tolerance and less fuss than modern iceberg types. A classic nineteenth-century French gardening reference even illustrated and described the variety, evidence of how far its reputation traveled. Its large old-fashioned heads are well suited to slicing for sandwiches, and it holds in the garden respectably before bolting. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Haogen Melon (Ogen Melon, Israeli Melon)
