description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun; Haogen is ready to harvest when the skin transitions from green to orange-yellow in patches and the fruits slip from the vine with minimal pressure — like all aromatic melons, it deteriorates rapidly after peak ripeness. Haogen (also spelled Ogen) was developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz in Israel and remains the most celebrated Israeli melon variety, known throughout the melon-growing world for its extraordinary flavor; the small to medium (1–3 lb), round fruits start with pale green skin that develops orange and gold patches and creeping yellow-green net as they ripen. The flesh is salmon-orange to greenish, with an intensely sweet, highly aromatic, complex melon fragrance and flavor with notes of honey and tropical fruit that many consider the finest melon eating experience available. Short shelf life after harvest (1–2 days at room temperature, 3–5 days refrigerated) means Haogen is fundamentally a garden and local market melon rather than a commercial shipping variety — its reputation rests on the incomparable quality of fruit eaten within hours of harvest. Widely grown in Israel, Netherlands, and by American melon enthusiasts. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Happy Giant Honeyberry (Large-Fruited Russian Haskap)
description: Happy Giant is a Russian-derived F3 selection valued for producing some of the largest fruit of any haskap, elongated berries reaching over an inch long with a sweet-tart, blueberry-like flavor and high sugar content at harvest. It blooms early and tolerates winter cold to roughly -40F, but the early flowers benefit from a sheltered site or row cover during hard late frosts. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and expect a vigorous, upright bush that reaches significant yields by its fourth or fifth growing season. Fruit ripens ahead of strawberries, giving gardeners one of the earliest fresh harvests of the season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Haralson Apple (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Heirloom Apple)
description: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1922, Haralson was bred specifically to survive winters that kill most other apple trees and became the most widely planted apple in Minnesota for much of the 20th century. The medium, deep-red fruit is firm and notably tart, holding its shape well in pies and sauce, with flavor that mellows somewhat in storage. Its extreme cold hardiness makes it a reliable choice where winter low temperatures rule out many popular commercial cultivars. Plant it in northern gardens as a dependable, disease-tolerant workhorse rather than for dessert-apple sweetness. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Harcot Apricot (Canadian Disease-Resistant Apricot, Northeast-Adapted Apricot)
description: Plant on a north-facing slope, elevated ground, or north side of a windbreak to delay bloom and reduce late spring frost damage to blossoms; Harcot is self-fertile; thin fruits to 4–5 inches after natural drop; fruit ripens in July producing medium to large, firm, orange fruits with very good sweet-tart flavor and above-average resistance to brown rot — a critical advantage in humid northeastern climates. Harcot apricot was released by Agriculture Canada's Harrow Research Station in Ontario in 1977 as part of a breeding program aimed at developing apricot varieties with improved cold-hardiness and disease resistance for production in eastern Canada and the northeastern United States, where the combination of cold winters, late spring frosts, and humid summer conditions had historically made reliable apricot production difficult or impossible. Harcot achieved a combination of characteristics that made it the premier recommended apricot for the northeastern states and eastern Canada: significantly better cold-hardiness than California-bred varieties (surviving winters in zone 4), self-fertility requiring no companion tree, above-average resistance to the brown rot disease that devastates apricots in humid climates, and good fruit quality — medium to large fruits with firm, orange flesh, a pleasant sweet-tart balanced flavor, and good fresh-eating quality. University cooperative extension services throughout the northeastern states from New England through the Mid-Atlantic list Harcot as their primary or sole recommended apricot variety for home orchards in the region, reflecting its exceptional combination of hardiness, disease tolerance, and quality under northeastern conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hardired Nectarine Tree
description: Hardired is a cold-tolerant, self-fertile nectarine known for smooth-skinned, freestone fruit and good resistance to bacterial spot and brown rot. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and thin the fruit to about 6 inches apart for larger nectarines. Prune each late winter to an open-center vase shape to maximize light and airflow. Consistent watering during fruit development keeps the flesh juicy and sweet. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hardy Chicago Fig (Widely Grown Cold-Hardy Home-Garden Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and mulch well over the root zone. Hardy Chicago is one of the most widely planted fig cultivars for home gardens across the country, prized for dependable, heavy production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, strawberry-red pulp, along with unusual root hardiness that allows it to resprout from the base and still produce a crop even after a winter cold enough to kill the top growth to the ground. This resilience has made it a favorite starter fig for gardeners in climates on the edge of reliable fig hardiness, though in the milder winters of the Gulf South it typically grows as a full, unpruned multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Harvest figs when they soften, droop on the stem, and develop full color, picking every day or two during the height of the season since ripe figs do not store well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hardy Kiwi
description: Hardy kiwi vines are dioecious — plant one male vine for every 6–8 female vines or choose a self-fertile cultivar such as 'Issai'. The vines can take 4–7 years to bear fruit but become very productive once established, requiring a pergola or heavy-gauge trellis rated to hold at least 200 lbs. Prune to a permanent framework of main arms and renewal spurs each late winter, cutting lateral shoots back to 2–4 buds. Harvest when smooth, grape-sized fruits yield slightly to pressure and taste sweet. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Hardy Orange (Trifoliate Orange, Japanese Bitter Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; hardy orange is deciduous (unusual for citrus) and leafless in winter. Poncirus trifoliata (trifoliate orange or hardy orange) is the most cold-hardy member of the citrus family — a deciduous, thorny Chinese shrub or small tree that survives temperatures to -10°F when dormant, making it the only citrus relative that can be grown permanently outdoors through USDA zone 5. The small, 1.5-to-2-inch, round, yellow fruits resemble a tiny orange but are intensely bitter and unpleasant raw (high limonin content) — technically edible as marmalade or preserves if the bitterness is accounted for, but not for fresh eating. The plant's primary horticultural importance is as a dwarfing, cold-hardy rootstock for grafting edible citrus — trifoliate orange rootstock limits tree size, improves cold hardiness, and increases fruit quality in grafted sweet oranges, grapefruits, and mandarins. As an ornamental, it is a thorny barrier or specimen plant with fragrant white flowers in spring (before the leaves emerge), attractive yellow fall fruits, and interesting green-barked, zig-zag winter branch structure. A novel cold-climate citrus curiosity. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Hardy Red Kiwi (Red-Skinned Red-Fleshed Kiwiberry)
description: Hardy Red is a female Actinidia arguta selection grown for cranberry-red-tinged skin and red-blushed flesh with a sweet, well-regarded flavor, distinguishing it from the mostly green-fruited hardy kiwi cultivars. Vines are vigorous twining climbers that need a strong permanent trellis or arbor and reliably tolerate winter temperatures down to around -25F. As with all Actinidia arguta, this is a dioecious cultivar and requires a separate male vine, such as a hardy male seedling or Issai, planted nearby to ensure fruit set. Expect a productive vine once established, ripening in fall alongside other hardy kiwi selections. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hardy Tapioca (Cold Hardy Cassava, Argentine Cassava)
description: Plant rooted stem cuttings in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; dies back to roots in freezes but regrows. Manihot grahamii (hardy tapioca or Argentine cassava) is a cold-hardy Argentinian relative of true cassava (M. esculenta) — closely resembling its famous edible cousin in leaf shape (deeply palmately lobed, tropical-looking) and stem structure but significantly more cold-tolerant, surviving hard freezes to zone 8 (approximately 15°F) by dying to the ground and regenerating from tuberous roots the following spring. In zone 8–11, it is grown primarily as an ornamental for its dramatically tropical-looking, deeply cut, dark-green leaves (8–12 inches across) — creating a convincing tropical garden effect at far lower temperatures than true cassava (zone 10+). The plant can reach 4–8 feet in a single growing season, creating rapid impact as a tropical accent. The roots are reportedly edible (similar to cassava) but much less developed than commercial cassava and require the same caution about proper preparation to remove cyanogenic glycosides. Hardy tapioca is drought-tolerant, grows rapidly on poor soil, and is extremely low-maintenance — simply cut to the ground after frost and let it regrow. A remarkably useful plant for zone 8–9 gardeners seeking a tropical aesthetic without the winter protection demands of true tropical plants. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Harglow Apricot (Self-Fertile Canker-Resistant Canadian Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Harglow was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada, valued for combining good cold hardiness with notably strong resistance to perennial canker, a bacterial disease that seriously damages many apricot trees in humid or variable climates. The small to medium, orange fruit has firm, richly flavored flesh with a good sweet-tart balance, excellent for fresh eating as well as preserving. The compact tree size makes it a practical fit for smaller home orchards, and its disease resistance gives it real staying power compared with more disease-prone apricot varieties in regions where canker and other bacterial issues are common. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets, and prune to an open form for good air circulation, which further reduces disease pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hargrand Apricot (Large-Fruited Harrow-Series Canadian Apricot)
description: Hargrand was released by the Harrow Research Station in Ontario, Canada, the same cold-hardy breeding program that produced Harcot and Harglow, and it is grown specifically for its exceptionally large fruit size relative to other hardy apricot selections. Skin is yellow-orange with a light red blush over firm, freestone flesh with good, well-balanced flavor for fresh eating and preserving. Because fruit set improves markedly with cross-pollination, plant Hargrand alongside another Harrow-series or mid-season apricot with overlapping bloom rather than relying on it as a stand-alone tree. As with other Harrow selections, winter cold is rarely the limiting factor; a planting site that avoids frost pockets during the early spring bloom period protects the crop far more than any additional winter protection. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Haritaki (Chebulic Myrobalan)
description: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; haritaki is a frost-tender tropical and subtropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. One of the most revered trees in Ayurvedic medicine, called the 'king of medicines,' it is a deciduous forest tree native from India to Southeast Asia bearing small, ribbed, olive-like fruit that is dried and used as one of the three fruits in the classic Ayurvedic formula triphala, valued in traditional practice for digestive support among many other uses. The tree needs many years of growth before fruiting begins and ultimately becomes a substantial shade tree, making it a long-term planting suited only to large tropical properties, botanical collections, or dedicated medicinal orchards rather than a typical home garden. Water regularly while young, reduce watering once established, and expect a long wait before the first harvestable fruit crop. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Hark Pecan (Cold-Hardy Northern Pecan)
description: Hark is one of the northern pecan cultivars bred for short-season climates, bearing a medium-sized, thin-shelled nut with good kernel fill well outside the traditional Gulf South pecan belt. Give it deep, uncompacted soil and full sun, and plant a second cultivar with an offsetting pollen-shed and receptivity schedule nearby, since pecans rarely self-pollinate effectively. Watch for zinc deficiency (rosette) in spring and apply foliar zinc if new leaves emerge small and crinkled. Because it matures its crop within a shorter frost-free window than southern selections like Desirable or Stuart, Hark is the better choice for growers north of the humid Gulf Coast who still want home-scale pecan production. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Harko Nectarine (Cold-Hardy Canadian Freestone Nectarine)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Harko was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada specifically to extend nectarine growing into colder climates than most varieties can tolerate, combining genuine cold hardiness with good resistance to bacterial spot, a disease that troubles many nectarines in humid regions. The medium-sized fruit has bright red skin over yellow, firm, freestone flesh with good sweet-tart flavor, ripening in midsummer on a reliably productive tree. Its combination of hardiness and disease tolerance has made it a popular choice for home orchardists in the northern half of nectarine-growing range who still want good eating quality without the extra winter losses less hardy varieties suffer. Thin fruit after natural drop, and maintain routine brown rot management common to all nectarines. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Harogem Apricot (Self-Fertile Early-Ripening Harrow-Series Apricot)
description: Like its better-known sibling Harcot, Harogem came out of Agriculture Canada's Harrow Research Station breeding program in Ontario aimed at combining northeastern cold hardiness with better disease resistance than California apricots typically offer. Fruit is medium-sized with orange skin blushed red and firm, flavorful flesh, ripening in a tight window just before Harcot in most seasons. The tree is self-fertile, so a single planting will bear fruit, and it carries useful tolerance to perennial canker and brown rot, diseases that are a persistent problem for apricots in humid eastern climates. Thin fruit after natural June drop and prune to an open center for good airflow, which further reduces disease pressure in wetter regions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Harris Model Parsnip
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil — parsnip requires the same deep, uncompacted growing conditions as carrots but needs even more space due to the larger root; Harris Model is the standard American parsnip variety, selected in the 1880s by the Joseph Harris Seed Company as a smooth, uniform improvement over the traditional English Hollow Crown parsnip — fewer hollow crowns, smoother skin, and better root uniformity make Harris Model the most widely grown American parsnip. The long, tapering, ivory-white roots develop a rich, complex flavor that is unmistakably its own: sweet and aromatic with earthy, celery-like, and nuttily caramelized notes when roasted — a flavor that lacks any close comparison among other vegetables. The signature technique for maximizing parsnip flavor is 'frosting' — leaving harvested or in-ground roots exposed to repeated hard frosts that convert starches to sugars, creating a dramatically sweeter root than summer-harvested parsnips. Roasted parsnips (with butter, herbs, and honey) are one of the great classic British-American root vegetable preparations, where high heat caramelizes the natural sugars and transforms the texture from firm-and-dense to tender and lightly crisp at the edges. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Harrison Apple (Historic Newark New Jersey Cider Apple)
description: Harrison built the reputation of the once-famous Newark cider of colonial and early Federal-era New Jersey, prized for its deep color and high alcohol content pressed from a single variety rather than a blend. The small, dry-textured, black-speckled yellow fruit is far too astringent and mealy for fresh eating but yields juice with excellent sugar and tannin balance. Nearly lost to cultivation, it was rediscovered in an old New Jersey orchard in the 1970s and has since been preserved by heritage cider growers. Choose it specifically for serious home cidermaking, not for a dessert or baking apple. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Harrow Delight Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Early Canadian Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Harrow Delight was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada, specifically for strong resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that is the single greatest threat to pear growing in warm, humid climates and can kill susceptible trees outright in a bad year. The medium, yellow fruit blushed with red ripens early in the season, ahead of many other pears, with sweet, juicy, smooth-textured flesh good for fresh eating. Its combination of disease resistance and early ripening has made it a practical, low-risk recommendation for home orchardists in the humid South and elsewhere where fire blight makes growing more susceptible heirloom pear varieties a genuine gamble. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Harrow Sweet Pear
description: Plant two different pear varieties for cross-pollination; in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Harrow Sweet pear was released in 1964 by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Harrow Research Station in Ontario specifically for its outstanding fire blight resistance (a major disease problem for European pears in humid eastern climates) combined with excellent fruit quality; the medium-large, short-necked, golden-yellow fruits with some russeting ripen in September and have sweet, juicy, buttery flesh with exceptional flavor and keeping quality — storing for 2–3 months in refrigerated storage. Harrow Sweet was selected to fill the gap between early-ripening Bartlett (poor storage) and late-ripening D'Anjou/Bosc types; it is particularly valuable in humid southeastern climates where fire blight pressure makes most European pears unreliable. Partially self-fruitful but yields better with a pollinator. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Harry Masters Jersey Apple (Bittersweet Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Harry Masters Jersey is a reliable, productive variety well suited to traditional cider blends. A West Country English cider apple prized for producing consistently high-tannin, well-structured bittersweet juice, it is one of the workhorse varieties of traditional Somerset and Devon cider blends, valued more for the reliable quality of its juice than for the tree's ornamental qualities. Its medium-sized, dull red-flushed fruit is grown exclusively for milling and pressing, and it pairs well in a blend with sharper, more acidic apples to round out the finished cider's structure. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is far too astringent for fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hart's Pennyroyal
description: Plant Mentha cervina in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates standing water and grows well at the margins of ponds, in bog gardens, or in any reliably moist position; contain in pots as with other mints to prevent spreading; harvest stems for fresh use throughout the growing season. Hart's Pennyroyal is a distinctive and underused culinary mint — rare in cultivation but increasingly recognized for its ornamental value and culinary merit. Unlike most mints, it is adapted to aquatic or near-aquatic conditions and grows naturally in the beds of seasonal streams that dry in summer and flood in winter across the Iberian Peninsula, southern France, and North Africa. The very narrow, almost rush-like leaves are unlike any other mint and give the plant a unique, fine texture in the water garden. Culinary use closely mirrors that of spearmint: the leaves have a clean, fresh, strong spearmint fragrance with overtones of peppermint, and can be used fresh in teas, cocktails (particularly in Iberian cuisine), desserts, and savory dishes. In Portugal and Spain, it is used to make 'hortelã-da-ribeira' tea (riverside mint tea). Unlike some Mentha species, it does not spread as aggressively as peppermint or spearmint; still, container culture is advisable in mixed herb gardens. A charming, refined, and genuinely useful mint for the aquatic herb garden. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Hart's Pennyroyal / Water Pennyroyal
description: Plant Hart's Pennyroyal in moist to seasonally wet soil along pond edges, rain gardens, or stream margins where its narrow, peppermint-scented foliage can spread freely. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding. Harvest stems for culinary or herbal use by cutting back to just above a leaf node, which encourages bushy regrowth. Although more drought-tolerant than common pennyroyal, it performs best when soil moisture remains consistent through summer. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Hartley Walnut
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing enough room for a large, vigorous, spreading canopy. Hartley is a long-established English walnut variety recognized for its large, elongated, smooth-shelled nuts and light-colored, mild-flavored kernel, and it was for decades a mainstay of California commercial walnut orchards. It has been largely replaced in new plantings by more disease-tolerant modern varieties, but mature Hartley trees remain productive and are still valued for nut size and quality in older orchards and home gardens. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Harvest Moon Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Icebox Watermelon)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms, and plant a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen seedless watermelons need to set fruit. Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for very uniform, round, icebox-sized fruit — a manageable size for a refrigerator, unlike the largest field watermelons — with exceptionally sweet, crisp, deep-red flesh and only small, soft, edible white seed traces rather than the hard black seeds of standard watermelon. Its consistent size and shape make it a strong choice for home gardeners who want reliable, high-quality fruit without needing to manage a huge sprawling harvest. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill reduces size and quality. Judge ripeness by the ground spot turning from white to yellow and a dull, hollow thump when the fruit is tapped. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Harvester Peach (Mid-South Early Freestone Peach, Gulf South Yellow Freestone)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit in April to 6–8 inches; Harvester matures early (late May to mid-June in most of the Gulf South), making it one of the earliest large-fruited peaches; prune annually to open-vase form; good for direct-market sales and home fresh eating — early ripening gives it a market window before the main-season varieties arrive. Harvester is an early-season yellow freestone peach variety developed by North Carolina State University and the USDA (released 1971) that became an important variety for mid-South commercial peach production throughout the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee, and the Gulf South for its ability to deliver large, well-flavored, fully freestone yellow peaches earlier in the season than the standard mid-season benchmarks like Elberta and Loring. Early-season peach varieties command premium prices in direct farm markets because consumers are eager for the first fresh peaches of the year, and Harvester's ripening time — typically late May to mid-June in zone 7–9 — puts it among the first significant-sized freestone peaches available in most markets. The fruits are medium to large, round, with an attractive red blush over yellow skin, firm yellow flesh, and a clean freestone pit at full maturity. The chill hour requirement of approximately 750 hours fits the mid-South and Gulf South climate well in most winters, making Harvester a reliable producer under typical zone 7–8 conditions. Trees are vigorous and productive with moderate disease susceptibility requiring a standard spray program for brown rot and other peach diseases. An excellent choice for home orchardists who want the earliest possible fresh peach harvest. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Haschberg Elderberry (European Black Elderberry)
description: Plant in fertile, evenly moist soil and prune out the oldest stems each dormant season to keep the multi-stemmed shrub productive, since fruit forms on both new and one-year-old wood. Haschberg is a European black elderberry selection widely grown across Central Europe for its heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries used in juice, syrup, and wine production. It produces broad, flat flower heads of creamy white blooms in early summer that are themselves used for cordials, followed by large, drooping fruit clusters in late summer. It is vigorous and consistently productive, and benefits from a second elderberry cultivar nearby for improved pollination and yield. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Haskap
description: Plant Haskap in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; always plant two or more compatible cultivars for cross-pollination; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; berries ripen 2–3 weeks before strawberries and should be harvested promptly. Lonicera caerulea var. edulis and its cultivated selections (Honeyberry or Haskap) represent one of the hardiest edible shrubs in cultivation — tolerating temperatures to -40°F or below in adapted varieties, and withstanding late spring frosts during bloom thanks to early-season cold-hardiness of the flowers. Two compatible cultivars are essential for reliable fruiting, as the species is largely self-incompatible; many named Canadian and Japanese breeding program selections are available for pairing. The elongated, dark blue-black berries are nutritionally similar to blueberries but with a distinctly more complex flavor — sweet-tart with blueberry, raspberry, and elderberry undertones and a pleasant tartness. The shrubs are extremely long-lived (50+ years), begin bearing in year 2–3 after planting, and require minimal pruning beyond removing deadwood. Excellent for northern gardens where blueberries struggle, and the extremely early ripening season makes them valuable for extending the fresh-fruit season. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hass Avocado Tree
description: The world's most popular avocado, Hass produces rich, buttery fruit with pebbly skin that darkens as it ripens. Grow in full sun with fast-draining soil, as avocados are extremely sensitive to soggy roots. Water deeply but infrequently and protect from frost, growing in a large pot indoors where winters are cold. It is partly self-fertile, though a second avocado nearby improves fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hasta La Pasta Spaghetti Squash (Large-Fruited Heirloom Spaghetti Squash)
description: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since the vigorous vines need considerably more room than a compact bush spaghetti type. Hasta La Pasta produces oblong, pale cream fruit that dwarfs standard spaghetti squash, often reaching 6 to 8 pounds per fruit, so a single squash can provide strands enough for several meals. Once baked or boiled, the flesh separates into the same long, mild, pasta-like strands that make spaghetti squash a popular low-carbohydrate substitute, but the increased size makes it a better fit for larger households or preservation. Harvest when the rind has toughened to a deep cream color and resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry location for two to three months. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Hasya Sapodilla
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hasya is the leading commercial sapodilla cultivar in Mexico, selected for extra-large, football-shaped fruit that can weigh close to a pound, with a reddish-brown blush through the grainy, malty-sweet flesh. The tree grows into a large, upright form and bears prolifically once mature, with fruit maturing over a long window from late fall through late spring in warm climates. Fruit must be harvested mature but firm and allowed to ripen off the tree for several days until it yields to gentle pressure, since sapodilla picked too green stays astringent with latex and never develops proper sweetness. Sapodilla is highly wind- and salt-tolerant and, once established, one of the most drought-resistant of the common tropical fruit trees. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Hatch Green Chile
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil rich in phosphorus after all frost risk has passed. Hatch green chile refers to New Mexico-style long green chiles — varieties such as NuMex Big Jim, Joe Parker, and the heritage 6-4 — bred at New Mexico State University and grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico; they produce 6–10 inch, elongated, thick-walled green pods with heat levels ranging from mild to hot depending on cultivar and growing conditions. The distinctive flavor comes from the dry, high-altitude climate, but home gardeners in zones 7–11 with hot, dry summers can produce excellent results in-ground. Harvest green when pods are fully sized and char-blister them on a grill or under a broiler; the roasted flavor is unmatched for green chile sauces, stews, and salsas. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Hatch Green Chile
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the New Mexico type chile, particularly Hatch and its relatives, is the defining pepper of Southwestern cuisine, eaten green (roasted), red (dried), or ground into chile powder. This long, mildly hot pepper (1,500–3,000 SHU) averages 6–8 inches and is the standard for roasting — the thick walls blister perfectly under a broiler or over an open flame, and the roasted, peeled chiles freeze beautifully for months. Harvest green through September, or leave some to ripen red for a fully different flavor profile. The Hatch designation technically refers to chiles grown in the Hatch Valley of New Mexico, but the variety performs excellently throughout zone 9. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Hausa Potato (Frafra Potato)
description: A close relative of Livingstone potato in the mint family, Hausa potato forms a much lower, more compact plant that produces dense clusters of small, pea- to walnut-sized tubers directly at its base rather than spread along trailing stems. It is a staple garden crop across West Africa, especially in Ghana and Nigeria where it is known as Frafra potato, and it is also cultivated in parts of southern India, where it goes by the name Chinese potato or koorka. Propagate from small whole tubers saved from the previous harvest, planted similarly to seed potatoes in loose, fertile soil. Harvest once the compact foliage yellows, usually four to five months after planting; the nutty, slightly resinous tubers store best left in the ground until just before use. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Haut Black Raspberry (Late-Ripening Maryland-Bred Black Raspberry)
description: Set out dormant canes or rooted tip layers in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow good air movement between canes. Haut came out of the University of Maryland's black raspberry breeding program and was released in 1984, valued mainly for ripening about three to five days behind earlier standards like Bristol and Jewel, which lets a home planting spread its blackcap harvest over a longer stretch of summer rather than concentrating it into a single flush. Head back the tips of vigorous new primocanes in midsummer to force the lateral branches that will carry the following year's crop, and cut spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest to reduce disease carryover into the next season. Because black raspberries are prone to cane diseases in humid weather, favor an open, breezy planting site and avoid working around wet foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Havasupai 60-Day Bean (Grand Canyon Fast-Maturing Heirloom)
description: Havasupai 60-Day is a fast-maturing common bean maintained by the Havasupai people of the Grand Canyon's Havasu Canyon, bred over generations for the short frost-free window and monsoon-dependent moisture of a high-desert canyon growing season. The compact bush plants set pods quickly and dry down within about two months, yielding small, mottled tan-and-brown seeds with a mild, earthy flavor typical of Southwestern dry beans. Because it was selected for arid conditions, it tolerates heat and irregular watering better than many bush dry beans, though a deep soak at flowering improves pod set. Harvest once pods are fully dry and papery, and save seed from the earliest-maturing plants to maintain the variety's signature speed. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Hawaiian Ipu Gourd (Ipu Nui)
description: This Hawaiian strain of bottle gourd is traditionally grown along the ground rather than on a trellis, which lets the fruit develop the rounder, double-bulbed form prized for carving the ipu heke gourd drum and other hula implements, rather than the elongated shapes that result from vertical training. Give the sprawling vine a generous patch of warm, fertile soil in full sun and water regularly through fruit set. Both a sweeter-fleshed strain historically used for food and a more bitter strain grown strictly for vessels have been selected over centuries, so flavor of immature fruit can vary by seed source. Harvest for craft use only after the fruit fully matures and the stem dries, then cure for several weeks in a dry, ventilated space until the shell hardens completely before hollowing and finishing. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Hawaiian Red Turmeric (Red-Stemmed Ornamental-Edible Turmeric)
description: Plant rhizome pieces 2-4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun. Hawaiian Red turmeric bears the same broad, canna-like paddle leaves as standard turmeric, but with striking red-tinged stems and leaf bases that add ornamental appeal to a tropical garden bed even before the pale flower spikes emerge from the leaf bases in summer, all while producing the same aromatic, deep orange-yellow edible rhizome used fresh or dried in cooking. Harvest rhizomes in fall after the leaves die back naturally, which signals the completion of rhizome development, and store a portion frost-free to replant the following spring in zones where the crown does not reliably overwinter. Turmeric grows best under the same warm, humid, partially shaded, consistently moist conditions favored by its ginger relatives. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Hawaiian Yellow Ginger
description: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in dappled shade to morning sun; hill soil up around the base as the plant grows, similar to potatoes, to encourage larger rhizome development. 'Hawaiian Yellow' is a distinct culinary ginger strain grown widely in Hawaii, prized for its thin brown skin covering bright golden-yellow flesh with a fuller, more pungent bite than typical grocery-store ginger. It can be harvested young in late summer for tender, mild 'stem ginger,' or left in the ground until foliage dies back in fall for fully mature, storable rhizomes. In zone 9, plants die back after frost but the rhizome survives if mulched; further north, treat as an annual or lift and store rhizomes indoors over winter. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Hawke's Champagne Rhubarb
description: Hawke's Champagne is a classic English forcing rhubarb known for pushing up exceptionally early, slender pink-red stalks when crowns are covered with a forcing pot or brought into a dark shed in late winter. Left unforced it still crops earlier than most maincrop varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners chasing the first rhubarb of the year. Its slender stalks are sweeter and less fibrous than the stalks of many later, thicker-stemmed cultivars, needing less added sugar in cooking. Rest forced crowns for a full season afterward so they can rebuild reserves before forcing again. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hawkeye Plum (H.A. Terry Iowa Heirloom American Plum)
description: Grow in full sun on well-drained soil with a compatible American plum planted nearby, since Hawkeye is self-incompatible and will not fruit reliably alone. Hawkeye was introduced around 1882 by pioneering Iowa plum breeder H.A. Terry of Crescent, Iowa, one of the most prolific selectors of native plum during the 19th-century Midwest plum-breeding era, and it became one of the more widely distributed named American plum varieties of its time. The medium to large fruit ripens red over yellow flesh with a sweet-tart flavor well suited to fresh eating as well as canning and preserves. As with other heirloom American plum selections, expect root suckering that can be managed by removing unwanted sprouts, and expect the tree to tolerate harsh winters and drought far better than European or Japanese plum types. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hayman Sweet Potato (Old-Time Southern Heirloom White-Fleshed Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun, ridging the row to keep the developing roots from sitting in wet soil. Hayman is an old-time Southern heirloom sweet potato, once one of the most widely grown varieties across the Carolinas and Georgia before modern commercial types like Beauregard displaced it, valued for its pale tan skin, dry, mealy, cream-white to pale-yellow flesh, and a mild, chestnut-like sweetness quite different from the moist orange-fleshed types now common in supermarkets. Vines are vigorous and heat-tolerant, sprawling widely and shading out weeds once established, and the roots store exceptionally well through winter when cured properly. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skins and convert starches to sugar, improving both flavor and keeping quality. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Hayward Kiwi (Classic Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Hayward is the classic commercial fuzzy kiwifruit cultivar behind nearly every kiwi sold in grocery stores, prized for its large size, bright green flesh, and well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. Like all fuzzy kiwi it needs a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days; it is dioecious, so a compatible male vine (roughly one male for every 6–8 female vines) must be planted nearby for pollination, since Hayward itself is a female-fruiting cultivar. Train vines on a sturdy T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each winter to control the vigorous growth and keep fruiting wood renewed. Harvest in late fall before hard frost once the seeds have turned black, and finish ripening the firm fruit indoors at room temperature. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Hazel Alder (Tag Alder, Smooth Alder)
description: Plant in consistently wet, moist-to-saturated soil along stream edges, pond margins, or low wet areas in full sun to partial shade; hazel alder is a multi-stemmed native shrub or small tree that thrives where few plants can, colonizing eroded stream banks and stabilizing them with a dense fibrous root system. Like other alders it hosts nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria in root nodules, enriching surrounding soil and supporting the broader riparian plant community. Reddish-purple male catkins emerge as early as February before any leaves appear, providing critical early-season pollen for queen bumblebees and other overwintered insects. The persistent woody seed cones persist through winter and are eaten by redpolls, goldfinches, and other seed-eating birds. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Hazelnut / Filbert
description: Hazelnuts require cross-pollination and are wind-pollinated, so plant at least two different cultivars within 20 feet of each other; pollen is shed in late winter before leaves emerge. American hazelnut (C. americana) is hardier and more disease-resistant than European types; many gardeners grow hybrid selections for both traits. Eastern filbert blight (Anisogramma anomala) is a serious fungal disease in the eastern United States — choose blight-resistant cultivars such as Jefferson or York for eastern plantings. Harvest in late summer when nuts begin to fall from the husks on their own. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: He-Shi-Ko Bunching Onion (Japanese Heirloom Scallion)
description: He-Shi-Ko is a traditional Japanese heirloom bunching onion that never forms a bulb, instead sending up tall, slender, silvery-white stalks that clump and multiply from the base as the plant matures. Sow thickly in rows and thin gradually, harvesting the largest stalks first and letting the remaining plants continue dividing for a repeated, cut-and-come-again supply through the season. Its mild, non-pungent flavor and tender texture make it a preferred variety for fresh eating raw or lightly cooked rather than for strong-flavored cooked onion dishes. He-Shi-Ko tolerates both cold and heat reasonably well, so gardeners often maintain a planting from early spring sowing through fall harvest without needing a second crop. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Head Cabbage
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant out 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; cabbage is a cool-season crop that tolerates hard frosts once established, and fall crops initiated in midsummer often produce the best heads as the crop matures into cool autumn weather. Space plants widely — 18–24 inches — as crowding produces smaller heads. Water consistently throughout head development, as irregular watering causes the heads to crack open; harvest immediately if heads show any cracking. Cabbage is susceptible to clubroot, cabbage worms, and aphids; row covers over young transplants provide excellent pest protection. Head types range from small early varieties (70 days) to large late storage types (120 days) suitable for long-term kraut fermentation. Matures in 70–120 days from transplant.

name: Head Lettuce (Butterhead)
description: Sow seed at 1/8 in depth and thin to 8–12 in once seedlings are 2 in tall; butterhead types form loose, tender heads with buttery inner leaves. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch to maintain cool root temperatures, as heat quickly triggers bolting. Harvest heads by cutting at the base when they feel moderately firm but before the center begins to elongate, which signals imminent bolting. Outer leaves can be removed as the head develops to stretch the harvest period over several weeks. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Headquarters Pecan (Alabama Scab-Resistant Elliott-Type Selection for Low-Spray Orchards)
description: Headquarters is an Alabama selection, likely a seedling of Elliott, identified by Alabama Extension horticulturists for its ability to crop heavily with no fungicide sprays in Alabama trials. Nuts resemble Elliott but are noticeably larger, though kernel quality runs somewhat behind Elliott, which led breeding programs to discontinue further testing of the cultivar. For Gulf Coast home growers who prioritize disease resistance and low maintenance over show-quality kernels, Headquarters remains a scab-resistant option worth sourcing from specialty nurseries. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Health Kick Tomato
description: Health Kick is a determinate saladette-paste hybrid bred by Seminis to concentrate roughly 50 percent more lycopene than a standard tomato while keeping a broad disease-resistance package that includes Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, tomato spotted wilt virus, and bacterial speck. Compact plants stay under three feet and need only minimal caging, making them well suited to smaller raised-bed plantings. The 3-5 ounce cylindrical fruits work equally well diced fresh, roasted, or cooked into sauce. Choose this variety when disease resistance and nutritional density matter as much as culinary versatility. Matures in 72–78 days from transplant.

name: Heartleaf Peppervine
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, organically rich soil at the base of a large, sturdy support structure, watering thoroughly and mulching to retain moisture through the first growing season while the root system establishes. Heartleaf peppervine is a vigorous deciduous vine native to floodplain forests and bottomland thickets of the southeastern US, recognized by its broad, bold, heart-shaped leaves and the showy clusters of small berries that ripen from green through turquoise to blue-black in fall, providing an important food source for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and other songbirds. This large-scale native vine is well suited to covering fences, large arbors, and the trunks of substantial trees in moist, lowland sites where vigorous growth is desired and space is not limiting. Once established on fertile, consistently moist soil, it requires no supplemental care and will cover its support structure rapidly; direct new growth as needed to keep the vine on its intended structure. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Heartnut
description: Heartnut is a variety of Japanese walnut bearing distinctively heart-shaped nuts that crack open cleanly along a suture to release a whole kernel — unlike black walnut, which requires significant effort to extract meat. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but yield better with a second tree; they begin bearing in 4–7 years from grafted stock. Heartnut is notably less allelopathic than black walnut, making it more garden-friendly as a specimen tree. Nuts fall in clusters in late summer to early fall; hull and dry for 2–3 weeks before cracking and storing. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Heartogold Sweet Potato (1947 LSU Heirloom, Tan Skin Bright Orange Flesh)
description: Heartogold is an early, heavy-yielding heirloom bred by Julian C. Miller at the LSU Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1947, producing tan-skinned roots with bright orange flesh on vigorous vining plants. It is one of the older Louisiana-bred varieties still maintained in germplasm collections, predating the Jewel-Beauregard-Covington succession of commercial standards. Sclerotial blight, a soil-borne fungal disease, tends to show up on Heartogold more readily than on many other varieties, so avoid planting in poorly drained or previously infected beds. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after harvest to develop full sweetness before storage. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Hearts of Gold Cantaloupe
description: A productive heirloom muskmelon well suited to short-season climates, bearing round 3-pound fruits with dark orange, firm, aromatic flesh. Direct sow into warmed soil after frost, or start indoors a couple of weeks early in cooler regions. Give vines room to sprawl and keep them evenly watered until the fruit begins to net and ripen. Harvest at full slip when the fruit releases from the vine with gentle pressure. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Hearts of Gold Melon
description: Hearts of Gold is a beloved heirloom cantaloupe with fragrant, honey-sweet orange flesh, usually maturing at two to three pounds. Sow directly into warm, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Keep moisture even during fruit set and growth, then reduce watering as the melons ripen to boost flavor. Harvest when fruit slips easily from the vine and gives off a strong sweet aroma. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Heat Wave II Tomato (Gulf South High-Heat Fruit-Setting Hybrid Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Heat Wave II is one of the most important tomato introductions for Gulf South gardeners — a hybrid specifically developed for heat tolerance to maintain fruit set during the high-temperature periods (daytime highs above 90–95°F) that cause standard tomato varieties to drop flowers without setting fruit. In zone 9, most standard tomato varieties produce well in spring (March–May) then cease fruiting when summer heat arrives in June; Heat Wave II's genetic ability to set fruit at high temperatures extends the productive season into summer conditions that defeat other varieties. The medium-large (6–8 oz), round, globe-shaped fruits have bright-red color, firm flesh, and good fresh-eating flavor — not the finest gourmet tomato, but extremely reliable production in conditions that eliminate the competition. Heat Wave II is a determinate (bush-type) tomato growing 4–5 feet that can be grown with minimal staking. Disease resistance includes V, F, FF, N, T — a comprehensive disease package for Gulf South conditions where soilborne disease pressure is high. For zone 9 gardeners who want tomatoes through the summer rather than only spring and fall, Heat Wave II is the primary recommendation. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Heath Speedwell (European Tea)
description: Veronica officinalis forms a low, ground-hugging mat of hairy, oval, scalloped leaves on trailing stems that root as they spread, sending up short spikes of small pale-blue to lilac flowers with darker veining in early summer. Native to dry heaths, moors, and open woodland across Europe, it was once dried and steeped as a substitute for imported tea, giving rise to the old name European tea, and used in folk medicine for coughs, catarrh, and minor skin irritations. Grow in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; overly rich or wet ground encourages rot and weakens the tight, mat-forming habit. Trim lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and encourage fresh rooting along the stems. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Heatmaster Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Heatmaster is a hybrid tomato developed specifically for gardeners in hot-summer climates (USDA zones 8–10) where standard tomato varieties drop their blossoms and fail to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F and daytime temperatures exceed 95°F. The proprietary Seminis breeding program tested hundreds of crosses before selecting a plant that maintains viable pollen and fruit set under extreme heat — making it one of the most important varieties for Gulf Coast, Southwest, and Deep South gardeners who struggle with the narrow spring window before heat arrives. Fruits are medium-large (8–10 oz), red, globe-shaped with good flavor and firm flesh. The indeterminate plant continues producing through periods of heat that stop Celebrity and Better Boy cold. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium, Tobacco mosaic virus, and nematodes. For zone 9 gardeners frustrated by tomatoes that stop producing in May, Heatmaster extends the harvest window by 3–5 weeks. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Heavy Hitter Okra (High-Yield Branching Oklahoma Heirloom Okra)
description: Sow seed directly in the garden after danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. Heavy Hitter was developed by grower Ron Cook of Dry Creek Farm in Oklahoma and selected specifically for extreme productivity, with well-branched plants reaching up to 7 feet tall that can set well over 100 pods per plant across a season. Because multiple pods form at each node rather than one at a time, plants need daily or near-daily picking once production ramps up to keep pods from fibering over and to keep the heavy-bearing plant setting new fruit. This branching habit makes Heavy Hitter a strong choice for gardeners who want maximum yield from a small number of plants. Matures in 56–65 days from seed.

name: Hedelfingen Cherry (Hedelfinger Riesenkirsche, German Heirloom Sweet Cherry)
description: Hedelfingen, known fully in Germany as Hedelfinger Riesenkirsche, is a 19th-century heirloom sweet cherry from the village of Hedelfingen near Stuttgart, bearing large, dark mahogany-red to near-black, heart-shaped fruit with rich, sweet flavor. It is self-unfruitful but blooms in the mid-to-late window that overlaps with many other sweet cherry cultivars, which has made it a long-standing standard pollinizer choice in commercial and heirloom orchards alike, including for late-season cultivars such as Regina. The fruit has moderate resistance to cracking compared with older, softer-fleshed heirlooms, though it is less crack-tolerant than modern firm-fleshed releases. Net trees against birds as fruit colors, and provide deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development to reduce splitting. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hedou Tiny Bok Choy
description: Direct sow shallowly and keep the soil surface consistently moist, since this micro bok choy's shallow roots dry out quickly compared to standard-sized types. Hedou produces miniature, whole heads barely larger than a bite, with pale stems and small tender leaves that need no chopping before cooking, and it thrives in the light shade of a container on a partly shaded porch or the dappled edge of a garden bed. Its small stature and fast pace make it forgiving of less-than-full sun, since a shorter daily light window still lets it reach harvest size before bolting becomes a concern. Pick whole heads at the base as soon as they firm up, and resow every few weeks for uninterrupted harvests through the cool season. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Heinz 1350 Tomato (Classic Canning Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Heinz 1350 is the classic determinate processing tomato developed by the H.J. Heinz Company, once widely grown commercially for ketchup production, that became a home garden favorite for anyone serious about canning, sauce-making, or tomato processing — it produces a concentrated set of uniform, medium-sized (5–6 oz), globe to slightly blocky, bright-red fruits with thick, meaty walls, small seed cavities, and very firm texture that holds up exceptionally well to cooking and reduces beautifully to rich tomato sauce without excessive water. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce the entire crop within a 3–4 week window, which is exactly what canners need — a predictable large harvest all at once rather than a continuous trickle. VF resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt) keeps plants healthy through the season. For zone 9, plant in late January to early February so the harvest window falls in late April through May before summer heat stresses the plants. An outstanding choice for serious home canning enthusiasts who want a reliable, high-yield processing crop. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Heirloom Gardens Mix Lettuce
description: A blend of four red and green lettuces including bibb, romaine, crisphead, and leaf types for varied color and texture in one bed. Direct sow in cool soil and thin as plants grow, eating the thinnings as baby greens. Keep the soil consistently moist and give afternoon shade in warm spells to slow bolting. Harvest outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again supply or cut whole heads at maturity. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Helenor Rutabaga (Purple-Top Storage Swede)
description: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to six to eight inches apart, giving the globes plenty of room to size up evenly. Helenor produces smooth, round roots with a purple-blushed shoulder above soil level fading to pale cream below, and dense, pale orange flesh with a fine texture and a mild, well-balanced flavor. Its coloring develops early and evenly, and mature roots hold their quality well in cool storage through winter. Leave roots in the ground into cooler fall weather before harvest, since a touch of cold noticeably sweetens the flavor. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Helios Radish (Golden-Yellow Spring Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Helios is a round spring radish with smooth, bright golden-yellow skin and crisp, mild white flesh, an eye-catching alternative to standard red radishes that adds warm color contrast to salads, relish trays, and mixed radish plantings. Flavor is clean and only mildly peppery, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Hemp (Grain/Seed)
description: Drill seed 3/4–1 in deep at 20–30 lb/acre for grain production (denser stands reduce branching and improve yield); hemp requires a federal or state license to grow legally in the United States. Plants are dioecious — female plants produce the seed-bearing flowers; for grain production allow plants to go naturally to seed and harvest when seeds are firm and no longer milky. Thresh and dry seed to below 10% moisture for storage; hulled hemp seed (hearts) is nutritionally rich in protein and balanced omega-3/6 fatty acids. Do not confuse grain hemp with high-THC varieties; certified grain cultivars contain less than 0.3% THC. Matures in 70–110 days from seed.

name: Henbit
description: Henbit is a low, square-stemmed winter annual in the mint family that carpets shaded and partly shaded garden beds, hedgerows, and orchard floors through the cold months with scalloped, clasping leaves and small purple-pink hooded flowers. The young shoots and leaves have a mild, faintly sweet, slightly minty flavor and can be tossed raw into winter salads or wilted briefly into soups and egg dishes, much like a gentler, softer-textured spinach. It thrives in the dappled shade under deciduous trees and shrubs where few other cool-season greens perform well, and self-sows so reliably that a single fall planting typically renews itself for years. Harvest whole young plants or pinch tips regularly before flowering, when the texture is most tender and least fibrous. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Henderson Bush Lima Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost in full sun, in fertile, well-drained soil; Henderson Bush Lima is the standard small-seeded bush lima bean, an heirloom selection dating to the 1880s that remains the most widely grown small white lima because of its outstanding heat tolerance, compact growth requiring no staking, and prolific production of small, tender, buttery beans in a compressed time frame. The small seed size means faster cooking than large limas and a creamier texture; it is excellent fresh, frozen, or dried as a dry bean. Space rows 18–24 inches apart for good air circulation and reduce disease pressure. Mulch to keep soil moist as pods develop. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Henderson Bush Lima Bean
description: This compact heirloom butterbean, introduced in the late 1800s, is loved for its reliability, mild flavor, and easy sprouting. Sow seeds directly into warm soil, as lima beans germinate poorly in cold or wet ground. The bushy plants need no staking and produce flat pods of small, creamy beans. Pick pods when plump for shelling fresh, or leave them to dry on the plant for storage beans. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Henderson Lima Bean (Baby Bush Lima, Heat-Tolerant Gulf South Butter Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest green for fresh use when pods are plump; leave to dry on the plant for dry beans. Henderson is a small-seeded bush lima bean — one of the most widely grown lima bean varieties in the American South and Gulf Coast region, where it is often marketed and sold as 'baby butter bean' or 'speckled butter bean' (referring to the speckled seed coloring of some strains). Henderson was introduced in the 1880s and has remained a staple in Southern gardening for over a century, valued for its small, tender seeds, heat tolerance, and reliable production in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf South that challenge larger-seeded lima types (such as Fordhook). The primary distinction between Henderson and Fordhook-type limas is seed size: Henderson produces small seeds roughly half the size of Fordhook, with a more tender skin and a creamier texture when cooked fresh or dried. In the Gulf South culinary tradition, 'butter beans' (the Southern name for fresh lima beans) are a staple of summer cooking — simmered low and slow with fatback or ham hock until very tender, the small Henderson seeds achieve a creamy, buttery texture that the variety's Southern common name accurately describes. Henderson also performs well as a dry bean: the small seeds dry quickly on the vine and cook to a smooth, creamy texture in soups and stews without requiring the long soaking and cooking time of larger bean types. The heat tolerance of Henderson is a practical advantage in zone 9: while cool-season beans (snap beans, peas) cannot be grown in summer, Henderson sets pods reliably in July-August temperatures that stop production in more sensitive varieties. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Hendre Huffcap Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Hendre Huffcap is one of the more precocious perry pears, bearing somewhat sooner than many other traditional varieties. A well-regarded Herefordshire perry pear producing large, elongated, aromatic fruit for the type, it yields fragrant, medium-tannin juice that makes for a softer, more approachable perry than the harshest bittersharp varieties, contributing floral aromatics valued by perry makers seeking a more delicate finished blend. Its comparatively earlier bearing age and good, consistent yields have made it one of the more commercially popular traditional perry pears for new plantings. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and develop aroma, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Henna (Egyptian Privet, Mehndi)
description: Lawsonia inermis is a many-branched, sometimes spiny shrub grown throughout the arid and semi-arid tropics for its leaves, which are dried and ground into the fine green powder used to dye hair, skin, fingernails, and textiles a reddish-orange to deep auburn color when mixed into a paste. The small, fragrant, cream-to-pink flower clusters are separately prized for perfumery. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well but need consistent warmth to thicken and produce a full canopy of harvestable foliage; in zones below 9 grow it in a large container and overwinter indoors near a bright window. Harvest mature leaves by hand-stripping branches once the shrub is well established, typically beginning in its second season, and allow the plant to regrow between harvests. Matures in 150–240 days from seed.

name: Hera Dill
description: Hera is a compact, uniform dill bred specifically for bunching and baby-leaf production, with attractive blue-green feathery foliage held on short, sturdy stalks. It bolts noticeably later than older market varieties, holding its leafy stage roughly two extra weeks before flowering, which gives growers a longer window to harvest whole bunches for market or kitchen use. The short internodes and dense foliage make it well suited to close spacing and container culture as well as field rows. Cut whole stems near the base for bunching, or shear the tips repeatedly for a steady supply of fresh dill weed. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Herb Robert (Red Robin)
description: Direct sow or allow to self-sow in moist, shaded, rocky or well-drained soil under trees, along walls, or in shaded garden beds; herb Robert is a dainty annual or biennial with deeply cut, ferny foliage that smells of turpentine when bruised — a scent that may repel insects, which accounts for part of its old folk-medicine reputation as a pest deterrent. The small, bright magenta-pink flowers appear from spring through fall and attract small native bees. In traditional European herbal medicine, the plant was used as an astringent and anti-inflammatory poultice; modern research has found antibacterial compounds in the leaf. In partly shaded rock gardens, walls, and woodland edges, herb Robert forms charming self-sustaining colonies without becoming aggressive. The foliage turns bright red in fall, giving rise to the common name 'red robin.' Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Herbemont Grape (Historic 1800s South Carolina Wine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Herbemont is a historic wine grape dating to the early 1800s in South Carolina, one of the older American hybrid grapes still valued today for its strong tolerance of Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection that has limited European wine grape production across the humid South for two centuries. It produces small, dark, sweet-tart berries used historically and still today for wine, offering a taste of the region's viticultural history along with genuine disease resilience that many modern hybrids still aim to match. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and airflow. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hercules Dill
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — do not transplant; Hercules is a compact, bolt-resistant dill variety developed for gardeners and market growers who need an extended leaf harvest before the plant flowers. Unlike standard dill that rushes to bolt in warm weather, Hercules delays flowering by 2–3 weeks under similar conditions, producing a longer window of dense, feathery, aromatic foliage harvest — the primary advantage over standard open-pollinated dill types. The plant grows to a more compact 24–36 inches rather than the 4–5 foot height of standard dill, making it easier to grow in containers or small spaces without the flopping and staking required for large dill plants. The leaf flavor is identical to standard dill — fresh, bright, anise-like — and is equally useful in all dill applications from cold fish preparations to tzatziki, potato salads, and dill pickles. In zone 9 the compact habit makes Hercules the better choice for the brief spring dill season before heat ends production. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Hercules Southern Pea (Large-Seeded Crowder Cowpea)
description: Hercules was released in 1981 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station, bred by longtime breeder Roy Ogle. It is a large-seeded crowder type with straight 8-9 inch pods held upright on a bushy, short-runnered plant, and coffee-colored crowder seed that shells easily. Matures around 75 days, later than most bush purple hull types, rewarding the wait with an especially large, meaty pea. Best suited to gardeners who want a heavier-seeded crowder flavor distinct from cream or blackeye types. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Herd's Mammoth Loquat (Extra-Large-Fruited Heirloom Loquat)
description: This old California heirloom loquat is grown chiefly for producing some of the largest individual fruits of any named loquat cultivar, with an orange, mildly sweet flesh and a correspondingly large seed cavity. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil with generous spacing, since the vigorous growth habit and heavy fruit clusters need room to develop without crowding. Thin fruit aggressively after fruit set to concentrate size and prevent limb sag, and stake or brace young scaffold branches during the first heavy crop. As with all loquats, protect the fall-to-winter bloom period from freezes, since flower loss is the main obstacle to consistent cropping in zone 8b. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Herefordshire Russet Apple (Disease-Resistant Nutty Russet Apple)
description: Herefordshire Russet was bred by the English nursery Frank P. Matthews from a cross involving Egremont Russet, aiming to combine classic russet flavor with stronger resistance to apple scab and powdery mildew than older russet varieties typically offer. The golden-brown, rough-skinned fruit ripens in mid fall with a dry, nutty, honeyed flavor characteristic of russet apples. Because it needs less fungicide intervention than many heirloom russets, it is a practical choice for home growers in humid regions where scab pressure is high. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hergo Sea Buckthorn
description: Hergo is a German-bred female sea buckthorn cultivar prized for producing some of the largest individual berries of any named selection, borne in tight orange clusters along the previous year's wood, which makes it a favorite for growers pressing juice or oil at a small commercial scale. It ripens in mid-season, generally a bit ahead of the largest Russian selections, and shares the thorny, silvery-leaved, nitrogen-fixing growth habit typical of the species. As a dioecious shrub it sets little or no fruit without a nearby male sea buckthorn in bloom at the same time. Because the tart berries cling firmly to the stem, most growers harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches and stripping or freezing them rather than picking individual berries by hand. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Heritage Raspberry
description: Plant 'Heritage' canes in well-drained loam enriched with compost, spacing them 2-3 feet apart in rows. This reliable everbearing (primocane) variety fruits on first-year canes in late summer and again the following early summer. For a single heavy fall crop, mow all canes to the ground each late winter. Provide a trellis or T-post support and keep beds mulched to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Herrenhausen Ornamental Oregano
description: Herrenhausen is an RHS Award of Garden Merit selection distinguished from other ornamental oreganos by near-black stems and bracts that make the rose-pink flower clusters appear to glow, and by a tidy, non-flopping habit that holds up from June through the first hard frost. The young foliage emerges with a purple flush before settling to grey-green, adding a second season of interest before bloom. It is grown for pollinators and dried-flower structure rather than the kitchen, since its essential oil content is much lower than culinary Greek oregano. Cut the spent flower stems back hard in late winter to keep the woody base compact for another season. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Herskovitz Pomegranate
description: Herskovitz is a small-fruited, early-season pomegranate from Israel commonly grown as a comparison cultivar alongside Acco and Wonderful in orchard trials. Its arils have a tangier, more tart-forward flavor than sweeter dessert cultivars and firmer seeds, which makes it a good choice for juicing or for gardeners who prefer a less cloying pomegranate. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil; the tree is naturally shrubby and compact, so it fits well in smaller Gulf Coast landscapes if given room to spread. Water deeply but infrequently once established, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size on the remaining fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hestia Brussels Sprout (AAS-Winning Heat and Cold-Tolerant Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants and top the growing tip once bottom sprouts reach marble size to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Hestia was named an All-America Selections Regional Winner for the Southeast specifically for its ability to tolerate the warmer fall temperatures typical of a Gulf Coast growing season while still developing tight, high-quality sprouts as the weather cools, and its sprouts resist bursting and rot better than many older varieties in humid conditions. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm, and expect flavor to sweeten after a light frost. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Hewes Virginia Crab Apple (Colonial-Era Cider Crabapple)
description: Grown at Monticello and documented by Thomas Jefferson himself, this small, hard, tannic crabapple was a workhorse of colonial Virginia cider production, adding astringency and complexity when blended with sweeter apples at the press. The tree is markedly tougher and more disease-resistant than standard dessert apples, tolerating poorer soil and less spray attention. Fruit is far too tannic and small to eat out of hand, so it is grown specifically as a blending variety for traditional heritage ciders. Choose it to recreate historically accurate colonial-style cider or to add backbone to a home cider blend. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hi Ho Silver Creeping Thyme
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil — creeping thyme fails in wet or heavy soils; Hi Ho Silver is a variegated creeping thyme (Thymus praecox) with silver-margined leaves that create a two-tone silver-and-green appearance across the mat-forming plant, making it one of the most ornamentally attractive thymes available for groundcover use. The tiny, silver-edged leaves are fragrant when brushed or crushed and are mildly culinary — suitable as a garnish and for light flavoring, though not as potently flavored as upright culinary thyme varieties. In spring (March–April in zone 9) the entire mat is covered with small pink-lavender flowers that are highly attractive to bees and beneficial insects. Hi Ho Silver is widely used in rock gardens, between stepping stones where foot traffic releases the fragrance, as an edging plant, and as a fragrant groundcover in herb gardens. The prostrate, spreading habit fills in gaps efficiently without becoming invasive in well-drained soils. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Hi-Crop Collards (Heat-Tolerant Hybrid Smooth-Leaf Collard)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this F1 hybrid was bred for commercial-style uniformity, producing tall, upright plants with smooth, dark blue-green leaves held tightly on a strong central stalk that resists lodging in wind. Hi-Crop tolerates late-summer heat noticeably better than heirloom Southern collards, allowing growers to set plants out a few weeks earlier in fall and still avoid the bitterness that heat stress causes in less tolerant types. Its uniform growth habit and heavy leaf set make it well suited to multiple-pass harvesting, where the lower leaves are stripped repeatedly over several months while the growing point continues producing new leaves at the top. Matures in 55–68 days from transplant.

name: Hican (Pecan-Hickory Hybrid, Bitternut Hican)
description: Plant grafted named-variety trees in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained bottomland soil in full sun; hicans are natural and intentionally bred hybrids between pecan (Carya illinoinensis) and various hickory species (most commonly shagbark or bitternut), combining traits of both parents — the nuts are usually larger and easier to crack than hickory but with a richer, more complex flavor than straight pecan, with less oil and a firmer, drier kernel. Trees are typically very vigorous and disease-resistant, combining pecan's productivity tendency with hickory's cold hardiness and adaptability. Suitable for zones 5–9 where pecan may be too tender or unreliable; an excellent choice for nut tree diversification in humid eastern forests. Requires cross-pollination from pecan or a compatible hickory nearby. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Hickory Cane Dent Corn (Pre-1875 Florida/Georgia Heirloom Field Corn)
description: Sow in blocks rather than single rows for good pollination, in fertile soil with steady moisture through tasseling and ear fill, since stalks of this variety can tower up to 15 feet. Hickory Cane predates 1875 and traces to corn grown in north Florida and south Georgia before spreading north through the Southern Appalachians as a staple grain corn. Plants typically carry one to two ears with large white kernels, and tightly wrapped husks help shield developing ears from weevils and earworms in the field.
