Left to dry fully on the stalk, the grain grinds into classic coarse white cornmeal and grits, and also makes excellent hominy. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Hickory King Corn
description: Hickory King is a historic heirloom white dent corn with unusually large kernels, ideal for grits, hominy, masa, and cornmeal. Sow directly into warm soil in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good pollination. Give plenty of nitrogen and steady moisture as the tall stalks develop. Let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvesting for grinding or long-term storage. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Hicks Everbearing Mulberry
description: Hicks Everbearing is a heritage North Carolina selection long thought lost before being rediscovered and reintroduced by fruit collector A.J. Bullard. It is more cold-hardy than black mulberry and drops slender, dark, mildly flavored berries continuously for up to four months, historically valued as a hog-forage tree as much as a table fruit. Plant in full sun on rich, moist soil and expect a long-lived, large-statured tree; it can live over a century. Because fruiting continues so long, plan for a mulched drop zone or plant it well away from walkways. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hidatsa Red Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6 inches apart along a trellis or the stalks of sweet corn in the traditional Three Sisters companion planting arrangement. Hidatsa Red is a Native American heirloom dry pole bean from the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region (present-day North Dakota), with deep maroon-red seeds that cook to a creamy, full-bodied texture with an earthy, robust flavor well-suited to soups and stews; the variety was collected and preserved through the work of Alfred Mandan and introduced more widely by Seed Savers Exchange. Allow pods to ripen and dry completely on the vine; pods are tan with dark mottling when ready. An important cultural heritage bean that rewards the grower with both excellent eating and connection to a long agricultural tradition. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Hidatsa Red Indian Bean (Plains Native American Dry Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Hidatsa Red is a bush dry bean that does not require staking; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery, typically 85–100 days from planting. Hidatsa Red is a traditional bean variety of the Hidatsa people (also called Minitari or Gros Ventre), a Native American nation of the upper Missouri River valley in what is now North Dakota, where they cultivated beans, corn, and squash in the fertile bottomlands for centuries before European contact; the bean entered American heirloom preservation networks through ethnobotanical work documenting traditional Plains agriculture and was distributed by the Seed Savers Exchange. The medium-sized, kidney-shaped seeds are an unusual deep brick-red to maroon-red color — distinctive enough to recognize immediately among other dry beans — and cook to a tender, creamy texture with rich, earthy, complex flavor somewhat similar to kidney beans but with more character. In traditional Hidatsa cooking, the beans were dried and stored for winter use, then slow-cooked in stews with dried meat and corn; they are equally excellent in modern preparations — chili, soups, slow-cooked bean dishes, and baked beans where the robust flavor is showcased. Well-adapted to short seasons and the variable conditions of the Northern Plains; good drought tolerance. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Hidatsa Shield Figure Bean (Native American Heirloom Dry Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent transplanting and rot readily in cold ground. Hidatsa Shield Figure is a Native American heirloom dry bean maintained by the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region, producing plump white beans strikingly marked with a dark maroon shield-shaped figure on one side, a traditional variety preserved and shared through indigenous seed-saving networks. Grown on sturdy bush plants, it is left on the vine until pods dry and rattle before harvest, then shelled for storage as a dry bean valued for its rich, creamy texture in soups and stews. Because it is open-pollinated and true-breeding, seed can be saved season to season, continuing a variety with deep cultural and agricultural history. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Hidatsa Squash
description: A traditional squash of the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River valley in present-day North Dakota, grown for generations as part of the Three Sisters companion planting system with corn and beans. Sow seeds directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vigorous vines are notably drought tolerant, reflecting their origin on the Northern Plains. Fruit is teardrop-shaped with salmon-pink skin and thick, deep orange flesh, typically ten to twenty inches long. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists puncture, then store in a cool, dry place, where its excellent keeping quality made it a reliable winter food source. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Hidcote English Lavender (Compact Deep-Purple English Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage (amended sandy or gravelly soil if needed) and avoid heavy clay or consistently moist soils; trim after flowering to maintain compact shape; in zones 8–9 plant in fall for establishment before summer heat; Hidcote lavender requires excellent air circulation to prevent fungal issues in humid climates. Hidcote is one of the most beloved and widely planted English lavender cultivars in the world, named for the famous English Arts and Crafts garden Hidcote Manor in Gloucestershire — a National Trust property renowned for its rare plants and structured garden design, where this compact, very dark-purple lavender was popularized. The cultivar has been a standard in English lavender since the early 20th century and is recognized by its distinctive characteristics: very compact, tightly mounding habit (12–18 inches rather than the 24–36 of open-pollinated English lavenders), intensely deep purple-violet flowers (darker than almost all other English lavender varieties), and silver-gray foliage. The deep color makes Hidcote one of the most visually striking lavenders for formal planting designs, knot gardens, edging borders, and formal herb gardens. The fragrance is intensely sweet in the characteristic English lavender style — considered by many perfumers to be the most refined and complex of all lavender types, with a floral-camphorous-sweet balance that is the reference fragrance for culinary lavender and lavender products. Hidcote is the lavender for people who want compact, tidy, deeply colored plants for formal or small-space settings. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Hidcote Pink English Lavender
description: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, matching the growing conditions of its parent 'Hidcote' but watching for shadier or damper spots that can wash out the delicate flower color. This compact selection shares the tight, mounding habit and silver-gray foliage of classic 'Hidcote' but bears soft pink-lilac flower spikes instead of deep purple, giving formal herb gardens and edging plantings a softer color option without sacrificing the well-known cultivar's neat form. Shear back after the main flush of bloom to keep the mound dense and to encourage a possible light rebloom later in the season. Good air circulation is essential in humid climates to prevent fungal disease common to tightly mounded lavenders. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Hidden Rose Apple (Airlie Red Flesh)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking young trees and watering deeply through the first two seasons while roots establish. Hidden Rose, also sold as Airlie Red Flesh, was discovered as a chance seedling near Airlie, Oregon, and is unusual for having rose-pink flesh throughout the fruit rather than just a blush near the skin, a trait that holds up well when the fruit is cooked or baked into rosy sauces and pastries. The medium apple has a green-gold skin overlaid with a dusty red-pink flush, and the dense flesh is crisp with a bright, tangy-sweet, berry-like flavor that fresh-eating fans and cider blenders both prize for its color and acidity. Fruit ripens in the second half of the season and keeps reasonably well in cold storage; thin the crop in early summer to improve fruit size and support annual bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Higgins Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil and provide a pollinator vine; Higgins is a Georgia Experiment Station-released muscadine variety renowned for producing fruits of extraordinary size — large white (bronze-skinned) muscadines reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter, among the very largest in the muscadine world. The large, pale bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, rich, floral muscadine flavor and a tender skin that makes fresh eating considerably more pleasant than older tough-skinned varieties. Higgins is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the impressive fruit size creates visual impact at farmers' markets and U-pick operations. As a female-flowered (pistillate) variety, Higgins requires a perfect-flowered pollinator nearby — without cross-pollination the vine sets little or no fruit. Plant alongside Ison, Triumph, or another self-fertile muscadine for reliable production. In zone 9 the long, warm summer provides ideal conditions for the large fruits to develop to their full potential size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Highbush Blueberry
description: Blueberries require acidic soil with a pH of 4.5–5.5; amend with elemental sulfur and use acidic mulch such as pine bark or wood chips 3–4 in deep. Plant at least two cultivars for cross-pollination and better fruit set. Prune out old canes older than 6 years at the base each late winter to stimulate productive new wood. Harvest when berries turn deep blue and detach with minimal resistance, typically 7–10 days after color change. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Highgate Banana (Jamaica Gros Michel Selection)
description: Highgate is a Jamaican-selected clone within the historic Gros Michel subgroup, the richly flavored dessert banana that dominated world trade before Panama disease devastated commercial plantings in the mid-twentieth century. It grows into a very tall, heavy plant and needs generous space, deep fertile soil, and steady irrigation to fill out its large bunches. Because it is among the least cold-tolerant of the widely grown banana types and remains highly susceptible to Fusarium wilt in poorly drained soil, treat it as a specialty planting for collectors rather than a dependable annual cropper in zone 9a. Site it in the warmest, most sheltered corner of the garden and mulch the base heavily before winter. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Highland Burgundy Red Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; this British heirloom is one of the few potato cultivars with deep burgundy-red flesh that runs solidly through the tuber rather than just tinting the skin. The color, driven by anthocyanin pigments, fades only slightly with cooking, producing striking pink-tinged mash, roasted wedges, and chips. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty with a moderately dry, floury texture suited to baking and roasting more than boiling. Grow it as a novelty maincrop alongside white- and yellow-fleshed varieties for a dramatic color contrast at harvest and on the plate. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Highland Cream Thyme
description: Highland Cream is a culinary common thyme cultivar with attractive cream-margined leaves that add ornamental interest without sacrificing the classic strong thyme flavor used in cooking. It grows best in poor to average, well-drained soil and full sun, and struggles in heavy, wet clay. Shear back by about a third after flowering to prevent woodiness and to keep the variegation fresh and dense. Harvest sprigs regularly through the growing season for the best flavor and to encourage compact new growth. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Highland Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, training young trees to an open-center or modified central-leader form for strong scaffold branches under a heavy crop load. Highland originated as a selection out of the Pacific Northwest pear industry and is grown as a productive, dependable alternative to straight Bartlett, ripening slightly later with firmer, longer-keeping flesh that holds up well in storage and shipping. It shares Bartlett's classic bell shape and greenish-yellow skin, and performs best with a mid-season pollinizer such as Anjou or Bosc nearby. Harvest while still hard and green, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best dessert texture. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Highlander Onion (F1 Hybrid Early Yellow Onion)
description: This extra-early long-day hybrid delivers large, uniform globes with light brown skin well before most main-season yellow onions are ready, making it a favorite for growers who want an early fresh-market crop. Direct-seed into fertile, well-worked soil as early as the ground can be tilled, thinning to final spacing once seedlings are a few inches tall. Because it bulbs quickly rather than storing long-term, plan to use or sell the crop within a few months of harvest rather than holding it over winter. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist through bulb formation for the largest, most uniform onions. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Hijinks Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Small Grooved Decorating Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow in hills after frost danger passes, giving the long vines, which can reach 15 feet, plenty of open ground or a sturdy trellis to climb. Hijinks was named an All-America Selections winner in 2011 for its unusually uniform 7-9 pound fruit, smooth deep-orange skin with distinctive grooves, and a strong, durable stem that makes an excellent handle. The variety shows notable resistance to powdery mildew and releases cleanly from the vine at harvest, both practical advantages in warm, humid growing regions. Pick once the rind has colored fully and hardened, leaving the handle intact, since Hijinks is prized as much for painting and porch display as for carving. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Hill Country Heirloom Red Okra
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in full sun in any well-drained soil; Hill Country Heirloom Red is a striking Texas heirloom okra with deep burgundy-red pods, stems, and leaf veins that make it as ornamental as it is productive. The pods are smooth with 5 ridges and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness; like all okra, the pods become fibrous if left to exceed 5–6 inches. The red pigmentation fades to green when cooked, similar to red-pod okra generally. Plants grow vigorously in the limestone soils and intense heat of Central Texas, where this variety has been grown by generations of families in the Hill Country region. Soaking seeds overnight in warm water before planting speeds germination. Harvest every 2–3 days in summer. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Hill Hardy Rosemary (Madalene Hill Cold-Hardy Rosemary)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; like other rosemary cultivars it dislikes rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages soft, frost-tender growth at the expense of cold hardiness. Hill Hardy is a cold-hardy rosemary selection associated with Madalene Hill, the pioneering Texas herb grower who also introduced Arp rosemary, and is prized alongside Arp as one of the more winter-tolerant named rosemary cultivars available to home gardeners in marginal climates. Its habit is semi-upright to spreading, somewhat looser than a compact culinary type, with the same piney, resinous fragrance and flavor as any standard rosemary, making it fully usable in the kitchen for roasting, grilling, and seasoning. Prune after flowering to maintain a dense, shapely plant, and avoid overwatering or heavy mulch against the crown, which invites root rot in humid Gulf South summers. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Hillary's Sweet Lemon Mint (Apple-Lime Hybrid Citrus Mint)
description: Bred from apple mint and lime mint parentage, Hillary's Sweet Lemon combines a sweet, fruity apple-mint aroma with a bright citrus edge that leans more toward lemon than either parent, making it a favorite for iced tea, fruit salads, and desserts. Like other aggressive running mints it is best confined to a container or a buried bottomless pot to keep its spreading rhizomes from overtaking neighboring beds. Give it rich, consistently moist soil and afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage lush and prevent scorching. Harvest and cut back regularly through the season to keep growth tender and to encourage a steady flush of fragrant new leaves. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Hillbilly Tomato
description: This West Virginia heirloom produces huge one-to-two-pound beefsteak fruits with striking yellow-and-red marbled coloring and sweet, low-acid flavor. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. The indeterminate vines can reach five feet or more and need sturdy staking or caging. Support heavy fruit clusters and harvest when the marbled fruits give slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Hillbilly Tomato (Appalachian Bicolor Yellow-Orange Striped Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Hillbilly (also called Hillbilly Potato Leaf) is a West Virginia heirloom beefsteak tomato of Appalachian origin — a large (12–24 oz), irregularly shaped, golden-yellow-orange fruit streaked and mottled with red to produce the characteristic bicolor pattern of this historic mountain heirloom. The Hillbilly's distinctive coloration differs from closely related varieties (Pineapple, Big Rainbow) in its specific yellow-orange background tone and the characteristic way the red streaking distributes across the fruit surface in bold, irregular patches. The flavor is outstanding: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a mild, rich character that has made Hillbilly one of the most enthusiastically recommended heirlooms by those who have grown it. 'Hillbilly Potato Leaf' plants display the characteristic potato-leaf (undivided, smooth-margined) foliage common among certain old Appalachian heirloom lineages. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type season after season. In zone 9, Hillbilly produces best in the spring window (February–June) before summer heat arrives — the very large fruits require the full spring season to reach their finest size and flavor quality. Sturdy support is required for the vigorous indeterminate vines. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Himbo Top Raspberry (Productive Swiss Fall-Bearing Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, and provide support for the tall, productive canes. Himbo Top was bred in Switzerland (its name drawn from the German word for raspberry, 'Himbeere') as a fall-bearing red raspberry, and it has become popular with commercial growers and home gardeners alike for combining very heavy yields with large, firm, well-flavored berries that hold their shape and quality well after picking. Producing fruit on current-season canes from late summer into fall, it can be managed with the simple annual mow-down pruning typical of primocane raspberries, making it a practical, high-yielding choice for gardeners who want strong production without complex cane management. Pick regularly during the fall fruiting window, since the heavy-bearing canes can set fruit faster than a light picking schedule can keep up with. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Himrod Grape (Cornell-Bred White Seedless Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Himrod was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and remains one of the most widely planted seedless table grapes for home gardens in cooler climates, producing loose clusters of amber-green, honey-sweet, crisp berries that ripen early in the season. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hinnomaki Red Gooseberry
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorny stems. Hinnomaki Red is a Finnish-bred gooseberry cultivar prized for combining reliable productivity, good mildew resistance, and outstanding fruit quality — the medium-sized berries ripen from green to a deep red-burgundy with a rich, sweet-tart flavor considered among the best of any gooseberry for fresh eating out of hand, as well as excellent for pies, jams, and fools. The compact, upright bush is more manageable and less sprawling than many older gooseberry varieties, and its Nordic breeding gives it strong cold hardiness alongside dependable disease resistance in cool, humid summer climates. Best suited to northern gardens with cool summers; in hot, humid zones the plant struggles with heat stress and powdery mildew regardless of afternoon shade. Zone 3–7. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hinnonmaki Red Gooseberry
description: 'Hinnonmaki Red' is a hardy Finnish gooseberry with dark-red, aromatic berries that are tart when green for cooking and sweet when fully ripe for dessert. It shows good mildew resistance and thrives in cool, moist conditions. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, well-drained soil and mulch to keep the roots cool. Prune to an open-centered bush in winter, removing crossing and low branches, and wear gloves when harvesting the thorny stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hinnonmaki Yellow Gooseberry
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open vase shape each winter for easier harvest among the thorns. Hinnonmaki Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the widely grown Hinnonmaki Red, bred in Finland from the same mildew-tolerant lineage and sharing its compact, upright, spiny habit. The translucent amber berries ripen a little later than the red form and carry a milder, honeyed sweetness many gardeners prefer straight off the bush, while both hold up well cooked into pies and preserves. Best suited to cool-summer climates, since heat and humidity bring on powdery mildew and fruit stress. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hiratanenashi Persimmon (Classic Flat Seedless Japanese Astringent Kaki)
description: Hiratanenashi, whose name translates roughly to flat and seedless, is a traditional Japanese cultivar formally recorded in the Shonai region of Yamagata Prefecture in 1887 and remains one of Japan's most widely grown persimmons. It is a strongly astringent, highly parthenocarpic type that reliably produces seedless, flattened fruit even without pollination, which is exactly why it is grown as a solo tree commercially. The juicy, somewhat watery flesh must be fully softened or artificially treated to remove astringency before eating; unripe fruit is unpalatable. Once treated or fully soft-ripe, the fruit is mild, sweet, and prized for fresh eating and drying. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ho-O Mulberry (Crinkled-Leaf Ornamental White Mulberry)
description: Ho-O is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown for its bizarre, tightly crinkled and crumpled foliage that bears almost no resemblance to typical mulberry leaves, giving it a strong conversation-piece texture in mixed borders and foliage-focused plantings. Left unpruned it can grow into a small tree to about 30 feet, but it is most commonly managed as a hard-pruned cutback shrub, cut nearly to the ground or to a low framework each late winter so it resprouts vigorously and tops out around 5 to 8 feet by season's end, since the most dramatically distorted, oversized leaves form on strong new growth. Fruiting is sparse and incidental; the cultivar is grown for foliage effect, not for a berry crop. Site in full sun to light shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and plan on an annual hard prune as routine maintenance rather than optional grooming. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hoary Blueberry (Appalachian Blueberry)
description: Plant in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry is a native Appalachian species of high-elevation heath and forest understory communities, distinguished by its distinctly hairy (hoary) twigs and leaf undersides — the fine hairs give new growth and undersides a grayish, woolly appearance. The plant is closely related to rabbiteye blueberry but adapted to cooler, higher-elevation sites. The blue-black berries are edible and well-flavored. In the garden, it performs well in moist, acidic shade conditions that suit other ericaceous plants like rhododendron and mountain laurel. An excellent native for the acid woodland garden in zones 5–8. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hoary Mountain Mint
description: Plant in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; hoary mountain mint is one of the most distinctive mountain mints, immediately recognizable by the striking silvery-white, downy (hoary) coating on the upper leaves and bracts surrounding the flower clusters — creating a bold, almost mealy-white appearance in midsummer that makes the plant ornamentally attractive even before and after bloom. The white bracts below the small lavender flowers are so conspicuous that they resemble petals, creating an unusual effect in the garden. Like all mountain mints, the flowers attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees — documented as supporting over 50 native bee species at a single planting. The aromatic foliage is repellent to deer. More tolerant of dry, rocky soils and partial woodland shade than Virginia mountain mint, hoary mountain mint is excellent in the transitional zone between sunny meadow and shaded woodland. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Hobblebush (Witch-hobble)
description: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, allowing generous spacing for the broad, arching form; hobblebush requires cool summer temperatures and consistent moisture, and is best suited to northern gardens or high-elevation sites where summer heat is moderate. Viburnum lantanoides produces large, heart-shaped leaves on low-arching branches that root where they contact the ground — the source of the name 'hobblebush,' as the rooted stems can trip unwary woodland walkers — and bears flat-topped clusters of showy white flowers in April and May followed by berries that ripen from red to black and attract thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Fall foliage color is among the most dramatic of any native shrub, turning rich crimson to claret-red in September, making hobblebush a multi-season standout for shaded northern woodland gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hog Peanut
description: Hog Peanut is a delicate, twining native legume vine of moist forest floors and shaded stream banks across eastern North America, producing two types of flowers: small lavender blossoms on climbing aerial stems that rarely set fruit, and inconspicuous cleistogamous flowers near the soil surface that produce fleshy, one-seeded pods underground — a remarkable adaptation for seed burial and dispersal. The underground fleshy seeds are rich, sweet, and bean-like in flavor, and were a significant food source for many Native American peoples including the Meskwaki, Cherokee, and Iroquois, who harvested them in fall; settlers called them hog peanuts because pigs eagerly rooted them from the soil. A nitrogen-fixing perennial that returns from taproots each spring in zones 5–9, Hog Peanut adds valuable biodiversity and soil health to shaded native plant gardens and woodland edges while providing food and cover for small wildlife. Direct sow after frost in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; established plants self-seed freely and colonize gradually. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Hog Plum (Wild Olive, Seaside Plum, Tallow Wood)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil — tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils exceptionally well once established; hog plum is a pantropical shrub or small tree with strongly fragrant white flowers and small oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow-orange then red, with thin skin, juicy sour-sweet flesh, and a large oily seed. The fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe but is very sour; it makes excellent jellies, juices, and fermented drinks popular across sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, and coastal Brazil. The seeds contain a high-quality oil used for cooking and cosmetics in West Africa. A superb drought- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting hedge plant for coastal gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Hoja Santa (Root Beer Plant)
description: Divide established clumps in spring by separating rooted suckers from the base of the mother plant and replanting in rich, moist soil. Hoja santa grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and prefers partial shade with consistent moisture; the enormous heart-shaped leaves can reach 12 in wide and emit a distinctive anise–root beer aroma from their essential oils. In Mexican cuisine the leaves are used to wrap tamales, season mole verde, and envelop fish for grilling. In zones 8–9, plants die to the ground after frost but reliably regrow from the roots; mulch heavily to protect the root zone through winter. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Hojiblanca Olive (Dual-Purpose Spanish Oil and Table Olive)
description: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer nearby. Hojiblanca, meaning 'white leaf' in Spanish for the strikingly silvery undersides of its foliage, is one of the most important olive varieties of Andalusia in southern Spain, valued for genuine dual-purpose flexibility, producing both good quality mild oil and firm, attractive table olives from the same tree depending on how the crop is used and harvested. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reasonably disease-tolerant, contributing to its widespread commercial planting across southern Spain. Harvest earlier and greener for table olive curing, or later for oil pressing, and remember that all olives require proper curing before eating fresh off the tree, since raw fruit is intensely bitter. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hokus Gherkin Cucumber
description: A gherkin cucumber producing seedless, bitter-free, uniform fruits perfect for cornichons and sweet pickles, best used from 1.5 to 4 inches long. Direct sow after the soil warms, spacing plants along a trellis for the vines that can reach 6 feet. Keep the soil evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress causes bitterness and misshapen fruit. Harvest small and often to keep the plant setting new cucumbers. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Hollow Crown Parsnip (Classic American Heirloom Parsnip Variety)
description: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in loose, deep, well-prepared soil; thin to 3–4 inches when 2 inches tall. Keep soil consistently moist during germination. Hollow Crown Parsnip is the standard American garden parsnip — an open-pollinated variety that has been the dominant parsnip type in American kitchen gardens and seed catalogs since at least the 1820s. The name 'Hollow Crown' describes a shallow depression or crown at the top of the root where the leaves emerge — a characteristic of this variety's root shape rather than an internal hollowness. The roots are long (10–16 inches), creamy-white, tapered, and aromatic — a distinctive sweet, earthy, and spicy character that is unlike any other common vegetable. Parsnip's flavor transformation with cold exposure is the most dramatic of any commonly grown root vegetable: fresh-dug roots in warm weather have a starchy, slightly bitter character, but roots exposed to several weeks of near-freezing temperatures convert their starch to sugar and develop a rich, complex sweetness with spicy, aromatic notes that make parsnips one of the great vegetables of the cold-season kitchen. Roasting parsnips at high heat caramelizes the surface sugars and creates the classic preparation: crisp, brown-edged exterior with creamy, sweet interior. Hollow Crown has remained the standard parsnip in American catalogs because no modern breeding has significantly exceeded its combination of good flavor, long roots, and reliable production. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Holstein Bloodred Rhubarb (Holsteiner Blutrot)
description: Holstein Bloodred is a German heirloom originating in the Holstein region, grown for stalks that run a deep, almost uniform red from base to tip, among the darkest-colored of the traditional European rhubarb strains. It is a heavy-feeding, vigorous grower that rewards an annual topdressing of compost or well-rotted manure with larger, more numerous stalks each following spring. The intense color makes it a favorite for preserves and rhubarb wine, both traditional uses in its region of origin, in addition to the usual pies and sauces. Keep the crown well mulched over winter in colder zones and divide every four to five years to maintain vigor as the clump matures. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Holt's Mammoth Sage
description: Root 3-4 in semi-ripe cuttings in a sharply drained mix in late summer, or set out nursery plants in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Holt's Mammoth is a robust culinary sage selected for its unusually large, 4-5 in gray-green leaves and fast, vigorous growth, making it a favorite of growers who need to harvest big quantities of leaf for drying. Flavor is fully typical of garden sage — warm, resinous, and savory — and the plant produces attractive violet-blue flower spikes in early summer. Cut back hard in spring to remove winter-damaged wood and keep growth dense. Matures in 80–110 days from transplant.

name: Holy Basil (Tulsi)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; holy basil (tulsi) is the sacred herb of Hindu worship and traditional Ayurvedic medicine, with an intensely spicy, clove-and-pepper scented flavor distinctly different from sweet Italian basil. The purple-stemmed Kapoor and Krishna varieties are most fragrant; the green-stemmed Vana type has a stronger, more medicinal flavor. Holy basil makes excellent Thai cooking, fresh teas, and pesto, and is reputed to have adaptogenic properties. Grow exactly as sweet basil — pinch flowers early and often to extend the harvest. In zones 10–12 it grows as a short-lived perennial; everywhere else it is grown as an annual. Seed is produced prolifically if a few flower stalks are allowed to mature. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Holy Basil / Tulsi
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix at 75–85°F; germination is swift when soil is adequately warm. Transplant after night temperatures stay above 55°F and pinch growing tips immediately to promote bushy growth. Regular pinching and removal of flower spikes prolongs the leaf harvest and delays bitterness; harvest leaves in the morning after dew has dried for the most aromatic result. Fresh or dried leaves are used in adaptogenic teas, Ayurvedic preparations, and as a sacred plant in Hindu tradition. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Home Green Sugarcane (Georgia Green Heirloom Dooryard Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Home Green is a long-grown Gulf South dooryard heirloom, green-stalked through summer and ripening to a golden yellow with red-blushed, sunset-like mottling as stalks mature in fall; the rind is soft and easy to peel, the juice notably greener than most other heirloom canes, and growers describe the flavor as a simple, syrupy sweetness reminiscent of old-fashioned cane syrup. It is valued as a dual-purpose variety, equally suited to fresh chewing and to pressing and cooking down into syrup, and was traditionally kept in home dooryard patches rather than grown commercially. As with other heirloom canes, propagation is entirely from saved stalk sets: healthy stalks are cut before the first hard freeze, bedded horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and covered with soil, pine straw, or plastic to hold them dormant through winter without freezing, then replanted the following spring. Harvest runs from the first light frosts of late fall, after cool nights have sweetened the stalks, through early winter. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Home Wood Mahonia (Columnar Winter-Flowering Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Home Wood is a large, upright, columnar Mahonia x media selection with dramatic, boldly pinnate leaves reaching nearly two and a half feet long, and slightly fragrant yellow flowers carried in ascending clusters up to 14 inches tall in late autumn and winter, followed by blue-black berries. Its imposing architectural scale makes it best suited to a spacious shaded border or woodland-edge planting rather than a tight foundation bed. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Homebell Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Homebell was one of the first named rabbiteye cultivars, released in 1955 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton from selections of wild rabbiteye stands, the same program that produced Gardenblue and Tifblue that same year. It carries a moderate chill requirement of roughly 350-450 hours below 45 degrees F and ripens early, coloring in late May to early June in the Gulf South, ahead of most modern cultivars. Berries are light blue, small to medium, and softer-skinned than newer selections, with mild, unremarkable flavor that made it more valuable historically for earliness than dessert quality; it has largely been superseded by cultivars like Climax and Premier that ripen just as early with better fruit. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark and keep it paired with a second early rabbiteye for fruit set, since it is self-unfruitful like all rabbiteye types. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Homemade Pickles Cucumber
description: A heavy-yielding pickling cucumber ready early, with the ideal interior texture for pickles though also good fresh, harvested anywhere from 1.5 to 6 inches long. Direct sow after frost into warm soil and mulch to hold moisture. The compact 4 to 5 foot vines do well in containers or on a small trellis. Pick frequently and evenly water to keep fruits crisp and the plant productive for canning batches. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Homestead 24 Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun, fertile soil with good drainage; Homestead 24 is a University of Florida IFAS heirloom bred at the Homestead Experiment Station in Homestead, Florida, selected for heat tolerance and disease resistance under South Florida's extreme subtropical growing conditions. The '24' designation indicates a selection within the Homestead series, the result of many generations of selection for performance in tropical heat and humidity. Determinate plants produce medium (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with good flavor, firm flesh, and resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. An important open-pollinated variety for zone 9b–12 gardeners who want to produce tomatoes reliably in hot, humid summer conditions where most varieties fail to set fruit — one of the trio of UF heirlooms (with Tropic and Walter) that carried South Florida vegetable gardening through decades before modern disease-resistant hybrids became available. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Homestead Guava
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Homestead is a South Florida dooryard guava selected for reliable production and good fruit quality in a home-garden setting, bearing medium-sized fruit with yellow skin and pink-tinged, sweet-tart flesh that is popular for fresh eating and for guava paste and juice alike. Like other guavas it fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the shrub-form tree productive and manageable in size rather than letting it grow into an unwieldy small tree. Guava roots generally tolerate brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit even when the canopy is killed back, so zone 9 gardeners should mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and expect to prune out and regrow frozen top growth in a hard year. In a favorable year with a long warm season, established plants can produce two overlapping flushes of fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Homestead Tomato
description: Transplant into fertile, deeply amended, well-drained soil and stake or cage; Homestead 24 is a determinate variety developed by the University of Florida that bears a concentrated crop of medium-large, smooth, red fruits ideal for canning and fresh use in hot, humid climates. Its primary attribute is heat tolerance — the variety was specifically selected to set fruit when night temperatures remain above 75°F, a condition that causes blossom drop in most standard varieties. Fruit size averages 6–8 ounces with good wall thickness for slicing or canning. This heirloom-type determinate variety has been a Southern garden standard since the 1950s and remains popular throughout the Gulf Coast. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Hon Tsai Tai
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; plants establish quickly in cool weather and are ready to harvest in about a month. Cut the entire plant at 3–4 inches above the soil or snap off individual stems with leaves and emerging flower buds, the most prized part. The vivid purple stems, dark green leaves, and yellow flower buds are equally edible — stir-fry briefly over high heat or blanch and toss with sesame oil. Flavor is mild and sweet before the plant bolts; harvest frequently to delay bolting. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Honan Red Persimmon (Chinese Heirloom Acorn-Shaped Persimmon)
description: Honan Red is an heirloom Chinese astringent-type Asian persimmon, introduced to the United States in the early 20th century and named for its origin in Henan (historically romanized Honan) province. The small-to-medium, round to acorn-shaped fruit ripens to a saturated red-orange with a large, stiff calyx cap, and stays firm and astringent until fully soft, at which point the flesh becomes smooth, moist, and richly sweet with essentially no fiber. Its low chill requirement lets it thrive across a wide range of climates, including warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens where higher-chill Japanese cultivars sometimes underperform, and the tree puts on vivid orange-red fall foliage before dropping its leaves to display the colorful fruit. Grow in full sun with good drainage; Honan Red is a specialty, home-orchard variety rather than a commercial crop, valued as much for its ornamental fall display as for its fruit. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Honduran Sarsaparilla
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with trellis or other support for climbing; Smilax ornata is adaptable to a range of conditions including full sun with consistent moisture and deep shade — mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and supply organic matter to the root zone. Smilax ornata (Honduran Sarsaparilla, Zarzaparilla) is a thorny, woody, perennial climbing vine in the Smilacaceae family native to humid tropical forests, forest edges, and riparian corridors of Central America — particularly Honduras, Guatemala, Mexico (Veracruz and Chiapas), Cuba, and Jamaica — where it climbs through the understorey using tendrils. The long, aromatic, reddish-brown rhizomes are the authentic source of 'true' sarsaparilla flavoring — the complex, vanilla-anise-wintergreen root flavor historically used in 19th-century American sarsaparilla beverages and root beer before artificial flavors displaced it. Medicinally, sarsaparilla root was a major export from Central America and the Caribbean to European pharmaceutical markets in the 16th–19th centuries for treatment of syphilis, psoriasis, rheumatism, and as a blood-purifying tonic. Modern phytochemical research confirms anti-inflammatory steroidal saponins (sarsasaponin, smilasaponin) in the rhizomes. The rhizomes are harvested by carefully digging, removing a portion, and replanting the crown; the vine regenerates. Excellent shade-tolerant medicinal vine for forest-garden and woodland-garden settings in zones 7–11. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Honeoye Strawberry (Cornell-Bred Cold-Hardy June-Bearer)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring with the crown level with the soil surface, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first season's blossoms so the plants put their energy into establishing strong roots and crowns before fruiting heavily the following year. Honeoye was bred at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station and released in the late 1970s, and it became a mainstay June-bearing variety across the colder parts of the Northeast, upper Midwest, and eastern Canada because of its outstanding winter hardiness and dependable, concentrated early-season crop. The berries are large, glossy bright red, and firm, with a bold, tangy-sweet flavor that many growers describe as more assertive than milder modern varieties, and the plants send out runners vigorously to fill in a matted row within a season or two. Honeoye ripens early to midseason and is frequently planted alongside later-fruiting varieties to stretch the harvest window in home gardens and pick-your-own plantings. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Honewort
description: Honewort is a shade-loving native edible herb, native to moist, rich woodlands and forest edges throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to Kansas, producing tender, edible leaves and stems in spring and early summer that taste mildly of parsley and celery — used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb. It is closely related to Japanese mitsuba (Cryptotaenia japonica) and can substitute for it in East Asian cooking; the young leaves are particularly flavorful in early spring. A self-seeding perennial that naturalizes freely in the shade garden, it fills in the difficult deep-shade spaces where most vegetables fail, providing a continuous harvest of tender greens from early spring to summer heat. Harvest outer leaves regularly to maintain plant vigor; allow some plants to set seed for natural self-renewal. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Honey 'n Pearl Sweet Corn (AAS-Winning Bicolor Supersweet Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows (rather than one or two long rows) for reliable wind pollination, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, after the soil has warmed to at least 65F. Honey 'n Pearl is an AAS-winning bicolor supersweet (sh2, shrunken-2 gene) corn, one of the landmark early supersweet varieties that changed home and commercial sweet corn breeding by holding its sugar content — and therefore its sweet flavor — for up to two weeks after harvest, far longer than older standard-sugary sweet corn varieties that begin converting sugar to starch within hours of picking. Ears are well-filled with a classic mix of yellow and white kernels. Because supersweet corn types can cross-pollinate badly with standard or sugary-enhanced corn and lose their sweetness, isolate plantings from other corn varieties by distance or timing. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during silking and ear fill, and side-dress with nitrogen when plants are about knee-high for the best ear development. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Honey and Cream Corn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Honey and Cream is a classic bicolor sweet corn producing attractive ears with alternating yellow and white kernels in the traditional American bicolor pattern — it was among the earliest widely available bicolor sweet corn varieties and remains popular for its straightforward, reliable, pleasant sweet corn flavor without the extreme sweetness of modern super-sweet types. Honey and Cream represents the standard sugary (su) bicolor corn flavor profile that defined American sweet corn for most of the 20th century — rich, substantial corn flavor with moderate sweetness and a tender, slightly milky kernel texture when eaten at peak ripeness. The reliable production, good ear appearance, and familiar flavor make it a trusted heirloom-style bicolor variety for home gardeners seeking a classic sweet corn experience. The ears are well-filled and typically 7–8 inches long — a proper size for fresh eating and corn-on-the-cob presentations. Matures in 78–84 days from seed.

name: Honey and Cream Sweet Corn
description: A bicolor sweet corn with a luscious blend of white and yellow kernels bursting with flavor and tenderness far above store-bought. Direct sow after the last frost once soil warms, planting in blocks of at least four rows so wind pollination fills the ears. Feed with nitrogen and keep well watered through tasseling and silking. Harvest at the milk stage when silks brown and kernels squirt milky juice when pressed. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Honey Babe Peach (Genetic Dwarf Container Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container of at least 15 gallons; Honey Babe is a genetic dwarf peach bred by Floyd Zaiger that naturally stays around 4–5 feet tall rather than being size-controlled by rootstock, yet still bears full-sized, richly flavored yellow freestone fruit that many home growers rate among the sweetest of the dwarf peach types. Its compact, densely branched form and showy pink spring blossoms make it as ornamental as it is productive, and it is self-fruitful, requiring no second pollinator tree. Thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart once set, since the small tree can easily overbear relative to its size, and prune lightly each dormant season to maintain an open, sunlit canopy. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Honey Bear Acorn Squash
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Honey Bear is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning acorn squash that produces a compact, semi-bush vine with small, single-serving fruits — typically 1 pound, the perfect size for splitting and roasting as one serving for two. The deep green, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruits have exceptionally sweet, dry, nutty flesh — rated significantly sweeter in taste trials than standard acorn squash types including Table King and Table Queen. The compact plant habit (3–4 feet spread versus 8–12 feet for standard acorn squash) makes Honey Bear one of the few winter squashes genuinely suitable for raised beds and smaller gardens. Each plant produces multiple fruits over the harvest season. Cure harvested fruits at room temperature for 10 days to convert starches to sugar and extend storage life to 3–4 months. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Honey Bee Honeyberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars, since nearly all commercial haskaps are self-infertile. Honey Bee is a University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred primarily as a universal pollinizer rather than for its own fruit production, chosen for heavy, well-timed flowering that overlaps with most other haskap cultivars' bloom windows. Its berries are edible and pleasantly flavored but smaller and less abundant than dedicated fruiting cultivars like Borealis or Aurora, so it is typically planted as roughly one bush in five or six. The bush is extremely cold-hardy and easy to grow, tolerating the same conditions preferred by other haskaps. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Honey Boat Winter Delicata Squash
description: A delicata-type winter squash with rich, golden-orange flesh and a sweet, nutty flavor that is excellent baked and buttered. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, giving the trailing vines plenty of room to run. Water steadily while fruit forms, then let the rinds harden as the plants wind down. Harvest before hard frost when the skin is tough, and cure in a warm spot to deepen the sweetness for storage. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Honey Dew Melon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — honeydew requires warm soil, abundant heat, and consistent moisture during fruit development; Honey Dew is the standard honeydew melon variety — a winter melon type (Cucumis melo, Inodorus group) producing large (5–8 pound), oval to round fruits with a distinctive smooth, creamy-white to pale green skin that develops a subtle gold or cream color at full ripeness. The flesh is pale green, firm but juicy, with a mild, clean, very sweet flavor that is quite different from the musty, complex, aromatic sweetness of cantaloupe — honeydew's sweetness is cleaner and more neutral, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too strong. Honeydew's longer shelf life and later harvest timing compared to cantaloupe made it historically important as a late-summer melon that could be stored and shipped where cantaloupe could not. Zone 9 is ideal for honeydew production — the extended summer heat and long growing season align perfectly with honeydew's need for consistently warm conditions over a long development period. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Honey Drip Sorghum (Southern Heirloom Syrup Sorghum)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in average, well-drained garden soil once the ground has warmed after frost, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Honey Drip is a Southern heirloom syrup sorghum that has been grown and re-selected in the region for generations, giving it strong heat and drought tolerance and dependable yields on soils too lean or dry for some other syrup canes. Plants top out shorter than many syrup sorghums, with upright, honey-colored seed heads, and reach cutting stage somewhat earlier in the season than late-maturing types. Harvest canes at hard-dough stage and press promptly, since the sweet, mellow syrup Honey Drip is known for depends on getting the juice to the evaporator soon after cutting. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Honey Gold Jackfruit
description: Bred as a dwarf selection and popular in both Florida and Australian home orchards, Honey Gold stays dense and prunable, bearing fruit along many lower limbs rather than concentrating it high in the canopy the way standard-sized jackfruit trees do. Fruit is medium at 10 to 12 pounds, with golden-yellow, crisp flesh that is notably sweet and aromatic, closer in texture to Black Gold than to the stringier flesh of unimproved seedling jackfruit. Its manageable size and heavy bearing on young wood have made it a favorite where full-sized cultivars like Black Gold or J-31 would outgrow the available space. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Honey Jar Jujube (Small Sweet Early Chinese Jujube)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Honey Jar is among the earliest jujubes to ripen (mid-August in many areas, 3–4 weeks before Li and Lang); the small fruits are best consumed fresh at peak ripeness rather than dried; trees are moderately compact compared to other jujube varieties. Honey Jar is widely regarded as the sweetest-tasting jujube variety available in American nurseries — the fruits are small (about 3/4 to 1 inch), round, and at perfect ripeness have a flavor described as pure concentrated honey with very little acidity and no bitterness, earning the variety its descriptive name. The small size, while meaning less fruit per piece, is actually an advantage in fresh eating situations where you want to pop a whole fruit in your mouth without cutting — Honey Jar is the jujube equivalent of a cherry tomato or Champagne grape, perfectly sized for snacking directly from the tree. The early ripening season (mid-August in zones 6–8, somewhat earlier in zone 9a) makes Honey Jar valuable for extending the fresh jujube harvest over the longest possible season when planted alongside the mid-season Li and the late-season Lang — a three-variety planting can provide fresh jujubes from late July through October. The trees are somewhat more compact than Li and Lang, making Honey Jar a good choice when space is limited. Cross-pollination with Lang or Li improves fruit set on Honey Jar trees significantly. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Honey Mesquite
description: Honey mesquite is the defining native tree of Texas plains and prairies, a thorny, nitrogen-fixing legume of unmatched drought resilience that has sustained both wildlife and indigenous cultures of the semi-arid Southwest for thousands of years — its sweet, nutritious seed pods were ground into mesquite meal (pinole) by many Southwestern and Gulf Coast tribes and are the source of distinctively flavored mesquite honey produced by Texas beekeepers from the abundant, fragrant yellow catkin flowers in spring and summer. The hard, dense wood is the premier smoking wood for Texas barbecue and is also used in flooring, furniture, and decorative woodworking; charcoal from honey mesquite burns hotter and longer than most other hardwoods. Honey mesquite is an important wildlife tree: the pods are consumed by deer, javelinas, coyotes, and dozens of bird species; the canopy provides nesting habitat for doves, mockingbirds, and scissor-tailed flycatchers across Texas ranchlands. Long-paired spines on the branches can be hazardous — site away from foot traffic, but within wildlife habitat and native plantings it is invaluable. Matures in 1825–5475 days from seed.

name: Honey Nut Squash (Cornell Mini Butternut Sweet Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Cure harvested fruits at 80–85°F for 2 weeks to harden skin, then store in cool, dry conditions. Honey Nut is a miniature butternut-type winter squash developed at Cornell University by plant breeder Michael Mazourek, introduced commercially around 2011–2015 — a squash that has rapidly gained status as one of the most innovative new vegetable introductions of the decade. The standard butternut squash (Waltham Butternut and similar) is widely considered one of the best-flavored winter squashes but weighs 3–5 lbs — more than most households can comfortably consume in one meal. Honey Nut produces single-serving-sized fruits of only 4–6 oz, with the same classic butternut shape (pear-shaped with a long cylindrical neck and round base) compressed to a palm-sized scale. Beyond the practical size advantage, Honey Nut has exceptional flavor that often outperforms standard butternut in blind tastings — the small size means the fruits must mature fully before harvest, when starches have converted to sugar, resulting in a consistently sweeter, more intense squash flavor. The deep orange flesh is very sweet, smooth-textured, and rich — ideal for roasting (a single halved fruit roasts in 30–35 minutes, faster than the 45–60 minutes for full-size butternut), soups, and purees. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Honey Punch Nectaplum (Nectarine-Plum Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer nearby with overlapping bloom time. Honey Punch is a Zaiger Genetics 'nectaplum,' an interspecific hybrid combining nectarine and plum genetics, producing smooth-skinned, deep red fruit with dense, richly flavored red-tinged flesh that carries the smooth skin and juiciness of nectarine along with the depth of flavor plum breeding contributes. As with other Zaiger interspecific stone fruit hybrids, the combination produces a genuinely distinctive eating experience different from either parent species grown alone, with concentrated sweetness and complex flavor prized by specialty fruit growers. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and fully colors for the best flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Honey Rock Melon
description: Honey Rock, an All-America Selections winner from 1933 also known as Sugar Rock, offers honey-sweet salmon-colored flesh and dependable performance. Direct sow seeds in warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Keep vines evenly watered during growth, then reduce moisture as fruit ripens to intensify sweetness. Harvest at full slip when the melon parts easily from the vine and smells fragrant. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Honey Select Sweet Corn (AAS-Winning Bicolor Synergistic Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress at knee height with nitrogen. Honey Select is a 1999 All-America Selections-winning bicolor sweet corn from Rogers Brothers/Syngenta that represents one of the most successful expressions of synergistic (sy or triplesweet) sweet corn genetics — a breeding system that places approximately 75% supersweet (sh2) kernels and 25% standard su kernels randomly across each ear, creating a flavor profile that integrates the long-lasting sweetness and slow starch conversion of sh2 types with the richer, more complex corn flavor that su kernels contribute. The resulting flavor is considered by many tasters to be more balanced, complete, and authentically corn-flavored than pure sh2 types (which can be very sweet but thin in traditional corn character) while retaining the extended harvest window advantage of sh2 genetics. The bicolor (yellow and white) ears are large (8–8.5 inches, 16 rows), well-filled, and visually attractive; the synergistic type's mixed kernel genetics produce slightly irregular but appealing ear fill. Honey Select has been a top-selling sweet corn variety since its release and remains one of the most consistent performers in home garden and market garden trials, with good disease resistance including tolerance to Stewart's wilt, NCLB, and SCLB. An outstanding all-around bicolor corn for any climate where premium flavor and extended postharvest quality are priorities. Matures in 78–84 days from seed.

name: Honey Stevia
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Honey Stevia is a named cultivar of stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) selected for a smoother, more honey-like sweetness compared to the standard species, which can have a distinct licorice-menthol aftertaste that some people find unpleasant in large quantities. The sweetening compounds in stevia (steviosides and rebaudiosides) are 200–350 times sweeter than sugar by weight, so only small amounts of fresh or dried leaf are needed to sweeten foods and beverages. The Honey cultivar has been selected to emphasize the rebaudioside-A fraction (which provides the cleaner, honey-like sweetness) relative to the stevioside fraction (associated with the bitter aftertaste) — making it the preferred variety for fresh leaf use in teas, lemonades, and fresh preparations where subtle sweetener differences are most noticeable. Leaves are used fresh in drinks and food, or dried and powdered for longer storage. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Honey Tangerine (Murcott Tangerine)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest available location in full sun; Honey tangerine (also called Murcott or Murcott honey mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored and sweetest commercial citrus varieties — the name 'Honey' reflects its extraordinary sugar content (Brix up to 14–16) and rich, honeyed, complex flavor that combines mandarin aromatics with tangerine sweetness and a characteristic mild tartness. The fruit is medium-sized, deep orange, with thin, peelable skin and tender, very juicy flesh. Ripening in January–March, Honey tangerines extend the citrus season into late winter and early spring when other citrus is winding down. They have seeded flesh (unlike some modern mandarins) but flavor more than compensates. Trees are productive and attractive landscape specimens; they can have alternate-bearing tendencies (heavy crop one year, lighter the next) that are managed by thinning in the on-year. Feed with citrus fertilizer; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Florida produces commercial quantities in Polk and Highlands counties. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Honeybaby Winter Squash
description: An All-America Selections winning butternut-type hybrid that is very productive, setting numerous 1 to 2 pound fruits on compact 2 to 3 foot vines with some powdery mildew resistance. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, thinning to the strongest seedlings per hill. The semi-bush habit suits smaller gardens; keep evenly watered through fruit set. Harvest when rinds turn tan and hard, then cure before storing. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Honeyberry (Haskap)
description: Plant two or more different cultivars for cross-pollination in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full sun; honeyberry is an edible-fruited honeysuckle native to boreal regions of Russia, Japan, and Canada that produces sweet-tart blue berries resembling elongated blueberries in late spring — the first fresh fruit of the season in cold climates. Plants tolerate temperatures to -40°F and the flowers survive spring frosts to -8°F. Fruit is borne on second-year wood, so avoid heavy pruning in the first three years. Cultivars 'Tundra', 'Indigo Gem', and 'Borealis' are among the most productive for North American gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Honeyberry / Haskap
description: Honeyberries are among the earliest fruits to ripen — often 2–3 weeks before strawberries — and flowers can survive temperatures as low as -4°F, making them ideal for short-season climates. Two compatible cultivars from the same breeding group must be planted for cross-pollination. Minimal pruning is needed for the first 5 years; thereafter, remove a few of the oldest, thickest canes annually to renew. Harvest when berries are entirely blue-purple inside (cut one open to check), as color alone can be misleading. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Honeybush Tea
description: Cyclopia subternata is a wiry, yellow-flowered legume shrub of the Cape fynbos, one of several Cyclopia species harvested for honeybush tea, a naturally sweet, caffeine-free herbal infusion made by fermenting the cut, needle-like leaves and stems until they darken and develop the tea's characteristic honey-like aroma. Bright yellow, sweetly scented, pea-like flowers appear in spring and give the plant its common name as much as the finished tea does. As with rooibos and other fynbos legumes, deep, nutrient-poor, acidic sandy soil and excellent drainage are essential; rich garden soil or wet feet quickly kill it. Established plants are cut back periodically to encourage the fine new growth used for tea production. Best suited to a dedicated fynbos or Mediterranean-climate herb bed rather than a conventional border. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Honeycrisp Apple Tree
description: Honeycrisp is beloved for its explosively crisp texture and balanced sweet-tart flavor, and it is notably cold-hardy. It needs a compatible pollinating apple variety and thrives in cooler northern climates. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and water steadily through the season. Thin fruit clusters and prune in late winter to promote large, well-colored apples and reduce disease pressure. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Honeydew Melon
description: Honeydew produces sweet, refreshing melons with crisp pale-green flesh that thrive in hot summer gardens. Sow seeds directly in warm soil and full sun after all frost has passed, giving the long-season vines ample room. Provide steady water during fruit development and a long, warm growing season for the fruit to sweeten fully. Unlike cantaloupe, honeydew does not slip, so harvest when the rind turns creamy and the blossom end softens slightly. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Honeydew Melon
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in hills of 4–5 seeds thinned to 2. Honeydew requires a longer, hotter season than cantaloupe; black plastic mulch is helpful in northern climates to boost soil warmth. Unlike cantaloupes, honeydews do not slip from the vine when ripe, so judge by skin color changing to creamy white, a waxy feel, and a sweet aroma from the blossom end. Cut fruits from the vine with a knife rather than pulling. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Honeydew Pawpaw (Large Freestone Melon-Flavored Kentucky Pawpaw)
description: Honeydew is a named freestone pawpaw discovered on a late-1800s orchard in Richmond, Kentucky, alongside its siblings Cantaloupe and Marshmallow, and released through England's Orchard by pawpaw enthusiast Woody Walker as an 'England's Orchard Introduction.' The large, well-formed, blunt-ended fruit, averaging around 10 ounces, has a tropical, melon-like flavor reminiscent of honeydew melon with a trace of banana, and the flesh ranges from soft chiffon to firmer texture depending on ripeness. Because it lacks a fibrous seed sack, seeds lift out cleanly, making the fruit easy to process, and it freezes exceptionally well for later use. Harvest by feel when the fruit yields to gentle pressure, and use or refrigerate promptly since pawpaws have a short fresh shelf life. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Honeynut Squash (Mini Intensely Sweet Butternut-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Honeynut is a landmark squash introduction from Cornell University and Row 7 Seed Company — a diminutive butternut-type squash (3–4 inches long, 6–8 oz) that is completely different from standard butternut squash in flavor intensity: the Honeynut's flesh has dramatically more concentrated sweetness, nuttiness, and butternut flavor than full-sized butternut because the ratio of flesh to seed cavity is much higher in the mini fruit. When roasted, the deep-orange flesh caramelizes beautifully and develops an intense, complex butterscotch-butternut flavor that has made Honeynut one of the most talked-about new vegetables of the 2010s since its public introduction in 2015. The small fruit size (one squash per serving) makes Honeynut practical for individual servings without the waste of a large standard butternut. As a Cucurbita moschata variety, Honeynut has better heat and disease tolerance (particularly vine borer resistance) than pepo-type winter squash — an important practical advantage in the Gulf South where squash vine borers and heat challenge pepo types in summer. In zone 9, direct sow in July–August for a fall harvest (September–November). Cure for 4–6 weeks after harvest to develop maximum sweetness. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Honeynut Winter Squash
description: A miniature butternut bred by crossing butternut with buttercup, giving intensely sweet 4 to 5 inch fruits with thin, edible skin that turns from green to terracotta at ripeness. Direct sow into warm soil after frost and let vines sprawl. Keep evenly watered while fruit develops, then ease off near harvest. Cut fruit when the rind is fully terracotta and cure to concentrate the rich, nutty flavor. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Honeysweet Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant USDA Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected from 137 seedlings screened for fire blight survival and winter hardiness at Purdue University and released by the USDA, it combines a comparatively high level of fire blight resistance, similar to Kieffer and notably better than Seckel, with genuinely sweet, dessert-quality flavor rather than the tough, mediocre-eating fruit typical of many blight-resistant pears. The medium-sized, classically pear-shaped fruit has yellow skin with russet freckling at maturity and white, fine-grained, very juicy, smooth flesh. Harvest in fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Honeywood Saskatoon (Vigorous Saskatchewan Fruit Cultivar)
description: Honeywood is a Saskatchewan-origin saskatoon selection known for its vigorous, upright growth habit and reliable heavy fruit set even on younger plants. The dark purple-blue berries have the classic sweet, nutty saskatoon flavor and hold well on the bush for a staggered harvest. Plant in full sun with good drainage; because the shrub grows tall and dense, allow generous spacing in a hedgerow planting and prune out older canes periodically to maintain vigor and light penetration. It is a common choice in commercial U-pick saskatoon plantings across the Canadian Prairies for its dependable productivity. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hong Kong Garcinia
description: Plant Garcinia oblongifolia in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled sun; maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid prolonged drought; protect young plants from temperatures below 32°F; established trees tolerate light frost. Hong Kong Garcinia is one of the more cold-hardy Garcinia species — adapted to the subtropical climate of South China and Hong Kong where winters can be cool with occasional brief frost — making it more tractable in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens than strictly tropical Garcinias. The ornamental value is high: the tree has a neat, dense, compact form with attractive, glossy, oblong, dark-green leaves and produces small clusters of bright orange-red fruits that are decorative on the tree. The fruits have a sweet-sour, juicy, translucent-white pulp somewhat resembling a small mangosteen in flavor — less rich than Purple Mangosteen but pleasant and refreshing. The tree is appreciated in Hong Kong and southern Chinese traditional culture both as an ornamental and for the edible fruits; it also has traditional medicinal uses in Chinese herbal medicine, particularly the dried rind of the fruit (similar to Garcinia cambogia). Relatively uncommon in Western cultivation but deserves wider planting in humid subtropical gardens as a hardy, attractive alternative to more tropical Garcinias. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Hong Kong Green Bitter Melon
description: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vines. This classic Cantonese-type cultivar produces oblong, blunt-ended fruit with a pale-green, gently warty surface that is larger and milder than typical Indian bitter melon types. Harvest fruit while still firm and light green, before the surface begins to yellow, for use in stir-fries, stuffed dishes, and soups where its characteristic bitterness is balanced with garlic, black bean, or egg. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Hong Kong Kumquat (Hong Kong Wild Kumquat)
description: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11. This dense, twiggy, thorny shrub from the rocky hillsides of southern China and Hong Kong bears masses of tiny, pea- to marble-sized round fruit with thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around intensely tart, seedy pulp, best nibbled whole rather than juiced. It flowers and fruits abundantly even as a small potted specimen, making it a popular choice for bonsai and container citrus collections as much as for the fruit itself, and its fine, small-leaved habit distinguishes it from the larger-leaved kumquats grown for eating fresh. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season, water deeply but infrequently, and prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hood Pear (Low-Chill Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hood is a low-chill European pear cultivar developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program, requiring only 100–150 hours of chilling — one of the lowest chill requirements of any successful pear. This makes Hood exceptional for zone 9 and even zone 9b–10a, where most European pear varieties fail to produce consistent crops. The fruit is large, greenish-yellow to yellow at maturity, with sweet, white, juicy flesh ripening in June–July in zone 9 — much earlier than conventional pear season. Flavor is mild and pleasant, suitable for fresh eating and canning. Fire blight can be a problem in humid conditions; prune out infected wood promptly and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Cross-pollination with Pineapple pear or Floridahome significantly improves yields. Hood is one of the three low-chill pears (with Orient and LeConte) most reliably recommended for Gulf Coast zone 9 home orchards where conventional Bartlett and Bosc fail to fruit. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hooker's Onion (Hooker Chives, Chinese Mountain Leek)
description: Set divisions with a few inches of intact root mass into loose, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone from drying out. Unlike most alliums, Hooker's onion is grown chiefly for its thick, faintly cumin-scented white roots as well as its flat, grass-like leaves, both of which are eaten fresh, pickled, or stir-fried in the cuisines of the eastern Himalayas and southern China where the plant originates.
