It spreads steadily into dense clumps in the moist shade or part shade of a woodland-edge bed and is one of the few alliums that genuinely thrives without full sun. Dig and divide congested clumps every year or two in spring, replanting a portion immediately to keep the patch productive and harvesting the rest roots and all. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Hooker's Sweet Indian Corn
description: Hooker's Sweet Indian was developed more than seventy years ago by Ira Hooker near Olympia, Washington, who worked from Native American corn strains to produce a sweet corn that would reliably ripen in a short, cool growing season. The short four to four-and-a-half foot stalks are unusually compact for a corn variety and typically set two ears per plant, five to seven inches long with 10-12 rows of kernels, starting out white and darkening through purple to a deep blue-black as they dry. Because it holds sweetness at the fresh eating stage and also grinds into flavorful cornmeal once fully dried, it works as a genuine dual-purpose corn for gardeners who want both a fresh crop and a grain harvest from the same planting. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Hooligan Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Bicolor Miniature Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, spacing hills so the compact vines have room to set their heavy load of fruit. Hooligan won an All-America Selections award for a striking two-tone pattern that splits each miniature pumpkin between deep orange and creamy white, a novelty look that has made it a favorite for fall tablescapes and porch displays rather than cooking. A single vine can produce dozens of the palm-sized fruits over the season, giving far more usable pieces per plant than standard-size decorative pumpkins. Harvest once the rind fully hardens and the color pattern has set, and the small size means the whole crop keeps well for weeks without curing. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Hope 13 Mayhaw (Large Dark Red Fire-Blight-Resistant Mayhaw)
description: Hope 13 is a western mayhaw selection prized for very large, dark red fruit approaching an inch across, among the largest of the named mayhaw cultivars. It carries good resistance to fire blight, a bacterial disease that can quickly kill susceptible mayhaw wood during warm, humid springs. Plant it on the moist to wet, acidic soil mayhaw naturally prefers, and site a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and a dependable crop. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Hope Mahonia (Slieve Donard Winter-Flowering Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Hope is a sister seedling of 'Charity' and 'Faith', raised at Windsor Great Park from open-pollinated 'Charity' seed, bearing fragrant yellow flower racemes from January into March above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by powdery blue-black berries. It is a somewhat more compact, cold-hardy selection than most other Mahonia x media clones, useful where a smaller-scale winter-flowering shade shrub is wanted. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hope Seedless Grape (Soft-Textured Green Table Grape)
description: Hope is a green-fruited seedless table grape bred by the University of Arkansas program from a 1983 cross, released together with Faith, Gratitude, and Joy. It carries a pleasantly fruity flavor and a notably soft texture, along with high production potential, ripening in mid-to-late August. The fruit is non-slipskin with good skin quality and resistance to splitting, and the vine has shown dependable winter hardiness and vine health in Arkansas trials. Its soft texture means Hope is best picked and eaten fresh at home or sold through short local-market channels rather than shipped any distance. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hope's August Pawpaw (Early-Ripening Ohio Selection)
description: Hope's August is a named pawpaw selection documented from Paint, Ohio, valued primarily for its early maturity, ripening ahead of most named cultivars and extending the pawpaw harvest toward late summer. It is one of a small family of related Ohio selections, including the similarly named Hope's September, cataloged in Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records. Like all pawpaws, it needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination since it cannot reliably set fruit alone. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Hopi Black Bean
description: Direct sow an inch deep once the soil has warmed well past last frost, since this bush-type dry bean sulks in cold, wet ground. Hopi Black has been grown for generations by Hopi farmers in the arid mesas of northeastern Arizona, selected over centuries for its ability to set a reliable crop of small, glossy black beans on minimal rainfall. Let pods dry fully on the plant before shelling, and expect a compact, drought-tolerant bush that needs no staking. The dried beans cook to a rich, dense texture well suited to stews and traditional Southwestern dishes. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Hopi Blue Corn (Traditional Native American Blue Flour Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4+ rows; harvest ears when husks are fully dry and brown (typically 3–4 weeks after the milk stage of sweet corn). Hopi Blue is a traditional open-pollinated flour corn grown by the Hopi people of the Colorado Plateau for centuries — one of the most culturally significant food plants in the Southwestern United States, where blue corn (technically any of several traditional pueblo corn varieties) is the foundation of traditional Hopi cuisine and ceremony. The deep blue-purple to near-black kernels are soft starch corn (flour type) ground into the fine blue cornmeal used for piki bread (the traditional thin, paper-like blue corn bread), blue corn tortillas, atole (blue corn porridge), and blue corn mush. The blue color comes from anthocyanin pigments in the aleurone layer, and the striking blue color is enhanced rather than destroyed by traditional lime processing (nixtamalization). Modern American markets for blue corn tortilla chips and blue corn products have dramatically increased interest in blue corn varieties. Hopi Blue requires isolation from other corn types to maintain kernel color purity; crossing with yellow or white sweet corn produces offspring with diluted color. The variety shows good drought tolerance adapted to its ancestral dry-mesa homeland. Matures in 78–90 days from seed.

name: Hopi Orange Watermelon (Drought-Tolerant Native American Heirloom)
description: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in warm hills spaced widely apart, thinning to the strongest one or two vines per hill; in dry-farmed desert tradition the seed is planted deeper still, up to 4-6 inches, to reach residual soil moisture, though garden beds with regular irrigation can plant at a normal depth. Hopi Orange is a Native American heirloom watermelon developed by the Hopi people of northern Arizona and preserved through seed banks such as Native Seeds/SEARCH, selected over generations for the ability to produce a crop with minimal supplemental water in arid, sandy soil. Fruit is medium-sized with light green rind and sweet, deep orange flesh that is less common among heirloom watermelons than the standard red. Vines are vigorous and sprawling and still benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set even though the variety tolerates drought once established. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to pale yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Hopi Pale Grey Squash (Ancient Southwestern Native American Squash)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, far-ranging vines generous room to spread. Hopi Pale Grey is a traditional Hopi heirloom squash grown for centuries in the arid Southwest, producing large, round to slightly oval fruit with smooth, pale bluish-gray skin and dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and traditional Hopi cooking. It is notably drought tolerant once established, reflecting its origins in a low-rainfall growing region, and stores exceptionally well, often keeping through much of the winter in a cool, dry location. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure for a couple of weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to long-term storage. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Hopi Red Dye Amaranth
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, neutral soil — amaranth grows in poor soils and does not need fertilization to thrive; Hopi Red Dye is an heirloom grain amaranth variety cultivated by the Hopi people of the American Southwest for centuries — the deep burgundy-red to maroon pigment extracted from the dried seeds and flowers was used as a traditional food dye for piki (paper-thin corn bread) and other ceremonial foods, creating a vivid magenta-red color central to Hopi cultural celebrations. The plant is simultaneously ornamental and productive: growing 5–7 feet tall with dramatic, deep burgundy-red seed heads and richly colored foliage that makes it one of the most striking large-scale garden plants for summer use. The small seeds (grain) are a nutritionally exceptional whole grain — very high in protein (13–17%), lysine (an amino acid deficient in most grains), and various minerals — usable as a cooked grain substitute for rice or quinoa, ground into flour, or popped like popcorn. Young leaves can be eaten as a cooked green similar to spinach. The drought-tolerance and heat-adaptability of amaranth make Hopi Red Dye one of the best grain crops for zone 9's challenging summer conditions. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Hops (Common Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hops is the perennial vine whose dried female flower cones ('hops') are the essential bittering and preserving agent in virtually all beer styles. Native to temperate North America and Europe, it is a vigorous, tendriled vine that dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15–20 feet on strings, trellises, or arbors. The soft green hop cones (strobiles) ripen in late summer; harvest when papery and fragrant, then dry immediately for use in home brewing. The young spring shoots emerging from the ground are edible as a vegetable, cooked like asparagus. The dried seed cones have traditional medicinal use as a mild sedative. Ornamental cultivars like 'Aureus' (golden-yellow foliage) are widely grown for their dramatic summer screening effect. Performs best in cool-summer climates (zones 3–7); struggles in the persistent heat of zone 8+. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Horapha Nanum Thai Basil (Compact Anise-Clove Thai Basil)
description: Horapha Nanum, nanum meaning dwarf, is a compact, bushy strain of Thai basil, named for horapha, the Thai term for this basil type, that stays noticeably smaller and denser than standard Thai basil selections like Siam Queen. Deep purple-brown stems carry olive-green, purple-tinged, slightly serrated leaves with the same pungent anise-clove flavor prized in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, and its small mulberry-purple flower clusters make it an attractive pot plant as well as a kitchen herb. The dwarf habit suits containers and small raised beds where a full-size Thai basil would sprawl. Pinch flower spikes to extend leaf harvest, and cut stems above a leaf pair to keep the plant branching. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Horehound
description: Surface-sow onto moist mix 6–8 weeks before transplanting; horehound germinates readily in warm soil but can be slow and erratic. Plant in dry, well-drained, even rocky or sandy soil where most plants would struggle — fertile, moist conditions cause leggy, weak growth. Harvest stems and leaves before flowering for the most potent bitterness, bundling for drying or infusing fresh into candy and cough syrups. Shear plants back in late summer to keep growth compact and prevent excessive self-seeding. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Horizontal Cocoplum
description: Horizontal Cocoplum is the naturally low, creeping coastal form of Florida's native cocoplum, selected for its dense, spreading habit and outstanding salt and wind tolerance compared to the taller, upright 'Red Tip' inland form. Its trailing branches root readily where they touch the ground, gradually knitting together into a dense mat that is excellent for stabilizing dunes, beach edges, and other exposed coastal sites prone to erosion. Plant in full sun in sandy, well-drained soil; once established it needs little supplemental irrigation and tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil far better than most fruiting shrubs. It still produces the species' small, edible, dark purple fruit, though its primary garden role is as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover for coastal landscapes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Horn's White Pawpaw (Unusually Pale-Fleshed Heirloom Selection)
description: Horn's White is an heirloom pawpaw selection prized for flesh that is unusually white and creamy rather than the typical yellow-orange, with tasting notes reminiscent of coconut and cherimoya alongside classic banana-custard pawpaw flavor. Fruit runs large, often around 12 ounces, and ripens late in the season. Like all pawpaws, Horn's White needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination, since it will not reliably set fruit alone. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Horse Apple (Large Southern Heirloom Cooking Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and plant a second apple cultivar nearby for pollination, since Horse Apple is not reliably self-fruitful. A large, old Southern heirloom of uncertain origin, Horse Apple produces big, greenish-yellow fruit with a coarse, tart flesh best suited to cooking, drying, and cider rather than fresh eating out of hand — its name reflects both its large size and its traditional use as livestock and orchard fruit as much as table fruit. Its low chill requirement and long history of successful cultivation across the Deep South make it one of the more reliable heirloom apples for Gulf Coast gardens, where many higher-chill Northern cultivars struggle to fruit consistently. Fruit ripens in mid to late summer and does not store especially well, so plan to process it into sauce, butter, or cider soon after harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Horse Gram (Kulthi, Hurali Bean, Madras Gram)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun after last frost; horse gram is a drought-tolerant legume grown across the dry regions of South and Southeast Asia, highly valued in Ayurvedic medicine and increasingly recognized as a nutritional powerhouse with very high protein, iron, and polyphenol content. The small, reddish-brown seeds are used in soups, stews, and sprouted for salads; in South Indian cuisines the seeds are used to make rasam, curries, and thick dals. One of the most heat-tolerant and drought-resistant food legumes available, capable of growing on thin, rocky, sandy soils with minimal inputs — an excellent candidate for permaculture systems and food forests in dry climates. Matures in 80–120 days from seed.

name: Horse Mint (Long-leaved Mint)
description: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, contained in pots or with root barriers to limit spreading; horse mint is a European native mint with long, lance-shaped, silver-green leaves that are more strongly and sharply aromatic than spearmint, with a mentholated, camphor-like fragrance. The dense, elongated spikes of small lavender flowers in late summer are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, honey bees, and numerous other pollinators. The leaves can be used as a tea, culinary seasoning, or insect repellent — the intense menthol content makes it more suited to teas and infusions than to fresh eating. In South Africa it is widely used as a traditional medicine and culinary herb (called 'ballerja'); it naturalizes in moist streamside habitats across North Africa, Europe, and western Asia. Contrast with 'horse mint' used in the US (Monarda punctata), which is an entirely unrelated native wildflower. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Horseradish
description: Plant 6–8 in root cuttings (thongs) at a 45-degree angle, 2–3 in deep, in deeply tilled, fertile soil; vertical planting produces rougher roots while angled planting encourages smoother, straight taproots. Horseradish is extremely vigorous and should be contained or given a dedicated bed where spreading is acceptable. Harvest main roots in autumn after the first hard frost triggers maximum heat and oil development. Save pencil-thick side roots to replant as next year's cuttings. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Hosui Asian Pear (Japanese Golden-Russet Round Asian Pear)
description: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; thin fruit clusters to one fruit per cluster when fruits are marble-sized for maximum size. Asian pears need no post-harvest ripening period. Hosui is a Japanese-bred Asian pear (nashi pear, Pyrus pyrifolia) — one of the finest Asian pear varieties available in North America for both flavor quality and adaptability to warmer zones (zone 5–9 with adequate chill). The fruit is large (8–12 oz), round to slightly oblate, with distinctive golden-brown russeted skin — the russet texture of Hosui's skin is one of its defining aesthetic characteristics, giving it a warm, autumn-toned appearance that differs from the smooth green or yellow skin of other Asian pear varieties. The flesh is the extraordinary feature: extremely crisp, almost crunchy — quite unlike the soft, butter-like texture of ripe European pears — with very high juice content and a sweet, aromatic, complex flavor with notes of honey and vanilla. Asian pears are eaten fresh at harvest, when crisp and juicy at peak quality; they do not improve with storage and are not used for cooking or canning the way European pears are. Hosui is among the most popular and widely planted Asian pear varieties in Japan and California, where its early ripening, excellent flavor, and moderate chill requirement make it adaptable to a wider range of climates than many Asian pear types. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hot and Spicy Oregano (Compact High-Oil Pungent Culinary Oregano)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct sow in spring; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil. Harvest stems for drying just as flower buds begin to open. Hot and Spicy Oregano is a compact cultivar of common oregano (Origanum vulgare) selected for higher essential oil content and more pronounced, pungent flavor compared to the bland, low-oil common oregano that grows widely in American gardens. Standard common oregano (Origanum vulgare) grown in the United States often has relatively low essential oil content and mild flavor — the reason that most dried commercial 'oregano' products in American grocery stores are a blend of Origanum vulgare with Greek oregano (O. heracleoticum) or marjoram. Hot and Spicy represents a more flavorful selection of the common oregano type, with significantly more essential oil and a more robust, peppery, slightly camphoraceous character approaching that of true Greek or Italian cooking oregano. The compact habit (10–15 inches), fine texture, and purple-tinged flowers make Hot and Spicy also ornamentally attractive in herb gardens and Mediterranean-style plantings. The variety is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in containers where watering can be controlled. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Hot Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80–85°F soil temperature — hot peppers need warm conditions to germinate and grow; transplant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil only after nights stay above 60°F consistently. Hot peppers range from mildly pungent (Anaheim, poblano) to fiercely hot (habanero, ghost pepper, Carolina Reaper) depending on variety, with heat measured in Scoville heat units (SHU). The capsaicin compound that produces heat is concentrated in the inner white ribs and seeds rather than the flesh. In zone 8–11 hot peppers are short-lived perennials that can be overwintered if protected from frost, often producing more prolifically in their second and third years than in their first. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: How Sweet It Is Corn (AAS-Winning White Sugary-Enhanced Sweet Corn)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. How Sweet It Is, a 1986 All-America Selections winner, produces pure white, sugary-enhanced kernels with outstanding sweetness and tenderness that hold their sugar content well after harvest rather than quickly converting to starch, giving a longer window of peak eating quality than standard sweet corn. Isolate from field corn, popcorn, or other corn types by at least 250 feet or two weeks of tasseling time to prevent cross-pollination from diluting sweetness. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly for the best flavor. Matures in 80–87 days from seed.

name: Howard Walnut
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to accommodate the tree's naturally compact, spreading form. Howard is a widely planted California commercial English walnut variety valued for its lateral bearing habit, which sets nuts along the length of each branch rather than only at the tips, boosting yields per acre. It produces a light-colored, high-quality kernel and buds out later than older varieties such as Hartley, reducing the risk of spring frost damage to the crop. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Howden Pumpkin
description: The quintessential carving pumpkin developed in 1970s Massachusetts, with bright orange skin, strong handles, and good storage. Direct sow after frost in hills with plenty of room for the sprawling vines. Feed richly and water deeply while fruit sizes up, tucking straw under developing pumpkins to prevent rot. Harvest when the rind is hard and fully colored, leaving a length of stem intact. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Howell Pear (Productive Connecticut Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Introduced from Connecticut in 1806, Howell bears medium to large, yellow, red-blushed pears with sweet, juicy, fine-grained flesh, and the tree became a widely planted commercial and home orchard variety through the 19th century thanks to its dependable, heavy annual bearing and relatively early start to production compared to many other pears of its era. It remains a solid, low-fuss choice for a home orchard wanting reliable fall pears without fussy care. Harvest while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Howes Cranberry (Heirloom Late-Season Storage Cranberry)
description: Howes was selected from the wild around 1843 by Eli Howes of East Dennis, Massachusetts, and became one of the foundational heirloom cultivars that built the New England cranberry industry, alongside Early Black and Searles. It ripens late in the season and produces small to medium, firm, deep-red berries with excellent keeping quality, historically prized for winter storage before modern refrigeration. Vines are moderately vigorous and well adapted to traditional bog culture with winter flooding and sanding. Because it ripens later than Early Black, Howes needs a fairly long, frost-free fall window to fully color, making it best suited to milder cranberry-growing regions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Hua Moa Banana (Samoan-Hawaiian Egg Banana)
description: Hua Moa is a traditional Samoan and Hawaiian table banana known for its short, plump, egg-shaped fruit and sweet flesh, grown in Pacific island dooryard gardens long before commercial Cavendish varieties arrived. The plant is somewhat more compact than the taller Iholena and Maoli types, making it a manageable choice for a home garden bed with rich soil and reliable irrigation. Grow it in full sun with heavy monthly feeding through the warm season, and expect a slow first fruiting from a young pup as with most edible bananas. In zone 9a it performs best as a warm-season specialty planting given winter protection rather than left to face a hard freeze unmulched. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Huacatay (Black Mint)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained soil after last frost; thin to 18–24 in apart as huacatay grows into a tall, upright plant. This Andean herb — essential in Peruvian cuisine for dishes like ocopa sauce and anticuchos marinades — has a complex flavor combining mint, tarragon, and citrus. Plants are day-length sensitive and flower in late summer to fall; harvest leaves and stem tips throughout the vegetative season before flowering commences. Grow in full sun with moderate fertility; the plant is drought-tolerant once established and spreads by self-seeding in warm climates. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Huang Jin Gui Tea (Golden Osmanthus Oolong)
description: Selected in Anxi County, Fujian, China, and ranked among that region's four historically celebrated oolong cultivars alongside Tieguanyin, Huang Jin Gui takes its 'golden osmanthus' name from an intensely sweet, floral fragrance in the finished tea reminiscent of osmanthus blossoms. It breaks bud notably early in spring compared to most Anxi cultivars, giving growers a jump on the harvest season, and it forms a relatively compact, manageable shrub. Provide the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and partial shade favored by other Fujian tea cultivars, and pick young flushes promptly once growth begins, since the cultivar's fragrance is most pronounced in the tenderest leaf. Light oolong processing best preserves its floral character. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Huauzontle (Mexican Tree Spinach, Aztec Broccoli)
description: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely covered after last frost in well-drained to average soil in full sun; huauzontle is a wild relative of lamb's quarters domesticated by the Aztecs and still a traditional food in Mexico, where the dense broccoli-like seed heads are harvested while still immature and green, dipped in egg batter, and fried in a fritter-like style, or simmered in tomato sauce. The young leaves are also excellent cooked like spinach. Highly drought-tolerant and heat-loving, it thrives in the same conditions as corn and requires little irrigation once established. Harvest seed heads while green and before seeds begin to harden for best eating quality; allow a few plants to set seed to guarantee a self-sowing colony. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Hubbard Squash
description: Plant 3–4 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in deeply worked, fertile soil, thinning to two vines after establishment. Hubbard squash produces very large, warty fruits with a hard blue-gray or orange shell and very sweet, dry, fine-grained flesh ideal for pie and soup. Allow vines to spread freely over 8–12 feet of ground, or train onto a very strong trellis and support individual fruits in slings. Fruits are ripe when the rind resists a fingernail, the skin has turned its characteristic color, and the stem is fully dry; cure for two weeks before storing. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Huffman Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Desirable Replacement, Large-Nut Pecan)
description: Huffman was released by the University of Georgia in 2012 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Pawnee and Desirable, selected at the UGA Horticulture Farm in Watkinsville as a scab-resistant replacement for Desirable. It produces a very large nut, 37-39 per pound, with 52-55% kernel and Desirable-like shape and color, and its scab resistance is markedly superior to Desirable's in Georgia trials. Huffman thins its own crop similarly to Desirable and needs little additional hand-thinning to bear consistently from year to year. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it near a Type II cultivar for good nut set. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Hugin Aronia (Compact Scandinavian Black Chokeberry)
description: Hugin is a Scandinavian-bred black chokeberry selected for a noticeably more compact, tidy habit than seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa, named for one of the two ravens of Norse mythology and well suited to smaller gardens where full-size aronia would sprawl. It flowers profusely in spring with white clusters that draw pollinators, then sets heavy loads of shiny black, tannin-rich berries best used for juice, syrup, or jam rather than fresh eating, since raw fruit is quite astringent. Fall color is a strong point, turning brilliant orange-red well before most other fruiting shrubs color up. It tolerates wet or boggy soil far better than most berry shrubs but performs poorly on shallow, chalky ground, so amend heavy alkaline soils before planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hull Thornless Blackberry (USDA Semi-Erect Thornless Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and tie the semi-erect, arching canes to a two-wire trellis to keep fruit clusters accessible and off the ground. Hull Thornless was developed by USDA-ARS breeders at Beltsville, Maryland and released in the early 1980s as part of a program aimed at combining the thornless trait with better cold tolerance and fruit quality than earlier thornless releases. The berries are medium-to-large, glossy black, and notably sweeter than many of its thornless predecessors, ripening over a fairly long midseason window with good yields once the semi-erect canes are established. Because it tolerates cooler winters better than many thornless trailing types, Hull Thornless became a popular home-garden choice for growers who wanted thornless canes without moving to a warmer climate zone. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Hull-less Barley (Naked Barley)
description: Drill or broadcast seed into cool, firm, fertile soil in full sun; hull-less barley grows exactly like the familiar covered feed-barley but its papery hull separates from the kernel during threshing instead of staying glued on, so home growers can dehull a season's grain by hand-flailing and winnowing rather than needing a commercial pearling mill. Harvest when the heads have dried tan and kernels are hard, cutting stalks and drying them under cover for a week or two before threshing. The naked kernels cook like pearled barley in soups and pilafs, or can be milled into a nutty, high-fiber flour. In the Gulf South, fall planting takes advantage of the mild winter growing window and lets the crop mature and dry down before summer humidity sets in. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Hull-less Oat (Naked Oat, Streaker Oat)
description: Broadcast or drill seed into cool, firm, fertile soil in full sun and rake in for good contact; hull-less oat grows and looks much like ordinary cereal oats but its grain separates cleanly from the hull during ordinary hand or flail threshing, skipping the abrasive dehulling step that makes standard Avena sativa impractical to process by hand. Harvest when the seed heads have dried to tan and the grain is hard, cutting whole stalks and letting them finish drying under cover for a week or two before threshing. Yields are somewhat lower than commercial oat varieties bred for hulled grain, but for a home patch the labor saved at threshing time more than makes up for it. In the Gulf South, fall sowing lets the crop bulk up over winter and mature before summer heat arrives. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Hummingbird Mint (Bubblegum Hyssop)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hummingbird mint is a native sage relative of the Texas-New Mexico border region with the most extraordinary foliage fragrance in the genus — a pure, sweet bubblegum-spearmint scent that fills the air when brushed. The deep rose-pink tubular flowers from summer through frost are consumed almost exclusively by hummingbirds, which are so attracted to the flowers that the plant earns its common name. It is genuinely drought tolerant and thrives in hot, dry conditions where it has excellent drainage. The plant self-sows modestly and is short-lived as a perennial (3–5 years); take cuttings in summer to maintain the garden. Deer resistant. An excellent choice for zone 8–9 pollinator gardens in full sun with excellent drainage. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Hummingbird Sage (Pitcher Sage)
description: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in partial shade; hummingbird sage is one of the most useful native California salvias for gardens, tolerating more shade than most salvias while producing large, striking, rose-magenta flower spikes on tall stems — among the largest flowers of any native California sage, strongly attractive to Anna's hummingbirds and rufous hummingbirds throughout the blooming season from late winter through spring. The large, crinkled, gray-green aromatic leaves smell strongly of fresh pineapple and sage when crushed. Spreads by rhizomes to form gradually expanding colonies that provide excellent, drought-tolerant groundcover under California oaks and in dappled shade. One of the best California natives for replacing invasive English ivy under trees while maintaining shade coverage and providing outstanding wildlife value for hummingbirds and native bees. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Black Pepper (Cold-Hardy Purple-Black Ornamental Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after the coldest weather has passed. Hungarian Black is a dual-purpose ornamental and culinary pepper with striking deep purple flowers and foliage that darkens to near-black, setting slender purple-black fruit that ripens through purple to bright red, giving the plant multicolor visual interest across a single growing season. Fruit carries mild to medium heat, roughly comparable to a jalapeño, and is entirely usable in the kitchen even though the plant is most often grown for its dramatic dark coloring in ornamental beds and containers. Among peppers it is notably more tolerant of cool temperatures than typical tropical types, allowing a slightly earlier transplant date and better performance into cool fall weather. Harvest at any color stage; purple fruit is milder and firmer, while fully red fruit is sweeter and slightly hotter. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Heart Tomato (Large Pink Oxheart Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably warm. Hungarian Heart is an oxheart-type heirloom traced to a village near Budapest around 1900, valued for producing pointed, meaty pink fruit that often exceeds a pound with very few seeds and little core. The dense flesh and low moisture content make it especially good for sauces and canning as well as fresh slicing. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vines well, since the heavy fruit clusters can pull down unsupported branches. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Hot Wax Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant to the garden once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F; Hungarian Hot Wax is a medium-heat open-pollinated pepper (5,000–10,000 Scoville units) that produces waxy, pale-yellow 5–7 inch fruits that ripen through orange to deep red, and it is among the most versatile peppers for pickling, stuffing, frying, and fresh eating. Fruits are ready to pick at the yellow stage for the mildest heat and thickest walls, or left to ripen red for maximum color and slightly more intensity. This variety is highly productive and disease-tolerant, thriving in both humid and dryer conditions; plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and avoid overwatering once plants are established. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Sweet Wax Pepper (Banana Pepper, Sweet Yellow Wax Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Hungarian Sweet Wax (also commonly called banana pepper, though this term covers both sweet and hot wax types) is one of the most widely grown pickling peppers in North America — a long (5–7 inch), tapered, waxy-skinned, pale yellow to golden-yellow pepper with very mild to no heat that has become the standard home pickle pepper for generations of American gardeners. The waxy, smooth skin characteristic gives these peppers excellent structure for pickling — the thin walls absorb brine quickly, the skin maintains its integrity through the canning process, and the mild flavor showcases the pickling brine without competition from pepper heat. Hungarian Sweet Wax is the standard banana pepper of pizza restaurants and deli sandwiches across the United States, where it appears in countless jar formats — whole, sliced into rings, or pickled in brine. Beyond pickling, the fresh peppers are excellent eaten raw (sweeter and crisper than bell peppers), stuffed with cream cheese, and sliced in salads. Prolific plants produce heavily throughout the summer, yielding more peppers per plant than bell types. The sweet type should not be confused with Hungarian Hot Wax (which has 1,000–15,000 SHU); both look nearly identical at the yellow harvest stage. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Wax Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm mix maintained at 78–82°F; germination is fastest and most even with bottom heat from a heat mat. Hungarian wax peppers produce thick-walled, banana-shaped fruits that ripen from pale yellow through orange to red; they range from mildly hot (1,000 Scoville) when yellow to moderately hot when fully red. Harvest yellow fruits at 65 days for pickling (the classic use), or allow to ripen through the color stages for fresh eating and sauces. Plants are heavy producers and benefit from a midseason application of balanced fertilizer to sustain yield. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Hungarian Wax Pepper
description: Start indoors and transplant to warm, fertile soil after last frost; Hungarian wax pepper produces elongated, 5–6 inch pale yellow (wax-colored) fruits that mature to red and have a medium heat level (2,500–10,000 SHU) — hotter than banana peppers but milder than jalapeños. The waxy, thick-walled fruits are outstanding for pickling (Hungarian pickled peppers are a traditional condiment), stuffing, grilling, and use in Hungarian goulash and paprikash. They are also excellent raw in salads and are often confused with banana peppers in grocery stores, though the two have different heat levels and slightly different flavors. The plants are extremely productive, producing dozens of fruits per plant through the growing season. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Hunt Fig (Texas-Bred Nematode-Resistant Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Hunt was developed in Texas and selected for genuinely good resistance to root-knot nematodes and several fig diseases that trouble other varieties in the warm, humid soils of the Gulf South, making it a particularly reliable, low-maintenance choice for Texas, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf Coast gardens. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, richly flavored pink-amber flesh, good for fresh eating and preserves, and the productive tree bears a heavy main crop in late summer. Its combination of regional disease resistance and dependable production has made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast home orchardists specifically dealing with the nematode-prone sandy soils common across the region. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hunt Muscadine Grape (Early-Ripening Black Female Cultivar)
description: Hunt is a black-skinned muscadine selected in 1920 at the Georgia Experiment Station in Experiment, Georgia, and remains a widely planted heirloom valued for its early ripening and high sugar content. The medium-large berries hang in good-sized clusters with medium-tough skin and rich, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating, juice, jelly, and wine. Hunt carries only female flowers, so a self-fertile pollinator such as Carlos or Cowart must be planted nearby to secure reliable crops. The vine is notably vigorous and tolerant of heat, drought, and the fungal diseases that trouble bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Hunterdon Hazelnut (Rutgers EFB-Resistant Eastern Filbert)
description: Hunterdon is a vigorous, upright hazelnut with a slightly spreading habit, one of four cultivars released by Rutgers University in 2020 for Eastern Filbert Blight resistance and productivity under Mid-Atlantic conditions. It carries a high level of blight tolerance, though somewhat less than sibling cultivars Raritan and Monmouth, and is prized for mostly round, medium-to-large kernels with outstanding flavor and excellent blanching. It is self-incompatible and among the earliest of the Rutgers releases to ripen, typically ready from late August into the first week of September. Grow it in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range, and plant a compatible pollenizer for dependable annual crops. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Huntington Carpet Rosemary (Extremely Prostrate Groundcover Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Huntington Carpet is among the most flat-growing, ground-hugging rosemary cultivars available, spreading widely while staying only a few inches tall, making it an excellent choice for covering a sunny bank or slope, cascading over a wall, or filling a large container where a true groundcover habit is wanted rather than an upright shrub form. It shares the same fragrant, culinary-quality foliage as other rosemary cultivars and produces small blue flowers in season. Excellent drainage is essential, since rosemary is highly prone to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soil, and it needs very little pruning to maintain its naturally flat, spreading form. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Hunza Apricot (Drought-Tolerant Heirloom Apricot from the Karakoram)
description: Hunza apricot originates from the arid Hunza Valley of the Karakoram range in northern Pakistan, where apricots are a dietary staple traditionally dried whole with the sweet, edible kernel left inside the pit. The small-to-medium fruit is sweet, richly flavored, and freestone, and the tree is notably drought-tolerant once established, reflecting its origins in a dry mountain climate. It is self-fertile, so a single tree bears fruit, though a second apricot nearby can improve set in a marginal year. In humid climates like the Gulf South, prioritize excellent drainage and airflow to reduce fungal disease pressure that this variety does not encounter in its native range. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Husky Cherry Red Tomato (Compact Cherry Tomato)
description: Transplant into full sun after the last frost, giving the sturdy, thick-stemmed vine a small cage to support its heavy cherry tomato clusters. Husky Cherry Red is an All-America Selections winner in the Husky series bred for a compact, potato-leaf indeterminate habit that concentrates energy into abundant 1-1.5 inch, deep-red, sweet-tart fruit rather than excess vine growth, making it a dependable choice for smaller gardens that still want continuous cherry tomato production. It is distinct from the larger-fruited Husky Red slicer in the same series. Matures in 60–65 days from transplant.

name: Husky Red Tomato (Compact Semi-Determinate Hybrid Tomato for Containers and Small Gardens)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake lightly. Harvest when uniformly deep red and gives slightly to pressure. Husky Red is a hybrid tomato variety bred for compact growing habit, good disease resistance, and productive fruit set in a semi-determinate plant that provides a midpoint between the sprawling unpredictability of indeterminate varieties and the one-time heavy crop of fully determinate types. The 'Husky' designation refers to the sturdy, self-supporting nature of the plant — Husky varieties were developed specifically to stand upright with minimal staking, making them practical for gardeners without room for large cage structures or tall stakes. The semi-determinate growth habit means Husky Red sets a substantial crop of fruits over a productive period and then slows significantly, unlike true indeterminate varieties that continue to grow and produce until frost. This concentrated production is an advantage for gardeners who want a substantial harvest over a defined period for preserving, canning, or fresh eating without managing continuous production throughout a long season. For container growing, Husky Red is one of the most practical full-sized slicing tomato varieties — its compact plant produces genuine slicing tomatoes (not just cherry or grape types) in a footprint manageable in a 15–20 gallon container. The VFNt resistance package provides meaningful protection against the soilborne diseases (Verticillium, Fusarium wilt, nematodes) and tobacco mosaic virus that limit tomato success in zone 9. Matures in 68–72 days from transplant.

name: Hutterite Soup Bean
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Hutterite Soup Bean is a pole bean heirloom preserved by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains and Canada — religious agricultural communities known for maintaining exceptional heirloom seed collections. The small, round, pale yellow seeds are outstanding soup beans with a creamy, slightly buttery, mild flavor and a texture that breaks down smoothly in long-simmered soups without becoming mushy — they were specifically selected and maintained by Hutterite cooks for soup making over many generations. The small seed size (similar to a navy bean) and mild flavor make Hutterite Soup Bean versatile in white bean soups, bean salads, and cassoulet-style dishes. The climbing pole bean vines are productive and the pods dry down cleanly for harvest. The Hutterite selection demonstrates exceptional adaptation to cool, short-season climates of the northern plains, but grows successfully in a wide range of conditions. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Hutterite Soup Bean (Yellow Hutterite Bean, Great Plains Heritage Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Hutterite beans tolerate short cool growing seasons (80–95 days makes them practical for zones 3–4 short summers); harvest dry pods when fully papery and rattle when shaken. Hutterite Soup Bean is an heirloom dry bean variety maintained by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains — communal Anabaptist communities of German and Austrian origin who settled the Montana, South Dakota, and Alberta regions in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, bringing their traditional agricultural varieties with them from Europe. The Hutterites maintain strict communal farming traditions including seed saving, and have preserved many heritage varieties of beans, grains, and vegetables that might otherwise have been lost. Hutterite beans have buff-yellow to light cream seeds with a mild, delicate flavor and an unusually thick, creamy texture when cooked — thicker than navy beans or great northern beans, with less tendency to break down or become mushy when simmered long. This creamy texture makes them particularly well-suited for thick soups and stews in the German-Russian culinary tradition of the Hutterite communities — served weekly in communal dining halls as 'bean soup Sunday.' The variety is adapted to the short, cool growing seasons of the northern plains, making it also excellent for short-season northern gardeners who struggle with longer-season dry beans. Good flavor for use in any white-bean recipe; outstanding in soups. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Hyacinth Bean
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; hyacinth bean is a fast-climbing, ornamental tropical vine producing deep purple stems, lavender to violet pea flowers in upright racemes, and shiny deep-purple seed pods that are among the most spectacular of any annual vine. Young pods and fresh seeds are edible when thoroughly cooked — raw or undercooked seeds contain toxic cyanogenic glycosides (phytohaemagglutinin) and must never be eaten without boiling; immature flat pods may be eaten like snap beans after thorough cooking. The vine reaches 10–15 feet in a single season and thrives in hot, humid summer conditions where it fixes nitrogen and provides dense ornamental coverage on structures. In tropical and subtropical climates (zone 9–11), plants may persist as perennials and develop a woody base. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Hyakume Persimmon (Gosho, Nearly Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume, also sold as Gosho, is a large, flattish Japanese kaki persimmon cultivar notable among astringent-type persimmons for a distinctive trait — when the flowers are pollinated and seeds form, the flesh develops streaks and flecks of brown, sugary tissue, and fruit with enough of this coloring can be eaten firm and crisp like a non-astringent type rather than requiring full softening. Unpollinated fruit without seeds remains fully astringent until soft-ripe, so planting near another kaki cultivar for pollination noticeably improves the eating experience. The fruit is large, pale orange, and mild-flavored with a pleasant, slightly spiced sweetness once the brown sugar-flecking develops. Trees are vigorous, productive, and, like most Asian persimmons, largely trouble-free once established, tolerating heat and a range of soils well. Harvest in fall as fruit colors fully; taste-test a fruit or two to judge whether the crop has enough pollination-driven flecking to eat crisp, or whether it needs to soften fully before eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Hybrid Amaranth (Slim Amaranth)
description: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; hybrid amaranth (also called slim amaranth, green amaranth, or quelite in Mexican Spanish) is one of the most important wild and cultivated leaf vegetables in the tropical and subtropical world — a coarse, weedy-to-cultivated annual of the amaranth family widely consumed as a cooked green leaf vegetable (called 'alefu' in Ethiopia, 'callaloo' in the Caribbean, 'rajgira' leaves in India) across Africa, South Asia, and the Caribbean. The tender young leaves and shoot tips are harvested and cooked like spinach — mild in flavor, nutritious, and fast-growing in warm weather. One of the parent species of the cultivated grain amaranths (Amaranthus cruentus and others) selected for large seed production. Self-sows prolifically and establishes easily in hot, dry, disturbed soil — one of the most adaptable and heat-tolerant leaf vegetables available. Harvest young leaves continuously through the summer; the plant bolts in heat to produce seed heads used as grain in traditional cultures. Matures in 55–80 days from seed.

name: Hyskin Onion
description: Hyskin is a hardy British heirloom onion grown from autumn-planted sets to give an earlier harvest the following summer than spring-planted types. Push the small bulbs into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving just the tip exposed, and mulch lightly in the coldest regions to protect against hard freezes. Growth resumes as days lengthen in spring, and the brown-skinned bulbs size up quickly ahead of standard maincrop onions. Because overwintered onions generally store less well than spring-planted maincrop types, plan to use Hyskin bulbs within a few months of the early-summer harvest. Matures in 240–280 days from seed.

name: Hyssop
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep indoors in warm starting mix; germination is fast and reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — hyssop is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in conditions similar to lavender. Prune plants back by about one-third after flowering to keep them from becoming woody and to promote a compact, bushy habit. Harvest leafy stems and flowers in the morning just as the blossoms begin to open, drying them for use in expectorant teas, culinary herb blends, and potpourri. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: I'itoi Onion (Sonoran Perennial Multiplier Onion)
description: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them 6-8 inches apart to give clumps room to multiply. I'itoi is a heirloom perennial multiplier onion long cultivated by the Tohono O'odham of the Sonoran Desert borderlands, and it is unusual among onions for tolerating both intense summer heat and winter cold, which lets it persist as a perennial clump in Gulf Coast gardens rather than needing yearly replanting. A single planted bulb divides into eight or more bulbs within a season, and gardeners typically harvest by pulling scallion-like greens continuously while leaving part of the clump to keep multiplying underground. Dig and divide the clump when the foliage dies back in summer dormancy, replanting a portion immediately to keep the planting going indefinitely. Matures in 84–112 days from transplant.

name: Ibis Celeriac (Smooth-Skinned Septoria-Resistant Celery Root)
description: Ibis is a fast-developing celeriac prized by market growers for its smooth, oval-round white globes that clean up with minimal peeling loss compared to older, knobbier types. Its strong field resistance to septoria leaf spot keeps the canopy healthy through the long season needed to size up a root, and its bolt-hardiness makes it a reasonable choice for an early start under cover. As with all celeriac, keep the bed evenly and continuously moist, since inconsistent watering cracks and hollows the developing globe, and strip away side shoots through summer to concentrate growth into the root. Harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing root with a clean, nutty celery flavor. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Icatu Coffee
description: Bred at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas beginning in 1950 by crossing tetraploid Robusta with Arabica and repeatedly backcrossing the progeny to Mundo Novo over many generations, Icatu was the first successful artificial Arabica-Robusta hybrid released for commercial planting and takes its name from a Tupi-Guarani word evoking calm after a storm. It inherited useful disease and nematode tolerance from its Robusta ancestry while keeping recognizably Arabica-quality cups with notes of chocolate and light citrus, and it typically out-yields older Brazilian cultivars like Mundo Novo by a healthy margin. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade with the same warm, frost-free conditions other Arabicas need, expecting a vigorous, tall-growing tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ice Cream Banana
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil with consistent moisture — banana requires abundant water, nutrients, and heat to produce fruit; Ice Cream banana (also called Blue Java) is a cold-tolerant banana cultivar notable for its distinctive blue-green to silvery-blue coloring on unripe fruits and the unusually rich, creamy flavor of ripe fruit described as reminiscent of vanilla ice cream — a flavor and texture quality that sets this cultivar apart from the standard Cavendish banana flavor most North Americans are accustomed to. The ripe fruits develop a pale yellow to creamy-white flesh with a particularly soft, smooth, melting texture and vanilla-banana flavor that is among the finest of all banana varieties for fresh eating. Ice Cream's relative cold tolerance compared to Cavendish and other commercial varieties (the rhizome surviving to approximately 22°F with mulching) makes it one of the most practical banana varieties for zone 9 Gulf South gardens where winter freezes regularly kill the above-ground pseudostem. In zone 9 the combination of the summer heat, humidity, and rain that banana requires, combined with the cold-hardiness that allows ratoon production from surviving rhizomes, makes Ice Cream banana one of the most rewarding tropical fruit plants available. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Ice Cream Banana (Blue Java Cold-Hardy Vanilla-Flavored Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Blue Java (Ice Cream banana) is one of the most cold-hardy banana cultivars available for Gulf South gardens — tolerating frost temperatures to approximately 20°F, allowing the rhizome to survive most zone 9 winters even when the pseudostem is frozen to the ground and regenerate productive new shoots in spring. The variety name 'Blue Java' refers to the distinctive blue-green color of the unripe fruit bunches; the 'Ice Cream' name describes the rich, creamy, vanilla-like flavor of the ripe fruit — a flavor profile distinctly different from the standard Cavendish banana of commerce and more complex, with smooth, creamy, slightly vanilla-custard characteristics that justify the evocative name. The medium-length (6–8 inch), pale-yellow ripe fruits have a soft, creamy texture that reinforces the ice cream comparison. In zone 9, Blue Java typically requires the full warm season (May–October) for pseudostem development, and established plants with multiple offsets may fruit in warm years with protection through mild winters. Even when pseudostems are killed by frost, the vigorous rhizome system regenerates multiple new shoots in spring, making Blue Java a reliable ornamental tropical even in years when fruit production is not achieved. Heavy mulching around the base protects the rhizome during cold snaps. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Ice Cream Banana Tree
description: Also called Blue Java, this banana yields creamy, vanilla-flavored fruit and tolerates more cold and wind than most bananas. Give it full sun, rich soil, and abundant water plus regular feeding to fuel its fast growth. The bluish fruit ripens to pale yellow and is best eaten fresh. In marginal climates grow it in a large container and overwinter the plant in a bright, frost-free spot. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Ice Cream Bean (Joaquiniquil)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — ice cream bean is a fast-growing Central and South American legume tree producing enormous pods (12–30 inches long) filled with white, cottony, sweet pulp that wraps the seeds and tastes unmistakably of vanilla ice cream. The white pulp is eaten fresh directly from the pod; it melts on the tongue with a sweet, mild, creamy vanilla flavor that surprises everyone who encounters it for the first time. Beyond the extraordinary fruit, ice cream bean is a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility, an excellent shade and windbreak tree (growing 30–40 feet), and a valuable component of agroforestry systems throughout the tropics. The fragrant white flower pompoms attract hummingbirds and native bees. It grows rapidly in the frost-free tropics and sub-tropics, beginning to fruit in 2–3 years from seed. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ice Plant (Crystal Ice Plant, Common Ice Plant)
description: Sow in fall in well-drained, sandy, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; the common ice plant is one of the most visually distinctive of all edible plants — the thick, fleshy, spatula-shaped leaves and stems are covered in large, glistening, fluid-filled papillae (water cells) that catch and reflect sunlight like tiny glass beads or ice crystals, giving the plant its enchanting name. The mildly salty, refreshing leaves are edible raw in salads, as a garnish, or as a substitute for spinach, with a texture somewhere between watercress and succulent. The plant is halophytic (salt-tolerant) and is often used to bind coastal sandy soils. It is a cool-season plant that grows through winter in zone 9–11 and dies in summer heat. The species is considered invasive in California coastal areas where it has altered soil chemistry — plant only in maintained garden areas. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Ice Queen Crisphead Lettuce
description: Also called Reine des Glaces, this 1883 Batavian summer-crisp lettuce is cold tolerant, heat tolerant, and slow to bolt, with frilly emerald leaves and crisp texture. Direct sow in cool soil and thin to give heads room to form. Keep evenly watered to avoid bitterness, and offer light afternoon shade during heat to extend the harvest. Cut whole heads at maturity or harvest outer leaves as needed. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Iceberg Lettuce
description: This heirloom crisphead forms compact, tight heads about eight inches across with firm, mild, refreshingly crunchy leaves. Sow in cool weather, either early spring or late summer, since heat triggers bolting and bitterness. Thin plants to give each head room to fill out and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest when heads feel firm and full, cutting at the base in the cool part of the day. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Ichang Lemon (Cold-Hardy Citrus)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the hardiest citrus species available, surviving winter conditions that kill standard lemons and limes outright. Citrus ichangensis (Ichang lemon, or Ichang papeda) is a wild citrus species native to the mountainous borderlands of China, prized by cold-hardy citrus breeders and enthusiasts as one of the parents behind many of today's cold-tolerant citrus hybrids, thanks to its unusual combination of true citrus flavor and genuine winter hardiness. The rough-skinned, lemon-like fruit is highly acidic and aromatic with a distinct floral note, used much like a true lemon for juice, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating out of hand. Its glossy, deep green, notably large-winged leaves and modest thorns give it strong ornamental value even apart from fruiting. A rewarding choice for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast who want to grow citrus outside the usual protected range, and a useful parent plant for anyone interested in breeding hardier citrus hybrids, zone 7–10. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ichang Papeda
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ichang Papeda (Citrus ichangensis, Ichang lemon) is a wild citrus species from the mountains of central China near Yichang on the Yangtze River — the hardiest true citrus species, capable of surviving brief temperatures near 0°F and making it valuable for cold-climate citrus experimentation far beyond the normal range. The large, fragrant, lemon-yellow fruits are highly aromatic but extremely acidic and seedy, used for juice, fragrance, and culinary flavoring rather than fresh eating. The distinctive winged petioles on the leaves identify the plant and give it an interesting ornamental appearance with an almost tropical look. In zone 9 Ichang Papeda grows vigorously and produces abundant, highly aromatic fruit with a distinctive floral-citrus fragrance used in Chinese cooking and perfumery. Ichang Papeda is a parent of the Yuzu lemon hybrid and has contributed cold hardiness to many important citrus breeding programs; it thrives in zone 9 as an ornamental citrus tree with exceptional cold insurance. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Ichi Ki Kei Jiro Persimmon (Self-Fertile Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and stake young trees until well established. Ichi Ki Kei Jiro is a compact, heavy-bearing Japanese persimmon cultivar belonging to the non-astringent group, meaning the fruit can be harvested and eaten crisp and sweet as soon as it reaches full orange color, unlike astringent Asian and American persimmons that must fully soften before they are palatable. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will produce a full crop without a pollinator, and its naturally smaller stature suits home orchards with limited space. Thin fruit if the tree sets an especially heavy crop to improve size, and harvest by clipping fruit from the branch rather than pulling, since the stem can tear the skin. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ichiban Eggplant (Japanese Eggplant, Long Slender Eggplant)
description: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun when night temperatures stay above 55°F; Ichiban is the classic Japanese-type slender eggplant — producing long (10–12 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter), cylindrical, deep purple-black fruits that are harvested young and tender with exceptionally thin, delicate skin, very few seeds, and mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh. The thin skin and low seed content of Ichiban-type eggplants produce a fundamentally different culinary result from standard oval Italian-type eggplants — the flesh is tender-soft rather than dense, the flavor is milder and sweeter, and the skin is thin enough to be eaten without peeling. This makes Ichiban particularly well-suited to quick stir-frying, grilling, and Asian cooking methods. In zone 9, Ichiban is one of the most heat-tolerant vegetables available — eggplants love the hot, humid Gulf Coast summer that defeats many vegetables, and Ichiban's slender fruit type tends to size up and set fruit more reliably in extreme heat than standard round or oval types. Harvest when the fruit skin is deep, glossy purple-black and before any softening or browning of the calyx — once the skin loses its gloss, the fruit is overripe. The plants can be maintained year-round as perennial shrubs in frost-free zone 10–11, and in zone 9 they often survive mild winters and produce prolifically in their second year. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Ichiban Nashi Asian Pear
description: Ichiban Nashi produces fine-textured, crisp fruit with a mellow butterscotch flavor, eaten fresh rather than cooked or stored to soften the way European pears are. The tree is noted for reliable, heavy production once established. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and, in common with most nashi cultivars, offers little inherent resistance to fire blight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Icicle Eggplant (AAS-Winning Spineless White Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest flavor and fewest seeds. Icicle is an AAS-winning eggplant producing long, slender, pure-white fruit on spineless plants, a genuine convenience for hand-harvesting compared to the sharp spines that guard the calyx of many eggplant varieties. It carries noticeably fewer seeds than typical white eggplant, giving a creamier, less bitter texture, and its tender skin needs no peeling. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season. Harvest regularly while fruit is still glossy and firm, since letting fruit overripen on the plant both reduces quality and slows further production; the plant responds to frequent picking with a steady stream of new fruit through the season. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: ICS 1 Cacao
description: Selected in Trinidad in the early twentieth century by the breeding program at the Imperial College of Tropical Agriculture, ICS 1 belongs to the historic 'Imperial College Selection' series of Trinitario-type clones prized for excellent chocolate flavor and still maintained in cacao germplasm collections worldwide. It has been used both as a direct planting material valued by fine-flavor chocolate makers and as parent stock in countless later breeding programs seeking to combine good flavor with improved vigor or disease resistance. Growth habit is moderately vigorous and upright, similar to other Trinitario selections. Grow it under the same filtered shade and rich, moist soil conditions favored by heirloom cacao types. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: ICS 6 Cacao (Imperial College Selection 6)
description: ICS 6 is another member of the Imperial College Selection series bred in Trinidad from Criollo and Lower Amazon Forastero parentage, part of the same twentieth-century breeding program that produced ICS 1 and ICS 95. It has long been maintained in cacao germplasm collections and used in breeding and comparative agronomy trials for traits including yield, vigor, and disease response, and it is occasionally planted directly for its Trinitario-type flavor contribution. Habit is moderately vigorous and upright, similar to its sister ICS selections. Provide the same filtered shade beneath taller companion trees and rich, moist, well-drained soil recommended for other Trinitario cacao types. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: ICS 95 Cacao (Imperial College Selection 95, CCN-51 Parent)
description: ICS 95 belongs to the historic Imperial College Selection series of Trinitario clones developed in Trinidad in the early twentieth century, combining genetic contributions from Criollo and Lower Amazon Forastero. It is best known today as one of the parent clones, alongside IMC 67, used to create the high-yielding CCN-51 hybrid that now dominates much of Ecuador's cacao production, though ICS 95 is also grown and studied in its own right for its agronomic performance and flavor contribution. Growth habit is vigorous and upright, typical of Trinitario-type selections, with moderate disease tolerance compared with pure Criollo lines. Cultivate it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, providing the same warm, humid, sheltered conditions favored by other heirloom and hybrid cacao types. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Icterina Sage (Golden Variegated Culinary Sage)
description: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring or summer and plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Icterina is a variegated culinary sage with soft gray-green leaves broadly edged in gold, giving a brighter, more luminous look to an herb garden or mixed border than plain green sage while carrying the same savory, slightly peppery flavor used in stuffings, poultry dishes, and herb butters. It stays a bit more compact than green garden sage, making it useful for edging or container plantings. Cut back hard in early spring to remove winter-worn growth and encourage fresh, well-colored new leaves. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Ida Lingonberry (Swedish Balsgård Cultivar)
description: Ida was developed at Sweden's Balsgård research station and stood out in USDA-ARS comparative trials for having notably higher anthocyanin content than several sibling Swedish cultivars, giving its berries a deeper red color. It forms the same low, glossy-leaved evergreen mat typical of the species, spreading gradually by rhizomes into a dense groundcover over a few seasons. Grow it in very acidic, humus-rich soil in the pH 4.5-5.5 range, ideally in the light shade of taller acid-loving shrubs like blueberry or rhododendron. Renew older plantings by shearing back hard every few years to stimulate fresh, more productive growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Idaho Silverskin Garlic (Softneck)
description: Idaho Silverskin is a softneck garlic strain adapted to the high desert growing conditions of southern Idaho, producing tightly wrapped, bright white bulbs with 12-18 small, densely packed cloves ideal for braiding. It stores exceptionally well, often keeping firm for 9-12 months past harvest, longer than most hardneck types. Because it lacks a hard central stalk, the flexible leaves make traditional garlic braids easy to weave for kitchen storage or gifting. Choose this variety for its outstanding shelf life and adaptability to warmer, drier growing regions where hardneck types underperform. Matures in 210–240 days from seed.

name: Idared Apple (Idaho-Bred Long-Storage Baking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Idared was bred at the University of Idaho and released in 1942 from a cross of Jonathan and Wagener, developed specifically to combine good eating quality with truly outstanding long-term storage life, and it remains one of the best-keeping apples widely available, often holding good quality for six months or more in cold storage. The bright, uniform red fruit has firm, crisp, white flesh that starts out notably tart and mellows into a pleasant, mild tartness in storage, making it a favorite for pies, sauce, and baking, since it holds its shape well under heat. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reliable, and the fruit's long shelf life makes it an especially practical choice for home orchardists wanting apples that last well into winter without special storage facilities. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Iditarod Red Tomato (Large-Fruited Compact Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Iditarod Red bears notably large, deep red beefsteak-style fruit for a dwarf tomato, often rivaling full-size indeterminate slicers in fruit weight despite growing on a compact, manageable plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its combination of big fruit and small plant footprint makes it a standout choice for gardeners short on space who still want a substantial slicing tomato. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Igloo Cauliflower
description: Igloo is a fast, open-pollinated cauliflower that reaches harvest in under two months, notably quicker than most named cauliflower cultivars. Its compact upright leaves naturally curl inward over the curd, giving a degree of self-blanching protection from sun exposure without extra tying. The speed and reliability of Igloo make it especially well suited to succession sowing through a cool season or to squeezing in a crop where the growing window is short. Select Igloo when quick, dependable snow-white curds are the priority over large head size. Matures in 50–58 days from transplant.

name: IHCAFE 90 Coffee
description: Released by the Instituto Hondureno del Cafe, IHCAFE 90 is a pedigree selection combining Hibrido de Timor with Caturra, giving it the same rust-resistant lineage as other Sarchimor and Catimor-type hybrids. It is a dwarf, high-yielding plant well adapted to the lower-elevation farms common in Honduras, where many traditional tall varieties struggle with disease pressure, though its cup profile, typically balanced, citrusy, and mild, trails behind flavor-forward heirloom varieties. Growers who take it to higher elevations and process it carefully can coax out noticeably better sweetness and clarity than the variety's reputation as a yield-focused workhorse might suggest. Culture follows other dwarf Central American arabica hybrids: rich, well-drained acidic soil, partial shade, and steady moisture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Iholena Banana (Hawaiian Heirloom Banana)
description: Iholena is a traditional Hawaiian and wider Polynesian banana grown for centuries as a dual-purpose fruit, eaten fresh when tree-ripened or cooked while still starchy and green. Its blunt, short fruit and reddish-tinged bracts distinguish it from the slender Cavendish types more commonly sold in stores, and older Hawaiian selections come in a range of skin colors from green to nearly maroon. Grow it in deep, fertile, well-watered soil in full sun, and expect a large, vigorous plant that benefits from wind shelter given its broad leaves. In a Gulf Coast garden it is best grown as a warm-season specialty planting protected from hard freezes rather than left to overwinter unprotected. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Ikaika Macadamia (HAES 333)
description: Ikaika (HAES 333) is a Hawaii-developed macadamia selection prized in commercial orchards for its unusually strong, compact branching structure, which holds up well to the strong trade winds common on Hawaii's macadamia-growing slopes where more brittle cultivars suffer limb breakage. It bears a reliable, moderate crop of good cracking-quality nuts on a vigorous tree and is often planted as a windbreak selection within mixed orchard blocks alongside higher-yielding cultivars. Like other macadamias it needs many years of warm, frost-free growth before significant bearing, along with a compatible cross-pollinator. Water regularly during nut development and allow nuts to fall naturally before harvest. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ilama
description: Ilama is a semi-deciduous Annona from Mexico and Central America that tolerates drier conditions than most of its relatives, preferring a pronounced dry season to trigger leaf drop and subsequent flowering. Like other Annonaceae, flowers are protogynous and benefit strongly from hand-pollination — collect pollen in the afternoon from half-closed male-stage flowers and dab onto receptive stigmas of newly opened female-stage flowers in the morning. Fruit comes in pink-fleshed and white-fleshed strains; the pink-fleshed type has a slightly acidic flavor while the white is sweeter and more custard-like. Harvest when the skin has slightly separated at the segment lines and the fruit gives to gentle pressure; shelf life at room temperature is only 1–2 days. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Illikomban Eggplant (Kerala Heirloom Long Green Snake Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55F; harvest fruit young and glossy for the sweetest flavor and most tender texture. Illikomban is a rare heirloom from the Onattukara backwater region of South Kerala, India, named for its resemblance to an elephant tusk and prized for producing glossy, light green fruit that can reach two feet or more in length.
