The silky, nearly seedless flesh has a sweet, nutty flavor that cooks down quickly, making it well suited to curries and stir-fries where the fruit is sliced and absorbs bold spices readily. As a variety selected for tropical growing conditions, it takes the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer in stride, continuing to set long fruit through the hottest stretch of the season when many Western eggplant types slow production. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Illini Hardy Blackberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Erect Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Illini Hardy is an erect, thorny blackberry developed at the University of Illinois specifically for reliable cane survival in cold northern winters where most blackberry varieties suffer significant winterkill, tolerating temperatures well below zero without winter cane protection. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening mid-to-late season with good yields once established. Because the canes are self-supporting and very cold-tolerant, Illini Hardy is a dependable choice for northern growers who want blackberries without the trellising and winter mulching that tender varieties require. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 6-8 per plant to keep the planting productive and manageable. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Illini Xtra Sweet Sweet Corn
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in blocks of at least four rows for dependable wind pollination. Illini Xtra Sweet was developed at the University of Illinois around the discovery and early commercialization of the shrunken-2 (sh2) gene, which keeps sugars from converting to starch after picking, giving it a longer sweet eating window than older sugary (SU) corns like Golden Bantam. Unlike most modern sh2 hybrids, it is open-pollinated, so seed can be saved from year to year as long as isolation from other corn types is maintained. Keep soil consistently moist from tasseling through ear fill, since the plant is somewhat less vigorous in cool or wet spring conditions than newer hybrid supersweets. Matures in 85–92 days from seed.

name: Illinois Everbearing Mulberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — mulberry is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and conditions; Illinois Everbearing is a hybrid mulberry (Morus alba x Morus rubra) that produces the longest fruit season of any widely available mulberry cultivar — harvesting over 6–8 weeks from late spring into early summer compared to the brief 2–3 week window of standard mulberry varieties. The large, cylindrical, 1–1.5 inch fruits ripen from red through dark purple-black over the extended season, with the sweet, mild, slightly bland flavor characteristic of mulberries — less complex than blackberries, softer-textured, and milder-tasting, primarily valued for fresh eating, smoothies, and baked goods where the abundant, easily harvested fruit compensates for the relatively mild flavor. The practical appeal of Illinois Everbearing is unambiguous: a single established tree produces quantities of fruit (hundreds of pounds in a mature tree) over an extended period with essentially zero cultivation requirements beyond harvesting. As a wildlife plant, mulberry is unparalleled — the fruit is consumed by more than 60 species of birds and dozens of mammal species — making it the single most productive wildlife-supporting tree available for home landscapes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Illinois Everbearing Mulberry (Long-Season Red Mulberry Hybrid, Eastern Standard Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile; the trees are fast-growing and begin bearing in year 2–3; fruit ripens over an extended 4–6 week season (June–July in zones 5–7) rather than dropping all at once; the long harvesting period makes it practical to collect ripe fruit repeatedly from the ground or by shaking branches. Illinois Everbearing mulberry is a naturally occurring or deliberately selected hybrid of Morus alba (white mulberry) and Morus rubra (red mulberry) that was selected and propagated in Illinois in the mid-20th century and subsequently became the standard recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern and midwestern United States. The variety combines the key qualities of both parent species: from Morus rubra, it inherits superior fruit flavor — significantly more complex and berry-like than the often bland white mulberry — along with better fresh-eating quality; from Morus alba, it inherits cold-hardiness to zone 4 and adaptability to a wide range of soils and climates. The most practically important feature reflected in its name is the extended ripening season — berries mature gradually and drop over a period of 4–6 weeks rather than all ripening within 1–2 weeks as many mulberry seedlings do. This extended season makes it much more manageable for home fruit harvesting and wildlife feeding, and reduces the dramatic mess that concentrated mulberry drop can create on driveways, paths, and patios. The fruit quality is good: long (1–1.5 inch), dark red to black-purple berries with sweet, mild, pleasant mulberry flavor — not as intensely sweet as Pakistan Mulberry but far superior to most seedling trees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Imbu
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil; Spondias tuberosa is exceptionally drought tolerant — the underground water-storage tubers allow the tree to survive months of total drought; overwatering or waterlogged soil is fatal. Spondias tuberosa (Imbu, Umbú, or Umbuzeiro) is a drought-deciduous, small to medium tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga (semi-arid thorny scrubland) of the northeastern states of Pernambuco, Bahia, Sergipe, Piauí, and Ceará — one of the most important and beloved wild fruit trees of the Brazilian Northeast. The tree's defining ecological adaptation is remarkable: a system of massive, water-filled, carrot-to-sweet-potato-sized underground storage tubers (technically water-storing roots) that can accumulate hundreds of kilograms of water, allowing the tree to survive the brutal, multi-month droughts of the Caatinga and burst into fruit production with the first rains — typically January through March. The small (1–1.5 inch), round, pale-yellow to yellow-green fruits have juicy, sweet-sour, tropical, mango-lychee-like pulp eaten fresh, made into the beloved Brazilian drink umbuzada (fruit pulp boiled with milk and sugar), jams, and fermented into Caatinga wine. The tree has become a symbol of northeastern Brazilian cultural identity and food resilience. Spondias tuberosa is well adapted to dryland gardens in zone 9–11 where excellent drainage and full sun are provided; it is one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: IMC 67 Cacao
description: Collected from a wild population on an island in the Amazon River near Iquitos, Peru during germplasm expeditions of the 1930s that formed the historic 'Pound collection,' IMC 67 (its name short for Iquitos Mixed Calabacillo) is a pure Upper Amazon Forastero type valued for strong resistance to witches'-broom, moniliasis, and black pod, along with early flowering and tolerance of periodic flooding. It has been used worldwide as breeding stock, most famously as one of the two parents of the high-yielding Ecuadorian clone CCN-51. Grow it like other cacao, in rich, moist, well-drained soil beneath taller shade trees, with steady warmth and humidity and protection from wind while young. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Impepho (Imphepho)
description: Helichrysum odoratissimum is a strongly aromatic, woolly-grey-leaved perennial of South African grasslands, widely known as impepho and burned as dried bundled foliage in Zulu, Xhosa, and other southern African traditions to honor ancestors and cleanse a space, one of the most culturally significant smudging herbs of the region, comparable in role to white sage or sweetgrass elsewhere. The felted, silver-green leaves release a warm, honey-curry-like scent when brushed or dried, and clusters of small, papery, everlasting, golden-yellow flowers appear in summer and hold their color well after drying, making the plant useful for dried arrangements as well as ceremonial bundles. It thrives in poor, gritty soil and full sun, tolerating drought far better than excess moisture, and benefits from an annual cutback to keep growth dense and prevent legginess. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Imperator 58 Carrot
description: This AAS-winning heirloom yields long, tapered orange roots with fine-grained texture, outstanding sweetness, and thin, easy-to-peel skin. Sow seeds directly into loose, stone-free soil so the long roots can grow straight. Keep the seedbed consistently moist during the slow germination period, then thin seedlings to prevent crowding. Harvest once roots reach full size and sweeten further after a light frost. Matures in 68–78 days from seed.

name: Imperator Carrot (Long Imperator)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in very deeply prepared, loose, stone-free soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Imperator is the long, slender carrot of the grocery store — 8–10 inches long with a tapered tip, thin skin, high sugar content, and the satisfying snap of commercial carrots eaten fresh from supermarkets. It requires deep, perfectly loose, stone-free soil to reach full size without forking; raised beds with sandy loam are ideal. The flavor of home-grown Imperators freshly harvested is dramatically better than commercial versions; the high sugar content makes them outstanding for juicing, fresh eating, and the carrot sticks in lunch boxes. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Imperial Epineuse Plum (Historic French Prune-Type European Plum)
description: Imperial Epineuse is a French heirloom European plum discovered near the Lot Valley prune-growing district of France and brought to American growers by a California nurseryman in 1883. It became a historic reference variety for prune flavor and is still grown for its rich, sweet flesh that dries into a prune without the lye-dip treatment many other plums require. The medium-to-large oval freestone fruit has thin skin mottled in red, purple, and yellow-green beneath a light natural bloom, and the firm, slightly fibrous flesh is juicy and full-flavored fresh or dried. As a European plum it blooms later than Japanese types, which improves frost avoidance, and it is generally self-fertile though a nearby pollinator can improve yields. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Imperial Gem English Lavender
description: Plant in full sun with lean, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or waterlogged ground, which invites root rot. 'Imperial Gem' is a compact English lavender bearing unusually dark violet-blue flower spikes on upright stems held above tidy silver-gray foliage, a color depth that has earned it an RHS Award of Garden Merit and made it a favorite for hedging and dried-flower production. Shear lightly right after the main flush of bloom to keep the mound dense and encourage a possible second flush. It tolerates heat and drought once established but resents humid, poorly ventilated sites. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Imperial Star Artichoke (Annual Seed-Grown First-Year Flowering Artichoke)
description: Start seeds indoors at 65–70°F; expose seedlings to 50–55°F for 10 days (vernalization) before transplanting. Harvest buds when still tight and before the scales begin to open. Imperial Star is the pioneering annual artichoke variety bred by Keith Mayberry of the University of California Cooperative Extension in Imperial County — the variety that made artichoke production as an annual possible for the first time. Traditional artichoke varieties (such as Green Globe) are perennials that produce their first commercial harvest in the second or third year after planting from divisions; they require mild winters to survive (zone 8–9), making them impractical or impossible in colder climates. Imperial Star changed this by introducing the genetic characteristic of first-year flowering when exposed to a period of cool temperatures (vernalization) — the same cold-stimulus mechanism that triggers biennial flowering in brassicas, adapted to artichoke. When properly vernalized, Imperial Star plants produce their first artichoke buds in the same season they are planted, allowing artichoke cultivation as an annual across a much wider range of zones and eliminating the 2–3 year establishment period. The artichokes produced are full-sized, rounded, traditional artichoke form — not meaningfully different in size, flavor, or eating quality from perennial types. Imperial Star remains the dominant annual artichoke variety decades after its introduction, maintained by Johnny's Selected Seeds and other specialty vegetable suppliers as the standard annual artichoke reference. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Impress Purple English Lavender (Compact Seed-Grown Lavender)
description: Impress Purple is a seed-grown English lavender bred for compact, uniform mounds and dependable first-year flowering, making it popular for bedding displays and mass plantings where growers need consistent germination and habit from seed. Sow it indoors under light, since seed needs light to germinate and benefits from steady warmth; transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil once frost danger has passed. Deep violet-purple spikes rise over silvery foliage from early summer, and shearing the plant back by about a third after the first flush encourages a strong second bloom. Keep water low once established, since good drainage matters far more to this cultivar's longevity than fertility. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Improved Brown Turkey Fig (Larger-Fruited Brown Turkey Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Improved Brown Turkey is a selection of the classic Brown Turkey fig valued for producing somewhat larger, bronze-brown fruit with sweet, amber-pink flesh compared to standard Brown Turkey, while keeping the same dependable cold hardiness and heavy, reliable production that has made Brown Turkey one of the most widely planted figs in home gardens. Like other figs it bears on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by the main crop in late summer, and it needs minimal care beyond routine mulching and occasional pruning to control size. In colder zones, grow in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Improved Celeste Fig (Larger-Fruited Celeste Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun, and mulch around the root zone to help protect against winter root injury in the northern part of its range. Improved Celeste is a selection of the classic Celeste fig chosen by growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than the standard cultivar while retaining Celeste's honey-sweet, rose-pink flesh and thin, violet-brown skin, along with its reputation for exceptional cold hardiness and dependable, heavy production in Deep South gardens. It ripens over the same mid-July through August window as standard Celeste and requires the same minimal care — established trees rarely need fertilizer and produce well without spraying. As with all Celeste-type figs, the small, closed eye at the base of the fruit helps deter souring insects and fruit spoilage common in open-eyed fig varieties in humid climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Improved Fertility Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. An improved sport selected from the older English variety Fertility, it retains its parent's hardiness and remarkably heavy, reliable cropping while offering somewhat better dessert quality, bearing medium-sized fruit that is very sweet and juicy with a melting texture. Its partial self-fertility makes it a forgiving choice for a small home orchard with room for only one or two pear trees, though cropping still improves with a second variety nearby. Harvest in early-to-mid fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Improved Golden Wax Bush Bean
description: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has warmed. Improved Golden Wax is an early-twentieth-century refinement of the old Golden Wax bean, bred to add resistance to common bean mosaic and improve pod straightness while keeping the same flat, buttery-yellow, stringless pods and compact bush habit. Pick pods young, while still slender and snapping cleanly, since wax beans quickly develop tough strings and a fibrous texture if left to mature on the plant. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed can be saved for the next season by letting a few pods dry fully on the vine. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Improved Meyer Lemon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — Meyer lemon requires excellent drainage, regular deep watering during the growing season, and full sun for maximum fruit production; Improved Meyer Lemon is the most widely grown home lemon tree in the United States — a hybrid between a true lemon (Citrus limon) and a mandarin or sweet orange (possibly Citrus sinensis) that produces fruit with significantly less acidity and more sweetness than commercial lemons, combined with a distinctively rich, complex, floral lemon fragrance that makes it the preferred fresh lemon for culinary applications requiring the full flavor profile rather than pure acidity. The thin, smooth, deep yellow to orange-yellow skin is edible and aromatic, zesting beautifully for baking applications where the combination of lemon oil and zest from a Meyer produces a more complex, rounded result than commercial Eureka or Lisbon lemons. The combination of cold hardiness (extending the range further north than most citrus), compact tree size (6–10 feet), heavy and recurrent fruit production, beautiful flowers, and superior culinary quality has made Meyer lemon the definitive home citrus tree across zones 8–11. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Improved Meyer Lemon Bush
description: A younger, bushier form of the classic Improved Meyer, this lemon-orange hybrid produces sweet-tart, thin-skinned fruit on a compact plant well suited to pots. Grow in full sun with fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during active growth. Let the top inch of soil dry between deep waterings to prevent root rot. Bring it indoors to a bright window before frost in cooler zones. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Improved Meyer Lemon Tree
description: Improved Meyer is a low-maintenance lemon-orange hybrid that bears masses of fragrant, sweetly tart fruit, and it is nearly thornless and disease-resistant. It fruits reliably even for beginners and works beautifully as a container specimen. Provide full sun, fast-draining acidic soil, and regular citrus feeding through the growing season. In cold-winter areas keep it potted and move it indoors near bright light before the first frost. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Improved Rugen Alpine Strawberry (Everbearing German Woodland Strawberry)
description: Improved Rugen is a German alpine strawberry selection named for the Baltic island of Ruegen, valued for producing larger-than-typical fruit on plants that send out only a few short runners, so it stays tidier than wild seedling strawberries while still filling in a bed over time. Sow indoors in late winter, surface-sowing the dust-like seed and keeping it consistently moist under bright light. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, siting plants where they get a half day of sun; established clumps flower and fruit continuously from late spring into fall. Harvest the aromatic red berries as they ripen, since they soften quickly and do not hold well once picked. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Imshu Heartnut
description: Imshu is a long-established named heartnut selection prized among nut growers for heavy, consistent production and nuts that split cleanly along the suture to release a whole heart-shaped kernel with relatively little effort. It bears in long clusters typical of heartnut and tends to come into production somewhat earlier than seedling trees. As with all heartnuts, it is far less allelopathic than black walnut, so it can be sited closer to garden plantings, though it still benefits from deep, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Inca Plum (Heart-Shaped Golden Heirloom Japanese Plum)
description: Inca has been grown in home orchards across the South since the early twentieth century and remains valued for its distinctive heart-shaped, golden-skinned fruit marked with magenta speckling and a rosy blush near the stem. Its roughly 250-hour chill requirement is low enough to satisfy most Gulf Coast zone 8-9 winters, and the flesh is dense, crisp, and notably tart-sweet compared to softer modern Japanese plums. Plant a second compatible Japanese plum cultivar, such as Methley or Morris, nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune annually in late winter to an open center to improve airflow and reduce the bacterial and fungal disease pressure common in humid Southern summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Inca Red Drop Pepper (Fruity Andean Hot Pepper with Small Elongated Red Fruits)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Inca Red Drop is a Capsicum baccatum pepper from the Andean tradition of Peru — the species group that also includes Aji Amarillo and Aji Cristal, characterized by the distinctly fruity, citrusy, tropical flavor profile that distinguishes Andean peppers from the more neutral heat of C. annuum varieties. Inca Red Drop produces small to medium (2–3 inch), elongated, pendant, bright-red fruits with a pointed tip — the 'drop' shape giving the variety its name. The heat level is medium to medium-hot (30,000–60,000 SHU) — more heat than a jalapeño but less than a habanero — with the fruity, berry-like undertones characteristic of quality C. baccatum selections. The fruit flavor combines the fruity complexity of the aji family with a clean, bright heat that builds persistently. In Peruvian and Bolivian cooking, aji baccatum varieties are used fresh, dried, and as the base for sauces and marinades where the fruity complexity is as important as the heat level. The long season to maturity (90–120 days from transplant) is well-suited to zone 9's extended warm season. The ornamental value of the small red pendant fruits on attractive plants makes Inca Red Drop equally at home in ornamental pepper displays and in dedicated vegetable gardens. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Incense Maypop (Hardy Fragrant Hybrid Passionflower)
description: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis or fence for climbing; Incense is a USDA hybrid passionflower combining native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with the more tender South American Passiflora cincinnata, bred to combine maypop's reliable cold-hardiness with larger, showier, more intensely fragrant deep-purple flowers than the straight native species. Like maypop, the vine dies back to the ground in winter through much of its hardiness range and resprouts vigorously from the roots in late spring — do not disturb or remove the crown before new growth appears, as it can be slow to emerge. Flowers are followed by egg-sized, aromatic fruit with sweet-tart pulp similar to tropical passionfruit, though fruit set is often lighter than the straight maypop species; plant more than one vine to improve cross-pollination and fruiting. Incense is also an important larval host plant for Gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies, adding pollinator-garden value beyond its fruit and ornamental flowers. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Incense Passionflower (Fragrant Deep Purple Hybrid Passionflower)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils. Incense is a hybrid passionflower bred from the cold-hardy native Passiflora incarnata and prized for its large, intensely fragrant, deep purple flowers with a dramatic fringed filament corona, combining showy color with a noticeably stronger scent than many other ornamental passionflower hybrids. It is considerably more cold-hardy than tropical passionflower species thanks to its native parentage, often surviving winters as a root-hardy perennial that dies back and resprouts from the ground each spring outside its evergreen range. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom through summer, and provide a sturdy support for the fast-growing, twining vine. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Inchelium Red Softneck Garlic
description: A large, mild softneck garlic with 8 to 20 cloves per bulb and a robust, taste-test-winning flavor, well suited to braiding and long storage. Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, and mulch heavily for winter protection. Keep beds weed-free and watered through spring, then stop watering as the lower leaves brown. Harvest in summer when several lower leaves have yellowed, and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Incredible Sweet Corn (Sugar-Enhanced Yellow Hybrid Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; apply balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Incredible is one of the most respected and widely grown sugar-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn hybrids in American home and market gardens — a Seminis-developed variety that consistently rates among the top performers for flavor, tenderness, and eating quality across multiple decades of university and commercial variety trials. The se (also called EH, everlasting heritage, or sugar-enhanced) gene doubles the sugar content at harvest compared to standard su varieties, and — critically — slows the conversion of sugar to starch after picking, giving se-type corn a 2–4 day postharvest quality window compared to the 24-hour window of su types. This extended holding quality made se types like Incredible a significant practical advance for home gardeners, allowing harvest and consumption at leisure rather than immediately. The 8–9 inch ears carry 16–18 rows of golden-yellow, tender, plump kernels with excellent flavor that is noticeably sweeter and more tender than older su types. Incredible consistently places first or second in tasting panels for yellow se corn and offers good disease resistance including northern corn leaf blight tolerance. An outstanding all-around sweet corn variety that has earned its perennial top-seller status. Matures in 77–82 days from seed.

name: Independence Almond (Self-Fertile Almond)
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most almond cultivars, Independence is self-fertile and can produce a good crop as a solid block planting without a separate pollenizer variety or heavy reliance on pollinator bees during bloom. It produces a semi-hard shell nut comparable in size and quality to Nonpareil, blooms later than many traditional varieties, and has become popular with growers seeking to reduce pollination costs and frost risk. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Independence Nectarine (Bright Red-Skinned California Freestone)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Independence is a widely grown California nectarine prized for its brilliant, nearly solid red skin and firm, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in midsummer on a vigorous, productive tree. The freestone pit and firm texture make it easy to prepare fresh or for preserving, and the fruit's excellent eating quality has kept it a standard commercial and home-orchard variety for decades. Like all nectarines, it shares peach genetics closely enough to suffer the same pest and disease pressures — particularly brown rot and peach leaf curl — so a routine dormant-season spray program is important for a clean crop. Thin fruit to four to six inches apart after natural drop for the best size and flavor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Index Cherry (Early-Season Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry)
description: Index is a Pacific Northwest-bred sweet cherry valued both for its own fruit and as a dependable early pollinizer for other cultivars sharing its bloom window, such as Chelan. Unlike most sweet cherries, Index is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit on its own, and because it flowers several days ahead of Bing it can pollinate a wide range of self-unfruitful varieties that bloom at the same early time. The fruit itself is large, glossy mahogany-red with medium-red flesh, similar in appearance to Bing but ripening several days earlier, with good firmness and rich, sweet flavor for fresh eating. Site the tree in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and choose a location with good air movement and some frost protection, since the very early bloom period carries real risk from late spring freezes. Water consistently as fruit develops to reduce cracking, and prune to an open-center form for good light penetration and airflow, which helps limit brown rot and other fungal problems in humid growing regions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Indian Almond (Tropical Almond, Beach Almond, Sea Almond)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — Indian Almond is extremely drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, making it one of the best trees for exposed coastal sites in zone 10-11. Terminalia catappa is a large, deciduous to briefly deciduous tropical tree of uncertain original native range (possibly the Malay Archipelago and Indian Ocean Islands) that has been transported and naturalized throughout tropical coastlines worldwide by human action over millennia, now found on virtually every tropical coast from South and Southeast Asia through the Pacific Islands, tropical Africa, the Caribbean, Central America, and South Florida. The tree has a distinctive tiered, horizontal branching pattern that creates a naturally formal, layered silhouette. Large, glossy, oval leaves (8–12 inches) turn spectacular shades of red, orange, and crimson before dropping twice per year (briefly deciduous in dry or cool periods), a display of fall color unusual in the tropics. The fruits are oval drupes (1.5–2 inches) containing a hard inner kernel that, when extracted and dried, has an almond-like flavor and is eaten throughout Asia and the Pacific — though the extraction requires significant processing. The large leaves are prized in aquarium and aquaculture for their tannins, which lower pH, release antimicrobial compounds, and replicate conditions of tropical black-water streams favored by certain fish. Matures in 730–2190 days from transplant.

name: Indian Chrysanthemum (Tea Chrysanthemum)
description: Set out divisions or transplants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, spacing plants 12–18 inches apart, and pinch stems through early summer to build bushy, floriferous plants. Chrysanthemum indicum is the wild East Asian species behind centuries of chrysanthemum tea (ju hua cha) and one of the parents of the modern florist mum, bearing masses of small, single, bright yellow daisy flowers on wiry stems from late summer into fall. Harvest flowers just as they open and air- or oven-dry them for tea, or leave them standing for pollinators — hoverflies and late-season bees depend on the nectar when little else is blooming. Divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to keep plants vigorous and floriferous. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Indian Coleus (Forskohlii)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; root cuttings readily in moist soil or water. Plectranthus barbatus (Indian coleus or forskohlii) is a fragrant-leaved tropical herb closely related to ornamental coleus, native to East Africa and tropical Asia and used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine under the name 'makandi' or 'coleus.' The roots of P. barbatus contain the diterpene compound forskolin, which has been extensively studied for its ability to activate the enzyme adenylate cyclase, increasing cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels in cells — a mechanism that has been researched for effects on weight management, glaucoma, and thyroid conditions. Forskohlii supplements (standardized root extracts) are widely sold in the herbal supplement market. As a garden plant, Indian coleus is an attractive, square-stemmed, aromatic, soft-leaved herb with pale-blue flower spikes in late summer — resembling a coarser-leaved version of its ornamental coleus relatives. It roots readily from stem cuttings and grows vigorously in humid, subtropical conditions. CAUTION: May interact with anticoagulants and medications metabolized by the CYP system; consult healthcare provider before medicinal use. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Indian Dill (Sowa)
description: Direct sow seeds in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian dill is a distinct species from the common European dill (Anethum graveolens), native to South Asia and widely used throughout Indian, Sri Lankan, and Iranian cuisines where it occupies a culinary role analogous to but distinct from European dill — the seeds are larger, more flattened, with a stronger, earthier, more camphoraceous aroma than common dill, and the fresh leaves have a more pungent, slightly different flavor profile that is essential to certain South Asian fish curries, lentil dishes, and the Persian herb-rice dishes that are among the oldest continuously prepared foods in culinary history. The whole plant is taller and somewhat coarser than common dill. The seeds are used both whole in tempering (bloom in hot oil to release aromatics) and ground in spice blends. The essential oil chemistry differs meaningfully from A. graveolens, containing higher carvone concentrations that give the seeds their more assertive character. It is used medicinally throughout South Asia as a carminative and digestive herb. Excellent for South Asian herb gardens and cross-cultural culinary herb collections. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Indian Frankincense
description: Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Native to dry, rocky hills across India, it is tapped for its fragrant resin, which hardens into aromatic amber 'tears' burned as incense and used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, closely related to the African and Arabian frankincense trees that supply the resin of biblical and ancient trade fame. The papery, peeling bark and sparse, compound leaves give the tree an open, drought-adapted silhouette suited to a xeriscape or succulent-collection planting in frost-free climates, where it can be grown as much for its unusual form as for eventual resin tapping. Water sparingly, provide maximum sun and heat, and avoid any risk of standing water at the roots, which quickly kills this dryland species. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Indian Free Peach (Red-Fleshed Heirloom Blood Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Indian Free is a distinctive American heirloom peach, likely of Native American cultivation origin, prized for its dramatic dark red, almost blood-colored flesh streaked through pale background flesh, and a rich, tangy-sweet, wine-like flavor unlike typical commercial peaches. It is a late-season variety, ripening well after most other peaches have finished, and shows notable resistance to peach leaf curl, a fungal disease that troubles many other peach cultivars in humid climates. The freestone fruit is best used fresh, in preserves, or in baking where its vivid color makes a striking presentation. Because it is an older, less commercially refined variety, fruit size and uniformity are more variable than modern hybrid peaches, but its unusual flavor and disease resistance have kept it popular among heirloom fruit collectors and home orchardists. Matures in 65–90 days from transplant.

name: Indian Jujube (Ber Fruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Indian jujube is one of the most widely cultivated fruits of the tropical and subtropical world, producing abundant crops of round to oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow, red, or purplish-black depending on cultivar — eaten fresh when crisp and apple-like, or dried when they become wrinkled and date-like in flavor. It is more heat-adapted and tolerant of alkaline soils than Chinese jujube, making it suited to south Texas, the Rio Grande Valley, and Gulf Coast zone 9–10 gardens. The fruit is one of the most important traditional fruits of South Asia, the Middle East, and West Africa, and is now gaining attention in the US as a dual-season crop that produces prolifically even under drought stress. Named cultivars such as 'Umran', 'Gola', and 'Seb' are selected for large fruit size and superior flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Indian Kale (Yautia Amarilla)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in partial shade to sun, giving the plant a full warm season to develop its corm. Xanthosoma atrovirens, known as Indian Kale or yautía amarilla, originated in Venezuela and has been cultivated across tropical America since pre-Columbian times, becoming especially favored in Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Jamaica. Unlike the other Xanthosoma species already in this dataset, its main edible organ is the central corm itself rather than the surrounding cormels — the corm is more tender than the tubers of most relatives, can weigh up to 2.5 kg (about 5.5 lb), and has yellow-orange flesh. As with all Xanthosoma, both corm and leaves must be thoroughly cooked before eating to break down irritating calcium oxalate crystals. Matures in 240–365 days from transplant.

name: Indian Long Bitter Melon
description: Indian Long is the slender, pointed-ended bitter melon type covered in sharp, jagged, triangular ridges rather than the smooth warts typical of Chinese and Taiwanese cultivars, and it carries the sharper, more assertive bitterness favored in Indian and Vietnamese cooking. Fruits are best picked young and firm, 6-9 inches long, while still glossy green, for use in stuffed karela, stir-fries, and curries; the intense bitterness mellows somewhat with salting, parboiling, or frying. The vigorous climbing vine performs well in Gulf Coast heat and humidity but benefits from a strong trellis and consistent moisture during fruit set to avoid stress-induced flower drop. Seeds have a hard, slow-to-imbibe coat, so nicking or an overnight soak speeds germination noticeably. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Indian Madder (Manjistha)
description: Indian madder is a scrambling, hook-bristled vining perennial in the same genus as European madder, grown across South Asia for the deep red-to-rust dye extracted from its slender roots and long valued in Ayurvedic medicine under the name manjistha. It climbs over neighboring supports using recurved prickles on its square stems and whorled leaves, so give it a trellis, fence, or shrubby companion to scramble through rather than staking it upright. Roots are dug in fall of the second or third year, washed, and either used fresh or dried and ground for dye extraction; the pigment (chiefly purpurin along with munjistin, distinct in balance from the alizarin-dominant palette of European Rubia tinctorum) gives warmer, more orange-leaning reds on alum-mordanted wool and silk than European madder's cooler brick reds. It tolerates a wider range of climates than its Mediterranean relative, growing successfully through warm-temperate and subtropical gardens where full-sun, alkaline-soil European madder can struggle in summer heat. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Indian Mulberry Root (Bai Ji Tian, Morinda Root)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; harvest roots after 3–5 years. Morinda officinalis (bai ji tian or Indian mulberry root) is a trailing and climbing vine from southern China and Southeast Asia in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and a plant used continuously in Chinese medical practice for over 2,000 years. The medicinal part is the dried root (bai ji tian in Chinese, meaning 'a hundred joints stretching to the sky') — starchy, slightly sweet, mildly warming — used in TCM specifically to tonify (strengthen) Kidney Yang energy, treating impotence, infertility, lower back and knee pain and weakness, fatigue, and osteoporosis from a TCM perspective. It is one of the principal herbs in many male reproductive tonifying formulas (like the classic Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan). The root contains anthraquinones, polysaccharides, and flavonoids with studied effects on testosterone levels, bone density, and adaptogenic activity. As a garden plant in zone 8–12, it is an attractive, semi-woody vine with glossy, ovate leaves and small white flowers in rounded clusters, followed by compound, white, aggregate fruits similar to noni (M. citrifolia) but smaller. Quite different from commercial noni in use and chemistry despite being in the same genus. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Indian Pearl Millet
description: Indian Pearl Millet is a grain-type strain of pearl millet grown for its distinctive blue-grey seed rather than for forage, producing corn-like stalks topped with dense, cattail-shaped seed heads. It is markedly drought-tolerant and grows quickly enough to take advantage of short windows of good weather, often outperforming corn or wheat in a poor season. The grain is naturally gluten-free and notably high in protein, potassium, and B vitamins, and can be ground into flour, cooked whole as a porridge grain, or left for backyard poultry to forage. Cut whole seed heads once the grain has hardened and dried, then thresh by rubbing the heads between gloved hands or over a screen. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Indian Plum
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia jangomas is drought tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils including lateritic, sandy, and slightly calcareous soils — water regularly only in establishment. Flacourtia jangomas (Indian Plum, Paniala, or Paniyala) is a thorny shrub or small tree native to South Asia from India and Sri Lanka east through Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, and Malesia, cultivated and semi-wild in village gardens and homestead agroforestry systems across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia for its clusters of small (0.5–1 inch), round, red-to-deep-purple, juicy fruits. The fruits are sweeter and less astringent than F. indica when fully ripe — tasting of a mild plum with slight tartness — and are eaten fresh, made into jams, chutneys, pickles, and preserves. Ripe fruits stain dark purple-red and can be fermented into a mild wine. The plant is dioecious (male and female on separate plants); at least one male tree is required among a group of female plants for fruit set. Flacourtia jangomas is very similar in growth habit and care to F. indica and makes a productive, low-maintenance fruiting shrub or edible hedge plant for zone 8–11 gardens in warm, sunny, well-drained conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Indian Plum (Osoberry, Oso Berry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Indian plum is a Pacific Northwest native deciduous shrub prized for being one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in February or March before leaves emerge, often while snow is still on the ground, providing an invaluable nectar source for early bees and hummingbirds. Small oval drupes (like tiny olives) ripen to blue-black with a single large stone; the flavor is astringent and bitter raw but palatable to birds and was eaten sparingly by many Native peoples. An excellent choice for wildlife habitat gardens, riparian buffers, and native plant landscapes in the Pacific Northwest and northern California. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Indian Prickly Ash (Triphal, Konkani Pepper Tree)
description: Zanthoxylum rhetsa is a large, thorny tree of South and Southeast Asia whose dried, split seed capsules are sold as triphal, a key spice in Konkani and Maharashtrian coastal cuisine used to flavor fish curries, pickles, and lentil dishes with the same tingling, numbing sensation found in Sichuan pepper. The bark and fruit are also used in traditional Ayurvedic preparations. It needs a long, warm growing season and considerable overhead and root room to reach fruiting size, making it a tree for spacious, essentially frost-free landscapes rather than a typical garden shrub border. Harvest the ripening capsules once they begin to split and dry them further indoors before storing in an airtight container for spice use. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Indian Sarsaparilla (Anantmul)
description: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, twining stems carry narrow, leathery leaves with a whitish midrib and small, purplish-brown flowers, but the plant is grown chiefly for its long, aromatic, cinnamon-scented roots, traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine and as a flavoring agent similar to true sarsaparilla, to which it is not closely related botanically. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and light levels once established, scrambling over low supports or trailing from a container, and roots are typically harvested for use after at least a year or two of growth. Water moderately, allowing soil to dry somewhat between waterings, and protect from any frost, which damages both foliage and roots. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Indian Shot (Achira, Canna Lily)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in warm soil (60°F+) in full sun to part shade in moist, humus-rich soil; in zone 8, mulch heavily in winter or lift and store rhizomes; the large starchy rhizomes can be harvested and eaten cooked. Canna indica (Indian shot or achira) is the wild species of canna from tropical America — the ancestor of modern hybrid ornamental cannas (Canna x generalis) that now dominate garden use worldwide — and a plant with a rich, ancient food history. The starchy rhizomes of Canna indica (and the closely related C. edulis, the 'purple arrowroot' or 'Queensland arrowroot') have been cultivated as a food crop by Andean indigenous peoples for an estimated 4,500–8,000 years, making achira one of the oldest cultivated food plants in the Americas. The large, starchy rhizomes are baked, boiled, or pit-roasted like sweet potatoes; the starch is uniquely large-grained (the largest starch granules of any plant), making achira starch distinctive in culinary applications. The seeds are among the hardest seeds in the plant kingdom (requiring scarification to germinate) and are traditionally used as natural beads and jewelry. As an ornamental, C. indica produces smaller flowers than modern hybrids (typically red or orange-red) but is equally spectacular, with bold, banana-like, green to sometimes bronze-purple leaves and abundant flowering on vigorous, rapidly-spreading rhizomes. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Indian Snakeroot
description: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants. Glossy, whorled leaves and small clusters of white flowers followed by small purple-black fruit grow on a compact forest-understory shrub native to South and Southeast Asian shade, historically significant as the original plant source of reserpine, one of the first modern drugs used to treat high blood pressure, and long used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine before that. Because unsustainable wild collection has made the species vulnerable across parts of its range, cultivated plantings from nursery-propagated stock, whether in a botanical collection or a home shade garden in a frost-free climate, help take pressure off remaining wild populations. Provide consistent warmth, humidity, and shade, and never attempt to self-medicate with plant material, since reserpine and related alkaloids have a narrow margin of safety and require professional medical guidance. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Indian Tobacco
description: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (do not cover) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost; Indian tobacco is a native annual wildflower of eastern North American woodland clearings and disturbed areas, recognized by its inflated, balloon-like seed capsules after the small, pale lavender-blue flowers fade. It is an important plant in the history of American botanical medicine — the leaves and seeds contain lobeline and related piperidine alkaloids that act as respiratory stimulants and were traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and 19th-century physicians for asthma, croup, and as an emetic. IMPORTANT CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic in quantity; it should be used medicinally only under professional guidance. Do not confuse with garden lobelia cultivars (L. erinus) which are ornamentals. Indian tobacco is primarily of botanical and ethnobotanical interest rather than general garden use. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Indigenous Cinnamon (Fragrant Cinnamon)
description: Endemic to the mountain forests of Taiwan, this cinnamon relative is prized because its leaves, rather than its bark, are the primary source of a high-cinnamaldehyde essential oil, making it possible to harvest cinnamon flavoring by repeated leaf pruning instead of destructively stripping bark. Individual wild trees vary widely in the dominant aromatic compound they produce (cinnamaldehyde, cinnamyl acetate, or camphor chemotypes), so named or clonal selections from cinnamaldehyde-type trees are preferred for culinary use. Grow in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; harvest and dry mature leaves for tea or as a ground cinnamon substitute, and prune to encourage flushes of new aromatic growth. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Indigo Apple Tomato (OSU Indigo Series Blue-Anthocyanin Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun for maximum anthocyanin expression — the blue-black pigmentation only develops in sun-exposed areas and fades entirely in shade. Indigo Apple is a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program led by Dr. Jim Myers, who developed the 'Indigo' series of tomatoes by crossing commercial tomatoes with a wild species (Solanum cheesmaniae from the Galapagos Islands) that carries genes for anthocyanin production in fruit tissue. The anthocyanins (the same pigments in blueberries and purple cabbage) accumulate in the skin of Indigo tomatoes when exposed to sunlight, creating a striking blue-black to deep purple coloration on the sun side while the shaded side remains red — a unique bicolor effect that changes as the fruit ripens and is genuinely unlike any other common tomato. Indigo Apple produces medium-sized (3–4 oz) round fruits that hang in clusters; the flesh inside is red and has good complex tomato flavor with moderate sweetness and acidity. Beyond the visual novelty, the anthocyanin compounds are genuine antioxidants of nutritional significance — the same compounds studied for potential health benefits in blueberries. Indigo Apple, Indigo Rose, Indigo Blue Berries, and other Indigo series varieties represent a fascinating example of targeted nutritional breeding combined with ornamental appeal. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Indigo Gem Honeyberry
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Indigo Gem sets almost no fruit alone. Bred at the University of Saskatchewan from Russian breeding stock, Indigo Gem is one of the earliest widely planted North American haskap cultivars, valued for its productive, compact bush and elongated, deep-blue berries with a tart, slightly grape-like flavor closer to the wild species than the sweeter modern releases. It is among the earliest fruits to ripen each year, often ahead of strawberries, which makes it a useful season-opener but also puts its early flowers at some frost risk in variable spring weather. Like all haskaps, it is extremely cold-hardy but performs poorly in hot, humid summers, so it is best suited to northern gardens and short-season climates rather than the Gulf South. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first few years to dead or crossing branches before starting renewal pruning of older canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Indigo Radicchio
description: This early-maturing F1 hybrid produces tight, softball-sized heads of glossy garnet-red leaves with crisp white ribs in as few as 55 to 65 days, making it one of the more dependable radicchios for gardeners outside the classic Italian growing regions. Unlike many open-pollinated Chioggia-type radicchios that need a hard freeze to redden and firm up, 'Indigo' forms well-blanched, uniformly colored heads even from a spring sowing, though a light fall frost still sweetens the flavor. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm to the touch, since they can split or bolt if left too long in warm weather. Its dependable heading habit and shorter cycle make it a good choice for succession planting through the growing season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Indigo Rose Pole Cherry Tomato
description: A deep purple-black cherry tomato bred at Oregon State to be rich in anthocyanin antioxidants, borne in clusters of 6 to 8 two-ounce fruits. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once weather warms. Stake or cage the 5-foot indeterminate vines and prune for airflow. Sun exposure deepens the purple color; harvest when the shoulders darken and the undersides turn red. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Indigo Treat Honeyberry
description: Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a different, overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora for reliable pollination and fruit set, since this cultivar is self-infertile. Indigo Treat is a midseason haskap from the University of Saskatchewan breeding program, selected for a sweeter, less tart flavor than earlier releases like Indigo Gem, with large, elongated, deep-blue berries. The upright, extremely cold-hardy bush breaks dormancy early, so late spring frosts during bloom are the main risk to cropping rather than winter cold itself. Expect fruit to ripen a week or two after the earliest haskap cultivars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Indigo Yum Honeyberry
description: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide consistent moisture during fruit development for the best size and flavor. Indigo Yum is one of the later-flowering cultivars in the University of Saskatchewan's Indigo series of haskaps, bred for a milder, sweeter flavor than earlier Indigo-series releases. Because its bloom period does not fully overlap with the earliest Indigo cultivars, it should be paired with a similarly timed pollinizer, such as Aurora or Borealis, to ensure adequate cross-pollination and fruit set. The compact, productive bush produces large, oblong blue berries with thin, tender skin well suited to fresh eating, jams, and baking. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: IndigoCrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Sweet University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulched heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. IndigoCrisp was bred by the University of Florida specifically for a distinctively crisp, firm bite that sets it apart from the soft flesh typical of most southern highbush blueberries, along with large berry size and a sweet, well-balanced flavor that holds up well after harvest. It ripens mid-season and carries a low chill requirement, making it a strong performer along the Gulf Coast where many older highbush cultivars underperform. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Indio Mandarinquat (Large Sweet-Skinned Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquat types, Indio Mandarinquat tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established, better than most true mandarins or oranges. It arose as an open-pollinated seedling beneath a Nagami kumquat tree and was later selected and named at a USDA date and citrus research station in Indio, California, for its unusually large, elongated, bell-shaped fruit. The thin, sweet, edible peel and tart, juicy flesh are eaten together like a kumquat, but the fruit is markedly bigger and juicier than standard Nagami or Meiwa types. Its kumquat parentage gives it cold hardiness comparable to the kumquats already grown successfully along the Gulf Coast, making it a novel option for gardeners who already grow Nagami or Meiwa. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ingrid Marie Apple (Danish Heirloom Parent of Elstar)
description: Ingrid Marie was discovered in Denmark around 1910, likely a seedling connected to Cox's Orange Pippin, and became a widely grown dessert apple across Scandinavia and northern Europe for its rich, aromatic flavor and attractive deep red-flushed skin over a yellow-green background. Dutch breeders crossed it with Golden Delicious to produce Elstar, passing along its crisp texture and complex, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor to that now-common commercial variety. The fruit stores respectably for a mid-season apple and is well suited to fresh eating, with dense, juicy flesh that holds its character for several weeks after harvest. The tree is a reliable, moderately vigorous bearer well adapted to the cool, maritime climates of its native range. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Instant Karma Elderberry (Compact Golden-Leaved Pink-Flowered Elder)
description: Site this compact selection where its chartreuse-to-gold foliage and deep pink flower clusters can be seen up close, ideally with some midday shade to prevent bleaching in hot summers. Water regularly during the first two seasons to establish a full root system, then reduce to moderate irrigation once mature. Plant a second, genetically distinct elderberry cultivar within pollination range to improve fruit set, since the small dark berries that follow the flowers are cooked-only edible and secondary to this cultivar's ornamental role. Cut back hard in late winter if a smaller, denser shrub is preferred, as it flowers on new wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Interior Serviceberry
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade on dry, rocky upland slopes or brushy hillsides across the northern Great Plains and Great Lakes region; interior serviceberry is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant clump-former that slowly spreads by root suckers to create a dense thicket of arching stems. White flowers in early spring emerge before the leaves and provide critical nectar for early native bees and overwintered butterflies when few other sources are available. The blue-black berries that ripen in early summer are sweet, flavorful, and high in antioxidants — excellent for fresh eating, jams, and pies, and consumed eagerly by fruit-eating birds before most gardeners can harvest them. It is one of the hardiest serviceberries available, making it a top choice for prairie-edge and windbreak plantings in zones 2–4 where other fruiting shrubs cannot survive. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Interlaken Grape (Cornell-Bred Early White Seedless Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Interlaken was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station as one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes available, producing sweet, crisp, pale green-gold berries in compact clusters well ahead of most other seedless varieties, an advantage for gardeners in shorter-season climates wanting a head start on the grape harvest. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Interspecific Squash Rootstock (Watermelon Grafting Rootstock)
description: This vigorous interspecific hybrid squash rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite watermelon, melon, or cucumber scion rather than eaten itself, providing a much larger, more aggressive root system that confers strong resistance to fusarium wilt and other soil-borne diseases along with improved tolerance of cool soil, drought, and salinity compared to a plant grown on its own roots. Widely used in commercial watermelon production in Asia and increasingly adopted by market and home growers elsewhere, grafted watermelon plants on this rootstock often show extended harvest windows, larger overall plant size, and better performance in soils with a history of vine crop disease. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, timing sowing so stem diameters match at grafting time, graft using a hole-insertion or splice technique, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun on raised beds or hills. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Invicta Gooseberry
description: 'Invicta' is a heavy-cropping green culinary gooseberry with outstanding resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The vigorous, spreading, and notably spiny bush yields large pale-green berries excellent for pies, jams, and preserves. Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil and space generously for airflow. Prune to an open goblet each winter to ease harvest among the sharp thorns and shorten leading shoots to encourage fruiting spurs. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Iochief Sweet Corn (Iowa State Heirloom Open-Pollinated Sweet Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows in fertile soil with consistent moisture during pollination for full, well-filled ears. Iochief was released by Iowa State University in the early 1950s as a productive, open-pollinated main-season yellow sweet corn, at a time when hybrid sweet corns were rapidly displacing older varieties, and it has survived among heirloom growers for its vigorous stalks, large ears, and genuinely excellent old-fashioned sweet corn flavor. It remains a solid choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year, something not possible with modern hybrid sweet corns. Matures in 85–94 days from seed.

name: Iona Shelling Petite Pea
description: A French petit pois variety producing peas half the usual size but packed with sweet flavor, often three dark-green pods per node. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost in cool, workable soil. The productive 28-inch vines are self-supporting but benefit from a low trellis, and the plant offers powdery mildew resistance. Harvest pods when plump and pick often for the tenderest baby peas. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Ira Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Ira is a Florida-bred rabbiteye released in 1970 with a comparatively high chilling requirement of roughly 700-800 hours, making it best suited to the cooler end of zones 7-9 rather than the deep Gulf Coast. It blooms about two days after Tifblue and has fruited reliably even in years when freeze damage reduced yields on many other rabbiteye cultivars in the Piedmont. Berries are medium-sized with average-to-good firmness and scar, ripening from mid-June to late July, but their relative softness means Ira is grown more for reliability under mechanical harvest conditions than for premium fresh-market fruit. Plant with Tifblue or another overlapping-bloom rabbiteye within about 50 feet, since Ira is not self-fruitful, and mulch heavily to protect its shallow roots. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Iran Winter Squash (Persian Heirloom Squash)
description: Iran is a rare heirloom winter squash originally collected in northeastern Iran in the 1940s and preserved in the USDA seed bank before being reintroduced to home gardeners by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Long, vigorous, heat- and drought-tolerant vines produce large round-oval fruits with silvery-green skin mottled in pale orange. The orange flesh is sweet and can be baked, roasted, or pureed like other Cucurbita maxima squash. Its notable heat and drought tolerance make it a useful choice for hot, dry-summer gardens. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Iranian Medlar (Large-Fruited Persian Heirloom Medlar)
description: Iranian is a large-fruited medlar accession originating from Persia, held in European fruit collections as a distinct genotype valued for fruit size and flavor rivaling the best Western European cultivars. The small, gnarled tree carries the same showy white spring flowers and open, twisting habit typical of the species, followed by hard, russet-brown fruit that must be bletted after harvest, stored in a cool spot for several weeks past the first frosts until it softens and darkens into a rich, spiced, wine-like pulp. It tolerates poor soils and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, fruiting best on a sheltered, sunny site where the spring blossom escapes late frosts. Harvest once fruit has colored fully and the calyx end has opened, then set aside to blet before eating fresh or cooking into preserves. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ireland Creek Annie Bean (Early Bush Dry Soup Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep directly in the garden once soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart in rows 18-24 inches apart. Ireland Creek Annie is a compact, heavy-yielding bush dry bean prized for its unusually early maturity and cool-tolerance, making it a reliable choice for short-season gardens. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling; the buff-yellow to mustard-colored seeds cook down quickly to a rich, creamy texture well suited to soups and purees. Keep beds weeded and evenly moist through flowering and pod set, then withhold water as pods mature and dry for harvest. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Irene Rosemary (Vigorous Trailing Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Irene is a vigorous, low-growing, trailing rosemary selection that spreads and cascades rather than growing upright, making it an excellent choice for spilling over a retaining wall, raised bed, or large container edge. It carries the same fragrant, needle-like foliage and culinary use as upright rosemary types, along with small blue flowers in spring, and it tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established. Good drainage is essential, since rosemary quickly develops root rot in heavy, wet soil, and only minimal pruning is needed to keep the trailing habit tidy. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Irish Cobbler Potato
description: Irish Cobbler is one of the oldest potato varieties still grown in North America, dating to the late 19th century and long valued as one of the earliest potatoes to reach harvestable size. The round-to-irregular tubers have thin, buff-tan skin with shallow eyes and dense white flesh that is excellent for boiling, mashing, and creaming, though it does not store as long as later-maturing varieties. Because it matures quickly, Irish Cobbler is a good fit for a Gulf Coast winter-planted potato crop that needs to finish before summer heat arrives. Plant certified seed pieces in late winter and hill the developing plants as they grow to keep tubers covered and prevent greening. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Irish Lace Marigold (Licorice Marigold)
description: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Irish lace marigold forms a low, dense mound of finely divided, thread-like foliage and needs no staking. Extremely fine, feathery, fern-like foliage carries a strong anise or licorice fragrance and flavor when crushed, used in parts of Mexico and Central America as a culinary herb and traditional flavoring, quite different from the coarser leaves and stronger, more medicinal scent of common marigold species. Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers appear over a long season, but this species is grown chiefly for its ornamental, lacy foliage texture and edible, licorice-scented leaves rather than a showy floral display. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it makes a fine edging plant or herb-garden filler, and harvested leaves can be used fresh or dried as a licorice-flavored seasoning. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Iron Clay Pea (Iron and Clay Cowpea)
aliases: Vigna unguiculata subsp. unguiculata 'Iron and Clay'
description: Broadcast at 40–80 lbs per acre (or 1 lb per 1000 sq ft) onto a loosened seedbed and rake in lightly; no inoculant is required in soil with prior cowpea history, but rhizobium inoculant greatly improves nitrogen fixation in new ground. Iron Clay is a hybrid between iron cowpea and clay cowpea types bred specifically as a summer cover crop and forage legume for the southeastern US. It is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant summer cover crops available, providing dense weed suppression, substantial nitrogen fixation (80–150 lbs N/acre under ideal conditions), erosion control, and wildlife habitat simultaneously. The vining, semi-prostrate plants knit together to form a dense ground cover; deer and other wildlife browse the foliage heavily, making it popular as a food-plot crop. Terminate before seed set by mowing or incorporation. In a garden context, till under green at peak vegetative growth for maximum nitrogen credit. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Iron Cowpea (Historic USDA Wilt- and Nematode-Resistant Southern Pea)
description: Iron cowpea is a tall, half-bush heirloom Southern pea with a landmark place in American crop breeding history — one of the earliest cultivars developed with genuine, durable resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea wilt, two soil-borne problems that devastated cowpea plantings across the South before its release in the early 1900s. Its resistance genetics went on to found much of the region's cowpea breeding, most visibly in the blended Iron and Clay mix still grown today as a cover crop and forage, and later in modern resistant releases such as California Blackeye 5. Grown as a food crop, Iron produces good yields of peas suited to fresh shelling or drying, performing reliably on sandy, nematode-prone soils where susceptible varieties decline mid-season. Like other Southern peas it fixes nitrogen as it grows, so it also serves well as a soil-building rotation crop between heavier feeding vegetables. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Iron Lady Tomato (Multi-Disease-Resistant Cornell F1 Hybrid Slicer for Humid Climates)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F; transplant after hardening off. Stake or cage immediately; Iron Lady is an indeterminate vine requiring vertical support. Iron Lady is a disease-resistant F1 hybrid tomato developed through the Cornell University Vegetable Program in collaboration with the Public Seed Initiative — a breeding program committed to developing open-access (non-patented) vegetable varieties for organic and conventional farmers. Iron Lady carries one of the most comprehensive disease-resistance packages available in a slicing tomato: confirmed resistance to Early Blight (Alternaria solani), Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans — the disease responsible for the Irish Potato Famine), Septoria Leaf Spot, and Fusarium and Verticillium wilt, plus tolerance to Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus. For Gulf South gardeners in zone 8–10, where the combination of high humidity, warm nights, and heavy summer rainfall creates near-ideal conditions for fungal tomato diseases, Iron Lady's disease package addresses the primary reason tomato plants fail prematurely in the region — not heat or drought, but the rapid defoliation by Early and Late Blight that kills plants before the crop is fully harvested. The tomatoes themselves are medium-sized (4–8 oz), round, deep red, with excellent flavor quality for a disease-resistant type — a notable achievement given that breeders historically faced trade-offs between disease resistance and eating quality. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Iron Man Pumpkin (F1 Hard-Shell Personal-Size Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow in hills once the soil has warmed, allowing the full, vigorous vines plenty of room to run through the second half of the growing season. Iron Man produces round, dark orange fruit only 6-7 inches across and 3-4 pounds, sized for painting projects, porch groupings, and small-space carving rather than large jack-o'-lanterns. The unusually hard rind resists Fusarium and Phytophthora fruit rot, an advantage in the wet, humid soils common along the Gulf Coast, and cured fruit stores for months without softening. Harvest once the shell has fully hardened and cannot be dented with a thumbnail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week before moving pumpkins into long-term storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Ironbark Pumpkin (Australian Heirloom Dark-Green Storage Pumpkin)
description: Ironbark is an Australian heirloom dating to the Victorian gold-rush era of the 1850s, prized for its thick, hard, dark blue-green bumpy rind that is notoriously difficult to cut, which gives the variety its name. The round, flattened, deeply ribbed fruits weigh roughly 5-18 lbs and are packed with dense, dry, bright orange flesh that is sweet and excellent baked or roasted. The exceptionally hard rind gives Ironbark outstanding storage life, often keeping well past other winter squash. It remains a popular home-garden variety in Australia but is still uncommon in North America. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Iroquois Beauty Chokeberry
description: Iroquois Beauty (trade name for the cultivar 'Morton') was selected at The Morton Arboretum for its dense, rounded, low-suckering habit that stays far more compact than the wild species, making it a good substitute for burning bush in small gardens. White spring flower clusters give way to glossy black berries in late summer, and the dark green summer foliage turns brilliant red-orange in fall. It tolerates both wet and dry soils and is largely untroubled by pests or disease once established, needing only an occasional thinning cut at the base to remove old canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Iroquois Melon (Iroquois Cantaloupe)
description: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 3 to 4 weeks before your last frost date, or direct sow once soil has warmed past 70°F, then thin or space plants generously to allow the sprawling vines room to run. Released by Cornell plant breeder Henry Munger in 1944 as a cross of 'Minnesota 99-36' and 'Bender's Surprise', Iroquois was the first muskmelon bred specifically for resistance to Fusarium wilt. Its thick, heavily netted rind covers deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, musky-sweet flavor, and its disease tolerance made it a long-time favorite for northern and Midwestern home gardens. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Irwin Mango (Florida-Origin Mango Popular Worldwide)
description: Irwin originated in the Miami area and, although developed in Florida, became especially popular in Asian mango-growing regions for its deep red, glossy skin and moderately compact tree habit. The small to medium fruit has mild, sweet, only lightly fibrous flesh and ripens relatively early in the season, making it a useful complement to later Florida cultivars. Its smaller stature compared to Kent or Tommy Atkins makes it somewhat easier to manage in a dooryard setting or large container. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from frost. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Isfahan Quince (Traditional Persian Culinary Quince)
description: Isfahan is a long-cultivated traditional quince selection from the orchards of Isfahan province in central Iran, where quince has been grown for centuries alongside other regional culinary fruits. Iranian horticultural researchers have studied it as one of several distinct named quince cultivars grown across the country's fruit-growing regions, valued locally for aromatic, golden fruit used in stews, jams, and preserves. As with other Cydonia oblonga selections, the fruit is hard and astringent when raw and must be cooked to bring out its rich, floral sweetness and characteristic color change. Grow in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest in mid to late fall once the fruit turns fully golden and develops a strong quince fragrance. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.
