name: Ishikura Bunching Onion (Japanese Non-Bulbing Scallion)
description: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart; hilling soil up around the base as plants grow blanches the shanks white and tender. Ishikura is a classic Japanese bunching onion, or negi, that forms a long, straight, pure-white shank without ever swelling into a bulb, staying tender and mild even as it grows tall. It is slow to bolt, tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, and can be harvested at scallion size or left to mature into thick, leek-like stalks. Because it does not form a storage bulb, Ishikura is best used fresh, sliced into stir-fries, soups, and as a raw garnish; cut-and-come-again harvesting of the outer leaves extends the picking season from a single planting. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Isis Candy Cherry Tomato (Striped Sweet Cherry Tomato with Gold Cat-Eye Markings)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when fully red with gold markings showing clearly at blossom end. Isis Candy is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety developed by Carolyn Male, a New York tomato enthusiast and breeder who spent decades collecting and evaluating heirloom tomato varieties and documented her work in the widely respected '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden.' Among cherry tomato varieties, Isis Candy stands out for both flavor quality and visual appeal: the flavor combines genuine tomato sweetness with a candy-like fruitiness and enough natural acidity to provide complexity rather than simple sweetness — the kind of balanced flavor profile that makes cherry tomatoes irresistible eaten directly off the vine. The appearance is striking: when ripe, the 1-inch round fruits display a candy-apple red with distinctive gold 'cat's-eye' markings — a golden-yellow circle centered at the blossom end — and sometimes faint pink striping on the red skin, creating a two-tone effect visible even from a distance in the garden. This visual distinction makes Isis Candy particularly attractive for multi-variety cherry tomato plantings where color diversity adds visual interest, and for farmers market and fresh-eating contexts where the unusual patterning captures attention. The variety is open-pollinated and stable, meaning saved seed reliably reproduces the variety's characteristics — an advantage over F1 hybrid cherry types that cannot be seed-saved. For zone 9 gardeners, Isis Candy's heat tolerance and prolific production throughout the Gulf Coast's long warm season make it a consistently productive choice among open-pollinated cherry varieties. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Isis Candy Tomato (Bicolor Gold-and-Red Cherry Heirloom)
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines for support. Isis Candy is a beloved heirloom cherry tomato producing round, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red, with a rich, sweet, well-balanced flavor that consistently ranks among the best-tasting cherry tomatoes in home garden trials. Plants are heavy, reliable producers over a long season, and the striking bicolor fruit makes an attractive addition to a mixed cherry tomato harvest or salad. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the best flavor, and water consistently to reduce splitting, since the thin skin is prone to cracking after heavy rain. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Islander Pepper (AAS-Winning Lavender-to-Red Ornamental-Edible Bell Pepper)
description: Islander is an All-America Selections-winning bell-type pepper bred for a striking color progression, with fruits maturing from ivory through lavender-purple before finishing orange and finally red, so the plant often carries several colors simultaneously. Start seed indoors in warm conditions and transplant after the soil has warmed, since fruit color development is strongest in full sun and consistent warmth. The compact, well-branched plants were selected as much for garden and container ornamental value as for eating quality, though the blocky fruit is genuinely sweet and crisp at any ripeness stage. Pick continually through the color stages both to enjoy the visual display and to keep the plant setting new fruit. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Ison Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ison is one of the most widely planted muscadine varieties in the Southeast, selected by Ison's Nursery in Georgia for its combination of very large, sweet, black-bronze-skinned fruits and self-fertility — the perfect-flowered habit means a single Ison vine sets full crops without requiring a separate pollinator vine. The large, round to slightly oval fruits ripen to deep bronze-black with a rich, sweet, complex muscadine flavor and relatively low tannin compared to older varieties. Ison is used for fresh eating, juice, wine, and muscadine jelly, where the large fruit size and good juice content are advantageous. The vine is vigorous and productive once established, with crops of 30–60 pounds per mature vine in good growing conditions. Unlike some muscadine varieties that have a thick, tough skin, Ison's skin is more tender and the slip-skin characteristic less pronounced, making fresh eating more pleasant. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Issai Hardy Kiwi
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Issai is a Japanese-selected cultivar of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) notable for being reliably self-fertile — unlike the species, which requires separate male and female vines for fruit production, Issai is a self-pollinating selection that sets fruit as a single plant. The small, smooth-skinned, grape-sized kiwiberry fruits ripen in September–October to a dark green with a delicate strawberry-kiwi flavor — eaten whole without peeling, unlike fuzzy kiwis (Actinidia deliciosa) that require peeling. Hardy kiwi fruits are considerably smaller than supermarket fuzzy kiwis but have a thin, edible skin and a sweet, complex, tropical flavor. Issai is less vigorous than most Actinidia arguta plants — a compact 15–20 foot climber rather than the 40+ foot sprawl of standard hardy kiwi — making it more manageable in garden settings. In zone 9 the vines experience mild winters and may have reduced dormancy; provide some shading in the hottest zones. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Issai Kiwi (Self-Fertile Kiwiberry)
description: Plant on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Issai is a self-fertile hardy kiwiberry cultivar, a rare trait among Actinidia arguta selections that are normally dioecious and need a separate male vine for pollination. This makes Issai a practical choice for a small garden with room for only one vine, though yields still improve somewhat with a male pollinator nearby if space allows. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten skin and all, with sweet green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. Issai also tends to fruit at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, often within two to three years of planting rather than the longer wait typical of the species. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous, twining growth and keep fruiting wood renewed, and provide a sturdy support structure from the start, since mature vines become heavy. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Issai Mulberry (Precocious Dwarf Self-Fertile Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact, naturally dwarf habit is a real advantage. Issai is a Japanese-bred mulberry selection prized for its exceptional precocity — plants commonly bear their first crop within a year of planting, far faster than seedling or standard-sized mulberry cultivars — combined with a compact, easily managed size well suited to small yards, espalier training, and container culture. The sweet, juicy, dark purple-black berries ripen over an extended season, and the plant is self-fertile, needing no second tree for pollination. Because of its smaller stature, Issai is easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand than full-sized mulberry trees, while still producing a generous crop relative to its size. Prune to control height and encourage branching if a bushier form is desired. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Italian Corn Salad (Hairy-Fruited Corn Salad)
description: Direct sow into fairly rich, well-drained soil in a sunny spot; unlike Valerianella locusta, this southern European species cannot be grown in shade and needs open sun to perform well. Italian corn salad is distinguished from common mâche by its softly hairy leaves and fruit and its greater tolerance of warm weather, making it a traditional choice in Italy and southern France where it does not run to seed as quickly as common corn salad during a hot spell. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than Valerianella locusta, so late sowings benefit from a sheltered site or row cover in colder gardens. Keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress hastens bolting and increases bitterness in the small, pale-blue-flowered rosettes. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Italian Flat Leaf Parsley
description: This heirloom flat-leaf parsley produces broad, dark green leaves with a clean, robust flavor prized in Mediterranean cooking. Soak seed overnight to speed the naturally slow germination, then sow shallowly and keep the soil consistently moist for the two to four weeks it takes to sprout. Thin seedlings to about eight inches apart in rich, well-drained soil and full sun. Harvest outer stems first so the plant keeps producing tender new growth through the season. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Italian Genovese Basil
description: Genovese is the classic Italian basil, offering the traditional fragrance and flavor that make it the top choice for pesto and countless summer dishes. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after the soil is warm and settled weather has arrived, as cold stunts young plants. Give it full sun, rich soil, and even moisture for lush growth. Pinch out flower buds and harvest from the top to keep plants leafy, tender, and productive all season. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Italian Heirloom Tomato (Large Ribbed Sweet Pink Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Italian Heirloom was preserved and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange network from a family's own long-held Italian seed stock, producing large, distinctively ribbed and slightly flattened, deep pink-red fruit with sweet, well-balanced, richly flavored flesh reminiscent of classic Italian slicing tomatoes. The pronounced ribbing and irregular shoulders give the fruit an old-world, rustic appearance that sets it apart from the smoother modern hybrids most gardeners are used to, while the vigorous indeterminate vine produces reliably through a long season. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking around the ribbed shoulders, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Italian Large Leaf Basil (Oversized Smooth-Leaf Classic Pesto Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Italian Large Leaf basil produces very large (3–4 inch), smooth, flat, slightly cupped, glossy leaves with the classic sweet, aromatic, clove-and-anise basil flavor of traditional Italian cooking — the preferred basil for pesto, where the large leaf size dramatically reduces the time and effort required to harvest sufficient leaf mass for a batch. The large, smooth leaves with their flat, relatively unwrinkled surface represent a distinctly different basil character from small-leaf and ruffled types — they are easier to clean, process, and stack, and produce a cleaner pesto with less stem fiber. The vigorous plants reach 2–2.5 feet with regular harvesting that removes flower buds and promotes continued vegetative growth. In zone 9, Italian Large Leaf basil grows throughout the warm season (April–October) and succession planting every 3 weeks maintains continuous fresh supply despite the tendency of summer heat to promote bolting in individual plants. For maximum leaf harvest, remove flower stalks immediately when they appear — flowering redirects plant energy from leaf production and quickly reduces the quality and flavor of remaining leaves. A single-season basil capable of producing many pounds of leaves from a short row under good management. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Italian Oregano (Hardy Italian Oregano)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Italian oregano (Origanum x majoricum) is a naturally occurring hybrid between sweet marjoram (O. majorana) and Greek oregano (O. vulgare subsp. hirtum) that combines the complex, warm sweetness of marjoram with the earthy intensity of oregano to produce the characteristically mild, aromatic flavor used in Italian cuisine — the flavor profile preferred for pizza, pasta sauces, and Italian-American cooking. It is more cold-hardy than sweet marjoram, more flavorful and complex than ordinary wild oregano, and easier to grow with consistent harvest quality. The small, oval, gray-green leaves are harvested before flowering for maximum essential oil content; dried Italian oregano is far more intensely flavored than the thin, often stale commercial product and vastly superior for cooking. Excellent for container growing and performs well in zone 9 heat if given good drainage and lean soil. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Italian Prune Plum (Fellenberg Plum, Pacific Northwest Prune Plum, Dried Prune Standard)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; Italian Prune is self-fruitful but benefits from cross-pollination; the oval blue-black fruits ripen in September in the Pacific Northwest; allow fruits to fully soften and develop their sweet flavor before fresh eating; for prune production, pick slightly underripe and dry at low heat (135–145°F) for 18–24 hours in a dehydrator. Italian Prune plum (also known as Fellenberg after a German horticulturist, and as 'Prune' or 'Italian' in the Pacific Northwest) is the foundational prune variety of the Pacific Northwest commercial prune and dried fruit industry — the variety responsible for making the Willamette Valley of Oregon the center of American prune production and the source of most of the dried prunes consumed in the United States. The tree was brought to the Pacific Northwest in the mid-1800s by European immigrants (primarily German and Italian settlers) for whom dried prunes were a staple preserved food, and the variety proved ideally suited to the mild, moderately humid climate of the Willamette Valley where warm, dry summers during ripening allowed on-tree drying and hand-harvest at low cost. The fruits are medium-sized, oblong, classic 'prune-shaped' with deep blue-purple to nearly black skin and amber-yellow to golden flesh that is firm, moderately dry (essential for making quality prunes), and freestone at full ripeness — all characteristics essential for the drying process. At fresh-eating maturity, Italian Prune is sweet, richly flavored, and excellent for preserves, tarts, and plum butter as well as fresh consumption. A traditional home garden plum throughout the Pacific Coast states and the Northeast. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Italian Red of Florence Bunching Onion
description: An Italian heirloom torpedo-shaped red onion used young as a mild scallion or grown on for elongated red bulbs. Direct sow thickly as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning for scallions and eating the thinnings. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist for tender stalks. Pull young for fresh use, or let plants mature and cure the bulbs for short-term storage. Matures in 60–100 days from seed.

name: Italian Roma Bush Tomato
description: A classic heirloom paste tomato with firm, meaty, few-seeded 3-inch oblong fruits on compact, very productive determinate vines. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply after the weather warms. Because most fruit ripens together, it is an excellent choice for canning and sauce. Provide a cage for support, water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot, and harvest when fully colored. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Italiko Red Dandelion
description: Despite its name, this is an Italian chicory with vivid burgundy stems and deeply lobed green leaves, grown for flavorful bitter greens. Sow directly in cool weather, spring or late summer, when the flavor is at its most balanced. Thin seedlings and keep soil moist to encourage tender leaves. Harvest young leaves for salads or let plants mature for cooking greens with a robust chicory bite. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Itasca Grape (Cold-Hardy Low-Acid White Wine Grape)
description: Itasca is a University of Minnesota-bred white wine grape released in 2017, the fifth cultivar from the program's cold-hardy breeding effort, surviving winter lows into USDA Zone 4. Its naturally low acidity and high sugar accumulation set it apart from earlier Minnesota releases like La Crescent, yielding a light straw-colored wine with pear, quince, melon, and violet aromas and a long finish. The vine shows strong field resistance to downy mildew, powdery mildew, and phylloxera, reducing the spray program needed compared to many cold-hardy hybrids. Because clusters ripen with unusually high sugar for a cold-climate grape, growers should monitor for sunburn and manage canopy density to protect fruit quality in hot late-summer stretches. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ithaca Lettuce (Cornell-Bred Tipburn-Resistant Crisphead)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Ithaca was bred at Cornell University for good resistance to tipburn, a physiological disorder that causes browning at leaf edges in crisphead lettuce under heat or irregular watering stress, along with a degree of heat tolerance that lets it hold quality longer into warm weather than many older iceberg-type varieties. The dense, crisp, pale green heads deliver the familiar crunchy texture prized in classic iceberg lettuce, well suited to sandwiches and salads calling for texture over deep flavor. Keep soil consistently moist through head formation to further reduce tipburn risk, and harvest once heads feel firm and solid when gently squeezed. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Ives Grape (Historic American Red Wine and Juice Grape)
description: Discovered in Ohio in the 1840s, Ives Seedling produces small, dark blue-black berries with intensely colored, slip-skin flesh that yields deeply pigmented juice and jam-like, foxy-flavored red wine. It remains grown in parts of Missouri and Arkansas, valued for its cold hardiness, heavy cropping, and resistance to many fungal diseases that trouble vinifera. Because clusters set thickly, thin fruit early to prevent overcropping and improve berry size and ripening. The vine is vigorous and long-lived, tolerating a wide range of soils once established on a cane-pruned trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ivory Teff (White-Seeded Food-Grade Teff)
description: Mix the dust-fine seed with dry sand for even coverage and surface-broadcast onto a firm, rolled seedbed, pressing lightly rather than covering, since ivory teff germinates poorly if buried. This is the pale-seeded food-grade class prized for producing lighter-colored injera and for grinding into a mild flour, in contrast to the stronger flavor of brown teff. Cut whole plants near the base once most of the fine seed heads have turned from green to golden-tan but before shattering begins in wind, then finish drying under cover for a week or more. Thresh gently by beating bundles over a smooth tarp and winnow in the lightest possible breeze, as the tiny ivory seed is easily lost. Matures in 75–120 days from seed.

name: Ivy Gourd (Tindora, Kovakka, Baby Watermelon)
description: Propagate from stem cuttings taken from female and male plants; plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil after soil warms above 70°F, providing a sturdy trellis or fence; ivy gourd is a perennial tropical vine widely grown across South and Southeast Asia for its tender young shoots and immature green fruits (tindora), used stir-fried, curried, or pickled with a mild flavor similar to young zucchini. The 2–3 inch fruits should be harvested green before they ripen to vivid red — fully ripe fruits are sweet but mushy and unsuitable for cooking. Caution: ivy gourd is invasive in Hawaii and parts of south Florida where it escapes cultivation and smothers native vegetation; grow in containers or managed plots where spread can be controlled. Young shoots and leaves are also edible as greens. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: IXL Pawpaw (Large Late-Season Davis x Overleese Pawpaw)
description: IXL is a historic named pawpaw resulting from a cross of two other well-regarded selections, Davis and Overleese, and it combines their traits into a tree that produces some of the largest fruit in the genus with a notably late ripening date, extending the pawpaw season into October in most climates. Because pawpaws are self-incompatible, plant IXL within about 20 feet of a second unrelated cultivar to ensure reliable cross-pollination and heavy fruit set. Give young trees part shade and consistent moisture for their first year or two, then transition them to full sun as they establish a deep taproot. The large, custard-textured fruit is best harvested when it begins to soften and give slightly at the stem end. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Izu Persimmon
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers. A Japanese non-astringent cultivar related to Fuyu, it bears small to medium, flattened, sweet fruit that can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree, ripening earlier in the season than most other non-astringent types. The naturally small, dense, spreading tree bears at a young age and stays compact even without heavy pruning, making it one of the better persimmon choices for a limited-space garden or large container. Persimmons need little spraying or care once established; thin heavy fruit set in early summer to prevent limb breakage and improve fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: J-31 Jackfruit
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, since jackfruit roots are very intolerant of standing water. J-31 produces large, irregularly lobed fruit with firm, deep-yellow flesh and a sweet, rich flavor and aroma that South Florida tropical fruit tasters consistently rank among the best of any named jackfruit selection, with bulbs that separate cleanly and rarely turn mushy or split on the tree. The tree has an open, spreading, fast-growing habit but responds well to pruning, allowing it to be kept to roughly 15 feet for easier harvest and home garden management. Established trees are prolific, often producing fruit outside the normal summer-to-fall season as well as during it, so support developing fruit on young limbs with slings to prevent limb breakage under the fruit's considerable weight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jaboticaba
description: Jaboticaba produces grape-like berries directly on its trunk and main branches (cauliflory) in dramatic clusters; the fruit ripens just 20–25 days after flowering and can bear several times per year in frost-free climates. It is self-fertile and requires well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5); chlorosis is common in alkaline soils and can be corrected with chelated iron and sulfur. Trees are slow-growing, making them well-suited to container culture where they can be overwintered in zone 8 or moved under frost protection. Harvest berries when they are entirely deep purple-black, soft, and sweet-tart — they ferment within 3–4 days at room temperature, so refrigerate or process promptly. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Jabotilla
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, acidic, organically rich soil; Jabotilla (also called Guavaberry or Rumberry in the Caribbean) is a medium to large Myrciaria species producing small, round, dark-purple to black berries directly on the trunk and main branches in the same cauliflorous pattern as Jaboticaba — but the fruit is smaller, more tart, and has a distinctive spiced, aromatic quality with notes of cloves, vanilla, and exotic spice that make it highly prized in Caribbean culinary traditions. In the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, jabotilla berries are the foundation of 'guavaberry rum' — a traditional Christmas liqueur in which the berries macerate in rum to produce a spiced, aromatic, deeply colored drink of cultural significance. The fresh berries are also eaten raw, made into jams and jellies, and used as a flavoring for drinks and sauces. The tree is ornamental year-round with attractive bark, shiny leaves, and the unusual cauliflorous fruiting pattern. In zone 9 it is a specimen fruit tree for collectors and enthusiasts. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jabuticaba (Brazilian Grape Tree)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, fertile, consistently moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), well-drained soil; jabuticaba is one of the most spectacular food plants in the world, producing dark purple to black grape-like fruits that burst directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches in a phenomenon called cauliflory, which causes the whole tree to turn dark with fruit clusters several times per year in its native Brazil. The fruits are eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest (they ferment rapidly on the tree), pressed into wine, or made into jelly and liqueur. The skin is thick and slightly astringent while the white flesh is sweet, gelatinous, and fragrant with a flavor suggesting muscadine grape. In zone 9 the tree benefits from a sheltered position and protection when temperatures dip below 26°F. Though extremely slow to fruit from seed — sometimes 5–10 years — air-layered or grafted plants can bear in 2–3 years. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Jack Be Little Pumpkin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jack Be Little is an All-America Selections award-winning miniature pumpkin producing perfectly proportioned, deeply ribbed, orange fruits only 2–4 inches across and weighing 3–8 ounces — a precisely scaled-down replica of a full-size pumpkin that has become one of the most popular autumn decorating elements for tabletop arrangements, wreaths, and centerpieces since winning its AAS award in 1989. The tiny fruits are also fully edible: halved and roasted in the oven or microwave, they produce a small amount of dense, sweet, pumpkin-flavored flesh that can be eaten directly from the shell — the shell becoming the natural serving bowl. The vine produces abundantly (often 10–15 fruits per plant) from a relatively compact plant footprint, making it highly space-efficient for ornamental pumpkin production. Jack Be Little became the defining mini pumpkin that launched the specialty ornamental squash market and has remained the most recognized mini pumpkin variety. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Jack Be Little Pumpkin
description: A tiny ornamental and edible pumpkin, 3 to 4 inches across and 2 inches tall, useful for decorating or as an individual stuffed-and-baked serving. Direct sow after frost into warm soil, with the compact 3 to 5 foot vines producing 6 to 10 fruits each. Keep evenly watered through fruit set and slip straw beneath the little pumpkins. Harvest when fully orange with a hardened rind, leaving a bit of stem for display. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Jack O' Lantern Pumpkin
description: This classic heirloom pumpkin has smooth orange skin, dependable size, and the perfect round shape for carving jack-o'-lanterns. Sow directly into warm, rich soil after frost, allowing the sprawling vines plenty of space. Feed and water consistently as fruit sets and swells, tucking a board or straw under each pumpkin to prevent rot. Harvest when rinds harden and turn deep orange, cutting with a length of stem attached for better keeping. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Jackfruit
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) is a fast-growing tropical tree from India and Bangladesh that produces the world's largest tree-borne fruit — massive, spiky green-to-yellow pods weighing 10–80 pounds that hang directly from the trunk and main branches in a spectacular display of cauliflory. The flesh (arils) surrounding each seed is sweet, fragrant, and fiber-rich, eaten fresh when ripe or cooked as a meat substitute when unripe — a use that has made jackfruit globally popular as a plant-based protein source. Trees grafted from superior selections begin fruiting in 3–4 years and can produce 100–200 fruits per year on mature specimens. Plant in well-drained soil, as jackfruit is highly susceptible to root rot in waterlogged conditions; once established, trees are moderately drought-tolerant and grow vigorously in the humid tropics. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Jackson Pecan (Scab-Tolerant Mississippi Gulf Coast Pecan, Type I)
description: Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving it room to grow into a large shade tree and siting a Type II pollinator nearby since pecans are wind-pollinated and set fruit far more reliably with a cross-pollinator present. Jackson traces to an early-1900s open-pollinated seedling selection from Ocean Springs on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, the same coastal nursery district that produced Stuart, Schley, and Forkert, and it carries the moderate scab tolerance typical of that old Gulf Coast selection group, making it a more forgiving choice than scab-susceptible standards like Burkett in Louisiana and Mississippi's humid summers. Nuts run 33-38 per pound with a good 52-56% kernel percentage and solid classic pecan flavor. Water deeply through nut fill in late summer and apply a foliar zinc spray each spring, since pecans are notoriously heavy zinc feeders on Gulf Coast soils. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Jackson Wonder Lima Bean
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jackson Wonder is a compact, bush-type speckled lima bean that has been the standard Lima for Southern kitchen gardens since the 1880s — it is heat-tolerant where other lima varieties fail to set pods and is the recommended lima bean variety for zone 8–9 gardens. The small-seeded beans are harvested green (fresh shelled) as baby limas at 50–60 days or left to dry on the vine for use as dried beans; the dried seeds are attractively speckled in purple and white. Inoculate seeds with lima bean rhizobia at planting for nitrogen fixation; no fertilization is needed beyond a light dose of phosphorus and potassium at planting. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Jackson Wonder Lima Bean
description: This historic dwarf bush butterbean, introduced in 1888, is prized for heat tolerance, resilience, and dependable yields in hot, dry conditions. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, since lima beans will not germinate in cold ground. The compact bush plants need no support and produce speckled, buttery-textured beans. Harvest young pods for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the plant for storage. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Jacob's Cattle Bean (Classic Maine Spotted Dry Bean for Baked Beans and Soup)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before harvesting. Shell and store in airtight containers. Jacob's Cattle Bean (also called Trout Bean or Dalmatian Bean in some regions) is a New England heirloom dry bean with one of the most visually distinctive appearances in the bean world — white beans irregularly splashed and dotted with maroon-red spots in a pattern that resembles the speckled coat of Jacob's Cattle described in the Book of Genesis, from which the variety's evocative name derives. The spotted appearance is due to anthocyanin pigmentation in the seed coat that creates the irregular, non-repeating pattern on each individual bean — a genetic expression that varies slightly bean to bean within the variety but maintains the distinctive red-on-white motif overall. Jacob's Cattle has been grown in Maine and New England since at least the mid-19th century, where it became the traditional bean for authentic New England-style baked beans: the creamy, meaty texture and moderately earthy flavor of Jacob's Cattle holds up beautifully in long, slow cooking with salt pork and molasses, developing richness without falling apart or becoming mushy. The beans are also excellent in soups, stews, and chili, where the spotted appearance adds visual interest to the finished dish. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved indefinitely from the best plants. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Jacob's Cattle Bean (Trout Bean, Dalmatian Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Jacob's Cattle is one of New England's oldest heirloom dry beans, with a distinctive white seed marked with dark red-maroon splotches in a bold, cattle-hide-like pattern that inspired its name. The beans are extraordinarily creamy and rich-flavored when cooked, with a texture that stays firm without becoming mushy — excellent in baked beans, soups, and cassoulet-style dishes. The traditional New England baked beans were made with this variety, slow-cooked with salt pork and molasses. A true bush bean, it grows compactly and requires minimal staking. The pods should be left to dry and yellow-brown on the vine; harvest when the seeds rattle loosely inside and cure indoors in a dry, ventilated area to finish drying before storage. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Jacob's Cattle Gold Bean
description: A stabilized cross between the classic maroon-and-white Jacob's Cattle bean and a paint-type bean, this variety produces oblong white seeds dotted with striking golden-tan spots instead of the traditional dark red. Sturdy bush plants stay compact and self-supporting, bearing 4 to 5 inch pods with 6 to 8 seeds each that should be left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down fully for storage beans. The golden speckled beans hold their shape well through long cooking and take on other flavors readily, making them a favorite for baked beans, chili, and soups. Because it is bush-habit and matures reliably within a single season, it suits gardeners who want a distinctive heirloom dry bean without trellising. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Jade Bean (Slender Dark Green French Filet-Style Bush Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a refined bush snap bean with slender, deep jade-green pods that occupies a quality niche between standard American snap beans and the more delicate French haricot vert types. The pods are round (not flat), uniformly dark green, stringless, and noticeably more tender and flavorful than standard bean varieties when harvested young at 4–5 inches — with a mild, sweet, delicate green bean taste and a fine texture that makes them excellent for light steaming, quick sautéing with butter and herbs, and all preparations where bean flavor is the centerpiece. Unlike the very slender haricot vert types (such as Maxibel or Espada), Jade has a slightly more substantial pod that is easier to harvest and handle in quantity, while still maintaining considerably more refinement than standard snap beans like Blue Lake or Provider. A popular choice for market gardeners, farm-stand vendors, and home gardeners who want a more elegant snap bean without committing to the exacting harvest schedule of true filet-type beans. Very productive and relatively heat-tolerant for a fine-podded bean. Matures in 53–60 days from seed.

name: Jade Bush Bean
description: A favorite green bean prized for long, straight, stringless dark-green pods that stay tender and sweet, held high on upright plants to avoid tip rot. Direct sow after the soil warms past 65F, spacing seeds a few inches apart. This variety tolerates heat and cold better than most, so it produces reliably across the season. Pick pods young and often to keep the plants setting new beans. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Jade Cross Brussels Sprout (AAS Heat-Tolerant F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost at 70–75°F; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip ('topping') to concentrate energy; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward when 1–1.5 inches across. Jade Cross is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that has been a reliable performer in American gardens since its introduction; it was specifically developed for improved performance in warmer fall conditions compared to the standard heirloom types. Standard Brussels sprouts (Long Island Improved, Catskill, etc.) require consistently cool temperatures (40–60°F) to develop tight, round, high-quality sprouts; in zones 7–9 where fall remains warm well into October, these traditional varieties often produce loose, bitter, or poorly formed sprouts. Jade Cross was selected for earlier sprout initiation at warmer temperatures, allowing it to begin developing sprouts before cool weather arrives and then perfect them as temperatures fall. The sprouts are uniform, round, tightly wrapped, and excellent in flavor — milder and sweeter than heirloom types, with the classic Brussels sprout character that intensifies after frost exposure. Jade Cross is the standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Louisiana State University AgCenter for Gulf South Brussels sprout production. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Jade Okra
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a spineless, open-pollinated okra producing straight, medium-green, ribbed pods with a texture and appearance valued in Asian cuisine — the name reflects its appeal in Chinese and Vietnamese cooking where the mild-flavored, tender pods are stir-fried, braised, and used in soups. The medium-height plant produces generous yields of pods that hold their quality for harvest at 3–4 inches without becoming fibrous as quickly as some varieties. The spineless habit makes harvesting considerably more comfortable than thorny-spine varieties and allows the plants to be handled without protective clothing. In zone 9 Jade okra thrives in the long, hot growing season and can be planted in spring for an early summer crop and again in late summer for a fall harvest — two full production cycles are achievable in zone 9. Matures in 53–60 days from seed.

name: Jade Pagoda Chinese Cabbage (Tall Columnar Napa Cabbage)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-tilled, fertile soil; thin to 12–15 inches for full-sized heads. Jade Pagoda is a tall, columnar Chinese cabbage (napa cabbage) that differs in form from the more squat, barrel-shaped types like Michihili and standard napa types — the heads are distinctly elongated (14–18 inches tall, 8–10 inches wide), with a compact, upright, tower-like form reminiscent of a pagoda spire, which gives the variety its name. The elongated form produces a higher proportion of the central, tightly blanched, pale yellow-green interior leaves relative to total head weight — the most tender and mildly flavored portion — compared to rounder, more compact types. Jade Pagoda has excellent storage quality: the tight, dense heads keep well in refrigeration (4–6 weeks) without significant quality loss. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and delicate — the characteristic Chinese cabbage flavor that is far milder than Western cabbage types — excellent raw in salads (particularly Korean kimchi-style preparations), cooked in stir-fries and soups, and in the braised Chinese preparations where the sweet, soft, cooked texture complements soy and ginger sauces. An excellent variety for gardeners who want to grow Chinese cabbage and experiment with Korean or Asian cooking traditions. Matures in 68–75 days from seed.

name: Jagua (Genipap, Marmalade Box)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, choosing the warmest and most wind-protected spot available since this tree resents any chill below the mid-40s. Keep the root zone consistently moist during establishment and expect a large, glossy-leaved tree that eventually bears heavy, applesauce-scented fruit with a pale, custard-like pulp. On the Gulf Coast it is realistically grown only in the warmest coastal pockets of south Florida or in a large container that can be moved into a greenhouse for winter. Young trees should be protected from any frost, as even brief freezes can kill wood back to the ground. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Jahn's Prairie Gooseberry
description: Jahn's Prairie is a cold-hardy gooseberry selection from Cornell University's Ribes breeding program, drawing on American prairie-type parentage to push hardiness and disease tolerance beyond many European dessert gooseberries. It carries good field resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot, the two diseases that most limit gooseberry culture in humid eastern gardens, making it a lower-spray option for home growers. Fruit ripens to an amber-pink blush with a sweet-tart flavor suited to fresh eating as well as preserves, borne on a moderately vigorous, upright-to-spreading bush. Site it in full sun to light shade with consistent moisture and a thick mulch layer, since gooseberries dislike hot, dry root zones. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Jalafuego Pepper (AAS-Winning Extra-Hot High-Yield Jalapeno)
description: Jalafuego produces glossy, blocky jalapenos that run noticeably hotter than standard types like Early Jalapeno, ripening on compact, well-branched plants that set fruit heavily over a long season. It earned an AAS award for combining that extra heat with high yield and good field tolerance to several strains of bacterial leaf spot, a disease that thrives in the Gulf South's humid summers. Harvest pods green for classic jalapeno heat and crunch, or let some ripen to red on the plant for a sweeter, even spicier finish. Consistent moisture and full sun keep plants productive and help prevent blossom drop during peak summer heat. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Jalapeno Pepper
description: This classic heirloom produces thick-walled, three-to-four-inch fruits with moderate heat and robust flavor for stuffing, slicing, or grilling. Start seeds indoors eight weeks before the last frost, as peppers need a long warm season. Transplant only after nights stay reliably above 55 degrees and the soil has warmed. Pick fruits green for typical jalapeno flavor, or let them ripen red for extra sweetness and heat. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Jalapeño
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in a warm starting mix and maintain soil temperature above 75°F for best germination. Transplant to the garden once nights are reliably warm and the soil is fully settled. For hotter fruit, allow stress by reducing water slightly as fruits mature. Harvest at 3–4 inches long while still firm and dark green, or leave on the plant until red for a milder, slightly sweeter heat. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Jalapeño Pepper (Classic Hot Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the soil has warmed thoroughly; Jalapeño is the most widely grown and most universally recognized hot pepper in American gardens and cuisine — a medium-heat (2,500–8,000 Scoville units) pepper with thick-walled, cylindrical to conical, dark-green fruits that turn red when fully mature. The glossy green jalapeños are harvested at 2.5–3.5 inches long before turning red for the classic fresh, pickled, and canned jalapeño used in Mexican, Tex-Mex, and American cooking. Red-ripe jalapeños are sweeter and somewhat hotter than green-harvested fruit. In zone 9, jalapeños thrive through the warm season and often survive mild winters as perennials, re-sprouting from the base to produce a large, established second-year plant with significantly higher fruit production than first-year plants. The compact, bushy habit requires no staking and makes jalapeños appropriate for container culture as well as garden beds. Harvest green jalapeños when the fruit is firm and full-sized; allow some fruits to turn red for a sweeter product. Excellent for fresh salsa, pickling, stuffing (chile poppers/jalapeños stuffed with cream cheese), and smoking (chipotles are dried, smoked jalapeños). Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee
description: A famous Typica-derived selection traditionally grown in Jamaica's cool, misty Blue Mountains, prized for a smooth, mild, low-acid cup with almost no bitterness. Home growers outside true high-elevation tropics won't replicate the legendary flavor exactly, but the plant itself performs well in bright, filtered light with rich, well-drained acidic soil and protection from hot, drying wind. It is slower-growing and lower-yielding than commercial hybrids, which suits its role as a specialty collector's plant rather than a high-volume producer. Keep humidity moderate to reduce fungal leaf disease, which this selection is somewhat prone to in humid lowland conditions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jamaican Caper (Bay-Leaved Caper)
description: Plant in well-drained, thin, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Jamaican caper (formerly Capparis cynophallophora) is a native Florida and Caribbean shrub or small tree related to the Mediterranean caper (Capparis spinosa), sharing the family's distinctive flowers — large, white, nocturnally fragrant blooms with numerous long, showy purple stamens that create a shaving-brush or firework appearance. The flowers open at night and are gone by mid-morning, attracting moths and long-tongued bees. The fruit, which resembles an elongated sausage, splits to reveal brilliant orange-red flesh containing the seeds — an attractive food source for white-crowned pigeons and other subtropical birds. A salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant native for coastal and hammock-edge gardens in south Florida. The young flower buds could theoretically be pickled like Mediterranean capers but this use is not traditionally practiced. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jamaican Hot Chocolate Pepper (Chocolate-Brown Fruity Habanero-Type)
description: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Jamaican Hot Chocolate bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen to a deep chocolate-brown, carrying the characteristic fruity, floral habanero aroma along with intense heat and a subtly smoky depth of flavor that distinguishes it from orange and red habanero types. It is a favorite among hot sauce makers for the complex flavor it lends alongside its heat. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; pick pods once fully colored for the best flavor. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Jambalaya Okra (Compact Dwarf Productive Okra for Small Gardens)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jambalaya is a compact, dwarf okra hybrid producing the full flavor and productivity of standard okra on a plant roughly half the height of traditional okra varieties — reaching only 3–4 feet versus the 6–8 feet of older varieties like Clemson Spineless. The compact size makes Jambalaya practical for raised beds, containers (5-gallon minimum), and gardens where standard-height okra would create shade problems or require staking. Despite the reduced height, fruit production per plant is excellent — the compact branching structure holds pods within easy reach without the ladder-or-bending situation that harvesting from full-height okra plants requires. The pods are standard green okra with the classic flavor, tender at 3–4 inches and maturing at the typical rapid okra pace (daily checking required at peak production). Jambalaya's compact habit also makes it attractive as a temporary summer ornamental — the large, lightly lobed leaves, yellow hibiscus-like flowers with red centers, and developing pods create a tropical visual effect that is ornamental as well as productive. In zone 9, Jambalaya thrives through the hottest Gulf South summer months when most other vegetables are stressed — okra is one of the few crops that genuinely performs at its best during July and August heat. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: James Grieve Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; James Grieve is a reliable, heavy-blooming pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties. Bred in Edinburgh, Scotland in the late nineteenth century, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red stripes and juicy, tender, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall as one of the more reliable early-to-mid-season dual-purpose apples for a cooler climate. Its good cold hardiness, heavy and reliable annual bearing, and value as a strong cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties have kept it a widely planted favorite in home orchards across the British Isles and other cool-summer regions for well over a century. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks, since the tender flesh does not store especially long. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: James Muscadine (Historic Large-Fruited Bronze Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis, and plant a self-fertile muscadine variety nearby for pollination, since James produces only female flowers. James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still widely grown, a historic bronze cultivar prized for very large, sweet berries with the classic musky muscadine flavor, harvested for generations across the Deep South for fresh eating, jelly, and wine. Its long track record in Southern gardens speaks to its reliability and adaptability across a range of soils and conditions. Like other muscadines it resists Pierce's disease and the major fungal diseases of the humid South without a spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: James Scarlet Intermediate Carrot
description: A Victorian-era English heirloom that became a staple of British kitchen gardens and allotments soon after its introduction in the 1880s, prized for combining a deep scarlet-orange color with reliably heavy yields. The roots are medium-long with a blunt tip, sitting between short stump-rooted carrots and the longest tapering types, which makes them adaptable to a range of soil depths. Direct sow into loosened, stone-free soil and thin early to avoid misshapen roots; roots hold well in the ground for late-season harvest. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Janet Muscadine Grape
description: Janet is a large, bronze-skinned muscadine released by Ison's Nursery in 1988 and named for Bill and Leola Ison's daughter, Janet Ison McClure. It is regarded as one of the more cold-hardy bronze female varieties and ripens late with an uneven, extended harvest window, so expect to pick over several weeks rather than all at once. The berries have a persistently wet stem scar that tears on picking, which keeps Janet out of commercial fresh-market packing lines but is a non-issue for home gardeners eating fruit straight off the vine or pressing it for juice. Because it is female-flowered rather than self-fertile, plant it alongside a perfect-flowered cultivar to ensure good fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jantar Cilantro (Extended-Harvest Central European Coriander)
description: Jantar is a Central European coriander cultivar bred for a longer productive leaf stage before bolting, developed for both fresh cilantro leaf and coriander seed production. In side-by-side trials it has held its leafy stage notably longer than common cilantro strains, giving growers extra harvest time from the same planting before plants run to flower. Its aromatic seed also has a good oil yield, so gardeners who let a planting go to seed get a worthwhile coriander spice harvest in addition to the fresh leaf crop. Grow it exactly as you would other cilantro: direct-sown, in full sun, kept evenly moist, and sown in fall or very early spring to avoid the heat that triggers bolting in zone 9. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: January King Cabbage
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the transplanting date (late summer, aiming for outdoor planting in August–September for a winter harvest) or direct sow in early summer for fall maturity. January King is a centuries-old French and British heirloom winter cabbage that produces medium-sized, semi-round, savoy-type heads with beautifully crinkled, reddish-purple-flushed outer leaves and green-white inner leaves; it is exceptionally cold-hardy, standing in the garden through temperatures well below freezing and becoming sweeter with each frost. Transplant into well-amended, deeply prepared, slightly alkaline to neutral soil and firm the seedling in well to prevent wind-rocking; collar or brassica cage against caterpillars and aphids which are the main pests. In zone 8–9, grow as an overwintering crop planted in September for harvest January through March. Matures in 180–210 days from seed.

name: Japanese Angelica Tree (Dureup)
description: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese angelica tree is a large, sparsely branched, spiny-stemmed understory tree grown throughout Japan and Korea for its highly prized spring shoots — known as dureup or taranome — which are snapped off while still tightly furled, blanched or lightly battered and fried as tempura, and valued for a distinctive bittersweet, slightly resinous flavor. Established plants sucker readily from the roots to form a spreading colony, and shoot harvest is timed to remove the terminal buds from two- and three-year-old suckers each spring, which also keeps the colony to a manageable size. Left unharvested it becomes a bold architectural small tree with huge, twice-compound leaves and large plumes of white flowers in late summer followed by black berries relished by birds; variegated ornamental selections are grown for foliage alone. Give it room to sucker and site it away from foot traffic, since both stems and leaf stalks carry sharp prickles. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Apricot
description: Plant grafted Japanese Apricot in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; prune to open vase shape after fruiting; harvest fruits green-yellow when firm for pickling (umeboshi), or wait for full yellow ripeness for eating fresh or making ume liqueur. Prunus mume is revered in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean culture as the herald of spring — its fragrant, five-petaled flowers in shades of white through deep rose appear January–March, often while snow still falls, making it one of the most poetically celebrated trees in East Asian art and literature. The fruits, called ume (Japanese) or mei (Chinese), resemble apricots but are sharply sour when ripe due to high citric acid content; they are almost always processed rather than eaten raw. Traditional umeboshi preparation involves salt-pickling the green fruits with red shiso leaves to produce a strongly sour, salty Japanese condiment used in rice balls, with noodles, and as a digestive aid — extraordinarily long-lasting, with some umeboshi aged decades or more. Umeshu (ume liqueur, often called plum wine) is made by steeping whole green fruits in shochu spirits with sugar. Many named ornamental cultivars exist with double flowers and deep pink to red color; fruiting varieties for culinary use include 'Nanko' and 'Kairyou Ouseibai'. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Black Trifele Tomato (Dark Pear-Shaped Rich Heirloom Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Japanese Black Trifele (also called Japanese Truffle) is a Russian heirloom producing unusual pear-shaped to truffle-shaped (the 'trifele' name references the truffle mushroom shape) fruits in a striking deep mahogany-black to brownish-red color with complex, rich, wine-like flavor that has made it one of the most celebrated dark-fleshed heirloom tomatoes in American seed-saving circles. The pear shape and dark color are both distinctive — the elongated, slightly rounded-bottom pear form with its near-black exterior creates an unusual appearance that is immediately recognizable at the farmers market and in the garden. The red-brown flesh has a rich, dense, complex flavor with deep savory undertones that differ from the fruity brightness of standard red or the simple sweetness of yellow tomatoes — a flavor profile well-suited to cooking, sauces, and combinations with cheese and herbs. Despite the 'Japanese' in the name, this variety was developed and preserved in Russia. The medium-sized fruits (4–6 oz) are more practical for everyday use than giant beefsteaks while still providing exceptional flavor. The dark color comes from anthocyanin production in the skin triggered by sun exposure. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Butterbur
description: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese butterbur (fuki) is a large, bold foliage perennial with rounded leaves that can reach 2–4 feet across on stiff petioles — producing one of the most dramatic tropical-looking foliage effects achievable with a cold-hardy plant in the shade garden. Before the leaves emerge in early spring, compact clusters of small, whitish flowers rise on stout scapes, producing the first bloom of the woodland season. The thick, edible leaf stalks (petioles) are a traditional Japanese vegetable — blanched, pickled (tsukudani), or cooked in miso soup as fuki — harvested in early spring before the leaves fully expand. The plant spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes in moist conditions and can colonize large areas rapidly; manage spread by installing buried barriers or confine to a naturally wet, shaded depression. An outstanding bold-leaf specimen for water garden margins, shaded stream banks, and large-scale woodland plantings. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Chestnut (Kuri)
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; Japanese chestnut is critically important in chestnut breeding programs as a source of resistance to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica), the fungal disease that virtually eliminated the American chestnut from eastern North American forests in the early 20th century. While Japanese chestnut is not immune to the blight, it carries resistance genes that allow infected trees to survive and produce nuts despite infection — a trait intensively incorporated into breeding lines for blight-resistant American chestnut restoration. The nuts are large (often larger than American chestnut), sweet, and excellent roasted or boiled in Japanese cuisine. Japanese chestnut has been cultivated in Japan for over 2000 years and is the source of many cultivated varieties. Requires cross-pollination; plant two or more trees. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Cornelian Cherry
description: Sow cleaned seeds in fall and be patient, as double dormancy means most seeds will not sprout until the second spring; mark the bed clearly and keep it weeded during the waiting period. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are adaptable to a range of soil types and tolerate summer heat better than its European relative Cornus mas. The clusters of tiny yellow flowers that stud the bare branches in late winter are among the earliest blooms of the year, providing a vital nectar source for early pollinators; the cherry-like fruits that follow ripen to bright red by midsummer and are edible fresh or made into jams and wines. With age, the exfoliating bark develops an ornamental patchwork of grey, brown, and orange, making this a genuinely four-season specimen plant for gardens across a wide range of climates. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Eggplant
description: Long, slender, thin-skinned fruit with tender flesh that cooks quickly and rarely needs peeling. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant into black plastic mulch to boost soil temperature in cooler regions. Feed with a balanced fertilizer and keep evenly watered to prevent bitter, seedy fruit. Cut fruit with pruners while young and glossy, typically at 6 to 8 inches long. These plants often outyield globe eggplants where summers are short or mild. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Flowering Quince
description: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; Japanese flowering quince is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay, drought, and pollution once established — excellent for slopes, hedges, and difficult urban sites. Chaenomeles japonica is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub that blooms in early spring before the leaves expand (often in February–March in mild climates), producing a spectacular display of vivid orange to scarlet-red, five-petaled flowers on bare stems — some of the earliest and most vivid spring color in the garden; the flowers provide critical early nectar for overwintered and emerging queen bumblebees. The hard, fragrant, yellow-green, apple-like fruits that follow in autumn are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, quince paste (membrillo), and homemade quince wine with excellent flavor and natural pectin content. More compact and cold-hardy than the larger C. speciosa. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Ginger (Myoga)
description: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in rich, moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese ginger (myoga) is a shade-thriving edible perennial rarely seen in American gardens despite being widely grown in Japan for its prized flower buds. The plant's ginger-scented strap leaves reach 24–36 inches in shade conditions, forming a handsome ground cover through the growing season. The harvest is the unopened flower buds, which emerge at soil level in August–September — these small, pink-tipped buds are sliced thin and used as a pungent, mildly spicy garnish in miso soup, sashimi, noodle dishes, and pickled in vinegar. Young spring shoots are also edible with a more delicate flavor. The flavor is distinctly gingery but milder and more aromatic than culinary ginger root. Plants naturalize slowly and are nearly care-free once established in a shaded spot with consistent moisture. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Hulless Popcorn
description: This compact heirloom reaches about five feet tall, making it well suited to smaller gardens while producing two or three short, full ears per stalk. Sow directly into warm soil in blocks of several rows to ensure good wind pollination. Keep it isolated from sweet or dent corn so the popping quality stays true. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure the tender, low-hull kernels further indoors before popping. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Japanese Indigo
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Japanese Indigo (Ai, Tade Ai) is the traditional indigo dye plant of Japan, used for over 1,500 years to produce the brilliant blue textile dye that colors traditional Japanese fabrics including indigo-dyed cotton, shibori tie-dye, and katazome stencil-printed cloth. The blue dye precursor indican is stored in the fresh leaves and requires a fermentation vat (sukumo) or direct fresh-leaf dyeing process to produce the indigo pigment that bonds to fiber. Unlike the tropical indigo plant (Indigofera), Japanese Indigo thrives in temperate garden conditions and is accessible to North American home growers. Fresh leaves yield blue dye directly when crushed and applied to cotton in the sun — a simple process known as 'leaf printing' that produces soft blue marks without a dye vat. The ornamental plants with reddish stems and oval, deep green leaves and pink flower spikes in fall are attractive in the garden and valuable to craft dyers, fiber artists, and natural dye enthusiasts. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Long Cucumber (Kyuri, Japanese Burpless Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straight fruits and good air circulation. Japanese long cucumber ('Kyuri' in Japanese) is the standard cucumber of Japanese cuisine and is distinct from both the thicker-skinned American slicing cucumber and the ribbed Chinese varieties — producing slender (1–1.5 inch diameter), uniformly dark green, smooth-skinned fruits 8–12 inches long with exceptionally thin, tender skin that needs no peeling, very small seed cavity, dense crisp flesh, and mild, sweet, refreshing flavor with virtually no bitterness. The thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it 'burpless' and highly digestible, and the crisp, dense flesh holds its texture remarkably well in sliced preparations. Japanese cucumbers are the standard for pickled cucumber preparations (as in the Japanese salted tsukemono tradition) because of their superior texture, and they are equally outstanding for fresh eating, in salads, and in Korean oi sobagi kimchi. Multiple varieties are grown in Japanese commercial and home horticulture, all sharing the smooth skin, thin wall, dense flesh, and mild flavor characteristics. Production is very heavy when vines are trellised and harvested regularly, and the plants perform well in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf South summer. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Japanese Loquat
description: The evergreen Japanese loquat offers handsome, bold foliage and clusters of sweet-tart, apricot-like fruit that ripen in spring. It flowers in autumn, so late frosts can damage the developing crop in colder zones. Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil and water regularly while young. Thin fruit clusters for larger loquats and prune lightly after harvest to shape the canopy. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Mahonia (Fragrant Winter-Flowering Shade Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Japanese Mahonia bears bold, holly-like, pinnately compound evergreen foliage and, in late fall through winter, pendant racemes of small, lemon-scented yellow flowers that are among the earliest nectar sources for winter-active pollinators, followed by tart, dusty-blue-black berries that can be used for jelly. Its architectural foliage and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes, since it needs little routine shaping. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Mint (Japanese Menthol Mint)
description: Plant rooted divisions in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, containing the spreading rhizomes in a pot or buried barrier. Japanese Mint is the specific menthol-type variety of corn mint that has been selected and cultivated for centuries in Japan, China, and India for industrial menthol crystal production, carrying a substantially higher menthol content in its essential oil than the wild Mentha arvensis species. The rounded, bright green leaves have an intensely strong, almost sharp peppermint aroma and flavor, more concentrated and cooling than either spearmint or standard peppermint, so it is best used sparingly for tea and flavoring rather than as a general cooking herb. Its dense clusters of small pale-purple flowers form tight whorls at the leaf axils in summer. Harvest and dry stems for menthol-rich tea or extraction; cutting the plant back hard before flowering maximizes both leaf yield and menthol concentration. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Oxheart Tomato (Meaty Pink-Red Oxheart Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Japanese Oxheart bears large, heart-shaped fruit in pink to pink-red with dense, meaty flesh and few seeds, the classic oxheart form prized for slicing and sauce alike, on productive indeterminate vines. Its rich, well-balanced flavor and substantial fruit size have kept it popular among heirloom tomato collectors. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 85–90 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Pepper Vine (Fuji Kadsura, Asian Pepper Vine)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; provide trellis or tree trunk support. Piper kadsura (Japanese pepper vine) is a Japanese and East Asian climbing vine in the pepper family (Piperaceae) — related to true black pepper (P. nigrum) but native to the humid, shaded forests of Japan, China, and Korea. The plant produces attractive, heart-shaped, deeply veined, dark-green leaves with conspicuous venation and a mildly spicy pepper aroma when crushed. Small, string-like flower spikes produce tiny, red to dark-purple peppercorns-like berries in fall that are mildly peppery-spicy and have been used as a seasoning and traditional medicine ingredient in East Asian cuisine and herbal practice. The vine climbs by adhesive stem roots similar to Virginia creeper and can attach to rough stone, brick, and wood surfaces. As a shade-tolerant ornamental vine for zone 9–12, it provides year-round interest with its attractive foliage and subtle fruiting display. Used in Japanese herbal medicine (kampo) for joint pain and circulation. Extremely rare in Western horticulture. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Quince (Flowering Quince, Maule's Quince)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained to moderately moist soil; Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica) is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub native to Japan, producing masses of brilliant red-orange to scarlet flowers on bare winter-spring branches — one of the most vivid early spring-flowering shrubs available. The small, apple-scented, greenish-yellow fruits that follow are too astringent to eat raw but make excellent jelly, jam, and cordial with a flavor combining quince, lemon, and apple; very high in pectin and requiring no added pectin when making preserves. The thorny habit makes it an effective barrier hedge. Extremely adaptable and long-lived, thriving in a wide range of soils and tolerating air pollution, drought, and neglect; a reliable garden shrub with multiple seasons of interest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Raisin Tree (Oriental Raisin Tree)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the Japanese raisin tree is an unusual and little-known deciduous tree from East Asia cultivated for its fleshy, branched fruiting stalks (peduncles) that swell and become sweet, raisin-like, and edible in fall when the actual seeds have dropped. It is the peduncles — not the small, round seeds — that are consumed; they have a mild, sweet flavor resembling dried figs or raisins and have been used in Japan, China, and Korea both as a food and as a traditional remedy for alcohol intoxication and liver protection. The tree is an attractive ornamental with large, tropical-looking leaves and fragrant white flowers in summer. In zone 9, it may bloom and fruit erratically due to insufficient winter chilling; it performs best in zones 6–8 where winter cold is reliable. An excellent and unusual fruit tree for the adventurous edible landscape. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Japanese Sweet Flag (Dwarf Sweet Flag, Grassy-Leaved Sweet Flag)
description: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or in containers in shallow water (up to 3 inches deep) in shade to part shade. Acorus gramineus (Japanese sweet flag or dwarf sweet flag) is a small, compact, grass-like aquatic-marginal perennial from Japan and China — a diminutive relative of the larger sweet flag (A. calamus) — producing dense tufts of narrow, grass-like, slightly arching, aromatic leaves in solid green or with variegated golden-yellow striping. The leaves, when crushed, release a mild, pleasant anise-cinnamon fragrance similar to (but softer than) the larger A. calamus. Several ornamental cultivars are widely grown: 'Ogon' (yellow-green striped leaves), 'Variegatus' (white-striped leaves), and the miniature 'Pusillus' (just 3–4 inches tall). Japanese sweet flag naturally grows along stream margins and in wet meadows in Japan and Korea, tolerating conditions from moist soil to shallow water up to 3 inches deep; it is an ideal marginal plant for water garden pots, pond edges, and shade rain gardens. In Japanese flower arranging (ikebana), the upright leaves provide linear structure. In Chinese and Japanese traditional medicine, the root and leaves are used as a mildly stimulating tonic and insect repellent herb. A wonderfully versatile plant for moist shade situations. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Japanese Walnut (Siebold's Walnut)
description: Plant fresh nuts in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Japanese walnut is an impressive large nut tree from the mountains of Japan, Hokkaido, Honshu, and Sakhalin — closely related to Persian walnut (Juglans regia) but growing in colder climates and producing rounder, harder-shelled nuts. The trees are immediately distinguished by their enormous compound leaves (the largest of any walnut — up to 4 feet long with 11–17 leaflets) and by the sticky glandular hairs covering young growth and fruit husks. The nuts are round to slightly oval, with a very hard, thick shell and rich, oily kernel. The variety 'cordiformis' (heartnut) produces a distinctively heart-shaped nut that cracks more easily than the round-nutted species. Used in Japanese cuisine and for nut oil. Like all walnuts, releases juglone from its roots that can inhibit many nearby plants. The closely related Manchurian walnut (J. mandshurica) is even hardier. An excellent, ornamental, large-canopy nut tree for cooler northern gardens. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Japanese Wineberry
description: Japanese wineberry is an Asian Rubus species with distinctive red glandular-hairy canes that are ornamentally attractive year-round. It fruits on floricanes in mid-to-late summer, bearing translucent orange-red to deep ruby berries enclosed in a sticky calyx that opens at ripeness — a feature that helps distinguish ripe from unripe fruit and reduces bird predation. Cut all fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and thin primocanes to 4–6 per hill for next year's crop. The species naturalizes aggressively in disturbed areas in the eastern U.S. and is considered invasive in several states; confirm legality before planting. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Jargonelle Pear (Historic Early-Season Dessert Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil, tolerant of cooler and shadier sites than most pears. One of the oldest pears still in cultivation, dating to at least the early 1600s and first recorded by John Parkinson in 1629, it likely originated in Anjou, France. The long, small, calabash-shaped fruit has tender, melting, juicy flesh with a distinctive musky flavor, ripening very early in August ahead of nearly all other European pears. The tree is notably hardy and long-lived, tolerating walls and cooler northern sites without full sun better than most pear varieties. Harvest in early August as the fruit softens, and eat promptly since it does not keep. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jarrahdale Pumpkin
description: An Australian heirloom pumpkin with striking silvery blue-grey skin, deep ribbing, and a drum shape, plus sweet, nutty, stringless orange flesh, in 6 to 12 pound fruits. Direct sow after frost into warm soil, giving the long vines plenty of room. Water deeply and feed richly while fruit sizes up, resting pumpkins on straw. Harvest when the rind hardens and coloring is complete, and cure for both decoration and cooking. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Jarrahdale Squash (Australian Heritage Blue-Grey Pumpkin with Dense Sweet Orange Flesh)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost; harvest when stem dries and skin is firm grey-blue. Jarrahdale Squash (also called Jarrahdale Pumpkin in its native Australia, where 'pumpkin' is the standard term for what North Americans call both pumpkin and winter squash) is an Australian heritage variety named after the town of Jarrahdale in the Darling Ranges southeast of Perth, Western Australia, where the variety was grown and maintained by local families before being recognized and distributed more widely. The Jarrahdale pumpkin belongs to a distinctive Australian heritage pumpkin group characterized by grey-blue skin — a color produced by a combination of pigmentation and a powdery wax bloom on the skin surface — that distinguishes these varieties from the orange and tan pumpkins dominating North American markets.
