This blue-grey color group, which includes Queensland Blue, Crown Prince (United Kingdom), and related European heritage varieties, represents a distinct aesthetic and culinary tradition in which the blue skin and dense, dry orange flesh are valued for specific culinary properties. The flesh of Jarrahdale is particularly dry and dense for a large pumpkin — significantly less watery than most carving pumpkins and many North American pie pumpkins — which makes it exceptional for preparations where moisture content affects texture: pumpkin soup (concentrated flavor without excessive water thinning), pumpkin curry, and baked preparations where excess moisture causes sogginess. The flavor is genuinely sweet and complex, with a depth that makes Jarrahdale one of the most culinarily respected heritage pumpkin varieties in Australian cooking and in North American heirloom vegetable circles. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Jasper Tomato (Blight-Resistant AAS-Winning Cherry Hybrid)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Jasper was named an All-America Selections winner for being one of the very few cherry tomatoes with resistance to both early and late blight, alongside resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, giving it an outstanding disease package for humid, disease-prone gardens. It produces heavy, extended clusters of small, deep red, exceptionally sweet cherry fruit with a crack-resistant skin that holds up on the vine. Because it keeps healthy foliage even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in a wet Gulf Coast summer, Jasper tends to remain productive well after less resistant cherry tomatoes have declined. Pick fruit as clusters ripen to full red color and harvest regularly to keep the vine setting new flowers. Matures in 60–65 days from transplant.

name: Jaune de Deux Saisons Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Jaune de Deux Saisons (Yellow of Two Seasons) is a French two-crop fig producing yellow-green to golden-yellow fruits in both the breba (early summer) and main crop (fall) seasons — one of the most productive two-crop fig varieties for home gardens because both crops are of comparable quality and size. The medium-sized, round to slightly pear-shaped fruits have golden-yellow skin and pale amber to pink-tinged flesh with a mild, honeyed sweetness and delicate flavor. The yellow color is distinctive and immediately identifiable among darker-skinned varieties. Two-crop figs like Jaune de Deux Saisons are particularly valuable in zone 9 where the long warm season allows both crops to mature fully — the breba crop in June provides early-season figs while the main crop extends harvest into October. The golden color makes this fig outstanding for fresh presentations and pale fig jam. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jaune Flamme Tomato (French Orange Heirloom)
description: A French heirloom prized for its abundant clusters of smooth, round, apricot-orange fruits about 2-3 ounces each, with thin skin and a balanced, fruity-sweet flavor often compared to a ripe apricot. Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, transplant into warm, fertile soil, and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines, which crop heavily and hold up well through Gulf South heat. Pick fruit as soon as it colors fully to keep the thin skins from splitting after summer rain, and expect steady production from early summer until frost. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Jaune Gros de Paris Pumpkin (Yellow of Paris)
description: Jaune Gros de Paris is a market-garden heirloom long grown around the French capital, prized for its enormous, flattened, lightly ribbed fruit in soft pastel yellow-pink that can weigh anywhere from 25 to well over 100 pounds. Sow into hills enriched with compost or aged manure and thin to two vigorous vines per hill, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling growth. The deep orange flesh is dense and moderately sweet, well suited to soups, gratins, and baked dishes rather than fresh eating. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry storage, where the fruit keeps for several months. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Jaune Paille des Vertus Shallot (Classic French Golden Storage Shallot)
aliases: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Jaune Paille des Vertus'
description: Plant individual bulb sets pointed-end-up, about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart, in fertile, well-drained soil, and keep the bed evenly moist through the growing season while easing off water as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over. Jaune Paille des Vertus, whose name translates roughly as "golden straw of Vertus," is one of the oldest documented French shallot varieties still in commerce, each set multiplying into a tight cluster of coppery-gold, papery-skinned bulbs with pale yellow flesh and the classic mild, sweet-sharp shallot flavor. It has long been regarded by French market gardeners as the standard keeping shallot, holding firm in storage for many months longer than most modern shallot varieties when properly cured. Harvest once the tops have fully collapsed and dried, cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for two to three weeks, and store the cleaned bulbs somewhere cool, dry, and dark. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Java Cardamom (Round Cardamom, Kapulaga)
description: Native to the lower hills of western Java and now cultivated across Sumatra and the Moluccas, this compact ginger-family relative forms clumps of upright, dark green reed-like pseudostems that stay smaller and tidier than true cardamom or black cardamom. The small, round, pale-skinned pods that form at the base of the plant are known as kapulaga in Indonesia, where they season rendang, gulai, and other spiced braises and are steeped into jamu herbal tonics. It prefers dappled shade under a tree canopy, steady warmth between roughly 50-95F, high humidity, and frequent rainfall, resenting both dry spells and direct sun. Because seed-grown plants are slow and inconsistent, most growers propagate by dividing rhizome clumps, and newly divided plants take a few years to reach flowering and bearing size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Java Citronella (Citronella Grass, Mahapengiri)
description: Plant clump divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; harvest leaves after 4–6 months and steam-distill or use fresh as repellent. Cymbopogon winterianus (Java citronella) is a large, clumping tropical aromatic grass that is the world's primary commercial source of citronella essential oil — one of the most commercially important aromatic crop plants globally, with the highest geraniol and citronellal content of any Cymbopogon species. Java citronella oil (named for its origin in Indonesian cultivation on Java) is the primary active ingredient in citronella candles, insect repellent products, and many natural insect-deterrent sprays worldwide. The plant is named for Cornelius de Winter, a Dutch botanist. Java citronella (C. winterianus) is distinct from Ceylon citronella (C. nardus) — Java citronella has significantly higher citronellal and geraniol content and produces a superior, more commercially valuable oil. The plant resembles lemongrass but has a more pronounced citrus-floral-rose fragrance (from geraniol content) rather than purely lemon. As a garden plant in zone 10–12, Java citronella forms an attractive, 4–6 foot clump of narrow, arching, blue-green leaves with a strong pleasant scent when crushed. Fresh stems placed around outdoor seating areas provide some mosquito deterrence, though less than the concentrated essential oil. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Java Olive (Tropical Chestnut, Bastard Poon Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; a fast-growing tree that requires ample space. Sterculia foetida (Java olive or poon tree) is a large, fast-growing tropical tree native from East Africa and India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, producing an impressive display of distinctive, star-shaped, woody, bright-red seed pods 4–6 inches across that split open dramatically to reveal 5–18 shiny black seeds with a high (55%) oil content. The common name 'Java olive' refers to the traditional use of the seeds as cooking oil and food in Java and other Indonesian islands — the seeds have a mild, slightly bitter, nutty flavor when roasted and can be pressed for a high-quality edible oil similar to olive oil in fatty acid composition. CAUTION: Raw seeds contain cyclopropene fatty acids that are mildly toxic; seeds should be roasted or heated before consumption. The tree has striking large, palmate leaves and produces flowers with a distinctive unpleasant odor ('foetida' = stinking) that attracts pollinating flies. An unusual specimen tree for large tropical landscapes where few food trees provide such dramatic seed pod displays. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Java Plum (Jambolan)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; Java plum (Syzygium cumini), also called jambolan or jamun, is a large, fast-growing evergreen tree from India and Southeast Asia in the Myrtaceae family that produces dense clusters of small, oblong, deep purple to nearly black fruits with a distinctive flavor that is simultaneously sweet, tart, and astringent — with a tongue-staining purple juice widely used in wines, vinegars, syrups, and preserves across South and Southeast Asia. The astringency is due to tannins that diminish when the fruit is fully ripe; fruits are also eaten fresh with a pinch of salt, which tempers the bitterness and heightens the sweetness. Java plum has a long history in Ayurvedic medicine, with seeds, bark, and fruit used in preparations for diabetes management, digestive complaints, and other conditions. Trees are vigorous, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably adaptable — growing in a range of soil types — but produce the best fruit quality with regular moisture and full sun. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Javanese Long Pepper (Cabe Jawa, Balinese Pepper)
description: Piper retrofractum is a woody, clinging-rooted climbing vine native to Java, Bali, and other islands of maritime Southeast Asia, where the small, cone-shaped fruiting spikes are harvested green and dried to produce 'cabe jawa,' the pungent Javanese long pepper essential to Indonesian jamu tonics and used to season rendang, sambal, and other regional dishes. Distinct from the related Indian long pepper (Piper longum), it delivers a hotter, more intensely peppery heat with warm, resinous undertones. Train young plants up a sturdy post or tree trunk in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright, dappled shade and keep consistently moist; established vines take two to three years to reach fruiting size. Harvest the spikes while still green and dry them fully before storage. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Javanese Turmeric (Temulawak, Java Ginger)
description: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep in loose, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; Javanese Turmeric (temulawak) is native to the island of Java and is a close but distinctly larger relative of common turmeric (Curcuma longa), producing bold, paddle-shaped leaves on stems that can reach 6 to 8 feet where soil and warmth are generous — far exceeding the culinary species in scale. The showy flowering spike emerges from the base with pale-yellow true flowers tucked among pink-flushed bracts, appearing before or alongside the foliage. Throughout Indonesia and Malaysia the large, deep-orange rhizome is valued in traditional herbal tonics and beverages such as jamu, and is harvested in the same way as culinary turmeric once the foliage dies back in fall. Because it is a true lowland tropical species, it is more cold-sensitive than C. longa and performs best as a warm-season landscape feature or large container specimen outside zone 10-11. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Javelin Parsnip
description: A canker-resistant parsnip that holds well in the ground, letting you leave roots to sweeten over a long 110-day season. Direct sow fresh seed shallowly into loose, stone-free soil, keeping the surface moist through the slow germination. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart for long, well-formed roots. Harvest after fall frosts, which convert starches to sugar for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Jazz Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jazz requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Gala and Braeburn, it produces medium-sized, densely crisp, juicy fruit with a distinctive sweet-tart flavor balance and a pear-drop aroma that sets it apart from its sweeter Gala parent, marketed commercially since the early 2000s as a premium eating apple. The tree bears reliably and the fruit stores exceptionally well in refrigeration, holding its crisp texture and flavor for months, which has helped make it a popular choice for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting a long-keeping late-season apple. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once the background color turns from green to yellow beneath the red blush for the best flavor balance. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jazzman Rice
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Jazzman is an aromatic long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter and bred to rival imported jasmine rice in fragrance and cooking quality, giving Gulf South growers a domestically adapted option for fragrant rice. The grain develops a distinctive popcorn-like aroma during cooking and a soft, slightly sticky texture similar to Thai jasmine rice, making it well suited to Southeast Asian and Cajun-Creole dishes alike. Keep the bed continuously saturated through the growing season, since consistent moisture through grain fill is especially important for developing the variety's signature aroma and flavor. Harvest when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry thoroughly before hulling and storing; aromatic rice varieties are somewhat more prone to losing fragrance in storage than standard long-grain types, so use home-hulled grain within the first several months for the best aroma. Matures in 110–135 days from seed.

name: Jean Davis Lavender (Pink English Lavender)
description: This English lavender selection is prized for its unusually soft, pale pink flower spikes, a rare break from the typical blue-violet lavender palette, held above compact, tidy gray-green foliage. It blooms a bit later than 'Hidcote' or 'Munstead' and holds its color best with some afternoon shade in hot summer climates, since intense heat can wash the pink toward white. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid overwatering or rich fertilizer, both of which encourage floppy growth and root rot. Shear lightly after the main flush to maintain a dense mound and encourage a possible rebloom. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Jeanne Gooseberry
description: Jeanne is a modern American-European hybrid gooseberry released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service, bred for high resistance to powdery mildew and other fungal diseases that commonly trouble older gooseberry cultivars. It produces medium-sized, deep maroon-red fruit with a full, sweet flavor considered an improvement over many traditional cultivars, ripening later in the season than most. The compact 2-3 foot bush bears reliably without a pollinator and is especially well suited to the Pacific Northwest and other cool, temperate climates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Jefferson Hazelnut (OSU Premium Large-Nut EFB-Resistant Filbert, OSU 2009 Release)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jefferson hazelnut requires a companion variety for cross-pollination; nuts ripen in September–October and drop naturally; harvest promptly from ground and dry immediately at low heat to cure and extend shelf life; Jefferson's large, well-filled nuts are suitable for roasting, confectionery, and fresh consumption. Jefferson hazelnut was released by Oregon State University in 2009 — named after Thomas Jefferson, who was an enthusiastic hazelnut grower at Monticello — and represents the flagship of OSU's first generation of EFB-resistant hazelnut varieties. Among the OSU 2009 releases, Jefferson stands out as the variety with the largest nut size and highest kernel quality comparable to the longtime commercial standard Barcelona, while adding the critical Eastern Filbert Blight resistance that Barcelona lacks. In Oregon and Washington State hazelnut orchards, Jefferson is being planted as a replacement for Barcelona both in existing orchards where EFB has arrived and in new plantings where EFB resistance is now considered standard. In the eastern United States, Jefferson has opened hazelnut production to a region that was essentially unable to grow commercial European hazelnuts due to the endemic EFB — Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern university variety trials show Jefferson performing strongly under heavy EFB pressure that devastates Barcelona in just 2–3 seasons. The nuts are large, round to oval, with a clean, thin shell and excellent sweet hazelnut flavor — considered among the best-tasting of any named variety, justifying the Jefferson name's association with culinary excellence. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jefferson Plum (Fine-Flavored American Golden Gage-Type Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Jefferson was raised in New York in the 1820s and became one of the most highly regarded American plums of the 19th century, producing large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with red and carrying rich, sweet, aromatic flesh often compared favorably to the classic European gage plums it descends from. The vigorous tree crops reliably and the large fruit size, combined with outstanding flavor, made it a standard for fine dessert plums in American orchards for generations. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets to maintain good size, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored for the best flavor, since Jefferson plums picked too early lack the full richness the variety is known for. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jelly Bean Dwarf Blueberry (Cold-Hardy Compact Container Blueberry)
description: Grow Jelly Bean in a container or compact raised bed filled with acidic, well-drained soil, taking advantage of its dense, tidy, rounded form for small-space edible landscaping. It is one of the more broadly climate-adaptable selections in the dwarf Bushel and Berry line, tolerating both colder winters and the mild, low-chill winters typical of the Gulf South, though fruit set in the warmest zones benefits from siting where it gets full winter sun exposure. Sweet, marble-sized berries ripen over several weeks in early summer on a self-fertile plant, though a second blueberry nearby improves yield. Keep the potting mix consistently moist and top-dress with acid-forming fertilizer each spring. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Jelly Fig (Mary Lane Seedless Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Jelly, marketed by some Gulf South nurseries as Mary Lane Seedless, produces a distinctive elongated, bottleneck-shaped fruit with thin yellow skin and clear amber flesh that is nearly free of viable seeds. The lack of seeds and high sugar content make it especially prized for fig preserves and jam, while the tender, sweet flesh is also excellent fresh. It ripens on a single main crop in late July into August and is grown as a cold-tolerant landscape and container fig further north than many named cultivars. As with other closed-eye types, its tight ostiole offers some resistance to the rain-driven souring that plagues open-eyed figs during humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jelly Palm (Pindo Palm)
description: Jelly palm is one of the hardiest fruiting palms, surviving temperatures down to 12–15°F, and is well-suited to zones 8–11 in well-drained soils ranging from sandy to clay. The tree is monoecious, with male and female flowers on the same large branched inflorescence, so a single specimen fruits reliably without a pollinator. It produces abundant clusters of small orange-yellow drupes in summer; the sweet-tart pulp is rich in pectin and classically used for jelly, wine, and preserves. Allow fruit to fall naturally or gently shake clusters when most fruit has colored; process quickly as the thin-skinned fruit ferments rapidly after harvest. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Jelly Palm (Pindo Palm)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; the jelly palm is one of the hardiest feather palms in cultivation, tolerating temperatures to about 12°F (-11°C) with minimal damage, making it reliable across zone 8b-10. The silvery-blue arching fronds give a dramatic tropical appearance while the plant chugs through drought and poor soils with little supplemental care once established. Clusters of small orange-yellow fruits ripen in summer and have a sweet-tart apricot-pineapple flavor prized for jellies, wine, and juice — harvest when the entire cluster begins to drop. Water deeply but infrequently during the first two years to encourage deep root development, then reduce irrigation significantly. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Jenkins Pecan (Mississippi Delta Scab-Resistant Pecan, Type II Gulf South Selection)
description: Jenkins originated as a chance seedling planted around 1977 by grower Travis Jenkins in Rena Lara, Mississippi, and was later evaluated by Auburn University, Mississippi State University, and the University of Georgia for its scab resistance and nut quality. Nuts are ovate with a rounded base similar to Success, run about 55 per pound, and fill to roughly 53 percent kernel, ripening a few days ahead of Stuart. Its good scab tolerance and strong fall foliage retention make it a solid low-spray option for Mississippi Delta and broader Gulf South backyard orchards. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Jenny Chinese Chestnut (Tall Early-Ripening Kintzel-Derived Selection)
description: Jenny was selected by chestnut breeder J.M. Nave as an open-pollinated seedling of the old West Virginia cultivar Kintzel, and has since been evaluated in Missouri chestnut trials. Unlike the broad, spreading orchard-type crown typical of many Chinese chestnut selections, Jenny grows as a tall, vigorous, erect tree with unusually large leaves, so it benefits from extra vertical space. It ripens early and drops its large, exceptionally flavorful nuts within a short window once the first ones fall, which simplifies harvest compared with cultivars that drop nuts over many weeks. Inheriting the blight resistance and cold hardiness of its Kintzel parent along with the natural resistance of Chinese chestnut generally, Jenny is only rarely troubled by chestnut blight. Because chestnuts will not self-pollinate, plant a second, unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within range for a reliable nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jenny Kiwi (Self-Fertile Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vigorous vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor system able to support its weight for decades. Jenny is a self-fertile fuzzy kiwifruit selection, a genuine practical advantage over the classic Hayward variety, which requires a separate non-fruiting male vine purely for pollination — Jenny produces a crop from a single plant, making it a far more space-efficient choice for smaller home gardens that can't accommodate two full-sized kiwi vines. Fruit is somewhat smaller than Hayward and yields are generally lighter without a dedicated pollinizer nearby, but a nearby male vine (of Jenny or another compatible variety) will still improve fruit set and size if space allows. Prune annually in the dormant season to control the vine's naturally vigorous, sprawling growth and keep fruiting wood productive. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Jenny Lind Melon (Early American Heirloom Ribbed Muskmelon)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Jenny Lind melons are small and compact compared to modern varieties, making them suitable for small gardens; harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the blossom-end softens slightly; the green flesh is unusual for American melons and has a delicate, sweet, slightly floral flavor. Jenny Lind is one of the oldest and most historically documented named melon varieties in American horticulture — it was listed in seed catalogs by the 1840s and became extremely popular in the northeastern states (particularly New Jersey, where it was widely grown for the Philadelphia and New York markets) during the latter half of the 19th century, remaining a garden standard well into the early 20th century before modern hybrids displaced it. The variety is named in honor of Jenny Lind (1820–1887), the Swedish opera singer known as the 'Swedish Nightingale,' whose American tour managed by P.T. Barnum in 1850–1851 created an extraordinary popular sensation — everything from hairstyles to trains to songs to garden plants were named for her in that era. Jenny Lind melon is distinctive in several ways: the small (typically 1–2 pound) round fruits are deeply ribbed with prominent ridges running from stem to blossom end, and the blossom end has a characteristic raised, button-like knob in the center of a depression — a 'turban' or 'navel' that is unique among common muskmelons. The flesh is a pale sea-green to apple-green color (not the familiar salmon-orange of modern cantaloupes) that is thin relative to the total fruit size but very sweet and floral in flavor. Jenny Lind ripens about 2 weeks earlier than standard cantaloupes, making it an excellent choice for short-season gardens. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Jericho Lettuce (Israeli Heat-Tolerant Romaine)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep; Jericho tolerates warmer soil and air temperatures than most lettuces, extending the spring sowing season by 2–4 weeks beyond the window suitable for other varieties; provide afternoon shade in the hottest weather; thin to 8–12 inches; harvest full heads or use as cut-and-come-again. Jericho is an Israeli-developed Romaine (Cos) type lettuce bred specifically for the extreme heat of the Jordan Valley and the Mediterranean climate of Israel, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 100°F and conventional lettuce bolts immediately. The variety was developed to remain productive longer into warm weather than any other Romaine, and delivers this through exceptional heat tolerance — it is typically the last lettuce still producing usable heads when spring heat arrives in mid-latitude gardens, and one of the earliest candidates for late-summer planting when other varieties would bolt immediately. The large, upright heads have crisp, pale green Romaine-style leaves with excellent flavor — sweet, slightly nutty, and refreshing — and the heads are notably larger than many other heat-tolerant varieties. For Gulf Coast gardeners (zones 8b–10), Jericho is the most valuable Romaine for the challenging transition from cool-season winter lettuce into warming spring, providing 2–4 extra weeks of production compared to standard varieties. Highly recommended by Territorial Seed and Johnny's for hot-summer and transition-zone gardens. Matures in 57–68 days from seed.

name: Jericho Romaine Lettuce (Israeli Heat-Tolerant Bolt-Resistant Cos Lettuce)
description: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting in early spring or fall; transplant to partial shade in warm seasons to extend the harvest. Harvest outer leaves or whole heads when compact and firm. Jericho Romaine is an Israeli-bred romaine (cos) lettuce developed by breeders working in the conditions of the Jordan Valley near the ancient city of Jericho — an arid, extremely hot agricultural region where the development of heat-tolerant lettuce was driven by practical necessity to extend the local growing season. The breeding produced a romaine variety with substantially better heat tolerance and bolt resistance than standard European and American romaine types, and Jericho has become one of the most recommended romaine varieties for warm-climate gardeners and for late-spring plantings in temperate zones where other romaine varieties rapidly bolt when temperatures rise. The heads are upright, tightly folded, medium-large, dark green, with the crisp, mildly bitter interior quality of classic romaine. For zone 9 gardeners, Jericho's heat-tolerance advantage translates to a 2–4 week extension of the spring romaine harvest window before heat triggers bolting — a meaningful extension in climates where the transition from cool to hot weather happens rapidly. Jericho is also appropriate for early fall planting when temperatures are still warm but declining. Matures in 57–70 days from transplant.

name: Jermor Shallot (French Banana Shallot, RHS AGM)
description: Plant individual sets about an inch deep and six to eight inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, and keep the bed weeded and evenly watered through spring growth. Jermor is a French 'banana' or échalion-type shallot bred in Brittany, producing clusters of medium to large, elegantly elongated bulbs with glossy rose-copper skin and pale pink-tinged flesh prized for its refined, mild-sweet flavor. Reduce watering once the foliage begins to yellow and fall over, then lift the bulbs and cure them in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks before trimming and storing. Well-cured bulbs keep for several months in cool, dry storage. Matures in 110–125 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Blueberry (Classic Northern Highbush Blueberry, New Jersey Standard Blueberry)
description: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat moss or pine bark; maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.2 for healthy growth and production; mulch heavily with pine bark or acid wood chips; fertilize with ammonium sulfate in early spring; Jersey ripens in August (late season) producing large, firm, light blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and excellent storage quality. Jersey blueberry is one of the oldest and most historically important highbush blueberry varieties in American commercial and home garden production — developed by Frederick Coville at the USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in 1928 from deliberate crosses with wild Vaccinium corymbosum selections from the Atlantic coastal plain. Jersey was one of the first named highbush blueberry varieties released and became the cornerstone of the New Jersey commercial blueberry industry (the first commercial blueberry industry in the United States), for which it was specifically developed. For several decades, Jersey was essentially THE commercial highbush blueberry of the American East Coast, dominating production in New Jersey, Michigan, and the other blueberry-producing states before the development of newer varieties with earlier ripening or larger fruit. Despite its age (nearly 100 years of commercial production), Jersey remains popular for several reasons: its late-season ripening (August) extends the fresh blueberry window after most other varieties have finished, its very large, firm, light blue berries store and ship exceptionally well (better than softer-berried varieties), and its mild, sweet flavor is reliable and consistent. Jersey is considered somewhat milder in flavor than Bluecrop or Elliott but produces reliably in a wide range of conditions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Devil Tomato (New Jersey Heirloom Banana Paste Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil after last frost. Stake or cage plants before or at transplanting. Jersey Devil is a New Jersey heirloom paste tomato with an immediately recognizable elongated, banana-shaped to horn-shaped fruit form: 5–8 inches long, tapered to a sharp point at the blossom end, with bright red skin and very dense, meaty flesh. The distinctive shape — sometimes described as resembling a long red chili pepper at a glance — makes Jersey Devil one of the most visually unusual paste tomatoes. The eating quality matches the visual appeal: the flesh is very dense and dry with minimal gel and seeds, a high solid content that makes it ideal for tomato sauce (concentrates quickly without extended cooking), sun-dried tomatoes, and oven-roasted preparations where the low moisture prevents the pan from becoming soupy. Jersey Devil is an indeterminate vine that produces heavily over a long season; the fruits ripen mid-season (78–88 days from transplant) and continue until frost. The variety is strongly connected to New Jersey, where it appears in the regional heirloom seed tradition alongside other East Coast paste types. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Gem Beach Plum (Rutgers-Bred Named Beach Plum Selection)
description: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun and site a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species sets fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Jersey Gem is a beach plum selection bred by Rutgers University in New Jersey and singled out, alongside a small number of other named clones such as Resigno and ECOS, for producing larger and better-flavored fruit than typical unselected wild seedling stands, where fruit quality and sweetness vary considerably from bush to bush. Its purple-red to blue-black drupes ripen in late summer and are well suited to the traditional beach plum jams, jellies, and preserves long made along the Jersey Shore and greater mid-Atlantic coast. As a true dune-adapted shrub, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress most other fruiting plants, needing only light pruning after bloom to stay productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Giant Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Hybrid Asparagus)
description: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge over the growing season. Jersey Giant is one of the Rutgers University all-male hybrid asparagus cultivars, bred so that plants never set seed and instead direct all their energy into producing thick, vigorous, high-yielding spears over a long productive lifespan. It also carries good resistance to Fusarium crown and root rot, a serious disease problem in older asparagus plantings, making it one of the more reliable modern choices for a home asparagus bed. Do not harvest any spears the first year and only lightly the second year, allowing the fern-like foliage to grow through summer to build a strong root system for many years of future harvests. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jersey King Asparagus
description: Jersey King is one of the Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus lines bred for resistance to Fusarium crown rot and asparagus rust while eliminating the volunteer seedlings that female plants produce. It sends up thick, uniform, deep-green spears with tightly closed tips over a long spring harvest window. Because energy is not diverted into seed production, established beds tend to build vigor faster than open-pollinated types like Mary Washington. Give plants a full season to establish before taking any harvest, and top-dress with compost each fall to sustain crown health for decades. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Knight Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Hybrid Asparagus for Southern Gardens)
description: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench; allow all fern growth in the first year. Feed annually with balanced fertilizer after harvest. Jersey Knight is an all-male F1 hybrid asparagus from the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station at Rutgers University — part of the 'Jersey' series of asparagus hybrids (including Jersey Giant and Jersey Supreme) that revolutionized asparagus production in the United States from the 1980s onward by introducing all-male genetics, disease resistance, and dramatically improved yield over the open-pollinated varieties that had been standard for a century. The key innovation of the Jersey series is their all-male genetics: asparagus is naturally dioecious (separate male and female plants), and female plants divert significant energy into berry and seed production that could otherwise go to spear production; all-male hybrids eliminate this energy diversion and direct all plant resources to the edible spears, resulting in 2–3× the yield of traditional open-pollinated varieties under the same conditions. Jersey Knight carries improved resistance to asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot — two diseases that significantly reduce the productive lifespan of traditional varieties in warm, humid climates. In zone 9, Jersey Knight is among the better-adapted of the Jersey hybrids due to its moderate heat tolerance and disease package; while asparagus is genuinely challenging in zone 9's warm winters, Jersey Knight has performed better in southern trials than many other varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Supreme Asparagus (Early High-Yield Rutgers Hybrid)
description: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. Jersey Supreme is a later-generation Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus bred for earlier spring spear emergence and higher overall yield than older selections like Jersey Giant, while retaining the same good disease resistance and long-term productivity that made the Jersey series a standard choice for home and commercial asparagus plantings. As an all-male hybrid it never sets seed, so all of the plant's energy goes into vigorous spear production over what can be a fifteen-to-twenty-year productive bed lifespan. Avoid harvesting the first year and harvest only lightly the second year to let the root system establish fully before full production begins. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jersey Wakefield Cabbage
description: This historic heirloom, dating to the 1840s, forms distinctive pointed heads with sweet flavor and matures early on compact plants ideal for small gardens. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant hardened seedlings in early spring. Cabbage tolerates light frost, so it can go out before tender crops. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest the conical heads when firm to avoid splitting. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Jerusalem Artichoke
description: Plant tuber sections 3–5 inches deep around the last frost date in any well-drained soil — Jerusalem artichoke is remarkably tolerant of poor soils, drought, and neglect, producing masses of crunchy, nutty, sweet tubers in autumn that can be harvested after frost improves their flavor by converting inulin to sugars. The plants reach 6–10 feet tall and produce small yellow sunflowers in late summer. Harvest tubers from fall through early spring by digging; leave some tubers in the ground to re-sprout and produce next year's crop. Note that inulin is not digested by most people and can cause significant gas — start with small servings and cook thoroughly to reduce this effect. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Jerusalem Artichoke Sunchoke (Native Perennial Sunflower Tuber Vegetable)
description: Plant 2–3 inch tuber pieces 4–6 inches deep in spring; harvest tubers in late fall through winter after tops die back. Jerusalem Artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus, also called Sunchoke) is a native North American perennial plant of the sunflower family — widely distributed across eastern and central North America where it was cultivated by Indigenous peoples as a staple starchy food long before European contact. The name is misleading: it has no connection to Jerusalem (possibly a corruption of the Italian girasole, meaning sunflower) and is not an artichoke (the flavor resemblance to artichoke heart inspired the name). The edible part is the knobby, irregular underground tuber — tan to purple-skinned with white, crisp flesh that tastes sweet, nutty, and faintly artichoke-like when eaten raw, and takes on a creamier, sweeter character when roasted or cooked. The distinctive carbohydrate of sunchoke tubers is inulin (not starch), a prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial gut bacteria — making sunchokes notable for their probiotic benefits. The plants themselves are spectacular: 6–10 feet tall by summer, topped with bright yellow sunflowers in late summer and fall. In zone 9, sunchoke thrives with minimal care in the summer heat, requiring no watering once established in reasonably good soil. Matures in 105–130 days from transplant.

name: Jerusalem Oak Goosefoot (Feather Geranium)
description: Sow directly in lean, well-drained soil after last frost and thin seedlings to 8-12 in apart; established plants tolerate heat and drought and need little care beyond occasional weeding. The deeply cut, oak-leaf-shaped foliage is covered in sticky glandular hairs that release a strong, sweet, resinous fragrance when brushed or crushed, and the branching flower spikes dry to a feathery, chartreuse-to-rust plume prized in dried arrangements and sachets. Cut whole flowering stems just as the tiny green flowers open and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy spot to preserve both scent and form. Historically the aromatic tops were also dried and used in traditional remedies for coughs and chest congestion, though it is grown today mainly as a fragrance and dried-flower herb. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Jet Star Tomato
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Jet Star is a popular indeterminate hybrid tomato introduced by Harris Seeds in the late 1960s that earned a lasting following among home gardeners for its combination of large, smooth, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with distinctively mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to people who find standard tomatoes too tart — the low-acid character makes Jet Star the variety of choice for those who love the fresh tomato experience without acid sensitivity. The smooth, crack-resistant fruits have few seeds and thick walls, making them excellent slicing tomatoes for sandwiches and salads; they also hold up well in cooking but are really at their finest fresh off the vine at warm room temperature. VF disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2) keeps plants productive through the season. Jet Star is a mid-season tomato (70–75 days from transplant) and bears continuously as an indeterminate variety — plants will need staking or caging as they can reach 5–6 feet. An excellent choice for gardeners who prefer mild, low-acid tomatoes, and a reliable producer in zone 8–10 spring and fall tomato seasons. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Jet Trail Flowering Quince (Compact Spreading White Quince)
description: Jet Trail bears clusters of pure white flowers opening on bare, thorny branches in late winter into early spring, on a low, spreading shrub that stays under 3 feet, considerably more compact than most flowering quince cultivars. Its low, wide habit suits mass plantings, low informal hedges, and banks where a spreading rather than upright quince is wanted, and small yellow-green quince fruit follows the flowers in fall, edible for preserves though quite tart and hard raw. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, and drought-tolerant once its roots are settled. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jetstar Tomato (Disease-Resistant Low-Acid Hybrid Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the indeterminate vine. Jetstar is a widely grown hybrid slicing tomato valued for its mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes, combined with good resistance to verticillium and fusarium wilts that helps it stay productive through a long growing season. It produces smooth, round, meaty red fruit with few seeds and good crack resistance. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot, and feed regularly through the season to keep the vigorous vine productive from early summer into fall. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Jewel Amethyst Eggplant
description: A container-friendly eggplant with a tidy habit and glossy oval purple fruits best picked at 3 to 4.5 inches long. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, then transplant once nights stay reliably warm. Keep evenly watered and mulched, and harvest regularly from this prolific plant to keep new fruit setting. Pick while the skin is glossy for the firmest, best texture. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Jewel Black Raspberry
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jewel is a Cornell University-released black raspberry (Rubus occidentalis) — an entirely distinct species from red raspberries with a different flavor, deeper color, and more intense aromatic character. Black raspberries produce jet-black, hollow drupes with an intensely rich, complex, wine-like flavor that differs dramatically from the lighter, brighter flavor of red raspberries — the dark color indicates very high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any commonly grown berry. Black raspberry flavor is described as a deep, earthy, complex fruitiness with more tannin and less overt sweetness than red raspberries, making them outstanding for jams, pies, syrup, black raspberry ice cream (a regional specialty in the Ohio River Valley), and liqueurs. Jewel is the leading commercial black raspberry variety, selected for large, firm fruits and good resistance to anthracnose disease. In zone 9 the June ripening precedes peak summer heat, making black raspberry production more feasible than red raspberry in warm climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jewel Blueberry (UF Very-Early Southern Highbush Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Jewel is a University of Florida IFAS very-early-ripening southern highbush blueberry that starts production 1–2 weeks ahead of Emerald and most other Gulf South varieties — providing the season's first fresh blueberries in February to March in zone 9, making Jewel particularly valuable for extending the blueberry harvest season when planted with later-ripening varieties. The medium-large, blue berries have good flavor and firm texture with a small dry scar — the fresh-eating quality is good for a very early variety, though some tasters find the peak flavor of mid-season varieties like Emerald and O'Neal slightly superior. Jewel's very low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–200 hours) makes it one of the best-adapted blueberries for the warmest zone 9 locations where winters are mild and chill accumulation is uncertain. Jewel is upright and moderately vigorous, reaching 4–5 feet with regular management. As with all southern highbush blueberries, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) is the fundamental requirement — plant in raised beds or containers with acidic media (50% pine bark plus peat) if native soil pH cannot be sufficiently lowered. Plant with Emerald, Southmoon, or O'Neal for cross-pollination that significantly increases berry size and total yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jewel Strawberry (Mid-Season June-Bearer, Premier New York Strawberry)
description: Plant in early spring; Jewel is a high-yielding, large-fruited mid-season June-bearer that peaks about 5–7 days after Earliglow; berries have excellent fresh flavor and store and process better than many June-bearers; remove flowers the first year; the plants are vigorous and winter-hardy in zones 3–7 with straw mulch. Jewel strawberry is a Cornell University-developed variety (released 1985) that became the dominant commercial and farm-stand strawberry in New York State and one of the most important strawberries in the northeastern United States. Cornell's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva bred Jewel specifically for northeastern growing conditions — the humid, cool summers and reliable winter cold of New York — and the variety's success reflects that targeted development: it performs exceptionally in zones 4–7 humid northeastern conditions where some varieties from drier or warmer climates show reduced vigor or disease problems. The berries are large to very large, consistently well-shaped, dark red throughout with outstanding fresh flavor — considered by many northeastern tasters to combine the best attributes of Earliglow flavor with Allstar size. Jewel is noted for holding flavor and firmness well across a range of weather conditions, producing consistently good berries even in the hot, humid spells that sometimes degrade the quality of other varieties during ripening. It is vigorous enough to be productive for 3–4 years in a well-managed bed, somewhat longer than many modern varieties. The standard strawberry at many northeastern U-pick farms and roadside stands. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Jewel Sweet Potato (1970 NCSU Orange Standard)
description: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms above 65°F; Jewel tolerates less-than-ideal soil conditions better than many newer varieties. Jewel was developed and released in 1970 by North Carolina State University as part of the USDA–state cooperative sweet potato breeding program and became the dominant American commercial sweet potato throughout the 1970s–1990s; it produced the standard against which American sweet potatoes were judged for two decades before Beauregard's introduction. The medium to large, elongated, smooth, coppery-orange to red-orange-skinned roots have intensely orange, moist, sweet flesh that softens to a creamy consistency when baked — an excellent texture for traditional sweet potato preparations. Flavor is sweet and complex with good caramel development during baking. Self-reliant and productive; excellent for Gulf Coast spring planting in late March through April and fall planting in June through July. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Jewels of Opar
description: Direct-sow seeds on soil surface in partial shade or full sun after frost; jewels of opar (Brazilian spinach, fameflower, pink baby's breath) is a tropical perennial succulent of the purslane family (Portulacaceae) that serves a dual role as an edible leafy vegetable and an ornamental plant — the fleshy, oval, bright-green leaves are eaten raw in salads (with a mildly astringent, spinach-like flavor) or cooked as a pot herb, while the plant itself produces an ornamental display of hundreds of tiny, rosy-pink to magenta, five-petaled flowers on widely branched, airy, 12–24-inch flowering stems, creating a delicate pink-mist effect above the succulent foliage. In warm climates it grows as a drought-tolerant, shade-tolerant annual or short-lived perennial that self-seeds freely to maintain permanent colonies in partially shaded garden beds, pathways, and edges. Unlike most leafy greens, it thrives in the combination of heat, drought, and partial shade that defeats most other edibles in Gulf Coast and tropical summers. An excellent dual-purpose plant for edible/ornamental shade gardens in zone 8–12. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Jiaogulan
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm, moist starting mix and provide a trellis or support on which the vigorous twining vine can climb; jiaogulan grows 10–20 ft if given the right conditions. Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates; consistent moisture promotes the most lush and harvestable leaf growth. In zones 7–8 the plant dies to the ground in winter but regrows from the root; in zone 9 and above it may be evergreen. Harvest the five-lobed leaflets throughout the growing season for fresh or dried tea; known as southern ginseng, the leaves contain saponins similar to those in Panax ginseng and are used in adaptogenic preparations. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Jicama
description: Sow scarified seeds 1 in deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil 2–4 weeks after the last frost once soil is thoroughly warm. Jicama is a vigorous vine requiring a sturdy trellis; pinch flower buds as they appear throughout the season — leaving flowers reduces tuber size dramatically since the plant diverts energy to seed set. Begin harvesting small tubers at about 5 months; larger tubers become more fibrous if left past 9 months. Only the roots are edible — all above-ground parts, including seeds and pods, contain rotenone and are toxic. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Jim Best Oregano (Trailing Golden Marbled Oregano)
description: Jim Best is an ornamental selection of common oregano prized for its gold-and-green marbled foliage on lax, trailing stems that spill attractively over the edge of a container or raised bed. Leaf variegation is most pronounced when plants get some relief from intense afternoon sun, making it a good candidate for a partly shaded herb pot or hanging basket rather than a full-sun bed. Unlike purely ornamental oregano hybrids, its leaves retain usable oregano flavor, though it is grown primarily for foliage color and trailing habit. Trim stem tips periodically to keep growth dense and prevent the trailing stems from becoming sparse and leggy. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Jim Gerdemann Chilean Guava (Large Crimson-Fruited Selection)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping soil more consistently moist than most Chilean guava selections tolerate. Named for the horticulturist in whose garden it was discovered by nurseryman Ian Barclay, this selection is a lower, shrubbier, more rounded-leaved form of Chilean guava than the typical species, responding especially well to hedging and clipped forms. It produces large crimson fruit that ripens later in the season than many other selections, with the species' characteristic intense strawberry-watermelon aroma and flavor. Hardy to around 10F once established, it is best suited to sheltered gardens at the milder end of its zone range, where its evergreen foliage and drooping white summer flowers also make it a handsome ornamental hedge. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jimmy Nardello Pepper (Sweet Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Jimmy Nardello is one of the most beloved heirloom sweet peppers in American home gardening — an Italian variety brought to Connecticut from Basilicata, Italy, by Giuseppa and Jimmy Nardello's family in 1887 and preserved in that family for nearly a century before being donated to the Seed Savers Exchange. The long, thin, curved, brilliant red fruits (8–10 inches, very thin walls) are among the sweetest of all peppers when fully ripe red — intensely concentrated sweet pepper flavor without any heat whatsoever. Jimmy Nardello is the premier sweet frying pepper: the thin walls mean the fruits cook in seconds in hot oil (traditional Italian fritto method) or over high heat on a grill, caramelizing immediately to a concentrated, smoky-sweet, almost jammy flavor that is entirely different from the fresh fruit character. The dried fruits are also exceptional for crushing into sweet paprika with excellent color and flavor. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved indefinitely and the variety preserved — Jimmy Nardello is recognized on the Slow Food Ark of Taste as a culturally significant food variety worth preserving. In zone 9, the plants are very productive from late spring through fall. The abundant, long, curved red fruits hanging from productive plants are visually beautiful and practically abundant. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Jimmy Nardello Sweet Pepper
description: Start these Italian heirloom frying peppers indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm at 70 to 90 degrees for reliable germination. Transplant seedlings out only after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. The long, tapered 6 to 12 inch fruits ripen from green to glossy red and are exceptionally sweet, making them ideal for frying. Provide consistent moisture and a light feeding once fruit sets to keep plants productive through the season. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Jimmy Nardello's Sweet Frying Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 75–80°F and transplant after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil. This Italian heirloom from Basilicata bears long, thin-walled, crinkled fruits that dangle in clusters and turn from green to brilliant red at maturity. The fruits are nearly heat-free and intensely sweet, making them outstanding for frying in olive oil, roasting, or drying. Harvest when fully red for peak sweetness, or dry on a string in a warm, airy location — the thin walls dehydrate rapidly and concentrate flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Jimmy Red Corn
description: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; let ears fully dry on the stalk for the deepest color and best grinding or distilling quality. Jimmy Red is a South Carolina heirloom dent corn with a dramatic history — the variety nearly vanished entirely, surviving through only a handful of ears kept by a single South Carolina farming family, before being rediscovered and reintroduced in the 2010s by chef and miller Glenn Roberts of Anson Mills and distiller Scott Blackwell, who used it to help revive heirloom Southern corn whiskey and grits production. The deep garnet-red, almost purple-black kernels grind into a rich, distinctively flavored meal and grits, and the variety has become especially prized by craft distillers for producing bourbon and moonshine with a uniquely deep, earthy character credited to the corn's high oil content and pigmentation. A striking, historically significant heirloom for gardeners interested in Southern foodways and heritage grain, zone 6–10. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Jindai Persimmon (Seedless Non-Astringent Semi-Dwarf Kaki)
description: Jindai is a Japanese non-astringent (PCNA-type) persimmon prized for its naturally compact, semi-dwarf growth habit, making it one of the easier kaki cultivars to keep manageable in a home orchard or even a large container without heavy pruning. Fruit is medium-sized, round to slightly flattened, orange-skinned, and virtually seedless when grown without a pollinator, and can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree since it never develops the mouth-puckering tannins that afflict astringent types. The tree bears young and reliably, tolerates the mild winters of the Gulf South on modest chill accumulation, and its smaller stature makes netting against birds and squirrels considerably more practical than on full-sized persimmon trees. Fall color is a attractive bonus, with foliage turning shades of yellow-orange before the bright fruit hangs on bare branches into late autumn. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Jing Orange Okra (Chinese Heirloom Orange-Red Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight before direct sowing an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra bearing vivid orange-red pods on stems and foliage tinged with the same warm color, making it as striking in the garden as it is productive, while retaining good tenderness a bit longer than typical green okra before pods toughen. Harvest at 2-4 inches for the best texture, picking every couple of days through the growing season to keep plants producing continuously in the Gulf South's long, hot summer. The colorful pods make an attractive addition to a mixed vegetable bed or ornamental edible border in addition to their culinary use in gumbo, frying, and pickling. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Jinsixiaozao Jujube (Golden Silk Small Jujube, Cangzhou Drying Jujube)
description: Jinsixiaozao produces small, slender, column-shaped fruit (about 7 grams) with thin skin, dense flesh, and a tiny pit, named for the fine golden threads of pulp that stretch out when a dried fruit is pulled apart. Sugar content is unusually high, reported from the high-20s to mid-30s Brix fresh and much higher once dried, giving it a honey-like intensity that makes it one of the best jujube cultivars for home drying and candying rather than fresh eating alone. Originating from Cangzhou in Hebei Province and released commercially in 2001, it was brought into US jujube collections in the following decade and remains a minor but distinctive selection compared to the mainstream Li, Lang, and Honey Jar types. The tree itself is smaller and less vigorous than most other jujube cultivars, so it suits gardeners with limited space, and like other jujubes it shrugs off Gulf Coast heat, poor soil, and drought once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jiro Persimmon (Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Jiro is the most widely grown non-astringent Japanese persimmon cultivar in California, Asia, and the Gulf South — producing large, slightly flattened, bright orange-red fruits that can be eaten crisp, firm, and crunchy directly from the tree without waiting for softening, making them much more approachable than astringent persimmons (like Hachiya) that must be fully soft before eating. The non-astringent quality means Jiro persimmons are eaten like apples — sliced, eaten fresh, added to salads, or simply eaten out of hand with no waiting for ripeness. The sweet, mild, honey-like flavor is pleasant and distinctive. In zone 9, Jiro ripens in October–November, adding late-season ornamental color when the bright orange fruits hang on the increasingly bare branches after leaf drop — a striking autumn display that has made ornamental persimmons popular landscape trees. The tree is naturally well-shaped and attractive with excellent fall foliage color. Jiro requires very little care once established — it is drought-tolerant, highly pest-resistant, and adapts to clay soils that challenge many fruit trees. One of the most productive and reliable fruit trees for Gulf South landscapes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jitlee Rambutan
description: Grow in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun protected from strong wind; Jitlee is a compact, heavy-bearing rambutan cultivar producing clusters of bright crimson, free-stone fruit, and is popular in Southeast Asian orchards for its reliable, intense flowering. It is a male-dominant flowering type best interplanted with a hermaphroditic cultivar such as Rongrien to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Because it stays smaller than many other rambutan selections it can be planted more closely and is a good option for growers with limited space in true tropical climates. Like all rambutan, it has no meaningful cold tolerance and requires warm, humid, frost-free conditions to thrive. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Joan J Raspberry (Thornless Primocane Everbearing Raspberry)
description: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring, and mow or cut all canes to the ground each winter for the simplest maintenance approach, since Joan J bears fruit on the current year's primocanes rather than needing overwintered floricanes. This thornless, everbearing raspberry produces a large early-summer crop plus a second flush in fall, with smooth, spine-free canes that make picking and pruning far more pleasant than thorny raspberry cultivars. It is notably vigorous and disease-resistant, producing large, firm, richly flavored berries over an extended harvest window. Support canes with a simple two-wire trellis if grown for the full season rather than mown annually, and harvest when berries pull cleanly from the plug with no resistance. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Job's Tears (Adlay Millet)
description: Direct-sow in moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Job's tears is a large, tropical grass from Southeast Asia grown both as a grain crop and as an ornamental and craft plant. The plant is unmistakable: large, corn-like leaves on tall stems produce pendulous clusters of hard, rounded, bead-like structures (involucres) containing the true grain, which ripen from green to white, gray, and sometimes blue-gray or black. These natural beads have a hole through the center and have been used for necklaces, rosaries, and ceremonial jewelry for thousands of years across Asia and the Pacific. The grain itself (adlay) is nutritious, with a mild, earthy flavor resembling barley, and is used in soups, porridges, teas, and brewing in China, Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia. It is considered medicinal in traditional Chinese medicine. In zone 9–11, the plant can grow as a short-lived perennial. It tolerates moist soil and partial shade better than most grain crops, making it suitable for wet areas of the garden. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Joe's Long Cayenne Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking plants if pod weight bends the stems. This Calabrian heirloom traveled from Italy to Italian-Canadian growers in Toronto and then to Joe Sestito of Troy, New York, whose name became attached to it when Dr. Carolyn Male introduced the variety to American gardeners through Seed Savers Exchange in 1996. Plants produce heavy clusters of slender, thin-walled cayenne-type pods that can reach up to a foot long, ripening from green to bright red with medium-high heat in the 30,000–50,000 Scoville range. The thin walls make whole pods easy to string into ristras for air-drying, and dried fruit grinds readily into pepper flakes or crushed cayenne. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Joey Avocado (Extreme Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters. Joey was discovered as a chance seedling near Uvalde, Texas, and stands out among avocado varieties for its cold tolerance, with mature trees reported to survive brief drops into the teens Fahrenheit that would kill most avocados. It is a Type B, Mexican-race avocado producing medium, egg-shaped fruit with thin purple-black skin and rich, creamy, nutty-flavored flesh that ripens in late summer through fall. Joey's combination of cold hardiness and dependable production makes it one of the better avocado choices for in-ground planting along the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast and coastal Texas. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jogranda Jostaberry (Large-Fruited Currant-Gooseberry Hybrid)
description: Jogranda was released in 1985 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer as a follow-up to the original Josta jostaberry, selected for violet-black berries that run noticeably larger than Josta's and ripen two to three weeks later, which stretches the jostaberry picking season into midsummer. The spreading, slightly drooping canes benefit from light staking or a simple wire support as the heavy fruit clusters develop, and the thornless growth habit keeps harvest and pruning far less prickly than picking true gooseberries. Flavor is tangy and full-bodied, closer to black currant than gooseberry, and the fruit holds up well for jam, syrup, and home winemaking. Jogranda crops most heavily when planted with Jostine or another jostaberry for cross-pollination, and like other jostaberries it tolerates Gulf Coast heat better than straight black currants provided it gets consistent moisture and some afternoon shade. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: John Elderberry
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to periodically wet soil; John is a named American elderberry cultivar selected at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva as part of the New York State elderberry improvement program — the same program that produced the widely-grown Adams cultivar. John was selected as a pollinator companion for Adams, producing profuse flowers slightly earlier than Adams to ensure cross-pollination during the Adams flowering period. The vigorous, upright shrub produces large, flattened flower corymbs (elderflower clusters) with abundant small white flowers in early summer, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer. John is particularly valued in mixed elderberry plantings where it improves Adams yields through cross-pollination; the two varieties are the most common pairing in eastern American elderberry plantings. In zone 9 both elderberry flowers and berries are produced abundantly in favorable moist conditions. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: John Rick American Persimmon (Large Sweet Indiana Persimmon Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun, ideally with a male American persimmon seedling or another pollinator cultivar nearby to ensure reliable fruit set; drought-tolerant once established. John Rick is a long-cultivated named American persimmon selection out of the Midwest, valued among heirloom fruit-tree collectors and permaculture growers for its large, richly flavored fruit and dependable productivity once a pollinator is present. The fruit ripens in fall and, as with all American persimmons, needs a hard frost or full ripening on the tree to shed its astringency, after which the deep orange flesh turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich with notes of caramel and dried fruit. It is commonly grafted onto native persimmon rootstock and grown alongside other named cultivars in mixed persimmon plantings to guarantee cross-pollination and a heavier crop. A good choice for zone 5–9 growers assembling a diverse American persimmon collection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: John's Elderberry (Large-Fruited Canadian Elderberry Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; pair with a second, genetically distinct elderberry cultivar within cross-pollinating range for a full crop, since John's does not set well on its own. John's is one of the oldest named Canadian elderberry selections, long grown as a classic pollinator and companion cultivar for Adams in commercial and home elderberry plantings — the two cultivars were historically recommended together as a standard cross-pollinating pair for decades before more recent university releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood became available. The tall, vigorous shrub produces large, flat-topped flower clusters in early summer, valued for elderflower tea, cordial, and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer used for jams, syrups, wine, and traditional elderberry preparations. Its long track record and reliable vigor make it a solid, time-tested choice for a home elderberry planting, especially paired with Adams for cross-pollination, zone 3–8. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Joi Choi Pak Choi (Vigorous Upright Bok Choy)
description: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; Joi Choi is the most widely recommended pak choi (bok choy) cultivar for American home gardens — an All-America Selections award winner producing an upright, well-formed head with crisp, white, thick, succulent stems and dark-green, smooth leaf blades in a clean, classic pak choi form. Joi Choi's excellence comes from the combination of very clean, upright growth habit (the stems don't spread outward messily like some varieties), exceptional bolt resistance for an early-maturing type (30–50 days), and excellent flavor — the stems are tender and mildly sweet, the leaves are tender with mild cabbage flavor, and the whole plant can be used in stir-fries, soups, and raw preparations. In zone 9, Joi Choi is grown September through April as a cool-season crop; in the heat of summer it bolts quickly. The bolt resistance is Joi Choi's key advantage — allowing it to be planted in late February and early March (early spring zone 9) before the heat arrives, with harvest extending a week or two longer than standard varieties. Harvest the whole head at soil level when it reaches full size (10–12 inches tall) or harvest outer leaves continuously for a prolonged cut-and-come-again harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Jojoba (Goatnut, Deer Nut, Pignut)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy desert soil; jojoba is a remarkable desert shrub native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California, and Mexico whose seeds produce a liquid wax (not technically an oil) used extensively in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and lubricants as a spermaceti whale-oil substitute. The seeds are edible but contain a waxy compound (simmondsin) that causes nausea if eaten in quantity; indigenous peoples roasted or ground them into a paste. The shrub is among the most drought-tolerant woody plants in North America, surviving on 10 inches of rainfall annually, and provides important cover and food for desert wildlife. Excellent for erosion control and dryland restoration in zone 8–11. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Jolant Leek (Mid-Season European Leek)
description: Jolant is a European mid-season leek bred to bridge the gap between quick summer types and the toughest overwintering varieties, giving a long stretch of harvest from late summer well into early winter. Plants form thick, well-blanched white shanks with a moderate flavor and hold in the ground without bolting or splitting for weeks once mature, which spreads out the harvest window instead of forcing a single cutting date. Moderate winter hardiness lets a fall-sown planting carry through the first hard frosts in milder climates, though it is not as cold-tolerant as dedicated winter leek strains. Hill soil around the base as the shanks thicken to maximize the tender white portion. Matures in 85–110 days from transplant.

name: Jolico Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Jolico is an Austrian selection prized for its unusually large, pear-shaped, bright red fruit, up to twice the size of the wild species, produced on a plant that still tolerates the dappled light of a woodland edge better than most fruiting shrubs. The tart-sweet, cranberry-like fruit ripens in late summer and is traditionally cooked into jams, syrups, and sauces, though fully ripe fruit can also be eaten fresh. A part-shade planting slows ripening slightly but the shrub remains healthy and productive, making Jolico a good fit for the partly shaded fringe of an edible landscape. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Jonafree Apple (Scab-Resistant Jonathan-Type PRI Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Jonafree was bred by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative program to capture the classic tangy-sweet flavor of the old Jonathan apple in a tree resistant to apple scab, powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust, sparing home growers the heavy fungicide schedule that susceptible heirloom apples like Jonathan itself require. The medium-sized, bright red fruit has crisp, juicy flesh with the familiar sprightly Jonathan flavor, good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. Because it combines classic flavor with broad disease resistance, Jonafree is a good choice for gardeners who love old-fashioned apple flavor but want a low-spray, low-maintenance tree. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jonagold Apple (Jonathan × Golden Delicious, Best-Flavor Commercial Apple)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; because Jonagold is triploid, plant it with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties — it needs two compatible pollinators and cannot pollinate other trees itself; thin fruit clusters in late spring for maximum size; Jonagold ripens mid-to-late season (October) producing very large fruit with outstanding sweet-tart flavor. Jonagold is widely considered one of the best-tasting apple varieties in the world — a cross of Jonathan and Golden Delicious developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1943 and released in 1968. The variety combines the aromatic, spicy sweet-tart character of Jonathan with the sweetness and crispness of Golden Delicious, resulting in very large, yellow-orange to red-blushed apples with exceptional, complex flavor that many apple connoisseurs consider among the finest eating apples available. Jonagold has become particularly important in European apple markets — it is one of the most widely planted apple varieties in Belgium and the Netherlands, and is highly regarded throughout European specialty apple production — in part because its substantial size and richly complex flavor profile make it stand out at specialty and farmers' market venues. In the United States, Jonagold is less prominent commercially than varieties with better storability (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) but widely recognized among apple enthusiasts as a flavor benchmark. An important practical consideration: Jonagold is a triploid variety (three sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two) — its pollen is sterile, meaning it cannot pollinate other apple trees and requires two compatible diploid varieties for its own fruit production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jonamac Apple (McIntosh x Jonathan Cross, Early Northeastern Apple)
