description: Jonamac was bred at Cornell University's Geneva research station from a cross of McIntosh and Jonathan and released in 1972, aiming to combine McIntosh's soft, aromatic, sweet-tart flesh with some of Jonathan's brighter tartness and slightly improved keeping quality. The medium-sized, deep red fruit ripens roughly a week to ten days ahead of standard McIntosh, giving Northeastern growers an earlier crop from a very familiar flavor profile. Like McIntosh, the flesh softens fairly quickly after harvest, so it is best used fresh or processed within a few weeks rather than stored long term. The tree is winter-hardy and productive across the cold-winter apple-growing regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that both parent varieties favor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jonathan Apple (Classic 1826 American Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Jonathan was discovered as a chance seedling in Woodstock, New York in 1826 and went on to become one of the most widely planted apple varieties in American history, remaining a dominant commercial and home-orchard apple for over a century. The medium-sized fruit ripens to a bright red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, aromatic white flesh balancing bright tartness with real sweetness, excellent for fresh eating, sauce, and pie alike. Jonathan is also historically significant as a parent variety, having been crossed with Golden Delicious to produce the modern Jonagold. Harvest when fruit colors fully and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist, and note that Jonathan is somewhat more prone to bitter pit and early softening in storage than some modern keeper varieties, so plan to use it within a few months of harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Jonkheer van Tets Red Currant
description: Jonkheer van Tets is a classic early-ripening red currant valued for its long, uniform strigs of bright red, tart-sweet berries that ripen ahead of most other red currant cultivars, extending the harvest window when grown alongside later types like Rovada or Red Lake. It sets fruit heavily and reliably, but the early bloom period makes it vulnerable to late spring frosts, so a site with some air drainage or light overhead protection during flowering helps secure the crop. Grow in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and prune out the oldest third of the wood each dormant season on an open, vase-shaped framework to maintain fruiting vigor. It performs best in regions with cool summers and struggles in hot, humid climates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Josephine de Malines Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site. Raised by Major Esperen at Malines, Belgium in 1830 and named for his wife, it bears heavy crops of small, conical, greenish-yellow fruit with a dark red flush, and smooth, melting, white flesh with a sweet, fine, aromatic flavor that earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. A late winter pear usable from November into December or January, it shows good resistance to pear scab and keeps well into the new year, though its lack of vigor and delicate skin reward a sheltered planting site and careful handling. Harvest in mid-to-late fall while still firm, store cool for several weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Josephine Raspberry
description: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Josephine is a Cornell University fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry selected for exceptional fruit quality — widely considered to have the finest flavor of any fall-bearing raspberry released by the Cornell small fruit breeding program, with very large, conical, bright red berries and a sweet, complex, intensely raspberry-flavored aroma and taste that rivals the best summer-bearing varieties. The primocane-fruiting habit provides a late-season crop in August–October from first-year canes, avoiding the May–June crowded harvest season when many other soft fruits are also ripe. The berries are soft and best for fresh eating or immediate processing — Josephine is not a commercial shipping variety, but for home garden fresh eating it represents the highest quality among fall-bearing raspberries. The vigorous, productive canes grow 4–6 feet tall and the plants are reliably productive once established, returning annually from the root system. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Josta Jostaberry (Original 1977 Black Currant-Gooseberry Hybrid)
description: Josta is the original jostaberry, released in 1977 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer after crossing black currant and gooseberry lines and doubling the chromosome count to stabilize a fertile hybrid; its name blends the German words for black currant (Johannisbeere) and gooseberry (Stachelbeere). Vigorous, thornless canes carry glossy, purple-black berries larger than a black currant but smaller than a gooseberry, with a mild, sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating, jam, and juice, and the plant shows strong natural resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf-spot diseases that trouble many gooseberries. Josta is more heat-tolerant than most true black currants, though it still fruits best with reliably moist soil and some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers. Prune out the oldest third of canes each dormant season to keep the naturally spreading, arching bush productive and open to light and air. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Jostaberry (Blackcurrant-Gooseberry Hybrid)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep roots cool, since this hybrid inherits its cool-climate preference from both currant and gooseberry parents. Jostaberry is a thornless hybrid bred in Germany from a cross of blackcurrant and gooseberry, combining the vigor and disease resistance of both parents into a productive, easy-care shrub that bears large, smooth, dark purple-black berries with a flavor described as a cross between the two — richer and less tart than gooseberry, milder and less musky than blackcurrant. The thornless canes make picking far easier than with true gooseberries, and the shrub is notably resistant to the powdery mildew and rust diseases that trouble many currants and gooseberries. It performs best in regions with cold winters and mild summers, generally struggling with the heat, humidity, and mild winters of the Deep South, so it suits cooler parts of the transition zone and the upper South far better than true Gulf Coast gardens. Prune out the oldest third of canes each winter to encourage strong new fruiting wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Jostine Jostaberry
description: Jostine is a thornless, disease-resistant jostaberry cultivar prized for its compact growth habit, making it well suited to small gardens or container culture. It produces medium-to-large, deep violet berries with a complex, tart-forward flavor that ripens slightly later than the original Josta cultivar, extending the harvest into midsummer. Fruit holds well on the bush after ripening, giving growers a longer picking window for fresh eating, jams, and pies. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Joy Seedless Grape (Soft Blue Table Grape)
description: Joy is a blue-skinned seedless table grape released by the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, one of four cultivars introduced together with Faith, Gratitude, and Hope for home and local-market growers. It ripens in the first to second week of August and is prized for exceptionally fruity flavor and very thin, tender skin with no noticeable astringency. Like its siblings, Joy is non-slipskin with good resistance to cracking and has shown solid winter hardiness and vine health in university trials. Its very soft texture makes Joy best suited to eating fresh off the vine rather than storage or shipping, so it fits dooryard plantings better than commercial production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jubilee Blueberry (Early-Midseason North Carolina Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Jubilee was bred in North Carolina and ripens early to midseason, producing large, firm, sweet, light-blue berries on a vigorous, productive bush well suited to warmer Southern growing conditions where lower-chill varieties are needed. The good heat tolerance for a highbush type makes it a solid choice for extending highbush blueberry production into milder climates than many Northern-bred varieties can handle. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jubilee Sweet Corn
description: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks; Jubilee is an SU type that benefits from block planting for good pollination and is best planted at least 400 feet from supersweet (SH2) types to prevent cross-pollination that reduces sweetness. Jubilee is a midseason (82–87 days) yellow sweet corn that has been widely grown in American gardens and markets since the 1950s and maintains a reputation for reliable production, excellent flavor, and adaptability to a wide range of climates from the Upper Midwest to the Gulf Coast; the large ears (8–9 inches) carry 14–16 rows of bright golden-yellow kernels with classic, rich sweet corn flavor — the balance of sweetness and traditional corn taste that makes fresh summer sweet corn a culinary experience distinct from the excessive sweetness of modern hybrid types. Jubilee has better disease resistance than many older varieties (including some tolerance to Stewart's wilt and common rust) and holds slightly longer in the field than older SU types. Outstanding in Gulf Coast gardens for both the spring crop (April–May planting) and fall crop (late July–August planting). Matures in 82–87 days from seed.

name: Jubilee Watermelon
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Jubilee is a Florida-developed heirloom watermelon introduced in 1963 by the Florida Agricultural Experiment Station, producing oblong, striped fruits weighing 25–40 pounds with bright red, crisp, sweet flesh and gray-green skin with dark stripes — one of the classic large Southern watermelons grown at commercial scale for roadside markets. The long, oblong shape distinguishes it from round varieties; the sweet, firm, seedless-type flesh holds up well for transport and has excellent flavor. Resistant to fusarium wilt, which historically decimated Southern watermelon crops. A traditional choice for gardeners in the Gulf South who want a truly large, impressive watermelon with Southern heritage adapted to regional heat and humidity. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Judge Amphlett Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Named for the Assizes court judge Richard Amphlett, one of several traditional Three Counties perry pears commemorating individuals, it is a medium sharp type with medium acidity and low tannin. Its bletted fruit is notoriously unpredictable, developing into either a rich, sweet, delicious pear or, if left too long, an antiseptic, unpleasant one, making it one of the trickier traditional perry pears to work with despite its good potential quality. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, monitor bletting closely, and mill and press for perry as soon as the fruit reaches its best condition. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Judión de La Granja Bean
description: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight through the season. Grown for centuries in the volcanic soils around La Granja de San Ildefonso in Segovia, Spain, it produces some of the largest bean seeds in cultivation — broad, flat, and ivory-white — traditionally simmered slowly into the region's celebrated judión stew. Like other runner beans it flowers and sets pods best where summer nights stay relatively cool, dropping blossoms in prolonged heat. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the outsized beans for storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Jujube
description: Jujube is exceptionally drought-tolerant and thrives in hot, dry climates where other fruits struggle; it prefers well-drained, even sandy soils and performs poorly with excessive moisture. Most cultivars are self-fertile, though a second variety increases yields. Li and Lang are the most widely planted in North America; Li produces large, round, date-like fruit while Lang is more elongated. Fruit is eaten fresh when crisp and apple-flavored or dried to a sweet, wrinkled date; harvest when skin turns from yellow-green to mahogany-red. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Julie Mango (Compact Caribbean Dooryard Mango)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Julie is a small, dwarf-habit mango of Caribbean origin, especially beloved in Jamaican and Trinidadian dooryard gardens for its compact size, precocious bearing, and intensely sweet, fiberless, deep orange flesh with a distinctive rich flavor that fans consider among the best of any mango. Because it stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars, Julie is one of the better choices for zone 9 gardeners growing mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter rather than risking an in-ground planting. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect trees from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Juliet Tomato (Grape Tomato)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Juliet is a 1999 All-America Selections winner widely regarded as the standard-setter for the grape tomato category. The oval, grape-sized (1.5–2 inch) fruits grow in large trusses of 30–40 tomatoes and have a particularly rich, complex flavor — a balance of sweetness and acidity often described as more 'adult' and interesting than the purely sweet cherry types. Juliet is notable for its outstanding crack resistance (thin-skinned cherry tomatoes frequently split in rain; Juliet resists this), its prolific production, and its reliable fruit set under warm conditions. The thick-walled, meaty fruits have an unusually long shelf life and hold on the vine for weeks without cracking, making them practical for casual harvesting. Disease resistance is strong. In zone 9, Juliet is especially valuable because it continues setting fruit at temperatures that shut down many indeterminate varieties; the heavy trusses of beautiful red grape tomatoes become a summer landmark in the garden. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Jumbo Hardy Kiwi (Large-Fruited Kiwiberry)
description: Jumbo is a female hardy kiwi selection bred for noticeably larger, smooth-skinned berries than most arguta cultivars, with individual fruit approaching an ounce and a sweet, citrus-tinged flavor eaten whole, skin and all, with no peeling needed. Vines are vigorous twining climbers that require a permanent, heavily built trellis or arbor and benefit from annual winter pruning to control size and renew fruiting wood. Plants begin bearing in their third or fourth year and are exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below zero once established. Harvest in early to mid fall by taste-testing a few berries, since the green skin shows little visible color change at ripeness. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jumbo Muscadine (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Jumbo is one of the largest-berried muscadine grape cultivars available — producing extra-large, 1–1.5 inch diameter, dark black to purplish-black berries that are significantly larger than standard muscadines and create a dramatic visual impression both on the vine and at harvest. The large size makes Jumbo berries outstanding for fresh eating, where the large, sweet, musky flesh provides a more substantial bite than smaller cultivars. The flavor is rich, sweet, and distinctly muscadine with the characteristic musky, fruity flavor that distinguishes muscadine grapes from bunch grapes. Jumbo ripens in mid to late season (September in zone 9) and is self-fertile — producing good crops without a pollinator. The vine is vigorous, productive, and well-adapted to Gulf South conditions including clay soil, heat, humidity, and the fungal disease pressure that affects European grapes in the Southeast. Muscadines are the most naturally disease-resistant grapes for the Gulf South — they have evolved in the region and require far fewer pesticide applications than bunch grapes in the humid Southeast. Jumbo is perfect for fresh eating, home juice, wine, and preserves. Train on a 5–6 foot high wire trellis and prune hard in winter, leaving only 2–4 lateral spurs per cane. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jumbo Romano Pole Bean (Italian Flat-Pod Romano Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; install a 6-foot support structure before planting. Harvest flat pods when 5–8 inches long — the wide, flat pods stay tender longer than round-pod snap beans. Romano-type flat-pod beans are the classic Italian snap bean — the distinctive wide, flat pods (0.5 to 0.75 inch wide, versus the round cross-section of standard snap beans) with a meaty, thick-walled character that gives them a very different cooking quality from American round-pod types. Romano beans are the traditional choice for Italian green bean preparations: braised with olive oil, garlic, and tomato (fagiolini al pomodoro), slow-cooked until completely tender and silky, or simply boiled and dressed with good olive oil and salt. The thick walls mean romano beans absorb oil and flavors particularly well during cooking, and the flat shape increases surface area contact with the cooking medium. Jumbo Romano is a large-podded version of the classic Italian romano pole type — pods reach 7–9 inches at full size while remaining tender — and one of the most widely available and productive romano-type beans in North America. The flavor when cooked is richer and fuller than round-pod snap beans — a deeper, more substantial bean flavor that makes romano beans a favorite of Italian cooks and everyone who discovers them. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Junami Apple (Swiss-Bred Crisp Aromatic Apple)
description: Junami was bred by the Swiss agricultural research institute Agroscope and selected for its crisp, juicy bite and aromatic, floral sweetness. The fruit has a distinctive bright red-orange blush over a pale yellow background and ripens in the mid-to-late fall. It handles cold storage well without losing its crunch and the tree crops at a moderate, manageable rate. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for the best size and to encourage annual rather than biennial bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: June Gold Peach (Early Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; June Gold is an early-season freestone peach cultivar that ripens in late May to early June in zone 9 — one of the earliest-ripening freestone peach selections available for Gulf Coast production. The medium-large, round fruit has yellow flesh with red coloring and a rich, full peach flavor with good sweetness. The early ripening season avoids the peak summer disease pressure (brown rot, oriental fruit moth) that damages later-ripening cultivars, and it extends the Gulf South peach season earlier. June Gold requires approximately 650 chill hours — reliably accumulated in zone 9a and most zone 9 climates during typical winters, and less frequently limiting than the 800–1000 hours required by standard northern peach cultivars like Elberta and Redhaven. The tree is vigorous and productive with proper annual pruning to an open-vase form. In zone 9, peaches are planted in January–February for the spring growing season, and the orchard management cycle includes dormant oil and copper sprays at bud swell, thinning to 6–8 inches between fruits after natural drop, and a preventive brown rot spray program as harvest approaches. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: June Plum (Ambarella, Hog Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; june plum (ambarella) is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree of the Pacific Islands and Southeast Asia, producing clusters of oval green-to-yellow fruits 2–3 inches long that are consumed at all stages of ripeness. Unripe fruits are prized throughout Asia and the Caribbean for their crisp, tart flesh, used in fresh salads, pickled condiments, and green mango-style preparations; ripe fruits are sweet-tart with a fibrous spiny seed and are eaten fresh or juiced. The tree is extremely fast-growing (10–15 feet in the first 2 years), the leaves are edible as salad greens when young, and the tree propagates easily from large hardwood cuttings that fruit in 2–3 years. It thrives in zone 9b–12 as a reliable, low-maintenance, highly productive tropical fruit tree and is one of the best 'beginner' tropical fruits for warm-climate gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jupiter Bell Pepper (Large Blocky Red-Ripening Sweet Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Jupiter is one of the largest and most productive open-pollinated bell pepper varieties — producing extra-large, four-lobed, thick-walled fruits that are larger and more blocky than standard California Wonder types. The fruits are harvested green for fresh use or allowed to ripen fully to a rich, sweet red (occasionally yellow to orange). Jupiter is prized for its combination of very large fruit size (often 4–5 inches long, 4 inches wide), thick walls that hold up well in cooking, and outstanding sweet flavor that improves markedly when allowed to ripen fully red. As an open-pollinated, non-hybrid variety, Jupiter seeds can be saved from the best fruits for replanting — an important advantage for seed-saving gardeners who want consistent results without purchasing new seed annually. Jupiter's disease tolerance (particularly to tobacco mosaic virus) represents an improvement over older open-pollinated varieties. In zone 9, bell peppers thrive in spring (late February through June) and even more productively in fall (August transplants through November) — the fall crop in zone 9 consistently produces the largest, most flavorful fruits as temperatures moderate from the summer peak. Zone 9 gardeners have two full productive seasons for bell peppers, providing fresh peppers for much of the year. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Jupiter Grape (Seedless Muscat-Flavored Table Grape)
description: Jupiter was released by the University of Arkansas breeding program and produces large, seedless, blue-black berries with a distinctive spicy muscat flavor on vigorous, productive vines. It ripens in mid-season and holds well on the vine, making it a favorite among home growers wanting a flavorful seedless alternative to standard labrusca types. Prune to a bilateral cordon system and thin crowded clusters early to encourage larger berry size. Vines benefit from a full season of heat to fully develop their characteristic sweetness and aroma. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Jupiter Rice (Louisiana Medium-Grain Rice)
description: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated through the growing season whether in a flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Jupiter is a widely grown Louisiana medium-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter, valued by commercial growers and home gardeners alike for high, dependable yields and grain that cooks up moist, tender, and slightly clingy in the style favored for jambalaya, risotto-style dishes, and sushi rice rather than the fluffy separate grains of long-grain types. The sturdy, semi-dwarf plants stand up well to wind and rain compared to older tall varieties, making it a practical choice for a home rice patch. Harvest when seed heads droop and the grain has turned golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling or storing. Matures in 115–135 days from seed.

name: Just Right Turnip (AAS-Winning Mild Non-Pithy Hybrid Turnip)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip ever introduced and remains notable for staying mild, sweet, and non-pithy even when its pure-white, flattened roots are allowed to grow to a large 5-6 inches across — most turnip varieties turn woody, hollow, or sharply pungent well before reaching that size, forcing gardeners to harvest small. This gives more flexibility in harvest timing and a bigger yield per root without sacrificing quality. The tender greens are edible as well and hold up well in the kitchen. In zone 9, grow it strictly as a fall and winter crop, since heat above the mid-70s causes turnip roots to become pithy and bitter regardless of variety; sow from late summer through early fall for a harvest running into winter. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Just Sweet Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Snacking Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Just Sweet is an AAS-winning snack-type sweet pepper bred for a compact, well-branched plant that produces heavy clusters of small, elongated, bell-flavored fruits that ripen quickly from green to bright red and are sweet and crunchy enough to eat straight off the plant. The small, tidy plant size makes it an excellent choice for large containers and patio growing, not just garden beds. Pick fruit continuously through the season, either green or fully ripe red, to keep the plant producing; the earlier and more often fruit is harvested, the more the plant sets. Feed lightly through the season, since heavy nitrogen encourages foliage over fruit. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Jwala Pepper (Indian Finger Hot Chili)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jwala ('flame' in Hindi) is one of the most widely grown chilies in India, prized as the classic Indian finger hot pepper for everyday cooking. Slender, curved, slightly wrinkled green pods grow 3–4 inches long in dense clusters and carry a fruity, sharp heat (roughly 25,000–50,000 Scoville units) well above a jalapeño. Pods are usually picked and used green — deep-fried whole for the popular mirchi bhaji snack, sliced into curries, or pickled — though left to ripen they turn red and can be dried. Prolific, compact plants perform well in containers as well as garden beds and keep producing through summer heat if picked regularly. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Jyunpaku Okinawan Pure White Bitter Melon
description: A Japanese Okinawan heirloom-type bitter melon grown for its smooth, creamy-white, blunt-ended fruit, typically 8-10 inches long, that carries noticeably milder bitterness than the common green Indian and Chinese types. As the fruit fully ripens it develops a sweet, bright-red seed coating that is considered the best-flavored of any bitter melon type when eaten out of hand. Okinawan bitter melon (goya) has long been associated with the traditional Okinawan diet and its reputation for longevity, and the pale, gently bitter fruit is well suited to raw preparations like thin-sliced salads as well as classic stir-fries such as goya champuru. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis and consistently moist, fertile soil for strong summer production in Gulf Coast heat. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: K7 Coffee
description: K7 was selected in Kenya from French Mission coffee stock tracing back to Bourbon, making it one of the traditional tall Kenyan cultivars alongside SL28 and SL34. It shows useful partial resistance to coffee berry disease and some leaf rust races that its more famous SL siblings lack, though yields run lower than newer compact hybrids. The tree grows tall and vigorous with a spreading habit, producing the bright, wine-toned acidity and floral aromatics characteristic of high-grown Kenyan arabica. Best suited to well-drained volcanic soils at elevation, with the same partial shade and rich organic feeding regime that suits other highland Kenyan varieties. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ka Pow Chilean Guava (Large-Fruited Selection)
description: Ka Pow is a vigorous Chilean guava selection popularized for bearing noticeably larger fruit than typical seedling plants, and for cropping while still young. Fragrant soft pink flowers appear over a long season and are followed by aromatic red berries with a flavor often compared to wild strawberries crossed with lily of the valley. It grows into a denser, more upright shrub than some older Chilean guava selections and tolerates light frost down to around 20°F once established, though a sheltered site is still recommended in marginal climates. Grow in lime-free, well-drained soil and use as a hedge, container specimen, or mixed-border shrub in mild coastal gardens. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kabocha Squash
description: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in deeply amended, compost-rich soil and thin to the strongest vine after the first true leaves appear. Kabocha is a Japanese winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species; its flattened, dark-green fruits have dense, dry, sweet orange flesh superior to many other squash types. Harvest when the skin is very hard, the stem corky and dry, and a small section of rind scratched with a fingernail shows no damage. Cure at room temperature for 10–14 days before storing; properly cured kabocha keeps four to six months in a cool, dry room. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Kabocha Squash (Japanese Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; kabocha is a Japanese-style winter squash with a dumpling-shaped, dark green (or orange in some types) skin and incredibly dense, dry, sweet bright-orange flesh that has a texture more like sweet potato or chestnut than watery summer squash. The flavor is distinctive — nutty, sweet, and complex — and kabocha is prized in Japanese, Korean, and Thai cuisines for tempura, braised dishes, soups, and desserts. It stores 3–5 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail puncture and the stem has dried and corked over. The flavor actually improves after 2–3 weeks of curing at room temperature as starches convert to sugars. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Kabosu (Japanese Sour Citrus)
description: Kabosu is a tangy, aromatic Japanese citrus grown chiefly in Oita Prefecture, closely related to but larger and more mellow than sudachi. Fruit is harvested green and unripe from late summer into autumn, when its juice is squeezed over grilled fish, sashimi, hot pot dishes, and noodles for a bright, minty-citrus tartness. The tree is moderately cold-hardy for citrus, and mature specimens can shrug off brief drops to around 20F, though young trees need frost protection. Grow it like other cool-adapted mandarin relatives, in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and regular feeding during the growing season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kabuli Chickpea (Large Cream-Colored Garbanzo Bean)
description: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep into well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, since chickpeas rot quickly in cold, wet ground and dislike heavy clay. Kabuli chickpeas produce the large, plump, beige-cream seeds most familiar to home cooks as garbanzo beans or hummus chickpeas, borne one or two per small, inflated pod on bushy, ferny-leaved plants that rarely need staking. The foliage and pods are covered in fine glandular hairs that exude a sticky, mildly acidic secretion, so wear long sleeves and gloves when working among mature plants to avoid skin irritation. Pick pods green and shell them for fresh eating like a shelling pea, or let the crop dry down fully in the field and harvest whole plants once most pods have turned tan and papery, then thresh, winnow, and store the dried seed in a sealed container. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Kadota Fig (Italian Honey Fig, Dottato Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Kadota is one of the oldest known fig cultivars, documented in Italian records since at least the 16th century and known as Dottato or Dottato Bianco in Italy, where it has been cultivated around Naples and in Calabria for over 400 years. The American name 'Kadota' is an Anglicized corruption of 'Dottato.' The fruits are small to medium, rounded, pale green to yellowish-white at maturity (not turning brown like most figs) with amber to violet interior flesh that is seedless (no viable seeds) and extraordinarily sweet — among the highest sugar content of any fig. The nearly seed-free flesh is ideal for fig preserves, dried figs, and fresh eating. Kadota is self-fertile, drought-tolerant, and among the most productive figs per tree. It is the most widely used commercial fig in California's Central Valley canning and drying industry. The pale, golden-green skin requires learning when it is ripe — pick when it bends at the stem and yields gently to pressure, the skin turns a barely perceptible yellowish hue, and the neck softens. Excellent for the Gulf Coast Zone 9 garden. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kaester Mulberry (California Black Mulberry Heirloom)
description: Kaester is a California-origin black mulberry heirloom selected for heavy, reliable cropping of deep purple-to-black fruit roughly an inch long, with a flavor balance that leans more toward sweet than the sharply tart edge found in many black mulberry seedlings. Trees grow into substantial specimens over time and bear over a fairly compact ripening window in midsummer rather than trickling fruit out over many weeks. Because ripe fruit drops and stains hard surfaces heavily, site the tree away from patios and driveways or plan to net and harvest promptly once color develops. Regular deep watering during fruit set improves both fruit size and juice content in hot, dry Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Kaffir Lime (Makrut Lime)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; makrut lime is grown primarily for its distinctive double-lobed leaves, which are the indispensable aromatic herb of Thai and Cambodian cooking, used in curries, soups, and stir-fries to impart an intensely floral, citrusy perfume that no other herb can substitute. The bumpy, knobbly green fruit has very little juice but extremely aromatic zest used in marinades and Thai curry pastes. Leaves can be harvested whenever new growth appears; young leaves have the strongest flavor. In containers (the most practical approach north of zone 9), use a quality potting mix, fertilize monthly with citrus fertilizer spring through fall, and overwinter indoors in a bright window above 50°F. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kagraner Sommer Lettuce
description: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces. Developed near Kagran outside Vienna, this Austrian heirloom butterhead is prized for exceptional heat tolerance and slow bolting, unusual traits among classic butterheads. It remains a benchmark variety for gardeners needing a butterhead that survives real summer heat. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Kaimana Lychee
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kaimana is a lychee cultivar developed at the University of Hawaii for its exceptional combination of large fruit size, outstanding flavor, and reliable production in subtropical conditions. The name means 'diamond' in Hawaiian and reflects the premium quality of the fruit. The large, dark red fruits have a very small ('chicken tongue') seed — a highly valued characteristic that means more of the edible white aril is present relative to seed volume. The translucent, white, juicy flesh has a complex, floral, honey-lychee fragrance and flavor. Kaimana ripens in June–July in zone 9, providing fresh lychee in a season when few other tropical fruits are available. As a relatively cold-tolerant lychee, Kaimana has gained popularity in zone 9 gardens from Florida's Gulf Coast to California's coastal areas, where the mild winters provide flower-inducing chilling without the destructive hard freezes that damage lychee trees. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Kaiteri Feijoa
description: Kaiteri takes its name from New Zealand's Golden Bay coastal region, an area associated with several modern feijoa breeding selections, and produces medium to large fruit with good eating quality and the classic sweet, aromatic, pineapple-guava-mint flavor of top dessert cultivars. The bush grows vigorously with a somewhat spreading habit, filling out into a substantial evergreen screen or informal hedge within a few years if left unpruned, or it can be kept tighter with an annual light shaping cut. Spring bloom is heavy and showy, with the typical white-petaled, crimson-stamened feijoa flowers whose sweet flesh is itself edible. Full sun, well-drained slightly acidic soil, and steady summer moisture bring out the best fruit size and flavor, and mature plants shrug off the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers with little complaint. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kajang Carambola (Kajang Starfruit)
description: Kajang was among the sweet carambola selections evaluated at the University of Florida's Tropical Research and Education Center and is regarded by many home growers as one of the sweetest, juiciest carambola cultivars available, with large, golden-yellow, crisp-fleshed fruit. The tree tends to stay more compact than standard carambola, which suits smaller yards and container culture. Like all carambola, it is frost-tender and needs a sheltered site in zone 9a, with protection during any hard freeze. Harvest fruit once it has fully colored to deep gold for the best sweetness, since carambola does not continue ripening much after picking. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kajari Melon
description: A striking Indian heirloom melon striped in green, orange, and cream with sweet, pale flesh. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay warm. Train vines with room to sprawl and mulch to keep fruit clean and warm. The dramatic rind color develops as the fruit ripens, and mature melons detach easily from the stem. Cut back on water near harvest to concentrate the sugars in the flesh. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Kakadu Plum (Gubinge, Billygoat Plum)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Kakadu plum requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal drought — water only in establishment first year, then rely on rainfall in tropical monsoonal climate. Terminalia ferdinandiana (Kakadu plum, gubinge, or billygoat plum) is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree native to the open woodland and savanna regions of the Northern Territory and northwestern Western Australia — and the producer of what is recognized as the single richest natural source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in the world. The small (1/2–1 inch), round, pale-green to olive-colored fruits contain an extraordinary 1,000–5,300 mg of ascorbic acid per 100g fresh weight — 20 to 80 times more vitamin C than oranges and roughly 100 times more than most commercial fruits. Aboriginal Australians across the Top End and Kimberley have eaten Kakadu plums as a traditional food and medicine for at least 65,000 years. The fruits are also remarkably high in ellagic acid and other polyphenol antioxidants. In contemporary Australian native food and cosmetics industries, Kakadu plum extract has become one of the most sought-after botanical ingredients for antioxidant skincare products, functional foods, and vitamin C supplements — and Kakadu plum jam, sauce, and fruit purée are premium native food products sold across Australia and internationally. The tree adapts well to tropical and subtropical low-humidity conditions with good drainage. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kakai Pumpkin (Styrian Hulless-Seed Pumpkin, Oil Seed Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set. This Austrian landrace from Styria produces medium orange pumpkins prized not for their stringy flesh but for their thin-hulled, dark-green naked seeds, which are roasted or pressed for the region's famous dark green pumpkinseed oil. Harvest when rinds harden and vines die back, then cure fruit briefly before scooping and drying seeds for eating or oil pressing. It has become a staple specialty crop among home seed-savers and oil producers in North America since the late 20th century. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Kakariki Feijoa
description: Kakariki takes its name from the Maori word for the small native green parakeet, a nod to the deep green skin the fruit keeps even at full ripeness rather than showing the pale or bronzed blush some other feijoa cultivars develop. Fruit is medium-sized and oblong with sweet, fine-grained, aromatic flesh that ripens in the mid-to-late season, and the shrub itself is compact and well-branched compared to older, ranker-growing feijoa cultivars, making it easier to keep tidy in a smaller garden or as a clipped hedge. It flowers heavily in spring with the typical showy white-and-crimson feijoa blossoms, whose sweet fleshy petals are edible and popular with foraging gardeners. Give it full sun and good drainage, and expect the toughness and low-maintenance character typical of the species once past its first year or two of establishment. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kakri (Indian Snake Melon, Khira Kakri)
description: Kakri is a slender, pale green to lightly mottled melon grown throughout North India and Pakistan not for sweetness but as a fresh vegetable, eaten raw in salads, juiced, or cooked in curries much like cucumber. Give the sprawling vine a trellis or let it run along the ground, keeping soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit set since irregular watering toughens the skin and turns the flesh bitter. Harvest fruit young and slender, typically 8 to 12 inches long, well before the interior seeds mature and the rind coarsens, and pick every few days to keep the vine setting new fruit rather than ripening old ones to full size. It thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that stress many true cucumbers, making it a reliable substitute crop for gardeners in punishing summer heat. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Kalamata Olive
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost. Native to and named for the region around Kalamata, Greece, this classic dual-purpose olive cultivar produces large, almond-shaped, deep purple-black fruit famous worldwide when brine-cured for eating, along with good-quality oil, making it one of the most recognizable named table olive varieties globally. Like other olives it thrives on neglect once established, tolerating poor, rocky, alkaline soil and long dry summers far better than regular watering and rich soil, and needs a genuinely Mediterranean-type climate with wet winters and hot, dry summers to fruit and ripen well. Raw olives straight from the tree are intensely bitter and inedible; fruit must be cured through brining, salt-curing, or lye processing before eating, a process requiring several weeks depending on the method used. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kale Microgreens
description: This Siberian kale germinates quickly, so sow it densely on a moist tray and blackout for just a couple of days. Once the stems stretch, uncover and provide bright light to build sturdy, deep-green shoots. Keep the surface evenly moist and give gentle airflow to discourage mold. Cut the tender, mild greens at the cotyledon or first-true-leaf stage after eight to ten days. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Kalettes (Flower Sprouts)
description: Kalettes are an open-pollinated cross between Brussels sprouts and kale, first bred by Tozer Seeds in the UK and released commercially in the early 2010s; the result is a tall stalk lined with loose, frilly, purple-green rosettes instead of the tight round buttons of a standard Brussels sprout. Grow exactly as you would Brussels sprouts: stake the tall stalks against wind, keep soil evenly moist, and top the growing point once the lowest rosettes reach marble size to concentrate energy in the remaining buds. Harvest rosettes from the bottom of the stalk upward as they firm up; flavor becomes noticeably sweeter and less bitter after a hard frost. A single stalk can be harvested over several weeks as rosettes mature sequentially up its length. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Kalibos Cabbage (Polish Heirloom Conical Red)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for transplanting out in late summer, since Kalibos develops its best color and flavor with a longer, cooler fall growing season. Kalibos is a Central/Eastern European heirloom cabbage, likely developed from the older Vysoky (Vysocke) type, distinguished by small, dense, cone-shaped heads of deep purple-red leaves that form a striking pointed rosette rather than the round or flattened heads of typical cabbage. The tender, crisp, juicy leaves are deep red to violet clear through to the core, making Kalibos as prized for its color in raw slaws and pickles as for its mild, sweet flavor. It stores for a moderate period after harvest and remains something of a novelty in North American gardens despite long popularity in Eastern Europe. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Kalluvally Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, training the vine onto a sturdy support. Kalluvally is another traditional Western Ghats landrace from Kerala, India, distinguished by unusually long spikes and heavier-than-average berry clusters that make it a favorite among smallholders seeking better yields without switching to formally bred hybrids. It performs particularly well on the lateritic soils common across its home region and is traditionally intercropped with areca palm or coconut, which double as its living climbing support. Provide consistent moisture, warmth above 60°F, and dappled shade, and expect steady production once the vine matures. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kalmegh (Green Chiretta, King of Bitters)
description: Direct sow or transplant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harvest aerial parts when plants begin to flower for maximum andrographolide content. Andrographis paniculata (kalmegh, green chiretta, or king of bitters) is one of the most important and widely researched medicinal plants in Asian traditional medicine systems — a tropical Asian annual herb producing intensely bitter leaves (among the bitterest of any plant) containing the bioactive diterpene compound andrographolide. Clinical research has documented significant efficacy for andrographolide in reducing the severity and duration of upper respiratory infections (common cold and flu) — it is one of the better-supported herbal remedies for viral respiratory illness. The plant is used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine (as kalmegh), traditional Chinese medicine, and Southeast Asian folk medicine for fever, liver conditions, and infections. Despite its extreme bitterness, the plant is consumed as an herbal tea, tincture, and tablet supplement throughout South and Southeast Asia. The plant grows as an upright, branching annual with lance-shaped leaves and small, white, pink-speckled flowers; it is well-adapted to hot, humid conditions and grows vigorously through Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Kalonji (Nigella, Black Seed)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly where they are to grow; kalonji has fine, thread-like foliage similar to its ornamental cousin love-in-a-mist and dislikes transplanting. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; the plant bolts quickly in summer heat, so time sowing for a cool-season harvest. Harvest the swollen seed pods when they begin to turn tan and paper-like, cutting whole stems into bags before the pods split and release the seeds. The intensely aromatic black seeds are used in South Asian cooking on naan breads and in spice blends, and have a long history of medicinal use; they are not to be confused with black cumin (Bunium persicum). Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Kamchatka Bilberry (Rossberry)
description: Kamchatka bilberry is a mat-forming, creeping deciduous subshrub from the cool forests of northeastern Asia, Japan, and Kamchatka, spreading by underground rhizomes to just a few inches tall. Its bright red, translucent berries are famous among foragers in its native range for an intense, pineapple-like fragrance and flavor unlike any other Vaccinium, traditionally eaten fresh or preserved in Japanese and Russian Far East folk cuisine. Extremely cold-hardy and adapted to short, cool growing seasons, it performs best as a shaded woodland-floor groundcover in consistently moist, peaty, acidic soil and struggles in hot summer climates. Once established it needs little care beyond an annual topdressing of leaf mold or pine needle mulch to maintain soil acidity. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Kamo Eggplant (Kamo Nasu, Kyoto Heirloom Round Eggplant)
description: Kamo Nasu is a traditional heirloom from the Kamo district of Kyoto, grown for its large, softball-sized round fruit with thick, dense flesh that stays creamy and never turns spongy even at full size. It is the classic eggplant used for dengaku, where thick slices are grilled or pan-fried and topped with sweet miso glaze, since the dense flesh holds together better than thinner-skinned slicing types. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture, as the large fruit can stress the plant if it dries out between waterings. Choose Kamo when you want an eggplant suited to grilling and roasting whole slices rather than the elongated Asian types more common in home gardens. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Kampong Mauve Sugar Apple
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in a warm, frost-free site; Kampong Mauve is a striking sugar apple selection with a distinctive dusty pink-to-mauve blush over its bumpy, segmented skin, standing out visually from the typical pale green sugar apple, while the sweet, creamy, custard-textured white flesh inside is classic sugar apple in flavor and texture. It is more cold-sensitive than cherimoya or atemoya and needs consistently warm, essentially tropical conditions to thrive, making it best suited to south Florida, south Texas, and similarly frost-free zones, or container culture that can be moved under cover in cooler areas. Hand-pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers in the evening or early morning when they are receptive, significantly improves fruit set in home garden settings where the tree's natural beetle pollinators may be scarce. Harvest when the segments on the fruit begin to separate slightly and the fruit softens, and eat promptly since ripe sugar apples do not store well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kanayamidori Tea
description: Kanayamidori is a registered Japanese green tea cultivar, selected from Yabukita lineage in Shizuoka and noted for an unusually rich, milky, creamy character in the finished sencha, tied to its elevated concentration of methylated catechins compared with the standard Yabukita cultivar. It grows as a dense, small-leaved China-type shrub and is processed the same way as other Japanese sencha cultivars, steamed shortly after picking to halt oxidation and preserve its bright green color. Give it the standard acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade tea camellias prefer, with protection from harsh afternoon sun in hot climates. It is grown as a specialty companion cultivar alongside Yabukita in several Japanese tea-producing regions. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kandahar Pomegranate
description: Kandahar is a historically significant Afghan pomegranate landrace named for the province where it has long been grown, and it is recognized by the international Slow Food Ark of Taste catalog for its exceptionally large fruit, which can weigh well over a pound apiece. Skin is deep red and the soft-seeded arils are notably sweet with balancing acidity, a flavor profile that made Afghan pomegranates historically prized as trade goods across Central and South Asia. It is a distinct regional selection from the unrelated 'Afghanistan' cultivar already grown elsewhere, having its own separate lineage tied specifically to Kandahar province orchards. Give it full sun and excellent drainage, and expect a long-lived, productive tree once past its multi-year establishment period. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kandil Sinap Apple (Ottoman-Era Turkish Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the young tree and watering deeply through establishment. Kandil Sinap is an old variety from the Black Sea region of Turkey and Crimea, long grown in Ottoman-era orchards and prized for its distinctive elongated, almost conical shape unlike most round apples. The thin yellow skin, often washed with a light red blush on the sun-exposed side, covers dense, crisp white flesh with a mild, honeyed, aromatic flavor and notably low acid for an heirloom. It is a strong keeper that stores well into winter in cool conditions, ripens late in the season, and is grown today mostly by heirloom orchardists and collectors for its history, form, and storage qualities rather than heavy production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kandy Korn Sweet Corn (EH-Type Traditional-Flavor Yellow Corn)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows; side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Kandy Korn EH is a yellow EH (Everlasting Heritage) or se-type sweet corn — a variety from the Illinois Foundation Seeds stable that occupies an important niche as a late-season yellow corn with a distinctive flavor profile that many traditional corn enthusiasts prefer to modern hybrid types. The 'EH' designation refers to 'Everlasting Heritage,' a genetic trait that increases sugar content and slows the sugar-to-starch conversion rate compared to standard su types but maintains more of the complex, traditional 'field corn' flavor notes that characterize classic American sweet corn — a richer, deeper, more complex corn flavor than the clean sweetness of modern se or sh2 types. Kandy Korn is particularly popular with older gardeners and those who grew up eating sweet corn from small farms and roadside stands, where the flavor of the corn itself (rather than just sweetness) was the primary quality attribute. The medium-large ears (7.5–8 inches, 14–16 rows) carry well-filled rows of golden-yellow, tender kernels with extended holding quality compared to standard su. At 85–92 days, Kandy Korn extends the sweet corn season to the later summer window when earlier varieties have finished. Matures in 85–92 days from seed.

name: Kanna (Kougoed)
description: Sceletium tortuosum is a mat-forming, jointed-stemmed succulent of the fig-marigold family, native to the dry Karoo and Namaqualand regions of South Africa, where the fermented leaf and stem material (traditionally called kougoed, or chew-stuff) has long been chewed, smoked, or brewed as a mood-lifting and appetite-suppressing traditional remedy. Small, star-shaped, pale yellow to white flowers open in sunny weather over succulent, fleshy, sometimes purple-tinged leaves. Grow it exactly as you would a hardy mesemb or ice plant: bone-dry, mineral soil, full sun, and minimal winter water, since rot rather than cold is the main threat in cultivation. Established plants tolerate long dry spells and light frost once mature. Container culture with a cactus-style mix is the most reliable approach outside its native climate. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Kanota Oat (Heirloom California Red Spring Oat)
description: Kanota is an open-pollinated red spring oat released in California in 1928 that has stayed in circulation among small grain growers and homesteaders ever since, valued for maturing only a few days behind the earliest oat varieties available. Broadcast or drill seed into firm, cool spring soil and rake it in shallowly for even emergence; the crop grows into a tall, leafy stand that heads out and ripens well before summer heat and humidity peak, which helps it dodge some of the rust and mildew pressure that hits later-maturing oats. Because Kanota is more susceptible than modern varieties to crown rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, and barley yellow dwarf virus, it is best suited to smaller-scale, closely watched plantings rather than large monoculture fields. Harvest when the panicles are fully dry and golden, then thresh and store the hulled grain for rolling, milling, or replanting. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Kanpyo Gourd (Japanese Dried Gourd Strip Bottle Gourd)
description: Kanpyo is the Japanese bottle gourd cultivar grown specifically to be peeled into long ribbons and sun-dried into the sweet-savory strips used in kanpyomaki sushi rolls and simmered dishes, distinct from gourds grown for eating fresh or for hard dried shells. Vines are vigorous and need a sturdy trellis or wide open ground, with large white flowers opening at dusk for moth pollination, so hand-pollinating with a small brush in the evening improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Harvest the pale green fruit while still immature and tender, before the seeds and rind harden, then peel it in one continuous spiral ribbon with a vegetable peeler or specialized gourd slicer and hang the strips to dry in a warm, airy spot out of direct sun. Because the plant is a heavy, sprawling grower that benefits from consistent warmth and moisture through fruit development, it performs best where summers are long and hot. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Kansas Muskmelon
description: Kansas Muskmelon is a Great Plains heirloom kept alive through regional seed savers and now offered by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, valued for holding up to humid weather and inconsistent rainfall better than many other old melon varieties. The oval, sutured, moderately netted fruits average about four pounds and ripen almost all the way out to the rind for little waste, with fine-textured, richly flavored flesh that has kept the variety in demand among heirloom growers. It also shows good resistance to sap beetles, a common pest that ruins fruit of other melon varieties late in the season. As with other open-pollinated melons, isolate plantings from other Cucumis melo varieties if you intend to save true seed. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Kanthari Chili Pepper (Kerala Bird's Eye Chili)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this compact, bushy frutescens landrace from Kerala, India, is prized in South Indian cooking for its small, marble-round, glossy red pods. Heat runs high (roughly 50,000-100,000 Scoville units) but dissipates faster than many other hot peppers, leaving a bright, citrusy flavor that's central to Kerala fish curries, chutneys, and pickles. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node through a long harvest season. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Kanza Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Mid-Season Pecan, Excellent for the Midsouth)
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually. Pair with a Type II pollinator within 150 feet. Kanza Pecan was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service (ARS) Pecan Breeding Program in 1984 as part of the Northern Pecan Testing Program — a cooperative breeding effort between the USDA and several state agricultural experiment stations to develop superior pecan varieties adapted to a wide range of conditions from the Gulf Coast northward through Oklahoma, Kansas, and Missouri. Kanza is notable for its excellent resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the most economically damaging disease of pecans in the humid Gulf South region, where high summer humidity and rainfall create ideal conditions for scab development on susceptible varieties. Standard commercial varieties like Desirable and Stuart have significant scab susceptibility and require intensive fungicide programs in humid regions; Kanza's improved scab resistance significantly reduces the fungicide inputs required for commercial-quality nut production. The nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and relatively thin shells, and they mature in mid-season — earlier than some standard varieties — allowing harvest before fall rains that can cause nut deterioration. For Gulf South pecan growers (backyard and small-scale), Kanza's disease resistance reduces management burden substantially compared to growing standard susceptible varieties. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Kanzi Apple (Gala x Braeburn Crisp Sweet-Tart Apple)
description: Kanzi was bred in Belgium from a cross of Gala and Braeburn, combining Gala's crisp sweetness with a firmer texture and a brighter, more tart edge from its Braeburn parent. Fruit ripens in mid-to-late season, well after Gala, and colors to a deep red blush over a yellow-green background. It stores considerably longer than Gala thanks to its dense flesh, and the tree crops reliably once established. Thin clusters to one fruit each in early summer for larger, better-colored apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kapoor Basil
description: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kapoor is a compact Indian sweet basil cultivar selected for high essential oil content and strong clove-camphor aroma with a distinctive spicy note absent from European Genovese varieties. The small-to-medium dark green leaves have a more robust, pungent flavor than Genovese basil and are used extensively in Indian cooking — in chutneys, raitas, and as a fresh herb added to dals and curries. Kapoor's compact habit and heat tolerance make it particularly suitable for year-round indoor container growing and for outdoor herb gardens in subtropical zone 9 where it often survives mild winters as a short-lived perennial. The slightly camphoraceous aroma also has medicinal uses in Ayurvedic tradition, closely related to but distinct from true holy basil (tulsi). Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Kapoor Tulsi
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kapoor Tulsi is a named variety of holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) selected for compact habit and exceptionally high eugenol content — the volatile oil component that gives tulsi its characteristic warm, clove-like fragrance is highest in the Kapoor selection, making it the preferred variety for medicinal use in Ayurvedic preparations where eugenol concentration matters. In Hindu tradition, Tulsi (also called Vrinda or the Holy Basil) is the most sacred plant in the home, representing Lakshmi and kept in a tulsi pot on the veranda of traditional Indian homes where it is tended daily. Beyond its religious significance, Kapoor Tulsi is used medicinally for digestive support, as an adaptogen for stress, in tea blends for respiratory health, and as an aromatic in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking where the clove-camphor notes are distinctly different from sweet basil. The compact Kapoor selection fits easily in container or herb garden cultivation and grows robustly in the warm conditions of the Gulf South. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Kaprao Holy Basil
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kaprao (กะเพรา in Thai, pronounced 'kra-pao') is the specific holy basil type used in Thai cooking — its clove-and-pepper-forward flavor with a faint anise note and spicy heat is the defining herb of pad kra pao (stir-fried basil), Thailand's most popular everyday dish. While all holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) has the characteristic clove-spice aroma from eugenol, the Kaprao type selected for Thai cooking has a particularly pungent, peppery quality and narrow, slightly serrated leaves that are used exclusively in their cooked form — unlike Italian sweet basil or Vietnamese basil, Kaprao is wilted into hot wok dishes where the heat activates and transforms the volatile oils. The fresh leaves cannot be substituted by Italian sweet basil in pad kra pao, as the clove-pepper flavor profile is essential to the dish. In zone 9 Kaprao thrives in the hot, humid summers that are close to its native tropical Thai climate, performing far better than sweet basil in the season's peak heat. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Kara Mandarin (California Heirloom Satsuma-King Hybrid)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot, since this cultivar can be shy-bearing in cooler coastal fog belts and benefits from reflected heat. Keep soil evenly moist and feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season to support its dense, spreading canopy. Kara fruit ripens late, often improving in flavor if left on the tree into late winter, developing a rich, aromatic sweetness with a soft, slightly fragile peel. It is a favorite among California backyard growers for its dessert-quality flavor, though it ships poorly and is rarely found in stores. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Karanda (Carandas Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; karanda is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree from India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia — widely used throughout South Asia as an impenetrable security hedge and as a productive fruit shrub. The small, oval fruits (1/2 to 1 inch) ripen from green through white to pink and finally red-purple or black, with the white stage being particularly popular for pickling (used extensively in Indian pickles, chutneys, and preserves) while the ripe red-black fruits are eaten fresh or used for jams. The fruits have a mild, slightly tart flavor when ripe. Extremely drought and heat tolerant — one of the tougher fruiting shrubs for hot, dry gardens in zones 8–11. More cold-tolerant than natal plum (Carissa macrocarpa), making it useful in the warmer parts of zone 8 where natal plum would be damaged. Exudes a milky latex sap when cut — wear gloves when pruning. Forms an excellent thorny security hedge. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Karikachi Edamame (Karikachi No. 3 Soybean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in full sun, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria for improved nitrogen fixation. Karikachi No. 3 is a compact, determinate Japanese heirloom bred on the island of Hokkaido for cool, short growing seasons, setting three large, sweet-flavored beans per pod on reliably productive, disease-resistant plants. Harvest whole pods once they are plump and bright green but before the shells begin to toughen or yellow. Blanch briefly in salted water before shelling and serving as a snack or in salads and stir-fries. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Karimunda Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing the vine to climb a sturdy support post or living standard. Karimunda is the traditional, most widely grown black pepper cultivar across Kerala, India, favored by smallholders for its dependable moderate yields, broad soil adaptability, and relative tolerance of foot rot compared to many other selections. Keep the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged, maintain warmth above 60°F with high ambient humidity, and mulch to conserve moisture between waterings. This adaptable, hardy standard is also commonly used as rootstock for grafting less vigorous but higher-quality pepper cultivars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Karla Rose Nectarine (Low-Chill White-Fleshed Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and thin developing fruit to a few inches apart to encourage larger, sweeter fruit. Karla Rose is prized for white, low-acid, semi-freestone flesh with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor that stands apart from typical yellow-fleshed nectarines. It is self-fertile and blooms attractively with showy pink flowers in early spring. Because it sets a heavy crop, an annual dormant-season prune helps maintain an open canopy and manageable size for home orchards. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Karma Bell Pepper (Mosaic Virus-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Karma is a hybrid bell pepper bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, letting it keep its foliage healthier through the aphid pressure that builds over a long, warm Gulf South growing season. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant longer. The compact, well-branched plant provides good leaf cover that helps shield developing fruit from sunscald during peak summer heat. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness, and keep picking to encourage continued fruit set. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Karmijn de Sonnaville Apple (Dutch Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)
description: Karmijn de Sonnaville was raised in the Netherlands in 1949 by Piet de Sonnaville from a cross of Jonathan and Belle de Boskoop, producing a russeted, red-striped apple prized among connoisseurs for its intensely rich, wine-like, sweet-tart flavor. The tree is somewhat vigorous and can bear biennially without careful thinning, and its Boskoop parentage leaves it more prone to scab than many modern cultivars. Because of its demanding growth habits it rewards attentive home orchardists more than commercial growers seeking easy, uniform crops. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the fruit develops its characteristic red blush over a green-gold background. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Karp's Sweet Quince (Eat-Fresh Cold-Hardy Quince)
description: Karp's Sweet is a cold-hardy quince selection notable for fruit mild enough to eat fresh out of hand, unlike most quince cultivars that require cooking to be palatable. Trees are compact, self-fertile, and produce fragrant, pear-shaped golden fruit in fall after a single showy spring bloom. Its hardiness makes it a good choice for northern growers where standard Smyrna-type quinces struggle with winter dieback. Site in full sun with good air circulation to reduce fire blight and leaf spot pressure, and thin fruit if branches appear overloaded. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kary Starfruit
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during the growing season — starfruit requires full sun and adequate water for consistent fruit production; Kary Starfruit is a superior sweet cultivar of Carambola (Averrhoa carambola), a tropical fruit tree originally from Southeast Asia that produces the distinctive 5-ribbed, translucent yellow-orange fruits that create the characteristic star cross-section when sliced. Unlike commercial starfruit varieties selected for high acidity and sour flavor, Kary was selected specifically for sweet eating quality — lower oxalic acid content, higher sugar content — producing fruits that are genuinely enjoyable eaten fresh without the puckering tartness that characterizes inferior varieties. The crisp, juicy flesh with a mild, sweet, tropical flavor combined with the visually stunning star-shaped cross section makes Kary starfruit both an eating and a culinary presentation fruit of first quality. In the warmest, most frost-protected zone 9 microclimates, starfruit can be grown successfully as a landscape tree with both ornamental value (pretty pink flower clusters, handsome tropical foliage) and substantial fresh-fruit production — providing a tropical fruit experience that very few other fruit trees can offer in zone 9. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kasandra Hybrid Persimmon (Self-Fertile Cold-Hardy Louisiana-Bred Hybrid)
description: Kasandra is a hybrid persimmon bred by Louisiana fruit breeder David Lavergne, produced by crossing the Asian cultivar Great Wall with an F2 seedling of the American-Asian hybrid Rosseyanka, then backcrossing toward American persimmon to combine cold hardiness with large, high-quality fruit. The tree closely resembles an Asian persimmon in appearance, with large, glossy leaves, and produces fruit nearly 3 inches wide that many growers rate among the best-tasting persimmons they have tried, with very high sugar content. Kasandra is self-fertile and reliably productive on its own, and it is notably cold-hardy for a kaki-type hybrid, tolerating temperatures to -10°F or below once dormant, which makes it a strong option for Gulf South and mid-South growers wanting Asian-persimmon fruit quality without the cold sensitivity of pure Diospyros kaki cultivars. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Kashi Anmol Chilli (Indian Dwarf Green Chile Pepper)
description: Developed by ICAR's Indian Institute of Vegetable Research through recurrent selection from a Sri Lankan introduction, Kashi Anmol is a determinate, dwarf chile with dark, pigmented nodes and slender green pods held upright in attractive pendant clusters. Its compact stature and short internodes make it productive in a small footprint, and it begins yielding earlier than many taller Indian chile types. Grow it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and pick pods green for the mild-to-moderate heat favored in everyday Indian cooking, or allow some to ripen red for drying. Because plants stay short and self-supporting, Kashi Anmol is a good choice for raised beds and container vegetable gardens. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Kashi Dhawal Ash Gourd
description: Kashi Dhawal is an ash gourd cultivar released by ICAR's Indian Institute of Vegetable Research in Varanasi, selected from a local landrace for its oblong fruit, thick white flesh, and unusually high flesh-to-rind ratio. Vines are long and vigorous, reaching well over 20 feet, and fruits mature in about 120 days into large, greenish-white, waxy-coated gourds commonly weighing 11-12 pounds. Its dense, high-recovery flesh makes it the preferred type for making petha, the popular Indian candied ash gourd sweet, though it cooks and stores like any other winter melon in curries and soups. Grow it exactly as you would standard winter melon, in full sun on deeply worked, fertile, moisture-retentive soil with a heavy-duty trellis or generous ground space to support the long vines and heavy fruit. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Katahdin Potato (1932 USDA Classic White Storage Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Katahdin is a main-season variety producing large, round to oval, smooth, buff-white-skinned, white-fleshed tubers of excellent quality. Katahdin was developed by the USDA Potato Research Laboratory in Presque Isle, Maine and officially released in 1932, named for the highest peak in Maine; for the next several decades it was the most widely grown potato in the northeastern and mid-Atlantic United States, valued for its consistent productivity, reliable storage quality, and disease resistance (including moderate resistance to late blight). The large, smooth, nearly round tubers have thin, buff to light tan skin and white flesh with a slightly waxy texture when young — excellent for boiling and potato salad — that transitions toward semi-floury when fully mature, making them good for baking and mashing as well; a genuinely all-purpose variety in the tradition of the great white American storage potatoes. Flavor is clean, mild, and characteristic of the best white potato types; stores 4–6 months under proper conditions (35–40°F, high humidity). Still grown commercially in the Northeast and available from heritage potato suppliers. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Katarina Cabbage (AAS-Winning Early Compact Mini Cabbage)
description: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Katarina is an AAS-winning cabbage bred for very early maturity and a small, tidy head about 4 inches across, forming a solid, sweet, light-green head faster than nearly any other garden cabbage — a useful trait for squeezing a crop into a short spring or fall window, or for a large container where a full-size storage cabbage would be impractical. Its small stature and rapid maturity also make it a good choice for succession planting through a cool season. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and dense, since even fast-maturing types can split if left too long once mature. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Katinka Parsley (Extra Curled)
description: Katinka is a Dutch-bred curled parsley selected for very tightly ruffled, mid-green leaves on short, sturdy stems that resist flopping and stay clean off the soil surface.
