It germinates and establishes somewhat more reliably than older curly strains, giving a quicker, more even bed for market growers and home gardeners alike. The compact habit and dense curl make it a strong choice for garnish production and container growing on a patio or windowsill. Regular cutting of outer leaves keeps plants productive for months before they bolt. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Katuk (Sweet Leaf, Star Gooseberry Shrub)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; harvest tender shoot tips and young leaves regularly for continuous production. Sauropus androgynus (katuk or sweet leaf) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub — native from India through mainland Southeast Asia to Indonesia — that produces one of the most nutritious and palatable leafy vegetables in the tropical world. The shoots and young leaves (the standard harvested part) contain exceptionally high levels of protein (6–8% by fresh weight — remarkably high for a vegetable), vitamins A and C, iron, and calcium; the fresh leaves taste mild, slightly sweet, and pea-like — quite different from the stronger, bitter flavors of many tropical leafy greens. In Malaysia (where it is called 'cekur manis'), Vietnam ('rau ngot'), and Indonesia, katuk is a standard, everyday vegetable used in stir-fries, soups, and as a cooked green. It is also extensively used in Singapore and among Southeast Asian diaspora communities worldwide. CAUTION: Very large quantities of raw juice (as consumed in some weight-loss protocols in Taiwan in the 1990s) caused severe pulmonary toxicity; katuk must be cooked before eating and should not be consumed raw in large amounts or as a supplement. Properly cooked as a vegetable in normal food quantities, it is safe and highly beneficial. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Katy Apple (Swedish Moderate-Low-Chill Red Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Katy, bred in Sweden and also sold as Katja, produces attractive, bright red, crisp apples with a pleasant, slightly tart, sweet flavor, ripening in mid to late summer, well ahead of most main-season apples. Its moderate chill requirement makes it one of the apple cultivars sometimes recommended for the milder end of Southern apple-growing country, though it needs somewhat more winter chill than the very lowest-chill Florida-bred selections. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to keep the canopy open for good air circulation. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Katy Apricot (Low-Chill Gulf South and Texas Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bred by Zaiger Genetics in California and selected specifically for regions with mild winters, Katy is one of the more dependable apricots for Texas and the Gulf South, where most northern apricot cultivars fail to set fruit due to insufficient winter chilling. It blooms quite early, so late cold snaps remain the main risk to the crop even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Fruit is medium, orange-blushed, and sweet-tart, ripening in late spring to early summer, and the tree is self-fruitful, needing no separate pollinator. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Katydid Tomato (Green-Striped Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Katydid bears medium fruit striped green over an amber-green background even when fully ripe, a striking novelty color pattern with tangy, well-balanced flavor typical of green-fleshed tomato types, on a compact plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its manageable size and eye-catching fruit suit raised beds and containers. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone won't signal ripeness in green-fleshed types. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Kaunching Quince (Rare Asian-Origin Heirloom Quince)
description: Kaunching is an uncommon, lesser-known quince selection maintained mainly in fruit-collector and germplasm circles rather than mainstream nursery trade, grown for its dense, hard, golden-yellow fruit and typical strong quince perfume once ripe. As with all quince, the fruit is astringent and inedible raw and must be cooked, at which point the flesh turns a warm rose to amber color and develops a rich, honeyed flavor suited to jelly, paste, and baking. The tree bears on an open, spreading framework and benefits from being trained to a vase shape for airflow, since crowded interior growth increases the risk of fire blight in humid regions. Because it is scarce in commerce, gardeners usually source it as scionwood from fruit-collector exchanges or specialty germplasm repositories rather than as finished nursery stock. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kava (Kava-Kava)
description: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kava is a Pacific Island understory plant that is sterile and propagated only from cuttings, and it needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun and wind. This large, heart-leaved shrub has been cultivated for centuries across Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia, where its thick roots are pounded and mixed with water to produce a traditional ceremonial and social beverage valued for its mild relaxant effect. It requires consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions and rich, well-drained soil in filtered light, essentially replicating the sheltered forest-garden conditions of its native Pacific islands, and struggles badly with cold, dry air or direct hot sun. Roots are typically harvested for use after three to five years of growth; further north than zone 10, it must be grown as a protected container plant moved indoors well before any cold weather. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kazake Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy Central Asian Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Kazake, originating from the cold-winter regions of Central Asia, is grown chiefly for its exceptional cold hardiness among fruiting pomegranate cultivars, tolerating winter temperatures that would damage or kill less hardy selections, which gives extra insurance against rare hard freezes in zone 8b-9a gardens. Fruit is medium-sized with dark red skin and tart-sweet, deep-red arils, ripening in fall for fresh eating and juicing. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and long-lived; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kañiwa (Cañihua)
description: Broadcast or sow seed shallowly in firm, well-drained soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 8–12 inches apart; kañiwa is an Andean pseudograin closely related to both quinoa and the already-familiar huauzontle, distinguished by tiny, dark reddish-brown seeds borne on a shorter, bushier plant. Unlike quinoa, its seed coat carries little to no bitter saponin, so it needs little or no rinsing before cooking or roasting, and the plant tends to shatter and self-sow readily once mature. Harvest when seed heads have dried and seed threshes free easily, then dry further indoors before storing whole grain in a sealed container. Roasted kañiwa (kañiwako) has a nutty flavor and is traditionally ground into a toasted flour called cañihuaco, used as a high-protein addition to porridges and baked goods. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Keecrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Mid-Late University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Keecrisp, a University of Florida cross between the earlier Sweetcrisp and Indigocrisp releases, inherits the notably crisp, firm texture that distinguishes the Crisp lineage from the softer flesh typical of most blueberries, giving the fruit excellent fresh-eating snap and good holding quality on the bush. It ripens mid-to-late season and carries a somewhat higher chill requirement than the earliest, lowest-chill UF releases, performing best in the cooler pockets of zone 8b-9a rather than the very mildest coastal winters. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Keeled Corn Salad
description: Sow seeds thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in late summer or early autumn into fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 4-6 inches apart. Germination is most reliable when soil temperatures have dropped below 65°F; cool nights after late-August sowings are ideal. Harvest entire rosettes by cutting at the base once they reach a few inches across, or pick outer leaves continuously throughout winter. Keeled corn salad has a mild, slightly sweet flavor well suited to winter salads alongside mâche and other cold-hardy greens. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Kei Apple (Umkokola, Wild Apricot)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Kei Apple tolerates poor, sandy, alkaline, and mildly saline soils and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. Dovyalis caffra is a large thorny shrub or small tree native to the coastal thornveld and thicket of South Africa's Eastern Cape province, named for the Kei River region where it grows wild. The formidable 2-inch spines make it one of the most impenetrable barrier plants available for zone 9 — a mature hedge is impassable to deer, livestock, and intruders. The small, round fruits (3/4 to 1 inch diameter) ripen in summer (July–September in zone 9) to a bright golden-yellow or amber color with paper-thin skin and juicy, very acidic pulp that is rarely eaten fresh but makes extraordinary jams, jellies, chutney, and preserves with a distinctive bright, tart flavor combining notes of apricot, plum, and citrus. The glossy, willow-like evergreen foliage is ornamentally attractive year-round. Kei Apple can be grown as a specimen tree (2–4 trunks) or planted 4–6 feet apart and clipped into a dense, absolutely impenetrable hedge. Drought tolerance, extreme heat resistance, and salt spray tolerance make it valuable for coastal Gulf South gardens. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Keiko Honeyberry (Late-Blooming Japanese Haskap)
description: Keiko belongs to the Japanese emphyllocalyx type of haskap and is among the latest-ripening honeyberries available, holding its rounded, heart-shaped fruit into late June or early July when most other cultivars have already finished. The delayed bloom is an asset in areas with unpredictable late frosts, since flowers open once pollinating insects are already active, which tends to improve fruit set. Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained soil and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and expect a spreading, twiggy bush that needs little pruning beyond removing dead wood in the first several years. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Keitt Mango (Late-Season Florida Mango)
description: Keitt was selected in the Homestead, Florida mango district and is notable for ripening very late in the season, often into September, well after most other major cultivars have finished. The large fruit stays green even at full ripeness, with little or no red blush, and its flesh is sweet, juicy, and largely fiberless, making it a favorite for fresh eating. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its late timing makes it a valuable addition alongside earlier cultivars like Haden or Tommy Atkins to extend a home harvest. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and protection from frost, since mango wood is easily damaged by cold. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kellogg's Breakfast Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a rich, well-drained site in full sun after frost danger has passed, burying the stem to the lowest leaves. Kellogg's Breakfast is an American heirloom orange beefsteak tomato that originated with William Kellogg of Michigan, introduced to the larger seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange, and has since become one of the most celebrated orange heirlooms for its extraordinary flavor — sweet, mild, and low-acid with a rich, fruity depth that makes it ideal fresh. Fruits weigh 1–2 pounds and have very meaty, almost seedless flesh that is deep orange throughout; they ripen relatively slowly but the wait is well worth it. Stake or cage plants firmly and thin to two or three main leaders for the largest fruits. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Kelsae Onion (Giant Exhibition Onion)
description: Kelsae is a British giant exhibition onion bred to produce enormous, mild-flavored globes that regularly place among the largest onions grown at horticultural shows. Start seed early under lights, prick out into individual pots, and transplant into deeply dug, heavily enriched soil with generous spacing so each bulb has room to reach show-winning size. Feed and water generously through the growing season, since exhibition size depends on sustained, uninterrupted growth rather than stress-hardening. Because the huge, thin-skinned bulbs are milder and less pungent than standard storage onions, they are best used soon after harvest rather than held for long-term storage. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Kelsey Plum
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Kelsey cross-pollinates with Santa Rosa, Shiro, Satsuma, and most other Japanese plums. Kelsey is historically significant as one of the first Japanese plums introduced to North America, brought from Japan in 1870 by John Kelsey of Berkeley, California and widely distributed through the California nursery trade in the late 19th century, where it contributed to Luther Burbank's subsequent Japanese plum breeding work. The very large (3–5 oz), heart-shaped to irregular, somewhat flattened fruits have distinctive mottled green and yellow skin with a red blush on the sun-exposed cheek, ripening to golden-yellow with a sweet, mild, honeyed yellow flesh. Kelsey is a late-season variety (August–September) with lower chill requirements than many Japanese plums (approximately 300–400 hours), making it well-suited to Gulf Coast zone 8 and mild California gardens; the flesh firms up during ripening, giving the fruit good keeping quality and making it one of the better shipping and storage plums for home orchardists. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kemangi (Indonesian Lalapan Basil)
description: Kemangi is the everyday table basil of Indonesia, grown less as a cooked cooking herb and more as a fresh vegetable — whole sprigs are served raw alongside cabbage, cucumber, and sambal as part of a lalapan plate, or tucked into fried fish and grilled chicken preparations to cut the richness. Its aroma sits apart from Thai basil's clove-anise punch, being lighter and more herbaceous with a gentle lime-like edge, which is exactly what makes it pleasant to eat by the sprig rather than just as a background seasoning. The thin stems and smaller leaves bruise and wilt quickly once cut, so harvest close to serving time and handle it gently. Pinch flower buds regularly to keep the plant leafy and productive through the growing season, and expect it to bolt readily in long summer daylength like other basils. Matures in 50–70 days from transplant.

name: Ken Taylor Rosemary (Arching Australian Hedge Rosemary)
description: Ken Taylor is an Australian-bred rosemary selection valued for its dense, mounding-to-arching growth habit, intermediate between fully upright culinary types and fully prostrate groundcover forms. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil and avoid overhead irrigation once established, since wet feet in winter are the primary cause of failure in all rosemary types. The long, gracefully arching stems make it a popular choice for informal hedges, low screens, and bank or slope plantings where its spreading mass can be shown off, and it tolerates hard pruning well if a tighter hedge form is wanted. Flowering is prolific and nearly continuous in mild-winter climates, with deep violet-blue flowers that draw bees through the cooler months when few other nectar sources are available. Leaves are fully edible and aromatic, though gardeners seeking the most refined culinary flavor typically still reach for upright cultivars like Tuscan Blue; Ken Taylor shines primarily as a dual-purpose landscape and kitchen plant. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Ken's Red Hardy Kiwi
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor. Ken's Red is a female hardy kiwi cultivar originating in New Zealand, distinguished from most other Actinidia arguta selections by its attractive reddish-purple fruit skin and red-blushed flesh near the skin, in addition to the sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi. The smooth skin means the small, grape-sized fruit can be eaten whole without peeling, and its distinctive red coloring makes it a visually striking choice for a home fruit planting or farmers-market crop. Like all Actinidia arguta, it is dioecious and needs a separate male vine nearby to ensure good pollination and a full fruit set. A flavorful, ornamental option for gardeners who want something visually distinct from standard green-fleshed hardy kiwi, zone 4–8. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ken's Red Kiwi (Red-Skinned Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred hardy kiwiberry cultivar notable for its smooth skin blushed red-purple over green, distinguishing it visually from the plain green skin of most kiwiberry cultivars, with sweet green flesh and rich kiwi flavor inside. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is eaten whole without peeling, like other kiwiberries. As with all Actinidia arguta selections, plants need a few years to reach full bearing size but then crop heavily and reliably for many years once established. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis or pergola from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within range for consistent pollination and fruit set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kenaf
description: Direct-sow seed 1/2–1 in deep at 25–30 lb/acre for fiber production (narrower spacing promotes taller, less branched stems); kenaf is a warm-season annual related to okra that can reach 14 feet in a single season. For fiber, harvest at early flowering before stems become too woody — cut at ground level and ret the stalks in water for 10–20 days to separate the long bast fibers from the woody core. The core material (hurds) is useful as animal bedding or biomass fuel, while the bast fibers make durable rope, sacking, and paper. Young leaves and shoots are edible and nutritious — commonly cooked as a green in West African cuisine. Matures in 90–140 days from seed.

name: Kennebec Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil; Kennebec is an All-America Selections winner introduced by the USDA in 1948 from a cross of B127 x USDA 96-56, named for the Kennebec River in Maine. For many decades it was the most widely grown potato in the eastern United States, dominating both fresh market and potato chip production because of its outstanding adaptability, disease resistance, and excellent culinary quality. The large, oval tubers have thin, buff-white skin and firm, white flesh that performs equally well baked, fried, mashed, or roasted — a true all-purpose potato. Kennebec shows good resistance to late blight and is tolerant of common scab, making it more reliable than many varieties in the variable conditions of Gulf Coast winter gardens. It remains a benchmark variety offered by heritage seed companies for its proven performance and consistent quality. In zone 9, plant January–February and harvest May–June before summer heat arrives. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Kensington Pride Mango (Bowen Mango)
description: Australia's leading commercial and backyard mango, Kensington Pride (also called Bowen after its main growing region in Queensland) is valued for a distinctively perfumed, sweet-tangy flavor and vibrant yellow flesh unlike the milder Florida cultivars grown elsewhere in this collection. Fruit is medium to large with yellow-orange skin blushed pink, and unusually for a named cultivar it is polyembryonic, meaning seed-grown trees are typically true clones of the parent. Yields are notably erratic from year to year, and the fruit is softer and more prone to internal breakdown in transit than firmer-fleshed cultivars like Keitt, which is why it remains mostly a domestic Australian variety rather than a major export type. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kent Beauty Oregano (Ornamental Hop-Flowered Trailing Oregano)
description: Kent Beauty is an ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its unusual dangling flower clusters, in which large, papery, chartreuse-to-rose-pink bracts overlap like tiny hops and gradually flush pink as they age, held above rounded, blue-gray, aromatic leaves on trailing stems. Unlike culinary oregano, it is grown chiefly for this striking flower display rather than for the kitchen, and it performs best trailing from a raised bed, rock garden pocket, or hanging container where the pendant flower clusters can be seen and admired at eye level. Give it lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since it is prone to rot in humid, poorly drained conditions, and expect it to be shorter-lived than standard oregano, particularly where summer humidity is high. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Kent Coffee
description: Selected in the 1920s from a single disease-tolerant tree found on the L.C. Kent estate near Mysore in southern India, this Typica-type Arabica became one of the first commercial cultivars bred specifically for partial resistance to coffee leaf rust. Its tall, upright growth and moderate yields resemble other heirloom Typica-derived lines, and it later served as one of the two parents behind the widely grown Indian hybrid S795. Give it the same dappled shade, warm humid air, and rich, well-drained acidic soil that other Arabica types need, and expect the same three-to-four-year wait before the first harvest. Because rust pressure has intensified since Kent's introduction, home growers in humid climates should still watch closely for orange leaf spotting even on this historically resistant line. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kent Elderberry (Early-Ripening Nova Scotia American Elderberry Cultivar)
description: Kent was selected at the Kentville Research Station in Nova Scotia from Adams-derived American elderberry stock and is best known for ripening its clusters 10-14 days ahead of Adams or York, giving growers an earlier start to the harvest window. Flat-topped cymes of small white flowers appear in late spring, followed by dense, drooping clusters of small, very sweet black berries that hold their flavor well whether used fresh-cooked, dried, or pressed into juice and syrup. In Gulf Coast heat, site Kent where afternoon shade or consistent soil moisture is available, since it was bred for a cooler maritime climate and benefits from extra irrigation during peak summer; plant it alongside a second American elderberry cultivar to ensure good pollination. Manage root suckers each season to keep the planting contained, and prune out the oldest canes in late winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Kent Mango (Rich-Flavored Florida Commercial Mango)
description: Kent originated in Florida in the mid-twentieth century and is regarded as one of the best-flavored large commercial mango cultivars, with rich, sweet, nearly fiberless flesh that has made it a favorite among mango connoisseurs. The large fruit has greenish-yellow skin with a red-purple blush and ripens later in the season than Haden or Tommy Atkins, extending the summer harvest. The tree is vigorous and productive, tending toward alternate bearing in some years, and benefits from post-harvest pruning to control its size and encourage new fruiting wood. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and protect from frost, as mango wood is killed by even brief freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kentish Cob Filbert (Lambert's Filbert, Classic English Cobnut)
description: Kentish Cob, also sold as Lambert's Filbert, is one of the oldest and best-known English cobnut cultivars, long grown commercially in Kent for its elongated, sweet-flavored nuts with a fine flavor. The tree produces its dangling yellow male catkins in late winter well before leaf-out, an attractive early-season feature, but the female flowers need pollen from a genetically distinct hazel to set a full crop, so pairing with Cosford or another compatible cultivar significantly improves yield and nut size. Prune to an open, multi-stemmed bush form and remove root suckers regularly to keep the plant manageable. Harvest in early autumn once husks brown and nuts loosen readily from their cases. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Beefsteak Tomato (Golden-Orange Low-Acid Appalachian Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6-8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. Kentucky Beefsteak, an heirloom collected from the hills of eastern Kentucky, produces large, meaty, golden-orange fruit with notably low acidity and a mild, sweet flavor, distinguishing it from the more common red and pink Southern beefsteak heirlooms. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive through a long summer season in hot, humid Southern conditions. Its low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and eating fresh for gardeners sensitive to the tang of more acidic tomato varieties. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Blue Pole Bean (AAS-Winning Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Kentucky Blue is a 1991 All-America Selections-winning pole bean that crossed two of the most beloved pole bean varieties — Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake — to combine the best traits of both parents. Kentucky Wonder contributes vigor, heavy production, excellent traditional pole bean flavor, and the characteristic meaty pod texture; Blue Lake contributes its renowned stringless quality, mild sweetness, and the refined, crisp texture that made it the gold standard of snap bean flavor. The resulting Kentucky Blue produces long (6–8 inch), round, deep green, completely stringless pods with excellent flavor that tasters consistently rate among the best of all snap beans — more substantial than filet beans but more refined than older Kentucky Wonder strains. Very productive vines climbing 6–7 feet continue bearing throughout the summer and fall when harvested regularly. The combination of classic pole bean character, genuine stringlessness, superior flavor, and heavy production has made Kentucky Blue one of the most popular and recommended pole beans in American gardens since its introduction. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Kentucky Champion Pawpaw
description: Kentucky Champion was discovered on a vigorous seedling tree near Richmond, Kentucky, and stands out among pawpaw cultivars for consistently ripening among the earliest of the commercially available named selections, often coloring up in September well ahead of many other cultivars. Fruit runs large, close to half a pound, with melon-orange flesh carrying a tropical flavor with a faint raspberry note, and a comparatively small proportion of seed to pulp that leaves more usable fruit per pick. The skin is thicker and more resistant to bruising and dark spotting than many older pawpaw selections, which helps it hold up better to handling and short-term storage. As with other pawpaw cultivars, young trees need light shade to establish before tolerating full sun, and pawpaw's odd, fly- and beetle-pollinated maroon flowers may need hand pollination with a small brush in gardens lacking those insects. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Colonel Mint (Classic Julep Spearmint)
description: Plant divisions in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally in a container or a bed edged with a root barrier, since mint spreads aggressively by rhizome and can quickly overrun a garden bed. Kentucky Colonel is a spearmint selection with unusually large, crinkled, dark green leaves and a smooth, sweet, mild mint flavor without the sharper bite of peppermint, making it the traditional choice among Southern bartenders and home mixologists for mint juleps and other cocktails where a clean, refined mint character matters. It is also excellent for iced tea, fresh garnishes, and simple syrups. Keep soil consistently moist, since mint wilts quickly in dry conditions, and cut back hard in mid-summer if growth becomes leggy to encourage a fresh flush of tender new leaves. In light shade the leaves stay more tender and less prone to leaf spot than in full, hot Gulf South sun. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Colonel Spearmint
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — mint thrives with consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Kentucky Colonel is widely considered the finest spearmint cultivar for culinary use, producing very large, broad, slightly crinkled, bright green leaves with a smooth, intensely sweet, clean spearmint fragrance and flavor that is more refined and less harsh than standard commercial spearmint. The large leaf size makes Kentucky Colonel practical for fresh cocktail garnishes (mint juleps, mojitos), cold drinks, and herb preparations where leaf presentation matters — the substantial leaves are picked individually for floating in glasses or bruising for infusions, rather than stripped from stems. The Kentucky Colonel name connects this variety to the classic bourbon-and-mint culture of Kentucky where spearmint was historically associated with the mint julep tradition — the sweet spearmint character complements bourbon's caramel and vanilla notes without the sharp mentholated edge of peppermint. Kentucky Colonel is also excellent in iced tea, fruit salads, desserts, and fresh herb sauces where a classic spearmint flavor is desired. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Legend Pawpaw (Large Firm-Fleshed England's Orchard Selection)
description: Kentucky Legend is a pawpaw introduction from England's Orchard and Nursery, the Kentucky nursery behind other named selections including Cantaloupe and Marshmallow. It produces large fruit, often reaching around 13 ounces, with firm-textured flesh and a notably low seed percentage comparable to the classic cultivar Sunflower. Kentucky Legend ripens mid-to-late season and, like other named pawpaws, requires a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kentucky Wonder Bean (Old Homestead Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; Kentucky Wonder is the most famous and most enduring American heirloom pole bean — an heirloom variety in continuous cultivation since the 1860s that remains one of the most widely grown and best-regarded pole beans in American home gardens. The vigorous climbing vines reach 5–8 feet and require a sturdy support structure — traditional pole, trellis, or fence. Kentucky Wonder produces heavy yields of long (7–9 inch), round-to-flat, stringless-when-young green pods with exceptional flavor — a rich, full, classic green bean taste that is considerably more complex and satisfying than modern bush beans bred for commercial production. Seed can be saved true-to-type from open-pollinated Kentucky Wonder. The dry seeds (beans) can be used as shell beans or dried for winter storage, giving the plant dual utility as both green snap bean and dry bean. In zone 9, the spring season (February–May) and fall season (August–October) provide two productive growing windows. The combination of outstanding flavor, prolific production, historical significance, and heirloom status makes Kentucky Wonder the gold standard of American pole beans. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Kentucky Wonder Pole Bean
description: Direct sow this vigorous 1800s heirloom pole bean once the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or pole 6 to 8 feet tall. Provide support early, as the climbing vines produce heavy crops of 9 inch curved, oval pods that are stringless when young. Pick regularly to encourage continued production and enjoy fresh, or leave pods to dry for shelling beans. Beans dislike root disturbance, so sow directly rather than transplanting and keep evenly moist during flowering and pod set. Matures in 65–72 days from seed.

name: Kentucky Wonder Wax Pole Bean (Yellow-Podded Heirloom Pole Bean)
description: Kentucky Wonder Wax is a yellow-podded selection of the classic brown-seeded Kentucky Wonder pole bean, offering the same vigorous climbing habit and heavy yields but with round, buttery-yellow pods instead of green. Pods run 7-8 inches, stringless and meaty, with a slightly sweeter, more delicate flavor than the green original, and they show up clearly against the foliage for easy picking. Like its parent variety, it climbs readily to 6-8 feet and needs a sturdy trellis, rewarding gardeners with continuous production when harvested every few days. It remains a favorite where gardeners want a wax bean with genuine pole-bean vigor rather than a compact bush habit. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Kepayang (Football Fruit)
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating. This large Southeast Asian rainforest tree produces football-sized fruit containing large seeds that, after a traditional fermentation and boiling process to remove naturally occurring toxic compounds, become the famous kluwak or keluak used to flavor the dark, earthy Indonesian dish rawon and Peranakan ayam buah keluak. The raw seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic and must never be eaten without proper traditional processing, which involves burying, boiling, and fermenting the seeds over an extended period to render them safe. Grow only as a specialty tree for a large tropical property or botanical collection, and never attempt to process or consume the fruit without expert traditional knowledge of the detoxification method. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Kepel Fruit (Burahol, Violet Deodorant Fruit)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; kepel fruit is slow-growing and best suited to zone 11–12 humid tropical conditions with consistent moisture. Stelechocarpus burahol (kepel fruit or burahol) is one of the world's most unusual and historically remarkable fruit trees — a medium-sized tropical tree in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) native to Java, Indonesia, where it has been deeply associated with the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta for centuries. The rounded, deep-brown, plum-sized fruits emerge cauliflourously in dense clusters on the trunk and main branches, and have a pleasant, sweet, melon-custard apple flavor. What makes kepel fruit uniquely extraordinary, however, is its documented effect on body chemistry: eating the fruits causes the sweat, breath, and urine of the consumer to take on a floral fragrance — reportedly reminiscent of violets or jasmine — for several hours. This effect was so prized in Javanese royal culture that kepel trees were traditionally planted exclusively in the gardens of the Kraton (royal palace), and common people were reportedly forbidden to grow or eat the fruit. The active compounds are thought to be terpenoids that are metabolized into aromatic volatiles excreted through the skin and kidneys. Kepel is extremely rare in cultivation outside Java; it is categorized as a vulnerable species due to limited habitat and restricted cultivation history. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Keraji Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Japanese Lemonade Mandarin)
description: Keraji is a small, cold-hardy mandarin developed in Japan and long grown on Kikai-jima island in the Ryukyus, prized among cold-hardy citrus hobbyists for a tart, distinctly lemonade-like flavor unlike typical sweet mandarins. The thornless, vigorous tree can reach 15 feet or more where winters stay mild, but responds well to pruning for a more compact dooryard or large-container size. Mature wood has been reported to tolerate brief drops to around 12°F, making it noticeably hardier than standard mandarins and a good candidate for pushing citrus culture into cooler pockets of zone 8b Gulf Coast gardens. The small, seedy, yellow-orange fruit ripens in winter and is used more often for juice and ade than fresh peeling and eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kerman Pistachio
description: Kerman is the standard commercial female pistachio cultivar grown across California's Central Valley, chosen for its large nut size and heavy production once mature, though trees can take 7-10 years to bear a full crop. It needs the same demanding climate as the species overall: 700-1000 hours of winter chill combined with long, blisteringly hot, low-humidity summers to fill and split the shells properly, which makes it a poor fit for humid Gulf Coast gardens even where winter cold is adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and expect strong biennial bearing, with a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter one the next. A male pollinator such as Peters must bloom at the same time and be planted nearby, since pistachio is wind-pollinated and entirely dioecious. Harvest when hulls loosen and nuts show the characteristic natural shell split, typically in early autumn. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Kermit Eggplant (Thai Round Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to ping-pong-ball size for the crisp, mild, seed-free texture prized in Thai cooking. Kermit is a small, round Thai eggplant with pale green skin streaked and mottled with cream-white striping, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh has very few seeds when harvested young and holds its shape well in curries, stir-fries, and stews — traditional uses in Thai cuisine, where round green eggplants are added whole or halved directly into simmering curry. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens, zone 4–12. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Kerr's Pink Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill generously, as this old Scottish cultivar produces a heavy crop of round to oval tubers with distinctive rose-pink skin and creamy white, floury flesh. Bred in Scotland in 1917, Kerr's Pink became a staple maincrop potato across Ireland and Scotland thanks to its reliable yields, good disease tolerance, and adaptability to poorer, wetter soils than many refined modern varieties tolerate. The floury texture makes excellent mash and roast potatoes but causes it to break apart in soups and stews, so reserve it for dry-cooking preparations. Grow it where a rustic, high-yielding heirloom maincrop with real cold-region pedigree is wanted over a fussier modern hybrid. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Kesar Mango (Gir Kesar Mango, Queen of Mangoes)
description: Grown at the foot of Gujarat's Girnar hills and holding Geographical Indication status in India, Kesar is named for its deep saffron-orange, non-fibrous pulp and regularly tests among the sweetest of Indian mango cultivars, often exceeding 22 Brix. Its aroma is rich and rounder than Alphonso, with less tang and a smooth, almost creamy mouthfeel. Fruit is medium-sized and roundish with thin, greenish-yellow, easily peeled skin, ripening on a moderately vigorous tree that needs a long, hot growing season to reach full color and sweetness. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kestrel Beet (Monogerm Bolt-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Kestrel is a widely grown market hybrid beet valued for its true monogerm seed, smooth dark-red globe roots, and dependable resistance to premature bolting when spring temperatures swing warm and cold. Sow thinly 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and keep the bed evenly moist through germination, since the single-seedling habit removes the usual thinning labor but still needs even moisture for uniform root size. Roots hold quality in the ground longer than older open-pollinated types, which makes Kestrel a dependable choice for succession plantings and for growers who bunch beets with their tops still attached. Harvest at 1.5-2.5 inches across for the sweetest, most tender roots. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Kestrel Blueberry (Very Early Low-Chill University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Kestrel is a southern highbush blueberry bred at the University of Florida specifically for the low winter chill of north and central Florida and the Gulf Coast, ripening its fruit very early, typically by April, well ahead of most other blueberry types, allowing home growers to harvest before the summer heat sets in and before many pest and disease pressures build. As a southern highbush type, it needs consistently moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil rather than the more forgiving conditions rabbiteye types tolerate. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ketembilla (Ceylon Gooseberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; ketembilla (Ceylon gooseberry) is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub from Sri Lanka producing small (1/2 to 1 inch diameter), round, reddish-purple to deep purple fruits with a tart, acidic, gooseberry-like flavor that makes them outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups — not particularly pleasant raw due to their sharp acidity, but among the best tropical fruits for processing. The plant is heavily thorned and makes an impenetrable hedge — widely used in Sri Lanka and tropical gardens for security hedging. Requires both male and female plants for fruit (dioecious). Grows quickly in warm, humid, well-drained conditions. The tart fruits are exceptionally high in vitamin C. In Florida it is occasionally grown as a specialty fruit and hedge plant. Underutilized as a jam fruit in the US — the intense, tart purple jam from ketembilla rivals the finest domestic berry jams. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ketter Pawpaw
description: Ketter traces to a 1916 pawpaw contest sponsored by the American Genetics Association, in which Mrs. Frank Ketter of Ironton, Ohio submitted fruit — shipped packed in excelsior and arriving in perfect condition — that judges rated among the best of roughly 75 trees entered, winning the contest's cash prize. The variety was propagated from her tree, and one of its own seedlings was later named and released as 'Fairchild', giving Ketter a real place in early pawpaw breeding lineage even though, like most of the 1916 contest winners, it never became a widely commercialized nursery item. Fruit is large and yellow with comparatively thick, tough skin that ships and handles better than most old-line selections, ripening early in the pawpaw season with flesh that matures evenly throughout the fruit and a mild but notably rich flavor. Because it predates modern disease-resistance screening, plant it as a genetic-diversity or historical-interest addition alongside a proven modern cultivar rather than relying on it alone for orchard production. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kettle River Giant Garlic (Porcelain Hardneck)
aliases: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'Kettle River Giant'
description: Kettle River Giant is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating from the Kettle River valley near the Washington-British Columbia border, prized for producing some of the largest bulbs of any hardneck strain, often exceeding 3 inches across with just 4-6 oversized cloves per head. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture through bulb sizing, and mulch heavily over winter in colder zones since Porcelain types are somewhat less cold-hardy than Rocambole strains. The flavor is strong and full-bodied with a lingering heat, and the tall, sturdy scapes make excellent garlic scape pesto in early summer. Choose this variety when garden space is limited but you still want big, easy-to-peel cloves for the kitchen. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Kew Gold Sage (Solid Golden-Leaved Culinary Sage)
description: Grow in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun, where strong light intensifies the leaf color; too much shade or overly rich soil causes the gold tone to fade toward green. Kew Gold is a low, mounding culinary sage selection with solid, even yellow-gold foliage that holds its color through the season more reliably than older gold-splashed selections such as Aurea, and it rarely flowers, keeping energy focused on leaf production. The flavor and aroma match standard culinary sage and the leaves can be harvested and used the same way. Its compact, non-flowering habit suits edging and container use as much as the kitchen garden. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Kew Red Spanish Lavender
aliases: Lavandula stoechas subsp. stoechas f. rosea 'Kew Red'
description: Kew Red stands apart from most Spanish lavenders for its distinctive coloring: deep pink-red flower cones topped with pale, almost white flag bracts that flutter above the blooms like small wings. It forms a well-branched, compact, free-flowering bush and blooms earlier and more heavily than many stoechas cultivars, repeating well if deadheaded. Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since it shares the family's intolerance of wet feet and humid, heavy clay. Shear lightly after each flush to maintain a dense shape and prevent the woody, splayed-open habit lavenders develop with age. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Key Lime
description: Key lime is a small, thorny tree distinct from the larger Persian lime (Citrus latifolia) — its fruit is smaller, more aromatic, more acidic, and nearly seedless at full yellow ripeness. It is self-fertile and bears prolifically in truly tropical conditions; the tree is damaged by any frost and requires zone 10–11 for outdoor culture, though it adapts well to large containers for zone 9 growers who can move it inside. Harvest fruit while still light green to yellow-green, before it turns fully yellow; yellow fruit is riper and less acid but also more perishable. Apply citrus fertilizer three times per year and ensure excellent drainage to prevent root rot. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Key Lime
description: Key lime, also called Mexican lime, produces small, intensely aromatic and juicy fruit beloved for pie, drinks, and marinades. This tender, somewhat thorny citrus stays compact and grows readily in a container that can shelter indoors in cold weather. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with excellent drainage and feed it a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the top of the soil dry between waterings, and protect it from any frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Key Lime Bush
description: A younger, compact form of the Key lime, this semi-tropical evergreen produces small, juicy green limes nearly year-round, famous for Key lime pie. Grow in full sun with fast-draining acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between soakings to avoid soggy roots. Its small size makes it perfect for patio pots that can be sheltered indoors in cold weather. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Keystone Resistant Giant Pepper (Pennsylvania Heirloom Stuffing Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun with consistent moisture and balanced fertility. Keystone Resistant Giant is a Pennsylvania-origin heirloom bell pepper that was one of the most important commercial bell pepper varieties in the eastern United States from the 1940s through the 1970s, valued as the largest-fruited TMV-resistant open-pollinated bell pepper available during a period when disease resistance was achieved only through strain selection rather than modern breeding techniques. The 'Keystone' name connects the variety to Pennsylvania (the Keystone State), where it was grown extensively by commercial growers, home gardeners, and the Pennsylvania Dutch communities who prize large, thick-walled peppers for stuffing with meat and rice. The fruits are distinctly large (4–5 inches tall, 3–4 inches wide), blocky, 3-4 lobed, dark green ripening to red, with moderately thick walls and an upright, pendant orientation on strong-stemmed plants. Keystone Resistant Giant represents the pre-F1-hybrid era of American pepper breeding and occupies an important place in American heirloom pepper history — it was the standard against which American bell peppers were measured for decades and remains a valued open-pollinated option for seed savers who want a true-breeding large stuffing pepper. The flavor at the red stage is rich, sweet, and classically bell-pepper, with none of the bitterness that characterizes some heirloom types. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Keystone Shellbark Hickory
description: Keystone is a named shellbark hickory selection valued by nut tree enthusiasts for producing the largest nuts of any North American hickory in a shell that, while still thick, cracks out with better kernel recovery than typical wild seedling shellbarks. Like all shellbark hickories it prefers deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soils and tolerates wetter sites than shagbark hickory. Grafted trees are slow to reach bearing age, often a decade or more, but produce sweet, richly flavored kernels once established, making this a long-term planting for patient collectors. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Kherson Oat (Heirloom Russian-Origin Spring Oat)
description: Kherson was brought into the United States in 1896 from the Kherson region of southern Russia by way of the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station, and within twenty years it had become one of the most widely sown oats across the Great Plains and Corn Belt thanks to its short season and unusual drought tolerance. Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring; the crop germinates in cool soil and races to maturity ahead of the worst summer heat, which is what made it so valuable on dry, marginal prairie ground before irrigation was common. It tillers modestly and stands a bit shorter than many modern oats, so it tolerates lean soil without lodging heavily. Harvest when straw and hulls turn pale gold, then thresh promptly since the loose hull shatters somewhat more readily than modern oat varieties. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Kidd's Orange Red Apple (Cox's Orange Pippin x Delicious, Parent of Gala)
description: Kidd's Orange Red was raised in New Zealand in the 1920s by orchardist J.H. Kidd from a cross of Cox's Orange Pippin and a red-skinned Delicious parent, inheriting the rich, aromatic, sweet-tart flavor of its Cox parent on a somewhat more reliably productive tree. It is best known today as one of the two parents of Gala, passing on its flavor heritage and red-flushed skin to that far more widely grown modern apple. Fruit is medium-sized with an orange-red flush over a yellow-green background and crisp, juicy, well-balanced flesh, ripening in early-to-mid fall and keeping reasonably well in cool storage for a few months. Give it a compatible pollinator and the same moderate winter chill and well-drained soil that Cox's Orange Pippin requires, since Kidd's Orange Red shares much of that parent's demanding, disease-prone nature in humid climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kieffer Pear
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Kieffer is an 1863 American pear hybrid (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) with extraordinary disease resistance and low chill hour requirements that make it the most reliably productive pear for hot-summer, mild-winter climates in the Southeast and Gulf South — regions where most European pear varieties fail from fire blight disease or insufficient winter chilling. The yellow-green to russet fruits with white, gritty, aromatic flesh are at their best when harvested slightly firm and allowed to ripen at room temperature for several days — the fresh eating quality improves dramatically with proper ripening off the tree. Kieffer pear is primarily a cooking and canning pear in American tradition: the firm, gritty flesh holds its shape beautifully in cooked preparations, and canned Kieffer pear preserves, spiced pears, and pear butter have been produced from this variety for over 150 years in Southern home kitchens. Exceptionally vigorous and productive once established, bearing full crops even in zone 9 conditions that exclude most pear varieties. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kieffer Pear Tree
description: Kieffer is a tough, adaptable pear valued for its heavy crops of crisp, gritty fruit that is excellent for canning, cooking, and preserves. It shows strong resistance to fire blight and tolerates a wide range of climates. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly while establishing. Prune in late winter to build a strong scaffold and allow light into the canopy for even ripening. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kikusui Asian Pear (Chrysanthemum Water Pear)
description: Kikusui is an early-1900s Japanese heirloom whose name translates to 'chrysanthemum water,' a reference to the fruit's exceptionally high juice content when bitten into. The skin is smooth and pale green-yellow rather than russeted, and the mildly sweet, watery flesh has a softer texture than firmer modern nashi cultivars. It bears less heavily than newer selections bred for commercial production, which keeps it mostly in the hands of heirloom collectors and home orchardists rather than commercial growers today. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kikuza Squash (Japanese Heirloom Black-Green Kabocha)
description: Kikuza is a Japanese heirloom kabocha-type squash bearing flattened, deeply lobed fruit with a dark green rind roughened by prominent grayish-tan warts and scarring, a distinctive look among the smoother-skinned kabocha commonly sold in supermarkets. The dry, dense flesh is deep orange-yellow and intensely sweet with the chestnut-like flavor characteristic of the finest kabocha strains, and it stores well for months when cured properly. Grow it as you would other maxima kabocha types, keeping vines evenly watered until fruit sets and then letting soil dry somewhat as the rind hardens and corking develops around the stem. Cure harvested squash in a warm, dry location for one to two weeks to toughen the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Killarney Raspberry
description: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing rows to allow good air movement through the thicket. Killarney was released by the University of Manitoba specifically for prairie and northern climates and remains one of the most cold-hardy red raspberry cultivars available, reliably surviving winters that would damage many modern varieties. It bears a single summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, firmly textured berries with classic sweet-tart raspberry flavor on floricanes, so spent canes should be cut to the ground after harvest. Its toughness makes it a dependable choice for short-season gardens where more tender cultivars struggle. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Killarney Red Garlic (Rocambole Hardneck)
description: Separate cloves shortly before planting and set them pointed end up about 2 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Mulch after planting to buffer winter temperature swings and remove mulch gradually as green shoots emerge in spring; cut off curling scapes in early summer to redirect energy into bulb growth. Killarney Red is a cold-hardy rocambole strain originating from Irish and Canadian growers, prized for its rich, full-bodied garlic flavor and easy-to-peel purple-blushed skins, though like other rocamboles it does not store as long as porcelain or silverskin types. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Killen American Persimmon (Self-Fruitful Native Persimmon)
description: Killen is a named native persimmon selection valued for its exceptionally sweet, blemish-free orange fruit and its self-fruitful habit, meaning a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator planted nearby. It is a somewhat smaller-statured American persimmon, typically maturing around 25 feet, which makes it easier to fit and harvest in a home orchard than many seedling-grown native persimmons. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, Killen fruit remains firm and astringent until fully ripened and softened by autumn frosts, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The tree is drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types, and well suited to the long, humid growing season of the Gulf Coast. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kimbrough Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Kimbrough is a cold-hardy satsuma mandarin selection developed and evaluated by the Louisiana State University AgCenter — selected specifically for superior cold hardiness compared to standard Owari satsuma, making it the recommended satsuma cultivar for zone 8a–8b gardens where occasional hard freezes occur. Satsuma mandarins are the most cold-hardy commonly grown citrus — Kimbrough extends the cold hardiness envelope even further, surviving brief exposure to 14–18°F without permanent damage when grown in well-drained soil (saturated roots dramatically reduce cold tolerance). The fruit is easy-peeling, seedless, and has the classic sweet-tart satsuma mandarin flavor that ripens early (October–November) — delivering fresh citrus fruit months before oranges and before the most demanding winter cold arrives in the Gulf South. In zone 9, Kimbrough satsumas perform reliably with minimal cold protection. Satsumas are fast to bearing — often producing some fruit in the second or third year — and are moderate-sized trees that fit comfortably in residential landscapes. Plant in the warmest, most protected microclimate (south-facing, near a wall or fence) for zone 8 plantings. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kincho Bunching Onion
description: Kincho is a Japanese non-bulbing bunching onion bred for reliable cold hardiness and improved resistance to pink root and botrytis leaf blight compared to older heirloom types. It forms upright, uniform stalks well suited to late-season and overwintered plantings where other bunching onions struggle. Sow thickly and thin gradually, harvesting outer plants first while allowing remaining stalks room to thicken. Its disease tolerance and cold resilience make it a dependable choice for extending green onion harvests into fall and winter in temperate climates. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: King David Apple (Wine-Flavored Arkansas Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. King David originated as a chance seedling discovered on an Arkansas farm in 1893, believed to be a natural cross of Jonathan and Winesap, and quickly gained a following for its rich, aromatic, distinctly wine-like flavor that many heirloom apple enthusiasts still rank among the best-tasting of the old Southern apples. Fruit is medium-sized, deep red over a yellow background, with firm, crisp, juicy flesh that holds up well for fresh eating, baking, and cider. Trees show good vigor and better resistance to common apple diseases than many high-chill Northern varieties of the same era, though it still needs a moderate winter chill and performs best in zone 5-8, becoming marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open, well-ventilated canopy that reduces disease pressure in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: King James Mulberry (Historic English Black Mulberry, syn. 'Chelsea')
description: King James traces its lineage to black mulberries planted in England in the early 1600s under royal patronage for a short-lived silk industry, and old specimens descended from those original plantings are still tended as historic trees; the cultivar is also sold under the synonym 'Chelsea' after the Chelsea Physic Garden. Trees have gnarled, textured bark and heart-shaped leaves that color yellow in fall, and they produce large, richly flavored, deep-purple-black fruit typical of true black mulberry (Morus nigra) — more intensely flavored than white or red mulberry types. Provide fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; established trees tolerate summer heat well but appreciate consistent moisture during fruit development. Because ripe fruit drops and stains heavily, site trees away from patios and walkways, and prune only lightly to maintain shape, since fruiting spurs persist for years on this species. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: King of Hearts Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Hybrid)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen this seedless triploid needs to set fruit. King of Hearts is an All-America Selections winning seedless hybrid producing large, oval, striped fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and only soft, edible white seed traces rather than hard black seeds, a genuine convenience for fresh eating. The vigorous vine is a reliable, heavy producer when properly pollinated, and the flavor and texture rank among the better seedless hybrids available. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot turns creamy yellow, since seedless watermelons give fewer reliable ripeness cues than seeded types and are easy to pick too early. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: King of the Garden Lima Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost with soil above 65°F; provide poles or strong trellising 6–8 feet tall for support. King of the Garden is a classic American pole lima bean introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1883 and considered for much of its history the finest large-seeded lima bean available; the plants are vigorous, 6–8 foot climbers that produce long, broad, flat pods with 4–6 very large (up to 1 inch), flat, creamy-white bean seeds with an extraordinarily rich, buttery, full lima bean flavor superior to most modern bush varieties. The large seeds require a relatively long, warm season to develop fully (85–95 days from seed); in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens the long growing season makes King of the Garden ideal for both spring and fall plantings. Excellent for fresh green lima use (harvested at the flat-but-not-yet-wrinkled stage when seeds are fully developed), freezing, and drying. One of the foundational American heirloom vegetables. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: King of the North Pepper (Heirloom Short-Season Sweet Bell Pepper with Zone 9 Fall Use)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost or in late summer for fall production. Harvest green or red. King of the North is an heirloom sweet bell pepper variety bred and popularized specifically for short-season, cool-climate gardens where standard bell pepper varieties (requiring 70–90+ days and substantial heat to develop fully) cannot be relied upon to ripen before fall frosts. The breeding goal of short-season bell peppers like King of the North is to compress the fruit development timeline while maintaining adequate size, wall thickness, and flavor — a challenging tradeoff since bell peppers that ripen quickly tend to be smaller and thinner-walled than late-maturing types. King of the North succeeds reasonably well at this balance: the fruits are large enough to be genuinely useful (3–4 inches, 3-lobed form), with walls adequate for stuffing and fresh use, and flavor that develops to full sweetness when ripened to red. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward, making it a practical choice for seed-saving gardeners. In zone 9, the short days-to-maturity of King of the North are most valuable for the fall growing season rather than spring: a late-July start from seed produces plants that can be transplanted in late August and begin producing before October heat drops, allowing harvest through November in a climate where long-season varieties started at the same time might not mature before plants are compromised by cool weather. This fall-planting application in zone 9 mirrors King of the North's primary value in zone 3–5 gardens — speed of production in a constrained growing window. Matures in 57–68 days from transplant.

name: King of the Pippins Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; King of the Pippins is a strong, reliable pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties, though it can bear biennially if not thinned. An old variety of uncertain French or English origin dating to at least the eighteenth century, it bears attractive orange-red-striped apples over a golden ground, with crisp, aromatic, sweet-sharp flesh that made it a widely planted commercial dessert apple across Europe for generations before more modern varieties took over the market. Its strong, abundant bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties in a mixed home orchard, though the tree has a tendency toward biennial bearing, alternating heavy and light crop years unless fruit is thinned in a heavy year. Harvest in mid-fall and eat within a couple of months, since it does not keep quite as long as some other classic dessert varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: King Philip Corn (Historic New England Flint Corn)
description: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows, and take advantage of its short season to succeed even in cool, short-summer regions of northern New England. King Philip is one of the oldest documented flint corns in cultivation, recorded in Massachusetts and Rhode Island since colonial times and traditionally said to honor the Wampanoag leader Metacomet, known to English colonists as King Philip. The eight-rowed ears bear hard, deep red-brown kernels that dry quickly on the stalk and grind into a flavorful, reddish cornmeal long used for johnnycake and other traditional New England cornbreads. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: King Richard Leek
description: Start King Richard leeks indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings the thickness of a pencil into the garden spaced 4 to 6 inches apart. This early variety produces extra-long white stems, so hill or trench the plants and mound soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. Leeks tolerate cold well and can be harvested from late summer through fall. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free for the best-quality stems. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: King Sieg Leek
description: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; King Sieg is a Belgian-bred leek cultivar selected for the mild winter climates of the maritime Pacific Northwest and Gulf South — specifically bred to produce long, thick, white-blanche shanks without premature bolting in mild, frost-free or light-frost winters. Standard leek cultivars selected for cold northern climates often bolt prematurely when grown in mild zone 8–10 winters because the mild temperatures signal the plant that spring has arrived; King Sieg has delayed bolting response, allowing harvest through February and March in zone 9 without quality loss. The thick, tender white shanks with a mild, sweet leek flavor are excellent in potato-leek soup, braised whole, sautéed as a vegetable side, or used in place of onions where a milder allium is needed. Earth up soil around the shanks as the plants grow to extend the white, blanched portion and reduce the proportion of green. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: King's Ransom Mahonia (Hybrid Oregon Grape with Bronze Winter Foliage)
description: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, where King's Ransom forms an upright-mounded hybrid Oregon grape with spiny, holly-shaped, bluish-green evergreen leaves that emerge burgundy in spring and turn bronze-red through winter. Showy, fragrant racemes of yellow flowers hang below the branches in early spring, followed by an abundant crop of attractive blue, grape-like berries from midsummer into fall that draw birds. Slow-growing and long-lived, it makes a durable specimen or background shrub for a shaded border. Prune only to remove dead or leggy canes at the base. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kingston Black Apple (Classic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, dark red-purple apple is the most celebrated of the true single-variety, or vintage, cider apples, prized as a rare bittersharp carrying both the tannin and acid balance needed to produce a complex, well-structured cider entirely on its own without blending. Its fruit is far too astringent and acidic for fresh eating, but its combination of tannin, sugar, and acid in a single apple has made it the benchmark variety against which other cider apples are measured. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and expect a light, sometimes biennial crop, since Kingston Black is well known among cider makers for being a difficult, temperamental tree to grow well. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kinnard's Choice Apple (Tennessee Heirloom Dessert Apple)
description: Grow as a standard tree in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage in heavy years. Kinnard's Choice originated in Tennessee in the 19th century and has long been prized by Southern heirloom apple collectors for its rich, aromatic, exceptionally sweet flesh, considered by many old-timers to be among the best-flavored dessert apples of the region. It ripens in late summer to early fall and is primarily grown today by small orchardists and heritage-fruit enthusiasts rather than commercial producers. Matures in 155–170 days from transplant.

name: Kinnow Mandarin (King x Willowleaf Hybrid Tangerine)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, choosing a well-drained site with at least eight hours of direct sun and protection from cold winds. Water deeply and regularly during establishment, then taper to consistent moisture during fruit development while avoiding standing water. This vigorous mandarin hybrid produces deep orange, intensely sweet-tart fruit with numerous seeds and a tight peel, ripening in mid to late winter. It tolerates brief dips into the high 20s F once established but performs best where winters stay mild, making it a favorite in low-desert and Gulf Coast citrus plantings. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kintzel Chinese Chestnut (Historic Ohio Blight-Resistant Selection, Parent of Jenny)
description: Kintzel is an old Ohio Chinese chestnut selection, documented under the breeding designations Byron 1-1 and 1-2 in a 1962 Northern Nut Growers Association Nutshell article, and long valued among nut-tree collectors for combining genuine resistance to chestnut blight with excellent winter cold hardiness. Its most lasting legacy is as the seed parent of Jenny, a tall, early-ripening open-pollinated selection chosen by breeder J.M. Nave and since evaluated in Missouri chestnut trials, which has been distributed far more widely than Kintzel itself. Kintzel is rarely offered by name in the nursery trade today, surviving mainly in historic breeding records and in specialty nut-tree collections, while gardeners wanting its blight resistance and hardiness in a currently available tree are more likely to find its offspring Jenny. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut selections. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kiowa Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Kiowa is a thorned, erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 1996 as part of the same breeding program that produced Natchez and Ouachita. It is distinguished principally by its extraordinary berry size — among the largest of any blackberry variety, often exceeding 10–14 grams per fruit — and its exceptionally long harvest season that can extend 6–8 weeks through June and July in zone 8–9. Flavor is sweet and complex. The upright, thorned canes are self-supporting and vigorous, producing heavily. Kiowa shows good adaptability to the South and mid-South, performing well in humid, hot climates where some varieties decline. The principal trade-off is the thorns — unavoidable when harvesting and pruning — but many growers consider this worthwhile for the combination of size, yield, and long season. Prune fruited floricanes to ground level after the last berries are harvested; tip primocanes at 36–42 inches in summer to promote lateral branching. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Kiowa Pecan (Precocious Large-Nut Type I Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with room for a large mature canopy. Kiowa is an Oklahoma State University release prized by home orchardists for its precocity, bearing well ahead of most named pecan varieties, and for its very large, attractive, thin-shelled nuts with excellent bright kernel color and good fill. It is a Type I pollinator, so pair it with a Type II variety for cross-pollination and heavier yields. Scab pressure is moderate; in the humid Gulf South a fungicide program during wet springs helps protect nut quality, while drier inland sites see less trouble. Thin overcrowded nut clusters in heavy-bearing years to reduce alternate bearing and keep nut size consistent season to season. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Kirby Cucumber
description: Kirby is the classic short, bumpy, thin-skinned pickling cucumber with crisp, dense flesh. Direct sow after the soil warms, either in hills or along a low trellis for cleaner fruit. Provide abundant, even water since pickling cucumbers are especially prone to bitterness and hollow centers under drought. Pick daily at 3 to 5 inches for pickling, as the vines produce heavily over a short window. Succession sowing every two to three weeks extends the harvest into late summer. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Kirsten Pawpaw
description: Kirsten is a named seedling selection bred by pawpaw enthusiast Tom Mansell at his 'Paw Paw Haven' planting on the bluffs above the Ohio River near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, from a cross of the older, widely grown Michigan selection 'Taytwo' and the clustered, smooth-fleshed Indiana selection 'Overleese'. It is catalogued alongside the Kentucky State University pawpaw program's compiled regional cultivar table as a named hybrid selection, though unlike the KSU-released cultivars it has not passed through formal multi-state variety trials, so growers should treat it as a collector's selection valued for combining the productivity of its Taytwo parent with the mild, smooth-fleshed dessert quality of Overleese. Trees tolerate deep shade for their first several years but should be given more sun as they mature to maximize fruit set. Because it sits near the northern, cooler end of Pennsylvania pawpaw range, it is a useful genetic option for growers assembling cold-hardy orchard blocks. As with all pawpaws, flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles drawn to their faint carrion scent rather than bees, so hand-pollination with a small brush during the dark maroon spring bloom improves fruit set in home plantings. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kishu Mandarin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–7.0) soil; Kishu mandarin (Kishu mikan) is a tiny Japanese mandarin producing small, round, intensely sweet, completely seedless fruits — typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, roughly the size of a large grape. The combination of total seedlessness and extraordinary sweetness makes Kishu the darling of high-end specialty markets, where the small size makes it a perfect one-bite citrus snack. The paper-thin skin peels effortlessly in a single piece, and the flavor is intensely sweet with rich tropical complexity that surpasses most commercial mandarins.
