Trees are compact and manageable at 6–10 feet, well-suited to zone 9 and container growing. Kishu ripens in December–January, slightly earlier than most clementine-type mandarins. Although small trees, they bear prolifically and a single established tree can produce hundreds of fruits. Avoid planting in frost pockets where cold air settles. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kiwano (African Horned Melon, Jelly Melon)
description: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; provide trellis support; kiwano tolerates more drought than most cucurbits once vines are established. Cucumis metuliferus (kiwano or African horned melon) is an extraordinary African cucurbit producing one of the most visually dramatic fruits in horticulture — an oblong, 3-to-5-inch fruit covered in prominent, rigid, pointed spines (horns), ripening from green to brilliant deep orange-gold that looks almost artificial in its intensity. The jelly-like interior flesh is lime-green and gelatinous, with a mild, refreshing flavor combining hints of banana, cucumber, and lime. Kiwano is grown commercially in New Zealand, Kenya, and California for specialty markets and upscale grocery stores where the exotic appearance commands premium prices. The fruit is eaten by scooping out the jelly-like flesh with a spoon, used in tropical fruit salads, blended into smoothies, or used as a dramatic edible vessel for other foods. As an annual vine, it is easy to grow in zone 9 summers — direct sow after the last frost, provide trellis support, and harvest when the skin turns deep orange. The vines are vigorous and productive under heat. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Kiwiberry
description: Kiwiberry is a compact-fruited selection of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) grown specifically for smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits that are eaten whole without peeling — they have the same flavor as standard kiwifruit but ripen 3–4 weeks earlier. Self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' and 'Ken's Red' allow single-plant production, but yields are higher when a male pollenizer is present. The extremely vigorous vines require a heavy-gauge trellis or pergola capable of bearing hundreds of pounds of vine and fruit; prune hard each dormant season to renewal spurs. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and taste sweet with no starchiness. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kiyomi Tangor (Satsuma-Orange Hybrid, Parent of Sumo Citrus)
description: Kiyomi is a Japanese-bred tangor, a cross of Satsuma mandarin and Trovita sweet orange developed at the Okitsu citrus research station, prized for exceptionally sweet, low-acid, richly aromatic juice with a deep orange rind and few seeds when grown in isolation from other citrus. It is best known as the parent of Dekopon/Sumo Citrus, but the fruit stands on its own merits for home orchardists wanting a specialty dessert citrus distinct from the more common Satsumas and navels already in wide cultivation. Kiyomi needs more heat and a longer frost-free season than Satsuma mandarins, so it suits warmer zone 9-11 gardens and container culture further north. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, since Kiyomi can overbear and produce undersized fruit the following year. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Klavdija Sea Buckthorn (Slovenian Near-Thornless Seaberry)
description: Klavdija is a female sea buckthorn cultivar valued for producing heavy quantities of orange-red fruit on a shrub that is nearly thornless, letting berry-laden branches be picked by hand rather than stripped or cut, as is often necessary with thornier seaberry selections. Like other named sea buckthorn cultivars it forms a large, upright, nitrogen-fixing shrub that tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils and drought that would stunt most other fruiting plants, while resenting waterlogged sites. The tart, vitamin-C-rich berries are used for juice, syrup, and preserves. Being dioecious, Klavdija needs a male sea buckthorn planted nearby, since female plants set no fruit without pollination. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kleckley Sweet Watermelon (Thin-Rind Southern Heirloom, Supreme Garden Eating Quality)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; allow 6–8 feet between hills. Harvest when tendril nearest fruit dries and ground spot turns yellow. Kleckley Sweet (also called Monte Cristo in some seed catalogs) is one of the great heirloom watermelons of the American South — a variety with an extraordinary reputation for eating quality that has been maintained by home gardeners and seed savers for well over a century, despite being completely impractical for commercial production due to its extremely thin rind. The rind of a ripe Kleckley Sweet is so thin that the fruit can crack simply from being set down too hard — a catastrophic liability for commercial shipping but an indication of the rind's extreme thinness that is part of what makes it so desirable for eating, where rind thickness is inversely proportional to flesh proportion per fruit. The flesh is brilliant red, dense and fine-grained, with very small seeds relative to the flesh volume, and of the highest natural sweetness of any standard-sized watermelon variety — the flavor is intensely, purely sweet with the clean watermelon taste that distinguishes vine-ripened, heat-grown Southern watermelons from the bland, watery specimens produced from short-season varieties in cool climates. The variety was introduced by W. Atlee Burpee around the 1890s-1900s and became one of the most popular garden watermelons in the South through the mid-20th century, maintaining a devoted following among heirloom gardeners long after commercial production shifted to thick-rinded shipping varieties. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Klondike Striped Watermelon
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Klondike Striped is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in hot, dry Western climates and Gulf Coast sandy soils. Klondike Striped was developed in early 20th century California, where it became the primary commercial watermelon for California's San Joaquin Valley and other Western growing regions; the medium-large (25–35 lbs), oblong fruits have attractive, uniform, alternating light and dark green stripes and firm, deep red to scarlet flesh with excellent, rich, sweet flavor and few seeds relative to its size. The variety became widely grown in the West and South for its reliable production, attractive appearance, and good quality; the firm flesh holds well after cutting, making it a practical variety for families and market growers. Days to maturity of 80–90 suit it well for both long-season Southern and moderately short Pacific Coast growing seasons. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Knuckle Head Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the sprawling vines. Knuckle Head is a hybrid novelty pumpkin from the Superfreak series, producing 12-16 pound, slightly tall, dark-orange fruit densely covered in gnarled warts that range from dark green through light green to orange; unlike some warty types, wart color is not a reliable ripeness indicator here. The variety carries useful powdery mildew resistance, which helps keep foliage productive through the fruit-finishing stage of the season. Grown almost exclusively for its shock-value texture at pumpkin patches and fall markets rather than for eating, it should be harvested once the rind is fully hard and stored in a cool, dry spot for display. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Knuckle Purple Hull Cowpea
description: This productive bush-type cowpea produces plump, succulent peas with a distinctive purple eye inside richly colored purple pods. Sow directly into warm soil, as cowpeas love summer heat and tolerate dry conditions. The compact plants need no staking and set a heavy crop of easy-to-shell pods. Pick pods when the hulls turn purple and the peas inside are full for fresh use, or leave them to dry for storage. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Knuckle Purple Hull Pea (Short-Season Compact Purple Hull Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Knuckle Purple Hull is a semi-determinate purple hull southern pea that matures faster and concentrates its pod set in a shorter window than standard indeterminate purple hull types — producing the characteristic purple-hulled pods on a compact, upright plant that reaches 18–24 inches without trailing vines, making it more manageable for raised-bed and intensive garden production. The name 'Knuckle' refers to the distinctive bunching habit of pod production — the pods tend to cluster near the stem joints ('knuckles') in groups rather than being spread along extended vining stems, which concentrates the harvest and makes picking more efficient. The peas themselves are the classic purple hull type: green hulls with purple coloring at maturity, and cream-colored seeds with the mild, sweet flavor characteristic of purple hull peas. At 55–65 days, Knuckle Purple Hull is also earlier than standard purple hull types (typically 65–75 days) — allowing earlier first harvests from spring plantings and more productive use of the warm season in zone 9 where succession planting through summer is common practice. The compact, determinate-tending growth habit requires no staking and makes Knuckle Purple Hull suitable for higher-density plantings than trailing types. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Knucklehead Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Warty Jack-O-Lantern Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, giving the vigorous vines ample room since fruit can reach 15 pounds or more. Knucklehead won an All-America Selections award for a texture unlike any standard carving pumpkin: dense, rounded warts cover the entire orange rind from stem to blossom end, creating a rugged, knuckled surface that stands out in any fall display. Despite the unusual texture the rind stays firm and workable, making the fruit suitable for both painting and light carving around the bumps. Harvest before hard frost once the color has fully developed and the warting has set, and expect a long-lasting fall display since the thick, tough rind resists rot better than smooth-skinned pumpkins. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Kobold Garlic Chives (Compact Container Selection)
description: Kobold is a compact, uniform garlic chive selection bred with thin, aromatic, flat stems and a noticeably tighter growth habit than standard Allium tuberosum, which typically sprawls wider and taller. This scaled-down footprint makes Kobold well suited to container culture, window boxes, and small kitchen-garden beds where standard garlic chives would quickly outgrow the space. Grow in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and harvest the flat, garlic-flavored leaves regularly by cutting near the base to encourage steady regrowth. Deadhead the white star-shaped flower clusters after bloom if self-seeding is a concern, since garlic chives can spread readily from seed even in a compact cultivar. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Kodiak Brown Mustard (High-Glucosinolate Biofumigant Cover Crop)
description: Broadcast or drill seed into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and mow or flail-chop the stand right at early flowering, then incorporate the shredded residue into the top few inches of soil immediately and irrigate to seal it in — the biofumigant effect depends on releasing volatile isothiocyanate compounds from the chopped tissue quickly, before they dissipate into the air. Kodiak was bred at the University of Idaho for an unusually high concentration of glucosinolates, the sulfur compounds that break down into natural soil fumigants capable of suppressing soilborne fungal pathogens, weed seed germination, and plant-parasitic nematodes, offering a lower-input alternative to chemical soil fumigation ahead of a susceptible vegetable crop. Beyond its biofumigant role, the fast, leafy growth smothers weeds and scavenges excess soil nitrogen, and the bright yellow flowers, if allowed to open, are attractive to early-season pollinators. Avoid planting into a bed just biofumigated with mustard for several weeks to allow residues to fully break down. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Kodo Millet (Kodra)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 6-10 inches when plants are established; kodo millet is a South Asian and West African grain grass valued for exceptional hardiness, tolerating both drought and temporary waterlogging better than almost any other cultivated grain, which has made it a traditional insurance crop in unpredictable growing conditions. The clumping plant produces slender seed spikes on branching stalks that ripen over an extended period; harvest by cutting mature heads as they brown and finishing the dry-down on a tarp in the sun before threshing by flailing or rubbing to release the small, hard seeds. Freshly harvested and properly dried kodo millet is safe and nutritious, but note that grain infected by a specific fungus (Aspergillus tamarii) during wet storage can become toxic, so dry and store the harvest promptly and thoroughly, a standard precaution long practiced by traditional growers. The grain is notably high in dietary fiber and has a mild, slightly nutty flavor when cooked whole like rice. Matures in 100–140 days from seed.

name: Koginut Squash (Chef-Bred Kabocha-Butternut Hybrid)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vine room to sprawl. Koginut combines the deep, nutty sweetness and dry, dense texture of kabocha squash with the smoother shape and easier peeling of butternut, developed through a chef-driven breeding collaboration specifically to concentrate flavor rather than yield or shelf appearance. The tan, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruit has an intensely sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that roasts especially well. Harvest when the rind hardens and dulls to a matte tan color, usually as the vine declines in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to further concentrate sweetness. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems for cucurbits in Gulf South gardens. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Kohala Longan
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Kohala is the most widely planted named longan cultivar in Hawaii and South Florida, selected at the University of Hawaii for consistently large, sweet, reliable fruit production in tropical and subtropical conditions. The large clusters of walnut-sized fruits with tan-brown papery shells and translucent white sweet flesh ripen in August–September — the classic longan flavor is a delicate sweetness with floral notes and a refreshing juicy texture, less intense and more floral than lychee. In zone 9 the mild winter temperatures provide the natural chilling that longan requires to initiate flower buds, making zone 9a an ideal longan climate. Kohala trees are vigorous growers that can eventually reach 30–40 feet in favorable conditions but are maintained smaller by selective pruning. The species produces abundantly once established, with mature trees bearing hundreds of pounds of fruit in a good year. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Kohlrabi
description: Direct sow seed 1/4 in deep in cool, fertile soil and thin plants to 5–8 in to give the swollen stem room to develop. Keep soil consistently moist, as drought stress causes the bulb to become woody and strongly flavored. Harvest when the swollen stem is 2–3 in across for best tenderness; larger bulbs become fibrous. Pull the whole plant and trim the leaves before storing in the refrigerator. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Kokuho Rose Rice (Heirloom California Medium-Grain Rice)
description: Kokuho Rose was bred by a family rice farm in California, crossing Japanese short-grain lines with a Middle Eastern long-grain parent to produce a semi-dwarf medium-grain rice with better flavor than the era's standard Calrose. The family has continuously grown and sold it since the 1960s, making it one of the longest-lived named rice selections still in commercial production in the United States. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or stock tank through the warm season, maintaining standing water while the plant tillers and fills, then draining as the panicles ripen and dry. Cooked grains turn creamy and slightly sticky with a mild sweetness, making this variety a longtime favorite for sushi rice and home rice cookery on the West Coast. Matures in 140–160 days from seed.

name: Kokum
description: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment. Kokum is dioecious, so both male and female trees are needed for fruit, and it is native to the moist forests of India's Western Ghats. The purple-rind fruit is sun-dried into the deep reddish-black souring spice used throughout Goan and Konkani cooking, such as kokum curry and solkadhi, and pressed into kokum butter; fresh pulp is also boiled into a tart, cooling summer syrup. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Kokuso Mulberry (Japanese Large-Fruited Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Kokuso is a Japanese mulberry cultivar bred specifically for dessert-quality fruit rather than the silkworm-feeding leaf production most Morus alba selections were traditionally grown for. The berries are notably large, dark purple-black, and richly sweet with good depth of flavor, ripening over a fairly extended summer window that spreads out the harvest rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Trees are vigorous and adaptable to a wide range of soils, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established with only occasional deep watering needed during extended dry spells. Because mulberries can grow quite large and dense if left unpruned, an annual shaping prune in late winter keeps the canopy at a manageable height for easier harvest. Site female-fruiting trees away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since ripe berries drop over an extended period and stain hard surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kolb's Gem Watermelon (American Rail-Shipping Heirloom)
description: Plant in deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun, watering consistently through fruit set and tapering off as melons approach ripeness to build sugar. Reuben Kolb of Alabama developed this variety around 1885, and its unusually tough, bruise-resistant rind made it one of the first watermelons durable enough for long-distance rail shipping, briefly making it a dominant commercial melon of the late 19th century before later shipping varieties displaced it. Fruits are large and nearly round, often reaching 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions, with sweet, deep red flesh prized for home and market eating. Because the rind is tougher than modern melon-market types, it also stores and travels unusually well for a home garden heirloom. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Kolibri Kohlrabi (Purple F1 Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seed ½ inch deep in early spring 2-4 weeks before the last frost, and again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Kolibri grows fastest and mildest in cool weather. Kolibri is a widely grown F1 hybrid noted as one of the most uniform and reliably deep-purple kohlrabi varieties available, forming a smooth, round, above-ground bulb with crisp, nearly fiberless white flesh beneath the vivid purple skin. Its rapid 45- to 50-day maturity and compact, neat habit make it well suited to succession planting, small-space beds, and early-season cloche or row-cover production. Harvest bulbs at about the size of a tennis ball for the sweetest, most tender texture, since kohlrabi can turn woody if left too long in the ground. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Komatsuna (Japanese Mustard Spinach)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep, thinning to 4 inches for baby greens or 8 inches for full-sized plants. Komatsuna is one of the most versatile Asian brassicas — milder than mustard, more heat-tolerant than spinach, and remarkably cold-hardy. Begin harvesting at 30 days for tender salad leaves, or allow plants to reach full size at 8–14 inches for stir-frying and braising. Water consistently to keep leaves mild and succulent. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Komodo Dragon Pepper (UK Superhot)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, and transplant only once the soil is thoroughly warm, since seedlings stall in cool conditions. Stake plants as the fruit load builds and keep moisture consistent to avoid blossom drop during heat spikes. Komodo Dragon was bred in the United Kingdom by chile grower Salvatore Genovese and is known as one of the hottest peppers developed in Britain, with elongated, ridged red pods and a sharp, intense burn. It is popular among superhot collectors for its productivity in cooler UK-style greenhouse growing. Matures in 95–120 days from transplant.

name: Konan Kohlrabi (AAS-Winning Compact Globe Kohlrabi)
description: Direct sow, or start transplants and set out 2-4 weeks before last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Konan is an AAS-winning kohlrabi bred for a compact plant habit and smooth, uniform, pale-green globes that stay crisp, sweet, and free of the woodiness or cracking that plagues older kohlrabi varieties even at a larger harvest size, giving gardeners a wider window to pick. The neat, upright plant fits well in small beds, raised beds, and large containers. Harvest bulbs when they reach 2-3 inches across for the best texture; peel the tough outer skin before eating raw in slaws or cooked. As a cool-season crop it can bolt and turn woody in summer heat, so grow it as an early spring or fall crop in zone 9. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Konjac
description: Plant corms in rich, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and dappled shade, mimicking the forest understory conditions of its native East Asia; each corm produces a single enormous compound leaf on a mottled stalk that can reach 6 feet tall in a single season. Corms grow slowly, increasing in size each year, and are typically harvested after 2–3 years when they can weigh 5–10 pounds; the raw corm contains calcium oxalate crystals and must be processed before eating. Traditional processing involves drying, grinding, and treating the flour with an alkaline solution to form the firm, gelatinous product used in shirataki noodles and konjac blocks. In zones 6–7 mulch the planting site heavily in autumn to protect corms through winter, or dig and store them frost-free. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Konstance Kohlrabi (AAS-Winning Crack-Resistant Purple Kohlrabi)
description: Direct sow, or start transplants and set out 2-4 weeks before last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Konstance is an AAS-winning purple kohlrabi bred from the same breeding line as Kolibri, improved with smoother skin, more upright foliage, and better resistance to fusarium, and it holds a vivid purple color that extends into the leaf stems. The crisp, sweet, peppery bulb stays crack-resistant and tender over a longer harvest window than older varieties, so a planting does not have to be picked all at once. Harvest bulbs at 2-3 inches for the most tender texture, and use young leaves as a cooked or raw green in addition to the bulb itself. Matures in 42–55 days from seed.

name: Koralle Lingonberry (Heavy-Bearing European Lingonberry)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Koralle is a classic Dutch-bred lingonberry cultivar, one of the earliest widely distributed named lingonberry selections and still valued for its heavy, reliable fruit production and vigorous, dense, low-growing habit. The glossy evergreen foliage forms an attractive year-round groundcover, topped with clusters of small white to pale pink bell-shaped spring flowers followed by bright red, tart berries used in Scandinavian-style jams, sauces, and preserves. Because lingonberries thrive in acidic soil and tolerate shade better than most fruiting shrubs, Koralle makes an excellent edible groundcover planted beneath blueberries, azaleas, or pines where soil is already acidic. Shear plants back lightly every few years to rejuvenate growth and maintain a dense, productive mat. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Korarima (Ethiopian Cardamom)
description: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; korarima, or Ethiopian cardamom, is a ginger-family relative whose aromatic seed pods are a key spice in Ethiopian cooking, most notably in berbere spice blend and in the traditional Ethiopian coffee ceremony, where whole pods are sometimes added to the roasting coffee. It is a distinct species from both true cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) and the West African spice grains of paradise (Aframomum melegueta), with its own warm, slightly citrusy-peppery, resinous flavor. The plant grows as a clumping, ginger-like perennial with broad leaves and produces its aromatic seed pods near the base of the plant close to the soil. It needs consistent warmth, humidity, and moisture year-round and is intolerant of any frost, so outside of zone 10–11 it is best grown in a large container that can be moved to a warm, bright indoor spot for winter. Harvest pods once they mature and dry to a deep reddish-brown, then dry further and store whole, grinding just before use to preserve aroma. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Korean Barberry
description: Korean barberry is a dense, extremely cold-hardy deciduous shrub from the Korean peninsula, grown for drooping clusters of fragrant yellow spring flowers, brilliant scarlet-red fall foliage, and bright red, elongated fruit that persists into winter. The tart berries are edible cooked into jelly or syrup in the same manner as European barberry, though they are astringent eaten raw. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for cereal stem rust, check local agricultural extension guidance before planting near wheat, barley, or oat fields. Give the shrub full sun for the best fall color and fruit set, though it tolerates part shade; little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood in late winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Korean Black Raspberry (Bokbunja)
description: Grow on a trellis or in a bounded bed in full sun, and prune out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the stand productive and accessible. Rubus coreanus, known in Korea as bokbunja, is a wild bramble species long harvested and increasingly field-cultivated for its firm, tart berries, most famously fermented into the traditional Korean fruit wine of the same name. The fruit ripens from red to a deep blackish-red, smaller and firmer than typical black raspberries, with a distinctly tart flavor valued in beverages, preserves, and traditional Korean herbal use. Plants form dense, arching, thorny thickets similar to black raspberry and root readily from cane tips that touch the soil, making propagation easy but also requiring management to keep the planting contained. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Korean Cucumber (Joseon Oi, Korean Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Korean cucumber (Joseon Oi or 'Korean local cucumber') is the traditional cucumber of Korean agriculture — a light green to whitish-green cucumber with a bumpy, spiny-warted surface (similar to pickling cucumbers but larger and paler), crisp, dense, mildly flavored flesh, very thin skin, and a shape that ranges from short and stout (about 6 inches) to long and slender depending on the local strain. It is the essential ingredient in oi sobagi (cucumber kimchi) where the crisp texture and thin skin allow quick pickling and absorption of spicy, garlicky brine without becoming soft or mushy — texture properties that make Korean cucumber distinctly superior to standard American slicing or pickling cucumbers for Korean-style preparations. The pale color and slightly different flavor profile also distinguish it from Japanese kyuri types; Korean cucumber has a slightly more pronounced flavor with a mild earthiness. Very heat-tolerant and productive under summer conditions; an excellent Asian specialty cucumber for Southern gardens with access to Korean or Asian seed suppliers. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Korean Giant Asian Pear (Olympic Pear, Jumbo Asian Pear, Large Korean Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Korean Giant requires a cross-pollinator; thin fruit clusters in May to 1 fruit per spur for maximum fruit development — this variety has the capacity to produce extremely large fruit when properly thinned; harvest in late September to October when skin color shifts from green to yellow-green and fruit gives very slightly to pressure. Korean Giant (also marketed as 'Olympic Pear' in American nursery trade, named for the 1988 Seoul Olympics) is a Korean variety that produces some of the largest Asian pear fruits available to home growers and specialty markets — single fruits commonly weigh 1–1.5 lbs and exceptional fruits can reach 2 lbs, making them dramatically larger than the typical 6–10 oz fruits of Hosui, Shinseiki, and Nijisseiki. The size is the variety's primary market distinction: Korean Giant pears make a striking visual impression at farmers' markets and gift fruit presentations, where the giant, pale gold-green to golden-brown skin and exceptional juicy-sweet flavor create a memorable product. The flavor at peak ripeness is excellent — sweet, refreshingly crisp, and juicy with a clean, mild pear flavor — and the very late ripening season (September–October) extends the fresh Asian pear harvest window well after early and mid-season varieties have finished. Korean Giant requires careful fruit thinning to develop full-sized individual fruits; without thinning, trees set too many fruits and individual nuts remain smaller. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Korean Long Hot Pepper (Slender Mild-to-Medium Cooking Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Korean Long Hot produces long, slender, pale to medium green pods with thin walls and mild-to-medium heat that can vary with growing conditions, a staple pepper in Korean cooking eaten fresh, dipped in ssamjang, sautéed, or stuffed. The plants are productive over a long summer harvest season, and pods can be picked green or allowed to ripen to red for a sweeter, hotter flavor. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Korean Melon
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Korean melon (chamoe, chamgwoe) is a small, oval to round melon of East Asian origin that ripens from green-striped to a brilliant golden-yellow with white stripes running longitudinally along the skin — visually distinct from any Western melon type. The small (4–8 ounce) fruits have crisp, white flesh with a delicate floral fragrance and exceptionally sweet flavor; the thin skin is edible and the seeds and surrounding gel are also consumed in Korean tradition. Unlike large Western muskmelons, Korean melons are picked at peak ripeness and eaten immediately — they do not store well, and the flavor deteriorates quickly after harvest. Grow on trellises for cleaner fruits or allow to sprawl on mulched ground. The fast maturity (60–75 days from transplant) makes Korean melon one of the quickest-maturing melons available, allowing multiple crops per season in zone 9. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Korean Mint
description: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean mint (Korean hyssop) is an East Asian culinary and medicinal herb with large, anise-mint-scented leaves used fresh in Korean, Vietnamese, and Chinese cooking — particularly in ssam (lettuce wrap), salads, and teas — and dense spikes of lavender-purple to pink flowers from midsummer through fall that attract extraordinary numbers of bees and swallowtail butterflies. Distinctly different from the North American native A. foeniculum (anise hyssop) in flavor and growing conditions, though botanically similar. More heat-tolerant and easier in southern gardens. Self-sows freely once established; leave some spent flower stalks for seed to maintain the colony. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Korean Mulberry
description: Plant Morus australis in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment, then reduce as the plant is drought-tolerant once established; prune in winter to shape and control size; harvest berries as they ripen and turn deep purple-black, as they stain readily. Korean Mulberry is the smallest-growing of the commonly cultivated mulberry species — typically maturing as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 5–15 feet tall — making it better suited to smaller gardens than the more vigorous White Mulberry (Morus alba) or American Red Mulberry (Morus rubra). The abundant small to medium berries are very sweet and richly flavored, ripening over several weeks in early to midsummer; birds are strongly attracted to fruiting trees so netting may be needed for a full harvest. In East Asian traditional medicine systems, the berries (sang shen), leaves (sang ye), bark (sang bai pi), and twigs (sang zhi) are all used in herbal preparations for treating conditions ranging from hypertension and diabetes to tinnitus and gray hair. The leaves are used for silkworm (Bombyx mori) cultivation like other mulberry species. Compact enough for container growing in large pots; prune annually to maintain size and maximize fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Korean Perilla (Kkaennip, Korean Sesame Leaf)
description: Sow seeds on the soil surface (they need light to germinate) or barely cover; Korean perilla self-seeds prolifically and will return each year once established — deadhead if you want to control spread. Perilla frutescens var. japonica (Korean perilla, kkaennip, also called Korean sesame leaf or Korean mint) is distinct from the Japanese shiso (var. crispa) in its larger size, rounder leaf shape, flat rather than crinkled leaf margin, thicker leaf texture, and stronger, more complex fragrance — a blend of anise, mint, basil, and sesame that is deeply characteristic of Korean cuisine. The large (3–5 inch), round-oval, bright green leaves (occasionally flushed with purple on the underside) are used in Korean cooking in numerous ways: as ssam wraps for grilled meats (samgyeopsal, bulgogi), as perilla kimchi (kkaennip kimchi), marinated in soy and sesame as a banchan side dish, fried in batter as pajeon ingredients, and as a culinary herb in soups and stews. Distinguished from Japanese shiso by larger leaf size and the more potent, less floral fragrance. Excellent for hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens where it thrives in summer heat; tolerates partial shade. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Korean Pine (Pine Nut)
description: Korean pine is a large, ornamental five-needle pine that produces the large, wingless pine nuts commonly sold in Asian markets — seeds are bigger than those of Italian stone pine and have a rich, buttery flavor. Trees are monoecious and bear cones that ripen over two growing seasons; significant cone production typically begins at 15–25 years from seed. Cones are harvested in early autumn when the scales begin to separate; spread cones on tarps to dry and then beat or tumble to dislodge seeds. The outer seed coat must be cracked to access the edible kernel, which is high in oil and should be refrigerated or frozen to prevent rancidity. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: Korean Radish
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches apart in loose, well-tilled, deep, fertile soil in full sun; Korean radish (mu, 무) is the standard radish of Korean cuisine — a large, stout, mostly white root with a green shoulder, shorter and more rounded than Japanese daikon but crisper, denser, and somewhat spicier. The typical Korean Giant root weighs 1–3 pounds with a firm, juicy, slightly peppery crunch used extensively in kimchi (kkakdugi, cubed radish kimchi), pickled banchan side dishes, and stir-fried radish sides (musaengchae). The flavor is richer and more assertive than mild daikon while remaining far milder than small European radish types. Young tops are also edible and used in soups and kimchi. Harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for the best texture — over-mature Korean radishes become pithy and hollow at the core. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Korean Red Garlic (Vigorous Cold-Hardy Asiatic Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Korean Red is a vigorous Asiatic-type hardneck garlic prized for its early maturity, reliable productivity, and strong, spicy-hot flavor with a pleasant lingering sweetness once cooked. Bulbs are medium-sized with glossy, deep reddish-purple-streaked skin and 6-10 cloves, and the plants tend to size up and mature earlier in the season than many other hardneck types, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early garlic harvest. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect energy into the bulb; the scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Harvest bulbs once the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming and storing; like most hardnecks, storage life is moderate, around 4-6 months. Matures in 230–260 days from transplant.

name: Korean Sancho (Mastic-Leaf Prickly Ash)
description: Korean sancho is a thorny deciduous shrub native to Korea, Japan, and China, closely related to Sichuan pepper and Japanese sansho but distinguished by finer, more feathery compound leaves and smaller, intensely aromatic reddish husks. The dried husks are ground into a numbing, citrusy spice used in Korean cooking, most notably in chueotang (loach soup) and other fish and meat dishes where its sharp, palate-tingling quality cuts through rich or fishy flavors. It is more shade-tolerant than many of its relatives and often grows as an understory shrub at woodland edges, making it adaptable to less-than-full-sun garden spots. Drought-tolerant once established, it fixes no nitrogen itself but is otherwise a low-input shrub, needing only occasional pruning to control size and remove old, unproductive wood. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Korintje Cinnamon (Padang Cinnamon)
description: Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Korintje cinnamon is an Indonesian species from Sumatra that is actually the most commonly sold type of cinnamon in the United States under the generic label 'cinnamon' — accounting for the majority of commercial cinnamon imports. Named for Kota Kerinci in Sumatra, it produces thick, dark-brown bark quills with a strong, mildly sweet flavor intermediate between Ceylon and Chinese cassia cinnamons. The bark is harvested from trees 3–4 years after planting by stripping young branches; coppicing the trees stimulates new shoot production for repeated harvests. Like all commercial cinnamon, the attractive, broad, three-veined leaves are also aromatic when crushed. In zone 9–11, it grows well outdoors as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree; regular harvesting of branches maintains a bushy, productive form suitable for the home garden. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Koroneiki Olive
description: Koroneiki is a productive Greek olive celebrated for generous harvests and a compact, easygoing habit that suits both orchards and patios. Its small fruit yields a robust, high-quality oil, and the silvery evergreen foliage lends year-round Mediterranean charm. Grow a young tree in full sun with sharp drainage and minimal water once established. Prune to keep light reaching the interior, and where winters are cold, grow it in a pot to move to shelter during freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Korsor European Elderberry (Danish Large-Berried Black Elder)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korsor is a Danish selection of European black elder bred for heavy clusters of large, dark, juicy berries and is among the most widely grown cultivars for commercial elderberry juice, syrup, and medicine production in Europe. Broad, flat-topped cymes of creamy white, fragrant flowers open in early summer and are prized for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy, pendant clusters of large blue-black berries ripening in late summer that are rich in anthocyanins. Korsor grows as a vigorous, multi-stemmed shrub to about 6-8 feet and benefits from renewal pruning of older canes each dormant season to maintain vigor and berry size. Provide consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set for the best yields. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Koseret (Ethiopian Culinary Herb)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after frost danger passes; koseret is an aromatic Ethiopian shrub whose dried, crumbled leaves are a foundational seasoning in Ethiopian and Eritrean cooking, most notably in kitfo (spiced raw or lightly cooked minced beef) and gomen (collard-style greens), lending a pungent, herbal, faintly citrusy-minty aroma unlike common Western culinary herbs. Leaves are typically harvested, dried in the shade, and crumbled into a fine seasoning rather than used fresh, concentrating their aromatic oils. The plant grows as a soft-wooded perennial shrub in frost-free tropical and subtropical climates and can be grown as a warm-season annual or container plant that overwinters indoors farther north. Harvest leafy stems regularly through the growing season to encourage bushy new growth, and dry the harvest in a warm, shaded, well-ventilated spot before storing in an airtight container for use throughout the year. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Koshiabura (King of the Sansai)
description: Site this slender understory tree where it gets filtered morning sun or dappled light all day, in loamy soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Once established, harvest the tightly furled terminal buds just as they begin to open each spring, snapping them off the way you would pick asparagus tips. The buds carry a clean, faintly bitter, almost nutty flavor prized across Japan for tempura and quick blanching, and many foragers rank it above other spring shoots for its delicacy. Because it thrives in the dappled light beneath larger trees, it fills a niche few other food crops can occupy in a wooded garden. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kosovo Tomato (Balkan Heirloom Meaty Pink Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Kosovo is a Balkan heirloom valued for large, smooth, pink-red, slightly oxheart-shaped fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor, and it is notably productive for a tomato of its size, setting a heavier crop than many other large-fruited heirlooms of similar fruit weight. The low acidity and thick, low-moisture flesh make it especially good for slicing and sandwiches, since the fruit holds together well without excess juice. The vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking to support the heavy fruit load; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Kossak Kohlrabi (Giant Kohlrabi Variety, Tennis Ball to Softball-Sized with Tender Flesh)
description: Direct sow or transplant in cool soil; keep consistently moist for best growth. Harvest from 3 inches up to 10 inches diameter. Kossak is an F1 hybrid kohlrabi variety developed and introduced by Bejo Seeds (Dutch seed company) specifically for the giant kohlrabi market — a category of extra-large kohlrabi varieties that can reach 6–10 inches in diameter while remaining tender and palatable, unlike standard kohlrabi varieties that become woodily fibrous above 3–4 inches. The distinction between Kossak and standard kohlrabi varieties is fundamental: standard types (Purple Vienna, White Vienna, Early White Vienna) must be harvested promptly at small size or become inedible, while Kossak was specifically selected for an extended harvest window at large sizes. This makes Kossak practical for gardeners who cannot monitor their garden daily, for home gardeners who want a few large plants rather than many small ones, and for fall gardeners who want kohlrabi that overwinters in the ground without quality loss. The bulbs are pale green (white type), extremely smooth-skinned, and can reach weights of 1–2 pounds or more while retaining the characteristic kohlrabi flavor — mild, sweet, slightly peppery, somewhere between broccoli stem and turnip — without the harsh bitterness and woodiness of overmature standard types. The flesh is very juicy and crisp, excellent raw in slaws and salads (where the sweetness is most apparent), roasted (where it caramelizes beautifully), or braised. Kossak is also more cold-hardy than many kohlrabi varieties, holding quality in the garden through light freezes, which extends its usability in zone 9 winter gardens. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Kosui Asian Pear (Early Sweet Japanese Pear, Small Golden Russet Asian Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Kosui requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in late July to August when the golden-brown russet skin reaches full color and fruit gives very slightly under thumb pressure; Kosui has somewhat shorter shelf life than later-season varieties — best consumed within 2–4 weeks of harvest; the small to medium size makes it ideal for single-serving eating straight off the tree. Kosui is a widely grown Japanese pear variety developed through deliberate cross-breeding at the National Institute of Fruit Tree Science in Japan and released in 1959, becoming one of the most popular fresh-eating Asian pear varieties in Japan and increasingly common in American specialty orchards and Asian-American community gardens. The variety's most important attribute for home orchardists is its early ripening season — Kosui typically ripens in late July to August in the Pacific Northwest and mid-Atlantic, 3–6 weeks before mid-season varieties like Hosui and 6–8 weeks before Korean Giant, allowing fresh Asian pear harvest to begin at the height of summer rather than early fall. The fruits are small to medium-sized with golden-brown russet skin and crisp, juicy, very sweet white flesh with a clean, refreshing flavor and aromatic quality. The sweetness and early ripening of Kosui — combined with its thin, tender skin that doesn't need peeling — make it an appealing variety for fresh eating directly from the tree. Productive and reliable in zones 5–9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kotata Blackberry
description: Train the long, trailing canes onto a wire trellis and thin out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the planting productive and easy to pick. Kotata is a vigorous trailing blackberry developed for the Pacific Northwest that produces large, firm, glossy black berries with a rich, tart-sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing into jams and baked goods. It ripens in mid-summer with good yields on second-year canes and holds up well to shipping compared to older trailing types. The canes carry thorns, so gloves and careful trellis training make harvest and maintenance easier. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Krausa Parsley (Curled)
description: Krausa is a German curly-leaf parsley selection known for exceptionally dense, tightly ruffled triple-curled leaves on strong, upright stalks that hold their bright to medium green color well through summer heat. It is notably vigorous and heavy-yielding compared to older curly types, giving multiple cuttings from a single planting. As a biennial it overwinters in mild climates and can be harvested through winter before it flowers and sets seed the following year. Its dense, crisp foliage keeps its texture well after cutting, making it useful both as a fresh garnish and for drying. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Krauter Vesuvius Purple-leaf Plum
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Krauter Vesuvius is one of the darkest-foliaged purple-leaf plum cultivars, unfurling deep purple-black leaves that hold their near-black color through the entire growing season with far less summer fading toward bronze-green than many other purple plum selections. Single, pale pink flowers open very early in spring — often in February in zones 7-9 — before the leaves emerge, followed by an oval, rounded crown of dramatic dark foliage that makes it one of the most striking specimen and accent trees in residential landscaping. It sets little to no fruit compared with the species and green-leaved cultivars, reducing cleanup and self-sown seedlings. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15-25 years) but very fast-growing and reliably floriferous. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Krewer Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Krewer is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh Southern blueberry harvest into midsummer after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, a valuable trait for home gardeners and market growers wanting to spread out the harvest season. The vigorous, productive bushes bear medium to large berries with good flavor and firmness. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Krewer requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other, choosing early- and mid-season partners to spread bloom timing and further extend the overall harvest. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Krishna Tulsi (Purple Holy Basil)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant bushy and productive. Krishna is the deep purple-leaved, purple-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), named for the Hindu deity traditionally depicted with dark blue-purple skin, and valued both for its striking ornamental coloring and its more intensely spicy, peppery, clove-forward flavor compared to the milder green Rama type. The rich purple foliage and purple-tinged flower spikes make it as much an ornamental accent for a sunny herb bed as a culinary and tea herb, and its stronger flavor makes it a favorite for those who prefer a more assertive tulsi tea. Like other holy basil types, it is considered sacred in Hindu tradition and is easy to grow in a warm, sunny herb garden through the summer. Zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Krobonko Luffa
description: This West African heirloom luffa is grown along the Gold Coast of Ghana for its dual harvest: young ridged fruit around 12 inches long can be sliced into soups and stews for a mild, slightly sweet flavor, while fruit left on the vine to fully mature and dry yields a fibrous sponge. Provide a sturdy trellis or arbor, since the vigorous vines can climb well over 15 feet in a single warm season. Give it full sun, evenly moist soil, and a long frost-free season of at least 90 days, switching to a phosphorus-heavy feed once flowering begins to support fruit set. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Krug Yellow Dent Corn (Foundation Iowa Heirloom Dent Corn)
description: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; this is a tall, vigorous dent corn that rewards a full-length warm season. Krug was developed by Iowa farm families in the second half of the 1800s through careful ear-to-row selection and became one of the most influential open-pollinated dent corns in American corn breeding, serving as parent stock for many of the early hybrid corn lines that transformed Corn Belt agriculture in the twentieth century. Its smooth yellow dent kernels grind into hearty cornmeal, and growing it today offers a direct link to the open-pollinated corns that underlie much of modern commercial corn genetics. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Krupnopladnaya Kolomikta Kiwi (Large-Fruited Russian Arctic Beauty Kiwi)
description: Krupnopladnaya (Russian for 'large-fruited') is a Russian selection of Actinidia kolomikta chosen specifically for fruit size well above the species average, while retaining the vine's exceptional cold hardiness. Grow it on a trellis, arbor, or fence in fertile, well-drained soil with dappled light, since strong afternoon sun can scorch the foliage in warmer climates. The grape-sized, smooth green kiwiberries ripen unevenly over several weeks in late summer and drop when ripe, so harvest daily from a tarp or by hand-picking softened fruit. Because the species is dioecious, pair one male vine with several Krupnopladnaya females for reliable, heavy fruit set. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Krymsk 86 Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Krymsk 86 is a semi-dwarfing understock bred for wet-soil and disease tolerance. Bred at a research station in Krymsk, Russia, from a cross of cherry plum and peach, this modern semi-dwarfing rootstock produces a tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a standard seedling peach tree, with notably better tolerance of heavy, wet, or poorly drained soils than most other peach and plum rootstocks, along with strong anchorage that generally does not require permanent staking. Its combination of size control, wet-soil tolerance, and good resistance to some soil-borne diseases has made it an increasingly popular choice for stone fruit orchards on less-than-ideal soils. Graft a desired named peach, plum, or apricot variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect strong, well-anchored growth even in soils too wet for many other stone fruit rootstocks. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: KSU-Atwood Pawpaw
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can handle full sun. KSU-Atwood is a Kentucky State University research program release bred from Atwood x Overleese parentage, chosen for consistently large, well-filled fruit with rich, sweet flesh and a relatively low seed count for the species. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, ripening their crop in the midseason window and holding fruit quality well compared to many wild seedling trees. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce in home gardens. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: KSU-Benson Pawpaw
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can tolerate full sun. KSU-Benson is a Kentucky State University pawpaw research program release, selected alongside sibling cultivars like KSU-Atwood for good fruit size and flavor from the university's decades-long regional germplasm evaluation program. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, bearing medium-to-large fruit with smooth, rich, custardy flesh in the late-summer harvest window typical of named pawpaw selections. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 50 feet, and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, faintly unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce around home gardens. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: KSU-Chappell Pawpaw (Kentucky State University Large-Fruited Selection)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, siting the tree in partial shade for its first few years before it can handle more sun as it matures. Released in 2018 by Kentucky State University's pawpaw breeding program, following the earlier KSU-Atwood and KSU-Benson introductions, KSU-Chappell is an extremely vigorous, high-yielding cultivar that in multi-year trials averaged notably larger fruit than the widely grown Susquehanna while carrying a comparably low percentage of seed by weight. The creamy flesh has a mild banana-pineapple flavor with floral notes that ripens mid-season, typically September into October. Like all pawpaws, it is self-incompatible and pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so plant a second, unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small brush to improve fruit set in a home orchard. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ku Shen (Shrubby Sophora Root)
description: Concentrated extracts of this root are not intended for prolonged internal use without professional guidance due to potential liver-related concerns. Scarify and soak the hard legume seed before starting indoors in early spring, then transplant out after frost into deep, well-drained soil, since the developing taproot resents later disturbance. Roots are harvested from plants three to four years old and traditionally decocted or used in topical washes in TCM to relieve itching and eczema-type skin conditions and as a folk antiparasitic. Matures in 1095–1460 days from seed.

name: Kuching Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, training the vine up a sturdy support post. Also known locally as Sarawak pepper, Kuching is the leading cultivar grown across Sarawak, Malaysia, prized internationally for producing unusually large, dense berry clusters that give Sarawak black and white pepper their reputation for superior pungency, aroma, and heavier grain weight than pepper from many other origins. It is a moderately vigorous vine that rewards the intensive fertilization typical of Malaysian pepper gardens with heavy, consistent yields. Maintain warmth above 60°F with high humidity and consistent soil moisture, and expect the vine to reach full production within a few years of establishment. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Kuganskaya Quince (Cold-Hardy Russian Heirloom Quince)
description: Kuganskaya is a quince selection out of southern Russia bred specifically for cold tolerance well beyond what most quince cultivars can survive, making it a rare option for growers in colder climates who still want a true quince harvest. The tree forms a compact, rounded small tree and blooms with the pale pink flowers typical of the species before setting medium-sized, golden-yellow, strongly aromatic fruit that ripens in the second half of fall. Like other quince, the raw flesh is dense and astringent and must be cooked to soften into the rosy, honeyed preserves, paste, and jelly the fruit is prized for. It is self-fertile and needs no second tree, and an open, well-pruned canopy helps guard against fire blight in humid regions. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kujo Negi Bunching Onion
description: Kujo Negi is a traditional Kyoto brand vegetable recorded since the Edo period, prized for its exceptionally dark green, tender, glossy leaves and mild, slightly sweet flavor compared to Western scallions. Sow thickly in a nursery row and transplant into trenches, hilling soil up gradually as the plants grow to blanch a long white base similar to a leek, or grow it more thickly spaced for a scallion-style harvest. It tolerates cold well and is traditionally harvested through Kyoto winters, when cold exposure sweetens the leaves for use in nabe hot pots, yakitori, and miso soup. Because it does not form a bulb, cut-and-come-again harvesting of outer leaves from an established clump extends the picking season. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Kuling Chinese Chestnut (Historic Early USDA Introduction, Dunstan Parent Stock)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Kuling holds a special place in American chestnut breeding history as one of the original Chinese chestnut selections introduced by the USDA in the early twentieth century in the search for blight-resistant chestnuts to replace the vanishing American chestnut, and its genetics were later used as founding parent stock in developing the widely planted Dunstan hybrid chestnut line. It carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight and produces medium-sized, sweet, reliably annual nut crops, dropping free of the spiny burr in October for easy collection. Space trees widely for their broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for best nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kumquat
description: Kumquats are the hardiest of the citrus family and the only ones whose entire fruit — sweet peel and tangy flesh — is eaten whole. They are self-fertile and well-suited to container growing in zones 7–8, where they can be overwintered indoors. Unlike other citrus, kumquats go dormant more readily in winter, which improves their cold hardiness. Fruit ripens from late autumn through winter; harvest when fully orange and sweet-peel is prominent. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kuno Wase Satsuma (Early-Season Cold-Hardy Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season. Kuno Wase ripens in October, among the earliest of the satsuma strains, with small-to-medium, seedless, loose-skinned mandarins of good sweet-tart flavor that reliably mature before the first hard freeze in Gulf Coast and lower-South climates. Mature, dormant trees tolerate brief drops to roughly 15-20F; protect young trees with frost cloth for the first two or three winters until the root system matures. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Kunth's Wild Onion (Texas Wild Garlic)
description: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Kunth's wild onion is one of the most widespread and important edible native alliums of Texas and the American Southwest — a spring-blooming, small wild onion native to the limestone hills, Rocky Mountain foothills, and Chihuahuan Desert mountains of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it has been harvested and eaten by indigenous peoples for thousands of years as a wild food plant. The bulbs and leaves both have a strong onion-garlic flavor and aroma, usable in the same ways as domestic onions and garlic — raw, cooked, pickled. The spring flowers are produced in small, rounded umbels of white to pale pink to deep pink star-shaped florets on stems 8–16 inches tall, serving as pollinators for native bees and beetles. In the garden it provides both a wildflower display in spring and an edible wild-food plant for harvesting — a dual-purpose native species for the Texas-Southwest edible landscape and native plant garden. The strong garlic-onion scent immediately identifies it as edible and distinguishes it safely from the non-scented, potentially toxic Nothoscordum bivalve (crow poison) with which it sometimes grows. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Kurinishiki Kabocha Winter Squash
description: Direct sow this compact Japanese kabocha after the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep in hills spaced 3 to 4 feet apart in full sun. Each vine produces small 3 to 4 pound fruits with sweet, fine-grained flesh reminiscent of sweet potato. Allow the squash to mature fully on the vine until the rind hardens and the stem corks, then cure in a warm spot to improve storage and flavor. Give the vines room to sprawl and provide steady moisture, especially while fruit is sizing up. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Kurle Pawpaw (Michigan Davis-Line Seedling Selection)
description: Kurle originated in Michigan as a seedling selection from the Davis pawpaw line, one of breeder Corwin Davis's influential mid-20th-century wild selections. Fruit is small to medium in size with yellow flesh and yellow skin, similar in character to its Davis parentage. Like other named pawpaws, Kurle needs cross-pollination from a genetically distinct second tree to set a reliable crop. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Kuroshinju Black Edamame Soybean
description: Sow seed an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean rhizobium if soybeans are new to the bed. Kuroshinju, meaning 'black pearl' in Japanese, is a rare heirloom edamame prized for its striking black seed coat and rich, nutty, sweeter-than-average flavor, borne two to three beans per pod on upright, 2 to 2.5 foot plants. Harvest at the green-shell stage, while pods are fully plump and still green with just a cast of black showing through, rather than waiting for the beans to dry and darken completely. Steam or boil briefly in salted water and pop the beans free of the pod for eating fresh. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Kurrat (Egyptian Leek)
description: Kurrat is the same species as leek and elephant garlic but is grown exclusively for its flat, garlicky-oniony foliage rather than a swollen shank or bulb, and it is a staple flavoring green in Egyptian and eastern Mediterranean kitchens. Broadcast or drill seed thickly into rich, well-drained soil, since plants are grown in dense clumps rather than as individually spaced bulbs. Once shoots reach 8–10 in, cut foliage back to about 2 in above the crown; the clump will resprout, allowing several successive harvests over the cool season. Established clumps can also be divided in fall to propagate new plantings vegetatively. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Kurt Creeping Lemon Thyme
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, since this thyme rots quickly in heavy, wet ground over winter. Kurt was collected in Thracia by Kurt Reschke and introduced into cultivation by German nurseryman Werner Simon around 2000, and it forms a dense, ground-hugging mat of small, dark green, distinctly lemon-scented leaves that stays lower and more prostrate than the broader-leaved species type. Clusters of pink-purple flowers splashed with dark crimson appear in summer and draw bees steadily, while the lemon-flavored leaves and flowers can season fish and vegetable dishes much like common lemon thyme. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and prevent the woody center from opening up, and use it between stepping stones or trailing over a wall where its low, spreading habit can be appreciated up close. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Kurtovska Kapia Pepper (Bulgarian Heirloom Sweet Pepper)
description: Kurtovska Kapia is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom sweet pepper from the Plovdiv area of central southern Bulgaria, recognized on Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a distinctive regional food. Plants stay relatively low and bushy but produce heavy, hanging clusters of large, flattened, heart-shaped pods that ripen from dark green to deep red with tender, juicy, notably sweet flesh. Its broad, meaty shoulders and pointed tip typify the wider kapia class of Balkan and Turkish sweet peppers used fresh, roasted, or preserved into spreads such as lutenitsa and ajvar. Because fruit is often left to fully redden before harvest for maximum sweetness, this variety benefits from a long, warm growing season. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Kuwini Mango (Fragrant Mango, Huani)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Kuwini mango is similar in requirements to common mango but more frost-sensitive. Mangifera odorata (Kuwini mango or fragrant mango) is a species in the Anacardiaceae family related to common mango (M. indica), native to the Malay Peninsula and the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, producing small to medium-sized, oval, green to yellowish fruits with extraordinarily intense mango-floral fragrance — the most powerfully aromatic of all Mangifera species. The fresh fruit has a strong turpentine-floral aroma detectable at a considerable distance, with yellow-orange flesh that is significantly more fibrous than commercial mangoes and with more resinous flavor notes. While less pleasant to eat out of hand than polished commercial mango varieties, Kuwini is prized in Malaysia and Indonesia for juice, juice blends, mango lassi-type drinks, ice cream, and traditional sambal sauces where the intense fragrance shines through processing. The skin of the fruit also yields a yellow dye. The tree is also notable as one of the parents in the natural hybrid origin of common mango's wild ancestors. In zone 11–12 tropical fruit collections, Kuwini is a valuable diversity addition for those wanting the full spectrum of Mangifera species. Very rare in cultivation outside Southeast Asia. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kwai Mi Lychee
description: One of the oldest and most historically important Chinese lychee cultivars, Kwai Mi forms a tall, upright, vigorous tree that matures a heavy flush of large clusters in May and June, with pink-to-red, bumpy-skinned fruit running around 30 to the pound. The flesh is sweet, fragrant, and juicy with a pleasing balance of crispness and tenderness, though bearing can be inconsistent outside of favorable years. New growth emerges coppery-bronze before turning dark green, and abundant yellow spring flower panicles give it an ornamental character distinct from smoother-leaved cultivars like Mauritius. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Kwik-Krop Black Walnut (Precocious Early-Bearing Selection)
description: Kwik-Krop is a long-circulated named black walnut selection prized chiefly for its precocity, beginning to set nuts within about six years of grafting, well ahead of most seedling trees and many other named cultivars that take a decade or more to reach bearing age. It has been used alongside cultivars such as Emma K and Sparks 127 in University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry flavor and quality evaluations of grafted black walnut selections. Plant it in deep, well-drained loam in full sun with generous room to mature into a large shade tree, and pair it with a second black walnut cultivar nearby to improve nut set through cross-pollination. Like all black walnuts, its roots, hulls, and leaf litter exude juglone, so keep tomatoes, apples, and other juglone-sensitive species well outside the eventual dripline. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Kwintus Pole Bean (Early Riser Dutch Flat-Podded Snap Bean)
description: Kwintus, also sold as Early Riser, is a Dutch-bred flat-podded pole bean that combines the buttery texture of an Italian Romano type with unusually early maturity for a climbing bean. Pods grow 8-10 inches long, broad and stringless, and stay tender and flavorful even as they size up on the vine, which makes for a more forgiving harvest window than narrow round-podded snap beans. Vigorous 6-9 foot vines need sturdy support and reward regular picking with continuous production through the season. Its combination of early cropping and long harvest tolerance has made it a favorite among market gardeners and home growers alike. Matures in 55–62 days from seed.

name: Kyona Mizuna (Japanese Feathery Mustard Green)
description: Sow seed thinly a quarter inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to reduce crowding once established. This selected mizuna strain produces dense clumps of finely serrated, feathery dark-green leaves with slender white stalks and holds flavor well without becoming overly pungent. Harvest outer leaves continually for salads and stir-fries, or cut the whole plant an inch above the crown for regrowth. Bolts in sustained heat, so it performs best as a spring or autumn crop. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Kyoto Market Bunching Onion
description: Kyoto Market is a vigorous, fast-growing Japanese bunching onion long associated with the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of the Kyoto region, prized for its long, straight white shanks and heavy, uniform yields. Sow seed directly and thin as stalks develop, harvesting young plants as slender scallions or letting them grow thicker without losing tenderness or flavor. Hilling soil around the base as the plants grow lengthens the blanched white portion for a more traditional Japanese-style leek-like scallion. Its disease resistance and tolerance of both heat and cold make Kyoto Market a reliable choice for extended-season plantings from spring through fall. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Kyoto Red Carrot (Kintoki, Japanese New Year Heirloom)
description: Sow seed thinly in deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart, since this variety needs a long, undisturbed taproot run to reach its full 10- to 12-inch length. Kyoto Red, also known as Kintoki carrot, is a traditional Japanese heirloom prized for its striking, uniformly deep red-orange color that holds even after cooking, along with a sweet, dense flesh valued in Japanese New Year dishes and simmered preparations. It grows more slowly than Western carrot types and performs best with a long, cool finish, so a late-summer sowing timed to mature through fall and winter gives the best color and flavor. Harvest once roots reach full size and store dug roots cool and slightly moist for extended keeping. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Kyzyl Shala Upland Rice
description: Kyzyl Shala is a landrace upland rice from Uzbekistan prized for being one of the earliest-ripening rices available to home growers, often setting harvestable grain within about three months of transplanting. Its long, colorful awns are a landrace trait that helps deter birds from stripping the ripening panicles, a useful feature for gardeners without netting. Plants stay compact and stand well without lodging, and the purplish hulls with light brown bran make it easy to spot at harvest time. Because it does not require flooding, it can be grown as a dryland crop with attentive watering rather than a true paddy. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: La Crescent Grape (Cold-Hardy Aromatic White Wine Grape)
description: La Crescent is a University of Minnesota-bred white wine grape prized for its intensely aromatic fruit, with apricot, citrus, and honeysuckle notes reminiscent of Muscat and Riesling. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its Minnesota-bred siblings, tolerating winter lows near -30°F, but ripens its fruit with very high sugar and high acid simultaneously, which winemakers use to produce off-dry or dessert-style wines. The compact clusters are prone to bunch rot in wet years, so growers benefit from leaf pulling around the fruit zone to improve airflow and sun exposure. Vigorous shoot growth means canopy management and cluster thinning are needed to avoid overcropping thin canes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: LA Early Satsuma (Louisiana Early Satsuma Mandarin)
description: LA Early was selected by the LSU AgCenter citrus breeding program from open-pollinated seedlings planted in the late 1960s at the Citrus Research Station in Port Sulphur, Louisiana, and released for its unusually early ripening window. Trees are medium-sized with a spreading, drooping, thornless habit and set fruit heavily and evenly through the canopy. Fruit is medium-to-large, oblate, thin-skinned, essentially seedless, and ready to pick from early September into mid-October, well ahead of standard Owari satsuma. As with other satsumas, cold hardiness is good for citrus but root zones should be mulched and young trees protected during hard freezes in zone 8b plantings. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: La Feliciana Peach
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; La Feliciana is a freestone peach developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1978, specifically bred for the Gulf Coast South and named for the historic peach-growing region around St. Francisville, Louisiana. With a chill requirement of approximately 450 hours, it is well-matched to the inland Gulf South (zones 7b–8b) where more heat-sensitive northern varieties struggle through summer but standard low-chill Florida varieties lack enough winter cold. Fruit quality is excellent — large, yellow-fleshed, fully freestone with rich, classic peach flavor ripening in late May to June in Louisiana and Mississippi. Trees are vigorous and productive, with good disease tolerance under Gulf Coast conditions. La Feliciana is considered a benchmark variety for Louisiana peach production and is widely sold at regional nurseries. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches in April for full-sized fruit; prune to an open center after leaf drop. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: La Festival Peach
description: Another LSU-bred freestone peach recommended for south Louisiana home orchards, ripening in late June with large yellow fruit streaked red and vigorous, productive trees. It pairs well with earlier-ripening La Peche to extend the harvest window on a small Gulf Coast home orchard.
