Site trees in full sun with excellent drainage, since peach roots are highly intolerant of standing water common after Gulf Coast summer downpours, and maintain a regular fungicide schedule to manage brown rot and scab in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: La Peche Peach
description: An LSU AgCenter release bred specifically for the low-chill winters of the Gulf South, producing heavy crops of medium-to-large, red-fuzzed, semi-freestone fruit with sweet golden flesh flecked red, ripening in mid-to-late June. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and prune to an open-center vase shape to let light into the canopy and reduce brown rot pressure in humid conditions. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart in April to improve size, and watch for bacterial leaf spot and peach tree borer, both common on Gulf Coast stone fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: La Ratte Fingerling Potato (Classic French Gourmet Fingerling)
description: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. La Ratte is a classic French fingerling potato long prized by chefs for its exceptionally rich, nutty, almost chestnut-like flavor and dense, waxy, pale yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled or roasted whole. The small, knobby, finger-shaped tubers mature over a somewhat longer season than standard round potatoes and yield less per plant, but the superior flavor has made it a long-standing favorite for specialty and high-end cooking. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and die back, and handle the thin-skinned tubers gently, since they bruise more easily than thicker-skinned storage potatoes. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Lacatan Banana (Historic Caribbean Cavendish)
description: Lacatan is a tall Cavendish subgroup clone that was the dominant Caribbean and Philippine export banana in the mid-twentieth century, valued for large bunches of sweet fruit before shorter, sturdier Cavendish clones like Grand Nain and Valery largely replaced it commercially. It grows into a large, heavy plant that benefits from deep fertile soil, generous spacing, and firm staking once the fruiting stalk begins to lean under bunch weight. Water deeply and feed through the growing season to support its broad leaf canopy, and expect a single bunch per pseudostem before cutting it back for a sucker. Given its height and lack of cold tolerance, grow it as a warm, sheltered specialty planting in zone 9a rather than an unprotected permanent planting. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Lacinato Dinosaur Kale
description: Sow this 18th-century Tuscan heirloom in early spring for a summer harvest or in mid to late summer for fall and winter greens, as its flavor sweetens after frost. Direct sow a half inch deep and thin seedlings to 12 to 18 inches apart. Harvest tender young leaves as salad greens in about 21 days, or let plants mature for full-size, strap-shaped dark blue-green leaves prized by cooks. Pick outer leaves first to keep plants producing over a long season, and provide steady moisture for tender growth. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Lacinato Kale
description: Also known as dinosaur or Tuscan kale, this heirloom features deep blue-green, bumpy-textured leaves with rich, mild flavor. Sow directly in spring or late summer, as it is a cold-hardy crop whose flavor sweetens after a frost. Thin plants to give the tall, upright rosettes room to develop. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up, letting the center keep producing for a long, continuous cutting season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Lacinato Kale
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost or start indoors in early spring; lacinato kale (also called dinosaur kale, Tuscan kale, or cavolo nero) forms tall, upright plants with long, strap-like, deeply puckered, blue-black to dark-green leaves with a more tender texture and milder, slightly sweeter flavor than curly kale. It is one of the foundational vegetables of Tuscan cuisine, essential in ribollita and minestrone. Harvest by removing outer leaves as needed, working from the bottom of the stem upward — plants will continue producing from fall through winter and into spring in mild climates. Flavor intensifies significantly after frost exposure. A more elegant, slower-maturing, and culinary-preferred alternative to curly kale for the kitchen garden. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Laciniata Elderberry (Cutleaf European Black Elderberry)
description: Laciniata is one of the oldest recorded elder cultivars, prized since at least the 17th century for its deeply cut, almost fern-like or parsley-like green foliage that gives the whole shrub a soft, airy texture unlike the coarse leaves of wild elder. Creamy white flat-topped flower clusters appear in early summer followed by small black berries, though it is grown chiefly as a foliage and texture accent in mixed borders rather than for harvest. Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the most finely divided leaves, and prune hard in late winter to renew vigorous, well-cut foliage each season, since older wood tends to produce coarser leaves. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lady Cream Pea (Lady Pea)
description: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in any well-drained, lean soil in full sun after last frost; Lady cream pea is a traditional Southern heirloom cowpea producing small, white, round peas with a notably sweet, mild, delicate flavor — milder and less earthy than crowder peas or black-eyed peas, and considered by many Southern pea aficionados to have the finest flavor of all the cream peas for fresh eating and freezing. The small size and mild sweetness make it the variety most often served to guests unfamiliar with Southern peas, as the flavor is more approachable and universally liked. A true bush-type plant that is drought-tolerant once established; performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast. Excellent boiled simply with butter and salt and served as a side dish, or incorporated into succotash, hoppin' John, and traditional Southern vegetable plates. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Lady Finger Banana (Sugar Banana, Fig Banana)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Finger banana (also called Sugar Banana, Sucrier, or 'Fig Banana') is an AAB genome group banana producing long, thin, elegant fruits (4–5 inches long but unusually slender) with delicate, thin, easily peeled skin and exceptionally sweet, rich, aromatic flavor — widely regarded as one of the finest-flavored fresh-eating bananas available, with a honey-like sweetness and floral aroma that surpasses standard Cavendish bananas. The fruits are produced in large bunches of 12–20 fingers per hand, and the delicate thin skin means they do not ship well commercially (hence their relative scarcity in supermarkets despite their superior flavor), making Lady Finger an excellent choice for the home gardener who wants superior banana flavor and can eat the fruits promptly at ripeness. The tall (12–18 foot) plants produce large ornamental pseudostems with broad tropical leaves; they are truly tropical and suffer pseudostem dieback in any freeze but the rhizomes can survive to about 28–30°F with heavy mulching in zone 9b. Grow in the warmest, most protected microclimate available in zone 9. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lady Godiva Pumpkin
description: This heirloom is grown for its unique hulless seeds, which are soft-shelled pepitas that need no peeling for roasting or snacking. Sow directly into warm, rich soil after frost, giving the vines plenty of room to spread. Keep moisture and nutrients steady as fruit develops. Harvest the mature pumpkins, then scoop and dry the green hulless seeds for a homegrown supply of pepitas. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Lady Lavender (AAS-Winning First-Year-Flowering English Lavender)
description: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination, and expect uneven sprouting over 1-3 weeks even under ideal conditions. 'Lady' won the 1994 All-America Selections award as the first lavender ever to receive the honor, prized for its ability to bloom in dense, fragrant violet-purple spikes within five to six months of sowing rather than requiring a full second season like open-pollinated English lavender. Its compact, tidy, upright habit and uniform seedling growth make it well suited to mass plantings, edging, and containers where consistent size matters. Once established, treat it like any English lavender: provide sharp drainage, full sun, and avoid overwatering, and it will persist as a hardy perennial well beyond its first flowering season in zones 5-9. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Lady Plymouth Rose Geranium
description: Root Lady Plymouth cuttings in lean, well-drained soil and grow in full sun to partial shade with light, infrequent watering, allowing soil to dry between waterings; overly rich soil or heavy shade will dull both the variegation and the fragrance. Pinch stems regularly to maintain a full, shrubby shape and remove any all-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegated pattern true. The finely dissected, rose-and-lemon-scented leaves are used exactly like standard Rose Geranium — infused in sugar, cream, and jellies, or added fresh to fruit salads and iced drinks — while the cream-edged foliage additionally makes this one of the most ornamental scented geraniums for mixed containers and hanging baskets. Bring indoors well before first frost as a houseplant, since it has no cold hardiness. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Lady Williams Apple (Late-Ripening Western Australian Parent of Pink Lady)
description: Lady Williams was discovered as a chance seedling near Donnybrook, Western Australia in the 1930s by orchardist A.G. Williams, and is remarkable for ripening later than almost any other apple, often hanging on the tree into early winter in its home climate. John Cripps used it as the pollen parent, crossed onto Golden Delicious, to breed both Cripps Pink (Pink Lady) and Sundowner, passing on its deep red color, dense storage-friendly flesh, and unusually low chill requirement for a full-sized apple. The fruit itself is small to medium, very firm, and tart when picked, mellowing into a crisp, tangy apple useful for fresh eating and cooking after some storage. Its low chill requirement and heat tolerance during the long finishing period make it one of the few apples that can be grown to full maturity in mild-winter, warm-autumn climates. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lady's Bedstraw
description: Galium verum is a slender, scrambling, rhizomatous perennial herb of dry grasslands and hedgerows throughout Europe and temperate Asia, producing whorls of very fine, needle-like, dark-green leaves along square stems and masses of tiny, four-petaled, honey-scented, bright-yellow flowers in dense, frothy panicles from early to mid summer; the whole plant when dried emits a pleasant, sweet, coumarin-like (new-mown hay) fragrance. Direct-sow seeds in fall in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline, calcareous soil in a sunny or lightly shaded position; seeds benefit from cold stratification and germinate most reliably after a natural winter cold period — established plants spread by shallow rhizomes to form loose, weed-suppressing mats. Lady's bedstraw has a rich history of traditional use: the flowering tops were used to curdle milk in cheese-making (especially for Cheshire and Gloucester cheeses, as a vegetable rennet substitute), and the roots yield a warm red to orange dye with an alum mordant, while the stems and flowers produce yellow; the dried plant was historically stuffed into mattresses and strewn underfoot for its pleasant scent and supposed flea-repelling properties. Tolerant of drought and coastal conditions once established; excellent for naturalizing in wild or meadow gardens with other dry-grassland species. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Lady's Thumb (Redshank)
description: Lady's thumb is a sprawling summer annual in the knotweed family, easily identified by the dark, thumbprint-shaped smudge on each narrow leaf and the small, bottlebrush-like pink flower spikes it produces from midsummer into fall. The young leaves and tender stem tips have a mild, slightly peppery flavor similar to a soft watercress and can be added raw to salads or cooked briefly as a potherb, though larger, older leaves turn tougher and are better cooked. It thrives in the moist, partly shaded, disturbed soil found at the edge of vegetable beds, compost areas, and rain gardens where few deliberately planted greens compete well, and self-sows freely once established. Harvest continuously through summer by pinching tips, which also helps limit how much the plant spreads by seed. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Lagos Spinach (Soko Yokoto, Edible Celosia Greens)
description: Lagos spinach is the same species as ornamental cockscomb and plumed celosia, but grown as a leaf vegetable across West Africa, where the mild, slightly peppery young leaves and tender stem tips known as soko yokoto are a staple green in soups and stews. Sow thickly and thin as you harvest, since crowding the plants slightly keeps the leaves tender and the plants from bolting to flower too quickly in long, hot days. Harvest by pinching young leaves and shoot tips starting around a month after sowing, which also delays flowering and keeps the plant producing tender new growth for weeks. It tolerates heat and some drought better than spinach or lettuce, making it a dependable summer green when cool-season leafy crops have failed. Cook briefly by steaming or sautéing, similar to amaranth greens, to preserve texture and nutrients. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Lakadong Turmeric
description: Lakadong is a high-curcumin turmeric selection originating from the Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, prized by growers and herbalists for curcumin content that runs well above ordinary supermarket turmeric. Plant finger rhizomes in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade once the soil has warmed in spring, and keep the bed evenly moist through the long frost-free growing season the crop needs to bulk up. Foliage dies back naturally in fall, signaling that rhizomes are ready to dig, cure, and either replant or process into powder; in zone 9a, lift and store rhizomes indoors over winter rather than relying on the ground to protect them. The deep-orange flesh and intense color make Lakadong a favorite for home turmeric powder as well as fresh-root use. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Lake Emerald Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Florida Wine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing extra space between vines since Lake Emerald is a vigorous grower recommended for wider row spacing than most other Florida bunch grapes. Developed by the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program at Leesburg, it is prized for strong resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by leafhoppers that has historically limited grape growing across the humid Gulf South, and it does not require grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in soils with a naturally high pH. It produces light green, juicy berries used mainly for wine and juice or jelly rather than fresh eating, ripening in midsummer just after the purple 'Blue Lake' cultivar. As with other Florida bunch grapes, a preventive fungicide spray program through the growing season is important to control the fungal fruit rots that thrive in hot, humid weather, and vines should be pruned hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lakeland Limequat (Cold-Hardy Round Kumquat-Lime Hybrid)
description: Lakeland was released in 1913 as one of three original USDA limequats bred by Walter Swingle from a cross of Key lime and round (Meiwa/Marumi-type) kumquat, sharing its exact parentage with the far more widely planted Eustis limequat from the same breeding batch. Like Eustis, the small, gold-orange fruit combines a genuinely tart lime-flavored interior with an edible, mild, sweet kumquat rind, so the whole fruit can be eaten out of hand, sliced into drinks, or preserved. It carries the same strong cold tolerance that makes limequats useful where true limes cannot survive outdoors, but nurseries propagated Eustis far more heavily over the following century, leaving Lakeland a comparatively rare named selection today. Grow it exactly as you would Eustis, in full sun and well-drained soil, with winter protection while young and full sun exposure to maximize fruit sweetness. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lakemont Grape (Seedless White Table Grape)
description: Developed at the Geneva, New York experiment station, Lakemont is one of the most widely planted seedless table grapes for home gardens in cold-winter regions, producing large, loose clusters of sweet, crisp, pale green berries. It ripens in early to mid-season and holds its quality well on the vine, making it forgiving for gardeners who cannot harvest the moment it peaks. The vine is vigorous and productive, so cluster and shoot thinning improve berry size and air circulation. It is considerably more cold-hardy than European seedless types like Thompson Seedless. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lakota Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Large-Nut Pecan)
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually and prune to maintain an open canopy for airflow and scab management. Lakota Pecan was released through the USDA Agricultural Research Service pecan breeding program as a scab-resistant alternative to older, disease-prone standards, combining good resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) with a large, attractive, thin-shelled nut and high kernel percentage that appeals to growers who want commercial-quality size without the heavy fungicide program that susceptible varieties demand in humid regions. The tree bears at a moderate age and produces consistent, mid-season crops of good-quality nuts well suited to both fresh eating and baking. Its disease resistance and nut size make it a strong choice for Gulf South and Midsouth home orchards and small commercial plantings seeking reduced-spray management, in zone 6–9. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Lakota Squash (Native American Heirloom Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after soil warms; provide 4–8 feet of vine space; harvest when the skin hardens completely and can no longer be dented with a fingernail, and the stem begins to dry and cork; cure at room temperature for 10–14 days after harvest to develop optimal flavor and maximize storage life. Lakota squash is an heirloom winter squash associated with the Lakota (Sioux) people of the Great Plains, one of the native peoples of North America who cultivated squash as a primary food staple long before European contact. The variety produces one of the most visually distinctive squashes in cultivation: teardrop or pear-shaped fruits with deep orange-red skin boldly marked with irregular splotches and streaks of dark green and near-black — a coloration so striking that Lakota is as ornamental as it is edible. The flesh is the intensely orange, dry, sweet, and finely textured type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties: rich enough to need nothing added beyond butter and salt, sweet enough to serve as dessert, and dry enough to bake or purée without becoming watery. The flavor is often compared favorably to kabocha and red kuri squash — comparable sweetness and dryness but with a distinctive terroir-like richness that differentiates it from commercial varieties. Lakota stores exceptionally well — 4–6 months under cool, dry conditions — making it a true long-keeping winter provision. Average fruits weigh 5–8 lbs with moderate vine length suitable for home gardens. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Lakota Winter Squash
description: Direct sow this vigorous heirloom squash in warm soil, planting in hills spaced well apart to accommodate 10 to 20 foot vines. Beyond its striking orange and green coloring, Lakota is a superior baking variety with fine-grained, sweet, nutty flesh. Let the pear-shaped fruits ripen fully and the rind harden before harvesting, then cure in a warm, dry spot to improve storage life. Give the sprawling vines full sun and consistent moisture while the fruit develops. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Lamb Black Walnut (High-Yield Nut-Quality Cultivar)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. Lamb is a named black walnut selection valued by nut growers for combining good kernel percentage and cracking quality with strong, consistent annual bearing, an important trait in a species that can otherwise produce heavily only every second year. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it grows into a large, long-lived shade tree over time, so it is best suited to a large property, orchard row, or field edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly to prevent kernel discoloration, and grafted trees typically begin bearing within six to ten years, considerably sooner than seedling trees. Rake and dispose of fallen husks away from lawns and walkways, since they stain concrete and skin on contact. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Lamb Hass Avocado
description: A Hass-type seedling selection, Lamb Hass is distinguished by flat, squared shoulders rather than Hass's smoothly curved profile, and by pebbly skin that stays very dark green before darkening further toward black as it fully ripens. Trees grow upright and compact but produce noticeably larger fruit than standard Hass, typically 10 to 18 ounces, and ripen later in the season, extending the black-skinned avocado harvest into early winter after Hass has finished. The rich, smooth, nutty flesh flavor closely echoes Hass itself, making Lamb Hass useful mainly as a season-extending companion rather than a flavor departure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lamb's Quarters
description: Scatter seeds on bare soil and press firmly; lamb’s quarters germinates readily and requires virtually no care once established. Harvest young leaves and stem tips continuously — they taste similar to spinach, raw or cooked, and are exceptionally high in vitamins A, C, and calcium. The mealy white coating on new leaves is a natural wax secretion. Allow a few plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-sowing colony; mature seeds can be dried and cooked like quinoa. Plants grow rapidly in rich soil and may reach 6 feet if left unchecked. Matures in 35–55 days from seed.

name: Lambkin Melon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Charentais-Type Melon)
description: Lambkin is a Burpee-introduced, All-America Selections-winning melon bred to bring French Charentais-style eating quality to a compact vine and an early, personal-size fruit about the size of a small cantaloupe. The smooth, lightly ribbed gray-green rind encloses deep orange, richly perfumed flesh with the concentrated sweetness and floral aroma typical of Charentais types, but on a plant far more manageable than the long-vining French heirlooms it descends from. Grow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture steady through fruit set and easing off as the small melons approach ripeness to intensify their sugars. Because Charentais-type melons slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily near the expected harvest window and watch for a softening and light cracking at the stem end as the surest sign of peak flavor. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Lambrook Silver Cotton Lavender (Fine-Leaved Gray Santolina)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this selection needs the same superb drainage as the species and will rot in wet or humid, poorly aerated soil. 'Lambrook Silver' is a widely grown cultivar selected for finer, more feathery, more intensely silver-white foliage than the species, giving it a softer, lacier texture that is especially prized in knot gardens and silver borders. It produces the same small, bright-yellow, button-like flower heads in midsummer, though many gardeners shear the flower buds off to keep the foliage effect uninterrupted. Trim after flowering (or in place of flowering) to maintain a dense, rounded habit and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Lambsquarters (Fat Hen, White Goosefoot, Pigweed)
description: Allow to grow voluntarily in garden beds or scatter seeds on soil surface in early spring; lambsquarters is arguably the most nutritious common garden weed available as a potherb, with leaves containing more calcium, iron, and vitamins A and C than most cultivated greens. The young growing tips and leaves have a mild, spinach-like flavor that is excellent raw in salads when small or steamed, sautéed, or added to soups and egg dishes when older. The mealy white coating on young leaves is normal and edible — it is not pesticide or mildew. The seed heads, when mature in late summer, can be eaten cooked as a grain similar to quinoa (they are closely related). Control by harvesting regularly before seed set; one plant can produce 70,000 seeds that remain viable for decades. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Lancashire Lad Gooseberry (Historic English Red Gooseberry)
description: Plant in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with some afternoon shade in warmer regions, and prune annually to an open shape since this is a naturally spreading, thorny bush. Lancashire Lad is a 19th-century English heirloom once among the most popular cultivars grown for the competitive gooseberry-showing clubs of Lancashire and Cheshire, prized for its large size as much as its flavor. The fruit is downy-skinned and dark red at maturity, tart enough for excellent cooking and preserving when picked slightly underripe, and mellowing to a richer flavor if left to fully color on the bush. Its heavy cropping and cold hardiness have kept it in cultivation among heirloom fruit collectors long after most Victorian-era show cultivars faded from commerce. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lancaster Surecrop Corn (Pennsylvania Dutch Heirloom Dent Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; this variety tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns, though it still performs best with even moisture during pollination. Lancaster Surecrop was developed by Pennsylvania Dutch farmers in Lancaster County and became, over generations of selection, the source of the Lancaster heterotic group that later proved foundational in commercial hybrid corn breeding across the eastern Corn Belt. Grown today, it produces sturdy stalks and well-filled ears of yellow dent kernels well suited to cornmeal and traditional livestock feed, preserving a genetic line with an outsized influence on modern corn. Matures in 105–115 days from seed.

name: Lancelot Leek (Early-Season Summer Leek)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 65–75°F; transplant outdoors after last frost, setting transplants 4–6 inches apart in a trench 4–6 inches deep to blanch the shafts; gradually backfill the trench as plants grow; harvest beginning at 1 inch shaft diameter for best tenderness. Lancelot is a European-bred early-season leek variety that fills an important niche in the leek production calendar: unlike the classic overwintering leek varieties (such as Bleu de Solaise or Giant Musselburgh) that require 130–150+ days from transplant and are intended to overwinter in the garden for winter and spring harvest, Lancelot matures in just 70–85 days from transplant and is harvested in late summer and early fall while stalks are still slender, tender, and at their best eating quality. The stalks are typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter at harvest — more refined in texture and milder in flavor than fully mature overwintering leeks — making Lancelot the superior choice for preparations where tenderness and delicate leek flavor are paramount: vichyssoise, leek gratin, braised leeks, and fresh leek salads where the young stalks are excellent raw. The blue-green foliage and cylindrical white shaft create an attractive plant in the garden from late spring through summer. Lancelot does not have the cold hardiness or overwintering capability of late types but excels as a summer-season leek in climates too hot for fall-planted overwintering types. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Lancer Parsnip (Canker-Resistant Smooth-Skinned Parsnip)
description: Direct sow shallowly into loose, deeply dug soil free of rocks and clods so the long roots can develop without forking, and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding. Lancer is valued by market gardeners for its smooth white skin, uniform wedge shape, and strong resistance to canker, a common fungal problem that disfigures many older parsnip varieties. Allow roots to remain in the ground after the first fall frosts to develop their full sweetness before digging for storage or immediate use. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Land Cress
description: Direct sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun as soon as soil can be worked in spring or in late summer for fall harvest; land cress (upland cress, American cress, creasy greens) is a biennial European native grown as an annual salad herb that provides a peppery, watercress-like flavor in ordinary, moist garden soil — without the stream or pond edge that true watercress (Nasturtium officinale) requires. The deeply lobed, rounded basal leaves have intense, hot, peppery bite that mellows considerably with cooking. Plants remain edible through light frosts and can often be overwintered under cold frames in zones 5–7, providing very early spring greens. Harvest outer leaves beginning at 4–6 inches in height; plants withstand multiple pickings before bolting in warm weather. Sow every 4 weeks for succession harvests through the cool season. Excellent raw in small quantities to add zip to salads, or blanched and wilted as a cooked green. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Landreth Stringless Bush Bean (1885 American Heirloom Snap Bean)
description: Landreth Stringless is an American heirloom bush bean first offered by the D. Landreth Seed Company in the 1880s and notable historically as one of the earliest widely marketed stringless snap beans, a trait that was a genuine novelty in that era. It produces medium-green pods a little over 5 inches long with a meaty texture and good flavor, backed by seeds in a rich chocolate-brown color. The plant matures quickly and yields heavily over a relatively short window, making it a reliable choice for succession planting and home canning. Its long, continuous availability from Landreth makes it one of the oldest still-commercially-offered American bean varieties. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Lane Muscadine Grape (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Lane is a modern University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its very large, glossy black berries with a thinner, more tender skin than many older black muscadines, along with sweet, richly flavored flesh well suited to fresh eating. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, ripening in the mid-to-late season, and its improved skin quality and berry size have made it a popular choice for both home gardens and u-pick plantings across the Gulf South. Keep vines well watered during fruit development for the best berry size, and thin overcrowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid weather. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lang Jujube (Pear-Shaped Chinese Jujube, Large Late Jujube)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — jujubes thrive in poor, alkaline, rocky soils where other fruit trees fail; Lang and Li are the classic companion pair for maximum fruit set; harvest fruits when they turn from green to mahogany-red and reach full size; air-dry excess harvest at room temperature for preserved 'dried dates.' Lang jujube is one of the two most important cultivated jujube varieties in American horticulture, planted alongside Li jujube (the other dominant variety) throughout the jujube-growing regions of the United States. Lang differs from Li in fruit shape and season: where Li produces round to oval fruits that ripen relatively early, Lang produces elongated, pear-shaped to teardrop-shaped fruits that are noticeably larger than Li (typically 1.5–2.5 inches long) and ripen later in the season. The larger, more elongated fruit shape of Lang also makes it particularly excellent for drying into Chinese-style red dates (hong zao / hóng zǎo), where the pear shape produces attractive elongated dried fruits with a pleasant chewy texture and concentrated honey-sweet flavor. Cross-pollination between Lang and Li is well-documented to significantly increase fruit set on both trees, making them the classic companion pair for backyard jujube plantings — planting one of each type provides mutual pollination benefits that result in substantially heavier crops than either variety planted alone. Like all jujubes, Lang is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant, thriving with no supplemental irrigation once established in most of the country. An exceptional choice for zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners who want a reliable, low-input fruit tree. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Langley Gage Gooseberry (Historic English Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Langley Gage is a small, historic English gooseberry maintained today mainly in heritage fruit collections, grown for its small, near-translucent pale greenish-white berries with an unusually sweet flavor that makes it one of the better gooseberries for eating fresh off the bush rather than cooking. As with other Ribes, confirm it is permitted in your state or county before planting, since gooseberries can carry white pine blister rust between white pines and their alternate hosts. The bush itself is notably compact and low-vigor compared to modern culinary gooseberries, so it suits a small border or container culture better than a production row. Give it cool, humus-rich soil, mulch to conserve moisture, and thin out crowded interior branches each dormant season to keep the small fruit clean and easy to reach among the thorny stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Langsat (Duku, Longkong, Lanzon)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Langsat is more shade-tolerant than most tropical fruit trees and performs well with overhead canopy protection when young, mimicking its native understory forest environment. Lansium parasiticum (formerly L. domesticum) is a medium tropical tree native to the Malay Peninsula, the Philippines, and Indonesia, where it is one of the most beloved native fruits — at once common enough to be sold from roadside carts throughout Southeast Asia and exotic enough to be a premium market item in Japan and specialty stores. The fruits are produced in long, grape-like clusters directly on the main trunk and branches (cauliflory), each fruit a small (1–2 inch) oval, pale yellowish-tan berry with thin, papery skin. Inside are 3–5 segments of translucent, juicy, sweet-tart flesh with a flavor variously described as combining grape, grapefruit, longan, and rose water — extraordinarily refreshing in tropical heat. The 'Duku' form (sometimes listed separately) produces larger, thicker-skinned, sweeter fruits than the standard Langsat; 'Longkong' is a selected clone from Thailand with very sweet, thin-skinned fruits highly valued in Southeast Asian markets. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Southeast Asia and rare specialty markets, Langsat is a coveted addition to zone 11 South Florida tropical fruit gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Lapins Cherry Tree
description: Lapins is a self-fertile sweet cherry producing large, firm, dark-red fruit without needing a pollinator, ideal for smaller gardens. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water steadily as fruit develops. Prune in late winter or after harvest to keep an open canopy and reduce disease. Netting the tree near ripening helps protect the crop from birds. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lara Carambola (Lara Starfruit)
description: Lara, selected in Homestead, Florida, is one of the sweet-flavored carambola cultivars recommended by University of Florida IFAS for home landscape planting alongside Arkin. It is notably precocious, fruiting at a young age, and grows into a bushy, rounded tree with attractive deep green foliage that works well as a small specimen or container plant. The waxy, five-ribbed yellow fruit is eaten fresh out of hand or sliced for its familiar star shape as a garnish. Because it shares the frost sensitivity typical of all carambola, Gulf Coast gardeners in zone 9a should plant it in the warmest available spot and be ready to protect young trees during freezes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Larac Asparagus (French Green Hybrid)
description: Larac is a French-bred green asparagus hybrid developed from INRA breeding lines and widely grown across French production regions for its reliable early emergence and consistent spear quality. Spears are medium to thick, cylindrical, and hold their tight tips well even during a fast spring flush, making the variety popular where harvest timing matters for fresh-market bunching. It shows solid tolerance to common rust and performs reliably across a range of soil types provided drainage is good. As with other named hybrids, resist harvesting until the crowns have had two full seasons to establish, then cut spears daily at ground level through the six-to-eight-week spring season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Large Leaf Basil
description: This sweet Italian basil is grown for its unusually large, aromatic leaves and slow-bolting habit that stretches the harvest for pesto and fresh cooking. Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and keep it warm, since basil resents cold soil. Transplant into rich, well-drained ground in full sun once nights stay reliably above fifty degrees. Pinch flowering tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and encourage a steady supply of tender leaves. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Large Leaf Tea Camellia (Tetraploid White Tea Selection)
description: Large Leaf is a tetraploid tea selection, originally distributed through a 1970s USDA introduction, distinguished by thick, leathery, strongly veined leaves up to 6 inches long and unusually large buds and flowers. Its natural tendency is to grow as a multi-trunked small tree rather than a rounded shrub, eventually reaching 10 feet or more, so give it more room than a typical China-type tea plant. The oversized buds make it a favorite among home tea growers specifically for white tea production. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic, and expect somewhat variable seed set, a known trait of tetraploid Camellia selections. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Large Red Cherry Tomato
description: This classic indeterminate variety yields abundant clusters of bright red cherry tomatoes with fresh, zesty flavor all summer. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. Stake or cage the vigorous vines and remove suckers if you want to manage the sprawl. Pick tomatoes as they ripen to keep the plants setting new fruit continuously through the season. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Large Sourplum (Wild Sourplum, Sour Plum)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — adapted to seasonally dry African bushveld. Ximenia caffra (large sourplum or wild sourplum) is a thorny deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savannas, bushveld, and woodland margins of eastern and southern Africa — native across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Tanzania, and Kenya. The plant produces small (1-inch), oval, single-seeded drupes that ripen from green to bright orange-red to scarlet, with very tart, astringent, vitamin C-rich flesh surrounding a large seed — eaten fresh across rural sub-Saharan Africa (often with salt to balance the sourness), and made into jam, chutney, beer, and preserved sour fruit drinks. The seed kernel has an almond-like flavor and is pressed for Ximenia oil (sour plum oil), one of the most sought-after African cosmetic oils, with excellent skin-conditioning properties rich in long-chain polyunsaturated acids — increasingly used in high-end African cosmetics, hair oils, and skin care. Distinguished from the smaller X. americana (tallow wood) by its larger fruits, larger leaves, and preference for drier, more seasonal climates. As a water-wise shrub for zone 9–11 gardens, large sourplum is extremely tough and attractive, with white, almond-scented flowers in spring. Matures in 1095–2920 days from transplant.

name: Large-Flowered Calamint
description: Calamintha grandiflora is the showiest of the calamlints, producing soft, aromatic, mint-scented foliage and large (for the genus), vivid pink, tubular, two-lipped flowers in whorled clusters from late spring through early fall that are extraordinarily attractive to bumblebees and are among the most bumblebee-visited ornamental herbs in British and European garden trials. The leaves and young shoots have a strong, pleasant, minty-oregano flavor and can be used fresh or dried as a seasoning and herbal tea; the flavor is similar to but more delicate than wild mountain oregano. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Laroda Plum (Large Late-Season Red California Japanese Plum with Rich Flavor)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters to 4–5 inches. Harvest when red skin is deep and fruit gives to gentle pressure. Laroda is a California-developed late-season Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) that has been grown in California commercial orchards and home gardens since the mid-20th century, selected from the same broad program of California stone fruit development that produced Santa Rosa, Friar, and other standard Japanese plum varieties. The name Laroda is of uncertain derivation — unlike Luther Burbank's poetically named plum introductions, Laroda was likely a station selection name from one of the California experiment station programs that systematically evaluated Japanese plum seedlings for commercial quality. The fruit is one of the largest Japanese plum types: large to very large globose fruits, 2–2.5 inches in diameter, with deep red to dark red skin that becomes almost black at full maturity. The skin has a slightly mottled appearance with a light bloom (waxy surface coating). The flesh is amber to yellow, firm and juicy with rich, full plum flavor and moderate sweetness — more complex and less bland than some of the large-fruited Japanese plums selected primarily for size. The late season (July-August in California, somewhat earlier in the humid South) means Laroda provides fresh plums after most other Japanese varieties have finished — a practical attribute for home orchard planning where sequential harvests are desirable. Cross-pollination from Santa Rosa plum or another compatible Japanese plum is needed for full crop set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lassen Pistachio
description: Lassen was released by the University of California, Davis pistachio breeding program as an alternative female cultivar to the industry-standard Kerman, bred to bear more precociously and produce a more consistent annual crop rather than Kerman's pronounced alternate-year bearing pattern. It requires the same demanding climate as any pistachio: hot, dry, low-humidity summers paired with sufficient winter chill to break dormancy uniformly, and it performs poorly in humid or marine climates even where cold hours are adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and pair with a male pollinizer that sheds pollen at the same time, since pistachios are entirely dioecious and wind-pollinated. Harvest in early autumn once the hulls loosen and the characteristic shell split appears; trees need roughly seven to ten years to reach significant production. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Late Flat Dutch Cabbage
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Late Flat Dutch'
description: Set transplants 24–30 inches apart in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the large, heavy heads need ample room and rich soil to size up properly over their long season. Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom prized for producing enormous, flattened, blue-green heads that commonly reach 10–15 pounds and can grow considerably larger under good conditions, with dense, crisp interior leaves that make it an outstanding keeper — heads store for months in a root cellar or cool garage, and the variety was historically favored for large-batch sauerkraut and winter storage before refrigeration was common. Its long season and excellent cold hardiness make it best suited to fall planting in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where the heads mature slowly through the cool months and can stand in the garden through hard freezes without splitting. A workhorse heirloom for gardeners who want maximum storage cabbage from a single planting, in zone 3–9. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Late Fry Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Late Fry is a University of Arkansas release bred as a black-fruited counterpart to the popular bronze variety Fry, producing very large, glossy black berries with the same thin skin and high sugar content that made Fry a favorite for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and ripens late in the season, filling out the tail end of the muscadine harvest after earlier black varieties are finished. Vigor and disease resistance are good across the humid Gulf South. Because it is one of the last muscadines to ripen, protect ripening clusters from birds and other wildlife, which concentrate on the few varieties still fruiting late in the season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Late Santa Rosa Plum
description: Late Santa Rosa is a later-ripening sport of the classic Santa Rosa Japanese plum, carrying the same reddish-purple skin and juicy, aromatic amber flesh but extending the harvest window several weeks beyond the standard cultivar. This makes it useful for orchards and home gardens that already grow Santa Rosa and want to stretch fresh plum season rather than concentrate the whole crop at once. Culture is identical to the parent cultivar: plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun, and though partially self-fruitful, plant a second Japanese plum nearby for a heavier, more reliable set. Prune to an open-center vase shape in the dormant season and thin heavy fruit sets to 4-6 inches apart to improve size and reduce limb breakage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Latham Raspberry (Classic Cold-Hardy Heirloom Red Raspberry)
description: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and support rows with a simple two-wire trellis. Released by the University of Minnesota in the 1920s, Latham became one of the most widely planted red raspberries in the northern United States for decades because of its exceptional winter hardiness and reliable, heavy midsummer crop of firm, bright red berries with classic tart-sweet raspberry flavor. It is a floricane-fruiting type, bearing on second-year canes, so remove spent canes to the ground right after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 4-6 per foot of row. Modern cultivars have surpassed it in disease resistance, but Latham remains valued in cold climates for its toughness and long track record. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Lattarula Fig (Sweet Pale-Skinned Italian Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Lattarula is a classic Italian heirloom fig producing pale yellow-green skinned fruit with intensely sweet, amber-honey colored flesh, considered by many growers to be among the sweetest and most reliably productive of the light-skinned fig varieties widely available in North America. The vigorous, hardy tree sets a good main crop in late summer and often a smaller early crop as well in warm climates, and its productivity and adaptability across a range of soils and conditions have made it a long-standing favorite for both home orchards and small-scale commercial fig growing. As with all figs, provide winter protection for the roots in the colder parts of its range, since the plant reliably regrows from the root system even after top dieback in a hard freeze. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Laurel Avocado
description: Plant Beilschmiedia pendula in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Laurel Avocado is one of numerous wild Lauraceae fruit trees related to the cultivated avocado — in the Beilschmiedia genus, distributed across tropical Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The Caribbean species B. pendula produces fruits that closely resemble small avocados in appearance and texture: oval to pear-shaped, 2–3 inches long, with dark greenish to purple-black skin and green, oily, smooth-textured flesh surrounding a single large seed. The flavor is avocado-like but distinctly different — the laurel-family heritage shows in a subtle aromatic note reminiscent of bay leaves, giving the fruit a more complex character than standard avocado. Eaten fresh with salt and lime, used in local Caribbean cooking as an avocado substitute, and occasionally used to press for oil. The tree grows naturally in humid Caribbean forest and coastal woodland environments and tolerates periodic flooding better than cultivated avocado. Of interest as a potential rootstock for avocado cultivation research and as a wild relative for avocado breeding programs. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Laurel-Leaved Currant (Evergreen Winter-Flowering Fragrant Currant)
description: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to mostly shade or high overhead shade, and shelter from harsh winter wind. Laurel-Leaved Currant is unusual among currants for being evergreen, holding leathery, glossy, laurel-like leaves year-round, and for flowering in the depths of winter, producing hanging clusters of small, sweetly fragrant, greenish-cream flowers from January into March that are a valuable early nectar source for the first bees of the season. Plants are dioecious, so both a male and a female are needed for the female to set its small, edible red-to-black currants, which ripen in early summer and can be used like other currants once fully colored. It is an easy, low-maintenance shrub for the shaded winter garden, valued as much for its fragrance and evergreen structure as for its fruit. Prune only lightly, right after flowering, to remove damaged wood and maintain shape. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Laurentian Rutabaga
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil; Laurentian is the standard North American rutabaga variety — a natural hybrid between turnip and cabbage producing large, round to slightly elongated roots with the characteristic purple shoulder above ground and yellow-tan below, with golden-yellow, dense, starchy flesh distinctly different from the white flesh of turnips. Rutabaga (called 'swede' in British English, reflecting its Swedish origin) has a richer, more complex flavor than turnip — the yellow flesh is denser, starchier, and more nutrionally robust with a sweeter, more earthy, complex flavor that becomes significantly more intense and sweet after hard frost exposure. The classic rutabaga preparations — mashed ('neeps' in Scotland, traditionally served with haggis), chunked in beef stew, roasted with butter and herbs, or pureed into soups — take full advantage of the dense, deeply flavored flesh that holds its shape better than potato while contributing its own distinctive sweetness and earthiness. Laurentian's large size (roots can reach softball size in good conditions), excellent storage quality (roots keep for months in cool storage), and consistent purple-top appearance make it the most reliable and widely grown rutabaga for home and market garden production. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Laurina Coffee (Bourbon Pointu)
description: Arising as a natural mutation of Bourbon coffee on Réunion Island (once called Île Bourbon) sometime in the 18th or 19th century, Laurina is prized for beans containing roughly half the caffeine of ordinary Arabica along with a delicate, low-acid, distinctly sweet cup with notes of stone fruit and honey. Its narrow, pointed beans (giving rise to the alternate name Bourbon Pointu) come from a smaller, more slender, lower-yielding plant that is markedly harder to grow and harvest than standard Bourbon, which keeps it rare and sought after among specialty roasters. Provide the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and filtered shade other Arabicas need, but expect slower growth and lighter harvests in exchange for its unusual low-caffeine cup. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lavandin (Provence Lavender)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lavandin is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) and spike lavender (L. latifolia) that has become the dominant commercial lavender worldwide — over 90 percent of the lavender essential oil sold globally comes from lavandin rather than true English lavender. It is larger, more vigorous, and more heat- and drought-tolerant than English lavender, with longer, more branched flower spikes and a stronger scent that is higher in camphor and has a slightly sharper, more penetrating quality than the pure English lavender fragrance. As a sterile hybrid, it produces no viable seed but blooms heavily and reliably. The cultivar Grosso produces the most oil and the largest, most dramatic dried bundles; Provence is the classic lavender-field cultivar of the Provence region of France. Excellent for mass planting, dried flower production, cut flowers, and herb gardens. Slightly less cold-hardy than English lavender but more heat-tolerant in zones 7-8. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Lavender Mint (Floral Peppermint-Lavender Hybrid Scent)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Lavender Mint layers soft, floral lavender notes over the classic cooling menthol scent of peppermint, an unusual fragrance combination that makes it a favorite for potpourri, herbal sachets, and fragrant tea blends beyond straightforward culinary use. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Lavewa Spinach
description: Sow Lavewa spinach directly in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since spinach bolts in heat and long days. This open-pollinated variety offers good heat tolerance and mildew resistance, rivaling hybrids for flavor. Thin seedlings to about 4 to 6 inches apart and keep the soil consistently moist and cool. Harvest outer leaves individually or cut whole plants, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest in warm weather. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Laxton's Progress Pea (Early English Heirloom Shelling Pea)
description: Laxton's Progress is an early-maturing English heirloom shelling pea bred by the historic Laxton Brothers nursery, valued for its short, sturdy vines and heavy set of well-filled pods on plants that need only light support. It was one of the two parent lines, alongside 'Perfection', that USDA breeders crossed in 1943 to create the heat-tolerant modern classic 'Wando'. Direct-sow into cool, workable spring soil as early as the ground can be prepared, since like all garden peas it grows and yields best well ahead of summer heat. The dwarf, self-supporting habit suits raised beds and smaller gardens where taller vining peas would need substantial trellising. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Laxton's Superb Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Laxton's Superb is a reliable, cold-hardy alternative to Cox's Orange Pippin for gardeners wanting similar flavor from a more forgiving tree. Bred in Bedfordshire, England in the early twentieth century from a Cox's Orange Pippin and Wyken Pippin cross, it bears medium, red-flushed russeted apples with rich, aromatic, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh reminiscent of its famous Cox parent, but on a tree that is notably hardier, more reliably productive, and more forgiving of less-than-ideal growing conditions than the notoriously finicky Cox. Its combination of excellent Cox-like flavor and much easier garden performance has made it a favored choice for gardeners wanting classic English dessert apple flavor without Cox's demanding cultural requirements. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months, during which the flavor continues to develop and improve. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Layeroka Chestnut (Gellatly Pacific Northwest Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Layeroka (Gellatly #1) is a European x Japanese chestnut hybrid selected by nurseryman J.U. Gellatly of Westbank, British Columbia, and it has become a mainstay of Pacific Northwest chestnut orchards for its productivity and cold hardiness rather than for strong blight resistance. It bears medium-sized, sweet nuts that drop free of the bur but do not store well, so plan to use or process the crop soon after the September harvest. Because Layeroka is pollen-sterile, it must be interplanted with a genetically distinct, overlapping-bloom pollinizer, growers commonly use the Gellatly selection Skioka for this purpose. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lazy Housewife Bean
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis, teepee poles, or corn stalks; provide 6 feet of vertical support for the vigorous vines. Lazy Housewife is one of America's most documented heirloom pole beans, appearing in American seed catalogs since at least 1810 and recorded by seed historian William Woys Weaver as a bean brought to America by German immigrants; the name refers to the ease of preparation — the pods are stringless when harvested young as snap beans, and the mature white seeds shell out of the dried pods with minimal effort, hence 'lazy housewife.' The pods are 5–7 inches long, round, and stringless, with plump white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye at maturity. Equally excellent as a snap bean (harvest young), shell bean (harvest green pods when seeds have filled), or dry bean; the cooked flavor of the mature seeds is rich, creamy, and outstanding. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Lazy Wife Pole Bean (Stringless German Heirloom Pole Bean, 1810 American Classic)
description: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost; provide tall support (6–8 feet). Harvest at 5–7 inches as snap bean or leave to dry for shell/dry use. Lazy Wife is a German immigrant heirloom pole bean that was introduced to American seed catalogs around 1810 and became one of the most popular snap beans in the 19th century — a status maintained until modern stringless hybrid varieties provided equivalent ease of preparation with higher yield. The name 'Lazy Wife' refers to the bean's stringless character: in the 19th-century farm kitchen where snap bean preparation required long sessions of stringing pods by hand before cooking, a truly stringless bean required no stringing at all — hence the tongue-in-cheek name suggesting the homemaker could be 'lazy' about bean preparation. The implied humor of the name was accepted in its era; the bean's quality was the real selling point. Lazy Wife produces broad, flat, pale green pods (5–7 inches long, 0.75 inches wide) with a somewhat different form than round-pod types — the flat pod shape and relatively thick walls give Lazy Wife a characteristic visual distinction from most modern snap beans. The pods are truly stringless through their snap-bean stage and have rich, full flavor that heirloom enthusiasts prize. The seeds are creamy-white and excellent as a shell bean (picked young) or dry bean (left to fully mature), giving Lazy Wife three-stage versatility as a snap, shell, or dry bean from a single planting. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Leaf Amaranth (Chinese Spinach, Callaloo, Joseph's Coat)
description: Sow seeds on the soil surface or barely 1/8 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; leaf amaranth germinates quickly in warm conditions and grows rapidly to a productive harvest-ready size in as little as 30 days. The young leaves taste mild and spinach-like when harvested small; older leaves are cooked like spinach, steamed, sautéed, or stewed into the Caribbean callaloo and West African soups that this plant anchors. It is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens for southern gardens, producing abundantly through summer temperatures that wilt most other greens. The tricolor varieties display striking red, gold, and green foliage useful as an ornamental. Pinch the growing tip frequently to encourage bushy lateral branching and delay seed formation; once the plant flowers heavily, leaf quality declines. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Leaf Lettuce
description: Scatter or row-sow seed on the surface or barely cover with 1/8 in of soil, as light aids germination. Thin to 6–10 in and use thinnings as baby greens in salads to avoid waste. Harvest outer leaves continuously once plants are 4–6 in tall, or cut the entire plant an inch above the soil line for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Bolting in warm weather makes leaves bitter; provide shade cloth in late spring to extend the season. Matures in 30–55 days from seed.

name: Leatherleaf Mahonia (Chinese Mahonia, Leatherleaf Oregon Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is a bold architectural evergreen shrub with some of the most striking foliage in the shade garden — stiff, upright canes bearing enormous compound leaves (18–24 inches) of dark, holly-like leaflets with viciously spiny edges that create a dramatic tropical effect in the deepest shade. Fragrant yellow flowers appear in winter in drooping grape-like clusters, followed by powdery blue-purple berries in spring that are edible (tart, used for jelly and wine). It is one of the few large shrubs that truly thrives in deep, dry shade — an outstanding barrier plant and shade specimen. NOTE: Mahonia bealei is listed as invasive in several southeastern states including Texas and Georgia — check local invasive species lists before planting; the native alternative Mahonia trifoliolata (agarita) is an excellent substitute in Texas. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lebanese Oregano (Cascading Oregano)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun, ideally where its trailing stems can cascade over the edge of a raised bed, wall, or hanging basket; Lebanese oregano is grown chiefly as an ornamental rather than a culinary herb, producing long, wiry stems draped with rounded, blue-green leaves and dangling clusters of papery, chartreuse-pink, hop-like bracts that persist attractively for weeks in mid- to late summer. The trailing habit and long-lasting bracted flower clusters make it a favorite for dry, sunny container plantings and rock wall crevices where its cascade can be fully appreciated. It is somewhat more tender than common culinary oregano, so provide winter protection or grow it as a container plant that can be moved to shelter in climates colder than its hardiness range. Trim lightly after the main flowering display fades to keep growth tidy, and avoid rich soil or excess water, both of which produce leggy, less floriferous growth. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Leccino Olive (Cold-Hardy Italian Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Leccino is one of Italy's most widely planted olive cultivars, valued for producing smooth, mild, buttery oil with low bitterness and pungency compared to more robust Tuscan cultivars like Frantoio, and for its comparatively good tolerance of cold winters and root rot among Italian olive selections, which has made it a popular choice in warm-temperate American olive trials including in the Southeast. Trees are vigorous, spreading, and heavy-bearing, typically beginning meaningful production within four to six years of planting. Harvest olives from green through purple-black depending on the oil style desired — earlier harvest yields a greener, more peppery oil, while later harvest gives a milder, more buttery result. Leccino is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and yield. Established trees tolerate drought and poor, alkaline soil well, needing supplemental water mainly during the first two years and during fruit development in dry summers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: LeConte Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; LeConte is a historic American hybrid pear (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) developed in the 19th century in the United States and named for John LeConte, Georgia naturalist. It was one of the dominant commercial pear varieties in the Deep South from the 1850s through early 20th century because of its combination of fire blight resistance (far superior to European Bartlett types), low chill requirement (150–200 hours), and productivity under Gulf Coast conditions. The large, yellowish-green pear-shaped fruits are crisp and mildly sweet — good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves, though not as richly flavored as Bartlett. Trees are vigorous, productive, and extremely long-lived; old LeConte pear trees planted before 1900 still stand and fruit in some Southern gardens. Modern pear growers in the humid South should choose LeConte over Bartlett specifically for its far superior fire blight resistance. Prune in winter to an open-center or modified central-leader form; remove water sprouts that attract fire blight. Harvest when fruit lifts easily from the branch but before fully soft. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lee Mandarin (Clementine x Orlando Tangelo Cross)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Lee was bred by USDA researchers in Florida from a cross of Clementine mandarin and Orlando tangelo, producing medium-sized, deep orange fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor that ripens in early to midseason, making it a useful bridge variety between the earliest and latest mandarins in a mixed home citrus planting. The tree is productive and the fruit easy to peel, with the fine, tender segments typical of good mandarin breeding, and while it contains some seeds it remains popular among Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its outstanding eating quality. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize regularly with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lee Okra (University of Arkansas Semi-Dwarf Spineless Okra)
description: Lee was bred at the University of Arkansas from Gulfcoast, Emerald, and Clemson Spineless parentage to give a semi-dwarf plant that stays largely free of side branches, which simplifies picking. Straight, spineless, bright green pods form close along the main stem and should be cut every couple of days at three to four inches for the best texture. The compact, upright habit lets gardeners plant Lee more densely than sprawling heirloom types without sacrificing airflow. Regular harvest keeps the short growing season this variety was bred for producing right up until fall's first cool nights. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Leek
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors in flats and thin to 2 in; transplant pencil-thick seedlings into 6-in-deep trenches, dropping each plant into a dibber hole and filling with water rather than soil to encourage a long white shank. Gradually fill trenches and hill up soil around stems as they grow to blanch the shanks. Leeks tolerate hard frost and can be left in the ground well into winter for a late harvest. Dig as needed once shanks reach 1 in or more in diameter. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Legacy Blueberry (Adaptable Highbush-Southern Highbush Hybrid)
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to maintain the moist, acidic soil conditions blueberries require. Legacy is a USDA release bred from a cross between northern highbush and southern highbush parentage, giving it unusually broad climate adaptability — it performs well from the upper South through much of the Gulf region, bridging the gap between cultivars suited only to cold winters and those needing very low chill. The semi-evergreen bush produces heavy crops of firm, sweet, richly flavored medium-sized berries over a fairly long mid-to-late season, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it easy to manage and harvest. Its adaptability and reliable production have made it one of the more versatile blueberry cultivars for gardeners uncertain whether a northern or southern highbush type suits their exact climate. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with productive new wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Legacy Southern Highbush Blueberry (Late-Season Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Legacy is a vigorous, productive, late-season highbush blueberry with relatively low chill requirements (approximately 400–600 hours) that extends the highbush blueberry season well into late summer and performs reliably in zone 8 and warmer parts of zone 9. Developed by USDA in New Jersey and released in 1993, Legacy produces medium to large, firm, sweet, aromatic berries with exceptional flavor that is considered by many blueberry connoisseurs to be among the finest-tasting highbush cultivars. The berries ripen late in the season (3–4 weeks after Bluecrop) and hold on the bush without dropping, extending the harvest window for the home garden. The vigorous, upright shrub produces attractive white spring flowers and outstanding red-orange fall foliage — one of the better blueberries for fall landscape interest. Legacy is semi-evergreen to evergreen in zone 9, which reduces winter chilling compared to deciduous cultivars — this is actually advantageous in zone 9 where chilling is the primary production limitation. For zone 9 production, pair with other low-chill southern highbush cultivars like Sunshine Blue or O'Neal. Soil pH management is critical: maintain pH between 4.5 and 5.5 using elemental sulfur treatments and acidic mulch such as pine bark or pine straw. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Legend Tomato (OSU Late Blight Resistant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage prevents fruit from resting on the soil; provides excellent production without fungicide sprays in conditions where late blight is present. Legend was released in 1996 by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University, culminating many years of breeding for late blight resistance in open-pollinated tomatoes; at the time of release it had the highest documented level of late blight resistance in any open-pollinated variety, making it a breakthrough for organic and low-spray gardeners in humid, blight-prone climates. The large (10–16 oz), round to slightly flattened, smooth, uniform deep red fruits have thick walls, good meaty texture, and classic sweet-balanced tomato flavor superior to most disease-resistant commercial varieties; the determinate plant ripens a heavy concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks rather than producing continuously. Legend performs exceptionally well in the Pacific Northwest and humid Eastern climates; it is also valuable in Gulf Coast gardens planted in fall (August–September) when late blight risk from summer thunderstorm humidity is highest. One of the most important contributions to open-pollinated tomato breeding in the late 20th century. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Lehman's Delight American Persimmon (Large Self-Fertile Indiana Selection)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in deep, well-drained to average soil; Lehman's Delight is self-fertile and will set a full crop on a single tree, though a second American persimmon nearby can further boost yields. Bred by Indiana persimmon breeder Jerry Lehman and also sold under its original breeding number, 100-46, it was one of Lehman's own favorite selections from thousands of controlled crosses for combining outstanding size, flavor, and productivity. The large, reddish-orange fruit — often exceeding two inches across — has smooth, clear pulp and an intensely sweet flavor once fully soft-ripe after frost, and mature trees are known as some of the heaviest-bearing American persimmon selections available. It stays comparatively compact for the species, tolerates the heat and clay soils common across zone 7-9 gardens, and needs little upkeep beyond removing root suckers once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Leikora Sea Buckthorn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — sandy, rocky, and coastal soils are ideal; Leikora is a German-selected female sea buckthorn cultivar bred for commercial berry production, selected at the Bundesanstalt für Züchtungsforschung as one of the heaviest-bearing named female cultivars with large, bright orange-yellow berries that ripen in August–September in dense clusters along the stems. Sea buckthorn berries contain extraordinary concentrations of vitamin C (up to 15 times that of oranges), vitamin E, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids — the nutritional profile has driven substantial commercial interest in sea buckthorn juice, oil capsules, and skincare products. The tart, acidic, tropical-citrus flavor of the fresh berries makes them challenging to eat raw but outstanding processed into juice (often blended with apple or honey to moderate acidity), jam, wine, and dietary supplements. Leikora is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant shrub adapted to harsh, exposed sites where few other fruiting plants survive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Leisure Cilantro (Classic Open-Pollinated Slow-Bolt Cilantro for Leaf Production)
description: Direct sow thinly in cool soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves successively before bolting. Leisure Cilantro is one of the most widely recommended open-pollinated cilantro varieties for home gardeners specifically wanting maximum leaf production before the plant bolts to seed. All cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) is genetically programmed to flower — it is an annual that must complete its seed cycle — but the timing and speed of this transition from vegetative (leaf-producing) growth to reproductive (flower/seed) growth varies considerably among cultivated varieties, and selecting for delayed bolting has been a primary breeding objective in cilantro improvement since leaf herb production became the primary commercial use of the crop in North America. Leisure was selected from open-pollinated cilantro populations for its consistent tendency to remain in vegetative leaf production mode longer than standard unselected populations, particularly as temperatures increase in spring. This character is not the same as the more dramatically extended bolt resistance of F1 hybrid varieties like Calypso, but it is meaningfully better than generic cilantro seed and substantially better than truly fast-bolting varieties. For zone 9 gardeners, the distinction matters: in the rapid spring temperature rise of the Gulf Coast (February through April), even 2–3 extra weeks of leaf production before bolting is a meaningful difference in total harvest. Leisure's open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from selected late-bolting individual plants to potentially improve the variety further for local conditions over successive generations. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Lemon
description: Lemons are self-fertile and can bloom and fruit year-round in frost-free climates; Eureka and Lisbon are the commercial standards, while Meyer lemon is hardier (damaged below 22°F) and better suited to containers in cooler climates. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year. In zones 8–9, grow in large containers and bring indoors when temperatures drop below 28°F. Fruit is ready when fully yellow, slightly soft, and the rind is thin — do not wait for it to fall off the tree. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Aspen (Australian Lemon Aspen)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; lemon aspen grows as a rainforest understory tree and performs best with some afternoon shade protection.
