Acronychia acidula (lemon aspen) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the tropical and subtropical rainforests of northeastern Queensland — one of the most distinctive flavor ingredients in Australian native cuisine and a rising star of the Australian native food industry. The tree produces small (1/2–3/4 inch), round, pale-yellow to white fruits with highly aromatic, intensely concentrated lemon-pine-eucalyptus flavor — a unique, complex, bright citrus character that is entirely different from true lemons (Citrus limon) but provides a distinctively clean, intense, herbal-citrus punch that chefs value highly. The flavor profile is often described as lemon with eucalyptus, thyme, and pine notes — a complexity that normal citrus lacks. Lemon aspen is entirely unrelated to true citrus but has evolved a remarkably similar citrus flavor independently through different chemistry. The fruits are too intense and sharp to eat fresh in quantity but are used in small amounts as flavor accents in dressings, seafood sauces, marinades, desserts, and beverages — both fresh and as preserves, oils, and freeze-dried powder. Commercially produced lemon aspen products are increasingly available in Australian specialty food stores and international gourmet markets. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Balm
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon balm tolerates more shade than most herbs and is one of the few culinary herbs that produces acceptable quality even in partially shaded sites. Melissa officinalis is a vigorous, lemon-scented European perennial in the mint family producing wrinkled, oval, toothed leaves with a delightful fresh lemon fragrance used in teas, lemonade, salads, fish dishes, poultry, desserts, and liqueurs; it is much milder and more pleasant than lemon verbena for fresh use. Cut plants back hard after flowering to prevent aggressive self-seeding and to stimulate a flush of fresh, fragrant new leaves; in the Gulf South it often dies back in summer heat but re-emerges in fall. Harvest before flowering for best fragrance and flavor. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Lemon Balm Aurea
description: Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; Lemon Balm Aurea (also known as Golden Lemon Balm or Variegated Lemon Balm) is a cultivar of common lemon balm distinguished by brilliant gold-splashed, yellow-green variegated foliage in spring and early fall — the leaves are irregularly mottled with golden-yellow against the base green, giving the plant an ornamental quality entirely absent from plain lemon balm. The lemon fragrance is identical to the species, and the leaves have the same culinary and herbal uses — teas, desserts, liqueurs, and salads — with the added benefit of attractive foliage that makes this herb garden-worthy as an ornamental. In hot zone 9 summers the gold variegation tends to fade to mostly green as the plant responds to heat stress; for the best color effect, grow in partial shade and harvest the brightest spring leaves for culinary use. The plant spreads by self-sowing in fertile soils; deadhead before seed set to prevent naturalizing. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Basil
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Lemon Basil is a hybrid basil (Ocimum basilicum x O. americanum) producing smaller, narrower leaves with a distinctive, intense lemon-citrus fragrance and flavor that is completely different from the clove-anise profile of sweet basil — substituting citrus brightness for the classic basil complexity. The lemon flavor is genuine and strong, derived from citral and other lemon-fragrance compounds in the leaf oils, making lemon basil specifically useful in preparations where lemon and herb flavors are desired simultaneously: Thai cuisine (where it is a traditional herb in certain dishes), lemon herb sauces, seafood seasoning, herbed rice, and tea. The compact, fine-textured leaves and upright, branching habit create a smaller, more refined plant than sweet basil — typically 18–24 inches tall with many small branches each tipped with the small, narrow, lemon-scented leaves. Lemon basil is one of the most immediately identifiable herb plants in the garden for visitors unfamiliar with it — the combination of basil's visual character and the unexpected lemon fragrance when leaves are touched creates a memorable sensory experience that makes it a particularly effective plant for teaching about herb gardens. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Lemon Basil
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm seed-starting mix at 70°F or above; germination is rapid once soil temperature is adequate. Transplant into rich, well-drained garden soil in full sun and pinch the growing tip early to encourage a bushy, multi-stemmed plant. Lemon basil is compact compared to sweet basil and has a distinct citrus fragrance from the presence of citral; it pairs well with fish, poultry, and Southeast Asian cuisines. Harvest by snipping stems just above a leaf pair once plants are well established, and pinch flower buds promptly to extend the harvest season. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Boy Tomato
description: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and providing a sturdy cage or stake from the outset. Lemon Boy is one of the most widely grown large yellow tomatoes, an F1 hybrid introduced in 1984 that remains a top performer for home gardeners seeking a reliable, large, lemon-yellow salad tomato; it produces 6–8 ounce round fruits with smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and mild, sweet, very low-acid flesh that is ideal for slicing fresh, for guests who find red tomatoes too acidic, and for adding visual contrast in salads and on plates. Disease resistance to verticillium, fusarium, and nematodes makes it particularly valuable in humid southern gardens. Water consistently and stake firmly as the indeterminate vines are tall and productive. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Catnip
description: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained starting mix and press in lightly; fresh seeds germinate readily in 1–2 weeks. Lemon catnip has all the nepetalactone chemistry of common catnip (making it equally irresistible to cats) but its foliage carries a pleasant lemon-mint scent suitable for tea and aromatherapy. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil; cut plants back by half after the first flush of flowers to encourage a second bloom and fresh aromatic foliage. Harvest stems before flowers fully open for the best flavor in herbal teas; dry quickly in a warm, airy spot and store in airtight containers. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Lemon Cucumber
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with trellis support; Lemon Cucumber is an 1894 American heirloom producing distinctive round to oval, lemon-sized fruits with pale yellow-white skin when ripe — the resemblance to a lemon is strictly visual, as the flavor is mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the tartness of actual lemon. The thin skin, small seeds, and crisp, sweet, very low-bitterness flesh make Lemon Cucumber one of the most palatable cucumbers for fresh eating without peeling — the skin remains tender and palatable throughout the eating-ripe stage (pale yellow to ivory) unlike the tough skins of slicing cucumbers. The round shape also makes Lemon Cucumber excellent for serving as a natural bowl — hollow out the round fruit and fill with dips, salads, or other fillings. The mild, sweet flavor and easy digestibility (lower cucurbitacin bitterness than many cucumbers) makes it popular for people who find regular cucumbers hard to digest. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Lemon Cucumber
description: This heirloom bears round, yellow, lemon-sized fruit with sweet, mild, non-bitter flesh. Sow seeds an inch deep in warm soil and grow on a trellis to keep the round fruit clean and easy to spot. Keep evenly watered to avoid bitterness and misshapen fruit during dry spells. Harvest while the skin is still pale yellow and before it turns deep gold and seedy. Frequent picking keeps the prolific vines producing until frost. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Lemon Cucumber (Crystal Apple Cucumber, Round Yellow Cucumber)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil reaches 65°F; thin or transplant to 18–24 inches; harvest when pale yellow. Cucumis sativus 'Crystal Apple' (Lemon cucumber) is a heritage cucumber variety — one of the best-loved heirloom types — producing distinctive round to oval, tennis-ball-sized fruits with pale cream to pale yellow skin and white flesh that is exceptionally mild, sweet, and non-bitter compared to most standard cucumbers. Despite the name, the flavor is not lemony — it tastes like a very mild, sweet, refreshing cucumber. The thin skin makes peeling unnecessary, and the mild flavor means the seeds and seed cavity are also mild and not bitter, unlike some full-sized cucumbers. Lemon cucumbers are extremely popular with home gardeners for several reasons: the unusual round shape is attractive and different from grocery store varieties; the mild, non-bitter flavor appeals to people who find standard cucumbers too strong; and the fruits are easy to spot when harvesting (by size and color rather than hunting in dense vines). The variety produces prolifically over a long season. Best harvested young — large, deep-yellow specimens tend toward bitterness and seedness. An excellent choice for fresh eating, quick pickles, and cucumber water. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Lemon Drop Chile Pepper
description: Start this Peruvian aji pepper indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, as baccatum peppers germinate slowly and need a long, warm growing season. Provide bottom heat and warm soil around 80 degrees for best germination, then transplant out well after frost when nights stay warm. The bright yellow, wrinkled pods rate 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units with a distinct citrus flavor and lemony aroma. Give plants full sun, stake them if they grow tall, and harvest fruits fully colored for the best flavor. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Drop Mangosteen
description: Plant Garcinia intermedia in fertile, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; provide consistent moisture throughout the year — Garcinia species do not tolerate prolonged drought; protect from cold below 40°F, especially in youth; dioecious species (both male and female plants needed for fruiting, or select self-fertile named varieties if available). Lemon Drop Mangosteen is one of the most exquisitely flavored of all Garcinia fruits — smaller than the Purple Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) but with a uniquely intense, sweet-tart, citrus-dominant flavor profile quite different from other Garcinias. The bright golden-yellow to orange, golf-ball-sized fruits contain translucent-white, juicy pulp segments of remarkable flavor — combining intense lemon, lime, and sweet tropical fruit notes in an almost sherbet-like profile. In Central America, the fruits are eaten fresh, used in drinks, and made into preserves; the yellow skin contains bitter compounds similar to other Garcinias and is not eaten. In zone 10–12 gardens and collections, Lemon Drop Mangosteen grows as a slow-growing, handsome ornamental tree with attractive, glossy, dark-green leaves; fruiting begins after 5–7 years from seed. An excellent greenhouse tree in cooler climates. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Drop Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lemon Drop is a Peruvian aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) producing small, wrinkled, bright lemon-yellow fruits that ripen from pale green through various shades of yellow with a distinctive fruity, citrusy, bright heat very different from the harsher burn of jalapeños or the floral heat of habaneros. The heat level is medium-hot (15,000–30,000 Scoville units) with a pronounced fruity, lemony flavor note that makes Lemon Drop one of the most culinarily versatile hot peppers — used in salsas, ceviches, hot sauces, and Peruvian-style pepper pastes where the citrus-forward flavor complements seafood and poultry. Capsicum baccatum species peppers are widely grown in South America and increasingly popular in North American specialty gardening. In zone 9 the perennial habit is a major advantage — the plant can grow to a small shrub 4–5 feet tall over multiple seasons, producing far more fruit than annual plantings. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Drop Pepper (Aji Limon)
description: Start indoors in warm conditions and transplant after frost danger has passed; lemon drop pepper (aji limon) is a Peruvian Capsicum baccatum cultivar producing small, tapered, bright yellow fruits 2–3 inches long with a distinctive intensely fruity, citrusy, lemon-like flavor combined with a clean, building heat (30,000–50,000 SHU). The lemon aroma and flavor make it quite different from other yellow hot peppers and it is used extensively in Peruvian cuisine — in ceviche, aji de gallina, and fresh salsas where its fruitiness and brightness are essential. The plants are productive and quite ornamental with their pendant yellow fruits. Fresh or dried and ground, it is one of the most versatile and distinctive of the South American aji peppers. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Drop Pepper (Fruity Lemon-Yellow Peruvian Hot Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Lemon Drop is a traditional Peruvian pepper (Ají Lemon in Peru) — a small (1–1.5 inch), thin-walled, conical fruit with a distinctive bright-lemon-yellow color at maturity and a unique combination of intense heat (15,000–30,000 Scoville units — comparable to a serrano but with more heat variability) and fruity, distinctly citrus-lemon flavor. The characteristic lemon flavor — a fruity, citrus-forward quality quite unlike the neutral heat of jalapeños or the fruity sweetness of habaneros — makes Lemon Drop one of the most flavorful hot peppers for cooking applications where heat AND flavor complexity are desired simultaneously. The dried and powdered fruit has an exceptional flavor that is widely used in traditional Peruvian cuisine for adding heat and bright citrus notes. As a Capsicum chinense species, Lemon Drop requires somewhat higher temperatures for germination (80–90°F) and a longer season than C. annuum peppers — start seeds 10–12 weeks before transplanting for adequate development time. The plant is productive in zone 9's long warm season, producing prolifically from late spring through frost. Fresh fruits, dried fruits, and powder form are all excellent culinary applications. The vivid yellow color and intense fruity aroma make Lemon Drop a distinctive addition to the pepper garden. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Frost Thyme (Variegated Lemon-Scented Groundcover Thyme)
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun. Lemon Frost is a variegated selection of lemon thyme, its small, gray-green leaves edged in creamy white for a frosted, two-tone effect that stands out clearly against plain green groundcovers and adds brightness to a rock garden or herb bed even before it flowers. Crushed foliage releases a strong, clean lemon fragrance along with the characteristic thyme aroma, and the leaves are fully usable in the kitchen anywhere a citrusy thyme flavor is wanted, from roasted chicken to herbal tea. Small pale lavender-pink flowers appear in early summer and attract bees, though the foliage color and fragrance remain the plant's main appeal through the rest of the season. Like other creeping thymes, it thrives in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and struggles in rich, moist, or poorly drained conditions, which promote rot and reduce the intensity of both flavor and fragrance. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, tidy mat and encourage fresh, brightly variegated new growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Geranium
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; lemon geranium is a South African scented-leaf pelargonium with intensely lemon-scented, small, crinkled, fan-shaped leaves that release a remarkably true, clean lemon fragrance — not the synthetic-citrus scent of lemon verbena but a pure, fresh, clear lemon aroma that is one of the finest natural citrus scents available in an herb garden plant. The leaves are used to flavor sugar, baked goods, tea, jellies, and custards; placed in the bottom of a greased cake pan before adding batter, they impart a delicate lemon perfume to pound cake and sponge cakes. Small, pale-pink to lavender flowers appear at intervals. Unlike most pelargoniums, lemon geranium tolerates partial shade acceptably, though it flowers most heavily in full sun. In zones 9–11 it grows as a perennial sub-shrub; elsewhere it is grown as a container plant brought indoors in autumn. 'Prince Rupert' (upright, strong-growing), 'French Lace' (compact, cream-variegated leaves), and 'Cy's Sunburst' are notable cultivars. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Gold White Sapote
description: Site Lemon Gold in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil and shelter from strong wind, since it is somewhat less vigorous than other white sapote selections and benefits from a protected spot. The tree tends toward repeated light bloom cycles rather than one big flush, so ripe fruit can be found across a longer window, with the main crop typically coming on in fall. Fruit is medium-to-large, thin-skinned, and turns yellow as it ripens, with smooth flesh carrying a sweet, custardy flavor that growers often describe as having a faint lemony or citrus note setting it apart from other white sapote cultivars. Because it holds flavor well even when picked slightly under-ripe and finished indoors, Lemon Gold is a forgiving choice for growers who want to beat fruit fly or bird pressure. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Guava (Yellow Strawberry Guava)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; lemon guava (yellow-fruited variety of strawberry guava) produces small, round to oval, yellow-skinned fruits with white flesh and a sweet, aromatic, guava-strawberry-lemon flavor that is milder and less acidic than the red-skinned strawberry guava (var. cattleyanum). The glossy, dark green, evergreen leaves and attractive smooth bark are ornamental year-round. Fruits eaten fresh, used in jams, jellies, and juices. Like the red strawberry guava, it is extremely adaptable and has become seriously invasive in Hawaii's native forests and in parts of Florida and the Caribbean, where it forms dense thickets that displace native vegetation. In cultivation outside of tropical areas (zone 8), it is well-behaved; in zone 9–11 it should be monitored for self-seeding. Birds are the primary seed dispersers. More cold-tolerant than tropical guava, growing in zone 8 with some frost protection. The lemon-yellow skin makes ripe fruits easy to identify for harvest. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Mint
description: Also called lemon bee balm or horsemint, this aromatic Monarda produces tiered whorls of lavender-pink blooms that draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Surface sow the seed where plants are to grow, pressing it in for good contact, and expect uneven germination over two to three weeks. It thrives in full sun and average, well-drained soil and self-sows to return year after year. Harvest fragrant foliage for tea and leave some flowers standing to feed pollinators. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Lemon Myrtle
description: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon myrtle is an Australian native rainforest tree with the most intensely concentrated lemon fragrance of any plant on Earth — the essential oil content of the leaves (95% citral) vastly exceeds that of lemon balm, lemon verbena, or lemon thyme. Fresh or dried leaves are used in cooking exactly as lemon is used, in teas, baked goods, sauces, marinades, ice cream, and fish dishes, with a clean, pure lemon flavor that holds up better to heat than actual lemon juice. It is increasingly popular as a culinary specialty herb in Zone 9–11 gardens in the US, particularly in coastal California and the Gulf Coast. The shiny, oval, evergreen leaves are attractive year-round, and small clusters of white flowers appear in summer. It makes an excellent large container specimen in colder zones that can be moved to protection before frost. Harvest leaves fresh as needed or dry for long-term use. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Perilla
description: Lemon perilla is the least commonly cultivated of the three recognized botanical varieties of Perilla frutescens, standing apart from the familiar leaf shiso (var. crispa) and Korean kkaennip (var. japonica) by its finer, noticeably hairy stems and leaves and a bright citrus note layered over the usual perilla mint-anise base. The lemon fragrance makes it a more delicate substitute for green shiso where a lighter, brighter aroma is wanted, torn fresh over cold noodle dishes, steeped for herbal tea, or used sparingly as a fish garnish. It is less vigorous and slower to bulk up than standard shiso, so give plants a head start with consistent moisture and a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage tender. Pinch flower spikes to extend leaf production, though a few plants can be left to seed for next year's crop since it self-sows readily once established. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Lemon Queen Cotton Lavender (Pale Creamy-Yellow Gray Santolina)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Lemon Queen' shares the finely dissected, woolly, silver-gray foliage of gray santolina but bears pale, creamy-lemon-yellow button flowers rather than the species' bright gold, giving it a softer look in pastel and silver-themed plantings. It requires the same superb drainage as the species and will rot in wet, heavy, or humid conditions without excellent airflow. Shear after flowering to keep growth compact and prevent the woody, gappy center that develops on unpruned plants. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Thyme
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lemon thyme provides the same low-growing, woody-stemmed, small-leafed thyme habit as common thyme but with distinctly and strongly lemon-scented foliage from the volatile oil constituents geraniol and linalool. The lemon fragrance is immediately apparent on touching the leaves and makes lemon thyme particularly valuable for fish dishes, roasted poultry, herb butters, cream sauces, and lemon-scented baked goods where a citrus-thyme combination is desired. Pale-pink to lavender-pink flowers in early summer attract bees and other pollinators. The variegated cultivars Aureus (golden-edged leaves) and Silver Queen (cream-variegated) add bright foliage color to the herb garden edge, rock garden, or container planting while retaining the full lemon-thyme culinary flavor. Grows identically to common thyme in its requirements for very well-drained, lean soil and full sun exposure. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Thyme (Citrus-Scented Thyme)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; Lemon thyme is a hybrid thyme with an intensely pleasant lemon-citrus fragrance and flavor overlaid on the traditional thyme aromatic — the combination of thyme's herbal character with a bright, clean citrus note makes lemon thyme one of the most useful and distinctive culinary herbs for fish, poultry, tea, desserts, and anywhere a citrus-thyme combination is desired. The low, spreading, mat-forming habit (4–8 inches tall, spreading 12–18 inches) is elegant in rock gardens, between stepping stones, and as a fragrant ground cover in well-drained, sunny areas. In summer, small pale-pink to lavender flowers attract bees. The most commonly grown lemon thyme cultivar is 'Silver Queen' — a variegated selection with silver-margined green leaves that adds ornamental value to the culinary utility. 'Aureus' (Gold Lemon Thyme) has yellow-variegated leaves. The plain green form provides the most intense flavor. In zone 9's summer humidity, lemon thyme is the most heat-sensitive common thyme — it benefits from afternoon shade during peak summer heat and absolutely requires sharp drainage to survive zone 9 summers. Container culture in a porous mix with excellent drainage is often the most reliable approach in Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Verbena
description: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in summer rather than from seed, which has poor viability; root cuttings in moist perlite under plastic until rooted. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil; in zones below 8 grow in containers that can be overwintered indoors in a cool, bright spot. Prune hard in spring when new growth emerges from what may look like dead wood — lemon verbena is often a slow riser after dormancy. Harvest leaves any time for intensely lemon-scented tea, dessert flavoring, and potpourri; fragrance peaks just before the plant begins to flower. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Winter Savory
description: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since seed-raised plants of this form can lose the true lemon character. Lemon Winter Savory forms the same tidy, semi-evergreen mound of narrow dark leaves as standard winter savory, but crushed foliage releases a clean, sweet citrus fragrance in place of the usual resinous, peppery savory smell, making it a workable substitute for lemon thyme in the kitchen. Because the lemon flavor fades under long cooking, add sprigs near the end of cooking for fish, poultry, or bean dishes rather than simmering them in from the start. Clip the plant back after its small summer flowers fade to keep the mound tight and encourage fresh, strongly scented new growth for the following season. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Lemon Zest Mango (Dwarf Container Mango with Citrusy Flavor)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover before frost. Lemon Zest is a true dwarf mango, bred specifically for container culture and small landscapes, staying compact enough to manage on a sunny patio while still bearing full-sized fruit. Its bright yellow, fiberless flesh carries a distinctive sweet-tart, citrusy note that gives the cultivar its name, setting it apart from the purely sweet flavor of most mango cultivars. Because it stays small, Lemon Zest is one of the more practical mango choices for zone 9 gardeners who want to grow mango in a container that can be sheltered through winter rather than risking an in-ground planting. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lemonade Berry (Lemonade Sumac, California Lemonade Berry)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean soil in fall or early spring; lemonade berry is a coastal chaparral shrub of southern California prized for edible red-orange berries (technically drupes) covered in a sticky, tart coating — the berries can be soaked in cold water for 15–30 minutes to make a refreshing, pink, lemonade-like drink that indigenous Chumash and Cahuilla peoples have used for centuries. The berry flavor is strongly acidic and lemony with a resinous undertone. Absolutely drought-tolerant once established, thriving on coastal rainfall with no supplemental water after the first year — an ideal California-friendly landscape plant combining edibility with low maintenance and excellent wildlife value. Makes an attractive hedge or screen and tolerates salt spray. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lemongrass
description: Propagate by placing fresh grocery-store stalks (with roots intact) in water until roots develop, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Lemongrass needs heat and consistent moisture; water deeply and regularly during the growing season. In zones below 10, grow in large containers and bring indoors before first frost, cutting back to 6 in tall. Harvest outer stalks by cutting or twisting at the base when they reach pencil thickness; use the pale, tender base for cooking. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Lemony Lace Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Ornamental Elderberry)
description: Lemony Lace is a compact, rounded ornamental elderberry selected for finely dissected, lacy, bright chartreuse-gold foliage held on contrasting near-black stems, a dramatic color and texture combination for a mixed border or foundation planting. Flat clusters of pinkish-white flowers appear in late spring, followed by small red berries that, like other red elderberries, are mildly toxic raw and should be cooked before any culinary use, or simply left for birds. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than wild red elderberry, needs only light shaping after bloom, and performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid, since foliage color and vigor decline in the most intense Deep South heat. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lena American Persimmon (Large Low-Astringency Claypool-Program Persimmon)
description: Lena, also recorded as L-104, is a named selection from James Claypool's Indiana American persimmon breeding program and has been propagated and passed along through collector orchards, including Jerry Lehman's persimmon research farm in Terre Haute, Indiana. It produces large fruit for the species with red-orange flesh, and it is noted among American persimmon growers for being especially low in astringency even before fruit is fully soft, though as with all Diospyros virginiana selections the best flavor and sweetness develop only after full ripening. Lena ripens late in the fall relative to earlier cultivars such as Early Golden, so it suits growers with a longer autumn season. The tree shares the general toughness of native persimmon, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soils once established, and needs little maintenance beyond removing root suckers. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Leningrad Garlic (Russian Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Leningrad is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic sourced from the historic seed collections of St. Petersburg, Russia, valued by cold-climate growers for exceptional winter hardiness and vigorous growth even after harsh, deep-freeze winters. Bulbs form with 4-6 large, easy-to-peel white-wrapped cloves and a robust, sharp flavor that mellows nicely when roasted. Because Porcelain types need a strong cold vernalization period, Leningrad performs best in northern gardens with reliably cold winters and struggles in warm-winter regions. Select this cultivar for its proven reliability in USDA zones 3-5 where many other garlic strains falter. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Lentil
description: Direct-sow lentils in early spring as soon as the soil is workable, planting seeds 1 inch deep in rows 12–18 inches apart; they germinate readily in cool soil and tolerate light frost. Choose a well-drained bed in full sun and avoid high-nitrogen soil, which promotes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Plants need little water once established and are highly drought-tolerant. Harvest when the lower pods turn tan and begin to rattle but before the stems dry completely; pull the entire plant and hang it upside down in a dry, airy space to finish curing before threshing. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Lentil
description: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that delay podding. The slender, branching plants benefit from brushy twigs as supports to keep pods off the ground and improve air circulation. Harvest the entire plant when the majority of lower pods have turned tan but before they shatter. Thresh by beating dried plants on a tarp and winnow lightly to clean seed before storage. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Leon Millot Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American Red Wine Grape)
description: A sibling seedling of Marechal Foch from the same Kuhlmann breeding program, Leon Millot ripens slightly earlier and produces deeply colored juice prized for blending into rustic, full-bodied red wines. Its compact clusters of small berries set reliably even in cooler, shorter growing seasons, and the vine shares its sibling's strong resistance to winter cold. Growers should watch for its tendency toward vigorous growth by shoot-thinning and opening the canopy to improve air movement and reduce fungal disease pressure. It performs best on a cane-pruned trellis system. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Leren (Sweet Corn Root)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in warm, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; leren is a Caribbean and northern South American relative of the ornamental Calathea houseplants, grown in dooryard gardens for the cluster of small, crisp, ivory-white tubers it forms around its base, which are boiled or steamed and eaten much like a delicate, sweet-flavored water chestnut or corn-flavored potato. The broad, upright, paddle-shaped leaves make it an attractive foliage plant for a shaded tropical bed in addition to its root crop, and clumps expand steadily by rhizome offsets that are simply divided to start new plantings or lifted for harvest. Keep soil evenly moist throughout the growing season, since dry spells check tuber development, and harvest by digging the whole clump eight to twelve months after planting once the foliage begins to decline. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Lesser Calamint
description: Calamintha nepeta is a compact, bushy, aromatic perennial of the mint family (Lamiaceae) native to dry, sunny grasslands, rocky hillsides, and chalky banks throughout southern and central Europe, producing small, softly hairy, gray-green, rounded leaves with an exceptionally pleasant minty-peppery-oregano fragrance and an unusually long succession of tiny, two-lipped, white to pale-lilac flowers from July through September that make it one of the single best perennial plants for attracting native bees, bumblebees, and other pollinators. Direct-sow seeds in spring in very well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline, preferably chalky or stony soil in full sun; it is summer drought-tolerant once established, requiring minimal irrigation in well-drained soils, and will decline in rich, moist, or waterlogged conditions. Lesser calamint has an ancient culinary history in Mediterranean Europe: the leaves and flowering tops are used fresh or dried as a flavoring for roasted meats (particularly in Italian cuisine, where it is sometimes called nipitella and used with porcini mushrooms), as a tisane, and as an aromatic addition to salads. Shear plants by about one-third after the first main flush of bloom to maintain tidiness and encourage a second flowering period; plants self-sow moderately and naturalize well on dry banks, gravel paths, and in dry-stone wall crevices. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Lesser Galangal (Small Thai Cooking Galangal Root Herb)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Lesser Galangal (Alpinia officinarum) is a rhizomatous herb from southern China and Southeast Asia grown for its aromatic rhizomes, which provide the distinctive peppery-gingery-citrusy flavor that is essential to Thai tom kha soup, Thai curries, Indonesian laksa, and numerous other Southeast Asian dishes. The flavor differs significantly from ginger — sharper, more peppery, with pine and citrus overtones — and from greater galangal (A. galanga) which is milder and more floral. The smaller stature of lesser galangal (2–3 feet) compared to the 5–6 foot greater galangal makes it more manageable in typical garden settings and suitable for large containers. The rhizomes can be harvested from the edge of established clumps after the first year without disturbing the entire plant — a sustained harvest approach that allows the clump to continue producing indefinitely. In Gulf South gardens, lesser galangal thrives in the warm, humid conditions similar to those of its native growing range. The ornamental narrow leaves and occasional small white-and-red flower spikes provide year-round interest as a foliage plant in partial-shade tropical herb gardens. The rhizomes freeze and can be grated directly from frozen state for cooking, making storage simple. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Lettuce Leaf Basil
description: This exceptionally productive sweet basil produces huge, light green leaves nearly the size of your hand that are more sweet than spicy. The broad leaves make an excellent lettuce substitute in wraps and sandwiches or a bold layer in a caprese salad. Start seed indoors in warmth and move to a sunny bed only after frost danger has passed. Keep soil evenly moist, pinch off flower spikes, and harvest whole leaves to encourage continued production. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Lettuce Microgreens
description: Sow lettuce seed thinly pressed onto the surface of a moist tray, since it germinates best in cooler conditions and with some light. Keep only a light cover for a day or two, then bring the seedlings into bright light to prevent leggy growth. Mist gently and avoid overwatering, as tender lettuce seedlings rot easily. Harvest the mild, sweet, crunchy greens after about ten days to two weeks once the cotyledons are fully expanded. Matures in 10–15 days from seed.

name: Leucocarpa Nanking Cherry (White-Fruited Nanking Cherry Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun alongside a second Nanking cherry for reliable cross-pollination. Leucocarpa is a distinct white-fruited sport of Nanking cherry, bearing the same abundant early-summer crop as the common red form but with translucent, ivory-white to pale-yellow fruit that ripens a shade later and tends to escape the notice of fruit-eating birds that quickly strip red-fruited plants. The flavor is sweet with less of the tartness typical of the red form, making it pleasant for fresh eating as well as preserves. Like other Nanking cherry selections it flowers very early on a dense, spreading shrub and shrugs off poor, dry, or alkaline soils that would stress most stone fruits; prune lightly after harvest to keep the canopy open and productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Leutschauer Paprika Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Leutschauer Paprika is a Slovak heirloom paprika pepper that produces elongated, pendant, 5–6 inch fruits with exceptionally thin walls and high sugar content — characteristics that make it one of the premier varieties for drying and grinding into fresh paprika. The bright red, fully ripe fruits are dried whole in strings (paprika ristras) or sliced and dehydrated before grinding. The flavor is sweet, slightly fruity, and aromatic — quite different from commercially ground paprika that has lost volatile compounds in processing. Plants are productive on fertile soil with consistent moisture; fruit set can stall during the hottest weeks in zone 9 but resumes in September. This is primarily a drying variety, though the fresh ripe fruits are also edible. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Levant Cotton (Old World Cotton)
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has thoroughly warmed; Levant cotton is one of the two Old World cultivated cotton species, historically grown across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia long before American upland cotton became the dominant commercial fiber crop, and it remains a favorite of heirloom-crop growers and fiber crafters for its distinct, shorter, coarser staple. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers open over summer and fade before dropping, revealing bolls that split open at maturity to expose the cottony lint, ready to hand-pick once fully open and dry. It generally matures a touch faster than upland cotton, making it a reasonable choice where the growing season runs a little shorter, and its compact, shrubby habit and smaller stature suit a raised bed or container planting as well as a row. Grow it as a curiosity, dye-garden, or spinning-fiber crop, and rotate its planting site yearly like any other cotton to limit soil-borne disease buildup. Matures in 140–170 days from seed.

name: Leveller Gooseberry
description: Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil, since Leveller needs steady moisture to size its fruit. This Victorian-era English dessert gooseberry, first raised in the 1850s, is still grown for its very large, pale yellow-green, thin-skinned berries with an exceptionally rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. It is a vigorous, somewhat spreading bush that is more prone to American gooseberry mildew than modern disease-resistant releases, so good airflow matters in humid climates. Best reserved for dedicated fruit growers in cool-summer regions willing to manage its mildew susceptibility for the sake of exceptional flavor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lewis Hazelnut (Improved Kernel-Quality Filbert)
description: Lewis was released by Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program in the late 1990s specifically to improve on the kernel quality and blanching performance of older commercial cultivars like Barcelona and Ennis, producing a good-sized, well-filled nut suited to confectionery use as well as fresh eating. Plant it in full sun and deep, well-drained soil alongside a compatible pollenizer cultivar, since hazelnut catkins shed pollen in late winter while female flowers on a genetically different plant must be receptive at the same time. Lewis predates the Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant OSU releases, so growers in blight-affected regions should scout canes yearly during the dormant season and prune out cankers to manage the disease. It remains a solid choice for home orchardists focused on nut quality where blight pressure is low or well managed. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Li Jujube
description: Li is a large-fruited jujube cultivar producing sweet, apple-crisp fruit that can be eaten fresh or dried like dates. It thrives in hot summers and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and neglect once established. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; a second cultivar such as Lang nearby improves fruit set. Prune in late winter to remove suckers and thin the canopy, and harvest when the fruit turns fully brown. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Liana Yardlong Bean
description: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous 10- to 12-foot vines to climb. Bred to be day-length neutral, Liana is one of the earliest-maturing yardlong bean types and performs reliably in both northern and southern gardens, tolerating heat and humidity better than many snap bean varieties. Harvest the slender green pods at 12-18 inches, well before they reach their full 23-inch potential, for the most tender texture in stir-fries and braised dishes. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Liberica Coffee (Barako Coffee, Liberian Coffee)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Liberica coffee grows as a larger tree than arabica and needs more space; tolerates slightly drier conditions than arabica. Coffea liberica (Liberica coffee or barako) is the rare third major commercial coffee species — a larger, bolder, more assertive plant than arabica (C. arabica) or robusta (C. canephora). Native to the lowland forests of Liberia and West Africa, C. liberica is a substantial tree reaching 20–35 feet (much taller than the 10–15 foot arabica shrub), with large, glossy leaves, large white flowers, and large, asymmetric, elongated coffee fruits (cherries) containing unusually shaped, irregular beans. The flavor of Liberica coffee is perhaps the most controversial in the coffee world: strongly fruity with jackfruit-like, slightly funky, floral-aromatic, sometimes smoky notes — entirely different from the clean, nuanced arabica profile or the bold-bitter robusta profile. Some specialty coffee drinkers consider Liberica's complex, funky, tropical fruit character uniquely wonderful; others find it off-putting. Liberica coffee is of particular importance in the Philippines, where it is known as barako (from a Tagalog word for a virile bull) and has strong cultural identity as the traditional Filipino coffee — once produced in significant quantities on Luzon until coffee rust devastated plantations in the 1880s. Today barako is a prized specialty product in the Philippines. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Liberty Apple (Disease-Resistant Organic Apple, Cornell Scab-Free Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Liberty is self-unfruitful and requires a nearby apple of a compatible variety for pollination; in disease-resistant plantings, pair with Freedom or Enterprise for cross-pollination; Liberty ripens in October producing medium to large, red-blushed fruit with good sweet-tart flavor — quality significantly above what one might expect from a disease-resistant variety. Liberty apple is a Cornell University-developed disease-resistant variety (released 1978) that has become one of the most important apple varieties for home organic production in the eastern United States, where the humid climate creates severe pressure from the four major apple diseases — apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew — that require intensive fungicide spray programs to manage on standard susceptible varieties like Fuji, Gala, and McIntosh. Liberty's multiple-disease resistance package was assembled through deliberate crosses at Cornell that combined resistance genes from multiple sources: the apple scab resistance comes from Malus floribunda 821 (the same source as the PRI disease-resistant breeding program), while fire blight and rust resistance come from other wild Malus species in the parentage. The result is an apple variety that can be grown essentially spray-free in home gardens — a significant advantage for organic-minded gardeners — while still producing attractive, well-flavored fruit that compares favorably with commercial varieties. The fruit is medium to large, red-striped over yellow-green skin, with crisp, juicy, moderately sweet flesh and a pleasant balance of sweet and tart flavor. Liberty has been the recommended variety for organic home orchards from Cornell Extension for over 40 years. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Licorice
description: Scarify seed coat lightly with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix; germination improves significantly with this treatment. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — licorice develops an extensive, deep root system and resents being moved. Roots are ready to harvest in the third or fourth autumn when they are at least pencil-thick, digging carefully to extract as much of the lateral root run as possible. The dried root is used medicinally as a demulcent and anti-inflammatory for digestive and respiratory conditions; note that excessive consumption raises blood pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from seed.

name: Licorice Basil
description: Transplant or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; licorice basil is a large-leaf sweet basil cultivar with an extraordinarily intense anise-licorice aroma — significantly more pronounced than standard Genovese basil — arising from exceptionally high methyl chavicol (estragole) concentration in the essential oil. The wide, dark green, slightly cupped leaves are 2–3 inches long with purple-tinged flower bracts that make the plant quite ornamental when in bloom. Licorice basil is prized for Thai-inspired cooking, Vietnamese-style salads, and beverages where a prominent anise note is desired — it is also used in cocktails, syrups, and infused vinegars. The flavor is distinctly different from Cinnamon or Thai basil types despite also containing high methyl chavicol. In zone 9 the plant performs best in spring and fall, but continues producing through summer with regular pinching and irrigation. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Licorice Mint Hyssop
description: Surface-sow indoors 8 weeks before last frost, leaving seed uncovered since light aids germination. This golden-leaved anise hyssop offers licorice-scented foliage for teas and blue flower spikes for pollinators. Transplant to full sun in well-drained soil, spacing to allow good airflow. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering into fall and prevent excessive self-seeding. Harvest leaves and flowers fresh or dried and cut plants back after frost. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Licorice Plant (Trailing Silver-Felted Foliage Plant)
description: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Helichrysum petiolare is a South African subshrub grown for its densely felted, round, silver-gray leaves that release a mild licorice-like scent when brushed, rather than for its small, insignificant white flowers, which are best pinched off to keep foliage full. Its vigorous, trailing stems make it a classic 'spiller' for mixed containers and hanging baskets, cascading a foot or more over the rim in a single season. Established plants tolerate drought well but benefit from regular watering in containers; where hardy, it forms a sprawling evergreen mound that can be cut back hard in spring to renew dense growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Licorice Root (Spanish Licorice, True Licorice)
description: Plant root divisions in deeply tilled, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep soil in full sun; harvest roots in fall of years 2–3. Glycyrrhiza glabra (licorice root or Spanish licorice) is the plant behind all licorice flavoring in candy, herbal teas, and medicine — a perennial Mediterranean and Central Asian leguminous herb producing sweet, tan-skinned taproot stubs extending 3–4 feet into the soil. The roots contain glycyrrhizin, a saponin compound approximately 30–50 times sweeter than sucrose, responsible for the characteristic sweet, anise-like, distinctive licorice flavor. Licorice root has been used medicinally for over 4,000 years — in ancient Egypt, China, India, and Greece — as a treatment for coughs, digestive disorders, and ulcers; it remains one of the most widely used herbal medicines worldwide, used in pharmaceuticals as a sweetening and flavoring agent for bitter medicines (the name 'licorice' comes from the Greek for 'sweet root'). CAUTION: Overconsumption of licorice root or glycyrrhizin can cause hypertension, potassium loss, and hormonal effects — not for excessive use, and problematic for those with high blood pressure or heart conditions. As a garden plant, licorice grows as a multi-stemmed, pinnately-leafed, attractive perennial shrub with pale lavender flowers — harvest roots in the fall of year 2 or 3 for best glycyrrhizin content. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lila Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Lila is a Mexican-race avocado cultivar valued for its combination of cold hardiness and rich, high-oil-content flesh with the classic anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race avocados, distinguishing it from the milder Guatemalan and West Indian races. Mexican-race avocados tend to have thinner, smoother skin and smaller fruit than Guatemalan types, but generally offer superior cold tolerance, an important trait for gardeners at the northern edge of avocado range. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lillian's Yellow Heirloom Tomato (Pale Yellow Tennessee Potato-Leaf Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the tall, vigorous potato-leaf vines. Lillian's Yellow was collected from a Tennessee grower and passed on for distribution through a Seed Savers Exchange yearbook; it requires a long season, typically 90-100 days from transplant, to produce its large, 12-20 ounce, pale yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed pink at the blossom end. The meaty, low-seed flesh is prized among heirloom growers as one of the finest-tasting yellow tomatoes, with a mild, citrusy sweetness distinct from more golden-orange yellow varieties. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Lily White Sea Kale (Vigorous Seed-Raised Forcing Strain)
description: Lily White is a named UK seed strain of sea kale selected over generations for producing especially pale, blanch-white forced shoots with minimal bitterness, along with more reliably true germination from seed than typical wild-collected sea kale seed. It forms the same billowing mounds of crinkled, blue-gray, cabbage-like leaves and honey-scented white summer flowers as the species, and is grown identically: choose a permanent bed for its long taproot, let plants establish for two to three years, then cover dormant crowns with a forcing pot in late winter to produce sweet, nutty, asparagus-textured shoots in early spring. Because plants are deep-rooted and drought-tolerant once established, they perform especially well in coastal gardens and sandy, low-fertility soils where few other vegetables thrive. Matures in 545–910 days from seed.

name: Lima Bean
description: Sow seeds 1 to 1.5 in deep in loose, warm soil with the eye of the bean facing downward. Lima beans are sensitive to drought during flowering; irregular moisture can cause blossom drop and reduced pod set. For fresh shell use, harvest pods when they are bright green and plump but before they begin to fade or yellow. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine for dry bean storage. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Limber Honeysuckle (Wild Honeysuckle)
description: Plant in well-drained, loamy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun along a trellis, fence, or forest edge; Limber Honeysuckle is a native twining vine found across northern and central North America from Quebec to British Columbia and south into the Ozarks and Appalachians, scrambling up shrubs and small trees along forest margins where it is an important nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring and early-summer residency. The flowers range from orange-yellow to red and appear in May–June in clustered whorls at the stem tips, followed by translucent red to orange berries in late summer that are eaten by thrushes, vireos, and other woodland songbirds. Like Lonicera prolifera, it has perfoliate leaves near the stem tips where the uppermost pair of leaves fuse into a disk, though in this species the leaves beneath the flower clusters are typically distinctly bluish-green. It is non-invasive and well-behaved in the garden, rarely exceeding 15 feet, making it one of the best native vine choices for small to medium trellises in northern gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Limbertwig Apple (Old Fashioned Southern Appalachian Heirloom)
description: Stake young trees loosely, since the cultivar takes its name from the distinctively supple, drooping branches that bend rather than break under a heavy crop. Limbertwig is really an old Southern Appalachian family name covering many closely related strains, so trees sold under this name can vary somewhat, but all share a rich, spicy-tart flavor that many growers feel improves after a few weeks in storage. It was a dooryard and cider staple across the Southern mountains through the 19th century and is still sought out by heirloom orchardists for its complex, old-fashioned flavor and long keeping quality. Matures in 160–180 days from transplant.

name: Lime
description: Key lime (C. aurantiifolia) is the most cold-sensitive common citrus and is reliable only in zones 10–11; Persian lime (C. latifolia) is somewhat hardier and suits zone 9 in sheltered spots. Both are self-fertile and produce almost continuously in warm climates with adequate water. Container culture in a large pot (25+ gallons) allows limes to be grown farther north and moved indoors during frost. Fruit is best harvested while still green and fully sized — if left to yellow on the tree it becomes dry and flavorless. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Lime Balm (Lime-Scented Lemon Balm)
description: Lime Balm traces to a wild population from Crete, sometimes classified as Melissa officinalis subsp. altissima, and is distinguished from ordinary lemon balm by its softly hairy, lime-green foliage that smells and tastes distinctly of lime rather than lemon, along with larger, showier light-lavender flower spikes that draw in bees. Site it in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil, giving it a little afternoon shade in hot-summer regions to keep the leaves from scorching. Harvest young leaves fresh for a citrusy herbal tea or infused syrup, and shear the plant back hard after flowering to encourage a flush of tender new growth and to prevent it from becoming leggy. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, since named selections like this one are best kept true by division rather than seed. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Lime Basil
description: Direct-sow after the soil warms past 65F, scattering seed thinly and thinning to a hand's width apart. The bright citrus scent makes this basil superb in Southeast Asian dishes and cold drinks. Give it full sun and steady moisture in rich, free-draining soil for the best oil content. Pinch growing tips early to build a bushy plant and delay bolting. Harvest leaves in the morning when the fragrant oils are most concentrated. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Lime Basil
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lime Basil is an Ocimum x citriodorum hybrid selected for an intense natural lime-citrus fragrance and flavor derived from high concentrations of limonene, citral, and related volatile compounds in the leaves — the aroma is strikingly and unmistakably lime, not just vaguely citrus as with some other basil varieties. The small, pointed bright green leaves have a fresh, bright citrus-lime character distinctly different from standard sweet basil (which contains primarily linalool and estragole). The lime flavor makes it a natural pairing for Thai and Vietnamese cuisines where lime leaves are traditional (dried Lime Basil can partially substitute for kaffir lime leaf), in fresh salsas, tropical fruit salads, seafood dishes, limeade, and cocktails. The compact, neat habit with small leaves is attractive in herb gardens. Like all basil, Lime Basil is frost-tender and performs best in warm weather, though it is somewhat more heat-tolerant than lemon basil. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Lime Mint (Bright Lime-Citrus Scented Spearmint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Lime Mint bears glossy green leaves with a sharp, bright lime-citrus scent and flavor rather than the classic menthol of spearmint or peppermint, prized for muddling into cocktails, iced tea, and other cold summer drinks where its citrus edge stands out. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Lime Thyme
description: Lime Thyme is a citrus-scented lemon thyme selection whose bright, tangy-lime aroma comes through strongly when the leaves are brushed or crushed, making it popular for teas, marinades, and citrus-forward dishes. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid rich or waterlogged ground, which encourages rot and dilutes flavor. Trim back hard after flowering to maintain compact, bushy growth and encourage fresh, aromatic new leaves. It combines well with other creeping thymes in a sunny path or container planting. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Limeberry (Myrtle Lime)
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; limeberry is frost-tender and best suited to sheltered dooryard plantings in zones 9b-11 or large containers moved indoors for winter further north. This small, thorny, trifoliate-leaved citrus relative bears intensely fragrant, orange-blossom-scented white flowers nearly year-round in frost-free climates, followed by small, oval, deep-red fruit with a sweet, thin skin over lime-tart, mucilaginous pulp traditionally used in preserves and candies rather than eaten fresh. Long grown as a dooryard and hedge plant across the tropics and subtropics, it tolerates shearing well and makes a fragrant, fine-textured, thorny barrier planting or specimen shrub near a patio where its flower scent can be enjoyed. Protect from frost, water regularly during dry spells, and prune lightly after flushes of bloom to maintain shape. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Limelight Licorice Plant (Chartreuse Trailing Foliage)
description: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; 'Limelight' carries the same soft, velvety, rounded leaves as the species but in a glowing chartreuse-to-lime-green that releases a warm licorice scent in hot weather. Its trailing stems make it a favored 'hot color' spiller for mixed containers, playing off purple and burgundy foliage companions. In regions with intense summer sun, a little afternoon shade helps prevent the pale foliage from scorching or bleaching; pinch stem tips periodically to keep growth dense rather than leggy. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Limequat
description: Limequat is a Key lime × kumquat hybrid combining the intense lime flavor of Citrus aurantiifolia with the cold hardiness of Fortunella, tolerating temperatures down to about 20°F — the hardiest of the lime-flavored citrus. Like kumquat, the entire fruit — sweet edible peel and sour juice pulp together — can be eaten whole or sliced into drinks and salads. Trees are self-fertile, compact, and well-suited to container culture in zones 7–8, where they can be moved indoors during hard freezes. The small oval to round fruits ripen from green to yellow in autumn through winter; harvest when fully yellow for the sweetest peel, or use while still green for the most intense lime flavor. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lincoln Leek (Dual-Purpose Baby and Full-Size Leek)
description: Start Lincoln leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Lincoln is a flexible, open-pollinated leek that rewards impatient gardeners as well as patient ones — pull it young at 50-60 days for slender, tender 'baby' or finger leeks with a mild, delicate flavor, or let it grow on to a full-sized 16-20 inch stalk for a heartier harvest later in the season. Hill or trench soil around the growing stems to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion as the plants mature. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free, and harvest through fall and into winter in mild climates, since leeks tolerate cold far better than onions. Matures in 50–130 days from transplant.

name: Lincoln Pea (Homesteader Pea)
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep, 2–4 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; direct seed as soon as soil can be worked in early spring. Lincoln (sold as Homesteader in Britain and by some American companies — both names refer to the same variety) is a mid-season American shelling pea considered by many gardeners and seed savers to produce the finest overall flavor and texture among commonly available bush peas; the compact plants produce blunt-tipped pods with 7–9 large, wrinkled (sweeter) peas each, ripening in 65–70 days from sowing. The wrinkled seed type indicates higher sugar content compared to smooth-seeded varieties; like all garden peas, Lincoln must be harvested at precise peak ripeness and eaten promptly before sugars convert to starch. An excellent variety for freezing as well as fresh eating; it remains the benchmark for shelling pea flavor among serious home gardeners. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Lingonberry
description: Lingonberries require acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and perform well as an ornamental groundcover in zones 2–7. They produce two crops per year — a smaller crop in midsummer and a larger one in fall. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants to 3–4 in every few years to rejuvenate. Harvest when berries are deep red and slightly tart; they store well refrigerated and are traditionally used in Scandinavian preserves and sauces. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Linnea Lingonberry (Swedish Seedling Selection)
description: Linnea was selected in Sweden from an open-pollinated seedling of the older wild-derived cultivar 'Sanna' and is grown as a somewhat newer, more refined alternative within the same Scandinavian lingonberry breeding line. Like its parent, it produces glossy evergreen foliage year-round and small pink-tinged bell flowers in late spring, followed by tart red berries in two flushes per season. It requires the same very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil as blueberry and performs best with light shade rather than baking full sun in warmer parts of its hardiness range. Because lingonberry spreads slowly by underground rhizomes, space plants closely if a solid groundcover is the goal, or wider if used as an edging plant. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lionel Fortescue Mahonia (Early-Blooming Upright Winter Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Lionel Fortescue, raised from the same Mahonia japonica x M. lomariifolia cross as 'Charity' and selected at The Garden House in Buckland Monachorum, Devon, is distinguished by unusually early bloom, with dense, stiffly upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers often opening in October, well ahead of most other x media selections, above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage. Its early flowering extends the winter garden's fragrant-shrub season and provides an early nectar source for late-active pollinators. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lipan Pecan (Scab-Resistant Annual-Bearing USDA-ARS Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun; Lipan is a Type II pollen shedder, so pair with a Type I cultivar such as Cape Fear or Pawnee for reliable cross-pollination. Released in 2011 by the USDA-ARS pecan breeding program at Brownwood, Texas from a Cheyenne x Pawnee cross, Lipan was specifically selected for excellent resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that most limits pecan production in humid climates, combined with regular, non-alternate annual bearing that avoids the boom-and-bust cycles common in older cultivars. Nuts mature roughly two weeks after Pawnee, extending the harvest window when the two are planted together, and the tree comes into bearing relatively young for a pecan. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and harvest once the shucks split open in fall. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Lipstick Pepper (AAS-Winning Sweet Pimento-Type Pepper, Compact and Prolific)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or red; red is sweeter. Lipstick Pepper is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the sweet pepper category, recognized for its combination of compact plant size, prolific productivity, and exceptional fruit quality in the pimento pepper class. The variety belongs to the pimento type — a group of sweet peppers distinct from bell peppers in fruit shape (heart-shaped, conical, or tapered rather than blocky), flesh thickness (very thick walls with small seed cavity), and flavor (sweeter, with less of the grassy quality of green bell peppers). Pimento peppers have a long history in American cooking: the red pimento paste used to stuff olives and fill pimento cheese sandwiches is made from this type, and the pimento's thick, sweet walls make it the preferred pepper for roasting, where the flesh caramelizes to an exceptional sweetness. Lipstick's AAS recognition was awarded specifically for its performance across diverse North American climates — including hot-summer regions where standard bell peppers underperform — making it a practical choice for gardeners in zone 9 who find that large bell peppers drop their blossoms or produce poorly during the Gulf South's summer heat peak. The fruit is medium-sized (3–4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), heart-shaped to conical with a small pointed tip, and ripens from green to a deep, brilliant red. The skin is thinner than a bell pepper and the flesh is proportionally thicker, with a small, easily removed seed cavity. The flavor at red-ripe stage is very sweet, almost candy-like, with none of the bitterness that some tasters detect in green bell peppers. Matures in 53–65 days from transplant.

name: Lipstick Sweet Pepper (Pimiento-Type Mini Sweet Bell Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost with spacing of 15–20 inches. Lipstick is a Burpee-developed pimiento-type sweet pepper that produces small to medium (3 x 3.5 inch), heart-shaped, very thick-walled fruits of the pimiento class — a pepper type characterized by a rounder, more compact form than standard bell peppers, extraordinarily thick walls relative to total size, very few seeds, and exceptional sweetness. The pimiento type has been prized by Spanish and Mediterranean cooks for centuries for its superior eating quality (pimientos are what give pimento-stuffed olives their distinctive flavor and the Spanish name 'pimiento' itself means pepper in Spanish). Lipstick delivers the classic pimiento character in a compact, prolific plant suitable for small gardens and containers: the fruits have very thick walls that hold up to heat, an extremely sweet, mild flavor with no heat, and the characteristic heart-shaped cross-section when sliced that makes them visually distinctive from bell peppers. The vivid, saturated red color at full ripeness is striking and the thick walls make Lipstick excellent for roasting, stuffing with cheese, and eating raw where the thickness provides a satisfying crunch. Ripens more completely and uniformly than many larger bell types, making it practical for gardeners who want to harvest primarily red-ripe peppers. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Lipstick Sweet Pimento Pepper
description: Start seeds at 75–85°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Lipstick is an early-maturing sweet pimento-type pepper that produces heart-shaped, 4-inch fruits with thick, candy-sweet walls, minimal seed cavity, and zero heat; they ripen from green to a brilliant lipstick red earlier than most pimentos, making it one of the better sweet pepper choices for northern gardens and short-season growers. The fruits are remarkably thick-walled and sweet when roasted, and they peel cleanly after charring, making them ideal for preserving as roasted red peppers. Compact plants are well-suited to containers. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Lisbon Lemon Tree
description: Lisbon is a vigorous, cold-tolerant lemon that fruits heavily and produces classic tart, juicy fruit almost year-round in warm regions. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. In zones colder than 9, grow in a pot that can be moved indoors or to a bright greenhouse for winter. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer during active growth and water deeply but allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Thin fruit lightly on young trees so the branches are not overloaded. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Listada de Gandia Eggplant
description: A Spanish heirloom with teardrop fruit striped purple and white and a notably sweet, mild flavor. Give it a long warm season, starting seed indoors early and transplanting into the warmest bed available. Fruit skin is thin and bruises easily, so handle carefully and harvest with shears. Pick when fruit is 5 to 7 inches and still shiny, before seeds harden. Steady watering prevents blossom-end problems and keeps flesh creamy. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Listada de Gandia Eggplant (Striped Italian Heirloom Eggplant)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Listada de Gandia is one of the most beautiful and visually distinctive eggplant varieties — a traditional Italian heirloom from the Valencia region of Spain producing oval to oblong, medium-large fruits with a stunning two-tone pattern of cream-white base with vivid purple-lavender stripes or splashes covering much of the surface. No two fruits have exactly the same pattern, making each harvest visually unique. Beyond its striking appearance, Listada de Gandia is prized for its exceptionally mild, tender, low-bitterness flesh — the thin skin and low seed content make it one of the finest eggplants for fresh preparations, grilling, and Italian dishes where eggplant bitterness would be unwelcome. The mild, creamy flesh has a slightly sweet, delicate flavor that is quite different from the stronger flavor of large black globe eggplants. Harvest at medium size (4–6 inches long) when the skin is shiny — the stripes fade and seeds become noticeable if left too long. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type. The ornamental quality of the fruits and foliage makes Listada de Gandia attractive even as an edible ornamental in mixed garden beds and containers. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables, thriving in the Gulf South summer. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Litchi Tomato (Morelle de Balbis, Sticky Nightshade)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; wear gloves when handling — plants are densely spiny. Solanum sisymbriifolium (litchi tomato or morelle de Balbis) is a South American tomato relative producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red berries resembling tiny tomatoes, enclosed in a spiny, papery calyx that peels back to reveal the glossy red fruit at maturity — the resemblance to lychee fruit when partially enclosed in its papery husk gives the plant its common name 'litchi tomato.' The flavor is sweet-tart, similar to a cherry tomato but with a distinct floral undertone; fruits are eaten fresh, used in jams, pies, and salsas, or dried. The plants are extremely productive in warm climates, bearing prolifically from midsummer through frost. The entire plant is covered with numerous, sharp, reddish-orange spines on stems, leaves, and calyces that make handling without gloves painful; despite this deterrent, the plants are interesting and productive specialty edibles. CAUTION: Like all nightshades, the leaves, stems, and unripe berries are toxic; consume ripe fruits only. The spiny character makes litchi tomato a useful barrier or living fence plant. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Little Angel Dwarf Variegated Burnet
description: Little Angel is a naturally dwarf sport of great burnet, forming a tight, low mat of small pinnate leaves edged in cream-white rather than the tall, airy clumps of the straight species, with the same cool, cucumber-like flavor prized in salad burnet. Wiry stems carry small maroon button flowers well above the foliage from mid- to late summer, giving a second season of interest to what is otherwise grown as a low edging or container herb. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain the tight habit and refresh vigor, since the variegation is a stable sport that holds true from division but not from seed. Harvest only the youngest inner leaves for eating, as older foliage toughens and the cucumber flavor fades. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Little Darling Watermelon (Compact Personal-Size Hybrid)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart since vines run only about 4-5 feet, considerably shorter than traditional watermelon varieties. Little Darling produces oblong, dark-striped fruits around 5 by 8 inches and 5-7 lbs, with crisp, sweet red flesh rating around 12 on the Brix sugar scale, making it a good choice for gardeners who want full-flavored, classic watermelon character without the space demands of large-vine heirlooms. Water deeply and consistently through flowering and fruit set, then reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip and by checking that the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned, since the compact plant can otherwise make ripeness easy to misjudge. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Little Finger Carrot
description: Direct sow this French baby carrot in loose, stone-free soil, since carrots dislike transplanting and forked roots result from compacted ground.
