Sow seed shallowly and keep the surface consistently moist until germination, which can take two to three weeks. Thin seedlings to about an inch apart so the slender 3 inch roots can size up sweet and crisp. Little Finger is ideal for shallow beds and containers and is best harvested young; succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Little Finger Eggplant (Slender Baby Asian Finger Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Harvest slender purple-black fruits at 3–5 inches. Little Finger is a slender, finger-shaped Asian eggplant — a compact variety producing clusters of elongated, narrow fruits (2–5 inches long, 0.5–1 inch in diameter) of the finger eggplant type. The finger eggplant category is distinct from the large, globe-shaped Italian types and the longer Asian slicers: finger eggplants are the smallest category, producing bite-sized to small fruits in prolific clusters on bushy plants. Little Finger's small fruits are characterized by very thin, tender skin; virtually no seeds; and mildly sweet, creamy flesh without the bitterness sometimes found in large-fruited types. The thin skin means no peeling is required — fruits can be cooked whole (roasted, grilled, or sautéed) without preparation. The compact cluster-fruiting habit makes Little Finger one of the most productive eggplants per plant for its size, making it excellent for small gardens and containers. The fruits are harvested frequently (every 2–3 days at peak production), and the small size makes them ideal for stir-fries, kebabs, and preparations where bite-sized pieces are desired. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Little Fingers Carrot
description: This heirloom baby carrot produces small, vibrant orange roots packed with sweet flavor, bred originally for canning but excellent fresh or in containers. Sow seeds directly into loose soil and keep the bed evenly moist during the slow germination. Thin seedlings so the short roots can size up cleanly. Harvest while the roots are still small and tender for the sweetest, most delicate flavor. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Little Fingers Eggplant (AAS-Winning Slender Asian-Type Eggplant)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Little Fingers, a 1985 All-America Selections winner, produces clusters of slender, finger-sized, deep purple Asian-type eggplant fruit that mature quickly and prolifically, giving a much faster and heavier harvest than large-fruited standard eggplant types. Its compact plant size and quick maturity make it a good fit for containers, small raised beds, or gardeners wanting an early eggplant harvest. Pick fruit young while still glossy and tender, several inches long, since Asian-type eggplant quickly becomes seedy and bitter if left to overmature, and harvest often to keep clusters coming through the season. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Little Gem Lettuce (Sucrine Lettuce)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50–70°F. Little Gem is a miniature romaine/butterhead cross producing small (4–5 inch), compact, upright heads with firm, crunchy outer leaves and a sweet, butter-cream interior heart — essentially a mini Caesar salad head in one plant. Also known as 'Sucrine' in France (from the French for 'sugar'), it has become extremely popular in restaurant and farmers market contexts as a whole-head salad lettuce grilled or served halved with dressings. The outer leaves have romaine's crunch while the hearts are as sweet and buttery as buttercrunch — the best of both types in a small, space-efficient package. 4-6 inch spacing allows intensive planting; harvest the whole head when firm and compact. More heat-tolerant than standard butterhead and holds well in the garden without bolting quickly. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Little Gem Mini-Romaine Lettuce
description: Sow this English heirloom mini-romaine directly in cool weather, barely covering the seed since lettuce needs light to germinate. The petite heads reach just 6 inches tall and 4 inches wide, forming the perfect size for a single-serving salad with tender, sweet, succulent leaves. Thin plants to 6 to 8 inches apart and keep them evenly moist to prevent bitterness and bolting. Succession sow every couple of weeks and give afternoon shade in warm weather to extend the harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Little Leaf Cucumber (H-19, Beetle-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Little Leaf, formally H-19, was developed by Cornell University plant breeders specifically for its diminutive foliage, a trait that exposes fewer leaf surfaces to cucumber beetles and their associated bacterial wilt while still allowing plenty of sunlight to reach developing fruit and improving disease airflow around the vines. It is gynoecious, so interplanting with a small percentage of a standard pollenizer variety, or relying on nearby bees for cross-pollination from other varieties, improves fruit set. Fruits are small, blocky, and dark green, ideal for classic dill pickles, and should be harvested every one to two days at 2-4 inches for best quality. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Little Lucy Okra (Dwarf Ornamental-Edible AAS Winner)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Little Lucy is a genuine dwarf okra, growing only about 2 feet tall with attractive maroon-veined foliage and burgundy-red pods, making it as much an ornamental accent for a small bed or large container as a food crop. Despite its small stature it produces a real, usable harvest of tender pods best picked young at 2-3 inches, since the compact plant sets pods close together on short internodes. Its diminutive size means it needs no staking and takes up a fraction of the space of full-size okra varieties, a practical advantage for small Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat makes okra one of the most reliable producers. Harvest every couple of days during peak summer heat to keep pods tender and encourage continued flowering. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Little Marvel Pea
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep; Little Marvel can be planted in raised beds at 15-inch row spacing due to its dwarf habit and needs only minimal support. Little Marvel pea won an All-America Selections award in 1934 and remains one of the most productive and most compact garden shelling peas available — the dwarf 15-inch plants are among the shortest of all shelling peas while producing an outsized crop of well-filled pods with 6–8 wrinkled, sweet peas each. The compact habit makes Little Marvel excellent for small raised beds, succession planting in containers, and tight-spaced intensive gardens where full-sized pea varieties would be impractical. Does not require staking even in wind, though a small 12–18 inch support fence improves harvestability. The 60–65 day maturity is relatively early for a sweet wrinkled-seeded pea. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: Little Marvel Petite Shelling Pea
description: Direct sow this compact heirloom shelling pea as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since peas thrive in cool weather. The short vines grow only 18 to 24 inches tall and do not require support, making them ideal for small gardens and containers. Plants produce an abundance of 3 to 4 inch pods filled with sweet, tender peas perfect for fresh eating. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill, and harvest promptly to encourage continued production. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: Little Millet (Samai)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 4-8 inches when plants are established; little millet is an ancient South Asian grain crop, among the earliest domesticated grasses on the subcontinent, valued today for its very short growing season (as little as 60 days to maturity), drought tolerance, and ability to produce a reliable crop on poor, marginal soils where other grains fail. The compact plant produces loose, open seed panicles that ripen unevenly, so many growers harvest by cutting whole panicles as they mature rather than waiting for a single uniform harvest date. Thresh by rubbing or flailing dried panicles to release the small seeds, then winnow to remove chaff; the tiny grains are hulled before cooking (whole grain, similar to other millets) and are notably high in fiber and micronutrients compared to rice or wheat. Its short season and drought tolerance make it a useful catch crop or dry-season grain trial in Gulf South gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Little Miss Figgy Fig Tree
description: Little Miss Figgy is a naturally dwarf fig reaching only about 4 to 5 feet, making it ideal for patios and small gardens. It produces sweet, deep-purple figs on new growth, often with a light second crop later in the season. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently while fruit is sizing up. In zones below 7, grow it in a container and move it to an unheated garage or shed during hard freezes. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the plant and encourage fruiting wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Little Napoli Tomato (AAS-Winning Dwarf Paste Tomato)
description: Little Napoli was named an AAS Winner for packing a full-size San Marzano-type paste tomato onto a true dwarf plant barely 18 inches tall, making it one of the few sauce tomatoes practical for a patio container or small raised bed. The compact, sturdy determinate plants stay tidy without staking and still produce a generous crop of elongated, meaty 2-3 ounce plum fruit with classic low-moisture paste texture suited to sauces and canning. Keep the container evenly watered since dwarf plants in small pots dry out faster than in-ground vines, and harvest as fruit turns fully red for the best sauce flavor. Matures in 60–68 days from transplant.

name: Little Ragu Sweet Bay
description: Little Ragu is a compact, upright form of culinary sweet bay with aromatic evergreen leaves used fresh or dried in soups and stews. It stays tidy at 6 to 8 feet and takes well to pruning or shaping in containers. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil and let the surface dry slightly between waterings, as it dislikes soggy roots. In cold-winter areas grow it in a pot and bring it into a cool, bright spot before hard frost. Harvest mature leaves any time and dry them for the strongest flavor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Little Rosie Pawpaw (Small-Fruited Indiana Selection)
description: Little Rosie is a named pawpaw selection documented from Evansville, Indiana, notable chiefly for its small fruit size relative to most named cultivars. It remains part of the historical record of regional wild-tree selections that Kentucky State University has cataloged alongside better-known Indiana cultivars such as Overleese. A genetically distinct second pawpaw tree is required nearby, as Little Rosie will not reliably set fruit on its own. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Littlehip Hawthorn
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to occasionally wet soil in full sun along river banks, flood plains, or moist forest margins; littlehip hawthorn is one of the most graceful of the southeastern native hawthorns, with an elegant form, attractive spatula-shaped to shallowly 3-lobed leaves, and masses of tiny (1/4-inch) brilliant red haws that ripen in fall and persist on the branches well into winter. The persistent fruit crop is exceptionally valuable to winter-resident thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other berry-eating birds when larger food sources have been exhausted. White flower clusters in spring provide pollen and nectar for native bees and early butterflies. The tree's smaller stature relative to other hawthorns makes it well suited to suburban wildlife gardens and riparian restoration plantings where a medium-scale fruiting tree is needed. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Littleleaf Linden (Small-Leaved Lime, Linden, Tilia)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil; littleleaf linden (Tilia cordata) is one of the most important medicinal trees of Europe, grown primarily for its fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters (collected with the distinctive wing-like bract) that are dried to make tilleul tea — one of the classic European herbal teas with a pleasant mild flavor and traditional use for relaxation, sleep, cold and flu, and anxiety. The flowers, which appear in June-July, are intensely attractive to bees and are considered one of the finest sources of honey in Europe; linden honey is a premium product. The tree itself is magnificent, developing deeply furrowed bark and a broad, rounded crown that provides excellent shade. Leaves are edible as salad greens in spring when young and tender. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: Littleleaf Miner's Lettuce (Showy Rock Montia)
description: Native from Alaska south to California along moist, rocky slopes, cliffs, and creek banks, littleleaf miner's lettuce is a low, stoloniferous perennial forming rosettes of small, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves topped by loose sprays of pink or white five-petaled flowers in spring and summer. It spreads by trailing stolons tipped with tiny rooting plantlets, gradually knitting together a groundcover mat well suited to a partially shaded rock garden, stone wall, or gravelly bed with reliable moisture. Like its relatives, the mild, slightly succulent leaves are edible raw in salads. This is a distinct, longer-lived perennial species, not to be confused with the annual Claytonia perfoliata, which is sometimes still sold under the older name Montia perfoliata. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Littleleaf Sumac (Desert Sumac)
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; littleleaf sumac is a small-leaved, drought-adapted native shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau of west and central Texas, recognized by its unusually tiny compound leaves with small, dark green, heat-tolerant leaflets. White flowers in early spring before leaf emergence are followed by small, sticky, tart red berries that are edible as a lemonade-like beverage (native peoples soaked them in water to make a refreshing drink, similar to other Rhus species). The persistent small red fruits are important food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other desert birds through summer. Outstanding fall color — brilliant orange-red — followed by attractive winter structure. An extremely drought and heat tolerant native shrub for xeric, rocky, alkaline gardens in central and west Texas and adjacent areas. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Livingston's Beauty Tomato (1880s Foundational American Heirloom)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, staking the vine as it grows. Livingston's Beauty was introduced in 1886 by Alexander W. Livingston of Reynoldsburg, Ohio, one of the most important early tomato breeders in American history, whose systematic selection work through the late 1800s helped transform the tomato from a distrusted curiosity into a smooth, reliably productive garden staple. The medium to medium-large fruit is a rosy pink-red, smooth, and globe-shaped with good, well-balanced flavor for its era — a marked improvement over the ribbed, irregular tomatoes common before Livingston's breeding program, and a variety that directly influenced the smooth, round tomato shape gardeners now take for granted. Grow it as a piece of American horticultural history as much as a garden tomato; water and feed evenly through the season for the best fruit set and flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Livingston's Paragon Tomato (1870 Foundational Smooth-Skinned Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, staking to support the heavy fruit set. Introduced by Ohio seedsman Alexander W. Livingston in 1870, Paragon is historically significant as the first tomato widely recognized for producing smooth, uniformly round, evenly red fruit without the deep ridges and cracking typical of tomatoes at the time, a breakthrough that helped popularize the tomato as a garden and market crop across 19th-century America. The plants are productive and disease-tolerant for an heirloom, yielding clusters of medium-sized red fruit with classic old-fashioned flavor suited to fresh eating and canning. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Livingstone Potato (Native Potato)
description: A minor but locally important root crop of the mint family, Livingstone potato is grown across the savanna belt of southern and central Africa for the small clusters of starchy, nutty-flavored tubers that form along its sprawling, square-stemmed, aromatic foliage. Because flowering and seed set are unreliable, it is propagated vegetatively from saved tuber pieces or leafy stem cuttings rather than from seed. Plants form a low, spreading mound and benefit from loose, well-drained soil that allows the tuber clusters to expand freely at the base of each stem. Dig tubers once the foliage yellows and dies back at the end of the growing season, handling them gently since the skins are thin and bruise easily. Matures in 180–210 days from transplant.

name: Lizzano Tomato (Trailing Cherry Tomato for Hanging Baskets)
description: Transplant into a hanging basket or rail-mounted container after the last frost and let the trailing stems spill downward rather than staking them upright. Lizzano is an All-America Selections winner noted for combining a true cascading habit with strong early blight tolerance, an unusual pairing that keeps foliage healthier through the season than most basket-type tomatoes. It produces abundant clusters of sweet, 1-inch red cherry tomatoes continuously from mid-summer until frost. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Lobjoits Green Cos Lettuce
description: Sow directly in cool soil; this classic English cos lettuce from the early twentieth century forms tall, upright, dark-green heads that fold in on themselves to blanch a firm, sweet heart. It is reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings in cooler climates. Long a favorite of British kitchen gardeners, it is still maintained by seed-saving groups as one of the best-flavored traditional cos varieties. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Lockwood de Forest Rosemary (Cascading Culinary Rosemary)
description: Lockwood de Forest is a low, spreading rosemary selected from a seedling found in a Santa Barbara garden of the same name, valued for cascading stems that trail 6 to 8 feet while staying under 2 feet tall. The narrow, resinous leaves carry the same high oil content as upright culinary types and can be snipped for cooking, though gardeners most often plant it to spill over raised beds, retaining walls, and large containers. It flowers on and off through fall, winter, and spring with the pale blue blooms typical of the species, drawing early-season pollinators when little else is in bloom. Give it lean, fast-draining soil and full sun; like other trailing rosemaries it declines quickly in heavy or poorly drained ground. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Locustberry
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys. Small, glossy, leathery leaves and delicate clusters of small flowers that open pink and fade to yellow give this native shrub extended seasonal interest, followed by small red berries that ripen to nearly black and are eaten by birds, while the foliage serves as a larval host plant for several native butterfly species. Highly tolerant of poor, rocky limestone soil, salt exposure, and drought once established, it is a valuable, low-maintenance shrub for a South Florida native landscape, coastal planting, or pollinator garden, requiring essentially no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first year. Prune lightly to shape if a more formal habit is wanted, though it naturally maintains an attractive, open form without regular pruning. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Loddon Blue English Lavender
description: Grow in full sun with fast drainage, ideally in slightly alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil amended for lavender's low fertility needs. A companion selection to 'Loddon Pink' raised at the same Berkshire nursery, 'Loddon Blue' stays low and dense with fine silver-green foliage and short, tightly packed spikes of rich violet-blue flowers held just above the mound. Its compact habit and reliable flower color have made it a long-standing choice for low hedging and formal edging in English cottage gardens. Prune immediately after flowering to keep the plant from becoming leggy and open at the center. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Loddon Pink English Lavender
description: Site in full sun in lean, gritty soil; heavy clay or consistently damp ground quickly kills this compact selection. One of the older English named cultivars raised at Loddon Nursery in Berkshire, it forms a low, tidy mound of gray-green foliage topped with soft lilac-pink flower spikes in midsummer. Shear the spent flower stems back to the foliage line once bloom fades to keep growth dense and to discourage the sprawling, woody base older lavenders develop. Its smaller stature suits edging, rock gardens, and containers where the more common blue-flowered types would crowd the space. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Loffani Pomegranate
description: Loffani is a soft-seeded pomegranate maintained in the USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, valued by fruit-tree collectors for its notably easy propagation — hardwood cuttings root at a high percentage compared to many other cultivars — and its distinctly green, vigorous foliage. Fruit is sweet with tender arils, and the shrub-like tree performs well across a range of warm climates when given full sun and sharp drainage. Because Loffani roots so readily from cuttings, it is a practical choice for gardeners propagating their own stock rather than relying solely on grafted nursery trees. Thin dense interior growth occasionally to improve airflow and reduce fruit-skin blemishing in humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Loganberry
description: Loganberry, a natural hybrid of blackberry and raspberry discovered in California in the 1880s, produces long, dark red, tart berries that are excellent for jams and wine. Train the vigorous trailing canes on a two- or three-wire trellis, weaving new primocanes along the wires during the growing season. After the summer harvest, cut all floricanes that bore fruit to the ground and secure the new primocanes in their place. The thornless 'LY59' strain is preferred for home gardens; in borderline zones, lay canes down and mulch after leaf drop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Lolla Rossa Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Lolla Rossa is an Italian looseleaf lettuce producing rosettes of tightly frilled, deeply ruffled, deep burgundy-red to crimson leaves — the most intensely frilled and ruffled of all red lettuces, with a texture often compared to coral or ruffled fabric. The heavy frilling maximizes surface area and catches dressings exceptionally well, making Lolla Rossa a favorite in mixed salad bowls and mesclun mixes where its dramatic appearance creates visual impact. The flavor is mild and tender with a slight bitterness from the red pigments that is barely perceptible in young leaves and becomes slightly more pronounced in older, larger leaves. The deep red color makes Lolla Rossa one of the highest-anthocyanin lettuces, providing significant antioxidant content. It is the standard red frilly lettuce in European market and supermarket displays, where it has been in continuous commercial production since the 1970s, and is equally valuable in North American specialty salad production and home gardens. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Lolla Rossa Lettuce
description: This Italian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce forms frilly rosettes of magenta-red and green leaves with mild flavor and striking color. Sow directly in cool weather, spring or late summer, since heat prompts bolting and bitterness. Sow in succession for a continuous supply of tender leaves. Harvest outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut whole rosettes when full, keeping soil evenly moist throughout. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Lollo Bionda Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Green Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or barely cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; maintain consistent moisture through germination. Lollo Bionda (Italian for 'blonde curly') is the green counterpart to Lollo Rosso — sharing the identical intensely frilled, ruffled leaf margin and open loose-leaf habit but expressing uniformly bright chartreuse-green to golden-green coloring throughout rather than the Rosso type's red pigmentation. The two varieties are frequently grown together in alternating rows or blocks, where the intense green-and-crimson contrast creates a visually striking planting that is both ornamental and practical. Mixed bags of Lollo Bionda and Lollo Rosso leaves form the foundation of the Italian insalata mista tradition. Like Lollo Rosso, Lollo Bionda has a mildly bitter, distinctly Italian loose-leaf character — more complex and interesting than flat-leafed American loose-leaf types — and the same extremely frilled, ruffled texture that gives the leaves visual and textural interest in salads. Lollo Bionda is somewhat more heat-tolerant than Lollo Rosso in some trials, extending the spring salad season by 1–2 weeks before bolting. Both Lollo types are excellent for cut-and-come-again harvesting, where the plant continues producing from the center after outer leaves are removed, providing multiple harvests from a single planting. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Lollo Rosso Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Red Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; keep moist until germination. Lollo Rosso is the defining Italian loose-leaf lettuce — a variety whose intensely frilled, ruffled, deeply cut leaf margins and vibrant crimson-red to dark wine-red coloring at the leaf tips (fading through red-purple to green at the base) have made it the visual centerpiece of European mixed salad culture and one of the most recognizable lettuce varieties in the world. The name means 'red curly' in Italian, describing both the color and the extraordinarily frilled leaf margin that distinguishes Lollo Rosso from all other common loose-leaf types. The frilling is dramatic and consistent — the leaf margins curl so tightly that they create a lace-like appearance when the lettuce is displayed whole, making Lollo Rosso not only a component of salads but a visual garnish in its own right. The flavor is mildly bitter in the Italian leaf lettuce tradition — more complex and interesting than bland American loose-leaf types but not unpleasantly so — and pairs well with vinaigrette-dressed salads where the slight bitterness provides welcome contrast. Lollo Rosso is the standard accompaniment to Italian prosciutto and melon, appears in mixed salad bags throughout Europe as the red accent component, and is excellent alone dressed simply with olive oil and sea salt. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Lomanto Grape (Texas Hill Country Disease-Resistant Bunch Grape)
description: Lomanto traces its parentage to the pioneering hybrid grape breeding work begun by T.V. Munson in Denison, Texas, which focused on combining native American Vitis species with European vinifera to create grapes tough enough for Texas heat, drought, alkaline soils, and Pierce's disease pressure. It bears clusters of small to medium dark red-black berries used mainly for juice, jelly, and home winemaking rather than fresh eating, with a tart, distinctly grapey flavor. Plant it on a sturdy trellis in full sun on well-drained soil, including thin, rocky, or alkaline sites where many other grapes struggle, since its American parentage gives it good drought tolerance and root vigor once established. It is a solid choice for home growers in the Texas Hill Country and greater Gulf South who want a low-input bunch grape without the spray program vinifera varieties demand. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Long Black Spanish Radish (Winter Storage Radish with Black Skin)
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fall in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when roots are 6–8 inches long; peel before eating as the black skin is tough and astringent. Long Black Spanish Radish is a winter storage radish with a very distinctive appearance: the long (6–10 inch), cylindrical root has deeply black skin — nearly jet black — contrasting with crisp, white flesh within. It is one of the oldest documented European radish varieties, with references dating to the 16th century; it was the standard large winter radish of European cuisine before the introduction of Asian types and remains common in Polish, German, and Ashkenazi Jewish food traditions where it appears in salads (grated with onion and oil) and as a medicinal digestive herb. The flavor is significantly sharper and more pungent than spring radishes — a biting, horseradish-adjacent pungency that mellows somewhat when the grated flesh is salted and rested. The winter storage capability distinguishes Long Black Spanish from spring radishes: properly harvested and stored in damp conditions near freezing, the roots keep for 3–4 months, providing a root vegetable throughout the winter. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Long Green Improved Cucumber
description: Dating to at least 1842, Long Green Improved was for decades the standard American slicing and pickling cucumber before modern hybrids took over seed racks, and it remains one of the longest-cultivated open-pollinated cucumbers still commercially available. Vigorous vines produce dark green, often faintly ribbed fruit that can be picked small for pickles or left to grow 8-10 inches or more for fresh slicing, with crisp, mild flesh that holds up well in hot weather. Because it is an old-style monoecious variety rather than a modern gynoecious hybrid, it needs both male and female flowers present for pollination, so plant a full row rather than just one or two hills to ensure good fruit set. Save seed from fully ripened (yellowed) fruit for a true-breeding crop next season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Long Island Cheese Pumpkin (Cheese Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2; Long Island Cheese Pumpkin is a large, flat, deeply ribbed, tan-buff heirloom that looks remarkably like a wheel of French cheese — hence its popular name. Developed by Long Island market gardeners in the 19th century, it was once the dominant commercial pumpkin variety in the northeastern United States because of its excellent eating quality, dense orange-yellow flesh with a smooth, rich, sweet flavor particularly prized for pumpkin pies (significantly better than jack-o-lantern types). Being a Cucurbita moschata variety, it is substantially more resistant to squash vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat than C. pepo types, making it one of the most practical large pumpkins for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast gardens where summer disease and pest pressure is high. Fruits weigh 8–15 pounds and store well for months. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Long Island Cheese Squash (Heirloom Flat Wheel-Shaped Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Long Island Cheese is a 19th-century New York heirloom named for its flattened, ribbed, buff-tan fruit that closely resembles a wheel of cheese, with dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata type, it shares that species' strong resistance to squash vine borer, a serious pest of pepo- and maxima-type squash in warm, humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks to concentrate sweetness and improve storage life, which can extend several months in a cool, dry space. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera 'Long Island Improved'
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders requiring substantial nitrogen throughout their long growing season; Long Island Improved is the standard open-pollinated Brussels sprouts variety — the classic 'compact' type (as opposed to taller, older varieties) that has dominated American horticulture since the early 20th century. The small, round, tightly packed miniature cabbage heads (sprouts) that form along the stem are harvested from bottom to top as they mature, with each stem producing dozens of 1–2 inch sprouts over several weeks of harvest. Brussels sprouts' reputation for strong, unpleasant flavor is entirely a product of poor growing conditions — specifically, heat stress — rather than the plant's inherent flavor. Brussels sprouts grown to maturity in cool weather with frost exposure are mild, nutty, sweet, and completely different from heat-stressed sprouts with the intense sulfurous off-flavors that give the vegetable its negative reputation. The conversion of starches to sugars after frost exposure transforms Brussels sprouts from a challenging, strong-flavored vegetable into a genuinely delicious one — a transformation that zone 9 gardeners rarely witness but that northern gardeners who harvest after repeated freezes experience routinely. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts
description: This time-tested heirloom from the late 1800s is valued for compact plants, dependable yields, and excellent cold tolerance. Start seeds indoors and transplant so the long-season crop matures into cool fall weather, when the sprouts taste sweetest after light frosts. Keep plants well watered and side-dress with nitrogen for steady growth. Harvest the firm sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch across. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts
description: Start this heirloom Brussels sprout indoors and transplant for a fall harvest, as the sprouts sweeten and firm up after light frosts. Give plants plenty of water, rich soil, and a long season, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. Row covers help protect young plants from cabbage worms and other pests. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch in diameter, and top the plants a few weeks before harvest to encourage uniform sizing. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Long Island Improved Dill (Classic Standard Dill Variety for Leaf and Seed Harvest)
description: Direct sow in cool soil; thin to 6–12 inches. For seed harvest, allow plants to flower and seed heads to mature and begin to brown. Long Island Improved Dill is a classic American named dill variety that has been one of the standard cultivars in the United States seed trade for many decades — one of the most widely available and commonly grown dill varieties in home and market garden production. The 'Long Island' designation reflects its association with New York's Long Island, which was a major center of market garden and specialty crop production in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with many vegetable varieties named for the region (Long Island Cheese Pumpkin, Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts). Unlike the more recent specialty dill cultivars selected for specific properties (Dukat for high leaf oil, Fernleaf for dwarf compact habit), Long Island Improved is a classic standard selection valued for its combination of good leaf production and excellent seed head development — the characteristic that makes it a true dual-purpose variety useful for both dill weed (fresh and dried leaf) and dill seed harvest. The seed heads of Long Island Improved are large, flat-topped umbels that dry well for use in pickling (dill seed is the primary flavoring agent in dill pickles), in dill vinegar, and as a dried floral/culinary ingredient. The seeds are held firmly in the umbel until fully ripe and begin to shatter as the seed head fully dries — harvest by cutting the entire seed head when seeds have changed from green to tan-brown but before significant shattering begins. For zone 9 gardeners wanting dill seeds for pickling their summer cucumbers, Long Island Improved's good seed head development makes it the classic choice. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Long Keeper Onion
description: Long Keeper lives up to its name as a pungent yellow storage onion selected specifically for exceptional shelf life, commonly holding firm for eight months to a year in a cool, dry pantry. Transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil and give plants full sun and consistent moisture through bulb formation, then reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall. Because the flavor is sharp and the flesh dense, it is best suited to cooked dishes rather than fresh raw use. Cure the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot for several weeks before storage, since a complete cure is what gives this variety its outstanding keeping quality. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Long Keeper Tomato (Winter Storage Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, caging or staking the semi-sprawling vines. Long Keeper is grown specifically for its ability to ripen slowly off the vine when picked mature-green to pale blush before the first fall frost, gradually coloring to an orange-red over weeks or months in cool, dark storage so gardeners can enjoy fresh tomatoes well into winter. The flavor is milder than a summer-ripened tomato but remains a valued novelty among gardeners who want to extend the tomato season past the growing year. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Long of Naples Squash
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Long of Naples (Lunga di Napoli, Serpentina di Napoli) is a renowned Italian heirloom squash from the Campania region surrounding Naples, producing extraordinarily long cylindrical fruits of 24–36 inches or more — occasionally reaching 4–5 feet under optimal conditions. At maturity the tan-to-buff skin covers dense, deep-orange flesh with a sweet, rich flavor similar to butternut but with a creamier texture and less watery flesh. Immature fruits at 12–18 inches can be harvested and used as a superior summer squash — far more flavorful than standard zucchini, with firmer flesh and more concentrated sweetness. Fully mature fruits cure well and store for 6–12 months in a cool, dry location. As a Cucurbita moschata type, Long of Naples shows excellent heat and humidity tolerance, resistance to vine borers, and superior performance in zone 9 compared to pepo-type squashes. The vines are vigorous and spreading — allow 8–12 feet per plant. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Long Orange Improved Carrot
description: A refined selection of the historic Dutch Long Orange carrot line that traces back to 17th-century Netherlands and was further developed by American seed houses in the 1800s, making it one of the direct ancestors of modern Danvers and Chantenay types. It produces long, tapered, deep-orange roots with a somewhat coarser core than modern Nantes hybrids but dependable yields in open garden soil. Direct sow into deeply worked beds and thin early for straight roots; it is a strong, old-fashioned keeper well suited to fall storage. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Long Pepper (Indian Long Pepper, Pippali)
description: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and grow in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled light; long pepper is the historical precursor to black pepper in European and Mediterranean cuisines, used extensively from ancient Rome through the medieval period before the black pepper trade displaced it. The elongated catkin-like fruits (1–2 inches long) have a rich, complex heat distinct from black pepper — sweeter, more aromatic, with a slight numbing quality and notes of cinnamon and ginger. A tropical climbing vine that needs support and high humidity; it performs year-round outdoors in zone 10–12 and makes an unusual and rewarding container plant moved inside during cool months. Harvest green or ripe red and dry completely for long storage. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Long Pie Pumpkin (New England Long Pie Squash)
description: Plant seeds in hills of two or three after frost danger passes, and let the long vines sprawl since the fruit is too heavy and elongated to trellis practically. Long Pie is an old New England heirloom, cylindrical rather than round, growing two to three feet long and resembling an overgrown zucchini more than a typical jack-o'-lantern pumpkin. Its smooth orange rind and dense, mild-flavored flesh make it a traditional substitute for butternut or sugar pumpkin in pies and baking, and its thick shell allows it to store for many months longer than most winter squash. Harvest before hard frost when the rind resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Long Purple Eggplant
description: Start this heirloom eggplant indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, providing bottom heat and warm soil for good germination. Transplant only after nights are reliably warm, as eggplant is very cold sensitive, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. The long, slender purple fruits are flavorful in countless dishes and are best harvested young when the skin is glossy. Stake taller plants, keep them evenly watered, and pick fruits regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Long Red Cayenne Pepper (Classic American Cayenne)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil; Long Red Cayenne is a vigorous grower that benefits from staking when loaded with fruit; pick all red and drying fruits promptly to encourage continued production through the season. Long Red Cayenne is the classic cayenne pepper — an old heirloom open-pollinated variety that represents the original 'cayenne' type from which the broad category of cayenne peppers takes its name (likely from Cayenne, French Guiana, where related chiles were grown). The fruits are distinctive: pencil-thin (1/2 to 3/4 inch in diameter), 6–8 inches long, wrinkled and irregular in cross-section, tapering to a point, and ripening to a bright red — characteristics that make Long Red Cayenne immediately identifiable and distinct from the smooth-skinned, shorter 'Ring of Fire' type. The heat level of 30,000–50,000 SHU is moderate-hot — significantly hotter than jalapeños but substantially milder than habaneros — in the range that defines 'cayenne heat' in American cuisine. Long Red Cayenne is the source (via cultivated strains) of commercial cayenne powder, an essential spice in Cajun and Creole cooking, Indian cuisine, and most dry spice blends; of Louisiana-style hot sauce; of the dried cayenne pods used in Chinese and Sichuan cooking; and of the classic sriracha-style sauces. Prolific production on vigorous plants (24–36 inches) in warm climates; excellent for drying on the plant or on strings. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Long Red Florence Onion
description: Long Red Florence is a traditional Tuscan heirloom onion grown for its elongated, torpedo-shaped bulbs of glossy deep-red skin and mild, sweet white-and-red flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and space plants closely enough to encourage the characteristic slender shape rather than a rounded bulb. It can be harvested at three distinct stages: pulled very young as a scallion-like salad onion, at mid-size for grilling whole, or left to mature into a full torpedo bulb for slicing raw over pizza and salads. Because its flesh is milder and higher in moisture than standard storage onions, plan to use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it in long-term storage. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Long Red Slim Cayenne Pepper (Classic Slender Drying Cayenne)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Long Red Slim is a classic, widely grown cayenne cultivar producing narrow, tapering, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to bright red, packing substantial heat in a lightweight, easily dried pod. The thin walls make it ideal for stringing into traditional pepper ropes (ristras) or oven-drying and grinding into homemade cayenne powder or crushed red pepper flakes. Plants are productive over a long season and tolerate heat well, making cayenne one of the more reliable hot peppers for Gulf South summers; pick pods at full red color for maximum heat and flavor when drying. Matures in 65–85 days from transplant.

name: Long Scarlet Short Top Radish
description: Broadcast or row-sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1 inch apart, since the short, upright tops leave little room for foliage to compete for light. Long Scarlet Short Top is a nineteenth-century market variety producing tapered, cylindrical scarlet roots 5-6 inches long, distinguished from other 'long scarlet' types by its notably reduced leaf growth, which was bred deliberately to permit tighter row spacing for commercial growers. Pull roots promptly once they reach usable size, as the slender shape can turn pithy and hollow faster than round varieties if left in warm soil. The tapered form and quick maturity made it a standard early-spring forcing radish before greenhouse culture became common. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Long Slim Cayenne Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Long Slim Cayenne is the standard form of cayenne pepper — the elongated, thin-walled, moderately wrinkled red pepper that is one of the most important culinary chile peppers in the world and the source of commercial cayenne pepper powder and red pepper flakes. The fruits are 4–6 inches long, pencil-thin, and bright red when fully ripe, with heat levels typically measuring 30,000–50,000 Scoville Heat Units — a penetrating, clean, sharp heat that has made cayenne the dominant hot pepper in Louisiana Cajun and Creole cuisine, Indian cooking, and dozens of other culinary traditions. Long Slim Cayenne dries easily and completely due to the thin walls, and the dried pepper grinds to the characteristic bright red powder of commercial cayenne spice. Fresh red cayenne peppers are also used in hot sauce production — Tabasco-style sauces use fermented cayenne-type peppers as their primary ingredient. In zone 9 the plants bear enormous crops of drying-quality peppers over the full warm season. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Long Standing Santo Cilantro
description: Also known as Chinese parsley, this variety is selected for excellent flavor, extra leafiness, and slow bolting, giving you a longer cilantro harvest. Direct sow into cool soil since the taproot resents transplanting, and make successive sowings every few weeks for a steady supply. Provide full sun in cool weather or light afternoon shade as temperatures climb to delay flowering. Let some plants bolt and set seed to harvest coriander for the spice rack. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Long White Cow Horn Turnip
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart; because much of the root pushes up out of the soil as it grows, mounding a little loose soil around the shoulders keeps the exposed portion from toughening or turning green. Long White Cow Horn is an early American heirloom named for its distinctive shape: a slender, curved, carrot-like white root that tapers to a point, growing half-exposed above ground rather than forming a globe. It matures faster than round white-fleshed turnips and was traditionally valued for both table use when young and livestock feed when left to size up. The exposed shoulders develop a slight green blush in sunlight, which does not affect the mild flavor of the flesh beneath. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Long White Reishi Bitter Melon
description: A striking, elongated white bitter melon that dangles from the vine like pale stalactites, reaching about 16 inches long with slender, smoothly ridged, faintly mint-green-tinged white skin. Its bitterness is notably gentler than green-skinned types, making it a good choice for fresh stir-fries and soups where a milder flavor is wanted. Beyond its culinary use, the long, glossy, pale fruit hanging against dense green foliage makes the vine a genuine edible ornamental for an arbor or fence-line trellis, drawing attention in the summer garden even before harvest begins. Give it a tall, sturdy support and steady moisture through the long fruiting season to develop full-length, well-formed fruit. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Long-leaf Ground Cherry
description: Long-leaf Ground Cherry is a hardy native husk tomato found across central and eastern North America in prairies, disturbed areas, and open woodlands, producing small yellow fruits enclosed in papery husks similar to a miniature tomatillo that are edible fresh or cooked. Direct sow seeds after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, as this perennial spreads vigorously from spreading rhizomes and will naturalize in favorable conditions. Plants are extremely drought-tolerant once established and require little care beyond occasional thinning to prevent them from crowding out neighboring plants. Harvest fruits when the husk has turned tan and dried, and the berry inside has dropped naturally, as this indicates peak ripeness and sweetness. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Longan
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in full sun; longan will not tolerate standing water or saturated roots. A brief winter cool-dry period — temperatures in the mid-40s°F for several weeks — is essential to trigger reliable flowering, making coastal south Florida and extreme south Texas the two viable zones in the continental United States. Fruit clusters ripen in summer and should be harvested by cutting whole panicles with scissors when the skin turns tan to light brown and the flesh is translucent and sweet. Prune annually after harvest to keep the canopy to a manageable height and promote new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Longevity Spinach
description: Root cuttings easily in water and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; the plant sprawls attractively as a groundcover or can be trained onto a low trellis. Harvest leaves and shoot tips regularly; the raw leaves have a crunchy, mild, slightly succulent texture and are popular in Southeast Asian salads and as an anti-diabetic traditional food. Unlike the closely related Okinawa spinach, this species has smooth (not wavy-edged) leaves without the purple underside. Bring cuttings indoors before first frost for overwintering; in frost-free areas it grows year-round and can be lightly sheared to encourage fresh growth. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Longfellow Flint Corn (New England Yellow Flint Corn)
description: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season makes it well suited to northern New England gardens where longer-season dent corns struggle to dry down before frost. Longfellow is an old New England eight-row yellow flint corn, kept in circulation by regional seed savers and small farms in Maine and neighboring states for its dependable yields and cold-season resilience. Ears dry hard and quickly on the stalk, and the kernels grind into a sweet, full-flavored yellow cornmeal typical of the flint corns that sustained early New England farm households through winter. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Longjing 43 Tea
description: Bred by the Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences near Hangzhou and released in the 1980s, Longjing 43 was selected specifically to produce the classic flat, jade-green, pan-fired Longjing (Dragon Well) tea for which the region is famous. Its standout trait is exceptionally early spring budbreak, giving growers a premium early-season harvest advantage over older Longjing-type bushes, along with a delicate, sweet, faintly chestnut-like flavor. Because of its importance to a protected-origin product, authentic Longjing tea from this cultivar commands strong prices in the Chinese domestic market. Grow it in the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil as other tea cultivars, harvesting the earliest spring flush by hand for top grade. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Longor Shallot (French Elongated Shallot)
description: Longor is a traditional French shallot valued for producing unusually long, slender bulbs with coppery skin and pink-tinged flesh, distinguishing it from the rounder Dutch-type shallots grown for the fresh market. Plant sets shallow with the tip just showing above the soil surface and keep the bed weed-free, since each set divides into a cluster of several elongated bulbs by midsummer. Reduce watering once foliage begins to yellow and topple, then lift, dry, and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storing. Longor is prized in French cooking regions such as Brittany for its slightly sweet flavor and long storage life, and gardeners choose it over rounder shallot types specifically for its distinctive shape and keeping quality. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Longue d'Aout Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Longue d'Aout is an old French heirloom fig variety named for its August ripening season, producing distinctive elongated, pear-to-tear-drop-shaped fruits with violet to purple-brown skin and amber to pink-tinged flesh with a sweet, mild, honey-fig flavor and very few seeds. The unusual elongated shape (2–3 inches long, narrowing to a pronounced neck) makes this variety immediately identifiable among more common round-fruited fig varieties and creates an elegant presentation at table. Longue d'Aout is a main-crop variety producing its primary harvest in August–September in zone 9. It grows as a moderately vigorous tree with good productivity once established. This variety is well-regarded in French fig traditions and has been grown for centuries in the south of France; its elongated form makes it particularly distinctive for display and specialty market use. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Longwood Thyme (Resinous Hybrid Groundcover Thyme)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like most thymes it resents heavy, wet soil and performs best in rock gardens, path edging, or containers. Longwood is a naturally occurring hybrid thyme first identified at a botanical garden, prized for a strong, resinous, camphor-and-thyme scent that is more pungent than common culinary thyme when the foliage is brushed or crushed. The small, narrow leaves form a low, wiry mound topped with pale lavender-pink flowers favored by pollinators in summer. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound dense and to prevent the center from opening up and going woody. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Loomis Muscadine Grape (Black Loomis)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Loomis, named for the USDA breeder who developed it, produces medium-large clusters of glossy black berries with unusually high sugar content (near 20 Brix) and rich, sweet flavor that place it among the best-tasting of the black muscadines. The vine is notably vigorous with disease-resistant foliage and ripens late in the season, extending the black muscadine harvest after earlier cultivars like Cowart and Ison have finished. Because Loomis carries only female flowers, it produces no fruit on its own and must be planted within pollination range of a self-fertile variety. Prune hard each winter back to short spurs on permanent cordons, and expect some unevenness in ripening within a cluster, which is typical of the variety. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Loquat
description: Loquat is an evergreen tree that flowers in fall and winter and ripens its fruit in late winter to early spring — one of the earliest fruiting trees of the season. Most varieties are self-fertile, though two trees increase crop size. Fruit clusters can be thinned at golf-ball size to produce fewer but larger fruit. Harvest when fruit is fully golden-yellow to orange, slightly soft, and sweet-tart; the thin skin is edible but seeds are large and should be discarded. Trees are cold-hardy to about 12°F but flowers and developing fruit are damaged below 28°F. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Lord Sea Buckthorn (Male Pollinator)
description: Lord is a hardy male sea buckthorn selection grown solely to supply pollen, since Hippophae rhamnoides is dioecious and fruits only when a male plant blooms nearby. It opens its small, petal-less catkins early and holds bloom for roughly ten days, long enough to overlap with most early- and mid-season female cultivars. Give it the same lean, sandy, well-drained site the females need, since it shares their nitrogen-fixing roots and dislikes rich, wet soil. Position it upwind of the planting block where practical to help wind-borne pollen reach the widest number of female shrubs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Loring Peach (Mid-South Commercial Standard Yellow Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit to 6–8 inches after petal fall for maximum fruit size; Loring ripens mid-season (late June to mid-July in zone 7–9) with large, well-colored yellow-fleshed freestone fruit; apply preventive fungicide starting at bud swell for brown rot and peach leaf curl control. Loring peach is one of the most widely planted commercial peach varieties in the mid-South and a benchmark mid-season variety throughout the southeastern United States, developed at the Missouri Agricultural Experiment Station (USDA collaboration) and released in 1944. The variety takes its name from Mount Loring, a traditional Missouri peach-growing area. For decades, Loring was the dominant commercial peach in Tennessee, Missouri, Arkansas, and adjacent southeastern states, praised for its reliable high yields, large fruit size, excellent flavor, and shelf life compared to other varieties of its era. The fruits are large to very large, round to slightly oblate, with a predominantly red skin over a yellow-orange background — very attractive at roadside markets and farm stands. The flesh is yellow, firm, and fully freestone at full maturity, with a well-balanced rich peach flavor that compares favorably with Elberta while generally producing larger, better-colored fruit under mid-South conditions. Loring's moderate chill requirement (approximately 750 hours) fits the climate of the mid-South better than Elberta (which needs 800–1000 hours) in years with insufficient winter cold. It has been partially replaced by newer varieties with improved disease resistance in commercial production, but remains a standard recommendation for home orchardists throughout the Southeast. Matures in 105–125 days from transplant.

name: Lorz Italian Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lorz Italian is a Washington State heirloom sweet frying pepper, a classic Italian-style variety with thin-walled, pendent fruits that are 8–10 inches long — among the longest sweet peppers available. The mild, sweet flesh is nearly seedless and ideal for the classic Italian-American preparation of frying in olive oil with garlic and salt (peperonata), as well as roasting, stuffing, and fresh eating. The thin walls roast and collapse beautifully without the wateriness of thicker-walled sweet peppers. Plants produce prolifically once established, with multiple fruits per branch; the long, elegant fruits are also ornamental hanging from the plant. Harvest green for crispest texture or allow to ripen red for sweetest flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Lorz Italian Softneck Garlic (Pacific Northwest Italian Immigrant Heirloom)
description: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall; softneck types like Lorz Italian can be planted over a wider window than hardnecks — from 4 weeks before first frost to a week or two after; mulch after planting; keep weed-free in spring; harvest when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly. Lorz Italian is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic with a remarkable Italian-American immigrant story: it was brought to the Walla Walla Valley of eastern Washington State by an Italian immigrant named Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 19th century, where it became a staple of the Italian immigrant farming community in the Columbia River valley region, passed down through family seed-saving for generations before being preserved by heirloom garlic collectors and specialist growers. The large, roundish bulbs typically contain 12–20 cloves arranged in multiple overlapping layers (characteristic of Artichoke types), with white to pale ivory outer skin; the cloves are plump, meaty, and moderately spicy — a full-flavored softneck with more character than commercial supermarket garlic but without the intensity of the finest Rocambole hardnecks. The great practical advantage of Lorz Italian and other Artichoke softnecks is excellent storage — bulbs typically keep 9–12 months in good conditions, far outlasting any hardneck type; the flexible stems also make it excellent for braiding. Adapted to a wide range of climates from cool Pacific Northwest conditions to warm Southern winters. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Lost Hills Pistachio (Early-Harvest Low-Chill Female Selection)
description: Lost Hills is a University of California-bred female pistachio cultivar developed from a 1989-1996 breeding program and released as an improvement on the industry-standard Kerman. It harvests four to sixteen days earlier than Kerman, produces individually larger nuts, and has a higher percentage of nuts with a fully split shell at harvest. Its most notable trait for marginal growing regions is a lower winter chilling requirement than Kerman, which improves the uniformity of bloom, pollination, and nut fill in years when chill accumulation falls short — a scenario common during the Gulf Coast's mild, inconsistent winters. As a female selection it still needs a compatible male pollenizer planted nearby, and growers should recognize that pistachio as a species performs best with hot, dry summers; Gulf Coast humidity substantially increases the risk of fungal disease on the hulls and foliage, so this cultivar is best treated as an experimental planting on the driest, most open site available with careful disease monitoring. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Loto Upland Rice
description: Loto is a short-grained, awnless upland rice from the Emilia-Romagna region of northern Italy, traditionally used for risotto rather than steamed rice. It tillers freely into compact clumps on lodging-resistant stalks and, unlike most rice grown in the United States, does not need to be flooded — consistent moisture and warm soil are enough to bring it to maturity in a single temperate growing season. Home growers in cooler climates have had success direct-seeding it alongside a nurse crop of fast-germinating radish to mark the slow-emerging rice rows. Its easy-to-thresh, easy-to-hull grain makes it a practical choice for small-scale growers without dedicated rice processing equipment. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Lotus Root
description: Plant intact rhizome sections (with at least one growing tip) horizontally in the mud bottom of a pond, tub, or container submerged under 12–18 inches of still water; never allow the growing tip to dry out. Full sun is essential — lotus will produce only foliage and few flowers in shade. Harvest rhizomes in fall once foliage dies back by reaching into the mud and carefully pulling out the chain of large, starchy sections; the distinctive lacy, hole-patterned cross-section is a signature feature. Rhizomes must be cooked before eating; they are eaten stir-fried, pickled, or braised throughout East and Southeast Asia and have a crunchy texture even after cooking. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Louisa Crabapple (Weeping Pink-Flowered Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Louisa bears clear pink flowers along gracefully weeping, cascading branches, creating a soft, fountain-like silhouette very different from the upright or rounded habit of most crabapple cultivars, making it a strong focal-point specimen near a patio or entry. Small yellow fruit follows the spring bloom, of modest interest to birds. It shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases including apple scab, though somewhat less bulletproof than top-tier resistant cultivars like Prairifire or Adirondack. Prune in late winter, if needed, to remove crossing branches and maintain the weeping form, taking care not to disrupt the graceful cascading habit that defines the tree. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Louise Bonne Pear (Louise Bonne of Jersey, Reliable French Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Louise Bonne, widely known in England as Louise Bonne of Jersey, is a French heirloom dating to the 1780s that became one of the most reliably productive and widely planted pears of the 19th century, valued for its dependable, heavy annual bearing as much as its fruit quality. The medium, greenish-yellow pear blushed with brownish-red has juicy, sweet, melting flesh with a good, well-balanced flavor, excellent for fresh eating and reasonably good for canning as well. The vigorous, precocious tree tends to bear young and heavily, sometimes needing fruit thinning to avoid limb breakage or biennial bearing. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best eating quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Louise Swenson Grape (Cold-Hardy White Wine and Table Grape)
description: Named for the wife of Minnesota breeder Elmer Swenson, this hybrid produces large clusters of pale green-white berries with a mild, fruity flavor suited to fresh eating as well as aromatic white wine. It is one of the more cold-hardy white hybrids available, tolerating harsh northern winters that would kill vinifera vines outright. The loose cluster architecture helps reduce bunch rot in humid climates, and the vine is moderately vigorous, benefiting from a cordon or cane training system. Home growers in short-season regions value it for combining table-grape appeal with reliable hardiness. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: Louise White Sapote
description: Plant Louise in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil protected from strong wind. Its main appeal is an extended, nearly everbearing cropping pattern that stretches from midwinter through late summer instead of dumping the whole harvest at once, so a single home tree can supply ripe fruit across many months of the year. The medium-sized fruit ripens to yellow with the typical smooth, custard-textured white sapote flesh and good sweet flavor. Because of this spread-out bearing habit and generally manageable size, Louise is frequently recommended over larger, heavier-cropping cultivars for gardeners who want a steady trickle of fruit rather than a single big harvest to process at once. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod Okra (Southern Heirloom with Extra-Long Tender Pods)
description: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod is a tall, vigorous Southern heirloom selected over generations for pods that stay tender even as they grow far beyond the length most okra turns woody. Give plants generous room since they build large leaves and reach considerable height, and consider staking in exposed sites prone to summer storms. Harvest ribbed green pods every day or two once they reach a usable size to keep the heavily branching plant setting new flowers all season. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from the driest, most mature pods for replanting the following year. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Louisiana Green Velvet Okra (Long Smooth Dark Green Southern Okra)
description: Soak seeds overnight before planting; direct sow 1 inch deep 12–18 inches apart after soil warms; harvest pods at 4–5 inches for the finest texture; once production begins, harvest every 2 days during peak summer heat as pods elongate rapidly. Louisiana Green Velvet is an heirloom open-pollinated okra variety with a strong association with Louisiana and Gulf Coast traditional food culture — it is one of the most historically prominent varieties in the region and has been grown by Louisiana gardeners for generations as the standard for gumbo okra and fresh summer side dishes. The pods are smooth, deep green, and slightly ridged rather than heavily ribbed like Clemson Spineless, with a velvety (not bristly) surface texture that makes handling comfortable and gives the variety its name. 'Green Velvet' pods remain tender at 4–5 inches under high summer temperatures — a practical advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat causes many okra varieties to become tough and fibrous quickly if not harvested every day. The variety is adapted to the humid, hot climate of coastal Louisiana and the Gulf South and performs especially well in the clay soils and high humidity of the Louisiana bayou region where it originated as a preferred variety. Louisiana Green Velvet is the traditional okra of Cajun and Creole cooking — most commonly used in gumbo, where the natural mucilage (thickening quality) of properly cooked okra is considered essential to authentic texture and flavor. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Louisiana Long Green Eggplant (Old South Elongated Green Eggplant)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Louisiana Long Green is a traditional old-South eggplant variety producing elongated, cylindrical fruits 8–12 inches long in an unusual pale green to light green-white color that stands in stark contrast to the standard purple-black American eggplant. The pale green color indicates ripe fruit — unlike purple-black types where color darkens as they ripen, Louisiana Long Green turns a light, creamy green to yellow-green when mature. The flesh is white, mild, and very low in bitterness — outstanding for frying, grilling, and the classic Louisiana preparation of eggplant dressing (a traditional Gulf South casserole combining eggplant with shrimp, crabmeat, bread crumbs, and Cajun seasonings). Louisiana Long Green is a regional heirloom that has been grown continuously in Louisiana and lower Mississippi kitchen gardens for generations — selected by Southern gardeners for its outstanding heat tolerance, prolific production in the Gulf South summer, and excellent culinary qualities in traditional regional recipes. Harvest when fruits are 8–10 inches long with pale, slightly shiny skin — over-mature fruits become yellowish and develop more seeds and bitterness. Plants are vigorous and can reach 4 feet tall in the long Gulf South growing season, requiring staking when heavily loaded with fruit. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Louisiana Purple Pod Bean (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis or pole support after the danger of frost has passed. Louisiana Purple Pod is a Deep South heirloom pole bean selected over generations for reliable production through the heat and humidity that stall many snap bean varieties, and it shows good resistance to common bean mosaic virus and rust compared to older commercial types. Pods emerge deep purple, which makes them easy to spot among the leaves at harvest time, and the color cooks away to ordinary green so the beans can be prepared exactly like any other snap bean. Pick pods at 5-6 inches long while still tender for the best snap texture, and pick regularly to keep vines producing; left longer, pods can also be shelled fresh or dried for winter storage. Vines climb vigorously and benefit from consistent moisture during flowering and pod set to prevent blossom drop during extreme heat. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Louisiana Purple Sugarcane (Heirloom Syrup Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Purple is an heirloom sugarcane variety with deep purple-to-maroon stalks, long grown in Deep South dooryard patches both for chewing fresh (stripping and gnawing the sweet fibrous stalk) and for cooking down into dark cane syrup. Its rich color makes it a popular choice for ornamental use along fences and property lines in addition to its culinary role. Traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, it is then stripped of leaves, crushed to extract the juice, and slow-cooked into syrup, a staple of Southern country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows vigorously from the root each spring, though a hard freeze can reduce syrup yield if it strikes before harvest. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Louisiana Ribbon Cane (Heirloom Striped Syrup Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Ribbon Cane is a historic heirloom sugarcane variety, distinguished from modern commercial hybrids by its slender, green-and-purple striped stalks, that has been maintained by Deep South farm families and seed savers for generations specifically for making cane syrup rather than refined sugar. It is traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, then stripped, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked down into dark, richly flavored cane syrup, a staple of Louisiana and Georgia country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass also makes a striking, fast-growing screen or accent planting; in zone 9 it typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze and regrows vigorously each spring. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Louisiana Short Okra
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the soil is thoroughly warm, since this late-season heirloom needs the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to hit its stride. Louisiana Short produces stocky, heavily branching plants bearing short, fat, dark green pods that stay tender at a larger diameter than slim-podded types, so pods can be picked at 3-5 inches without turning woody. The compact branching habit keeps fruit within easy reach and yields hold up right until a hard frost, making it one of the more forgiving okra choices for gardeners who cannot pick every single day during peak heat. Originally maintained by an Oklahoma seed saver and preserved through Midwest heirloom seed banks, it performs reliably in the humid, clay-heavy soils common along the Gulf Coast. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Louisiana Sweet Satsuma (Gulf South Cold-Hardy Mandarin)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and give young trees frost cloth protection on the coldest nights until they are several years established. Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma mandarin selection grown and promoted along the Gulf Coast for combining good cold hardiness with consistently sweet, low-acid flavor even in years when cooler, cloudier falls can leave other citrus tart. Fruit is medium-sized, nearly seedless, and easy to peel, ripening in the standard satsuma window from October into December ahead of most other citrus. As with all satsumas, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization late in the season, which delays the hardening off trees need to withstand winter cold, and mulch well to protect the root zone. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lovage
description: Levisticum officinale is a bold, statuesque perennial herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to the mountains of southern Europe, producing deeply divided, dark, glossy-green leaves with a powerful, unmistakable flavor of intensified celery — a single large plant can supply a household with celery-like flavoring throughout the growing season from every part: leaves, stems, seeds, and roots. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in moist, deeply dug, fertile, well-drained to moisture-retentive soil in full sun or light partial shade; seed viability drops sharply after the first year, so always sow the freshest seed available. Once established, lovage grows to 4–6 feet tall with hollow, celery-scented stems and large umbels of small, greenish-yellow flowers in early summer — plants should be cut back hard after flowering to encourage a second flush of tender, flavorful young foliage. Harvest young leaves and stems freely throughout the season for use in soups, stocks, stews, and salads where celery flavor is desired; seeds can be used as a spice and dried roots are used in traditional herbal preparations. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Lovell Peach Rootstock
description: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock. A long-standing standard peach seedling rootstock widely used across commercial and home orchards for its reliable vigor, good compatibility with a broad range of peach and nectarine varieties, and adaptability to a range of well-drained soil types.
