It produces a full-sized, vigorous tree without the size control offered by modern clonal dwarfing rootstocks, making it best suited to a home orchard with ample space for a standard-sized peach tree. Graft a desired named peach or nectarine variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide well-drained soil, since peach rootstocks in general are notably intolerant of wet, poorly drained conditions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lovett Loquat (Early-Ripening Florida Seedling with Honey-Sweet White Flesh)
description: Lovett is a Florida seedling selection known for honey-sweet, white-fleshed fruit of medium size, ripening in early spring ahead of many standard cultivars. Like other loquats, Lovett blooms in fall and early winter, leaving its flowers and small developing fruit exposed to occasional hard freezes that can reduce Gulf Coast harvests in a cold winter. The tree performs well in the humid Gulf South climate where it originated and is grown as a dooryard fruit tree valued for its mild, dessert-quality flavor. Loquats are generally self-fertile, though fruit set is often heaviest when more than one tree is nearby. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Low Scape Mound Chokeberry
description: Low Scape Mound is a dwarf, mounding sport of black chokeberry bred for use as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover rather than for berry production, though it still bears the species' white spring flowers, small black fruit, and fiery red fall color on a dense, spreading form under two feet tall. It handles wet, dry, salty, or clay soils and urban pollution better than most low shrubs, making it useful for parking-lot islands, slopes, and mass plantings where mowing is impractical. Trim lightly after flowering only if a tighter shape is wanted; otherwise it requires no routine pruning. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Low Scape Snowfire Chokeberry (Heavy-Blooming Dwarf Black Chokeberry)
description: Low Scape Snowfire is a Proven Winners selection of black chokeberry bred as the heaviest-flowering plant in the Low Scape series, blanketing its low mounded form in white spring blossoms that draw a steady stream of pollinators before setting a heavy crop of dark blue-black berries. The compact, spreading habit tops out around two feet, with glossy dark green summer foliage that turns deep red and purple in fall. It accepts clay, alkaline, wet, or drought-stressed soils with equal ease and tolerates road salt, making it a practical choice for roadside plantings, coastal landscapes, or mass groundcover use. Beyond an occasional light shearing to maintain a neat mound, the shrub requires no routine maintenance. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Low Serviceberry
description: Sow fresh seeds in fall directly into sandy, well-drained soil, as Low Serviceberry is adapted to dry, rocky ground and performs poorly in rich or consistently moist conditions. Winter cold provides the stratification seeds need, and seedlings emerge in spring when soil temperatures warm to 40–55 degrees Fahrenheit. This spreading, colony-forming shrub is excellent for naturalizing slopes, stabilizing sandy soils, and providing wildlife habitat; allow adequate space for root-sprouting colonies to develop. Expect the first berry crop 2–5 years after transplanting; the sweet, dark blue fruits ripen in midsummer and are relished by birds and mammals. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Low's Champion Bean
description: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained garden soil after frost danger has passed; the compact bush habit needs no staking, making it an easy dry bean for smaller gardens. Low's Champion is a New England bush bean introduced in 1884 by the Aaron Low Seed Company of Boston and believed to derive from an older Abenaki variety, producing broad, flat pods that can be picked young as tender snap beans or left to mature into glossy mahogany-red oval dry beans. Its dual usefulness as both a green bean and a soup bean made it a dependable staple in old New England kitchen gardens. Harvest pods regularly if using fresh to keep plants productive, or let the whole crop dry down at season's end for winter storage beans. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Lowbush Blueberry
description: Lowbush blueberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and spread by underground rhizomes to form colonies. Manage in a two-year cycle: mow or burn half the planting to the ground each year so alternating sections produce a full crop annually. Harvest in midsummer when berries are deep blue-purple and sweet. Drought-tolerant once established, but irrigation during fruit fill improves berry size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lower Salmon River Squash
description: A rare Pacific Northwest heirloom preserved by home gardeners along the Lower Salmon River in Idaho and later distributed through Slow Food Ark of Taste seed-saving networks. Sow directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vines are relatively compact and early-maturing compared to many winter squash. Fruits are round with peach-to-orange skin, occasionally showing faint turban shaping, and average five to seven pounds. Harvest when the rind is hard and stem has begun to dry, then cure briefly before storing; the thick skin resists rot and rodent damage, allowing fruit to keep for many months. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Loxton Lad Tomato (Orange Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the thick, rugose-leafed stems lightly for support. Loxton Lad bears large, smooth, oblate orange beefsteak fruit with well-balanced, delicious flavor, notably bigger than its sibling release Loxton Lass. It originated from a 2009 Rosella Purple x orange heirloom cross made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized over several seasons by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers, and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for peak sweetness. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Loxton Lass Tomato (Orange Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)
description: Loxton Lass bears smooth, oblate orange beefsteak fruit with the same well-balanced, rich flavor as its sibling release Loxton Lad, but on a noticeably smaller-fruited plant. It shares the same origin as Loxton Lad: a 2009 cross of Rosella Purple and an unnamed orange heirloom made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, rugose-leafed stems lightly for support. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: LSU Gold Fig (Louisiana Gold Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; LSU Gold is a golden-yellow fig cultivar developed by the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center's renowned fig breeding program — one of several outstanding cultivars released by LSU specifically for Gulf Coast garden conditions. The medium-sized fruits have golden-yellow to amber skin and rich, sweet, amber-colored flesh with excellent flavor and lower acidity than common brown-skinned fig varieties. The golden skin and rich, honey-sweet taste make LSU Gold particularly attractive for fresh eating and fresh presentations where the unusual color adds visual appeal. LSU Gold ripens with a main crop in July through September in zone 9 and often produces a lighter breba (early crop) in June. LSU-developed figs are specifically selected for performance in the hot, humid Gulf South — resistance to fig mosaic virus, quality fruit production in high heat and humidity, and productivity in the long Gulf South growing season. Figs are among the easiest and most productive fruit trees for Gulf Coast gardens — drought-tolerant, naturally pest-resistant, fast to bearing (often fruiting in the second year from cuttings), and requiring minimal care beyond keeping the soil moist during fruit development. Propagate easily from dormant hardwood cuttings taken in late winter. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: LSU Purple Fig
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; LSU Purple fig was developed by Louisiana State University specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, where high humidity, summer rains, and soil fungal diseases typically prevent figs from performing as reliably as in Mediterranean or California climates. It produces an abundant main crop in summer of medium-sized, deep purple-skinned figs with a rich, sweet, dark-red interior. The variety has superior resistance to fruit splitting and souring — common problems in humid regions where rain during ripening ruins the crop on other varieties. It ripens earlier than most, avoiding the worst of hurricane season. An outstanding choice for zone 8‑9 gardeners in the humid Southeast. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: LSU Scott's Black Fig (Mississippi-Grown Deep Red-Fleshed Fig)
description: Plant a rooted cutting or container tree in spring after frost danger in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soil but reward good drainage and consistent moisture during fruit development. Scott's Black is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter's fig breeding program in the 1950s and, like its siblings LSU Gold and LSU Tiger, was selected specifically for vigor and fruit quality in hot, humid Gulf South conditions. The self-fertile tree produces small to medium figs with deep purple-to-black skin and intensely flavored, strawberry-pink flesh, ripening on a late main crop from September into October. Scott's Black stands out for continuing to produce good-quality fruit into cool, rainy fall weather after many other fig varieties have finished for the season. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: LSU Tiger Fig
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; like its LSU AgCenter sibling releases, LSU Tiger fig was bred specifically to perform reliably in the humid, disease-prone conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Its most distinctive feature is its striking immature fruit — young, unripe figs are boldly striped in yellow-green and dark green, giving the variety its 'Tiger' name — before ripening to a bronze-brown skin with sweet, richly flavored, amber-to-strawberry-colored flesh. The variety carries useful resistance to fruit splitting and souring, common problems for figs grown where summer rains fall during ripening, and its ornamental striped immature fruit makes it a conversation piece in the garden even before harvest. A good choice for Gulf South growers who want the LSU program's disease resistance along with a visually distinctive fruit, zone 7–11. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lucknow 49 Guava (Sardar)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Lucknow 49 (also sold as Sardar) is India's most widely planted commercial guava cultivar, selected for its round to ovate fruit with smooth, primrose-yellow skin and firm, sweet, aromatic white pulp with relatively few, soft seeds. The tree is notably vigorous and productive, with attractive smooth bark that flakes away in patches to reveal pink and green new bark beneath. It bears two main crops per year in subtropical climates and fruits nearly continuously in frost-free tropical conditions, making it a heavy, reliable producer for home orchards. Regular pruning after harvest encourages the flush of new growth on which guava fruit is borne, keeping trees productive and manageably sized. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Lucky Boy Angled Luffa
description: Lucky Boy is a named cultivar of ridged (angled) luffa grown for its deeply ten-ribbed, dark-green fruit, harvested young at 6-8 inches when the flesh is still tender, mild, and free of the fibrous skeleton that develops later. It is favored in South and Southeast Asian home gardens and by Florida growers for heavier, more reliable fruit set through hot, humid summers than smooth luffa types, and it climbs vigorously on a trellis, fence, or arbor. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine productive continuously from early summer through fall in Gulf Coast conditions. Young shoots and leaves are also edible and used in some Southeast Asian cooking, though the fruit is the primary crop. Matures in 50–80 days from seed.

name: Lucky Cross Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the large, heavy fruits. Lucky Cross is an exquisite heirloom bicolor tomato producing large, 1–2 pound beefsteak fruits with golden-yellow to orange skin blushed with a red blush at the blossom end and extraordinarily beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh that is as ornamental sliced on a plate as it is delicious — the flavor is sweet, low-acid, and tropically fruity with exceptional richness. Its rarity and stunning appearance make it a prize at farmers' markets and seed saving circles. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; harvest when fruit softens at the blossom end and the skin transitions fully from green. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Lucques Olive (Crescent-Shaped Languedoc Table Olive)
description: Lucques is the crescent-shaped green table olive of the Languedoc region of southern France, prized for its firm, fine-textured flesh and mild, nutty flavor once cured. It is only partially self-fertile, so planting it alongside a compatible cultivar such as Manzanilla or Leccino improves fruit set. The distinctive curved, pointed olives are harvested green in early fall specifically for brine-curing rather than oil pressing, since the crescent shape and clean flesh are central to the variety's culinary appeal. Provide full sun and well-drained, lean soil, and protect young trees from hard freezes until they are well established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lucretia Dewberry (Heirloom Southern Trailing Bramble)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy loam and train the sprawling, thorny canes onto a low trellis or wire to keep the large fruit off the ground. Lucretia is one of the oldest named dewberry cultivars still grown in the South, prized in Texas and the Gulf region in the early twentieth century for producing unusually large, glossy, sweet-tart fruit far earlier in the season than blackberries. Because dewberries flower and ripen so early, protect blossoms from late cold snaps and expect a short, intense harvest window rather than the extended cropping of modern blackberry cultivars. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to keep the sprawling planting from becoming an unmanageable thicket. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Lucullus Chard (Heirloom White-Stemmed Large-Leaf Swiss Chard)
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full-sized production. Harvest outer leaves regularly from 40 days onward; the plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months with consistent harvesting. Lucullus is one of the oldest and most established Swiss chard varieties in American cultivation — named after Lucullus, the Roman general and gourmet famous for his extravagant feasts, a name that captures both the impressive size of the plant and the generous quality of its harvest. Lucullus produces very large (18–28 inch tall), broadly spreading plants with thick, heavily crinkled, dark green leaves and thick, ivory-white to pale green stems and ribs — a classic white-stemmed chard in the traditional style before the development of colored-stem varieties. The large, deeply savoyed leaves have substantial texture and rich, minerally chard flavor that is excellent cooked — wilted with olive oil and garlic, added to soups and pasta, or incorporated into quiches and casseroles. The very large leaf size makes Lucullus impractical for baby salad mixes (too coarse when young) but exceptionally productive for cooked greens — a single plant at peak production can provide a large bundle of cooking greens per week. Lucullus is often noted for better heat tolerance than some other chard varieties, making it one of the more productive summer leaf vegetables in hot climates. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Lucuma (Egg Fruit Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in a frost-free location; lucuma is a Peruvian fruit tree native to the Andean valleys, where it has been cultivated since ancient times and was called the 'Gold of the Incas.' The large, oval fruits (3–4 inches) have a dry, starchy, bright orange-yellow flesh with an extraordinary flavor — intensely sweet with a rich, complex caramel-maple-sweet potato quality that is completely unlike any familiar fruit. The taste is so distinctive and rich that lucuma powder (dried, ground lucuma flesh) is used as a natural sweetener and flavoring for ice cream, smoothies, pastries, and confections in Peru, where lucuma ice cream outsells chocolate and vanilla in many surveys. The flavor is particularly popular as a low-glycemic sweetener alternative. Fresh lucuma is eaten locally in Peru and Chile but ships poorly, so it is rarely found fresh outside its home region. An exceptional specialty fruit tree for collectors in frost-free zones. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Luffa / Sponge Gourd
description: Nick or soak seeds for 24 hours before sowing 1/2 inch deep indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost to give this long-season crop a head start. Provide a very sturdy trellis, as vines can reach 15 feet and carry heavy fruit. For eating, harvest young fruits at 4–6 inches before the fibrous skeleton hardens. For sponges, allow fruits to fully mature and dry on the vine until the skin browns, then soak in water, peel, and rinse out the seeds. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Luffa Gourd
description: This vigorous climbing gourd serves two purposes: harvest young fruits as a tender, okra-like vegetable, or let them mature and dry into natural loofah sponges. It needs a long, hot season, so start seeds indoors and transplant onto a sturdy trellis once soil is warm. The heavy vines produce long, hanging fruits that require strong support. For sponges, leave the gourds on the vine until the skin browns and the interior fibers dry, then peel, shake out the seeds, and rinse. Matures in 120–200 days from transplant.

name: Luffa Sponge Gourd
description: Grow on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence — luffa vines are extremely vigorous and can cover a large structure in a single season. The large yellow flowers are showy and attract bees and pollinators. Young fruits at 4–6 inches long are eaten as a tender vegetable in Asian cuisines (similar to zucchini but with a silkier texture); for sponge production, allow fruits to mature fully on the vine until the skin turns brown and papery, then soak in water to loosen and remove the outer skin, revealing the fibrous interior skeleton. Dry the sponge in the sun and rinse several times until the fiber is clean and pale yellow. Each vine can produce dozens of sponges. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Lula Avocado
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — avocados are extremely sensitive to root rot in poorly drained or clay soils; Lula is a historic Florida avocado cultivar developed by George Lula in Homestead, Florida in the 1920s and valued for its combination of good cold hardiness, large fruit size, and excellent fresh-eating quality. The large fruits (often 12–18 ounces) have smooth green skin that remains green when ripe — ripeness is determined by giving the fruit a gentle squeeze, not by color change. The flesh is pale yellow-green, creamy, and mild-flavored with good avocado oil content. Lula is classified as a hybrid between West Indian and Guatemalan race avocados, inheriting moderate cold tolerance from its Guatemalan genetics and fruiting reliability from its West Indian parentage. In zone 9 Lula is one of the more reliable cultivars for home production; the long, warm growing season develops the oil content that gives mature fruits their buttery richness. Cross-pollinate with a Type A avocado such as Bacon for best fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Lumina White Pumpkin
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-amended soil, spacing hills 5–6 feet apart; Lumina is a vigorous vine type that needs plenty of room and full sun. Lumina is the most widely grown white pumpkin, producing round, 10–20 pound fruits with a smooth, creamy-white to ghostly-white exterior rind that makes it one of the most sought-after decorative pumpkins for Halloween and fall displays; the interior flesh is orange, sweet, and of good quality for cooking and pies — better than many orange carving pumpkins. The white skin provides an excellent canvas for painting, engraving, or decorative carving. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin resists puncture with a thumbnail; cure for 1 week and store in a cool, dry location for 2–3 months. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Lunar White Carrot (Pale Ivory Sweet Carrot)
description: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, loose, sandy loam free of rocks and clumps, keeping the surface consistently moist until the slow-germinating seedlings emerge. Lunar White produces smooth, tapered, ivory-white roots with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor free of the slight bitterness some white carrots carry, making it a popular addition to mixed-color carrot bunches for market and home use. Because it lacks the orange and purple pigments of most carrots, it shows soil staining and surface blemishes more readily, so grow it in well-worked, debris-free soil for the cleanest roots. Thin seedlings early to prevent crowded, twisted roots, keep beds weeded while carrots are young and slow to establish, and harvest once roots reach full size, since white carrots left too long in the ground can develop a coarser texture. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Lunchbox Pepper (Snack-Size Sweet Pepper Series)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lunchbox is a popular sweet pepper series bred to produce large numbers of small, thin-walled, crunchy, sweet fruit about the size of a large grape or small egg, perfect for snacking whole, tossing into lunchboxes, or adding to salads without any need to slice. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and work well in both garden beds and containers. Harvest continuously as pods ripen to their full color (red, orange, or yellow depending on the specific variety) to keep the plant producing more fruit. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Luscious Pear (Cold-Hardy Sweet Melting-Flesh Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Luscious was bred by South Dakota State University specifically for the harsh northern Great Plains climate, combining excellent cold hardiness and good fire blight resistance with genuinely good eating quality, living up to its name with sweet, juicy, melting flesh comparable to much less hardy European dessert pears. The medium-sized, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in early to mid fall and should be picked while still firm, then ripened at room temperature indoors for the best texture, as with most European-type pears. Its combination of hardiness and flavor has made it a favorite recommendation for northern home orchardists who want a genuinely good fresh-eating pear without relying on tender varieties bred for milder climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Luther Hill Sweet Corn (Historic White Sweet Corn)
description: Luther Hill was bred by New Jersey farmer Luther Hill in 1902 and became the most popular sweet corn in parts of New Jersey for half a century before serving as a direct parent of the later hybrid 'Silver Queen'. Plants stay relatively compact at around five and a half feet, typically producing two small, tender white-kerneled ears per stalk plus extra ears on the vigorous suckers if given room to spread. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in blocks for dependable pollination. The flavor is notably sweet and rich even by modern standards, which is why breeders have continued to draw on its genetics long after more productive hybrids replaced it commercially. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Lutz Green Leaf Beet (Winter Keeper Storage Beet)
description: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody roots. Lutz Green Leaf, also called Winter Keeper, is a classic American heirloom beet bred to grow to a large size (often 3-5 inches or more) without becoming woody, fibrous, or losing its sweet flavor the way most beets do when oversized — a trait that makes it uniquely suited for fall harvest and long winter root-cellar storage. The tender, mild, sweet flesh holds its quality even at full size, and the abundant deep green tops are excellent cooked as beet greens. Because it needs a longer season to develop its full storage-quality size, plant it in time to mature before hard frost, then harvest and store roots in damp sand or a root cellar for use well into winter. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Lychee
description: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) in a site sheltered from salt spray and drying winter wind; lychee cannot tolerate waterlogged roots at any age. Trees require a cool-dry stress period of 4–6 weeks in late autumn — nights reliably below 59°F — to trigger flower bud development, so hold irrigation during that window rather than watering on a regular schedule. Fruit clusters develop rapidly after bloom and benefit from thinning to 3–5 fruits per panicle when marble-sized to improve final fruit size and reduce limb stress. Harvest clusters when the rough, bumpy skin has turned fully red to pinkish-red and the aroma is distinctly floral and sweet, typically 90–112 days after bloom. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Lychee Tomato (Litchi Tomato, Morelle de Balbis)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — lychee tomato is remarkably drought-tolerant and thrives in poor soils where other nightshades would struggle; provide gloves when handling since the entire plant is covered in sharp spines up to 1.5 inches long. The cherry-sized, bright red fruits are enclosed in spiny green husks that split open at full ripeness, revealing smooth, glossy berries with sweet-tart, lychee-flavored flesh containing small seeds. Fruits are delicious eaten fresh when fully red or cooked into sauces, jams, and pies. In zone 8–9 this perennial-in-origin plant often naturalizes and re-seeds, becoming a productive self-sustaining patch. It is also studied as a biocontrol host against nematodes and as a trap crop for Colorado potato beetle. Wear thick gloves during any maintenance or harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: M111 Apple Rootstock (Malling-Merton 111)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M111 is grown as a semi-dwarfing to semi-standard understock, not for its own fruit. One of the classic Malling-Merton series rootstocks developed in England, it produces a vigorous, semi-standard-sized tree that develops a large, sturdy, self-supporting root system needing no permanent staking, along with good drought tolerance and adaptability to a wide range of soil types compared to the smaller, more demanding fully dwarfing rootstocks. Its self-supporting, low-maintenance root system and tolerance of poor or dry soil have made it a traditional standard for larger home orchard trees and for growers unwilling or unable to install permanent trellising for dwarf trees. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the eventual tree ample room, since it grows nearly as large as a full seedling tree. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: M26 Apple Rootstock (Malling 26)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M26 is a semi-dwarfing understock that benefits from staking in its early years. Another classic East Malling selection, it produces a semi-dwarf tree roughly 40-50 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, notably hardier and more cold-tolerant than M9 while still offering meaningful size control and precocious early fruiting, making it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards wanting a manageable tree size. Its root system is sturdier than M9 but still benefits from staking for the first several years until the tree is well established, and it performs best in fertile, well-drained soil, showing some susceptibility to fire blight and collar rot in poorly drained sites. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, stake for the first few years, and expect a compact, productive tree well suited to a small home orchard in a colder climate. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: M7 Apple Rootstock (Malling 7)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M7 is a semi-dwarfing understock that is largely self-supporting once established. A long-standing East Malling selection producing a semi-dwarf tree roughly 50-60 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, it develops a sturdier, more self-supporting root system than the more fully dwarfing M9 and M26 rootstocks, generally needing staking only while young rather than for the tree's entire life. It has a tendency to produce root suckers that should be removed periodically, and it shows good tolerance of a range of soil types along with reasonably good cold hardiness, making it a reliable choice for a home orchard tree of moderate, easy-to-manage size. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, remove root suckers as they appear, and expect a productive tree that needs only temporary staking while establishing. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: M81E Sorghum (Light Amber Syrup Sorghum)
description: Sow seed roughly an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has thoroughly warmed, thinning to final spacing as seedlings establish. M81E is a tall, late-season Mississippi-bred syrup cultivar with brown seed heads that needs a longer stretch of hot weather than earlier varieties like Dale to fully mature, making it especially well suited to the long warm season along the Gulf Coast. Harvest when the canes reach hard-dough stage in the seed head and the lower leaves begin to dry, then press and boil the juice quickly into a mild, light amber syrup. Because of its late maturity, gardeners in shorter-season areas should get it in the ground as early as safely possible after frost to ensure the stalks finish sweetening before fall's first cold snap. Matures in 130–145 days from seed.

name: M9 Apple Rootstock (Malling 9)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M9 is a fully dwarfing understock requiring permanent staking or trellising. Selected at England's East Malling Research Station in the early twentieth century, it remains the benchmark fully dwarfing apple rootstock against which most modern rootstocks are compared, producing a small tree roughly 25-30 percent the size of a standard seedling tree that bears fruit remarkably early and heavily for its size. Its brittle, shallow root system anchors poorly and requires permanent staking or trellising for the life of the tree, and it demands consistently fertile, well-drained soil and regular irrigation to perform well, making it best suited to intensively managed high-density plantings rather than a low-maintenance home orchard. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, provide permanent support, and expect an extremely compact, easy-to-harvest tree bearing within two to three years. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Maayan Apple (Israeli Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Maayan was bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at the Rehovot experiment station in Israel specifically for hot, low-chill growing regions, and needs about 450 hours of winter chilling — well matched to Gulf Coast Texas and Louisiana winters. It ripens mid-season, later than Anna, with round-oblong fruit that is yellow with more than half its surface flushed red. The flesh is notably crisp and highly juicy, making it a good fresh-eating choice among the Israeli low-chill introductions. It keeps reasonably well in storage compared to some of its lower-chill counterparts. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mabel Grey Pelargonium (Intensely Lemon-Scented Geranium)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, letting the top of the soil dry slightly between waterings. Mabel Grey is widely considered the most intensely and purely lemon-scented of all the scented geraniums, its deeply cut, rough-textured, sharply pointed leaves releasing a strong citrus fragrance at the lightest touch, far more potent than milder lemon-scented cultivars. Small lavender-pink flowers appear but are incidental to the plant's main appeal as a fragrance and culinary herb; the leaves can flavor teas, baked goods, and sugars, or be crushed and rubbed on skin as a natural citrus-scented insect deterrent. Pinch stems to keep it bushy and encourage fuller growth, and take cuttings easily to propagate; it is frost-tender, so bring containers indoors to a bright window before the first freeze. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Mac Black Raspberry (Late-Season Michigan Black Raspberry)
description: Plant dormant canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and train the tall, vigorous canes onto a trellis or wire support, since Mac Black grows noticeably taller and more upright than older black raspberry standards. Originating in Michigan from parentage that was never clearly recorded, Mac Black is prized chiefly for ripening about a week to ten days after most other blackcap cultivars have finished, giving gardeners who also grow an early type like Bristol or Jewel a meaningfully longer overall black raspberry season. The medium-to-large berries are firmer than many blackcaps, holding up well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserves, and the canes show useful field tolerance to anthracnose. Remove spent floricanes right after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per hill to keep the planting productive and easy to pick. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mac's Golden Wooly-leaf White Sapote
description: Grow Mac's Golden in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, mulching the root zone and providing winter protection in the cooler parts of zone 9 as with other woolly-leaf white sapote trees. This Carlsbad, California-origin selection is prized among Casimiroa tetrameria seedlings for producing notably large, elongated-oval, golden-yellow fruit with a distinctive rich aroma and fewer seeds than typical, giving a higher proportion of edible custardy flesh per fruit. The flavor is sweet and buttery, similar to common white sapote but often considered richer by growers who have tasted both. Because it is a grafted selection rather than an unnamed seedling, it offers more predictable fruit quality and size than growing Casimiroa tetrameria from seed. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Maca (Peruvian Ginseng)
description: Sow seeds directly into deep, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in a cool climate or cool season, barely covering them and keeping the seedbed consistently moist until germination; maca is a compact, low-growing brassica relative native to the high Andes above 13,000 feet, where it produces a flat, radish-like hypocotyl in colors ranging from cream and yellow to red, purple, and near-black. The edible hypocotyl has a butterscotch-malt flavor when fresh and intensifies to a deeper, richer taste when sun-dried — the traditional Andean preparation — and is used in porridges, stews, baked goods, and fermented drinks. In temperate lowland gardens, maca is challenging but achievable in cool-summer climates; gardeners in maritime regions of the Pacific Northwest, the UK, and New Zealand have had the most consistent success. Harvest when the central rosette begins to decline, usually in autumn of the planting year. Matures in 180–270 days from seed.

name: Macadamia
description: Macadamias are self-fertile but cross-pollination between two or more varieties meaningfully increases yields; grafted trees start bearing at 3–5 years, while seedlings can take 10–15 years. The tree prefers well-drained, slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) and is sensitive to root disturbance — plant without disturbing the root ball. Trees produce racemes of cream-white flowers that fall and create a slippery surface; harvesting is done by collecting nuts that have dropped naturally as the green husk splits and the nut falls. Shell and dry nuts for 3–4 weeks before cracking; the shells require a commercial or heavy-duty nut cracker as they are among the hardest of any food nut. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Macadamia Nut (Smooth-Shell Macadamia)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; protect from frost below 26°F until established; plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination and better yields. Macadamia integrifolia (smooth-shell macadamia) is one of the world's most celebrated nut trees and the only major food crop originating in Australia — native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland. The macadamia nut is universally recognized as one of the finest-flavored nuts in the world: round, ivory-white, buttery-smooth, with an extraordinarily rich, creamy, sweet flavor unlike any other nut. The fat content (75%) is predominantly monounsaturated, making macadamia oil one of the most desirable culinary and cosmetic plant oils. The smooth-shell species (M. integrifolia) is the primary commercial macadamia — most Hawaiian, Australian, South African, and Kenyan commercial orchards are primarily or entirely M. integrifolia or its hybrids. Trees are evergreen, grow slowly to 25–35 feet, produce dark-green, glossy, leathery leaves, and begin bearing in 5–7 years from grafted stock. The extremely hard shell (requiring 300+ psi to crack) requires a specialized macadamia cracker. Zone 9b–11, damaged below 26°F. Hawaii, California, and South Florida can grow macadamia commercially; zone 9a gardens can succeed with protected sites. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: MacBeth Loquat (Large-Fruited Late-Season Loquat)
description: Plant in compost-rich, well-drained loam in full to partial sun; MacBeth is self-fertile and does not require a second loquat for fruit set, though nearby trees can improve yield. The tree has a handsome, symmetrical growth habit and can reach around 20-30 feet at full maturity if left untrained, so prune annually to keep fruit within easy reach in a home orchard. MacBeth ripens later than early cultivars like Gold Nugget and produces exceptionally large, orange-skinned fruit with creamy flesh that balances sweetness and acidity, often compared to notes of plum; the size and flavor have made it one of the most sought-after loquat cultivars among backyard growers and collectors. Like other loquats, MacBeth blooms in fall and ripens fruit in late winter to spring, and open flowers and young fruit are more cold-tender than the mature tree, so a warm, sheltered planting site near a south-facing wall improves crop reliability at the cooler edge of its range. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: MacDonald Rhubarb (Cold-Hardy Canadian Heirloom Rhubarb)
description: Plant dormant crown divisions in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, setting the bud eyes 1-2 inches below the soil surface in a bed enriched with aged manure or compost. Space plants generously and avoid harvesting stalks the first year so the crown can establish a deep root system for winter survival. MacDonald was developed by a Canadian prairie breeding program specifically to withstand the extreme winter cold and short growing seasons of the Canadian plains, and it remains a favorite in Manitoba and Saskatchewan home gardens for its reliability where many other cultivars struggle. Its stalks are medium-thick and rosy-pink to red, with a balanced tart flavor well suited to pies, sauces, and preserves. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: MacGregor's Favorite Beet
description: A Scottish heirloom bunching beet, grown for over a century, notable for its striking dark magenta-purple leaves as much as its slender, conical red roots. Bred for rapid early growth so it can be harvested young in bunches rather than left to bulk up like a storage beet. The dramatic foliage doubles as an attractive edible green, sauteed like chard, while the roots are sweet and tender when pulled small. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Mache (Corn Salad)
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed at 1/4 in depth in cool soil and keep moist; mache is extraordinarily cold-tolerant and grows slowly through winter in mild climates. Thin to 4–6 in for well-formed rosettes, though closer spacing produces acceptable baby greens. Harvest entire rosettes by cutting at the soil line, or pinch individual rosettes for salad use. Mache does not tolerate heat and will quickly bolt and disappear as spring temperatures rise; enjoy it as a winter green. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Machiaw Eggplant (Asian Hybrid Long Pink-Purple Eggplant)
description: Machiaw is an Asian-type hybrid bearing slender fruit that ranges from pale purple to a striking deep pink, typically 10-12 inches long and about 1-1.5 inches thick. The skin stays thin and tender even as the fruit lengthens, giving mild, non-bitter flesh that needs no peeling or salting before cooking. Plants set fruit continuously through hot weather, making Machiaw a dependable choice for a long Gulf Coast harvest season. Pick fruit while the color is bright and the surface glossy, since the thin skin toughens and dulls quickly once fruit is left to over-mature. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Macoun Apple (Beloved Northeast Eating Apple, McIntosh-Type Geneva Station Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; requires cross-pollinator; thin biennial crops by hand-removing half the fruit clusters in early summer to encourage annual bearing; Macoun ripens October and must be harvested at peak ripeness — slightly soft at the stem end, fully red, and with characteristic spicy aroma — as it deteriorates quickly after peak. Macoun apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva from a cross involving McIntosh, and named for W.T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturalist of Canada who made significant contributions to fruit breeding and evaluation — released in 1923, making it roughly contemporary with McIntosh's commercial rise. Among apple connoisseurs of the northeastern United States, Macoun occupies a unique status: it is considered by many the finest-eating apple of any variety available in New York and New England, with a complex, spicy-sweet, intensely aromatic flavor at peak ripeness that exceeds even McIntosh in intensity and depth. The fruit is medium-sized, dark red (often nearly all-red with a purple-red hue at full maturity), with pure white, tender, very juicy flesh and the characteristic McIntosh floral fragrance amplified. Macoun's intense flavor comes with a significant limitation: the variety has a very short window of peak eating quality — typically 1–2 weeks at the height of ripeness in October — after which the flesh softens rapidly and flavor diminishes. This poor keeping quality has limited Macoun's commercial viability but made it a cult variety among farmers' market customers who know to seek it out during its brief peak season. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mad Hatter Pepper (Unique Flying-Saucer-Shaped Mild Pepper)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mad Hatter is an All-America Selections winner grown for its unusual, whimsical, flattened flying-saucer-shaped pods with distinctive lobed edges, a shape unlike almost any other common pepper, combined with a mild, sweet, subtly citrusy flavor reminiscent of its Capsicum baccatum relatives like aji peppers. It works well fresh in salads, pickled whole for a striking presentation, or lightly cooked, and the productive plants continue setting fruit over a long summer season. Harvest at any color stage from green to ripe yellow-orange, since the mild heat and flavor are enjoyable throughout ripening. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Mad-dog Skullcap (Blue Skullcap)
description: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near pond edges, rain gardens, or low woodland spots; does not tolerate prolonged drought. Scutellaria lateriflora (mad-dog skullcap) is a native wetland and streamside perennial in the mint family, grown for its small blue-to-violet, two-lipped flowers that line the leaf axils in a distinctive one-sided (lateriflora) arrangement, and for the aerial parts, which are harvested at flowering and dried for traditional calming herbal preparations. Despite the common name, the plant is not associated with rabies — the name stems from historical folk use as a treatment for rabid-animal bites. It spreads by rhizomes into loose colonies in reliably damp ground and is a good choice for the moist partial-shade margins of a rain garden or bog bed, where it also attracts small native bees. Zone 3–9. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Madake Bamboo
description: Plant with strong, deep rhizome barrier (30-inch HDPE sheet) to prevent running — Phyllostachys bambusoides sends rhizomes 20–30+ feet in a season and will colonize large areas without containment; install barrier before planting and inspect annually for rhizome escape. Phyllostachys bambusoides (Madake, Japanese Giant Timber Bamboo, or Matake) is one of the largest and most culturally important bamboos in the world — native to China but cultivated in Japan for at least 1,500 years, where it is the premier timber bamboo of Japanese traditional crafts. The culms grow to extraordinary dimensions in optimal conditions: 50–75 feet tall and 4–6 inches in diameter, with thick, straight, dense walls, outstanding tensile strength, and beautiful, lustrous, deep-green color that ages to golden-yellow. Madake is the traditional material for shakuhachi (Japanese end-blown flutes), kendo practice swords (shinai), fishing rods, scaffolding, architectural elements, and fine bamboo furniture — the culm quality is unsurpassed among temperate bamboos. The young spring shoots are edible. As a Phyllostachys (running bamboo), however, it produces aggressive, far-traveling monopodial rhizomes that can penetrate asphalt, damage foundations, and invade neighbor properties if not properly contained by deep rhizome barriers. Never plant without barriers in place. Extremely cold hardy to zone 5 when established. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Madame Jeanette Pepper (Surinamese Lantern Pepper, Intensely Hot Caribbean Capsicum chinense)
description: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully yellow. Madame Jeanette is a Surinamese Capsicum chinense variety that is one of the most important chiles in Dutch-Caribbean cuisine — particularly in the culinary traditions of the Surinamese and Antillean communities that immigrated to the Netherlands beginning in the mid-20th century. The pepper is named after a legendary entertainer from Paramaribo, Suriname's capital, and carries strong cultural significance in Surinamese cooking, where it is used to season traditional dishes such as pom (tayer root casserole) and various rice preparations. Morphologically, Madame Jeanette produces elongated, lantern-shaped to irregular pendant fruits — 2–3 inches long, tapering to a point — that ripen from green to yellow (occasionally to orange or red in some strains). The shape is somewhat different from the round, wrinkled habanero and the bell-shaped Scotch bonnet, falling between those types and the elongated fatalii in form. The heat level is substantial (estimated 150,000–300,000 Scoville units) with the characteristic fruity, floral habanero-type aroma of C. chinense — sweet, tropical, and intensely fragrant. The flavor that accompanies the heat is distinctly fruity and aromatic with apricot-like qualities that distinguish C. chinense from the more neutral heat of cayenne. In zone 9, Madame Jeanette performs exceptionally well — the heat and humidity that challenge cool-season crops are ideal conditions for this tropical species, which can produce abundant fruit through summer and fall. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Madder
description: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply loosened soil in full sun; Rubia tinctorum tolerates drought once established and benefits from calcium-rich soils — add lime to acidic soils and avoid waterlogging. Rubia tinctorum (Madder or Dyer's Madder) is a rambling, rhizomatous, rough-stemmed perennial climbing herb in the Rubiaceae (coffee) family native to the eastern Mediterranean, Turkey, and Central Asia, now widely naturalized across Europe and cultivated by natural dyers worldwide. For more than 5,000 years — documented in Egyptian tomb textiles dating to 1500 BCE, Indian trade records, and Islamic textile traditions — Madder root was the primary source of red, orange, and coral dyes for textiles, wool, silk, and cotton worldwide. The roots contain alizarin (1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone) and purpurin, which when mordanted with alum produce clear reds, with iron produce purples and browns, and with other mordants produce a full spectrum from coral to brick-red to burgundy. Madder root cultivation was an enormous agricultural industry in the Netherlands, France, Turkey, and India from the medieval period until the synthesis of alizarin from coal tar by Perkin in 1869 collapsed the natural dye industry almost overnight. Today Madder is grown by natural dyers, craft textile artists, and historical recreationists who value plant-based dyes. The plants need 2–3 years to produce roots of harvestable size. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Madeira Vine
description: Plant Anredera cordifolia tubers or divisions in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a trellis, fence, or other support as it is a vigorous climber; water regularly during active growth; harvest young, tender leaves as needed throughout the warm season; contain carefully as the aerial tubers can spread and the plant is invasive in warm climates. Madeira Vine is native to tropical South America and has spread as a culinary crop throughout Asia, where the leaves are eaten as a nutritious cooked green vegetable in the same manner as spinach or Malabar spinach — particularly popular in the Philippines (alugbati companion), Taiwan, and Indonesia. The succulent, heart-shaped leaves are harvested continuously from the vigorous vines and cooked briefly in stir-fries, soups, and wilted salads; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to New Zealand spinach. The plant produces numerous small, warty aerial tubers along the stems as well as underground tubers, all of which are edible cooked. WARNING: Madeira Vine is classified as a serious environmental weed in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and some US states; never plant near natural areas, and dispose of all plant material including tiny aerial tubers carefully, as even small fragments can establish new plants. Grow in containers or in contained raised beds in frost-free areas. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Madison Peach (Cold-Hardy Virginia Heirloom Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Madison is self-fruitful; thin fruit in spring to 6–8 inches; this variety is particularly valuable where late spring frosts endanger developing blossoms — its cold-hardy flower buds and frost resistance make it among the most reliable peach varieties in colder zones. Madison peach was developed at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (released 1963) as part of a program to develop peach varieties combining high fruit quality with improved cold-hardiness of the flower buds — addressing the primary limitation on peach production in the colder parts of the South and the lower Midwest where late spring frosts can destroy the blossoms of standard varieties like Elberta even in years when winter temperatures are adequate for the trees to survive. The key innovation of Madison is its extraordinary flower bud cold-hardiness: Madison buds have been documented surviving temperatures of -5°F to 0°F with minimal damage in some trials, making it significantly more frost-resilient than Elberta (whose buds are damaged at 28–30°F during bloom). This characteristic translates to reliable cropping in zones 4–6 where other varieties fail every few years due to late frost blossom kill. The fruits are medium to large, red-blushed over golden-yellow skin, with firm, yellow, fully freestone flesh and a well-flavored, balanced sweet-tart peach quality. Madison ripens in mid-season (late July to mid-August in its Virginia homeland, somewhat earlier in warmer zones). It remains one of the most important variety recommendations for cold-region home orchardists in the Mid-Atlantic, Appalachian, and upper Midwest states. Matures in 105–125 days from transplant.

name: Madonna Elderberry (Gold-Margined Variegated Black Elderberry)
description: Madonna is a compact, brightly variegated elder cultivar with broad green leaves boldly edged in creamy gold, lighting up a shaded corner of the border more strongly than older gold-margined forms. Flat clusters of white, faintly fragrant flowers open in early summer and mature into small black berries, but the shrub is grown as a foliage specimen rather than for fruit. Site it in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun to prevent the variegated margins from browning, and prune out any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the variegation strong. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Maekawa Jiro Persimmon (Early-Ripening Non-Astringent Jiro Sport)
description: Maekawa Jiro, sometimes sold as Early Jiro, is a Japanese sport of the classic non-astringent Jiro persimmon selected to finish ripening about a week ahead of standard Jiro, which helps the fruit develop full sweetness and flavor in regions where cool fall weather can otherwise limit ripening. The large, seedless, conical fruit can be eaten firm and crunchy, with a clean, sweetcane-like flavor, or allowed to soften further for a richer texture, and it colors up bright orange in late fall. The tree is compact and cold-hardy, typically staying under about 12 feet, and is self-fertile, producing full crops without a second persimmon nearby. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Maestro Pea (Disease-Resistant High-Yielding Shelling Pea)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing light support such as pea netting or twiggy brush. Maestro is a modern shelling pea bred for reliable, heavy yields of dark green, well-filled pods carrying good resistance to powdery mildew and fusarium wilt, two of the most common diseases that shorten a pea harvest, particularly as the season warms toward summer. The sweet, tender peas inside are excellent fresh, frozen, or cooked, and the disease resistance helps the vine keep producing later into the season than many older, more disease-susceptible varieties manage. Pick pods promptly once well filled but before peas inside turn starchy, and keep the vine picked clean to prolong the harvest window as long as cool weather allows. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: Magana Mamey Sapote
description: Grow this Cuban-origin, grafted mamey sapote cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for a large, long-lived tree. It is valued by south Florida growers for reliably producing smooth-skinned fruit with dense, sweet, salmon-pink flesh often compared to sweet potato or pumpkin custard. Young trees are noticeably cold-tender and can lose leaves or twigs at temperatures in the mid-30s, so Gulf Coast growers stick to the warmest coastal locations or grow smaller trees in large containers that come indoors for winter. Mature trees take several years to bear their first crop, and fruit is harvested firm and then ripened off the tree at room temperature. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Magda Squash (Lebanese Cousa-Type Summer Squash, Superior Nutty-Sweet Flavor)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best flavor; up to 6 inches for stuffing. Magda is a cousa-type Lebanese summer squash — a form of summer squash with a fundamentally different eating character from the Italian zucchini types (such as Black Beauty, Costata Romanesco) that dominate American garden squash production. The cousa squash group, originating in the Middle East and Mediterranean, produces fruits that are pale sage-green to celery-green, cylindrical to club-shaped with a distinctively bulging blossom end, and with a pale, waxy skin surface that is noticeably different in appearance and texture from the darker, shinier skin of Italian zucchini types. The defining characteristic of cousa squash flavor — and the reason Magda has a devoted following among cooks — is a nutty, creamy sweetness distinctly different from the mild, slightly vegetal flavor of standard zucchini. Cousa squash flesh has a firmer, drier texture and more pronounced sweetness than Italian types, making it the preferred squash for Middle Eastern preparations: the primary culinary use of cousa squash in Lebanese, Syrian, and Egyptian cooking is kousa mahshi (literally 'stuffed squash') — the small fruits cored and filled with a spiced meat and rice mixture before being simmered in tomato sauce, a preparation where the firmer flesh and nutty flavor of the cousa type are essential to the dish's character. Magda is an F1 hybrid cousa-type that produces prolifically with good uniformity, adapts well to North American growing conditions, and provides the cousa flavor character more reliably than open-pollinated Middle Eastern varieties. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Magdal Loquat (Major Spanish Commercial Sweet-Flavored Loquat)
description: Magdal is one of only a handful of loquat cultivars grown commercially at scale in Spain, particularly in Andalusia, where it is valued alongside Golden Nugget for its notably sweet flavor. Fruit ripens with the orange skin and flesh typical of top commercial Mediterranean cultivars, and sensory panels have consistently rated Magdal among the sweeter-tasting loquats compared to tarter selections like Algerie. As with all loquats, Magdal blooms in autumn and winter, so a hard freeze during bloom or early fruit development can severely reduce or eliminate that year's harvest. Grafted trees typically need two to three years after transplanting before first fruiting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Magdalena Big Cheese Pumpkin (Sonoran Desert Heirloom)
description: Magdalena Big Cheese is a Sonoran Desert heirloom pumpkin with roots in Sonora, Mexico, grown by Southwestern gardeners and maintained by regional seed-saving organizations. It produces large, flattened, wheel-shaped fruits weighing 15-30 lbs with light orange, ribbed skin resembling a wheel of cheese. The dense, fine-grained flesh is richly sweet and well suited to soups, purees, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries useful resistance to squash vine borer and tolerates heat well, fitting arid Southwestern growing conditions. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Magic Carpet Creeping Thyme
description: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery divisions into sharply drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun. Magic Carpet forms an exceptionally dense, low mat of tiny gray-green leaves that all but disappears under a heavy midsummer flush of lavender-pink flowers, one of the showiest and most uniform bloom displays among the creeping thymes and a strong pollinator draw. It tolerates light foot traffic once established, releasing a faint aromatic scent when brushed or stepped on, making it a favorite filler between flagstones and pavers and along the edges of gravel paths. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and encourage a fuller second flush; avoid heavy, poorly drained soils where the shallow roots are prone to rot. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Magic Lantern Pumpkin (F1 Jack-o'-Lantern Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the vigorous vines. Magic Lantern is a hybrid carving pumpkin producing classically shaped, medium-ribbed fruit in the 16-24 pound range with bright orange skin and a sturdy, well-attached handle that holds up through harvest and transport to market. Its uniform round-to-slightly-tall shape and consistent sizing make it a dependable choice for growers selling by the piece at pumpkin patches and farm stands. Harvest when the rind has fully colored and hardened, before the first hard frost, and cure briefly in a warm, dry spot to toughen the skin for longer display life. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Magic Molly Potato (Deep Purple High-Anthocyanin Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow to boost yield and prevent tuber greening. Magic Molly is a striking purple potato with deep violet-black skin and vivid, uniform purple flesh throughout, prized for its exceptionally high anthocyanin content, dense, moist texture, and rich, earthy flavor that some describe as slightly nutty. Unlike some older blue and purple varieties, Magic Molly holds its intense color well through cooking, making mashed potatoes a striking lavender-purple and roasted wedges deep violet inside. The medium-sized, round-to-oval tubers form in good numbers per plant, and the variety performs reliably across a range of climates. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait until vines die back for full-sized, better-storing tubers. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Magical Michael Basil (Compact Disease-Resistant AAS Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture. Magical Michael, a 1996 All-America Selections winner, bears dark green leaves on a compact, uniform, notably disease-resistant plant that holds up better against common basil ailments than many older cultivars, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where basil downy mildew and other foliar diseases are frequent problems. Its tidy, container-friendly size and improved disease resistance make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a small herb garden or patio pot. Pinch flower spikes as they form to keep the plant producing tender new leaves, and harvest regularly to encourage continued growth. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Magness Pear (Exceptional-Flavor Fire-Blight-Resistant USDA Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it near two other pear cultivars since Magness produces sterile pollen and cannot pollinate itself or other pears, though other pears can pollinate it. Magness is a USDA-released pear celebrated among fruit growers for its outstanding dessert quality, with smooth, buttery, exceptionally sweet flesh often ranked among the best-tasting of all pear cultivars, paired with strong resistance to fire blight that makes it a dependable choice for humid Southern growing conditions. Because of its sterile pollen, plant it alongside two compatible, fertile pear cultivars to ensure good fruit set on all three trees. Prune to an open framework for good air circulation, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well into clean wood below the damage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Magnolia Blackeye Cowpea (Disease-Resistant Mississippi Blackeye Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, checking plants regularly since pods are not always held well above the foliage and can be easy to miss at harvest. Magnolia Blackeye is a Mississippi State University release bred from a cross involving Extra Early Blackeye, Bunch Purple Hull, and Dixielee, combining a compact, medium-sized bush habit with strong resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode along with tolerance to common cowpea viruses. Pods are light green-yellow at the green-shell stage, holding cream-to-light-green peas marked with the classic black eye, and the seed coat is notably smoother and less wrinkled than most other blackeye-type southern peas. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix nitrogen, and the plant's disease resistance package makes it a practical choice for Gulf South gardens where nematode or wilt pressure has limited other blackeye varieties. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Magnolia Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Magnolia is a USDA-developed self-fertile bronze muscadine grape, bearing medium to large bronze-to-copper-colored fruits with a mild, sweet flavor and thin, tender skin — one of the more elegant-tasting muscadine varieties for fresh eating, without the strongly musky, foxy character of older selections. The perfect-flowered Magnolia vine can pollinate female-only varieties like Carlos and Fry planted nearby, making it doubly useful as a multi-variety vineyard anchor. Fruits ripen in late August to September in most zone 8–9 plantings, later than some early-season varieties. The vines are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 15–20 pounds per vine at maturity. Train on a 4-wire trellis system, prune back to 2–3 buds per spur in late winter, and fertilize lightly in early spring. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Magnolia Southern Highbush Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines before planting; Magnolia was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service breeding program at Poplarville, Mississippi, specifically for the coastal plains of the southeastern United States, and carries a moderate chilling requirement of about 500 hours. It blooms roughly 5 to 12 days after the earliest rabbiteye cultivars but its fruit often ripens 5 to 14 days ahead of them, giving growers an early harvest while reducing exposure to late-winter freeze damage during bloom. For best production, interplant Magnolia with another Southern highbush cultivar rather than growing it as a single variety block. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw to keep the shallow root system cool and moist through Gulf Coast summers, and skip lime and phosphorus-heavy fertilizers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Magnum Bonum Apple (North Carolina Piedmont Heirloom Fall Apple)
description: Old Southern nurseries once marketed Magnum Bonum as 'the standard fall apple' and 'king of all fall apples,' and it was a fixture of Southern orchards from the 1830s through the 1930s. The medium, roundish fruit has thin, smooth, pale greenish-yellow skin with a light crimson blush and faint darker stripes, surrounding white, fine-grained, tender, juicy flesh that is mildly subacid and aromatic. It ripens in mid-to-late summer across most of the South and is prized as a dessert apple as well as a good keeper for its season, with a vigorous, productive, disease-tolerant tree habit that made it a dependable dooryard choice. Provide a compatible pollinizer such as Horse, Yates, or Shockley, since Magnum Bonum sets fruit best with cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Magnus Blueberry (Early Hand-Harvest University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and evenly moist through the growing season. Magnus was released by the University of Florida as an early-season, hand-harvest cultivar prized for large, firm berries comparable in size to Emerald, though the fruit is not firm enough to hold up under mechanical harvesting equipment. It has performed consistently across seasons and under both hydrogen-cyanamide and non-cyanamide bud-break management, making it a dependable choice for growers who apply dormancy-breaking sprays as well as those who do not. Because its chilling requirement runs a bit higher than many low-chill southern highbush releases, it rewards sites with reliably cool winters within the Gulf Coast growing region rather than the very mildest microclimates. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Magoon Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Bronze Breeding-Stock Muscadine)
description: Released from Mississippi's muscadine breeding program, Magoon is a self-fertile bronze muscadine long grown in home gardens across the Gulf South for fresh eating, juice, and wine, and has also served as breeding stock in university grape-improvement programs, including as a parent of interspecific hybrid muscadine selections developed at the University of Florida. Vines are vigorous and productive once established on a strong trellis, ripening their bronze-gold berries through late summer alongside other classic self-fertile bronze cultivars like Carlos. As with other muscadines, Magoon shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal diseases that trouble European bunch grapes in humid climates, so a home planting typically needs no fungicide program. Prune back hard to short spurs on permanent cordons each winter to keep the vine productive and manageable. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mahan Pecan (Historic Very Large-Nutted Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. One of the earliest widely planted named pecan cultivars, dating to the early 1900s, Mahan is known for producing exceptionally large nuts, among the biggest of any pecan cultivar, though the kernel fill and disease resistance lag behind modern breeding selections. It remains of historical interest and is still grown in some older orchards and by collectors of heirloom pecan varieties for its striking nut size, even though it has largely been superseded commercially by higher-yielding, more scab-resistant cultivars. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Maher Black Sapote
description: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Maher is a Florida-selected black sapote valued for its large, round, apple-green fruit that ripens to a dull olive-brown and reveals dark, chocolate-brown, custard-smooth flesh once fully soft — hence the common name 'chocolate pudding fruit.' Unlike astringent persimmons, black sapote is only palatable when completely soft-ripe, at which point the mild, sweet flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon or blended into puddings, smoothies, and baked goods. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate light shade better than most fruit trees, making them useful in mixed edible plantings. Harvest fruit while still firm and green and allow it to fully soften indoors over one to two weeks, as tree-ripened fruit is quickly taken by wildlife. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mahlab (Mahaleb Cherry, St. Lucie Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mahlab, or mahaleb cherry, is a small ornamental cherry species native to the Mediterranean and Middle East, grown far more for the fragrant kernel inside its small, bitter cherry pits than for the fruit's thin, tart flesh, which is not typically eaten fresh. The dried, ground kernels — called mahlab or mahleb — have a distinctive bitter-almond, floral, faintly cherry aroma used to flavor Middle Eastern, Greek, and Mediterranean pastries and breads, including Greek tsoureki, Cypriot flaounes, and Middle Eastern ka'ak. To harvest the spice, collect ripe pits, crack them to remove the kernel inside, and grind the kernels just before use, since their aroma fades quickly once ground. The tree itself is small, fragrant-flowered in spring, and notably drought- and alkaline-soil-tolerant, which is also why it is widely used as a rootstock for grafting sweet and sour cherries in regions with dry, calcareous soils unsuited to standard cherry rootstocks. It tolerates heat and poor soil well once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mahua (Indian Butter Tree, Honey Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; mahua is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on poor soils. Madhuca longifolia (mahua or Indian butter tree) is a large, slow-growing tropical tree native to the forests of central and southern India, deeply woven into the culture and economy of indigenous tribal communities across Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh. The tree provides multiple distinct food, economic, and cultural products: the fleshy, sweet, cream-colored flowers (corollas) that drop prolifically in spring are edible and extremely sweet — they are eaten fresh (tasting like a mild honey-flower combination), sun-dried and used as a sweetener, fermented into mahua wine, and distilled into mahua liquor, one of India's most important traditional tribal spirits and an important livelihood product. The seeds contain 30–40% mahua butter (a semi-solid vegetable fat) with a composition similar to cocoa butter, used in traditional cuisine, soap-making, and cosmetics. The leaves provide fodder; the bark and flowers have Ayurvedic uses. Mahua is considered a 'tree of life' by many Indian adivasi (tribal) communities — the flowers are economically critical, often constituting a significant fraction of tribal household income in forest villages. A remarkable tree with enormous cultural depth and genuine multiple-use value. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Maiden Blush Apple (Early American Heirloom Dual-Purpose Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator, since Maiden Blush is not reliably self-fruitful. First noted in New Jersey in the late eighteenth century, Maiden Blush became one of the most widely planted American heirloom apples of the nineteenth century for its striking pale lemon-yellow skin marked with a rosy pink blush on the sun-exposed side, a color pattern early writers likened to a blushing cheek. The crisp, tart-leaning flesh cooks down into a pale, delicately flavored sauce and dries well, while a fully ripe apple mellows enough for pleasant fresh eating, making it a genuinely dual-purpose variety by the standards of its era. It ripens over a fairly early late-summer window and does not keep as long in storage as later-season heirlooms, so plan to use or process the crop within a few weeks of picking. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to improve size and reduce biennial bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Majestic Hardneck Garlic
description: Plant this Porcelain-type hardneck garlic in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, so cloves establish roots before winter. Separate the bulbs into individual cloves just before planting and set them pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 to 8 inches apart, then mulch heavily. Each bulb yields 4 to 7 jumbo cloves with an assertive flavor. In early summer, snap off the curling scapes to direct energy into the bulbs, and harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy spot. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Majesty Muscadine Grape
description: Train onto a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Majesty was bred by Dr. Jiang Lu at Florida A&M University from a 'Supreme' x 'Triumph' cross and released in 2008, and it is notable for producing some of the largest berries of any released muscadine cultivar, with an attractive glossy black skin and excellent, sweet flavor. Because Majesty carries only female flowers it will not set fruit on its own, so a nearby self-fertile black or bronze muscadine is essential for pollination. Yields run lighter than the heaviest-cropping commercial cultivars, which is why Majesty is grown mainly by home gardeners chasing exceptional dessert-quality fruit rather than by growers prioritizing volume. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Majesty Pole Bean
description: Direct sow this AAS-winning purple pole bean once the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep at the base of a tall trellis or pole. The vigorous climbing vines produce striking 5 to 6 inch pods with rich purple skins and tender green interiors that offer sweet, crisp flavor. The purple color also makes the pods easy to spot at harvest. Pick regularly to keep the vines productive, and provide full sun with consistent moisture during flowering and pod set. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Majorca Pink Rosemary
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — excellent drainage is more important than soil fertility for rosemary; Majorca Pink is a named cultivar of culinary rosemary distinguished by its delicate pink flowers in contrast to the blue-purple blooms of most rosemary varieties, making it equally valuable as an ornamental flowering shrub and a culinary herb. The upright to slightly spreading habit and profuse pink spring bloom (February–April in zone 9) create a spectacular display in herb gardens, Mediterranean-style landscapes, and edible ornamental borders. The foliage flavor and aroma of Majorca Pink is equivalent to standard rosemary — potent, resinous, piney, with notes of camphor — and it can be used in all the same culinary applications: roasting meats and vegetables, infused oils, herb breads, and as a fresh garnish.
