In zone 9 Majorca Pink is particularly drought-tolerant and heat-adapted, thriving in the intense summer sun that would stress less robust varieties. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Makok Sapodilla
description: 'Makok' is a Thai sapodilla selection introduced to Florida collector orchards for its small, round, olive-shaped fruit borne in heavy clusters, distinct from the larger single fruits typical of most Florida cultivars. The flesh is smooth-textured, sweet, and low in grit, making it a favorite for fresh eating in Southeast Asian cuisine. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; the tree is moderately vigorous and, like other sapodilla selections, extremely tolerant of drought, wind, and salt once established. Fruit should be picked while still firm and allowed to ripen off the tree for several days at room temperature, since sapodilla harvested too early remains astringent with latex. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Makrut Lime (Kaffir Lime, Thai Lime)
description: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Citrus hystrix (makrut lime, formerly and controversially called kaffir lime) is a Southeast Asian citrus grown primarily for its extraordinary, hourglass-shaped double leaves — two leaves joined end to end — which have an intensely aromatic, complex lime-floral fragrance unlike any other citrus and are indispensable to the flavor profiles of Thai, Indonesian, Cambodian, and Lao cuisines. The fresh or dried leaves flavor curries, soups (Tom Yum), coconut-milk dishes, and rice; they are among the most important flavoring ingredients in Southeast Asian cooking. The small, warty, dark-green, rough-skinned fruits are highly acidic and used primarily for their zest (makrut lime zest is a key ingredient in Thai curry pastes) rather than their juice. The plant is an extremely popular container herb in Thai and Southeast Asian communities across the Gulf South — grown in pots for easy access to fresh leaves year-round and brought indoors when cold threatens. Makrut lime is also used in some natural beauty products for its essential oil. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Malabar Chestnut (Money Tree, Guiana Chestnut, Saba Nut)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar chestnut is best known to most people as the ornamental 'money tree' with braided trunks sold as a houseplant across the world, but it is also a genuine food plant producing 12-inch oval pods filled with 20–25 large, edible seeds that taste remarkably like chestnuts or roasted peanuts when cooked — the seeds can be roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, and the young leaves and flowers are edible as vegetables. As a landscape tree in zone 9b–12 it can reach 30–40 feet in the ground with a spreading tropical canopy, but is easy to keep pruned to 10–15 feet. The large, palmate leaves and buttressed trunk give it outstanding ornamental character. Native to the seasonally flooded forests of Central and South America, it tolerates both dry periods and extended flooding — a rare combination that makes it valuable for challenging low-lying sites. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Malabar Nut (Vasaka)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar nut, known as vasaka in Ayurvedic medicine, is a fast-growing evergreen shrub from South Asia long used in traditional respiratory remedies, with the leaves brewed into teas and syrups historically employed for coughs, bronchitis, and asthma-like symptoms. The plant forms an attractive, dense, leafy shrub with large, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves and showy white flowers marked with purple-veined lower lips, produced in short spikes mainly in spring, that attract pollinators despite the plant's primary reputation as a medicinal rather than ornamental subject. It tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to nearly full sun and adapts well to average garden soil once established, needing only routine watering during dry spells. In the Gulf South, Malabar nut can be grown as a woody perennial shrub in sheltered zone 9 gardens, cut back hard after a hard freeze to resprout from the base, or grown further north as a container specimen brought indoors for winter. Prune periodically to maintain a bushy shape and encourage fresh leaf growth for harvest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Malabar Nutmeg (Bombay Nutmeg, Wild Nutmeg)
description: Plant seedling or grafted trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained forest loam in the dappled shade of taller canopy trees, keeping humidity high year-round. Native to the Western Ghats of India, this wild relative of true nutmeg produces a larger fruit than Myristica fragrans, and its bright red, waxy aril is dried and sold as a distinct spice known as Bombay mace or rampatri, historically used as a cheaper substitute or adulterant for true mace and valued in its own right in Konkani and Malabar coastal cooking for a resinous, less sweet flavor. The seed kernel itself is bitter and not used as a nutmeg substitute the way the aril is. The species is now assessed as vulnerable due to habitat loss, and smooth, greenish-black to reddish bark distinguishes the mature trunk from true nutmeg. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Malabar Spinach
description: Sow direct or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting, placing seeds in warm soil after last frost and providing a trellis, fence, or other support — Malabar spinach is a vigorous twining vine that can climb 10 feet or more in a single season. Basella alba is an excellent warm-season substitute for true spinach in hot, humid climates where conventional spinach bolts; the thick, fleshy, glossy leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture when cooked and hold up better than spinach in stir-fries, soups, and curries, and the young leaves are pleasant eaten raw. It grows rapidly in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile soil and high humidity, making it ideal for gulf-coast and tropical gardens. Harvest by snipping young stem tips every 1–2 weeks to encourage bushy regrowth; the plant is killed by the first frost but self-seeds freely in frost-free zones. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Malaga Violet Radish (French Purple-Skinned Spring Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Malaga Violet is a classic French heirloom radish valued for its striking, uniform violet-purple skin over crisp white flesh, a distinctive color that stands out clearly from the more common all-red or bicolor spring radishes. The round to slightly oval roots have a clean, mild, only lightly peppery flavor, and the purple skin holds its color well even as the radish sizes up, unlike some varieties that fade. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Malagueta Pepper
description: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 1–3 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed in full sun; Malagueta pepper is a heavy-yielding, upright frutescens type similar to tabasco pepper that continues producing through summer heat. Capsicum frutescens 'Malagueta' is the iconic hot pepper of Brazilian cuisine, prized for the tangy, piri-piri-style hot sauce and pepper-infused vinegar (molho de pimenta) served at Brazilian steakhouses, producing prolific clusters of small, slender, upward-pointing fruit that ripen from green through yellow-orange to red with intense, sharp heat around 60,000–100,000 Scoville units. Plants form a bushy, productive shrub over the growing season and, like other frutescens peppers, tolerate heat and humidity well, making them reliable producers through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer. In frost-free zones plants can be overwintered as a short-lived perennial shrub; elsewhere grow as a warm-season annual and harvest continuously to encourage further fruit set. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Malanga
description: Plant cormels or divide corms in moist, humus-rich, fertile, deep soil in partial shade; malanga (yautia, cocoyam, tannia, new cocoyam) is a tropical American root crop closely related to taro (Colocasia esculenta) and widely cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Central and South America, and tropical Africa as a major starchy staple food. The underground corms and cormels are large, starchy, and nutritious — boiled, baked, fried, or mashed in a broad range of Caribbean and Latin American dishes including Cuban malanga fritters (frituras de malanga), pasteles, soups (sancoche), and as a potato substitute. Unlike true taro, malanga corms are generally considered easier to digest and are less irritating to people with taro sensitivities. The above-ground plant is ornamental in itself — the large, arrowhead-shaped, deep-green leaves on tall, mottled petioles create an impressive tropical foliage display while the roots develop. It grows well in partial shade and moist, fertile, organically rich soil. Harvest corms 8–10 months after planting when the lower leaves begin to turn yellow. An important crop in Caribbean communities and a worthwhile tropical edible for zone 9–12 food gardens. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Malanga (Cocoyam)
description: Plant corms in fertile, loose, consistently moist but well-drained soil in partial shade; malanga grows naturally in Caribbean and South American forest edges and is more tolerant of shade than taro. The arrow-shaped leaves are ornamental as well as edible (properly cooked), and the large starchy corms have a nuttier, creamier flavor than taro. All parts must be thoroughly cooked before eating as raw malanga contains calcium oxalate crystals. Harvest corms when leaves begin to yellow and die back, typically 7–9 months after planting; the central corm and surrounding cormels can all be harvested. In zone 9 store unharvested corms with heavy mulch over winter or dig and store indoors above 50°F. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Malay Apple (Mountain Apple, Jambu Bol, Rose Apple Tree)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple grows most rapidly with regular watering and fertilization in the warm humid conditions of zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida. Syzygium malaccense is a large, fast-growing, evergreen fruit tree native to Malaysia and the Indonesian islands, now cultivated throughout the tropics from the Pacific Islands to Central America, Africa, and the Caribbean. The tree is doubly ornamental: in spring, it produces spectacular displays of crimson-red to deep rose-purple flowers that emerge directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches (cauliflory), creating an extraordinary effect of flowers growing from the wood — dozens to hundreds of 1-inch flowers with brush-like clusters of bright crimson stamens covering the trunk in a fiery display. These flowers are followed by the fruits: dark red to magenta, pear-shaped, 2–3 inch fruits with white, spongy, mildly sweet flesh and a faint floral flavor — eaten fresh throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands and used in jams and beverages. The tree is an important crop and dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical Oceania and Southeast Asia. The Hawaiian name 'Ohia Ai' (mountain apple) reflects its long cultivation history in the Hawaiian Islands. In zone 10-11 South Florida landscapes, it serves as both an ornamental shade tree and a productive home fruit tree. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Malayan Dwarf Coconut Palm (Compact Early-Bearing Selection)
description: Plant container-grown seedlings or a partly husked seed nut in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Malayan Dwarf is the most widely planted dwarf coconut selection, valued for its compact 20-30 foot mature height (roughly half that of tall varieties), earlier bearing at just 4-6 years from planting, and moderate resistance to lethal yellowing disease that has devastated tall coconut plantings throughout Florida and the Caribbean. Because it is naturally self-pollinating, seed nuts come true to type, making it easy to propagate reliably from seed. The shorter stature also makes harvesting and hurricane cleanup considerably safer and easier than with tall varieties. Golden, green, or yellow-fruited strains are all sold under the Malayan Dwarf name. Extremely frost-sensitive — restricted to USDA zones 10-12 in the continental US, chiefly southern Florida and Hawaii. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Malayan Kumquat (Limau Pagar, Swingle's Kumquat)
description: Native to Hainan Island in China and to Peninsular Malaysia, where it is known locally as limau pagar, this species is one of the least commonly grown kumquats in Western gardens and is distinguished by an unusually thin, smooth, aromatic peel relative to fruit size compared to the more familiar Nagami and Meiwa kumquats. Fruit is small and globose, roughly an inch across, ripening to a bright orange or golden-yellow and typically divided into four to six segments, and like other kumquats the sweet peel is eaten along with the tart pulp. The tree stays more compact and shrubby than standard kumquat cultivars, which suits container culture, but it is also more cold-sensitive, making it best suited to the warmest Gulf Coast microclimates or protected container growing rather than an unprotected zone 9a landscape planting. Its rarity outside botanical citrus collections makes it more of a specialty conversation piece than a mainstream dooryard fruit. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Malbec Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes. Originally a minor Bordeaux blending grape in France, this deeply colored red variety found its true expression in the high-altitude vineyards of Mendoza, Argentina, where abundant sunshine and cool nights produce the rich, plush, dark-fruited wines with soft tannins that have made Malbec Argentina's signature grape and an internationally beloved red wine style. It is somewhat prone to coulure (poor fruit set in cool, wet spring weather) and benefits from a warm, sheltered site with reliable sunshine through flowering and fruit set. Provide full sun and a warm site sheltered from late spring cold snaps, prune to a moderate crop load for the best concentration, and harvest when tannins are ripe alongside sugar development. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Malibu White Sapote
description: Developed in Malibu, California in 1981, this selection produces round, yellow fruit that ripens in fall, typically October to November, well after many earlier white sapote cultivars have finished. It takes noticeably longer than average to come into bearing, but growers who plant it consider the wait worthwhile for its rich, custard-like flavor and consistent fall crop once the tree matures. Site it in full sun on deep, well-drained soil with wind protection, since white sapote wood is brittle and prone to breakage in storms. Let harvested fruit soften fully at room temperature for several days, since it does not ripen properly if picked hard and refrigerated. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Malta Fig (Small Sweet Early-Ripening Mediterranean Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Malta is a small, dark purple-brown Mediterranean heirloom fig grown for ripening notably early in the season, giving gardeners a reliable, dependable crop of sweet, richly flavored fruit even where the growing season isn't long enough for later-ripening varieties to fully mature a full crop. The compact, manageable tree size makes it a practical choice for container culture or smaller garden spaces, and the fruit's small size and thin skin make it excellent for fresh eating straight from the tree, though it does not ship or store as well as firmer, larger fig varieties. As with all figs, protect the roots with heavy mulch in winter in the colder parts of its range, since the top can die back in hard freezes but typically regrows from the root system. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mama Mia Giallo Pepper (Early Yellow Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Mama Mia Giallo is a modern Italian frying pepper bred for earliness and productivity, bearing slender, tapering fruits that mature from green to a glossy golden yellow with the thin walls and sweet flavor typical of classic Italian corno-type peppers. Market growers favor it for its ability to set fruit heavily even under cooler, less-than-ideal conditions, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom frying types. Harvest at the yellow stage for peak sweetness, or pick some pods green for a milder, more vegetal flavor. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Mambo Watermelon (AAS-Winning Personal-Sized Dark-Rind Watermelon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after the last frost, in hills spaced to allow the vigorous vines to sprawl, or trellis to save space. Mambo is an AAS Edible-Vegetable Award winner bred as a personal-sized icebox watermelon, producing dark green, dark-striped 4–6 pound fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and notably good disease tolerance for a home garden variety. Its compact fruit size and relatively fast maturity make it a practical choice for smaller gardens, raised beds, or trellised growing where full-sized watermelon varieties are impractical. Consistent watering through fruit development is important for good sugar content and to prevent hollow heart, and fruit is ready to pick when the tendril nearest the stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Mamey Apple (Mammee Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is a large, stately fruit tree native to the Caribbean, Mexico, and northern South America, producing round to oval fruits 3–8 inches across with a thick, rough, bitter brown-russet skin enclosing firm, apricot-orange to yellow flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavor suggesting apricot, vanilla, and almond — quite unlike most other tropical fruits. The flavor is complex and distinctive: the outer flesh directly under the skin can be slightly bitter, while the inner flesh is sweet and aromatic. The tree is magnificent as a landscape specimen — densely leafy, with thick, glossy, oval leaves and a formal, dome-shaped crown. Small, white, fragrant flowers appear on the branches directly. The timber is dense and valuable. Not to be confused with Mamey Sapote (Pouteria sapota), an entirely different fruit despite the similar name. Mamey apple was a staple food of the Taino people of the Caribbean before European contact and was described by Columbus's men. It is now primarily grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mamey Sapote
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) is a majestic Central American tree in the Sapotaceae family that produces one of the most beloved tropical fruits in Caribbean and Latin American cuisine — a large, russet-brown, football-shaped fruit with vivid salmon-to-brick-red flesh of exceptional richness, sweetness, and smooth texture, often compared to a pumpkin-sweet potato-almond fusion. The fruit is eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes and batidos (a staple across Miami's Cuban community and throughout the Caribbean), made into ice cream, and used in desserts. Only grafted trees of named selections should be planted, as seedling trees can take 10–15 years to fruit and produce variable quality; grafted trees begin bearing in 3–5 years. Mamey sapote is moderately drought-tolerant once established but produces larger, higher-quality fruit with consistent irrigation and regular fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mammoth Basil
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Mammoth basil is prized for its extraordinarily large leaves, regularly reaching 4–6 inches long and 3–4 inches wide — far larger than standard Genovese varieties. The oversized leaves are ideal for making whole-leaf Caprese salad arrangements, individual-leaf wraps, and for presentations where a single perfect leaf is the feature rather than chiffonade. Flavor is standard Genovese-type — sweet, clove-like, aromatic — with no sacrifice in quality for the size increase. The relatively compact plant habit for a large-leaf variety makes Mammoth more manageable than some other large basil types. Pinch flower buds as soon as they appear to maintain leaf production; in zone 9 the plant will bolt in May–June but often rebounds for fall production. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Black Twig Apple (Paragon, Arkansas Black Twig)
description: Give this vigorous tree plenty of room and prune annually to keep the spreading, upright canopy open to light and air. Originating in Arkansas in the 1830s as a Winesap seedling, Mammoth Black Twig became a popular commercial apple across the South and lower Midwest for its large size, dark red color, and firm, tart-sweet flesh that stores well into winter. It is a distinct cultivar from the unrelated Arkansas Black and is grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors seeking a taste of 19th-century Southern apple culture. Matures in 165–180 days from transplant.

name: Mammoth Dill
description: Mammoth dill lives up to its name, reaching at least three feet and sometimes towering to five, with feathery foliage prized for cooking and pickling. Its large flower umbels are magnets for beneficial pollinators, and the plants readily self-sow once seed matures. Direct sow into full sun since the taproot dislikes being moved, and sow in succession for a continuous supply of leaves. Provide staking or a sheltered spot for the tallest plants, and harvest foliage before flowering for the best flavor. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Feijoa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Mammoth is an older New Zealand-selected feijoa cultivar named for its unusually large, elongated fruit, which can weigh well over 4 ounces and sometimes tops the size chart among common home-garden feijoa varieties. The flesh is aromatic and juicy with the classic pineapple-guava-mint flavor, though quality is somewhat more seed-heavy toward the fruit's center than in top dessert cultivars like Apollo. Mammoth ripens mid-to-late season, extending harvest when planted with earlier cultivars, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it useful as an informal evergreen screening hedge as well as a fruiting shrub. Because Mammoth sets fruit poorly on its own pollen, interplanting with a second cultivar is essential for a worthwhile crop; the showy white-and-crimson spring flowers and edible sweet petals are ornamental bonuses either way. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mammoth French White Sunchoke (Large White-Skinned Heirloom Jerusalem Artichoke)
description: Plant tuber sections 3-5 inches deep in a dedicated, well-drained bed, since sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground and this vigorous heirloom is difficult to fully eradicate once established. Mammoth French White is an old French-derived heirloom strain valued for producing notably large, pale tan-to-white tubers substantially bigger than wild-type or unnamed sunchoke stock, which means fewer tubers are needed to fill a basket and less scrubbing per pound at harvest, though the tubers still carry some of the knobbiness typical of the species rather than the smooth club shape of Fuseau-type strains. Plants grow tall and coarse, 6-9 feet, topped with small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back with frost; tubers are ready to dig once tops are killed and can be harvested through winter into early spring as needed. A light frost is said to sweeten the flavor by converting stored inulin into simple sugars. Leave a portion of tubers in the ground each year to regenerate next season's crop, and rotate or contain the bed to keep the planting from spreading into unwanted areas. Matures in 125–150 days from transplant.

name: Mammoth Long Island Dill
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — do not transplant; Mammoth Long Island Dill is the classic tall, open-pollinated dill variety grown for over a century in the truck-farming regions of Long Island, New York, and is still the standard for dill pickle production. The large plants reach 4–5 feet with broad, flat seed heads (umbels) 6–8 inches across carrying hundreds of seeds — the seed-head size is the key advantage over compact varieties when the goal is fresh dill seed for pickling, dill vinegar, or dill oil. The seed flavor is stronger, more pungent and aromatic, and more concentrated than leaf dill flavor, and Mammoth Long Island is timed and sized to produce mature seed heads concurrent with cucumber harvest. Both the fresh foliage (dill weed) and the mature seeds are usable. The very tall habit makes the plants dramatic in the back of the herb or vegetable garden and provides early habitat for swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed exclusively on Apiaceae family plants. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Long Island Dill (Tall Classic Dill for Pickling and Abundant Seed Heads)
description: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammoth Long Island is the tall, large-seed-head dill cultivar traditionally grown for pickling and dill seed production — producing the largest seed heads and highest seed yields of common dill varieties, along with an abundance of feathery foliage for fresh and dried dill weed use throughout the season. The name reflects the cultivar's origins in Long Island, New York pickling operations where large seed heads were needed to efficiently pack dill into pickle jars — those large, flat compound umbels of yellow flowers and, later, of aromatic dill seed are the defining feature of the variety, producing proportionally more seed per plant than dwarf and compact varieties. The tall habit (3–5 feet) provides visual presence in the herb garden and creates the feathery, vertical texture that makes dill an attractive ornamental companion for low-growing vegetable crops. In Gulf South zone 9, dill is best grown as a cool-season herb: fall-sown plants establish through the cool months, producing foliage for harvest through winter and spring, then flower and set seed in March–April before summer heat. Fall-grown plants self-sow freely, naturalizing the dill into the garden as a self-renewing herb. Dill foliage is the host plant for black swallowtail butterfly larvae — accepting this graciously means dill does double duty as both herb and butterfly garden plant. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Melting Snow Pea
description: Direct sow this heirloom snow pea in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, since peas prefer cool conditions. The vigorous vines reach 5 to 6 feet tall and benefit from a trellis or netting to keep pods clean and easy to pick. Harvest the large, sweet, tender flat pods before the peas swell for the best flavor in stir-fries and fresh eating. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod development, and pick frequently to prolong the harvest. Matures in 65–72 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Melting Sugar Pea (Snow Pea)
description: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost, providing 4–5 feet of netting or trellis support; Mammoth Melting Sugar is the most widely grown heirloom snow pea, an heirloom variety documented since at least the early 1900s producing large (4–6 inch), flat, tender pods with a delicate, melt-in-the-mouth texture when harvested young and cooked lightly in stir-fries or eaten raw. The pods are stringless when young and the standard against which other snow peas are judged for tenderness and flavor. Harvest when pods are 3–4 inches long and absolutely flat with no seed bulge visible for the premium eating experience. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Mammoth Red Rock Cabbage
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Mammoth Red Rock'
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Mammoth Red Rock is a large, late-season red cabbage heirloom that forms very dense, dark red-purple heads of 8–10 pounds — among the largest and densest of red cabbage types. The firm, tightly-packed heads have a robust, slightly peppery flavor that mellows to rich sweetness after frost exposure and is perfect for braised red cabbage with apples and vinegar (the classic Scandinavian and German preparation), coleslaw, sauerkraut, and long-storage use. Red cabbage keeps far longer than green cabbage — 3–4 months in cold storage at near-freezing temperatures — making Mammoth Red Rock particularly valuable for homesteaders and home food preservation. The deeply saturated red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are natural pH indicators, turning more blue-purple in alkaline cooking water and more red in acidic conditions (add vinegar to fix the red color when braising). In zone 9 Mammoth Red Rock is a fall-planted crop that matures through the winter months. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify (Vegetable Oyster Edible Root, Biennial Cool-Season Novelty)
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in deeply loosened soil; thin to 3–4 inches. Do not transplant — the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Harvest roots at 1 inch diameter or larger by carefully loosening the soil with a fork. Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify is the standard American garden salsify — a biennial root vegetable in the daisy family grown as an annual for its long, tapering, white-skinned edible root. Salsify occupies an unusual position in the vegetable world: it is one of a handful of vegetables whose flavor genuinely resembles a different food — in this case, oysters. The cooked root has a subtle, oceanic, slightly mineral quality reminiscent of mild oysters, earning salsify its traditional common name 'Vegetable Oyster' and giving it appeal in preparations that highlight this unusual flavor character. Salsify was widely grown in American kitchen gardens in the 18th and 19th centuries when root vegetables formed a much larger portion of the winter diet than today, and Mammoth Sandwich Island was the primary named variety in this period. The roots are peeled (the skin oxidizes brown immediately, like artichokes — drop into acidulated water) and boiled, roasted, or prepared like other root vegetables. In zone 9, salsify provides a distinctive cool-season root that few gardeners grow, offering variety from the more standard parsnip, turnip, and carrot roots. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Mamoncillo (Spanish Lime)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free climates; mamoncillo (Spanish lime, quenepa, genip) is a large tropical tree native to Central America and the Caribbean that produces clusters of golf-ball-sized green fruits with a brittle outer skin concealing a translucent, salmon-colored pulp clinging tightly to a large seed. The flavor is a unique combination — simultaneously sweet-tart, tropical, and faintly lime-like with a passionfruit quality — that is utterly distinctive among tropical fruits. Fruits are eaten by biting through the skin and sucking the pulp off the seed, which is the traditional way to consume them across the Caribbean. They are also made into juice, fermented into wine, and processed into candy. Mamoncillo is an important street-food fruit in Puerto Rico, Colombia, Cuba, and throughout the Caribbean, where it is eaten fresh out of hand in large quantities. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and very long-lived. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Manalucie Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Manalucie was developed by the University of Florida in the 1950s and named for the Manalucie experimental farm in Homestead, Florida — one of several important tomato varieties developed by UF plant breeders for subtropical Florida conditions. An indeterminate variety producing large, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with solid flesh, good flavor, and outstanding resistance to gray leaf spot (Stemphylium solani), a fungal disease that is especially destructive in Florida and humid Gulf Coast conditions but for which most tomato varieties have no resistance. Manalucie was for decades the standard large beefsteak-type tomato for Florida home gardens because of this specific disease resistance. It remains valuable today for any gardener in zone 8b–11 who has struggled with leaf spot diseases in tomatoes. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Manchester Market Turnip (English Heirloom Green-Top Turnip)
description: Manchester Market is a 19th-century English field and market turnip named for the city where it was widely grown for sale, producing a creamy white, globe-shaped root topped with light green, edible foliage. It carries a stronger, more peppery bite than modern salad turnips once roots size up past tennis-ball diameter, which suits it well to stews and long-cooked dishes rather than raw eating. It is notably forgiving of a later sowing date than many turnip varieties, making it a practical choice for filling a gap after an earlier crop is cleared. Harvest at a moderate size for the best balance of texture and flavor, since older roots turn fibrous. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Manchurian Wild Rice (Water Bamboo)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water up to 6 inches deep in full sun; Manchurian wild rice spreads by rhizome into large colonies and is best grown in a submerged container to control spread. Tall, broad, bamboo-like leaves rise from the water's edge, and in East Asia the swollen base of stems infected by a specific smut fungus is harvested as a prized vegetable known as jiaobai or gaobai, with a mild, sweet, water-chestnut-like crunch used widely in Chinese cooking. Grown mainly as an ornamental water-garden accent in Western gardens for its bold, architectural foliage, it also serves the same erosion-control and habitat role at a pond margin as other tall emergent grasses, providing cover for waterfowl and other wildlife. Confine the spreading rhizomes to a large submerged container in most garden ponds to prevent it from overtaking the entire margin. Matures in 150–240 days from transplant.

name: Mandan Bride Bean
description: Sow seed directly after all frost danger has passed and provide poles, a tepee, or sturdy netting for this vigorous climbing habit. Mandan Bride descends from beans grown along the upper Missouri River by the Mandan people, prized as much for its dramatically streaked and mottled seed coat — ranging through maroon, tan, and cream in a single pod — as for its flavor. Keep the vines evenly watered through flowering and podset, then allow pods to dry completely before shelling for storage. It is best treated purely as a dry bean, since pods are fibrous and not suited to snap eating. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Mandan Bride Corn
description: Mandan Bride is an heirloom flour corn attributed to the Mandan people of the upper Missouri River, grown historically alongside beans and squash in traditional Three Sisters plantings. Each ear carries an unpredictable mix of red, orange, black, yellow, and white kernels, and because the whole kernel is soft and starchy rather than hard-hulled like flint corn, it grinds easily into flour once fully dried. Leave ears on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are rock-hard before harvesting, then cure indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before grinding or storing. Beyond its culinary use, gardeners often grow it for its striking multicolored ears, which make excellent autumn braids and decorations. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Mandan Pecan (USDA Early-Maturing Scab-Resistant Pecan)
description: Mandan was released by the USDA-ARS Pecan Breeding Program in 2009 from a cross of BW-1 and Osage (tested as USDA 85-1-2), selected for its combination of high scab resistance, late budbreak, and excellent tree strength. Nut maturity is very early, about a week ahead of Pawnee, producing a large, high-quality nut with a good proportion of halves and large pieces suitable for the retail trade. Mandan is a Type I pollen shedder and needs a Type II pollinator planted nearby, and its high scab resistance makes it a good low-input choice for humid Gulf South plantings. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Mandarin / Tangerine
description: Mandarins (including tangerines, clementines, and satsumas) are the most cold-hardy of the common sweet citrus, with satsumas surviving to about 15°F and thriving in zone 8. Most are self-fertile, though some varieties set more fruit with a compatible pollinator nearby. Fruit tends to ripen earlier in the season than oranges — from October through January depending on variety — and the loose peel and sweet-tart flavor make them popular for fresh eating. Avoid overwatering, as mandarins are somewhat drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mandarin Orange (Mandarin, Common Tangerine)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Citrus reticulata is the species encompassing all mandarins, tangerines, satsumas, clementines, and most mandarin-type hybrids — a diverse group of loose-skinned, easily peeled, aromatic citrus originating in Southeast Asia and southern China that includes hundreds of named varieties ranging from tiny, seedless clementines to large, deeply flavored Ponkans. As a group, mandarins are the most cold-hardy common citrus (Satsuma types tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established) and one of the most adaptable to Gulf South conditions, performing well in zones 8b–11 where sweet oranges or grapefruit might struggle with cold or humidity-related issues. Key mandarin varieties for Gulf South gardens include Satsuma (most cold-hardy), Owari Satsuma, Owens Navel, Clementine, Ponkan, Murcott (Honey mandarin), and Dancy tangerine. Most mandarins ripen November through February, and the loose skin that peels easily by hand makes them the most user-friendly fresh citrus. The species is very adaptable to container culture, making it practical for zone 8 gardeners who want moveable citrus. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Manganji Pepper (Kyoto Sweet Togarashi)
description: Grow like a sweet pepper in warm, well-drained soil with steady moisture to keep pods tender and mild. Manganji is a traditional Kyoto vegetable cultivar producing large, glossy, thin-walled pods similar in shape to shishito but noticeably bigger and generally sweeter, though occasional fruits turn hot under heat or drought stress. Harvest young and green for pan-frying or grilling whole, a popular preparation in Kyoto cuisine. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Mangel-Wurzel (Mangold, Stock Beet, Field Beet)
aliases: Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris var. crassa
description: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in deeply worked, loose, fertile to moderately fertile soil after last frost; mangel-wurzel is a large-rooted beet developed in Europe for winter livestock feed and human food in times of scarcity, producing enormous roots (up to 20 lbs) with reddish-yellow or white flesh that stores through winter in a root cellar. Young leaves are edible as greens, and the roots (when young, under 3 lbs) can be cooked and eaten like regular beets with a slightly coarser, starchier flavor. Of growing interest to market gardeners, homesteaders, and traditional food preservers for its extraordinary storage qualities and very high yields per square foot. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Mangkokan (Shell Leaf, Cup Saucer Plant)
description: Plant rooted stem cuttings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; mangkokan is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Round, cupped, saucer-shaped leaves with scalloped edges give this Southeast Asian shrub its common name, and the young, tender leaves are eaten raw as a salad green or wrapped around other foods in Indonesian and Malaysian cooking, traditionally valued for supporting milk production in nursing mothers. Easy to grow and propagate from stem cuttings, it tolerates the light shade beneath larger trees or shrubs and produces usable leaves within a few months of rooting, making it a practical addition to a warm-climate edible landscape. Harvest young leaves continuously as needed, and protect from any frost, since cold quickly damages or kills the plant. Matures in 120–200 days from transplant.

name: Mango
description: Plant grafted trees of named cultivars (Kent, Tommy Atkins, Haden, Keitt) rather than seedlings; grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years and produce fruit true to type. Mangoes require a cool-dry period of 4–6 weeks during winter — nights below 60°F without frost — to trigger uniform flowering; excess rainfall during bloom causes anthracnose and poor fruit set. Prune after harvest each year by removing one-quarter to one-third of the outer canopy to keep the tree at a manageable height and promote fresh fruiting wood. Fruit is ripe when the shoulders near the stem fill out, color develops according to the cultivar, and the flesh yields slightly to pressure; the stem end is often the last to color. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mango Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Curcuma amada is dormant in winter — cut back dead foliage after frost, mulch the root zone heavily in zone 8–9 to protect against freezing, and replant or divide in spring. Curcuma amada (Mango Ginger or Amba Haldi) is a clumping, rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to subtropical India (West Bengal, Odisha, northeast India) and cultivated throughout South Asia for its plump, whitish to pale-yellow rhizomes — valued for the extraordinary raw green mango scent and flavor profile unique to this species within the Curcuma genus, with no heat or turmeric bitterness. The fresh rhizomes are sliced, pickled, or grated in South Indian and Sri Lankan seasonal preparations — particularly the South Indian festival pickle ambahaladi or amada pachadi — and are sold fresh at South Asian markets during the brief harvest season (October–January). The flavor is genuinely mango-like, mild, slightly sour, and entirely distinct from all other gingers. Mango Ginger is an excellent culinary novelty for partial-shade herb gardens in zone 8–11, dying back completely in winter and re-emerging reliably from its persistent rhizome in spring. The inflorescences are also ornamentally attractive: pale-pink, cone-shaped spikes that emerge before the foliage in spring. Matures in 210–300 days from transplant.

name: Mango Pawpaw
description: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Mango Pawpaw is a named USDA-selected cultivar known for producing fruits with a distinctly tropical, mango-like flavor quality that is more pronounced than in typical seedling pawpaws — a richer, more aromatic, tropical sweetness beyond the standard banana-vanilla pawpaw flavor. The medium to large fruits weigh 6–12 ounces with bright yellow flesh and a creamy, custard-like texture. Mango is considered one of the finest-flavored named pawpaw cultivars in the Corwin Davis breeding tradition and is widely used in taste trials as a benchmark for outstanding pawpaw flavor. Like all pawpaw cultivars, Mango requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar — plant alongside Overleese, Wells, or NC-1 for reliable fruit set. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be refrigerated or eaten within a few days; the short shelf life is inherent to the species. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Mango Turmeric
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in rich, well-drained, moist, humus-rich soil; Mango Turmeric (Curcuma amada) is an Indian ginger-family plant producing rhizomes with a pronounced raw mango aroma and flavor when cut — distinctly different from the warm, earthy, peppery flavor of regular turmeric (Curcuma longa). When the fresh rhizomes are sliced, they release a strongly fruity, tropical aroma with pronounced mango-citrus notes, making them a completely different culinary ingredient from turmeric despite their similar appearance. In Indian cuisine, Mango Turmeric rhizomes are used primarily as a pickle vegetable — sliced and preserved in salt, lemon juice, or vinegar where the bright mango flavor develops into a tart-fruity preserve used as a condiment. The plant is also used in Ayurvedic medicine (called Ambi Haladi in Sanskrit) for its anti-inflammatory and digestive properties. The attractive flowering tropical foliage with large, paddle-shaped leaves adds ornamental value to partially shaded garden areas in zone 9. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Mangosteen
description: Mangosteen is one of the slowest-growing and most demanding tropical fruit trees, requiring deep, rich, well-drained, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5), humidity above 80%, and temperatures that never fall below 40°F or rise above 100°F. It is apomictic — seed-grown trees are genetically identical to the mother, eliminating the need for pollinators, though fruit set is parthenocarpic in cultivation. Young trees require shade for the first several years; gradually transition to full sun as the canopy develops. Harvest when the thick purple rind has deepened to a dark maroon-purple and yields slightly to thumb pressure, typically 5–6 months after fruit set. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Manicata Passionflower (Scarlet Andean Passion Vine)
description: Native to the cool, humid cloud forests of the northern Andes, Passiflora manicata tolerates cooler nights and brief cold spells better than most scarlet-flowered passionflowers from the lowland tropics, making it worth trying against a warm, sheltered wall in a zone 9 Gulf Coast garden. Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun with a trellis or fence, and expect a somewhat shrubbier, less rampant habit than vigorous lowland vines like Passiflora coccinea or P. vitifolia. The brilliant scarlet flowers, each centered with a ring of deep purple-blue filaments, open over a long season and are magnets for hummingbirds. Where winter lows dip into the low 20s F, mulch the root zone heavily and expect topgrowth dieback, with new shoots emerging from the base once temperatures warm in spring. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Manila Tamarind
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — Manila Tamarind is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, sandy, even compacted soils where most fruit trees fail; Manila Tamarind (also known as guamúchil, Madras thorn, or camachile) is a thorny, tropical legume tree from Mexico and Central America that produces coiled, bright red-and-white seed pods containing sweet, fibrous white pulp surrounding shiny black seeds. The sweet-tart, cotton-candy-like flavor of the fresh white aril (the edible fleshy layer around the seeds) is popular in Mexican street food markets and throughout tropical Asia where the tree has naturalized. Despite the common name, Manila Tamarind is not related to true tamarind (Tamarindus indica) but belongs to the legume family with nitrogen-fixing roots. The tree is highly productive and drought-tolerant, making it valuable for edible landscape use in hot, dry zone 9 conditions. Pods are harvested when the husks split open to reveal the red-pink exterior and white interior with sweet pulp. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Manoa Sweet Acerola (Barbados Cherry)
description: Manoa Sweet was bred at the University of Hawaii and released in 1963 as a low-acid, mild-flavored acerola suited to eating fresh rather than only juicing, unlike sharply tart seedling Barbados cherries. The upright, spreading shrub is very productive, bearing repeated flushes of orange-red fruit through the warm season, and it reaches a larger mature size than compact selections like 'B-17', so give it more room in the landscape. Grow in full sun and well-drained fertile soil; the shrub takes light pruning well and can be shaped into a dense hedge or specimen. Fruit is thin-skinned, juicy, and highly perishable once ripe, so harvest and refrigerate or process it within a day or two. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mantanghong Watermelon Radish
description: Sow this Chinese beauty-heart radish in summer or early fall, as it needs cool weather and shortening days to develop its large, mild roots. Direct sow a half inch deep and thin seedlings to 3 to 4 inches apart to give the 3 inch round roots room to swell, some reaching up to a pound. The greenish-white exterior hides a vivid fuchsia interior that is crisp and mildly sweet. Keep the soil evenly moist for tender roots and harvest before hard freezes. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Mantovano Fennel (Italian Heirloom Florence Fennel)
description: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil, since fennel resents root disturbance; Mantovano is a traditional Italian heirloom named for the Mantua region, valued for its large, flattened, very white bulbs and a sweeter, more assertively anise-forward flavor than many other Florence fennel strains. It matures earlier than most bulbing fennel and has an unusual habit of continuing to bulk up in the ground for weeks after reaching harvest size rather than splitting or turning woody, which gives growers real flexibility in harvest timing. Mound soil lightly around the base as the bulb swells to keep it pale, and use young bulbs raw in salads or slice and roast larger ones for a milder, caramelized flavor. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Manzanilla Olive (Spanish Table Olive Standard, Green Martini Olive, Seville Table Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Manzanilla is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for green table olives in October when fully sized but still green; harvest for black table olives in November–December when fully ripe; home-cured Manzanilla olives require brine treatment for 6–12 months to remove bitter oleuropein before eating. Manzanilla (meaning 'little apple' in Spanish, for the round fruit shape) is the dominant commercial table olive variety in the world — the variety behind the iconic green olives stuffed with pimentos found in cocktail jars and martini glasses throughout the Western world, and a major component of Spanish, American, and Mexican table olive production. Its origin is in the Seville region of Spain (particularly the province of Huelva), where it has been the foundation of the Spanish table olive trade since the 1800s, and it was introduced to California (where it is called 'Manzanillo') in the 19th century with California's Spanish-mission heritage, becoming established in the central California olive-growing regions (Fresno, Madera counties) and eventually as the dominant commercial table olive variety in the United States. The olives are medium-sized, round to slightly oblate, with firm, meaty flesh and a relatively small pit that makes them ideal for stuffing — the characteristic American 'green olive' of commercial production is almost always a Manzanilla cured at the green stage. The trees are medium-sized (15–25 feet), productive, and adapted to a wide range of California and Gulf South conditions with adequate drainage and minimal rainfall during the ripening period. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Manzanillo Olive (Classic Spanish Table Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Manzanillo is a classic Spanish olive cultivar and the most widely grown table olive variety in the world, valued for its large, plump, meaty fruit with a favorable flesh-to-pit ratio that makes it the standard choice for brine-cured green and black table olives found in grocery stores worldwide. The tree bears heavily and reliably, and while it can also be pressed for oil, its primary use and reputation is as a table olive. Harvest green in fall for green-cured olives, or let fruit ripen to black for black-cured olives, then cure in brine or lye solution for several weeks to months to remove natural bitterness before eating; olives are inedible straight off the tree. The tree grows to a more traditional, larger size than modern compact cultivars, so allow ample space. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Manzano Banana (Apple Banana, Finger Banana)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Manzano banana (also called Apple Banana, Finger Banana, or 'Bocadillo' in Colombia) is a widely grown short-fruited banana popular throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, producing plump, stubby fruits (3–5 inches long, broader in proportion than Cavendish) with a distinctive, complex flavor reminiscent of strawberry and apple when fully ripe — a significantly more aromatic and interesting eating experience than a standard Cavendish. The fruits turn bright yellow and then develop black skin patches as they ripen, and the flesh remains firm even when sweet and fully ripe, giving them better shelf life than many banana types. Manzano banana plants are more compact than Cavendish (8–12 feet versus 12–20 feet) making them practical for smaller yards. Manzano is moderately susceptible to Black Sigatoka and should be grown in well-drained, well-fertilized conditions with regular irrigation; it thrives in Gulf Coast conditions (zones 9b–11) but pseudostems are killed by even brief freezes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Manzano Pepper (Rocoto)
description: Start indoors early and transplant after all frost danger has passed; Capsicum pubescens is a unique pepper species easily identified by its distinctive purple flowers, hairy leaves and stems, and black seeds — features shared by no other cultivated Capsicum. The apple-shaped (manzano = apple in Spanish) fruits ripen from green to red, orange, or yellow and contain extremely hot flesh (100,000–200,000 SHU) with a thick, fruity wall — quite different from the thin, papery walls of most hot peppers. In Peru and Bolivia, rocoto is used whole to make rocoto relleno (stuffed pepper), as the thick walls hold up to cooking. Unlike other Capsicum species, it tolerates light frost and can survive as a perennial in mild climates. The black seeds are distinctive in culinary use. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Maqui (Chilean Wineberry, Maqui Berry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui berry is a Chilean native shrub prized for its small, intensely purple-black berries with the highest reported anthocyanin content of any known berry — significantly higher than acai, blueberries, or pomegranates, giving it extraordinary antioxidant properties. The berries have a pleasant sweet-tart flavor with herbal overtones; they are eaten fresh, made into juice, jams, and wine, and used extensively in Mapuche traditional medicine. It grows naturally in the coastal and Andean ranges of Chile and Argentina, tolerating mild frost, and adapts to a Mediterranean climate with dry summers. An emerging superfood crop with increasing commercial cultivation in Chile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mara des Bois Strawberry (French Day-Neutral Wild-Flavored Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in loose, well-drained soil, and remove flowers for the first few weeks to allow the compact, day-neutral plants to establish a strong root system before continuous fruiting begins through summer and into fall. Mara des Bois was developed in France in the early 1990s by combining garden strawberry lines with genetics from the wild alpine strawberry, giving it a fruity, perfumed aroma reminiscent of wild strawberries that sets it apart from typical supermarket varieties. The berries are small to medium, soft, and highly aromatic rather than large and firm, which makes them a favorite of chefs and farmers-market growers but less suited to long-distance shipping. Because it is day-neutral, Mara des Bois produces a steady trickle of fruit from late spring through fall frost rather than one concentrated June crop. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Maradol Papaya (Mexican Papaya, Giant Papaya)
description: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Maradol is the dominant commercial papaya of Mexico and the variety most commonly sold in American supermarkets, producing very large, oblong fruits (3–8 pounds, sometimes to 10 pounds) with distinctive salmon-red to deep orange flesh, moderate to high sweetness, and a mild, pleasant, non-musky flavor that appeals to consumers who find tropical Solo papayas too strongly flavored. The skin turns from green to yellow-orange at ripeness, with clear indicator spots appearing near the stem. 'Maradol' plants are dioecious (separate male and female plants) which means planting multiple trees is necessary to ensure fruiting; approximately one-third of seedlings are male. The tall plants (10–18 feet under optimal conditions) bear heavily from the main trunk, with fruits maturing in dense clusters below the umbrella of large leaves. Originally developed in Cuba, 'Maradol' is now the main papaya in Mexico's Veracruz and Tabasco production regions and thrives in Gulf Coast conditions — hot humid summers, mild winters, and fertile lowland soils of zone 9b–11. Matures in 270–365 days from seed.

name: Maragogype Coffee (Elephant Bean)
description: A natural giant-leaved mutation discovered in Brazil, grown by home coffee enthusiasts mainly as a novelty for its unusually large leaves, cherries, and beans, which are roughly double the size of standard Arabica. It is lower-yielding and slower to bear than compact modern cultivars, so patience is required before the first harvest. Grow in bright, dappled shade with rich, acidic, well-drained potting mix, and protect from any temperature below 50F. Its dramatic size makes it a popular specimen plant in home greenhouses and sunrooms even where fruit production is modest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Marang (Johey Oak, Green Pedalai, Tarap)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, rich, consistently moist, well-drained tropical soil; marang (Artocarpus odoratissimus) is a close relative of breadfruit and jackfruit, native to Borneo and Mindanao, producing rounded, yellow-green fruits about the size of a small jackfruit with an extremely sweet, creamy white flesh surrounding large, edible seeds — many who have tasted it rank it among the finest tropical fruits, with a rich, sweet, almost vanilla-custard flavor with a fragrant aroma. The seeds are also edible when cooked (roasted, boiled, or ground) and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor. Strictly tropical and not tolerant of any frost; best suited for south Florida and Hawaii collections and food-forest enthusiasts in zone 11+. Less well-known outside Southeast Asia but increasingly available from specialty nurseries. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marathon Broccoli (Cold-Tolerant Overwintering Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer for a fall and winter crop, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Marathon is a broccoli hybrid recognized industry-wide for exceptional cold tolerance, holding up through hard frosts and cold snaps that would damage less hardy varieties while continuing to develop a large, dense, tightly beaded blue-green head. This cold hardiness makes it especially well suited to the Gulf South's mild winter growing window, where it can be grown as a true overwintering crop instead of racing to beat summer heat. After the main head is harvested, the plant produces a strong flush of side shoots for continued picking. Cut heads while the buds are still tight, before any yellow flower color shows. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Marathon Mandarin (Seedless UF/IFAS Daisy x Kishu Mandarin Hybrid)
description: Marathon is a modern University of Florida mandarin release, a cross of Daisy mandarin and Seedless Kishu, valued for fruit that is completely seedless under any pollination conditions, easy to peel, and able to hold on the tree from October into January without becoming puffy or dry. It shows useful tolerance to citrus greening (HLB), an increasing concern for dooryard citrus. Cold hardiness is typical of standard mandarins rather than the exceptional range of satsuma or the UGA Frost series citrus, so plant in a warm microclimate and protect during hard freezes. Its parentage and extended on-tree storage distinguish it from the older Florida mandarin hybrids such as Sunburst, Robinson, Lee, and Nova already grown on the Gulf Coast. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Maraval Chestnut (French Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Maraval is a European x Japanese hybrid chestnut from the same French breeding program that produced Marigoule and Marsol, grown for its large, glossy nuts and reasonably vigorous growth on a tree that tolerates ink disease better than pure European chestnut. It buds and flowers a little later than some sibling selections, which can help nuts escape early-season frost in marginal sites. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby to ensure a full nut set. Harvest burs as they split and fall in early autumn, and collect promptly since fallen nuts spoil quickly on the ground. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Maraş Pepper (Kahramanmaraş Turkish Biber)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maraş Pepper is a landrace long grown around Kahramanmaraş in southeastern Turkey, where sun-dried, coarsely crushed pods become the fragrant, oil-glossed red pepper flake known as pul biber. The 3–4 inch, moderately wrinkled pods ripen to a deep brick red and carry a mild-to-moderate heat, generally around 4,000–8,000 Scoville units, with a rich, slightly sweet, faintly smoky flavor distinct from the tangier Aleppo pepper it is often compared to. Traditionally pods are partially sun-dried, seeded, and crushed while still a little moist, which is what gives Maraş flakes their characteristic dark color and oily texture rather than the bone-dry look of standard chili flakes. A single productive plant can supply a household's pepper flakes for a year; harvest fully red pods and dry in a low oven or dehydrator if humid outdoor air prevents full sun-drying. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Marblehead Squash (Yakima Marblehead)
description: Marblehead was introduced in 1896 out of Massachusetts as a selection valued for the stony hardness of its smooth grey-green rind, a trait that earned it the name and made it one of the longest-storing winter squashes of its era. Sow in enriched hills and let the vigorous vine sprawl over six to eight feet, watering steadily through the growing season to size up the large, rounded fruit. The deep orange flesh is fine-grained and flavorful, holding up well in soups and baked dishes even after months of storage. Because the shell is so hard, cure fruit for two to three weeks in a warm spot before moving it to a cool, dry root cellar or pantry, where it can keep considerably longer than thinner-skinned squash. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Marbrite Fig (White-Fleshed Green-Skinned Italian Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Marbrite is an Italian fig cultivar bearing medium-sized figs with pale green to yellow-green skin and sweet, translucent amber to white flesh, a lighter-colored departure from the deep pink and red interiors of Gulf Coast standards like Celeste and Brown Turkey. It typically produces two crops in warm climates: a smaller breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer, followed by a larger main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Figs fruit on both second-year wood and current-season growth, so avoid heavy winter pruning, which removes the breba crop; light shaping after the main harvest is sufficient. Trees are vigorous and productive once established and rarely need fertilizer, though a layer of mulch over the root zone helps in zone 7-8 where occasional hard freezes can damage unprotected roots. Harvest when fruit softens and the neck bends over, since figs do not ripen further once picked. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Marcona Almond (Spanish Queen of Almonds, Round Blanched Premium Almond)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile soil (calcareous or sandy loam preferred) in full sun; Marcona requires a companion pollenizer variety; harvest in late summer when hulls begin to split; the round, flat kernels are best roasted in olive oil and sea salt in the traditional Spanish preparation — the rich, buttery texture of roasted Marcona is distinctly different from any California variety. Marcona is a Spanish almond variety traditionally grown along the eastern Mediterranean coast of Spain (the Valencian Community and Murcia region) that has become known internationally as the 'queen of almonds' for its extraordinarily rich, buttery flavor and distinctive round, flat shape that makes it immediately recognizable on a charcuterie board or tapas spread. The flavor difference between Marcona and California varieties (Nonpareil, Mission, Carmel) is significant and immediately apparent to tasters: Marcona has a much higher fat content and a softer, more buttery texture with a sweeter, more intensely almond-flavored profile — often described as having hints of marzipan and fresh sweetness that California varieties cannot replicate. The traditional preparation — blanched (skin removed), roasted in olive oil, and salted — is the standard presentation in Spanish tapas and increasingly common in American specialty food and charcuterie culture. Marcona's very low chill requirement (200–300 hours) makes it the almond most adapted to warm-winter zones 8–10 where standard California varieties may also grow, but Marcona's flavor sets it apart for culinary use. Not as productive as California commercial varieties in California growing conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Marconi Pepper (Classic Sweet Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75-80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Marconi is a classic Italian heirloom sweet pepper producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruit that ripens from green to red, prized for a sweet, mild flavor and a thin flesh that chars and caramelizes quickly when roasted or fried, much like its well-known relative Corno di Toro. It is a traditional variety in Italian-American gardens, used roasted for antipasto, sautéed in olive oil, or stuffed. The vigorous, productive plants bear over a long season through summer heat; harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for maximum sweetness, and pick regularly to keep plants producing. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Marconi Red Pepper
description: This classic Italian heirloom produces long, slender six-to-eight-inch peppers with thin skin, tender flesh, and sweet mild flavor, excellent roasted or grilled. Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm. Support the plants as the heavy fruits develop. Harvest green for a milder taste, or let the peppers ripen to deep red for their fullest sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Marconi Red Sweet Pepper (Italian Frying Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Marconi is productive and begins bearing early for a long sweet pepper; the fruits can be harvested green or left to ripen fully red for the sweetest, richest flavor. Marconi Red is an Italian heirloom sweet frying pepper producing long, tapering, deeply lobed, 6–8 inch fruits that ripen from green to brilliant red; unlike blocky bell peppers, Marconi has thin, tender walls with very sweet, rich, slightly smoky pepper flavor that intensifies dramatically when fried in olive oil or roasted over a flame. Used throughout Italian and Mediterranean cooking as the classic 'frying pepper' for peperonata, antipasto, and pan-fried pepper dishes. The thin walls mean the fruits cook quickly and evenly without becoming tough; they also need minimal or no skin removal after roasting. Marconi is one of several related Italian frying pepper varieties (along with Corno di Toro and Jimmy Nardello) that together represent the tradition of Italian long sweet peppers, each with slightly different fruit shape, texture, and flavor profile. Very productive plants set fruit continuously through summer. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Marechal Foch Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American Red Wine Grape)
description: This early-ripening French-American hybrid was bred by Eugene Kuhlmann and produces small, dark clusters used for light, fruity red wines with an earthy, sometimes smoky character. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter lows that damage most vinifera, and has long been a mainstay of northeastern and Canadian vineyards. Because it fruits heavily and buds early, growers should balance crop load through cluster thinning and protect young growth from late spring frosts. Prune to a cane system and expect reliable production once the vine is established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Marfax Bean
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, spacing 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; Marfax germinates quickly in warm soil and the compact bush plants require no staking or support. Marfax is a New England heirloom bush dry bean with attractive tan-and-brown mottled seeds that are smaller and rounder than kidney-type beans and have a creamy, buttery texture when cooked with a mild, nutty flavor excellent in baked beans, soups, and salads. Allow pods to fully mature and begin to yellow and rattle before harvesting; if a wet spell threatens, pull plants and hang them under cover to finish drying. Marfax stores well for a year or more when dried thoroughly and kept in an airtight container at room temperature. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Marge Elderberry
description: Marge is a prolific European elderberry prized for heavy yields of dark berries used in syrups, jams, and wine. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil and keep it well watered, as elderberries are shallow-rooted and thirsty. Fruit set improves dramatically with a second, different elderberry variety planted nearby for cross-pollination. Prune out the oldest canes each late winter to keep the plant vigorous and productive. Always cook the berries before eating, since raw fruit and other plant parts can cause stomach upset. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Marglobe Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes and stake plants early. Marglobe, introduced by the USDA in 1925 and awarded the first All-America Selections Gold Medal, was the standard American home and market tomato for much of the twentieth century; bred at the Arlington, Virginia USDA experiment station to resist Fusarium wilt and nailhead rust, it was the first widely successful disease-resistant tomato and allowed commercial tomato production to expand dramatically into areas where disease pressure had previously made growing difficult. The fruits are medium-sized (6–8 oz), round to slightly globe-shaped, smooth, bright red, and of solid, crack-resistant construction with a firm skin and classic tomato flavor; Marglobe Supreme is a later improved selection. Grows as an indeterminate vine; productive over a long season and well-suited to home gardens, canning, and fresh market. Matures in 73–80 days from transplant.

name: Maria's Joy Pawpaw (Award-Winning Large Late-Season Lehman Selection)
description: Maria's Joy is a Davis x Prolific cross bred by noted pawpaw breeder Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana, and named in tribute to a friend and mentor; it produces some of the largest fruit of any named pawpaw cultivar, with medium-to-large, kidney-shaped fruit weighing 8-14 ounces and sometimes reaching a full pound. The yellow flesh is exceptionally sweet and flavorful, often described as mango-pineapple with notes of bubblegum, and the cultivar won the Ohio Pawpaw Festival's Biggest Pawpaw Contest in 2012. Maria's Joy ripens late in the pawpaw season, typically late September into October, and is notably cold-hardy, tolerating temperatures to about -20°F once dormant. Plant at least two genetically distinct named cultivars for reliable cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mariachi Pepper (AAS-Winning Mild Fruity Pepper with Multicolored Cluster Fruits)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at ivory-yellow for mild flavor or let ripen to red for maximum sweetness. Mariachi Pepper is a 2006 All-America Selections winner in the vegetable category, developed for its extraordinary visual display of multicolored fruits at different ripeness stages and its mildly spiced fruity flavor that makes it accessible to a wide range of palates. The name 'Mariachi' evokes the colorful, festive nature of the plant at peak production, when ivory, yellow, orange, and red fruits appear simultaneously in clusters on the same compact plant — the visual effect is immediately striking. Unlike standard bell pepper development where fruit transitions from green to fully ripe (green→red, green→yellow, etc.), Mariachi's fruit transition from ivory cream through progressive warm tones to red creates a more complex visual palette on the plant. The heat level of Mariachi is technically mild rather than sweet — at 500–600 SHU (Scoville Heat Units), it is substantially less hot than a jalapeño (2,500–8,000 SHU) but not as completely heat-free as a standard bell pepper. This small amount of heat adds a fruity warmth that enhances the flavor without causing heat discomfort for most people, making Mariachi useful in both sweet pepper contexts (fresh eating, salads) and mild chili contexts (salsas, roasting, stuffed preparations). The compact plant habit (24–30 inches) and prolific production of Mariachi's clusters make it an excellent candidate for container growing on patios and decks where the ornamental and culinary value combine effectively. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Marianna's Peace Tomato (Czechoslovakian Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost risk has passed. Marianna's Peace is a Czechoslovakian family heirloom carried to the United States after World War II and later introduced commercially in honor of the woman whose story gave the variety its name. The potato-leaved, indeterminate vines produce large pink beefsteak fruit with a rich, well-balanced sweet flavor and relatively few seeds. Give it sturdy staking and a full growing season, as the heavy fruit and long maturity window reward patient care. Matures in 85–90 days from transplant.

name: Maridonne Chestnut (INRA Ink-Disease-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Maridonne was bred by French chestnut researchers as a European-Japanese hybrid combining large, high-quality nuts with strong resistance to Phytophthora ink disease, a root and collar rot that thrives in the heavy, wet soils common across much of the Gulf South. It flowers in midseason and is commonly paired with other European-Japanese hybrid cultivars for cross-pollination, since chestnuts rarely set a full crop without a compatible partner nearby. Grow it in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and improve drainage on heavier clay sites to further reduce ink disease pressure. Harvest nuts from the ground as burrs split in autumn, and cure briefly before eating to allow the starches to convert to sugars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marigoule Chestnut (Disease-Resistant European-Japanese Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. Bred in France from a cross of European and Japanese chestnut, Marigoule combines good resistance to chestnut blight and ink disease with large, easy-to-peel nuts and a precocious habit, often bearing within a few years of planting. It has become a popular choice in North American chestnut orchards specifically because its hybrid vigor and disease tolerance let it thrive where the straight American chestnut has been devastated by blight. The tree is moderately vigorous and more compact than a full-sized American chestnut, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or food forest planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marina di Chioggia Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost, or start 3–4 weeks early indoors; plant in hills of 2–3 seeds per mound spaced 5–6 feet apart and thin to the strongest plant. Marina di Chioggia is a prized Italian heirloom winter squash from the Chioggia lagoon region, producing large 8–15 pound fruits with deeply ridged, blue-green skin covered in grey-green bumps and warts, and brilliant orange flesh that is dense, sweet, nutty, and nearly stringless — among the finest-flavored winter squashes.
