Cure fruits for 2 weeks in a warm, dry location after harvest to harden the skin and concentrate the sugars; properly cured fruits store for 4–6 months. The large vines need ample space; train them onto a trellis or let them sprawl in open ground. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Marino Cilantro (Organic Slow-Bolt Cilantro)
description: Marino is an organic cilantro selection bred for slow bolting and a growth habit close to the widely grown Santo strain, but with a slightly spicier, more peppery edge to the leaf flavor than standard cilantro. Plants stay in the leafy stage longer before sending up flower stalks, which stretches the harvest window during the cool months when cilantro grows best in zone 9. Direct sow into the bed rather than transplanting, since the taproot is easily damaged, and succession sow every few weeks through fall and winter for a steady supply. Once plants do bolt, leave a few to flower and set seed, which can be harvested and used whole or ground as coriander spice. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Marion Blackberry (Marionberry)
description: Marion is the trailing blackberry that put Oregon berry breeding on the map, released in 1956 from a 1945 USDA cross of 'Chehalem' and 'Olallie' and named for the county where it was first field-trialed. Its long, thorny canes need a sturdy trellis but reward the extra work with small, deeply complex, wine-toned berries prized by processors and bakers well above most modern thornless cultivars. Marion's superior flavor became the benchmark that later thornless USDA-ARS releases like Black Diamond, Black Pearl, and Nightfall were bred to approach without the thorns. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and train the current season's primocanes onto the wires for next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Marion Tomato (NC State Southern-Adapted Disease-Resistant Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50°F, staking or caging the compact determinate plants as fruit sets. Marion was bred at North Carolina State University and released for Southern gardens, combining Fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot resistance with reliable fruit set under the hot, humid conditions that cause many slicing tomatoes to falter. The medium-sized, deep-red fruit has firm flesh and balanced flavor well suited to fresh eating and canning. Because it sets a concentrated main crop, it remains a dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want an early, disease-resistant harvest before peak summer heat shuts down fruit set. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Marionberry
description: Marionberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (Chehalem x Olallie) developed by Oregon State University and is the most widely grown blackberry in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its deep, complex, slightly tart flavor. The thorny, vigorous canes must be trained along a two-wire trellis; weave new primocanes along the lower wire during the summer and tie them to the upper wire the following spring. After the mid-summer harvest, remove all fruited floricanes at the base and train the new primocanes into their place. Marionberries are sensitive to freezes below about 10°F; in colder areas, protect canes over winter. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Maris Piper Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in deep, loose, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing rows generously since this vigorous variety produces a heavy underground spread. Maris Piper was bred in Britain in the 1960s and became the standard chip-shop and baking potato across the UK, prized for its high dry-matter content, floury texture, and thin cream-colored skin that crisps well when fried. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to prevent tuber greening, and expect a longer season than early varieties before the vines die back and tubers can be lifted for storage. Choose this cultivar over a general baking potato when a reliably fluffy, low-moisture interior for chips, roasting, and baking is the priority. Matures in 85–110 days from transplant.

name: Marjoram
description: Sweet marjoram is a Mediterranean culinary herb with a warm, gently spicy flavor softer than its relative oregano. Surface sow the fine seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost, pressing it into the mix and keeping it warm and lightly moist. Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants around ten inches apart. Grown as a tender perennial, it is best treated as an annual in cold climates or potted up to overwinter indoors. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Marketmore 70 Cucumber
description: Marketmore 70 was bred by Henry Munger at Cornell University as an early strain in the Marketmore breeding line, preceding the widely grown 1976 release Marketmore 76, which improved on it with a broader disease-resistance package. It set the vining, productive growth habit later carried forward by its successors: vigorous vines bearing straight, dark green, cylindrical slicing cucumbers with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp white flesh. Grow it on a trellis or fence where possible, since vertical training improves airflow and keeps fruit straighter and easier to pick. Harvest at 7-8 inches while still firm and uniformly dark green, checking vines daily during peak production since oversized fruit turns the plant's energy away from setting new cucumbers. Matures in 62–70 days from seed.

name: Marketmore 76 Cucumber
description: Direct sow 3–4 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, then thin to the 2 strongest seedlings; trellis to maximize air circulation and fruit quality. Marketmore 76 is the Cornell University-developed standard slicing cucumber, bred for disease resistance to multiple fungal and viral pathogens including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, and powdery mildew — resistance that makes it especially valuable in humid Southern gardens. The smooth, dark-green fruits are 8–9 inches long with crisp, bitter-free flesh and very small seed cavity. Consistent, even watering is the most critical cultural practice — irregular moisture leads to bitter-tasting fruits. Harvest daily when fruits reach full size before they yellow. Matures in 67–75 days from seed.

name: Marketmore 80 Cucumber (Disease-Resistant Standard Slicing Cucumber)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Marketmore 80 is a Cornell University slicing cucumber introduction that has become one of the most widely grown home garden cucumbers in America — producing straight, cylindrical, 8–9 inch, deep-green cucumbers with excellent fresh-eating flavor, thin skin, and small seed cavities. The significant disease resistance package — scab, cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), and angular leaf spot resistance — makes Marketmore 80 substantially more reliable in Gulf South gardens where summer humidity drives disease pressure. The 'Marketmore' series from Cornell represents a succession of improvements beginning with the original Marketmore in the 1960s; Marketmore 80 was selected for improved scab resistance and CMV tolerance critical for humid-climate production. The non-bitter fruits have classic cucumber flavor and good crispness. Plants are indeterminate vines that perform best on a trellis or fence where air circulation reduces disease and fruits hang straight. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring season (March–May) and fall season (August–October) — summer heat causes reduced fruiting and increased disease. Succession sowing every 2–3 weeks through spring extends the harvest window. Harvest fruits at 6–9 inches for best flavor; over-mature cucumbers become bitter and seeds harden. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Marketmore Cucumber
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost risk has passed, in hills of 3–4 seeds thinned to 2, or in rows 12 inches apart against a trellis; cucumbers germinate quickly in warm soil and grow fast — do not plant in cold ground. Marketmore 76 was developed at Cornell University and released in 1976 as an improvement on the original Marketmore line, and for decades it has been the benchmark slicing cucumber for home gardeners: a vigorous, disease-resistant vine producing straight, dark green, 8–9 inch fruits with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp, mild white flesh that stays productive over a long harvest window. The variety carries resistance to cucumber mosaic virus, angular leaf spot, powdery mildew, and scab. Pick fruits when uniformly dark green and firm, before any yellowing begins, to encourage continued production; cucumbers left on the vine too long signal the plant to stop setting new fruit. Matures in 67–75 days from seed.

name: Marlhac Chestnut (French Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Marlhac is another member of the French hybrid chestnut group that includes Marigoule and Marsol, selected for a productive, disease-tolerant tree bearing good-sized nuts suited to the fresh and processing chestnut markets. Like its sibling cultivars it carries meaningful resistance to chestnut blight and improved tolerance of Phytophthora ink disease compared with pure European chestnut. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and a genetically distinct pollenizer, and expect burs to ripen and split in early to mid autumn. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marquette Grape (Extreme Cold-Hardy Red Wine Grape)
description: Marquette is a University of Minnesota-bred red wine grape descended in part from Pinot Noir, valued for surviving winter lows near -30°F with only minor cane damage. Vines are vigorous and require an early, thorough trellis training program along with cluster thinning to manage heavy fruit set. The grapes produce a deeply colored, medium-bodied red wine with notes of black cherry, black pepper, and spice, and the variety shows good resistance to downy mildew though it can be prone to black rot in humid seasons. Site vines with good air circulation and avoid low frost pockets to protect the early-breaking buds from late spring freezes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Marquis Wheat (Historic Canadian Hard Red Spring Wheat)
description: Marquis was bred by a Canadian agronomist from a Red Fife and Hard Red Calcutta cross, and released around 1909-1910 as a spring wheat that matured one to two weeks earlier than Red Fife while keeping its outstanding bread-baking strength. That earlier ripening let wheat farming push much further north and west across the Canadian Prairies and the U.S. Northern Plains, and by 1920 Marquis accounted for the great majority of hard red spring wheat grown on the continent. Sow it in early spring into a firm, fertile seedbed; it performs best where summers are not too long or humid, ripening ahead of the worst rust and heat pressure. Because it was never patented, home millers and small grain growers can still source and replant true Marquis seed today as a living piece of agricultural history. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Marron Medlar (Large Chestnut-Flavored Heirloom Medlar)
description: Marron takes its name from the French word for chestnut, a nod to the deep russet-brown color and rich, nutty-sweet character its bletted flesh develops, setting it apart from sharper, more austere medlar selections. Like all medlar, the fruit is rock-hard and unpalatable when picked and must be left on the tree until after hard frost, or stored several weeks in a cool spot, until it softens, browns, and takes on the soft, spiced, wine-and-date flavor typical of bletted medlar. The tree keeps the same small, picturesquely gnarled habit and showy white spring flowers common to the species, making it as much an ornamental specimen as a fruiting one. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun, prune only lightly to remove damaged or crossing wood, and harvest once the calyx end has fully opened and fruit color has deepened in fall. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Marrowfat Bean (White Egg Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained soil after frost danger passes; the sturdy bush plants carry four-inch pods that need no support. Marrowfat, also known as the White Egg bean for the plump, egg-shaped form of its seed, is a mid-1800s New England baking bean recognized by Slow Food USA's Ark of Taste for its creamy texture and rich, almost bacon-like savoriness when cooked. It was once a mainstay of the region's baked-bean tradition before falling out of common cultivation, and is now kept alive mainly by small seed savers and heirloom specialists. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before shelling, and store the beans in a cool, airtight container for baking and soups through winter. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Mars Grape (Disease-Resistant Southern Seedless Blue Grape)
description: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Mars was bred at the University of Arkansas specifically for good disease resistance and reliable performance in the warm, humid Southern climates where many other seedless table grapes struggle with fungal disease pressure, combining that practical resilience with sweet, blue-black, seedless berries carrying a mild, classic grape flavor. The compact, manageable vine is well suited to home garden trellises and arbors, and its combination of hardiness and disease tolerance has made it one of the more dependable seedless grape choices for Southern home gardeners. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter to control vigor, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mars Seedless Grape (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blue Table Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Bred at the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in the 1970s, Mars combines good disease resistance with genuinely seedless, blue-black berries and a sweet, fruity, slip-skin flavor reminiscent of Concord but milder. Its compact vine habit and strong resistance to common grape diseases make it far easier to grow without a heavy spray program than European wine grapes, especially in humid climates. Prune hard each winter to a few renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Marseillais Basil
description: Marseillais is a traditional dwarf French basil that packs classic, intensely essence-of-basil flavor into a tight, mounded 8-10 inch plant, making it one of the most space-efficient basils for a kitchen windowsill or small container. Its leaves are proportionately large for such a compact plant, and the dense branching habit means frequent light harvesting keeps it productive for months rather than bolting quickly like larger basils. Pinch the growing tips regularly once the plant reaches 4-6 inches to encourage the bushy, rounded form that gives this cultivar its French market-garden reputation. Choose it over Genovese-type basils when growing space is limited but full basil flavor is still the goal. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Marsellesa Coffee
description: Selected by the French agricultural research center CIRAD from Sarchimor lineage, Marsellesa is a pure-line, non-hybrid rust-resistant cultivar that has been widely distributed across Nicaragua, Honduras, and other Central American coffee regions as a more affordable, seed-saveable alternative to F1 hybrids. Because it breeds true from seed, smallholders can maintain their own planting stock without repurchasing hybrid seed each generation, a significant practical advantage over cultivars like Ruiru 11 or Centroamericano. Cup quality is generally considered good for a rust-resistant selection when grown at adequate elevation. Provide the same filtered shade, steady moisture, and rich acidic soil that other Sarchimor-derived cultivars need. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Marsh Grapefruit (Seedless White Grapefruit, Marsh Seedless)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Marsh grapefruit (introduced commercially around 1860 from a seedling found in Florida) is the foundational white grapefruit of the citrus industry — virtually all seedless white grapefruits sold commercially today are Marsh or descended from it. The large, round, pale-yellow fruits (4–5 inches diameter) are nearly or completely seedless (a major practical advantage over older seedy varieties like Duncan), with pale-cream to light-yellow flesh, balanced sweet-tart grapefruit flavor, and abundant juice. The flavor is the benchmark classic grapefruit flavor — moderately tart with characteristic bitterness from naringin — excellent eaten fresh (halved and sectioned with a serrated spoon), juiced, or used in salads and cocktails. The large tree (15–20 feet when mature, larger on vigorous rootstocks) is cold-hardier than many citrus and can tolerate brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established. Marsh grapefruit is the parent of most modern grapefruit varieties, including Ruby Red (a bud sport of Marsh) and Thompson Pink. Ripens November through May in Florida; the fruits hold on the tree exceptionally well, improving in flavor through winter. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marsh Mallow
description: Marsh mallow is a tall perennial herb with soft gray-green foliage and pale pink flowers, long valued for its soothing roots and leaves. The seed germinates best after a cold period, so sow outdoors in fall or cold-stratify before a spring sowing. Give it full sun and consistently moist soil, reflecting its natural home in damp meadows and marshy ground. Plants may be slow the first year but form deep roots that can be harvested from established clumps. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Marsh Woundwort
description: Stachys palustris is a circumboreal mint-family perennial of wet meadows, ditch banks, and pond margins, bearing soft, hairy, nettle-shaped leaves (without any sting) and whorled spikes of dusky pink-purple flowers through summer. Old herbals rank fresh-crushed marsh woundwort leaves among the most effective traditional first-aid poultices for stopping bleeding and speeding the healing of cuts and wounds, a reputation some herbalists held in even higher regard than betony. The slender, knobby white tubers are edible and related in flavor to the cultivated Chinese artichoke, though smaller and more fibrous. Plant in reliably moist to wet, full-sun soil; the running rhizomes spread readily in favorable conditions, so give it room or a barrier in smaller gardens. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Marsh Yellowcress (Bog Yellowcress)
description: Direct sow onto exposed wet mud or very moist, fertile, high-organic-matter soil near pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens from a few weeks before last frost through late summer; marsh yellowcress is a watercress relative that germinates readily on bare damp ground and needs constant moisture, not standing shade. This fast-growing native annual to short-lived perennial forms rosettes of glossy, deeply lobed leaves with a mild, peppery, watercress-like bite that is best harvested young, before the small four-petaled yellow flowers and narrow seed pods appear on branching stems. It thrives on disturbed, muddy, nutrient-rich ground such as pond margins, streambanks, and seasonally flooded low spots where few other food crops will grow, self-sows readily, and can be treated as a cut-and-come-again green through a moist summer. Harvest leaves regularly to delay bolting and keep the planting from spreading beyond the intended wet area. Matures in 35–55 days from seed.

name: Marshmallow
description: Scarify or soak seed overnight before sowing 1/4 in deep; marshmallow appreciates consistent moisture, particularly during its establishment period. Plant in deep, moderately moist soil as the tap root grows substantial in mature plants. Harvest leaves and flowers in summer for use in soothing teas and poultices; the fleshy root is the most mucilaginous part and is best dug in the plant's second or third autumn. The dried root can be sliced, powdered, or made into a cold-water infusion to extract its slippery mucilage for throat-coat and digestive preparations. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Marshmallow Pawpaw (Sweetest of the Kentucky Freestone Pawpaws)
description: Marshmallow is a named freestone pawpaw discovered on the same late-1800s Richmond, Kentucky orchard as its siblings Cantaloupe and Honeydew, and released through England's Orchard by pawpaw enthusiast Woody Walker. Of the three related freestone selections, Marshmallow is described as the sweetest, with plump, well-formed, medium-sized fruit (roughly 7-9 ounces) and a light, chiffon-to-custard textured flesh that carries a tropical melon flavor with sweet, honeyed undertones. As with its siblings, the fruit lacks a fibrous seed sack, so seeds lift out cleanly, and it freezes exceptionally well. Marshmallow ripens in the early part of the pawpaw season; harvest when the fruit yields to gentle pressure and eat or process promptly since pawpaws are highly perishable. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Marsol Chestnut (Vigorous French Hybrid, Ink Disease and Rust Tolerant)
description: Marsol, also recorded as Maraval 07, is an open-pollinated selection from France's INRA chestnut breeding program at Lalevade-d'Ardeche, part of the same European x Japanese hybrid family that produced Marigoule, Maridonne, and Precoce Migoule. It is prized above all for its vigor and outstanding graft compatibility, which has made it a leading rootstock choice, more vigorous than the related Maraval and on par with Bouche de Betizac and Comballe, but it also bears attractive, large reddish nuts, averaging roughly 26 grams each, with good flavor and easy peeling. As a sativa x crenata hybrid, Marsol carries meaningful resistance to chestnut blight and chestnut rust, and its roots show some tolerance of ink disease (Phytophthora), a soil-borne pathogen that has damaged pure European chestnut plantings. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut cultivar nearby for a full nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Martian Jewels Sweet Corn
description: Direct sow this open-pollinated corn in warm soil, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good wind pollination. The purple stalks and husks yield ears with white kernels and a traditional, slightly-less-sweet corn flavor, rich in anthocyanins. Give plants full sun, fertile soil, and steady moisture, especially during tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when the silks brown and the kernels are plump and milky for the best eating. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Martin Pawpaw
description: Martin originated in Springfield, Ohio and is recorded in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar table as a large-fruited selection with yellow flesh of superior eating quality, noted specifically for withstanding cold well. That documented cold tolerance makes it of particular interest to growers at the northern edge of pawpaw hardiness in zone 4b-5 who have struggled with dieback or crop loss on cultivars bred mainly for the Ohio Valley and points south. As with other historic Ohio-region selections it has not gone through the formal multi-state disease and yield trials that the modern KSU-released cultivars have, so it is best planted as a cold-hardy diversity addition to an orchard rather than the sole named cultivar. Mulch young trees well and provide winter wind protection for the first few years in the coldest end of its range. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Martin Saskatoon (Serviceberry)
description: Martin produces some of the largest berries among the older Alberta-origin saskatoon selections, with a vigorous upright growth habit that suits both hedgerow and orchard-row plantings. Fruit clusters ripen fairly uniformly, making a single hand-harvest practical for home growers. Established plants sucker readily, so allow room for the clump to widen over time. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Martini Manuka (Compact Double-Pink New Zealand Tea Tree)
description: Martini is a compact, densely branched manuka selection prized for smothering itself in small, fully double, soft-pink flowers over a long late-winter-into-spring bloom season, with a tidier, more restrained habit than the species that makes it well suited to smaller borders, large containers, and rock gardens rather than the open shrubbery manuka typically forms. Plant in lean, gritty, slightly acidic soil with excellent drainage in full sun; like all Leptospermum, it is markedly more tolerant of drought and poor soil than of wet feet, and root rot in heavy or poorly drained ground is the most common cause of failure. Because the fully double flowers produce little accessible nectar or pollen, Martini offers less value to foraging bees than single-flowered manuka, so gardeners wanting both ornament and pollinator value should pair it with species plants or other single-flowered cultivars nearby. Trim lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, compact form. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Maru Persimmon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Maru is a Japanese persimmon cultivar that exemplifies the PVA (pollination-variant astringent) type — uniquely, the flavor and texture of its fruit changes dramatically based on whether the flower was pollinated. Unpollinated Maru fruits are uniformly orange-colored and astringent until fully ripe-soft; pollinated fruits develop dark brown or black spots and streaks in the flesh (called 'chocolate flesh') around the seeds, and these dark regions are sweet, jelly-like, and completely non-astringent while still firm — a prized texture and flavor combination. Fully pollinated Maru fruits may have most of the flesh dark-colored and sweet, making them among the most interesting persimmon-eating experiences available. In zone 9 Maru produces reliable crops of medium-sized, round to slightly oblate fruits ripening in October–November. The dark flesh and sweet, pudding-like texture of cross-pollinated fruits makes Maru an outstanding garden and fresh-market variety. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Maruba Santoh
description: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Maruba Santoh is a Japanese mustard green distinct from other Asian brassicas in having smooth, round, paddle-shaped leaves rather than the lobed or frilly leaves of most mustard types — the name 'maruba' means 'round leaf' in Japanese. The flavor is much milder than standard mustard greens, with a mild, slightly mustardy-sweet taste closer to bok choy or spinach, making it one of the most versatile and approachable cool-season greens for raw use in salads, stir-fries, soups, and braising. The smooth, non-frilly texture of the leaves holds dressings well without wilting and is preferred over crinkled-leaf types in delicate preparations. Maruba Santoh is faster-maturing than most brassicas and can produce a baby green harvest in 25–30 days from sowing. In zone 9 it is an excellent gap-filler for the fall and winter garden, tolerating light frosts and growing through the cool months without the bitterness that develops in other mustard greens exposed to heavy cold. Matures in 35–50 days from seed.

name: Marula (Elephant Tree, Jelly Plum, Maroela)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil of any type — Marula is remarkably adaptable to poor, sandy, or rocky soils and intensely drought-tolerant, thriving in conditions that challenge most fruit trees. Sclerocarya birrea subsp. caffra (Marula) is a large, spreading, deciduous African fruit tree native to the woodlands and savannas from Ethiopia and Nigeria south to South Africa, famous throughout sub-Saharan Africa as one of the most important traditional food and beverage trees of the continent. The plum-sized fruits (1–1.5 inches diameter) ripen in December–March in South Africa; in zone 9 they ripen in late summer–fall. When ripe, the thin, pale yellow skin covers soft, extremely juicy, intensely aromatic flesh with a rich, complex flavor combining tropical fruit notes reminiscent of mango, pineapple, and lychee — prized fresh, fermented into a traditional beer, and distilled into the popular Amarula Cream liqueur (produced commercially in South Africa). The large, brown, extremely hard seeds inside each fruit contain edible kernels with a rich, nutty flavor and high oil content used in traditional African cosmetics. Elephants travel great distances to feed on fallen marula fruits, giving rise to the folklore that they become inebriated — a myth, though the fruits do ferment rapidly when fallen. Marula is increasingly grown as an edible landscape tree in zone 9b–11. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Marumi Kumquat (Round Kumquat)
description: Marumi is the round-fruited kumquat species, forming a denser, more compact and thornier shrub than the oval-fruited Nagami kumquat. The small, orange-round fruit has a thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around noticeably tart, seedy pulp, so it is usually eaten whole rather than juiced. The tree is self-fertile and heavy-fruiting even as a young container specimen, and along with Nagami it is one of the parent species behind most modern kumquat hybrids. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season and site in the warmest microclimate available in zone 8b-9a, since hard freezes below the high teens can damage wood. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Marumi Kumquat (Round Sweet-Skinned Kumquat)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Marumi is one of the oldest kumquat cultivars grown, producing small, round fruit with thin, sweet, edible skin surrounding a tarter, seedier pulp, eaten whole rather than peeled. It is among the more cold-hardy kumquats and, being a naturally small, dense shrub, adapts well to container culture and can be moved under cover during hard freezes in the cooler parts of its range. Fruit ripens in winter and holds on the tree for weeks without dropping, giving a long, flexible harvest window; established plants are otherwise low-maintenance and require only routine citrus fertilizing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Marvel of Four Seasons Butterhead Lettuce
description: Sow this 1800s French butterhead directly in cool weather, barely covering the seed since it needs light to germinate. The tender, sweet leaves are green at the base and turn a beautiful cranberry-red, forming a crinkly rosette that resembles a flower. Keep plants consistently moist to preserve the coloring and prevent bitterness, and thin to about 8 to 10 inches apart. This adaptable variety performs across the seasons; give it afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Marvel of Four Seasons Lettuce (Merveille des Quatre Saisons)
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A classic French heirloom whose name translates to 'Marvel of the Four Seasons,' this butterhead forms attractive heads with bronze-red outer leaves surrounding a pale, blushed-pink, buttery interior, valued for holding quality and reliable heading across spring, summer, and fall plantings better than many single-season lettuce varieties. Its rich color and sweet, tender texture have kept it popular in French market gardens and home plots for well over a century. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Marvel Stripe Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake early as plants produce large, heavy fruit on indeterminate vines. Marvel Stripe is a large bicolor heirloom tomato of reported Mexican (Oaxacan) origin, producing very large (1–2 pound), oblate fruits with a striking golden-yellow exterior streaked and flamed with red and orange that is visually one of the most dramatic tomatoes in the garden or at a farmers market; when sliced, the interior shows a beautiful bicolor pattern of orange-gold and red. The flavor is mild, sweet, and tropical with notably low acidity — more fruity and candy-like than most large red tomatoes — making it particularly appealing to those who find red tomatoes too sharp. An outstanding choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and market display where visual drama matters. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Mary Foos Johnson Pawpaw (Historic Vigorous Named Pawpaw Selection)
description: Set out a grafted tree in spring in rich, well-drained soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before letting them mature into full sun. One of the earliest widely propagated named pawpaw selections, Mary Foos Johnson is valued for its vigorous, heavy-cropping habit and medium-to-large fruit with smooth, well-flavored yellow flesh. Gardeners choose it as a reliable, historically proven pollinator partner and producer alongside newer cultivars like Sunflower or Susquehanna, giving an extended pawpaw harvest window in late summer and early fall. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mary Washington Asparagus
description: Mary Washington is a classic heirloom asparagus producing thick, straight green spears with a faint purple blush at the tips. Start seed indoors early and transplant seedlings or crowns into a deeply worked, well-drained permanent bed. Resist harvesting for the first two seasons so plants build strong root reserves, then cut spears for several weeks each spring. A single planting can yield reliably for fifteen years or more with annual mulching and feeding. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Maryland Dittany (Stone Mint)
description: Plant in dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Maryland dittany — also called stone mint or wild oregano — is a low-growing native perennial herb of dry, rocky woodland edges and open, thin-soiled habitats across the eastern United States. It produces small lavender-pink flowers in late summer when most other native herbs have finished blooming, making it valuable for late-season nectar. The entire plant is strongly aromatic with a fresh, oregano-like fragrance when bruised, reflecting its culinary history as a wild herb — the dried leaves can be used as a substitute for oregano or dittany in cooking and teas. One of the few native mints that blooms in late summer and fall, providing critical resources for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season native bees. Extremely drought tolerant once established in appropriate dry, rocky conditions. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Masai Bush Bean (French Filet Bush Bean, AAS Winner)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 3-4 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest every 1-2 days once pods reach 4-5 inches and are still pencil-thin. Masai is an American Award of Merit-winning French filet bush bean, prized for combining the slender, tender, seedless-tasting pods typical of haricots verts with a compact, upright, easy-to-harvest bush habit that needs no trellising. The plants hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, making picking fast and keeping pods cleaner and less prone to soil-splash disease than sprawling bush types. Because filet beans mature quickly from flower to overgrown pod, harvest frequently to maintain the fine, tender texture; pods left even a day or two too long become coarser and more fibrous. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the season for a continuous harvest, since bush types produce a concentrated flush rather than the extended season of pole filet beans. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Mascara Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Mascara is a deeply red-colored romaine-type lettuce producing upright, compact heads of dark wine-red to nearly black-red leaves with the crisp, crunchy texture and pronounced midrib of romaine — combining the structural quality of cos-type lettuces with an extreme depth of red pigmentation that rivals the darkest red looseleaf varieties. The dramatic, almost black-red color maintains well through the warm fall temperatures that cause most red lettuces to lighten; Mascara's consistent dark color regardless of temperature makes it valuable for market growers who need reliable color in variable fall conditions. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — very similar to standard romaine in taste despite the striking color difference. In mesclun and mixed salad plantings, the very dark Mascara leaves provide the strongest color contrast against green lettuces. The intense red-black coloring indicates very high anthocyanin content and corresponding antioxidant value. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Mascotte Bean (AAS-Winning Compact Container Filet Bean)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since the compact habit does not need the room a pole bean requires. Mascotte, a 2014 All-America Selections winner, was bred specifically for container growing, holding its slender, straight, tender filet-type pods well above the tidy, upright foliage where they are easy to spot and pick without stooping or digging through leaves. It matures quickly and produces a concentrated, heavy set of pods over a shorter window than many pole beans, making it well suited to succession planting in small beds or pots on a patio. Harvest pods young and slender for the best filet-bean texture, picking every day or two once production begins to keep new flowers coming. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Mashed Potatoes Acorn Winter Squash
description: Direct sow this compact white acorn squash after the soil warms, planting in hills spaced a couple of feet apart. Its restricted vines reach only about 45 inches, making it a good choice for smaller gardens, and each plant usually sets three to four fruits. Let the squash mature fully until the rind hardens, then harvest with a bit of stem attached and cure in a warm spot for storage. Provide full sun and steady moisture while the fruits are developing. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Mashua (Anu, Tuberous Nasturtium)
description: Plant tubers in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mashua is one of the 'lost crops of the Andes' — a climbing nasturtium relative that produces edible tubers at the base of its twining stems. It is the most productive of the Andean tuber crops (producing more calories per unit area than potato under appropriate conditions) and is naturally resistant to insects and some nematodes through bitter compounds in its tissues. The tubers have a distinctive sharp, peppery, mustard-like raw flavor that mellows dramatically when cooked (especially by frost exposure) to a sweet, starchy taste similar to parsnip. The attractive red and orange tuberous nasturtium flowers are edible and ornamental. Mashua is a short-day plant that forms tubers only when days shorten in fall — it performs best in zone 7–9 where frost is not severe but fall days are distinctly short. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Mason's Superberry Mayhaw (Texas Superberry, Early-Blooming Western Mayhaw)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland native that tolerates the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most other fruit trees decline. Also sold as Texas Superberry, this East Texas selection of western mayhaw is one of the earliest-blooming named cultivars, opening flowers ahead of most other mayhaws in late winter, and produces large, deep red fruit with pink flesh that ripens by early May and hangs on the tree unusually long before dropping. The heavy, reliable crop and long hang time make harvest more forgiving than with cultivars that drop fruit quickly once ripe, though deer and other wildlife are drawn to it as readily as gardeners are. Expect bearing to begin within three to five years, with yields improving steadily as the tree matures. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Massandra Jujube
description: Massandra originated at the Nikita Botanical Garden near Yalta on Ukraine's Crimean coast, part of a Black Sea breeding tradition that also produced several other jujube selections grown for cold tolerance. The fruit is notably large for an early-ripening cultivar, with glossy, dark-brown skin at full maturity and a sweet, flavorful flesh that many growers compare favorably to standard Chinese selections. Trees bear heavily once established and tolerate the same poor, well-drained soils and drought that make jujube generally easy to grow, needing supplemental water mainly in the first year or two. Because Massandra shares ancestry with other Black Sea-region cultivars, plant it alongside a genetically distinct variety such as Li or Lang if maximizing fruit set is a priority. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Masterwort (Alpine Masterwort, Imperial Masterwort)
description: Not to be confused with the unrelated ornamental Astrantia major, which shares the English name masterwort, Peucedanum ostruthium (formerly classed as Imperatoria ostruthium) is a robust Apiaceae relative of angelica and lovage native to the mountain meadows and pastures of central and southern Europe. It produces broad, deeply divided leaves and flat umbels of small white flowers atop hollow stems, with a pungently aromatic rhizome long chewed or infused by alpine herders as a digestive bitter and traditionally credited with easing the effects of high-altitude exertion. Its dried root remains a flavoring component in some traditional European herbal bitters and mountain liqueurs. Grow in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun; plants resent hot, dry summers and perform best in climates that mimic their subalpine origin. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years to maintain vigor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mastic Tree (Lentisc)
description: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; mastic tree is the source of the original mastic gum — the resinous, pine-scented exudate collected by scoring the bark of trees on the Greek island of Chios, used for at least 2,500 years as a chewing gum, food flavoring, incense, varnish, and medicine. Greek mastic ('Chios masticha') is a protected designation of origin product used in the liqueur Mastika, Greek chewing gum, breads, pastries, and Turkish delight. As a landscape plant, mastic tree is an outstanding drought-tolerant, evergreen shrub for Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens, producing aromatic, glossy, pinnate leaves and small clusters of red to black berries that attract birds. It is excellent for coastal gardens due to its salt tolerance and thrives in the hot, alkaline, well-drained conditions of the Texas Hill Country and Gulf Coast. A relative of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera). Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Matador Spinach
description: Sow Matador spinach directly in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop, as spinach bolts quickly in heat. This variety offers good heat tolerance and holds a while before bolting, with smooth, dark green oval leaves suited to salads and cooking. Thin seedlings to 4 to 6 inches apart and keep the soil cool and evenly moist. Harvest baby leaves for salad mixes or let plants mature for cooked dishes like risotto. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Matico (Spiked Pepper)
description: Matico is a fast-growing, multi-stemmed Amazonian shrub whose crushed leaves have long been applied topically as a folk wound dressing and brewed as a digestive tea. Propagate from nodal stem cuttings, which root readily in moist, humus-rich media, since seed is rarely available commercially. Site in bright, filtered light under taller canopy in humid, frost-free gardens, and keep soil consistently moist but well drained. Once established the shrub tolerates brief dry spells and can be cut back hard to encourage bushy new growth for repeated leaf harvest. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Matina Cacao
description: Named for Costa Rica's Matina Valley on the Caribbean coast where it has been grown by smallholders for generations, Matina (formally the clone Matina 1-6) is today the most widely cultivated cacao type in the world, forming the backbone of Costa Rican and much of Central American cacao production thanks to its dependable yields and pleasant, well-balanced flavor. Its importance to the global crop made it the subject of one of the first complete cacao reference genomes sequenced by international researchers. Grow it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, with the same warm, humid conditions and frost protection other cacao types require. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Matina Tomato (German Heirloom Ultra-Early Small-Medium Red Salad Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage plants. Harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Matina is a German open-pollinated heirloom tomato from the Quedlinburg region of Saxony-Anhalt — a historically important German seed-saving and plant breeding center that preserved many traditional German vegetable varieties through the 20th century. Matina is among the most respected early tomatoes in European heirloom tomato tradition: a variety that consistently delivers ripe, flavorful tomatoes earlier in the season than almost any other indeterminate heirloom, making it a first-pick benchmark for season extension and early production. The fruits are small to medium (2–3 oz), round, smooth, and deep red at full ripeness — the classic small salad tomato form used throughout Germany and much of northern Europe for sliced tomatoes, salads, and fresh eating where the relatively small size provides good proportionality for whole slices. The flavor is exceptional for an ultra-early variety: sweet with a good acid balance and genuine tomato complexity that many early-maturing hybrid tomatoes lack. Early-ripening tomato varieties often sacrifice flavor to achieve early maturity; Matina demonstrates that early harvest and excellent flavor are compatible. In zone 9 gardens, Matina's ultra-early ripening makes it particularly practical: the variety delivers its best production before the June-July heat that suppresses fruit set in most tomato varieties, allowing harvest of the critical first tomatoes of the season before summer limits production. Matures in 58–65 days from transplant.

name: Matsumoto Wase Fuyu Persimmon (Early-Ripening Fuyu Bud Sport)
description: Matsumoto Wase Fuyu yields flattened, oblate fruit with firm, sweet, non-astringent flesh that can be eaten while still crisp, just like the standard Fuyu it sprouted from. Trees are compact and moderately vigorous, generally staying smaller than seedling persimmons, which suits smaller home orchards. It is self-fruitful and sets a reliable crop without a pollinator, and its early ripening window helps fruit finish before the heaviest fall rains in humid coastal climates. Tip-cracking, a common issue in flat non-astringent types, is notably reduced in this selection. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Matsumoto Wase Satsuma (Extra-Early Cold-Hardy Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Site Matsumoto Wase in full sun with excellent drainage and mulch the root zone to buffer soil temperature swings through winter. This compact, precocious satsuma strain is prized for ripening its seedless, easy-peel fruit several weeks ahead of standard Owari trees, which lets home growers in marginal zone 8b-9a areas get a full crop in before the first significant cold snap. The small, glossy-leaved tree bears young and stays manageable in size, making it a popular choice for espalier or large containers as well as open-ground planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Matt's Wild Cherry Tomato (Wild-Type Tiny Red Cherry)
aliases: Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme 'Matt's Wild Cherry'
description: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Matt's Wild Cherry is an extremely vigorous grower requiring sturdy staking; the pea-sized fruits are prone to cracking when ripe and should be harvested frequently; self-sows readily in mild climates — may reappear without replanting. Matt's Wild Cherry is a tomato variety with an interesting origin: it was collected by Matt Liebman from a wild or semi-wild population (possibly a naturalized escape) in the Hidalgo state of Mexico — an area near the center of origin of the domestic tomato — and introduced to North American seed-saving networks through the Seed Savers Exchange and similar organizations. The variety is classified as Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme, the wild cherry tomato type considered ancestral to all cultivated tomatoes, and it displays many wild-type characteristics: extremely small fruits (pea-sized, only 3/8 to 1/2 inch in diameter), prolific production (literally hundreds of fruits per plant), high seed-to-flesh ratio, thin skin prone to cracking, and exceptional flavor intensity that is quite different from cultivated cherry tomatoes. The flavor is extraordinarily complex for such small fruits — intensely tomato-ish, with high acidity balanced against good sweetness, and a deep, earthy, wild tomato character that reflects the original tomato flavor before centuries of breeding selected for larger, milder, less acidic fruits. For flavor enthusiasts and tomato purists, Matt's Wild Cherry offers a connection to the ancestral tomato that no commercial variety can provide. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Matua Kiwi (Male Pollinizer for Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis positioned to pollinate nearby female fuzzy kiwi vines. Matua is a New Zealand-bred male fuzzy kiwi selection grown exclusively to provide pollen for female vines like Hayward, which cannot set fruit without a compatible male nearby, since kiwifruit plants are dioecious with separate male and female vines. Matua blooms relatively early and vigorously, and one male vine can typically pollinate several female vines when well positioned within the planting, making efficient use of garden space for the non-fruiting pollinizer. Because Matua itself never produces fruit, prune it primarily to encourage abundant flower production and to keep its size manageable relative to the fruiting female vines it supports. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Mauka (Chago)
description: Plant root sections or divisions in deep, well-drained, fertile soil after danger of hard frost has passed, setting them 3-4 inches deep in a site that receives full sun but stays cool through summer; mauka is a striking Andean perennial in the four-o'clock family (Nyctaginaceae), producing large, somewhat fleshy leaves on multi-branched stems above a cluster of thick, parsnip-like storage roots that can reach 12-18 inches in length under ideal conditions. The roots are not edible raw — they contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense oral irritation — but a traditional sun-curing process of several days substantially reduces the oxalate content and transforms the flavor to a mildly sweet, starchy quality reminiscent of parsnip. In the high Andes, mauka was once a staple crop of the pre-Columbian era but is now rare even in its native range; outside of botanical gardens and specialty growers in cool-climate gardens, it is extremely uncommon in cultivation and represents a living piece of agricultural heritage worth preserving. Harvest roots in autumn after the first frost kills the tops, and save a few root sections in cool, dry storage to replant the following spring. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Maurino Olive (Cold-Hardy Italian Oil Olive)
description: Maurino is an Italian oil olive noted for early, precocious bearing and comparatively strong cold hardiness within the Olea europaea cultivar group, which has made it a popular choice for growers testing olives at the cooler margins of their range. Plant in full sun in well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil, and expect Maurino to begin cropping earlier in tree life than many traditional Italian varieties. It is partially self-fertile but produces a heavier, more consistent crop with a cross-pollinator such as Frantoio or Pendolino nearby. Harvest fruit in late fall as color shifts from green to purple for oil production, and irrigate sparingly since Maurino, like most olives, tolerates drought well once its root system is established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mauritius Lychee
description: Mauritius is a productive lychee bearing rough-skinned red fruit with sweet, fragrant, translucent flesh. It needs a frost-free subtropical or tropical climate with a brief cool, dry period to trigger flowering. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil and protect young trees from wind and cold. Water generously during flowering and fruit development but ease off during the winter rest period. Mulch heavily to keep the shallow roots moist and feed with a balanced fertilizer through the growing season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mauritius Raspberry (Roseleaf Bramble)
description: This slender, nearly thornless bramble stays compact and shrubby rather than sprawling, and it holds its foliage through mild winters where hardy, making it useful as a shade-tolerant edge planting under fruit trees or along a woodland path. It flowers and fruits nearly continuously in warm climates, producing small, soft, sweet-tart red raspberries that are eaten fresh, though they are more delicate and less productive per cane than temperate raspberries. Give it half-day shade and evenly moist soil, and thin out older canes each year to keep new fruiting wood coming. It offers gardeners in humid subtropical and tropical shade gardens a genuine raspberry-family fruit where classic raspberries fail from heat stress. Matures in 300–545 days from transplant.

name: Maverick Spelt (Modern Semi-Dwarf Winter Spelt)
description: Maverick was bred to give organic and specialty grain growers a spelt option with a shorter, sturdier straw than older heirloom lines like Oberkulmer, cutting down on lodging losses in wet or windy years while still delivering the hulled kernel and nutty flavor spelt is grown for. Sow into a firm, well-worked seedbed in mid-fall, using a slightly heavier seeding rate than for common wheat since spelt tillers less. Plants overwinter low to the ground and resume vigorous growth in spring, typically heading out and ripening around the same window as other winter spelt lines. Because the tough hull remains fused to the kernel at harvest, plan on a dedicated dehuller or mill built for spelt rather than a standard combine setup used for free-threshing wheat. Matures in 260–290 days from seed.

name: Max's Gold Summer Squash
description: Direct sow this golden zucchini after the soil warms, planting a couple of seeds per hill and thinning to the strongest plant. The long, straight fruits have a small seed cavity and firm, flavorful flesh, and their bright color makes them easy to spot for harvest. Pick fruits young at 6 to 8 inches, checking daily during peak season since summer squash grows fast. Give plants full sun, rich soil, and consistent moisture, and harvest frequently to keep the plant producing. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Maxibel Filet Bush Bean
description: Direct sow this French filet bush bean after the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep in full sun. The compact plants need no support, making them well suited to containers and small beds. Harvest the slender, stringless haricots verts at their peak between 6 and 8 inches long and about a quarter inch wide for the best texture and flavor. Pick every couple of days to keep the plants productive, and sow in succession for a steady supply through the season. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Maxifort Rootstock Tomato
description: This exceptionally vigorous interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite heirloom or hybrid tomato scion, not eaten itself, offering a much larger and more disease-resistant root system that in turn boosts scion vigor, fruit size, total yield, and season length compared to an ungrafted plant on its own roots. Widely used in commercial greenhouse and high tunnel tomato production, it carries broad resistance to soil-borne diseases including fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and corky root rot, extending productive plant life well past what many own-root tomatoes achieve in intensive production. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick using a tube or splice graft, keep grafted plants in a humid, shaded healing chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy staking or trellising to support the extra vigor. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Maxima Elderberry (Giant-Flowered American Elderberry)
description: Maxima is an old selection of American elderberry in which every part of the plant is scaled up from the wild type — the fragrant white flower clusters can reach a foot or more across, and the resulting clusters of purple-black berries are correspondingly larger and heavier than standard wild-collected elderberry. Because flowering wood is produced fresh each year, gardeners willing to cut the whole plant back hard in late winter are rewarded with fewer stems but dramatically oversized flower heads by midsummer; left unpruned, it simply grows into a large multi-stemmed shrub with above-average flower and fruit size. Fruit is used the same way as any American elderberry, for jelly, syrup, and wine, and the plant spreads by suckers over time if not managed. It performs well through Gulf Coast summer heat provided soil moisture stays consistent during flowering and fruit set. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Maxine Mayhaw (Late-Blooming Fire-Blight-Resistant Western Mayhaw)
description: Maxine is a western mayhaw selection found growing wild near DeRidder, Louisiana, and named for the finder's wife; it was chosen for combining above-average fruit size with a naturally open, umbrella-shaped canopy that needs little corrective pruning. It blooms later than early selections such as Royal Star, which helps its flowers dodge Gulf South late frosts, and it carries good field resistance to fire blight, the disease that most often limits mayhaw orchards in the humid South. Like other mayhaws, it thrives on wet, poorly drained, acidic ground where few other fruiting trees perform well, and it sets a heavier crop when planted with a second mayhaw cultivar for cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Maxine Pear (Starking Delicious Fire Blight-Resistant Southern Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maxine cross-pollinates well with Moonglow, Orient, Kieffer, and most other fire blight-resistant Southern pear varieties. Maxine, also marketed as Starking Delicious, was developed for good disease resistance and reliable production in the humid Southeast, where fire blight quickly kills susceptible European pear varieties like Bartlett. It produces large, smooth, yellow-green fruit with sweet, juicy, only lightly gritty flesh, notably larger than many of its fire-blight-resistant peers, ripening in late summer. Like most Southern-adapted pears, it should be picked while still firm and green and ripened off the tree in a cool spot for the best texture and flavor, since fruit left to ripen on the tree tends to soften unevenly from the core outward. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the strong disease resistance means Maxine needs little to no fungicide spraying to produce a reliable crop in Gulf South conditions. Plant with another European pear variety for best cross-pollination and yield. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: May Duke Cherry (Historic Sweet-Tart Duke Cherry)
description: May Duke is one of the oldest named Duke cherries, a naturally occurring group of hybrids between sweet and sour cherry grown in Europe since at least the 1600s and long favored in English gardens. The medium, dark-red fruit is tart when it first colors but sweetens considerably if left to hang until fully ripe, making it useful both fresh and for cooking. It is partially self-fertile and ripens earlier than most sweet cherries, giving it its name. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil, and prune to an open vase shape in late winter to keep the compact, upright growth productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: May Queen Lettuce (Maikönig)
description: Sow directly as early as soil can be worked, or start under cold frame protection for an even earlier crop, since it tolerates light frost well. This German heirloom butterhead, also called Maikönig or May King, dates to before the 1880s and was bred to be the very first lettuce ready in spring, producing tender, rosy-blushed rosettes in under two months. Market gardeners historically relied on it to fill the earliest gap in the spring salad season. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Maya Nut (Breadnut Tree)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil — including rocky, limestone-based soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; Maya nut (Brosimum alicastrum) is a towering canopy tree in the Moraceae family that the ancient Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples relied upon as a critical famine food for thousands of years, with seeds that are extraordinarily nutritious — high in protein, calcium, potassium, iron, zinc, and B vitamins — and can be boiled, roasted, dried, and ground into flour. The ripe purple-skinned fruits are also edible fresh, with a sweet, fig-like flavor, and the abundant leaves serve as high-quality livestock fodder. Trees are long-lived, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and grow naturally in limestone-rich soils where other fruit trees may struggle. Though primarily a large timber and food tree rather than an orchard crop, Maya nut is gaining recognition as an exceptionally valuable multipurpose agroforestry species, with first seed harvests typically beginning 5–10 years after planting. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mayflower Bean
description: Mayflower, sometimes called the Amish Knuttle Bean, is a long-cultivated heirloom pole bean grown chiefly for its small, oval seeds marked with maroon-and-white or rose speckling on a white background. Pods can be picked young as snap beans, but the variety is best known and most valued as a dry shelling bean with rich, dense flavor well suited to baking, soups, and long-simmered dishes. Train the vigorous vines up 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis and leave pods on the plant until they rattle and the pods turn tan and papery before harvesting for storage. Its long history and vigorous, reliable production make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a dual-purpose bean with strong heirloom provenance. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Mayhaw (May Haw, Eastern Mayhaw)
description: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun; mayhaw thrives in the heavy, wet, acidic soils of the Gulf Coast plain that frustrate most fruit trees. Crataegus aestivalis (mayhaw) is the iconic native fruit tree of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-like fruits in April–May (hence 'may haw' — haw is an old name for hawthorn fruit) that are traditionally harvested by spreading sheets under the tree or raking from the water's surface when the tree grows over ponds and bayous. Mayhaw jelly is a Southern culinary tradition — the vivid, translucent, coral-red jelly with a unique tart-sweet, apple-berry flavor is considered a regional treasure and a gift-worthy specialty product throughout Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. The tree is also highly ornamental — producing masses of white flowers in February–March (often among the first spring blossoms), followed by the distinctive April berry crop, then good fall foliage color. Named cultivars for improved fruit production include 'Big Red,' 'Crimson,' 'Super Berry,' and 'Texas Star.' Mayhaw grows naturally in wet bottomland forests, bayou margins, and pond edges throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mayhaw (Western Mayhaw, May Haw)
description: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw naturally grows in wet bottomlands and tolerates seasonal flooding. Crataegus opaca (Western mayhaw or May haw) is a native hawthorn of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a small to medium deciduous tree growing in the wet, seasonally flooded bottomlands, bayous, and boggy depressions of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia. It is the source of one of the most prized and distinctively Southern traditional preserves: mayhaw jelly, made from the small (1/2-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-flavored fruits that ripen in April and May (hence 'mayhaw' — haw ripening in May). Mayhaw jelly has a uniquely mild, apple-quince-like flavor with subtle floral notes that makes it a beloved regional specialty — spread on hot biscuits, it represents the taste of the Gulf South spring. The fruits must be harvested from the ground or water (they drop when ripe, sometimes into shallow water) and are processed immediately — too sour and dry to eat fresh, but exceptional for jellies, preserves, and syrup. Many improved fruiting cultivars have been selected in Louisiana, Texas, and Georgia; 'Super Berry,' 'Texas Star,' and 'Crimson' are productive modern selections. Mayhaw is notably tolerant of wet soils and occasional flooding, making it valuable for rain gardens and wet spots in Gulf Coast landscapes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Maypan Coconut Palm (Lethal-Yellowing-Resistant Hybrid Coconut)
description: Maypan is a hybrid coconut developed in Jamaica by crossing the compact, precocious Malayan Dwarf with the larger, more vigorous Panama Tall, bred specifically to combine dwarf-parent resistance to lethal yellowing disease with taller-parent vigor, nut size, and yield after lethal yellowing devastated Jamaica's tall coconut plantations in the 20th century. It reaches an intermediate mature height, taller and more vigorous than pure Malayan Dwarf plantings but well short of unimproved tall varieties, and begins bearing somewhat later than Malayan Dwarf alone, typically five to seven years from planting. Maypan was widely distributed throughout Florida, the Caribbean, and other lethal-yellowing-affected regions starting in the 1970s-80s as the standard replacement variety for susceptible tall coconuts, though growers should note that resistance to lethal yellowing is relative rather than absolute and newer disease strains have reduced its reliability in some areas over time. Extremely frost-sensitive and restricted to the warmest USDA zones in the continental US. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Maypole Columnar Crabapple (Compact Flowering and Fruiting Pollinator Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maypole is a columnar crabapple in the Ballerina series, sharing the same narrow, single-trunk growth habit as its larger-fruited siblings while producing a spectacular flush of deep pink spring blossoms followed by small, cherry-sized, deep red crabapples that hang on the tree well into winter, valued both ornamentally and for jelly-making. Its extended, reliable bloom period makes it a useful pollinator partner for other columnar or standard apple cultivars planted nearby, extending cross-pollination coverage in a small orchard or container grouping. The narrow, upright form fits easily into a large container, tight garden bed, or closely spaced row, and needs only minimal pruning — removing occasional stray side shoots is usually all that is required to maintain the columnar shape. Small fruit can be left for winter birds or harvested for crabapple jelly once fully colored in fall. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Maypop (Native Passionflower)
description: Maypop (Passiflora incarnata) is a North American native passionflower that is cold-hardy to zone 6, distinguishing it clearly from the tropical Passiflora edulis (passionfruit). The ornamental lavender flowers are stunning and the egg-sized yellow-green fruits have sweet, aromatic pulp similar to tropical passionfruit. Plants die back to the roots in zone 6–7 winters and re-sprout vigorously in late spring — do not remove the crown before new growth appears. Plant cross-pollinators nearby (more than one plant) for reliable fruit set. Harvest when fruits turn yellowish-green and fall or detach easily. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Maypop Passionflower
description: Direct-sow seeds or plant transplants in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil against a trellis, fence, or arbor; maypop is one of the most ornate native vines of the Southeast, producing intricately structured lavender-and-white flowers all summer followed by fragrant, egg-sized, yellow-green edible fruits that ripen in fall and make excellent juice and jam with a tropical guava-like flavor. The vine spreads vigorously by underground runners and can colonize an area quickly — provide a sturdy trellis and monitor spread, or allow it to naturalize along a fence row. Maypop is the sole or primary host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae in the Southeast, making it one of the most ecologically valuable native plants for zone 5–9 pollinator gardens. Despite top growth dying back in zone 5–7, the deep roots re-emerge dependably each spring. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Mazzard Cherry Rootstock
description: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Mazzard produces a full-sized, long-lived tree. A wild sweet cherry seedling selection and the traditional standard rootstock for grafted sweet and sour cherry trees for well over a century, it produces a large, vigorous, deep-rooted, long-lived tree with excellent anchorage and broad compatibility across cherry varieties, without the size control offered by modern dwarfing rootstocks like the Gisela series. Its reliability, wide soil adaptability, and long productive lifespan have kept it in use even as smaller, more precocious rootstocks have become popular, particularly where a large, permanent shade-producing cherry tree is desired. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the eventual tree ample permanent space, since it grows nearly as large as a wild, ungrafted cherry tree. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: McAllister Black Walnut
description: McAllister is a named black walnut selection valued among nut growers for vigorous growth and heavy, consistent nut production on a grafted tree. It produces a good-sized nut with kernel quality comparable to other widely propagated named selections, bearing years earlier than an unselected seedling tree. Site it in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with plenty of room clear of gardens sensitive to juglone. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: McCallister Hican (Vigorous Pecan-Hickory Hybrid)
description: McCallister is among the most widely grafted hican selections in hobbyist nut-tree circles, prized for its exceptionally large, showy nuts on a vigorous tree. Fill percentage and seed viability are variable, a trait typical of pecan-hickory hybrids, so growers usually plant it for novelty, breeding stock, and diversified nut plantings rather than for consistent commercial yield. It needs the same deep, well-drained soil and cross-pollination partner as pecan, and tolerates colder winters than straight pecan does. Expect a long establishment period before the tree reaches bearing age. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: McCaslan Pole Bean (Georgia Heirloom Snap Bean)
description: McCaslan traces to a Georgia family garden bean grown before 1900, later refined and released commercially as 'McCaslan 42' by the Corneli Seed Company in 1962. The heavy-producing vines climb readily on a pole or trellis and set slightly flattened, meaty pods up to 8 inches long that stay stringless and fine-grained when picked young. Left longer on the vine, pods can be shelled fresh or dried for ivory-white beans, giving the variety a useful two-stage harvest. McCaslan is prized in Deep South gardens for its heat tolerance and reliable yields through summer conditions that slow down less vigorous pole beans. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: McConnell's Blue Rosemary (Dwarf Trailing Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. McConnell's Blue is a low, spreading rosemary that reaches only about a foot tall while spreading two to three feet wide, with broad dark green needles and clear deep blue flowers that appear in flushes from late winter into summer in mild climates. The fully flavored foliage works in the kitchen just as well as any upright culinary rosemary, but the trailing habit makes it especially suited to draping over a raised bed edge, retaining wall, or large container. Like all rosemary it is intolerant of wet feet, so plant in a raised or sloped spot if garden soil is heavy, and where winters dip below the mid-teens Fahrenheit, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: McCormack's Green Glaze Collard (Gullah Geechee Heirloom Collard)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'McCormack's Green Glaze'
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. This variety was preserved by the McCormack family and is one of dozens of distinct named greasy-leaf collards documented through the Heirloom Collards Project, a collaboration between Seed Savers Exchange and Southern seed keepers that has traced individual family lines of collards across the Carolinas and Gulf South back for generations. Its rounded, glossy, deeply dentate leaves carry the same waxy sheen found in other 'glaze' collards, giving natural resistance to leaf-chewing pests, and the plant is slow to bolt and holds well through cold snaps without heading. Because it survives today as a small, actively regenerated seed stock rather than a mass-market variety, gardeners who grow it out and save seed are directly helping preserve a piece of African American Southern foodways. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: McDill White Sapote
description: Plant McDill in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind; it is a large, vigorous tree that grows quickly and takes readily to grafting, making it a popular choice for growers wanting a dependable, early-bearing selection. Fruit is oblate in shape, greenish-yellow at maturity, and counts among the largest-fruited white sapote cultivars, with rich, custard-like flesh and excellent flavor. The crop ripens in early autumn, somewhat ahead of many other cultivars, giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the harvest season before cooler weather sets in. Because the tree bears at a young age relative to seedling trees, it is a good option for growers wanting a quicker return from a newly planted grafted specimen. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: McDonald Hazelnut (OSU 880.027, Eastern Filbert Blight-Resistant Peeling Filbert)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; McDonald requires a compatible pollenizer variety; nuts drop naturally when ripe, typically about 14 days earlier than the older standard 'Barcelona,' allowing growers to complete harvest before Willamette Valley autumn rains begin, which lowers drying and cleaning costs. McDonald was developed within Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program and tested under the designation OSU 880.027, a cross of 'Tonda Pacifica' and 'Santiam,' before being released and patented in January 2014. The tree is a vigorous, heavy producer of medium-small, high-quality kernels prized for the peeled hazelnut market, with an excellent shelled-nut recovery around 52%, and it carries strong resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight, the canker disease that devastated older 'Barcelona' plantings across the Pacific Northwest. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: McFarlin Cranberry
description: McFarlin originated in Massachusetts in the 1870s and became the dominant commercial cranberry cultivar across the Pacific Northwest and Wisconsin bogs for much of the twentieth century before being largely replaced by Stevens. It produces large, firm, dark-red berries with good storage quality and was historically one of the parent cultivars used to breed Stevens. Vines are vigorous and productive but somewhat more susceptible to false blossom disease than newer cultivars, so growers should watch for leafhopper vectors and remove infected plants promptly. It remains of interest to home growers and heirloom collectors for its historical significance and reliable regional performance in cooler bog climates. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: McIntosh Apple (Mac Apple, Original Red Apple, Northeastern Apple Classic)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; McIntosh requires cross-pollination; ripens early season (early September in New York), making it the first major commercial apple of the fall; fruit should be harvested when fully red and slightly soft to pressure — McIntosh doesn't firm up like later-season apples and is at its best when slightly tender and very aromatic. McIntosh apple is the foundational variety of the northeastern American apple industry and for decades was the dominant commercial apple in New England, New York, and eastern Canada. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling on John McIntosh's farm in Dundas, Ontario (near present-day Morrisburg) around 1811 — one of the most consequential accidental apple discoveries in North American horticultural history.
