The young seedling was found growing on his property, probably a wild seedling from a previous homestead planting, and John McIntosh and his son Allan grafted and propagated the tree beginning around 1835, eventually distributing trees throughout eastern Canada and New England. McIntosh produces distinctively aromatic fruit with a characteristic sweet-tart flavor and very soft, juicy, bright white flesh that is immediately recognizable to anyone who grew up in the Northeast. The red-green skin deepens to full red with harvest, and the flesh is softer than modern popular apples (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) — McIntosh is what older generations mean when they say 'the way apples used to taste' — a tender, juicy, very fragrant apple with complex flavor. McIntosh is also the primary parent of many important modern apple varieties including Cortland, Empire, Jonamac, Macoun, and others. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: McKenzie Aronia (North Dakota-Bred Black Chokeberry)
description: McKenzie is a North Dakota-selected black chokeberry valued for its taller, more vigorous growth and heavy annual fruit set compared to more compact aronia cultivars. The glossy black berries ripen in late summer and are extremely high in anthocyanins, making them popular for juice, syrup, and jam production despite their astringent raw flavor. Plant in full sun for the best fruit yield and fall color; the species tolerates poor, wet, or compacted soils that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and it needs little more than occasional thinning of old canes to stay productive. Its exceptional cold hardiness suits it well to short-season northern climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: McMillan Pecan (Highly Scab-Resistant Native-Type Gulf South Pecan)
description: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually to prevent rosette symptoms common in Gulf South pecan production. McMillan is a native-type pecan selection out of Mississippi long favored by Gulf South growers for its outstanding, near-immune resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) — the single most damaging disease of pecans in the humid Southeast — which allows it to produce consistent, high-quality crops with little or no fungicide input, unlike scab-susceptible standards such as Desirable and Stuart. The nuts are smaller than many commercial cultivars, in keeping with its native-type parentage, but the kernel quality and flavor are excellent, and the tree bears reliably and precociously. Because of its disease resistance, McMillan is frequently recommended for backyard, homestead, and low-input orchard plantings across the Gulf South where fungicide spraying is impractical, and it pairs well with a Type I pollinator for full production. Zone 7–9. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Meader American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Self-Fertile Native Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, taking care with the taproot since American persimmon does not transplant well once established. Meader was selected in New Hampshire and is notable for extending American persimmon culture well north of its typical native range, combining reliable cold hardiness with self-fertile, seedless fruit that a single tree can produce without a pollinator. The medium orange fruit ripens in fall and, like all American persimmon, must soften fully before eating or it will be unpleasantly astringent. It also grows vigorously and fruits reliably in the milder, longer growing seasons of the Gulf South, tolerating heat and a range of soils once established. Water during the first two seasons to establish the taproot, then expect the tree to need little care beyond removing root suckers. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Meader Hardy Kiwi (Male Pollinator)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis; site centrally within pollinating distance of the female vines it is meant to serve. Meader is a male hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivar selected by Professor Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, prized specifically for its exceptional cold hardiness — among the most cold-tolerant hardy kiwi selections available, able to survive winter conditions that damage or kill less hardy male cultivars. As a male vine, it produces abundant flowers but no fruit; its sole purpose in the garden is to provide pollen for nearby female cultivars, and because Actinidia arguta is dioecious, at least one male vine is essential wherever female vines are grown for fruit. Its outstanding hardiness makes it the standard pollinator choice for northern hardy kiwi plantings, ensuring the pollinator survives winters that a female cultivar chosen for fruit quality alone might not, zone 3–8. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Meader Kiwi (New Hampshire Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Meader is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar bred at the University of New Hampshire and named for horticulturist Elwyn Meader, selected for exceptional cold hardiness and a shorter growing season requirement that lets it ripen fruit reliably even in northern New England summers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good kiwi flavor, ripening earlier in the season than many other kiwiberry selections. This early ripening and strong cold tolerance make Meader a dependable choice anywhere the growing season is on the short side for other hardy kiwi cultivars. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for consistent fruit set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Meadow Garlic (Wild Onion)
description: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; meadow garlic naturalizes readily by bulbils (produced instead of seeds in many populations) and will colonize moist meadows and woodland edges over time. Allium canadense is a native North American wild onion found across the eastern and central US in moist meadows, open woodlands, and disturbed areas; it produces slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and 12–24-inch stems bearing rounded umbels that typically produce bulbils (small bulbs) rather than flowers or a mixture of both in spring. All parts are edible and have a mild onion-garlic flavor; the leaves, young bulbs, and bulbils were widely used by Native Americans and are excellent as a wild substitute for chives or green onions in cooking. It is extremely adaptable and tolerates light shade, wet soils, and neglect, making it one of the easiest native edibles to establish. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Meadowlark Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system. Meadowlark is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for only about 200 chill hours, so it reliably leafs, blooms, and ripens even after unusually mild Gulf Coast winters that leave higher-chill cultivars sparse. It is one of the earliest-ripening blueberries available, often ready well ahead of standard rabbiteye types, though it benefits from a second early low-chill cultivar nearby for best pollination. Prune out old canes each winter and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring to keep plants vigorous. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Meadowsweet
description: Filipendula ulmaria is a tall, elegant perennial native to wet meadows, riverbanks, and marshy ground throughout Europe and temperate Asia, producing pinnate, dark-green leaves that are white-downy beneath and spectacular, frothy, cream-white, almond-honey-scented flower plumes from mid to late summer; it thrives only in permanently moist or wet soil and is not suitable for dry or well-drained conditions. Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in rich, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — it will grow in standing water at the margins of ponds and streams and is one of the finest plants for naturalizing in wet, wild garden areas. Meadowsweet has deep historical and pharmacological significance: the flower buds contain salicylates (including salicylic acid and methyl salicylate), the compounds that served as the chemical model for the synthesis of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) in 1897 — the name 'aspirin' is derived from 'Spirin,' from the plant's former Latin name Spiraea ulmaria. Traditionally the flowers were strewn on floors to perfume rooms, used to flavor mead and wines, and taken as a remedy for fever, pain, and digestive complaints; harvest flowers in full bloom for herbal preparations. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Medallion Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Medallion is a mini-romaine type lettuce producing compact, upright, 5–6 inch heads with tightly wrapped inner leaves and crisp, crunchy texture — the small-head format that has become standard in grocery produce departments and upscale food service. Mini-romaine heads like Medallion are harvested at one-quarter to one-third the size of full-sized romaine but with the same crunchy, mild, slightly sweet romaine flavor in a single-serving portion size. The compact heads also allow significantly closer spacing (6–8 inches) than full-sized romaine, making them more efficient in raised beds and small gardens. The crisp, upright inner leaves hold dressings exceptionally well for Caesar-style preparations, and the compact whole head can be split lengthwise and grilled or broiled as a dramatic presentation. Medallion has been widely adopted in restaurant supply chains precisely because the single-serving size reduces food waste compared to large head lettuces. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Medana Tayberry
description: Medana is a thornless tayberry selection bred in Scotland at the former Scottish Crop Research Institute, carrying the same long, conical, deep purple-red fruit and rich raspberry-blackberry flavor as the classic tayberry on completely spineless canes. Fan-train the trailing canes along wires, keeping the current season's primocanes apart from the fruiting floricanes so post-harvest cleanup stays simple. Remove fruited canes to the ground immediately after harvest and tie the new primocanes onto the trellis for next year's crop. In cooler parts of its range, unclip the canes from the wires after leaf drop and cover with straw mulch or row cover for winter protection. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Medjool Date Palm
description: Plant Medjool Date Palm offshoots (tissue-culture plants or basal offshoots from certified, disease-free sources) in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; requires hot, dry summers (ideally above 95°F) for fruit development and very low humidity during the fruit ripening period — high humidity causes fungal problems with the developing fruit clusters; irrigate deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry between waterings. Medjool dates are among the most commercially valuable date palm products in the world — large, soft, caramel-brown dates with rich, complex sweetness described as a combination of honey, caramel, and dried fruit; they are the 'fresh date' sold in upscale markets and gourmet stores. Originally from the royal date gardens of Morocco and the Middle East, Medjool was brought to the United States in 1927 by Walter Swingle of the USDA, who rescued eleven offshoots from a diseased date garden in Morocco; this small genetic founder population gave rise to the entire US commercial Medjool industry centered in the Coachella Valley of California and the Yuma area of Arizona. For fruiting in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens, Medjool requires the dry, intensely hot summers of desert climates; in humid coastal areas like Houston, fruiting is unreliable but the palm grows magnificently as an ornamental. Must be hand-pollinated by transferring pollen from male palm flowers to female date clusters to ensure fruit set in home gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Medlar
description: Medlar is a small, gnarled tree that tolerates a wide range of soils and needs minimal pruning beyond removing crossing branches; it is largely self-fertile and rarely needs a pollinator. Fruit is harvested in late autumn after the first light frost when the skin has turned brown and slightly wrinkled, then 'bleted' (stored at room temperature for 2–4 weeks) until the flesh softens to a custard-like consistency and loses its harsh astringency. The bletted fruit tastes of apple butter with wine overtones and is traditionally made into jelly or cheese. Few pests bother medlar, making it one of the easiest heritage fruits for a low-spray garden. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Meech's Prolific Quince (Classic American Heirloom Quince)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Meech's Prolific is a nineteenth-century American heirloom quince, long documented in historic US pomology references as one of the heaviest-bearing and most reliable quince cultivars available, producing large, bright golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, jelly, paste, and baking. As the name suggests, it is notably precocious and prolific, often bearing well within just a few years of planting and continuing to crop dependably year after year. Like all quince the fruit is hard and astringent raw and is meant to be cooked, which transforms the pale flesh to a rosy pink and develops the complex floral-honey flavor quince is prized for. Prune in late winter to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the best defense against fire blight, the primary disease risk for quince in humid regions. Harvest in fall once fruit has turned fully golden and developed its characteristic strong perfume; quince stores well in a cool location for weeks after picking. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Meeker Raspberry
description: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and train the canes to a two-wire trellis, since the long, productive canes bend heavily under a full crop. Meeker is the classic Pacific Northwest commercial red raspberry, bred at Washington State University and long the dominant processing variety in Washington and Oregon, valued for its consistently large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor for both fresh eating and freezing. It fruits on floricanes, so remove spent canes to the ground after harvest each year and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest shoots. It performs best where summers are mild and winters are not severely cold, and can be prone to root rot in poorly drained soils. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Meerlo Variegated Lavandin
description: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil; the variegated foliage is more prone to winter injury than plain-leaved lavandins, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range benefit from a sheltered spot and light winter protection. 'Meerlo' is grown chiefly for its foliage, with gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy gold that provide season-long color even before the pale lavender-blue flower spikes appear in summer. It makes an eye-catching accent or low hedge where variegated foliage is wanted alongside typical lavender fragrance. Trim after flowering and again lightly in late winter to keep the variegation fresh and the habit compact. Matures in 100–150 days from transplant.

name: Megaton Leek (F1 Hybrid)
description: Megaton is a vigorous F1 hybrid leek grown for its exceptional uniformity and speed to maturity compared with older open-pollinated types, producing long, thick, upright shanks under wide dark green leaves. Its hybrid vigor means less outer-leaf cleaning is needed at harvest to reveal a straight, market-ready stalk, which makes it popular with growers who sell bunched leeks. Give plants rich, consistently moist soil and hill soil around the base as they thicken to extend the blanched white shank. Because Megaton matures earlier than winter-hardy heirloom leeks, it suits gardeners wanting a heavy early-to-mid fall harvest rather than a leek held in the ground through deep winter. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Megatron Jalapeno Chile Pepper
description: Start this large jalapeno indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm for reliable germination. Transplant seedlings out only after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. Megatron produces extra-large, thick-walled peppers up to 4.5 inches long and matures earlier than many jalapenos, giving an abundant crop ideal for stuffing. Provide consistent moisture and a light feeding once fruit sets, and harvest green or let peppers ripen red for a sweeter, hotter flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Mei Qing Choi (Compact Hybrid Bok Choy)
aliases: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Mei Qing Choi'
description: Direct sow, or start indoors and transplant, in early spring after the last hard freeze, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since Mei Qing Choi bolts quickly in long, hot days. Mei Qing Choi is a compact, vase-shaped hybrid pac choi with thick, pale jade-green stems and glossy, rounded dark green leaves, bred for a uniform, tightly packed miniature head that is smaller and more tender than standard-sized bok choy. It combines useful heat and cold tolerance with strong bolt resistance for a bok choy of its type, giving gardeners a wider planting window than many other Asian brassica greens. Harvest whole heads at baby size for salads or at full size for stir-fries, cutting at the base just above the soil line. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Meigetsu Asian Pear
description: Meigetsu is a pleasantly sweet Japanese nashi cultivar with fruit and aroma often compared to pineapple, watermelon, and butterscotch. Unlike most nashi pears prized for a hard, crunchy bite, Meigetsu's flesh is comparatively soft, giving it a texture closer to a ripe European pear while still being harvested and eaten fresh rather than after a storage ripening period. It is not self-fertile and, like other Asian pear cultivars, is vulnerable to fire blight in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Meiling Chinese Chestnut (Historic Large-Nut USDA Introduction)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Meiling is a sister selection to Kuling among the early twentieth-century USDA Chinese chestnut introductions that helped establish blight-resistant chestnut breeding in America, valued for producing unusually large, sweet nuts of good eating quality on a tree that carries the strong natural blight resistance characteristic of Chinese chestnut. It bears reliably within a few years of planting, with nuts dropping free of the spiny burr at maturity in October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate their broad mature canopy and the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Meiwa Kumquat (Large Round Kumquat)
description: Meiwa is thought to be a natural hybrid between the round Marumi and oval Nagami kumquats, combining a thicker, sweeter rind with lower-acid, less seedy pulp than either parent, which makes it the kumquat most people prefer for eating fresh out of hand. The nearly thornless, rounded shrub is slightly smaller and less vigorous than standard Nagami, and it bears heavily on short spurs from late fall into winter. It is self-fertile and does well in large containers as readily as in the ground, and like other kumquats it benefits from a citrus-specific fertilizer and a slightly dry rest period before flowering. Whole fruit, rind and all, can be eaten fresh, candied, or preserved. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Meiwa Kumquat (Round Sweet Kumquat)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Meiwa is self-fruitful and does not require a pollinator. Meiwa kumquat (also spelled Miehua or called 'Sweet Kumquat') is a round-fruited species hybrid distinct from the elongated Nagami, with notably thicker, sweeter edible peel and somewhat less acidic interior flesh than Nagami — making it the most approachable and pleasant kumquat for direct, whole-fruit eating without the sharp pucker of standard types. The round to slightly oval, golden-orange fruits (approximately 1 inch in diameter) ripen November through February and hold well on the tree. Meiwa trees are somewhat more compact than Nagami and are among the most cold-hardy citrus available, tolerating brief temperatures to 16–18°F. An outstanding ornamental container citrus for temperate climates and an excellent Gulf Coast landscape tree. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Meiwa Kumquat (Sweet Round Kumquat)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Meiwa is the sweetest and most widely recommended kumquat cultivar for fresh eating — a round-fruited kumquat (distinct from the oval Nagami kumquat) with notably sweeter, thicker, nearly non-acidic edible skin and sweet-tart flesh. The sweet skin makes Meiwa kumquats the superior choice for eating whole — both skin and flesh are consumed together, and the sweetness of the Meiwa skin dramatically reduces the puckering tart bite that makes Nagami less pleasant for casual snacking. The small, round, golden-orange fruits appear in clusters on a compact, attractive, evergreen tree that makes an outstanding ornamental specimen even when not in fruit. Kumquats are among the most cold-hardy true citrus — surviving to 18–22°F — which makes them excellent choices for the entire Gulf South and even zone 8b gardens with minor winter protection. The trees are naturally compact and can be maintained at 6–10 feet for easy harvesting. Meiwa kumquat fruit is excellent fresh, sliced in salads, made into marmalade, and candied. The attractive, shiny, dark-green foliage and white, fragrant flowers make it an excellent landscape specimen year-round. Excellent container plant for patios and small gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Melinjo (Gnemon Tree, Indonesian Joint Fir)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; melinjo grows slowly and tolerates light shade when young. Gnetum gnemon (melinjo or paddy oat) is one of the most botanically unusual food plants in cultivation: it belongs to the Gnetaceae, a group of gymnosperms (cone-bearing plants related to conifers) rather than flowering plants — making it one of very few non-angiosperm food trees (alongside ginko, cycads, and pines). Despite looking superficially like a tropical flowering tree with broad, opposite, shiny green leaves and red seed pods, it is more closely related to conifers than to any fruit tree. In Indonesia and Malaysia, both the leaves and seeds of melinjo are important food ingredients. The young leaves are used in Javanese vegetable stews (sayur asem) and soups; the seeds, after roasting and pounding flat, are fried to make emping melinjo (also called emping crackers or gnemon chips) — thin, translucent, slightly bitter crackers that are a standard accompaniment to Indonesian nasi goreng, rijsttafel, and as a snack. The ripe red fruits (technically the sarcotesta, a fleshy seed coat rather than true fruit) are boiled and the starchy, mildly bitter seeds inside are peeled, pressed flat, and sun-dried before frying. CAUTION: High in purines — not recommended for gout sufferers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Melissa Lilac Lavender (Pastel English Lavender)
description: A softer-flowered sport of the pink-toned lavender group, this cultivar carries long spikes in a pale lilac-pink wash over compact gray-green foliage, giving a gentler, pastel effect than standard violet-blue English lavenders in mixed borders. It shares the toughness of its species, tolerating heat and drought once established but resenting humid or waterlogged soil. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, avoid heavy mulch against the crown, and shear back after the first flush of bloom to keep growth dense and encourage a second, lighter round of flowers. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Melitopolski Watermelon (Russian Heirloom Watermelon)
description: Sow directly into warm soil once frost danger has passed, and provide consistent moisture while vines establish and fruit sizes up. This heirloom traces to the Melitopol region of southern Ukraine, a historic melon and watermelon growing district, and was bred for a relatively short, reliable season compared to many large Southern watermelon types. Fruits are round with dark green striping and crisp, sweet pink-red flesh, making it a favorite among gardeners in cooler climates who still want an authentic watermelon harvest. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Melody Spinach (AAS-Winning Smooth-Leaf Spinach)
description: Direct sow seed a half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Melody, a 1971 All-America Selections winner, produces smooth to slightly savoyed, dark green leaves with good disease resistance to common spinach ailments, on plants that are somewhat more heat- and bolt-tolerant than many older spinach varieties, useful for extending the harvest a bit later into spring in the Gulf South. Its smooth leaves are easier to clean of grit than heavily crinkled savoy-type spinach. Harvest outer leaves as needed for cut-and-come-again picking, or cut the whole plant at once for a single harvest, and provide light afternoon shade as the weather warms to delay bolting. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Melogold Grapefruit (UC Melogold, Sweet White Grapefruit)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Melogold is a pomelo x white grapefruit hybrid developed by the University of California alongside Oro Blanco from the same breeding program (both released 1980), but with a subtly different flavor — where Oro Blanco has a pomelo-forward character with slightly dry, mealy flesh, Melogold has juicier flesh and a flavor closer to a very sweet, very mildly bitter grapefruit, with somewhat more grapefruit character and slightly more juice than Oro Blanco. Like Oro Blanco, Melogold lacks the bitter naringin flavanone that makes standard grapefruit bitter, but retains more of the characteristic grapefruit aroma and slight tartness, making it a good bridge between grapefruit lovers and those who normally avoid grapefruit bitterness. The large, greenish-yellow to pale-yellow fruits (4–6 inches) ripen October through February and must be tasted to judge ripeness since the skin stays green or pale yellow even when fully ripe. The very large tree is suitable for large home landscapes and the Southern California and Gulf Coast climate in zones 9–11. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Melrose Apple (Ohio State Apple, Jonathan x Delicious Cross)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Melrose was bred by Ohio State University and the USDA from a cross of Jonathan and Red Delicious, released in 1944 and later named the official state apple of Ohio, developed with the specific goal of combining Jonathan's rich flavor with Red Delicious's storage life and size. The large, firm fruit has red-striped skin over a green-yellow background, and the crisp, dense flesh offers a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well both fresh and in the kitchen, equally good for eating out of hand, baking, and sauce. Melrose stores notably well for a mid-century American apple, often keeping several months in good cold storage, and the vigorous, productive tree has made it a lasting favorite for Midwestern home orchards even as many contemporary releases have faded from popularity. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Melrose Pecan (Precocious Early-Bearing Louisiana Pecan)
description: Melrose arose as a chance seedling discovered near Melrose Plantation in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, and was propagated for its unusually precocious habit of bearing a full crop years earlier than most named pecan cultivars. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil with plenty of room to spread, and provide a cultivar with an opposite pollen-shed pattern nearby to ensure full nut set. The medium-sized, well-filled nuts crack out easily and have good flavor, making Melrose a popular dooryard and home-orchard choice across the Gulf South even though it can show more scab susceptibility than newer disease-resistant releases in very humid seasons. Because it fruits so young, growers often use Melrose as a filler tree between longer-lived cultivars, removing it once the permanent trees begin bearing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Melrose Pepper (Utica-Style Italian-American Heirloom Frying Pepper)
description: Sow seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Melrose is an Italian-American heirloom frying pepper long cultivated by home gardeners in central New York's Mohawk Valley, prized for the elongated, thin-walled, pale green fruits that mature to red and carry a sweet flavor with only the faintest whisper of heat. The tender walls cook down quickly when sautéed in olive oil with garlic, making it the traditional pepper folded into Utica-style braised greens alongside hot cherry peppers, breadcrumbs, and provolone. Pick some pods green for a milder, grassier flavor and let others ripen fully red on the vine for maximum sweetness. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Menditoo Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Menditoo was released in 1969 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in the same batch as Briteblue, Delite, and Southland, and it was bred specifically to push ripening earlier in the rabbiteye season. Chill requirement runs about 350-400 hours below 45 degrees F, and fruit colors very early, often ahead of Beckyblue in zone 7-9 plantings. Berries are small to medium with a soft texture and only fair, somewhat tart flavor, which is why it was valued mainly for extending the front of the harvest window rather than for fresh eating, and it has mostly been dropped from modern nursery offerings in favor of Climax and Premier. Give it full sun and acidic, well-drained soil high in organic matter, and expect a productive but short shelf-life crop best used quickly after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Meraviglia di Venezia Pole Bean (Marvel of Venice Yellow Romano Bean)
description: Meraviglia di Venezia, known in English as Marvel of Venice, is an Italian heirloom pole bean bearing flat, lemon-yellow Romano-type pods up to 10 inches long with a buttery texture and no stringiness. It is an early-maturing, white-seeded strain of this classic Venetian bean, ready to pick in about 55 days, notably fast for a climbing variety. The meaty pods hold their quality well even as they lengthen on the vine and are traditionally sliced and dressed simply with lemon, olive oil, and herbs. Because it has become uncommon in commercial production, it is listed on the Slow Food Foundation's Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Merengo Celery
description: Start Merengo celery indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, as the seed germinates slowly and needs a long season; barely cover the tiny seeds since they need light. Transplant hardened seedlings out around the last frost, spacing them 8 to 12 inches apart. Celery is a heavy feeder that demands consistently moist, rich soil to produce tender, flavorful stalks free of stringiness. Water generously and mulch to retain moisture, and harvest whole plants or individual outer stalks as needed. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Merit Corn (Classic Early-Midseason Yellow Hybrid Sweet Corn)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. Merit is a classic standard-sugary yellow hybrid sweet corn that has been a dependable home-garden and market variety for decades, valued for consistent, heavy ear production and good, traditional sweet corn flavor on a vigorous, adaptable plant. Its early-to-midseason maturity makes it a good choice for a first planting in a succession sweet corn schedule through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly, since standard sugary sweet corn converts sugar to starch faster after picking than sugary-enhanced or supersweet types. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Merlin Beet (Downy Mildew-Resistant Bolt-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Merlin is a hybrid beet bred with intermediate resistance to downy mildew and Cercospora leaf spot, two fungal diseases that can blemish and weaken beet tops in humid, wet conditions, along with high resistance to bolting even through a swing of cool-to-warm spring weather. It produces smooth, uniformly round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and good, dark green tops usable as cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 55–62 days from seed.

name: Merlot Lettuce (Deep Burgundy Frilled Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Merlot is a loose-leaf lettuce grown as much for its striking appearance as for eating, producing deeply ruffled, glossy leaves in one of the darkest, most saturated wine-red colors available in lettuce, deepening further with cool nights and bright light. The flavor is sweet and mild despite the intense color, and the ruffled texture and dramatic hue make it a standout addition to salad mixes and a popular choice for edible landscaping in ornamental beds and containers. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole loose head once it reaches full size; like most leaf lettuces it bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plan plantings for the cooler shoulder seasons. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Merlot Pepper
description: Merlot is an early, compact F1 sweet bell hybrid grown for its unusual color sequence, shifting from green to white before purple stripes spread and merge into a deep wine-purple fruit that finishes red if left on the plant. Its short, sturdy habit and disease tolerance make it dependable in both cool springs and hot, humid summers, and the thick walls hold up well for stuffing or fresh slicing. Choose it for a striking, out-of-the-ordinary bell pepper color in mixed vegetable and ornamental edible plantings. Regular harvesting at the purple stage encourages continued fruit set through the season. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Merlot Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Merlot is one of the great Bordeaux red wine grapes, historically blended with Cabernet Sauvignon but equally prized as a varietal wine in its own right, producing softer, rounder, fruit-forward wines with plum and blackberry notes and generally gentler tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon. The vine buds and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, which can be an advantage in shorter growing seasons but also increases the risk of spring frost damage to young growth and demands closer attention to disease management, since the thinner-skinned berries are more susceptible to bunch rot in wet or humid weather. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for airflow around clusters, and monitor closely as harvest approaches, since Merlot can lose acidity quickly once sugar accumulation begins in earnest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Merrylegs Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. One of a number of old West Country perry pears whimsically named for the reputed effects of their potent drink, it is classified as a sweet type with low tannin and low acid, yielding an easy-drinking, mellow perry with less of the harsh astringency typical of the bittersharp varieties. Like other true perry pears it bears hard, astringent fruit of no value for fresh eating, grown purely for fermenting into traditional English perry. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Merton Pride Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. Raised in 1941 by M.B. Crane at the John Innes Horticultural Institute in Merton, London, from a cross of Glou Morceau and Double Williams, it was renamed Merton Pride in 1957 after initially being called Merton Favourite. The large, conical to pyriform fruit has rough green skin ripening to yellow with variable brown russet, and creamy white, soft, smooth, very juicy flesh with excellent sweet, melting texture and good pear flavor. The tree is a moderate cropper with some biennial tendency, ripening its fruit in September. Harvest in September while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Merton Thornless Blackberry (Historic English Thornless Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous, semi-trailing canes onto a two-wire trellis, tying in new growth through the growing season. Bred in England from a thornless mutation, Merton Thornless was one of the first commercially grown thornless blackberry cultivars and became the parent of many later thornless releases, including some of the early Arkansas breeding lines. Fruit is medium-sized, glossy black, and moderately firm with a classic tart-sweet blackberry flavor, ripening in mid-to-late summer. Prune out spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and select the strongest new canes to retie for the following season. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Merveille de Bollwiller Hazelnut (Hall's Giant, Historic European Filbert)
description: Selected in Germany in the late eighteenth century and also sold under the name Hall's Giant, this is one of the oldest named hazelnut cultivars still commercially grown, valued for its large, sweet, thin-shelled nuts and for its long-flowering, purple-blushed catkins that make it a useful cross-pollinator for many other cultivars. The tree is late to leaf out in spring, which helps its young growth avoid frost damage, and it is vigorous and reliably productive once established. Because it is only partially self-fertile, plant it alongside a genetically distinct hazel such as a wild hedgerow hazel or another named cultivar for the heaviest nut set. Harvest in early to mid autumn as the husks color and nuts release freely. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Merveille des Quatre Saisons Lettuce (Marvel of Four Seasons, French Red Butterhead)
description: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 10–12 inches apart; Merveille des Quatre Saisons produces its most stunning red coloration when nights are cool (45–55°F); succession sow every 3 weeks for continuous harvest; harvest full heads by cutting at the base or harvest outer leaves as cut-and-come-again. Merveille des Quatre Saisons is a classic French butterhead heirloom lettuce with roots in the traditional potager (kitchen garden) of France, where it has been grown and selected for generations as both an ornamental and culinary variety of exceptional beauty. The heads are distinctly bicolor: the outer leaves are deep crimson to mahogany-bronze with the red intensifying dramatically in cold weather, while the inner leaves are creamy pale yellow-green — the contrast between brilliant red outer leaves and golden interior makes this one of the most photographed and admired lettuces in the garden. The 'quatre saisons' (four seasons) name reflects its traditional use throughout the growing year in French kitchen gardens. The flavor is excellent: sweet, buttery, and mild with the silky tenderness characteristic of well-grown butterhead types. The name and variety appear in French seed catalogs dating to at least the 1880s, making it among the oldest continuously cultivated lettuce varieties still widely available. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Mesa Queen Squash (AAS-Winning Compact-Vine Kabocha-Type Squash)
description: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to suit the shorter-running vines. Mesa Queen won an All-America Selections award for producing deeply ridged, dark orange-red kabocha-type squash on a plant noticeably more compact than typical maxima vines, making it a practical option for gardeners who want kabocha's dense, dry, sweet flesh without a sprawling vine. Fruit averages 3 to 4 pounds, a convenient size for roasting or steaming whole halves. Harvest once the deep grooves and rich color have fully developed and the rind resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry spot. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Metcalfe Walnut (Cold-Hardy Carpathian Persian Walnut)
description: Metcalfe is a cold-hardy Carpathian-strain Persian walnut selection identified in Canada and valued by northern growers for surviving winter temperatures that kill less hardy English walnut cultivars. It produces a medium, thin-shelled nut with good kernel quality on a tree that tolerates the shorter growing seasons of USDA zone 5 better than California-bred selections such as Chandler. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, provide a compatible pollenizer, and site away from low frost pockets to protect the relatively early spring bloom. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Metechi Hardneck Garlic (Republic of Georgia Rocambole Heirloom)
description: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Metechi is a Rocambole-type hardneck heirloom brought out of the Republic of Georgia, grown for its rich, robust, full-bodied garlic flavor and large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single ring around a hard central stalk. Like other Rocamboles it sends up a distinctive coiling scape in early summer, which should be cut once it curls to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size, and the bulbs store only moderately well compared to porcelain or silverskin types, so plan to use this variety earlier in the storage season. It demands a genuine cold winter to break dormancy and form full-sized bulbs, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens rather than the Deep South. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Meteor Tart Cherry (Cold-Hardy Compact Pie Cherry)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile sour cherry needs no second tree to set fruit. Released by the University of Minnesota, Meteor is a naturally dwarf, extremely cold-hardy tart cherry bred to survive winters too harsh for Montmorency, the standard commercial pie cherry, while producing similar bright red, juicy, tart fruit for pies, preserves, and juice. Its compact, rounded habit tops out well below standard sweet cherry trees, making it easier to net against birds and to harvest without a ladder. Fruit ripens in a concentrated window in midsummer; harvest by cutting or gently pulling clusters, and net the tree as fruit colors up since birds find it just as appealing as gardeners do. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Methley Plum (Red-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Methley is one of the best Japanese plum cultivars for warm climates — a highly productive, self-fertile tree requiring only 250–350 chill hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable plum choices for zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens where most other plum cultivars fail due to insufficient winter cold. The medium-sized fruit has red-purple skin and distinctive red flesh with a sweet-tart, juicy flavor. Methley is an early-season plum that ripens in May or June in zone 8–9, which allows the harvest to be completed before summer heat and disease pressure peak. It is also an effective pollinizer for many other Japanese plum cultivars. Trees are vigorous and productive, beginning to bear 2–3 years after planting. Prune annually after harvest to maintain tree structure and control size. A consistent performer in the Gulf Coast South where it is one of the standard recommendations from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Metolius Blackberry (Extra-Early Trailing Fresh-Market Cultivar)
description: Metolius is a trailing blackberry from the USDA-ARS breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, prized as one of the earliest-ripening trailing cultivars available, well ahead of older Pacific Northwest standards. Breeders selected it for fruit firm enough to hold up to wholesale fresh-market shipping, a trait uncommon among the earliest-ripening trailing types, and it has been evaluated for cold hardiness and machine-harvest suitability in Pacific Northwest trials. The long, sprawling canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous row spacing to manage their trailing growth. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and train in the season's new primocanes, and provide full sun with good air movement, since trailing blackberries bred for the cool, dry Pacific Northwest can be more disease-prone in hot, humid climates. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Metro PMR Butternut Squash
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Metro PMR is a butternut squash hybrid bred specifically for high resistance to powdery mildew, so foliage stays greener and more productive later into summer than standard butternut varieties, which typically succumb to mildew before the crop has fully sized and cured. It produces the classic tan, bottle-shaped butternut fruit with dense, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and purees. Let fruit mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for one to two weeks; properly cured squash stores for several months in a cool, dry pantry. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Mexican Bay Leaf (Mexican Avocado Leaf, Hoja de Aguacate)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harvest leaves as needed throughout the growing season and dry for storage. Persea drymifolia (Mexican bay leaf or hoja de aguacate) is a Mexican and Central American tree in the avocado family (Lauraceae) grown primarily for its strongly aromatic leaves, which have a complex, distinctive fragrance and flavor combining anise (star anise), cinnamon, and sassafras. The leaves are not related to European bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) but occupy a similar culinary role in southern Mexican cooking — they are an essential, non-substitutable ingredient in Oaxacan mole negro, tasajo, estofado, and tamales, where they are toasted on a comal (griddle) before use to intensify their flavor and then added whole to slow-cooked dishes. The trees also occasionally produce small, avocado-like fruits that are inedible but closely resemble tiny avocados. In zone 9–11, the tree grows as a small to medium ornamental specimen; the leaves can be dried and stored for use. Dried Mexican bay leaves can be purchased at Mexican grocery stores but fresh-from-the-tree leaves are far more fragrant. A unique culinary herb tree that no serious Oaxacan cooking enthusiast should be without. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Cream Guava (White-Fleshed Sweet Guava)
description: A favorite fresh-eating guava across South Texas and Florida dooryards, this cultivar bears thin yellow skin over creamy white, very sweet, low-acid flesh with comparatively few seeds. It fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the shrub-form tree compact and stimulates a fresh flush of fruiting growth. Roots generally survive brief dips to around 28°F even when the canopy freezes back, so zone 9 gardeners should mulch heavily and expect to regrow top growth after a hard freeze; in warm years the plant can produce two overlapping harvests. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Elderberry / Blue Elderberry
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moderately moist soil; Mexican elderberry is more drought-tolerant than eastern common elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established and adapts well to the neutral to alkaline soils of the Southwest, California foothills, and the intermountain West. Sambucus mexicana (syn. Sambucus nigra subsp. cerulea) is the native elderberry of California, the Southwest, and the Pacific Northwest mountains, forming a large, fast-growing, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with massive, flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) of creamy-white blossoms in late spring that are irresistible to native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. The flowers are followed by heavy drooping clusters of small, powdery-blue to blue-black berries in late summer — excellent for elderberry syrup, jelly, wine, and traditional medicine. CAUTION: cook berries before eating; raw berries, bark, and leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides. An outstanding wildlife plant — the berries are consumed by dozens of bird species including waxwings, robins, and thrushes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Mint (Cuban Oregano)
description: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in water or moist perlite at room temperature; Mexican mint roots quickly and is one of the easiest herbs to propagate. The thick, velvety leaves have an intense oregano-thyme-sage fragrance much stronger than true oregano — a small amount seasons an entire dish. It is used widely in Caribbean, Indian, and Southeast Asian cooking for meat marinades, bean dishes, and stuffings. The plant tolerates heat and drought extremely well, making it ideal for hot, humid Gulf Coast conditions. Bring containers indoors before frost; a single overwintered plant provides cuttings to replant each spring. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Oregano
description: Lippia graveolens is the true oregano of Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking — a shrubby, woody perennial native to dry, rocky hillsides from northern Mexico through Central America whose strongly aromatic, slightly rough-textured leaves have a more intense, earthy, and complex flavor than Mediterranean oregano (Origanum vulgare), making it the preferred herb in authentic salsa, mole, chili, and carne asada recipes. Propagate from semi-hardwood stem cuttings, which root readily in moist perlite or sand; Mexican oregano is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in full sun, hot conditions, and lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil — rich, moist soils reduce essential oil concentration and can cause root rot. In zones 9-11 it grows as a multi-stemmed shrub 2-4 feet tall, bearing small, white, tubular flowers attractive to bees and butterflies throughout the warm season; in zone 9 a hard freeze may kill top growth, but established plants typically regrow vigorously from the roots in spring. Harvest leafy branch tips at any time during the growing season; the flavor is most concentrated just before flowering and the leaves dry well, intensifying in aroma much like Mediterranean oregano. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Oregano
description: Poliomintha longiflora is a strongly aromatic shrubby herb native to the Chihuahuan Desert and south Texas, widely prized in Mexican regional cuisine as the true 'Mexican oregano' — its flavor is more complex and citrusy than Mediterranean oregano and is considered essential for authentic mole sauces, tamales, and chili con carne. Plant in the hottest, driest, most well-drained spot in the garden; once established it requires little to no supplemental water and thrives on neglect in rocky, alkaline soils. The long, lavender-pink tubular flowers produced from summer through fall are highly attractive to hummingbirds and are among the best late-season nectar sources in xeric gardens. In zone 9 and warmer the plant is evergreen and can be harvested year-round; in zone 7-8 it may die back to the roots in hard winters but re-sprouts reliably in spring. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Pinyon (Three-needle Pinyon)
description: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; Mexican pinyon is the most widely distributed of the Mexican pinyon pines — a three-needle pinyon (three needles per bundle, distinguishing it from the two-needle Colorado pinyon) of the dry mountain ranges of Mexico and into trans-Pecos Texas, southeastern Arizona, and southern New Mexico. The most important commercial pine nut tree in Mexico and an important food plant for Indigenous peoples of northern Mexico. More heat-tolerant than Colorado pinyon, extending into warmer, drier climates of zones 6–9 in the Southwest — an excellent xeriscape tree for hot, dry Texas Hill Country, west Texas, and similar climates where Colorado pinyon is marginally hardy. The nuts are smaller than Colorado pinyon nuts but comparable in flavor and nutritional quality. Slow-growing but long-lived — old trees develop picturesque, gnarled forms on rocky, exposed slopes. An underused edible landscape tree for dry southwestern gardens. Matures in 730–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Pitaya (Dagger Cactus, Pitaya Agria)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican pitaya is a large, multi-stemmed columnar cactus native to the dry coastal and lowland regions of Venezuela, Colombia, the Caribbean islands, and Mexico, grown for centuries in tropical America for its edible fruits — the pitayas are oval to round, 2–3 inches long, with a thin, red or yellowish skin studded with clusters of spines and translucent white to reddish, sweet, refreshing flesh surrounding the seeds, with a flavor combining gentle sweetness with a slightly acidic, wine-like finish. In Oaxacan markets, fresh pitayas are a beloved seasonal delicacy sold from June through August. The plant grows as an upright, branching, candelabra-shaped cactus that makes an impressive landscape specimen reaching 10–20 feet. The white, night-blooming flowers are adapted for bat pollination. Different from the pitahaya/dragon fruit (Selenicereus undatus) in being a columnar cactus rather than a climbing vine cactus. An outstanding ornamental and edible cactus for zone 9–12 landscapes. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Plum (Big Tree Plum, Creek Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Mexican plum tolerates rocky, shallow, limestone soils that defeat most fruit trees. Prunus mexicana (Mexican plum or big tree plum) is the largest native plum of Texas and a landscape-worthy ornamental tree as well as a valuable food plant — more tree-like in form than the suckering Chickasaw plum, growing to 15–25 feet as a single-trunked specimen with attractive, exfoliating, reddish-brown bark. The 1-to-1.5-inch, dark-red to purple-red plums ripen in August–September with a rich, sweet-tart flavor excellent for jams, jellies, preserves, and fresh eating. Clouds of fragrant white flowers smother the bare branches in February–March, making it one of the most spectacular early-flowering native trees in the Texas landscape. Mexican plum is self-fertile, requiring no cross-pollination; it is also one of the most limestone and drought-tolerant of the native plums, thriving in the alkaline, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Post Oak Savanna. Wildlife value is high — the large fruits are consumed by deer, foxes, raccoons, and many bird species. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Mexican Sour Gherkin (Cucamelon, Mouse Melon)
description: Transplant or direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the thin, wiry, climbing vines, which are more delicate looking than standard cucumber vines but grow just as vigorously in heat. Mexican Sour Gherkin, also called cucamelon or mouse melon, is a distinct species related to cucumbers, native to Mexico and Central America, that produces an enormous number of grape-to-thumb-sized fruit with the striped look of a tiny watermelon and a crisp, tangy, cucumber-with-a-citrusy-sour-edge flavor, eaten whole, skin and all. The heat-loving vines shrug off the humid Gulf Coast summer far better than standard cucumbers and keep producing steadily through conditions that stall out most other cucurbits, with harvest starting once fruits reach about an inch long and firm. Pick regularly, since the tiny fruits go from perfect to overripe quickly, and the vigorous vines benefit from vertical support both to save space and to keep the abundant fruit clean and easy to spot. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Mexican Tarragon (Mexican Mint Marigold)
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in warm starting mix or propagate by stem cuttings, which root readily in moist perlite. Mexican tarragon thrives in the same hot, humid summers that kill French tarragon and delivers a very similar anise-like flavor; harvest foliage throughout the season by pinching stem tips. It blooms in fall with small golden-yellow flowers that attract butterflies — you can allow blooming or deadhead to maintain leaf production. In zone 9–11 the plant is perennial; cut back hard in early spring to stimulate fresh growth. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Mexico Midget Tomato (Tiny-Fruited Heirloom Currant Tomato)
description: Transplant into warm soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the sprawling vines since a single plant can carry hundreds of tiny fruit clusters by midsummer. Mexico Midget is a wild-type heirloom currant tomato collected in Mexico, producing an explosion of pea-sized, intensely sweet-tart red fruits in loose clusters continuously from early summer to frost. The tough little vines shrug off the heat, humidity, and disease pressure that slow down larger-fruited tomatoes, making this one of the most productive and trouble-free tomatoes for Gulf South gardens. Fruits are best picked and eaten straight off the vine or tossed whole into salads, since their small size makes stemming tedious for cooking; a light monthly feeding and consistent watering keep the sprawling plants producing all season. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Mexicola Avocado (Most Cold-Hardy Avocado, Mexican Race Black Avocado, Edible-Skin Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexicola is more compact than most avocados; plant with a Type B companion (Fuerte, Bacon) for best fruit set; harvest August–October (earlier than most avocados) when the small fruits turn glossy purple-black; the thin, papery skin is edible and contributes an anise-herb flavor to the fruit; slice and eat with skin on for the full flavor experience. Mexicola avocado is a pure Mexican race avocado (Persea americana var. drymifolia) with remarkable cold-hardiness traceable to its highland Mexican origin, where ancestors of this variety grew at elevations above 6,000 feet where frost is common — making Mexicola and its relatives the most frost-tolerant avocados that produce edible fruit, with documented survival at 18–22°F that no Guatemalan-race variety (Hass, Reed) can approach. This cold-hardiness has made Mexicola the recommended avocado for zone 8b gardens in the Gulf South, California's inland valleys, and anywhere else where an extra 6–8°F of frost protection would make the difference between avocado success and failure. Mexicola's distinctive features beyond cold-hardiness include small fruit size (3–6 oz compared to Hass's 6–12 oz), very thin, edible skin with an anise or licorice flavor that is typically eaten along with the flesh, and a very high oil content with a rich, complex flavor. The trees are relatively compact (15–25 feet) compared to standard avocados. Mexican race avocados like Mexicola also produce aromatic leaves used as a culinary herb in Oaxacan and other Mexican cuisines. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mexicola Grande Avocado (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexicola Grande is a larger-fruited selection out of the classic Mexicola avocado line, retaining the same remarkable cold-hardiness that makes Mexican-race avocados the only avocados worth attempting in zone 8b–9, while offering noticeably bigger fruit than the original Mexicola. Like its parent, Mexicola Grande is a pure Mexican-race avocado (Persea americana var. drymifolia) with thin, edible skin carrying a distinctive anise or licorice note, rich, high-oil flesh, and a compact tree form compared to tropical Guatemalan-race cultivars like Hass. Established trees tolerate brief drops into the high teens °F with wood damage but often survive and resprout, whereas standard nursery avocado cultivars are killed outright at those temperatures. Plant with a Type B pollinator such as Fuerte, Bacon, or Zutano for improved fruit set, and harvest in late summer to fall once fruit reaches full size and skin darkens to near-black; slice and eat with the thin skin on for the full anise-inflected flavor. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Meyer Lemon
description: Meyer lemon is a natural hybrid between a lemon and either a mandarin or sweet orange, resulting in a thinner-skinned, less acidic, and more cold-tolerant fruit than standard lemon varieties; it tolerates brief dips to about 22°F once established. It is self-fertile, blooms nearly year-round in frost-free climates, and is exceptionally well-suited to container culture — a 20-gallon pot allows the plant to be moved indoors in zones 7–8. Plant in fast-draining citrus mix or well-amended garden soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer. Fruit is ripe when the skin turns deep golden-yellow and yields to gentle pressure; the rind is thin and zests well for culinary use. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Meylan Walnut (Grenoble AOC French Persian Walnut)
description: Meylan is a traditional French Persian walnut cultivar long grown in the hills around Grenoble as part of the Noix de Grenoble appellation, prized for its large, attractive nut and mild, sweet kernel flavor. It leafs out relatively late in spring, reducing frost damage risk to the flowers in the cool foothill climate where it is traditionally grown. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, provide a compatible pollenizer, and allow ample room for a broad mature canopy. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mi Lan Xiang Tea (Honey Orchid Dan Cong)
description: Mi Lan Xiang, literally 'honey orchid fragrance,' is the single most widely planted of the named Phoenix (Feng Huang) Dan Cong cultivars from the Chaozhou highlands of Guangdong, China, chosen for oolong processing that brings out sweet, nectarine-like fruit and orchid aromatics with a lingering honeyed finish. It grows as a large-leaved, upright arbor-type shrub, distinct from the small compact China-type bushes used for most green teas, and traditionally develops into a substantial small tree if left unpruned at high elevation. Processing follows classic oolong methods, withering, bruising, partial oxidation, and roasting, to develop its signature aroma, so home growers wanting the characteristic flavor should replicate oolong rather than green-tea processing. Give it warm, humid conditions and the same acidic, well-drained soil required by other tea camellias. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mibuna
description: Direct sow in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun 4 weeks before last frost in spring or 8–10 weeks before first frost in fall; mibuna is a Japanese mustard green that produces smooth, narrow, rounded-tip, dark-green leaves distinctly different from the deeply lobed, feathery leaves of its close relative mizuna — the mild, slightly peppery, clean flavor of mibuna is excellent raw in salads and wilted in stir-fries, soups, and noodle dishes. It is harvested by cut-and-come-again method — cut outer leaves at 4–6 inches tall, leaving the center growing point intact, and plants regrow multiple times. Extremely cold-tolerant (withstands light frost) and among the fastest-maturing of all brassica greens. Bolt-resistant in cool conditions but seeds quickly in heat. Outstanding value as a winter salad green in zones 7–10 where it can be grown year-round with cold frame protection. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Michal Apple (Israeli Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Michal was developed by breeder Chanan Oppenheimer in Israel and is conditionally recommended by University of Florida trials as a mid-season companion to earlier Gulf South standards like Anna and Ein Shemer. It requires roughly 425 chill hours and ripens later in summer than Anna, extending the harvest window into the humid, disease-pressured part of the Gulf Coast season. Fruit is medium-sized, round to slightly oblate, and notably crisp compared to many other low-chill selections. Growers should watch closely for scab and fire blight given its later ripening into wetter conditions. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Michigan State Kiwi (Cold-Hardy MSU-Selected Kiwiberry)
description: Michigan State is a female hardy kiwiberry selection developed at Michigan State University and grown for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating winter lows that damage many other Actinidia arguta cultivars. Fruit is grape-sized with smooth green skin and sweet flesh, ripening in early to mid fall. Being dioecious, it requires a separate male arguta vine nearby for pollination and fruit set. Provide a heavy-duty trellis and prune each winter to remove old wood and maintain an open, productive canopy. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Michurinska-10 Fig (Bulgarian Cold-Hardy Fig)
description: Michurinska-10 originated near the town of Michurin on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and is grown chiefly for exceptional cold hardiness among quality-fruited figs. Fruit is medium-sized with a bright, sweet, berry-toned flavor, produced as an early breba crop followed by a main crop. Its key advantage over most Gulf South cultivars is that it reliably sets a main crop even on new growth pushed after a hard freeze kills the top of the tree back to the ground, so a single unusually cold winter is far less likely to cost a full year's harvest. Because it was selected for far colder climates than the Gulf Coast, treat its heat and humidity tolerance here as unproven rather than assumed. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mickylee Watermelon (Early Disease-Resistant Icebox Watermelon)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mickylee was released by the University of Florida and bred for early maturity and reliable resistance to fusarium wilt, a soil-borne disease that can devastate watermelon plantings in warm, humid growing regions where the fungus persists in the soil for years. The round, medium-small icebox-type fruit has sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a thin rind, making a single melon a manageable size for a small household without leftovers going to waste. The compact vines and early ripening window make it a good choice for shorter growing seasons or for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest than larger, later-maturing watermelon varieties provide. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries, and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Micmac Strawberry (Historic Kentville Cold-Hardy Strawberry)
description: Micmac is an early-to-mid-season strawberry released by the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia, valued through the mid-20th century for outstanding winter hardiness and reliable cropping in the short-season, cold-winter regions of Atlantic Canada. Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and mulch the planting heavily over winter in the coldest parts of its range. The berries run small to medium with firm flesh well suited to preserves, and plants throw vigorous runners that fill in a matted row quickly. Though long superseded by later Kentville and Ottawa introductions for fresh-market use, Micmac's hardiness made it valuable breeding stock, contributing to later cold-tolerant cultivars such as Glooscap. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Micro Tom Tomato (Ultra-Dwarf Research and Container Tomato)
description: Sow seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a small pot once true leaves appear, since the plants never need staking and stay compact from seed to fruit. Micro-Tom was bred at the University of Florida from a cross of 'Florida Basket' and 'Ohio 4013-3' and carries a mutation that stunts its growth to just a few inches tall with a life cycle of only a few months, making it one of the most widely used model organisms in tomato genetics research worldwide. Home gardeners grow it mainly as a novelty for windowsills and tiny containers, where it still produces a modest crop of small, edible red fruit. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Mid-Pride Peach (California Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach with Excellent Flavor)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches when marble-sized for maximum fruit size. Harvest when skin background has transitioned from green to yellow-orange and fruit gives slightly to firm pressure. Mid-Pride is a California-developed low-chill peach variety considered by many low-chill peach enthusiasts to be among the finest-flavored low-chill varieties available in North America. The variety was selected from University of California breeding programs that worked systematically to reduce chill hour requirements while maintaining the fruit quality characteristics (flavor complexity, sugar-acid balance, flesh texture) that distinguish premium peaches from the bland, fibrous fruit that many early low-chill releases produced. The fruit is medium to large, with yellow skin blushed red and yellow freestone flesh — the freestone character (flesh separates cleanly from the pit at full ripeness) makes Mid-Pride practical for fresh eating, canning, preserving, and freezing without the effort of separating clingstone flesh. The flavor is genuinely excellent for a low-chill variety: sweet with good acid balance, peach aroma, and the melting, juicy flesh texture that characterizes premium peaches. For Gulf Coast zone 9 gardeners, Mid-Pride represents one of the most reliable paths to growing truly excellent-quality peaches in a climate that limits most other stone fruit production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Middletown Pawpaw
description: Middletown is one of the older named pawpaw selections, tracing to Middletown, Ohio, and documented in historic cultivar surveys compiled by Kentucky State University. It performs well as a dooryard tree in the Ohio Valley climate it originated in. Provide part shade while young, since pawpaw is naturally an understory species, then transition to more sun once the tree is fruiting-age. Feed lightly with a balanced organic fertilizer in early spring and keep the root zone consistently moist through fruit development. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Midget Summer Savory
description: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for an extra-early container crop. Midget is a compact, densely branched selection of summer savory that stays only about 10 to 12 inches tall with proportionally more leaf mass per plant than standard seed strains, making it well suited to pots, window boxes, and tight raised-bed edges. Its narrow, dark green leaves carry the same peppery, thyme-and-mint-tinged summer savory flavor as the full-sized species and can be harvested continuously through the season. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep the dense habit tidy and to delay flowering, which lets flavor hold longer than it does on unpinched plants. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Midknight Valencia Orange (Nearly Seedless Late-Season Sweet Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate, feeding with a citrus fertilizer program three times a year as with any Valencia-type orange. Midknight is a bud sport of Valencia that originated in South Africa and was selected specifically because it produces far fewer seeds, typically none to a handful per fruit, while keeping the deep orange color, abundant juice, and classic sweet-tart Valencia flavor. Like standard Valencia, it ripens uniquely late in the season, holding on the tree from spring into early summer after navels and other oranges have finished, which makes it a good way to stretch home dooryard citrus harvest into the hottest months. It shares Valencia's relatively good cold tolerance for a sweet orange, tolerating brief dips into the mid-20s F once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Midland Hawthorn (English May, Woodland Hawthorn)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; midland hawthorn tolerates heavier clay soils and partial shade better than common hawthorn. Crataegus laevigata (midland hawthorn or English May) is a native European hawthorn species closely related to — and often confused with — common hawthorn (C. monogyna), but botanically distinguished by having 2–3 styles per flower (instead of one in C. monogyna), deeply lobed but less deeply cut leaves, and preferring the partial-shade, moist-soil woodland-edge habitat rather than open scrub and hedgerows. Both species are called 'May' or 'May blossom' in England, referring to the masses of white (or in cultivated forms, pink or red) flowers in May that were traditionally brought into homes for May Day celebrations. The deep-red to scarlet fruits (haws) are similar to those of C. monogyna: small, oval, containing 2–3 seeds, with a mild, floury, slightly sweet-tart flavor. In European herbal tradition, hawthorn berries and flowers are among the most important cardiovascular herbs — widely used in European phytomedicine for mild heart conditions, improving coronary blood flow, and supporting healthy blood pressure. The double-flowered pink ornamental forms ('Paul's Scarlet' and 'Rosea Flore Pleno') are among the most popular ornamental flowering trees in British gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Midnight Cascade Blueberry (Trailing Vanilla-Flavored Hanging-Basket Blueberry, 'FC12-187')
description: Midnight Cascade is a patented Bushel and Berry companion to Sapphire Cascade, sharing the same trailing, downward-arching habit bred for hanging baskets rather than a traditional upright bush form. Its deep-blue, medium-sized berries ripen in midsummer with a distinctive hint of vanilla in the flavor, setting it apart from most other blueberry cultivars. It is self-fertile and bears a crop on its own, though pairing it with Sapphire Cascade or another low-chill blueberry nearby can improve pollination and yield. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Midnight Snack Tomato (AAS-Winning Indigo Anthocyanin Cherry Tomato that Changes Color at Ripeness)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when underside turns fully red to match upper blue-red skin. Midnight Snack Tomato is one of the most visually distinctive cherry tomato varieties available — a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program's work on anthocyanin accumulation in tomato fruit skin. Anthocyanins are a class of pigments responsible for blue, purple, and red colors in many plants (blueberries, purple cabbage, red grapes, black currants), and OSU researchers identified and bred for a trait that causes anthocyanins to accumulate in tomato fruit skin in response to light exposure. In Midnight Snack, the sun-exposed upper portion of each cherry develops a dramatic deep blue-black to dark indigo color while the shaded underside remains the conventional cherry-red of a ripe tomato — creating a two-toned fruit unlike any traditional tomato variety. When fully ripe, the red color from the underside gradually encompasses the fruit, providing a visual cue: as the red progresses upward to meet the darkening blue-black, the fruit is at peak ripeness. The flavor combines genuine sweetness with a fruity, complex quality that reflects the improved eating quality bred into OSU's anthocyanin lines beyond their visual novelty. Beyond appearance, the high anthocyanin content of Midnight Snack skin provides measurable antioxidant value — anthocyanins contribute to the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant capacity associated with blueberry and dark fruit consumption — with zone 9's intense sun exposure maximizing anthocyanin production in the fruit. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Midori Giant Soybean
description: Midori Giant is a compact heirloom edamame that sets large, plump pods packed with tender, protein-rich beans.
