Sow seed directly into warm soil in full sun once frost danger has passed, spacing plants a few inches apart in rows. The bushy plants stay tidy and are well suited to smaller gardens and raised beds. Harvest pods when they are bright green and full but before they yellow, then steam or freeze promptly. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: MidSouth Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Mississippi Bunch Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the moderately vigorous canopy. MidSouth was released by Mississippi State University in 1981, tracing back to USDA breeding work begun in the late 1930s at the Meridian, Mississippi field station, and it remains valued today for its exceptional tolerance of Pierce's disease across Mississippi, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf South states. Its self-fertile vines produce clusters of dark blue-purple berries covered in a heavy waxy bloom that ripen in late July to mid-August in the southern part of its range, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor carrying a hint of raspberry; the seeded, slip-skin berries are best suited to jelly and juice rather than fresh table use. The vine is more susceptible to fungal disease and root-knot nematodes than to Pierce's disease itself, so a regular fungicide program and nematode-aware site selection help keep plantings productive. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons to keep cluster and berry size from declining. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Midyim Berry (Midgen Berry)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery liners in spring in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving light afternoon shade where summers run hot. This low, spreading Australian bush-food shrub produces small white flowers followed by white, red-freckled berries with a spicy, blueberry-like flavor over a long summer-to-fall season, forming a durable, drought-tolerant edible groundcover once its roots are established. It has almost no frost tolerance, so treat it as a container plant that can be moved under cover anywhere winter lows dip much below freezing. A light shearing after each fruiting flush keeps the mat dense and encourages the next round of flowers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mighty Fine Muscadine Grape
description: Mighty Fine (selection AM-70) was released in fall 2025 by the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture's fruit breeding program, named for retired breeder John Clark's favorite phrase of approval. It is a self-fertile, black-skinned muscadine with notably large berries bred for fresh eating, and it carries better cold tolerance than most Southern-bred muscadines, extending the crop's range further north than older varieties like Carlos or Noble. In 2022 field-day taste trials it beat out the long-standard Supreme cultivar as attendees' favorite fresh-eating muscadine. Give it full sun and a sturdy trellis; as a very new release, long-term disease performance outside Arkansas trial plots is still being documented. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mignonette Alpine Strawberry (French Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)
description: Mignonette is a compact French heirloom alpine strawberry, considered an improved selection of the old Reine des Vallees type, grown for its dainty pointed red berries and rich woodland-strawberry perfume rather than for size or yield. Plants form neat, semi-evergreen mounds without runners and often produce a light crop the first season from an early indoor sowing. Grow in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; it tolerates partial shade but sets more fruit with several hours of direct sun. Because the berries are small, soft, and quick to perfume a whole bowl, they are best used fresh for snacking, garnishing desserts, or infusing drinks rather than for preserving. Matures in 85–110 days from transplant.

name: Miho Satsuma (Early Compact Gulf South Satsuma)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Another early-ripening Japanese satsuma selection similar in season to Okitsu, Miho has become one of the most commonly sold satsuma cultivars in Gulf Coast nurseries because of its naturally compact, rounded growth habit and dependable early crop of small, sweet, essentially seedless fruit. Fruit typically colors and ripens in October, ahead of standard-season satsumas, with loose rind that peels away easily in segments. The tree's smaller stature also makes it a good option for large containers that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Miike Giant Mustard (Giant Red Japanese Heirloom Mustard)
description: Miike Giant is a Japanese heirloom mustard prized for its huge, savoyed leaves that emerge green and develop striking bronze-purple coloring and deep-cut, ruffled margins as they mature. Direct sow into fertile soil and thin generously, since mature plants form large, dramatic rosettes over two feet across. Young leaves are milder and good raw, while mature leaves carry substantial heat and are best braised, stir-fried, or used in kimchi-style ferments. The plant's size and color also make it a striking addition to ornamental vegetable plantings. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Milam Apple (Drought-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Keeper)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Milam is a Southern heirloom apple, likely originating in Virginia or North Carolina in the early 1800s, valued historically for a rare combination of drought tolerance, disease resistance, and reliable annual bearing that made it a dependable choice for Southern farmsteads without irrigation or modern spray programs. The small to medium red fruit has crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh and keeps reasonably well in cool storage, useful for extending fresh apple availability into winter. The tree's genuine toughness and adaptability to less-than-ideal growing conditions have kept it valued among heirloom orchardists in the South even as more demanding, higher-input modern varieties have become common elsewhere. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Milenio Coffee
description: Milenio is an F1 hybrid variety created by cooperative Central American coffee research programs from a cross between a Sarchimor-derived line and the Ethiopian landrace Rume Sudan, part of a wave of F1 coffee hybrids bred for vigor and climate resilience rather than being fixed, true-breeding lines. It combines coffee leaf rust resistance with tolerance of coffee berry disease, strong yields, and a distinctive cup noted for dark chocolate, cane sugar, and citrus notes that exceed what older rust-resistant hybrids typically offer. Because it is an F1 hybrid, seed-grown plants show more variability than clonally propagated varieties, so commercial plantings are usually established from tissue-cultured or grafted plantlets rather than open-pollinated seed. It performs best in shaded agroforestry systems at higher elevation, and otherwise wants the same rich, well-drained, partially shaded conditions favored by other highland arabica. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Miles Choice Bay Laurel
description: Miles Choice is a selection of common bay laurel bred for a denser, more upright habit than the species, with smaller, more crowded glossy dark-green leaves that make it especially forgiving of regular shearing. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and let the top few inches dry between waterings once established. Because it holds a tidy shape with less pruning effort than seed-grown bay, it is favored for clipped hedges, screens, and formal standards, though the aromatic leaves can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like ordinary bay laurel. In marginal zones grow it in a container and shelter it from hard freezes and drying winter wind. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Milk Thistle
description: Direct sow 1/4 in deep in early spring; milk thistle germinates readily in cool, moist conditions and self-seeds vigorously once established. Plants become quite large and spiny — space generously and wear gloves when tending them. Monitor flower heads closely as seeds ripen quickly and can be scattered by wind; harvest heads when the fluffy pappus begins to appear but before seeds fully disperse. Dry seed heads on a tray, then thresh to separate the hard achenes, which are ground or extracted for their silymarin content in liver-supportive preparations. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Milkberry (Snowberry, West Indian Snowberry)
description: A sprawling, semi-woody vine-shrub of Florida and Gulf Coast maritime hammocks, milkberry produces small fragrant white tubular flowers followed by glossy white berries that persist through much of the year and are relished by birds. It scrambles over neighboring shrubs or can be kept as a loose mounding groundcover shrub with occasional pruning. Grow in partial shade to filtered sun in humus-rich, well-drained soil typical of coastal hammock understories, and provide some wind protection when young since it is not a true front-dune plant. Its salt and drought tolerance once established make it useful as a naturalizing understory shrub in restored maritime forest plantings. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Milky Oats
description: Grown as milky oats, this Avena sativa is harvested at the soft, immature seed stage prized in herbal wellness, and it also serves as a soil-building cover crop. Broadcast or drill the seed into cool, moist spring soil and rake it in, keeping the bed evenly watered until it establishes. It grows quickly in full sun and average ground, tolerating light frost. Watch the developing seed heads and gather the tops when they exude a milky sap for the traditional harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Millennia Blueberry (Early-Midseason University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Millennia is a University of Florida southern highbush release from the Lyrene breeding program, first released in 2001 and since become one of the most widely planted low-chill blueberry cultivars in north-central Florida. The vigorous, upright bush blooms and ripens in the early-to-midseason window and carries a moderate chilling requirement for a southern highbush selection, letting it perform reliably through the mild, unpredictable winters typical of the Gulf Coast. Plant alongside another southern highbush cultivar with an overlapping bloom period to improve fruit set and berry size. Prune out the oldest canes each winter and keep the shallow root zone mulched with pine bark to conserve moisture through the humid growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Miller American Persimmon
description: Miller is grown for producing some of the largest fruit known among American persimmon selections, regularly exceeding two and a half inches across, with color ranging from light yellow-orange to a deeper orange-red depending on the season and ripeness. The tree tends toward a multi-stemmed, wide-spreading form with drooping branches and foliage that give it a looser, almost tropical look compared with the more upright habit of many other native persimmon cultivars. It is vigorous and comes into bearing relatively early for the species, typically by its third year, and produces heavy annual crops once mature. Like all American persimmon, fruit must fully soften on the tree or be sweetened by a hard frost before eating, since unripe fruit is strongly astringent; drop typically runs from October into late November depending on region. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Millionaire Eggplant (Vigorous Slender Asian Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Millionaire is a widely grown Asian-type hybrid eggplant producing long, slender, glossy dark purple fruit with tender, nearly seedless flesh and thin skin that needs no peeling. It bears exceptionally early and heavily, often setting its first harvestable fruit faster than most other eggplant types, and continues producing steadily through hot, humid summer weather that can slow other varieties. The slim fruit is well suited to quick-cooking methods like stir-frying and grilling, since it cooks through fast without the bitterness or heavy seediness of larger globe eggplants. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm, about 6-9 inches long, since overripe fruit turns dull and develops tougher skin and larger seeds. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Millionaire Japanese Eggplant
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Millionaire is a Japanese-type hybrid eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, deep purple-black fruits of exceptional quality and high yields — the name reflects its extraordinary productivity under good growing conditions. The thin, tender skin and nearly seedless, non-bitter flesh make it ideal for slicing, stir-frying, and grilling without peeling or salting. It is a high-yield variety developed in Japan and widely grown in zone 9 commercial and home gardens for the Southern Asian food market. The plants are vigorous and productive from summer through fall, with fruit set continuing reliably even in the peak heat of Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when skin is deep purple and glossy at 6–8 inches — fruits become seedy and bitter if allowed to grow to full size. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Millionaire Okra (Early Prolific F1 Hybrid Okra)
description: Millionaire is an F1 hybrid bred from Clemson Spineless lines to mature earlier and set pods more heavily than many open-pollinated okra varieties. Sturdy, medium-large plants hold up well to wind and heavy fruit load, producing flavorful pods best cut at three to four inches for peak tenderness. Its early start makes it well suited to regions with a shorter warm season, since it begins yielding before many heirloom types hit their stride. Frequent picking through the heat of summer keeps this vigorous hybrid setting new flowers rather than diverting energy into oversized, fibrous pods. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Miner's Lettuce (Winter Purslane)
description: Direct-sow in fall in moist, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; miner's lettuce is a western North American native cool-season annual producing the most distinctive leaf form of any salad green — later-produced stem leaves are perfectly round, like a disc, with the stem growing through the center of the leaf, giving the appearance of a small lily-pad with the flower stalk emerging from the middle. Earlier leaves are long-stalked and spade-shaped. The plant was a critical winter and spring food source for California Native Americans and was later eaten by gold rush miners (hence the name) to prevent scurvy. The flavor is mild and succulent, similar to spinach or purslane, and the entire plant is edible raw or cooked — leaves, stems, and small white flowers. It thrives in shade where most vegetables fail, making it invaluable for shaded vegetable gardens. In zone 8–10, it grows abundantly through fall, winter, and spring and dies back in summer heat. Self-sows reliably to maintain a self-perpetuating colony that requires no maintenance. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Mini Love Watermelon (Personal-Size Crack-Resistant AAS Winner)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Mini Love is a personal-size seeded watermelon bred for early maturity and crack resistance, producing round, 3-6 pound fruit with sweet, crisp, deep red flesh perfect for a single small household to finish in one sitting. Its shorter vines and lighter fruit make it a good candidate for growing up a trellis with fruit slings for support, saving ground space in a small garden. Because it matures faster than standard full-size watermelon, it also fits well into a shorter spring or fall planting window. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Mini Red Bell Sweet Pepper
description: Start this compact mini bell pepper indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm for reliable germination. The plant stays a tidy 24 inches tall, making it well suited to containers and small spaces. Transplant out after nights warm and space plants 12 to 18 inches apart in full sun. Each little pepper is about 1.5 inches with smooth, thick, juicy flesh; harvest them fully red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage more fruit. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Mini White Habanero Pepper
description: This rare Peruvian heirloom produces petite creamy-white pods roughly three-quarters to two inches long with intense, fruity habanero heat. Start seed indoors under warm conditions well before your last frost, as germination is slow and needs consistent warmth. Transplant into full sun once nights are reliably warm, and the ornamental, productive plants thrive in containers. Wear gloves when handling the ripe pods, which are excellent in salsas and hot sauces. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Minicor Carrot
description: A Dutch Nantes-type carrot bred with an especially small core, giving straight, uniform roots with fine grain and reliable sweetness. It matures quickly enough to be pulled small as a baby carrot or left slightly longer for full-size roots without losing tenderness. Its short stature and forgiving root shape make it a good fit for heavier or shallower garden soils that stunt longer carrot types. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Minimus Dwarf Culinary Sage (Little Leaf Sage)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Minimus' is a tightly compact dwarf selection of common culinary sage, valued for its narrow, fine-textured, aromatic gray-green leaves and abundant lavender-blue, white-lined flowers in late spring. Because it produces little to no seed, it stays tidier and less weedy over time than straight species sage, and its dense mounding habit tolerates somewhat heavier soil than other sage cultivars while remaining drought-tolerant once established. Its small stature makes it well suited to rock gardens, herb garden edging, and containers where a full-size sage would sprawl. Harvest leaves as needed for cooking and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent legginess. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Minneola Tangelo (Honeybell Tangelo)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Minneola tangelo is a hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine developed by USDA breeders at the University of Florida in 1931, producing the largest and most dramatically flavored tangelo available — large (3–4 inch diameter), deep reddish-orange fruits with a characteristic knobby protrusion at the stem end (giving them the nickname 'Honeybell' from their bell-like silhouette) and intensely aromatic, sweet-tart juice that is considered by many citrus enthusiasts to be among the finest citrus flavors of any variety. Minneola typically ripens January–March in Florida and California (one of the latest-ripening citrus), and the fruits hold on the tree for 2–4 weeks allowing flexible harvest. The skins peel easily (a peel-and-eat citrus), and the flesh separates into 10–12 clean segments with very few seeds. The tree is medium-sized (8–15 feet), moderately vigorous, and somewhat cold-hardy for a tangelo. Minneola requires cross-pollination — plant a Temple orange, Dancy tangerine, or Orlando tangelo within 50 feet for adequate fruit set; trees planted alone may produce poorly. Outstanding for Gulf Coast gardens in zone 9–11. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Minnesota Midget Cantaloupe
description: Direct sow this compact heirloom melon in warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks early in short-season climates. Introduced in 1948, it produces loads of small 4 inch fruits that are sweet and juicy right to the rind, on short vines well suited to small gardens and containers. Give plants full sun and steady moisture while fruits develop, then ease off watering as they ripen to concentrate the sugars. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and smells fragrant. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Minnie Royal Cherry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, always alongside its dedicated pollinizer Royal Lee, since neither cultivar reliably sets fruit on its own. Minnie Royal was bred specifically to satisfy fruit-bud chilling with only about 200 to 400 hours below 45 degrees Fahrenheit, opening sweet cherry growing to warm winter regions of the South that are far too mild for standard sweet cherry cultivars like Bing. Fruit is medium-sized, dark red, and ripens notably early, often well ahead of traditional sweet cherries, giving Gulf South and coastal growers a genuine shot at a home cherry crop. Because bloom is early, choose a site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the flowers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mino Early Daikon
description: Mino Early is an old open-pollinated Japanese heirloom prized for producing long, slender white roots weeks faster than standard Minowase types, with late-developing pithiness that keeps texture crisp even at full size. Work soil deeply and stone-free before sowing, since the smooth cylindrical roots can reach 14-16 inches and require loose ground to grow straight. Its combination of speed, heat tolerance, and mild, tender flavor makes it a dependable choice for growers wanting daikon without the long season standard winter types demand. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Minowase Daikon (Classic Long White Japanese Radish)
description: Thin seedlings early to prevent forked roots, and keep soil evenly moist to avoid splitting as the roots elongate. Minowase is the foundational Japanese daikon type behind many named strains, producing smooth, pure-white roots 18-24 inches long that taper only slightly. It is the traditional choice for takuan pickles as well as fresh grating and simmering, valued for its mild, clean flavor and dependable uniformity. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Mint Julep Peppermint (Sterile Triploid Cocktail Peppermint)
description: Set out divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates to keep leaves tender and prevent scorch. Mint Julep carries a bold, clean peppermint flavor with a faint spicy warmth that holds up well when muddled or steeped, making it a favorite for the classic Kentucky cocktail as well as iced tea and desserts. Because the plant is a sterile hybrid that rarely if ever flowers or sets seed, all of its vigor goes into leaf and stem production, so pinch tips regularly through the season to keep growth bushy and delay the tendency of mint stems to flop and root wherever they touch soil. Water deeply during dry spells, since mint wilts fast once the soil dries out, and cut the whole planting back hard in midsummer to refresh the foliage. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Minutina (Erba Stella, Buck's Horn Plantain)
description: Direct sow in cool weather in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; minutina (erba stella, or 'star grass') is one of the most unusual and sought-after Italian salad greens, producing rosettes of narrow, deeply toothed, antler-like leaves that have a pleasantly mild, slightly nutty to salty flavor and a satisfying crunch — a standout texture in any mixed salad. Unlike most salad greens, minutina is very tolerant of light frost and can be harvested almost year-round in mild climates; in the Southeast it is a fall-through-spring crop that withstands temperatures down to the mid-20s°F. The leaves are cut at the base and the plant regrows from the crown for multiple harvests. It tolerates partial shade better than most salad crops, making it productive in spots that receive only 3–4 hours of direct sun. Slow to bolt even in cool, bright conditions. Outstanding in the cut-and-come-again salad garden. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Mioga Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in shade or deep partial shade; mioga ginger is a Japanese culinary plant of major importance in traditional Japanese cooking and is distinguished from all other commonly grown gingers by its exceptional tolerance of deep shade — it is among the very best shade-tolerant edibles available to gardeners in zones 6–9, thriving under deciduous tree canopy where most vegetables and herbs fail entirely. The edible product is the compact, tightly packed, pale-yellow to pinkish flower buds (called 'myoga') that emerge directly from the ground at the base of the plant in summer and fall, separate from the leafy stems; these buds are harvested just before they open and used in Japanese cuisine as a garnish and flavoring for cold tofu, somen noodles, miso soup, and pickled preparations, with a flavor that is milder, more floral, and more delicate than culinary ginger rhizome. The plant goes fully dormant in winter and is reliably cold-hardy well into zone 6; established clumps expand steadily and can be divided every few years. One of the most underutilized shade-garden edibles in North American horticulture. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mirabelle Plum
description: Mirabelles are small, round, golden plums famed in Lorraine for tarts and eau-de-vie. Plant in full sun on fertile, free-draining soil and provide shelter from late frosts that can damage the early blossom. Most are self-fertile, so a single tree will crop, though a European plum companion boosts yields. Thin the abundant fruit set and prune lightly in summer to keep the canopy open. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Miracle Berry (Miracle Fruit, Miraculous Berry)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in part shade; water with rainwater or filtered water — chlorinated tap water and alkaline water damage the plant. Synsepalum dulcificum (miracle berry or miracle fruit) is a West African evergreen shrub that produces the most remarkable edible berry in the botanical world: small (1-inch), red, olive-shaped berries containing a glycoprotein called miraculin, which temporarily binds to sour taste receptors on the tongue and causes sour, acidic foods to taste intensely sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating a single berry. The berries themselves have virtually no sugar content and a bland flavor — the effect is entirely on taste perception, not on the food itself. After eating a miracle berry, lemons taste like lemon candy, vinegar tastes sweet, sour cream becomes sweet cream, and Tabasco sauce tastes like hot doughnut glaze. Miracle berry parties (where participants eat the berry and sample unusual flavor combinations) have become a culinary novelty. The plant is native to West African rain forest understory and requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist, part-shade conditions as blueberries — it is extremely pH-sensitive and will decline rapidly in alkaline soil or water. In zone 10–12, it can be grown outdoors; in zone 8–9, best in a pot brought indoors in winter. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Miracle Fruit
description: Plant in highly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5), which is critical — miracle fruit performs poorly above pH 6.0 and the leaves turn chlorotic in alkaline conditions. It requires consistently warm temperatures and suffers at any temperature below 40°F; container culture in large pots using acidic potting mix is the most practical approach outside zones 10–11. The small red berries contain miraculin, a glycoprotein that binds to taste receptors and makes sour foods taste sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating one fruit; harvest when berries are fully red and soft. Although individual plants are self-fertile, cross-pollination by insects improves berry set, so grow multiple plants together. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Miracle Fruit Vine
description: Plant in deep shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil; Thaumatococcus daniellii is adapted to the humid tropical rainforest floor and suffers in direct sunlight, dry conditions, or cold below 55°F — provide a consistently shaded, humid microenvironment and water regularly to maintain soil moisture. Thaumatococcus daniellii (Miracle Fruit Vine, Katemfe, or Katamfe) is a large, rhizomatous, forest-floor monocot in the Marantaceae family (prayer plant family) native to the humid rainforests of West and Central Africa from Sierra Leone east through Nigeria and Cameroon to the Congo Basin. Its common name 'Miracle Fruit Vine' is somewhat misleading — it is not a vine, but a large, clumping, ground-level herb with broad, long-stalked, oval leaves resembling a giant prayer plant. The small, triangular, red fruits (about 1 inch long) contain thaumatin — a naturally occurring protein recognized as the sweetest natural substance on earth, approximately 2,000–100,000 times sweeter than sucrose on a weight basis — used traditionally in West Africa to sweeten bitter foods and fermented beverages. Thaumatin (E957) is approved as a natural sweetener in the EU and many countries and is commercially extracted for use in food products and chewing gum. The plant requires conditions mimicking deep African rainforest understory — deep shade, high humidity (above 70%), consistent moisture, and warm temperatures year-round; it does not tolerate cold or dry spells. Note: not to be confused with Synsepalum dulcificum (miracle berry), a separate shrub with a different taste-modifying effect. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mirai 301 Bicolor Sweet Corn
description: Bred in Japan and marketed under the Mirai trademark, this bicolor hybrid is prized for exceptionally thin, tender pericarps and very high sugar content that many gardeners describe as fruit-like sweetness eaten raw off the cob. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through silking, since the thin-walled kernels are more sensitive to stress cracking than standard sh2 supersweets. Ears fill out to the tip reliably with 7 to 8 inch cobs on sturdy stalks, and the variety holds refrigerated quality in the husk for up to two weeks, longer than most sweet corn. Choose this cultivar when the priority is the sweetest possible fresh-eating experience rather than maximum yield or field storability. Matures in 74–79 days from seed.

name: Mirliton (Chayote)
description: Plant the entire fruit whole — chayote has a single large seed that cannot be separated from the flesh and the whole fruit is the planting unit. Dig a hole 4 inches deep and set the fruit at an angle with the narrow stem end barely covered. Once sprouted, provide a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor; the vine grows 20–40 feet and is extremely productive in zones 9–11 where it overwinters and bears fruit in fall and again in early spring. In New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, a single vine can produce hundreds of mirlitons per season. Fruits are eaten at all stages: stuffed and baked when large, stir-fried or pickled when small. The tender young leaves and shoot tips are edible greens, and the large starchy tubers that develop on established plants are edible as well. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Misato Rose Radish (Beauty Heart Radish, Rose Heart Radish)
description: Direct sow in late summer or fall; thin to 4–6 inches for full root development; Misato Rose grows to 3–4 inches in diameter over 60–70 days — much longer than spring radishes; harvest before hard freeze; the vivid interior color intensifies in cool fall weather; slice thin to showcase the color in salads. Misato Rose is a traditional Japanese winter radish (daikon type) from the Misato region of Japan, where it has been grown for centuries as a specialty vegetable known for its extraordinary interior color. The exterior of the root is pale green to greenish-white — completely unremarkable from the outside — but when the root is cut crosswise, the interior reveals a brilliant ring of vivid rose to magenta-pink extending from the interior outward, with a paler white core and a narrow white zone just inside the green skin. The effect is striking: the pink-fleshed cross-section looks like a small decorative disc with a rose-colored center zone. The vivid pink color comes from betalain pigments similar to those in beets and watermelon radishes, and it intensifies dramatically in the cooler temperatures of fall growing. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — much milder than the small red spring radishes most American gardeners know, and excellent for slicing thin in Japanese-style pickles (where the pink color turns the pickling liquid a beautiful deep rose), for raw salads where the color provides visual drama, and for Korean-style seasoned vegetable preparations. Also called 'Beauty Heart Radish' in some markets. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Mish Muscadine Grape (Heirloom Black Female Cultivar)
description: Mish is one of the old heirloom black muscadines selected from wild Southeastern vines generations before modern university breeding programs began, historically grouped with other early favorites such as Flowers, James, and Thomas for its combination of vigor, productivity, and dessert-quality fruit. The dark-skinned berries carry the rich, musky-sweet flavor prized in traditional muscadine cookery and fresh eating. Because Mish bears only female flowers, it needs a nearby self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to pollinate its blooms and set a full crop. Give it a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis in full sun, where this tough, long-lived heirloom vine will thrive with minimal disease pressure through Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mishirasu Asian Pear (Hokkaido Giant Russet Pear)
description: Mishirasu produces some of the largest fruit of any nashi cultivar, often exceeding a pound, with russet brown-gold skin and crisp, juicy, sweet flesh eaten fresh rather than cooked, unlike soft European pears. It stores unusually well for an Asian pear. Like most nashi cultivars it is not self-fertile and needs a different Pyrus pyrifolia cultivar blooming at the same time for a full crop, and it carries the fire blight susceptibility typical of most Asian pear varieties. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Misome (Komatsuna-Tatsoi Hybrid Savoyed Asian Green)
description: Misome is a relatively recent Japanese cross between komatsuna and tatsoi, combining tatsoi's glossy, savoyed, rounded leaf with a more upright, komatsuna-like growth habit that is easier to harvest cleanly. The thick, tender leaves and stems have a sweet, mild flavor raw that turns more robust and mustardy once cooked, and the plant holds up well in the field without turning tough or bitter. It matures quickly from direct sowing and shows good tolerance of both heat and cool weather, making it a flexible filler green for spring, summer, and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or take outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again crop. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Miss Blanc Grape (Mississippi-Bred White Wine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Miss Blanc was released by Mississippi State University in 1982, bred by USDA researcher N.H. Loomis specifically for Pierce's disease tolerance, and produces white grapes well suited to wine and juice production across the Gulf South where the disease limits most traditional wine grape choices. Its interspecific hybrid parentage gives it the disease resistance needed to thrive in the region's warm, humid growing conditions without the heavy spray program European wine grapes require. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce fungal disease risk. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Miss Blue Grape (USDA/Mississippi-Bred Pierce's Disease-Prone-Region Bunch Grape)
description: Miss Blue was developed by USDA researcher N.H. Loomis at the Meridian, Mississippi field station alongside the sister releases Miss Blanc and MidSouth, both bred specifically for the Deep South's severe Pierce's disease pressure. The dark-blue berries form in open, well-aerated clusters and are recommended for juice and jelly rather than fresh eating, typically ripening from late July into mid-August. Unlike Pierce's disease, anthracnose is the main disease concern for this variety, so a regular fungicide program is needed to keep the fruit clean. Grow on a sturdy trellis in full sun with good air circulation, and prune hard each winter to renewal spurs to maintain fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Miss Jessopp's Upright Rosemary (Tall Hedging Rosemary)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; avoid heavy, wet soils and overhead watering, which promote root and foliar disease. Miss Jessopp's Upright is a long-cultivated English rosemary selection prized for its tall, narrow, strongly vertical branching, which holds its shape naturally and makes it one of the best rosemary cultivars for clipped hedges, screens, and formal topiary shapes rather than a sprawling border plant. Culinary quality is excellent and identical in use to any standard rosemary — piney, resinous leaves for roasting, grilling, and seasoning — while pale blue flowers appear along the upright stems in late winter and spring, attracting bees. Prune after flowering to maintain a tight hedge form, and in zone 9 give it a warm, sheltered, sharply drained site, since it is somewhat less cold-hardy than selections like Arp or Hill Hardy. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Miss Jessup Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in sharply drained, average to lean soil in full sun; rosemary is highly intolerant of wet feet, so raised beds or slightly sloped sites help in areas with heavy clay or high rainfall. Miss Jessup is a long-cultivated rosemary selection known for its tall, strongly upright growth habit, reaching four to six feet with age, which makes it one of the best rosemary cultivars for training into a low hedge, topiary, or vertical accent plant, distinct from the many low, spreading, or mounding rosemary types more commonly sold for groundcover use. The narrow, aromatic, needle-like leaves are fully useful in the kitchen, and the pale blue flowers in late winter to spring draw early-season pollinators. Prune regularly to maintain shape and encourage bushy new growth, and avoid overhead watering, since rosemary performs best on the dry side once established. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Miss Katherine Pink English Lavender
description: Give this lavender full sun and sharply drained soil, since pink-flowered selections are just as prone to root rot in wet ground as any English lavender. Bred by Downderry Nursery in Kent and named for the breeder's daughter, 'Miss Katherine' produces clear rose-pink flower spikes over compact silver-green foliage, a rare break from the usual blue-violet lavender palette that has earned it an RHS Award of Garden Merit. Trim back hard after flowering to maintain a neat mound and prevent the woody, gappy habit that develops when lavender is left unpruned. Afternoon shade in very hot climates helps the pink tone hold rather than fade toward white. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Miss Kim Mulberry
description: Miss Kim is a Southern-selected white mulberry valued for large, richly flavored, sweet berries and notably strong tolerance of heat and humidity, making it well adapted to Gulf Coast summers. Trees begin bearing within two to three years of planting and require little maintenance once established beyond an occasional shaping prune to keep the canopy at a manageable size. Give it full sun and average, well-drained soil; established trees tolerate drought well and need only supplemental water during prolonged dry spells. Because ripe fruit drops over an extended harvest window and can stain pavement, site it away from walkways, patios, and parked cars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Miss Kim Persimmon (Compact Weeping Cold-Hardy Asian Persimmon)
description: Miss Kim is a naturally compact, self-fertile Asian persimmon prized for its weeping form and long, tropical-looking foliage that turns deep red in fall, making it as much a landscape specimen as a fruit tree. It is an astringent-type cultivar, so the large, round, reddish-orange fruit must soften completely, becoming tender like a ripe tomato, before it loses its puckery tannins and turns sweet and flavorful. Miss Kim leafs out earlier than most other Asian persimmon cultivars and ripens early, beginning in October and continuing on the tree into the cooler months. It has also proven hardier than many kaki cultivars in cold snaps, and trees typically begin bearing within two to three years of planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mission Almond (Texas Mission Almond, California Mission, Hard-Shell Commercial Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mission is partially self-fruitful but benefits from a companion variety; harvest in late August to September — later than Nonpareil — when hulls split naturally; the thick, hard shell requires a nutcracker rather than the light hand pressure sufficient for Nonpareil; kernels are round, plump, and darker than Nonpareil with a richer, slightly more intense almond flavor. Mission almond (also called Texas Mission) is one of the oldest continuously grown named almond varieties in California, historically associated with the California Spanish mission system and possibly introduced to California with Spanish colonization in the late 1700s — though the exact origins are contested. It was one of the first California almond varieties to reach commercial significance and for many years was the second most planted California variety after Nonpareil. Mission's hard, thick shell — a significant disadvantage for fresh-cracking and processing — became an asset in the shell-on almond market, where the hard shell protects the kernel during shipping and storage, and in the roasted-in-shell specialty market. Mission almonds also have a distinctly different flavor from the mild Nonpareil — slightly richer, with a more intense almond character — making them preferred by some specialty roasters and confectioners. The variety's later bloom time (1–2 weeks after Nonpareil) reduces spring frost risk at the critical blossom stage, a practical advantage in frost-prone almond sites. In Texas, Mission is the primary recommended almond variety where it often goes by the name 'Texas Mission.' Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mission Olive
description: The Mission olive, first cultivated in California, is a versatile favorite valued for both flavorful oil and classic table olives. It is a hardy, resilient evergreen that adapts to a range of conditions and delivers reliable harvests for home growers. Plant a young tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water sparingly once it establishes. Prune for an open canopy and good airflow, and in cold-winter regions grow it as a container specimen that can be sheltered from hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mississippi Cream Pea (Traditional Gulf South Small-Seeded Cream Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mississippi Cream is a traditional Gulf South cream pea variety — producing small to medium-sized, cream-white seeds with the mild, sweet, nutty flavor characteristic of cream peas that distinguishes them from the earthier, bolder flavor of blackeye peas and cowpeas. Mississippi Cream is a semi-bush type with good productivity in Gulf South conditions and excellent heat tolerance — continuing to produce through the summer heat of zone 9 when most cool-season vegetables have ended. As a cream pea type, Mississippi Cream has slightly smaller seeds and a sweeter, more delicate flavor than standard crowder or blackeye types — the creamier texture and milder flavor of cream peas generally makes them preferred for certain traditional preparations including fresh summer pea succotash, cream peas and okra, and fresh peas braised with ham or fatback. Southern peas as a group are the most important summer legume vegetable of Gulf Coast traditional gardens — providing fresh protein through the hottest months when other vegetables fail. The nitrogen-fixing root system enriches garden soil for subsequent crops. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage (well-filled hulls but still green) for fresh eating or continue to dry maturity for storage. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Mississippi Crowder Southern Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any reasonably well-drained soil; Mississippi Crowder is a bush-type crowder pea with tightly packed seeds that turn light brown at maturity. It is a traditional Mississippi variety well-adapted to the heavy clay soils common along the Gulf Coast and Mississippi Delta, where it tolerates temporary waterlogging better than many other cowpea types. The crowder seeds develop a creamy texture when cooked with excellent flavor for fresh-shell eating, and they also dry well for storage as dried beans. The vigorous vines shade out weeds effectively once established, and the roots fix substantial nitrogen, improving soil for the following season. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Mississippi Hot Pickle Pepper
description: This old Mississippi dooryard heirloom produces slender, tapered fruit that ripen from pale yellow-green through orange to bright red, with a medium heat similar to a cayenne. It was passed down among home gardeners specifically for pickling whole in vinegar brine, and the thin-walled pods also dry and grind well for homemade hot pepper flakes or vinegar-pepper sauce. Compact, heavily branched plants handle Deep South humidity and heat well and keep setting new pods through summer if picked regularly rather than left to fully color on the plant. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other annuum peppers by distance if you intend to save true seed. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Mississippi Nemaheart Pepper (Nematode-Resistant Pimiento)
description: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55 degrees F. Mississippi Nemaheart was released by Mississippi State University in 1966 as an open-pollinated pimiento-type pepper bred by recurrent backcrossing into 'Truhart Perfection,' and it remains historically significant as the original source of the dominant N gene that confers resistance to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes in modern pepper breeding. Plants are moderately vigorous with heart-shaped, thick-walled sweet fruit that ripens from green to deep red and is well suited to canning, roasting, and pimiento cheese. Because root-knot nematodes are endemic in the sandy, poorly drained soils common across the Gulf Coast, this cultivar performs far more reliably there than standard susceptible pimiento types, though its plants can be somewhat weaker-growing than modern hybrids bred from it. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull Pea (Virus-Resistant Deep South Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in rows 24-30 inches apart, thinning to 4-8 inches; like other cowpeas it fixes its own nitrogen and needs little to no supplemental fertilizer. Mississippi Pinkeye is a semi-crowder Southern pea bred with resistance to fusarium wilt, root-knot nematode, and several strains of blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, distinguishing it from older purple hull types that lack that disease package. Pods emerge light green with a distinct pink 'eye' blush, then color to deep purple at the green-shell stage, and the upright plant habit holds pods above the foliage for easier hand harvest. Shell at the purple-podded green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage peas with the characteristic cream seed coat and maroon-pink eye. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Mississippi Purple Hull Pea (Deep South Garden Crowder Cowpea)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in rows 24–30 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. No fertilizer needed on most soils — cowpeas fix nitrogen. Harvest at the green shell stage for the best fresh flavor. Mississippi Purple Hull Pea is a Southern pea (cowpea, Vigna unguiculata) — a warm-season legume that is one of the most historically important and widely grown vegetables of the American Gulf South and Deep South, where the hot summers that challenge many other vegetables are actually the conditions Southern peas thrive in. The name 'purple hull' describes the distinctive coloration of the pods at harvest: the pods are vivid purple-red, making the harvest stage visually unmistakable in the garden and distinguishing purple hull types from the silver/green pods of cream peas and the tan pods of blackeye peas. Mississippi Purple Hull is a crowder-type pea (the seeds are crowded tightly in the pod, creating the characteristic dimpled, round shape of the shelled peas) — crowder types are considered by many Gulf South cooks to have the richest, meatiest flavor of the Southern pea types, ideal for the slow-cooked preparations that are central to Gulf South foodways. Southern peas are nitrogen-fixing legumes that improve soil fertility while producing — one of the most productive and soil-improving summer crops for zone 8–10 gardens. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Mississippi Silver Cowpea (Silver-Hulled Crowder Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods once they turn from green to a silvery, pale green-white color at the crowder stage. Mississippi Silver is a productive crowder-type cowpea whose closely packed, squarish peas fill the pod so tightly they are pressed ('crowded') against one another, developing a rich, hearty flavor prized in traditional Southern cooking. Its pale, silvery pod color at harvest makes ripeness easy to spot, and the variety is noted for good tolerance to common cowpea diseases and heat stress, producing reliably through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables decline. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the silver-green stage for fresh shelling, or allow pods to dry fully for long-term storage. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Mississippi Silver Southern Pea (Silver-Hull Crowder Pea)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun, well-drained soil; Mississippi Silver can be succession-planted every 3–4 weeks from spring through late summer for continuous production; plants fix atmospheric nitrogen and require no supplemental fertilizer in average garden soil; harvest at the green-shell stage when pods are well-filled and slightly silvery-tan in color. Mississippi Silver is a traditional open-pollinated Southern pea variety that derives its name from the distinctive silvery-tan to pale buff color of its mature pods — a different visual marker from the purple-hull and black-eyed types more familiar to outside the South. The variety is classified as a crowder type because the seeds are tightly packed ('crowded') inside the pod, causing them to develop flat sides from pressing against each other — the classic crowder characteristic that gives the type its name. The seeds are cream-colored with purple or red-purple speckled markings that fade to a uniform tan when cooked, as with most field peas, and the flavor is the rich, earthy, savory character of Southern field peas that is quite different from garden peas or snap beans. Mississippi Silver is one of the most widely recommended varieties by Mississippi State University Extension and LSU AgCenter for home garden Southern pea production — consistently rated highly for both yield and eating quality in regional trials. Like all Southern peas (Vigna unguiculata), it thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South through summer months when most other vegetables have ended, making it one of the primary summer food crops of the region. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Missouri Gooseberry
description: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Missouri gooseberry is a thorny, arching Midwestern and Great Plains native shrub found wild along woodland edges, fencerows, and thickets, tolerating more shade than most fruiting berries while still producing a reliable crop. Small, greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers in early spring give way to smooth, purple-black berries by early summer that are tart-sweet and excellent fresh once fully ripe, or cooked into pies, jams, and preserves while still slightly underripe and firmer. It is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than European gooseberry cultivars, and its wide native range makes it naturally adapted to variable continental climates from hot summers to severe winters. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to renew vigor, and watch for the sharp spines at each leaf node when harvesting or pruning. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Missouri Wonder Pole Bean (Heirloom Cornfield Climbing Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, giving vines a tall pole, fence, or living corn stalk to climb since plants can reach six to eight feet. Missouri Wonder is a traditional cornfield bean from the early twentieth century, grown intercropped with corn so the climbing vine needed no separate support, a companion-planting approach once common across Southern and Midwestern subsistence farms. The thick, slightly curved pods stay stringless and tender while young, making excellent snap beans, while mature seed can be dried for use as a hearty soup bean through winter. It is notably tolerant of heat and garden stress compared with many bush varieties, and steady daily picking keeps the vigorous vines producing over a long harvest window. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Misty Blueberry (Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, sandy loam in full sun with another southern highbush cultivar for cross-pollination; Misty is an outstanding low-chill southern highbush blueberry cultivar developed by the University of Florida — requiring only 150–300 chill hours, making it one of the best blueberry choices for the Gulf Coast, Central Florida, and other warm-winter regions where northern highbush varieties consistently fail to produce. Misty is additionally distinctive for having attractive ornamental value beyond its fruit production — it has an elegant, upright habit with attractive dark-green foliage that turns red in fall, and in spring produces showy clusters of white to pink, urn-shaped flowers before leaf-out. The medium to large, light-blue fruits ripen in April through May in zone 9, with a somewhat mild but pleasant blueberry flavor. As a very early ripening variety (among the earliest of all southern highbush types in zone 9), Misty gives Gulf Coast gardeners fresh blueberries in April when markets charge premium prices. Plant Misty in raised beds or in containers with acidified peat-based potting mix — most Gulf Coast clay and native soils are too alkaline and must be heavily amended or blueberries will fail regardless of cultivar. Pair with O'Neal or Sharpblue for best cross-pollination and maximum yields. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mitchell Pawpaw
description: Mitchell originated as a wild selection found in Franklin County, Illinois, and was later included in Kentucky State University's regional pawpaw variety trials alongside Sunflower and KSU-Atwood. It sets fruit reliably on a vigorous, disease-resistant tree and benefits from cross-pollination with a genetically distinct cultivar planted nearby. Grow in deep, moist, well-drained soil and mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool. Hand-pollinate with a small paintbrush in home orchards if fruit set is sparse, since pawpaw flies attract few natural pollinators. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mitsuba
description: Direct sow Cryptotaenia japonica in cool weather in moist, humus-rich soil in part to deep shade; keep evenly moist and succession-sow every 3–4 weeks for continuous harvest; harvest individual leaves and stems as needed, or cut entire plants to 2 inches above the crown for regrowth; plants self-sow readily in favorable conditions. Mitsuba (Japanese for 'three leaves', referring to its three-leaflet compound leaves) is an essential herb in Japanese cooking — used fresh, never cooked at length — as a garnish and subtle flavoring in osuimono (clear soup), chawanmushi (savory egg custard), nabemono (hot pot), and as a fresh addition to salads and scattered over finished dishes. The flavor is uniquely delicate: more complex than parsley, less anise-forward than chervil, with a clean, fresh quality that bridges East Asian and Western herb traditions. Unlike most herbs that demand full sun, Mitsuba thrives in the deep shade of a woodland garden or the north side of a building — making it one of the most valuable herbs for shaded kitchen gardens. In zone 7 and warmer it can be semi-evergreen; in zone 4–6 it dies back to the root in winter but regrows reliably in spring. The plant self-sows freely in suitable conditions and can naturalize under trees or along shaded borders. Etiolated (blanched) stems grown in darkness are particularly prized for their milder, more delicate flavor. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Miwa Tea (Red-Stemmed Narrow-Leaf Selection)
description: Miwa is an ornamental tea selection best recognized by its reddish-brown new stems, which contrast strikingly with narrow, dark-green leaves only about an inch wide. It grows into a rounded shrub roughly 6 feet tall and wide over a decade, making it a manageable size for home tea gardens. The fine-textured foliage suits it to both landscape use and light tea production. Provide consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and begin harvesting the top two leaves and a bud once the plant is well established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Miyagawa Satsuma (Classic Early-Season Cold-Hardy Satsuma)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, choosing a warm, sheltered site since even cold-hardy satsumas benefit from added winter protection at the northern edge of their range. Miyagawa is one of the oldest and most widely propagated satsuma strains, a Japanese selection prized for consistently early ripening, seedless fruit with the loose, easy-peeling skin and sweet, low-acid, nearly seedless flesh that makes satsumas so popular for fresh eating and for introducing children to citrus. The compact, naturally dwarfing tree bears young and heavily, and its combination of good cold tolerance and dependable early production has made it one of the standard satsuma selections offered by Gulf Coast citrus nurseries. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Miyashige White Daikon Radish
description: Sow this Japanese daikon in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since it is a winter radish that needs cool weather and shortening days to size up. Direct sow in loose, deeply worked soil so the long white roots can grow straight, and thin seedlings to 4 to 6 inches apart. Keep the soil evenly moist for tender, mild roots with a lightly spicy flavor. Harvest before hard freezes; use young roots shredded fresh, or pickle and cook mature roots in stir-fries and soups. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Miz America Mizuna
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep into fertile, well-drained soil in early spring or, better, six to eight weeks before the first fall frost, since this deep-red F1 mizuna holds its uniform maroon color and mild, non-bitter flavor best in cool weather. Thin seedlings to allow the deeply serrated, feathery leaves room to form their signature vase-shaped rosette, and harvest whole heads or individual leaves for cut-and-come-again picking. Its consistent color on both leaf surfaces makes it popular for baby-leaf salad mixes, garnishes, and mixed ornamental plantings as well as stir-fries. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Mizuna (Japanese Mustard Greens)
description: Direct sow in cool weather in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mizuna is one of the most popular Japanese salad greens and one of the fastest, easiest cool-season crops available, producing deeply cut, feathery, pale green leaves with a mild, slightly peppery, refreshing flavor that is pleasantly tender when harvested young. It is one of the most cold tolerant of all the Asian brassicas and continues growing through light freezes, making it an outstanding fall and winter crop in zones 7–9. Begin harvesting as baby leaf at 21 days by cutting the outer leaves; the plant regrows for multiple harvests before bolting in warm weather. Bolt resistance is better than arugula, and the plant handles light shade well, making it productive in partly shaded plots. Red-leaved mizuna cultivars ('Red Kingdom', 'Mikado Red') add color to salad mixes. An outstanding addition to spring and fall salad mixes, stir-fries, and as a garnish in Japanese cuisine. Matures in 21–45 days from seed.

name: Mock Strawberry (Indian Strawberry, False Strawberry)
description: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, average soil — mock strawberry is one of the most shade-tolerant edible groundcovers available for difficult spots under trees. It spreads vigorously by runners, forming a dense weed-suppressing carpet of trifoliate leaves studded with small yellow flowers from spring through fall followed by round, bright red berries. The fruits are edible and safe but mild and nearly tasteless compared to true strawberries — they lack the complex aroma that makes true strawberry irresistible. They are best used in jams or flavored beverages rather than eaten fresh. The plant does well in lawn edges, woodland paths, and shaded slopes where it outcompetes many weeds while providing interest through yellow flowers and bright fruit. May naturalize aggressively; divide to control spread. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Mockernut Hickory (White Hickory, Bigbud Hickory)
description: Plant young container or bare-root trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, moderately fertile to fertile soil in spring; mockernut hickory is the most common hickory in the eastern United States and among the most beautiful, with dramatic large compound leaves that turn brilliant golden-yellow in fall. The nuts are enclosed in a very thick husk (giving the 'mockernut' name — the husk 'mocks' the nut inside), and the kernel is small but has a rich, full, classic hickory flavor. A critical wildlife tree, providing extremely high-value mast for deer, turkey, squirrels, and many other species; the very dense, strong, flexible wood is commercially valuable for tool handles and sporting goods. An outstanding native shade tree for large properties that also provides excellent wildlife food. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Modello Sapodilla
description: Plant grafted Modello sapodilla trees in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, using the same culture as other Manilkara zapota selections; trees are evergreen and drought-tolerant once established but suffer serious dieback below the upper 20s F. Modello bears elliptic-to-ovate fruit with light brown, moderately scurfy skin and smooth, whitish-tan flesh of good dessert quality, ripening mainly from late winter into late spring in South Florida. Yields are only fair compared with heavier-cropping cultivars like Brown Sugar or Alano, so Modello is grown more for its refined flavor and low-grit texture than for sheer volume. Harvest when the skin turns dull and scurfy and let the fruit soften at room temperature for several days before eating. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Modi Apple (Gala x Liberty Disease-Resistant Apple)
description: Modi was bred in Italy from a cross of Gala and Liberty, pairing Gala's sweet, crisp eating quality with Liberty's strong resistance to apple scab. The deep red, almost fully colored fruit ripens in the fall a few weeks after Gala and holds its crunch well in storage. Its disease-resistant parentage lets home growers get a clean, attractive crop with far less fungicide spraying than scab-susceptible varieties require. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mogette de Vendée Bean (Vendée White Bean)
description: Mogette de Vendée is a Protected Geographical Indication white kidney bean from France's Atlantic-coast Vendée region, where it is the traditional accompaniment to local ham and is celebrated every autumn at regional mogette festivals. The plump, pure-white seeds cook to a smooth, mild-flavored, creamy finish that absorbs butter, garlic, and herbs readily, making it a staple of simple rustic French cooking. Allow pods to dry fully and turn pale tan before harvest, then shell and finish curing indoors for a week or two. Give vines full sun, steady moisture during pod fill, and a tall, sturdy support since plants can reach 8 feet. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Mogi Loquat (Classic Small-Fruited Japanese Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mogi is one of the oldest and most historically significant Japanese loquat cultivars, originating from Nagasaki and serving as a parent or foundation selection behind many later loquat cultivars developed in Japan and California. Fruit is smaller and rounder than modern large-fruited selections, with pale orange, juicy, sweet-tart flesh and a thin skin. Though newer cultivars have surpassed Mogi in fruit size, it remains valued by collectors and heritage-fruit growers for its productivity, reliability, and historic significance in loquat breeding. Trees bloom in fall and fruit ripens in spring, so protect open flowers and developing fruit from hard freezes with row cover during cold snaps in zone 8, where loquat is at the edge of its reliable range. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a range of soil types well, needing only routine care once past the first two years. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mohler American Persimmon
description: Mohler is a named American persimmon selection distributed through the efforts of pomologist Lee Reich of New Paltz, New York, and valued chiefly for ripening unusually early even in cool northern climates, with fruit coloring and softening by late August to early September rather than after the first hard frosts typical of the species. The glowing deep-orange fruit develops rich, sweet flavor once fully soft, while unripe fruit remains strongly astringent like all Diospyros virginiana. The tree responds well to pruning to keep it in a manageable 15-25 foot range for home orchards, and it produces vivid orange and yellow fall foliage color in addition to its fruit crop. Mohler is a useful choice for gardeners in shorter-season or colder regions (zones 5-9) who want an American persimmon that reliably finishes ripening before autumn frosts arrive. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mojito Mint
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — mint tolerates a wide range of conditions but is most productive with consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Mojito Mint (also called Cuban Mint or Hierba Buena) is the specific mint variety traditionally used in Cuban mojito cocktails and throughout Latin American cuisine where the common name 'hierba buena' (good herb) refers to this distinctive spearmint type. The large, soft, round, slightly fuzzy leaves have a distinctive mint character that is milder and fruitier than standard peppermint — less cool and piercing, with sweet spearmint notes and a smooth, rounded flavor that makes it the preferred mint for beverages where a harsh mint punch would overpower the other ingredients. The mojito's balance of rum, lime, sugar, and mint depends on this softer mint character to support rather than dominate. Mojito Mint also works excellently in fresh summer drinks, desserts, herb sauces, and anywhere a gentle, approachable mint flavor is desired over the assertive cool of peppermint. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Mokka Coffee (Maui Mokka, Low-Caffeine Dwarf Coffee)
description: Mokka arose as a naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon and has been cultivated since at least the early twentieth century, prized for a compact, densely branched habit that looks more like a clipped hedge than a typical coffee tree. Its narrow leaves and diminutive cherries yield beans containing roughly half the caffeine of standard arabica cultivars, while still producing a heavy-bodied, chocolaty cup often noted for dried-fruit and spice character, especially when natural-processed. The naturally short internodes keep mature plants under six feet, making it one of the few coffee selections well suited to large-container or patio growing outside true tropical climates. Give it the same rich, humus-heavy, slightly acidic soil and filtered light preferred by other arabica types, and expect several years of growth before the first useful harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mokum Carrot
description: Direct sow this Nantes-type hybrid carrot in loose, stone-free soil, since carrots dislike transplanting and rocky ground causes forked roots. Sow shallowly and keep the surface evenly moist until the slow-germinating seeds sprout, then thin seedlings to about an inch apart. Mokum stays sweet even in warmer weather and its slim, nearly coreless roots are crisp whether pulled as baby carrots or grown to a full 6 to 8 inches. Provide steady moisture and full sun for smooth, snappy roots. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Molix Sapodilla
description: Grow this heavy-bearing grafted sapodilla cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing it well away from structures since mature trees become quite large and dense. It is grown commercially in south Florida for producing abundant crops of medium-sized fruit with grainy, malt-and-brown-sugar-flavored flesh once fully ripened off the tree. Established trees tolerate brief light frost better than many tropical fruits but still suffer leaf and twig damage below the upper 20s, so Gulf Coast growers reserve it for the warmest zones or keep young trees containerized for winter protection. Fruit must soften fully before eating, as unripe sapodilla is astringent with latex. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mollar de Elche Pomegranate (Spanish Soft-Seeded Pomegranate)
description: Mollar de Elche is Spain's most widely grown pomegranate cultivar, historically centered on the city of Elche in Alicante province, and is prized for very large fruit with rare, genuinely soft and edible seeds and an intensely sweet, low-acid flavor. Rind color ranges from pale cream-pink to deep red depending on growing conditions, and its soft-seeded quality has made it a parent in modern breeding programs aiming to combine that trait with the darker skin of cultivars like Wonderful. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; as a Mediterranean-bred selection it appreciates the same hot, relatively dry ripening period that benefits other Old World soft-seeded cultivars, so extra airflow and prompt removal of any humidity-damaged fruit helps it perform in humid Gulf Coast summers. Established plants are drought-tolerant and benefit from light annual pruning to renew fruiting wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Molle (Peruvian Pepper Tree, Pink Peppercorn)
description: Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen from the Peruvian Andes develops graceful, weeping, willow-like branches and clusters of small berries that ripen from green to bright rose-pink. The dried berries are sold commercially as pink peppercorns and add a fruity, mildly resinous heat to pepper blends, sauces, and infused oils, though botanically the tree is unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Handle fresh fruit and sap with care, as some people develop mild skin or respiratory irritation, and check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mollie's Delicious Apple (Low-Chill Sweet Red Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station from a multi-way cross involving Golden Delicious parentage and released in 1966, Mollie's Delicious carries a Red Delicious-style name and blush but is genetically unrelated to that variety. It needs around 400 chill hours or less, well within Gulf Coast winters, and ripens mid-to-late August with a sweet, aromatic flavor and red-blushed yellow skin. Because it is not self-fruitful, plant it alongside Fuji, Granny Smith, or Beverly Hills for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Molokai Purple Sweet Potato
description: Molokai Purple is a Hawaiian-origin heirloom sweet potato named for the island of Molokai, producing roots with dark purple to nearly black skin over dense, vividly purple flesh that holds its color well through baking and steaming. The vines are vigorous and trailing with purple-tinged foliage, and the roots are somewhat smaller and more irregular in shape than mainstream commercial purple varieties, reflecting its heirloom, unselected background. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since rich soil favors vine growth over root development; the vine tolerates the heat and humidity of a long warm season well. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to firm the skin and develop full sweetness before storing in a cool, dry place. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Molokhia
description: Also called Egyptian spinach or jute mallow, molokhia is a heat-loving green that thrives when other leafy crops bolt. Direct sow after the soil is thoroughly warm, since seedlings need heat and stall in cool weather. Pinch the growing tips to encourage bushy branching and a continuous supply of young leaves. Harvest the tender upper leaves and stems, which turn silky and thicken soups and stews when cooked. Keep it well watered through summer, and pick regularly to delay flowering. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Momotaro Tomato
description: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Momotaro is Japan's most celebrated fresh tomato — an indeterminate, pink-fruited hybrid with exceptionally low acidity and high sugar content that has dominated the Japanese fresh tomato market since Sakata Seed Company introduced it in 1985. The smooth, round, 6–8 ounce fruits have thin, tender skin, almost no gel around the seeds, and a dense, sweet, mild flesh that requires no sugar addition in cooked preparations and is prized for fresh eating. The plant produces steadily over a long season and shows better resistance to blossom-end rot than many large-fruited varieties. In zone 9 the flavor is best in spring and fall crops; the fruits produced through peak summer heat tend toward milder, less complex flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Monaco Sweet Potato (Disease-Resistant Rose-Skinned NC State Release)
description: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; Monaco is a North Carolina State University release valued for a broad disease-resistance package — it stands up to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode, an emerging pest in parts of the South. Its rose-pink skin fades somewhat in storage over dark orange flesh, and the plant grows in a dense, upright habit rather than sprawling widely, which helps it shade out weeds within the row once established. Monaco needs a longer season than standard varieties like Covington — plan on two to three extra weeks in the ground — and while its disease resistance makes it a strong option for low-spray or organic plantings, expect somewhat lower yields than top commercial varieties. Cure roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and develop full sweetness before storing. Matures in 120–135 days from transplant.

name: Monastrell Bulb Onion
description: Start Monastrell onions indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant the seedlings out several weeks before the last frost since onions are cold tolerant when young. This late-season variety forms uniform, slightly flattened red globes 3.5 to 4 inches across with strong sunscald resistance. Match the variety to your latitude, as onion bulbing is triggered by day length. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist, then stop watering once tops fall over and cure the bulbs for storage of up to six months. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Moneta Beet (Monogerm No-Thin Beet)
description: Direct sow thinly in early spring or late summer, since each seed ball contains only a single embryo and germinates as one seedling rather than the tangled cluster typical of most beets. Moneta is an All-America Selections winner valued for this true monogerm trait, which eliminates the tedious thinning normally required for beets and makes precision seeding practical for both home gardeners and small-scale growers. It produces smooth, uniformly round, deep-red roots with sweet flavor and tender greens suitable for salad mixes. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Money Maker Pecan (Historic Late-1800s Prolific Pecan)
