description: Selected in the closing years of the 19th century, Money Maker earned its name from its reputation as a remarkably prolific bearer, often setting such a heavy crop that nut size and shell thickness suffer without regular thinning or fertilization. It was one of the mainstay commercial cultivars of the early Gulf South pecan industry before scab-resistant 20th-century releases largely replaced it in new plantings. The nuts are small to medium with a moderately thick shell, and the tree is more prone than modern cultivars to biennial bearing if not managed with attentive fertility and crop-thinning practices. Today it is grown mainly in older heritage orchards and by collectors interested in preserving historic pecan germplasm. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Money Tree (Malabar Chestnut, French Peanut)
description: Plant in moist to wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; money tree tolerates periodic flooding and poor drainage. Pachira aquatica (money tree or Malabar chestnut) is a Central American tropical tree famous in two quite different contexts: as a beloved ornamental houseplant (braided trunk forms sold under the 'money tree' name, associated in Feng Shui with prosperity) and as a significant wild and semi-cultivated food tree in its native tropical Central and South American habitat. The tree produces large, distinctive, 5-to-7-fingered, palmate leaves and spectacular, large (8–12 inch), creamy-white flowers with hundreds of long, red-tipped, brush-like stamens — one of the showiest flowers of any tropical tree. The large, woody fruits contain edible seeds (Malabar chestnuts) with a nutty flavor when roasted or boiled — eaten throughout Central America as a nutritious food. Braided trunk forms (produced by braiding multiple young seedlings while soft) have become extremely popular houseplants worldwide. In zone 10–12, money tree grows as a large landscape tree; in zone 9, it requires frost protection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Moneymaker Pecan (Reliable Annual-Bearing Texas Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer variety nearby for the best nut set. Moneymaker is an early 20th-century Texas pecan valued above all for its dependable, consistent annual production, avoiding the pronounced alternate-year bearing pattern (heavy crop one year, light the next) that plagues many other pecan varieties and makes yields far less predictable. The medium-sized nuts have a thin shell and good kernel quality, and the tree shows solid resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that is the single biggest production challenge for pecans in humid Southern climates. Because of its reliability, Moneymaker has remained a popular choice for home orchards over more than a century, even as many showier, larger-nutted varieties have come and gone. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the first significant nut crops five to seven years after planting. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Moneymaker Pole Tomato
description: Start this indeterminate heirloom indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply once nights warm, burying part of the stem to encourage strong roots. Moneymaker earned its name through uniform, reliably heavy yields of medium-sized, meaty, sweet fruits. Provide a tall stake or cage since the vines keep growing all season, and prune suckers to improve airflow. Water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and harvest fruits as they ripen to keep the plant producing. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Monk Fruit (Luo Han Guo)
description: Grow this dioecious perennial vine on a strong arbor or fence, planting at least one male vine for every six to eight female vines to ensure fruit set. The round green fruits, picked in autumn and dried, contain mogrosides that make them intensely sweet with none of the calories of sugar, and gardeners in zone 8-10 areas often treat the vine as a cut-back perennial that resprouts from the crown after light winter dieback. It prefers rich, well-drained soil high in organic matter and benefits from the same humid summer heat that suits muscadine grapes. Home use is mainly for steeping into tea or extracting a home sweetener rather than fresh eating, since the raw fruit is bitter until dried and cured. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Monkey Jack
description: Plant Monkey Jack in deep, fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water well during establishment and dry seasons; harvest fruits when they turn golden-yellow and yield to gentle pressure — use gloves as the latex sap stains skin and clothing. Artocarpus lacucha produces round to irregularly shaped compound fruits 3–6 inches across — structurally similar to small jackfruits, formed from fused fruitlets on a central core — with golden-yellow to orange-red skin studded with small bumps and sweet-sour, aromatic, slightly astringent yellow flesh. The flavor is described as a complex blend of mango, pineapple, and slightly acidic tropical notes; the fruits are eaten fresh, pickled, cooked in curries, and used in chutneys and preserves throughout its native range. The starchy seeds are also edible when boiled or roasted, similar to jackfruit seeds. Various parts of the tree are used in traditional Ayurvedic and Thai medicine — the bark yields a yellow dye used for dyeing Buddhist monk robes in Thailand and Myanmar. A productive and ornamentally handsome tree for large tropical gardens, with attractive compound leaves and interesting fruits hanging from the main trunk and larger branches. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Monkey Jack (Pingan, Terap Hutan)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; monkey jack is more shade-tolerant than jackfruit and suited to multi-story food forest understory planting. Artocarpus rigidus (monkey jack, pingan, or terap hutan) is a tropical Artocarpus species from the lowland dipterocarp forests of Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines — one of several dozen Artocarpus species in the breadfruit and jackfruit genus, most of which produce edible composite fruits through cauliflory (fruiting on the trunk and main branches). Monkey jack produces round to oval, 2–4 inch composite fruits with a spiny-bumpy, green exterior and orange-yellow, sweet, somewhat sticky flesh surrounding multiple seeds. The flavor is sweet, fruity, and pleasant when fully ripe, though less refined in flavor than the closely related cempedak (A. integer) or jackfruit (A. heterophyllus). It is primarily a forest fruit eaten opportunistically in Malaysia and Indonesia rather than a major cultivated crop, and is notable mainly to tropical fruit collectors and ethnobotanists documenting the edible Artocarpus species of Borneo. As a garden tree, monkey jack is smaller and more manageable than jackfruit, with good shade tolerance making it useful in food forest designs. Restricted to zone 11–12 humid tropics. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Monkey Puzzle Tree (Pehuen)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun with plenty of room, since this striking Chilean and Argentine conifer eventually becomes a very large, unmistakable tree with thick, reptilian, spirally arranged branches covered in sharp, overlapping, scale-like leaves — an architectural specimen unlike anything else commonly grown. Native to the cool temperate rainforests and volcanic slopes of the southern Andes, it is the sacred tree of the Indigenous Mapuche and Pehuenche peoples, whose name for the tree, pehuen, gave the Pehuenche people their name as "people of the pehuen," reflecting the tree's central place in their diet and culture for millennia. Female cones take about three years to mature and release large, edible, chestnut-like seeds (piñones) that are traditionally roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, but a tree needs both a male and female cone-bearing tree nearby and several decades of growth before it produces a nut crop, making it a multigenerational planting rather than a quick food source. It tolerates cold well but resents the sustained summer heat and humidity of the Gulf South, performing best in cool-summer, mild-winter climates such as the Pacific Northwest or higher elevations. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Monmouth Hazelnut (Rutgers EFB-Resistant Eastern Filbert)
description: Monmouth is a moderately vigorous, slightly spreading hazelnut released in 2020 by Rutgers University as part of the first wave of Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant cultivars bred for Mid-Atlantic growing conditions. It is a high-yielding, early-blooming selection producing medium, round kernels that blanch very well after roasting, making it well suited to confectionery use as well as fresh eating. Because it is self-incompatible, pair it with a compatible pollenizer such as Raritan or Somerset for consistent nut set, and harvest in the first to second week of September when nuts drop free of the husk. It is recommended for USDA zones 6-7, reflecting its New Jersey breeding and trial origins. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Monroe Avocado (Late-Season Florida Avocado)
description: Monroe is a vigorous Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid grown in South Florida chiefly for its very late harvest, with large, round fruit typically maturing in early winter after most other cultivars have finished. The thick, leathery skin protects moderately oily, rich-flavored flesh that holds well after picking, and the tree's late timing makes it a useful complement to earlier-ripening cultivars like Simmonds or Choquette in a home planting. Its size makes it best suited to larger properties, and like other Guatemalan-influenced hybrids it tolerates a bit more cool weather than pure West Indian types, though it still cannot take frost. Grow in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Monstera (Swiss Cheese Plant, Fruit Salad Plant)
description: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in deep to bright indirect shade; monstera is one of the world's most recognizable houseplants in temperate climates but grows as a large, vigorous outdoor vine in zone 10–12, where it can climb 20 feet or more up trees, walls, and structures by aerial roots. In the wild it migrates from deep shade toward brighter light as it matures, producing the characteristic deeply lobed and perforated leaves only in brighter conditions — deeply shaded plants have smaller, unlobed juvenile leaves. The edible 'fruit' is actually a cone-like cluster of hexagonal segments that ripens from the base upward over 10–12 months; fully ripe segments slip off cleanly and taste like a blend of pineapple, banana, and coconut. Unripe fruit contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense mouth irritation — harvest only segments that have separated naturally from the base. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Monstrueuse Medlar (Giant French Heirloom Medlar)
description: Monstrueuse is an old French cultivar selected for producing some of the largest fruit of any medlar, on a small, picturesque, twisting tree that also carries showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is picked hard in late fall and then bletted, meaning it is stored in a cool spot for several weeks until the flesh softens and browns into a soft, spiced-apple-and-date flavor before eating. The tree needs little pruning beyond removing crossing or dead wood and tolerates poor soil far better than most orchard fruit, though it fruits best with a reasonably sunny site. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree will set a full crop without a pollinizer. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Monstrueux de Viroflay Spinach
description: This large French heirloom spinach produces enormous smooth leaves and is known for fast, heavy yields. Sow seed half an inch deep in cool soil as early as it can be worked, since heat prevents germination and triggers bolting. Thin to 6 inches and keep beds evenly moist and rich in nitrogen for lush leaves. Harvest whole plants or pick outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again supply. Sow again in late summer for a fall crop that sweetens with frost. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Montana Gold Melon
description: Montana Gold was originally offered as an ultra-early cantaloupe for gardeners coping with high elevation and short, cool growing seasons. Its compact vines set small fruit with notably thick, sweet flesh, ripening well ahead of the 85-90 day eastern cantaloupe standards most catalogs offer. It remains a practical choice anywhere summers run too short or too cool for full-season melons, though its fruit size and yield are modest compared with longer-season heirlooms. The variety persists today mainly through small regional seed-saving networks rather than large commercial suppliers. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Montana Zemo Hardneck Garlic
description: Plant this vigorous Porcelain-type hardneck garlic in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, so the cloves root before winter. Break the bulbs into individual cloves just before planting and set them pointed end up 2 inches deep and 6 to 8 inches apart, then mulch heavily for winter protection. Each bulb yields 4 to 7 large, pink-wrapped cloves with a buttery, nutty, low-heat flavor. Remove the scapes in early summer to boost bulb size, and harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Montauk Sweet Corn (Jumbo-Ear Cool-Soil Bicolor Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Montauk is a synergistic-type bicolor sweet corn hybrid, blending sugary-enhanced and supersweet genetics for excellent flavor and good cool-soil vigor at germination, letting Gulf Coast gardeners plant slightly earlier than standard supersweet types allow. It produces large, jumbo-sized ears packed with tender yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for well-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Montebianco Fennel (Finocchio Montebianco)
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin seedlings to their final spacing, since bulbing fennel does not transplant well once its taproot is established. Montebianco is a heritage Italian bulbing fennel, its name referencing Mont Blanc, selected for producing mid-sized, very round, solid white bulbs that mature somewhat earlier than many other Florence types. It is prized among Italian heirloom growers for holding a tight, crisp bulb shape without the hollowing or splitting that affects some older strains, and for tolerating the changeable summer weather typical of the UK and Ireland better than most open-pollinated fennels. Mound soil around the swelling bulb base as it develops to keep the flesh pale and tender rather than green and woody. Harvest by cutting the bulb at ground level once it has filled out, and use the feathery foliage as a bonus fresh herb. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Monterey Almond (Large Late-Blooming Soft-Shell Almond)
description: Monterey is a California-bred almond cultivar developed as a heavy-yielding, large-kerneled companion to Nonpareil, valued for its bigger nut size and later bloom that reduces frost risk compared with earlier-flowering cultivars. The soft-shelled nuts are attractive and uniform, making them popular for the in-shell and snack market as well as shelled use. It is not self-fertile and depends on overlapping bloom with a compatible pollinizer for a full crop, so orchard rows typically alternate Monterey with Nonpareil or another midseason cultivar. Grow it in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with the low water needs typical of almond, and harvest by shaking the tree once hulls split in late summer to early fall. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Monterey Strawberry (Day-Neutral UC Davis Heavy-Fruiting Strawberry)
description: Plant bare-root or plugs in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil; mulch with straw to maintain moisture and keep fruit off the soil. Monterey is a day-neutral strawberry developed by the University of California at Davis and released in 2009 by plant breeders Douglas Shaw and Kirk Larson — a variety bred to combine the high-productivity and large berry size of California commercial strawberries with the continuous-production advantage of day-neutral types. Day-neutral strawberries (unlike traditional June-bearing types) produce fruit throughout the growing season regardless of day length — triggered to bloom and fruit by temperature rather than day length. This gives Monterey a very long harvest window in zone 8–10, where it can produce from early spring through late fall with a summer break during the hottest months. The berries are large (1–1.5 inch diameter), firm, and very flavorful — significantly more aromatic and sweet than many commercial varieties, though with the large size that makes them visually attractive. Monterey was developed for California coast conditions (mild summers, year-round production) and performs exceptionally well in Gulf Coast fall and spring conditions that mimic coastal California temperatures. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Monterrey Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Texas Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator such as Orient or Hood, since Monterrey sets fruit best with a second variety nearby. Like other Kieffer-type hybrid pears bred for the South, Monterrey combines strong resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates many European dessert pears in the humid Gulf region, with a low chilling requirement that suits mild zone 8-9 winters. Fruit is firm, gritty-textured, and best used cooked, canned, or in preserves rather than eaten fresh off the tree, and it keeps well after harvest, softening gradually in storage. The vigorous, disease-resistant tree needs little spraying compared to European dessert pears, making it a practical low-maintenance choice for home orchards in hot, humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Montgomery Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Mid-Season Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Montgomery is a vigorous rabbiteye blueberry cultivar developed for Southern growing conditions, producing a reliable mid-season crop of medium to large, firm berries with good flavor. The bushes are notably vigorous and productive, establishing quickly and bearing well once mature, making Montgomery a dependable choice for filling out a mid-season harvest window alongside earlier and later rabbiteye selections. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, it requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Monthong Durian (D159)
description: Monthong (Thai for 'golden pillow') is Thailand's leading commercial durian cultivar and the variety most commonly exported worldwide, known for large fruit, thick pale-yellow flesh, a relatively mild odor and sweetness compared to other cultivars, and a small proportion of seed to flesh. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with high humidity and warm year-round temperatures; the tree flowers at night and depends primarily on bats for pollination, so avoid pesticide applications near dusk. Fruit develops over roughly 3-5 months and should be left to drop naturally rather than cut from the tree, both for safety around the spiny husk and for proper ripening. Monthong trees are large and long-lived, eventually reaching great size where climate allows sustained outdoor growth. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Monticello White Chayote
description: Monticello White is a cream-to-pale-skinned chayote cultivar, one of the two commercially cloned selections most commonly sold at Florida garden centers alongside Florida Green, and named for the north Florida city near the research station associated with its selection. Its smooth, ivory fruit is slightly milder and more tender-skinned than the common green types, and it is prized in home gardens both for fresh eating and for its ornamental pale coloring on the vine. Like all chayote it needs a season of six months or more of warmth to fruit heavily, so Gulf Coast growers should plant as early as safely possible after frost and provide a large, strong trellis. The vine's large starchy tuberous root, which develops after a full growing season, is also edible and can be dug and cooked like a yam once the vine dies back for winter. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Montmorency Cherry
description: Montmorency is the classic self-fertile tart pie cherry, so a single tree will crop heavily on its own. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding frost pockets that damage the early bloom. It is more compact and cold-hardy than sweet cherries, making it well suited to northern gardens. Prune to an open center in late winter and net the ripening fruit against birds. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Montreal Market Melon
description: Sow directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost, or start indoors in short-season climates and transplant carefully to avoid root disturbance. This heavy-feeding Quebecois heirloom was cultivated by market gardeners around Montreal in the late 1800s and prized for producing enormous, heavily netted, nutmeg-type melons that could reach 10-15 pounds under generous manuring and glass-frame protection. Its green flesh is exceptionally sweet and aromatic, though the variety demands rich soil and a long, warm season to reach its famous size. Nearly lost to commercial cultivation, it survives today largely through heirloom seed-saving networks. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Montreal Muskmelon
description: Sow in deeply enriched, well-drained hills after last frost; Montreal Muskmelon is a large, demanding variety that needs rich soil and ample space — traditional Montreal growers would excavate three-foot-deep planting holes and fill them with aged manure before planting. Montreal Muskmelon was the most celebrated North American melon from roughly 1850 to 1920, grown on the Island of Montreal (particularly in the Rivière-des-Prairies area) in intensively managed, manure-enriched beds and shipped to Montreal, New York, and Boston as a luxury fruit commanding premium prices; the Ferme Onésime Pépin operation shipped 11,000 melons daily at peak production. The large (10–15 lb), deeply ribbed, heavily netted fruits have orange flesh with a rich, intensely sweet, musky perfume that made it the yardstick by which all other melons were judged. It went extinct in commercial production by the 1940s but was revived from Seed Savers Exchange members; now being recultivated by slow food advocates in Montreal. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Monty Kiwi (Late-Season California Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a sturdy arbor or T-bar trellis capable of supporting many years of vigorous growth. Monty was among the original fuzzy kiwifruit cultivars grown commercially in California alongside Hayward, Bruno, Abbott, and Allison, and it is noted for consistent heavy yields and a harvest season that runs later than Hayward, helping spread out the fresh-eating window. As with all fuzzy kiwi, Monty is dioecious and a female vine will not fruit without a compatible male pollinizer blooming nearby at the same time. Prune hard in winter to manage the vine's fast, sprawling growth and to keep fruiting wood accessible, and provide consistent irrigation through the growing season since kiwi vines are shallow-rooted and drought-sensitive. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Moon and Stars Watermelon (Star-Speckled Heirloom Watermelon)
description: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness. Moon and Stars is a striking American heirloom watermelon, first documented in the late 1800s and rescued from near-extinction in the 1980s after seed saver Merle Van Doren shared surviving seed with Kent Whealy of Seed Savers Exchange, reviving a variety that had all but vanished from commerce. Its dark green rind is scattered with one large yellow 'moon' spot and many smaller yellow 'star' speckles, a genetically distinctive and instantly recognizable pattern; the leaves also show smaller yellow speckling, making the plant ornamental even before fruiting. Flesh is sweet, deep red, and classic in flavor, and large fruits commonly reach 20-40 pounds. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners who want to preserve genetic and horticultural history alongside a tasty harvest. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Moonglow Pear
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Moonglow cross-pollinates well with Seckel, Bartlett, Harrow Sweet, and most other European pear varieties. Moonglow pear was released by the USDA in 1960 from a breeding program targeting soft-fleshed, early-ripening pear varieties for Southern gardens; it produces medium-large, pyriform (classic pear-shaped), pale yellow to greenish-yellow fruits that ripen in late July to August — the earliest of the commonly grown European pears. The flesh is white, very soft, mild, and sweet without the grittiness of some older pear varieties; it is a dessert pear best for eating fresh as it does not hold well after picking (must be ripened off the tree like Bartlett). Good fire blight resistance makes it more reliable than Bartlett in humid southeastern gardens. Partially self-fruitful; cross-pollinate with another European pear for best yields. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Moongold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Apricot, Sungold Pollinizer Pair)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, always alongside a Sungold apricot, since Moongold cannot pollinate itself and the two varieties were specifically bred and released together by the University of Minnesota as a compatible pollination pair for cold climates. The medium-sized, yellow-orange fruit has sweet, juicy flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves, produced by a genuinely cold-hardy tree that extends apricot growing well into regions too harsh for most other varieties. As with most cold-hardy northern apricots, the tree's biggest challenge is not winter cold but early spring bloom, which can be damaged by a late frost even though the tree itself survives severe winter temperatures without difficulty; a site that avoids low-lying frost pockets helps protect the crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Moorcroft Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Classified among the bitter, high-tannin, low-acid perry pears, it can be difficult to work with thanks to its narrow ripening window and the sheer height of its trees, but the resulting juice is prized by perry makers, with well-bletted fruit described as tasting somewhere between fresh dates and a bakewell tart with custard. Its high tannin content gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, making it a valued component of traditional Three Counties perry blends. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in fall, let it sweat and blett for several days, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Moore Pecan (Historic Texas Heirloom Pecan, Parent of the Apalachee Cultivar)
description: Moore is a historic Texas heirloom pecan long grown in the San Saba and Hill Country region, prized in its day for a notably light-colored, good-flavored kernel. It carries breeding significance as one of the parents, crossed with Schley at Brownwood, Texas in 1948, of the modern cultivar Apalachee. Because mature Moore trees are prone to alternate bearing and inconsistent nut quality, and the variety lacks the scab resistance of newer releases, it suits heirloom orchards and breeding collections better than a primary planting in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Moorpark Apricot (Classic English Heirloom Apricot, Large-Fruited Heritage Apricot)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Moorpark requires a cross-pollinator; thin heavy crops to 4–6 inches after natural fruit drop for maximum size; harvest when fruit is deep orange, fully colored, and gives slightly to pressure — Moorpark is at its best consumed fresh within days of picking, as the extraordinarily rich, honeyed flavor at peak ripeness is what makes this variety historically important. Moorpark apricot is one of the great classical apricot varieties of the English-speaking world, an heirloom dating to at least the early 1600s in England and named for Moorpark House in Hertfordshire where it was grown extensively — though its origins may be even earlier and possibly Italian or Continental European. For centuries, Moorpark was the standard of apricot excellence in England, appearing in historic orchards of country houses and kitchen gardens throughout the British Isles, and was the variety which set the benchmark against which all other apricots were evaluated. The fruits are large (for the era), round to oval, deep orange to orange-red with a distinctive dark blush, with firm, richly sweet-tart, intensely flavored orange flesh that is considered among the finest flavors of any apricot variety even by modern standards — a rich, honeyed, complex flavor that distinguishes it from the milder, blander commercial varieties selected for shelf life. Moorpark is not self-fertile and requires cross-pollination; the spring blossoms appear very early and are vulnerable to late frosts, making site selection on a frost-protected slope or south-facing wall important for reliable fruiting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Morado Yacon (Purple-Skinned Andean Ground Apple)
description: Morado is a traditional Andean strain of yacon distinguished from the common tan-skinned type by its deep reddish-purple tuber skin and correspondingly purple-flushed stem bases, though the crisp, juicy, pear-like flesh inside remains cream to pale yellow. Grow it exactly as standard yacon: propagate only from the knobby rhizome crowns at the base of last season's stalks (never from the large storage roots, which lack buds and will not sprout), and give it a long, frost-free season of at least five to six months to bulk up its tubers. Many growers who maintain both types report Morado yields slightly smaller but more numerous roots than pale-skinned strains, with a similar sweet, watery crunch that intensifies after a week or two of post-harvest curing in a warm, sunny spot. Because it is an old landrace rather than a registered cultivar, plant vigor and skin color can vary somewhat between sources. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Moranga Pumpkin
description: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in deeply amended, fertile soil and thin to the strongest plant when 3 inches tall; Moranga is a large, flat-ribbed, orange-red Brazilian pumpkin (Cucurbita maxima) with deep orange, dense, sweet flesh used throughout Brazil as the traditional vessel for stuffed shrimp dishes (camarão na moranga) and as a soup tureen. The large fruits, averaging 15–25 pounds, are oval to flat with a warty, orange skin and extraordinarily thick, starchy-sweet flesh with minimal seed cavity. The Moranga type is closely related to Hubbard squash and has been cultivated in Brazil for centuries. The flesh makes exceptional purées, soups, and savory stuffings. Store cured fruits for 3–4 months in cool conditions. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Moreland Pecan (Scab-Resistant Gulf South Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Selected for reliable production and notably good resistance to pecan scab, a fungal disease that is a major limiting factor for pecan growing in humid Gulf Coast climates, Moreland has long been a dependable choice for growers in Louisiana, Mississippi, and neighboring states where less resistant cultivars require heavy fungicide programs. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality, and the tree is a consistent annual bearer under good management, making it a solid choice for growers prioritizing lower-input disease tolerance over maximum nut size. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Morello Cherry (English Morello, Dark Sour Cherry, Culinary Sour Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun or partial shade; Morello is self-fertile; the dark red to nearly black fruits ripen in late July to August — later than most sweet cherries — and are very tart, intended for cooking, preserves, and culinary preparations rather than fresh-eating; harvest when fully black for maximum color in jams and liqueurs. Morello cherry is the classic European culinary sour cherry — a dark-skinned, dark-fleshed variety with deep red to nearly black skin and dark red juice that distinguishes it from the clear-juiced Montmorency type — grown for centuries in English, Dutch, and German cottage gardens as the primary cherry for preserves, pies, tarts, cherry brandy, and the fermented cherry preparations traditional in continental Europe. The dark flesh and juice of Morello give it distinct advantages over Montmorency in certain culinary applications: cherry jam, jelly, and liqueurs (including the famous Schwarzwälder Kirschwasser of the Black Forest and the maraschino cherry liqueur of Central Europe) derive their deep red-purple color from Morello's dark pigments, producing a dramatically richer-colored product than would result from clear-juiced cherries. Morello is also notable for being one of the few cherry varieties that will bear adequate crops in partial shade — a practical advantage in British and northwestern European cottage gardens where full sun is not always available. The fruit is very tart at all stages of ripeness, with a complex sourness and rich cherry flavor that intensifies with cooking and makes it the definitive variety for traditional European cherry cookery. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Morgan Pear (Highly Fire-Blight-Resistant University of Tennessee Pear)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Morgan, the companion release to Carrick from the University of Tennessee's 1950s fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program, was rated highly resistant to fire blight in USDA Beltsville, Maryland evaluations, making it one of the more dependable pear choices for humid Southern gardens where fire blight regularly damages susceptible European cultivars. Fruit has the firm, reliable qualities typical of Southern-bred pears, suited to fresh eating once ripened off the tree as well as canning and preserving. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions typical of home orchard management. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Moringa (Drumstick Tree, Miracle Tree, Horseradish Tree)
description: Direct sow or plant stem cuttings in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; moringa is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually performs better in poor, dry soil than in rich, wet conditions. Moringa oleifera (moringa, drumstick tree, or miracle tree) is a North Indian native now cultivated throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide as one of the most nutritionally dense multipurpose food trees known — virtually all parts are edible and extraordinarily nutritious: the young leaves are exceptionally high in vitamins A, C, B6, calcium, iron, potassium, and protein and are eaten steamed, added to soups and curries, or dried and powdered as a nutritional supplement; the immature green seed pods (drumsticks) are used in curries; the mature seeds are pressed for edible, high-quality oil (moringa or ben oil); and the roots have a flavor similar to horseradish and are used as a condiment. In zone 9, moringa grows as a fast-growing perennial that may die back to the roots in hard freezes but resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 10–12, it is a permanent tree. Cut back to 4–5 feet annually to maintain productive, harvestable leaf growth rather than letting it become a large tree. Matures in 90–240 days from seed.

name: Moro Blood Orange (Red-Flesh Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Moro is the deepest-colored blood orange cultivar — a Sicilian selection producing dramatic, dark crimson to near-black flesh with a striking red-streaked rind exterior. The flavor is distinctly more complex than standard sweet oranges, with a pronounced berry-like, raspberry-blackberry tone layered over the sweet orange base — a flavor unlike any other citrus. The deep red color comes from water-soluble anthocyanin pigments that develop only when cool nights (below 55°F) occur during fruit development; in very warm winters the flesh may show less red coloration but still produces the characteristic flavor. In zone 9, Moro blood oranges ripen in December through February — the coolest months — when the anthocyanin development is most favorable. The small to medium, round to slightly oval fruits have a thin, smooth rind. Blood oranges are highly valued in cooking for their dramatic color in fresh-squeezed juice (which turns deep ruby-red to purple), salad dressings, sauces, and cocktails. The juice color provides a culinary application that no other citrus can replicate. Protect from temperatures below 28°F; site in thermally protected areas of zone 9 gardens. Matures in 270–330 days from transplant.

name: Moroccan Cilantro
description: Moroccan coriander is a fast-growing, four-in-one herb, giving a quick flush of leaves, edible white flowers for beneficial insects, and, above all, large aromatic seeds. It is especially valued for its heavy yield of round coriander seed used in baking and spice blends. Direct sow into cool soil since the taproot resists transplanting, and let plants flower and set seed for harvest. Provide full sun and even moisture, then cut seed heads once they turn tan and dry them fully before storing. Matures in 45–90 days from seed.

name: Moroccan Mint (Classic Culinary Spearmint for Tea)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Moroccan Mint is the classic spearmint selection traditionally used for Moroccan mint tea, prized for its clean, sweet, true spearmint flavor without the sharper menthol bite of peppermint, making it the standard choice for hot mint tea sweetened with sugar as well as for cocktails like mojitos and juleps. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather to prevent wilting, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut the planting back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage for the rest of the growing season. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Morris Burton American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Indiana Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and undemanding of fertile soil. Morris Burton is a named American persimmon cultivar out of Indiana grown for its combination of dependable cold hardiness, early bearing age, and consistent production of medium, seedless orange fruit without requiring a nearby male tree. The fruit ripens in mid-fall and, like other American persimmons, must fully soften on the tree or after a hard frost to lose its raw astringency, at which point the flesh turns sweet, thick, and richly flavored — excellent fresh, or processed into persimmon pudding, bread, and butter. Its good cold tolerance and self-fruiting habit make it a popular choice for northern-edge persimmon growers and for gardeners who want a single reliable tree without pollination logistics, in zone 5–9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Morris Heading Collards
description: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24–30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wider spacing than most collards is needed because Morris Heading forms a loose, cabbage-like head rather than a simple open rosette of leaves. This old Southern heirloom collard is distinctive among collard varieties for its semi-heading habit — the inner leaves cup and fold inward to form a loose head reminiscent of a savoy cabbage, while the outer leaves remain harvestable individually as with any collard. The smooth, tender, blue-green leaves have a sweeter, milder flavor than many open-leaf collard varieties, and the heading habit helps blanch and protect the inner leaves from cold and insect damage. Long grown in home gardens across the Carolinas and Georgia, it is well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, where fall-planted crops can be harvested over many months. Zone 6–10. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Morris Plum (Texas A&M Low-Chill Self-Fertile Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; prune to open-center form. Thin fruit heavily at marble size for maximum size and quality. Morris Plum is a Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) developed at the Texas A&M University Agricultural Experiment Station in Montague County, Texas — one of the primary low-chill Japanese plum varieties released specifically for the hot, humid climate of the South and Gulf Coast region where most standard Japanese plum varieties from California require too many chilling hours or fail to set fruit reliably. Morris carries a low chilling requirement (400–450 hours) that is reliably met throughout most of zone 7–9, and the variety's self-fertile nature (it can pollinate itself and set a full crop without a second plum nearby) makes it particularly practical for home gardeners with space for only one tree. The fruit is medium-sized, round, with mahogany-red skin and amber to yellow flesh — freestone at full ripeness — with good sweet-tart plum flavor. Morris is notably productive for a low-chill plum, bearing heavily in most years when the chilling requirement is met. Texas A&M's stone fruit breeding program (which also produced Bruce plum and other Gulf South stone fruit varieties) made commercial and home plum production viable across zone 7–9 of Texas and the surrounding Gulf South. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mortgage Lifter Lima Bean
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mortgage Lifter lima bean is an Appalachian heirloom from Virginia and West Virginia — an exceptionally productive, large-seeded pole lima with big, flat seeds that can reach half an inch across and fill the pod tightly with 3–5 massive seeds per pod. The sheer yield of these large limas made the variety valuable for subsistence gardeners who could shell, cook, and preserve enormous quantities of butter beans from a small planting, historically giving the variety its name. Fresh-shelled Mortgage Lifter limas have an exceptionally creamy, buttery, starchy flavor — richer than most commercial lima beans and similar in quality to the best Virginia butter beans. Like all limas, they thrive in Gulf Coast heat and continue producing through summer when most other legumes have failed. Harvest pods when plump and the seeds inside are full but still green for fresh eating; allow to fully dry on the vine for dry beans. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Mortgage Lifter Pole Tomato
description: Start this classic indeterminate beefsteak indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes, burying part of the stem for strong roots. The Halladay strain produces hefty 1 to 2 pound pink beefsteak fruits with crack-resistant skin on vigorous vines. Provide a sturdy tall cage or stake, prune suckers for airflow, and water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot. Harvest the big fruits as they ripen to keep the plant setting more. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Mortgage Lifter Tomato
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, amended soil after frost risk passes; Mortgage Lifter is a legendary American heirloom developed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia in the 1930s by crossing four large tomato varieties over six years — the resulting tomatoes sold so well at 50 cents each that he paid off his mortgage in six years, giving the variety its unforgettable name. Fruits are very large (1–2 pounds), pink-red, with meaty flesh, few seeds, and a mild sweet flavor excellent for fresh eating and slicing. One of the most reliable and high-yielding large heirloom beefsteak types, with better disease tolerance than many heirlooms. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Mortgage Lifter Tomato
description: Mortgage Lifter is a famous indeterminate heirloom beefsteak known for enormous, meaty pink-red fruits that often top two pounds. The rich, mild, low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and sandwiches. Start seed indoors several weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the soil is warm, burying the stem deeply. Provide sturdy staking or caging, since the tall vines carry very heavy fruit and keep producing until frost. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Morton Citrange (Cold-Hardy Orange-Flavored Citrus Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for citrus, with mature wood able to withstand temperatures well below what standard sweet orange trees survive, thanks to trifoliate orange parentage. Morton citrange is a hybrid between trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) and sweet orange, bred primarily to extend cold-hardy citrus growing further north than standard oranges allow. The fruit is tart, seedy, and more acidic than a true sweet orange, generally used for juice, marmalade, or as an ade rather than fresh eating out of hand, though well-ripened fruit mellows considerably. Trees show the trifoliate parent's deciduous or semi-deciduous habit in colder winters and small, three-part leaves, along with light thorns typical of trifoliate hybrids. Because of its unusual hardiness, Morton citrange has been of particular interest to cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing the edible citrus range into zone 6-7, well beyond where standard citrus survives. Protect young trees for the first few winters; established trees are considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored for the best balance of sweetness and acidity. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mosaic Hops
description: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Mosaic is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2012, this vigorous, high-yielding American hop produces cones with an unusually complex aroma profile combining tropical fruit, citrus, pine, and berry notes all at once, living up to its name by contributing a shifting mosaic of different flavor impressions depending on how it is used in a beer recipe. Its complexity and versatility across both bittering and late-addition aromatic brewing uses have made it one of the most in-demand hop varieties among craft brewers since its release, commanding premium prices and frequently being in short supply. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Moskvich Pole Tomato
description: Start this early Russian indeterminate indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes. Bred in the early 1970s near Moscow, Moskvich withstands cool weather and is often the first tomato to ripen, offering round, deep-red fruits with rich flavor. Provide a tall stake or cage since the vines keep growing all season, and prune suckers for better airflow. Water consistently at the base and harvest as fruits color up to encourage continued production. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Moso Bamboo (Giant Bamboo)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained loamy soil in full sun; moso bamboo is the most economically important bamboo in the world — the source of most commercial bamboo timber, flooring, furniture, textiles, and paper produced globally. It also produces the most prized bamboo shoots in Chinese cuisine, harvested in spring when they emerge from the ground. The new shoots can be harvested before they emerge from the soil (the pale, tender, underground form) or just as they break the surface. ALWAYS install a deep root barrier (24 inches minimum) before planting — moso is an aggressive running bamboo that can devastate surrounding plantings and structures without physical containment. The towering, green culms with their distinctive white waxy powder on new growth reach 40–90 feet tall, creating a dramatic grove effect reminiscent of Chinese mountain paintings. Once established, a well-managed grove produces an annual harvest of both timber culms and edible shoots. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Moss Curled Parsley
description: This curled parsley forms dense, ruffled rosettes of deep green that garnish plates beautifully and pack in vitamins A, B, and C. Cold-tolerant, it can be grown as an annual that carries on through fall and into mild winters. Parsley seed is famously slow to sprout, so soak it overnight and be patient, keeping the soil consistently moist. Grow in full sun to part shade with steady water and harvest outer stems first to keep the plant producing. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Mostoller Wild Goose Bean
description: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, training vines up a tall pole, corn stalk, or trellis rather than a light fence. Mostoller Wild Goose is a Pennsylvania heirloom pole bean with a famous origin story: seed was reportedly found in the crop of a wild goose shot in the 1860s and has been passed down through the Mostoller family ever since. The plump, kidney-shaped white beans with a faint pink blush cook to a smooth, creamy texture that many gardeners favor for baking and hearty winter soups. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, and expect strong vigor and heavy yields from a relatively small planting. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Moth Bean
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hot, dry conditions; moth bean is one of the most drought-tolerant grain legumes in the world, capable of producing a crop on as little as 8 inches of annual rainfall. The small, cylindrical pods contain tiny tan or speckled seeds prized in South Asian cooking — sprouted or cooked whole in dal preparations, ground into flour for papadums, and used in the Rajasthani specialty moth ki dal. The spreading, leafy vines make an excellent cover crop for hot, arid, or sandy soils with the added benefit of nitrogen fixation. An outstanding plant for warm, dry climates where most legumes struggle; ideal for zone 9–11 summer gardens. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Mother of Thyme (Creeping Thyme)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential — plants will rot in waterlogged soil. Thymus praecox is a low, mat-forming thyme of central and southern European rocky terrain, producing very flat carpets of tiny, dark-green, aromatic leaves 1–4 inches tall that bear a profusion of bright magenta-pink to lilac flowers in early summer smothered with honeybees; it forms a tighter, denser mat than wild thyme (T. serpyllum) and is the preferred species for most ground-cover, stepping-stone, and lawn-substitute plantings. The aromatic leaves are fully culinary-quality; the plant tolerates foot traffic and shearing well. Subsp. arcticus (with cultivars 'Coccineus', 'Purple Creeping') offers deep red-purple flowers for ornamental use. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Motherwort
description: Direct sow in early spring or late autumn and allow natural freeze-thaw cycles to stratify the seed over winter for strong spring germination. Motherwort thrives in partial shade and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, often naturalizing along hedgerows and woodland margins. Harvest the upper third of flowering stems just as the lower flowers begin to open, using aerial parts fresh or tinctured in alcohol. Wear gloves when harvesting as the prickly calyces are sharp; avoid use during pregnancy due to its uterine-stimulating properties. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Motueka Hops
description: Motueka is a New Zealand aroma cultivar, originally released under the name Stichbury's Seedling, bred from an open-pollinated Saaz-type seedling crossed with local wild hop stock, giving it bright lime, lemon, and tropical citrus aromatics unlike its noble-hop ancestor. Its comparatively low alpha acid content suits it mainly to late-kettle and dry-hop additions rather than bittering. The bine performs best in mild, maritime-influenced climates with consistent moisture and struggles in prolonged summer heat. Provide full sun, a tall trellis, and even watering through cone development to preserve its delicate citrus character. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Mouli Pomegranate (Florida Heirloom Pomegranate)
description: Mouli produces medium-sized fruit with a red hull blushing to pink at the shoulder, enclosing clear arils with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and moderately firm seeds. It ripens in late September, later than many commercial cultivars, which helps stagger the harvest in a home orchard. The shrub grows with multiple upright canes typical of Deep South heirloom pomegranates, and its documented decades-long survival in Florida dooryard plantings speaks to strong resilience against regional heat, humidity, and disease pressure. It was preserved and named through Florida heirloom fruit conservation efforts rather than commercial breeding. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Moulin Rouge Beet (Uniform Cylindrical Hybrid Beet)
description: Sow half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly shaped roots. Moulin Rouge is a modern hybrid cylindrical beet, similar in form to heirloom cylindrical types like Forono but bred for more uniform root shape, smoother skin, and reliable germination and sizing, making slicing and pickling more efficient with less trimming waste. The deep red, sweet, tender flesh holds its color well when cooked, and the long, straight roots make it a favorite for home canning and pickling where consistent slice size matters. Because the roots grow mostly upright rather than wide, plants can be spaced somewhat closer than round beet varieties for the same yield. The greens are also edible and good cooked as beet greens. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Mount Hood Hops
description: A low-alpha noble-type aroma hop bred from German Hallertau stock at Oregon State, prized by home brewers for clean, mild spicy-herbal character in pilsners and lagers. Give it deep, well-drained, fertile soil and a sturdy 12-18 foot support, since bines climb aggressively once established. Cut the first-year crown back hard after frost and mulch heavily to protect the root system through winter. Expect only a token harvest the first year, with full cone production arriving by year three. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mount Royal Plum (Canadian Cold-Hardy European Freestone Prune Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mount Royal is self-fruitful and very cold-hardy; the round to oval blue-purple fruits ripen in late August to mid-September; flavor is rich, sweet, and high-quality — one of the best-tasting cold-hardy European plums; suitable for fresh eating, preserves, cooking, and drying. Mount Royal plum is a Canadian-origin European prune plum (Prunus domestica) that has been widely grown in Quebec and the northeastern states since its selection in the Montreal area (likely in the late 19th century), where it consistently demonstrated the cold-hardiness and reliable self-fruitfulness that make it particularly valuable in zones 4–5 where standard European plums like Stanley and Italian Prune may suffer winter damage or require cross-pollination to set adequate crops. The name reflects its Canadian origin — Mount Royal (Mont-Royal) is the mountain in the heart of Montreal, and the variety's proven performance in that zone 5 climate is its primary recommendation. Mount Royal produces medium-sized, round to slightly oval, blue-purple to dark blue fruits with firm, yellow-green, freestone flesh and a sweet, rich European plum flavor with balanced acid and sugar that makes it excellent for all purposes: fresh eating at peak ripeness, preserves and jam, plum butter, cooking in tarts and cakes, and drying into prunes. It is considered one of the best-tasting cold-hardy European plums available, with quality comparable to Stanley but with significantly better cold-hardiness and self-fruitfulness. An essential variety for home orchards in zones 4–5 where plum options are limited. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mount Vernon Asian Pear (WSU Research Station Selection)
description: Mount Vernon was identified by Raintree Nursery as the best of many open-pollinated Asian pear seedlings trialed at the Washington State University Mount Vernon Northwestern Washington Research and Extension Station, making it a Pacific Northwest regional selection bred for maritime climates. It bears large, round, cream-colored fruit in mid-season with crisp, juicy flesh and excellent flavor, eaten fresh rather than stored to soften. It is not self-fertile and needs a compatible Asian pear cultivar for cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Fresh Plus Tomato (Southern Disease-Resistant Slicer)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Mountain Fresh Plus is a North Carolina State University-bred determinate hybrid tomato from the Mountain series (which also includes Mountain Merit, Mountain Spring, and Mountain Pride), developed to combine excellent fruit quality with broad disease resistance for Southern and transitional-climate production. The large (8–12 oz), globe, bright red fruits have firm, crack-resistant skin, good internal color, and balanced sweet-acid flavor — a reliable all-purpose slicing tomato without the flavor complexity of heirlooms but with vastly superior disease resistance and shelf life. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes (races 0, 1, 2, 3) — one of the broadest resistance packages available in a Southern-bred tomato. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 home gardens and market growers who need reliable, marketable tomatoes with broad disease protection in humid, challenging Southern conditions. Matures in 77–83 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Huckleberry (Black Huckleberry)
description: Mountain huckleberry naturally colonizes the filtered light beneath conifer forests in the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, so give it acidic soil, steady moisture, and the dappled shade of nearby trees rather than open, exposed sun. Established plants spread slowly by underground rhizomes and reward patience with intensely flavored, dark purple berries in late summer that are considered by many foragers to be the finest of all the huckleberries for pies, jam, and eating fresh. It is notoriously slow to establish from nursery stock, so plant it where it can be left undisturbed for years. This is a true forest-floor crop, offering a genuinely shade-adapted alternative to sun-loving blueberries. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Magic Tomato (Disease-Resistant Cherry-Cocktail Hybrid)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Mountain Magic was bred by Dr. Randy Gardner at North Carolina State University specifically to combine outstanding disease resistance with excellent flavor, standing up to late blight, early blight, and septoria leaf spot far better than most home-garden tomatoes. It produces heavy clusters of 1-2 ounce, deep red cocktail-sized fruit with rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor prized by growers who find most disease-resistant hybrids bland by comparison. Because it keeps producing healthy foliage and fruit even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in humid Gulf Coast summers, it is an especially good choice for gardeners who have struggled with blight on other varieties. Pick fruit as it ripens to bright red and keep harvesting regularly to encourage continued production through the season. Matures in 66–75 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Merit Bush Tomato
description: Start this determinate slicer indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes, burying part of the stem. As a 2014 All-America Selections winner, Mountain Merit offers strong disease resistance including to Fusarium wilt and produces a beautiful red beefsteak on compact plants suited to containers. Its condensed harvest period is handy for preserving a large batch at once. Support the plants with a cage, water consistently at the base, and harvest fruits as they ripen. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Mint
description: Plant divisions in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 18–24 inches apart; mountain mint is a native Eastern North American herb whose square stems and small white flowers appear in mid-to-late summer and are among the most powerful pollinator attractors in the native plant palette, drawing dozens of bee, wasp, and butterfly species simultaneously. The foliage has an intense peppermint-spearmint fragrance when brushed and can be dried for tea, used fresh in beverages, or as a culinary mint substitute. Plants spread vigorously by underground rhizomes — contain in raised beds or mow surrounding areas annually to limit spread. Fresh or dried leaves repel insects effectively. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Papaya
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Vasconcellea pubescens is remarkably cold-tolerant compared to common papaya (Carica papaya) — tolerating brief temperatures to 26–28°F when established, making it the best papaya-like fruit tree for zone 8 climates — water regularly, fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer, and prune to maintain tidy form. Vasconcellea pubescens (Mountain Papaya, Chamorro, or Chihualcan Papaya) is a small to medium-sized, fast-growing, short-lived tree in the Caricaceae (papaya) family native to the Andean highlands of Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Colombia at elevations of 1,500–3,200 meters, where the cool, moist, frost-prone mountain climate would immediately kill common papaya (Carica papaya). As one of the papaya family's most cold-hardy species, V. pubescens withstands light frosts that damage the common papaya — making it the most appropriate papaya relative for cultivation in mild-winter zone 8–10 climates across southern North America and the Mediterranean. The clusters of small (2–4 inch), oblong, yellow-orange, smooth-skinned fruits contain firm, white, strongly aromatic, papaya-like flesh with a distinctive, sharp, tropical-citrus-sour flavor — eaten raw, cooked in stews and soups (popular in Chilean cocina criolla), juiced, and made into jam and preserves across its Andean native range. Plants are typically dioecious and very fast to first fruit (1–2 years from seed), making them productive even as short-lived trees. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Papaya (Andean Papaya)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mountain papaya is a cool-climate relative of common papaya from the Andes of Colombia and Ecuador, adapted to elevations of 5000–10,000 feet where it tolerates light frost to 28°F — considerably more cold-hardy than the common papaya (Carica papaya). The small, yellow-green fruits are high in papain enzymes — even higher than common papaya — and must be cooked before eating, as the raw fruit is too enzyme-active to eat comfortably. Cooked, the flesh is used in jams, jellies, and stews throughout the Andes. In zone 9, mountain papaya can be grown outdoors year-round and provides a more climate-appropriate alternative to common papaya. The plant is dioecious; obtain plants of both sexes for fruiting. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Mountain Pennyroyal
description: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in early summer and root them in a gritty, fast-draining mix before setting plants out in spring in their permanent location of full sun and extremely well-drained, lean soil. This exceptionally fragrant mounding subshrub is native to rocky slopes and mountain meadows of the American West, where it produces dense heads of pinkish-purple flowers in summer that are avidly worked by native bees and hummingbirds. Once established it is highly drought-tolerant and demands little supplemental water, making it an outstanding choice for xeric rock gardens and dry slopes in western gardens. Avoid overwatering or clay soils, which quickly cause root rot; treat it as a Mediterranean herb by cutting back lightly in early spring to remove winter-killed tips and encourage fresh growth. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Pepper (Fragrant Litsea, Maychangberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; litsea grows naturally as an understory tree in subtropical forest and tolerates partial shade well. Litsea cubeba (mountain pepper, fragrant litsea, or maychangberry) is a small to medium-sized deciduous to semi-evergreen tree in the laurel family (Lauraceae) native to the subtropical mountain forests of central and southern China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. The tree produces small (1/4-inch), round, pepper-like black fruits (cubeba = resembling cubeb pepper) with an extraordinarily intense, clean, lemon-floral-citrus aroma — one of the most concentrated natural sources of citral (60–80% of essential oil content), the same aromatic compound found in lemongrass (Cymbopogon), melissa, and other citrus-scented plants. The essential oil of L. cubeba (may chang oil or litsea oil) is extracted commercially and used extensively in high-end perfumery, soap, and cosmetic formulations, and as a natural food flavoring. The dried fruits can be used as a spice — adding a bright, lemony, floral-pepper note to dishes — in a culinary style similar to Sichuan pepper or pink peppercorn. In Taiwan and southern China, the fruits, leaves, and bark are used in traditional mountain tribal cuisine as a distinctive aromatic spice. The tree also has documented antimicrobial activity from citral. It performs well in zone 8–11 subtropical gardens as an aromatic specimen or food forest understory tree. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Pepper (Tasmanian Pepperberry, Native Pepper)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Tasmannia lanceolata (mountain pepper or Tasmanian pepperberry) is a native Australian alpine shrub from the cold, moist rainforests and alpine heathlands of Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales — the most important native Australian spice plant and a signature ingredient of contemporary Australian native cuisine. Both the black, ripe berries and the dried, ground leaves are intensely peppery-hot, with a heat that is initially sharp and then evolves into a prolonged, warming burn distinct from black pepper's heat — the primary pungent compounds (polygodial and drimanyl acetate) belong to a different chemical class from piperine (black pepper's heat compound) and interact differently with the tongue. The dried leaves have a complex, eucalyptus-clove-pepper aroma and are used in Australia as a seasoning rub for lamb, game, and seafood; the berries are used whole or crushed as a distinctive peppercorn substitute. Mountain pepper has become a centerpiece of the Australian 'bush tucker' (native food) movement and is increasingly available in gourmet food markets internationally. The plant is dioecious — plant male and female shrubs for berry production. In cultivation outside Australia, it requires cool, moist, acidic, shaded conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Pride Tomato (Early North Carolina State Disease-Resistant Determinate)
description: Mountain Pride was released by North Carolina State University's vegetable breeding program in 1979 as one of the earliest entries in what became the Mountain series, bred as a determinate hybrid carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt and Fusarium wilt for more reliable production in the humid Southern Appalachians. Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after frost danger passes, staking or caging the relatively compact plants to keep the developing fruit off the ground. It sets a concentrated main crop of firm, medium-large red globes with good old-fashioned tomato flavor over a shorter harvest window than later Mountain-series introductions bred for extended production. Though largely superseded in modern trials by Mountain Spring and its descendants, Mountain Pride is still offered by a few heirloom-minded seed companies for gardeners wanting the original Mountain-series disease package. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Rose Potato (Red-Fleshed All-Purpose Potato)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep 4–6 weeks before last frost, after curing cut surfaces for 1–2 days; Mountain Rose is a striking and delicious red-fleshed potato — the skin is red, but when cut, the flesh is also vivid rose-red to pink throughout, distinguishing it from standard red-skinned potatoes (like Red Pontiac) that have white flesh inside. The rosy-red flesh is high in anthocyanin antioxidants (the same pigments that color red cabbage, blueberries, and beets) and retains some color through cooking, making baked, mashed, and roasted Mountain Rose potatoes visually dramatic. The flavor is rich and earthy with good potato character; the texture is medium-moist and moderately waxy, excellent for baking, roasting, and boiling. Mountain Rose is a versatile all-purpose potato that performs well in both Southern cool-season production and in more northerly climates, and its beautiful color makes it outstanding for farmers' markets and gourmet home cooking. The red flesh fades somewhat during boiling or steaming but is better maintained when roasted or baked. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Soursop (Guanábana Cimarrona)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun — mountain soursop is the larger-fruited relative of common soursop (Annona muricata), native to the rainforests of the Amazon basin, and is considered more vigorous and faster-fruiting than its more common relative. The spiny, ovoid fruits (3–6 inches) have white, fibrous, juicy flesh with a strong tropical flavor used to make juice, ice cream, and desserts similar to soursop. The tree is faster-growing than common soursop and shows slightly greater cold tolerance. Like all Annona species, the flowers produce heat and attract beetle pollinators overnight — cross-pollination with another tree improves fruit set significantly. The handsome, large, dark-green glossy leaves make it an attractive ornamental even when not in fruit. A productive, fast-bearing tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12 gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Spring Tomato (North Carolina State Disease-Resistant Determinate Slicer)
description: Mountain Spring followed Mountain Pride out of the North Carolina State University breeding program, released in 1991 with broader disease resistance and a heavier, more concentrated fruit set that made it a standard commercial and home-garden slicer across the Southeast through the 1990s. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun, staking the sturdy determinate plants to carry the crop of large, firm red globes. It carries resistance to Verticillium wilt and multiple races of Fusarium wilt along with useful field tolerance to early blight, a combination that kept foliage productive later into the season than older Southern-bred tomatoes of its era. Mountain Spring was eventually followed by newer Mountain-series releases such as Mountain Fresh and Mountain Merit, but it remains a dependable, widely adapted choice for home gardens across USDA zones 6-9. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Mountain Sweet Yellow Watermelon
description: This heirloom yields large oblong melons of 20 to 35 pounds with sweet, juicy yellow flesh inside a dark green striped rind. Give each hill rich, well-drained soil and full sun, and allow long vines plenty of room to sprawl. Water steadily while fruit sets, then ease off as melons ripen to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit dries and the ground spot turns creamy. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Mountaineer Half Runner Bean (West Virginia Heirloom Half-Runner)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after last frost, providing light support such as a low trellis or twiggy brush for the heaviest yields. Mountaineer is a West Virginia Appalachian heirloom half-runner bean, a growth habit intermediate between bush and pole types that produces short climbing runners while still setting a concentrated, earlier harvest more like a bush bean. The tender, stringless, flavorful pods are a favorite for fresh eating and traditional Appalachian canning and pickling ('leather britches' style stringing and drying is also common with half-runner types), and the plants tend to keep producing over a longer window than most bush beans. Pick regularly once pods reach full size but before seeds bulge visibly inside, since frequent picking is the single most effective way to keep any snap bean, including half-runners, producing longer. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Mouse Melon Cucamelon
description: These grape-sized fruits look like miniature watermelons but taste like tart cucumber, perfect for pickling or garnishing drinks. Vines can reach 10 feet, so provide a trellis for tidy growth and easy picking. Harvest fruits when firm and about the size of a grape, before they soften and turn sour. Plants tolerate heat well and produce steadily until frost. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Mr. Big Pea (AAS-Winning Large-Podded Shelling Pea)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner prized for its unusually large, plump, sweet pods, often 4-5 inches long and packed with 9-10 large peas, produced heavily on vigorous vines over a fairly long harvest window for the cool season. Its exceptional pod size makes shelling faster and more rewarding than many standard shelling peas. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking every couple of days to encourage continued production before summer heat ends the crop. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Mr. Snow Tomato (Ivory-White Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Mr. Snow bears medium fruit in a pale, creamy ivory-white with mild, low-acid, sweet flavor typical of white tomato varieties, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant that brings this unusual color to a small-space garden. Its pale fruit stands out strikingly against green foliage and in a mixed harvest basket. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint cream-yellow tone, since it never colors red. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Mr. Stripey Tomato (Large Bicolor Yellow-Red Striped Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Mr. Stripey is a large bicolor heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (10–20 oz), somewhat flattened, irregularly shaped fruits with a yellow-to-golden exterior prominently striped and mottled with red or pink-red in an irregular, abstract pattern across the fruit surface. The bicolor exterior reveals a matching interior when sliced — yellow and red-tinted flesh arranged in an irregular pattern that makes each fruit slightly different in cross-section. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity — characteristic of yellow-dominant bicolor tomatoes — and with a melon-like, fruity quality that is outstanding in fresh eating. Mr. Stripey is an indeterminate heirloom with vigorous vines requiring sturdy support throughout the season.
