The very large size of the fruits makes them slow to mature — zone 9 gardeners should start seeds early (8 weeks before last frost) and plant out as early as safely possible to maximize the spring growing window before summer heat arrives. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, the thin skin requires careful handling. Not to be confused with the British variety 'Tigerella' which shares a similar name but is a much smaller (4–6 oz), earlier-maturing, red-with-yellow-striped variety of completely different character. Matures in 80–92 days from transplant.

name: Mridula Pomegranate
description: Mridula was bred at an Indian agricultural research station as an improvement on the older Ganesh cultivar and quickly became one of Maharashtra's major commercial pomegranates alongside Bhagwa and Ganesh. Fruit carries a deep red skin and deep red, soft-seeded arils with a sweeter, less tart flavor profile than Ganesh, and trees are notably more vigorous and productive than their parent. As with other Indian selections, Mridula rewards a hot, dry ripening season, so in humid Gulf Coast gardens prioritize full sun, sharp drainage, and generous spacing to reduce fungal pressure on ripening fruit. Expect several years of establishment growth before a substantial first harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mrs. Burns' Lemon Basil (New Mexico Heirloom Lemon Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Mrs. Burns' Lemon is a New Mexico heirloom lemon basil long saved and passed along by seed keepers for its unusually intense, true lemon fragrance and flavor, stronger and cleaner than many other lemon basil selections, on plants that grow taller and more vigorously than typical lemon basils even through Gulf South summer heat. The bright citrus flavor makes it outstanding in teas, fish and seafood dishes, fruit salads, and infused vinegars or oils. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and keep the plant bushy and productive, and harvest leaves often since frequent picking encourages fuller, more branched growth through the season. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Mrs. Cooksey Loquat (Large Yellow-Fleshed New Zealand Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting the tree where late-winter bloom and the developing spring crop are sheltered from the coldest north winds, since freezing temperatures during flowering or early fruit set are the main threat to a reliable harvest along the Gulf Coast. Mrs. Cooksey is a long-cultivated New Zealand loquat variety prized for its large fruit, typically running up to about 1.5 inches long and 1 inch in diameter, notably bigger than many older loquat selections. The flesh is a rich yellow color with very good, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, and the tree bears reliably once established. Like other loquats it flowers in fall to winter and ripens over a short window in late winter into spring, so a warm microclimate or wall planting helps protect the bloom in zone 8 gardens; established trees tolerate light freezes, but open flowers and small green fruit are damaged well above the hardiness threshold of the wood itself. Thin heavy fruit clusters after set to improve individual fruit size, and harvest when fruit has fully colored and softens slightly, since loquats do not continue to ripen after picking. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Mt. Atlas Pistachio
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, lean, rocky or sandy soil; Pistacia atlantica is remarkably drought tolerant and thrives in conditions too harsh for most fruit trees — avoid clay, overwatering, and excess fertility, which promote lush growth at the expense of drought adaptation and cold hardiness. Pistacia atlantica (Mt. Atlas Pistachio, Mastic Pistachio, or Bene) is a large, long-lived, drought-adapted deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia, and extending across the Middle East to Central Asia — the wild pistachio tree most widely used as the cold-hardy rootstock upon which commercial Pistacia vera (edible pistachio) varieties are grafted, conferring exceptional drought tolerance, deep-rooting habit, and disease resistance to the scions. The tree itself produces small clusters of small, pea-sized, resinous, edible nuts resembling tiny pistachios — edible and pistachio-flavored when roasted, historically used as a seasoning and oil source across the Middle East and North Africa. Pistacia atlantica is also the source of a gum-resin historically used as a primitive chewing gum and incense in the Middle East. As an ornamental landscape tree, it is exceptional: extremely long-lived, deeply drought-tolerant, with elegant pinnate foliage and spectacular orange-red-purple autumn color in cooler climates. Planted in California's pistachio-growing regions as a street and shade tree for its drought tolerance. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: Mt. Washington Tomato (Ultra-Early Cold-Tolerant Cherry)
description: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Mt. Washington is a compact, determinate-type cherry tomato that does not require staking; the plants concentrate production in a relatively tight window (good for canning or preserving in quantity); harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Mt. Washington is an ultra-early cherry tomato selected specifically for cold-tolerance and short-season performance, named for Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — famous for its extreme weather (the site held the world record for the highest surface wind speed ever recorded at 231 mph in April 1934) and the notoriously harsh conditions of its summit area. The variety produces small, round, red cherry tomatoes (about 1 inch) with good, sweet-tart flavor in 52–60 days from transplant — one of the fastest-maturing cherry tomatoes available. The compact, determinate plants (24–36 inches) are appropriate for container growing and produce a compressed flush of fruit ideal for gardeners who want to can or preserve cherry tomatoes in quantity rather than harvest over an extended season. Cold tolerance allows fruit set at nighttime temperatures approaching 45°F, making this variety one of a handful suitable for truly short growing seasons with cold nights throughout the summer. Matures in 52–60 days from transplant.

name: Mucho Nacho Jalapeño Pepper (Extra-Large AAS Jalapeño)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Mucho Nacho is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast and Southern growing seasons. Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning jalapeño developed specifically to produce extra-large (4–5 inch long), thick-walled jalapeño fruits that are large enough for easy stuffing for jalapeño poppers and have enough surface area for maximum nacho topping use — the name directly references its intended use. The heat level (10,000–12,000 SHU) is somewhat hotter than many standard jalapeño varieties and significantly hotter than TAM Jalapeño, making it authentic jalapeño heat in a much larger package. The very thick walls (up to 1/4 inch) make Mucho Nacho excellent for grilling whole (the thick walls hold up without burning through) and for stuffing with cream cheese or other fillings. Ripens from dark green to red; can be harvested and used at the green stage (most common) or allowed to ripen red for a slightly different, sweeter flavor. High productivity and disease resistance make it one of the most reliable jalapeño varieties for home garden use. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Mugwort
description: Plant root divisions in any well-drained soil; mugwort is extremely vigorous and can become invasive via rhizomes, so consider installing a root barrier or growing in a contained bed. The deeply lobed, silver-backed leaves are strongly aromatic with a bitter, sage-like scent used in traditional European and East Asian medicine. Harvest leafy stems just before flowering in midsummer for use in moxibustion, digestive bitters, dream pillows, and traditional holiday flavoring of fatty meats. Cut plants back hard in late summer to control spread and prevent self-seeding. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Muir Lettuce
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; thin to 6–10 inches and harvest as cut-and-come-again or as full heads. Muir is a French heirloom oakleaf-type loose-leaf lettuce developed as a heat-tolerant selection, producing a loose, upright rosette of thick, savoyed, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctively crisp, succulent texture and mild, sweet flavor that holds up better than most leaf lettuces once temperatures start climbing. Its unusually thick, crinkled leaf texture also makes it more forgiving of the wilting summer sun than thinner-leafed varieties, and it is slower to turn bitter as it approaches bolting. A useful bridge variety for gardeners who want fresh salad greens into the early part of a Gulf South summer before switching to heat-adapted greens, in zone 3–10. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Mukunuwenna
description: Root stem cuttings or direct-sow in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade; mukunuwenna (sessile joyweed, dwarf copperleaf, alternanthera) is a pantropical low-growing perennial herb widely consumed as a leafy vegetable throughout South and Southeast Asia — the young shoots and leaves are a staple green vegetable in Sri Lanka (where it is a major ingredient in mallung, a coconut-based herb salad), and in Indian, Thai, and Vietnamese cooking. The mild, slightly crunchy leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked briefly in stir-fries, curries, and soups. The plant is exceptionally shade-tolerant for a warm-season leafy green, maintaining vigorous production in partial shade where spinach and lettuce would bolt in summer heat, making it a highly practical leafy green for Gulf Coast and tropical summer shade gardens. It grows along the margins of streams, ponds, and wet ditches in its natural habitat and tolerates wet, waterlogged soil conditions. Multiple harvests per season are obtained by tip-pruning. In zone 9–12 it persists as a perennial; elsewhere it is grown as a summer annual. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Mulato Isleno Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato Isleno is a poblano-type dried chile grown specifically for its distinctive chocolate-brown dried form rather than for fresh use — unlike the more common ancho (dried red poblano), the mulato is harvested at a later stage when fruits turn from green directly to dark brown, producing a darker, smokier, more complex dried chile with chocolate, coffee, and dried fruit undertones. It is one of the three chiles traditionally used in mole negro (with ancho and pasilla), contributing a smoky depth that neither ancho nor pasilla provides alone. Dry fully ripe, dark-brown fruits in a dehydrator or low oven for 2–4 hours until leathery and pliable. Plants are productive on fertile soil in zone 9 and tend to be tall with upright growth habit. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Mulato Pepper (Mulato Isleno, Dried Mulato)
description: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato is a Mexican dried chile closely related to poblano but from a distinct gene pool (the seed color is tan, versus black for poblano/ancho) that produces heart-shaped, medium-large fruits, dark green turning dark brownish-black (rather than red) when fully ripe and dried. In dried form, mulato is one of the trio of chiles (together with ancho and pasilla) used in traditional Mexican mole negro sauce — its distinctive contribution is a dark, chocolate-tobacco, raisin-like complexity that makes mole negro deep and bittersweet. Heat level is mild to moderate (500–2,500 Scoville). Fresh mulato fruits are used in chiles rellenos and sauces; dried mulatos are rehydrated for mole and enchilada sauces. The plants are productive in zone 9's warm season and the fruits dry naturally on the plant in hot, dry conditions or can be dried in a dehydrator. An essential ingredient for serious Mexican cooking and home food preservers. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Mulberry
description: Red mulberry (native to eastern North America) and white mulberry (Morus alba, from Asia) are both grown for fruit; white mulberry is more tolerant of heat and alkaline soils. Most mulberries are self-fertile or near-enough so that a single tree crops well. Trees require very little care once established — no regular spraying or thinning is needed. Fruit ripens over several weeks and drops when ripe; lay a tarp beneath the canopy for easy collection, as the juice stains pavement and clothing permanently. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mulberry Wine Chilean Pernettya (Dark Magenta-Fruited Prickly Heath)
description: Mulberry Wine is a female Chilean pernettya cultivar grown for its unusually large, rounded berries that ripen from pink through a deep wine-red to purple, giving the plant its name. Because the species is dioecious, a male seedling or male-flowered cultivar must be planted within pollinator range for Mulberry Wine to set its showy fruit each autumn. The low, mounding evergreen habit and small, glossy, needle-like leaves make it a useful acid-soil groundcover or edging shrub in a woodland border, where the fruit persists into winter after the foliage of nearby perennials has died back. Grow it exactly as other ericaceous shrubs — moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled shade, with a thick organic mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Mule Team Tomato
description: Mule Team belongs to a small family of Americana-named heirloom tomatoes developed by the same hobbyist breeder as Box Car Willie, and the seed nearly disappeared before being rediscovered stored in glass jars decades later and grown out by tomato collector Dr. Carolyn Male. The sturdy, drought-tolerant indeterminate vines are abundant producers of eight to twelve ounce beefsteak fruit with rich, juicy, zippy-sweet flavor, and the plants keep fruit quality consistent from the first harvest through the last frost of the season rather than tapering off in late summer heat. It is a dependable choice for gardeners who want a hearty slicing tomato without the fussiness of some other large-fruited heirlooms. Matures in 78–82 days from transplant.

name: Mulgoba Mango (Historic Indian Parent of Haden)
description: Mulgoba is the celebrated Indian mango that USDA plant introduction agents brought to Florida in 1889, with one of the original trees planted on Captain John Haden's Coconut Grove homestead, where a chance seedling from it later became the famous Haden cultivar. The medium-sized, oval fruit ripens to a yellow ground color heavily blushed orange-crimson, enclosing rich, only lightly fibrous flesh long admired among Indian mango connoisseurs for its complex, aromatic sweetness. Like many older Indian cultivars it tends toward alternate bearing and sets fruit most reliably when a dry, sunny bloom period limits anthracnose pressure. Give it excellent drainage and shelter young trees from frost, since mango wood is easily injured by cold below the mid-30s Fahrenheit. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mullein
description: Mullein is a striking hardy biennial that forms a rosette of soft, silver-green leaves the first year and sends up a tall yellow-flowered spike the second. Surface sow the dust-fine seed onto disturbed soil and leave it uncovered, as it needs light to germinate. It thrives in poor, well-drained ground and full sun with minimal water, making it ideal for lean sites. Allow a few plants to set seed and it will naturalize, returning on its own from year to year. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Mullica Queen Cranberry (Rutgers Late-Season High-Yield Processing Cultivar)
description: Mullica Queen was released from the Rutgers P.E. Marucci Center cranberry breeding program in New Jersey's Pine Barrens and named for the Mullica River that runs through the region's historic bog country, joining Crimson Queen as one of the newer high-yield hybrids developed for the modern processing and juice trade. It ripens later in the season than most named cultivars, extending the harvest window for growers and giving berries additional time to build size and color, and it has shown good fruit-rot tolerance and vine vigor in New Jersey bog trials. Cultivation follows the same demanding requirements as all cranberries: acidic, peaty, constantly saturated soil (pH 4.0-5.0), a sand-topped bog bed, and full sun, with vines taking several years to establish before cropping heavily. As with other Rutgers 'Queen' series selections, it is grown almost exclusively in commercial New Jersey, Wisconsin, and Pacific Northwest bogs rather than home gardens, and is unsuited to warm-winter climates lacking sustained cold dormancy. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Multicaulis Mulberry / King's White Mulberry
description: Propagate from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter and root in a well-drained propagation mix under plastic film, or take semi-softwood cuttings in early summer; plant rooted cuttings out in spring after the last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Multicaulis mulberry is a vigorous, large-leaved variety of white mulberry selected in China for its enormous leaves — up to 12 inches long — that historically supported the silk industry; in the food garden it channels that same vigor into abundant, sweet white to pale-pink berries that ripen weeks ahead of most mulberries. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils including clay, heat, and urban conditions, and once established is drought-resilient while performing best with consistent moisture during fruiting. Harvest berries over several weeks as they ripen unevenly, spreading a sheet beneath the canopy and shaking branches gently to collect ripe fruit. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Multipik Squash (Virus-Tolerant Yellow Straightneck Hybrid)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Multipik is a widely grown yellow straightneck summer squash hybrid valued for heavy, sustained production and for its 'precocious' gene, which masks the green mottling that mosaic viruses normally cause, so fruit keeps its attractive, uniform bright yellow color for market and table even under virus pressure. The compact, open bush habit produces slender, smooth-skinned fruit best picked young at 5-6 inches for the most tender texture. Because summer squash is highly attractive to aphids that spread mosaic viruses in humid Gulf Coast gardens, Multipik's cosmetic virus tolerance helps keep the harvest looking good even in a bad aphid year. Check plants daily during peak production and pick promptly, since squash left on the vine quickly grows oversized and seedy. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Multiplier Onion (Potato Onion)
description: Plant small sets 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; multiplier onions are a perennial system that perpetuates itself through vegetative division rather than seed. One planted bulb will produce a cluster of 4–12 bulbs at harvest; sort the cluster at harvest, eating the largest and replanting the smallest to maintain the planting year after year. The flavor is milder and sweeter than common onions, and the green tops can be harvested as scallions throughout the growing season. In zone 9 they perform best planted in fall; in hot, dry summers the tops die down and the bulbs go dormant, much like garlic. This heirloom vegetable was once widely grown in kitchen gardens before commercial onions became cheap. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Muncher Cucumber
description: Muncher is a burpless heirloom cucumber prized for mild, low-acid flavor and thin, tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest fruits young at four to six inches for crisp snacking, or let them size up to eight or nine inches for slicing. Direct sow in warm soil in full sun after frost, or start early indoors, and grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Pick regularly and keep the plants evenly watered to prevent bitterness. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Muncher Persian Cucumber
description: This mini slicing cucumber produces tender, burpless, thin-skinned fruits with a crisp bite, best picked around 5 inches long. High yields come from steady moisture and full sun, so water consistently to avoid bitterness. Train vines on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive throughout the season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Munchkin Pumpkin (Miniature Orange Decorative Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun; harvest when rind has hardened completely and is uniformly deep orange. Munchkin is a 1996 All-America Selections-winning miniature pumpkin that produces perfectly proportioned, small (4–5 inches in diameter, 3–5 oz) pumpkins with the classic Halloween pumpkin shape — deeply ridged, round, bright orange, with a proportionally large corky stem — in quantities of 8–15 per vine. The scale and perfect form of Munchkin pumpkins have made them the dominant decorative miniature pumpkin in the American market: they look like standard pumpkins shrunk to one-tenth their normal size, with all the visual appeal intact. Their most popular use is as tabletop decorations, door step arrangements, and centerpieces for autumn events; the small size and hard rind give them good postharvest longevity (4–8 weeks in cool conditions) for extended decorative use. Munchkin also has the distinction of being edible — the sweet, dense flesh makes excellent pumpkin puree, though the small size means significant work for a small yield — but most growers treat it purely as a decorative crop. Very productive and highly marketable at farm stands, farmers markets, and pumpkin patches where customers specifically seek miniature varieties. A top-selling item for autumn specialty crop producers. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Mundo Novo Coffee
description: A natural Brazilian hybrid of Typica and Bourbon discovered in the 1940s, valued for combining a robust, disease-tolerant constitution with excellent cup quality. It grows noticeably larger and more vigorously than dwarf cultivars like Caturra, so home growers need generous container size or in-ground space with good headroom. Provide bright, filtered light, steady warmth above 60F, and rich, well-drained acidic soil, and expect a longer wait to first harvest than compact modern hybrids. Its vigor and disease tolerance make it one of the more forgiving Arabica types for home cultivation. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Mundu (Sweet Mangosteen, Egg Tree)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Garcinia dulcis is slow-growing and prefers consistent moisture. Garcinia dulcis (mundu or sweet mangosteen) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia — a member of the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae) and related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) but distinctly different in fruit character. Mundu produces round, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits with smooth, thin, golden-yellow to orange-yellow skin and bright-yellow, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh with a flavor profile combining apricot, mango, and a slight citrus note — pleasant, refreshing, and more accessible in flavor than mangosteen's complex floral-tropical character. The yellow latex (gamboge) in the skin and pith is mildly bitter and slightly resinous (as in all Garcinia species) — peel carefully and avoid including the skin in the edible flesh. Mundu is significantly easier to grow than true mangosteen, which is notoriously difficult and slow; mundu is faster-maturing, more forgiving of less-than-perfect conditions, and more productive. The tree is also useful as a rootstock for grafting true mangosteen in regions where mangosteen is difficult to grow on its own roots. In the Philippines, the fruit is eaten fresh and made into jam; the large seeds contain a fat used in traditional cosmetics. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Mung Bean (Green Gram, Moong Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; inoculate with Rhizobium legume inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Vigna radiata (mung bean or green gram) is among the most widely consumed legumes in the world — a staple of Indian, Chinese, Southeast Asian, and Korean cuisines in its many forms: whole cooked beans in dal and soups, split (moong dal) for creamy lentil dishes, sprouted (bean sprouts) as a fresh vegetable, ground into flour for cheela pancakes, and processed into bean thread (glass) noodles. The bean is particularly nutritious — high in protein, folate, magnesium, and iron — and easier to digest than many other legumes, producing less flatulence. Mung beans are also the most common source of fresh bean sprouts: seeds germinate and develop edible sprouts in just 3–5 days at room temperature, making them one of the few vegetables that can be produced entirely indoors year-round. In the garden, mung bean grows as a fast-maturing, upright, bushy annual producing small, cylindrical black or brown pods with 8–15 seeds each, harvested when pods turn black-brown and dry. Matures in 55–80 days from seed.

name: Mung Bean Microgreens
description: Soak mung beans overnight so they swell and sprout rapidly, then spread them in an even layer on a tray or in a sprouting jar. They germinate within a day or two and thrive in warmth, so keep them covered and rinse or mist frequently to prevent souring. If growing as tray microgreens, give them light once shoots appear to green them up slightly. Harvest the crunchy, protein-rich shoots after roughly a week, or eat earlier as classic bean sprouts. Matures in 5–9 days from seed.

name: Mung Bean Sprouts
description: Mung beans are prized for quick, protein-rich sprouts used in stir-fries, egg rolls, and salads. Soak seeds overnight, then rinse and drain two to three times daily in a sprouting jar kept out of direct sun. Sprouts are ready to eat in four to seven days once the shoots are an inch or two long. Keep them moist but well-drained to prevent souring. Matures in 4–7 days from seed.

name: Munger Black Raspberry (Historic Commercial Black Raspberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and tip-prune new canes at about 24-30 inches during the summer to force branching, since black raspberries fruit on lateral shoots off last year's canes rather than on the cane tips. Munger was selected in the late 1800s and went on to become the backbone of the commercial black raspberry industry in Oregon and the Midwest for decades, prized for its productivity, vigor, and the deep, wine-dark, firm berries that hold up well to picking and processing. The flavor is intensely rich and slightly tart, excellent for jam, syrup, and baking, and the arching canes root readily wherever an unpruned tip touches soil, so stake or tip-prune to keep the planting from wandering. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to the strongest four or five per hill each spring. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Munich Bier Radish (German Beer Garden Radish)
description: Sow seed directly half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to a few inches apart, since this variety forms a substantially larger root than typical salad radishes. Munich Bier is an old German heirloom traditionally served whole, sliced, or spiraled and lightly salted as a salty, crunchy snack alongside beer in Bavarian beer gardens, a use quite different from the quick-growing salad radishes most American gardeners know. Its large white roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even at full size, resisting the pithiness and heat that ruins many radishes left in the ground too long. Harvest once roots reach 3-4 inches across, and keep soil evenly moist throughout growth for the best crisp, mild-flavored roots. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Munstead English Lavender
description: Munstead is a compact, early-blooming English lavender prized for its sweet fragrance and tidy habit that suits containers and small gardens. Chill the seed for a few weeks, then surface sow indoors under light and be patient, as germination is slow and uneven. Transplant into sharply drained, even gritty soil in full sun, since lavender rots in wet ground. Prune lightly after flowering to keep plants dense and harvest the fragrant flower spikes for culinary or craft use. Matures in 90–200 days from seed.

name: Munstead Lavender
description: Introduced in 1916 and named for Gertrude Jekyll's garden at Munstead Woods, this compact English lavender blooms earlier than most and stays neatly mounded. Its sweet flowers are among the best for culinary use as well as sachets and dried bouquets. Cold-stratify seed before sowing, then start indoors and transplant to full sun with sharp drainage. Keep water low once established, trim after flowering to maintain a tidy shape, and avoid rich or soggy soil. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Muntries (Emu Apple, Native Cranberry)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly, coastal-type soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established; avoid clay or poorly drained soils. Kunzea pomifera (muntries, emu apple, or native cranberry) is a prostrate, ground-hugging Australian native shrub from the coastal heathlands, mallee scrub, and sand dunes of South Australia and western Victoria — one of the most remarkable and underappreciated Australian native food plants. The plant spreads slowly as a low (6–18 inch), dense, aromatic groundcover with tiny, dark-green leaves and small white bottlebrush-like flowers, eventually producing clusters of small (1/4–1/2 inch), round berries that ripen from green to red-purple in late summer. The berries have a unique, complex, sweet-spicy flavor combining apple, cinnamon, and a subtle eucalyptus note — quite unlike any other berry. Nutritionally, muntries are exceptional: ORAC (antioxidant) values four times higher than blueberries by weight, with high vitamin C, flavonoids, and polyphenols. Aboriginal Australians historically ate muntries extensively as a major food source across the southern Australian coast. In the modern Australian native food industry, muntries are used in jams, sauces, ice creams, and gourmet berry products, and are increasingly available from specialty nurseries. As a garden plant, muntries serves as an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover that also produces an edible crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Murasaki Fioretto Cauliflower (AAS-Winning Purple Long-Stem Sprouting Cauliflower)
description: Start transplants and set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Murasaki Fioretto is an AAS-winning stick-type cauliflower that first forms a compact purple head, then elongates into loose, bunchable, tender-stemmed florets that can be harvested at 3-4 inches for bagging or left to reach 8 inches for bunching, similar in habit to broccolini. Its vivid violet-purple color is heat tolerant and stays vibrant through cooking, shifting to fuchsia when pickled and to golden brown when roasted or sautéed. The mild, sweet flavor and tender stems need no peeling, and the compact plant holds in the field well past typical cauliflower harvest windows without declining in quality. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Murasaki Sweet Potato (Japanese Purple Sweet Potato)
description: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; murasaki (purple in Japanese) sweet potato is a Japanese-origin variety producing long, slender tubers with striking dark purple skin and off-white to cream-colored flesh — a distinct and useful contrast to the Okinawan purple-flesh type, with a dry, chestnut-like sweetness and firm texture that holds up beautifully in roasting, frying, and sautéing where orange-flesh sweet potatoes would become too soft. The flavor is rich, mildly sweet, and nutty with a savory quality that makes it more versatile in non-sweet preparations than moist orange types. Widely grown in Japan and increasingly popular in the United States as interest in Asian sweet potato varieties grows; excellent for Japanese-style roasted sweet potatoes, tempura, and savory preparations that benefit from a firmer texture. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Murasaki-29 Sweet Potato (Nematode-Resistant Purple-Skin White-Flesh LSU Release)
description: Murasaki-29 was bred by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station from an open-pollinated cross with the female parent L89-72 as a specialty white-flesh alternative to orange-fleshed dessert types like Beauregard. It has purple skin and white flesh, with shorter, elliptical, non-lobed storage roots compared to Beauregard. Unlike many other white-flesh specialty types such as O'Henry, Murasaki-29 carries useful resistance to southern root-knot nematode, comparable to Covington, Evangeline, and Jewel. Its firmer, less sweet flesh suits roasting and savory preparations rather than the moist, syrupy texture of orange-fleshed baking types. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Murcott Honey Tangerine (Murcott, Honey Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Murcott honey tangerine (also called Murcott mandarin, Honey mandarin, or Spring mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available — a complex tangor (mandarin x sweet orange hybrid) with deep reddish-orange skin, extremely sweet, rich, honey-like juice with excellent aromatic complexity, and medium-thick skin that peels relatively easily. The fruits are medium-sized (2.5–3.5 inches), slightly flattened, and typically contain 15–25 small seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor profile that many citrus enthusiasts consider the finest of all mandarin types. Murcott ripens late in the season (January–March in Florida; February–April in California), and the fruits hang on the tree well, gradually increasing in sweetness through the winter; the tree can be used as a reliable late-season fresh citrus source when earlier varieties have finished. The California Citrus Research Board markets Murcott as 'Honey mandarin' and sells significant quantities at premium prices. Trees are moderately cold-sensitive (damaged at 28°F) and are best in the warmest sites in zone 9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Musang King Durian (D197)
description: Musang King (registered as clone D197 in Malaysia) is currently the most sought-after commercial durian cultivar in the world, commanding premium export prices for its thick, deep-yellow to golden flesh, small seed, and rich, custardy, bittersweet flavor with a lingering finish. Trees need deep, fertile, well-drained soil, high humidity, and warm temperatures year-round; flowers open at night and rely heavily on bats and other nocturnal pollinators, so avoid dusk pesticide use and encourage nearby night-pollinator habitat. Fruit takes roughly 3-5 months to mature after flowering, and the heavy spiny husks should be allowed to fall naturally rather than being cut, both for safety and because Musang King is known to ripen poorly if harvested green. As with all durian, plant only where extended winter cold is not a risk. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Muscadine Grape
description: Muscadine grapes are native to the southeastern U.S. and far more heat- and disease-resistant than European or labrusca types. Train to a single trunk with two permanent lateral cordons on a high-wire trellis at 5–6 ft; spur-prune cordons each dormant season to 2–3 bud spurs spaced 4–6 in apart. Many cultivars are not self-fertile, so check pollination requirements before purchasing. Harvest by shaking or hand-picking individual berries when they reach full color and slip easily from the skin. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Muscat Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Muscat grapes are among the oldest cultivated grape varieties and are unusual for producing wines that actually smell and taste distinctly of fresh grapes. One of the oldest and most widespread grape families in the world, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is prized for its intensely floral, distinctly grapey aroma, unusual among wine grapes for producing wine that actually smells and tastes like fresh table grapes, used to make everything from light, lightly sparkling Moscato d'Asti to sweet fortified dessert wines. The grapes are also excellent eaten fresh off the vine, giving this variety dual value as both a wine and table grape in a home garden setting. Provide full sun and good air circulation, thin clusters if fruit set is heavy to concentrate the distinctive floral aromatics, and pick based on desired sweetness level, since Muscat can be used for both dry and sweet wine styles depending on harvest timing. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Music Garlic (Extremely Popular Large-Clove Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Music is a Canadian-origin porcelain hardneck that has become one of the most popular garlic varieties in North America, producing large bulbs with just four to six exceptionally big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, and a rich, full, well-balanced flavor that holds up well raw or cooked. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; Music has moderate storage life, typically five to seven months under good conditions. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Music Hardneck Garlic
description: This porcelain hardneck cultivar produces very large bulbs with 4 to 6 big, easy-to-peel cloves and excellent cold tolerance. Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, mulch heavily, and let them overwinter. Snip the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy spot for storage. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Musica Romano Pole Bean (Wide Flat Italian-Style Pole Bean with Exceptional Tenderness)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide a sturdy trellis or poles to 7 feet and harvest pods when flat and full-length (8–10 inches) but before seeds develop prominently inside. Musica Romano Pole Bean is a Dutch commercial variety developed specifically to combine the flat Romano-style pod shape beloved in Italian cuisine with the productivity and extended harvest window of a modern pole bean. The flat pod shape — wide (nearly 1 inch across) with a slightly rectangular cross-section rather than round — is the defining characteristic of the Romano bean type, which originated in Italy and represents a fundamentally different pod morphology from the round, pencil-thin beans of French filet types or the oval cross-section of standard American snap beans. Romano types are prized for a distinctive beany, almost meaty flavor that is more pronounced than round-podded types; this flavor intensity comes partly from the thicker pod walls and slightly higher dry matter content of the flat pod structure. Musica improves on older Romano varieties in two key ways: pods remain tender and stringless at large sizes (a significant practical advantage, since older Romano types become stringy once pods exceed 6–7 inches), and the plant produces heavily over an extended harvest window rather than the concentrated burst typical of bush bean types. The vigorous climbing plant (to 7 feet) is highly productive in warm conditions and particularly well-suited to zone 9's long warm season, where it can continue producing through fall when given a midsummer break from heat. Steam or blanch briefly for the best texture; Musica also holds up well in longer-cooked dishes like minestrone where flat Romano beans contribute body without dissolving. Matures in 60–68 days from seed.

name: Musk Mallow (Muskmallow)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; musk mallow is a tropical Asian relative of okra and hibiscus grown primarily for the musky-aromatic seeds used in perfumery, liqueurs, and traditional medicine across South and Southeast Asia. The seeds contain ambrette seed oil, which has a rich, nutty-musky fragrance closely resembling animal musk — used as a natural, ethical alternative to animal musk in fine perfumery and as a fixative in high-end fragrance. The seeds are also used medicinally in Ayurveda and are added to the Egyptian spice blend 'beharat'. The large, showy, hibiscus-like flowers in yellow to red are highly ornamental. The entire plant — seeds, leaves, and roots — is edible, with the young leaves used as a cooked green. In zone 9, it behaves as a warm-season annual that may overwinter in protected spots. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Musk Strawberry (Hautbois Strawberry)
description: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; musk strawberry is a European native species and one of the most historically important cultivated strawberries before the modern hybrid garden strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) replaced it in the 19th century. The medium-sized fruits have an intense, musky-aromatic fragrance far more complex and perfumed than modern strawberry varieties — often described as combining strawberry with pineapple and rose. The plant uniquely tolerates partial shade, making it one of the few berry crops for understory or semi-shaded settings. Most cultivated plants are of a single sex (plants were traditionally vegetatively propagated), so both male and female plants must be obtained for fruiting. 'Capron Royal' and 'Profumata di Tortona' are heritage Italian cultivars. The berries are soft and must be eaten immediately after harvest. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Musquee de Provence Pumpkin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, rich, slightly acidic soil; Musquee de Provence (Musk of Provence) is a magnificent French heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region, producing large, deeply ridged, flat-round fruits with a muted tan to bronze-brown skin that develops rich russet-copper tones when fully mature. The deep orange-yellow flesh is exceptionally sweet, dense, and aromatic — the 'musquee' (musky) name refers to the intensely sweet, rich, slightly musky fragrance and flavor of the ripe flesh, considered among the finest-flavored of any large pumpkin. Fully matured fruits from this Cucurbita moschata variety develop complex flavor notes beyond ordinary pumpkin sweetness. The large, photogenic fruits (often 12–20 pounds) are classic French market pumpkins seen in Provençal farmers' markets in fall. In zone 9 the summer heat and humidity are well tolerated by this C. moschata type, which is more disease-resistant in warm climates than C. maxima varieties. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Musquée de Provence Pumpkin (Fairytale Pumpkin, Cheese Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2) after last frost in warm, rich soil; Musquée de Provence is a spectacular heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region of southern France that produces deeply ribbed, flat-lobed, heavily textured fruits that turn from dark green to a rich tan-bronze at maturity, resembling giant rounds of aged cheese (it is often sold under the marketing name 'Fairytale Pumpkin' in the US). The large fruits (10–20 pounds, sometimes to 30 pounds) are as stunning ornamentally as they are culinarily valuable — the deep orange, dense, sweet flesh is comparable to butternut squash in flavor (Musquée de Provence is Cucurbita moschata, the same species as butternut) with excellent sweetness, minimal stringiness, and superb flavor when roasted, pureed into soups, or made into pie. The thick skin and hard rind give outstanding storage life (6–12 months in a cool, dry location), and the impressive size and dramatic appearance make the fruits valuable for both Thanksgiving decorations and serious cooking. Well-adapted to the heat and humidity of Gulf South summer production and a rewarding long-season crop in zone 8–11. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Musselburgh Leek
description: This hardy Scottish heirloom leek withstands hard freezes and can be harvested through winter in many climates. Start seed indoors early, then transplant seedlings into deep dibble holes so the shanks blanch white. Hill soil around the stems or drop plants into holes to lengthen the tender white portion. Keep well watered and side-dress with nitrogen midseason for thick shanks. Dig leeks as needed all winter, lifting the last before spring regrowth begins. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Mustang Grape
description: Plant against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large tree in well-drained soil in full sun; mustang grape is one of the toughest and most vigorous native grapes of Texas and the Gulf South, tolerating extreme heat, drought, poor soil, and disease pressure that eliminates most cultivated bunch grapes in the region. Leaves have a distinctive dense white to rust-colored woolly underside, and the vine climbs aggressively by tendrils, quickly covering large structures if not managed. Small, tart, dark purple to black grapes ripen from midsummer into fall and are prized locally for jelly, juice, and wine once sweetened, though the juice is intensely acidic and the skins can irritate skin and eyes on contact, so handle fresh fruit with care. Prune hard each winter to control size and improve air circulation, since the vine's vigor can quickly overwhelm nearby structures and trees if left unchecked. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Mustard Greens
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring, or 4–6 weeks before first fall frost for the preferred fall crop; mustard greens are a staple leafy vegetable of Asian and Southern US cuisines, prized for their pungent, peppery, mustardy flavor that ranges from mildly spicy to intensely sharp depending on variety. Young leaves are used raw in salads; mature leaves are braised, stir-fried, or cooked with salt pork and vinegar in Southern tradition. They bolt quickly in summer heat but tolerate light frosts, improving in flavor after cold exposure. In zone 7–10 fall-planted mustard greens can produce through winter; Southern flat-pod varieties like 'Florida Broadleaf' and Asian varieties like 'Mizuna' and 'Red Giant' are popular choices. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Mustard Microgreens
description: Sow mustard seed dry and dense on a moist tray, since it develops a gel coat when wet that makes presoaking messy. It sprouts fast, so keep the blackout period short and move it into bright light within a couple of days. Mist to keep the surface moist and provide airflow to keep the fast growth healthy. Harvest the zesty, peppery greens at the cotyledon stage in about a week for maximum heat and aroma. Matures in 6–10 days from seed.

name: Mutsu Apple (Crispin, Large Honeyed Japanese-Bred Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties nearby, since triploid cultivars cannot pollinate themselves or each other. Bred in Aomori Prefecture, Japan from a cross involving Golden Delicious and released in the late 1940s, Mutsu produces very large, greenish-yellow fruit with dense, juicy flesh and a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. It is sold in Britain and parts of Europe under the name Crispin. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the fruit holds its shape well when baked, making it a favorite for pies alongside fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Muña (Andean Mint, Muña Muña)
description: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, replicating the rocky Andean slopes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador where muña grows wild at elevation. This shrubby mint relative has hairy, serrated, intensely camphor-mint-scented leaves traditionally added to cooking beans and potatoes to reduce flatulence and brewed as a digestive tea. Harvest leafy stems just before flowering for the strongest aroma, and use fresh or air-dried in place of huacatay or regular mint in Peruvian stews and ceviche marinades. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: My Joanie Okra (Mississippi Heirloom Pink-Blushed Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once soil is reliably warm; harvest pods at 3-4 inches every couple of days to keep plants productive. My Joanie is a Mississippi heirloom okra passed along through home gardeners before being preserved by Midwest seed-saving growers, distinguished by a dusky rose blush that washes over its grass-green pods rather than the solid red found in burgundy-type okra. Plants stay a manageable 4 feet tall and hold up well in a Kerr Center trial of heirloom okra varieties, where it out-yielded many taller types despite being marketed as a late producer. The mix of ornamental color and heavy yield makes it a good double-duty choice for a Gulf Coast vegetable bed that also needs to look good. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Myoga (Japanese Ginger)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; myoga is the only ginger species that genuinely prefers shade, making it one of the most valuable edible plants for the shaded food garden. The edible parts are the flower buds and young shoots that emerge directly from the ground in late summer and fall — they are sliced and used as a fresh garnish in Japanese cuisine with a mild ginger-citrus flavor. The tall, arching reed-like stems make attractive foliage throughout summer. In zone 7–11 the roots are winter-hardy and re-emerge each spring, slowly spreading to form a clump; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. An outstanding shade-garden edible for Gulf Coast gardens where deep shade under trees is otherwise difficult to plant productively. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Myoka Chestnut (Gellatly Chinese Chestnut Pollinizer)
description: Myoka is a Chinese chestnut seedling selection made by J.U. Gellatly in British Columbia and is valued in Pacific Northwest orchards primarily as a reliable pollinizer for other regional chestnut cultivars. As a Chinese chestnut selection it carries the species' generally good natural resistance to chestnut blight. Plant it alongside pollen-sterile hybrids such as Layeroka or Skookum to ensure a full nut set across the planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Mysore Banana (Cold-Tolerant Indian Dessert Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Mysore is a widely grown Indian banana cultivar valued in Gulf South plantings for better cold tolerance and more consistent fruiting than many purely dessert-type bananas, while still producing sweet, thin-skinned fruit with a pleasant, slightly tart edge good for fresh eating. The clump grows vigorously and suckers readily, and like other cold-tolerant bananas the pseudostem typically dies back to the ground with hard freezes in zone 8b–9 but resprouts from the surviving rhizome in spring, often reaching fruiting size again within a single long growing season. Feed heavily with a balanced, nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season and provide consistent irrigation, since bananas are shallow-rooted, fast-growing plants that suffer quickly under drought stress. Mulch the root zone deeply going into winter for extra cold protection, and thin excess pups to one or two per clump to concentrate energy into fruiting stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Mysore Raspberry (Hill Raspberry, Ceylon Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Mysore raspberry is the premier fruiting bramble for subtropical gardens — the only raspberry-type fruit that thrives and produces abundantly in zone 9–10 conditions where standard raspberries fail from summer heat and disease. Native to the hills of South Asia, it produces arching, thorny canes 5–8 feet tall with attractive silver-backed leaves and large clusters of small, dark-red to black berries with an intense raspberry flavor from October through April. Unlike temperate raspberries, it fruits on second-year canes (floricanes) but in a warm-climate evergreen pattern. Cut canes to the ground after fruiting; the plant regrows vigorously. It can be invasive outside cultivation where conditions suit it — avoid planting near natural areas. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Mâche (Corn Salad, Lamb's Lettuce)
description: Sow direct from late summer through fall (or in early spring in cold climates) in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; thin to 4–6 inches apart and harvest the outer rosettes, or pull entire plants at 45–70 days. Valerianella locusta is the premier winter salad green for cold-hardy production; a small-rosette-forming annual with smooth, oval, soft, blue-green leaves and a distinctively mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavor quite unlike any other green — the taste that makes genuine French salade de mâche so sought-after in winter bistros. It is among the most cold-hardy of all salad crops, surviving temperatures to 10°F under light row cover or as low as 20°F with cold frames; in the Gulf South (zones 8–10) it can be harvested from October through April as a continuous cool-season salad. It self-seeds readily and often naturalizes in garden beds. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: München Bier Radish (German Beer Garden White Radish)
description: Sow 1/2 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart (important for large root development); keep consistently moist to prevent cracking; harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for best flavor — overripe roots become pithy and hot. München Bier is a traditional Bavarian radish variety with an intimate connection to German beer garden culture: in Munich's famous outdoor beer gardens and throughout Bavaria, a 'Radi' (the Bavarian German word for radish) served alongside a Masskrug (liter) of beer is as traditional and culturally fixed as pretzels and sausages. The Bavarian Radi is always München Bier or a similar large, white, round variety — never the small red radishes of American experience — and it is served in a specific traditional way: the entire large root is scored with a spiral cut from top to bottom using a special tool (a Radihobel), accordioned apart to fan out into a long, beautiful spiral, rubbed with salt to draw out the juices, and eaten slice by slice as an accompaniment to beer. The flavor is mildly peppery and refreshing, with good crunch and juiciness, and the large size allows the elaborate spiral cutting presentation impossible with small radishes. München Bier is one of the few radish varieties specifically sized and textured for this presentation; it is also excellent sliced thick for salads, grated for German-style radish salads with vinegar and oil dressing, or pickled. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Nabechan Bunching Onion (Negi)
description: Nabechan is a traditional Japanese negi-type bunching onion grown for its long, thick, upright white shanks that resist splitting and curling even in hot weather. Sow into a shallow furrow and gradually mound soil around the base every few weeks as the plants grow, which blanches the lower stalk into the long white shaft prized for hot pot dishes. The sweet, mild flavor and non-bulbing habit make it equally useful sliced raw as a garnish or cooked whole in soups and nabemono. It tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, allowing extended harvest windows in most temperate gardens. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Nacional Cacao (Arriba Nacional)
description: An heirloom Ecuadorian cacao renowned among chocolate makers for its distinctive floral, jasmine-like 'arriba' flavor note found in no other cacao type. It is more disease-susceptible and lower-yielding than modern hybrid clones, so home growers should prioritize excellent drainage, high humidity, and dappled shade under taller canopy trees or shade cloth to reduce stress. Keep young trees sheltered from wind and direct sun, and maintain consistently warm, humid conditions year-round since this variety has no cold tolerance whatsoever. Best suited to true tropical home gardens or heated greenhouse collections rather than casual container culture in temperate climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nacono Pecan (Elongated Banana-Cluster USDA-ARS Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, and plant a compatible Type I pollinator such as Cape Fear or Pawnee nearby, since pecans require cross-pollination from a genetically distinct cultivar for best nut set. Nacono, a USDA release from a Cheyenne x Sioux cross, is visually distinctive among pecan cultivars for its unusually elongated nut clusters, which hang in long, curved, banana-like bunches rather than the more rounded clusters typical of most cultivars, containing nuts with bright, attractive straw-colored kernels and good flavor. Harvest occurs around early October once the shucks split open. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and provide the deep, loose, well-drained soil pecans need for healthy taproot development. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Nadia Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Glossy Italian Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Nadia is a widely grown hybrid eggplant producing glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with tender, non-bitter flesh and few seeds, on a vigorous, high-yielding plant especially valued for continuing to set fruit through peak summer heat when many other eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, soft skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and tougher flesh. Regular harvesting every few days keeps the plant productive over a long season, and staking helps support the heavy fruit load on the branches. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Naga Morich Pepper (Snake Pepper, Bangladeshi Naga)
description: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost, providing bottom heat to speed the naturally slow chinense germination, and pot up seedlings before setting them out in warm soil. Give plants a long, hot growing season and steady moisture for the heaviest pod set. Naga Morich is a traditional Bangladeshi and northeastern Indian pepper closely related to bhut jolokia, prized for its intense heat and slightly fruity aroma, and it is a parent of several later superhot hybrids. Pods ripen from green to a wrinkled orange-red and should be handled with gloves. Matures in 95–120 days from transplant.

name: Naga Viper Pepper (UK Superhot Hybrid)
description: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with consistent bottom heat, then harden off and transplant once nights stay warm, since this hybrid resents cool, wet soil. Keep the compact plants evenly watered and staked once fruit sets heavily along the branches. Naga Viper was bred in England by crossing Bhut Jolokia, Naga Morich, and Trinidad Scorpion lines, and it briefly held recognition as the world's hottest pepper around 2011 before later superhots surpassed it. The knobby pods ripen from green to red and carry a sharp, lingering heat. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Nagami Kumquat (Oval Kumquat)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; kumquats are more cold-hardy than most citrus and can tolerate temperatures briefly to about 18–22°F when mature. Nagami kumquat is the most widely grown kumquat worldwide, producing oval (1–1.5 inch long), bright orange fruits with a sweet, aromatic edible peel and intensely sour-tart flesh and juice — the unique flavor is experienced by eating the entire fruit in one or two bites, allowing the sweet peel flavor to intermingle with the tart interior. The contrast of sweet and sour in a tiny package is delightfully surprising and different from any other citrus. Nagami fruits from November through January and holds on the tree for 3–4 months; the laden branches are extraordinarily ornamental and the trees make outstanding large container specimens that can be moved indoors in zones north of 8 for winter protection. Self-fruitful; no pollinator needed. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nagasakiwase Loquat (Earliest-Ripening Japanese Deep-Orange Loquat)
description: Nagasakiwase is a classic Japanese loquat cultivar and one of the earliest-ripening varieties available, producing medium to large fruit with deep orange, exceptionally juicy flesh and a high flesh-to-seed ratio. The flavor combines apricot and pineapple notes with a mild tang, and in warm subtropical climates the tree can produce two crops per year. Because loquats bloom in fall and winter, Nagasakiwase's early habit means its flowers and young fruit are exposed to the coldest part of the Gulf Coast winter, so a late freeze can still damage the crop despite the tree's overall vigor. Grafted trees are fast to bear, often fruiting within two to three years of transplanting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nagoonberry
description: The nagoonberry (arctic raspberry) is a low-growing, rhizomatous Rubus native to Alaska, Scandinavia, and northern Russia, bearing small, deep rose-red berries in early summer that are considered among the finest-flavored wild berries in the boreal world — exceptionally fragrant, rich, and complex. Plants require cool, moist, acidic bog or tundra-edge conditions (pH 4.5–5.5) and cool summer temperatures; they will not survive heat and are rarely successful south of zone 5 except at high elevations. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in early spring. The Finnish-bred cultivar 'Mespi' (a nagoonberry x Arctic raspberry hybrid) shows improved yield and adaptability while retaining the outstanding flavor of the wild species. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nam Doc Mai Mango (Thai Honey Mango)
description: This classic Thai cultivar produces slender, curved fruit with thin golden-yellow skin blushed pink and exceptionally sweet, fiberless, low-acid flesh once ripe, though it is also prized green for eating with sticky rice or salt-chili dip while still tart and crisp. Its comparatively moderate vigor and manageable size make it one of the better mango cultivars for containers and small yards. Humid climates favor anthracnose on flowers and young fruit, so maintain an open canopy through annual pruning and consider a copper fungicide program through bloom. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Namwa Banana (Thai Banana, Nam Wa)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Namwa (also spelled 'Nam Wa', 'Kluai Nam Wa' in Thai, meaning 'water banana') is an ABB genome banana that is among the most widely grown commercial and home garden bananas in Southeast Asia, particularly Thailand, where it is the dominant fresh market variety. Its great popularity stems from its compact size (8–12 feet tall), reliable productivity, good flavor (sweet, slightly tangy, slightly firmer than Cavendish), and significantly greater drought and cold tolerance than Cavendish types — the ABB genome contributes Musa balbisiana cold and stress resistance that allows the rhizome to survive temperatures to about 22–25°F, making Namwa useful in zone 8b–9 Gulf South gardens. The medium-sized, plump, round-tipped fruits (5–6 inches) ripen to creamy yellow with a thin skin and dense, sweet, slightly chalky-creamy flesh; they are excellent fresh, and the slightly starchy texture when green-ripe makes them suitable for cooking or frying as well. A productive, compact, and cold-resilient choice for Gulf South banana cultivation. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Namwah Banana (Pisang Awak, Cold-Tolerant Thai Cooking Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Namwah, also known as Pisang Awak, is a Thai banana cultivar widely recommended by Gulf South extension programs for home growers because it combines good cold tolerance, resistance to Panama disease and other common banana ailments, and dependable fruiting even in a shortened growing season after winter dieback. The medium-sized fruit has a sweet, slightly tangy flavor good for fresh eating, and the vigorous, disease-resistant plant tends to sucker freely, quickly forming a productive clump. Like other cold-hardy bananas grown in zone 8b–9, expect the pseudostem to die back to the ground in hard freezes and resprout from the root system in spring; mulch heavily over the root zone in fall for extra insulation. Feed heavily and water consistently through the growing season, since bananas are fast-growing, heavy feeders that respond strongly to rich soil and regular moisture. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nana Alba Dwarf White English Lavender
description: Plant in full sun with excellent, sharp drainage, and avoid heavy clay or consistently damp soil that leads to root rot. 'Nana Alba' is a dwarf English lavender selection, first recorded in Perry's Hardy Plant Farm catalog in 1928, grown for its short, tidy silvery-green mounds topped with pure snow-white flower spikes in mid- to late summer, a striking contrast to the more common blue-purple lavender varieties. Its compact size makes it ideal for edging paths, white or moon gardens, and containers where a full-size lavender would overwhelm the space. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody, and site it where reflected heat from paving or gravel can help it dry out quickly after rain. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Nana Dwarf Pomegranate (Compact Ornamental Fruiting Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; this dwarf pomegranate is far more tolerant of poor, dry, and alkaline soils than most flowering shrubs of similar size. Nana is a naturally compact, densely branched pomegranate selection that reaches only 2-3 feet tall and wide, retaining the species' narrow, glossy foliage and bright orange-red, trumpet-shaped flowers borne over a long summer season, followed by small, tart, seedy fruit that is edible but grown mainly for ornament rather than harvest. Its small mature size makes it useful in foundation plantings, rock gardens, low informal hedges, and containers or bonsai culture where a full-size pomegranate tree would be unmanageable. Established plants shrug off heat and drought and need only an occasional light shaping prune, since like all pomegranates it flowers and fruits on new wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nance
description: Nance is a tough, drought-tolerant shrub-tree native to tropical America that thrives on poor, acidic, sandy or rocky soils where other fruit trees struggle, and is among the most fire-tolerant tropical fruit plants. It is partially self-fertile, but fruit set improves significantly when multiple plants are grown together; bees are the primary pollinators. The small yellow drupes ripen over an extended season and have a distinctive pungent, waxy, cheese-like aroma that intensifies when processed; they are consumed fresh, frozen in syrup, fermented into a popular Central American drink called chicha, or cooked into preserves. Harvest when the fruit has fully yellowed and drops freely from the clusters, then refrigerate or process immediately. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Nancy Hall Sweet Potato (Moist Southern Heirloom)
description: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is a Deep South heirloom variety grown since the early 20th century for pale copper-pink skinned tubers with soft, exceptionally moist, deep-orange flesh that cooks up custardy rather than dry or mealy, a texture many older Southern gardeners still prefer to modern commercial types like Beauregard. Vines are long and vigorous and tubers form somewhat irregularly shaped, so hill soil up generously and harvest carefully to avoid bruising the tender skin. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall, before the first frost, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin, heal nicks, and sweeten the flesh before storing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Nancy Howard Rosemary
description: Nancy Howard is a semi-trailing rosemary prized for its unusual pale pink flowers, a rare break from the typical blue-flowered forms, set against gray-green, mildly variegated foliage. Grow in full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, and let the soil surface dry between waterings. It tolerates light shearing for culinary harvest but blooms best if pruning is limited mostly to right after flowering. Overwinter container specimens indoors in a bright, cool spot where marginal. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Nankeen Cotton (Heirloom Naturally Brown Cotton)
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following the same culture as any upland cotton. Nankeen is one of the oldest documented naturally colored cotton types, its warm tan-to-brown lint historically spun and woven into the durable buff-colored cloth that gave Nanjing, China's export cotton -- and eventually the color name "nankeen" -- its fame; Thomas Jefferson is recorded growing nankeen cotton in his Monticello gardens in the early 1800s. The lint's natural color eliminates the need for dyeing and tends to darken slightly with washing and UV exposure over the life of the finished cloth. Showy pale yellow flowers fade to pink before dropping to reveal green bolls that split open at full maturity, exposing the naturally tan lint; pick promptly once open to keep it clean and free of weathering stains. Rotate the planting site yearly and watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures as other cotton. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Nanking Cherry
description: Nanking cherry is one of the hardiest fruiting shrubs available, reliably surviving temperatures below -40°F and tolerating poor, dry, or alkaline soils. The abundant small red cherries ripen in early summer and have a sweet, slightly tart flavor excellent for jams, juices, and fresh eating. Two or more plants are needed for cross-pollination; plants flower very early in spring and may need frost protection of blossoms in zones 3–4 during cold snaps. Prune after harvest to remove dead wood and open the canopy; the shrub is generally very healthy with minimal pest and disease problems. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nanking Chinese Chestnut (Historic USDA Blight-Resistant Selection)
description: Nanking descends from one of the original USDA Chinese chestnut introductions brought into the United States in the early twentieth century as breeders searched for blight-resistant replacements for the dying American chestnut. Surviving trees of this stock later supplied scionwood used in several of the twentieth century's most influential chestnut breeding programs in the eastern United States. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a second genetically distinct chestnut nearby, since Chinese chestnut is largely self-incompatible. It bears younger and more reliably than American chestnut, and its resistance to Cryphonectria blight makes it far more durable in the humid Southeast. Collect nuts from the ground as spiny burrs split in early fall, and refrigerate briefly to sweeten the kernels before eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nanko Ume (Nankou Japanese Apricot, Premier Umeboshi Cultivar)
description: Nanko is the most widely grown fruiting Japanese apricot cultivar in Japan, prized around its home region of Minabe in Wakayama Prefecture for large, thin-skinned, richly flavored fruit that yields an exceptionally high percentage of flesh to pit, the standard by which other umeboshi-grade ume cultivars are judged. Like other Prunus mume selections it flowers in late winter to early spring on bare branches, opening pale pink, fragrant blossoms well before leaf-out, followed by green-yellow fruit that ripens to gold through late spring into early summer. Because Nanko is only partially self-fruitful, plant a second Japanese apricot cultivar nearby to ensure a heavy crop for salt-pickling into umeboshi or steeping in shochu for umeshu. Prune to an open vase shape after fruiting to maintain airflow and fruiting wood, and harvest fruit while still firm and green-yellow for traditional pickling, or let it fully ripen to gold for fresh eating or liqueur. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nannyberry
description: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets. Viburnum lentago is a large native viburnum of the northeastern and central United States, producing shiny, deeply veined, finely toothed leaves and flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that are outstanding for native bees; the abundant, blue-black, berry-like drupes in fall and winter provide critical food for migrating and overwintering songbirds — particularly cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes — and are also edible for humans, with a sweet, date-raisin flavor when fully ripe. The fall foliage turns rich wine-red to purplish-red; the plant often sends up suckers and gradually forms a thicket. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nansemond Sweet Potato (Virginia Heirloom Since 1850)
description: Nansemond is a 19th-century heirloom named for Nansemond County in Southside Virginia, where it has been a favorite home-garden variety since 1850. It produces yellow-fleshed roots on vigorous vines, with a red-skinned subvariety also historically grown in the region. Regionally it has traditionally been baked into sweet potato pies, sometimes made with toasted peanuts or peanut flour worked into the crust. Along with Southern Queen and Hayman, it remains one of the dependable pre-1900 sweet potato varieties still maintained by heirloom seed preservationists. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Nansho Daidai (Taiwanica Cold-Hardy Sour Orange)
description: Nansho Daidai, botanically Citrus taiwanica, is a vigorous, thorny sour orange type that the Japanese named and popularized during their administration of Taiwan, valued today by cold-hardy citrus growers for its exceptional toughness. Documented specimens in the Deep South have come through winter lows near 0°F with little to no leaf drop, placing it among the hardiest evergreen citrus grown in the United States, on par with Thomasville citrangequat and trifoliate orange hybrids. The orange-sized, acid-bitter fruit is not eaten fresh but substitutes well for lemon or sour orange juice in ades, marinades, and sauces, and the tree is also used as an understock for other citrus. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage and expect a large, vigorous, well-armed tree that needs little winter protection once established in zone 8 Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nantahala Raspberry (Heat-Tolerant Southern Red Raspberry)
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool through summer heat, since red raspberries generally struggle south of the mountains. Nantahala was bred at North Carolina State University specifically to extend red raspberry production into warmer parts of the Southeast, combining better heat tolerance with good fruit size and quality than older Northern-bred varieties typically manage in Southern gardens. It bears its primary crop on second-year floricanes in early summer, ahead of the worst heat, and benefits from consistent irrigation and a site with some afternoon relief in the hottest zone 8-9 gardens. Even with its improved heat tolerance, red raspberry remains a marginal crop in the Deep South, so gardeners in zone 9 should treat it as an experiment best sited in the coolest, most sheltered spot available. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nantes Carrot (Half-Long Nantes, Scarlet Nantes)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches when 2 inches tall; Nantes is the most widely grown home garden carrot type, originating in Nantes, France — producing 6–7 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical carrots with remarkably sweet, crisp, virtually coreless flesh and thin skin that doesn't require peeling. The standard against which other home garden carrots are judged for flavor and tenderness. Requires loose, deep, stone-free soil for best shape; rocky or compacted soils produce forked, stunted roots. Excellent raw, steamed, or roasted; also one of the best for juicing. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Nanticoke Squash (Native American Heirloom Winter Squash)
description: Nanticoke is an heirloom landrace squash grown for generations by the Nanticoke people of the Delmarva Peninsula, Delaware and the Eastern Shore of Maryland, and is one of the few surviving Native American winter squash lines from the Eastern Woodlands. Fruits have a mottled, speckled green rind that cures to a hard protective shell suited to long winter storage. The flesh is rich golden-orange, dense, fine-grained, and sweet, good for baking and roasting. It is maintained today primarily by seed-preservation and Indigenous seed-rematriation projects.
