Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Nantucket Serviceberry
description: Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nantucket serviceberry is one of the most compact and low-growing serviceberries in cultivation, native to coastal pine barrens, heathlands, and sandy outwash plains from Cape Cod and Nantucket south through the mid-Atlantic — conditions that most other fruiting shrubs find inhospitable. Its small scale makes it one of the few fruiting native shrubs suited to tight urban lots or coastal cottage gardens where larger serviceberries would overwhelm the space. White flowers appear in early spring and sweet blue-black berries ripen in early summer, attracting catbirds, robins, and warblers. Because it is endemic to a restricted range and specialized habitat, sourcing plants or seed from reputable native plant nurseries rather than wild-collecting is strongly encouraged to protect remaining natural populations. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nanum Dwarf Oregano (Compact Non-Flowering Edging Oregano)
description: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, such as a rock garden pocket, trough, or path edging. Nanum is a miniature form of common oregano that forms a dense, tight mound only a few inches tall, rarely producing the flower spikes typical of full-sized oregano, so its appeal is as a neat, low edging plant rather than a flowering ornamental. The tiny, aromatic leaves have a milder version of standard oregano flavor and can be snipped sparingly for cooking. Its slow, compact growth means it needs little pruning beyond an occasional trim to keep the mound even. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Napa Cabbage
description: Direct sow 1/4 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 12–18 in once seedlings are 3–4 in tall. Water regularly, as dry spells encourage premature bolting in warm weather. Fall planting generally produces better-quality heads with fewer pest problems. Harvest when heads feel firm and compact, cutting at the base before temperatures drop below 20°F. Matures in 50–80 days from seed.

name: Napa Cabbage Blues
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Blues is a high-performing napa cabbage hybrid selected specifically for resistance to tipburn and premature bolting — the two primary failure modes for napa cabbage in warmer regions. The compact, upright heads weigh 4–6 pounds with tightly wrapped, pale yellow-green interior leaves and crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flavor that is ideal for fresh eating, kimchi, stir-fries, braises, and raw slaws. Blues develops solid heads without the loose, poorly-wrapped outer structure common in heat-stressed napa cabbage; the improved tip-burn resistance means more marketable heads per planting. In zone 9 fall is the primary season — transplant in September for harvest from November through January. Consistent soil moisture is critical for head development; water stress causes loose, poorly-filled heads and encourages premature bolting. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Napa Cabbage Michihili
description: This Michihili-type Napa cabbage forms tall, barrel-shaped heads of tightly wrapped, mild, tender leaves ideal for kimchi and stir-fry. It grows best as a fall crop; sow in mid to late summer so heads mature in cool weather, since spring heat and long days trigger bolting. Keep the soil consistently moist and rich in nitrogen for fast, uniform growth. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, and cut before hard freezes. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Napoletano Basil (Italian Large-Leaf Lettuce-Leaf Neapolitan Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil after last frost. Pinch flower buds as they appear to maintain leaf production. Napoletano (also called Italian Large-Leaf or Lettuce Leaf Basil) is the traditional basil of Neapolitan cuisine — a variety with exceptionally large, broadly oval, slightly crinkled, aromatic leaves that can reach 4–6 inches across in good growing conditions, two to three times the size of standard Genovese basil leaves. The very large leaf size makes Napoletano particularly well-suited to certain traditional Italian preparations: the leaves are large enough to use whole as a pizza topping without chopping, attractive as a garnish or salad base, and produce impressive yields of leaf area per harvest. The flavor is rich, sweet, and classically basil — virtually identical to Genovese in fragrance and taste, as the large leaf size is a morphological rather than a chemical difference between the varieties. Napoletano performs well in zone 9's warm summers and is one of the basil varieties that handles Gulf South heat and humidity acceptably, though like all basil it bolts in response to day length and hot temperatures — regular pinching extends productive life. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Napoli Carrot (Early Spring Nantes-Type Hybrid Carrot)
description: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in loose, well-amended soil; thin to 2–3 inch spacing when plants are 2 inches tall. Napoli is a Bejo Seeds Nantes-type hybrid that has earned a strong reputation among market gardeners and home growers as one of the most consistent early-season carrots available — reliably producing smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots 6–7 inches long with rich orange color, good internal uniformity, and the clean, sweet Nantes flavor in just 58–68 days. The Nantes type is distinguished from other carrot forms by its nearly cylindrical shape (minimal taper from shoulder to tip), blunt end, almost coreless interior with minimal differentiation between phloem and xylem, and clean, crisp texture that makes it the most versatile shape for both fresh eating and cooking. Napoli's early maturity makes it especially valuable for areas where the growing season is short or where spring planting must be followed by summer crops. The roots have good storage quality and hold well in the ground after reaching maturity without significant quality loss. Napoli has been a consistent top performer in university carrot variety trials across the northeastern United States and Europe, where its combination of earliness, quality, and reliable stand establishment have made it a standard recommendation. A dependable all-purpose Nantes carrot well suited to both home garden and small-farm production. Matures in 58–68 days from seed.

name: Naranjilla (Lulo)
description: Start seeds in warm, moist seed mix at 75–80°F; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a location sheltered from strong afternoon sun, as the large tropical leaves burn easily. This Andean highland fruit naturally grows at elevations where temperatures rarely exceed 85°F — it prefers the cool tropics and will struggle in humid Gulf Coast summers; maritime California and high-altitude zones 9–10 are ideal. The orange, tomato-like fruits are covered with soft hair when immature and ripen over several months; the intensely tart, aromatic pulp is used for juices, smoothies, and ice cream in Colombia and Ecuador. Prune to remove dead or crossing branches after harvest. Matures in 180–270 days from seed.

name: Narrowleaf Cattail
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches depth) or saturated soil in full sun; narrowleaf cattail is a cosmopolitan aquatic native with narrower leaves than broadleaf cattail (T. latifolia) and a distinctive gap between the male and female portions of the brown, sausage-like seed head — a reliable identification feature. Like all cattails, it provides extraordinary wildlife value: the fluffy seed cotton is used for nest lining by ducks and wrens; the seed heads provide food for marsh wrens and red-winged blackbirds; the dense rhizome mats provide spawning habitat for fish and shelter for amphibians. All parts of cattail are edible — the young spring shoots taste like cucumber; the green male flower heads can be cooked like corn on the cob; the pollen is a protein-rich flour substitute; and the rhizomes yield a starchy flour. Spreads rapidly — contain in pots sunk in water or with barriers to prevent unwanted spread. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Nashville Prickly Pear (Southeastern Clumping Prickly Pear)
description: Root a callused pad section in gritty, sharply drained, limy soil in full sun, choosing a rocky or gravelly bed rather than heavy garden loam. Unlike the sprawling mats of its close relative eastern prickly pear, Nashville prickly pear grows in tighter, more upright clumps of pads and is native to limestone glades, cedar barrens, and rocky open woodlands through the interior Southeast, including Tennessee, Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. Pale yellow flowers open in late spring atop the pad margins, followed by reddish-purple fruit that ripens by late summer and can be used like other edible pricklypear tunas once the glochids are removed. Its tufted, clump-forming habit makes it a good choice for rock gardens and glade-style plantings where a less sprawling native cactus is wanted. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Natacha Escarole
description: Natacha is a French-bred escarole selected for large, heavy heads packed with abundant, tender leaves surrounding a creamy, well-blanched heart. It stands out for its strong resistance to bolting, tipburn, and bottom rot, which lets it hold in the garden longer than many older escarole types, especially in hot or humid weather. As with other broad-leaved endives, gathering and tying the outer leaves a week or two before harvest deepens the self-blanching of the heart and mellows the characteristic mild bitterness. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Natal Orange (Kaffir Orange, Spiny Monkey Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; very drought-tolerant once established; the thorny nature deters browsing animals. Strychnos spinosa (Natal orange, spiny monkey orange, or kaffir orange) is a thorny deciduous tree from sub-Saharan Africa — native to the savanna, bushveld, and dry woodland regions of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and eastward to Kenya and Tanzania. The tree bears the most remarkable fruits in the genus: large (3–4 inch diameter), perfectly round, hard-shelled, bright yellow-green when ripe, strongly resembling oranges externally despite being completely unrelated (in the Strychnaceae family). IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unlike Strychnos nux-vomica (the strychnine tree, which has highly toxic seeds), S. spinosa fruit pulp is edible — the sweet-acid, jelly-like, cream to yellow flesh surrounding the large seeds inside has a pleasant, fruity, somewhat date-like flavor and is widely eaten in rural southern Africa. The seeds are bitter and should be avoided. The extremely hard shell of the dried fruit has been used for millennia as a container, bowl, and decorated gourd throughout sub-Saharan Africa. The roots, bark, and leaves have extensive traditional medicinal applications in southern African herbalism. A remarkably tough, drought-resistant tree for dry subtropical collectors' gardens in zone 9–11. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Natal Plum
description: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; natal plum is a South African native shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves armed with forked spines, fragrant white flowers like large jasmine blooms, and cranberry-sized red to deep-crimson fruits that are among the finest edible berries available in zone 9–11 landscapes. The fruit has a rich, sweet, somewhat cranberry-like flavor and is excellent for jams, jellies, juices, and fresh eating. Plants bloom and fruit nearly year-round in frost-free climates. Salt-tolerant, drought-resistant, and excellent as a security hedge or coastal planting. Note: only the ripe red fruits are edible — all other plant parts including unripe fruits are toxic. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Natchez Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5); Natchez is a semi-erect, thornless blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2007, widely considered one of the finest named varieties for the Gulf Coast and mid-South. It is the earliest-ripening major thornless variety, typically producing its first berries in late May to early June in zones 8–9 — a full 2–3 weeks before Ouachita and other Arkansas releases. Berries are very large (9–12 grams), elongated, jet-black, sweet, and aromatic with excellent fresh-eating quality. Yields are high, and the self-supporting semi-erect canes need only minimal trellising. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select 4–6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for next year's crop. Natchez is susceptible to double-blossom rosette disease in areas with high disease pressure; avoid overhead irrigation. In zone 9a, provide afternoon shade or plant on a north-facing slope to reduce heat stress during fruiting. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: National Pickling Cucumber
description: National Pickling is an open-pollinated heirloom bred for firm, blocky fruits about five to six inches long that are perfect for pickling and canning. The productive vines set fruit heavily and quickly, so pick often to keep new cucumbers coming. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun after frost and keep evenly watered for crisp, uniform fruit. Harvest at the size you want, from small gherkins to larger slicing cucumbers. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Natural Mystic Dragon Fruit
description: A white-fleshed dragon fruit selection favored by growers for reliable self-fertility and good yields without hand-pollination between different plants, though hand-pollinating night-blooming flowers still improves fruit set and size. Fruit is medium to large with red-pink scaled skin and sweet, mildly floral white flesh studded with tiny black seeds. As an epiphytic cactus it needs gritty, fast-draining soil and infrequent deep watering rather than a regular irrigation schedule, plus excellent air circulation to avoid stem rot. Provide a stout post or trellis at planting, since the three-ribbed stems climb by aerial roots and become heavy as the plant matures. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Navaho Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Navaho is a thornless erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program and released in 1988. The large, glossy, jet-black berries are among the sweetest of any commercial blackberry variety — significantly sweeter than most thorned varieties and with a more balanced sweet-tart flavor than the extremely tart early-season varieties. The high sugar content and mild, pleasant flavor make Navaho berries exceptional for fresh eating without added sugar and for preserves where reduced sugar is desired. The thornless, erect habit makes harvesting unusually practical: no thorns to navigate and no extensive trellis infrastructure required. Navaho produces mid-to-late season, ripening in late June–July in zone 9, providing fruit after the earlier erect varieties have finished and extending the fresh blackberry season. The firm berries have good post-harvest shelf life, remaining harvestable for several days without softening if kept cool. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Navaho Blackberry
description: 'Navaho' is an erect, thornless blackberry that produces firm, very sweet berries with excellent shelf life on self-supporting canes. Because it grows upright it needs little or no trellising, though a single wire helps in windy sites. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep suckers thinned to maintain a manageable hedgerow. Prune out fruited floricanes each fall and tip new primocanes to encourage branching. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Navajo Yellow Cantaloupe
description: This drought-tolerant heirloom, originally grown by the Navajo people, produces 3 to 7 pound melons with sweet orange flesh and a yellow rind. It thrives in poorer soils and hot, dry conditions where other melons struggle. Give it full sun and room to sprawl, watering deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and develops a fragrant aroma. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Navel Orange
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the Washington Navel is the world's most widely grown eating orange, identifiable by the small secondary fruit (the 'navel') embedded in the blossom end of each fruit. Navel oranges are seedless, easy to peel, and have exceptionally rich, sweet, non-bitter flavor when fully ripe. They ripen in winter (November through March), making them a precious fresh fruit at a time of year when few other fruit trees are bearing. Trees are self-fruitful and require no pollinators. Feed monthly with a citrus fertilizer, maintain good drainage, and protect from frost — even brief exposure to 28°F will damage fruit. In zone 9 the trees are hardy but fruit may be damaged in hard freezes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Navy Bean (Haricot Bean, Boston Bean, White Pea Bean)
description: Sow 1–2 inches deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; navy beans are the small, oval, ivory-white dried beans of New England baked beans, Senate bean soup, and countless European cassoulet and bean dishes. The compact bush plants are highly productive and concentrate their pod set for a single, efficient harvest period — more practical for dry bean production than many spreading pole types. Allow pods to turn yellow-brown and papery before harvest; pull the entire plant and dry in a warm, well-ventilated location for 1–2 weeks, then shell. Navy beans are rich in fiber (19g per cup) and folate. In zone 9a, spring plantings avoid the hottest summer weather; flowers drop in temperatures above 90°F, so early planting is key to a full harvest. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Nazemetz Feijoa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Nazemetz is a California-selected feijoa (pineapple guava) cultivar prized for producing the largest fruits of any commonly available named variety — round to slightly pear-shaped fruits typically reaching 4–8 ounces, significantly larger than the 2–4 ounce fruits of unnamed seedling plants. The rich, complex, aromatic flavor combines pineapple, mint, guava, and strawberry notes into a unique tropical flavor that is highly distinctive and unlike any other common fruit. Feijoa (Acca sellowiana) is a South American fruit increasingly popular in California, New Zealand, and the Gulf South for its exceptional zone 8–10 adaptability, drought tolerance, and ornamental value — the spring flowers with white petals and red stamens are edible and delicious eaten directly from the plant as a sweet-spicy spring treat. In zone 9 Nazemetz produces fruit reliably with minimal care; the fruit drops naturally when ripe and is harvested by collecting fallen fruits. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: NC-1 Pawpaw
description: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; NC-1 is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ontario, Canada by Richard Campbell and subsequently widely adopted in North American pawpaw cultivation for combining two usually separate virtues: exceptional cold hardiness (rated to USDA zone 4) and superior fruiting productivity in the upper part of its range. The medium-large fruits (8–14 ounces) have cream-to-yellow flesh with a rich, complex, sweet flavor rated highly in Kentucky State University pawpaw taste evaluations. NC-1 is noted for its consistent, reliable fruiting on young trees — often beginning to bear meaningfully in 3–4 years from transplant, ahead of the 5–7 year wait common for seedling pawpaws. Its northern Canadian selection history means it leafs out slightly later in spring, reducing the risk of late frost damage to flowers — a significant advantage for zone 9 gardeners where erratic late-winter weather can damage early flowers. Cross-pollinate with Mango, Overleese, or Shenandoah for best results. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: NC-10 American Persimmon (Campbell NC10, Cold-Hardy Seedless Persimmon)
description: NC-10, also sold as Campbell NC10, arose as a seedling of the classic Early Golden cultivar selected in Ontario's Niagara region and has since been distributed by cold-climate specialty nurseries as one of the hardier named American persimmon selections. It bears medium-sized, oval fruit, seedless when grown without a male pollinator nearby, that ripens over a long window from mid-September through late October. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections the fruit is firmly astringent until fully soft, at which point it develops a very sweet, rich flavor and pudding-like texture. NC-10 is valued particularly by growers at the northern edge of American persimmon's range for its reliable ripening and good winter hardiness. Site trees in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and avoid disturbing the taproot when transplanting. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: NC-113 Pawpaw (Davis x Overleese Numbered Selection)
description: NC-113 is a numbered seedling selection from the same Davis x Overleese cross that also produced the well-known commercial cultivar NC-1, but it is a genetically distinct individual selected and documented separately in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar records rather than a synonym for NC-1. Fruit is documented at roughly 10 to 12 ounces, few-seeded, with yellow flesh and yellow skin, consistent with its Davis x Overleese parentage but never commercially released the way NC-1 was. Because it shares grandparentage with NC-1, avoid pairing the two together for pollination — pick a more distantly related cultivar instead. NC-113 is best suited to collectors and gene-bank-style plantings interested in preserving the wider range of seedlings that came out of the historic Davis x Overleese cross rather than home growers who simply want the single most productive tree. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ne Plus Ultra Almond (Historic California Soft-Shell Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety with overlapping bloom time is planted nearby. Ne Plus Ultra is one of the oldest named California almond varieties still in cultivation, its name Latin for 'nothing further beyond,' reflecting the confidence of its 19th-century breeders in its quality, and it remains valued for a long, slender, soft-shell kernel with good sweet flavor. Historically an important variety in the early development of California's commercial almond industry, it has since been surpassed in commercial volume by more productive modern releases but is still grown by home orchardists and specialty producers who appreciate its distinctive nut shape and historic pedigree. Water deeply through the growing season, especially during kernel fill, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nebbiolo Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Nebbiolo is the noble red grape of Piedmont, Italy, source of the legendary Barolo and Barbaresco wines, prized for pale color that belies powerful, high-tannin, high-acid wines with distinctive aromas of rose, tar, and dried cherry that develop remarkable complexity with age. The grape buds early, exposing it to spring frost risk, yet ripens very late in the season, one of the last major wine grapes harvested each year, and it is notoriously particular about site, generally performing best on specific hillside exposures that concentrate warmth — a real challenge for growers outside its native Piedmont. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize a warm, well-exposed site, and be prepared for a long hang time before tannins and flavors reach full ripeness. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nebraska Wedding Tomato (Pioneer-Era Orange Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed, providing support for the fruit-laden branches. This variety was carried by pioneer families from Minnesota to the Nebraska plains in the late 1800s, and tradition held that a pinch of its seed was given to Nebraska brides as a wedding gift so they could grow it in their own gardens. The plants yield deep orange, globe-shaped fruit with a rich, sweet flavor and few seeds, and the variety was later documented and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Necta Zee Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Container Nectarine)
description: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, in the ground or in a large container of at least 15–20 gallons, and thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart when marble-sized, since the naturally dwarf, densely fruiting tree can easily overset relative to its small size. Necta Zee is a genetic dwarf nectarine, naturally compact rather than grafted onto dwarfing rootstock, reaching only about 5–6 feet tall with a dense, bushy habit, yet still producing full-sized, sweet, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with the classic smooth nectarine skin in mid-summer. Its true dwarf stature makes it one of the very few stone fruits practical for a patio container, small urban yard, or anywhere a full-sized 15–20 foot peach or nectarine tree would be impractical, while requiring the same full sun, sharp drainage, and moderate chill (around 500 hours) as standard nectarine varieties. Prune lightly to maintain an open center for light and air circulation, and watch for the leaf curl and brown rot diseases common to nectarines in humid climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nectarine
description: Nectarines are essentially smooth-skinned peaches and share the same culture — self-fertile, open-center pruning, and annual heading-back of one-year-old wood. Because nectarines lack the peach's fuzzy skin barrier they are somewhat more susceptible to brown rot and bacterial spot in humid climates, so good air circulation is critical. Chill requirements range from 250 to 900 hours depending on cultivar; select accordingly. Fruit is ready when it gives slightly to thumb pressure and the background color has shifted from green to creamy yellow. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Neem Tree
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; neem is one of the most multipurpose trees in tropical horticulture, revered for thousands of years in India where virtually every part of the tree is used: the seeds yield neem oil, widely used as an organic pesticide and insect repellent containing azadirachtin, a potent botanical insecticide; the leaves are used medicinally for their antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic properties; young shoots and leaves are eaten as a bitter vegetable in some South and Southeast Asian cuisines; and the twigs are traditionally used as disposable toothbrushes (chew sticks). The tree itself is a spectacular ornamental — fast-growing with a broad, spreading crown of dense, pinnate leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers beloved by bees. It is one of the most drought-tolerant trees available and tolerates alkaline, poor soils that support little else. The organic pesticide market for neem oil products has created significant commercial cultivation in Florida and Hawaii. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Negret Hazelnut (Avellana de Reus DO Filbert, Catalan Hazelnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Negret requires a compatible pollenizer and benefits from monitoring for iron chlorosis on alkaline soils; the tree is naturally low-vigor with a spreading, suckering habit and bears relatively late in its establishment compared to other commercial cultivars. Negret is the dominant hazelnut cultivar of Spain, accounting for roughly 70% of Spanish commercial hazelnut orchards, and is the principal variety behind the 'Avellana de Reus' Designation of Origin in the Tarragona province of Catalonia. The kernels are highly regarded by the confectionery and kernel-roasting market for their flavor and processing qualities. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Negro Pepper (Grains of Selim, Ethiopian Pepper, Hwentia)
description: Plant seedlings in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with full sun to partial shade, giving the tree ample room since it eventually reaches a slender, tall canopy form. Negro pepper is an aromatic evergreen tree native to the humid lowland forests and savanna transition zones of West and Central Africa, grown for its finger-like, slightly twisted seed pods that are sun-dried and often smoked before use. The dried pods and their small seeds carry a warm, smoky, camphor-and-pepper flavor used whole or ground in West African soups, stews, and spice blends, and are also valued in traditional medicine and smoked-fish preparation. Because it is slow to bear, most growers outside Africa treat it as a long-term agroforestry or specimen tree rather than a quick spice crop; young trees benefit from light shade and should be protected from strong wind while establishing. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Nellie Kelly Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Nellie Kelly is a purple passionfruit cultivar popular in Australian and subtropical home gardens for its combination of good disease resistance, heavy cropping, and rich, tangy flavor. The vine grows quickly and begins fruiting within its first year, producing abundant deep-purple fruit that drop naturally from the vine when ripe. Give the vigorous vine a sturdy trellis or fence and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage lateral branching, which increases the fruiting wood. In zone 9, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden and mulch heavily over winter, since purple passionfruit types tolerate cold less well than the hardier Possum Purple hybrid and can be killed back or outright by a hard freeze. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Nelly Chives (Fine-Leaf Bunching Chive)
description: Nelly is a fine-to-medium leaf chive with a uniform, upright habit and slender, dark green leaves, a leaf profile favored for bunching and fresh use because it gives a refined, delicate appearance when snipped over a finished dish. It performs well in containers as well as garden beds, making it a good option for a kitchen-window herb pot. Flavor is the classic mild onion taste typical of common chives, and the pale purple pompom flowers that follow are edible and attractive to pollinators if left to bloom. Harvest by snipping leaves near the base regularly to keep the clump producing tender new growth, and divide every few years in spring as clumps become congested. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Nelson Carrot (Heat-Tolerant Sweet Nantes Hybrid)
description: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2-3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall. Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type hybrid carrot specifically noted for retaining good, consistent sweetness even when grown through warmer weather than most carrots tolerate well, since heat typically pushes carrots toward a stronger, more bitter flavor and woody texture. The smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange with a small core and crisp, juicy texture. In zone 8-9, sow in late winter for an early spring harvest and again in late summer for a fall crop, and expect Nelson to hold its sweet flavor through a wider harvest window than standard carrot varieties. Matures in 58–68 days from seed.

name: Nelson Sauvin Hops
description: Named for its uncanny resemblance to Sauvignon Blanc wine grapes, this New Zealand hop delivers intense tropical fruit, gooseberry, and white-wine aromatics that home brewers use heavily in New Zealand and West Coast IPAs. It performs best in mild, maritime-influenced climates and appreciates protection from intense midday heat in hot inland regions. Provide a tall trellis, rich soil, and consistent irrigation, since inconsistent moisture noticeably dulls its signature aroma. Pick cones promptly at peak ripeness, as its delicate aromatics fade quickly if harvest is delayed. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nemagold Sweet Potato
description: Nemagold was developed in the mid-20th century as an improved, root-knot-nematode-resistant strain within the Puerto Rico type of sweet potato, released to protect Gulf South growers from nematode damage that plagued earlier orange-fleshed varieties. The moist, deep-orange flesh and coppery-orange skin closely resemble Beauregard and Puerto Rico in flavor and texture, producing smooth, blocky roots that store and cure well. Because it tolerates the sandy, nematode-prone soils common across the Gulf Coast, Nemagold remains a dependable heirloom choice for gardeners battling nematode pressure in older vegetable beds. Set slips after the soil has warmed in late spring and let the long, warm Gulf Coast season fully mature the crop before the first fall frost. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Nemaguard Peach Rootstock
description: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock; Nemaguard is bred specifically for root-knot nematode resistance. Bred specifically for strong resistance to root-knot nematodes, a serious soil-borne pest that stunts and kills peach trees on susceptible rootstocks in warm, sandy-soil growing regions, it has become the standard rootstock for peach and nectarine production across the sandy soils of the Southeast, Gulf South, and California. Its nematode resistance makes it a far more reliable choice than ordinary seedling rootstocks for a home orchard on sandy or previously peach-planted soil, where nematode populations often build up over time. Graft a desired named peach or nectarine variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and note that it is somewhat less cold-hardy than other peach rootstocks, best suited to zone 7 and warmer. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nendran Banana (Kerala Dual-Purpose Plantain)
description: Nendran is one of the most widely grown AAB-genome bananas of Kerala, India, valued as a true dual-purpose cultivar: the long, thick, slightly curved fruit is cooked as a starchy vegetable, notably fried into chips, when green and eaten as a sweet dessert banana when fully ripe. It grows into a tall, vigorous, wind-resistant plant and needs deep fertile soil and generous irrigation to fill out its characteristically large, elongated fruit. It has no notable cold tolerance and should be reserved for the warmest, most sheltered parts of a zone 9b-11 garden. Feed heavily through the growing season, since it is a heavier feeder than many dessert-type bananas. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Neon Eggplant (Smooth Hot-Pink Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Neon produces smooth, glossy, vividly hot-pink to magenta fruit that stands out sharply against the plant's foliage, with mild, tender, nearly seedless flesh similar to standard Italian eggplants. It matures notably early for an eggplant and sets fruit heavily on a relatively compact plant, making it a productive choice for smaller gardens and containers as well as open beds. Harvest at 4-6 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since fruit left too long dulls in color and toughens. Its striking coloring also makes it a popular market and specialty-produce variety. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Neos Frisée Endive
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun once seedlings have several true leaves. Neos is a hybrid frisee endive selected for a compact, upright habit and finely cut, curled leaves that shade the heart naturally, producing a pale, tender center with little need for tying. It matures faster and more uniformly than many open-pollinated curly endives, which makes it a favorite among market growers for consistent harvests. Use the mildly bitter, delicate leaves raw in composed salads such as salade lyonnaise, or briefly wilted with warm bacon dressing. Matures in 50–65 days from transplant.

name: Nepal Tomato (Himalayan Pink Potato-Leaf Heirloom)
description: Collected from a Himalayan village garden, this heirloom is distinguished by soft, blue-green, potato-leaf foliage and heavy clusters of smooth, pink-red, medium-large globe fruits with few seeds and a rich sweet-tart flavor. The vigorous indeterminate vines are reliably productive through hot, humid conditions and have shown good foliage disease tolerance in Gulf South trial gardens compared to many other pink heirlooms. Stake or cage plants well, since the potato-leaf vines are dense and heavy once fruit sets, and pick at full color for the best flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Neptune Tomato (Heat-Set Gulf South Hybrid)
description: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Neptune is a heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida as part of a long-running Southeastern breeding effort to keep fruit set going once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s, a point at which most standard hybrids stop setting fruit. The medium-to-large, round, red fruits have solid, well-balanced flavor and enough firmness to ship and hold well, making Neptune a dependable choice for a continuous summer harvest rather than a single early flush. Plants carry good resistance to common Southern tomato diseases, but a preventive fungicide or copper spray schedule still helps in the humid Gulf South. Stake or cage plants early, since they grow vigorously, and keep watering consistent to avoid blossom end rot in the region's heavy summer rains followed by dry spells. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Nero Aronia
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist soil — tolerates periodic wet feet better than most fruiting shrubs; Nero is a Czech-selected black chokeberry cultivar widely used in European commercial aronia production, selected for slightly more compact growth habit than Viking with comparable or superior berry yield relative to plant size. The medium to large, round, blue-black to jet-black berries ripen in late August–September with the characteristic high-tannin, astringent flavor of the species — intensely purple when juiced and among the highest known plant sources of anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins. Nero is the most widely grown aronia variety in European commercial production, where aronia juice and concentrate are major products. The compact, upright-to-rounded shrub fits well into mixed border plantings and provides four-season interest with spring flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, heavy late-summer berry crops, and outstanding fall color. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nero di Milano Zucchini
description: Nero di Milano, meaning 'black of Milan,' is a traditional Italian zucchini from Lombardy prized in home gardens for its very dark, near-black-green skin and compact, open bush growth habit that makes fruit easy to spot and pick. It is among the earliest zucchini to begin bearing, and fruit is best harvested young at 6-8 inches, when the skin is tender and the flavor sweetest. The tidy, non-sprawling plant produces steadily over a long season, making it a practical choice for gardeners who want continuous zucchini without the vine sprawl of many other summer squash types. As an open-pollinated Italian heirloom, its seed can be saved true from year to year. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Nero di Toscana Kale
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. palmifolia 'Nero di Toscana'
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nero di Toscana (also known as Lacinato kale, Dinosaur kale, or Cavolo Nero) is the traditional Italian black kale of Tuscany, producing long, strap-like leaves with a deeply blistered (savoyed) surface and an almost blue-black dark green color — the darkest of all kale types. The texture is firmer and the flavor is more savory, mineral, and complex than curly kale, with less bitterness and a sweeter, earthier depth that develops most fully after frost. Nero di Toscana is the authentic ingredient in ribollita (Tuscan bread and vegetable soup), farinata di cavolo nero, and braised Tuscan kale side dishes where curly kale cannot substitute. The long, upright growth habit exposes the lower leaves for continuous harvest while the growing tip extends upward — a productive cut-and-come-again pattern that provides months of harvest from a single planting. Remove individual outer leaves for harvest to allow continuous new growth from the center growing point. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Nero Tondo Radish
description: Nero Tondo, Italian for round black, is a refined selection of the old Black Spanish type bred for rounder, more uniform roots and notably better bolt tolerance than the traditional heirloom strain. The rough, matte-black skin conceals dense, snow-white flesh with a sharp, peppery bite that mellows into an earthy sweetness when roasted or braised. Because the roots hold in the ground and in storage far longer than spring radishes, gardeners grow it as a keeper crop, pulling roots through fall and into winter for slaws, pickles, and cooked preparations. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Nesbitt Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood on a two-wire trellis or arbor. Nesbitt is a University of Georgia-released muscadine selected for its combination of very large, deep purple-black fruit, vigorous productive vines, and reliable self-fertility, making it a popular home-garden choice that needs no separate pollinator vine. The fruit has a thin, tender skin for a muscadine, sweet juicy flesh, and good flavor for fresh eating, with fruit size among the largest of the widely grown self-fertile varieties. The vigorous vine bears heavily once established and holds its crop well, tolerating the humid, disease-prone conditions of Gulf South summers better than bunch grapes. A dependable, high-yielding choice for a home muscadine arbor in zone 7–9. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nessberry
description: The nessberry is an old dewberry-raspberry cross developed for the hot South, producing dark, wine-red berries with a sprightly flavor. Its trailing canes benefit from a low trellis and adapt well to heat and heavier soils where standard raspberries struggle. Plant in full sun in well-drained ground and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Remove spent floricanes after the summer crop and train fresh primocanes for the following season. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Netted Gem Melon (Ancestor of the Modern Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced around 1881, Netted Gem produces small, round, densely netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh, and its heavy netting pattern and reliable sweetness made it enormously influential in American melon breeding — most of the netted cantaloupe types sold in grocery stores today trace back to selections made from this variety. The compact vines are productive and well suited to home gardens. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the netting has fully developed, indicating peak ripeness and sweetness. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Netted Pawpaw (Flag Pawpaw)
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, choosing a site that mimics the pine flatwoods and scrub where this pawpaw grows wild. Large, fragrant, creamy-white to maroon flowers open in spring before or alongside the new leaves, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit that ripens smaller than common pawpaw but is sweet and edible fresh. The shrub spreads slowly by root suckers into low colonies and tolerates the sandy, low-fertility, seasonally wet-then-dry soils typical of the Gulf Coast pine belt far better than most fruiting shrubs. It is also a larval host for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, adding pollinator and wildlife value to a native fruit or naturalized planting. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Netzer Elderberry (Missouri-Selected American Elderberry Ecotype)
description: Netzer is a wild-selected Missouri ecotype of American elderberry that was carried into replicated University of Missouri and Missouri State University cultivar trials alongside Bob Gordon, Wyldewood, and Adams, where it consistently proved well adapted to hot, humid, southern-Midwest growing conditions. It bears the typical broad, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by heavy sets of small, dark purple-black berries in mid- to late summer, and its native Ozark origin gives it good tolerance of the heat and humidity that stress northern-bred cultivars. Because it grows and fruits on a similar schedule to other American elderberry selections, Netzer cross-pollinates readily with cultivars such as Adams, Bob Gordon, or Wyldewood when planted in the same bed. Cut back the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and control root suckers to prevent the planting from spreading into an unmanaged thicket. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nevada Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Nevada is a French batavian-type lettuce selected specifically for heat tolerance and slow bolting — it holds usable quality in warm spring conditions 1–2 weeks longer than standard butterhead or looseleaf varieties before flowering, providing a meaningfully extended harvest window in warm climates like zone 9. The large, crisp, slightly frilly green leaves form a dense, semi-heading rosette similar to a looseleaf but with better structure and more crunch than floppy butterhead types. The flavor is fresh, mild, and slightly crisp — closer to iceberg in texture but without the blandness, and closer to looseleaf in flavor but with more body. Nevada is widely used by commercial producers in California and the Southwest who need a heat-tolerant green-leaf lettuce for late spring production windows. In zone 9 it is one of the most reliable lettuces for bridging the February–May spring season before summer heat ends production. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Neves Azorean Red Tomato (Portuguese-American Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and provide sturdy staking, since the vigorous indeterminate vines carry a heavy load of large fruit. Neves Azorean Red traces to Azorean immigrant families who brought tomato seed with them to New England and California and kept it going in home gardens for generations before it entered the wider heirloom seed trade; the deep pinkish-red beefsteak fruit is prized for its dense, meaty flesh, relatively small seed cavities, and low acidity, which makes for a tomato with almost no watery waste when sliced. Individual fruits commonly reach a pound or more on well-grown plants, and the rich, well-balanced flavor holds up in sandwiches and fresh salads as well as in sauce. As an open-pollinated heirloom it saves true from seed with basic isolation, letting gardeners keep the family line going the same way it has been passed down for decades. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: New Big Dwarf Tomato (Heirloom Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)
description: New Big Dwarf was introduced by the Livingston Seed Company in 1917 as an improvement on earlier dwarf tomato lines, combining a compact, potato-leaf, non-sprawling habit with unusually large fruit for its class. Mature pink beefsteak-type tomatoes can approach a pound, with smooth shoulders and rich, well-balanced flavor on plants short enough to grow without a full cage. Its early-20th-century dwarf, rugose-leaved genetics made it a natural choice for modern hybridizers, and it stands behind later Dwarf Tomato Project crosses, including as a parent of Tasmanian Chocolate alongside Paul Robeson. Harvest as fruit fully colors and softens slightly at the blossom end for best flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: New Guinea Basil
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; New Guinea Basil is an uncommon, small-statured basil type with narrow, arrow-shaped leaves only about 1.5-2 in long, dark green on top with a distinct dark-purple wash and purple leaf veins and undersides, topped by showy violet flower spikes. Its fragrance is unusual among basils — a strong, sweet licorice scent layered with mint and spice notes rather than the clove-anise character typical of Genovese or Thai basil. Because of its compact size, colorful foliage, and striking flowers, it is grown as much for its ornamental value in pots and border edges as for culinary use, though the aromatic leaves can be used sparingly wherever a licorice-mint basil note is wanted. It performs best as a container or edging plant rather than a large cutting-production basil. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: New Hampshire Midget Watermelon (Ultra-Compact Short-Season Icebox Watermelon)
description: Bred at the University of New Hampshire and released in 1951, this is one of the earliest true short-vine watermelons ever developed, making it a workhorse for northern gardeners and anyone with a short frost-free window. Vines stay compact enough for a large container or a small raised bed, and the round 4-6 pound fruits with pale flesh mature fast rather than for exceptional sweetness. Keep soil evenly moist through fruit set, then ease off watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate what sugar they do develop. Its main value is reliability where longer-season Southern varieties simply run out of summer. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: New Hanover Southern Highbush Blueberry (Disease-Resistant Low-Chill NC State Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. New Hanover, released by North Carolina State University in 2007, needs relatively little winter chill and ripens in early-to-mid June, offering a valuable combination of low-chill suitability for the Gulf South alongside notably good resistance to stem blight and canker, the fungal diseases that most often shorten the productive life of southern highbush blueberry bushes in humid climates. This disease tolerance makes it a lower-maintenance choice than many low-chill selections that trade hardiness for early ripening. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out any affected wood promptly despite its improved resistance. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: New Mexico No. 6-4 Green Chile (Classic Hatch-Style Mild Roasting Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake lightly. Harvest green pods at full size before any color break for roasting, or allow to ripen to deep red for drying. New Mexico No. 6-4 is the chile pepper variety that defined an entire regional food culture: the mild, thin-walled roasting pepper grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico and marketed under the 'Hatch Chile' designation that drives an enormous annual harvest festival and roasting tradition every August and September in New Mexico and throughout the American Southwest. The variety was developed by Dr. Roy Harper at New Mexico State University in Albuquerque in the 1950s through selection from the original New Mexico No. 6 variety, with the '6-4' designation referring to the parents used in the cross. The resulting variety became the commercial standard for New Mexico green chile production because it combined the mild-to-medium heat level preferred by most consumers with a pod shape and size (6–8 inches long, 1.5–2 inches wide) that roasts evenly on a flame or in a large drum roaster without burning before the flesh is fully cooked through. Thin walls and high moisture content allow steam to separate the charred skin from the flesh during roasting, enabling the characteristic step of peeling the blackened skin to reveal the moist, mildly pungent chile beneath. Home gardeners can replicate commercial roasting by placing whole pods under a broiler or directly on a gas burner flame, turning until charred on all sides, then placing in a sealed plastic bag for 10–15 minutes to steam before peeling. For red chile production, allow all pods to fully ripen to deep red on the plant or allow to ripen after harvest in a warm, dry location before drying whole or grinding to powder. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: New Queen Watermelon (Yellow-Fleshed Icebox Watermelon)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed, or start transplants a few weeks early to get a jump on the season, and thin to strong single plants once vines begin to run. New Queen was named an All-America Selections winner in 1999 for its early, compact icebox-sized fruit and its unusual bright orange-yellow flesh, a departure from typical red-fleshed watermelons of its era. The globe-shaped fruits typically weigh 5 to 6 pounds and offer crisp, honey-sweet flavor well suited to small gardens. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: New Red Fire Leaf Lettuce
description: This flame-tipped green leaf lettuce holds its flavor even in summer heat and resists downy mildew, bottom rot, and tipburn. Its slow-to-bolt habit lets you harvest over a long window. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist for tender leaves. Pick outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head, and provide light afternoon shade in hot weather to extend the season. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: New Red Fire Lettuce (Improved Heat-Tolerant Red Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. New Red Fire is a loose-leaf lettuce bearing large, ruffled, deep red-tinged leaves over a green base, an improved selection bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf lettuce varieties, which makes it noticeably more forgiving for gardeners in warm climates trying to stretch the lettuce season into early summer or start it earlier in late winter. Because it is a loose-leaf type, it never forms a tight head, and outer leaves can be harvested continuously while the center keeps producing new growth, extending the useful harvest window from a single planting. Flavor is mild and pleasant even as leaves size up, without the pronounced bitterness that develops quickly in less heat-tolerant lettuce under stress. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to further delay bolting as temperatures climb. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: New York Improved Eggplant (New York Spineless)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm since eggplant germinates poorly below 70F, then transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm. Give plants full sun, even moisture, and a stake or cage to support the heavy fruit load once pods set. This is one of the oldest American commercial eggplant selections, dating to the late 1800s, prized for its large glossy purple-black fruit and mild, tender flesh, and it stands as a direct ancestor of many modern hybrids sold today. Because it lacks the disease tolerance bred into newer types, gardeners often see best results with crop rotation and floating row cover early in the season. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: New York White Garlic (Heirloom Porcelain Hardneck)
aliases: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'New York White'
description: New York White is a long-preserved heirloom Porcelain hardneck strain maintained in northeastern American seed-saver collections for generations, valued for dependable bulb formation in cold Northeast winters and clean, glossy white wrappers. Bulbs typically produce 4-6 large cloves with a hot, pungent raw bite that sweetens dramatically when roasted or slow-cooked. As a true Porcelain type it needs a sustained cold period to vernalize properly, so gardeners in mild-winter climates should choose a different type. Grow it for its regional heirloom story and its reliability as an old New York homestead strain that has outlasted many modern hybrids. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: New Zealand Spinach
description: Sow direct after all danger of frost has passed in warm, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; soak seeds 12–24 hours in warm water before sowing to soften the hard seed coat and improve germination — thin to 18–24 inches apart. New Zealand spinach is the premier heat-tolerant, summer-substitute for true spinach, producing a sprawling, succulent-leaved groundcover of succulent, triangular, bright-green leaves with a mild, slightly salty flavor that can be harvested continuously by tip-pruning throughout summer and fall without bolting; it is ideal for the Gulf Coast and similar hot, humid climates where true spinach is impossible in summer. Despite the common name it is not closely related to spinach; it is in the family Aizoaceae. Frost-tender but can naturalize in zone 9–10 from self-seeding. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: New Zealand Tea Tree (Manuka)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; New Zealand tea tree is one of the most important plants of Maori tradition and modern apiculture — the intensely antibacterial nectar from manuka flowers produces the famous manuka honey, scientifically documented for its exceptional wound-healing and antibacterial properties. The leaves were used by Maori as a medicinal tea. In the garden, manuka is a handsome small to medium shrub covered in masses of small, open flowers — white in the species, pink to deep crimson in many cultivars — in late winter through spring. The tiny, heather-like aromatic leaves are evergreen. Many ornamental double-flowered cultivars are available ('Martini', 'Red Damask', 'Crimson Glory') that are showy but produce less nectar for bees. Full drainage is essential — root rot in wet soil is the primary cause of failure. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Newcastle Apricot (Ultra-Low-Chill Firm-Fleshed Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Newcastle needs under 300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any apricot cultivar in commerce, allowing it to set a reliable crop in mild-winter zone 8-9 regions where most apricots fail from insufficient winter chilling. Fruit is medium and firm-fleshed, good for fresh eating as well as canning and drying, ripening mid-to-early season. As with other very-low-chill apricots, its early bloom remains vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree tolerates the region's warm winters well. The tree is generally self-fruitful. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Newe Ya'ar No. 4 Sage (High-Oil Israeli Culinary Sage)
description: Set rooted cuttings or divisions into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, since excess moisture dilutes the oil concentration this clone was bred to maximize. Newe Ya'ar No. 4 is a selected culinary sage line developed by Israeli agricultural researchers specifically for consistently high essential-oil yield in commercial distillation and dried-herb production, rather than for ornamental leaf color or flower display. The gray-green leaves and habit closely resemble common culinary sage, but the plant is grown primarily where a dependable, laboratory-verified oil chemotype matters more than novelty. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage dense new growth and harvest leaves for drying just before bloom, when oil content peaks. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Newport Flowering Plum (Cold-Hardy Purple-Leaf Ornamental Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Newport is a compact, cold-hardy purple-leaf plum selection prized for foliage that emerges reddish-purple in spring and holds its color through the season better in cool climates than many purple-leaf plum cultivars, sometimes fading toward bronze-green in extreme summer heat. Single, light pink flowers open in very early spring before the leaves, on a smaller, rounder-headed tree than the species. Small, purplish-red fruit forms in summer and is technically edible, though the tree is grown almost exclusively as an ornamental. Newport's standout trait is cold hardiness — it tolerates winters into zone 4, making it one of the few purple-foliage flowering plums reliable in the Upper Midwest and Northeast, where less hardy purple-leaf cultivars are prone to dieback. Short-lived compared with many landscape trees (15-25 years) but fast-growing and dependably floriferous; prune to remove crossing or damaged branches after flowering. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Newtown Pippin Apple (Albemarle Pippin, Thomas Jefferson's Apple, First American Exported Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Newtown Pippin requires a cross-pollinator; the greenish-yellow to yellow fruit with some russet ripens very late (October–November) and benefits from 4–6 weeks of cold storage before eating, during which the flavor mellows, sweetens, and develops complex aromatic notes; an outstanding cider apple as well as a fresh eating variety. Newtown Pippin is one of the oldest American apple varieties in continuous cultivation, discovered as a chance seedling in the early 1700s in what was then the town of Newtown on Long Island, New York (now the neighborhood of Elmhurst in Queens), and is distinguished by a historical record rivaling any apple variety in the world. Benjamin Franklin shipped Newtown Pippin to England as early as the 1750s, where it was received with acclaim; it was later selected as the apple to be presented to Queen Victoria in the early 19th century — and became so popular in England that the British Parliament waived the apple import duty on American Newtown Pippins, the only American apple to receive such distinction. Thomas Jefferson planted Newtown Pippin at Monticello, where the variety is now called 'Albemarle Pippin' for its long association with Albemarle County, Virginia, and still grown in the restored Monticello orchard today. The fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to yellowish with russet patches, with crisp, dense, moderately tart, richly flavored flesh that becomes complex and aromatic after storage — nutty, slightly spicy, and quite unlike most commercial varieties. An important cider variety as well. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ney Poovan Banana (Honey Banana)
description: Ney Poovan is a diploid AB-genome dessert banana grown widely across India, prized for consistently high sweetness and a distinctive thin, sometimes lemon-yellow skin. It is one of the few edible banana groups to carry a wild Musa balbisiana contribution alongside acuminata parentage, giving it somewhat tougher foliage than pure AA or AAA dessert types. The plant grows tall and slender with a fairly long cycle to first bunch, so it rewards a full frost-free season, rich soil, and steady irrigation and feeding. It has no significant cold tolerance and should be treated as a warm-season specialty planting in zone 9 and sheltered from wind given its height. Matures in 305–455 days from transplant.

name: Niagara Grape (White Concord, Golden Grape, American White Table Grape)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun in well-drained soil; train to a 4-arm Kniffin system or similar; cane-prune in late winter; Niagara ripens 1–2 weeks before Concord in most regions (late August to early September); the berries are pale green to amber-gold at full ripeness, very juicy, with the classic musky Labrusca fragrance and flavor. Niagara is the second most important American Labrusca grape after Concord, developed in Lockport, New York in 1872 by C.L. Hoag and B.W. Clark as a cross of Concord and Cassady — two Labrusca-type grapes. Where Concord produces blue-black fruit with the iconic musky-sweet Concord flavor, Niagara produces pale green to golden-amber fruit with an equivalent but distinct flavor: the same Labrusca 'foxiness' but in a lighter, more delicate package that is closer to traditional white grape flavors when eaten fresh, yet unmistakably American in its musky, aromatic character. Niagara has been widely grown in the northeastern and midwestern states since its introduction and is the standard white-fruited companion to Concord in home vineyards across the grape belt of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, and similar regions. The grapes are seeded (like Concord) with the same slip-skin characteristic — the skin separates easily from the pulp — and produce excellent fresh-eating fruit, white grape juice (with a distinctive musky-sweet flavor that distinguishes American white juice from European-style products), and white jellies and preserves with a characteristic Labrusca fragrance. The vines are vigorous and highly cold-hardy, equivalent to Concord in frost resistance, and similarly require adequate chilling hours that limit their usefulness in zones 9+. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nichols Fig (Cold-Hardy Louisiana-Bred Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nichols is a fig selection developed in Louisiana and long grown across the Gulf South for its reliable production of medium-large, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber-pink flesh, along with good cold hardiness that lets it recover well after occasional hard freezes common at the northern edge of fig-growing country. Like other figs it fruits on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and needs minimal care once established beyond an annual mulch layer and light pruning to manage size. Established plants regrow readily from the base if winter cold kills back the top growth in an unusually harsh year. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nickajack Apple (Summerour, Big Hill, Wonder)
description: Plant in full sun with good air movement, since this large, vigorous tree was historically valued for its toughness and reliability rather than fussy care. Nickajack was one of the most widely planted apples in the antebellum and postbellum South, grown from the Appalachians to Texas for its large greenish-red fruit, dependable annual crops, and good keeping quality in a root cellar. Flavor is mildly subacid rather than showy, making it best suited to cooking, drying, and cider as well as fresh eating once fully ripe. Matures in 155–175 days from transplant.

name: Nickajack Bean
description: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom. Nickajack traces its name to a historic Cherokee community in the Tennessee River valley of the southern Appalachians, and it has been passed down among mountain gardeners as a reliable dual-purpose bean, with large, flat pods that can be picked young for snapping or left to mature into tan, speckled dry beans. Harvest at the snap stage for the tenderest eating, around 70 days, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a longer-season soup bean. The vines are productive and well adapted to the humid summers of the Southern Appalachians. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Nicoline Flowering Quince (Bright Scarlet Semi-Double Quince)
description: Nicoline is a densely branched flowering quince selection covered in vivid scarlet-red, cup-shaped flowers with a bright cluster of yellow stamens at the center, opening directly on the thorny bare stems from late winter into early spring. Its bushier, more upright growth than many of the low-spreading quince cultivars gives it good presence as a specimen or informal flowering hedge, and small, hard, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom in fall, usable for jelly and preserves. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and quite drought-tolerant, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Night Shadow Eggplant (Reliable Classic Black-Skinned Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Night Shadow is a hybrid eggplant bred for reliable, sustained production of classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, vigorous plant that tolerates the heat of a Gulf South summer well. It is listed among Cornell University's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant selections, giving it an edge in the humid, disease-prone conditions common across the Southeast. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull, hard fruit signals it has gone past peak quality and developed more seeds and bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist and pick regularly to encourage the plant to keep setting new fruit through the season. Matures in 62–72 days from transplant.

name: Nightfall Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Processing Cultivar)
description: Nightfall is a thornless, trailing blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University alongside two sibling releases, 'Black Diamond' and 'Black Pearl', as part of an effort to give growers machine-harvestable, thornless alternatives to the thorny industry-standard 'Marion'. Like its siblings it produces firm, dark fruit suited to both fresh use and commercial processing. The long trailing canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous spacing to manage their sprawling growth, so fan-train fruiting canes along the wires each season. Remove spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest and tie in the new primocanes, and give the planting full sun with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure in humid climates. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Niitaka Asian Pear
description: Niitaka is a Japanese-bred nashi pear noted for producing some of the largest fruit of any commonly grown Asian pear cultivar, often exceeding a pound once thinned to one fruit per spur cluster. The round fruit carries a warm brown russeted skin over crisp, very juicy flesh with a mild, sweet flavor and none of the graininess of unripe European pears. Trees ripen fruit in September and, unlike European pears, the fruit should be picked when fully colored since it will not continue to ripen or improve once removed from the tree. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nijisseiki Asian Pear (20th Century Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires cross-pollination with another compatible Asian pear. Nijisseiki (20th Century, in Japanese literally 'twentieth century') is perhaps the most historically significant Asian pear cultivar, discovered as a chance seedling in Matsudo, Chiba Prefecture, Japan in 1888 by Chuhei Matsudo and eventually named for the approaching new century; for most of the 20th century it was Japan's most widely grown pear and still accounts for significant commercial production. The fruits are large (8–12 oz), perfectly round, smooth-skinned, pale yellow-green, and juicy with a mild, refreshing, lightly sweet flavor and crisp, white flesh. Reasonably low chill requirement (approximately 400–500 hours) makes it viable in California, Gulf Coast, and mild Southern gardens. Ripens in August; stores well for 2–4 months refrigerated. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nikita White Mulberry
description: Nikita is a self-fertile white mulberry selection notable for ripening earlier than most other white-fruited cultivars, giving Gulf Coast gardeners an earlier start to the mulberry harvest. It stays naturally smaller and more compact than typical seedling mulberry trees, which makes it a better fit for home landscapes with limited space. Fruit is large, juicy, and very sweet, and the tree shows good resistance to pests along with solid drought tolerance once established. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect fruiting to begin at a young age with minimal care required beyond occasional pruning. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nikita's Gift Persimmon (American-Asian Hybrid Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Nikita's Gift is notably drought-tolerant when established and thrives without supplemental fertilization in most soils — avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that encourage excessive vegetative growth. Nikita's Gift was hybridized at the Nikita Botanical Garden (Nikitsky Botanic Garden) in Yalta, Crimea, Ukraine by crossing the cold-hardy American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) with the large-fruited Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki); the goal was to produce a persimmon with fruit size, quality, and non-astringency approaching the Japanese cultivars while withstanding the much harsher winters of continental and cold-temperate climates where standard Asian persimmons die back or fail to fruit. The result is a very cold-hardy tree (to approximately -25°F when fully dormant) producing large (6–12 oz) fruits with reddish-orange to brick-red skin resembling the appearance of Asian varieties; the fruits are astringent when unripe but become non-astringent and sweet after frost or artificial treatment (the PVNA type characteristic of some Asian varieties). The flavor of fully ripe Nikita's Gift is rich, sweet, and honeyed — superior to American persimmon and comparable to the finest Japanese types. Self-fruitful; produces best without a pollinator. One of the most important persimmon introductions for cold-climate gardeners. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Nikitskaya Bordovaya Hybrid Persimmon (Self-Fertile Crimean Custard-Flavored Persimmon)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nikitskaya Bordovaya is a Crimean-bred hybrid persimmon, crossing Asian kaki persimmon back onto the American species (in the lineage of the well-known Rosseyanka), combining the American parent's cold hardiness and vigor with fruit quality closer to Asian persimmon: large, deep red-orange fruit with a rich, custard-smooth texture and a distinctive honeyed, peach-like flavor once fully soft-ripe. It is self-fertile, setting a reliable crop without a second tree nearby, though yields can improve with a pollinator present, and it shows good adaptability across a wide hardiness range, performing well in both the humid Gulf South and considerably colder climates. Fruit ripens in October and, like other hybrid and American persimmons, should be allowed to soften fully before eating to avoid astringency. An easy, low-input tree once established, tolerating heat, drought, and a range of soils. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nikitski Ranni Pomegranate (Crimean Cold-Hardy Early Pomegranate)
description: Nikitski Ranni traces its breeding to Crimea's Nikita Botanical Garden, drawing on Azerbaijani parent material to combine unusually strong cold hardiness with early ripening; established plants are reported to tolerate temperatures well below what most pomegranate cultivars survive. Fruit is large, up to about six inches across, with light pink skin and red arils balancing sweet and tart flavors, ripening in September–October with good resistance to rind cracking. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; its cold tolerance makes it useful insurance for gardeners at the colder edge of pomegranate range or in years with an unexpected hard freeze. It is carried by several Southeastern specialty fruit-tree nurseries as a reliable choice for an early, crack-resistant harvest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nine Star Perennial Broccoli
description: Transplant to deeply dug, richly amended soil in full sun; nine star is a remarkable perennial broccoli variety that sends up multiple small white or pale yellow broccoli-like heads in early spring, year after year, for up to 4–5 years from a single planting. The key to maintaining the perennial habit is to harvest all the heads before any can flower and set seed — once a plant is allowed to flower, it may cease to perennial and become biennial. The heads are smaller than commercial broccoli (tennis ball-sized) but very numerous on established plants, and the flavor is excellent. After harvesting the heads, the plant sends up side shoots producing cut-and-come-again broccoli for weeks. Feed heavily after harvest to support the following year's growth. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Nipa Palm
description: Plant Nypa fruticans propagules (the large, floating seeds germinate readily and can be pressed into waterlogged soil) in tidal freshwater to slightly brackish mudflats or pond margins with permanently saturated soil in full sun; the rhizome spreads horizontally underground and produces new upright frond clusters periodically; plants tolerate some saltwater intrusion but grow best in low-salinity or freshwater tidal conditions. Nipa Palm is one of the most ancient and ecologically important palms in the world — with a fossil record extending back 70 million years to the Cretaceous period — and is the only member of the subfamily Nypoideae, making it botanically unique among all living palms. Unlike all other palms, Nypa is essentially stemless: its massive, horizontal trunk lies underground or just at the water surface, sending up large, pinnate fronds 10–15 feet tall directly from the horizontal stem. The spherical, rugose fruit clusters yield young, jelly-like endosperm (kaong or palm toddy in the Philippines) eaten fresh or preserved in syrup; the developing floral stalks are tapped for sap (up to 8 liters/day) fermented into palm wine (tuba) or boiled to make palm sugar (gula atap). Millions of acres of Nipa stands form critical tidal mangrove habitat across Southeast Asia, storing substantial carbon and protecting coastlines from erosion.
