Cultivation outside its natural range requires a very wet, frost-free environment. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Nipplewort
description: Scatter seeds shallowly on the soil surface or cover with no more than 1/8 inch of soil in a partially shaded spot in early spring; nipplewort is one of the few edible annuals that performs well in the shade of hedges or woodland edges. Thin or transplant seedlings to 6-12 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist through cool weather. Harvest the young, tender basal leaves and shoot tips before the plant bolts, cooking them briefly like spinach to reduce their mild bitterness. Allow a few plants to self-seed at the end of the season; nipplewort will reliably return each year with no further effort. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Nippon Orangequat (Thornless Kumquat-Mandarin Hybrid)
description: Nippon orangequat produces small, sweet, deep-orange fruit with an edible peel, eaten whole like a kumquat but with a milder, more orange-like flavor than Nagami or Meiwa. The tree is notably thornless even when young, making it pleasant to work around and harvest, and it holds fruit attractively through winter. It shares the cold hardiness typical of kumquat-derived hybrids, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established. Grow it as a specimen or large container plant, feeding with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and providing winter protection north of zone 8b. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nishimura Wase Persimmon (Early-Ripening Japanese Astringent Persimmon)
description: Nishimura Wase is a Japanese astringent persimmon whose main distinction from cultivars like Hachiya and Tanenashi is timing: it colors and ripens several weeks earlier in the season, extending the harvest window into late summer in warm climates. The medium-large, acorn-shaped fruit has deep orange-red skin and, like other astringent types, must be allowed to fully soften on the counter or after a hard freeze before the tannins mellow into a sweet, rich flavor. It is grown alongside later-ripening cultivars in California's Central Valley to spread out the persimmon harvest season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nkruma Tenten Okra (Ghanaian Tree Okra)
description: Known in Ghana as tall okra, this West African heirloom can tower 8 to 12 feet given a long enough hot season, making it one of the largest okras a gardener can grow. Red-tinged stems and huge, tender leaves top a slow-starting plant that, once established, produces thick-walled, deep green pods often tinged with red continuously until frost. Beyond the pods, its large leaves are traditionally cooked like a mucilaginous spinach among cooks in West Africa. In frost-free tropical climates it behaves as a short-lived woody perennial for years, but in a zone 9a garden it is best grown as a single tall-season annual with plenty of room to spread. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: No Mai Tsze Lychee (Glutinous Rice Lychee)
description: Widely regarded by connoisseurs as the finest-tasting of all lychee cultivars, No Mai Tsze produces intensely crisp, super-sweet flesh around an unusually minute seed, leaving nearly the whole fruit edible. Fruit runs smaller than Brewster or Sweetheart, and the tree's irregular growth habit and inconsistent fruit set outside ideal climates have kept it a rare specialty planting rather than a commercial mainstay. It rewards patient growers willing to trade reliability for exceptional flavor over cultivars bred for consistent yield. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Noble Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Noble is a black-skinned muscadine released by North Carolina State University in 1971 and named for James Noble, an early muscadine researcher. It is the standard against which black muscadine wine varieties are measured: the deep purple-black berries are extraordinarily high in anthocyanins, resveratrol, and other polyphenols that give muscadine wine and juice its distinctive deep color and purported health benefits. Flavor is rich, musky, and complex — more intensely flavored than bronze varieties — producing deep-colored wine, juice, and jelly with earthy, berry notes. Fresh-eating quality is good but not as mild as bronze types; the thick skin and seeds are more pronounced. Noble is self-fertile and produces consistently high yields even as a single vine. Its exceptional disease resistance and adaptability make it one of the best black muscadines for the humid Gulf South. Harvest when berries are fully black and yield easily to gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Noble Muscadine Grape (Large Dark-Purple Self-Fertile Gulf South Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Noble is one of the most widely planted and highly regarded purple muscadine grape cultivars for Gulf South home gardens and small vineyards — a vigorous, productive vine producing large (1–1.5 inch), round, deep purple-black to dark purple grapes with thick, slightly tough skin and sweet, musky, richly flavored flesh that is the definition of classic muscadine flavor. Muscadine grapes (Muscadinia rotundifolia) are the grape of the American Southeast — a separate species from European and California wine grapes, native to the coastal plain from Florida to Virginia, and extraordinarily well-adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Gulf South summers that devastate Vitis vinifera varieties. Noble bears perfect (hermaphroditic) flowers and is self-fertile, a major advantage over the older cultivars that required a male or bisexual pollinator; it is also an excellent pollinator for female-flowered cultivars like Fry and Higgins. The large grape clusters ripen in August–September and are harvested individually as grapes ripen separately within each cluster — a distinctive feature of muscadine harvesting. Noble is used for fresh eating, juice, jelly, wine, and vinegar. The thick skin and seeds are the main characteristics distinguishing muscadine from table grapes — some people find them unpleasant, while others consider them inseparable from the authentic flavor experience. Noble wine produces a characteristically sweet, richly flavored muscadine wine very different from European wine styles. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nocellara del Belice Olive (Sicilian Table Olive, Castelvetrano-Style)
description: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Nocellara del Belice comes from the Belice Valley of western Sicily and is the source of the large, bright green, mild, buttery table olives sold in North America as 'Castelvetrano-style' olives, prized for a sweet, almost fruity flavor with none of the sharp bitterness of many other green table olives. While excellent for eating fresh-cured, the variety also produces good quality olive oil, giving growers dual-purpose flexibility from a single tree. The tree is a strong, dependable producer well adapted to Mediterranean-climate growing conditions; harvest for table use while still green and firm, and allow appropriate curing time, since fresh olives straight off any tree are intensely bitter and inedible without curing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Nodding Onion
description: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; nodding onion is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates poor, dry, rocky soils where most alliums would struggle. Allium cernuum is a native wildflower of dry prairies, rocky slopes, and open woodlands across much of North America, named for its distinctive drooping, nodding flowerhead — the flower stalk curves or bends at the top so the umbel of small, pink to white, bell-shaped flowers faces downward in a charming, pendant cluster in mid-summer. All parts are edible with a mild onion flavor, and the plant was an important food source for many Native American peoples; it is also an excellent pollinator plant, attracting native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. Outstanding in rock gardens, dry meadows, and native prairie restorations; it self-seeds freely without being invasive. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Noga Basil
description: Noga basil balances heavy yields with classic Genovese flavor, producing tall, uniform plants that grow fast and stand up to repeated cutting. Its large, glossy, dark green leaves perform well in the field, greenhouse, or a patio container. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil has warmed thoroughly. Provide full sun, steady moisture, and frequent harvests, pinching out flower buds to keep leaf production high. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Noir de Bourgogne Black Currant (Classic French Heirloom Black Currant)
description: Noir de Bourgogne is the historic black currant of Burgundy, France, long prized as the traditional base for cassis liqueur and still regarded by many growers as the benchmark for rich, aromatic black currant flavor. It is an early-season cultivar that carries long strigs of large, intensely flavored black berries with a distinctive musky-resinous aroma, and it is self-fertile though yields improve with a second cultivar nearby. Noir de Bourgogne is quite susceptible to powdery mildew and needs a substantial number of winter chill hours to flower and fruit well, so it is a poor match for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens and is better reserved for cold-winter regions. Where it is well adapted, prune out about a third of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous, high-yielding young wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Noir de Spain Mulberry (Noir of Spain Black Mulberry)
description: Noir de Spain is a long-cultivated black mulberry selection prized among fruit collectors for an unusually complex, aromatic flavor that balances sugar and acid more evenly than most other mulberries, with fruit that ripens to a deep red-black rather than the jet black of some other Morus nigra selections. Established trees typically don't bear a full crop until two to three years after planting but then settle into consistent annual production. Because rooted cuttings of true black mulberry are notoriously slow and unreliable, plants sold under this name are almost always grafted, so buy grafted nursery stock rather than attempting to propagate from cuttings at home. Give the tree full sun and consistent moisture through fruit ripening in midsummer, and expect heavy bird interest once fruit begins to color. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Noir des Carmes Cucumber (Heirloom Black-Spined French Cucumber)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Documented in French seed catalogs since the mid-1800s, Noir des Carmes produces short, chunky, dark-green fruit that ripens quickly and is covered in distinctive black spines when young, an old-world trait bred out of most modern cucumbers. It is one of the fastest-maturing open-pollinated cucumbers available, ready in under two months from sowing, making it a good choice for short-season succession planting through the summer. Pick fruit small and young for the sweetest, least bitter flavor, and harvest frequently to keep vines productive. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Noir des Carmes Melon (Black Rock Melon)
description: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in warm, enriched, well-drained soil; Noir des Carmes performs best with reduced watering as the fruits approach maturity — drying out slightly at the end concentrates the sugars and perfume. Noir des Carmes (Black of the Carmelites, named for the dark-robed Carmelite friars who reportedly cultivated it) is a French heirloom muskmelon first listed in catalogs in 1883 and described by Vilmorin-Andrieux in their famous 1885 The Vegetable Garden; the young fruits are dark green to nearly black (the 'noir'), ripening to orange-yellow at maturity with a pronounced perfume. Inside, the flesh is deep orange, very sweet, and extraordinarily fragrant in the way characteristic of the finest Charentais-type melons of Poitou-Charentes. One of the earliest European muskmelons (70–80 days from seed), making it suitable for shorter seasons. Somewhat rare but increasingly available from specialty seed companies. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Noire de Caromb Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Noire de Caromb is a French dark-skinned fig from the Caromb commune in Vaucluse, Provence — part of the rich fig heritage of Provence where the warm, dry Mediterranean climate has sustained diverse fig cultivation for millennia. The medium-sized, round to slightly flattened fruits have very dark purple to nearly black skin and deep red-to-garnet flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet flavor with pronounced winey depth that characterizes the best Provençal dark figs. Noire de Caromb is considered one of the finest-flavored dark-skinned fig varieties by European fig enthusiasts, though it remains less well-known in North American markets than brown Turkey or Celeste. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast heat produces fig flavor of excellent quality, and Noire de Caromb performs well in the long, warm growing season. Its primary advantage over more common dark-skinned figs is the depth and complexity of flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Noiret Grape (Cornell-Bred Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)
description: Released by Cornell's breeding program in 2006 from complex hybrid parentage including Steuben and Chancellor, this variety produces small dark-skinned berries that yield a deeply colored, peppery red wine with good tannin structure for a hybrid. It buds late, which helps it dodge spring frost damage, and shows strong resistance to fungal diseases common in humid eastern vineyards. Vines are vigorous and benefit from shoot thinning early in the season to manage canopy density and improve fruit ripening. It ranks among the more cold-hardy options for growers wanting a serious hybrid red rather than a juice or fresh-eating grape. Matures in 150–165 days from transplant.

name: Non-Tough Half Runner Bean
description: Non-Tough Half Runner is a preserved Appalachian bean selected and maintained by Dr. Bill Best of the Sustainable Mountain Agriculture Center after decades of commercial half-runner seed losing the tenderness that once made the type popular, as seed producers had inadvertently bred in a toughening trait to extend shelf life. Its plump pods stay tender-eating even when the seeds inside swell to full size, which sets it apart from most modern half-runners that toughen quickly, and it remains a favorite for traditional leather-britches drying as well as fresh snap use, canning, and freezing. The half-runner growth habit sends out short runners beyond a bush frame, so light support or brush keeps pods off the ground and easy to pick. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Noni
description: Plant in well-drained sandy, rocky, or infertile soil — including saline and coastal soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; noni (Morinda citrifolia) is a small, fast-growing evergreen tree in the Rubiaceae family native to Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands that has been one of the most important plants in Pacific Islander traditional medicine for over 2,000 years, with virtually every part of the plant — fruit, leaves, bark, seeds, and roots — used in traditional preparations throughout Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. The distinctive, lumpy, pale greenish-white to translucent fruits have an extremely pungent, cheese-like odor when ripe that makes them challenging to consume fresh, yet the juice has become a globally marketed health supplement product worth billions of dollars annually, prized for antioxidant compounds including iridoids, scopoletin, and various polysaccharides. Trees produce fruit year-round in frost-free tropical conditions, bear their first crop remarkably quickly — within 1–2 years of transplanting — and are exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, requiring irrigation only during establishment. Noni is one of the most salt- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it well suited to coastal planting in South Florida and the Gulf Coast. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nonpareil Almond (California Commercial Standard Almond, The World's Almond)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Nonpareil requires two cross-pollinating companion varieties for fruit set; irrigate deeply but infrequently once established; harvest in late July to August when hulls split open naturally; shake trees to dislodge nuts and allow to dry on tarps for 1–2 days before hulling and drying. Nonpareil is the most widely planted almond variety in the world and the variety that defines the global almond market — approximately 40–50% of California's almond production, which itself supplies roughly 80% of the world's almonds, comes from Nonpareil trees, making it the single most economically important tree nut variety on earth. The variety was selected in California in the 1870s by A.T. Hatch and propagated by Sexton & Lewelling Nurseries of San Leandro, California, quickly becoming the commercial standard because of its combination of easily-shelled, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (around 62–65%), excellent kernel quality (smooth, flat shape ideal for processing and sliced almonds), and early ripening that opens the harvest season before other varieties. Nonpareil kernels set the price benchmark in global almond markets — the Nonpareil grade commands the highest premiums for direct consumption, whole roasted almonds, and retail packaging because of the variety's consistent appearance, mild sweet flavor, and thin, papery shell. The variety is not self-fertile and requires two companion varieties with overlapping bloom times for reliable nut set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nootka Rose Garlic (Rocambole Hardneck with Rich Flavor)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Nootka Rose is a rocambole-type hardneck garlic prized for rich, full-bodied flavor and attractive bulbs wrapped in rose-tan skin over large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. Its rich flavor comes with the tradeoff of shorter storage life typical of rocamboles, generally four to five months, so plan to use it earlier in the storage season relative to porcelain or softneck types. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Nootka Rose Softneck Garlic
description: This widely adapted softneck heirloom from the San Juan Islands stays productive from wet to arid and cool to hot climates, forming bulbs with 12 to 20 cloves. Plant cloves in fall, mulch, and let them overwinter for a summer harvest. Softneck types store especially well and can be braided. Harvest when the lower leaves yellow, then cure in a shaded, airy place before storing. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Nopales (Edible Prickly Pear)
description: Allow a pad cutting to callus (dry) for one week before planting in sandy or rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; overwatering is the most common cause of failure. Young pads (nopales) are harvested when 6–8 inches long and still tender, using tongs and a sharp knife to remove glochids (small barbed spines) by scraping before cooking. The pads are eaten grilled, in tacos, scrambled with eggs, or in soups, with a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture. The pear-shaped red or yellow fruits (tunas) that ripen in late summer are sweet and edible; wear thick gloves when harvesting as glochids penetrate skin on contact. Established plants are extremely drought and heat tolerant and require virtually no care. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Nora Pepper (Dried Spanish Sweet Pepper for Romesco)
description: Nora is a small, round, thick-fleshed sweet pepper grown mainly in Murcia and Valencia in eastern Spain, where the deep red, fully ripe fruit is sun-dried whole rather than ground into powder, giving it a distinctively wrinkled, tomato-like appearance in the kitchen. Its heat is negligible, well under 1,000 Scoville units, so its value lies entirely in a sweet, earthy, almost raisin-like dried flavor that develops through slow drying and forms the flavor backbone of romesco sauce, arroz negro, and many Murcian and Valencian braises and rice dishes. Fruit should be harvested only after turning fully red and slightly soft, then air-dried or dehydrated over several weeks until the skin is leathery and the pepper rattles faintly with loose seeds, similar in method to the Mexican cascabel. Because Nora needs a long season to reach full red ripeness, gardeners outside mild climates should start plants early and grow them in the warmest, sunniest spot available. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Nordic Raspberry (Extremely Cold-Hardy Minnesota Fall-Bearing Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun. Nordic was bred at the University of Minnesota specifically for extreme cold hardiness, giving it a genuine advantage in the harshest northern growing regions where many other raspberry varieties suffer significant winter cane damage or fail outright. As a fall-bearing (primocane) type producing fruit on the current season's new canes, it can be cut entirely to the ground each winter, a simple, low-maintenance pruning approach well suited to gardeners in cold climates who want a reliable, straightforward raspberry crop without fussing over selective cane pruning. The compact, sturdy canes produce good yields of flavorful red berries from late summer into fall, right up until hard frost ends the season. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nordmann Seedless Kumquat (Seedless Nagami-Type Kumquat)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil, as this compact selection stays smaller and denser than standard Nagami kumquat. Water deeply during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat. Nordmann bears an abundance of small, oval, orange fruit with sweet edible skin and tart flesh, and unlike standard Nagami it produces few to no seeds, making it easier to eat out of hand. It is among the more cold-hardy true citrus types, tolerating brief drops into the upper teens F once mature, and is popular for Gulf Coast and lower Southeast gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Norris Che (Seedless Female Mandarin Melon Berry)
description: Norris was discovered growing near Norris Dam in Tennessee and, like 'Darrow', is a female che selection that sets a heavy, fully seedless crop without needing a male pollinator nearby. The maroon-red, bumpy-skinned fruits run one to two inches across and ripen to a sweet flavor often likened to a fig with a hint of watermelon. Grow it as you would 'Darrow': full sun, unfussy well-drained soil, and room for a thorny-when-young large shrub or small tree that responds well to formative pruning for easier harvest. Planting Norris alongside 'Darrow' or a male che is unnecessary for fruiting but can extend the ripening season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: North and South Okra (Sand Mountain Alabama Heirloom Okra)
description: North and South is a Southern heirloom okra preserved by gardening families on Sand Mountain in northeast Alabama, grown for slim, ridged green pods that stay tender well past the size most okra turns woody. Direct sow after the soil is reliably warm, since okra seedlings are slow to establish in cool soil, and thin plants to give them room to branch. The tall, productive plants keep setting pods over a long summer season if picked every day or two at 3-4 inches. As an open-pollinated heirloom it is easy to save seed from, helping keep a piece of Alabama foodways history in circulation. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: North Georgia Candy Roaster (Southern Appalachian Cherokee Heritage Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns salmon-pink and develops waxy bloom. North Georgia Candy Roaster is one of the most historically significant Appalachian heirloom vegetable varieties — a large winter squash that has been grown in the mountain regions of North Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and adjacent Appalachian areas for centuries, with the variety associated with Cherokee and Scots-Irish Appalachian agricultural traditions of the southern mountain region. The 'candy roaster' name is shared by several closely related Appalachian squash varieties that differ somewhat in size, color, and shape but all share the characteristic of extraordinary sweetness when roasted — the candy-like sweetness that develops when the dense, high-starch flesh is slowly baked or roasted until caramelized. The specific 'North Georgia' designation distinguishes this variety from the similar but distinct 'Tennessee Candy Roaster,' 'Big Orange Candy Roaster,' and other regionally-named selections, with the North Georgia type typically producing cylindrical to elongated fruits with characteristic salmon-pink to apricot skin. The squash can reach enormous sizes: typical fruits are 15–20 lbs, and exceptional specimens exceed 30 lbs, making this one of the largest winter squash varieties in heirloom cultivation. The flesh — thick, dense, bright orange-yellow — is exceptional in nutritional value (very high beta-carotene) and flavor, with a sweetness and complexity that rewards the long growing season required. The variety has been maintained by Appalachian farming families and seed-saving organizations including the Seed Savers Exchange as an important cultural heritage variety of the southeastern mountain region. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: North Pole Columnar Apple (Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; North Pole is one of the original Ballerina-series columnar apples bred in England, growing as a single narrow, upright trunk studded directly with short fruiting spurs rather than spreading lateral branches — a genetic dwarfing trait, not just a pruning technique, that lets a full-sized apple crop grow in a space barely wider than a fence post. This makes it an excellent choice for a large container, a narrow side-yard bed, or planted in a tight row as a productive, space-efficient hedge or espalier substitute. Fruit is medium-sized, red-skinned, crisp, and sweet-tart, ripening in early fall. Because columnar apples still need a genetically compatible pollinator, plant North Pole with another columnar or standard apple cultivar blooming at the same time within about 20–50 feet. Little to no pruning is needed beyond removing the occasional stray side shoot, though very light annual thinning of overcrowded spurs can improve fruit size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: North Pole Lettuce (Cold-Hardy Overwintering Butterhead)
description: Sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quick spring harvest; North Pole thrives in cold, short-day conditions and largely stops growing once winter cold sets in, then resumes as days lengthen. Small, unprotected plants can survive temperatures well below freezing, and with the light protection of a cold frame or row cover it reliably carries a crop of compact, buttery, lime-green heads through winter in cold climates. It resents summer heat and bolts quickly if grown in warm conditions, so it is best reserved for the coldest part of the lettuce calendar. Harvest whole heads once they feel dense, or pick individual leaves through the winter for a slower, extended harvest. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: North Star Cherry (Dwarf Sour Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; North Star is a naturally dwarf tart cherry developed at the University of Minnesota that reaches only 8–12 feet tall — significantly smaller than standard sour cherry trees — making it manageable for home gardens and usable on semi-dwarfing rootstocks for even smaller trees. The fruit is tart, dark-red, with a short stem that makes hand harvesting easier than Montmorency. It is self-fertile, needing no pollinizer, and is exceptional for its hardiness — surviving zone 3 winters reliably. Like all tart cherries, North Star fruit is used primarily for pies, jams, juices, and preserves rather than fresh eating, but the intense cherry flavor is prized in those applications. Trees bear heavily and begin producing within 2–3 years of planting. North Star is more disease-resistant than sweet cherries, requiring less intensive management. An excellent choice for the northern home orchard where sweet cherries may be unreliable. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northblue Blueberry (Half-High Cold-Hardy Highbush Blueberry, Northern Half-High)
description: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.2) with excellent drainage; mulch with pine bark 3–4 inches deep to protect roots and maintain moisture; fertilize with acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) in spring; Northblue ripens mid-season (July in Minnesota and Wisconsin) producing large, dark blue berries with excellent highbush flavor — larger and better-flavored than lowbush but hardier than standard highbush. Northblue blueberry is one of the University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry varieties that transformed blueberry growing in zones 3–5 of the upper Midwest, making reliable blueberry production possible in climates where standard highbush varieties (which are typically hardy only to about -20°F with snow cover) suffered severe dieback or winter-killed entirely. The half-high blueberries were developed by crossing standard highbush Vaccinium corymbosum (for berry size and quality) with the ultra-cold-hardy native lowbush blueberry Vaccinium angustifolium (for hardiness) — and Northblue represents one of the earliest and most successful results of this breeding work. Northblue plants grow 2–3 feet tall — intermediate between lowbush (6–18 inches) and highbush (4–6 feet) — and produce large, dark blue berries with a distinctly better flavor and larger size than wild lowbush berries, closer to highbush quality. The combination of cold-hardiness to -35°F (with some snow cover and mulching), compact size, and genuinely good fruit quality (not just acceptable — actually good by highbush standards) makes Northblue one of the most important blueberry varieties for cold-climate gardeners. Cross-pollination with another half-high variety (Northcountry, Northsky, Polaris) is required for best fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northcountry Blueberry (Half-High Minnesota Cold-Hardy Blueberry, Twin Cities Blueberry)
description: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.2); mulch heavily; fertilize lightly with ammonium sulfate; Northcountry ripens slightly earlier than Northblue (late June to early July in Minnesota), making it valuable for extending the blueberry season from the beginning; berries are medium-sized, sky-blue, with a mild but pleasant flavor and good sweetness; the plants have attractive red-orange fall color. Northcountry blueberry is a companion half-high variety to Northblue from the same University of Minnesota breeding program, released together as a pair that complements Northblue's mid-season ripening with an earlier season (typically ripening 1–2 weeks before Northblue). The pairing of Northcountry (early) with Northblue (mid) or Northsky (late) is the standard recommendation from University of Minnesota Extension for home blueberry plantings in zones 3–5, providing a 3–4 week fresh blueberry season from one combined planting. The cross-pollination between these varieties also improves fruit set on both plants. Northcountry plants grow slightly more compact than Northblue (typically 24–36 inches rather than 36–48 inches), with a dense, mounded habit that makes them particularly attractive as landscape shrubs in addition to their edible fruit value. The berries are medium-sized (slightly smaller than Northblue), sky-blue in color, with a good sweet-mild flavor and good shelf life for a half-high variety. The extreme cold-hardiness — tested to -30°F with snow cover — and early ripening season make Northcountry one of the most important blueberry varieties for northern Minnesota, North Dakota, and other severe cold-climate gardening situations. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northern Bayberry
description: Sow seeds in fall after rubbing away the waxy seed coating, or provide a 60–90 day cold stratification period before spring sowing; northern bayberry grows naturally in coastal dunes, sandy thickets, and open woods from Newfoundland to North Carolina and thrives in lean, acidic, sandy or loamy soils with excellent drainage. This nitrogen-fixing native is highly tolerant of salt spray, wind, and drought, making it an exceptional choice for coastal landscapes and difficult sites where more refined shrubs fail. The aromatic, blue-gray waxy berries cluster tightly along the branches and persist into winter, historically rendered for bayberry candles; in the garden they provide excellent winter interest and food for birds such as yellow-rumped warblers. Northern bayberry spreads slowly by root suckers to form naturalistic colonies and requires both male and female plants for berry production. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Northern Bedstraw (White Bedstraw)
description: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; northern bedstraw is an attractive native perennial of prairies, open rocky meadows, and woodland edges across northern North America and Eurasia, producing whorled leaves in groups of four and dense clusters of tiny, bright white, fragrant flowers in early to midsummer — among the most floriferous of the native Galium species. Unlike the scrambling, sticky-stemmed cleavers (G. aparine), northern bedstraw is upright and well-mannered, forming attractive clumps that spread slowly by rhizomes. The dried plant was historically used to stuff mattresses (giving the genus its common name 'bedstraw'), and the seeds can be roasted as a coffee substitute — the genus Galium is closely related to coffee (Coffea). The small white flowers are heavily visited by small native bees, flower flies, and beneficial wasps. A good, underused native for dry to average, rocky meadow gardens. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Northern Blueberry (Alpine Blueberry)
description: Plant container-grown divisions in early spring into acidic, sandy to peaty, well-drained soil in full sun; northern blueberry is a diminutive, mat-forming species native to windswept alpine barrens, coastal headlands, and subarctic tundra of northern New England, the Maritimes, and eastern Canada, where it hugs the ground to survive harsh, exposed conditions. Its small, sweet, powder-blue berries ripen in mid to late summer on a plant rarely taller than knee height, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a low, dense groundcover on lean, acidic soil. Because it is adapted to a short, cool growing season and needs sustained winter cold to perform well, it is a specialty planting for far-northern or high-elevation gardens rather than a general-purpose landscape blueberry, and it will not thrive in hot, humid summer climates. Grow it as a rock-garden or barrens-style planting in sharply drained, lean, acidic soil, and avoid rich garden loam or added fertilizer, which favor weeds over this slow-growing native. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northern Brewer Hops
description: A reliable dual-purpose hop with woodsy, minty-resinous character, popular for California common (steam) beer, brown ales, and smoked beers. It is notably vigorous and more tolerant of cool, damp climates and less-than-ideal soil than many aroma cultivars, making it a forgiving choice for first-time hop growers. Give it a sturdy 15-20 foot support since mature bines produce heavy cone loads. Side-dress with compost each spring and watch for aphids, which this variety attracts more than most. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Northern California Black Walnut (Hinds Walnut)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in deep, well-drained soil with a full sun exposure and ample room for a broad, spreading canopy. This California native walnut tolerates heavier soils, summer heat, and some drought better than English walnut, and was historically the dominant rootstock onto which commercial English walnut orchards in California were grafted. Left ungrafted, it produces a heavy crop of small, thick-shelled, strongly flavored nuts that are more work to crack than commercial walnuts but valued for wildlife forage and rootstock breeding. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Northern Dewberry
description: Northern Dewberry is a low-trailing native of dry, open, sandy or rocky ground and thin-soiled barrens throughout eastern North America, distinguished from upright blackberries by its prostrate, creeping canes that root at the tips to form low, dense, ground-covering mats. Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring into dry, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart; individual canes will trail and root freely to expand coverage over a wide area. White flowers appear in spring and ripen into sweet, black, aggregate drupes in late May to June, making Northern Dewberry one of the earliest-fruiting native brambles and a critical early-summer food source for bluebirds, mockingbirds, towhees, and box turtles. This species excels in sandy, infertile, full-sun sites where taller brambles and most garden fruits cannot survive, making it a uniquely useful edible ground cover for difficult dry spots. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Northern Spicebush
description: Plant in moist, average to rich soil in partial to full shade; northern spicebush is one of the few large shrubs truly native to the forest understory, making it invaluable for shaded landscapes. The tiny yellow flowers in early spring appear before the leaves and provide early nectar for native bees; the brilliantly yellow fall foliage is outstanding. Bright red, oil-rich berries on female plants in fall are devoured by migratory thrushes and are the primary larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail butterfly. The dried berries are edible with a complex allspice-bay-pepper flavor once used as a colonial-era spice — they can replace allspice in recipes. All parts are intensely aromatic when crushed. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northern Spy Apple (Classic New York Pie Apple, Late-Season Northeastern Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pair with McIntosh, Cortland, or Empire for cross-pollination; thin fruits in June for maximum size; Northern Spy ripens October–November — later than almost all other apple varieties — producing very large, greenish-yellow to red-striped fruits with exceptional crispness, complex sweet-tart flavor, and outstanding keeping quality. Northern Spy apple was discovered as a chance seedling in East Bloomfield (Ontario County), New York around 1800, taking its unusual name from political associations of the era; it was introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s and rapidly became one of the most important commercial and home orchard apples of the northeastern United States and Canada. The variety has characteristics that make it consistently beloved by serious apple enthusiasts: very large size (sometimes exceeding one pound per fruit), exceptional crispness and juiciness, a complex, rich sweet-tart flavor with floral notes that compares favorably with any modern variety, and excellent keeping quality (fruits store 3–5 months under proper conditions). Northern Spy is the definitive pie apple of the northeast American tradition — the variety that old-time New England and New York pie recipes specify by name — because its firm flesh holds structure through baking and its tart, complex flavor creates an extraordinary pie filling. The trees are notably long-lived and become very large, with documented trees 150+ years old still producing; the long juvenile period (5–10 years to significant bearing) is a trade-off for extreme longevity. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Northern Star Artichoke (Cold-Hardy Perennial Selection)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed after frost danger passes. In cold-winter regions apply a thick winter mulch over the dormant crown to help the root system survive freezing temperatures and resprout the following spring. Northern Star was selected specifically for the ability to survive winters far colder than traditional Mediterranean-bred artichoke varieties can tolerate, extending true perennial artichoke growing into regions that previously had to treat the crop strictly as an annual. It produces medium-sized green buds with good flavor, and growers in cold climates report it returning from the crown for multiple seasons when given adequate mulch protection. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Northland Blueberry (Extremely Cold-Hardy Half-High Type)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Northland was bred at Michigan State University by crossing highbush and lowbush blueberry species, resulting in a compact, spreading 'half-high' bush notable for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters too harsh for standard highbush varieties. The medium-sized berries have good, classic sweet blueberry flavor and ripen reliably even in short northern growing seasons, and the naturally lower, denser habit makes the bush useful as an informal hedge or foundation planting in addition to its fruiting value. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter to remove the oldest wood, and plant with a second variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Northline Saskatoon (Early-Ripening Prairie Saskatoon Cultivar)
description: Northline is a prairie-bred saskatoon selection valued for producing very large, sweet, almond-scented berries earlier in the season than many other named cultivars. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow air movement and reduce foliar disease, and mulch to conserve moisture through establishment. It suckers moderately to form a multi-stemmed thicket over time, so remove wayward suckers if a tidier hedge form is wanted. The extreme cold hardiness of this cultivar makes it a staple of Canadian Prairie saskatoon orchards, where fruit is picked for fresh eating, pies, and preserves. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Northsky Blueberry (Dwarf Half-High Cold-Hardy Blueberry)
description: Northsky is one of the most compact of the University of Minnesota half-high blueberries, growing only 10 to 18 inches tall, which makes it well suited to foundation plantings, containers, and rock-garden-style edible landscapes in severe-winter regions. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its half-high siblings, tolerating temperatures near -35°F when snow-covered, and ripens medium-sized, light-blue, sweet berries in mid- to late summer. Because the plant is so low-growing, mulching and consistent moisture are especially important to prevent root stress during dry spells. Plant alongside another half-high cultivar such as Northblue or Polaris to improve pollination and fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Norton Grape (Cynthiana, Flagship Ozark Native American Red Wine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the vigorous canopy. Norton, also sold under the name Cynthiana, is a pure native American grape (Vitis aestivalis) with exceptional resistance to Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that limit many other wine grapes across the humid South and lower Midwest, and it served historically as the flagship red wine grape of the Ozark and Missouri wine industry before Prohibition. It produces small, dark, high-acid berries that make deeply colored, full-bodied red wine, though the fruit is generally considered too tart and seedy for fresh eating. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, since Norton is a vigorous grower that needs regular canopy management to keep fruit quality high. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Norton's Gold Oregano (Golden Ornamental Marjoram)
description: Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in full sun but the plant tolerates light shade better than most golden-leaved herbs. Norton's Gold forms a low, rounded mound of smooth, bright yellow-gold leaves that stay more evenly colored through summer heat than many golden oregano selections, which tend to green up as temperatures rise. Small pale pink flower clusters appear in mid to late summer, adding a second season of interest without detracting from the foliage display. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and encourage fresh gold new growth. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Nothstine Dent Corn (Wisconsin Yellow Dent Heirloom Corn)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin heirloom yellow dent corn passed down within a single farm family for generations before being preserved and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange, valued for reliable yields of good-quality meal and feed corn adapted to short-season Upper Midwest growing conditions. Its relatively short season to maturity makes it a practical choice for regions with a shorter frost-free window than the Gulf South typically has. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels for grinding or seed. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Nottingham Medlar (Classic Bletted European Medlar Tree for Unusual Jelly and Wine)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nottingham Medlar is the best and most widely grown cultivar of one of the most unusual and historically significant fruits in the European garden tradition — the medlar (Mespilus germanica) is a small deciduous tree that produces brown, apple-like fruits with an open calyx end that must undergo 'bletting' (controlled softening through frost damage and fermentation) before becoming edible. Freshly picked medlar fruits are hard, astringent, and unpleasant; after bletting — either on the tree after frosts or stored in a cool location for several weeks — they transform into soft, brown, date-like paste with a rich, wine-like flavor combining apple, date, and brown sugar notes that is quite unlike any other fruit. Bletted medlar flesh is used for medlar jelly (a beautiful, rose-colored preserve with complex flavor), medlar wine, and eaten fresh as a confection. The tree itself is ornamentally beautiful: a small, naturally gnarled and picturesque deciduous tree (10–15 feet) with large white flowers in spring, handsome broad leaves that color well in autumn, and the unusual open-calyx brown fruits hanging from the branches through fall and into winter. The late-season beauty and ancient cultural history — medlar appears frequently in medieval and Renaissance English literature and was a common kitchen-garden tree for centuries — give this fruit exceptional interest for historically minded gardeners. Zone 9 is at the warm edge of its range. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Nouveau Poiteau Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. An old French and Belgian heirloom pear named for the French botanist and pomologist Antoine Poiteau, it is valued above all as a reliable, heavy-cropping variety, with good if not outstanding dessert flavor and texture. Its consistent, generous yields made it a long-standing orchard staple in Europe even though showier or better-flavored varieties were available. Harvest in fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nova Easygro Apple (Low-Spray Scab-Resistant Nova Scotia Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Nova Easygro was released by the Nova Scotia agricultural research program specifically for scab resistance and generally easy, low-input growing, living up to its name by requiring far less fungicide intervention than scab-susceptible standard varieties to produce clean, attractive fruit. The medium, red-striped apple has crisp, juicy flesh with a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and general cooking use. Its combination of disease resistance and straightforward care requirements has made it a practical recommendation for home orchardists in humid, scab-prone regions who want to grow apples with a minimal spray program, particularly those interested in organic or low-chemical fruit production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nova Elderberry (Early-Ripening High-Yield Canadian Elderberry Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a Canadian elderberry cultivar developed by Agriculture Canada that produces large, dense, heavy berry clusters ripening one of the earliest in the American elderberry season — typically 7–10 days earlier than Adams and other mid-season cultivars. The large, heavy clusters of very dark purple-black berries — dense and pendant when fully ripe — combine good fresh eating quality with excellent processing characteristics for elderberry syrup, juice, wine, and jelly production. Nova produces abundant flat-topped flower clusters in June–July, providing one of the most productive native pollinator resources in the early summer garden — elder flowers are visited by extraordinary numbers of native bees, small native bees, and beneficial insects that use the pollen and nectar. The compact cyme structure of Nova clusters makes harvesting somewhat easier than looser-clustered varieties. Nova's combination of early ripening, high production, and compact plant habit (slightly smaller than some other cultivars at 5–10 feet) makes it a practical choice for home gardens. As with all American elderberry, Nova spreads by root suckers to form colonies — plan for the suckering habit and remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Nova Pear (Cold-Hardy Zone 3 Fresh-Eating Pear)
description: Nova was introduced by St. Lawrence Nurseries in northern New York, one of the oldest cold-climate fruit nurseries in North America; unlike the Manitoba- and Saskatchewan-bred Ussurian hybrids such as Ure, Rescue, and David, Nova's exact parentage was never formally documented, and it has long circulated in cold-climate nursery trade based on performance rather than pedigree. It is reliably hardy to zone 3 and has proven successful even in parts of Alaska, tolerating winters that eliminate most European pear cultivars. Nova stands out among cold-hardy pears for genuine fresh-eating quality, described by growers as flavorful whether picked slightly green or left to fully ripen, a comparatively rare trait among the often gritty, astringent Ussurian-derived hardy pears. It is also self-fertile, though fruit set and size improve with a second hardy pear planted nearby. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nova Raspberry (Cold-Hardy Vigorous Canadian Red Raspberry)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis or wire support to keep the vigorous canes upright. Bred in Nova Scotia, this summer-bearing red raspberry was selected for outstanding winter hardiness and strong resistance to common cane diseases, making it a reliable choice for gardeners in colder climates where less hardy cultivars struggle. It produces firm, medium-large, bright red berries with good flavor on tall, vigorous, spine-covered canes over a midsummer harvest season. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting and thin new canes each spring to maintain airflow and fruit quality. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Nova Red Raspberry
description: Nova is a hardy, disease-resistant red raspberry that stands up to harsh winters and yields firm, flavorful berries. Plant dormant canes in early spring in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow airflow and easy picking. Provide a trellis or support to keep the fruiting canes upright. This summer-bearing type fruits on second-year canes, so remove spent floricanes after harvest while leaving new primocanes for next season. Mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Nova Tangelo (Clementine-Orlando Tangelo Hybrid Mandarin)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed, siting them in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and room for a moderately vigorous canopy. Provide steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set, and fertilize with a balanced citrus formula during the growing season. Nova produces deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with a rich, honeyed flavor that ripens early in the mandarin season, though a pollinator variety nearby improves fruit set and reduces seediness. It suits home orchards across Florida, the Gulf Coast, and coastal California where winters stay above the low 20s F. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Novaria Banana (Cold-Hardy Hybrid Fruiting Banana)
description: Novaria is a hybrid banana bred specifically for cold-climate growers, crossing hardy Himalayan and hardy Asian banana lineage to combine better winter root survival with a better chance of edible fruit than pure Musa basjoo offers. In the Gulf South it behaves much like other root-hardy bananas: the above-ground stalk is usually cut back or killed by winter cold, but a deep mulch layer over the corm lets the plant resprout vigorously each spring. Because it needs a long, warm growing season to actually bloom and set fruit, treat fruiting as a bonus in favorable years rather than a guarantee, and prioritize its ornamental value and reliable perennial return instead. Give it full sun, rich moist soil, and heavy summer feeding to maximize both size and the odds of a fruiting cycle. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Novella Pea (Self-Supporting Semi-Leafless Shelling Pea)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sowing a bit thicker than usual so plants can lean on and support one another. Novella is a semi-leafless ('afila') type pea in which most of the normal flat leaflets are replaced by curling tendrils, causing plants to knit themselves together into a dense, self-supporting tangle that stands mostly upright with little or no staking, a real convenience compared to conventional pea vines that flop without support. The reduced foliage also means better airflow and light penetration through the planting, which can reduce fungal disease pressure, while still producing a solid crop of sweet, tender shelling peas in well-filled pods. Pick regularly once pods fill out for the best flavor, and enjoy the relatively low-maintenance, self-supporting habit that sets this type apart from standard pea varieties. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Nozawana (Japanese Turnip Greens, Nozawana Pickled Leaf Turnip)
description: Direct sow in late summer or early fall in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; nozawana (also called 'nozawa-na' or 'nozawana turnip') is a cool-season Japanese brassica grown primarily for its large, textured, dark-green leaves rather than its turnip root (the root is small and incidental) — the leaves are the classic ingredient in nozawana-zuke, the Nagano Prefecture traditional pickle that is one of Japan's most beloved preserved vegetables. The large, crinkled, somewhat coarse-textured leaves (larger and more substantial than most Asian greens) are harvested whole and salt-pickled in large crocks over winter, developing a complex, slightly funky, fermented flavor that is eaten alongside rice and miso soup throughout Nagano winters. Fresh young leaves can also be blanched and stir-fried or used in miso soup. In zone 9, nozawana grows as a reliable fall-to-winter crop; it tolerates frost well and improves in sweetness after cold weather. A wonderful specialty brassica for gardeners interested in Japanese fermentation traditions and Asian vegetable diversity. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: NS1 Jackfruit
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; NS1 forms a dense, upright, medium-vigor canopy that stays far more compact than seedling jackfruit and can be held to roughly 8-10 feet with routine annual pruning, making it one of the more manageable named selections for a home dooryard. Trees are heavy, reliable bearers, and fruit are dark green and blocky with blunt, flattened spines that open as the fruit ripens, enclosing firm, dark-orange flesh with a rich, sweet flavor. Because NS1 begins fruiting on relatively young, small trees, thin the first one or two crops to just a few fruit per tree so the young trunk and root system can establish before carrying a full load. Harvest when the spines flatten and the fruit develops a hollow sound when tapped, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for a day or two before cutting. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Nubia Eggplant (Purple and White Variegated Italian-Type Hybrid Eggplant)
description: Nubia produces oval fruit boldly variegated in purple and white, growing 6-7 inches long and 3-4 inches across, with dense, cream-colored flesh and a mild, semi-sweet flavor. Because it fills out its fruit over a slightly longer window than many hybrids, keep plants evenly watered and well fed through the back half of summer rather than expecting an early flush. Slicing the flesh and salting it briefly before cooking helps draw out moisture and firms the texture for roasting, grilling, or caponata. Pick fruit while the variegated skin is still glossy, since it dulls noticeably once past peak ripeness. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Nubiana Plum (Self-Fruitful Black-Skinned California Japanese Plum)
description: Nubiana is a California-bred Japanese plum valued for its large, firm, slightly flattened fruit with deep purplish-black skin and sweet amber flesh that has very little tartness even near the pit. It ripens in mid-to-late summer, generally a few weeks after Black Amber and ahead of late-season types like Angeleno, filling out the middle of the harvest calendar. Unlike many Japanese plums, Nubiana is usually described as self-fruitful, though fruit set and size typically improve with a second Japanese plum planted nearby. Its moderate chilling requirement makes it a reasonable candidate for milder zone 8 and warmer zone 9 orchards that still receive some winter chill. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Nude Sheath Bamboo (Snow Bamboo)
description: Phyllostachys nuda is among the most cold-tolerant of all timber bamboos, with rhizomes that can survive extreme winter lows even where top growth dies back, making it a good running-bamboo choice for gardeners at the cold edge of bamboo culture. Culms are a dark, glossy green with a distinctive pale ring below each node, and mature groves reach a moderate height compared to giant timber species, staying more manageable in smaller landscapes. The spring shoots are considered outstanding for eating, with a sweet flavor and low bitterness, and should be cut just below the soil surface while still short. Because it spreads by rhizome like all Phyllostachys, install a barrier or plan for regular rhizome pruning to keep the grove contained. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Nufar Basil (Fusarium-Resistant Genovese Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once the garden has thoroughly warmed. Nufar was bred specifically to combine the classic large, glossy, sweet-scented leaves of Genovese basil with resistance to fusarium wilt, a soilborne disease that can devastate basil plantings, especially in beds where basil has been grown repeatedly. Its robust, upright plants hold up well through a full season of repeated pinching and harvesting for pesto and other Italian cooking. Regularly removing flower spikes keeps the plant leafier and extends its productive life into fall. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Nugget Hops (High-Alpha American Bittering Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Nugget, released by the USDA in 1982, is a reliable high-alpha American hop grown chiefly for its strong bittering power and productive, vigorous growth, with a robust herbal, slightly piney aroma that makes it a workhorse bittering hop in many American beer styles. It is valued by home growers in part for being an especially heavy yielder and easy to grow compared with some finicky aroma cultivars. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Big Jim Pepper (World's Longest Chile Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture for maximum fruit size; NuMex Big Jim is most famous when roasted over open flame or under a broiler in the New Mexico tradition. NuMex Big Jim was developed at New Mexico State University's Chile Pepper Institute by Dr. Roy Nakayama and released in 1975 as a breakthrough in Hatch/New Mexico green chile breeding; it holds the Guinness World Record for the world's longest chile pepper, with individual fruits measured up to 13 inches in length and 2–2.5 inches in diameter — fruit of this size are capable of being stuffed whole (for chile rellenos) without cutting, which drove the commercial appeal. The heat level is moderate (500–2,500 SHU — from virtually nil to mild-moderate depending on growing conditions, with hotter summers producing hotter fruit), characteristic of New Mexico green chiles rather than the sharp heat of jalapeños or serranos. The flavor when roasted is rich, smoky, earthy, and complex with characteristic New Mexico chile character — the basis of authentic Hatch green chile sauce, the iconic topping of New Mexico cuisine from green chile cheeseburgers to burritos and sopapillas. One of the most important American regional chile varieties. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Easter Pepper (Color-Changing Ornamental Chile)
description: NuMex Easter was released by the New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute and named a 2014 All-America Selections winner for its striking clusters of small, upright, teardrop-shaped fruit that shift through pastel lavender, cream, and yellow before finishing bright orange, often showing several colors on the same compact plant at once. The dense, fasciculate fruiting habit and dwarf stature, typically under a foot tall and about as wide, make it one of the most reliable ornamental peppers for small containers, window boxes, or mixed spring bedding displays. The fruit carries real heat, roughly in the cayenne-to-habanero range, and is technically edible, but it is grown almost exclusively for its ever-changing color display rather than culinary use. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and light monthly feeding to keep fruit set continuous through the season. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Heritage Big Jim Hatch Chile Pepper
description: This improved Hatch-type chile offers thick flesh, large flavorful pods, and consistent mild-to-medium heat ideal for fire roasting. Start seeds early indoors since peppers need a long warm season, and transplant only after the soil is thoroughly warm. Feed lightly and water evenly to size up the pods. Harvest green for roasting or leave to redden for deeper, sweeter flavor. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Joe E. Parker Anaheim Chile Pepper
description: This productive Anaheim-type pepper bears thick-walled, uniform 6 to 8 inch fruits with few seeds, excellent for roasting, stuffing, or canning. Mild heat around 500 to 2,500 Scoville units makes it versatile in the kitchen. Start seeds indoors early and set out sturdy transplants once nights are warm. Peppers ripen from green to red, so pick at whichever stage suits your recipe. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Joe E. Parker Pepper (Standard New Mexico Green Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun, deeply watered soil after last frost. NuMex Joe E. Parker is one of the most commercially important New Mexico chile varieties — a New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute release named in honor of Joe E. Parker, a former NMSU Board of Regents member. The variety occupies the essential middle ground of New Mexico chile heat: mild to medium-hot, approximately 500–2,500 Scoville Heat Units, hot enough to have authentic New Mexico chile character but mild enough for broad consumer acceptance. Joe E. Parker is the standard commercial variety for Hatch-brand green chile operations, grown across thousands of acres in the Rio Grande Valley and producing the long (7–9 inch), flat, meaty-walled green fruits used for fresh-roasted whole chiles, canned green chile, green chile stew, and freezing. The fruits roast exceptionally well: thick walls hold up under direct flame, the skin blisters and chars cleanly, and the interior steams to the silky texture essential for authentic New Mexico green chile preparations. When left to mature to red and dried, NuMex Joe E. Parker produces the bright, papery-red pods used in New Mexico ristras and traditional dried red chile. For gardeners who want to grow the authentic Hatch valley chile experience, NuMex Joe E. Parker is the single most representative variety — it defines the flavor and character that New Mexico green chile has meant to American Southwestern cuisine for generations. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Joe Parker Pepper
description: NuMex Joe E. Parker was released in 1990 by New Mexico State University's chile breeding program and named for a longtime agricultural evaluator who helped select it; it is one of the standard named cultivars behind commercial Hatch green chile alongside NuMex Big Jim. Pods run six to eight inches, thick-walled and mild to medium in heat, and are traditionally picked green for roasting and stuffing or left to ripen red for drying and sauces. The plants are productive and relatively compact for a New Mexico-type chile, making them a manageable choice for home gardeners who want authentic Hatch flavor without the largest-fruited varieties. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Lemon Spice Jalapeno Chile Pepper
description: This colorful jalapeno from the Chile Pepper Institute ripens from green to bright yellow with full jalapeno heat and a citrus undertone. Pick pods at either the green or yellow stage for a varied jar of pickled peppers. Start seeds indoors well before your last frost, then transplant into warm, sunny beds. Steady watering and a light feeding keep the compact plants cranking out fruit. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Suave Orange Pepper
description: NuMex Suave Orange was bred at the New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute as a companion to NuMex Suave Red, combining the classic wrinkled, lantern-shaped habanero pod and citrusy, apricot-toned chinense aroma with almost none of the heat, typically measuring under a thousand Scoville units. The plump pods ripen from green to a rich orange over a long, warm growing season, so give plants the full run of summer and avoid letting nighttime temperatures dip into the 50s while fruit is setting. Because so little capsaicin is present, cooks can use whole or pureed pods generously in salsas, marinades, and fruit-forward hot sauces to capture authentic habanero flavor without overwhelming heat. Rich, well-drained soil and consistent watering through fruit set keep yields high on the compact, bushy plants. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Suave Red Pepper
description: NuMex Suave Red was released by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as a nearly heatless habanero, measuring only a few hundred Scoville units yet retaining the same fruity, tropical aroma prized in hot habaneros. Plump, wrinkled fruit ripens from green to a deep red on productive plants that need a long, warm season to reach full size. Because the pepper carries little to no burn, it lets cooks use habanero flavor generously in salsas and sauces without overwhelming heat. Give it the same rich soil, consistent watering, and full sun that other chinense peppers require to perform well. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: NuMex Twilight Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental-Edible Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Twilight is compact enough for containers (8–12 inches) and makes an outstanding patio plant both for ornamental color and edible use. NuMex Twilight was developed at New Mexico State University's internationally renowned Chile Pepper Institute as part of their ornamental-edible pepper breeding program; the variety takes its name from the brilliant multicolor sky of a New Mexico twilight that it is said to evoke — each plant produces upright clusters of small (1–2 inch), conical fruits that transition through the colors purple (immature) → yellow → orange → red (fully ripe), with all four colors simultaneously visible on a mature, productive plant. The heat level is approximately 50,000–75,000 SHU — significant but not extreme, in the range of cayenne peppers — and the small fruits are fully edible at any color stage; purple fruits are mildest, red fruits are hottest. As an ornamental plant, NuMex Twilight is among the most stunning of all edible plants, combining constant visual interest through the growing season with genuine culinary utility for dried chile flakes, hot sauces, and fresh use. Outstanding in containers, as a border plant, or as an annual focal point in vegetable and ornamental beds. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Nutmeg Geranium (Spice-Scented Geranium)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; nutmeg geranium is a compact hybrid scented-leaf pelargonium with small, roundish, slightly gray-green, softly hairy leaves that release an unmistakable warm, spicy nutmeg-and-pine fragrance when touched or rubbed — quite different from the rosy fragrance of P. capitatum or the lemony notes of P. crispum. The fragrance is immediately recognizable as nutmeg with a fresh, slightly turpentine-woody undertone. Small, white, pink-veined pelargonium flowers appear in spring and early summer. A traditional cottage and kitchen garden herb grown for centuries for the use of its fragrant leaves in cooking (particularly in pound cakes, custards, and sugar syrups where a leaf placed in the bottom of the pan imparts its fragrance), for herbal sachets, and as a fragrant window-sill plant. Very easy to grow from cuttings, which root readily and were traditionally passed between neighbors and friends — the most common mode of propagation for all scented geraniums, which are grown almost exclusively as cutting-propagated plants rather than from seed. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Nutmeg Hickory
description: Nutmeg Hickory is the rarest of the true hickories native to North America, found scattered in moist to wet bottomlands, alluvial flats, and river swamps of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina west to southeastern Texas, where it reaches its greatest abundance in Louisiana and Mississippi. The round, dark nuts — resembling nutmegs in shape and borne in thick, 4-parted husks — are smaller than those of most hickories but are relished by squirrels, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys, and were historically gathered and eaten by Native Americans. Plant fresh nuts directly in fall in deep, moist, slightly acidic loamy soil in full sun, allowing 90–120 days of cold stratification over winter before spring germination; the deep taproot that forms in the first growing season makes older trees virtually impossible to transplant. Trees grow steadily in bottomland soils and develop spectacular golden-yellow fall color and deeply furrowed gray bark that make them outstanding additions to naturalized floodplain or riparian plantings. Matures in 3650–7300 days from seed.

name: O'Gosho Persimmon (Compact Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
description: O'Gosho is a non-astringent Japanese persimmon that stays notably more compact than standard Fuyu, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards or espalier training. The fruit is smaller and rounder than Fuyu with a slightly flattened shape and orange-red skin, and it can be harvested and eaten crisp like an apple as soon as full color develops. Being self-fruitful, a single tree sets a complete crop without a separate pollinator variety nearby. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: O'Henry Sweet Potato (White-Skin White-Flesh Beauregard Sport)
description: O'Henry arose as a natural sport of Beauregard, sharing its parent's vigor and productivity but with cream-white skin and white flesh in place of Beauregard's copper skin and orange flesh, giving a milder, less sweet, drier-textured potato favored by cooks who want a sweet potato that behaves more like a baking potato. Vines are vigorous and trailing, producing heavy yields of smooth, uniform, blocky roots under the same growing conditions Beauregard thrives in. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storage to heal skin cuts and convert starches to sugars, improving both flavor and keeping quality. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: O'Neal Southern Highbush Blueberry (Low-Chill Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; O'Neal is widely considered the finest-tasting southern highbush blueberry cultivar — a North Carolina State University release with remarkably low chill requirements (200–400 hours) that makes it appropriate for zone 9 and even warmer parts of zone 8, where northern highbush cultivars receive insufficient chilling. The large, medium-blue berries have exceptionally complex, aromatic, rich blueberry flavor — consistently rated among the best-tasting of all blueberry cultivars in taste trials by the North Carolina breeding program. The flavor profile is described as rich, aromatic, and complex with a good balance of sweetness and acidity. O'Neal is an early-season cultivar, ripening in April–May in zone 9, which helps avoid peak summer heat and provides early-season fruit at a premium time. The bush grows vigorously to 5–7 feet with attractive white urn-shaped flowers in late winter and outstanding fall color (orange to red) that makes it an ornamental landscape plant as well as a fruiting shrub. Plant with at least one other southern highbush cultivar (Legacy or Sunshine Blue) for cross-pollination, which dramatically increases berry size and total yield. Maintain strict soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 — blueberries fail in soils above pH 6.0. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: O'Rourke Fig
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; O'Rourke is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter and named for Dr. Ed O'Rourke, the Louisiana fruit breeder who led decades of fig research at LSU. Released in the late 20th century, it was bred specifically for Louisiana and Gulf Coast conditions, where the challenges of summer rain, humidity, and insect pressure at the eye (ostiole) cause fruit souring and internal pest damage in many standard varieties. O'Rourke has a distinctively tight, nearly closed eye that greatly reduces fruit souring caused by rain entering the ostiole and internal splitting — making it one of the best varieties for humid Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to tan at maturity with amber-pink flesh, very sweet with complex fig flavor. The breba crop on old wood in June is modest; the main crop in August–October is abundant. Trees are vigorous and well-adapted to heavy clay soils when drainage is adequate. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Oak Leaf Lettuce (Green Oak Leaf)
description: Scatter seed thinly on the soil surface and firm in; keep consistently moist until germination at 50–70°F. Oak Leaf lettuce is one of the most recognizable and popular looseleaf lettuces in American home gardens, with deeply lobed, ruffled leaves that resemble the silhouette of an oak leaf — a form distinct from the curled frill of Lollo Rosa types or the smooth curves of Butterhead. The bright green (or burgundy, in the 'Red Oak Leaf' variety) deeply cut leaves form loose, open rosettes that can be cut-and-come-again repeatedly; the leaf texture is tender and buttery, and the flavor is mild with excellent heat tolerance compared to most lettuces. It was one of Thomas Jefferson's preferred salad plants at Monticello and has been grown in American gardens continuously since the colonial era.
