Outstanding for cut-and-come-again salad production in spring and fall. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Oak-Leaf Geranium (Almond-Scented Geranium)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; oak-leaf geranium is a boldly distinctive scented-leaf pelargonium species prized for two features — its unusually large, deeply lobed, oak-leaf-shaped leaves (which give the plant its species name quercifolium, Latin for 'oak-leaved') and the strong, pungent, bitter-almond to balsamic fragrance released when the sticky, glandular leaves are handled, distinctly different from the rose or citrus notes of other scented pelargoniums. The leaves are large and rough-textured compared to most pelargoniums, sticky to the touch, and the plant becomes a large, somewhat gawky but aromatic shrub in warm climates. Small rose-pink to magenta flowers appear in spring and summer. Used in the fragrance industry and in potpourri for its balsamic notes. In zones 9–11 it can grow into an impressive specimen shrub with an overwhelming presence when the foliage is disturbed in the breeze. 'Fair Ellen' is a widely available cultivar with particularly deep-cut, decorative leaves. A plant grown more for fragrant-foliage effect than ornamental flowers — one of the most botanically interesting of the diverse scented pelargonium group. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Oakleaf Lettuce
description: Oakleaf is a classic loose-leaf heirloom lettuce with tender, deeply lobed leaves that resemble oak foliage. It is a reliable cut-and-come-again type, letting you harvest outer leaves while the center keeps growing. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, giving it full sun in cool weather or partial shade to slow bolting in heat. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest young for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Oaxacan Green Corn (Mexican Heirloom Flour and Tortilla Corn)
description: Sow in blocks of at least four rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Oaxacan Green is a tall, traditional Zapotec heirloom corn from the Oaxaca region of Mexico, grown for large ears of pale green kernels that dry to a soft cream-green color and grind into a flour prized for tortillas, tamales, and masa-based dishes with a distinctive sweet, complex corn flavor. It grows notably tall, often exceeding 8 feet, reflecting its origins in traditional milpa polyculture systems where it was often interplanted with beans and squash in a Three Sisters-style planting. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk before harvesting, then cure further indoors before grinding or storing whole. Isolate from other corn varieties by distance or planting-date offset to keep the strain true from seed saved for replanting. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Oaxacan Green Dent Corn (Traditional Mexican Blue-Green Flour Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows; harvest when husks are completely dry and papery. Oaxacan Green Dent is a traditional flour and dent corn from the valley of Oaxaca, Mexico — a staple landrace corn of the indigenous Zapotec and Mixtec agricultural traditions maintained over centuries in the high-altitude valley environment of southern Mexico. The most visually striking characteristic is the kernel color: at maturity, the kernels are an unusual blue-green to aqua-blue, sometimes with silvery-white highlights — a color found in few other corn varieties and quite distinct from the blue-black of Hopi Blue or the rainbow of Glass Gem. The color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments that color other colored corns, but in a combination that expresses specifically in the blue-green range. In traditional Oaxacan cuisine, Oaxacan Green corn is used as masa for the deep green, smoky-flavored specialty tamales and tlayudas, where the colored masa produces a visually distinctive product unlike standard yellow or white corn preparations. The ears are medium to large, somewhat irregular in kernel arrangement as expected of a landrace variety, and the plants are tall. Oaxacan Green is maintained and distributed by Native Seeds/SEARCH and the Seed Savers Exchange as part of preserving Mesoamerican corn diversity. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Obatã Coffee (IAC Obatã)
description: Developed at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas from a cross between the breeding line IAC 1669-20 and Yellow Catuaí, Obatã combines a compact, dwarf growth habit with strong resistance to coffee leaf rust and consistently high cup quality, a combination that has made it popular with Brazilian growers looking to replace older, disease-prone cultivars. Its short stature allows closer spacing and easier hand harvesting than tall heirloom types, while its late maturation spreads out the picking season. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade, giving it the same warm, frost-free care as other dwarf Arabica cultivars like Catuaí. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Oberkulmer Rotkorn Spelt (Swiss Heirloom Winter Spelt)
description: Oberkulmer Rotkorn is a Swiss landrace spelt prized for its genetic purity, having never been crossed back into common bread wheat the way many modern spelt lines have. It grows quite tall, easily reaching five to six feet, and is deliberately grown lean: skip added compost or fertilizer, since excess nitrogen and rich soil cause this old variety to lodge before harvest. Sow into weed-free ground in mid-fall so plants overwinter as a low rosette, then resume growth in spring and ripen for a late-summer harvest. The red-husked grain threshes with more effort than free-threshing wheat because the tough hull clings to the kernel, but it rewards the work with flour that heritage bakers describe as unusually flavorful and easy to digest. Matures in 280–310 days from seed.

name: Obsession Sweet Corn (Vigorous Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Obsession is a supersweet bicolor sweet corn hybrid bred for vigorous stalk growth and consistent ear quality under warm Southern growing conditions. It produces well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels that stay sweet in storage longer than standard sugary-type corn thanks to its supersweet genetics. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage leads to poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Obsidian Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Bramble with Marion-Like Flavor)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the vigorous, thornless trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since the sprawling growth habit needs support to keep fruiting laterals off the ground. Obsidian was released in 2005 by the USDA-ARS breeding program working with Oregon State University, bred from Marion, Olallie, and Boysen parentage to combine thornless canes with fruit quality much closer to the industry-standard 'Marion' than earlier thornless trailing types like 'Waldo'. The berries are large, glossy black, firm, and richly flavored, ripening early in the trailing-blackberry season around mid-to-late June. Its combination of thornless canes and excellent dessert and processing quality has made Obsidian one of the more widely planted modern replacements for thorny Marion. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Oca (Andean Wood Sorrel, New Zealand Yam)
description: Plant seed tubers 3–4 inches deep in loose, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; oca is the second most important Andean root crop after potato, cultivated for thousands of years across the Andes from Colombia to Argentina at elevations of 7,000–13,000 feet, where its tangy, lemony tubers are boiled, roasted, freeze-dried into 'caya', or left in the sun for several days to mellow the oxalic acid and develop sweetness. Tubers come in striking colors — white, yellow, orange, pink, red, and near-black — and range from pleasantly tart to mild and starchy depending on cultivar and post-harvest sun exposure. Harvest after the first light frost kills the foliage, which signals peak tuber development; in frost-free zones, cut back the vines in November to trigger dormancy. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Oceanside Spinach
description: This spinach yields deep green, easy-to-clean leaves that are ready as baby greens in about 25 days and full size in 40. Sow directly in cool spring or fall soil since heat triggers bolting. Keep the bed evenly moist and thin seedlings for good airflow. Harvest baby leaves with scissors or pull whole plants, and provide afternoon shade to stretch the harvest into warmer weather. Matures in 25–45 days from seed.

name: Ochlockonee Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season UF Blueberry)
description: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the long southern summer. Ochlockonee is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry named for the Ochlockonee River in the Florida Panhandle, valued for ripening late in the season, after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, which lets home growers stretch fresh blueberry harvest into July. The vigorous, upright bush produces firm, medium-to-large, good-flavored berries in heavy clusters, and its low chill requirement makes it well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and remove old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Oconee Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Southeastern Pecan, Type I Mid-Season Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained to moderately moist fertile soil; Oconee is a mid-season variety (ripening October in the Gulf South) with large nuts and good kernel fill; its scab resistance makes it particularly valuable in the humid southeastern states from Virginia through the Gulf Coast; trees are moderately vigorous and productive. Oconee pecan is a University of Georgia-developed variety (released in the 1990s) that has become one of the most highly recommended pecan cultivars for the southeastern United States, specifically bred and selected for performance under the humid conditions, disease pressure, and climate of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf South. The breeding program at the University of Georgia's Tifton Campus has focused on developing pecan varieties with significantly improved scab resistance compared to the older standard commercial varieties (Desirable, Stuart, Schley) while maintaining nut quality comparable to those benchmarks — and Oconee represents one of the successful outcomes of this program. The nuts are large (40–48 per pound), well-filled, with good kernel percentage (58–62%), and produce a clean, sweet, buttery pecan flavor that compares favorably with the best commercial varieties. Oconee's most important attribute is its considerably better scab resistance than Desirable or Schley in the humid conditions of Georgia, Alabama, and the Gulf South — in UGA variety trials under disease pressure, Oconee consistently shows significantly lower scab infection rates on leaves and shucks, resulting in cleaner nuts and more consistent yields without the intensive fungicide programs that scab-susceptible varieties require. A premier choice for home orchard planting throughout the Gulf South. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: October Bean
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy pole or trellis support; October Bean is an Appalachian mountain heirloom shellout bean (also called 'fall bean', 'shelly bean', or 'October shellout') that has been grown in Southern Appalachian kitchen gardens continuously for generations — the bean is named for its traditional harvest period in September and October when the seeds have filled the pods but before autumn frosts dry the plants down. The large, tan to cream-colored, maroon-streaked seeds inside swollen pods are shelled and cooked fresh like a combination between fresh lima beans and dry beans — with a rich, meaty, potato-like texture and earthy, slightly sweet flavor quite different from green snap beans or fully dried beans. The freshly shelled October bean is a cornerstone of traditional Appalachian cooking, served with cornbread, potatoes, and green onions. The climbing vines produce abundantly over a long season, and any mature pods that escape the fresh-shelled harvest can be allowed to dry for a dried soup bean with excellent winter storage. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: October Bean (Peanut Butter Bean, Speckled Pole Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing 4–6 feet of vertical support; October bean is a traditional Appalachian heirloom pole or half-runner bean whose primary value is as a shelling bean — harvested when pods are fully filled but still green to slightly dried ('fall colored'), when the speckled tan-and-maroon seeds shell out easily and cook quickly with a rich, creamy, almost peanut-buttery flavor. Named for October when they traditionally matured in the mountain regions of the southern Appalachians, the plants produce best when planted in late spring to mature into cooler fall temperatures. In zone 9 a June planting produces a September–October shell bean harvest with ideal timing. The shelled beans cook in 45–60 minutes without soaking, absorbing seasoning beautifully, and are outstanding cooked with ham hocks and served over cornbread. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Ocumare Cacao
description: Named for the Ocumare valley along Venezuela's Aragua coast, this fine-flavor Criollo-type landrace has been propagated there as a series of numbered clonal selections prized by chocolate makers for bright, fruity, low-bitterness flavor notes distinct from the more floral Porcelana strain grown further west. Like other true Criollo cacaos it is thin-shelled, slow to establish, and notably more vulnerable to fungal pod disease than robust Forastero-type trees, so it rewards attentive humidity and airflow management. Plant seedlings in spring beneath the canopy of taller shade trees in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and keep air temperatures reliably above 60F year-round. Expect a long wait of four to five years before the tree produces a meaningful first harvest of pods. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Odorless Bayberry
description: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions. Myrica heterophylla is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native bayberry of the southeastern coastal plain, closely related to wax myrtle but lacking the characteristic aromatic fragrance; it produces similar small waxy berries that attract overwintering songbirds and provides dense cover in wet to moist habitats where few other shrubs thrive. This species is an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet swales, and pond margins in the Southeast, where its compact form and wildlife value make it a workhorse of native planting designs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ogle Southern Pea (Clemson-Bred Purple Hull Pea)
description: Ogle was bred by longtime Clemson horticulturist Roy (W.L.) Ogle, the same breeder behind the classic Colossus and Hercules southern peas, and was released commercially by Clemson University decades after he first developed the line. It is a purple hull type selected for a large eating seed, strong yield, and resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a disease that has historically limited purple hull production in humid climates. Like other purple hull peas it can be picked green for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage peas. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Oh My! Muscadine Grape (Seedless Bronze Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Oh My! is the first muscadine bred to reliably produce full-sized, seedless bronze fruit, the result of a multi-decade breeding effort by North Carolina grape breeder Jeff Bloodworth and protected under U.S. utility patent, so home gardeners should buy vines from a licensed nursery rather than propagate cuttings. The tender-skinned berries are unusually high in sugar and eat almost like a table grape, without the tough hull and swallow-or-spit seeds of a typical muscadine. Self-fertile, it needs no separate pollinator vine and ripens in early to mid-September in the Gulf South. Like other muscadines, the vine carries strong native resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures of humid summers, so it needs no spray program beyond routine winter pruning to short spurs on permanent cordons. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ohelo Berry (Hawaiian Blueberry)
description: Grow this low, wiry-branched shrub in gritty, well-drained, acidic soil that mimics its native volcanic cinder habitat, and avoid rich garden soil or heavy watering that can encourage rot. Ohelo produces small, tart-sweet, cranberry-like berries in shades of red, yellow, or orange, borne alongside dainty urn-shaped pink or yellow flowers typical of the blueberry family. Native to high-elevation Hawaiian volcanic slopes, it tolerates poor, rocky ground and strong sun but is sensitive to wet, poorly drained conditions and to frost. The tangy fruit is traditionally used fresh or cooked into jams and sauces. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ohio Black Walnut (Historic Named Selection)
description: Ohio is one of the oldest named black walnut cultivars still in circulation, selected in the early twentieth century for a thinner shell and better flavor than typical wild seedling trees. It remains a benchmark cultivar in regional nut variety trials and is often planted alongside newer releases for comparison. Give it deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and wide spacing to accommodate its eventual size, and locate it away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to root-zone juglone. Plant a second distinct black walnut nearby to improve pollination, and harvest nuts as soon as hulls loosen to reduce staining and kernel darkening. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: OHxF 97 Pear Rootstock (Old Home x Farmingdale 97)
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired pear variety onto the young rootstock; OHxF 97 is a semi-dwarfing, fire blight-resistant understock, not grown for its own fruit. Bred from a cross of the fire blight-resistant Old Home pear and Farmingdale pear at what is now Oregon State University, this rootstock in the widely used OHxF series produces a semi-dwarf to semi-standard tree around 75-85 percent the size of a standard seedling pear tree, valued above all for outstanding resistance to fire blight, one of the most destructive diseases of pear in humid growing regions. Its combination of moderate size control, strong anchorage that needs no permanent staking, and disease resistance has made the OHxF series the standard modern choice for pear rootstocks in North America, largely displacing the fire blight-susceptible quince rootstocks used in parts of Europe. Graft a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect a sturdy, disease-resistant, moderately sized tree well suited to humid-climate pear growing. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Oka Melon
description: Oka was bred in the early twentieth century at the Trappist monastery of Oka, Quebec, as a deliberate cross of the Montreal Melon and the Banana Melon, aimed at combining rich flavor with a shorter season than the giant Montreal type required. It produces small, flattened, roughly ten-ribbed fruit with aromatic, sweet orange flesh well suited to Quebec's cool summers. It fell out of wide commercial circulation by mid-century as industrial melon varieties took over, only to be rediscovered decades later from seed preserved near Montreal. It is grown today largely through Quebec heirloom seed farms working to keep the revival going. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Okahijiki (Land Seaweed, Saltwort)
description: Direct sow seeds shallowly in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in fall or early spring; thin to 3–4 inches. Salsola komarovii (okahijiki or land seaweed) is a Japanese saltwort vegetable — an annual succulent herb related to the Russian thistle (tumbleweed), grown in Japan for its tender, crisp, spiny young shoots that are bright green, cylindrical, and highly reminiscent in texture and mild, slightly salty flavor of sea vegetables (seaweed). The 'okahijiki' name literally means 'land hijiki,' comparing the plant to hijiki (a Japanese seaweed); the 'land seaweed' comparison reflects both the plant's mild marine-like flavor and its coastal saltmarsh habitat. Young shoots are harvested at 3–6 inches when most tender and used in salads, blanched as a side vegetable, or incorporated into Japanese cuisine as a seasonal vegetable; the texture is pleasantly crisp and slightly mucilaginous. The plant is extremely drought-tolerant and grows in salty, lean, sandy soils where most vegetables fail. As it matures, it becomes increasingly spiny and fibrous; harvest young for best eating quality. An unusual and underutilized cool-season specialty vegetable for adventurous gardeners. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Okinawa Pink Okra (Ribless Smooth-Podded Pink Heirloom Okra)
description: Sow seed a half inch deep directly in the garden once soil is thoroughly warm, thinning seedlings to a foot or more apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Okinawa Pink is a heirloom from Okinawa, Japan valued for smooth, ribless, rosy-pink pods that resist the toughening and stringiness common in other okra as pods pass the ideal picking size, making the harvest window more forgiving for home gardeners. Pods are best cut at three to six inches long for eating fresh, pickled, or sauteed, though the pink color fades to green when cooked. Harvest every day or two once plants begin producing to keep the compact, branching plants flowering steadily through the heat of summer. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Okinawa Spinach
description: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; they strike quickly at warm temperatures and are ready to transplant in 10–14 days. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade — full afternoon shade is ideal in hot climates, where the ornamental two-toned leaves (dark green above, vivid purple beneath) are most striking. Harvest young leaves and stem tips continuously; the raw leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture and are eaten as salad greens or briefly stir-fried. In zones 9–11 the plant grows as a sprawling perennial; in cooler climates bring cuttings indoors over winter. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Okinawa Sweet Potato
description: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, slightly sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Okinawa sweet potato is a Japanese heirloom variety with cream-colored skin and brilliantly purple flesh — the vibrant purple color comes from exceptionally high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any food crop. The slightly sweet, nutty, dry-textured flesh holds its purple color through roasting, steaming, and baking (though water boiling may leach some pigment). Okinawa sweet potato is a staple of the Okinawan diet, studied extensively as part of the traditional diet associated with unusual longevity on the island. The flavor is subtly sweet and starchy with an earthy, slightly nutty aftertaste. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and 90% humidity for 10 days before eating or storing to develop sweetness and heal any cuts. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Okinawan Spinach
description: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; Okinawan spinach (Cholesterol spinach, edible velvet plant, han tsai tai) is a tropical perennial leafy vegetable from Southeast Asia and Okinawa that is one of the most productive and effortless greens for subtropical gardens in zones 9–12 — the plant grows continuously year-round in frost-free climates, producing an inexhaustible supply of young, tender growing tips that are harvested by snipping and regrowing for months. The leaves are bicolored — dark green on the top and deep purple-red underneath, with a velvety, slightly hairy texture — creating an attractive ornamental plant that functions simultaneously as an edible garden specimen. Young leaves and tips are eaten raw in salads (pleasant, mild flavor) or briefly sautéed. The plant is rich in antioxidants and flavonoids associated with the traditional Okinawan diet. Tolerates partial shade better than most vegetables, making it valuable for shaded garden beds where conventional leafy greens would bolt. Distinct from the related Gynura procumbens (longevity spinach) in its ornamental bicolored foliage. Matures in 30–60 days from transplant.

name: Okinawan Spinach (Cholesterol Spinach)
description: Grow in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Okinawan spinach thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9 summers when cool-season greens have long since bolted. The dark green leaves with purple undersides are harvested young and eaten raw in salads, lightly stir-fried, or blended into smoothies; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture and are rich in antioxidants. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep plants bushy and productive; the sprawling stems root at nodes when they touch moist soil, making propagation effortless. This species is distinct from Okinawan sweet potato — it is a member of the daisy family and produces small yellow flowers. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Okinawan Sweet Potato (Purple Sweet Potato, Hawaiian Purple Yam)
description: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Okinawan sweet potato has creamy-white skin concealing spectacularly vivid purple-violet flesh — the deep purple color comes from extremely high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any sweet potato), making it a genuine superfood with powerful antioxidant properties. The flavor is mildly sweet, slightly nutty, and drier than orange-flesh types; it is prized in Hawaiian cuisine (where it's called 'Hawaiian purple sweet potato'), Japanese cuisine, and modern farm-to-table cooking for its dramatic color that holds remarkably well through most cooking methods. Excellent roasted, steamed, in ice cream, and in colorful desserts. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Okitsu Satsuma (Early-Ripening Sweet Japanese Satsuma)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected at Japan's Okitsu horticultural research station as an early-ripening sport of common satsuma, this cultivar produces small, flattened, deep-orange fruit that colors and sweetens several weeks before standard satsuma, often ready by October. The seedless, loose-skinned segments are tender and richly sweet with low acidity, and the compact tree bears reliably from a young age. Its early ripening window makes it especially useful in areas where an early hard freeze can threaten later-maturing citrus. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Oklawaha Blackberry (Low-Chill Central Florida Trailing Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, sandy soil and train the long, thorny, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since they will not stand upright on their own. Oklawaha was released by the University of Florida alongside 'Flordagrand' in the 1950s, bred specifically to serve as its cross-pollenizer, since both cultivars are largely self-unfruitful and set their best crops when planted in alternating rows together. Like its companion, Oklawaha needs only a low number of winter chilling hours, stays evergreen through mild Central Florida and Gulf Coast winters, and produces large, attractive berries that ripen in April and May. It remains valued by Deep South gardeners as the traditional pollenizer partner for Flordagrand in low-chill home plantings. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Okumidori Tea
description: Bred in Shizuoka Prefecture and registered in Japan in 1966, Okumidori has become the second most widely planted tea cultivar in the country after Yabukita, prized by growers for the deep emerald color and rounded, mellow sweetness it lends to shade-grown gyokuro and high-grade sencha. Its late budbreak, roughly a week behind Yabukita, spreads out the spring harvest window and helps growers avoid losing an entire crop to a single late frost. The cultivar's name translates roughly to "deep green," a nod to the intense color of both the living leaf and the finished liquor. Grow it under the same acidic, humus-rich conditions recommended for other Camellia sinensis cultivars, and prune into a rounded hedge to encourage the dense flush growth needed for hand or machine plucking. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Olallieberry
description: The olallieberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (a cross involving loganberry and youngberry parentage) popular along the California coast for its rich, sweet-tart flavor. Its long, sprawling canes must be trained onto a trellis and are best separated by fruiting year for easier pruning. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with regular irrigation through the dry season. Prune out fruited canes after the early-summer harvest and tie in the new canes for next year. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Old Fashioned Ragged Edge Mustard (Hen Pecked Heirloom Mustard Green)
description: Also sold under the folk names Hen Pecked Mustard and Ragged Edged Mustard, this black-seeded, open-pollinated type is an old standby of Southern home gardens grown both for salad and cooking greens and for its own seed. The long, narrow leaves are deeply cut and ruffled along the margin, giving the variety its ragged edge name and setting it apart from the broader, less-dissected leaves of Southern Giant Curled or Florida Broadleaf. Flavor is notably sharp and aromatic, with a horseradish-like bite that mellows somewhat when cooked, and the short days-to-maturity make it a reliable fast crop for both spring and fall sowings. Matures in 40–45 days from seed.

name: Old German Tomato (Mennonite Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Old German is an heirloom beefsteak tomato of Mennonite German ancestry — producing very large (1–2 lb), deeply flattened, lobed beefsteak fruits with a striking bicolor pattern of golden-yellow skin marked with deep-red and orange streaks, marbling, and patches distributed across the fruit surface in irregular patterns. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this German heirloom tradition: yellow and red sectors arranged in a beautiful mosaic pattern that is outstanding in sliced fresh presentations — the multicolored cross-section of Old German makes it one of the most visually beautiful tomatoes when displayed on a cutting board or serving plate. The flavor follows the pattern of the best bicolor heirlooms: very sweet, extremely low-acid, with a complex, fruity, mild quality that makes it exceptional for fresh eating. Old German is most clearly distinguished from similar bicolor heirlooms (Pineapple, Hillbilly, Big Rainbow) by the specific distribution and proportion of its red-and-yellow coloring — the exact pattern varies somewhat from fruit to fruit but consistently produces the beautiful bicolor marbled effect. An open-pollinated heirloom with saveable seed. In zone 9, grow as a spring crop for best results before summer heat. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Old Home Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant European Pear)
description: Plant in full sun with good air circulation, and prune lightly since vigorous new growth is the most blight-susceptible tissue on a pear tree. Old Home was released by USDA breeders in Oregon in the early 20th century and is famous chiefly for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates most European pears in the humid Southeast, and it is widely used as a parent of blight-resistant rootstocks as well as a scion cultivar in its own right. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit is firm and good for canning and baking, and a second pear cultivar such as Bartlett or Moonglow should be planted nearby for reliable pollination. Matures in 150–165 days from transplant.

name: Old Ivory Egg Tomato (Pale Ivory Egg-Shaped Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the abundant fruit set. Old Ivory Egg produces small, egg-shaped, 2-3 ounce fruit that ripens from pale ivory to a soft creamy yellow, with a mild, sweet flavor carrying a hint of citrus, and is prized for its striking pale coloring in salads and mixed cherry-tomato plates. The variety was distributed in a mid-1980s Seed Savers Exchange yearbook by a Wisconsin member who traced the seed stock back to Australia. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Old Timey Blue Collard (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and thin or transplant to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves. Old Timey Blue is a traditional Southern heirloom collard, one of many regional strains passed down and re-saved within families for generations before being preserved by seed-saving organizations, valued for its dependable vigor, good cold tolerance, and classic blue-green collard flavor that sweetens after a frost. Tall, productive plants yield heavily over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again, taking outer leaves while the center keeps producing. Fertilize with a balanced or nitrogen-rich feed through the season for the best leaf growth, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, managing with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide if needed. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Old Timey Green Collard (North Carolina Heirloom Non-Heading Collard)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously since this heirloom spreads wide and low rather than growing into a tall, upright stalk collard. Old Timey Green is a rare non-heading North Carolina family strain, saved for decades before passing into seed-bank preservation efforts, and it remains scarce in cultivation today, distinct from the separately preserved Old Timey Blue strain. Leaves are broadly elliptic with a wavy edge and only light blistering, often carrying purple tinting at the stem and leaf base, and cook up with a notably strong, earthy flavor and a bit more bitterness than milder modern collard hybrids. Harvest outer leaves continually through the cool season, and consider saving seed from vigorous plants to help keep this dwindling family heirloom in circulation. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Old Tokyo Komatsuna
description: Direct sow into fertile soil and thin progressively, eating the thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants develop into full-sized rosettes. Old Tokyo carries the smooth, glossy, dark green leaves and mild, faintly sweet, spinach-like flavor typical of heirloom komatsuna, with a slightly milder bite than many modern hybrid strains. It grows well in the dappled light under taller crops or along the partly shaded edge of a bed, needing less direct sun than full-sized napa cabbage or mustard greens to size up properly. Harvest outer leaves continuously from about a month after sowing, or cut whole rosettes at the base once they reach full size; cold weather sweetens the flavor further. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Oldham's Bamboo (Giant Timber Bamboo)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Oldham's bamboo is one of the most important timber and edible bamboos for warm-climate gardens in zones 8b–12, producing straight, strong culms 3–4 inches in diameter and 30–50 feet tall that are used in construction, furniture, and crafts. Unlike the running (monopodial) bamboos that spread aggressively by underground rhizomes, this is a tight-clumping (sympodial) species that expands slowly and predictably without invasive spreading — making it safe to plant near structures and property boundaries. The large, young shoots in spring are edible — milder and less bitter than many bamboos. An excellent choice for tall tropical screening, erosion control on slopes, and sustainable bamboo production in the warm Southeast. Water generously in summer to support rapid growth of new culms. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ole Timey Blue Collards (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ole Timey Blue'
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom collard with broad, blue-green leaves, representing the traditional dooryard collard type grown throughout the Deep South long before modern compact hybrids became widely available. Plants grow quite tall over a long season, and the leaves carry the classic robust, full-bodied collard flavor that sweetens further after the first light fall frosts. Because it is a genuine open-pollinated landrace rather than a stabilized commercial variety, some plant-to-plant variation in leaf shape and color is normal and part of its heirloom character, and seed can be saved from the best plants to maintain the strain. Harvest outer and lower leaves as needed, leaving the central growing point intact so the plant continues producing fresh leaves from the top through a long cool-season harvest. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Olesh Tres Fine Endive
description: Also called frisee, this endive forms lacy, finely cut leaves with a mild flavor that dresses up a salad or serves as an ornamental. Sow in cool weather and keep evenly watered to reduce bitterness. Blanch the center by tying up outer leaves a week or two before harvest for a pale, sweeter heart. Harvest before hard frost, cutting whole heads at the base. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Olive
description: Olives thrive in the classic Mediterranean climate — hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters — and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, but they require 200–400 chill hours to set fruit reliably. Most cultivars are self-fertile, but cross-pollination with a second variety improves yields significantly. Trees are long-lived and slow-growing; minimal pruning is needed beyond thinning for light penetration. For table olives, harvest when fruit is still green-to-straw colored; for oil, pick when about half the fruit has turned black. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Olive Tree
description: The olive is a slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen with silvery foliage, gnarled character, and small fruit ripening from green to black. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and needs a stretch of winter chill to set fruit well. Plant in full sun in fast-draining, even rocky soil and water deeply but infrequently once established. In zones below 8, grow it in a large pot and move it to a cool, bright indoor space during hard freezes. Prune in late winter to open the canopy and cure the fruit before eating, as fresh olives are bitter. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Oliver Brussels Sprout (Very Early F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, rich, consistently moist soil; stake tall plants against wind; remove the growing tip when bottom sprouts reach marble size to encourage rapid maturing of the rest; harvest from the bottom upward when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Oliver is an F1 hybrid Brussels sprout bred for early sprout initiation — one of the earliest-maturing Brussels sprout varieties commercially available — that produces uniform, round, high-quality sprouts beginning earlier in the fall season than standard types. The relatively compact plants (24–30 inches) with short internodes produce sprouts packed closely on the stem in tight, uniform clusters that are excellent for harvest. The early initiation of sprout development makes Oliver particularly valuable in two challenging situations: in zones 3–5 where the growing season is short and standard Brussels sprouts often don't finish before hard freeze, and in zones 7–9 where the goal is to get sprout harvest completed before the arrival of hot spring weather. Oliver's flavor is mild and sweet, comparable to other modern hybrid Brussels sprouts, with the characteristic improvement in flavor and sweetness after frost exposure. A practical, reliable choice for gardeners who want Brussels sprouts without the 100–120 day wait of heirloom types. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Oliver Loquat (Historic Sweet Orange-Fleshed Gulf Coast Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting the tree where late-winter blooms and developing spring fruit are shielded from the coldest north winds. Oliver produces medium to large, orange-skinned fruit with pale orange flesh that is notably sweet and carries only one or two seeds per fruit, making it an easy, low-waste loquat for fresh eating. It grows as a compact small to medium tree, generally topping out shorter and denser than many other loquat cultivars, which suits it to smaller dooryard plantings along the Gulf Coast. Fruit ripens over a relatively short window from March into May; thin heavy clusters early to encourage larger individual fruit, and expect the developing crop, not the tree itself, to be the most cold-sensitive stage of the growing cycle. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Olosapo
description: Plant Couepia polyandra in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; trees begin fruiting at 5–8 years and can produce heavy crops of excellent-quality fruit once mature. Olosapo is a member of the Chrysobalanaceae family (relatives of coco plum) native to the Pacific coastal lowlands of Mesoamerica, where it is a traditional food tree in local communities in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Costa Rica. The russet-brown to olive-green, oval fruits (resembling a small russet potato externally) contain very rich, creamy, yellow-orange flesh surrounding a single large seed; the texture is smooth and buttery, not unlike a ripe avocado, and the flavor is sweet and complex — combining notes of sweet potato, almond, and a mild tropical richness. The fruit is eaten fresh out of hand (removing the thin skin) or processed into beverages. The tree produces attractive, large, oval, glossy leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by the distinctive fruits. Rarely seen outside its native range but considered by those who know it to be one of the finest-flavored Pacific coast Mesoamerican fruits; deserving wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens in Florida, Hawaii, and southern California. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Olympia Spinach (Slow-Bolt Smooth-Leaf Hybrid)
description: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings once true leaves appear, harvesting outer leaves or whole plants as needed. This hybrid produces smooth to lightly crinkled, dark green leaves on a slow-to-bolt plant, making it a reliable choice for stretching the spring harvest window a bit longer than older heirloom types. It performs well as both a baby-leaf and full-size crop and holds quality in cool, short-day conditions common to winter gardening in the Gulf South. Matures in 40–48 days from seed.

name: Olympian Fig (Exceptionally Cold-Hardy Brown-Skinned Productive Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is a fig cultivar noted for exceptional cold-hardiness and reliable productivity — it is one of the hardiest named figs commercially available, surviving temperatures well below those that damage other cultivars, making it the preferred choice for gardeners at the northern edge of fig culture (zone 6-7) and an extremely reliable fruiting tree throughout zone 8-10. The medium to large fruits have brown to brown-violet skin, amber flesh with reddish tones, and a pleasant sweetness — not as dramatically flavored as Violette de Bordeaux but consistently good and productive. Olympian typically produces a breba (early summer) crop on previous year's wood in addition to the main crop on current year's wood, extending the harvest season. The cold-hardiness advantage of Olympian is most significant in zone 9a and northward, where occasional cold snaps below 20°F would damage less-hardy cultivars; in zone 9b-10, it provides a comfortable margin of cold tolerance safety. Self-fertile, like all common figs, and a vigorous, productive tree that begins bearing in its second or third year from planting. The large, distinctive lobed leaves of all figs provide attractive tropical-looking foliage through the growing season. Figs produce two crops in warm climates: the early breba crop in June and the main crop in late summer through fall. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Omar Arab Tomato (Syrian Heirloom Tomato)
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Omar Arab is a Syrian heirloom tomato with elongated, ribbed or lobed, deep red to crimson fruits 8–12 ounces in weight with a distinctive beaked tip and meaty, near-seedless flesh with very few gel pockets that makes it outstanding for traditional Levantine-style stuffed tomatoes (mahashi), where the tomato is cored, filled, and cooked whole; the balanced, savory-sweet flavor is excellent fresh as well. Adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean-type climates, it performs reliably in zone 8–11 high-summer conditions where other heirlooms drop flowers or crack. Seed was collected and introduced more widely through the work of heritage seed savers in the Arab world. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Omar's Lebanese Tomato (Middle Eastern Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes, spacing plants generously to allow air movement around the sprawling vine. Omar's Lebanese is a Middle Eastern heirloom brought into wider American circulation through the Seed Savers Exchange network, grown for enormous, smooth, pale to deep pink beefsteak fruit that regularly reaches one to two pounds with a mild, low-acid, juicy sweetness. The indeterminate vines are notably productive for such a large-fruited variety, setting fruit steadily through summer heat where many other big pink slicers slow down. Provide even moisture and consistent feeding, since fruit of this size draws heavily on the plant, and support the heaviest clusters to prevent limb breakage. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Omny F1 Daikon
description: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin generously, since this Sakata-bred hybrid produces unusually large, heavy roots that need more room than typical spring radishes to size up properly. Omny is grown through spring and summer for a dependable harvest of smooth white daikon suited to grilling, baking, stir-frying, or simmering as well as fresh salads. Keep soil consistently moist as roots swell to prevent splitting, and harvest before roots become oversized and woody. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: On Deck Sweet Corn (Compact Container Corn)
description: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows, even in a large container, once the soil has warmed to ensure adequate cross-pollination between the short stalks. On Deck is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for small-space and container gardening, reaching only about 4-5 feet tall while still producing two 7-8 inch bicolor ears per stalk with classic sweet corn flavor. Its shrunken stature makes it one of the few sweet corn varieties genuinely practical for a patio or deck planter. Matures in 63–68 days from seed.

name: Onaway Potato
description: Onaway was released by Michigan State University in the 1950s and remains prized among home growers as one of the earliest potatoes available, often ready for new potatoes within about ten weeks of planting. The round, white-skinned tubers have shallow eyes and white flesh with good flavor, best used fresh rather than for long-term storage. Its rapid maturity makes Onaway a strong choice for a quick Gulf Coast spring crop planted in late winter, allowing harvest well before the region's summer heat sets in. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to protect the shallow-set tubers from sunlight and pests. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: One Ball Squash (Round Yellow Hybrid Summer Squash)
description: One Ball is the bright yellow counterpart to the dark green Eight Ball and pale Cue Ball round squash, bred by Hollar Seeds to round out a trio of billiard-themed globe-shaped summer squash. The vigorous, disease-resistant bush plant sets shiny yellow fruit best picked at 2-3 inches across for the crispest texture and nuttiest flavor, well before the rind toughens. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is valuable in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens where these aphid-vectored viruses are common late-season problems. The compact habit and small mature fruit size make it a good choice for succession planting in raised beds through a long Texas growing season. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: One Kilo Slow Bolt Napa Cabbage
description: This napa cabbage forms tight, creamy-yellow heads with a delicate flavor and texture between lettuce and regular cabbage. Its slow-bolt habit lets it hold in the garden longer, and it grows most reliably as a fall crop. Keep the soil consistently moist and fertile for solid heads. Protect young spring plantings from cold snaps, which can trigger premature bolting. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: One-rowed Watercress (Small-leaf Watercress)
description: Grow in cold, clean, slow-moving to still water or in consistently saturated soil at the water's edge — ideal conditions are a spring-fed stream with a gravel substrate and constant cool temperatures below 70°F; One-rowed Watercress is closely related to the common watercress (Nasturtium officinale) sold in grocery stores and is harvested and eaten in the same way, but its flavor is noticeably more peppery and pungent, making it preferred by those who want a stronger bite in salads, sandwiches, and garnishes. It can be distinguished from common watercress by its smaller, rounder leaflets and, botanically, by its seeds being arranged in a single row inside the seed pod rather than the double row of N. officinale. Like common watercress, it is best harvested in cool weather — spring and fall — as summer heat triggers bolting and intensifies bitterness. Only harvest from water sources confirmed to be free of agricultural runoff, animal grazing upstream, and waterborne pathogens such as Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke), which can colonize watercress in contaminated streams; thoroughly cook the greens if water quality is uncertain. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Ong Choy (Water Spinach, Morning Glory Greens, Kangkong)
description: Direct sow or plant rooted cuttings after last frost in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ong choy (also called water spinach, kangkong in Southeast Asia, or 'rau muống' in Vietnamese) is the principal summer green of tropical Asia — a remarkably productive, fast-growing vining plant that produces enormous quantities of tender, mild, spinach-like shoots and arrow-shaped leaves in hot, humid conditions where temperate greens fail. Ong choy is the go-to summer stir-fry green across all of East and Southeast Asia and is extraordinarily common in Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, Filipino, and Malaysian cooking — most famously in the Thai preparation 'phad phak bung fai daeng' (morning glory cooked with garlic, oyster sauce, and roasted chilies over high flame) and in Vietnamese simple stir-fries with garlic. The flavor is mild, spinach-like, and slightly mucilaginous; stems are hollow (hence the name water spinach, as it grows in or near water in its native habitat), and tender enough to eat whole including stems. Harvest by snipping growing tips; plants regenerate vigorously and yield continuously through the hot season. IMPORTANT: Ipomoea aquatica is a federal noxious weed in the US — confirm local regulations before cultivating outside a contained area. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Onondaga Pear (Swan's Orange, New York Fall Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Also known historically as Swan's Orange, Onondaga is a New York heirloom bearing large, yellow, lightly russeted pears with juicy, sweet, aromatic flesh that ripens in fall, filling the gap between summer pears and the long-keeping winter varieties. The vigorous, productive tree was a staple of upstate New York orchards through much of the 19th century. Harvest while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Onslow Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Productive Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Onslow is a rabbiteye blueberry cultivar released for the Southeast, valued for exceptional plant vigor and consistently heavy production of medium to large, good-flavored berries. Its strong growth makes it well suited to establishing a productive planting relatively quickly, and it performs reliably across the range of soil conditions typical of Southern blueberry patches, provided the acidic, well-drained requirements common to all rabbiteye types are met. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Onslow requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Onyx Red Ornamental Pepper (AAS-Winning Purple-Black Foliage Pepper Ripening Red)
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after all danger of frost; Onyx Red is an AAS-winning ornamental pepper bred for striking near-black, glossy purple foliage that provides season-long color contrast even before fruiting begins. Small, upright, conical fruits emerge dark purple-black and ripen through red-orange to bright red, often showing several colors on the plant at once against the dark leaves, creating a dramatic, jewel-toned display in beds, borders, and mixed containers. The compact, uniform mounded habit and heat tolerance make it a reliable performer through the full Gulf South growing season, needing only light, regular feeding to keep the color intense. Fruits are technically edible and quite hot, but the variety is bred and marketed primarily as an ornamental rather than a culinary pepper. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Ooharabeni Asian Pear (Red-Blushed Japanese Hybrid Pear)
description: Ooharabeni is an unusual cross between European Red Bartlett and an Asian pear parent, ripening red-blushed, medium, round fruit in late August to early September with a flavor sweeter and more aromatic than typical nijisseiki-type nashi pears. Its compact tree opens with red spring foliage that turns green by summer, and the fruit is noted for good resistance to scab. Like other Asian pear-type cultivars, fruit is best picked and eaten crisp rather than ripened further in storage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Opal Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Opal requires a moderate chill period, good disease resistance for a modern apple, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A Czech-bred cross between Golden Delicious and the scab-resistant Topaz, it produces smooth, bright golden-yellow fruit with dense, crisp, exceptionally slow-browning flesh and a sweet, mild flavor, marketed since the 2010s as a naturally non-browning apple achieved through conventional breeding rather than genetic modification. The tree carries good genetic resistance to apple scab, a significant fungal disease that plagues many apple varieties, reducing the need for fungicide spraying in a home orchard setting. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once fruit reaches full golden-yellow color for the best sweetness and texture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Opal Artichoke (Fast-Maturing Purple AAS Winner)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Opal is an F1 hybrid bred for fast, dependable first-year bud production and stands out for the striking violet-purple color of its rounded, tender buds, which hold their color well even after light cooking. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining strong ornamental appeal with genuine first-year productivity from seed, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want both a harvest and a bold accent plant among vegetables or in a mixed border. Plants are moderately compact for an artichoke and produce a good number of secondary buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest buds while still tightly closed, since the purple color and tender texture are both best before scales begin to loosen. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Opal Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or temporary cover. Opal is a Mexican-race cold-hardy avocado cultivar grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists as part of the small group of named selections that make in-ground avocado growing possible north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and richly flavored, with the anise-scented foliage characteristic of Mexican-race avocados, ripening through late summer and fall. Cross-pollination with a complementary Type A or Type B flowering cultivar planted nearby generally improves fruit set over a single isolated tree. Established trees tolerate brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit with minimal damage, though young trees remain frost-tender and need winter protection for their first two or three years. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Opal Basil
description: Opal basil is an ornamental sweet basil with glossy, deep violet leaves and delicate pink blooms that make it as decorative as it is flavorful. Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm to trigger quick germination. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun once nights are reliably warm, spacing plants about a foot apart. Pinch flower buds to prolong leaf production and preserve the vivid purple color for garnishes and infused vinegars. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Opal Plum
description: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen. A Swedish-bred dessert plum from a Victoria and Oullins Golden Gage cross, it bears reliably heavy crops of medium, reddish-purple fruit with sweet, juicy, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening notably early in the plum season, well ahead of Victoria, which makes it a valued choice for extending the home orchard's fresh plum harvest earlier into summer. Its good cold hardiness relative to many English and French plum varieties, combined with reliable self-fertile heavy cropping and precocious young bearing, has made it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards across northern Europe and the northern United States. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size in a heavy-cropping year. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Opalka Tomato (Polish Paste Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Opalka is a Polish heirloom paste tomato (named for the Opalka family who brought it to America) producing distinctively long, tapering, banana-pepper to Italian horn-shaped fruits of 4–8 inches with a pointed blossom end and the distinctive characteristic of exceedingly thick, dense walls surrounding very small seed cavities — the result is a paste tomato with more dry matter per pound than virtually any other variety, producing sauce with exceptional body and concentrated tomato flavor without hours of reduction time. The flavor fresh is rich and complex, with more sweetness and less tartness than most red paste types; the thick walls and dry flesh make Opalka exceptionally well-suited to drying (dried Opalka are comparable to sun-dried tomatoes in Italy). An indeterminate plant that bears a large late-season crop; very productive in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens in spring and fall seasons. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Opo Squash (Upo, Filipino Bottle Gourd)
description: Opo, also called upo in the Philippines and known across Southeast and East Asian cuisines as a mild, absorbent summer vegetable, is a shorter, plumper, club-shaped bottle gourd cultivar harvested young and tender rather than left to mature and dry like ornamental or dipper-type gourds. Train the sprawling vine onto a trellis or overhead arbor so fruit hangs straight instead of curling on the ground, and hand-pollinate at dusk with a soft brush where moth activity is low, since the large white flowers open only in the evening. Harvest fruit at 10 to 14 inches long while the skin is still glossy and easily pierced with a fingernail; overmature fruit develops a tough rind and spongy, seedy flesh unsuitable for cooking. Peeled and sliced, the mild flesh readily takes on the flavor of broths, stir-fries, and sautés, making it a staple in Filipino sinigang and ginisang upo as well as Vietnamese and Chinese home cooking. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Optimus Blueberry (Machine-Harvest Early-Season Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Optimus is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for a very low chilling requirement of roughly 150 to 200 hours, an early bloom period, and good natural leafing, all of which suit the mild, unpredictable winters of the Gulf Coast. The firm, round, medium-sized berries were selected with machine harvesting in mind, and the vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes have shown good field resistance to stem blight and Phytophthora root rot. Home growers get the benefit of a reliable, early-season crop on a tough plant that shrugs off the humid Southern growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Orach (Mountain Spinach)
description: Press seeds firmly into soil no deeper than 1/4 inch; germination is improved by pre-soaking seeds for a few hours before sowing. Orach grows quickly into an upright plant with red, gold, or green leaves that can substitute for spinach in any cooked preparation. Pinch the central growing tip when the plant is 12 inches tall to encourage bushy side growth and delay bolting. Harvest young leaves frequently; once flower stalks emerge, leaves become less palatable. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Orange
description: Sweet oranges (Citrus sinensis) are self-fertile; navel oranges and many blood oranges are seedless because they are parthenocarpic. Most oranges need warm nights to develop sweetness and cannot be grown outdoors north of zone 9; the Hamlin and Navel types are slightly more cold-tolerant. Fruit can stay on the tree for weeks to months after ripening, extending harvest, but may re-green in warm weather without losing quality. Apply a balanced citrus fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer for best production. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Orange Balsam Thyme
description: Propagate from cuttings to preserve the distinct orange-balsam fragrance of this thyme. The narrow grey-green leaves lend a citrusy note to poultry, fish, and marinades. Set plants in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun and keep water to a minimum. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain a tidy mound and prevent the base from going woody. Harvest sprigs throughout the season and protect crowns with gravel mulch over winter. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Orange Banana Tomato (Heirloom Orange Paste Tomato)
description: Orange Banana is an open-pollinated heirloom paste tomato from Elberta, Alabama, grown for its elongated, curved, banana-shaped fruit in a bright tangerine orange rather than the usual red or yellow of most paste types. The dense, meaty, low-moisture flesh with few seeds makes it excellent for sauces, salsas, and drying, and the striking color adds visual interest to canned goods and mixed-color tomato dishes. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vine well, and pick fruit as it colors fully to avoid the splitting that heavy paste-type fruit can suffer after a sudden rain. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Orange Bell Pepper
description: This heirloom bell pepper ripens from green to a bright, juicy orange with a crisp, sweet flavor ideal for salads, stuffing, and fresh snacking. Start seed indoors well before the last frost and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably warm. Peppers need steady warmth, even moisture, and moderate feeding to size up well. Allow fruits to fully color on the plant for the sweetest taste, then harvest to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Orange Blaze Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Orange Mini Bell Pepper with Early Production)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at full orange for maximum sweetness; can harvest at green stage but flavor improves considerably at full ripeness. Orange Blaze Pepper won the All-America Selections award in 2010 for its compact plant habit, early production of fully mature (orange-colored) fruit, and excellent flavor quality in a category (orange sweet bell peppers) where most available varieties required exceptionally long growing seasons that limited their usefulness in many North American climates. Standard orange bell peppers are derived from bell pepper varieties with the genetic trait for orange ripening (rather than red or yellow), and this trait is typically associated with an extended maturation period: the fruits must first reach full green bell size before beginning the color transition, and the transition from green to full orange requires additional time beyond what red peppers need for their color change. The result is that many orange bells require 80–95 days from transplant to reach edible orange maturity — too long for gardens with short warm seasons, and even in zone 9 limiting the productive harvest period. Orange Blaze's AAS recognition reflected its ability to achieve full orange maturity 10–15 days earlier than other orange bell varieties while maintaining good fruit size and quality, expanding the practical use of orange bell peppers in home gardens. For zone 9 spring gardens where April–May transplanting targets a June–July harvest before extreme summer heat, Orange Blaze's earlier maturity maximizes the productive harvest window within zone 9's optimal pepper-growing period. Matures in 65–72 days from transplant.

name: Orange Cherry Tomato
description: This indeterminate cherry tomato bears heavy clusters of vibrant golden-orange fruits with a sweet, mild, almost tropical flavor. Start seed indoors several weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once soil is warm, setting plants deep. The tall vines need staking or a cage and keep bearing right up to frost. Pick the small fruits as they ripen fully for the best sweetness and to encourage more production. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Orange Fantasia Swiss Chard
description: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches apart. Orange Fantasia stands out among chards for its vivid, saturated carrot-orange stalks, midribs, and veining, a deeper and more solidly orange tone than the paler gold seen in yellow-stemmed chards, set against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves. It is slow to bolt and holds its color well when cooked, making it a favorite for both the ornamental vegetable garden and the kitchen. Harvest baby leaves at about a month for salads, or let plants mature for six to eight weeks and harvest outer stalks continually, since the plant regrows from the center through a long season. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Orange Flame Mahonia (Orange-Red New Growth Oregon Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding exposed sites with harsh winter wind. Orange Flame is a patented Oregon grape selection prized for its striking new growth, which emerges vivid orange-red before aging to glossy green through summer and turning wine-red again in fall and winter. Clusters of bright yellow flowers open in spring, followed by dusty, glaucous-blue, tart, edible berries on the same spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage typical of the species. Its multi-season color makes it a strong accent in a shaded shrub border. Prune only to remove dead or leggy canes at ground level. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Orange Frost Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Changsha-Satsuma Hybrid Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally in a sheltered, south-facing spot near a wall or structure for extra winter warmth; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar-designated cold-hardy mandarin, a hybrid between Changsha tangerine and satsuma bred to survive colder winters than standard satsuma varieties can tolerate, extending reliable in-ground citrus growing into zone 8 with proper siting and young-tree protection. It produces small, sweet, easy-peel orange fruit with the classic satsuma-type flavor in fall and early winter. Young trees still need frost protection — cover or use string lights on hard-freeze nights for the first several winters — but a well-established, mature tree in a good microclimate can survive cold snaps that would kill less hardy citrus outright. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and fruit development, and avoid heavy fertilizing late in the season, which can push tender new growth vulnerable to frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Orange Habanero Pepper
description: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness. This classic habanero selection produces small, lantern-shaped fruit that ripens from green through yellow to a vivid bright orange, carrying an intense, fruity, floral heat in the 100,000-350,000 Scoville range that has made habanero peppers a staple of Caribbean, Yucatecan, and hot sauce cuisine. The compact, bushy plants are heavy producers over a long season and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions favored by many tropical Capsicum species, continuing to set fruit through the hottest part of summer when some other peppers slow down. Harvest fruit at full orange color for maximum heat and flavor, wear gloves when handling, and avoid touching your face or eyes after working with the fruit. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Orange Habanero Pepper
description: The classic orange habanero delivers intense heat with a fruity, tropical sweetness that shines in salsas and hot sauces. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, as germination is slow and demands consistent warmth. Transplant into full sun only after nights are reliably warm, and the productive plants do well in containers. Handle the ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly once they turn deep orange. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Orange Mint
description: Propagate from stem cuttings or divisions, since named mints do not come true from seed. This citrusy peppermint variety perfumes teas, desserts, and cocktails with orange-bergamot notes. Plant in moist, rich soil in partial shade and confine roots to a buried pot or bottomless container. Water frequently and shear plants back after flowering to renew fresh leafy growth. Divide clumps every two or three years to keep the patch vigorous. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Orange Quince (Classic Round Golden American Heirloom Quince)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Quince is a long-established American heirloom cultivar producing large, round, golden-orange fruit with a strong, sweet fragrance, among the most widely planted quince cultivars in home orchards for its reliable production and good flavor when cooked into preserves, jelly, and paste. Like other quince it is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, blooming with attractive pale pink flowers in spring before the hard, aromatic fruit develops and ripens in fall. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and needs only routine pruning to maintain an open form that allows good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight, the main disease concern for quince in humid regions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Orange Smoothie Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Smooth-Rind Small Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small-to-medium pumpkin distinguished by an unusually smooth, nearly rib-free rind — most pumpkins have pronounced vertical ridges, but Orange Smoothie's clean, rounded surface gives it a distinctive look for decoration and makes it especially easy to carve or paint without ridges interrupting the design. The fruit is a good size for both decorative use and cooking, with reasonably good flesh quality for pies and purees. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or fall display. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Orange Strawberry Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Orange Strawberry (also known as Strawberry Oxheart Orange) is an oxheart-type heirloom tomato producing large, elongated, pointed fruits with a distinctive heart or strawberry silhouette in vivid, deep orange — the 'strawberry' in the name refers to the fruit shape, not the flavor. The thick, meaty, deep orange flesh is extraordinarily dense and nearly seedless, with a small hollow interior cavity common to oxheart types — the low water content and minimal seed-gel gives Orange Strawberry one of the meatiest, most substantial textures of any tomato type, with a concentrated, rich, fruity-sweet tomato flavor that becomes even more intense when the dense flesh is sliced for sandwiches or diced for salads. Orange tomatoes are distinguished by their lycopene profile — beta-carotene and tetra-cis-lycopene rather than the all-trans lycopene of red tomatoes — which is more bioavailable than the red form and contributes to the characteristic rich, fruity sweetness of orange-fleshed varieties. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Orange Sun Pepper (Fully Orange-Ripening Sweet Bell Pepper, Early and Productive)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Allow to fully color orange before harvesting for best flavor. Orange Sun is an F1 hybrid bell pepper variety selected for fully orange fruit at maturity — the distinctive bright orange color of an orange-ripe bell pepper rather than the mixed red-orange of incompletely ripened red varieties harvested early. Orange bell peppers as a category occupy an intermediate position in the bell pepper maturity and flavor spectrum: green peppers are harvested immature, red peppers are harvested fully ripe (or harvested orange-yellow then gassed), yellow and orange peppers represent distinct genetic selections that color differently from red-maturing types. True orange varieties like Orange Sun have the genetics to produce stable, uniform orange coloring at maturity — different from red varieties picked early, which produce a mottled, inconsistent orange appearance and inferior flavor. The walls of Orange Sun are thick and firm, excellent for fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing. The flavor at full orange ripeness is notably sweeter and more complex than green bells from the same plant, as the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids during ripening is accompanied by conversion of starches to sugars and development of aromatic compounds. Orange Sun is early-maturing for a bell pepper, reaching the green harvest stage approximately 70 days from transplanting and full orange ripeness a few weeks later — making it practical for the Gulf South's spring production window before summer heat limits continued setting. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Orange Sun Sweet Pepper
description: This large bell pepper ripens from green to glowing orange with thick, sweet, juicy walls. Pick fruit at either stage to boost overall production and add color to meals.
