Start seeds indoors well ahead of your last frost, then set sturdy transplants into warm soil. Stake heavily laden plants and water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: OrangeGlo Watermelon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, fertile, slightly acidic soil; OrangeGlo is an heirloom watermelon producing large, oblong fruits with striped yellow-green skin and vivid deep orange flesh — the orange color results from high beta-carotene content rather than the lycopene responsible for red watermelon flesh, giving OrangeGlo significantly higher vitamin A precursor content than conventional red varieties. The flavor is sweet and mild with a distinctive tropical, honey-melon note that many tasters describe as sweeter and less watery than red watermelons — the orange flesh has a slightly different sugar profile and flavor that creates a tropical-fruity sweetness. OrangeGlo has been selected from an heirloom lineage for consistent large size (typically 20–30 pounds), high sugar content, and the distinctive orange flesh color that makes it immediately striking when cut open at the table. The unusual orange interior creates a dramatic visual contrast in fruit arrangements and makes OrangeGlo watermelon a reliable conversation piece at summer gatherings. Matures in 90–95 days from seed.

name: Orangeglo Watermelon
description: Orangeglo is a beloved heirloom watermelon with brilliant orange flesh and a crisp, exceptionally sweet, tropical flavor. The large oblong fruits ripen on vigorous vines over a long, warm season. Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger, giving the vines ample room to run. Water consistently while fruit develops, then reduce watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Orangered Apricot (California Breeding-Parent Apricot)
description: Orangered is a California apricot cultivar notable chiefly as a breeding parent, contributing its early ripening and bright orange-red blushed skin to later California selections. Fruit is medium-sized with firm, deep orange, freestone flesh and good sweet-tart flavor, ripening early in the apricot season ahead of many standard varieties. It is not consistently self-fruitful in all plantings, so a compatible pollenizer with overlapping bloom improves yields. As with most apricots, the early bloom period leaves flowers vulnerable to a late frost, so choose a planting site with good cold-air drainage away from low spots. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Orangetti Spaghetti Squash (Orange Spaghetti Squash, Golden Spaghetti Squash)
description: Direct sow after last frost; Orangetti is semi-compact with shorter vines than standard spaghetti squash; harvest when the outer skin is a uniform deep orange and the rind is firm; bake halved at 375°F for 40–50 minutes and scrape the interior with a fork to produce the characteristic pasta-like strands that give spaghetti squash its name. Orangetti is a distinctive type of spaghetti squash developed in Israel through breeding work at the Negev branch of the Agricultural Research Organization, selected for its vivid orange skin color (versus the pale cream-yellow of standard spaghetti squash), higher beta-carotene content in both the skin and the stranded flesh, and slightly earlier maturity than most spaghetti squash varieties. The vegetable has the same characteristic feature that makes all spaghetti squash unique — the interior flesh separates into long, pasta-like strands when cooked — but the Orangetti variant produces strands that are slightly yellower-orange than the pale yellow of standard varieties, reflecting the higher pigment content. The flavor of Orangetti is considered by many cooks to be sweeter and more complex than standard white spaghetti squash, though still with the mild, somewhat neutral quality that makes spaghetti squash a versatile pasta substitute for low-carbohydrate diets. The compact, semi-bush vine habit is more manageable than standard spaghetti squash in small gardens. Orangetti typically yields 3–5 fruits per vine weighing 2–4 lbs each. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Orca Bean (Killer Whale Bean, Half-and-Half Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; harvest for dry beans when pods are fully dry and papery on the vine; in humid climates pull whole plants before complete drying and hang in a sheltered, airy space to finish drying to prevent mold on pods. Orca beans are a relatively modern open-pollinated dry bean variety that quickly gained wide popularity among seed savers and heirloom gardeners for their extraordinary visual appearance: each bean is precisely two-toned, with exactly one half black and one half white in a pattern that closely resembles the distinctive black-and-white coloring of the orca whale — hence the common names 'Orca Bean' and 'Killer Whale Bean.' The coloring is remarkably consistent across all seeds from a plant, though the exact position of the color boundary and the ratio of black to white can vary slightly between individual seeds. The seeds are medium-sized, slightly plump, and oval. When cooked, the dramatic two-tone coloring fades and the beans become a more uniform dark brown to black, as with most vividly colored beans — the show is in the seed, not the cooked dish. The flavor is mild and creamy, similar to black beans, with a pleasantly earthy character. Orca beans are excellent in soups, stews, rice dishes, and any preparation where black beans are used. They are often added to seed displays and mixed bean soups specifically for visual interest, and the raw seeds make a striking addition to craft projects, seed collages, and botanical displays. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Orchard Baby Sweet Corn (Compact Canadian Heirloom Corn)
description: Bred in Canada and introduced commercially in the 1940s by a North Dakota seed house, this extra-dwarf sweet corn nearly disappeared after the original seed house closed before being rescued and preserved by heirloom growers. Stalks stand a compact 3 to 5 feet yet still carry two ears each, with small five- to six-inch ears bearing eight to ten rows of tender yellow kernels and old-fashioned, mildly sweet flavor rather than the intense sweetness of modern hybrids. Its short stature and fast finish make it one of the better sweet corns for small gardens, raised beds, or large patio containers. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other corn varieties if you intend to save true seed. Matures in 60–67 days from seed.

name: Oregano
description: Oregano is a hardy Mediterranean perennial with bold, aromatic leaves that are a cornerstone of Italian and Greek cooking. Surface sow the fine seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, keeping it barely moist until sprouts appear. Transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where the plant develops its strongest flavor. Harvest sprigs regularly and shear plants back after flowering to keep them compact and productive for years. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Oregano-Scented Thyme (Broadleaf Thyme Selection)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where this vigorous, mounding thyme tolerates poor, rocky ground better than richer garden soil. Oregano-Scented is a broadleaf thyme selection prized for shiny, dark green leaves that carry a savory, oregano-like fragrance layered over the typical thyme aroma, distinguishing it from the plainer scent of common culinary thyme. Clusters of lilac flowers cover the mounded plant in midsummer and are a strong draw for honeybees and other pollinators. Use the leaves anywhere a recipe calls for either oregano or thyme, and shear lightly after bloom to keep the habit dense and encourage fresh growth for continued harvest. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Oregon Champion Gooseberry
description: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Oregon Champion is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry long favored in the Pacific Northwest for combining decent mildew tolerance with the classic tartness of European-type gooseberries. The medium-sized, pale yellow-green berries have a smooth, faintly fuzzy skin and hold their tang well, making them as useful for pies and preserves as for fresh eating once fully ripe. The vigorous, spiny bush handles the region's cool, damp summers better than many English exhibition varieties. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Oregon Giant Snow Pea
description: This snow pea produces some of the largest, crispest, sweetest flat pods you will grow, on vines that stay under 30 inches and need little support. It carries strong resistance to powdery mildew, Fusarium wilt, and pea enation mosaic virus. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep evenly moist. Harvest pods young and flat, before the seeds swell, to keep plants producing. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Oregon Grape
description: Oregon grape is a native Pacific Northwest evergreen shrub with holly-like spiny leaves that produces clusters of tart, powder-blue berries in midsummer — one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant edible-fruiting shrubs available. The berries are too tart to eat fresh in quantity but are excellent for jellies, syrups, and wine when sweetened; they are high in berberine, a compound with traditional medicinal use. Plant in groups of three or more for best cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune by removing the oldest, leggiest canes at the base every few years to encourage compact, multi-stemmed growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Oregon Spring Tomato (Cold-Tolerant Early Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden with minimal staking needed, since the compact determinate plants stay under three feet. Oregon Spring was bred by Dr. James Baggett at Oregon State University from a cross involving the cold-adapted Russian variety Severianin, and it was released in 1984 specifically for short, cool growing seasons in the Pacific Northwest and similar climates. The nearly seedless, medium-sized fruit sets even when nights stay chilly, giving gardeners in short-season regions a dependable early, low-acid harvest. Matures in 58–68 days from transplant.

name: Oregon Sugar Pod II Pea
description: Oregon Sugar Pod II is a productive snow pea bearing crisp, sweet, flat pods that are delicious raw or lightly cooked. The compact vines resist common pea diseases and crop heavily over the cool season. Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and provide short netting or twiggy supports. Pick pods young and often, before the peas inside swell, to keep the plants producing. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Oregon Sugar Pod II Snow Pea
description: This heavy-yielding snow pea bears large numbers of 4 inch flat pods on manageable 28 inch vines that resist mildew, pea enation virus, and leaf roll. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep the bed moist. A short trellis or brush keeps vines upright and pods clean. Pick pods while flat and tender, before the peas inside develop, for the best flavor. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Oregon Sugar Pod Snow Pea
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; provide a 2–3 foot trellis or fence for support. Oregon Sugar Pod pea won the All-America Selections award in 1971 and remains one of the most widely grown and most reliable snow peas, selected for both outstanding pod quality and resistance to pea enation mosaic virus (PEMV), a significant disease problem in humid growing regions. The semi-dwarf plants produce large (4–4.5 inch), flat, very sweet pods harvested when the pod wall is still translucent and peas inside are just barely beginning to swell — the 'snow pea' harvest window when the entire flat, stringless pod is eaten. Used in stir-frying, sautéing, and raw in salads, where the flat pods retain their crisp texture and bright color well when cooked quickly over high heat. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Oregon Thornless Blackberry (Thornless Cutleaf Evergreen Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis for the long, trailing, thornless canes, which are more vigorous than most upright blackberry cultivars. Oregon Thornless is a thornless sport of the cutleaf or 'Evergreen' blackberry, distinguished by deeply cut, fern-like leaflets that give the plant an almost ornamental appearance in addition to its fruit crop. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart, ripening late in the season and holding well on the vine after ripening. Because canes are highly vigorous and can root wherever tips touch soil, prune hard after harvest and keep tips off the ground to prevent the planting from spreading beyond its trellis. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Organ Pipe Cactus
description: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun in zones 9–12; organ pipe cactus is a multi-stemmed columnar cactus native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, Mexico — the signature species of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. The dark green, 20+ ribbed columns eventually reach 15–20 feet in height in a candelabra form. The night-blooming, pale lavender to pink-white flowers are pollinated by long-nosed bats, which migrate northward from Mexico specifically to feed on cactus blooms. The reddish-purple, spiny fruits — the pitaya dulce (sweet pitaya) — are among the most important traditional foods of the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert, eaten fresh or dried into fruit leather. A freeze-sensitive cactus (damaged below 26°F) best suited to the warmest, driest areas of zone 9 and the true desert Southwest. Matures in 3650–7300 days from seed.

name: Orient Express Eggplant (AAS Early Japanese-Type Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Orient Express benefits from staking in windy locations; harvest fruits when 6–10 inches long and the skin is glossy dark purple — do not allow to over-ripen; continuous picking encourages continued fruit production. Orient Express is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Japanese-type eggplant that combines the long, slender fruit shape, thin skin, and tender flesh of Asian eggplant varieties with very early maturity (58–68 days from transplant) — a combination that makes it highly productive across a wide range of climates. The long (8–10 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter) fruits have glossy, near-black purple skin and white, very tender flesh with minimal seeds and virtually no bitterness — the thin skin makes Orient Express excellent for eating with skin on in stir-fries, Japanese-style preparations (nasu dengaku — miso-glazed grilled eggplant), grilling, and dishes where the skin texture would be noticeable in a thick-skinned globe eggplant. The early maturity is particularly valuable for Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners who want to get the eggplant harvest in before peak summer heat reduces fruit set, and for northern gardeners who need production in 60–70 days rather than 80–90 days. Highly productive — a well-grown plant can produce 6–10 fruits at once — and the early season timing allows for multiple successive harvests. Matures in 58–68 days from transplant.

name: Orient Nanking Cherry (Historic Self-Fertile Large-Fruited Bush Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Orient, a self-fertile Nanking cherry selection released by the University of Minnesota in 1925, bears unusually large, oval, sweet-tart red fruit on a vigorous, dense, multi-stemmed shrub, offering a genuinely heat-tolerant bush-cherry alternative to true sweet and sour cherries, which generally fail in the Deep South's mild winters and humid summers. Ripening in early summer, the fruit is excellent fresh, for jam, or for wine, though birds compete heavily for the crop. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain an open, productive form, since Nanking cherry blooms and fruits on one-year-old wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Orient Pear
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Orient is a hybrid between European and Asian pear species released by the USDA in 1945 and one of the most recommended pears for zone 7–9 because of its exceptionally low chill requirement (100–150 hours), outstanding fire blight resistance, and reliable productivity in the humid South. The large, yellow-brown, russeted fruits are sweet and juicy with a slightly gritty, Asian pear texture — firm enough to eat fresh immediately after harvest (unlike European varieties that must ripen off the tree) and excellent for canning, preserves, and cooking. Orient trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively easy to grow in zone 9. The early ripening (July–August in most of the Gulf South) makes fresh pears available in midsummer — a time when pear production from the northern states is still weeks away. Orient is considered slightly more fire blight resistant than Kieffer and a better fresh-eating pear. One of the most reliably productive pear choices for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 home orchards. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Orient Pear
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil — like the Kieffer, Orient pear tolerates the heavier clay soils common in the Gulf South better than most fruit trees; Orient is a Southern-bred pear hybrid (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1945, developed specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the American Southeast. The large, golden-yellow, round to bell-shaped fruits are among the largest of any pear variety commonly grown in the South, with smooth, butter-textured, mildly sweet flesh that ripens earlier than Kieffer (August rather than September-October). Orient's exceptional resistance to fire blight — the bacterial disease that devastates pears in humid southern climates — was the primary breeding objective that made it a success in the Southeast. The combination of large fruit size, fire blight resistance, adequate flavor, and low chill hour requirement makes Orient one of the most reliably productive pears for zone 9 conditions in the inland South. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Orient Wonder Pole Yard Long Bean
description: Also called Chinese long beans, this dark green pole variety produces smooth, slender pods that stay tender because the seeds develop slowly. It tolerates weather swings from cool and dry to hot and humid better than common beans. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous vines. Harvest pods young at 12 to 18 inches, picking often to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Oriental Photinia
description: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia is adaptable to a range of soil types and is notably more disease-resistant than the commonly planted red-tipped photinia. Photinia villosa is a deciduous shrub or small tree from East Asia offering outstanding multi-season interest: flat clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by persistent bright red berries that last well into winter, and the foliage turns a brilliant red-orange in autumn that rivals the best fall color of any shrub in the temperate garden. Birds, particularly thrushes and waxwings, relish the persistent berries through late winter, making this an excellent choice for a wildlife-supporting mixed shrub border. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Orinoco Banana (Very Cold-Hardy Cooking and Eating Gulf South Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Orinoco is among the most cold-hardy banana cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a large, vigorous variety with remarkable rhizome hardiness that allows reliable regrowth from the roots even after severe freezes that kill the pseudostem entirely. The cold hardiness is Orinoco's primary practical advantage over most other banana cultivars in zone 8b–9: while the aboveground pseudostem is typically killed in hard freezes below 25–28°F, the underground rhizome system survives temperatures into the upper teens (°F), regenerating aggressively in spring and frequently reaching full pseudostem height again within a single growing season. Orinoco produces medium-large, thick-skinned, angular-ribbed fruits that are excellent for cooking when green (plantain-like, with a slightly starchy, mild flavor that takes on seasonings well in frying, baking, and sautéing) and sweet for fresh eating when fully ripe and yellow to black. The thick skin provides good shelf life and handling resistance. The very large, bold tropical foliage (8–12 foot pseudostems with 4–6 foot leaves in Gulf South conditions) creates dramatic tropical landscape impact even in years when fruit production is not the priority. Orinoco has been grown in Gulf South gardens for generations and is particularly favored in coastal Louisiana where its heat and humidity tolerance are well-matched to the climate. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Oriole Persimmon (Low-Chill Korean Astringent Persimmon)
description: Oriole is a Korean-bred Asian persimmon valued for its very low chilling requirement, making it one of the more reliable astringent-type kaki selections for the mild winters of Gulf Coast gardens where many higher-chill cultivars bloom poorly. The tree bears heavy crops of large, deep red-orange to nearly black-fleshed fruit with an intensely sweet flavor once fully soft-ripe. Because Oriole is an astringent type, the fruit must soften completely to a jelly-like texture before eating, unlike non-astringent Fuyu-type persimmons that can be eaten while still firm. Provide consistent summer moisture to prevent premature fruit drop and grow in full sun on well-drained soil for the best production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Orion Florence Fennel
description: Orion is a hybrid Florence fennel selected for improved bolt resistance and uniform, rounded bulb formation, making it more reliable than open-pollinated types for both spring and fall sowings. Bulbs develop a tight, flattened-round shape with tender, sweetly anise-flavored flesh and stay in good condition in the field longer than older cultivars before splitting or flowering. Give it consistent moisture and full sun to encourage smooth, well-formed bulbs, and harvest promptly once bulbs reach baseball to tennis-ball size. Gardeners who have struggled with fennel bolting in variable spring weather choose Orion for its dependability across a wider sowing window. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Orlando Seedless Grape (First Pierce's Disease-Resistant Seedless Bunch Grape)
description: Plant grafted vines in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, since Orlando Seedless requires grafting onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock for satisfactory growth and yield rather than growing on its own roots. Bred from interspecific crosses at the University of Florida's Agricultural Research Center in Leesburg, it was the first bunch grape to pair genuine seedlessness with resistance to Pierce's disease, the leafhopper-spread bacterial infection that devastated Florida's historic bunch grape industry. Its white, seedless fruit has good eating quality and fresh-market appeal, though the variety is notably more susceptible to anthracnose than other Florida-bred cultivars and can suffer berry shattering as clusters mature, so a consistent fungicide spray program from bud break onward is important. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to reduce disease pressure and improve berry size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Orlando Tangelo (Grapefruit-Tangerine Hybrid Citrus)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and site a compatible pollinizer citrus within about 50 feet since Orlando sets poorly on its own. This USDA-bred hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine, developed in Orlando, Florida, produces medium-sized, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with juicy, mildly sweet flesh that ripens in midseason, generally ahead of its offspring cultivar Minneola. The tree is vigorous, moderately cold-hardy for a tangelo, and productive once established. It is one of the parent cultivars behind several modern tangelo hybrids but is less commonly planted itself today, making it a good candidate for home orchards seeking classic mid-century Florida citrus. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Orleans Reinette Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Orleans Reinette is a classic French dessert apple that stores well and develops fuller flavor after a few weeks off the tree. An old French variety documented since the eighteenth century, it bears medium-to-large, golden-orange, russet-dappled apples with dense, rich, nutty-sweet flesh long considered among the finest-flavored dessert apples grown in continental Europe, comparable in reputation to Cox's Orange Pippin in Britain. Its excellent, complex flavor and good keeping qualities have kept it a favorite of European apple connoisseurs and heirloom orchardists for centuries, even as it remains less widely known in North America than its English counterparts. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for several weeks to a couple of months, during which the rich, nutty flavor continues to deepen. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Orleans Sweet Potato
description: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Orleans is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release developed as a modernized alternative to the industry-standard Beauregard, bred for higher yields, improved resistance to soil-borne diseases, and a slightly longer storage life after curing. Skin and flesh are both a rich orange, with smooth, uniformly shaped roots that store and cure well. Like all sweet potatoes, newly dug roots are starchy rather than sweet; cure at 85-90F and 85-90% humidity for 5-7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches into the sugars that give sweet potatoes their characteristic flavor. Plant certified, virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery-store roots to avoid introducing sweet potato virus disease, which reduces yield over successive seasons. Well suited to Louisiana's long, humid growing season and heavy summer rainfall. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Ormskirk Late Cabbage (Lancashire Winter Savoy Cabbage)
description: Start seed in a nursery bed or trays and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, timing planting so heads mature through the cool season. Ormskirk Late is a traditional Savoy-type winter cabbage bred in the town of Ormskirk in Lancashire, England, valued for its deeply crinkled, dark blue-green leaves and dense, sweet-flavored heads that improve in flavor after exposure to frost, and for standing in the garden through hard winter weather without splitting. It is well suited to a long, cool fall-to-winter growing season in mild climates like the Gulf South. Harvest heads once firm, cutting at the base and leaving the outer wrapper leaves in the garden. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Ornamental Kale
description: Ornamental kale, a flowering cabbage, forms compact rosettes of frilly leaves in pink, purple, cream, and white that light up cool-season beds and containers. Start seed in mid to late summer so plants color up as temperatures drop, since the vivid hues develop with cold. Give full sun and steady moisture for full, dense rosettes. Frost only deepens the color, making this a standout for fall and winter displays; the leaves are edible but grown mainly for looks. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine
description: Purchase rooted slips or start cuttings from overwintered tubers and transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; ornamental sweet potato vine is one of the most dramatic foliage plants for containers, hanging baskets, and ground cover use in warm-season gardens, producing an exuberant cascade of heart-shaped to deeply lobed leaves in purple-black, chartreuse, bronze, or tricolor combinations depending on cultivar. Growth is vigorous in summer heat, easily spreading 4–6 feet per season to fill containers and cascade elegantly over walls. The small tubers that form underground are edible but bland compared to culinary sweet potato varieties; the ornamental appeal is entirely the foliage. In zone 9–11 leave tubers in the ground year-round as a perennial; elsewhere dig tubers after the first light frost and store overwinter in a cool, dry location. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Oro Blanco Grapefruit (Oroblanco, White Gold)
aliases: Citrus grandis x C. paradisi 'Oro Blanco'
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oro Blanco ('White Gold' in Spanish) is a remarkable hybrid of pomelo (Citrus grandis) and white grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) developed by University of California breeders in the 1950s and released in 1980, producing pale greenish-yellow to yellow fruits that appear externally unripe but are actually fully ripe and extraordinarily sweet — completely lacking the bitter notes of standard grapefruit due to the absence of the flavanone naringin, the compound responsible for grapefruit's characteristic bitterness. The result is a large citrus (slightly larger than grapefruit) with thick, spongy peel, white, juicy flesh, and a flavor that is pure sweet citrus without any bitterness — outstanding for people who love grapefruit flavor but dislike the bitterness, and for those who take medications contraindicated with grapefruit. Fruits ripen October through February (one of the earliest-ripening grapefruits) and hold on the tree for months; the thick peel insulates the flesh and extends storage life. The large tree (12–18 feet) is handsome in the landscape and produces heavily. A superb and under-known citrus for Gulf South zone 9 gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Oro de Valle Quinoa (Southwestern Heirloom Golden Quinoa)
description: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun. Oro de Valle, meaning 'gold of the valley,' was developed in Arizona specifically to adapt quinoa to hot, arid, low-elevation growing conditions unlike the cool highland climate quinoa traditionally requires, making it one of the more heat-tolerant quinoa selections available for warmer American gardens. It produces bright golden seed heads on tall, upright stems, valued for both grain production and its striking garden presence. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Oroblanco Pomelo
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil with consistent deep watering during the growing season — Oroblanco citrus requires full sun, good drainage, and regular irrigation for fruit production; Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid (Citrus x paradisi) developed at UC Riverside specifically to combine the large, sweet, low-acid flesh of pomelo with the familiar grapefruit flavor profile — producing a fruit that is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than standard white or pink grapefruit while retaining the clean, refreshing citrus character that makes grapefruit family fruits distinctive. The large, pale yellow-green to yellow fruit (5–6 inches in diameter) has a thick rind and abundant, juicy, very pale yellow-white flesh with the reduced bitterness that makes Oroblanco accessible to consumers who find standard grapefruit too bitter without sugar. Oroblanco is one of the most productive and consistent hybrid citrus varieties for zone 9 — the combination of large fruit size, high juice content, and notably superior eating quality compared to bitter grapefruit types makes it a practical and rewarding home citrus tree in the warm, protected microclimates of zone 9 where adequate winter temperatures allow year-round outdoor culture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Orpine
description: Root cuttings or divide clumps in well-drained, average to poor, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; orpine (live-forever, stonecrop) is a European edible succulent perennial and one of the oldest known medicinal plants, used for wound healing throughout northern Europe since ancient times. Now correctly classified as Hylotelephium telephium, it produces attractive fleshy, blue-green, oval, toothed succulent leaves (edible raw in salads with a mild, slightly acidic flavor, or cooked) on upright stems, topped in late summer and fall by large, flat-headed clusters of star-shaped flowers in shades of deep-rose-pink, crimson-red, or white. The late-summer flowering season (August–October) makes it particularly valuable as a late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies, bumblebees, and migrating painted ladies. Extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived. It is the parent of the Hylotelephium 'Herbstfreude' (Autumn Joy) hybrid — one of the most widely planted autumn-flowering perennials in temperate gardens. 'Matrona' (purple-flushed foliage, dark stems, rose-pink flowers) and 'Purple Emperor' (deep-purple foliage) are outstanding cultivars. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Orpine (Live-Forever, Witch's Moneybags)
description: Orpine grows happily in light shade beneath shrubs or trees, tolerating drier, leaner soil than most edible greens, and its thick gray-green leaves hold moisture the way its Sedum relatives do. Pinch young leaves and stem tips through the growing season and add them raw to salads for a crisp, faintly lemony, cucumber-like bite, or steam them briefly as a minor cooked green in the old Northern and Eastern European tradition of eating this plant. Because it needs so little water and shrugs off shade that defeats lettuce and spinach, it earns a spot in the low-input corners of a woodland food garden. Deadhead the pink late-summer flower clusters if you prefer to keep the plant compact and leafy. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Orrin Chestnut (Good Blight-Resistant Chinese Chestnut Selection)
description: Orrin is a Chinese chestnut selection made by O.S. Good and carries recorded resistance to chestnut blight. It bears modest-sized nuts, around 8 grams, with good flavor, ripening from mid- to late September. Plant it with a genetically distinct second chestnut cultivar for reliable cross-pollination and a full nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Osage American Persimmon
description: Osage is a 21st-century Oklahoma selection valued for heavy, reliable bearing of medium-sized, flavorful fruit that ripens earlier than many older American persimmon cultivars. Its early ripening makes it a good match for shorter-season regions or gardeners who want to beat the first hard freeze. Plant in full sun and resist the urge to over-irrigate mature trees, which are naturally drought tolerant thanks to a deep taproot. Thin heavy fruit sets in vigorous years to reduce limb breakage. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Osage Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Osage is a University of Arkansas-released thornless semi-erect blackberry selected for early ripening (among the first thornless erect blackberries to ripen in June in zone 9) and exceptional flavor — rated by Arkansas evaluators as the best-flavored of their thornless erect releases, with a rich, sweet, complex blackberry flavor and balanced sugar-to-acid ratio that surpasses the milder flavor of some other University of Arkansas varieties. The large berries are firm, glossy, and jet-black with excellent shelf life after harvest. The early ripening of Osage is a meaningful advantage in zone 9 where the blackberry harvest window can be shortened by early summer heat — getting the bulk of the crop in late May to mid-June avoids the worst of the heat. In zone 9 Osage is planted alongside mid-season varieties like Apache to extend the harvest over a longer period. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Osage Melon (Miller's Cream)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained hills after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest seedlings and training vines with room to spread. Osage is an early twentieth-century American heirloom muskmelon, also offered under the name Miller's Cream, distinguished from netted-rind types like Hearts of Gold by its comparatively smooth, faintly ribbed skin and its exceptionally sweet, deep salmon-orange flesh. Water consistently while vines establish and fruit sizes up, then reduce moisture as the melons approach ripeness to intensify flavor. Harvest at full slip, when the stem releases from the fruit with gentle pressure and the blossom end gives slightly and smells sweetly fragrant. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Osage Orange (Hedge Apple, Bois d'Arc)
description: Plant in virtually any well-drained soil in full sun — osage orange is extraordinarily tough and tolerates drought, flooding, extreme heat, alkaline soils, heavy clay, and compaction better than almost any other large deciduous tree; it was originally native to a small area of Texas and Oklahoma but was spread across much of North America in the 19th century for use as a living fence (a hedge of osage orange is literally 'horse-high, bull-strong, and hog-tight'). The dense, thorny branches form impenetrable barriers; the orange-colored heartwood is one of the most rot-resistant and hardest of any American wood, traditionally used for fence posts, bows (the tree's French name 'bois d'arc' means 'bow wood'), and railroad ties. The large, lumpy yellow-green fruits (osage oranges or hedge apples) are not edible for humans but are consumed by squirrels and, historically, by mammoths and ground sloths — the tree is a relic of the Pleistocene megafauna era. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Osage Pecan (USDA Native-Named Series Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and pair with a compatible pollinator of the opposite pollen type for full production, since pecans do not reliably self-pollinate. Osage belongs to the USDA pecan breeding program's family of cultivars named for Native American nations, developed to give growers better disease resistance and more consistent bearing than many older heirloom pecans, particularly in humid regions where pecan scab is a persistent problem. It produces medium-sized, good-quality nuts with a solid kernel percentage on a tree that begins bearing at a relatively young age for a pecan. As with other pecans, deep, well-drained soil and a large amount of room to grow are essential, since mature trees can eventually reach well over sixty feet with a comparably wide canopy. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poor kernel fill. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Osaka Purple Mustard (Japanese Purple Leaf Mustard)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 6–12 inches for mature plants or sow thickly for baby leaf harvest at 3–4 inches; the rich purple color intensifies dramatically as temperatures cool (40–55°F); harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again production or harvest whole plants at the baby leaf stage. Osaka Purple is a Japanese mustard green variety with notably different characteristics from the large-leaved American mustard green types — rather than elongated, flat leaves, Osaka Purple produces compact, round, slightly blistered leaves (mildly puckered like a miniature Savoy cabbage) with an intense purple-red color on the upper surface that deepens in cold weather, making it among the most visually attractive winter vegetables for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 'Osaka' name references Japan's second-largest city and its long vegetable-growing tradition. The flavor is milder and more delicate than large-leaved mustard greens — a gentle mustard note and pleasant sweetness that make it excellent raw in salads and fresh spring rolls, as a substitute for radicchio in salad mixes, or lightly stir-fried in Japanese and Korean cooking. Osaka Purple is one of the most visually useful plants for fall and winter salad mixes, providing intense purple-red color that contrasts beautifully with pale green lettuces and white mizuna; it pairs particularly well with arugula, watercress, and baby spinach for color and flavor contrast in mesclun-style mixes. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Osborn Prolific Fig (Heavy-Bearing Purple-Brown Heirloom Fig)
description: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Osborn Prolific is a long-grown English heirloom fig noted for exceptionally heavy, consistent crops of medium purple-brown fruit with sweet, strawberry-pink flesh and good flavor even in cooler summers. It is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, and its relatively strong cold hardiness for a fig — regrowing reliably from the roots or lower trunk after a hard winter — makes it a forgiving choice at the cooler edge of fig-growing range as well as in the milder Gulf South. Fruit ripens over a long midsummer-to-fall window rather than all at once, which spreads out the harvest for home use. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and shape the tree; heavy pruning reduces the following season's breba crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Osborne Prolific Fig (San Francisco Bay Fig, Cool-Climate California Fig)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Osborne Prolific is drought-tolerant once established and requires minimal fertilization; prune in late winter to maintain desired size; fruits ripen brownish-purple to dark reddish-purple and should be harvested when completely soft and sweet — they do not store or ship well and are best eaten immediately. Osborne Prolific is an heirloom California fig variety of unknown but apparently pre-1900 California origin, named for and associated with the nursery trade of the San Francisco Bay Area region where it became the standard recommended fig for maritime and cool-summer Pacific Coast gardens. Its primary distinguishing attribute is its ability to ripen fruit adequately in the cool, foggy summers of the Pacific Coast, where the heat units accumulated from May through October are significantly lower than in the Sacramento Valley or Central Valley fig-growing regions — conditions under which varieties like Calimyrna, Kadota, and Brown Turkey may fail to fully sweeten or ripen the main crop before autumn. Osborne Prolific's adaptation to cool conditions appears to involve both earlier ripening of the main crop and a reliable breba (first) crop in early summer that provides fruit even if the main crop is delayed by a cool summer. The fruits are medium-sized, brownish-red to dark reddish-purple, with amber to strawberry-pink flesh and an excellent rich, sweet, honey-fig flavor that is considered one of the finest of any California fig variety. Very productive and reliable — living up to the 'Prolific' in its name — it is also a good choice for mild-winter coastal gardens in the Southeast. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Oscar Mulberry
description: Oscar is a red-white mulberry hybrid named for naturalist Oscar Clark, prized for early-ripening fruit that can be picked at the red stage for a tart, raspberry-like flavor or left to fully darken for a rich, blackberry-like taste. It is a fast-growing, easy-care tree that responds well to pruning and training, making it practical to keep at a manageable home-orchard height despite naturally vigorous growth. Ripening runs through mid-to-late summer, and the tree tolerates cold well into USDA zone 5. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Osceola Blueberry (Southern Highbush Large-Berry Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Plant in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil; acidify if necessary with sulfur or peat moss. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw. Osceola is a southern highbush blueberry developed in Florida through the University of Florida breeding program — a hybrid of northern highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) and the native southern rabbit-eye relative (Vaccinium darrowi) that produces a plant adapted to the warm, humid conditions and low chilling hours of the Gulf South. The challenge of growing blueberries in the Deep South is chilling requirement: most northern highbush varieties need 800–1,200 hours below 45°F per winter to break dormancy and fruit properly, a requirement never met in zone 8–10 winters where chilling hours typically run 150–400. Osceola and other southern highbush varieties were specifically bred for low chilling requirements (150–200 hours), allowing reliable fruiting in zone 8–10 where northern varieties fail. Osceola produces large, firm, high-quality berries with excellent flavor — among the largest of the southern highbush varieties — ripening mid-season (May–June in zone 9). It is one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden blueberries in Florida and along the Gulf Coast. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Osha (Porter's Lovage)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun (in cool climates); osha is one of the most important medicinal plants of the Southwest and Rocky Mountain Native American healing traditions — the pungent, dark-brown, shaggy-coated roots with their distinctive, strong, celery-fennel fragrance were used for centuries by Pueblo, Navajo, and other western peoples for respiratory conditions, immune support, and as bear medicine (bears seek out and roll in the roots emerging from hibernation, and the plant is sometimes called bear root). The large, finely divided, carrot-family foliage is attractive in the garden, and in summer the plants produce typical flat-topped umbel flowers in white. It grows naturally in cool, moist, mountain meadows of the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to Wyoming at high elevations where cool summer temperatures persist. In lowland gardens it requires the coolest, most protected, shadiest positions available and adequate moisture. A plant of great ethnobotanical significance and unique aromatic character. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Osmin Basil (Compact Dark Purple Basil, Ornamental and Culinary Dwarf Purple Variety)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F or direct sow after last frost. Pinch growing tips frequently to maintain compact form. Harvest leaves as needed. Osmin Purple Basil is a compact, dark-purple ornamental-culinary basil variety selected specifically for consistent, uniform deep-purple coloration and a dwarf, tidy growth habit smaller than the standard Dark Opal and other large purple basil varieties. The name Osmin may reference Ottoman or Turkish naming conventions, reflecting the Central Asian and Middle Eastern origins of purple basil cultivar development. Purple basil varieties derive their color from anthocyanin pigments — the same class of compounds responsible for purple coloration in red cabbage, blueberries, and eggplant skin — and have been cultivated for centuries both for their visual distinction and for the herb's culinary uses. In the ornamental garden context, Osmin's uniformly purple foliage and compact size make it one of the most useful purple basil varieties for edging, formal herb garden designs, and container arrangements, where the consistent dark color provides a reliable foil for green herbs and bright flowers. The culinary value of purple basil is in the distinctive peppery, slightly clove-flavored fragrance (same family as green sweet basil but somewhat less intensely sweet) combined with the visual effect of purple-tinted vinegars (one of the most popular uses of purple basil), herbed oils, and fresh presentations where the purple leaf color adds visual interest. Osmin's smaller leaf size compared to Dark Opal means individual leaves are more delicate in presentations and salads. The flavor and fragrance are typical of the purple basil group: spicy, mildly clove-like, and sweet with less of the intense Italian character of Genovese. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Oso Grande Strawberry (Extra-Large California Short-Day Classic)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Oso Grande was released in the late 1980s by the University of California strawberry breeding program and became one of the standard short-day, extra-large-fruited cultivars grown across the mild-winter South and California for decades. Its very large, firm, glossy conical berries hold their size and shape well through a long picking season, and the sturdy fruit ships and stores better than many older, softer-fruited cultivars. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual, setting out fresh crowns in October or November for a harvest that runs from late winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to limit the disease pressure common in humid Gulf Coast strawberry plantings. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Ostrich Plume Mustard (Heirloom Fringed-Leaf Curled Mustard)
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ostrich Plume is a long-grown American heirloom curled mustard named for its finely cut, deeply frilled, feather-like leaf margins that resemble ostrich plumage more than the coarser curling seen in many mustard types. The tightly ruffled bright green leaves make an attractive garnish planting as well as a cooking green, and young leaves are mild enough for fresh salad use before the plant matures into fuller mustard heat. Like other curled mustards, it is fast to bolt once day length and temperature increase, so successive small sowings through the cool season give a steadier harvest than one large planting. Older, larger leaves develop a stronger peppery bite and are best suited to cooked greens rather than raw eating. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Otaheite Gooseberry (Star Gooseberry, Malay Gooseberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; tolerates short dry periods once established. Phyllanthus acidus (Otaheite gooseberry or star gooseberry) is a pantropical small tree native to Madagascar and widely grown throughout Southeast Asia, India, and the Caribbean, producing dense clusters of tiny (1/2-inch), deeply ribbed, 6–8 angled, pale cream to yellow fruits that grow directly from the branches and main trunk in a striking display of cauliflory. The fruits are extremely sour and high in vitamin C — almost inedibly tart fresh — but excellent when cooked with sugar to make preserves, pickles, chutney, and a distinctive sour relish used in Filipino and Southeast Asian cooking as a souring agent (similar to tamarind) in soups, stews, and curries. In India, the fruits are pickled in salt and used in rice dishes. The tree is ornamental in its own right — the delicate, deciduous, compound-leafed branches resembling fine fern fronds contrast with the heavy clusters of waxy fruits on the bare branches. In zone 9, the tree may be damaged by hard freezes but usually recovers from the roots. A neglected tropical food tree that produces abundantly with minimal care in warm climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Otto File Corn (Tuscan Eight-Row Corn, Otto Fila Giallo)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-prepared, fertile soil; Otto File is an eight-row flint corn that produces compact ears with exactly 8 rows of golden-yellow kernels; allow ears to dry fully on the stalk; stone-grind for the authentic coarse-textured, deeply flavored polenta that is standard in Tuscany and distinguishes Italian-style polenta from American cornmeal mush. Otto File (Italian: otto fila = eight rows) is the traditional polenta corn of Tuscany, the Italian region where polenta — while less dominant than in the Venice region of northeastern Italy — has been made from this specific eight-row flint corn for generations. The variety name precisely describes the defining characteristic of the ear: each cob bears exactly eight rows of kernels, a consistent genetic trait that is visible at harvest and that Italian farmers used for centuries as a way to identify and maintain the variety. The yellow flint kernels are deeply golden to amber-yellow at maturity, and when stone-ground they produce a meal with a rich, nutty, complex flavor and a pleasantly coarse, somewhat granular texture that gives polenta its characteristic hearty body. Otto File is shorter-season than the Floriani Red Flint (90–110 days versus 100–120) and adapts well to a wide range of climates including the humid Southeast and Gulf South. The compact plant height (5–7 feet) makes it somewhat easier to manage in wind-prone garden situations than taller heritage corns. Otto File is prized by Italian-American home cooks and professional chefs who seek the authentic grain for traditional polenta preparations. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Otto Quast Spanish Lavender (Compact Rabbit-Ear Lavender)
description: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; like other Spanish lavenders, Otto Quast tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity far better than English lavender, but it still fails quickly in wet or heavy clay. This compact, free-flowering selection produces an unusually heavy show of purple flower spikes topped with prominent lavender-pink rabbit-ear bracts, blooming earlier in spring and repeating through the season more reliably than the straight species. Its tidy, rounded habit suits containers, border edges, and rock gardens where taller lavenders would flop. Shear back by about a third after each bloom flush to keep growth dense, and avoid heavy mulch or fertilizer, both of which encourage the rot that kills most garden lavenders. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Ouachita Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained acidic soil; Ouachita is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2003 — one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in the mid-South and Gulf Coast because of its outstanding combination of productivity, fruit quality, and disease resistance. Berries are medium-large (7–9 grams), glossy black, firm, and mildly sweet with a pleasant balanced flavor and small seeds. Yields are among the highest of any named blackberry variety, and the plants show good resistance to orange rust and anthracnose — a meaningful advantage in the humid South. Canes are self-supporting but benefit from a simple T-trellis for row plantings. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; thin primocanes to 4–6 per plant and tip at 36 inches in late summer to encourage lateral branching that will carry next year's fruit. Ouachita's mid-season ripening (about 2 weeks after Natchez) makes it an excellent partner variety for an extended harvest window. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Outredgeous Lettuce (Deep Red Romaine, First Lettuce Grown in Space)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Outredgeous is an open-pollinated romaine lettuce selected for intensely dark red-burgundy outer leaves that shade to green toward the crisp, upright heart, giving each head striking two-tone color as well as classic romaine crunch and mild, sweet flavor. It gained widespread recognition in 2015 as the first food crop grown, harvested, and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station as part of NASA's Veggie experiment, chosen partly for its rich anthocyanin pigmentation and reliable performance. In the home garden it is simply a vigorous, dependable, good-flavored red romaine, harvested either as whole heads once firm or as individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again approach. It bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best quality in zone 9, providing afternoon shade for plantings that overlap with warm weather. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Oval-Leaf Blueberry (Early Blueberry)
description: Native across the cool coniferous forests of Alaska, the Pacific Northwest, and northern Japan, this blueberry relative is remarkably tolerant of dense shade and thrives in the same acidic, mossy understory conditions that defeat most fruiting shrubs. Its pale pink spring flowers give way to soft blue berries by midsummer, among the earliest wild blueberries to ripen, with a mild sweet flavor traditionally gathered fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast and interior. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic and avoid any lime or wood ash near the roots. For a genuinely shade-loving berry crop under established evergreens, this species outperforms almost any cultivated blueberry. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Overleese Pawpaw
description: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Overleese is a named pawpaw cultivar selected by Charles Zimmerman from southern Indiana, producing very large, high-quality fruits — among the largest of any named pawpaw variety at 6–16 ounces per fruit, with a distinctive elongated shape. The creamy, custard-like yellow flesh has a rich tropical flavor combining notes of banana, vanilla, and mango with a dense, smooth texture and relatively few, large seeds. Overleese is regarded as one of the premier flavor varieties in the Corwin Davis and Neal Peterson selection programs and produces heavy crops on mature trees. Pawpaws are the largest edible fruit native to North America and require cross-pollination from a different named variety — plant two or more cultivars within 50 feet, or hand-pollinate using a brush to transfer pollen between flowers on different trees. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be eaten or refrigerated within a week; they do not ship well, which is why pawpaws remain a local specialty. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Owari Satsuma
description: The Owari satsuma is the early bird of citrus, ripening juicy, seedless, easy-peel mandarins in early winter. It is among the most cold-tolerant citrus, making it a good choice for growers in warm-temperate regions or in containers that overwinter indoors. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply but allow the surface to dry between waterings, and give some frost protection during hard cold snaps. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Owari Satsuma Mandarin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, sandy loam soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Owari Satsuma is the most widely grown mandarin in the Gulf Coast region and one of the best-adapted citrus for zones 8–9 where its exceptional cold hardiness (among the hardiest of all edible citrus) allows reliable production in climates that would damage other mandarin varieties. The medium-sized, flattened-globe fruits with loose, easily peeled orange skin and nearly seedless, exceptionally sweet, aromatic flesh begin ripening in October — well before navel oranges and most other citrus — providing fresh homegrown citrus through December from a single, low-maintenance tree. The loose peel (puffy skin that separates easily from the fruit segments) makes Satsumas the easiest-to-eat citrus variety for fresh consumption, requiring no knife and no mess — a significant practical advantage over oranges and grapefruits. Owari Satsuma's cold hardiness has made it the standard citrus for the Gulf South, where it is grown commercially in Louisiana and Texas as well as throughout zone 9 home gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Own Choice Macadamia
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit. This Australian-bred cultivar is prized for a naturally more compact, self-shaping growth habit that needs little pruning to maintain a manageable size compared to larger, more sprawling macadamia varieties, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or smaller property with limited space. It produces reliable crops of good-quality, high-oil-content nuts and, like other named macadamia cultivars, benefits from cross-pollination with a second variety planted nearby to maximize nut set. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and allow nuts to fall naturally from the tree at full maturity before collecting and drying them for storage or cracking. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Oxheart Carrot (Guérande Carrot)
description: A French heirloom, known in its homeland around Guérande in Brittany, bred specifically for heavy clay and stony soils that defeat long, tapered carrot types. The blunt, conical roots grow only 4-5 inches long but swell wide at the shoulder, so they size up reliably without forking where deep, loose ground is unavailable. Sow direct and thin early, since crowded roots distort quickly given their broad shape; the dense orange flesh is sweet and stores well through fall. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Oxheart Pink Tomato
description: Oxheart Pink is a vigorous indeterminate heirloom producing large, heart-shaped fruits with smooth skin, deep pink flesh, and a firm, meaty texture with few seeds. The dense flesh makes it excellent for sauces as well as fresh slicing. Start seed indoors before the last frost and transplant into full sun in warm soil, planting deeply. Provide strong support for the heavy fruit and keep watering even to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Oxheart Pole Tomato
description: This Italian heirloom, also known as Cuore di Bue, bears heart-shaped, meaty fruits that are dense with few seeds and cook down into a robust sauce. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and need staking or caging. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water evenly to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot. Prune suckers lightly to improve airflow and fruit size. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Oyster Nut
description: Plant Telfairia pedata seeds in fertile, deep, well-drained, moist soil in full sun; provide the sturdiest support structure possible as this vine can climb 30–50 feet and bears massive, heavy fruits; water deeply twice weekly during active growth; harvest mature fruits when the skin yellows and splits; dry and shell seeds before eating. Oyster Nut is among the most impressively large of all tropical vines — a forest-margin climber capable of ascending trees to 100 feet and producing enormous, football-shaped to cylindrical gourds that can weigh 40–70 kilograms (100–150 lbs), making them among the largest fruits of any plant. The fruits contain 30–100 large, flat, ovoid seeds (resembling giant sesame or pumpkin seeds) with a thin, papery shell and rich, oily, protein-dense kernel. The seeds are roasted and eaten as a snack, ground into a protein-rich paste for cooking (similar to egusi), or pressed for a cooking oil with a mild, distinctive flavor. In East Africa, particularly in Tanzania and Kenya, Oyster Nut is an important food security crop and commercial oil crop; efforts are underway to expand cultivation. The vines require massive, strong trellises or tree support and will break lightweight structures; plant near a sturdy tree or build a purpose-made strong support before planting. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Oz Hunter Ozark Chinquapin (Precocious Blight-Resistant Selection)
description: Oz Hunter is a patented Ozark chinquapin selection produced from a controlled cross of two blight-tolerant parent trees from Missouri and Arkansas research plots, chosen for outstanding precocity and heavy, dependable annual crops. Burs typically hold one to six small, sweet, high-protein nuts, and it grows notably faster than wild Ozark chinquapin seedlings even without fertilizer or soil amendment, reaching bearing age well ahead of typical wild stands decimated by chestnut blight. Nut drop begins in early-to-mid September and continues over several weeks, so plan on repeated ground collection through the harvest window. Site it on the same dry, rocky, acidic, well-drained ground favored by wild Ozark chinquapin, since it does not tolerate wet or heavy clay soils. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ozark Beauty Strawberry (Reliable Everbearing Strawberry for Home Garden Production)
description: Plant bare-root crowns in late winter–early spring (or fall in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Ozark Beauty is one of the most widely grown and long-proven everbearing strawberry varieties for home gardens — producing two to three crops annually (spring, summer, and fall in cooler regions; spring and fall in the Gulf South) versus the single annual spring crop of June-bearing types. The everbearing fruiting habit provides strawberries across a much longer season than June-bearers, making Ozark Beauty the preferred choice for home gardeners who want a sustained harvest rather than the concentrated single-season production of June-bearing varieties. The medium-to-large fruits are bright red, firm, and sweet — not quite the exceptional fresh flavor of the best June-bearing varieties (like Chandler) but reliably good across all crop flushes. The everbearing habit is maintained by growing the plant without harvesting runners during the first year, allowing energy to concentrate in fruit production rather than vegetative spread. In zone 9, Ozark Beauty performs best when planted in fall (October–November) to allow establishment during the cool season — spring transplants in zone 9 have limited time to establish before summer heat reduces productivity. Mulching with straw or pine straw conserves soil moisture, maintains even soil temperature, and keeps fruit clean. Remove runners from plants dedicated to fruit production to maintain fruiting energy. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Ozark Chinkapin
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Ozark chinkapin is a native chestnut relative endemic to the Ozark Highlands of Arkansas and Missouri, historically less severely impacted by chestnut blight than the eastern American chestnut and still producing viable nuts in remnant populations. The tree occupies a niche on dry, rocky, acidic Ozark ridges where it was a valuable food resource for both wildlife and people — the sweet, thin-shelled nuts were gathered and eaten raw, roasted, and dried for winter storage. Like other American Castanea species, it is threatened by chestnut blight, though some individual trees show variable resistance. Conservation organizations actively collect seeds from resistant individuals for propagation and restoration. The nuts are smaller than Japanese chestnut but excellent in flavor, with a rich, sweet taste. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Ozark Giant Pepper
description: Ozark Giant is an old regional heirloom prized for producing some of the largest bell peppers a home gardener can grow, with fruit commonly reaching six inches or more in length on sturdy, heavy-bearing plants. The thick, crisp flesh ripens from green to red and is noted for a flavor considered sweeter and more robust than many modern bell hybrids. Because the plants carry an unusually heavy fruit load for their size, staking helps prevent branches from snapping once peppers begin to size up. It performs especially well through hot, humid Southern summers, making it a strong choice for gardeners in the region where it originated. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Ozark Gold Apple (Early-Season Golden Delicious-Type Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Released by the University of Missouri as an early-ripening improvement on Golden Delicious, Ozark Gold produces medium to large, smooth, yellow-gold fruit with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh, ready for picking in mid to late summer well ahead of its parent. Its early ripening and heat tolerance have made it a long-standing favorite for southern and midwestern home orchards where summer heat can push standard Golden Delicious to ripen unevenly. Like other Golden Delicious types, the thin skin bruises easily, so handle fruit gently at harvest, and thin clusters to one apple each in late spring to improve size and reduce biennial bearing. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ozark Premier Plum (Large Red Japanese-Type Plum)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart along the branch to encourage larger size and prevent limb breakage from a heavy crop. Developed in Arkansas and long a favorite in Southern orchards, Ozark Premier is a vigorous Japanese-type plum producing very large, round, red-skinned fruit with firm, juicy, amber-yellow flesh and a rich, sweet-tart flavor that holds up well for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. It ripens in mid to late summer and is partially self-fruitful, though yields improve significantly with a second compatible plum variety nearby for cross-pollination. The tree is vigorous and productive with moderate disease resistance for the region, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South home orchards where lower-chill plum selection is important. Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and fruit quality. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ozark Razorback Cowpea (Calico-Seeded Climbing Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis, fence, or tall stakes since Ozark Razorback is a true climbing cowpea rather than the semi-bush habit of most Southern pea varieties. It is an Ozark Mountain heirloom prized for outstanding drought tolerance and the ability to produce reliably on thin, poor soils where richer garden peas struggle. Each dried seed carries a distinctive calico pattern, with mottled color covering roughly half the seed coat, making saved seed easy to identify from season to season. The fresh-shelled peas cook up creamy and richly flavored, similar to a black-eyed pea, and the vigorous vines also work well as a nitrogen-fixing summer cover crop when a section of the garden is resting between plantings. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Ozarkblue Blueberry (Cold-Hardy Southern-Adapted Northern Highbush)
description: Plant in full sun in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system. Ozarkblue was developed by the University of Arkansas and stands out among northern highbush blueberries for its unusual heat tolerance and adaptability to warmer regions that would stress most other northern highbush cultivars, while still delivering the large size, firm texture, and excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor the group is known for. It ripens late in the blueberry season, extending the harvest window when planted alongside earlier-ripening cultivars. Cross-pollination with a second highbush cultivar improves fruit set and size. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old canes each winter to keep the bush productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ozette Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ozette is descended from fingerling potatoes brought to the Pacific Northwest coast by Spanish explorers in the late 1700s and preserved for generations by the Makah Tribe near Neah Bay, Washington. The tubers are long, narrow, and knobby with tan skin and dense, waxy, slightly nutty yellow flesh that holds together well when steamed or roasted whole. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a culturally significant heirloom variety worth preserving in home gardens. Grow it for its genuine Indigenous heritage and distinctive narrow fingerling shape rather than for high yield, since production is modest compared to modern cultivars. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: PA Golden Pawpaw (Pennsylvania Selection with Rich Golden Flesh)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; PA Golden is a Pennsylvania-origin pawpaw selection prized for its rich, deep golden-yellow flesh, smooth fiber-free texture, and intensely sweet, tropical flavor that many growers rank among the best-tasting named cultivars available. The medium-to-large fruits ripen over a relatively long window in the mid-to-late season, and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer once established. Because of its outstanding flavor and reliability, PA Golden is one of the more widely recommended cultivars for new home pawpaw plantings. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, and plant with a second distinct cultivar such as Sunflower, Shenandoah, or Susquehanna for cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pablo Lettuce (Dark Red Romaine Hybrid)
description: Sow seed shallowly and keep the bed consistently moist for even germination, then thin seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear. Pablo is a dark burgundy-red romaine hybrid that holds its rich color and upright, well-filled head shape more reliably than many open-pollinated red romaines, with a crisp texture and mild flavor typical of romaine types. It tolerates a bit more heat before bolting than many red lettuces, giving it a somewhat longer productive window into late spring, though it still performs best in the cool shoulder seasons in a Gulf Coast garden. Harvest whole heads once fully formed, or pull individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest over several weeks, and provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture to further delay bolting as temperatures rise. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Pacamara Coffee
description: Developed by Salvadoran coffee researchers by crossing the dwarf Pacas with the giant-leaved, giant-beaned Maragogipe, Pacamara inherited its Maragogipe parent's notably oversized beans along with a more moderate, manageable stature from Pacas. The huge beans and complex, often fruit-forward cup have made it a favorite of specialty roasters and competition entrants, though yields tend to run lower than more workaday commercial hybrids. It needs the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica types and benefits from consistent feeding to fill out its oversized cherries. Expect a medium-tall shrub and the first harvest after roughly three to four years of growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pacas Coffee
description: Discovered in 1949 as a naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon on the Pacas family farm in El Salvador, this compact, densely branched Arabica selection bears heavily for its small stature and is now one of the most widely planted varieties in Central America. Its short habit allows closer spacing than tall heirloom Arabicas and suits container culture well, though heavy bearing on a small frame means it needs regular feeding to sustain both plant vigor and cup quality. Pacas is also the dwarf parent of the large-beaned Pacamara hybrid, passing on its manageable size to that cross. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica coffees and expect the first cherries after three to four years. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pace Mamey Sapote
description: Pace bears precociously and heavily on a somewhat smaller, more manageable tree than many older mamey sapote selections. Fruit runs on the small side for the species, with sweet orange-red flesh, and ripens in an early-spring window when few other fresh tree fruits are available on the Gulf Coast. Young trees are still frost-tender and benefit from wind shelter and trunk wraps their first several winters, though established trees tolerate brief dips into the low 30s better than most other named cultivars. Harvest fruit while still firm and let it finish softening at room temperature indoors. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pache Colís Coffee (Caturra-Pache Dwarf Hybrid)
description: Pache Colís is a deliberate cross between Caturra and Pache Común, combining two separate dwarfing lineages into a plant that grows even shorter and more compact than either parent. The extremely reduced stature suits very high density plantings and easy hand-picking, characteristics that made it popular among Guatemalan smallholders looking to maximize yield on limited land. Cup quality tracks closely with its Typica- and Bourbon-derived parentage, generally clean and well balanced rather than especially distinctive. Grow it exactly as you would other compact arabica selections, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade and steady moisture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pache Común Coffee (Pache Comun, Guatemalan Dwarf Typica)
description: Pache Común is a spontaneous dwarf mutation of Typica first documented at Finca El Brito in Guatemala, where a single recessive gene compresses internode length and produces a noticeably shorter, more compact tree than standard Typica. That reduced stature lets growers plant it at higher density and harvest more easily by hand, without sacrificing the clean, balanced, classically Typica-like cup quality the variety is known for. It remains one of the most widely planted arabica selections in Guatemala's highland coffee zones, typically grown alongside Caturra and Catuaí under similar management.
