Provide rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, filtered overhead shade, and consistent moisture, and expect a first meaningful harvest roughly three to four years after transplanting. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pacific Purple Asparagus (New Zealand-Bred Sweet Purple Asparagus)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in a trench 6-8 inches deep, spreading roots over a mound of loose soil and backfilling gradually as spears emerge over the season. Withhold harvest for the first two years to let the extensive root system establish fully. Pacific Purple was bred in New Zealand from purple-skinned asparagus germplasm and is notable for spears with a naturally higher sugar content and lower fiber than most green cultivars, giving it a mild, sweet flavor that many gardeners enjoy raw as well as cooked. The purple pigment fades to green when spears are cooked, but the tenderness and sweetness carry through, and the thick spears also tend to be less fibrous and easier to trim than many green varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Packham's Triumph Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping. Bred in New South Wales, Australia in the nineteenth century from a Bartlett seedling, it has become one of the most important commercial pear varieties in the Southern Hemisphere and a significant global export pear, bearing knobbly, irregular, pale green fruit that ripens to yellow-green with sweet, juicy, Bartlett-like flavor and notably good storage and shipping qualities. Its productive, reliable bearing and adaptability to a somewhat wider climate range than more cold-demanding European pears have made it a valued choice for warmer-winter home orchards seeking a Bartlett-type dessert pear. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best sweet, juicy dessert texture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Packman Broccoli (AAS-Winning Early Hybrid Broccoli)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 60–75°F; Packman broccoli is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning hybrid that remains one of the most widely grown garden broccoli varieties — an early-maturing variety (65–75 days from transplant) producing large, blue-green central heads with a domed, attractive appearance and good flavor. After the central head is harvested, Packman produces generous side shoots that continue through the season, extending harvest considerably beyond what determinate, single-head broccoli types provide. The early maturation is particularly valuable for zone 9 gardeners who need a broccoli that produces before summer heat terminates the season, and for northern gardeners who want to beat early fall frosts. Packman is dependable, widely available, and well-adapted to a range of growing conditions — making it an excellent beginner's broccoli and a reliable backbone variety for any broccoli production. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Padang Cassia (Indonesian Cinnamon)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in full sun; Padang cassia grows vigorously once established in frost-free conditions and begins producing harvestable bark on young shoots within 2–3 years after planting. Cinnamomum burmannii is an Indonesian native and the species that provides the majority of "cinnamon" sold in North American grocery stores and spice jars; it is harvested by stripping the bark from young branches and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills, and has a strong, sweet-spicy, slightly more pungent flavor and higher coumarin content than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The tree is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen with oval, three-veined, cinnamon-scented leaves and can be grown as a landscape ornamental in zone 9–10; harvest bark from young shoots 1–2 years old and re-coppice to regenerate the plant cyclically for ongoing production. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Padre Almond (Late-Blooming Frost-Avoidant Pollinizer Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety such as Nonpareil is planted nearby with overlapping bloom time. Padre is a California almond variety notable for blooming later than most, which gives it valuable protection against the late-winter and early-spring frosts that can devastate the crop of earlier-flowering varieties, and it is widely used specifically as a pollinizer partner for Nonpareil orchards for this reason. The medium, hard-shell nut has good flavor and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer, valued in commercial orchards as much for its reliable pollination role as for its own direct nut production. Water deeply through the growing season, especially during summer kernel fill, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer to early fall. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Padron Chile Pepper
description: This early, thin-skinned Spanish pepper is a classic tapas appetizer, mostly mild but with the occasional fiery pod for a game of Spanish roulette. Pick fruits small at 1 to 1.5 inches for the best texture and flavor. Start seeds indoors early and transplant into warm, sunny beds. Harvest frequently while green, blistering the pods in hot oil for the traditional dish. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Padrón Pepper (Spanish Tapas Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. A traditional pepper from the Galicia region of Spain, Padrón is grown almost exclusively for the classic tapas dish 'pimientos de Padrón' — small peppers quickly blistered whole in hot olive oil and finished with coarse salt — and is famous for its unpredictable heat, where most fruit stay mild but roughly one in ten packs a surprising, sharp bite, a trait tied to growing conditions and picking size. Harvest fruit small and green, at 2–3 inches, well before they mature to red, since flavor and the traditional use are built around the small, immature stage. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season, rewarding frequent picking. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Page Mandarin (Page Tangerine)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Developed by USDA researchers in Orlando, Florida in 1963 from a cross of Minneola tangelo and Clementine mandarin, Page produces small, deep reddish-orange fruit with very sweet, richly flavored, easy-peeling segments. The compact, dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be moved to shelter during hard freezes. Fruit ripens from December into February, and the tree benefits from thinning in years of especially heavy fruit set to maintain size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pagoda Dogwood
description: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark. Cornus alternifolia is the only native eastern dogwood with alternate (rather than opposite) leaves, and it produces one of the most distinctive and elegant branching patterns of any native tree — distinctly horizontal, tiered layers of branches that create a pagoda-like architectural silhouette outstanding in winter; its small, fragrant, flat-topped white flower clusters are followed by showy blue-black berries on red pedicels that are consumed by dozens of migrating bird species. Four-season interest: layered winter form, white spring flowers, summer fruit, and red-purple fall foliage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Painted Hill Sweet Corn
description: This colorful open-pollinated sweet corn was bred from a cross of Luther Hill sweet corn and Painted Mountain flour corn, giving it kernels in many hues and adaptation to short, cool seasons. Sow in warm soil in blocks of at least four rows so wind pollinates the ears well. Keep evenly watered, especially as tassels and silks form. Harvest in the milk stage when kernels are plump and juicy. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Painted Lady Runner Bean (Bicolor Red-and-White Flowered Runner Bean)
description: Sow seeds 2 inches deep at the base of a robust trellis or obelisk at least 6 feet tall; this vigorous climber needs a sturdy support and will overwhelm light structures. A 19th-century English heirloom, Painted Lady is grown as much for its striking bicolor red-and-white flowers as for its edible pods, the two-toned blossoms making it a favorite for cottage gardens and pollinator plantings as well as the vegetable patch. Hummingbirds and bumblebees visit the flowers heavily, and the tender young pods can be picked at 6–8 inches for fresh eating, while pods left to mature yield large, attractively mottled purple-and-cream dry beans. Pick pods frequently to keep the vigorous vines flowering and producing over a long season. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Painted Mountain Corn
description: Sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Painted Mountain is shorter than most corns and somewhat drought-tolerant once established. Painted Mountain corn was developed over 30 years by Dave Christensen of Montana through selection from hundreds of traditional Native American and pioneer corn varieties, specifically to produce an open-pollinated flour corn that matures in 65–85 days in the short growing seasons of Montana mountain communities; the resulting variety is extremely early-maturing, cold-tolerant, and drought-resistant compared to most corns. The ears are 6–8 inches long with strikingly beautiful, multi-colored kernels in a palette of crimson, blue, gold, yellow, orange, and white that can produce rainbow-like color gradients even on a single ear. The flour ground from Painted Mountain has sweet, complex flavor; the variety is also grown as a ornamental corn and for whole-grain cooking. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Painted Pony Bean (Speckled Heirloom Dry Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; allow pods to fully mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. Painted Pony is a visually spectacular heirloom dry bean producing medium-sized beans with a beautiful swirled pattern of deep maroon-red, tan, and cream — each bean unique in its markings, resembling the coat of an Appaloosa or pinto horse, which gives the variety its evocative name. The ornamental markings unfortunately fade significantly when cooked (as with most colorfully marked dry beans), but the flavor is excellent — rich, slightly earthy, and starchy with the substantial body that makes it outstanding in soups, chilis, stews, and baked bean preparations. Painted Pony beans hold their shape reasonably well when cooked, making them suitable for preparations where bean integrity matters. A productive bush-type bean (no staking required) that fits well into small gardens and is an outstanding choice for seed saving due to its distinctive and reliably reproduced markings. An excellent heirloom variety for bean enthusiasts who value genetic and visual diversity in their garden and pantry. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Painted Serpent Cucumber (Striped Light-and-Dark Green Armenian Cucumber)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; provide a trellis for the straightest fruit shape and harvest at 12-18 inches for the best texture. Painted Serpent bears the same extraordinarily long, curling fruit typical of Armenian cucumber, but distinguished by striking alternating stripes of light and dark green running the length of the fruit, an eye-catching heirloom pattern that sets it apart in the garden and at market. Like other Armenian cucumbers it is botanically a muskmelon rather than a true cucumber, giving it notably better heat tolerance through Gulf Coast summers than standard cucumbers, with thin, edible skin and mild, non-bitter, faintly melon-scented flesh. Harvest regularly to keep vines productive, since old, oversized fruit develops tougher skin and more prominent seeds. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Pajaro Strawberry (Historic California Short-Day Cultivar)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Pajaro was released in 1979 by the University of California strawberry breeding program and was, for much of the 1980s and 1990s, one of the most widely planted short-day strawberries in California, valued for its glossy, dark red, firm conical berries and good flavor. Though newer patented cultivars have largely replaced it in commercial production, Pajaro remains available to home gardeners and small growers in mild-winter regions who appreciate its dependable vigor and old-fashioned strawberry flavor. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual, setting out fresh crowns in October or November for a harvest running from late winter into spring. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Pak Choi (Bok Choy, Pac Choi)
description: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in spring or late summer in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 6–12 inches depending on desired head size. Pak choi (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) is the quintessential Chinese white-stemmed leafy vegetable grown throughout East Asia for thousands of years and now foundational in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cooking; the distinctive appearance — a rosette of smooth, deep-green leaves on broad, crisp, white to pale green, fleshy stems — is immediately recognizable. Both the leaves and stems are edible and have different textures: the stems are crisp, juicy, and mild; the leaves are tender and slightly more bitter. Used in stir-fries, soups (pho, hot pot, won ton), dumplings, and braised dishes throughout Asian cuisines. Bolts quickly in heat but is excellent as a fall-through-spring crop in zones 8–11. Baby pak choi (harvested at 3–4 inches) is increasingly popular for microgreens and market sales. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Pak Wan (Sweet Leaf Tree)
description: Plant seedlings after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pak Wan is frost-tender and slow-growing, realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a container plant brought indoors for winter. Native to Thailand and mainland Southeast Asia, this small tree produces tender young shoots and leaves prized as one of the most highly regarded wild vegetables in Thai cuisine, with a naturally sweet flavor (giving the plant its Thai name, which translates as 'sweet vegetable') typically stir-fried or added to soups and omelets. It grows slowly and can take several years to reach a size worth regular harvesting, and it has historically been difficult to propagate and cultivate outside its native range, so wild-collected shoots remain more common than cultivated ones even within Thailand. Harvest young, tender shoot tips regularly once the plant is established, and provide the warm, humid, partly shaded forest-edge conditions of its native habitat for the best growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pakistan Mulberry (Giant Mulberry, Long Mulberry, Sweet Giant Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pakistan Mulberry is drought-tolerant once established; trees bear in year 2–3 from transplant; fruit ripens May–June, producing very long (2–3 inch), deep red to black-purple mulberries with extraordinary sweetness — far more intensely sweet than red or white mulberry; spread a sheet under the canopy and shake branches to harvest ripe fruit. Pakistan Mulberry is a named selection of Morus macroura (the long mulberry of South Asia and Central Asia) introduced and popularized in American home orchards in the late 20th century, valued almost entirely for its exceptional fruit size — the berries of Pakistan Mulberry are dramatically longer than any other mulberry variety, with ripe fruits reaching 2–3 inches in length, nearly twice the length of the longest standard mulberries. This extreme length gives Pakistan Mulberry a visual impact unlike any other berry and a practical advantage in harvesting and fresh eating — the long, cylindrical berries are easy to pick individually and contain more juice and sweetness per fruit than shorter mulberries. The flavor of ripe Pakistan Mulberry is exceptional: intensely sweet, deeply fruity, and far richer than the wild red or white mulberry, with a complex sweetness that improves significantly on the flavor of seedling-grown mulberry trees. The trees are large and vigorous (30–40 feet on standard, smaller with pruning), adapting well to the hot summers of the Gulf South, central California, and the lower Midwest. In zone 9a, Pakistan Mulberry performs very well and has become one of the most-sought specialty fruit trees at Gulf Coast nurseries. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Paku Miding (Climbing Swamp Fern)
description: Plant divisions after last frost in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade near a support to climb; Paku Miding is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Unlike most edible ferns, this Southeast Asian species climbs by scrambling over shrubs and trees in swampy forest, and its young, tender, reddish fiddleheads and shoot tips are harvested as a popular vegetable across Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, typically stir-fried with garlic and chili or added to soups. It thrives in the same wet, swampy, semi-shaded conditions favored by many tropical wetland edibles, spreading by rhizome in consistently moist to wet soil at a pond margin or bog garden. Harvest young shoot tips regularly to encourage continued production, and provide a trellis or nearby shrub for the scrambling fronds to climb. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Paladin Bell Pepper (Phytophthora Blight-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Paladin was one of the first commercially significant bell pepper hybrids bred with meaningful resistance to Phytophthora blight, a fast-moving soil-borne disease that can wilt and kill an entire pepper planting within days after heavy rain leaves soil saturated, as commonly happens in Gulf Coast summer storms. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good flavor and sweetness if left on the plant. Because good drainage alone cannot fully protect against Phytophthora in a wet season, Paladin's genetic resistance gives it a real advantage in low-lying or poorly drained garden beds. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Pale Horsemint
description: Direct sow in fall onto dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral, very well-drained soil in full sun, allowing winter temperatures to cold-stratify seed naturally before spring germination. Once established, thin plants to 18-24 inches and provide no supplemental irrigation, as this species is adapted to the parched mountain slopes and canyon edges of New Mexico, Arizona, and adjacent Mexico where it is native. Dense, upright spikes of pale pink to lavender-pink, anise-scented tubular flowers appear from summer through fall and draw hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, and native bumblebees in great numbers. The broad, aromatic leaves carry a pleasant anise-mint flavor and can be dried and brewed as herbal tea; this species is far more drought-tolerant than Agastache foeniculum and thrives where other hyssops fail. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Pale Pawpaw (Flag Pawpaw)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a shrubby member of the custard apple family endemic to dry sandhills, sandhill scrub, and dry oak-pine woodland of northern and central Florida and southern Georgia — a very different habitat than the moist bottomlands of common pawpaw (A. triloba). The white flowers with pale cream to white petals are produced before leaf emergence, showy against the bare stems in late winter to early spring. The small, oval fruits are edible and custard-flavored like common pawpaw but smaller. The larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus) feed exclusively on Asimina species, making all pawpaws critically important for this distinctive butterfly. A rare and threatened species in its native Florida sandhill habitat, valuable for ecological restoration of dry, sandy, native ecosystems. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Palillo (Yellow Guabiroba, Gabiroba Amarela)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Campomanesia lineatifolia (palillo or yellow guabiroba) is a Colombian, Peruvian, and Ecuadoran tropical fruit tree in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) — the same plant family as guava, feijoa, and jaboticaba — producing small, round to oval, bright-yellow-orange fruits with smooth, thin, aromatic skin and a small quantity of cream to golden, very fragrant, sweet-rich flesh surrounding a few small seeds. The flavor is described as combining guava, mango, and custard in one fruit — aromatic, sweet, with pronounced tropical fragrance. The fruit is eaten fresh or made into juice, ice cream, and preserves; it is an important traditional food of indigenous Andean communities in Colombia and Peru. The genus Campomanesia encompasses many species of native Brazilian and South American myrtle-family trees — some famous (like guabiroba, C. xanthocarpa), most virtually unknown outside their native regions. Palillo is the Colombian and Peruvian name for C. lineatifolia; the tree is an important ornamental in Bogotá urban parks. Extremely rare in cultivation outside South America. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Palla Rossa Chicory
description: Palla Rossa is an Italian radicchio-type chicory that forms tight, round heads of deep burgundy leaves with crisp white ribs and a pleasantly bitter flavor. It grows best as a fall crop; the cool weather colors up the heads and mellows their bitterness. Direct sow in mid to late summer in full sun and thin to give each plant room to head up. Harvest when heads feel firm, and a light frost only improves flavor and color. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Palla Rossa Mavrik Radicchio
description: This radicchio forms firm red heads whose color and flavor develop best in cool fall weather, and it overwinters well in zone 4 and warmer. The mildly bitter leaves sweeten after frost. Sow in mid to late summer for heading in autumn, keeping soil evenly moist. Cut heads at the base, and if cut correctly the plants may regrow a second flush. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Palmarosa (Gingergrass, Rose Grass)
description: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; palmarosa is drought-tolerant once established. Cymbopogon martinii (palmarosa or gingergrass) is a tall, tropical Indian aromatic grass closely related to lemongrass (C. citratus), citronella (C. nardus), and vetiver (Chrysopogon zizanioides) — grown commercially as one of the world's most important perfumery and aromatherapy raw material crops. The leaves and stems distill to a pale-yellow essential oil with a soft, sweet, floral-rose fragrance with undertones of geranium — the compound geraniol (up to 90% of the oil) is responsible for the characteristic rose-like smell. Palmarosa oil is used extensively in perfumery as a low-cost rose substitute or adulterant, in cosmetics, soaps, and aromatherapy (antibacterial, skin-conditioning properties), and as a flavoring in some food products. The plant itself resembles a coarser, more upright lemongrass with narrower leaves and a somewhat less pronounced citrus scent — though the leaves are pleasantly fragrant when crushed. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, palmarosa is ornamental and easy to grow; fresh leaves can be used to scent soaps, sachets, and infused oils at home. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Palmarosa Grass (Rosha Grass)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; palmarosa grass is an Indian aromatic grass in the same genus as lemongrass and citronella, cultivated throughout tropical Asia and Madagascar for its essential oil — one of the most widely used in perfumery. The essential oil, distilled from the leaves and tops, is dominated by geraniol (70–85%), giving it a sweet, rose-like fragrance with floral and earthy undertones. It is used extensively in cosmetics, soaps, food flavorings, and aromatherapy and is one of the most popular natural geraniol sources in the fragrance industry. The grass has traditionally been used to adulterate or substitute for expensive attar of roses in Indian perfumery — a use reflected in the common name. In the home garden, it provides an attractive clumping grass that can be harvested by cutting back and steam-distilling the biomass for aromatic purposes. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Palmer Mango (Elongated Florida Commercial Mango)
description: Palmer originated in South Florida in the mid-twentieth century and became a popular commercial cultivar for its distinctive elongated fruit with a deep wine-red to purple blush and its consistent, heavy bearing. The flesh is mild, sweet, and moderately fibrous, and fruit ripens mid- to late season, filling a harvest window between earlier cultivars like Haden and later ones like Keitt. The tree is naturally vigorous but responds well to pruning after harvest, which keeps it manageable in a dooryard setting. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, and protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is easily killed by cold. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Palmetto Southern Highbush Blueberry (University of Georgia Flavor-Standard Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Palmetto, released by the University of Georgia in 2003, needs a moderate 400 to 450 chill hours and ripens in early May, and has long been regarded by Southern blueberry growers as something of a flavor standard among southern highbush cultivars, prized for rich, well-balanced sweetness alongside a vigorous, productive, disease-tolerant bush. It performs reliably across a range of Gulf South soils and climates within its chill requirement, making it a dependable choice for home orchards seeking classic blueberry flavor. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor and fruit quality. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Palmyra Palm (Toddy Palm, Doum Palm)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Palmyra palm is remarkably drought-tolerant once established. Borassus flabellifer (Palmyra palm or toddy palm) is one of the oldest cultivated plants in Asia — documented in Tamil literature for over 2,000 years — and one of the most economically important multi-use palms in the tropics. The tree is the national tree of Cambodia and the state tree of Tamil Nadu (India), reflecting its profound cultural and economic significance. The sap (toddy) tapped from the immature flower stalks is an extremely important product: fresh, it is a sweet, mildly alcoholic fermented drink; boiled down, it produces palm jaggery (tan-neera sugar), one of the most traditional sweeteners of South and Southeast Asia; left to ferment fully, it produces palm wine. The young, firm, jelly-textured fruit segments inside the unripe fruit are 'ice apples' (nungu) — refreshing, mildly sweet, hydrating; eaten as a summer cooling food throughout South India. The ripe orange-yellow outer flesh is edible; seeds are cooked and eaten when young. The leaves are used for traditional palm-leaf manuscripts (the medium of Southeast Asian scripture and literature for millennia), baskets, mats, and roof thatching. A truly remarkable plant of civilization. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Palora Yellow Dragon Fruit (Golden Pitahaya)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Palora is a yellow-skinned dragon fruit selection originally from Ecuador, grown for fruit that is generally sweeter and more intensely flavored than red-skinned Selenicereus undatus types, with crisp white flesh and small edible black seeds. Unlike many dragon fruit cultivars, Palora is self-fertile and does not require hand pollination or a second plant to set fruit, which simplifies home cultivation, though the spiny, ridged yellow skin needs more careful handling at harvest than smooth-skinned red types. As an epiphytic cactus, give it a sturdy post or trellis to climb and cactus-like watering rather than the frequent irrigation a conventional fruit tree would need. Palora is generally slower-growing and somewhat more cold-sensitive than red dragon fruit types, so zone 9 gardeners should plan on container culture with winter shelter rather than in-ground planting except in the very warmest, most protected microclimates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pam Muscadine Grape
description: Pam is a heavy-bearing bronze muscadine known for very large, loose clusters that can carry a dozen or more berries, among the biggest cluster counts of the female-flowered bronze varieties. Fruit runs sweet with notably high sugar content and pulls free with a dry stem scar, which helps individual berries keep their shape and quality for several days after harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-tolerant, and productive once established, making Pam a good choice for a pick-your-own row or a home arbor with plenty of room to spread. Because it bears only female flowers, plant it near a self-fertile variety such as Carlos or Nesbitt to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Panache Fig (Tiger Fig, Striped-Skin Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally sheltered from strong wind; Panache, also sold as Tiger Fig for its striking green-and-yellow striped skin, is a French heirloom fig grown as much for its ornamental fruit as for eating, with each ripe fig displaying bold longitudinal stripes over deep red, strawberry-jam-colored flesh. The breba (first) crop on old wood tends to be the more strongly striped and ornamental of the two annual crops, while the main crop on new wood ripens later in the season with slightly less pronounced striping. Fruit is sweet but not among the richest-flavored figs, so it is often grown as a conversation piece and fresh-eating novelty alongside more productive workhorse varieties like Celeste or Brown Turkey. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and control size, and protect young plants from hard freezes their first few winters, since Panache is somewhat less cold-hardy than common Gulf South fig standards. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Panache Parsnip (Canker-Resistant Hybrid Wedge-Rooted Parsnip)
description: Panache is a vigorous modern F1 parsnip that produces long, wedge-shaped roots with notably smooth white skin and sweet, creamy flesh, developed as a rival to show-quality types while remaining practical for ordinary garden use. It combines good field resistance to canker with strong storage quality, holding well in the ground or in cool storage after harvest. Sow shallowly into loosened, stone-free soil and keep the seedbed consistently moist, since parsnip germinates slowly and unevenly and dry spells reduce stands further. As with all parsnips, delay harvest until after one or more hard frosts, which convert root starches to sugars for noticeably sweeter roots. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Panache Tiger Fig (Ornamental Yellow-Green Striped Fig with Strawberry-Like Flavor)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache (Tiger Fig, Strawberry Fig) is one of the most visually distinctive and ornamentally beautiful fig cultivars — producing medium-sized fruits with unmistakable yellow-to-green and darker-green vertical striping on the skin that resembles the pattern of a tiger or the appearance of a watermelon rind, creating an arresting visual display unlike any other commonly grown fig. The striped skin pattern is formed by differential ripening of the fruit skin, with the yellow portions ripening ahead of the green stripes and both shifting gradually toward gold-and-green as the fruit matures. The interior flesh is light strawberry-red to pale rose — the flesh color and an unusually sweet, almost strawberry-like flavor that gives 'Strawberry Fig' its other common name. The ornamental quality of Panache at all stages of fruit development makes it an outstanding specimen tree for edible landscape use — the striped fruits hanging in clusters from late summer through fall are genuinely decorative. Production is somewhat lower than some other cultivars — Panache prioritizes flavor quality over quantity. In zone 9, Panache is grown successfully as a standard landscape fig tree; it is somewhat less cold-hardy than varieties like Celeste and may need frost protection below 20°F. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Panama Berry (Jamaica Cherry, Calabura)
description: This extremely fast-growing pioneer tree bears small, soft, cotton-candy-sweet red berries almost continuously in warm weather, often fruiting within its first year or two from seed. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established but is reliably hardy only in zone 10-11, so Gulf Coast growers farther north typically grow it in a large pot that can be sheltered indoors during freeze events. Fruit is eaten fresh, dropping by the handful onto the ground when ripe, and it draws strong bird and wildlife interest, making it a useful fast-establishing pollinator and wildlife planting in warm-climate food forests. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Panama Gold Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Gold is a yellow-skinned passionfruit selection bred alongside Panama Red, producing notably large, thick-rinded fruit with abundant, tart-aromatic golden pulp well suited to juicing as well as fresh eating. The vine is vigorous and heavy-bearing, climbing quickly and beginning to fruit within its first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant. Unlike many yellow (flavicarpa-type) passionfruit, which generally require cross-pollination between genetically distinct vines, growers should plant two Panama Gold vines or interplant with another compatible passionfruit to ensure reliable fruit set. Provide sturdy support and regular tip-pruning, and mulch the root zone heavily going into winter in zone 9, since this cultivar remains sensitive to hard freezes. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Panama Red Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Red is a purple-red-skinned passionfruit selection valued for producing larger fruit than many standard purple passionfruit types, with rich, aromatic, tart-sweet pulp well suited to both fresh eating and juicing. The vigorous vine climbs quickly and begins bearing within its first year from a rooted cutting, dropping ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to harvest. Provide sturdy support and pinch new growth periodically to keep the vine directing energy into fruiting wood rather than unchecked vegetative sprawl. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily each winter, since this cultivar shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Panamint Nectarine (Low-Chill Freestone Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Panamint is a low-chill freestone nectarine developed for mild-winter growing regions, producing medium-to-large, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit with a sweet-tart balance typical of good dessert nectarines. Its comparatively low chilling requirement lets it flower and fruit reliably in areas like the Gulf South and lower South where standard high-chill nectarines fail to leaf out and bloom evenly. The tree is self-fruitful and ripens in early-to-mid summer; thin fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in years of heavy set to improve size and reduce limb strain. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pancho Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and shield young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or a temporary structure. Pancho is a Mexican-race avocado bred for cold hardiness, part of the small group of dooryard cultivars (alongside Joey, Lila, and Fantastic) that Gulf Coast and Texas growers rely on for in-ground avocado production outside the traditional Florida and California growing regions. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and rich in flavor with the anise-scented foliage typical of the Mexican race. Because avocados bear more reliably with cross-pollination between a Type A and Type B flowering cultivar, plant Pancho alongside a complementary flowering-type variety where space allows. Established trees tolerate brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit with only minor damage, though young trees need protection their first two or three winters before developing full cold tolerance. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pancho Cold Hardy Avocado
description: Pancho is a cold-hardy Mexican-type avocado that shrugs off chills that would damage tender varieties, extending avocado growing into cooler regions. It is low-maintenance and rewards patient growers with creamy, homegrown fruit. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with deep, fast-draining soil, since avocados are extremely sensitive to soggy roots and root rot. Water regularly but never let the tree stand in water, mulch well, and protect young trees during their first few winters. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pandan (Screwpine)
description: Propagate by removing rooted basal suckers from an established plant and potting into rich, moist, well-drained potting mix; cuttings without roots should be allowed to callous before planting. Pandan is a tropical Southeast Asian herb that rarely sets seed in cultivation and must be grown vegetatively; the long, strap-like leaves impart a distinctive vanilla-like, grassy fragrance used throughout Southeast Asian sweets, rice dishes, and drinks. Grow in bright indirect light or dappled shade with consistent moisture and high humidity; in temperate climates it makes an excellent houseplant or conservatory specimen. Harvest mature outer leaves by cutting at the base; knot or tie leaves before use in cooking to release their fragrance, or blend with water to make an extract. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Pandan Leaf
description: Root Pandanus amaryllifolius offshoots or stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; keep evenly moist at all times; in zone 10–12 grow in the ground in a sheltered, partially shaded position; in cooler zones grow in a large container brought inside in winter. Pandan Leaf is the vanilla of Southeast Asia — the green, aromatic leaves of this compact pandanus screwpine are as fundamental to Southeast Asian cooking as vanilla is to Western baking, providing an intensely fragrant, green, vanilla-coconut aroma and flavor to an extraordinary range of foods. The long, stiff, bright-green leaves (tied in knots and simmered in dishes, or juiced and blended into batters) flavor coconut rice (nasi lemak), ketan (sticky rice cakes), chiffon cakes, kaya jam, onde-onde, and countless other Southeast Asian sweets and desserts. Pandan juice (squeezed from crushed leaves) provides a vivid natural green color and strong flavor to pandan chiffon cake and kueh (traditional sweets). The active flavor compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline — the same compound found in basmati rice and jasmine flowers — explaining its distinctive, reminiscent aroma. Unlike most Pandanus, this species is known only from cultivation (never found in the wild) and reproduces entirely vegetatively by offshoots; it is believed to be a sterile cultigen developed in ancient Southeast Asian agriculture. Indispensable for any garden serving Southeast Asian cuisine. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Panniyur-1 Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, training the vine up a sturdy living or artificial support post. Panniyur-1 was released in 1961 by the Pepper Research Station in Panniyur, Kerala, India, as the first officially released high-yielding black pepper hybrid, valued for heavier fruit clusters and greater productivity than traditional local types. Maintain consistent humidity and warmth above 60°F year-round, water regularly without letting the root zone dry out, and provide light shade especially while the vine is young and establishing. Vines typically begin bearing three to four years after planting and continue producing for many years with proper support and fertility management. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Panniyur-2 Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, training the vine up a sturdy living or artificial support post. Released by the Pepper Research Station in Panniyur, Kerala, India as a successor to the original Panniyur-1 hybrid, Panniyur-2 was bred specifically for improved tolerance to Phytophthora foot rot, the most economically damaging disease of cultivated black pepper, while retaining good yield potential. It is commonly recommended for growing sites with higher disease pressure where Panniyur-1 alone proves too vulnerable. Maintain consistent humidity, warmth above 60°F, and even soil moisture without waterlogging, and expect bearing to begin three to four years after planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pantano Romanesco Tomato (Ribbed Roman Heirloom Slicer)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Pantano Romanesco bears medium-to-large, deeply ribbed red-pink fruit with a flattened shape and rich, complex flavor prized in Roman home cooking for both fresh eating and sauce, the pronounced ribbing and slightly irregular form typical of many traditional Italian heirloom slicers. Its productive vines and well-adapted heat tolerance suit warm growing regions. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Pantin Mamey Sapote
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil with room for a large canopy; Pantin is one of the oldest and most widely planted named mamey sapote cultivars in South Florida, tracing to early Cuban plantings in Miami-Dade County, and remains a benchmark for commercial-quality fruit. The large, football-shaped fruit has rough, russet-brown skin and dense, salmon-pink to brick-red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor often described as a cross between pumpkin, sweet potato, and almond. Trees are vigorous, long-lived, and eventually very large, so site them well away from structures and power lines. Harvest by scratching the skin lightly — ready fruit shows green beneath the russet surface — then ripen at room temperature for several days to a week until it yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Papalo
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in the garden once soil is warm and all frost danger has passed; papalo does not transplant well due to its taproot. This Mexican culinary herb is used raw, added at the table rather than during cooking — heat destroys its unique flavor, which blends notes of cilantro, rue, and citrus. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates heat and moderate drought admirably, making it valuable as a summer substitute for cilantro. Harvest young leaves and stem tips regularly while the plant is in vegetative growth; use very sparingly as the flavor is more intense than cilantro. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Papaloquelite (Poreleaf, Quilquiña, Mexican Coriander)
description: Sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; papaloquelite is a traditional Mesoamerican culinary herb used throughout Mexico, Central America, and Bolivia with a distinctive aroma that combines cilantro, rue, and a strong, almost petroleum-like note that is at once exotic and intensely savory — the flavor used extensively in Mexican salsas, pozole, tacos de canasta, and Oaxacan cooking as a bolder, heat-stable alternative to cilantro. Unlike cilantro, which wilts when heated, papaloquelite retains flavor when briefly cooked and is used as a fresh herb added at the end of cooking or stirred into hot soups tableside. The oval, glandular-dotted leaves on the blue-green stems are harvested by pinching stem tips regularly. In zone 9 it grows as a warm-season annual that self-seeds freely in favorable sites; drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the heat that limits cilantro production in Gulf Coast summers, making it a superb cilantro substitute for tropical-climate gardeners. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Papaya
description: Papaya is one of the fastest-bearing fruit plants — grafted or transplanted seedlings can fruit within 6–12 months of planting. It is highly sensitive to frost, waterlogged soil, and root disturbance; plant in well-raised, excellently drained beds and never let roots sit in water even briefly. Most commercial papaya is hermaphroditic (self-fertile), allowing a single tree to produce fruit; dioecious types require a male plant within 20 feet. Cut the growing tip back at 3–4 ft to encourage a compact, easily harvested form. Harvest when at least one-quarter of the skin has turned yellow; ripen fully at room temperature and refrigerate only after fully ripe. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Papaya Pear Squash (Small Pear-Shaped Ornamental-Edible Gourd)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb. Papaya Pear is a small, distinctively pear-shaped squash with pale, mottled skin, harvested young at three to four inches as a tender, mild summer squash for cooking, or left to mature into a firmer, longer-keeping fruit valued as a novelty ornamental for fall displays alongside gourds and pumpkins. This dual-purpose flexibility — usable young in the kitchen or later as an attractive harvest decoration — makes it a fun addition to a vegetable garden looking for something beyond standard zucchini and yellow squash. Pick young fruit every few days for the best culinary texture, or leave select fruit to fully mature and harden for fall display and longer storage. Matures in 50–90 days from seed.

name: Papuan Nutmeg (Fakfak Nutmeg)
description: Plant seedling trees in spring in deep, humid, well-drained soil under partial canopy shade, replicating the equatorial rainforest understory of Papua and West Papua, Indonesia, where this species is endemic. Also called Fakfak nutmeg for the district where it is most heavily harvested, Myristica argentea yields a seed and aril that are traded regionally as a nutmeg and mace substitute with a milder, less resinous aroma than true nutmeg, and the fat-rich seed is additionally pressed into 'nutmeg butter,' a semisolid oil used in traditional medicine, soap, and perfumery rather than as a culinary spice on its own. The tree's silvery-backed leaves, giving rise to the species name argentea, help distinguish it from other regional wild nutmegs. Wild populations are assessed as vulnerable, making cultivated specimens valuable for both spice interest and conservation. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Par-Cel Celery (Leaf Celery)
description: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Par-Cel is grown for its leaves rather than a blanched stalk and is much easier and faster to raise than standard stalk celery. This cutting-type celery produces a bushy clump of thin, dark green, flat-leaf-parsley-like stems and foliage with full, concentrated celery flavor, cut and used as a seasoning herb rather than eaten as a crunchy stalk vegetable. It resists bolting and disease better than conventional celery, tolerates the light shade and humidity of a Gulf South summer far better than blanched celery, and regrows readily after cutting for a season-long harvest. Snip outer stems as needed for soups, stocks, and stuffing, always leaving the center growing point intact to keep the plant productive. Matures in 55–80 days from seed.

name: Parade Bunching Onion
description: Direct sow thinly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Parade is a bunching onion (Japanese-type scallion or green onion) producing straight, uniform, single-stemmed plants with bright white bases, upright green tops, and a clean, mild, sweet flavor — the ideal scallion for fresh eating, garnishing, and all uses where an attractive, uniform appearance matters. Unlike multiplying types that form clusters of small bulbs, Parade produces a single straight stem that is easier to harvest, wash, and present. The non-bulbing, perennial-type Allium fistulosum species tolerates more cold, heat, and wet soil than common bulbing onions, making it well-suited to zone 9 year-round production. Parade is widely used in commercial food service and restaurant settings precisely because the straight, single-stem habit provides uniform portions without the cleaning and sorting of cluster types. In zone 9 plant Parade in fall for the cleanest, sweetest harvest through winter and spring. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Paradise Mulberry
description: Paradise is a thornless, self-fertile mulberry that stays a compact, broad-canopied small tree rather than growing into the large shade tree many mulberry seedlings become, making it easier to manage and harvest in a home garden. Fruit is ivory-colored with a light purple blush at full ripeness, medium-sized, and very sweet, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the mulberry season. It handles heat and humidity exceptionally well and tolerates drought once established, though it should be sited with some protection from deer browsing, since young growth is palatable. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil for the heaviest fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Paradise Nut (Zabucajo, Monkey Pot, Sapucaia Nut)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic, deep soil; Paradise Nut Tree grows best in conditions that approximate the humid, fertile soils of its native Amazonian rainforest habitat — deep, moist, well-drained, organic-rich soil with regular rainfall. Lecythis zabucajo is a large, majestic tropical tree from the Amazon Basin (Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), grown for its edible seeds and as a remarkable ornamental specimen. The tree is closely related to the Brazil Nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and produces similar large, round, woody pods — but with a crucial difference: the pod of L. zabucajo has a natural operculum (lid) that opens at maturity to release the seeds, while the Brazil Nut pod does not open and must be cracked. The open-lidded pods ('monkey pots') have a narrow neck opening that is a natural primate trap: a monkey can reach in and grab a nut, but cannot withdraw its closed fist, and must release the nut or remain trapped — a phenomenon documented and described by naturalists since the 16th century. The Paradise Nuts themselves — large, brown, oily, rich — are considered by those who have tasted both to be superior to Brazil Nuts in flavor and richness. In zone 10-11 collections and botanical gardens, L. zabucajo is grown as both an edible nut tree and an ornamental specimen for its year-round beauty, including attractive pink flowers. Matures in 1095–3650 days from transplant.

name: Paradise Tree (Aceituno)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; paradise tree is a multipurpose tropical tree from Central and South America producing large, pinnately compound leaves that create a lush, tropical canopy effect. Small, fragrant, yellowish flowers produce clusters of small, dark purple olives containing seeds with 60–75% oil content — one of the highest vegetable oil contents of any plant, approaching the palmitic/oleic profile suitable for both food use and biodiesel production. The tree is extremely fast-growing (20+ feet per year in tropical conditions), drought-tolerant once established, and being actively developed as a low-input bioenergy crop in tropical developing countries. The red-and-yellow immature fruits and the dark purple ripe fruits are ornamentally attractive. Of very limited landscape use in the US outside zone 10–11 Florida, but grown as an agroforestry specimen. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Paradiso Fig (Historic Neapolitan Heirloom)
description: Paradiso is an old Neapolitan variety recorded in early-19th-century Italian pomological literature and long grown around the Mediterranean under regional names such as Brogiotto and Albero d'Oro. It is an early-ripening, two-crop fig with green-to-yellow skin and dark red pulp carrying an intense strawberry-berry sweetness. Because the name was widely reused by different growers over the centuries, several distinct strains circulate in today's collector trade under different labels, so expect some variation between sources. Even accounting for that uncertainty, well-sourced Paradiso trees are consistently praised for rich flavor and reliable early cropping. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Paradox Walnut Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root seedlings in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; Paradox is a vigorous hybrid understock, not grown for its own nuts. A hybrid between Northern California black walnut and English walnut, first noticed for its unusually vigorous, fast growth compared to either parent species, it has become the standard rootstock for commercial English walnut production in California, imparting notably greater vigor, earlier bearing, and better tolerance of a range of soil conditions than seedling English walnut rootstock. Traditional seedling-grown Paradox is genetically variable since it arises from open-pollinated crosses, which has driven development of named clonal selections such as RX1 and VX211 for more uniform, disease-resistant performance. Graft a desired named English walnut variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the resulting tree ample permanent space, since walnut on Paradox rootstock grows into a very large, long-lived tree. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Parainema Coffee
description: Bred by IHCAFE in Honduras from a cross between Villa Sarchi and Hibrido de Timor, Parainema belongs to the Sarchimor family and carries strong resistance to coffee leaf rust inherited from its Timor parent. Unlike many rust-resistant hybrids that sacrifice cup quality for disease resistance, Parainema has earned specialty-grade recognition when grown at good elevation, a legacy of the well-regarded Villa Sarchi side of its parentage. The plant stays compact and dwarf, similar in stature to Caturra, which lets growers set trees closer together and increase yield per hectare on the medium-altitude farms across Honduras, Nicaragua, and El Salvador where it now thrives. Grow it as other dwarf Central American arabica selections, with rich, well-drained acidic soil and dappled shade. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Paramount Parsley (Triple-Curled)
description: Paramount is an older American curled parsley bred for dense, thick, triple-ruffled leaves on plants noticeably taller than most curly types, giving it a bold, upright presence as a border or edging plant as well as a kitchen herb. The heavy curl holds up well as a plate garnish while still delivering good fresh parsley flavor for cooking. Because the plants grow tall and full, space them slightly wider than compact curly cultivars and harvest outer stems regularly to keep new curled growth coming from the crown. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Parfianka Pomegranate (Central Asian Premium Pomegranate, Soft-Seeded Supreme)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat — ideal for zone 9a; harvest when the skin deepens to full deep red and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped (late September–November in the Gulf South); Parfianka arils are strikingly deep red and the juice intensely colored. Parfianka is a Central Asian pomegranate variety (originally from Uzbekistan or the broader Turkestan region, where pomegranates have been cultivated for millennia) that has become the acknowledged gold standard of pomegranate flavor among American pomegranate enthusiasts, consistently winning blind tasting competitions at California Rare Fruit Growers Society events and receiving the highest ratings in UC Cooperative Extension pomegranate variety trials. The arils are brilliant deep crimson-red — darker and more richly colored than Wonderful (the commercial standard) — and have a flavor combination that separates Parfianka from other varieties: intensely sweet with balanced acidity, complex fruity aromatics, and remarkably soft, almost undetectable seeds. The seed softness (characteristic of the 'soft-seeded' varieties from Central Asia) means the arils can be eaten whole without the crunching sensation that bothers some pomegranate consumers. The juice is vivid deep red, exceptionally flavorful, and produces the finest pomegranate juice of any commercially available variety. For zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners willing to invest in the best possible fresh-eating pomegranate, Parfianka is the clear first choice — a tree that rewards with the finest-quality pomegranates available in home production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Paris Market Carrot
description: This round French heirloom carrot forms golf-ball-sized roots that thrive in clay or rocky ground where long carrots struggle. Sow seed thinly and shallowly, keeping the surface damp until the slow seedlings emerge. Thin to 2 inches to allow the little globes to plump up evenly. Because roots are short, they mature quickly and are excellent for containers. Harvest young at about 1 to 1.5 inches across for the sweetest, most tender roots. Matures in 50–68 days from seed.

name: Parisian Carrot (Tonda di Parigi Round French Heirloom Carrot)
description: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fine, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently moist until seedlings establish, since carrot seed germinates slowly and unevenly. Parisian, also sold as Tonda di Parigi, is a 19th-century French heirloom grown for round, roughly golf-ball-sized roots rather than the long tapered shape of most carrots, which makes it a reliable performer in the shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils that deform standard long carrots. The sweet, tender orange flesh and small size also make it an excellent choice for container growing on patios and small raised beds. Thin seedlings to two to three inches apart for well-rounded roots, and harvest as soon as they reach full size, since the round shape can turn woody if left too long in warm soil. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Parisian Pickling Cucumber (Cornichon de Paris)
description: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil, and provide a low trellis or ample ground space for the compact vines. Parisian Pickling is a traditional French cornichon cucumber grown for centuries around Paris and other French market gardens, producing an abundance of small, bumpy, dark green fruit that must be picked daily, often at under two inches long, to catch them at the ideal size for classic French cornichon pickles served alongside pâté and charcuterie. The vines are prolific once picking begins in earnest, since frequent harvest of the smallest fruit encourages continuous new fruit set through the season. Flavor is crisp and mild even at the smallest sizes, distinguishing true cornichon types from cucumbers merely picked young. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Parkhill Saskatoon (Serviceberry)
description: Parkhill is a U.S.-origin saskatoon cultivar that has been widely adopted in Canadian commercial plantings for its large, deep blue, tangy-sweet fruit borne in long, heavy clusters. Its later bloom time reduces frost damage to flowers compared with earlier-blooming cultivars, improving fruit set reliability in variable spring weather. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and give it plenty of space, since mature plants can reach 15 feet tall and wide. Harvest in clusters once berries turn deep blue and detach easily, similar to picking blueberries. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Parris Island Cos Romaine (Classic Upright Tall Romaine Lettuce)
description: Transplant or direct sow; thin to 8–10 inches for full heads. Harvest whole head or pull outer leaves. Parris Island Cos is a tall romaine (cos) lettuce — named for Parris Island, South Carolina, from the coastal region where the variety was developed and popularized — that became the dominant commercial romaine type in the United States during the mid-20th century and has remained the standard against which other romaine varieties are measured. Romaine (cos) lettuce differs from butterhead and loose-leaf types in its characteristic tall, upright, tightly folded form — the outer leaves are held upright and pressed together, creating a tall, narrow head with a pale, creamy, slightly blanched interior of great crispness and sweetness that is unavailable in the more loosely arranged butterhead types. The inner heart leaves of Parris Island Cos are the hallmark of a proper Caesar salad — the firm-textured, slightly bitter, crisp interior ribs and pale yellow-green heart that define the authentic Caesar experience. Parris Island Cos has good bolt resistance for a romaine (better than some other varieties) and thrives in the cool fall-through-spring window of Gulf South gardens in zone 8–9, where it produces high-quality heads with the sweetness and crispness that makes this variety so widely planted. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Parris Island Cos Romaine Lettuce
description: This classic romaine, developed by the USDA and Clemson around 1950, forms upright 10 to 12 inch heads with crunchy sweet leaves and a buttery green heart. It shows good heat tolerance and vigor. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist for tender leaves. Harvest whole heads or pick outer leaves, and offer light shade in summer heat to delay bolting. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Parris Island Romaine Lettuce
description: Parris Island is a classic romaine (cos) heirloom forming large, upright heads up to a foot tall with firm green outer leaves and tender, blanched hearts. It shows good heat resistance for a lettuce, making it dependable into early summer. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, keeping soil consistently moist. Give full sun in cool weather, and harvest whole heads when firm or take outer leaves as needed. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Parry Pinyon Pine (Four-Leaf Pinyon)
description: Plant in dry, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking the arid desert-mountain slopes of the southern California and Baja California peninsular ranges where this species naturally occurs. Parry pinyon is unusual among pinyons for bearing needles in bundles of four rather than the more typical one or two, giving rise to its alternate name of four-leaf pinyon, and it forms a slow-growing, rounded small tree well adapted to poor, thin desert soils. It produces large, wingless, edible seeds similar in size and quality to other pinyon pines and has long been harvested by Indigenous peoples of the Colorado Desert region. Extremely drought tolerant once established and essentially intolerant of summer irrigation or heavy soils. Matures in 730–3650 days from transplant.

name: Parsley Italian Giant
description: Italian Giant is a robust flat-leaved parsley prized by cooks for its strong, fresh flavor and easy-to-chop leaves. Grown as an annual, it produces large, dark green leaves ideal for soups, stews, and garnishes. Sow seed directly or start indoors, keeping the soil consistently moist since germination is slow and can take up to three weeks. Give it full sun to part shade and harvest outer stems first so the plant keeps producing. It tolerates light frost and can be grown in containers on a sunny windowsill. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Parsnip
description: Sow 3 seeds per station 1/2 in deep in very deeply dug, stone-free soil and thin to the strongest seedling; long taproots will fork in compacted ground. Parsnip germination is notoriously slow and erratic — sowing radish seed in the same row acts as a quick-germinating row marker. Leave roots in the ground through autumn frosts, which convert starches to sugars for a sweeter harvest. Wear gloves when handling foliage in bright sun to avoid phototoxic sap burns. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Parson Brown Orange (Oldest Commercial Florida Sweet Orange)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parson Brown is the earliest-ripening common sweet orange, ready from October, and is notably more cold-tolerant than later-season Florida oranges, which historically made it valuable for the northern edge of the citrus belt. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Partenon Zucchini (Parthenocarpic Seedless-Set Hybrid Squash)
description: Because Partenon sets fruit without pollination, it can be sown a bit earlier than standard zucchini and grown successfully under row cover or in a high tunnel where pollinator activity is limited. Direct sow or transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants about 30 inches apart. The dark-green, cylindrical fruit is exceptionally uniform, making Partenon a favorite among market growers who need consistent size and shape for bunching. Harvest young at 6-8 inches, since parthenocarpic zucchini can size up quickly once fruit set begins. Matures in 48–50 days from seed.

name: Paseante Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)
description: One of five Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes released by UC Davis in 2019, Paseante Noir was bred by Dr. Andy Walker using marker-assisted selection to move resistance from the wild Vitis arizonica into a predominantly vinifera vine. The resulting wine is described as similar in style to Zinfandel, with good fruit character despite the vine's mostly-wild disease-resistance parentage. Gulf South and Texas growers facing severe glassy-winged sharpshooter and Pierce's disease pressure are beginning to trial it as an alternative to susceptible European varieties. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun and expect limited nursery availability while the variety is still being multiplied commercially. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pasha Male Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Ornamental Kolomikta Pollinator)
description: Pasha is a male Actinidia kolomikta selection grown specifically as a pollinator for female Arctic Beauty kiwi vines, since the species is dioecious and female vines will not set fruit without a nearby male. Rather than producing fruit itself, Pasha is prized for its strikingly ornamental foliage, splashed with pink, white, and green variegation, making it an attractive vine in its own right on a trellis or arbor. It is exceptionally cold hardy, reportedly tolerating winter lows to around -40F, among the hardiest of all Actinidia selections. A single well-placed Pasha vine can pollinate multiple female kolomikta vines within range. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pasilla Bajio Chilaca Chile Pepper
description: The fresh chilaca pepper dries into the dark, wrinkled pasilla that is essential to traditional mole and adds depth to enchilada sauces and salsas. Heat runs a mild 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units. Start seeds indoors early and set transplants into warm soil in full sun. Let pods ripen to dark brown for drying, or use them fresh, harvesting regularly to keep plants productive. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Pasilla Bajio Chile (Chilaca Pepper)
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. Pasilla Bajio — meaning 'little raisin from the lowlands' — is the dried form of the fresh chilaca chile, producing narrow, 6–9 inch, wrinkled dark green to near-black fruits that dry to a very dark reddish-black with a distinctive fruity, dried-fruit, earthy flavor and medium heat (1,000–2,500 SHU). Pasilla is one of the three essential dried chiles used together in authentic Mexican mole negro (along with mulato and ancho) and is used extensively in Oaxacan and central Mexican cooking. The tall, upright plants produce cascading clusters of long, drooping fruits; harvest green for fresh use or allow to ripen fully dark and dry on the plant. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Pasilla de Oaxaca Pepper (Smoke-Dried Oaxacan Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Pasilla de Oaxaca produces elongated, dark green pods that ripen to deep red-brown and are traditionally cured over wood smoke before drying, a regional Oaxacan specialty distinct from the standard pasilla (chile negro) grown elsewhere in Mexico and prized in stews and moles for its smoky, fruity heat. The plants bear well over a long warm season in a climate similar to their native highland Oaxacan growing region. Harvest pods once fully colored for drying and smoking, or use fresh while still green. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Pasilla Mixe Pepper (Oaxacan Smoked Chile)
description: Give plants full sun, warm nights, and moderate consistent water; the tall bushy plants benefit from staking once fruit-heavy. This landrace is grown in the highlands of the Mixe region of Oaxaca and traditionally left to ripen to a deep brownish-black before being slow smoke-dried over wood fires, producing a chile with intense smoky, fruity, tobacco-like depth and considerable heat. Use dried pods rehydrated into moles, adobos, and salsas where a smokier alternative to chipotle is wanted. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Pasilla Negro Pepper (Mexican Mole Chile, Long Dark-Fruited Dried Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Pasilla Negro (also called Chile Pasilla, Chile Negro, or Pasilla Bajío) is a long, narrow, dark-fruited Mexican chile pepper that, when dried, becomes one of the essential dried chiles of Mexican cuisine alongside ancho and mulato. The fresh pepper is 6–9 inches long, narrow (1–1.5 inches diameter), and deep dark green to near-black at the harvest stage — the name 'Pasilla' (little raisin) refers to the wrinkled, dark, raisin-like appearance of the dried pepper. The heat level is mild to medium (1,000–2,500 Scoville units) — substantially milder than serrano or jalapeño — making the peppers appropriate for use in larger quantities in sauces and moles. The flavor is rich, earthy, and slightly fruity with a complex character that makes pasilla one of the most important 'flavor' peppers in Mexican cooking rather than primarily a heat source. Mole negro, the complex black mole of Oaxaca and southern Mexico, typically uses pasilla negro (along with mulato and ancho) as its primary chile base, and the dried, toasted pasilla contributes the dark color and deep, earthy flavor that defines the sauce. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Passe Crassane Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Passe Crassane ripens very late and needs weeks of cold storage before the gritty flesh softens and sweetens. A classic French winter pear bred in Normandy in the mid-nineteenth century, it was for generations the standard Christmas and New Year's market pear across France, bearing large, round, russeted fruit with dense flesh that is notably gritty and unpalatable straight off the tree but softens into rich, sweet, fine-textured flesh after a long period of cold storage. Its very late ripening and exceptional keeping ability once properly stored made it historically important for extending the fresh pear season deep into winter, well after other varieties had finished. Harvest quite late in fall while still very hard, store cool for many weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature until the flesh softens fully before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Passionfruit
description: Passionfruit is a vigorous, tendril-climbing vine requiring a sturdy wire trellis or fence. Train the main stem vertically and allow lateral shoots to drape horizontally from the top — these laterals bear the flowers and fruit. Prune heavily after fruiting to rejuvenate the vine and maintain productive growth. Harvest when the fruit skin begins to wrinkle and the fruit falls or detaches easily; purple cultivars are generally more cold-tolerant than yellow types. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Passport Melon (Early French Charentais-Type Hybrid)
description: Passport is a compact-vined hybrid bred to bring true French Charentais eating quality within reach of gardeners with shorter or cooler summers than the Charentais region of France. Fruit is small and round, about 2-3 pounds, with smooth gray-green skin faintly ribbed at the blossom end and deep orange, intensely aromatic flesh with a very high sugar content. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only when fully ripe, check daily near the expected harvest window and cut fruit that shows a slight crack or softening at the stem rather than waiting for it to detach on its own. Its shorter vines and earlier maturity make it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting restaurant-quality melon flavor without a long, hot growing season. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Pataste
description: Plant Herrania mariae in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil with consistently high humidity; maintain soil moisture year-round; protect from all frost and dry winds. Pataste is a close relative of cultivated cacao (Theobroma cacao) in the same subfamily Byttnerioideae, sharing cacao's characteristic cauliflorous pod production — the colorful, oval to elongated pods emerge directly from the trunk and major branches rather than at the branch tips. The pulp surrounding the seeds is white, translucent, and sweet (similar to cacao pulp, eaten fresh or fermented for beverages); the seeds themselves are bitter and high in theobromine like cacao, and have historically been used by Amazonian peoples as a cacao substitute or mixed with true cacao for chocolate preparation. Herrania is a genetically diverse cacao relative of significant interest to cacao breeders for disease-resistance genes, and several species produce viable chocolate-flavored pods. Growing in the deep, humid, understory shade of Amazonian forests, Pataste is adapted to conditions of very high humidity, no frost, and dappled to deep shade — making it a perfect choice for shaded positions in zone 10–12 tropical gardens where true cacao may grow poorly in full exposure. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pataste (Mocambo Cacao, Two-Colored Cacao)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in part shade; pataste grows naturally as an understory tree and requires shade protection, especially when young. Theobroma bicolor (pataste, mocambo cacao, or two-colored cacao) is a close relative of chocolate cacao (T. cacao) — one of the approximately 20 edible Theobroma species native to the tropical Americas — and one of the most historically significant secondary cacao species. Like T. cacao, it is native to the humid forests of Mesoamerica and the Amazon basin and produces large, ribbed, gourd-like fruits containing seeds embedded in white, sweet, edible pulp. The seeds of T. bicolor were used by the pre-Columbian Maya and Aztec as a cacao substitute and flavoring in chocolate beverages — often blended with T. cacao to modify flavor, reduce cost, or add specific aromatic notes. The seeds can be fermented and processed similarly to cacao beans to produce a chocolate-like paste and beverage. The white, sweet, mucilaginous fruit pulp surrounding the seeds (similar to the cacao pulp used in Colombia and Ecuador) is pleasantly sweet-acid and is eaten fresh or processed into juice, ice cream, and fermented beverages. T. bicolor was once more widely cultivated than it is today; it is currently grown in home gardens and small farms across Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico, but has been largely displaced by T. cacao in commercial production. A fascinating collector's tree connecting to chocolate's deep pre-Columbian history. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Patchouli
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite at 75°F and provide high humidity during rooting; commercial patchouli rarely sets viable seed and is almost universally propagated vegetatively. Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun.
