The broad, irregularly toothed leaves release the characteristic heavy, earthy patchouli fragrance when touched or bruised, a scent that intensifies as leaves dry and ferment. Harvest branches before flowering for maximum essential oil content by cutting stems back to a node; the plant re-sprouts vigorously. Essential oil is steam-distilled from dried leaves and used widely in perfumery and aromatherapy. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Patience Dock (Herb Patience, Monk's Rhubarb)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; patience dock is a large, handsome perennial with broad, spinach-like leaves that are harvested as a pot herb from earliest spring through late fall. Unlike the sharply acid sorrel (Rumex acetosa), patience dock has a mild, slightly earthy flavor with very little oxalic acid bitterness, making it more broadly useful as a cooked green. The huge leaves (up to 12 inches long) are excellent sautéed with garlic and olive oil, stirred into pasta, or used in savory pies in the way southern Europeans have used them for centuries. The plant has been cultivated in European cottage gardens for hundreds of years and was historically considered one of the most valuable early-spring pot herbs. Divide large clumps every 3-4 years to keep them productive. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Patillo Guava (Cold-Hardy Pink-Fleshed Guava)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after all frost risk has passed; Patillo is a small to medium guava tree valued for bright pink, fragrant flesh with a fruity, tangy-acidic flavor that suits fresh eating, juice, and preserves alike. Pink-fleshed guava selections such as Patillo are generally reported to tolerate cold better and resprout more readily from the roots after a hard freeze than white-fleshed types, a useful trait for gardeners at the northern edge of guava-growing country. As with other guavas, fruit forms on new growth, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the tree compact and encourages a strong flush of fruiting wood each season. Mulch the root zone heavily going into winter, since top growth is more cold-sensitive than the root system and often regrows after being frozen back. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Patio Baby Eggplant (AAS-Winning Compact Container Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or a large container with good drainage; Patio Baby is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for compact, spineless, well-behaved growth that fits easily on a patio or in a small raised bed while still producing a heavy crop of glossy, deep-purple, egg-sized fruit. It bears notably early and continues producing over a long season, with tender, mild, nearly seedless flesh typical of good eating quality eggplant. Harvest fruit at 2-3 inches long while glossy and firm, and its small stature and prolific habit make it a favorite for container vegetable gardens with limited space. Matures in 45–55 days from transplant.

name: Patio Choice Yellow Bush Cherry Tomato
description: This compact determinate bush tomato is ideal for containers and small spaces, yielding abundant sweet half-ounce yellow cherry tomatoes. Its tidy habit needs little staking, making it good for patios and mixed pots. Start seeds indoors, transplant after frost, and water evenly to keep fruit from splitting. Pick ripe tomatoes often to encourage a steady flush. Matures in 45–55 days from transplant.

name: Patio Pride Pea
description: Patio Pride is an early, compact heirloom shelling pea that grows just eight to twelve inches tall, making it ideal for containers, window boxes, and small raised beds. Despite its small stature it produces a generous early crop of sweet peas. Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, sowing thickly since the dwarf plants support each other. Harvest promptly once pods fill for the best flavor, and enjoy a quick turnaround for succession planting. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Patio Pride Snap Pea
description: This early snap pea is a 2017 All-America Selections winner, ready in about 40 days on compact plants perfect for containers. It yields sweet, uniform 2 to 3 inch pods that are tender when picked young. Sow directly in cool soil for a quick spring or fall crop and keep evenly moist. Harvest pods when plump but still crisp to keep the vines producing. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Patio Snacker Cucumber (Compact Container-Friendly Snacking Cucumber)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Patio Snacker is a compact, semi-vining cucumber variety selected for container and patio growing — producing shorter, more manageable vines (18–30 inches) than standard cucumber varieties while maintaining prolific fruit production of small (3–4 inch) snacking-size cucumbers. The small fruit size and compact plant habit are ideally matched for patio container growing: the cucumbers are sized for fresh snacking without slicing, and the plant fits in a large container (5-gallon minimum, 10-gallon ideal) with a simple stake or small trellis. Patio Snacker produces crisp, thin-skinned, nearly seedless cucumbers with mild, sweet flavor and no bitterness — characteristic of the modern small-cucumber/snacking types bred for fresh eating without the preparation steps (peeling, seed removal) required for large slicing varieties. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring shoulder season (February–April) and the fall shoulder season (August–September) — summer heat reduces fruiting and increases disease pressure. The compact size and container suitability make Patio Snacker particularly useful for zone 9 gardeners who can move containers to optimize microclimate conditions during the challenging summer transition period. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Patio Star Summer Squash
description: Patio Star is an All-America Selections winner bred for its dwarf, tidy bush habit, making it one of the only pattypan-type squash that performs well in a large pot or half-barrel rather than a garden bed. Plants stay compact and open, setting pale green to creamy-white, flying-saucer-shaped fruit that hold their tender texture and mild, buttery flavor even when a few are missed at the ideal 2-3 inch picking size. Harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since the small plant size means missed fruit can slow overall production more noticeably than on a sprawling vine type. Feed container-grown plants regularly, since frequent watering in a pot leaches nutrients faster than in garden soil. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Patio Tomato (Classic Compact Container Tomato)
description: Sow indoors and transplant into a sunny patio container or garden bed once frost danger has passed, keeping the compact plant evenly watered since small pots dry out quickly. Patio, an early All-America Selections winner, was one of the original dwarf tomato hybrids bred specifically for container growing, staying under 24 inches tall while still bearing clusters of 3-4 ounce round red fruit with reliable, old-fashioned tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark heirloom-era patio variety that predates the many modern compact hybrids it inspired. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Patrecia Blueberry (Early Firm-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants for the upright, spreading habit this cultivar develops as it matures. Patrecia was developed from a cross of 'Star' and 'Springhigh' and released by the University of Florida for its early-to-mid season ripening, large and very uniformly ripening berries, and late bloom that reduces exposure to spring freeze damage compared with earlier-flowering cultivars. The fruit's picking scar runs larger than ideal and can tear during harvest, so growers hand-pick rather than machine-harvest this selection, and yields respond well to a hydrogen-cyanamide bud-break program. Fertilize with an acid-forming blend in early spring, mulch heavily with pine bark to hold soil moisture and acidity, and remove the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Patriot Blueberry (Cold-Hardy Northern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun with at least one other blueberry cultivar for cross-pollination; Patriot is a cold-hardy northern highbush blueberry cultivar developed by the University of Maine — selected for extreme cold hardiness (to -20°F), compact upright habit, and good resistance to root rot (Phytophthora cinnamomi), which makes it more adaptable to heavier or less-than-perfectly-drained soils than most highbush cultivars. The large, firm, aromatic, medium-blue berries ripen in early-to-midseason (July in zone 5–6) with a sweet, excellent blueberry flavor and very good shelf life. Patriot is widely grown in the Northeast and upper Midwest where its cold hardiness is the decisive advantage. In zone 8 it performs well with sufficient soil acidification — a reliable producer where winter temperatures regularly drop below 10°F. In zone 9, Patriot's 800–1000 chill hour requirement is not reliably met in the warmest locations; southern highbush cultivars (Misty, O'Neal, Sharpblue) are better adapted to zone 9. Patriot is a good pollination partner for Bluecrop, Blueray, and other midseason northern highbush varieties. Amend soil with peat moss, sulfur, or acidifying fertilizers to maintain the essential low pH. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Patterson Apricot (California Standard Cannery Apricot)
description: Patterson is a widely grown California canning apricot named for Patterson, California, long known as a self-proclaimed apricot capital. It became the standard commercial replacement for Blenheim in many orchards because of its reliable heavy bearing and firm, all-purpose fruit suited equally well to canning, drying, shipping, and fresh eating. The medium-sized, golden-orange freestone fruit ripens in mid-to-late June and the tree is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set a full crop without a pollinator. Patterson needs a moderate amount of winter chill, so it performs best in zone 6 through 9 gardens with a real, if mild, winter. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Patterson Onion (Long-Day Yellow Storage Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; space 4–6 inches apart in rows 12–18 inches apart; Patterson is a long-day variety requiring 14+ hours of daylight to form bulbs — performs in zones 3–8 north of the 35th parallel; harvest when 80% of tops fall naturally and cure 3–4 weeks in a warm, dry location with good airflow. Patterson is a long-day hybrid yellow storage onion widely considered one of the gold standards for reliable, high-yielding yellow onion production in northern gardens (zones 3–8); it has been a staple recommendation of Johnny's Selected Seeds — the primary commercial source — and university extension services throughout the Northeast and Midwest for its combination of high yield, consistent bulb quality, and exceptional storage performance. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have smooth, dark golden-amber skins that cure tightly and resist breakdown in storage; the flesh is white, firm, moderately pungent, and full-flavored in the traditional yellow onion style — excellent for all cooking purposes: caramelizing, soups, stews, roasting, and pickling. The standout characteristic that makes Patterson the choice of serious northern vegetable gardeners is storage life: under ideal conditions (33–40°F, low humidity, good airflow), Patterson onions store 8–12 months — essentially the full year from one harvest to the next — with far less deterioration, sprouting, or softening than most other onion varieties. This durability in storage is the result of tight, multiple layers of dry outer scales that seal the bulb against moisture and pathogens. Matures in 104–118 days from transplant.

name: Pattypan Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost; pattypan (also called scallop or flying-saucer squash) is a bush summer squash producing flat, round, scallop-edged fruits in white, yellow, green, or bicolored versions that look entirely different from the cylindrical zucchini or yellow straightneck. Harvest at 2–3 inches in diameter for the most tender flesh; larger fruits become tough and seedy. The hollow center makes them ideal for stuffing: scoop out the interior, fill with cheese, herbs, or seasoned meat, and bake. The compact bush habit makes pattypan suitable for smaller gardens. 'Sunburst' (yellow) and 'Patio Star' (white) are popular named cultivars. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Pattypan Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil in hills of 2–3 seeds, thinning to the strongest plant. Consistent moisture at the root zone keeps the bush compact and productive throughout the season. Pattypan's distinctive flying-saucer shape makes sizing easy. Harvest when fruits are 2–3 inches across for the most tender flesh; over-mature fruits become tough and seedy. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Paul Robeson Tomato (Complex Deep Brick-Red Russian Dark Heirloom)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Paul Robeson is a celebrated Russian heirloom tomato that is consistently rated by connoisseurs as one of the finest-flavored dark tomatoes available — producing medium-large (7–10 oz), round to oblate fruits in a distinctive deep brick-red to mahogany-brownish-purple color with dark-green shoulders that is the hallmark of the 'black' Russian tomato aesthetic. The flavor is remarkable: deeply complex, rich, smoky, and earthy with a balanced sweetness and moderate acidity that creates a dimensional, wine-like flavor profile that many experienced tomato tasters consider superior to any other tomato type. The flavor intensity — often described as the most complex and layered of all dark heirloom tomatoes — makes Paul Robeson outstanding for fresh eating (particularly with nothing more than salt and olive oil), in Caprese-style presentations, and in cooking where the rich, smoky character concentrates further. Paul Robeson was introduced to American seed savers from a Russian collection by Marina Danilenko in the 1990s and has become one of the most respected and sought-after heirlooms in the American seed-saving community. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type. In zone 9, Paul Robeson produces best in the spring growing window (February–June) and requires the long spring season to develop its finest fruit quality. Matures in 74–85 days from transplant.

name: Paul's Scarlet Hawthorn (Crimson Cloud, Double Red English Hawthorn)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Paul's Scarlet, also sold in North America as Crimson Cloud, arose as a sport of the older double-pink midland hawthorn Rosea Flore Pleno found in an English garden in the 1850s, and it quickly became one of the most popular flowering hawthorns in cultivation, later earning the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. In mid-to-late spring the thorny branches are smothered in fully double, deep rose-red to scarlet flowers carried in dense clusters, a far showier and more saturated display than the simple white or pale pink blooms of the wild species, followed in autumn by dark green foliage that turns red. Because the flowers are double and largely sterile, the tree sets few if any of the small red haws typical of single-flowered hawthorns, so its garden value rests almost entirely on the spectacular spring bloom and on its dense, twiggy, thorny branching, which still offers good nesting cover for birds. It tolerates a wide range of soils from acidic to alkaline and adapts to both moist and fairly dry sites once established. As a grafted named clone it must be propagated vegetatively, since seedlings revert to single flowers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Paulista Jaboticaba
description: Paulista is one of the two most widely grown jaboticaba selections in Brazil alongside 'Sabara', distinguished by noticeably larger fruit and thicker, more leathery purple-black skin. Like all jaboticaba, the grape-like fruit erupts directly from the trunk and older branches in dense clusters, and the tree typically produces one large main flush per year rather than the near-continuous cropping seen in 'Sabara'. New foliage emerges an attractive salmon-pink before maturing to deep green, adding ornamental value alongside the fruit. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a slow-growing but very long-lived tree that rewards patience with sweet, translucent pulp for fresh eating or preserves. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Paulk Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and give the vine generous trellis space; Paulk is a self-fertile muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program and has quickly become popular for producing some of the largest berries of any muscadine cultivar, with glossy black-purple skin and a sweet, mild flavor good for fresh eating. Vines are notably vigorous and heavy-bearing, often needing more aggressive winter pruning than older varieties to keep the canopy in bounds and light penetrating to the fruiting spurs. Train young vines to a single trunk and permanent cordon along a wire, then prune all lateral growth back to short spurs each winter, since fruit forms on new shoots from that spur wood. Harvest from late summer into early fall as berries turn fully black and detach freely from the stem; because Paulk berries are large and thin-skinned relative to older varieties, pick promptly at ripeness to avoid splitting after rain. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pawnee Pecan (Early Maturing Large Pecan)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Pawnee is one of the finest pecan cultivars for the Gulf South — a USDA Agricultural Research Service introduction that has become one of the most widely planted pecans in the region for its combination of outstanding nut quality, large nut size, excellent kernel percentage (55–57%), early maturity, and partial scab resistance. Pawnee's most significant attribute is its very early maturity: it ripens 2–3 weeks earlier than Desirable, Stuart, and other standard cultivars, meaning Pawnee nuts are falling in late September to early October in zone 9 — well ahead of the alternating wet/dry weather cycles of mid-fall that cause many pecan cultivars to develop scab and quality losses. The large, thin-shelled nuts have excellent quality with bright, sweet-tasting kernels and very good percentage fill. Pawnee is a Type II pecan (protandrous pollen shedding) — it produces pollen when its own female flowers are not yet receptive, requiring cross-pollination from a Type I cultivar (like Desirable) for maximum yields. This cross-pollination requirement is easy to meet in the Gulf South where multiple pecan cultivars are commonly grown in close proximity. Pawnee is moderately susceptible to pecan scab — preventive fungicide applications during leaf-out and through spring are important in humid Gulf South conditions. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Pawpaw
description: Pawpaws require two genetically distinct seedlings or named cultivars for cross-pollination; hand-pollinating flowers with a small brush greatly improves fruit set. Young trees need shade for the first one to two seasons — plant under a light canopy or use a shade cloth — but mature trees prefer full sun to fruit well. The taproot makes transplanting difficult, so use container-grown stock and disturb roots as little as possible. Fruit ripens in late summer to fall and goes from firm to custardy-soft within days; refrigerate immediately after picking as shelf life is very short. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Payne English Walnut (Early-Leafing Precocious Heavy Bearer)
description: Payne is a long-established California walnut cultivar prized for extremely precocious, heavy bearing on a comparatively small, spreading tree, making it a popular choice for higher-density plantings. Its very early leafing and bloom give it a long growing season and abundant clustered nuts, but the same trait leaves flowers vulnerable to spring frost in colder or frost-prone sites. Nuts are medium-sized with a light-colored, good-flavored kernel, though the thin shell can be more prone to insect damage than tougher-shelled cultivars. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and away from low frost pockets, and harvest as hulls split in early fall. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Payroll Squash (Disease-Tolerant Hybrid Zucchini)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Payroll is an early, high-yielding hybrid zucchini bred with tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, letting it hold healthy foliage and keep setting fruit later into the season than many older varieties once disease pressure builds. It produces uniform, dark green, cylindrical fruit on a compact, open bush habit that makes spotting and harvesting fruit easy even as the plant fills out. Pick at 6-8 inches for the best eating quality, checking daily during peak summer production since zucchini left on the plant even a day or two too long quickly grows oversized and seedy. Matures in 45–52 days from seed.

name: Pea Microgreens
description: Soak the pea seed overnight so it germinates quickly and evenly, then spread it thickly across a moist tray. Keep the seeds covered under weight for a couple of days to encourage strong, upright shoots, then bring them into bright light. Water from below to keep the dense mat hydrated without inviting rot. Harvest the sweet, tender pea shoots at three to six inches tall; many growers get a second cutting from the same tray. Matures in 8–14 days from seed.

name: Pea Shoots Baby Greens
description: Harvested young, pea shoots are a tender, versatile green for salads, sandwiches, soups, and stir-fries. Sow the seeds thickly in a container or garden bed and keep them evenly moist. Snip the shoots with scissors when a few inches tall, cutting above the lowest leaves so plants can regrow for a second cutting. They grow quickly in cool conditions and tolerate part shade. Matures in 14–21 days from seed.

name: Peach
description: Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, but they need 600–1000 chill hours — choose low-chill varieties (below 400 hours) for zones 8–9. Train to an open-center (vase) shape to allow sunlight deep into the canopy, and prune out about one-third of last year's growth each dormant season because peaches only fruit on one-year-old wood. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart after June drop to size up remaining fruit and reduce limb breakage. Harvest when the green ground color fades to cream and the fruit yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Peach Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Peach Ghost Pepper)
description: Peach Bhut Jolokia ripens to a warm apricot-peach hue instead of the classic red, on the same wrinkled, thin-fleshed pods and blistering heat associated with ghost peppers. Growers often note a subtly sweeter, fruitier aroma compared to red strains, though the Scoville load remains firmly in superhot territory. Give plants full sun, rich well-drained soil, and consistent watering to avoid blossom drop during fruit set. Use gloves when harvesting and processing pods, since capsaicin oils are persistent on skin. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Peach Chinese Chestnut (Fuzzy Peach-Skin-Textured Reliable Chestnut)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Peach, a modern selection from Ohio's Empire Chestnut Company, takes its name from the faintly soft, fuzzy texture of its shell surface, reminiscent of a peach skin, a distinctive tactile trait among Chinese chestnut cultivars, and is valued as a reliable, consistent annual producer of good-flavored nuts. Like other Chinese chestnut selections, it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in late September to mid-October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely for the broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Peach Habanero Pepper (Pale Peach-Fruity Habanero Variety with Full Heat)
description: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully peach-colored. Peach Habanero is a color variant of the habanero pepper group (Capsicum chinense) producing fruits that ripen to a distinctive peach to pale apricot-cream color rather than the familiar orange of standard habanero. The heat level is comparable to orange habanero (100,000–350,000 Scoville units) — full habanero-class heat that demands careful handling and measured use — but the flavor character is perceived by many tasters as slightly different: more floral, sweeter, and with a pronounced fruity quality that some describe as reminiscent of apricot or tropical fruit. The habanero group includes color variants ranging from white through yellow, orange, peach, red, chocolate, and nearly black, with all variants sharing the distinctive fruity-floral habanero aroma that distinguishes Capsicum chinense from the more neutral Capsicum annuum species. Peach Habanero is valued by hot sauce makers, hot pepper enthusiasts, and gardeners interested in the visual diversity of the habanero color spectrum — the pale peach fruits are visually striking against the deep green foliage and make an attractive presentation in fresh pepper mixes and hot sauce. In zone 9, Peach Habanero is one of the most productive hot peppers available: the combination of the species' heat and humidity tolerance with the long Gulf Coast growing season produces prolific crops of fruits through summer and into fall. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Peach Palm (Pejibaye)
description: Peach palm is clump-forming, producing multiple spiny stems from the base; plant suckers or container-grown plants in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent irrigation. It is dioecious in the wild but many cultivated selections are monoecious and self-productive; planting in clusters of 3–5 stems improves pollination and yield. The starchy, oily orange-red drupes are rich in beta-carotene and must be boiled or roasted before eating as raw fruit contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals. Harvest bunches when fruit has turned fully orange to red and softens slightly; boil or cook within a few days as the starchy fruit does not store well raw. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Peach Sage
description: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and water consistently through the establishment period, then maintain moderate irrigation as the plant is sensitive to prolonged drought but equally intolerant of waterlogged roots. The enormous, velvety leaves emit a sweet peach fragrance when brushed, and tall spikes of bright magenta-pink flowers appear in late fall and winter, drawing hummingbirds throughout the cool season. Pinch stem tips during the growing season to promote bushy, compact growth and delay flowering until the plant is well branched. In zone 9, cut back frost-damaged stems to the ground in late winter and the plant will resprout vigorously from established roots. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Peach Sorbet Dwarf Blueberry (Compact Container Blueberry with Colorful Foliage)
description: Grow Peach Sorbet in a large container or raised bed filled with an acidic, well-drained azalea-and-camellia mix, since its compact, mounding habit makes it as much a landscape or patio accent as a fruiting shrub. New spring foliage emerges a soft peachy-pink before turning green for summer, then shifts back to shades of orange and purple as nights cool in fall, giving three seasons of color in addition to the berries. Being self-fertile, a single plant will set fruit, though yields improve with a second nearby blueberry for cross-pollination. Water deeply and regularly since containers dry out faster than garden beds, and top-dress with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Peaches and Cream Sweet Corn (Bicolor Sweet Corn)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate cross-pollination; Peaches and Cream is the most popular bicolor sweet corn cultivar in American home gardens — producing medium-large ears with yellow and white kernels in a random bicolor mosaic pattern that gives the variety its name and provides both sweet varieties in a single ear. The flavor is typically described as rich, sweet, and complex — the combination of white (typically sweeter) and yellow (typically more 'corny' in flavor) kernels in each bite creates a distinctive eating experience that many gardeners prefer to all-yellow or all-white varieties. Peaches and Cream is an 'SE' (sugar-enhanced) sweet corn type — sweeter than standard su sweet corn but not as sweet or tender-skinned as sh2 (supersweet) types. The SE type is more forgiving of growing conditions and holds its sweetness longer after harvest than standard sweet corn. In zone 9, sweet corn is a spring and fall crop — plant in late February for June harvest and in late July for October harvest. The hot summer is too demanding for quality corn. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder — side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer when plants are 12 inches tall and again when tasseling. Corn earworms are the primary pest and must be managed with Bt applications at silk emergence. Matures in 79–86 days from seed.

name: Peanut
description: Shell peanuts and plant seeds 2 in deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil; heavy clay prevents proper peg penetration and pod development. After flowering, keep the area around plants free of weeds and loosen surface soil lightly so fertilization pegs can easily enter the ground. Harvest when foliage begins to yellow and the inner shell veins turn dark, by lifting the entire plant with a fork. Cure plants upside-down in a warm, airy location for 2–3 weeks before removing pods. Matures in 100–150 days from seed.

name: Peanut Butter Fruit
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zones 9–12; peanut butter fruit earns its name from the distinctive flavor of the ripe orange-red fruits — the flesh surrounding the seeds has a rich, somewhat sticky texture and flavor uncannily reminiscent of peanut butter, combined with subtle sweet notes. Native to Peru and the Andes, this ornamental shrub is surprisingly adaptable to Gulf Coast conditions in zones 9–11, where it fruits prolifically on an almost continuous basis in warm seasons. The small, bright yellow flowers are attractive and produced repeatedly throughout the year in warm climates. The fruit are eaten fresh from the shrub or used in smoothies, ice cream, and desserts throughout South America. Unusually shade-tolerant for a fruiting tropical — it can produce reasonably well in the bright filtered light beneath a high canopy, making it valuable for partially shaded garden positions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Amazon Peanut Butter Tree, Peanut Butter Plant)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Peanut Butter Fruit is adaptable to a range of soil types and is moderately drought tolerant once established, performing reliably in zone 9b-12 as an evergreen fruiting shrub-tree. Bunchosia glandulifera is an evergreen to semi-deciduous, large shrub to small tree native to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, and the Amazon basin in the Malpighiaceae family — the same family as Acerola (Malpighia emarginata), from which the distinctive wing-petaled yellow flowers of Bunchosia are recognizable. The plant produces ovate, dark-green, glossy leaves and clusters of small (0.5-inch) yellow flowers with the characteristic wing-petaled (fringed petal margin) form typical of the Malpighiaceae. The flowers are followed by oval fruits, 1–1.5 inches long, that ripen progressively from pale green through yellow-orange to deep red-orange. The ripe flesh of Bunchosia glandulifera fruit is thick, sweet, slightly dry in texture, and has a flavor that is remarkably and unmistakably reminiscent of smooth peanut butter — sweet, rich, and nutty, without any actual peanut content. The fruit can be eaten fresh at the ripe orange-red stage (before it becomes overripe), blended into smoothies, used as a natural sweet spread on crackers, or incorporated into desserts. Plants are highly productive in warm climates and begin fruiting within 1–2 years from a large transplant or seedling. An unusual and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 9b-12 gardens. Non-toxic. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Silver-Leaved Bunchosia, Gold Cherry)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Peanut Butter Fruit grows and fruits well in partial shade, making it useful for under-story tropical food garden positions under larger fruit trees. Bunchosia argentea is a fast-growing, evergreen shrub or small tree from Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the family Malpighiaceae, widely grown as a dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical America and increasingly available in South Florida and zone 10-11 Gulf Coast fruit collections for one of the most remarkable flavor descriptions in the tropical fruit world: the flesh of the ripe fruit has the precise taste and texture of smooth commercial peanut butter — sweet, nutty, slightly dry, and unmistakably peanut-like, despite having no botanical relationship to Arachis hypogaea (the peanut). The fruits are small (half to 1 inch), oval to oblong, and ripen from yellow-orange to orange-red, produced in clusters along the branches from the warm months. A single ripe Bunchosia argentea fruit consumed fresh is a memorable culinary experience — the resemblance to peanut butter is genuine and immediate. The plant is a rapid grower that begins bearing fruit within one to two years of planting and produces through the warm months. The silver leaf undersides (the 'argentea' — 'silvery') give the plant an attractive bi-colored appearance. An excellent, unusual addition to any tropical or subtropical home food garden. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pear
description: European pears require 700–1200 chill hours and almost always need a second compatible cultivar for adequate pollination; Bosc and Anjou cross well with each other. Pears are prone to fire blight, so choose resistant varieties and prune out any infected wood well below the canker margin. Train to a central leader and avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes lush growth susceptible to blight. Pick pears while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature — they go mealy if left on the tree too long. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pearl Glam Beautyberry (Dark Purple Foliage Compact Beautyberry)
description: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; American beautyberry tolerates a wide range of conditions and needs little supplemental water once established. Pearl Glam bears striking dark purple-black foliage through the entire growing season, a departure from the plain green leaves of the straight species, paired in fall with the same eye-catching clusters of vivid purple berries that encircle the stems and persist after leaf drop, providing food for songbirds through winter. Its dark foliage color adds ornamental interest for months before the berry display even begins, and its more compact size fits smaller gardens than seedling-grown beautyberry. Prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth, since flowers and berries form on new wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pearl Goya Bitter Melon
description: Pearl Goya is an Okinawan selection that produces round, pearl-white fruit closer in shape to a golf ball than the typical elongated bitter melon, with a milder, almost umami flavor that suits simple soups. Grow it on a tall trellis in full sun with consistently moist, compost-rich soil, training vines vertically and pruning lateral shoots to keep air moving through the foliage. Harvest fruit while still pale and firm, picking early and often to extend the fruiting season. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Pearl Onion
description: Tiny pearl onions are grown deliberately crowded so each bulb stays small and round for pickling and boiling. Direct sow densely in a wide band and skip thinning, since competition limits bulb size. Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free during the short growing period. Harvest when tops yellow and fall, then cure the little bulbs before storing or pickling. Blanching the cured bulbs in hot water makes peeling far easier. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Pearl River Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Pearl River is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the LSU AgCenter specifically for Gulf South dooryard and commercial plantings, selected for consistent production under Louisiana's mild winters and low-to-moderate chill hours. The medium-sized, light blue berries ripen mid-season and have a firm texture and mild, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating and freezing. Plants are vigorous and moderately disease-tolerant, though they benefit from mulching with pine bark or pine straw to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. Not self-fruitful, so plant with at least one other rabbiteye cultivar within 50 feet for reliable cross-pollination and full-sized fruit. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pecan
description: Pecans are protandrous or protogynous depending on variety — pollen shed and receptive female flowers rarely overlap on the same tree — so always plant at least two cultivars of opposite types (Type I with Type II) to ensure cross-pollination. Northern varieties (Hark, Kanza, Lakota) are bred for shorter growing seasons and suit zones 5–7; southern varieties need 250+ frost-free days. Pecans are heavy zinc feeders; apply zinc foliar spray in spring if leaves show rosette symptoms. Harvest when shucks split open in autumn and nuts fall freely. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Pecan Tree (Native Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pecans require at least 30–40 feet of space in all directions and are best suited to large properties with deep, loamy soil. Carya illinoinensis (pecan) is the iconic native nut tree of the American South and Southwest — the only major North American nut to have achieved worldwide commercial importance — producing sweet, buttery, thin-shelled nuts from September through November that are consumed fresh, candied, in pies (pecan pie is the most iconic Southern dessert), and in a vast range of confectioneries and baked goods. The pecan is native to the Mississippi-Ohio River basin and Gulf Coastal Plain, reaching 60–100 feet tall and living for centuries; established trees are drought-resistant and incredibly long-lived. Two trees with different bloom times (Type I — shedding pollen before receptive to it; Type II — the opposite) are needed for reliable cross-pollination and maximum nut production. Named varieties for the Gulf South include 'Desirable,' 'Candy,' 'Caddo,' 'Cheyenne,' 'Kiowa,' and 'Oconee' — all selected for disease resistance to pecan scab, the primary disease problem in humid southeastern climates. The trees also have significant wildlife value as a mast crop for deer, turkeys, and squirrels. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Peerless Almond (Large-Kernel California Commercial Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety with overlapping bloom time is planted nearby, since almonds are self-unfruitful. Peerless is a long-established California commercial almond variety producing large, plump, soft-shell kernels with good flavor, historically planted widely for its productivity and reliable performance in California's Central Valley almond-growing regions. The tree blooms relatively late compared to some other varieties, offering some protection against early spring frost damage to the crop, a real practical advantage in marginal or frost-prone sites. Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, particularly during kernel fill in summer, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer to early fall, allowing nuts to dry before storage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Peking Black Southern Pea (Vigorous Black-Seeded Heirloom Cowpea)
description: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep and provide a trellis at least 4 feet tall, since Peking Black is a vigorous climbing Southern pea rather than a compact bush type. Vines reach about 5 feet and bear abundant 8-9 inch pods that mature to fully black, glossy seed, giving high shelled yields for drying and storage. Like other cowpeas it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established, thriving through the hottest weeks of the Southern summer that slow down snap beans and other legumes. Trellising keeps pods clean and off the soil, and also makes the long harvest season easier to manage than letting the vines sprawl. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Pellitory of Spain (Spanish Chamomile)
description: Anacyclus pyrethrum forms a low, feathery-leaved mat of finely divided foliage topped with chamomile-like daisy flowers whose petals are white above and deep maroon-red beneath. It is not the same plant as insecticidal pyrethrum (Tanacetum cinerariifolium) despite the shared common name; the pungency here comes from the root, which contains a numbing, saliva-stimulating compound that has made it a classic Mediterranean and North African remedy chewed fresh or dried to relieve toothache and dry mouth. Plant in gritty, low-fertility, sharply drained soil in full sun; standing winter wet is the most common cause of failure. Harvest roots from established two-year-old plants in autumn for drying. Matures in 150–240 days from seed.

name: Peluche Loquat (Large Sweet Spanish Commercial Loquat)
description: Peluche is a Spanish loquat cultivar grown commercially in the Mediterranean and recognized as one of the largest and sweetest loquat varieties available, with fruit weighing around 70 grams and notably high sugar content. Like other loquats, Peluche flowers in fall and winter, so its blossoms and developing fruit can be damaged by a hard freeze, a real risk during Gulf Coast cold snaps even in zone 9a. The deep orange skin and flesh are typical of the sweeter Mediterranean cultivars, and the fruit ripens mid-to-late season. Peluche is grown alongside cultivars like Algerie in Spain's loquat-producing regions. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pembina Saskatoon (Serviceberry)
description: Pembina was selected in North Dakota for its earlier ripening window compared to many prairie saskatoon cultivars, giving gardeners in short-season regions a head start on the harvest. The shrub forms a dense, rounded multi-stem clump with reliable annual bloom and good resistance to late spring frosts at flowering. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes each winter to keep fruiting wood vigorous. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pencil Cob Corn (Ashworth Corn)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of 4+ rows for good pollination; thin to 9–12 inches within the row. Pencil Cob corn (sometimes called Cob Corn or Ashworth type) is a distinctive Appalachian and Midwestern heritage flour corn named for the distinctive narrow, slender cob (roughly pencil-diameter, compared to the fist-thick cobs of modern hybrids) that is densely covered in small, tightly packed kernels; the cobs are long for their diameter (8–12 inches) and produce flour corn with a fine-grained texture and delicate, sweet corn flavor that is different from the coarser, more assertive flavor of modern hybrid cornmeal. Ground into a fine, cream-colored meal that makes exceptionally tender and flavorful cornbread; many Southern cornbread enthusiasts claim it produces the finest cornbread of any heritage variety. Also used for hominy, grits, and polenta. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Pencil Pod Black Wax Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest through spring. Pencil Pod Black Wax is an American heirloom wax bean introduced around 1880, named for its distinctive round, cylindrical pods (resembling a pencil in shape — round rather than flat) and black seeds; the 'wax' designation refers to the golden-yellow color of the pods, which are more ornamentally attractive than standard green beans and have a somewhat different, milder flavor. The pods are harvested at 4–6 inches when crisp and tender; like all wax beans, the yellow color holds through cooking and canning better than green beans, making the finished product more visually appealing in jars. Black Wax beans were a standard American commercial canning variety in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; now maintained by heirloom seed companies. One of the most productive and reliable early wax beans for succession planting. Matures in 52–58 days from seed.

name: Pender Blueberry (Machine-Harvest NC State Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, spacing bushes to allow airflow and eventual mechanical harvest access down the row. Released by North Carolina State University's blueberry breeding program, Pender ripens early to mid-season with smaller berries than most modern fresh-market southern highbush cultivars, reflecting its partial wild highbush parentage and its intended use for processing rather than fresh sale. It fits growers who want a dependable, mechanically harvestable cultivar for juice, jam, or IQF processing rather than premium hand-picked fruit. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, keep a heavy organic mulch in place, and prune out the oldest canes each dormant season to sustain productive new growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pendolino Olive (Weeping Italian Pollinizer Olive)
description: Pendolino is a classic Tuscan olive cultivar grown chiefly as a highly effective, long-blooming pollinizer for other Italian varieties, though its own fruit also produces good-quality oil. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil, and site it within bee-flight range of Frantoio, Leccino, or Maurino to maximize cross-pollination across the planting. The tree's distinctive weeping, willowy branch habit gives it ornamental value beyond fruit production. Pendolino shows reasonable cold tolerance for an Italian olive variety, making it a workable choice for zone 8b-9 Gulf Coast plantings where a dedicated pollinizer tree improves overall grove yield. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pennsylvania Blackberry
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing generously to accommodate rapid spread by root sprouts; Pennsylvania blackberry is one of the most common and widespread wild blackberries of the eastern United States, forming stout, heavily armed, upright to arching canes in old fields, fencerows, and forest edges. White flowers open in late spring, followed by large, firm, sweet-tart black drupes that ripen over a long midsummer season and are excellent fresh or in preserves. Its vigorous, thicket-forming habit makes it valuable for wildlife cover and erosion control on a bank or hedgerow but requires regular management (cutting root suckers or mowing a defined perimeter) in a maintained garden setting to prevent it from spreading beyond its intended space. After harvest, remove spent second-year floricanes at ground level to make room for the current season's new primocanes, which will fruit the following year. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pennsylvania Dutch Crookneck Winter Squash
description: This Pennsylvania heirloom is a long-necked butternut type with rich, smooth flesh and excellent keeping quality. The elongated necks are nearly solid flesh, ideal for roasting and soups. Give the vigorous 6 to 8 foot vines full sun and plenty of room to sprawl. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot to deepen flavor and improve storage life. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Pennyroyal
description: Surface-sow seeds onto moist starting mix as they need light to germinate, keeping the medium evenly moist throughout germination. Pennyroyal spreads by creeping stems and works well as a fragrant ground cover in moist, partially shaded spots; it spreads less aggressively than other mints. The intensely peppermint-scented leaves are used fresh or dried as a traditional flea-repelling herb for pet bedding and as a strewing herb. Caution: pennyroyal oil is highly toxic and internal use carries serious risk — use the dried herb only in small quantities for tea and keep away from pregnant women and pets. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Pentland Brig Kale (Scottish Dual-Purpose Leaf-and-Spring-Shoot Kale)
description: Sow directly or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow the tall, semi-open habit room to develop. Pentland Brig was bred in the 1960s at the Scottish Plant Breeding Station from a cross of Thousand-Head kale and curly kale, combining loose, lightly frilled, medium-green leaves with an unusual second act: overwintered plants send up abundant tender flowering shoots in early spring that are harvested and cooked exactly like sprouting broccoli. This dual-purpose habit, cut-and-come-again leaves through autumn and winter, then a flush of sweet flower shoots in the notorious late-winter hungry gap before other vegetables are ready, is what has kept it a favorite kitchen-garden variety in Britain for decades even though it remains uncommon in American seed catalogs. The flavor is notably mild and sweet for a kale, without the toughness of older curly types, and both the leaves and the immature flower buds are good raw or lightly cooked. Choose Pentland Brig where reliable winter survival and an early-spring harvest gap-filler matter more than a single big autumn leaf crop. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Peperone di Senise (Basilicata Sweet Drying Pepper)
description: Peperone di Senise takes its name from the town of Senise in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, where farmers have long selected this thin-fleshed sweet pepper and it now carries a protected geographical indication. Pods are elongated and tapering, hooked or twisted depending on the strain, and their unusually thin flesh dries quickly on strings hung in the sun without rotting. Once fully dried, the pods are known as peperoni cruschi, deep-fried briefly until shatteringly crisp and used as a garnish or snack throughout Basilicata, or ground into a red seasoning. Because the whole point of the variety is easy sun-drying, it performs best where summers are long, hot, and relatively dry. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Pepino (Pepino Melon)
description: Pepino melon is a perennial fruiting shrub from the Andes of South America, belonging to the same genus as tomatoes and eggplants — its smooth-skinned, oval fruits are pale golden-yellow with distinctive purple streaks when ripe, with sweet, mild, melon-like flesh that has been compared to a blend of cantaloupe and cucumber. The plant blooms and sets fruit best in cool to mild temperatures (50–75°F) rather than peak summer heat, making the fall through early spring season the most productive in the subtropical Gulf Coast; in zone 9 it often survives mild winters to fruit again the following cool season. Propagate easily from stem cuttings like tomatoes — a rooted cutting can fruit within 75–100 days of transplanting. Stake plants like a tomato or pepper to keep fruits off the ground; harvest when fruits develop a fully golden background color and give slightly to thumb pressure, typically 3–4 months after transplanting; let fully ripen at room temperature after picking for peak sweetness. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Pepino Dulce
description: Plant Pepino Dulce in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; water consistently and feed monthly with balanced fertilizer; stake or cage as plants sprawl; harvest fruits when fully colored and aromatic, giving slightly to gentle pressure. Solanum muricatum is a domesticated Andean crop related to tomato, potato, and eggplant — one of the less commonly grown members of the Solanaceae family that produces a genuinely delicious and distinctive dessert fruit. The oval fruits, ranging from 2–4 inches long, develop beautiful purple streaking on a pale yellow base as they ripen, and the flesh has a mild, sweet flavor combining melon, pear, and cucumber notes with very low acidity — a refreshing warm-season treat eaten fresh, chilled, or in fruit salads. Propagation from stem cuttings is faster and more reliable than from seed, yielding fruiting plants within the same season; plants grown in zone 9–11 behave as short-lived perennials and may be cut back after fruiting for regrowth. In frost-prone zones it is grown as a warm-season annual from transplants started indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Pepino Melon
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; pepino melon is a relative of tomato and eggplant that produces cream to pale-purple-striped fruits shaped like a pear or egg, with flesh tasting of a mild blend of melon and cucumber. Grow on a stake or trellis to keep fruit off the ground and improve air circulation. The plant benefits from regular fertilization with a tomato-type fertilizer and consistent watering; fruit quality declines with drought stress. Harvest when fruits turn golden yellow with purple stripes and yield slightly to pressure — they are eaten fresh, in fruit salads, or as a savory side dish in Andean cuisine where they originate. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Pepitas Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Hull-Less Seed Snacking Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Pepitas is an AAS-winning pumpkin bred specifically as a seed crop — the medium-orange fruit is filled with abundant naked, hull-less green seeds (the same type sold commercially as pepitas), which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly with no shelling needed, unlike the tough-hulled seeds of most pumpkin varieties. It is a fun, productive choice for gardeners who want a real harvest of roastable snacking seeds without buying store pepitas, and the flesh, while secondary to the seed crop, is still usable in cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to decline, then scoop and separate the seeds from the pulp before rinsing and roasting or drying them for storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Peppadew Pepper (Piquanté Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay warm; Peppadew is the trademarked name for a piquanté pepper discovered as a chance seedling in a South African garden in the 1990s and now grown commercially worldwide for pickling. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling Capsicum baccatum shrub that produces small, round, tomato-shaped fruit that ripens from green through orange to deep red, carrying a sweet-tart flavor with a mild, tingling heat far gentler than most hot peppers. Because it needs a long, warm growing season to size up and color fully, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed extra early and expect the first ripe fruit late in the season; in the Gulf South's long summers it has time to produce a heavy crop. Pick fruit once fully colored and pickle or roast to mellow the skin, as Peppadew is traditionally eaten cured rather than fresh off the plant. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F soil temperature — peppers need warm soil to germinate and grow; transplant after nights consistently stay above 55°F in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Water consistently but do not overwater — even moisture is essential for preventing blossom drop and fruit set; inconsistent watering causes blossom drop during pollination. Peppers are one of the most productive vegetables for hot-summer climates, producing continuous harvests from midsummer through frost. Green peppers can be harvested at any time; allowing them to mature to red, yellow, or orange increases sweetness and vitamin C content significantly. In zone 8–11 peppers can be overwintered as perennials if protected from frost. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Pepper X (World's Hottest Certified Chile)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using a heat mat to keep soil near 85F, since chinense types germinate unevenly and slowly compared to annuum peppers. Transplant into warm soil only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F, and stake plants as the heavy fruit load develops. Pepper X was bred by Ed Currie of PuckerButt Pepper Company and was certified by Guinness World Records in 2023 as the hottest pepper ever measured, surpassing the Carolina Reaper. Handle ripe pods with gloves, as the capsaicin level is extreme even by superhot standards. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Pepper-Bark Tree
description: Native to woodlands of southern and eastern Africa, this evergreen tree bears leaves and bark with a sharp, peppery bite, used fresh or dried as a chili-pepper-like seasoning as well as in traditional medicine, which has driven heavy wild harvesting and left the species classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Garden specimens should be grown from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected material, and only leaves (not bark) should be harvested from cultivated trees to keep the tree healthy, since debarking easily kills it. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; the tree is moderately drought-tolerant once established and produces small greenish flowers followed by purple-black fruits. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Peppermint
description: Peppermint is a vigorous, cool-flavored perennial beloved for teas, desserts, and savory dishes. Press the fine seed onto the surface without covering, as it needs light to germinate, and keep it warm and evenly moist. It thrives in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to part shade and spreads aggressively by runners, so grow it in a container or a contained bed. Harvest sprigs anytime and cut plants back before flowering to keep the foliage flavorful. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Peppermint
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; contain in buried pots or with root barriers sunk 12 inches into the soil as peppermint spreads aggressively by underground stolons and will colonize a large area if uncontained. Mentha × piperita is a sterile hybrid between water mint (M. aquatica) and spearmint (M. spicata) that is propagated vegetatively; it is the mint whose essential oil (menthol) is used in toothpaste, confections, medicine, cosmetics, and a vast range of products, and whose leaves are used for peppermint tea, juleps, mojitos, and as a culinary flavoring. Black peppermint (var. piperita) has purple-tinged stems and the strongest menthol flavor; white peppermint (var. officinalis) has greener stems and is slightly milder. Both types prefer moist, fertile soil and appreciate afternoon shade in hot climates. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Peppermint Chard (Candy-Striped Pink Stem Chard)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Peppermint chard produces glossy, savoyed green leaves on stalks striped in bands of pink and white, resembling the candy for which it is named and giving it strong visual appeal both in the garden and sliced into salads. Flavor is typical of Swiss chard, with tender leaves that cook down like spinach and crisp stalks that can be prepared like celery, and the coloring holds reasonably well when lightly cooked. Harvest outer leaves regularly as needed to keep the plant productive, and expect continued cropping over a long cool-season harvest window with cut-and-come-again picking. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Peppermint Geranium
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade; peppermint geranium is the most shade-tolerant and large-leaved of the scented pelargoniums — its enormous, densely hairy, velvety, gray-green, rounded leaves give the plant a soft, textural, spreading quality unlike any other herb, and crush the leaves to release an intensely fresh, clear peppermint-eucalyptus fragrance that is one of the most pleasant and cooling herb scents available. The velvety, felt-like texture of the large leaves is as much a tactile as a visual pleasure. It spreads by lax, trailing stems to cover considerable ground in partial shade, making it useful as a low, scented groundcover in shaded containers, window boxes, and garden edges. Small, white, purple-spotted flowers appear at intervals. Leaves are used to flavor sachets, tea, and baked goods. It is more water-tolerant than most scented pelargoniums. The most commonly grown cultivar for ground coverage and shade tolerance is the straight species; 'Chocolate Mint' (dark-spotted center) is an attractive variant. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Pepperoncini (Tuscan Pepper, Golden Greek Pepper)
description: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pepperoncini is the classic Italian pickling and frying pepper, widely grown throughout Tuscany and the Greek Peloponnese for centuries and the pepper that fills the olive bar jars in every American grocery store. The thin-walled, mildly hot (100–500 Scoville), wrinkled fruits are harvested at 2–3 inches when bright green for pickling in white wine vinegar — the standard preparation produces the distinctive brine-pickled pepperoncini familiar from Italian sub sandwiches and antipasto. When allowed to ripen fully red, the fruits sweeten considerably and are excellent fresh or roasted. The plants are productive and undemanding, bearing heavily over a long season in full sun with consistent moisture. In Italian cooking, fresh pepperoncini are used whole in pasta sauces (arrabbiata), braised with olives and capers, and roasted under poultry. The Greek variety (often called 'Golden Greek' or 'Greek Golden') is essentially the same pepper and is the primary type pickled for commercial sale in the US. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Pepperwort (Dittander, Perennial Cress)
description: Plant rooted divisions in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; pepperwort (Lepidium latifolium) is a vigorous, spreading, perennial cress with large, thick leaves that have a strong, peppery to horseradish-like flavor much more intense than common garden cress — used as a horseradish substitute in medieval European cooking and still used traditionally in parts of Britain and Scandinavia. Young leaves can be eaten raw in small amounts as a condiment or added sparingly to salads and sandwiches; older leaves and the roots are used cooked as a flavoring. Caution: the plant is listed as an invasive weed in parts of the western United States where it colonizes riparian areas and wetlands; plant only in contained situations in those regions. Produces masses of small white flowers attractive to bees. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Pequi
description: Plant Caryocar brasiliense in deep, well-drained, sandy, acidic, very lean cerrado soil in full sun; the tree is adapted to nutrient-poor savanna soils and performs poorly in rich, fertilized conditions; water moderately during establishment, then sparingly — it is drought-adapted. CAUTION: the inner seed coat (endocarp) is covered with sharp spines; eat the oily flesh from the outside of the seed coat with extreme care, using a scraping motion, or you will be impaled. Pequi is an ingredient of such cultural importance in Minas Gerais and the Cerrado of central Brazil that it has been called 'the soul of sertanejo cooking.' The intensely aromatic, golden-yellow oily flesh surrounding the spiny inner stone is eaten by scraping with the front teeth — a culturally specific technique that everyone from the region knows — in dishes like Galinhada com Pequi (chicken and rice with pequi), pamonha, and various cerrado preparations. The flavor is extraordinary and polarizing: powerful, complex, unmistakably distinctive, combining notes of ripe mango, roasted nuts, pungent tropical cheese, and a rich, almost buttery oiliness. The fruit oil is pressed for cosmetics, cooking, and traditional medicine. A crucial food for wildlife in the Cerrado: jaguars, tapirs, and many birds consume the fallen fruits. The tree is the symbol of Minas Gerais state and a cultural keystone of the cerrado region. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Pequin Pepper
description: Start indoors and transplant to well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pequin pepper (also spelled piquin) is a wild-type species pepper native to South Texas and northeastern Mexico, where it grows as a woody perennial shrub in dry, rocky, calcareous soils — often under the shade of mesquite, oak, and other native trees. The tiny, egg-shaped fruits (1/4 to 1/2 inch) pack an intense concentrated heat (40,000–100,000 SHU) with a distinctive citrusy, nutty flavor beloved in Tex-Mex cooking, particularly in traditional Mexican salsas and vinegar-based hot sauces. Wild-harvested pequin peppers are prized over cultivated ones in parts of northern Mexico. Birds that eat the fruits are immune to capsaicin and disperse the seeds. An excellent native plant for hot, dry, alkaline Texas and Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Peredovik Black Oil Sunflower (Russian High-Oil Bird-Feeding and Oil-Production Sunflower)
description: Direct sow 0.5–1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest when seed heads are completely dry and brown. Peredovik (also spelled 'Peredovik') is a Russian open-pollinated oilseed sunflower developed in the Soviet Union specifically for oil production — one of the most widely planted sunflower varieties in the world and the standard variety used in commercial sunflower oil production globally before the development of modern high-oleic hybrids. The Peredovik breeding emphasized oil percentage over seed size: the thin, black seeds contain 42–45% oil by weight (compared to 24–28% for striped ornamental/snack sunflower types), and this high oil content is what gives 'black oil sunflower' its distinct value. In the bird-feeding context, black oil sunflower seeds (Peredovik or similar black-seeded varieties) are universally recommended as the premier wild bird food: the thin, easy-to-crack shell is accessible to a wider range of small songbirds than the thick-shelled striped types, and the high oil content provides superior energy density for birds — particularly important for overwintering and migratory species. For wildlife food plots in the Gulf South, Peredovik-type black oil sunflower is one of the primary dove and songbird attractants planted specifically for the September-October dove season. The seeds are also excellent for human consumption (roasting, pressing for oil) though small in size. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Perennial Basil
description: Root stem cuttings in water or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; perennial basil (African basil, East Indian basil, spice basil) is a tropical perennial species grown in Gulf Coast and subtropical gardens for its superior performance in the heat and humidity that causes standard sweet basil (O. basilicum) to bolt and decline rapidly in midsummer — perennial basil withstands zone 9–12 summer heat, continues producing through the hottest months, and in frost-free climates grows as a large, multi-stemmed perennial shrub to 3–4 feet that persists for several years. The flavor is similar to sweet basil but carries an additional spicy, clove-like note that distinguishes it in cooking. Like all basils, the culinary quality is best before flowering; tip-prune regularly to delay bolting. It roots readily from stem cuttings placed in water, making it easy to propagate and share. Excellent in containers and mixed herb borders as a large, bushy accent. In zones below 9, grow as a long-season annual or bring cuttings indoors in fall to overwinter. Matures in 45–75 days from transplant.

name: Perennial Basil (East African Basil, Tree Basil)
description: Start from seed or cuttings and plant in full sun after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; perennial basil (Ocimum gratissimum, also called East African or tree basil) is a large woody-based perennial subshrub native to tropical Africa and Asia that grows year-round in frost-free gardens, eventually reaching 4–6 feet tall and requiring no replanting. The flavor is more pungent and medicinal than sweet basil — strongly clove-like with hints of eucalyptus and camphor — and is the basil of choice in West African, Southeast Asian, and South American cooking rather than Italian cuisine. Used fresh or dried in stews, soups, bean dishes, and rice preparations. An excellent container plant for northern gardeners overwintered indoors on a sunny sill. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Perennial Glasswort (Woody Glasswort)
description: Sow seed or plant divisions in sandy, well-drained, saline to brackish soil in full sun; perennial glasswort is a close relative of annual Salicornia, sharing the same leafless, jointed, succulent green stems and briny, oceanic flavor prized as 'sea beans' or samphire in gourmet cooking, but distinguished by its perennial habit — the base of the plant becomes woody and persists through winter, resprouting fleshy new stems each spring rather than dying back to seed like annual glasswort. This makes it a useful low, spreading edible groundcover for a genuinely saline coastal garden bed, salt marsh restoration planting, or tide-edge landscape where few other edible plants survive, and once established it slowly forms a dense, low mat rather than requiring reseeding each year. Harvest the tender young stem tips through the growing season with scissors, leaving the tougher, woodier base intact to keep producing; flavor and texture are best on actively growing spring and early summer growth before stems begin to harden. Like its annual cousin, it tolerates direct seawater irrigation and thrives in salinity that would kill ordinary vegetables. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Perfection Apricot (Large-Fruited California Heirloom Requiring a Pollenizer)
description: Perfection is an early-twentieth-century California apricot bred for exceptionally large fruit size, among the biggest of the traditional apricot varieties, with golden-orange skin and juicy, mild-flavored flesh best suited to fresh eating rather than drying. Unlike self-fertile modern varieties, Perfection will not set a reliable crop on its own and needs a compatible pollenizer, typically Blenheim, planted within pollinating distance and blooming at the same time. The tree tends to set fruit heavily in good years, so thin aggressively while fruit is still small to prevent limb breakage and to keep the remaining fruit at full large size. Because it is an older variety selected before modern disease-resistance breeding, watch for brown rot and bacterial canker in humid conditions and prune for an open canopy to improve air circulation. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Perfection Fennel
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to final spacing, since fennel taproots resent disturbance. Perfection is a long-standing open-pollinated bulbing fennel prized for producing some of the largest, most uniform bulbs among non-hybrid Florence types, with crisp white flesh and a clean, sweet anise flavor. It is often grown as a reliable, seed-saveable alternative to F1 hybrids like Zefa Fino where growers want to select and replant their own seed year to year. Mound soil around the base of the swelling bulb as it enlarges to keep it pale and tender rather than green and fibrous. Harvest by cutting the bulb at soil level once it reaches a good hand-sized girth, before the center begins to push up a flower stalk. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Perfection Pea (Heirloom Wrinkled Shelling Pea, Parent of Wando)
description: Perfection is an early-20th-century heirloom shelling pea, one of the smooth-podded, wrinkled-seeded 'marrow' dessert types once widely offered in market and home garden seed catalogs before modern hybrid peas became dominant. Sow seed directly into cool, workable spring soil, since like all garden peas it germinates and grows best well ahead of summer heat. The vigorous vines climb readily with light brush or netting support and set pods over several weeks of cool weather, yielding sweet, full-flavored peas typical of the wrinkled-seed dessert type. Perfection is historically notable as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Laxton's Progress, crossed by USDA breeders in 1943 to create the heat-tolerant Wando pea. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Perfection Red Currant (Classic American Heirloom Red Currant)
description: Perfection is an early-twentieth-century American red currant selection, raised from a Fay's Prolific by Cherry cross, that has stayed in commerce for over a century because of its large, long, easy-to-strip clusters of bright red, tart berries. Bushes are vigorous and self-fertile, producing heavy crops on long strigs that make hand-picking faster than on many other red currant cultivars, and the fruit is well suited to jelly, syrup, and baking as well as fresh eating once fully ripe. Like most red currants, Perfection needs a meaningful number of winter chill hours and cool summer nights to perform well, so it should be treated as an experimental, likely underperforming choice in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast plantings rather than a dependable crop. Where climate allows, keep roots cool with mulch, prune out canes older than three years each winter, and pick full clusters rather than individual berries to preserve fruit quality. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Perilla (Shiso)
description: Surface sow on moist soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; perilla (shiso) is the essential Japanese herb with large, ruffled leaves in green or deep purple-red that have a distinctive flavor combining cinnamon, anise, cloves, and mint — unique in the herbal palette. Green shiso (ao-jiso) wraps sushi, flavors salads, and garnishes sashimi; red/purple shiso (aka-jiso) colors umeboshi pickled plums and makes the vivid magenta shiso juice (yukari). Both forms are ornamentally striking, especially the 'Britton' frilly-leafed type. Plants self-seed extremely prolifically — thin seedlings carefully and pull unwanted volunteers before they go to seed, as it can naturalize aggressively in favorable climates. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Perique Tobacco (Aztec Tobacco)
description: Transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Nicotiana rustica is a shorter, broader-leaved, much more potent species than common tobacco, historically grown by the Choctaw and later by Acadian farmers along the Mississippi River in St. James Parish, Louisiana, where its cured leaf became the base for Perique, a uniquely fermented tobacco with a distinctive dark, fruity, spicy character produced by packing the cured leaf under heavy pressure in wooden barrels for months, a traditional process protected as a geographic specialty of the region. The broad, crinkled, yellow-green leaves are harvested and air-cured much like common tobacco before undergoing the distinctive pressure-fermentation that sets Perique apart from other tobaccos. This species is also of historical significance as one of the tobaccos originally cultivated and traded by Indigenous peoples of North America prior to European contact. All parts of the plant contain nicotine at notably higher concentrations than common tobacco and are toxic if ingested, so keep well away from pets, livestock, and children, and wear long sleeves when handling mature plants to avoid skin absorption. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Perkins Dwarf Okra (Compact Southern Heirloom Long-Pod Okra)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm; harvest at 3-5 inches for the most tender eating, though pods stay usable up to 8-9 inches longer than most okra. Perkins Dwarf is a compact-growing strain within the old Perkins okra family, bred down from the tall Southern heirloom standard to a manageable 3-5 foot plant while keeping the same ribbed, dark green pods and early, heavy production. The shorter stature means less staking and easier picking through the peak of a Gulf Coast summer, and the extended window of pod tenderness gives more forgiveness if a hot spell delays harvest by a day or two. It remains an excellent choice for canning, pickling, and frying, and its early start lets Gulf Coast gardeners begin harvesting well before many full-size heirloom types come into production. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Perkins Long Pod Okra (Classic Tall Southern Heirloom Okra)
description: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F.
