Perkins Long Pod is a traditional Southern heirloom okra grown for generations before the spineless Perkins strains were selected from it, producing heavy yields of long, ribbed, dark green pods on tall, vigorous plants that can reach 6 feet or more by season's end. Harvest pods every two to three days at 2-4 inches long for the most tender eating, since larger pods quickly turn woody and fibrous; regular picking keeps the plant producing continuously through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer. Stake or support plants in windy sites, and remove any overgrown pods promptly to keep new flowers and pods coming. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Perkins Mammoth Long Pod Okra
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is warm; soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an heirloom okra variety introduced in the 1890s that produces exceptionally long (6–10 inch) ribbed green pods with a more tender quality at larger sizes than most okra varieties — meaning the pods remain acceptable for eating somewhat longer than standard varieties, which quickly become fibrous and tough once they exceed 3–4 inches. The plants are vigorous (5–8 feet), highly productive, and heat-tolerant, performing well throughout the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Harvest pods at 4–6 inches for optimal tenderness; though the pods can be eaten somewhat larger, regular harvesting every 1–2 days in hot weather is essential to keep production high — missed pods left on the plant stop production quickly. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Perla Negra Chayote (Dark Green Smooth Spineless Chayote)
description: Perla Negra is a dark green, smooth-skinned, spineless chayote selection, distinguished from common pale-green mirliton by its deeper color and glossier, blemish-free skin, traits favored in Mexican and Central American fresh markets. Plant the whole fruit at an angle in well-worked soil with the narrow stem end barely covered, since chayote's single large seed cannot be separated from the flesh and the entire fruit is the planting unit. Provide a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor, since the vigorous vine can run 20-40 feet and becomes extremely productive once established in zones 9-11, typically bearing in fall and again in early spring. Fruit, tender young shoots, and leaves are all edible, and mature plants develop large starchy edible tubers as well; harvest fruit young and firm for the mildest flavor and most tender texture. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Perle Hops
description: Perle is a German aroma cultivar developed at the Hop Research Center in Hüll from Northern Brewer parentage, bred to offer a milder, spicy, minty aroma close to noble-hop character while resisting Verticillium wilt and other diseases far better than true landraces like Hallertauer Mittelfruh. It has since become a mainstay in both German and Pacific Northwest hop yards, valued for its dependable vigor. Full sun, deep fertile soil, and a tall, sturdy trellis suit its steady, moderately vigorous bine growth. It makes a good lower-maintenance substitute where authentic Hallertau proves too disease-prone for a home garden. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Perlette Grape
description: Released by UC Davis in 1946, Perlette is one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes, producing small to medium, round, pale green berries with a crisp, neutral-sweet flavor on compact clusters. Its very early harvest window makes it popular with home gardeners wanting fresh grapes before most other varieties are ready. Vines are moderately vigorous and clusters tend to be tightly packed, so thinning berries when they are pea-sized helps prevent splitting and rot in humid weather. It has good cold tolerance for a vinifera type but still needs a warm, sunny site to ripen well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Perpetua Everbearing Dwarf Blueberry (Reblooming Two-Harvest Container Blueberry)
description: Give Perpetua a large container or raised bed of acidic, well-drained soil, since it grows a bit larger than the other dwarf Bushel and Berry selections while still staying compact enough for a patio or small yard. What sets it apart is a genuine second bloom and fruit set in late summer, so gardeners get an early-summer crop followed weeks later by a smaller fall harvest, on a self-fertile plant. This reblooming habit makes it especially useful in a mild Gulf Coast climate where the growing season is long enough to ripen both flushes before frost. Deadhead spent fruit clusters after the first harvest to encourage the second bloom, and feed with acid-forming fertilizer after each fruiting cycle. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Perpetual Spinach
description: Perpetual spinach is actually a leaf chard grown for tender, mild leaves that eat like true spinach but far more heat- and bolt-resistant. As a cut-and-come-again crop it produces for months, and being biennial it can carry over for a second season in mild areas. Direct sow in spring in full sun to partial shade and keep evenly watered. Harvest outer leaves regularly and the plant will keep pushing out new growth well into fall. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Perpetual Spinach (Spinach Beet, Leaf Beet)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Perpetual Spinach is an old English strain of leaf beet grown specifically as a heat- and bolt-resistant substitute for true spinach, with smaller, smoother, thinner-stalked leaves than standard Swiss chard and a milder, more spinach-like flavor when cooked. Unlike true spinach, which bolts quickly in warm weather, this leaf beet keeps producing tender new leaves through much of the growing season, giving gardeners a reliable spinach-flavored green across a far longer window. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect the plant to keep cropping for months with regular cutting. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Perpetual Spinach Swiss Chard
description: Despite its name this thin-ribbed Italian heirloom is a Swiss chard grown for its tender, spinach-like leaves, and it is slow to bolt in hot weather. Sow directly and thin seedlings, then harvest outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing new growth for months. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed occasionally for lush leaves. It tolerates both spring and fall conditions and mild frost. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Perry Pear
description: Perry pears are tannic, high-acid cultivars grown to ferment into perry, the pear equivalent of cider. These are famously long-lived, slow-to-fruit trees that eventually reach great size, so give them ample space and patience. Plant at least two varieties for pollination in deep soil and full sun. Little pruning is required once a strong framework is established; harvest the astringent fruit slightly underripe and let it sweat before pressing. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Persian Basil
description: Persian Basil, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, produces large, soft silvery-green leaves with an assertive spicy flavor combining clove, anise, and a hint of lemon that sets it apart from sweeter Genovese-type basils. The sturdy, upright plants are notably slow to bolt, holding good flavor and tender texture well into summer while many other basils turn bitter once they flower. It is the traditional basil of Persian cuisine, eaten fresh as part of sabzi khordan herb platters and stirred into stews, rice dishes, and grilled meats. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and harvest by pinching stem tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and delay flowering even longer. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Persian Bearss Lime Tree
description: Persian Bearss is a prolific, thornless lime producing juicy, seedless fruit perfect for cooking and drinks. It is one of the more cold-tolerant limes but still needs protection below freezing. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. Water deeply and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, feeding with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. In zones colder than 9, grow in a large pot that can move to a bright indoor location for winter. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Persian Catmint (Mussini Catmint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Persian catmint blooms most freely with good drainage and lean, somewhat dry soil — avoid rich, moist soil which produces lush but less floriferous plants. Nepeta mussinii is a low, aromatic, mounding European catmint with soft, gray-green, scalloped, strongly fragrant leaves and prolific spikes of small, lavender-blue flowers from late spring through early summer; shear plants by half after the first flush of bloom to stimulate a second flowering period in mid- to late summer. Unlike the commonly grown N. × faassenii (a sterile hybrid), N. mussinii is the true species from the Caucasus; it is slightly smaller than faassenii and sets viable seed. Attractive to bees, butterflies, and cats; resistant to deer and rabbits. Use as a low, billowing border edger or path-side planting. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Persian Cress (Ornamental Garden Cress)
description: Persian cress is a distinct, upright-growing strain of garden cress grown less for cutting as salad microgreens and more for its tall, airy sprays of tiny silvery seed pods, prized by floral designers as a delicate cut-flower filler. Left to mature past the baby-leaf stage, plants send up branched, wiry stems topped with small white flowers that quickly form the decorative seed heads for which the variety is grown. Direct sow in cool weather into average, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings a few inches apart to give the branching stems room to develop. Succession sow every few weeks in spring and fall for a continuous supply of cutting stems, since plants bolt and decline quickly once summer heat arrives. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Persian Lime (Tahiti Lime, Bearss Lime)
description: Plant in excellent drainage in full sun; Persian lime is the lime sold in virtually every grocery store worldwide — the standard 'lime' of commerce in the United States and Europe. The large, seedless, thick-skinned fruits (much larger than Key lime) are harvested green and provide the characteristic lime flavor of margaritas, guacamole, and countless beverages. Unlike Key lime, Persian lime is technically a triploid (3 sets of chromosomes), which makes it seedless and somewhat more vigorous and cold-tolerant than Key lime. It produces fruit year-round in tropical climates and has peak seasons in spring and fall in zone 9. Trees are also more cold-tolerant than Key lime (surviving to 26°F vs. 28–30°F for Key lime) and are larger and more productive under zone 9 conditions. Feed 3–4 times yearly with a complete citrus fertilizer; supplement with chelated micronutrients if leaves show yellowing. Freeze protection below 28°F is recommended; wrap trunks with frost cloth or move container trees indoors. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Persian Melon
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Persian melon requires hot, dry conditions for best sweetness and is most successful in California, Arizona, Texas, and Gulf Coast gardens. Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon of Middle Eastern origin that became a California commercial standard in the early 20th century; the large (8–15 lb), round to slightly oval fruits have a thick layer of fine, closely woven gray-green netting over dark green skin that transitions to golden-green at maturity, with deeply aromatic, thick, deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, spicy sweetness. Persian melon is rounder and larger than cantaloupes and has thicker, denser flesh with a more pronounced, spicy aromatic complexity than American cantaloupe types. It requires a longer season (90–100 days) and performs best in hot, dry conditions; California's Central and Imperial Valleys have historically produced most commercial Persian melons sold in Western markets. The thick rind and firm flesh give Persian melon better shipping quality than more delicate muskmelon types, and it stores 1–2 weeks refrigerated after harvest. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Persian Star Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Samarkand Heritage)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch after planting; keep weed-free and consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl; harvest in early to midsummer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure in a warm, dry, airy location. Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe-type hardneck garlic with a remarkable provenance: it was collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan — the ancient Silk Road city at the crossroads of Central Asia — by John Swenson, a garlic enthusiast and Seed Savers Exchange member who traveled to the former Soviet Union in 1989 collecting traditional garlic varieties grown in the region for centuries. The provenance from Samarkand, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a center of Central Asian agricultural tradition, gives Persian Star historical and botanical significance as a window into the genetic diversity of garlic in its center of diversity (Central Asia is believed to be the region where cultivated garlic first developed). The bulbs are 2–3 inches across with 8–12 cloves; the outer skin is white with subtle purple striping typical of the Marbled Purple Stripe group, while the inner clove skins are often vivid violet-purple — beautiful when peeled. The flavor is rich, earthy, moderately pungent, and complex — slightly different from Rocambole types with a distinctive minerality. Storage life is better than Rocambole (5–7 months) but less than softneck types. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Persimmon Tomato
description: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and staking or caging firmly. Persimmon is a Ukrainian heirloom beefsteak tomato with fruit that resembles the color of a ripe persimmon — vivid golden-orange — with very meaty flesh, a small seed cavity, extraordinarily sweet, low-acid, fruity flavor, and fruits weighing 10–16 ounces; it is among the finest-tasting orange or golden beefsteak heirlooms and has been prized by serious tomato growers since its introduction through Seed Savers Exchange. The vigorous indeterminate vines produce steadily through the season; stake firmly and maintain consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and yield slightly to pressure at the blossom end. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Perth Pride Tomato (Australian-Bred Red Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Perth Pride, developed through the Australian arm of the international Dwarf Tomato Project, bears deep red, beefsteak-style fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact plant, combining full-size tomato quality with a footprint suited to small gardens and containers. It reflects the collaborative, worldwide nature of the Dwarf Tomato Project breeding effort. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Peruano Bean (Mayocoba Bean)
description: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination. Also sold as Mayocoba or canary bean, Peruano is a pale golden-yellow bean central to everyday Mexican and Mexican-American cooking, valued for a creamy texture and mild flavor that holds up well in refried preparations. The compact bush habit needs no staking and produces a concentrated harvest suited to home drying. Let pods mature fully and dry on the plant before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry, airtight container. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Peruque Pecan (Historic Early-Ripening Missouri Native Pecan)
description: Peruque was discovered growing wild in the Mississippi River floodplain near St. Charles, Missouri, and was brought to national attention in the 1950s for its precocious, reliably annual bearing habit. It produces a medium-sized, thin-shelled nut, about 80 per pound, that ripens in mid-September, among the earliest of any named pecan, which makes it valuable for far-northern growing regions with short frost-free seasons. Peruque is notably scab-susceptible compared to modern resistant releases, and its thin shell makes the crop a favorite target for crows and jays, so plan on bird deterrence at harvest. As a Type I pollen shedder, it needs a Type II pollinator planted nearby. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Peruvian Apple Cactus
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean cactus or sandy soil in full sun; Peruvian apple cactus is a large, multi-branched columnar cactus native to South America and widely planted as an ornamental, living fence, and fruit tree throughout the Caribbean, tropical America, and the Mediterranean. The stout, blue-green to gray-green columns branch freely to form impressive upright clumps reaching 10–25 feet, with prominent ribs and clusters of short spines. In summer, it produces large, showy, white funnel-shaped flowers up to 6 inches across that open at night and are pollinated by bats and hawk moths — a remarkable natural spectacle. The flowers are followed by the edible 'Peruvian apples' — oval red to dark-magenta fruits 2–3 inches long with sweet, translucent white flesh and small black seeds, having a mild, pleasant flavor. Related to and confused with the queen of the night and night-blooming cereus, but distinct. Excellent as a living fence, architectural garden specimen, or screening plant in zone 9–11 landscapes. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Peruvian Purple Pepper (Ornamental Edible Hot Pepper with Purple Foliage and Upright Fruits)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest fruits at any stage from purple-black (immature, high heat) to fully red (ripe). Peruvian Purple Pepper is a compact ornamental-edible hot pepper variety distinguished by its unusual anthocyanin-rich foliage — a deep purple-black that makes the plant visually dramatic from seedling stage through maturity. The purple coloration in the leaves and immature fruits results from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to high light intensity; the same plant grown in reduced light will show less purple coloration and more green foliage, making sun exposure a direct visible factor in the plant's ornamental effect. Fruits emerge deep purple-black and upright — pointing skyward rather than pendant — which is a characteristic of many small ornamental hot pepper types and adds visual interest as the small fruits are held prominently above the purple foliage. As fruits ripen to full maturity they transition through a mottled purple-and-red stage before reaching solid vivid red; many gardeners harvest throughout this color progression since the flavor and heat level remain high at all stages. The heat level is substantial for a Capsicum annuum variety — comparable to Thai or bird's eye types — and is proportional to the small fruit size, as capsaicin concentration tends to increase as fruit diameter decreases within the species. Culinary uses mirror those of other small hot peppers: used fresh in salads, salsas, and stir-fries; pickled; or dried whole for later use. As a compact container plant with dramatic foliage, Peruvian Purple also functions effectively as a purely ornamental annual in mixed containers where its purple leaves provide contrast against chartreuse, silver, or deep green companions. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Pescadero Red Garlic (Fisherman's Garlic, Mild Coastal Creole Type)
description: Pescadero Red, also called Fisherman's Garlic for its coastal California origins near Pescadero, is a Creole-type softneck garlic grown for its symmetrical bulbs wrapped in brilliant burgundy-streaked skins and a mild, mellow garlic flavor with far less bite than typical hardneck varieties. It is an unusually vigorous grower for a Creole, often producing bulbs larger than its relatives, with 8-12 plump cloves arranged in the tight circular pattern characteristic of the group. Because it needs minimal cold exposure to form bulbs, it thrives in the same mild Gulf South and coastal winters where northern Rocambole and Porcelain garlics routinely fail. Harvest in early summer when the lower leaves brown and 4-5 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; well-cured bulbs store from early summer through winter into mid-spring. Matures in 180–220 days from transplant.

name: Pesto Perpetuo Basil (Variegated Non-Flowering Columnar Basil)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun after last frost; pinch occasionally to maintain compact form — unlike most basil, Pesto Perpetuo never flowers and never needs pinching for flower removal. Root 4-inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix. Pesto Perpetuo is a unique sterile basil hybrid — a cross between Ocimum basilicum and Ocimum citriodorum — that distinguishes itself from all other basil varieties by never flowering and never setting seed. Standard basil becomes progressively less productive, more bitter, and eventually dies after flowering and setting seed; the entire management practice of regular pinching (removing flower buds before they open) is devoted to delaying this flowering. Pesto Perpetuo's sterility eliminates this entirely: it produces leaves continuously throughout the entire growing season without any flower development, making it the most consistently productive basil for a full-season harvest without intervention. The leaves are small to medium, oval, with a distinctive cream-white to ivory variegated margin around a green center — an ornamental quality unlike any other basil type. The flavor is lemon-basil in character — aromatic, mildly sweet, with distinct citrus notes alongside the standard basil character — very pleasant fresh but somewhat different from classic Genovese pesto basil. The columnar habit (upright, narrow, 18–30 inches) makes it ideal for containers, herb pots, and edible ornamental arrangements. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Petai (Stink Bean, Bitter Bean, Twisted Cluster Bean)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; petai requires a long growing season with warm temperatures year-round. Parkia speciosa (petai or stink bean) is a large, tropical legume tree of Southeast Asia producing distinctive, long (12–18 inch), flat, twisted seed pods containing 10–18 large, flat, bright-green seeds with an intensely pungent, sulfurous odor (similar to but stronger than garlic and fenugreek combined) that is a celebrated ingredient in Malaysian, Indonesian, and Thai cooking. The seeds are eaten raw, stir-fried with shrimp, added to curries and sambals, or mixed with garlic, chili, and shrimp paste — those accustomed to the flavor consider it a prized delicacy despite (or because of) its extreme pungency. Like asparagus with certain compounds, petai causes urine to smell strongly of its sulfurous compounds for several hours after eating — considered a normal, if somewhat inconvenient, effect. The tree is a nitrogen-fixer (fixing atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules) and has been used in agroforestry systems throughout Malaysia and Indonesia. Rarely available in the continental US except in specialty tropical fruit nurseries. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Peter Davis Thyme (Compact Lemon-Scented Pink-Flowered Alpine Thyme)
description: Peter Davis is a compact, mat-forming thyme with soft grey-green, lemon-scented foliage that holds a neat, cushiony habit rather than sprawling flat like common creeping thyme. Pale pink-mauve flowers cover the mound in late spring and summer, drawing bees, and the tidy, slightly domed shape suits rock gardens, alpine troughs, and border edging where a well-behaved, non-invasive thyme is wanted. It shares the same demand for lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil and full sun as other thymes, but is somewhat less cold-tolerant than common garden thyme and benefits from a gritty mulch and dry winter footing. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain the compact mound and encourage repeat bloom. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Peter Pan Pattypan Squash (AAS-Winning Green Scallop Summer Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches diameter for best eating quality. Peter Pan is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning pattypan (scallop) summer squash — an early-maturing, bush-habit variety producing pale green, disc-shaped fruits with the characteristic scalloped, fluted edges of the pattypan type. The distinctive flat, disc-like shape with scalloped margins distinguishes pattypan squash from all other summer squash types (zucchini, yellow crookneck, yellow straightneck) and has no equivalent in other vegetable categories — the shape makes individual fruits look like tiny flying saucers or UFOs and creates an unusually attractive presentation on the plate when halved or stuffed whole. Peter Pan's light green color is gentler and less common than the white pattypans that dominated before its introduction. The flavor is mild and slightly sweet — similar to other summer squash but with a distinctive nuttiness that develops in the scallop varieties at the ideal 3–4 inch harvest size. The bush habit (24–36 inch spread vs. the 6–8 foot spread of vining squash) makes Peter Pan practical for smaller raised beds and gardens. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Peter Pan Squash (AAS-Winning Pale Green Scallop Squash, Early and Compact)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when pale sage-green and tender. Peter Pan Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the summer squash category, honored for its early production, compact plant habit, and the distinctive pale sage-green to silvery-blue-green color of the scallop-shaped fruits. The AAS recognition confirmed Peter Pan's performance advantage over other scallop squash varieties of its time in trials across multiple growing regions and climates. The scallop squash form — a flat, disc-shaped fruit with distinctively scalloped or fluted edges — is one of the oldest American summer squash forms, with historical precedent in both Native American cultivation and early colonial American gardens. Peter Pan's F1 hybrid vigor contributes to both its compactness (more manageable plant than many bush zucchini) and productivity (abundant fruit set throughout the season). The color is a notable characteristic: the pale, muted sage-green to silvery green of Peter Pan is unlike the darker green of standard zucchini or the yellow of Sunburst, occupying its own distinctive color space that many gardeners find attractive for mixed variety plantings and market displays where color diversity is valued. The flat scallop form also makes Peter Pan an exceptionally attractive stuffed squash: the naturally hollow interior of the scallop form (relative to the solid flesh core of zucchini) allows more filling capacity per fruit when halved for stuffing, and the shallow depth of the squash makes even cooking possible at the small sizes most suitable for stuffing preparations. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Peter Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; stake taller plants if heavily loaded with fruit. Peter Pepper is a well-known Southern heirloom hot pepper, famous for its unmistakably novelty shape, which has made it a popular curiosity and conversation piece for generations of home gardeners across Texas and Louisiana. The medium-heat fruits (roughly 10,000–25,000 Scoville units, comparable to a strong jalapeño or mild cayenne) ripen from green to red and carry a fruity, tangy flavor good in salsas, pickling, and hot sauce once the novelty value has been enjoyed. Plants are productive and reasonably compact, performing well in containers as well as garden beds, and the fruit's thick walls hold up nicely to stuffing or pickling whole. A fun, genuinely productive heirloom for gardeners who want something distinctive alongside their standard pepper lineup, in zone 4–11. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Peter's Honey Fig (Small Yellow-Green Sweet Fig)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate poor soil but grow and fruit best with consistent moisture during fruit development. Peter's Honey is a fig cultivar collected and popularized among southern fig enthusiasts for its small-to-medium, pale yellow-green fruit with a honeyed, richly sweet flavor that belies its modest size and unassuming skin color. The tree is productive and vigorous, producing a light breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer followed by a heavier main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Because the fruit does not need to color up to signal ripeness, harvest by feel — ripe figs soften and the neck droops — rather than by color change. Prune in late winter to control size and remove any winter-killed tips, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Peters Pistachio (Male Pollinator)
description: Peters is the standard male pollinator paired with Kerman and other female pistachio cultivars in commercial and home orchards; it produces no nuts itself but times its pollen shed to overlap with Kerman bloom, which is essential since pistachio is entirely wind-pollinated and dioecious. Grow it under the same demanding regime as female pistachio trees: deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, 700-1000 winter chill hours, and hot, dry summers, conditions that make the species a poor match for humid climates regardless of cultivar. In a home planting, a single Peters tree, sited centrally or upwind of the prevailing spring breeze, is usually enough to pollinate several female trees. Because it carries no fruit load, Peters tends to grow a bit more vigorously and can be pruned harder to keep its canopy from overtopping the females it is meant to serve. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Petit Gris de Rennes Melon (French Heirloom Gray-Green Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to gray-green (the characteristic 'petit gris' color) and the stem cracks slightly at the base — this muskmelon type does not 'slip' from the vine like American cantaloupes but has a less decisive harvest cue. Petit Gris de Rennes (small gray of Rennes) is a traditional French muskmelon heirloom from Brittany, the coastal region of northwestern France, where it has been grown for centuries as the area's distinctive local melon. In France, Petit Gris de Rennes has Slow Food Ark of Taste recognition as a threatened traditional variety of significant cultural importance. The small to medium (1–2 lb) round fruits are distinguished by their unusual grayish-green to slate-green skin coloration with shallow ribs and fine, irregular netting — a very different appearance from the tan-netted American cantaloupe standard. The deeply orange, firm-textured, extremely sweet and aromatic flesh has a rich, complex character that many tasters consider superior to standard Western cantaloupe types — more complex in flavor, with floral and spicy notes beyond simple sweetness. Petit Gris de Rennes represents the French horticultural tradition of flavor breeding, where appearance is secondary to eating quality, and is a fascinating variety for gardeners interested in growing traditional European melon types beyond the standard muskmelon. Matures in 72–82 days from seed.

name: Petite Aubique Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Petite Aubique is a French compact fig variety producing small to medium, teardrop-shaped fruits with violet to brown skin and amber flesh — a mild, delicate, honey-sweet flavor suitable for fresh eating and preserves. The compact tree habit (smaller than most standard fig varieties) makes Petite Aubique one of the better options for container growing in large pots or half-barrels on patios and decks. The smaller plant size does not compromise productivity significantly; established container-grown Petite Aubique can produce 50–100 fruits annually. The small fruit size (1–1.5 inches) makes them a good all-in-one fresh-eating fig — no slicing required. In zone 9 the compact habit and full-sun requirement make it an excellent choice for warm south-facing walls or enclosed courtyards where reflected heat can accelerate ripening. The name 'Petite Aubique' is also found in the literature as 'Petite Grise,' indicating possible synonym use in some regions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Petite Negra Fig
description: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage and at least 8 hours of sun for maximum fruit production; Petite Negra is a naturally compact, dwarf fig cultivar producing small, round to pear-shaped fruits with dark purple to nearly black skin and amber to red, rich, sweet flesh — delivering the characteristic fresh fig flavor at a manageable plant scale that makes fresh fig production accessible to gardeners with limited space. The dwarf habit (3–5 feet in the ground, 2–3 feet in containers) is the primary distinguishing feature: Petite Negra produces full-sized, high-quality fruit on plants small enough to grow as container specimens on patios, to fit in small garden beds, or to overwinter indoors in containers in marginally cold climates. Container-grown fig culture allows gardeners outside the traditional fig belt (zones 7–10) to grow figs by moving plants indoors or into garages during winter; zone 9 gardeners can grow Petite Negra in the ground as a permanent, productive perennial shrub or in large containers for patio display. The self-fruitful nature (no cross-pollination required) and rapid return to bearing (often in the first or second year) make Petite Negra one of the most immediately rewarding fruit plants available. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Petite Pearl Grape (Cold-Hardy Dark Red Wine Grape)
description: Bred by Minnesota grape breeder Tom Plocher and released in 2010, this hybrid produces small clusters of tiny, thick-skinned dark berries that concentrate color and tannin for a deeply pigmented red wine unusual among cold-hardy hybrids. It combines strong winter hardiness with good resistance to fungal disease, and its naturally low yields concentrate flavor without extensive crop thinning. The compact clusters also reduce bunch rot risk in humid seasons. It has become popular among small-scale and hobby winemakers in the northern United States seeking a hybrid capable of real varietal red wine character. Matures in 145–160 days from transplant.

name: Petite Sirah Wine Grape (Durif)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Petite Sirah, more accurately known by its French name Durif after the botanist who discovered it as a chance cross of Syrah and the obscure Peloursin grape in the 1800s, produces small, thick-skinned, intensely dark berries despite the confusingly similar name to Syrah, which it is genetically related to but distinct from. Wines are deeply colored, high in tannin, and robust, often used both as a standalone bold red and as a blending grape to add color, structure, and backbone to lighter varieties. The unusually thick skin gives the variety real practical resilience against bunch rot and splitting in humid or rainy conditions, an advantage over many thinner-skinned fine wine grapes. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the naturally vigorous canopy for airflow, and pick once tannins are ripe as well as sugars, since underripe Petite Sirah can taste harshly astringent. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Petite Treat Watermelon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Seedless Melon)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply pollen for this seedless triploid to set fruit. Petite Treat is an All-America Selections winner bred for genuinely personal-sized fruit, producing round melons small enough for one or two people to finish in a single sitting, with sweet, crisp, deep red, seedless flesh and a thin rind. The compact vine takes up less garden space than standard large-fruited watermelon varieties, and the smaller fruit size means a shorter time from pollination to harvest-ready ripeness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the fruit turns creamy yellow, the most reliable ripeness indicators for seedless types. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Petrowski Turnip
description: A Central/Eastern European heirloom turnip grown historically in Poland and Russia for its round, golden-skinned roots with pale yellow flesh, a distinct look and flavor compared to the purple-top white types common in American gardens. It was traditionally valued for dual use as both a table vegetable and livestock forage. Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor and reduces the sharper bite common in summer-grown turnips. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Pettingill Apple (Ultra-Low-Chill Coastal Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pettingill was found as a chance seedling near Long Beach, California, and introduced in 1949; its chill requirement of roughly 100 hours makes it one of the lowest-chill named apples available, suited to areas where even Anna and Dorsett Golden struggle to accumulate enough winter cold. Fruit ripens late in the season, from late September into mid-October, later than most other low-chill selections, giving Gulf Coast growers a fall harvest option. The large red-over-green apples are crisp and juicy with well-balanced sugar and acid. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Phalsa (Indian Sherbet Berry)
description: Phalsa is a fast-growing shrubby tree from South Asia that tolerates drought, heat, and a range of soils, fruiting reliably within 1–2 years of planting — one of the quickest-bearing subtropical fruits. In traditional cultivation it is heavily pruned (nearly to the ground) each year after fruiting, which promotes vigorous new fruiting wood; in zone 9 this also serves as winter frost management. The small, dark purple-red drupes ripen over several weeks in summer and have a refreshing sweet-sour flavor prized in Indian cooling drinks (phalsa sherbet) and jams. The fruit is extremely perishable — harvest when fully dark purple and soft and use within 24 hours; it does not store or ship well. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Phenomenal Lavender (Heat-Humidity Tolerant Lavandin for Southern Gardens)
description: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; in humid climates amend clay soil with coarse sand or gravel; excellent air circulation is essential; in zones 7–9 with humid summers, plant in fall for establishment; Phenomenal resists the root rots and fungal diseases that kill standard lavenders in humid heat, making it essentially the only lavender that can be grown reliably as a long-lived perennial in the humid South. Phenomenal is a lavandin hybrid (Lavandula × intermedia) that was selected specifically for exceptional performance in hot, humid climates — a characteristic set that very few lavender varieties possess, since most lavenders originate from the Mediterranean region and are adapted to hot, dry summers rather than the humid heat of the American Southeast. The selection and introduction of Phenomenal represented a significant advance for Southern gardeners who had long struggled to grow lavender as a lasting perennial in zones 7–9 with high summer humidity — the conditions that cause root rot and crown fungal diseases in English lavenders within 1–3 years. Phenomenal's superior disease resistance in humid conditions comes from a combination of its thicker, more robust stems, greater inherent resistance to Botrytis and Phytophthora, and possibly greater ability to shed moisture from the crown. The plants are large, vigorous, and productive, with long silver-gray spikes and a strongly fragrant, slightly camphor-accented scent. For zone 9a Texas and Gulf Coast gardens, Phenomenal is the practical choice when other lavenders have repeatedly failed. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Philippine Spinach (Waterleaf)
description: Sow seed shallowly in warm, moist soil; talinum is an exceptionally heat-tolerant tropical leafy vegetable used across West Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia as a spinach substitute that thrives in hot weather that destroys most other greens. The thick, succulent leaves and stems cook quickly and have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to purslane. Harvest by cutting stem tips with young leaves regularly; plants regenerate vigorously from the base. In zones 9–11 it becomes a woody perennial subshrub 2–3 feet tall; cut back to 6 inches periodically to keep growth tender. Very drought-tolerant once established and requires little fertilizer. Also known as Lagos spinach and waterleaf. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Phoenicia Pomegranate
description: Phoenicia is one of the pomegranate cultivars evaluated in University of California variety trials as a potential alternative to the industry-dominant Wonderful, producing medium to large fruit with a distinctive yellowish, pale pink rind rather than the deep red skin of most commercial cultivars. In coastal California consumer taste trials it was rated more favorably than Wonderful for its balance of sweetness, tartness, and softer seeds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, giving it the same deep, infrequent watering and light annual pruning used for other pomegranates to encourage new fruiting wood. Its lighter skin color makes it a visually distinct addition to a home orchard growing several cultivars side by side. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Phoenix Tears Goji Berry (Compact High-Yield Goji Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Phoenix Tears is a named goji cultivar selected for heavy, reliable fruit production and elongated, bright red-orange berries with the tart-sweet flavor typical of the species, on arching, slightly thorny canes that can be left as a loose shrub or trained to a central leader with staking. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals for the following season. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling directly on the fruit, since the sap can stain skin and clothing. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Phoenix Tomato (Heat-Set Texas A&M Tomato)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent watering reduces blossom end rot in humid conditions. Phoenix is a tomato variety developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife vegetable breeding program specifically to keep setting fruit through the extreme heat of a Texas and Gulf South summer, when night temperatures above 75°F cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in most standard varieties. The medium-sized, firm, deep red globe fruits also carry useful resistance to common soilborne diseases and cracking, and the vines continue producing through the hottest stretch of summer that typically causes a production gap in southern tomato gardens. It also carries a degree of protection against sunscald thanks to good foliage cover. A dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want tomatoes to keep coming through July and August rather than stalling out, in zone 4–11. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Physical Graffiti Dragon Fruit
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil against a sturdy post, fence, or trellis for the climbing stems to grip with their aerial roots; Physical Graffiti is a Florida-bred dragon fruit selection that has become a favorite among collectors and backyard grafters for its deep magenta flesh and unusually high sugar content compared with more common commercial varieties. As with other dragon fruit, flowers open only at night and typically need hand pollination with a small brush to reliably set fruit, transferring pollen between blooms of the same or a different self-compatible plant. Treat the plant more like a succulent than a conventional fruit vine — water deeply but infrequently, let the soil dry between waterings, and protect the fleshy stems from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can cause serious damage. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Picholine Olive (French Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Picholine is a classic French olive cultivar from the Languedoc region, valued as a dual-purpose variety producing both high-quality table olives — elongated, firm, green-cured olives with a distinctive nutty flavor — and good oil with a peppery, herbaceous character typical of southern French olive oils. The tree is notably vigorous and relatively cold-hardy for an olive, tolerating brief winter dips better than some more tender cultivars, which has made it a popular choice for marginal olive-growing climates. Harvest green in fall for classic Picholine table olives, curing in a lye or brine solution over several weeks to remove bitterness, or allow fruit to ripen further for oil pressing in early winter. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pick a Bushel Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container with a small trellis. Pick a Bushel is an AAS-winning pickling cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit, producing full-size yields of crisp, uniform, 3-5 inch pickling cukes on a plant small enough for patios, raised beds, and tight garden spaces where a standard vining pickler would sprawl out of bounds. It bears heavily and continuously over a relatively short, concentrated season, ideal for gardeners who want a big pickling harvest all at once for a canning batch. Pick fruit at the size wanted for the pickle style being made — small gherkins to full-size dills — and harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since oversized cucumbers slow down further production. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitter or misshapen cucumbers. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Pickering Mango (Compact Florida Dooryard Mango)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Pickering is a Florida-bred mango descended from Alampur Baneshan, developed as a compact, heavy-bearing dooryard cultivar for home gardeners with limited space. Fruit is medium-sized with a rich, sweet, aromatic, fiberless flesh and a flavor many growers rank among the best of the Florida dooryard mangoes, ripening over a fairly long summer window that extends the harvest compared to single-flush cultivars. Its naturally compact size and tendency toward heavy annual bearing make it a strong choice for zone 9 gardeners planning to grow mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter. Reduce watering as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from any frost or freeze, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold snaps. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pickle Bush Cucumber (Compact Bush-Habit Pickling Cucumber for Small Spaces)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush is a bush-type pickling cucumber producing compact, self-supporting vines 18–24 inches across rather than the sprawling 4–6 foot vines of standard pickling cucumbers — making it the preferred choice for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where trellises are impractical and space is limited. The short (3–4 inch), blocky, warted, pickling-type cucumbers mature very early (48–55 days) in prolific clusters that concentrate harvest in a short window ideal for batch processing and canning. Pickling cucumbers are specifically bred for thin, tender skin that absorbs brine quickly, mild-to-bland flavor that allows pickle seasonings to dominate, and firm flesh that maintains crunchiness through the pickling process — qualities that distinguish them from slicing cucumbers in important culinary ways. In zone 9, the very early maturity (48–55 days) of Pickle Bush is a practical advantage — it completes its production cycle before summer heat drives cucumbers into bitter, poor-quality fruit stage. The bush habit allows high-density planting in raised beds (18 inches apart) compared to the 3–4 foot spacing required for trellised vining types. AAS Honorable Mention recognized Pickle Bush's outstanding performance in the small-space home garden category. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Pickling Cucumber
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun 1–2 weeks after last frost, thinning to 12–18 inches apart; pickling varieties such as National Pickling, Calypso, and Boston Pickling bear shorter, blockier, thinner-skinned fruits than slicing types and set fruit more uniformly over a compressed harvest window — ideal for making dill pickles and bread-and-butter chips in a single session. Harvest at 2–4 inches for gherkins, 4–5 inches for standard dills; leaving even one overripe fruit on the vine significantly slows further production. Keep soil evenly moist — irregular watering causes bitter fruits. Succession-plant every 3 weeks for a season-long supply. Matures in 48–60 days from seed.

name: Picolino Cucumber (Seedless Mini Snacking Cucumber)
description: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed, training vines onto a trellis or cage for straighter, cleaner fruit. Picolino is a parthenocarpic mini cucumber, meaning it reliably sets thin-skinned, seedless, 3-4 inch fruit without needing pollinator activity, making it dependable even in low-bee conditions or under row cover. The skin is tender enough to eat without peeling and the flavor is mild and non-bitter, making it a popular choice for lunchbox snacking and pickling whole. Because fruit sizes up quickly, plants need picking every day or two at peak season to prevent cucumbers from overgrowing and to keep the vine setting new fruit. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Picual Olive (World's Most Planted Oil Olive, Jaén Spain Olive, Stable High-Polyphenol Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Picual is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for oil production in November–December when olives shift from green to purple-black; Picual oil is known for its stability and resistance to oxidation — it keeps significantly longer than most olive oils and maintains its flavor profile without going rancid. Picual olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world, accounting for approximately 20% of total global olive production — concentrated primarily in the province of Jaén in Andalusia, Spain, which alone produces more olive oil than the entire country of Greece. The variety's global dominance is built on a combination of practical attributes: very high oil content (22–27% by weight, among the highest of any variety), exceptional oil stability and shelf life (Picual oil has very high oleic acid and polyphenol content that makes it resistant to oxidation — a critical commercial advantage since most olive oil goes rancid within 1–2 years), strong cold-hardiness relative to other major varieties, and vigorous, productive trees adaptable to the challenging calcareous, poorly-drained soils of the Spanish meseta. Picual oil has a distinctive flavor profile: robust, fruity, slightly bitter and peppery in the fresh-pressed (unfiltered) state — characteristics that reflect its high polyphenol content (polyphenols provide both the peppery sensation and the health benefits of olive oil). For home oil production, Picual's high oil content and excellent stability make it the most efficient variety for pressing, and its robust flavor is well-suited to the strong tastes associated with premium extra-virgin olive oil. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Piel de Sapo Melon (Spanish Toad-Skin Winter Melon)
aliases: Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Piel de Sapo'
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis with slings to support the heavy fruit. Piel de Sapo, meaning 'toad skin' in Spanish, is a classic Spanish winter melon named for its distinctive mottled dark and pale green rind, an oblong fruit that hides sweet, crisp, pale green-white flesh with a mild, delicate flavor. Unlike musky cantaloupe types, this inodorus-group melon develops little to no aroma at the stem even when fully ripe, so growers judge readiness by days from planting, a slight softening at the blossom end, and a duller rind color rather than by scent, and the fruit also stores notably longer after harvest than most melons. Water deeply but infrequently once fruit begins sizing up, and reduce watering in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sugars. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Piennolo del Vesuvio Tomato (Vesuvius Hanging Cluster Storage Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small, oval red tomato grown for centuries on the mineral-rich volcanic soils of the Mount Vesuvius region near Naples, its thick skin and low water content allowing whole trusses to be hung in bunches ('piennoli') and stored through winter without refrigeration, slowly concentrating in flavor as they cure. The tangy, intensely tomato flavor makes it prized in Neapolitan cooking, especially for a quick, bright sauce. Harvest whole clusters when fully colored and hang them in a cool, airy spot to store, checking periodically and using fruit as it continues to ripen. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Pieper American Persimmon (Named Female Midwestern Persimmon Cultivar)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained to average soil; Pieper is adaptable to clay, sandy, or poor soils and very drought-tolerant once established; harvest by collecting fallen fruits from the ground after frost softening — fruits that separate easily from the calyx are ready; ripe fruit is completely soft and uniformly orange. Pieper is a named American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) selection that has been propagated through Midwestern and eastern nurseries as a reliable female cultivar with above-average fruit size and consistent productivity — characteristics that distinguish it from seedling trees of variable quality. American persimmon is a dioecious species, meaning most trees produce only pollen (male) or only fruit (female), so named female cultivars like Pieper must be planted alongside a male tree or a self-fertile cultivar (Meader) for reliable cropping. Pieper produces medium to large American persimmon fruits (1.25–1.75 inch) that ripen in October–November following hard frosts, developing the characteristic sweet, honey-apricot flavor of excellent American persimmon at peak ripeness. The trees are vigorous, drought-resistant once established, and productive across the range of Midwestern soils — making them a practical native fruit for home orchards where Asian persimmon would be marginally hardy. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pierce Cherimoya
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Pierce is a California-selected cherimoya cultivar valued for its smooth-skinned, relatively small-to-medium fruit that ripens later in the season than many other named selections, helping extend the cherimoya harvest window into winter. The white, custardy flesh is very sweet with the classic pineapple-banana-vanilla flavor typical of good cherimoya, and the fruit's smaller size makes it convenient for single-serving eating. Like all cherimoya, hand-pollination by transferring pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers with a small brush in the morning greatly improves fruit set, since the flowers' timing rarely allows a single flower to self-pollinate and natural pollinators are scarce outside the tree's native Andean range. Grafted Pierce trees begin bearing within two to four years and need protection from frost while young. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pigeon Pea
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; pigeon pea is a deep-rooted, drought-tolerant shrubby legume that is one of the world's most important tropical food crops — the yellow, green, or red seeds (arhar dal, toor dal) are a dietary staple across the Caribbean, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, used in dals, stews, rice dishes, and soups. The plants fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and thrive in poor soils without supplemental fertilizer; overly rich or wet soils reduce pod production. Harvest green pods when plump for fresh use or allow to fully dry on the plant for dried dal; in zone 9–12 plants become woody perennial shrubs and will continue producing pods for several years if pruned back hard after the main harvest to stimulate new growth. In zone 8 and below, grow as a warm-season annual and expect a single late-season harvest. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Pigeon Plum
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in sandy, well-drained soil; pigeon plum is a native Florida and Caribbean understory tree related to sea grape (Coccoloba uvifera) that produces dark purple, grape-like fruits in hanging clusters that ripen in fall and winter — an important food source for birds and wildlife. The small fruits have a thin, sweet skin covering minimal flesh around a large seed, similar to wild grape, and are used in the same ways as sea grape fruits: fresh eating, jelly, wine, and juice. The tree is highly salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and pollution-resistant, making it valuable for coastal landscapes where other fruit trees struggle. Leaves are evergreen and smaller than sea grape. Best suited to south Florida and the Keys outdoors; zone 9a requires frost protection. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pignut
description: Sow Conopodium majus seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; plants are slow to establish and the small underground tubers take 2–3 years to reach harvestable size; avoid disturbing the soil around plants once growing; harvest small tubers with a trowel in summer as foliage dies back. Pignut is one of the most charming native edibles of British and European woodlands — a slender, graceful plant of meadows, hedgerows, and open woodland that has been gathered for its sweet, nut-flavored tubers by country people for centuries. The small, round to irregularly shaped tubers (technically a corm-like swelling of the underground stem) are covered in brown skin and have cream-colored, very sweet, crunchy flesh with a flavor reminiscent of sweet chestnut or hazelnut — edible raw or cooked. Foragers prize them but they are difficult to dig without following the thin, brittle stem underground without breaking it (hence their reputation for elusiveness). Wild populations are protected in Britain, but cultivation from seed is permitted and encouraged for those wishing to grow them. The plant is an important food source for dormice, wild boar, and other wildlife in European woodland ecosystems. A genuinely rare and unusual woodland garden plant with culinary value and strong ecological connections. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Pignut Hickory
description: Pignut Hickory is a stately, long-lived native nut tree, native to the dry to mesic upland forests and ridges of eastern North America from Ontario and New England south to Florida and west to Kansas, where it is a dominant component of the oak-hickory forest communities of the eastern United States. The small, pear-shaped nuts — borne in thin, pear-shaped husks that split into four sections at maturity — are intensely bitter to humans but form a critical fall and winter food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, squirrels, blue jays, and wood ducks, making Pignut Hickory one of the most ecologically important native nut trees in the eastern forest. Rich, golden-yellow fall foliage and deeply furrowed gray bark provide ornamental interest in all seasons; the hard, dense wood is among the toughest and most shock-resistant of any North American tree. Direct sow fresh nuts in fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the deep taproot that forms in the first year makes mature trees virtually impossible to transplant. Matures in 3650–7300 days from seed.

name: Pikanta Summer Savory (Spicy Bush Summer Savory)
description: Pikanta is a Central European seed strain of summer savory selected for a dense, upright, bushy habit and a notably more intense, spicier flavor than common garden-strain summer savory, packing more peppery punch per leaf into bean, lentil, and meat dishes. Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings so the compact plants have room to branch fully. Its small oval leaves release a strong spicy aroma when brushed or crushed, and the plant's tidy dense form suits containers and small raised beds as well as open garden rows. Harvest whole stems for drying right as the small white-to-lilac flowers begin to open, when the essential-oil concentration and flavor intensity peak. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Pike White Sapote
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind; Pike is a California-selected white sapote cultivar valued for combining good cold tolerance with rich, high-quality fruit, making it a popular alternative where growers want more reliable cropping than some of the less flavorful ultra-hardy selections offer. The medium to large, thin-skinned fruit ripens from green to pale yellow-green and has smooth, custard-like flesh with a sweet flavor often described as a cross between banana and vanilla pudding. Trees grow quickly and can become large, so allow ample room and prune after harvest to keep the canopy manageable and encourage branching for the following year's crop. Pick fruit once it softens slightly at the stem end and finish ripening at room temperature for a few days before eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pilgrim Cranberry
description: Pilgrim is a USDA-bred cranberry cultivar valued for producing some of the largest, deepest-red berries of any commonly grown cultivar, making it popular for fresh-market and specialty use. It ripens later in the season than Stevens, so it is best suited to regions with a long enough fall growing season to fully color before hard freezes. Vines are moderately vigorous with a somewhat more open growth habit than Stevens, requiring the same acidic, saturated bog conditions and coarse sand mulching used for other cranberry plantings. Established vines take three to four years to reach significant production but then bear reliably for many years with minimal maintenance beyond consistent moisture and acidic fertility. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pili Nut (Philippine Nut, Elemi Nut)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained tropical soil; pili nut (Canarium ovatum) is the premier nut crop of the Philippines, producing large, elongated, olive-shaped brown nuts with an extremely rich, buttery, almond-cashew flavor and high oil content (70–80% fat, similar to macadamia) that many food experts rank among the most delicious nuts in the world. The tree is a close relative of elemi resin trees and produces fragrant, semi-translucent resin used in varnishes. Nuts are eaten raw, roasted, candied, or pressed for cooking oil; the pulp surrounding the nut shell is also edible, used in Filipino cuisine for cooking and flavoring. Increasingly cultivated in Hawaii and south Florida as a high-value specialty nut crop by tropical fruit enthusiasts. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Pimento L Pepper
description: Pimento L is a compact, open-pollinated pimiento-type sweet pepper long grown in home gardens for its heart-shaped, thick-walled fruit and reliable tobacco mosaic virus resistance, a trait that made it a dependable choice before modern hybrid pimientos were widely available. Fruits run about four and a half inches long, ripening from green to a glossy bright red with very few seeds and exceptionally sweet, mild flesh (under 500 Scoville units). The short, tidy plants make this a good fit for small beds or containers, and the thick walls hold up well for stuffing, roasting, or slicing raw into salads. Matures in 90–95 days from transplant.

name: Pimento Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and transplant to fertile, well-drained garden soil once the risk of frost has fully passed. The heart-shaped, thick-walled fruits ripen from green to deep red and are sweeter and more aromatic than most bell peppers, with a rich, almost spicy fragrance that is distinct to the type. Harvest at full red for fresh use, or roast and peel for preserving in oil — pimento is the classic stuffing for green olives. High yields from compact plants make this a productive choice for containers or small beds. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Pimiento Pepper (Classic Sweet Thick-Walled Pimento Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pimiento (also spelled pimento) is the traditional thick-walled sweet pepper of Spanish and Southern American tradition — producing heart-shaped to rounded, medium-sized (3–4 inches) fruits with exceptionally thick, sweet, juicy walls and very mild, sweet flavor with no heat. The thick walls and very sweet, low-acid flesh are the defining qualities that distinguish pimiento from other sweet peppers: the wall thickness (often twice that of standard bell peppers) makes pimiento ideal for roasting, stuffing, and jar-packing, while the sweetness and mildness make it the original pepper for stuffed olives and the authentic ingredient in Southern pimiento cheese. The fruits ripen from green to a deep, vivid red and are at their best flavor when fully red. Pimiento is less commonly found in grocery stores than bell peppers (most commercial pimiento production goes to food processing), making it a particularly worthwhile home garden variety for cooks who want the authentic ingredient. The plants are productive, compact, and well-adapted to Gulf South growing conditions. In zone 9, pimiento peppers have two productive seasons: spring planting (February–March transplant, harvest May–July) and fall planting (August transplant, harvest October–November). The rich red color and exceptional thick-walled quality make pimiento one of the finest peppers for roasting whole. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Pin Oak
description: Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; pin oak is the most widely planted native oak in urban landscapes because of its symmetrical pyramidal form, fast growth (1–2 ft/year when young), ease of transplanting, and tolerance of clay and periodic flooding. The deeply lobed leaves turn brilliant red in fall, and the tree retains many of its dead lower branches in a distinctive downswept arrangement — a characteristic silhouette. Pin oak strictly requires acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5); in high-pH soils the tree develops iron chlorosis with yellowing leaves and declining vigor. Avoid high-pH soils or amend with elemental sulfur before planting. The small acorns are among the most important wildlife foods in eastern North America, consumed by over 100 bird and mammal species. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Pinata Apple (Sonata, Scab-Resistant Cox-Type Apple)
description: Pinata, also sold as Sonata in some markets, was bred in Germany from parentage that includes Cox's Orange Pippin, Duchess of Oldenburg, and Golden Delicious, and it was selected specifically for durable resistance to apple scab. The yellow-orange, red-striped fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with a sweet, aromatic flavor reminiscent of its Cox ancestry, though milder and less complex. It stores reasonably well for a mid-season apple and crops reliably once established. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pindo Palm (Jelly Palm)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pindo palm is the most cold-hardy feather palm (pinnate-leaved, as opposed to fan-leaved) in general cultivation — a native of the open grasslands and woodland edges of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina that tolerates winter temperatures down to about 12–15°F (-11 to -9°C) when established, providing reliable cold hardiness through most of USDA zone 8 and all of zone 9. The arching, recurved, pinnate leaves are a beautiful blue-gray to gray-green, the whole crown developing into a graceful, somewhat symmetrical hemisphere of arching blue-gray feather fronds with an instantly recognizable tropical character that tolerates conditions (dry, cold, lean soil) far beyond the range of most feather palms. The palm earns the common name 'jelly palm' by producing annually — in summer — large, hanging clusters of small, round to oval, orange-yellow to apricot-red drupes, each about 1 inch across with a thin skin, juicy orange flesh of sweet-tart, tropical flavor often described as pineapple-apricot-mango, and a large central seed. The fruits are genuinely edible fresh but highly perishable; they are most commonly cooked into jellies, wines, and preserves — 'pindo jelly' being a traditional product in the coastal Carolinas, Georgia, and the Gulf States where the palm is widely planted. The combination of exceptional cold hardiness for a feather palm, handsome blue-gray ornamental foliage, and genuinely edible, annually produced fruit makes it an outstanding dual-purpose landscape and edible plant for zone 8–11 Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple
description: Plant crowns or slips in very well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; pineapple is a bromeliad that grows terrestrially, producing a rosette of stiff, spiny-edged leaves from which a single fruit-bearing stalk emerges from the center. It is surprisingly easy to grow from the crown of a grocery store fruit — simply twist it off, dry the base for a few days, and plant in sandy, well-drained soil. Fruit matures in 18–24 months from crown planting, or 12–15 months from slips (the small plantlets that grow along the fruit stem). After fruiting, cut the old plant but leave the ratoon shoots that sprout from the base — these produce a second and often third crop in less time than starting over. In zone 9a, grow in a large container in full sun and bring indoors or to a greenhouse when frost threatens; pineapple is frost-sensitive at 28°F. Matures in 540–720 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Crush Alpine Strawberry (White-Fruited Pineapple-Flavored Woodland Strawberry)
description: Pineapple Crush is a white-fruited alpine strawberry whose creamy, blush-tinged berries carry a distinctive tropical pineapple aroma rather than the typical wild-strawberry flavor. Like other alpine types it forms tidy, runnerless mounds that fruit continuously from early summer through fall once established, making it a good edging or container plant as well as a producer. Because the pale fruit doesn't visually signal ripeness to birds the way red berries do, losses to birds are usually lighter than with red alpine strawberries, though the soft fruit still bruises easily and should be picked and eaten promptly. Transplant seedlings into humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot regions. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Gem Feijoa
description: Pineapple Gem is one of the few genuinely self-fertile feijoa selections, so a single plant can set a worthwhile crop without a second cultivar nearby, unlike most feijoas that need cross-pollination for heavy fruiting. The compact, rounded shrub carries silvery evergreen foliage year-round and edible, sweet spring flowers before setting small, intensely aromatic fruit in fall. It suits gardeners with limited space who still want reliable feijoa production, or a large container that can be moved to shelter in the coldest zone 8 winters. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit with only minor twig damage. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Ground Cherry
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pineapple Ground Cherry is a named selection of the ground cherry (Physalis pruinosa) grown for its small (1/2–3/4 inch), golden-yellow fruits enclosed in dry, papery, tan husks (lantern-like husks much smaller than tomatillo husks) with an intensely sweet, tropical flavor reminiscent of pineapple, vanilla, and caramel — completely unlike tomatillos in flavor despite being related. The fruits drop from the plant when fully ripe and are gathered from the ground (hence the name); this drop-when-ripe characteristic is the easiest ripeness indicator. Extraordinarily productive in warm weather, with hundreds of fruits per plant. Delicious eaten fresh, in pies (often compared to cape gooseberry pies), in jams, and dried like raisins. A charming and unusual fruit for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that is barely known to most gardeners. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Guava (Feijoa)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; pineapple guava tolerates drought, coastal salt spray, and moderate alkalinity better than most subtropical fruits. Most selections set better crops with a second nearby cultivar for cross-pollination, though some are self-fruitful. The showy red-stamened flowers are edible and mild-flavored — harvest petals before they fall for salads. Fruits drop naturally when ripe in autumn; check the ground daily and collect before birds and insects take them, then ripen indoors for 3–5 days until they yield to gentle pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Mayhaw (Western Mayhaw, Opaca Hawthorn)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil — this tree tolerates periodic flooding better than most fruit trees and thrives in Gulf Coast bottomland conditions; pineapple mayhaw (Crataegus opaca) produces the largest fruits of all native mayhaws — round, bright red, 1-inch berries with a distinctive fruity, pineapple-like aroma that distinguishes it from the more common Eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis). The tart, cranberry-like berries ripen in April–May and are prized across the Deep South for mayhaw jelly, syrup, and wine; an excellent crop in zones 6–9 Gulf Coast gardens. Largely overlooked by commercial horticulture despite the outstanding jelly quality; a critical food source for wildlife including cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and wood ducks. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Mint
description: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, containing in a buried pot to limit spread; pineapple mint is a variegated form of apple mint with cream-edged, textured, rounded leaves that carry a fruity, tropical fragrance somewhere between pineapple and mint that makes it popular in fruit salads, cocktails, mojitos, and desserts. The plants are striking enough to use as ornamental container plants, with the white-edged leaves providing bright contrast in shade gardens. Not as aggressively invasive as spearmint or peppermint, but still spreads by rhizome and benefits from containment. Harvest regularly to keep growth compact and fresh. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Muscadine (Self-Fertile Bronze Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine grown by home gardeners and small vineyards for its distinctive flavor — a mild, sweet, tropical pineapple note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste, unusual enough among muscadine varieties to have earned the fruit its name. Being self-fertile, one vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety planted nearby, making it an easy choice for a single-vine home planting. As with other muscadines, it resists Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European wine grapes difficult to grow in the humid South, so no regular spray program is needed. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest berries as they ripen and slip easily from the cluster. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Orange (Classic Florida Sweet Orange with Aromatic Juice, Historical Commercial Variety)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil with full sun. Water regularly in establishment year; tolerates some drought once established. Harvest January–March when rind is fully orange and fruit is fragrant.
