Pineapple Orange is one of the historically significant Florida orange varieties that shaped the state's commercial citrus industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries — at its commercial peak, it was one of the leading sweet orange varieties grown in central Florida's ridge region, particularly in Polk and Orange Counties where the well-drained sandy loam soils and warm nights produced the highest-quality fruit. The name refers to the distinctive pineapple-like aroma of freshly squeezed Pineapple Orange juice — a volatile ester profile distinct from other orange varieties that creates a complex aromatic quality prized by juice connoisseurs. Florida horticulturists identified the variety in the 1860s–1870s as particularly valuable for its juice quality, and it became an important commercial variety until it was gradually displaced by Navel oranges (which offer better fresh-eating convenience with their seedless character) and Valencia oranges (which hold on the tree longer for extended harvest seasons). Despite its loss of commercial dominance, Pineapple Orange remained a beloved home garden and specialty variety in Florida, maintained by homeowners and small growers who valued its juice quality over the commercial virtues (navel convenience, Valencia storage) that made other varieties dominant. For zone 9a Gulf Coast gardeners, Pineapple Orange remains one of the most rewarding sweet orange varieties for home juice production — the fruit sets reliably in zone 9's warm winters, ripens to exceptional sweetness and flavor in January–March when fresh citrus is most welcome, and the tree's moderate size makes it manageable in home landscapes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Pear (Gulf South Low-Chill Heirloom Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pineapple pear is one of the most widely grown and historically important heirloom pear varieties in the Gulf South, deeply rooted in the orchard traditions of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida — a Pyrus communis selection known for its unusually low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–250 hours) that makes it productive in Gulf Coast winters that defeat most European pear varieties. The medium-large, yellowish-green to golden-tan fruits have a distinctly sweet, rich, aromatic quality with a subtle pineapple-like fragrance and flavor that distinguishes them from blander pear types; the flesh is moderately juicy and slightly gritty (typical of P. communis), excellent for fresh eating and very good for canning and preserves. Pineapple pear shows useful fire blight resistance — critical in the humid Gulf South where fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) devastates susceptible varieties — and the trees are productive and long-lived in appropriate climates. Ripens in late July through August in the Gulf South. This variety has sustained Southern home orchards and farmstead preserving traditions for generations and remains one of the recommended low-chill pear varieties for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast production. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Pole Tomato
description: This high-yielding beefsteak ripens to yellow-orange marbled with red streaks running through the meaty, low-acid flesh. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and need strong staking or caging. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water consistently to reduce cracking on the large fruit. Prune suckers lightly to boost airflow and support ripening of these big tomatoes. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Quince (Fragrant Sweet Large-Fruited Quince for Gulf South Preserves)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pineapple Quince is the most popular and widely grown quince cultivar in North America — producing large, round to pyriform, golden-yellow fruits with a distinctive sweet, pineapple-like fragrance and flavor that sets it apart from tarter, more typical quince. Quince (Cydonia oblonga) is one of the oldest cultivated fruits, native to the Caucasus region and grown throughout the Mediterranean for millennia — the golden fruit of ancient mythology may have been a quince rather than an apple. The raw fruit is astringent and usually not eaten fresh, but becomes transformed by cooking: quince turns a beautiful ruby-red to deep rose color when cooked slowly with sugar, developing a rich, sweet, floral flavor for quince paste (membrillo), quince jelly, and quince preserves that are among the most distinctive of tree-fruit preparations. 'Pineapple' is selected for sweeter, less astringent raw flavor than most quince — it can be eaten fresh when fully ripe (golden-yellow with red cheeks), though cooking still brings out the most complex flavor. The spring bloom — large, cup-shaped, pale pink to white flowers — is ornamentally beautiful and provides excellent bee forage. In zone 9, quince performs best in the cooler, northern parts of zone 9 (zone 9a) where it receives adequate winter chilling (150+ hours below 45°F); southern zone 9 may provide insufficient chilling for reliable fruiting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Sage
description: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix in spring and plant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; pineapple sage is a large-leaved Mexican native with a striking, true pineapple fragrance that makes it one of the most popular ornamental-culinary herbs for Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 gardens. The soft, bright-green leaves are used fresh in fruit salads, herbal teas, cocktails, and desserts where the pineapple-mint flavor adds an unexpected tropical note; the long stems are also attractive in floral arrangements. Brilliant scarlet tubular flowers appear in late fall and winter in warm climates, making pineapple sage one of the best late-season hummingbird plants for southern gardens. In zone 8 it may freeze to the ground but re-emerges from the roots in spring; take cuttings before first frost in colder climates to overwinter indoors. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Tomatillo
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pineapple Tomatillo is a named selection of Physalis ixocarpa that ripens to a distinctive golden-yellow rather than the standard tomatillo green, with a noticeably sweeter, more tropical flavor that includes a pineapple-like brightness absent from green-fruiting types. The medium-sized fruits, typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, fill and split the papery husk as they ripen to gold, at which point they are at peak sweetness. The sweeter profile makes Pineapple Tomatillo less acidic than standard green tomatillos and more suitable for fresh eating out of hand, in fruit salsas, or in preparations where a less tart tomatillo flavor is desired. Standard green tomatillos provide better classic salsa verde acidity; Pineapple works best where a milder, sweeter, more unusual tomatillo experience is the goal. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Tomato (Giant Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pineapple is one of the most visually spectacular heirloom beefsteak tomatoes — producing enormous (1–2 lb), irregular, slightly ribbed fruits with a stunning bicolor pattern of golden-yellow base skin marked with bold red and orange streaking and marbling that creates a stained-glass appearance when sliced. The cut surface reveals a similarly bicolor red-and-yellow flesh pattern — an ornamental quality that makes Pineapple outstanding for fresh salads and sliced presentations where the visual effect can be appreciated. The flavor matches the visual quality: intensely sweet, fruity, and complex with a low-acid, tropical quality that justifies the variety's evocative name — the combination of golden-yellow color and sweet, fruity flavor genuinely suggests tropical fruit. Large, vigorous indeterminate plants require sturdy support (minimum 6-foot cage or stake). As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from the most characteristic fruits for replanting. In zone 9, Pineapple produces best in the spring season (March–June) before summer heat arrives; the very large fruits require a relatively long, cool growing period for maximum development. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Pineapple Weed (Wild Chamomile)
description: Scatter seeds on compacted, lean, disturbed, sunny to partly shaded soil and allow to naturalize; pineapple weed is a small annual of the chamomile tribe, native to northeastern Asia but widely naturalized as a weed of paths, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout North America. Unlike true chamomile, the tiny dome-shaped flower heads lack white ray petals — only the central yellow-green disc flowers are present, giving the plant a distinctive button-like appearance. When crushed, the entire plant releases an intense, sweet pineapple-chamomile fragrance that is unmistakable and charming. The flower heads can be brewed into a pleasant, mild, pineapple-scented herbal tea similar to chamomile tea but with a tropical twist. The plant typically colonizes compacted, poor soils where it often grows in path edges, gravel driveways, and worn turf without any encouragement. Gather the button-like heads for tea when fully yellow-green and fragrant. Matures in 45–90 days from seed.

name: Pineberry
description: Pineberry is a white-fruited strawberry cultivar (largely derived from the South American species Fragaria chiloensis crossed with F. x ananassa) that produces pale cream-white berries with red achenes and a distinctive pineapple-like aroma when fully ripe. Pineberries have low self-fertility and require a red-fruiting strawberry variety planted nearby as a pollinator for adequate fruit set. Grow exactly as you would a june-bearing or everbearing strawberry, removing blossoms the first season to build root strength. Harvest when berries are white to pale pink with red seeds and give off a sweet pineapple fragrance. Matures in 365–425 days from transplant.

name: Pinecone Ginger (Shampoo Ginger)
description: Plant rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; pinecone ginger (shampoo ginger, wild ginger) is a spectacular tropical ginger grown for its unusual inflorescences — tight, compact, cone-shaped flower heads that look exactly like green pinecones on thick stems, which mature from green to brilliant red as the season progresses. The small, yellow flowers emerge briefly from between the bracts. The ripe, red cones produce a fragrant, slightly slimy liquid when squeezed that has been used as a hair conditioner and shampoo in Pacific Island and Asian cultures for centuries — the liquid has a pleasant, gingery fragrance and actually conditions hair effectively. The rhizomes are edible with a slightly bitter, medicinal ginger flavor and are used in Southeast Asian cooking. In zone 9 the tall, bamboo-like stems die back completely in winter and regrow from rhizomes in spring, providing both edible, fragrant, and ornamental value throughout the warm season. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Ping Tung Long Eggplant (Taiwanese Heirloom Slender Purple Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches and still vivid lavender-purple. Ping Tung Long (named for Pingtung County in southern Taiwan where it originates) is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant representing the classic Asian long eggplant type at its finest — producing exceptionally long (12–16 inch), slender, slightly curved, vivid lavender-purple to violet fruits with thin, tender skin. The variety is among the most widely grown and highly regarded long Asian eggplants in Taiwan and throughout the Chinese-American gardening community in the United States, where it has been maintained as an open-pollinated heirloom for multiple generations. The fruits are characterized by extremely thin, tender skin (no peeling needed), virtually no seeds, and very sweet, mild flesh with no bitterness — a flavor profile considered superior for raw preparations and quick stir-fries where the tender skin softens immediately without extended cooking. The vivid lavender-purple color is particularly attractive in the garden and at the table. Ping Tung Long's heat tolerance and prolific production in hot conditions make it especially well-suited to southern gardens. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Pingtung Long Eggplant
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pingtung Long is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant that produces slender, 12–18 inch fruits in a vibrant lavender-purple, among the longest eggplant fruits available. The skin is exceptionally thin and tender with minimal bitterness, making it prized for quick stir-fries and grilling without peeling. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, continuing to set fruit through the hot zone 9 summers when other eggplant varieties may pause. Harvest fruits young when skin is glossy and before seeds develop; overripe fruits become seedy and bitter. A heavy producer that may need light staking to support the long, heavy fruits. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Pink Banana Winter Squash
description: Pink Banana is a large heirloom winter squash producing elongated, pink-skinned fruits with sweet, tender orange flesh on vigorous vines that can run fifteen feet. The big fruits store well for months in a cool, dry place. Direct sow into warm, rich soil in full sun after frost, giving the sprawling vines plenty of space. Harvest when the rind hardens and skin turns pink, then cure the squash before storing. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Pink Beauty Possumhaw Viburnum (Heavy-Fruiting Smooth Witherod)
description: Pink Beauty is prized among possumhaw viburnum selections for producing the most abundant, densely packed berry clusters of any widely sold cultivar, opening creamy-white flower cymes in early summer that give way to rounded hemispheres of fruit passing from pink to blue to blackened purple as they ripen. The heavy fruit set makes it an especially valuable songbird feeding station in fall, when migrating and resident birds strip the color-shifting clusters over several weeks. Like other Viburnum nudum selections it tolerates wet, poorly drained soil far better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and low spots in a partly shaded border. Planting a second, genetically distinct viburnum nearby further improves fruit set and berry abundance. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Beauty Radish
description: An All-America Selections-winning open-pollinated radish prized for round roots in a clear bright pink over crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably gentle and mild rather than sharp, making it a favorite for market growers selling to customers who find standard radishes too peppery. Strong tops make it easy to bunch for market, and the roots resist splitting even when left in the ground a few extra days. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Pink Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato (Marbled Pink-Green Striped Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Pink Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern open-pollinated variety related to the original green Berkeley Tie Dye, bred by Wild Boar Farms and prized for its striking exterior of pink and green streaks and blushes, which give way when sliced to a marbled, jewel-toned interior of pink, red, and gold swirled together in a genuinely tie-dye pattern. Beyond the visual novelty, the flavor is rich, sweet, and complex, ranking among the better-tasting of the modern striped 'tie dye' tomato series that has become popular with heirloom and specialty tomato growers. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once the distinctive coloring fully develops. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Pink Bourbon Coffee (Bourbon Rosado)
description: First identified among farms in Colombia's Huila department in the early 2010s, Pink Bourbon takes its name from the blushing peach-pink color of its ripe cherries, a hue that falls between the classic red and yellow Bourbon types and may reflect a natural hybrid origin rather than a simple color mutation. It has become a favorite of specialty coffee producers for cups showing pronounced florals and juicy stone-fruit sweetness, though yields are modest and mother trees are still relatively scarce outside a handful of Colombian growing regions. Cultivate it like other Bourbon-type Arabicas, with rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, filtered shade, and consistent moisture, and be patient waiting for wider availability of true-to-type plants. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pink Brandywine Tomato
description: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost, burying 2/3 of the stem, and stake or cage immediately — Pink Brandywine produces tall, sprawling, potato-leaved vines that are challenging to support and slow to set fruit. Pink Brandywine (distinct from the yellow Brandywine and red Brandywine strains) is widely considered by heirloom tomato enthusiasts to be the definitive Brandywine — a large (12–24 oz), oblate to irregular, deep pink-skinned, pink-fleshed tomato with extraordinary, complex, sweet-rich flavor that lacks the sharp acidity of red tomatoes; many growers consider it the best-tasting tomato they have ever grown. The Sudduth and Platfoot strains (the two main documented lineages preserved by Seed Savers Exchange) are both potato-leaved (a genetic marker associated with the true Brandywine) and behave similarly in the garden. A notoriously slow, difficult, but rewarding grow — plants are late to mature and require long, warm seasons, but the fruit quality when conditions are right is unmatched. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Pink Bumble Bee Tomato (Striped Pink Cherry Tomato)
description: Pink Bumble Bee is a member of Wild Boar Farms' Bumble Bee series of striped cherry tomatoes, bearing small round fruit in rosy pink overlaid with fine gold stripes that radiate from the stem end. The thin-skinned fruit has an intense, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of the series, and the heavy-yielding vine produces in long clusters through most of the season. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate growth and pick fruit promptly at full color, since ripe cherry tomatoes soften and can crack quickly in wet weather. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Pink Champagne Currant
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; this cultivar performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity. Pink Champagne is a popular pink-fruited selection of red currant, producing long, well-filled strigs of translucent, pale rose-pink berries that are noticeably milder and sweeter than typical red currants, making them pleasant for fresh eating straight off the bush rather than only for cooking. The self-fertile bush is vigorous and reliably productive, ripening its blush clusters in midsummer alongside or slightly ahead of most red currant cultivars. Culture is identical to red currant: grow in cool, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil with a pH of 6.0-6.5, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune each late winter to retain 8-12 mixed-age canes, removing wood older than five years since fruit forms best on younger spurwood. Net ripening clusters against birds, which find the pale, glowing fruit just as attractive as red currants. Check state Ribes restrictions before ordering, since currants are regulated in some areas as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Chilean Guava (Ugni candollei)
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ugni candollei is a rare, small evergreen shrub endemic to the coastal regions of central and southern Chile, growing in habitat similar to its better-known relative Ugni molinae (Chilean guava). It stays lower and denser than Chilean guava, typically reaching only 2 to 2.5 feet, with small white five-petaled flowers followed by edible, pink to light-orange berries, a paler color and slightly different flavor than the deep-red fruit of Ugni molinae. Grow it as a specimen or low hedge in mild, humid, acidic-soil gardens, and protect from hard freezes, since it has cold tolerance limits similar to Chilean guava. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Chintz Thyme (Fuzzy Gray-Green Creeping Thyme)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or gritty, lean soil; thyme rots quickly in wet or heavy ground. Pink Chintz is a low, mat-forming creeping thyme with soft, fuzzy, gray-green leaves that give the foliage a distinctive downy texture, covered in a heavy flush of small salmon-pink flowers in late spring to early summer that draw bees in large numbers. Its dense, mat-forming habit makes it a favorite for planting between stepping stones and pavers, where light foot traffic releases its herbal fragrance, as well as for draping over rock walls and border edges. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense new growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Pink Currant
description: Pink currants are naturally occurring or selected mutations of red currant (Ribes rubrum) producing pale rose-pink to blush-colored berries that are milder and sweeter than the typical red forms — popular cultivars include 'Pink Champagne' and 'Gloire de Sablons'. Culture is identical to red currant: plant in cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5 and prune each late winter to retain 8–12 mixed-age canes, removing any older than 5 years. The translucent pink strigs are ornamentally striking and ripen slightly earlier than most red currants. Check state Ribes restrictions before ordering. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Eye Purple Hull Pea (Classic Gulf South Dual-Color Summer Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull is one of the most widely grown and deeply traditional southern pea varieties of the Gulf South — a semi-bush to vining type producing distinctive purple-hulled pods that make harvest timing and identification visually clear (green hulls shade to purple as the peas approach maturity), with cream-white peas marked by a distinctive pink to rose-colored 'eye' or hilum that gives the variety its evocative name. The pink eye is the identifying mark: when a pot of fresh-shelled Pink Eye Purple Hull peas is spread on the counter, the cream peas with their small pink-rose eye marks are immediately recognizable as this specific variety. The flavor is excellent — classic southern pea quality with a rich, earthy, beany sweetness that is characteristic of the Gulf South summer pea tradition. Pink Eye Purple Hull is extremely productive in Gulf South conditions, continuing to produce through summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables. It is among the most important vegetable crops of the traditional Gulf South summer garden, providing fresh food through July, August, and September when garden production from other crops has ended. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. The purple hulls are ornamentally attractive in the garden and make identifying ripe pods easy and unambiguous. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Pink Fir Apple Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil, and be patient, since this is a true late-season variety and tubers will not fully knobble and size up until the last weeks of the growing season. Pink Fir Apple is a Victorian-era heirloom fingerling named for its long, narrow, knobbly tubers with pink-blushed skin and waxy, nutty, pale-yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled whole. It remains a favorite of chefs and home cooks for cold potato salads because the dense waxy texture does not turn mealy or fall apart. Choose it over a modern fingerling hybrid when a genuinely old salad-potato flavor and the classic irregular fingerling shape are the goal. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Pink Frost Grapefruit (UGA Cold-Hardy Pink-Fleshed Grapefruit)
description: Pink Frost is a University of Georgia-released grapefruit bred by Wayne Hanna for reliable production at the cooler northern edge of the citrus range, and is reported hardy as far north as Tifton, Georgia, noticeably farther north than the standard grapefruit cultivars, which are among the least cold-tolerant citrus types. Fruit carries a deep pink blush on the rind over pink flesh, with a long harvest window running from late November through March. It fills a gap left by the grapefruit cultivars already in wide use (Marsh, Ruby Red, Star Ruby), which are generally recommended only for the mildest parts of zone 9b-10 rather than the cooler zone 8b-9a Gulf Coast. As with other grapefruit, protect young trees from hard freezes and expect several years before a substantial first crop. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pink Hyssop
description: Sow Pink Hyssop indoors in a warm, well-drained starting mix; transplant after hardening off into lean, dry to moderately moist, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun. Prune back hard after the first flush of bloom to maintain a dense, bushy shape and to encourage rebloom later in the season. The rose-pink flower spikes are showier in the border than the species type and equally attractive to bees and butterflies, while the strongly camphor-scented leaves are harvested the same way as standard hyssop for use in bittering liqueurs, savory meat rubs, and traditional expectorant teas. Being a seed strain rather than a clone, plants show some minor variation in exact flower shade from pale to deep rose; select and propagate the best-colored individuals by cuttings if uniform color is desired. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Pink Ice Finger Lime (Pink-Blushed Caviar Lime Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Pink Ice bears fruit with a distinctive rosy blush on the rind and pink, caviar-like pulp vesicles inside, adding visual appeal beyond the tangy citrus flavor common to all finger limes. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than seedling-grown plants when purchased grafted. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh as a garnish for seafood, cocktails, and desserts, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pink Icing Dwarf Blueberry (Compact Container Blueberry with Blue-and-Pink Foliage)
description: Site Pink Icing in a container or small raised bed of acidic, well-drained soil where its blue-green summer foliage and pink-to-purple fall color can be appreciated up close near a patio or entryway. The compact, rounded habit stays small enough for tight garden spaces yet still produces a respectable crop of sweet, powder-blue berries in early to midsummer on a self-fertile plant. Because container-grown blueberries dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat, check soil moisture often and never let the root ball go bone-dry. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and refresh the potting mix every couple of years as it breaks down. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Lady Flowering Quince (Rich Pink Early-Spring Quince)
description: Pink Lady is a flowering quince selection bearing rich, rose-pink, cup-shaped blossoms that open from darker pink buds in profusion along the thorny, leafless branches in late winter and early spring, ahead of most other flowering shrubs. Its dense, bushy, tangled habit spreads wider than it grows tall, giving it good presence as an informal hedge, barrier planting, or flowering specimen, and small, hard, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom in fall that can be used for jelly and preserves. It tolerates poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil and is quite drought-tolerant once established, asking for little beyond good drainage. Because flower buds form on the previous year's growth, prune only right after flowering finishes to avoid cutting off the next season's display. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pink Lemonade Blueberry
description: 'Pink Lemonade' is an ornamental rabbiteye-type hybrid bearing translucent pink berries with a mild, sweet flavor that deepen in color as they ripen. It offers attractive white-pink spring blooms and fiery fall foliage in addition to novelty fruit. Grow in full sun in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) kept evenly moist with a pine-bark or pine-needle mulch. Yields improve with a second blueberry variety nearby for cross-pollination; prune lightly after the third year to renew fruiting wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pink Lipstick Chard (Vivid Magenta-Stemmed Savoy Chard)
description: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil and thin to final spacing, watering consistently to keep leaves tender through summer heat. Bred for its intensely saturated hot-pink stalks and veins, this selection stands out even among rainbow chard mixes and holds its color well after cooking. Its heavily crumpled, deep green leaves are produced over a long season, and repeated cutting encourages continued new growth from the crown. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Pink Passion Chard (Vivid Hot Pink Stem Chard)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Passion is a modern chard cultivar bred for exceptionally vivid, saturated hot-pink stalks and midribs that stand out strongly against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves, making it a favorite for ornamental edible plantings as well as the kitchen. Both leaves and stalks are edible with classic chard flavor, the leaves cooking down like spinach and the crisp, colorful stalks holding their hue reasonably well when sautéed or roasted. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect strong production through the cool season with regular cutting. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Pink Pearl Apple (Pink-Fleshed Etter Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering deeply and regularly while the young tree establishes. Pink Pearl was bred by Northern California nurseryman Albert Etter and released in 1944, part of a series of hybrids he made specifically to breed pink and red flesh color into eating apples rather than just skin color. The thin greenish-yellow skin, sometimes brushed with a light pink blush, hides vivid magenta-pink flesh that turns heads when the fruit is sliced, and the flavor is notably tart and lively with berry-like, almost strawberry-scented overtones. It ripens mid to late season and is best used fresh, in sauce, or blended into hard cider for both its acidity and its color; the tree bears fairly young and benefits from thinning to keep fruit size up. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pink Ponderosa Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy staking; Pink Ponderosa (also called 'Henderson's Pink Ponderosa') is a late 19th-century American heirloom tomato introduced by the Henderson seed company around 1891, noted for producing enormous, beefsteak-type fruits of a distinctive deep rose-pink color — the 'pink' refers to the red flesh showing through the colorless (no yellow pigment in skin) skin, creating the characteristic pink-red appearance of traditional beefsteak-type heirlooms. The very large fruits (often 1–2 pounds each) are meaty, low-acid, and juicy with a mild, sweet, rich tomato flavor that made Ponderosa-type tomatoes the standard fresh-eating tomato for most of the 20th century before uniform-color commercial hybrids replaced them. The indeterminate vine produces continuously until frost and can be especially productive in zone 9's long growing season. The mild, low-acid flavor makes Pink Ponderosa particularly appealing for sliced tomatoes where the full fruit flavor is experienced without cooking. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Pink Purslane
description: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade as soon as soil can be worked; pink purslane (Siberian miner's lettuce) is a small, delicate annual or biennial native to Siberia and the Pacific Coast of North America that produces a rosette of fleshy, pale-green, succulent leaves and distinctive stems that pierce directly through their paired leaves (perfoliate, like its American relative Claytonia perfoliata), topped with clusters of small, pink, five-petaled flowers in spring. All parts are edible — the tender leaves, stems, and flowers are mild, slightly succulent, and pleasant in salads. Unlike most salad greens, pink purslane grows enthusiastically in full shade and can be naturalized as a self-sowing edible groundcover in shaded woodland gardens and under deciduous trees, where it self-sows to provide a recurring supply of early spring greens. Goes to seed quickly in heat but will resow for fall crops. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Pink Trumpet Tree (Rosy Trumpet Tree, Pink Tabebuia)
description: Plant container-grown specimens in full sun in well-drained soil; pink trumpet tree (Tabebuia rosea) is one of the most spectacular flowering trees of the tropics, producing masses of large, pink to lavender-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late winter to early spring when the tree is briefly leafless — creating a breathtaking cloud of color before new leaves emerge. Native to Central America and widely planted across the Caribbean and Gulf Coast, it is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and thrives in the alkaline limestone soils of south Florida. The wood is among the hardest and most durable of any tropical tree. Plant as a specimen tree, street tree, or focal point; the brief but spectacular bloom period makes it one of the most admired flowering trees in zone 10–12 landscapes. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Pinkerton Avocado
description: Easily identified by its elongated, curved neck and pear shape, Pinkerton is a Guatemalan-leaning Type A avocado with thin, pebbled green skin, a notably small seed, and a high flesh-to-seed ratio that yields more edible fruit per pound than round-fruited cultivars like Reed. It blooms and ripens earlier than Hass, filling the harvest gap from late winter into early summer before mainseason cultivars come on, though the flesh takes noticeably longer to soften after picking. Flavor is creamy and nutty but somewhat milder and less rich than Hass, making it a useful early-season complement rather than a direct substitute. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pinkeye Purple Hull Cowpea (Southern Pea, Purple Hull Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; Pinkeye Purple Hull is the most widely grown and most beloved Southern pea (cowpea) cultivar in Gulf South gardens — a semi-vining bush variety producing pods with a distinctive purple hull (pod exterior) that turns from green to vivid purple-magenta at the ideal harvest stage for fresh-shelling, making it easy to identify perfect harvest timing. The peas inside have the distinctive pink 'eye' (hilum marking) characteristic of this type, with a rich, full, starchy-creamy flavor that is the authentic taste of Southern cooking — distinctive, earthy, and satisfying in ways that fresh garden peas cannot replicate. Cowpeas are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables in cultivation and actually perform best during the hottest summer months when most other crops fail — the Gulf South summer that defeats beans, cucumbers, and squash is ideal cowpea growing weather. They fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule bacteria, enriching the soil for follow-on crops. For fresh eating, harvest when the majority of the pod has turned purple and feels firm and fully rounded but before the pod dries. For dried peas, allow the pods to turn tan and dry completely on the vine. The dried peas store indefinitely and are the foundation of traditional Southern New Year's black-eyed pea dishes. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Pinkie Rosemary (Pink-Flowered Trailing Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, ideally on a slope, wall, or raised bed where the trailing stems can cascade freely. Pinkie is a low, spreading rosemary selection distinguished from most other trailing rosemary cultivars by its soft pink flowers rather than the usual blue or violet, blooming heavily in cooler months. The narrow, dark green leaves have the same pungent culinary aroma as upright rosemary and are fully usable in cooking. Because it is more cold-sensitive than hardier upright types, protect container-grown plants from hard freezes or treat it as a seasonal ornamental-culinary plant in colder zones. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Pinks Mammoth Atemoya (Extra-Large-Fruited Historic Atemoya)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Pinks Mammoth is one of the oldest and most historically significant atemoya cultivars, an early Queensland-bred hybrid known for producing some of the largest fruit of any atemoya selection, occasionally exceeding two pounds, with rich, sweet, custard-white flesh. Cropping tends to be less regular than modern cultivars like Gefner, and fruit can show some irregular shape or blemish, but the exceptional size and flavor keep it popular with home growers chasing a standout specimen fruit. Hand pollination in the morning, moving pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, markedly improves fruit set and helps the tree reach its full potential fruit size; harvest as the fruit softens slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pinnacle Blueberry (Early Large-Fruited NC State/USDA Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained, organic-matter-rich soil amended with pine bark, since Pinnacle performs best on the kind of moisture-retentive 'blueberry soils' historically favored for highbush production. Developed jointly by NC State University and USDA-ARS breeders, Pinnacle is grown for early ripening, large, light-blue, firm berries with excellent shelf life that hold up well to shipping and handling. The self-fertile flowers produce abundant pollen and the semi-upright bush is only moderately vigorous, so routine pruning of older wood each winter helps keep new fruiting canes coming without letting the plant become overcrowded. Fertilize with an acid-forming blend in early spring and maintain a thick pine-bark or pine-straw mulch to hold the soil acidity and moisture this cultivar needs. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pinot Gris Wine Grape (Pinot Grigio)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Gris is a genetic mutation of Pinot Noir and shares that variety's preference for cooler growing climates. A pinkish-gray-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, this white wine grape produces two distinctly different wine styles depending on region and winemaking approach: light, crisp, neutral wines when labeled Pinot Grigio in the Italian style, or richer, more aromatic, fuller-bodied wines when labeled Pinot Gris in the Alsatian French style. It shares much of Pinot Noir's cold hardiness and preference for cooler climates, along with a similar susceptibility to fungal disease in humid conditions, requiring attentive canopy management for airflow. Prune for an open canopy to reduce disease pressure in humid climates, and decide on harvest timing based on the intended wine style, since earlier picking favors the crisper Pinot Grigio style and later picking favors richer Pinot Gris character. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pinot Noir Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Noir prefers cooler growing regions and is notoriously demanding, susceptible to fungal disease and sensitive to heat and site conditions. One of the world's most celebrated but challenging red wine grapes, it produces thin-skinned, tightly clustered grapes prone to rot in humid or wet conditions, making it best suited to cooler, drier climates with good air circulation rather than hot, humid regions like the Gulf South. Its thin skins and tight clusters demand vigilant canopy management, leaf pulling for airflow, and prompt disease treatment, and it is generally considered one of the more difficult grape varieties for a home vineyard to grow successfully compared to more disease-resistant hybrid grapes. Site vines on a well-drained slope with good air movement, prune for an open canopy to reduce humidity around the fruit, and monitor closely for powdery and downy mildew through the growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pinotage Wine Grape (South African Pinot Noir x Cinsaut Cross)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Pinotage was created in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then locally known as Hermitage), combining the two into a distinctive grape now considered South Africa's signature red wine variety, producing deeply colored wines with bold red and dark fruit character often accompanied by a distinctive smoky, earthy, sometimes rubbery note that divides wine drinkers but has become part of the grape's identity. The vine is considerably more vigorous and heat-tolerant than pure Pinot Noir, adapting well to warmer growing regions where its more finicky parent would struggle, and it produces reliably heavy crops if not deliberately restricted. Train to a permanent trellis, thin crop for concentrated flavor if quality wine is the goal, and manage canopy carefully, since overcropped Pinotage can accentuate unwanted rubbery, volatile aromas. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pinova Apple (Crisp Sweet-Tart German Modern Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pinova was bred in Germany in the 1980s from crosses tracing back to Golden Delicious and Clivia, released for its crisp, dense, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh and attractive red-striped skin over a yellow background, quickly gaining popularity across Europe as a quality dessert apple with genuinely good storage life. The vigorous, productive tree bears reliably, and fruit holds its crisp texture and flavor well in cold storage for months, making it a satisfying choice for home orchardists wanting fresh apples well past the immediate harvest season. Harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the longest keeping quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pinto Bean
description: Pinto is a heat- and drought-tolerant bush bean grown as a dry bean, producing pods of speckled beans on upright plants with short runners. Direct sow after frost into warm soil in full sun, and let the pods dry fully on the plant. Water moderately during flowering and pod set, then ease off as pods mature. Harvest when pods are brown and brittle, then shell and dry the beans further for storage. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Pinto Bean
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinto beans are the most widely grown dry bean in the United States, accounting for nearly half of all dry bean production, and the foundation of Southwestern and Mexican cooking — the primary bean in refried beans (frijoles refritos), bean soup, and chili. The tan seeds with reddish-brown speckles (the Spanish name 'pinto' means 'painted') turn uniformly tan-brown when cooked, at which point the flavor is rich, earthy, and starchy with a creamy texture that falls apart when mashed. Bush-habit pinto plants are compact and self-supporting, producing a single concentrated harvest suitable for home-scale production and storage. The dry beans store for 2–3 years in a cool, dry location. In zone 9 the plants are susceptible to bean rust in humid conditions; provide adequate spacing for air circulation. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Pinyon Pine (Colorado Pinyon)
description: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; pinyon pine is the most ecologically and culturally important small tree of the American Southwest — the source of the highly prized and commercially valuable piñon nuts (pine nuts) that are a cornerstone of both Native American foodways and southwestern cuisine. A two-needle pine (two needles per bundle) forming dense, round-crowned, picturesque small trees in the classic piñon-juniper woodland that dominates millions of acres of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin at 4,500–8,000 feet elevation. Pinyon nut harvests are a major economic and cultural event across the Southwest — harvested by Native peoples and marketed commercially for centuries. The large, wingless nuts are rich in protein, fat, and calories. Drought tolerant to an extraordinary degree — essentially requiring no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate Southwest climates. Trees live 200–1,000 years. Pinyon jays are entirely dependent on pinyon nuts as their primary food source. An excellent, slow-growing, low-water landscape tree for hot, dry, rocky gardens in zone 4–8. Matures in 730–3650 days from transplant.

name: Pioneer Cornelian Cherry
description: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; Pioneer is a fruit-selected cultivar of Cornus mas, a small multi-stemmed tree that opens clusters of tiny yellow flowers on bare branches in very early spring, weeks before forsythia. Its oblong, cherry-red fruits ripen in midsummer and drop as they soften, so most growers harvest by shaking the tree onto a tarp or gathering fallen fruit daily; the tart, plum-like flesh is used for syrup, jam, liqueur, and traditional Eastern European preserves. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerates urban conditions and a range of soils, and is largely untroubled by pests or diseases that plague other stone fruit. Pioneer bears earlier and more heavily than unselected seedlings, typically fruiting within three to four years of planting. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pipestone Plum (University of Minnesota Cold-Hardy Hybrid Plum)
description: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible Japanese-American hybrid pollinizer such as Superior or Toka nearby, since Pipestone is not reliably self-fruitful. Pipestone was released by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program from a cross of Burbank with a Prunus salicina x Wolf seedling, part of the same long-running Minnesota plum-breeding effort that combined Japanese plum quality with the extreme cold hardiness of native American plum to fill a gap for northern gardeners where standard Japanese and European plums winter-kill. Pipestone bears very large, red-skinned, clingstone fruit with sweet, juicy yellow flesh under a notably thick, tough skin that holds firm until it splits open in a burst of juice at full ripeness. The tree is exceptionally productive and among the hardiest named plums available, making it a dependable choice for the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains where many stone fruits fail. Thin heavy fruit sets to improve size and reduce limb breakage, and prune in late winter to an open form for good light and air circulation. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pipicha (Slender Poreleaf)
description: Sow seeds after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pipicha is a strongly aromatic Mexican herb native to the dry, mountainous regions of Oaxaca, Puebla, and Guerrero, used in Oaxacan cuisine as one of the distinctive flavoring herbs — recognizable by its very narrow, linear leaves dotted with visible oil glands (the 'porophyllum' = pore-leaf name refers to these), which release a pungent, complex aroma combining elements of rue, cilantro, and anise when bruised or used in cooking. It is used in tlayudas, quesillo dishes, soups, black beans, and as a fresh herb scattered over completed dishes. Pipicha is closely related to papalo (Porophyllum ruderale) which is already more widely known in US markets, but has narrower, more pungent leaves and a slightly different flavor profile preferred by cooks from the Oaxacan Valleys. In regions with good Mexican grocery supply, both pipicha and papalo can sometimes be found fresh. Grow as a warm-season annual in most of North America. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Pipsissewa (Prince's Pine)
description: Plant in dry to moist, highly acidic, humus-rich, conifer-needle duff soil in full shade beneath pines or oaks; pipsissewa is a small, semi-woody, evergreen native of dry conifer and mixed forests across the Northern Hemisphere, recognized by its whorled, dark green, glossy, toothed leaves with pale midribs and its nodding clusters of waxy, pink-white, fragrant flowers in summer. Like spotted wintergreen (C. maculata) and other Pyrola relatives, it is mycoheterotrophic — partially dependent on mycorrhizal fungi for nutrition and extremely difficult to establish in garden conditions without intact fungal partners. The plant has a long history of use in traditional Native American medicine and was an ingredient in the original commercial root beer formulas. Do not collect from wild populations. Best appreciated as a feature of intact native forest rather than a cultivated garden plant. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Piquillo Pepper (Spanish Roasting Pepper, Lodosa Piquillo)
description: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost danger passes; piquillo plants are compact and productive, setting numerous small, triangular fruits; harvest at full vivid red maturity; roast over open flame or under a broiler until charred, steam to loosen skin, peel and seed for the classic preparation. Piquillo is the defining preserved pepper of northern Spain, particularly the Navarra region around the town of Lodosa (in the Ebro River valley) where the Denomination of Origin 'Piquillo de Lodosa' protects the traditional pepper and its preparation. The pepper is small (2–3 inch), triangular to slightly flattened-conical with a characteristic pointed 'beak' tip (piquillo = 'little beak'), vivid scarlet-red at maturity, and sweet to very mildly pungent with no significant heat. The flesh is thin but intensely sweet and slightly fruity, with a subtle bitterness that is balanced by the roasting process — fire-roasting is inseparable from the piquillo's culinary identity. The traditional preparation involves hand-roasting individual peppers over wood fires, peeling and seeding each one by hand without any water washing (to preserve flavor and sugars), and packing them in their own juices in jars or tins without any additional preservation except salt. The result is one of the most refined and flavorful preserved vegetables in world cuisine. Jarred piquillo peppers are a staple of Spanish kitchens and are used stuffed with salt cod or cheese, arranged on pintxos, layered in pasta dishes, and pureed into smooth sauces. Growing piquillo at home and roasting them yourself produces a quality that commercially jarred peppers rarely match. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Piracicaba Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant Brazilian Sprouting Broccoli for Warm Climates)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant to garden in fall for zone 9 winter harvest. Harvest loose florets continuously. Piracicaba Broccoli originated at the Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) and agronomic research stations near Piracicaba, a city in São Paulo state, Brazil — a major center of Brazilian tropical agricultural research. The variety was developed specifically to address the fundamental incompatibility between standard broccoli breeding (which targets cool-climate heading formation) and the subtropical conditions of southern Brazil and other warm-climate growing regions. Standard broccoli varieties were bred primarily in Europe and California's cool coastal fog belt, where temperature ranges precisely suited to head development allow reliable production; in warm climates, standard broccoli heats prematurely, forms loose, open heads of poor quality, or bolts before any marketable crop develops. Piracicaba's breeding solution was to select for a sprouting growth habit that produces continuously rather than forming a single marketable head — an approach that converts the temperature sensitivity of head formation from a problem into an advantage. Since the plant never forms a central head to be ruined by heat, there is no precise temperature window to miss, and the plant produces usable florets across a much broader temperature range. The florets of Piracicaba are small and tender, with a delicate texture superior to the sometimes-coarse texture of oversized main-head broccoli, and the continuous harvest over weeks or months provides far greater total yield per plant than single-harvest heading types in favorable conditions. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Piri Piri Pepper (African Bird's Eye)
description: Start indoors early and transplant to warm, well-drained soil; piri piri is an African cultivar of Capsicum frutescens (the same species as tabasco pepper) producing small, erect, vivid red to orange fruits 1–2 inches long with an intense, bright heat (50,000–175,000 SHU). It is the essential ingredient in the famous Portuguese piri piri sauce, brought to Portugal from its colonies in Angola and Mozambique in the 1500s, and is now central to Portuguese, South African, and Mozambican cuisines. Nando's Peri-Peri sauce is based on this pepper. The fruits are blended with garlic, lemon, and oil to make a marinade-sauce for grilled chicken. Plants become perennial subshrubs in zones 9–11 and produce prolifically year-round. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Pisang Mas Banana (Golden Finger Banana)
description: Pisang Mas, or 'golden banana,' is a small, intensely sweet dessert banana widely grown across Malaysia and Singapore, prized for its short, thin-skinned fruit that ripens to a bright gold with a rich, almost honeyed flavor unlike the milder Cavendish. It is naturally more compact than most edible bananas, which makes it a good candidate for a large patio container that can be moved to shelter before frost. Grow it in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive soil and steady feeding through the growing season, and expect a somewhat faster cycle to first bunch than tall commercial cultivars. It has no particular cold hardiness, so protect the corm or bring the container indoors well before the first freeze in zone 9a. Matures in 305–455 days from transplant.

name: Pisang Raja Banana (Southeast Asian Dessert Banana)
description: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, feeding heavily through the growing season since bananas are gross feeders. Pisang Raja, meaning 'king banana' in Malay and Indonesian, is one of the most widely grown and highly regarded dessert bananas in Southeast Asia, prized for its dense, creamy, richly aromatic flesh with a distinctive honeyed flavor that many consider superior to Cavendish-type bananas for fresh eating. The moderately sized fruits have thick yellow skin with characteristic black spotting when fully ripe. In zone 9a, where winter freezes routinely kill the pseudostem to the ground, treat it as a root-hardy perennial: mulch heavily over winter and expect regrowth from the rhizome in spring, though a freeze-free run of 12-15 months is typically needed to reach fruiting size, so a large container that can be moved to shelter improves the odds of a crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Pistachio
description: Pistachio is dioecious — you must plant at least one male tree (typically Peters variety) for every 8–10 female trees; pollen is wind-carried. The tree requires 700–1000 chill hours in winter and blisteringly hot, dry summers (100°F+ is ideal) to ripen nuts properly, making it poorly suited to humid or mild-summer climates. Trees are extremely drought-tolerant and actually prefer alkaline, well-drained soils. Nuts are ready when hulls turn from green to red-pink and slip off easily; harvest by shaking limbs and collect nuts off tarps laid below. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Pistou Basil
description: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Pistou Basil is a French compact dwarf basil named for the Provençal paste pistou — the French equivalent of Italian pesto made with fresh basil, garlic, olive oil, and sometimes cheese and tomatoes. The plant forms a naturally round, globe-shaped mound of small to medium-sized aromatic leaves with a rich, clove-spicy basil flavor slightly sweeter and less anise-forward than Italian sweet basil. The compact habit (8–16 inches, self-branching) makes Pistou ideal for container growing, window boxes, and herb gardens where space is limited. Unlike Fino Verde with its tiny, fingernail-sized leaves, Pistou produces slightly larger leaves that are easier to harvest individually and better-suited to chopping for pistou paste, compound butter, and herb-infused oils. The two cultivars — Pistou and Fino Verde — are distinctly different: Pistou is more upright and globe-forming, Fino Verde is a lower spreading mound with smaller leaves. In zone 9 both provide an excellent warm-season herb harvest. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Pitmaston Pineapple Apple (Small Pineapple-Flavored English Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pitmaston Pineapple is an English heirloom dating to 1785, named for a genuinely distinctive tropical, pineapple-like flavor and aroma that sets it apart from every other common apple variety, a quality that has kept it a beloved curiosity among heirloom apple collectors for well over two centuries. The small, golden-yellow, lightly russeted fruit is far smaller than a typical dessert apple, more the size of a large crabapple, but the intensity of its unusual flavor more than compensates for its modest size, making it a favorite for fresh eating in small quantities and an interesting addition to hard cider blends. The compact tree bears reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect a short storage life typical of many aromatic heirloom dessert apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pitomba (Pitomba Amarela, Brazilian Cherry)
description: Plant in full sun in rich, moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in frost-free conditions; pitomba is a small to medium Brazilian Eugenia producing clusters of golden-orange round to ovoid fruits about cherry-sized with smooth thin skin and juicy sweet-acidic orange flesh surrounding a single large seed — the flavor blends apricot, mango, and peach with a pleasant tartness. Trees are slow to mature but once established bear heavy crops excellent eaten fresh, juiced, or preserved as jams. Slightly more cold-tolerant than many tropical Eugenias, tolerating brief dips near 30°F on established trees. A rewarding and unusual addition to the zone 10–12 food garden. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Pix-Zee Genetic Dwarf Peach (True Dwarf Container Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container; Pix-Zee is a true genetic dwarf peach, meaning its compact 5–8 foot mature size is controlled by the tree's own genes rather than achieved through a dwarfing rootstock or heavy pruning — a genuinely different growth mechanism from popular container peaches like Bonanza or Bonfire that are simply naturally shorter standard-type trees. This makes Pix-Zee well suited to a large patio pot, small urban yard, or anywhere a full-sized peach tree would be impractical, while still producing normal, full-sized, freestone yellow-fleshed fruit with good sweet peach flavor. It is self-fertile, so a single tree sets fruit without a second pollinator variety nearby. Thin fruit to about 4–6 inches apart once set to improve size and prevent limb breakage, since the compact branches can be overwhelmed by a heavy crop. Provide full sun and consistent moisture, especially for container-grown trees, which dry out faster than trees planted in the ground. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pixie Crunch Apple (Compact Disease-Resistant Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Pixie Crunch, also released as Co-op 33 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program, combines genetic immunity to apple scab with a naturally denser, more compact growth habit than most other apple varieties, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards or higher-density plantings where a full-size tree would be too much. The fruit is medium-size, crisp, and juicy with a lively sweet-tart flavor and good storage quality, ripening in the fall alongside other mid-season scab-resistant varieties. Because the tree naturally stays more compact, it requires somewhat less aggressive pruning to control size than typical apple varieties, though annual pruning to maintain an open canopy and good light penetration is still recommended for fruit quality and disease control in humid climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pixie Mandarin (California Heirloom Seedless Late-Season Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Pixie is a longstanding California heirloom mandarin valued for small, easy-peel, essentially seedless fruit with rich, sweet flavor, and for an unusually late ripening window that stretches into spring and even early summer, well past when most other mandarins have finished, giving a long tail to the citrus season. The tree tends to be moderately vigorous with a somewhat spreading habit. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pixwell Gooseberry (Easy-Pick Reduced-Thorn Gooseberry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Pixwell was bred specifically to make gooseberry picking less painful, holding its pale green, ripening-to-pink berries on longer stems that dangle clear of the thorny branches, unlike older cultivars whose fruit clusters tightly among the spines. The berries have the classic tart gooseberry flavor, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, and the plant is vigorous, cold-hardy, and self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, and site with some afternoon shade in warmer climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: PKM-1 Moringa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — moringa is extremely drought tolerant once established and is one of the few productive food trees that thrives in poor, dry, neglected sites; PKM-1 is an improved selection of Moringa (Moringa oleifera, the 'miracle tree') developed specifically for high pod yield and early production — bearing its first edible pods within 6–8 months of sowing from seed compared to the 12–18 months typical of seedling-grown moringa. The leaves, young pods (drumsticks), and flowers of moringa are all edible and among the most nutritionally dense plant foods available — the leaves contain protein, vitamin C, calcium, iron, and a range of antioxidants at concentrations that have made moringa a focus of nutritional research and a widely promoted food security crop. In zone 9 moringa grows as a rapidly resprouting tender perennial — killed to the ground by frost but regenerating vigorously from the root in spring and often reaching 10–15 feet before the next frost. The soft, ferny, compound leaves are harvested continuously throughout the growing season by cutting branch tips, and the long, angular seed pods (the 'drumsticks' of Indian cuisine) are harvested when young and tender for cooking in curries, soups, and stir-fries. Matures in 180–240 days from seed.

name: PKM-2 Moringa (Extra-Long-Pod High-Yield Annual Moringa)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; extremely drought-tolerant once established. PKM-2 is an Indian agricultural selection bred specifically for pod production, producing markedly longer pods than PKM-1 with more flesh relative to seed, and abundant horizontal lateral branching that makes both pods and leaves easier to harvest by hand. It blooms roughly 100-110 days from sowing with first pod harvest around 170-180 days, and leaves have scored well in taste comparisons against other moringa selections. In zone 9, grow as a fast-resprouting tender perennial killed back by frost each winter and regrown from the root or reseeded in spring; commercial growers in India often treat it as an annual, replacing plants after one to two seasons of harvest for peak productivity. Matures in 170–240 days from seed.

name: Placentia Loquat (Historic Large-Fruited Late-Season Loquat)
description: Placentia traces back to seed introduced from Japan and planted in Placentia, California between roughly 1880 and 1900, making it one of the oldest named loquat selections still grown in the United States. It bears large, oblong to rounded fruit with tough orange-yellow skin dotted with numerous small white flecks, enclosing thick, firm, juicy orange flesh with a sweet, apricot-like flavor. Fruit is borne in small clusters of only a few loquats each rather than the large hanging trusses typical of some cultivars, and the thick skin lets Placentia fruit keep and ship better than thinner-skinned types. It ripens late in the loquat season and is self-fertile, so a single tree bears reliably on its own. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Plains Bee Balm
description: Plains bee balm is the drought-tolerant Monarda of the southern Great Plains, growing naturally on dry, sandy, rocky soils of the short-grass and mixed-grass prairies of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Colorado where rainfall is too scarce and the climate too extreme for other bee balms to survive. The plant is intensely aromatic — a strong, pleasant oregano-like scent rises from the leaves when brushed — and it has been used by indigenous peoples and settlers as a culinary herb and tea plant; it makes an excellent substitute for Mexican oregano in southwestern cooking. Small, pink to lavender whorled flowers appear on branching stems in summer and are heavily visited by native bees and small butterflies for nectar; the aromatic oils deter deer and most mammalian herbivores. In dry, sunny native garden situations and xeriscape designs, plains bee balm provides both ornamental interest and aromatic culinary value with essentially no irrigation required once established in sandy, well-drained soil. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Plainsman Amaranth (Early USDA-Bred Grain Amaranth)
description: Plainsman came out of the grain amaranth breeding work done at the Rodale Research Center in the early 1980s, part of the push to turn amaranth into a viable modern US grain crop rather than strictly a garden curiosity. It bears tan to golden upright seed heads on tall, sturdy plants and was selected in large part for maturing reliably within a single Midwestern growing season, a trait that made it a common choice in early commercial grain amaranth trial plots. Sow shallowly in warm soil once frost danger has passed, thin to a wide spacing, and let plants grow largely unattended through summer heat. Harvest once the seed heads dry and shed seed readily when rubbed between the hands, then thresh and winnow thoroughly, since amaranth seed is small and light. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Plantain (Cooking Banana, Starchy Banana)
description: Plant suckers in deeply cultivated, rich, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; keep consistently moist, feed heavily with high-potassium fertilizer, and mulch the root zone heavily in winter in zones 8–9. Musa paradisiaca (plantain banana) is the starchy, cooking banana — botanically a giant herbaceous perennial growing from a massive underground corm, producing a 10–20 foot pseudostem (not a true trunk, but a compressed stem made of overlapping leaf sheaths) topped with enormous, paddle-shaped leaves up to 9 feet long; fruiting occurs 10–18 months after planting when the plant produces a pendant inflorescence that develops into a bunch containing 5–12 hands of 10–20 plantain fruits each. Unlike dessert bananas, plantains are harvested and consumed at all ripeness stages: green plantains are starchy and firm, used for tostones, chips, and savory dishes; yellow plantains are semi-sweet; and fully ripe, black-skinned plantains are sweet enough for desserts. In zone 9, established corms reliably resprout each spring after winter dieback and fruit every 12–18 months from established stools. Plantains are a dietary staple across the Caribbean, West Africa, and Latin America. Matures in 300–540 days from transplant.

name: Planters Jumbo Cantaloupe (Classic 1930s Netted Melon)
description: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Planters Jumbo is an heirloom cantaloupe dating to the 1930s, once a standard commercial variety grown widely across the South before modern hybrid melons largely replaced older open-pollinated types, prized for heavily netted rind and sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Platinum Blonde Lavandin (Variegated Cream-Edged Foliage Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry, neutral-to-alkaline soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind. Platinum Blonde was discovered as a sport by a Spanish breeder and was nominated for Plant of the Year at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show; it is grown chiefly for its striking variegated foliage, narrow, grey-green leaves edged in creamy yellow, which provides season-long color even between bloom cycles, topped in summer by fragrant spikes of soft blue flowers. Like other lavandins it grows larger and more vigorously than English lavender, so allow extra space for airflow, and shear lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, compact mound. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Pleas Hican (Historic Bitternut-Pecan Hybrid)
description: Pleas is a bitternut hickory x pecan cross long documented in Northern Nut Growers Association records and considered one of the outstanding hican selections for cold hardiness, retaining a distinctly hickory-shaped nut with a rich flavor and ample kernel. As with other hicans, kernel fill and cracking quality vary by season, so it is grown chiefly by collectors and diversified nut-orchard hobbyists rather than commercial producers. Site it in deep, well-drained soil with a compatible pecan or hickory pollinator nearby, and be patient; hicans are typically slower to reach bearing age than standard pecan cultivars. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Plein Blanc Inerme Cardoon (French Spineless White Cardoon)
description: Plein Blanc Inerme is a traditional French cardoon selected for broad, fleshy leaf ribs that carry almost no spines, unlike most cardoon strains whose sharp-edged leaves make harvest and blanching an unpleasant task. Plants form an imposing architectural clump of long, deeply cut, silvery-gray foliage a yard or more tall and wide before the ribs are ready to bundle and blanch in autumn. Wrap the outer leaves around the stalks and cover with cardboard, straw, or black plastic for several weeks before harvest to sweeten the ribs and reduce bitterness. Give it deep, rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture through the growing season for the tenderest stalks. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Pleurisy Root
description: Sow in fall or cold-stratify seed for four weeks before spring sowing to break dormancy. This drought-tough native milkweed has a deep taproot historically used for respiratory ailments. Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid moving it once established. The brilliant orange flowers are a magnet for butterflies and native bees. Water only during severe drought and harvest roots from mature plants in autumn. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Plum
description: European plums (Prunus domestica) are often self-fertile, but Japanese plums (P. salicina) generally need a compatible pollinator planted nearby within 50 feet. Prune European types to a central leader and Japanese types to an open center; remove crossing branches each dormant season. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches apart after natural fruit drop to encourage larger size. Pick when fruit achieves full color and yields gently to pressure — overripe plums are soft and ferment quickly. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Plum Pine
description: Plant Podocarpus elatus in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; female plants bear the edible receptacles only when a male tree is planted nearby for pollination. Plum Pine is one of the most ecologically and gastronomically interesting of all Australian rainforest trees — a conifer (in the Podocarpaceae family, relatives of pines) whose 'fruit' is technically the swollen, fleshy, purple-black stem (receptacle) that develops beneath the actual seed. The edible receptacles are about 1–2 cm across with dark purple-black skin and rich, soft, slightly jammy flesh with a distinctive, complex flavor that combines sweetness, tartness, and a subtle piney, resinous note unlike any other fruit. Aboriginal Australians used the receptacles as a food source; today Plum Pine is a celebrated ingredient in Australian native food (bush tucker) cuisine — used in jams, sauces, cocktails, and gourmet desserts. Commercial cultivation is expanding in subtropical Australia. In the garden, it is a handsome, slow-growing evergreen tree with dense, narrow, yew-like foliage; it tolerates urban conditions well and makes an excellent shade tree or screen. Dioecious — both male and female trees needed for fruit production. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Plum Regal Tomato (Disease-Resistant Plum Paste Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Plum Regal is a determinate plum-type paste tomato developed by Cornell University's tomato breeding program specifically to improve on the disease susceptibility of heirloom Roma and similar paste types while maintaining the thick walls, dense flesh, and low moisture content that make plum tomatoes superior for sauce-making and processing. Plum Regal carries resistance to late blight (Phytophthora infestans) — the disease that wiped out heirloom paste tomatoes across much of the Northeast during the late blight epidemic of 2009 — as well as Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt. The medium-large (3–5 oz), deep red, oval fruits have very thick walls, small seed cavities, and excellent sauce-making characteristics with rich, concentrated tomato flavor. An outstanding choice for humid-climate paste tomato production, for home canners who want reliable crops without the disease susceptibility of traditional paste heirlooms, and for any gardener growing tomatoes where late blight or Fusarium are recurring problems. Matures in 72–78 days from transplant.

name: Pluot
description: The pluot is a complex plum-apricot hybrid skewed toward plum, prized for intensely sweet, richly flavored fruit. Plant in full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and provide a suitable Japanese plum or another pluot for cross-pollination. Train to an open vase form and thin fruit to 4-6 inches apart to prevent overbearing. In cold regions protect the early blooms from frost, as flowering can precede that of many plums. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: PMR 45 Cantaloupe (Powdery Mildew Resistant 45)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, spacing hills 24-36 inches apart in rows several feet apart. PMR 45 produces medium-sized, well-netted, oval fruits with thick, sweet orange flesh, and was a landmark release in melon breeding as the first commercial cantaloupe bred specifically for resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that had caused catastrophic losses in California melon fields during the 1920s. Its resistance genes have since been used extensively by breeders to create many modern mildew-resistant melon hybrids, making it a historically significant variety as well as a solid, productive open-pollinated choice for home gardens. Water consistently through vine growth and fruit development, then taper off as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Poblano Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and provide bottom heat around 80°F to speed germination. Transplant to fertile, well-drained soil once nights are consistently above 55°F.
