Water deeply but infrequently to encourage deep rooting and reduce disease pressure. Harvest dark green fruits at 4–5 inches long for fresh use, or allow to turn red and dry them for ancho chiles. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Poblano Pepper (Ancho Pepper, Mulato Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Poblano is the classic Mexican culinary pepper — a mildly hot (1,000–2,000 Scoville units), wide, heart-shaped to triangular pepper that is the foundational ingredient in chiles rellenos, mole negro, and dozens of traditional Mexican dishes. Harvested green (poblano) or dried red (ancho or mulato depending on variety), these peppers have a rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor with moderate heat that defines the deep, layered character of traditional Mexican cuisine. The large, thick-walled fruits reach 4–5 inches long and 2.5–3 inches wide, with deep green color maturing to red-brown. Poblano is one of the most heat-tolerant culinary peppers and performs exceptionally well in zone 9's summer temperatures — unlike many sweet bell peppers, poblano tolerates the high summer heat of the Gulf South and continues producing through the hottest months with consistent irrigation. In zone 9, the plant can become a perennial woody shrub if protected from hard freezes, producing for 2–3 years from a single planting. Dry ripe red-brown poblanos to make ancho chiles — a key ingredient in red mole — by hanging in bundles in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Pocahontas Elderberry (University of Missouri Vigorous High-Yield American Elderberry)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pocahontas was selected from a wild population near Pocahontas, Arkansas, and released by the University of Missouri Elderberry Improvement Program in 2019 after multi-year replicated trials showed it consistently out-yielding the widely grown 'Bob Gordon' cultivar. It is the most vigorous and fastest-growing of the university's releases, producing large flower and berry heads on tall, sturdy canes, with flat-topped cymes of white flowers opening later in the season than most American elderberry cultivars, followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries used for syrup, juice, wine, and jelly. As with all American elderberry, Pocahontas spreads by root suckers to form colonies — remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to encourage strong new fruiting wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Poinsett 76 Cucumber
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; provide support or allow vines to sprawl with 3–4 feet between hills. Poinsett 76 was developed by the Clemson University vegetable breeding program in South Carolina and released in 1976 as an improved selection of the original Poinsett cucumber (released 1966) — both named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian who brought the poinsettia plant from Mexico. Poinsett 76 is distinguished by its outstanding disease resistance package (angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, mosaic, and powdery mildew resistance) and heat tolerance that makes it the cucumber of choice for hot, humid Southeastern gardens where most varieties decline quickly in summer; fruits are 7–8 inches long, dark green, cylindrical, and of good eating quality. An open-pollinated, seed-saveable classic that remains one of the best choices for Gulf Coast and Deep South summer cucumber production. Matures in 63–70 days from seed.

name: Poinsett Cucumber (Original 1966 Multi-Disease-Resistant Slicer)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost danger has passed, and provide a trellis or allow the vigorous vines to sprawl on 3-4 feet of row spacing. Named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian diplomat who introduced the poinsettia to the United States, this cucumber was a genuine breeding milestone: it was among the first commercial slicers to stack resistance to angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, and mosaic virus into one dependable open-pollinated line, which sharply reduced losses in the humid Southeast. Fruits are dark green, cylindrical, and 7-8 inches long with good flavor, though the plant is somewhat less heat-tolerant in peak midsummer than the 1976 selection later bred from it. Save seed from fully mature, yellowed fruit for a true-breeding crop the following year. Matures in 62–68 days from seed.

name: Pointed Gourd (Parwal, Patol)
description: Propagate from rooted stem cuttings or root sections, planting male and female plants together (ratio of 1 male per 4–6 females); train on a strong trellis in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; pointed gourd is one of the most popular vegetables in Bengali, Odia, and North Indian cuisine, prized for its tender 2–6 inch elongated fruits with green-and-white striped skin that are stuffed, curried, fried, or used in sweets when fully mature. Distinct from snake gourd (Trichosanthes cucumerina) in being much smaller, more compact, and preferred for cooking fresh and stuffed. Plants in zone 9 may freeze to the ground in winter but resprout from the roots in spring; mulch heavily in the first winter. Harvest fruits when they reach 3–4 inches for best culinary quality. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Pokey Joe Cilantro (Dwarf Slow-Bolt)
description: Pokey Joe is a dwarf cilantro selected for a low, dense, mounding habit and a notably slow transition to flowering compared with standard cilantro. Its short stature keeps the fine-cut leaves close together and easy to shear for repeated cutting, and the compact size suits small beds, edging, and containers where taller cilantro would flop or crowd neighbors. Because it holds in leaf production longer before bolting, it extends the harvest window of a single spring sowing further into warm weather than older varieties typically allow. Succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply, and let a few plants flower and set seed for coriander. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Polana Raspberry
description: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Polana is a Polish-bred, fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry producing its main crop on first-year canes in autumn — earlier than most other fall-bearing varieties, beginning to ripen in August–September in most climates. The earlier fall ripening is a significant advantage because it means more of the crop matures before winter freezes end the season in northern areas, and in zone 9 the earlier ripening of Polana compared to later fall-bearing types like Heritage means the crop starts before the hottest September weather. The firm, conical, dark red berries have excellent flavor — well-balanced sweet-tart with rich raspberry aroma. Polana is one of the most productive fall-bearing varieties per area; the compact, self-supporting primocane habit (no trellis needed) makes it practical for small gardens. In zone 9 fall raspberries are more reliably successful than summer varieties because the October ripening occurs in cooler conditions. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Polar Bear Pumpkin (Giant White Exhibition Pumpkin)
description: Start seed indoors ahead of the last frost, then transplant into deeply worked, richly amended soil with plenty of room, since fruit can reach 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions. Polar Bear stands out among giant pumpkins for its smooth, pure white rind, a striking contrast to the orange skin of most large exhibition types, making it a favorite for painted or decorated giant-pumpkin displays as well as competitive weigh-offs. Keep soil consistently moist during vine growth and fruit set, and remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine if maximum size is the goal. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has fully hardened and the vine has begun to decline, handling the heavy fruit carefully to avoid cracking the shell. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Polar Jewel Honeyberry (Russian Haskap)
description: Plant in well-drained loam or sandy loam in full sun alongside a compatible pollinizer, since Polar Jewel is self-infertile and will not crop well alone. A vigorous Russian-bred haskap selection, it produces large, elongated, dark blue berries with powdery bloom in an early-to-mid bloom group, ripening to a sweet flavor often described as a cross between blueberry and raspberry, good for fresh eating, jam, jelly, and baking. The upright, rounded bush reaches roughly 4 to 5 feet tall and wide at maturity and is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter lows well below -40F, but like all haskaps it struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is a poor fit for Gulf Coast gardens. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes once mature to sustain fruit production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Polaris Blueberry (University of Minnesota Cold-Hardy Half-High Blueberry)
description: Polaris is a University of Minnesota half-high blueberry, bred from a cross of lowbush and highbush parentage to combine extreme cold hardiness with a larger, more productive plant than pure lowbush types. It is among the earliest-ripening half-high cultivars, producing medium-sized, light blue, sweet-flavored berries in a concentrated early-summer harvest window. Compact and low-growing, it is well suited to cold-climate home gardens and container culture where taller highbush cultivars would not survive winter, but plant it with a second half-high or highbush cultivar nearby, since cross-pollination improves berry size and yield even though Polaris will self-pollinate to some degree. Mulch with pine bark or sawdust to maintain the acidic soil blueberries require, and prune out only dead or weak wood for the first several years to let the compact framework fill in. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Polish Linguisa Tomato (Sausage-Shaped Polish Heirloom Paste Tomato)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost, staking early to support the long fruit clusters. Polish Linguisa is a Polish heirloom paste tomato named for its distinctive elongated, curved, sausage-like fruit shape, which sets it apart from the blockier Roma and San Marzano types most gardeners know. The deep red fruit is dense and meaty with very little seed cavity or juice, cooking down quickly into a thick, richly flavored sauce or paste with minimal simmering. The vigorous indeterminate vines are heavy producers over a long season; pick fruit as it colors fully and process promptly, since the thin skin is more prone to splitting after heavy rain than dedicated modern paste hybrids. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Polish White Softneck Garlic (Eastern European Heirloom Artichoke Garlic)
description: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall from 4 weeks before first frost to shortly after; Polish White performs well in both cold northern climates and mild southern winters; harvest in summer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly before storage; braid the flexible stems for attractive long-term storage. Polish White is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic originating in Poland and the broader Eastern European garlic-growing tradition, where garlic has been a staple culinary and medicinal crop since ancient times; it entered the North American heirloom garlic collection through the immigrant communities and seed-saver networks that preserved traditional European agricultural varieties throughout the 20th century. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) with tightly packed multiple layers of cloves (10–16 per bulb) in the characteristic Artichoke arrangement, with clean white to ivory outer skins and a compact, rounded shape. The flavor is full, moderately pungent, and satisfying — not as complex as the finest Rocambole or Marbled Purple Stripe hardnecks, but very reliable and versatile for all cooking uses from fresh salsas and aioli to long-cooked soups, stews, and roasted garlic. The primary virtues of Polish White are reliability (excellent performance in a wide range of climates), productivity (high-yielding compared to hardneck types), and outstanding storage life of 10–12 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark) — making it the garlic of choice for those who want a year-round supply from a single fall planting. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Polka Raspberry
description: Plant dormant canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and mow all canes to the ground in late winter for the simplest management, since Polka is a primocane type that fruits reliably on first-year wood. Bred in Poland at the Brzezna research institute, Polka is a heavy-yielding fall raspberry known for large, firm, glossy conical berries with a pleasant sweet-tart flavor and good shelf life, making it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. It ripens over a long fall window and holds up well to light rain without excessive fruit softening. Good air circulation and consistent moisture during fruiting help maximize berry size and reduce disease pressure. Matures in 110–140 days from transplant.

name: Pollmix Sea Buckthorn (Male Pollinator)
description: Pollmix is a German-bred male sea buckthorn selection grown specifically to supply pollen for female fruiting cultivars such as Leikora and Titan, since Hippophae rhamnoides is dioecious and female plants set little or no fruit without a nearby male. It bears no berries itself but produces abundant, early-shedding catkins and grows as vigorously as the fruiting cultivars, with the same silvery narrow foliage, thorny branching, and nitrogen-fixing roots that let it thrive in poor, sandy, or coastal soils. One Pollmix plant can pollinate a substantial block of female shrubs, so it is typically planted upwind of the orchard or hedge to aid pollen dispersal. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pollock Avocado (Historic Large-Fruited Florida Avocado)
description: Pollock is among the earliest named avocado cultivars grown commercially in South Florida, a West Indian race selection prized for producing some of the largest fruit of any dooryard avocado, frequently exceeding a pound and a half. The smooth green skin encloses pale, mild, watery-textured flesh with low oil content, characteristic of pure West Indian heritage, and fruit ripens early, generally in mid- to late summer. Because it has no meaningful cold hardiness, Pollock is best suited to true tropical and near-tropical dooryards rather than the colder margins of zone 9. Give it deep, well-aerated soil and consistent moisture during fruit development, but avoid waterlogging, which quickly promotes root rot. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Polyanna Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis. Polyanna was released by the University of Florida in 1998 from a 'Fry' x 'Southland' cross and stands out for its good resistance to fruit rot, a real advantage in the humid Gulf South where berry rot is a constant threat late in the season. The red-black berries are medium to large and self-fertile, so a single vine will set a full crop without a separate pollinizer. Because ripening is late and spread unevenly across the cluster, plan on picking over several weeks rather than in one pass, which actually extends the harvest season for a home vineyard. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Polynesian Arrowroot (Pia)
description: Plant rhizome pieces in humid, tropical or subtropical gardens in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this Pacific island staple grows naturally in coastal and forest-edge habitats from East Africa to Polynesia. The deeply lobed leaves are attractive, and by 6–9 months the underground rhizomes are large enough to harvest; raw rhizomes are bitter and mildly toxic due to tannins and must be grated, washed repeatedly in water, and dried to yield a pure white starch. The fine arrowroot-like starch, called pia in Hawaii and Polynesia, was a critical famine food and is used to thicken sauces and puddings; it is entirely gluten-free and easily digestible. Outside zones 10–12 grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter, maintaining warmth and humidity. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Polynesian Arrowroot / Pia
description: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, organically rich, well-draining soil in a partially shaded location, spacing them 3-5 feet apart to accommodate the large, deeply lobed umbrella-like leaves. Water moderately and consistently through the growing season, allowing the top inch of soil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent tuber rot. The plants go dormant during dry seasons, so reduce water and allow the tops to die back naturally before lifting or leaving tubers in place in frost-free areas. To process tubers for starch, grate and thoroughly wash the flesh through multiple changes of water, then allow the settled starch to dry completely before use as a fine, high-quality thickener. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Polyphant Ornamental Oregano
description: Polyphant is a UK-raised ornamental oregano selection grown chiefly for its striking young foliage, which emerges cream-white and gradually flushes soft pink at the leaf margins before settling toward gray-green, giving the plant a long season of color interest well before the pale pink summer flower clusters appear. It forms a tidy, low mound and is best used at the front of a border, in a rock garden, or trailing over a container edge where the variegation can be appreciated up close. Provide lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or damp conditions weaken the variegation and encourage rot. Shear back after flowering to keep growth compact and to encourage fresh, brightly variegated new foliage. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Polyvert Chives (Uniform Dark Green Culinary Chive)
description: Polyvert is a market-garden chive selection bred for highly uniform, medium-sized, dark green leaves that are slightly thinner than those of comparable field varieties, giving an even, tidy stand well suited to bunching for market or steady cutting in the home garden. Flavor is the standard mild, oniony chive taste, good snipped fresh over eggs, potatoes, or salads. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest by cutting leaves an inch or two above the base, which encourages continuous regrowth through the season. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Pomegranate
description: Pomegranates are self-fertile and thrive in hot, dry conditions with well-drained soil; they tolerate drought but produce sweeter, larger fruit with regular deep watering from bloom through harvest. In zone 7, mulch the root zone heavily and site against a south-facing wall to protect against winter kill. Allow plants to develop as a multi-stemmed shrub or train to a single trunk by removing suckers. Fruit is ready in fall when it turns deep red, sounds hollow when tapped, and the crown (calyx) is prominent. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Pomegranate Crunch Lettuce (Red Romaine)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 8-10 inches; Pomegranate Crunch is a medium-size red romaine bred for a texture between crisp romaine and tender butterhead, with thick, glossy cherry-red outer leaves wrapped around a heart that often blushes pink toward the center. It grows faster and more uniformly than many older red romaines while showing good resistance to downy mildew, making it a dependable choice for gardeners who want striking color without giving up productivity. The balance of sweetness and a light bitter edge suits both whole-leaf salads and Caesar-style preparations. Harvest as a full head once dense, or take outer leaves individually for an extended harvest. Matures in 50–57 days from seed.

name: Pomelo
description: Pomelo is the largest citrus fruit — often the size of a large cantaloupe — and the ancestor of the grapefruit. It is less bitter than grapefruit, with a sweeter, milder flavor, and a very thick pith that insulates the segments. Trees are self-fertile but cross-pollination with another variety increases fruit set. Pomelos require heat to develop sweetness and need a longer season than most citrus — fruit set in spring is ready from October through February of the following year. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually and maintain consistent moisture during fruit development; drought stress during sizing causes dry, pithy fruit. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Ponca Baby Butternut Squash (AAS-Winning Mini Butternut)
description: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing to allow moderate vine spread, and keep soil evenly moist to support a heavy set of small fruit. Developed by breeders at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and named an All-America Selections winner in 2021, this butternut produces compact, single-serving fruit under a pound with tan skin and dense, nutty-sweet orange flesh, bred with organic and small-farm production in mind. Its shorter vines and high fruit count per plant make it productive even in modest garden spaces. Allow fruit to fully harden on the vine before harvest, then cure for improved storage and flavor. Matures in 105–115 days from seed.

name: Ponca Blackberry (High-Sugar Thornless Erect Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the upright canes onto a simple two-wire trellis for support. Released by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Ponca is one of the newer thornless erect blackberry cultivars, notable for exceptionally high sugar content and small seed size that give it outstanding fresh-eating flavor compared to older, tarter cultivars. The compact, upright canes need less trellising than sprawling semi-erect types, and the plant produces a concentrated harvest over a relatively short picking window in early summer. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to make room for the canes that will fruit the following season. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Poncho Avocado (Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Poncho is one of several Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado cultivars bred and trialed for cold hardiness at the northern limit of where avocados can survive outdoors, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. Its selection reflects decades of Texas home-gardener efforts to identify avocado seedlings that survive occasional hard freezes with only minor damage. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pond Apple (Alligator Apple)
description: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; pond apple (Annona glabra) is a native Florida Annona that holds the distinction of being the only member of its genus adapted to flooded, swampy, and periodically inundated soils — growing naturally along the edges of ponds, marshes, and Everglades sloughs where it often forms dense thickets. The round to oval, apple-sized fruits are bland compared to other Annonaceae relatives, with a pale yellow to cream custard-like flesh that is edible but not widely prized for fresh eating; they are consumed by wildlife and occasionally used in preserves or as rootstock for grafting more flavorful Annona species such as cherimoya and soursop. Trees reach 20–40 feet at maturity and produce dense, evergreen canopies well suited to wildlife habitat, riparian buffers, and edible landscape plantings in consistently wet, low-lying sites. Pond apple requires no irrigation once established in suitable wet conditions and is tolerant of brackish water and poor, waterlogged soils. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ponderosa Lemon Tree
description: Ponderosa is a lemon-citron hybrid famous for enormous, grapefruit-sized, thick-skinned fruit with tart, seedy flesh. It is compact and free-fruiting, making it a rewarding container tree for patios and sunrooms. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and keep the graft union above the soil surface. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between waterings, and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9, bring the pot indoors to a bright spot before frost arrives. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ponderosa Red Tomato (Classic Large Red Potato-Leaf Beefsteak)
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake the heavy vine well before fruit sets. Ponderosa Red is a classic American heirloom beefsteak dating to the late 1800s, grown for very large, deep red, meaty fruit with a dense, low-moisture, few-seeded interior that made it a favorite for slicing thick, generous sandwich rounds long before modern hybrid beefsteaks existed. The potato-leaf foliage typical of Ponderosa strains sets it apart visually from regular-leaf tomatoes, and the plant carries a genuinely old-fashioned, rich tomato flavor prized by heirloom growers over the milder taste of many modern varieties. Water evenly to reduce cracking on the large fruit, and support heavily, since individual tomatoes commonly exceed a pound and can snap unsupported branches. Matures in 85–90 days from transplant.

name: Ponkan Mandarin (Chinese Honey Orange, Taiwanese Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ponkan (also called 'Chinese Honey Orange', 'Warnurco', or 'Batangas' in the Philippines) is one of the most widely grown mandarin varieties in the world, dominant in China, Taiwan, Brazil, Japan, and throughout Southeast Asia — though less well known in North America than Satsuma or Clementine types. It produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly flattened, loose-skinned fruits (the skin slips off in large intact pieces much more easily than tighter-skinned mandarins) with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid juice and deeply orange, highly fragrant flesh divided into 10–13 segments with typically few seeds. The flavor profile emphasizes sweetness and intense mandarin aroma more than tartness, making Ponkan distinctively different from the more acid Clementine and Satsuma — excellent for people who prefer very sweet citrus. Ripens November through January in subtropical climates. The tree is medium-large and productive under good subtropical conditions in zone 9–11; it is moderately cold-hardy (tolerates brief temperatures to 26–28°F when established). An outstanding landscape and edible tree for Gulf South gardens. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Poona Kheera Cucumber (Indian Heirloom Color-Changing Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep and provide a trellis for best production; harvest at any stage from white (mild, crisp) to apple-yellow (sweetest, most complex) to russet (mellow, slightly sweet and aromatic); the yellow-to-russet stage is the traditional eating stage in India but many American gardeners prefer the pale yellow stage for fresh salads. Poona Kheera is an heirloom cucumber from the Pune (formerly Poona) region of Maharashtra state in western India, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary cucumber of the region and is still widely available in Indian markets. The most distinctive characteristic of this variety is its remarkable color change through the maturation cycle: young fruits are white or pale ivory, then transition to pale yellow, apple-yellow, golden-yellow, and finally to a warm russet-tan at full maturity — no other commonly grown cucumber goes through such a dramatic color progression. The flavor also changes with color: white fruits are mild, crisp, and relatively bland; yellow fruits have developed characteristic cucumber fragrance, sweetness, and complexity; russet fruits have an almost apple-like sweetness and aroma distinct from young cucumber flavor. In the Indian culinary tradition, the yellow-to-russet stage is preferred for eating raw out of hand, in raitas, and for cooking; American gardeners often prefer the yellow stage for salads where the flavor is sweet and the flesh remains crisp. Poona Kheera has good heat tolerance compared to standard slicing cucumbers and adapts well to Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Poorman Gooseberry (Mild-Flavored American Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch and reduce mildew pressure). Poorman is a long-cultivated American gooseberry hybrid, valued for combining good disease resistance with berries that are sweeter and milder than many European gooseberry cultivars, making them pleasant for fresh eating as well as pies, jams, and preserves. The medium-sized fruit ripens from green to a rosy red-pink blush, and the bush, while still thorny like most gooseberries, is comparatively less vicious to harvest from than many older European types. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on both old and new wood; prune out the oldest canes each winter and thin crowded growth to improve air circulation, since gooseberries are prone to powdery mildew in humid, poorly ventilated plantings. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Popcorn
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for proper wind pollination, isolating from sweet corn to prevent cross-pollination that ruins eating quality. Side-dress with nitrogen at knee-height and again when tassels appear. Leave ears on the stalk past eating stage until husks are completely brown and papery; pull husks back and hang ears in a dry, ventilated spot for 4–6 weeks until kernels release from the cob easily. Kernels are ready to pop when moisture content drops to around 14%. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Popoulu Banana (Hawaiian Cooking-Eating Banana)
description: Popoulu belongs to the same Hawaiian Iholena grouping of Polynesian-introduced bananas and is notable for its orange-tinted flesh and dense, starchy texture even when fully ripe, making it a versatile fruit for both fresh eating and cooking. It grows into a robust, wide-leafed clump similar in stature to Iholena and shares its broad-leaf sensitivity to wind damage. Provide deep, humus-rich soil, full sun, and consistent moisture, and expect a long time to first fruiting from a young pup. Because it is a warm-climate heirloom without special cold tolerance, Gulf Coast growers should reserve it for a sheltered bed or large container that can be protected from hard freezes. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Porcelain Doll Pumpkin (F1 Pink Cinderella-Type Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to give the vigorous vines room to spread. Porcelain Doll is a hybrid Cinderella-type pumpkin producing flattened, deeply ribbed fruit in the 20-24 pound range that shifts from pale yellow to cream and finally to a distinctive soft pink as it fully ripens on the vine. Beneath the showy pink rind lies a thick wall of sweet, dense, edible flesh that holds up well for roasting and pureeing, making this variety popular with both farmstand growers and cooks. Harvest once the rind has fully hardened and colored, then cure for one to two weeks before moving to cool, dry storage. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Pork Chop Pole Tomato
description: Bred by Wild Boar Farms, this true-yellow beefsteak has a sweet flavor with citrus notes and slightly flattened 8 to 12 ounce fruits. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and benefit from sturdy staking. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water evenly to prevent cracking. Let fruit ripen fully to yellow for the sweetest flavor, picking regularly to sustain production. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Porter Tomato (Porter's Pride)
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Porter tomato is a Texas heirloom introduced around 1897–1900 by the Porter & Sons seed company of San Antonio, developed or selected specifically for the demanding conditions of Texas summers — heat, drought, and alkaline soils that would destroy most Eastern varieties. The small to medium (4–6 oz), pinkish-red, slightly oval fruits grow in clusters and have rich, concentrated flavor enhanced by mild water stress. Porter is genuinely drought tolerant and produces in Texas summer heat when standard varieties quit blooming. Historically the most important garden tomato in Central and South Texas, where generations of families grew it through conditions that would kill Brandywine or Cherokee Purple. For any gardener in the hot, dry interior South or Southwest struggling with summer tomato production, Porter is the essential starting point. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Porto Rico Sweet Potato
description: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, slightly sandy soil amended with organic matter in full sun; Porto Rico is one of the oldest named American sweet potato varieties, recorded since the early 1900s and widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, and the Gulf Coast region for generations before the introduction of Beauregard and Covington. The medium-sized, copper-skinned tubers have bright orange, moist flesh with a rich, sweet, creamy flavor — considered by many Southern gardeners to have superior taste to modern commercial varieties. The vining plants spread widely, up to 10 feet, and should be positioned in open areas or at garden edges. Cure harvested roots at 85°F with high humidity for 7–10 days before storage to maximize sweetness and shelf life. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Portola Strawberry (Vigorous UC Davis Day-Neutral Strawberry)
description: Plant on raised, well-drained beds in full sun and feed regularly through the season, since Portola's heavy, near-continuous fruit set draws down soil fertility faster than a typical June-bearer. Released by the University of California, Davis breeding program, Portola is a day-neutral cultivar known for beginning to fruit earlier after planting and producing a notably large early crop compared to older day-neutral varieties, with good-sized, attractive, well-flavored berries throughout the season. It has become a widely grown commercial variety in California for its vigor and productivity, and it performs well for home gardeners willing to keep up with its water and fertility demands. In mild-winter regions it can be planted in fall for a strong spring crop or in spring for summer-into-fall production; renew plantings every one to two years as yields taper off. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Portugal Quince (Large Highly Aromatic Heirloom Quince)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ideally in a warm, sheltered spot; Portugal is an old European heirloom quince long grown in American heritage orchards, prized above most other quince cultivars for its very large, intensely aromatic fruit and, uniquely among quinces, flesh that cooks down to a rosy-red color with a smoother, less gritty texture than most quince varieties — traditionally considered the finest quince for jelly and paste making. It is a somewhat shier, slower bearer than heavier-cropping cultivars like Meech's Prolific or Orange, and performs best with a warm site and attentive care in its early years, but the exceptional fruit quality has kept it in cultivation for centuries despite more productive alternatives. As with all quince, fruit is hard and astringent raw and must be cooked to develop its rich, honeyed, floral flavor. Prune to an open form for good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk, and harvest in fall once fruit turns golden-yellow and is strongly fragrant. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Portuguese Kale (Tronchuda Kale, Couve Tronchuda, Caldo Verde Cabbage)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to well-enriched, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Portuguese kale (couve tronchuda) forms large, loose heads with broad leaves featuring wide white midribs that are milder and more tender than common kale — both the leaf blades and the thick midribs are cooked, the midribs simmered until very tender in the traditional Portuguese soup caldo verde where the leaves are sliced into thin chiffonade with potatoes and chouriço. More heat-tolerant than most kales and excellent in zone 8–10 gardens where it can be grown nearly year-round; harvest leaves from the outside in, leaving the center growing point intact. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Portuguese Pink Rosemary (Upright Pink-Flowered Culinary Rosemary)
description: Portuguese Pink is an upright culinary rosemary similar in size and habit to Tuscan Blue, but distinguished by soft pink flowers marked with darker pink veining instead of the usual blue-violet. The glossy deep-green foliage is fully aromatic and flavorful, making it as useful in the kitchen as any standard rosemary while adding a less common flower color to the herb border. Its tall, dense growth habit lends itself to hedging, topiary, and use as a specimen shrub, much like other large upright rosemary cultivars. Grow it in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune after flowering to maintain a tight form. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Posey Pecan (Historic Thin-Shelled Indiana Native Pecan)
description: Posey traces back to a large native pecan tree that grew on the bank of the Wabash River in Gibson County, Indiana, famous in the late 1800s for its large size and thin shell; the named cultivar was propagated from that tree's seedlings in the early 1900s. It is among the thinnest-shelled of the northern-grown pecans, with a distinctively rough, winged shuck and a vigorous, heavy-bearing tree that develops shaggy, hickory-like bark with age. Posey has performed as a large, vigorous grower in regional Kansas and Missouri variety trials alongside Kanza, and has shown only slight scab susceptibility in those far-northern trial sites, though it has not been widely tested under humid Gulf South disease pressure. Match it with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Possum Purple Passion Fruit
description: Train this vigorous, purple-fruited passion vine onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during dry spells to keep production steady. It is grown for its noticeably better cold tolerance than typical yellow passion fruit selections, often resprouting from the root crown after the top growth is cut back by a freeze. On the Gulf Coast growers mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and treat the vine as a root-hardy perennial that regrows each spring even where hard freezes are common. Ripe fruit, which drops naturally from the vine, has an intensely aromatic, tart-sweet pulp used fresh or for juice. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Possumhaw Holly
description: Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw holly is a multi-season native shrub that blooms with small white flowers in spring attractive to native bees, then develops abundant bright-orange to red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter to provide critical food for cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other frugivorous birds. A male pollinator must be planted nearby for fruiting; nurseries often sell named female selections (Warren's Red, Council Fire) paired with a male. Tolerates the periodic flooding and clay soils common to Gulf Coast lowland sites. Exceptional as a wildlife garden shrub, in rain gardens, and along creek margins. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Possumhaw Viburnum (Smooth Witherod)
description: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum (also called smooth witherod) is a native shrub of swamp margins, streambanks, and wet coastal plain forests that provides one of the most remarkable fall berry displays of any native shrub. The berry clusters ripen in stages through August–November, with individual berries changing from apple-green to blush-pink to rose to blue-black on the same cluster simultaneously — creating a stunning multi-colored mosaic of color that extends for weeks. The berries provide essential fall nutrition for migrating and resident birds. The glossy, deep green leaves turn burgundy-red in fall. The cultivar 'Winterthur' is particularly floriferous and berry-laden. Plant in rain gardens, bog borders, or any consistently moist location. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Pot Marjoram (Turkish Oregano, Cretan Oregano)
description: Propagate from stem cuttings or divisions in spring; plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — pot marjoram is a Mediterranean native that dislikes heavy, moist soils and grows best in conditions similar to its native rocky hillside habitats. Origanum onites is distinct from both sweet marjoram (O. majorana) and common Greek oregano (O. vulgare subsp. hirtum), occupying a middle flavor ground between the two: it is more aromatic and peppery than sweet marjoram but less aggressively pungent than the intense Greek species used on pizza. In Turkish and eastern Mediterranean cooking it is the standard 'kekik' (thyme/oregano) used on meat, in köfte, on lahmacun, and in herb blends; the white to pale pink flowers in summer are smaller than many oregano species. Hardy only to about 5–10°F (zone 7); treat as an annual or pot plant in cooler climates. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Pot-a-peno Pepper (Compact Container Jalapeño, AAS Winner)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into a large container or garden bed after danger of frost has passed. Pot-a-peno was bred specifically to solve a common problem with growing jalapeños on a patio or balcony — most jalapeño varieties grow too large and sprawling for small containers — by combining a genuinely dwarf, compact plant habit with full-sized, full-flavored jalapeño fruit and strong productivity. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining container-friendly size with reliable yield and classic jalapeño heat and flavor, unlike many ornamental dwarf peppers bred for looks rather than culinary use. Fruits mature from green to red if left on the plant, with red fruits noticeably sweeter and slightly hotter than green. Because the plant is so compact, it benefits from a slightly richer potting mix and more frequent watering and feeding than an in-ground pepper, since a small root zone dries out and depletes nutrients faster. Harvest fruits at the green stage for classic jalapeño flavor or let them ripen to red for a sweeter, smokier heat, useful for chipotle-style drying. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Potato Onion
description: Plant individual bulbs 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile soil — large bulbs planted in fall will multiply into a cluster of 8–12 medium onions, while small bulbs tend to produce fewer but larger bulbs. Potato onions are a multiplier onion type that propagates entirely by bulb division, forming a cluster of bulbs in the same way shallots do; no seed is needed or typically produced. Allow tops to fall over and begin to yellow before harvesting the entire cluster; cure in a warm, airy spot for 2–3 weeks. Save the smallest bulbs from the cluster for replanting, perpetuating the variety indefinitely without seed purchases. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Potomac Hazelnut (Gellatly Hybrid Filbert)
description: Potomac is one of the Gellatly-bred hybrid hazelnuts developed in British Columbia from crosses between cold-hardy American hazelnut and larger-nutted European hazelnut, part of the same historic breeding effort that produced Bixby and Faroka. It has been valued mainly as parent stock in later cold-climate hazelnut breeding programs rather than as a widely sold orchard cultivar, though it remains available through specialty nut nurseries. Site it as a multi-stemmed shrub in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer for reliable nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Potomac Pawpaw (Productive Peterson Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun at fruiting age; Potomac is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected by breeder Neal Peterson for dependable, heavy production alongside good flavor and size — a combination that has made it a popular choice for growers who prioritize consistent yield in a home or small-orchard planting. The rich, custardy flesh has the classic pawpaw flavor profile reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard, best eaten fresh once the fruit yields to gentle thumb pressure and has developed full aroma. As with all pawpaws, Potomac is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and full fruit set. Pawpaws thrive as an understory tree when young, so give newly planted trees light shade for the first year or two before they adjust to more direct sun, and provide steady moisture through establishment. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Potomac Pear
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune out any blighted shoots well below visible discoloration as soon as they appear. Potomac came out of the same USDA fire blight resistance breeding effort that produced Blake's Pride and Sunrise, and it is valued for producing a larger, more Bartlett-like fruit than most of the other resistant selections from that program, with good flavor for fresh eating and canning. Give it a compatible mid-season pollinizer, since it is only partially self-fruitful. Harvest while the fruit is still hard and green-yellow, then ripen it indoors for the best dessert texture. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Pound Sweet Apple (Pumpkin Sweet, Giant New England Baking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pound Sweet, also called Pumpkin Sweet for its large, rounded, greenish-yellow fruit, is an old New England heirloom grown for exceptionally large, mild, sweet apples with dense, coarse flesh that holds its shape and flavor beautifully when baked whole, a traditional preparation that takes full advantage of both the apple's size and its low acidity. Unlike sharper cooking apples that need added sugar, Pound Sweet's natural sweetness makes it a classic choice for simple baked apple desserts and old-fashioned New England apple dishes calling for a mild, sugary apple rather than a tart one. The tree is notably cold-hardy, reflecting its New England origins, and reliably productive; harvest in fall once fruit reaches full size and color. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Powder Blue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Heavy-Bearing Gulf South Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil at the same depth as the nursery container; mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Do not fertilize with standard garden fertilizers — use acid-specific fertilizers (ammonium sulfate or azalea/camellia formulas). Powder Blue is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium virgatum, formerly classified as V. ashei) released in 1978 by North Carolina State University — one of the most widely planted and highest-yielding rabbiteye varieties across the Southeast. Rabbiteye blueberries are the blueberry species native to the Gulf South — the wild Vaccinium virgatum grows naturally throughout the coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana — and they are dramatically better adapted to the heat, humidity, and acidic sandy soils of the Gulf South than the northern highbush blueberries that dominate the commercial blueberry market. Powder Blue produces very large berries for a rabbiteye — medium-firm, light blue (giving the variety its name), with a mild, sweet flavor. The late-season ripening (July in zone 8–9) means Powder Blue fills the end of the Gulf South blueberry season after earlier-ripening varieties have peaked, extending the household fresh blueberry window into midsummer. Established rabbiteye plantings (plants reach bearing age in 3–5 years and can remain productive for 30–50 years) are highly cost-effective long-term investments for Gulf South home fruit gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Powderblue Blueberry (Productive Mid-Season Rabbit-Eye Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Powderblue is one of the most widely planted and highly regarded rabbit-eye blueberry varieties — producing large, light-blue to sky-blue, firm berries with excellent flavor and good fresh-eating and processing quality on a vigorously productive, heat-adapted bush that is among the most reliable blueberry types for zone 9 conditions. Rabbit-eye blueberries (Vaccinium virgatum, also classified as V. ashei) are the blueberry type most naturally adapted to the Gulf South — native to the coastal plain and Piedmont of the southeastern US, rabbit-eye varieties tolerate heat, drought, clay soils, and the region's soil conditions better than northern highbush types and are generally more productive and longer-lived in zone 9 landscapes. Powderblue is mid-season to mid-late season (June in zone 9), ripening after the early southern highbush varieties (Emerald, Jewel) and extending the blueberry harvest season. The vigorous, upright to spreading bushes reach 6–10 feet at maturity — larger than southern highbush varieties but very productive and long-lived, with established Powderblue bushes commonly producing for 30–50+ years. As with all blueberries, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) is essential — rabbit-eye varieties may tolerate slightly higher pH than southern highbush but still require highly acidic conditions for nutrient availability and healthy growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Powderblue Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Powderblue is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry valued for its vigorous, upright, disease-resistant growth habit and dependable, heavy production of firm, small-to-medium, powder-blue berries with excellent shelf life and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and freezing. It ripens mid-to-late season, several weeks after Climax and Premier, helping extend the rabbiteye harvest window into July in most Gulf Coast plantings. The upright, vigorous canes tend to sucker less than some rabbiteye varieties, keeping the planting tidier, and the bush shows good tolerance of the humid, disease-prone conditions typical of southeastern summers. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through fruit development, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer at bloom and again after harvest. Zone 6–9. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prague Citrandarin (Cold-Hardy Mandarin-Trifoliate Orange Hybrid)
description: Prague is one of a small group of citrandarins USDA breeders produced by crossing cold-hardy trifoliate orange with mandarin to push edible citrus further north than pure mandarins can survive. The small, tart, seedy fruit is more useful for juice, ade, or marmalade than fresh peeling, and the tree carries the trifoliate parent's semi-deciduous habit and light thorns. Grow it as a curiosity for pushing the cold edge of dooryard citrus in the Gulf South, siting it in a warm microclimate and protecting young trees for their first few winters. Established trees tolerate hard freezes that would kill a standard orange or mandarin outright. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Dawn American Persimmon (Early-Ripening Seedless Claypool Selection)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Prairie Dawn sets a crop on its own but bears more heavily with a second American persimmon or a known male tree planted nearby for cross-pollination. Bred by Illinois hobbyist Jim Claypool under the designation H55A, Prairie Dawn was selected for cold hardiness well beyond what most Southern growers need, but that same toughness translates into vigorous, dependable growth and disease resistance through the long, humid summers of zone 7-9. It is one of the earliest-ripening American persimmon cultivars, coloring up by late September with large, seedless, orange-yellow fruit that is sweet and firm rather than watery. Prune annually to hold the naturally tall tree to a manageable 12 feet or so, since it can reach 20 feet or more if left alone, and expect the first meaningful crops within two to three years of planting a grafted tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Fire Crabapple
description: Prairie Fire is an ornamental crabapple that puts on a spectacular show of magenta spring blossoms followed by fiery fall foliage and small persistent fruit that feeds birds. Disease-resistant and adaptable, it makes a durable landscape tree for cold and temperate gardens. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, and enjoy the tiny fruit as wildlife forage or for jelly. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Flameleaf Sumac (Texas Sumac, Limestone Sumac)
description: Plant in full sun in alkaline, rocky, well-drained limestone or caliche soil; prairie flameleaf sumac (Rhus lanceolata) is the primary sumac of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, a large shrub to small tree with narrow, willow-like leaflets that turn brilliant flame-red in fall — one of the best fall color plants native to Texas and the Gulf Coast. The small, densely clustered red berries can be used to make a tart sumac lemonade or dried and ground as a spice, and are a critical winter food source for birds across the Gulf Coast. Exceptionally heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and adapted to the shallow, alkaline limestone soils of central and south Texas where other plants struggle. Provides dense thicket habitat for wildlife and butterfly larval host for several species. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Gem American Persimmon (Tender-Fleshed Seedless Claypool Selection)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in average to well-drained soil; Prairie Gem produces fruit on a single tree but crops more heavily with a second American persimmon or a male seedling nearby to complete pollination. A sibling selection to Prairie Dawn from Jim Claypool's Illinois breeding work, Prairie Gem carries the same exceptional cold hardiness but ripens its light orange, seedless fruit slightly later, typically in the early-to-mid fall window. The tender, sweet flesh softens to a texture much like a ripe tomato when ready to eat, and trees are notably free of the pests and diseases that trouble many other fruit species in humid Southern gardens. Keep it pruned to about 12 feet for easy harvest, since Prairie Gem will otherwise grow taller, and expect bearing to begin within two to three years of setting out a grafted tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Ground Cherry
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant to a dry, sunny location with sandy or well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. This compact native perennial produces small, sweet-to-tart yellow berries enclosed in papery husks that ripen from midsummer through fall. It is notably more drought-tolerant than tomatillo or cape gooseberry and thrives on neglect once established. Plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies, making them a productive and low-maintenance addition to dryland food gardens or prairie restoration plantings. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Onion
description: Plant bulbs in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; prairie onion is a native North American allium of the central prairies and upper South, producing attractive spherical clusters of rose-pink to lavender flowers in late summer when few other bulbs bloom. All parts are edible — bulbs, leaves, and flowers — with a mild onion flavor used by Plains indigenous peoples as a wild food and flavoring. The upright, flat leaves emerge in spring, provide texture through summer, and the flowers appear in August and September when hummingbirds and late-season butterflies are active. It is both a functional edible garden plant and a beautiful native wildflower for dry, sunny prairie or meadow gardens. Increases steadily by bulb division and self-seeding. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Sun American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Early-Ripening Claypool Selection)
description: Prairie Sun, designated Claypool A-33, is a cold-hardy American persimmon selection bred by Jim Claypool and rated hardy to roughly -25F, well beyond the needs of most Southern growers but a mark of the tree's overall vigor and reliability. It is self-fertile, setting abundant crops of seedless, firm, yellow-orange fruit without a second tree, though fruit is astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point it turns sweet and flavorful. Prairie Sun is one of the earlier-ripening American persimmon selections, with harvest typically beginning in late September to October, and the tree can be kept compact at 10-12 feet with regular pruning. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a wide range of soils with minimal care. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prairie Turnip (Tipsin, Breadroot)
description: Sow in very well-drained, lean, prairie-type soil in full sun; prairie turnip (tipsin, breadroot) is one of the most important food plants of the North American Plains tribes — a critical starch staple for the Lakota, Blackfoot, Comanche, and many other Plains peoples, who harvested, dried, and braided the turnip-like starchy roots for winter storage. The roots, which resemble parsnips with a brown outer skin and white starchy interior, were eaten raw, boiled, roasted, or ground into flour. Lewis and Clark documented trading for them with the Mandan people. The plant itself is small and unobtrusive — a low-growing perennial with gray-green, divided leaves and small clusters of lavender-blue pea flowers in late spring. The root can reach 2–4 inches in diameter and 4–8 inches in length on mature plants. As a nitrogen-fixing legume of the dry prairie, it improves lean, poor soils. An important plant for food forest, edible prairie, and cultural heritage gardens and for ecologically-minded gardens on the Great Plains. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Prairifire Crabapple (Disease-Resistant Purple-Foliage Deep Pink-Red Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Prairifire bears deep pinkish-red flower buds that open to vivid dark pink-red flowers, one of the most saturated colors in the genus, followed by small, glossy dark red-purple fruit that persists into winter as a food source for birds. New foliage emerges reddish-purple before settling to a bronze-green, adding a further color dimension. It is among the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a standard recommendation from extension services across the country. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Praying Hands Banana (Fused-Finger Novelty Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Praying Hands is a novelty banana whose individual fingers fuse together in pairs along most of their length, opening only at the tips, so each fused pair resembles a pair of hands pressed together in prayer. The fruit itself is sweet and fully edible, similar in flavor to a standard dessert banana, but it is grown chiefly as a talking-point specimen for its unusual form rather than for volume production. Plants have the typical bold, tropical Musa acuminata habit and need the same rich, moist soil, full sun, and heavy feeding as other dessert bananas to fruit well. Cold tolerance is limited, so in zone 9 grow it in a large container that can be sheltered over winter, or provide substantial protection to the rhizome if planting in the ground, since a hard freeze can kill the below-ground growing point outright rather than allowing simple resprouting. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Precoce Migoule Chestnut (Early-Ripening European-Japanese Hybrid)
description: Precoce Migoule is a vigorous French hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut, discovered at an orchard near Brive-la-Gaillarde and prized for ripening its medium-to-large, glossy nuts up to two weeks ahead of Colossal and other later hybrids. That early harvest lets growers in shorter-season regions get a crop in before fall frost damages burs still on the tree, and the tree is also a heavy, well-timed pollen source for other sativa-type cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since a single chestnut tree will not produce nuts. Harvest in early-to-mid fall as spiny burs split open and nuts drop free. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Prelude II Okra (Short-Season Hybrid)
description: Prelude II is a hybrid okra bred to set pods reliably in shorter, cooler growing seasons where classic Southern heirloom okra often struggles to mature a full crop before fall's first frost. Its compact, earlier-flowering plants begin producing spineless green pods notably sooner than tall heirloom types, making it a practical option for northern gardens and short-summer regions that still want a real okra harvest. Soak seed overnight before sowing to speed germination in cool spring soil, and harvest pods every one to two days at two to three inches for the most tender texture. Because the plant stays shorter and more compact than traditional Southern varieties, it tolerates closer spacing and needs less staking in exposed sites. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Prelude Raspberry (Very Early Cold-Hardy Summer-Bearing Red Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, and support upright canes with a trellis or wire system. Prelude was bred at Cornell University's New York research station for exceptionally early ripening, opening the summer raspberry season days to weeks ahead of most other floricane (summer-bearing) varieties, a genuine advantage for gardeners eager for the first fresh raspberries of the year. The medium-sized, firm, richly flavored red berries are borne on vigorous, cold-hardy canes well suited to northern growing conditions. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest each summer to make room for new cane growth, and thin canes to the strongest four to six per foot of row for the best fruit size and air circulation. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Preludio Florence Fennel
description: Preludio is an early-maturing hybrid Florence fennel bred to size up quickly into smooth, glossy white bulbs while resisting the premature bolting that plagues fennel sown in lengthening spring days. Its speed makes it a favorite for the first fennel planting of the season, when growers want a harvestable bulb well before summer heat sets in. The flesh is crisp and mildly sweet with the characteristic anise flavor, equally good raw in salads or roasted. Choose Preludio specifically for early-season plantings where bolt resistance and a short days-to-maturity window matter most. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Premier Beach Plum (Plum Island Named Beach Plum Selection)
description: Site in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun and plant beside a different named beach plum cultivar, since seedling beach plum stands and single clones fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Premier was selected on Plum Island, Massachusetts, during the early-to-mid 20th-century burst of interest in developing beach plum as a commercial New England crop, and it was long regarded as one of the best-flavored named selections available, though it is more prone to brown rot than some of its contemporaries. Its fruit ripens in late summer to a deep purple color prized for jams, jellies, and the traditional Cape Cod and Long Island beach plum preserves. As a true coastal native shrub, it withstands salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soil that would stress or kill most other fruiting plants, and light pruning after flowering is enough to keep it productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Premier Blend Kale
description: This blend mixes Dwarf Blue Curled, Dwarf Siberian Improved, Lacinato, and Red Russian kale for a range of colors, textures, and flavors. Harvest baby greens in about 25 days or let plants size up for full leaves. Sow directly in cool soil and thin as they grow, picking outer leaves so plants keep producing. Frost sweetens the flavor, making it a great fall and winter crop. Matures in 25–60 days from seed.

name: Premier Blueberry
description: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.0) amended with pine bark, peat, or sulfur; Premier is an early-to-mid-season rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1978, valued particularly for its very large berry size — among the largest of the rabbiteye types — and excellent fresh-eating flavor. Berries are light blue, mild, sweet, and ripen from late May through June in zone 8–9. The spreading, vigorous plant is one of the more open-canopied rabbiteye varieties, giving better air circulation that reduces disease problems. Premier is a perennial favorite for u-pick operations and home gardens in the Gulf Coast South because the large berries are showy and harvest quickly. Fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or cottonseed meal) in early spring and again in late spring; avoid high-nitrogen applications after July. Prune to remove crossing branches and old unproductive wood after the third year of growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Premier Loquat (Florida Premier Loquat, Gulf Coast Orange Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil, avoiding heavy clay or areas where water stands; Premier loquat blooms in October–November and ripens fruit in February–April in zone 9–10; thin fruit clusters to 4–6 per cluster for better-sized fruit; harvest when skin is fully golden-orange and slightly soft; store refrigerated for up to 2 weeks. Premier is the principal commercial loquat variety of Florida and one of the most reliable fruiting loquats for the Gulf Coast region, selected by the University of Florida extension system for its consistent performance in Florida's hot, humid, subtropical climate. The fruits are medium to medium-large, rounded to slightly pear-shaped, with warm orange to golden skin and orange flesh that is sweet, mildly acidic, and typically richer-flavored than Champagne (which is milder and more delicate). The variety bears consistently and prolifically in the Florida and Gulf Coast climate — more reliably than many California selections that may be adapted to a drier summer climate — and is the standard recommendation from UF IFAS Extension for home and commercial loquat production in Florida. Premier trees are moderately vigorous, reaching 15–20 feet at maturity, and are considered one of the best-adapted loquats for the humid subtropical conditions of zones 9–10 including the Gulf South, Louisiana, and coastal Texas. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Premier Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Premier is the standard early-season rabbiteye blueberry for zone 7–9, producing large, light blue, mildly flavored berries beginning in late May in most Gulf Coast plantings — up to 3 weeks before mid-season varieties. The upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet with age and are among the most productive of the early-season rabbiteyes. The berries have a larger size than most other early varieties but a thinner skin than mid-season types; harvest promptly after coloring to prevent skin softening. Premier has a chilling requirement of approximately 350 hours, making it reliable in zone 8–9 without the risk of premature bloom during January warm spells. Cross-pollinates well with Brightwell, Climax, Centurion, and Tifblue. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Premium Crop Broccoli (AAS-Winning Classic Hybrid Broccoli)
description: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Premium Crop, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, has remained a benchmark hybrid broccoli for decades, prized for exceptionally large, dense, uniform blue-green central heads and reliable heading even under variable growing conditions that can cause other broccoli to head poorly. After the main head is harvested, the plant produces a useful flush of smaller side shoots, extending the harvest for several more weeks. Cut the central head while buds are still tight and before any yellow flowers show, and keep harvesting side shoots as they develop. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Premium Late Flat Dutch Cabbage
aliases: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Premium Late Flat Dutch'
description: Start indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, giving plants extra room since this is one of the larger-headed cabbages. Premium Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom line prized for its very large, flattened, blue-green heads that can reach ten pounds or more and hold together tightly rather than splitting. Its long time to maturity and dense, thick leaves make it an excellent late-season crop for slaw, kraut, and cold storage, where whole heads keep for months in a cool root cellar. Because of its size, allow it a full, uninterrupted season of growth and avoid crowding neighboring plants. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Prescott Fond Blanc Melon (White-Bottomed French Cantaloupe)
aliases: Cucumis melo var. cantalupensis 'Prescott Fond Blanc'
description: Start seed indoors in short-season regions or direct sow into warm soil after frost, spacing vines generously to allow good air circulation and reduce fungal disease pressure. Prescott Fond Blanc is a traditional French market melon named for its deep, warty ribbing and the pale, creamy patch, or fond blanc, where the fruit rests on the ground as it ripens. The orange flesh is dense, sweet, and highly perfumed, and the variety has long been prized in Provençal markets as one of the most flavorful of the old French cantaloupe types. Harvest when the stem begins to crack and separates cleanly from the fruit, the classic slip stage that signals full sweetness. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: President Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Classic Green Zucchini)
description: President was one of the first hybrid zucchinis to combine early vigor with a long, productive harvest window, and it remains a benchmark against which newer hybrid zucchinis are still compared. The upright, semi-open plant carries glossy, dark green, cylindrical fruit that stay tender even a bit past the ideal 6-8 inch harvest size, giving gardeners more forgiveness than many modern types. Its reliable, heavy set makes it a solid choice for gardeners who just want zucchini without babying a temperamental variety. Keep fruit picked regularly to prevent the plant from slowing production. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: President Plum (Late-Season English Dessert Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. President is a classic English European plum valued for ripening notably late in the season, well after most other plums have finished, which extends the fresh plum harvest into early fall for home orchards growing several varieties. The large, deep purple-blue fruit has firm, greenish-yellow flesh with a good sweet-tart balance, holding its texture and quality well both for fresh eating and for cooking and preserves. The tree is reliably productive and the firm-fleshed fruit keeps and handles better than many earlier, softer-fleshed plum varieties, making President a practical choice for gardeners who want to stretch the plum season and have fruit that travels well from tree to kitchen. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Preston's Prolific Fig
description: An English heirloom selected for reliability in cool, short-season climates, Preston's Prolific produces medium-sized, brown-purple fruit with sweet amber flesh and is prized for setting a dependable breba crop even where summer heat is limited. Plant in full sun against a south-facing wall or in a warm microclimate to maximize ripening in marginal areas, and mulch the root zone well for winter protection. It fruits readily on both old and new wood, so light annual pruning to remove crossing branches is usually all that's needed. This cultivar is a good choice for gardeners in cooler temperate regions who want fruit without a heated greenhouse. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Priam Apple (Scab-Immune Disease-Resistant French Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Priam is a French-bred apple carrying genetic immunity to apple scab, one of the most damaging and widespread apple diseases, particularly troublesome in humid climates where standard varieties require regular fungicide applications to produce clean fruit. The medium-sized, red-blushed fruit has crisp, juicy, well-balanced flesh suitable for both fresh eating and cooking, and while it may not match the absolute peak flavor of the finest dessert apples, its dramatically reduced spray requirements make it an attractive option for organic growers and home gardeners wanting to minimize chemical inputs. As with other scab-immune apples, some resistance can erode with new scab races over time, so continued monitoring is worthwhile even on a genetically resistant tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Price Almond (Soft-Shell California Pollinizer Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety with overlapping bloom time is planted nearby. Price is a California almond selected in the Ne Plus Ultra lineage, producing a similar long, slender, soft-shell kernel with good sweet flavor, and it has historically been planted as a reliable pollinizer partner for other soft-shell varieties in mixed orchard plantings. The tree is a consistent producer, and its soft shell makes for easy hand-cracking, a practical advantage for home orchardists processing a home harvest without commercial equipment. Water deeply through the growing season, especially during summer kernel fill, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer to early fall, drying nuts thoroughly before storage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prickly Water Lily
description: Direct sow Euryale ferox seeds in warm, still, shallow water in full sun; press seeds into heavy clay loam at the pond bottom or in sunken aquatic pots, spacing plants 5–10 feet apart to accommodate the enormous leaves; fertilize with aquatic tablets monthly for maximum leaf and seed production. The Prickly Water Lily is an annual or short-lived perennial aquatic in the Victoria family, native to southeastern Asia from India to Japan — the only species in its genus. Its enormous spiny floating leaves (up to 5 feet across, dark green above and deep purple-red below), covered in sharp prickles on both surfaces, are among the most dramatic of all aquatic plants. The seeds — dried and popped to make makhana (fox nuts) — are a prized crop in the Mithila region of Bihar and widely consumed across India, Nepal, and China for their high starch content and nutty flavor. In warm climates, the plant grows extremely fast and can form a dense, nearly impenetrable floating mat; harvest seeds in late summer as seed pods ripen and begin to sink. In zone 8, it may self-sow from seeds that overwinter in pond mud; in zone 10–12, it may behave as a short-lived perennial. Matures in 120–180 days from seed.

name: Pride of Wisconsin Melon (Queen of Colorado Muskmelon)
description: Start seeds indoors a few weeks ahead of the last frost to give this melon a head start in shorter growing seasons, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. Originally sold as 'Queen of Colorado' in the early 1920s before being reintroduced under its current name in 1937, this heirloom produces oval, 4 to 8 pound melons with apricot-orange flesh that is notably sweet with little of the musky aftertaste typical of many muskmelons. It was long grown as a market melon for Milwaukee before nearly disappearing from trade, and it remains valued today for good powdery mildew tolerance. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Priestly Atemoya (Large-Fruited Cold-Tolerant Older Cultivar)
description: Priestly is an older atemoya cultivar prized for producing very large, heart-shaped fruit with a bumpy, thick-skinned rind and dense, creamy flesh carrying the classic atemoya flavor profile of custard, vanilla, and pineapple. It bears less consistently than the widely planted Gefner, so growers should plan to hand-pollinate flowers with a small brush during the brief evening window when they are receptive in order to get a worthwhile crop.
