Its main claim to relevance for Gulf Coast gardeners is a reputation for handling cooler temperatures somewhat better than many other atemoya selections, which can matter in zone 9a where winter cold snaps are the main limiting factor for growing Annona successfully outdoors. Harvest when the fruit's skin segments begin to separate slightly and the green color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature indoors for several days before eating. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prilop Pecan (Historic Scab-Resistant Texas Native Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby. Prilop originated as a native pecan seedling growing along the Lavaca River south of Halletsville in Lavaca County, Texas, and was propagated and preserved by grafters after the original tree was destroyed in a 1940 flood; it is sometimes also found under the names Steffek or Kallus after growers who helped keep the selection in circulation before wood was sent to the USDA-ARS pecan collection. Like many Texas native-type selections, Prilop produces a smaller nut than large modern commercial cultivars but is notably scab-resistant, an important trait for low-spray home orchards in the humid Gulf South, and it was recognized as a Texas Pecan Show state champion native selection. It remains a solid, low-maintenance choice for East Texas and similar Gulf Coast growing conditions, though it is generally considered less productive overall than higher-yielding modern releases like Caddo or Oconee. Correct zinc deficiency with a spring foliar zinc spray and water deeply during nut fill in late summer for the best kernel development. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Prima 1216 Pawpaw
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons before exposing them to full sun. Prima 1216 is one of the oldest named pawpaw selections still in commerce, originally chosen from wild Michigan trees by pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis decades before the modern named-cultivar boom, and it remains valued for early, reliable ripening and consistent, medium-sized fruit with mild, smooth-textured flesh. It tends to bear at a younger age than many other named selections, making it a good anchor tree for a new pawpaw patch. Interplant with a genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Wabash for cross-pollination, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom if fruit set seems light in early years. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Prima Donna Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Prima Donna is a southern highbush blueberry selected by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery for its combination of high fruit quality and strong plant vigor in warm-climate conditions. The medium-large berries are firm, flavorful, and sweet with a pleasant balance of sugar and acid that makes them superior for fresh eating. Prima Donna's primary advantage is a high-quality, consistent fruit that stores and ships better than softer varieties — the firm texture retains quality for 2–3 weeks under refrigeration, significantly longer than some other southern varieties. In zone 9 home gardens this means less pressure to consume the harvest immediately after picking. Prima Donna is popular in commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast precisely because the firm berries withstand handling by customers without bruising. The plant habit is vigorous and upright, producing good yields without excessive vegetative growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Ark 45 Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Prime-Ark 45 is the premier primocane-fruiting blackberry for the Southeast from the University of Arkansas, producing very large (among the biggest primocane-fruiting blackberries), firm, sweet, intensely flavored berries on both first-year (summer) and second-year (spring) canes. The fruit quality is significantly higher than earlier primocane blackberry releases — larger, firmer, sweeter berries that are excellent for fresh eating and hold well after harvest. Prime-Ark 45 is thorny, unlike the thornless Prime-Jan, but the superior fruit quality compensates for the harvesting difficulty. The number '45' in the name refers to internal University of Arkansas breeding program designation. In zone 9 the fall primocane crop matures in August–September when few other berries are available, providing fresh blackberries in a season gap that no other easily-grown small fruit fills. The spring floricane crop in May–June follows the standard blackberry season timing. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Ark Freedom Blackberry
description: 'Prime-Ark Freedom' is the first thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry, capable of bearing very large berries on first-year canes. It offers an early summer crop on floricanes and a late-summer-to-fall crop on new primocanes. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, and support the canes on a trellis in windy locations. In hot climates the fall crop yields the sweetest fruit when temperatures moderate; soft-tip the primocanes to boost lateral fruiting. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Ark Horizon Blackberry (Extended-Season Primocane-Fruiting)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Prime-Ark Horizon is the newest primocane-fruiting blackberry from the University of Arkansas breeding program, meaning that unlike traditional blackberries it fruits on the current season's new canes in addition to the usual second-year floricanes, extending the harvest window into fall. It produces larger fruit with a good sugar-to-acid balance and was bred to push the primocane fruiting season later than the earlier Prime-Ark releases. Because it retains thorns, unlike Prime-Ark Freedom and Prime-Ark Traveler, handle canes with care and consider glove use during pruning and harvest. To get both a summer floricane crop and a fall primocane crop, leave some canes unpruned; for a fall-only crop, mow all canes to the ground in late winter. Matures in 200–365 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Ark Traveler Blackberry (Thornless Machine-Harvestable Primocane Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and provide a sturdy trellis, since this vigorous primocane-fruiting cultivar produces fruit on first-year canes in addition to the traditional second-year floricane crop. Bred by the University of Arkansas specifically for firmness that withstands mechanical harvesting and shipping, Prime-Ark Traveler also performs well as a home-garden thornless blackberry, producing a first crop on primocanes in late summer and fall in addition to the normal early-summer floricane harvest. Because it fruits on both first- and second-year wood, pruning decisions affect which crop you prioritize: cutting all canes to the ground in winter sacrifices the floricane crop but still allows a fall primocane harvest, while leaving some canes standing provides both crops. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Jan Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Prime-Jan is a University of Arkansas thornless erect blackberry notable for its primocane-fruiting (fall-bearing) character — unlike conventional blackberries that produce fruit only on second-year canes (floricanes), Prime-Jan produces fruit on first-year canes in late summer and fall (August–September) as well as a conventional floricane crop in spring (May–June). This dual-cropping habit provides two distinct harvest windows per season, approximately doubling the period of fresh blackberry production from a single planting. The primocane crop in late summer fills the gap between the spring blackberry season and fall, when no other thornless erect blackberries are producing. In zone 9 both crops ripen reliably, and the late-summer primocane crop avoids the rush of the spring berry season when many other fruits are also ripe. The fruit quality is comparable to other University of Arkansas erect varieties — medium to large, sweet-tart, jet-black berries with good flavor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Prime-Jim Blackberry (Original Thorny Primocane-Fruiting Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil and provide a simple wire support for the upright, thorny canes. Released in 2004 alongside Prime-Jan by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Prime-Jim was the first primocane-fruiting (fall-bearing) blackberry cultivar ever developed, a genetic breakthrough that made possible the later thornless Prime-Ark series. It produces two crops from one planting: a conventional floricane harvest in early summer and a second primocane harvest on new canes in late summer and fall. Remove all canes to the ground after the fall harvest if only the primocane crop is wanted, or leave canes standing over winter to also collect the following spring's floricane crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Primrose Gem Green Santolina (Compact Pale-Yellow Lavender Cotton)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Primrose Gem' forms a neat, rounded mound of bright emerald-green, feathery foliage studded in midsummer with soft primrose-yellow button flowers, staying noticeably more compact than the straight green santolina species. Its tidy size makes it well suited to low edging, gravel gardens, and rockeries where a larger santolina would overwhelm the scale. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent the bare, woody centers that develop on neglected plants. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Primus White Currant
description: Primus is a classic Dutch white currant selection valued for its long, evenly filled strigs of translucent, pale gold berries with a milder, less acidic flavor than red currants. It is largely self-fertile and productive on a compact, upright bush, making it a good choice for smaller garden beds or espalier training. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and prune out the oldest wood each winter to maintain strong new fruiting shoots. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prince Albert Rhubarb (Historic Early English Rhubarb)
description: Set crown divisions into rich, deeply dug soil in early spring, positioning the growing bud level with or just below the soil surface. Mulch around, but not over, the crown to conserve moisture and suppress weeds while the plant establishes. Prince Albert is one of the oldest named rhubarb cultivars still in cultivation, dating to the early nineteenth century in England and named for the consort of Queen Victoria, and it is notable for pushing up some of the earliest stalks of the season. Its early, tender pink-red stalks made it historically popular for the first forced rhubarb of spring, and it remains valued by heirloom growers for its long cultivation history and reliable early cropping. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prince Charles Serviceberry (Early-Blooming Hybrid Serviceberry)
description: Patented from a plant found at the University of Wisconsin Arboretum, Prince Charles is a densely branched serviceberry selection notable for opening its full flush of white flowers before the leaves unfold, giving a cleaner, more concentrated bloom display than typical seedling serviceberries. Bronze-purple emerging foliage matures to green through summer and shifts to yellow, orange, and red in fall, while the sweet purple-black June berries are quickly stripped by birds if not netted or picked early. It can be grown as a large multi-stemmed shrub or limbed up into a small single- or multi-trunk tree, and performs best in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade. It combines well with other spring-flowering natives in a woodland-edge or mixed border planting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prince Rupert Lemon Geranium (Vigorous Upright Scented Pelargonium)
description: Prince Rupert is a historic, strong-growing lemon geranium cultivar dating to the eighteenth century, distinguished from the species by larger, more coarsely crinkled leaves and a more vigorous, upright habit that quickly fills out into a substantial sub-shrub. The crushed foliage releases the same clean, true lemon fragrance prized in lemon geranium generally, used to flavor sugars, cakes, and teas, but Prince Rupert's bigger leaves make for faster, more generous harvests than the species type. Root stem cuttings in a well-drained mix or plant container specimens in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates a bit more shade than most pelargoniums but flowers and grows most vigorously with several hours of direct sun. In zones 9-11 it persists outdoors as a woody perennial; elsewhere grow it in a container and bring it indoors to a bright window before frost, pinching regularly to keep its vigorous growth in a manageable, bushy form. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Prince William Serviceberry (Compact Suckering Shadblow)
description: Prince William is a compact, bushy, suckering selection of shadblow serviceberry that stays well under the size of the straight species, making it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller shade gardens. It is self-fertile and produces unusually heavy crops of sweet, blue, blueberry-like fruit that ripen in early summer and are excellent fresh, baked, or left for birds. Bronze-toned new growth matures to green and finishes the season in a mix of yellow, orange, red, and purple. Give it moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade for the best flowering and fruit set, and thin out excess suckers periodically if a tighter clump is desired. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prince's Feather Amaranth
description: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; amaranth is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant grain crops available and requires little supplemental water once established. Amaranthus hypochondriacus was one of the three staple crops of Aztec civilization (along with maize and beans), consumed as grain in porridge and flatbreads (tamales de alegría) and in ritual religious offerings to Huitzilopochtli; the Spanish conquistadors banned its cultivation as part of their campaign against Aztec religion, contributing to the decline of amaranth as a staple food. The grain is nutritionally exceptional — 14–18% protein with a balanced amino acid profile including lysine — and is now being rediscovered as an important gluten-free alternative grain. The dramatic tall stems with enormous, feathery, dark-red to magenta to gold plumes are visually spectacular in the garden and support abundant seed for birds in autumn. Matures in 75–100 days from seed.

name: Princess Diana Serviceberry (Compact Hybrid Serviceberry with Brilliant Fall Color)
description: Princess Diana is a hybrid serviceberry cultivar selected for clean, disease-resistant foliage and some of the most vivid red-orange fall color of any Amelanchier selection, often outperforming Autumn Brilliance in cooler climates. Clusters of white flowers open in early spring before the leaves, followed by small, sweet, blueberry-flavored fruit in early summer that is quickly taken by birds if not netted. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; its somewhat more compact, rounded habit suits smaller landscapes better than larger serviceberry types. It requires minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing branches after bloom. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Princess Kay Flowering Plum (Double-Flowered Canada Plum)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil where its extreme cold hardiness can be put to use in far northern landscapes that cannot support most other flowering plums. Princess Kay was discovered as a wild sport with fully double flowers in Itasca County, Minnesota, by Catherine Kay and Robert Nyland, and was released by the University of Minnesota in 1986 as an ornamental selection of the native Canada plum. Unlike the species and unlike fruiting native plum cultivars, it produces no fruit and needs no cross-pollinator, since its double, fragrant white flowers that age to pale pink are sterile; the tradeoff is an exceptionally showy, weeks-long spring bloom set off by smooth blackish bark. Because it is a Canada plum selection, it tolerates winter cold to roughly -40 degrees Fahrenheit that would kill most other ornamental flowering trees. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Princess Persimmon
description: Plant Princess Persimmon in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; minimal pruning needed — mainly to shape; the tiny fruits persist through winter and are best left for ornamental effect and wildlife. Diospyros rhombifolia is a gem of the East Asian ornamental plant palette — a compact, slow-growing tree or large multi-stemmed shrub that transforms dramatically in autumn. The tiny round persimmon fruits (barely 0.5 inch across) ripen to vivid orange-red and are produced in such abundance that entire branches become festooned with bright baubles, creating one of the most spectacular ornamental displays of any small tree in the autumn and early winter garden. The fruits are technically edible once fully ripe and soft — very sweet, but seedy and small — though most gardeners leave them for wildlife and ornamental effect. Autumn foliage also turns attractive shades of red-orange before leaf drop, leaving the brilliant fruit display on bare branches well into winter. An excellent subject for container growing, bonsai, and small garden spaces where a larger persimmon tree would be impractical. Dioecious (male and female plants separate) — fruiting plants are female; ensure at least one male plant is within pollination range for reliable fruit set. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Principe Borghese Tomato (Prince Borghese)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Principe Borghese is the traditional Italian tomato for sun-dried tomatoes, a compact determinate vine bearing enormous clusters of small (2–3 oz) plum to egg-shaped fruits with thick dry flesh, thin skin, few seeds, and very low moisture content — the characteristics that make it ideal for halving and drying in the sun or dehydrator. The variety's name refers to the Borghese family of Rome who historically grew them on terraced hillsides; the dried product is intensely flavored and chewy. It bears all at once in a concentrated flush, making it excellent for large-batch canning and preserving as well. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Prinz Celeriac (German Smooth-Skinned Bolt-Resistant Celery Root)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile soil; Prinz is a German-bred celeriac valued for producing rounded, smooth, light-skinned globes that clean up easily compared with the rougher-skinned older varieties, with dense, firm, pure white interior flesh. Its strong resistance to premature bolting makes it more forgiving of an early start under row cover or plastic than most celeriac, while it also performs reliably as a later, unprotected planting. The flavor is a clean, nutty, concentrated celery essence, equally good raw and grated into rémoulade or cooked into soups, purees, and roasts. As with all celeriac, keep the soil evenly moist throughout the long growing season and remove small side roots from the developing globe to encourage a smooth, well-formed root. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Priscilla Apple (Scab-Resistant Early PRI Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Priscilla was introduced in 1972 by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program and rates very resistant to apple scab while also resisting fire blight and cedar apple rust, letting a home orchard get by with little or no fungicide spraying. The medium-sized, red-striped fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall. As one of the earlier disease-resistant apple releases, Priscilla helped establish the case that good disease resistance and good eating quality did not have to be a trade-off. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prisma Shallot
description: Prisma is a modern Dutch shallot cultivar bred for uniform, copper-skinned, round-to-oval bulbs and dependably heavy yields, making it one of the more widely available shallots in the commercial seed trade. Plant sets shallowly in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a tight cluster of several bulbs by midsummer. Keep the bed evenly moist during active growth and taper off watering once the foliage begins to yellow and topple over. Cure the harvested cluster in a warm, airy, shaded spot for a couple of weeks before separating and storing, where well-cured Prisma bulbs keep respectably for a shallot, typically several months. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Pristine Apple (Early Disease-Resistant Yellow Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois program, Pristine is immune to apple scab and shows good resistance to fire blight and powdery mildew, making it a dependable low-spray choice for an early crop. The clear yellow, medium-sized fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh best enjoyed fresh soon after picking, since it does not store as long as the program's later-season siblings. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's harvest window well before fall apples come in. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prize Choy Pak Choi
description: Prize Choy is an open-pollinated pac choi tracing back to Alf Christianson Seed Company breeding from an era when major companies still maintained open-pollinated Asian brassica lines. It forms vase-shaped, 15-18 inch plants with celery-like white stems and tender, glossy green leaves, and is notably uniform and slow to bolt for an open-pollinated type. Grow it as a substitute for napa cabbage in stir-fries and soups, harvesting whole heads at full size or picking outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again baby crop. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Prizehead Leaf Lettuce
description: This heirloom leaf lettuce dating to at least 1881 forms large, loose green leaves with bronze-red margins and an upright habit. Slow to bolt with good heat tolerance, it offers a tender texture and mild sweet flavor. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist. Harvest outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop, and shade lightly in summer heat to prolong the harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Prizehead Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Prizehead is a classic American heirloom looseleaf lettuce developed by W. Atlee Burpee Company in the 1880s and still widely grown for its exceptional flavor and striking red-bronze tipped leaves. The large, frilly, bright green leaves are broadly and dramatically tipped in red-bronze to burgundy at the leaf edges, creating a distinctly two-toned effect that makes Prizehead one of the most ornamental of all heirloom lettuces and an enduring favorite in kitchen gardens. The flavor is superb — mild, tender, and buttery with a crisp texture that surpasses many newer commercial varieties in taste trials — and the quick maturity (45–55 days to full size) allows it to be harvested before summer heat arrives. The frilly, slightly ruffled leaf texture holds dressings well. In zone 9 Prizehead is equally at home in spring and fall gardens; the red tips intensify in cooler weather and provide the most dramatic color in fall plantings. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Prizetaker Leek (Lyon Prizetaker, Heirloom)
description: Prizetaker, also sold as Lyon Prizetaker, is an English heirloom leek dating to the 1880s that was bred for exhibition size, producing some of the thickest, tallest shanks of any leek variety while staying remarkably tender for its bulk. Give it wide spacing and rich, deeply worked soil so roots have room to support the plant's large stature, and hill soil progressively around the base through the season to blanch a long white shank. Its dark green leaves and pure white, solid base have made it a favorite for county-fair and garden-show exhibitors for over a century, but it performs equally well as a substantial main-season leek for the kitchen. Because it needs a long growing season to reach full size, start it early and expect a later harvest than quick early-season types. Matures in 110–135 days from transplant.

name: Prizewinner Pumpkin (Prize Winner Giant Pumpkin Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors a few weeks before the last frost to maximize the growing season, then transplant into deeply enriched soil with generous room for the vines to sprawl, thinning each plant down to a single developing fruit for maximum size. This F1 hybrid giant pumpkin was bred for exhibition growers chasing very large fruit, with mature specimens commonly reported in the 100 to 300 pound range under attentive feeding and watering. Its smooth, glossy orange rind and classic rounded pumpkin shape make it as suitable for display as it is for competition. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Prizm Kale (AAS-Winning Compact Tender Kale)
description: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Prizm is an All-America Selections-winning kale bred for a compact, dense, more uniform habit than older kale varieties, with tender, tightly curled, blue-green leaves that hold good quality and mild flavor even as the plant matures. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to containers and smaller garden beds, and the tender texture requires less cooking time than some older, tougher kale cultivars, making it popular for salads as well as cooked greens. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production, and like other kale, flavor sweetens after light frost in a fall crop. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Procimequat (Dwarf Ornamental Limequat-Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Procimequat was bred by crossing Eustis limequat with Hong Kong kumquat (Fortunella hindsii) to combine tart lime flavor with the tiny, ornamental fruiting habit of the wild kumquat parent. The naturally dwarf plant is a triploid, so it rarely if ever sets viable seed, but it flowers and fruits abundantly regardless, covering itself in small, pale orange, marble-sized fruit useful more for pickling, garnish, and ornamental interest than fresh eating. Keep it in a container of well-drained citrus mix in full sun and bring it under cover during hard freezes, since this rare hybrid is grown almost entirely by citrus collectors rather than commercial growers. Light, frequent feeding with citrus fertilizer through the growing season keeps the compact plant productive. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Profusion Chives (Sterile Non-Seeding Ornamental Chive)
description: Plant divisions in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Profusion produces an exceptionally heavy, long-lasting flush of pale purple pompom flowers over slender, mild-flavored leaves, without the risk of unwanted self-seeding that troubles many chive plantings, since the flowers are sterile and set no viable seed. Its extended bloom period makes it as valuable for pollinator gardens and cut-flower use as for the kitchen, and clumps stay tidy rather than spreading into surrounding beds. Harvest leaves regularly by snipping from the outer edge of the clump to encourage fresh, tender growth. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Profusion Sorrel (Sterile Non-Flowering Perennial Sorrel)
description: Profusion is a naturally occurring sterile selection of garden sorrel that never bolts to flower or set seed, so all of the plant's energy stays in leaf production and it can only be increased by dividing an established clump. Plant divisions in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in early spring, spacing them roughly a foot apart in a permanent bed since the plants are long-lived perennials. Because it never diverts energy into flowering, Profusion keeps producing tender, fleshy, mildly tart leaves later into summer heat than seed-grown sorrel, which typically turns tough and bitter once it sets flower stalks. Harvest outer leaves continually through the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants. Matures in 45–60 days from transplant.

name: Progress #9 Shelling Pea
description: This heavy-producing heirloom shelling pea, also called Laxton's Progress #9, fills each 5 inch pod with 7 to 9 plump, sweet peas. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep evenly moist for good pod fill. The compact vines need little support. Harvest when pods are rounded and full but still bright green, shelling promptly for the freshest flavor. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Progress No. 9 Garden Pea (Laxton's Progress Classic English Wrinkled Shell Pea)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart; thin to 2–3 inches. Support with short twiggy branches or a low string trellis. Shell pods when plump and round; do not allow to over-mature. Progress No. 9 (also called Laxton's Progress or simply Progress) is a classic English garden pea with a history in British kitchen gardens extending back to the work of Thomas Laxton, the 19th-century English plant breeder who made significant improvements to pea varieties through systematic cross-breeding. The variety produces heavy yields of large, dark green, round pods containing 6–9 large, sweet, wrinkled peas — the wrinkled seed (rugose type) is a characteristic of sweeter, higher-sugar garden peas versus the smoother seeds of field peas, and Progress No. 9 exemplifies the sweet, tender, wrinkled-pea style. The semi-dwarf habit (18–24 inches) makes Progress No. 9 more manageable in home gardens than the tall pole peas like Alderman (Telephone) that require 4–5 foot trellises, while still producing full-sized, well-filled pods of excellent quality. Progress No. 9's early maturity (60–68 days) is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the window between suitable pea-growing temperatures and summer heat is brief — earlier-maturing varieties like Progress complete their harvest before heat stress arrives. Matures in 60–68 days from seed.

name: Prok American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)
description: Plant a bare-root or container-grown tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; American persimmon develops a long taproot, so set young trees carefully and avoid transplanting older ones. Prok is a well-known named selection of the native American persimmon valued for its unusually large fruit for the species, along with reliable, heavy, self-fertile production that does not require a second tree for pollination. Orange fruit ripens in fall and is intensely sweet and rich once fully soft-ripe, but astringent and unpalatable if eaten before that point, so wait until fruit is soft to the touch or has dropped naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and a wide range of soils once established, needing little care beyond occasional watering during establishment and removal of root suckers that can form a thicket if left unchecked. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Prolific Hardy Kiwi
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade and train onto a sturdy trellis or pergola, since vines are vigorous twiners that live for decades. Prolific lives up to its name as a heavy, dependable bearer of smooth, grape-sized, edible-skinned fruit with a sweet flavor high in vitamin C, and unlike most hardy kiwi it can set fruit without a male pollinizer, though a nearby male still boosts yield. Like all Actinidia arguta it is far more cold-hardy than fuzzy kiwi, tolerating winter lows well below what would kill Actinidia deliciosa outright. Pick fruit while still slightly firm in late summer to fall and finish ripening at room temperature for the best flavor and to avoid losses to birds. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Prolific Hardy Kiwi
description: Prolific is a self-fertile, cold-hardy hardy kiwi bearing sweet, grape-size fruit with smooth green skin you can eat whole, no peeling required. Train the vigorous vine onto a strong trellis or arbor in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Water consistently during the growing season and prune in winter to control its rampant growth and encourage fruiting spurs. Fruit typically arrives two to three years after planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Prolific Pawpaw (Heavy-Bearing Named Pawpaw Cultivar)
description: Plant in partial shade while young, since pawpaw seedlings and young trees are naturally understory plants that scorch in full sun, and transition the tree to more sun as it matures and begins bearing. Prolific is one of the longer-established named pawpaw cultivars grown for grafted orchards, valued less for exceptional fruit size than for its dependable, heavy annual crops of medium fruit with good flavor, making it a useful workhorse variety in a mixed planting. Like all pawpaws it needs cross-pollination from a genetically distinct cultivar to set a full crop, since a pawpaw's own pollen rarely fertilizes its own flowers well, so plant it alongside a different named variety or seedling tree flowering at the same time. The maroon, unpleasant-smelling flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, and hand pollination with a small brush can improve fruit set in a planting with poor natural pollinator visits. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Prolific Sapodilla
description: Grow in full sun on deep, well-drained soil that can be sandy, rocky, or calcareous; 'Prolific' is valued by South Florida growers chiefly for its dependable, heavy annual crops of small to medium round fruit rather than for exceptional size. The grainy tan flesh has the classic malty, brown-sugar sweetness typical of good sapodilla selections, and the tree bears at a relatively young age for a grafted cultivar. Because it sets fruit so heavily, thinning is rarely needed but trees benefit from occasional light fertilization during the growing season to sustain production. Like other sapodilla cultivars it is highly drought- and wind-tolerant once established and is best reserved for zone 10-11 or the warmest protected pockets of zone 9b, since young wood is damaged below the low 30s F. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Proso Millet (Broomcorn Millet)
description: Drill or broadcast seed 1/2 in deep at roughly 20–25 lb per acre in home-scale rows and thin to 4–6 in; proso millet germinates quickly in warm soil and produces an open panicle of seed in just 60 days, making it practical even in short-season gardens above zone 4. Harvest entire stalks when the lower seeds are hard and the panicle begins to droop; hang bundles upside-down over a tarp for 2 weeks to finish drying. Thresh by beating bundles against the inside of a barrel and winnow outdoors; the hull is loose and comes free with light rubbing in warm water. Proso millet is gluten-free and has the lowest water requirement of any grain crop. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Prospera Basil (Downy-Mildew-Resistant Genovese-Type Basil)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Bred through conventional breeding to carry strong resistance to downy mildew, Prospera keeps the familiar large-leaved, classic sweet flavor and growth habit of Genovese basil while standing up far better to the humid conditions that favor mildew outbreaks in traditional pesto basil. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushy growth and harvest whole stems above a leaf node, removing flower buds promptly to keep the leaves tender. Its disease resistance makes it a strong choice for humid Gulf South gardens where standard Genovese basil often declines by midsummer. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Prosperosa Eggplant (Round Violet Italian Heirloom)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Prosperosa is a traditional Italian heirloom producing large, round to oval fruit in deep violet-purple with faint pale striping near the calyx, and dense, creamy, mild-flavored flesh well suited to grilling, roasting, and classic Italian preparations like eggplant parmesan. Plants are vigorous and productive, often needing staking to support the weight of the large fruit, and perform reliably through a long, hot growing season. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since overripe fruit develops a bitter edge and coarser seeds. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Prostrate Rosemary (Trailing Rosemary)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; prostrate rosemary is the trailing, spreading form of rosemary that grows horizontally rather than upright, producing long, cascading stems that hug the ground or spill dramatically over walls, retaining walls, raised beds, and the lips of containers. The culinary use, flavor, and aromatic quality are identical to upright rosemary, but the growth habit is fundamentally different — prostrate rosemary reaches 1-2 feet tall and spreads 3-6 feet wide in a flowing groundcover form, making it an outstanding choice for erosion control on sunny slopes, as a cascading element in large containers, or as a low-water groundcover between stepping stones. Flowers are typically a deeper blue-violet than many upright forms and are produced freely from fall through spring in mild climates, providing nectar for honeybees and native bees during the cooler months. The salt tolerance makes it particularly valuable in coastal landscapes where few other herbs thrive. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Provence Lavandin (Sweet Culinary-Grade Lavandin)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil, spacing plants generously to allow for its broad, mounding size. Provence is a lavandin hybrid (a cross between English lavender and spike lavender) selected for a sweeter, less camphorous fragrance than the widely grown Grosso, making it one of the preferred lavandin cultivars for culinary use, sachets, and light perfumery where a purer floral scent is wanted. Its long, gracefully arching flower spikes hold pale lavender-blue blooms and, like other lavandins, it inherits better heat and humidity tolerance from its spike lavender parentage than pure English lavender, making it a more forgiving choice for Gulf South gardens. Shear spent flower spikes after bloom to prevent the plant from becoming woody and sprawling, and harvest stems just before flowers fully open for the best fragrance and flavor. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Provence Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy French Sweet-Tart Pomegranate)
description: Provence is a French pomegranate selection grown for its combination of good cold hardiness and consistently sweet-tart, well-balanced fruit, making it a useful choice at the cooler edge of pomegranate country. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils well, though even moisture during fruit development improves size and reduces splitting. Fruit is medium-sized with a reddish-pink rind and juicy, pink-red arils that ripen in early-to-mid fall. Prune out dead or crossing wood in late winter and remove root suckers to maintain a single- or multi-trunk shrub form suited to home garden spacing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Provence Quince Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince. A long-used traditional French quince selection, it has historically served as a dwarfing rootstock for pear, producing a tree slightly larger than the more common Quince A or Quince C rootstocks while still offering good precocity and size control compared to seedling pear rootstocks. As with other quince rootstocks, many pear varieties are graft-incompatible with it, so an interstem of a compatible pear variety is often bench-grafted between the Provence rootstock and the desired scion. It is hardy to about -10°F, suiting it to zones 6 through 8. Graft or double-work a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and reserve it for growers wanting a somewhat larger tree than Quince A or BA29 provide. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Provence Thyme (Provençal Thyme)
description: Provence is a selected culinary thyme grown for its high proportion of thujanol in the essential oil, giving a rounder, fruitier, less medicinal flavor than ordinary common thyme, which is why it is prized specifically for herbes de Provence blends. It grows into a broader, more sprawling woody mound than upright French thyme, with wiry intertwining stems and small grey-green leaves. Shear back hard after the spring flowering flush and again in late summer to prevent the center from opening up and going woody, and replace plants every three to four years as vigor declines. Because it forms a wider mat than most culinary thymes, it also works well cascading over a raised bed edge or low wall. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Providence Sweet Corn (Disease-Resistant Bicolor TripleSweet Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Providence is a bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with supersweet-level sugar content, bred with disease resistance including tolerance to bacterial mottle, a bacterial disease that can streak and discolor kernels in warm, wet conditions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on sturdy stalks over a main-season 82-day maturity. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best results. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Provider Bean (Cold-Tolerant Dependable Bush Snap Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep; Provider is one of the most widely grown and recommended bush snap bean varieties in the United States — a 1965 release that has remained a cornerstone home garden and commercial variety for 60 years due to its combination of reliable production, consistent quality, and unusually cold-tolerant germination. Provider's ability to germinate reliably in cooler soils (down to about 50°F, compared to the 60°F minimum for most beans) allows it to be planted 1–2 weeks earlier than standard beans in spring and later into fall, giving it a significant practical advantage for extending the bean season in both directions. The round, medium-length (4–5 inch), dark green pods are harvested when young and tender and have clean snap-bean flavor — honest, straightforward, and pleasant rather than refined. A vigorous, upright bush habit requires no staking and produces heavily over a 2–3 week period per planting; successive sowings every 2–3 weeks provide continuous harvest. Provider has been the standard reliable bush bean against which others are compared — not glamorous, but dependable, productive, and universally adaptable from the earliest spring planting to late fall production in virtually any vegetable garden climate. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Provider Bush Bean
description: Provider is an early, dependable bush snap bean valued for germinating well in cooler soil and adapting to a wide range of climates. It sets straight, stringless, tender pods with good flavor in a heavy early flush. Direct sow after frost, or slightly earlier than most beans since it tolerates cool soil, in full sun. Pick pods young and often to keep the plants producing over several weeks. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Pruden's Purple Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil. Pruden's Purple was saved by William Pruden of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina and entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1980s; it is a large, indeterminate, potato-leaved (smooth, undivided leaf form, as in Brandywine) beefsteak tomato producing very large (12–24 oz), flattened, lobed, dusky rose to purple-pink fruits with dense, meaty, sweet, complex flesh with the rich, full tomato flavor characteristic of the best pink beefsteak heirlooms. Many tomato growers consider Pruden's Purple slightly more productive and reliably earlier than Brandywine Sudduth while producing nearly identical flavor; the two make excellent companions in the garden. Days to maturity of 65–80 from transplant make it one of the earlier large beefsteak heirlooms. A consistently excellent performer in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Précoce d'Argenteuil Asparagus (Classic Early French Heirloom)
description: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, forgoing any harvest in the first year to build the root system. Précoce d'Argenteuil is a classic 19th-century French heirloom named for the asparagus-growing town of Argenteuil near Paris, historically prized for thick, tender spears with purple-tinged tips that emerge notably earlier in spring than most varieties, giving the earliest asparagus harvest of the season. Because it is an open-pollinated variety rather than a modern all-male hybrid, yields run lower than modern hybrids and plantings include both male and female plants, with the females producing red berries in summer that should be removed before they scatter volunteer seedlings through the bed. It remains popular with heirloom growers and in traditional French cuisine for its rich, distinctive flavor; harvest spears once they reach 6–8 inches by snapping or cutting at soil level. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Puerto Rico Okra (Tall Tropical Heirloom Okra)
description: Puerto Rico okra is a striking tropical heirloom that towers over most garden okra, often reaching 8-12 feet in a long, warm growing season, with correspondingly large leaves and pods that need to be picked young to stay tender. Give it plenty of room and rich soil, since the plant puts substantial energy into its height and canopy before pods come on in quantity. It thrives in the long, hot, humid summers of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, where shorter-season okra varieties can start to slow down in peak heat. Choose it as a dual-purpose plant, since the tall, leafy stand also works as a temporary summer privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Puerto Rico Sweet Potato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, slightly acidic, moderately fertile sandy soil — sweet potatoes require loose soil for the roots to expand and develop properly; Puerto Rico was the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States for much of the 20th century, and under various synonyms ('Southern Queen', 'Vineless Puerto Rico') it formed the backbone of American sweet potato production in the Southeast, where it became the foundation of Southern sweet potato cuisine. The moist-flesh, orange sweet potato familiar as a Thanksgiving side dish, sweet potato pie filling, and candied yam is essentially the Puerto Rico type — the moist, sweet, orange-fleshed character that most Americans think of as the defining sweet potato quality. The large, uniform, blocky-to-slightly-tapered roots have deep orange skin and vivid orange flesh with an intensely sweet, moist, smooth texture after curing and baking. Puerto Rico is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions and produces very large yields in zone 9's long, warm growing season with minimal care. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Puget Gold Apricot (Pacific Northwest Maritime Apricot)
description: Site trees against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available to maximize summer heat and ripening in cool coastal climates. Puget Gold is self-fertile and was developed at Washington State University's Puyallup research station specifically to succeed where most apricots fail in the region's damp, late springs, thanks to a later bloom period that dodges frost and better tolerance of humid growing conditions. Fruit is medium-large, golden-orange, and freestone with good flavor for a cool-summer climate. Thin fruit after the natural June drop to improve size and reduce limb stress. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pulasan (Kapulasan, Wild Rambutan)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained tropical soil; pulasan (Nephelium ramboutan-ake) is a close relative of rambutan (Nephelium lappaceum) native to the Malaysian peninsula, producing clusters of oval, red fruits with short, thick, blunt protuberances (versus rambutan's long, flexible hairs) — distinguishing it from rambutan at a glance. The white, translucent, sweet, juicy flesh is widely considered sweeter and better-flavored than rambutan, and the seed of pulasan is also edible (unlike rambutan's bitter seed) — roasted or boiled with a flavor similar to cocoa or almond. A premium tropical fruit rarely available commercially outside Southeast Asia; highly prized by tropical fruit collectors. Requires high humidity, consistent moisture, and no frost. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Pulverulenta Elderberry
description: Pulverulenta is a Victorian-era heirloom elderberry grown purely for its striking foliage, which appears dusted or marbled with fine white speckling across each leaflet, giving the whole shrub a frosted, variegated look distinct from any other elder in cultivation. It is noticeably slower-growing and less vigorous than green- or purple-leaved elderberry cultivars, so it rarely needs the aggressive annual cutback other ornamental elders require, and it still produces the flat white flower clusters and small black berries typical of the species. Give it some afternoon shade and steady moisture, since the pale leaf tissue is more prone to sunburn and drought stress than fully green foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Pumpkin
description: Sow 3–4 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in deeply worked, compost-rich soil once soil temperature is at least 65°F, then thin to the 2 strongest seedlings. Large-vined types need 6–10 feet of space per plant; choose bush types for smaller gardens. Place a piece of cardboard or straw under developing fruits to prevent rot. Harvest when the shell is fully orange, the rind is hard throughout, and the stem has begun to dry and cork. Matures in 75–120 days from seed.

name: Pumpkin on a Stick Ornamental Eggplant
description: This 1800s ornamental eggplant produces clusters of small, ribbed fruits that look like tiny pumpkins, prized for fresh and dried fall arrangements. Grow it like eggplant, starting seeds indoors early and transplanting into warm, sunny soil. The fruits ripen from green to orange-red on sturdy branching plants. Cut stems when the little fruits color up, and hang to dry for lasting decorations. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Punarnava (Red Spiderling, Spreading Hogweed)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; punarnava spreads readily by seed and can naturalize in warm climates. Boerhavia diffusa (punarnava or red spiderling) is a tropical prostrate or spreading perennial herb found throughout the tropics and subtropics of India, Africa, Asia, and the Americas — simultaneously one of the most widespread tropical 'weeds' and one of the most important medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine. In Ayurveda, punarnava ('the one that renews the body') is one of the top-ranked diuretic, liver-protective, and kidney-supporting herbs, with documented clinical studies supporting its hepatoprotective (liver-protective) and anti-inflammatory effects. The leaves are also eaten as a pot herb in India and West Africa — boiled like spinach, with a mildly mucilaginous texture and bland-earthy flavor. The plant produces tiny, attractive, magenta-pink flowers throughout the warm season, followed by small, glandular, sticky seeds. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, punarnava is a low, spreading, self-seeding herb that naturalizes readily in disturbed areas and lean soils. It tolerates drought and poor soils that few other herbs can survive. The red-stemmed spreading growth creates a soft, groundcover-like effect in dry garden areas. An important herb for those interested in Ayurvedic herbal practice. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Puntarelle (Catalogna Chicory, Asparagus Chicory)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and thin to 18–24 inches; puntarelle is a treasured Italian winter vegetable from the Lazio region, prized for its hollow, asparagus-like inner shoots that emerge from the center of the large chicory head. After harvest, the shoots are shaved or sliced thin, soaked in cold water to curl and reduce bitterness, and served raw in the classic Roman preparation with anchovy-garlic-lemon dressing. The outer leaves are also edible and mildly bitter in the chicory style. Sow in late summer for fall and winter harvest — in zone 8–10 this is an excellent late-season crop that matures when few other vegetables are producing. The plant is a biennial that sends up a tall flower stalk in its second spring; grow as an annual for the best eating shoots. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Puntarelle Chicory (Catalogna Chicory, Asparagus Chicory)
description: Direct sow in late summer in rich, well-drained soil; thin to 12–18 inches once established. Puntarelle is the Italian Catalogna-type chicory grown for its distinctive hollow, asparagus-like inner shoots that emerge from the crown in fall and winter and are the centerpiece of the classic Roman winter salad — thin strips of the shoots are soaked in cold water to curl them, then tossed with a pungent anchovy, garlic, and olive oil dressing in one of Rome's most iconic dishes. The outer leaves are cooked like bitter greens or braised, while the inner shoots and their hollow stems (the puntarelle themselves) are harvested by cutting just above the root crown. In warm-climate gardens (zones 8–11), puntarelle is an outstanding cool-season crop that fills the winter vegetable gap when few other greens are available. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Punting Pole Bamboo
description: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Bambusa tuldoides is a clumping bamboo that does not run — safe to plant in most garden settings without rhizome barriers; water deeply in establishment and regularly during shooting season for maximum edible shoot production. Bambusa tuldoides (Punting Pole Bamboo, Canton Bamboo, or Greenstripe Bamboo) is a medium to large, fast-growing, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to Taiwan and southeastern China (Guangdong, Fujian), widely cultivated across subtropical Asia and naturalized in many tropical regions. The culms are straight, thin-walled, and lightweight — traditionally harvested as punting poles for river transport in Guangdong and as construction material, scaffolding, and utility poles — yet flexible and strong. The spring shoots are among the most commercially important edible bamboo shoots in China, produced in large quantities as an important culinary ingredient. Bambusa tuldoides performs reliably as an ornamental landscape bamboo in zones 8–11, forming dense, attractive clumps 15–35 feet tall with glossy, dark-green foliage. Considerably smaller and more garden-appropriate than B. oldhamii while still producing excellent edible shoots. Excellent as privacy screen, windbreak, and edible bamboo grove plant for Gulf Coast and similar warm subtropical gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Purple Apple Berry
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub as support; Billardiera longiflora is a light, delicate twiner that does not require heavy support — it weaves through shrubs naturally and benefits from an organic mulch layer to keep the root zone cool and moist. Billardiera longiflora (Purple Apple Berry or Climbing Blueberry) is a dainty, evergreen, twining vine native to cool, moist forests and mountain gullies of Tasmania, Victoria, South Australia, and New South Wales, where it climbs through the understory layer on fences and shrubs to produce small, nodding, narrowly bell-shaped, pale greenish-yellow to cream flowers in spring and early summer, followed in autumn by oblong, shiny, deep-purple berries roughly the size and shape of a large olive. The berries are entirely edible and were a prized bush food of southeastern Aboriginal peoples — sweet, slightly glutinous, with a mild, pleasant flavor reminiscent of a mild grape-berry combination. Billardiera longiflora is well-suited to cool-temperate and mild-temperate gardens in zones 8–10, thriving in sheltered, partially shaded positions in moist, well-drained, organically enriched soil. An excellent choice for cool-climate cottage gardens, shaded fences, and native wildlife gardens attracting insects and small birds. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple Beauty Bell Pepper
description: Purple Beauty is a striking heirloom bell pepper with thick-walled, four-inch fruits that ripen from green to a deep glossy purple, then to red if left longer. The crisp, mild flesh is as ornamental as it is tasty. Start seed indoors well before the last frost and transplant into full sun once nights are warm. The compact plants suit containers; harvest at the purple stage for color or leave to sweeten fully. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Beauty Bell Pepper (AAS-Winning Dark Purple Blocky Sweet Bell Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at 78–85°F; transplant after last frost. Compact plants do not require staking. Harvest peppers at full purple color for best appearance. Purple Beauty is a 1990 All-America Selections-winning bell pepper — a fully blocky, 4-lobed, medium-large sweet bell pepper that matures to a deep purple-violet color rather than the standard red, yellow, or orange of typical bell pepper types. The purple coloration comes from anthocyanin pigments produced in the skin (not the flesh, which remains pale green-white), and the purple color intensifies as the pepper approaches maturity, creating one of the most striking visual effects in the summer garden among vegetables. Purple Beauty is frequently planted in ornamental-edible garden designs and kitchen garden borders where the dark purple fruits contrast dramatically with the green plant and with neighboring yellow and orange peppers. The flavor is standard sweet bell pepper — no heat, with a clean, slightly grassy-sweet taste similar to green bell peppers (purple bell peppers are harvested at the same maturity stage as green bells in terms of flavor development). Purple Beauty's compact plants (18–24 inch) set fruit heavily and are among the earlier-maturing bell peppers, making them well-suited to short-season gardens and zone 9 spring plantings before summer heat affects fruit set. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Beauty Pepper (Sweet Purple Bell Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors under grow lights or a warm sunny window 6–8 weeks before the last frost, and harden off before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. Pick fruit at the deep purple stage for a mild, crisp bell flavor, or leave on the plant to ripen fully to red for a sweeter finish. Purple Beauty is a compact, high-yielding bell pepper cultivar that produces blocky, medium-sized fruit that emerges green, matures to a glossy deep purple, and eventually ripens to bright red if left on the plant, giving gardeners three color and flavor stages from a single planting. The eye-catching purple stage retains crisp texture and holds up well raw in salads or on a crudité tray, and the plants tend to be sturdy and productive in home garden conditions across a wide range of climates. Because purple pigment can fade to green when cooked, Purple Beauty is best showcased fresh. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Purple Beauty Sweet Pepper
description: This bell pepper shifts from creamy lime to deep purple and finally red, with a contrasting lime-green interior that is both ornamental and tasty. The compact, very early plants adapt to many climates. Start seeds indoors and transplant into warm soil in full sun. Pick peppers at the purple stage for color or let them redden for sweetness, and water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Bergamot
description: Plant in moist to average, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; purple bergamot is a natural hybrid monarda occurring where the ranges of scarlet beebalm (M. didyma) and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa) overlap, producing intermediate flowers in rich purple-lavender tones. The plant is more vigorous and mildew-resistant than pure M. didyma in many gardens and produces large, showy whorled flower heads that are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, ruby-throated hummingbirds, and fritillary butterflies. The bergamot fragrance of the crushed leaves is distinctive and pleasant. Spreads by rhizomes to form substantial colonies in moist, fertile conditions — divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and control spread. An outstanding native pollinator plant that bridges the gap between the red and lavender monarda color spectrum in native plant gardens. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Purple Calabash Tomato (Ruffled Deep-Purple Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking well to support the sprawling vines. One of the oldest known tomato heirlooms, Purple Calabash produces small to medium, deeply ruffled and pleated fruit that ranges from dusky pink-burgundy to dark purple-brown, believed to closely resemble tomatoes as they looked before generations of breeding smoothed and enlarged the fruit. The flesh is complex and tangy with a distinctive rich flavor, and the variety was preserved and distributed through Seed Savers Exchange in the early 1990s. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Carpet Creeping Thyme (Dense Mat-Forming Groundcover Thyme)
description: Plant in average to dry, sharply drained soil in full sun to part shade. Purple Carpet forms a fast-growing, dense, low mat of tiny aromatic leaves that stays under three inches tall and knits together quickly to make an attractive, walkable groundcover between stepping stones or along the edge of a path. Masses of small rose-purple flowers cover the foliage in early summer and are a strong draw for bees. It dislikes excessive moisture and poor drainage far more than it dislikes drought or foot traffic, and tends to decline in heavy clay or wet winter soil. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and encourage fresh growth for the following season. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Carrot
description: These anthocyanin-rich carrots range from purple skin with orange cores to solid purple throughout. Sow the fine seed a quarter inch deep in deep, loose, stone-free soil and never let the surface dry during germination. Thin seedlings to 2 to 3 inches so roots develop without forking or crowding. Purple pigment intensifies in cool weather, so fall crops often show the deepest color. Harvest when shoulders reach three-quarters of an inch and store in cool, humid conditions. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Purple Carrot (Cosmic Purple Carrot, Anthocyanin Carrot)
description: Direct sow seeds thinly (1/4 inch deep) in deeply tilled, loose, stone-free, lean soil in full sun; thin to 2–3 inches; harvest at 6–8 inches for best color and flavor. Daucus carota 'Cosmic Purple' (purple carrot or anthocyanin carrot) is an open-pollinated purple-rooted carrot variety developed by the USDA Agricultural Research Service — one of the most richly pigmented and nutritionally dense carrot varieties available to home growers. The root has deep purple to nearly black outer skin from very high anthocyanin concentrations (the same antioxidant pigments found in blueberries and red cabbage) with orange interior flesh, creating a dramatic color contrast when sliced. The flavor is significantly different from standard orange carrots: 'Cosmic Purple' is notably sweeter, with a mild, distinctive flavor complexity from both sugars and secondary compounds. Anthocyanins in the skin are heat-labile and can fade during cooking — roasting at high heat preserves them better than boiling or steaming. Eating purple carrots raw in salads or quick-pickling with vinegar (which intensifies the purple to fuchsia-red) are excellent ways to enjoy both flavor and color. In zone 9, purple carrots are planted in fall for winter harvest when cool temperatures concentrate sugars; spring-planted carrots in warm areas tend to be less sweet and may bolt before fully sizing. A beautiful addition to diverse carrot sowings alongside orange, yellow, and white types. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Purple Cauliflower
description: The vivid purple curds come from anthocyanins and do not require blanching like white types. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before transplanting and set plants out in rich, moisture-retentive soil. Keep growth steady and unchecked, since any stress from heat, drought, or transplant shock can cause premature small heads. Harvest while the head is still tight and dome-shaped, before the curds begin to separate. The color softens somewhat when cooked but stays vibrant if steamed briefly. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Chokeberry (Hybrid Chokeberry)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil; purple chokeberry (Aronia prunifolia) is a naturally occurring hybrid between black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) and red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia), often found growing where the two parent species overlap. The dark purple to purple-black berries are intermediate in size and flavor between the parent species, with very high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any berry), strong tart-bitter flavor excellent for juices, jams, and wine, and exceptional antioxidant properties that have driven significant commercial interest. The shrub offers year-round interest: white flowers in spring, dark glossy leaves in summer, brilliant red to purple fall color, and persistent berries attractive to birds through winter. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple de Milpa Tomatillo
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide staking or caging as plants become sprawling. Purple de Milpa is a traditional Mexican tomatillo variety grown in the traditional milpa polyculture system; it produces small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round fruits with papery husks that burst and split when ripe, ripening to purple-green to deep purple-green rather than the standard yellow-green of commercial tomatillos. The flavor is more concentrated, fruitier, and tangier than standard green tomatillos, with a more complex background of citrus, herbs, and earthiness that many Mexican cooks and chefs consider superior for salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and mole verde when an authentic deep flavor is desired. Plant in pairs or groups as tomatillos need cross-pollination for best fruit set; highly productive in warm weather. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Delight Basil
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Purple Delight produces some of the darkest, most saturated near-black purple leaves of any basil cultivar, holding its intense coloration even in the interior of the plant rather than fading to green-purple like many older purple selections. The taller, more vigorous habit than Dark Opal or Osmin makes it useful both as a dramatic landscape accent and as a productive cutting herb. The flavor is a strong, classic sweet-basil profile with a mild peppery edge, well suited to purple-tinted vinegars, infused oils, and garnish where maximum color saturation is the goal. Pinch flower spikes regularly to prolong leaf production and prevent the plant from bolting in peak summer heat. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Purple Dewberry (Northern Dewberry)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, acidic soil; northern dewberry is a trailing native blackberry that runs along the ground rather than forming erect canes, with individual canes spreading 3–6 feet from the crown. It is among the first bramble fruits to ripen in summer — often a full month before other blackberries — producing glossy, deep black, juicy, intensely sweet-tart fruits excellent for fresh eating and preserves. The trailing habit makes it suitable for slopes, embankments, and naturalized woodland edges; it thrives under open forest canopy where cultivated blackberries would languish. Unlike erect blackberries it does not sucker aggressively but can spread by cane-tip rooting. The canes have sharp prickles; wear gloves for harvest and management. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Purple Dragon Carrot
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Dragon is among the darkest-colored purple carrots available, producing 6–7 inch Chantenay-type roots with an almost purple-black exterior of extraordinary depth — the highest anthocyanin content of the major purple carrot varieties on the market, with the deep pigment extending well into the shoulder of the carrot. The interior flesh is vivid orange, creating a dramatic two-toned cross-section when sliced that makes Purple Dragon the most visually striking carrot in a rainbow mix. The flavor is earthy and subtly spicy with good sweetness, distinctly more complex than standard orange carrots. Raw eating shows the anthocyanin benefits and full visual impact; cooking at high heat fades the exterior purple toward brown, but moderate-heat roasting preserves considerable color. Outstanding raw in salads, crudités, and juicing where the deep purple color makes an impression. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Purple Flash Pepper (Texas Superstar Variegated Ornamental Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container. Purple Flash is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental pepper valued mainly as a striking foliage plant — its leaves are marbled in near-black purple, deep green, and creamy white, giving it a bold variegated presence unmatched by most other heat-loving bedding plants, and it holds this dramatic coloring through the hottest part of summer when many foliage plants fade. It does produce small, round, very hot purple-to-red fruit, but flowering and fruiting are secondary to its role as a colorful accent in mixed beds and containers. It performs best in full sun, where the foliage color intensifies, and tolerates heat and drought once established better than many variegated foliage plants. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier shape. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Gage (Reine Claude Violette, Aromatic Purple-Skinned French Gage Plum)
description: Purple Gage, or Reine Claude Violette, is a long-grown French dessert plum distinguished from the classic green Reine Claude by its dusky purple-red skin over sweet, richly aromatic, amber flesh. It is one of the most intensely flavored of the gage plums, prized in France for eating fresh and for preserves. Largely self-fertile, it still benefits from a second European plum planted nearby for a fuller crop. Thin the fruit if it sets heavily to keep the characteristically small gage fruit from becoming undersized, and prune in late winter to maintain an open, airy canopy. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Purple Giant Filbert (Purple-Leaf Hazelnut)
description: Purple Giant Filbert is grown as much for its deep maroon-purple spring foliage, which mellows toward green-purple by late summer, as for its edible filbert-type nuts borne in husked clusters each fall. It makes a striking specimen shrub or informal hedge and colors best with several hours of direct sun daily, though it tolerates light shade. Plant a second, genetically distinct hazel nearby for reliable nut set, since Corylus is wind-pollinated and self-incompatibility is common. Prune out old, crowded stems in late winter to renew vigor and maintain strong leaf color on fresh growth, and rake up and destroy any leaves showing eastern filbert blight cankers. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Purple Giant Hyssop
description: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; purple giant hyssop tolerates partial shade better than most agastaches and adapts to the moist, fertile soils of woodland edges and naturalized meadow gardens. Agastache scrophulariifolia is an impressive, tall (4–6 feet) native perennial of eastern North American open woodlands and forest edges producing large, mint-scented, heart-shaped leaves and tall, dense spikes of violet-purple flowers in mid- to late summer that are outstanding for native bees (especially bumblebees), butterflies, and hummingbirds. The plant is one of the most prolific native pollinator plants available for the North American garden; it self-seeds moderately to naturalize in favorable spots and is excellent at the back of native plant borders, along fence lines, and in naturalized meadow plantings. The leaves and flowers are edible and were used medicinally by several Native American peoples. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Purple Giant Passion Fruit
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Purple Giant is valued for producing noticeably larger, rounder fruit than typical purple passionfruit, with heavy, rich pulp and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, self-pollinating readily on fragrant white-and-purple crowned flowers. Vines are fast to establish and often fruit within their first year from a rooted cutting, considerably quicker than seed-grown plants, and ripe fruit drops naturally from the vine at around 80 days from flowering. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mound mulch over the crown going into winter, since a hard freeze can kill purple passionfruit vines to the ground or outright. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Purple Glazer Garlic (Glazed Purple Stripe Hardneck Heirloom)
description: Plant cloves pointed end up, about two inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Glazer is a Glazed Purple Stripe heirloom out of the Republic of Georgia, prized for its striking bulb wrappers of deep violet-purple washed with a metallic gold or silver sheen, wrapping six to nine plump, easy-to-peel cloves with a rich, balanced flavor that starts sweet and finishes with a gentle, lingering warmth. Like other hardnecks it sends up a coiling scape in early summer that should be cut once curled to redirect energy into bulb growth, and the scapes are excellent chopped into pesto or stir-fries. It stores respectably for a hardneck and performs best in regions with a genuinely cold winter to break dormancy, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Purple Gromwell (Murasaki, Japanese Dye Root)
description: Purple gromwell, known in Japan as murasaki, is grown for its thick, woody taproot, whose outer bark layer contains shikonin, a naphthoquinone pigment that yields a distinctive deep reddish-purple dye once used for imperial court robes and prized kimono silk. The plant itself is an unassuming hairy-leaved perennial with small white summer flowers, giving little hint of the color locked in its root; because the taproot needs two to three years of growth before it holds enough pigment to be worth harvesting, this is a patience crop rather than a quick dye plant. Dig roots in fall of the second or third year, wash them, and either dry them whole for storage or process fresh — the dye is extracted with alcohol rather than water, since shikonin is only poorly water-soluble, and the resulting dyebath is used on silk and wool with an acidic mordant. It prefers loose, well-drained soil in light shade to full sun and resents root disturbance once established, so direct-seed or transplant into its permanent bed while still small. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Purple Haze Carrot
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Haze is an All-America Selection Edible Vegetable winner with striking purple-skinned, orange-fleshed 10-inch carrots that turn purple skin orange when cooked (the purple color fades with heat), with slightly higher anthocyanin content than orange carrots. When eaten raw, the purple exterior provides both visual drama and a hint of earthiness that complements the sweet orange interior. Excellent for rainbow carrot mixes, farmers markets, and home gardens looking for an unusual and conversation-starting variety with genuinely good flavor. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Purple Haze Dragon Fruit
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Haze is a dragon fruit cultivar grown for its deep magenta-purple flesh, one of the most intensely colored selections available, with a sweeter, more aromatic flavor profile than the classic white-fleshed types. As an epiphytic cactus it needs a sturdy post or trellis to climb and support its long, three-ribbed, succulent stems, along with excellent drainage rather than the regular watering a conventional fruit tree would need.
