Flowers open at night and close by dawn, so for best fruit set hand-pollinate after dark by transferring pollen with a small brush between open flowers, since many dragon fruit selections are only partially self-fertile. Zone 9 gardeners in the warmest, most frost-protected locations can attempt in-ground planting, but most should grow Purple Haze in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot whenever a freeze threatens, since even brief cold exposure damages the succulent stems. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple Heart Pomegranate (Deep Purple-Red Aril Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat, harvesting when the skin deepens to full color and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Purple Heart bears fruit with a deep purple-red skin blush and arils that run notably darker than the bright ruby-red of most pomegranate cultivars, with rich, sweet-tart flavor and juice that stains a deep, saturated purple-red. Its striking dark coloring makes it a distinctive choice among pomegranate cultivars both for fresh eating and for juice with an unusually deep color. Prune to an open, vase-shaped form in the early years and remove root suckers regularly, since pomegranates sucker readily from the base; established trees are long-lived and require little routine care. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Purple Hull Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; purple hull peas are exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and require no added fertilizer on moderately fertile ground since they fix atmospheric nitrogen. The distinctive purple-hull pods flush violet-pink to purple at maturity, making them easy to spot at harvest time — pick pods when the hull is fully colored but before it begins to dry and yellow. Fresh-shelled purple hull peas cook faster than dried beans and have a richer, earthier flavor than black-eyed peas; they are a staple of Southern cooking, particularly New Year's Day hoppin' john and summer side dishes. The vines sprawl moderately — plant in wide rows or support with short stakes for easier harvest. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Purple Karma Barley (Tibetan Hull-less Barley)
description: This six-row hulless barley traces back to a single seed sample collected in Tibet in 1924 and deposited in the USDA seed repository, where it sat unnoticed for decades before researchers rediscovered and propagated it under the name Karma. Its deep purple-black kernels carry an anthocyanin-rich bran layer, and because the hull is only loosely attached, most of it falls free during ordinary threshing rather than requiring a pearling mill. Sow in early spring into well-drained soil; the plant is notably drought-tolerant once established and performs well on modest, low-input ground. Harvest when heads are fully dry and kernels are hard, then thresh and winnow to reveal grain that cooks up chewy and nutty, similar to pearled barley but with substantially more fiber, zinc, and B vitamins than hulled white barley. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Purple Kohlrabi Sprouts
description: These purple kohlrabi sprouts add eye-popping color and crunch to salads and sandwiches with a classic brassica flavor and spicy note. Sprout the seeds indoors in a jar or shallow tray, rinsing and draining two to three times daily. They are ready to eat in four to seven days once the shoots stand an inch or so tall with tiny leaves. Keep them moist but drained to avoid mold. Matures in 4–7 days from seed.

name: Purple Lady Bok Choy
description: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Lady holds its color and resists bolting better in the shorter days of fall than in the heat and long days of spring. Glossy, deep purple-black leaves top pale green petioles in a compact, upright rosette, giving this bok choy strong ornamental value alongside its mild, sweet, crisp flavor, and it holds its rich color whether cooked or eaten raw in salads. Bred as a hybrid for uniform heads and improved bolt resistance compared to open-pollinated purple pak choi types, it matures quickly enough for two full crops in a single spring-to-fall season in most climates. Harvest whole heads at full size or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again harvest, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest window into warmer weather. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Purple Magic Broccoli (AAS-Winning Purple-Headed, Purple-Stemmed Broccoli)
description: Start transplants and set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or midsummer. Purple Magic is an AAS-winning broccoli notable for carrying purple color not just in the head but through the stems and leaves as well, a first among broccoli breeding, driven by a high anthocyanin content that also gives the roughly 1-pound domed heads a sweeter taste than green broccoli. The uniform, well-domed crowns hold their vivid color well after harvest and even through light cooking. Harvest the central head while buds are still tight, then keep picking side shoots as they form to extend the season; the plant tolerates heat stress better than many broccoli varieties, easing timing in warmer regions. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Purple Majesty Potato (Deep Purple Skin and Flesh Specialty Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Purple Majesty is a Colorado State University potato introduction producing tubers with dramatic deep-purple skin and equally vivid deep-purple flesh throughout — not a surface tint or partial coloring but consistently, intensely purple from skin to center in every tuber. The purple coloration comes from high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments that are the same class of antioxidants found in blueberries and acai — Purple Majesty has among the highest anthocyanin levels of any potato variety tested, providing both the extraordinary visual quality and the health-attributed benefits associated with anthocyanin-rich foods. The color partially survives light cooking — steamed or microwaved Purple Majesty retains much of its striking purple appearance, while hard-boiled or oven-roasted preparations create dramatic visual presentations unlike any other potato. The flavor is mild and pleasant — comparable to other specialty potatoes — with the skin adding a slightly earthy complexity. Purple Majesty is oblong-shaped with smooth skin and produces well under typical potato growing conditions. In zone 9, plant in January–February for spring harvest. The vivid color makes Purple Majesty outstanding in mixed potato salads where the purple tubers contrast dramatically with red, gold, and white varieties. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Majesty Sweet Potato (Deep Purple Flesh, High-Anthocyanin NC State Release)
description: Plant certified slips in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Purple Majesty is a North Carolina State University release with dark purple skin and equally dark purple flesh throughout, colored by a high concentration of anthocyanin pigments that give cooked roots a moderately dry texture and mild sweetness. It produces uniform, elliptic roots and performs especially well on sandy ground, reaching harvest in around 100 days from transplanting. The variety resists Fusarium wilt but remains susceptible to Streptomyces soil rot and both southern and guava root-knot nematodes, so rotate away from beds with a recent history of those problems. Purple Majesty ships and stores well after curing, but it does poorly in wet or flooded soil, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained ground rather than low-lying areas prone to standing water after heavy rain. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Purple Mitsuba (Purple Japanese Wild Parsley)
description: Direct sow in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple mitsuba self-sows readily in a shaded herb bed once established and naturalizes as a woodland-edge perennial herb. This ornamental purple-leaved form of Japanese wild parsley (mitsuba) carries deep burgundy-purple, three-lobed leaves on slender stems, combining the same mild parsley-celery-anise flavor prized in Japanese cooking with striking, season-long foliage color for a shaded herb or ornamental border. Unlike most culinary herbs, it thrives in full shade and actually prefers it to hot sun, making it a useful flavor and color addition to the deep-shade parts of a garden where few edible herbs perform well. Harvest young leaves and stems continuously for soups, salads, and garnishes, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Purple Mustard Greens (Crinkle-leaf Purple Mustard)
description: Direct sow in late summer for fall harvest or very early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple mustard greens (varieties include 'Red Giant', 'Osaka Purple', and 'Crimson Forest') produce large, crinkled or frilly, deep burgundy-red to purple-red leaves with a pleasant, pungent, spicy mustard flavor. The purple color is most intense in cool temperatures and fades slightly in warm weather. Extremely fast to harvest — baby leaves ready in 3–4 weeks, full size in 5–7 weeks. The flavor is spicier than milder Asian greens but milder than mature yellow mustard plants. Use in salad mixes for color and spice, stir-fry when young and tender, or braise the mature leaves Southern-style with pot liquor. Overwintering plants in zones 7–9 produce early spring regrowth before bolting. A staple of Asian-American vegetable gardens and increasingly popular in American farmers markets for its dramatic color and quick harvest. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Purple of Romagna Artichoke (Violetto di Romagna Heirloom)
aliases: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Purple of Romagna'
description: Set out rooted offshoots or nursery transplants in spring after danger of frost, into deeply worked soil enriched with compost. In mild-winter regions plants persist for several years as a true perennial; in colder zones, mulch heavily over winter or grow as an annual from an early indoor sowing with a cold treatment. This classic Italian heirloom from the Romagna region produces elongated, spineless purple buds that are notably tender at a small, immature size, which is why they are traditionally harvested young and eaten raw, thinly sliced, in salads such as pinzimonio rather than only cooked whole like larger green cultivars. Its purple coloring and slender bud shape distinguish it visually from rounder green types like Green Globe. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple Passion Asparagus
description: Plant 1-year crowns 6–8 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil amended with compost in full sun; Purple Passion is a New Zealand-bred asparagus cultivar that produces vivid deep-purple spears with 25–40% higher sugar content and significantly lower fiber than standard green varieties — the purple color comes from anthocyanins concentrated in the outer tissues. The raw spears are noticeably sweeter and more tender than green asparagus and can be eaten raw in salads and crudités where the color is preserved; cooking turns the spears green as the anthocyanins break down under heat. Flavor is superior to most green varieties whether raw or cooked. Established beds are productive for 15–25 years. In zone 9 the plant benefits from a sandy, well-drained location and may require supplemental irrigation in the long, dry spring. Skip the first two seasons' harvest to allow crown development; thereafter harvest only the first 4–6 weeks of the spring flush. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Purple Passion Fruit
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a strong trellis or chain-link fence; the purple passion fruit vine grows rapidly and requires physical support for the tendrils. Unlike the cold-hardy native maypop (P. incarnata), this is a true tropical vine that produces the familiar large, purple, wrinkled fruits of commerce, intensely aromatic with sweet-tart yellow pulp. Fruits ripen and fall to the ground when ready — simply collect them from the ground. In zones 9b–11 plants produce heavily twice yearly, in spring and fall. The spectacular 3-inch flowers with purple, white, and yellow corona filaments are among the most intricate in the plant world and are visited by bumblebees, which are the most effective pollinators. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple Passion Sweet Potato
description: Purple Passion is a specialty heirloom sweet potato grown as a distinct named selection within the loose group of purple-skinned, purple-fleshed sweet potatoes maintained by small seed-saving farms, producing roots with purplish skin over moderately deep purple flesh and a drier, denser texture than orange-fleshed mainstream varieties. Flavor is mildly sweet and earthy, holding its purple color best when roasted or steamed rather than boiled in acidic water, which fades the pigment. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and keep fertility moderate, since excess nitrogen pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation; sprawling, purple-tinged vines tolerate a long, hot growing season well. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure at warm temperature and high humidity for a week or two to heal skin wounds and develop full sweetness before moving roots to cool, dry storage. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Purple Passionflower (Maypop, Wild Apricot)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or wire support; allow some room for root sucker spread. Passiflora incarnata (purple passionflower or maypop) is the cold-hardy native passionflower of the eastern United States, producing the most extraordinarily ornate flowers in temperate horticulture — each 3-inch flower displays five white petals and five sepals framed by a crown of lavender to purple, fringed, radiating filaments arranged in concentric rings, the whole structure appearing more like an alien artifact than a flower. Flowers bloom from June through September and are followed by edible, golf-ball-sized, yellow-green to orange fruits (maypops) with a sweet-tart, guava-like flavor used for jams, jellies, and drinks. The vine is the obligate host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae — caterpillars consume the leaves, making it exceptional for butterfly gardens. Passiflora incarnata is cold-hardy to zone 5 (dying to the ground in winter but resprouting vigorously from roots), and in zones 7–10 it is virtually indestructible once established, spreading from root suckers. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Purple Peacock Broccoli (Ornamental Kale-Broccoli Cross)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Peacock is an open-pollinated cross between purple broccoli and Russian kale, producing deeply lobed, ruffled, purple-veined leaves along with small, tender purple broccoli-like side shoots rather than one large central head. Both the ornamental foliage and the small flowering shoots are edible, making it a dual-purpose plant valued equally for cut-and-come-again greens and for its striking, frost-enhanced color in the fall and winter garden. Harvest outer leaves and side shoots regularly to encourage continued production, and expect the purple coloring and flavor to intensify after the plant experiences a light frost. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Purple Pershore Plum (Classic English Cooking and Jam Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Purple Pershore takes its name from the English town of Pershore in Worcestershire, historically the center of a major English plum-growing and jam-making industry built substantially around this variety, prized for consistently heavy crops of small to medium, deep purple, tart-fleshed fruit that cooks down into excellent jam, chutney, and stewed plum preparations. The fruit is generally considered too tart and firm for fresh eating out of hand but excels once cooked with sugar, developing rich, deep plum flavor that made it a commercial jam standard for generations in England. The tree is notably reliable and productive, an important trait for a variety grown primarily for volume processing rather than fresh market appeal; harvest once fruit fully colors and yields slightly to pressure. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Purple Peruvian Fingerling Potato (Andean Purple Heritage Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces (whole small tubers work best for fingerlings) 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; fingerling potatoes produce many small, elongated tubers that benefit from slightly closer planting than large-tuber varieties. Purple Peruvian fingerling potatoes come from the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, the center of origin of the domestic potato (Solanum tuberosum), where indigenous Quechua and Aymara peoples developed thousands of diverse potato cultivars over 8,000+ years — the wild ancestral diversity of potatoes in this region dwarfs the few dozen varieties commonly grown in North America. Purple Peruvian produces long (2–4 inch), slender, finger-shaped tubers with intensely dark purple to near-black skin and uniformly deep purple to violet flesh throughout; the color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments found in Adirondack Blue and All Blue but at high concentrations. The texture is waxy and the flavor is earthy, slightly nutty, and distinctly more complex than commercial potato varieties — reflecting centuries of selection in high-altitude Andean environments. The fingerling shape makes them visually dramatic on the plate and ideal for roasting whole (the skin caramelizes beautifully), potato salads, and presentations where the purple color adds visual impact. High in antioxidants. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Petra Basil
description: Purple Petra offers a mild, sweet basil flavor without the peppery bite of some varieties, making it a favorite for those who prefer gentle herbal notes. Its deep purple foliage doubles as an ornamental accent and tints vinegars and oils a lovely pink. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after frost, giving plants full sun and rich, moist soil. Pinch tips regularly to encourage bushy growth and keep the vivid leaf color coming. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Purple Plum Radish
description: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Plum is a round, globe-shaped spring radish with uniformly deep violet-purple skin — a dramatic and attractive departure from the familiar red-and-white Cherry Belle type, with the rich purple skin creating an unusual ornamental effect in the radish row and on vegetable platters. When sliced, Purple Plum reveals clean white flesh with only the thin purple skin providing color — the interior is typical crisp, juicy, peppery radish with the same satisfying bite as standard spring radishes. The flavor is classic spring radish: pungent, peppery, slightly sweet when very fresh, and progressively hotter as the root ages or the weather warms. The round, smooth shape and uniform size make Purple Plum excellent for sliced vegetable platters, salads, and garnishes where the deep purple skin creates visual contrast with other vegetables. As one of the fastest-maturing vegetables available, radishes including Purple Plum are often direct-sown between slow-growing transplants (tomatoes, peppers, squash) to use the space productively while the main crop establishes. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Purple Plum Radish
description: Direct sow 'Purple Plum' seeds 1/2 inch deep and thin seedlings to about 1-2 inches apart for well-formed, violet-skinned roots. This fast-maturing radish is ready in roughly a month and stays crisp and mild even as bulbs enlarge. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent pithiness and cracking, and harvest promptly once roots reach about 1 inch across. Tolerant of cool weather and containers, it thrives in full sun to partial shade. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Purple Podded Pole Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost at base of a trellis, poles, or fence that will support 6–8 foot vines; thin to 4–6 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Purple Podded Pole bean is an old American heirloom snap bean with the dramatic characteristic of deep purple pods that develop against the green foliage — a striking visual contrast in the garden that makes this one of the most ornamentally interesting of all vegetable plants. The long (6–8 inch), round-sectioned pods are deep maroon-purple when raw and suitable for fresh eating or canning; however, the anthocyanin purple pigment is water-soluble and the pods turn standard green when cooked in water, a characteristic that surprises many gardeners. The flavor is excellent, similar to other pole snap beans; the raw purple pods are also edible in salads where the color can be appreciated. Very productive and continuous bearing through summer; the purple color also makes the beans somewhat easier to spot for harvesting against the green foliage. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Purple Pony Purple-leaf Plum
description: Purple Pony is a purple-leaf plum cultivar grown for the same rich burgundy-purple foliage and very early single pink flowers that define the group, opening before or alongside the emerging leaves in late winter to earliest spring. Like its better-known relatives Thundercloud and Krauter Vesuvius, it holds its dark foliage color through most of the growing season before fading somewhat by fall, and produces small, sparse, edible reddish plums that are secondary to its ornamental value. Plant it in full sun and well-drained soil as a small flowering accent or specimen tree, expecting the same fast early growth and relatively short 15- to 25-year lifespan typical of purple-leaf plum selections. Water regularly through the first year or two of establishment, then rely mainly on rainfall except during extended drought, and prune lightly after bloom to remove crossing or damaged branches. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Purple Prickly Pear (Long-Spine Cactus)
description: Plant callused pads in very well-drained, dry, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — purple prickly pear is one of the most ornamentally striking native cacti of the Chihuahuan Desert and Texas prairies, valued for the brilliant reddish-purple to wine-red coloration that develops on its blue-green pads during cold weather and drought stress, providing some of the most vivid winter color of any cactus or succulent in cultivation. The yellow flowers with red centers in spring are beautiful; the edible purple-red fruits (tunas) follow in late summer and fall. Long, 3–4 inch white to gray spines give the plant a dramatic, bold texture. The distinctive purple winter color is the result of anthocyanin pigments produced as a cold-stress response — pads return to blue-green in summer warmth. An outstanding xeriscape and dry garden plant for hot, dry, alkaline soils of the southern Gulf Coast and Texas. Edible pads and fruit used as other prickly pears. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Purple Ruffles Basil (AAS-Winning Ornamental Deep-Purple Frilled Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Purple Ruffles is an All-America Selections gold medal-winning basil combining exceptional ornamental quality with full culinary utility — producing large, deeply ruffled, deeply frilled leaves in rich dark-purple to reddish-purple coloration that is immediately striking in the herb garden or as an ornamental annual. The large, heavily ruffled leaf margins — with deeply incised, wavy, almost lace-like edges — distinguish Purple Ruffles from other purple basils whose leaves are smooth or only slightly ruffled. The ornamental quality is outstanding: the combination of the vivid dark-purple color and elaborate leaf texture creates a decorative impact far beyond most culinary herbs. The basil flavor is good — a full, classic basil flavor with a slight spicy-anise character and a pleasant mild bitterness from the purple anthocyanins — suitable for pesto, salads, and infused oils where the purple color creates a striking visual effect (purple basil vinegar is particularly beautiful). In zone 9, purple basil grows through the warm season from April–October but often bolts (flowers) quickly in summer heat; pinch flower buds promptly and repeatedly to extend the harvest season. The purple leaf color makes excellent contrast with silver herbs (artemisia, horehound) and chartreuse-leaved companions in herb garden designs. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Purple Sage
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — culinary sage rots in heavy, wet soils; Purple Sage is a cultivar of common culinary sage (Salvia officinalis) selected for its ornamental foliage — the leaves are a soft, velvety purple-gray rather than the standard gray-green, creating a striking two-tone ornamental effect when the plant is in growth. The culinary flavor and fragrance are identical to standard sage — the same warm, resinous, camphor-and-pine aroma and savory flavor used in Thanksgiving stuffing, sage butter for pasta, sausage seasoning, and Italian cooking — making Purple Sage a practical dual-use plant where ornamental value complements culinary function. The lavender-blue flowers in spring (April–May) add a third color to the already-attractive plant, and both the flowers and the purple-gray foliage are used in dried wreaths, herbal sachets, and potpourri. Purple Sage retains the same beneficial compounds as common sage (ursolic acid, rosmarinic acid, thujone) used medicinally for generations. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Purple Sage
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; purple sage is a handsome ornamental-culinary cultivar of common garden sage whose young leaves emerge in rich purple tones that soften to purple-green as they mature. The flavor is fully equivalent to common sage — warm, peppery, slightly bitter, and intensely aromatic with notes of camphor and eucalyptus — and it can be used as a complete substitute in all sage-seasoned dishes. The purple foliage provides attractive contrast in herb gardens where it pairs visually with silver thyme and golden oregano. It requires the same excellent drainage and full sun as common sage and is equally deer-resistant. Trim lightly in spring to prevent woodiness and promote compact, leafy new growth. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Purple Sage (Coastal Sage, Gray Sage)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; water sparingly — established plants need summer dry conditions to thrive. Salvia leucophylla (purple sage or coastal sage) is a California native aromatic shrub from the coastal sage scrub and chaparral communities of coastal and inland California. The plant produces aromatic, wrinkled, silver-gray to white-felted leaves with a strong, distinctive fragrance — more complex and resinous than common garden sage (S. officinalis), with additional notes of camphor, eucalyptus, and warm spice. The soft, gray foliage creates a beautiful silvery landscape effect, especially dramatic when paired with purple lavender and other Mediterranean-climate plants. In late spring through early summer, it produces whorled clusters of pink to light-purple flowers on white-felted stems — both fragrant and attractive to hummingbirds and bumblebees. Purple sage is a classic plant of the California chaparral and is notable for producing volatile allelopathic compounds (camphor, 1,8-cineole) from its leaves that inhibit the germination and growth of competing plants beneath its canopy — a natural herbicide effect. The leaves are traditionally used by California indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging, and can be used as a culinary sage substitute (though stronger). Drought tolerance once established is extreme. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Purple Shiso (Red Perilla, Aka Shiso)
description: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering (light aids germination) after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; purple shiso is the red-leafed cultivar group of perilla, with deep burgundy leaves essential in Japanese pickling — umeboshi (pickled plum) gets its characteristic pink-red color and complex flavor from red shiso leaves layered with the salted plums. The entire plant is strongly aromatic, blending mint, anise, and basil; in Korean cuisine the leaves (kkaennip) are used to wrap grilled meats or pickled in soy sauce. Allowed to flower and set seed, it self-sows freely and returns each summer; use leaves whole or finely chiffonaded. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Purple Splendor Sweet Potato (Color-Fast Purple Flesh NC State Release)
description: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants a bit wider than usual since Purple Splendor produces slips prolifically and quickly crowds a tightly spaced row; Purple Splendor is a North Carolina State University release notable for purple flesh pigment that stays vivid through cooking rather than fading the way many purple sweet potato varieties do. Roots form uniform blocky to round-elliptic shapes and stay compact even in deep sandy soil, with a moderately dry texture and moderate sweetness once cured. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode. Purple Splendor stores and ships well but cannot tolerate flooded or poorly drained fields, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained soil rather than low spots that collect water after summer storms. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Purple Sprouting Broccoli
description: This hardy overwintering broccoli produces many small purple spears in early spring rather than a single central head. Start seed indoors in mid to late summer and transplant in early fall so plants establish before cold sets in. Provide steady moisture and rich soil, and mulch heavily to protect crowns through winter in zones 6 and 7. Harvest spears when buds are tight and cut regularly to encourage continued side-shoot production. Exposure to winter chill is what triggers the abundant spring flush. Matures in 150–220 days from transplant.

name: Purple Star Apple (Caimito)
description: The purple-skinned form of star apple is the more widely traded of the two color types, prized for its glossy, deep violet rind that ripens to nearly black and encloses sweet, milky, translucent flesh; when sliced crosswise the seed cavities form the pale star pattern that gives the fruit its name. Purple-fruited selections tend to have a denser, slightly firmer texture than the green form and travel a bit better after picking. Grow in full sun on fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil, and pick when the skin develops a uniform dull sheen and yields slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit does not ripen further once removed from the tree. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within 3-5 years. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Purple Sweet Potato
description: Plant slips 2–3 weeks after last frost in loose, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Purple Sweet Potato produces better tubers in slightly poor, loose soil rather than heavily amended rich soil — excess nitrogen encourages vine growth at the expense of tuber development; harvest 90–120 days after transplanting when the vines begin to yellow. Ipomoea batatas 'Purple' (Purple Sweet Potato, Okinawan Sweet Potato, or Stokes Purple Sweet Potato) encompasses a group of purple-fleshed sweet potato varieties — including 'Okinawan,' 'Japanese Purple' (Satsumaimo), and 'Stokes Purple' — sharing the characteristic of producing tubers with deep violet-purple flesh caused by exceptionally high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments (cyanidin and peonidin glycosides). These anthocyanins give purple sweet potatoes one of the highest antioxidant levels of any commonly eaten vegetable — ORAC values 2–3 times higher than blueberries — and have generated significant interest in functional food and nutraceutical research. Purple-fleshed sweet potatoes retain their vibrant purple color when baked or boiled (better than in acidic cooking), are somewhat drier and nuttier in texture than orange sweet potatoes, and are traditional in Okinawan Japanese cuisine (where they are called 'beni imo'), Hawaiian cuisine (Okinawan sweet potato poi), Filipino cuisine, and increasingly in American superfood markets. Grow exactly like standard sweet potato: loose, sandy soil, full sun, long warm season. Slips (not tubers or seeds) are the standard planting material. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Purple Tomatillo
description: Start purple tomatillo seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil in full sun. Plant at least two seedlings to ensure cross-pollination, since tomatillos are largely self-incompatible. The sprawling plants benefit from staking or caging; harvest fruit when the papery husk splits open and the berry turns deep violet for the sweetest flavor. Keep watering consistent through fruit set to encourage a heavy crop. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple Top Milan Turnip
aliases: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top Milan'
description: A traditional Italian heirloom prized for being one of the fastest turnips to reach the table, producing flattened white discs capped in bright purple-red in as little as five to six weeks. Its speed makes it ideal for very early spring sowing before other crops are ready, or for a quick fall catch crop after summer vegetables finish. The flesh is notably tender and mild when harvested young and small, becoming pithier if left to size up, so pull roots promptly at 2-3 inches across. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Purple Top Rutabaga
description: American Purple Top rutabaga produces large five- to six-inch roots with purple shoulders and smooth ivory flesh that is sweet, mild, and fine-textured. Grown as a fall crop, it stores exceptionally well for winter use in mashes and stews. Direct sow in mid summer so roots mature in cool weather, and thin generously to size up. A light frost sweetens the roots; harvest before the ground hard-freezes and store in a cool, humid place. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Purple Top Strap Leaf Turnip
description: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 4-6 inches, using thinnings as tender greens. Purple Top Strap Leaf is a nineteenth-century dual-purpose heirloom distinguished from ordinary purple-top turnips by its smooth, non-lobed 'strap' leaves, which grow upright rather than sprawling and stay cleaner in wet weather, making them a preferred choice for market growers selling bunched turnip greens alongside the roots. The flattened globe roots are white below the soil line with a purple-red crown above, mild-flavored when harvested young. This foliage trait, rather than root shape or color, is what sets it apart from other purple-top selections still common in seed catalogs. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Purple Top Turnip
description: Purple Top is the classic heirloom turnip, forming smooth white roots with bright purple shoulders plus tender, nutritious greens. Both roots and tops are edible, giving a dual harvest from one planting. Direct sow in early spring for a fast crop or in late summer for sweeter fall roots, thinning to give roots room. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest roots young at two to three inches for the mildest flavor. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip
aliases: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top White Globe'
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Purple Top White Globe is the definitive American turnip variety — the standard against which all other turnip cultivars are measured, with over a century of continuous cultivation making it the most widely recognized turnip appearance in North America. The smooth, round roots develop their characteristic two-tone coloration from the soil surface: the shoulder (exposed to light above ground) develops a rich, vivid purple-violet pigmentation while the buried portion stays clean creamy white, creating the immediately recognizable bicolor that defines the visual identity of a turnip. Both the roots and the large, hairy, dark green leaves (turnip greens) are edible — the mild, slightly sweet, pleasantly peppery roots can be eaten raw at small size or cooked in soups, stews, and roasted vegetable preparations, while the greens are a classic Southern potherb simmered with smoked pork and eaten alongside collards and mustard. Fall-planted turnips develop the finest flavor in zone 9 as cool temperatures concentrate sugars and reduce any harshness in the roots. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip
description: Direct sow 'Purple Top White Globe' 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3-4 inches apart for smooth, globe-shaped roots with purple shoulders and white bottoms. This classic heirloom is dual-purpose: harvest young greens for cooking and pull roots at about 3 inches across before they turn woody. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, sweet roots, and grow in cool spring or fall weather. Turnips store well in a cool, humid place through winter. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip (Standard American Turnip)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Purple Top White Globe is the classic American turnip — an old open-pollinated variety that has been the standard American garden turnip for generations and remains by far the most widely grown turnip variety in both home gardens and commercial production. The medium-large globe roots (3–4 inches diameter at ideal harvest size) have a distinctive two-tone appearance: the upper portion (exposed above the soil line) turns vivid purple to purple-red in sunlight, while the lower portion remains white. The firm, crisp, sweet-peppery flesh is mild when harvested young (under 3 inches) and becomes stronger and more pungent as roots age and enlarge — harvest promptly at desired size for best quality. The tender, nutritious greens (tops) are equally valuable: they are among the best-flavored of all Southern cooking greens, prized in traditional Gulf South cooking simmered with pork and seasonings. In zone 9, Purple Top White Globe is strictly a fall and winter crop — heat above 75°F causes the roots to become pithy, bitter, and tough. Sow from August through early October and harvest from October through February. Turnips are extremely fast-maturing and exceptionally cold-hardy — they tolerate freezes to the mid-20s°F without damage and flavor actually improves after frost exposure. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Purple Vienna Kohlrabi
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Purple Vienna Kohlrabi is the standard purple-skinned kohlrabi, identical in flavor and culture to white-stemmed types but with a striking deep purple-red skin color that makes it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The interior flesh is white, mild, and sweet — identical to white kohlrabi in texture and taste despite the purple exterior. The purple color, from anthocyanin pigments, is present only in the skin and does not penetrate the flesh; peeled Purple Vienna looks and tastes exactly like White Vienna. The visual contrast between the purple skin and white interior makes it popular for raw preparations like kohlrabi slaws, crudités, and salads where slicing reveals the striking bicolor cross-section. In zone 9 kohlrabi is primarily a fall vegetable transplanted in September–October; it withstands light frosts and can be harvested from November through February. Remove leaves and store harvested kohlrabi in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Purple Vienna Kohlrabi
description: Purple Vienna is a cool-season heirloom kohlrabi forming deep purple bulbs above the soil with crisp, tender, mildly sweet flesh similar to a turnip. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, thinning to give the swelling stems room. Keep growth steady with even moisture, since stress can make the bulbs woody. Harvest when bulbs reach two to three inches across for the best texture, before they turn fibrous. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Purple Vienna Kohlrabi
description: Sow 'Purple Vienna' kohlrabi 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart so the purple, edible swollen stems develop cleanly. The bulbs are best harvested at 2-3 inches in diameter while crisp and sweet; larger bulbs turn tough and fibrous. Grow in the cool weather of spring or fall in full sun, keeping moisture even to avoid cracking. Both the bulb and young leaves are edible raw or cooked. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Purple Viking Potato (Purple-Skinned White-Flesh Storage Potato)
description: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Purple Viking produces large, oval tubers with striking purple-splashed pink skin over dense, moist, pure white flesh that holds together well when boiled, making it a favorite for potato salad as well as roasting and mashing. The vigorous plants are heavy yielders and the thick skin gives the tubers good storage life compared to thinner-skinned varieties. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to keep developing tubers covered and prevent greening, and harvest after the vines die back for the best storage tubers. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Purple Wild Angelica (Vicar's Mead)
description: 'Purpurea', distributed in the nursery trade as both 'Purpurea' and 'Vicar's Mead' (the two names refer to the same selection), intensifies the purplish stem tinting of the wild species into deep, glossy purple-black stems and leaf ribs that persist through the whole plant, topped by the same rounded umbels of white to pink-flushed flowers in summer. The striking dark stems have made it a favorite of naturalistic and 'new perennial' style planting design, where its architectural height and moody coloring pair well against airy grasses and pale-flowered companions in a damp, partly shaded border. Sow fresh seed in fall — viability drops quickly in storage — in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil at a woodland edge, streamside bed, or other consistently damp, partly shaded site. Like the species it is monocarpic, dying after flowering and setting seed in its second or third year, but self-sows reliably enough to maintain a colony of purple-stemmed plants once established, provided at least some seedlings are allowed to mature and set seed each cycle. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Purple Winter Savory (Illyrian Savory)
description: This Balkan subspecies of winter savory forms a low, dense, semi-woody mound of narrow dark leaves that stays noticeably shorter and tighter than typical winter savory, and it produces an unusually heavy show of violet-purple summer flowers that draw bees and other pollinators more visibly than the pale blooms of the straight species. It was selected for gardens as much for ornamental value as for the kitchen, working well as a xeric border edge or rock-garden specimen, though the leaves carry the same resinous, peppery savory flavor prized with beans and roasted meats. Grow it in poor to average soil with excellent drainage, since rich or damp conditions quickly lead to root rot and loose, sprawling growth. Shear back lightly after flowering to maintain its tight mounded shape and encourage fresh foliage for the following season. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Purple Yam (Ube, Water Yam, Winged Yam)
description: Plant tuber sections in loose, deep (18–24 inches), well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with strong trellis support; purple yam (ube) is the most widely cultivated yam species in the world and a treasured ingredient in Filipino cuisine, where its vivid violet-purple flesh and sweet, mildly nutty flavor are used in ube halaya (jam), halo-halo, ice cream, pastries, and a growing global trend in purple foods. Originating in Southeast Asia and now grown pantropically, D. alata produces large (up to 20 lb), winged-stemmed vines that require a full 9–12 month season for maximum tuber development; in frost-prone zones grow in the longest available frost-free window and harvest after vine dieback. The distinctive purple color comes from anthocyanins and deepens with cooking; unlike taro, the flesh is not irritating raw. Tubers store well for several months in cool, dry conditions. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Purple Zebra Tomato (Small Purple-Red Striped Tomato)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Purple Zebra is a small, round striped tomato in the same family of striped varieties as the well-known Green Zebra, but ripening to a deep purple-red base color striped with contrasting gold-green, giving fruit an eye-catching jewel-toned appearance both on the vine and sliced on a plate. The flesh carries a bright, tangy-sweet flavor typical of striped 'zebra' tomatoes, with a bit more acidity than fully ripe solid-colored types, making it a favorite for salads and mixed heirloom tomato platters where visual variety matters. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; harvest once the stripe pattern and base color are both fully developed, and water evenly to reduce cracking on the thin skin. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Purple-Flowering Raspberry
description: Purple-flowering raspberry is a thornless native North American Rubus producing large, showy rose-purple flowers attractive to pollinators followed by broad, flat, raspberry-like fruits in midsummer. The berries are edible but dry and seedy — more appealing to wildlife than humans — making this species primarily grown as an ornamental fruiting shrub for naturalizing woodland edges and native plantings. It spreads vigorously by root suckering and can colonize large areas; control spread by removing suckers as needed at the perimeter. No trellising is required; prune out older, dying canes to the ground in late winter to encourage fresh, vigorous shoots. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Purple-leaf Plum (Cherry Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple-leaf plum (cherry plum) is a small Asian ornamental tree and one of the most widely planted landscape trees in North America for its combination of very early white to pale pink spring flowers — often blooming in February in zones 7–9 — and the dramatic burgundy-purple foliage retained through the summer. The species itself has green leaves, but the purple-leaved cultivars 'Atropurpurea', 'Thundercloud', 'Krauter Vesuvius', and 'Newport' are among the most common ornamental trees in American residential landscaping. Small, round, yellow to red plums are produced in summer and are edible, making acceptable jam and jelly. Self-sows readily and some cultivars can become invasive outside gardens in mild climates. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15–25 years) but very fast-growing and reliably floriferous. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Purple-Podded Asparagus (Yardlong) Bean
description: Distinct from the common Red Noodle type, this asparagus bean produces slender pods up to 18 inches long in a deep, glossy purple that holds its color well even after light cooking or stir-frying. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis, since vines climb vigorously and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions that stress common snap beans. Harvest pods young and pencil-thin, well before the seeds inside swell, checking plants every day or two during peak season since pods lengthen quickly. This variety tolerates heat, humidity, and many common bean pests and diseases better than Phaseolus beans, making it a reliable warm-season substitute where snap beans struggle in midsummer. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Purplette Onion
description: This Dutch heirloom produces round, golf-ball-sized bulbs with glossy burgundy skin that fades to a soft pastel pink once cooked or pickled. Because it matures far faster than standard storage onions, it can be harvested young as a purple-tipped bunching onion or left to size up into a small mild bulb. The flavor is notably gentle, making raw slices in salads or quick pickles a popular use. Cluster plantings closely since bulbs stay small even at maturity, and harvest as soon as tops begin to fall for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Purslane (Verdolaga)
description: Sow direct 2–4 weeks after last frost in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; purslane requires warm, loose soil (70°F+) to germinate and thrives in heat and drought that would wilt most salad greens. Portulaca oleracea is one of the world's most widespread wild plants, a succulent, mat-forming annual with thick, water-storing, paddle-shaped leaves and reddish stems; in the Middle East, Mexico, and much of Europe and Asia it is cultivated as a valued summer vegetable — snipped stems and leaves are eaten fresh in salads (particularly Greek salads and Mexican ensalada), lightly sautéed, pickled, or added to soups and stews for a mild, slightly lemony, slightly mucilaginous texture. Purslane is extraordinarily rich in omega-3 fatty acids for a leafy green, and is one of the highest plant sources of ALA. It naturalizes aggressively in warm climates — harvest regularly to prevent unwanted spreading. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Pusa Makhmali Okra (IARI Parent Line, Light Green Indian Okra)
description: Pusa Makhmali is an open-pollinated okra selected by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute for smooth, light green pods on tall, productive plants well suited to warm-season cropping. Unlike its own offspring Pusa Sawani, which was specifically bred for resistance, Pusa Makhmali is highly susceptible to yellow vein mosaic virus, a whitefly-transmitted disease that can devastate plantings in regions with heavy vector pressure, so it performs best where okra pests and this virus are not a persistent problem. Pick pods every couple of days at 4-5 inches long, before the ribs toughen, to keep plants setting new fruit through the season. Give plants wide spacing and consistent moisture during flowering and pod set for the heaviest, most tender harvest. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Pusa Purple Long Brinjal (Indian Long Eggplant)
description: Bred and released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa Purple Long is a widely grown Indian brinjal variety valued for its glossy, light purple, slender fruit reaching 10 to 12 inches long with smooth, tender skin and few seeds. Plants are early and heavy yielding, well suited to both spring and autumn plantings in warm climates, and the long, uniform fruit is prized for slicing into rounds for frying or grilling as well as for classic Indian preparations like baingan bharta. Give plants rich, well-drained soil, steady moisture, and support if fruit loads get heavy, and harvest while skin is still glossy, since dull skin signals over-mature, seedier fruit. Its long harvest window and reliable production make it a staple variety across Indian home gardens and market farms. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Pusa Sawani Okra
description: Released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute as a cross between IC-1542 and Pusa Makhmali, Pusa Sawani is a vigorous, open-pollinated okra with medium-tall, short-jointed plants that adapt to a wide range of warm climates and cropping seasons, and it carries resistance to yellow vein mosaic virus, a damaging disease of the crop. Its dark green, smooth, five-ridged pods reach best eating quality at 4 to 5 inches long, well before they toughen, so frequent picking every couple of days keeps plants productive. The tall, sturdy plants benefit from wide spacing and steady moisture during pod set, and because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year if plants are isolated from other okra. It remains one of the most widely grown okra varieties across South Asia for its reliability and wide climatic adaptability. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Pusillus Dwarf Sweet Flag (Miniature Japanese Sweet Flag)
description: Pusillus is an extremely diminutive, solid-green cultivar of Japanese sweet flag, forming dense tufts of fine, grass-like leaves only two to three inches tall — among the smallest named selections of the species in cultivation. Its miniature scale suits container water gardens, trough plantings, bonsai underplanting, and other small-scale settings better than open pond margins, where larger cultivars like 'Ogon' or 'Variegatus' are more typical. Divide congested clumps in spring and replant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil or shallow standing water in shade to part shade. Unlike its gold- and white-variegated relatives, Pusillus is grown purely for its tiny scale and fine texture rather than leaf color. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Pyrethrum (Dalmatian Chrysanthemum, Dalmatian Pellitory)
description: Start seed indoors under light, since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; pyrethrum forms a low mound of finely cut, silvery-gray, aromatic foliage similar in texture to feverfew, and from late spring into summer sends up wiry stems topped with cheerful white, daisy-form flowers with yellow centers. This is the source plant of natural pyrethrin insecticide, which is concentrated in the still-closed flower heads and traditionally harvested just as the outer ring of petals opens, then dried quickly out of direct sun to preserve potency before grinding into powder. As an ornamental it needs only average care: good drainage is the one non-negotiable requirement, since wet winter soil is far more likely to kill it than cold. Plants are relatively short-lived, usually productive and vigorous for three to four years before they benefit from division or replacement. Deadhead spent flowers not being harvested to keep the plant tidy and encourage further bloom. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Qing Chestnut (Blight-Resistant Chinese Chestnut Cultivar)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Qing is a widely planted Chinese chestnut cultivar selected for strong resistance to chestnut blight, dependable annual production, and a manageable, relatively compact tree form compared with seedling Chinese chestnuts; nuts are medium-large, glossy mahogany-brown, and sweet, dropping free of the burr for easy harvest in September-October. It is a mainstay of southern nut-orchard and food-forest plantings because it tolerates heat and humidity far better than American or European chestnut, sets a heavy crop at a young age, and shows good resistance to the ambrosia beetle and gall wasp pressure that troubles many other chestnut selections in the Gulf South. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Qingxin Tea (Ruan Zhi Oolong, Green Heart)
description: Also called Ruan Zhi ('soft stem') or Green Heart, Qingxin is Taiwan's most important high-mountain oolong cultivar and the source of prized styles such as Dong Ding, Alishan, and Lishan oolong, valued for a delicate, creamy, floral cup at elevation. It is less vigorous and more demanding than heavier-yielding modern cultivars like Jin Xuan or Si Ji Chun, growing best on cool, misty high-elevation sites where slow growth concentrates flavor, and it can be more susceptible to leafhopper damage at lower elevations. Plant it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and expect a more modest yield than sturdier cultivars in exchange for its reputation among Taiwan's finest oolongs. Hand-pluck only the youngest leaves and bud for the best-quality lightly oxidized tea. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Quadrato d'Asti Pepper (Piedmontese Blocky Sweet Frying Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks ahead of the last frost, keeping soil warm for even germination, then transplant once frost danger has passed. Quadrato d'Asti ('square from Asti') is a traditional Piedmontese sweet pepper named for its home region in northern Italy, producing blocky, deeply four-lobed fruits with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to golden yellow or red depending on the strain grown. The dense flesh holds its shape well when roasted, grilled, or stuffed, and the flavor turns notably sweeter and richer as the fruit fully colors. Give plants sturdy support in windy gardens, since the heavy fruit can weigh down brittle branches. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Quaker Delight Pawpaw
description: Quaker Delight was selected at Wilmington College in Ohio and has placed well at the Ohio Pawpaw Festival tastings for its creamy texture and mild flavor. It ripens earlier than many named pawpaws, typically by early September, making it useful for extending the home harvest window when paired with later cultivars. Plant a second unrelated cultivar nearby for pollination, since pawpaw is self-incompatible. Mulch well and avoid waterlogged sites, as roots are sensitive to standing water. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Quedlinburger Niederliegende Lemon Balm (Procumbent High-Oil Lemon Balm)
description: This traditional German seed strain, named for the town of Quedlinburg near the Harz mountains, grows low and procumbent along the ground in its first year before shifting to a more upright habit in its second season, making it useful as a dense, aromatic groundcover as it matures. It carries a notably higher citronellal and essential-oil content than common lemon balm, giving a sharper lemon punch in teas and dried-herb blends, and it has proven more winter-hardy in trials than standard seed-grown lemon balm. Grow it exactly as you would ordinary lemon balm, in moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates, and shear plants back after their pale yellowish-white flowers fade to renew fragrant foliage and curb self-seeding. Divide congested clumps every few years once the plant settles into its upright second-year form. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Queen Ann Plum (Large Sweet Dark Purple California Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Queen Ann is a California Japanese plum producing large, dark purple-black fruit with sweet, juicy, amber flesh, prized for its substantial size and dependable, heavy production in commercial and home orchard settings. The tree is vigorous and well suited to standard Japanese plum growing conditions, delivering fruit with good flavor balance and firm enough texture to handle well from harvest to table. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to maintain good size, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and reaches full dark color for the sweetest, best-developed flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Queen Anne's Pocket Melon (Dudaim Melon, Pomegranate Melon)
description: Sow an inch deep in warm soil after frost danger passes, and let vines ramble along the ground or train them up a light trellis, since the fruit is small and light enough not to need slings. This heirloom, grown in Victorian and earlier gardens more for its intense perfume than for eating, produces palm-sized striped orange-and-yellow fruit that was traditionally carried in a pocket or reticule to scent a room or a handkerchief drawer. The flesh is edible but mild and mealy rather than sweet, so most modern gardeners grow it as a fragrant curiosity and conversation piece rather than a dessert melon. It is closely related to modern snake melons and has been kept in circulation mainly by heirloom seed stewards for its novelty and historical interest. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Queen of Siam Basil
description: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Queen of Siam basil is an ornamental and culinary hybrid producing striking dark purple-stemmed plants with large, green leaves and purple-flushed undersides, topped by spectacular spikes of deep purple to magenta flower bracts — one of the most ornamentally dramatic of all basil types. The flavor combines the clove-sweet base of sweet basil with a distinct anise and licorice note similar to Thai basil, making it suitable for both Italian and Southeast Asian cooking. The bolt-resistant, continuously flowering habit produces an extended season of ornamental bloom that makes this basil equally valuable in the flower garden as in the herb garden. The deep purple flower spikes are excellent as cut flowers. In zone 9 the heat tolerance and continuous flower production through summer make Queen of Siam the most reliably ornamental basil for summer landscapes, where it continues flowering attractively even after the flavor of the leaves has declined with heat. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Queen of the Night Cereus
description: Plant in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun in zones 9–12; the 'Queen of the Night' name is shared with several night-blooming cacti, but this species — the monstrose cereus sold commonly in garden centers and grocery stores as 'peruvian apple cactus' (now distinguished from C. repandus) — is a large, multi-ribbed columnar cactus from South America that becomes a substantial, multi-stemmed specimen in frost-free conditions. The large, white, intensely fragrant flowers open at night for a single evening in summer — a dramatic event attracting moths and night-pollinators. The fruits that develop are round, red to yellow, with white, sweet, refreshing flesh surrounding black seeds, eaten raw in South America where they are called 'pitaya' or 'tuna.' More cold-tolerant than most tropical cacti, this species survives brief temperatures down to about 25°F in zone 9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Queensland Blue Pumpkin (Australian Heirloom Blue-Gray Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the vigorous vines. Queensland Blue is a classic Australian heirloom pumpkin, developed in the 19th century and still one of the most widely grown pumpkin varieties in Australia, valued for its distinctive, deeply ribbed, slate-blue-gray rind — a color that stands out dramatically against typical orange pumpkins in a fall display — and its dense, dry, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and pies. The hard rind, while tough to cut into, is also the reason for the variety's outstanding keeping quality; well-cured fruit routinely stores for six months or longer in a cool, dry location, among the best storage life of any winter squash. Fruits typically run 8-12 pounds with a flattened, ribbed shape. Vines are vigorous and productive given full sun, fertile soil, and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and resists a fingernail, and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to sweeten over the following months. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Quick Snack Cucumber
description: 'Quick Snack' is a compact, parthenocarpic cucumber bred for 6-8 inch pots on a sunny windowsill, counter, or balcony. Because it sets fruit without pollination, it produces well indoors with no bees needed; keep it in bright light and evenly moist soil. Harvest the smooth, dark green fruits young at 1.5-2.5 inches long for the best sweet, crisp flavor and to keep the plant producing. Feed lightly and provide a small trellis or let vines trail over the pot rim. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Quickpick Pinkeye Cowpea (Compact Top-Set Purple Hull Pea)
description: Quickpick was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a compact pinkeye purple hull type bred for resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus. Pods are dark purple, 7-8 inches long, and set simultaneously at the top of the plant, giving the variety its name and making a single harvest pass practical. Seeds are cream colored with a large maroon eye, larger than older purple hull standards, and cook up with classic pinkeye flavor. Matures quickly at around 60 days, making it useful for a second planting later in the Gulf Coast summer. Matures in 60–65 days from seed.

name: Quinault Strawberry (Day-Neutral Everbearing Pacific Northwest Strawberry)
description: Plant in spring in a rich, well-prepared bed; do not remove flowers from Quinault in the first year — as a day-neutral type it will produce fruit on new plants; allow fall runners to fill in the bed for subsequent seasons; remove runners in summer to redirect energy to fruit production. Quinault strawberry is a Washington State University-developed day-neutral (everbearing) variety (released 1967) that produces fruit regardless of day length, yielding crops in spring, mid-summer (briefly), and fall rather than the concentrated June-bearing harvest of standard varieties. This fruiting pattern is genuinely different from both June-bearing (single spring crop) and older everbearing (two main crops, spring and fall) varieties — true day-neutral varieties like Quinault produce small but continuous fruit throughout the growing season whenever temperatures are moderate (below 80°F). The practical implication for home gardeners is that Quinault plants bear fruit in their first growing season from spring plantings, providing immediate gratification without waiting through an entire growing year before harvesting. This first-year fruiting makes Quinault a particularly good variety for children's gardens, community gardens, and impatient gardeners. The variety was developed at Washington State University for Pacific Northwest conditions (mild, cool summers), where it has been widely grown since its release. The berries are large, red, and soft with a sweet flavor similar to alpine strawberries — best for fresh eating rather than processing. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Quince
description: Quince is self-fertile and one of the easier tree fruits to grow, tolerating heavier and wetter soils than apples or pears. It needs 300–500 chill hours, which suits zones 5–9 broadly. The fruit is astringent and almost always cooked rather than eaten raw; it turns pink when heated with sugar and is prized for marmalade, paste (membrillo), and jelly. Harvest in late autumn when the fruit turns fully golden-yellow and fragrant, before the first hard freeze. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Quince BA29 Pear Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; BA29 is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit. A French quince selection long used as a dwarfing pear rootstock in European orchards, it produces a smaller, more precocious tree than seedling pear rootstocks, roughly 50-65 percent of standard size, though it is somewhat less cold-hardy and more prone to iron chlorosis on high-pH soils than the seedling and OHxF pear rootstocks more commonly used in North America. Because many pear varieties are graft-incompatible with quince, an interstem of a compatible pear variety such as Old Home is often bench-grafted between the quince rootstock and the desired scion variety. Graft or double-work a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and reserve this rootstock for milder climates and growers specifically wanting a smaller, earlier-bearing pear tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Quinoa
description: Broadcast or sow seed 1/4 in deep in firm, well-drained soil and thin to 12–18 in when seedlings are 3–4 in tall; quinoa is highly drought-tolerant once established and prefers cool, dry weather through seed fill. The colorful seed heads (red, orange, or cream) are ready to harvest when the seed falls easily from the panicle when rubbed — typically after the first light fall frost has dried the plant. Cut the seed heads into paper bags, dry for 1–2 weeks in a warm airy space, then thresh by rubbing heads between hands and winnow away the chaff outdoors in a breeze. Rinse seed thoroughly before eating to remove bitter saponins from the seed coat. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: R134 Rambutan (Malaysian Selection)
description: Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from wind; R134 is one of the principal commercial rambutan selections released by Malaysian breeding programs, valued for medium-sized round fruit with soft green-tipped spinterns, a high percentage of edible aril, and a good sugar-to-acid balance. Unlike lychee and longan, rambutan has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, humid conditions with no dry-season stress to fruit well, which limits reliable outdoor cultivation in the US to South Florida and Hawaii. Trees are large and need considerable room to reach full bearing size, typically beginning to fruit four to six years after planting a grafted specimen. Keep soil consistently moist — unlike many tropical fruit trees, rambutan is intolerant of drought stress at any stage of growth. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun with at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination; rabbiteye blueberry is the blueberry of the Gulf Coast South — native to the coastal plain from Texas to Florida and naturally adapted to hot summers, mild winters, and the low-chill conditions (below 45°F hours) that prevent highbush blueberries from fruiting reliably in zone 8–9. The name 'rabbiteye' refers to the pale, pinkish color of the unripe berries before they turn deep blue-purple at maturity. Plants are large, vigorous, and long-lived — potentially producing for 40–50 years — with spring flowers that attract early native bees, summer berries that ripen over an extended period from May through August depending on cultivar, and attractive red-orange fall foliage. A fundamental food plant for Gulf Coast edible gardens that produces abundantly with minimal care in appropriate acidic soil conditions. The primary challenge in the Gulf Coast is achieving and maintaining the necessary soil acidity; soil acidification with sulfur or planting in raised beds filled with peat, pine bark, and acidic compost is often necessary. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Racemosa Passionflower (Red Cluster-Flowered Passion Vine)
description: Give this Brazilian native a warm, sheltered site with a sturdy trellis or arbor, since Passiflora racemosa is considerably more cold-sensitive than hardy garden passionflowers like maypop or blue passionflower and is best treated as a container plant that can be moved under cover, or planted only in the mildest, most protected corners of a zone 9b-10 garden. Unlike most passionflowers, which bear solitary flowers at each leaf axil, racemosa produces its vivid scarlet-red blooms in pendant, elongating clusters that can each carry a dozen or more flowers over several weeks, making it one of the showiest passionflowers for a warm patio or conservatory. Grow in rich, well-drained soil with light shade during the hottest part of the day to prevent leaf scorch, and water regularly through the growing season while letting the soil dry slightly between waterings in winter. Hummingbirds are frequent visitors to the tubular red flowers, and the vine can be cut back hard in late winter to control size without sacrificing the coming season's bloom. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Racer Pumpkin (F1 Extra-Early Jack-O-Lantern Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds directly in hills once soil has warmed, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill spaced roughly three to four feet apart. Racer was developed through a University of New Hampshire and Johnny's Selected Seeds breeding collaboration for exceptionally rapid ripening, producing blocky 12-16 pound fruit with dark green handles well before most other jack-o'-lantern types color up. In Gulf Coast gardens the short vine and early finish are real advantages, letting fruit set and mature before the worst of late-summer humidity drives powdery mildew and vine borer pressure. Harvest once the rind has hardened to a deep, uniform orange and cure in a warm, airy spot for about a week before moving pumpkins to cooler storage. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Radar Onion (Overwintering Onion)
description: Radar is a widely grown F1 overwintering onion bred to give gardeners a bulb harvest weeks ahead of spring-sown types by getting a head start on root growth before the ground freezes. Set out young bulbs in firmed, well-drained soil in early autumn, leaving the tip just above the surface, and keep beds weed-free through the mild winter growth period. The straw-yellow, semi-globe bulbs bulk up rapidly once spring days lengthen, typically ready weeks earlier than spring-set maincrop onions. Because overwintered bulbs are generally milder and less firm than maincrop storage onions, use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it long term. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Radicchio
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep and thin to 10–14 in; radicchio produces loose, green summer foliage before forming its characteristic red and white tight head as days shorten and temperatures fall. Cut back summer foliage to about 1 in when plants look tired and cool temperatures arrive; new heads will form from the crown within 3–4 weeks. Harvest compact heads by cutting at the base once they feel firm and the color is deep burgundy. Hard frost may damage outer leaves but the inner head often survives. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Radicchio Rossa di Verona
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Verona is the classic round-headed radicchio from the Verona region of Italy and the dominant variety in world commerce — the compact, baseball-sized heads of deep red-purple leaves with white midribs are the defining image of radicchio. The bitter, slightly sweet flavor is characteristically Italian and develops most fully after light frost exposure, which converts some starches to sugars and intensifies the red-purple anthocyanin pigmentation. In zone 9 plant in August–September for a fall-through-winter crop; the heads form and mature in cool weather from October through February. For sweeter flavor, blanch heads by loosely tying outer leaves over the center 1–2 weeks before harvest, reducing bitterness 30–40%. Rossa di Verona is excellent grilled (the bitterness mellows dramatically under high heat), used in risotto bianco, or eaten raw in Gorgonzola and walnut salads where the bitter note is a feature rather than a flaw. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Radish Microgreens
description: Radish is one of the fastest and most forgiving microgreens, germinating within a day or two of dense sowing on a moist tray. Keep the blackout period short, then give bright light to develop sturdy stems and, in some varieties, a pink or purple blush. Mist regularly and provide airflow to keep the vigorous growth clean. Harvest the crisp, boldly peppery shoots in about a week at the cotyledon stage. Matures in 6–10 days from seed.

name: Rainbow Blend Pole Cherry Tomato
description: This color-coded blend produces cherry tomatoes in orange, yellow, brown, red, and green, mixing mostly indeterminate pole types with one determinate. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm soil in full sun. Provide sturdy stakes or tall cages for the vining plants and pinch suckers to keep them manageable. Harvest the sweet, bite-sized fruits as each color ripens for a colorful, all-summer supply. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Rainbow Carrot
description: This F1 hybrid produces white, yellow, orange, and coral roots from a single sowing, each 7-9 inches long, uniform and conical. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination period. Thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart so roots size up evenly, and harvest this early-season Nantes x Imperator type once shoulders reach full color. Cool weather sweetens the flavor. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Rainbow Chard
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Rainbow Chard is a mixture of Swiss chard varieties with stalks in multiple vivid colors — red, yellow, orange, gold, pink, white, and bicolors — creating one of the most visually striking vegetable plantings possible in a kitchen or ornamental garden. The broad, crinkled, dark green leaves and brilliantly colored stalks make Rainbow Chard simultaneously one of the most productive and most ornamental vegetables available. Nutritionally, Swiss chard is among the most nutrient-dense vegetables: extremely high in vitamins K, A, and C, iron, calcium, and magnesium. The mild, spinach-like flavor of young leaves is pleasant raw in salads; older leaves and the colorful stalks are best sautéed, stir-fried, or added to soups where the color partially fades but the substantial flavor and nutrition remain. The partial shade tolerance makes Rainbow Chard one of the best vegetables for gardens with limited full-sun exposure. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Rainbow Chard (Five-Color Silverbeet)
