description: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil, thinning to 6–12 inches; rainbow chard is a mixture of white, yellow, orange, red, and vivid pink-stemmed chard varieties grown together, producing an exceptional display of color in the garden while providing the same mild, earthy leaves as single-colored chard. The stems of different colors have slightly different flavor intensities (red-stemmed are earthier, white-stemmed milder) but all are equally nutritious and versatile in cooking. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep plants productive for months. An outstanding cut-and-come-again green for the productive ornamental garden. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Rainbow Papaya (PRSV-Resistant Transgenic Hawaiian Papaya)
description: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting or sow directly in warm soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Rainbow is the transgenic, papaya ringspot virus-resistant papaya developed in Hawaii after the virus devastated nearly all of the state's main papaya-growing region in the early 1990s. Researchers engineered papaya lines carrying a gene for the virus's own coat protein, which triggers a resistance response in the plant; the resulting transgenic line became the parent cultivar SunUp. Rainbow itself is a bisexual F1 hybrid produced by crossing SunUp with the traditional, non-transgenic Kapoho cultivar, combining reliable ringspot virus resistance with Kapoho's familiar yellow-orange, sweet, small-seed-cavity fruit quality. Rainbow and SunUp were released to Hawaiian growers in 1998 and are widely credited with saving Hawaii's papaya industry from collapse within a few years of release. The compact tree begins bearing within roughly seven to ten months of germination in warm conditions, and fruit should be picked as the skin begins to turn from green to yellow, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature. As with other papayas, protect from frost and provide consistent moisture and a balanced fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality. Matures in 210–330 days from seed.

name: Rainbow Pillar Serviceberry
description: Selected by Edward Losely from a group of Amelanchier canadensis seedlings and sold as Rainbow Pillar, this strongly columnar serviceberry stays only 8-10 feet wide while reaching 15-20 feet tall, making it useful as a narrow street tree, screen, or vertical accent where a spreading serviceberry would not fit. It carries the same white spring flower clusters, edible red-to-purple June berries beloved by birds (and usable in pastries and preserves), and vivid multi-colored fall foliage as its wide-crowned relatives, with foliage that is notably unaffected by powdery mildew. Grow it in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and expect it to tolerate the occasional dry spell once established. Because it is a patented, propagated clone, buy named plants rather than seedlings to guarantee the columnar habit. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rainbow Swiss Chard
description: Soak the corky seed clusters overnight to speed germination, then sow half an inch deep directly in the garden. Thin seedlings to 6-12 inches, since each cluster can produce several plants. The vivid red, pink, yellow, orange, and white stems hold their color best in full sun with steady moisture. Harvest outer leaves regularly on a cut-and-come-again basis and the plant will keep pushing new growth well into fall. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Rainforest Pearl Finger Lime (Pale Pink-White Caviar Lime Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Rainforest Pearl bears slender, dark green fruit filled with pale pink to white, translucent, caviar-like pulp vesicles that burst with tangy citrus flavor, a color combination especially prized by chefs for garnishing seafood and desserts. It is self-fertile and, like other finger lime cultivars, bears at a younger age on grafted rootstock than most seedling-grown plants. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh as a garnish, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rainier Cherry (Blushing Cherry, Yellow Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Rainier is considered the premium sweet cherry cultivar — producing large, blush-yellow to golden-red fruit with creamy yellow flesh that is exceptionally sweet, almost honeylike, with delicate flavor considered superior to the firmer, darker varieties. It was developed at Washington State University in 1954 and named for Mount Rainier. The firm, thick skin makes Rainier more resistant to cracking than some sweet cherries, but the pale color means bird damage can be severe — netting is often necessary. Rainier requires 700–800 winter chill hours (hours below 45°F) to fruit reliably, limiting it to zones 5–8; in warmer climates, performance is inconsistent. A pollinizer (Bing, Black Tartarian, or Lapins cherry) planted within 50 feet is necessary for full crop production. Prune during dormancy to maintain an open-center or modified central-leader form. Bears fruit on spurs that persist for many years — avoid pruning productive spur wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Raja Puri Banana (Fast-Fruiting Dwarf Banana)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Raja Puri is a dwarf, fast-fruiting banana cultivar especially popular with Gulf Coast and Florida home growers because its short 4–7 foot pseudostem reaches flowering size and produces a bunch within one warm growing season — a critical advantage over taller bananas that need more than a year of frost-free growth to reach fruiting size, since a hard freeze that kills the pseudostem each winter resets a tall variety's clock but barely slows a fast, compact grower like Raja Puri. Fruit is medium-small, sweet, and good for fresh eating, borne in bunches lower to the ground than most bananas, which also makes bunches easier to bag and protect from wind damage. Provide consistent moisture and heavy monthly feeding through the growing season, since bananas are fast, heavy feeders. In zone 8b–9, mulch the root zone deeply in fall to protect the rhizome through winter, and expect the pseudostem to die back with hard freezes and resprout from the root system in spring. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Rajapuri Banana (Compact Indian Dessert Banana, Cold-Tolerant Edible for Zone 9)
description: Plant divisions in spring in full sun, rich soil. Maintain moisture and fertilize regularly. Cut fruited pseudostems to ground after harvest; allow pups to develop for next year's crop. Rajapuri Banana is a traditional cultivar from the Indian subcontinent where it is one of the most popular dessert bananas — cultivated in home gardens and small plantations throughout India, particularly in Maharashtra and other banana-growing states, for its excellent flavor and manageable plant size. In the Gulf South context, Rajapuri offers several practical advantages over the more common edible bananas: its compact height (8–12 feet) is more appropriate for most home landscapes than the 15–20 foot height of tall cultivars, making management of the pseudostems easier; its cold tolerance is better than most Cavendish types, improving survival in zone 9's occasional freezes; and its fruit quality — shorter, chubby fingers with extremely sweet, rich, creamy flesh — is considered superior to supermarket Cavendish bananas by most fresh-tasting evaluations. The fruit is typically ready to pick when the skin is still green-yellow (watch for the ridges to round out and the skin to lighten) and ripened indoors to full yellow with a pronounced aroma. For zone 9 Gulf Coast home gardeners with full sun and space for 8×10 feet of planting, Rajapuri is one of the most rewarding fruiting plants that can be grown — producing large bunches of genuinely excellent bananas within 12–18 months of planting a good-sized pup. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Rakkyo (Chinese Onion, Bakeri)
description: Plant small bulbs in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; rakkyo (Allium chinense) is a small, perennial allium grown throughout Japan, China, and Southeast Asia specifically for pickling — one of Japan's most beloved preserved foods, pickled rakkyo (rakkyo no su-zuke) are the sweet-tart, crispy pickled bulbs served as a condiment alongside curry rice, bento boxes, and traditional Japanese meals. The small, elongated bulbs are harvested in early summer, cleaned, and pickled in vinegar with sugar and salt. They have a milder, more delicate onion flavor than regular onions, with a distinctive crispy texture retained through the pickling process. The plant itself is an attractive ornamental — the purple-pink flowers appear in fall on upright stems and are followed by the edible bulbs that multiply underground like shallots. In mild climates it naturalizes readily and provides bulbs year after year with minimal care. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Ralls Janet Apple (Late-Season Virginia Heirloom, Parent of Red Delicious and Fuji)
description: Ralls Janet dates to 18th-century Virginia and became famous in 20th-century Missouri and Illinois orchards for its ability to shrug off harsh winters and heat waves alike. Very late bloom time helps the flowers dodge spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering apples, and the small, firm, tart-sweet fruit stores in a root cellar into late winter. It is one of the two parents of Red Delicious and, through a Japanese breeding program, a grandparent of Fuji, making it an interesting living link for gardeners who grow both modern and heirloom apples. Choose it for its toughness and storability rather than fresh-eating size, since the fruit is on the small side compared to modern dessert apples. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rama Tulsi (Green Holy Basil)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant productive and bushy through the season. Rama is the classic green-leaved, green-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), considered by many Ayurvedic practitioners to be the mildest and sweetest-flavored of the traditional tulsi types, with a fragrant, clove-and-pepper aroma softer than the more pungent purple Krishna form. It is the variety most commonly dried for tulsi tea, prized for its balanced, adaptogenic-reputed flavor, and is also used fresh in Thai and Indian cooking. The vigorous, upright plants produce abundant foliage over a long warm season and, like other tulsi, are considered sacred in Hindu tradition and often grown near the home for both culinary and spiritual purposes. A rewarding, productive warm-season herb for tea and cooking, zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Ramapo Tomato (Rutgers Jersey-Style Heirloom-Flavor Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vine. Ramapo was bred at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station in 1968 and quickly became beloved throughout the New Jersey area for its rich, well-balanced, old-fashioned tomato flavor, but it fell out of commercial availability for decades until gardener demand led Rutgers to bring seed back into production through its 'Rediscover the Jersey Tomato' program. It combines much of the deep, sweet-tart flavor complexity associated with heirloom tomatoes with the disease resistance and reliability of a modern hybrid, producing medium-to-large red slicing fruit over a long summer season. Prune suckers lightly on the lower part of the plant for better airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture consistent, which reduces cracking and blossom-end rot on the larger fruit. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Rambai (Burmese Grape)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–11; rambai is a medium-sized Southeast Asian fruit tree in the Phyllanthaceae family that produces large, pendulous clusters of small, grape-like fruits — ranging in color from pale yellow to deep pink or red — borne on the branches and trunk in the cauliflorous habit shared by many tropical rainforest species. The translucent, sweet-tart flesh surrounds relatively large seeds and is eaten fresh or made into juices, wines, and pickles across Myanmar, Bangladesh, Thailand, and Malaysia, where the fruit is a beloved seasonal treat sold in local markets. Trees are dioecious, meaning separate male and female trees are required for fruit production, so plant at least two seedlings or obtain a confirmed female tree grafted onto a rootstock. Maintain high humidity and consistent moisture for best growth, and apply a thick layer of organic mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist throughout the year. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Rambai (Rambeh, Betanbar)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruit production — rambai is dioecious. Baccaurea motleyana (rambai or rambeh) is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree native to the humid lowland forests of the Malay Peninsula, Thailand, and Borneo — closely related to langsat (Lansium domesticum) in lifestyle and fruit appearance, though in a different botanical family (Phyllanthaceae). The tree produces long, pendulous clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), thin-skinned, yellow to pale-orange fruits directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), similar in habit to cacao and jackfruit. The sweet-acid, translucent-white, jelly-like flesh has a pleasant, mild, tropical flavor — somewhat sweet, gently tart, with a slight astringency when slightly underripe. Rambai is eaten fresh in Malaysia and southern Thailand, and is also used in traditional cooking and beverages. The tree requires genuinely hot, humid, tropical conditions without frost — suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental US (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). It is dioecious, requiring both a male and female tree for fruit production; grafted female trees are occasionally available from specialty tropical nurseries. Almost entirely unknown outside Southeast Asia in cultivation; an exceptional and very rare find for the dedicated tropical fruit collector. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rambutan
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in a frost-free location; rambutan is damaged at any temperature below 40°F and is one of the most cold-sensitive common fruit trees. Most cultivars bear both male and hermaphrodite flowers on separate trees, so plant at least one male tree alongside female or hermaphrodite fruiting trees to ensure pollination. Trees require consistent rainfall or irrigation — roughly 60–150 inches of annual precipitation equivalent — especially during fruit development, with a short dry period to stimulate flowering. Harvest clusters when the leathery spines (soft spinterns) have turned fully red or yellow depending on variety and the flesh is translucent, sweet, and separates cleanly from the seed. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ramie
description: Plant root divisions 2–3 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Boehmeria nivea spreads aggressively by rhizome — contain with deep edging or grow in a dedicated plot; harvest stems when 36–50 inches tall by cutting at ground level, typically 2–4 harvests per year in warm climates. Boehmeria nivea (Ramie, China Grass, or White Ramie) is a robust, rhizomatous, herbaceous perennial in the Urticaceae (nettle) family native to subtropical to tropical East Asia — China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and the Indo-Chinese peninsula — where it has been cultivated for textile fiber for at least 6,000 years, making it one of the oldest cultivated fiber crops on earth. The bast fiber extracted from the long, upright stems is among the strongest, longest (individual fibers can reach 4–6 inches), and most lustrous of all natural textile fibers — stronger than flax (linen) and comparable to cotton in softness but with a silky sheen — and is used for high-quality clothing, table linens, lace, canvas, industrial fiber, and blended with cotton and silk. Processing ramie for spinning is labor-intensive (requiring degumming), which limited commercial adoption in the West, but in China, Korea, Japan, and the Philippines, Ramie clothing production is substantial. Leaves of Boehmeria nivea are also nutritious (20–27% crude protein) and fed to livestock and fish (particularly carp) in China as a high-protein fodder. An ornamental value in the large, white-undersided leaves. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Rampion Bellflower (Rapunzel Root, Edible Bellflower)
description: Press seeds onto the soil surface without covering (light required for germination); keep the seedbed consistently moist until germination; thin to 4–6 inches apart; harvest roots in fall of the first year or early spring of the second year by digging carefully with a fork; the slender white roots are eaten raw or cooked, and the young leaves and shoots are used in salads. Rampion (Campanula rapunculus) is a European biennial wildflower and traditional kitchen garden vegetable that is best known as the plant at the center of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale 'Rapunzel': the story's plot hinges on a pregnant woman's craving for the rampion growing in the enchanted garden next door, her husband's theft of the plant to satisfy the craving, and the consequence of giving up their daughter as payment — 'Rapunzel' is simply the German and Italian name for Campanula rapunculus. The real rampion is a slender-rooted biennial native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, whose edible taproot (resembling a small, white parsnip or radish) was eaten raw in salads (with a mild, slightly nutty, turnip-like flavor) or cooked in soups and stews in French, Italian, and German kitchen gardens from medieval times through the 1800s. The young leaves are also edible — mildly sweet and tender — and were used in spring salads. Rampion largely disappeared from cultivation as more productive root vegetables (parsnips, turnips, carrots) displaced it, but the plant is still grown by kitchen garden historians and edible plant collectors. In its second year it sends up 2–4 foot spikes of pale violet-blue, bell-shaped flowers typical of the bellflower family. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Ramps
description: Plant bulb divisions in early fall in moist, very rich, leaf-mold-enriched, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade under deciduous hardwoods — the classic habitat is slopes with sugar maple, beech, and tulip poplar; ramps are a celebrated foraged edible of eastern North American forests with broad, smooth, rich-green leaves (like lily of the valley) and a small, white, garlic-like bulb with an intense, complex garlic-wild onion flavor that has become a culinary phenomenon. Both leaves and bulbs are edible; leaves emerge in early spring before the canopy closes and die back by June. Harvest no more than one leaf per plant per year, and never take more than a third of any colony to ensure sustainable harvest. Slow-growing: colonies planted from bulb divisions become harvestable in 3–5 years and persist indefinitely in suitable shaded conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ramsey Grape Rootstock (Salt Creek, Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Nematode-Resistant Understock)
description: Ramsey, also marketed as Salt Creek, is a Vitis champinii rootstock selection, from the same tough native Texas species behind the Dog Ridge and Tampa rootstocks already grown across the Gulf South. Its deep, vigorous root system gives grafted vines strong drought tolerance and the ability to perform in poor, sandy, or high-pH caliche soils, while its champinii parentage confers useful field tolerance to Pierce's disease and strong resistance to root-knot nematodes. Growers bench-graft or bud a named bunch grape cultivar onto young Ramsey rootstock rather than growing it for its own fruit, which is small, seedy, and of no culinary interest. It is one of the standard rootstock choices in hot, humid, nematode- and Pierce's disease-prone vineyard sites in Texas and the wider Gulf Coast. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ramsons (Bear's Garlic)
description: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade, or plant bulb offsets 2–3 inches deep in fall; ramsons naturalizes readily by seed and offsets to form dense colonies under deciduous trees, though the foliage dies back completely by early summer and must be located carefully to avoid disturbing the dormant bulbs. Allium ursinum is a European native wild garlic with broad, glossy, bright-green, strap-shaped leaves (resembling lily of the valley) that carpet the woodland floor in spring and bear strong garlic flavor and aroma; the leaves, bulbs, and the attractive white, star-shaped umbel flowers in late spring are all edible and highly prized in European culinary traditions — the fresh leaves can be used exactly like garlic in pestos, soups, salads, and compound butters. It naturalizes to form spectacular carpets under deciduous trees and is one of the finest and most useful edible groundcovers for partial to full shade; plant away from lily of the valley (Convallaria) which is toxic and has similar foliage. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Ranch Elderberry (Missouri-Bred American Elderberry Cultivar)
description: Ranch is an American elderberry selection developed through the University of Missouri's elderberry improvement program alongside better-known releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood, chosen for productive, well-formed clusters and reliable performance in commercial-scale plantings. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil, and keep well watered during establishment since elderberries are shallow-rooted and drought-sensitive. Large, flat-topped white flower clusters appear in early summer and can be harvested for elderflower cordial, followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in late summer used for syrup, jam, and wine after cooking. Prune out the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the shrub vigorous and productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Randy Pistachio (Early-Pollen-Shedding Male Pollinizer)
description: Randy is a male pistachio selection grown solely as a pollen source, bearing no nuts itself but shedding pollen earlier than the older standard male cultivar 'Peters', which helps it better overlap with the bloom of widely planted female cultivars like Kerman. Site male trees evenly through a planting, or in a block upwind of prevailing spring winds, so pollen reaches female trees efficiently. Culture is identical to fruiting pistachio: deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and good heat during the growing season, with minimal water once established since pistachio is notably drought tolerant. Prune to an open form in early years to establish strong scaffold branches, since the tree needs no fruit-thinning attention. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Ranger Blackberry
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ranger is a mid-20th-century erect, thorny blackberry from the early era of USDA bramble breeding, valued today mostly for its toughness, cold hardiness, and productivity under low-input conditions rather than for the largest berries. Fruit is medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, well suited to jam, jelly, and cobbler more than fresh eating. The upright canes are self-supporting in home gardens, though a simple wire trellis keeps rows tidier and eases picking. Prune out spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest and thin new primocanes to 4-6 per plant, tipping them at about 36 inches in late summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry next year's crop. Its old-fashioned toughness and reliable cropping make Ranger a good pick for a low-maintenance hedgerow planting rather than a showcase bed. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Rangpur Lime
description: Rangpur lime is actually a mandarin-lime hybrid (not a true lime) prized for its mandarin orange appearance, intensely sour juice, and significantly greater cold-hardiness than Key or Persian limes, making it a practical choice for zone 8 citrus gardens and container culture. It is self-fertile, productive as a single tree, and bears fruit nearly year-round in warm climates; fruit ripens to a deep orange-red color similar to a tangerine. Use the juice as a direct substitute for regular lime juice in cocktails, marinades, and curries — it is slightly more complex and aromatic. Harvest when the fruit has turned fully orange-red and yields to gentle pressure; fruit can be held on the tree for several weeks after ripening without significant quality loss. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rapiah Rambutan
description: Rapiah has been one of the dominant rambutan cultivars planted in Java since the 1930s, distinguished from most other cultivars by unusually dry, firm, sweet flesh with lower juice content, which some growers prefer for out-of-hand eating because it separates cleanly from the seed with little mess. Fruit is medium-sized with soft red spines and a mild, consistently sweet flavor. Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with wind protection, providing steady irrigation through bloom and fruit fill despite the cultivar's drier flesh, since the tree itself still requires abundant moisture to crop well. Rapiah has no cold tolerance and is limited to the warmest, most humid tropical and near-tropical sites. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rapini (Broccoli Raab)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rapini (broccoli raab, cime di rapa) is an Italian-heritage cool-season brassica grown for its tender stem tips, leaves, and immature flower bud clusters harvested before the yellow flowers fully open. Harvest the central stem with 6 inches of stem, leaves, and tight bud cluster when buds are still green and closed — this is the prime eating stage. The characteristic pleasantly bitter flavor (due to glucosinolates) intensifies in heat and with age. Rapini is a staple of southern Italian cooking — used in pasta, sautéed with garlic and olive oil, and in sausage dishes throughout Campania, Apulia, and Calabria. Succession sow every 2 weeks from late summer into fall for a continuous harvest through October–November in zone 7+. After the main head is cut, side shoots continue to produce smaller edible buds for several additional weeks. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Rapini (Broccoli Rabe, Cime di Rapa)
description: Direct sow thinly in early spring or late summer in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; thin to 6 inches. Rapini (broccoli rabe, cime di rapa, or in dialect rabé) is a fast-growing cool-season vegetable in the Brassica rapa family, more closely related to turnips than to true broccoli; the tender stems, small leaves, and unopened flower buds are harvested together as a bundle when the buds are still tightly closed (40–60 days from seed). The flavor is distinctive — pleasantly bitter, peppery, and slightly nutty — and is considered an essential element of Italian-American and southern Italian cooking: rapini sautéed with garlic, olive oil, and red pepper flakes is the classic accompaniment to sausage, pasta, and orecchiette in Pugliese and Neapolitan traditions. In warmer climates (zones 8–11) it is an outstanding cool-season crop for fall-through-spring production, bolting quickly in heat. Matures in 42–60 days from seed.

name: Rapini Broccoli Raab
description: Rapini, or broccoli raab, is grown for its tender stems, leaves, and small budding florets with a pleasantly bitter, peppery flavor. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart, growing in the cool weather of spring or fall to avoid rapid bolting. Harvest the whole plant or cut budding shoots just before the small yellow flowers open, when flavor is best. Fast to mature, it can be succession sown for repeat harvests. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Rappahannock Pawpaw (Early-Ripening Peterson Pawpaw)
description: Rappahannock is one of Neal Peterson's seven named Peterson Pawpaw selections and is notable for ripening earlier than its siblings, typically in mid-September, which spreads the harvest window and gets fruit off the tree before early fall storms. The flesh is a brighter yellow than most pawpaws, low in fiber, and unusually low in seed count for the genus, making it a favorite for fresh eating. Like all pawpaws it is self-incompatible, so a second, genetically distinct cultivar or seedling must be planted nearby for pollination and fruit set. Expect grafted trees to begin bearing in four to six years, with best performance where winters deliver reliable chilling but summers stay long and warm. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Raritan Hazelnut (Rutgers EFB-Resistant Eastern Filbert)
description: Raritan is a vigorous, upright hazelnut released in 2020 by Rutgers University, one of the first cultivars bred specifically to combine strong quantitative resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight with high yields under Mid-Atlantic growing conditions, where the disease had long prevented commercial European hazelnut production outside the Pacific Northwest. It produces medium, round, well-blanching kernels and ripens early, typically ready to harvest in the first to second week of September. Because it is self-incompatible, plant it with a genetically compatible pollenizer such as Monmouth or Somerset, sited so their bloom periods overlap. It performs best in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range, reflecting its breeding and testing focus on New Jersey and the broader Mid-Atlantic region. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rat Tail Radish (Edible-Pod Radish, Podding Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/2 inch deep after last frost; allow plants to grow and bolt (flower); harvest pods when 3–6 inches long and still crisp and tender — before the seeds inside develop fully; harvest daily once production begins as pods become fibrous when overripe. Rat Tail Radish (Raphanus sativus var. caudatus) is a Southeast Asian and South Asian radish cultivated specifically for the edible seed pods it produces after bolting, rather than for the root — a striking reversal of the usual reason for growing radishes. When most radishes bolt, the gardener curses the heat and pulls the plant; with Rat Tail Radish, bolting is the point. The plants grow to 24–36 inches tall, produce small flowers (white or pale violet), and then develop long, slender, arching or pendant seed pods typically 4–8 inches long with a characteristic curved tip that gives the variety its common name. The pods are harvested young and tender (before full seed development) and have a crunchy, snappy texture and peppery, radish-flavored taste that is excellent raw in salads, pickled, stir-fried in Asian cooking, or used in Indian chutneys and curries where the peppery pod flavor is prized. The purple-podded forms (the most commonly grown) are visually dramatic and the pods are mildly ornamental on the plant. A practical advantage: Rat Tail Radish tolerates summer heat that destroys root radish production, providing fresh radish flavor throughout summer months. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Rat's Tail Radish
description: Unlike ordinary radishes, 'Rat's Tail' is grown for its abundant slender, edible seed pods borne above ground on tall 2-5 foot plants. Direct sow 1/2 inch deep, thin to 6-12 inches apart, and give the plants room and support as they grow large. Harvest the crisp, spicy pods young at 3-5 inches long while still tender, picking often to keep new pods forming. Heat tolerant, it produces through summer when other radishes bolt. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Ratoli Hazelnut (Spanish Eastern Filbert Blight Resistance Source)
description: Ratoli is a traditional Catalan hazelnut landrace long grown in the Reus-Tarragona region of northeastern Spain, an area that accounts for the great majority of Spanish hazelnut production. Its lasting importance to modern growers comes from a single dominant resistance gene to Eastern Filbert Blight, mapped to a different chromosome location than the Gasaway-derived resistance used in most Pacific Northwest breeding, which makes Ratoli valuable for diversifying the genetic sources of blight resistance in new cultivars. Rutgers University drew on this Ratoli-derived resistance in developing its blight-resistant release Somerset, which has shown no blight infection in New Jersey field trials. Ratoli itself remains a minor cultivar grown mostly in its traditional Catalan homeland and used elsewhere chiefly as breeding and resistance-screening germplasm rather than as a widely planted orchard variety. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rattlesnake Pole Bean (Classic Purple-Streaked Heirloom Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy pole or trellis for the vigorous climbing vines. Rattlesnake is a classic heirloom pole snap bean named for the purple streaking that mottles its green pods, an old Southern favorite valued for good production even in hot, humid summer conditions that stress many other snap beans, along with reliable flavor and good tolerance of drought once established. The purple markings fade during cooking, leaving a green bean with excellent flavor. Harvest pods young and tender for the best snap bean texture, picking every couple of days to keep the vigorous vines setting new pods through the long growing season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Rave Apple (MN55 / First Kiss)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator apple within range for good fruit set. Developed by David Bedford and James Luby at the University of Minnesota from a cross of Honeycrisp and the University of Arkansas selection AA44, this cultivar (breeding number MN55) was selected in the late 1990s and released commercially by Stemilt Growers in 2017 under the trade name Rave, while fruit grown within Minnesota is marketed separately as First Kiss. It is one of the earliest-ripening apples in the Honeycrisp lineage, typically ready in mid-to-late August, several weeks before Honeycrisp itself, while sharing a similarly crisp, juicy texture and sweet-tart flavor. Because it ripens over an extended window, growers often pick over the tree in multiple passes rather than in one harvest, and it suits the cold winters of the Upper Midwest that the University of Minnesota breeding program targets. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Raven Zucchini (AAS-Winning Dark-Green Disease-Tolerant Compact Zucchini)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raven is an All-America Selections-winning zucchini hybrid notable for its very dark green to nearly black-green skin color, compact open plant habit, excellent flavor, and improved disease tolerance. The extremely dark skin — darker than standard dark-green zucchini — is the most visually distinctive quality: Raven zucchini are nearly black-green at harvest size, creating a visually striking contrast with yellow and light-green squash in market displays and mixed vegetable presentations. The compact, open plant habit (non-vining, upright-spreading, with good air circulation through the plant canopy) reduces powdery mildew pressure in Gulf South humid conditions where powdery mildew often devastates standard bush-type zucchini by mid-season. The earlier maturity (48–55 days) compared to many other zucchini allows faster first harvest and more production within the spring window before summer heat. In zone 9, plant in February–March for spring production and again in August–September for fall production. Harvest Raven at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — the dark skin makes it slightly harder to judge size at a glance, so check plants frequently during peak production. An outstanding choice for Gulf South summer gardens where disease pressure is the primary limitation of zucchini production. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: RazzMatazz Muscadine Grape (Seedless Muscadine-Vinifera Hybrid)
description: RazzMatazz is a patented hybrid between muscadine grape and European wine/table grape (Vitis vinifera), bred to combine muscadine-type disease resistance with the seedless berries and thin skin of a bunch grape. Fruit is deep red with crisp flesh and a sweet flavor, and unlike most muscadines the self-fertile vines flower and ripen berries continuously from midsummer until frost rather than in a single concentrated harvest window. It ripens earlier than most straight muscadine cultivars and has shown strong resistance to the fungal diseases that trouble bunch grapes in humid Southern climates, allowing it to be grown with minimal spraying. Train on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a more compact, less sprawling vine than typical full-size muscadine cultivars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rea's Mammoth Quince (Giant-Fruited American Heirloom Quince)
description: Rea's Mammoth is a nineteenth-century sport of Orange Quince selected in California for fruit that runs noticeably larger than typical quince, often exceeding a pound apiece, with bright yellow skin and firm, intensely fragrant flesh well suited to jelly, paste, and baking. The self-fertile tree crops reliably on a compact frame, making it a practical choice for small orchards or a single dooryard specimen where space for a second pollinizer tree is not available. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune lightly each winter to keep an open canopy that sheds humidity and reduces fire blight pressure. Pick in mid-to-late fall once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic heavy quince perfume, and expect the raw flesh to remain hard and tart until cooked. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Really Red Deer Tongue Lettuce (Red-Blushed Pointed-Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A red-leaved selection of the classic Amish Deer Tongue type, Really Red Deer Tongue forms upright rosettes of triangular, pointed leaves flushed deep burgundy-red over green, the red intensifying in cool weather and full sun, adding strong color contrast to salad mixes and garden beds alike. Like its green counterpart, it is notably heat-tolerant and slow to bolt for a loose-leaf lettuce, holding good quality longer into warm weather than most lettuce varieties. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop for a steady, colorful supply. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Rebecca's Gold Pawpaw (Historic Golden-Fleshed Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Rebecca's Gold is one of the older named pawpaw selections, predating the modern Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and long maintained in pawpaw germplasm collections for its rich, deep-golden flesh and excellent sweet flavor. It is a productive, reliable tree that has stood the test of decades of cultivation among pawpaw enthusiasts and collectors, valued alongside historic selections like Overleese and Sunflower as part of the foundation on which today's larger-fruited cultivars were bred. As with all pawpaws, Rebecca's Gold is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set; hand-pollinating between two open flowers of different cultivars with a small brush can improve yield where natural fly and beetle pollinators are scarce. Provide consistent moisture through the first two seasons while the shallow root system establishes, and expect the tree to fruit within four to eight years from a grafted start. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rebel Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Rebel is a southern highbush blueberry developed by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, released specifically for its combination of very large fruit size and excellent flavor — the berries are among the largest available in southern highbush blueberries, and their rich, sweet-tart, complex flavor rivals northern highbush varieties that are not adapted to zone 9 conditions. The vigorous, productive plant produces heavy crops of these exceptional large-caliber berries with a firm texture that holds up well in packing, shipping, and storage. Rebel's fruit quality has made it popular among commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast where premium large berries command top prices. In zone 9 home gardens it provides exceptional fresh eating quality — the large berries are satisfying to pick and eat fresh from the bush. Cross-pollinate with Flordablue, Biloxi, or Windsor for maximum crop set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rebelski Tomato (Comprehensive Disease-Resistant Beefsteak Hybrid)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or trellis the tall, vigorous indeterminate vines; Rebelski was bred for greenhouse and high-tunnel growers and carries one of the broadest disease-resistance packages available in a beefsteak-type tomato, including Fusarium crown and root rot, Fusarium wilt, powdery mildew, multiple races of leaf mold, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt. It produces large, crack-resistant, deep red beefsteak fruit with excellent classic tomato flavor on a plant that continues setting fruit reliably even under heavy disease pressure. In an open Gulf South garden, this extensive resistance package helps the vines stay productive later into the humid summer than most beefsteak varieties. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep vines pruned and tied to their support for the best air circulation and fruit quality. Matures in 68–78 days from transplant.

name: Red & Yellow Pear Blend Pole Cherry Tomato
description: This heirloom blend combines 'Red Pear' and 'Yellow Pear', indeterminate vines bearing small, firm, pear-shaped fruit with sweet, mild, low-acid flavor. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun beds. The vigorous vines need tall stakes or cages and regular pinching of suckers. Harvest the bite-sized fruits all summer for snacking, salads, pickling, or preserves. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Red Ace Beet (Early Disease-Tolerant Hybrid Globe Beet)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, fertile soil with consistent moisture; thin to 4–6 inch spacing. Red Ace is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid beet that has become one of the most widely recommended standard beet varieties for home gardens and commercial production alike — a globe-shaped, smooth, uniformly sized hybrid that consistently produces high-quality roots with reliable stand establishment, uniform maturity, and excellent disease tolerance (particularly for Cercospora leaf spot, the fungal disease that causes disfiguring brown leaf spots in humid regions). The roots are uniformly round to slightly oval, medium-large (2.5–3 inches diameter), with very smooth, deep red-purple skin, excellent internal uniformity and color (consistently dark red throughout with minimal zoning), and a tender, sweet, earthy-sweet flavor that compares favorably with the best heirloom types while delivering the hybrid advantages of uniformity, consistency, and disease resistance. Red Ace is an all-season variety that performs reliably in spring, fall, and winter production, holds well in cold storage, and has excellent greens quality for dual-purpose use (root plus cooking greens). One of the most practically reliable and consistently productive beet varieties available, recommended by university extension services across North America as a benchmark hybrid against which other beets are evaluated. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Red Acre Cabbage
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Acre is a classic open-pollinated red cabbage variety producing firm, round, 5–7 inch heads with deep red-purple to burgundy outer leaves and a bright magenta-red interior — the characteristic vivid color that makes red cabbage one of the most ornamental vegetables and the most visually distinctive cole crop. The red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are pH-sensitive: the same compound that makes red cabbage turn blue when cooked with alkaline water is stabilized and brightened by adding acid (vinegar, apple juice) during cooking — a useful culinary fact for maintaining the vivid color in braised preparations. Red Acre's flavor is slightly stronger and more peppery than green cabbage, with a firmer texture that holds up extremely well to long braising, pickling, and fermentation. Braised red cabbage with apples, vinegar, and spices (the classic German Rotkohl) and quick-pickled red cabbage for tacos and grain bowls represent the two most common culinary applications, both of which take advantage of the vivid color and firm texture that make Red Acre specifically valuable. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Red Acre Cabbage
description: Start seeds indoors six weeks before setting out, then transplant hardened seedlings into rich, well-drained soil. This compact heirloom forms dense, deep-purple heads around 3-4 pounds and tolerates cold well, making it a good choice for tight spaces and raised beds. Keep moisture even to prevent the round heads from splitting as they firm up. Harvest when heads feel solid, and enjoy the crisp, colorful leaves fresh, in slaws, or lightly cooked. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Acre Cabbage
description: 'Red Acre' forms solid, deep-red heads early on compact plants, making it a strong pick for small gardens and containers. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before setting out, then transplant into rich, full-sun soil spaced 12-18 inches apart. Keep moisture steady to prevent splitting and harvest heads once firm and about 5-7 inches across. This cool-season variety offers good storage and resistance to yellows. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Amaranth
description: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 12–18 inches and sidedress with nitrogen at 30 days for best grain production. Amaranthus cruentus is a remarkable dual-purpose annual producing enormous, showy, red-purple to magenta flower plumes from midsummer through fall while simultaneously growing highly nutritious seeds (up to 20% protein with a complete amino acid profile including lysine) that can be harvested as a pseudo-grain and popped, ground into flour, or cooked like porridge; the young leaves and shoots are also edible as a nutritious cooking green high in iron and calcium. The bold, often dark-red to bronze-red foliage is highly ornamental; selected grain varieties include 'Burgundy', 'Hot Biscuits', and 'Hopi Red Dye'. Young leaves are an excellent spinach substitute in hot weather when true spinach bolts. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Red Amaranth Microgreens
description: Scatter the very fine amaranth seed on the surface of a moist tray without burying it, and keep the medium warm to trigger germination. It grows more slowly than brassicas and prefers extra heat, so be patient during the first week. Mist gently to keep the delicate seedlings from drying out while avoiding standing water. Harvest the vivid crimson, mild-sweet microgreens once the cotyledons color up, usually around two weeks, for an elegant gourmet garnish. Matures in 12–20 days from seed.

name: Red Amposta Bulb Onion
description: 'Red Amposta' is an intermediate-day onion producing large, reddish-purple globes with sweet, snappy flavor and attractive red-and-white rings. Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings 3-4 inches apart in fertile, full-sun soil. Keep the shallow-rooted plants weed-free and evenly watered until the tops begin to fall over. Cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Red and Yellow Blend Biquinho Chile Pepper
description: These small, teardrop 'little beak' Brazilian peppers are tangy, sweet, and smoky with only a whisper of heat, ripening from green to red or yellow. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, as germination is slow, and transplant only when nights stay warm. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and light feeding; the compact plants do well in containers. Harvest fully colored pods for fresh eating, pickling, or drying. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Anjou Pear (Red-Skinned Firm Winter Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Anjou is a red-skinned bud sport of the classic D'Anjou pear, carrying the same dense, firm, sweet, low-fiber flesh and outstanding storage life as the parent variety, wrapped in a deep burgundy-red skin that adds visual appeal without altering flavor or texture. Like other Anjou-type pears, the fruit does not change color noticeably as it ripens, which makes checking for ripeness by color unreliable — instead, press gently near the stem end and harvest or eat once that area yields slightly to pressure. Anjou-type pears are prized for exceptionally good long-term cold storage, often holding good quality for months, making Red Anjou a satisfying choice for home orchardists who want fresh pears well into winter. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Banana Passionfruit (Curuba de Indio)
description: An Andean cloud-forest species valued for its spectacular pendant, tubular scarlet-red flowers that draw hummingbirds, followed by elongated yellow-orange, banana-shaped fruit with sweet aromatic pulp. Unlike lowland tropical Passiflora, it performs best with cool nights and moderate summer heat, so gardeners outside its native highland range should site it with afternoon shade and grow it against a sturdy trellis with excellent drainage. It is markedly less heat- and humidity-tolerant than Passiflora edulis, and prolonged temperatures above the mid-90s°F can cause bud drop, so a shaded, breezy location extends its usefulness in warm-summer gardens. Mulch heavily and protect the root zone in any winter approaching freezing, since top growth is damaged well above the hardiness limits of hardier native passionflowers. Matures in 240–365 days from transplant.

name: Red Barberry (Southwest Barberry)
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; red barberry is a dense, spiny-leaved evergreen shrub of the desert Southwest, its holly-like, blue-gray foliage giving way in spring to small, fragrant, bright yellow flower clusters that draw bees. Clusters of tart, juicy red berries follow in summer, edible fresh in small quantities and traditionally used to make jelly, syrup, and a tart, refreshing beverage similar to that made from the related algerita (Berberis trifoliolata). The dense, thorny branching makes it a useful barrier or wildlife hedge planting, offering cover and food for birds while deterring foot traffic. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and requires minimal care beyond occasional shaping, needing supplemental water only during the driest extended stretches. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Baron Onion
description: Red Baron is a compact, early-maturing intermediate-day storage onion with deep red-purple skin and firm, pink-tinged white flesh with a moderately pungent, well-balanced flavor. Its smaller bulb size and quick maturity make it a favorite for gardeners who want reliable red onions without a long growing season, and its skins hold color and firmness well in storage for several months. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, keeping beds weed-free since onions compete poorly with weeds during bulb sizing. Choose Red Baron where garden space or season length is limited but a dependable, good-keeping red onion is still wanted. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Red Bartlett Pear (Red-Skinned Sport of Classic Bartlett)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Bartlett is a naturally occurring red-skinned sport of the classic green Bartlett pear, discovered as a bud mutation and propagated for its striking burgundy-red skin, while retaining the same sweet, juicy, melting flesh and classic pear flavor that made Bartlett the standard American pear for over a century. Because the tree and fruit share Bartlett's genetics apart from skin color, growers get the familiar reliable flavor with added ornamental interest in the orchard and a more eye-catching fruit for fresh eating, gift baskets, and market sales. Harvest while still firm and green-tinged with a hint of red blush, then finish ripening at room temperature indoors, since pears ripen from the inside out and develop the best texture and flavor off the tree rather than fully ripened on the branch. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Bay (American Bay Laurel)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; red bay is the native American aromatic bay of the coastal Southeast and Gulf Coast, producing glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with the same aromatic oils and culinary bay-laurel fragrance as the Mediterranean bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) — the leaves are used identically in Southern cooking for seasoning gumbos, soups, stews, and bean dishes. In fact, red bay has traditionally been used in Gulf Coast cuisine (particularly in Louisiana) for generations as the local bay leaf. It is a fast-growing native tree of coastal hammocks and stream margins that provides excellent wildlife value — the blue-black fruits are important food for migrating songbirds, and the palamedes swallowtail butterfly uses red bay as its exclusive larval host plant. Tragically, laurel wilt disease (spread by an invasive ambrosia beetle) has killed the vast majority of red bay trees throughout the Southeast — consult local extension services before planting. Matures in 730–3650 days from seed.

name: Red Beard Bunching Onion (Red-Tinted Cold-Hardy Scallion)
description: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart for straight, uniform stalks. Red Beard is a non-bulbing bunching onion selected for shanks that develop an attractive reddish-pink blush, especially in cool weather, adding color contrast to salads, garnishes, and stir-fries beyond standard all-green scallions. It is cold-hardy and can be sown in late summer for a fall and winter harvest in mild climates, standing in the garden through cool weather without bolting. Harvest at scallion size for the best color and tenderness, or let a portion mature further for thicker stalks; successive small sowings every few weeks keep a continuous supply through the cool season. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Red Brandywine Tomato
description: Sow seeds indoors about six weeks before your last frost, then transplant deeply, burying much of the stem to encourage strong roots. These indeterminate Amish heirloom vines are large and sprawling, so provide tall stakes or heavy cages for support. The rosy-red, deeply lobed beefsteak fruits are sweet, low-acid, and best eaten fresh in slices. Water consistently and mulch to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot on the big fruits. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Brussels Sprout
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant into firm, fertile soil, giving each plant plenty of room and support in windy sites. This striking heirloom produces purple-red sprouts along tall stalks with a nutty-sweet flavor that deepens after frost. The long season means patience is required, so plan the planting date backward from your first fall frost. Harvest sprouts from the bottom up as they firm to about an inch, and the color intensifies with cold weather. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Red Burgundy Okra
description: Direct sow after soil warms to 70°F+ in full sun, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; harvest pods at 3–4 inches for best tenderness; Red Burgundy produces excellent fresh pods and makes a very beautiful ornamental edible garden plant. Abelmoschus esculentus 'Red Burgundy' is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom okra variety selected for its striking deep red-burgundy to near-black pod color — one of the most visually dramatic okra varieties available. The compact, 4–5-foot plants produce deep-red stems, leaf veins, and pods that create a stunning ornamental effect in the edible garden or mixed border. The pods are tender, flavorful, and productive at 3–4 inches; they have the same culinary properties as green okra but with the added visual appeal of the deep color. The color is caused by anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple sweet potatoes; like other anthocyanin-rich vegetables, Red Burgundy okra pods lose most of their red color and turn green when cooked, though the anthocyanins are still consumed. The flavor and texture are essentially identical to high-quality green okra. Red Burgundy is productive in the long, hot Gulf Coast summer and was a 1988 AAS winner — one of the most enduringly popular colored okra varieties in American seed catalogs. Matures in 49–60 days from seed.

name: Red Burgundy Okra
description: Soak seeds overnight and sow one inch deep only after soil is thoroughly warm, since okra hates cold. This 1988 All-America Selections winner grows into tall five-foot plants with deep-red stems and burgundy pods that add ornamental appeal. Harvest pods young, at about three to four inches, snipping every day or two to keep the plants productive and the pods tender. The rich color can fade with cooking but the plants remain handsome all season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Red Burgundy Onion
description: Start seeds indoors two to three months before transplanting, as onions need a long lead time. This short-day variety forms bulbs when days reach 10-12 hours, so it suits southern and mild-winter gardens best. Set transplants a few inches apart in loose, fertile soil and keep them weed-free and evenly watered. The glossy red bulbs reach about four inches with sweet, mild white flesh ringed in pink, and are best used fresh rather than for long storage. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Red Candy Lingonberry (Compact Heavy-Fruiting Cultivar)
description: Red Candy is a Dutch-bred patented lingonberry selection prized for its dense, compact, mounding habit and unusually heavy flower and fruit set relative to its small size, typically staying under a foot tall while spreading into a tidy evergreen mat. Loose clusters of nodding, pink-blushed white spring flowers give way to abundant bright scarlet berries that ripen earlier and more prolifically than many older lingonberry cultivars. It shares the acidic, humus-rich soil preferences of blueberries and makes an excellent edible groundcover beneath other ericaceous shrubs. Shear plantings back lightly every few years to renew vigor and maintain dense, productive growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Catawissa Walking Onion (Red Tree Onion)
description: Red Catawissa is a color-selected strain of the historic Catawissa walking onion, distinguished by a reddish-bronze blush on its topset bulbils and sometimes the base of the stalks, while sharing the same loose, open bulbil clusters and occasional true flowers that set true Catawissa apart from the common Egyptian walking onion. As the aerial bulbils swell and grow heavy, the seed stalk bends toward the ground and roots the bulbils wherever they touch soil, allowing the clump to slowly migrate through the bed year after year with no replanting needed. Harvest green shoots through the season like scallions, dig underground bulbs once tops begin to yellow, and collect or replant the colorful topset bulbils to expand the planting or share with other gardeners. Divide congested clumps every few years to keep vigor and bulbil production high. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Red Champagne Finger Lime (Reddish-Pink Caviar Lime Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Red Champagne bears fruit with a reddish-tinted skin and vivid pink-to-red, caviar-like pulp vesicles that burst with tangy citrus flavor, one of the more colorful finger lime selections available and popular with chefs for garnishing. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than seedling-grown plants when purchased grafted. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Choi Bok Choy
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil; Red Choi is a red-leafed bok choy (pak choi) selection producing compact rosette plants with deep burgundy-red to purple-red leaves with contrasting white or pale pink midribs — visually striking in both the garden and on the plate. The flavor is identical to standard green bok choy — mild, slightly mustardy, very tender — but the anthocyanin pigments in the red leaves indicate additional antioxidant content. Red Choi performs best and shows the deepest color in cool weather; warm temperatures cause the plants to green up and bolt quickly. The compact size and partial-shade tolerance make it ideal for intercropping under taller crops, growing in containers, or filling shady corners of the fall garden where other vegetables would fail. Harvest the whole head at 45–55 days or cut outer leaves for continuous baby green harvest. Stir-fry briefly to preserve some color, or use raw in salads where the red color provides striking visual contrast. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Red Chokeberry
description: Red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia) is a taller, more upright native shrub than its black-fruited relative, bearing bright red berries that ripen in fall and persist well into winter, providing exceptional wildlife food and four-season ornamental interest. The berries are intensely astringent fresh but soften after frost and are suitable for jellies, juices, and wines with added sweetener. The cultivar 'Brilliantissima' is widely grown for its especially vibrant fall foliage and heavy fruit set. Prune oldest canes to the ground every 3–4 years to control suckering and maintain vigor. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Red Clover Microgreens
description: Sow the small clover seed densely and evenly across a moist tray, or grow it in a sprouting jar with regular rinsing. It germinates quickly and grows fine, upright stems, so uncover early and provide bright light. Mist frequently to keep the delicate mat hydrated without souring. Harvest the mild, fresh-tasting green shoots after about a week to ten days at the cotyledon stage. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Red Clover Sprouts
description: Red clover sprouts are grown indoors in a jar or sprouting tray, offering a crisp, mild flavor and easy-to-hull seed coats similar to alfalfa. Soak seeds several hours, then rinse and drain two to three times daily in indirect light. Harvest in about 5-7 days once the sprouts show tiny green leaves, then refrigerate. They add crunch and nutrition to sandwiches, salads, and green drinks. Matures in 5–7 days from seed.

name: Red Cored Chantenay Carrot
description: 'Red Cored Chantenay' produces thick, blunt, 6-inch roots that reliably size up even in heavy or shallow soils where longer carrots struggle. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and keep the seedbed moist through the slow germination, then thin to 2-3 inches apart. The heavy-yielding, split-resistant roots are excellent for juicing, canning, freezing, and cooking, and they store well. Cool weather deepens their sweetness. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Red Creole Onion
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Creole C-5 is the predominant short-day red onion of the Gulf South, widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and Alabama and a staple of Gulf Coast kitchen gardens for generations. Unlike the mild, low-pungency sweet onions prized in other regions, Red Creole is a distinctly pungent, storage-type red onion — strongly flavored, with a sharp, assertive onion bite that makes it preferred for Creole and Cajun cooking where onion flavor needs to stand up through long cooking in jambalayas, étouffées, and red beans. The medium-sized, somewhat flattened bulbs cure well and keep for several months in a dry, well-ventilated location. Red Creole bolts in long days, so it MUST be grown on the short-day winter schedule in zone 9 (planted October–December, harvested March–April). It is heat-tolerant once past the bulbing stage and handles the warming temperatures of spring well. A foundational vegetable of Louisiana foodways alongside celery and bell pepper in the Cajun 'holy trinity.' Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Red Currant
description: Red currants fruit heavily on spurs of wood two years old and older; prune each late winter to keep 8–12 canes of mixed ages and remove any cane older than 5 years. They tolerate more shade than most fruits and appreciate afternoon shelter in hot climates. Harvest entire strigs (clusters) when berries are uniformly bright red and slightly translucent. Check state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Red Currant (Junifer)
description: Junifer is a Dutch red currant selected for early ripening and long, well-filled fruit clusters (strigs) that make picking faster than with many other red currant cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush carries glossy bright red berries with the classic tart flavor used in jellies, sauces, and baking. It shows good resistance to common currant leaf diseases under the cool, humid conditions typical of its native growing regions. Junifer performs best where winters are reliably cold and is not recommended for warm, low-chill climates. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Red Dacca Banana
description: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive, fertile soil; Red Dacca (also called Red Banana, Claret Banana, or Pisang Raja Udang in Southeast Asia) is a distinctive red-skinned banana cultivar producing medium-sized fruits with deep maroon to reddish-purple skin when unripe that turns dark yellow-orange when fully ripe. The flesh is creamy white with a slightly firmer, sweeter, and more aromatic flavor than standard Cavendish bananas — often described as having hints of raspberry or tropical fruit notes beyond the typical banana flavor. The entire plant is ornamentally striking, with dark red-purple pseudostems, contrasting green leaf tops and red-purple leaf undersides, and the colorful fruit clusters adding exceptional visual interest. Red Dacca is widely grown as a dual-purpose ornamental and edible banana in zone 9-11 gardens and is popular in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cuisine both fresh and cooked. The fruits are ready to harvest when the skin color begins to lighten from deep red toward orange-red. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Red Damask Manuka (Classic Double Dark-Red New Zealand Tea Tree)
description: Red Damask is a long-established, vigorous manuka cultivar covered in late winter through spring with masses of small, fully double, deep crimson-red flowers that give the whole shrub a rich, dark-red glow from a distance — a dramatic contrast to the white flowers of the wild species. It grows larger and more upright than many newer compact manuka selections, making a substantial evergreen accent or informal hedge in mild-winter gardens. Grow in lean, gritty, slightly acidic soil with sharp drainage in full sun; the fine, heather-like foliage and tolerance of coastal wind and salt spray make it a reliable choice for exposed sites, but it will not tolerate waterlogged soil. Like other double-flowered manuka cultivars, its dense, ruffled flowers offer bees far less accessible nectar than the species, so plant it as an ornamental accent rather than a bee-forage shrub. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Red Deadnettle (Purple Deadnettle)
description: Sow in any garden soil in fall or early spring in partial shade to full sun; red deadnettle is a common European winter annual now naturalized worldwide, growing as a charming winter and early spring wildflower in lawns, gardens, and disturbed areas. The small, purple-hooded flowers, which appear from late winter through spring, are one of the earliest nectar sources for queen bumblebees emerging from winter dormancy — a service of significant ecological value. The purplish-tinged young leaves are edible raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb, high in vitamins and minerals. The plant germinates in fall and overwinters as a low rosette, making it valuable as a living mulch and green cover during winter months. It does not compete with summer crops and dies naturally as temperatures rise. Embrace this plant as a beneficial winter ground cover rather than treating it as a weed. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Red Delicious Apple (Hawkeye Apple, Most-Planted American Apple, Classic Red Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Delicious requires cross-pollination from a compatible diploid apple variety; harvest when the background color turns fully yellow-green under the red and the calyx basin softens slightly — Red Delicious harvested too late becomes mealy, while picked at proper maturity it is firm and pleasantly mild. Red Delicious is the most historically planted apple variety in the United States, dominating American commercial apple production for most of the 20th century and serving as the iconic image of an apple in American culture — the deep red, elongated, five-pointed shape was for decades what millions of Americans pictured when they thought 'apple.' The variety originated as a chance seedling discovered by farmer Jesse Hiatt on his farm near Peru, Iowa around 1872; Hiatt named it 'Hawkeye' and sent samples to a Stark Brothers Nurseries competition in 1893, where it won first prize and was renamed 'Delicious' (later 'Red Delicious' to distinguish it from Golden Delicious). Over the following century, commercial selection pressure for maximum red color and long shelf life produced the modern market strains with deep, all-red skin and elongated shape — but these selections simultaneously reduced the flavor quality that made the original Hawkeye notable. By the early 2000s, Red Delicious had become widely criticized for waxy skin, mealy texture, and mild flavor — a cautionary example of how breeding for appearance at the expense of eating quality can undermine a variety's standing. However, heritage strains and home-grown Red Delicious harvested at correct maturity are noticeably better than commercial examples. Highly productive and disease-tolerant in its home range of zones 5–8. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Deuce Tomato (Commercial-Grade Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicer)
description: Red Deuce is a determinate hybrid slicer bred for commercial fresh-market production in the Southeast that has become a popular choice for home gardeners wanting a tough, reliable main-crop tomato. It produces large, smooth, deep-red 10-12 ounce globes on a compact, high-yielding plant with resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus. Stake or cage the sturdy determinate vines to keep the heavy fruit clusters clean and off the soil, and expect a concentrated main harvest typical of determinate types. Matures in 72–78 days from transplant.

name: Red Dragon Fruit
description: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy, gritty, low-fertility soil — red dragon fruit is a cactus and will rot rapidly in rich, wet, or clay soils; Red Dragon Fruit (Selenicereus costaricensis, formerly Hylocereus costaricensis) is the red-fleshed species of dragon fruit, producing large, oval, deep red-skinned fruits with vivid magenta-red flesh flecked with tiny black seeds. The deep crimson flesh color comes from betacyanin pigments (the same class as beet pigments) that turn smoothies, yogurt, and beverages a dramatic pink-red color. The flavor is mild and sweet with a watermelon-like freshness that is more subtle than the appearance suggests. Red dragon fruit typically ripens 30–35 days after the large, white nocturnal flowers open — the flowers must be pollinated on the night they open (by hand or by nocturnal pollinators) for fruit to set. In zone 9 the long warm season provides ideal conditions for multiple fruiting cycles per year, typically producing 4–6 fruit-set periods from May through November. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Dragon Fruit (Red-fleshed Pitaya)
description: Plant cuttings in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12, with trellis support; red-fleshed dragon fruit differs from the common white-fleshed variety (S. undatus) in producing fruits with vivid deep magenta to crimson flesh — dramatically more colorful and considered by many to have superior flavor with sweeter, slightly more complex notes. The spectacular, white, night-blooming flowers up to 12 inches across are among the largest of any cactus, pollinated by moths and bats. Like all pitayas, this species vines with aerial roots along support structures and requires staking when young. The red-pigmented flesh contains high levels of betacyanins — potent antioxidants responsible for the vivid color. Multiple self-fertile clones exist; 'American Beauty' and 'Physical Graffiti' are popular red-flesh varieties. Needs at least 2 years from cuttings to first fruit; grafted plants begin producing sooner. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Red Drumhead Cabbage (Drumhead Red Savoy)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 3–4 weeks before last frost (cabbage tolerates light frost); space 18–24 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Red Drumhead is a traditional European heirloom red cabbage with a distinctive flattened or slightly convex head shape — broader and flatter than the round heads of varieties like Red Acre or Mammoth Red Rock — that packs very tightly with dense, waxy, deep red-purple leaves. The name 'Drumhead' refers to this characteristically wide, flat shape reminiscent of a drum (a category designation historically used for flat-headed cabbages in both red and green forms). The flavor is bold, earthy, and slightly peppery when raw — excellent for traditional German red cabbage dishes (braised with apples and vinegar), pickling, sauerkraut, and coleslaw; the purple pigment (from anthocyanins) is water-soluble and will turn the cooking liquid blue-purple, traditionally corrected by adding vinegar or apple to keep the red color. Individual heads weigh 4–8 lbs at full maturity; the dense heads resist splitting and store well in cool conditions (35–40°F) for 3–4 months after harvest. Excellent cold hardiness — can withstand frosts to 20°F, making it suitable for overwintering in mild climates. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: Red Elderberry
description: Red Elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of cool, moist forests, rocky slopes, talus, and ravines across the northern United States and Canada, valued for its dramatic pyramid-shaped white flower clusters in spring and vivid red berry clusters in early summer that ripen weeks before American Elderberry. The berries are relished by over 50 species of birds including thrushes, waxwings, grouse, and tanagers, making Red Elderberry among the most important native berry shrubs for wildlife in northern gardens. Unlike the closely related American Elderberry, Red Elderberry berries are mildly toxic when eaten raw due to cyanogenic glycosides and should be cooked before any culinary use; fully cooked berries have been used for jams, wines, and syrups in both traditional and modern kitchens. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Elderberry is more shade-tolerant than American Elderberry and thrives at cool woodland edges and in dappled understory light. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Express Cabbage (Early Small Red Cabbage for Fall Production)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Red Express is an early-maturing red cabbage that matures 2–3 weeks faster than standard red varieties like Red Acre or Ruby Ball, producing small to medium (1.5–3 lb), nicely rounded, deep purple-red heads in just 63–72 days from transplant. Red cabbages in general contain significantly more anthocyanin antioxidants than green types and have a characteristic slightly sharper, more peppery flavor profile; Red Express delivers these attributes in an early-maturing, compact form well-suited to small gardens and fall production windows where there may not be time for the standard 80–85 day maturity of most red cabbage varieties. The red-purple pigmentation intensifies with cool fall temperatures — heads started in late summer and maturing in fall have dramatically deeper, more saturated color than spring-grown heads. Red Express holds well in the garden after reaching maturity and stores very well in refrigeration (4–6 months at 32°F), making it an excellent variety for gardeners who want to put up a supply of red cabbage for winter coleslaw and braised preparations.
