Matures in 63–72 days from transplant.

name: Red Fife Wheat (Canadian Heirloom Hard Red Spring Wheat)
description: Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring, since Red Fife is a spring wheat that needs a cool start and a short, reliable growing season to head out before the heat of summer. Ontario farmer David Fife is credited with selecting this variety from a chance seed lot in the 1840s, and its earliness and hardiness made it the dominant wheat of the Canadian prairies for decades, underpinning the growth of the wheat trade that built Winnipeg and much of western Canadian agriculture. The kernels mill into strong, flavorful bread flour with a distinctive nutty character prized by heritage-grain bakers, and the variety is enjoying a revival among small growers seeking flavorful, regionally adapted wheat. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Red Fuseau Sunchoke (Red-Skinned Fingerling Jerusalem Artichoke)
description: Plant tuber pieces in a dedicated, well-drained bed in full sun, since this vigorous heirloom spreads readily by underground tubers and can be difficult to eradicate once established. Red Fuseau is a long-grown French heirloom sunchoke prized for its elongated, finger-shaped, red-skinned tubers, which are smoother-skinned and easier to scrub clean than the knobby tubers of many other varieties, and its nutty, sweet-earthy flavor is well regarded among heirloom growers. The tall plants produce cheerful small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back with frost, which signals it is time to dig the tubers; cold exposure is said to sweeten the flavor by converting stored inulin to sugar. Harvest from fall into early spring as needed, and leave a portion of tubers in the ground each year to regenerate next season's crop while thinning the bed to keep it contained. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Red Gem Goumi
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of average to poor fertility; heavy nitrogen fertilization is unnecessary and can suppress fruiting in this nitrogen-fixing shrub. Red Gem is a goumi selection valued for producing an especially heavy crop of small, silvery-speckled scarlet berries on a compact, easy-to-manage bush, making it a good choice where space is limited but a full-size goumi's yield is still wanted. The tart-sweet, faintly astringent flavor mellows as the fruit ripens fully in late spring, and berries are equally good eaten fresh off the bush, cooked into jam or syrup, or dried. Like other Elaeagnus, Red Gem fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, improving soil fertility for neighboring plants, and its dense, silvery-leaved habit doubles as an attractive, wildlife-friendly hedge or windbreak component in a food forest planting. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Giant Mustard (Purple Japanese Mustard)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Red Giant is the most widely grown purple mustard green — a Japanese mustard variety with large, deeply frilled to semi-smooth leaves in a striking deep burgundy-purple to reddish-purple color that makes it simultaneously ornamental and edible. The bold purple color intensifies with cool temperatures and frost exposure, making Red Giant one of the most visually dramatic cool-season vegetables for the Gulf South garden — combining beautifully with green kale, white cauliflower, and orange-flowered pansies in the fall edible landscape. The flavor is distinctly pungent and spicy with a mustard heat that develops more fully in mature leaves; young leaves at 4–6 inches are milder and excellent for salads and slaws. In hot weather, the plant bolts and the leaves become extremely pungent and bitter — in zone 9, grow strictly as a fall/winter/spring crop. The purple color partially transfers to cooking liquid and mixed dishes, giving cooked dishes a beautiful purple-tinted sauce. The combination of culinary value and ornamental purple foliage makes Red Giant an excellent choice for edible landscape plantings where vegetables serve double duty as ornamentals. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Red Globe Grape
description: Released by UC Davis in 1980, Red Globe produces very large, round, rose-red berries in big, heavy clusters with a mild, sweet flavor and firm, crisp flesh that stores exceptionally well. It is a late-season variety, ripening well after most other table grapes, which makes it valuable for extending the harvest into fall. Vines are vigorous and need generous spacing and a strong support system to carry the weight of its oversized clusters, plus cluster thinning to prevent overcropping. It has seeds, distinguishing it from most modern supermarket table grapes, but its size and long storage life have kept it a mainstay variety for decades. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Habanero Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors early with consistent warmth, since habaneros germinate slowly and need a long, hot season to ripen. As tender perennials they can be grown year-round outdoors only in frost-free zones. Transplant into full sun after nights stay warm, and support the branching plants as the crimson pods develop. These are among the hottest habaneros with a fruity flavor, so handle the ripe red pods with gloves when harvesting for salsa and hot sauce. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Habanero Pepper Heirloom
description: Sow seeds indoors eight or more weeks before transplanting, using bottom heat to coax the slow-germinating seeds along. This heirloom Capsicum chinense produces bright red, extremely hot, fruity pods perfect for salsas and Caribbean cooking. Move plants outdoors only after the weather is settled and warm, spacing them for good air circulation. Ripen fruits fully to deep red for maximum heat and flavor, wearing gloves whenever you handle them. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Hickory (Sweet Pignut Hickory)
description: Plant seedlings in deep, well-drained upland soil in full sun, allowing room for a tall, straight-trunked tree. Red hickory is a native eastern North American species closely related to pignut hickory, distinguished by its reddish twigs and a husk that splits more readily and completely from the nut at maturity. Its kernels are notably sweeter and less bitter than those of true pignut hickory, and the tree is a valuable wildlife mast producer as well as a source of dense, strong wood. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Red Hubbard Squash (Large Traditional Orange-Red Winter Storage Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits 2 weeks at warm temperature before cool storage. Red Hubbard is a classic large Cucurbita maxima winter squash — one of the largest commonly grown winter squash types, producing fruits typically weighing 10–15 lbs with distinctive warty, orange-red to brick-red-orange skin and a teardrop to large, irregular form with a knobby, pointed blossom end. The Hubbard class of squash has a long American horticultural history, dating to the mid-19th century when the Blue Hubbard type was brought to New England and became a regional storage squash staple. Red Hubbard is a warmer-colored variant with orange-red skin rather than the Blue Hubbard's steel-blue-gray. The very thick, hard shell provides exceptional storage capability (stored roots keep 4–6 months) and was important in pre-refrigeration households where squash served as an important carbohydrate source through winter. The deep orange flesh is very dense, dry, and sweet — the classic winter squash flavor in concentrated form, excellent for pies, soups, and roasted preparations where the flavor holds up to extended cooking. Matures in 92–105 days from seed.

name: Red Huckleberry
description: Red huckleberry is a Pacific Northwest native that naturally colonizes rotting conifer stumps and logs, requiring extremely acidic conditions (pH 4.0–5.0) and excellent drainage with abundant organic matter. The bright scarlet berries ripen in summer and are tart — excellent for jams, syrups, and pies — and are an important wildlife food for birds and bears. Established plants spread slowly by rhizomes and require minimal pruning; remove only dead or crossing branches in late winter. Difficult to transplant as a wild specimen; use nursery-grown container stock for best results. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Impact Sweet Pepper (AAS-Winning Lamuyo-Type Bull's Horn Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed. Red Impact is an AAS-winning Lamuyo-type sweet pepper bearing large, roughly 7-inch tapered fruit that ripens from green to deep red, with unusually thick, sweet walls even before the fruit fully colors. Plants grow upright and tidy with a strong disease-resistance package, setting a heavy load of uniform fruit that finishes reliably. Harvest green for a milder, crisper pepper or let fruit ripen fully to red for the sweetest flavor and best eating quality; consistent watering during fruit set helps prevent thin walls and blossom-end rot. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Jaboticaba (Jaboticaba Vermelha)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; jaboticabas are slow-growing and may take 5–8 years to first fruit but eventually produce multiple crops per year. Plinia trunciflora (red jaboticaba or jaboticaba vermelha) is one of several species in the jaboticaba group of Brazilian native fruit trees — distinct from the commonly cultivated Plinia cauliflora (the dark-purple or black jaboticaba) by producing smaller fruits that ripen red to deep ruby-red rather than purple-black, with thinner skin, slightly sweeter flavor, and a somewhat shorter delay before first flowering after planting in good conditions. Like all jaboticabas, P. trunciflora produces its fruits cauliflourously — directly on the bark of the trunk and main branches, covering the tree's lower structure with dense clusters of round, grape-like fruits that appear to erupt directly from the wood, creating one of the most visually spectacular fruiting displays in subtropical horticulture. The fruits are eaten fresh or made into wine, liqueur, and jam in Brazil; they are thin-skinned enough that the entire fruit (including the somewhat tannic skin) can be popped into the mouth. Jaboticabas produce multiple crops per year in warm, humid conditions. P. trunciflora is noted as marginally more cold-tolerant than some jaboticaba relatives, making it a candidate for protected zone 9 microclimates. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Red Japanese Sweet Potato (Reddish-Purple Skin, Dry White-Flesh Heirloom)
description: Red Japanese produces deep reddish-purple skin over creamy white flesh, with a drier, denser texture than common moist orange varieties and a sweet, nutty flavor suited to roasting, steaming, frying, and baking. It is a vigorous, disease-resistant vine that reaches maturity in about 95 days, a shorter season than many dry-fleshed sweet potatoes require. Its adaptability to a range of summer climates has made it a long-standing offering among heirloom seed exchanges. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after digging to firm the skin and develop full flavor. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Red Jewel Crabapple (Upright White-Flowered Red-Fruited Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Red Jewel produces pure white spring flowers from pale pink buds, followed by an abundant crop of bright, glossy red, jewel-like fruit that holds on the branches into winter, providing striking color against bare branches and snow long after most ornamental trees have finished their season of interest. Its narrower, more upright-oval form than many crabapple cultivars fits smaller landscapes and tighter planting spots where a wide-spreading crabapple would not fit. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Red Kingdom Mizuna
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Kingdom is a red-leaved selection of mizuna (Brassica rapa var. japonica) that combines the deeply cut, feathery leaf shape of traditional green mizuna with vivid deep ruby-red to burgundy-purple leaf color — creating one of the most ornamental salad greens available for kitchen garden beds and mixed containers. Mizuna is a Japanese mustard green with a mild, slightly peppery, pleasantly tangy flavor that is substantially less harsh than red mustard or arugula, making Red Kingdom one of the most approachable and versatile peppery greens for fresh salads. Baby leaves harvested at 2–3 inches have a particularly mild and delicate flavor that works well in mixed salad blends; mature leaves develop more pronounced peppery notes similar to mild arugula. The vivid red-purple color is most intense in cool weather and fades somewhat as temperatures rise in spring — a cool autumn or winter planting in zone 9 produces the most visually striking, deeply colored leaves. Red Kingdom's partial shade tolerance makes it a productive salad green for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Red Kitten Spinach (Red-Veined Baby-Leaf Hybrid)
description: Broadcast or row sow seed thickly and shallowly, keeping the bed consistently moist for even germination, then cut leaves with scissors once they reach salad size. This smooth, arrow-shaped hybrid is distinguished by its bright pink-red midribs and veins running through tender green leaves, adding color and a mild, slightly sweet flavor to fresh salad mixes. It resists bolting better than many baby-leaf types and regrows readily for repeat cuttings. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Red Knight Bell Pepper (Hybrid Thick-Walled Red Bell Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil after last frost. Red Knight is a premium F1 hybrid bell pepper from PanAmerican Seed that has become one of the most consistently recommended thick-walled, high-quality bell peppers for both home gardens and commercial production in the eastern United States — a large (4 x 4 inch), blocky, 4-lobed bell pepper with very thick walls (0.3–0.35 inch) that set it apart from thinner-walled standard bell types. The thick walls are the key eating-quality trait: they provide a satisfying crunch, substantial texture for stuffing (the walls hold up to heat without collapsing), and a longer postharvest shelf life than thin-walled types that wilt rapidly after picking. Red Knight ripens from deep, dark green to a uniformly rich red with clean, complete color change. The fruit flavor at the red stage is noticeably sweeter and more complex than at the green stage — the extended ripening time converts starches and develops sugars, creating a pepper that many cooks use specifically in the red stage for roasted red pepper, jarred pimento-style preparations, and raw salads. Disease resistance includes Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), which can devastate pepper plantings in summer heat — a practical advantage in zone 8–10 summer production. Matures in 65–85 days from transplant.

name: Red Komatsuna (Purple-Leaved Japanese Mustard Spinach)
description: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin to final spacing for full-sized rosettes or grow tightly spaced for a cut-and-come-again baby-leaf harvest. Red Komatsuna is a purple-red-leaved selection of komatsuna, the fast-growing, cold-hardy Japanese mustard spinach, offering the same tender, mild, slightly mustardy flavor as the standard green form but in leaves flushed deep maroon-purple, especially vivid in cool fall and winter growing conditions. It is a productive, quick-maturing green well suited to a fall or early-spring planting, tolerating light frost better than true spinach while adding striking color contrast to salad mixes and stir-fries. Harvest whole young plants or pick individual outer leaves for a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest, since the plant regrows readily from the crown after cutting. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Red Kuri Squash
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Red Kuri (also known as Red Hokkaido, Orange Hokkaido, or Uchiki Kuri) is a Japanese heirloom winter squash producing distinctive, medium-sized, pear-to-teardrop-shaped fruits with deep reddish-orange skin and bright orange, dry, starchy flesh. The flavor is described as a rich chestnut-like sweetness with buttery, nutty notes and an exceptionally dense, dry texture that distinguishes it from the moister, stringier flesh of butternut and acorn squash. The dry, starchy texture makes Red Kuri outstanding for soups and purees (where it thickens naturally), Japanese-style simmered preparations (kabocha), and stuffed squash presentations where watery flesh would dilute the flavor. The medium size (5–8 pounds) is more practical for home cooking than very large winter squash. Red Kuri has been popular in French and Japanese cuisine for decades and is now widely grown in American specialty gardens and farmers markets. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Red Kuri Squash
description: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in compost-enriched soil and thin to one or two vines per hill once established. Red Kuri is a teardrop-shaped Cucurbita maxima with vivid orange-red skin and nutty, chestnut-flavored, dry flesh that is among the finest of all winter squash. Harvest when skin is deep orange-red and hard; the stems will be beginning to dry and the skin will resist a thumbnail. Cure for 10–14 days at room temperature before storing; fruits keep well for three to four months under cool, dry conditions. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Red Kuri Winter Squash
description: 'Red Kuri', also called Orange Hokkaido, yields teardrop-shaped 3-4 pound fruits with smooth, sweet, chestnut-like flesh. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl in full sun. Keep watering steady while fruit develops, then cure harvested squash to build sweetness and storage life. Cut fruit once the rind hardens and the stem dries, leaving a stub of stem attached. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Red Lady Papaya (F1 Hybrid Papaya)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow in warm soil in full sun after frost passes; 'Red Lady' is a commercially successful Taiwanese F1 hybrid papaya developed by Known-You Seed, widely sold in tropical and subtropical regions around the world and favored for its tolerance of Papaya Ring Spot Virus (PRSV), the most devastating papaya disease, which allows it to maintain productivity in areas where most other papayas fail. The bisexual (hermaphrodite) flower type means a single plant can self-pollinate and fruit without needing a separate male, a practical advantage for home gardens with space for only one or two trees. Fruits are medium-large (2–4 pounds), round to slightly oblong, with thin yellow skin blushed with orange-red at maturity and deep, salmon-red flesh with exceptional sweetness and fragrance. 'Red Lady' is an earlier-bearing variety than most papayas, producing fruits within 7–10 months from seed under good growing conditions, and is particularly productive in hot-summer climates like Gulf Coast zone 9. An excellent choice for any zone 9b–12 food garden seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant, self-fruitful papaya. Matures in 210–300 days from seed.

name: Red Lake Currant (Classic American Red Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. Red Lake is a classic American red currant, released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s and long the standard home-garden red currant, valued for its long, uniform strigs (clusters) of large, bright red, tart-sweet berries that are self-fertile and productive without a second bush. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, and the tart flavor mellows somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit on spurs of older wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework in winter and remove wood older than three years to keep the bush productive. Net the bushes at ripening, since birds find currants highly attractive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Red LaSoda Potato (Red Pontiac Type)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil; Red LaSoda is a red-skin, white-flesh potato variety developed at Louisiana State University specifically for Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions — it is one of the few potato varieties bred with the hot, humid Deep South in mind rather than the cool Pacific Northwest or Northeast where most commercial varieties originate. The round, attractively smooth, deep-red skinned tubers have firm, white, waxy flesh excellent for boiling, potato salads, and roasting — the waxy texture holds shape during cooking rather than falling apart. Red LaSoda shows better tolerance of warm temperatures, clay soils, and the wet winters common to the Gulf South than most commercial varieties. It is the most widely recommended red potato for Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Texas Gulf Coast gardens, and is a staple offering at Southern feed-and-seed stores each January. Harvest as new potatoes when plants bloom; for storage potatoes, harvest after vines begin yellowing and dying back. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Leaf Amaranth (Chinese Spinach)
description: Scatter seeds thinly on the soil surface — they need light to germinate — then press gently and keep moist; thin seedlings to 6 inches apart, using thinnings as baby greens. Leaves are brilliantly colored in shades of red, purple, and green and are mildly flavored, used in stir-fries, soups, and as a cooked green throughout South and Southeast Asia. Harvest outer leaves or cut entire young plants at 6–8 inches tall to encourage regrowth; plants that are allowed to flower and set seed will readily self-sow for the following year. This species thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that cause true spinach to bolt immediately. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Red Leaf Lettuce
description: Sow seed thinly on the surface and press in gently; lettuce seeds need light to germinate and should not be covered more than 1/8 inch deep; keep moist until germination. Red leaf lettuce encompasses looseleaf types with varying degrees of red-to-burgundy pigmentation in the leaves, including classics like 'Lollo Rossa,' 'New Red Fire,' 'Red Sails,' and 'Oak Red' — the anthocyanin pigmentation develops best in cool temperatures and direct sunlight, with heat causing color to fade and bitterness to increase. Red leaf lettuces are the most commonly grown looseleaf types in American home gardens, valued for their visual appeal, nutritional density (the red pigment is anthocyanins with antioxidant value), and ease of growing as cut-and-come-again salad plants. Harvest outer leaves when 4–6 inches long, leaving the center to continue growing; provide shade cloth (30%) in warm climates to extend the season. Interplant with taller vegetables for natural afternoon shade. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Red Long of Tropea Onion
description: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Long of Tropea (Cipolla Rossa di Tropea) is the iconic long, elongated red onion of the Calabrian coast town of Tropea in southern Italy, with IGP protected status as a geographic-origin food product. The bulbs are strikingly elongated — cylindrical to torpedo-shaped rather than globe-shaped — with brilliant deep-magenta-red skin and white-to-light-pink flesh with exceptionally low pungency and high natural sweetness. The Tropea onion is the standard for Italian raw onion preparations — sliced thin on bruschetta, dressed with olive oil and herbs, or pickled in vinegar — where the mild, almost sweet flavor allows the onion to be eaten raw without the harsh bite of standard globe onions. The visual appeal of the deep red, elongated shape makes it a striking addition to salads and charcuterie boards. In zone 9 it bulbs up reliably through the mild winter and produces excellent results in the sandy loam soils typical of Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Red Malabar Spinach
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil — Red Malabar Spinach tolerates partial shade better than most warm-season vegetables and grows productively in dappled light; Red Malabar Spinach is the magenta-stemmed ornamental form of Malabar spinach (Basella), a tropical Asian climbing vine whose thick, succulent leaves and stems provide a heat-tolerant alternative to true spinach (Spinacia) for hot-summer gardens. While true spinach bolts and becomes unusably bitter within days of warm weather arriving, Red Malabar Spinach actively thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9 summers, producing increasingly large quantities of glossy, thick, mild-flavored leaves through the entire warm season. The mild, slightly mucilaginous, neutral flavor of the leaves works well in stir-fries, soups, green smoothies, and anywhere true spinach would be used — the slight mucilage (similar to okra) actually serves as a natural thickening agent in soups and stews. The striking red-purple stems and glossy dark green leaves make the vine ornamentally attractive climbing a fence or trellis. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Red Malabar Spinach (Red Vine Spinach, Malabar Nightshade Red)
description: Direct sow seeds or plant rooted stem cuttings in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; provide trellis or fence for the vining stems. Basella rubra (red Malabar spinach or red vine spinach) is the red-stemmed form of Malabar spinach, with strikingly beautiful deep-crimson to purplish-red stems and petioles contrasting with glossy, dark green, somewhat succulent, heart-shaped leaves. Botanically, red (B. rubra) and green (B. alba) Malabar spinach are sometimes treated as separate species, sometimes as forms of the same species — both are grown identically and used the same way. The ornamental value of red Malabar spinach is substantial: the crimson stems winding up a trellis create a dramatic tropical display throughout the warm season. The leaves are cooked like spinach — slightly mucilaginous (slippery) in texture, mild in flavor, wilting quickly in heat — used in stir-fries, soups, curries, and as a spinach substitute throughout South and Southeast Asia. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial vine; in colder zones, a summer annual. It is one of the very few spinach-type leafy greens that performs well in high heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast summer, bridging the gap when cool-season greens have failed. Stem cuttings root easily. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Red Malaysian Guava
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Red Malaysian Guava is a striking cultivar producing fruits with a red-blushed skin and deep salmon-pink to red flesh — the most colorful of the common guava cultivars, with a vibrant internal color that is dramatically vivid when the fruit is sliced. The flavor is rich, aromatic, and sweet with the characteristic guava fragrance, perhaps slightly less musky than standard pink guava types. The red flesh color is due to lycopene, the same antioxidant pigment as in tomatoes, and red-fleshed guavas contain significantly more lycopene than pink-fleshed varieties. Red Malaysian guava is visually impressive at the market and on the table — the vivid red cross-section makes it one of the most photographed fresh tropical fruits. In zone 9 the trees produce multiple crops annually and fruit most heavily in late summer–fall and late winter–spring. Fruits ripen from green to a yellow-red skin color and should be eaten when fully soft. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Marconi Frying Pepper (Italian Open-Pollinated Sweet Roasting Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Red Marconi is the classic Italian open-pollinated sweet frying/roasting pepper — a traditional heirloom variety that produces long (6–8 inch), moderately tapered, thick-walled, slightly ridged fruits of the Italian frying type, ripening from medium green to deep, vivid red. Unlike the Giant Marconi hybrid (AAS 1997), Red Marconi is open-pollinated, allowing seed to be saved and maintained from year to year — the preservation choice for gardeners who want a self-sustaining seed supply. The traditional Italian frying pepper form is distinctive: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a slightly irregular, ridged exterior and relatively thick, meaty walls. At the green stage, the flavor is mild, fresh, and subtly sweet — the standard for Italian sautéed peppers (peperoni fritti) where the pepper is sliced and cooked in olive oil until tender. At the red stage, the flavor concentrates into a sweet, rich, complex character ideal for roasting, peeling, and incorporating into antipasto, stuffed preparations, or the classic Italian peperonata. Red Marconi plants are tall (30–42 inches), productive, and require staking when loaded with fruit. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Red Margin Bamboo (Temple Bamboo)
description: Phyllostachys rubromarginata is one of the fastest-growing temperate running bamboos, valued for its straight, thick-walled culms and the reddish blush that appears on new shoots and emerging leaves, which is the source of its common name. It tolerates alkaline soils and windy sites better than many Phyllostachys, and it is exceptionally cold hardy, holding up to temperatures well below zero once established. Because it is a monopodial runner, it needs a buried rhizome barrier or generous isolation to prevent it from invading nearby beds or neighboring yards. Harvest spring shoots for eating when they are a few inches above the soil, and thin older culms every few years to keep groves vigorous and to harvest poles for garden stakes or building projects. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Red Mizuna
description: Scatter seeds thinly and cover with 1/4 inch of soil in a cool, moist seedbed; germination is rapid in cool conditions. Red mizuna has the same deeply-cut, feathery leaf form as green mizuna but with vivid burgundy-red stems and leaf coloring that intensifies in cool weather, making it as ornamental as it is edible. Harvest outer leaves continuously once plants reach 4 inches, or cut the entire plant 1 inch above the base to allow regrowth; flavor is peppery and nutty, similar to green mizuna but with slightly more bite. Fall sowings consistently outperform spring plantings in flavor and color intensity as frost sweetens the leaves. Matures in 20–40 days from seed.

name: Red Mombin (Spanish Plum, Jocote)
description: Plant large hardwood cuttings directly in well-drained soil in full sun — red mombin is a small tropical plum tree of Central America and the Caribbean notable for two things: the flavor of its egg-shaped, wine-red to dark purple fruits (a thin skin over sweet-tart orange flesh with an enormous seed, eaten fresh or in agua fresca throughout Mexico and Central America where it is called 'jocote') and its ability to propagate from large cuttings stuck directly in the ground — even fenceposts made from the wood can sprout. The deciduous tree drops its leaves in the dry season, then blooms and leafs out simultaneously in the rainy season. It is remarkably drought tolerant and is grown in poor, dry soils throughout the tropics. The small reddish fruits ripen over a long season and are consumed by birds and wildlife. An excellent low-water, easy-care tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Mulberry
description: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the red mulberry is the only mulberry native to eastern North America and produces berries superior in flavor and nutrition to the introduced white mulberry — richer, more complex, and deeply red to black when fully ripe. It is an ecologically critical plant, providing fruit for hundreds of wildlife species at a critical early-summer period. The berries are edible fresh or made into pies, jams, wine, and dried fruit; harvest is best done by spreading a tarp and shaking the branches, as berries stain everything they touch. Red mulberry is distinguished from white mulberry by its leaves, which are rough on the upper surface (smooth in white mulberry). It unfortunately hybridizes readily with the invasive white mulberry where the two grow together, threatening the genetic integrity of pure wild populations; purchasing certified native red mulberry trees from reputable nurseries is important. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Red Noodle Asparagus Bean
description: Provide a sturdy 7-8 ft trellis before sowing, as vines climb aggressively and produce deep burgundy pods up to 18 inches long. Direct sow two weeks after last frost when soil reaches at least 70 F, planting seeds 1 inch deep. Harvest pods young and tender at pencil thickness for best flavor and to keep plants productive. Pick every two to three days during peak season to prevent pods from becoming fibrous. Feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer since heavy nitrogen reduces pod set. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Red Noodle Yard-Long Bean (Striking Deep-Red Extra-Long Asian Pole Bean)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Red Noodle is a striking red-podded yard-long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis) producing deep burgundy-red to dark red pods 18–24 inches long — the dramatic red color and extraordinary length combine to make this one of the most visually spectacular edible climbing plants available for Gulf South summer gardens. Yard-long beans (also called asparagus beans or Chinese long beans) are a tropical subspecies of cowpea adapted to hot, humid conditions that make them particularly suitable for Gulf South summer production when standard snap beans decline. The pods should be harvested at 12–18 inches for best tenderness and flavor — they become tough and fibrous when allowed to develop past 20 inches. Red Noodle maintains its red color when raw and in raw preparations but turns greenish-brown when cooked — similar to the color loss in Burgundy snap beans and Red Russian kale. The cooking texture is similar to standard yard-long beans: slightly firmer and less watery than snap beans, holding texture well in stir-fries and sautés. The vines grow vigorously to 8–12 feet in Gulf South heat and require substantial trellis support (minimum 5–6 foot fence or trellis height) — the trailing red bean clusters hanging from overhead structures create a dramatic ornamental and productive display simultaneously. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Red Noodle Yardlong Bean (Burgundy Asparagus Bean, Red Long Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after the soil reaches 70°F or more (1–3 weeks after last frost) at the base of a sturdy trellis 6–8 feet tall; Red Noodle bean is extremely heat-tolerant and actually performs best in the hottest summer conditions — it continues producing during summer heat that stops most beans from setting pods. Red Noodle is a cultivar of the yardlong bean (also called asparagus bean, long bean, or snake bean), which is the same species as the cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) but selected for long pod production — the typical yardlong bean produces green pods 18–24 inches long; Red Noodle produces pods of the same length but in a spectacular deep burgundy to crimson-red color that is unique among commonly grown beans and makes the loaded trellis a visual centerpiece of the summer garden. The flavor is similar to standard green yardlong beans — somewhat starchier and with more umami than fresh Phaseolus beans — and is excellent stir-fried in Chinese cooking (the primary culinary tradition that uses yardlong beans), in pad thai, in Southeast Asian salads and pickles, or simply sautéed with garlic and soy. The dark color fades significantly when cooked, but remains visually interesting as a dark grayish-purple. Yardlong beans including Red Noodle are far more heat-tolerant than any Phaseolus bean variety and are ideal for Gulf Coast gardeners in zones 8b–10 who want continuous summer bean production through July and August when other beans fail. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Red Norland Potato (Very Early Smooth Red-Skinned White-Flesh Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Norland is one of the finest early-maturing red potato varieties for home garden production — producing attractive, smooth, bright-red-skinned, white-fleshed tubers that mature in only 70–80 days from planting, making it the best choice for Zone 9 gardeners whose spring potato window closes when summer heat arrives. The smooth red skin (without the russeting or rough texture of some red varieties) and excellent appearance make Red Norland outstanding for presentation at harvest — new Red Norland potatoes dug fresh from the garden have bright color and clean appearance. The white flesh is excellent for boiling, steaming, and potato salad — waxy enough to hold its shape when cooked, with a moist, creamy texture and mild potato flavor that excels in salads, soups, and boiled presentations. In zone 9, plant seed potatoes in January–February for a May–June harvest before summer heat makes potato production impractical. Hill soil over the developing plants 2–3 times as they grow to ensure tubers do not green from light exposure. Red Norland has been one of the most widely grown early red potato varieties in American home gardens since its introduction in the 1950s — a reliable, consistent producer of high-quality fresh-eating potatoes. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Red Oak Leaf Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Red Oak Leaf is the red-leafed counterpart to the classic green Oak Leaf lettuce — producing deeply lobed, sinuate leaves with an outline resembling the characteristic deeply-indented silhouette of an oak leaf, in deep burgundy-red to bronze-red coloring. The deeply-indented, non-frilly leaf form distinguishes Oak Leaf types immediately from the more common looseleaf lettuces with wavy or ruffled edges. The flavor is mild, tender, and slightly nutty — one of the better-flavored looseleaf lettuces with a soft, non-bitter quality. Red Oak Leaf lettuce is notably heat-tolerant and slow-to-bolt compared to most red lettuces, making it particularly valuable for extending the spring harvest season in zone 9 and for reliable color retention in warm fall conditions when other red varieties revert to green. The striking leaf form and consistent deep-red color make it one of the most popular lettuces for mesclun mixes and specialty salad blends. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Red Onion
description: Grow identically to yellow onions, starting seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting or planting sets as early as soil can be worked in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; red onions get their distinctive color from anthocyanin pigments concentrated in the outer layers and are the premier choice for fresh use in salads, salsas, pickles, and raw preparations where their mild, slightly sweet flavor and dramatic purple-red color provide visual impact alongside their culinary role. The color fades when cooked, making them less suitable for long-cooked dishes than yellow onions. Popular varieties include 'Red Burgundy' (short-day, for zone 7–10), 'Red Wethersfield' (long-day, for zone 3–6), and 'Redwing' (intermediate-day). Quick-pickled red onion in lime juice or vinegar is one of the most versatile condiments in modern cooking. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Red Orach (Red Mountain Spinach)
description: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; red orach is a striking annual with wine-red to burgundy foliage that makes it as ornamental as it is edible. The arrow-shaped leaves have a flavor similar to spinach — mild, slightly salty, and earthy — and are excellent raw in salads when young or lightly cooked when larger. Unlike spinach, orach is more heat-tolerant and slightly less cold-tolerant. The upright habit and vivid red color make it an excellent backdrop plant in the kitchen garden. Self-sows freely where happy, so either deadhead before seeds ripen or allow to naturalize. Young seedlings that sprout the following spring can be transplanted to preferred locations. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Red Orache (Mountain Spinach)
description: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in any reasonably fertile, well-drained to moist, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; orache germinates and grows extremely rapidly in cool conditions and can be harvested as baby leaf greens in 3 weeks or as full plants at 40–60 days. Atriplex hortensis is a large, fast-growing cool-season annual producing striking red, gold, or green arrow-shaped to triangular leaves with a mild, slightly salty, spinach-like flavor excellent for salads, stir-fries, and as a spinach substitute; the red form ('Rubra') is especially ornamental, growing to 3–6 feet tall and making a dramatic statement in the potager. It self-seeds prolifically and can naturalize in gardens; in the Gulf South it is best grown in fall, winter, and spring as a cool-season crop. Related to quinoa and lamb's quarters; all parts including the young seed heads are edible. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Red Passionflower (Red Granadilla)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in frost-free zones (10–12) or grow in containers that can be protected from frost in zones 9 and below. Passiflora coccinea is a Brazilian tropical passionflower vine with large, heart-shaped to deeply lobed, oblong leaves and brilliant scarlet, orange-red, or vermilion flowers with a prominent corona of white-banded filaments from late spring through fall in tropical climates; it is one of the finest plants for attracting hummingbirds in tropical gardens. The small, edible fruits are yellow-green when ripe with soft, sweet, aromatic pulp. Related to P. vitifolia but with somewhat different leaf shape and flower proportions; both are outstanding for tropical garden collections and large container culture. Excellent on arbors, fences, and trellises in frost-free climates. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Red Pear Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide sturdy caging or staking as Red Pear is an indeterminate vine that reaches 5–7 feet and produces abundant clusters of small fruit through the season. Red Pear is the red-fruited version of the classic pear tomato type, producing small (1–1.5 inch), distinctively pear-shaped, bright red fruits in prolific hanging clusters from midsummer through frost; the flavor is sweet and mild, slightly less complex than larger tomatoes but ideal for snacking directly from the vine, halved in salads, and as a colorful contrast to yellow or orange cherry types. Like Yellow Pear, Red Pear is indeterminate and extremely vigorous, producing continuously until frost and sometimes overloading cages with fruit weight; the plants may need supplemental tying. Resistant to cracking even in wet conditions. Popular in children's gardens for the playful shape and snacking appeal. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Red Pearl Chilean Guava (INIA Chile Murtilla Selection)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltering from hard freezes in the cooler end of its range. Red Pearl is a patented selection released by Chile's national agricultural research institute (INIA) from a domestication program that began in the 1990s to bring wild-harvested murtilla into cultivated production, and it was chosen for dark red berries notably larger and more uniform than typical seedling Chilean guava. The compact, bushy, evergreen shrub bears its intensely aromatic, sweet-tart fruit over an extended late-season window, and the small, dark-green leaves make it as useful for clipped hedging as for fruit production. Harvest when berries are fully dark red and slightly soft for the best flavor, and expect several years of establishment before the plant reaches full bearing size. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Pearl Lingonberry
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions; Red Pearl is a Dutch-selected lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea) cultivar renowned as one of the most productive named varieties, producing two crops of bright red berries per season rather than the single crop of most species plants — the first crop ripens in August and the second in October, significantly extending the fresh lingonberry harvest. The glossy, bright scarlet berries have the characteristic lingonberry flavor: tart, slightly bitter, and astringent when raw, transforming into the quintessential lingonberry jam flavor when sweetened and cooked. Lingonberry jam is the traditional accompaniment to meatballs and other Scandinavian dishes and is a major commercial product in northern Europe. The low-growing, evergreen, spreading habit makes Red Pearl an excellent edible groundcover for shady acidic spots under blueberries, azaleas, rhododendrons, and pines where few other fruiting plants thrive. Spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a dense carpet. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Pontiac Potato (Red Skin Waxy Potato)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost, after cutting to egg size with 1–2 eyes and allowing cut surfaces to cure for 1–2 days. Red Pontiac is the most widely grown red-skinned potato in the United States for over 50 years — a late-season, round, medium to large potato with smooth, dark red skin and white, waxy to slightly waxy flesh with moderate moisture content that holds its shape when boiled (making it excellent for potato salad, boiled potatoes, and roasting) while also mashing reasonably well. The bright red skin is attractive when left on for roasted preparations, and the firm texture keeps it together in soups and stews. Red Pontiac produces large, impressive tubers and is very productive in a wide range of soils, making it a reliable choice for home gardeners who want attractive, versatile red potatoes with a genuine all-purpose cooking character. In zone 9, plant in late January or early February and harvest in late April through May before summer heat causes plant decline. Matures in 75–95 days from transplant.

name: Red Power Cabbage
description: 'Red Power' forms uniform, 1.5-2 pound pointed heads of tightly wrapped magenta leaves on a compact, upright plant ideal for small gardens. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before setting out and transplant into rich, full-sun soil. Keep moisture even to prevent splitting and harvest once heads feel firm. The sweet, mild flavor and striking color make it excellent raw in salads, stir-fried, or braised. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Red Pride Bush Tomato
description: 'Red Pride' is a determinate bush tomato that yields a heavy set of firm, 10-ounce red fruits on vigorous, compact plants. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun soil. Its strong disease-resistance package covers Alternaria stem canker, gray leaf spot, Fusarium wilt, and Verticillium wilt, making it low-fuss. A short cage or stake supports the concentrated fruit load; harvest when fully red. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Red Princess Hardy Kiwi (Red-Fleshed New Zealand Kiwiberry Hybrid)
description: Red Princess is a New Zealand-bred female hardy kiwi selection, a cross of the Actinidia arguta type Cordifolia with A. melanandra, grown for smooth-skinned, oval, grape-sized fruit with striking red flesh and a sweet, concentrated kiwi flavor eaten whole without peeling. Fruit ripens mid to late fall, later than many arguta cultivars. Being dioecious, it requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine growing within pollinating range to set fruit. The vigorous vine is hardy to roughly -25F and needs a strong permanent trellis or arbor to support its twining growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Racer Tomato (Nematode-Resistant AAS-Winning Cocktail Hybrid)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F; Red Racer is a compact, determinate cocktail-sized tomato recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally early maturity and broad disease resistance, including root-knot nematodes, a soil pest that stunts and weakens tomato roots and is a persistent problem in the sandy soils common across the Gulf Coast. It produces an early, concentrated crop of round, deep red, 2-3 ounce fruit with good, well-balanced flavor on plants compact enough for containers or small raised beds. Because of its resistance to nematodes as well as Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt, Red Racer performs reliably even in garden soil where other tomatoes have struggled. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color for the best flavor. Matures in 55–62 days from transplant.

name: Red Raripila Mint
description: Set divisions into moist, humus-rich soil and confine the roots with a buried barrier or grow in a large container, since this vigorous three-way mint hybrid runs as aggressively as its parent species. The reddish stems and leaf veins are the plant's calling card, and coloration intensifies with more sun exposure, but it actually performs best with light shade during the hottest part of the day, making it a good pick for a partially shaded herb bed where other mints struggle. The mild, sweet spearmint-like flavor works well in teas and cold drinks. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh, tender regrowth and keep the red stem color vivid. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Ripper Pea (Red Ripper Cowpea)
description: Direct sow in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving with minimal irrigation through the hottest, driest part of the Gulf South summer. Red Ripper is a vigorous, long-vining heirloom cowpea grown across the South since the 19th century both as a food crop and as a dependable summer cover crop and livestock forage, valued for its toughness in poor soil and drought that would fail most other legumes. The sprawling vines carry deep red-brown, kidney-shaped seeds in long pods over an extended late-summer season, continuing to set new pods until the first frost, which makes it one of the longer-producing Southern peas for a continuous late-season harvest. Beyond the table, Red Ripper is prized as a nitrogen-fixing green manure and grazing forage crop, tilled or turned under at the end of the season to build soil fertility for the following year. A dual-purpose, low-input heirloom well suited to the toughest garden conditions, zone 5–11. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Red Ripper Southern Pea (Red Ripper Cowpea, Old Timer Pea)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; Red Ripper is semi-vining and may need minimal support or can be left to sprawl; for cover crop use broadcast at 5–10 lbs per 1000 sq ft; harvest pods at green-shell stage for fresh eating or allow to fully dry for storage as dry peas. Red Ripper is one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant Southern pea varieties available, valued for both its role as a food crop and its exceptional performance as a summer cover crop in the hot, dry conditions of the Southern Plains and Gulf Coast. The plants are semi-vining (not quite as bushy as modern varieties, not as long-vining as pole types) and produce prolifically under conditions that would reduce the yield of more refined modern varieties — poor, sandy soil, minimal rain, and sustained heat above 95°F. The seeds are distinctive: larger than many Southern peas, reddish-tan to brown with darker mottling, with a hearty, earthy cowpea flavor when cooked. As a cover crop, Red Ripper builds nitrogen at high rates (80–120 lbs N/acre under good conditions), suppresses summer weeds aggressively with its spreading canopy, and its large biomass decomposes quickly in the warm soil to build organic matter. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter recommend Red Ripper as one of the top summer cover crops for the Gulf South. For food production, Red Ripper is an old heirloom with deep roots in Southern and Texan food traditions — used as fresh shelled peas, dried peas, and as the source of pot likker in traditional Southern cooking. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Red Robin Micro Tomato (Patio Container Micro-Dwarf Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; grow in 6–8 inch containers or hanging baskets. Red Robin is a micro-dwarf determinate tomato — one of the smallest tomato plants available to gardeners, typically reaching only 8–14 inches tall and 8–12 inches wide at maturity. The extreme compact size distinguishes Red Robin from standard 'patio' tomatoes (which reach 24–36 inches) and makes it the tomato of choice for situations where space is extremely limited: kitchen windowsills, apartment balcony pots of any size, children's garden projects, hanging baskets, and window box plantings. Despite its tiny size, Red Robin produces red, round, 1-inch cherry tomatoes of acceptable sweet-tangy flavor in small but meaningful quantities — a single plant might produce 30–50 fruits over its harvest period, sufficient for salads and snacking. The determinate habit means the plant stops growing at its genetic maximum size and sets a crop over a 2–3 week window, making it ideal for succession planting (start a new plant every 3 weeks from late winter through late summer for continuous small harvests). Red Robin requires no staking, no pruning, and no trellising — it simply grows into a self-supporting mound and fruits. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Red Romaine Lettuce
description: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. This Cos-type heirloom forms upright heads of sturdy, crisp leaves in a rich burgundy that fades to pale green at the heart. Keep the soil evenly moist and provide some afternoon shade in warm regions to delay bolting. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole heads once they are full and firm. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Red Rubin Basil (Purple Basil, Red Basil)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Rubin is the finest and most consistent deep-purple basil cultivar — an improved selection of 'Dark Opal' basil that produces more uniformly dark, deep burgundy-purple leaves across the entire plant with a richer, more saturated color than older purple basil selections. The deep crimson-purple foliage provides striking ornamental value in the herb garden and the edible landscape — the dark leaves contrast beautifully with green herbs, chartreuse foliage, and brightly colored flowers. Red Rubin basil has the same classic sweet basil fragrance and flavor as green Genovese-type basils and can be used interchangeably in cooking, where its purple color creates dramatic purple-tinted basil oil, purple pesto, and deep-toned herb vinegars that standard green basil cannot produce. The purple color also migrates to other ingredients when the fresh herb is used — providing a subtle tinting effect in salads. In zone 9, Red Rubin grows vigorously through the warm season. Regular harvest by pinching the upper leaves and flower buds maintains the bushy habit and delays flowering. Once the plant bolts and sets seed, leaf production diminishes — cut back hard or compost the plant and start fresh. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Red Rubin Holy Basil (Deep Purple-Red Sacred Tulsi Basil for Tea and Ritual Use)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Red Rubin Holy Basil is a deeply colored cultivar of tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum, holy basil) — the sacred plant of Hinduism, considered the most important of the sacred plants (tulsi) present in virtually every Hindu household as a revered manifestation of the goddess Lakshmi. The deep purple-red to burgundy-red foliage of 'Red Rubin' is substantially more ornamental than standard green tulsi, combining the sacred herb's distinctive aromatic qualities with a plant form visually comparable to red basil varieties used in Western herb gardening. The aroma of holy basil is distinctly different from sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) — a complex, spicy-clove-mint-camphor fragrance with earthy, slightly medicinal undertones rather than the purely sweet-anise of Italian basil. This aroma makes tulsi specifically suited for herbal teas (tulsi tea is a traditional Ayurvedic beverage), aromatherapy, and as a basil flavor component distinct from sweet basil in fusion cooking. In zone 9, Red Rubin Holy Basil grows as a vigorous warm-season annual from spring through fall, potentially self-seeding in sheltered positions. Regular harvest of stem tips prevents bolting and maintains vegetative growth. The ornamental purple foliage and small lavender-pink flowers make it equally valuable as a garden ornamental and as an herb with the distinctive tulsi fragrance. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Red Rubine Brussels Sprout (Heirloom Purple)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants out roughly 12-16 weeks ahead of the first fall frost so the long-season crop matures in cool weather. Red Rubine is a Dutch open-pollinated heirloom dating to the mid-20th century, prized for its striking purple-red buttons and matching purple-veined foliage, a dramatic contrast to standard green Brussels sprouts. Its sprouts are smaller and yields somewhat lighter than modern green hybrids, but the flavor is rich and nutty and intensifies with sweetness after hard frost, and the purple color often persists lightly even after cooking. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making Red Rubine a favorite of heirloom seed savers and gardeners seeking ornamental as well as edible value in the fall garden. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Russian Kale
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Russian Kale is widely considered the most versatile and palatable kale variety for fresh and minimally processed use — the flat, deeply indented, gray-green leaves with red-purple stems and leaf margins have a tenderness and mild sweetness that allows them to be eaten raw in salads (particularly baby leaves) without the fibrous toughness and bitterness that makes many kale varieties unpleasant uncooked. Unlike the curly kales that require extensive massage to soften for salad use, Red Russian baby leaves can be used directly in mixed green salads, smoothies, and fresh preparations. The flavor is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than curly kale, with a mild earthiness and peppery undertone that becomes even more pleasant after frost — cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, dramatically improving the sweetness of all kale but especially Red Russian. The partial shade tolerance makes Red Russian one of the better kale choices for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Red Russian Kale
description: This oleracea-type kale has flat, frilly gray-green leaves with purple stems and is notably tender and sweet. Direct sow half an inch deep and thin to 12 inches, or harvest thinnings as baby greens. It tolerates both heat and cold better than curly kale, making it a good four-season crop. Snap off outer leaves as needed and the plant will keep pushing new growth from the center. A light frost improves its mild, sweet flavor. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Red Russian Kale Baby Greens
description: Grown as baby greens, 'Red Russian' kale delivers tender, flat, purple-veined leaves loaded with vitamins A and C plus calcium and iron. Sow seeds thickly in shallow rows or trays and harvest by cutting leaves at about 3-4 inches tall, allowing regrowth for repeat cuttings. It grows quickly indoors any season or outdoors in cool weather, tolerating light frost. Snip young for salads or a quick saute. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Red Rustproof Oat (Heirloom Southern Winter Oat)
description: Red Rustproof arrived in the Deep South around 1849, reportedly carried home from the Mexican War, and by the early 1900s it was the dominant winter oat grown from Georgia through Texas because of its strong immunity to crown rust, a disease that regularly wiped out other oat stands. Drill or broadcast in fall into worked ground; the crop overwinters as a leafy rosette on cotton-worn soils and resumes vigorous growth once days lengthen in late winter. It is markedly less cold-hardy than northern oat types, so it belongs in mild-winter regions rather than areas with hard, prolonged freezes. Cut and thresh in early summer once the panicles dry to gold, saving the light, thin-hulled grain for livestock feed or replanting the following fall. Matures in 210–240 days from seed.

name: Red Sails Leaf Lettuce
description: 'Red Sails' is a loose-leaf lettuce with soft, buttery, bronze-red leaves that resist bitterness even in warm weather. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them since light aids germination, and thin to 8-12 inches for full heads. Harvest baby greens in 2-3 weeks or full heads in about 6 weeks, or pick outer leaves for a continuous supply. Its heat tolerance and slow bolting make it a reliable choice for extended harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Red Sails Lettuce (Red Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Red Sails is a 1985 All-America Selections winner red leaf lettuce that has remained one of the most widely grown and recommended loose-leaf lettuces for over 40 years, valued for its combination of attractive deep burgundy-red to bronze coloring, excellent flavor, and — most practically — its slow bolting characteristic that gives it several weeks longer in the garden before going to seed than most lettuces under warming spring conditions. The large, ruffled, wavy leaves are moderately to deeply red throughout, with a mild, sweet lettuce flavor that is pleasant and non-bitter even in moderate heat. As a loose-leaf type, Red Sails can be harvested by removing outer leaves continuously (cut-and-come-again), or the entire plant can be cut at once. Red Sails is excellent for mixed salad bowls and provides visual contrast when grown alongside green lettuce varieties. In zone 9, it excels in the fall-through-winter season (September–February) when temperatures are cool enough for crisp lettuce production. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Red Salad Bowl Lettuce
description: Scatter seeds thinly and press lightly into the soil surface, as they germinate best with light. This loose-leaf heirloom forms large open rosettes of frilly burgundy-red leaves with a crisp, mild flavor. It is notably heat-tolerant, so it holds longer than many lettuces before bolting in warm weather. Harvest leaves individually on a cut-and-come-again basis for a steady supply of baby or full-size greens. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Red Samurai Carrot (Scarlet Japanese Nantes-Type Carrot)
description: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in deeply tilled, loose, rock-free soil; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall, keeping thinnings for salads. Red Samurai is a Japanese-bred Nantes-type carrot (developed by Takii Seeds of Kyoto) that stands apart from most modern carrot varieties through its extraordinary deep scarlet-red to crimson skin and pinkish-red interior flesh, coloration that comes from lycopene — the same red pigment in tomatoes — rather than from the beta-carotene responsible for orange carrot color. The rich red color makes Red Samurai visually striking in the garden (the feathery tops are standard-green, revealing nothing of the flamboyant root below), stunning when sliced for salads and crudités, and exceptionally nutritious from a lycopene perspective. The roots are long (7–8 inches), slender, tapered in the classic Nantes style, with excellent sweet, mild flavor that compares favorably to the best orange Nantes varieties — the red pigmentation does not negatively affect flavor. Red Samurai is one of the most ornamentally distinctive of all carrot varieties and serves as an outstanding conversation piece in CSA boxes and farmers market displays where its unusual color draws immediate attention. Grows best in cool weather when the roots develop their deepest color; summer-grown roots are paler and somewhat less flavorful. An excellent addition to rainbow carrot mixes or grown on its own for maximum visual impact. Matures in 72–80 days from seed.

name: Red Santol
description: Red santol is the form most widely grown and sold commercially throughout Southeast Asia, historically distinguished as its own species (Sandoricum nervosum) before taxonomists merged it with the yellow type into a single species, Sandoricum koetjape, differentiated chiefly by its old leaves turning red rather than yellow before dropping and by a thicker rind around a thinner, more tart layer of pulp. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing ample room for the tree's eventual large canopy, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for best fruit set. Grafted selections come into bearing within a few years, whereas seedling trees take considerably longer. Harvest the round, downy, yellow-brown fruit once fully colored and slightly soft, and use the tangy, cottony pulp fresh or cooked into preserves and candied treats, as is traditional in the Philippines and Thailand. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Red Savina Habanero Pepper
description: Germinate on a heat mat at 85°F and grow under strong grow lights until transplanting outdoors after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Red Savina grows as a compact, bushy plant and does best with consistent moisture and fertilization in full sun. Red Savina was developed by Frank Garcia in Walnut, California as a selected sport of the standard orange habanero and registered with the US Plant Variety Protection office; from 1994 until 2006 it held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper at 350,000–580,000 Scoville Heat Units — since surpassed by even hotter superhot varieties but still among the most intensely hot widely available peppers. The fruits are classic habanero-shaped, medium-sized, bright red at maturity, with the characteristic fruity, apricot-like habanero aroma and overwhelming heat. Often grown by heat enthusiasts who want a genuinely hot habanero with well-established provenance and consistent heat levels. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Red Shiso
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Shiso (Perilla frutescens var. purpurea) is the red-purple-leaved form of Japanese shiso — a herb central to Japanese and Korean cuisine with a distinctive flavor combining anise, mint, basil, and cinnamon in a complex, aromatic profile unlike any other commonly grown herb. The deep red-purple to burgundy leaves are used fresh in Japanese food preparations: wrapping nigiri sushi and maki rolls, as a garnish for sashimi, mixed into rice, and used in the traditional preparation of umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums) where red shiso provides the characteristic color and flavor of the classic pink umeboshi. Red shiso produces the vivid red pigment (anthocyanin perillins) that colors umeboshi and red shiso juice — the brilliant magenta-red natural dye is water-soluble and stable enough for food and beverage coloring. Beyond Japanese and Korean applications, red shiso's ornamental burgundy foliage makes it valuable in kitchen garden designs where its striking color provides contrast against green vegetables, and the self-seeding habit provides a reliable annual return once established. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Red Shiso (Japanese Purple-Leaf Culinary and Pickling Herb)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; red shiso (Aka Shiso) is the purple-red-leafed variety of the Japanese culinary herb perilla — one of the foundational herbs of Japanese cuisine, used fresh in sushi (wrapped around rice and fish), as a garnish and flavoring for sashimi, in Japanese pickles (umeboshi ume plums pickled with red shiso leaves which provide both color and flavor), and as a tempura vegetable. The deeply colored, crinkled, rounded leaves in vivid burgundy-purple to dark-red-purple create striking ornamental foliage as well as excellent culinary value — red shiso is one of the most ornamentally attractive culinary herbs for the garden. The flavor is uniquely complex: simultaneously minty, anise-like, citrusy, and herbaceous with a spicy undertone that has no direct Western equivalent and is immediately recognizable as distinctly Japanese in character. Red shiso produces its most intense color and flavor in full sun; partial shade lightens the leaf color to red-green but maintains culinary quality. In zone 9, red shiso grows as a warm-season annual (April–October), tolerating Gulf South heat and humidity well. Allow plants to set seed at season end — shiso self-seeds prolifically, establishing a self-renewing naturalized patch that provides leaves season after season without replanting. Fresh young leaves are the primary harvest; flowers are also edible. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Red Spanish Pineapple (Heirloom Fresh-Market Pineapple)
description: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Red Spanish is an heirloom pineapple cultivar with a squat, barrel-shaped fruit and tough reddish-orange skin that historically made it a favorite for shipping and fresh market sale before modern refrigerated transport, since the thick rind resists bruising and handling damage. Flesh is pale yellow, firm, and tangy-sweet with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving alike. Like other pineapples, the low rosette of stiff, often spiny leaves takes about 18-24 months to mature a single fruit at its center, after which offset suckers can be detached and replanted. Pineapple has virtually no cold tolerance, so zone 9 gardeners should grow Red Spanish in a large container that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse before the first freeze and returned outside once nights stay reliably above 50F. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Red Spy Apple (Red-Skinned Northern Spy Sport, Cornell Breeding Parent)
description: Red Spy is a deeper-colored, more evenly blushed bud sport of the classic New York heirloom Northern Spy, selected for improved red skin coloring while retaining the parent's very large fruit size, crisp dense flesh, and exceptionally long storage life. Cornell breeders at the Geneva research station used it as a parent alongside Golden Delicious to produce Spigold, passing on its size and firm texture to that cross. The tree shares Northern Spy's slow-to-bear habit and long lifespan, so plan for a multi-year wait before significant production begins. Thin fruit in years of heavy set to reduce biennial bearing and support fruit size on this large-fruited strain. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Tip Cocoplum
description: Red Tip Cocoplum is the upright inland form of the native Florida cocoplum, grown as much for its ornamental flush of bright red to orange-bronze new leaves as for its small, dark purple, plum-like edible fruit used in jellies and preserves. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it grows larger and less salt-tolerant than the low, spreading 'Horizontal' coastal form, making it better suited to hammock-style gardens and hedges than beachfront plantings. Established plants tolerate heat, humidity, and periodic flooding well, and respond to shearing with dense, twiggy regrowth, making it a popular clipped hedge or screen throughout South Florida landscapes. Clusters of small white flowers appear through summer, followed by fruit that ripens over an extended season and should be picked as it colors fully for the best flavor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red Toch Garlic (Artichoke Softneck)
description: Collected near Tochliavri in the Republic of Georgia in the late 1980s, Red Toch is an Artichoke-type softneck valued among garlic growers for the striking red and pink streaking on its clove wrappers. Plant cloves pointed-end-up in fertile, well-drained soil in fall and mulch to protect against winter heaving. It forms the overlapping, many-layered cloves typical of Artichoke garlics, with a flavor that is well balanced rather than sharply hot, making it popular both raw and cooked. Harvest once the lower leaves have dried while four or five green leaves remain, then cure for three to four weeks before storing. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Red Torpedo Onion
description: This elongated torpedo-shaped Italian onion has a mild, sweet flavor ideal for fresh eating and grilling. Start indoors and transplant early, giving each bulb room to elongate in loose, fertile soil. Maintain even moisture through bulbing to develop full size, then taper off as tops lodge. Because it is a fresh-use onion, it stores only a few weeks compared with storage types. Harvest when most tops have fallen and cure briefly before use. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Red Treviso Radicchio
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Treviso (Red Treviso Radicchio) is the elongated, cone-to-torpedo-shaped Treviso type of radicchio, producing pointed heads of 10–14 inches long with deep wine-red to burgundy leaves with prominent white midribs — visually distinct from the round, compact Rossa di Verona radicchio. The naturally-heading (non-forced) Treviso type forms its distinctive elongated shape through the cool-weather growing process without requiring the dark forcing period of Tardivo, making it accessible to home growers who want Treviso-type radicchio without the complexity of forcing. The flavor is bittersweet and complex — similar to Rossa di Verona but with the elongated form lending itself to halving and grilling (the standard preparation for Treviso-type radicchio) where the heads can be placed directly on the grill without splitting apart. In zone 9 it is planted in fall and harvested November through February, with color and flavor improving with each frost. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Red Valerian
description: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; red valerian (Jupiter's beard, fox's brush, kiss-me-quick) is a Mediterranean perennial that has naturalized on rocky coastal cliffs, stone walls, and dry limestone outcrops throughout Europe and warm-climate North America — its ability to root into the smallest crevices of dry stone walls and cliff faces, producing clouds of intensely fragrant, deep coral-red, rosy-pink, or white flower clusters from late spring through summer, makes it a classic companion to stone walls, gravel gardens, and dry, chalky slopes. The young leaves and roots are edible (leaves used in salads in France and Italy as a raw herb with a mild, slightly bitter flavor), and the large, fluffy seed heads provide excellent cut material for dried arrangements. It self-seeds freely into any available dry, alkaline crack or gravel area, naturalizing remarkably quickly. Excellent in dry stone wall gardens, Mediterranean-style plantings, and hot, dry coastal gardens. 'Albus' (white), 'Coccineus' (deep crimson-red), and 'Rosenrot' (rose-pink) are named cultivars. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Red Velvet Okra
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Red Velvet is well-suited to the edible landscape as both a productive vegetable and ornamental plant with dramatic color. Red Velvet okra is one of the most ornamentally striking of all vegetable plants, producing intensely pigmented deep burgundy-red to crimson-velvet pods, stems, leaf veins, and even young leaves that make it outstanding as an edible ornamental in landscape plantings and containers; the yellow hibiscus flowers with purple-red centers add additional ornamental value. The pods are edible and flavorful at 3–4 inches, with a taste and texture identical to standard green okra; when cooked they unfortunately lose much of their dramatic red coloring (it leaches into the cooking water, which turns bright pink — interesting for certain preparations like red okra pickles). Plants are more compact than many okra varieties (4–6 feet), making them practical for smaller gardens. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Red Warty Thing Pumpkin
description: 'Red Warty Thing', descended from the 1897 heirloom 'Victor', bears bumpy, thick, red-orange 10-20 pound pumpkins with fine-textured, flavorful flesh. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the sprawling vines ample space in full sun. Water deeply and feed the heavy-feeding plants through the long season. The thick rind lets these fruits store for many months and doubles as striking fall decor. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Red Wethersfield Onion (Large Red Wethersfield)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall; direct seed outdoors can also be attempted in early spring when soil is workable.
