Red Wethersfield (also called 'Large Red Wethersfield') is perhaps the oldest onion variety with documented continuous American cultivation, grown commercially in Wethersfield, Connecticut since the late 17th century; colonial-era records describe the Wethersfield onion trade as one of the most profitable agricultural enterprises of early New England, with flat-bottomed boats (called 'onion sloops') carrying Wethersfield red onions to New York, Boston, and West Indies markets. The medium to large (3–4 inch), flattened-globe bulbs have deep red-purple to dark crimson skin and white-to-pinkish flesh with a moderately pungent flavor that mellows to mild sweetness when cooked. A long-day variety suited to zones 3–7 northern growing conditions where summer day length exceeds 14–16 hours; the thick skin provides excellent storage quality with bulbs keeping 4–6 months when properly cured in a warm, dry location before transferring to cool storage. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Red Windsor Apple (English Red-Skinned Cox-Flavored Dessert Apple)
description: Red Windsor is a modern English dessert apple selected for combining a richly aromatic, Cox-like flavor with a much more reliable, heavier-cropping habit and a fully red-flushed skin that colors easily even in cooler summers. Fruit ripens in mid-to-late fall with firm, juicy, sweet-tart flesh that holds its quality well in storage. It tends to bear consistent annual crops rather than the biennial pattern common in older Cox-type apples. Harvest once the skin has fully colored and the fruit separates easily from the spur. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Red Wine Velvet Sweet Potato (Deep Red-Skin Orange-Flesh Heirloom)
description: Plant slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil ridged up for good drainage, and avoid heavily nitrogen-rich amendments that favor foliage over root bulking. Red Wine Velvet is a mid-season, normal-leaf vining heirloom sweet potato prized for its deep wine-red skin wrapped around moist, richly colored orange flesh, offering a striking contrast to the paler skin of standard commercial types like Beauregard. Yields run average rather than exceptional, which is part of why the variety has stayed a small-grower specialty rather than a commercial staple, but the flavor is sweet and the deep-red roots make an eye-catching addition to a home harvest basket. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and cure in warm, humid conditions for one to two weeks before storing to sweeten the flesh and toughen the skin. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Red Zinger Roselle (Tea Hibiscus)
description: Grow Red Zinger in full sun and warm, well-drained soil, spacing plants generously since the tall, reddish-stemmed bushes branch widely by late summer. It is a short-day plant that holds off flowering until the days begin to shorten in late summer, then quickly loads its branches with the thick, tart, deep-red calyces that give the tea blend bearing its name its characteristic color and tang. Harvest calyces within a week or two after the petals drop, while they are still crisp, since they toughen and lose quality if left too long on the plant. Dry the harvested calyces thoroughly for tea, or use fresh for syrups, jams, and sauces before the first frost ends the season. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Red-Fleshed Durian (Durian Merah, Borneo Durian)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; requires genuinely tropical, humid, frost-free conditions; a collectors' tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts. Durio kutejensis (red-fleshed durian, durian merah, or kuning) is one of approximately 30 Durio species native to the forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — and considered by many tropical fruit connoisseurs to produce superior-quality fruit to the common commercial durian (D. zibethinus). The fruits of D. kutejensis are smaller than commercial durian (typically 2–4 lbs) and covered with shorter, broader spines; the flesh is distinctively bright red-orange to golden-yellow — dramatically different from the pale cream-yellow flesh of common durian. The flavor is often described as richer, sweeter, more complex, and less sulfurous than D. zibethinus — with strong caramel, butterscotch, and tropical fruit notes without the overwhelming, polarizing odor that makes commercial durian controversial. The relative mildness of the aroma compared to D. zibethinus is one of the key reasons D. kutejensis is considered by Southeast Asian fruit lovers to be among the finest of all wild durian species. Wild animals in Borneo (orangutans, civets, bearded pigs) are major consumers and dispersers of durian fruits; D. kutejensis provides critical nutrition to Borneo wildlife. Extremely rare in cultivation outside Borneo. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Red-flowering Currant
description: Plant in moist to dry, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; red-flowering currant is a Pacific Northwest native shrub and one of the most spectacular early-spring-blooming shrubs for Pacific Coast gardens, producing pendulous clusters of deep rose-red to carmine-pink flowers in March and April before the leaves emerge. It is the first major nectar source for returning rufous hummingbirds on their northward spring migration, and hummingbirds converge on flowering specimens in large numbers. The timing of its bloom — earliest of any showy ornamental shrub in coastal Pacific Northwest gardens — combined with its value to hummingbirds and other early pollinators makes it ecologically as well as ornamentally outstanding. The flowers are followed by small, blue-black, bloom-covered berries attractive to birds. The maple-like, aromatic leaves are attractive through summer and the shrub develops an open, graceful form. Highly drought-tolerant once established and naturally adapted to the summer-dry Pacific Coast climate. The cultivar range includes colors from white through all shades of pink to deep crimson. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Red-Veined Sorrel
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in moist, well-drained soil and thin to 9–12 in apart; red-veined sorrel germinates readily in cool soil. The lance-shaped leaves with vivid crimson veins are ornamentally striking and have a mild lemony-tart flavor suitable for salads, garnishes, and light sautés. Remove flower stalks promptly to prevent self-seeding and to keep the plant producing tender new foliage throughout the season. Harvest outer leaves when they are young and vibrant; flavor and texture deteriorate in the largest, oldest leaves. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Redbor Kale
description: 'Redbor' is a strikingly ruffled, deep purple kale that is both ornamental and delicious, with color and curl intensifying as temperatures drop. Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Extremely cold hardy, plants sweeten in fall and can survive hard freezes for late-season harvest. Pick outer leaves as needed, letting the center keep producing. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Redchief Strawberry
description: Redchief was released in 1968 by the USDA Beltsville station working with the Maryland Agricultural Experiment Station and became an important early-midseason cultivar for growers battling red stele root rot, resisting several known races of the pathogen. It also carries moderate resistance to verticillium wilt, leaf scorch, and powdery mildew, giving it broader disease tolerance than many older cultivars of its era. Berries are medium-large, sweet, and attractive, produced on vigorous plants that runner freely to fill in rows. Rotate planting sites and avoid old strawberry ground even with resistant cultivars like Redchief to limit buildup of other soilborne problems. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Redfree Apple (Scab-Immune Early-Season PRI Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Redfree was released by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program in 1981 and is field-immune to apple scab while also resisting the other major fungal and bacterial apple diseases, making it one of the most reliably low-spray apples available. It ripens earlier than most disease-resistant varieties, giving a mid-to-late-summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, crisp, juicy fruit with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh eating. Because it is one of the earliest scab-immune apples to ripen, Redfree is a good choice for gardeners who want disease resistance without waiting until fall for the harvest. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and pick fruit once it has developed full color and separates easily from the spur. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Redhaven Peach (Early-Season Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Redhaven is one of the most widely grown and consistently performing freestone peach cultivars in American horticulture — an early-season variety ripening in late May through mid-June in zone 9, which is 2–3 weeks ahead of the main-season peach crop. The medium-large, round fruit has attractive red-blushed skin over yellow background color, with yellow, firm, freestone flesh of excellent quality and rich, aromatic flavor. The early ripening is a significant advantage — early fruit escapes the worst of the summer disease pressure from brown rot and oriental fruit moth that builds through the season. The vigorous tree produces reliably heavy crops with good thinning practices. Redhaven requires approximately 950 chill hours, which is well-suited to zone 7–8 and marginal in zone 9 — growers in lower zone 9 or inland zone 9a should evaluate local chill hour accumulation data (available from county extension offices) before planting. In borderline chill-hour years, Redhaven may set a reduced or irregular bloom. Annual pruning to an open-vase form and consistent summer disease management are necessary for reliable production. Matures in 65–90 days from transplant.

name: Redheart Plum (Red-Fleshed Heirloom Blood Plum)
description: Redheart is an old American-bred plum grown chiefly for its striking deep red flesh, which runs from skin to pit rather than staying pale like most dessert plums. The flavor is sweet with a pleasant tang, and the vivid color makes it especially good for jams, jellies, and preserves that keep their color when cooked. It is a vigorous, reliably productive tree that tolerates a wide range of soils as long as drainage is good. Site with another plum for best pollination and fruit set, and thin the crop if it sets heavily to improve fruit size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Redlands #4 Jujube
description: Redlands #4 traces back to a chance seedling found on an old homestead in Redlands, California, and is grown chiefly for producing some of the largest round fruit of any jujube cultivar, exceeding the size of the widely planted Li. The flesh is crisp and richly flavored when harvested at the green-to-yellow stage for fresh eating, with texture and sugar content that hold up well through the mahogany-brown stage if left to fully ripen and semi-dry on the tree. Because jujube trees sucker readily from root fragments, plant Redlands #4 where root disturbance from nearby digging or tilling can be avoided, and pair it with a second cultivar such as Li or Lang to encourage heavier fruit set through cross-pollination. Once established, the tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with little intervention, making it a low-maintenance choice for a large specimen jujube. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Redlands Tropic Star Passion Fruit
description: Redlands Tropic Star was released by University of Florida breeders working near the Redland agricultural district south of Miami and combines the fragrant, deep-purple fruit of common passion fruit with improved tolerance of the fungal diseases that plague vines in Florida's humid growing season. It is a vigorous, self-fertile climber that needs a strong trellis or arbor, since a single plant can cover a large structure within its first year. Fruit ripens over a long summer-to-fall season and drops when fully ripe, signaling harvest time without guesswork. Choose this cultivar over unnamed seedling passion fruit when disease pressure has been a recurring problem in the garden. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Redskin Peach (Mid-Century Firm Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Redskin was released by the USDA in the mid-1940s and went on to become a widely planted mid-20th-century commercial and home orchard peach, valued for firm, yellow, freestone flesh under an attractive skin heavily blushed with red, holding up well to handling and processing while still delivering good, classic peach flavor fresh off the tree. The reliable, productive tree set the standard for decades before being gradually supplanted by newer disease-resistant cultivars, but it remains a solid, dependable choice for home orchards wanting an old-fashioned, well-proven variety. Prune to an open-vase form and follow a routine dormant-season spray program for peach leaf curl and brown rot, which affect Redskin as they do most peach cultivars. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Redstone Cornelian Cherry (Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Redstone is a fruit-improved selection of Cornus mas chosen for larger, deep-red, heavier-cropping fruit compared to unselected seedlings. Like the species, it opens small yellow flower clusters on bare branches in very early spring, well ahead of forsythia, then ripens its tart, plum-flavored fruit by midsummer, dropping as it softens so most growers gather it from a tarp shaken beneath the tree or by daily hand-picking. The fruit is prized for syrup, jam, sauces, and Eastern European-style preserves, and the tree itself tolerates poor soils, urban pollution, and drought once established with minimal pest or disease pressure. Plant it alongside another cornelian cherry cultivar for the fullest fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Redventure Celery (Modern Red-Stalked Heirloom Celery)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; Redventure is a stabilized modern breeding-line celery developed by plant breeder Frank Morton in the early 1990s from a cross of the tough, strongly flavored heirloom Giant Red celery and the smoother, more tender Ventura celery. The result combines brilliant red-to-magenta stalks and luminous emerald leaves with a chewy but non-stringy texture and a more intense, concentrated celery flavor than typical green cultivars. Because the flavor and color are so pronounced, Redventure is especially well suited to soups, stocks, and braises where its stalks and leaves add both color and depth rather than being eaten raw on their own. It is notably cold-tolerant for a celery, extending the usable harvest window well into fall. Matures in 95–105 days from transplant.

name: Redwing Onion (F1 Hybrid Long-Storage Red Onion)
description: Bred for the market grower who needs a red onion that actually lasts through winter, Redwing forms uniform, hard globes with thick, deep-red skins that resist bruising in storage. Start seed indoors under lights and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to encourage full-sized bulbs. Its late maturity means it needs a full season, but the payoff is a storage onion whose color and firmness actually improve over months in a cool, dry room. Reduce watering as tops begin to fall and cure thoroughly before bagging for storage. Matures in 104–110 days from transplant.

name: Redwood Sorrel (Oregon Oxalis)
description: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in zones 7–9; redwood sorrel is native to the floor of coastal conifer forests from the California redwoods north to British Columbia, where it forms dense, lush carpets of clover-like trifoliate leaves in one of the deepest shade environments in North America. The leaves close and fold downward in bright light — a nyctinastic response also seen in clover — and reopen in shade or at night. Small white to pale pink flowers bloom from spring through early summer. The foliage is edible in small quantities as a salad ingredient or garnish, with a bright, lemony flavor from oxalic acid; consume in moderation as large quantities can interfere with calcium absorption. Provides one of the best groundcovers for deep, moist shade under mature conifers or where dense tree canopy suppresses most other plants. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Reed Avocado
description: Reed is a round, grapefruit-sized Guatemalan-type avocado with thick, pebbled green skin that never darkens, distinguishing it visually from Hass and its black-skinned relatives at a glance. The flesh is exceptionally creamy and buttery, with 18 to 20 percent oil content and a small seed relative to fruit size that leaves an unusually high proportion of edible flesh. It ripens through the heat of summer into early fall, well after spring-ripening cultivars like Fuerte and Zutano have finished, and the tree's narrow, upright form fits smaller yards better than spreading Guatemalan types. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rees Pawpaw (Small-Seeded Heirloom Selection)
description: Rees is an older named pawpaw selection noted in Kentucky State University's historical cultivar records for its pale-yellow flesh, good flavor, and notably small seeds relative to most pawpaws, a trait that increases the proportion of edible flesh per fruit. Exact origin and ripening timing were not well documented when the selection was first cataloged, but it remains of interest to collectors seeking low-seed heirloom genetics. A genetically distinct second tree is required nearby for cross-pollination and fruit set. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Regal Lingonberry (University of Wisconsin Dwarf Groundcover Selection)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Regal was developed by the University of Wisconsin from open-pollinated seed of Finnish origin and selected for an unusually flat, prostrate habit, standing only two to four inches tall while spreading roughly two feet, making it one of the lowest-growing named lingonberry selections available for use as a true edible carpet groundcover. In warm-enough spring weather it can produce both a modest summer crop and a larger fall crop of medium-large berries, though yields are sparser than upright cultivars given the plant's diminutive size. Since lingonberries tolerate more shade than most fruiting plants, Regal works well tucked beneath blueberries, azaleas, or conifers where the soil is already suitably acidic; shear lightly every few years to keep the mat dense and vigorous. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Regal Sweet Potato (Disease-Resistant Southern Baking Type)
description: Regal was jointly developed by the USDA and the South Carolina and Texas agricultural experiment stations as a reliable, disease-resistant sweet potato for Southern home gardens and market growers. Its light orange skin and flesh give a classic sweet, moist baked texture, and broad resistance to common soil diseases and insect pests makes it more forgiving than many older heirlooms in beds that have grown sweet potatoes before. It matures a bit faster than many standard orange cultivars, which is useful insurance in a Gulf Coast garden where an early tropical storm can end the season abruptly. Grow it the same way as Beauregard or Centennial, in loose, well-drained, ridged soil in full sun. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Regale Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Regale is a University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its large, glossy black berries with a thinner skin and juicier, sweeter flesh than many older black muscadine cultivars, making it well suited to fresh eating as well as juice and wine production. Vines are vigorous and productive, ripening a heavy mid-season crop that holds up well on the vine without excessive splitting in wet weather, a common problem with thinner-skinned muscadines. Regale is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, though as with other muscadines, planting several varieties together tends to boost overall yield. It shows good disease resistance typical of muscadine grapes in humid Gulf South conditions, requiring far less fungicide input than bunch grapes. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure; expect the vine to reach full production three to four years after planting on a sturdy two-wire trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Regent Juneberry
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Regent is a compact, dwarf saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia) selected by South Dakota State University, producing a shrub typically 3–5 feet tall rather than the 8–12 foot height of standard saskatoon varieties — making it the most practical Amelanchier for small residential gardens, containers, and formal edible landscape plantings where size is a constraint. The sweet, blueberry-like berries ripen in June–July in clusters of 5–10 and are among the most delicious of any native North American fruit — eaten fresh, made into pies, jams, and wine, or dried like raisins. The flavor is richer and sweeter than blueberry with almond-like notes from the tiny edible seeds. Regent blooms very early in spring (March–April in zone 9), providing one of the first nectar sources for bees and early pollinators. The white flower clusters, attractive summer foliage, and orange-to-red fall color make Regent exceptional as an edible ornamental. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Regent Serviceberry (Compact Shrub-Form Fruiting Serviceberry)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Regent is a compact selection of saskatoon serviceberry, bred specifically as a fruiting shrub rather than a landscape specimen tree, producing heavy crops of sweet, blueberry-like berries on a manageable-sized bush well suited to home orchards, hedgerows, and edible landscaping. It shares the white spring flowers and good fall color of its tree-form relatives but stays considerably smaller, making it easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand. It is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and low-maintenance, needing only occasional removal of the oldest stems to keep the planting vigorous and productive. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Regiment Spinach (Fast-Maturing Semi-Savoy Hybrid)
description: Direct sow thinly into cool, moist, fertile soil as early as the ground can be worked, since Regiment germinates and establishes unusually well in cold soil. It produces dark green, semi-savoyed, arrowhead-shaped leaves on a fast-bunching plant that reaches harvest size in as little as five to six weeks, one of the quickest turnarounds among savoy-type spinach. Strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races keeps quality high through humid spring weather, and the leaves stay tender even as plants size up, reducing the pressure to harvest at a small stage. Cut whole plants at the base for bunching or pick outer leaves for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest. Matures in 37–45 days from seed.

name: Regina Cherry (Crack-Resistant Late-Season German Sweet Cherry)
description: Regina is a German-bred late-season sweet cherry valued commercially for its very firm, large, dark-red fruit and outstanding resistance to rain-cracking near harvest, a common problem in humid climates. It is self-unfruitful and needs a compatible pollinizer such as Sam or Hedelfingen blooming at the same time. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water evenly through fruit development, and prune annually to maintain airflow and fruiting wood. Its long hang time and firm flesh make it a favorite for growers wanting to spread out the cherry harvest window. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Reichardia / Bright-eyed Scorzonera
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in full sun into well-drained, moderately fertile soil; plants thrive in the same rocky or sandy conditions that challenge most vegetables. Once established, reichardia is remarkably drought-tolerant and requires minimal irrigation, making it an excellent choice for dry summer gardens in the Mediterranean climate zone. Harvest basal leaves as needed throughout the cooler months, cutting back to encourage fresh, tender regrowth; the plant is perennial in frost-free zones and will produce for several years from a single sowing. Young leaves are mild enough for raw salads, while older leaves are better cooked briefly as a spinach substitute. Matures in 45–80 days from seed.

name: Reid's Yellow Dent Corn (Historic Foundation Dent Corn)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and keep the crop consistently watered through tasseling, silking, and kernel fill for full ears. Reid's Yellow Dent traces to a farm in Illinois in the 1840s and became, through decades of careful ear-to-row selection in the late 1800s, one of the most influential open-pollinated corn varieties in American agricultural history, serving as foundational breeding stock behind much of the hybrid corn later developed across the Corn Belt. It produces tall, sturdy stalks with well-filled ears of smooth, deep-yellow dent kernels, valued for grinding into cornmeal, livestock feed, and general grain use, with a rich flavor typical of good open-pollinated dent corn. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk, or pull and cure them indoors on a dry rack, before shelling and storing the grain in a cool, dry, rodent-proof container. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Reine des Vallees Alpine Strawberry (Classic French Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)
description: Reine des Vallees ('Queen of the Valleys') is a 19th-century French heirloom alpine strawberry long prized for its intensely perfumed, slender conical red berries, considered by many growers among the most flavorful of the runnerless alpine types. Plants form neat, compact clumps well suited to edging borders, herb gardens, or containers, and bear continuously from early summer into fall without needing to manage runners. Set transplants in rich, well-drained soil with a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates, and pick berries often since the delicate fruit softens quickly once ripe. Division of established clumps every few years helps maintain vigor and fruit size. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Reinecke Commercial White Sapote
description: Grow Reinecke Commercial in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil away from strong wind, as with other white sapote selections. As the cultivar name suggests, it was selected with commercial handling in mind: the fruit is somewhat irregular in shape, runs around five ounces, and turns a distinctive golden-orange as it ripens. Its standout trait among white sapote cultivars is better-than-average keeping quality, since many white sapote selections soften and spoil quickly after harvest, making Reinecke Commercial a useful choice for growers who want a few extra days of shelf life before the fruit must be eaten. Harvest when the skin has colored fully and the fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure, then hold at room temperature to finish ripening. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Reisetomate Tomato (Traveler Tomato)
description: A German novelty heirloom grown less for yield than for its bizarre fruit form: individual tomato segments fuse together as they develop into a lobed, rose- or brain-like cluster that can be broken apart by hand into bite-sized pieces, each with its own thin skin. The red-orange fruit is thin-walled and only moderately flavorful, so Reisetomate is best treated as a conversation-piece crop for gardeners with room for a vigorous, heavy-vining indeterminate plant rather than a primary sauce or slicing tomato. It needs a full, warm season to size up and is most reliable where summers are long and hot, making it a good fit for a Gulf South vegetable garden with space to spare. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Reiter's Red Creeping Thyme
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown starts in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun. Reiter's Red forms a very low, wiry mat of small dark green leaves topped with a dense, deep rose-red flower display in early summer that reads redder than most other creeping thyme cultivars, and it has a reputation among xeriscape growers for outperforming other red-flowered thymes in hot, dry, high-altitude conditions. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and is a good choice for gravel gardens, dry stone paths, and the gaps between flagstones in full-sun sites where many other groundcovers struggle. Shear lightly right after bloom to maintain a tight mat and prevent the center from opening up and going woody; avoid rich or consistently damp soil. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Reka Blueberry (Early-Season New Zealand Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Reka is an early-to-midseason highbush blueberry bred in New Zealand, valued for its compact, vigorous, upright bush and large, firm berries with a bright, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that ripens ahead of many standard highbush varieties. The early ripening window makes it useful for extending the front end of a home blueberry harvest when paired with midseason and late varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and overall yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Reliance Grape (Cold-Hardy Pink Seedless Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Reliance was bred at the University of Arkansas and is prized for its outstanding cold hardiness among seedless grapes, along with medium-sized pink-red berries that are sweet, tender-skinned, and easy to eat fresh off the cluster. It ripens in midseason and is self-fruitful, though thinning clusters improves berry size and vine longevity. Because it needs sustained winter chill to perform well, it is best suited to northern and mid-South gardens rather than the humid, mild-winter Gulf Coast, where muscadines and Pierce's-tolerant hybrids are more reliable. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Reliance Peach (Ultra-Cold-Hardy Northern Peach, New Hampshire Freestone)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; thin to 6–8 inches in spring; Reliance is self-fruitful and requires no cross-pollinator; the trees are vigorous and productive, delivering reliable crops in zones where other peach varieties fail due to winter cold; fruit ripens early-mid season (late July to mid-August in zones 4–6). Reliance peach is the most cold-hardy named peach variety in widespread cultivation in North America, developed by F.H. Emerson at the University of New Hampshire (released 1964) specifically for the challenging peach-growing conditions of New England and the northern United States where standard peach varieties like Elberta, Loring, and Madison lose their flower buds to winter cold or late spring frosts too frequently to be reliable crops. The extraordinary cold-hardiness of Reliance is its defining characteristic: dormant wood has survived -25°F in New Hampshire orchard trials, and the flower buds show significantly better cold-tolerance than most other varieties. In comparative cold-hardiness tests, Reliance consistently outperforms all other widely-available named peach varieties, giving it a unique market niche as 'the peach you can actually grow in the North.' Fruit quality is good but not exceptional compared to premium mid-South varieties — the fruits are medium-sized, round to oval, with a red blush over yellow background, and a pleasant yellow-fleshed, sweet, fully freestone flavor. The flavor is somewhat mild compared to full-sun, high-quality southern peaches, reflecting the shorter, cooler northern growing season. However, for gardeners in zones 4–6 where reliable peach production from standard varieties is difficult or impossible, Reliance delivers consistent, acceptable-quality fresh peaches from a tree that simply survives winters that would kill other varieties. Matures in 90–115 days from transplant.

name: Reliance Seedless Grape (Red Seedless Home Garden Grape, Hardy Seedless)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun; spur-prune in late winter to 2 buds per spur; Reliance is self-fruitful; fruit ripens mid-August in most zones; the medium-sized, rose-red to red berries are seedless, tender-skinned, and sweet with a mild, pleasant flavor more subtle than Concord; excellent for fresh eating, fruit salads, and home winemaking. Reliance seedless grape is a University of Arkansas-bred red seedless table grape (released 1982, bred by James Moore) that became the most widely planted cold-hardy seedless home garden grape in the United States, filling a genuine need for a sweet, seedless fresh-eating grape that could be grown reliably in zones 4–8 where the California-bred Thompson Seedless and Flame Red Seedless (developed for California's mild winters and low humidity) perform poorly or inconsistently. The breeding background of Reliance includes multiple American Labrusca and hybrid species crosses selected for cold-hardiness, which gives the variety a very cold-tolerant profile — mature canes are hardy to -15°F and the variety tolerates late spring frosts reasonably well. The berries are medium-sized, red-rose to medium red (lighter than dark blue varieties like Mars), round to slightly oval, and truly seedless with a tender, non-slip skin (unlike the slip-skin character of Concord and Niagara). The flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasantly fruity without the strong Labrusca 'foxiness' of slip-skin varieties — closer to the flavor profile of commercial seedless grapes but with its own mild aromatic quality. Reliance is a productive, reliable variety that earns its place as the standard seedless home garden grape for most of the northern and central United States. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rendidora Tomatillo (Upright High-Yield Tomatillo)
description: Rendidora is a Mexican-improved tomatillo selection bred for a notably upright, self-supporting growth habit rather than the sprawling vines typical of most tomatillo varieties, making it easier to manage and harvest in a small garden bed without extensive staking. Its name, roughly translating to high-yielding, reflects its reputation for heavy, dependable fruit set: round, slightly flattened, pale yellow-green fruit that fills its papery husk fully at maturity with the classic tart, citrusy tomatillo flavor. The more compact, upright plants can be spaced closer together than standard sprawling tomatillo types, making Rendidora a good choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast vegetable gardens where space for wide-spreading vines is limited. As with all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals to ensure cross-pollination and fruit set. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Renegade Spinach (Downy Mildew and Mosaic Virus-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Renegade is a spinach hybrid bred with resistance to numerous races of downy mildew along with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus, giving it a broader disease package than most spinach varieties and helping it stay productive through the damp, changeable weather of a Gulf South winter. It also shows good bolt tolerance, holding a harvestable rosette longer into warming spring weather than many varieties. The upright, dark green leaves are well suited to both fresh eating and cooking. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Republic of Texas Fig (Cold-Hardy Brown Sugar Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Republic of Texas is among the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant fig cultivars grown in Texas home orchards, tolerating both harder winter freezes and drier soil than many other figs. Fruit is medium-sized with brownish-purple skin and sweet, deep amber-pink flesh with a rich, honeyed flavor, ripening over a long harvest window from summer into fall. Even where winter cold kills the top growth to the ground, the vigorous root system reliably resprouts and fruits again the following year, making it a forgiving choice for the cooler edge of fig-growing range. Prune to control size and remove winter-killed wood in spring once new growth reveals what survived. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Republic of Texas Lime (Cold-Hardy Thornless Lime)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be sheltered during hard freezes; Republic of Texas is a nearly thornless lime of uncertain hybrid parentage that has become a favorite dooryard and patio citrus across the Gulf South because it is noticeably more cold-tolerant and heat-tolerant than true Key lime, while still delivering a strongly aromatic, classic lime flavor. Trees are vigorous, heavy-bearing, and begin fruiting young, producing abundant small to medium, thin-skinned, seedy fruit that ripens from pale green to yellow — harvest while still green for the brightest acidity, since fully yellow fruit turns sweeter and less lime-like. It is self-fertile and does not need a pollinizer. In zone 9a, site trees against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection and wrap or cover young trees during freeze events; established in-ground trees recover from light freeze damage by resprouting from the trunk. Fertilize with a citrus-specific blend three times during the growing season and keep the root zone mulched but not piled against the trunk. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rescue Pear (Early Canadian Cold-Hardy Prairie Pear)
description: Rescue was one of the earliest cold-hardy pear cultivars bred in Canada from Ussurian pear parentage, selected specifically to survive prairie winters that kill standard European pear cultivars outright. It blooms later than most pears in spring, helping its flowers escape many late-frost events that damage earlier-blooming fruit trees in northern climates. The medium, round, yellow-green fruit ripens in late summer with a mild, somewhat gritty texture better suited to canning, sauce, and preserves than fresh eating, though well-ripened fruit softens to acceptable fresh dessert quality. Like other Ussurian-derived pears, Rescue shows good resistance to fire blight, an important advantage over European pears in humid growing regions, and benefits from a second cold-hardy pear such as 'Ure' planted nearby for cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Resigno Beach Plum (Named Beach Plum Selection for Improved Fruit)
description: Site in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun and plant beside a different named beach plum cultivar, since seedling beach plum and single clones set fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Resigno is one of a small group of named beach plum selections, along with Jersey Gem and ECOS, chosen from wild coastal populations for producing larger and better-flavored fruit than typical unimproved seedling stands, in which individual bushes can vary from sweet to notably sour or bitter. Its fruit ripens in late summer to shades of red, purple, or blue-black and is prized for the traditional New England and mid-Atlantic beach plum jams and jellies. As a true coastal dune native, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soil that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and needs only light pruning after flowering to remain productive. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Resina Calendula
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Resina is a calendula cultivar specifically selected by the Heritage Seed Program for maximum resin content rather than ornamental appeal — the flower heads are visibly more resinous and sticky than standard ornamental calendula varieties, with a higher concentration of the triterpenoid saponins and flavonoids that make calendula one of the most important herbs in traditional and contemporary herbal medicine. The high-resin flowers are the preferred type for making calendula-infused oil (used in salves, lip balms, and skin care products), tinctures, and medicinal teas where the active compound concentration per flower is significantly higher than in standard varieties. Resina flowers are single to semi-double in pale to deep orange and yellow, with the characteristic sticky feel of the bracts when harvested. In zone 9 the cool-season planting from October through February produces the most productive and resinous flower crop. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Resina Calendula
description: Resina calendula was bred for exceptionally resin-rich petals, making it the go-to variety for herbalists preparing salves and infused oils. Its bright yellow, daisy-like blooms shine in the garden and are so frost tolerant they may keep flowering into the snow. Direct sow and cover the seed well, since darkness aids germination, in a sunny spot with average soil. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and harvest fully open flower heads on a dry morning for the best medicinal quality. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Restharrow (Cammock)
description: Ononis spinosa is a wiry, spine-tipped European legume subshrub of dry chalk grassland and roadside verges, named for its tenacious, tough taproots that were said to catch and stop a horse-drawn harrow. Small pink pea flowers appear along the spiny stems in mid to late summer, followed by small pods, and the plant fixes its own nitrogen, thriving in poor, lean, unamended ground. The dried root bark has a long folk history as a mild diuretic used for gravel and minor urinary complaints. Grow in full sun on sharply drained, even gravelly, low-fertility soil; rich or damp ground produces lank, floppy growth and shortens the plant's lifespan. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Reveille Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early Mechanical-Harvest NC State Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Reveille, released by North Carolina State University in 1990, ripens early, typically by the beginning of May, and was originally bred with mechanical harvest and fresh-market shipping in mind, giving it a firm, well-formed berry that holds up to handling. It is unpatented and has long been available to home growers as an early, dependable southern highbush option, though the fruit can be prone to cracking if heavy rain falls just as berries approach full ripeness, so harvest promptly once color develops. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Revival Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Hybrid)
description: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Revival is an American-Chinese hybrid chestnut developed as part of the blight-resistant breeding lineage that also produced the well-known Dunstan chestnut, combining some of the American chestnut's tree form and nut quality with the Chinese chestnut's resistance to chestnut blight. Trees bear precociously, often within a few years of planting, and produce medium to large, sweet nuts that drop free of the burr for easy harvest in fall. Because it carries genuine blight resistance rather than simply avoidance, Revival can be planted with more confidence in areas with a history of chestnut blight pressure than pure American chestnut. Good heat tolerance makes it a reasonable choice for Gulf South food-forest and small-orchard plantings, though as with all chestnuts, well-drained soil and good air circulation help minimize disease pressure in humid summers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Revolution Bell Pepper (Bacterial Spot and Phytophthora-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Revolution is a bell pepper hybrid bred for an unusually broad disease package, combining resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus and Phytophthora root rot, a soil-borne disease that thrives in the heavy rain and poorly drained spots common in Gulf Coast gardens. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant. Because it resists both a major foliar disease and a major root disease, Revolution tends to hold up better than many varieties through a wet, humid growing season. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or allow fruit to fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Rexrot Gooseberry (Large-Fruited Mildew-Resistant Red Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Rexrot is a large-fruited European gooseberry cultivar from German nursery breeding, prized for heavy, reliable yields and good resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that plagues many older gooseberry cultivars in humid conditions. Fruit is large and round, ripening by midsummer from a yellowish-green base to a red blush on the sun-exposed side, with a rich, aromatic, sweet-tart flavor well suited to fresh eating, pies, and preserves; the high, efficient yield per bush also makes it popular for pick-your-own operations. Like other European gooseberries, Rexrot prefers cool summers and consistently moist, well-drained soil, and benefits from afternoon shade and mulch to keep roots cool where summers run hot and humid; expect diminished vigor in the Deep South and similarly warm, humid climates. Prune out the oldest canes each winter and thin crowded growth to maintain the open framework that keeps mildew pressure low and eases harvest from the thorny wood. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Rezista Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rezista is a heat-tolerant, slow-bolting European butterhead lettuce selected specifically for warm-climate production — it remains productive 2–3 weeks longer than standard butterhead varieties under heat stress before bolting, providing a meaningfully extended spring harvest window in zone 9 and making it one of the most useful warm-season lettuces for Gulf Coast gardeners. The medium-sized butterhead heads have soft, mild, tender leaves typical of the butterhead type, with a flavor and texture that are difficult to distinguish from standard butterhead when grown in cool weather. Rezista's key value is in the warm-spring transition period (March–May in zone 9) when most lettuces have given up but cool-season crops are still preferred over summer alternatives. Partial shade from established transplants or shade cloth reduces heat stress further during this critical period. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through winter maximize the productive season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Rhode Island Greening Apple (Classic Colonial-Era Tart Pie Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Rhode Island Greening dates to around 1650, one of the oldest apple varieties native to New England, and it became one of the most celebrated American cooking apples of the 18th and 19th centuries, prized for large, green to yellow-green fruit with firm, tart, aromatic flesh widely considered among the very best for pie-making, since it holds its shape and delivers bright, well-balanced flavor when baked. The vigorous, spreading tree bears heavily once established, and the fruit keeps reasonably well in cool storage through much of the winter. While less commonly planted commercially today than in its heyday, Rhode Island Greening remains a favorite among heirloom orchardists and bakers who specifically seek out its superior pie-apple qualities. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rhodos Escarole (Batavian Endive)
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to allow heads room to fill out. Rhodos is a modern Batavian-type escarole bred for a fast, uniform habit with semi-savoyed, dark green outer leaves surrounding a naturally pale, self-blanching heart, sparing gardeners the need to tie leaves for blanching. It resists bolting and tipburn better than many older escarole strains, making it reliable for both spring and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a milder, less bitter flavor than curly frisee types. Matures in 48–60 days from seed.

name: Rhubarb
description: Plant root divisions 3–4 in deep in deeply dug, compost-enriched soil, setting buds just at the soil surface. Do not harvest any stalks in the first year, and take only a few in year two so the crown can establish a deep root system. From year three onward, harvest stalks when they are 12–18 in long and 3/4 in thick by pulling and twisting at the base; remove any flower stalks that appear immediately to prevent weakening the crown. Note that only the stalks are edible—the leaves contain high concentrations of oxalic acid and are toxic. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Rhubarb Chard (Ruby Red Swiss Chard, Classic Red-Stemmed Chard)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in fertile, moist, well-amended soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued growth — leaving some inner leaves promotes sustained production. Rhubarb Chard (also called Ruby Red Swiss Chard or simply Red Chard) is the classic red-stemmed form of Swiss chard, grown for centuries for both its striking ornamental appearance and excellent culinary value. The deep, vivid crimson-red to ruby-red stems and ribs contrast dramatically against the dark green, deeply crinkled leaves, creating one of the most visually attractive vegetables in the edible garden and making Rhubarb Chard a staple in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings. The name references the stems' resemblance in color (but not flavor) to rhubarb. The red pigmentation comes from betalain pigments — the same compounds in red beets — which are vibrant raw but bleed into cooking water, giving a pinkish tint to any cooking liquid and fading the stems somewhat when cooked. The leaves are excellent cooked like spinach or kale (sauté with garlic and olive oil is the classic preparation), and young leaves are delicious raw in salads. Rhubarb Chard is more heat-tolerant than spinach and more cold-tolerant than basil, occupying a useful niche as a year-round leaf vegetable in zone 8–9 gardens where it often grows through the winter as an important fresh green when other vegetables are unavailable. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Riberry (Small-Leaf Lillypilly, Clove Lilli Pilli)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry can be pruned as a formal hedge or left to grow as a specimen small tree. Syzygium luehmannii (riberry or small-leaf lillypilly) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the subtropical and warm-temperate rainforests of New South Wales and Queensland — one of the most commercially important of the Australian lilly pilly (Syzygium) species in the native food industry. The tree produces abundant clusters of small (1/2-inch), teardrop-shaped, vivid magenta-crimson fruits, and is one of the most prolific and reliable fruiting lilly pillies in the genus. The riberry flavor is unique and highly prized: sour, fruity, and sweet with distinctive warm cinnamon-clove spice notes from the high eugenol content — a flavor combination with no equivalent in European or American fruits. In Australian native food (bushfood) cuisine, riberries are used in jams, sauces, wines, ice creams, vinegars, and as a garnish for savory dishes — particularly with game, lamb, and cheese. As a landscape plant, riberry is compact, attractive, and responds very well to formal clipping into hedge shapes; the coppery-red new growth flushes make it ornamentally outstanding. Its combination of ornamental and food value makes it one of the best lilly pillies for zone 9–12 edible landscapes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ribier Grape (Historic Large Black Seeded Table Grape)
description: Ribier, grown in Europe under the name Alphonse Lavallée, is a historic French black table grape once a mainstay of the California fresh-market grape trade before seedless varieties largely displaced seeded types in supermarkets. Its very large, round, thick-skinned, jet-black berries have mild, sweet, unassuming flavor rather than intense complexity, but their impressive size and striking color made them a favorite for fruit bowls and holiday displays for much of the twentieth century. Vines are vigorous and productive, ripening late in the season, and the thick skin gives the berries useful resistance to cracking and rot compared with thinner-skinned varieties. Train to a permanent cordon system, prune hard each winter, and thin developing clusters to a manageable number of berries, since Ribier tends to overset and undersized fruit loses the variety's main visual appeal. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ribston Pippin Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby. Raised in Yorkshire, England around 1707 and one of the two parent varieties of the famous Cox's Orange Pippin, it bears medium, orange-red-flushed, lightly russeted apples with rich, aromatic, sharp-sweet flesh that made it one of the most celebrated English dessert apples of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries before its own offspring largely eclipsed its popularity. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination, and it can be a somewhat biennial, uneven bearer from year to year. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks, during which the rich, sharp flavor continues to develop and mellow slightly. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rice
description: Start seeds in shallow flats of moist potting mix at 70–80°F, then transplant 6–9-inch seedlings to flooded paddies, water gardens, or large containers filled with heavy garden soil and submerged under 2–4 inches of standing water; upland (dry-land) varieties can be grown in moist garden beds without flooding but require consistently wet soil throughout the season. Rice matures in 90–150 days depending on variety — grain is ready when the panicle droops and grains turn golden-yellow. Drain standing water 3–4 weeks before harvest and allow the plant to dry on the stalk before cutting. Threshing by hand is practical for small plots. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Rice Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil; rice bean is a heat-tolerant tropical legume widely grown across Southeast and South Asia, where it is often intercropped with rice and maize. The small, oval seeds range from yellow to red to brownish-red and are cooked in the same ways as adzuki beans — in soups, dals, sweet red bean paste, and as a dried bean staple. The plant is semi-vining or bushy and fixes atmospheric nitrogen. It is one of the more underutilized warm-season legumes for Gulf Coast and tropical climates where cowpeas and yard-long beans already perform well. Nutritionally the seeds are high in protein (20–25%) and iron. Young pods may also be eaten as snap beans. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Rice Paddy Herb (Vietnamese Herb, Limnophila)
description: Root stem cuttings in water or wet soil in partial shade to full sun; rice paddy herb is the fresh herb most responsible for the distinctive, complex aroma of Vietnamese pho and many other Southeast Asian soups — the crushed leaves have a remarkably layered fragrance combining cumin, rice, lemon, and a unique floral quality that is difficult to describe but instantly recognizable in a bowl of authentic pho. It is used fresh as a tableside herb for hot soups and spring rolls in Vietnamese cuisine, where it is called rau om. The plant grows naturally in rice paddies and flooded fields throughout tropical Asia, requiring consistently wet to aquatic conditions — it will not thrive in typical garden soil that dries between waterings. Plant at pond margins, in water gardens, or in containers kept sitting in 1–2 inches of water for reliable production. In zone 9–10 it persists as a perennial through mild winters; harvest regularly by pinching stems to keep plants bushy and productive. Matures in 30–60 days from transplant.

name: Rich's Dwarf Quince (Compact Dwarf-Habit Quince for Small Orchards)
description: Rich's Dwarf is valued chiefly for its naturally reduced, compact stature compared with standard quince selections, staying small enough for a large container or a tight backyard corner while still producing typical hard, aromatic, golden fruit each fall. Like other quince, the raw fruit is dense and astringent and needs cooking to develop its floral, honeyed character for jelly, paste, and preserves. Its smaller mature size means less pruning is needed to keep the canopy open, though thinning out crowded interior growth still helps reduce fire blight pressure in humid climates. Because the tree stays compact, it is a practical choice for gardeners who want a quince harvest without dedicating the footprint a full-sized tree requires. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Richmond Green Apple Cucumber
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Richmond Green Apple is an Australian heirloom cucumber producing small, round, apple-shaped fruits of 2–3 inches diameter with smooth, pale green to ivory-green skin and crisp, exceptionally sweet, very mild, lightly perfumed white flesh with minimal seeds. The round shape and pale coloration are genuinely apple-like, and the name is descriptive — the flesh has a fresh, delicate sweetness with a faint floral note unlike the somewhat vegetal flavor of standard slicing cucumbers. The skin is thin and does not require peeling; the whole fruit can be eaten like an apple or sliced into salads where its elegant shape makes for attractive presentation. Richmond Green Apple has a reputation for very low bitterness and is considered by some cucumber enthusiasts the sweetest and most refined of the heirloom cucumber types. In zone 9 it performs well in the spring and fall cucumber seasons; the small fruit size and productive vines make it excellent for container growing on a small trellis. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Ridge Gourd (Angled Luffa)
description: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in warm soil after last frost and provide a trellis or fence immediately, as vines climb vigorously by tendrils. Ridge gourd differs from smooth luffa in having ten prominent sharp ridges running the length of the fruit and slightly more tender flesh when young. Harvest fruits at 6–9 inches long while skin is still soft and the ridges are firm and green — the young flesh is mild, slightly sweet, and commonly used in Indian dal, stir-fries, and curries. Like smooth luffa, fruits left to fully mature develop a tough fiber skeleton and can serve as a scrubbing sponge. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Ridged Luffa (Angled Loofah, Ridge Gourd)
description: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide strong trellis — ridged luffa is a vigorous climber. Luffa acutangula (ridged luffa or angled loofah) is the more tender, edible species of luffa — a tropical Asian cucurbit vine grown throughout South and Southeast Asia as a primary vegetable crop. Ridged luffa is distinguished from smooth luffa (L. aegyptiaca) by its deeply ridged, angled, dark-green fruits (hence 'ridged' and 'angled' in the name) and by being significantly milder, more tender, and less bitter when eaten young. At 6–8 inches, young ridged luffa fruits have a mild, delicate flavor similar to mild zucchini with a slightly slippery texture — excellent stir-fried, in curries, soups, and Indian sabzi. It is an extremely productive vine in the Gulf Coast heat, producing continuous fruit through summer. The vine also produces attractive, bright-yellow flowers. If fruits are allowed to mature fully and dry, they produce a natural fiber loofah (the vascular skeleton of the mature fruit) — both varieties produce usable loofahs, but ridged luffa fibers are softer. In Indian, Filipino, and Southeast Asian cuisines, ridged luffa is preferred over smooth for vegetable use. Matures in 50–80 days from seed.

name: Riesentraube Tomato (Giant Bunch of Grapes)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking, caging, or trellis support as plants grow vigorously to 6–8 feet; Riesentraube benefits from pruning to 1–2 leaders for best cluster development and air circulation. Riesentraube is a German heirloom cherry tomato documented in American seed catalogs by the 1850s and one of the oldest cherry tomato varieties maintained in continuous cultivation; the name 'Riesentraube' translates as 'giant bunch of grapes,' which perfectly describes the plant's most distinctive characteristic — enormous, pendulous clusters of 20, 30, or even 40+ small (1–1.5 oz) round, red fruits hanging in tight, cascade-like grape formations from the indeterminate vines. Each individual fruit has a pointed blossom end, which together with the cluster arrangement gives the plant an unmistakable profile compared to modern cherry tomatoes. The flavor is rich, tangy, and well-balanced with classic cherry tomato sweetness; the pointed fruits with thicker skin crack less than many cherry types and hold on the cluster longer after ripening. Riesentraube is both ornamentally spectacular in the garden (the cascading clusters are genuinely striking) and extremely productive, with harvests continuing from midsummer through first frost. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Riesling Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties. Late-ripening, aromatic, and capable of producing wines ranging from bone-dry to intensely sweet depending on when the grapes are picked, it retains bright, food-friendly acidity even at high sugar levels, a hallmark that has made it one of the most versatile and food-pairing-friendly white wine grapes grown worldwide. Its relatively high tolerance for winter cold makes it a realistic choice for home vineyards in cooler regions where more tender vinifera varieties struggle to survive, though it still needs a long growing season to fully ripen. Prune for an open canopy to promote airflow and reduce disease pressure, and consider harvest timing carefully, since flavor and sweetness profile change significantly the longer fruit hangs on the vine. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ring of Fire Cayenne Pepper (AAS Early Compact Cayenne)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost into warm, well-drained soil; Ring of Fire is compact enough for containers (5-gallon minimum) and makes an excellent patio pepper both for culinary use and as an ornamental with upright clusters of ripening red fruits. Ring of Fire is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning cayenne pepper introduced by Park Seed that distinguished itself in AAS trials for its early maturity and compact plant habit compared to standard Long Red Cayenne types. Where standard Long Red Cayenne reaches 24–36 inches and takes 70–80 days from transplant, Ring of Fire is more compact (18–24 inches) and earlier (60–75 days), making it better suited for containers, shorter growing seasons, and gardeners who want cayenne peppers without managing large, sprawling plants. The fruits are classic cayenne in form — pencil-thin, 4–5 inches long, tapering to a point — and ripen from green through yellow to red in an attractive cluster that gives the variety its name; fruits remain attached to the plant well through ripening, making the loaded plant highly ornamental. Heat level is typical cayenne range (70,000–85,000 SHU) — significantly hotter than jalapeños and suitable for use in all traditional cayenne applications: fresh salsa, hot sauce, cayenne powder, drying into ristras, and as a heat element in cooking. Ring of Fire is particularly well-suited to Gulf Coast home gardeners who want a reliable cayenne producer through the long warm season. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Rio Caribe Cacao
description: Named for the colonial port town on Venezuela's Paria Peninsula where it has been grown and traded since colonial times, Rio Caribe is a Trinitario-type cacao descended from local Criollo stock and ranks among the most sought-after fine-flavor beans in the world. Its fermented, dried beans are known for deep chocolate intensity paired with nutty, low-acid, faintly coffee-like undertones rather than the brighter fruit notes typical of many other Venezuelan cacaos. The trees grow in the humid coastal lowlands of eastern Venezuela, traditionally beneath mixed shade canopy alongside other food crops in small-holder plots. As with Carenero, Rio Caribe is primarily a regional trade designation rather than a single registered clone, so plant material is typically sourced as regional seed or budwood. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rio Grande Peach (Texas-Bred Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred in Texas for roughly 400-500 chill hours, Rio Grande is a dependable mid-season choice for the warmer half of zone 8 into zone 9 where many standard peaches underperform. It produces large yellow freestone fruit with a red blush, ripening in June with rich, classic peach flavor. Self-fertile and heat-tolerant, it needs hot, sunny summers to size its fruit properly and can disappoint in cooler, cloudier growing seasons. A good mid-season companion to earlier ultra-low-chill selections for a longer harvest window. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rio Red Grapefruit
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, the warmest available location; Rio Red is a grapefruit cultivar developed at Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis of Ruby Red stock and released in 1984 — and has since become the dominant commercial grapefruit variety in Texas, replacing both Ruby Red and Star Ruby on most commercial acreage. The fruit is the gold standard for Texas red grapefruit: large, with yellow skin blushed deep red-pink, and flesh that is deep crimson-red, very sweet (low acidity), with complex flavor and very few seeds. Rio Red's flesh has the deepest, most consistent red color of any commercially significant grapefruit variety, a characteristic valued by both fresh market buyers and for appearance when halved. The trees are vigorous and productive. Feed with citrus fertilizer 3–4 times annually and supplement with zinc and manganese chelate if leaves show deficiency symptoms on alkaline soils. Protect below 28°F. In zone 9 the long hot summers develop excellent sweetness and color in the fall crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rio Verde Cabbage (Heat-Tolerant Blue-Green Fall Cabbage)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 15-18 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart, and keep moisture even as heads begin to fill out. Rio Verde is a main-season hybrid cabbage bred for exceptional tolerance of heat and humidity, producing large, slightly flattened, dense blue-green heads that commonly reach 4-6 pounds without splitting even when harvest is delayed. It has been a long-running recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter for southern fall gardens because it germinates and establishes reliably in late-summer heat that stalls many other cabbages, then finishes with good size and quality through the cooler months. Choose Rio Verde where a proven, widely adapted variety with a long track record in hot, humid climates matters more than novelty. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Rio Zape Bean (Hopi Purple String Bean, Ancient Aztec Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost at the base of sturdy poles or trellises in full sun; Rio Zape is an ancient bean of Aztec and Hopi origin with distinctive dark purple-brown seeds streaked and spotted with maroon or lavender markings that fade to a deep chocolate color on cooking. It has an exceptional rich, chocolatey-earthy flavor with complex undertones — often called the best-tasting dry bean by chefs who discover it — and a creamy texture excellent in tacos, soups, and refried beans. Drought-adapted from its desert Southwest heritage; it performs well in hot, dry conditions where other beans struggle. A prized heirloom for serious bean enthusiasts. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Ripbor Kale (Tall Frilly Red-Purple Hybrid Curly Kale)
description: Direct sow or start indoors and transplant, giving plants ample room to reach their full upright height, and harvest lower leaves first as the plant continues growing from the top. This hybrid was bred as a red-purple counterpart to the popular green curly hybrids, with tightly ruffled maroon-purple leaves on tall, sturdy stems. Cold exposure deepens its color and sweetens its flavor, and its height makes it a striking option for both the vegetable garden and cut-foliage use. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Riverbank Grape (Frost Grape)
description: Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy soil in full sun along riverbanks, fences, and arbors; riverbank grape is native to streambanks and forest edges across most of North America, from Quebec to Texas, and is one of the most cold-hardy wild grapes — surviving to zone 2. The small, highly fragrant flowers in spring are intensely honey-scented and attract numerous pollinators. The small, blue-black, tart grapes ripen after the first fall frost (hence 'frost grape'), becoming slightly sweeter and less astringent with cold exposure. This species has been critically important in wine breeding — it is a parent of numerous cold-hardy wine grape cultivars including 'Marquette', 'Frontenac', and 'Frontenac Gris' developed for cold northern climates. Also an important source of phylloxera-resistant rootstock for European wine grapes. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Riverside Giant Rhubarb (Vigorous English Heirloom Rhubarb)
description: Plant crown divisions in early spring, allowing extra spacing beyond typical rhubarb cultivars since Riverside Giant produces unusually large leaves and stalks. Work generous compost into the planting hole and keep young plants well watered until established. This traditional English allotment variety is grown chiefly for its exceptional vigor and heavy yields, throwing thick green-to-pink stalks large enough to have made it a favorite for exhibition growers as well as home cooks wanting a high volume of stalks for freezing and preserving. Its productivity comes with a mild, less intensely tart flavor than some red-skinned cultivars, so it is often paired with strawberries or extra sugar in desserts. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rivoli Radish (AAS-Winning Large Non-Pithy Radish)
description: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked. Rivoli is an AAS-winning radish notable for growing to a substantially larger round size than most globe radishes — up to 2 inches or more across — while keeping its white flesh dense and crisp rather than turning pithy or hollow the way an oversized radish typically does, giving gardeners a bigger harvest window and more flexibility about exact pick timing. Its bright red skin and clean round shape make it visually appealing for slicing and garnishing as well as eating whole. Keep soil consistently moist for the best size and texture, and it was, at the time of its award, the first radish AAS winner in several decades — reflecting a genuinely useful improvement over standard varieties rather than just a color or shape novelty. Matures in 28–35 days from seed.

name: Roaring Lion Gooseberry (Historic Red Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Roaring Lion is a historic English gooseberry cultivar that was carried in the American Pomological Society's fruit catalog from 1873 to 1897, bearing medium-sized, smooth, light red, subacid berries good for pies and preserves. Older trial records note it can lack vigor and is somewhat prone to mildew compared with tougher modern cultivars, so it suits heirloom collectors more than large-scale production. Like other European gooseberries, it needs a substantial winter chill and struggles in the mild, humid winters of the Gulf South. Grow it in full sun to light shade on fertile, well-drained soil, pruned to an open habit for good airflow. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Robada Apricot (Early-Season Red-Blushed California Apricot)
description: Robada is a California apricot bred from a cross of Orangered and a University of California breeding selection, prized for its striking bright red blush over golden-orange skin and deep orange, firm freestone flesh. It ripens very early, among the first apricots of the season in early June, and the firm flesh handles shipping better than many older early varieties. Robada is not reliably self-fruitful in most plantings, so pair it with Patterson, Castlebrite, or another apricot with overlapping bloom for a full crop. Its moderate chilling requirement suits zone 7 through 9 gardens that receive a real winter but still want an early, richly colored apricot. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Robert Feijoa (Self-Fertile South American Selection)
description: Robert traces to South American feijoa stock and has long been grown in California as a dependable self-fertile cultivar, meaning a single bush can set a worthwhile crop without a second variety planted for cross-pollination, a real advantage for gardeners with room for only one feijoa. Fruit is medium in size with smooth skin and sweet, juicy flesh carrying the classic pineapple-guava-mint flavor, ripening across a fairly long mid-season window rather than all at once. The shrub is a strong, reliable grower with the typical silvery-backed evergreen foliage, taking well to hedging, screening, or espalier against a sunny wall. Because it is self-fertile but still improves with a partner, gardeners who later add a second cultivar such as Wiki Tu or Anatoki nearby will usually see a further bump in yield and fruit size on both plants. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Robert Grimm Sage (Dwarf Mat-Forming Culinary Sage)
description: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it plenty of room to spread since this selection forms a broad, low mat rather than the upright clump of standard culinary sage. The small, silvery-gray leaves have the same bold, savory sage flavor as full-size garden sage but are easier to harvest in small pinches for fresh use, and spikes of blue flowers appear above the foliage in late spring. Because the plant spreads outward rather than up, it works well as a fragrant, edible groundcover along a path edge or spilling over a low wall. Cut it back by about a third in early spring to remove any winter dieback and keep the mat from opening up in the center. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Robin Beet
description: 'Robin' was bred for harvesting at baby size, delivering well-rounded, tender, sweet 1 to 1.5 inch roots with high bolt resistance. Direct sow the seed clusters 1/2 inch deep and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart, since each cluster can produce several plants. Keep moisture even for crisp, crack-free roots, and harvest young for the best texture. The tender baby greens are also excellent raw or cooked. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Robin Hill Serviceberry (Pink-Blushed Hybrid Serviceberry)
description: Robin Hill is a hybrid serviceberry cultivar distinguished from most white-flowered types by its deep pink flower buds that open to a pale pink that fades toward white as the blooms mature, giving a two-toned effect on the shrub in early spring. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade for the strongest bloom and best orange-red fall color. Like other Amelanchier x grandiflora selections, it produces sweet, blueberry-like fruit in early summer that draws songbirds quickly, so gardeners hoping to harvest berries should net the plant or watch it closely as fruit ripens. It works well as a specimen tree or in a naturalized shrub border. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Robinson Tangerine (Early-Season Florida Hybrid Mandarin)
description: Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil enriched with organic matter. Keep the root zone evenly moist during establishment and reduce watering slightly as fruit begins to color to concentrate sugars. Robinson bears loose-skinned, richly flavored orange fruit that ripens earlier than most mandarins, often by early fall, but it tends toward seediness unless grown in isolation from other citrus. It is popular with Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its dependable early harvest and moderate cold tolerance. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.
