name: Robust Pop R400MR Popcorn
description: 'Robust Pop R400MR' produces large, round popped kernels sturdy enough to hold coatings, unlike the more common butterfly popcorn. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good wind pollination. Give plants full sun, steady moisture, and rich soil through the long season. Let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvesting, then cure the kernels further before popping. Isolate from sweet corn to keep quality true. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Robusta Banana
description: Robusta is the Cavendish subgroup clone that dominates banana production across India, chosen by growers there for its stout, wind-resistant stalk and dependable bunch size. It sits between Dwarf Cavendish and Grand Nain in height, which gives it a bit more resistance to wind lodging than taller Cavendish clones while still producing full-size dessert fruit. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil with consistent deep watering and monthly feeding through the warm season, and expect a single fruiting cycle per pseudostem before cutting it back for a replacement sucker. In zone 9a it fruits best as a container specimen that can be moved to shelter before the first hard freeze. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Robusta Coffee (Canephora Coffee, Congo Coffee)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee grows naturally as an understory shrub and performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates. Coffea canephora (robusta coffee or Congo coffee) is the second major commercial coffee species, accounting for approximately 40% of world coffee production — ranking second only to arabica (C. arabica) but distinctly different in origin, physiology, flavor, and agricultural use. C. canephora is native to the humid tropical forests of central and West Africa (particularly the Congo Basin region — hence 'Congo coffee'), where it grows as a spreading, multi-stemmed understory shrub. Robusta coffee has several significant differences from arabica: it is more disease-resistant (particularly to coffee leaf rust — Hemileia vastatrix — the devastating fungal disease that has devastated arabica crops worldwide); it is more drought-tolerant; it contains approximately twice the caffeine content of arabica (2–4% vs. 1.2–1.5%); and it can be grown at lower elevations and in hotter, more humid climates than arabica. These traits make robusta the preferred crop for hot, humid, lower-elevation tropical regions including Vietnam (the world's largest robusta producer), India, Ivory Coast, Uganda, and Indonesia. The flavor profile of robusta — stronger, more bitter, earthier, with woody and chocolate-cocoa notes — suits espresso blends (where it adds body and crema), instant coffee, and cold brew. In zone 10–12 gardens, both coffee species can be grown for home production and as ornamental shade-tolerant specimens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Robusto Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Vigorous Japanese Plum)
description: Robusto came out of the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program in Byron, Georgia, the same research station behind Byrongold and Ruby Sweet, and produces a tall, upright, semi-spreading tree that bears heavily. Fruit is red-skinned with yellow flesh and ripens early, in late May to early June, ahead of most other Southeastern plums. Its chill requirement runs 400-500 hours, higher than the true ultra-low-chill Gulf series plums, so it performs best in interior zone 8 orchards rather than the mildest coastal fringe. It is not reliably self-fruitful, so plant it with a second compatible Japanese plum, such as Morris or Methley, for cross-pollination and consistent fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rocambole Garlic (Hardneck Garlic)
description: Plant pre-chilled cloves 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rocambole is considered by most garlic connoisseurs to be the finest-flavored garlic group — rich, complex, deeply savory, and mellow with a characteristic lingering warmth and almost chocolate-like earthiness that no other garlic group fully matches. Named varieties include 'Spanish Roja,' 'German Red,' 'Killarney Red,' and 'Music.' The medium-sized, brownish-purple skinned bulbs contain 8–12 cloves per head arranged in a single layer. The paper wrapping is loose, almost shaggy, and the inner skins of individual cloves are characteristically streaked with purple-brown. Rocambole is a hardneck garlic producing a central flower stalk (scape) that should be removed in June to direct energy into bulb formation; scapes are edible and delicious in stir-fries and pestos. In zone 9, Rocambole requires refrigerator pre-chilling of cloves for 6–8 weeks before October planting, or better yet, substitute Creole garlic, which is naturally adapted to mild winters without chilling. Rocambole stores only 3–5 months. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Rock Hyssop (Dwarf Alpine Hyssop)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the fine seed, then transplant into lean, sharp-draining, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. This dwarf subspecies of common hyssop stays low and tightly mounded rather than upright and shrubby, making it far better suited to rock garden crevices, dry stone walls, and border edging than the taller species type. The same strongly camphor-scented, needle-like leaves and short spikes of blue flowers appear from midsummer on, drawing bees just as reliably as standard hyssop. Once established it tolerates poor, gritty soil and drought extremely well, and only needs a light shearing after bloom to keep the mat neat. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Rock Palm (Sombrero Palm)
description: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, lean soil — this native of dry Mexican limestone mountains thrives on neglect and is one of the most drought-tolerant palms available for zone 8-9 gardens. The silvery-blue fan leaves are similar to other Brahea species and provide striking year-round color; the palm is slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Small, dark, date-like fruits are produced in pendant clusters and are sweet and edible, though they are used mainly by local communities in Mexico for food, wine, and traditional crafts. Once established, reduce irrigation to near zero; overwatering is the most common cause of failure with this species. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Rock Samphire (Sea Fennel)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; rock samphire is a historical edible coastal herb that was once widely gathered and pickled throughout coastal Europe — Shakespeare referenced its dangerous collection by cliff-hangers in King Lear ('half-way down hangs one that gathers samphire; dreadful trade!') and it was a common market vegetable in London through the 18th century. The finely divided, succulent, gray-green, carrot-family foliage has a strong, distinctive, aromatic flavour combining fennel, anise, and iodine — intensely herbal and marine. It produces flattened umbel flowers in summer followed by seeds. The young shoots are used fresh in salads, cooked as a vegetable, or pickled in vinegar. It grows naturally on sea cliffs, rock crevices, and shingle beaches of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, clinging to completely vertical cliff faces and experiencing salt spray, full sun, and total drought. In the garden it requires similarly lean, well-drained, open conditions. Excellent in rock gardens, coastal gardens, and as a maritime-flavored culinary herb for adventurous cooks. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Rockit Apple (Miniature Columnar Snack Apple)
description: Rockit was developed in New Zealand as a naturally dwarf, columnar apple that produces clusters of small, snack-sized fruit along a single upright trunk rather than wide spreading branches. The fruit is sweet, crisp, and red-striped, sized to be eaten in a couple of bites, and the compact habit makes it one of the few apple cultivars practical for container growing on a patio. Because it stays narrow, plant it closer than a standard apple and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set. Thin overcrowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rocky Arugula / Wild Rocket
description: 'Rocky' is a fast-growing wild-type arugula forming a compact rosette with a stronger, more complex, nutty-peppery flavor than salad arugula. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 4-6 inches, harvesting leaves young and often for the mildest taste. It tolerates cold well and behaves as a short-lived perennial in USDA zones 6-10, resprouting after cutting. Grow in cool weather and shear back before flowering to prolong tender leaf production. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Rocky Ford Cantaloupe (Colorado Classic Heirloom Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; harvest when stem slips easily from the vine ('slip' stage) and the blossom end is slightly soft. Rocky Ford is the historic heirloom cantaloupe variety that made the Arkansas River Valley around Rocky Ford, Colorado famous for melon production in the late 19th century — producing medium-sized, netted, round to slightly oval fruits with bright green skin under tan netting and pale green to orange flesh with exceptional sweetness and classic old-fashioned cantaloupe flavor. The variety was so famous that 'Rocky Ford' became synonymous with high-quality cantaloupe across America in the early 20th century, and special rail cars shipped Rocky Ford melons to Chicago, New York, and other major cities during the peak season. Rocky Ford performs best in dry climates with hot days and cool nights (like the high-altitude semi-arid conditions of Colorado) where low humidity reduces fungal disease and water-stressed plants concentrate sugars at maturity. In humid Gulf Coast conditions it requires careful disease management, but dedicated heirloom melon enthusiasts appreciate its distinctive flavor, which has a more complex, old-fashioned character than modern hybrids. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Rocotillo Pepper (Caribbean Seasoning Pepper)
description: Germinate on a heat mat at 80°F; transplant outdoors after frost when soil is warm and nights are above 60°F. Rocotillo is a Capsicum chinense seasoning pepper of Caribbean origin that looks remarkably like a miniature, squashed habanero with its distinctive ribbed, round, flattened form — but carries minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) while retaining the intensely fruity, tropical, citrusy habanero aroma that makes this species unique; it is used in Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Venezuelan cooking wherever the habanero flavor without the fire is desired. The small, round, ribbed fruits ripen from green through yellow to orange or red and are used fresh in sofrito, salsas, sauces, and seasoning blends. Related to and sometimes confused with the aji dulce (sweet habanero) and cachucha peppers of the Caribbean. Highly productive in hot weather; perennial in zone 9b–12. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Rocoto Canario Pepper (Yellow Rocoto)
description: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature its blocky, irregularly shaped fruit. Pods hold black seeds and thick, juicy flesh typical of rocoto, ripening to a bright yellow with heat ranging from moderate to fiercely hot (roughly 10,000-60,000 Scoville units). Plants form a more compact bush than typical rocoto and, like other pubescens types, set fruit best where summer nights stay relatively cool. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Rocoto Chocolate Pepper (Brown Rocoto)
description: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost, giving this rare rocoto selection the long, patient start every pubescens variety demands. Medium-sized fruits mature to a distinctive chocolate-brown, with the thick, crunchy walls and fruity, apple-like heat characteristic of the species. Because pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F, plants perform best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat in hot-summer regions. Matures in 100–140 days from transplant.

name: Rocoto Pepper (Manzano)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep at a cooler 65–70°F — unlike other peppers, Capsicum pubescens actually germinates better in cooler soil and is damaged by excessive heat. This Andean species is unique among cultivated peppers for its purple flowers and distinctive black seeds; it tolerates light frost better than any other pepper species. Transplant to a position with afternoon shade in hot climates, as rocoto stops setting fruit when temperatures exceed 90°F — coastal or mountain gardens suit it best. Fruits resemble small apples (hence 'manzano') and ripen to yellow, orange, or red with thick, sweet flesh and intense, burning heat. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Rocoto Perón Pepper (Pear-Shaped Andean Rocoto)
description: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate. Unlike the round, apple-shaped manzano rocoto, the Perón type produces elongated, pear-shaped pods with thick, juicy walls that hold up especially well to stuffing and roasting. Deep purple flowers and fuzzy, hairy foliage distinguish the plant from every other cultivated pepper species, and it tolerates cooler nights better than typical warm-season chiles. Matures in 100–140 days from transplant.

name: Roger's Red Grape (Ornamental Fall-Color California Grape)
description: Roger's Red is a fast-growing deciduous ornamental grape discovered by horticulturist Roger Raiche near an old homestead in Northern California and named for him, prized above all for its dramatic autumn color, when the broad leaves turn a saturated scarlet-crimson well before most other fall foliage plants. Although long sold as a straight selection of the native California wild grape, later genetic testing found Roger's Red actually carries wine-grape ancestry alongside its Vitis californica parentage, which likely explains its unusually intense red fall color compared with the species. It bears small, tart, blue-black grapes in loose clusters that are edible but grown mainly for wildlife value rather than fresh eating, since the true ornamental draw is the vine's vigorous habit and spectacular foliage display. Train it onto a strong arbor, fence, or pergola where its twining habit and fall color can be appreciated, and prune hard each winter to keep its vigorous growth in bounds; established vines are drought-tolerant and need little summer irrigation. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rogow Hardy Kiwi (Polish Mini-Kiwi Kiwiberry)
description: Rogow is a prolific female hardy kiwi selected at the Warsaw University of Life Sciences arboretum in Rogow, Poland, bred for reliable cropping in a cold-continental climate. It produces small, oval, grape-sized berries with edible skin and good flavor, ripening notably late in the season, from late September into October. As a dioecious selection it requires a separate male Actinidia arguta vine planted within pollinating range to set fruit. The vigorous twining vine needs a strong permanent trellis and performs well in the same cold-hardy range as other named A. arguta cultivars. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rojo Brillante Persimmon (Spanish Astringent Kaki, CO2-Treated 'Sharon Fruit' Type)
description: Rojo Brillante is Spain's dominant commercial persimmon cultivar, grown at enormous scale around Valencia under the Ribera del Xúquer designation and marketed internationally after a brief post-harvest carbon-dioxide treatment strips the astringency while the flesh stays crisp and apple-firm rather than jelly-soft, a trait that sets it apart from most other de-astringed kaki types. Fruit is large, deep orange-red, and glossy, with a thick skin that ships and stores unusually well for a persimmon. The tree is vigorous and productive, bearing reliably on second-year wood, and its relatively low chill requirement makes it a strong fit for Gulf Coast winters that rarely deliver much cold. Growers without CO2 treatment equipment can still enjoy the fruit by letting it soften completely on a windowsill, at which point the astringency resolves into rich, honeyed sweetness like any other soft-ripe persimmon. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rollinia (Biriba)
description: Rollinia / biriba is an Annona relative from Amazonia that prefers deep, fertile, consistently moist soil and produces fruit faster than cherimoya or soursop under hot, humid conditions. Like other Annonaceae, the flowers exhibit protogynous dichogamy — the female stage opens first, closes, then reopens in the male stage — so hand-pollination at the correct time greatly increases fruit set: collect pollen from half-open flowers in the afternoon and apply to fully open receptive stigmas the following morning. The soft, custard-flavored fruit is covered in soft yellow spines and must be handled very gently — it bruises and ferments within hours of reaching peak ripeness. Harvest when the spines have softened and yellowed and the fruit gives noticeably to pressure; consume immediately or refrigerate for no more than 24 hours. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rollinia (Biribá, Wild Sugar Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; rollinia (biribá) is a South American tropical tree in the custard apple family, native to the Amazon basin and considered by fruit connoisseurs one of the finest fruits in the Annonaceae family — potentially superior to cherimoya and sugar apple in flavor. The fruits are large (often 4–6 inches across) and round to heart-shaped with distinctive, pointed tubercles (bumps) on the yellow-green exterior that turn golden-yellow at maturity. The interior is snow-white, sweet, translucent, and juicy — much moister and more refreshing than cherimoya — with a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and caramel with a sweet lemon-custard quality. The texture is extremely delicate, almost like thick cream, and it must be eaten immediately after harvest as it deteriorates within 1–2 days of ripening. Rollinia is faster-growing and more prolific than most Annonaceae and is better adapted to humid tropical conditions. It tolerates wet soils and high humidity better than cherimoya or atemoya. An important and growing orchard crop in tropical South America. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Roma II Bush Bean
description: 'Roma II' is a bush-type Italian flat snap bean with a rich, nutty flavor rarely found in stores, borne on compact plants that need no support. Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, spacing them 3-4 inches apart in full sun. The 4-5 inch pods stay tender and slow to develop fiber, so harvest regularly to keep plants producing. Excellent fresh, frozen, or canned; good in containers. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Roma Tomato
description: Sow indoors six weeks ahead of transplanting and set plants deep to build strong roots. Roma is a compact, determinate paste tomato producing firm, meaty three-inch fruits with few seeds, ideal for sauces and canning. A single stake or small cage supports the tidy vines, which set most of their fruit in a concentrated window. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot, and expect a heavy flush of fruit that ripens over a few weeks. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Romaine Lettuce
description: Sow seed at 1/8 in depth in cool soil and thin to 8–12 in; romaine forms an upright, elongated head that needs slightly more space than loose-leaf types. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent tip burn, which appears as brown leaf edges due to calcium deficiency from moisture stress. Harvest by cutting the whole head at soil level when it is 8–10 in tall and the inner leaves feel firm. Outer leaves can be removed individually as the head develops to extend the harvest period. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Roman Beauty Rosemary (Chef's Choice Compact Culinary Rosemary)
description: Roman Beauty, marketed under the trademark Chef's Choice, is a compact, slow-growing culinary rosemary selected for a noticeably higher essential-oil content than standard rosemary, giving a spicier, more concentrated flavor from the same amount of leaf. Its dense, finely textured gray-green foliage and pale blue flowers hold a tidy, upright habit that stays under 3 feet, making it a good choice for containers, herb-garden borders, and small kitchen beds where sprawling rosemary cultivars would outgrow the space. Like other culinary rosemaries it thrives on neglect, wanting lean soil, full sun, and minimal supplemental water once established. Harvest sprigs throughout the growing season; the concentrated flavor means a little goes further in cooking than with milder rosemary types. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Roman Chamomile
description: Chamaemelum nobile is a low-growing, apple-scented perennial chamomile native to western Europe, producing fine, feathery, bright-green foliage and small white daisy flowers with yellow centers from early summer through early fall; the crushed foliage releases a distinctive sweet, fruity, apple-like scent that distinguishes it from the taller German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla). Surface-sow seeds in early spring directly in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun or light partial shade; seeds require light to germinate and should not be covered — press them lightly onto the soil surface and keep evenly moist until germination occurs in 7–14 days. The non-flowering cultivar 'Treneague' is propagated vegetatively and used as a fragrant, low-maintenance lawn substitute that releases its apple scent when walked upon; it requires no mowing but does best in well-drained, sunny sites. Harvest flowers by hand when fully open for use in herbal tea; flowers and foliage have traditional uses for soothing teas, topical rinses, and as a mild sleep aid. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Roman Hyssop / Za'atar Rumi
description: Establish plants in the sunniest, driest spot in the garden, as this Eastern Mediterranean subshrub is evolved for calcareous, rocky soils and intense summer heat; poor drainage is the primary cause of failure. Harvest leafy stem tips before or just as the whorled pink-purple flowers open, when the essential oil content peaks, then dry in bunches to use in homemade za'atar spice blends. Trim lightly after each harvest and cut back by a third following the main flowering period to maintain a bushy form and prevent the base from becoming too woody. In zone 7, provide a light mulch around the crown in winter and site plants against a south-facing wall for additional warmth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Roman Wormwood (Small Absinth)
description: Native to southeastern Europe, Artemisia pontica forms a low, finely cut, silver-gray colony of aromatic foliage that is markedly less bitter than common wormwood, making it prized historically as a gentler flavoring herb in the production of vermouth and certain herbal bitters and cordials. Its old English name Roman wormwood distinguishes it from both true wormwood and mugwort. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it spreads slowly by rhizome to form an attractive weed-suppressing patch; rich, damp soil causes floppy, sprawling growth. Shear plants back hard in early spring to keep the silvery foliage dense and prevent the clump from thinning at the center. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Romance Nantes Carrot (Very Sweet Crack-Resistant Bejo Hybrid Carrot)
description: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in loose, deep, well-worked soil free of rocks and clods; thin to 2–3 inches. Keep soil consistently moist until germination. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid carrot from Bejo Seeds, a Dutch vegetable breeding company with a long history of Nantes-type carrot refinement. The Nantes type — originating in the Nantes region of western France — defines a carrot form that differs fundamentally from the long Imperator types common in grocery stores: Nantes carrots are shorter (6–8 inches vs. 9–11 inches), blunt-tipped rather than tapering to a point, rounder in cross-section, and notably sweeter with more tender, less fibrous flesh. Romance carries Nantes-type characteristics to a high standard: the roots are uniformly 7–8 inches long with a clean, blunt Nantes tip, bright orange interior color throughout (no pale core), very high sugar content, and notably fine-textured, tender flesh that makes Romance excellent for eating raw as well as cooked. The crack resistance that gives Romance particular value means that unlike some other sweet, high-sugar varieties that develop radial cracks if left in ground too long, Romance holds well after reaching maturity — a practical advantage for home gardeners harvesting over weeks rather than in a single commercial harvest. Fall-grown carrots in zone 9 achieve maximum sweetness as cold nights concentrate sugars in the roots. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Romanesco
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant date; romanesco demands consistent temperatures between 60–65°F during head formation or it fails to produce proper fractal spirals. Transplant into deeply amended soil and water evenly throughout the season, as any moisture stress affects head quality. Harvest the single central head when the spiral turrets are sharp and well-defined but before any yellowing begins. Unlike broccoli, romanesco rarely produces usable side shoots after the main head is cut. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Romanesco (Romanesco Broccoli, Roman Cauliflower)
description: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before transplanting; plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; cover heads as they develop to maintain lime-green color if desired. Brassica oleracea var. botrytis 'Romanesco' (Romanesco or Roman broccoli) is a variety of Italian origin — known since the 16th century in Rome — that produces one of the most visually spectacular vegetables in existence: a tightly packed head of lime-green, spiraling conical florets arranged in a precise logarithmic spiral following the Fibonacci sequence, creating a fractal pattern of remarkable mathematical beauty. Each floret replicates the overall head shape at a smaller scale, in a perfect example of self-similar fractal geometry visible to the naked eye. The flavor is equally noteworthy: milder, sweeter, and nuttier than both standard broccoli and cauliflower, with a crisp-firm texture that holds up well when roasted or steamed. Romanesco requires similar growing conditions to cauliflower — it is the most temperature-sensitive of the three major brassica heading types, requiring consistent temperatures during head formation for proper development; heat causes premature bolting or loose, irregular heads. In zone 9, grow as a fall crop, planted September–October for December–February harvest. The stunning heads make excellent centerpiece dishes and are highly popular at farmers markets. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Romanesco Artichoke (Roman Round-Headed Heirloom)
description: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil worked with compost, siting plants in full sun with room to form a large clump. Romanesco is a classic Italian heirloom type from the countryside around Rome, producing broad, rounded, purple-flushed green buds with fleshy, nearly spineless scales and a tender heart, the type traditionally used for carciofi alla romana. As a true perennial type it is slower to reach full production than seed-grown annual hybrids, generally needing an established second-year crown for its heaviest harvest, though in mild coastal climates it can be grown as a long-season annual from an early transplant. Cut buds while the scales are still tightly closed and before they begin to spread open for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Romanesco Broccoli
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant into rich, consistently moist soil, giving each plant ample room to develop. This Italian heirloom forms mesmerizing lime-green heads of spiraling Fibonacci cones with a mild, nutty flavor. It grows slowly and prefers cool conditions, so time plantings so heads mature before summer heat or in the cool of fall. Harvest the whole head while the fractal spirals are tight and firm, cutting with several inches of stem. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Romanesco Cauliflower
description: 'Romanesco' produces mesmerizing chartreuse, fractal-spiraled 5-6 inch heads with a delicate, nutty flavor between broccoli and cauliflower. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before transplanting and set plants 18-24 inches apart in rich, full-sun soil. Steady moisture and cool weather are essential for well-formed heads, so it often performs best as a fall crop. Harvest while the spirals are tight and firm. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Romanesco Fennel
description: 'Romanesco', a Florence (bulbing) fennel, forms a crisp, anise-flavored bulb prized raw, sauteed, or in soups and pasta, with feathery edible foliage. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 6-12 inches, keeping the plants evenly watered to encourage plump bulbs and discourage bolting. Mounding soil around the base as bulbs swell keeps them tender and pale. Grow in the cool ends of the season and harvest bulbs once they reach the size of a fist. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Romanian Red Hardneck Garlic
description: Romanian Red is a porcelain hardneck garlic that yields large, dense bulbs of usually 4-5 easy-to-peel cloves with a hot, robust flavor and excellent storage. Separate bulbs into cloves just before planting and set each clove pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in fall. Mulch heavily after the ground cools to protect against heaving over winter. Snap off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb sizing. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot for two to three weeks. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Romano Pole Bean (Italian Flat Bean)
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; provide a 5–6 foot trellis or teepee for the vines and begin harvesting when pods are flat and 4–5 inches long, before they string. Romano is the classic Italian flat-podded or 'Italian flat bean,' a pole type with wide, flat, 5–7 inch pods that have a different texture and flavor profile from standard round snap beans when cooked — more tender, less fibrous, with a rich, earthy, slightly nutty flavor that makes them the preferred snap bean for Italian sautés (fagioli in padella), long-braised dishes with olive oil and garlic, and agrodolce preparations. The flat pods become stringy if left to mature too long; harvest when pods are still flat and not yet showing bean bulges. A bush Romano type is also available. Highly productive in warm climates; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall bean production. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Rome Beauty Apple (The Baking Apple, Ohio Heirloom Baker, Rome)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is the classic baking apple and benefits from being cooked rather than eaten fresh — its firm, low-acid flesh holds structure beautifully under heat; harvest in October when fully colored deep red, typically after McIntosh and Empire are finished; baked whole apples with butter and brown sugar are the signature preparation. Rome Beauty (often sold simply as 'Rome') is an Ohio heirloom apple discovered as a branch sport on a seedling tree near Rome, Ohio (Lawrence County) by Joel Gillett around 1816, propagated by his neighbor Alanson Gillett, and introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s where it rapidly became one of the most important American commercial apples of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The variety has an unusual characteristic that defines its culinary use: the flesh is relatively low in acid and somewhat dry in texture compared to most eating apples, which means it is not the most interesting variety for fresh consumption but becomes exceptional when baked — the firm flesh holds its shape without collapsing, the mild, sweet flavor concentrates under heat, and the large round shape makes it the ideal vessel for a whole baked apple filled with butter, sugar, and spices. For a century, 'Rome' and 'baking apple' were nearly synonymous in American cookery. The round, symmetrical, deep red to all-red appearance also made Rome Beauty particularly popular with retailers when unblemished fruit mattered; a barrel of large, perfectly round, uniformly deep-red Romes was among the most visually impressive of any apple variety. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Romeo and Juliet Cherry
description: Romeo and Juliet are a pair of compact, extremely cold-hardy bush cherries that produce sweet, robust fruit good for snacking and baking. Plant both varieties near each other in full sun with well-drained soil to improve cross-pollination and yields. Space plants 5-8 feet apart and water consistently while young to establish strong roots. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain an open, productive shape. These dwarf trees stay small enough for backyard gardens and fruit reliably even in harsh winter regions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ronde de Bordeaux Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Ronde de Bordeaux (Round Bordeaux) is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region producing small, round, dark-purple to nearly black-skinned fruits with brilliant deep red to garnet-colored flesh — one of the most richly colored of all fig varieties. The dark skin and brilliant interior make Ronde de Bordeaux a spectacular fresh eating fig and an equally attractive fig for jam and preserves where the deep color produces richly-hued products. The flavor is very sweet, rich, and slightly winey with the complexity associated with dark-skinned fig varieties. The compact tree habit makes Ronde de Bordeaux one of the most practical figs for home gardens and container growing — it produces prolifically despite its modest size. It is an early-maturing variety with the main crop ripening in late July–August in zone 9, among the earliest of the dark-skinned European fig types. This fig has become very popular among fig enthusiasts in zone 9 and zone 10 for its combination of early ripening, outstanding flavor, and manageable tree size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ronde de Nice Zucchini (Round French Zucchini)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in well-amended, well-drained soil after last frost in full sun; Ronde de Nice is a bush-type that needs 2–3 feet of space and no support. Ronde de Nice is a French heirloom round summer squash of Provençal origin, the classic stuffing squash of Niçoise cuisine (courgettes rondes farcies à la niçoise) and one of the oldest and most culinarily significant French kitchen garden varieties still in regular cultivation. The fruits are perfectly spherical, 2–4 inches in diameter, with smooth, thin, pale to medium green skin and tender, mild, cream-colored flesh that has a somewhat denser texture than elongated zucchini — well-suited to stuffing as it holds its shape better during cooking. Harvest at 2–3 inches for fresh eating and 3–4 inches for stuffing; slightly larger fruits (4–5 inches) can still be stuffed but become seedy. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall production. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Rondo F1 Florence Fennel
description: Direct sow shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear. Rondo is a modern F1 Florence fennel bred for a fast, even bulbing habit, producing rounded, uniform white bulbs that stay tight and resist splitting even under less-than-ideal watering. It shows notably strong bolt resistance compared to older open-pollinated bulbing fennels, which lets gardeners get a reliable crop from both spring and late-summer sowings. Hill soil slightly around the swelling bulb base as it develops to keep the flesh blanched, pale, and tender. Harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball by cutting at the base, leaving roots in place to often resprout a smaller secondary harvest of feathery fronds. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Rongai Lablab (Late-Flowering Vining Warm-Season Legume Cover Crop)
description: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, inoculating seed with a cowpea-type Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation in fields with no prior lablab history. Rongai is a vigorous, twining lablab selection valued as a summer cover crop for its late, photoperiod-triggered flowering, which keeps the plant putting energy into leafy vine growth and root nodulation for months rather than shifting early to seed production, producing an unusually heavy mat of biomass that smothers weeds and builds organic matter. It climbs readily on trellis, fence, or companion crop and can also be grown as forage or green manure, mowed or rolled and left as mulch, or turned under ahead of a fall planting. As a legume, it fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and tolerates heat and drought once established, making it a reliable warm-season soil builder for the Gulf South growing season. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Rongrien Rambutan
description: Rongrien is the most widely planted rambutan cultivar in Thailand and the variety most commonly recommended for South Florida growers, prized for its hermaphroditic flowering, which allows reliable self-pollination and fruit set without a separate pollinator tree. Grafted Rongrien trees come into bearing markedly faster than seedling rambutan and produce clusters of bright red, soft-spined fruit with sweet, easily separated flesh. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun protected from strong wind, keeping soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit development since drought stress during these stages sharply reduces yield. Like all rambutan, it has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions, making it suitable only for the warmest parts of zone 10b and above. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rooibos (Red Bush Tea)
description: Soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to soften its hard coat, sow into acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and grow seedlings on for about two months before transplanting into their permanent full-sun position. Rooibos is a fine-needled legume shrub found only in South Africa's Cederberg mountains, where hot dry summers and cool wet winters shape its narrow native range. Harvested stems are cut, bruised, and left to oxidize before drying, turning the leaves the deep red-brown that gives the naturally caffeine-free, sweetly earthy tea its color and name. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Root Chicory
description: Sow seeds shallowly in loose, deep soil so the taproots can grow long and straight. This hardy, drought-resistant perennial produces nutrient-dense greens and thick roots traditionally roasted as a coffee substitute. Thin seedlings to give each plant room, and keep beds weeded while young plants establish. Dig roots in fall of the first year for coffee-style use, and enjoy the bitter young leaves in salads throughout the season. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Roquette Arugula
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Roquette is the Italian heirloom arugula variety — the specific selection used for millennia in Italian cuisine that gave arugula its character and reputation as the quintessential Italian salad green. The deeply lobed, dark green leaves have the intense peppery, nutty, slightly bitter flavor that defines the arugula experience — more pronounced than milder modern selections. The flavor becomes sharper and more assertive as the weather warms (approaching bolting), while young winter-grown leaves are milder and more delicate. Roquette's use in Italian cooking spans from the simple classic of arugula, shaved Parmesan, and lemon in a pizza topping, to fresh salads with olive oil, to pasta dishes and antipasto plates across Italy. The small, lobed leaf shape and strong flavor make Roquette the most authentic form for Italian culinary preparations. The partial shade tolerance allows it to be grown under taller plants in a kitchen garden, extending the season slightly. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Rosa Bianca Eggplant
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in the warmest available position; Rosa Bianca is an Italian heirloom eggplant producing large, round to slightly oval fruits with a beautiful rosy-lavender and creamy-white skin that lightens to nearly white at eating maturity — the name means 'pink and white' in Italian and accurately describes the distinctive pastel bicolor appearance that makes Rosa Bianca the most visually elegant of heirloom eggplant varieties. The white to very pale cream flesh has the mildest, least bitter flavor of any eggplant variety — traditional eggplant bitterness is largely absent in Rosa Bianca, which has a delicate, sweet, slightly creamy taste that has made it the preferred eggplant of Italian chefs for generations. The flesh does not need salting before cooking as most other eggplant varieties require. The large, bulbous fruits (6–8 inches across) have a spongy, moist texture that absorbs olive oil and seasonings beautifully in roasted, grilled, and baked preparations — particularly in traditional Italian dishes like caponata, parmigiana, and grilled vegetable preparations. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Rosa Bianca Eggplant
description: 'Rosa Bianca' is an Italian heirloom eggplant bearing plump, scalloped 4-6 inch fruits in pinkish-purple with white streaks, with mild, creamy, seedy-free flesh and no bitterness. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, transplanting only after nights warm up. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and warmth, staking the plants as fruit sets. Harvest while the skin is glossy for the best texture. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Rosalie Roselle (Compact High-Yield Hibiscus)
description: Sow Rosalie in warm, fertile soil after the soil has warmed well past 70°F, since roselle seedlings are frost-tender and slow to establish in cool conditions. This selection branches low and fills out into a dense, rounded bush that carries a heavier concentration of plump, deep red calyces per plant than taller heirloom roselle types, making it a good fit for smaller vegetable beds or large containers. Like other roselle, it is day-length sensitive and begins setting flowers and calyces as days shorten in late summer, so harvest continues from late summer until frost. Pick the fleshy calyces about a week after the petals fall, while still tender, for fresh use, drying, or syrup. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Rosborough Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Developed by the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program, Rosborough was selected specifically for reliable performance in the hot, humid conditions of Texas and the Gulf South, producing good yields of medium-to-large, flavorful berries in early-to-mid summer. It has thorns, unlike many newer cultivars, but its regional heat tolerance and disease resistance have made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast growers who prioritize proven regional performance over the novelty of thornlessness. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting vigorous and productive. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Rose Apple (Malay Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; rose apple (Syzygium jambos) is a medium-sized evergreen tree in the Myrtaceae family native to Southeast Asia that produces waxy, pale yellow to cream or blush-pink, oval fruits with a uniquely crisp, crunchy texture and a delicate, unmistakable flavor of rose water — floral, lightly sweet, and aromatic in a way unlike any other fruit. The fruits are primarily eaten fresh out of hand, and their distinctive rose fragrance also makes them popular for flavoring drinks, syrups, and desserts across Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. The tree produces spectacular ornamental flower clusters of long, creamy-white stamens resembling shaving brushes before fruit development, making it a dual-purpose landscape tree. Rose apple is adaptable, moderately fast-growing, and performs well with consistent moisture and regular balanced fertilization. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rose de Berne Tomato (Swiss Heirloom Pink Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost risk passes. Rose de Berne is a classic heirloom from the Bern region of Switzerland, often described as the European counterpart to Brandywine for its reputation as one of the best-tasting pink tomatoes grown in France, Germany, and Switzerland. The smooth, deep-rose fruit has thin but durable skin and creamy, richly sweet-tart flesh. The vigorous 6-8 foot vines need firm staking and reward a long warm season with heavy, reliable yields. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Rose de Lautrec Garlic
description: Rose de Lautrec is a celebrated French softneck garlic named for the town of Lautrec, where it has earned Protected Geographical Indication status for its rose-pink-blushed skin and distinctive, refined flavor. Plant cloves pointed end up in loose, well-drained soil in fall, mulching lightly in colder regions to buffer winter temperature swings. Keep beds weed-free through spring and reduce watering as the lower leaves begin to brown ahead of harvest. Because it is a softneck type, the flexible stems can be braided for storage, and well-cured bulbs are prized in French markets for their long shelf life and delicate, slightly sweet garlic flavor. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Rose Finn Apple Potato (Rose-Skinned Heirloom Fingerling)
description: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Rose Finn Apple is a Scandinavian heirloom fingerling potato with rose-pink to tan skin and creamy yellow flesh, valued for its smooth, dense, waxy texture and sweet, rich flavor that holds up especially well in roasting and potato salads. The elongated, knobby tubers form in loose clusters and the plant is a dependable, moderately productive grower. Being a later-maturing variety, it benefits from a full growing season; dig for tender new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let the vines die back naturally for mature tubers with better storage qualities. Like other fingerlings, its low-starch flesh keeps its shape well through cooking rather than turning mealy. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Rose Geranium
description: Root Rose Geranium stem cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; avoid overwatering — the plant prefers to dry out between waterings and is highly susceptible to root rot in wet conditions; prune regularly to maintain compact, bushy shape and encourage continuous fresh, fragrant foliage; fertilize lightly. Rose Geranium is the primary commercial source of geranium essential oil — steam-distilled from the leaves and stems — and is one of the most important fragrance crops in the world, with major production in Egypt, China, South Africa, and Réunion Island. The oil is used extensively in fine perfumery (often blending as a rose substitute or modifier), aromatherapy, and high-end skin care products. In the culinary garden, the intensely rose-fragrant leaves are used fresh: layered in sugar (rose geranium sugar) to transfer their scent; pressed into the bottom of cake tins before baking (rose geranium pound cake); infused in cream for ice cream; floated in lemonade and iced tea; and used to scent herb vinegars and syrups. The flavor is a delicate rose with a slight leafy, green note — distinctive and sophisticated. A well-drained, hot, sunny position suits Rose Geranium perfectly in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens; it grows vigorously in the long warm season and tolerates light frost with some protection. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Rose-Scented Geranium
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; rose-scented geranium is a South African coastal dune native and the primary commercial source of geranium essential oil — one of the most important fragrance materials in perfumery, used to round out and fix rose notes in countless fine fragrances. The deeply lobed, velvety, gray-green leaves release an immediately recognizable, rich, rosy-citrusy fragrance when touched — often described as a green rose or rose combined with mint — that is more complex and interesting than an actual rose. The small, pink, pelargonium-type flowers appear in clusters through the growing season but are secondary to the extraordinary aromatic foliage. In zones 9–11 it grows as a substantial, spreading sub-shrub. The oil is extracted by steam distillation of the green stems and leaves; commercial production centers on the island of Réunion and South Africa. Excellent as a container herb for patios where the fragrant foliage can be brushed when passing. Dried leaves retain fragrance well for sachets and potpourri. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Rosea Flore Pleno Double Pink Hawthorn (Double Pink May)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; 'Rosea Flore Pleno' is one of the most popular ornamental flowering forms of midland hawthorn, smothering itself each May in fully double, rich rose-pink flowers carried in dense clusters along the branches — a striking contrast to the simple white or pale pink single flowers of the wild species. Because the flowers are double, they produce little or no fruit, so the tree's ornamental value rests entirely on its spectacular spring bloom and, secondarily, on its dense, twiggy, thorny branching habit, which still provides good nesting cover and winter structure for birds. It shares the species' tolerance of heavier clay soils and partial shade, and makes an excellent flowering specimen, hedgerow, or small ornamental tree in gardens too small for larger flowering trees. Being a grafted named clone, it must be propagated vegetatively to preserve its double flower form, as seedlings will revert to single flowers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rosea Sage (Pink-Flowering Culinary Sage)
description: Root semi-ripe stem cuttings in late summer, or plant container-grown starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Rosea sage is a low, bushy culinary sage selected for its pale lilac-pink flower spikes rather than the species' usual blue-purple, produced over a long season on typical wrinkled, aromatic gray-green leaves. Leaves are fully edible with the classic warm, savory flavor of common sage. Trim after flowering and again in spring to maintain a compact habit and prevent legginess. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Rosea Tea Camellia (Pink-Flowered Burgundy-Leaf Selection)
description: Rosea is grown chiefly as an ornamental tea camellia, notable for pale pink autumn flowers with bright pink filaments and for red pigment that runs through the whole plant, from roots to new burgundy-tinted growth. Its tiny, dark, smooth-textured leaves and slow growth rate make it well suited to containers or a fine-textured tea hedge for patient gardeners. It corresponds to a botanical form first described in Japan and later introduced to American cultivation through South Carolina plant-introduction channels. Provide the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rosella Purple Tomato (Compact Dusky Purple-Pink Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Rosella Purple bears medium fruit in a rich, dusky purple-pink, the deep, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomato varieties, on a compact plant from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom-quality flavor to gardens without room for a full-size indeterminate vine. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Roselle
description: Start seeds indoors or sow directly after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; roselle is a tropical hibiscus grown primarily for its deep-red, fleshy calyces that envelop the seed capsules after the flowers fade in fall — these calyces are harvested fresh or dried to make hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica), syrups, jams, and wines with a bright cranberry-like tartness. Plants grow rapidly to 4–8 feet tall and are ornamental throughout the season with attractive burgundy-tinged stems and lobed leaves. Harvest calyces when they are plump and fully colored but before they dry on the plant; check plants every few days as the harvest window is short. A single plant can yield 1–3 pounds of fresh calyces. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Rosemary
description: Rosemary is an aromatic Mediterranean perennial with needle-like leaves that bring a warm, piney flavor to roasts, breads, and herb blends. Start seed indoors ten or more weeks early and be patient, as germination is slow and often spotty. Transplant into sharply drained soil in full sun, since rosemary dislikes wet feet, and water only when the soil dries. In colder climates grow it in a pot and bring it indoors before hard frost, as it is only reliably hardy in mild zones. Matures in 120–200 days from seed.

name: Rosenkuppel Ornamental Oregano (Wine-Stemmed Purple-Bracted Oregano)
description: Rosenkuppel is an RHS Award of Garden Merit ornamental oregano prized for near-black, wine-red stems and bracts that set off dangling clusters of rosy-purple flowers from midsummer into fall. The dusky purple cast carries into the young foliage before it matures to grey-green, giving the plant a moodier color palette than green-stemmed oregano cultivars. It is grown for bees and dried-flower structure rather than the kitchen, since flavor is secondary to ornamental impact in this selection. Cut the flowering stems back hard in late winter to keep the semi-woody base tidy and encourage a fresh flush the following season. Matures in 70–100 days from transplant.

name: Roseroot
description: Divide rhizomes or direct-sow in well-drained, poor to average, rocky or gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; roseroot (golden root, Arctic rose) is a circumpolar arctic and alpine succulent perennial of the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that is one of the most extensively studied adaptogenic herbs in modern phytotherapy — the thick, fragrant rhizome (smelling of roses when cut, hence the name) contains rosavins and salidroside, compounds that have been demonstrated in clinical trials to reduce fatigue, improve physical and mental performance under stress, and support mood in states of mild anxiety and depression. It has been used in Scandinavian, Siberian, and Tibetan traditional medicine for at least 3,000 years as a stamina- and stress-resistance herb, and modern Scandinavian military and sports research has documented its adaptogenic effects. The plant itself is an attractive dwarf succulent with fleshy, toothed, blue-green leaves and clusters of small, bright-yellow to yellow-green, star-shaped flowers in late spring. It is extremely cold-hardy (surviving to zone 1) but requires cool summers and excellent drainage; it fails in warm, humid, poorly drained conditions. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Rosette Pak Choi (Tai Sai, Flat Cabbage, Taisai)
description: Direct sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 10–12 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall; rosette pak choi (tai sai) forms a distinctive flat, spreading rosette of dark green spoon-shaped leaves with broad white midribs — entirely different in shape from upright pak choi but equally tender and excellent in stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. The flat growth habit makes it wind-tolerant and very space-efficient as a cut-and-come-again crop or whole heads spaced wider for full size. Extremely fast to harvest at baby stage (25–30 days); cold-hardy to about 22°F and less bolt-prone than standard pak choi. Grows well in light shade, making it suitable for interplanting under taller crops in spring. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Rosette Tatsoi Bok Choy
description: Tatsoi forms a flat, decorative rosette of spoon-shaped, dark green leaves with a mild, slightly mustardy flavor and high calcium and vitamin content. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 6-10 inches apart, or harvest crowded plants young as baby greens. It thrives in the cool weather of spring and fall and tolerates light frost, which sweetens the leaves. Cut the whole rosette or pick outer leaves for salads, stir-fries, and soups. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Rosie Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Purple Basil for Containers)
description: Sow indoors and transplant after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow directly in containers. A 2022 All-America Selections winner, Rosie produces small, glossy, deep-purple leaves on a dense, compact, uniform mound that holds its color and shape more consistently than older purple types like Dark Opal. Pinch flower spikes and harvest young leaves regularly for salads, garnishes, and vinegars to keep the plant bushy and productive. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Rosita Eggplant (Rutgers-Bred Puerto Rican-Type Lavender Eggplant)
description: Rosita produces blocky, egg-shaped fruit with pale lavender-pink skin and creamy white flesh that stays mild and tender even as fruit sizes up, a trait bred in by Rutgers to suit fresh-market growers serving Caribbean and Latino communities. The vigorous, heat-loving plants set fruit reliably through hot, humid summers and hold up well without staking in most home gardens. Pick fruit while still glossy at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, since the thin skin means it bruises more easily than thicker-skinned purple types. Its milder flavor and lower seed count make it a good choice for cooks who find standard purple-black eggplant too bitter or seedy. Matures in 62–75 days from transplant.

name: Rossa di Chioggia Radicchio
description: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden and firm up as temperatures drop, with a light frost sweetening the flavor. Named for the lagoon town of Chioggia near Venice, this classic Italian radicchio forms tight, round, cabbage-like heads of deep wine-red leaves once cool autumn nights trigger the pigment. It is one of the most widely grown radicchio types in Italy and forms the template most people picture when they hear the word radicchio. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Rossa di Milano Onion
description: A centuries-old open-pollinated onion from the countryside around Milan, prized for its teardrop-shaped bulbs with deep garnet skin and pink-streaked white flesh. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through bulb swell, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and topple. Cure bulbs in a warm, airy location for two to three weeks before storage; this variety is noted for holding firm and flavorful well into winter. The rich, slightly sharp flavor mellows nicely when roasted or grilled. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Rosseyanka Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Non-Astringent American-Asian Hybrid Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, staking young trees until established. Rosseyanka is a hybrid between the native American persimmon and Asian persimmon, developed in Ukraine to combine the cold hardiness of the American species with fruit quality closer to Asian persimmons, notably becoming non-astringent and pleasant to eat while still firm rather than requiring the full softening American persimmons need. It is a productive, vigorous tree well suited to a wider hardiness range than most pure Asian persimmon cultivars while still offering good fruit size and flavor. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest by clipping the fruit from the branch to avoid tearing the skin at the stem. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rossiyanka Persimmon (Russian Hybrid Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established trees are drought-tolerant and need little supplemental fertilization beyond a light annual feeding. Rossiyanka is a Russian-bred hybrid between the native American persimmon and the Asian kaki persimmon, developed to combine the extreme winter hardiness of the American parent with fruit size and eating quality closer to Asian types. The medium-large orange fruits are strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point they turn sweet and jammy with a rich, honeyed flavor; frost or a period of cold storage speeds the softening. Self-fruitful and reliably productive once established, it is a good choice for growers who want Asian-persimmon-quality fruit in a climate too cold, or on a rootstock too marginal, for standard kaki cultivars, and it also performs well in the milder Gulf South. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Rostov Sunflower (Russian Black-Seeded Oilseed Sunflower)
description: Rostov is a traditional Russian oilseed sunflower bred for a single sturdy stalk topped by one large head up to 10 inches across, densely packed with small black seeds carrying an unusually high oil content compared to snacking types. It matures faster than many oilseed cultivars, typically finishing within about ten to thirteen weeks, which suits it to shorter growing seasons or a late-summer succession planting. Harvest once the back of the head turns from green to yellow-brown and the seeds rattle loosely, then cut the head and hang it to finish curing in a dry, airy, rodent-proof space before threshing. Whole seed can be cold-pressed for oil, roasted for snacking, or offered whole to backyard poultry and wild birds. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa Eggplant (Italian Heirloom Blushed White Egg-Shaped Eggplant)
aliases: Solanum melongena 'Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa'
description: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa is an Italian heirloom producing large, rounded, egg-to-pear-shaped fruit 5-6 inches across, with creamy white skin that gradually takes on a soft lavender-pink blush as it ripens. The firm, creamy white flesh is sweet and free of the bitterness found in many older eggplant types, so it needs no pre-salting before cooking. Its classic rounded shape and thick flesh walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and baking whole, in addition to standard slicing preparations. Harvest as soon as the rosy blush develops fully across the skin, since fruit left on the vine longer turns fully rose-colored and the texture coarsens. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Rou Gui Tea (Cinnamon Oolong)
description: Named for the warm, cinnamon-spice aroma it develops during roasting, Rou Gui originated in the Wuyi Mountains of Fujian, China, and has become one of the two most widely planted Wuyi rock oolong cultivars alongside Shui Xian. It is a vigorous, adaptable shrub that tolerates a somewhat wider range of growing sites than the more finicky heirloom Wuyi cultivars, which has helped it spread well beyond its home cliffs into general commercial plantings. Grow it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil with partial shade and consistent moisture, and prune it into a manageable hedge for repeated hand plucking. Its leaf is typically harvested slightly more mature than delicate green-tea cultivars, since the traditional roasted-oolong process favors sturdier leaf. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Roucaneuf Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant French-American Hybrid)
description: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Roucaneuf is a complex French-American hybrid grape carrying genes from several wild American Vitis species alongside European vinifera, giving it real resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South within a few seasons. It is one of a small group of Pierce's-disease-resistant varieties recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for gardeners and small growers in the region who want to make wine or juice without the constant disease losses that come with standard vinifera grapes. Harvest clusters once berries have colored and developed good sugar content, and expect the vigorous vines to need regular summer pruning to manage growth in a warm, humid climate. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rouge d'Hiver Lettuce (Red Winter Romaine)
description: Sow in late summer in rich, moist, well-drained soil and thin to 9–12 inches; Rouge d'Hiver tolerates hard frost and is best grown as a fall-to-winter crop in mild climates, or with cold frame protection in colder zones. Rouge d'Hiver (Red Winter) is a French heirloom romaine-type lettuce bred for extreme cold tolerance — a critical trait in French kitchen garden tradition where gardeners have long maintained winter salad production under cloches and frames. The upright, elongated, semi-cos heads develop deep bronzy-red to burgundy coloring that intensifies in cold weather, with firm, crunchy texture and rich, slightly nutty flavor that is superior to most warm-season lettuces. In zones 8–10 it can be grown outdoors through winter without protection; in zones 6–7 it thrives in cold frames or low tunnels. One of the most valuable and underused lettuces for Gulf Coast and Southeastern winter salad gardens where it will produce from October through March. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Rouge d'Hiver Romaine Lettuce
description: This 1800s French heirloom romaine forms a compact, 12-inch head with a tender green heart wrapped in bronze-red leaves and a rich, buttery flavor. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, and thin to 8-12 inches apart in full sun to partial shade. True to its name meaning 'Red Winter', it is quite cold tolerant and good for fall and mild-climate overwinter crops. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest heads before hot weather brings bitterness. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Rouge et Noir Southern Pea (Red-and-Black Louisiana Heirloom Cowpea)
description: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep after the soil has warmed; Rouge et Noir ('red and black') is a Louisiana heirloom Southern pea traditionally grown in Washington Parish, named for its seed color change from vivid red when freshly shelled to glossy black once fully dried. Long, slender pods up to about 10 inches hold as many as 18 seeds and can be picked young and cooked whole like a snap bean, or left to fill out for shelling and drying. The vigorous, drought-tolerant bush habit produces long running vines that sprawl well beyond the main crown, so allow generous row width or provide a low support. In Louisiana foodways this variety is traditionally simmered together with lima beans and fresh green peanuts, and the dried seed has also been roasted as a coffee substitute. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Rouge Grenobloise Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rouge Grenobloise is a French heirloom butterhead lettuce from the Grenoble region of southeastern France, selected for exceptional cold-hardiness in the alpine climate of the French Alps — its ability to withstand temperatures to 15–20°F makes it one of the most cold-tolerant butterhead lettuces available. The large, loose heads have deeply red-bronzed outer leaves with green-to-yellow-green interior leaves, creating a bicolor head that is visually striking at harvest. The flavor is the classic buttery, tender, mild butterhead type with a slight sweetness that intensifies with cold exposure — the deep burgundy-red outer leaves have a richer, slightly more complex flavor than the green interior. In zone 9 Rouge Grenobloise provides the most reliable fall-to-winter butterhead harvest of any lettuce variety, forming substantial heads from October plantings that are ready from November through February. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a continuing harvest. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Rouge Vif d'Etampes Pumpkin (Cinderella Pumpkin)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, hills spaced 6–8 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Rouge Vif d'Etampes — 'vivid red of Etampes,' the French market town where it was sold — is a century-old French heirloom pumpkin famous for its dramatically flattened, deeply ribbed, vivid red-orange form that resembles the coach from the Cinderella fairy tale; fruits weigh 15–35 pounds and have brilliant orange, fine-grained, dry, sweet flesh of outstanding quality for soups, gratins, and tarts in the French culinary tradition. Cure for 2 weeks at warm temperatures after harvest and store in a cool, dry place for up to 4 months; the unusual shape makes it a dramatic autumn centerpiece as well as an excellent culinary pumpkin. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Rougeon Grape (Teinturier French-American Hybrid Wine Grape)
description: A Seibel-bred French-American hybrid, Rougeon is a teinturier variety whose flesh, not just its skin, is deeply pigmented, producing intensely colored juice used both for blending into red wines and boosting color in lighter batches. Its productive, compact clusters ripen reliably in mid-season and the vine is well suited to the cooler climates where it has long been grown for juice and blending wine in the northeastern United States and Quebec. Prune to a cane system and thin crop load in vigorous years to maintain wine quality. It tolerates cold winters better than vinifera reds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rough-Shell Macadamia (Prickly-Leaf Macadamia)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; M. tetraphylla is slightly more cold-tolerant than M. integrifolia and may succeed in protected zone 8b sites. Macadamia tetraphylla (rough-shell macadamia or prickly-leaf macadamia) is the second of the two commercially important macadamia species — closely related to the smooth-shell macadamia (M. integrifolia) but distinguishable by its prickly-edged leaves arranged in whorls of four (the species name 'tetraphylla' means 'four-leaved'), and by the rough, ridged texture of its nut shell. Both species produce equally delicious, buttery, rich macadamia nuts with the same world-class flavor, and in commercial macadamia production, the two species and their hybrids are grown side by side with little practical flavor difference noted by consumers. The practical distinction for home growers is cold tolerance: M. tetraphylla is marginally more cold-hardy than M. integrifolia, typically tolerating temperatures of 24–26°F in established trees — potentially extending the range to protected zone 8b–9a microclimates in warm-wall or frost-pocket-free sites. M. tetraphylla is also slightly smaller in tree size. Both species benefit from cross-pollination, and planting one of each species is commonly recommended to ensure good nut set. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Round Black Spanish Radish
description: 'Round Black Spanish' is a large winter radish with rough black skin and pungent, crisp white flesh grown in the U.S. since the 1800s. Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since winter radishes need a longer season and cooler weather than spring types. Thin to 4-6 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist for smooth, non-woody roots. The spiciness mellows when cooked, and roots store exceptionally well through winter. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Round Melon (Tinda, Indian Round Gourd)
description: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches across before skin hardens. Praecitrullus fistulosus (round melon or tinda) is an Indian subcontinent cucurbit — closely related to but distinct from watermelon — that is an important summer vegetable throughout India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. The small, round, pale-green, slightly fuzzy fruits (2–4 inches across when harvested young) have a mild, delicate flavor and a slightly spongy, moist texture when cooked; they absorb spices and sauces well, making them excellent for Indian curries (tinda masala), stuffed preparations, and stir-fries. The plant is compact and less vigorous than many cucurbits — it can be grown on a small trellis or allowed to sprawl as a groundcover. The fruits must be picked when young and tender; overripe fruits become pithy and seedy. It grows best in the hot summer conditions of zone 8–12 and is rarely available in North American grocery stores, making home growing especially rewarding for Indian cooking enthusiasts. An essentially unknown vegetable in Western horticulture that deserves wider recognition. Matures in 50–75 days from seed.

name: Round Winter Melon (Round Wax Gourd)
description: A round-fruited strain of winter melon that develops large, globe-shaped fruit up to 14-22 pounds, in contrast to the more common oblong wax gourd types. As fruit matures it develops the characteristic waxy white bloom on pale green skin that gives the vegetable its storage-friendly reputation; whole melons can keep for months in a cool, dry spot after harvest. Its round shape and generous size make it the traditional choice for the banquet presentation known as dong gua zhong, where the entire hollowed melon is steamed and served as a soup tureen. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room or a very sturdy trellis with fruit slings, since ripe melons are heavy. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Round Zucchini
description: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm, fertile soil, planting a couple of seeds per spot and thinning to the strongest. This heirloom summer squash produces charming globe-shaped fruits about three to four inches across that are ideal for stuffing. Keep the plants well watered and harvest fruits young, when they are tender and the skin is still glossy. Picking frequently keeps the productive plants setting new fruit throughout the warm season. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Round Zucchini Summer Squash
description: This round zucchini bears tender, ball-shaped fruits especially suited for stuffing or serving as individual soup bowls. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the bushy plants full sun and room to spread. Harvest fruits young at 3-4 inches wide for the best flavor, picking often to keep the plant productive. The edible blossoms are delicious fried, and consistent watering supports steady fruit set. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Roundleaf Serviceberry
description: Harvest berries when fully dark blue-black and extract seeds by mashing and rinsing before sowing in fall into lean, well-drained soil in a sunny outdoor bed. The round, coarsely toothed leaves that give this species its name are a useful identification feature as seedlings mature through their first growing seasons. Roundleaf Serviceberry tolerates shallow, rocky soils and gravelly barrens far better than most shrubs, making it a strong candidate for challenging landscape sites. Plants begin bearing their sweet, dark berries within 2–5 years of transplanting and attract a wide variety of frugivorous birds during the midsummer ripening period. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rovada Red Currant
description: 'Rovada' is a late-season red currant that bears exceptionally long strigs of bright, uniform berries prized for jelly and fresh use. It flowers late, escaping frost, and crops reliably even in cooler summers. Unlike black currants, red currants fruit on spurs of older wood, so prune to an open goblet framework and shorten new growth in winter. Grow in partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch, and net the bushes to protect ripe fruit from birds. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Roxanne Radish (AAS-Winning Uniform Red Globe Radish)
description: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; Roxanne is an AAS-winning globe radish producing uniform, bright-red, smooth roots with crisp, mild white flesh, bred for unusually strong resistance to the pithiness and hollow centers that often develop in radishes that sit in the ground a few extra days past ideal harvest size or face a warm spell. This forgiveness makes it a good choice for gardeners who cannot harvest on the exact first day of readiness. It matures quickly, in as little as 24 days, allowing several successive plantings through a spring or fall cool season. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, fast-sizing roots, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across for the crispest texture. Matures in 24–30 days from seed.

name: Roxburgh Fig (Timla, Elephant Ear Fig)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig grows rapidly and produces large clusters of edible figs. Ficus auriculata (Roxburgh fig or timla fig) is one of the most ornamentally dramatic and useful fruiting figs in tropical horticulture — a large, fast-growing tree from the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia producing the largest leaves of any commonly cultivated Ficus: enormous (12–24 inch), rounded, dark-green, slightly hairy leaves with a bold, tropical texture that gives the plant a genuinely dramatic visual presence, resembling a cross between a giant philodendron and an elephant ear.
