The figs are equally remarkable: large (1.5–2.5 inch), distinctly ribbed, brownish-red when ripe, produced in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) — the same unusual fruiting pattern as jackfruit. The figs are sweet, moist, seedy, and pleasant to eat fresh when ripe, with a mild, sweet flavor; they are also eaten as a cooked vegetable when unripe in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking (stewed, pickled, or curried). In Himalayan and hill-station gardens in India, Roxburgh fig is grown as a major multi-use tree; in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens, it is an outstanding bold-textured ornamental that also produces an edible crop. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Roxbury Russet Apple (Oldest Documented American Apple Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. First recorded in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s, this is the oldest apple cultivar documented as having originated in North America, predating the country itself by well over a century. The medium, dull yellow-green fruit is almost entirely covered in rough golden-brown russet, with firm, crisp, sweet-tart flesh well suited to fresh eating, cider, and long winter storage, since the thick skin sheds moisture slowly and resists shriveling. It ripens in mid-fall and was historically prized precisely because it kept so well through the winter months before refrigeration existed. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Roy's Calais Flint Corn (Vermont Abenaki Flint Corn)
description: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; this is among the most cold-adapted flint corns available and reliably dries down even in short, cool Vermont-style growing seasons. Roy's Calais Flint traces to Abenaki agriculture in the Calais, Vermont area and was preserved through the twentieth century by farmer Roy Fair before seed steward Sylvia Davatz continued growing and distributing it, making it one of the best-documented survival stories among Northeastern landrace corns. Ears show a striking mix of yellow, red, and burgundy kernels on the same cob, and the corn is prized both for cornmeal and for polenta with a distinctively rich, sweet flint-corn flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Royal Ann Cherry (Napoleon Cherry, Classic Light Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Royal Ann, known in Europe by its original name Napoleon, is a historic light-colored sweet cherry with pale yellow skin blushed with red and firm, sweet, translucent flesh, and it holds particular commercial significance as the primary variety historically used for maraschino cherries, since its light color takes dye and processing well. Beyond processing, Royal Ann is an excellent fresh-eating cherry, with a classic sweet flavor and firm texture that also makes it good for canning. The vigorous tree requires cross-pollination from another sweet cherry variety and grows quite large without size-controlling rootstock, so plan orchard spacing accordingly; harvest when fruit reaches full color and sweetness, since light-skinned cherries like Royal Ann do not continue ripening once picked. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Royal Burgundy Bush Bean
description: Direct sow seeds one inch deep once frost danger has passed and soil is warm, with no trellis needed for these compact plants. The 15-20 inch bushes are well suited to containers and small gardens, producing deep-purple, stringless pods that stand out against the foliage. The pods turn green when cooked, making harvest easy since the purple is simple to spot. Pick regularly while pods are young and tender to keep the plants producing. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Royal Burgundy Bush Bean (Purple Pod Snap Bean That Turns Green When Cooked)
description: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, thinning to 4–6 inches apart; Royal Burgundy is a bush snap bean producing vivid deep-purple pods that are immediately striking in the garden and make harvesting easy — the bright-purple color stands out against green foliage so ripe pods are much easier to spot than the green pods of standard snap beans. The purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when the beans are cooked — pods turn a standard snap-bean green when blanched or boiled, which is useful to know so the color loss is not mistaken for poor quality. The flavor is excellent: full, classic snap bean flavor with slightly more robust character than some modern hybrids. Royal Burgundy is notably cold-soil tolerant for a snap bean — germinating reliably in soil temperatures down to 60°F (versus the 65°F+ preferred by most snap beans), making it a good choice for early spring and fall plantings in zone 9 where soil temperatures can be borderline for bean germination. The bush habit (18–24 inches, no staking required) and reliable early productivity (50–60 days) make Royal Burgundy one of the more practical ornamental-vegetables for Gulf South kitchen gardens, combining harvest efficiency with decorative garden impact. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Royal Corona Bean (Giant White Gigante-Style Runner Bean)
description: Royal Corona was developed and popularized by California heirloom seed company Rancho Gordo as a domestically grown alternative to Italy's prized gigante beans, selecting a large-seeded white runner bean strain grown in Mexico's highlands for exceptional size and a dense, creamy texture. The oversized white seeds swell further when cooked, becoming meltingly tender while holding their shape, a texture prized for simple olive-oil-and-herb preparations that let the bean's quality shine. As with other runner beans, give plants tall, sturdy supports and consistent moisture, since shallow roots make the vines quick to stop setting pods in hot, dry conditions. Let pods dry fully on the vine before harvest, then shell and cure before storage. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Royal Crimson Cherry (Self-Fruitful Low-Chill Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike most sweet cherries, Royal Crimson is self-fruitful, so a single tree can produce a crop without a separate pollinizer, though a nearby second tree improves yields. Bred from the same low-chill program that produced Minnie Royal and Royal Lee, Royal Crimson needs only about 200 to 300 chill hours, allowing it to fruit reliably in warm-winter Southern gardens where classic sweet cherries fail to break dormancy properly. The tree bears large, crimson-red, sweet fruit in early to mid-spring, ahead of most other sweet cherries. Because the crop ripens and blooms so early, choose a well-drained site with good air movement to protect flowers from late frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Royal Crown Turnip (Purple-Topped Dual-Purpose Hybrid Turnip)
description: Royal Crown is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip grown for both its roots and its abundant dark green tops, making it a genuine dual-purpose crop rather than a greens-only or roots-only type. The slightly flattened, globe-shaped roots are smooth and creamy white with a bright purple-blotched crown, and stay sweet and mild if pulled small rather than left to size up. Because the leafy top is unusually productive relative to the root, it is a good choice for gardeners who want a steady cutting of turnip greens alongside a modest root harvest. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin early, since crowded roots become misshapen. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Royal Gala Apple (Deeper-Red Striped Sport of Gala)
description: Royal Gala arose in New Zealand as a more deeply and evenly colored bud sport of the original Gala apple, showing bright red striping over a larger portion of the fruit's surface than the parent strain. It colors reliably even in seasons with less pronounced day-night temperature swings, which made it the preferred strain for commercial orchards worldwide — most apples sold simply as 'Gala' in supermarkets today are actually the Royal Gala strain rather than the original 1934 release. Flavor, texture, and chill requirement are essentially identical to standard Gala: crisp, fine-grained, sweet, and low in acidity, with fruit ripening in the early-to-mid season. Provide a compatible pollinizer such as Fuji or Golden Delicious within about 50 feet for reliable fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Royal Guard Rusty Blackhaw Viburnum
description: Introduced by the former Cole Nurseries of Circleville, Ohio, 'Royal Guard' is a narrow, upright selection of the native rusty blackhaw viburnum, reaching up to 12 feet tall while staying only 6-8 feet wide, considerably narrower in spread than typical seedlings. Like the species, it bears flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by fruit that ripens from green through pink to blue and persists into winter, plus deep burgundy fall foliage. Plant in well-drained, average to dry, well-drained loam in full sun to part shade; it is highly drought-tolerant once established and, in warmer parts of its range, appreciates light afternoon shade. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Royal Lee Cherry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and always pair with Minnie Royal for pollination, since Royal Lee will not set a usable crop alone. Like its companion, Royal Lee needs only around 200 to 400 chill hours, making it one of the few sweet cherries genuinely worth trying south of the traditional cherry belt, including parts of the Gulf Coast and lower South with mild winters. Fruit is firm, dark red, and ripens early in the season, roughly two weeks ahead of Bing, giving Southern growers a short but real cherry harvest window. Select a sunny, frost-protected planting site, since the trees' early bloom leaves flowers exposed to any late cold snaps. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Royal Limbertwig Apple (Warm-Climate Southern Limbertwig Strain)
description: Royal Limbertwig is one of the best-regarded of the more than one hundred Limbertwig strains documented by Lee Calhoun, singled out among heirloom nurseries as a high-quality apple that grows well in the warmer areas of the South, making it a more Gulf-Coast-friendly choice than many mountain-bred Limbertwig selections. Fruit is medium to large with yellow skin overlaid with red, and the fine-grained, juicy, tender flesh is mildly subacid with the rich, old-fashioned flavor the Limbertwig family is known for. It ripens in October and keeps well, making it useful for fresh eating, cooking, and cider alike. Like other Limbertwigs it is not self-fruitful, so plant a second apple cultivar within pollination range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Royal Medlar (Classic English Bletting Medlar)
description: Royal is a traditional English medlar cultivar grown for centuries for its russet-brown, apple-shaped fruit that must be bletted, or softened by frost and storage, before eating, developing a soft, spiced, wine-like flavor. Trees are small, gnarled, and self-fertile, producing single white blossoms in late spring followed by fruit that ripens hard on the tree into autumn. Harvest fruit after the first hard frost and store in a cool, dark spot for two to three weeks until the flesh softens and darkens before use in preserves or eaten fresh. The species tolerates a range of soils and needs little pruning beyond removing crossing or damaged branches. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Royal Raindrops Crabapple (Cutleaf Purple-Foliage Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Royal Raindrops is a distinctive ornamental crabapple with deeply cut, purple-red, finely serrated foliage unlike the broad, rounded leaves of most crabapple cultivars, opening with a heavy flush of magenta-pink spring flowers followed by small, persistent red fruit that hangs on into winter as forage for birds. It shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases — apple scab, fire blight, cedar-apple rust — that plague many older crabapple cultivars, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a small flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; the small, hard fruit persists well into winter, providing months of ornamental and wildlife value beyond the spring bloom. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Royal Rosa Apricot (Zaiger White-Fleshed Low-Chill Apricot)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid frost pockets, since early bloom makes flowers vulnerable to late cold snaps. Royal Rosa is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and thinning developing fruit to a few inches apart improves size and prevents limb breakage. It is prized for pale creamy-white to blush-pink skin and sweet, low-acid, aromatic white flesh that distinguishes it from standard orange-fleshed apricots. Its unusually low chill requirement makes it a go-to choice for gardeners in mild-winter regions where Blenheim and Moorpark can bloom unevenly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Royal Star Mayhaw (Early-Blooming Thornless Purple-Red Mayhaw)
description: Royal Star is an early-blooming western mayhaw selection valued for its nearly thornless, upright branching, which makes mowing and harvesting beneath the canopy far easier than with thorny seedling mayhaws. Its fruit ripens to a deep red verging on purple, giving jelly and syrup an unusually dark, rich color compared with the brighter red of most mayhaw cultivars. Because it flowers early in the season, it needs another early-blooming mayhaw such as Spectacular planted nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Grow it, like other mayhaws, on moist to wet, acidic ground in full sun. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Royal Velvet English Lavender
description: Grow in full sun in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil; avoid rich beds and irrigation systems that keep the crown wet. 'Royal Velvet' produces long, straight stems topped with dense, deep violet-blue flower spikes that are prized for cutting and drying, standing taller than compact English lavenders like 'Hidcote' or 'Munstead' while keeping a tidy, upright habit. The strong stems and saturated color make it a favored variety for cut-flower bouquets and craft use. Shear the plant back by about a third after the main flowering flush to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new growth for the following season. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Royalty Mayhaw (Named Eastern Mayhaw Selection)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a native wetland tree that thrives in the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most fruit trees struggle. Royalty is a named selection of eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis), grown as a smaller, more spreading tree than many western mayhaw cultivars, producing clusters of bright red fruit in spring that ripen into the classic tart, aromatic berries prized for mayhaw jelly across the Gulf South. Like other mayhaws it can be affected by cedar-apple rust where eastern redcedar grows nearby, so siting away from cedars helps keep fruit and foliage clean. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar to ensure good cross-pollination, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years of planting. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Royalty Purple Pod Bean (AAS-Winning Purple Bush Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long, while still tender and before the purple color begins to fade. Royalty Purple Pod is a 1976 All-America Selections-winning bush bean known for its striking deep purple pods — an unusual color in the snap bean world and a practical advantage because the vivid pods are easy to see against green foliage during harvest. The purple color results from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when cooked, leaving behind the standard green of cooked snap beans — a fact that surprises first-time growers who expect to retain the purple color. The flavor of Royalty is notably good — richer and slightly more complex than many modern bush bean hybrids — and the plants show slightly better cool-soil germination tolerance than green-podded snap beans. Royalty Purple Pod has maintained its status as a respected open-pollinated variety for nearly 50 years since its AAS award, used both as a practical garden bean and as a visual accent in edible landscapes where the purple-podded plants contrast attractively with green foliage. Matures in 51–60 days from seed.

name: Royalty Purple Raspberry
description: 'Royalty' is a hybrid of red and black raspberry yielding large, richly flavored purple berries excellent for jam and baking. The tall, sturdy canes do not sucker as aggressively as red types and are best tip-pruned in summer to encourage lateral branching. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and remove old floricanes after fruiting. Plant at least 300 feet from wild or black raspberries to reduce viral disease pressure. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: RST-04-106 Rootstock Tomato
description: This widely used interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite tomato scion variety rather than eaten itself, valued by home and market growers for moderate, manageable vigor along with broad resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts, root-knot nematodes, and corky root rot that substantially extends productive plant life in soils with a history of these problems. Its more restrained growth compared to the most aggressive rootstock cultivars makes it a favorite for home high tunnel and small-scale market growers who want the disease resistance and yield benefits of grafting without an overly rampant root system demanding constant pruning. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Rubicon Napa Cabbage (Disease-Resistant Barrel-Type Hybrid)
description: Transplant into rich, consistently moist soil, keeping plants well watered to prevent tipburn and premature bolting. Rubicon forms dense, barrel-shaped heads with good resistance to fusarium yellows, making it a reliable choice where soilborne disease has hurt other napa types. Harvest when heads feel firm and heavy; the tight wrap holds well in the field and in cold storage. Its balanced sweet-mild flavor suits both fresh kimchi and quick stir-fries. Matures in 56–60 days from transplant.

name: Rubina Aronia (Hungarian Large-Fruited Black Chokeberry)
description: Rubina is a Hungarian-bred black chokeberry selection resulting from a cross of 'Viking' with a Russian aronia variety, chosen for producing notably large berries and ripening earlier than most other black chokeberry cultivars. Its vigorous, upright growth habit yields heavy clusters of glossy black fruit that are slightly sweeter and less astringent than typical seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa, making them popular for fresh eating as well as juice, syrup, and jam. White flower clusters open in mid-spring and draw a wide range of pollinators before the summer foliage matures to deep green, then turns vivid orange-red in fall. Rubina tolerates wet or periodically saturated soils far better than most fruiting shrubs but performs poorly in shallow, chalky ground, so amend heavy alkaline soils before planting and mulch to retain even moisture. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rubinette Apple (Intensely Aromatic Swiss Dessert Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Rubinette is a Swiss apple with parentage tracing through both Golden Delicious and Cox's Orange Pippin, and it is widely regarded by connoisseurs as one of the most intensely aromatic and best-flavored modern apples available, delivering a complex, richly perfumed sweet-tart flavor reminiscent of its Cox heritage in a smaller, russet-blushed, red-striped fruit. The tree is only moderately productive compared with high-yield commercial varieties, a common tradeoff with exceptionally flavorful apples, but home orchardists focused on eating quality over sheer yield consider it well worth growing. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and enjoy fresh, since the fruit's aromatic complexity is best appreciated soon after harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ruby American Persimmon (Named Native Persimmon Selection)
description: Ruby is a named selection of the native American persimmon propagated by collectors and specialty nurseries alongside other named cultivars such as Meader, Morris Burton, and Prok. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, its orange fruit remains firm and strongly astringent until fully soft-ripened by cool autumn weather, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The species is dioecious, so siting a male tree or another fruiting cultivar nearby helps ensure reliable pollination and fruit set. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a wide range of soils, needing little maintenance beyond periodic removal of root suckers to prevent thicket formation. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Chard
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ruby Chard is the classic red-stemmed Swiss chard variety with deep crimson-red midribs and stems against dark, slightly crinkled green leaves — one of the most ornamental of all vegetables and a perennial favorite in both kitchen gardens and edible ornamental designs. The striking color contrast of red stem against dark green makes Ruby Chard effective as a garden border plant, in containers, and in ornamental beds where most vegetables would look out of place. The same mild, slightly earthy, spinach-like flavor of all Swiss chard makes Ruby excellent for sautéing with garlic, adding to soups, and wilting into pasta dishes where the vibrant red stems retain some color even after cooking. As a dual-use ornamental and culinary vegetable, Ruby Chard demonstrates that the most productive kitchen garden plants need not sacrifice ornamental appeal. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the better vegetables for partially shaded kitchen garden spaces. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Ruby Crush Tomato (Texas Superstar Compact Disease-Resistant Grape Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar-designated determinate grape tomato, compact enough for smaller garden beds and large containers, bred with a broad package of disease resistance that helps it hold up through the humid, disease-prone conditions of a Texas and Gulf South growing season. It produces heavy clusters of sweet, crack-resistant red grape tomatoes over a concentrated harvest window typical of determinate varieties, making it a good choice for gardeners who want a big, manageable crop for fresh eating or canning without the sprawling growth of an indeterminate vine. A light stake or cage helps keep the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the plant productive through its season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Ruby June Strawberry (Southeast-Bred Disease-Resistant Short-Day)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Ruby June is a short-day strawberry bred specifically for the Southeast and Gulf region, combining disease resistance with a compact, tight plant architecture that keeps beds tidy and makes picking easier than more sprawling cultivars. The berries are deep ruby-red both inside and out, with high early-season yield that gets a Gulf South winter strawberry planting off to a strong start. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure typical of humid Gulf Coast strawberry production. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Ruby King Pepper
description: Ruby King is an American heirloom sweet bell pepper documented since at least 1902 and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network after a 1977 donation. It sets heavy clusters of blocky, thick-walled fruit that ripen from green to a deep glossy red, with a mild, sweet flavor that holds up well fresh or cooked. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture, and stake or cage heavily loaded branches since the large fruit can weigh down stems. Its earlier maturity than many modern giant bells makes it a reliable choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Perfection Cabbage (AAS-Winning Red Cabbage)
description: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop. Ruby Perfection, an All-America Selections winner, forms dense, round, deep reddish-purple heads that hold their color and quality well, both in the garden and in storage, on a compact plant bred for uniform heading and dependable performance across varying growing conditions. Its rich color makes it a striking addition to salads, slaws, and pickled preparations in addition to standard cooked use. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm and dense to the touch. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Queen Beet
description: Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings so each root has a few inches to swell. This 1957 All-America Selections winner produces round, dark-red roots with mild, sweet flavor and tender texture. Keep soil evenly moist for smooth, non-woody roots, and do not skip thinning, since each cluster yields several plants. Harvest roots when they reach two to three inches, and enjoy the nutritious greens as an added bonus. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Ruby Queen Sweet Corn
description: Ruby Queen is a sugary-enhanced hybrid grown as much for its deep ruby-red kernels as for its old-fashioned corn flavor, with 8 inch ears carrying 16 to 18 rows on 7-foot stalks. Harvest at the blush stage for the sweetest eating, or let ears ripen further to full red for a richer, more traditional corn taste; steam, grill, or microwave rather than boil to keep the color from fading into the cooking water. The red tassels and husks make the standing plants attractive in the garden and useful for fall decorating even before the ears are picked. Choose it when a gardener wants a novelty-colored sweet corn that still delivers genuinely good fresh eating rather than an ornamental-only variety. Matures in 73–78 days from seed.

name: Ruby Red / Rhubarb Swiss Chard
description: 'Ruby Red' is an 1850s heirloom chard with vivid red stems and veins that beautifies the garden and provides greens from early summer into fall. Direct sow the seed clusters 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6-12 inches apart for full-size plants. This vigorous, long-season grower keeps producing when outer leaves are harvested regularly. Use young leaves raw in salads and mature leaves and stems cooked; it tolerates light frost. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Ruby Red Chard (Rhubarb Chard, Red-stalked Chard)
description: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 6–9 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously. Beta vulgaris 'Ruby Red' (Ruby Red chard or Rhubarb chard) is a variety of Swiss chard selected for its dramatic, brilliant red stems (petioles) and red-veined dark-green to red-flushed leaves — making it simultaneously one of the most ornamental and one of the most nutritious crops in the vegetable garden. The vivid crimson stems get their color from betalain pigments (the same pigment group responsible for red beet color) which have antioxidant properties. The flavor is mild and slightly earthy, similar to spinach with a slightly stronger taste; the stems are firmer and need slightly longer cooking than the leaves. In zone 9, Ruby Red chard is a superb fall-through-spring crop, sown from September through November for harvest from November through May — it tolerates light frost and performs through the cool season until summer heat bolts it. The ornamental value is substantial: planted in rows or mixed borders, the glowing red stems create strong visual impact, making this one of the few vegetables that earns a place in ornamental beds. As with all chard, cut-and-come-again harvest extends production for months. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Ruby Red Grapefruit (Original Texas Pink Grapefruit, First US Plant Patent Recipient)
description: Plant grafted tree in full sun, deep well-drained soil; mulch for moisture retention. Protect from frost in zone 9. Ruby Red is the original pink/red-fleshed grapefruit variety and one of the most historically significant citrus varieties in American horticulture: it holds the distinction of being the first variety to receive a US plant patent, issued February 4, 1930 (US Plant Patent 1), when Bonnie Nance's discovery of a pink bud sport on a Thompson grapefruit tree in Weslaco, Texas in 1929 was submitted by Stark Brothers Nursery. The story of Ruby Red begins in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas — one of the finest grapefruit-producing regions in the world — where the combination of warm days, cool nights, and alkaline soil produces grapefruit of exceptional sweetness and flavor. Ruby Red's pink flesh coloration comes from lycopene (the same pigment in tomatoes and watermelons) — a pigment that accumulates in the fruit's flesh during the cool nights of the growing season. The variety has less red pigmentation than its descendants (Rio Red and Star Ruby, which were developed specifically for deeper coloration), but it was the original breakthrough that made pink grapefruit a distinct commercial category. The fruit is large (3–5 inches), mildly fragrant, with blushed pink skin and sweet, mildly acidic, aromatic flesh that made pink grapefruit the preferred fresh-eating grapefruit variety in American markets through the mid-20th century. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Red Onion
description: Start seeds indoors about two months before transplanting, since onions require a long growing season. This long-day variety forms bulbs as summer days lengthen, making it well suited to northern gardens. Set transplants into loose, fertile soil and keep them weeded and evenly watered as the bulbs size up. The medium to large globes have firm white flesh and burgundy skins that store well after proper curing. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Red Rhubarb Swiss Chard
description: Soak seed clusters overnight and sow half an inch deep, then thin the seedlings since each cluster produces several plants. This heirloom chard shows off deep ruby stems against glossy green leaves, adding bold color to the garden. Harvest tender baby leaves for salads or let leaves mature for cooking, always taking the outer ones first. With steady moisture and regular picking, the plants keep producing through the season on a cut-and-come-again basis. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Ruby Red Swiss Chard (Classic Deep-Red Stem Rhubarb Chard)
description: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly, leaving the growing center intact. Ruby Red Swiss Chard (also called Rhubarb Chard for the resemblance of the brilliant crimson stems to culinary rhubarb stalks) is the original and defining red-stemmed chard — the variety from which all colored-stem selections and rainbow chard blends derive. Ruby Red produces large, dark green, heavily crinkled and savoyed leaves on vivid crimson to ruby-red stems and midribs — a color combination that makes the plant one of the most ornamentally striking vegetables in the cool-season garden, visually dramatic against the dark green leaf tissue. The crimson pigment in Ruby Red's stems is betacyanin — the same class of pigment found in red beets (Beta vulgaris, the same genus) — a natural antioxidant with deep red to violet-red coloration. Ruby Red has longer American cultivation history than most colored chard types, appearing in American seed catalogs under 'Rhubarb Chard' nomenclature for well over a century. The flavor is classic chard — mild and slightly earthy-sweet when young, more substantial and beet-adjacent in mature leaves. The red stem color is retained reasonably well through steaming but bleeds in boiling water; roasting or sautéing in fat preserves the best color. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Ruby Rhubarb
description: Ruby is an older English-raised rhubarb selection valued for stalks that stay a rich wine-red well up their length rather than fading to green partway, giving a more visually striking harvest than many all-purpose varieties. Flavor is bright and tart with the moderate acidity typical of good culinary rhubarb, making it well suited to pies, sauces, and preserves where color matters as much as taste. Divide crowns every four to six years once the center of the clump begins to thin, replanting divisions with at least one strong bud each. Skip harvest the first year after planting and take only a light cutting the second spring to let the crown build reserves for a long productive life. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Seedless Grape
description: A USDA release from 1968, Ruby Seedless bears medium, oval, reddish-purple berries with a sweet, slightly tart flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen mid-to-late season. The berries can be slow to color fully, developing deeper red tones as they hang longer on the vine in warm weather. Vines are vigorous and productive, so annual dormant pruning to a permanent cordon and early-season cluster thinning help keep berry size and quality consistent. It thrives with a long, hot, dry growing season and is prone to fungal problems in humid climates. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Streaks Mustard (Red Frills Mustard, Deeply Cut Red Mustard)
description: Broadcast seed thinly or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches (2–3 weeks); for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves or cut the whole plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; the pungent flavor mellows with cooking. Ruby Streaks is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with deeply incised, almost pinnately cut leaves that create a lacey, frilly appearance dramatically different from the broad flat or ruffled leaves of traditional Southern mustard varieties — the leaf form is sometimes compared to flat-leaf parsley or baby arugula but scaled up and colored an intense burgundy-red to dark purple-red throughout. The name describes the appearance perfectly: the stems and veins are ruby-red while the deeply cut leaf tissue is a rich burgundy-maroon that becomes most intense in cold weather, making Ruby Streaks one of the most visually dramatic cool-season greens available for garden beds and mesclun mixes. The flavor is strongly mustardy with a sharp, spicy edge that makes it an excellent salad mix component providing flavor contrast to milder greens (lettuce, spinach, mild arugula) and visual color interest; young leaves (3–4 weeks) are mild enough for raw eating while mature leaves (5–6 weeks) have significant heat that benefits from brief cooking or a vinegar-dressed wilted salad. Ruby Streaks is one of the standard components of the premium mesclun salad mix sold under names like 'Braising Mix' and 'Asian Salad Mix' in American specialty markets. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Ruby Supreme Guava
description: Ruby Supreme is a tropical guava that bears fragrant fruit with sweet, pink-red flesh rich in flavor and nutrition. This fast-growing evergreen fruits young and adapts well to containers, making it accessible even where winters are cold. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and feed regularly during the warm season for the heaviest crops. Keep the soil evenly moist, prune to maintain a manageable size, and bring potted trees indoors before frost. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ruby Sweet Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Red-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
description: Ruby Sweet resulted from a 1968 cross of Mariposa and Methley made by USDA breeder W.R. Okie at the Byron, Georgia research station, and was selected for markedly better flavor and disease tolerance than older Southeastern plums like Stanley. The fruit is medium to large with deep ruby-red skin and juicy red flesh, ripening in early-to-mid summer. It is not self-fruitful, so plant it alongside another Japanese plum such as Methley or Santa Rosa within pollinating range for reliable fruit set. Its chill requirement of roughly 400 hours runs toward the higher end for Gulf Coast zone 9a, so it is most reliable in the cooler pockets of the region and in years with a fuller winter chill; gardeners on the mildest coastal fringe should pair it with a very-low-chill variety as insurance. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rubybor Kale (AAS-Winning Purple Curly Kale)
description: Direct sow or start transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Rubybor is an AAS-winning curly kale that scored a Gold Medal in both ornamental and vegetable trials, an unusual double distinction, thanks to finely frilled leaves with deep purple stems and veining that hold their color even through summer heat. The leaves stay tender and mild enough for raw salads while remaining sturdy enough for cooking, and the compact, bushy plant produces roughly twice the yield of older red kale varieties. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up as needed, and expect improved sweetness in leaves picked after a light frost. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: RubyCrisp Muscadine (Firm-Flesh Table Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. RubyCrisp is a modern University of Georgia muscadine bred to address the main complaint fresh-market shoppers have about muscadines — thick, tough skin — with noticeably firmer flesh and thinner, more tender skin that make the deep red-to-black berries far more pleasant to eat out of hand, closer to the experience of a bunch grape while keeping the intense, musky-sweet muscadine flavor. Like other muscadines it is naturally resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and the fungal diseases that plague European wine grapes in the humid South, so home gardeners can grow it without a spray program. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety nearby if RubyCrisp is female-flowered, or check with the nursery on flower type at purchase, since muscadine cultivars vary between self-fertile and female-only. Prune hard in late winter, leaving short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as individual berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: RubyFrost Apple
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator apple within range for good fruit set. RubyFrost (bred as NY2) was developed by Susan Brown at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a cross of Braeburn and Autumn Crisp, taking roughly seventeen years to reach commercial release in 2013 alongside its sibling SnapDragon. It ripens late in the season, after SnapDragon, and is notable for unusually high vitamin C content along with firm, dense flesh and a tangy-sweet flavor that holds up exceptionally well in cold storage, often keeping quality for months. It is best suited to the cold-winter apple regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that the Geneva breeding program targets, and its thick skin and dense texture also resist bruising during handling. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ruddy Sweet Potato
description: Ruddy is a fresh-market sweet potato released by North Carolina State University's breeding program, selected for its notably darker, deeper rose-red skin than Jewel or Beauregard, which makes it stand out visually at market and in home harvests. The flesh is moist, deep orange, and sweet, with smooth, uniform roots and good resistance to several common sweetpotato diseases. It grows vigorously in the long, hot Gulf Coast season and produces heavily from a modest planting of slips. Harvest before soil temperatures drop in fall and cure promptly to bring out its full sweetness and deepen the skin color further. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Rudolf Radish (Extra-Early Bright Red Spring Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Rudolf is bred for extremely fast maturity, often ready to harvest in as little as three weeks from sowing, among the quickest radishes available, making it an excellent choice for gardeners wanting the fastest possible turnaround or squeezing in an extra succession planting before summer heat arrives. Roots are smooth, round, and bright cherry-red with crisp white flesh and a clean, mild flavor typical of quick-maturing spring radishes. Because it matures so fast, timing the harvest promptly is especially important, since even quick radishes turn pithy and hollow if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Matures in 21–28 days from seed.

name: Rue
description: Sow seed 1/8 in deep indoors in a warm spot; rue germinates best at around 68°F. Plant in poor, well-drained, alkaline soil and avoid overhead watering to prevent fungal issues in the bluish-green foliage. Always wear gloves and long sleeves when handling rue, as the sap can cause severe phototoxic skin burns when exposed to sunlight. Harvest small sprigs of foliage before flowering for traditional uses as a strewing herb or insect deterrent; internal use requires professional guidance due to toxicity at high doses. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Rufous Mayhaw (Florida Mayhaw, Rusty Hawthorn)
description: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, acidic soil in full sun to light shade, siting trees in low ground, pond margins, or swampy depressions where they will not be short of water during summer. Crataegus rufula is the third and least-known of the Gulf South mayhaws, a naturally occurring hybrid intermediate between eastern mayhaw (C. aestivalis) and western mayhaw (C. opaca) that arose where the ranges of its two parent species overlap along the Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia, and adjoining south Alabama. The reddish pubescence on the undersides of the leaves, especially along the veins, gives the species its 'rufous' or rusty-hawthorn name and distinguishes it in the field from the two parent mayhaws. Like its relatives it bears clusters of small, bright red, tart pome fruit in late spring that can be substituted for eastern or western mayhaw in jelly and syrup making, and its dense thorny branching, showy white spring bloom, and tolerance of wet, flood-prone ground make it valuable both as a wildlife food source and as a fruiting tree for low, poorly drained corners of Gulf South landscapes that would sour most other fruit trees. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Rugosa Friulana Squash (Italian Bumpy-Skinned Heirloom Pumpkin)
description: Rugosa Friulana is a traditional Italian heirloom from the Friuli region prized for its warty, tan-beige rind and remarkably dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh, long favored in northern Italy for filling tortelli di zucca and other stuffed pastas. The pear-to-oblong fruit develops a rough, bumpy skin as it matures, a trait that distinguishes it visually from the smoother Marina di Chioggia despite both being Cucurbita moschata types from neighboring regions. Vines are vigorous and productive, so provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development, then reduce watering as the rind hardens to concentrate sugars. Cure fruit in a warm spot for a couple of weeks after harvest before storing to further develop its characteristic sweetness. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Rugosa Rose
description: Plant in well-drained soil including poor sandy or salty soils where few shrubs survive; rugosa rose is extraordinarily tough and requires almost no maintenance once established. The intensely fragrant single or semi-double flowers in magenta, pink, or white bloom repeatedly from late spring to fall, followed by the largest and most nutritious rose hips of any commonly grown species — orange-red to scarlet tomato-shaped hips up to 1 inch in diameter that are exceptionally rich in vitamin C. Hips are harvested after the first frost when fully soft and red for rosehip tea, syrup, jam, and wine. The dense, thorny habit makes an excellent barrier hedge. Remove only dead wood; avoid hard pruning, which disrupts repeat flowering. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ruiru 11 Coffee
description: Released in 1985 by Kenya's Coffee Research Foundation, Ruiru 11 was the first Arabica cultivar bred with combined resistance to both coffee berry disease and leaf rust, the two most destructive coffee diseases in East Africa, and its dwarf, highly compact habit allows far denser planting than traditional Kenyan selections like SL28. It is an F1 composite hybrid, so seed must be sourced from the breeding program rather than saved from open-pollinated trees. Cup quality is respectable but historically ranked below the legendary SL28 and SL34, a gap that later prompted the breeding of the successor cultivar Batian. Grow it in filtered shade with rich, well-drained soil and expect early, heavy bearing. Matures in 1095–1400 days from transplant.

name: Rukam (Indian Prune, Rukam Manis)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, fertile soil in humid tropical lowland conditions; rukam is a large Southeast Asian fruiting tree in the same genus as governor's plum but bearing larger, rounder fruits (3/4–1 inch) with dark red to purple-black skin and acidic flesh that sweetens with full ripeness and can be eaten fresh or preserved. A handsome ornamental tree with large glossy leaves, it is grown in home gardens across Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines as both ornamental and fruit tree. Much less commonly grown than governor's plum but produces superior fruit quality and larger individual fruits. Slow to bear from seed — grafted plants fruit several years earlier. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Runner Bean
description: Sow seeds 2 in deep at the base of a robust trellis or obelisk at least 6 ft tall; runner beans are vigorous climbers and will overwhelm light supports. The scarlet flowers attract hummingbirds and are themselves edible. Pick pods frequently at 6–8 in before they become stringy; pods left to mature inhibit further flowering. In frost-free climates, tuberous roots can be overwintered and will regrow the following spring. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Running Conch Cowpea (Vining North Florida Cream Pea)
description: Sow directly in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, and let the long vines climb a trellis or scramble over corn or sorghum stalks in the old co-cropping style. Running Conch belongs to the Conch group of cream-seeded southern peas, first documented along the St. Johns River in north Florida in the late 1800s and likely introduced from the West Indies. The narrow, slender pods hold medium-sized cream-colored peas prized for a delicate flavor and notably fast, easy cooking compared with other dried peas. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling once they fill out, or leave them on the vine to dry fully for storage peas; like other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Running Serviceberry (Low Juneberry)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; running serviceberry is the low-growing, colony-forming native serviceberry of the northeastern US and Appalachians, spreading by stolons to form attractive low thickets 1–3 feet tall on rocky slopes, woodland edges, and open forests. Like all serviceberries, it produces masses of white flowers in early spring that are an important nectar and pollen source for early-emerging native bees, followed by sweet, blueberry-like June berries in early summer that are excellent fresh, dried, or cooked into pies and preserves. The low, suckering habit makes it more useful as a shade-tolerant groundcover or erosion control plant than as a specimen shrub. It colors brilliantly orange-red in fall. An ideal native edible shrub for shaded slopes, woodland edges, and low-maintenance natural landscapes in the Northeast and Appalachians. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Runway Arugula
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly into cool, moisture-retentive soil for fast, even germination. Runway produces smooth, rounded, dark green leaves with a clean, moderately spicy flavor and was selected by seed breeders for a notably slower bolt response, letting growers hold plantings longer into warm weather before they turn bitter and go to seed. It performs well both as a quick baby-leaf crop for salad mixes and, with wider spacing, as a full-size bunching arugula. Succession sow every couple of weeks for continuous cutting through the cool season. Matures in 25–40 days from seed.

name: Rush American Hazelnut (1917 J.F. Jones Selection, Foundation Parent of Modern Hybrid Hazels)
description: Rush was selected around 1917 by nurseryman J.F. Jones of Lancaster, Pennsylvania from an unusually prolific wild plant of native Corylus americana, and released under the clonal name 'Rush' for its heavy, reliable yields. Its greater historical significance lies in breeding: starting in 1919 Jones used Rush as the seed parent to cross with European hazelnut (Corylus avellana) clones including Barcelona, Cosford, Daviana, Italian Red, and Kentish Cob, producing the first American-European hybrid hazels; USDA breeder Clarence A. Reed and later programs continued using Rush as foundation breeding stock. The Rush resistance source has held up against Eastern Filbert Blight in the eastern US and Ontario since the 1940s, and its genes underlie a large share of modern EFB-resistant hybrid hazelnut breeding lines, including material behind the Rutgers New Jersey releases. Nuts are smaller than European hazelnut but flavorful and produced in dependable quantity even in cold climates, ripening in late summer to fall. Rush is not self-fertile and requires a second, genetically distinct hazelnut nearby for cross-pollination; it is more susceptible to hazelnut bud mite than some later selections. The shrub suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket and can be grown directly as a durable native nut shrub or valued by breeders and collectors as a living link to the foundation of hybrid hazelnut breeding. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rusk Citrange (Historic Cold-Hardy Swingle-Bred Orange Hybrid)
description: Rusk citrange dates to Walter Swingle's earliest USDA hybridization trials, crossing sweet orange with trifoliate orange in 1897 in response to the catastrophic Florida freezes of the 1890s, and was named for J.M. Rusk, the first U.S. Secretary of Agriculture. Compared with many other citranges bred in the same trials, Rusk fruit was noted for holding up better in fresh use, though it still carries more acid and seed than a true sweet orange and shines brightest in ade, marmalade, or juice. The tree takes on the trifoliate parent's light thorns and semi-deciduous winter habit, dropping some leaves in hard cold, and tolerates freezes well beyond what a standard orange survives once wood is mature. Give young trees a sheltered site and winter protection for their first two or three seasons in the Gulf South before letting them fend for themselves. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Russell Sapodilla
description: Grow Russell like other named sapodilla selections, planting a grafted or air-layered tree in full sun on well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in a frost-free South Florida-type landscape; established trees shrug off drought and salt wind but hard freezes below the upper 20s F cause serious damage. Selected from a seedling tree in the Florida Keys, Russell produces some of the largest fruit of any named sapodilla cultivar, nearly round, up to four inches across, with brown, scurfy skin and soft, reddish-tan, richly sweet flesh. Unlike heavier-cropping selections such as Brown Sugar or Prolific, Russell is an inconsistent bearer, so it suits growers chasing fruit size and flavor as a specimen tree rather than orchard volume. Expect several years of growth before the first crop, and harvest fruit only once the skin dulls and softens slightly, then finish ripening it at room temperature for a few days. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Russet Buffaloberry (Soopalallie, Canadian Buffaloberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established; the plant fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. Shepherdia canadensis (russet buffaloberry or soopalallie) is a deciduous native shrub of Canada, Alaska, and the northern United States — one of the most cold-hardy native fruiting shrubs on the continent, thriving in zone 2–6 conditions where few fruiting plants survive. The plant produces small (1/4-inch), translucent, red-orange to yellow, elliptic berries in summer that are bitter and astringent when eaten raw due to saponin content, but become edible after frost or cooking. The most famous traditional use is as 'sxusem' or 'soopalallie' (in Chinook jargon) — the indigenous peoples of British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest whipped the raw berries with water to produce a frothy, bright-red, bitter-sweet foam similar to meringue, traditionally sweetened with berries or honey and eaten as 'Indian ice cream.' The high saponin content is what enables the foam to form — the same compounds that make dish soap foam. The berries are also used for jelly, syrup, and beverages. Shephaerdia canadensis is a dioecious nitrogen-fixer (requires separate male and female plants, and fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis), making it valuable in cold-climate food forest systems as a soil-building shrub with an edible berry crop. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Russet Buffaloberry / Soopolallie
description: Sow seeds in fall directly in the garden or cold-stratify for 60–90 days before planting in spring; plant in dry, rocky, or sandy soil with excellent drainage in full sun, as russet buffaloberry naturally colonizes forest edges, rocky slopes, and open woodlands from Alaska to the northeastern United States. This dioecious nitrogen-fixer requires both male and female plants to produce its small, tart red berries, which ripen in midsummer. The berries were a prized food source for many indigenous peoples and can be whipped with a small amount of water and a touch of sweetener into a stable foam traditionally called 'sxusem' or Indian ice cream. Established plants are extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once rooted, making russet buffaloberry an excellent low-maintenance native for challenging northern and high-altitude sites. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Russet Burbank Potato (Classic Idaho Baking Potato, Most Widely Grown US Potato)
description: Plant certified seed potato pieces in trenches 4 inches deep; hill soil around plants as they grow. Harvest when tops die back. Russet Burbank is the most economically important potato variety in the United States — the potato that defined American french fry culture and continues to be the dominant variety grown commercially in Idaho, Washington, and Oregon. The variety's history traces to Luther Burbank, the famous plant breeder of Lunenburg, Massachusetts, who developed the 'Burbank' potato in 1875 — a white-skinned, prolific variety. A natural bud sport of the Burbank with netted russet skin emerged in the late 19th century and was selected for its superior baking qualities: the russet skin variety produced the floury, high-starch, dry flesh that makes for the ideal baked potato — a fluffy interior with a crisp, well-cured skin that holds its shape. The high starch content of Russet Burbank also makes it the preferred variety for making french fries: when fried, the high starch content produces the crispy exterior and fluffy interior texture that defines the classic fast-food french fry. McDonald's adopted Russet Burbank (specifically the 'Russet Burbank' and later selected clones) as the basis for their standardized french fry program, and this relationship made the variety synonymous with American potato processing. The tubers are very large (often 8–16 oz), oblong, with rough russet-brown skin and bright white flesh — the visual standard for 'Idaho potato' that most Americans associate with baked potatoes. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Russet Norkotah Potato
description: Russet Norkotah was released by North Dakota State University in 1987 and quickly became one of the most widely grown russet potatoes in North America, prized for its uniform, oblong tubers, attractive netted brown skin, and consistent yields. The dry, fluffy white flesh is a classic baking and frying russet that holds up well in storage after curing. Though bred for the northern Plains, it can adapt to a Gulf Coast winter-planted crop if seed pieces go in early enough to mature before summer heat arrives. Hill the plants as they grow to prevent sunburned, green-shouldered tubers and harvest once the vines die back. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Russian #2 Jujube (Black Sea, Earliest-Ripening Compact Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established. Russian #2, also known as Black Sea, is a compact-growing jujube cultivar prized for producing the earliest-ripening fruit of any commonly grown jujube selection, with small, sweet, teardrop-shaped fruit ready to harvest by midsummer, well ahead of later-season cultivars, extending the jujube harvest window when planted alongside them. Its smaller mature size also makes it a practical choice for tighter home garden spacing. As with other jujubes, it thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South and needs minimal care once established. Prune only lightly, and manage root suckers, which can be left to form a thicket or removed to keep a single-trunk form. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Russian 26 Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy Productive Pomegranate)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate poor, alkaline, and clay soils far better than most fruit trees. Russian 26 is one of several numbered cold-hardy pomegranate cultivars brought into North American cultivation from Russia and Central Asia, prized for combining good winter hardiness with heavy, precocious production of medium-sized fruit. The rind is typically pink to red and the arils are juicy, sweet-tart, and well flavored, ripening in early-to-mid fall. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and long-lived, and the compact, multi-stemmed shrub form makes it easy to manage as a large shrub or small espaliered tree. In the Gulf South, Russian 26 fruits reliably and its cold tolerance provides insurance against occasional hard freezes that can damage less hardy pomegranate selections. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Russian Banana Fingerling Potato
description: Plant whole small tubers or cut pieces 3–4 inches deep in loose, rich soil; Russian Banana is the most widely grown fingerling potato in the United States, an heirloom variety brought from Eastern Europe (likely Latvia or Russia) by immigrants in the early 20th century. The distinctive, curved, 3–4 inch tubers with smooth, pale yellow skin and deep golden-yellow flesh look remarkably like small bananas when harvested and rinsed — hence the name. Flavor is exceptional: buttery, nutty, and intensely potato-tasting with the creamy texture of a waxy potato that holds its shape beautifully when roasted, boiled, or pan-fried with herbs. Russian Banana fingerlings have become the premium specialty potato at farmers' markets and upscale restaurants because of their appearance, flavor, and versatility. Harvest when plants begin to die back; fingerlings store well in a cool, dark location after curing. In zone 9, plant January–February for April–May harvest. The small size makes them quick to cook — roasted whole with olive oil and rosemary, they are outstanding. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Russian Comfrey
description: Plant root cuttings 3–4 inches deep in moist, fertile soil in sun to part shade; Russian comfrey (Symphytum x uplandicum) is a hybrid between common comfrey and tuberous comfrey, producing a much more vigorous and productive plant than either parent — it is the preferred comfrey for permaculture systems and organic gardening as a dynamic accumulator, deep-rooting perennial that mines subsoil minerals (particularly potassium, phosphorus, calcium, and nitrogen) and concentrates them in its large, hairy leaves that can be cut 3–5 times per year and used as a mulch, liquid fertilizer (composted in water to make comfrey tea), or composted directly. The leaves decompose rapidly and are an outstanding activator for compost piles. The purple-blue flowers are beloved by bumblebees. Unlike common comfrey, 'Bocking 14' does not set viable seed and is non-spreading except through root division, making it the gardener's preferred choice for a controlled, productive stand. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Russian Olive (Oleaster)
description: Russian olive is an extremely cold-hardy, nitrogen-fixing shrub or small tree from Eurasia, grown historically for windbreaks, erosion control, and its silvery, drought-tolerant foliage. The small, mealy, olive-like fruits ripen tan to reddish in fall and are edible fresh or dried, with a dry, sweet-astringent flavor traditionally used in Central Asian cooking. It tolerates poor, saline, and alkaline soils that few other fruiting shrubs can handle, and the fragrant, inconspicuous yellow spring flowers are attractive to pollinators. Because it spreads readily by seed via birds and can outcompete native cottonwood and willow along waterways, it should only be planted where it is not restricted, and ideally kept away from natural riparian areas; where legal, choose an isolated garden site rather than a location near streams or wild land. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Russian River Coyote Mint
description: Russian River is a compact, densely mounding selection of coyote mint originating from wild populations along California's Russian River, prized for tidier, more uniform growth than seed-grown plants along with a long season of soft lavender-purple bloom. Root softwood cuttings in a fast-draining mix in summer, then set plants out in fall or early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. The strongly mint-and-oregano-scented gray-green foliage and abundant flower heads draw large numbers of native bees and butterflies through the warm months. Once established, water only occasionally during the driest part of summer, and shear lightly after the first bloom flush to maintain its neat mounded form and prompt a second round of flowers. Matures in 120–240 days from transplant.

name: Russian Tarragon
description: Unlike French tarragon, Russian tarragon grows readily from seed and forms a vigorous perennial with a milder, anise-like flavor. Surface sow the seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, then transplant into well-drained soil in full sun. It is hardy, drought tolerant, and grows larger than its French cousin, so give it space at the back of an herb bed. Harvest young leaves for the best flavor and cut plants back to keep them from becoming leggy. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Ruston Red Peach (Louisiana Heirloom Clingstone Peach for Gulf South Gardens)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit when marble-sized to 6–8 inches apart. Ruston Red is an heirloom peach variety associated with Ruston, Louisiana — a city in Lincoln Parish in north Louisiana that became famous for its peaches and has celebrated an annual Peach Festival since 1951. Ruston is located in a sweet spot for peach production in Louisiana: elevated enough above the Gulf Coast to accumulate adequate winter chill hours for most peach varieties, yet with a long enough warm season for fruit development, making the area one of the most productive peach regions in the Deep South. Ruston Red is a clingstone variety (the flesh adheres to the pit, making fresh eating more effortful but canning and preserving easier), with deep red skin and yellow to orange flesh, good sweetness, and the rich peach flavor associated with tree-ripened southern peaches. The variety has been grown in Louisiana for multiple generations and represents the type of locally-adapted, regionally-specific heirloom fruit variety that is increasingly important to preserve as commercial agriculture standardizes toward nationally-marketed varieties. Ruston Red's reputation in Louisiana is one of strong local association and pride: the name carries the flavor of place, as fruit varieties often do in American agricultural tradition, linking the eating experience to a specific region's history and soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Rusty Blackhaw (Southern Blackhaw)
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; rusty blackhaw is one of the most beautiful and underused native fruiting shrubs of the Southeast, producing spectacular flat clusters of creamy white flowers in early spring, followed by clusters of dark blue-black berries with a raisin-like, sweet-tart flavor that can be eaten fresh or used for jelly and wine. The leaves have rusty-red fuzzy undersides (giving the species name) and turn deep burgundy-red in fall. It grows naturally on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and woodland edges and is extremely drought tolerant once established. The berries provide fall food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and thrushes. It can be trained as a specimen shrub or allowed to develop into a small multi-trunk tree. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rusty Coat Apple (Heavily Russeted Southern Heirloom Keeper)
description: Rusty Coat was, by the 19th century, a name applied broadly to any old Southern apple whose greenish-yellow skin was heavily overlaid with coarse, dry russet, but the strain preserved by today's heirloom orchards has become the standard bearer for the type. Fruit is small to medium with faint red striping showing through the rough russet coat, and the crisp, tender flesh is somewhat dry with a pleasant, sweet, nutty flavor rather than sharp acidity. It ripens in late September to early October and is an outstanding long keeper, historically used for drying and as a late-winter dessert apple once smoother-skinned varieties had gone soft in storage. Its thick russet coat also gives it more resistance to cracking and disease pressure than many thin-skinned Southern heirlooms, a useful trait in humid Gulf South summers. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Rutabaga
description: Sow seeds 1/2 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil; rutabagas need more time and space than turnips to produce their large storage roots. Thin to 6–8 in once seedlings are established and keep soil evenly moist to prevent splitting. Flavor is significantly improved by frost, so aim to leave roots in the ground until after the first hard freeze. Harvest before the ground freezes solid and store in a cool, humid root cellar for several months. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Rutgers Beacon Asparagus (Early Rutgers Polycross Hybrid)
description: Rutgers Beacon is an early dioecious asparagus hybrid developed at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, part of the university's long-running asparagus breeding program that later produced the all-male Jersey series. Unlike the all-male supermale hybrids bred afterward, Rutgers Beacon includes both male and female plants, so some volunteer seedlings can appear in an established bed over time. It was grown across the Midwest and East Coast for its solid field performance before being largely superseded by higher-yielding all-male hybrids, and its male lines were themselves used as breeding stock for later Rutgers supermale releases such as Eros, Atlas, and Apollo. Give crowns two full seasons to establish before harvesting, then cut spears daily during the spring flush to keep the plant signaling new growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Rutgers Obsession Basil (Compact Downy-Mildew-Resistant Purple Basil)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Rutgers Obsession was bred at Rutgers University for deep, uniform purple leaf color, a compact, well-branched habit that fits containers and small garden spaces, and strong resistance to the downy mildew that has become a major problem for basil growers in humid climates. Its purple leaves add striking color contrast to garden beds and containers as well as flavor and color to vinegars, pestos, and garnishes. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushy growth and remove flower buds promptly to keep leaves tender and productive through the season. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Rutgers Obsession DMR Basil
description: Sow indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50°F, spacing plants a foot apart in fertile, well-drained soil. This compact Genovese-type basil was bred at Rutgers University and released for its resistance to basil downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii), the fungal disease that devastates conventional Genovese basil in humid, wet, or overcast conditions, making it a reliable choice for gardeners in the Southeast and other mildew-prone regions. It grows more compactly and slower to establish than sibling releases like Devotion DMR, but the dark green, glossy, sweetly aromatic leaves hold their classic Genovese flavor for pesto, caprese salads, and general Italian cooking over a long season of repeated cuttings. Pinch flower spikes regularly to keep leaf production high through the season. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Rutgers Passion DMR Basil
description: Direct-seed or transplant into full sun after soil has warmed, keeping plants evenly moist but never waterlogged. Part of the Rutgers basil breeding program's suite of downy-mildew-resistant Genovese-type basils, Rutgers Passion DMR carries resistance genes that keep foliage clean and productive even in the warm, humid, low-airflow conditions that trigger downy mildew outbreaks in older heirloom Genovese strains. Leaves are large, glossy, and intensely aromatic, well suited to fresh pesto, infused oils, and drying. Harvest by pinching stem tips just above a leaf pair to encourage continuous branching and delay flowering. Matures in 55–68 days from transplant.

name: Rutgers Thunderstruck DMR Basil
description: Sow indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once the weather is reliably warm. Thunderstruck DMR is one of the later Rutgers University sweet-basil releases, bred and selected specifically for vigorous, high-yield production suited to bunching, microgreens, and processing markets rather than just fresh-market leaf sales; it carries the same downy mildew resistance as its Rutgers sibling releases (Devotion, Obsession, Passion) but was bred with faster regrowth and heavier cutting yields in mind. The medium-to-large leaves are slightly ruffled and bright green with the classic sweet, clove-and-anise Genovese aroma. Because it resists Peronospora belbahrii, Thunderstruck DMR keeps producing clean, marketable leaf through the humid conditions that typically shut down conventional Genovese basil for repeated cut-and-regrow harvests. Matures in 55–68 days from transplant.

name: Rutgers Tomato (Classic Heirloom Slicing Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Rutgers tomato is a historically significant American heirloom, developed in 1934 as a joint project between Rutgers University and the Campbell Soup Company, that became the dominant processing and fresh-market tomato in America from the 1940s through the 1970s — the reference standard for what a traditional American garden tomato should taste like. The medium-large (6–8 oz), slightly flattened, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have a firm but yielding texture with balanced sweet-acid traditional tomato flavor that is widely praised as a benchmark for real tomato taste in contrast to modern flavorless commercial varieties. Rutgers is neither the most disease-resistant nor the highest yielding tomato today, but it remains a beloved open-pollinated heirloom for gardeners who want authentic vintage tomato flavor, the ability to save seeds, and a piece of American agricultural history. The indeterminate plants reach 4–5 feet and benefit from staking; Rutgers is well-suited to the Northeast and mid-Atlantic where it was developed but grows well in most climates including the Gulf South in spring and fall seasons. Matures in 74–80 days from transplant.

name: RX1 Walnut Rootstock
description: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; RX1 is a disease-resistant clonal understock, not grown for its own nuts. Developed by the University of California walnut breeding program as a clonally propagated hybrid rootstock, it was bred specifically for strong resistance to Phytophthora root and crown rot and to lesion nematode, two of the most damaging soil-borne problems limiting walnut orchard longevity on the traditional seedling Paradox rootstock, while offering the genetic uniformity that open-pollinated seedling Paradox lacks. Its combination of disease resistance and vigor comparable to Paradox has made it an increasingly popular modern choice for new commercial walnut plantings on disease-prone or replant sites. Graft a desired named English walnut variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect vigorous, disease-resistant growth well suited to sites with a history of walnut root disease. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: S795 Coffee (Selection 795)
description: Released by Indian coffee researchers as a cross between the rust-tolerant Kent selection and the Ethiopian landrace Tafarikela, S795 combines good cup quality with sturdier disease tolerance than older heirloom Typica and Bourbon lines. It has become one of the most widely planted Arabica cultivars across South India, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea for its dependable yields and adaptability to a range of elevations. Grow it like other Arabica coffees, with filtered shade, evenly moist, well-drained acidic soil, and protection from any temperature below 55F. Its moderate vigor and manageable size make it a reasonably forgiving choice for a large container or greenhouse planting. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Saanichton 12 Kiwi (Cold-Hardy British Columbia Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis, and plant a compatible male pollinizer vine nearby, since Saanichton 12 is a female-only selection that will not set fruit without cross-pollination. Bred at the Saanichton research station on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, this fuzzy kiwifruit selection was developed for improved cold hardiness and reliable ripening in cooler coastal climates than typical California-bred kiwi varieties tolerate well, extending fuzzy kiwi growing into marginal regions. Fruit quality is good, comparable to standard fuzzy kiwifruit, once pollination is properly managed with a nearby male vine. Prune annually during dormancy to control vigorous vine growth and maintain productive fruiting wood. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Saaz Hops
description: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Saaz is a lower-yielding traditional variety compared to modern high-alpha hops. One of the original four European 'noble hop' varieties, grown for centuries in the Žatec region of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), it imparts the mild, spicy, earthy, floral bitterness that defines classic Czech and German pilsner beer styles, a subtle character quite different from the bold citrus and tropical fruit notes of modern American hop varieties. It is a lower-yielding, more disease-susceptible variety than many modern hybrid hops, reflecting its long, unimproved heritage, and rewards patient, attentive growing rather than the vigorous, high-output performance of newer cultivars. Train young bines up a sturdy support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and expect a lighter yield than modern high-alpha varieties in exchange for its classic, historic flavor profile. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Saba Banana (Philippine Cooking Banana, Sab-a)
description: Saba is the everyday cooking banana of the Philippines, prized for its blocky, squared-off fruit and starchy texture whether fried, boiled, or grilled green. Its ABB genome gives it noticeably tougher, more weather-resistant foliage and better drought and wind tolerance than dessert-type Cavendish bananas, and Gulf Coast growers report it recovering from winter dieback more reliably than thin-leafed AAA cultivars. Give it full sun, deep rich soil, and heavy irrigation through summer, then cut the frozen stalk back after a hard freeze and let the corm resprout in spring. Bunches take over a year to mature but the plant is a vigorous, heavy producer once established as a clump. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Sabara Jaboticaba
