description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — jaboticaba tolerates a wider pH range than most tropical fruits and performs well in amended Gulf Coast soils; Sabara is the most widely grown jaboticaba cultivar, a selection of the Brazilian grape tree (Plinia cauliflora) renowned for its unique and visually remarkable fruiting habit — the small, grape-like fruits emerge directly from the trunk and main branches of the tree rather than on terminal shoots, covering the bark in dense clusters of dark purple fruits that look like the tree has been decorated with purple grapes. The fruits are eaten fresh (popped open to reveal the sweet, translucent white pulp inside a thick purple skin), or processed into jams, wines, and liqueurs. Jaboticaba trees fruit multiple times per year in zone 9 after triggering by rain or irrigation following a dry period, providing periodic fresh fruit throughout the growing season. Sabara is the highest-quality eating variety, with sweet, rich, complex fruit flavor and good fresh-eating skin-to-pulp ratio. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sabro Hops
description: Sabro is a trademarked American cultivar prized for a distinctive aroma combining coconut, tangerine, and stone fruit unlike most other hop varieties. Unlike the typical single-leader climbing habit of most hops, Sabro throws unusually long lateral side-arms, so growers should provide extra horizontal space or a wider trellis in addition to standard vertical support. It is a relatively recent, fast-growing release that has become a favorite for hazy and tropical-style IPAs. Full sun, rich soil, and steady moisture during cone development help it reach its full aromatic potential. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Sacajawea Hazelnut (EFB-Resistant Pollenizer Filbert)
description: Sacajawea is a more recent Oregon State University release bred with resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight, the canker disease that devastated the older Barcelona-dominated Willamette Valley hazelnut industry. It is grown mainly as a pollenizer, shedding pollen at a timing that complements resistant main-crop cultivars like Jefferson, though its round, good-quality nuts are also perfectly usable. Give it full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, and prune out any blighted cankers promptly even though the resistance greatly reduces disease pressure compared to older varieties. Because it needs a genetically distinct pollen partner nearby, plant at least two compatible cultivars together for a dependable annual crop. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sacha Inchi (Inca Peanut, Mountain Peanut, Star Nut)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun with a strong trellis for support; Sacha inchi (also called Inca peanut, star nut, or sacha mani) is a high-altitude Amazonian climbing vine (Plukenetia volubilis, family Euphorbiaceae) native to the cloud forests and montane tropics of Peru, Colombia, and Bolivia, grown for its remarkable star-shaped seed capsules (typically 4-lobed, looking like geometric 4-pointed stars) containing large, oil-rich seeds with an extraordinary nutritional profile — the roasted seeds contain 48–54% oil (the highest of any cultivated edible nut, higher than macadamia) with exceptionally high omega-3 fatty acid content (49% of the oil by weight), making it among the richest plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid. The oil is marketed internationally as a premium cooking and supplement oil with a pleasant, nutty flavor. The seeds are eaten roasted (raw seeds contain alkaloids that are destroyed by roasting) and have a mild, pleasant flavor similar to peanuts. Sacha inchi grows vigorously in humid tropical to subtropical conditions (zones 9b–12) and produces the decorative star-shaped green to brown capsules approximately 6–9 months after planting; the fruits are attractive in the landscape as well as productive. Matures in 180–270 days from seed.

name: Sacred Fig (Bodhi Tree, Peepal Tree, Bo Tree)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Sacred Fig grows vigorously in tropical and subtropical conditions and should be sited away from all structures, pipes, and paving. Ficus religiosa is a large, semi-deciduous fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, one of the most sacred plants in human history. It is the tree under which Siddhartha Gautama achieved enlightenment, becoming the Buddha, at Bodh Gaya in present-day India — an event considered so significant that the tree, and its descendants propagated from that original specimen, are venerated throughout the Buddhist world. The plant is equally sacred in Hinduism and Jainism. Its distinctive heart-shaped to ovate leaves have an extraordinarily elongated drip tip — sometimes 2–3 times the length of the leaf blade — that evolved to channel water rapidly off the leaf surface in the heavy monsoon rains of its native habitat. These trembling, long-tipped leaves create a distinctive rustling sound in the slightest breeze, a quality noted in both botanical and spiritual literature. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Sacred Fig is grown as a significant landscape specimen and street tree. In zone 9, it is best maintained as a large container tree or bonsai subject, moved to protected locations in winter. Small, inedible figs are produced and consumed by birds. Matures in 1095–7300 days from transplant.

name: Sacred Lotus (Indian Lotus, Pink Lotus)
description: Nick the hard seed coat and soak in warm water until sprouting; transplant to a wide, shallow tub of heavy clay soil submerged 2–6 inches below the water surface in full sun — sacred lotus is one of the most magnificent aquatic plants on Earth and one of the most culturally significant plants in human history, sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, and ancient Egyptian tradition. The enormous, water-repelling leaves (2 feet across) on tall stems and fragrant, luminous pink or white flowers up to 12 inches wide rising 4–6 feet above the water are incomparably beautiful. Every part is edible: the crunchy, lace-patterned rhizomes (lotus root) are a prized vegetable in Asian cuisine, the seeds are eaten raw when young or dried and roasted, the large leaves are used to wrap food for steaming. The lotus is winter-hardy in zone 5–10 if the rhizomes are protected from freeze. It grows best in a large (15+ gallon) container sunk in a pond or placed in full sun. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Sadandy Southern Pea (Early Purple Hull Cream Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows and thinning if needed. Sadandy is a Louisiana heirloom purple hull-type southern pea prized for its unusually early maturity and heavy, concentrated fruit set on compact, bushy plants, letting gardeners get a full picking in one or two passes rather than the extended trickle typical of many purple hulls. Pods mature to a deep purple that shows clearly against the green foliage, signaling when the cream-colored peas inside are ready to shell, and the pods hold well without shattering even in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Like other cowpeas its roots fix nitrogen, so it also serves well as a quick-turnaround soil-building crop between spring and fall vegetables. Harvest at the purple-pod stage for fresh shelling or let dry fully on the vine for storage peas. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Saemidori Tea
description: Saemidori was bred at Japan's Makurazaki research station in Kagoshima by crossing the dominant Yabukita cultivar with Asatsuyu, registered in 1990 as Tea Norin No. 40. It buds out earlier in spring than Yabukita and is especially prized for shaded-culture teas such as gyokuro and tencha (matcha base leaf), where its naturally sweet, low-astringency character and vivid green color are considered top-tier. The shrub carries small, glossy dark leaves on a compact, upright frame. Cultivate it exactly as other Japanese sencha-type cultivars, with acidic, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and shade cloth or overhead shading in the weeks before harvest if grown for gyokuro-style leaf. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Safari Zucchini (Disease-Resistant High-Yield Hybrid Zucchini)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Safari is a modern hybrid zucchini bred for a strong disease-resistance package, including tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, which helps the compact, open bush stay productive and healthy later into the season than many older open-pollinated varieties manage in humid climates. The smooth, dark green, cylindrical fruit has tender, mild flesh typical of good zucchini, and the plant's heavy, sustained yield makes it a solid choice for gardeners who have struggled with squash bugs, vine borers, or mildew shortening the productive life of past plantings. Pick at six to eight inches long for the best texture, and harvest every day or two once fruit begins setting to keep the vigorous plant in steady production. Matures in 48–52 days from seed.

name: Safflower (Oilseed)
description: Plant seed 1 in deep at 6–10 in apart in rows 18–24 in wide; safflower needs a long growing season so early planting in cool soil is critical. The plant grows a large rosette in the vegetative phase, then bolts to form spiny, branching heads with brilliant orange or yellow florets. Harvest when the heads are dry and papery — cut and place in cloth bags to finish drying, then thresh by rubbing to release the seed. Safflower oil is prized for its high linoleic acid content and heat stability; the petals can also be used as a saffron substitute. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Saffron Crocus
description: Plant corms (not seeds) 3–4 in deep in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun during late summer to early autumn; good drainage is critical as corms rot quickly in waterlogged soil. Each corm produces lilac-purple flowers in autumn of the first year; within each flower are three vivid red stigmas — these are saffron. Harvest the flowers as soon as they open in the morning and carefully pluck the three red stigmas from each blossom, drying immediately on a warm screen or in a low oven. Corms multiply each year; lift and divide every 3–4 years to prevent overcrowding and maintain flowering vigor. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Safou (African Pear, Bush Butter Tree)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; young trees benefit from partial shade and consistent moisture. Dacryodes edulis (safou, African pear, or bush butter tree) is one of sub-Saharan Africa's most culturally and nutritionally important indigenous food trees, native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Cameroon, Nigeria, Gabon, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The fruits are produced in large pendant clusters directly on the branches: deep purple-blue to violet, oval-oblong, 2–4 inches long, resembling a fat olive. The fruit is not eaten raw — the hard, firm flesh must be boiled or flame-roasted to soften, at which point it transforms into a rich, buttery, smooth, avocado-like consistency with a unique, savory-nutty flavor profile. The fruit pulp contains 35–55% oil with a composition similar to olive oil and palm oil combined, making safou one of the most calorie-dense and nutritionally complete forest fruits in Africa. It is also a significant protein source compared to most fruits. In its native range, safou is widely eaten alongside corn, cassava, and plantain as a major dietary fat source, and is sold extensively in West African urban markets. Outside Africa, safou is almost entirely unknown but is gaining interest as a potential food security crop and agroforestry tree in tropical regions worldwide. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Sage
description: Press seeds 1/8 in into well-drained seed mix and keep at 60–70°F; germination is steady but takes two to three weeks. Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; wet, poorly drained soil is the leading cause of sage death. Prune hard in early spring once new growth shows at the base to prevent the plant from becoming too woody. Harvest young leaves throughout the season, cutting stems back by no more than one-third at a time. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Sago Palm
description: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in tropical conditions; Metroxylon sagu thrives in peat swamp conditions with consistently high water table — it tolerates seasonal flooding and requires consistently moist to wet soil; do not allow the root zone to dry out. Metroxylon sagu (Sago Palm) is a large, clustering, monocarpic palm native to the peat swamps, freshwater swamps, and lowland swamp forests of the Malay Archipelago — Borneo, Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, the Moluccas, and Papua New Guinea — where it is the primary source of 'sago,' a powdery starch extracted from the pithy interior of the trunk immediately before the palm flowers and dies. Each trunk accumulates up to 150–300 kilograms of starch over 7–15 years before flowering, fruiting, and dying (monocarpic); the clusters produce multiple offshoots (suckers) that replace the mother stem, so the clump persists indefinitely. Sago is a fundamental caloric staple for millions of people across Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, and the Pacific Islands — prepared as papeda (sago porridge), sago pancakes, sago noodles, and diverse traditional foods. It has been called 'the staff of life of swamp peoples' and feeds communities in areas too wet, flooded, or acidic for rice or other crops. Globally important as a swamp-agroforestry tree for waterlogged, acidic, peat-swamp soils where no other major food crop survives. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Saharanpur Mulberry (White Shahtoot Giant Mulberry)
description: Saharanpur produces long, slender white-to-pale-yellow fruit that can reach three to four inches, with a dense, honey-sweet flavor and almost no tartness. The berries ripen in succession over several weeks in late spring and early summer, extending the harvest well past typical black mulberry types. Trees grow vigorously and can reach substantial size if left unpruned, but respond well to annual pruning to keep fruit within reach. This selection has shown good tolerance of the leaf and stem diseases that trouble many mulberries in humid, high-rainfall climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Saigon Cinnamon (Vietnamese Cinnamon)
description: Plant seed-grown saplings in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive but freely draining soil, in full sun or dappled partial shade in the northern Vietnamese highlands' cooler subtropical climate. Saigon cinnamon carries the highest cinnamaldehyde and coumarin concentration of any commercially traded cinnamon, giving it a hotter, sweeter, more intensely spicy punch than Ceylon, Chinese, or Padang types, and it is prized for baking and confectionery where a small amount of bark goes a long way. Bark of real commercial quality is not stripped until trees reach ten to twelve years of age, far longer than the three-to-four-year coppice cycle used for Padang cassia, which is why true Saigon cinnamon has historically fetched a premium price and much of the crop is still gathered from semi-wild trees. The species is now assessed as vulnerable in the wild, adding conservation value to garden or nursery-grown specimens. Matures in 3650–4380 days from transplant.

name: Saijo Persimmon (Slender Yellow Astringent Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Saijo is an astringent Japanese persimmon of Japanese origin — widely considered one of the finest-flavored of all persimmon cultivars, with elongated, narrow, yellow-orange to orange fruits and exceptional rich, honey-sweet flavor that persimmon enthusiasts describe as superior to any non-astringent variety. Saijo is astringent when firm — meaning the fruit must fully ripen and soften to a jelly-like texture before the astringency disappears and the full sweetness and flavor develop. This is not a defect but a different style of persimmon use: fully ripe Saijo is spooned from the skin like a pudding. Saijo ripens in September to October in zone 9, requiring only 100–200 chill hours, making it one of the lowest-chill persimmon cultivars and extremely well adapted to Gulf Coast climates. The tree is handsome, drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably free of serious pests and diseases — one of the easiest fruit trees for Gulf South gardens. The striking orange fruit and vivid orange fall foliage create exceptional ornamental value in the landscape. Saijo can be dried (hoshigaki) to make the traditional Japanese dried persimmon candy — a process that concentrates the intense natural sweetness into a complex, mellow confection. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Saint Valery Carrot (Heritage French Long Orange Carrot)
description: Direct sow in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Saint Valery is one of the oldest and most prestigious heritage carrot varieties — a 19th-century French heirloom from the Normandy coast town of Saint-Valery-en-Caux, producing long (8–10 inches), tapered, vivid deep-orange roots with a smooth skin, blunt tip, and sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that is considered among the finest-flavored of all heirloom carrot varieties. The deep, saturated orange color (more vivid than many modern varieties) comes from very high beta-carotene content, giving Saint Valery both excellent flavor and outstanding nutritional quality. The long, tapering root form requires deep, loose, stone-free soil for straight, well-formed roots — in shallow or compacted soil, the roots fork and twist around obstacles. Raised beds filled with deep, friable, sandy loam produce the best specimens. In zone 9, Saint Valery is a fall and winter crop: sow in August or September for harvest from November through February when the cool temperatures bring out the characteristic sweetness that makes heritage carrots like Saint Valery memorable. Carrots actually improve in flavor after light frost exposure — the cold converts starches to sugars, intensifying sweetness. Leave in the ground and harvest as needed through winter rather than pulling the entire crop at once. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Sakura Cherry Tomato (High-Yield Crack-Resistant Red Cherry)
description: Sakura is a widely grown F1 red cherry tomato prized by market growers and home gardeners alike for its combination of very heavy, early yields and fruit that resists splitting after rain far better than most cherry types. The small, round, bright red fruit hangs in long trusses with good classic cherry-tomato sweetness and holds well on the vine without over-softening. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate vine, prune to a few main leaders for easier harvest, and pick regularly to keep the heavy-bearing trusses coming. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Sakura Sweet Potato (Fast-Maturing Purple-Skinned Louisiana Release)
description: Plant certified slips in well-drained, loose garden soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to allow vines room to run; Sakura is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release named for its deep purple skin wrapped around an unusual light purple flesh, giving cooked roots a soft lavender color rather than the deep violet of typical purple sweet potatoes. Its standout trait for Gulf Coast growers is speed — Sakura roots reach harvestable size in roughly 90 days from transplanting, well ahead of the 110-120 days most varieties need, which lets gardeners get a crop in even from a late-set planting or squeeze in an earlier harvest before hurricane season disruptions. Like other LSU AgCenter releases bred for the region, it carries resistance to southern root-knot nematode, a persistent problem in sandy Gulf Coast garden soil. Cure harvested roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Sakurajima Daikon (Giant Japanese Winter Radish)
description: Sow directly since the massive taproot resents transplanting, and thin aggressively to give each plant a full 2-3 foot circle of loose, deeply tilled soil. Named for the volcanic island near Kagoshima where it originated, this cultivar can swell to 40-100 pounds while staying surprisingly dense and low-fiber compared to other giant radishes. Harvest before hard freezes and store in a cool root cellar; despite its size the flesh stays sweet and is prized locally for simmered dishes and pickling. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Salad Bowl Blend Leaf Lettuce
description: This blend combines award-winning 'Green Salad Bowl' and 'Red Salad Bowl' loose-leaf lettuces for a colorful, flavorful, heat-tolerant mix. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them since light aids germination, and thin to 8-12 inches or grow densely for baby greens. Harvest young leaves in a few weeks or pick outer leaves for a continuous cut-and-come-again supply. Its heat tolerance and slow bolting extend the picking season into warm weather. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Salad Burnet
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-drained, alkaline or neutral soil; salad burnet tolerates poor, thin soils and performs well on chalky or limestone ground. As an evergreen perennial, it provides fresh cucumber-flavored leaves through mild winters when little else is harvestable. Remove flower stems as they appear to keep the plant producing the most tender, flavorful leaves rather than diverting energy into seed production. Harvest the youngest leaves at the tips of each stem for the freshest cucumber taste in salads, cool drinks, and herb butters. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Salad Bush Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Container Slicer)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; no trellis required for bush types, though light support improves air circulation and fruit quality. Salad Bush is a 1988 All-America Selections-winning slicing cucumber selected specifically for compact, bush-type growth that makes cucumber growing accessible in small gardens, raised beds, and large containers. Standard cucumber vines sprawl 5–8 feet in diameter and require significant trellis support; Salad Bush was bred to produce a compact plant (vines spreading only 24–30 inches) that fits in a large container or small raised bed section without consuming excessive space. The compact habit comes without sacrificing fruit quality: the 8-inch, dark green fruits have the same smooth, mild, sweet flavor and tender skin of the best standard slicing cucumbers, with good disease resistance including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, angular leaf spot, and powdery mildew. Fruit production is concentrated over a shorter window than vining types but can be extended with succession sowings 2–3 weeks apart. Salad Bush remains one of the most practical cucumber choices for balcony, patio, and small-space gardeners who want fresh cucumbers without a large garden footprint. Matures in 57–63 days from seed.

name: Saladmore Bush Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Slicing Cucumber)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Saladmore Bush is an AAS-winning slicing cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit that still delivers a full-size harvest of straight, dark-green, 8-inch slicing cucumbers with crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor, on a plant that fits easily into small beds and large pots where a standard vining slicer would sprawl. It also carries strong resistance to several common cucumber diseases, giving it good vigor through a long summer season in humid climates. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitterness and misshapen cucumbers, and harvest regularly once fruiting begins to keep the plant productive. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Salak (Snake Fruit, Sala)
description: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in frost-free tropical conditions; salak (snake fruit) is a dramatic spiny clustering palm from Indonesia and Malaysia producing clusters of pear-shaped fruits with distinctive reddish-brown scaly skin that closely resembles a snake's skin — hence the common name. The fruit has three lobes of crisp, dry, sweet-acidic flesh (texture somewhat like a dry apple) with a complex flavor variously described as sweet, astringent, honey-like, and reminiscent of cinnamon, varying considerably by variety. The most prized variety is 'Salak Bali' from Bali. High humidity and consistent moisture are essential; this is one of the most challenging tropical fruits to grow outside its native range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Salak Bali (Bali Snake Fruit)
description: Salak Bali is the traditional snake fruit of Bali, grown for centuries around villages in the island's eastern regency of Karangasem, and is distinguished from the Java-bred Pondoh type by its larger fruit and moist, crunchy, juicier flesh with a sweet-tart flavor rather than Pondoh's dry, crumbly texture. Like other salak, it is a low, clumping, viciously spined palm best grown in the filtered light of an open woodland canopy in rich, constantly moist, well-drained soil; full tropical heat and humidity are essential, and the palm will not tolerate any frost. Because salak is dioecious, keep a male plant or take cuttings of male inflorescences nearby for hand pollination to guarantee heavy fruit set on female clumps. Manage clumps by removing excess suckers and old fronds, and harvest fruit in tight clusters once the snakeskin-like scales are fully colored and the fruit yields slightly to pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Salak Pondoh (Sweet Snake Fruit)
description: Salak Pondoh is Indonesia's most widely planted salak selection, originating from the Sleman district of Yogyakarta, valued for dry, crumbly-textured flesh that is sweet and only mildly acidic even before full ripeness, unlike the sharp, astringent bite of unimproved seedling salak. Grow this clumping, spiny-trunked palm in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of taller trees, since salak is naturally an understory plant of humid tropical forests. Female plants need a male pollinator nearby, or hand pollination, to ensure good fruit set, and mature clumps should have excess suckers and spent leaves removed regularly to keep the planting productive and manageable. Harvest fruit clusters when the overlapping reddish-brown scales lift slightly and the fruit gives a bit to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Salal
description: Salal is an evergreen native shrub of the Pacific Northwest coast, found beneath conifers from central California to Alaska, where it forms dense thickets on acidic, well-drained forest soils. The dark blue-purple berries are similar in size to a blueberry but have mealy, mildly sweet flesh and were an important food source for coastal Indigenous peoples, eaten fresh or dried into cakes. Salal is propagated by division or from container-grown nursery stock; seed germination is slow and unreliable. The glossy foliage is commercially valuable in the floral trade, and home growers can cut leathery stems for arrangements without harming the plant. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Salamander Lettuce (19th-Century Cabbaging Heirloom Lettuce)
description: Salamander was among the most widely grown lettuces of the nineteenth century, a black-seeded cabbaging type that forms a dense head of thick, heavily savoyed, deep green leaves. Its crinkled leaf texture and firm heart gave it good heat tolerance for its era, letting nineteenth-century gardeners hold it in the garden longer than many delicate butterheads of the time. The mature heads have a satisfying crunch and mild flavor typical of old cabbage-type lettuces, distinct from the smoother butterheads more common today. It is a worthwhile variety for gardeners wanting to taste a lettuce type that has largely fallen out of modern seed catalogs. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Salanova Lettuce (Compact Cut-and-Come-Again Salad Lettuce Series)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Salanova is a lettuce series bred specifically to solve the labor problem of harvesting baby salad greens leaf by leaf: each Salanova head grows as a tight rosette of dozens of small, uniform, bite-sized leaves attached at a single central core, so cutting the plant once at the base instantly yields a full bowl of ready-to-eat, pre-washed-looking salad leaves rather than a single lettuce head that needs chopping. It comes in multiple types — butterhead, oakleaf, and incised (frilly) forms in both green and red — allowing gardeners to plant a mix for varied color and texture in a single cutting. Because the leaves are already small, individual heads can be spaced fairly closely for high-density production, and successive sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply coming through the cool season. It bolts readily in summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best results in zone 9, and provide afternoon shade for any late-spring or early-fall plantings that overlap with warm weather. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Salavatski Pomegranate
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils; Salavatski (also spelled Salavatsky, Salavatskij) is a Central Asian pomegranate from the Caucasus region of Russia and Azerbaijan, valued primarily for its exceptional cold hardiness among fruiting pomegranate varieties — it survives temperatures to 10–15°F that would kill most other cultivars, making it the go-to choice for zone 7b–8 growers and providing extra insurance in zone 9a. The large, deep-red to garnet fruits ripen in September–November with tart-sweet, ruby-red arils surrounding tender seeds — the flavor is typically more tart than softer varieties like Wonderful, which suits pomegranate juice, grenadine, and Persian cooking better than fresh eating. Trees are extremely drought-tolerant once established and long-lived; established specimens may produce fruit for decades or even centuries. In zone 9 pomegranates produce heavily and reliably; Salavatski offers cold-hardiness insurance for zone 9a gardens where rare hard freezes occasionally occur. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Salem Rosemary (Cold-Hardy Upright Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Salem is a compact, upright rosemary selected for good cold hardiness alongside strong, classic culinary flavor, making it a reliable choice for cooks in climates where standard rosemary cultivars struggle to overwinter outdoors. Pale blue-lavender flowers appear in spring on a tidy, dense, shrubby plant, and regular harvesting throughout the growing season encourages fuller, bushier growth. Prune lightly after flowering to keep the plant shapely, and give it sharply drained soil, since standing water in winter is a far greater threat to rosemary than cold temperatures alone. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Salicornia (Sea Beans, Glasswort, Sea Asparagus)
description: Sow seeds after last frost in sandy, well-drained soil; salicornia is one of the few vegetables that can be watered with dilute seawater or grown in genuinely saline soil where other vegetables die; harvest bright green stems by snipping with scissors when 3–6 inches long for the most tender eating quality. Salicornia (also called sea beans, glasswort, sea asparagus, samphire — not to be confused with rock samphire, Crithmum maritimum) is an annual succulent halophyte — a plant not merely tolerant of salt but actually thriving in salty, coastal environments — native to salt marshes, coastal mudflats, and tidal edges around the world. The plant is entirely leafless: instead of conventional leaves, it consists of jointed, fleshy, cylindrical green stems that branch repeatedly, creating a plant that looks like bright green coral or a miniature cactus. These stems are the edible part — crunchy, bright green, and naturally seasoned with sea salt stored in the plant tissues, with a distinctive briny, fresh, oceanic flavor and a crisp texture that makes raw eating possible without additional seasoning. Salicornia is prized in gourmet cooking as 'sea beans' — sautéed briefly in butter (excellent with fish and shellfish), pickled, used raw in salads for their crunch and natural seasoning, or served alongside seafood dishes where the marine flavor echo is an elegant touch. The plant was historically used in glass-making in coastal areas (hence 'glasswort' — the burned ash was used as an alkali source for soda-lime glass production). For Gulf Coast gardeners in zones 8b–10, salicornia can be grown in garden soil without salt amendment, or cultivated in genuinely saline coastal conditions where nothing else will grow. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Saline Mayhaw (Late-Blooming Western Mayhaw Cultivar)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since like all mayhaws Saline is adapted to the poorly drained bottomlands and bayou margins of the Gulf Coastal Plain where conventional fruit trees struggle. Saline is a named western mayhaw (Crataegus opaca) selection valued among east Texas and Louisiana growers for its late bloom period in late winter to early spring, a trait that reduces crop loss from the late cold snaps that can wipe out the flowers of earlier-blooming mayhaw cultivars, with fruit following in late April to early May. The fruit itself is notably large and firm, with reddish skin over pinkish-orange flesh, and holds well on the tree without dropping prematurely, giving growers a wider harvest window than more fragile-fruited selections. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar for reliable cross-pollination and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Salmonberry
description: Salmonberry is a Pacific Northwest native shrub that thrives in moist to wet, shaded sites along streams and forest edges, making it one of the few fruiting canes suitable for boggy ground. Fruits ripen very early — often in May or June — in shades from yellow-orange to deep red-salmon, with a mild, slightly bland flavor best suited to fresh eating or jams. Thin old canes to the ground each year after fruiting to maintain vigor, as the plant spreads by rhizomes and can form dense thickets. Wildlife value is extremely high; berries attract birds and bears within days of ripening. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Salsify (Oyster Plant)
description: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in deeply dug, stone-free soil; salsify develops long taproots that fork and deform in rocky or compacted ground. Thin to 3–4 inches after germination and keep weed-free, as salsify's grass-like tops are easily overwhelmed early on. Roots are ready in autumn when they reach pencil thickness and finger length; flavor improves markedly after hard frost. Roots can overwinter in the ground and be harvested as needed through winter in mild climates, or dig all roots in late fall and store in damp sand. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Salt and Pepper Cucumber (AAS-Winning White Speckled Seedless Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when speckles are visible. Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid cucumber that received All-America Selections recognition for its distinctive appearance and exceptional eating quality. The fruit skin is white to pale cream with characteristic dark green to near-black speckles distributed across the surface — the 'salt and pepper' pattern that gives the variety its name and makes it immediately visually recognizable. Unlike heirloom types with similar light-colored skin (such as Boothby's Blonde), Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid bred for the parthenocarpic (seedless) character that allows fruit set without pollination — the interior is nearly seed-free and extremely tender, with no tough seed cavity. The resulting texture is among the finest of any outdoor cucumber: exceptionally crisp, with virtually no bitterness, tender skin that requires no peeling, and very high water content producing a refreshing fresh-eating quality. Salt and Pepper produces abundantly and early — with the first ripe fruit typically appearing 57 days from direct sowing, making it one of the earliest-producing cucumbers available. For zone 9 gardeners, the early maturity and heat-set ability allow the variety to produce heavily in spring before summer heat becomes limiting, and the fall planting typically produces prolifically through October or November. The seedless character and very thin skin make Salt and Pepper one of the few cucumbers that market gardeners can sell without refrigeration for brief periods, as the intact skin and low seed cavity reduce the moisture loss that causes conventional cucumbers to shrivel. Matures in 57–62 days from seed.

name: Saltwort (Turtleweed, Pickleweed)
description: Plant rooted cuttings directly into consistently wet, saline to brackish sand or mud in full sun along tidal flats, salt marsh edges, or artificially salted raised beds; saltwort is one of the few true halophytes grown for food, an edible succulent similar in use to samphire or sea beans. Jointed, cylindrical, fleshy stems form a low, spreading, olive-green mat, and the crisp, salty-tangy young stem tips are harvested and eaten fresh in salads, pickled, or lightly sautéed. It naturally colonizes the upper edges of salt marshes and mangrove fringe, tolerating regular tidal inundation and salinity that would kill nearly any other vegetable crop, but it needs that salinity to compete against weeds and grow vigorously. Harvest tips regularly to encourage bushy branching, and expect the planting to spread steadily by rooting stems across suitable wet, saline ground. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Sam Cherry (Canadian-Bred Dark Sweet Cherry and Pollinizer)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Sam was bred at the Canadian federal research station in Summerland, British Columbia, and produces large, firm, dark mahogany-red to black sweet cherries with rich, classic sweet cherry flavor similar in style to Bing, along with good resistance to fruit cracking after rain, a genuinely useful trait in humid or rain-prone climates. Beyond its own fruit quality, Sam is widely planted as a reliable pollinizer for other sweet cherry varieties, since its bloom timing overlaps well with many popular cultivars. The tree is vigorous and productive; net against birds as fruit colors, and pick once fully dark and firm, since sweet cherries like Sam do not ripen further after harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sam Houston Peach (Low-Chill Freestone Peach for the Gulf Coast)
description: Set out bare-root trees in late winter in full sun and well-drained soil, then prune young trees to an open, vase-shaped form to maximize light and airflow through the canopy in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Sam Houston is a Texas A&M-developed freestone peach bred for reliable fruiting in the low-chill winters around Houston and the upper Texas Gulf Coast, producing medium-sized, yellow-fleshed fruit with a red-blushed skin and good flavor considering its low chilling requirement. The tree is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit, but siting it away from low-lying frost pockets helps protect the early bloom from a late freeze. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart when they reach marble size to improve size and quality, and watch for the humidity-related fungal diseases common to peaches in the Gulf South, treating preventively if brown rot or leaf curl has been a problem in the area. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Samdal Elderberry (Danish Large-Cluster Black Elderberry)
description: Samdal is a Danish commercial black elderberry selection bred for unusually large flower and fruit clusters, giving a heavier harvest per bush than most older European elder cultivars. New shoots emerge vigorously from the crown each season and typically fruit the following year, so renewal pruning should favor one- and two-year canes while removing the oldest, least productive wood each dormant season. The lush green foliage and broad, creamy-white flower umbels make it attractive as a dual-purpose fruiting hedge as well as a productive orchard shrub. Berries ripen dark and glossy in late summer and are used for syrup, wine, and jelly, but like all elderberry, fruit should be cooked before eating and never consumed with the stems, leaves, or unripe berries attached. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sampo Elderberry (Nordic Elderberry Juice Cultivar)
description: Sampo is a Danish-bred European black elderberry cultivar developed alongside Samyl for the Scandinavian and Central European processing industry, and researchers studying elderberry juice cultivars have found it produces a distinct anthocyanin pigment profile from Samyl, giving processors two complementary options for blending juice color and flavor. Plants produce the broad, flat clusters of white, fragrant flowers typical of European elderberry in early summer, followed by heavy clusters of small black berries by late summer that are cooked before use, as with all Sambucus nigra fruit. It has been grown commercially in Sweden and Germany in addition to its native Denmark. In Gulf Coast gardens, treat it as a specialty planting rather than a low-maintenance shrub, since it will need afternoon shade and steady soil moisture to get through the region's long, humid summers. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sampson Tangelo (Historic Swingle-Bred Dancy-Bowen Hybrid)
description: Sampson was the first tangelo ever produced, bred by Walter Swingle in 1897 at Eustis, Florida by crossing Dancy tangerine with pollen from Bowen grapefruit, decades before the more familiar Orlando and Minneola tangelos followed from similar parentage. The medium, globose, thin-skinned fruit is juicy and tangy with a distinctive bittersweet tang and a heavy seed count, prized more by citrus historians and collectors than commercial growers, though it remains an interesting dooryard curiosity and occasional rootstock. Cold hardiness falls between its tangerine and grapefruit parents, tolerating brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit but needing more winter protection than satsuma or true mandarins in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil as a conversation-piece heirloom alongside more productive modern citrus. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Samyl Elderberry (Danish High-Anthocyanin Juice Cultivar)
description: Samyl was released from the elderberry breeding program at Denmark's Aarslev horticultural research center specifically for commercial juice and cordial production, and it has since been planted commercially across Denmark, Germany, and Sweden. Its main advantage over older European black elderberry selections is an unusually high concentration of anthocyanin pigments in the fruit, which gives pressed juice a deeper color and a sweeter, less astringent flavor than many wild-type black elderberries. Large, flat-topped white flower clusters open in early summer and are themselves used for cordial and syrup before the berries ripen to black in late summer. Because European black elderberry generally prefers cooler, more evenly moist conditions than the Gulf South provides, give this cultivar afternoon shade and supplemental irrigation through summer heat. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: San Andreas Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral Everbearing with Excellent Summer Flavor)
description: Plant crowns with crown at soil surface; mulch with straw. Pick when fully red. San Andreas Strawberry was released by the University of California Davis strawberry breeding program around 2009 as part of a sequence of day-neutral variety releases (Albion, Seascape, San Andreas, Monterey) that established UC Davis as the primary source of commercial day-neutral strawberry genetics in North America. The UC Davis program, which has produced many of the most important commercial strawberry varieties in the world over the past several decades, focused San Andreas specifically for improved performance in California's commercial production regions — the Watsonville and Salinas Valley coastal areas that produce the majority of California's fresh-market strawberries. Day-neutral varieties (also called everbearing in older terminology) distinguish themselves from June-bearing types by initiating flower production regardless of day length: standard June-bearers require specific short-day conditions to trigger flowering, restricting their production season, while day-neutral varieties flower whenever temperatures are favorable (roughly 35–85°F). San Andreas produces medium to large, conical fruits with bright red skin, firm flesh, and excellent sweet flavor with good acid balance — qualities that place it at the premium end of commercial strawberry flavor, closer to the flavor of Albion than many other commercial varieties. The skin is moderately firm, allowing several days of shelf life after harvest, and the flesh is red throughout without the white core common in lower-quality commercial varieties. For zone 9 fall-winter planting, San Andreas's day-neutral character and good heat tolerance make it one of the better choices for a productive winter-through-spring strawberry season. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: San Joaquin Jalapeño Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact High-Yield Jalapeño)
description: Start seed indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after all frost danger has passed into full sun. San Joaquin is an AAS-winning jalapeño bred for a tidy, determinate bush habit that concentrates its heavy fruit set into a shorter window, often producing dozens of thick-walled, crack-resistant, roughly 4-inch pods per plant. Peppers hold mild jalapeño heat and can be picked green for classic use or left to ripen to red for a sweeter, still-mild flavor. The sturdy, compact plant needs little staking and performs well in containers, making it a good choice for smaller gardens wanting a big jalapeño harvest for pickling and stuffing. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: San Marzano Broccoli Raab
description: Direct sow seeds shallowly in cool soil and thin lightly, as this fast crop is grown for its leaves, stalks, and buds rather than large heads. Also called rapini or rabe, it develops a bold, pleasantly bitter flavor prized in Italian cooking. Harvest when the flower buds appear but before they open, cutting the whole plant near the base. Because it grows quickly and prefers cool weather, succession sowing keeps a steady supply of tender greens. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: San Marzano Roma Pole Tomato
description: 'San Marzano' is the legendary Italian paste tomato, an indeterminate pole type bearing meaty, low-seed plum fruits ideal for sauce and canning. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun soil. Support the tall vines with sturdy stakes or cages and prune suckers to focus energy on fruit. Consistent watering helps prevent blossom-end rot; harvest when fully red for peak flavor. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: San Marzano Tomato
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake as San Marzano is a vigorous indeterminate vine reaching 5–6 feet or more. The elongated, plum-shaped fruits with pointed blossom ends are the gold standard for pasta sauce and canned tomatoes — they are low in moisture, dense in flesh, mildly acidic, and have few seeds, making them ideal for reduction into rich sauces. Prune to 2–3 main stems for the largest individual fruits; unpruned plants produce more fruits but smaller. This Italian heirloom from the Campania region near Naples has DOP status in Italy, though the variety sold in the U.S. performs very differently from its Italian counterpart under different soil and climate conditions. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: San Piero Fig (Teardrop Purple Italian Fig)
description: San Piero is a vigorous heirloom Italian fig, also grown under the synonym names Turkish Brown and Negro Largo, prized for its medium-to-large teardrop-shaped fruit with deep purple skin and richly sweet, strawberry-pink flesh. As a common-type fig it sets a reliable crop without pollination, typically producing a light early-summer breba crop and a heavier late-summer main crop. The tree is notably vigorous and productive, reaching 15-25 feet if left unpruned, but responds well to hard annual pruning to keep it manageable in home orchards and containers. San Piero tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity well and is closely related to the fig widely sold in warm-climate nurseries as 'Brown Turkey', sharing much of that cultivar's toughness and reliability. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sanbokan (Japanese Winter Citrus)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and protect young trees from hard freezes since this citrus is less cold-hardy than satsuma or kumquat. Sanbokan is a traditional Japanese citrus long grown around Wakayama Prefecture, believed to be a natural hybrid with pomelo-type ancestry; it bears large, thick-rinded, pale yellow-orange fruit with a mild, only lightly acidic flavor that sits between an orange and a grapefruit. Fruit ripens in winter but is typically picked and cured in a cool, dry spot for a few weeks before eating, which softens the rind and mellows any lingering bitterness. Feed lightly with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season, keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and thin heavy fruit sets to encourage larger, better-flavored fruit the following year. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sand Blackberry
description: Sand Blackberry is a low-growing native blackberry of dry, sandy, acidic open ground across the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, identified by its broadly wedge-shaped leaflets with distinctive white-felted undersides. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 3 to 5 feet apart to allow for natural spreading by root sprouts into a dense, wildlife-supporting thicket. White flowers appear in spring on second-year canes, followed by small but sweet, glossy black drupes in early summer that are excellent for jams, pies, and fresh eating. Remove spent floricanes after harvest each season and allow vigorous new primocanes to develop; this species is far more drought-tolerant than Rubus allegheniensis or R. argutus and thrives where heavier soils would cause root rot. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sand Cherry
description: Sand cherry is a small, sprawling native North American shrub bearing small dark purple to black cherries in midsummer with a flavor ranging from pleasantly tart to bitter depending on provenance and ripeness stage. The fruits are consumed fresh, dried, or processed into pemmican and preserves and were an important food source for Plains Indigenous peoples. The plant is extraordinarily cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, spreading by root suckers to form low thickets excellent for erosion control. Harvest when berries are fully dark and soft; cross-pollination between multiple plants improves fruit set significantly. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Sand Grape (Rock Grape)
description: Plant in sandy, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; sand grape is a compact, shrubby wild grape native to gravel bars and rocky streambanks across the south-central United States, distinguished from most other native grapes by its low, bushy, non-climbing to weakly climbing habit and small, glossy, coarsely toothed leaves. The small, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, generally more valuable to wildlife and home winemakers blending with sweeter grapes than for fresh eating on their own. Its greatest significance is historical and genetic: sand grape's exceptional drought tolerance and resistance to grape phylloxera made it one of the key wild American species used to breed phylloxera-resistant rootstock in the late 19th century, helping save European wine grape production after the phylloxera epidemic devastated Old World vineyards. In the garden or native planting, it is a tough, low-maintenance vine well suited to lean, sandy, or rocky sites where other grapes struggle, and it provides food and cover for wildlife. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sand Hickory
description: Sand Hickory is a native nut tree specially adapted to the dry, sandy, acidic soils of pine-oak barrens, sandhills, and upland forest margins across the southeastern coastal plain from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Kansas, where it thrives in conditions too infertile and dry for most other nut trees. The compound leaves are distinctively pale and silvery-hairy on the undersides — a useful field character separating it from the similar Pignut and Mockernut hickories — and produce brilliant gold fall color. Nuts are moderately thin-shelled with mildly bitter to slightly sweet kernels eaten by squirrels, white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and black bears; direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, allowing 90 days of cold stratification before spring germination. Once established, Sand Hickory is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation, making it the ideal native nut tree for dry, infertile, xeric sites. Matures in 3650–7300 days from seed.

name: Sand Pear
description: The sand pear is a vigorous, disease-resistant Asian pear species valued for its gritty, juicy fruit and tolerance of hot, humid summers. Plant two compatible cultivars for cross-pollination in full sun and deep, well-drained soil. Train young trees to a central leader and thin fruit clusters to one per spur to improve size. Its strong fire-blight resistance makes it a dependable choice where European pears fail. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sandalwood
description: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. This slow-growing tropical tree produces the fragrant, dense, oil-rich heartwood prized for centuries in incense, perfumery, and religious ceremonies across South and Southeast Asia, but the tree must be interplanted with a suitable host species from an early age, since its roots form haustoria that tap into a neighboring plant's roots for water and nutrients even as it also photosynthesizes on its own. Decades of growth (typically fifteen years or more) are needed before the valuable, densely aromatic heartwood develops in commercially useful quantity, making it a long-term, multi-generational planting rather than a quick garden project, and wild populations have historically been overharvested, making legally sourced plantation-grown seedlings the responsible choice. Water young trees regularly during establishment, choose a nitrogen-fixing or otherwise compatible host species to plant alongside it, and be prepared for a very long wait before any wood harvest. Matures in 5475–9125 days from transplant.

name: Sandia Pepper (New Mexico Green Chile, Medium-Hot Roasting Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; Sandia is a New Mexico State University-developed chile variety named after the Sandia Mountains near Albuquerque, bred to fill a flavor and heat niche between the mild Anaheim-type peppers and the hotter NuMex Big Jim — producing long (6–8 inch), meaty, thick-walled green chiles with a medium heat level (approximately 1,000–2,500 Scoville units) that provides a pleasant warmth without overwhelming heat and excellent roasted green chile flavor. The thick walls and dense flesh roast beautifully — the skin blisters and chars evenly while the interior steams to a silky, rich texture — making Sandia an excellent choice for all traditional New Mexico green chile preparations including green chile stew, chile rellenos, and roasted chiles packed in the freezer for winter use. As the fruits mature to red and dry, Sandia provides good red chile powder with medium heat and authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Sandia performs well in a wide range of climates including the humid Gulf South, where its thick-walled flesh resists decay better than thinner-walled varieties. One of the most important green chile varieties in the New Mexico tradition alongside NuMex Big Jim, Hatch, and Numex Joe E. Parker. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Sandy Lettuce (AAS-Winning Compact Oakleaf Lettuce)
description: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning to about 8-10 inches apart since Sandy forms a compact, uniformly mounded loose head rather than a large sprawling plant. Named an All-America Selections winner as the first lettuce to earn the award since 1985, Sandy is an oakleaf type with a multitude of sweet, frilly, dark green lobed leaves, notable disease resistance (especially to powdery mildew), and a strong tolerance for heat and heat-stress bitterness that lets it hold quality well past when older lettuces would bolt. Its compact 10-12 inch mounded habit fits neatly into a flowerpot, raised bed, or tight garden row. Harvest by cutting whole loose heads at maturity, or pick outer leaves cut-and-come-again style for baby leaf salads in as little as 30 days. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Sangiovese Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangiovese is a late-ripening variety that needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature. The most widely planted red wine grape in Italy and the backbone of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, it produces medium-bodied, high-acid, savory red wines with notes of tart cherry and dried herbs that pair especially well with food, reflecting the grape's central role in Tuscan cuisine and culture. It is a genetically variable and somewhat finicky grape, with dozens of recognized clones differing in cluster size, vigor, and quality potential, making clone selection an important consideration for a home vineyard planting. Prune to manage its naturally vigorous growth, thin fruit clusters if needed to concentrate flavor, and be prepared for a long hang time on the vine, since it ripens later than many other red varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sangre Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangre is a Colorado-bred round red potato developed for the western US fresh-market trade, prized for its smooth, bright red skin and shallow eyes that make for clean, attractive market tubers. The white flesh is moderately moist and holds its shape well when boiled, making it a solid choice for potato salads, roasting, and general table use. It bulks up earlier than many maincrop reds, making it a good option where an early harvest of good-looking red new potatoes is wanted. Grow it alongside a russet or yellow variety for a mixed-color early harvest. Matures in 80–95 days from transplant.

name: Sangria Watermelon (Classic Southern Shipping Hybrid)
description: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Sangria is a widely grown seeded watermelon hybrid bred with resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt, giving it reliable performance in the hot, humid disease pressure typical of a Gulf South summer. It produces large, oblong, dark green-striped fruit in the classic 20-24 pound shipping-melon range, with firm, deep red, sweet flesh that holds up well to handling and short-term storage. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably over a long harvest window. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned. Matures in 82–90 days from transplant.

name: Sanguinelli Blood Orange (Spanish Seedless Blood Orange)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and water deeply and regularly through summer while fruit sizes up. Sanguinelli arose in Spain in the late 1920s as a bud mutation of the older Doblefina blood orange and is valued for being essentially seedless while still developing the streaked red rind and red-mottled flesh characteristic of blood oranges. Its pigmentation is more moderate and more dependable in warm-winter climates than the deeply colored Moro, since Sanguinelli does not require as many cold nights to color well, and its flavor carries a milder raspberry-like note over a standard sweet-orange base. Fruit ripens mid-season in winter and has a notably thin, smooth rind that peels easily for fresh eating. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sanguinolenta Passionflower (Compact Blood-Red Passion Vine)
description: Native to the cloud forests of Ecuador and Peru, Passiflora sanguinolenta is a noticeably more compact, restrained climber than most tropical passionflowers, making it a good fit for a small trellis, hanging basket, or patio container rather than a large arbor. It flowers over a long season with small but intensely colored, blood-red blooms centered by a contrasting corona, and its modest size keeps it manageable for gardeners without room for a sprawling vine. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, grow it as a container plant kept in dappled shade during the hottest part of the day, watering regularly through summer, and bring it under cover or into a bright indoor spot whenever temperatures threaten to fall much below 40 F. Repot every year or two into fresh, humus-rich, well-drained mix to keep the compact root system vigorous. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Sanna Lingonberry (Swedish Wild-Strain Selection)
description: Sanna is a foundational Swedish lingonberry selection made directly from a superior wild strain rather than through controlled crossing, and it later served as the seed parent behind the newer cultivar 'Linnea'. It grows as a compact, spreading evergreen groundcover with the species' typical small, leathery, boxwood-like leaves and clusters of tart red berries produced in two harvests a season. Provide the same acidic, moisture-retentive conditions favored by blueberries and cranberries, ideally with a mulch of pine needles or acidic compost to maintain soil pH. Light afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hotter parts of its hardiness range, while full sun in cooler climates produces the heaviest fruit set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sansho (Japanese Pepper, Japanese Prickly Ash)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in a sheltered position; sansho is the Japanese pepper of Japanese cuisine, an aromatic shrubby tree of the citrus family unrelated to black pepper but producing a similar numbing, tingling 'hot' sensation on the tongue from compounds called hydroxyl-alpha-sanshool — the same effect as Sichuan pepper from the related Zanthoxylum bungeanum. The ground green unripe berries are sprinkled on broiled eel (unagi), miso soup, and grilled dishes; the fresh aromatic young leaves (kinome) are used to garnish spring dishes. Both male and female plants are needed for berry production. A unique and rewarding specialty crop for culinary enthusiasts. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Santa Barbara Macadamia
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Barbara macadamia is somewhat more cold-tolerant than Macadamia integrifolia cultivars but still needs a largely frost-free climate to thrive. A rough-shelled macadamia cultivar selected in coastal California, it belongs to the Macadamia tetraphylla species, which is generally hardier and better suited to California's cooler coastal climate than the smooth-shelled Macadamia integrifolia cultivars more commonly grown in Hawaii and Australia, producing flavorful, high-quality nuts with a thicker, more difficult-to-crack shell. Its improved cold tolerance relative to other macadamia species has made tetraphylla cultivars like this one the more practical choice for California growers outside the warmest coastal microclimates. Water regularly during nut development, provide the most sheltered, frost-free site available, and allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest and shelling. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Santa Claus Melon (Christmas Melon, Piel de Sapo)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Santa Claus melon requires 90–110 days to maturity, so start early or choose a long-season location; it is well-suited to Gulf Coast and California gardens. Piel de Sapo (literally 'Toad's Skin') is a Spanish winter melon variety widely grown throughout the Iberian Peninsula and used as the Christmas melon (melon de invierno) because its extraordinary keeping quality — 3–6 months at room temperature without refrigeration — allows harvest in October to be enjoyed fresh through December and January. The large (8–15 lb), elongated-oval fruits have mottled green and yellow skin with irregular markings resembling a toad's skin (the Spanish common name); the flesh is pale green to white-cream with a sweet, mild, refreshing flavor different from the aromatic intensity of muskmelon types. Sold in American markets as 'Santa Claus melon' and widely available in Hispanic grocery stores year-round due to its storage ability. Requires full sun and a long, warm season; sets fruit reliably in Gulf Coast and Western gardens. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Santa Cruz Oregano (Trailing Ornamental Hop-Flowered Oregano)
description: Santa Cruz is a vigorous, spreading ornamental oregano selected for its showy, hop-like flower clusters rather than kitchen use, since its small upright foliage carries very little of the typical oregano fragrance. Violet, trumpet-shaped flowers with pink overtones and lime-green calyces appear at the stem tips from midsummer through fall, tumbling attractively over rocks, walls, and slopes, and holding their color well when cut and dried for wreaths and arrangements. It tolerates heat and drought once established, making it a good choice for a low-water border or xeriscape planting. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade with moderate to occasional watering, and shear back after flowering to keep growth dense and tidy. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Santa Fe Grande Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Santa Fe Grande is a versatile wax-type pepper that ripens through yellow, orange, and finally red, with heat levels ranging from very mild at the yellow stage to moderately hot at full red maturity (500–1,000 SHU). This variety is particularly valued by Southern gardeners for its exceptional summer productivity — the plants set fruit even in high heat and humidity and continue producing well past the point where most pepper varieties slow down. The thick, waxy, cone-shaped fruits are 3–4 inches long with a crisp texture excellent for pickled peppers, fresh eating, and stuffing. Excellent disease resistance including tobacco mosaic virus. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Santa Fe Southern Highbush Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines well before planting; Santa Fe was released by the University of Florida in 2000 with one of the lowest chilling requirements among Southern highbush cultivars, around 350 hours, making it a strong fit for zone 8-10 Gulf Coast winters that are often too mild for higher-chill blueberries. Plants are vigorous and upright, ripening medium-to-large, dark blue berries with excellent scar, firmness, and flavor from early to late May. Because it is somewhat difficult to root, buy nursery-propagated plants rather than attempting hardwood cuttings at home, and interplant with another early-blooming Southern highbush cultivar such as Star, Windsor, or Rebel for the strongest fruit set. Keep roots consistently moist with drip irrigation and a heavy pine bark mulch, since blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems intolerant of drought. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Santa Rosa Plum
description: Plant this popular Japanese plum in deep, well-drained loam and full sun, setting the graft union a few inches above the soil line. Though partially self-fruitful, yields improve dramatically with a second Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination. Prune to an open-center vase shape during the dormant season to admit light and air. Thin heavy fruit sets to 4-6 inches apart to size up the crop and prevent limb breakage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Santaka Chile Pepper
description: 'Santaka' is a hot Japanese chile, just 2 inches long but delivering 40,000-50,000 Scoville units of spicy heat. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with warm soil for reliable germination, then transplant once nights stay warm. Grow in full sun with even moisture and light feeding; the compact plants do well in containers. Harvest peppers red for full heat, and dry them for use in stir-fries and soups. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Santana Eggplant
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Santana is a Dutch-bred hybrid eggplant selected for verticillium wilt tolerance and a heavy, extended set of glossy, deep-black, oval fruit on a vigorous, productive plant, making it a favorite of market growers who need consistent yields through a long season. The dense white flesh has few seeds and holds up well to roasting, grilling, and frying without becoming watery. Keep soil evenly moist and side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer as fruiting begins to sustain production over the full harvest window. Matures in 70–76 days from transplant.

name: Santiam Hazelnut
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Santiam is an Oregon State University release bred for strong resistance to eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that has devastated susceptible hazelnut orchards, while also carrying blight-immune 'Gasaway' resistance genetics distinct from some earlier resistant releases, which helps slow the disease's ability to overcome a single resistance source when multiple resistant cultivars are planted regionally. Trees are moderately vigorous and productive, bearing medium-large, round, good-flavored kernels well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Like other European hazelnuts, Santiam needs winter chilling and is intolerant of the hot, humid, disease-pressured conditions of the Gulf South, performing best in the Pacific Northwest and other cool-summer, moderate-winter regions. Because hazelnuts are self-incompatible and pollinated by wind-borne pollen in late winter, plant with a bloom-compatible pollinizer cultivar for a reliable crop, and expect the first significant harvest around year four to five after planting. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Santol
description: Santol is a fast-growing Southeast Asian tree bearing round, downy fruit with sweet-sour, cottony pulp surrounding large seeds. It requires a hot, humid, frost-free climate and deep, fertile, well-drained soil with steady moisture. Plant in full sun, allowing ample space for the large canopy to develop. Grafted trees fruit within a few years; harvest when the skin turns yellow and use the pulp fresh or in preserves and candies. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Santé Onion
description: Santé is a widely grown European storage onion producing firm, semi-globe bulbs with tight straw-yellow skin and pungent, long-keeping flesh. Plant sets or young transplants in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow full bulb development, and keep the row weeded since onions are shallow-rooted and slow to establish. It has good field tolerance to downy mildew and onion white rot compared with many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice in humid climates. Harvest once most tops have fallen over, cure thoroughly in a warm, airy location, and expect several months of firm storage from well-cured bulbs. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Sapodilla
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — including sandy, rocky, and calcareous soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) is a long-lived, slow-growing Mesoamerican tree that ranks among the most drought- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it exceptionally well adapted to South Florida's coastal sandy soils, salt air, and seasonal dry periods. The small to medium-sized, rough brown-skinned fruits reveal a translucent, grainy, caramel-brown flesh of extraordinary sweetness — often described as tasting of brown sugar, pear, and malt — that must be fully ripe and soft before eating, as unripe fruits are astringent from tannins. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Prolific' and 'Tikal' begin bearing in 4–6 years; seedling trees may take 8 years or more. The tree also has historical industrial significance as the source of chicle, the natural latex once used as the base of chewing gum, harvested by the Mesoamerican chiclero tradition for centuries. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Sapphire Cascade Blueberry (Trailing Self-Fertile Hanging-Basket Blueberry, 'FC12-029')
description: Sapphire Cascade is a patented Bushel and Berry introduction bred specifically for hanging baskets, with branches that arch outward and trail downward rather than growing upright like a typical blueberry bush. It is self-fertile and produces a classic sweet-tart blueberry flavor on medium-sized berries in early to midsummer, with deciduous foliage that takes on red tones in new growth and again in autumn. Grow in an acidic, well-drained mix in a basket or wide container, and water more frequently than an in-ground planting since hanging baskets dry out quickly in Gulf Coast summer heat. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sapucaia (Paradise Nut, Monkey Pot Tree)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sapucaia requires genuinely tropical conditions and a long time to first fruiting — a tree for patient collectors in zone 11–12. Lecythis pisonis (sapucaia or paradise nut) is a massive canopy tree of the tropical rainforests of Brazil, Venezuela, and the Guianas — in the lecythis family (Lecythidaceae), closely related to Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and sharing its remarkable botanical story. The tree produces large, barrel-shaped, very heavy woody capsules (4–6 inches wide) that remain on the branches and open via a detachable 'lid' at the top — these are the famous 'monkey pots' or 'monkey cups': animals (monkeys, squirrels, agoutis) reach into the narrow opening to grab the nuts, but if they grab too many, their fist is too large to withdraw, trapping them. The nuts inside (5–40 per capsule) are considered by nut connoisseurs to be superior to Brazil nuts: milder, creamier, less waxy, with an exceptionally smooth texture and rich flavor, very high in healthy fats similar to macadamia oil composition. Sapucaia nuts are almost entirely unknown in commerce despite their exceptional quality, because they do not store as well as Brazil nuts (the high oil content means they go rancid quickly) — making them a fresh-nut delight available primarily near their source. A magnificent collector's tree for zone 11–12 tropical gardens. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Sarah's Choice Cantaloupe (High-Sugar Disease-Resistant Muskmelon)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4-5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Sarah's Choice is a widely respected muskmelon bred by Dr. Brent Loy's public breeding program at the University of New Hampshire, selected for unusually high sugar content — commonly 14-15% Brix, well above many commercial cantaloupe varieties — along with resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt, two of the most common disease problems that shorten the productive life of melon vines. The medium-sized, heavily netted fruit has firm, deep-orange, aromatic flesh with excellent flavor. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars further. Ripe melons develop a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure — the classic 'full slip' sign of peak ripeness. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause fruit to split. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Saratoga Bay Laurel
description: Plant Saratoga bay laurel in full sun to part shade in ordinary, well-drained soil; it tolerates lean or poor soil and, once established after about two years, needs only infrequent irrigation. This compact, naturally tidy selection of common bay laurel produces glossy, rounded, olive-green leaves that emerge with a reddish blush, along with small pale yellow flowers in late winter and early spring; because it is a male selection it never sets the messy black fruit of seed-grown bay laurel. It shows better resistance to laurel psyllid and soft scale than the species and is popular trained as a clipped standard, multi-trunk patio tree, or clean, low-litter hedge. Left unpruned it can reach 20 to 25 feet, but it responds well to shaping and is equally at home sheared tight or grown loose as a specimen. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sarchimor Coffee
description: Developed by crossing the dwarf Villa Sarchi with the rust-resistant Hybrido de Timor, Sarchimor carries the same disease resistance as Catimor but from a different dwarf parent, and it has become the foundational lineage behind many newer rust-resistant varieties such as Marsellesa, Costa Rica 95, and IHCAFE90. Growers and roasters generally regard Sarchimor-derived selections as capable of better cup quality than straight Catimor lines when grown at good elevation and carefully processed. It forms a somewhat taller, more open shrub than Catimor and bears reliably once established.
