Provide the dappled shade, steady moisture, and rich, well-drained acidic soil favored by other highland Arabicas. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sargent Crabapple
description: Sargent crabapple is a true wild species from Japan, introduced to Western cultivation by Arnold Arboretum director Charles Sprague Sargent, for whom it is named, after he collected it on a plant-hunting expedition in the 1890s. Unlike most tree-form crabapples, it grows as a dense, wide-spreading, mounded shrub, usually broader than tall, making it useful where a crabapple's flowers and fruit are wanted without the scale of a full-sized tree. Fragrant white flowers open from pink-tinged buds in mid-spring, followed by abundant small, dark red fruits that persist into winter and are heavily used by birds. Its compact, shrubby habit and reliable disease resistance suit it to foundation plantings, mixed borders, or mass plantings where a lower-growing flowering and fruiting accent is needed. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sarsaparilla Vine
description: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full shade to partial sun; dwarf smilax is a coastal plain specialist adapted to the dry, shady conditions beneath longleaf pine and live oak canopies where few other evergreen groundcovers thrive. Smilax pumila is a low, trailing, spiny evergreen vine native to the pinelands and oak hammocks of the southeastern coastal plain, producing attractive glossy foliage that remains green through winter and showy clusters of bright red berries in late winter and early spring when wildlife food is scarce — making it exceptionally valuable for birds and small mammals during the hungry gap. Use it as a weed-suppressing groundcover under open-canopied native trees, where it will spread gradually into dense mats that require virtually no maintenance once established. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Saskatoon (Serviceberry, Western Serviceberry, Pacific Serviceberry)
description: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil; saskatoon (Amelanchier alnifolia) is the primary serviceberry of the Great Plains and Canadian prairies, producing abundant clusters of sweet, blueberry-flavored, dark purple berries in June that have been one of the most important food plants of the North American plains — used fresh, dried, and in pemmican by indigenous peoples including the Cree, Assiniboine, and Blackfoot, and now commercially cultivated across western Canada as 'saskatoon berries' for pies, jams, and wine. One of the most cold-hardy edible berry shrubs available, surviving to -40°F. Named cultivars including 'Thiessen', 'Smoky', and 'Martin' produce particularly large, sweet fruits. An outstanding prairie food-forest plant and edible landscape shrub. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Saticoy Cantaloupe (Disease-Resistant California Commercial Melon)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Saticoy is a California commercial cantaloupe variety bred with good resistance to powdery mildew and fusarium wilt, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm growing regions, helping the vine stay healthy and productive through a full summer season. The uniform, well-netted, orange-fleshed fruit has good sweet flavor and consistent size, traits that made it a reliable choice for commercial growers and equally useful for home gardeners wanting dependable production. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the rind's netting has turned from green to tan, and hold off on extra watering in the final week before harvest for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Satin Leaf
description: Plant Satin Leaf in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees tolerate brief cold to 28°F; protect young plants from hard frost; no significant pruning required. Chrysophyllum oliviforme is among South Florida's most striking native trees, instantly recognized by the extraordinary bicolor leaves — dark glossy green above and covered with dense, copper-golden, silky hairs below — that shimmer and catch light dramatically when wind moves through the canopy. The tree grows in South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks alongside Gumbo Limbo, Strangler Fig, and Pigeon Plum, and is a highly recommended native alternative to non-native ornamental trees for South Florida landscapes. Small clusters of tiny white flowers give rise to small, dark purple, oval fruits (less than 1 inch) — technically edible and sweet when fully ripe, similar in structure to small star apples (in the same family), though the thin flesh makes them a minor snack rather than a major crop. The fruits are enthusiastically consumed by mockingbirds, robins, and migrating warblers in winter. An excellent shade tree for South Florida native gardens, providing year-round color interest through the glinting copper undersides of its foliage. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Satinleaf
description: Satinleaf is one of the most visually striking native trees of south Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks, native to coastal hammocks, marl prairies, and pinelands from Brevard and Hillsborough counties south through the Keys and into the Caribbean, recognized immediately by its distinctive two-toned leaves — rich, dark, glossy green on top and brilliant coppery-golden on the undersides — that shimmer and flash in the breeze with each passing gust. Small white flowers produce small, dark purple to black berries (1–1.5 cm) that are sweet and edible and an important food for mockingbirds, robins, and migrating warblers; the fruit is also edible for people, with a flavor reminiscent of a mild grape. In south Florida native landscapes it works beautifully as a specimen tree, understory tree under larger canopy, or informal screen in partial shade; it tolerates the thin, rocky, alkaline marl and limestone soils of Miami-Dade County where many plants struggle. Grow in well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun in zones 9b–11. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Satputia (Clustered Ridge Gourd)
description: Satputia is a semi-domesticated relative of ridge gourd, distinct enough to be classified as its own species, valued in parts of northeastern India for bearing several smooth, unribbed young fruit together in a single cluster rather than one at a time along the vine. The plant's hermaphrodite flowers set fruit more readily than typical monoecious luffa, often giving noticeably heavier yields per vine over a shorter, more compact fruiting season. Provide a trellis or fence for the twining vine and harvest fruit young and tender, well before the skin toughens or ribs develop, for use exactly as you would ridge gourd in stir-fries and curries. Because it thrives in hot, humid conditions, it performs especially well through a long, warm Gulf Coast summer. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Satsuma Mandarin
description: The satsuma is a nearly seedless, cold-hardy mandarin that ripens early and peels with ease. It survives brief dips near the low twenties Fahrenheit once established, making it the best citrus for marginal areas. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and protect young trees during hard freezes. Harvest promptly when the rind colors, as the fruit puffs and loses quality if left too long on the tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Satsuma Plum (Blood Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Satsuma cross-pollinates best with Santa Rosa, Beauty, Methley, or other Japanese plums. Satsuma is a distinctive Japanese plum selection of early 20th century origin whose most striking characteristic is its blood-red to deep crimson-purple interior flesh — unlike most plums with yellow or amber flesh, Satsuma's flesh is the same deep red as the skin, producing richly pigmented juice and a distinctive wine-like, full-flavored sweetness with more depth and richness than most yellow-fleshed Japanese plums. The medium-large, round fruits have deep red to maroon-black skin; they ripen in late July to August. With only approximately 200–300 chill hours required, Satsuma is one of the most reliably productive Japanese plums for Gulf Coast zone 8 and similar low-chill climates. The deep red flesh makes spectacular jam, preserves, and fresh eating; the color intensifies when cooked. Outstanding for Gulf Coast, Texas, and Central and Southern California gardens where insufficient chill makes most European plums unproductive. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Saturn Apple (English Scab-Resistant Golden Delicious-Type Apple)
description: Saturn was bred in England as part of a disease-resistance breeding program and carries strong resistance to apple scab, one of the most damaging fungal diseases of apples in humid climates. The medium-sized, red-flushed fruit over a pale yellow-green background ripens in early-to-mid fall with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor reminiscent of Golden Delicious. Its clean disease record makes it a dependable choice for organic and low-input home orchards. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Saturn Summer Savory
description: Direct sow shallowly into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed, thinning seedlings to stand 8 to 12 inches apart. Saturn is a Polish-bred field cultivar of summer savory developed for industrial essential-oil extraction, and its foliage carries an unusually high concentration of carvacrol and gamma-terpinene, giving a sharper, more concentrated peppery-herbal bite than an average garden-strain summer savory. In the kitchen it is used exactly like common summer savory in bean, lentil, and sausage dishes, but because of its stronger oil content it can be used a bit more sparingly. For the most concentrated flavor and oil content, cut whole plants for drying right at the start of flowering. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Sauvignon Blanc Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sauvignon Blanc is vigorous and productive but benefits from canopy management to control its naturally sprawling growth. One of the world's most popular white wine grapes, it produces small, thick-skinned green grapes prized for wines with pronounced herbaceous, citrus, and 'green' aromatic character that vary noticeably by growing region and ripeness at harvest, from grassy and tart in cool climates to tropical and riper in warmer ones. Vigorous and adaptable to a range of soils and climates, it is one of the more forgiving wine grapes for a home vineyard, tolerating moderate disease pressure better than some of its more delicate relatives. Prune to control the vine's vigorous, sprawling growth habit, thin leaves around fruit clusters to promote airflow and even ripening, and harvest based on flavor and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Savage Citrange (Historic Cold-Hardy Sweet-Orange-Type Hybrid)
description: Savage citrange came out of the same 1897 sweet orange x trifoliate orange hybridization work by USDA botanist Walter Swingle that produced Rusk, Morton, and the other early named citranges, all bred to push edible citrus north of where true oranges reliably survive. USDA citrus researcher Herbert Webber singled Savage out among that group as coming closest to a true sweet orange in size, color, and fresh-eating quality, though the fruit still carries more seeds and tartness than modern orange cultivars. Trees inherit trifoliate orange's cold hardiness and semi-deciduous habit along with modest thorns, tolerating hard freezes well past the point that would kill standard orange trees outright. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and shelter young trees through their first couple of winters in the Gulf South before treating them as an established, self-sufficient planting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Savanna Guava
description: Plant Psidium guineense in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun; once established it is highly drought-tolerant — one of the most drought-resistant of all Psidium species — and performs well in sandy, poor soils where common guava struggles; prune lightly after fruiting to maintain a manageable size. Savanna Guava is the wild guava of the Brazilian cerrado (tropical savanna) — a shrubby, fire-resistant, drought-adapted species that has co-evolved with the deep-rooted, seasonally dry ecosystems of central Brazil. The small (golf-ball-sized to slightly larger), yellow-green fruits are produced in abundance from a relatively young age; the flavor is sweet-tart with an assertive, complex guava aroma — often described as more intensely flavored than common guava — and the fruits are eaten fresh, used for juice, made into jellies, and fermented into guava wine. The plant's tolerance of poor, sandy, acidic soils and periods of summer drought make it an excellent choice for Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens where common guava might be marginal; it is hardy to about 25–27°F with protection. The white, four-petaled flowers are attractive and produced throughout the warm season; birds relish the ripe fruits. A productive, low-maintenance, wildlife-supporting fruit shrub for hot, dry garden conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Savanna Hybrid Mustard
description: Savanna is a fast-growing F1 hybrid mustard bred for exceptionally tender, smooth leaves and stems that stay mild and non-fibrous even as plants size up, letting the whole leaf and stem be harvested without trimming. It grows quickly enough to cut for baby salad greens within three weeks or left longer for a traditional cooked green, and its slow-bolting habit keeps it productive across a wider temperature range than older open-pollinated Southern mustards. Home gardeners and market growers choose it for cut-and-come-again harvesting, since new leaves regrow readily after cutting through the cool season. Matures in 20–30 days from seed.

name: Savoy Ace Cabbage (AAS-Winning Crinkled-Leaf Savoy Cabbage)
description: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, spacing plants to allow full head development. Savoy Ace, an All-America Selections winner, forms attractive, deeply crinkled, blue-green leaves wrapped into a dense, tender head, with the savoy type's characteristically milder flavor and more tender texture compared with smooth-leaf cabbage, making it excellent for salads as well as cooked dishes. It heads reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions that can cause other savoy cabbages to form loose or split heads. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Savoy Cabbage
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply prepared soil; savoy cabbage is distinguished from standard green or red cabbages by its deeply wrinkled, crinkled, blistered leaves that form a less tightly packed, more loosely structured head — the deeply textured leaves are more tender, delicate, and sweet than smooth-leaved cabbages and are prized for raw salads, braising, stuffed cabbage rolls, and colcannon. The plant is markedly more cold-hardy than standard cabbages, tolerating hard frosts below 20°F when mature, and improves considerably in sweetness after exposure to frost. The spring crop tends to be less satisfying than fall-harvested heads; time fall planting so heads mature in cool autumn temperatures. Excellent varieties include 'Savoy Express' (early, compact), 'Savoy King' (large, late), and 'Deadon' (very cold-hardy). Rotate brassica family crops on a 3-year cycle to prevent clubroot buildup. Matures in 80–110 days from transplant.

name: Savoy Express Cabbage (Early Compact Crinkle-Leaf Savoy Cabbage)
description: Savoy Express is a fast-maturing, compact savoy cabbage bred to bring the deeply crinkled, tender-leaved character of savoy types to gardeners in far less time than standard savoy cultivars, forming smallish, round, moderately dense heads in about two months from transplant. Its early maturity and small footprint make it a good fit for succession planting, small raised beds, and gardeners in short-season climates who still want the delicate, sweet flavor and tender texture savoy cabbage is prized for. Like other savoy types it tolerates hard frost well and improves in sweetness after cold exposure, though its quick maturity also lets it beat summer heat in a spring planting where standard cabbages would bolt or turn bitter. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and rotate with non-brassica crops on a three-year cycle to prevent clubroot buildup. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Savoy King Cabbage (AAS-Winning Savoyed Crinkled-Leaf Hybrid Cabbage)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Savoy King is a 1965 All-America Selections-winning savoy (crinkle-leaved) cabbage — a type that differs fundamentally from standard smooth-headed cabbages in leaf texture, flavor, and culinary applications. Savoy cabbage produces the characteristic deeply blistered, puckered, crinkled leaves that make the head appear almost frilly compared to the smooth-skinned heads of standard green or red types. The crinkled texture comes from the faster growth rate of the leaf blade relative to the midrib — the excess blade tissue buckles and folds into the distinctive savoy pattern. Flavor-wise, savoy cabbage is notably sweeter, more tender, and less sulfurous than standard round cabbages — the crinkled leaves have a more delicate character that makes savoy preferred for raw salads (the soft, tender leaves wilt pleasantly rather than staying tough) and for elegant stuffed cabbage preparations where the flexible leaves wrap easily around fillings. Savoy King produces large (4–6 lb), well-domed, attractive heads with deep blue-green coloring and the decorative crinkled surface that makes it one of the most ornamental cabbages in the winter garden. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: Sawtooth Blackberry (Southern Blackberry)
description: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; sawtooth blackberry is one of the most common and widespread native blackberries of the eastern and southeastern US — a vigorous, thorny-caned shrub with large, deeply sawtooth-toothed compound leaves and masses of white flowers in spring followed by sweet-tart black drupelets in midsummer. One of several eastern blackberry species (along with Rubus allegheniensis and others) forming the backbone of wild blackberry patches in woodlands, old fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas from New England to Florida. The fruit is sweet-tart and excellent for fresh eating, jams, cobblers, and pies. In the natural garden, sawtooth blackberry forms important wildlife thickets — the thorny canes provide nesting sites and escape cover for songbirds, rabbits, and ground-nesting animals; the berries feed more than 100 species of birds and mammals. More tolerant of partial shade and moist soils than many other native blackberries. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sayamakaori Tea
description: Sayamakaori is a registered early-ripening Japanese green tea cultivar selected in 1958 at Saitama Prefecture's tea experimental station, developed for the cooler, more northerly Sayama tea-growing region where it is especially prized for its pronounced, distinctive aroma. Its comparatively good cold tolerance for a China-type cultivar makes it a useful choice outside Japan's warmest tea belts. The shrub produces small, narrow leaves typical of fine sencha cultivars and buds early in spring, giving growers a head start on the first flush. Cultivate with the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade other China-type tea selections require. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sayamusume Edamame Soybean
description: Sow seed about an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean-specific rhizobium if soybeans haven't grown in the bed before. Sayamusume is a Japanese edamame heirloom valued for its large, elongated, light-green beans and reliably sweet, tender flavor, carried on upright plants with pods clustered two to four per cluster. Pick pods while still bright green and fully plump for fresh edamame, or leave plants to dry down further for shelling as dry soybeans. Steam or boil harvested pods briefly in well-salted water, then pop the beans free to eat as a snack or use in salads and stir-fries. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: SCA 12 Cacao (Peruvian Witches'-Broom-Resistant Clone)
description: SCA 12 is a cacao accession collected in Peru that, together with its sister clone SCA 6, has served for decades as a primary reference source of resistance to witches' broom disease (Moniliophthora perniciosa), one of the most damaging fungal diseases affecting cacao in the Americas. Breeders have used SCA 12 as a parent in a very large share of the improved, disease-resistant cacao varieties held in international germplasm collections, though its resistance has shown regional variability and has occasionally broken down against certain local disease strains. Growth habit is vigorous and upright, similar to other resistant breeding clones. Because it is grown mainly for breeding and disease-resistance trials rather than fine flavor, home growers plant it more for genetic interest than eating quality; provide it with the same filtered shade, rich moist soil, and warm humid conditions used for other cacao selections. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: SCA 6 Cacao
description: Collected in Peru in the early twentieth century as one of the 'Scavina' upper Amazon Forastero-type clones, SCA 6 is significant chiefly as one of the two parent clones, alongside IMC 67, used to breed the high-yield, disease-resistant CCN-51 hybrid that transformed Ecuadorian cacao production. On its own it contributes strong resistance to witches'-broom disease and notably vigorous, fast growth compared to heirloom Criollo or Trinitario types. Its beans are considered workmanlike bulk cacao rather than fine flavor. Grow it in the same warm, humid, partially shaded conditions as other cacao selections, expecting rapid early growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Scallop Blend Summer (Patty Pan) Squash
description: This colorful patty pan blend combines the heirlooms 'Early White Bush', 'Bennings Green Tint', and 'Yellow Bush' for a bowl-worthy mix of scalloped summer squash. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and space the bushy plants 24-36 inches apart in full sun. Harvest fruits young at 2-4 inches across when tender and flavorful, picking frequently to keep the plants producing. Steady moisture and rich soil support a heavy summer crop. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Scallopini Squash (AAS-Winning Hybrid Bush Scallop Squash)
description: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk. Introduced in the mid-1970s as an All-America Selections winner, this cross between zucchini and pattypan types yields small, dark-green scalloped fruit with a mild, nutty flavor and tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest young at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, picking every day or two once plants begin producing heavily. Its compact, non-vining habit made it a popular choice for small-space and container vegetable gardens when it was introduced. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Beauty Plum (Ultra-Low-Chill Japanese Plum for the Deep Gulf South)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, since plum roots decline quickly in standing water. Developed by a Florida plant breeder for the state's mildest winters, Scarlet Beauty carries one of the lowest chill requirements of any Japanese-type plum, letting it flower and set fruit dependably where higher-chill plums bloom sparsely or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized with red-streaked amber flesh and ripens in May, ahead of most other plums in the same garden. Thin fruit clusters when marble-sized to reduce limb breakage and improve fruit size, and plant a second low-chill Japanese plum nearby to boost yields even though the tree is partly self-fruitful. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Scarlet Emperor Pole Runner Bean
description: Scarlet Emperor is a vigorous pole runner bean prized for its brilliant clusters of edible red flowers as well as its rich-flavored pods. Sow seeds 1 inch deep and 4-6 inches apart at the base of a tall trellis, fence, or pole after the soil warms in spring. Pick young pods for tender snap beans, or leave them to mature and shell for green or dried beans. Keep vines watered during flowering and harvest regularly to keep new pods forming. This variety doubles as an ornamental screen thanks to its showy blooms that attract hummingbirds. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Emperor Runner Bean
description: Erect a tall trellis or teepee before sowing, since these vigorous vines climb up to ten feet. Direct sow seeds one to two inches deep after frost, and enjoy the showy scarlet blossoms that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. This ornamental heirloom is both beautiful and productive, yielding plenty of edible pods over the season. Pick pods young for tender eating, or let them mature to harvest the large seeds for cooking. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Frills Mustard (Deep Maroon Frilled Mustard)
description: This ornamental-edible mustard produces deeply fringed, almost lacy leaves in a rich burgundy-maroon that intensifies in cool weather and full sun. Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin to final spacing, using thinnings as spicy microgreens. Leaves can be harvested young for salad mix, where the color and frilled texture stand out, or left to mature for a peppery cooked green. Plants are attractive enough for mixed ornamental beds as well as the vegetable garden, but bolt quickly once summer heat arrives. Matures in 21–45 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Kadsura
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zones 7–10; scarlet kadsura is a semi-evergreen to evergreen twining vine native to Japan, Korea, and southern China, valued for exceptional seasonal interest across multiple seasons: glossy, dark green, leathery leaves that may turn burgundy in cool weather; small, pale yellow, fragrant flowers in summer; and spectacular, showy clusters of scarlet-red, coral-like fruiting bodies in fall — each cluster up to 2 inches in diameter and resembling a bunch of tiny rubies. The fruits are edible and used in traditional Chinese medicine. It grows naturally in shaded forest understories and tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines — one of its most valuable garden traits. An outstanding shade vine for zone 7–10 gardens where its combination of handsome evergreen foliage, fragrant flowers, and dramatic red fruit clusters provides year-round ornamental interest in difficult, shaded positions. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Scarlet Kale
description: Sow seeds half an inch deep and thin plants to give the upright rosettes room to grow. This edible and ornamental heirloom produces curly leaves in brilliant scarlet, magenta, and deep purple that stand two to three feet tall. Cool weather deepens both the color and the sweetness, making it a standout in the fall and winter garden. Harvest outer leaves as needed, and the plants will keep pushing new growth for months. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Lingonberry (Dwarf Groundcover Pollinizer Selection)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Scarlet is a dwarf, evergreen lingonberry selection standing just four to eight inches tall, producing a reasonable quantity of medium-sized, cranberry-flavored red berries on its branch tips while also serving as a dependable pollinizer that boosts fruit set on neighboring lingonberry cultivars. Its diminutive, spreading habit makes it as useful for ornamental edging and container growing as for harvest, and like other lingonberries it tolerates more shade than most fruiting plants provided the soil stays consistently acidic. Shear lightly every few years to rejuvenate growth and keep the planting dense. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Scarlet Nantes Carrot
description: Sow seed shallowly directly in the garden and thin seedlings to about 2 inches apart once they reach a couple inches tall. This sweet, nearly coreless heirloom develops best in deep, loose, well-drained soil free of rocks that can fork the roots. Keep the seedbed evenly moist during the slow germination period, which can take up to three weeks. Harvest when roots reach about six to seven inches and full color for the tenderest, sweetest flavor. Successive sowings from spring through midsummer extend the harvest. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Ohno Revival Turnip (Red-Leafed Dual-Purpose Japanese Turnip)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart for best root development; harvest at 2–3 inches diameter for the sweetest, mildest eating quality; the red coloration intensifies in cool weather; the leaves can be harvested as greens throughout the season. Scarlet Ohno Revival (sometimes marketed as 'Scarlet Queen Turnip') is a Japanese turnip variety with striking visual characteristics: the round roots have vivid scarlet to magenta-red skin with pink-red flesh throughout — much more deeply and uniformly colored than the more common 'Tokyo' types — and the broad basal leaves have dramatic red-tinged stems and midribs that make the plant ornamental in the garden as well as functional. The turnip was selected from an older Japanese variety ('Ohno Scarlet') by seed savers and represents a revival of an older type that had become rare. At harvest size (2–3 inches), the roots have a mild, slightly sweet turnip flavor quite different from the sharp, peppery bite of older turnip types — the Japanese breeding tradition favors mild, salad-turnip types that can be eaten raw, and Scarlet Ohno follows this tradition. The roots are excellent sliced thin into salads (the red color is dramatic against green lettuce), quick-pickled in the Japanese style (the red pigment turns the pickling brine a beautiful deep pink), roasted with the skin on (which deepens the color), or used in any turnip recipe where visual impact is valued. Matures in 35–50 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Royal Grape
description: Another David Ramming USDA release, introduced in 2006, Scarlet Royal produces large, firm, bright-red seedless berries with a sweet, crisp bite on very large clusters that ripen late in the season. It reliably develops strong red color even under warm-night conditions that leave some other late red grapes pale, making it a dependable choice for extending the red seedless harvest into fall. Vines are vigorous and productive, so cluster thinning and a sturdy permanent cordon system help manage the heavy crop load. It needs a long, hot growing season to size and color properly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Scarlet Runner Bean
description: Direct sow after frost danger in fertile, moist soil on a tall trellis in full sun; scarlet runner bean is a dual-purpose ornamental and edible vine native to the mountains of Central America, producing brilliant scarlet (occasionally white or bicolor) flowers beloved by hummingbirds throughout the growing season, followed by long flat pods with striking maroon-speckled white seeds. Pods are harvested young as snap beans (very similar to pole beans in texture and flavor) or allowed to mature for the attractive dried beans used in soups and stews. The plant is a perennial in zones 7–11, where established tuberous roots resprout each season; in cooler zones treat as an annual. In zone 9a spring plantings often stop producing in summer heat — plant a second succession in late August for fall harvest. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Scarlet Sentinel Columnar Apple (Red Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Scarlet Sentinel is the red-skinned counterpart within the Ballerina series of columnar apples, sharing the same naturally dwarfing, single-trunk growth habit as North Pole and Golden Sentinel — the tree grows as one narrow, upright stem lined directly with short fruiting spurs rather than spreading branches, staying only about 2 feet wide at full height. Fruit is crisp, juicy, and well-colored deep red, ripening in early to mid fall with good, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. The narrow, columnar form makes it well suited to a large container, a tight side-yard bed, or a closely spaced productive row, and it can also be used as a striking, fruiting vertical accent in an ornamental edible landscape. Plant with a second compatible apple cultivar nearby for pollination, since columnar apples still require cross-pollination despite their compact size. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any stray side shoots and occasionally thinning crowded fruiting spurs. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Scarlet Turnip White-Tipped Radish
description: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1-2 inches apart; harvest promptly once roots reach 1 inch across, as the globe shape turns pithy faster than elongated types if left in the ground. Scarlet Turnip White Tipped is an old French and American market-garden heirloom distinguished by its round, turnip-like shape rather than the oblong 'half-long' form of French Breakfast, with bright scarlet skin fading to white at the root tip. It was cultivated as a distinct forcing and early-market variety well before French Breakfast rose to prominence, and the two were listed as separate cultivars in nineteenth-century French seed catalogs. Its crisp texture and mild bite make it a good choice for growers wanting a quick round radish with more color contrast than solid-red types. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Scarlett Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and train onto a single-wire or double-curtain trellis; Scarlett is a self-fertile muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected for its reddish-bronze skin color, above-average berry size, and reliable self-pollination, making it a good choice for a home planting with limited space for a separate pollinizer vine. The flavor is sweet with the classic musky muscadine character, and the vine is vigorous and productive once established, typically bearing its first meaningful crop in year three. Prune hard every winter back to spurs on the permanent cordon, since muscadines fruit on new growth from the current season's canes. Harvest berries individually as they ripen and detach easily from the stem, over a multi-week window in late summer, and provide consistent moisture during fruit swell to reduce splitting after heavy rain. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Scented Geranium (Rose Geranium, Lemon Geranium)
description: Root cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; scented geraniums are a diverse group of Pelargonium species grown primarily for their extraordinary aromatic foliage rather than their flowers. The rose-scented P. graveolens is the classic, with deeply lobed leaves smelling of rose-lemon; other varieties offer scents of peppermint, cinnamon, nutmeg, coconut, apple, apricot, pine, and many other aromas, achieved by rubbing or crushing the leaves. The dried leaves are used to flavor sugar, pound cake, jams, and teas; fresh leaves infuse a subtle rose flavor into cream, sorbet, and pound cake. They are more heat-tolerant than zonal geraniums and can survive Gulf Coast summers in partial shade with adequate water. All scented geraniums root easily from cuttings taken in late summer to bring indoors for the winter in zone 8a. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Schley Pecan (Classic Thin-Shelled Papershell Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Schley became one of the foundational commercial pecan cultivars of the 20th-century South and is still valued for its thin, easily cracked papershell and rich, high-quality kernel. It has been widely used as a parent in breeding programs that produced many of today's more disease-resistant cultivars, since it passes along excellent nut quality even though the tree itself is fairly susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and may need fungicide protection in wet years. It remains a good choice in drier pecan-growing regions or where scab pressure is manageable. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Schoon's Hard Shell Melon (Heirloom Shipping Cantaloupe)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, allowing ample room for the vigorous vines to sprawl. Schoon's Hard Shell is a long-season heirloom muskmelon producing large, oval, heavily netted fruits, 7-8 inches long and 5-8 lbs, encased in an unusually thick, tough rind that made it an outstanding shipper and field-stander in an era before refrigerated transport, while the thick red-salmon flesh ripens to an intensely sweet, richly aromatic flavor. Because it is slow to mature relative to modern hybrids, gardeners in shorter-season regions may want to start it a bit earlier or choose a warm, sheltered planting site. Keep soil consistently moist through vine growth and fruit development, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit. Matures in 88–95 days from seed.

name: Scintilla Blueberry (Ultra-Low-Chill Mid-Spring University of Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Scintilla is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred with an unusually low chill requirement of only about 200 to 300 hours, allowing it to break dormancy and fruit reliably even after the mild, warm winters typical of the immediate Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida where standard highbush and even many southern highbush cultivars fail to accumulate enough winter chill. It ripens over several weeks from mid-April into mid-May. As a southern highbush type, it needs consistently moist, highly acidic soil. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Scorzonera (Black Salsify)
description: Sow direct as soon as soil can be worked in spring in deep, stone-free, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double-dig or use raised beds as scorzonera needs at least 12–18 inches of loose, unobstructed soil for long, straight roots — rocky or compacted soil produces forked, misshapen roots. Scorzonera hispanica is an underappreciated European root vegetable with long, black-skinned, white-fleshed taproots with a delicately sweet, oyster-like flavor that can be harvested in the first year but improves dramatically if left to mature for 18–24 months; the white sap that oozes from cut surfaces (a latex) can be rinsed away with cold water. Unlike most root vegetables, scorzonera is a true perennial that can be harvested selectively over multiple years; the young spring leaves and flower buds are also edible in salads. A gourmet vegetable widely popular in Belgium and the Netherlands. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Scotch Bonnet
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in moist starting mix, maintaining soil at 85°F for best germination results; this Capsicum chinense type is among the slower starters. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil only after the garden is fully warm, and consider black plastic mulch to boost soil temperatures in cooler climates. The bonnet-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the strain and carry a distinctive fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Use gloves when handling ripe fruits; they are essential in Caribbean jerk seasoning and hot sauces. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Scotch Bonnet Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors eight or more weeks before the last frost, as this Caribbean chile needs warm soil and a long season to ripen. Transplant into the warmest part of the garden after the soil and nights have settled into the 60s. The fiery, fruity fruits mature from green to bright yellow-orange or red, so wait for full color for maximum heat and flavor. Consistent watering and a steady feed produce the heaviest yields. Wear gloves when handling the exceptionally hot pods. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Scotch Bonnet Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil and nights have thoroughly warmed; the Scotch bonnet is the defining pepper of Caribbean cuisine, particularly Jamaican jerk and Trinidadian cooking, with a distinctive fruity-floral heat (100,000–350,000 SHU) and a unique, tropical, almost fruity aroma that separates it from habanero despite the close botanical relationship. The small, flattened, wrinkled fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and red, and can be used at any ripe stage — the green stage has the most vegetal flavor while red fruits are sweetest and hottest. Unlike habaneros, genuine scotch bonnets have a more complex, sweeter aroma profile with notes of cherry and apple. The plants are tall and bushy, very productive in warm conditions, and benefit from staking as fruit clusters become heavy. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Scotch Lovage (Sea Lovage)
description: Ligusticum scoticum, known as Scotch lovage or sea lovage, is a compact, hardy, aromatic perennial of the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to coastal cliff tops, rocky shores, and seaside grasslands of Scotland, northern England, Iceland, Scandinavia, and northeastern North America, where it grows in some of the most exposed and salt-swept maritime habitats imaginable; the glossy, dark-green, divided leaves have a strong, pleasant aroma and flavor closely resembling lovage (Levisticum officinale) and celery, and were eaten by coastal peoples as a potherb and flavoring herb long before cultivated celery was available. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in well-drained, gritty or stony, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in a cool, sunny to partly shaded position; it is a cool-climate coastal plant that prefers excellent drainage and good air circulation and is not well-suited to hot, humid summers. Young leaves and stems can be harvested in spring and used as a celery-flavored potherb in soups and stews; historically important to the diet of remote coastal and island communities in Scotland and Scandinavia, where it was one of few flavoring herbs available and was also used as a green vegetable. Scotch lovage is rarely offered commercially but is a unique and culturally significant culinary herb for northern gardens and maritime heritage plantings. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Scotch Spearmint (Smooth Sweet Commercial Oil-Production Mint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Scotch Spearmint, a hybrid cultivar long grown for commercial mint oil production, offers a smoother, sweeter spearmint flavor with less of the sharper bite found in native spearmint, making it a favorite for candy, gum, and toothpaste flavoring as well as home culinary use. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Scotia Elderberry (Cold-Hardy Canadian Elderberry)
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; elderberries tolerate wet sites better than most fruiting shrubs and are well suited to low or seasonally damp spots in the garden. Scotia is a Nova Scotia-origin American elderberry selection valued for its very early ripening and large, showy fruit clusters of small, dark purple-black berries, borne on a vigorous, suckering shrub. Berries must be cooked before eating, as raw elderberries and other plant parts contain compounds that can cause stomach upset; ripe, cooked fruit is traditionally made into syrup, jelly, wine, and pie, and the broad, flat flower clusters can also be used fresh or dried for elderflower cordial and fritters. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew the shrub, since elderberries fruit best on relatively young wood, and cut the whole planting back hard every few years to keep it a manageable size. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Scout Apricot (Hardy Manchurian-Derived Prairie Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Scout is another Saskatchewan-developed apricot bred from cold-hardy Manchurian apricot stock, part of a small group of extreme-hardy prairie apricot selections developed to give northern growers a genuine option for growing apricots where standard varieties cannot survive winter. Fruit is small to medium with orange skin and flesh, tarter and less refined than warm-climate apricots but entirely usable for fresh eating, drying, and preserves, and a genuine novelty for gardeners in short-season, harsh-winter climates. As with other prairie apricots, the tree's cold hardiness is exceptional, but flowers open early and remain vulnerable to spring frost, so site selection to avoid frost pockets matters more for the annual crop than winter survival does. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Screwbean Mesquite (Tornillo)
description: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; screwbean mesquite is immediately recognizable by its uniquely coiled, spiral seed pods — tightly twisted into a tight helix resembling a screw or corkscrew — unlike the straight or gently curved pods of other mesquites. The common name 'tornillo' (Spanish for screw) reflects this distinctive pod shape. The pods are edible, sweet, and nutritious, and were processed into food by Sonoran Desert indigenous peoples. The tree grows naturally along desert washes and dry riverbanks of the Southwest, tolerating the highly alkaline, sometimes saline soils of desert floodplains. The cream-colored flower spikes are fragrant and heavily visited by native bees. Increasingly rare in some areas due to agricultural development of desert floodplains. A distinctive, drought-tolerant native for desert Southwest gardens with excellent wildlife value. Matures in 730–1825 days from seed.

name: Scrub Hickory
description: Scrub Hickory is a rare and imperiled native nut tree endemic to the ancient, fire-maintained Florida scrub habitats of the central Florida ridge, where it grows in pure white sand soils of extremely low fertility that are inhospitable to most other plants. A small tree rarely exceeding 25 feet, it produces small, round, thick-shelled nuts with bitter kernels that are eaten by Florida Scrub-Jays, fox squirrels, gopher tortoises, and other scrub wildlife, making it a keystone component of the Florida scrub food web. Plant fresh nuts in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained soil in full sun — excessive water, clay, or organic matter quickly kills this species. In cultivation, Scrub Hickory performs best in open xeric settings that mimic native scrub conditions, and benefits from the periodic, low-intensity fire that characterizes and maintains the Florida scrub ecosystem. Matures in 2555–5475 days from seed.

name: Sculpit Stridolo
description: Direct-sow in early spring in well-drained soil, covering seed lightly and thinning young plants. This Italian wild green, also called bladder campion, has a mild sweet-grassy flavor for risottos and omelets. Grow in full sun with moderate water where it forms tender leafy rosettes. Harvest young shoots and leaves before flowering for the best texture and taste. Let a few plants flower to self-sow for a continuing patch. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Scuppernong Grape
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Scuppernong is a bronze-skinned muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) that is arguably the oldest cultivated grape in North America — the original 'Mother Vine' on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, is estimated to be over 400 years old and still produces fruit. It is the ancestral cultivar of the entire muscadine grape industry in the southeastern United States. Scuppernong grapes are large (1–1.5 inches), round, bronze-green to golden when ripe, with a distinctively musky, sweet, complex flavor very different from European grapes — they are used for fresh eating, wine, juice, and preserves. Muscadines are extremely well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf South, where they naturally resist Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that devastate Vitis vinifera grapes. Vines are vigorous and long-lived, requiring a strong overhead arbor or high-wire trellis. Harvest in late August–September when berries drop from the cluster at a touch. Prune heavily each winter, leaving only short spurs on the permanent arms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sea Apple
description: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Syzygium grande is fast-growing and tolerates brief waterlogging and coastal conditions — water regularly in establishment, then water deeply and infrequently once the tree is established. Syzygium grande (Sea Apple or Jambu Bol) is a large, handsome, fast-growing evergreen tree native to the coastal and freshwater-edge rainforests of the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, Sumatra, and the Philippines — one of the most important and beautiful tropical street and shade trees of Singapore and Peninsular Malaysia, where it is widely planted in parks, streets, and public spaces as one of the city's signature urban trees. The tree is spectacular in flower: enormous, cloud-like masses of small, white, 'powder-puff' flowers (characteristic of the Syzygium genus) cover the tree canopy in brilliant white floral displays multiple times per year. The round, green-to-pink-red fruits — 1–2 inches across, resembling small apples — are crisp, watery, mildly sweet, and edible fresh in the same way as the related rose apple (Syzygium jambos), though less flavorful. The fruit is also attractive to birds and wildlife. Syzygium grande is among the fastest-growing and most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the large Syzygium species and is well-suited to the humid tropical climate of coastal south Florida and Hawaii. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sea Aster
description: Sow directly or set out divisions in moist, full-sun ground, ideally in a low spot that stays damp; sea aster is a short-lived but self-renewing perennial of European salt marshes now grown as a specialty vegetable, especially prized by Dutch and Scandinavian chefs under names like zeeaster or strandaster. The somewhat fleshy, narrow leaves and young stems have a pleasantly sweet-salty, mineral flavor reminiscent of samphire, and are harvested repeatedly through the season for use raw in salads, quick-pickled, or lightly steamed as a side vegetable. Unlike samphire, sea aster tolerates ordinary damp garden soil without true tidal salinity, though a light annual dressing of sea salt improves flavor and keeps the foliage tender. Cut plants back hard after their late-summer lavender-blue daisy flowers fade to encourage fresh basal growth and to keep the clump vegetative for the following year's harvest; older clumps can be lifted and divided every few years to maintain vigor. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Sea Beet (Wild Beet)
description: Sow seeds in coastal, sandy, or well-drained soil in full sun; sea beet is the wild ancestor of all cultivated beet varieties including table beet, chard, sugar beet, and mangelwurzel — the original plant from which millennia of selection produced all these crops. It grows naturally along European and North African coastlines in dry, sandy, often saline soils and is remarkably tolerant of salt, drought, and poor soil. The glossy, dark green leaves are edible exactly like chard, with an excellent fresh flavor that is actually more tender and less strongly flavored than cultivated chard. The fleshy root is small and woody compared to cultivated beets but edible. A fascinating plant for edible garden history and for coastal gardens where most vegetables struggle. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Sea Buckthorn
description: Sea buckthorn is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing shrub that thrives in poor, dry, sandy soils where most fruits struggle. It is dioecious and requires male plants for pollination — one male per 5–7 females; sex is not identifiable until first flowering, so purchase sexed plants. The tiny berries are borne directly on the branches in dense clusters and are difficult to harvest without damaging the plant; a common approach is to cut fruiting branches in fall and strip berries indoors or by freezing and shaking. The tart, orange berries are extremely high in vitamin C. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sea Grape
description: Sea grape is dioecious — male and female plants must both be present for fruit production — so purchase nursery plants that have been confirmed female, or graft from a known fruiting specimen and include a male pollinator nearby. It is one of the most wind- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting trees available and naturally colonizes beach dunes and coastal scrub; it thrives on sandy, alkaline soils where most fruit trees fail. The grape-like clusters of purple-red fruits ripen in late summer to fall and are used to make a tart, mild jelly; individual fruits must be fully purple before picking as unripe fruit is astringent. Sea grape is legally protected in some coastal states — confirm local regulations before heavy pruning. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sea Island Cotton (Pima Cotton)
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm; Sea Island cotton is the extra-long-staple cotton species historically grown along the coastal Sea Islands of Georgia and South Carolina and now the source of premium Pima and Egyptian cotton fiber, distinct from the shorter-staple upland cotton grown across most of the Cotton Belt. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, revealing bolls that mature more slowly than upland cotton and split open to reveal exceptionally long, silky, fine fibers prized by hand-spinners for their smooth, lustrous quality. It requires a longer, warmer, more humid growing season than upland cotton to fully mature its bolls, making it best suited to the Gulf Coast and Deep South rather than shorter-season northern climates. Watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures common to cotton generally, and rotate planting location yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup. Matures in 160–190 days from seed.

name: Sea Island Red Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; the Sea Island Red Pea is a semi-vining, dark-red-to-brown speckled cowpea that was the foundation of Gullah/Geechee cuisine on the sea islands of Georgia and South Carolina from the colonial period through the early 20th century. The variety served as the original ingredient in hoppin' john and purloo dishes before black-eyed peas replaced it in most recipes. It is an exceptional-flavored cowpea with earthy, rich, deeply savory notes and a dense, creamy texture when fresh-shelled that surpasses commercial black-eyed peas in the estimation of many who have tasted both. The vine habit is moderate — plants sprawl 2–3 feet and may benefit from short supports. Revived through efforts by the Anson Mills and Slow Food USA Ark of Taste programs. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Sea Kale
description: Sow seeds direct in early spring in deep, sandy to gravelly, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; sea kale has a very long taproot and deeply resents transplanting — choose its permanent location carefully. Crambe maritima is a spectacular, ornamental-as-well-as-edible native of European coastal shingle beaches, producing large, blue-gray, crinkled, cabbage-like leaves and billowing clouds of tiny, honey-scented white flowers on 24–36-inch stems in early summer that are outstanding in the border; the young, blanched shoots are the edible crop, harvested in early spring by covering the dormant crown with a forcing pot or dark bucket 4–6 weeks before harvest, producing pale, sweetly nutty, asparagus-like shoots. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and long-lived, thriving in poor, well-drained soils in coastal and hot, dry inland gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Sea of Red Lettuce (Deep Red Frilly Oakleaf Lettuce)
description: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Sea of Red is an oakleaf-type lettuce prized for deeply lobed, ruffled, deep burgundy-red leaves that stay glossy and appetizing-looking even as outer leaves are repeatedly harvested, making it a favorite for cut-and-come-again baby leaf production as well as full-head harvest. It holds its rich color and resists premature bolting and the bitterness that develops in many red lettuces once temperatures climb, giving it a somewhat longer productive window than more heat-sensitive varieties, though it still performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons in zone 9. Harvest outer leaves as needed for continuous production, or cut the whole loose head at once for a single larger harvest. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings to further delay bolting as the weather warms. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Sea Purslane
description: Plant stem cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this remarkable halophyte naturally colonizes tidal flats, beach margins, and coastal dunes where few other edibles survive, tolerating periodic saltwater flooding and saline spray. The succulent, bright-green to purplish leaves and stems have a pleasantly salty, crisp flavor — rinse before eating to reduce saltiness — and are excellent raw in salads, briefly stir-fried, or used as a sea-vegetable garnish. The plant forms a dense, prostrate mat that suppresses weeds and helps stabilize sandy soils against erosion. In zone 9–11 it is a reliable perennial that can be harvested throughout the year. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Sea Rocket
description: Sow seeds shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, directly into sandy or well-drained soil in a sunny position in early spring. Sea rocket is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, coastal winds, and drought once established, requiring very little supplemental water. Harvest young, succulent leaves and stems regularly for use raw in salads where they contribute a pleasant peppery bite; young seed pods are also edible and can be added to salads or pickled. Allow some plants to set seed for reliable self-seeding in subsequent years. Matures in 45–70 days from seed.

name: Sea Wormwood
description: Native to salt marshes, shingle beaches, and estuary flats of coastal Europe and the steppes of Central Asia, sea wormwood is a low, mounding subshrub with finely cut, silver-gray foliage and a sharper, more resinous scent than common wormwood. Central Asian populations were historically the commercial source of santonin, an anthelmintic compound extracted from the dried, unopened flower heads before synthetic alternatives replaced it. In the garden its salt tolerance and compact silver mass make it a useful edging plant for coastal gravel gardens, and it has also been used in small quantities to flavor regional bitters. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and prevent the base from becoming woody and open. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Seagrape
description: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; seagrape is one of the most iconic plants of Florida and Caribbean coastal areas — a native evergreen shrub or small tree with enormous, nearly round leaves 6–12 inches across with distinctive red veining that deepen to a rich burgundy in winter. It grows naturally in coastal dune scrub and maritime hammocks, one of the very few trees adapted to grow in pure beach sand with salt spray exposure. The clusters of grape-like fruits ripen to deep purple in late summer and fall, eaten fresh (moderately tart) or made into jelly and wine. Seagrape is critical habitat for coastal wildlife and an important sea-turtle nesting beach plant; it is legally protected in Florida — never collect from wild populations. It is used extensively as a hedge, screen, and windbreak in zone 10–11 coastal gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Searles Cranberry (Heirloom Wisconsin Cranberry)
description: Searles was discovered as a wild seedling in 1893 near Wisconsin Rapids, Wisconsin, and went on to become one of the historically dominant heirloom cultivars of the North American cranberry industry, still accounting for a meaningful share of Wisconsin bog acreage today. It is a medium-early ripening selection producing large, bright red berries, though the fruit does not store as long as Howes and is generally used soon after harvest rather than kept for winter storage. Vines are vigorous and well suited to the cooler bog conditions of the upper Midwest, tolerating traditional winter flooding for cold protection. As with all cranberries, success depends on strongly acidic, saturated bog soil and a reliable irrigation or flood source. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Seascape Strawberry
description: 'Seascape' is a day-neutral strawberry that produces large, firm, sweet berries continuously from late spring through fall regardless of day length. Set crowns at soil level so the growing point is neither buried nor exposed, spacing plants about a foot apart in raised beds or containers. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist with drip irrigation and straw mulch. Pinch off early flowers for the first few weeks after planting to build strong plants, then allow continuous fruiting. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Seashore Mangosteen (Beach Mangosteen)
description: Seashore mangosteen thrives in the tough coastal conditions its name suggests: plant it in full sun to partial shade in sandy or rocky, well-drained soil, where it tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil far better than true mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana). Native to the coastal forests of Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam, it is a small to medium tree bearing smooth, beaked, pinkish-red fruit with segmented, juicy white pulp that tastes tart and citrusy with a faint banana note, milder and more sour than purple mangosteen. Botanists consider it one of the likely wild parents involved in the natural origin of true mangosteen, making it an interesting collector's tree in addition to an edible one. It has essentially no frost tolerance and needs sustained warmth and humidity, but its drought and salt tolerance make it a good option for tropical coastal gardens where G. mangostana would fail outright. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Seaside Spinach (Heat-Tolerant Savoy Hybrid)
description: Direct sow into well-drained beds and thin to stand a few inches apart, keeping soil consistently moist to support quick establishment in warm soil. This hybrid was bred with above-average heat tolerance and downy mildew resistance, allowing it to be sown earlier in fall or later into spring than many spinach types without bolting prematurely. Its dark green, savoyed leaves hold good texture and flavor even as temperatures rise, making it a strong pick for extending the cool-season window along the Gulf Coast. Matures in 40–45 days from seed.

name: Sebring Blueberry (Very Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry for Deep South Gardens)
description: Set out dormant bushes in winter into strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil, siting plants where cold air won't pool, since Sebring's very low chill requirement pushes bloom unusually early. Developed by the University of Florida blueberry breeding program, Sebring was selected specifically for the mild, often chill-deficient winters of central and south Florida, making it one of the better southern highbush choices for the warmest pockets of zone 9-10 where many other blueberry cultivars fail to break dormancy reliably. Berries are medium-sized with good flavor, and though partially self-fertile, fruit set improves with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar planted nearby. Because Sebring flowers so early, protect open blooms from occasional late cold snaps and keep the root zone consistently moist through the Florida dry season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Seckel Pear
description: Seckel is a small, intensely sweet American dessert pear often called the sugar pear. It shows useful resistance to fire blight and crops reliably in home orchards. Plant a second European pear such as Bartlett nearby for cross-pollination, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Train to a central leader, thin the abundant fruit, and pick while still firm to ripen in cool storage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Seematjan Rambutan
description: Seematjan is a long-established Indonesian rambutan cultivar from Java, grown for medium-sized, red, softly spined fruit with sweet, very juicy, easily separating flesh -- a texture many growers rate above the firmer commercial exports like Rongrien. It is an older selection that has been a dooryard favorite for generations but is less commonly grown commercially outside Southeast Asia because the soft fruit bruises and ships poorly. Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from wind, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit development, since rambutan is intolerant of drought stress at any life stage. Like all rambutan, Seematjan is strictly tropical and has essentially no frost tolerance. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Segundo Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Red-Skinned Japanese Plum)
description: Segundo was developed by the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program in Byron, Georgia, the same station that produced Byrongold and Ruby Sweet, and bears red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit that ripens mid-to-late June, somewhat later than earlier Gulf-series selections. The fruit is soft-textured and best used fresh shortly after harvest rather than stored. Its chill requirement of roughly 400-500 hours places it toward the upper end of what the Gulf South can reliably deliver, so it is best reserved for zone 8 gardens with fuller winter chill rather than the warmest coastal zone 9 sites. Plant a second compatible Japanese plum cultivar nearby, since Segundo is not dependably self-fruitful. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Self Blanche Cauliflower (Classic Self-Wrapping-Leaf Cauliflower)
description: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower variety whose outer leaves naturally curl inward to cover the developing head as it forms, largely eliminating the tedious task of hand-tying leaves over the curd to keep it white, a labor-saving trait especially appreciated by home gardeners growing more than a plant or two. It produces solid, well-formed white heads of good size and quality with this convenient self-blanching habit doing most of the work automatically. Check occasionally to make sure leaves are covering the head adequately, tying loosely if needed, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before curds begin to separate or yellow. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Self-Heal
description: Surface-sow seeds onto moist soil in early spring; a 2–3 week cold stratification in the fridge before sowing can improve germination rates. Self-heal spreads by stolons and will naturalize into a dense mat in moist, partly shaded spots; it tolerates light foot traffic and can work as a lawn substitute. Harvest aerial parts — leaves, stems, and flowers — when plants are in full bloom throughout summer, using them in poultices, teas, and infused preparations traditionally associated with wound healing. The purple flower spikes are also attractive and pollinator-friendly, making self-heal a useful dual-purpose ground cover. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Selma Fino Fennel (Florence Bulbing)
description: Selma Fino is an Italian Florence fennel cultivar selected for large, heavy, uniform white bulbs and strong resistance to bolting when sown in cool spring conditions. Sow directly and thin seedlings so bulbs have room to swell, then hill soil around the base as the bulb develops to keep it blanched, tender, and mild. Its sweet, pronounced anise flavor makes it popular for both raw and cooked preparations, and it holds in the garden longer than many older bulbing strains before splitting or flowering. A fall sowing timed to mature in cool autumn weather often produces the largest, most tender bulbs. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Selma Zebra Pole Bean (Purple-Streaked Early Snap Bean)
description: Selma Zebra is a distinctively marked pole snap bean, its green pods streaked with purple zigzag patterning that fades somewhat when cooked but makes for an eye-catching harvest basket. It matures notably early for a climbing bean, and the tender, fleshy pods are best picked young for fresh snap use. Like other regionally maintained heirlooms, it is kept alive mainly through small seed companies and seed-saver networks rather than large commercial catalogs. Give it a sturdy trellis and pick often to encourage continued pod set through the growing season. Matures in 55–62 days from seed.

name: Selma Zesta Pole Bean (Zelma Zesta Heirloom Snap Bean)
description: Selma Zesta, also circulated under the spelling Zelma Zesta, is a Southern heirloom pole snap bean maintained in small-scale seed exchange circles rather than mass commercial production. Vigorous climbing vines produce rounded, fleshy pods with good snap-bean flavor and texture, harvested young for fresh eating in the tradition of Appalachian and Southern cornfield-style pole beans. It is a good candidate for gardeners looking to grow out and help preserve a regionally distinct heirloom that has not been widely commercialized. Provide a tall, sturdy support and pick regularly to keep vines productive through the season. Matures in 62–70 days from seed.

name: Semanggi (Indonesian Water Clover)
description: Plant divisions after last frost into wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; Semanggi spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container or contained bog bed. Small, four-lobed leaves resembling a four-leaf clover float or stand just above the mud of rice paddies and shallow wetlands across Indonesia, where the tender young leaves and stems are harvested and traditionally steamed as the key ingredient in the East Javanese dish pecel semanggi, tossed with a spicy peanut sauce. This true fern (not a clover, despite the resemblance) spreads readily by creeping rhizomes across wet mud, forming a low, dense mat useful for the shallow-water margin of a bog garden or paddy-style planting. Harvest young leaves and stems regularly for the best eating quality, and keep the planting confined to prevent it from spreading beyond the intended wet area. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Seminole Pumpkin
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Seminole pumpkin is a historic Native American heirloom cultivated by the Seminole people of Florida for generations and is exceptionally well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where most pumpkins and butternut squash struggle with vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat collapse. It produces tan-buff, round to pear-shaped fruits weighing 5–10 pounds on very vigorous vines that can reach 15–20 feet — the vines are traditionally trained up trees or fences in Florida to keep the fruits off the moist ground. The buff-orange flesh has excellent butternut-like flavor, keeping quality of months, and outstanding resistance to diseases and insects that devastate other squash. Once established, vines are genuinely drought-tolerant. One of the most important heirloom vegetables for sustainable subtropical gardening. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Seminole Tangelo (Self-Fertile Duncan Grapefruit x Dancy Tangerine Hybrid)
description: Seminole is a historic USDA-bred tangelo (Duncan grapefruit crossed with Dancy tangerine) valued for richly flavored, deep reddish-orange, very juicy flesh that many growers consider among the best-tasting of all tangelos, though the fruit is seedy and better suited to fresh eating and juicing than to easy peeling. Unlike Orlando and Minneola tangelos, Seminole is self-fertile and sets a full crop without a second citrus variety planted nearby. Fruit ripens later than most Gulf Coast citrus, typically hanging on the tree from late winter into spring and extending the home harvest season. As with other tangelos, cold hardiness is moderate rather than exceptional, so protect trees during hard freezes in zone 9a. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Seneca Pecan (USDA Compact Cold-Hardy Northern Pecan)
description: Seneca was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service, patented in 2023, from a 1997 cross of two northern-origin selections, NC-2B and NC-4, themselves derived from the classic native pecans Colby and Peruque. It was bred specifically for the northern edge of the pecan range: the tree is compact, breaks bud late in spring, and stops growth early in fall, giving it strong freeze tolerance in regions where standard Gulf South cultivars struggle. Seneca produces high-quality, cream-kerneled nuts early in the season and carries useful resistance to pecan scab. Its size and hardiness make it a good fit for northern gardeners well outside the traditional Gulf Coast pecan belt. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Seneca White Corn (Haudenosaunee White Flour Corn)
description: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow for stability, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling. Seneca White is a traditional white flour/flint corn central to Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) agriculture in what is now upstate New York, grown for generations alongside beans and squash in the Three Sisters planting system. The soft, starchy white kernels are traditionally parched, ground, or simmered into corn soup, and community-led seed-saving efforts such as the Iroquois White Corn Project have kept this culturally vital variety in cultivation after it nearly disappeared from wider circulation in the twentieth century. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Senegal Date Palm (Multistem Date Palm)
description: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Senegal date palm is the most important palm of tropical Africa — a naturally multi-trunked, suckering palm (producing clusters of arching trunks that grow to 25 feet and lean outward from a common base) native to riverbanks, lake margins, and moist savannas across tropical Africa from Senegal to Tanzania. The multi-stemmed, arching, clustering growth habit creates an instantly recognizable, lush tropical silhouette quite different from the single-trunked date palms. The small date-like fruits are edible, used locally for food and wine. More cold-hardy than most Phoenix species other than the Canary Island date palm, tolerating brief temperatures to about 22°F when mature and established — making it one of the hardiest of all fruiting palms. An outstanding ornamental for large spaces where its spreading, multi-stemmed habit can develop. Widely naturalized and invasive in Florida. Matures in 1095–3650 days from seed.

name: Senposai (Japanese Heat-Tolerant Hybrid Leafy Green)
description: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 8–14 inches apart; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again from about 30 days; Senposai is mild enough to eat raw as well as cooked; spring plantings should go in very early since it bolts in sustained heat. Senposai is a hybrid leafy green developed in Japan by crossing common cabbage (Brassica oleracea) with komatsuna or Japanese mustard spinach (Brassica rapa var. perviridis), producing a vigorous, fast-growing green that combines characteristics of both parents — the large, smooth, broadly oval leaves of cabbage with the faster maturity, milder flavor, and somewhat greater heat tolerance of komatsuna. The resulting hybrid fills a useful niche in both Japanese home gardens and warm-climate gardens worldwide: it is ready for harvest significantly faster than heading cabbages (40–60 days versus 80–120), produces continuously as a cut-and-come-again crop rather than requiring a single heading harvest, and tolerates heat better than most brassicas while retaining the mild, slightly sweet, cabbage-family flavor without the sharpness of mustard greens. Senposai is versatile in the kitchen — the large, smooth leaves are excellent raw in salads, quickly stir-fried or sautéed, braised in Japanese-style dashimono or miso soup, or used like savoy cabbage leaves for wrapping. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Senposai is most valuable as a fall-through-spring cool-season green, sown from September through February for harvest from October through April. Available from Kitazawa Seed Company and other Asian vegetable seed specialists. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.
