name: Sensational! Lavender (Giant Long-Spiked Lavandin)
description: Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, amending heavy soil with coarse sand or gravel; Sensational! is a robust lavandin hybrid bred for exceptionally large size, with vigorous silvery foliage and some of the longest, most strongly fragrant flower spikes available in a garden lavender, held well above the foliage on tall, sturdy stems. Its bigger stature and heavier bloom make it a strong choice as a specimen plant, low hedge, or cut-flower and dried-lavender crop where scale and bloom quantity matter. Like other lavandins it is more tolerant of humidity than pure English lavender, though good air circulation and lean, fast-draining soil remain essential to prevent crown rot. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to maintain a tidy mound and encourage a second, lighter bloom later in the season. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Sentinel Blueberry (Vigorous Early-Season University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Sentinel is a vigorous, high-yielding southern highbush blueberry approved for release by the University of Florida in 2020 and bred for early-season production with no known significant disease issues. Its firm berries have scored well above older standard varieties like Emerald in consumer taste panels, and the bush's naturally good leafing habit means it typically does not require hydrogen cyanamide defoliation sprays to break dormancy evenly, simplifying management for home growers. The upright, productive plant suits both hand harvest and mechanical picking and has performed consistently across Florida growing regions. Provide highly acidic, well-drained soil and pair with another early-season southern highbush cultivar for best pollination. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: September Sun Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Variegated Fruiting Kolomikta Kiwi)
description: Plant a rooted cutting of September Sun in spring against a sturdy trellis or fence in humus-rich, well-drained soil, and pair it with a male Actinidia kolomikta vine nearby since this cultivar is a fruiting female that needs a pollinator to set fruit. Give it a site with dappled or filtered light rather than harsh all-day sun, which keeps the foliage's dramatic pink-and-white variegation from scorching while the vine still ripens its small, smooth-skinned, sweet kiwiberries in late summer. The grape-sized fruit tastes like a sweeter, thinner-skinned version of grocery-store kiwifruit and can be eaten skin-and-all straight off the vine. Because it thrives with part-shade protection and doubles as an ornamental accent, September Sun suits a partly shaded arbor or fence where both fruit and foliage color are wanted. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sequoia Strawberry (California Large-Fruited Heat-Tolerant Winter Strawberry)
description: In warm climates (zones 8–10), plant in fall for a spring harvest; in cooler climates plant in early spring; Sequoia produces very large, sweet berries with tender flesh that is best consumed fresh — it has less firmness than modern commercial varieties, making it ideal for home gardens where immediate consumption is the goal rather than shipping. Sequoia strawberry is a University of California variety (released 1953) that became one of the most widely planted strawberries in California commercial production in the mid-20th century and has remained popular in California and mild-winter gardens for its large, intensely flavored berries that represent the ideal of the fresh-eating home garden strawberry. The variety was developed by Dr. Harold Thomas at UC Riverside specifically for California's mild-winter, warm-spring growing conditions — conditions very different from the cool, humid eastern states where most strawberry varieties were bred. Sequoia produces berries that are exceptionally large (often double the diameter of standard varieties), vivid red, with a characteristic deep sweetness and complex strawberry fragrance that makes them among the most intensely flavored of any readily available variety. The flesh is somewhat soft — Sequoia berries bruise easily and have short shelf life (2–3 days maximum), which is why this variety essentially disappeared from commercial production as the industry shifted toward firmer-berried shipping varieties — but this same softness contributes to the intense, yielding, jam-like texture that makes Sequoia exceptional for fresh eating. For zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardens, Sequoia performs well as a fall-planted winter strawberry, producing its harvest in late February through April before summer heat arrives. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Serbian Gold Quince (Leskovac, Highly Productive Balkan Quince)
description: Serbian Gold, also sold under its original local name Leskovac, is a heavy-cropping Balkan quince cultivar selected in Serbia in the early twentieth century and now widely distributed through European and North American nurseries for its reliability and good resistance to leaf blight compared with many older quince selections. It forms a broad, low-domed small tree with attractive pale pink spring blossom followed by large, aromatic, golden-yellow fruit that ripens in early to mid autumn. The tree is self-fertile and consistently productive on its own, making it a good single-tree choice for a home garden. Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and harvest once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic strong quince fragrance; the raw flesh remains firm and astringent and is best cooked into jelly, paste, or preserves. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Serendipity Sweet Corn (Bicolor TripleSweet Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Serendipity is a widely grown bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with the high sugar content and slower sugar-to-starch conversion typical of supersweet types, giving it both excellent eating quality and good holding time after picking. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 82–88 days from seed.

name: Serr English Walnut (Vigorous Early-Bearing Precocious Walnut)
description: Serr was released by the University of California in the 1960s as a fast-growing, notably precocious walnut cultivar that begins bearing at a younger age than older selections such as Franquette. Large, thin-shelled nuts with good kernel quality are borne in clusters on vigorous wood, and heavy early crops sometimes need thinning or extra bracing to prevent limbs from breaking under the weight. It leafs out fairly early in spring, so it is best sited away from frost pockets where late freezes could damage new growth and flowers. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and harvest as hulls begin to split in early fall. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Serrano Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors about six to eight weeks ahead of transplanting and provide bright light and warmth for sturdy seedlings. Move plants outdoors once the soil warms and frost danger has passed, spacing them about a foot and a half apart. These prolific plants set many slender, spicy peppers used green for salsas and pico de gallo. Pick fruits green for the classic sharp heat, or leave them to ripen red for a slightly sweeter kick. Steady moisture and full sun keep production high through the season. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Serrano Pepper
description: Start seeds indoors with warm soil about eight weeks before transplanting, since peppers need heat to germinate. Move seedlings outdoors only after nights are reliably warm, spacing plants for good airflow. This heirloom produces slender 3-4 inch peppers with medium heat around 10,000 to 25,000 Scoville units and a bright, crisp flavor. Harvest green for classic salsa heat, or let the pods ripen to red for a slightly sweeter, hotter bite. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Sertaneja Acerola (BRS 152)
description: Sertaneja, registered as BRS 152, is one of a series of acerola cultivars released by Brazil's EMBRAPA agricultural research agency, bred for reliable production and good fruit quality in the hot, drought-prone growing regions of Brazil, the world's leading acerola-producing country. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, watering regularly during establishment and through flowering and fruit set, though the cultivar tolerates brief dry spells better than many other tropical fruiting shrubs once established. Like other acerola selections it flowers and fruits in repeated flushes through the warm season, yielding small, bright red, extremely vitamin C-rich fruit that must be harvested and used within a day or two of ripening. Light pruning after each fruiting flush keeps the shrub compact and encourages continued flowering. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Service Tree
description: Collect ripe fruits in autumn and extract seeds, then sow directly in a prepared outdoor seedbed or in deep pots left outside to receive natural winter chilling. Seeds require 90–180 days near freezing to break dormancy and will not germinate reliably without this cold period. Transplant seedlings to their permanent location in well-drained soil once they reach 6–12 inches tall, ideally in their second or third year. Patience is essential: trees take 7–15 years to bear their first crop of small, astringent sorbets, which soften and sweeten after a frost or brief bletting period. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Serviceberry (Juneberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full to partial sun; serviceberry tolerates wet sites and woodland edges better than most fruiting shrubs. No cross-pollinator is required, though planting two or more selections increases yield. Fruits ripen in late spring to early June, turning from red to deep purple-blue when fully sweet — birds will compete for them, so netting is advisable. Prune crossing or crowded stems in late winter to maintain an open, multi-stemmed form and remove root suckers to control spread. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sesame
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in rows 18–24 in apart after soil reaches at least 70°F; sesame seed is very small, so mixing with dry sand aids even distribution and prevents clumping. Thin to 6–12 in once plants are 3 in tall and keep well-weeded until the canopy closes. The upright plants produce attractive tubular flowers along the stem that develop into rectangular seed capsules; the key challenge is timing harvest before 'shattering' — when ripe capsules split and scatter seed spontaneously. Cut entire stalks when the bottom capsules begin to yellow, invert plants into large paper bags, and allow to dry for a week indoors; the capsules then split easily and seed falls into the bag when shaken. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Seto Satsuma (Flat, Thin-Peeled Texas Superstar Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and feed and water regularly through the growing season to size up the crop. Seto produces distinctly flat, smooth, thin-skinned fruit that ships and stacks better than rounder satsuma types, with virtually seedless, easy-peeling segments carrying a sweet, slightly tangy flavor. Once established, mature trees tolerate brief drops to roughly 10-15F, making Seto one of the more cold-tolerant satsuma selections recommended for zone 8b-9a dooryard citrus. Site it in a warm microclimate and protect young trees with frost cloth for the first two or three winters until the root system matures. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Seuri Asian Pear
description: Seuri produces round, medium-size fruit with yellow-brown skin and crisp flesh that is sweet with a touch of tartness and a hint of apricot, considered by growers to be among the most flavorful of the nashi pears rather than the milder taste typical of many Asian pear cultivars. Its unusually early bloom time is its most distinctive trait and requires a compatible cross-pollinator flowering in the same window. As with most Asian pears, fruit is picked crisp and eaten fresh rather than ripened off the tree, and the tree is generally susceptible to fire blight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Seven Top Turnip (Leafy Greens Turnip for Gulf South)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top is a turnip variety grown exclusively for its prolific, tender, flavorful greens (tops) rather than its roots — the roots of Seven Top are small, tough, and not typically eaten, but the plant produces an extremely vigorous canopy of large, lush, tender, deeply flavored greens that are among the most productive and flavorful of all Southern cooking greens. The variety's name describes its characteristic of producing an exceptionally dense canopy of seven or more vigorous shoots per plant — creating a tall, productive leafy mass that yields far more greens per plant than Purple Top or other root-type turnips when grown for tops. Seven Top is a staple of traditional Gulf South fall and winter gardening — it's the turnip greens variety most commonly grown for pot greens in Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, and Georgia gardens where a large quantity of flavorful cooking greens from a small space is the primary objective. The greens are best harvested young and tender (6–10 inches tall) and become progressively more robust in flavor as they mature — a quality that appeals to those who prefer the traditional strong, minerally flavor of Southern cooking greens. Seven Top tolerates temperatures well into the teens once established. Cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting to 4 inches, allowing regrowth) produces multiple flushes through the cool season. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Seven Year Love Squash (Long-Storage Japanese Heirloom Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed after the last frost, spacing hills to give the sprawling vines room to run, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage a strong root system. Seven Year Love is a Japanese heirloom moschata squash, named and prized above nearly all other winter squash for its exceptional keeping ability — properly cured fruit stored in a cool, dry spot can remain sound and good to eat for many months, and the name reflects a reputation for storage life that far outlasts typical winter squash. The tan to buff, hard-shelled fruit has dense, sweet, deep orange flesh that, like other moschata types, holds its quality and flavor well even after long storage rather than turning stringy or bland. Cure fruit in a warm, dry location for one to two weeks after harvest to harden the rind and improve storage life, then keep in a cool, dry, well-ventilated space out of direct sun. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Severn Sea Rosemary (Compact Semi-Trailing Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Severn Sea is a compact, semi-trailing rosemary cultivar with gracefully arching branches, striking a middle ground between the tall, upright habit of culinary types like Tuscan Blue and the fully flat, prostrate groundcover forms. It produces an especially heavy show of deep violet-blue flowers in spring, showier than many other rosemary cultivars, in addition to fragrant, flavorful foliage suitable for cooking. It performs well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden where its arching form can spill attractively over an edge, and like all rosemary it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Sevillano Olive (Large-Fruited Spanish Table Olive)
description: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sevillano is a Spanish-origin olive cultivar known in California and other American growing regions as the classic large-fruited table olive, producing some of the biggest olives of any commonly grown cultivar — prized for canning and curing as whole table olives rather than for oil, where its low oil content is a disadvantage. Trees are vigorous and grow considerably larger than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina, so give Sevillano plenty of room to reach its full spreading form. Harvest green for classic Spanish-style brine-cured green olives, or allow fruit to ripen to black for a milder cured product; either way, fresh-picked olives are intensely bitter and must be cured in lye or long brine soaks before they are palatable. Sevillano is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second olive cultivar nearby improves both fruit set and yield. Established trees are drought-tolerant and long-lived, tolerating the alkaline, low-fertility soils typical of much of the Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Seychelles Pole Bean
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is warm, planting alongside a sturdy trellis or pole seven to nine feet tall. This All-America Selections winner bears clusters of tender four-to-six-inch pods well ahead of many standard pole beans. Pick pods young and often to keep the vines producing over a long season. Even, moderate watering during flowering and pod set gives the best yields. Avoid handling the plants when wet to reduce the spread of disease. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Seyval Blanc Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)
description: This French-American hybrid produces tight clusters of small green-white berries used for crisp, high-acid white wine and is valued in cooler regions where vinifera struggle to ripen. It shows good resistance to downy and powdery mildew compared to vinifera but is prone to bunch rot in humid climates, so canopy management and cluster thinning improve air circulation. Prune to a cane or cordon system and expect vines to reach full production by the third or fourth year. It is more cold-hardy than most vinifera, tolerating winter lows that would damage traditional wine grapes. Matures in 150–165 days from transplant.

name: Shadblow Serviceberry (Downy Serviceberry)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; shadblow tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most Amelanchier species — excellent for rain gardens, streambanks, and moist woodland edges. Amelanchier canadensis (shadblow serviceberry or downy serviceberry) is one of the most widespread native Amelanchier species of the eastern United States, growing naturally in bogs, streambanks, wet woods, and swampy thickets from Maine to Georgia and inland to the Great Lakes. The plant flowers in earliest spring — often the first woody plant to bloom, sometimes even before forsythia — with spectacular clusters of pure white, 5-petaled flowers on bare branches that open as the leaves begin to emerge. The flowers are followed in June by small (1/3-inch), round, purple-black to dark blue-purple berries with a mild, sweet, almond-apple flavor distinctly different from blueberries — produced abundantly enough that a mature shrub can yield several quarts of fruit. The berries are excellent fresh, in pies, jams, pancake syrup, and anywhere blueberries are used. The name 'shadblow' (also written shad-bush or shad-blow) derives from the colonial observation that the tree bloomed when alewife and shad fish began running up rivers from the sea — a reliable calendar indicator for early spring fishing. Notable for better tolerance of wet soils than smooth serviceberry (A. laevis). Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Shady Acres Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Hedge Rosemary)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants for a hedge line if grown as a boundary planting. Shady Acres is a vigorous, strongly upright rosemary cultivar that grows noticeably taller and narrower than many culinary rosemary selections, making it a popular choice for tall herbal hedges and topiary rather than groundcover use. The narrow, dark green leaves carry the classic strong culinary rosemary flavor and can be harvested year-round in mild climates. Light pale-blue flowers appear mainly in winter and spring; prune after flowering to maintain a dense, upright form. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Shagbark Hickory
description: Shagbark hickory is a stately native North American tree recognized by its exfoliating, shaggy gray bark; it produces small, round nuts with thin shells and exceptionally sweet, richly flavored kernels prized over pecans by many nut connoisseurs. Trees are monoecious and wind-pollinated; two or more trees improve nut set but a single tree can produce modest crops. Seedlings bear unpredictably and may take 10–20 years to fruit; grafted improved selections (Grainger, Wilcox) begin bearing in 5–7 years. Nuts drop in autumn when the four-sectioned husk splits open; collect promptly before squirrels take them and cure for 2–3 weeks before cracking. Matures in 2920–5475 days from transplant.

name: Shallot
description: Separate shallot clusters into individual cloves and plant each with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, 1 in deep, in fertile, well-drained soil. Each clove multiplies into a cluster of 6–12 new bulbs by season's end, so generous spacing pays off. Harvest when most of the green tops have toppled and turned papery. Dry clusters on screens in good airflow for 2–3 weeks and store in a cool, airy spot; well-cured shallots keep for 6 months or more. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Shaman's Blue Popcorn
description: Shaman's Blue was the first widely offered dark-blue hybrid popcorn, bred for large, tender kernels that pop bright white despite their deep bluish-purple hull color, unlike the small, chewy kernels typical of older open-pollinated blue popcorns. Leave 8 inch ears on the stalk until husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, then cure indoors before shelling and storing in a sealed container to preserve popping moisture. The anthocyanin-rich hull gives raw kernels a deeper color than yellow popcorns, which growers selling at farmers markets often use as a selling point alongside its reliably fluffy pop. Choose this variety when a gardener wants the visual novelty of blue corn without sacrificing tender, large-kernel popping performance. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Shandong Hardneck Garlic
description: Break bulbs into individual cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes. This early-maturing Turban-type hardneck yields white bulbs with six to eight cloves and matures noticeably faster than most hardnecks. Mulch after planting to protect the cloves through winter and conserve moisture. Cut the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb sizing. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Shanghai Pak Choi (Shanghai Bok Choy)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; keep evenly watered, since any dry stress speeds bolting. Shanghai pak choi is a compact, fast-maturing bok choy type with pale jade-green, spoon-shaped petioles and glossy dark green leaves that form a tidy, vase-shaped rosette — smaller and quicker to mature than standard white-stemmed bok choy varieties, and prized for its exceptionally tender, mild, sweet stems that need no peeling or trimming before cooking. Its speed and compact size make it ideal for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season, providing a steady supply of baby greens for stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. In warm-winter climates like the Gulf South it can be grown nearly through the whole cool season, from fall through early spring, before rising temperatures push it to bolt. Zone 2–10. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Shangri-La Mulberry (Everbearing Compact Gulf South Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shangri-La is a compact, everbearing mulberry selection valued for Gulf South gardens where the combination of heat tolerance, low chill requirement, extended fruit production, and moderate size makes it one of the most practical fresh fruit trees for zone 9 home landscapes. The long, cylindrical, dark-purple to black fruits (1.5–2 inches) are sweet, juicy, and excellent for fresh eating, jam, jelly, and freezing — the rich, complex mulberry flavor is one of the finest of any easily grown fruit tree. 'Shangri-La' fruits over an extended season (typically March through June in zone 9, with some additional fall fruiting) rather than in a single compressed flush — providing weeks of fresh mulberry harvest rather than an overwhelming glut. The tree's smaller mature size (8–12 feet compared to 20–30 feet for seedling mulberries) makes it manageable in typical home landscapes and allows netting to protect fruit from birds, which are very competitive with human harvesters for mulberry fruit. Mulberries in the Gulf South require very few chill hours (100–200 hours) and fruit reliably in warm winters that defeat other tree fruits. Established trees are highly drought-tolerant and require minimal care — the most significant maintenance is the control of surface root spread and the cleanup of fallen fruit on paved surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Shankhpushpi
description: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; shankhpushpi is a low, spreading groundcover that tolerates poor, dry soil and needs minimal supplemental water once established. Small, hairy, gray-green leaves and delicate, pale blue to white, funnel-shaped morning-glory-like flowers cover a low, sprawling groundcover native to dry open ground across India, harvested whole (leaves, stems, and flowers together) for use in traditional Ayurvedic preparations valued for their calming properties. Its low, spreading habit and drought tolerance make it a workable, unfussy groundcover for a warm-climate medicinal or ethnobotanical garden bed, tolerating heat and poor soil with little care once established. Harvest above-ground growth as needed through the growing season, and expect the plant to die back in any significant cold, behaving as a tender perennial in the warmest zones or an annual further north. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Shanxi Li Jujube (Large Pear Jujube)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Shanxi Li shrugs off drought, poor soil, and the humid heat of a Gulf South summer far better than most fruit trees, and is naturally resistant to most pests and diseases that trouble other orchard crops. Named for its native Shanxi province in northern China, this heirloom selection produces the largest fruit of the Li-type jujubes, with shiny reddish-brown, date-shaped fruit that can reach over 2 inches long. The crisp, sweet flesh is excellent eaten fresh off the tree and turns into a chewy, date-like treat when dried. Self-fruitful, it will set a good crop on its own, though yields improve with a second jujube cultivar nearby, and the tree handles winter temperatures well below zero once dormant. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sharlyn Melon (Sweet Orange-Fleshed Honeydew-Cantaloupe Hybrid)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sharlyn is a hybrid melon combining traits of honeydew and cantaloupe, with smooth, pale ribbed skin like a honeydew but sweet, aromatic, pale orange flesh with the rich flavor of a cantaloupe, giving it an unusual combination of exterior and interior appearance that often surprises gardeners who haven't grown it before. Unlike true cantaloupe, ripe fruit does not slip easily from the vine, so judge ripeness by a color shift toward pale cream-yellow and a sweet fragrance at the blossom end rather than by fruit separation. It stores somewhat better after harvest than standard cantaloupe, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting a melon that holds a bit longer at peak quality. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Sharp Velvet Pomegranate (Sharp's Velvet)
description: Sharp Velvet is a California selection prized for its very dark red-to-purple skin and deeply colored, soft-seeded arils with a rich sweet-tart flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, bearing large fruit comparable in size to Wonderful but with a notably darker rind and juice, making it popular for fresh juicing where deep color is desired. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it is drought-tolerant once established and, like most pomegranates, is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator. It suits warm-summer regions where fruit can fully color and sweeten before fall harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sharpblue Blueberry
description: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) amended with peat or composted pine bark; Sharpblue is a Southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program and released in 1976 as one of the first cultivars specifically bred for extremely low-chill environments — it requires only 150–200 chill hours and thrives in zone 9–10 where rabbiteye varieties often fail to fruit consistently. This makes it particularly valuable for gardeners in coastal zone 9b, south Florida, and similar climates where winter chill accumulation is marginal. Berries are medium-sized, dark blue, very flavorful and aromatic — quality rivals highbush varieties grown in cooler climates. The plant is slightly tender and may be damaged by hard freezes below 15°F, though it recovers quickly. It is nearly evergreen in frost-free areas and can produce two crops per year in very warm locations. An excellent container blueberry for patios in the deep South. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sharwil Avocado
description: A Guatemalan-Mexican hybrid bred in Australia and now closely associated with Hawaii's Kona coast, Sharwil is unusual for staying green-skinned and bumpy even at full ripeness rather than darkening like Hass or Lamb Hass. Its flesh runs remarkably high in oil, 15 to 25 percent, giving a rich, nutty, almost meaty flavor and an unusually high flesh-to-seed ratio. As a Type B bloomer it ripens through the winter months, filling a harvest window that complements Type A cultivars such as Hass and Pinkerton rather than competing directly with them. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shasta Gold Mandarin
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Shasta Gold is a University of California-developed mandarin hybrid combining the superior flavor of Murcott mandarin with improved disease resistance and the late-season ripening of Encore — producing large, orange, flattened fruits with a very low seed count (typically 2–5 seeds), deep-orange flesh, and a rich, complex sweetness that many citrus experts rate among the finest mandarins available. The fruit holds on the tree without internal quality loss for 6–8 weeks after ripening (January–March), allowing extended harvest over a long window. The moderate-sized tree is easy to manage and produces heavy crops once established. In zone 9 Shasta Gold benefits from afternoon heat reflected from walls or pavement to ensure full fruit ripening; place against a south-facing wall in marginal locations. Trees are typically grafted onto trifoliate or flying dragon rootstock for cold hardiness. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shatavari (Wild Asparagus, Indian Asparagus)
description: Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or nearby shrub for the scrambling, thorny stems to climb, as this relative of garden asparagus can sprawl or vine several feet. Fine feathery foliage and small white flowers give way to red berries, but the plant is grown primarily for its clustered tuberous roots, traditionally harvested at one to two years and used in Ayurvedic tonics. It is frost-tender and best treated as a container specimen or annual outside zones 9-11, overwintered indoors in a bright spot where winters are cold. Keep soil evenly moist during the growing season and reduce watering once roots go dormant in cooler months. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Shawnee Blackberry (University of Arkansas Large Late-Season Thorned Blackberry)
description: Plant bare-root canes 3–4 feet apart in rows 8–10 feet apart; tip-prune new canes at 3–4 feet in summer to encourage lateral branching. After fruiting, remove second-year (fruited) canes at ground level. Shawnee is a University of Arkansas erect blackberry released in 1985 — part of the legendary Arkansas blackberry breeding program led by Dr. James N. Moore that produced the majority of the blackberry varieties grown commercially and in home gardens across the eastern United States. The Arkansas program's systematic approach to blackberry improvement — selecting for large fruit size, good flavor, and erect cane habit suitable for mechanical harvesting — transformed blackberry production from a minor cottage-scale enterprise to a significant commercial crop. Shawnee produces very large, firm, glossy black berries (among the largest of the Arkansas releases in its era) with excellent flavor — described as rich and sweet with good balance, not overly tart. The late-season ripening of Shawnee means the fruits develop during the hottest part of the Gulf South summer (June–July in zone 9), and adequate irrigation during fruit development is important to maintain size and quality. The erect cane habit (no sprawling) makes Shawnee manageable in home gardens with a simple 2-wire T-trellis at 3 and 5 feet, providing a contained, productive planting in moderate space. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Shawnee Pecan (Early-Ripening Scab-Resistant USDA Release)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Shawnee is a USDA-released pecan bred for good resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most serious losses in humid, high-rainfall pecan-growing regions, combined with notably precocious bearing, meaning young trees begin producing meaningful nut crops earlier than many older varieties. The medium to large nuts have good kernel quality and ripen relatively early in the fall, an advantage in areas where hurricane season or early frost can threaten a late-ripening crop still on the tree. The moderately vigorous tree is well suited to home orchards wanting a scab-resistant option without the extreme size of some larger pecan cultivars. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the first significant crops within five to seven years of planting. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: She Chuang Zi (Monnier's Snowparsley)
description: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; She Chuang Zi is grown as a cool-season annual and is harvested for its seed once the flat seed umbels turn brown and dry. Finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat-topped clusters of small white flowers, typical of the carrot family, are followed by small, ribbed, aromatic seeds that are the part collected and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, historically applied topically for skin conditions. An easy, weedy annual related to Queen Anne's lace and wild carrot, it grows quickly from seed in ordinary garden soil with minimal care and self-sows readily if seed heads are left standing. Harvest seed umbels once they have dried and turned brown on the plant, and thresh the small seeds free before storing in a cool, dry place. Matures in 100–140 days from seed.

name: Shea Tree (Shea Butter Tree, Karite)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep, sandy-loam soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — shea is a true savanna tree adapted to seasonal drought; requires decades to reach full production. Vitellaria paradoxa (shea tree or karite) is one of the most culturally and economically important trees in sub-Saharan Africa — a long-lived (200–300 years), slow-growing deciduous tree native to the dry savanna and Sudan zone from West Africa east to Uganda and Ethiopia. For millennia, shea has been a tree of extraordinary importance: the large seeds (shea nuts) yield shea fat (shea butter or karite butter), a solid, ivory-colored fat with exceptional cosmetic properties — outstanding skin and hair moisturizing ability, high stearic acid content, resistance to rancidity — that has become one of the most sought-after cosmetic ingredients worldwide and is also a major cooking fat and chocolate substitute in West African cuisine. Shea butter is one of the primary cooking fats across the West African Sahel. The sweet, green, plum-like fleshy fruit surrounding the shea nut is also edible fresh — tasting mildly sweet with a date-like softness. The tree is considered sacred in many West African cultures and is legally protected in several countries — it may not be cut down without authorization. Almost never cultivated outside Africa due to its extremely slow growth and extremely long time to first production (15–30 years from seed); a truly generational investment tree. Matures in 5475–9125 days from transplant.

name: Sheep Sorrel (Red Sorrel, Common Sorrel)
description: Direct sow in lean, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; sheep sorrel is a diminutive native of Eurasia, now naturalized as a common weed across North America in sandy, acidic, infertile soils. The small, arrowhead-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes are more strongly acidic and citrusy than common sorrel (R. acetosa), with a bright lemon-sour flavor from oxalic acid. Young leaves are excellent in salads, soups, and sauces — the same culinary uses as garden sorrel — and the plant has a long history of use in traditional medicine as a spring tonic herb. Consume in moderation as with all oxalic-acid-containing plants. The plant spreads by both seed and underground rhizomes and becomes a persistent presence once established in appropriate acidic, lean soil; treat it as a semi-wild foraged herb rather than a crop requiring intensive management. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Sheepnose Pimento Pepper (Ohio Amish Heirloom Sweet Pimento)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into the garden after soil has warmed and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Sheepnose Pimento is a cherished Ohio Amish heirloom named for its squat, heart-shaped fruit, which ripens from green to a glossy deep red and is prized for exceptionally thick, meaty walls and an intensely sweet, almost sugary flavor. Sturdy, bushy plants are highly productive over a long season, yielding abundant fruit well suited to roasting, stuffing, canning, and fresh eating. Keep soil evenly moist and fertile through fruit set, and harvest at full red ripeness for the best flavor and thickest flesh. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Sheldon Pear (Aromatic Wayne County New York Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Discovered growing on the farm of Major Sheldon in Wayne County, New York around 1815, this heirloom bears medium, round, russet-tinged pears with intensely aromatic, sweet, richly flavored flesh that once made it one of the most highly regarded fall dessert pears in the Northeast, prized by connoisseurs even though it never became a major commercial shipping variety. The tree is hardy and productive under typical Northeastern growing conditions. Harvest while still firm in early fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shellbark Hickory (Big Shellbark, Kingnut Hickory)
description: Plant in deep, moist but well-drained bottomland or alluvial soil in full sun, allowing ample space for this eventually massive tree; shellbark hickory bears the largest nuts of any hickory — up to 2.5 inches wide — with a rich, sweet, buttery flavor prized as the finest native hickory nut. It is a slow-growing but very long-lived bottomland tree of river floodplains; young trees may require 5–10 years before setting significant crops, but established trees become reliable producers for 150 years or more. The bark develops characteristic loose, curling, shaggy plates even more pronounced than shagbark hickory. Plant in deep organic-rich soil with consistent moisture; drought stress in the first few seasons significantly delays establishment and nut production. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Shelling Pea
description: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart and provide support for tall types. Consistent moisture from flowering through pod fill is critical; drought during this window sharply reduces yield. Harvest when pods are well rounded and the peas inside feel firm through the pod wall; sugar converts rapidly to starch after picking, so chill or eat immediately. Shell and freeze any surplus the same day for best sweetness. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Shenandoah Apple (PRI Disease-Resistant Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Shenandoah came out of the cooperative Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistant apple breeding program, which focused on combining genetic resistance to scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew into apples that also deliver good eating quality, reducing the spray program needed to produce clean fruit in humid, disease-prone regions. The fruit is crisp and well flavored, with red-striped skin over a yellow background, suitable for fresh eating and general kitchen use. For home orchardists in the humid South and Mid-Atlantic dealing with heavy disease pressure, multi-resistant PRI-program apples like Shenandoah offer a meaningfully easier path to a clean home apple crop than many older, disease-susceptible heirloom varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shenandoah Pawpaw (Sweet, Large-Fruited Named Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade when young (seedlings require shade protection) transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Shenandoah is one of the finest named pawpaw cultivars — selected by Kirk Pomper at Kentucky State University for its large, sweet, beautiful fruit with vanilla-custard flavor and minimal strong aftertaste that characterizes some inferior seedling-grown trees. Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is the largest tree fruit native to North America, producing fruits 3–6 inches long with yellow-green skin, creamy-yellow flesh, and a unique tropical flavor reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard combined — sometimes called 'the custard apple of the North.' Shenandoah was specifically selected for mild, sweet flavor without the bitterness or sourness that reduces the palatability of some pawpaw seedlings. The large, heavy fruits ripen in September–October in zone 7–8 and must be picked when they yield slightly to pressure — they do not ripen off the tree well and have a very short shelf life (2–3 days at room temperature, 2–3 weeks refrigerated). Pawpaws require cross-pollination from a different named cultivar; two or more plants are needed for reliable fruit production. The flowers have a faint unpleasant odor to attract fly and beetle pollinators — supplemental hand pollination or adding flowering road-killed meat near the trees during bloom significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaw performs in the northern portions; the deep South's heat and lack of winter chill can limit performance. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sheng Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Astringent Kaki)
description: Sheng is an astringent-type Asian persimmon, meaning the fruit is mouth-puckering and inedible while firm and must be allowed to soften completely to jelly-ripe before eating, at which point it turns rich, nutty, and very sweet. Fruit is notably large, flattened, and squarish with four lobes, ripening early in September through October and often holding well on the tree. The tree grows as a dwarf to semi-dwarf, upright, irregularly branched form with large glossy leaves, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards, and it is markedly more cold-tolerant than typical Asian persimmon cultivars, extending kaki growing into cooler zones than most non-astringent types can handle. Like other kaki persimmons it is self-fruitful and reliably productive once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shepherd's Purse
description: Because of its traditional use to stimulate uterine contractions, it should be avoided in pregnancy except under professional supervision. Direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring or again in fall; this fast-growing, cold-tolerant mustard-family plant self-seeds readily and often persists as a low-maintenance garden edge herb. The flowering aerial parts are traditionally dried and used as a styptic tea or tincture to help slow minor bleeding and to support postpartum recovery. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Sheridan Grape (Late-Keeping Blue Juice and Table Grape)
description: Released from the Geneva, New York breeding program, Sheridan ripens late in the season and is prized for its exceptional storage life, keeping in good condition for weeks longer than most American hybrid grapes after harvest. Its small to medium clusters of blue-black berries have a rich, wine-like flavor good for fresh eating, juice, and jelly. Because it ripens late, it needs a full growing season to reach peak sweetness, and cluster thinning helps ensure even maturity. The vine is cold-hardy and productive once established on a cane-pruned trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sherry Loquat (Semi-Dwarf Low-Acid Homestead Loquat)
description: Sherry was selected by Hugh Sherry at the USDA facility in Homestead, Florida in 1950 and is distinguished by an unusually high pulp-to-seed ratio, typically carrying only one to three small seeds compared to the four or five larger seeds common in many loquat cultivars. The thick yellow skin covers white to pale-yellow flesh with a Brix reading around 11, giving a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor with notes reminiscent of peach and apricot. Fruit ripens early, typically March through April in Florida, ahead of many later-season cultivars, which helps spread out the loquat harvest window for Gulf Coast growers who plant multiple cultivars. Because the tree stays compact, it is easier to net against birds and to hand-thin fruit clusters than larger loquat cultivars, and its dwarfing habit also makes winter cold protection more practical during rare Gulf Coast freeze events. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sherwood Jujube (Louisiana Jujube, Gulf Coast Large-Fruited Jujube)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Sherwood is vigorous and productive in the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where some Chinese jujube selections may show reduced vigor; harvest at the red-mahogany stage for best fresh eating; the round, relatively large fruits are excellent for fresh eating and air-drying. Sherwood jujube is a Gulf Coast-adapted variety that originated as a chance seedling in Louisiana — making it an American selection rather than one of the Chinese-originated varieties (Li, Lang, Honey Jar) that dominate the market. This local origin is significant: the Sherwood tree's parents were jujubes that had already adapted to the climate of coastal Louisiana over multiple generations, and the resulting variety demonstrates the kind of humid-heat tolerance and disease resistance that matters in zone 9a and Gulf Coast conditions. Jujubes are generally very adaptable and drought-tolerant, but Chinese selections optimized for the dry summers of northern China sometimes show reduced performance in the hot, humid summers of the Gulf South. Sherwood's local Louisiana heritage makes it a logical first choice for Gulf Coast gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Li and Lang combination. The fruits are large (comparable to Li), round, and flavorful at full mahogany-red maturity. Trees are vigorous and productive with good disease resistance in humid conditions. An important variety for preserving and developing Gulf Coast-adapted jujube germplasm. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sherwood Red Okra (Red Okra 98, Tennessee Heirloom)
description: Donated to Southern Exposure Seed Exchange by a Tennessee grower in the late 1970s, this fast-growing, non-prickly okra bears fat, four-inch red-and-green pods on plants with striking red stems and leaf veins. Its low mucilage keeps pods tender even when allowed to grow larger than most varieties, which forgives a missed picking day or two during peak summer harvest. The colorful pods are excellent fried and add both color and mild flavor when sliced raw and young into salads. As with most heirloom okras, its color fades toward green once cooked, but the ornamental red-tinged plants remain a garden standout all season. Matures in 53–60 days from seed.

name: Shi Hu (Dendrobium officinale)
description: Mount on bark or rock, or pot in coarse orchid bark mix, in bright, indirect light in a warm, humid location; Shi Hu is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a greenhouse or indoor orchid. Slender, jointed, cane-like stems bear narrow leaves and small, fragrant, pale yellow-green to white flowers, but the plant is prized chiefly for its thick, mucilage-rich fresh or dried stems, one of the most highly valued tonic herbs in traditional Chinese medicine and historically among the most expensive due to its slow growth and vulnerability to overharvesting in the wild. Cultivated commercially on rock faces or tree bark in parts of China to relieve pressure on rapidly declining wild populations, it can be grown similarly in a home setting mounted on bark or grown in an orchid-appropriate bark mix with good humidity and air movement. Water regularly during active growth, allow the mount or mix to dry somewhat between waterings, and maintain high humidity and warmth year-round for the best growth. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shin Kuroda Carrot
description: Sow seed shallowly in loose, deep soil and keep the surface moist during the slow germination. Unlike many carrots, this heat-tolerant Kuroda type can be sown well into late spring and summer for fall harvests. Thin seedlings to about two inches so the tapered five-inch roots with broad shoulders can size up. Steady moisture prevents cracking and keeps the roots sweet and tender. Harvest before roots become oversized for the best texture. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Shin Li Asian Pear
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Shin Li is a patented Asian pear bred from a cross of Kikusui and Tsu Li, producing medium-to-large, round-oblate fruit with smooth yellowish-green skin flecked with russet and firm, extremely juicy white flesh carrying a distinctive sweet, spicy, faintly cinnamon-like aroma. The tree grows notably more vigorously than many other Asian pear cultivars and has performed reliably even in heavy clay soils in zone 8 trial orchards, ripening a heavy crop in mid-to-late September. Cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar is required, since Shin Li will not set a good crop on its own. Keep an eye out for fire blight strikes during humid spring bloom and remove infected wood promptly, cutting well below any visible discoloration. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shinko Asian Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Russet Japanese Pear)
description: Set the bare-root tree in well-drained soil with the graft union above grade, then train to an open-center or central-leader form and thin developing fruit to one per cluster for larger size. Shinko is prized among Asian pear growers for its unusually strong resistance to fire blight, a major limitation for pear culture in humid climates, while still producing sweet, mildly tangy, crisp bronze-russeted fruit. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the fruit slips easily from the spur, and expect a productive, long-lived tree once established. Matures in 150–165 days from transplant.

name: Shinseiki Asian Pear (New Century Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; requires a pollinator — plant with Nijisseiki, Hosui, or another compatible Asian pear variety for good fruit set. Shinseiki (Japanese for 'New Century') is one of the most important commercial and home-garden Asian pear cultivars worldwide, bred in Japan in 1945 and widely grown in California, Oregon, and southern states; it produces medium-large (6–10 oz), round, smooth-skinned, pale yellow to cream-yellow fruits in August with crisp, white, juicy flesh and mild, refreshing, lightly sweet flavor. Low-chill requirement (approximately 300 chill hours) makes it excellent for Gulf Coast, Texas, and California gardens where traditional European pears fail. Fruits store well for 2–3 months refrigerated; highly productive and relatively disease-resistant compared to European pears. Cross-pollinate with Nijisseiki, Hosui, or another Asian pear for best yields. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shinsui Asian Pear (Early Red-Skinned Juicy Nashi)
description: Shinsui is a Japanese-bred Asian pear valued for ripening earlier than most nashi cultivars, giving gardeners a russet-bronze, red-blushed fruit with exceptionally juicy, sweet, crisp flesh well ahead of the main late-summer pear harvest. The tree bears young and reliably, and thinning developing fruit clusters to one or two pears per spur improves final fruit size. Grow it exactly as other Asian pears, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer such as Hosui or Kosui planted nearby. Pick fruit when it releases easily from the spur and the background skin color has turned from green to bronze, since unlike European pears, Asian pears ripen fully on the tree. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Shiny Blueberry
description: Shiny Blueberry is the low-growing native blueberry of the Florida peninsula and southeastern coastal plain, native to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained flatwoods, scrub, and longleaf pine savannas from South Carolina to Florida and west to Mississippi, forming dense, rhizome-spreading colonies under open, sunny conditions. The small, glossy, dark green leaves are evergreen in zones 8–9, giving the plant its common name, and the small, sweet, dark blue berries ripen in spring — earlier than most other blueberries — providing fruit for birds and gardeners alike. Unlike the taller highbush blueberries, Shiny Blueberry is a groundcover-scale plant that works well as an edible lawn substitute in acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; it requires the same highly acidic soil conditions as all blueberries and benefits from cross-pollination with additional plants for heavy fruiting. Excellent for edible native landscape designs in the lower South. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shiny Bush (Clearweed Peperomia, Ikmo-Bundok)
description: Direct sow or transplant seedlings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; allow to self-seed for a continuous supply. Peperomia pellucida (shiny bush or clearweed) is a tiny, semi-succulent tropical annual or short-lived perennial herb — a member of the pepper family (Piperaceae) related to black pepper — native to tropical South and Central America but naturalized throughout the tropical world in shaded, moist, disturbed areas, including the floors of tropical markets, along walls, and in garden beds. The plant produces translucent-stemmed, bright-green, heart-shaped, succulent leaves just 1–2 inches across with a mild, slightly peppery, watercress-like flavor and juicy, tender texture when fresh. The entire plant — leaves, stems, and all — is edible raw in salads or lightly cooked as a pot herb; in the Philippines (where it is called 'pansit-pansitan'), it is eaten fresh as a salad green and cooked in soups; in Brazil (where it is called 'erva-de-vidro') and throughout Latin America, it is used as a mild culinary herb and folk remedy for arthritis and skin conditions. Peperomia pellucida is one of the easiest and most useful shade herbs for warm, humid gardens: it self-seeds abundantly, grows in deep shade under trees where little else will grow, and provides a continuous harvest of mild salad greens from a minimal footprint. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Shiro Plum (Yellow Japanese Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires a pollinator — plant with Santa Rosa, Methley, Beauty, or another Japanese plum for best fruit set. Shiro plum was introduced in 1899 by Luther Burbank, America's preeminent fruit breeder, as part of his extensive Japanese plum improvement program; it remains one of the most popular and widely grown Japanese plums more than 125 years after its introduction, prized for very early ripening (late June to July), consistent heavy production, and large, round, golden-yellow fruits with thin, transparent yellow skin and sweet, mild, honey-flavored yellow flesh. Chill requirement is approximately 400–500 hours, making it suitable for zones 5–9 but less reliable in the lowest-chill Gulf Coast areas. The large crops ripen quickly and have short shelf life; fruit should be harvested when skin turns fully yellow and fruit gives to gentle pressure. An excellent pollinator for other Japanese plum varieties. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shirofumi Edamame Soybean
description: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this open-pollinated Japanese heirloom edamame needs consistent summer warmth to fill its pods. Plants set heavy clusters of two- to three-bean pods on compact, well-branched bushes and are valued in trials for their reliably smooth, sweet, nutty-flavored beans. Harvest whole pods when plump but still green, then steam or boil briefly in salted water for a classic edamame snack; being non-hybrid, seed can be saved from healthy plants for replanting. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Shishigatani Squash (Kyoto Heirloom Kabocha)
description: Shishigatani is a traditional Kyoto heirloom squash and one of the certified Kyo-yasai heritage vegetables, developed in the 19th century from chrysanthemum-type pumpkins brought south from Tsugaru in northern Japan. Fruits develop a distinctive bumpy, waisted, gourd-like snowman shape rather than the rounded form of typical kabocha. The squash carries deep cultural significance in Kyoto, where Anraku-ji Temple holds an annual squash-blessing ceremony each summer, and it is traditionally simmered in shojin ryori Buddhist vegetarian cooking. It remains a rare specialty variety outside Japan. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Shishito Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out after the soil warms. This popular Japanese frying pepper produces heavy sets of slender two-to-four-inch fruits with a mild, citrusy, slightly smoky flavor. Harvest peppers green and small for the best flavor when blistered in a hot pan or on the grill. Roughly one in ten pods surprises with mild heat, adding to the fun. Pick frequently to keep the highly productive plants setting new fruit. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Shishito Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; shishito peppers are a slender, thin-walled Japanese variety harvested green at 3–4 inches long, when they are mild and sweet with an occasional — roughly 1 in 10 — surprisingly hot fruit that keeps diners guessing. Plants produce prolifically once they begin fruiting and require consistent moisture and monthly fertilization with a balanced vegetable fertilizer to maintain production. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive; once fruits redden they become hotter and the plant redirects energy away from new fruit. The standard preparation is to blister whole fruits in a dry or lightly oiled cast-iron skillet over high heat until charred and softened, then finish with sea salt and a squeeze of lemon. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Shiso (Japanese Basil, Red Perilla)
description: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (needs light to germinate) in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; shiso self-seeds prolifically once established. Perilla frutescens var. crispa (shiso or Japanese basil) is an East Asian annual herb — one of the most important culinary herbs in Japanese cuisine — with large, ruffled, deeply crenate (toothy-edged), intensely aromatic leaves in green (ao-shiso) or red-purple (aka-shiso) forms, each with a distinctive, complex flavor combining basil, mint, anise, cinnamon, and fresh herbal notes unlike any other culinary herb. In Japanese cooking, green shiso leaves are used fresh and whole to wrap sashimi and sushi (providing a fresh, aromatic counterpoint to raw fish), cut into chiffonade as a garnish for cold noodles and soups, and fried whole in tempura batter. Red/purple shiso leaves are used to color and flavor umeboshi (salt-pickled sour plums) a bright magenta-pink, to make perilla vinegar, and in Korean cuisine to make kkaennip kimchi (perilla leaf kimchi). The seeds are also edible and are used in Japanese cooking as a condiment. Shiso tolerates partial shade better than most herbs and thrives in the heat and humidity of Southern summers; it self-seeds abundantly in warm climates, effectively naturalizing in the garden once established. The plant is nutritionally rich in vitamins A and C, rosmarinic acid, and luteolin. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Shiso (Perilla)
description: Surface-sow seeds (they need light to germinate) directly in the garden around last frost or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier in trays, transplanting after frost danger has passed into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Perilla frutescens (green shiso) is an annual herb used as a vegetable throughout East Asian cooking — the large, ruffled, vivid green, anise-and-clove-scented leaves are used to wrap sashimi, roll rice and pickles in, scatter over noodles and salads, and deep-fry as tempura; it is a fundamental ingredient in Japanese cuisine. Shiso self-seeds prolifically and often becomes a welcome recurring presence in the garden without any replanting effort; deadhead promptly if you do not want it to naturalize. Harvest individual leaves as needed from the outside of the plant, or snip whole stem tips to encourage bushier growth. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Shiso / Perilla
description: Refrigerate seeds for a few days before sowing to break dormancy, then surface-sow or cover with 1/8 in of soil after the last frost. Grow in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; shiso tolerates partial shade but growth is less vigorous. Pinch flower spikes promptly to extend leaf production, or allow a few to go to seed for next year's volunteer plants. Harvest the large, ruffled leaves at any stage; young leaves are most tender and aromatic for fresh use. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Shlomit Apple (Israeli Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Also bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at Rehovot in Israel, Shlomit has the lowest chill requirement of the Israeli low-chill group at roughly 375 hours, blooming as early as March in warm climates. It ripens from late June through mid-July, ahead of Michal, Elah, and Maayan but slightly behind Anna. Fruit is large and round with light-to-medium yellow skin brushed with a rusty red blush over about a quarter of its surface, and the crisp, highly juicy flesh makes it a solid fresh-market choice for Gulf South backyard orchards. It shares bloom timing closely enough with Anna and Dorsett Golden to serve as a useful cross-pollinator. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shockley Apple (Long-Storing Georgia Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Shockley is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early 1800s, once one of the most widely planted commercial apples in the South before refrigerated shipping and storage made its greatest strength less essential: fruit stored in a cool root cellar could reportedly keep in good eating condition into the following spring, an almost unmatched keeping quality among apples of any era. Fruit is small, yellow with a red blush, firm and crisp with a mildly sweet, slightly tart flavor that some describe as unremarkable fresh off the tree but that mellows and improves markedly in storage, developing a richer, more complex flavor over weeks and months. Trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively disease-resistant for an older Southern heirloom, ripening late in the season. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shogoin Turnip (Mild Japanese Dual-Purpose Turnip)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is a Japanese heirloom turnip cultivar that is outstanding in two distinct ways: it produces unusually mild, sweet, tender-fleshed white roots appropriate for fresh eating and light cooking, and simultaneously produces exceptionally mild, tender, palatable greens that are significantly less pungent than the traditional American turnip greens grown for Southern cooking. This dual mildness — both roots and tops — makes Shogoin the turnip of choice for those who find standard American turnips too strongly flavored but want to grow a dual-purpose root vegetable for fall and winter. The pure-white, globe-shaped roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — smaller and more tender than Purple Top White Globe when harvested young. The roots are outstanding raw in salads and slaws, steamed or roasted with light seasoning, and pickled (Shogoin is commonly used for Japanese-style pickled turnips). The tender greens can be used raw in salads when young, stir-fried, or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, Shogoin is a fall and winter crop — sow from August through October for harvest from October through February. The mild flavor makes Shogoin an outstanding variety for introducing turnips to gardeners and cooks unfamiliar with or averse to the pungency of traditional varieties. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Short-toothed Mountain Mint (Clustered Mountain Mint)
description: Sow seed in early spring or fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — short-toothed mountain mint is widely regarded as one of the single most valuable native plants for pollinators in the eastern US, producing dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white to pale pink flowers whose nectar is irresistible to a remarkable diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, flies, and butterflies. The silvery-white leaf bracts surrounding each flower cluster give the plant a striking frosted appearance at bloom time. Strongly mint-scented throughout, it repels deer and rabbits. Unlike most mountain mints, it tolerates partial shade and moist soils well, making it more adaptable than the narrow-leaved species. Spreads by rhizome to form a colony; divides easily to share. An outstanding native herb for mixed borders, rain gardens, and any setting where maximum pollinator support is the primary goal. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Shortleaf Fig (Wild Banyantree)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; shortleaf fig is the native banyan tree of south Florida and the Florida Keys — a hemiepiphytic strangler fig in the Moraceae family that begins life as an epiphyte in the crevices of trees or walls before sending down aerial roots that fuse around the host, eventually forming a trunk that can outlive the original host. Related to and similar in growth habit to the more commonly planted Florida strangler fig (Ficus aurea), shortleaf fig is distinguished by its somewhat smaller, more oval-rounded leaves with a distinctive drip tip. The small, rounded figs produced on short stalks are consumed by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other subtropical birds. A critically important food source for south Florida's native bird community. More cold-sensitive than strangler fig, and restricted to zone 10–12. Used in native-plant gardening in Dade and Monroe Counties for habitat restoration. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Shoya Long Eggplant (Japanese Hybrid Long Purple Eggplant)
description: Shoya Long is a Japanese-type hybrid bred for exceptionally long, slender fruit with glossy deep-purple skin and a matching dark calyx, often reaching 14-16 inches with tender, nearly seedless flesh. The upright, vigorous plant habit keeps the long fruit off the ground and makes picking easier than with sprawling heirloom types. It matures early and yields heavily over a long harvest window, staying productive through the hottest stretch of a Gulf Coast summer. Harvest while the skin still has a bright sheen, since fruit left too long on the plant dulls and toughens. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Shrubby Blue Sage (Mejorana)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in zones 8–11; shrubby blue sage is a woody native salvia of southern Texas and northern Mexico, producing bright lavender-blue flowers in loose terminal spikes over a very long season — from early spring to hard frost in warm climates — making it one of the most persistently flowering native sages in the South Texas garden. The strongly aromatic, gray-green, woolly-felted leaves have a distinctive strong fragrance and have been used traditionally in Mexico as a tea herb (mejorana is a traditional name in northern Mexico). The shrubby, semi-evergreen habit and extreme drought tolerance make it valuable as a foundation plant or informal hedge in alkaline, dry landscape conditions where few shrubs thrive. Consistently attractive to migrating hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, and native bees throughout its long blooming season. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Shui Jin Gui Tea (Golden Water Turtle)
description: Shui Jin Gui, or "Golden Water Turtle," rounds out the Wuyi Mountains' Si Da Ming Cong alongside Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, and Bai Jiguan, and takes its name from a legend describing an original bush's leaves gleaming like a golden turtle after rain. It is noted among the four for comparatively high yield and vigor and for a lighter, sweeter, more floral cup than the deeply roasted Da Hong Pao style, making it a popular everyday yancha oolong as well as a collector's cultivar. As with the other Wuyi rock-tea cultivars, it performs best in the mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils and partial shade of its native terrain, developing more pronounced yan yun "rock rhyme" character with age. Harvest semi-mature leaves for oolong-style processing, expecting the multiple roasting rounds typical of traditional Wuyi production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shui Xian Tea (Narcissus Oolong)
description: One of the oldest and most extensively grown cultivars in Fujian, China, Shui Xian is the backbone of both Wuyi rock oolong and the distinct compressed oolong cakes made in Zhangping further south, valued for a soft, orchid-like fragrance that gave rise to its 'narcissus' name. It grows into a notably larger, more sprawling shrub than most named tea cultivars, with bigger leaves that support strong, dependable yields even on modest sites. Plant it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and give it more room than compact cultivars like Jin Xuan or Tieguanyin. Because it tolerates a fairly wide range of elevations and soils, it is a forgiving choice for growers experimenting with oolong-style processing at home. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Shungiku (Chrysanthemum Greens)
description: Broadcast seed or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; shungiku is a cool-season Asian vegetable in the chrysanthemum family grown for its highly aromatic, slightly bitter leaves that are fundamental to Japanese hot pot (nabe), sukiyaki, and Korean soups. The flavor is herbal, slightly medicinal, and distinctly chrysanthemum-like — beloved in East Asian cooking, particularly in winter one-pot dishes where the leaves add fragrance as well as nutrition. Harvest outer leaves when plants reach 6–8 inches; or cut whole plants at soil level for a cut-and-come-again crop. It bolts quickly in heat, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers — these are also edible as a garnish. Sow in succession for continuous harvest through cool seasons. Matures in 30–50 days from seed.

name: Shunkyo Semi-Long Radish (Japanese Rose-Pink Heirloom Radish)
description: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding. This Japanese heirloom produces rose-pink, tapered roots four to five inches long with crisp, notably sweet and mild flesh that holds its quality and stays crisp longer than typical round spring radishes as temperatures fluctuate. Its extended harvest window and resistance to turning pithy or overly hot in warm soil make it a reliable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners working with a short, mild winter rather than a true hard freeze. Both the roots and the peppery young leaves are edible. Matures in 30–35 days from seed.

name: Shvelisi Garlic (Georgian Porcelain Hardneck)
description: Set cloves 2 inches deep in loose, fertile soil and mulch well for the winter, uncovering gradually as spring shoots appear. Cut the curling scape in early summer to focus growth into the bulb, then cure harvested heads in a dry, shaded, airy location for a few weeks. Shvelisi is a Republic of Georgia heirloom porcelain hardneck brought to the United States by garlic researcher Ron Engeland, known for its tall stature, large white bulbs, and rich, warm flavor that reflects its Caucasus mountain origins. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Si Ji Chun Tea (Four Seasons Spring Oolong)
description: Selected by a Taiwanese grower and named for its ability to be harvested in four or more flushes a year rather than the one or two typical of finer high-mountain cultivars, Si Ji Chun ('Four Seasons Spring') is prized for vigorous, dependable growth and a strongly floral, almost lily-like aroma. Its heavy-cropping habit makes it a favorite for everyday, affordably priced oolong production, though connoisseurs generally rank its refinement below slower-growing cultivars like Qingxin. Grow it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and take advantage of its extended harvest window by plucking new flushes as they mature throughout the growing season. It also tolerates lower elevations and warmer conditions better than many prestige Taiwanese cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Siam Queen Basil (Thai Basil, Clove Basil)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Siam Queen is the 1997 All-America Selections Herb Award winner — the premier Thai basil cultivar for American gardens, producing a compact, well-branched plant with deeply fragrant, dark-green, slightly crinkled leaves and a distinctive spicy-clove fragrance that is sharply different from sweet Italian basil. The clove-anise-pepper flavor profile of Siam Queen is essential to authentic Thai, Vietnamese, and other Southeast Asian cuisines — it is the correct basil for Thai basil chicken (gai pad krapao), pho, green papaya salad, and spring rolls. Unlike sweet basil cultivars, Siam Queen's flavor and fragrance remain strong even after the plant flowers, giving it a longer useful harvest window. The ornamental purple flower spikes and purple stems add visual interest beyond the herb's culinary value. In zone 9, Siam Queen grows vigorously through the long warm season and handles the summer heat better than many sweet basil cultivars — pinching the flowering stems back regularly prolongs the harvest but the herb remains usable even when flowering. The compact plant is well-suited to container growing where it can be positioned conveniently near the kitchen for ready harvesting. Excellent in containers and raised beds. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Siam Ruby Banana (Striking Red-and-Green Striped Ornamental Banana)
description: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, watering generously and feeding regularly through the growing season to support the fast, lush growth typical of ornamental bananas. Siam Ruby is prized above all for its spectacular foliage, with broad leaves striped and mottled in deep wine-red over green in an ever-shifting pattern that makes it one of the showiest tropical-look foliage plants for a Gulf South summer landscape, whether in a large container or planted directly in a bed. While it can produce small bananas in long, warm growing seasons, it is grown primarily as an ornamental rather than for reliable fruit in most of its hardiness range. In zone 8-9 gardens the top growth is usually killed by winter frost but the underground rhizome often survives with heavy mulching, resprouting in spring; in colder areas, dig and overwinter indoors or grow in a large movable container. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Siamese Bitter Melon
description: This slender Thai type produces small, deeply ridged fruit with a notably assertive bitterness prized in Southeast Asian cooking. Provide a tall trellis in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest young and often, since frequent picking of immature fruit keeps the vigorous vine flowering and setting new fruit. Left unpicked, fruit ripens to orange and splits open to reveal red-coated seeds, which can be saved after a short drying period. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Siberian Chives / Giant Chives
