description: Allium schoenoprasum var. sibiricum, commonly called Siberian chives or giant chives, is a robust, cold-hardy variety of common chives native to the harsh continental climates of Siberia, northern China, and Alaska, distinguished by its noticeably broader, thicker, hollow leaves and larger, showier lavender-pink flowerheads that make it both a more productive culinary herb and a bolder ornamental plant than standard chives. Propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring or fall, replanting divisions at the same depth in moderately fertile, consistently moist but well-drained soil in full sun; Siberian chives are more tolerant of cold, wind, and dry conditions than common chives and are an excellent choice for exposed northern gardens. Harvest leaves by cutting 1-2 inches above soil level, repeating every 3-4 weeks throughout the growing season; the flavor is essentially identical to common chives — mild onion — with the advantage that the broader leaves are easier to harvest in quantity. The large, globe-shaped flowerheads in late spring are highly attractive to native bees and can be used fresh as a garnish or steeped in vinegar; deadhead after flowering to maintain leaf production and prevent excessive self-seeding. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Siberian Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Cold-Climate Heritage)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch heavily after the ground cools (especially important in zones 3–4); keep consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl and straighten; harvest in early to midsummer when lower leaves yellow. Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic originating in Russia and introduced to North American garlic culture through seed-saver networks and specialist garlic growers in the 20th century; it is particularly valued for its exceptional cold hardiness, with reliable performance in zones 3–4 where many garlic varieties struggle with winterkill or produce reduced bulb size. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) and typically contain just 5–9 large, easy-to-peel cloves — fewer than most garlic types but each clove is substantial in size, making them easy to use in cooking. The outer skins are cream-colored with distinctive purple-violet streaking and spotting characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe group; the flavor is rich, moderately pungent, and earthy with good complexity — similar in character to Persian Star and other Marbled Purple Stripe types. Siberian is an excellent choice for northern gardeners in zones 3–5 who struggle with hardneck variety performance, and for seed-saving gardens that want geographic diversity in their garlic collection. Storage life of 5–7 months under good conditions. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Siberian Kale (Early Curled Siberian Kale)
description: Siberian kale is an old, extremely cold-hardy strain of Brassica napus grown across northern Russia and Siberia long before it reached North American seed catalogs, and it stands behind many of the popular 'Russian' type kales, including the purple-stemmed Red Russian selections bred from it. Unlike the tightly curled Scots kales of Brassica oleracea, Siberian kale has flat, deeply lobed, blue-green leaves with a milder, sweeter flavor that improves further after frost. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to about a foot apart, and harvest outer leaves continually as the plant regrows from the center. It tolerates hard freezes better than almost any other garden brassica, often surviving under snow cover well into winter. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Siberian Miner's Lettuce (Candy Flower)
description: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian miner's lettuce is a Pacific Northwest and northern Asian native cool-season green, closely related to the round-leaved miner's lettuce but with pointed, spade-shaped leaves and dainty pink-veined white flowers held in loose sprays above the foliage from late winter into summer in cool, shaded gardens. The tender leaves and flowers have a mild, slightly tart, spinach-like flavor and are eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked, and the plant tolerates deeper shade than nearly any other salad green. Unlike annual miner's lettuce, it spreads by shallow rhizomes as well as self-seeding, gradually forming a low, semi-evergreen groundcover in a consistently moist, shaded woodland garden or the north side of a building. Thin or divide congested patches in fall to keep it in bounds, and expect it to die back in extended summer heat, returning with cooler fall weather. Matures in 45–65 days from seed.

name: Sibley Squash (Pike's Peak Heirloom Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the long, vigorous vines. Sibley squash, introduced in the 1880s and also sold as Pike's Peak squash, is an American heirloom valued by generations of gardeners for its unusual teardrop or pear shape, thin, smooth, blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-textured deep orange flesh with almost no fiber, a texture and flavor that many long-time growers rank above modern hybrid winter squash. Fruits typically run 6-10 pounds, large enough to serve a crowd, and the thin rind, while making the squash slightly more vulnerable to handling damage than thick-shelled types, also makes it easier to peel and cook than harder-shelled Hubbard-type squash. Vines are long and productive given full sun and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before storing in a cool, dry spot, where well-cured fruit keeps for several months while its sweetness continues to improve. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Sichuan Pepper
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sichuan pepper (not related to black pepper or chili peppers) is the dried husk of the fruit of Zanthoxylum shrubs, whose defining characteristic is a numbing, buzzing sensation on the tongue caused by the compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool — a sensation called ma (tingling/numbing) that is the foundation of the ma-la (numbing-spicy) flavor profile of Sichuan Chinese cuisine. Harvest the small red fruits in fall when fully ripe, then dry and separate the husks from the black seeds — only the husks are used, as the seeds are bitter and gritty. The shrub is spiny and produces attractive clusters of small red fruits on female plants. Plant at least one male for pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sicilian Artichoke Softneck Garlic
description: Separate bulbs into cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall. This Artichoke-type softneck forms twelve to twenty cloves per bulb with classic pearl-white papery skin sometimes streaked purple. Softnecks store especially well and are ideal for braiding, and they perform reliably in milder-winter regions. Mulch for winter protection and keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist through spring. Harvest when the lower leaves yellow, then cure in a dry, ventilated spot before storing. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Sidra Coffee (Ecuadorian Specialty Varietal)
description: Sidra rose to prominence on farms in Ecuador's Pichincha province before spreading into Colombia's specialty coffee scene during the 2010s. Its exact parentage is debated: growers have long described it as a cross of Typica and Red Bourbon, while genetic testing on some material points instead to Ethiopian landrace ancestry, and both explanations may apply to different Sidra populations now in circulation. The plant is notably vigorous, with an unusually thick trunk and a mature height well above compact dwarf cultivars, typically grown at 1,650-1,800 meters elevation. It has earned a following among specialty roasters for a complex, floral, fruit-forward cup that stands out in competition lots. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade, allowing extra room for its taller, more vigorous habit compared with dwarf varieties like Caturra or Pacas. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sierra Blanca Onion (Super Star Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this intermediate/short-day hybrid needs a southern winter's shorter daylight to bulb well. Sierra Blanca is an All-America Selections-winning white onion widely grown across the Southwest and Gulf South for its large, globe-shaped bulbs, crisp white flesh, and consistently mild, sweet flavor, making it a favorite for fresh eating as well as cooking. It bulbs reliably and stores somewhat better than the thinnest-skinned sweet onions, though it is still best used within a few months for peak quality. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and ease off watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Sierra Lettuce (Batavian Lettuce)
description: Sow seed on or just below the soil surface in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sierra is a batavian-type lettuce combining the crisp texture of a crisphead with the loose, outer-leaf harvest convenience of a loose-leaf type — producing green, ruffled, tender-crisp heads with outstanding bolt and heat resistance that extends the spring lettuce season significantly later than butterhead or loose-leaf types. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 gardeners where spring heat arrives quickly, giving a several-week extension window before quality declines. Harvest heads when firm but before any heat stress causes bitterness. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Sierra Plum (Klamath Plum)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sierra plum is a thicket-forming small tree or large shrub native to the mountains of California and southern Oregon, valued by home orchardists and native plant gardeners for its drought tolerance, fragrant white spring flowers, and small, tart-sweet red-to-purple plums that ripen in late summer. Fruit quality is variable from seed, so growers who want reliable, larger fruit often select and propagate superior wild clones by cuttings or grafting. The species is tough and adaptable to rocky, thin mountain soils and needs little supplemental water once established, but it suckers readily and can form dense thickets if not managed. Fruit is traditionally used fresh, for jam and jelly, and was an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and California. Matures in 1095–1825 days from seed.

name: Sieva Bean (Baby Lima Bean, Carolina Lima Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide support for pole types; pick pods when full and plump but still green. Phaseolus lunatus var. sieva (sieva bean or baby lima bean) is the small-seeded form of lima bean — traditionally called 'butter beans' across the South — that has been cultivated in the southeastern United States for centuries, adapted to the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South where the large-seeded Fordhook-type limas are far less reliable. Sieva beans are smaller (1/3 to 1/2 the seed size of Fordhook), have thinner seed coats, cook more quickly, and are more heat-tolerant at pollination — a critical advantage in Gulf Coast summers where high night temperatures (above 70°F) cause heavy-seeded limas to drop flowers and fail to set pods. Heritage varieties like 'Florida Speckled' (with beautiful purple-speckled green seeds), 'Henderson Bush,' and 'Christmas Butter Bean' are treasured in Southern heirloom seed collections. Fresh sieva beans (butter beans) are a beloved Southern side dish — simmered with fatback or butter until creamy-tender, they have a rich, buttery, starchy flavor distinct from Northern-style green limas. Also excellent dried and shelled for winter use. Matures in 65–85 days from seed.

name: Sihong Jujube (Dense Crisp Caramel-Flavored Fresh-Eating Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established. Sihong is one of the most highly regarded jujube cultivars grown in the United States, consistently rated by fruit collectors and evaluation trials among the best-tasting available, prized for its dense, exceptionally crisp texture and rich, caramel-like sweetness that develops fully as the fruit ripens to a mahogany-brown color in September. It bears within its first few years and, like other jujubes, tolerates Gulf South heat, humidity, and periodic drought with minimal input once established. Harvest at the fully colored, slightly wrinkled stage for peak sweetness, and expect vigorous root suckering, which can be managed by mowing or used to propagate additional trees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sikkim Blue Chives (Himalayan Blue-Flowered Allium)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Sikkim blue chives is a Himalayan meadow native prized for nodding umbels of true violet-blue, bell-shaped flowers in late summer, an unusually vivid and rare color within the onion genus. Its narrow, mild-flavored leaves are edible in the same way as common chives, though it is more often grown as a choice rock-garden or border ornamental for its flower color. It prefers slightly cooler, more evenly moist conditions than drought-tolerant ornamental alliums and benefits from a summer mulch in hot climates. Divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Silas Woods Sapodilla
description: Silas Woods is a naturally dwarf, compact sapodilla selection out of Homestead, Florida, staying under about 20 feet even planted in the ground, which makes it a good fit for small yards and large containers; grow it in full sun on well-drained soil and shield young trees from any freezing temperatures. Grafted trees are remarkably precocious, often producing their first fruit within one to two years of planting and cropping twice a year on roughly a six-to-eight-month cycle once mature. The round, smooth, brown-skinned fruit, two to four inches across, has a grainy, pear-like texture and a sweet, brown-sugar flavor typical of the best sapodilla selections. Because of its small stature and fast fruiting, it is one of the more practical sapodilla choices for home growers without room for a full-sized tree. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Siletz Tomato (Oregon Early Beefsteak)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Siletz can be transplanted 1–2 weeks before last frost in mild climates due to its cold tolerance for a tomato; it is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage helps manage the heavy fruit load. Siletz was developed by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University as part of the Pacific Northwest vegetable breeding program, named for the Siletz River in Oregon's Coast Range; it was released specifically to address the challenge of growing tomatoes in the cool, overcast summers of the Pacific Coast where nighttime temperatures regularly fall below the fruit-set threshold of standard varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, bright red fruits have good meaty texture and pleasant, balanced sweet-acid flavor — not the most complex among heirloom varieties, but reliably excellent given its exceptional earliness and cold tolerance. In Gulf Coast gardens, Siletz makes an outstanding early-season variety when planted in February–March, producing ripe fruit well before the onset of summer heat that terminates most tomato production. Its determinate growth habit allows clean harvest before the hot season, with plants ripening a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks. Matures in 52–65 days from transplant.

name: Siling Labuyo Pepper (Philippine Bird's Eye Chili)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this Filipino landrace grows into a shrubby perennial in frost-free climates but performs well as a warm-season annual elsewhere. The tiny, tapering pods — among the smallest of any cultivated chile — pack intense heat around 80,000-100,000 Scoville units and are used both fresh and dried in staples like sinigang, bicol express, and vinegar-based dipping sauces; young leaves are also edible and used in some regional dishes. Harvest frequently to keep the compact, heavily branching bush setting new fruit. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Silk Hope Mulberry (Southern Heirloom Black Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Silk Hope is a Southern heirloom black mulberry, named for the small North Carolina community where it was long cultivated and passed down among home orchardists for its rich, deep-purple-black fruit and dependable production. The elongated berries are intensely sweet with a wine-like depth of flavor considered by many mulberry enthusiasts to surpass the milder white and red mulberry types more commonly sold. Like other black mulberries it is somewhat slower-growing and less cold-hardy than white mulberry hybrids, but well suited to Gulf South heat and long growing seasons once established. Trees tolerate poor soil and drought once established, needing little more than occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Site female-fruiting trees well away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended summer harvest window and stain hard surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Silky Dogwood
description: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; silky dogwood grows naturally in streamside thickets, wet meadows, and pond margins and is one of the best native shrubs for stabilizing stream banks and rain gardens. Cornus amomum is a loosely branched, multi-stemmed native shrub with soft, somewhat silky-haired leaves, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in June that are outstanding for native bees and small butterflies, and blue-black berry-like drupes in fall that are among the most heavily consumed native fruits by migrating songbirds — particularly wood thrushes, robins, and waxwings; the red-purple winter stems provide dormant season interest. Plant in groupings for best berry production and wildlife impact. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Silvan Blackberry
description: Silvan is an Australian-bred trailing blackberry (from the Victoria, Australia breeding program) known for very early ripening, large, glossy, dark-red-to-black berries, and rich, intense flavor closer to a wild blackberry than many milder modern cultivars. Unlike several newer trailing types, Silvan retains thorny canes, so heavy gloves are essential when fan-training the vigorous canes along a sturdy multi-wire trellis. Cut fruited canes to the ground right after harvest and tie in the current season's new primocanes for next year's crop. Silvan performs best in regions with cool, relatively dry summers; in humid climates give it full sun and excellent air circulation to limit fungal disease pressure on the ripening fruit. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Silver Anouk Spanish Lavender
description: Site in full sun in gritty, poor-to-average soil with excellent drainage; Spanish lavenders rot quickly in humid or waterlogged conditions and are hardy only to the warmer edge of English lavender's range. A silvery-foliaged sport of the popular 'Anouk', this selection carries the same compact, rounded habit and dense purple flower heads topped with showy upright purple bracts resembling rabbit ears, but with distinctly silver-gray leaves that add contrast in the border. It blooms earlier in the season than English lavenders and often continues sporadically through summer with deadheading. In marginal zones grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for winter. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Silver Buffaloberry
description: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; silver buffaloberry is a spiny, thicket-forming native shrub of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain West with distinctive silvery-gray foliage and clusters of brilliant orange-red to red berries that ripen in summer and fall. The plant is dioecious — male and female flowers appear on separate plants — so both sexes must be planted for fruit production. Berries are tart but edible, historically used by Plains nations to make pemmican and sauce for buffalo meat (hence the name). Plants fix nitrogen through root nodules, tolerate extreme cold, drought, alkaline soils, and salt — among the most rugged food-producing shrubs for difficult Great Plains conditions. Excellent wildlife hedge. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Silver Creek Pawpaw (Illinois Heirloom Selection)
description: Silver Creek is a wild-tree selection documented from Millstadt, Illinois, and cataloged among Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records. It produces medium-sized fruit and represents the many regionally significant heirloom pawpaw selections that circulated among enthusiasts before the modern KSU and Peterson breeding programs. Plant it alongside a genetically distinct second pawpaw tree, since cross-pollination is required for fruit set. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Silver Date Palm
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, alkaline-tolerant soil; Phoenix sylvestris is drought tolerant once established and adapts well to alkaline, calcareous, and slightly saline soils — water regularly only in establishment; excellent for hot, dry, alkaline landscape positions in zone 8–11. Phoenix sylvestris (Silver Date Palm, Indian Date Palm, or Wild Date Palm) is a large, majestic, single-trunked feather palm native to the plains and hills of the Indian subcontinent — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka — where it is one of the most culturally and economically important wild palms. The silvery-gray crown of long, recurving, pinnate fronds gives the palm a distinctively glaucous, blue-silver appearance that differs from the common date palm (P. dactylifera). The fruits are small (1 inch), orange-to-brown dates — edible but less sweet and more fibrous than commercial dates. The primary economic use is 'toddy' production: tapping the crown to collect sweet sap, which is fermented into palm wine, distilled into arrack, or boiled into jaggery (palm sugar). Phoenix sylvestris is substantially more cold-hardy than many date palms — tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established — making it excellent for zone 8b–9 date-palm landscapes. Outstanding ornamental and shade palm for Gulf Coast, Southwest, and Mediterranean-climate gardens. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Silver Dust Tea (White-Speckled Variegated Selection)
description: Silver Dust is grown primarily as an ornamental tea camellia for containers or small garden beds, valued for white speckling across its leaf surface and for a first spring flush that can emerge nearly pure white before greening with age, as is typical of leaf variegation. Its slow growth rate and naturally mounded form keep it compact and tidy without much pruning. A small test batch of tea made from the white shoots has been described as very mild with little bitterness, though it is chosen mainly for foliage interest rather than yield. Grow it in the same acidic, evenly moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias require. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Silver Lace Society Garlic (Variegated Society Garlic)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this South African native is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in zone 9–10 gardens. Silver Lace is a variegated society garlic selection, its strap-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white, adding season-long foliage interest to the near-year-round clusters of lavender, garlic-scented flowers typical of the species. Like the plain green form, leaves and flowers carry a mild garlic flavor without lingering breath and make a useful, ornamental garlic substitute in the kitchen, while the flowers reliably draw bees and small pollinators. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor and clean variegation. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Silver Queen Lemon Thyme (Silver-Variegated Lemon-Scented Thyme)
description: Silver Queen is the most widely grown variegated lemon thyme, forming a tidy, mounded plant of small dark-green leaves edged in soft silver-white, brighter and cooler in tone than the gold-leafed lemon thyme cultivars. It carries the same clean lemon fragrance and flavor as green lemon thyme, so it earns a spot at the herb-bed edge or rock garden for both a citrus-thyme seasoning and pale, frosted foliage color. Give it very well-drained, lean soil and full sun, since wet or overly rich ground quickly causes the woody base to rot and the variegation to fade. Shear lightly after the summer bloom to keep the mound dense and prevent woodiness. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Silver Queen Okra (Pale Ivory-Green Ornamental Okra)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Silver Queen is an heirloom okra valued for its pale, silvery ivory-green pods and foliage, a striking, almost ghostly color that sets it apart from the deep green of most okra varieties and makes it as much an ornamental curiosity as a productive vegetable. The tender pods have the classic okra flavor and texture, well suited to frying, gumbo, and pickling, and the plant produces reliably through the heat of a Gulf South summer. Harvest young, at three to four inches, for the best tenderness, and pick regularly to keep the plant producing over a long season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Silver Queen Sweet Corn (Classic White Sweet Corn Standard)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Silver Queen is perhaps the most historically influential and recognizable white sweet corn variety in American horticulture — an su (standard sugar) white hybrid introduced around 1955 that rapidly became the benchmark white sweet corn against which all others were measured for decades. The large, 8–9 inch ears carry 14–16 rows of pure white, tender, milky kernels with the classic, unmistakable sweet corn flavor that made Silver Queen famous across the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states, where roadside stands and home gardens grew Silver Queen as the late-summer corn of choice for multiple generations of cooks who planned their summer around it. At 88–94 days, Silver Queen is a late-season variety that reaches peak quality in the hottest part of summer, a timing that traditionally marked the height of summer corn season in the South and Midwest. The flavor at peak maturity — kernels plump, skins tender, sugar at maximum before starch conversion begins — is the standard by which many older gardeners still evaluate all corn. Silver Queen must be harvested and consumed or preserved within a narrow window (1–3 days after peak) as the su type converts sugar to starch more rapidly than modern se or sh2 types. In the Gulf South, Silver Queen is a classic late-spring-to-early-summer variety with a dedicated following among gardeners who grew up eating it. Matures in 88–94 days from seed.

name: Silver Rose Garlic (Fast-Maturing Silverskin Softneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Silver Rose is a silverskin softneck garlic prized for maturing earlier than many other varieties and for exceptional storage life, often keeping 9 months or longer in a cool, dry pantry when properly cured. Bulbs form tight, papery white to rose-blushed wrappers around a good number of small to medium cloves with a strong, well-rounded flavor that mellows considerably when cooked. Like other silverskins, it tolerates mild winters far better than hardneck types, making it one of the more dependable garlics for zone 8-10 gardens. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store. Matures in 200–240 days from transplant.

name: Silver Shield French Sorrel
description: Silver Shield is an ornamental selection of buckler-leaf French sorrel grown as much for its dense mat of shiny, silver-mottled, shield-shaped leaves as for its tart, green-apple flavor. It thrives in sun to fairly deep shade and tolerates poor, dry soil once established, spreading steadily by creeping rhizomes to form a low groundcover along paths and border edges. Snip young leaves regularly for salads, which also curbs its naturally rampant spread and keeps foliage tender. Divide congested mats every couple of years in spring to renew vigor and to share or contain the planting. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Silver Thyme
description: Grow this variegated thyme from cuttings or division to keep the silver-edged leaf pattern true. It offers standard culinary thyme flavor along with attractive frosty foliage. Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun and water sparingly once established. Trim after flowering to prevent woodiness and encourage fresh compact growth. Harvest sprigs any time and mulch the crown in cold-winter regions. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Silver Vine
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun on a sturdy support, since this is a vigorous twining vine related to kiwifruit; silver vine is best known in the West as a potent feline attractant, with dried leaves, wood, and galls used in cat toys because most cats respond to its nepetalactol compounds even more strongly than to catnip. Left to grow, it produces heart-shaped leaves that often develop a distinctive silvery-white blaze in summer, small white fragrant flowers, and yellow-orange fruit on female vines pollinated by a male plant; the normal fruit is edible though mild and rarely prized, while galled fruit caused by a gall wasp has a long history of use in traditional Japanese medicine. Because the vine is very vigorous and twining, give it a sturdy arbor or fence well away from smaller plants it could overwhelm, and expect enthusiastic garden cats to rub, chew, and roll on any part of the plant they can reach, which can slow young vines' establishment. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Silver White Softneck Garlic
description: Plant individual cloves pointed end up about two inches deep in the fall. This California-bred silverskin softneck yields ten to twelve cloves per bulb and is prized for consistent performance and high yields. It adapts well across cold, hot, humid, and coastal climates and offers excellent long-term storage. Mulch after planting, then keep the bed evenly moist through the spring growing period. Harvest when lower leaves brown and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place for months of storage. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Silver-seed Gourd
description: Direct sow Cucurbita argyrosperma seeds in hills 4–6 inches apart after soil warms to 70°F in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; provide ample space as vines spread 10–15 feet; water deeply once or twice weekly and side-dress with compost at vine set; harvest when rinds are hard and stems begin to cork. Silver-seed Gourd is the least-known of the four domesticated Cucurbita species but arguably the most heat-tolerant — better adapted to hot, dry summers of the US Southwest, Mexico, and Central America than C. pepo or C. maxima. It encompasses the familiar Cushaw squash (large, curved-neck, striped with light and dark green) and many traditional Mexican varieties grown specifically for their large, flat, silverish seeds (pepitas) used in the classic Mexican mole negro, pepita oil production, and traditional candies (dulce de pepita). The flesh of the large fruits is mild and sweet, excellent for pies and tamale fillings; the seeds are dried, shelled, and used as a significant protein and oil source in Mexican cuisine. Cushaw squash resists vine borers and powdery mildew better than many other Cucurbita species and performs excellently in zone 8–12 heat. Several named heirloom varieties are available including 'Green Striped Cushaw', 'White Cushaw', and 'Jonathan' (round-fruited). Matures in 85–110 days from seed.

name: Silverhill Jujube (Alabama Gulf Coast Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Silverhill, named for the jujube-growing community of Silverhill, Alabama, is a heat- and humidity-adapted selection well suited to Gulf South conditions. This historic American jujube selection traces to the early twentieth-century Gulf Coast jujube plantings around Silverhill and Fairhope, Alabama, where USDA plant introductions from China were trialed and locally adapted decades before jujube saw its recent surge in popularity. It bears medium, round to oval fruit with crisp, sweet, apple-like flesh at the green-mature stage, sweetening further and wrinkling like a date as it ripens to mahogany-brown, and the tree is notably tolerant of the humid, disease-prone summers that can trouble jujube varieties bred for drier climates. Once established the tree is extremely drought-tolerant, largely pest-free, and requires only light pruning to maintain an open shape; harvest fruit in stages from crisp-green through fully wrinkled-brown depending on preferred texture. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Silverhill Satsuma (Historic Coastal Alabama Satsuma)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it in a warm microclimate such as near a south-facing wall in the cooler parts of its range. This satsuma selection takes its name from the historic citrus-growing community of Silverhill in Baldwin County, Alabama, once a center of satsuma production shipped north by rail in the early 20th century. Like other satsumas, the small, deep-orange fruit is essentially seedless with loose, easy-to-peel skin and sweet, mild flesh, ripening from October into December. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a satsuma, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once mature, which made it a mainstay of small Gulf Coast dooryard orchards. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Silverweed
description: Plant in moist, sandy or gravelly, open soil in full sun along coastal margins, wet meadows, and disturbed open ground; silverweed is a cosmopolitan coastal and temperate wildflower with distinctive pinnate leaves that are silver-silky on the underside — providing a striking two-toned effect as the wind turns the leaves. The bright yellow five-petaled flowers in summer attract numerous small native bees. The starchy taproots were historically an important famine food in coastal Scotland, Ireland, and in Indigenous communities across the Pacific Northwest, where they were boiled, roasted, or dried for winter storage. The roasted roots have a pleasant, slightly sweet, parsnip-like flavor. Spreads rapidly by runners and can become a weed in garden settings — best planted where it can naturalize on moist, open disturbed ground. Also listed as Argentina anserina in some taxonomic systems. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Silvery Fir Tree Tomato (Russian Heirloom with Distinctive Ferny Silver-Green Foliage)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. No staking needed for compact plants. Harvest when fruits are uniformly red and slightly soft. Silvery Fir Tree is a Russian heirloom tomato of exceptional visual distinction — the variety is immediately recognizable in the garden by its foliage, which is finely dissected and ferny in appearance, closely resembling carrot leaves or fir tree needles rather than the broad, palmately lobed leaves of standard tomato types. The silvery-green color of the leaves (more gray-green than the typical bright green of most tomato foliage) reinforces the fir tree visual impression and gives the variety its English common name. Botanically, the finely cut leaf form is a recessive mutation in leaf architecture that has been maintained in this Russian variety through traditional seed saving — the same mutation appears occasionally in other tomato varieties but rarely becomes the defining characteristic of a named variety. The plants are determinate and compact (24–30 inches), producing clusters of small-medium red round fruits (2–3 oz each) that ripen in a concentrated season-appropriate window. The flavor is excellent for an early determinate — sweet, well-balanced, genuine tomato character without the flatness that sometimes characterizes early-season determinate types. Silvery Fir Tree has become popular in North American heirloom tomato cultivation not only for its early production and good flavor but also as an ornamental garden plant: the unusual ferny foliage makes it visually striking in container plantings, edible landscapes, and kitchen gardens where visual diversity among plants adds character. Matures in 58–65 days from transplant.

name: Silvia Brussels Sprouts
description: Start seed indoors in early to midsummer and transplant sturdy seedlings for a long-season fall crop. Brussels sprouts need a lengthy, cool finish, and a light frost actually sweetens the tight little sprouts. Space plants generously and stake tall stalks in windy sites to keep them upright. Remove yellowing lower leaves as sprouts form to improve air flow and size. Harvest from the bottom of the stalk upward once sprouts are firm and about an inch across. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Simacan Rambutan
description: Simacan is a long-standing Javanese rambutan cultivar, historically one of the two dominant selections (alongside Rapiah) planted in Indonesian home orchards since the 1930s. Fruit is medium to large with red skin and soft spines, and the flesh is juicy and sweet with good separation from the seed. Grow grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind, and maintain consistent soil moisture year-round, since even brief drought during flowering can cause significant fruit drop. Simacan requires warm, humid, essentially frost-free conditions and is best suited to zone 10b and warmer in the continental United States. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Simcoe Hops
description: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Simcoe is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in the early 2000s, this high-alpha dual-purpose hop delivers a distinctive combination of passionfruit and pine aromas alongside earthy, dank undertones that became a signature flavor of the West Coast IPA style, and its high alpha acid content also makes it effective as a clean bittering hop. Its unique aroma profile and versatility for both bittering and late-addition dry-hopping uses have made it a foundational variety in modern American craft brewing since its introduction, prized enough that supply is often constrained relative to brewer demand. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture and full sun through the growing season. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Simka Plum (Large Dark-Skinned Amber-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
description: Simka produces some of the largest fruit of any common Japanese plum, with a dark maroon-purple skin covering firm amber flesh that is sweet and only mildly tart. Because it is only partially self-fruitful, plant it alongside Santa Rosa or another mid-season Japanese plum to ensure a full crop. The tree is vigorous and needs early, deliberate thinning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy fruit load, and its large fruit size makes it a favorite for fresh eating out of hand. Harvest when the deep color has developed fully over the entire fruit and the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Simmonds Avocado (Historic Florida West Indian Avocado)
description: Simmonds is one of the oldest named Florida avocado cultivars, a West Indian race selection from the Miami area that helped establish South Florida's dooryard and commercial avocado culture in the early twentieth century. It bears large, glossy green, thin-skinned fruit with mild, buttery, relatively low-oil flesh typical of West Indian parentage, ripening early in the season during mid- to late summer. As a true West Indian type it has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, frost-free conditions, but it tolerates the humid, high-rainfall summers of the Gulf Coast better than California-bred Guatemalan cultivars. Provide deep, well-drained soil and avoid overwatering, since avocado roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in heavy or poorly drained ground. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Simpson Chestnut (Blight-Resistant Chinese-European Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Simpson is a Chinese x European chestnut hybrid selected by W. Simpson and carries recorded resistance to chestnut blight. It produces good-flavored nuts around 11 grams each, though some nuts have multiple embryos, and it ripens later than many selections, from late September into early October. Plant it with a genetically distinct second chestnut cultivar for reliable cross-pollination and a full nut set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Simpson Elite Lettuce (AAS-Winning Improved Black Seeded Simpson)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Simpson Elite, an All-America Selections winner, improves on the classic heirloom Black Seeded Simpson looseleaf lettuce with notably better resistance to bolting in warm weather, extending the harvest window later into spring and giving Gulf South gardeners more usable growing time before summer heat sets in. It forms loose, tender, light green frilled leaves ready for cut-and-come-again harvest within weeks of sowing. Harvest outer leaves as needed while the center continues to produce, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest weeks of the season to further delay bolting. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Simpson Stopper (Twinberry, Naked Wood)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; simpson stopper is a Florida-native small tree or large shrub with flaking cinnamon-colored bark, glossy dark green oval leaves, and small white flowers with prominent stamens that have a pleasant spicy fragrance — the flowers are followed by small, orange to red, berry-like fruits that are edible and have a pleasantly spicy, aromatic flavor used for wildlife food, flavoring, and nibbling fresh. The peeling bark is one of the most distinctive features, revealing warm salmon-cinnamon tones beneath. Native to the coastal hammocks, pine rocklands, and tropical hardwood hammocks of South Florida and the Florida Keys, it is exceptionally well-adapted to the calcareous, well-drained soils of peninsular Florida and tolerates salt spray, drought, and partial shade. An important nectar source for butterflies and the berries are eaten by many species of birds and wildlife, making it an outstanding Florida native wildlife plant for landscapes in zone 9b–11. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sin Pepe Pomegranate (Pink Ice, Soft-Seeded Fresh-Eating Pomegranate)
description: Sin Pepe carries pale pink arils so soft-seeded they can be chewed and swallowed whole, with a mild, fruit-punch-like sweetness and almost no tartness or astringency. Its light coloring and non-staining juice make it especially good for fresh eating and juicing without the mess of darker-fruited cultivars. The shrub grows in the typical multi-stemmed pomegranate habit and can be trained as a small tree or left as a dense hedge-like shrub. It is a newer soft-seeded selection maintained in the USDA pomegranate germplasm collection and increasingly offered by specialty fruit nurseries in the Gulf South. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Singleleaf Pinyon Pine
description: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to very dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; singleleaf pinyon pine is the botanical oddity of the pine family — the only pine in the world with one needle per fascicle (bundle) rather than the 2–5 needles typical of all other pines. The stout, curved, single needle is one of the most distinctive identification features in the western flora. The dominant tree of the Great Basin at mid-elevations — forming the classic Nevada and Utah basin-and-range piñon-juniper woodland with Utah juniper (Juniperus osteosperma) across millions of acres of the intermountain West. Produces large, wingless, edible pine nuts (piñon nuts) comparable in size and quality to the two-needle pinyon's nuts — both species' nuts are harvested commercially and by Native peoples. The nuts are an essential fall food for many Great Basin birds and mammals, including pinyon jays, Clark's nutcrackers, and mule deer. An exceptional xeriscape tree for hot, dry, rocky Great Basin and Mojave-edge gardens. Matures in 730–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sinton Citrangequat (Cold-Hardy Citrange-Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Sinton was bred alongside the better-known Thomasville and Telfair citrangequats in the early 1900s by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle, crossing cold-hardy citrange (trifoliate orange x sweet orange) with kumquat to create an edible-skinned, tart-sweet novelty citrus for the coldest edge of the citrus range. Small, rounded, orange fruit has an aromatic marmalade-type flavor best suited to preserves and candying rather than fresh eating. The tree is a compact, thorny large shrub well suited to Gulf Coast hobbyist plantings where standard citrus struggles to survive hard freezes. Give it full sun, good drainage, and winter protection for young trees to get established. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sioux Pecan (High Kernel-Percentage Type I Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sioux, released from the USDA breeding program in Texas, produces small to medium nuts but is valued for an exceptionally high kernel percentage and rich, sweet flavor that makes it a favorite among home growers for eating fresh out of hand. Its smaller, more manageable tree size compared to old-line pecans like Stuart makes it a good fit for home orchards with limited space. It is a Type I pollinator and needs a Type II variety nearby for good nut set. Scab susceptibility is a real concern in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so Sioux performs best in drier inland areas or with a fungicide spray program during wet springs; irrigate deeply during nut fill for the best kernel quality. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Sioux Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake or cage early — Sioux is an indeterminate variety that sets fruit continuously through the season. Sioux was introduced by the University of Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station in 1944, bred specifically for heat tolerance and disease resistance in hot, humid, continental climates; it remains one of the most reliably productive tomatoes for hot Southern summers and Gulf Coast conditions where other varieties drop blossoms during heat waves — Sioux continues setting medium-sized (6–8 oz), round, bright red fruits even when nighttime temperatures stay above 75°F. The flavor is classic, balanced, and mildly acidic — a dependable slicer with good disease resistance and continuous production from early summer until frost. Highly recommended for gardeners in zones 8–11 who struggle to keep tomatoes producing through midsummer. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Sirenevyi Pomegranate (Cold-Hardy Lilac-Skinned Russian Pomegranate)
description: Sirenevyi is a Russian-bred pomegranate cultivar named for the distinctive lilac-purple blush of its rind, which sets it apart visually from typical red-skinned pomegranates. Bred for cold hardiness, it is a good option for growers on the cooler fringe of the Gulf Coast pomegranate range who still want reliable fruiting. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and expect a compact, multi-stemmed shrub habit that responds well to light annual pruning. Fruit has a tart-sweet flavor typical of Central Asian and Russian pomegranate breeding lines; harvest in fall once the rind fully colors and a metallic ring is heard when fruit is tapped. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sirola Sea Buckthorn (Upright Low-Thorn Seaberry)
description: Sirola is a female sea buckthorn selection noted for its upright, relatively narrow growth habit and comparatively few thorns compared with older wild-type selections, which makes hand harvest noticeably easier. It bears heavy clusters of large, sweet-tart orange berries on long stalks that hang somewhat clear of the foliage, another trait that speeds picking. Like all sea buckthorn it is dioecious and needs a male plant nearby for pollination, and its nitrogen-fixing roots let it thrive in lean, sandy, or coastal soils where little else fruits well. Established plants are extremely drought and wind tolerant and need almost no supplemental feeding once settled in. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sirora Pistachio (Even-Bearing Australian-Bred Selection)
description: Sirora was developed by Australia's CSIRO from open-pollinated seed of the Red Aleppo pistachio and has become the dominant cultivar in Australian orchards, planted on roughly half of the country's pistachio acreage. Its main advantage over Kerman is more consistent year-to-year cropping rather than a pronounced alternate-bearing cycle, and total yield across seasons can be substantially higher even though individual nuts run smaller than Kerman's. It also ripens earlier, which helps growers finish harvest before fall rains in variable climates. Sirora still needs roughly 1000 hours of winter chilling below about 45°F along with a hot, dry summer to properly fill and split its shells, and dry conditions during summer and fall are important to prevent fungal problems — conditions the Gulf Coast's humid summers do not naturally provide, so treat this as a high-risk experimental planting reserved for the driest, most exposed, best-draining site on the property. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Sivan Melon (Israeli Galia-Type Hybrid Muskmelon)
description: Sow 3-4 seeds per hill after soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, thinning to two vigorous plants per hill, or transplant tender young seedlings if a short growing season demands a head start. Sivan is a Galia-type F1 hybrid melon bred in Israel, popular there and across the Mediterranean and Middle East for its round, heavily netted rind that shifts from green to golden yellow at ripeness and its highly aromatic, pale green, sugary flesh that develops flavor unusually fast for a muskmelon, typically ready 75-85 days from sowing. Grow it like other Galia types on black plastic mulch to warm the root zone and suppress weeds, keep watering consistent through fruit set, then taper off as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with gentle pressure and the blossom end gives off a strong sweet fragrance. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Six Basil Blend
description: This blend gathers six basils, including Genovese and large-leaf types for pesto, Dark Opal for colorful vinegars, plus lime and lemon basils for oils, sauces, and sorbets. Because every type in the mix is a form of Ocimum basilicum, they share the same warm-weather culture and can be grown together for a diverse harvest. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after frost into full sun with rich, moist soil. Pinch flower buds and harvest often to keep the range of scents and flavors at their peak. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Six Weeks Purple Hull Pea
description: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and one of the fastest-maturing Southern peas available, ready to pick as fresh shell peas in as little as six weeks. Six Weeks Purple Hull is a classic, widely grown heirloom cowpea prized above all for its speed — the compact, semi-bush plants set pods and fill out quickly, making it the go-to variety for gardeners who want an early first picking or need to squeeze in extra succession plantings between other summer crops. The pods mature to a deep purple that makes ripe pods easy to spot against the green foliage, and the cream-colored peas inside have the classic mild, earthy purple hull flavor, excellent fresh-shelled and cooked down Southern-style with a bit of pork or simmered as a simple pot of field peas. Reliable, heat-tolerant, and fast, it is a Gulf South garden staple for a quick, dependable pea crop, zone 5–11. Matures in 42–55 days from seed.

name: Skeena Cherry (Self-Fertile Late-Season Dark Sweet Cherry)
description: Skeena was released from a British Columbia breeding program and is prized for its large, firm, dark mahogany-red fruit with excellent flavor and good resistance to rain-cracking. It is self-fertile and ripens about a week after Bing, extending the mid-to-late season sweet cherry harvest for home orchards. Give it deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and consistent moisture as fruit sizes up to avoid splitting. Prune to an open center or central leader in late winter and net trees as fruit colors to deter birds. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Skioka Chestnut (Gellatly Chinese Chestnut Pollinizer Selection)
description: Skioka (Gellatly #2) is an open-pollinated Chinese chestnut seedling selected by J.U. Gellatly in British Columbia and is grown chiefly as a dependable, heavy pollen producer rather than for its own nut crop. It is commonly interplanted with pollen-sterile Pacific Northwest hybrid selections, such as Layeroka, to ensure full pollination and a reliable nut set on those trees. Skioka itself also produces nuts and, as a Chinese chestnut seedling, benefits from the species' generally good resistance to chestnut blight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Skirret
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-prepared, deeply cultivated soil; skirret produces a cluster of multiple sweet, carrot-like roots that need loose ground to develop well. Keep well-watered through summer as drought stress causes woody, fibrous roots with an unpleasant core. Harvest in autumn after frost, washing and separating the finger-sized roots; any woody central strings are removed before eating. Divide clumps in early spring to propagate, replanting the outer sections and discarding the old center. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Skookum Chestnut (Gellatly-Schildgen Pacific Northwest Hybrid)
description: Skookum is a Gellatly-lineage hybrid chestnut selected by W. Schildgen and grown in Pacific Northwest orchards for its good nut flavor and regional adaptation. Blight resistance records for Skookum are mixed rather than fully resistant, so it is best sited where blight pressure is manageable or combined with other resistant cultivars in a planting. Because it is pollen-sterile, Skookum must be planted alongside a genetically distinct, overlapping-bloom pollinizer to produce nuts. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Skullcap
description: Cold-stratify seed in moist peat in the refrigerator for 4 weeks before surface-sowing onto a warm starting mix; germination is slow and erratic. Plant in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil that mimics its woodland-edge native habitat. Harvest aerial parts — stems, leaves, and small flowers — in full bloom during summer, using them fresh or dried for tinctures and teas valued for their calming properties. Divide established clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Skunk Currant
description: A low, sprawling, thornless currant native to cool, moist forests and streambanks across boreal Canada and the northern Appalachians, Skunk Currant is among the most shade-tolerant of all Ribes species, thriving even in fairly dense conifer shade where few other fruiting shrubs persist. The small red berries are covered in gland-tipped bristles and, like the foliage, release a distinctly skunky odor when bruised or crushed, which limits their appeal for fresh eating but does not prevent their use cooked into jam or jelly. Give it consistently damp, humus-rich soil and cool root conditions, as it struggles in heat or dry sites. It spreads gradually by low, rooting branches rather than aggressively, making it a manageable native choice for a shaded, moist woodland edge. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Skyphos Lettuce (Red Butterhead)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant out once seedlings have several true leaves, spacing 8-10 inches apart in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Skyphos is a European-bred red butterhead prized for forming reliably dense, well-rounded heads even in variable weather, unlike many red butterheads that head loosely or split. Its deep burgundy-red outer leaves wrap around a contrasting lime-green heart, with color intensifying in cool weather and softening to more green in heat, and the buttery texture holds a mild, sweet flavor. It is a good choice for gardeners who want the visual drama of a red lettuce without sacrificing the reliable heading habit of a classic Boston type. Matures in 47–55 days from transplant.

name: SL28 Coffee
description: Selected in the 1930s by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya from a single drought-tolerant tree, this tall, vigorous Arabica selection is renowned among specialty roasters for an intensely bright, blackcurrant-like acidity and full, syrupy body that few other varieties match. It is deep-rooted and notably tolerant of dry spells once established, but it lacks resistance to coffee berry disease and leaf rust, so watch new growth for spotting and treat promptly if either appears. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions favored by other highland Arabicas, feeding regularly through the growing season, and expect a tall, open-branched shrub that begins bearing after three to four years. Because of its height it suits large containers, conservatories, or in-ground planting in zones 10-11 rather than tight patio pots. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: SL34 Coffee
description: Selected alongside its sister cultivar SL28 by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya, SL34 shares much of the same French Mission Bourbon ancestry and produces a similarly rich, wine-toned, high-quality cup, though it tends to perform better in wetter highland sites and bears somewhat more heavily. Like SL28 it is a tall, open-growing Arabica with limited resistance to leaf rust and coffee berry disease, so it rewards attentive scouting and prompt treatment of any fungal spotting on leaves or cherries. Provide the same warm, humid, dappled-shade conditions as other highland Arabica types, feed regularly, and expect first cherries after roughly three to four years. Its larger eventual size makes it best suited to spacious containers or in-ground planting in zones 10-11. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sleeping Giant Chestnut (Blight-Resistant Connecticut Complex Hybrid Chestnut)
aliases: Castanea mollissima x (crenata x dentata) 'Sleeping Giant'
description: Sleeping Giant is a complex mollissima x (crenata x dentata) hybrid selected by Arthur H. Graves at the Sleeping Giant chestnut plantation in Hamden, Connecticut, part of the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station's early chestnut breeding program. It has recorded resistance to chestnut blight and produces medium-sized nuts, roughly 15 grams each, with excellent, sweet flavor and good pellicle (skin) removal, ripening from mid- to late September. Plant it with a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby, since Sleeping Giant will not reliably set a crop on its own. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sleeping Lady Tomato (Pink-Fruited Alaskan-Named Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Sleeping Lady bears medium pink fruit with sweet, well-rounded flavor on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant, named for the Sleeping Lady mountain near Anchorage, Alaska, home to one of the breeding program's participating gardeners. Its manageable size and reliable production suit raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Slender Amaranth (Livid Amaranth, Chinese Spinach)
description: Broadcast or drill seed thinly into warm, fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart for continuous baby-leaf harvest. Slender amaranth grows quickly into low, branching plants with tender, mild, spinach-like leaves that hold up to heat and humidity far better than true spinach, making it a reliable summer green in hot climates where cool-season greens have already bolted. Harvest by pinching young shoot tips and outer leaves regularly, which encourages fresh branching growth and delays the onset of flowering; older plants become slightly coarser but remain edible when cooked. It self-sows readily in disturbed garden soil, so remove spent plants before seed drop if volunteer seedlings are not wanted the following season. Cook briefly like spinach or chard, as the leaves wilt down substantially and have a mild, slightly earthy flavor. Matures in 30–55 days from seed.

name: Slicing Cucumber
description: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; slicing cucumbers are bred for fresh eating with smooth, glossy, dark-green skins, mild flavor, and few seeds compared to pickling types. Provide a trellis for vining varieties to keep fruits straight and clean and improve air circulation; bush types are more compact and work well in raised beds. Water deeply and consistently — inconsistent moisture causes bitter fruit and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest when fruits are 7–9 inches long before the skin yellows or seeds harden. Pick frequently — leaving overripe fruits on the vine signals the plant to stop producing. Cucumber beetles are the primary pest; row covers until flowering provide effective protection. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Slim Jim Eggplant
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into a sunny spot or a large container after the last frost, keeping the compact plants consistently watered since their smaller root systems dry out faster than standard eggplant. Deadheading spent fruit encourages continued production through the season. Slim Jim produces slender, finger-sized purple fruit on a small, bushy plant, making it a popular choice for patio containers and small gardens where space is limited. Its petite size and attractive purple flowers also make it a common pick for ornamental-edible plantings. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Slimleaf Pawpaw (Small-flowered Pawpaw)
description: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands. Narrow, willow-like leaves and creamy white to pale yellow, nodding flowers set this small shrubby tree apart from the common pawpaw, and it bears small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit with the characteristic custardy pawpaw flavor, though smaller and less commonly harvested than named common pawpaw cultivars. Native to the fire-maintained sandhill and scrub habitats of Florida, Georgia, and the western Gulf coastal plain, it is well adapted to the region's characteristic dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and periodic natural fire, resprouting readily from its root system after top damage. It serves the same role as other pawpaws as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies and needs little supplemental water once its extensive root system is established in sandy soil. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Slo-Bolt Lettuce (Classic Heat-Resistant Looseleaf Lettuce)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Slo-Bolt lives up to its name as one of the most heat-resistant looseleaf lettuces available, holding good flavor and resisting the bitterness and premature flowering that end the harvest of most lettuce varieties once temperatures climb, making it a favorite for extending the spring lettuce season deeper into the Gulf South's warm months. It produces medium green, slightly frilled leaves in a loose, open rosette well suited to cut-and-come-again harvest. Pick outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing, and provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to push the harvest window even further. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Sloe (Blackthorn)
description: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in any well-drained soil — poor, thin, alkaline, or rocky — in full sun to partial shade; blackthorn is one of the most adaptable and tough woody plants available, tolerating exposure, drought, poor soil, and neglect. Prunus spinosa is a very thorny, dense, suckering European native shrub that flowers brilliantly in early spring with masses of small, white blossoms on bare black stems before the leaves appear, creating a spectacular display; the flowers are followed by small (1/3–1/2 inch), round, blue-black fruits (sloes) with a white bloom, astringent flesh, and complex flavor that is unpalatable raw but transforms with frost and sugar into excellent jams, jellies, wine, and the essential ingredient of sloe gin. The dense, thorny thickets provide superb nesting habitat for birds and small mammals. Harvest sloes after the first frost for best flavor. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Slow Bolt Arugula
description: Direct sow seed shallowly in cool weather and keep the bed moist for quick, even germination. As the name suggests, this variety resists bolting longer than standard arugula and tolerates a bit more heat. Harvest young leaves for microgreens or baby greens, or let plants reach full size for peppery salad leaves. Cut outer leaves and let the center regrow for repeated harvests. Successive sowings every couple of weeks keep a steady supply of tender greens. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Slow Bolt Cilantro
description: Direct sow seed where plants are to grow, as cilantro has a taproot and dislikes transplanting. This beginner-friendly variety is bred to stay leafy longer before bolting to seed, extending the harvest of flat, flavorful leaves. Plants reach about twelve to twenty-four inches and respond well to successive sowings every few weeks. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage fresh growth and delay flowering. If plants do bolt, let them go to seed to collect coriander. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Small Black Blueberry (Deerberry Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), lean soil in partial shade to full sun; small black blueberry is a dwarf, spreading native vaccinium of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine flatwoods, closely associated with longleaf pine habitat. The small, very dark blue-black berries ripen in early summer and, while tiny, are intensely flavored and sweet — eaten fresh or used in preserves and baked goods in the traditional Southern way. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form low colonies and provides important food for dozens of bird species. In the native range, it grows in the precise habitat type (sandy, dry, very acidic) that is among the most threatened ecosystems in North America. An excellent species for naturalized longleaf pine ecosystem restoration in the Gulf Coastal Plain. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Small Coastal Germander (Dwarf Germander)
description: Sow directly into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; small coastal germander is a diminutive, aromatic mint-family annual to short-lived perennial found on coastal sands and shell middens from Texas and Louisiana to Florida. Its lobed gray-green leaves and tiny white to pale blue speckled flowers stay low and inconspicuous, making it best suited to a sunny gravel path, dune restoration planting, or the gaps between coastal paving stones rather than a formal bed. It tolerates the long, humid Gulf Coast growing season without irrigation once established and self-sows into bare sandy patches, filling niches too dry and infertile for most other groundcovers. Matures in 60–100 days from seed.

name: Small Cranberry (Bog Cranberry)
description: Plant in constantly moist to saturated, strongly acidic, peaty soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally in a lined bog bed amended heavily with peat moss; small cranberry is a circumboreal wild relative of the commercially grown large cranberry, with wiry, thread-like trailing stems, tiny evergreen leaves, and delicate pink, backward-swept flowers in early summer. It bears smaller, more strongly tart fruit than cultivated cranberry, ripening from late summer into fall and usable in the same jellies, sauces, and baked goods, though yields are lighter than commercial varieties. Because it is adapted to genuine sphagnum bog habitat, it needs sustained moisture and acidity that most garden soils cannot provide without significant modification, making a dedicated peat bog bed or large lined container the most realistic way to grow it outside its native cold, wet peatlands. Mulch with additional peat or pine needles each year to maintain acidity, and avoid any liming or alkaline amendments nearby. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Small Leaf Tea Camellia (Compact China-Type Tea Selection)
description: Small Leaf is a classic small-leaved China-type (var. sinensis) tea selection, propagated by specialty camellia nurseries from a long-cultivated Southeastern stock plant, and grown for its compact, container-friendly, densely branching habit. Leaves stay under about 4 inches long, giving a fine-textured hedge and a milder, more delicate cup than larger-leaved types. Provide morning sun with afternoon shade, keep the soil consistently moist and acidic, and expect a rounded shrub reaching roughly 3 to 6 feet in a decade. Begin light plucking of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Small Sugar Pumpkin
description: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm, fertile soil, planting in hills and thinning to the strongest plants. This classic heirloom pie pumpkin produces compact, deep-orange fruits with sweet, fine-grained flesh perfect for baking. Give the vines plenty of room to run and keep them well watered as fruits develop. Harvest in fall when the rind is hard and fully colored, then cure the pumpkins for a week or two to improve storage and flavor. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Small Viburnum (Walter Viburnum)
description: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; small viburnum is an underused evergreen to semi-evergreen native of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, valued for its small, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves, masses of tiny white flower clusters in early spring before most plants awaken, and the bright red to dark purple-black drupes that provide exceptional wildlife food in summer and fall. Unlike many large viburnums, small viburnum stays naturally compact, to 6–8 feet in cultivation, and responds well to pruning — it can be maintained as a low hedge or specimen shrub. Very drought tolerant once established despite its riparian origins. The cultivar 'Mrs. Schiller's Delight' stays under 3 feet with particularly glossy foliage. An excellent choice for shaded understory positions and moist areas in zone 8–10 landscapes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Small Wonder Spaghetti Squash (Compact Personal-Size Hybrid)
description: Small Wonder is a hybrid spaghetti squash bred for a compact, space-saving vine that still delivers high yields of personal-sized fruit, each weighing roughly 1.5 to 2 pounds, about half the size of standard spaghetti squash. The oval fruit yield the same pale-yellow, stringy flesh that separates into spaghetti-like strands when cooked, making it well suited to single servings without the leftovers a full-sized fruit produces. Because the vines take up notably less garden space than traditional spaghetti squash, it is a practical choice for smaller vegetable beds or intensive plantings. It also matures somewhat earlier than many full-sized spaghetti squash varieties, giving a head start in shorter growing seasons. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Smallage (Cutting Celery)
description: Surface sow seed on moist starting mix at 65°F and provide bright light; smallage is the ancient, semi-wild form of celery with thin, hollow stems and very intensely flavored leaves — flavor is perhaps 10 times stronger than modern celery and reminiscent of the finest celery seed spice. It is grown primarily for its leaves, not its stalks, and a small amount goes a long way in soups, stews, and sauces. Unlike stalk celery, smallage is relatively easy to grow, tolerates partial shade, and does not require blanching. It is the celery of most historical European recipes before hybridization for thick stalks. A biennial or short-lived perennial that self-sows readily to establish a permanent presence in the herb garden. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Smaragd Mahonia (Compact Bronze-New-Growth Oregon Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding exposed sites with harsh winter wind and afternoon sun. Smaragd is a dense, low-mounding Oregon grape selection staying under 2 feet tall, with bronze new foliage maturing to deep glossy green through summer and turning purple-red in winter. Dense clusters of yellow flowers open in spring, followed by dusty blue-black, tart, edible berries on spiny, holly-like evergreen leaves. Its compact scale suits foreground plantings in a shaded shrub border or as a flowering groundcover under high shade. Prune only to remove dead or leggy canes at ground level. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Smith Fig (Texas BA-1)
description: Smith is a heirloom fig long maintained in the Becnel family of Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, and later used briefly as breeding stock in fig improvement work in Louisiana. Fruit is large and somewhat flattened, yellow skin blushed with brown, opening to deep red flesh with a distinctive drop of honey at the eye and outstanding sweetness. The cold-hardier reselection sold as Texas BA-1 traces back to this same variety and is a good option where Smith itself proves less reliable through winter. Like most Southern heirloom figs it is self-fertile, easy-care, and productive with minimal attention once established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Smitten Apple (New Zealand Bred Sweet Crisp Apple)
description: Smitten was bred by Plant and Food Research in New Zealand and selected for its dense, juicy crunch, honeyed sweetness, and appealing bright yellow skin with a pink-red blush. It ripens in the early-to-mid fall harvest window and keeps its crisp texture well in cold storage. The tree tends to bear at a relatively young age once established. Thin fruit clusters in early summer to improve fruit size and reduce the tendency toward biennial bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Smokehouse Apple (Reliable Pennsylvania All-Purpose Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Smokehouse originated in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, reportedly discovered as a seedling growing near a farm smokehouse, and it became a widely planted, dependable all-purpose apple across the Mid-Atlantic for over a century. The medium to large fruit has yellow skin streaked and blushed with red, and the crisp, firm, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that performs equally well fresh, baked, and pressed for cider, a genuine multipurpose apple in the old farmstead tradition. The vigorous, productive tree bears reliably and holds fruit reasonably well in storage, making it a solid choice for home orchardists who want a historic variety without the finicky habits of some rarer heirlooms. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Smokey Bronze Fennel
description: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun where the plant can remain undisturbed for years, since bronze fennel builds a deep taproot and returns from the crown each spring in mild-winter climates. Smokey is a selected bronze-leaved strain valued for especially rich, smoky copper-purple filigreed foliage that holds its dark coloring through the season better than seed-grown bronze fennel populations, which often fade toward green. The tall plumes of foliage are topped in summer by wide, flat umbels of small yellow flowers that draw enormous numbers of pollinators and serve as a favored host plant for swallowtail butterfly caterpillars. Harvest feathery leaves continuously for a sweet anise flavor in fish and salad dishes, and collect the ripening seed heads in late summer for use as a spice or tea; deadhead some umbels before seed drop if self-sowing is not wanted. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Smoky Saskatoon (Serviceberry)
description: Smoky is one of the oldest named saskatoon selections, prized for consistent heavy fruiting and reliably sweet, dark purple berries on a suckering multi-stem shrub.
