It tolerates extreme prairie winters and thrives in a wide range of soils provided drainage is adequate. Thin out old canes periodically to keep the clump productive and encourage new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Smooth Boy Luffa
description: Smooth Boy is a widely available named cultivar of smooth luffa, recommended by University of Florida gardening programs for home dual-purpose growing: young fruit picked at 6-8 inches has mild, zucchini-like flesh good for stir-fries and soups, while fruit left on the vine to mature and turn brown yields the classic fibrous bath and cleaning sponge once peeled and cured. It produces cylindrical, smooth to faintly ribbed fruit on a fast-climbing vine that thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity, and it flowers with showy bright-yellow blossoms that attract pollinators. Give it a tall, strong trellis or arbor, since vines readily reach 15-20 feet, and keep soil evenly moist through fruit set for the straightest, best-formed sponges. Matures in 60–100 days from seed.

name: Smooth Cayenne Pineapple (Classic Commercial Pineapple)
description: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Smooth Cayenne is the classic commercial pineapple cultivar grown throughout the tropics for its large, cylindrical, juicy, sweet-tart fruit with relatively smooth, spineless leaf margins that make handling far easier than older spiny pineapple types. Plants form a low rosette of stiff, strap-like leaves and take 18-24 months from planting to produce a single fruit at the center of the rosette, after which side suckers can be removed and replanted to start new plants. Because pineapple has essentially no frost tolerance, zone 9 gardeners should grow it in a large container that can be moved to a greenhouse, garage, or bright indoor spot before the first freeze, bringing it back outside once nights stay reliably above 50F. Full sun, warmth, and free-draining soil or potting mix are the main requirements for good fruit size and flavor. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Smooth Hawk's Beard
description: Surface-sow or barely cover seeds in full sun in early spring, thinning to 6-10 inches once seedlings are established; smooth hawk's beard germinates quickly and is ready to harvest within a month of sowing. Cut young rosette leaves when they are 3-4 inches long for the mildest flavor, using them raw in salads or wilting briefly in a pan with olive oil and garlic. Plants can be cut back to within an inch of the crown and will regrow for additional harvests before bolting triggers the small yellow flower heads. Self-seeding is prolific in disturbed ground, making smooth hawk's beard a low-maintenance, cut-and-come-again addition to the productive garden. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Smooth Luffa (Loofah, Sponge Gourd, Vegetable Sponge)
description: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 2–4 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained, deeply cultivated, moist, fertile soil on a very sturdy trellis or fence — luffa vines become heavy and must have strong support. Luffa aegyptiaca (smooth luffa or vegetable sponge) produces dual crops: the immature fruits (3–5 inches long) are eaten as a vegetable throughout Asia and Africa — tasting like a mild, slightly sweet zucchini — while the fully mature, dried fruits are harvested for their fibrous interior skeleton, which dries into the familiar luffa or loofah bath sponge. The vine produces large, bright-yellow flowers (4–5 inches, excellent for pollinators) and cylindrical fruits 18–24 inches long that must be allowed to ripen fully on the vine until the skin yellows and shrivels before harvesting for sponges. To process sponges: cure dried gourds in the sun, peel off the papery skin, shake out seeds (save for next year), wash, and bleach lightly if desired. Zone 9 provides the long, hot season luffa requires to complete its full lifecycle and produce dry, mature sponges. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Smooth Sumac
description: Plant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; smooth sumac is the most cold-hardy North American sumac, naturally colonizing roadsides, old fields, and dry slopes throughout most of the continent. It is distinguished from staghorn sumac (R. typhina) by its smooth stems — staghorn has velvety, fuzzy new growth resembling a stag's antler in velvet. The brilliant, fire-engine-red fall color of smooth sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub, often turning color before most other plants. The large, upright, cone-shaped clusters of fuzzy, dark red berries persist through winter and are critically important food for numerous birds including robins, catbirds, mockingbirds, and cedar waxwings. Spreads by root suckers to form thicket colonies — an excellent native for erosion control on dry slopes but needs containment near formal gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Smooth Sweet Cicely
description: Sow Osmorhiza longistylis seeds in fall directly in the garden — seeds are slow to germinate and require cold stratification; alternatively cold-stratify in damp paper towels in the refrigerator for 60–90 days before spring sowing; plants self-sow freely once established and can naturalize into a fragrant woodland groundcover. Smooth Sweet Cicely is an elegant, airy, native woodland herb that fills the shaded understory with its finely divided, carrot-family foliage and pervasive anise fragrance throughout the growing season — the roots especially smell strongly of sweet anise when bruised. All parts are edible: young spring leaves used as a mild anise flavoring in salads, fish dishes, and desserts; the thick, carrot-like taproot grated or eaten raw for its strong anise flavor; the immature green seeds used as a spice. Multiple Indigenous nations used Osmorhiza roots as food and medicine — the Cheyenne as a cold remedy, the Ojibwe as an eye wash, and the Iroquois as a root vegetable cooked with meat. The white, flat-topped flower clusters attract numerous small native bees, wasps, and flies. An excellent companion for ferns, wild ginger, and trilliums in naturalistic woodland gardens; once established, it requires no care beyond controlling spread if self-sowing becomes excessive. Matures in 60–120 days from seed.

name: Smooth Witherod, Possumhaw Viburnum
description: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; viburnum nudum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, and low areas where standing water occasionally occurs. Viburnum nudum produces one of the most spectacular fall berry displays of any native shrub: the abundant berry clusters transition through pink, rose, blue, and finally blue-black as individual berries ripen at different times in September and October, creating a multi-colored cluster that is breathtaking and irresistible to migrating songbirds; the berries are consumed within days of full ripeness by cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other species. The glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage turns rich burgundy-red in fall; white, fragrant flower clusters in May attract native bees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Smyrna Quince (Classic Large Fragrant Turkish Quince)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Smyrna is one of the classic Old World quince cultivars, originating in Turkey and long grown commercially in the eastern Mediterranean, producing large, golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, quince paste (membrillo), and poaching, since the hard, tart flesh is rarely eaten raw. The tree is self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator, and blooms with attractive pale pink spring flowers before setting fruit that ripens in fall. Quince trees are generally low-maintenance once established, tolerating a range of soil types, though good air circulation helps reduce fire blight risk in humid climates. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Snake Gourd
description: Nick the seed coat or soak seeds 24 hours before sowing 1/2 inch deep to improve germination rates in this heat-demanding tropical. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis or overhead structure — vines can exceed 12 feet and produce pendulous fruits that must hang freely to grow straight, reaching 1–3 feet in length. Harvest young fruits at 12–18 inches while skin is still soft and pale green-striped white; the tender young fruit is used like summer squash in South and Southeast Asian cooking. Overripe fruits develop an unpleasant bitter compound and turn orange-red, signaling they should be discarded rather than eaten. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Snap Ginger / Indian Cardamom Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions 2-3 inches deep in moist, organically rich, well-draining soil in partial to full shade, spacing clumps 24-36 inches apart to allow the lance-shaped, aromatic foliage to fill in naturally. Water consistently throughout the growing season to maintain even soil moisture, and apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer in spring to fuel vigorous growth. In zone 8 gardens, mulch the root zone heavily after the first frost to protect the rhizomes through winter, as the tops will die back but the roots typically survive. Harvest young leaves and rhizomes as needed for culinary use in Sri Lankan and South Asian cooking, where both impart a mild cardamom-like fragrance to curries and rice dishes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Snap Pea
description: Sow seed 1 in deep as soon as the ground can be worked and provide twiggy brush or mesh netting for vines to climb. Pre-soaking seeds overnight can improve germination in cold soil. Harvest when pods are plump, fully filled, and glossy; snap peas pass their peak quickly in warm weather. Powdery mildew is common late in the season — choose resistant varieties when available. Matures in 58–70 days from seed.

name: SnapDragon Apple
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator apple within range for good fruit set. SnapDragon (bred as NY1) was developed by Susan Brown at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a 1998 cross of Honeycrisp and the advanced Cornell selection NY 752, reaching commercial release in 2013 alongside its sibling RubyFrost after about a decade of evaluation. It ripens in early-to-mid fall, ahead of RubyFrost, and is prized for an extremely crisp, dense bite along with a sweet flavor carrying a distinctive spicy note inherited from its Honeycrisp parent. It is best suited to the cold-winter apple regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that the Geneva breeding program targets, and it stores well under refrigeration, though not as long as the later-ripening RubyFrost. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Snow Crown Cauliflower (AAS-Winning Early Hybrid Cauliflower)
description: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Snow Crown, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is one of the fastest-maturing cauliflower varieties available, reliably forming smooth, dense, pure white heads well ahead of many other cultivars, an important advantage in the Gulf South where cauliflower's narrow cool-season window can cut short slower-maturing varieties. Its early maturity also makes it more forgiving of the unpredictable spring warm-ups that can stall cauliflower head formation. Tie or fold outer leaves over the developing head once it is a couple of inches across to blanch it and keep the curds bright white, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before they begin to separate or discolor. Matures in 50–60 days from transplant.

name: Snow Pea
description: Press seeds 1 in deep into cool, well-drained soil and erect support netting before the vines need it. Snow peas are harvested when pods are flat, bright green, and the seeds inside are barely visible; even slight bulging means the pod is overripe for stir-fry use. Keep pods picked daily during peak production to sustain cropping. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush foliage at the expense of pods. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Snow White Bok Choy
description: Direct sow thinly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning seedlings once true leaves appear; Snow White is a tall heirloom bok choy type distinguished by unusually broad, glistening white petioles topped with crisp, dark green leaves. Unlike many bok choy types that need full sun to size up quickly, Snow White holds its quality and resists premature bolting when given afternoon shade during the warmer edges of the growing season, making it a useful pick for beds that only get partial light. Harvest whole heads once the thick white stems have filled out, or take outer stalks individually for a longer cut-and-come-again season; the crunchy stems are good raw, and both stems and leaves hold up well in stir-fries and soups. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Snow White Cherry Tomato (Pale Ivory Sweet Cherry)
description: A pale ivory-yellow cherry tomato with such low acidity and high sugar that it is regularly ranked among the sweetest cherry tomatoes grown, with a near-translucent skin over blushing golden flesh. The heavy-yielding indeterminate vines set long clusters of one-inch round fruit continuously through the season and benefit from steady, even watering, since the thin skin cracks readily after a dry spell followed by heavy rain. Its mild, sugary flavor and pastel color make it a favorite for fresh eating and mixed cherry-tomato salads rather than cooking. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Snowball Cauliflower
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant into rich, evenly moist soil, since cauliflower needs steady growth without checks. This early-maturing heirloom forms uniform, snow-white heads with excellent flavor. When the curds reach the size of an egg, tie or fold the outer leaves over them to blanch and protect the head from yellowing. Harvest while the heads are firm and tight, before the curds begin to loosen or separate. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Snowball White Turnip
description: Direct sow seeds a quarter to half an inch deep and thin seedlings so roots have room to round out. This reliable heirloom produces smooth, round white roots with a mild, sweet flavor, and its tender greens are edible too. Keep the soil evenly moist for fast, crack-free growth in the cool seasons. Harvest roots young, at about two to three inches, when they are sweetest and most tender. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Snowball White Turnip Heirloom
description: Sow seeds shallowly directly in the garden and thin the seedlings to a few inches apart for well-formed roots. This timeless heirloom yields smooth, round white roots with a mild, sweet taste, and both roots and greens are good eating. Provide steady moisture so the roots stay crisp and do not turn woody in warm spells. Pull turnips while young and tender for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Snowball Y Cauliflower
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — cauliflower requires more nitrogen and consistent moisture than any other Brassica; Snowball Y is one of the classic open-pollinated white cauliflower varieties — an improved selection from the Snowball strain that has defined the white-headed cauliflower in American horticulture for a century. The compact, round, pure white heads (when properly blanched) represent the culmination of cauliflower development — the plant's edible curd is composed of densely packed, malformed (fasciated) flower buds arrested before they develop, creating the characteristic curded texture of cauliflower. Unlike broccoli, where the flower buds are visible and intact, cauliflower's curd represents a complete developmental halt before budding — a botanical curiosity that produces one of the most unusual vegetable textures available, simultaneously firm and mealy, dense and delicate. Cauliflower's reputation for difficulty is warranted — it requires the most specific temperature range (50–70°F) of any commonly grown vegetable, failing in heat or extreme cold. In zone 9 this restricts successful cauliflower to a narrow fall window of September–December planting. Matures in 55–68 days from transplant.

name: Snowball Y Cauliflower
description: Start seed indoors and transplant sturdy seedlings into rich, evenly moist soil for a spring or fall crop. This dependable variety forms flavorful six-inch snow-white heads in about seventy to eighty days, making it well suited to short-season gardens. The leaves naturally curl around the head for self-blanching and protection from sun scald. Keep water and nutrients steady, since stress can trigger loose or off-color curds. Mature heads hold well in the garden, so they need not all be cut at once. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Snowbird Pea (Early Dwarf Shelling Pea for Southern Gardens)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Snowbird is a short, self-supporting dwarf shelling pea bred to mature very quickly, an important trait in the Gulf South where the cool-season pea window is narrow before summer heat arrives and stops pod production. Its compact vines need little to no staking, and the concentrated, early harvest lets gardeners get a pea crop in before spring warms up too much. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking regularly to encourage the plant to keep flowering during its short productive window. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Snowcap Bean
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Snowcap is a bush-type bean that needs no support and can be direct-seeded in rows 18 inches apart. Snowcap is an heirloom bush dry bean producing attractive, round-to-oval seeds that are white with a distinctive cap of maroon-red coloring concentrated around the seed scar (hilum) — the 'snowcap' pattern from which it takes its name. The flavor is rich, buttery, and creamy when cooked, with a thin skin that doesn't need pre-soaking for most applications; it is outstanding in soups, chilis, and bean salads where its firm-yet-creamy texture holds up well. An attractive plant for the vegetable garden with modest height and compact habit; the ornamental seeds are a bonus when drying for seed saving. One of the most beautiful and best-flavored heirloom dry beans in the Seed Savers Exchange collection. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Snowcap Chives (Semi-Dwarf White Spherical-Bloom Selection)
description: Snowcap is a semi-dwarf chive selection bred for its pristine white, tightly spherical flower heads held just above a low, mounding clump of finely textured, gray-green leaves, a striking contrast to the lilac-pink blooms of ordinary chives. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, where the compact habit performs well as edging or in rock gardens without sprawling into neighboring plants. Snip leaves regularly for the same mild onion flavor as standard chives, and shear back spent flower stalks after bloom to encourage a tidy second flush of foliage. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain the tight, uniform mound this cultivar is prized for. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Snowchaser Blueberry (Earliest-Ripening Commercial Florida Southern Highbush)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Snowchaser is an extremely low-chill southern highbush blueberry bred to capture the earliest possible market window, with fruit ripening throughout April, among the earliest of any commercial blueberry cultivar. This early-ripening advantage comes with a tradeoff: the cultivar is more prone to stem blight than sturdier southern highbush selections and benefits from careful site selection, good drainage, and prompt removal of any blighted canes to maintain long-term plant health. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and monitor closely for stem dieback, pruning out affected wood as soon as it is noticed. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Snowcloud Serviceberry (Vigorous Upright Allegheny Selection)
description: Snowcloud is a single-trunk selection of Allegheny serviceberry chosen for markedly faster growth and a tidier, more upright oval form than typical seedling A. laevis. Bronze-red new foliage unfurls beneath heavy drooping clusters of white flowers in early spring, followed by June berries that ripen from red through purple to near-black and are good for fresh eating or baking if harvested ahead of the birds. Foliage holds up well through summer heat and humidity before turning coppery orange to red in fall. Site it in full sun to light shade and moist, well-drained soil, and use it as a specimen or street tree where a single clean trunk is preferred over a multi-stemmed clump. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Snowdrift Crabapple
description: Snowdrift bears an exceptionally heavy spring flush of pure white flowers opening from red buds, covering the rounded canopy so thoroughly that the branches are barely visible during peak bloom. Small, orange-red fruits about a third of an inch across follow and persist into winter, holding their color and drawing flocks of cedar waxwings and other fruit-eating birds after most other food sources are gone. It is widely planted for its strong resistance to apple scab and reliable annual flowering, making it a dependable, low-maintenance choice for a front-yard specimen or street tree. Prune young trees lightly in late winter to establish a strong branch framework, since mature specimens need little further shaping. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Snowdrift Creeping Thyme (White-Flowered Mat-Forming Groundcover Thyme)
description: Plant in moist but sharply draining soil in full sun. Snowdrift is a low, evergreen, mat-forming thyme selection with small dark green leaves and dense clusters of pure white flowers in summer, giving it a cooler, brighter effect in the garden than the more common pink- and purple-flowered creeping thymes. It is well suited to rock gardens, gravel paths, and the joints between paving stones, where its flat habit tolerates light foot traffic once established. Bees visit the flowers readily. Like other creeping thymes it resents wet, poorly drained soil and heavy shade; shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: SnowSweet Apple (University of Minnesota Non-Browning White-Flesh Apple)
description: SnowSweet was released by the University of Minnesota apple breeding program and is distinguished by its unusually slow-browning white flesh, which stays fresh-looking far longer than most apples once cut, making it popular for lunchboxes and fruit trays. The mildly sweet, low-acid flavor and dense, crisp texture pair with a red-blushed skin over a pale background, and fruit ripens in the fall. The tree is bred for the extreme winter cold of the Upper Midwest and is reliably hardy well into colder zones than most dessert apples. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples and more consistent annual bearing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Snowy Eggplant
description: Start seeds indoors with bottom heat about eight weeks before transplanting, as eggplant loves warmth. Set plants out only after the weather is settled and warm, spacing them for good air movement. This variety produces firm, sweet white eggplants up to eight inches long with meaty flesh that holds up to grilling and roasting. Harvest fruits while the skin is glossy and the flesh is firm, cutting rather than pulling to avoid damaging the plant. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: So Jujube
description: So is a relatively recent Chinese cultivar prized for fruit that many jujube growers rank among the sweetest of any variety, though it carries a distinctive tart undertone that sets it apart from straightforwardly sugary types like Honey Jar. The round fruit stays small, under an inch across, and the tree itself grows compact and naturally tidy, making it a good option where space is limited. Unlike many jujube cultivars that benefit from a cross-pollinator, So sets a reliable crop on its own, simplifying planting decisions for a single-tree yard. Harvest at the crisp yellow-green to tan stage for the best balance of sweetness and tang, since the tart note fades and the fruit turns simply sweet as it fully browns. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Soap Tree (Soapberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; soap tree is a small evergreen to semi-evergreen tree of the Caribbean and south Florida with pinnately compound leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by translucent, fleshy, amber fruits containing high concentrations of saponins — natural soap compounds. The crushed or moistened fruits lather readily in water and have been used throughout the Caribbean for centuries as soap for washing clothes and hair. Unlike the more common western soapberry (S. drummondii) of the southern plains, soap tree is a subtropical to tropical species better adapted to the hot, humid conditions of south Florida. The fruits are also used in some ayurvedic traditions and in natural cleaning products. A drought-tolerant, low-maintenance native tree providing both ornamental interest and functional soap production for eco-conscious gardeners in zone 9–11. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Soapberry (Wingleaf Soapberry, Wild China Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; soapberry is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, alkaline soils. Sapindus saponaria (wingleaf soapberry or wild China tree) is a native Texas, Caribbean, and tropical American tree producing clusters of small, round, translucent, amber-gold berries in fall that contain saponins — the natural soap compounds that give the genus its Latin name (Sapo = soap, Indus = Indian, originally referring to 'soap nut from the New World'). When the berry flesh is worked with water, it creates a genuine, biodegradable, soap-like lather that has been used by indigenous peoples and settlers for washing clothes, hair, and skin for centuries; the berries are the same 'soapnuts' sold in natural products stores as a biodegradable laundry detergent. The tree is a handsome, medium-sized shade tree with pinnately compound leaves, small white flowers, and attractive amber berries that persist into winter. The hard, black seeds inside the berries have traditionally been used as beads. Outstanding for low-maintenance, drought-tolerant landscaping in the Gulf South, especially on alkaline soils. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Soapwort
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil; soapwort is extremely adaptable and tolerates poor, dry soils once established, spreading by both seed and rhizome. The entire plant — especially the roots — contains saponins that create a soapy lather when bruised and agitated in water, making it historically valuable for washing delicate textiles and woolens. Harvest roots in autumn and foliage before flowering for use in gentle natural soap preparations; the lather cleans without the harshness of detergents. Deadhead spent flowers to limit self-seeding, or allow a few to naturalize for a low-maintenance informal planting of clove-scented pink blooms. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Sochan (Cutleaf Coneflower)
description: Grow in moist, humus-rich soil along a woodland edge or shaded bed; sochan is a tall native perennial in the sunflower family long gathered by the Cherokee and other Southeastern tribes as one of the first spring greens, still harvested today in the Great Smoky Mountains under a treaty-protected gathering right. The deeply cut, lance-shaped basal leaves are picked young in early spring before flowering stalks rise, then cooked like a mild, slightly nutty spinach or wild green — raw leaves can cause stomach upset in some people and are best cooked. Established clumps spread by rhizome and can be divided every few years to renew vigor and expand the patch; leave some growth uncut so plants can flower and support pollinators in mid-to-late summer, when tall yellow daisy-like blooms appear well above the foliage. Cut plants back hard after flowering to encourage a fresh flush of tender basal leaves for a second harvest window in fall. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Sochi Tea (Cold-Hardy Tea Cultivar)
description: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; Sochi is a cold-hardy tea cultivar originally developed for the Black Sea coastal tea-growing region of Russia, the northernmost commercial tea-producing area in the world, and is widely sold in the US specifically because it tolerates significantly colder winters than typical tea plants, with reports of surviving briefly into the single digits °F once well established. This makes it the go-to choice for tea growers in cooler zones than the Gulf South, such as the mid-South and lower Appalachians, though it also performs well in the milder winters of zone 8–9. Leaves and growth habit are similar to standard small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for the same green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch heavily to protect the acid-loving root system through winter in the colder end of its range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Society Garlic
description: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; society garlic is a South African native perfectly adapted to Gulf Coast heat and drought, producing strappy blue-green foliage and clusters of lavender-pink flowers almost continuously from spring through fall. Despite the name, it lacks the offensive breath component of garlic while retaining a mild garlic flavor — the leaves, flowers, and bulbs are all edible and used in salads, stir-fries, and as a cooked vegetable in South African cuisine. It is a superb low-maintenance edging plant for sunny borders, extremely tolerant of heat, reflected heat, poor soil, and dry conditions once established. Deer and rabbits avoid it completely. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Soft Ground Cherry
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant to a full-sun site with sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. Native to the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, this softly hairy perennial ground cherry produces papery-husked yellow berries from late summer through fall that are sweet and pleasant when fully ripe. Plants require excellent drainage and tolerate drought well once established, making them well-suited to xeric southern food gardens. They spread by rhizomes to form loose colonies over time and may die back to the roots in cooler parts of zone 7. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Soissons Bean
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost, and set poles or a trellis at planting time, since this semi-climbing French heirloom benefits from support to keep its long pods off the ground. Named for the town of Soissons north of Paris, this large, flat, ivory-white bean has been the traditional centerpiece of French cassoulet for generations, valued for its creamy texture and its ability to hold shape after long, slow cooking. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry place. A single planting yields a substantial harvest of beans well suited to soups, stews, and braises. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Solano Walnut (Early-Season UC Davis Persian Walnut)
description: Solano is an older University of California Persian walnut release grown chiefly for its early harvest window, ripening well ahead of standard-season cultivars like Chandler and Howard. The tree bears reliably on a spreading, moderately vigorous framework, though its once-wide use in the Sacramento Valley has declined as growers shifted to higher-yielding, disease-tolerant modern releases. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and site it away from frost pockets since earlier leafing can expose young growth to spring cold. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Solar Eclipse Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Black-and-Orange Miniature Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing hills to allow the productive vines to spread. Solar Eclipse produces palm-sized pumpkins whose deep, near-black coloring on the upper half of the fruit fades into bright orange toward the base, a striking pattern that gave the variety its name and earned it an All-America Selections award for novelty color. Plants set a heavy number of the small fruits over a long harvest window, making it useful for gardeners assembling mixed miniature pumpkin displays rather than growing for eating. Pick once the color pattern has fully developed and the rind has hardened, and the small fruits need no curing before use in fall arrangements. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Solar Fire Tomato (AAS-Winning Heat-Adapted Gulf South Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Solar Fire is an All-America Selections-recognized tomato hybrid developed at the University of Florida for superior performance in hot climates — combining good heat tolerance for extended fruit set with excellent fresh-eating flavor, disease resistance, and attractive fruit appearance. The medium-large (8–10 oz), round, firm, bright-red fruits are well-suited to Gulf South conditions — they hold well on the vine and in post-harvest storage better than some softer hybrid types. Solar Fire carries resistance to the major tomato diseases of the humid Gulf South including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), Alternaria stem canker, Gray leaf spot, and Nematodes — a disease package that significantly reduces the fungicide and nematicide inputs required for production. The determinate to semi-determinate growth habit reaches 4–6 feet with moderate staking requirements. Solar Fire typically performs well for zone 9 gardeners in both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The spring crop produces the largest volume of fruit before summer heat; the fall crop frequently produces the best-quality fruit as temperatures cool. An excellent choice for Gulf South gardeners seeking a reliable, productive, disease-resistant red tomato with better heat tolerance than standard commercial varieties. Matures in 72–82 days from transplant.

name: Solar Set Tomato (UF Heat-Setting Gulf South Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Solar Set is a determinate hybrid tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically to address the most critical failure point in Gulf Coast tomato production — the inability of most varieties to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F. In standard tomatoes, high night temperatures destroy pollen viability and prevent fruit set even when flowering is abundant, causing the characteristic 'drop-out' where plants flower profusely but set no fruit as spring transitions to summer. Solar Set was bred to maintain viable pollen and fruit set at higher temperatures than standard varieties, extending the productive window by 2–4 weeks in warm spring conditions — a significant advantage in zone 8–11 where the spring growing window is narrow. The medium-large (6–10 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have good flavor and adequate disease resistance including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and gray leaf spot. Solar Set is not as widely known as Solar Fire or Heatmaster but performs a similar heat-set function and has been a reliable variety in UF variety trials for Gulf Coast spring production. Best suited to spring and fall production in zone 8b–11 where heat-setting capacity provides measurable yield advantages. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Solar Yellow Carrot
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Solar Yellow is a bright lemon-yellow carrot with Nantes-type cylindrical shape and excellent flavor — somewhat milder and less earthy than orange carrots with a clean, slightly sweet taste and better carotene stability (it holds its yellow color both raw and when cooked, unlike purple carrots that fade to orange). Rich in xanthophylls rather than beta-carotene, with distinct nutritional benefits associated with yellow pigments. An excellent variety for multicolored carrot mixes alongside orange, purple, red, and white types for maximum visual and nutritional diversity. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Solbunch Bunching Scallion Onion
description: Direct sow seed thickly in shallow rows in early spring and keep the bed evenly moist. This specialty bunching onion forms uniform, sweet, tender stalks with only a small bulb at the base, prized for grilled cebollitas asadas. Vigorous and easy to grow, it can also be started indoors and transplanted in clumps. Hill a little soil around the stalks to lengthen and blanch the white bases. Harvest whenever stalks reach usable size, pulling entire plants as needed. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Soldier Bean (Johnson Bean)
description: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; soldier bean is a bush type that performs best in cool to moderate summer climates (zones 3–7) but is grown across a wide range. Soldier bean is a New England heirloom dry bean with a long history in Maine and New England, documented in American seed catalogs for well over a century; the seeds are large, kidney-shaped, and pure white with a striking red figure near the hilum that — with some imagination — resembles a soldier or musketeer with a distinctive hat and cloak, making it one of the most visually interesting of all heirloom beans. The cooked flavor is mild, creamy, and rich, similar to navy beans but larger; soldier beans are the traditional bean of New England baked beans, Boston baked beans, and bean soups and make excellent succotash. An outstanding heirloom for seed saving, showing true and breeding reliably from year to year. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Solent Wight Garlic
description: Solent Wight is a British hardneck garlic developed on the Isle of Wight and grown for its large, purple-streaked bulbs and strong, well-rounded flavor suited to the cooler, damper UK climate. Plant cloves pointed end up in fall in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and mulch after the ground cools to guard against frost heaving. As with other hardnecks, cut off the curling scape in early summer to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size. Harvest once the lower leaves have browned, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy, shaded spot for a few weeks before trimming and storing. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Solo Honeyberry (Yezberry Japanese Haskap)
description: Sold under the Proven Winners Yezberry trademark, 'Kapu' descends from purely Japanese Lonicera caerulea strains rather than the Russian and Kuril lines behind most other haskap breeding, giving it a more compact, rounded form and large, tangy fruit borne over a longer harvest window than many single-flush cultivars. It tolerates winter cold to roughly -30F and needs very little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in its first several years. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; while it is marketed as capable of some self-fruiting, yields are markedly higher with a genetically distinct haskap cultivar blooming nearby at the same time. As with all haskap, it flowers extremely early in spring and performs best in cool-summer regions rather than the humid South. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Solo Papaya (Hawaiian Papaya, Kapoho Solo)
description: Sow seeds directly or start transplants in warm soil in full sun after frost danger passes; 'Solo' papaya is the classic Hawaiian commercial papaya developed at the University of Hawaii, the standard against which most commercial papayas are measured — a compact tree producing pear-shaped to round fruits averaging 0.5–2 pounds with deep orange-yellow flesh, exceptional sweetness, and a very small seed cavity. The 'Solo' name refers to being a manageable single-serving size (as opposed to the enormous Mexican papayas). 'Solo' plants may be hermaphrodite (bisexual, which set cylindrical fruits and are preferred for fruit quality), female (which require a male pollinator and produce more spherical fruits), or occasionally male (identified by long dangling chains of tubular flowers and producing no fruit). Plant 2–3 plants and remove males unless one is needed for pollination; bisexual plants are preferred and produce the finest fruit shape. In zone 9, 'Solo' papaya grows as a productive short-lived perennial but needs frost protection; it fruits within 6–10 months from seed, producing continuously in warm weather. The University of Hawaii's 'Rainbow' Solo is the transgenic PRSV-resistant variant widely grown commercially in Hawaii. Matures in 240–365 days from seed.

name: Somerset Hazelnut (Rutgers EFB-Resistant Compact Eastern Filbert)
description: Somerset is the most compact of the four Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant hazelnut cultivars released by Rutgers University in 2020, reaching only about two-thirds the size of its sibling Raritan at maturity, which makes it a good fit for smaller home orchards. Its resistance comes from a distinct vertical resistance gene inherited from the European hazelnut 'Ratoli' and has held up with no observed blight in Rutgers field trials. It is a reliably heavy bearer even on young trees, producing small-to-medium, round kernels with an excellent kernel percentage and good blanching, harvested in the first to second week of September. Being self-incompatible, plant it with a compatible pollenizer such as Raritan or Monmouth, and grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil within its recommended zone 6-7 range. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Somerset Redstreak Apple (Historic Bittersweet Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing. A traditional West Country English cider apple distinct from the unrelated old Redstreak variety once famous in Herefordshire, it produces a reliable crop of medium, red-streaked bittersweet fruit valued by cider makers for good, well-balanced tannin and juice yield in a full-flavored traditional English-style cider blend. Its vigorous, spreading growth habit and reliable annual bearing have kept it in cultivation in traditional Somerset cider orchards for generations, even as many other historic regional varieties have become rare. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Somerset Seedless Grape (Extremely Cold-Hardy Spicy-Sweet Red Grape)
description: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Somerset Seedless was bred by pioneering grape breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, developed for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters far too harsh for most table grapes, while still producing small, red, seedless berries with a sweet flavor carrying a distinctive light spiciness reminiscent of some native American grape species in its parentage. This combination of genuine cold hardiness and good eating quality has made it one of the standard recommendations for far-northern home gardeners wanting a real seedless grape harvest. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Soncoya
description: Plant Annona purpurea in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; water regularly during establishment and during fruiting; the tree is more drought-tolerant than Cherimoya or Sugar Apple once established; hand-pollinate flowers with a small brush during the female phase (when petals are slightly opening) to ensure fruit set, as natural pollinators may be absent outside the native range. Soncoya is the largest of the commercially relevant Annona fruits — with individual fruits commonly weighing 2–5 kg and occasionally much more — distinguished from the better-known custard apples by its dark-green, spiny surface (resembling a chestnut or sea urchin) and very dense, deep-orange to apricot-yellow flesh. The aroma is powerful and characteristic: sweet, musky, and fruity, sometimes described as a combination of mango, pineapple, and vanilla custard. The flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon scooped from the halved fruit; the flavor is very sweet and rich, though the large brown seeds must be removed. Soncoya is native to tropical dry forests of the Pacific coast of Central America and Mexico, making it better adapted to a pronounced dry season than most other Annonas; it performs well in zones with a dry winter season (zone 10–12 in Florida, Hawaii, and South Texas). Rarely seen in cultivation outside its native range but occasionally available from rare fruit nurseries. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Soncoya / Wild Custard Apple
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent moisture during the growing season; Soncoya is intolerant of frost and prolonged waterlogging but handles the heat and humidity of tropical climates better than its relative cherimoya. The large, spiny, orange-brown fruits weigh up to several pounds each and develop on the branches and trunk; they are ready to harvest when the skin begins to soften and the segments start to separate. The orange, fibrous interior pulp is most commonly processed into drinks, sorbets, and frozen desserts rather than eaten fresh due to its strong flavor. Hand pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers on different trees, can significantly improve fruit set. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Song Zhong Tea (Song Dynasty Dan Cong)
description: Song Zhong ('Song cultivar') traces its name to old tea trees on Guangdong's Wudong Mountain believed to descend from stock identified during the Song Dynasty roughly 900 years ago, making it one of the most storied of the Phoenix Dan Cong cultivars, an F1 relative of Shui Xian. It is a large-leaved arbor-type tea tree that, left unpruned in its native high-elevation habitat, can grow into a substantial small tree over centuries; garden plants stay far more manageable with regular pruning. The cup carries a classic orchid character with subtle stone-fruit and light spice notes when processed as oolong through the standard withering, bruising, oxidation, and roasting steps. Provide the acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and warm, humid conditions common to all tea camellias. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sonora Almond (Early-Blooming Soft-Shell Sweet Almond)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible early-blooming pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Sonora is a California almond variety valued for large, attractive, very soft-shell kernels that crack open easily by hand, along with sweet, well-flavored nutmeat that makes it popular for home orchards and specialty markets alike. The tree blooms early, which gives it a head start on the growing season but also increases exposure to spring frost risk during flowering, so site selection matters for reliable annual crops. Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, especially during kernel development, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer, allowing the nuts to dry thoroughly before storage to prevent mold. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sonora Wheat (White Sonora Wheat, Historic Southwestern Heirloom Wheat)
description: Sow in fall in the low desert Southwest, where it grows through the mild winter and matures before the onset of intense spring heat; in cooler regions it can also be sown as an early spring wheat. Sonora wheat was brought to the Sonoran Desert missions by Spanish colonists in the 1700s and became the dominant wheat of California and the Southwest well into the 1800s, prized for thriving with minimal water on desert soils. Its soft, low-protein white kernels mill into a fine, tender flour especially suited to tortillas and pastries rather than yeasted bread, and the variety has been actively revived by Southwestern seed-saving organizations after nearly vanishing from cultivation in the twentieth century. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Sops of Wine Apple (Ancient English Red-Fleshed Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Sops of Wine is an English heirloom dating back before the 1600s, one of the oldest named apple varieties still in cultivation, taking its evocative name from the old English custom of soaking bread ('sops') in cider or wine, since the flesh of this apple is streaked with a distinctive pink-red color reminiscent of wine-soaked bread when cut. The medium-sized, red-skinned fruit ripens early in the season, well ahead of most storage apples, with tart, aromatic flesh well suited to cooking and cider blending, and it has historically been valued for both its early ripening and its striking, unusual flesh color. As a variety carried by some of the earliest American colonists, it also has genuine historical significance for orchardists interested in colonial-era American fruit growing. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sora Radish (Heat-Tolerant Round Radish)
description: Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots; Sora is a round red radish notable for holding good quality in warmer soil than most radish varieties tolerate well, resisting the pithy, hollow centers that quickly ruin radishes grown too far into rising spring heat. This heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for extending the Gulf South radish season later into spring or for an earlier-than-usual fall planting while soil is still warm. Keep soil evenly moist for the crispest texture, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across, since even heat-tolerant radishes eventually turn woody if left too long. Matures in 24–30 days from seed.

name: Sorcerer Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Semi-Bush Jack-O-Lantern Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Sorcerer is an AAS-winning jack-o-lantern pumpkin bred with a semi-bush habit, taking noticeably less garden space than traditional sprawling pumpkin vines while still producing a full-size crop of classic round, deep-orange, 10-12 pound carving pumpkins with the strong, smooth handle and even shape prized for jack-o-lanterns. Its more compact vine makes it a practical choice for smaller vegetable gardens that still want to grow real carving-size pumpkins rather than miniatures. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached rather than pulling it, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two to improve storage life before Halloween display. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sorrel
description: Sow seeds shallowly in spring and thin plants to about a foot apart in a permanent bed, since sorrel is a long-lived perennial. It is one of the first greens to emerge in spring, offering a bright, tart, lemony flavor to salads and soups. Harvest outer leaves regularly and remove flower stalks to keep the plant producing tender new growth. In hot weather the leaves can turn tougher and more sour, so pick young for the best flavor. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Soundwave Jalapeno Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once frost danger passes. This F1 hybrid produces extra-large, dark green, thick-walled four-inch jalapenos with a slightly above-average heat around 6,500 Scoville units. The disease-resistant plants are high yielding and the fruit has an exceptional shelf life. Pick peppers green and firm for classic use, or let some ripen red for added sweetness. Steady water and full sun keep the heavy sets coming all season. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Soup Celery
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting (seeds need light — do not cover); set transplants in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; soup celery (cutting celery, leaf celery, smallage) is the ancestral form of cultivated celery, grown for its intensely flavored, aromatic leaves and slender stems used as an herb rather than a stalk vegetable. Plants produce dense, bushy clumps of dark-green, deeply cut celery-flavored leaves throughout the growing season, cut repeatedly like parsley. A single plant provides an essentially unlimited supply of celery flavor for soups, stews, salads, and stocks without the exacting cultural demands of stalk celery — no blanching is needed, and the plant tolerates some heat, drought, and partial shade that would devastate standard celery. Can be grown year-round in mild-winter climates (zones 8–10) and will self-sow in suitable conditions. 'Afina' and 'Amsterdam Cutting' are reliable selections. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Sour Cherry
description: Sour (tart) cherries such as Montmorency are self-fertile, reliably productive, and significantly hardier than sweet cherries, making them the better choice for zones 4–6. They require 1000–1200 chill hours and tolerate heavier soils than sweet cherries do. Thin lightly to maintain canopy airflow and prune in early summer to manage brown rot pressure in humid climates. Harvest when fruit is fully red and slightly soft — tart cherries rarely sweeten on the tree and are best for cooking, preserving, or juice. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sour Orange
description: The sour or Seville orange yields bitter, aromatic fruit that is the classic base for marmalade and its fragrant blossoms for perfume. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from frost, and note that it is also widely used as a hardy, disease-resistant rootstock. Water deeply and feed during the growing season for steady growth. Harvest the deeply colored fruit in winter and use the tart juice and peel rather than eating it fresh. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Soursop (Guanabana)
description: Soursop is a rapid-growing small tree bearing the largest fruit of the Annona genus — sometimes exceeding 10 pounds — with spiny dark-green skin and white, fibrous, intensely aromatic pulp that is used primarily in beverages and desserts. Like its relatives (cherimoya, sugar-apple), soursop flowers have a specialized pollination mechanism that benefits greatly from hand-pollination using a small brush or cotton swab in late afternoon. The tree prefers deep, well-drained loam and is sensitive to standing water, drought stress, and cold below 32°F. Harvest when the skin has darkened from bright green to dull olive-green, the spines soften, and the fruit yields to gentle pressing; ripen at room temperature for 1–2 days. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: South African Geranium (Umckaloabo)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; South African geranium is a low-growing pelargonium from the semi-arid grasslands and rocky hillsides of South Africa that has achieved global commercial significance as a medicinal herb: the dried, powdered root extract — sold under the names Umcka, Umckaloabo, and EPs 7630 — is one of the best-studied herbal supplements for upper respiratory tract infections, with multiple clinical trials supporting its efficacy for reducing the duration and severity of acute bronchitis and the common cold. As a garden plant, independent of its medicinal significance, it is quietly attractive: the velvety, rounded, silver-gray to blue-gray leaves with deeply scalloped edges form a soft, spreading, woolly-textured mound, and above this cloud of silver foliage appear, in late spring through summer, clusters of small, dark, wine-red to almost-black maroon, five-petaled flowers — one of the most unusually dark-colored flowers of any pelargonium. The combination of silver foliage and very dark maroon-purple flowers is sophisticated and distinctive. It grows from a thick, tuberous, carrot-like root that survives significant drought and moderate frost. An interesting, medicinally significant herb for the zone 9 herb garden. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: South American Sapote
description: Plant Quararibea cordata in fertile, moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water consistently throughout the year, maintaining soil moisture without waterlogging; the tree grows rapidly under good conditions and can begin fruiting in 3–5 years from a good-sized transplant. South American Sapote (chupa-chupa in Amazonian Colombia, where the name likely derives from the act of sucking the sweet flesh off the large seed) is one of the truly outstanding tropical fruits — combining the rich creaminess of mamey sapote with the bright tropical flavor of ripe apricot and mango in a way that is entirely its own. The orange-fleshed, salmon-skinned, football-sized fruits produced in large quantities on mature trees are eaten fresh out of hand or blended into juices, shakes, and ice creams. The tree is in the Malvaceae family (related to chocolate and kapok) and shares the fast growth and large size of its relatives. Fruiting is precocious for a tropical tree — beginning at 3–5 years from a good-quality transplant — and production can be heavy, with large trees bearing hundreds of fruits per season. Currently little-known outside Colombia and adjacent Amazonian countries but considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts as one of the best-tasting of all Neotropical fruits; wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens is warranted. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: South Pearl Chilean Guava (INIA Chile Murtilla Selection)
description: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltering from hard freezes in the cooler end of its range. South Pearl was released alongside Red Pearl under a plant patent from Chile's national agricultural research institute (INIA) as part of the same program to domesticate wild murtilla for commercial production, and shares the same compact, evergreen, hedge-friendly habit typical of cultivated Chilean guava selections. It bears the species' characteristically aromatic, sweet-tart berries, reminiscent of strawberry and guava, over a long ripening season into fall. As with other Chilean guava selections, several years of establishment are needed before the plant reaches full fruiting size, and a sheltered microclimate helps it perform at the cold edge of its hardiness range. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Agastache (Hummingbird Mint)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; southern agastache is a compact hyssop-mint native to dry, rocky, calcareous slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert region in west Texas and adjacent New Mexico and Mexico. The small but attractive rosy-pink to salmon-red flower spikes are produced from midsummer through fall and are magnets for hummingbirds and large bumblebees throughout the blooming period. More drought-tolerant than most agastaches and adapted to the thin, rocky, alkaline soils of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, making it an excellent choice for dry, rocky, calcareous gardens in zone 9. Unlike many agastaches that decline in the summer heat and humidity of the Gulf South, southern agastache thrives in the hot, dry conditions of west Texas and is more durable in drier zone 9 gardens than humid-adapted species. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Southern Bartlett Pear (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Bartlett Sport)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of the classic Bartlett pear discovered on an old Louisiana homestead and selected specifically for its low chilling requirement, letting it set fruit reliably in the mild Gulf Coast winters that leave standard Bartlett trees short on the cold hours they need to flower well. It bears the same classic bell-shaped, buttery, sweet pear fruit familiar from Bartlett, ripening in mid to late summer. Like most European pears grown in the humid South, it remains more vulnerable to fire blight along the immediate Gulf Coast than truly blight-resistant Southern selections such as Warren or Ayers, so prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth blight favors. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow, then ripen off the tree at room temperature for the best buttery texture and flavor. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Southern Belle Nectarine (Deep South Very-Low-Chill Nectarine)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Southern Belle is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer. Bred for the Gulf South, it produces yellow-fleshed fruit early in the season, giving warm-climate gardeners a nectarine option where most standard cultivars cannot accumulate enough winter chill to fruit well. Thin fruit after natural drop to improve size, and watch for brown rot and plum curculio, both common challenges for stone fruit in the humid Deep South. It performs best with a regular fungicide program suited to warm, humid summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Blackhaw (Rusty Blackhaw)
description: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; very drought-tolerant once established — one of the most adaptable native shrubs for difficult sites. Viburnum rufidulum (southern blackhaw or rusty blackhaw) is a native deciduous shrub or small tree of the southeastern United States — found naturally in dry rocky woods, cedar glades, roadsides, and forest edges from Virginia south to Florida and west to Texas — and one of the most ecologically important and underused native fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast wildlife gardens. The plant is distinguished from blackhaw (V. prunifolium) by its larger size, glossy dark-green leaves, and the distinctive rusty-red to reddish-brown fuzz (rufidulum = rusty) that covers the buds, new twigs, and leaf undersides. It produces large, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in spring, followed by large clusters of 1/3-inch, dark blue-black drupes (berries) in fall. The berries have a remarkable, sweet, prune-raisin-like flavor when fully ripe after frost — uniquely pleasant among native berries, and used by indigenous southeastern peoples for food. Birds (especially mockingbirds, bluebirds, and cedar waxwings) consume the fruit enthusiastically. The plant provides outstanding fall color (glossy burgundy-red), excellent winter bark interest, and remarkable drought tolerance — among the most xeric-adapted native shrubs for alkaline, rocky, and dry sites in the Southeast. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Southern Cattail (Narrow Leaf Cattail)
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet soil or shallow water at pond or wetland margins in full sun; southern cattail spreads aggressively by rhizome and may be invasive in small water features — best for large ponds or natural wetland restoration. Typha domingensis (southern cattail) is the dominant native cattail of the Gulf Coastal Plain, replacing common cattail (T. latifolia) in warm-climate marshes and ditches from the Carolinas through Florida and Texas. It is distinguished from common cattail by its narrower leaves (hence 'narrow-leaf cattail') and the characteristic gap between the female and male portions of the cigar-shaped flower spike — the two sections are separated by a visible gap in T. domingensis, while they are contiguous in T. latifolia. Cattails are among the most important edible wild plants of temperate and subtropical North America: the young shoots (peeled) are eaten like asparagus in spring; the green flower spikes are boiled and eaten like corn on the cob; the pollen is collected as a golden flour rich in protein; the starchy rhizomes can be processed into flour. They also provide outstanding wildlife habitat — nesting material and cover for numerous marsh bird species, seeds for waterfowl, and dense stands shelter fish. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Southern Comet Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant Hybrid AAS Broccoli)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 3 feet between rows to give the large frame room to develop. Southern Comet is an All-America Selections-winning F1 hybrid selected specifically for its ability to hold up to heat and humidity better than most broccoli, forming dense, deep-green 8-inch domed heads that resist the loose, ricey curd broccoli often develops when temperatures spike during head formation. Its strong side-shoot production after the main head is cut extends the harvest window considerably, an advantage in southern fall gardens where the cool season is often shorter than the plant's full production potential. Keep soil evenly moist and side-dress with nitrogen after the first head is harvested to sustain shoot production into winter. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Southern Crabapple (Narrowleaf Crabapple)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; southern crabapple is the native crabapple of the southeastern United States, producing a spectacular display of intensely fragrant pink flowers in early spring and small (1/2–1 inch) yellow-green to red crabapples in late summer and fall. The crabapples are too tart to eat fresh but make outstanding jelly, cider, and preserved fruit with excellent pectin content. The flowers are superb for native bees; cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and deer consume the fruit through fall and winter. It tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 better than most crabapple cultivars and produces cleaner foliage with fewer disease problems in the warm South. A self-fertile tree, so only one is needed for fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Dewberry (Common Dewberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; southern dewberry is a trailing or low-arching native bramble of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, producing large, juicy, black berries in late spring that are among the most flavorful of any native Rubus. The berries are excellent for eating fresh, preserving, and making wine and cobblers. The trailing canes root where they touch the soil, naturally colonizing disturbed, sandy, open habitats. Unlike upright blackberries, the low, trailing canes of dewberry are less showy but provide excellent wildlife value — the berries are consumed by birds, small mammals, and box turtles. In zone 9a, dewberry is one of the first fruits to ripen in spring (typically April–May), well before blackberries and blueberries. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Southern Flame Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Container Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, in the ground or in a large container, and thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart once marble-sized, since this naturally compact tree can overset relative to its small stature. Southern Flame is a genetic dwarf nectarine, part of the same Zaiger-bred family of true dwarf stone fruit as El Dorado and Necta Zee, growing only about 5–6 feet tall while still producing full-sized, freestone fruit with red-blushed yellow skin and sweet, richly flavored yellow flesh in mid-to-late summer. It is self-fruitful and needs no separate pollinator, and its dense, naturally rounded form suits a patio container or small garden bed where a standard nectarine tree would be impractical. As with other nectarines, watch for leaf curl and brown rot in humid Gulf Coast conditions and prune lightly each winter to keep the canopy open. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Frost Navel Orange (UGA Cold-Hardy Seedless Navel Orange)
description: Southern Frost is a seedless navel orange released by the University of Georgia and bred by researcher Wayne Hanna for improved cold tolerance beyond standard navel oranges such as the Washington Navel already grown on the Gulf Coast. Fruit offers classic sweet navel orange eating quality and ripens in late fall. Growers and university trial reports describe the tree surviving temperatures as low as 15 degrees F with limited damage, making it one of the more freeze-tolerant sweet oranges available for zone 8b-9a dooryard planting, though hard freezes still call for protection. It was released alongside UGA's companion Frost series citrus, including Pink Frost grapefruit and Sweet Frost tangerine, as part of a coordinated effort to expand citrus options for Deep South gardeners. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Giant Curled Mustard Green
description: Broadcast seeds and rake in lightly, or sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–15 inches; Southern Giant Curled is the classic all-purpose mustard green of the American South, grown for over a century in Gulf Coast and Southeastern gardens and still the standard by which other mustard greens are judged for traditional Southern cooking. The large, heavily ruffled and curled, bright yellow-green leaves are pungent and mustardy, with a characteristic bite that is best tamed by long, slow cooking with pork (a smoked ham hock or fatback) in the traditional Southern style. The big, broad leaves are also excellent braised in olive oil with garlic for a more Mediterranean preparation, or wilted into beans and soups. Flavor improves dramatically after a frost — the cold converts starches to sugars and mellows the pungency, making fall mustard greens distinctly better than spring. In zone 9, plants sown in October are typically at their peak in December–January. Harvest outer leaves for continuous production; entire heads can also be cut at once for batch cooking. An exceptionally easy, productive, nutritious cool-season crop. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Southern Giant Mustard Green
description: Direct sow seeds a quarter inch deep and thin seedlings so the large plants have room to spread. This heirloom produces giant, frilled green leaves with a bold, spicy flavor and good heat tolerance for warm climates. It grows quickly, so harvest outer leaves young for milder taste or let them mature for a stronger bite. Keep the soil moist to slow bolting, and sow in succession for a continuing supply of spicy greens. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Southern Highbush Blueberry
description: Southern highbush blueberries are interspecific hybrids bred for low chill-hour requirements (150–500 hours below 45°F), making them the only highbush-type blueberry suitable for Gulf Coast, Florida, and mild-winter California climates. Maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.5 with pine bark mulch and acidifying fertilizers; do not use lime. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination and improved fruit size. Prune lightly for the first three years, then begin removing the oldest, least productive canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new wood. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Home Muscadine (Ornamental Hybrid Muscadine)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy arbor or pergola, where the vine doubles as an ornamental landscape feature. Southern Home is a distinctive interspecific hybrid between muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) and traditional bunch grape (Vitis vinifera), bred at the University of Georgia specifically for its uniquely ornamental, deeply lobed, almost oak-leaf-shaped foliage that sets it visually apart from the simple rounded leaves of standard muscadine varieties, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for a decorative fruiting arbor. The self-fertile vine produces medium-sized, black, muscadine-flavored fruit in loose bunches more reminiscent of a traditional grape cluster than the typical loose, few-berried muscadine set, and it carries good resistance to Pierce's disease inherited from its muscadine parentage — a critical advantage over standard bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South and Southeast, where Pierce's disease kills most vinifera and many hybrid grapes outright. An excellent choice for gardeners who want both fruit and ornamental landscape value from the same vine, zone 6–9. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Southern Jewel Muscadine Grape
description: Southern Jewel is a self-fertile black to deep-purple muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross of the bronze cultivar Granny Val and a large black selection. Its most distinctive trait is fruiting habit: berries form in tight bunches of roughly six to twelve that cling firmly to the stem rather than dropping individually, so whole clusters can be picked and handled like bunch grapes instead of gathering loose berries off the ground. The thin, tender skin and crisp, crunchy flesh make it especially well suited to fresh eating, with good disease resistance and heavy yields under humid Southern conditions. Grow on a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun, and expect this warm-climate selection to perform best in the Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida heat it was bred for. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern King Pear (Low-Chill Self-Fruitful Gulf Coast Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern King is a low-chill Asian-European pear hybrid popular around Houston and the Gulf Coast of Texas, valued for reliable fruiting even after mild winters that leave higher-chill pears short on bloom, along with strong resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pear cultivars in humid Southern climates. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set fruit, though planting a second low-chill pear nearby can improve yields. Fruit is medium-sized with the sweet, mild flavor typical of Asian-pear influenced hybrids. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to improve air circulation and further reduce fire blight risk, removing any blighted shoots promptly by cutting well below visible damage. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Southern Mountain Cranberry (Elliottberry)
description: Found naturally in the deep, cool shade of high-elevation spruce-fir and northern hardwood forests along the Appalachian spine, this deciduous shrub tolerates more shade than most fruiting blueberry relatives, making it a good candidate for cool, acidic woodland gardens at higher elevations or in northern climates. Its bright red, tart, cranberry-like berries ripen in late summer and are traditionally used in jellies and sauces rather than eaten out of hand. As with other Vaccinium species, it needs consistently moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil and struggles in hot, humid lowland gardens outside its cool native range. Plant nursery-propagated stock, since seed germination is slow and erratic without extended cold stratification. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Southern Pea (Cowpea, Black-eyed Pea, Field Pea)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; thin to 4–6 inches. Vigna unguiculata (southern pea, cowpea, or black-eyed pea) is the most heat-tolerant major legume in North American horticulture and an absolute staple of Southern gardens and cuisine — encompassing black-eyed peas, crowder peas, cream peas, pink-eye purple hull peas, lady peas, and Iron-and-Clay peas in a single species with hundreds of named varieties grouped by pod color, seed markings, and intended use. All share the capacity to fix atmospheric nitrogen (greatly enriching soil when the crop residue is turned under), exceptional heat and drought tolerance, and thrive in the humid, hot conditions of Gulf Coast summers when other legumes fail. Fresh 'green' (immature) southern peas are shelled and cooked like shell beans; dry peas are stored for long-term use. 'California Black-eye' (classic black-eyed pea), 'Pinkeye Purple Hull,' 'Iron-and-Clay' (cover crop type), 'Mississippi Silver,' and 'Texas Cream' are widely grown named varieties. In zone 9, southern peas can be planted from April through August for continuous production. Matures in 55–85 days from seed.

name: Southern Queen Pear (Low-Chill Fire-Blight-Resistant Mississippi Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern Queen, a low-chill pear selected in south Mississippi, is grown throughout the Gulf South for its large, bell-shaped fruit with russet-bronze skin and its excellent resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many European pear cultivars in the region's warm, humid conditions. It ripens with the mild, sweet flavor typical of Southern low-chill pear selections and pairs well with a second low-chill pear nearby for improved cross-pollination and yield. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to maximize air circulation, and cut out any fire blight-infected shoots promptly well below the visible damage to prevent the disease from spreading into older wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Southern Queen Sweet Potato (19th-Century White-Skin White-Flesh Heirloom)
