description: Southern Queen is a vining 19th-century heirloom, introduced into the United States from South America around 1870, that produces long, narrow tubers with white skin and white, dry-cooking flesh. Sometimes called the White Yam, it is one of the oldest sweet potato varieties still maintained in American cultivation, alongside Nansemond and Hayman. Its dry, starchy texture and mild flavor make it well suited to traditional Southern cooking styles that favor a less-sweet, more potato-like sweet potato. It matures in roughly 100-110 days and adapts to a wide range of growing conditions. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Southern Red Oak (Spanish Oak)
description: Plant in well-drained to dry, acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; southern red oak is a dominant canopy tree of the southeastern US Coastal Plain and Piedmont, thriving in the dry, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soils that characterize much of the region. The distinctive leaves have a broadly lobed base with a narrow middle and a multi-lobed apex — sometimes described as bell-shaped — turning dark red in fall. The tree is a significant mast producer with small, round, bitter acorns consumed by deer, wild turkeys, squirrels, and many other wildlife species. It is more drought-tolerant and better adapted to dry sandy soils than northern red oak (Q. rubra), making it a preferred choice for tough Coastal Plain sites. Historically valuable as a timber tree and important in the ecology of southeastern pine-oak communities. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Southern Sensation Seedless Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Table Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southern Sensation is a Texas Superstar-designated table grape, a joint release from Texas A&M and University of Arkansas breeding programs, bred to combine yellow, thin-skinned, seedless fruit with strong flavor and years of demonstrated resistance to Pierce's disease — the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European-type table grape varieties within a few years across the humid South and has long limited backyard grape growing in Texas and the Gulf region. It has outperformed standard seedless varieties like Flame Seedless in regional trials specifically for disease survival and fruit quality in southern conditions. Prune to a permanent cordon system in late winter, and thin crowded fruit clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation, which helps reduce fungal disease pressure in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southern Stoneroot
description: Plant tuberous root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in zones 7–10; southern stoneroot is a mint-family perennial of the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain — found naturally in moist, shaded bottomlands and rich upland forests of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, and adjacent states — that produces large, coarsely toothed, opposite leaves with a distinctive lemon-horse-balm fragrance and branching panicles of small, pale yellow flowers in late summer and fall. The large, knotty, tuberous root system gives the plant its common name and was used in traditional herbal medicine for digestive complaints, as with the related C. canadensis. It tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–10 better than its northern relative and is a useful large-leafed foliage plant for shaded southern gardens where few fragrant herbs thrive. Pair with native gingers, beautyberry, and spicebush for a fragrant native shade border. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Southernwood (Lad's Love)
description: Root 4–6 in semi-ripe cuttings in late summer in gritty, moist propagating mix; cuttings root readily without hormone treatment. Southernwood is a woody, feathery-leaved Artemisia with a sharp lemon-camphor fragrance historically used as a moth repellent and insect deterrent in drawers and linen presses. Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; like most artemisias it suffers in wet or rich conditions and prefers slightly alkaline soil. Cut back hard to within 6 in of the ground in early spring to prevent excessive woodiness and stimulate a fresh flush of aromatic silver-green growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Southland Muscadine Grape
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Southland is a University of Georgia release valued for its large, dark reddish-black berries with a thin skin and sweet, rich muscadine flavor good for fresh eating as well as juice and wine. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and consistently productive, with solid disease resistance across the humid Gulf South. Mid-season ripening makes Southland a dependable companion to earlier black varieties like Cowart and later ones like Ison, spreading harvest over a longer window. Prune annually in late winter while dormant to renewal spurs to keep the vine productive and manageable on the trellis. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southland Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur well before planting; Southland is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release grown across zones 7B-9A, valued for producing large numbers of sweet, large berries over a long mid-to-late season harvest window rather than one heavy flush. Plants are vigorous and reliably productive in the humid Gulf South once established, but fruit set and berry size improve substantially with a second, overlapping-bloom rabbiteye cultivar planted within about 50 feet, since Southland is not self-fruitful. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summer heat, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southland Raspberry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 9, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Southland is one of the few red raspberry cultivars bred specifically for adaptation to mild southern winters, with a low chilling-hour requirement that lets it flower and fruit where standard northern raspberries decline within a season or two from insufficient winter chill. It produces a light-to-moderate crop of medium-sized, sweet-tart red berries in late spring, with some plants also producing a smaller fall crop on primocanes. Yields are modest compared with northern raspberry cultivars grown in their ideal climate, but Southland remains one of the more dependable options for gardeners in zone 8-9 who want to try growing red raspberries. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to maintain airflow and reduce disease in humid conditions. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Southmoon Blueberry (UF Mid-Season Large-Berry Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Southmoon is a University of Florida IFAS southern highbush blueberry introduction valued for its large berry size, excellent flavor, higher-pH tolerance than most highbush varieties, and vigorous upright growth habit that makes it one of the most productive and commercially successful southern highbush varieties. The large, light-blue to sky-blue berries are firm with a small, dry picking scar — the combination of large size, good flavor, and excellent firmness makes Southmoon outstanding for both fresh market and home garden production. Southmoon's relative tolerance for soil pH up to 6.0 (compared to the strict 4.5–5.5 requirement of most blueberries) is practically significant for Gulf South gardeners who have difficulty reducing clay soil pH — Southmoon performs in slightly less-acidic conditions where other varieties would show severe nutrient deficiency. Southmoon is mid-season (April–May in zone 9), producing its main crop after the early varieties (Jewel, Emerald) and before the latest-ripening types, making it valuable for extending the blueberry season as part of a multiple-variety planting. The vigorous, upright habit reaches 6–7 feet and benefits from annual post-harvest pruning to maintain productive, manageable size. A primary recommendation from University of Florida extension for Gulf South blueberry production. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Southport Red Globe Onion
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall and pencil-width. Southport Red Globe is a long-day heirloom red onion from Southport (now part of Fairfield), Connecticut, where it was the commercial foundation of one of the most important onion-growing regions of 19th-century America — the Connecticut shoreline towns of Southport, Wethersfield, and Granby exported enormous quantities of dried storage onions to markets up and down the Eastern Seaboard and into the Caribbean. The medium to large (3–4 inch diameter), globe-shaped bulbs have deep red-purple skin and white flesh lightly tinged with red at the outer rings; the flavor is moderately pungent when raw, milder when cooked, with a typical red onion character. As a long-day type, Southport Red Globe performs best in northern gardens (zones 3–7) where the long summer days trigger good bulb development; in Gulf Coast gardens (short-day conditions), use short-day red onion varieties instead. Excellent storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 4–6 months. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Southport White Globe Onion (Classic American Long-Storing Heirloom)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep beds weed-free and evenly watered through the bulbing period. Southport White Globe is a 19th-century American heirloom that became the standard of the old Southport, Connecticut onion-growing district, producing perfectly round, pure-white, mild-flavored bulbs with thin papery skin over crisp white flesh. It is a long-day type best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength, and while its white skin makes it more prone to sunscald and bruising in storage than yellow or red types, well-cured bulbs still keep respectably for a winter storage onion. Stop watering once tops begin to yellow and fall over, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks, and store the largest, firmest bulbs for later use. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Southport Yellow Globe Onion
description: Southport Yellow Globe is a nineteenth-century American heirloom onion from Southport, Connecticut, and the yellow-skinned counterpart to the better-known Southport White Globe and Southport Red Globe. It forms well-rounded, medium-large globes of tan-gold skin over firm, pungent, long-storing flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and keep the bed weeded, since this open-pollinated heirloom is slower to establish than modern hybrids. Harvest once most of the tops have fallen and dried, cure fully in a warm, airy spot, and expect good keeping quality typical of the classic Southport globe strains. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Space Spinach
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — spinach benefits from afternoon shade protection in warmer climates to delay bolting; Space is an F1 hybrid spinach developed specifically for exceptional downy mildew (Peronospora spinaciae) resistance — the most significant disease of fresh-market spinach. The smooth, slightly cupped, dark green, upright leaves are the commercial fresh spinach leaf type: uniformly sized, easy to wash without the texture trapping of savoy (crinkled) types, and attractive in fresh salads and smoothies. Unlike savoy-type spinach that requires multiple washings to remove soil from the heavily crinkled leaves, Space's smooth, upright leaves release dirt easily and drain well in salad spinners. The F1 hybrid vigor produces noticeably more uniform and productive plants than open-pollinated varieties. Space's disease resistance makes it the practical choice for zone 9 fall spinach where warm, humid conditions can destroy less resistant varieties; the resistance ratings cover multiple races of downy mildew, providing durable protection across multiple seasons. Matures in 39–45 days from seed.

name: Space Spinach
description: Direct sow seed in cool soil in early spring or late summer and keep the bed consistently moist. This upright, compact spinach produces smooth to lightly savoyed, medium-green leaves that are excellent fresh or sauteed. High resistance to downy mildew and good bolting tolerance make it dependable across seasons. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole plants at the base for a full crop. Successive sowings extend the harvest before summer heat triggers bolting. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Spacemaster 80 Cucumber
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is thoroughly warm, or start indoors in peat pots for an early start. This compact variety carries full-sized slicing cucumbers on short two-to-three-foot vines, making it ideal for small beds and containers. Keep plants evenly watered, especially during flowering and fruiting, to avoid bitter or misshapen cucumbers. Harvest fruits young and often to keep the vines productive. A little support keeps fruit clean and straight even in tight spaces. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Spacemaster Cucumber
description: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm soil, and take advantage of the compact, bush-type habit that thrives in containers and small spaces. Despite their short vines, the plants produce full-size 7-8 inch cucumbers with crisp, mild flesh. Keep the soil evenly moist to prevent bitterness and misshapen fruits during the warm season. Harvest cucumbers regularly while they are firm and dark green to encourage continued production. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Spadona Chicory (Catalogna Dandelion Chicory)
description: Sow directly in spring for a quick cutting crop or in late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, cutting leaves at the base to encourage regrowth. An Italian dandelion-leaf chicory of the Catalogna group, with long, smooth, sword-shaped serrated leaves and a mildly bitter, herbaceous flavor best known cooked but also usable young in salads. It has long been a staple green in southern Italian cooking, traditionally sautéed with garlic and olive oil. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Spaghetti Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, compost-enriched hills, placing 3 seeds per hill and thinning to 1–2 plants. Give vines ample room to spread, or train onto a strong trellis and support heavy fruits with a sling. The rind turns from pale green to golden yellow when mature and will feel hard when pressed. Allow picked fruits to cure in a warm spot for 1–2 weeks before using or storing; they keep for several months in a cool, dry room. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Spaghetti Squash
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Spaghetti Squash (also called Vegetable Spaghetti) is a unique winter squash whose cooked flesh separates naturally into long, thin strands closely resembling spaghetti pasta — when halved and baked cut-side down, the flesh is scraped out with a fork to produce a pile of mildly sweet, slightly crunchy, pasta-like strands. The mild, neutral flavor serves as an effective low-carbohydrate substitute for pasta under tomato sauces, pesto, or any pasta topping, and has become one of the most popular low-carb vegetables for health-conscious cooks since the 1970s. The oblong, cream-to-golden fruits (4–8 pounds) are a Cucurbita pepo type with the same excellent disease resistance and productivity as other C. pepo squash. In zone 9 the long warm season is ideal for spaghetti squash, which requires the full warm season to develop and cure properly on the vine. Matures in 88–100 days from seed.

name: Spalding Pear (Fire-Blight-Tolerant Louisiana Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Spalding is explicitly recommended by the LSU AgCenter for southern Louisiana home orchards, prized for its fire-blight tolerance in the humid Gulf South and for ripening in mid-September, later than early-season selections like Hood and Flordahome, which extends the fresh pear harvest into fall. Fruit is used both fresh and for canning, with the firm, gritty texture typical of Southern-adapted pear selections bred more for reliability than the buttery texture of European dessert pears. Prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth fire blight favors. Harvest while still firm, then ripen off the tree at room temperature. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Cherry (Bakul, Bullet Wood, Tanjong Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy soil in full sun; Spanish cherry is slow-growing but long-lived and very low-maintenance once established. Mimusops elengi (Spanish cherry, bakul, or tanjong tree) is a slow-growing, long-lived tropical evergreen tree native to India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, and the Pacific Islands — one of the most beloved ornamental and fragrance trees of the Indian subcontinent. The tree produces small (1/2-inch), white, star-shaped flowers with deeply fringed petals that emit an extraordinarily intense, sweet, jasmine-like fragrance — particularly at night. Remarkably, the fragrance of the flowers intensifies dramatically as they dry: fallen bakul flowers can perfume an entire courtyard for days after dropping, and dried bakul flowers are strung into garlands, threaded into women's hair (a classic Indian tradition), used in temple offerings, and dried for pot-pourri and perfume production. The sweet-acid, olive-sized, orange-red to orange fruits (the 'Spanish cherry') are edible — sweet, slightly astringent, with a pleasant, mild flavor — eaten fresh or used in preserves across the plant's native range. The hard, dense wood (bullet wood) is extremely durable. In zone 10–12 tropical gardens, bakul is an outstanding shade tree and long-term ornamental investment valued as much for its fragrance as its appearance. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Lavender (French Lavender, Butterfly Lavender)
description: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Spanish lavender (L. stoechas) is the most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the lavenders, making it the best choice for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where English lavender (L. angustifolia) typically fails from summer humidity. It produces distinctive flowers topped with long, rabbit-ear-like purple bracts in spring, with a repeat bloom in fall. Like all lavenders it requires perfect drainage — root rot in wet or heavy soil is the most common cause of death. Plant in a raised bed or on a slope in amended sandy soil. Harvest stems when flowers are half-open; dry hanging upside down for wreaths and sachets. Shear by one-third after each bloom flush to maintain compact growth. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Lime
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Melicoccus bijugatus is drought tolerant and adapted to calcareous, rocky, and coastal soils typical of the Caribbean — water regularly only in establishment and during flowering and fruit set. Melicoccus bijugatus (Spanish Lime, Genip, Mamoncillo, Quenepa, or Limoncillo) is a large, stately, long-lived evergreen tree native to Colombia, Venezuela, and the Lesser Antilles, now widely naturalized and cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Central America, and parts of Florida and Hawaii. The common name 'Spanish Lime' describes the fruit's appearance — small (1–1.5 inch), perfectly round, lime-green, thin-shelled, resembling a small lime — but the flavor is a sweet-sour, tropical, guava-lychee combination with firm, translucent salmon-to-orange jelly-like pulp clinging tightly to the large seed. Fruits are sold in street markets in enormous clusters of hundreds — eaten by cracking the thin shell between the teeth and sucking or scraping the juicy pulp from the seed. Spanish lime is one of the most beloved street foods and market fruits of the Caribbean, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Colombia. The ripe fruits are also made into juice, jams, wine, and fermented beverages. Trees are dioecious (separate male and female plants), so plant at least one male per several females for fruiting. Very long-lived — specimens 100+ years old still fruit productively. Well adapted to South Florida's alkaline limestone soils where many tropical fruits perform poorly. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Oyster Plant (Golden Thistle)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Spanish oyster plant is a Mediterranean native chicory-family perennial that has been grown as an edible root vegetable since at least medieval times throughout Spain, Italy, and southern France, where its long, white, deeply growing taproot is harvested in late spring and cooked like salsify or parsnip — boiled, roasted, or sautéed in olive oil. The cooked root has a pleasant, mild, artichoke-like or oyster-like flavor that makes it an interesting, underused culinary vegetable. The plant in the garden is a bold, deep-green, heavily spined thistle-like perennial with golden-yellow, star-shaped composite flowers in summer that are attractive to pollinators. The spines on stems and leaf margins are sharp and require careful handling. A drought-tolerant, deep-rooted perennial for Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens where its cool-season root-development period suits the mild winter conditions. Once harvested, it is generally treated as an annual or biennial. Grown in Spain and southern Europe as an artisan market vegetable. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Spanish Roja Garlic (Classic Rocambole with Superior Flavor)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Spanish Roja is a classic rocambole-type hardneck garlic, brought to the Pacific Northwest by Spanish settlers generations ago, and widely considered by garlic growers and chefs to have some of the finest, most complex flavor of any garlic variety — rich, hot, and full without being harsh. Bulbs have a distinctive rich reddish-brown skin over 8-12 large, very easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it produces a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. The main tradeoff for its superior flavor is shorter storage life than porcelain or softneck types, typically only 4-5 months, so plan to use Spanish Roja earlier in the storage season. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Ruby Pomegranate
description: Spanish Ruby is an older American heirloom pomegranate long recommended by Gulf South and Florida extension programs as a dependable choice for humid subtropical growing conditions where premier California commercial cultivars are more prone to fruit splitting and rot. Fruit is medium-sized with ruby-red skin and juice, offering a balanced sweet-tart flavor suited to fresh eating and juicing alike. Its practical value lies less in exceptional size or sweetness than in consistent performance and better disease tolerance under rainy, high-humidity conditions than many showier named cultivars. Site it in full sun with good air movement and well-drained soil for the healthiest fruit set. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Sage
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in spring in sharply drained, poor to average soil in full sun; Spanish sage is a Mediterranean subshrub with narrow gray-green, lavender-scented leaves that are interchangeable with garden sage in the kitchen and are considered superior for making herbal extracts and infusions. It is more drought-tolerant, more compact, and harder to kill than Salvia officinalis, performing well in dry gardens, rock gardens, and gravel paths where the soil drains quickly even in winter. Trim lightly after each flush of small blue-purple flowers to maintain shape and prevent woodiness. Avoid heavy clay soils — perfect drainage is essential to year-round survival. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Thyme (Jamaican Oregano, Puerto Rican Oregano)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; harvest stems frequently to maintain compact, bushy growth. Lippia micromera (Spanish thyme or Jamaican oregano) is a small, woody, aromatic shrub native to the dry limestone hills of Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, producing small, densely crowded, grey-green, strongly thyme-oregano scented leaves. The plant occupies the culinary niche of thyme and oregano in Caribbean cooking — the dried or fresh leaves are used in jerk seasoning blends, seasoning rubs for meats and fish, and traditional Caribbean herbal teas (sooshal, orosul). It is notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than either European thyme (Thymus vulgaris) or Mediterranean oregano (Origanum vulgare), making it well-suited to hot, dry, tropical and subtropical gardens where those herbs struggle. Lippia micromera belongs to the verbena family (Verbenaceae) and is distinct from Plectranthus amboinicus (Cuban oregano, also sometimes called 'Spanish thyme') — both are Caribbean oregano substitutes but from unrelated plant families. The essential oil is rich in thymol and carvacrol, the same primary compounds responsible for thyme and oregano's characteristic aroma. Excellent in containers in subtropical gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Spanish Wood Marjoram / Mastic Thyme
description: Establish rooted cuttings in fast-draining, alkaline to neutral soil in a location with maximum sun exposure, mirroring its native Spanish hillside habitat. Water sparingly once established; the camphor-rosemary-marjoram scent is most concentrated in dry conditions and will diminish if the plant is overwatered or grown in shade. Trim back by one-third after the white fluffy flower heads fade to keep the plant bushy and to prevent it from becoming overly woody at the base. Protect from prolonged hard freezes with a cloche or cold frame, as it is less cold-hardy than common thyme. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Sparkle Strawberry (Classic Late-Season Heirloom June-Bearer)
description: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown at soil level in a sunny, well-drained bed, and remove the runners during the first season if a larger single-crown hill is preferred over a spreading matted row. Sparkle was released in the late 1940s and went on to become the benchmark late-season, high-flavor strawberry for home gardeners across the northeastern and midwestern United States for decades. The berries are medium-sized and comparatively soft-fleshed, ripening at the tail end of the June-bearing season, with an intensely aromatic, old-fashioned strawberry flavor that many gardeners still seek out for fresh eating and preserves. Although firmer, more disease-resistant modern cultivars have largely displaced it from commercial fields, Sparkle remains popular with heirloom growers who prioritize flavor over shipping durability. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Sparkleberry (Farkleberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), poor to average sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; sparkleberry is the largest native blueberry relative in the Southeast, growing to 25 feet as a gnarly, multi-trunked small tree with distinctive exfoliating gray-brown bark that reveals warm cinnamon-red underbark — one of the most ornamental native bark patterns in southern woodland plants. The white bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, persistent dark black berries that, while dry and astringent compared to commercial blueberries, are eagerly consumed by wood thrushes, mockingbirds, foxes, and other wildlife throughout fall and winter. It grows naturally in dry, sandy upland forests and longleaf pine savannas. An outstanding specimen tree for dry, sunny or partly shaded naturalistic landscapes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sparkler Radish (Red-Top White-Tipped Bicolor Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart; Sparkler matures very quickly (22–30 days) and becomes pithy and hollow if left too long in the ground — harvest promptly when roots reach 3/4 to 1 inch in diameter; succession-plant every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply. Sparkler is a classic American heirloom spring radish that dates to the late 19th century and remains a popular choice in home gardens for its distinctive bicolor appearance: the round, smooth roots are vivid scarlet-red on the upper portion and a clean, bright white on the lower third to half — a sharp, clean color transition that gives the radish a visually appealing two-toned look unlike the solid red of Cherry Belle or the pure white of White Icicle. The name 'Sparkler' is apt — the red-and-white coloring is eye-catching and festive in a salad bowl or on a relish tray. The flavor is crisp and mildly peppery, slightly milder than some all-red varieties, and the texture at perfect maturity is ideal — firm, juicy, and snap-crisp. Like all spring radishes, Sparkler bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather (spring and fall); in zone 9a, the fall season (September through November) and very early spring (January through March in coastal areas) are the practical growing windows. Sparkler is valued by gardeners who want visual variety in their radish plantings beyond the standard all-red types. Matures in 22–30 days from seed.

name: Sparks 127 Black Walnut (Spur-Type Precocious Selection)
description: Sparks 127 was selected from a tree found by Archie Sparks in Iowa and is distinguished by a spur-type fruiting habit, in which nuts cluster on short lateral spurs rather than spreading along the full length of the shoot, a trait linked to earlier and heavier bearing than typical seedling black walnuts. It has become a benchmark cultivar in University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry black walnut variety trials and flavor studies, often evaluated alongside Emma K and Kwik-Krop. Give it deep, well-drained soil in full sun with wide spacing to accommodate its eventual size as a shade tree, and plant a second cultivar nearby since black walnut sets larger crops with cross-pollination. Keep tomatoes, peppers, and other juglone-sensitive plants well outside the mature dripline, as the roots and hulls release the growth-inhibiting compound juglone. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sparrow Black Walnut
description: Sparrow is a long-cultivated named black walnut selection recognized among nut growers for producing unusually large nuts with good kernel fill for the species. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it bears years earlier than seedling trees and produces more uniform crops. Deep taproots make bare-root or containerized grafted stock the practical planting choice, and trees should be sited well clear of gardens sensitive to juglone. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Spartacus Asparagus
description: Start seed indoors early, as germination is slow and warmth-dependent, then transplant to a permanent, weed-free bed after frost. This vigorous, all-male hybrid produces eight-to-ten-inch spears and, being male-sterile, channels its energy into strong crown and root growth rather than berries. Patience pays off, since harvest begins in the third year but a healthy bed can produce for up to twelve years. Feed and mulch the bed annually and let ferns grow after harvest to build the crowns. Harvest spears for only a few weeks the first productive year, then longer as plants mature. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Spartan Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Spartan is a cold-hardy, reliably productive apple well suited to northern climates. Bred in British Columbia, Canada in the 1920s from a McIntosh and Yellow Newtown Pippin cross, it bears medium, deep purple-red apples with crisp, snow-white, juicy flesh and a sweet flavor with the light, distinctive tang inherited from its McIntosh parent, ripening in early-to-mid fall as a reliable, attractive dessert apple. Its excellent cold hardiness, reliable annual bearing, and good disease resistance compared to many other apples have made it a longstanding favorite for northern and Canadian home orchards where more tender varieties struggle. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up deeply and pulls easily from the spur, and expect good storage life of a couple of months under cool conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Spartan Blueberry (Early-Season Large-Fruited Michigan Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Spartan was bred at Michigan State University and remains one of the most flavorful early-season highbush blueberries available, producing very large, firm, intensely sweet berries widely regarded by growers as among the best-tasting of any early blueberry variety. The tradeoff for that exceptional flavor is a genuine sensitivity to soil conditions — Spartan performs best in well-drained, properly acidic soil and can struggle in heavier or poorly prepared sites where more forgiving varieties would tolerate the conditions fine. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sparx Lettuce (Heat-Tolerant Romaine for Hearts)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest whole hearts once the upright heads have filled out. Sparx is a modern romaine bred for the fresh-market 'hearts' trade, producing dense, uniform, upright heads of crisp, sweet leaves on a plant noted for holding quality through hot spells that cause many other romaine types to turn bitter or bolt prematurely. Its dependable performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings makes it a practical choice for Gulf Coast gardeners looking to stretch romaine production beyond the short cool-season window most lettuce requires. Provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to further slow bolting and preserve leaf quality. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Spearmint
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; spearmint tolerates light shade better than most culinary herbs and is one of the better mints for partially shaded kitchen gardens. Mentha spicata is the garden mint of European tradition with smooth, bright-green, wrinkled leaves and a sweet, relatively cool, characteristic mint flavor (from carvone rather than menthol) used in mint sauce with lamb, jelly, juleps, mojitos, tabbouleh, and Middle Eastern cuisine. Unlike peppermint (M. × piperita) which is a sterile hybrid, spearmint sets viable seed and can be started from seed (though vegetative propagation produces more reliable, uniform plants). It is generally considered a milder, sweeter mint than peppermint and is the preferred choice in savory cooking and cocktails; cultivars 'Kentucky Colonel' and 'Moroccan' are popular selections with especially fine flavor. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Speckled Butter Bean (Sieva Bean, Carolina Butter Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep at the base of a fence, trellis, or pole teepee in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Speckled Butter Bean (also called Sieva or Carolina Sieva) is a small-seeded, pole-type lima bean of a different genetic character from the large-seeded butter bean types — it traces ancestry to indigenous lima varieties of the American South and Caribbean and has been cultivated in the Gulf South for centuries. The flat, cream-colored seeds are distinctively speckled with purple-maroon markings that fade during cooking. Flavor is extremely buttery, nutty, and rich — many Southern gardeners consider the Speckled Butter Bean to have a more complex, 'butter' flavor than large Fordhook-type limas. The vining plants are highly heat-tolerant and thrive through Gulf Coast summers that stop most shell beans cold, continuing to set pods at temperatures that wilt other legumes. Harvest fresh for the traditional Southern preparation: shell and cook with a piece of fatback or smoked sausage and season with salt and pepper. Dried seeds also cook into excellent soups and stews. A true Southern heirloom with deep historical roots in Gulf Coast foodways. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Speckled Cutshort Bean
description: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods young and tender for snap use, or let mature for a flavorful dry soup bean. Speckled Cutshort is a member of the Appalachian 'cutshort' family of heirloom pole beans, so named for the short, blunt, somewhat flattened pod tip characteristic of the type, and passed down for generations among mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and the Carolinas, with many named strains maintained within individual families and communities. The pods are speckled with purple-brown markings while developing, turning fully green as they mature, and the tender, meaty texture makes them excellent as a snap bean; left to dry, the attractively speckled seeds cook into a rich, traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous and productive on a sturdy support, it is a genuine piece of living Appalachian food heritage for gardeners who want an authentic regional heirloom, zone 4–10. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: Speckled Hound Pumpkin (Green-Speckled Orange Heirloom Baking Squash)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the vigorous vines room to sprawl, since Speckled Hound belongs to Cucurbita moschata, the same heat- and pest-tolerant species as butternut squash and generally outperforms Cucurbita pepo pumpkins in hot, humid Southern gardens. The medium-sized, slightly flattened fruit has a striking dark green speckled pattern over deep orange skin, and the moist, dense, sweet flesh is well suited to pies, soups, and roasting, holding its flavor and texture through long storage better than most jack-o'-lantern types. Moschata squash also tends to shrug off vine borers better than pepo types, a real advantage in the Gulf South where borers are a persistent problem. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail scratch and the stem has begun to dry, and cure fruit in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Speckled Hound Squash (Chef-Bred Sweet Delicata-Type Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room to spread. Speckled Hound was bred by Row 7 Seed Company in collaboration with chefs specifically for improved flavor over standard delicata squash, producing oblong, cream-colored fruit speckled and streaked with green, with notably sweet, dense, richly flavored orange flesh and a somewhat tougher rind that stores longer than typical delicata types. Harvest when the rind hardens and speckled coloring fully develops, usually as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Like other Cucurbita pepo squash, watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs in Gulf South gardens. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Speckled Purple Hull Pea (Old Timer Semi-Crowder Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Speckled Purple Hull, an old Southern heirloom also known as Old Timer, bears curved, rich purple pods about seven inches long, shelling out to reveal cream-colored peas mottled with distinctive tan-brown speckles, a semi-crowder texture prized for the classic flavor it brings to a pot of Hoppin' John. Its purple pods turn a deeper shade as they mature, making picking time easy to judge, and like other cowpeas it thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Speckled Roman Tomato (Striped Roman)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Speckled Roman tomato was discovered by Doreen Howard in Illinois and is distinguished from virtually all other paste tomatoes by its dramatically striped appearance — the fruits have alternating red and orange stripes (or speckles when young) that persist to full ripeness, making them visually striking among the usually uniformly red paste types. The foliage is similarly striped, with green and yellow banding on the leaves. Beyond the ornamental appeal, Speckled Roman produces exceptionally flavorful paste tomatoes with more complexity and better texture for fresh eating than standard San Marzano or Roma types while retaining the meaty, low-moisture flesh needed for sauce and paste production. Medium-large (4–8 oz), cylindrical to elongated-oval fruits. Outstanding for both fresh use and preserving, and a beautiful conversation piece in the garden. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Speckled Swan Hard-shelled Gourd
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors to gain time in short seasons. These vigorous vines need a long, warm season and benefit from a strong trellis that lets the swan-necked fruits hang and shape naturally. The emerald green shells speckled with light green make striking autumn displays. For crafts, let gourds mature fully on the vine, then cure them in a dry, airy place for weeks to months until the shells harden. Cured hard-shelled gourds last indefinitely and take paint and carving well. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Speckles Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Speckles is an Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce distinguished by large, soft, pale-green leaves heavily spotted and speckled with red-maroon freckles — a distinctive appearance unlike any other lettuce. The speckle pattern varies from plant to plant, and no two heads are identically spotted, making it one of the most visually interesting lettuces for mixed salads and fresh presentations. The flavor is classic butterhead — tender, buttery, mild, and slightly sweet — without the bitterness of some red-pigmented lettuces. Speckles is a slow-to-bolt Austrian type that holds quality in the garden longer than many butterhead varieties before heat causes it to flower. The unique spotted appearance makes it highly marketable at farmers' markets and popular in mesclun mixes where the speckled leaves stand out visually. In zone 9 it produces excellent fall-through-winter heads with the speckle pattern intensifying in cool temperatures. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Spectacular Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Early-Blooming Mayhaw)
description: Spectacular is an early-blooming western mayhaw selection bred for unusually large fruit, running up to about 0.85 inch across, noticeably bigger than wild-collected mayhaw. Because it blooms early, it requires a second early-flowering cultivar such as Royal Star planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination and a full crop. Give it the same wet, acidic, full-sun conditions favored by all mayhaws, since it is no more tolerant of dry, upland soil than its relatives. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Spelt
description: Drill or broadcast seed at 80–100 lb per acre (approximately 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft) in fall to 1 in depth; spelt is taller than modern wheat and slightly more susceptible to lodging in rich soils, so avoid high-nitrogen amendments. It tolerates clay and compacted soils better than most small grains and has reasonable resistance to rust diseases. Harvest at hard dough stage in early summer by cutting, sheaving, and drying for a week before threshing; spelt retains a tough hull (spikelet) that requires a dedicated pearler or dehuller before milling. The resulting flour has a mild, nutty flavor and is widely used by those who tolerate ancient wheats better than modern varieties, though it does contain gluten. Matures in 250–280 days from seed.

name: Spice Islands Rosemary (Classic Strongly Flavored Culinary Rosemary)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Spice Islands is a long-established culinary rosemary cultivar bred for strong, classic, pungently resinous rosemary flavor and fragrance, considered one of the most reliably flavorful rosemary cultivars for everyday cooking use. It grows into a dense, upright, well-branched shrub with the typical narrow, needle-like, dark green leaves and pale blue flowers of standard rosemary, making it equally useful as a culinary herb, an evergreen landscape shrub, or a low informal hedge. Like other rosemary, it thrives in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil and full sun, and is far more likely to suffer from overwatering and poor drainage than from drought or neglect. Harvest sprigs anytime for fresh use, or cut and dry larger quantities for winter storage. Prune lightly after flowering, or anytime during the growing season when harvesting, to maintain a full, bushy shape and encourage continued tender new growth. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Spice Zee Nectaplum (Genetic Dwarf Nectarine-Plum Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, Spice Zee is a genetic dwarf nectaplum, a nectarine-plum interspecific hybrid, that naturally stays compact enough for a large patio container or small-yard planting while still bearing full-sized, sweet, richly flavored fruit with a flavor many describe as somewhere between a nectarine and a plum. The reddish-purple young foliage in spring, aging to bronze-green, makes it an attractive small ornamental tree even outside of fruiting season, and its self-fertile flowers mean a single tree can set a full crop without a second pollinator. Fruit ripens in early summer, and the naturally dense, rounded canopy benefits from light annual thinning to keep light reaching the interior and to manage fruit size. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Spicy Globe Basil (Globe Basil, Bush Basil)
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Spicy Globe is a compact, naturally mounded basil variety that forms a near-perfect sphere shape 10–14 inches in diameter without any pruning or training. The tiny, fine-textured leaves are intensely fragrant and spicy — more intensely basil-flavored than large-leaf Genovese types — with a sweet, warm, clove-like spice note that makes Spicy Globe excellent for herbes de Provence blends, compound butters, and infused oils. The self-regulating globe shape and compact 10–12 inch height make it an ideal container plant, a neat edging for herb beds, and a productive houseplant in a sunny window. In zone 9's warm season it thrives April–October; the tiny leaves wilt at the first frost. Harvest by snipping 1/3 of the plant at a time to maintain the globe shape; never remove more than 1/3 at once. The dense, tight growth resists bolting slightly better than Genovese types, giving a longer leaf-harvest window before flowers appear. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Spicy Orange Thyme (Orange Spice Groundcover Thyme)
description: Spicy Orange, sometimes sold as Orange Spice thyme, is a low, mat-forming culinary thyme whose crushed foliage releases a bright, sweet-orange scent and flavor distinct from the more balsamic, resinous Orange Balsam cultivar. Its trailing, groundcover habit sets it apart from upright culinary thymes, making it useful for edging paths, tumbling over walls, or filling gaps between pavers where the scent releases underfoot, while pink summer flowers draw bees. Snip fresh sprigs to flavor poultry, fish, or fruit-based glazes, and shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage new tender growth. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Spigold Apple (Cornell Red Spy x Golden Delicious Cross)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Spigold was bred at the Cornell University research station in Geneva, New York, from a cross of Red Spy and Golden Delicious, combining Red Spy's large size and crisp texture with Golden Delicious's sweetness in one of the largest apples commonly grown, with fruit that can rival a softball in size. The skin is yellow-green heavily striped and blushed with red, and the crisp, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in storage. The tree tends toward biennial bearing (heavy crops every other year) if not thinned properly, so thin fruit in heavy-set years to encourage more consistent annual production, and stake young trees, since the very large fruit puts real strain on branches. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Spike Lavender (Broadleaved Lavender)
description: Spike lavender is a heat-loving Mediterranean species native to lower, warmer elevations than English lavender, and it is one of the two parents that give rise to sterile lavandin hybrids such as 'Grosso' and 'Provence.' Its broader, gray-green leaves and camphor-rich scent set it apart from the sweeter, narrower-leaved English lavender, and its oil is prized more for industrial and cleaning-product fragrances than for fine perfumery. Plant in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; it tolerates heat and drought better than English lavender but is noticeably less cold-hardy. Shear back after the summer flush of pale lavender-blue flower spikes to keep the rounded shrub from sprawling and to encourage denser regrowth. Matures in 180–300 days from transplant.

name: Spiked Speedwell
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; spiked speedwell is one of the most reliably beautiful summer perennials in the European tradition, producing dense, tapering spikes of tiny flowers in intense shades of violet-blue, lilac, or white (depending on cultivar) that bloom from midsummer into fall. The plant is extremely tough and drought tolerant once established, thriving in lean, well-drained soil where it is long-lived, but declining in rich, moist conditions where it becomes floppy and short-lived. Popular cultivars include 'Royal Candles' (deep violet, compact), 'Icicle' (white), 'Red Fox' (deep pink), and 'Heidekind' (rose-pink). An excellent front-of-border perennial that combines beautifully with ornamental grasses, sedums, and rudbeckia in late-season gardens. Attracts numerous small butterflies and bumblebees. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Spilanthes (Toothache Plant)
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in warm, moist seed-starting mix at 75°F; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture. Spilanthes is notable for spilanthol, a compound in the flowers and leaves that causes an intense, numbing tingle on the tongue — hence the common name toothache plant; it has uses in local anesthetic preparations and salivation-stimulating tinctures. The distinctive red and yellow, cone-shaped flower heads are harvested fresh or dried for tinctures and topical preparations; even a small piece of flower head produces a pronounced oral sensation. Grow in full sun with moderate moisture; deadhead regularly to encourage continuous flowering throughout the warm season. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Spinach Baby Greens
description: Sow seed densely in shallow rows or broad bands and keep the surface moist for even germination. Fast-growing baby spinach leaves add flavor and nutrients to salads, sandwiches, smoothies, and pesto. This crop can be grown indoors at any time of year, so move containers as needed for the best light and cool temperatures. Harvest leaves young, when just a few inches tall, by cutting above the growing point so plants regrow. Successive sowings keep tender baby leaves coming through the cool seasons. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: Spineless Beauty Hybrid Zucchini (Commercial-Grade Itch-Free Zucchini)
description: Spineless Beauty is a widely grown commercial-grade hybrid zucchini bred with smooth, nearly spine-free petioles, sparing gardeners the itchy rash that comes from brushing bristly zucchini foliage during harvest. The open, mounding plant sets glossy, speckled medium-green fruit that hold quality even when picked slightly larger than typical zucchini, at 6-8 inches. Because powdery and downy mildew can move fast through humid Gulf Coast gardens, growers should keep foliage dry with drip irrigation and watch closely during rainy spells since this variety carries no built-in mildew resistance. Regular harvest every two to three days keeps the vigorous, heavy-yielding plant productive through the season. Matures in 48–53 days from seed.

name: Spineless Nopal Cactus
description: Plant paddles upright with the cut end 2–3 inches deep in gritty, extremely well-drained soil — wet soil in any season will cause rot. Opuntia ellisiana is the premier spineless edible nopal cactus for home gardens, prized because even young pads lack the large spines of most prickly pears, though fine glochids still develop on mature pads. Harvest only young, tender spring pads (nopales) at 4–6 inches before glochid development; use gloves and scrub pads under running water to remove any remaining tiny spines before cooking. Nopales taste mildly tangy and have a mucilaginous texture when cooked — excellent grilled, scrambled with eggs, in tacos, or pickled in escabeche. The plant survives full drought periods once established and requires no irrigation or fertilization in zone 8–9 soils. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Spineless Prickly Pear
description: Root a calloused Opuntia pad cutting in dry, coarse, sandy soil in full sun; allow the cut end to dry for 1–2 weeks before planting to prevent rot; plant only 2–3 inches deep; water sparingly until established (3–4 months), then infrequently; harvest young pads in spring and ripe fruits in late summer/fall. Spineless Prickly Pear cultivars lack the dangerous glochid clusters that make wild and spiny Opuntia so irritating to work with, making the harvest of both young pads and ripe fruits safe and practical with only minimal care (lightweight gloves recommended). Young pads (nopales), harvested in spring when 4–6 inches long, are a major vegetable in Mexican cuisine — grilled, diced into salsa, cooked into soups, or scrambled with eggs; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous, tart-green flavor. The ripe fruits (tunas) in late summer and fall range from yellow to red to deep purple depending on variety; the sweet, melon-like flesh makes excellent juice, sorbet, jam, and candy. The spineless form was famously promoted by Luther Burbank in the early 1900s as a drought-resistant livestock fodder crop for arid lands — though that particular venture was not entirely successful commercially, his selections remain the basis of modern spineless cultivar lines. An outstanding plant for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where heat, drought, and alkaline soils challenge most edibles. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Spiny Chayote (Chayote Espinoso, Prickly Chayote)
description: Unlike the smooth, spineless chayote types more common in US markets, this traditional Mesoamerican and Caribbean varietal group bears fruit covered in soft to firm spines and is often preferred in Mexican, Central American, and Caribbean cooking for its firmer texture. Grow it exactly as common chayote, planting the whole fruit at a slight angle in rich soil and training the vigorous vine onto a heavy-duty trellis or arbor, since a single plant can cover 400 square feet or more. Wear gloves when handling and harvesting the fruit, as the spines can be sharp on some selections, though many are only softly bristled. In frost-free zones the vine is a long-lived perennial that also produces an edible starchy tuberous root after a few seasons. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Spiny Chicory (Prickly Succory)
description: Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; spiny chicory is a Cretan and eastern Mediterranean coastal plant — native to the rocky, wind-exposed, salt-spray-drenched sea cliffs of Crete and other Greek islands — that is one of the most important traditional wild food plants of Cretan cuisine. The young shoots and basal leaves are collected in late winter and spring, before the plant develops its characteristic spiny character, and prepared as horta — the classic Greek-Cretan tradition of boiling or sautéing wild greens in olive oil with lemon. The flavor is pleasantly bitter in the chicory family tradition. In the garden it forms a low, spiny, somewhat cushion-like perennial with small, pale-blue chicory flowers in summer. Extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and wind-resistant — qualities that make it outstanding for coastal and exposed Mediterranean-climate gardens where the combination of salt spray, wind, and lean, rocky soil defeats most ornamentals. An authentic plant for a Greek or Mediterranean-themed herb garden. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Spiny Gourd (Kantola, Teasle Gourd)
description: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide strong trellis or fence support; plant both male and female plants (approximately one male per 3–5 females) for fruit set. Momordica dioica (spiny gourd, kantola, or teasle gourd) is an important seasonal vegetable in India, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia — a perennial climbing vine in the cucurbit family that stores energy in underground tubers through dry or cool seasons and produces vigorous new growth annually. The small, 2-to-3-inch, oval fruits are densely covered in soft spines (the 'spiny gourd' name) and harvested young and green for cooking — their flavor is distinctively bitter-sweet, similar to bitter melon but milder and less intensely bitter, making them more versatile for sautéing, stuffing, curries, and stir-fries. In Indian cuisine, kantola is considered a delicacy and commands premium prices in markets. The plant is dioecious (separate male and female individuals) — an unusual trait in cucurbits — requiring both sexes for fruit production. The tubers can be left in the ground through zone 9 winters if mulched. Spiny gourd is a nutritious vegetable rich in protein, iron, and phytonutrients. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Spirit Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Semi-Bush Dual-Purpose Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds directly in hills once the soil has warmed, thinning to two or three plants per hill; the compact, semi-bush vine allows closer spacing than traditional long-vined field pumpkins. Spirit was named an All-America Selections winner in 1977 for producing bright orange, deeply oval fruit averaging 10-15 pounds on a plant that stays far more contained than open-pollinated heirlooms. The thick, meaty flesh makes it genuinely dual-purpose, equally suited to a classic jack-o'-lantern face and to being baked down for pumpkin puree. Harvest once the rind has hardened and colored fully, cure briefly in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location out of direct sun. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Splash Pluot (Yellow Skin with Red Splash Pattern)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Splash is a Zaiger Genetics pluot with pale yellow skin marked by irregular red splashes and streaks, giving each fruit a slightly different, hand-painted appearance, and it produces sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh typical of the best pluot selections. The tree is a reliable producer within the pluot family, and the fruit's bright, cheerful coloring along with its excellent eating quality has made it a popular choice among specialty fruit growers and farmers market vendors. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to concentrate flavor and size, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and the splash pattern has fully developed. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Splendor Lingonberry (Balsgård Research Station Cultivar)
description: Splendor emerged from the Balsgård fruit breeding program in southern Sweden, the same research station responsible for several other named lingonberry selections evaluated side by side in North American trials. It shares the species' dense, low, evergreen habit and produces small white to pale pink spring flowers followed by glossy red berries prized for their sharp, cranberry-like tartness in Scandinavian preserves. Because lingonberry roots are shallow and fine, keep the planting bed consistently moist but never waterlogged, and avoid cultivating around the base to prevent rhizome damage. A topdressing of acidic mulch each spring helps maintain the low soil pH the plant needs to take up nutrients effectively. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sponge Gourd (Smooth Luffa)
description: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun; sponge gourd is best known as the source of the loofah sponge — the fibrous interior skeleton of the mature fruit that becomes the natural bath and scrubbing sponge found in health food stores worldwide. The fruits are edible when young and immature (before the fibrous network fully develops) — harvested at 4–6 inches long and cooked like zucchini or opo squash, with a mild, slightly mucilagenous texture popular in East Asian and South Asian cuisine (called 'ghi tow' in Chinese, 'louki' or 'turai' in Hindi). To harvest loofahs, allow the fruit to mature and dry completely on the vine until the outer skin turns brown and papery and rattles when shaken — then peel the dry skin, shake out the seeds (save some for replanting), and rinse the fibrous sponge. A highly productive vine requiring a long, hot summer; grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel in short-season climates. The ornamental yellow flowers attract pollinators. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Spookie Pumpkin
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm, rich soil, planting in hills with plenty of room for the vines to run. This small pie pumpkin, a 1966 heirloom crossing Sugar Pie and Jack O'Lantern, averages six to seven inches tall with sweet, fine-textured yellow-orange flesh. Give plants steady water and consistent feeding for good fruit set and size. Harvest when the rind hardens and turns fully colored, leaving a length of stem attached. Cure the fruit in a warm spot to improve flavor and storage life. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Spring Cress (Bulbous Cress)
description: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; spring cress is a native American Cardamine (mustard family) of woodland springs, seeps, and shaded stream banks — one of the earliest edible wild plants of the year, producing rosettes of smooth, edible leaves in late winter with a pleasant, mild watercress-like flavor, followed by masses of small white 4-petaled flowers in early spring. Both leaves and flowers are edible fresh in salads or as a potherb. It grows naturally in the same wet, shaded, cool conditions as watercress and is an excellent native alternative in the shaded water garden or boggy woodland edge. The small bulb-like stem base gives it the common name 'bulbous cress.' A beloved early spring edible in Appalachian foraging tradition. Naturalizes to form showy colonies in appropriate conditions. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Spring Glow Cornelian Cherry (Low-Chill Southern Cornelian Cherry Dogwood)
description: Spring Glow is an introduction from the J.C. Raulston Arboretum selected for its notably low chilling requirement, extending the range of cornelian cherry into warmer parts of the South where most European-bred Cornus mas cultivars bloom poorly or fail to set fruit. Hundreds of small, bright yellow flowers smother the bare branches in late winter to early spring, weeks ahead of forsythia, followed by glossy, leathery dark-green summer foliage and oblong, cherry-red fruit that ripens in midsummer. The tart, plum-like fruit drops as it softens and is best gathered daily from a tarp or the ground for use in syrups, jams, and preserves. This small multi-stemmed tree tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soils, and is largely free of the pests and diseases that trouble other stone fruits, making it a low-maintenance choice for southern edible landscapes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Spring Snow Crabapple (Fruitless White-Flowered Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Spring Snow is prized for producing essentially no fruit at all, a genetic trait that makes it a popular choice where the messy fruit drop of ornamental crabapples is unwelcome — around patios, walkways, and driveways — while still delivering the classic crabapple spring show of dense, fragrant, pure white flowers covering the tree before the leaves fully emerge. Its clean, tidy habit and lack of fruit litter have made it one of the most widely planted flowering crabapples for urban and residential landscapes. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; watch for occasional fire blight and apple scab in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Springhigh Southern Highbush Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun, and pair with another early-blooming southern highbush variety for best pollination and fruit set. Developed by the University of Florida's blueberry breeding program, Springhigh was selected for an unusually low chilling requirement that lets it flower and fruit reliably in the mild winters of the Deep South, where many northern blueberry types fail to break dormancy evenly. It ripens very early in the season, often the first blueberry to color up in the garden, giving growers a jump on the market and on fresh eating alike. Keep soil consistently moist during bloom and fruit development, since southern highbush types have shallow root systems that dry out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Springwide Southern Highbush Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines well before planting; Springwide is a patented low-chill Southern highbush blueberry with medium plant vigor and a habit between erect and spreading, producing large, medium-blue berries with a good picking scar, firm texture, and mild flavor suited to fresh eating. Its low chilling requirement makes it a candidate for zone 8-10 Gulf South winters where Northern highbush types often underperform. Southern highbush cultivars including Springwide are self-fertile but set more and larger fruit with a second, overlapping-bloom cultivar nearby, so plant at least two varieties together. Keep the shallow, fibrous roots consistently moist with drip irrigation and a thick pine bark or pine straw mulch, and avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sprouting Broccoli
description: Start seeds at 65–75°F in small pots and grow under bright light to prevent leggy transplants; harden off over 7–10 days before setting in the garden. Unlike heading broccoli, sprouting types produce many small floret clusters on branched side shoots rather than a single large central head — harvest shoots when tight and before flowers open, cutting with 4–6 inches of stem to encourage continued production. Regular harvesting extends the season for weeks; uncut shoots quickly flower and the plant stops producing. Mulch heavily for overwintering in zones 6–8 to harvest the earliest spring shoots, often before any other fresh vegetable is available. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Sputnik Upland Rice
description: Sputnik is a modern awnless upland rice bred in Primorsky Krai in the Russian Far East, a region with a climate cool enough that it has proven workable for temperate North American gardens. It produces a short-grain brown rice and tillers vigorously, giving good yields per plant, though its taller stature makes it somewhat prone to lodging in wind and heavy rain. Start seed indoors and transplant it out once the soil has warmed, since like most upland rices it is slow to establish from seed and needs a head start against weeds. It is best suited to gardeners already growing other upland rice types who want a taller, higher-tillering variety to diversify their planting. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Squashberry / Mooseberry
description: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Squashberry is native to the understory of boreal and subarctic forests and performs best where it receives filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Maintain even soil moisture, especially during summer, by applying a generous layer of organic mulch around the root zone. Clusters of translucent orange-red berries ripen in late summer and were historically harvested by indigenous peoples of the north for fresh eating, jam, and pemmican. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer, treated with rooting hormone and kept in a humid environment; division of established clumps in early spring is also effective. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Squibnocket Beach Plum (Named Cape Cod Beach Plum Selection)
description: Squibnocket is a named beach plum selection identified from wild coastal populations for its reliable cropping and better-than-average fruit size, part of a group of named clones evaluated for improving on typical unselected seedling beach plum. Shrubs produce abundant white blossom in mid-spring followed by tart-to-sweet purple-red plums in late summer, prized for jams and jellies. Beach plum is naturally adapted to sandy, salt-sprayed, wind-exposed coastal soils and needs excellent drainage rather than rich garden soil to thrive. Because most beach plum is only partially self-fertile, planting more than one genetically distinct shrub greatly improves fruit set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sri Chompoo Longan (Pink Longan)
description: Sri Chompoo, also called Chompoo, is a Thai longan cultivar named for the faint pink blush of its aril -- an unusual trait among longan, which is normally translucent white throughout. The fruit is medium-sized with light brown, slightly rough skin, a small seed, and thick, aromatic, sweet flesh that many growers rate above standard cultivars for eating quality. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil, allowing the tree a period of relative dryness and cool nights in winter to encourage strong flowering the following spring. As with all longan, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization during the winter chilling period, since lush new growth in place of flower buds is a common problem in overfed trees. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sri Kembangan Star Fruit (Carambola)
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Sri Kembangan is a Malaysian carambola selection grown for elongated, deep orange-yellow fruit with thin, waxy skin and firm, very sweet, low-acid flesh that eats well fresh with few seeds. It is a smaller, more manageable tree than many carambola seedlings and can be kept to a compact size with regular pruning, making it well suited to home gardens and large containers. Flowering and fruiting occur over an extended season, with the heaviest crop from late summer through winter in warm climates. Fruit color and sugar content develop best with full sun exposure; trees in part shade tend to produce paler, more acidic fruit. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: St. Croix Grape (Extreme Cold-Hardy Red Wine and Juice Grape)
description: Bred by Minnesota grape breeder Elmer Swenson, this early-ripening hybrid tolerates winter temperatures well below zero without significant cane damage, making it a staple for northern growers who cannot overwinter vinifera or many other hybrids. Clusters of medium blue-black berries ripen early in the season and are used for both juice and light red wine with a mild, fruity character. The vine is naturally productive and needs cluster thinning in its early years to avoid overcropping, which can stunt future growth. Its combination of cold hardiness and early ripening makes it a dependable choice for short-season gardens. Matures in 135–150 days from transplant.

name: St. Edmund's Pippin Apple (Aromatic English Russet Dessert Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. St. Edmund's Pippin originated in Bury St Edmunds, England, in the 1870s, prized as one of the finest early russet dessert apples, with golden-yellow, rough-textured russeted skin covering crisp, aromatic, richly flavored flesh with a distinctive nutty sweetness characteristic of the best russet apples. It ripens earlier than most other russets, extending the season for gardeners who enjoy this distinctive style of apple beyond the typical late-fall russet harvest. The tree bears reliably and the fruit, while not a long keeper, offers exceptional eating quality fresh off the tree, making it a favorite among heirloom apple enthusiasts and collectors of English dessert apple varieties. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: St. John Wort (Common St. John Wort)
description: Surface sow seeds in early spring (press lightly into soil but do not cover — seeds require light for germination) in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; thin or transplant to 18 inches. Hypericum perforatum (St. John's wort) is the most important medicinal herb in the Western world after echinacea — a Eurasian perennial producing cheerful, 5-petaled, bright-yellow flowers with numerous golden stamens from June through August, on upright, two-winged, branching stems with small, oval, opposite leaves dotted with translucent oil glands (the characteristic 'perforations' visible when the leaf is held to light). Standardized Hypericum extracts are among the best-documented herbal treatments for mild to moderate depression, with multiple clinical trials showing efficacy comparable to conventional antidepressants. The flowers and upper leaves are harvested at peak bloom and tinctured or dried for medicinal use. The plant is easy to grow in lean, well-drained soils and self-seeds prolifically — it has naturalized across North America and is considered an invasive weed in some western states; grow responsibly. CAUTION: St. John's wort causes photosensitivity in fair-skinned people and may interact with numerous prescription medications including birth control, antidepressants, and anti-rejection drugs. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: St. John's Wort
description: Surface-sow seeds onto moist mix; cold stratification for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator prior to sowing can improve germination, especially with older seed. Plants thrive in poor, well-drained soil and become weedy in fertile conditions — resist the urge to fertilize. Harvest flower buds and newly opened blossoms around the summer solstice, when hypericin content peaks; rub a bud between your fingers and look for a red-purple stain confirming good potency. Dry flowers quickly on screens to preserve the active compounds. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: St. Julien A Plum Rootstock
description: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired plum or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; St. Julien A is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit. A selection of the wild bullace or damson-type plum long used as the traditional English standard rootstock for grafted plums, gages, and apricots, it produces a semi-vigorous tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a full seedling tree, with good compatibility across most plum and apricot varieties and reasonable tolerance of heavier soils compared to some other stone fruit rootstocks. Its long track record of reliable size control and broad graft compatibility has kept it in wide use for both commercial and home orchard plum and apricot production. Graft a desired named plum or apricot variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect earlier bearing and a more manageable tree size than on a vigorous seedling rootstock. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Stalked Water-horehound
description: Lycopus rubellus thrives in saturated or inundated soils and is an excellent choice for rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and streambank stabilization plantings where standing water is common in spring. The small white flowers appearing in summer attract native bees and are characteristic of the mint family; the plant is strongly aromatic when the leaves are crushed. Historically, the starchy tubers were eaten by indigenous peoples of the Southeast, and the plant remains an important habitat species supporting wetland food webs. Plant in partial shade with consistently wet roots, and divide every two to three years to maintain vigor. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Stambaugh Black Walnut
