description: Stambaugh is a named black walnut selection grown for a good percentage of easily extracted kernel meat relative to unselected wild trees, making it a practical choice for home nut growers who process their own harvest. Grafted trees establish bearing several years sooner than seedling black walnuts and crop more uniformly from year to year. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from juglone-sensitive plantings. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Stampede Jerusalem Artichoke
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Jerusalem artichoke is forgiving of poor soil and minimal care; Stampede is an early-maturing selection of Jerusalem artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus) that was developed for northern short-season gardens where standard varieties may not mature tubers before killing frost. The smooth, relatively uniform, white-to-tan tubers are significantly easier to clean and prepare than the knobby irregular tubers of wild-type plants, and the early maturity reduces the waiting period before harvest. Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke) tubers have a crunchy, slightly sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of water chestnuts when eaten raw, and a creamy, buttery quality when roasted or pureed — they are used in soups, stir-fries, gratins, and roasted as a potato substitute. The tubers store inulin (a prebiotic fiber) rather than starch, making them lower-glycemic than potatoes but causing digestive discomfort in some people — the nickname 'fartichoke' reflects this effect, which diminishes with acclimation. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Stampede Sunchoke (Early-Maturing Jerusalem Artichoke)
description: Plant tuber pieces in well-drained soil in a dedicated bed, since sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground and are difficult to fully remove once established. Stampede is prized among Jerusalem artichoke growers for maturing its large, smooth-skinned tubers earlier than most other varieties, allowing an earlier fall harvest and giving northern growers a reliable crop even where the growing season is on the short side. Foliage grows tall and topped with small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back after frost, at which point the tubers are ready to dig; a light frost is said to improve their sweet, nutty flavor by converting stored inulin into simple sugars. Harvest tubers from fall through early spring as needed, leaving a few in the ground to resprout the following year, and rotate or contain the bed to keep the planting from spreading into unwanted areas. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Standing Ovation Serviceberry
description: Standing Ovation is a narrow, upright saskatoon selection marketed under the First Editions brand, forming a tidy column reaching about 15 feet tall on a 3-foot spread, making it an unusually space-efficient native fruiting shrub. Bronze new growth matures to green and turns brilliant orange, red, and purple in fall, alongside small, sweet, edible blue-black berries in early summer. Plant in full sun for the best fruit set and fall color, in average, well-drained soil. Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead or crossing wood, since the naturally columnar form needs little shaping. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Stanley Plum (European Prune Plum, American Standard Freestone Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prune annually to an open-center form; thin heavy fruit crops to 3–4 inches apart after natural fruit drop; Stanley ripens in late August to September in most of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic; harvest for fresh eating when fully ripe and soft, or pick slightly firm for drying into prunes; self-fruitful but plant with a companion European plum for best yields. Stanley plum is the most important and widely planted European prune plum (Prunus domestica) in the eastern United States, developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1926 and released in the 1930s. For decades, Stanley was synonymous with 'prune plum' throughout the eastern states — the word 'Stanley' and 'prune' were used interchangeably by many orchardists and home growers, reflecting its dominance as the only widely-grown European-type freestone plum in the region. The fruits are large to very large (for prune-type plums), oval to oblong, with deep blue-purple to nearly black skin and golden-yellow, firm, freestone flesh with a rich, sweet, slightly winey plum flavor. They are excellent for fresh eating at peak ripeness, cooking in preserves and tarts, and the definitive prune-type plum for drying — the firm, dry flesh and freestone characteristic make them ideal for dehydrating into prunes. Stanley requires approximately 800 chill hours and is reliably productive in zones 4–7, with reliable but sometimes marginal performance in zone 8 in mild-winter years. It is partially self-fruitful, producing some crop when grown alone but yielding significantly more when cross-pollinated with other European plum varieties. The trees are moderately vigorous and productive, with moderate disease susceptibility under humid conditions. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Stanza Red Currant (Late-Season Norwegian Red Currant)
description: Stanza is a Norwegian-bred red currant selected for ripening several weeks later than standard cultivars, which makes it a useful choice for stretching the fresh currant harvest into late summer or for cooler northern gardens where early cultivars ripen unevenly. Like other Ribes, it can be regulated as a white pine blister rust host, so check state or county rules before adding it to the garden. The upright, hardy bush is self-fertile and holds its glossy red berries well on the strig without splitting, which makes for a cleaner harvest and less fruit loss to rain. Grow it in full sun to light shade in evenly moist, fertile soil, and prune out the oldest quarter of the wood each dormant season to keep new, productive spurwood coming. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Star Anise
description: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade. True star anise is a slow, long-lived subtropical evergreen native to southern China and northern Vietnam that needs six to eight years of consistent warmth and humidity before it forms its first harvestable star-shaped seed pods. Pods are picked while still green, then sun-dried until they turn the familiar deep reddish-brown, and are essential to Chinese five-spice powder, pho broth, and mulled wine. Do not confuse it with the toxic ornamental anise relatives (Illicium floridanum, I. anisatum) sold for landscaping — only I. verum pods are safe to eat. Matures in 2190–2920 days from transplant.

name: Star Apple (Caimito)
description: Plant grafted trees in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; star apple is a highly ornamental tropical fruit tree native to the West Indies, producing beautiful round fruits 2–4 inches across in purple or green skin with a distinctive star pattern in the cross-section of the white, gelatinous, sweet, milk-filled flesh — the 'star' that gives the fruit its name. The leaves are distinctively two-toned: dark glossy green above, silky golden-bronze beneath, creating a shimmering display when the breeze moves through the canopy. The fruit is eaten fresh by cutting in half and scooping the sweet, creamy flesh; the latex in the skin and rind is astringent and should not be consumed. Grafted trees begin producing in 3–5 years. The sweet, mild flavor is a favorite in the Caribbean and South Florida. An outstanding ornamental and fruiting tree for zone 10–12 gardens. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Star Gooseberry (Otaheite Gooseberry, Malay Gooseberry)
description: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; star gooseberry is a productive tropical fruit tree widely grown throughout Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, bearing clusters of ribbed, waxy, pale yellow to white drupes — each resembling a miniature star when cut cross-section — directly on the trunk and older branches in a distinctive cauliflorous pattern. The tart, acidic fruit has a crisp, translucent flesh somewhat reminiscent of a sour apple or green gooseberry and is consumed fresh (with salt and chili in Southeast Asia), pickled, candied, or made into jams and juices. Trees reach 10–30 feet in frost-free conditions but are easily maintained smaller through pruning. In zone 9 they may be damaged by frost below 28°F but typically recover from light frost damage at the root. Prolific bearers that fruit twice yearly in good conditions. The unusual trunk-fruiting habit and fine-textured, pinnate foliage are ornamental assets in the tropical garden. A worthwhile and underused edible tree for zone 9–11 gardens. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Star of David Okra (Israeli Okra)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; soak seeds 12–24 hours for faster, more uniform germination. Star of David okra (also called Israeli okra or Giant Israeli okra) is a Middle Eastern heirloom producing fat, broadly triangular, six-ridged pods that create a hexagonal or Star-of-David shape in cross-section; the pods are substantially wider in diameter (1.5–2 inches) than the slender American varieties, making them excellent for stuffing whole (halved lengthwise and filled with seasoned meat and rice in the Middle Eastern manner, or stuffed and baked with tomato sauce). The flavor is mild and tender at 3–4 inch harvest size; the large pod diameter keeps them from becoming stringy at slightly larger sizes than standard okra. Plants are very tall (6–9 feet), vigorous, and ornamental with large yellow hibiscus flowers. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Star Ruby Grapefruit (Pink Grapefruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest location with maximum sun exposure; Star Ruby is a red-fleshed grapefruit variety developed by Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis and released in 1970 — the variety that set the standard for deep-red, sweet, low-acid grapefruit. Texas Rio Grande Valley grapefruit production is dominated by Star Ruby and its offspring Rio Red (1984), both producing the deep ruby-red flesh and low-acid, sweet flavor that made Texas red grapefruit internationally famous. The fruits are large, with thin, yellow-blushed skin and deep crimson flesh that is sweeter and less bitter than white grapefruit — so sweet they are often eaten without added sugar. Star Ruby requires a long, hot growing season to develop maximum sweetness and color: in zone 9, summer heat is critical. Trees are vigorous, productive once established, and moderately cold-tolerant to about 26°F. Feed with citrus fertilizer (especially nitrogen and zinc) 3–4 times per year. An excellent landscape tree in warm zone 9 that provides both ornamental value and substantial food production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Star Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Ripening Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and provide consistent moisture through spring fruit development for the best berry size. Star is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued for its very early ripening, often among the first blueberries ready to harvest in Gulf South gardens, bearing firm, flavorful, medium to large berries on a vigorous, productive bush. Its low chill requirement and early season make it a good choice for extending the front end of the blueberry harvest, particularly useful when paired with a mid- or late-season rabbiteye or southern highbush cultivar to spread the crop over a longer window. Plant with a second compatible southern highbush variety for the best fruit set, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Starbor Kale (Compact Dwarf Curly Hybrid Kale)
description: Sow seed a half inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing, side-dressing with compost as plants size up. This compact, uniform hybrid produces tightly curled, dark blue-green leaves on short stems, making it well suited to close spacing and mechanical or hand bunch harvesting. Its short, dense habit and slow bolting have made it a standard choice for market growers wanting a tidy, consistent curly kale. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Starbrite Watermelon (Classic Disease-Resistant Striped Hybrid)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starbrite is a widely grown hybrid watermelon producing large, oblong fruit with the classic dark and light green striped rind most gardeners picture when they think of watermelon, and sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a small, manageable seed cavity. The vigorous vine carries good resistance to fusarium wilt and anthracnose, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm, humid growing regions, helping the plant stay healthy and productive through a long summer season. As a dependable, well-proven hybrid with a long track record, it remains a solid standard choice for gardeners wanting a classic, reliable watermelon without the added complexity of seedless triploid pollination requirements. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy yellow. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Starfruit (Carambola)
description: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; purchase grafted trees for earlier bearing — seedling trees may take 5–7 years to fruit while grafted trees can bear in 1–2 years after planting. Averrhoa carambola is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree producing the unique, deeply 5-ridged, golden-yellow, translucent fruit known as starfruit or carambola that when sliced crosswise yields the distinctive five-pointed star shape; the fruit ranges from very tart to sweet depending on cultivar and is excellent fresh, in fruit salads, as a garnish, and in tropical beverages. Trees bloom and fruit multiple times per year in tropical climates, producing an almost continuous harvest in zones 10–11; in zone 9 they need frost protection and may lose leaves in cold winters but often recover. Sweet cultivars 'Arkin', 'Kari', and 'Fwang Tung' are the most popular for home orchards. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Starkrimson Pear (Red Clapp's Favorite Sport)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett. Discovered as a brilliant crimson-red bud sport of Clapp's Favorite by Adrian G. Kalle of South Haven, Michigan, and introduced under the trademarked name Starkrimson by Stark Bro's Nursery in 1970, it is also known informally as Red Clapp's. The fruit has striking, glossy red skin with a thick, stocky stem and dense white flesh, offering a mild, sweet flavor with a subtle floral aroma and smooth, juicy texture. As an early summer pear it is typically among the first fresh pears of the season, ready from August. Harvest while still firm and deeply colored in late summer, then ripen at room temperature for a few days and eat promptly. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Starmaya Coffee
description: Bred jointly by CIRAD and ECOM Sustainable Management Services and released around 2018, Starmaya was the first F1 Arabica hybrid that could be propagated economically by seed rather than requiring costly embryo-culture or clonal cutting propagation, making the vigor and yield benefits of F1 hybrids accessible to smallholders for the first time. It combines a dwarf, compact growth habit with strong vigor, reliable production, and good cup quality reported by early adopters in Nicaragua and Mexico. Because it is still a hybrid, seed should be sourced from certified programs to maintain its traits. Grow it under filtered shade in rich, well-drained soil like other Arabica selections. Matures in 1095–1400 days from transplant.

name: Staro Chives (Thick-Leaf Freezing and Drying Cultivar)
description: Staro is a European market-garden chive selection bred for thicker, larger leaf blades than standard chives, a trait developed so the harvested leaf holds its color, texture, and flavor after freezing or dehydrating rather than turning limp or discolored. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest by cutting outer leaves close to the base every few weeks to keep the clump producing tender new growth. The heavier leaf structure also makes Staro easier to chop cleanly for fresh use than the thinner-leaved standard chive types. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and prevent the center of the clump from dying out. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Starship Zucchini (Pale Cream-White Summer Squash)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starship is a distinctive pale, cream-white zucchini that stands out visually from the far more common dark green types, with smooth, cylindrical fruit and tender, mild flesh good for all standard zucchini preparations, from grilling to sautéing to baking into bread. Beyond its novelty color, the compact, productive bush is a reliable, disease-tolerant performer well suited to home gardens wanting to diversify a summer squash planting beyond the usual green varieties. Pick fruit at six to eight inches for the best eating quality, and harvest frequently once production ramps up, since oversized fruit turns seedy and tough quickly, a trait shared by all zucchini types regardless of skin color. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Stauntonia (Mube, Japanese False Akebia)
description: This evergreen woody vine is unusual among fruiting plants for genuinely preferring shade to partial shade, making it one of the few climbers suited to a north-facing wall or the dim understory of a garden pergola. Train the twining stems onto a trellis or fence and be patient, since named or grafted plants fruit far sooner than seedlings, which can take years to bear. In autumn the vine produces oblong purple fruit similar to its relative akebia, splitting to reveal a sweet, milky-white pulp studded with small black seeds that is eaten fresh by hand in Japan. Plant two vines for best pollination and fruit set, since a single plant fruits sparsely on its own. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Stayman Apple (Stayman Winesap, Rich Wine-Flavored Keeper Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Discovered in Kansas in 1866 by Dr. J. Stayman as a seedling of the older Winesap apple, this cultivar keeps the tangy, wine-like flavor of its parent in a larger, more productive fruit. The dark red skin covers dense, juicy flesh that holds up well in storage and in cooking, and the tree has long been a Mid-Atlantic and Southern favorite for cider and pie making. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the background color turns from green to yellow-green. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Stella Cherry (First Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry, Canadian Self-Fertile Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Stella is self-fertile and will set a crop without a pollenizer — it will also cross-pollinate many other sweet cherry varieties as a companion tree; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting; Stella ripens mid-season (late June to early July) producing large, dark red to nearly black fruits with good sweet flavor. Stella sweet cherry was bred by Dr. Karl Lapins at the Summerland Research Station in British Columbia, Canada, and released in 1968 — it became historically significant as the first widely available self-fertile sweet cherry variety, a characteristic that transformed home garden cherry growing by eliminating the requirement for two compatible cherry trees with overlapping bloom times. Before Stella, growing sweet cherries required careful selection of compatible pollinating pairs (cherry pollination compatibility is complex and variety-specific), which limited practical cherry growing to gardeners with space for at least two trees and the knowledge to select compatible varieties. Stella's self-fertility made sweet cherries accessible for single-tree planting in small gardens throughout its zone range. The fruits are large (similar to Bing in size), dark red to nearly black at full ripeness, with firm, juicy, sweet flesh and excellent flavor — somewhat less complex than Bing by some evaluations, but reliably good and productive. Stella also serves as a pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties, making it a valuable companion in mixed plantings where Bing or other varieties need cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sterling Hops
description: Sterling is an American aroma cultivar released by the USDA-ARS breeding program specifically to give home and craft brewers a hardier, more disease-resistant substitute for true Saaz and other noble European hops, while retaining a similar mild, spicy, herbal-floral character. It establishes and yields more reliably than the finicky noble landraces, making it a good choice for gardeners in cooler climates who still want authentic lager and pilsner aromatics. Give it full sun, moderate consistent moisture, and a sturdy trellis for its climbing bines. Harvest when cones are dry and fragrant, and dry promptly to preserve its delicate spice-floral aroma. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Sterling Muscadine (Self-Fertile Bronze Juice Muscadine)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Sterling is a self-fertile bronze muscadine released jointly by North Carolina State University and USDA-ARS, bred with juice production as the primary goal — the berries are consistent, productive, and well suited to pressing, though they are equally good eaten fresh. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety nearby, simplifying the planting for a home gardener who only has room for one plant. Like other muscadines it shrugs off Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European grapes difficult in the humid South, needing no regular spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster; a light dropcloth under the vine makes fallen ripe fruit easy to gather during peak harvest. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Steuben Grape (Cornell-Bred Spicy Blue Table Grape)
description: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, pruning heavily each winter with a cane-pruning system. Steuben was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is grown for its blue-black, slip-skin berries with a rich, spicy-sweet, almost wine-like flavor that many growers consider superior to Concord for fresh eating, though it also makes excellent juice and jelly. It is a reliable, productive vine that ripens in midseason and stores unusually well for a labrusca-type grape. As a high-chill northern grape, it is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters favor muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Stevens Cranberry
description: Stevens is a USDA-bred hybrid cranberry cultivar (a cross of Vaccinium macrocarpon selections McFarlin and Potter) that has become the standard commercial variety across North American cranberry-growing regions, prized for large, uniform, deep-red berries, vigorous upright vines, and consistently heavy yields that outperform most older cultivars and many wild bog selections. It requires the same strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), constant moisture, and sandy-peat substrate as other cranberries, mimicking the native bog habitat, and benefits from a 3-4 inch layer of coarse sand mulch to suppress weeds and maintain the ideal rooting surface. Vines take three to four years to establish a meaningful crop but then produce reliably for decades with minimal input beyond consistent moisture and acidic fertility. Harvest in fall once berries turn deep red and bounce when dropped; home growers typically hand-pick rather than using the wet-harvest flooding method of commercial operations. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Stevia
description: Sow seeds shallowly, just pressing them into moist seed-starting mix, as light aids germination; note that germination rates for stevia seed can be inconsistent. Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil after temperatures are reliably warm, and water consistently—stevia is sensitive to both drought and waterlogging. Pinch growing tips early to encourage a bushy form with more harvestable leaf area. Harvest leaves before the plant flowers, when glycoside content (sweetness) is at its peak; dry or use fresh. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Stevia / Sweet Leaf
description: Stevia rebaudiana is a tender perennial herb native to the subtropical highland borderlands of Paraguay and Brazil, where indigenous Guarani peoples have used its intensely sweet leaves for centuries as a sweetener and medicinal plant; the steviol glycosides in its leaves are 30-300 times sweeter than sucrose, making even a few fresh leaves a potent, calorie-free sweetening agent for teas, lemonades, and desserts. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date by surface-sowing onto moist, sterile seed-starting mix — seeds need light to germinate and must not be covered; germination is often erratic, and cuttings from established plants root readily and produce more uniform plants than seed-grown specimens. Transplant hardened seedlings into well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; stevia dislikes waterlogged conditions but benefits from consistent moisture and regular feeding during the growing season. Harvest leaves throughout summer by pinching branch tips to encourage bushiness; dry harvested leaves completely before crumbling them for storage as a concentrated sweetener, or use fresh leaves directly in beverages. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Stewart's Zeebest Okra
description: Sow directly into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods every 1–2 days at 3–4 inches, since this tall, heavy-yielding variety puts on pods quickly in summer heat and older pods turn woody fast. Stewart's Zeebest is a Louisiana heirloom okra, grown for generations by home gardeners in the Gulf South for its tall, vigorous plants and heavy, extended production of smooth, tender, dark green pods with excellent flavor and relatively low fiber even at a slightly larger picking size than typical spineless varieties. The tall habit (commonly 6–8 feet by late summer) makes it useful as a seasonal privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden in addition to its culinary value, and the plants shrug off the heat and humidity that stress many garden crops in July and August. A reliable, long-producing regional heirloom for Gulf South okra lovers, zone 5–11. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Stickless Wonder Yardlong Bean (Bush Asparagus Bean)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil; unlike nearly every other yardlong bean, Stickless Wonder grows as a compact, self-supporting bush rather than a climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and matures noticeably faster than pole-type long beans. Pods still reach an impressive 12-15 inches even without the extra growing time a vine gets, and they hold a good tender texture if picked young. Because the plants stay low and open, watch more closely for pods hiding under the foliage so none are missed and left to toughen. A light stake can still help keep top-heavy plants upright in windy Gulf Coast summer storms, even though the vines themselves need no support to climb. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Sticky Currant
description: Native to coniferous forest understories across the interior Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, this deciduous currant gets its common name from the sticky, gland-covered hairs coating its leaves and stems, which release a resinous fragrance when touched. Its cream to pale pink, tubular flowers are notably fragrant and attract early-season pollinators, and the resulting black berries are edible, if somewhat dry and seedy, and were historically eaten fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the region. It adapts well to the partial shade of a mixed conifer-hardwood planting and, once established, handles the dry summers typical of its native montane range better than many currants bred for garden fruit production. Prune out a portion of the oldest stems each winter to keep the shrub open and productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sticky Groundcherry (Prairie Groundcherry)
description: Direct sow or plant divisions into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Sticky groundcherry is a low, spreading native perennial of coastal dunes, sandy prairies, and disturbed sandy soils across the southeastern and Gulf Coastal Plain, its finely hairy, gently sticky foliage and stems giving the plant its common name. Small, nodding, pale yellow flowers with a darker throat appear from spring through fall, followed by round yellow fruit enclosed in a papery, lantern-like husk typical of the groundcherry group; the ripe fruit is edible once the husk dries and browns, with a mild, slightly tart flavor. It spreads steadily by underground rhizomes in loose, well-drained sandy soil, making it useful for stabilizing a sunny sandy bank or naturalized dune-edge planting, and it tolerates drought, heat, and poor soil with ease once established. Matures in 80–120 days from seed.

name: Sticky Sage (Jupiter's Distaff)
description: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; sticky sage is a woodland native of mountain forests across central and southern Europe and Asia Minor — one of the very few salvias genuinely adapted to shade, making it uniquely valuable as a large, flowering herb for shaded sites where virtually all other sages would fail. The large, hairy, somewhat sticky (glandular) leaves are strongly aromatic when rubbed, with an odor somewhat like oregano mixed with damp vegetation. In summer the tall stems produce whorled clusters of pale lemon-yellow to soft yellow flowers with a darker reddish-brown spot in the throat — smaller than many cultivated salvias but distinctive in their soft yellow color (unusual among salvias, which are most commonly blue, purple, or red). The sticky-hairy texture of the plant is responsible for the common name 'sticky sage' and makes the leaves adhesive to the touch. It self-sows modestly in appropriate shaded conditions to maintain small colonies. A rare example of a shade-adapted Salvia, outstanding combined with hostas, ferns, and woodland wildflowers in moist, cool, semi-shaded positions. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Stinging Nettle
description: Surface-sow onto moist, nitrogen-rich soil in a dedicated bed with underground barriers if possible, as nettles spread aggressively by rhizome. Always wear thick gloves and long sleeves when handling plants, as the hollow stinging hairs inject formic acid on contact. Harvest young growing tips in early spring before plants reach knee height, using them in soups, teas, and nutritive infusions — cooking or drying neutralizes the sting completely. Cut plants back to the ground two or three times per season to encourage fresh new growth throughout the year. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Stink Currant
description: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in fall along a shaded, consistently moist site such as a streambank planting or the north side of a building, mimicking the understory ravines this Pacific Northwest native calls home. The tall, upright canes carry long drooping racemes of small black currants that ripen through summer, with foliage that releases a distinctly musky, skunky aroma when brushed against or crushed. Berries are tart and best cooked into jams or sauces rather than eaten fresh, and the shrub also serves as valuable cover and forage for wildlife. Keep the root zone consistently damp, since it struggles in dry shade despite tolerating low light well. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Stinkwood Plum
description: Plant Gustavia superba in partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil; maintain consistent moisture and protect from temperatures below 40°F; the tree is a good candidate for large containers in warm greenhouses in cooler climates. Gustavia superba is in the Lecythidaceae family — the same family as the Brazil nut and Cannonball Tree — and shares the family trait of producing extraordinarily ornamental, large, spectacular flowers; in Gustavia superba, the flowers can reach 10–12 inches across, with broad white to pink petals and a dramatic ring of hundreds of pink stamens forming a flower of breathtaking beauty. The common name 'Stinkwood' refers to the strong, pungent scent of the cut wood; the fruit name 'membrillo' (Spanish for quince) describes the pumpkin-shaped, brownish fruits. The orange-yellow, fibrous, mango-flavored flesh surrounding the large seeds is eaten locally in Colombia and Panama by both people and wildlife; it is not widely commercialized. The tree is exceptionally ornamental at every stage and stage-of-growth — its unusual, club-shaped leaves, spectacular flowers, and ornate fruits make it one of the most showstopping specimens for tropical garden collections. Rarely seen in cultivation outside botanical gardens and specialist collectors in zone 10–12. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Stockbridge Arrow Rhubarb
description: Stockbridge Arrow is a modern British-bred maincrop rhubarb selected for long, straight, uniformly deep-red stalks and strong disease resistance, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It holds its color and firm texture well into midsummer rather than fading to green like many older varieties, which makes it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. Vigorous, disease-resistant crowns establish quickly and produce heavy yields once mature. Divide congested clumps every four to six years in dormancy to keep stalk quality high. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Stockton Red Onion (California Heirloom Red Storage Onion)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and water evenly through the growing season. Stockton Red is an old California heirloom onion, named for the San Joaquin Valley growing district around Stockton, producing flattened, deep-red-skinned bulbs with pink-tinged white flesh and a flavor milder than many storage reds, making it good for both fresh eating and cooking. It is an intermediate-day type with somewhat more latitude flexibility than strict long-day heirlooms, and it stores respectably for a red onion when properly cured. Taper off watering once the tops begin to yellow and topple, then pull the bulbs, cure in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks, and store in a cool, dry spot out of direct light to preserve color and firmness. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Stokes Purple Sweet Potato (Deep Purple Ultra-High Anthocyanin)
description: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil after soil warms above 65°F; Stokes Purple needs its full 110–125 days to develop; harvest after first frost threat in cooler climates. Stokes Purple was developed by Stokes Tropicals nursery in Lafayette, Louisiana from crosses involving Asian purple-flesh sweet potato types and selected specifically for American growing conditions and maximum anthocyanin content; the resulting variety has skin ranging from deep purple to nearly black and flesh that is uniformly rich purple-violet throughout — the highest level of anthocyanin pigments of any readily available sweet potato cultivar, higher per serving than blueberries or Concord grapes. The flavor is less sweet and more starchy than orange-flesh types, with an earthy, wine-like complexity and dense texture suited to roasting, savory preparations, smoothies, and applications where the dramatic color matters most. The vivid purple holds reasonably well through cooking, making dishes visually spectacular. Now grown commercially in California and Hawaii; available in health food stores and some major grocery chains. Matures in 110–125 days from transplant.

name: Stone Mountain Mint
description: Grow in shallow, mineral, sharply drained soil over rock in full sun to light shade, mimicking the granite outcrops and mafic glades of Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Tennessee where this rare mountain mint survives in scattered small populations. The purple-spotted summer flower clusters, like those of its more common relatives, are exceptionally attractive to a wide range of specialist and generalist native bees. Because natural populations are sparse and vulnerable, gardeners in its native range who succeed with it are contributing a meaningful conservation planting rather than simply another mint for the border. Avoid fertile, water-retentive soils, which favor competitors it cannot tolerate in the wild. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Stone Mountain Watermelon
description: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Stone Mountain is a classic early 20th-century Southern heirloom watermelon, grown for generations across the South for its large, oblong, dark green fruit and exceptionally sweet, deep red, fine-grained flesh with relatively small seed count for an old-time variety. The vigorous vines are productive and well adapted to the long, hot growing season of the Gulf South, and the tough rind travels and stores reasonably well for a heritage variety, a trait that made it a popular market melon in the era before modern shipping cultivars took over. Its rich, old-fashioned flavor and reliable performance in southern heat and humidity have kept it a favorite among heirloom gardeners who want the taste of a bygone-era watermelon, zone 4–11. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Stone Pine (Italian Stone Pine)
description: Stone pine is the classic Mediterranean umbrella-form pine grown for the large, richly flavored pine nuts (pignoli) used in pesto, pastries, and Middle Eastern cuisine; it is monoecious, self-fertile, and pollen-heavy — individual trees produce both male and female cones. Cones take three years to mature from pollination to seed release, so a productive tree has three overlapping cone crops at any given time. Harvest brown, closed cones by hand or after they fall naturally in late autumn, then sun-dry or gently heat them until the scales open and release the papery-shelled nuts inside. The tree thrives in sandy, well-drained, alkaline to acidic soil and is extremely drought-tolerant once the taproot is established. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Stone Tomato (Livingston's 1889 Heirloom Canning Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking the vigorous vines. Introduced by Livingston Seed Company in 1889 from a market grower's field near Grandville, Ohio, Stone produces dense, heavy, 6-8 ounce red fruit with an old-fashioned tangy acidity that made it a favorite for canning, juice, catsup, and chili sauce in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name references the notable density and weight of its fruit compared to other varieties of the period, and the plants show better foliage disease resistance than many contemporaries. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Stonehead Cabbage (AAS-Winning Compact Early Green Cabbage)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil. Stonehead is a 1969 All-America Selections-winning hybrid cabbage that earned recognition for combining early maturity with compact plant size — producing well-formed, 3–5 lb solid round heads on plants that occupy roughly half the space of standard cabbage types. The 'stone' in the name refers to the rock-solid firmness of the tightly packed, dense heads — when thumped, a properly matured Stonehead sounds and feels like a stone ball. The compact habit (spread of 12–15 inches vs. the 18–24 inches of standard types) at 12-inch spacing allows 25–30% more plants per row, making Stonehead one of the most space-efficient cabbage varieties for home gardens. The heads are round, attractively formed, medium blue-green with smooth skin (not savoy-type), and crack-resistant — holding in the garden for an extended period after reaching maturity without splitting. The mild, tender cabbage flavor is excellent raw in coleslaw, fermented as sauerkraut, or cooked; the dense texture holds up well in both applications. Stonehead remains one of the most widely recommended cabbage varieties in the United States more than 55 years after its AAS recognition. Matures in 67–75 days from transplant.

name: Stoneroot / Horse Balm
description: Sow seed in fall into deeply amended, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees where the site remains consistently moist but not waterlogged. Cover seed lightly with sifted leaf mold and allow the winter chill to stratify the seed naturally before spring germination. Stoneroot grows large with age and benefits from generous spacing so that its broad, lemon-scented leaves can spread without crowding neighboring plants. Once established, it is a long-lived woodland fixture that needs little care beyond maintaining soil moisture and a mulch of decomposing leaves. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Storage No. 4 Cabbage (Danish Long-Keeper)
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, timing the crop to mature in the cooler days of fall. Storage No. 4 is a Danish-type cabbage bred above all for keeping quality, forming dense, hard, pale green heads that resist splitting in the field and hold their crispness for months in cold, humid storage such as a root cellar. Its heads are somewhat smaller and firmer than fresh-market types, a trait that directly supports its long shelf life. Harvest before hard freezes settle in and store whole heads with roots trimmed for the longest keeping. Matures in 95–105 days from transplant.

name: Stover Grape (Early Self-Fertile University of Florida Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Stover was released by the University of Florida in 1968 and remains a standard early-ripening bunch grape for the Deep South, producing self-fertile crops of white-to-green, tart-to-sweet fruit good for table use, juice, and wine, ripening well ahead of many other bunch grape cultivars. Its early season lets growers harvest before the peak of summer disease and pest pressure builds. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and reduce fungal disease risk in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Stowell's Evergreen Corn (Classic White Heirloom Late Sweet Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize well at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Stowell's Evergreen is one of the oldest and most important heirloom sweet corn varieties in American gardening tradition — a white su (standard sugary) corn introduced before 1848 by Nathan N. Stowell of Burlington, New Jersey, who reportedly sold the variety for $4 (a substantial sum) before it was propagated and spread widely by seed companies. The variety dominated American sweet corn production and home gardens throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, remaining one of the most popular sweet corn varieties in America for over 100 years before hybrid varieties began displacing open-pollinated types in the mid-20th century. The 'Evergreen' in the name refers to the variety's characteristic long harvest window in the milk stage — the kernels remain tender and edible for longer than most corn before converting sugar to starch, a property especially valuable before refrigeration when fresh corn had to be consumed quickly. Stowell's Evergreen produces large (8–9 inch) ears with 14–20 rows of pure white kernels that are tender, sweet (for an su type), and deeply flavored with the rich, starchy-sweet character of traditional open-pollinated corn that many old-timers consider superior to modern hybrids for preserving, canning, and creamed corn preparations. An irreplaceable heirloom variety with a direct connection to the entire American sweet corn tradition. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Stowell's Evergreen Sweet Corn
description: Sow 1–2 inches deep in blocks of at least 3–4 rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stowell's Evergreen was introduced in 1848 by Nathan Newman Stowell, originally a hybrid between a white field corn and an early sweet type. It was the dominant home garden sweet corn throughout the latter half of the 19th century and remained popular well into the 20th. The tall (7–8 feet) plants produce 8–9 inch ears with white kernels in 16–20 rows, each kernel deep and richly flavored with classic sweet corn taste. The name refers to an actual characteristic: unlike many older sweet corns where the milky eating stage lasts only a few days, Stowell's Evergreen holds at milk stage for 1–2 weeks — a valuable trait before refrigeration and the dominant reason for its century-long popularity. The tall stalks require some wind protection in exposed sites. An important heirloom for corn breeding and a satisfying producer for gardeners who prioritize old-fashioned flavor and the ability to harvest over an extended window. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Straight Eight Cucumber
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines up a trellis for cleaner fruits or let sprawl in ample space. Straight Eight won the All-America Selections Gold Medal in 1935 and for decades became the definitive American garden cucumber — named for its uniform, straight, exactly 8-inch, dark green fruits with rounded tips, blunt blossom ends, thin skin, crisp flesh, and reliable productivity. It remained the standard garden slicing cucumber through the mid-twentieth century and was the one cucumber every American seed company carried. While modern hybrids have surpassed it in disease resistance and uniformity, Straight Eight remains a beloved heirloom for gardeners who want a reliable, seed-saveable, classic slicer. Produces well in warm conditions; good for Gulf Coast spring and fall production. Matures in 57–66 days from seed.

name: Straight Eight Cucumber
description: Sow Straight Eight seeds about 1 inch deep once soil temperatures reach at least 70F, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart or in hills of three to four seeds. This heirloom slicer yields uniform, smooth 6 to 8 inch dark green fruits with crisp, tender flesh. Provide a trellis to keep vines tidy and fruit straight, and water consistently to avoid bitterness. Harvest cucumbers young and often to keep the vines producing through summer. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Straightneck Squash
description: Plant seeds 1 inch deep in warm, loose, well-drained soil enriched with aged compost. Thin to one plant per hill and keep the bed consistently moist throughout the growing season. Monitor frequently for squash vine borers and squash bugs, which are the most serious pests. Harvest fruits at 6–8 inches long while the skin is still soft and pale yellow for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 48–65 days from seed.

name: Straightneck Summer Squash
description: Plant Straightneck seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to one strong plant every 24 to 36 inches on a bushy, space-saving habit. This early yellow summer squash produces smooth, tapered fruits with tender skin and mild sweetness. Harvest fruits at 6 to 8 inches long while young for the best texture, picking frequently to keep new squash forming. Keep soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs and vine borers during warm spells. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Strata Hops
description: Strata is a public cultivar released by Oregon State University's hop breeding program, known for a pungent, resinous aroma layered with notes of blackberry and passionfruit that has made it a favorite in hazy and West Coast-style IPAs. The bine shows good vigor and above-average disease tolerance compared with many aroma cultivars, making it a reasonably forgiving choice for home growers. It performs best in full sun on a tall, sturdy trellis with rich, well-drained soil. Because its aroma compounds are especially potent, brewers and home growers alike tend to use it in smaller quantities than older varieties. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry (June-Bearing)
description: Plant bare-root crowns in spring with the crown at soil level, setting runners into a matted-row system 12–18 in apart. Pinch all blossoms the first year to build root vigor; harvest begins the following June when berries are uniformly red and pull easily from the stem. Renovate beds immediately after harvest by mowing foliage to 3–4 in and thinning plants to 4–6 per square foot. Mulch crowns with straw in fall in zones 4 and colder. Matures in 365–425 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Ground Cherry
description: Start Strawberry Ground Cherry seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun after frost; water regularly; fruits are ready when husks turn tan and papery and fruits drop to the ground — collect daily. Physalis pruinosa is the dwarf cousin of the taller Cape Gooseberry and common Ground Cherry (P. peruviana, P. heterophylla), distinguished by its compact, sprawling habit and intensely sweet, strawberry-vanilla flavored fruits inside papery husks. The plant is more compact than other groundcherries, topping out at 1–2 feet, making it easier to manage in small gardens and containers. Like all groundcherries, the ripe fruits naturally drop from the plant when fully ripe — the papery husk keeps them clean and extends shelf life for weeks at room temperature. The flavor is distinctly different from tomato or tomatillo: sweet, fruity, and aromatic, reminiscent of strawberry jam with vanilla undertones. Used fresh in fruit salads, made into preserves and pie filling, or dried like raisins. Extremely productive and easy to grow, self-seeding reliably in warm gardens once established. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Guava
description: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava (cattley guava, cherry guava, purple guava) is a Brazilian evergreen small tree or large shrub that produces small, round, dark-red to burgundy-purple fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a distinctive strawberry-guava flavor — sweet, aromatic, and mildly acidic — that are excellent eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, juice, and desserts, or dried. The fruits ripen from late summer through fall and fall when fully ripe, making harvest simple. The plant is one of the most attractive year-round fruiting shrubs for zone 9–11, with smooth, mottled, tan and brown peeling bark, glossy, thick, oval, dark-green leaves, and small, white, fragrant guava flowers that precede the fruit. Hardy to approximately 22°F, it is more cold-tolerant than tropical guava (Psidium guajava). However, strawberry guava is listed as a highly invasive species in Hawaii and parts of Florida, where it spreads rapidly in natural areas, and should not be planted near natural habitats in those regions. In drier Gulf Coast areas it is better behaved and is a productive, attractive, low-maintenance small fruit tree. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Guava (Cattley Guava)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava is a highly productive and flavorful small fruit tree or large shrub that produces abundant crops of 1-inch round fruits in red (the classic form) or yellow (Psidium cattleyanum var. lucidum, lemon guava) with an intensely sweet, slightly strawberry-like flavor — arguably the finest-flavored guava species, often preferred over the larger common guava by people who taste it. The glossy, dark-green evergreen leaves and smooth, mottled reddish-brown bark provide year-round ornamental value. In zone 9 it may suffer light frost damage but typically recovers well. It is extremely drought, heat, and poor-soil tolerant once established and produces fruit with minimal care. Important note: strawberry guava is listed as one of the world's 100 worst invasive species in subtropical humid regions — do not plant where it can escape to natural areas in Hawaii, Florida, and similar climates. In drier Gulf Coast locations it is less problematic. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Hedgehog Cactus (Texas Pitaya)
description: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; Texas pitaya is a robust, clump-forming hedgehog cactus native to the Chihuahuan Desert and South Texas brushlands, forming large sprawling mounds of thick, blue-green stems that can eventually spread several feet across. Large magenta-purple flowers open in mid-spring, followed by egg-sized, spiny red fruit that ripens in early summer and, once the spines are removed, has a sweet flavor reminiscent of strawberries — long harvested by regional residents as a wild treat, giving rise to the Spanish common name pitaya. It is more cold-hardy than many South Texas cacti and tolerates the milder winters of zones 7 through 10 as long as drainage is excellent, making it a good dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting choice for a xeriscape or rock garden planting. Matures in 730–1460 days from seed.

name: Strawberry Loquat (Tangy Bright-Flavored Loquat)
description: Strawberry loquat takes its name from a distinctive bright, tangy-sweet flavor reminiscent of the namesake fruit, setting it apart from milder cultivars. Grow in full sun on well-drained, organically rich soil, and water regularly during fruit development to maximize juiciness and reduce fruit-splitting. The orange-fleshed fruit ripens in a compact cluster in late winter to early spring; harvest by clipping whole clusters or picking individual fruits as they fully color, since loquats do not sweeten further after picking. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain an open canopy that promotes air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Mint (Fruity Strawberry-Scented Small-Leaf Mint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Strawberry Mint bears small, fine-textured leaves with a distinctly fruity strawberry aroma layered over a mild mint base, a fun, kid-friendly fragrance that makes it a popular garnish for desserts, fruit salads, and summer drinks. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Popcorn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — corn is a heavy feeder requiring nitrogen-rich soil and consistent moisture during ear development; Strawberry Popcorn is an heirloom ornamental and edible popcorn variety producing tiny, round, deep burgundy-crimson ears that are remarkably realistic miniature strawberry look-alikes — the round, plump shape and rich dark red color create an almost uncanny resemblance to a strawberry when the ear is viewed with fresh eyes. The small ears (2–3 inches long) are produced one to two per stalk on compact (4–5 foot) plants, making Strawberry Popcorn both a space-efficient popcorn crop and one of the most attractive ornamental corn varieties for fall decoration. The dark red kernels pop into white popcorn — the kernel color disappears in the heat of popping — producing popcorn with the same light, airy, slightly sweet flavor as standard popcorn. The ornamental appeal (dried ears make excellent fall table decorations, wreaths, and displays) combined with the culinary value (genuinely edible popcorn) makes Strawberry Popcorn one of the best dual-purpose plants for the home garden, particularly appealing to children who delight in both the process of growing them and the surprise of popping the dramatic red kernels into white popcorn. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Strawberry Popcorn
description: Sow Strawberry Popcorn seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good wind pollination. This dwarf heirloom grows compact 3 to 4 foot stalks bearing small, cone-shaped ears packed with jewel-toned deep red kernels. Let the ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure them further indoors before shelling for popping or ornamental use. Keep it isolated from other corn types to preserve its distinctive color and popping quality. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Strawberry Popcorn Corn
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows to ensure good pollination. Each compact four-foot stalk produces two or more ruby-red, strawberry-shaped ears two to three inches long. The ornamental foliage and ears look striking at the back of a border as well as in the vegetable patch. Let the ears dry fully on the stalk, then harvest and cure the kernels before popping. Keep this popcorn separated from other corn types to avoid cross-pollination. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Strawberry Spinach
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Strawberry Spinach (also called strawberry goosefoot or blite) is a unique dual-purpose edible plant that provides both tender, spinach-like young leaves and bright red, strawberry-resembling berries on the same plant — the plant is grown first for its spring leaf harvest (mild, slightly earthy flavor used raw in salads or cooked like spinach) and then for the clusters of small, fleshy, bright red fruits that develop up the stem in a pattern that closely resembles a miniature strawberry. The berries are edible, mild, and slightly sweet but lack the intense flavor of true strawberries — they are used as a colorful garnish, in fruit salads, and as an ornamental edible curiosity. The plant is a cool-season annual from North America and Europe that tolerates partial shade better than most garden vegetables, making it useful for growing in dappled light under trees or in partly shaded beds. Strawberry Spinach is a reliable self-seeder that naturalizes easily in suitable conditions, providing a low-maintenance perennial food source once established. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Strawberry Tree (Killarney Strawberry Tree)
description: Plant in poor, very well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the strawberry tree is a beautiful, slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen that produces clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers in fall and winter simultaneously with the ripening of the previous year's strawberry-like red and orange fruits — a unique garden spectacle of flowers and ripe fruit coexisting on the tree. The rough-textured red fruits are edible but taste nothing like a strawberry: they are mealy, mildly sweet, with a somewhat gritty texture, best used for jams, jellies, and wine rather than eating fresh (the name refers only to their appearance). The bark is a beautiful cinnamon red and exfoliating. The dwarf cultivar 'Compacta' stays 5–6 feet; 'Elfin King' is an ultra-compact form. Excellent drought-tolerant, deer-resistant evergreen for zone 7–10. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Strawberry Watermelon
description: Strawberry Watermelon was selected from an older Florida heirloom by grower Walt Childs and introduced by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange in 1989, making it a relatively recent release built on genetics already adapted to hot, humid Southern conditions. The long, dark green striped fruits reach 15-25 pounds when well fed and watered, with vivid strawberry-red flesh, white seeds, and very good disease resistance for an heirloom watermelon. It shows good tolerance of common Southern disease pressure compared to many older watermelon heirlooms, making it a practical choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Give vines ample room to run and consistent moisture while fruit is sizing for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 80–89 days from seed.

name: Strike Bush Bean (Early Disease-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Strike is an early, disease-resistant bush snap bean prized for a long, sustained harvest window rather than a short, concentrated flush of pods like many bush varieties. It holds up well to summer heat, continuing to set new pods over an extended period when many other bush beans slow down. Pods are straight, tender, and best picked young before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall. Harvest every couple of days to encourage continued flowering, and succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for an even longer supply of fresh beans. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Striped German Tomato (Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Striped German is a classic bicolor beefsteak heirloom — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped, old-fashioned beefsteak type with golden-yellow skin striped and mottled with red, creating a vibrant, contrasting bicolor appearance on the exterior. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this variety: red and yellow sectors arranged in alternating patterns that create an artistic cross-section pattern — a visually striking effect that makes Striped German outstanding for fresh sliced presentations. The flavor is exceptional — sweet, rich, low-acid, and complex in the tradition of old German beefsteak heirlooms. Striped German is believed to have originated in Appalachia from German immigrant seed stock and has been maintained by Appalachian seed savers for generations before entering the commercial heirloom seed trade. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, Striped German produces best in the spring season in zone 9 (March–June) and can be challenging to grow in the high summer heat that damages large fruit quality. The combination of visual beauty, excellent flavor, and historical significance makes Striped German one of the most rewarding heirlooms for zone 9 spring production. Matures in 78–88 days from transplant.

name: Stripetti Squash (Striped Spaghetti-Delicata Cross)
description: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines moderate room to spread. Stripetti combines the stringy, noodle-like flesh texture of spaghetti squash with the sweeter, richer flavor of delicata, and the cream skin striped in dark green makes it easy to identify at harvest or on a market table. The strands separate cleanly when the cooked flesh is scraped with a fork, but taste noticeably sweeter and less bland than standard spaghetti squash, appealing to cooks who want the low-carbohydrate pasta substitute without sacrificing flavor. Pick once stripes darken and the rind resists denting, and use within a couple of months since it does not store as long as full-season winter squash. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Stuart Pecan
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stuart is an old heirloom pecan variety originating in the Gulf South before the Civil War and one of the most historically important named pecans — it was among the first varieties to be systematically propagated by grafting and was widely planted throughout the Southeast from the 1880s through mid-20th century. Nuts are very large (45–50 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage, rich flavor, and attractive appearance that made Stuart the standard commercial variety for much of the 20th century. Though partially supplanted by more scab-resistant modern varieties in humid commercial orchards, Stuart remains extremely popular for home planting in zone 7–9 because of its large, beautiful nuts, adaptability to a wide range of soils, and long productive lifespan — well-established Stuart trees may continue producing heavily for 100+ years. The principal weakness is moderate scab susceptibility in very wet years; in most zone 9 home orchards, this is manageable without spraying. An excellent choice for the Gulf Coast gardener who wants large, flavorful nuts from a landscape tree. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Stubby Okra (Compact Heirloom with Short Stumpy Pods)
description: Stubby is a shorter heirloom okra, staying noticeably more compact than rangy Southern types while still producing steadily through summer heat. Its blunt, stumpy pods should be picked young, around two to three inches, since the thick shape can turn fibrous quickly once past prime size. The lower profile makes this variety easier to manage in smaller plots or where wind exposure would otherwise call for staking taller okra. Keep pods picked frequently to prevent the compact plant from shutting down seed-pod production early. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Student Parsnip
description: Bred in England in the mid-1800s through deliberate selection from wild parsnip stock, Student was one of the first named parsnip cultivars developed with a scientific breeding approach rather than simple farm selection. It produces smooth-skinned, creamy white roots with strong vigor and reliable germination for a crop notorious for erratic sprouting. Sow fresh seed shallowly as early as the soil can be worked, and leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert stored starches to sugar and sweeten the harvest considerably. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Stump of the World Tomato
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stump of the World is a Russian heirloom tomato preserved by Seed Savers Exchange, producing abundant clusters of small to medium (2–3 ounce) round to slightly oval red fruits with a rich, sweet-tart old-fashioned tomato flavor. The prolific, indeterminate vines are particularly valued for their consistent production even during hot, humid periods when many larger-fruited heirlooms stop setting — a significant advantage in zone 9 where the growing season is compressed and productivity through heat stress is paramount. The firm-skinned fruits hold well on the vine and in storage longer than thin-skinned heirlooms, and their medium size makes them versatile for fresh eating, salads, and saucing where small cherry tomatoes are too small and large beefsteaks are too large for single-use. The Russian origin suggests cold-climate breeding priorities — early maturity and prolific production — that translate to better zone 9 heat performance than many European heirloom varieties. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Stupice Tomato (Czech Early Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after danger of frost passes; Stupice is unusually tolerant of cold nighttime temperatures and can be transplanted somewhat earlier than standard heat-loving varieties. Stupice (pronounced 'STOO-peet-seh') originates from the village of Stupice in what is now the Czech Republic and was brought to the Seed Savers Exchange network by gardener Dr. Carolyn Male in the early 1990s, where it rapidly became one of the most popular heirloom tomatoes in cold-climate gardens of the Pacific Northwest, Canada, and Northern states. It is a potato-leaved, indeterminate variety producing clusters of small to medium (2–4 oz), round, uniformly deep red fruits — not large by beefsteak standards, but remarkable for their combination of earliness (ripening weeks before most other varieties) and rich, full-flavored, sweet-tart tomato character that is often absent in other very-early varieties. The ability to set fruit in cool temperatures makes Stupice the first choice for short-season gardeners in coastal climates and high altitudes; it also makes an excellent spring variety for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens planted early in the season. Matures in 52–65 days from transplant.

name: Sturmer Pippin Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sturmer Pippin needs a long, warm growing season to ripen and store well, and performs best where autumns stay mild. Bred in Suffolk, England in the early nineteenth century from a Ribston Pippin and Nonpareil cross, it bears firm, greenish-yellow apples with dense, crisp, sharply flavored flesh that ripens very late in the season and keeps exceptionally well, sometimes into late winter or early spring under good storage conditions, making it one of the longest-keeping traditional apples grown. Its late ripening and long storage life made it especially popular in Southern Hemisphere growing regions like Australia and New Zealand, where the extended warm autumn allows the fruit to mature fully; in cooler, shorter-season climates it can struggle to ripen well before frost. Harvest as late in fall as the season allows, letting the fruit hang as long as possible, and store cool for a remarkably long keeping period. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sturon Onion
description: Sturon is one of the most widely planted Dutch maincrop onion cultivars, grown from sets for its round, golden-brown-skinned bulbs and dependably heavy yields. Plant sets shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil and firm the soil around them so birds cannot pull the sets loose, then keep the row weed-free while bulbs size up over summer. It is valued as a strong keeper, with well-cured bulbs commonly holding firm in storage for several months past harvest. Bend or wait for tops to fall over naturally before lifting, then dry the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot before trimming and storing. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Stuttgarter Giant Onion (Stuttgarter Riesen)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant sets directly in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost at 2–4 inches apart; for seed-grown bulbs, thin to 4–6 inches in rows 12–18 inches apart. Stuttgarter Riesen (literally 'Stuttgart Giant') is a traditional German heirloom onion named for Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg and widely grown throughout Central Europe as the standard yellow storage onion; it is recognized by its distinctive flattened or slightly disc-shaped globe form (wider than tall), straw-yellow to golden-brown thin papery skin, and crisp white flesh with a mild-sweet flavor that is less pungent than many other yellow storage types. The relatively flat shape and thin skin were historically valued because the flatter bulbs cured and dried quickly without molding, and the thin skin peeled easily — practical advantages that made Stuttgarter both the preferred home-garden and commercial variety. Now widely grown from sets (small bulblets sold by the bag) as well as from seed; set-planted Stuttgarter is often the earliest onion to mature in northern gardens. Exceptional storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 6–9 months in cool, dry conditions. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: Subpeltata Passionflower (Fragrant White Naturalized Passion Vine)
description: Plant rooted cuttings or seed-grown transplants after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade, giving this vigorous South American vine a trellis, fence, or arbor to climb. Passiflora subpeltata bears intensely fragrant, pure white flowers with a fine corona banded in white and pale violet, followed by small, egg-shaped green fruits that ripen to pale yellow and are edible but mild and seedy rather than richly flavored. Naturalized throughout much of the Gulf South and other warm-temperate regions worldwide, it self-sows readily where happy and can spread beyond where it's wanted, so site it where volunteer seedlings are welcome or deadhead spent flowers to limit spread. Like other Passiflora species it serves as a larval host for Gulf fritillary and other heliconian butterflies, and its roots survive brief winter freezes into zone 8 to resprout vigorously each spring. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Success Pecan (Early 20th-Century Heirloom Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Success was among the important early named pecan cultivars that helped establish the commercial pecan industry in the South, valued in its day for good nut size and quality. It has largely been replaced in modern commercial orchards by more disease-resistant, higher-yielding cultivars, since it is fairly susceptible to pecan scab and other diseases common in humid climates, but it remains of historical interest and is still found in older plantings and heirloom nut collections. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Success PM Squash (Powdery Mildew-Resistant Yellow Squash)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Success PM is a yellow summer squash bred to carry meaningful resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that coats squash leaves in a white, dusty film and typically shuts down production in a Gulf South garden by midsummer, well before the season would otherwise end. Because the foliage stays healthier and photosynthesizing longer, plants tend to keep setting good-quality fruit later into the summer than mildew-susceptible varieties. Harvest fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized if missed for even a couple of days. Matures in 48–55 days from seed.

name: Success Saskatoon Serviceberry (Historic Early-Ripening Western Serviceberry)
description: Success is one of the oldest named saskatoon cultivars still grown today, selected generations ago from wild Amelanchier alnifolia stands on the Canadian prairies for its heavy, reliable cropping rather than for exceptional berry size. Clusters of white flowers open in early spring on multi-stemmed, upright shrubs, followed by sweet, mild, purple-blue berries that ripen several days to two weeks earlier than newer cultivars like Northline or Parkhill, making it useful for spreading out a harvest window. Fruit is smaller than modern selections but produced in heavy quantity, and the plant suckers readily to form a productive thicket over time. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it is exceptionally cold-hardy and requires little care beyond periodic removal of old canes to keep new, more fruitful wood coming. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sucrine du Berry Squash
description: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars. Originating in the Berry region of central France, this squash produces flattened, deep-orange, lightly ribbed fruit with notably dense, dry, sweet flesh reminiscent of chestnuts, making it a favorite for soups and roasting. It shares ancestry with Musquée de Provence but stays smaller and matures faster, fitting gardens with shorter seasons. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to harden the rind and intensify flavor before storing. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Sucrine Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Sucrine is a French mini-romaine lettuce producing compact, upright, 4–5 inch heads with thick, crunchy, deeply green leaves and an exceptional sweetness that is apparent even in the name — 'sucrine' derives from the French 'sucre' (sugar). It is considered by many French market gardeners to have the best flavor of any small lettuce, combining the crunch and structure of romaine with a delicate sweetness entirely absent from full-sized romaine varieties. The small, compact heads are the right size for a single salad portion, and the thick leaves hold up to dressings without wilting — ideal for individual Caesar salads and composed appetizer plates. Sucrine is the standard small romaine type in French markets and has become highly popular in North American specialty food markets and upscale restaurants. The tight, compact head formation and small size allow close spacing (6–8 inches) that maximizes production from small garden spaces. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Sudachi (Japanese Sour Citrus)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sudachi is self-fruitful and produces tiny, green fruits that are harvested before they ripen to yellow for the most aromatic juice. Sudachi (Citrus sudachi) is a small, intensely aromatic souring citrus virtually unknown outside Japan but recently gaining attention in American culinary circles for its exceptional flavor; native and endemic to Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku island (which produces approximately 98% of Japan's sudachi), the small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round, green fruits are always used before they ripen to yellow when their intense, fragrant juice and zest are at peak. The flavor is tart, fragrant, and floral with a complexity and intensity that surpasses lime or lemon — used by Japanese chefs exclusively for its aromatic quality as a garnish squeeze over grilled fish, mushrooms, soba noodles, and in ponzu sauce alternatives. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Japan; growing your own is the only way to access fresh sudachi in the US. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.
