name: Suebelle White Sapote (Self-Fruitful Compact White Sapote)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm, wind-sheltered spot since young trees are more cold-sensitive than mature specimens. Suebelle stays more compact than seedling white sapote trees, generally topping out around 15 to 20 feet, and it is self-fruitful so a single tree can set a full crop without a pollinator. The smooth green-to-yellow fruit has a custardy, banana-and-pear flavor prized by growers from the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast into Central Florida, and established trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F that would seriously injure many other subtropical fruits. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Suffolk Red Grape (Seedless Red Table Grape)
description: Bred at the Geneva, New York experiment station, Suffolk Red is one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes suited to cold-winter gardens, producing medium clusters of sweet, crisp, reddish berries. Its early ripening makes it a reliable choice where the growing season is too short for European seedless varieties to mature. The vine is moderately vigorous and productive, and cluster thinning helps maintain consistent berry size across the crop. It tolerates winter cold well and is a popular choice for northern home vineyards wanting seedless fruit. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Ann Dwarf Pea
description: Direct sow Sugar Ann seeds 1 inch deep and 2 to 3 inches apart as soon as the soil is workable in spring. This early, compact snap pea forms short 24 to 30 inch vines that need little or no support, making it ideal for containers and small beds. Harvest the plump, sweet pods when they fill out but are still crisp, picking regularly to prolong production. Provide steady moisture and enjoy the harvest before summer heat shuts the plants down. Matures in 52–62 days from seed.

name: Sugar Ann Snap Pea
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Sugar Ann is the first snap pea cultivar to achieve a compact, self-supporting, bush habit — it was awarded the All-America Selections award in 1984 for this breakthrough characteristic, which made snap pea growing practical for small gardens and container growing where the typical 4–6 foot Sugar Snap vines require substantial trellis infrastructure. The pods are genuine snap peas (edible pod, no strings in the eating-ripe stage) with sweet, crunchy, crisp pod walls and rounded, sweet peas inside — the classic snap pea flavor that has made snap peas one of the most popular garden vegetables since their introduction in the late 1970s. At only 52–56 days to maturity, Sugar Ann is also the fastest-maturing of the main snap pea varieties, providing an early crop before hot weather ends the pea season. In zone 9 the bush habit and fast maturity make Sugar Ann particularly valuable for the short cool-season window available. Matures in 52–56 days from seed.

name: Sugar Apple (Sweetsop)
description: Sugar apple is a semi-deciduous small tree that drops leaves during the dry season — a natural dormancy that can be encouraged in cultivation by reducing water in late autumn to trigger uniform bloom flush in spring. Like other Annona species, the flowers are bisexual but dichogamous; hand-pollinate using a soft brush to transfer pollen from male-stage flowers (petals separating but pollen not yet shed) to female-stage flowers (stigma sticky and receptive). Fruit is composed of loosely packed segments that separate when ripe; harvest when skin segments begin to separate and the fruit yields to light pressure. Trees are fast-growing and benefit from annual pruning after fruit set to maintain canopy density and manageable size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Baby Watermelon
description: This compact icebox watermelon produces round 8 to 10 pound fruit with sweet red flesh on shorter vines. Start seed indoors or direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm, and use black mulch in cool regions. Water steadily during vine growth and fruit set, then ease off as melons ripen to intensify sweetness. Signs of ripeness include a yellowing ground spot and a dried tendril nearest the fruit. Because it matures relatively quickly, it succeeds even where summers are short. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Baby Watermelon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral sandy or loamy soil — watermelons require deep, loose, well-drained soil and abundant heat to develop properly; Sugar Baby is the classic icebox watermelon variety — the small, round, dark-green fruits (7–10 pounds) that fit neatly into a home refrigerator, in contrast to the large oblong types (20–30+ pounds) traditional in Southern watermelon culture. The small fruit size makes Sugar Baby the most practical watermelon for small family gardens where a single large watermelon represents more than could be consumed before spoiling. The bright red, crisp, very sweet flesh with few seeds has made Sugar Baby one of the most popular home garden watermelons for decades — reliable, productive, and delivering the classic watermelon experience in a manageable size. As a true tropical fruit, watermelon is perfectly suited to zone 9's long, hot summers — in fact, the consistent 90°F+ temperatures of June through August produce the sweetest, most flavorful watermelons possible, as the combination of intense sun and heat maximizes sugar development in the fruit. Matures in 73–80 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Beet
description: Sow sugar beet seeds about half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 4 to 8 inches apart to give the large roots room to swell. This heirloom biennial forms sucrose-rich white roots up to 12 inches long with leafy tops nearly two feet tall. Keep the soil loose, evenly moist, and free of competition so the roots grow smooth and full. Harvest in late fall before hard freezes for home sugar extraction, livestock feed, or soil improvement. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Sugar Belle Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Honeybell-Type Mandarin)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; Sugar Belle is a University of Florida-bred mandarin cross prized for its distinctive bell-like shape, deep orange rind, and rich, intensely sweet, honeybell-style flavor, combined with better cold tolerance and canker resistance than many older mandarin varieties. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree without becoming puffy or losing flavor, giving a longer harvest window than many mandarins. Water deeply but let the soil surface dry between waterings, mulch to protect the root zone, and provide frost protection for young trees during their first couple of winters until they gain size and hardiness. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Bon Pea (AAS-Winning Dwarf Snap Pea)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Sugar Bon, an All-America Selections winner, combines the sweet, crisp, whole-pod-edible quality of snap peas with an unusually compact, dwarf vine that needs little to no staking, making it a convenient choice for small gardens, containers, or gardeners who want to skip trellising. It sets pods heavily and matures quickly, an advantage in the Gulf South's relatively short cool-season pea window before summer heat arrives. Harvest pods once they fill out but are still tender and glossy, picking every couple of days to encourage the vine to keep producing through its productive window. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Sugar Buns Sweet Corn (Early Cool-Soil Sugary-Enhanced Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Sugar Buns is an early, sugary-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn valued for reliable germination in cooler soil than many other sweet corn types tolerate well, letting Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the spring planting window. It produces 7-inch ears with tender, sweet, deep yellow kernels that hold their eating quality well for several days after picking. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage causes poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 68–75 days from seed.

name: Sugar Bush (Sugar Sumac)
description: Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sugar bush is an evergreen sumac native to chaparral and dry, rocky slopes of the California Coast Ranges and Baja California, one of the most reliable and ornamental drought-tolerant shrubs for California-climate gardens. The large, bold, leathery, ovate leaves are folded lengthwise like a taco shell — a distinctive feature that sheds rain and reduces water loss. The small, red, waxy-coated berries produced in summer are coated with a tart, malic-acid-rich white sugar that was mixed with water by indigenous peoples to make a refreshing, lemonade-like drink — hence the common name 'sugar bush.' A cornerstone shrub for California native and Mediterranean-climate gardens, providing year-round evergreen screening, early spring flowers for native bees, summer berries for birds, and outstanding drought tolerance. Never irrigate in summer once established — it prefers natural summer drought. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Cane (Noble Cane)
description: Plant stalk cuttings (billets) with 2–3 nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sugar cane (Saccharum officinarum) is the world's largest crop by tonnage and one of the most important agricultural plants in human history, providing approximately 70% of the world's sugar supply. In Louisiana, the Gulf Coast's sugar cane belt, it is a significant commercial crop harvested each fall. For home gardeners in zone 9, sugar cane serves multiple purposes: as a dramatic ornamental grass growing 8–12 feet tall with thick purple, green, or striped stalks; as a source of fresh-pressed cane juice (simply feed stalks through a sugar cane press or juicer); and as chewing cane, where stalks are peeled and chewed to extract the sweet juice — a traditional treat throughout the Gulf South and tropics. Commercial varieties include 'LCP 85-384,' 'HoCP 96-540,' and ornamental types like 'Pele's Smoke' (dark purple) and 'California Striped.' Louisiana cooperative extension services offer specific variety recommendations for the Gulf South. In zone 9, the cane may freeze to the ground in severe winters but returns from rhizomes in spring. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Cane Jujube (Extra-Sweet Crisp Jujube)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established. Sugar Cane is a jujube cultivar valued for its exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, refreshing texture, similar to biting into a small, sweet apple, best enjoyed fresh at the green-to-mahogany transitional stage when both sweetness and crunch are at their peak. Fruit can also be left to fully ripen and wrinkle on the tree for a chewy, date-like texture and flavor if a different eating quality is preferred. The tree is largely self-fertile, extremely low-maintenance, and one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available, making it a good fit for the hot, dry margins of a Gulf South orchard. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Cube Melon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Sweet Cantaloupe)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to maximize sugar concentration. Harvest at full slip or when the stem end yields to gentle pressure and the typical musky cantaloupe aroma is detectable. Sugar Cube is a 2000 All-America Selections-winning personal-size cantaloupe from Burpee that produces small (1.5–2.5 lb), round, heavily netted fruits — perfectly sized for a single serving, an individual lunch, or a couple's dinner without leftover melon. The personal melon size (compared to the 4–8 lb fruits of standard cantaloupe varieties) addresses the practical issue of melon waste in smaller households: a 6-lb cantaloupe purchased for one or two people must be stored cut for multiple days, losing quality rapidly, while a 2-lb Sugar Cube is consumed in one sitting at peak freshness. Beyond the practical size advantage, Sugar Cube produces exceptional flavor — dense, aromatic, intensely sweet orange flesh with the classic cantaloupe character that earned it AAS recognition. Each plant typically produces 4–6 fruits per vine, ripening over 2–3 weeks rather than all at once, providing a longer harvest window than some single-headed varieties. Sugar Cube also has the advantage of being growable on a trellis (the small fruits can be supported in fabric slings), making it one of the few viable trellis-grown melons for gardens where horizontal space is limited. Matures in 78–86 days from seed.

name: Sugar Daddy Snap Pea
description: Direct sow seed as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since peas thrive in cool weather. Bred by the developer of the original snap pea, this improved variety offers stringless three-inch pods, shorter vines, and better disease resistance. The compact plants need only light support and produce sweet, crunchy edible pods. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and yield. Pick pods often while young and plump to keep the plants producing. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Sugar Drip Sorghum (Heirloom Syrup Sorghum)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Sugar Drip is a classic Southern heirloom sweet sorghum, grown not for grain but for its tall, juicy canes, which are cut, crushed, and boiled down into sorghum syrup — a traditional sweetener across the rural South before cane sugar became widely available and still prized today for its distinctive, robust, molasses-like flavor. Plants grow into tall, cane-like stalks resembling corn, topped with a grain head that can be left for birds or harvested for feed once the syrup-bearing stalks are cut. Harvest when seed heads reach the hard-dough stage and stalks are packed with sweet juice, typically signaled by the lower leaves beginning to dry; press stalks promptly after cutting, since sugar content declines quickly once cut canes sit. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Sugar Dumpling Squash (Small Sweet Winter Squash with Cream-and-Green Stripes)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 36–48 inches. Harvest when skin shows orange or cream color without green and stem begins to dry. Sugar Dumpling Squash is a miniature winter squash variety in the Cucurbita pepo species that combines the sweet, dry, chestnut-flavored flesh of the best small winter squash types with an individual serving size (1–2 lbs, 4 inches diameter) that makes it supremely practical for home cooking. Unlike large winter squash varieties that require days of eating to finish once cut, Sugar Dumpling's small fruits provide a single meal's worth of squash for 2–4 people when halved and baked — eliminating the challenge of storing cut large squash and the quality loss that comes with refrigerating cut raw winter squash. The skin is a distinctive cream-white with thin green stripes that transition as the squash matures, eventually showing more orange-cream at full maturity (a ripeness indicator). The flesh is deep orange-yellow, very sweet, with the dense, dry texture that characterizes the best winter squash for baking and stuffing rather than the watery texture of summer squash types. Sugar Dumpling's vines are shorter (4–5 feet) than large pumpkin or Hubbard varieties, making the variety more practical for smaller garden spaces. For zone 9 fall production, plants started in late July can produce ripe squash by October–November, well-timed for the fall harvest and holiday table. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sugar Hubbard Squash
description: Developed in the late 1940s as a cross between Blue Hubbard and Sweet Meat squash, this heirloom keeps the rich, sweet flesh of its parents in a more manageable, thinner-shelled fruit. Sow directly in well-amended hills spaced widely apart, since vines are vigorous and long-running. Fruits have blue-gray, lightly warted skin and grow to fifteen pounds or more. Harvest before the first hard freeze once the rind is fully hardened, cure for a week in a warm room, and store in a cool, dry location, where it will keep for months longer than standard Blue Hubbard. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Sugar Kiss Melon (AAS-Winning High-Sugar Hybrid Cantaloupe)
description: Sugar Kiss is a modern hybrid cantaloupe bred by Sakata Seed and recognized with an All-America Selections award for combining exceptionally high sugar content with a compact, manageable vine that suits smaller home gardens better than traditional sprawling cantaloupe types. Fruits are heavily netted, medium-sized, and ripen with a strong sweet aroma at the blossom end, developing flesh that consistently tests sweeter on the brix scale than many older open-pollinated cantaloupe varieties. Sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost and keep moisture consistent through flowering and fruit set, then ease back on watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with gentle pressure and the netted rind has taken on a golden cast beneath the netting. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Sugar Lace II Snap Pea (Semi-Leafless AAS Winner)
description: Sugar Lace II is a semi-leafless snap pea, meaning many of its leaflets are replaced by extra curling tendrils that let neighboring plants hook together into a self-supporting mass, reducing or eliminating the need for a trellis. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining good disease tolerance, including resistance to powdery mildew, with heavy sets of sweet, crisp, stringless pods that are eaten whole. Direct sow early in cool soil and keep evenly moist through flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and texture. Harvest when pods are plump and glossy but before they lose their bright green color. Matures in 65–70 days from seed.

name: Sugar Loaf Chicory
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sugar Loaf Chicory (Pain de Sucre) is a French chicory producing tall, upright, cylindrical heads similar in shape to a Belgian endive or small romaine — but green throughout rather than blanched white. The name reflects the characteristic sweetness of this chicory type: the tightly-wrapped leaves are significantly milder and less bitter than radicchio or loose-leaf chicories, making Sugar Loaf accessible to people who find standard chicory too bitter for raw salad use. The crisp, substantial leaves with a mild, slightly bitter, refreshing flavor are excellent raw in salads, braised, or used as a sturdy wrap for composed appetizers. Sugar Loaf tolerates storage better than most lettuces — wrapped heads keep 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator, providing fresh salad greens long after harvest. In zone 9 the fall-through-winter growing season produces excellent Sugar Loaf chicory from October plantings harvested through February, when mild winters allow unprotected outdoor overwintering. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Magnolia Snap Pea
description: Direct sow seed in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked and set up a tall, sturdy trellis. This striking variety bears tender, fine-flavored purple edible pods and lovely purple flowers on six-to-seven-foot vines. Long hypertendrils act as extra supports, helping the vigorous plants cling to their trellis. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set for the best flavor. Harvest pods young and often while the vines climb, picking before they toughen. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Sugar Mountain Blue Honeyberry
description: Selected by nurseryman Jim Gilbert of One Green World from Russian Kamchatka-type Lonicera caerulea stock, Sugar Mountain Blue is prized for unusually large, oblong berries with a sweeter, less astringent flavor than many older haskap selections. It ripens very early, often several weeks before most other soft fruit, and needs an unrelated pollinizer variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop. Grow in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the upright bush tolerates extreme winter cold but performs poorly in hot, humid summer regions. Renewal-prune out the oldest canes after the first few years to keep yields high. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Mountain Kuma Honeyberry (Pollinator)
description: Released by One Green World from the same Russian Kamchatka-type breeding line as Sugar Mountain Blue, Kuma was chosen as its dedicated pollinizer partner because its bloom period reliably overlaps with Blue's very early flowering. Kuma also produces a worthwhile crop of its own, smaller and tarter than Sugar Mountain Blue, useful fresh or for preserves. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; like other haskaps it is extremely cold-hardy but struggles in hot, humid summer climates. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood until the bush is established, then thin older canes periodically to maintain vigor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Nut Melon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Cantaloupe)
description: Sugar Nut is a personal-size muskmelon bred for small households and small gardens, producing heavily netted, orange-fleshed fruit that average just under 2 pounds so a single melon serves one or two people without waste. Its compact vines and shorter internodes let it perform well in raised beds and large containers compared with sprawling standard cantaloupe types. High sugar content and a small seed cavity give a favorable flesh-to-seed ratio for its size, and its early maturity suits gardeners in shorter-season regions who struggle to ripen full-size cantaloupe. Vine to a trellis or let it sprawl, keeping fruit off wet soil to prevent rot. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Sugar Palm (Black Fibre Palm, Aren Palm)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sugar palm tolerates some shade when young. Arenga pinnata (sugar palm or aren palm) is one of Southeast Asia's most culturally and economically important palms, native to tropical Asia from India through Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, and the primary source of aren sugar (gula aren or gula jawa) — a distinctive, rich, deeply caramel-flavored, dark-brown palm sugar that is the traditional sweetener of Indonesian, Filipino, and Malay cooking. The palm produces sweet sap (neera) by cutting the flower stalks; the fresh sap is collected daily, boiled down to produce palm sugar, or allowed to naturally ferment to produce palm wine (tuak) and then palm vinegar. Beyond sugar, the tree produces fibrous black leaf-base material (ijuk fiber) used for centuries in Indonesia as a natural roofing thatch and rope material — renowned for durability and water resistance. The starchy pith of the trunk trunk is processed into a primitive palm starch (aren starch). The fruits contain three seeds each surrounded by a thick, starchy gel coating that is caustic when raw (irritating calcium oxalate) but edible when processed; young seed gel is used in Southeast Asian desserts (kolang-kaling). A monocarpic palm — it flowers once, over many years, then dies after seed set. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Pie Pumpkin
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm, rich soil, planting in hills with ample space for the vines. This heirloom, a standard since the 1800s, produces small six-to-seven-inch fruits with sweet flesh ideal for pies, soups, muffins, and casseroles. The compact fruits also work for small carving jack-o'-lanterns. Provide steady water and feeding for good fruit set, and harvest when the rind is hard and fully colored. Cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry place. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Sugar Pine
description: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; sugar pine is the largest and longest-coned pine in the world — individual trees reach 200–270 feet in height, and the cones (hanging from branch tips on stalks) measure 10–26 inches long, the longest cones of any conifer. John Muir called it 'the king of the conifers.' The species has the largest seed (pine nut) of any western pine, and the seeds were an important food source for Sierra Nevada Native peoples. The common name comes from the sweet, sugary sap or resin that exudes from wounds, tasting like brown sugar and used as a sweetener by indigenous peoples. Native to the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Range from Oregon through central California, the species is unfortunately threatened by white pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) — plant blister-rust-resistant selections when available. The five-needle bundles, massive trunk, and extraordinary long cones make it one of the most impressive trees in North America. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Sugar Rush Peach Pepper
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this modern baccatum selection, first found as a natural mutation of a South American aji type, needs the long, warm season typical of the species to size up. The glossy, peach-colored pods bring a habanero-adjacent heat wrapped in intense sweetness, with tropical and citrus notes that make them popular fresh in salads and ceviche or fermented into hot sauce. Plants grow tall and rangy, so stake or cage them and provide consistent moisture through fruit set. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Rush Red Sunrise Pepper
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost. This variety arose as an off-type selection within Sugar Rush Stripey plantings and ripens to a solid, glossy red rather than the parent's stripe pattern, with a milder heat range of about 5,000-45,000 Scoville units. It shares the same sweet, tropical-fruit flavor profile as its siblings and works well fresh, fermented, or dried. Provide staking for the tall, productive plants and harvest regularly to prolong the season. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Rush Stripey Pepper
description: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and give this vigorous baccatum plenty of vertical support — it can top 5 feet in a single season. Fruits begin lime green and ripen through a striking peach-and-red striped pattern that stays fairly stable from seed, with a Scoville range of roughly 25,000-100,000 that leans hotter than most other aji types. The flavor combines sweet, fruity, citrus, and stone-fruit notes, making it a favorite for colorful hot sauces and fresh garnishes. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Sugar Snap Pea
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Sugar Snap Pea was bred by Calvin Lamborn and introduced in 1979, winning the All-America Selections award and transforming the edible-pod pea category — it combined the thick, succulent, fleshy pod of snow peas with the full, plump, sweet peas inside, creating a pod that is outstanding eaten raw, pod-and-all, with no tough strings to remove at the right harvest stage. The crisp snap when a mature pod is broken — and the burst of sweetness from the swollen peas inside — made Sugar Snap immediately distinctive from flat snow peas. Harvest when pods are round and full but still bright green before the pod skin begins to wrinkle; at this stage the natural sugars are at their peak. Overmature pods develop a tough string along the suture and the peas inside become starchy. In zone 9 Sugar Snap pea is primarily a January–April crop that provides the most rewarding fresh vegetable of the cool season. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Sugar Snap Snap Pea
description: Direct sow seed as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring and provide a trellis for the tall vines. This All-America Selections winner produces an extended harvest of thick, crunchy three-inch edible pods bursting with sweet flavor. The vigorous plants have some heat tolerance but still perform best in cool weather. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill for tender, sweet pods. Pick regularly while young to encourage continued production and enjoy them fresh off the vine. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Sugar Sprint Pea (Sugar Sprint Snap Pea)
description: Sow seeds an inch deep in double rows along a low trellis or netting, since the compact vines benefit from light support even though they stay shorter than many climbing snap peas. This variety was bred for extra earliness and a concentrated harvest window, producing thick, crisp, stringless pods that are sweet enough to eat whole straight off the vine. Its shorter, sturdier vines make it a good choice for windy sites or gardeners who want snap peas without tall trellising, and it shows good tolerance to powdery mildew compared to older snap pea varieties. Pick pods promptly once they fill out to keep plants productive and pods tender. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Sugar Tyme Crabapple (Fragrant Pink-Bud White-Flowered Crabapple)
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Sugar Tyme is a heavy, reliable bloomer, its deep pink buds opening to abundant, fragrant white flowers each spring, followed by a persistent crop of small, bright red fruit that holds through winter and draws birds when other food sources are scarce. It is one of the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a widely recommended low-maintenance choice by extension services across many regions. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sugarberry
description: Plant in moist to wet, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Celtis laevigata is an exceptionally adaptable native tree tolerating periodic flooding, clay soils, silt, calcareous substrates, and seasonal drought once established — one of the few large trees naturally adapted to Gulf Coast bottomland conditions. Celtis laevigata (Sugarberry or Southern Hackberry) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous native tree of the southeastern United States, ranging from the coastal plain of Virginia and Maryland south through Florida and west to Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas — a dominant tree of river bottomlands, floodplains, moist woodland slopes, and disturbed sites across the South. The common name 'Sugarberry' references the small, round, thin-skinned, reddish-orange to dark-purple to black fruits (technically drupes) that ripen in late summer and fall — sweet, date-raisin-like in flavor, tiny but edible and historically eaten by indigenous peoples across its range. The wildlife value is extraordinary: the berries are consumed by at least 25–30 bird species including mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, wood thrushes, bluebirds, and yellow-rumped warblers, and by raccoons, opossums, foxes, and white-tailed deer. As a native habitat tree, Sugarberry also supports the larvae of several butterfly species including the Hackberry Emperor (Asterocampa celtis) and Tawny Emperor (A. clyton), whose caterpillars feed exclusively on Celtis foliage. An outstanding choice for native wildlife plantings, riparian buffers, and restoration plantings in the Southeast. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sugarcane
description: Plant cane cuttings ('seed cane') horizontally 3–4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; sugarcane is an enormous, bamboo-like tropical grass that has been cultivated for thousands of years for its sugar-rich stems. In the Gulf Coast home garden it is harvested in fall (October–November) when the stems are at peak sweetness, cut at ground level, and either pressed for fresh juice or chewed directly. The 'ratoon' growth from established root clumps often produces for several years before replanting. Most home gardeners in zone 9a treat it as an annual or protect the root clumps over winter with heavy mulch. Heirloom varieties popular in the Gulf South include 'Louisiana Purple,' 'Green German,' and 'Home Green,' all available from local growers and Southern specialty nurseries. Excellent as a tall seasonal privacy screen in the vegetable garden. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Sugaretti Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Sweet Spaghetti Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Sugaretti is an AAS-winning spaghetti squash bred for a genuinely compact, bush-type habit that fits into much smaller garden spaces than traditional sprawling spaghetti squash vines, while also improving on the flavor of standard spaghetti squash with noticeably sweeter, less bland flesh once the strands are separated after cooking. The fruit is a good single-family size, with pale-yellow, oval, ridged rind. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep golden-yellow; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest before storing or cooking. Roast, bake, or boil the whole squash, then scrape the cooked flesh with a fork to separate it into spaghetti-like strands. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sugargate Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune to a well-spaced fruiting framework each winter. Sugargate is a University of Georgia-released black muscadine grown almost entirely for exceptional fresh-eating quality — its large, tender-skinned fruit carries the highest sugar content and richest, sweetest flavor of any widely planted muscadine cultivar, making it a favorite among home growers and muscadine enthusiasts who prioritize taste over yield. The vine is somewhat less vigorous and productive than heavier-bearing varieties like Nesbitt or Supreme, so it is often planted as a specialty dessert selection alongside a more prolific cultivar rather than as the sole vine in a planting. Give it full sun, good drainage, and attentive care to get the best from its outstanding flavor, zone 7–9. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sugargloss Muscadine Grape (Glossy Sweet Bronze-Pink Muscadine)
description: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun. Sugargloss produces bronze to pinkish-bronze muscadine fruit with a distinctively glossy skin and an unusually high sugar content, making it one of the sweeter muscadine selections available, well suited to fresh eating for gardeners who prioritize sweetness over the more traditionally tart-edged muscadine flavor. The vine is a solid, productive grower under standard Southern muscadine growing conditions. Harvest as berries fully color, develop their characteristic glossy sheen, and detach easily from the stem with a gentle tug, typically over an extended late-summer to early-fall ripening window characteristic of muscadine grapes. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sugarloaf Chicory (Pan di Zucchero)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart, thinning to 12 inches when seedlings are established; Sugarloaf or Pan di Zucchero is a distinctive Italian chicory that forms an upright, elongated pale green head resembling a light-green romaine lettuce — quite different in form from the compact red Chioggia or the torpedo-shaped Treviso radicchios. The flavor is characteristically chicory-bitter when young, but sweetens considerably after several frosts or cold nights, becoming almost endive-like in the inner white heart. The heads can be stored after harvest for several weeks in a cool, humid location; the outer leaves are removed and the inner pale heart is eaten fresh in salads or braised. Self-blanching as the tight leaves exclude light from the interior; no additional blanching is required. Matures in 80–100 days from seed.

name: Sugarsnax 54 Carrot (Ultra-Sweet Imperator Snacking Carrot)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in very deeply tilled, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; water consistently through germination (10–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches when plants are 2 inches tall. Sugarsnax 54 (developed by Harris Moran Seed Company) is an Imperator-type hybrid carrot bred specifically for maximum sweetness at minimum days-to-maturity — its name reflects the two core attributes, 'sugar' for sweetness and '54' for the early maturity date that brings exceptionally sweet carrots to harvest in just 54–60 days. The roots are long and slender (8–9 inches) with a tapered Imperator shape, smooth bright-orange skin, and orange flesh that is noticeably sweeter than most other carrot varieties when grown under ideal cool conditions — the elevated sugar content is a breeding trait rather than solely a growing-condition effect, though cool weather amplifies it further. Sugarsnax is one of the most popular carrots for direct fresh-eating, CSA bunching, and farmers market premium carrot sales because customers can taste the difference: the sugar content is high enough to be perceptibly sweeter than standard storage carrots when eaten raw. The slender shape and smooth skin make Sugarsnax particularly attractive in bunched presentation with the green tops attached. Requires loose, deep soil to develop full-length roots without forking; heavier soils produce shorter, sometimes misshaped roots. Matures in 54–60 days from seed.

name: Sugraone Grape (Superior Seedless)
description: Marketed commercially as Superior Seedless, Sugraone is an early-ripening white seedless grape bearing large, oblong, pale green-yellow berries with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor on large, loose clusters. Its early maturity makes it one of the first seedless table grapes ready for harvest each season, well ahead of Thompson Seedless. Vines are vigorous, so berry and cluster thinning early in the season improves size and reduces the tight, compact clustering the variety is prone to. Gibberellic acid treatments are commonly used commercially to loosen clusters and enlarge berries, though home growers can rely on hand thinning instead. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sui Jujube (Historic USDA-Chico Introduction, Small Round Chinese Date)
description: Sui is one of the original jujube selections brought into the United States through the USDA's early-1900s plant introduction program and trialed at the Chico, California experiment station alongside Lang, Li, So, and Silverhill, making it one of the oldest named jujube cultivars still in American cultivation. Fruit is small to medium, round, and sweet with a crisp, apple-like texture when harvested at the mahogany-brown stage, and it dries into a wrinkled, date-like fruit if left to fully mature and shrivel on the tree. The tree shares the species' extreme drought tolerance and indifference to poor, alkaline, or compacted soils that defeat most other fruit trees, and it shrugs off Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity with essentially no disease pressure. Its long history in American orchards makes it a useful genetic and flavor comparison point alongside the more commonly planted modern jujube cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sultan Medlar (Large-Fruited Dutch Medlar)
description: Sultan is a large-fruited Dutch medlar cultivar grown for abundant crops of fruit up to two inches across, larger than many older medlar selections. Like all medlars, the hard, astringent fruit must be bletted — left on the tree through a hard frost or stored in a cool place for several weeks until the flesh softens and browns — before it develops its rich, wine-like flavor suited to jellies, sauces, and eating fresh as a confection. The tree is self-fertile, ornamental, and undemanding, tolerating poor soils better than most tree fruits, though it fruits best in full sun with good air movement. Pick fruit after the first hard frost of autumn and set it aside to blet before use. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Suma (Brazilian Ginseng)
description: Suma is a vigorous, climbing perennial from the Amazon basin grown for its deep, sweet-tasting root, prized in traditional medicine as a general tonic and adaptogen thanks to its saponin and ecdysteroid content. It thrives in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil under the dappled light of a humid tropical or subtropical garden, scrambling over neighboring shrubs or a trellis as it matures. Roots are left undisturbed for several growing seasons to bulk up before harvest, similar in patience required to true ginseng. Protect from any frost and mulch heavily to keep the root zone consistently warm and moist through the growing season. Matures in 730–1460 days from seed.

name: Sumbar Pomegranate (Turkmen Soft-Seeded Cold-Hardy Pomegranate)
description: Sumbar is a Central Asian pomegranate selection named for the river valley of its origin in Turkmenistan, prized among cold-climate pomegranate growers as one of the hardiest cultivars available while still producing well-flavored fruit. The pale orange-red skin encloses bright red, soft-seeded arils with a balanced sweet-tart flavor and juice suited to both fresh eating and juicing, ripening earlier in the season than many larger-fruited cultivars. Because its Central Asian steppe origin gives it tolerance for both cold winters and hot, dry summers, it handles Gulf Coast heat with the same ease it shows in cooler climates, provided drainage is good. Plant in full sun and prune lightly each dormant season to remove suckers and open the canopy, since fruit forms on new growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Summer Cross No. 3 Daikon
aliases: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus 'Summer Cross No. 3'
description: Bred by Takii as a Minowase-type hybrid for the summer sowing window, Summer Cross No. 3 combines a distinctive white-shouldered, cylindrical root with strong tolerance to heat, virus, and Fusarium wilt that ordinarily plague daikon planted before cool fall weather sets in. Direct sow into deeply worked soil and thin to a wide final spacing so roots can size up straight and unforked. Growers who want daikon in mid-to-late summer, rather than waiting for a fall-only crop, choose this hybrid specifically for its ability to hold quality and resist bolting through hot conditions that would ruin open-pollinated types. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Summer Delight Pawpaw (Very Early-Ripening Low-Seed Pawpaw)
description: Site in partial shade for the first season or two, moving to full sun as the tree matures, and plant a second, genetically different pawpaw cultivar nearby, since Summer Delight needs cross-pollination to bear a full crop. Bred by Kentucky nurseryman Cliff England as a cross of two respected parents, Sunflower and Overleese, this selection was developed specifically to ripen weeks ahead of most pawpaw cultivars, often coloring up in late July in warm climates and giving Southern growers the earliest homegrown pawpaws of the season. The 7 to 12 ounce fruits have notably thick, durable skin, a very low seed count, and rich golden flesh with a balanced mango-pineapple flavor rather than the heavier sweetness of some late-season types. Because it ripens so early, Summer Delight is a useful complement to mid- and late-season cultivars for extending the pawpaw harvest window in zone 7-9 orchards. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Summer Fest Komatsuna
description: Summer Fest is a Japanese F1 hybrid mustard spinach bred to resist bolting through the heat of summer, when most other Asian greens fail. Sow seed directly and thin as needed; leaves can be cut at baby-salad size in about three weeks or left to size up into full bunching plants within five to six weeks. Its glossy, rounded leaves have the mild mustard-spinach flavor typical of komatsuna, and afternoon shade during peak summer heat further extends the harvest window before the plants eventually bolt. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Summer Grape (Pigeon Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained to average soil of any pH in full sun; summer grape is one of the most widespread wild grape species in eastern North America, climbing high into the forest canopy from New England to Florida and west to Nebraska. The large, deeply lobed leaves resemble European wine grape leaves and provide dense, ornamental screening on arbors and fences. Clusters of small, blue-black, seedy but sweet-tart grapes ripen in late summer to fall and are consumed by over 90 species of birds and mammals. The grapes are edible for humans and have been used to make juice, jelly, and wine — they are tart when underripe but improve after frost. Summer grape is a host plant for multiple moth and butterfly species including the grapeleaf skeletonizer. Prune back in late winter to a few buds on the main stems to encourage fruiting shoots. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Summer Rambo Apple (Ancient 16th-Century French Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Summer Rambo, also known by its original French name Rambour, dates to at least the 1500s in France, making it one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation today and a variety that traveled to North America with some of the earliest European settlers. The large, somewhat flattened fruit has pale greenish-yellow skin streaked with red, and the crisp, juicy, notably tart flesh cooks down quickly into excellent sauce and is well suited to pies and other baked goods, though it can also be eaten fresh by those who favor a sharper apple. True to its ancient origins as a working farm variety, the tree is vigorous, disease-tolerant, and reliably productive; fruit ripens in mid to late summer, well ahead of most fall storage apples, and should be used within a few weeks since it does not keep long. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Summer Raspberry
description: Summer raspberries fruit on floricanes — canes produced in year one that overwinter and bear fruit the following summer. After harvest, cut all fruited floricanes to the ground and thin new primocanes to 4–6 per linear foot for best airflow. Support canes on a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft. Harvest when berries pull cleanly from the plug with no resistance, typically over 3–4 weeks in early summer. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Summer Savory
description: Sow seeds directly on the surface of well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost; summer savory germinates quickly in warm conditions and thins to 12–15 inches apart for best branching. It has a peppery, thyme-like flavor with slightly more intensity than its perennial relative winter savory, and it is the classic herb for seasoning fresh or dried beans (in German it is called Bohnenkraut, bean herb), as well as poultry, sausages, stuffings, and herb vinegars. Harvest regularly by cutting stem tips to keep plants bushy and delay flowering, as flavor declines after bloom; leaves are most aromatic just before the small pink or white flowers open. Dry whole sprigs tied in small bundles in a warm, well-ventilated place — summer savory dries well and retains excellent flavor. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Summer Squash
description: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in groups of 2–3 after last frost when soil is warm — squash seeds rot in cool, wet soil; thin to the strongest plant. Summer squash (zucchini, yellow crookneck, patty pan) is the most productive vegetable in the summer garden and is one of the easiest to grow, producing an abundant harvest within 50–65 days. Harvest frequently when fruits are small and tender (6–8 inches for zucchini) to encourage continuous production — fruits overlooked for even a few days become enormous and tough, and the plant stops producing. Water consistently at the base and avoid wetting the leaves to reduce powdery mildew. Squash vine borer is a major pest in the eastern US; row cover early in the season provides protection. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Summercrisp Pear (Cold-Hardy Crisp-Eating Early Pear)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Summercrisp was bred by the University of Minnesota for extreme cold hardiness and good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pears, making it a reliable choice for northern growers who struggle with more tender pear varieties. Unlike most European pears, which must be picked hard and ripened off the tree, Summercrisp is meant to be eaten while still firm and crisp, straight off the tree or shortly after picking, with sweet, juicy flesh and a flavor reminiscent of a crisp Asian pear crossed with a European one. Fruit ripens early, in mid to late summer well ahead of most storage pears, giving northern growers a reliable pear harvest even in regions where longer-season varieties may not fully mature. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Summerfest Komatsuna
description: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil and thin young plants for baby-leaf harvest or wider spacing for bunching-size heads; Summerfest is an upright hybrid komatsuna bred specifically for heat and disease tolerance, so it can be sown through the warmer months when standard mustard spinach types would bolt. The smooth, spinach-like dark-green leaves and pale stems have a mild flavor that holds up well in stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. Successive small sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply of tender greens. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Summertime Green Tomato (Sweet Green-Fleshed Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Summertime Green bears medium fruit that ripens to a translucent amber-green, the flesh staying green even at full ripeness, with a sweet, mild flavor typical of green-when-ripe tomato types, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant bred to bring specialty tomato flavor to small-space gardens. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where indeterminate vines would be impractical. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint amber blush, since color alone won't signal ripeness. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Summertime Lettuce (Slow-to-Bolt Heat-Tolerant Crisphead)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Summertime is a crisphead lettuce bred specifically to resist bolting under the lengthening days and rising heat of late spring and early summer, holding its tight, crisp head and mild flavor for a longer harvest window than most iceberg-type lettuces manage before turning bitter and sending up a seed stalk. The dependable heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for stretching the fresh lettuce season further into warm weather on the Gulf Coast than most crisphead varieties allow. Harvest once heads feel firm and solid, and monitor closely as temperatures climb, since even heat-tolerant lettuce will eventually bolt once conditions become too warm. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Summit Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Summit is a southern highbush blueberry released by the University of Georgia for its outstanding combination of large, flavorful berries and good disease resistance to the humid-summer conditions of the Southeast. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor — sweet and complex with good sugar-to-acid balance — and a dry scar that reduces the tendency to leak after picking, improving storage quality. Summit is specifically bred for disease resistance to mummy berry (Monilinia vaccinia-corymbosi) and to stem blight, which are the primary fungal diseases limiting blueberry production in the humid Gulf South. This disease package makes Summit particularly valuable in zone 9 conditions where wet summers favor fungal diseases. The mid-season ripening (late May–June) slots Summit between the earliest varieties and the latest-season types, contributing to an extended home harvest season when planted with Biloxi, Flordablue, and Windsor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Summit Muscadine (Large Bronze Self-Fertile Muscadine Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Summit is a bronze (amber-green) muscadine grape cultivar released by the University of Georgia — selected for its combination of large berry size, excellent fresh-eating quality, self-fertility, and late-season ripening. Bronze muscadines are generally milder and sweeter in flavor than black muscadines, making Summit particularly outstanding for fresh table use, wine production (bronze muscadines produce white/rosé wines), and juice. The large, uniform berries ripen in mid-to-late season (September in zone 9) in loose clusters that fall into collection bags or tarps for easy harvesting — a distinct muscadine characteristic compared to bunch grapes. Summit's self-fertility makes it an excellent standalone vine for gardeners with limited space, though yields are typically improved with a male or other self-fertile pollinizer within 50 feet. Muscadines are the native grapes of the southeastern United States — naturally adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure that make European (Vitis vinifera) grapes impractical without intensive spray programs. Summit is disease-resistant, long-lived, and productive — established vines 20–30 years old commonly produce 30–50 pounds of fruit per year. The vine becomes a significant landscape feature as it ages, with thick, gnarled main canes and attractive fall foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sumner Pecan (UGA Release Large-Nut Type II Southeastern Commercial Pecan)
description: Plant grafted trees in deep well-drained soil; pair with Type I pollinator. Apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually. Harvest when husks split and nuts fall. Sumner Pecan was released by the Georgia Agricultural Experiment Station (now part of the University of Georgia) as a named cultivar selected for the southeastern United States — a region that represents one of the traditional heartlands of US pecan production, with Georgia consistently among the top pecan-producing states nationally. Sumner is classified as Type II (protogynous) in the pecan flowering system that categorizes varieties by the relative timing of pistillate and staminate flower emergence: Type II varieties have pistillate (female) flowers ready to receive pollen before the same tree's catkins shed pollen, creating a natural cross-pollination requirement and making mixed-type plantings more productive than single-variety blocks. The nuts are large to very large for a southeastern pecan variety, with a good shell thickness-to-kernel ratio and above-average kernel quality — the kernel is plump, well-filled, and has good flavor. Sumner's relatively good resistance to pecan scab (compared to varieties like Desirable and Curtis, which have significant susceptibility) has made it a practical choice for home orchards and small commercial operations in humid areas where fungicide application is difficult to maintain consistently. The variety is widely available from Gulf South and southeastern nurseries and has remained in commercial production for decades despite the introduction of newer scab-resistant varieties. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sumo Mandarin (Dekopon, Shiranui Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin — sold under the trademarked name 'Sumo Citrus' in North America and known as 'Dekopon' in Japan and 'Shiranui' by its cultivar name — is a premium mandarin hybrid (Kiyomi tangor x Ponkan mandarin) developed in Japan and widely considered one of the finest fresh mandarin fruits in the world: extraordinarily sweet (very high Brix), completely seedless, easily peeled with thick, bumpy, loose skin, and so large (typically 3–4 inches in diameter) that a single fruit is a generous one-person serving. The characteristic topknot bump at the stem end and enormous size make Sumo instantly recognizable in markets, where it commands premium prices ($3–5 per fruit or more). The flavor is intensely sweet with very low acid and a honey-like aromatic quality unlike any other mandarin, and the peel comes off in large easy-to-remove sections. Sumo/Dekopon trees are slow to come into full production (4–5 years from grafted trees to reliable crops), somewhat demanding in their cultural requirements, and require fruit thinning to produce the signature large fruits — but the result is exceptional. A wonderful specialty tree for zone 9–11 home orchards and edible landscapes. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sumor Sweet Potato (Dry White-Fleshed Baking Type)
description: Sumor stands apart from most named sweet potato cultivars by being dry and mild rather than sweet and moist, with tan-to-yellow skin and firm white to pale yellow flesh that holds its shape when cooked. It behaves in the kitchen more like a russet potato than a typical Southern sweet potato, making it a useful choice for cooks who want a starchy, low-sugar substitute for regular potatoes in a Gulf Coast garden too hot for real potatoes in summer. The vines are vigorous and the roots show good field resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both common headaches in Southern sweet potato beds. Because it is slower to mature than orange types, get slips in the ground as early as the last frost date allows. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Sun Gold Cherry Tomato (Orange Cherry Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sun Gold is widely considered the finest-tasting cherry tomato ever developed and consistently ranks as the top-rated cherry tomato in taste trials — a Japanese hybrid producing small (3/4-inch), round to slightly elongated, deep orange fruits with exceptional sweetness, complex fruity-tropical flavor notes, and almost no acidity. The fruity, candy-sweet flavor of Sun Gold is distinctly different from other cherry tomatoes — a tropical, almost perfumed sweetness that makes it irresistible eaten directly from the vine. In zone 9, Sun Gold can be expected to produce continuously from transplanting in February through June and again from September through frost in the fall — the summer heat above 95°F temporarily stops fruit set but the plant remains and produces heavily once temperatures moderate. The vigorous, indeterminate vine requires a sturdy cage or staking to 5–8 feet and sets fruit in prolific clusters (trusses) of 10–20 tomatoes simultaneously. Sun Gold is a patented F1 hybrid — seed cannot be saved true-to-type. The attractive orange fruit color and extraordinary flavor make it one of the most popular and most widely recommended garden tomatoes. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Sun Gold Pole Cherry Tomato
description: Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out after frost danger passes. This indeterminate favorite produces long clusters of plump, tangerine-colored cherry tomatoes that are exceptionally sweet and juicy. Provide a tall stake or cage, since the vigorous vines easily reach six feet or more. Keep watering even to reduce cracking and pick fruit at peak color, or a bit early to finish ripening indoors. These low-acid tomatoes are rarely found in stores and are a special garden treat. Matures in 57–65 days from transplant.

name: Sun Gold Tomato (Sungold Cherry Tomato, Orange Cherry Tomato)
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with strong support; harvest clusters of cherry tomatoes when bright tangerine-orange. Solanum lycopersicum 'Sun Gold' (Sun Gold cherry tomato) is arguably the most beloved cherry tomato in home gardening — a Japanese F1 hybrid that consistently receives top ratings for flavor in nearly every comparative tasting. The fruits are small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oblong, brilliant tangerine-orange when ripe, and remarkably sweet — consistently the highest sugar content among widely grown cherry tomato varieties — with a complex, aromatic flavor combining intense sweetness with tropical-fruit and apricot notes and just enough acid to balance. The flavor is so intense that eating a ripe Sun Gold warm from the vine is often cited by gardeners as a transformative experience — the difference from a grocery store tomato is dramatic. 'Sun Gold' is an indeterminate vine that grows vigorously (staking required), produces prolifically throughout the season, and sets fruit reliably in a wide range of conditions. The thin skin causes occasional cracking near harvest in wet conditions — harvest promptly when ripe. In Gulf Coast zone 9, grow in spring (March–June harvest) and again in fall (September–November harvest), skipping the hottest summer months when fruiting stalls. A must-grow for anyone who wants to understand what a truly great tomato tastes like. Matures in 57–65 days from transplant.

name: Sun Leaper Tomato (NC State Heat-Set Hybrid)
description: Sun Leaper was bred at North Carolina State University from the heat-tolerant breeding line NC HS-1 specifically to keep setting fruit when nighttime temperatures stay warm — a common failure point for standard slicing tomatoes across the Deep South. The determinate vines carry thin foliage that sheds heat well, so give plants a stake or cage and moderate afternoon shade in the hottest zone 9 gardens to reduce sunscald on the shoulders. Fruit are large, firm, deep red with a small blossom scar, and hold up better against cracking and rough-scar disorders than comparable heat-set hybrids like Solar Set. Because it is determinate, plan a second late-summer transplanting for a fall crop rather than relying on a single planting to carry through the whole season. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: Sun Sugar Cherry Tomato (Extremely Sweet Orange F1 Cherry Tomato, Japan Tokita Seed)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest clusters when uniformly orange. Sun Sugar is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Tokita Seeds of Japan — one of the premier vegetable seed breeding companies in the world — and became widely popular in North America through distribution by companies including Park Seed and Renee's Garden Seeds, where it is sometimes sold under the Park Seed exclusive name 'Sun Sugar.' Sun Sugar consistently ranks among the highest-rated cherry tomato varieties for sweetness and flavor in home garden and market garden trials — its Brix (sugar content) measurements frequently exceed 10 (compared to 6–8 for standard slicing tomatoes), and the flavor combines this exceptional sweetness with mild acidity and what tasters frequently describe as a complex, almost citrus-tropical fruitiness distinct from standard red cherry types. The color — orange to golden-orange, slightly more orange than Sungold (which is from Takii Seeds, a different Japanese company) — is part of the flavor differentiation: orange cherry tomatoes in this category contain different proportions of carotenoids than red types, often with higher beta-carotene content and lower lycopene, contributing to their distinctively fruity, mild-acid flavor. Sun Sugar's crack resistance in the field is a practical advantage that Sungold (its main competitor) has been criticized for lacking — the characteristic of splitting when water uptake increases rapidly after drought periods plagues many cherry tomato varieties, and Sun Sugar's better resistance reduces the frustration of finding split fruit after rain events. Matures in 62–70 days from transplant.

name: Sunbest Nectarine (Early Low-Chill University of Florida Nectarine)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2001, Sunbest needs only about 225 chill hours, making it one of the few reliable nectarines for zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and north-central Florida. It ripens very early, typically by early May, several days ahead of the widely grown Sunraycer, with yellow melting semi-freestone flesh under 90-100 percent red-blushed skin. Trees are self-fertile and heavy-bearing, though like most low-chill nectarines they need close monitoring for bacterial and fungal leaf spot in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunburst Cherry (Self-Fertile Mid-Season Sweet Cherry)
description: Sunburst was released from a British Columbia breeding program and is one of the older self-fertile sweet cherries still widely planted in home orchards. It bears large, glossy red-black fruit at midseason with good flavor, though it is somewhat more prone to cracking after rain than newer firm-fleshed introductions. Because it is self-fertile it can be grown as a single tree, but yields improve with a compatible pollinizer nearby. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water steadily as fruit matures, and prune annually to an open habit for good light penetration and easy harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunburst Pattypan Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Sunburst is a bush-type pattypan that requires no support and takes up significantly less space than vining squash. Sunburst is an All-America Selections award-winning summer squash producing vivid golden-yellow, flying-saucer-shaped pattypan fruits with slightly scalloped edges and tender, mild, buttery white flesh that is best harvested at 3–4 inches when the skin is still soft and the seeds are immature; left to grow larger the skin toughens and flavor diminishes. The compact bush plants are highly productive in hot weather and are excellent for Gulf Coast gardens where the fast harvest window allows planting in both spring and early fall. Sunburst is virtually identical to Bennings Green Tint but with consistent bright yellow rather than pale green coloring. Matures in 52–60 days from seed.

name: Sunburst Scallop Squash (Bright Yellow AAS-Winning Patty Pan Squash)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sunburst is a widely grown hybrid patty pan (scallop) squash producing cheerful, bright golden-yellow, saucer-shaped fruit with the classic scalloped edge, best harvested small, at two to three inches across, when the skin is tender and the flavor is sweetest. Picking regularly, every day or two during peak season, keeps the compact, bushy plants productive over a long summer harvest and prevents fruit from becoming tough and seedy. Like other summer squash it is a heavy producer and benefits from consistent moisture and monitoring for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common pests in Gulf South gardens. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Sunburst Squash (AAS-Winning Golden Yellow Pattypan, Compact and Prolific Summer Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 2–3 inches when golden-yellow and edges still tender. Sunburst Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning summer squash recognized for its distinctive golden-yellow color, compact plant habit, and excellent productivity in home garden conditions. The pattypan or scallop squash form (a flattened disc with scalloped edges, sometimes called 'flying saucer' for its distinctive shape) represents an older squash form that predates the elongated zucchini in American kitchen garden history; pattypan varieties were among the first summer squash grown widely in early American gardens, and the distinctive scalloped shape remains one of the most visually attractive squash forms. Sunburst's breakthrough was producing the pattypan form in a vivid, uniform golden-yellow rather than the pale yellow, white, or green of earlier pattypan varieties — the bright color made it immediately eye-catching at farmers markets and in garden displays, and its AAS recognition reflected consistent performance across trial locations. The flavor of small Sunburst squash is mild and slightly sweet, with a firmer texture than zucchini at comparable sizes — the denser flesh of scallop types holds up better in sauté, roasting, and stuffed preparations than the waterier flesh of standard zucchini. For zone 9 gardeners, the compact plant size and abundant production of Sunburst make it one of the more practical summer squash choices for space-limited raised beds and containers, where a standard zucchini plant's 3–4 foot spread would be excessive. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Sunburst Tangerine (Deep Orange-Red Florida Hybrid Mandarin)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1979 from a cross of Robinson and Osceola mandarins, Sunburst produces medium-sized fruit with a strikingly deep orange-red rind and sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh with relatively few seeds. It is one of the more widely planted modern mandarin cultivars in Florida and the Gulf South because of its dependable, heavy annual production and attractive fruit color. The tree bears young and can overbear, so removing some fruit in spring helps maintain fruit size and reduce alternate-year bearing. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Suncoast Nectarine (University of Florida Low-Chill Nectarine for the Gulf Coast)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, siting them where good air movement helps foliage dry quickly after Gulf Coast humidity and rain. Suncoast is a University of Florida low-chill release with yellow, semi-clingstone flesh, a red blush covering most of the fruit, and notably better resistance to bacterial spot on leaves and fruit than many older nectarine varieties, an important trait in humid growing conditions where bacterial spot is a persistent problem. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set, and expect harvest in late April to early May, among the earliest tree fruit of the season in a Gulf Coast garden. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Suncrest Peach (California Freestone Prized for Exceptional Flavor)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Suncrest was bred in California by peach breeder Fred Anderson in the 1950s and became famous, decades later, through farmer-author David 'Mas' Masumoto's writing about the variety's near disappearance from commercial markets despite exceptional flavor, because its relatively short shelf life made it unsuited to long-distance commercial shipping in the era of firm, durable supermarket peaches. The yellow, freestone flesh is richly aromatic, intensely sweet, and complex, widely considered among home orchardists and flavor-focused growers to rank with the best-tasting peaches available, even if it will never win a shipping-durability contest. Grow it as a backyard or local-market tree where fruit can be picked and eaten at full ripeness rather than shipped hard and green, and maintain routine peach leaf curl and brown rot management with dormant-season spraying. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Suncrisp Apple (Rutgers-Bred Late-Season Sweet-Tart Apple)
description: Suncrisp was developed by the Rutgers University apple breeding program in New Jersey and released for its yellow, sometimes red-blushed fruit with a sweet-tart, Golden Delicious-like flavor and notably crisp, juicy flesh. It ripens late in the season, generally after Golden Delicious, and stores exceptionally well in cold storage, holding its texture and flavor for months. The tree tends to bear heavily and may need fruit thinning in early summer to keep fruit size up and prevent limb breakage. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sundowner Apple (Cripps Red, Late-Season Low-Chill Keeper Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps at the Western Australian Department of Agriculture from the same Golden Delicious x Lady Williams cross that produced Cripps Pink (Pink Lady), Sundowner (also sold as Cripps Red) is an even later-ripening sibling selected for its deep red-purple skin and exceptionally dense, firm flesh that keeps in cold storage for many months longer than most dessert apples. The sweet-tart, crisp fruit needs a long, warm autumn to fully color and mature, making it well suited to mild-winter growing regions where standard high-chill apples struggle to ripen before frost. Its lower chill requirement and heat tolerance during fruit finishing make it one of the more workable late-season keeper apples for the Gulf Coast South. Harvest late in the season once the fruit reaches full deep red color, and store cool for outstanding long-term keeping quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunflower (Oilseed Type)
description: Plant seed 1 in deep and 8–12 in apart in rows spaced 24–30 in; oilseed varieties like 'Peredovik' or 'Rostov' are grown more densely than confection types to reduce branching and produce a single large head per plant. Harvest when the back of the head turns yellow to brown and the seeds are hard — cut heads and hang upside-down in a covered, airy space to cure. Rub seeds out over a screen, then cold-press for oil or roast and use as a whole food. Birds are the main pest; protect ripening heads with netting or paper bags. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Sunflower Microgreens
description: Soak the black oil sunflower seed for several hours, then sow densely across a shallow tray of moist growing medium. Keep the tray covered and dark until the seedlings push up, then move to bright light to green up. These nutrient-dense greens are high in iron, calcium, protein, and healthy fats and can be grown indoors year-round. Harvest by snipping the stems just above the soil once the first true leaves begin to show, usually within about ten days. Keep the medium evenly moist and provide good airflow to prevent mold. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Sunflower Pawpaw (Yellow-Fleshed Ohio Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, full sun at maturity; Sunflower is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ohio from wild seedlings notable for its large, somewhat self-fertile nature (better fruit set when grown alone than most pawpaw cultivars), medium-large fruit size, and rich, sweet, yellow-gold flesh with excellent banana-custard flavor. The 'sunflower' name refers to both the yellow-gold flesh color and the cultivar's tendency to produce better solo fruit set than most pawpaws, though production is still significantly improved with a cross-pollinator. Sunflower's partial self-fertility is its most important practical attribute for gardeners who have space for only one tree — it will produce some fruit without a pollinator while most other pawpaw cultivars produce little or none. The medium-to-large fruits (4–6 oz average) have green to yellowish-green skin that softens slightly and turns more yellow-toned when fully ripe; the rich, sweet, banana-custard flesh is among the most popular of named pawpaw selections. Harvest by feel rather than appearance — ripe pawpaws yield to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. As with all pawpaws, the very short post-harvest shelf life (2–5 days at room temperature) makes them a specialty fruit for home gardeners and local direct-sale; they cannot be commercially distributed through standard grocery supply chains. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sungold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Apricot, Moongold Pollinizer Pair)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, always alongside a Moongold apricot, since Sungold cannot pollinate itself and the two varieties were released together by the University of Minnesota specifically to pollinate one another in cold climates. The medium, golden-yellow fruit has sweet, tender flesh good for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree carries the same excellent cold hardiness as its pollination partner, allowing apricot production in regions well north of where most other varieties can survive winter. Because spring frost during the tree's early bloom is a greater practical risk than winter cold itself, site the pair away from low frost pockets and, where possible, in a slightly elevated or air-draining location to reduce frost damage to the flowers that determine the year's crop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: SunGold Cherry Tomato (Takii Seed Golden-Orange F1 Cherry)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after last frost; SunGold is an indeterminate vine that benefits from strong staking or a tomato cage at least 5–6 feet tall; remove suckers for concentrated fruiting or allow to develop for maximum production; harvest when golden-orange and slightly soft. SunGold is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Takii Seed of Japan and first introduced to American gardeners in the early 1990s; it has since become the most widely grown and most frequently praised cherry tomato in American home gardens, consistently ranked first or near-first in taste comparisons by extension services, seed companies, and tomato enthusiasts for its exceptional sweetness and complex flavor. The small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oval fruits ripen from green through yellow to a distinctive rich golden-orange color; the flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinary — intensely sweet, with brix values of 9–10 or higher (far above standard tomato sweetness), and distinct tropical-fruity notes (mango, passion fruit, tangerine) that are unique among tomatoes and make SunGold recognizable in a blind taste test.
