The indeterminate vines are extremely productive, bearing prolific clusters of 15–30 fruits from early summer until frost; the fruits are crack-resistant for a cherry type. Not an open-pollinated heirloom (seed saved from SunGold will not come true), but the exceptional flavor makes it a standard in virtually every serious home garden. Matures in 57–65 days from transplant.

name: Sunki Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Sour Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunki is an exceptionally cold-hardy sour mandarin, tolerating brief dips into the low teens F once well established, well beyond what a standard satsuma or sweet orange survives. The small, seedy fruit is too tart and sour for most people to eat fresh, but it makes excellent marmalade, ade, and juice for cooking, and the tree's extreme hardiness has made it one of the parents behind many of the cold-hardy citrus hybrids bred for the Southeast. Sunki is also planted specifically as a dwarfing, cold-tolerant rootstock for grafting less-hardy scion varieties, which is how many home gardeners in zone 7-8 encounter it even without seeking out the fruit itself. Give young trees winter protection for their first few years; mature, well-established wood is considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored, and expect to use it in the kitchen rather than eating it fresh off the tree. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunmaster Tomato
description: Transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Sunmaster is an indeterminate heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically for production in hot, humid climates where daytime temperatures regularly exceed 90°F. Unlike many tomato varieties that drop blossoms at high temperatures, Sunmaster sets fruit reliably even when nights stay above 75°F, giving zone 9 gardeners a productive window from early May through June and again in September–November from fall plantings. The large, smooth, red globe fruits average 8–10 ounces with good flavor and crack resistance. Consistent watering is essential — irregular moisture leads to blossom-end rot and fruit cracking in the summer heat. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: Sunny Sea Buckthorn (Low-Thorn Latvian Seaberry)
description: Sunny is a Latvian-origin female sea buckthorn selection bred for unusually large, mild, less-acidic berries and notably fewer thorns than older Russian types, making harvest by hand somewhat easier. Give it lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the nitrogen-fixing roots actually perform poorly in rich garden loam and prefer sandy or gravelly sites. As a dioecious shrub it produces no fruit without a nearby male vine in bloom at the same time, so plan for a pollinator from the start. Because Latvian-bred stock tends to tolerate erratic winter freeze-thaw cycles better than some German cultivars, it is a solid choice for continental climates with unpredictable late-winter warm spells. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunraycer Nectarine (Low-Chill Nectarine for Warm Winters)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with deep, well-drained soil; nectarines share peach culture but their smooth skin makes them more prone to fruit-scarring insects and bacterial spot, so a warm-humid Gulf Coast planting benefits from an open, breezy site. Sunraycer sets a heavy early crop of medium-to-large fruit with bright red skin and sweet-tart yellow flesh, typically ripening ahead of most peaches in the same yard. Thin fruit clusters to one nectarine every 4-6 inches once they reach marble size to prevent limb breakage and improve final fruit size, and prune annually to an open, low vase shape after harvest to renew the one-year wood nectarines fruit on. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunred Nectarine (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf South Nectarine, Florida-Texas Nectarine)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sunred is self-fertile; thin fruits to 6 inches after natural drop; Sunred ripens early (May in zone 8–9, one of the earliest nectarines available), producing medium-sized, bright red, freestone fruits with yellow flesh and good sweet-tart flavor — the first fresh nectarines of the season in Gulf Coast markets. Sunred nectarine is the primary low-chill nectarine for Gulf South and Florida gardening, selected for its exceptionally low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–200 hours) that allows it to bloom and fruit reliably in the mild winters of Houston, New Orleans, Tampa, and similar Gulf Coast cities where the 400–600 chill hours required by standard California nectarines are rarely accumulated in a typical year. The variety was developed through University of Florida and related southern breeding programs specifically to fill the gap in the Gulf South stone fruit palette, where peaches had low-chill options (Flordaking, Florida Crest) but the nectarine category was essentially absent for warm-climate gardeners. Sunred ripens in May in zone 8–9 — among the very earliest of any nectarine — providing a fresh stone fruit harvest at a time when nothing else is ripe, giving it a clear market window at Gulf Coast farmers' markets and specialty farm stands. The fruits are medium-sized, bright red, with yellow freestone flesh and a pleasant sweet-tart nectarine flavor that, while not matching the complex richness of premium California nectarines in cool growing conditions, is excellent for the region. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sunrise Pear
description: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and site the tree with good air movement to keep humidity around the foliage down. Sunrise is one of the earliest-ripening pears to come out of the USDA's fire blight resistance program, producing a small to medium yellow fruit with soft, juicy flesh well ahead of Bartlett and most other European pears. That early harvest window is a real practical advantage in humid climates, since the tree spends less of the growing season vulnerable to blight infection during active shoot growth. Pick fruit while still firm and ripen it indoors, and pair it with another early to mid-season pear for pollination. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sunrise Rhubarb (Seed-Grown Red-Stalked Rhubarb)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings into a permanent, well-drained bed once soil is workable in spring. Because Sunrise is a seed strain rather than a division-propagated clone, expect some natural variation in stalk color and vigor among seedlings, though most produce attractive red-tinged stalks in their first full season. Sunrise was selected to reach usable harvest size faster than older seed-grown rhubarb strains, giving gardeners who cannot source crown divisions a practical way to start a rhubarb patch from seed. Its flavor is bright and tart, typical of the species, and plants continue to improve in yield for several years after establishment. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sunset Torch Tomato (AAS-Winning Striped Flame Grape Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vine well since it is a tall, vigorous indeterminate grower. Sunset Torch is an AAS National Winner prized for fruit that ripens through a striking flame-like progression — green fruit color up in streaks of gold, orange, and finally red as they mature, so a single cluster shows several colors at once and individual fruits look hand-painted. The oblong grape-type fruits are sweet and crack-resistant, produced in long, heavy clusters over a long harvest window. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the sweetest flavor; because color develops gradually, clusters can be harvested a few fruits at a time as each one finishes ripening. Prune suckers lightly to keep air moving through the dense foliage in humid climates. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Sunshine Blue Blueberry
description: 'Sunshine Blue' is a compact, semi-dwarf southern highbush blueberry that is self-fertile and needs only about 150 chill hours, making it ideal for warm regions and pots. It tolerates a slightly higher soil pH than most blueberries but still performs best in acidic, well-drained media. Grow in full sun, water consistently, and feed with an acid-formulated fertilizer during the growing season. Its tidy habit and showy pink-to-white flowers make it a productive ornamental for patios and small gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sunshine Kabocha Squash (AAS-Winning Orange Kabocha-Type Winter Squash)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in a warm, well-prepared bed; Sunshine squash vines are moderately vigorous and less sprawling than giant winter squash types; harvest when the stem corks and the skin is uniformly bright orange and resists fingernail denting; flavor improves significantly with 2–4 weeks of curing after harvest. Sunshine is a kabocha-type F1 hybrid winter squash that won the All-America Selections award in 2004 for outstanding garden performance — its combination of attractive appearance, reliable productivity, and outstanding eating quality made it an immediate success with home gardeners across the country. The squash belongs to the kabocha type (Cucurbita maxima), an East Asian tradition of winter squash with dry, dense, intensely sweet flesh that is considered the finest eating quality among all winter squash types. While traditional Japanese kabocha cultivars have dark green or grey skin with pale stripes, Sunshine was selected for brilliant orange skin that is instantly attractive and visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The flesh is the characteristic kabocha type: intensely deep orange, very dry, sweet, and starchy — so dense and sweet that it bakes without becoming watery, purées into thick soups without thickening, and can be used in dessert preparations. The compact 3–4 pound fruit size is practical for household use (one squash makes 2–4 servings without left-over waste) and the moderate vine size makes it manageable in home gardens with less space than butternut or hubbard types. Excellent storage for 3–4 months under cool conditions. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sunshine Squash (AAS-Winning Bright Orange Kabocha with Rich Sweet Flesh)
description: Direct sow in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when fully vivid orange and stem begins to dry. Sunshine Squash is an F1 hybrid kabocha-type winter squash that received All-America Selections recognition for its exceptional productivity, vibrant visual appearance, and excellent eating quality in the kabocha class — a category of Cucurbita maxima squash that includes some of the highest-rated winter squash varieties for flavor intensity, flesh texture, and sweetness. Kabocha squash (from the Japanese name for pumpkin, itself derived from 'Cambodia' in Portuguese, reflecting the trade route by which the squash reached Japan) have been developed in Japan into a distinctive style — typically flattened globe form, dense, dry, sweet orange to yellow-orange flesh, and rich, complex chestnut-like flavor — that differs substantially from the North American traditions of summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) and large pumpkin (C. maxima). Sunshine's orange skin sets it visually apart from the dark green and grey-green Japanese kabocha types that inspired it — the vivid orange exterior makes it immediately recognizable at harvest and provides a decorative harvest-season display function alongside its culinary utility. The flesh is dense, dry (low water content), very sweet at full maturity, and with the characteristic kabocha texture that some cooks describe as between sweet potato and chestnut — a distinctive dry, starchy sweetness that makes kabocha the preferred squash for soups, tempura, and Japanese-inspired preparations where excess moisture would dilute the flavors. Matures in 95–100 days from seed.

name: Super Berry Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Western Mayhaw Selection)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland-adapted native tree that thrives on low, poorly drained ground unsuitable for most conventional fruit trees. Super Berry is a named western mayhaw selection valued by Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than wild-collected trees or many older seedling selections, packed into heavy clusters of bright red, tart, aromatic berries that ripen in May. The larger fruit size speeds hand harvest for home jelly-making, one of the enduring food traditions of the Gulf South. Plant alongside a second mayhaw cultivar, such as Texas Star or Crimson, for the best cross-pollination and yield, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years, becoming increasingly productive as it matures over the following decade. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Super Fantastic Tomato (Burpee F1 Hybrid Large Vigorous Disease-Resistant Slicer)
description: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage immediately. Super Fantastic is a Burpee F1 hybrid tomato released in 1978 — one of the most successful and widely sold hybrid tomatoes of the latter 20th century, bred at the W. Atlee Burpee Company by Dr. Elwyn Meader's breeding program. Super Fantastic hit the market at a time when home gardeners were increasingly adopting the first generation of disease-resistant hybrid tomatoes, and the combination of large fruit size (fruits commonly 12–16 oz), vigorous plant growth, early maturity (70–80 days), and dual disease resistance (VF designation) made it extremely popular in the American home garden market through the 1980s and 1990s. The fruits are classic large red beefsteak form — round to slightly oblate, firm, meaty, with relatively few seeds and good thick walls — the standard large slicing tomato character for sandwiches, burgers, and fresh eating. Super Fantastic remains in production and widely sold despite the explosion of alternative hybrid and heirloom beefsteak types since its introduction, maintained in home garden seed racks and catalogs by its reputation for reliable, heavy production and disease resistance across a wide range of conditions. For zone 9 gardeners, the VF disease resistance tag is particularly relevant in humid soils where Fusarium and Verticillium wilt are common causes of premature plant death. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Super Sochi Tea (Enhanced Cold-Hardy Selection)
description: Super Sochi was selected from within the classic cold-hardy Sochi tea population for individuals with noticeably larger leaves and more vigorous growth, while retaining Sochi's Black Sea coastal heritage and cold tolerance. It suits growers who want to push tea cultivation into the cooler end of zone 6 while still harvesting enough leaf for meaningful batches of green, oolong, or black tea. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias need, with good winter mulch in its coldest growing zones. Expect a broad, multi-stemmed shrub reaching roughly 8 feet in a decade under good conditions. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Super Sugar Snap Pea (Improved High-Yield Snap Pea)
description: Super Sugar Snap is an improved selection bred from the original Sugar Snap pea to offer stronger vigor, better tolerance of powdery mildew, and a few days' earlier, heavier first flush of pods. The tall vines still need a sturdy trellis or fence but reward the extra support with thick-walled, sweet, fully edible pods over a longer harvest window than the older strain. Pick every two to three days once pods are round and glossy to keep plants producing and to catch pods before the pod wall starts to toughen. Because it holds up well to warm spring weather, it is a good choice for gardeners in regions where the cool pea season is short. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Super Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Red Cherry Cluster Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Super Sweet 100 is one of the most prolific and most frequently recommended cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — a hybrid producing massive, long clusters (trusses) of 20–30 small (1-inch), round, brilliant red cherry tomatoes with exceptional sweetness and high sugar content that makes each fruit taste like concentrated tomato candy. The 'Sweet 100' line was introduced in the 1970s and immediately became one of the best-selling tomato varieties; 'Super Sweet 100' is an improved hybrid with better disease resistance. In zone 9, Super Sweet 100 produces from February or March transplanting through June, and again from September through November transplanting for a fall crop — two productive growing windows that can yield hundreds of fruits per plant. The enormous, arching clusters of brilliant red tomatoes draping from a well-established vine are a spectacular sight. The high Brix (sugar content) makes Super Sweet 100 outstanding for snacking, caprese salads, and any use where raw tomato sweetness is the primary quality desired. Vigorous growth requires staking or caging — an established Super Sweet 100 vine can reach 8 feet or more and must be supported to prevent collapsing under the weight of developing fruit clusters. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: SuperBlue English Lavender (Compact Deep Blue-Purple Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, avoiding heavy clay or consistently moist soils that quickly cause root rot in lavender. SuperBlue bears richly colored, deep blue-purple flower spikes on a compact, tidy plant that blooms earlier and often more heavily than many other English lavender cultivars, with the classic sweet, refined fragrance the species is prized for in culinary and craft use. Its small, dense size fits edging, container growing, and small formal gardens where larger lavender or lavandin types would be out of scale. Trim lightly after the main flush of bloom to maintain a compact shape and encourage a possible second flush, and provide excellent air circulation to reduce fungal disease risk in humid climates. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Superbo Basil
description: Superbo is an Italian-bred Genovese-type basil selected specifically for plant-to-plant uniformity, giving growers a medium-compact, evenly sized crop that is easier to manage than open-pollinated Genovese strains. The broad, spoon-shaped leaves are a brilliant deep green and hold their glossy sheen and flavor well after cutting, which is why this cultivar became a standard for commercial bunching and pesto processing in Italy. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to extend the harvest window and prevent the leaves from turning bitter. Grow it side by side with a standard Genovese basil if you want to compare uniformity and leaf shape, since the two share nearly identical flavor profiles. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Superdukat Dill
description: Superdukat is a Danish selection bred as an improved version of the classic Dukat dill, combining the same high leaf-oil content with an even more pronounced resistance to bolting. Plants stay compact and productive in the leafy foliage stage for weeks longer than standard dill before switching over to flower, which extends the fresh dill weed harvest window considerably. The dense, blue-green ferny foliage holds up well for cutting and is prized for its intense, unmistakably dill aroma in sauces, pickles, and fish dishes. Because it is slower to flower, gardeners who also want dill seed for pickling brine should let a portion of the planting bolt naturally rather than harvesting every plant. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Superior Plum
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Superior is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier crops cross-pollinated with Toka, Pipestone, or another Minnesota plum hybrid. Superior plum was released in 1957 by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program, which developed a series of plum hybrids combining Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) quality and fruit size with the extreme cold hardiness of native American plum species (Prunus americana); these hybrids fill an important niche for gardeners in zones 4–6 where winters regularly kill Japanese plums or prevent adequate chill hours for European varieties. Superior produces large (2–3 inch), dark red-maroon, round fruits with yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor — one of the largest and best-flavored of the Minnesota hybrids and clearly superior in fruit quality to earlier hybrid selections. Very cold-hardy (surviving to –40°F) and blooms late enough to avoid most late spring frosts. A large, vigorous, productive tree suited to the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains where most stone fruits struggle. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Superschmelz Kohlrabi (Giant German Heirloom Kohlrabi)
description: Sow into fertile, well-drained soil with wide spacing, since Superschmelz — German for super melter — is bred to swell to eight or ten pounds while staying crisp and tender rather than turning woody like most oversized kohlrabi. Keep watering consistent through the growing season to avoid splitting the enlarging stem, and side-dress with compost as the bulb sizes up. Harvest young for a milder, thinner-skinned bite, or let it grow to full giant size for slicing, roasting, or long winter storage. Matures in 80–130 days from seed.

name: Supersett Crookneck Squash (Powdery Mildew Resistant Hybrid Yellow Crookneck)
description: Supersett is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash bred for improved tolerance to powdery mildew, a disease that shuts down foliage and yield on older open-pollinated crookneck varieties by midsummer in humid climates. Its compact bush habit and heavy, sustained fruit set make it a productive choice for gardeners who have struggled with mildew collapse on standard crookneck squash, particularly in the humid Southeast and Gulf South where warm, humid nights favor the disease. Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; harvest young at 5-6 inches long for the best tenderness, picking every day or two during peak production since crookneck squash left on the plant quickly becomes tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow production. Scout regularly for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which affect Supersett the same as other Cucurbita pepo crooknecks despite its improved mildew tolerance. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Supersonic Tomato (Large Crack-Resistant Red Beefsteak Hybrid Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Supersonic is a classic large-fruited beefsteak-type hybrid tomato developed for outstanding crack resistance — one of the most crack-resistant large-fruited tomato varieties available, a quality of significant practical importance in Gulf South gardens where irregular rainfall and alternating wet-dry conditions cause cracking in thin-skinned large varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have classic fresh-eating and slicing quality — Supersonic produces the large-scale, meaty beefsteak tomato slices valued for sandwiches and fresh presentations. Supersonic is an indeterminate variety reaching 5–7 feet that requires sturdy staking or caging throughout the season. The crack resistance advantage comes from a thicker skin and firmer flesh than many large-fruited varieties — the practical benefit is significantly less fruit loss during wet periods that would crack softer-skinned types. Supersonic carries V and F disease resistance. In zone 9, Supersonic is best grown as a spring crop (February–May) to maximize the early harvest before summer heat affects fruit set on large-fruited types. The variety has been in continuous production since its introduction in the 1970s — maintained by home gardeners who value the reliable production of large, crack-resistant, good-quality red slicing tomatoes. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Superspur Mayhaw (Heavy-Bearing Spurred Mayhaw Cultivar)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland native that tolerates the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most other fruit trees decline. Superspur is a named western mayhaw selection valued by Gulf South growers for the unusually dense, short fruiting spurs that line its branches, packing on a heavier crop of small, tart, aromatic red berries than many seedling or older cultivars produce. Fruit ripens in May, giving the tree its common name, and is harvested from the ground or by shaking branches over tarps for the classic mayhaw jelly of Louisiana, Mississippi, and east Texas. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar for best cross-pollination and yield, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years and to keep improving in production for decades. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Supersteak Tomato (Giant Hybrid Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, providing sturdy staking or caging since this vigorous vine bears exceptionally heavy fruit. Supersteak is a Burpee hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for some of the largest fruit of any tomato variety, often exceeding a pound per tomato, with meaty, flavorful flesh well suited to thick slices for sandwiches. Its designation as VFN indicates built-in resistance to verticillium wilt, fusarium wilt, and nematodes, helping it stay productive through a long, humid Gulf South growing season. Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking on the large fruit, and feed generously to support the heavy crop load. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Supersweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Classic Sweet Indeterminate Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong support and consistent, even watering to prevent blossom end rot. Supersweet 100 is one of the most important cherry tomato varieties ever developed — a Petoseed hybrid released in the 1980s that set the standard for sweet cherry tomatoes and has remained one of the top-selling cherry tomatoes in America for over 40 years based solely on its exceptional eating quality. The name states the performance promise: 'super sweet' flavor from fruits with approximately twice the sugar content of beefsteak types, and '100' (now sold as 'Supersweet 100 F1') referencing a very early working name for the variety's productivity. The red, round, 1-inch fruits are produced in long, abundant clusters of 20–50+ tomatoes per cluster on indeterminate vines that require staking or caging and continue producing until frost. The flavor is memorably sweet, bright, and richly tomato-forward — thin-skinned enough to burst slightly on the palate, sweet enough to eat like candy, and balanced with just enough acidity to be complex rather than cloying. Supersweet 100 has also demonstrated excellent virus resistance for a variety of its era, which contributes to its continued commercial success. Every tomato gardener who grows cherry tomatoes should try Supersweet 100 as the benchmark against which other cherry varieties are compared. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Supreme Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with a perfect-flowered pollinator vine; Supreme is a USDA-released dark (black-skinned) muscadine producing the largest black-skinned fruits of any commercially available muscadine variety — round to slightly oval berries reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter with deep blue-black to jet-black skin and rich, deeply flavored, sweet-tart purple flesh. The combination of very large fruit size, deep color, and late ripening (September–October in zone 9) makes Supreme particularly valuable for extending the fresh muscadine season after most other varieties have finished. The deep color indicates high anthocyanin content and the associated antioxidant capacity that has made muscadine grapes a focus of nutritional research. Supreme is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the very large individual berry size and attractive appearance make it outstanding for fresh market and U-pick use. As a pistillate variety, it requires a self-fertile pollinator nearby for any fruit production. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Supremo Bush Roma Tomato
description: Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out once frost danger passes. This determinate Roma sets a dependable mid-season crop of large, uniform paste tomatoes even in heat. The concentrated harvest is ideal for making sauce or paste, and the meaty fruits also chop well for salads and salsas. As a bush type it needs only light support and produces most of its fruit over a short window. In long-season areas a successive planting extends the harvest. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Suran (Elephant Yam, Whitespot Giant Arum)
description: Plant corm sections with at least one bud 4–6 inches deep in loose, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil; suran is a major root crop of South and Southeast Asia — a different species from konjac (Amorphophallus konjac) and much more important as a direct food source, producing starchy corms that can weigh 2–5 kg and are used extensively in Indian cooking as suran or oal, in Indonesian cooking as iles-iles, and across tropical Asia in curries, stews, and chips. The corm must be cooked before eating to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals that cause irritation when raw — boiling, roasting, or frying renders the corm safe and gives a texture similar to taro or potato with a mildly earthy flavor that absorbs spices beautifully. The plant emerges in spring as a single dramatic mottled petiole supporting an enormous, deeply divided leaf canopy 3–5 feet wide — extraordinary as a tropical foliage accent in the garden. Corms multiply readily and can be divided each year, building a productive patch. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Surecrop Strawberry (Widely-Adapted Disease-Resistant June-Bearer)
description: Plant dormant crowns in early spring with the crown even with the soil line, in full sun and well-drained soil, and remove first-year blossoms to build a stronger root system before the main fruiting season. Surecrop was developed by USDA breeders and released in the early 1950s, and it earned its name from an unusually broad range of climate adaptability, performing reliably from the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest into the upper South at a time when most varieties were narrowly suited to a single region. The berries are large, firm, and slightly tart, ripening mid-season, and the plants show strong resistance to red stele root rot and Verticillium wilt along with better-than-average drought tolerance for a June-bearer. Because of this combination of toughness and adaptability, Surecrop was widely planted for decades and used as breeding stock in numerous later strawberry-improvement programs. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Surefire Tomato (Texas Superstar Heat-Setting Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Surefire is a Texas A&M AgriLife release and Texas Superstar-designated tomato bred specifically to hold fruit set through the punishing high nighttime heat of a Central and South Texas summer, when most tomato varieties stop setting fruit almost entirely — a trait directly useful across the wider Gulf South wherever midsummer heat causes the familiar tomato slump between the spring and fall crops. The compact, determinate plant produces a concentrated, heavy crop of medium-size, firm, flavorful red fruit over a shorter, more manageable staking and pruning window than a sprawling indeterminate vine. Because it is bred to keep fruiting through heat rather than avoid it, it is a good choice to extend the harvest into the hottest stretch of a zone 9 summer where other varieties stall. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Surinam Cherry (Pitanga, Brazil Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are drought-tolerant but produce best fruit with consistent moisture during the fruiting period. Eugenia uniflora is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree native to tropical South America, widely naturalized in Florida, the Gulf Coast, Hawaii, and subtropical regions worldwide; the deeply ribbed, round, eight-segmented fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally to deep red or nearly black, with a distinctive sharp-sweet, resinous flavor that is immediately distinctive — excellent fresh when fully ripe (dark red to black stage), in juices, jellies, ice cream, and fermented beverages. The foliage is beautifully aromatic when crushed. It is commonly planted as a fast-growing hedge or screening shrub in zone 9–12 and has become naturalized (and invasive in some areas of Florida). Hardy to about 28°F; protect from frost in zone 9a. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Surinam Spinach (Waterleaf)
description: Direct sow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade after temperatures warm; surinam spinach (also called Philippine spinach or waterleaf) is a heat-loving tropical leafy vegetable used throughout West Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia, where the succulent leaves and stems are harvested young and cooked in soups, stews, and stir-fries. In zone 9–11 it is remarkably productive in the hot, partially shaded spots where most greens fail completely, filling a critical gap for summer leafy vegetable production under trees or on north-facing beds. It is tender to frost but self-sows prolifically in warm climates to return each year. Harvest the tender growing tips regularly to encourage continuous bushy production. The small magenta flowers are ornamental and attract bees. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Surprise Mayhaw (Craft-Selection Scarlet-Fruited Mayhaw)
description: Surprise is a western mayhaw selection developed by longtime Louisiana mayhaw breeder Billy Craft, producing clusters of scarlet fruit that ripen in May. It is grown alongside other Craft selections such as Maxine and Double G as part of an ongoing effort to replace wild-collected mayhaw with named, more productive cultivars. Site it on wet to moist, acidic ground in full sun, and plant a second mayhaw cultivar nearby to ensure good cross-pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Suruga Persimmon
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile soil; Suruga is a large-fruited astringent persimmon from Japan, producing brilliant deep-orange fruits of 8–14 ounces with smooth, thin skin and exceptionally rich, complex, honey-sweet flavor when fully bletted (softened to near-liquid jelly consistency). Astringent persimmons like Suruga contain high tannin levels when unripe that create an intensely mouth-puckering sensation; the astringency disappears completely when fruits are allowed to ripen and soften fully on or off the tree. Suruga is specifically valued in Japan for hoshigaki — traditional Japanese dried persimmon — where peeled fruits are hung on strings and massaged daily over 4–6 weeks to produce a sweet, concentrated dried fruit with a crystalline sugar bloom on the surface. In zone 9 Suruga trees are productive and long-lived, with spectacular fall foliage adding ornamental value. The large fruits are less susceptible to fruit fly damage than non-astringent types because they are harvested firm and ripened off the tree. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Susanville Garlic (Adaptable Artichoke-Type Softneck)
description: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Susanville is an artichoke-type softneck improved from California Early stock, valued for a wide climate range and dependable bulbing even where winters are too mild to satisfy hardneck garlic's chilling needs. Bulbs form in a layered, artichoke-like pattern with a good number of easy-to-peel cloves in white to lightly purple-streaked wrappers, carrying a robust flavor that mellows nicely when roasted or cooked. As a softneck it braids easily and cures into long-storing bulbs. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store for use through much of the year. Matures in 200–240 days from transplant.

name: Susquehanna Pawpaw (Large-Fruited Peterson Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Susquehanna is one of the flagship 'Peterson Pawpaws' — the group of named cultivars selected and introduced by Neal Peterson from decades of pawpaw breeding aimed at developing the largest, sweetest, and most productive cultivars available. Susquehanna produces some of the largest individual pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with exceptional fruits reaching 12–16 ounces — two to three times the average size of a good seedling-grown pawpaw — on a productive, healthy tree. The extraordinarily large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with rich banana-custard-vanilla character, and low seed-to-flesh ratio (maximum edible flesh per fruit) make Susquehanna the top choice among pawpaw enthusiasts seeking maximum yield from a home orchard planting. Cross-pollination from Shenandoah, Wells, or another unrelated cultivar is required for reliable production — plant two or more different named cultivars within 50 feet. Because pawpaw flowers have an unusual pollination mechanism (receptive to pollen only briefly, with fly/beetle pollinators), hand-pollination using a small brush to transfer pollen between flowers at different stages significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaws perform in the northern portions of the zone; deep South heat and insufficient winter chilling can limit production in zones 9b and warmer. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sussi Lingonberry
description: Sussi is a Swedish-bred lingonberry cultivar developed for compact, dense growth and heavy fruit set, making it a popular choice for edible groundcover plantings and container culture. Like other named European lingonberry selections, it produces a smaller summer crop followed by a larger, more concentrated fall crop of small, tart, bright-red berries used in Scandinavian jams and sauces. The low, spreading, evergreen habit tolerates part shade better than most fruiting shrubs, and plants perform best in the same very acidic, humus-rich soil favored by blueberries and other ericaceous plants. Light shearing every few years keeps plantings dense and productive. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sutherland Gold Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Red Elderberry)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the golden foliage color develops best without scorching; it tolerates more sun than most gold-leaved shrubs but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Sutherland Gold, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is a finely dissected, cutleaf selection of red elderberry whose lacy, fern-like leaves emerge coppery-red in spring before maturing to a bright chartreuse-gold that holds color through summer, creating a strikingly textured, glowing accent in the partly shaded border. Clusters of creamy spring flowers are followed by small, bright red berries that ripen in summer, providing food for songbirds, though the raw fruit and other plant parts contain compounds that are toxic to people unless properly cooked. Prune hard in late winter to encourage the largest, most vividly colored new foliage, since the best leaf color and texture appear on vigorous young growth. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sutton's Seedless Rhubarb
description: This classic English heirloom was selected specifically for its reluctance to bolt, so it channels far less energy into flower stalks than older rhubarb strains and instead keeps producing thick, tender leafstalks through most of the season. Divide and replant crowns every four to six years once the clump becomes congested, discarding the woody center and replanting vigorous outer sections. Top-dress heavily with compost or well-rotted manure each spring since rhubarb is a hungry, long-lived perennial, and remove any flower stalks promptly to redirect energy into stalk production. Stop harvesting by mid-summer to let the plant rebuild root reserves for the following year, and always discard the toxic leaf blades, using only the petioles. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Suwannee Grape (Early Disease-Tolerant University of Florida Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy to help manage humidity-driven fungal disease. Suwannee was released by the University of Florida in 1983 as a companion to Stover, matching its early ripening while offering comparable resistance to Pierce's disease, anthracnose, and powdery mildew, making it a dependable bunch grape option for the Deep South where European wine grapes typically fail. Fruit is used for fresh eating, juice, and home winemaking. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and reduce disease pressure in humid weather. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Suyo Long Cucumber (Chinese Long Cucumber)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines up a trellis to keep the long fruits straight and prevent rot — trellising is particularly important for Suyo Long to develop straight fruits. Suyo Long is a traditional Chinese slicing cucumber producing very long (12–18 inch), slightly ribbed, tapered fruits with a distinctive light green, slightly warted skin and an interior that is almost entirely flesh with very few seeds; the flavor is exceptionally mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the bitterness common in cucumbers grown in heat stress. It is the burpless cucumber par excellence — the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it highly digestible and virtually non-gassy even when eaten in large quantities. Extremely productive in hot weather and much more heat-tolerant than European greenhouse cucumbers; outstanding for Gulf Coast and Southern summer production. Best trellised vertically for straight fruits and improved air circulation. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: Suzhou Baby Bok Choy
description: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil and thin to allow heads room to fill out into their characteristic tight, rounded form. Suzhou Baby forms a dense, compact rosette of pale green petioles and rounded, glossy leaves that stays tender and mild-flavored well past the size where many baby bok choy types turn fibrous, and it shrugs off both a warm spell and a light cold snap better than most spring-planted greens. Because it needs only a partial day of direct sun to size up properly, it performs well tucked into beds that get shade from taller neighboring crops for part of the day. Harvest whole heads at the base once they feel firm, or pick outer leaves progressively for a steady kitchen supply. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Suziblue Blueberry (Early-Season Southern Highbush Blueberry)
description: Plant in strongly acidic, well-drained soil generously amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Suziblue is a University of Georgia-bred southern highbush blueberry selected for a relatively low chilling requirement suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, ripening its crop of large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor early in the blueberry season, ahead of many other southern highbush varieties. Like all blueberries it needs consistently acidic soil and will struggle or fail in neutral to alkaline ground; test soil pH before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed. Plant it with a second, compatible southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination, berry size, and total yield, since cross-pollination generally outperforms a single variety planted alone. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, and water regularly during dry spells and through fruit development. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sverkhranniy Pomegranate (Super Early Pomegranate)
description: Bred in Russia and named for its unusually early ripening, Sverkhranniy ('super early') produces medium-large red-and-pink fruit with sweet, soft-seeded arils by early August, well ahead of most other named pomegranate cultivars. Its Central Asian breeding background gives it above-average root cold-hardiness compared to warm-climate selections, though top growth still needs winter protection or dieback management outside its adapted zones. For Gulf Coast gardeners, the chief appeal is dodging the humid, rain-prone late-season window that causes fruit splitting and fungal spotting on later-ripening cultivars. Prune to an open, multi-trunk shrub form and thin fruit clusters to encourage larger individual fruit size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Swaar Apple (Dense Spicy-Sweet Hudson Valley Dutch Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Swaar traces to the Dutch settlers of New York's Hudson Valley in the colonial era, taking its name from the Dutch word for 'heavy,' a direct reference to the unusually dense, weighty flesh of the fruit for its size. The large, dull yellow-green apple has rich, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh considered by heirloom apple enthusiasts to be among the finest-flavored of the old Dutch-American varieties, and it stores exceptionally well, holding quality for months in proper cold storage. The tree is moderately vigorous and hardy, reflecting its long history of cultivation in the cold winters of the Hudson Valley; harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the best keeping. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Swamp Black Currant (Prickly Currant)
description: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; swamp black currant is a densely bristled, thorny shrub native to cool, moist forests, streambanks, and swamp edges across northern North America and the Rocky Mountains. Small, saucer-shaped, maroon to pinkish flowers dangle in spring, followed by dark purple-black, glandular-bristled berries that are edible but have a musky, somewhat unpleasant raw flavor most foragers find best transformed into jelly or syrup with enough sugar to balance it. The fine, sharp prickles covering the stems make careful handling and gloves worthwhile at pruning and harvest time. It fills a valuable niche for shaded, consistently moist planting sites too wet or shady for most other fruiting shrubs, and is a useful streambank or rain garden edge planting where the goal is habitat and food value as much as fruit quality. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Swamp Fly Honeysuckle (Oblong-leaved Honeysuckle)
description: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp fly honeysuckle is a native shrub honeysuckle of northern boggy habitats — a deciduous shrub with paired, yellowish-white flowers in late spring and attractive paired red berries in summer. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle vine (Lonicera japonica), this is a well-behaved native shrub that does not spread aggressively. The berries, while not favored as human food, are consumed by numerous bird species in summer and early fall. The shrub provides nesting structure for a variety of native birds in boggy habitats. An excellent native choice for consistently moist to wet, acidic, partially shaded sites in the cold-hardy northern zones 2–6. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Swamp Red Currant (Wild Red Currant)
description: Plant in consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; swamp red currant is a low, spineless native currant of wet, mossy northern woods, streambanks, and boggy conifer forest ranging from New England across Canada into Alaska, thriving in the cool, damp, shaded conditions typical of that habitat. Dangling clusters of small greenish flowers in spring ripen to bright red, tart currants in summer, smaller than cultivated red currants but usable the same way in jellies, syrups, and preserves, and readily eaten by songbirds if left unpicked. Because it comes from a cold, wet, northern habitat it struggles in hot, humid, or dry summer conditions and is best suited to gardens in its native cold-hardiness range with reliably moist, shaded, woodsy soil rather than a typical sunny fruit garden bed. Mulch with leaf litter to keep roots cool and moist, and expect a modest, informal, spreading shrub rather than a heavy commercial-style producer. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Swedish Brown Bean (Öland Heirloom Soup Bean)
description: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after the last frost date, spacing compact bush plants 4-6 inches apart; the low, sturdy habit needs no support. Swedish Brown, also sold as Öland Swedish Brown, is a Scandinavian heirloom dating to at least the 1890s that produces short pods holding five to seven glossy tan-brown seeds marked with a small white eye. Leave pods on the plant until they dry and rattle, then shell and store the beans, which cook to a nutty, dense texture well suited to baked bean dishes and hearty soups. The short, stocky plants tolerate cooler summers better than many bean varieties, reflecting their northern European origin. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Swedish Whitebeam
description: Harvest berries in early autumn and mash to separate seeds from pulp, then rinse seeds thoroughly before sowing to remove germination inhibitors in the flesh. Sow in a prepared seedbed or deep containers left outdoors to experience natural winter cold, which substitutes for manual stratification. Swedish Whitebeam is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates coastal winds, compacted urban soils, and exposed hillsides better than most ornamental trees. Move seedlings to their permanent site by the second year, choosing a location with full sun and good drainage where the tree can develop its distinctive white-backed foliage. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Classic Ultra-Productive Sweet Red Indeterminate Cherry)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and provide minimum 6-foot stake. Harvest clusters when uniformly red. Sweet 100 is one of the most famous and historically significant cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — an F1 hybrid first introduced in the early 1980s that set a new standard for cherry tomato productivity and established the category of 'sweet cherry tomato' as distinct from larger slicing tomato types. Before Sweet 100, cherry tomatoes were typically valued for novelty and ease of snacking rather than for the combination of extremely high productivity and genuinely sweet, complex flavor that Sweet 100 provided. The variety produces long, branching clusters with an extraordinary number of fruits per cluster — sometimes 50–100 per cluster, as the name implies — with uniformly round, 1-inch red fruits and a flavor that combines sweetness with the right amount of acidity to create what many gardeners consider the definitive cherry tomato flavor. The flavor balance of Sweet 100 — sweet but not cloying, with genuine tomato acid and complexity — made it the reference standard against which subsequent cherry varieties were judged for a generation. Sweet 100's high vitamin C content (documented to be substantially higher than larger slicing tomatoes) and prolific production made it popular both as a garden plant and as a crop for farmers markets where volume production of cherry tomatoes was economically important. Several improved varieties building on Sweet 100's genetics followed, including Sweet Million (improved crack resistance), Supersweet 100 (same name but improved disease package), and others — but the original Sweet 100 remains widely grown and available. Matures in 65–70 days from transplant.

name: Sweet 100 Tomato (Classic Prolific Hybrid Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, providing a tall, sturdy cage or trellis for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Sweet 100 is a classic F1 hybrid cherry tomato introduced in the 1980s, prized for producing extraordinarily long clusters of small, intensely sweet, bright red fruit in such abundance that a single healthy plant can yield hundreds of tomatoes over the season, giving the variety its name. Its exceptional sweetness, disease tolerance, and reliable heavy production made it one of the most widely grown cherry tomatoes for home gardens and remains a benchmark variety against which many newer cherry tomato hybrids are compared. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production, since the plant sets new clusters rapidly throughout a long summer season. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Adelaide Tomato (Pink Ruffled Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, tree-like stems lightly for support. Sweet Adelaide bears meaty pink fruit ranging from round to boat-shaped with somewhat ruffled shoulders, prized for its excellent, well-balanced sweetness on a compact plant. It descends from a New Big Dwarf x Paul Robeson cross and was named by Patrina Nuske Small, one of many collaborative releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom flavor to small-space gardens. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 75–88 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Alice Pawpaw
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving them toward full sun as they mature. Sweet Alice is a historic Indiana-origin pawpaw prized for exceptionally large, sweet fruit with a mild, low-astringency flavor that many tasters rank among the best of the older named selections, though it can bear somewhat irregularly compared to more modern, heavier-cropping cultivars. Trees are vigorous with the typical pyramidal pawpaw habit and glossy drooping foliage, and they tolerate the wet-but-drained bottomland soils pawpaw favors in the wild. Because pawpaws require cross-pollination, plant Sweet Alice with a genetically unrelated cultivar such as Shenandoah or Wabash, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom to improve fruit set in home settings where natural pollinators are scarce. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Ann Strawberry (Large-Fruited Day-Neutral Organic-Favorite Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Sweet Ann is a day-neutral strawberry bred by Lassen Canyon Nursery, prized for very large, richly flavored fruit with an excellent balance of sugar and acidity that has made it a favorite among organic growers. It flowers and fruits over a long season rather than concentrating into one winter flush, which suits a spring-planted Gulf Coast strawberry patch well. It carries resistance to most common strawberry diseases, though it remains susceptible to fusarium wilt, so avoid planting in soil where fusarium-susceptible crops have struggled and practice good bed rotation. Maintain consistent drip irrigation, raised beds, and remove runners regularly to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Annie (Annual Wormwood)
description: Broadcast the dust-like seeds onto a weed-free seedbed and press in without covering; they require light to germinate and will not sprout if buried. Sweet Annie grows rapidly into a large, feathery-leaved annual with an intensely sweet, camphor-like fragrance widely used in wreath-making and dried floral arrangements. The plant is the natural source of artemisinin, a compound researched extensively for anti-malarial properties; harvest aerial parts when the plant begins to flower for the highest artemisinin content. Self-seeds prolifically in warm climates, so deadhead spent plants before seeds fully ripen if reseeding in the garden is not desired. Matures in 120–150 days from seed.

name: Sweet Banana Pepper
description: Start Sweet Banana seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost, keeping the soil warm for even germination. Transplant seedlings 12 to 18 inches apart once nights stay warm. This heirloom produces long, slender fruits that ripen from pale yellow to orange and red with a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest at any stage for fresh eating, pickling, or stuffing, and keep plants evenly watered to support steady fruit set. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Banana Pepper (Classic Long Yellow Sweet Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Banana is one of the most popular sweet pepper varieties in American home gardens — a long (6–8 inch), tapering, banana-shaped pepper with thin to medium walls and very mild, sweet flavor with absolutely no heat at any stage of maturity. The fruits ripen from pale creamy-yellow through orange to red, with the best flavor for fresh eating at the orange to red stage and the best texture for pickling at the pale yellow stage. Sweet banana peppers are the standard pepper for the famous deli-style pickled banana peppers — the crunchy, mildly tangy, bright-yellow pickled pepper slices ubiquitous on Italian subs, pizza, and in Greek salads. Home-pickled banana peppers from fresh-harvested yellow fruits are far superior in flavor and crunch to commercially processed versions. For fresh use, allow to ripen fully red — the red stage develops sweeter, richer flavor approaching the sweetness of roasted red pepper. The productive, upright, sturdy plants are easily distinguished by the numerous hanging yellow peppers at varying stages, creating a colorful harvest display. In zone 9, sweet banana peppers are among the most productive warm-season vegetables — the long growing season allows multiple picks per plant from spring through late fall. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Banana Sweet Pepper
description: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes. This 1941 Hungarian heirloom is the traditional pickling type, bearing long, bright yellow, thick-walled sweet peppers. Enjoy the fruits fresh as a snack, in salads, grilled, or in any recipe calling for sweet pepper. Left on the plant, the peppers ripen through orange to red and grow even sweeter. Keep plants evenly watered and pick regularly to encourage a heavy set. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Beauty Watermelon (AAS-Winning High-Brix Icebox Watermelon)
description: Sweet Beauty is a small-space, single-serving icebox watermelon that won an All-America Selections award for consistently outscoring other compact varieties in sugar content during trials, with recorded Brix readings above 11. Fruits are oblong, 5-7 pounds, with dark green rind and medium green stripes and dense, sweet red flesh, and the vines stay manageable at roughly 8-10 feet, making the variety a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens. Grow it with full sun and even moisture through fruit development, then cut back watering as fruits ripen to keep the sugar concentration high. Its combination of compact vine habit and top-tier flavor makes it an easy choice for gardeners who don't have room for sprawling full-size Southern types but still want genuinely sweet, crisp melon. Matures in 77–80 days from seed.

name: Sweet Broom (Carpenter's Herb, Tilo)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun; sweet broom is a low, spreading tropical American herb long used across the Caribbean and South America as a folk remedy for coughs, colds, and respiratory complaints, brewed as a sweet, vanilla-and-hay-scented tea from the fresh or dried leaves, which contain coumarin, the aromatic compound also found in sweet woodruff and tonka bean. The small, narrow, bright-green leaves release their characteristic sweet fragrance most strongly once cut and dried, making it a plant grown as much for scent and tea as for garden appearance. It thrives in the dappled shade of a tropical understory planting and tolerates the humidity of a Gulf South summer well, though it has no frost tolerance and needs to overwinter indoors or under cover outside of zone 10-11. Harvest stems as needed for fresh tea, or cut and hang-dry bundles for longer storage; regular light harvesting encourages bushier regrowth. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Calabash (Sweet Granadilla, Hard-Shell Passion Fruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide very strong trellis or arbor support. Passiflora maliformis (sweet calabash or sweet granadilla) is a passionflower native to the Caribbean islands and northern South America that produces one of the sweetest and most intensely aromatic of all passionfruits. The fruits are rounded to slightly apple-shaped, roughly 2–3 inches across, with a hard, woody, yellow-brown to dark-brown shell when ripe (much harder than purple or yellow passionfruit shells), protecting an extremely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow pulp with a flavor that combines passion fruit, apricot, and guava with a honeyed sweetness rarely found in cultivated passionfruits. The hard shell makes it less susceptible to insect damage than thin-shelled species, and the fruits can be stored for weeks at room temperature. To eat, crack the hard shell and scoop out the aromatic pulp with seeds; the juice is excellent mixed with water as a tropical drink. Sweet calabash is prized in Caribbean home gardens and is occasionally grown in tropical botanical gardens worldwide; it remains very little known in commercial cultivation despite its outstanding fruit quality. The attractive, divided leaves and intricate blue-and-white flowers are typical of the genus. In zone 10–12, the vine is vigorous and productive in full sun. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Charlie Strawberry
description: Plant dormant crowns with crown at soil level in well-drained, amended beds in full sun; Sweet Charlie is a short-day strawberry cultivar released by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences in 1992, bred specifically for warm climates and the production systems of the Gulf South and Florida. It consistently ranks as one of the earliest and sweetest commercial strawberries in Florida and the Gulf South — often the first variety to ripen by 2–3 weeks over Chandler, with exceptional flavor characterized by very high sugar content and intensely sweet berry aroma. The medium-sized fruits are softer than Chandler (limiting shelf life for commercial distribution) but deliver superior fresh-eating flavor — the classic choice for local farmers' markets and u-pick operations where fruit is eaten the same day. Sweet Charlie is popular with home gardeners who prefer flavor over shipping durability. It shows good tolerance of Florida's warm winters and performs well in zone 9 planted on the October–November schedule. Manage irrigation carefully — overwatering increases disease; underwatering reduces berry size. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Cherry
description: Sweet cherries require 700–1100 chill hours and are among the least self-fertile of the stone fruits — always plant at least two compatible varieties, choosing cultivars from the same incompatibility group (or self-fertile types such as Stella and Lapins). They prefer well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and dislike wet feet, which promotes root rot and crown rot. Protect ripening fruit with bird netting. Harvest when fruit is deeply colored, fully sweet, and the stem parts cleanly from the spur. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Cherry Pepper
description: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in warm starting mix; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and soil temperature reaches 60°F. Sweet cherry peppers produce round, apple-sized fruits 1.5–2 inches in diameter that ripen from green to deep red and have thick, sweet, crisp walls with mild to no heat, making them among the best peppers for stuffing, pickling, and eating fresh off the plant. The compact, bushy plants are ornamental and prolific, producing dozens of round fruits per plant over a long season. Stuff raw fruits with cream cheese or pickled vegetables for appetizers, or pack them whole into brine for a classic Italian condiment. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Chocolate Pepper
description: Sow Sweet Chocolate seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks ahead of the last frost and transplant when the soil has warmed. This heirloom bell ripens from green to a striking deep mahogany-brown with crisp, mild, sweet flesh. Space plants 12 to 18 inches apart in full sun and stake if fruit load gets heavy. Harvest peppers once they turn fully brown for the richest flavor, and keep watering consistent to prevent blossom-end rot. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Cicely
description: Myrrhis odorata is one of the finest shade-tolerant culinary herbs available to the northern-hemisphere gardener, thriving in the dappled shade of woodland edges, hedgerows, and north-facing borders where few aromatic herbs will grow; the large, finely divided, fern-like, bright-green leaves emit a strong, sweet anise-licorice scent and flavor when crushed, making them prized in the kitchen for flavoring fruit desserts, salads, and herbal liqueurs. Sow fresh seed immediately in fall directly in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moisture-retentive, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; the seed has a hard coat and requires a prolonged cold period (at minimum 8–12 weeks) to germinate — stored seed rapidly loses viability, so fresh fall sowing is essential. Plants grow 2–4 feet tall and spread to form attractive, long-lived clumps with flat-topped, white umbel flowers in late spring followed by large, ridged, glossy-brown seeds; they will self-sow freely in suitable conditions once established. All parts are edible and anise-flavored: the leaves, young seeds (excellent chopped into salads), and sweet, parsnip-like roots; the sweetness of the leaves means they can be used to reduce sugar needed in recipes for rhubarb and tart fruits. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Sweet Daisy Tomato (High-Yielding Compact Grape Tomato)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, providing a cage or stake for support. Sweet Daisy is a modern grape tomato bred for exceptionally heavy, early, and sustained production of small, sweet, crack-resistant fruit on a compact, well-branched plant that fits well into smaller garden beds and large containers. The reliable disease tolerance and continuous fruit set through summer heat have made it a popular choice for gardeners wanting a low-maintenance, high-yield snacking tomato without the sprawling size of full-scale indeterminate vines. Harvest fruit as clusters fully color, picking regularly to keep the productive plant setting new fruit throughout a long summer season. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Dani Lemon Basil (AAS-Winning Strongly Lemon-Scented Large Basil)
description: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Dani is an All-America Selections award-winning lemon basil (Ocimum x citriodorum) recognized for its exceptional lemon fragrance, large plant size, and outstanding performance as both a culinary herb and ornamental annual. The intense lemon scent — produced by the citral compounds that distinguish lemon basil from sweet basil — is significantly stronger in Sweet Dani than in standard lemon basil varieties, filling a small garden area with citrus fragrance when brushed or harvested. The large, medium-green, slightly textured leaves have a complex flavor combining sweet basil aromatics with a bright, clean lemon note that is outstanding for lemon pasta sauces, fish preparations, lemon-herb vinaigrettes, herb teas, and potpourri. Sweet Dani is substantially larger than older lemon basil varieties — reaching 24–30 inches versus the compact 12–15 inches of some lemon basil selections — producing more harvestable leaf mass per plant. The plants bolt to flower in late summer in zone 9 heat but regular pinching of the growing tips delays this and extends the harvest season. The white flowers attract numerous bee species when allowed to bloom. Lemon basil provides a valuable flavor dimension distinct from standard sweet basil in herb garden collections and culinary applications where citrus brightness is desired. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Sweet Delight Honeydew Melon
description: Start seed indoors in peat pots a few weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once the soil is warm, giving vines plenty of room. This honeydew ripens to an unbelievably sweet, almost wine-like flavor far superior to store-bought melons. Each seven-by-eight-inch fruit weighs about seven to eight pounds with light green flesh and skin. Water consistently while vines grow and fruit sets, then ease off as melons ripen to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the blossom end softens and the rind lightens to creamy color. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Dumpling Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in compost-enriched hills 2–3 weeks after last frost, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Sweet Dumpling is one of the most popular small winter squash varieties, producing cream-colored, deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits weighing 1–2 pounds with distinctive dark green stripes and flecks that turn orange at full maturity. The single-serving-size fruits are among the sweetest of all winter squash — the pale yellow-orange flesh is dry, fine-textured, and sweet enough to eat simply baked with butter and a touch of salt, making it an outstanding small family vegetable garden variety for households that do not need the large quantity of a full butternut or Hubbard. Harvest when the rind is fully hard and the green striping has faded to cream or begun turning orange; cure for 1–2 weeks at room temperature before storing. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sweet Favorite Watermelon (AAS-Winning Classic Striped Picnic Watermelon)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Sweet Favorite is a long-established AAS-winning watermelon, producing large, oblong, classically striped fruit in the traditional picnic-watermelon style, prized above all for exceptional sweetness that has kept it a favorite for decades since its introduction. Fruit commonly reaches 15-25 pounds with crisp, bright-red flesh and a good, thin-but-sturdy rind for handling and short-term storage. Its large size makes it well suited to feeding a crowd at a summer gathering, in keeping with its classic picnic-watermelon role. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, ample space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development, since drought stress during fruit fill causes smaller fruit and hollow heart. Judge ripeness by the ground spot yellowing, the tendril nearest the fruit drying and curling, and a dull, hollow thump when tapped. Matures in 80–85 days from seed.

name: Sweet Fennel
description: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun — do not transplant; Dulce (Sweet) fennel is the culinary fennel grown for its fine, feathery, anise-flavored fronds and seeds — the herb fennel of Italian and Mediterranean cooking used in fish preparations, sausages, salads, and as a garnish, distinct from Florence fennel (finocchio) which forms the swollen bulb base. The tall, graceful, blue-green fronds have an intensely sweet anise-licorice flavor and fragrance; both fresh and dried fronds are used throughout Italian and Provençal cooking. The seeds (technically a double achene) are the primary flavoring in Italian sausage, Tuscan salumi, the spice mixes of southern French cooking, and liqueurs including pastis and absinthe. Dulce fennel is perennial in zone 9 and zone 10, returning from roots each spring; in colder zones it is grown as an annual. Site carefully as fennel inhibits the growth of many neighboring vegetables through allelopathic root exudates — keep it at least 3 feet from tomatoes, peppers, and beans. Matures in 65–90 days from seed.

name: Sweet Frost Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Seedless Changsha-Type Tangerine)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights. Sweet Frost is a University of Georgia release bred from Changsha tangerine specifically to make a hardier, more dependable citrus for gardeners as far north as zone 8b, well beyond where most mandarins survive outdoors. The small to medium fruit is easy-peeling and notably sweeter and less seedy than standard Changsha, ripening in fall into early winter. Mature trees have shown better cold tolerance in trials than satsuma, making Sweet Frost a strong option for pushing citrus culture into the cooler fringes of the Gulf Coast. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Goldenrod (Anise-scented Goldenrod)
description: Sow seed on the surface of dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in early spring; sweet goldenrod is unique among goldenrods for its exceptionally strong anise-licorice fragrance in the leaves and stems — when the foliage is crushed or brushed, the pure, clean anise scent is released. This fragrance comes from trans-anethole, the same compound that flavors anise seed, licorice, and tarragon. Historically, sweet goldenrod was used as an anise tea substitute known as 'Blue Mountain Tea,' and the leaves are still used to make an herbal tea with a pleasant anise flavor. Like all goldenrods, the flowers are an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarchs, native bees, and butterflies. It tolerates partial shade and dry, poor soils — performing in conditions where many goldenrods fail. The only goldenrod with significant culinary and herbal value. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Sweet Granadilla (Grenadia, Sweet Passion Fruit)
description: Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun with wire or trellis support; sweet granadilla is widely considered the sweetest and most delicately flavored of all passion fruits, with a brittle hard shell that rattles when ripe and a translucent sweet-gelatinous interior pulp eaten with a spoon — the dominant commercial species in Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela. It differs from P. flavicarpa in preferring cool highland conditions (3,000–8,000 feet elevation in the tropics, or mild Mediterranean climates); excessive heat reduces sugar content significantly. Harvest when the shell becomes brittle and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. A single established vine on a strong trellis can yield 100 or more fruits per season. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Granite Melon
description: Sweet Granite was released by a University of New Hampshire plant breeding program as one of the earliest-ripening eastern-type cantaloupes available at the time, developed specifically for gardeners in short-season northern, coastal, and mountain climates. The oblong fruit carries light netting over sweet, orange flesh and averages about three pounds, smaller than many long-season commercial cantaloupes but far more reliable where summers run cool or short. It remains a dependable option today for gardeners north of the traditional cantaloupe belt who still want genuine muskmelon flavor. Give it full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, tapering off as melons approach full slip. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Sweet Hungarian Pepper
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian is a classic frying and pickling pepper producing long, tapered, light yellow-green to red fruits of 5–8 inches with thin, tender walls, very mild heat (500–1,000 SHU), and a sweet, slightly tangy flavor that makes them the preferred pepper for Hungarian paprika production, pickled peppers, stuffed peppers, and traditional frying preparations. The thin-walled, tapered fruits cook quickly without the wateriness of thick-walled bell peppers, making them excellent for sautéing whole in olive oil, frying until blistered, stuffing with rice and ground meat, or pickling in brine. The fruit color progression from yellow-green through orange to brilliant red allows harvest at multiple stages — yellow-green for crisp, mild frying, red for maximum sweetness and paprika production. In zone 9 the compact, productive plants withstand summer heat far better than bell peppers and continue producing through the warmest months. Matures in 65–78 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Hungarian Wax Pepper
description: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian Wax is the mild counterpart to the hot banana pepper — a waxy, thick-walled, banana-shaped variety that ripens from pale yellow through orange to red and carries virtually no heat (0–500 SHU). The sweet, crisp, 5–7 inch fruits are outstanding for pickling, fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing, and their attractive color progression makes them ornamental on the plant. Harvest at yellow to orange stage for the sweetest, mildest flavor; the fully red fruits are slightly sweeter but softer. This variety is particularly valued for pickling operations as the thick walls hold their crunch through the canning process. Plants are compact and tidy, ideal for raised beds and container growing. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Jade Kabocha Squash (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Kabocha)
description: Direct sow in warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, giving the semi-compact vine room to ramble.
