Sweet Jade is an AAS-winning kabocha bred by Johnny's Selected Seeds for a personal-serving size, yielding round, 1 to 2 pound fruit with a jade-green, lightly speckled rind that encloses deep orange, richly sweet flesh often compared to a blend of pumpkin, sweet potato, and roasted chestnut. Let fruit fully harden on the vine before cutting, then cure in a warm spot for a week or two to concentrate sugars before moving to cool storage. Its smaller fruit size makes it easy to portion a whole squash per person for roasting or stuffing. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Sweet Jenny Muscadine Grape (Very Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Sweet Jenny is a University of Georgia muscadine release notable for producing some of the largest fruit of any black muscadine cultivar, with sweet, mild-flavored flesh and a skin tender enough for easy fresh eating rather than just juice or wine. The self-fertile vine is vigorous, productive, and ripens over an extended mid-to-late season window, making it a favorite for home gardeners who want big, showy fruit without needing a second pollinator vine. Water consistently during fruit sizing for the largest berries, and thin crowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid Gulf South conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Lavender Mulberry (Honey-Sweet Lavender-Blushed White Mulberry)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sweet Lavender is a large, spreading white mulberry that produces heavy, reliable crops of honey-sweet fruit with essentially no detectable acidity or the tannic berry bite found in many mulberries, and the pale fruit blushes lavender in patches when fully ripe. Because the light-colored juice does not stain like black mulberries, it is a good choice for planting near patios and walkways where dropped fruit is a concern. Self-fertile and heat-tolerant once established, with minimal care needed beyond initial establishment watering; fruit ripens over several weeks in early summer and is excellent fresh, dried, or made into jam, juice, or wine. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Lifeberry Goji (Compact High-Yield Goji Cultivar)
description: Sweet Lifeberry is a compact, self-fertile goji cultivar selected from breeding work aimed at improving fruit flavor and plant habit over wild-type Lycium barbarum, which is native to temperate Asia and naturalized widely across Europe. Unlike the sprawling, wide-arching canes of seedling goji, this selection forms a dense, rounded mound only a few feet tall, so it fits into smaller beds, patio containers, or low hedges rather than requiring the trellising many goji plants need. It flowers on new wood through summer, setting clusters of bright orange-red berries that ripen continuously into fall and are noticeably sweeter and less bitter than typical wild-collected goji. Grow it in full sun in lean, well-drained, even alkaline soil, and avoid overwatering or heavy fertility, both of which encourage rank, floppy growth at the expense of fruit. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Lime
description: Sweet lime yields mild, low-acid fruit prized in South Asia and the Mediterranean for fresh juice. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from any frost, or keep it in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and water deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the rind turns pale yellow-green and the fruit yields slightly to pressure. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Mace
description: Sow seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, barely covering it and keeping flats warm. This anise-scented marigold serves as a tarragon substitute and yields golden fall flowers for tea. Transplant to full sun in well-drained soil once the weather settles and nights warm. It tolerates heat and drought better than French tarragon, thriving where that herb fails. Pinch stems for bushier growth and harvest leaves through the season, drying flowers for winter tea. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Mama Kabocha Squash
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Mama is an All-America Selections-winning kabocha-type squash selected for exceptional sweetness and a compact vine habit. The small, flattened, dark green fruits (3–4 pounds) have brilliant deep-orange flesh with an almost impossibly sweet, nutty, dry flavor — more concentrated and dessert-like than butternut or acorn squash. When cut open the flesh is so dense and dry that it steams and bakes with a chestnut-like texture, and the sugar content is high enough to caramelize beautifully on cut surfaces. The thin edible skin softens when cooked, eliminating the need for peeling. Sweet Mama's superior flavor comes from its Japanese kabocha parentage, which Japanese breeders developed over decades specifically for sugar content and dry, flavorful flesh. In zone 9 harvest when the stem has dried and corked over and the skin has hardened — squeezing should produce no give in the flesh. Cure 2–4 weeks at room temperature before eating for best flavor development. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Sweet Marjoram
description: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost date in well-drained, slightly alkaline seed mix; seeds are tiny and slow to germinate — do not cover deeply. Transplant outdoors after all frost risk has passed in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, spacing 9–12 inches apart; sweet marjoram is frost-tender and is grown as an annual in all but the mildest climates. Origanum majorana is the sweeter, more delicate culinary counterpart to wild oregano, with a complex, warm, floral-herbal flavor that is the defining ingredient in many European sausage and stuffing recipes, and is used extensively in French and German cooking where oregano would be too pungent; the flavor diminishes sharply after cooking, so add at the end. Harvest branch tips frequently before flowering to keep plants producing fresh foliage through summer; in zones 9–11 it persists as a perennial shrublet. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Sweet Marjoram Erfo
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and press it onto the surface without burying, since light triggers germination. This improved culinary strain offers sweeter, milder flavor than wild oregano relatives. Transplant to a sunny, well-drained bed once frost danger passes, spacing plants closely. Pinch tips regularly to promote branching and harvest just as flower buds form for peak aroma. Bring a potted plant indoors over winter in colder climates. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Sweet Meat Squash (Oregon Homestead Sweet Meat, Gray Hubbard-Type)
description: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Sweet Meat requires a long vine (8–12 feet) and ample space; harvest when the skin is fully gray-blue and rock-hard; it stores exceptionally well (6–8 months in cool, dry conditions) and the flavor improves with several months of storage as starches convert to sugars. Sweet Meat squash is a prized heirloom of the Pacific Northwest, where it has been grown in Oregon and Washington for generations as the gold standard of winter keeping squash — valued above all other varieties for the combination of very long storage life, exceptional flavor, and high-quality flesh. The fruits are large (8–15 lbs), somewhat flattened round to oval, with a smooth, dry, slate-blue to gray-green skin that turns distinctly grayish-blue at full maturity — a color that is characteristic of the very best long-storing Cucurbita maxima varieties. The flesh is uniformly deep orange, very dry, dense, and extremely sweet — with a characteristic thick, starchy quality that makes it ideal for baking, puréeing, and any preparation where flavor concentration and dry texture are paramount. The famous Oregon home economist and food writer Carol Deppe championed Sweet Meat squash extensively in her book 'The Resilient Gardener' as the ideal squash for serious food gardeners seeking long storage life and superior flavor; her advocacy brought Sweet Meat to wider national attention. Unlike most winter squash that peak at harvest and slowly decline in storage, Sweet Meat actually improves for the first 2–3 months in storage as the chemistry continues to develop, making it the ideal squash for a Thanksgiving centerpiece planted in late spring. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Sweet Million Cherry Tomato (F1 Red Cluster Cherry)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; stake or cage early as Sweet Million produces vigorous indeterminate vines; the fruits ripen in large clusters of 15–30 and can be harvested cluster by cluster. Sweet Million is an F1 hybrid red cherry tomato developed as an improved successor to the classic Sweet 100 cherry tomato — retaining Sweet 100's exceptional productivity and sweet flavor while adding meaningfully better crack resistance, improved disease resistance (including resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts), and more uniform fruit sizing than the original Sweet 100. The fruits are small, round, and uniformly 3/4 to 1 inch, ripening a brilliant red; the flavor is classic cherry tomato — sweet, high in sugar relative to acids, bright and fruity with good tomato character. The vines are indeterminate and extremely productive, bearing what appears to be a literally endless succession of clusters from midsummer through frost — the name 'Sweet Million' suggests the volume of fruit a well-grown plant produces. Sweet Million is an outstanding choice for home gardeners who want maximum production of reliable, sweet red cherry tomatoes for fresh eating, salads, and snacking; it is particularly recommended for humid climates (including the Gulf Coast) where crack-prone cherry varieties fail in summer rains. Disease-resistant foliage is an advantage in humid zone 8–10 conditions. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Olive Tomato (Very Sweet Small Oval Grape-Type Cherry Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Olive is a grape-type cherry tomato — small (1–1.5 inch), oval to elongated, bright-red fruits with thick skin and meaty, low-moisture flesh that gives this type better handling durability, shelf life, and crack resistance than round cherry tomatoes. The grape-type classification refers to the oval, elongated shape resembling table grapes rather than the classic round cherry tomato form. The flavor is very sweet and concentrated — the firm, meaty flesh with lower water content intensifies the sweetness-per-bite relative to juicier round types. Sweet Olive produces large trusses of fruit on vigorous indeterminate vines. The thick skin and oval shape make grape-type tomatoes like Sweet Olive particularly practical for container growing, patio harvesting, and fresh snacking — the fruits don't burst when squeezed gently and hold their quality well at room temperature for several days after harvest. In zone 9, grape-type cherry tomatoes are among the most reliable summer producers because the thick skin provides some protection against cracking from uneven moisture that affects large-fruited and thin-skinned types. An excellent choice for continuous production through the warm season in zone 9 gardens. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Paprika)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; sweet paprika peppers are harvested when fully red and then dried whole (traditionally strung on twine and air-dried) or split and dehydrated before grinding. Sweet (édes) paprika peppers are a cultivar group of Capsicum annuum developed in Hungary for the production of paprika spice, the defining seasoning of Hungarian cuisine and a cornerstone of Central and Eastern European cooking; the peppers themselves are characterized by exceptionally high carotenoid content (primarily capsanthin and capsorubin) that produces both the brilliant deep red color of dried paprika and its characteristic sweet, slightly fruity, mildly smoky flavor with zero heat. Fresh sweet paprika peppers can be eaten like any sweet bell pepper — they have a somewhat thicker, crunchier texture and a distinctive paprika aroma even when raw. For making paprika powder, dry the fully ripe red fruits at 140–160°F until brittle, then grind; freshly ground home paprika is dramatically more vivid in color and flavor than commercial imported paprika. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Potato
description: Ipomoea batatas is a tropical American vine domesticated in Central or South America before 2500 BCE and now grown worldwide as one of the most nutritious staple vegetables — the orange-fleshed varieties are among the richest plant sources of beta-carotene, vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber. Grow from slips (rooted stem cuttings) purchased in spring or sprouted from a store-bought tuber in a jar of water; harvest after 90-120 frost-free days when vines begin to yellow, digging carefully to avoid cutting the roots. In zone 9-10, slips left in the ground may overwinter and produce a perennial planting; cure harvested tubers at 85-90°F for 1-2 weeks before storage to convert starch to sugar and heal surface cuts. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Rambai (Jentik-Jentik, Kemang Manis)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruiting — Baccaurea dulcis is dioecious. Baccaurea dulcis (sweet rambai or jentik-jentik) is a small tropical fruit tree from the humid lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — one of the sweetest and most pleasant of the Baccaurea fruit species (the species name 'dulcis' means sweet in Latin). The tree is a compact size compared to other Baccaurea relatives, making it somewhat more suitable for home tropical gardens. Like other Baccaurea species, the fruits are cauliflorous — forming in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and main branches in the distinctive pattern shared with cacao, jackfruit, and related tropical trees. The small (1/2-inch), round to oval fruits ripen to yellowish to orange-red with thin skin and translucent, white, jelly-like flesh; the flavor is genuinely sweet and mild, with less of the tartness characteristic of other rambai relatives (B. motleyana). The tree is dioecious, requiring both male and female plants for fruit production. Sweet rambai is largely unknown in cultivation outside its native Borneo and Malaysian range; a rare collectors' fruit tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts in zone 11–12. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sweet REBA Acorn Squash
description: Sweet REBA (Resistant Early Bush Acorn) is a Cornell University release bred for a truly compact, non-vining bush habit combined with earliness and improved powdery mildew tolerance, making it well suited to short-season and small-space gardens. Despite its small footprint, plants set heavy yields of dark green, ribbed, one-to-one-and-a-half-pound fruit with notably sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh. Its bush form allows closer in-row spacing than sprawling acorn varieties, so it fits well in raised beds or intensive plantings. Choose Sweet REBA when garden space is limited but you still want reliably sweet, early-maturing acorn squash for fall roasting. Matures in 78–85 days from seed.

name: Sweet Romance Lavender (Proven Winners First-Year-Flowering English Lavender)
description: Sweet Romance is a Proven Winners English lavender selection forming dense, compact mounds of silvery-grey foliage topped with rich violet-purple flower spikes from early summer into early fall, and it is notable for its ability to bloom the first year from a young plant with little or no cold vernalization required. It is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in hot, dry, gravelly sites where many perennials struggle. Shear the foliage back hard in early spring to rejuvenate growth, but avoid heavy fall pruning since the woody structure protects the crown through winter. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Sandwich Onion (F1 Long-Storage Sweet Onion)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once frost risk has passed, spacing them to allow bulbs room to size up. Maintain even moisture through the growing season and let foliage fall over naturally before curing bulbs in a dry, ventilated space. Sweet Sandwich is a long-day hybrid bred for a rare combination of mild, sweet flavor and genuinely good storage life, addressing the usual tradeoff where sweeter onions typically spoil faster than pungent storage types. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Scarlet Goumi
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — poor and lean soils are acceptable as the nitrogen-fixing roots improve fertility over time; Sweet Scarlet Goumi is a named cultivar of the Japanese goumi bush (Elaeagnus multiflora), a nitrogen-fixing shrub producing clusters of small, oval, bright scarlet-red berries with silvery speckles — the appearance is immediately distinctive and unlike any common North American fruit. The ripe berries have a tart-sweet, astringent flavor similar to a cranberry crossed with a sour cherry, with resinous notes and a unique aromatic quality. The astringency decreases and sweetness increases as the berries ripen fully in late May–June. Goumi berries are high in lycopene (the red carotenoid), vitamins A and C, and contain higher protein than most berries. They are eaten fresh when fully ripe, made into jams, juices, and wine, or dried. Sweet Scarlet is specifically selected for sweeter fruit than many other goumi selections. As an Elaeagnus species, the shrub fixes nitrogen and is an excellent companion plant near fruit trees in a food forest design. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Siberian Watermelon
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Sweet Siberian can germinate in soils as cool as 60°F (compared to 70°F+ needed by most watermelons), making early establishment easier in northern gardens. Sweet Siberian is a Russian heirloom watermelon developed for the short, cool growing seasons of Siberia and Central Russia, where conventional watermelon varieties fail to ripen before fall frost; it is one of the most cold-tolerant watermelons for germination and early growth while maturing in 65–75 days from seed — roughly 15–25 days earlier than most mainstream varieties. The small to medium fruits (8–15 lbs) have pale green, lightly striped skin and unusual salmon-orange to pale yellow flesh that is surprisingly sweet and fragrant with a distinctive aroma different from standard red-fleshed varieties. Compact vines suit smaller gardens. An outstanding variety for northern zone 3–5 gardeners who have given up on watermelons, and produces a fast summer crop in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens as well. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Sweet Slice Cucumber (AAS-Winning Burpless Slicer)
description: Sweet Slice is a burpless-type slicing cucumber that grows long, slender, mild fruit with thin, tender skin that rarely needs peeling. Its low cucurbitacin content keeps the flesh sweet and free of the bitterness and burping aftertaste that can come with standard slicers, making it popular for fresh eating and salads. The vigorous vines benefit from trellising, which keeps fruit straighter and easier to pick while improving air circulation in humid Gulf Coast summers. Pick fruit regularly once it reaches full length to keep vines producing over a long harvest season. Matures in 62–65 days from seed.

name: Sweet Sorghum (Sorghum Cane, Sorgo)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; sweet sorghum is grown for its tall, juicy, sugar-rich stalks rather than for grain — the canes are milled to extract sweet sap that is then boiled into sorghum molasses (sorghum syrup), a traditional Southern sweetener with a distinctive robust, complex flavor quite different from sugar cane molasses. The tall canes reach 6–15 feet with loose seed heads at the top; they are harvested at soft dough stage before the seeds fully harden. Children can chew raw pieces of stalk as a field snack with mildly sweet, refreshing juice. Growing your own sweet sorghum for syrup is a true farm-to-table tradition in the Appalachian South and Gulf States, requiring a simple press or roller mill to extract the juice and an outdoor evaporating pan to boil it into syrup. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Sweet Success Cucumber (AAS-Winning Burpee Seedless Slicer)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a vertical support for best fruit quality and air circulation. Sweet Success is a 1983 All-America Selections-winning burpless cucumber from Burpee that was among the first parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination) cucumbers released for home garden use — a trait that allows fruit production in greenhouses, screen porches, or early in the season when pollinators are scarce, without any compromise in fruit quality. The long (10–14 inch), thin, dark green fruits have tender, smooth skin that doesn't require peeling, virtually no seeds when harvested at the right size, and the characteristically mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor of 'burpless' cucumber types — the term referring to reduced cucurbitacin content that causes the bitterness and digestive upset some people experience with older cucumber types. Sweet Success carries resistance to cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, and angular leaf spot. The thin, tender skin and virtually seedless flesh make Sweet Success excellent for fresh eating and sandwich slicing, with a crisp, sweet quality that compares favorably to expensive English greenhouse cucumbers. A landmark variety in the development of the American burpless-seedless cucumber category and still a strong performer nearly 40 years after its introduction. Matures in 54–60 days from seed.

name: Sweet Thai Basil
description: Thai basil is a cornerstone of Southeast Asian cooking, prized as the aromatic garnish served alongside Vietnamese pho and stirred into curries and stir-fries. Its anise-scented leaves hold their flavor and texture better through cooking than sweet basils, and its purple stems and flower spikes add ornamental appeal. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil warms. Grow in full sun with even moisture, pinching flower spikes to prolong tender leaf production. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Treat Pluerry (Plum-Cherry Hybrid, Red-Skinned Cherry-Flavored)
description: Sweet Treat was the first named pluerry, a Zaiger Genetics interspecific hybrid predominantly of plum and sweet cherry parentage with traces of apricot and peach further back in its breeding, combining cherry-like sweetness with a plum's summery tang. Fruit is small, about the size of a ping pong ball, with red skin and yellow flesh, ripening from late June through July and able to hang on the tree for several weeks as sugars continue to build. It has a low chill requirement of roughly 200 to 300 hours, making it a good fit for mild-winter regions where many cherries fail to fruit reliably. The tree is not self-fertile and needs cross-pollination from Santa Rosa plum, Burgundy plum, or Flavor King pluot; expect a moderate, rounded tree reaching about 12 to 15 feet at maturity if left unpruned. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sweet Wormwood / Sweet Annie
description: Artemisia annua is a strongly camphor-scented annual from China that has become globally important as the source of artemisinin, the active compound in the most effective modern antimalarial drugs; the plant is now grown at large scale throughout Africa and Asia for pharmaceutical production. In gardens it is grown as an intensely fragrant ornamental annual with feathery, bright-green foliage and masses of tiny yellow flower heads in late summer; the dried branches retain their sweet, camphorous scent for months and are used in dried arrangements, herbal sachets, and potpourri. It self-seeds prolifically in mild climates. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Sweet Zellow Tomato (AAS-Winning Yellow Snacking Tomato)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking or caging the vine as it grows. Sweet Zellow was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally sweet, crack-resistant small yellow fruit borne in long, heavy clusters on a vigorous indeterminate vine, producing snacking tomatoes over a long season with far less splitting than many older yellow cherry types. The mild, low-acid, sugary flavor makes it a favorite for eating straight off the vine, and the tough but tender skin holds up well to handling and short-term storage. Pick fruit as it fully colors to golden-yellow for the sweetest flavor, and keep the vine well supported, since clusters can get heavy as they fill in. Even watering helps prevent the fruit cracking that plagues less crack-resistant yellow cherry tomatoes in wet weather. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Sweet-Ark Immaculate Blackberry (Late-Ripening Firm Thornless University of Arkansas Release)
description: Plant rooted canes or tissue-culture transplants in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; prune floricanes to the ground after harvest to maintain plant vigor. Immaculate, marketed as Sweet-Ark Immaculate, is one of the newest releases (2023) from the University of Arkansas blackberry breeding program that also produced Apache, Arapaho, Navaho, Kiowa, and Ouachita, distinguished by its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh blackberry harvest well past when earlier Arkansas cultivars have finished, and by exceptional post-harvest firmness that holds up unusually well in storage and shipping compared to older, softer varieties. The thornless, self-supporting canes make harvest easy and scratch-free. As with other Arkansas program releases, it has proven well suited to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South growing season. Water consistently during fruit development for the best size and flavor. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: SweeTango Apple (Honeycrisp x Zestar! Cross)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby, since apples are not reliably self-fertile. Developed by the University of Minnesota from a cross of Honeycrisp and the earlier-ripening Zestar!, SweeTango combines Honeycrisp's signature explosive crunch and juiciness with a sweeter, more complex, slightly spicy flavor and a harvest window about three weeks ahead of its famous parent. The tree bears at a younger age and more heavily than Honeycrisp, though the fruit is prone to bitter pit and benefits from consistent watering and calcium availability during fruit development. Because it is a managed variety, most trees are sold under license through Next Big Thing Growers, but home gardeners can still plant and grow it for personal use; thin fruit to one per cluster for the best size and to reduce biennial bearing. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sweetcrisp Southern Highbush Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Low-Chill Blueberry)
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain the moist, acidic conditions southern highbush blueberries require. Sweetcrisp is a University of Florida southern highbush release notable for its unusually firm, crisp berry texture — distinct from the softer bite of most blueberries — paired with high sugar content and good flavor, along with very low chill requirements that make it one of the most reliable blueberry choices for the Deep South and coastal Gulf region. The compact, productive bush ripens over a fairly long mid-season window, and its firm texture holds up especially well for fresh eating and short-term storage. Plant with a second southern highbush cultivar for best cross-pollination and yield, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush vigorous. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Sweetgrass (Vanilla Grass, Holy Grass)
description: Plant divisions into damp, low-lying soil near a pond edge, ditch, or consistently irrigated bed, since this native grass naturally grows in moist meadows and spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a loose colony. It tolerates full sun in reliably wet ground but appreciates part shade where soil dries out more. The blades carry a sweet vanilla-like fragrance, especially when cut and dried, and have long been braided and burned in Indigenous North American ceremonies, woven into baskets, and steeped as a fragrant herbal tea or used to flavor bison-grass-style spirits. Divide and replant crowded clumps every few years to keep the planting vigorous. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Sweetheart Cherry (Late-Season Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry)
description: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting and avoid low, frost-prone planting sites. Sweetheart is a Canadian-bred sweet cherry from the Summerland research station in British Columbia, valued for being self-fertile — unlike Bing and many other sweet cherries, it sets a reliable crop without a separate pollinizer tree, making it a practical choice where space allows for only one cherry tree. It ripens notably late in the sweet cherry season, extending fresh harvest well after earlier cultivars like Bing and Rainier have finished, with medium-large, bright red, firm, sweet fruit of good flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its self-fertility combined with late ripening has made it a popular choice for home orchards and small commercial plantings alike. Provide consistent moisture during fruit development to avoid cracking, especially if rain falls as fruit nears full ripeness. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Sweetheart Lychee
description: Sweetheart is a widely recommended Florida and Gulf Coast lychee cultivar prized because it is self-fertile and sets a reliable crop even in climates too marginal to trigger consistent flowering and fruit set in less adaptable cultivars such as Brewster. It bears clusters of medium-sized, bumpy-skinned red fruit with sweet, juicy, aromatic flesh and a comparatively small seed. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil, sheltered from strong wind, and protect young trees from any frost since even brief freezes can kill unestablished plants. Lychee needs a brief, cool, relatively dry period in winter to initiate flower buds, so avoid heavy fertilizing or irrigation in late fall and winter; once flowering begins, water and feed generously through fruit development. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sweetheart Passion Fruit (Self-Fertile Purple-Gold Hybrid Passionfruit)
description: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Sweetheart was bred in Australia as a cross between purple and golden passionfruit types and is prized by home gardeners because a single vine reliably sets a full crop without a separate pollinator. Fruit is medium-sized with dark reddish-purple skin and the tart-sweet aromatic pulp typical of purple passionfruit, ripening within the first year or two from a rooted cutting. Provide sturdy support and tip-prune regularly, since the vine grows fast and can quickly overwhelm a small trellis if left unchecked. Like other purple-type selections it is more cold-sensitive than Possum Purple, so in zone 9 plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot and mulch heavily before winter. Matures in 270–545 days from transplant.

name: Sweetie Cherry Tomato (Classic Open-Pollinated Small Sweet Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; cage or stake before growth gets away from support. Sweetie is an open-pollinated small cherry tomato that has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1970s — one of the classic heirloom small cherry tomatoes alongside Sweet 100 and Gardener's Delight. The round, 0.75–1 inch fruits are produced in large clusters of 15–25 or more on long, indeterminate vines, and have a flavor profile that lives up to the name: very sweet, with high sugar content relative to acid, and the concentrated pure tomato essence that has made small cherry tomatoes universally popular. Sweetie is open-pollinated, meaning seed can be saved from year to year to maintain a self-sustaining garden supply — an advantage over Sweet 100, which is a hybrid. The plants produce heavily from midsummer through frost, providing abundant cherry tomatoes for snacking, salads, roasting, and pasta for the entire season. Sweetie is particularly well-suited to gardeners who want to maintain their own seed from a reliable, high-quality cherry tomato variety. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Sweetie Pie Blackberry (Rosette Disease-Resistant Thornless Trailing Type)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, providing a trellis for the trailing canes to climb; Sweetie Pie is a thornless trailing blackberry developed at the USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred specifically for resistance to rosette disease (double blossom), a fungal disease that deforms flowers and ruins fruit set and is one of the most serious blackberry problems across the hot, humid South. It produces sweet, well-flavored berries on canes that need training to a trellis since the trailing habit does not stand upright on its own. Because rosette disease spreads through infected plant tissue and is difficult to control with fungicides alone once established, Sweetie Pie's genetic resistance is a real practical advantage for Gulf South growers who have struggled with the disease in other varieties. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Sweetshoot Bamboo
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, contained with a rhizome barrier; sweetshoot bamboo earns its name from its exceptional culinary qualities — the spring shoots are notably less bitter than most bamboos and sweet enough to be eaten raw in thin slices, without the blanching required for most species. The shoots are harvested in spring as they emerge from the soil, before the sheaths open, when they are at peak sweetness and tenderness. Mature culms reach 15–25 feet and 1–2 inches in diameter, providing attractive screening material and lightweight bamboo poles. Like all Phyllostachys species, it spreads by underground rhizomes and requires containment. The coppery-bronze color of new culm sheaths in spring is ornamental. Plant in groves of 3 or more for heavier shoot production. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Swenson Red Grape (Cold-Hardy Northern Table Grape)
description: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Swenson Red is another cold-hardy northern grape developed by breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, producing medium, pinkish-red table grapes with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a tender skin, considered by many Northern growers to be one of the best-tasting hardy grapes available, even though it retains seeds unlike some of Swenson's later seedless introductions. The vigorous vine is a reliable producer in climates too cold for most vinifera or Southern-bred hybrid grapes, extending quality fresh grape growing well into regions with harsh winters. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if the vine sets a heavy crop for the best berry size and flavor. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Swingle Citrumelo (Rootstock Citrus)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Swingle citrumelo is a grapefruit x trifoliate orange hybrid that became the standard commercial citrus rootstock across much of Florida and the Gulf South after older rootstocks succumbed to citrus blight and tristeza virus, valued for disease resistance, cold hardiness well beyond standard sweet orange, and good compatibility with most common scion varieties. Its own fruit is bitter, seedy, and essentially inedible, so it is used as understock for grafting a named orange, grapefruit, mandarin, or lemon variety rather than being grown for fruit. Trees show trifoliate-influenced foliage with small, three-part leaves and light thorns, especially on young wood. Home gardeners most often encounter Swingle citrumelo already grafted beneath a named citrus at the nursery rather than planting it directly, but it can also be grown from seed to produce rootstock trees for home grafting projects. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Swiss Chard
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade as early as spring soil can be worked; Swiss chard is the most heat-tolerant and adaptable of the cool-season leafy greens, bridging the gap between the cool spring lettuce season and the fall crops by continuing to produce through summer heat that would bolt most other leafy greens. Each chard seed cluster contains 2–4 seeds; thin to one seedling per 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves continuously, leaving the growing center to continue producing — a well-tended planting can produce for 6 months or more. Rainbow chard types with red, orange, yellow, and pink stems are highly ornamental as well as edible. Mildly earthy flavor that is more versatile than spinach. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Swiss Mint (Very High-Menthol Confectionery Mint)
description: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Swiss Mint carries an unusually high menthol content and an intensely cooling flavor, historically favored for confectionery and lozenge production where a strong, sharp mint punch is wanted rather than the softer flavor of culinary spearmint types. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Sword Bean (Overlook Bean)
description: Direct sow after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis, in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun — sword bean is a vigorous tropical climbing annual from Asia and Africa, producing enormous, curved, sword-shaped pods up to 18 inches long that are among the most dramatic in the legume family. When harvested young (3–4 inches long), the whole immature pods can be cooked and eaten like snap beans; the mature seeds can be eaten when thoroughly cooked through multiple water changes (raw seeds and undercooked beans contain canavanine, a toxic amino acid, and must be thoroughly boiled). In traditional Southeast Asian and African cuisines, the young pods are stir-fried, pickled, and used in curries. The plant is a prolific nitrogen-fixer used as a cover crop and soil improver in tropical agriculture. An ornamental conversation-piece in the summer garden where its enormous pods hanging from a trellis never fail to impress visitors. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Sylvesta Lettuce (Heat-Tolerant French Batavian Lettuce)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce forming loose, semi-crisp heads with a texture between soft butterhead and crunchy iceberg, valued for holding good quality and resisting premature bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as spring temperatures rise, extending the harvest window into warmer weather. The pale green leaves have a mild, sweet flavor and good crispness that holds up well in salads. Harvest as a loose head or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest part of the season to further extend its quality. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Sylvester Date Palm (Silver Date Palm, Wild Date Palm)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — clay, sand, alkaline, or loam — Sylvester Date Palm is broadly adaptable and extremely drought-tolerant once established; avoid waterlogged soils. Phoenix sylvestris (Wild Date Palm or Silver Date Palm) is native to Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka, where it is heavily tapped for the sweet sap used to produce date palm jaggery, a prized molasses-like sweetener throughout South Asia. In Gulf Coast zone 9 landscapes it is one of the most dramatic and widely-planted feather palms, prized for its striking silvery blue-green fronds — significantly more silver-blue than the commercial Date Palm (P. dactylifera) — and its distinctive diamond-patterned trunk that becomes increasingly textured and photogenic with age. Unlike P. dactylifera, Sylvester Date Palm tolerates more cold (zone 8b, to about 20–22°F with brief exposure), adapts to the high humidity and rainfall of the Gulf South, and resists the root and crown rots that plague commercial date palms in wet climates. The palm produces clusters of small, yellow to orange-red date-like fruits that ripen in fall and are edible fresh or used for making jaggery syrup. An outstanding statement palm for large residential properties and commercial streetscapes in zone 9, frequently planted in staggered triple groups for maximum visual impact. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Sylvetta Wild Arugula (Wild Rocket)
description: Scatter seed thinly over cool, fertile soil and cover lightly, since Sylvetta germinates best when kept consistently moist. This named selection of wild arugula produces smaller, more deeply lobed leaves than the species and a denser, more compact rosette that regrows readily after cutting. Its flavor is intensely nutty and peppery, sharper than salad arugula, and it holds up in heat and resists bolting far longer than Eruca types, making it a mainstay of Italian-style mesclun mixes. In mild-winter regions it behaves as a short-lived perennial and can be harvested for several seasons from the same planting. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Syrah Wine Grape (Shiraz)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Syrah (called Shiraz in Australia and South Africa) is a vigorous, heat-loving variety well suited to warm growing regions. This bold, deeply colored red wine grape produces small, dark-skinned berries that yield rich, full-bodied wines with dark fruit, pepper, and smoky notes, thriving in warm, sunny climates from France's Rhône Valley to Australia's Barossa Valley where it has become that country's signature red grape under the Shiraz name. Vigorous and generally reliable in warm regions, it tolerates heat well but is susceptible to bunch rot in humid conditions, making canopy management for airflow important in more humid growing areas. Train to a trellis system that supports its vigorous growth, thin fruit if overcropping to concentrate flavor, and provide full sun and warmth for the best ripening. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Syrian Oregano (Za'atar)
description: Surface-sow seeds on moist, gritty seed-starting mix and keep at 68–72°F; tiny seeds need light so do not cover. Syrian oregano is the primary botanical ingredient in the Middle Eastern spice blend called za'atar; its flavor is strongly oregano-thyme with a hint of marjoram. Grow in very well-drained, poor to moderate soil in full sun — it is native to rocky limestone slopes and rewards lean conditions with the most aromatic foliage. Harvest young stems and leaves throughout the growing season, drying them for use in the za'atar spice blend or using fresh in flatbreads, salads, and dips. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Syrup Mill Pecan (Exceptionally Scab-Resistant Alabama Gulf Coast Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and pair with a compatible Type II cultivar for cross-pollination; Syrup Mill was found in Mobile County on the Alabama Gulf Coast and has shown even higher resistance to pecan scab than the long-standard Elliott in university disease trials, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for humid coastal home orchards. The tree is notably vigorous and holds clean, healthy foliage through the growing season, which supports steadier nut fill in wet years when scab-prone cultivars are already defoliating. Nuts run smaller than many named cultivars, around 65 per pound, with roughly 47% kernel, so it suits growers who prioritize dependable low-input production and disease resistance over maximum nut size. Trees begin bearing within about seven years of planting; water deeply during nut fill and correct zinc deficiency with an annual spring foliar spray. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Szego Chestnut (Nave Large-Nutted Blight-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)
description: Szego is a hybrid chestnut selected by chestnut grower J. Michael Nave and carries recorded resistance to chestnut blight. It stands out for its unusually large, single-embryo nuts, around 40 grams each, and excellent flavor, and it is reported to graft readily onto a wide range of chestnut rootstocks. As with other chestnuts, plant it with a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby to ensure reliable cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Szukis American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Selected Native Persimmon Cultivar)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade; American persimmons tolerate poor, dry, acidic soils that challenge most fruit trees. Allow fruit to ripen fully and become very soft before harvesting. Szukis is a selected cultivar of the American Persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) — a native North American tree with a natural range from Connecticut to Florida and west to Nebraska and Kansas, making it one of the most widely distributed native fruit trees in eastern North America. The American persimmon was an important food for Indigenous peoples and early European settlers, who ate the ripe fruit fresh, dried, and fermented into persimmon beer; persimmon pudding remains a traditional Appalachian and Midwestern dessert made from the pulp of ripe fruit. Szukis was selected from the wild by Larry Szukis for its exceptional fruit size for an American persimmon — the fruits can reach 1.5–2.5 oz, substantially larger than typical wild American persimmon fruits. The flavor of fully-ripe American persimmon is dramatically different from the popular Asian persimmons (Diospyros kaki) — more complex, intensely sweet, winey, and honey-like, with a jammy quality that many consider superior to the blander sweetness of the kaki types. As a native plant, Szukis/American persimmon provides exceptional wildlife value: the fruits are eaten by deer, raccoons, foxes, and over 40 bird species. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Sémillon Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Sémillon is a Bordeaux white wine grape best known as the primary variety behind the legendary sweet dessert wines of Sauternes, where its thin skin readily allows infection by Botrytis cinerea, the 'noble rot' fungus that concentrates sugars and adds distinctive honeyed, apricot flavors to the shriveled berries; the same grape also makes excellent dry white wine, often blended with Sauvignon Blanc, with a rounder, waxier, honeyed character. Because the thin skin that enables noble rot production is a liability for growers aiming to make dry wine in humid climates, site selection and vineyard management differ significantly depending on the intended wine style. Train to a permanent trellis, and decide harvest timing based on style: pick at standard ripeness for dry wine, or allow extended hang time under the right humid autumn conditions if noble rot development is the goal. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tabasco Greenleaf Pepper
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed. Bred at Auburn University in the 1970s to replace tobacco-mosaic-susceptible stock, this cultivar produces the same slender, upward-facing, fiery fruit as classic tabasco but on virus-resistant plants, making it a more dependable choice for home growers and small producers. Pods ripen from pale yellow through orange to red, and are traditionally mashed and aged into vinegar-based hot sauce, though they work equally well fresh or dried. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Tabasco Pepper
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and provide consistent heat of 80°F until seedlings emerge. Transplant to well-drained soil in the sunniest garden position, as Capsicum frutescens types thrive with maximum heat accumulation throughout the season. Distinctive erect fruits ripen from yellow-green through yellow and orange to red; harvest at the red stage for the highest capsaicin concentration. Plants are short-lived perennials in frost-free climates and can be overwintered in pots to produce a second heavy crop. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Tabi Coffee (Typica-Bourbon-Timor Hybrid Cross)
description: Tabi is a three-way cross of Typica, Bourbon, and Timor Hybrid released by Cenicafé in 2002; its name means "good" in the Guambiano language of southwestern Colombia. The Timor Hybrid parentage contributes durable resistance to coffee leaf rust, while Bourbon lends sweetness and rounded acidity and Typica adds clarity and refinement to the cup, giving Tabi a reputation for above-average quality among rust-resistant varieties. Cherries are large and elongated, ripening slowly at higher elevations where the extra time on the tree helps build sugars and organic acids. Plants grow taller and more open than dwarf Caturra-type selections, closer in stature to Typica and Bourbon. Provide rich, moist, well-drained soil, filtered shade, and protection from temperatures below 55°F. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Table Ace Acorn Squash
description: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Table Ace is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid acorn squash with a compact, semi-bush habit that takes up considerably less garden space than standard vine-type acorn squash. The dark green, 1–2 pound fruits have the classic acorn shape with ridged skin and deep orange, dry, sweet flesh that pairs well with butter and brown sugar. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail pressure and the underside rind in contact with the soil turns orange; fruits left on the vine too long become fibrous. Store cured fruits in a cool, dry location for up to 3 months. The semi-bush habit makes Table Ace the preferred choice for gardeners who want acorn squash flavor in a space-efficient plant. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Table Gold Acorn Squash (Golden Acorn Squash)
description: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger has passed, and keep plants evenly watered through fruit set for the best flavor. Table Gold was bred by horticulturist Dr. Oved Shifriss, known for his work developing compact bush-type squash, and produces bright golden-yellow acorn-shaped fruit on space-saving vines. The tender flesh has a notably nutty, sweet flavor that distinguishes it from the more common dark-green acorn types. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: Table Grape
description: Table grapes require a robust trellis capable of supporting 15–30 lbs of fruit per vine; the two-wire Kniffin system or a pergola are common choices. Train a permanent trunk and 2–4 fruiting arms during the first 3 years; thereafter, annual dormant pruning should remove 90% of the previous year's growth, leaving spurs or canes with 2–4 buds each. Thin clusters after fruit set to improve berry size and airflow. Harvest when berries reach full color, the tendrils nearest the cluster have dried, and sugar is confirmed by taste. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Table King Acorn Squash
description: Sow Table King seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to the strongest plant every 24 to 36 inches. This All-America Selections winner grows as a compact dwarf bush rather than a sprawling vine, so it fits smaller gardens. It yields dark green, sweet, nutty-flavored acorn squash on tidy plants. Harvest when the rind is hard and dull, cure briefly, and store the fruits for winter meals. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Table King Acorn Winter Squash
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots for an early crop. This bush-type acorn squash matures early on compact four-foot vines, making it great for small gardens, large containers, and short seasons. The fruits offer the rich, sweet flavor of baked winter squash prized on cool autumn days. Water steadily during vine growth and fruit set, then let the rinds harden fully before harvest. Cure and store the squash in a cool, dry place for use through fall and winter. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Table Queen Acorn Squash (Classic Dark-Green Heirloom Acorn Squash)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Table Queen is the classic American acorn squash — an heirloom variety that has defined the acorn squash category since its introduction in the 1890s and remains one of the most widely recognized winter squash forms in American cooking. The deeply ribbed, dark-green to nearly black fruits (1.5–2 lb, 4–6 inches long) have dense, golden-yellow, sweet flesh with a nutty, slightly dry texture that is outstanding for baking: cut in half, brush with butter, season with brown sugar and cinnamon, and bake until caramelized — the classic American acorn squash preparation. The deep ribs and dark color are distinctive enough that 'acorn squash' has become synonymous with Table Queen's specific shape. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from season to season. Table Queen stores well for 1–2 months at cool room temperature after proper curing (10 days at 80°F). In zone 9, acorn squash is most reliable as a fall crop (August planting, October–November harvest) — the spring planting often struggles in early summer heat. The fall crop benefits from the cooling temperatures of fall that improve the sweetness and flavor of the flesh. Space plants generously as the vines spread 6–8 feet in all directions. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Table Star Acorn Squash (AAS-Winning Semi-Bush Acorn Squash)
description: Direct sow in hills after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants for the semi-bush habit rather than a full sprawling vine. Table Star won an All-America Selections award for combining a compact plant with an unusually high yield of dark green, deeply ribbed acorn squash, often setting more fruit per plant than older acorn varieties while reaching harvest earlier in the season. The sweet, fine-grained orange flesh is well suited to roasting halves or stuffing, and the smaller plant footprint makes it a good fit for raised beds. Harvest once the rind has darkened fully and the underside patch has turned from white to yellow-orange, then use within a couple of months since acorn types are not long-term keepers. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Table Top Ground Cherry
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil after danger of frost has passed. Table Top was selected for a low, mounding, self-supporting habit that stays far more contained than the wide-sprawling growth typical of ground cherries, so it fits neatly into small raised beds or a large patio pot without staking. Plants still bear the same small, sweet-tart, husk-wrapped golden fruits and drop them naturally when ripe, so spread a light mulch or row cover beneath plants to make gathering the fallen fruit easier and cleaner. Productive over a long summer season; pinch off any wayward stems if an especially neat, dwarf profile is wanted for container growing. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Tacaco
description: Grow tacaco exactly as you would chayote, since the two are close cucurbit relatives: plant a mature fruit on its side with the stem end barely covered in warm, rich, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, and train the vigorous climbing vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor. This species is essentially endemic to Costa Rica's highlands, with a small range extending into western Panama, and is almost never found outside that region, so homegrown or specialty seed stock is the main way to obtain it. The small, oval green fruit, only about three inches long, is harvested immature and boiled, giving a flavor often compared to a blend of zucchini and avocado with nutty undertones; the young shoots and leaves are eaten as greens as well. Like chayote, tacaco is a frost-tender perennial vine that resprouts from its root each year in frost-free gardens, though it remains a little-known, underexploited crop even in its home range. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Tadorna Leek (Cold-Hardy Fall and Winter Leek)
description: Start Tadorna leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or start seed in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Tadorna is a dependable open-pollinated leek that produces long, thick, blue-green stalks with excellent cold tolerance, standing well in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough or bitter, and shows good resistance to common leek diseases. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, Tadorna can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Tafarikela Coffee (Ethiopian Rust-Resistance Landrace)
description: Tafarikela is a heirloom Arabica landrace selected from wild and semi-wild coffee populations in Ethiopia, the species' center of origin, and long valued locally for its durable field tolerance rather than any single showcase trait. Indian coffee researchers crossed it with the Kent selection to breed S795, one of the most widely planted Arabica cultivars across South India and Southeast Asia, making Tafarikela an important but rarely cultivated-by-name ancestor behind that lineage. Rather than being sold as a distinct commercial cultivar, it survives mainly in Ethiopian farm gardens and germplasm collections maintained for coffee breeding. Grow it like other tall heirloom Arabica types, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade with steady warmth and moisture. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tah Tsai
description: Direct sow in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Tah Tsai (also spelled Tatsoi or Ta Tsai, Brassica narinosa or B. rapa var. rosularis) is an Asian brassica that forms a distinctive flat, ground-hugging rosette of dark green, spoon-shaped leaves radiating outward from the center — an almost architectural form entirely unlike the upright habit of bok choy or komatsuna. The very dark, glossy leaves have a mild flavor similar to spinach with a gentle mustardy note, making Tah Tsai one of the most versatile winter greens for raw use in salads, baby green mixes, braising, and stir-fries. The flat rosette form protects the growing center from frost and allows Tah Tsai to survive temperatures that would kill most other leafy greens — down to 10–15°F. In zone 9 it is one of the most reliably productive cool-season greens, thriving through the entire fall-winter-spring season from September sowing through April before bolting in summer heat. The flat habit allows it to grow in partial shade beneath other plants in the fall garden. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Tahitian Melon Squash (Tahitian Butternut)
description: Tahitian Melon Squash grows a huge, pale blue-green, club-shaped fruit that can reach 2 feet long and 20-plus pounds, with dense, deep orange flesh notably lower in fiber and sweeter than most butternut types, closer in eating quality to a sweet potato. The extremely long, vigorous vines need generous space or a strong trellis to support the developing fruit off the ground. Despite its huge size, a single fruit stores well for months and yields a lot of smooth, easily pureed flesh for soups and baking. A conversation-piece squash for gardeners with room to let vines ramble and a taste for very sweet, low-fiber winter squash. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Tahitian Spinach
description: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; Tahitian spinach (arrowleaf elephant ear, belembe) is a South American tropical aroid grown throughout the Pacific Islands, Caribbean, and tropical Africa as an important leafy vegetable — the large, glossy, arrow-shaped, deep-green leaves are regularly harvested and prepared like spinach or taro leaves: briefly cooked (the raw leaves contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals that disappear with cooking) in soups, stews, coconut milk curries, and as a wilted side vegetable. A mature plant can produce a steady supply of large, nutritious leaves throughout the warm season. It is one of the most productive leafy green vegetables for hot, humid, partially shaded growing conditions, thriving in the summer heat and partial shade that would cause spinach, chard, and most temperate leafy greens to bolt and fail. The plants spread by underground rhizomes and produce offsets that extend the colony. In zone 9–10 it is often frozen back in winter but regrows from the rhizomes in spring. An underused and highly productive tropical leafy vegetable for zone 9–12 edible gardens. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Tahitian Vanilla (Tahiti Vanilla)
description: Root stem cuttings containing 3–4 nodes in moist, organic, fast-draining medium in part shade; hand-pollinate the flowers as they open; harvest beans after 9 months on vine when tips turn yellow. Vanilla tahitensis (Tahitian vanilla) is a separate species from the dominant commercial vanilla (Vanilla planifolia) — distinguished botanically and aromatically by several key differences: the beans are shorter, plumper, and contain more moisture; the primary aromatic compound is heliotropin (piperonal) — a floral, anise-cherry compound — rather than the vanillin-dominated aroma of V. planifolia; and the overall scent profile of Tahitian vanilla beans is more complex, fruity, and intensely floral, with distinctive cherry, anise, and licorice notes absent from Mexican or Madagascar vanilla. These aromatic differences have made Tahitian vanilla the preferred choice of French pastry chefs and many gourmet bakers for delicate preparations where the distinctive floral complexity can shine — French vanilla ice cream, pastry creams, and fine chocolates. Tahitian vanilla is grown primarily in Tahiti and French Polynesia, with smaller production in Papua New Guinea. Like V. planifolia, V. tahitensis requires hand-pollination in cultivation outside its native range, as the natural pollinators (specific bees and hummingbirds) are absent. The vine climbs strongly on trees or supports in humid tropical conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tai Guo Bitter Melon
description: A widely grown Chinese-type hybrid bitter melon producing large, cylindrical, glossy dark-green fruit with thick, crisp flesh, typically 9-11 inches long and up to 3 inches across, with individual fruits often weighing a pound or more. Its size and thick walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and to the stir-fries and braises common in Cantonese and other Chinese preparations, where the mild-to-moderate bitterness pairs with garlic, black bean sauce, or egg. The vigorous vine grows quickly in hot weather and benefits from a tall, sturdy trellis to support both its rampant growth and the weight of the large fruit. Harvest while the skin is still firm, glossy, and fully dark green, before any yellowing begins, for the best texture and flavor. Matures in 50–55 days from transplant.

name: Tainung Papaya (Tainung No. 1, Taiwan Papaya)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting or sow directly in warm soil in full sun after frost; Tainung No. 1 ('TN1') is a bisexual F1 hybrid papaya developed by the Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute that has become the leading papaya variety in Taiwan and is widely grown throughout East and Southeast Asia for its combination of early bearing, excellent fruit quality, and bisexual flower type that allows single-plant fruiting. The compact trees (8–14 feet) begin fruiting at a very low trunk height (1–2 feet from the ground), allowing easy harvest and a shorter time from planting to first fruit than many papaya varieties. Fruits are medium-large (2–4 pounds), oblong-cylindrical, with moderately thick yellow-orange skin and deeply orange to salmon flesh with high sugar content (Brix 12–14°), excellent fragrance, and small seed cavity. Tainung No. 1 has reasonable tolerance of cooler subtropical conditions and is less sensitive to temperature fluctuations than some papaya varieties, making it a useful choice for zone 9 where temperatures occasionally drop in winter; the tree is killed by frost but seeds easily and can be replanted each year as a productive warm-season fruiting crop in frost-marginal climates. Matures in 210–330 days from seed.

name: Taioba (White Yautía, Caracu Cocoyam)
description: Plant in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to sun. Xanthosoma caracu is the source of most white-fleshed cultivated tannia in the Caribbean, distinguished from the yellow-orange-fleshed corms of X. atrovirens and X. sagittifolium and the deep purple petioles of X. violaceum already in this dataset by its numerous grey-brown, club-shaped corms with pale white flesh. Its glossy, bluish-green leaves with paler undersides are themselves an important vegetable in Brazil, where young leaves are chopped and simmered as the traditional dish taioba, in addition to the corm harvest used across Mexico, the Caribbean, and northern South America. Cook both leaves and corms thoroughly, as with all Xanthosoma, to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals before eating. Matures in 210–300 days from transplant.

name: Taishu Persimmon (Early-Ripening Pear-Textured Non-Astringent Persimmon)
description: Taishu produces medium to large oblate fruit with pale golden-orange flesh that stays crisp and dense even at full ripeness, giving it a pear-like bite rather than the jelly-soft texture of astringent types. Because it is pollination-constant non-astringent, the fruit can be eaten firm straight off the tree without any bletting period, and it typically carries just two or three small seeds. The tree bears young and ripens earlier than Fuyu, helping spread out the harvest window for growers who already have later persimmon cultivars. Its modest chill requirement and tolerance of humid summers make it a strong low-chill choice for zone 9a gardens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Taiwanese Flat Cabbage (A Choy, Chinese Flat Cabbage)
description: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or direct sow in fall for cool-season production; Taiwanese flat cabbage is a classic East Asian cabbage variety producing distinctly flat, wide, loosely-structured heads (12–16 inches in diameter but only 4–6 inches tall) with extremely tender, delicate leaves — a completely different texture and flavor experience from the dense, hard European round-head cabbages. The tender leaves are less pungent and more delicate than round cabbage, with a slightly sweet, mild flavor that holds up beautifully in quick-cooked preparations like stir-fries, hot pots, and braised dishes, while also working well in fresh preparations like slaws and salads. The flat shape and loose construction mean the heads do not store as long as round types but they are extraordinarily tender and pleasant to eat. Very popular in Taiwanese and Chinese fresh markets, restaurant kitchens, and among Asian-American home gardeners; the quick maturation (60–80 days from transplant) and cool-season preference make it an excellent fall-to-spring crop in the Gulf South. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Takanotsume Pepper (Japanese Hawk's Claw Chile)
description: Named for its resemblance to a hawk's talon, Takanotsume is a small, slender Japanese chile that sets fruit pointing upward in dense clusters rather than hanging, distinguishing it from similar Japanese types like Santaka. Fruits ripen from green to bright red and carry moderate heat with a clean, fruity flavor, historically dried for storage and ground into shichimi togarashi and other spice blends. Grow it like other hot peppers in full sun with even moisture, and harvest red for maximum heat and the best drying results; whole dried pods keep well for months. Its compact habit and heavy, ornamental fruit set make it a good choice for containers and small gardens. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Tall Hairy Agrimony
description: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tall hairy agrimony is the most common of the native North American agrimonies — a tall, erect perennial with pinnately compound leaves and slender, tapering spikes of small yellow flowers throughout summer. The entire plant is covered in soft, spreading hairs (glandular on the stems), giving it a pleasantly tactile, soft-textured appearance. The distinctive burr-like fruits with hooked hooks cling readily to clothing and animal fur — a classic hitchhiker in the summer garden. Like European agrimony (A. eupatoria), the native species has a long history in traditional American herbal medicine as an astringent herb used for throat conditions, wounds, and digestive complaints. The dried herbage makes a pleasant, slightly astringent, aromatic tea. An excellent low-maintenance native for naturalized, semi-wild garden areas and hedgerow plantings. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Talladega Tomato
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Talladega is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces large harvests of smooth, firm, 8–10 ounce red globe tomatoes with excellent shelf life and crack resistance. It was bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid South, where disease pressure from early blight, grey leaf spot, and bacterial spot is severe — Talladega carries broad disease resistance that keeps foliage healthy through the summer months when other varieties defoliate. The concentrated fruiting habit of this determinate variety makes it easy to time a large harvest for canning or preserving. Fall plantings in late July–early August often produce the heaviest yields as the fruits ripen into the cooler October–November weather. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Tallahatchie Pawpaw (Low-Seed Peterson Pawpaw Selection)
description: Plant in partial shade while young, transitioning the tree into full sun as it matures, and site alongside a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar since Tallahatchie will not set fruit on its own. Selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from a seedling growing in his Maryland research orchard, Tallahatchie produces medium-large fruit averaging around 9 ounces with an unusually low seed content and a smooth, silky texture that has made it a favorite for pawpaw ice cream and custard. Its floral, mellow flavor ripens mid-to-late season, and the tree tends to set fruit in generous clusters of five or more, so growers in warm zone 7-8 gardens may want to thin heavy clusters for more even ripening. Give it deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during establishment, since pawpaw's fleshy taproot resents both drought and transplant disturbance. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Talpiot Artichoke (Israeli-Bred Annual Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Talpiot is an Israeli-bred F1 hybrid developed alongside Tavor for seed-propagated, first-year annual production, forming a large, vigorous, spineless plant that sets medium green buds over a long harvest window. It shares the strong heat tolerance of other Israeli annual artichoke selections, making it a dependable choice for hot-summer growing regions, and continues to push side buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the season and cut buds while the scales are still tight, before they begin to loosen and spread. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: TAM Dew Melon (Texas A&M Downy Mildew-Resistant Honeydew)
description: TAM Dew was released by Texas A&M's melon breeding program to give southern growers a honeydew with better resistance to downy mildew than older honeydew varieties, which historically struggled in humid southern conditions. Vines carry smooth, creamy-white rinds around thick, sweet, light green flesh on fruit that typically run 4-6 pounds at harvest. Like other honeydew types it does not slip from the vine, so watch for the rind to shift from a hard green-white to a softer creamy yellow-white and the blossom end to yield slightly to gentle pressure. Give it the full length of a hot summer and consistent moisture through fruit sizing for the best sugar content at harvest. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper (Texas A&M Mild Jalapeño)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. TAM Jalapeño-1 was developed by Texas A&M University's pepper breeding program in cooperation with the USDA and released in 1992 specifically for the commercial food processing industry, which required a jalapeño with the characteristic jalapeño flavor, uniform size (3–4 inches), and appearance for use in products like jalapeño poppers, nachos, and salsas — but without enough heat to cause consumer complaints when consumed in quantity. The resulting variety has the same thick, meaty walls, dark green color, and characteristic jalapeño aroma as standard jalapeños but only 400–1,500 SHU (compared to 2,500–8,000 SHU in standard varieties), making it easily tolerable for most heat-sensitive individuals. TAM Jalapeño is an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want to grow their own jalapeños for cooking without excessive heat, and for making fresh salsa, pico de gallo, and pickled jalapeños accessible to children and heat-sensitive family members. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper (Texas A&M Mild Jalapeño, Low-Heat Jalapeño)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; TAM Jalapeño is compact, productive, and easy to grow as a warm-season annual in any vegetable garden. TAM Mild Jalapeño I is a Texas A&M University release (developed in 1992 by the university's vegetable breeding program) that addressed a specific and widely held preference: many cooks and eaters want the distinctive fresh, grassy jalapeño flavor that defines Tex-Mex and Southwestern cooking without the significant heat of a standard jalapeño. Standard jalapeños test at 2,500–8,000 Scoville Heat Units — enough to be noticeably and persistently hot for heat-sensitive eaters; TAM Jalapeño measures approximately 1,000–3,500 SHU, a 70–80% reduction in heat while retaining the characteristic jalapeño aroma and flavor profile. The fruits are indistinguishable from standard jalapeños in size and appearance — medium-large (3–4 inches), dark green to red, thick-walled, and blocky — making them ideal for all jalapeño applications where the full flavor is wanted without the burning heat: nachos, salsa, pickled jalapeños (called escabeche), jalapeño poppers, and fresh eating. TAM Jalapeño is widely grown in Texas for processing and fresh market and has developed a devoted following among home gardeners who cook frequently with jalapeños and want to moderate the heat for family members of different heat tolerances. Very productive plants with a long harvest window from green through red ripeness. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Tam Kam Persimmon (Very Sweet Non-Astringent Korean Persimmon)
description: Tam Kam is a non-astringent (PCNA) Asian persimmon originating from Sunchow in Korea; its name translates roughly as 'very sweet,' a fair description of the flat-lobed, deep orange fruit, which can be eaten crisp and firm straight off the tree with none of the puckering astringency of the astringent-type kaki cultivars. It is an early-ripening, high-yielding, essentially seedless cultivar on a medium-sized tree, with leaves that turn a bright orange in fall. Because it does not need to soften before eating, Tam Kam is convenient for fresh eating and easy to judge for ripeness by color and firmness alone. Grow in full sun with good drainage; the tree is self-fertile and productive without a second persimmon for pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: TAM Mild Jalapeno Pepper (Low-Heat Texas A&M Jalapeno)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, and harvest fruit at any stage from glossy dark green through fully ripe red. TAM Mild Jalapeno was developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife breeding program specifically to lower the capsaicin content of a standard jalapeno to a mild 500-2,500 Scoville units, roughly a tenth the heat of a typical jalapeno, while keeping the same thick-walled, classic jalapeno shape, size, and flavor that makes it useful for salsas, poppers, and pickling. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate Southern heat well, though heat and moisture stress can occasionally nudge individual peppers hotter than the variety's baseline. It's a good choice for gardeners, and especially families with children, who want the jalapeno's flavor and crunch without much of its punch. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.
