name: Tamarillo (Tree Tomato)
description: Start seeds in warm, moist potting mix at 75–80°F and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from cold wind and afternoon heat; tamarillos are frost-sensitive but also dislike sustained temperatures above 90°F, thriving best in cool subtropical climates such as coastal California, highland tropics, or mild maritime zone 10. The smooth-skinned red or yellow egg-shaped fruits ripen 18 months from seed and have a rich, complex flavor — tangy and tomato-like — excellent in salsa, chutneys, smoothies, and cooked dishes. Shallow roots make the tree drought-sensitive; water deeply but infrequently. Prune after harvest to maintain a manageable 6–8 foot height. Matures in 540–730 days from seed.

name: Tamarind
description: Tamarind is a massive, long-lived tropical tree that can take 6–8 years from seed or 3–5 years from grafted stock to begin bearing the distinctive hard-shelled brown pods. It is self-fertile and thrives in hot, dry conditions; it is one of the most drought-tolerant tropical fruit trees. The interior pulp surrounding the seeds is intensely sour when young and sweet-sour when fully ripe; pods are harvested when the shell is brittle and the pulp is sticky, fibrous, and deep brown. Trees require no significant pruning and are largely pest-free in the continental U.S.; remove only dead or crossing wood. Matures in 2190–4380 days from transplant.

name: Tamopan Persimmon (Large Ringed Chinese Astringent Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Tamopan is a distinctive Chinese persimmon cultivar known for its unusually large size and a visible constriction ring around the middle of the fruit that gives it a pumpkin- or acorn-like shape unlike most other persimmons. The deep orange fruit is strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point the flesh becomes sweet, thick, and custard-like, well suited to fresh eating and baking. The tree is vigorous and productive, and because individual fruits can grow quite large and heavy, thinning excess fruit helps prevent broken branches in a heavy year. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tampa Grape Rootstock (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Florida Bunch Grape Understock)
description: Tampa is a rootstock selection bred at the University of Florida's grape breeding program specifically to address Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by glassy-winged sharpshooters and other leafhoppers that has historically made growing many bunch grape varieties on their own roots impractical across Florida and the Gulf South. Grafted onto Tampa, susceptible fruiting cultivars such as Orlando Seedless gain meaningfully better tolerance of Pierce's disease along with the vigor needed to perform in Florida's warm, humid growing conditions and sandy native soils. It is used alongside the similarly bred Dog Ridge (Dogridge) rootstock as one of the standard understock choices for Florida bunch grape production, with growers choosing between the two largely on vigor and soil-type compatibility rather than fruit-quality differences, since the rootstock itself bears no fruit of horticultural interest. Bench-graft or bud a named bunch grape cultivar onto young Tampa rootstock in late winter or spring, and grow on in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tampiqueno Serrano Pepper (Classic Mexican Hot Serrano)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Tampiqueno is a widely grown, classic serrano pepper cultivar producing small, slender, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to red, packing more heat than jalapeno in a smaller package, and used extensively fresh in salsas, pico de gallo, and other Mexican dishes where a bright, grassy heat is wanted. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate heat well, making serrano peppers one of the more reliable hot pepper choices for Gulf South gardens. Harvest pods at any stage of ripeness, though full red pods have somewhat more sweetness alongside the heat. Matures in 65–85 days from transplant.

name: Tampoi (Greater Tampoi, Kapul)
description: Tampoi is a small to medium Bornean rainforest tree grown for its golden-yellow, spherical fruit borne in small clusters directly on the trunk and branches, each containing soft, juicy, off-white flesh ranging from sweet to pleasantly sour. As an understory species of humid lowland forest, it grows best in the dappled or partial shade of taller trees rather than in open, exposed sun, and needs rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil to thrive. Trees begin fruiting within two to three years of planting and require relatively little maintenance beyond regular watering during dry spells and periodic light fertilizing. Harvest fruit clusters once the skin turns fully golden-yellow and gives slightly to pressure, and eat the fresh pulp out of hand, since tampoi does not ship or store well. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tan Cheese Pumpkin
description: One of the oldest documented American pumpkin varieties, dating to before 1824, this heirloom produces a flattened, wheel-of-cheese shaped fruit with smooth tan skin and moderate ribbing. Sow directly in hills after the soil warms, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling vines. Fruit is ready when the rind hardens and takes on a uniform tan color; harvest with several inches of stem attached. The deep orange flesh is dense, sweet, and stores exceptionally well through winter, making it a reliable keeper for pies and baking. Matures in 105–115 days from seed.

name: Tanaka Loquat (Large Late-Ripening Japanese Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tanaka is a classic Japanese loquat cultivar, long regarded as a benchmark variety in Japanese and California loquat breeding for its large, rounded, russet-orange fruit and firm, sweet, mildly tangy flesh. It ripens later than most other loquat cultivars — typically extending the harvest into late spring — which makes it a valuable companion to earlier-ripening selections for growers wanting a longer fresh-loquat season. The fruit holds well on the tree without over-softening, giving some flexibility in harvest timing compared to more delicate cultivars. Trees are vigorous and moderately cold-hardy for a subtropical fruit, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once established, though open flowers and young fruit are damaged by hard freezes — plant in a warm microclimate in zone 8 for the most reliable crops. Thin heavy fruit clusters to two or three fruits per cluster shortly after fruit set to improve individual fruit size. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tanenashi Persimmon (Large Seedless Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tanenashi is the most widely planted Japanese persimmon cultivar in the American South — an astringent persimmon variety that produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly conical, bright orange-red fruits without seeds when grown without pollination. The seedless quality is one of Tanenashi's most important practical attributes — all commercial packing persimmons are seedless, and home-garden fresh eating quality improves without seeds in the soft, jellylike flesh. As an astringent persimmon, Tanenashi must be fully ripe (soft, completely yielding to pressure, like a water balloon) before eating or the tannins create an unpleasant mouth-puckering sensation; picking at the orange-red but still-firm stage and allowing to ripen at room temperature completes the conversion. The rich, sweet, pumpkin-like flavor of a fully ripe Tanenashi has no equivalent in temperate fruits. In zone 9, Tanenashi ripens in October through November and is one of the finest fall orchard fruits for the Gulf South — virtually pest-free, drought-tolerant once established, and producing heavily within 3–5 years of planting. The tree itself is ornamental: attractive dark-green summer foliage, spectacular orange-red fruit display in fall, and good fall foliage color before leaf drop. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Tangelo
description: The tangelo is a juicy, loose-skinned cross between a mandarin and a grapefruit or pomelo, often bearing a distinctive neck at the stem. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil in a frost-protected location, and note that some cultivars set better crops with a pollinizer nearby. Water deeply and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Harvest when the fruit is fully colored and heavy with juice, typically from midwinter onward. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tango Celery (Compact Disease-Resistant Modern Celery)
description: Start seed indoors well ahead of transplanting, since celery germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before warm weather arrives. Tango is a modern celery cultivar bred for compact size, crisp, stringless stalks, and good resistance to common celery diseases that plague older cultivars in humid climates, producing dark green, flavorful stalks over a somewhat shorter growing season than heirloom types. Consistent, even soil moisture is essential throughout the growing season, since celery stalks turn stringy and bitter under moisture stress. In hot-summer regions it does best as a fall or early spring crop rather than attempting to carry it through peak summer heat, since celery bolts and becomes bitter in prolonged high temperatures. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Tango Lettuce (Frilly Deeply-Cut Green Leaf Lettuce)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Tango produces densely frilled, deeply cut, curly bright green leaves that hold up well as a cut-and-come-again crop, regrowing quickly after repeated light harvests for baby leaf salads and mesclun mixes. Its crisp, mild flavor and attractive ruffled texture make it a popular addition to mixed salad greens, and it tolerates cool weather well, making it a strong choice for both an early spring and a fall crop in zone 8-9 gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head an inch above the crown to allow regrowth for a second and sometimes third harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Tango Mandarin (Seedless Afourer-Type UC Riverside Mandarin)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Tango, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, is a seedless sport of the popular Afourer (W. Murcott) mandarin, bred specifically to stay seedless even when planted near other citrus, unlike its parent which becomes seedy from cross-pollination, while retaining the same rich, sweet-tart flavor and easy-peel skin. It ripens in winter, providing fresh citrus during the cooler months. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tangor
description: A tangor is a mandarin-sweet orange hybrid, combining easy peeling with rich, full orange flavor. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and protect it from frost, which readily damages leaves and fruit. Apply a balanced citrus feed in spring and summer and mulch to conserve soil moisture. Harvest when fully colored and sweet, and prune lightly after cropping to remove crossing or weak wood. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tanner Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Early-Harvest Desirable Replacement Pecan)
description: Tanner was released by the University of Georgia in 2015 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Wichita and Pawnee, one of three scab-resistant Desirable replacements developed alongside Huffman and Whiddon. It produces a large, slightly oblong nut, 40-45 per pound, with 52-55% kernel, harvesting early, around September 20 in south Georgia trials, similar to Byrd and Treadwell. Field evaluations describe scab resistance as good in well-cared-for orchards and superior to Desirable's, though testing has been more limited than for the older standard cultivars. Tanner sets relatively few nuts per cluster, which growers report reduces the need for hand-thinning; as a Type I pollen shedder it should be planted with a Type II cultivar such as Lakota nearby. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Tansy
description: Plant divisions in any well-drained soil in full sun; tansy is a vigorous, drought-tolerant perennial that spreads by rhizome and can become invasive — site it where its spread can be managed or grow it in a contained bed. The finely cut, strongly aromatic foliage contains thujone, which is toxic in large doses, so tansy should not be consumed internally and should be handled with care. Harvest leafy stems and flat-topped clusters of button-like yellow flowers throughout summer for use as a traditional insect-repelling strewing herb, moth-deterring sachets, and companion-planting aromatic barriers. Deadhead promptly to reduce the copious self-seeding that can make tansy weedy in favorable conditions. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Tar Heel Pole Bean
description: Tar Heel is an old pole bean reportedly carried west by North Carolina natives from the Jackson/Haywood county area who migrated to Washington state for timber work around the turn of the twentieth century, taking on the Tar Heel name in honor of that origin. The vigorous climbing vines are heavy yielders of five to six inch, flattened pods that bulge as the seeds inside develop, with a hearty, old-fashioned flavor reminiscent of a greasy bean even though the pod surface itself is not shiny. It is a good pick for gardeners who want a traditional pole snap bean with real heirloom character rather than a modern high-production hybrid. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Tara Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Tara is a University of Georgia-released bronze muscadine grown for its consistently high fruit quality — large, uniform, golden-bronze berries with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a relatively tender skin — combined with a self-fertile, productive vine that bears reliably without a separate pollinator variety. It ripens earlier in the season than many bronze muscadines, extending the harvest window when planted alongside later-ripening varieties, and the fruit holds well on the vine without excessive cracking or splitting in humid weather. Widely recommended for both fresh eating and home winemaking, Tara is a strong choice for a Gulf South home muscadine planting, zone 7–9. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tara Rabbiteye Blueberry (Early-Season Light-Blue Blueberry)
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to retain the consistent soil moisture rabbiteye blueberries need for good fruit size. Tara is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release prized for its early ripening and consistently light, sky-blue berries with excellent flavor and a small, dry picking scar that resists splitting and leaking, an important trait for fresh-market and pick-your-own plantings. The bush is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the sandy, acidic soils of the Gulf South, extending the early end of the rabbiteye blueberry season when planted alongside later-ripening cultivars. Plant with a second compatible rabbiteye variety for good cross-pollination, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Taraw Palm
description: Plant Taraw Palm in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; water regularly during establishment and in dry seasons; young plants tolerate partial shade for the first few years; mature palms are self-cleaning (old fronds drop cleanly) and require no pruning. Livistona saribus is among the larger and more majestic members of the Livistona genus — the widespread Asian fan palm group represented in cultivation by the Chinese Fan Palm (L. chinensis) and Australian Fan Palm (L. australis). The Taraw Palm develops a single straight gray-brown trunk up to 40–80 feet tall, topped by a graceful crown of large, deeply divided fan leaves whose drooping tips give the crown a characteristic pendulous, elegant character. A fast grower by palm standards in good conditions, it is widely used as a landscape palm in Southeast Asian cities and is gaining favor in zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical gardens globally. In its native range, the leaves are traditionally harvested for weaving baskets, mats, and hats; the blue-black clustered fruits are eaten by local wildlife and occasionally by people as a minor food. An excellent large specimen palm for tropical gardens where a dramatic, fountain-crowned palm silhouette is desired. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Tarbais Bean (Classic French Cassoulet Bean)
description: Sow after last frost near a trellis, fence, or tall pole in full sun; Tarbais is the classic French heirloom bean of Gascon cuisine, historically grown climbing up corn stalks in the countryside around Tarbes in southwestern France, and it is the traditional bean specified in authentic cassoulet, the slow-cooked white bean and meat casserole of the region. The dry beans are creamy white, thin-skinned, and known for cooking up exceptionally tender and creamy while holding their shape, absorbing the rich flavors of the pork, duck, and sausage traditionally simmered with them in cassoulet. While best known dried, pods can also be picked earlier at the plump green shell-bean stage for a more delicate fresh bean dish. Let pods mature and dry fully on the vine for the classic dry-bean harvest, picking before fall rains can cause mold, and finish drying indoors in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Tardivo Radicchio
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tardivo is the most prized and most expensive radicchio in Italy — a Treviso-type radicchio that requires a traditional forcing process in which the plants are dug after fall frosts, packed in darkness, and allowed to produce elongated, curved white-and-red leaf chicons resembling a firework spray or an open hand. The resulting forced Tardivo heads have long, narrow, spoon-shaped, curling red-and-white leaves with a dramatic, sculptural appearance that makes them a luxury vegetable in Italian restaurants and specialty markets — they are served raw in salads, grilled whole, braised, or used as striking garnishes. The bittersweet flavor is the most refined of all radicchio types, with the forcing process reducing bitterness while concentrating sweetness. Tardivo commands the highest price of any radicchio in Italian markets; in home gardens the complex forcing requirement is rewarded with a genuinely special vegetable unlike any other readily available. Matures in 100–130 days from transplant.

name: Tarminiana Banana Passionfruit (Curuba, Tacso)
description: This high-elevation Andean vine produces elongated, bright yellow fruit filled with aromatic orange pulp, prized in Colombia and Ecuador for juice and desserts under the name curuba. It was only recently split taxonomically from the closely related Passiflora tripartita var. mollissima and Passiflora mollissima, and it struggles in prolonged summer heat, preferring a cool-summer or high-elevation subtropical climate. Give it a sturdy arbor or fence, humus-rich soil, and consistent moisture, and expect the first fruit roughly one to one-and-a-half years after planting a rooted cutting or seedling. Because it can naturalize aggressively in mild, moist climates, check local invasive-species lists before planting. Matures in 270–540 days from transplant.

name: Taro
description: Plant small cormels or divided corm sections 2–4 inches deep in deep, organic-rich, consistently wet to moist soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost risk has passed and soil temperatures exceed 70°F; taro tolerates and even thrives in standing water, making it suitable for rain gardens, swales, and pond edges. Colocasia esculenta is one of the world's oldest cultivated crops, grown throughout tropical Asia, the Pacific Islands, Africa, and the Caribbean for its starchy, edible corms — all parts of the raw plant contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense oral irritation, so corms and leaves must always be thoroughly cooked (boiling, steaming, or roasting for at least 30–45 minutes) before eating. The corms are the source of Hawaiian poi, taro chips, and cocoyam fufu, and have a distinctive, pleasantly earthy, slightly sweet, starchy flavor; the large, dramatic, heart-shaped leaves are used in Pacific Island cooking as wrappers (lau lau) and are edible after extended cooking. In zones 8b–9, plants may survive a mild winter with heavy mulching over the crown but should be treated as annuals in cooler climates, with corms lifted and stored above 50°F after the first frost. Matures in 180–210 days from transplant.

name: Tarocco Blood Orange (Italian Half-Blood Sweet Orange)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above freezing, in full sun with deep, well-drained soil. Water deeply and consistently through the growing season, and expect the best red pigmentation where winter nights are cool but frost-free, as in coastal and inland California valleys. Tarocco fruit is nearly seedless with tender, aromatic flesh streaked or fully blushed red-purple and a flavor prized for its balance of sweetness and berry-like tang. It is considered the finest-flavored of the widely grown blood oranges but is more cold-sensitive than standard sweet oranges. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tarwi (Andean Lupin, Pearl Lupin)
description: Sow in well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; tarwi is a highland Andean lupin domesticated in Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador thousands of years ago and grown as a protein- and oil-rich grain legume, with seed protein content rivaling soybean. The plant produces attractive blue-to-purple pea-family flower spikes followed by pods containing pale, disc-shaped seeds that are intensely bitter and contain alkaloids in their raw state, requiring a traditional debittering process before eating — seeds are boiled, then soaked in several changes of running or repeatedly refreshed water for several days until the bitterness is leached out, after which they are eaten much like a lupini bean, added to soups and stews, or ground into flour. Like other lupins, the deep taproot fixes atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil fertility, and the plant tolerates poor, thin mountain soils and considerable drought once established. Harvest pods once they dry and rattle, then thresh and process the seed before use; never eat the raw, unprocessed seed, as the alkaloid content can be harmful undiluted. Matures in 150–210 days from seed.

name: Tasmanian Chocolate Tomato (Purple-Black Dwarf Beefsteak)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking to support the plant as it can grow taller than most dwarf-indeterminate releases. Tasmanian Chocolate bears oblate, beefsteak-style fruit in a deep purple-black hue with well-balanced, rich flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes. It resulted from a 2006 cross of New Big Dwarf and Paul Robeson made by Patrina Nuske Small in Australia, selected and named by Linda Reid of Tasmania, and released through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Tasmanian Waxberry
description: Tasmanian waxberry is an upright evergreen understory shrub from the cool temperate rainforests of Tasmania, bearing small white spring flowers followed by plump, waxy-white to pale pink berries that were eaten fresh by Tasmanian Aboriginal peoples and remain a foraged bush food today. The berries have a mild, watery-sweet flavor and are best enjoyed fresh rather than processed. As a true rainforest-floor species it needs the cool, humid, sheltered conditions of a shaded woodland garden with consistently moist, acidic soil and protection from drought and strong sun, making it a good companion for rhododendrons and other broadleaf evergreens. Mulch annually with leaf litter or pine bark to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and avoid any hint of summer drought, which quickly stresses the shallow root system. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tasti-Lee Tomato (University of Florida High-Lycopene Red Slicing Tomato with Superior Flavor)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red-orange and gives to slight pressure. Tasti-Lee Tomato was released by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) around 2010, developed through a breeding program that specifically targeted the combination of high lycopene content, improved flavor, and Gulf South disease resistance in a single red slicing tomato variety. The UF/IFAS vegetable breeding program, one of the most active in the southeastern United States, has produced multiple important commercial tomato varieties for Florida's significant commercial tomato industry; Tasti-Lee represents a branch of that program targeting quality attributes (flavor, nutrition) rather than the shipping durability and uniformity that commercial Florida tomato breeding has primarily emphasized. The variety's elevated lycopene content — documented by UF/IFAS researchers as substantially higher than industry-standard slicing tomatoes — combined with higher-than-typical sugar content and genuine tomato flavor creates a profile closer to the flavor of a well-grown heirloom tomato than most disease-resistant hybrid varieties provide. The variety has been noted by home gardeners and researchers for producing genuinely good-flavored tomatoes in zone 9's challenging summer heat, a combination difficult to achieve with either heirloom varieties (which lack disease resistance) or standard commercial varieties (which sacrifice flavor for durability). Tasti-Lee is sold through specialty seed companies and has been grown for research comparisons confirming its superior flavor and nutritional profile relative to commercial standards. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Tasty Green Cucumber
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots to gain a head start. This Japanese-type cucumber bears slender, long, burpless fruits with thin, sweet, non-bitter skin and very few tiny seeds. Grow the highly productive plants on a trellis to save space and encourage straight, clean fruit. Keep watering even to prevent bitterness and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest frequently while fruits are still young and tender to keep the vines producing. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tasty Jade Cucumber
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Tasty Jade is an AAS Award-winning Asian burpless cucumber hybrid producing very long (10–12 inch), slender, uniformly dark green fruits with thin, tender, virtually seedless flesh and an exceptionally mild, non-bitter flavor. Unlike slicing cucumbers that can be bitter and require peeling, the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content of Tasty Jade makes it excellent for eating without peeling — just wash and slice. The crisp, sweet, mild-flavored fruits are ideal for fresh eating, salads, sushi accompaniments, and quick pickling. Tasty Jade's All-America Selections award recognized its superior flavor, production, and disease resistance compared to competing Asian cucumber types. In zone 9 the vigorous vines produce abundantly in spring and again in fall; summer production may slow during the hottest weeks of July–August but resumes as temperatures moderate in September. Matures in 54–62 days from seed.

name: Tasty Red Fruit Snacks Apple
description: Tasty Red is a narrow, columnar apple that produces sweet, bite-sized red fruit with a refreshing crunch while taking up very little space. Its upright growth habit makes it ideal for containers, patios, and small yards, and several can be planted close together. Set the tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly during establishment. Plant a second apple variety nearby for cross-pollination and better yields. Minimal pruning is needed thanks to the naturally compact columnar form. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tatar Bread Plant (Tartar Crambe)
description: Direct sow into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting the plant permanently since its thick taproot resents transplanting once established. Native to the dry steppes of Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Tatar bread plant produces a large basal clump of blue-green, cabbage-like foliage that can be treated exactly like sea kale — the young spring leaves and emerging shoots are cut and cooked as a potherb, with a flavor milder than cultivated cabbage. What sets it apart from other perennial crambes is its thick, sweet, starchy root: eaten raw in salads, cooked as a root vegetable, or dried and ground into a flour that was historically mixed into bread dough during lean harvests in Russia and Ukraine, which is the origin of the common name. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, thriving on poor, dry soils where few other perennial vegetables persist, and require little more than an annual mulch of compost. Matures in 545–730 days from seed.

name: Tatsoi
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and thin to 6–12 inches for full rosettes; closer spacing produces baby greens for salad mix. Tatsoi forms a flat, ground-hugging rosette of dark spoon-shaped leaves and is remarkably cold-hardy, surviving temperatures into the low 20s°F under row cover. Harvest whole plants when 4–6 inches across or pick outer leaves progressively. Avoid planting in summer as heat causes immediate bolting. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Tatume Squash (Tatuma, Mexican Globe Squash)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; tatume is a traditional Mexican summer squash producing round to slightly oval, smooth, dark green fruits 3–5 inches in diameter that are harvested young (before the rind hardens) for use as a summer squash, or left to mature fully into a yellow-tan winter squash. Young fruits have mild, tender flesh similar to zucchini but firmer and slightly sweeter; mature fruits have dry, pale orange flesh similar to a butternut squash. This dual-use quality, combined with exceptional heat tolerance that keeps plants productive through Texas and Gulf Coast summers when standard zucchini quits, makes tatume one of the most practically useful squash for hot-climate gardeners. Extremely popular in Mexican American communities in Texas, where it is used in caldos, guisados, and stuffed as chiles rellenos de calabaza. The vining plants produce abundantly over a long season. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Taunton Deane Perennial Kale (Cottager's Kale)
description: Set rooted stem cuttings into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake young plants in windy sites; Taunton Deane is a centuries-old English heirloom perennial kale from Somerset, traditionally called cottager's kale for its long history in small kitchen gardens. It develops into a sprawling, thick-stemmed woody shrub that can eventually reach 6-7 feet tall and as wide, distinguishing it from the smaller, more upright Daubenton's kale, yet its leaves stay remarkably tender for such a large plant and are harvested continuously as a cut-and-come-again green. Because it flowers and sets viable seed only rarely, propagation is done almost exclusively by rooting stem cuttings taken any time during the growing season. Prune hard every couple of years to rejuvenate leggy stems and keep the plant productive; in favorable sites a single specimen can supply greens for a decade or more, making it a cornerstone perennial for food forest and permaculture kitchen gardens. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Tavares Limequat (Cold-Hardy Oval Kumquat-Lime Hybrid)
description: Tavares was released in 1913 alongside Eustis and Lakeland as part of Walter Swingle's original USDA limequat introductions, but unlike its round-kumquat-parented siblings, Tavares was crossed from Key lime and oval (Nagami-type) kumquat, giving it a somewhat different fruit shape and rind character. Like other limequats, the whole fruit is edible skin and all, with a tart, aromatic lime-flavored flesh inside a thin, kumquat-sweet rind, useful sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved. It shares the group's strong cold hardiness relative to true limes, tolerating freezes that would seriously damage or kill Key lime or Persian lime trees, though it remains less commonly propagated commercially today than Eustis. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, protect young trees through their first winters, and expect a compact, productive shrub-like tree well suited to large containers or small Gulf Coast garden beds. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tavera Filet Bush Bean
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is warm, planting in rows or blocks for easy picking. This French filet bean, or haricot vert, is at its best when harvested young and slender and picked frequently. The disease-resistant bush plants need no staking and grow well in containers. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set for tender, straight pods. Pick every couple of days at petite size to keep the plants producing over a long window. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Tavor Artichoke (Vigorous Green Annual Hybrid)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Tavor is a vigorous Israeli-bred F1 hybrid selected for heavy, reliable production of medium, tightly closed green buds on a large, upright, spineless plant, and it is widely favored by growers in hot, dry-summer climates for its strong heat tolerance and steady yield of multiple side buds after the central bud is cut. Like other seed-grown annual types it flowers and produces a usable first-year harvest without needing the extended cold vernalization that older perennial varieties require, though a short cool spell after transplanting still improves bud set and uniformity. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the growing season, and cut buds while still tight and firm, well before the scales begin to loosen and spread. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Taxi Tomato (Bright Yellow Early Determinate Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Taxi is a determinate yellow tomato that produces a concentrated crop of uniformly bright taxi-yellow, medium (6–8 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits with a smooth, attractive appearance and mild, sweet, low-acid tomato flavor — the distinctive mellow sweetness typical of most yellow tomatoes, which have lower levels of the malic and citric acids that give red tomatoes their sharpness. The low-acid character makes Taxi an excellent choice for gardeners and eaters who find standard red tomatoes too acidic, for children who prefer milder flavors, and for fresh applications where the visual contrast of bright yellow adds interest to a salad or platter. The meaty flesh has a good firm texture that holds up in sliced presentations without becoming watery. Taxi is practical, productive, and early enough to complete its crop before the worst Gulf South summer heat; its concentrated set makes it useful for batch processing or sharing. A reliable, attractive yellow option for home gardens where some visual and flavor variety beyond standard red tomatoes is desired. Matures in 64–68 days from transplant.

name: Tayberry
description: Tayberry is a Scottish-bred hybrid (blackberry x raspberry) with long, conical, deep purple-red berries that ripen in mid-summer; the flavor is richer and sweeter than loganberry. Train the long trailing canes fan-style along wires, keeping current-year primocanes separate from fruiting floricanes to simplify post-harvest cleanup. After harvest, remove all fruited canes to the ground and tie in the new primocanes. In zone 5–6, protect canes over winter by detaching them from wires and covering with straw mulch or a frost-cloth tunnel. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Taylor Dwarf Horticultural Bean (Cranberry Bush, Shell Bean)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest as shell beans when pods have mottled tan-and-red coloring and beans are plump. Taylor Dwarf Horticultural is a classic New England and Mid-Atlantic heirloom horticultural (shell) bean — one of the oldest and most storied varieties in American seed saving tradition, producing beautiful red-streaked, cream-and-crimson pods and plump, cranberry-red-speckled beans that are used primarily at the fresh-shelled stage, when they have a rich, creamy, potato-like flavor and a velvety texture that is quite different from the firmer, drier character of the same beans when fully dried. Fresh-shelled horticultural beans are a seasonal delicacy that was once far more common in American cooking — they require no soaking, cook in 20–30 minutes, and have a rich, substantial flavor and a dense, satisfying texture that is superior to the canned or dried equivalents. Taylor Dwarf is compact (14–20 inches), making it well-suited to small gardens, and produces abundantly over a 2–3 week harvest window. As a dry bean it is also excellent (the same as a cranberry or borlotti bean), providing versatility across the whole season. A foundational heirloom with genuine culinary value and beautiful pod markings. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Taylor Pawpaw
description: Taylor is one of the older named pawpaw selections predating the modern Kentucky State University and Peterson breeding programs, and it later served as the seed parent of the widely grown Taytwo cultivar, making it of interest to growers who want to trace pawpaw lineage or diversify an orchard's genetics. Trees are moderately vigorous with the typical pyramidal pawpaw habit and tolerate deep shade during their first several years, though they should be moved into fuller sun exposure as they mature to maximize fruiting. Fruit is medium-sized with smooth, custard-like flesh and a mild, sweet flavor typical of the classic older selections rather than the very large fruit size bred into more recent cultivars. Because pawpaws are self-incompatible, pair Taylor with an unrelated cultivar such as Sunflower, Susquehanna, or NC-1 planted nearby, and consider hand-pollinating with a small brush during the dark maroon spring blooms since the flowers' carrion scent attracts few reliable pollinators. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Taynton Squash Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Taynton Squash is among the oldest documented perry pear cultivars and one of the largest, most long-lived trees in the group. Named for the village of Taynton in Gloucestershire and documented since at least the seventeenth century, it is considered one of the oldest surviving named perry pear cultivars in England, producing a reliable crop of small, mid-tannin fruit on a tree capable of growing to an immense size and living for well over a century under good conditions. Its ancient pedigree and reliable cropping have kept it in cultivation in traditional Gloucestershire perry orchards continuously since long before named fruit varieties were commonly propagated by grafting elsewhere in Europe. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Taytwo Pawpaw (Taylor #2 Pawpaw)
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Taytwo is a historic Ohio-origin pawpaw selection long grown for its heavy, dependable production and medium-sized fruit with good, smooth-textured flavor, and it remains one of the most widely planted older cultivars for home orchards because it crops reliably even in cooler seasons. Vigorous, cold-hardy trees form the classic pyramidal pawpaw shape and tolerate the deep shade of establishment years better than most fruit trees, though full sun once mature produces the heaviest crops. Because pawpaws will not self-pollinate, plant a second unrelated cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the maroon spring bloom for the most consistent fruit set. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tazumal Mamey Sapote
description: Tazumal traces to a seedling tree brought to Homestead, Florida from El Salvador in 1949 and remains prized for fast growth and heavy annual bearing, often producing a light second flush in summer alongside its main winter-to-spring crop. Fruit is medium-sized with rich pink flesh of excellent flavor, carrying a few more seeds than some competing selections. Grow it as you would other mamey sapote: deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and room for a large long-term canopy, expecting several years to first fruiting even from a grafted tree. Its vigor makes Tazumal a useful pollinizer companion planted alongside a primary eating cultivar. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tea Plant (Tea Camellia)
description: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; water regularly as tea plants are sensitive to drought but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Camellia sinensis is the plant species from which all true tea is made; the young leaves and leaf buds ('flush') are harvested and processed differently to produce green tea (unoxidized), oolong (partially oxidized), or black tea (fully oxidized) — the same plant, processed differently. Home tea gardens are feasible in zones 7–10 where the plant grows as a reliable evergreen shrub; in the Gulf Coast and Southeast United States (zone 8–10) it performs particularly well in the moist, acidic conditions similar to its natural subtropical mountain habitat in China and Southeast Asia. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once the plant is 3–4 years old and 2–3 feet tall; regular harvesting keeps the plant productive and bushy. Small white flowers in fall are fragrant. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tea Tree
description: Plant Melaleuca alternifolia in full sun to light shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to occasionally wet soil; it tolerates periodic waterlogging and moderate drought once established; prune after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense growth; harvest leaves in late summer to early fall when terpinen-4-ol content is highest. Tea Tree is the world's most commercially important medicinal Melaleuca — grown on a large scale in the coastal plains of northeastern New South Wales, Australia, where its essential oil is steam-distilled from the leaves and young stems. Tea tree oil is one of the most thoroughly researched of all plant essential oils, with well-documented antibacterial (effective against MRSA and other resistant strains), antifungal, and antiviral properties; it is used in skin care products, toothpastes, wound antiseptics, and household cleaning products worldwide. In the garden, it is an attractive small tree or large shrub with papery, peeling whitish bark, fine needle-like leaves, and showy cream-white bottlebrush flower spikes that are excellent for native bees and other pollinators. Tolerates poorly drained and seasonally wet soils better than most ornamentals, making it useful in low-lying areas of Gulf Coast gardens; it performs best in zone 9–10 in the United States. Caution: tea tree oil is toxic if ingested and should not be used internally. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Teabreeze Tea (Fountain-Form Green Tea Selection)
description: Teabreeze stands out among tea camellias for its arching, fountain-like growth habit, eventually reaching 8 to 15 feet, with narrow, deeply lacquered dark-green leaves up to 4 inches long. Lightly fragrant white flowers appear in fall against the glossy foliage, giving it strong ornamental appeal alongside its usefulness for green tea production. Because of its ultimate size, give it more room than a typical compact China-type selection, and site it where its graceful form can be appreciated as a specimen or informal screen. Maintain the same acidic, evenly moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias require. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Teapot Jujube (Chahuzao, Protuberant-Shaped Ornamental-Edible Jujube)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; like other jujubes, Teapot is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect. Its standout trait is fruit shape: medium-sized fruit develop one to five irregular protuberances on the shoulder, most commonly two, giving each fruit a whimsical resemblance to a miniature teapot with a spout and handle, a strong conversation-piece and edible-landscape planting for Gulf Coast gardens. Despite the odd shape, the fruit is very sweet and ripens mid-to-late season, making it a good companion to earlier cultivars like Li or Honey Jar for a longer jujube harvest window. Vigorous, upright tree habit. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Teas Weeping Mulberry (Weeping Fruiting Mulberry)
description: Named for 19th-century Kansas nurseryman John Teas, this heat-loving dwarf weeping form of white mulberry stays compact at a fraction of the size of a seedling mulberry tree while still bearing a genuine crop of sweet, blackberry-shaped fruit each early summer. The twisted, cascading branches sweep to the ground and give the tree strong winter sculptural interest even when bare of leaves. Fruiting habit and fast growth make it more of a working fruit tree than the strictly ornamental Chaparral clone, so plan for bird pressure and some fruit drop staining beneath the drip line at harvest. It performs reliably in Gulf Coast heat and humidity as long as it has full sun and even soil moisture through fruit development. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Tecumseh Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Long-Storing Asian Persimmon)
description: Tecumseh was named and selected by Dr. Jim Shanks of the University of Maryland, likely from seed of the hardy astringent cultivar Great Wall, and shares that parent's cold-hardiness and reliable productivity. As an astringent-type persimmon it must fully soften before eating, but it is unusual for holding ripe fruit on the tree deep into winter, often into January or February, extending the harvest window well past most other cultivars. The fruit is good fresh, dried, or frozen, and the tree is long-lived, self-fertile, and notably resistant to common pests and diseases while tolerating drought once established. Its small stature makes it a practical choice for home orchards with limited space. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Teddy Dill (Compact High-Density Leaf Dill)
description: Teddy is a compact dill bred for dense, finely feathered leaf production, with short internodes that pack thick leaflets tightly around each stem for a lush, full appearance even on a small plant. It is faster-growing and more productive for leaf harvest than the older compact standard Fernleaf, while still being slower to bolt than large field-type dills, extending the fresh-cut window. Its small stature makes it well suited to pots, window boxes, and tight garden spaces where a full-size dill would flop or crowd neighbors. Harvest leaves continuously for dill weed; allow a few plants to flower if seed heads are wanted for pickling. Matures in 35–60 days from seed.

name: Teff (Grain)
description: Surface-broadcast seed — it is extremely small (poppy-seed sized) and must not be buried; mix seed with sand to achieve even distribution at roughly 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, then press lightly with a roller or board for good soil contact. Teff tillers prolifically and forms a graceful, open canopy with hundreds of fine panicles per plant; harvest the entire plant at the base when the majority of seeds have turned brown but before they shatter in a breeze. Thresh by beating bundles over a smooth tarp and winnow carefully in a gentle airflow — the seed is light and easily blown away. Teff grain is naturally gluten-free and is the basis for Ethiopian injera flatbread. Matures in 75–120 days from seed.

name: Tehama Mulberry (California Heirloom Black Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Tehama is a California heirloom black mulberry named for Tehama County, prized among fruit collectors for producing some of the largest berries of any black mulberry selection, often two inches or more in length, with an intensely rich, wine-dark, sweet-tart flavor typical of Morus nigra at its best. Like other black mulberries it grows more slowly and stays somewhat more compact than the vigorous white mulberry hybrids, making it a reasonable choice where space is limited, though it still eventually forms a substantial shade tree. Trees tolerate heat, drought, and average soil once established, needing only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Site female-fruiting trees well away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended summer harvest window and stain hard surfaces. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tejpat (Indian Bay Leaf, Malabathrum)
description: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives. The glossy, distinctly three-veined leaves carry a warm cassia-cinnamon-clove aroma entirely different from true bay laurel and are picked and sun-dried once the tree is a few years established. Tejpat is essential to North Indian garam masala, biryani, and dal tadka, and should not be substituted with Mediterranean bay leaf, which lacks its cinnamon character. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Telegraph Cucumber (Victorian English Long Greenhouse Cucumber)
description: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil, then train vines up a trellis for the straightest fruit and easiest picking. Telegraph is a Victorian-era English heirloom, originally bred for greenhouse culture, that produces long, slender, dark green fruit twelve to eighteen inches at full size, with thin, tender, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor prized for slicing. It performs well outdoors in warm climates given a trellis and consistent moisture, though fruit is best picked at eight to twelve inches for the crispest texture, since fully mature fruit can turn coarse. Keep watering even throughout fruit development, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of bitterness and misshapen fruit in this and most cucumber varieties. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Telegraph Improved Cucumber
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots for an early crop. This English-type heirloom from the 1800s bears long, thin-skinned, burpless fruits up to eighteen inches with very small, soft seeds. Originally bred for greenhouses, it now thrives outdoors and produces best when trained up a trellis. Keep watering even to keep fruit straight and free of bitterness. Harvest the long cucumbers while young and tender for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Telephone Pea (Alderman Pea, Grande Telephone)
description: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep and 2–3 inches apart in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Telephone pea (sold in Britain as Alderman) is the classic tall heirloom main-crop shell pea, a vigorous climber to 5–6 feet that produces large, curved dark-green pods with 8–10 sweet, tender peas per pod — significantly more productive per plant than bush varieties and the pod size that made it famous in Victorian kitchen gardens. Requires strong netting or pea sticks for support. Harvest when pods are well-filled and peas are young and sweet; productivity drops rapidly if pods are left to mature fully on the vine. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Telfair Citrangequat (Historic Swingle-Bred Cold-Hardy Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Telfair citrangequat was bred by USDA scientist Walter Swingle in the early 1900s alongside the better-known Thomasville and Sinton citrangequats, crossing a Willits citrange (trifoliate orange x sweet orange) with Nagami kumquat to push edible citrus culture into colder climates. The small, rounded, thin-skinned orange fruit is tart with a mild kumquat sweetness in the peel, best suited to marmalade, candied peel, or ade rather than fresh eating out of hand. Mature wood tolerates temperatures down into the single digits Fahrenheit, similar to its Thomasville sibling, making it a hardy novelty planting for Gulf Coast gardeners who want citrus outside the usual protected range. Give young trees a sheltered, sunny site with excellent drainage and winter protection for their first two or three seasons. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Teltow Turnip (Teltower Rübchen)
description: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 2-3 inches apart, since this variety forms small, slender, finger-sized roots rather than a large globe. Teltow Turnip is a German heirloom from the sandy soils around Teltow near Berlin, historically prized enough that it was reportedly shipped to Weimar for Goethe's table, and it remains catalogued in European heirloom seed-saving collections today. The roots are pale yellowish-white with a dense, waxy texture and an intense, nutty flavor unlike the milder taste of larger globe turnips, traditionally used in slow-simmered stews rather than eaten raw. Growing it in poor, sandy ground rather than rich garden soil is essential to concentrating its distinctive flavor. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Temple Orange (Royal Mandarin, Tangor)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with some wind protection, since Temple is more cold-sensitive than sweet oranges. First found growing in Jamaica and brought into Florida commerce in the early 1900s, it is classed as a tangor, a natural mandarin-orange hybrid, and produces a deep reddish-orange, easy-peeling fruit with an exceptionally rich, aromatic, sweet flavor that many consider superior to either parent type. It ripens January through March, later than most satsumas, giving a late splash of fresh citrus in the garden. Trees are moderately vigorous and benefit from regular citrus fertilizer and consistent moisture during fruit development. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tempranillo Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tempranillo is an early-ripening variety, an advantage in regions with shorter growing seasons or early fall rains. Spain's noble red wine grape and the foundation of Rioja and Ribera del Duero, its name derives from the Spanish word 'temprano' (early), reflecting its tendency to ripen earlier than many other red varieties, producing medium- to full-bodied wines with notes of red fruit, leather, and tobacco that develop further complexity with oak aging. Its earlier ripening window makes it a practical choice for regions with shorter growing seasons or a risk of early autumn rain damaging late-ripening varieties still on the vine. Prune to a moderate crop load for concentrated flavor, provide full sun and good air circulation to reduce disease pressure, and take advantage of its earlier harvest window in climates where fall weather can be unpredictable. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Temuco Quinoa
description: Temuco is a lowland coastal quinoa selected from an isolated population near Temuco in Chile's Araucania region, and it has proven to be one of the easier quinoas for cool, maritime climates because it sets seed reliably at low elevation and short day length. Its small, pale, cream-colored seed carries unusually little bitter saponin coating compared to many other quinoas, which cuts down on the rinsing needed before cooking. Grow it like other quinoas in average, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give plants room to branch, and watch for birds as the heavy seed heads ripen and dry in late summer. Cut whole panicles once the leaves have dropped and seed rubs free easily, then dry further indoors before threshing. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Ten Degree Tangerine (Extreme-Cold-Hardy Clementine x Yuzu Hybrid, Clemyuz 2-2)
description: Ten Degree Tangerine (Clemyuz 2-2), a Clementine x Yuzu hybrid developed by Texas backyard citrus breeders, is grown mainly for extraordinary cold hardiness rather than dessert quality — the tart, lemonade-like flavored fruit is a bonus on a tree reported to have survived temperatures in the single digits Fahrenheit with only minor damage, notably hardier than satsuma, kumquat, or any other mandarin hybrid grown on the Gulf Coast. It has become a favorite among cold-hardy citrus hobbyists in south-central and southeast Texas, where winters occasionally drop below what satsuma or kumquat can reliably survive. Fruit ripens in late fall into early winter and, given its sharp, yuzu-influenced acidity, is more often used for juice, marmalade, or lemonade-style drinks than eaten fresh. Because it originated from hobbyist breeding rather than a university release, availability is limited mainly to specialty cold-hardy citrus nurseries. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tender and True Parsnip (English Heirloom Smooth-Skinned Parsnip)
description: Sow seed shallowly into deeply worked, stone-free soil, since forked or stunted roots result from compacted ground; keep the seedbed evenly moist through slow germination and thin seedlings to a few inches apart. This long-standing English heirloom is prized for roots that are smooth-skinned, nearly coreless, and unusually tender for a full-season parsnip, with good field tolerance to canker. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert starch to sugar and give the roots their signature sweet, nutty flavor. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Tenderette Bush Bean (Tenderette Green Bean)
description: Plant seeds an inch deep directly in warm garden soil, thinning to a few inches apart so bushy plants have room to fill out without crowding. This long-popular bush bean produces slender, rounded, curved pods that are notably tender and stay stringless even at a fairly large size, giving gardeners a wider harvest window than many snap beans. Plants are heat tolerant and continue setting pods reliably through summer warmth, making this a dependable choice for extending the fresh bean harvest. Pick regularly to encourage continued flowering and pod set throughout the season. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Tendergreen Burpless Cucumber
description: Direct sow seed after the last frost, though this variety tolerates cooler soil better than most cucumbers. The thin-skinned, sweet, burpless, acid-free fruits are a delight harvested at eight inches or shorter. Pick early for pickling or let fruit grow to full size as a slicer, since it works well for both. Tendergreen resists powdery mildew, adding to its reliability in the garden. Keep watering even and harvest frequently to keep the vigorous vines productive. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tendergreen Mustard Spinach
description: Direct sow seed shallowly and keep the bed moist for quick germination. This versatile Japanese green, also called komatsuna, is milder than most mustards and very easy to grow. It quickly produces flat, smooth, dark, glossy green leaves and tolerates both heat and cold better than spinach. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole plants young for tender greens. Successive sowings from spring through fall keep a steady supply for stir-fries and salads. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Tendersweet Carrot
description: Sow seed shallowly, about a quarter inch deep, directly in deeply worked, loose soil so the long imperator-type roots can grow straight. Keep the seedbed consistently moist during the slow germination period and thin plants to a couple inches apart once seedlings are established. Harvest these long, slender, nearly coreless roots at around 8 to 9 inches for the sweetest flavor; the deep orange-red color holds up well to steaming, baking, and freezing. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Tendersweet Orange Watermelon
description: Sow Tendersweet Orange seeds 1 inch deep in warm hills, thinning to the two strongest vines per hill. This heirloom produces large 30 to 35 pound melons with vivid orange flesh, exceptional sweetness, and a thick, durable rind that stores and ships well. Give the vigorous vines plenty of room and water deeply while fruit sizes up. Harvest when the ground spot turns yellow and the nearby tendril withers. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Tenjin-gosho Persimmon (Seedless Japanese Astringent Kaki)
description: Tenjin-gosho is a historic seedless astringent cultivar from Nara Prefecture, Japan, valued for large, elongated, acorn-shaped fruit with a distinctive pointed tip and deep orange color once fully ripe. Because it sets fruit without a pollinator and stays seedless under normal Gulf Coast growing conditions, the flesh softens evenly all the way through, giving smooth, honey-sweet pulp once astringency resolves rather than the harder pockets sometimes found in seeded types. The tree is vigorous, spreading, and productive, tolerating the region's mild winters on low chill accumulation, and the oversized fruit makes an especially striking specimen hanging on bare branches after leaf drop. Home growers can eat it soft and spoon-ripe, or peel and air-dry it into a dense, chewy dried persimmon in the same tradition as other astringent Japanese cultivars. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tennessee Candy Roaster (Southern Appalachian Heritage Winter Squash)
description: Tennessee Candy Roaster is one of several closely related, regionally maintained Appalachian candy roaster strains, distinguished from the salmon-pink North Georgia type by generally more elongated, tapered fruit with tan to golden-bronze skin and less pronounced blue bloom at maturity. Like other candy roasters it carries dense, deep orange-yellow flesh with exceptionally high sugar content that concentrates further with roasting, the trait that gives the whole candy roaster group its name and its devoted following among Appalachian home gardeners and seed savers. Give the long, vigorous vines ample room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and cork, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry spot before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to improve for months. Matures in 95–115 days from seed.

name: Tennessee Red Cob Corn (Appalachian Heirloom White Dent Corn)
description: Sow directly in well-drained soil in blocks for reliable pollination, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest since this is a grinding corn rather than a fresh-eating sweet corn. Tennessee Red Cob is a long-grown Appalachian and upland Southern heirloom prized by home millers for producing a notably white, fine-textured meal, with the vivid red cob making it easy to sort visually from other corn at harvest. Plants tolerate the hot, humid conditions and periodic dry spells typical of Southern summers reasonably well once established, and the variety has a long history of on-farm seed saving. Store dried ears in a mouse-proof container with good airflow, and shell only what you need for milling at a time to keep meal fresh. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Tennessee Sweet Potato Squash (Southern Cushaw-Type Heirloom)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills in full sun, allowing generous room for the sprawling vines. Tennessee Sweet Potato is an old Southern heirloom squash bearing pear- to bell-shaped, buff-tan fruit with a smooth rind and dense, sweet, fine-textured orange flesh reminiscent of sweet potato, a resemblance that gives the variety its name. As a moschata-type squash it shows good resistance to squash vine borer and performs reliably through hot, humid Southern summers, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South gardens where other winter squash struggle. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure for a couple of weeks in a warm, airy spot to concentrate sweetness before moving to cool, dry storage. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Tennis Ball Lettuce (Thomas Jefferson's Monticello Heirloom Butterhead)
description: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Tennis Ball is a small, dense, dark-green butterhead lettuce documented in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden records from the early 1800s, forming tight, tennis-ball-sized heads with a sweet, buttery, mild flavor and crisp inner leaves. Its small, quick-maturing heads make it well suited to close spacing, containers, and succession planting for a steady supply of tender lettuce through the cool season. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade as temperatures rise in late spring to delay bolting. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Tennosui Asian Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Texas Pear)
description: Tennosui was bred from a cross of the Tennessee pear and Hosui Asian pear by a Harris County, Texas extension horticulturist and released by Texas A&M in 2004 specifically for humid, fire blight-prone regions of the South. Its bell-shaped fruit ripens early, from late July into August, with crisp flesh that resists browning after cutting, a trait growers value for fresh eating. Unlike many nashi cultivars, Tennosui shows notably good field resistance to fire blight, and it is self-fertile, though cross-pollination with another pear cultivar can improve crop size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tepary Bean
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in very well-drained, low-fertility, sandy or rocky soil in full sun well after soil has warmed; tepary bean is the most drought-tolerant domesticated bean in the world, an ancient crop of the Sonoran Desert developed over thousands of years by the O'odham and other indigenous peoples of the American Southwest and northern Mexico. Plants complete their entire life cycle — from germination through harvest — on as little as 8 inches of rainfall and perform poorly in heavily irrigated or rich, wet soils where they become disease-prone. Both bush and semi-vining types exist; small seeds come in white, brown, tan, buff, and speckled patterns and are high in protein, soluble fiber, and resistant starch. Harvest entire plants when most pods have dried and turned tan, thresh to release seeds, and cure in a dry, well-ventilated location before storage. An outstanding crop for hot, dry garden conditions where common beans fail. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Terebinth (Turpentine Tree, Cyprus Terebinth)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, poor to moderately fertile soil; terebinth is an ancient Mediterranean tree whose small red fruits (similar to tiny pistachios) have been consumed since prehistoric times and are still eaten in Greece and Turkey, where they are roasted, ground into a coffee-like drink, used to flavor spirits, and pickled in brine. The tree also historically yielded the original terebinth resin (turpentine) used in ancient medicine and as a paint vehicle. Closely related to the pistachio (Pistacia vera) and sometimes used as a pistachio rootstock. Extremely drought-adapted, thriving on poor limestone hillsides where little else will grow. The autumn foliage turns brilliant red before leaf drop. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Terebinth Tree (Turpentine Tree, Bith)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — a true Mediterranean xerophyte. Pistacia terebinthus (terebinth or turpentine tree) is an ancient wild Mediterranean tree in the cashew family — the wild relative of the commercial pistachio (P. vera) — native to the dry hillsides, maquis, and garrigue scrublands of the Mediterranean basin from Portugal and Morocco east through Turkey and the Levant. The terebinth is one of the most historically significant trees of the ancient world: it appears in the Hebrew Bible (the 'elah' of the story of David and Goliath), in Greek mythology, and throughout classical Mediterranean literature. It produces small (1/4-inch), olive-shaped drupes that dry from red to dark brown-purple — the 'terebinth berries' or 'menengiç' used in Turkish cuisine as a traditional spice and, most distinctively, as a caffeine-free coffee substitute: roasted and ground terebinth berries are brewed exactly like coffee (menengiç kahvesi — terebinth coffee), producing a thick, rich, slightly bitter, nutty, resinous beverage beloved in southeastern Turkey and the Levant. The tree also produces a historical resin (Chian turpentine) used in medicine and varnishes in antiquity. As a garden plant, terebinth is an attractive, hardy, drought-tolerant Mediterranean small tree or large shrub with graceful pinnate leaves turning brilliant red-orange in autumn. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Terenzo Tomato (AAS-Winning Trailing Tumbler Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, window box, or large container filled with fertile, well-drained potting mix in full sun. Terenzo is an AAS-winning cherry tomato bred as a true tumbler type — a compact, mounding, self-branching plant that spills gracefully over the edge of a container rather than climbing, producing a heavy, non-stop crop of small, sweet red cherry tomatoes without any staking, caging, or pruning. Its small scale and container-ready habit make it one of the easiest tomatoes for a patio, balcony, or small-space garden with no in-ground bed at all. Water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil, and feed every couple of weeks through the season to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Terry Plum (H.A. Terry Heirloom American Plum)
description: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil alongside a second American plum for cross-pollination, since this variety sets little to no fruit without a compatible pollen source nearby. Terry originated from the plum-breeding work of H.A. Terry of Crescent, Iowa, one of the era's most active selectors of native American plum, and was distributed alongside his other introductions during the 19th-century prairie plum boom; it was later used as a parent in early Prunus salicina x americana hybridizing programs in the northern plains. The fruit is medium-sized with the tangy, rich flavor typical of well-selected native plum, good for fresh eating once fully ripe and excellent cooked into jams and sauces. Like other heirloom native plum selections, it suckers from the roots and shrugs off cold, drought, and poor soil that would damage most orchard fruit trees. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tetra Dill
description: Tetra is a bushy, late-flowering dill bred for heavy leaf production, so it stays leafy longer before running to seed. Its heat tolerance makes it slow to bolt, letting you pick fresh, aromatic foliage through the warmer months. Direct sow in full sun where plants will grow, since the taproot dislikes being disturbed, and sow in succession for a steady supply. Harvest leaves before flowering for peak flavor, and leave a few plants to bloom for pollinators and seed. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Tetsukabuto Squash (Kabocha-Butternut Hybrid)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after all danger of frost has passed, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to accommodate the exceptionally vigorous vines. Tetsukabuto is a hybrid cross between a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima and a moschata parent, prized by growers for hybrid vigor that shrugs off vine borers and powdery mildew far better than either parent species alone. Fruits are near-round, 4-6 pounds, with dark, mottled black-green skin and deep orange-yellow flesh that is dry, dense, and nutty-sweet, closer in eating quality to a fine kabocha than a butternut. Cure in a warm spot for a week after harvest before moving to cool storage, where the fruit keeps remarkably well, often into the following spring. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Tettnang Hops (Tettnanger)
description: A traditional Bavarian noble hop from the Tettnang region, related to Saaz and used for its subtle, spicy-floral aroma in lagers, pilsners, and Belgian-style ales. Like other noble varieties it yields modestly compared to American hops and appreciates deep, fertile soil with good drainage to reduce root disease risk. Train bines clockwise up strings each spring and remove the weakest shoots to focus energy into two or three strong bines per crown. Harvest when cones are dry, springy, and lupulin-rich at the base of the petals. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Texas 1015 Sweet Onion (Texas Super Sweet)
description: Set transplants 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in October–December for Gulf Coast and South Texas; Texas 1015 (Texas Super Sweet) is the premier commercial and home garden short-day sweet onion of Texas and the Gulf Coast, developed by Texas A&M AgriLife Research and named for its recommended planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley. The large, globe-shaped, golden-yellow onions have exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pyruvate flesh with virtually no sharpness — one of the mildest onions grown anywhere in the world, comparable to Vidalia and Walla Walla in sweetness and suitable for eating raw in salads, sandwiches, and fresh salsas without the bite of storage onions. It has the distinctive pale yellow, thin skin and high moisture content of sweet onions. Harvest when tops fall over naturally; cure in a warm, airy location for 2 weeks before storing in a cool, dry spot (sweet onions have shorter storage life than sharp onions due to high moisture and sugar content). Matures in 170–200 days from transplant.

name: Texas 1015Y Supersweet Onion (Texas A&M Short-Day Gulf Coast Sweet Onion)
description: Start transplants indoors in September–October at 60–70°F; set out in the garden mid-October in zone 9. Apply nitrogen fertilizer every 2–3 weeks through winter and spring. Texas 1015Y Supersweet (the name means: Texas, October 15 planting date, Yellow skinned) is the signature short-day sweet onion of the Gulf Coast and South Texas — a variety developed at Texas A&M University by Dr. Leonard Pike and released in 1983 that became the defining onion of Gulf Coast commercial and home production. The '1015' refers to the optimal planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, where the variety's potential is most fully realized — planted on that date, the onions experience the precise seasonal day-length and temperature progression that produces the largest, sweetest bulbs. Texas 1015Y is the Vidalia of the Gulf Coast: producing enormous (3–5 inch diameter), slightly flattened, sweet, mild bulbs with very low pungency and high water content — a mild enough onion to eat like an apple. The sweetness comes from low pyruvic acid content (the compound responsible for onion bite and tear-inducing character); 1015Y has some of the lowest pyruvic acid levels measured in onion varieties. It stores only moderately (2–3 months) due to the high moisture content that gives the sweet flavor, distinguishing it from pungent storage types. Matures in 170–200 days from seed.

name: Texas Black Persimmon (Mexican Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; once established, Texas black persimmon requires little to no supplemental water. Diospyros texana (Texas black persimmon or Mexican persimmon) is a native small tree or large shrub of rocky Texas Hill Country limestone and the brushlands of south Texas and northern Mexico, producing small, 1-inch, round, jet-black fruits in July–September that taste intensely sweet — like dark plums or figs with a honey-like richness — and stain everything they touch with deep-purple-black juice (historically used as a fabric dye by Native Americans and early settlers). The tree is highly ornamental in addition to its fruit value: an attractive, multi-stemmed form with flaky, pale-gray bark that exfoliates to reveal silvery, cream, and pale-orange patches; small, glossy, semi-evergreen leaves; and outstanding fall-winter structural interest. It is adapted to full sun and extreme drought and alkaline soils where most fruit trees struggle. Wildlife (deer, wild turkey, quail, and many bird species) consume the fruits eagerly. Texas persimmon is dioecious (separate male and female trees needed for fruit); plant at least one male per 3–5 female trees. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Texas Black Walnut (Little Walnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, rocky, chalky, or limestone-derived soil in full sun in central and south Texas; Texas black walnut is the small, drought-tolerant walnut native to the rocky limestone hills and creek drainages of central Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico. Unlike the towering eastern black walnut (J. nigra), this species stays at 20-30 feet with a spreading, multi-stemmed habit. The small nuts are round and dark-shelled with a proportionally small but edible, walnut-flavored kernel — historically gathered and cracked by Indigenous peoples and early settlers. The tree produces juglone in its roots and leaves like all walnuts, inhibiting the growth of some nearby plants, especially tomatoes, peppers, and certain other species.
