An excellent native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the Texas Hill Country and adjacent areas where eastern black walnut cannot thrive. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Texas Blue Giant Fig (Large Purple-Black Texas Fig)
description: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; figs benefit from consistent moisture during the fruiting season to size fruit well and avoid splitting. Texas Blue Giant is a large-fruited fig popular among Texas and Gulf South fig growers, producing sizeable, deep purple-black fruit with sweet, richly flavored strawberry-red flesh on a vigorous, spreading tree. Its large fruit size and dark, attractive skin color make it a favorite for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree is well adapted to regional heat and humidity, cropping over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to manage its vigorous size and remove any winter dieback, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system through summer heat and occasional winter cold snaps. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Texas Cream 40 Cowpea (Compact Early Cream Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they lighten from green to a pale cream color. Texas Cream 40 is a compact, bush-type cowpea bred for a short, roughly 55–65 day maturity and a concentrated pod set well suited to gardeners who want an early, efficient harvest without the sprawling vines of older heirloom cowpea types. The smooth, cream-colored peas have a mild, sweet flavor and tender texture prized for fresh shelling, and the plant's compact size makes it a good fit for smaller garden beds or closer spacing than rangier Southern pea varieties. Its short season also allows two or more successive plantings through the Gulf South summer for an extended harvest window. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for the next crop. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Texas Cream 40 Pea (Extended-Harvest Cream Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is part of the Texas A&M cream-type southern pea breeding series, selected for a longer, more extended pod set than the earlier-released Texas Cream 8, giving home gardeners a steadier trickle of pods for fresh picking rather than one concentrated flush. Seeds are creamy-white with the mild, delicate, slightly sweet flavor typical of cream peas, prized for fresh shelling and quick cooking. Plants are semi-vining and slightly more sprawling than Texas Cream 8, so allow a bit more row width or provide light support for easier picking. Pick pods while still slightly immature and the seeds are plump but not hardened for the best fresh-shell texture; pods left to fully dry make good storage peas as well. Consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill improves yield in the Gulf Coast heat of midsummer. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Texas Cream 8 Pea (Compact High-Yield Cream Pea for Gulf South Gardens)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 8 is a compact, high-yielding cream southern pea selected through the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program — producing uniform, cream-colored seeds in short, upright plants that are self-supporting and well-suited to intensive raised-bed production. The 'Cream 8' number designation indicates its classification in the cream-type southern pea category, where seeds are creamy-white to tan without the eye coloring of black-eyed peas or the mottled colors of crowder types. Cream peas have a mild, sweet, delicate flavor considered more refined than the earthier crowder types — they are prized for their tender texture when fresh-shelled and their clean, creamy appearance in finished dishes. Texas Cream 8 has performed consistently well in Gulf Coast trials for productivity, uniformity, and disease resistance. The compact, semi-determinate bush habit allows closer spacing (3–4 inches in rows) than standard sprawling cream peas, increasing productivity per garden square foot. The concentrated pod set makes Texas Cream 8 practical for batch shelling and freezing — the defined harvest window means a larger quantity of pods reaches maturity simultaneously, enabling more efficient processing than the trickle harvest of indeterminate types. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Texas Early Grano Bulb Onion
description: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out once the ground can be worked, spacing them four to five inches apart for large bulbs. This is a short-day variety, so grow it in southern regions where it forms bulbs as days lengthen only slightly; the sweet, mild bulbs can reach up to a pound. Keep the soil evenly moist and weed-free, then cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing. Matures in 100–168 days from transplant.

name: Texas Elderberry (Mexican Elder, Blue Elderberry, Tapiro)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil; Texas Elderberry adapts to a wide range of soil types from sandy loam to limestone caliche, and is more drought-tolerant than the Eastern Common Elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established. Sambucus mexicana (also listed as S. nigra subsp. canadensis var. mexicana and S. caerulea in western references) is the native elderberry of Texas, the Desert Southwest, Mexico, and Central America, ranging from the western Edwards Plateau of Texas through the Rio Grande Valley. It overlaps geographically with S. canadensis to the east but is adapted to the more alkaline, hotter, drier conditions of central and south Texas and the Mexican highlands. The plant produces large, flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers (excellent nectar source for native bees and butterflies) followed by clusters of small, blue-black to dark purple berries similar to common elderberry. The berries ripen in late summer–fall and are used to make elderberry wine, juice, jelly, and the traditional folk medicine elderberry syrup for immune support. CAUTION: Raw berries, bark, leaves, and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries thoroughly before consumption; do not eat raw. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Texas Everbearing Fig (Texas Everbearing Brown Turkey)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established Texas Everbearing figs are drought-tolerant and require minimal care; protect roots with 4–6 inches of mulch in zones 7–8 where temperatures occasionally drop below 15°F. Texas Everbearing is a fig variety specifically selected and propagated in Texas for its exceptional performance in the hot, humid climate of the Gulf Coast and Central Texas, where it is the most commonly grown and recommended home garden fig; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension has long listed it as a top variety for the region. The medium to large, pear-shaped fruits have brownish-purple to brown skin (similar to but distinct from standard Brown Turkey) with strawberry-pink to amber flesh; the flavor is rich, honeyed, and sweet with the characteristic caramel-fig quality characteristic of the best common-type figs. As an everbearing type, Texas Everbearing produces two crops: breba fruits on previous year's wood in early summer (June) followed by the main crop on current season's wood from late summer through frost (August–November); this extended fruiting season is a practical advantage over single-crop types for home garden production. Excellent fresh, dried, or preserved; very productive in Gulf Coast zone 8–10 conditions. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: Texas Gourdseed Corn
description: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and well adapted to the heat of a long Texas or Gulf South growing season. Texas Gourdseed is an old Southern dent corn named for the distinctive deep, thin, wedge-shaped indentation at the crown of each dried kernel, resembling the shape of a small gourd seed — a hallmark trait of the historic 'Gourdseed' corn family that was among the most widely grown field corns across the antebellum and postbellum South before hybrid corn displaced open-pollinated varieties in the 20th century. The tall, vigorous stalks are well adapted to hot, humid Southern summers and produce a reliable grain crop even under the drought stress that limits many other corns, grinding into a flavorful, traditional cornmeal and grits. A genuine piece of Southern agricultural history for gardeners interested in growing and preserving heritage field corn, zone 6–10. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Texas Grano Onion (Classic Gulf South Short-Day Sweet Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in the fall in mild-winter areas, since Texas Grano is a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing rather than the long summer days farther north. Developed in Texas in the early 20th century, it became one of the foundational sweet onion cultivars of the Gulf South and is a direct ancestor of many modern short-day sweet onions, including some of the parent lines behind Vidalia-type onions. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have straw-yellow skin and mild, sweet flesh with low pungency, best used fresh rather than stored long term since sweet onions generally keep less well than pungent storage onions. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb formation and reduce water as tops begin to fall over before harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Texas Legend Onion (Disease-Resistant Short-Day Storage Onion)
description: Texas Legend is a Texas A&M AgriLife release bred as a sturdier, longer-storing alternative to older Grano-type short-day onions like Texas 1015Y. It forms globe-shaped, straw-colored bulbs with a somewhat firmer texture and more pungency than the sweetest Texas onions, which helps it hold up in storage for weeks after curing rather than needing quick use. The variety also carries improved field tolerance to Fusarium basal rot and pink root, both persistent problems in warm, humid Gulf Coast onion beds. Set out transplants in fall through early winter so the short-day bulbs have time to size up before lengthening spring days trigger bulbing. Matures in 110–120 days from transplant.

name: Texas Mulberry (Mountain Mulberry)
description: Plant container-grown trees or hardwood cuttings in spring in dry to moderately moist, rocky, sandy, or caliche soils in full sun to light shade; Texas mulberry once established is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation in zone 7–10. Texas mulberry is a small native tree or large shrub (8–20 feet) of the dry Hill Country, Trans-Pecos, and Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and New Mexico, with smaller leaves and a more drought-tolerant constitution than any other native American mulberry; the sweet, dark purple to black mulberries ripen in late spring and are an extremely important food source for numerous bird species including cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and orioles, as well as mammals from foxes to deer. Excellent as a water-conserving landscape tree for dry zone 7–10 gardens where conventional mulberries may struggle; the fruit is edible and excellent fresh or in pies and preserves. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Texas Persimmon (Mexican Persimmon)
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Texas persimmon is a small native multi-trunked tree of the Texas Hill Country and Rio Grande Plains with distinctive smooth, peeling gray bark revealing white-green underbark (one of the most beautiful native bark patterns in the Southwest). The small round fruits ripen jet black in August–September and are intensely sweet when fully ripe, though the black pulp stains everything permanently — including lips, fingers, and clothing. They are eaten fresh, dried, or cooked into syrup and are an important food for coyotes, bears, gray foxes, and birds. The tree is extremely drought tolerant once established and requires alkaline, well-drained soil. Both male and female trees are needed for fruit production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Texas Pink Pomegranate
description: Texas Pink is a pomegranate valued for its large rosy-pink blushed fruit and its ornamental, gnarled bonsai-like bark and bright orange-red flowers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing plenty of room for the shrubby tree to develop. Once established, it is quite drought-tolerant and needs only occasional deep watering. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a patio container and move it to shelter over winter. Prune to a single trunk or multi-stemmed form and thin fruit to improve size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Texas Pistache (American Pistache)
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline, limestone-based or rocky soil in full sun; Texas pistache is a handsome small multi-trunked native tree of the limestone canyons of southwest Texas and northeast Mexico, prized for one of the most spectacular fall color displays of any native Texan woody plant — the compound leaves turning brilliant shades of orange, red, and scarlet before dropping. Small red fruits are eaten by birds and wildlife, and the tree is often suggested as a superior native alternative to the widely planted Chinese pistache (Pistacia chinensis). It is extremely drought tolerant once established and well suited to xeric landscapes, parking lot edges, and small residential lots in zones 7–10. Growth is slow to moderate, so purchase the largest container specimen available for faster landscape impact. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Texas Scarlet Flowering Quince (Compact Red-Orange Flowering Quince)
description: Texas Scarlet is a compact, spreading flowering quince selection covering itself in brilliant red-orange flowers directly on the bare, twiggy stems in late winter and very early spring, well before the leaves emerge, making it one of the earliest color displays of the gardening year. Its low, mounding habit stays well under 4 feet, more manageable than many older flowering quince cultivars, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, edible when cooked into jelly or preserves though rarely eaten raw. Extremely adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and quite drought-tolerant, it blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Texas Star Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Western Mayhaw Cultivar)
description: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil where the tree's native wetland preference lets it thrive on low, poorly drained ground unsuitable for most other fruit trees. Texas Star is a named western mayhaw selection prized among east Texas and Gulf South growers for fruit that runs noticeably larger than wild-collected mayhaw, borne in heavy clusters of bright red, tart, aromatic berries that ripen in May. The larger fruit size makes hand harvest more efficient for home jelly-making, one of the enduring regional food traditions of the Gulf South. Plant alongside a second mayhaw cultivar for best cross-pollination, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years, becoming increasingly productive as it matures. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Texas Supersweet Onion (Mild Short-Day Onion for the Gulf South)
description: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Texas Supersweet needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly. Texas Supersweet produces large, globe-shaped, pale yellow bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and low pungency, bred as a regional alternative to Georgia's Vidalia-type onions for growers in Texas and across the Gulf South. Its short-day requirement and heat tolerance make it well matched to zone 9 growing conditions, where long-day storage onion types typically fail to bulb at all. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location; like other sweet onions it has a shorter storage life than pungent long-day types and is best used within a few months of harvest. Matures in 150–175 days from transplant.

name: Texas Wild Rice
description: Texas wild rice survives naturally only in the upper stretch of the San Marcos River in Hays County, Texas, where constant-temperature spring flow lets it grow as a true perennial instead of the annual habit of its northern relatives Zizania aquatica and Zizania palustris. It anchors itself in flowing water over gravel or sand, sending up long, ribbon-thin submersed leaves that stream downstream while a separate flowering culm reaches above the surface to set seed. Listed as federally endangered since 1978 because of reduced spring discharge, recreational trampling, and competition from non-native aquatic vegetation, it should never be collected from the wild; conservation nurseries propagate it by division for reintroduction and research plantings. Its dense underwater foliage stabilizes streambed sediment and shelters the endangered fountain darter and San Marcos salamander, making it a keystone species of one of the most biologically unique spring ecosystems in North America. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: TexFirst Peach (Texas A&M Ultra-Low-Chill Early Yellow Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing trees 15–20 feet apart for an open-vase canopy. TexFirst was selected at Texas A&M's College Station breeding program from open-pollinated seedlings and released for its very early ripening, yellow ground color with heavy red blush, and firm handling quality — traits that suit both dooryard and small commercial plantings in zone 8–9 Gulf gardens. Because it flowers and leafs out extremely early, site it away from low-lying frost pockets to protect the bloom from a late cold snap. Thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart within a few weeks of bloom and maintain a regular dormant-season fungicide program, since warm, humid Gulf Coast springs favor brown rot and peach leaf curl on early-ripening cultivars. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: TexStar Peach (Texas A&M Very Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun on well-drained soil, since peach roots are very susceptible to rot in wet ground; prune to an open-vase shape the first year to let light into the canopy. TexStar was released by Texas A&M AgriLife specifically for the low-chill needs of the Texas Gulf Coast, producing a medium to large, yellow-fleshed freestone peach with attractive red-blushed skin and good flavor for a low-chill selection. It is self-fertile and does not need a second peach for pollination, though bloom can still be lost to a late hard freeze after an especially warm winter, so avoid low frost pockets when siting the tree. Thin fruit to one every 6-8 inches along the branch once they reach marble size to improve final fruit size, and fertilize lightly in spring and again after harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Thai Basil
description: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix and transplant after the last frost when soil has warmed; Thai basil withstands heat slightly better than sweet basil. The glossy, dark-green leaves with purple stems carry a spicy anise-clove flavor that holds up better during cooking than sweet basil, making it ideal for stir-fries, curries, and pho. Pinch out purple flower spikes as they emerge to maintain vigorous leaf production, though the flowers are edible and attractive to pollinators. Harvest stems above a leaf node; plants branch densely and remain productive throughout the warm season. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Thai Bird Chili (Bird's Eye Chile, Tiny Ultra-Hot SE Asian Cooking Pepper)
description: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. A single plant produces abundantly — dry excess peppers for storage. Thai Bird Chili (Bird's Eye Chile, Phrik Khi Nu in Thai) is the foundational hot pepper of Thai, Vietnamese, and Southeast Asian cuisines — small (0.5–1 inch), thin, pointed, upright peppers that measure 50,000–100,000 Scoville heat units, making them significantly hotter than jalapeños (8,000 SHU) and approaching the lower range of habaneros. The name 'Bird's Eye' or 'Bird Chile' refers to the upright-pointing, small fruit that resembles a bird's eye, and also to the belief that birds (which lack capsaicin receptors) eat the peppers and spread seeds — a genuine ecological relationship that explains why the plant produces small, highly visible peppers. Thai Bird Chili is not a single variety but a group of similar Capsicum frutescens and Capsicum annuum types grown across Southeast Asia under various local names. The peppers are used in Thai cooking in virtually every form of heat addition — fresh sliced in curries and soups, dried and ground in chili pastes, pickled, or dried whole for fish sauce preparations. For Gulf South gardeners, Thai Bird Chili is one of the most productive and low-maintenance hot peppers in the summer garden: the plant thrives in heat and humidity that challenges most other pepper types, setting fruit prolifically even in July-August conditions that cause many pepper varieties to drop flowers. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Thai Bird's Eye Pepper (Phrik Khi Nu, Bird's Eye Chile)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–90°F; Thai bird's eye pepper (called 'phrik khi nu' — literally 'mouse dropping pepper' — in Thai, or simply 'bird's eye chile' across Southeast Asia) is the small, intensely hot pepper that provides the backbone of heat in Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and Cambodian cuisines. The tiny fruits (1/2 to 3/4 inch long, narrow, conical) start green and ripen to vivid red, with heat levels measuring 50,000–100,000 Scoville units — substantially hotter than jalapeños but less scorching than habaneros — and a clean, bright, fruity heat without the floral overtones of chinense-type peppers. The small size means many peppers are sliced directly into dishes or pounded whole in mortars; Thai bird's eye peppers carry their heat through both flesh and seeds with essentially no mild portion, making them one of the most reliably fiery culinary peppers. Capsicum frutescens produces smaller, more compact plants than C. annuum with multiple upright-pointing fruits on each branch — the characteristic upright fruit habit distinguishes it from most common peppers. In zone 9+, plants become woody perennial shrubs (2–3 feet tall and wide) producing enormous numbers of peppers continuously from summer through fall and into winter during warm years. Production per plant is staggering once established — a mature zone 9 plant produces thousands of peppers per season, far more than most families can use fresh. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Thai Black Banana (Black-Stemmed Ornamental Banana)
description: Thai Black stands out among ornamental bananas for its dark, near-black pseudostem and leaf midribs, which read as deep aubergine to black against the plant's green blades and make it a striking specimen or backdrop plant in a tropical-look border. It wants the same rich, steadily moist, well-drained soil and heavy feeding that other fast-growing ornamental Musa need to reach full size in a single season. Full sun brings out the darkest stem color, though a little afternoon shade is tolerated in hot climates. It has no more cold tolerance than most acuminata- and balbisiana-type ornamentals, so gardeners outside the warmest zones should plan to dig and overwinter the rhizome indoors or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover before frost. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Thai Chili Pepper (Bird's Eye Chili)
description: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 82–85°F; Thai chili needs more heat for germination than most C. annuum types. Plants are compact and extremely productive, bearing dozens of small (1–2 inch) upright fruits that ripen from green to bright red and carry intense heat of 50,000–100,000 Scoville units. Harvest red-ripe fruits for maximum heat and full flavor; the plants can be brought indoors as houseplants before frost and often survive multiple seasons. Excellent for drying — the small fruits air-dry on the plant or can be strung and hung in a warm spot. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Thai Eggplant
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 80–85°F and maintain consistent heat throughout the seedling stage; Thai eggplant germinates and grows faster than larger-fruited types. Transplant to a warm, sheltered bed after last frost and mulch heavily to retain soil warmth. The round, golf ball-sized fruits ripen from white-striped green to fully white or yellow depending on the cultivar, and are harvested while still firm and slightly underripe for use in Thai green curry. Overripe fruits become bitter; check plants every 2–3 days and harvest promptly to keep plants productive. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Thai Extra Long Sponge Luffa
description: Selected in Thailand for exceptional length, this smooth luffa can produce fruit exceeding four feet if left to mature, though it is best picked at 12-18 inches for cooking, when the flesh is still tender and mild like zucchini. Because it needs a long 120-130 day warm season and vines that can reach 15-25 feet, give it the tallest trellis or arbor available and start seed indoors where summers are short. Allow a portion of the crop to fully ripen and dry on the vine for use as natural bath and cleaning sponges, peeling and rinsing the skin away once it turns brown and papery. Matures in 120–130 days from seed.

name: Thai Green Eggplant (Small Striped Round Eggplant for Curry)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to small-egg size for the crisp, mild, low-seed texture prized in Thai cooking. Thai Green is a small, round eggplant with pale to medium green skin lightly streaked with cream, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh holds its shape well when simmered whole or halved directly into Thai green curry, a traditional use where the small green fruit is added along with pea eggplants and other aromatics. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Thai Hot Chile Pepper
description: Start seed indoors with warm bottom heat several weeks before the last frost, since these peppers need heat to germinate well. Transplant the compact, mounding 8-inch plants outdoors only after all danger of frost has passed and nights are warm. Each plant carries dozens of upright, slender 1.5 to 3 inch fruits that ripen from green to red at the same time for a very ornamental, very spicy display; they do well in containers. Matures in 85–105 days from transplant.

name: Thai Hot Pepper
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Thai Hot (also called Thai Bird Pepper or 'prik kee noo' in Thai, meaning 'mouse droppings pepper') is the standard small, intensely hot pepper used in authentic Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and broader Southeast Asian cuisines. The thin, pointed, upright fruits (1–2 inches long, pencil-thin) ripen from bright green through red, with clusters of fruits in different ripening stages creating an ornamental display. The heat level of 50,000–100,000 Scoville Heat Units produces the sharp, penetrating, instant heat characteristic of Thai cuisine — different in character from the deeper, slower-building heat of dried Mexican chiles. Both green (unripe) and red (ripe) fruits are used in Thai cooking — green fruits appear in green curry paste, papaya salad, and stir-fries; red fruits are used in red curry paste and dried for chile flakes. The highly prolific plants bear continuously through warm weather, producing far more peppers than most home cooks can use fresh. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Thai Kang Kob Pumpkin
description: Thai Kang Kob was brought from Thailand to the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds' Andrew Kaiser in 2006 and has since become popular for its productivity and disease resistance. The heavily ribbed, warted fruits are sea-green at harvest and age to chestnut brown in storage, weighing about 6-8 lbs. The deep orange flesh is sweet and fragrant, traditionally used in Thai coconut curries, soups, and stir-fries, as well as the custard-filled dessert sangkaya. Vines tolerate squash bugs and common cucurbit pests and diseases better than many winter squash. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Thai Lessard Sugar Apple (Ultra-Sweet Green-Skinned Sugar Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this vigorous but manageably sized selection room to branch into a small rounded tree. Thai Lessard is prized for exceptionally sweet, soft, juicy flesh inside its bumpy, pale green skin, and for bearing a heavier and more reliable crop than many older sugar apple selections. It defoliates and drops fruit in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor a sheltered, south-facing microclimate or keep young trees in containers that can be moved under cover for winter. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning, transferring pollen from newly opened male-stage flowers to receptive female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set in home gardens where the tree's natural beetle pollinators are absent. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Thai Long Green Eggplant (Slender Pale-Green Asian Eggplant)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Thai Long Green produces slender, curved, pale jade-green fruit up to a foot long with a mild flavor and few seeds, a traditional Southeast Asian type widely used in stir-fries, curries, and grilling, where the thin skin and tender flesh cook quickly without needing to be peeled. The productive, heat-loving plants continue setting fruit through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many Western eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit young and glossy for the best texture — overripe fruit turns dull and develops tougher flesh and larger seeds — and pick every few days to keep plants producing. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Thai Red Roselle
description: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Thai Red is a deeply pigmented roselle cultivar from Southeast Asia, selected for extraordinarily high anthocyanin content that produces calyces (the fleshy red structures around the seed pod) of an intense ruby-red that yields a dramatic magenta-crimson juice when steeped. Harvest calyces when they are plump, firm, and fully red — typically 5–7 days after the flower petals drop — by snapping them off the branch. Thai Red calyces produce a more intensely flavored, darker red hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica) than standard roselle varieties, and are prized for naturally colored beverages, syrups, jellies, and dried flower teas. The tall, bushy plants are as ornamental as they are productive, with attractive red-veined leaves and showy flowers. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Thales Loquat (Large Orange-Fleshed Loquat)
description: Thales produces large, orange-fleshed fruit with a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and is valued as a reliable, moderately vigorous grower for home orchard plantings. Site trees in full sun on well-drained soil and provide even soil moisture through the late-winter bloom and spring fruit development period, since drought stress at fruit set can reduce yield. Thin clusters to improve individual fruit size and stake young trees carrying their first heavy crop to prevent branch breakage. As with all loquat cultivars, a sheltered microclimate away from cold pockets improves cropping consistency in the cooler end of its Gulf Coast range. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Thayer Carambola
description: Thayer is an older Florida carambola selection valued more for reliable vigor and disease tolerance than for exceptional fruit size, producing a steady crop of medium, ribbed, yellow-gold fruit with a mild, tart-sweet flavor that improves with full ripening on the tree. It is a useful pollinizer and dooryard tree where growers want production insurance alongside sweeter dessert cultivars like Arkin. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, water deeply and consistently during dry spells, and prune lightly after each harvest flush to keep fruiting wood within reach. Fertilize several times a year with a balanced fruit-tree formula, as carambola is a heavy feeder relative to its modest size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: The Sutton Fava Bean (Dwarf English Heirloom Broad Bean)
description: Bred by Suttons Seeds in England in the 1920s and still carrying a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, this is the classic dwarf broad bean, reaching only about a foot to eighteen inches tall while still setting a full crop of well-filled pods holding three to five beans apiece. The short, sturdy stems rarely need staking even in exposed or windy gardens, and the compact footprint makes it a favorite for raised beds, containers, and small-space plots where standard tall favas would sprawl. Sow directly into cool soil as early as it can be worked, spacing plants closely so they lean on one another for support, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Harvest pods young for tender fresh shelling or let some dry fully on the plant for winter storage. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: Theis Sorghum (Late-Season Mid-South Syrup Sorghum)
description: Sow seed about an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has fully passed, thinning seedlings to allow thick, sturdy canes to develop. Theis is a Mid-South heirloom syrup sorghum distributed through Mississippi's foundation seed program, growing noticeably taller and maturing later than standard varieties like Dale, and it holds up well to some of the organophosphate insecticides sometimes used on nearby cotton fields. Let the canes stand until the seed heads reach hard-dough stage before cutting and pressing, since Theis is valued for producing a notably mild, high-quality syrup once the juice is boiled down. Because of its long season, it performs best where summers run hot and frost-free well into fall. Matures in 120–140 days from seed.

name: Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash (Missouri Heirloom Acorn-Type with Sweet Nutty Flesh)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin is tan-cream and stem has dried. Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash is a Missouri heirloom winter squash with an unusually devoted following among winter squash enthusiasts — one of the open-pollinated acorn-type squashes most frequently cited for superior eating quality among the many heirloom varieties preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network. The variety produces oval to oblong fruits, 6–8 inches long, with smooth to lightly ridged cream to tan skin that turns uniformly tan at full maturity. The name 'sweet potato squash' references the flesh character: the texture is drier and denser than standard acorn squash, with a sweet, slightly dry, nutty quality reminiscent in some ways of baked sweet potato — particularly the way the flesh separates into fibrous, sweet sections when baked. This dry, dense texture is highly valued by cooks who find standard acorn squash flesh too watery: Thelma Sanders bakes to a fluffy, dry interior that absorbs butter and seasonings distinctly better than wet-fleshed varieties, and the sweetness at full maturity is exceptional. The flavor is genuinely complex — sweet, nutty, slightly starchy — in a way that distinguishes it from hybrid acorn types selected for uniformity and yield rather than flavor depth. Thelma Sanders' origin traces to an individual Missouri gardener of the same name who maintained the seed through her personal gardening before sharing it through the Seed Savers Exchange community. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Thermidrome Garlic (French Softneck)
description: Thermidrome is a softneck garlic that traces to the Drome valley of southeastern France, long favored there for its earliness and reliability in a maritime climate. Plant individual cloves pointed end up about 2 inches deep, mulch over winter, and keep beds weeded through spring since garlic competes poorly with weeds. Because it matures earlier and stores well into the following year, it is a dependable choice for gardeners in milder, wetter winter regions where hardneck types can rot. The flavor is notably milder than most hardnecks, making it popular for raw use. Matures in 210–240 days from transplant.

name: Theta Hazelnut (Eastern Filbert Blight-Resistant Hazelnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinator cultivar planted within about 50–60 feet for reliable cross-pollination, since hazelnuts require wind transfer of pollen between genetically compatible trees. Theta was developed by Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program and released with strong resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that has devastated susceptible hazelnut orchards, allowing more reliable production without the intensive disease management older, susceptible cultivars require. It produces medium to large, well-filled, high-quality nuts on a vigorous, productive tree, harvested in early fall as they naturally drop from the husk. Hazelnuts perform best in regions with cool, humid growing seasons and moderate winter chill, making them a better fit for the upper South and Pacific Northwest-like climates than the hot, humid Deep South, where summer heat and disease pressure limit success. Rake and collect fallen nuts promptly to prevent rodent loss and mold. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Thiessen Juneberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Thiessen is a named saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia) cultivar selected in Alberta, Canada, widely regarded as one of the best-flavored named saskatoon varieties with very large berries (among the largest of any named cultivar) and a sweet, rich, complex flavor with prominent almond notes from the edible seeds. The very large, round, dark purple-blue berries ripen in early to mid-June — among the earliest of the named cultivars, making Thiessen valuable for extending the fresh fruit season into late spring when few other fruits are available. The upright, vigorous shrub can reach 12–14 feet in height at maturity, forming a small multi-stemmed tree form. Thiessen is popular in commercial saskatoon orchards in the Canadian Prairie provinces, where the saskatoon berry industry produces fruit for fresh market, U-pick, frozen, dried, and processed products. The species is among the most cold-hardy edible fruits in cultivation, surviving temperatures below -40°F. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Thimbleberry
description: Thimbleberry is a large-leafed, thornless native Rubus that thrives along woodland edges and mountain slopes from Alaska to Mexico, tolerating more shade than almost any other fruiting cane. The soft, bright red berries resemble a wide, shallow thimble and have a delicate, sweet flavor but are extremely fragile — they must be eaten or processed within hours of harvest. Propagate by dividing root clumps in spring; seed germination is erratic and requires cold stratification. Allow the plant to naturalize in a semi-wild planting rather than managing it as a formal fruiting cane. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Thomas Black Walnut (Classic Large-Nutted Eastern Black Walnut)
description: Plant grafted trees into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from vegetable gardens and shade-sensitive plants since black walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Thomas is one of the oldest and most widely planted named black walnut cultivars, selected in Pennsylvania in the 1880s and still valued for its consistently large, well-filled nuts, relatively thin shell, and good cracking quality compared with wild seedling trees. The vigorous, long-lived tree needs several years to reach bearing age but then produces reliably for decades, with nuts maturing and dropping in fall for hulling, curing, and cracking. Keep young trees watered during establishment, and protect the trunk from mower and string-trimmer damage; mature trees need little care beyond an occasional light fertilization and removal of any dead or crossing limbs. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Thomas Laxton Pea (Heirloom English Main-Crop Shelling Pea)
description: Thomas Laxton was introduced in England in 1898 by the Laxton Brothers breeding firm as an improved early-to-main-season shelling pea and has remained popular with seed savers ever since for its reliable yields and classic sweet English pea flavor. Vines are shorter and easier to manage than tall telephone-type peas but still produce well-filled pods over a solid harvest window. Sow early for the sweetest peas, and pick pods promptly once they fill out, since flavor declines quickly as peas mature and starch content rises. Its heirloom status and open-pollinated seed make it a good choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Thomas Muscadine Grape (Historic Black Female Cultivar)
description: Thomas is a historic black muscadine selected from the wild well before the twentieth century, and it served as one of the foundational female parents in the University of Georgia's muscadine breeding program launched in 1909, contributing to the pedigree of later cultivars such as Magoon and, through further crosses, Noble. The dark, richly flavored berries retain the authentic musky-sweet character that defines classic Southern muscadine. Because Thomas is female-flowered, it must be planted alongside a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Nesbitt to ensure pollination and fruit set. This vigorous heirloom vine remains available from specialty nurseries for gardeners who want a direct link to the earliest cultivated muscadines. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Thomasville Citrangequat
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a fruiting citrus, tolerating hard freezes that would kill standard citrus outright, though a sheltered microclimate still improves fruit set and tree vigor. Thomasville citrangequat is a three-way citrus hybrid — a cross of citrange (trifoliate orange × sweet orange) with kumquat — developed by USDA citrus breeder Dr. Walter Swingle in Thomasville, Georgia in the early 20th century specifically to push the boundary of cold-hardy edible citrus northward out of Florida. The small, oval, orange-yellow fruits have an aromatic, tart-sweet, marmalade-quality flavor with edible skin in the kumquat tradition, best used for marmalade, candying, or juice rather than fresh peeling and eating. The tree also carries attractive small trifoliate-influenced leaves and light thorns, and its extreme hardiness has made it a mainstay of cold-hardy citrus hobbyist plantings from the Gulf Coast through the Southeast. A rewarding novelty citrus for growers pushing the cold edge of the citrus range, zone 7–10. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Thompson Pink Grapefruit (Original 1913 Pink-Fleshed Sport of Marsh)
description: Thompson Pink was discovered in 1913 in Oneco, Florida as a pink-fleshed bud sport growing on a branch of an otherwise ordinary white Marsh grapefruit tree, making it the first commercially propagated pink grapefruit. The fruit matches Marsh in size, seediness, and tree habit, but the flesh carries a soft pink blush from pigment accumulation rather than the pale cream of the parent, with a similar balanced sweet-tart flavor. Thompson Pink became the direct ancestor of the deeper-colored Ruby Red, discovered as a further bud sport in Texas in 1929, and stands behind most pink and red grapefruit grown commercially today. Grow it exactly as Marsh grapefruit, in full sun on well-drained soil, and expect fruit to hold well on the tree through winter without losing quality. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Thompson Seedless Grape (Sultanina)
description: Set vines against a sturdy trellis or arbor in deep, well-drained soil, spacing plants widely to allow for vigorous cane growth, and prune hard each dormant season to renew fruiting wood. This old California cultivar, also known as Sultanina, produces small, oval, amber-green berries in loose to medium clusters with no seeds and thin, sweet skin. It is the classic grape dried into raisins and is equally popular fresh, but it needs a long, hot growing season to ripen and size up well. Vines are vigorous and productive but more cold-tender than American-type grapes, so winter protection is worthwhile at the cooler edge of its range. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Thorn Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Thorn is a reliably productive, widely grown traditional Gloucestershire perry pear. One of the classic Three Counties perry pears traditionally grown across Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, and Worcestershire, it produces a reliable crop of small, hard, astringent fruit prized for well-balanced tannin and good juice yield, and it remains a component of a number of well-regarded commercial English perry blends. Like most true perry pears it is grown solely for fermenting into perry rather than fresh eating, and it shares the group's characteristically slow growth to first significant bearing. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Thornfree Blackberry (Historic USDA Thornless Blackberry)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the sprawling semi-erect canes onto a sturdy two-wire trellis. Released by the USDA in 1966, Thornfree was one of the first genuinely thornless blackberry cultivars to reach home gardeners and commercial growers, and its introduction helped launch the modern era of thornless bramble breeding that led to today's widely planted cultivars. It bears firm, glossy, medium-to-large black fruit with good flavor over a fairly long midsummer harvest window, on vigorous canes that need tying and support since the plant does not grow fully upright on its own. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting productive. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Thornless Blackberry Prime-Ark Freedom
description: Prime-Ark Freedom is a thornless, primocane-fruiting blackberry that bears large, sweet berries on first-year canes, giving a summer crop that can extend into fall. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or support for the vigorous canes. Because it fruits on new wood, you can mow floricanes to the ground in late winter for a single heavy late-season crop, or leave them for two harvests. Keep soil evenly moist during fruit development and mulch to suppress weeds. Feed in early spring with a balanced fertilizer. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Thornless Boysenberry
description: Thornless Boysenberry is a spineless sport of the classic boysenberry, carrying the same rich, deep maroon-purple, winey-flavored fruit but on canes free of the vicious thorns that make standard boysenberry a challenge to prune and pick. Yield and berry size run slightly behind the thorny original in most trials, and the thornless canes can be a touch less vigorous, but the dramatically easier hand harvest and maintenance make it the preferred choice for home gardens. Train canes to a trellis at 3 and 5 feet, cut all fruited canes to the ground right after summer harvest, and tie in the new season's canes to the wires for the following year's crop. In the cooler end of its range, canes can be unclipped from the wires and laid on the ground under mulch for winter protection. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Thornless Loganberry
description: Thornless Loganberry is a spineless bud-sport of the original loganberry (itself a natural blackberry-raspberry hybrid), producing the same long, tart, dark red fruit on canes that are dramatically easier to train, prune, and hand-harvest. Weave the vigorous primocanes along a two- or three-wire trellis through the growing season, then cut the floricanes that just fruited to the ground right after summer harvest and tie the new canes into their place. Because it lacks the parent's thorns, this strain is the preferred choice for home gardens and u-pick plantings where hand contact is frequent. In borderline-hardiness areas, detach canes from the wires after leaf drop and lay them on the ground under mulch for winter protection. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Thorogreen Lima Bean (Green-Seeded Bush Baby Lima)
description: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Thorogreen is a bush-type baby lima bean prized for seeds that stay a pale green color even after cooking, rather than the more common cream or white of most lima beans, giving finished dishes an appealingly fresh, vibrant appearance. The compact plant sets pods over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of bush lima types, making it convenient for a single main harvest for canning or freezing, and the small, tender seeds cook quickly with a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled, and pick promptly once pods mature, since lima pods left too long on the plant can toughen. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Thousand Fingers Banana (Musa Chiliocarpa)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Thousand Fingers is a novelty banana famous for producing an enormous bunch made up of hundreds to over a thousand tiny, finger-length fruits packed densely around a long, extended stalk, making it more of a conversation piece and ornamental curiosity than a practical fruiting banana. The individual fingers are small, mildly sweet, and mostly seedless in cultivated forms, edible but not a substantial harvest compared to standard dessert bananas. The plant itself is tall and vigorous with typical bold tropical banana foliage, and the extraordinarily long bloom stalk with its cascade of tiny fruit is the main reason gardeners grow it. Like most tropical Musa acuminata types it has little cold tolerance in zone 9, so plan on container culture or heavy winter protection, and give it full sun, high heat, and consistent moisture and feeding through the long growing season it needs to bloom. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Three-cornered Garlic
description: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; three-cornered garlic is named for its distinctively triangular stem cross-section, visible when the stem is cut. This Mediterranean allium is one of the most useful for shade gardens because it genuinely thrives under trees where garlic and chives fail. The small white bell flowers in spring are pendulous and nodding, borne in a one-sided umbel, and all parts — leaves, stems, flowers, and bulbs — have a mild garlic flavor and are fully edible. Leaves can be harvested like chives throughout fall and winter in mild climates; use them raw in salads, cooked in omelets, or as a mild garlic substitute wherever a delicate garlic presence is wanted. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Three-leaf Akebia
description: Plant Akebia trifoliata at the base of a sturdy trellis, pergola, or fence in partial to full sun; plant two or more seedlings of different genetic origin for cross-pollination and reliable fruiting; water regularly; harvest pods in autumn when they split open along the seam. Three-leaf Akebia is a fascinating edible ornamental vine producing unusual fruits that are rarely seen outside Japan and China but are gaining interest among adventurous Western growers. The pale purple to lavender sausage-shaped pods (3–5 inches long) split open in autumn to reveal sweet, translucent white pulp — the pulp is eaten fresh by scooping around the embedded seeds, which are not eaten. The flavor is mildly sweet, subtle, and aromatic — not intensely flavored but pleasantly unique. Beyond the fruit, young spring shoots are blanched and eaten as a vegetable (akebi no tsuru) in Japanese mountain cuisine. The intricate, three-leaflet foliage on twining stems is ornamentally attractive, and the small, dark purple flowers in spring are fragrant with a vanilla scent. A related species, Akebia quinata (Five-leaf Akebia), is very similar but with five leaflets and is widely grown ornamentally — both are vigorous and need substantial support. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Three-Leaf Sumac (Skunkbush, Lemonade Berry, Squawbush)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil from rocky to clay; three-leaf sumac (Rhus trilobata) is a wide-ranging, cold-hardy western sumac producing small, sticky, red-orange berries used identically to lemonade berry — soaked in water to make a tart, refreshing beverage — and was one of the most important wild food and medicinal plants of western Native American tribes from the Great Plains to California. The flexible young branches were traditionally used for basket weaving by many indigenous peoples. Exceptional for erosion control on dry slopes, with beautiful orange-red fall color, excellent wildlife value, and extraordinary drought tolerance. Does not sucker aggressively. The common name 'skunkbush' refers to the strong, somewhat pungent smell of the crushed foliage. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Threeleaf Akebia
description: Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 5–9; threeleaf akebia is closely related to the more commonly grown fiveleaf akebia (A. quinata) but is distinguished by having only three leaflets per leaf (vs. five in A. quinata) and generally larger fruits — the sausage-shaped, blue-purple pods can reach 4–5 inches long in good specimens. The pale purple, vanilla-fragrant flowers in spring are striking and ornamental. The ripe fruits split open along one side to reveal white, jelly-like pulp surrounding black seeds — the pulp is eaten fresh, tasting sweet and somewhat like lychee, while the empty pods are used as a vegetable in Japan. A vigorous, somewhat twining vine that can be invasive in some regions; grow on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence where its vigor can be managed by pruning. A productive edible vine for the partial shade garden in zones 5–9. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Thriller Winter Squash
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after the danger of frost has passed, or start indoors a couple weeks early and transplant carefully. This compact vine saves garden space while producing uniform 1 to 1.25 pound fruits with creamy-white rinds boldly striped in green and orange. Let fruits fully mature and cure the hard rinds before storing; the smooth, sweet flesh is as good for eating as the striking rinds are for autumn displays. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Thumbelina Carrot (AAS-Winning Round Baby Carrot)
description: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up. Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, produces small, round, sweet roots about the size of a golf ball rather than the long tapered shape of standard carrots, making it uniquely well suited to shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils where long-rooted carrots often grow forked or stunted, as well as to container growing. Its quick maturity and compact size also make it a fun, kid-friendly carrot for small gardens. Harvest as soon as roots reach full size, since round carrots can become woody if left in the ground too long, and keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender roots. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Thumbelina Leigh Dwarf English Lavender
description: Give this dwarf lavender full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; small, tightly mounded lavenders are especially prone to rot if planted too deep or kept damp. Bred in Australia and among the smallest widely sold English lavender cultivars, 'Thumbelina Leigh' forms a dense, rounded cushion of narrow gray-green leaves only about a foot tall, with plump, deep purple-blue flower spikes held on short stems just above the foliage. Its diminutive scale suits container growing, rock gardens, and edging where full-size lavenders would overwhelm the design. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain the tight habit and encourage repeat bloom. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Thunderbird Evergreen Huckleberry
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Thunderbird is a more compact, heavier-fruiting selection of evergreen huckleberry bred for improved garden and orchard performance. Small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves emerge bronze-red on new growth, covering a naturally more compact, dense shrub than the wild species, which produces small, sweet-tart, dark purple berries in late summer and fall prized for pies, jams, and fresh eating, historically an important traditional food for Pacific Coast Indigenous peoples. Native to coastal forests from British Columbia to California, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland understory, and its glossy evergreen foliage is also cut and sold commercially in the florist trade. Mulch with pine needles or acidic compost to maintain soil pH, water regularly during establishment and fruit development, and expect the heaviest fruit set with a bit of morning sun. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Thundercloud Elderberry (Purple-Leaved Ornamental Elder)
description: Thundercloud is grown chiefly as an ornamental elder, its deeply cut, dramatic burgundy-purple foliage set off by broad flat-topped clusters of bright pink flowers in early summer that mature into small dark purple-black berries by late summer. The rich leaf color holds best with several hours of direct sun daily and can fade toward green in heavy shade. Cut a portion of the oldest stems to the ground each winter to keep the naturally arching habit compact and to encourage the strongest, most vividly colored new growth, since the best foliage color appears on vigorous young canes. Berries are edible once fully ripe and cooked but are secondary to the shrub's landscape value here. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Thundercloud Purple-leaf Plum
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Thundercloud is the most widely planted purple-leaf plum cultivar in North America, valued for single, light pink spring flowers that open very early — often in February in zones 7-9 — just before the reddish-purple foliage emerges, which then deepens to a rich dark purple through summer before fading somewhat by fall. Its rounded, dense crown and reliable floriferousness make it a mainstay flowering and accent tree for residential landscapes, street plantings, and mixed borders. Small, round, dark red plums are produced in summer and are edible, though they are typically sparse and secondary to the ornamental display. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15-25 years) but very fast-growing; can self-sow in mild climates. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Thursby Loquat (Historic Florida Medium-Late Pear-Shaped Loquat)
description: Thursby is a historic Florida heirloom selected by Isabel Thursby of Orange City and introduced by the USDA's Tropical Research and Education Center in 1949, making it one of the older named loquat cultivars still in circulation in the Southeast. The pear-shaped fruit has thick, leathery, dark yellow to orange skin and dark yellow flesh with a mildly sweet-tart flavor, ripening medium-late in the loquat season and thereby stretching the harvest window on properties that also grow earlier types like Christmas or Advance. The notably thick skin, while less delicate for fresh eating out of hand than thinner-skinned cultivars, holds up better to handling and to the drenching spring rains common on the Gulf Coast, reducing losses to fruit splitting. Trees are vigorous and well adapted to Florida and Gulf Coast humidity, and as with all loquats, thinning fruit clusters after fruit set improves individual fruit size. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Thyme
description: Thyme is a hardy, low perennial with tiny fragrant leaves that season soups, roasts, and sauces and also make an aromatic groundcover. Surface sow the very fine seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, keeping it just barely moist until it sprouts. Transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it develops the best flavor and resists rot. Trim plants after flowering to keep them tidy, and harvest sprigs anytime through the growing season. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Tiara Cabbage (Early Mini Green Cabbage)
description: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since Tiara is bred specifically for high-density planting. It forms small, dense, round green heads of about 1-2 pounds in a notably short season, one of the fastest-maturing cabbages commonly grown, which lets gardeners fit in an extra planting or squeeze a crop into a narrow spring or fall window between other vegetables. The compact head size also suits smaller households better than a large storage cabbage does. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and solid, since fast-maturing types can split if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South. Matures in 45–55 days from transplant.

name: Tice Mulberry
description: Tice originated in the Ft. Myers, Florida area and is prized as one of the most nematode-resistant mulberries available, making it a favored rootstock as well as a fruiting selection for sandy Gulf Coast soils. It produces large, sweet-tart, juicy berries on a vigorous, wide-canopied tree with notably large leaves and weeping outer branches. Give it full sun and irrigate during establishment; once rooted it is quite drought tolerant. Net or harvest promptly, as ripe fruit drops heavily and stains hardscape below. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tie Luo Han Tea (Iron Arhat)
description: Tie Luo Han, or "Iron Arhat," is one of the Wuyi Mountains' Si Da Ming Cong ("Four Great Bushes"), the small group of heirloom rock-tea cultivars that, alongside Da Hong Pao, Bai Jiguan, and Shui Jin Gui, anchor the most prized yancha oolongs of Fujian Province. Local legend traces the original bushes to Huiyuan Cliff and credits the tea with folk-medicinal uses long before it became famous as a premium oolong source. Like its Wuyi siblings it performs best in mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils with partial shade, developing the mineral, roasted "rock rhyme" character prized in traditionally charcoal-fired processing. Harvest semi-mature leaves typical of oolong production rather than the youngest buds used for green tea. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tifblue Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Tifblue is a rabbiteye blueberry developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (Tifton, Georgia) and released in 1955, becoming the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the world for most of the 20th century. Though newer varieties (Climax, Premier, Brightwell) have larger or earlier-ripening fruit, Tifblue maintains a loyal following as the definitive late-season rabbiteye: its berries ripen in late July through August in zone 8–9, extending the blueberry season 4–6 weeks past early varieties. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, mildly sweet, with a firm texture that makes them excellent for shipping, freezing, and baking where texture is important. Tifblue is also one of the most important pollinators for other rabbiteye varieties, its abundant, late-season pollen highly compatible with Fry and other non-self-fertile varieties. Plants are vigorous, productive, and cold-hardy for a rabbiteye (surviving 10–15°F without significant damage in established plants). As a historical benchmark variety and reliable late-season producer, Tifblue remains valuable in zone 7–9 blueberry plantings. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tifblue Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Tifblue was the rabbiteye blueberry standard for decades — a large, vigorous, upright shrub with good berries and excellent adaptability. Released by the USDA-ARS Tifton, Georgia station, it produces medium to large, light blue, firm, mild-flavored berries in late June to July, extending the harvest season after early and mid-season varieties have finished. The berries have excellent shelf life due to their firm texture. However, Tifblue's higher chilling requirement (500–600 hours) makes it a less reliable choice in the warmer parts of zone 8–9 where chilling hours may not accumulate sufficiently in mild winters. Best suited to zone 6–8 where more consistent chilling ensures reliable bloom and full fruit set. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tifleaf Pearl Millet (High-Yield Summer Cover Crop and Wildlife Food Plot Grass)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained to moderately moist, average to fertile soil in full sun; Tifleaf Pearl Millet is the premier summer cover crop and wildlife food plot annual grass for Gulf South gardens and farms — a rapidly growing warm-season grass developed by the University of Georgia that establishes extremely quickly in warm conditions, producing dense, tall (5–8 foot) stands within 6–8 weeks of planting. The rapid establishment makes pearl millet exceptionally effective as a summer cover crop in Gulf South gardens that experience the challenging June–August gap between spring vegetable harvest and fall planting — a period when bare soil erodes, weeds proliferate, and soil organic matter degrades under summer sun. Tifleaf 3 is one of the most productive of all cover crop grasses for total biomass per acre in summer conditions, providing substantial green manure when terminated by mowing or incorporation before fall planting. The tall, dense stand also creates an effective summer screen, privacy hedge, or windbreak for garden areas. For wildlife gardeners, pearl millet provides outstanding deer forage and dove attractant — the seed heads produced in late summer are among the most palatable of all wildlife food plot plantings for mourning doves. Drought-tolerant once established. Terminated easily by mowing at the soil surface — the shallow root system decomposes quickly, improving soil organic matter. Grows as a warm-season annual, killed by first frost. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: Tiger Baby Watermelon (Striped-Rind Icebox Hybrid)
description: Tiger Baby gets its name from the dark gray-green rind striped with bold tiger-like markings, wrapped around a compact 7-8 pound icebox-size fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. Its shorter maturity window compared to full-size Southern heirlooms makes it a good pick for gardeners north of the traditional watermelon belt who still want a full-flavored melon. Fertilize modestly since excess nitrogen favors vine growth over fruiting, and thump or check the ground spot for creamy yellowing to judge ripeness. The single-serving size makes it easy to chill whole and slice fresh without leftovers going to waste. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Tiger Eye Bean
description: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tiger Eye is a stunning heirloom bush bean with large seeds in a rich golden-yellow to tan background covered with auburn to deep brown streaking and marbling — the pattern resembles a tiger's eye gemstone and retains some color on cooking. The flavor is particularly rich and buttery for a dry bean, often described as creamy with a hint of chestnut, making it excellent in soups and stews or as a simple side dish. A productive and reliable bush bean that dries beautifully on the plant and stores well. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Tiger Tooth Jujube (Deeply Serrated-Leaf Elongated Sweet-Tart Jujube)
description: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established, making them outstanding low-input choices for Gulf South heat. Tiger Tooth takes its name from its distinctively deep, sharply pointed leaf serrations, a visually unmistakable trait among jujube cultivars, and produces 2- to 3-inch elongated fruit with a crisp, apple-like texture and sweet-tart flavor when harvested at the tan, semi-dry stage in late summer to early fall. It bears within its first two to three years and, like other jujubes, shrugs off the heat, humidity, and periodic drought of a Gulf Coast summer with little complaint. Prune only lightly to remove crossing or damaged branches, and expect vigorous root suckering, which can be mowed or dug and transplanted to propagate new trees. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tigerella Tomato
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before last frost in a warm, moist seed-starting mix kept at 70–85°F; transplant deeply after frost danger has passed, burying the stem up to the lowest leaves to encourage a strong root system. Tigerella is a British heirloom also sold under the name Mr. Stripey in the UK, producing heavy clusters of 2–3 ounce fruits with vivid red skin and irregular gold-yellow stripes and a tangy, balanced flavor that is excellent fresh or in sauces. Stake or cage plants early and begin harvesting when the fruit is firm but fully colored at the blossom end; unlike many striped types it ripens evenly and does not crack easily. Regular irrigation helps maintain even soil moisture and reduces blossom-end rot. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Tigernut
description: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, loose, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; tigernut (chufa, earth almond) is a cultivated sedge grown for its small, starchy, walnut-flavored underground tubers — the basis of the traditional Spanish drink horchata de chufa — that are rich in fiber, healthy fats, and natural sugars and may be eaten raw, roasted, or processed into milk, flour, or oil. Plants produce a dense clump of grass-like, bright-green leaves with triangular stems (a sedge, not a grass). The tubers multiply prolifically underground and are harvested after the foliage dies back in fall. Excellent as a forage crop for wildlife food plots (ducks and deer are attracted to tigernuts) or as a human snack crop. Distinct from the wild weed form (C. esculentus var. esculentus) which is an invasive nuisance; always plant only the cultivated var. sativus. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: TigerPaw-NR Habanero Pepper (Nematode-Resistant Habanero)
description: Germinate on a heat mat at 80-90 degrees F and transplant outdoors only after nights stay reliably warm. TigerPaw-NR was released by USDA-ARS in 2006 after a recurrent backcross program moved a dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from a Scotch Bonnet accession into a habanero-type line, producing the first commercially available habanero cultivar resistant to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes. Plants are compact and productive, bearing attractive lantern-shaped orange fruit that is extremely pungent, in the same fiery range as standard habaneros. The resistance package makes it a strong choice for home gardeners and small-scale growers along the Gulf Coast, where nematode pressure in light, sandy soils often stunts unprotected habanero plantings. Matures in 95–110 days from transplant.

name: Tigger Melon
description: Sow in hills after last frost in warm, well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow vines to sprawl or train on a sturdy trellis with sling support for fruits. Tigger is a Central Asian or Middle Eastern heirloom melon with one of the most striking exteriors in the melon world — the smooth, round to oval, medium-sized (1–2 lb) fruits are a brilliant golden-yellow with dramatic crimson-to-orange zigzag stripes, spots, and splashes that make them resemble the fictional tiger character they are named for. The flesh is cream-colored to pale orange with a sweet, spicy, slightly fruity aroma that is pleasant rather than intensely musky; more of an ornamental conversation-piece melon than a flavor standout, but still delicious and perfectly edible. Extremely heat-tolerant and productive in hot climates; outstanding as a farmers market novelty and ornamental edible. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Tikal Sapodilla
description: Named for the ancient Maya city in Guatemala within the species' native range, 'Tikal' is a Central American sapodilla selection grown in South Florida for its good-quality, medium-sized fruit with fine-grained, sweet, brown-sugar-flavored flesh and comparatively few grit cells. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; the tree is vigorous and productive once established, tolerating the alkaline, rocky soils common to South Florida plantings. As with all sapodilla, harvest fruit while still firm but showing the characteristic dull, scurfy skin, then let it soften at room temperature for several days before eating, since unripe fruit is astringent with latex. Mature trees withstand brief dips into the upper 20s F with only leaf damage, but young wood needs frost protection. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tillamook Goumi
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-moderately-fertile soil — avoid over-fertilizing as excess nitrogen suppresses fruit production in this nitrogen-fixing shrub; Tillamook is a Raintree Nursery-selected goumi cultivar known for producing larger, sweeter fruit than most other goumi selections, with a berry size approaching that of a small cherry and a flavor noticeably sweeter and more pleasant for fresh eating than the more astringent wild-type goumi. The large, bright scarlet to deep red berries ripen with the distinctive silvery speckle pattern characteristic of Elaeagnus species, and the mature ripe fruit has a sweet-tart flavor with less of the mouth-puckering tannin that makes less-ripe goumi berries challenging to eat raw. Tillamook was selected from plants grown at Raintree Nursery in Morton, Washington — a Pacific Northwest selection that nonetheless performs well in zone 9 given its cold hardiness and drought tolerance. Like all goumi, it fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility for neighboring plants in a permaculture or food forest context. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tilton Apricot (California Canning Apricot, Late-Season Commercial Apricot)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Tilton is self-fertile; thin to 3–5 inches after June drop; Tilton ripens mid-to-late season (July in California), about 2 weeks later than Blenheim, providing a fresh apricot harvest window after the main-season varieties finish; firm flesh holds quality after picking and is excellent for drying, canning, and jam. Tilton apricot is a California variety with origins in the San Joaquin Valley community of Tilton (now part of Hanford), from which it takes its name, and it was one of the primary commercial canning apricot varieties in California's Central Valley from the late 19th century through much of the 20th century alongside Blenheim. Where Blenheim is the benchmark for fresh-eating quality, Tilton became the commercial preference for processing — its firmer flesh holds structure better through the heat of canning and cooking than the softer, more aromatic Blenheim, producing intact apricot halves that maintain attractive color and firmness in the can. Tilton fruits are medium-sized, round to oval, pale orange to golden-orange with a slight reddish blush, with firm, moderately sweet, mildly tart flesh and a pleasant though not exceptional apricot flavor. The variety blooms somewhat later than Blenheim and Moorpark — an advantage in regions with late spring frost risk — and the firm flesh makes it better for shipping and home drying into dried apricots. A solid production variety for home orchards where a large canning crop is desired. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Timor Hybrid Coffee (Híbrido de Timor)
description: Discovered growing spontaneously on the island of Timor in the early twentieth century, this naturally occurring cross between Arabica and Robusta combines Arabica's cup quality with Robusta's resilience, carrying broad-spectrum resistance to coffee leaf rust and coffee berry disease that has made it the single most important disease-resistance donor in modern coffee breeding. Rather than being planted commercially on its own, it lives on mainly as the hidden ancestor behind rust-resistant cultivars like Catimor and Sarchimor, though pure Timor Hybrid plantings still persist in Timor-Leste's mountain forests. Give it the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica types, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a vigorous, disease-tolerant plant that shrugs off pressures that devastate less hardy varieties. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Timperley Early Rhubarb (Classic Forcing Rhubarb)
description: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is a long-established English rhubarb cultivar bred and selected specifically for forcing — covering the crown in late winter with an upturned pot or forcing jar to exclude light produces exceptionally early, pale pink, sweet, tender stalks weeks ahead of an uncovered planting, a traditional practice in British kitchen gardens. Left unforced, it is simply an early-cropping, reliable garden rhubarb with slender, bright red-pink stalks and good flavor.
