As with all rhubarb, it performs best where winters provide real cold to satisfy its chilling requirement, so it is more reliable in temperate and upper Southern gardens than in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, always leaving several stalks per plant to sustain it, and never eat the leaves, which contain toxic levels of oxalic acid. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Timut Pepper (Timur, Nepal Pepper)
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins, tolerating winters at elevation across Nepal and northern India. The dried, husked berries deliver an intense citrus-grapefruit aroma alongside the characteristic tongue-tingling numbness of the genus, and are ground fresh for Nepali achar, momo dipping sauces, and spice blends. Harvest ripe berry clusters in autumn and dry them whole before grinding just before use to preserve the volatile citrus notes. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tiny Tim Tomato
description: Sow Tiny Tim seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then move seedlings to their final container or bed once frost danger passes. This dwarf determinate reaches only about 12 inches tall, making it perfect for patios, windowsills, and indoor pots. It sets an early, generous crop of bright cherry tomatoes on compact plants that need little or no staking. Give it plenty of light and steady moisture, and harvest the fruit as it ripens fully red. Matures in 45–55 days from transplant.

name: Titan Parsley
description: Titan is a flat-leaf (French) parsley bred for compact, weather-resistant growth and a profusion of small, finely divided, dark green leaves. Its flavor is notably stronger and sweeter than curly-leaf types, making it a favorite for cooks who want intense parsley taste rather than just a garnish. The tidy, uniform habit tolerates close spacing and holds up well to repeated cutting without becoming ragged. Grown as an annual, it can overwinter in milder zones into a biennial second year, though leaves coarsen and flavor declines once the plant begins to bolt and flower. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Titan Rabbiteye Blueberry (Extra-Large-Fruited Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Titan is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry celebrated for producing exceptionally large berries, among the biggest of any rabbiteye cultivar available, with good firmness and a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor that makes for an impressive fresh-eating harvest. The vigorous, upright bushes are productive and ripen mid-to-late in the rabbiteye season, extending the harvest window when paired with earlier cultivars like Alapaha or Premier. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Titan requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Titan Raspberry (Extra-Large-Fruited English Red Raspberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, and stake or trellis canes securely to support the exceptionally heavy fruit. Titan is an English-bred summer-bearing red raspberry known for producing some of the largest raspberry fruit commonly grown, with individual berries noticeably bigger than most standard varieties, making it popular for exhibition growing as well as home fresh eating. The vigorous, thorny canes are productive and reliable, though the sheer size and weight of the fruit clusters make sturdy support more important than with smaller-fruited varieties, since overloaded canes can bend or break without it. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest each summer, and thin new canes to the strongest for the best fruit size the following season. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Titan Sea Buckthorn (Large-Fruited Russian Seaberry)
description: Titan is a Russian-bred female sea buckthorn selection known for unusually large, orange-red berries produced in dense clusters along the branches, borne on thornier growth than some newer German cultivars. As a dioecious shrub it needs a male Hippophae rhamnoides plant within about 50 to 100 feet for pollination and reliable fruit set. Its nitrogen-fixing roots let it thrive in poor, sandy, or gravelly soils where few other fruiting shrubs succeed, and established plants tolerate drought and coastal wind well. Harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches and freezing them, since the tart berries cling tightly to the stem and are difficult to pick by hand when ripe. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Titania Black Currant
description: 'Titania' is a vigorous, disease-resistant black currant valued for strong resistance to white pine blister rust and mildew. It produces long strigs of large, glossy berries over an extended ripening window, making harvest easier. Grow in full sun to light shade in fertile, moisture-retentive soil enriched with compost. Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer in spring and prune out the oldest quarter of the wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Titania Currant (Vigorous Disease-Resistant Black Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Titania is a Swedish-bred black currant selected for strong vigor, heavy and consistent yields, and good resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew compared with older black currant cultivars. The large, glossy berries carry the classic intense, aromatic black currant flavor, best used cooked into jam, syrup, cordial, and baked goods rather than eaten fresh. The upright, vigorous bush establishes quickly and bears well from a young age. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so remove the oldest, least productive canes each dormant season to encourage the strong young growth that will carry next year's crop, and net the bushes as fruit ripens, since birds are highly attracted to currants. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Titicaca Quinoa (Danish-Bred Short-Season Quinoa)
description: Titicaca was developed through a Danish university breeding program aimed at bringing quinoa into higher-latitude, shorter-summer climates where standard Andean lines fail to ripen before fall frost. It grows notably shorter and more compact than most heirloom quinoa strains, an advantage for reducing lodging in windy gardens, and its day-neutral flowering habit lets it set seed reliably regardless of daylength. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun and thin to a wide enough spacing for the plants to bulk up their seed heads. Cut whole plants once the seed heads dry and rattle, then thresh and rinse the harvested seed thoroughly to strip the bitter saponin coating before cooking or storing. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Tivoli Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Spaghetti Squash for Small Gardens)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest when skin is cream-yellow and thumps with a hollow sound. Tivoli Squash was developed by W. Atlee Burpee and received All-America Selections recognition in 1991 specifically for solving one of the primary practical limitations of spaghetti squash production in home gardens: the sprawling, space-consuming vine habit of standard spaghetti squash varieties makes them impractical for most garden spaces. While standard vining spaghetti squash can trail 6–10 feet in multiple directions from a single plant, requiring 40–80 square feet per plant for uncrowded production, Tivoli's compact bush habit limits the footprint to approximately 3–4 feet in diameter — manageable within a raised bed or small garden plot. The fruits produced by Tivoli are standard-sized spaghetti squash (4–5 lbs, 8–10 inches long, cream-colored skin), with the same characteristic flesh that separates into noodle-like strands when cooked — a texture that makes spaghetti squash one of the most popular vegetable substitutes for pasta. For zone 9 gardeners, spaghetti squash performs well in spring (transplanted or direct sown in March–May for a June–August harvest) and in fall (planted in late August for October–November harvest), with the compact bush habit of Tivoli making both planting windows practical in average-sized raised bed gardens. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Tixia Gooseberry
description: Tixia is a Swiss-bred gooseberry raised from a cross with Invicta as the female parent, selected for large, bright red, sweet-tart berries on a vigorous, upright, mildew-resistant bush. A distinguishing trait is fewer thorns on first-year wood, and the thorns that remain stay soft, making picking substantially more comfortable than on traditional gooseberry cultivars. It performs best in regions with cool summers and consistent moisture, and struggles in prolonged heat or drought. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Tobacco
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; tobacco is a fast-growing annual grown for its large, broad leaves, which are harvested, cured, and fermented into the leaf used in cigars, cigarettes, and pipe tobacco. As flower buds form, most growers 'top' the plant by removing the flowering tip, which redirects energy into leaf size and thickness, and then remove the side shoots ('suckers') that sprout below the cut, though some plants can be left to flower for their tall spikes of pink, trumpet-shaped blooms if seed saving or ornamental effect is the goal. Harvest leaves progressively from the bottom of the stalk upward as they mature and turn pale yellow-green, then cure them by hanging in a warm, well-ventilated, shaded space for several weeks before further fermentation. All parts of the plant contain nicotine and are toxic if ingested by pets, livestock, or children, and the sticky leaf hairs can cause skin irritation (green tobacco sickness) in sensitive individuals during handling, so wear long sleeves when working with mature plants. Matures in 90–130 days from transplant.

name: Todd's Mitcham Peppermint (Verticillium-Tolerant Commercial Peppermint)
description: Todd's Mitcham is an improved strain of the classic Black Mitcham peppermint, released in the 1970s from an irradiation breeding program at Brookhaven National Laboratory specifically to improve field resistance to Verticillium wilt, the disease that devastates commercial mint plantings. It carries the same strong, high-menthol peppermint flavor and aroma prized for tea, confections, and oil distillation as standard Black Mitcham, but with better resilience in soils where wilt has been a problem. Like other peppermints it spreads aggressively by rhizome, so garden plantings should be contained in pots or sunk barriers. Harvest stems just before flowering, when menthol content and flavor peak, for the best fresh or dried leaf. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Toddy Fishtail Palm (Wine Palm, Jaggery Palm)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; note that Caryota urens is monocarpic and dies after completing its single flowering sequence. Caryota urens (toddy fishtail palm or wine palm) is a large, single-stemmed Indian and Sri Lankan palm remarkable for several unique characteristics: it is one of very few palms with bipinnate leaves (doubly compound — each leaf divided into segments, each segment then further divided into individual fishtail-shaped leaflets), giving it a dramatically different appearance from most other palms; and it is monocarpic — it flowers only once in its life, then dies. The flowering sequence begins at the top of the trunk and proceeds downward over several years (from the highest leaf axil to the lowest), with the entire tree dying when the last inflorescence at the base completes seed set — a spectacular but terminal process. The palm is the primary source of kithul jaggery in Sri Lanka (considered the finest quality palm sugar in Asia) and a major source of toddy (palm wine) in South India. The sap from tapped flower stalks is collected daily; fresh it is sweet and mildly fermenting; processed it produces kithul honey, jaggery, and vinegar. The seeds and unripe fruits contain oxalate crystals — do not eat raw. The palm is ornamentally outstanding — unique bipinnate fronds create an unmistakable tropical texture. Matures in 2555–5475 days from transplant.

name: Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn (Desert-Adapted Sonoran Flour Corn)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn is a remarkably fast-maturing flour corn developed by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, bred to reach maturity in about two months so a crop could be planted and harvested within the brief window of the summer monsoon rains. Its speed and drought adaptation make it valuable for short-season gardens or a fast succession planting anywhere. Harvest and dry ears fully before grinding the kernels into flour for traditional dishes like pinole and tortillas. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tokinashi Daikon
description: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into loose, deeply cultivated soil free of stones so the long, tapering white roots can grow straight and unforked. Tokinashi is a traditional Japanese heirloom valued for its unusual all-season adaptability and its resistance to becoming pithy, allowing roots to be left in the ground to reach 15-18 inches without losing quality. The firm, crisp, assertively pungent flesh is a staple for grating, pickling, and simmering, and the variety is a reliable open-pollinated choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Tokyo Bekana
description: This tender Asian green forms loose, frilly, pale chartreuse leaves used raw in salads or lightly cooked. Direct sow shallowly and thin to about 8 inches, or harvest thinnings as baby greens. It grows very fast and prefers cool weather, bolting quickly once temperatures climb. Keep soil evenly moist to maintain the crisp, mild leaves and prevent bitterness. Sow in early spring and again in late summer for tender harvests bracketing the heat of summer. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Tokyo Cross Turnip (AAS-Winning Hybrid Salad Turnip)
description: Tokyo Cross is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip, an All-America Selections winner bred from the open-pollinated Tokyo Market type, valued for producing smooth, pure-white globes that stay tender, mild, and crack-free even if left in the ground past ideal size. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin to a few inches apart, keeping the bed consistently moist for the fastest, sweetest roots. Both the crisp roots and the tender young tops are edible, making it a dual-purpose crop for salads, quick pickles, or braising greens. Its speed and heat tolerance for a turnip make it well suited to succession planting through much of the season. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Tokyo Long White Bunching Onion
description: Sow Tokyo Long White seeds a quarter inch deep and thin plants to about an inch apart for tall, tender green stalks. This non-bulbing Asian heirloom forms long white shanks topped with mild green tops rather than a round bulb. It tolerates cold well and can be grown in containers or resown every few weeks for a continuous supply. Harvest whole plants when they reach usable size, or trim tops as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Tokyo Market Turnip (Japanese Fast-Growing Salad Turnip)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 3–4 inches apart; harvest at 2–3 inch diameter for finest quality (overripe roots become pithy and strongly flavored); both roots and tender greens are edible. Tokyo Market is a Japanese-type salad turnip closely related to (but distinct from) Hakurei — both belong to the mild, sweet, fast-maturing Japanese turnip tradition that is quite different from the traditional European turnip types grown for cooking. Tokyo Market matures in just 30–40 days from direct seeding, producing smooth, round, pure white roots with a mild, slightly sweet, and almost fruity flavor that is excellent raw — sliced thin into salads, served with dipping sauces, or eaten out of hand like an apple in the garden. Unlike European cooking turnips (which are generally too sharp and starchy to eat raw), Japanese salad turnip types like Tokyo Market and Hakurei have been bred for low pungency and high sugar content, making them the most accessible and enjoyable turnips for most modern palates. The tender, mild young greens are equally edible — excellent in salads, stir-fries, and anywhere turnip greens are used with a preference for milder flavor. Tokyo Market is preferred in farmers market growing for its consistent, uniform appearance and rapid turnover; for home gardeners it provides the fastest-maturing turnip option for succession planting every 3–4 weeks. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Tolman Sweet Apple (Classic New England Sweet Baking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Tolman Sweet is a New England heirloom dating to the early 1800s, one of the classic old-fashioned 'sweet apple' varieties once grown widely across colonial and early American orchards specifically for their low-acid, honeyed sweetness, distinct from the tart-sweet balance of most familiar modern apples. The pale yellow-green skin, sometimes lightly blushed with red near the stem, covers firm, dry, mild, sugary flesh that is exceptional baked whole, since the sweetness needs no added sugar, and it was also historically valued as a good keeper and a favorite for livestock feed and cider blending. The tree is notably cold-hardy and dependable, and while sweet apples have fallen out of fashion compared with tart-sweet modern varieties, Tolman Sweet remains a worthwhile piece of American orchard history for gardeners interested in historic baking apples. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tom Thumb Lettuce (Miniature Heirloom Butterhead Lettuce)
description: Direct sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile soil with barely 0.125 inch coverage; keep consistently moist through germination. Tom Thumb is an English heirloom butterhead lettuce that produces perfectly proportioned miniature heads — fully formed, well-blanched butterhead-type lettuce compressed into a head 3–4 inches in diameter and 4–6 inches tall at maturity, roughly one-quarter the size of a standard butterhead like Buttercrunch or Boston. The miniature scale is not a compromised or immature form of standard lettuce; Tom Thumb is a true miniature variety that completes its growth cycle and forms a proper, compact head with the characteristic blanched, cream-colored inner leaves and tender, buttery texture of butterhead types. The small head size makes Tom Thumb exceptionally practical in multiple ways: it can be spaced 6 inches apart rather than 10–12 inches, fitting significantly more plants in a given area; it produces one serving per head, eliminating the common problem of leftover half-heads wilting in the refrigerator; and it is particularly suited to container growing, window boxes, and very small raised beds where a full-sized lettuce would be overwhelming. Tom Thumb has been grown in English kitchen gardens since at least the 19th century and represents the miniaturization approach to vegetable breeding that has recently become popular again in urban and space-limited gardening. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tom Thumb Pea
description: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly, making it one of the earliest garden peas to harvest. Bred in England in the mid-1800s as a compact alternative to the era's towering pea vines, Tom Thumb tops out under a foot tall, which has made it a longtime favorite for small beds, cold frames, and containers. Because the plants are so short, keep them weed-free, as taller neighbors will shade them out quickly. Harvest pods as soon as they plump for the sweetest flavor, since this small-statured variety produces a modest but concentrated crop over a short window. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: Tom Thumb Popcorn (Dwarf Heirloom Strawberry-Type Popcorn)
description: Sow in blocks in average garden soil or containers; its dwarf habit lets it thrive in small spaces where a full-size popcorn would be impractical. Tom Thumb is a diminutive heirloom popcorn reaching only three to four feet tall, producing small, deep-red ears reminiscent of miniature Strawberry Popcorn but on an even more compact plant. Left to dry fully on the stalk, the small hard kernels pop up light and tender, and the short ears and petite plants also make this variety popular for autumn ornamental displays as well as a genuinely productive novelty popcorn for the home popper. Matures in 85–90 days from seed.

name: Tom Watson Watermelon (Classic Georgia Heirloom, Very Large Southern Picnic Watermelon)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; space hills 6–8 feet apart. Harvest when tendril dries and ground spot turns creamy yellow. Tom Watson is one of the most historically important American watermelon varieties — a large, oblong, Southern heirloom that was the dominant commercial watermelon in the southeastern United States from approximately 1906 through the mid-20th century, and that is named (with slight uncertainty as to whether intentionally or as a coincidence of personal name similarity) after one of Georgia's most prominent politicians of the era. Tom Watson melons are large to very large (typically 25–50 lbs), oblong with mottled medium-dark green skin and faint lighter stripes, with red to deep red flesh and moderate seed content. The flavor at full maturity is excellent — sweet, richly flavored, and typifying the character of old-style Southern watermelons grown in sandy, hot-summer soil. Tom Watson was particularly prized for its performance in the sandy, well-drained soils of the Georgia and Carolina coastal plain, where the warm nights, deep sandy loam, and long growing season produced melons with exceptional sweetness and the size that made watermelons the centerpiece of summer picnics, church suppers, and community celebrations throughout the South. The variety's historical significance extends beyond flavor: Tom Watson represents a type of community and agricultural identity in the South where the production of very large, high-quality melons was a point of regional pride and a staple of summer social life in farming communities. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Toma Verde Tomatillo
description: Start Toma Verde seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings 24 to 36 inches apart in warm soil. This early-maturing variety produces bright green fruit in papery husks with the classic tart flavor prized for salsa verde. Plant at least two tomatillos, since they need cross-pollination to set fruit well. Harvest when the fruit fills and splits its husk, and stake the sprawling plants to keep fruit off the ground. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Tomatillo (Mexican Husk Tomato, Husk Tomatillo)
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; set transplants in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; plant at least two for pollination. Physalis philadelphica (tomatillo) is the green or purple, husked fruit essential to Mexican salsas, mole verde, and enchilada sauce — a fruity, tart, citrusy tomato relative encased in a papery, lantern-like calyx that expands as the fruit develops and splits open to signal ripeness; harvest when the husk fills tightly and the fruit turns from green toward yellow, or use green for maximum tartness in salsa verde. Tomatillos are extremely productive warm-season annuals that bear heavily in zone 9 through summer and fall; they are more heat-tolerant than tomatoes and continue producing when summer temperatures exceed 90°F. The plants sprawl considerably and benefit from caging or staking; prune to 2–3 main stems for higher yields. 'Verde Puebla' and 'Gigante' are large-fruited green types; 'Purple de Milpa' has purple-tinged fruits. Unlike tomatoes, tomatillos must be planted in pairs or groups because they are self-incompatible — single plants produce no fruit. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Tomcot Apricot (Early-Season Large-Fruited Apricot)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit after natural drop to prevent overbearing on this heavy-setting cultivar. Tomcot is valued commercially and by home growers for ripening two to three weeks ahead of most other apricots, filling the earliest slot in the harvest season with large, firm, richly colored fruit. It is self-fertile and also serves as an excellent pollinizer for other apricot varieties thanks to its abundant, early bloom. Because it flowers so early, plant in a site with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to blossoms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tomhannock Lettuce (Historic American Speckled Butterhead)
description: Documented as far back as an 1837 English gardening magazine, Tomhannock traces to French seed distributed through the London Horticultural Society but became far more popular in American gardens than in England. Nineteenth-century American seedsmen sold the same lettuce under other names as well. It forms a butterhead-type, somewhat savoyed and blistered head of medium green leaves with distinctive reddish-brown speckling, giving it a decorative look beyond its eating quality. This old dual-purpose butterhead is a good option for gardeners wanting a lettuce with genuine nineteenth-century American roots. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Tommy Atkins Mango (Widely Grown Commercial Florida Mango)
description: Tommy Atkins is a Florida-origin seedling selection that became the most widely planted commercial mango cultivar in the world thanks to its heavy, reliable bearing and unusually good resistance to anthracnose and rough handling during shipping. The fruit is large with a strikingly showy skin blushed red, orange, and yellow, but the flesh is moderately fibrous and milder in flavor than heirloom cultivars like Haden or Carrie. Growers in humid Gulf Coast climates appreciate its disease tolerance, though home gardeners prioritizing eating quality often prefer pairing it with a richer-flavored cultivar. Give the tree full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a large, vigorous canopy unless it is pruned regularly after harvest. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tommy Toe Tomato (Australian Heirloom Salad Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support the vigorous vines. Tommy Toe is a beloved Australian heirloom producing an abundance of round, golf-ball-sized fruit larger than a typical cherry tomato but smaller than a standard slicer, with rich, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor that many gardeners rate above modern cherry hybrids for taste. Its heavy, sustained production over a long season and good disease tolerance have made it a favorite for fresh eating, salads, and snacking straight off the vine, occupying a useful middle ground in size between cherry and full-sized tomatoes. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the prolific vines setting new fruit throughout the summer. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Tomuri Kiwi (Late-Blooming Male Pollinizer for Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis positioned to pollinate nearby female fuzzy kiwi vines. Tomuri is a New Zealand-bred male fuzzy kiwi selection notable for blooming later than Matua, making it a useful complementary pollinizer planted alongside Matua to extend the overlap with female Hayward bloom across a longer window and improve overall pollination reliability, since kiwi bloom timing between individual vines can vary from year to year with weather. As with all male kiwi vines, Tomuri itself never sets fruit, existing solely to provide pollen for female vines. Prune to encourage strong, abundant flowering and to keep the vine's size proportional to the fruiting female vines it services within the planting. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Tonatico Cherry Tomato (AAS-Winning High-Yield Round Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Tonatico is an AAS regional winner producing round, bright red, roughly 1.5-inch cherry fruit with a notably high sugar content and juicy, sweet flavor, carried on long, easy-to-harvest trusses that can number up to 200 fruits per plant over the season. Fruit resists cracking and the plant shows good disease resistance, so the uniform clusters hold up well through variable watering and weather. Pick trusses as fruit fully colors for the sweetest eating, and maintain consistent moisture to keep the high yields coming. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Tonda di Giffoni Hazelnut (Italian PGI Round Hazelnut)
description: Tonda di Giffoni is one of Italy's most celebrated hazelnut cultivars, grown around Giffoni in Campania and protected under EU Protected Geographical Indication status for its round, easily-peeled, richly flavored kernels favored by confectioners for roasting and chocolate production. The tree is moderately vigorous, precocious, and notably productive, with good tolerance of both cold winter temperatures and common fungal pressures compared to many other European cultivars. It performs best where summers are warm and dry enough to ripen the crop fully, similar to its native growing region. Harvest from early September into mid-October once husks brown and nuts drop or twist free easily. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tonda di Parigi Carrot
description: Sow seed shallowly in loose soil as soon as the ground can be worked, keeping the bed evenly moist through the slow germination. This Italian heirloom, whose name means Round of Paris, forms deep-orange, golf-ball-shaped roots that are sweet and tender. Its short, round shape means shallow roots, so it thrives in shallow beds and containers where longer carrots would struggle; harvest young for the best texture. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tonda Gentile delle Langhe Hazelnut (Piedmont Hazelnut)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollenizer variety nearby, since this hazelnut is not self-fertile. Tonda Gentile delle Langhe is the classic hazelnut of Italy's Piedmont region, celebrated for its round shape, thin shell, and rich, sweet, highly aromatic kernel that is the traditional standard for fine chocolate-hazelnut confections. Like most European hazelnut cultivars it is quite susceptible to eastern filbert blight in humid North American climates, so it performs best in drier growing regions or where the disease pressure is low. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tonda Gentile Romana Hazelnut (Tonda Romana, Nocciola Romana DOP Filbert)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tonda Gentile Romana requires a compatible pollenizer; nuts ripen from late August to late September and are collected from the ground as they fall, with fine, thin shells that split easily during processing. Tonda Gentile Romana (also called Tonda Romana) is one of the principal cultivars behind the Nocciola Romana DOP, an Italian Protected Designation of Origin hazelnut grown chiefly in the province of Viterbo and parts of Rome in the Lazio region, with cultivation dating back to at least the 15th century. The nuts are small, round, with pale, delicately flavored kernels, and the cultivar is prized in the Italian confectionery industry for chocolate and traditional sweets. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tonda Pacifica Hazelnut (OSU 228.084)
description: Tonda Pacifica was bred at Oregon State University from a cross of the celebrated Italian cultivar Tonda Gentile delle Langhe and an OSU breeding selection, then released in 2010 as a named commercial cultivar rather than pure breeding stock. It produces a smaller, more yield-efficient tree than the old industry standard Barcelona, bearing smaller nuts with an unusually high kernel percentage and few defects that suit the blanched-kernel, chocolate, and baking trade. Like Barcelona it remains susceptible to Eastern Filbert Blight, so growers in blight-prone regions should pair it with a resistant rootstock or maintain a fungicide program rather than counting on Tonda Pacifica's own disease tolerance. It also carries breeding significance as the female parent, crossed with Santiam, of the EFB-resistant OSU release McDonald. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tongkat Ali
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic, forest-type soil in partial shade to deep shade; Eurycoma longifolia requires the warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture of a tropical rainforest environment — avoid cold, drought, or standing water, and provide forest-floor-type organic mulch to mimic its natural habitat. Eurycoma longifolia (Tongkat Ali, Longjack, or Malaysian Ginseng) is a slender, dioecious, understory tree native to the lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, Vietnam, and the Philippines, recognized as the most commercially important and widely exported medicinal plant of Southeast Asia by trade value. The long, slender, deeply penetrating taproots — sometimes over 6 feet long and difficult to harvest — are the medicinal part, dried, powdered, and used in traditional Malay, Indonesian, and Vietnamese medicine as a bitter tonic for fatigue, stress, fever, and debility. Modern phytochemical research has identified quassinoids (eurycomanone) and other bioactive compounds with adaptogenic, testosterone-supporting, anti-fatigue, and antimalarial properties, driving a large international dietary supplement industry. Tongkat Ali is now one of the most over-harvested wild medicinal plants in Southeast Asia — Malaysia has established cultivation standards and sustainable harvesting programs to prevent wild population collapse. Cultivation from seed is slow; plant in deep, organically rich, moist, shaded conditions similar to rainforest understory. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Tongue of Fire Bean (Borlotto Lingua di Fuoco)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Tongue of Fire is an Italian heirloom bean with extraordinary visual appeal — the pods are cream-colored with vivid red-orange streaks and splashes, as if painted with fire. The seeds inside are cranberry-colored with dark red stripes. The beans are harvested green as a snap or shell bean, or left to dry for storage as a dry bean. As a fresh shell bean the flavor is rich, creamy, and nutty — superior to most commercial beans. The striped coloring unfortunately fades when cooked, but the flavor more than compensates. An excellent choice for Italian and Mediterranean-style cooking, particularly in minestrone, pasta e fagioli, and bean salads. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Tongues of Fire Bean (Lingua di Fuoco, Italian Shell Bean Heirloom)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; Tongues of Fire is a bush bean that can also be harvested as a snap bean at 5–6 inches (though the pods are somewhat coarse) — harvest as a shell bean when pods are plump and fully developed (60–70 days) or allow to dry completely for a dry borlotto bean (75–85 days). Tongues of Fire (Lingua di Fuoco) is a traditional Italian borlotto bean with some of the most dramatically beautiful pods in the vegetable garden — the medium-length pods are a creamy or pale yellow background completely covered with irregular streaks, splashes, and flames of scarlet-red that give the variety its evocative Italian name. The raw pods are so visually striking that harvesting them from the plant is genuinely exciting; unfortunately (from a visual standpoint), both the red pod markings and the speckled cream-and-red seed coloring fade completely when the beans are cooked, resulting in uniform tan to brownish seeds. The flavor of shell-stage Tongues of Fire beans is excellent — rich, earthy, and starchy in the characteristic Italian borlotto style that makes them the preferred bean for ribollita soup, pasta e fagioli, and other classic bean dishes of central and northern Italian cooking. Borlotti are used across Italy as the fresh shell bean equivalent of cranberry beans in New England cooking — they are always shelled before cooking, never eaten as whole pods. Tongues of Fire is reliable and productive in summer gardens throughout the US. Matures in 60–85 days from seed.

name: Toothache Plant
description: Surface-sow seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost and keep warm and bright until sprouts appear. The gold-and-red buds contain spilanthol, which produces a numbing, tingling sensation when chewed. Transplant into rich, moist soil in full sun after frost, spacing plants for their sprawling habit. Deadhead spent buds to keep new ones coming and pinch stems to encourage bushiness. Harvest flower buds fresh for medicinal use or to add a buzzing zing to salads. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Top Bunch 2.0 Collards
description: Sow seed directly or start transplants for spring and late-summer crops, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart. This vigorous hybrid produces tall, upright plants with slightly savoyed leaves and regrows quickly for repeated cut-and-come-again harvests. Collards are cold hardy and grow well far beyond the South; a light frost actually sweetens the nutritious, vitamin-rich leaves, so leave plants standing into cold weather. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Top Crop Bush Bean (AAS-Winning Classic Heirloom Bush Snap Bean, Early and Dependable)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; space 4–6 inches in rows 18 inches apart. Harvest at 5–6 inches before seeds bulge. Top Crop is one of the historically significant All-America Selections winners in the vegetable category, recognized in 1951 for performance and quality that exceeded the bush bean standard of the era. At the time of its AAS recognition, Top Crop represented a meaningful improvement over other widely grown bush bean varieties in terms of pod quality (straight, stringless, and uniform), plant habit (upright and compact, making harvest easier), and importantly for southeastern gardens — its tolerance for warm, humid growing conditions that cause many bean varieties to set pods poorly or produce stringy, misshapen pods. The variety became one of the most widely grown bush snap bean varieties in American home and market gardens through the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s, establishing itself as a regional standard especially in the South where the heat tolerance advantage mattered most. Top Crop produces round, stringless pods (the 'Top Crop' designation reflects the goal of beans that crop densely at the top of the plant, making harvest efficient) that are firm, tender at optimal harvest size (5–6 inches), and of classic, straightforward snap bean flavor. The variety is open-pollinated and remains available through seed companies as a historical heirloom standard. For zone 9 spring and fall gardens, Top Crop's heat tolerance and early maturity (49–54 days) make it practical for getting a bean crop harvested before summer heat peaks or after it subsides in fall. Matures in 49–54 days from seed.

name: Top Hat Blueberry (Dwarf Container Blueberry, Patio Blueberry)
description: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) or containers filled with peat-based mix; fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or azalea fertilizer) in early spring; Top Hat requires two plants for best pollination and fruit set; berries ripen mid-season (July in zones 5–6) — medium-sized, sweet, and flavorful; does not need pruning for first 4–5 years. Top Hat is the most widely grown dwarf container blueberry and the standard recommendation from extension services for gardeners wanting to grow blueberries in containers, small raised beds, or on patios where the 4–6 foot size of standard highbush varieties is impractical. The variety is a University of Michigan-developed dwarf highbush × lowbush half-high cross that was specifically selected for its unusually compact habit — plants grow only 18–24 inches tall and wide, far smaller than either highbush (4–6 feet) or lowbush (6–12 inches, spreads widely). This intermediate compact size makes Top Hat ideal for large container culture in a way that no other named blueberry variety achieves: large enough to be productive, small enough to manage easily in a 15–20 gallon container, and cold-hardy enough to survive winters outdoors in zones 4–7 on a patio or protected corner. The berries are medium-sized, deep blue, and well-flavored for a half-high type — sweeter and more aromatic than wild lowbush berries and with good quality comparable to standard highbush varieties. The plants are also attractive ornamentally: brilliant red fall foliage makes Top Hat an attractive container plant throughout the growing season. One of the most important blueberry introductions specifically designed for urban and suburban small-space gardening. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Top Mark Cantaloupe (Classic Western Shipping Melon)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of two to three plants in full sun once soil has warmed well past last frost, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. Top Mark produces slightly oblong, well-netted, 3-4 lb fruits with thick, firm, sweet salmon-colored flesh, and was long grown as a standard commercial shipping melon in California's Imperial Valley thanks to good tolerance of powdery and downy mildew. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit with light pressure and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Top Pick Brown Crowder Southern Pea (Easy-Harvest Crowder Type)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil is thoroughly warm. Top Pick Brown Crowder is an improved brown crowder-type Southern pea bred, like the related Top Pick Pinkeye, so pods set concentrated near the top of the plant instead of scattered through the foliage, letting a picker fill a basket quickly during the heaviest part of the summer flush instead of hunting for hidden pods. The tightly packed, squarish brown seeds develop the rich, hearty flavor traditional to crowder-type field peas, and plants hold up well through the hottest, most humid stretch of the season when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil fertility as the crop grows. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage for fresh shelling, or let them dry fully on the plant for long-term storage. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Top Pick Pinkeye Southern Pea (Easy-Harvest Purple Hull Type)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; Top Pick Pinkeye is an improved pinkeye purple hull southern pea bred so that pods set concentrated near the top of the plant rather than scattered throughout, letting a picker harvest a full basket quickly without hunting through foliage — a meaningful advantage during the heavy summer flush when Southern peas are at their most productive. The cream-colored peas with a distinctive pink eye have the classic mild, slightly sweet flavor prized in Southern cooking. Harvest pods when they've turned the characteristic purple-pink color and the peas inside have filled out but are still tender for fresh shelling, or let pods dry fully for storage. Like other Southern peas, the plant fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf South summer. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Topaz Apple (Scab-Resistant Czech Tart-Sweet Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Topaz was bred in the Czech Republic specifically for genetic resistance to apple scab, one of the most damaging and widespread apple diseases, giving it a real practical advantage for organic and low-spray home orchards in humid climates where scab pressure is heavy. The medium, yellow-green fruit blushed with orange-red has firm, crisp, notably tart-sweet flesh with good aromatic complexity, well regarded among disease-resistant modern apple varieties for genuinely good eating quality rather than resistance alone. The tree is productive and reliable; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect good storage life in proper cool conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Topper Turnip (Smooth-Leaf Heat-Tolerant Greens Turnip)
description: Direct sow into fertile, loose soil in full sun and thin lightly, since this variety is grown for its leaves rather than a marketable root and tolerates closer spacing than globe-type turnips. The smooth, broad, dark green leaves grow rapidly and regrow readily after cutting, making Topper well suited to a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest schedule rather than a single whole-plant pull. It resists the bitterness and rapid bolting that hot weather causes in many greens turnips, giving Southern gardeners a wider planting window than strictly cool-season varieties allow. The small, often forked roots are edible but are not the point of growing this variety, so gardeners aiming for a good turnip root should choose a globe type instead. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Torasan Komatsuna
description: Torasan is a Japanese F1 komatsuna prized for dark, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves and a sturdy, upright habit that holds up well to cutting. It grows quickly from direct-sown seed and tolerates both cool spring conditions and light autumn frost, which sweetens the leaves and mellows their mustard-spinach bite. Because it bolts readily once days lengthen and warm, gardeners in hotter regions do best sowing it in a partly shaded bed or as a fall crop rather than pushing it through summer. Matures in 30–40 days from seed.

name: Tormentil (Septfoil)
description: Plant in lean, acidic, well-drained to dry soil in partial shade to full sun; tormentil is a creeping, low-growing European perennial of heathlands and acidic meadows, recognized by its distinctive four-petaled yellow flowers (most Potentilla have five petals) and deeply divided leaves with 3–5 leaflets. The roots are exceptionally rich in tannins and astringent compounds — among the highest tannin content of any European herb — and have been used for centuries in traditional medicine as an anti-diarrheal remedy, wound herb, and tea substitute. The root was also historically used in leather tanning and as a red dye. In the garden, tormentil makes a charming low groundcover for dry, acidic, heather-garden conditions where few ornamental plants thrive. The yellow flowers bloom profusely from early summer through fall. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Toro Blueberry (Large-Fruited Vigorous Midseason Highbush)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Toro was bred at Rutgers University and released for its exceptionally large, firm, sweet, light-blue berries carried on a vigorous, upright, well-branched bush that stands up well to mechanical harvesting as well as home picking, with good resistance to several common blueberry diseases. Ripening in midseason, it produces heavy, concentrated crops that hold well on the bush without softening quickly, giving a wider picking window than some earlier varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and overall yield. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Toro Rice (Louisiana Clingy-Texture Long-Grain Rice)
description: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Toro is a specialty long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station near Crowley, bred with low amylose content and a low gelatinization temperature that give the cooked grain a soft, clingy, jasmine-like texture despite its long-grain shape — unlike the fluffy, separate-grain texture of standard American long-grain rice. Unlike aromatic Louisiana specialty rices such as Della and Jazzman, Toro carries no distinctive fragrance; its value is purely in cooking texture, making it popular for dishes and cuisines that call for a stickier grain. The tall plants perform well through the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain turns golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before storage or milling. Matures in 110–130 days from seed.

name: Torvum Vigor Rootstock Eggplant (Turkey Berry Rootstock)
description: This wild, thorny relative of eggplant is grown as a grafting rootstock rather than for its own small, bitter fruit, valued for an exceptionally vigorous, deep root system that confers strong resistance to bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and root-knot nematodes, all serious soil-borne problems that shorten the productive life of own-root eggplant in warm, humid climates. Grafting a favorite eggplant scion onto this rootstock is a traditional practice in parts of Asia and is gaining adoption among home and market growers in the humid Gulf South seeking longer-lived, more disease-resistant eggplant plants without resorting to soil fumigation or long rotations. Start rootstock seed well ahead of the scion, since germination is slower and less even than standard eggplant, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Totem Strawberry
description: Totem was released by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Pacific research station and became a dominant processing strawberry across the Pacific Northwest for decades, prized for firm, glossy, deep-red fruit that holds up well to freezing and machine harvest. It is a vigorous, high-yielding June-bearer with good resistance to red stele root rot, making it a dependable choice in cool, wet coastal growing regions. Berries are excellent for jam, freezing, and preserves, with slightly less fresh-eating sweetness than dessert-type cultivars. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to maintain productivity in following seasons. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Totem Witloof Chicory (Forcing Belgian Endive)
description: 'Totem' is a later-maturing F1 witloof chicory bred for growers who want to stagger their Belgian endive harvest well into winter, since its roots hold in cold storage and continue to force well after several months. Direct sow in late spring and grow through summer to develop a thick, straight taproot; in fall, trim the foliage to an inch above the crown, lift the roots before hard freezes, and store them cold and dark until needed. Force a batch every few weeks by replanting roots upright in moist sand or soil in complete darkness at 50-60F, and expect compact, ivory-white chicons in three to four weeks. Compared to earlier-maturing forcing hybrids, its slightly longer field season produces larger roots that can support a second, smaller flush of growth if the first chicon is cut and the root is forced again. Matures in 115–125 days from seed.

name: Touchstone Gold Beet
description: Direct sow the corky seed clusters as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to three or four inches apart since each cluster yields several plants. This golden beet holds its bright color when cooked and is notably sweet and mild, with less of the earthy flavor of red types. Harvest roots when they reach two to three inches across, and enjoy the nutritious tops as cooked greens. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Toy Choy Bok Choy
description: Direct sow seed in cool weather for spring and fall crops, thinning to about four to six inches apart. This miniature variety grows just 5 inches tall and is ready to harvest in as few as 30 days, with thick white stems and glossy dark green leaves. It tolerates warm weather better than most bok choy, but grow it quickly and keep it evenly watered to discourage bolting; its compact size suits containers well. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Toyo Nishiki Flowering Quince (Multicolor Pink-White-Red Flowering Quince)
description: Toyo Nishiki is a classic flowering quince cultivar famous for producing white, pink, and red flowers all at once on the same branch, and sometimes even within a single blossom, an unpredictable multicolor mix that makes each spring's bloom slightly different from the last. It flowers directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, forming a large, vigorous, arching shrub, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, valued for jelly and preserves rather than fresh eating. Highly adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and notably drought-tolerant, it makes an effective thorny barrier hedge in addition to its ornamental value. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Toyon
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in extremely well-drained, lean soil — avoid summer irrigation once established; Toyon (California Holly, Christmas Berry) is a large, handsome, evergreen shrub native to California chaparral and oak woodland, producing spectacular clusters of brilliant red to orange-red berries in November–January — the traditional holiday decoration plant of coastal California and the plant thought to have inspired the name 'Hollywood.' The berries have a slightly bitter, astringent flavor when raw but become edible and pleasant when fully ripe and soft after frost or light cooking; indigenous Californians ate them roasted, fermented into cider, or dried. The white flower clusters in summer attract bees, and the winter berries support mockingbirds, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds through the season when few other fruiting plants are active. Toyon is one of the most ornamentally rewarding California natives for gardens in the dry western zones and Mediterranean climates; its tolerance of the Gulf Coast requires excellent drainage and restrained irrigation. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Trader Mulberry (Extreme-Cold-Hardy North Dakota Black-Fruited Mulberry)
description: Trader is a US-patented (USPP28,932) black-fruited mulberry discovered in 2000 as the sole survivor of a grove of Morus alba seedlings that a German immigrant family named Trader planted near Oriska in Barnes County, North Dakota, around 1892; the original tree has since endured winter lows to -44 degrees F. Propagated on its own roots from cuttings rather than grafted, it bears abundant dark purple-to-black, nearly seedless fruit about 1 to 1.5 inches long with a flavor that starts tart at first color and sweetens within days, ripening sequentially over an extended midsummer-to-fall window rather than all at once. Mature trees develop an open, spherical crown and can eventually reach 30 feet or more, though most home plantings are kept smaller with routine pruning. Its combination of USDA zone 4 hardiness, self-fertility, and good resistance to spotted-wing drosophila makes it one of the very few reliably fruiting mulberries for northern gardeners where standard black mulberry (Morus nigra) cannot survive. As with other mulberries, ripe fruit stains heavily, so site it away from patios, decks, and walkways. Matures in 365–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tradition Serviceberry (Single-Leader Shadblow Selection)
description: Introduced by Lake County Nursery, Tradition is valued because it naturally grows a single dominant trunk rather than the multi-stemmed clump typical of shadblow serviceberry, making it a practical choice for street tree plantings, standards, and formal specimen use. Late-April clouds of white flowers give way to heavy crops of blue-black June berries that draw songbirds and can be picked for jams and baking if reached first. Fall color runs orange to red, and the tree tolerates a range of soils as long as drainage is reasonable. Plant in full sun to light shade and water regularly through the first two seasons to establish its central leader form. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Trafalgar Brussels Sprout (Late Mid-Season F1 Hybrid)
description: Start seeds indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil and stake the medium-tall stems against wind; top the plants once lower sprouts reach marble size to even out ripening, and harvest from the bottom up as sprouts firm up. Trafalgar is a British-bred F1 hybrid valued for producing abundant, uniformly round, tightly wrapped sprouts with a sweet, low-bitterness flavor that holds up well through a long late-season harvest window running from mid-autumn into the new year. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew and reliable, heavy-yielding habit have made it a standard late mid-season choice in UK trial and market gardens, and the sprouts stand well on the stalk without splitting, giving flexibility about exactly when to pick. Choose Trafalgar when the goal is a long stretch of classic, mild-flavored sprouts spanning Thanksgiving through the winter holidays rather than a single early flush. Matures in 100–110 days from transplant.

name: Trailing Rosemary
description: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil — rosemary rots in heavy, wet soil and thrives in conditions that would kill most other herbs; Prostratus is the trailing, prostrate form of rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) that cascades naturally over walls, slopes, and raised planters rather than growing upright — a different growth habit from the shrubby upright rosemary but with identical culinary flavor and fragrance. The woody, spreading stems reach 4–6 feet across while remaining only 1–2 feet high, creating an extensive ground cover with the characteristic needle-like, intensely aromatic rosemary leaves and lavender-blue flowers that appear in late winter and spring. Trailing Rosemary is particularly useful in zone 9 landscapes for covering slopes and dry, sunny, hard-to-maintain areas where conventional ground covers fail — the combination of extreme drought tolerance, deer resistance, salt tolerance, and attractive year-round appearance makes it one of the most practical landscape plants for these challenging conditions. The culinary quality is identical to upright rosemary: harvest sprigs of the strong, resinous, pine-and-camphor-scented leaves for roasting meats, flavoring breads, making herb oils, and the full range of Mediterranean herb applications. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Traminette Grape (Cornell-Bred Aromatic White Wine Grape)
description: Traminette was developed at Cornell University from a cross of Gewürztraminer with the French-American hybrid Joannes Seyve 23.416, combining Gewürztraminer's spicy floral aroma with much better cold tolerance and disease resistance than its vinifera parent. The vine buds out relatively late, which helps it dodge spring frosts, and it is widely planted across the mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Northeast for its lychee, rose, and clove-scented white wine. It shows good resistance to powdery mildew and moderate resistance to bunch rot compared with straight vinifera cultivars, though crop loads should still be managed through cluster thinning for wine quality. Train on a vertical shoot-positioned trellis and prune to spurs or short canes for consistent yields. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Trapp Avocado (Early Florida Commercial Avocado)
description: Trapp was one of the first avocado cultivars planted commercially in Miami-Dade County in the early 1900s and helped launch Florida's avocado industry decades before Lula and Waldin became standard. It produces medium to large, rounded, glossy green fruit with pale, mild, buttery flesh typical of the West Indian race, ripening in the fall, later than Simmonds or Pollock. The tree is vigorous and long-lived but, like other West Indian types, has virtually no frost tolerance and needs a warm, sheltered, frost-free site. Maintain deep mulch and well-drained soil, since avocado trees decline quickly in wet feet or compacted ground. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Trask Feijoa (Historic Large-Fruited California Pineapple Guava)
description: Trask is one of the earliest named feijoa selections from California, dating to the early twentieth century, and remains valued for producing medium-large, oblong fruit with good aromatic flavor. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a second cultivar to improve pollination and yield, since Trask sets fruit more reliably with a cross-pollinator nearby. The silvery-green evergreen foliage and showy edible-petaled spring flowers make Trask a useful dual-purpose edible landscape shrub. Harvest fruit as it drops naturally in fall, and prune lightly after harvest only to shape, since fruit forms on the current season's wood. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Traveler 76 Tomato (Heat- and Crack-Resistant Arkansas Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors in warm starting mix and transplant into full sun after frost risk passes; Traveler 76 was released by the University of Arkansas in 1976 as an improved successor to the original 1930s-era Traveler variety, bred specifically to correct that older tomato's tendency to crack in Southern humidity. The determinate plants set uniform, medium-sized, deep-pink globes with a well-balanced, low-acid flavor and skin that resists splitting after summer rains far better than most heirlooms. It shares the same heat-set reliability that makes Arkansas Traveler famous in Gulf Coast gardens, continuing to produce through the punishing midsummer stretch that causes many varieties to drop blossoms, but its firmer, more uniform fruit and improved crack resistance made it a favored market grower's choice across the mid-South. Matures in 75–80 days from transplant.

name: Traveler Tomato (Original 1930s Arkansas Heat-Set Heirloom)
description: Start seed indoors in warm starting mix and transplant into full sun once frost risk has passed, spacing plants generously for good air movement in humid climates. Traveler was bred to keep setting fruit through the same brutal midsummer heat that stops many tomatoes from pollinating, a trait that made it a dependable choice for Arkansas and mid-South gardeners decades before modern heat-set hybrids existed. Its medium-sized, pink, globe-shaped fruits have good old-fashioned flavor, but the skin is noticeably more prone to splitting after summer rain than later selections bred from this line. Because it predates the disease and cracking improvements added in 1976, it is now grown mainly by heirloom seed savers rather than commercial producers. Matures in 78–85 days from transplant.

name: Traviata Eggplant (High-Yielding Italian-Type Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Traviata is an early-maturing, high-yielding Italian-type eggplant hybrid bred for vigor and improved disease resilience, producing a heavy, sustained crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with few seeds and tender, mild flesh. Its early maturity lets Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the harvest before summer disease pressure builds, and the sturdy, well-branched plant continues setting fruit steadily through the season. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep soil consistently moist, since eggplant grown under drought stress develops tougher skin and a more bitter flavor. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Trazel Hazelnut (Tree-Form Blight-Resistant Hybrid Hazelnut)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, allowing 15-25 feet between trees for their eventual size. Trazels are named for their parentage — a cross between the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) and the Turkish tree hazel (Corylus colurna) — combining the American parent's cold hardiness and blight resistance with the Turkish parent's strong single-trunk, tree-like growth habit, unlike the suckering thicket form typical of most hazelnuts. This tree form makes Trazels far easier to manage in an orchard row or as a landscape specimen than shrubby hazelnut types, and their resistance to Eastern filbert blight — a fungal canker disease that has devastated commercial plantings of European hazelnut (C. avellana) across much of the eastern and midwestern United States — makes them one of the more dependable hazelnut options outside the Pacific Northwest. Nuts are borne in husked clusters and ripen in late summer to early fall; because most Trazel seedlings show variable nut size and quality, growers select and propagate individual trees for improved nut characteristics. Plant two or more seedlings for best pollination, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and largely self-incompatible. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Trebi Barley (Heirloom Russian-Origin Six-Row Barley)
description: Trebi was collected by USDA plant explorer Mark Carleton in Russia in the early 1900s and released after testing by the USDA Office of Cereal Investigations, quickly becoming a benchmark six-row spring barley across irrigated valleys of the Western United States for its high yield and strong straw. Sow into a firm, fertile seedbed in early spring; it responds especially well to irrigation but also holds up under rain-fed Northern Plains conditions. The stiff-strawed plant resists lodging better than many barleys of its era, letting it carry a heavy head of grain without falling over before harvest. Cut and thresh once the heads dry to straw-gold, and use the plump kernels for livestock feed, malting trials, or seed increase. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Tree Collard
description: Root 6–8 inch stem cuttings from an existing plant in moist compost; tree collard is a long-lived perennial brassica that grows as a woody shrub 4–8 feet tall, producing continuously harvestable blue-green to purple leaves with the same flavor as regular collard greens. Unlike annual collards that must be replanted each season, a single tree collard plant can produce edible leaves for a decade or more. They are propagated only by stem cuttings, never true to seed. In hot climates, tree collards perform best with some afternoon shade. Two main types exist: green-leaved (more vigorous) and purple-leaved (more ornamental). An outstanding plant for permaculture and food forest systems where perennial productivity is valued over annual yields. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Tree Collards
description: Root stem cuttings 6–8 inches long in moist potting mix or directly in garden soil; tree collards are essentially perennial collards that develop a woody trunk over time and can produce harvestable leaves year-round in mild-winter climates. The purple-leaf variety is the most common and most ornamental, with deep blue-green to purple foliage that intensifies in color after cool weather. Harvest the large lower leaves from the bottom of the plant up, leaving the growing tip intact; consistent harvest keeps plants productive and prevents them from becoming leggy. Unlike annual collards, tree collards do not bolt and can remain productive for 5–10 years with occasional hard pruning to rejuvenate the growth. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Tree Spinach
description: Direct-sow seeds in average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tree spinach (magenta spreen, giant goosefoot) is a Himalayan annual of the goosefoot family grown as an ornamental and edible plant — it grows remarkably tall (4–10 feet) for an annual leafy vegetable, producing large, deep-green, arrowhead-shaped leaves that are eaten raw or cooked in exactly the same way as spinach or lamb's quarters, with a mild, pleasant, slightly mineral flavor. The ornamental distinction of the species is the vivid, magenta-pink meal (a waxy powder similar to that on lamb's quarters) that coats the youngest emerging leaves, shoot tips, and stems, creating a strikingly colorful display at the growing tips that fades on older leaves to plain green. The plant self-seeds freely, ensuring persistent garden colonies once established. It grows rapidly, is tolerant of partial shade, is highly nutritious (rich in protein, calcium, and iron, like other Chenopodium species), and provides both an ornamental feature and a productive edible leafy green from a single plant. An underused dual-purpose annual for the edible landscape. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Tree Tomato
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Solanum betaceum grows fast but has brittle branches — provide wind protection and stake when young; water deeply and regularly and fertilize monthly for maximum fruiting; prune after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new productive growth. Solanum betaceum (Tree Tomato or Tamarillo, syn. Cyphomandra betacea) is a fast-growing, soft-wooded, small tree in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family native to the semi-arid and sub-humid Andean highlands of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Colombia, and northern Chile at elevations of 5,000–10,000 feet. The tree produces prolific clusters of glossy, egg-shaped, thin-skinned fruits — deep red, orange, or yellow depending on cultivar — with tangy-sweet, intensely flavored flesh combining tomato, passion fruit, and tropical notes, surrounding a central core of dark-purple seeds. Tamarillos are extensively eaten fresh (the skin is typically removed), made into juice, jams, chutneys, salsas, and cooked sauces across Ecuador, Peru, Colombia, and especially New Zealand, where the industry was developed from Andean introductions in the mid-20th century. Trees fruit prolifically in 1–2 years from transplants, providing remarkable returns for a tree-fruit crop. The plants are susceptible to tobacco mosaic virus, cold below 28°F, and water stress — they perform best in cool, frost-light subtropical conditions (zone 8b–10) with consistent moisture. Named a 'new world food' candidate for its high vitamin C, antioxidant, and nutritional content. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Tres Fine Endive
description: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tres Fine (Very Fine) is the most elegantly cut of all frisee endive varieties, producing an open, flat rosette of very finely divided, thread-like, deeply lacinated leaves with a delicate, airy, almost moss-like texture — more finely cut than standard frisee types and considered the premium grade for restaurant use. The characteristic pale yellow to cream heart forms naturally as the outer leaves shade the center; for maximum blanching, loosely tie the outer leaves 10 days before harvest. The very fine leaf cutting makes Tres Fine endive the lightest, most delicate-textured of the endive family in the salad bowl, where it provides a feathery contrast to dense leaves and holds vinaigrette dressings in the finest leaf surfaces. The flavor is gently bitter with a clean, slightly nutty edge. Tres Fine is widely used in French and Italian fine dining as the benchmark frisee for composed salads and the traditional salade lyonnaise. Matures in 55–70 days from transplant.

name: Tres Fine Maraichere Frisee Endive
description: Tres Fine Maraichere, sometimes sold as the Olesh strain, is an old French heirloom frisee endive valued for its petite size and quick growth compared to standard curly endives. Its narrow, deeply cut outer leaves curl into a naturally self-blanching rosette around a tender, creamy heart, and tying the outer leaves closed about a week before harvest whitens the center further. It can be cut young as a frilly, mildly bitter baby green for salad mixes or allowed to fill out into a full head, and it attracts relatively few pests along the way. Matures in 48–58 days from seed.

name: Treviso Basil (AAS-Winning Slow-to-Bolt Anise-Note Basil)
description: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Treviso is an AAS-winning basil with a compact, dense, highly branched habit and leaves carrying a subtle anise note alongside classic basil sweetness. It is notably slow to bolt and holds tender, non-bitter leaf quality later into the season than many culinary basils, with good heat tolerance and foliage that resists browning or oxidizing after cutting. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive, harvesting leaves anytime once established for fresh use or pesto. Matures in 60–75 days from transplant.

name: Treviso Radicchio (Late Treviso)
description: Sow seeds in summer for fall harvest, thinning to 10–12 in apart when seedlings are established; Treviso radicchio forms elongated, torpedo-shaped heads with deep red leaves and contrasting white veins, quite different in form from the round Chioggia-type radicchio. Flavor is intensely bitter before cold exposure, then sweetens significantly after several frosts. Some gardeners cut the plant back to 1 inch above the crown after initial growth, then allow it to resprout for tighter, sweeter heads — a technique called 'forcing.' In zone 9, the best crops are grown from September sowing, harvested November through January. The grilled heads, split lengthwise and drizzled with olive oil, are a classic Italian preparation. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Triamble Pumpkin (Australian Trefoil Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, giving the sprawling vines 6-8 feet of room. Triamble is an Australian heirloom dating to at least the 1820s, named for its distinctive tri-lobed, clover-like shape formed by three fused lobes curving back toward the stem; the tough, slate-blue-grey rind gave rise to its nickname 'Ironbark pumpkin.' Fruits average around 8 pounds and hold sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh similar in quality to Queensland Blue. The hard rind makes Triamble notably difficult to cut but also gives it outstanding keeping quality, with properly cured fruit reported to store for a year or more in a cool, dry space. Matures in 105–120 days from seed.

name: Tribulus (Gokshura, Puncture Vine)
description: Tribulus is a low, trailing warm-season plant native to dry, sandy, disturbed ground across Africa, southern Europe, and Asia, grown commercially for its spiny, star-shaped fruit capsules (gokshura in Ayurveda, bai ji li in Chinese medicine) rather than its foliage. Direct sow after the soil has warmed into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; small yellow flowers appear within weeks and are quickly followed by the hard, thorny seed capsules that give the plant its common name puncture vine. Harvest capsules as they dry and turn tan, before they fully harden and disperse, since mature spines are sharp enough to puncture bicycle tires and bare feet — contain plantings to a dedicated bed, as the species self-sows aggressively and is classified as a noxious weed in parts of the western United States. Grow as a warm-season annual in most gardens; it persists as a short-lived perennial only in essentially frost-free zones. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: Tribute Strawberry (Day-Neutral Everbearing Strawberry)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tribute is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar, valued for producing a steady, moderate harvest of medium-large, firm, well-flavored berries from late spring through fall rather than a single concentrated June crop, extending the home strawberry season significantly compared with traditional June-bearing types. It shows good resistance to several common strawberry diseases, including red stele and verticillium wilt, making it a dependable choice in a range of soil conditions. Because day-neutral types put continuous energy into fruiting rather than runner production, they produce fewer runners than June-bearers, and removing flowers for the first several weeks after planting helps establish a stronger root system for sustained production through the season. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Tricolor Sage (Purple-Pink-White Variegated Culinary Sage)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Tricolor is grown as much for ornamental value as for the kitchen, with soft, gray-green leaves irregularly splashed in cream and edged in rosy purple-pink, especially vivid on new growth, giving the plant a decorative look that stands out in an herb border or mixed container far more than plain culinary sage. The leaves are fully usable in cooking with the same flavor as green sage, though the plant is generally somewhat less vigorous and less cold-hardy than the species, so it benefits from winter protection or container culture where winters are severe.
