Harvest leaves as needed through the growing season, and cut the plant back by about a third in spring to remove winter dieback and encourage fresh, well-colored new growth. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Trifoliate Orange
description: The hardy trifoliate orange is a deciduous citrus relative bearing small, aromatic, seedy fruit used for marmalade and flavoring. Remarkably cold-tolerant, it survives well below freezing and is widely used as a dwarfing rootstock for other citrus. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; its dense, fiercely thorny growth makes an effective barrier hedge. Harvest the downy yellow fruit in autumn, using the tart juice and rind rather than eating it fresh. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Trinidad Moruga Scorpion Pepper
description: Germinate at 85–90°F on a heat mat — germination can take 3–4 weeks for superhot varieties; grow under bright lights and transplant only when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 60°F. Trinidad Moruga Scorpion originated in the Moruga district of Trinidad and was certified by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as the world's hottest pepper in 2012, with an average heat of 1.2 million SHU and individual samples reaching 2 million SHU — making it one of the hottest naturally occurring chile varieties ever measured. The fruits are round to elongated with a characteristic tail or 'stinger,' ripening to red (sometimes yellow or chocolate depending on the phenotype), with intense fruity tropical flavor beneath the extraordinary heat. Widely grown by superhot enthusiasts for hot sauce and extreme culinary use; handle seeds and fruits with nitrile gloves and eye protection. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Trinidad Perfume Pepper (Heatless Aromatic Habanero-Type Pepper)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Trinidad Perfume is a heatless selection within the Capsicum chinense species, the same species as habaneros and Scotch bonnets, bred to capture the intensely fruity, floral, almost apricot-and-citrus aroma and flavor characteristic of that species without any of the fiery heat, making it usable in far larger quantities than a true habanero for salsas, sauces, and dishes where habanero flavor is wanted but the heat is not. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits look nearly identical to a habanero, ripening from green to orange or red, and can be used fresh, dried, or blended into sauces for a burst of tropical fruit flavor. Plants are productive and grow similarly to other Capsicum chinense peppers, benefiting from a long, warm growing season. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Trinidad Scorpion Pepper (Original Strain)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since germination can be slow and irregular, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger passes. Stake plants and prune early flowers to build a stronger frame before letting the heavy fruit set develop. This is the original Trinidad Scorpion strain from which the later 'Butch T' selection was bred, named for the narrow curled tail at the pod's tip and known for ferocious, lingering heat. Wear gloves when harvesting and processing the ripe red pods. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Trinidad Seasoning Pepper
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the plants are productive and reasonably compact, doing well in raised beds or large containers. Trinidad Seasoning Pepper is a habanero-relative (Capsicum chinense) grown not for heat but for its intense, distinctively fruity, floral habanero-type aroma without the accompanying pungency — a genetic quirk that produces essentially all of the characteristic C. chinense flavor with almost none of the capsaicin heat. It is a foundational ingredient in Trinidadian and broader Caribbean cooking, where it is blended into 'green seasoning' marinades, curries, and sauces to deliver deep habanero-family flavor that can be used generously without overwhelming heat. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the specific strain. An essential, distinctive pepper for gardeners interested in Caribbean cuisine who want the flavor of a habanero without the fire, zone 8–11. Matures in 90–110 days from transplant.

name: Trinitario Cacao
description: This natural hybrid arose in Trinidad after hurricanes and disease devastated the island's original Criollo plantations in the eighteenth century, allowing surviving Criollo trees to cross-pollinate with later-introduced Forastero stock. The result is a genetically diverse group of trees that blend much of Criollo's fine, aromatic flavor with Forastero's sturdier disease resistance and productivity, making Trinitario a favored planting across Trinidad, Venezuela, and parts of Cameroon and Papua New Guinea. Because it arose from repeated crossing rather than a single fixed line, individual Trinitario trees vary noticeably in flavor, pod color, and vigor, so growers often select cuttings from proven trees rather than relying solely on seed. Give it the same warm, humid, shaded understory conditions as other cacao and expect several years of growth before the first pod harvest. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Trinity Sweet Corn
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has warmed. Trinity is a synergistic (SY) bicolor hybrid that combines sugary-enhanced and supersweet genetics on the same ear, giving tender, creamy kernels with good sweetness retention without the tough pericarp of straight sh2 types. It is among the earliest-maturing bicolor hybrids available, germinating well in cooler soil than most supersweet corn and making it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting the first fresh corn of the season. Water consistently from tasseling through ear fill to ensure full, well-formed ears. Matures in 67–70 days from seed.

name: Triomphe de Farcy Bean (French Haricot Vert Heirloom)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; harvest when pods are 4–5 inches long and pencil-thin for the finest haricot vert quality; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production; the red-violet streaking on raw pods fades to a uniform green when cooked. Triomphe de Farcy is a French heirloom bush bean dating to the 1880s, when it was listed in Vilmorin's famous seed catalog as one of the finest haricots verts — the slender, pencil-thin snap beans of French cuisine that differ fundamentally from the round, plump beans favored in American cooking. The variety is named for its triumphal quality (triomphe = triumph in French) and the Farcy region of Brittany where a similar bean type was cultivated. The pods are distinctive: slender (3/8 inch diameter at most), long (5–7 inches), and marked with beautiful irregular red-violet streaks and flecks on a pale green background — the coloration is reminiscent of a speckled trout and makes raw pods strikingly beautiful in the kitchen; the markings fade completely to solid green when cooked. The flavor is characteristically French haricot vert — tender, fine-grained, buttery, and subtly sweet — quite different from the starchier, coarser texture of standard American snap beans harvested at the same age. Triomphe de Farcy is the bean for gardeners who want authentic French-style haricots verts; harvest young and often, steam or blanch briefly, and serve with good butter. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Trionfo Violetto Pole Bean
description: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet. Long grown in Italian kitchen gardens, Trionfo Violetto is prized for its double ornamental value — deep violet flowers followed by glossy purple pods — as much as for the table, and the pods turn a deep green when cooked, losing their color but keeping excellent flavor and tenderness. Pick pods young and often, around five to six inches, to encourage continued production and to catch them before they toughen. The striking purple pods also make the plants easy to spot for harvest against their green foliage. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Triple Crown Blackberry
description: 'Triple Crown' is a thornless semi-erect blackberry famed for high yields of large, sweet, glossy-black fruit in mid to late summer. Train the vigorous canes onto a sturdy T-trellis and tip the primocanes at about four feet to promote fruiting laterals. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent summer moisture during ripening. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for next year's fruiting wood. Matures in 365–550 days from transplant.

name: Triple Curled Parsley (Dense Dark-Green Garnish Parsley)
description: Soak seeds overnight before sowing 0.25 inch deep; thin to 8–12 inches. Triple Curled parsley (also called Extra Curled or Triple Moss Curled) is the standard garnish parsley of American restaurant and commercial use — a Petroselinum crispum variety selected for the densest, most tightly packed curling of the leaves, creating a compact, almost moss-like texture in the leaf heads that makes neat, visually attractive garnishes. The triple curling (each leaf curled multiple times rather than the single curl of standard curly parsley) creates a denser, darker green head with more surface area and a more formal, decorative appearance than less-curled types. The flavor of curly parsley types is milder and slightly less complex than flat-leaf Italian parsley — less aromatic oils, less intense flavor — which is why many serious cooks prefer flat-leaf for cooking while curly types dominate in garnish applications where appearance is primary. Triple Curled produces compact, upright plants with excellent visual appeal in both ornamental and kitchen herb gardens. As a biennial, parsley lives through its first winter (when harvested from), sets seed in the second year, and dies — a growth cycle that supports fall planting in zone 9 for winter and spring harvest. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Triple Treat Pumpkin (Hulless-Seed Pie Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill. Triple Treat produces a 6 to 8 pound jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin whose flesh is sweeter and less watery than typical carving pumpkins, but the real distinction is its naked, hull-less seeds, which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly without the tough seed coat found in most pumpkin varieties. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week before moving to cool storage. Because it excels at carving, baking, and snacking all from one fruit, it rewards gardeners who want maximum use from a single vine. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Tristar Strawberry (Compact Day-Neutral Everbearing Strawberry)
description: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tristar is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar bred alongside Tribute, valued for its compact, tidy plant habit and continuous production of small-to-medium, sweet, glossy red berries from late spring through fall, making it a favorite for hanging baskets, containers, and small raised beds where a sprawling June-bearer would be impractical. It shows good disease resistance for a day-neutral type, including tolerance to red stele root rot, and its everbearing habit means a small planting can supply a steady trickle of fresh berries all season rather than one large harvest. Pinch off runners as they form to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production rather than spreading. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Triumph Apple (MN80)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator apple within range for good fruit set. Triumph (breeding number MN80) was selected in 2004 by the University of Minnesota apple breeding program from a 1990 cross of Honeycrisp and Liberty, and it was released to nurseries starting in 2021 after extensive evaluation for disease resistance. It carries two distinct genetic sources of resistance to apple scab along with low-to-moderate susceptibility to cedar apple rust, making it well suited to organic growers and low-spray home orchards. Fruit ripens in late September, around the same time as or slightly after Honeycrisp, with attractive coloring and occasional russeting near the stem, and the tree is confirmed hardy to USDA zone 4. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Triumph Feijoa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Triumph is a long-established feijoa cultivar, historically one of the standard commercial pollinator partners for Mammoth, producing medium-large, egg-shaped fruit with a thicker skin and firmer, slightly grittier flesh than dessert-focused modern selections. The flavor is good and aromatic though generally ranked a step below top-tier cultivars like Apollo or Unique, making Triumph best grown as a reliable cropping and pollinating partner rather than the star of the planting. It ripens mid-to-late season and stores and ships a bit better than softer-fleshed cultivars because of its firmer texture. The evergreen, silvery-backed foliage and edible spring flowers make it a handsome dual-purpose hedge or specimen shrub regardless of fruit rank. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Triumph Muscadine
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Triumph is a bronze-skinned (white) muscadine grape selected by the University of Georgia for large, sweet, bronze-gold fruits with an exceptionally sweet flavor and low acidity — one of the sweetest muscadine varieties available and a benchmark for fresh-eating quality among bronze muscadines. The large, round fruits (1–1.25 inches) ripen to a deep bronze-gold color and have a thin, tender skin with less of the tough slip-skin character that makes some muscadine varieties less appealing for fresh eating. The sweet, mild, slightly floral flavor with classic muscadine aromatic notes makes Triumph outstanding for fresh eating, and the golden color produces beautiful pale-gold juice and jelly. Triumph is a self-fertile (perfect-flowered) variety that sets crops reliably without a pollinator. In zone 9 the vine is vigorous and productive; provide generous spacing (20+ feet) for the mature vine's spread. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Triumph Persimmon (Sharon Fruit)
description: Triumph is an astringent persimmon bred in Israel and marketed commercially worldwide under the trade name Sharon Fruit after a de-astringency treatment, though home gardeners can simply let the fruit ripen fully soft on the counter as with any other astringent cultivar. The medium, round, orange fruit is nearly seedless and develops a mild, honeyed flavor once fully ripe, without the pronounced tannins of firm fruit. It performs especially well in hot, dry summer climates and has become an important commercial cultivar in Israel, Spain, and California's Central Valley. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Triumph Summer Squash
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, spacing plants for good airflow. This zucchini has an open growing habit on compact bush-type plants with reduced spines, making harvest much easier on the hands. It offers intermediate resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus and watermelon mosaic virus; pick the tender fruits young and frequently to keep plants producing. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Trocadero Lettuce
description: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces and holds quality through warm spells. A French Batavian heirloom dating to the 1880s, Trocadero forms loose, crunchy pale-green heads with a crisp, sweet, faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of iceberg but grown far more easily. It was long grown in French market gardens as a reliable source of crisp texture without the fuss of true crisphead types. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Trombetta di Albenga Squash
description: Trombetta di Albenga is a climbing zucchetta-type summer squash from the Ligurian coast of Italy, related to the more widely known Tromboncino but grown and selected as its own distinct regional strain around the town of Albenga. The curved, trumpet-shaped fruit reaches twelve to fifteen inches and is prized for its firm, nearly seedless flesh concentrated in the long neck (seeds sit only in the small bulbous end), with a mild, artichoke-like flavor that holds up better than typical zucchini when sliced and sauteed. Because it is a true climber, giving it a trellis rather than letting it sprawl saves garden space and produces straighter, easier-to-harvest fruit; left on the vine past the summer-squash stage it also matures into a nutty-flavored winter squash. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Tromboncino Squash
description: Sow seeds and train the vine up a strong trellis or chain-link fence; tromboncino is an Italian heirloom climbing zucchini with long, curved fruits shaped like a trombone — reaching 20–30 inches when mature — harvested young at 10–15 inches as a summer squash substitute with a nutty, buttery flavor. Being Cucurbita moschata rather than C. pepo, tromboncino has excellent resistance to squash vine borer — the borer does not prefer this species, making it the best choice for gardeners who have lost zucchini crops to this destructive pest. It also tolerates heat and humidity better than most summer squash. Fruits left to mature fully develop into golden winter squash with superb flavor; the seeds are also edible roasted. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Tromboncino Squash
description: This Italian moschata squash produces long curved fruit eaten green like zucchini or ripened tan for winter storage. Direct sow in warm soil and trellis the vigorous climbing vines to save space and keep fruit straight. Harvested young at 8 to 12 inches, the dense flesh has few seeds and resists getting mushy when cooked. Its moschata parentage gives it strong resistance to squash vine borers. Left to ripen fully, the mature fruit stores for months like butternut. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Trompo Canistel
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to sandy soil; Trompo takes its name from the distinctive top-shaped (trompo) form of its fruit, which is noticeably larger than typical seedling canistel, often 8-15 ounces, with smooth yellow skin and dense, deep-orange pulp. The texture is drier and more custard-like than most tree fruit, frequently compared to sweet potato or pumpkin pie filling, and is popular blended into milkshakes and flans throughout South Florida. Trees bear heavily through winter with an occasional light summer crop, so thin small fruit clusters on young trees to avoid limb breakage from the fruit's substantial weight. Harvest when the skin turns fully glossy yellow-orange and let fruit finish softening at room temperature for several days, since canistel is unpalatable until fully soft. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tronchuda Cabbage (Portuguese Cabbage, Sea Kale Cabbage)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant 18–24 inches apart in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil; harvest outer leaves progressively to extend the harvest season; the large white midribs can be cooked separately and have a flavor somewhat resembling chard. Tronchuda (Brassica oleracea var. costata) is a traditional Portuguese vegetable with centuries of cultivation in Portugal, particularly in the Azores and coastal regions of Portugal where it is a staple of Caldo Verde (the famous Portuguese green soup) alongside the more familiar Galician version using curly kale. Tronchuda is classified as a distinct variety of Brassica oleracea that sits between cabbage, kale, and kohlrabi — it produces a large, loose rosette of heavily crinkled, gray-green leaves (not forming a tight head like cabbage) with exceptionally prominent white midribs that can be quite thick and juicy. The flavor is notably sweet and mild compared to other brassica vegetables, with the characteristic savoy/collard family character but more delicate and buttery — considered superior to standard kale for soups and slow-cooked brassica dishes by Portuguese cooks. Tronchuda is cold-hardy, producing some of its finest quality after light frosts, and it can be harvested over an extended season by removing outer leaves while the center continues to produce. Also called 'sea kale cabbage' in some English references (not to be confused with true sea kale, Crambe maritima). Matures in 50–75 days from transplant.

name: Tropea Rossa Tonda Onion
description: Start Tropea Rossa Tonda seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and transplant the seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This long-day Italian heirloom forms deep rose-red, globe-shaped bulbs with sweet, mild flesh and high sugar content. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and keep the bed weed-free while bulbs size up. Harvest when the tops fall over and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Beauty Apple (Early-Ripening Florida Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Beauty is a Florida-bred low-chill apple cultivar requiring roughly 150–250 chill hours, among the lowest chill requirements of any apple in common cultivation, and is prized in Gulf Coast home orchards for ripening earlier in the season than most other low-chill selections, often just after Dorsett Golden. Fruit is medium-sized with a red blush over a yellow-green background and crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh — pleasant for fresh eating, though like most low-chill apples the flavor is milder and less complex than high-chill Northern cultivars. Plant with Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer for cross-pollination, since Tropic Beauty is not reliably self-fruitful. Prune annually to an open center to maintain good light penetration and air circulation, which helps limit fire blight and apple scab, the two disease pressures that most commonly trouble apples in the humid Gulf South. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Beauty Peach (Low-Chill Southern Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Tropic Beauty is a University of Florida-developed low-chill peach cultivar requiring only 150 chill hours — making it adapted to the warmest portions of zone 8b, all of zone 9, and zone 10 in protected locations. Tropic Beauty produces medium to large fruits with yellow flesh and good sweet peach flavor, ripening in late April to May in zone 9 — one of the earliest-ripening yellow-flesh peaches available and a particularly valuable trait in Gulf South climates where spring arrives early and summer heat quickly limits the harvest window. The tree has an upright, vigorous growth habit and adapts well to the pruning required to maintain an open center structure for air circulation in humid climates. Like all peaches in the Gulf South, Tropic Beauty requires preventive fungicide management (copper at dormancy, follow-up fungicides through bloom) for disease control in the humid climate. Self-fertile — produces without a pollinizer, though cross-pollination with another low-chill variety improves yield. Thin fruit aggressively to 6 inches after June drop for maximum fruit size and quality; unthinned trees produce many small fruits that are commercially worthless and exhaust the tree. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Gold Apricot (Self-Fruitful Firm Orange-Fleshed Low-Chill Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Tropic Gold was bred and marketed specifically for mild-winter regions, needing only about 350 chill hours to set a reliable crop, bearing medium-to-large, firm, juicy, orange-fleshed fruit on a self-fruitful tree that needs no separate pollinizer. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Prince Peach (Texas A&M Ultra-Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Prince naturally reaches 15–20 feet but responds well to summer pruning that keeps it at a manageable 10–12 feet for easier harvest and spraying. Ripening in late April to early May, roughly 85–90 days after bloom, the semi-freestone fruit has juicy, sweet, yellow melting flesh over a red-blushed skin. Because bloom occurs very early in the Gulf South, avoid frost-prone low ground and watch forecasts during late-winter cold snaps. Regular thinning of the heavy natural fruit set is essential to reach good fruit size, and a dormant copper spray helps manage bacterial spot and leaf curl common in humid winters. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Snow Peach (White Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Snow is a low-chill white-flesh peach developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program, requiring approximately 200 chill hours. It is one of the earliest-ripening white peaches in zone 9, typically producing fruit in mid-April — sometimes the first peach of the season in Gulf Coast gardens. The medium-sized fruits have creamy white flesh with a red-blushed, white skin, a freestone pit, and a distinctive sweet, low-acid flavor with floral, honeyed notes characteristic of the finest white peaches. Flavor quality is superior to most yellow-flesh peaches when eaten at perfect ripeness. The trees are productive and self-fertile. White peaches were historically preferred by many southern peach connoisseurs over the higher-acid yellow types, and Tropic Snow is one of the best white varieties for low-chill climates. Prune to an open-center form in late winter; thin fruitlets to 6 inches apart in early spring for full-sized fruit. Protect blooms from late cold snaps. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Sweet Apple (Large Sweet Low-Chill Gulf South Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tropic Sweet is a University of Florida low-chill apple introduction specifically developed for production in zone 8–10 gardens where chill hours are insufficient for standard northern apple cultivars. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Tropic Sweet is adapted to the winter climate of zone 9a where standard apple varieties cannot break dormancy properly. The fruits are large, round, yellow with a light blush, and distinguished by outstanding sweetness with very low acid content — a flavor profile that differs from the balanced sweet-tart quality of northern apples and appeals strongly to those who prefer sweet, mild apples. Tropic Sweet ripens in June in zone 9 — the June ripening window is well ahead of most summer fruit production and provides fresh orchard fruit at a time when few other tree fruits are ready. Like all low-chill apples, Tropic Sweet performs best when cross-pollinated with another low-chill cultivar such as Dorsett Golden or Anna. Proper dormant pruning (in late January–February) and fire blight management (preventive copper sprays during bloom) are the primary cultural practices for Gulf South apple production. The outstanding sweetness and large size make Tropic Sweet one of the finest fresh-eating apple choices for Gulf South gardeners willing to manage fire blight, which is the primary disease challenge in the humid Gulf South climate. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Tropic Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Tropic tomato was developed at the University of Florida IFAS and released in 1963 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates — the most durable, disease-resistant open-pollinated tomato for zone 8b–12. It continues setting fruit at temperatures where most tomatoes stop, has resistance to fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and gray leaf spot (the diseases that devastate most tomatoes in South Florida's humid heat), and produces good-sized (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with solid, meaty flesh and good flavor from spring well into summer. For Gulf Coast and Florida gardeners who struggle with tomato diseases and summer heat, Tropic remains the benchmark open-pollinated variety after 60 years because no other variety has combined its disease resistance and tropical performance as consistently. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Tropical Sunset Pole Cherry Tomato
description: Start seed indoors about six weeks before your last frost and transplant seedlings out once nights stay warm. This indeterminate cherry vine keeps growing all season, so give it a tall stake or trellis and prune as needed. Each ripe 1.5 inch fruit is nearly translucent and golden with orange-to-pink stripes, bright, fruity, and very sweet with a long shelf life; harvest continuously to encourage new fruit set. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Tropical Treat Pawpaw (Early-Season Mango-Flavored Long-Keeping Pawpaw)
description: Tropical Treat is a Woody Walker selection released through England's Orchard and widely regarded as one of the best-tasting pawpaw cultivars available, with rich flavor often described as mango with a hint of pineapple. Fruit is medium-sized, 6-11 ounces and up to 6 inches long, with yellow-green skin, yellow flesh, and a notably thick skin that gives it better keeping quality in cold storage than most pawpaw cultivars. It carries a fairly large seed relative to its flesh but makes up for it with exceptional flavor. Tropical Treat ripens early in the pawpaw season, around mid-August in Kentucky, extending the harvest window ahead of most other named cultivars. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Tropical White Guava
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — guava is adaptable to a wide range of soils and is drought tolerant once established; Tropical White is a white-fleshed guava cultivar producing medium-sized, round to oval fruits with pale green to yellow skin at full ripeness and cream-white to pale yellow flesh with a mild, sweet, aromatic flavor and a texture ranging from smooth to granular depending on harvest timing. The flavor of white-fleshed guava is milder and less intensely tropical than pink-fleshed varieties — appealing to consumers who find the strong, musky, distinctive guava flavor of red-fleshed types overpowering. Common guava (Psidium guajava) is one of the most productive and easily grown tropical fruit trees in zone 9 — adapting to a wide range of soils, producing fruit year-round, and growing rapidly from a young tree to full bearing size. The highly aromatic fruit — which contains more vitamin C per gram than citrus — is consumed fresh, in juice, paste (guava paste is a classic Latin American confection), jam, and desserts across the tropical world. In zone 9 the combination of easy culture, fast production, and highly aromatic fruit that cannot be found in commercial distribution makes guava one of the most rewarding tropical fruit trees available. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: TropicSnow Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill White Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the early years to let light into the canopy. TropicSnow was released by the University of Florida breeding program as one of the lowest-chill white-fleshed peaches available, developed to give far-southern and even subtropical growers a genuine tree-ripened peach where standard varieties fail to bloom reliably. The medium-sized freestone fruit has creamy white skin blushed with red and sweet, low-acid white flesh, a flavor profile many gardeners prefer to the tangier yellow-fleshed low-chill peaches bred for the same region. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart when marble-sized to improve size and quality, and expect an early harvest, typically in late spring, well ahead of summer heat. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: TropicSweet Apple (University of Florida Low-Chill Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; TropicSweet is a low-chill apple cultivar developed by the University of Florida specifically for subtropical apple production, requiring roughly 250–300 chill hours — low enough to fruit reliably through most of zone 9 and the warmer parts of zone 8b where standard apple cultivars fail to bloom consistently. It joins Anna, Dorsett Golden, and Ein Shemer as one of the small handful of apples bred or selected specifically for the Deep South and Gulf Coast, and performs best when planted alongside one of those cultivars for cross-pollination, since it is not reliably self-fruitful. Fruit ripens in early to midsummer with a sweet, mild flavor and crisp texture typical of low-chill apple selections, which tend to be less complex in flavor than high-chill Northern apples but offer the major advantage of actually fruiting in a warm-winter climate. Maintain good air circulation through pruning to reduce fire blight and apple scab pressure, both significant disease concerns for apples grown in humid Southern conditions. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Trovita Orange (Low-Chill California Sweet Orange)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed, in a warm, sunny site with well-drained soil, since this cultivar was selected for reliable fruiting in low-heat, low-humidity climates. Water regularly during establishment and reduce slightly as fruit matures to help concentrate flavor. Trovita produces medium-sized, thin-skinned oranges with juicy, sweet flesh and fewer seeds than many Valencia-type oranges, ripening in winter to early spring. Originating as a Washington Navel sport bred for desert and coastal Southern California conditions, it remains a dependable choice where summer heat is moderate. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Troyer Citrange Rootstock
description: Troyer citrange was produced in 1909 by USDA breeder E.M. Savage under Walter Swingle's direction at Riverside, California, crossing Washington Navel orange with trifoliate orange, and takes its name from the Alabama grower who received the first fruiting budwood. It became a cornerstone rootstock during California's mid-20th-century tristeza virus crisis, when UC Riverside's Bill Bitters screened hundreds of rootstock-scion combinations and found Troyer, along with its sister selection Carrizo from the same navel orange x trifoliate parentage, resistant to the disease that was devastating sour-orange-rooted groves. Troyer imparts strong cold tolerance, good tristeza resistance, and vigorous, well-anchored growth to whatever citrus variety is grafted onto it, though it is more sensitive than Carrizo to certain heavy or poorly drained soils. Home growers wanting a hardy, disease-resistant understock for grafting favorite citrus in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting can use Troyer much as they would Carrizo, providing full sun and good drainage for best results. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Truchas Mini-Romaine Lettuce
description: Sow seed shallowly in cool weather, since lettuce needs light and cool soil to germinate; make successive sowings for a continuous harvest. This deep-red mini-romaine is compact and easy to grow in small spaces, with uniform, upright leaves that stay clean and are perfect for Caesar salads. It carries disease resistance to downy mildew and lettuce dieback, and part shade helps it hold quality in warmer weather. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Trucker's Favorite Corn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with good air circulation; Trucker's Favorite is an open-pollinated Southern heirloom corn variety that was the standard large-eared roasting corn sold at Southern roadside stands, farmers markets, and farm stands for much of the 20th century — the 'trucker' in the name refers to produce truck farmers who grew it as their preferred selling variety because the large ears (8–10 inches, white to yellow-white kernels) made an impressive and reliably satisfying roasting ear crop. At the roasting-ear stage (about 20 days after silk), the white to cream-colored ears are tender, starchy-sweet, and deeply flavored with the old-fashioned, rich, full corn character that modern hybrid sweet corns bred for extreme sugar content often lack — a more complex, substantial corn flavor similar to mid-century American corn. As a dual-purpose variety, Trucker's Favorite dried to an excellent yellow cornmeal with full corn flavor prized for Southern cornbread, grits, and polenta. Matures in 85–95 days from seed.

name: Trucker's Favorite Tomato (Pre-1900 New Jersey Heirloom Pink Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking to support the vigorous vines. Trucker's Favorite is a pre-1900 heirloom traced to Burlington County, New Jersey and offered commercially by W. Atlee Burpee before 1899; it was named for its popularity among market gardeners hauling produce to city markets. The plants set clusters of 3-4 crack-resistant, 6-12 ounce pink beefsteak-type fruit with a rich, sweet, old-fashioned flavor and notably good foliage disease resistance for an heirloom of its era. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Truckers Favorite White Corn (Market Garden White Dent Corn)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for good pollination; thin to 8–12 inches; Truckers Favorite is tall and produces 1–2 ears per stalk; harvest at the milk stage (when kernels exude a milky liquid when punctured) for best fresh-eating quality; allow to dry on the stalk for grinding into grits or cornmeal. Truckers Favorite White Corn is a classic Southern open-pollinated white dent corn that has been grown in the American South since before the Civil War and takes its name from the small-scale produce farmers ('truckers') who grew and hauled vegetables to regional markets throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries — the same context that gave rise to terms like 'truck farming' and 'market gardening.' The variety was selected over generations specifically for the combination of early-maturing roasting ear quality (harvested at the milk stage for fresh eating) and excellent flour/grits quality when allowed to dry fully. The white kernels are large and doughy at the roasting ear stage, sweet enough for fresh eating but not as sugary as modern sweet corn varieties — the characteristic semi-sweet, starchy quality that old-fashioned cornbread and grits recipes were designed around. In the Gulf South, Truckers Favorite White is particularly valued as a heritage Southern cornbread corn — ground into coarse grits or fine meal, it produces the authentic white stone-ground cornmeal preferred in traditional Southern cooking. Plants are tall (7–9 feet), productive, and heat tolerant, maturing in the relatively modest time of 85–95 days that suits the Gulf Coast growing season. Matures in 80–95 days from seed.

name: True Cinnamon (Ceylon Cinnamon)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained, sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; true cinnamon (Ceylon cinnamon) from Sri Lanka is considered the 'real' cinnamon of culinary tradition — lighter, sweeter, and more delicate than the cassia cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) sold in most North American supermarkets. True cinnamon has very low coumarin content compared to cassia, making it safer for regular consumption. The cinnamon spice is harvested from the inner bark of shoots cut from coppiced trees — the thin bark curls into the familiar quills as it dries. In the home garden, the tree provides an ornamental, fragrant, tropical presence; the young leaves can be used as a bay leaf substitute. In zones 9 and below, grow in a large container and harvest leaves and small stems for culinary use. Coppice regularly to keep the plant at a manageable size. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: True Gold Sweet Corn
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after frost, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row to ensure good wind pollination. This old-fashioned sugary (su) corn produces large 9 inch ears that are very sweet and tender. The plants resist stalk-lodging and are less likely to bend or kink in windy areas; keep them well watered and harvest at the milk stage for peak sweetness. Matures in 75–85 days from seed.

name: True Greek Oregano
description: True Greek oregano is the genuine culinary type prized by Italian and Greek cooks for its intense, pungent aroma and flavor. It elevates tomato sauces, marinated vegetables, meats, fish, and poultry, and grows compactly enough for containers. Surface-sow the fine seed indoors since it needs light, then transplant to full sun with lean, well-drained soil. Keep water on the low side to concentrate the essential oils, and shear plants after flowering to maintain dense, flavorful growth. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: True Hyssop
description: True hyssop is an easy-care perennial that flowers in its first year and lights up the late-summer garden with spikes that draw bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. This ancient herb has long been valued for culinary and medicinal use as well as its ornamental blue blooms. Start seed indoors and transplant to full sun with well-drained soil, where it tolerates dry conditions once established. Trim after flowering to keep plants tidy, and grow it near vegetables to attract pollinators. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: True Indigo (Indigo Plant)
description: Sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; true indigo is the historical source of indigo blue dye — one of the oldest and most important natural pigments in human history, used for 6,000 years to dye textiles from ancient Egypt and India to colonial America, where indigo was South Carolina's most valuable colonial export crop. The blue compound (indigotin) is extracted from the leaves through a multi-step fermentation and oxidation process. The plant itself is a tropical shrub or subshrub with small, pinnate leaves and inconspicuous small pink-mauve pea flowers. It is nitrogen-fixing and improves soil fertility. Indigo dye has experienced a revival among natural dye artists and sustainable textile producers. In zone 9–11, the plant grows as a perennial shrub and can be harvested multiple times per season; in cooler climates it is grown as an annual specifically for dye production. Woad (Isatis tinctoria) provides the same dye compound but from a European temperate plant. The pure, rich blue of indigo dye is not achievable from any other widely cultivated plant. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: True Nutmeg (Nutmeg Tree)
description: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere. Native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, this evergreen tree bears apricot-like fruit that splits open to reveal a hard seed wrapped in a bright red, lacy covering; the seed itself is dried and ground into nutmeg, while the red aril is separately dried and ground into mace, making a single fruit the source of two distinct spices. Trees are dioecious, so both a male pollinator and a female fruiting tree (or a grafted tree combining both) are needed for fruit production, and trees typically take seven to nine years to begin bearing and up to twenty years to reach full production. Grow in the dappled shade of taller trees as it would experience in its native rainforest understory, keep humidity high, and protect from any cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: True Red Cranberry Bean (Heirloom Speckled Shell Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since this is a vigorous climbing variety. True Red Cranberry is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s, producing plump, cream-colored pods streaked in deep red-maroon that shell out to reveal beans mottled in burgundy and cream, cooking up to a rich, nutty flavor and creamy texture prized for baked beans and soups. Pick pods at the shell-bean stage for the best flavor and texture, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for long-term storage as a dry bean. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved season to season to continue the variety. Matures in 65–100 days from seed.

name: True Sichuan Pepper (Hua Jiao)
description: Zanthoxylum bungeanum is the deciduous, thorny shrub responsible for the bulk of the 'hua jiao' peppercorns used in Sichuan cooking, somewhat less cold-hardy and more heat-loving than its frequently substituted relative Z. simulans. Site it in full sun on lean, sharply drained soil, since wet feet in winter are the most common cause of losses. Harvest the small red husks in early autumn once they split open, then dry them fully before grinding away the bitter black seed to release the intensely citrusy, numbing sanshool compounds. Expect several years of establishment before a young plant produces a meaningful peppercorn harvest, and keep at least two seedlings if grown from seed since fruit set improves with cross-pollination. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Truhart Perfection Pimiento Pepper (Classic Georgia Canning Pimiento)
description: Truhart Perfection traces to a single outstanding plant selected from the original 1913 Perfection pimiento introduction, and the Georgia Experiment Station's pedigree breeding program refined it into the thick-walled, carmine-red, heart-shaped fruit that defined jarred pimientos and pimiento cheese for most of the twentieth century. Unlike its later nematode-resistant derivative Truhart-NR, the straight Truhart Perfection line carries no built-in resistance to root-knot nematode, so gardeners on sandy, nematode-prone soils should rotate plantings or solarize beds between crops. The blocky, three-lobed fruit ripens from green to deep red with sweet, dense flesh well suited to roasting, canning, and stuffing. Stake or cage plants once fruit loads heavily, and pick at full red color for the richest flavor and color in preserved pimientos. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Truhart-NR Pepper (Nematode-Resistant Pimiento)
description: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed. Truhart-NR was developed by USDA-ARS through a backcross program that introduced the dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from Mississippi Nemaheart into the 'Truhart Perfection' pimiento background, and it was released in 2009 after field trials showed it outyielding its susceptible parent with heavier, longer, thicker-walled fruit. The blocky, three-lobed pimiento fruit ripens to deep red with sweet, thick flesh suited to fresh eating, roasting, and pimiento cheese. It is particularly valuable for organic and specialty growers along the Gulf Coast who lack easy access to chemical nematicides and garden in nematode-infested sandy soils. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Truly Tiny Banana
description: Truly Tiny is a miniature Dwarf Cavendish banana that stays compact enough for a container or a bright corner indoors while still producing edible fruit. Its bold tropical leaves make it an ornamental standout, and its small size suits patios and sunrooms. Grow from a potted plant or pup in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive soil, feeding heavily during active growth. Keep the soil consistently moist since bananas are thirsty, shelter it from wind, and move it indoors before frost. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Tsaoko Cardamom (Chinese Black Cardamom, Cao Guo)
description: Amomum tsaoko is a large, clump-forming ginger relative native to the forested mountain slopes of Yunnan Province in southern China and adjacent northern Vietnam, where it is cultivated as a major cash crop at elevation under the dappled shade of forest canopy. Flowers form directly on the rhizomes near the soil surface, followed by large, ridged, reddish-brown seed capsules that are smoke-dried over open fires to develop the deep, smoky, camphor-and-eucalyptus aroma prized in Sichuan and Yunnan braises, marinades, and hot pot spice blends. Coarser and considerably taller than true cardamom, with broad glossy canes reaching 6-10 feet, it prefers cool, humid, sheltered shade and rich, constantly moist soil. Propagate by dividing established rhizome clumps in spring; plants take three to four years to reach bearing age. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: TSH 565 Cacao
description: TSH 565 is one of the Trinidad Selected Hybrids bred at Trinidad's cacao research station from a cross of SCA 6 and ICS 1, combining a witches'-broom and black-pod-tolerant parent with a classic Trinitario flavor line. Fermentation studies have shown it develops a full, traditional chocolate flavor profile through the action of its own indigenous microbiota, and it has been adopted well beyond Trinidad, including on estates in Brazil and the Andes. Unlike some self-compatible cacao clones, TSH 565 requires cross-pollination from a genetically compatible partner tree to set a full pod load, so orchard planning should include compatible neighboring clones. Give it the warm, humid, shaded understory conditions and rich, well-drained soil that all fine-flavor cacao selections need. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tsu Li Asian Pear (Chinese Pear)
description: Tsu Li is a Chinese heirloom pear grown widely across the Gulf South, valued for a chilling requirement low enough to fruit reliably where many other Asian pear cultivars fail to set a full crop in mild winters. The bottle-shaped fruit has smooth green-yellow skin and firmer, less crisp flesh than typical round nashi types, with a mild sweet flavor that leans closer to a European pear than to crunchy cultivars like Hosui. Trees show good field resistance to fire blight, a major disease pressure in the humid Southeast, and are commonly recommended alongside cultivars like Orient and Southern King for home orchards in Texas and Louisiana. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tsurunoko Persimmon (Crane's Egg Persimmon)
description: Tsurunoko is an old Japanese heirloom whose name translates to 'crane's egg,' describing the fruit's distinctive elongated shape with a pointed tip unlike the flatter or acorn-shaped fruit of most other persimmon cultivars. The deep orange skin covers flesh that becomes exceptionally sweet and jelly-soft once the astringency fully resolves after ripening. It remains a specialty planting favored by home orchardists and heirloom collectors rather than a mainstream commercial cultivar. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tulameen Raspberry (Premium Late-Season British Columbia Raspberry)
description: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and support the tall canes on a two-wire trellis. Bred in British Columbia, Tulameen is a premium fresh-market red raspberry known for unusually large, firm, glossy berries with excellent sweet flavor and a notably long harvest window that extends well into late summer. It is a floricane-fruiting type, so remove spent canes to the ground after the season and thin new primocanes to the strongest shoots to maintain fruit size and quality. Because the canes are tall and heavily laden when fruiting, secure them well to the trellis to prevent wind and fruit-weight breakage. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Tulare Walnut (Early-Bearing UC Davis Persian Walnut)
description: Tulare is an early-bearing University of California Persian walnut selection named for the San Joaquin Valley county where much of the state's walnut industry is concentrated. Trees begin cropping earlier in their life than many later-maturing commercial cultivars, producing a large, thin-shelled nut with good kernel quality, though careful framework training when young helps offset a tendency toward weak-angled lateral branching. Give it deep, well-drained soil in full sun and a compatible pollenizer for a consistent crop, and expect nuts to mature in the same general September harvest window as other California Persian walnuts. Matures in 1460–3285 days from transplant.

name: Tulip Prickly Pear (Twistspine Prickly Pear)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tulip prickly pear is one of the most widely distributed native cacti of the American Southwest and southern Plains, producing large, satiny, lemon-yellow flowers with orange centers in May and June that are among the most beautiful cactus flowers — 2–3 inches across, silky-textured, and glowing in full sun. The pads are flat, blue-green, and covered with clusters of spines. The fruits (tunas) ripen from green to deep red-purple in late summer and fall and are edible fresh or cooked into juice, jelly, candy, and syrup, having a sweet, watermelon-like flavor. The young pads (nopales) are also edible as a vegetable when the spines are removed. This species is one of the most cold-hardy prickly pears, surviving to zone 4 in well-drained conditions. It naturalizes across the Southwest and Texas and is an important wildlife plant — the fruit feeds desert tortoises, coyotes, javelinas, and birds. CAUTION: the tiny glochid spines embed invisibly in skin and cause intense, persistent irritation. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)
description: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; tulsi is more heat and humidity tolerant than sweet basil but equally frost-sensitive. Pinch flower buds as they form to prolong leaf harvest and maintain essential oil concentration in the foliage; once plants flower the leaves become more pungent and may turn slightly bitter. The clove-scented leaves are used in Indian cooking (especially in Hindu religious rituals), Ayurvedic medicine, and increasingly in Western herbal teas. In zone 9 tulsi often self-seeds, and seedlings can persist from year to year as tender perennials if protected from the rare hard frost. Matures in 50–75 days from transplant.

name: Tulsi Holy Basil
description: Known as the Queen of Herbs in India, tulsi or holy basil is treasured for its sacred status and prized for tea and wellness uses. This kapoor or temperate type is fast-growing with a distinctive bubble-gum fragrance and better cold tolerance than most basils. Surface-sow seed indoors in warmth since it needs light to germinate, then transplant to full sun after frost. Pinch flower spikes to prolong leaf harvest, though many growers let it bloom to attract pollinators and gather leaves and flowers for tea. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Tumbling Tom Tomato (Cascading Container Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into a hanging basket, window box, or large container with rich, well-draining potting mix. Water consistently (containers dry out faster than in-ground plantings) and fertilize every 2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer for best production. Tumbling Tom is a compact, pendulous-stemmed cherry tomato developed specifically for container and hanging basket growing — the first cherry tomato variety widely distributed with 'tumbling' in the name to describe its characteristic cascading habit, where the naturally trailing stems drape over pot edges and hang 18–24 inches below the rim, making it one of the most dramatic edible container plants available. Unlike most cherry tomatoes, which require staking and training on indeterminate vines that climb 5–8 feet, Tumbling Tom is a bushy, pendent type that requires no staking, no caging, and no training — just water, light, and fertilizer. The plants produce abundant clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), round, bright red cherry tomatoes with good sweet tomato flavor on the pendulous stems; a large hanging basket with a well-established Tumbling Tom plant loaded with red fruits is a genuinely beautiful and productive edible ornamental display. Available in both red and yellow strains ('Tumbling Tom Red' and 'Tumbling Tom Yellow'). Ideal for balconies, patios, decks, and any space where in-ground gardening is not possible. Matures in 55–70 days from transplant.

name: Tumbling Tom Yellow Tomato (Cascading Container Cherry Tomato)
description: Tumbling Tom Yellow is the yellow-fruited strain sold alongside standard red Tumbling Tom, sharing the same compact, naturally trailing, pendent growth habit bred specifically for hanging baskets, window boxes, and large containers rather than staking or caging. Plants stay small, under a foot wide, but the cascading stems drape 12 to 18 inches over the basket rim, loaded with abundant small, sweet, fruity golden-yellow cherry tomatoes that ripen a few days later than the red strain. Because containers dry out faster than garden soil, water consistently and feed every 1-2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set. No staking, caging, or pruning is needed; simply keep picking to encourage continued flowering, and pair it with the red strain in matched baskets for a two-tone display. Matures in 65–72 days from transplant.

name: Tummelberry
description: The tummelberry is a Scottish-bred Rubus hybrid developed at the Scottish Crop Research Institute from a tayberry cross, selected specifically for greater cold hardiness and easier mechanical harvest than its parent. It produces large, dark red to maroon conical berries slightly smaller than tayberries in midsummer with a rich, aromatic flavor well suited to preserves, juices, and desserts. Train the long, semi-trailing canes on a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; cut all fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes for the following year. It is substantially hardier than tayberry and performs reliably in zones 4–5 with minimal winter protection. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Tundra Honeyberry
description: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Tundra will not set a worthwhile crop alone. Released by the University of Saskatchewan breeding program as a mid-to-late-season pollinizer partner for Borealis, Tundra bears firm, mild-flavored, elongated blue berries that hold their shape well and are less prone to splitting after rain than some earlier cultivars, making them good for both fresh eating and processing. The upright, vigorous bush is easy to hand-harvest and tends to crop reliably once established. Tundra is extremely cold-hardy, surviving winter lows well below -40F, but like all haskaps it performs poorly in hot, humid summer regions and is not recommended for the Gulf South. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep production high. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Tung Oil Tree (China Wood Oil Tree)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; tung oil tree is a Chinese tree cultivated throughout zone 8–11 for its seeds, which yield tung oil — a fast-drying, water-resistant drying oil used extensively in paints, varnishes, wood preservatives, and wood finishing products. The spring flower display is spectacular — large clusters of white flowers with red or pink veining cover the bare branches before leaf emergence, followed by bold, large, heart-shaped leaves. The golf-ball-sized fruits contain 3–7 seeds with 50–60% oil content. The entire plant is poisonous if consumed — the seeds, leaves, and oil are toxic. The Gulf South has abandoned remnant tung orchards from a failed commercial industry of the mid-20th century. Now a naturalized, occasionally invasive ornamental/landscape tree notable for its spring flower show. Caution: all plant parts are toxic. Matures in 1095–1825 days from seed.

name: Tupy Blackberry (Brazilian Heat-Tolerant Erect Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Tupy is a vigorous, thorny, erect blackberry developed by the Brazilian agricultural research agency EMBRAPA from Arkansas breeding lines, and it has become one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in warm-climate regions of Latin America because of its exceptional heat tolerance and productivity under conditions too warm for many U.S.-bred varieties. Berries are large, glossy black, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening early in the season with a long harvest window and heavy yields. Because canes are thorny, plan for careful pruning and picking; remove fruited floricanes after harvest and tie in 4-6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for the following year. Tupy tolerates the intense heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast better than many thornless northern-bred varieties, making it a strong choice for zone 9-10 growers. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Turban Squash (Turk's Turban Squash)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in rich, well-amended soil in full sun; provide 6–8 feet of space for sprawling vines. Turban squash (also called Turk's Cap, Turk's Turban, or French Turban) is one of the most visually distinctive of all winter squash, producing medium to large (5–10 lb) fruits with a dramatic secondary lobe or 'cap' protruding from the blossom end in a shape resembling a Turkish turban or Ottoman fez — this unusual morphology is a Cucurbita maxima trait that occasionally appears in several varieties but is most pronounced and reliable in this dedicated 'Turban' selection. The skin is spectacularly patterned in orange, cream, and green with mottled, swirling patterns that vary between fruits; the ornamental quality makes Turban squash one of the most popular fall decorative squashes alongside regular pumpkins. The flesh is edible with a mild, somewhat dry, floury texture and pleasant squash flavor well-suited to stuffing — the cap portion is often removed and used as a natural serving bowl for soups or stuffings. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Turga Parsnip (Hungarian Heirloom Long Parsnip)
description: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, stone-free soil, keeping the bed evenly moist through the slow, erratic germination and thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once established. Turga is a Hungarian heirloom valued for producing stout, smoothly tapered roots that size up reliably even in soils too heavy or shallow for some other parsnip types, with a dense, creamy-white interior and a rich, distinctly sweet flavor. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts before digging, since the cold converts starches to sugar and gives Turga its full sweet, almost nutty character. Because parsnip seed loses viability quickly, always start with fresh seed for the season. Matures in 110–125 days from seed.

name: Turk's Turban Squash (Turban Squash, French Turban, Giraumon Turban)
description: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after last frost in a fertile, well-drained bed; Turk's Turban produces medium-length vines of 6–8 feet; harvest when the skin is fully hard and the color has developed to its mature orange-red with green and white swirling markings; cure at room temperature for 2–3 weeks to harden the rind and improve flavor. Turk's Turban is one of the most visually spectacular squashes in cultivation — an heirloom Cucurbita maxima variety that has been grown in American and European gardens since the 19th century, renowned for the extraordinary shape of its fruits: a squat, flattened orange-red primary body topped by a rounded, turban-like secondary lobe that protrudes from the blossom end, often striped or mottled in contrasting shades of green, cream, and orange. The distinctive shape comes from an unusual growth pattern in which the secondary floral section of the fruit expands outward from the blossom end, creating the appearance of a hat or turban imposed on top of the primary fruit body. No two Turk's Turban fruits are exactly alike in their color patterning — each shows a unique arrangement of orange, green, cream, and white in swirls and stripes that makes them natural art objects. The flesh beneath is the dense, sweet, orange type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties; at full maturity after curing, the flavor is rich and sweet with a dry, starchy texture excellent for baking, soups, and puréeing. While widely grown as a purely ornamental squash for autumn display, Turk's Turban is fully edible and good-flavored — it deserves to be eaten rather than simply displayed. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Turkey Berry
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; turkey berry is a sprawling tropical nightshade shrub producing prolific clusters of small (marble-sized) green berries that are an essential ingredient in Thai green curry — they add a distinctive bitter, slightly crunchy texture and are used whole or halved. In Caribbean and West African cooking the cooked berries appear in stews and salt fish dishes, including the Jamaican classic susumber in salt fish. Unlike many nightshades, the berries are always cooked before eating. In zone 9–11 the shrub becomes a large multi-stemmed perennial that produces year-round; in zone 8 it may dieback and resprout from the roots. The stems have scattered spines — wear gloves when harvesting. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Turkey Craw Bean (Cutshort Turkey Craw)
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing low supports of 2–3 feet for the semi-vining plants; Turkey Craw is an Appalachian heirloom snap bean dating back at least to the 19th century, named for seeds reportedly found in the crop (craw) of a wild turkey shot by a hunter — the story illustrating how food plants spread naturally through the American South via birds and early farmers. It is a cutshort type, meaning the seeds are crowded together in the pod and shortened in length to accommodate more seeds — the characteristic shape that identifies many traditional Southern snap beans. The pods are tender and flavorful when harvested young as snap beans, or the plants can be allowed to mature for dry bean use. Excellent heat tolerance and prolific production make it a dependable Southern garden bean; the seeds' tan and brown mottling is distinctive and appealing. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Turkey Red Wheat (Historic Kansas Hard Red Winter Wheat)
description: Drill or broadcast in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so seedlings establish a strong root system and low rosette before winter dormancy, then resume growth and head out in late spring. Turkey Red was carried to Kansas by Mennonite immigrants from the Crimea and southern Russia in the 1870s, and its exceptional cold hardiness and drought tolerance helped transform the Great Plains into the wheat-growing heartland of the United States, effectively founding the American hard red winter wheat industry. The bran-red kernels mill into strong, high-protein bread flour with a robust, slightly sweet flavor, and the variety remains popular today among heritage-grain bakers and small growers for its resilience on marginal, low-input land. Matures in 240–270 days from seed.

name: Turkish Hazel
description: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, even dry or compacted soil in full sun; Turkish hazel is the most drought-tolerant and urban-adaptable of all hazelnuts, renowned in the horticultural trade as one of the few large nut trees that tolerates dry, alkaline soils, compacted city conditions, and air pollution — a remarkable feat for any tree. It is used as a rootstock for grafting cultivated filbert and hazelnut varieties, and the straight species produces small edible nuts enclosed in deeply fringed husks. The distinctive corky, deeply ridged bark and broadly pyramidal form make it an ornamental specimen tree even when not in nut. Long-lived and very low-maintenance; used extensively in European forestry and urban planting programs. Matures in 1825–3650 days from seed.

name: Turkish Orange Eggplant (Round Heirloom Orange-Fruited Eggplant)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest at the orange stage when fruits are 2–3 inches in diameter for full flavor development. Turkish Orange is an heirloom eggplant from Turkey that produces compact, round fruits 2–3 inches in diameter that ripen from green to a deep, vibrant orange-red — a color completely unlike any other common eggplant and more reminiscent of a small tomato or tomatillo than a traditional eggplant. This color difference signals a different flavor profile: Turkish Orange eggplants are slightly sweeter than standard purple types, with less bitterness and a slightly more complex, slightly acidic note at the ripe orange stage. The plants are productive and ornamental — clusters of round, orange fruits hanging from attractive, somewhat spiny plants create a striking garden display that frequently prompts questions from visitors unfamiliar with the variety. The flesh is firm, white to cream-colored, and suitable for all standard eggplant preparations; the round shape makes them particularly interesting for stuffing whole, hollowing and filling with rice-and-meat preparations in the Turkish culinary tradition from which the variety originates. Matures in 72–85 days from transplant.

name: Turkish Rocket (Hill Mustard)
description: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline, deeply cultivated soil in full sun to partial shade; Turkish rocket is one of the most productive and versatile perennial vegetables for the four-season food garden — a member of the mustard family (Brassicaceae) with an edible flavor profile that shifts through the season. The young spring leaves are used raw in salads with a mild, arugula-like flavor; as they age and before flowering they develop a stronger, mustardy bite better suited to cooking as a potherb. The young flower buds and flowers are eaten like broccoli raab. After flowers open, the distinctive warty, corky, two-seeded pods are produced. The plant is extremely long-lived, drought tolerant, and cold hardy once established, and produces earlier in spring than almost any other perennial vegetable. Self-seeds freely — deadhead after flowering if spread is unwanted. An outstanding low-maintenance perennial vegetable for the permaculture food garden. Matures in 60–365 days from seed.

name: Turmeric (Indian Saffron)
description: Plant fresh rhizome sections with viable growing points 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; turmeric is the ancient golden spice of South Asian cooking and traditional medicine — the underground rhizome that when harvested, dried, and ground yields the vivid, saturated, warm-golden-yellow powder that gives curry its characteristic color, imparts a mild, earthy-peppery-slightly-bitter flavor, and delivers the curcumin compound that has become one of the most researched natural anti-inflammatory substances in modern phytomedicine. Native to tropical South Asia (most likely India or Southeast Asia), it has been cultivated throughout the tropical world for at least 4,000 years as both spice and dye (it provided the yellow color in Asian textiles long before synthetic dyes). The garden plant itself is a handsome, lush, tropical-looking Zingiberaceae (ginger family) member with large, paddle-shaped, bright-green, distinctly ribbed and veined leaves similar to those of cannas or gingers, reaching 3–4 feet in height and providing excellent tropical effect in the part-shade garden throughout the growing season. The rhizomes are internally a vivid, saturated orange-yellow (the curcumin pigment) and stain anything they contact that same bright orange-yellow. Harvest the fresh rhizomes in fall after the aerial stems die back; they can be used fresh (milder, more aromatic), dried and ground (the familiar powder), or replanted for next season. A highly rewarding dual-purpose ornamental and culinary/medicinal herb for zone 8–11 shade gardens. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: Turnip
description: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring, or 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; turnips are among the fastest-maturing root vegetables available, producing edible roots in 40–60 days and providing both edible roots and edible greens from a single planting. The roots are sweetest and most tender when harvested at 2–3 inches in diameter — larger roots become pithy and bitter. In zone 7–10 fall-planted turnips can overwinter in the ground and are sweetened by frost exposure. The greens of varieties like 'Seven Top' and 'Purple Top White Globe' are prized in Southern cooking and highly nutritious. Turnips also function as a quick-maturing catch crop, cover crop, and forage plant. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Turnip Greens
description: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in fertile soil; turnips are among the fastest-germinating brassicas and begin producing harvestable greens within a month. Thin to 4–6 in if growing for both greens and roots, or leave closer together for greens-only production. Begin harvesting outer leaves when plants are 6–8 in tall, leaving the crown to continue growing. Fall-harvested greens are noticeably sweeter than spring greens due to the conversion of starches to sugars in cool temperatures. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Turnip Tops (Turnip Greens, Cima di Rapa)
description: Broadcast or row-sow seeds thinly and cover with 1/4 inch of soil, thinning to 4–8 inches for greens production; when grown specifically for greens rather than root turnips, dense spacing produces tender young leaves more quickly and the roots remain small and edible as a bonus harvest. Turnip greens are one of the most nutritious and productive winter vegetables for the Southern garden — far superior in flavor after frost than when cut in warm weather. The traditional Southern pot of turnip greens slow-cooked with a smoked hock concentrates their earthy, slightly bitter, mineral richness into a deeply savory dish. Whole young plants can be harvested, roots and all, or cut repeatedly above the crown for ongoing regrowth. Italian cima di rapa strains are grown specifically for the tender florets and top leaves and are harvested before the flower buds fully open. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Turnip-rooted Chervil
description: Sow Chaerophyllum bulbosum seeds fresh in fall directly where they are to grow — seeds lose viability quickly and are best sown immediately after harvest; thin seedlings to 4–6 inches apart and keep soil moist but not waterlogged throughout the cool growing season; harvest roots in early to midsummer as foliage yellows and dies back. Turnip-rooted Chervil is among the rarest and most intriguing of all heirloom root vegetables — an annual or biennial carrot-family plant with delicate, ferny foliage and small, grey-skinned tubers with exceptionally delicate, nutty, chesnut-sweet flavor. It requires cold stratification to germinate (hence fall sowing is essential) and tolerates partial shade well — performing in spots where carrots or parsnips would not thrive. The roots are at their best when small, around an inch in diameter; larger roots can become pithy. Their flavor has been compared to a cross between chestnut, sweet potato, and parsley root — distinctive and prized by those lucky enough to taste them. Auguste Escoffier featured turnip-rooted chervil in classic French cuisine; it fell from fashion in the 20th century as it does not store or ship well and demands specific growing conditions. Fresh seeds from specialty heirloom seed suppliers are essential as germination rates drop sharply after a few months. The feathery foliage is also edible and mildly anise-flavored, usable as a garnish like regular chervil. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Turnpike Bell Pepper (Broad-Spectrum Bacterial Spot-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Turnpike is a bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to a wide range of bacterial leaf spot races along with Phytophthora blight and tobacco mosaic virus, giving it one of the broadest disease packages available in a commercial bell pepper and making it especially well suited to the combination of heat, humidity, and rainfall pressure found across the Gulf South. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good eating quality if left on the plant. Because it resists so many distinct disease pathogens at once, Turnpike tends to hold healthy foliage and continue setting fruit through conditions that would knock back less resistant varieties. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Tuscan Blue Rosemary
description: Tuscan Blue is a robust, upright rosemary that grows into an aromatic evergreen shrub prized for both cooking and Mediterranean-style landscaping. Its stiff, fragrant stems are ideal for skewers and roasting, while blue flowers draw pollinators. Because rosemary is slow and erratic from seed, it is best established from a live plant or cutting set out after frost. Give it full sun and fast-draining soil, water sparingly once established, and shelter or overwinter indoors in cold-winter zones. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Tuscan Blue Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Rosemary with Deep Blue-Violet Flowers)
