description: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; Tuscan Blue is the classic tall, strongly upright rosemary cultivar — one of the most commonly grown culinary rosemaries in Gulf South herb gardens, selected for its vigorous, columnar-upright habit, robust culinary fragrance and flavor, and particularly vivid deep blue-violet flowers that are more intensely colored than many other rosemary cultivars. The tall, strictly upright habit (4–6 feet) makes Tuscan Blue distinctly different from spreading and prostrate rosemary forms, functioning as a narrow, evergreen vertical accent in herb and kitchen garden designs rather than a low-spreading groundcover. The strongly aromatic, narrow, needle-like leaves are the standard culinary rosemary used in Mediterranean cooking — with the same powerful resinous rosemary scent and flavor as the straight species. In Gulf South zone 9, Tuscan Blue grows as a long-lived evergreen perennial that thrives in the heat and dry conditions that characterize Mediterranean-climate herbs. Well-drained soil is the critical requirement: rosemary in heavy clay or poorly drained soil declines rapidly. The fragrant blue flowers in late winter (February–March in zone 9) provide important early nectar for honeybees and native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Tuscan Blue can be trained as a formal herb garden accent, clipped as a low hedge, or grown as a specimen shrub. Prune after flowering to maintain a compact habit; avoid cutting into old, woody, leafless stems. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Tuxana Sweet Corn (Open-Source White Sweet Corn)
description: Tuxana is a modern, open-pollinated white sweet corn developed in southern Oregon by stabilizing a cross between an Anasazi flour corn landrace and a sugary-enhanced hybrid, now maintained and distributed as an Open Source Seed Initiative-pledged variety. Seven-foot stalks generally produce two eight-inch ears with twelve to sixteen rows of large, deep kernels that cook up rich, creamy, and sweet without the cloying intensity of supersweet hybrids. Because it breeds true, gardeners can save seed year to year, making it a good option for anyone wanting hybrid-level ear quality in a variety they can maintain themselves. Isolate from other corn types at pollination time to keep seed pure. Matures in 78–88 days from seed.

name: Tuxedo Sweet Corn (Bicolor Supersweet Sh2 Hybrid Corn)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil (65°F minimum) in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen at knee height. Isolate from other corn varieties (including other sh2 types) by 250+ feet or stagger planting dates by 2+ weeks. Tuxedo is a bicolor (white and yellow kernel) supersweet (sh2) hybrid that has become one of the most popular bicolor fresh-market and roadside stand corns in the eastern United States — a Syngenta/Rogers Brothers variety that delivers the maximum sweetness possible from the sh2 gene type combined with a visually appealing bicolor kernel appearance that many consumers associate with premium sweet corn. The sh2 (shrunken-2) mutation creates corn with up to 4 times the sugar content of standard su types at harvest, and unlike se types, sh2 varieties retain their sweetness for 5–7 days after picking under refrigeration — a major commercial advantage that has made sh2 types dominant in the fresh sweet corn market. Tuxedo produces large (7.5–9 inch), well-filled ears with 16–18 rows of alternating white and yellow kernels; the kernels are very tender with thin skins and intensely sweet flavor when harvested at peak. The bicolor appearance in uniform, well-filled ears of Tuxedo is particularly attractive for roadside stand and farmers market sales where visual appeal drives purchasing decisions. One of the most commercially successful bicolor sh2 varieties of the past two decades. Matures in 74–78 days from seed.

name: TV1 Tea (Tocklai Vegetative Clone 1, Assam)
description: TV1 was released in 1949 by the Tocklai Tea Research Institute in Assam, India, as the first vegetatively propagated commercial tea clone, and it remains one of the most widely planted clones in Assam's tea belt, prized for producing a consistent, high-quality CTC (crush-tear-curl) black tea. It is a broad-leaved, vigorous Assam-type selection and shows moderate tolerance of common tea pests and diseases relative to older seedling plantings. In cultivation it wants warm, humid conditions, acidic well-drained soil, and regular pruning to maintain a low plucking table. Its long commercial track record makes it a useful reference clone for comparing yield and cup quality against other named tea selections. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Twenty Ounce Apple (Massive American Heirloom Cooking Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Twenty Ounce is a 19th-century American heirloom named quite literally for its enormous fruit size, with individual apples commonly reaching well over a pound, making it one of the largest apples in common cultivation and a genuine novelty at the dinner table. The green-yellow skin, heavily striped and blushed with red, covers coarse, tart, juicy flesh best suited to cooking, baking, and sauce rather than fresh eating out of hand, since the sharp acidity and large size make it primarily a kitchen apple. A single Twenty Ounce apple can fill a whole pie shell on its own, a practical advantage that kept it popular in home orchards for generations of American cooking. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, since branches can be genuinely strained by fruit of this size. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Twickel Purple Lavender (Dutch Heirloom English Lavender)
description: Plant in full sun with sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil; amend heavy or clay soil with coarse sand or gravel, and avoid overhead watering or mulch touching the crown. Twickel Purple is a long-cultivated Dutch heirloom English lavender, named for the historic Twickel estate in the Netherlands, valued for its compact, tidy, rounded habit and deep violet-purple flower spikes with the classic sweet, floral fragrance and flavor of true English lavender, prized for culinary use, sachets, and potpourri. Because true English lavenders are more prone to root and crown rot in hot, humid conditions than lavandin hybrids, plant Twickel Purple in the driest, sunniest, best-draining spot available and consider it a shorter-lived perennial in the Gulf South compared with more heat-tolerant lavandins like Phenomenal or Grosso. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain shape and prevent the plant from becoming woody and open in the center. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Twilight Blackberry (Semi-Erect Thornless USDA Release)
description: Twilight is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program in cooperation with Oregon State University, selected from a cross of the thornless 'Ouachita' with a thornless USDA breeding selection. It ripens relatively early for a semi-erect type and is valued for large, very firm berries with tough skin and a distinctively crisp texture that holds up well to shipping. Canes are vigorous and largely self-supporting, though a simple trellis keeps heavily laden fruiting laterals off the ground and makes harvest easier. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest each year and tie in the current season's primocanes, which will carry next year's crop. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Twister Cauliflower
description: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings for a spring or fall crop, keeping plants evenly watered and never letting them check from stress. This self-blanching variety has well-wrapping leaves that curl over the developing curd, shielding the snowy-white heads from sun scald and rain discoloration. It reliably produces uniform, dense, medium-large heads and tolerates heat, so in mild climates it can even be grown nearly year-round. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Two Star Lettuce (Slow-Bolt Dark Green Leaf Lettuce)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Two Star is a dark green, savoyed leaf lettuce bred as a slower-bolting improvement on the classic Waldmann's Green type, holding its mild, sweet flavor and tender texture longer into warm weather before turning bitter and running to seed. The loose, upright rosette of ruffled leaves is well suited to cut-and-come-again harvesting, letting a single planting supply salads over several weeks. Provide afternoon shade during hot spells to further slow bolting, and keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress speeds up flowering in any leaf lettuce. Sow successively every 2-3 weeks through the cool season for a steady, continuous harvest. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Tycoon Tomato
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Tycoon is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces concentrated harvests of large, smooth, firm red globe tomatoes averaging 10–12 ounces. Its compact determinate habit keeps the plant manageable in the garden while still delivering excellent yields suited to canning, slicing, and fresh eating. Bred for Southern growing conditions, Tycoon sets fruit reliably when temperatures climb into the upper 80s and maintains production longer than many other large-fruited varieties. Strong disease resistance package including resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), and root-knot nematodes makes it especially valuable in zone 9 soils where these pathogens are widespread. Matures in 68–76 days from transplant.

name: Tyee Spinach (AAS-Winning Semi-Savoy Disease-Resistant Spinach)
description: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing as seedlings develop and use thinnings in salads. Tyee is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning spinach that has maintained its status as one of the most recommended disease-resistant spinach varieties for over 35 years — a semi-savoy (slightly crinkled leaf) hybrid that combines excellent productivity with broad disease resistance. The 'semi-savoy' designation means the leaves have moderate crinkle — more texture and surface area than flat leaf types but less crinkle than fully savoy varieties, striking a balance between the ornamental quality of savoy and the easy washing of flat types. Tyee's most important attributes are its comprehensive disease resistance: it carries resistance to five races of downy mildew (Peronospora farinosa), the primary fungal disease that terminates spinach crops early in humid and wet conditions. This resistance profile extends the productive season dramatically compared to susceptible varieties that collapse when mildew strikes. The dark green, upright, medium-large leaves are tender and mild-flavored with the classic, clean spinach taste. Tyee remains the benchmark spinach variety against which others are evaluated in university trials, consistently placing at or near the top for yield, disease resistance, and leaf quality. Matures in 42–50 days from seed.

name: Tygress Tomato (TSWV-Resistant Beefsteak Hybrid)
description: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Tygress is a beefsteak-type hybrid tomato and All-America Selections vegetable winner bred with strong resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV), a thrips-vectored disease that can devastate warm-climate tomato plantings with little warning. Fruits are large, meaty, and red with the classic beefsteak texture prized for slicing and sandwiches, produced on vigorous indeterminate vines that need sturdy staking or caging. Because TSWV pressure is worst where thrips populations build up in hot weather, Tygress is a particularly useful choice for Gulf South gardens that have struggled with sudden wilting and bronzed, ring-spotted fruit in past seasons. Keep watering even to avoid cracking and blossom end rot, and scout for thrips on new growth even though the plant tolerates the virus they carry. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Typica Coffee
description: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Considered the original Arabica coffee variety from which nearly all other Arabica cultivars ultimately descend, having spread from Yemen through European colonial cultivation to become the ancestral genetic base of the world's coffee industry, it is still valued today for its classically sweet, clean, well-balanced cup quality despite its taller, more open growth habit and lower yield and disease resistance compared to modern hybrids. Its lanky, open branching habit and susceptibility to coffee leaf rust and other diseases have led most commercial growers to switch to higher-yielding, more disease-resistant hybrid varieties, but heirloom Typica plantings remain prized by specialty coffee producers for their traditional flavor profile. Provide the same dappled shade, consistent moisture, and good drainage other Arabica coffees need, and expect the first harvest after three to four years of growth. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Tyson Pear (Honeyed Colonial-Era American Pear)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Discovered as a chance seedling on Jacob Tyson's Pennsylvania farm in 1794, Tyson bears small to medium yellow pears with a distinctive honeyed sweetness and fine, melting texture that made it a favored dessert pear among American orchardists for generations, even though its modest size kept it from ever becoming a major commercial variety. The tree is notably vigorous, productive, and disease-resistant compared to many European pears of its era, qualities that helped it persist in old homestead orchards long after flashier varieties fell out of favor. Harvest while still firm in late summer and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Uber Arugula
description: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly (about 1/8 inch deep) into cool, moist soil for quick, even germination. Uber produces fast-growing, deeply lobed leaves that give it the refined look of wild arugula while keeping the speed and uniformity of a standard salad-type strain, with a mild, nutty, peppery flavor. It performs especially well as a winter crop in high tunnels or cool greenhouses and tolerates cold better than many salad arugulas. Cut leaves about an inch above the soil line for quick regrowth, and cover new plantings with floating row cover to keep flea beetles off young seedlings. Matures in 21–35 days from seed.

name: UC 157 Asparagus (Classic California Commercial Hybrid Asparagus)
description: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. UC 157 is a long-standing, widely planted hybrid asparagus developed by the University of California, prized for producing spears in a more concentrated, uniform flush than many older varieties, along with good heat tolerance that suits warmer growing regions better than some Northeastern-bred cultivars. It has been a mainstay of commercial asparagus production for decades and performs well in home gardens too, given deep, well-drained soil and full sun. As with other asparagus, avoid harvesting the first year and harvest lightly the second year to let the crown establish a strong root system for many years of future spring harvests. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Udo (Japanese Spikenard)
description: Plant in moist, rich, humus-heavy soil in part to full shade; udo is a large, bold Japanese perennial vegetable native to shaded mountain valleys and forests of Japan, Korea, and China — one of the few perennial vegetables that genuinely thrives in deep shade and also functions as a dramatic ornamental. The emerging spring shoots — harvested when 6–12 inches tall by covering the crown to force blanched growth — are prepared in Japanese cuisine as a crisp, pleasantly bitter vegetable resembling white asparagus in texture, eaten raw in salads, pickled, or lightly cooked. When not harvested for food, the plant develops into an enormous, deeply tropical-looking perennial 6–10 feet tall with compound leaves nearly 3 feet across and clusters of small cream flowers in summer, followed by small black berries. The dramatic architectural scale makes it a remarkable ornamental for shaded woodland gardens. An ancient Japanese vegetable with no close Western analog, combining edible usefulness with the visual impact of a large tropical foliage plant in deep shade. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Udumalapet Eggplant
description: Sow indoors and transplant into full sun once the weather is reliably warm, giving plants sturdy stakes since the fruit can grow quite large and heavy. Regular, deep watering helps produce tender, sweet flesh. Udumalapet takes its name from a town in Tamil Nadu, India, and is grown for its large, rounded fruit with pale green skin marked by faint white striping. Home cooks favor it for curries and roasting because of its mild flavor and relatively few seeds. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: UF-613 Cacao
description: Selected in Costa Rica among the early twentieth-century United Fruit Company cacao trials, UF-613 became one of the most widely planted clones in Central America thanks to its large pods, good bean size, dependable disease tolerance, and strong yields. Recent genetic studies have found that it carries an unusually distinct ancestry compared to other Upper Amazon Forastero selections, suggesting it preserves lineage not well represented in most other commercial cacao. Cultivate it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, providing the warm, humid, frost-free conditions cacao needs throughout the year. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFBeauty Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first year to establish good light penetration and easy harvest access. UFBeauty is a University of Florida release from the same low-chill peach breeding program that produced Flordaking and TropicBeauty, bred specifically to bloom and fruit reliably where standard peach varieties fail to accumulate enough winter chill, ripening medium-large, attractive red-blushed yellow freestone fruit of good quality in late spring. Its very low chill requirement makes it one of the most dependable peach choices for the warmest parts of zone 9, where many older peach cultivars bloom too early, too late, or too erratically to set a reliable crop. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart when marble-sized to improve size and quality, and provide full sun and sharp drainage, since peach roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet soil. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFBest Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting trees away from low frost pockets since bloom can begin in December during mild winters. UFBest is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill peach releases, developed to give growers south of the traditional Gulf Coast peach belt a dependable home-orchard option despite winters too warm for standard varieties. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good sugar and a bright red blush, ripening in mid-to-late April. Because such a low chill requirement makes bloom erratic and extended in unusually warm years, watch closely through late winter and be ready to cover young trees if a hard freeze threatens; otherwise care follows standard peach practice — thin fruit to about 6 inches apart and prune annually to an open, low vase shape to keep the tree productive and easy to harvest. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFGem Peach (Low-Chill Yellow Clingstone Florida Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFGem, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville alongside UFGlo and other low-chill selections, requires only a small number of chill hours, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after a mild Gulf Coast or Florida winter. It bears firm, yellow, non-melting clingstone flesh with good sweetness and mild acidity, ripening in early May and holding up well for fresh eating or short-distance transport. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life and smaller fruit size than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program for brown rot and bacterial spot, both of which are aggressive in humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: UFGlo Peach (Low-Chill White Non-Melting-Flesh Florida Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; because UFGlo needs so few chill hours, it is one of the few peach cultivars reliable in the immediate Gulf Coast and Florida climate where winters may not deliver enough cold for standard peach varieties to bloom and fruit properly. Bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville, UFGlo requires fewer than 150 chill hours below 45°F, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after mild subtropical winters, then ripens by early May, well ahead of most Southern-adapted peaches. The white flesh is firm and non-melting, holding its texture well for fresh eating, canning, or short transport, with a mild, sweet flavor. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a shorter productive lifespan and somewhat smaller fruit than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program, since brown rot and bacterial spot pressure is high in humid Gulf Coast summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: UFGold Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Non-Melting-Flesh Peach)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first couple of years to keep light reaching the interior wood. UFGold is a low-chill University of Florida release with firm, non-melting yellow flesh, a texture that holds up well for canning and preserving in addition to fresh eating, unlike the soft melting flesh of most low-chill dessert peaches. Its roughly 200-hour chill requirement lets it set a reliable crop through the mild winters typical of the Gulf Coast, where bloom on high-chill peach varieties is often erratic. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size, and watch for a hard late freeze during an unusually warm bloom period, since low-chill peaches can flower earlier than the local last-frost date in some years. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFOne Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; UFOne is part of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill peach breeding program, developed to extend peach growing well south of where the fruit was traditionally thought possible, into areas that see only 100-150 hours of winter chill each year — far too little for standard or even most other Gulf South low-chill varieties. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good flavor for such an early-ripening, low-chill selection, typically ready in early spring. Because it flowers so early, a late cold snap can occasionally damage blooms even in mild climates, so a somewhat sheltered planting site helps protect the crop. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart once set, and prune to an open-center vase shape after harvest to maintain airflow and light penetration through the humid growing season. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFQueen Nectarine (Ultra-Low-Chill Nectarine)
description: UFQueen is a University of Florida-bred nectarine selected from among about eighty seedlings for its very low chilling requirement of roughly 250 hours, making it one of the earliest and most reliably fruitful nectarines for mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit ripens quite early in the season and has firm, non-melting yellow flesh under red-blushed skin, giving good handling and shelf life compared to soft melting-flesh types. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and be prepared for the smooth skin to need extra attention to thinning and pest management, since nectarines are more susceptible to fruit-boring insects than fuzzy-skinned peaches in humid climates. Prune annually to an open center to maintain good light penetration and airflow. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFRoyal Nectarine (Vivid Red-Skinned Very Low-Chill Nectarine)
description: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFRoyal, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville for the subtropical Deep South, needs only about 250 chill hours to break dormancy reliably, making it well suited to zone 8b-10 winters too mild for most standard nectarines. Its skin colors an especially striking, nearly solid deep red over firm, non-melting yellow flesh, giving it strong fresh-market eye appeal, and the fruit ripens quickly, roughly 85 days from bloom, in early May. As with other nectarines, it is more susceptible to brown rot than fuzzy-skinned peaches in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through fruit development and ripening. Expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life than higher-chill Northern cultivars, typical of very-low-chill stone fruit breeding. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: UFSharp Peach (Firm Non-Melting-Flesh Low-Chill Clingstone Peach)
description: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2006 with an estimated 325 chill unit requirement, UFSharp suits zone 8-9 gardens wanting a mid-to-late-season low-chill peach. Unusual among low-chill types, its flesh is firm and non-melting rather than melting, holding up well to handling, with 50-70 percent red blush over yellow-orange skin. Trees are vigorous, self-fertile, semi-spreading, and productive, ripening in late May in north-central Florida trials. The firmer texture makes it a useful option for growers who want a low-chill peach suited to fresh market handling or preserving. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: UFSun Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, choosing a site without a low-lying frost pocket since bloom can begin as early as December in warm winters. UFSun is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill releases, bred to extend backyard and commercial peach production into areas of central and south Florida too warm for even the Texas 'Gulf' series. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with a mild, sweet flavor and an attractive red blush, ripening in April, well ahead of most other peach varieties. Because bloom happens so early, protect trees from a late hard freeze with row cover if a cold snap threatens, and thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size. Prune annually to an open-center vase shape after harvest to keep the canopy low and to renew the one-year-old wood that peaches fruit on. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ugli Fruit (Jamaican Tangelo)
description: Ugli fruit is a naturally occurring Jamaican tangelo, a chance hybrid between grapefruit and mandarin parentage found growing wild in a Jamaican dooryard planting in the early twentieth century and later marketed commercially under the trademark UGLI. The rough, loose, puffy, greenish-yellow rind that gives the fruit its name belies a remarkably sweet, low-acid, juicy interior with the easy-peeling, segmented character of a mandarin rather than the tighter rind of a true grapefruit. Fruit typically ripens in winter and holds reasonably well on the tree, sweetening further the longer it hangs. Grow it much like other tangelos, with a warm, sheltered, frost-free site, since it shares the cold sensitivity typical of grapefruit-mandarin hybrids. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ugni Blanc Grape (Trebbiano, Cognac and Armagnac Distilling Grape)
description: Ugni Blanc, known in Italy as Trebbiano Toscano and historically as Saint-Emilion in the Cognac region, is among the most widely planted white grapes on earth, prized less for varietal wine than for producing the thin, high-acid, neutral-flavored base wine that is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac brandy. Its naturally high acidity, low sugar accumulation, and productivity are exactly the traits distillers want, since a lean, acidic base wine distills cleanly and ages well in oak, while the same neutral character makes it a workhorse blending and everyday table wine grape across Italy and southern France. The vine buds and ripens late in the season, which helps it dodge spring frost but means it needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature its large, productive clusters. It shows good resistance to many fungal diseases relative to thinner-skinned fine wine grapes, though bunch rot can still develop in wet years with dense canopies. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the vigorous canopy for good air movement, and harvest based on acid retention rather than sugar level if the goal is a base wine for distillation. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Ujukitsu (Japanese Semi-Sour Citrus)
description: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season. Ujukitsu bears large, pale orange-yellow fruit with a loose, easy-peeling rind and a mild, semi-sour flavor milder than a true orange but more assertive than a sweet mandarin, ripening in mid-to-late winter. It is grown chiefly in specialty and heirloom citrus collections rather than commercial production, and performs best in the warmer parts of zone 9 and in zones 10-11 where hard freezes are rare. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ulam Raja (King's Salad, Cosmos Herb, Wild Cosmos, Purple Cosmos Herb)
description: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Ulam Raja is a fast-growing, easy-care tropical annual that germinates rapidly and begins producing harvestable young leaves and shoot tips within 6–8 weeks of seeding. Cosmos caudatus is a tropical annual herb native to Mexico and Central America in the Asteraceae family that has become widely naturalized and deeply embedded in the food cultures of Southeast Asia — particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines — where it is consumed daily as an 'ulam,' the term for raw herbs and vegetables eaten fresh alongside cooked rice meals. The young leaves, tender shoots, and flower buds are eaten raw in salads, combined with other 'ulam' herbs, or used as a garnish and vegetable in cooking — the flavor is pleasantly sour, slightly bitter, and distinctly herbal, reminiscent of a more complex watercress. Research by Malaysian institutions has documented exceptionally high levels of antioxidants, phenolic compounds, and nutrients in the young foliage, and traditional Malay medicine credits the plant with anti-aging properties that are reflected in its honorific common name 'Ulam Raja' — 'the king's herb/salad.' The plant also produces the characteristic fine-petaled pink to magenta flowers of the Cosmos genus throughout the warm months. Self-seeds abundantly and naturalizes in zone 9-11 gardens as a continuously productive edible green. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Ulluco (Papa Lisa, Melloco, Olluco)
description: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in loose, moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; ulluco is a creeping, succulent-stemmed Andean tuber crop in the family Basellaceae, domesticated in the Andes over 5,000 years ago and second only to potato in importance across Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia where it is called 'papa lisa' (smooth potato). The tubers are waxy, colorful (yellow, orange, pink, red, purple), and retain their shape when cooked, making them excellent for stews such as the Bolivian dish 'soltero de ulluco'. Unlike potato, ulluco has never suffered a catastrophic blight and is rich in protein, calcium, and carotenoids. Harvest after first light frost kills back the vines; plants are almost entirely propagated vegetatively as fertile seed is rare. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Uluru Ochre Tomato (Orange-Green Ruffled Dwarf Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Uluru Ochre bears ruffled, oblate fruit with orange flesh tinged in green, giving each tomato an amber, earthy appearance that inspired its name after the Australian landmark; the flavor is rich and complex when the plant is at its best. It began as a cross between an orange heirloom and Rosella Purple made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized by a team of Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers, and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Umami Asian Blend Microgreens
description: Sow the seed densely across a shallow tray of moist growing mix and keep it evenly moist under bright light. This Asian blend of savory and spicy brassica-type greens is harvested very young, when the first true leaves appear, roughly one to three weeks after sowing. Snip the tender shoots at soil level with scissors and use the complex, umami-rich mix as a garnish for Asian dishes; sow in succession for a steady supply indoors year-round. Matures in 10–21 days from seed.

name: Umpqua Broccoli (Oregon Open-Pollinated High-Yield Broccoli)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 14-20 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart. Umpqua is an open-pollinated variety developed at Territorial Seed Company in Oregon and named for the Umpqua River; it is prized for producing large, uniform, dark-green 5-8 inch heads with big beads that size up quickly, then continuing to yield heavily from side shoots over an unusually long harvest window. Because it is open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, home gardeners can save true-to-type seed from year to year, making it a good choice for growers who want to build a self-sufficient seed-saving rotation into their fall brassica planting. Its long production season rewards steady feeding and consistent moisture, since plants left to dry out or run short on nitrogen will cut the side-shoot harvest short. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Umran Indian Jujube (Large-Fruited Ber for South Texas and the Gulf Coast)
description: Umran is one of the most widely grown named selections of Indian jujube (ber), prized in its native South Asia for producing unusually large, round to oval fruit that ripens from green to a mottled yellow-brown and is eaten fresh while still crisp and apple-like, well before it wrinkles into a date-like dried stage. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil, since Umran resents wet feet and performs best with infrequent, deep watering once established. The tree bears young and heavily, often within two to three years of planting, and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils far better than most temperate fruit trees, making it a productive dual-season option for the hottest, driest microclimates of zone 9-10 Gulf Coast gardens. Thin overcrowded fruit clusters in years of heavy set to improve individual fruit size, and protect young trees from any frost since Umran has little cold tolerance compared to Chinese jujube (Ziziphus jujuba). Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Uncle Tom Pawpaw (Historic First Named Pawpaw Cultivar)
description: Uncle Tom is historically significant as, by most accounts, the first pawpaw selection ever given a cultivar name, predating the organized breeding programs of the 20th century by decades. It was named and propagated by 19th-century Indiana pawpaw and persimmon enthusiast James A. Little of Cartersburg, Indiana, who also established what is considered the first dedicated pawpaw orchard on record. In Little's own descriptions the tree was an extremely heavy bearer, at times fruiting so abundantly that limbs broke under the load, producing large fruit of delicious flavor that ripened around the middle of September and held in good condition on the tree for about a month. Because it predates modern cultivar trials and disease screening, treat Uncle Tom as a living piece of pawpaw breeding history — a genetically distinct, heavy-cropping heirloom worth growing for its story and productivity — and pair it with a proven modern cultivar for the most reliable eating-quality fruit alongside it. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Underway Mahonia (Robust Early-Blooming Winter Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Underway, a hybrid of Mahonia japonica and M. lomariifolia raised at the historic Slieve Donard Nursery in Northern Ireland, is one of the largest and most vigorous of the x media selections, bearing bright yellow, fragrant flower spikes in late autumn — earlier than most other mahonias — above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by powdery blue-black berries. Its outsized eventual scale makes it best suited to a spacious shaded border or woodland-edge planting rather than a tight foundation bed. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Unique Feijoa
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Unique is a self-fertile New Zealand feijoa cultivar that reliably sets a good crop as a single plant, making it the best choice for gardeners with room for only one bush. Fruits are medium-large, pear-shaped, and smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic, low-seed flesh and a good balance of pineapple-guava flavor, ripening across a fairly long mid-to-late season window rather than all at once. Because it does not depend on a pollinator partner, Unique is a popular choice for small urban gardens, patios, and hedgerows where only one feijoa can be fit in, though a second cultivar nearby will still increase yield and fruit size. The compact, dense, evergreen habit takes well to hedging or espalier, and the edible spring flowers are a bonus harvest in their own right. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Unryu Contorted Mulberry (Twisted-Branch Ornamental Mulberry)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Unryu, meaning 'dragon's claw' in Japanese, is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown chiefly for its strikingly twisted, corkscrew-contorted branches, a dramatic sculptural feature that is most visible and prized in winter after leaf drop, and which also makes the cut branches valued by florists and flower arrangers. It produces small, sweet, mild-flavored white-to-pinkish mulberries in season, a secondary bonus to its main ornamental appeal. Because the twisted branch character can be lost in overly vigorous growth, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, and prune minimally, removing only dead or crossing wood, to preserve the natural contorted form. Like other mulberries, ripe fruit drops and stains, so site it away from paved areas. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Upland Cotton
description: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has thoroughly warmed; upland cotton is the classic Southern row crop, grown by home gardeners today mostly as a novelty, dried-arrangement, or heirloom fiber crop rather than for commercial-scale harvest. Showy, pale yellow to cream flowers resembling a hibiscus bloom (a close botanical relative) open over midsummer and fade to pink before dropping, revealing a green boll that swells over several weeks and eventually splits open to expose the fluffy white — or, in naturally colored heirloom varieties, tan, green, or brown — lint prized by spinners and fiber crafters. Because it needs a long, hot, frost-free season to fully open its bolls, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed as early as safely possible after last frost and choose an early-maturing variety. Watch for cotton's classic pest pressures, including boll weevil and aphids, and rotate planting location yearly to reduce soil-borne disease buildup. Matures in 150–180 days from seed.

name: Upland Cress
description: Sow seed densely in a tray for microgreens or thinly outdoors in cool soil to grow as a peppery leafy green. Also called creasy greens, upland cress is high in vitamins A and C and delivers a sharp, watercress-like bite without needing running water. Keep it consistently moist, since dryness makes it more pungent and prone to bolting; harvest microgreens at the true-leaf stage or pick mature outer leaves for sandwiches and salads. Matures in 10–21 days from seed.

name: Upland Cress (Early Yellowrocket)
description: Direct sow in late summer or fall for winter harvest in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; upland cress (early yellowrocket) is a European biennial grown as a cool-season salad green, long cultivated in British kitchen gardens as a dry-land substitute for watercress in gardens without access to streams. The dark green, round-lobed leaves are similar to watercress in appearance and have a pleasant, mild peppery flavor when young and harvested before flowering — less bitter and more refined than winter cress (B. vulgaris). Produces pickable leaves very quickly in cool weather, from fall through early spring. Allowed to bolt, the spring flower buds can be harvested like tender broccoli. An old and underappreciated cool-season salad green that thrives when other salad crops fail in cold weather. Well-suited to fall and winter salad gardening in zones 5–9 where it overwinters reliably. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: Ure Pear (Extreme-Cold-Hardy Prairie Pear)
description: Ure was bred in Manitoba at Canada's Morden Research Station from Ussurian pear parentage crossed with a European pear, combining the species' extreme cold hardiness with noticeably better fruit size and quality than straight Pyrus ussuriensis selections. Trees survive winter temperatures well below -40 degrees F and set reliable crops even in the short growing seasons of the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, where standard European pear cultivars cannot be grown at all. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit has a mild, sweet flavor acceptable for fresh eating when fully ripe, though most growers favor it for canning, sauce, and preserves like other ultra-hardy prairie pears. Plant with a second Ussurian-derived pear such as 'Rescue' for best pollination, and expect a vigorous, disease-resistant tree that needs little spraying even in humid climates. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Urfa Biber Pepper (Turkish Sun-Dried Smoky Raisin Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, then let fruit ripen fully to deep red before harvesting for drying. Urfa Biber takes its name from the city of Sanliurfa in southeastern Turkey, where the pepper is traditionally processed by day-drying the ripe fruit in the sun and wrapping or covering it at night so it sweats and partially reabsorbs moisture, a cycle repeated over several days that develops its signature near-black color, raisin-like sweetness, and mild, smoky, wine-like heat around 30,000-50,000 Scoville units. The moist, oily flakes it produces are a staple spice in Turkish and increasingly in Western kitchens, used to finish roasted vegetables, meats, and eggs where a coarser, sweeter, less sharply hot flavor than crushed red pepper is wanted. A single well-grown plant can produce enough fruit for a good supply of home-dried flakes, and the peppers can also be strung and air-dried in a covered, well-ventilated spot if a controlled sweating setup isn't practical. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: US Early Pride Navel Orange
description: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; US Early Pride is a modern navel orange selection bred for an early ripening window, often ready for harvest well ahead of standard Washington navels, and produces sweet, low-seed, easy-to-peel fruit with the classic navel form. Water deeply but allow the soil surface to dry between waterings, and mulch to protect the shallow root zone from summer heat. Give young trees frost protection through their first winters, and expect a light first crop within a few years of planting a grafted tree, building to full production as the tree matures. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: US-119 (USDA Cold-Hardy Sweet-Orange-Flavored Citrus Hybrid)
aliases: Citrus paradisi x Poncirus trifoliata x Citrus sinensis 'US-119'
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a protected spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter buffering in zone 8-9 gardens. US-119 was developed by USDA breeders from a cross of citrumelo and sweet orange, giving it roughly one-quarter trifoliate orange parentage and correspondingly greater cold tolerance than a true sweet orange, while retaining a genuinely sweet, orange-like flavor rather than the sharp bitterness typical of many trifoliate hybrids. Fruit has a smooth, attractive orange peel, relatively few seeds, and juicy flesh with just a hint of the trifoliate parent's distinctive aftertaste. Because of its unusual hardiness for citrus with real dessert-orange flavor, it has become popular among cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing sweet citrus north of the traditional growing range; protect young trees through their first few winters, since mature specimens are considerably tougher. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: US-852 Citrandarin (Cold-Hardy Changsha Mandarin-Trifoliate Hybrid)
description: US-852 was bred in 1965 by USDA researcher Joe Furr at the Indio, California field station, crossing Changsha mandarin with a large-flowered trifoliate orange selection to combine mandarin flavor with trifoliate orange's exceptional cold hardiness. Among the citrandarin group of USDA cold-hardy citrus hybrids, US-852 is regarded as one of the better-flavored for fresh eating, with a sweeter, less bitter profile than many trifoliate crosses, though fruit remains seedy and more tart than a standard mandarin. The tree shows the trifoliate parent's light thorns and part-deciduous winter habit and tolerates temperatures near 0 degrees F once wood is fully dormant and hardened off, well beyond what any true mandarin survives. Give it full sun and good drainage, and protect young trees through their first winters before relying on their cold tolerance in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: US-897 Citrandarin (Semi-Dwarfing Cold-Hardy HLB-Tolerant Rootstock Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and protect young trees during their first winter or two while cold hardiness develops. US-897, released by the USDA-ARS citrus breeding program in 2007 from a cross of Cleopatra mandarin and trifoliate orange, was developed primarily as a semi-dwarfing rootstock but has also drawn interest for direct planting because of its combination of good cold hardiness, inherited from its trifoliate parent, and documented tolerance to huanglongbing (citrus greening), the disease that has devastated citrus production across Florida and the Gulf South. Fruit is tart and seedy, more useful for juice or marmalade than fresh eating, similar to other citrandarin hybrids. As with other trifoliate-derived hybrids, expect a semi-deciduous habit and light thorns in colder winters. Established trees tolerate significantly colder temperatures than standard mandarin or sweet orange. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ussurian Pear (Harbin Pear)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear tolerates temperatures to -40°F and is the hardiest pear species available, making it the only viable pear for zones 2–3 where European pears cannot survive. Pyrus ussuriensis is a large, ornamental, extremely cold-hardy pear species from northeastern China and Siberia; it bears masses of white flowers in early spring before the leaves, followed in fall by small (1–2 inch), round, green to yellow-green, gritty-fleshed fruits with a rough texture that are best cooked or used for preserves rather than fresh eating. Its primary agricultural value is as a rootstock for grafted pear varieties and as a breeding parent for cold-hardy pear cultivars (e.g., 'Ure', 'Rescue', 'David', 'Nova') developed by Canadian and university breeders for the northern Great Plains. The glossy, dark-green leaves turn brilliant red in fall, making it an outstanding ornamental even where fruit quality is secondary. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Utah Celery
description: Start indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Utah 52-70 is the standard commercial and home garden celery in North America — an improved Utah-type celery producing tall, upright stalks of thick, crisp, rounded (not hollow) pale-green to cream-colored ribs with a classic, full celery flavor. The '52-70' designation refers to the original development period. Utah-type celery has largely replaced older Pascal types in commercial production because of superior rib thickness, crunchiness, and reduced stringiness compared to older varieties. Celery is among the most demanding vegetables in terms of water and fertility requirements; it grows naturally in moist, fertile wetland soils and demands consistent irrigation and rich soil throughout its long growing period. Blanch by earthing up or wrapping paper around the stalks 2 weeks before harvest to lighten the color and reduce bitterness. In zone 9 celery is exclusively a cool-season vegetable, transplanted in fall and harvested through winter. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Utah Celery
description: Start the tiny seed indoors 10 to 12 weeks before transplanting, pressing it into the surface since it needs light to germinate and is slow to sprout. Celery grows best in climates with long, mild-temperature seasons and demands consistently rich, moist soil to develop tender stalks. Harvest individual stalks when they reach about 6 inches, or wait for the full bunch to mature; keep the plants well watered throughout to avoid stringy, bitter stems. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Utah Serviceberry
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun to light shade; Utah serviceberry thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the West and Great Basin where other serviceberries would fail. Amelanchier utahensis is a native shrub of dry foothills, rocky slopes, and canyon walls from the Great Basin west, producing white spring flowers, small (1/3 inch) dark-blue berries with a sweet, mild, blueberry-like flavor in early summer (ripe very early, often by late May-June), and outstanding fall color in shades of orange and red. The berries are an extremely important wildlife food — essentially every frugivorous bird and mammal in the arid West relies on serviceberries during the brief ripening window. Extremely drought- and cold-hardy, this is the recommended serviceberry for xeric and high-altitude western gardens. Use for wildlife plantings, erosion control, and native landscaping. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Utah Sweet Pomegranate (Extra-Sweet Soft-Seeded Pomegranate)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; pomegranate is highly drought-tolerant once established and performs well on minimal irrigation in well-drained Gulf South soils. Utah Sweet is valued for pink-tinged skin and pulp with a notably sweeter, less tart flavor than the widely grown Wonderful pomegranate, along with softer, more tender seeds that make the arils easier to eat fresh without the firmer crunch typical of many other pomegranate cultivars. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will fruit, though yields can improve with cross-pollination from a second cultivar. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then ease back as fruit nears ripeness to help prevent splitting, and harvest when the fruit gives a dull, metallic sound when tapped. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Uthirankotta Black Pepper
description: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing the vine to climb a living or artificial support post. Named for its village of origin in Kerala, India, Uthirankotta is a traditional landrace selection valued by South Indian growers for consistently high yields and better tolerance of common pepper diseases than many older local types, along with good adaptability across the varied soils of the Western Ghats pepper belt. Its medium-length spikes carry a dense set of berries that mature reliably under the humid, filtered-shade conditions of traditional homestead pepper gardens. Keep the root zone evenly moist and mulched, and provide a living standard such as areca palm for the vine to climb. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Uvaia (Ubaía, Uvaia-do-Mato, Brazilian Cherry)
description: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia (Eugenia pyriformis) is a beautiful Brazilian Myrtaceae tree closely related to Surinam cherry and pitanga, producing pear-shaped to round yellow fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a juicy, aromatic, sweet-acidic flesh — the flavor is often described as a complex blend of passion fruit, citrus, and Eugenia aromatics with a pleasant acidity that makes the fruit excellent fresh, as juice, in ice cream, and as jams. The tree has attractive bronze-red new growth and small white flowers. Increasingly popular among Brazilian native fruit enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors in south Florida and Hawaii; one of the finest of the genus Eugenia for flavor. Fruits appear in clusters along the branches and trunk. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Uzbek Garlic (Turban Hardneck)
description: Uzbek is a Turban-group hardneck garlic traced to Uzbekistan and brought into North American seed stock decades ago; Turban types are named for the way their bulb wrappers twist and swirl like fabric wound around the cloves. It is among the earliest garlics to mature, with shiny purple-streaked skins over big, earthy-flavored cloves that carry a surprising spicy kick. Because Turban types generally store more briefly than Porcelain or Silverskin garlic, plan to use Uzbek bulbs within a few months of curing rather than holding them for a full year. Give it the same fall planting, spring scape removal, and full-sun culture as other hardnecks. Matures in 200–230 days from transplant.

name: Valdosta Mulberry (Extra-Large Black-Fruited Deep South Mulberry)
description: Valdosta originated from a tree near Valdosta, Georgia, close enough to the Gulf Coast climate zone to perform reliably in coastal gardens further south and west. It is best known for unusually long fruit, reaching up to two inches, colored deep black-purple with a rich, sweet flavor, borne on a fast-growing, large-leaved tree with a broad, spreading canopy similar in vigor to other big Deep South mulberry selections. Fruit ripens in a concentrated flush in mid-spring rather than trickling in over weeks, so plan for a short, heavy harvest window. Give it full sun, well-drained fertile soil, and room to spread; established trees need only light structural pruning to remove crossing or damaged limbs. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Valeene Beauty American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Precocious Indiana Claypool Selection)
description: Valeene Beauty, also recorded as Claypool I-94, is an Indiana-origin selection from a cross of Mitchellena and Early Golden made by James Claypool. It is notably precocious and a regular heavy producer, bearing large fruit 2.25 to 2.5 inches across that is low in fiber and high in pulp compared to many wild-type persimmons. As with all Diospyros virginiana cultivars, fruit is astringent and unpalatable until it softens fully, after which it becomes rich and sweet. The tree has an upright growth habit and can be pruned to hold it at 15 to 20 feet, tolerating the heat, drought, and variable soils typical of native persimmon once established. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Valencia Orange
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun in the warmest available location; Valencia is the world's most important juice orange and the benchmark orange of Florida's commercial citrus industry. The medium-large, thin-skinned, deep-orange fruits mature in March–June — uniquely late for citrus, which is why Valencia becomes the dominant fresh-market and juice orange in late spring when all other oranges have finished. The juice is abundant, sweet-tart, and intensely flavored. Valencia is known for re-greening: mature ripe fruit turns orange during cool weather, then re-greens as temperatures warm in spring — this does not affect juice quality but can confuse growers expecting a uniformly orange skin. In zone 9, Valencia is one of the most cold-tolerant sweet oranges and often survives temperatures to 25°F with minimal damage; below 20°F the tree may be severely damaged. Feed with citrus fertilizer (including zinc, iron, and manganese) three times per year and maintain a 3–4 inch citrus mulch ring. Excellent fresh or for juice. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Valencia Peanut (Tennessee Red Valencia)
description: Plant shelled, unroasted seeds about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since heavy clay makes it hard for pegs to penetrate and form pods. After yellow flowers fade, the plant sends down slender pegs that bury themselves and swell into pods, so hilling loose soil around the base at flowering time helps maximize pod set. Valencia is distinguished from other peanut types by clusters of three or four seeds per pod covered in a thin, bright reddish skin, and its notably sweet flavor makes it the classic choice for boiled peanuts across the South. Plants grow as an upright bunch rather than sprawling, so they fit well in raised beds and smaller garden rows. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Valencia Pride Mango
description: Bred in Delray Beach, Florida, this cultivar bears very large, elongated fruit with orange-yellow skin blushed red and rich, fiberless, sweet flesh with a relatively small seed. It shows notably better field tolerance to anthracnose than many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Fruit typically ripens early to midsummer; harvest when the shoulders swell and a few fruits begin to color, then allow the rest of the crop to finish ripening at room temperature indoors. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Valencia Tomato (Bright Orange Sweet Low-Acid Open-Pollinated Heirloom)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Valencia is one of the finest and most widely grown orange-fruited heirloom tomatoes — an open-pollinated variety producing medium-large (6–8 oz), round to slightly oblate, smooth, vivid orange fruits with meaty, dense flesh in an orange-gold color and characteristically low acid content combined with fruity sweetness that creates a very clean, mild, sweet flavor quite different from the sharper acid quality of standard red tomatoes. The vivid orange exterior color is striking in the garden and at market — Valencia's clear, bright-orange skin lacks the russet or reddish tones of some orange varieties and produces a consistent, pure-orange appearance across the crop. The low-acid quality makes Valencia particularly appealing to people sensitive to tomato acidity, and the sweet, fruity flavor is excellent in fresh eating, mixed tomato salads (where the orange color provides contrast to red and yellow types), and in light cooking where the low-acid character is preserved. As an open-pollinated heirloom, Valencia produces reliable seed that comes true to type, allowing gardeners to maintain a permanent seed supply. Valencia is an indeterminate variety requiring staking and producing consistently through the season rather than in a single concentrated flush. In zone 9, Valencia performs best in spring (February–May) before summer heat reduces fruit quality. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Valentine Bush Cherry (Cold-Hardy Romance Series Dwarf Cherry)
description: Valentine is one of the University of Saskatchewan's Romance series dwarf sour cherries, bred from crosses of Mongolian cherry and sour cherry to withstand prairie winters far colder than most tree cherries tolerate. The compact, multi-stemmed bush produces good yields of large, dark red, sweet-tart fruit good for fresh eating, juice, and baking. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil; it tolerates poor soils and drought once established but fruits best with consistent moisture during ripening. Prune out older, less productive stems every few years to renew the bush and keep it fruiting heavily. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Valentine Rhubarb (Deep Red Sweet-Tart Heirloom)
description: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun. Valentine is a widely grown American rhubarb variety valued for producing thick, deep-red stalks with good color even in the first year or two after planting, when many other rhubarb varieties are still mostly green, and for a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in pies, sauces, and preserves. It is a heavy, dependable producer of large stalks on vigorous plants, and the color intensifies further with consistent cold winters and full sun exposure. Harvest by pulling individual outer stalks with a firm twist rather than cutting, leave at least a third of the stalks on the plant at all times to keep it vigorous, and always discard the leaves, which contain oxalic acid and are not safe to eat. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Valentine Tomato (AAS-Winning Sweet Red Grape Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vigorous vine well before it needs support. Valentine is an AAS National Winner producing deep red, oblong grape tomatoes with an exceptionally sweet, well-balanced flavor and a notably early, heavy first flush of fruit compared to most grape tomatoes, extending the harvest window at both ends of the season. The disease-resistant vine is highly productive over a long season and holds up well to the heat and humidity of a full Gulf South summer. Harvest fruit as it fully colors for the best sweetness, and pick regularly to keep new clusters setting; the crack-resistant skin makes fruit more forgiving of uneven watering than many cherry and grape types. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Valerian
description: Use the freshest seed available, as viability declines within a year; surface-sow and keep cool and moist for best germination. Plants grow very tall in their second year and may need staking in windy locations; keep soil consistently moist and add compost annually. Remove flower heads in the first year to direct energy into root development. Harvest roots in the second autumn after the tops die back, washing and slicing them for drying; the characteristic musky odor intensifies as the root dries. Matures in 150–180 days from transplant.

name: Valery Banana
description: Valery is a taller Cavendish subgroup clone long grown commercially across Central America and Colombia for its heavy bunches of sweet, thin-skinned dessert fruit. Its height makes it more prone to wind toppling than dwarf Cavendish types, so a sheltered planting site and firm staking of the fruiting stalk matter in exposed Gulf Coast yards. Feed generously and water deeply through the growing season, since Valery's large leaf canopy transpires heavily in summer heat. Because it carries no more cold tolerance than other Cavendish clones, treat it as a container or greenhouse-protected specialty planting in zone 9a rather than a permanent in-ground banana. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Valley Girl Tomato (Heat-Set Disease-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous semi-determinate vines; Valley Girl combines resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt with an unusually reliable ability to set fruit under heat stress, when high nighttime temperatures cause many tomato varieties to drop their blossoms without setting fruit. It produces medium-sized (6-8 oz), round, deep red fruit with well-balanced, classic tomato flavor over a long harvest season. Because it keeps fruiting through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer that stalls many other varieties, Valley Girl helps bridge the gap between the spring and fall tomato crops. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep the vines picked regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 65–75 days from transplant.

name: Valor Plum (Productive Blue-Skinned Canadian Prune Plum)
description: Valor is a Canadian-bred European prune plum known for heavy, reliable production and large, blue-black fruit with sweet amber flesh. It ripens later than Stanley, giving a late-summer harvest for jam, baking, or fresh eating out of hand. The tree is self-fertile but benefits from a second European plum for a fuller set, and its vigorous growth means it needs annual pruning to keep the canopy open. Thin the fruit if it sets a heavy crop, since Valor is prone to overbearing, which can reduce fruit size in a given year. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Valvin Muscat Grape (Cornell-Bred Aromatic White Wine Grape)
description: Released by Cornell University's grape breeding program, Valvin Muscat brings the intensely floral, musky-sweet character of muscat grapes into a cold-hardy hybrid capable of surviving harsh northeastern and Midwestern winters. It produces medium clusters of golden berries used for aromatic dessert and dry white wines, as well as fresh eating in home gardens. The vine crops reliably and benefits from cluster thinning to concentrate its signature aromatics. It is best trained to a cane-pruned system and shows good tolerance of cold beyond what vinifera muscat types can withstand. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Van Cherry (Canadian Firm Dark Sweet Cherry and Pollinizer)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Van was bred at the Summerland research station in British Columbia, Canada, and remains a widely grown dark sweet cherry valued for firm, glossy, deep red-black fruit with rich flavor and good resistance to cracking, along with a bloom period that overlaps well with many other sweet cherry varieties, making it a dependable pollinizer choice throughout the industry. The tree is vigorous, cold-hardy, and productive, bearing reliably once established, and the firm fruit texture holds up well to handling for both fresh eating and processing. Net trees against birds as fruit begins to color, and harvest once cherries reach full dark color and firmness, since sweet cherries do not continue ripening after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Van Deman Quince (Historic USDA-Named Heirloom Quince)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Van Deman is a historic American quince cultivar named for USDA pomologist Henry E. Van Deman, documented in older state and federal pomology references among the notable named quince selections grown in American orchards in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It produces large, aromatic, golden-yellow fruit with the classic hard, tart flesh that transforms into a fragrant, rosy-pink preserve or paste once cooked with sugar. Like other quince, it is self-fertile, needs no separate pollinator, and begins bearing within a few years of planting on a young tree. Prune to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the primary defense against fire blight, the main disease risk for quince in humid climates. Harvest fruit in fall once it has turned fully golden and developed its strong, characteristic perfume, and store in a cool, dry spot, where quince keeps considerably longer than most tree fruit. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Van Dyke Mango (Compact Florida Dooryard Mango)
description: Van Dyke is a Florida-origin mango cultivar known for its semi-compact growth habit and dependable, consistent annual bearing, qualities that made it a long-standing favorite among South Florida dooryard growers. The small to medium fruit has deep red-orange skin and moderately fibrous, sweet flesh, ripening in mid-summer. Its smaller stature relative to full-size commercial cultivars makes it a reasonable option for gardeners with limited space or for large container culture in zone 9. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness, and protect the tree from any frost. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Vana Tulsi (Wild Holy Basil)
description: Surface-sow or press seeds 1/8 in into warm seed-starting mix; maintain 70–80°F for best germination. Vana tulsi (forest holy basil) is the most clove-like and pungent of the tulsi varieties, with green leaves and a more open, branching habit than Rama tulsi; it is revered in Ayurvedic practice and used widely in adaptogenic herbal teas. Pinch growing tips early to encourage branching, and remove flower spikes as they emerge to extend vegetative leaf production throughout the season. Harvest by cutting stem tips; dry leaves at low temperature to preserve the volatile eugenol-rich essential oils. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Vanessa Grape (Cold-Hardy Canadian Seedless Red Table Grape)
description: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Vanessa was bred in Ontario, Canada, for cold hardiness and reliable production of seedless red table grapes even in shorter, cooler growing seasons than many seedless varieties tolerate. The medium-sized, crisp, firm berries carry a bright, sweet, well-balanced flavor and hold well on the vine without splitting, making them good for fresh eating straight off the vine as well as for juice. The vigorous, productive vine is a solid choice for northern home gardens wanting a genuinely good-tasting seedless grape without relying on less cold-hardy varieties bred for milder climates. Train to a permanent trellis system, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size and flavor. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Vanguard Bell Pepper (Bacterial Spot and Root Rot-Resistant Hybrid)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Vanguard is a bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to multiple races of bacterial leaf spot along with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus and Phytophthora root rot, a combination that has made it a strong performer in university disease-pressure variety trials across the humid Southeast. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant. Because it resists both a major foliar bacterial disease and a major soil-borne root disease, Vanguard tends to hold up better than many varieties through a wet, humid Gulf South growing season. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Vanilla (Common Vanilla)
description: Plant stem cuttings in coarse, well-drained, slightly acidic organic bark mix in heavy shade with a support structure for aerial roots to climb — vanilla is the only edible-fruiting orchid and the world's second most expensive spice (after saffron), native to the tropical forest understory of Mexico and Central America where it climbs into the forest canopy in deep shade. The pale yellow-green flowers open one at a time for only a few hours and in most cultivated gardens must be hand-pollinated (the natural pollinators, stingless bees of the genus Melipona, are restricted to Mexico). Successfully pollinated flowers develop into the familiar vanilla bean pods (technically seed capsules) over 9–10 months. After harvest, the pods undergo a complex curing process (blanching, sweating, drying) to develop the characteristic vanilla flavor from the compound vanillin. An extraordinary container or greenhouse specimen for warm-climate gardeners who want to grow their own vanilla extract. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Vaquero Bean (Black and White Appaloosa-Pattern Dry Bean)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 60F, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart on a bush habit that needs no staking. Vaquero produces striking black-and-white speckled dry seeds reminiscent of an Appaloosa horse's coat, with a light, faintly earthy flavor and a texture often described as potato-like when cooked. Let pods mature and dry fully on the plant before harvesting, then shell and cure the beans in a warm, airy spot for another week or two before storing. This variety cooks into a rich, dark broth and holds its shape well through long, slow simmering, making it a favorite for chilis and pot beans. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Vardaman Sweet Potato (Bush Porto Rico)
description: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Vardaman is a compact, short-vined sweet potato (24–30 inch vines versus 6–10 feet for standard varieties) developed at Mississippi State University specifically for the home garden, where its restrained spread and ornamental purple foliage make it an attractive edible landscape plant. The orange-flesh tubers are typically smaller than commercial varieties but have excellent rich, sweet flavor and moist texture. An outstanding choice for container growing, raised beds, and small garden spaces where standard sweet potatoes would overwhelm their neighbors. Keeps well in storage and is the most popular sweet potato for the home garden in the southeastern United States. Matures in 85–110 days from transplant.

name: Variegata Borage (White-Mottled Borage)
description: Variegata is an RHS-recognized variegated strain of common borage in which the coarse, hairy green leaves carry an irregular white mottling and marbling across the leaf surface, distinct from the bolder cream-splashed blotches of the 'Bill Archer' strain. It otherwise grows and flowers like ordinary borage, producing the same brilliant blue, star-shaped blooms on a bristly annual plant. Direct sow where it is to grow, since the taproot is easily damaged, and remove any all-green seedlings early to keep the planting showy. Harvest the young leaves and flowers for the same mild, cucumber-like flavor prized in the species, and allow a few plants to self-sow if a repeat patch is wanted the following year. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Variegata Cornelian Cherry (White-Margined Variegated Cornus mas)
description: Variegata is a slower-growing, more compact sport of cornelian cherry grown chiefly as a foliage specimen, with leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten shaded corners of the garden through the growing season. Like the species it opens tiny yellow flowers on bare stems in late winter, well ahead of the foliage, and can still set the typical tart red, cherry-like drupes if a compatible pollinator is nearby, though fruiting is generally lighter than on green-leaved cultivars. Because variegated foliage is more prone to scorch, site it out of hot afternoon sun in warmer zones. Otherwise it shares the species' tolerance for a wide range of soils, drought once established, and urban conditions, and its slower, denser habit suits it well to smaller gardens. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Calamondin (Ornamental Variegated-Leaf Calamondin Orange)
description: This sport of the standard calamondin displays leaves irregularly splashed with cream and white, and even the young green fruit shows attractive light striping before ripening to orange. It is grown chiefly as a compact ornamental houseplant or patio specimen, its variegated foliage and abundant small, tart fruit making it a favorite for containers. Care matches the plain calamondin: full sun, rich well-drained soil kept evenly moist, and regular citrus fertilizer through the growing season. Variegated growth is often somewhat slower and less vigorous than the green-leaved form, so avoid overpotting and protect it from hard frost. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Cuban Oregano
description: Grow from cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Variegated Cuban Oregano ('Variegatus') is a cream-and-green variegated selection of Plectranthus amboinicus with the identical strong oregano-thyme aroma and flavor of the plain green type, but with striking ornamental foliage — the irregular cream margins on each thick, succulent leaf give the plant a luminous quality in shaded garden spots that plain Cuban oregano lacks. It is one of the more useful dual-purpose (culinary and ornamental) plants for zone 9 gardens and container plantings. The thick, succulent leaves retain the distinctive pungent aroma that Caribbean, Indian, and Cuban cooks use in sofrito, black beans, marinades, and rice dishes. The partially succulent nature of the leaves makes the plant somewhat drought-tolerant once established, and the trailing habit makes it excellent for hanging baskets and container combinations. Flavor intensity decreases if plants are too heavily shaded — partial sun gives the best balance of ornamental appearance and aromatic leaf quality. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.
