name: Variegated Horseradish
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — deep, loose soil produces the straightest, most harvestable roots; Variegated Horseradish is an ornamental form of standard horseradish (Armoracia rusticana) with leaves that are boldly splashed and streaked with irregular cream-white markings against green, creating a dramatically two-tone foliage effect throughout the growing season. The ornamental value is high — the large, wavy, cream-splashed leaves are attractive in herb borders and edible landscape designs where standard all-green horseradish might seem too utilitarian. The roots have the same intensely pungent, sinus-clearing horseradish flavor and heat as the standard species — the variegation is purely a foliar characteristic with no effect on root quality. Horseradish root is freshly grated or processed with vinegar to make prepared horseradish sauce; the pungency from allyl isothiocyanate is highest immediately after grating and dissipates over time, which is why freshly grated horseradish is dramatically more powerful than commercial prepared products. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Licorice Plant (Cream-and-Gray Marbled Trailing Foliage)
description: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in partial sun to bright, open shade; 'Variegatum' has felted, gray-green leaves irregularly marked with cream, the variegation often showing more strongly in cooler weather and settling to a softer silvery cream in summer heat. It is noticeably less vigorous and more compact than the plain green species, making it useful for scaled-down containers, window boxes, and shaded entry pots where its pale foliage brightens a dim corner. Pinch tips occasionally to encourage branching, and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly, since they grow faster and can overtake the variegated portions of the plant. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Pink Lemon (Pink Eureka Lemon, Eureka Variegated Pink)
description: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon (sold as 'Pink Eureka Lemon' or 'Eureka Variegated Pink') is a striking sports mutation of the standard Eureka lemon, valued both as a productive lemon and as a highly ornamental landscape or container specimen. The foliage is distinctively variegated in green and cream-white patterns that remain attractive year-round; the unripe fruits are dramatically striped in green and yellow (somewhat like a watermelon in miniature), and the flesh is pale pink when cut — a surprise and visual delight that makes this lemon memorable and photogenic. As the fruit ripens to full yellow, the pink-flesh color fades but remains just slightly pink in fully ripe fruit; the flavor is standard Eureka lemon — tart, aromatic, excellent for culinary use in anything requiring fresh lemon juice, zest, or slices. Production is good but somewhat lighter than standard Eureka. An outstanding choice for container culture, ornamental edible gardens, and any setting where visual interest in the plant matters as much as production. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Society Garlic (Cream-Striped Edible Tulbaghia)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated Society Garlic is the ornamentally superior form of Tulbaghia violacea — a South African bulbous perennial producing narrow, strap-like leaves with a striking cream to cream-white longitudinal stripe along the center or edge of each leaf. The two-tone cream-and-green variegated foliage has significantly higher ornamental value than the solid-green species and creates a bright, light-catching effect particularly valuable in partial shade. The long bloom season (May through October in zone 9, often year-round in frost-free winters) produces clusters of small, tubular, lilac-pink to rose-violet flowers on slender scapes 12–18 inches tall — the pink flowers above the cream-variegated foliage create an outstanding three-season color combination. The leaves, stems, and flowers are all edible with a mild garlic-chive flavor — milder than either garlic or chives individually — appropriate for salads, garnishes, and any dish where a delicate garlic note is desired. The common name 'society garlic' reflects this mild, socially acceptable garlic flavor (lacking the persistent breath odor of true garlic). Variegated Society Garlic is drought-tolerant, deer-resistant (due to the garlic scent), and virtually pest-free. In zone 9, it is evergreen year-round in mild winters and recovers quickly from any frost damage. An outstanding dual-purpose plant for the Gulf South garden. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Sweet Marjoram
description: This sport of sweet marjoram carries an irregular cream-to-white margin on each small oval leaf, giving mounded plants a frosted, two-tone look that reads more ornamental than the golden form while retaining the same delicate sweet-marjoram flavor in the green portion of the leaf. Some afternoon shade helps prevent the pale leaf margins from scorching in hot climates, unlike plain sweet marjoram, which tolerates full sun more readily. It is grown as a tender perennial in mild climates and as a container or annual herb elsewhere, and can be brought indoors over winter where space allows. Propagate only from stem cuttings, since seedlings do not reliably retain the variegated pattern. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Thyme (Silver Posie Thyme, Gold Thyme)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; clip lightly after flowering to maintain compact mound shape. Thymus vulgaris 'Variegatus' (variegated thyme) encompasses several cultivated varieties of common garden thyme selected for ornamental variegated foliage rather than just culinary use. The two primary types are: silver-variegated ('Silver Posie,' 'Silver Queen') with small, dark-green leaves edged in silver-white, creating a soft, frosted effect; and gold-variegated ('Gold,' 'Aureus') with leaves edged in yellow-gold, brightening the herb garden considerably. Both retain the characteristic thyme fragrance and flavor of common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) and can be used identically in cooking — the variegated leaves look beautiful in cooking and as garnishes. Variegated thyme cultivars tend to be slightly less vigorous than solid-green common thyme but grow readily under the same cultural conditions: excellent drainage, lean soil, hot sun, and minimal water. They are especially effective in herb garden borders, rock gardens, and as edging plants where the contrast between the dark green leaf centers and the cream, silver, or gold margins can be appreciated at close range. Also excellent in containers or topiaries. In hot, humid zone 9 climates, variegated thyme benefits from excellent air circulation to prevent fungal problems. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Variegated Vanilla
description: This ornamental sport of common vanilla carries irregular cream-to-white streaking down its thick succulent leaves and climbing stems, making it a striking foliage specimen even before it reaches flowering size. Because its variegated tissue contains less chlorophyll than the plain green species, it generally grows more slowly and wants brighter, more filtered light than standard vanilla to keep the variegation vivid without scorching the leaves. Like its parent it is a climbing epiphytic orchid that must be trained onto a moss pole, coco pole, or tree trunk in a shaded to lightly lit spot, and flowering-size vines still require hand pollination to set the bean pods that are cured into vanilla flavoring. Collectors grow it primarily as a striking houseplant or greenhouse specimen, with any pods it eventually sets treated as a bonus. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Varna Leek (Fast-Maturing Summer/Baby Leek)
description: Named for the Bulgarian city where the type originated, Varna is a quick-cycling summer leek prized for reaching usable size well ahead of longer-season winter storage leeks. Because it matures so fast, gardeners can crowd seedlings three or four inches apart and pull the whole planting young as slender, sweet salad leeks, or space them wider and let a portion size up into full stalks for cooking. The blue-green foliage tops slim, mild-flavored white shanks that blanch readily with light hilling. It handles a light frost but is best harvested through summer and early fall rather than overwintered, since it lacks the cold hardiness bred into dedicated winter leek types. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Vates Collard
description: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 9 plant fall transplants October–November for harvest December through March; Vates is the classic Southern collard variety developed at the Virginia Truck Experiment Station in the 1950s and for decades was the standard garden collard of the South — compact, slow to bolt, very cold hardy (surviving temperatures well below 20°F with frost actually improving the flavor by converting starches to sugars), and producing thick, blue-green leaves of the authentic Southern collard flavor. The name 'Vates' (meaning 'prophet' in Latin) was chosen by the Virginia researchers. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the growing tip to continue producing; plants that are allowed to keep their lower leaves become leggy and produce smaller, tougher leaves. The slow-bolt characteristic makes Vates substantially more useful in cool-season gardens than older varieties that rush to flower. Matures in 60–80 days from transplant.

name: Vates Collards (Compact Slow-Bolt Virginia Station Collard)
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Vates is an open-pollinated collard developed at the Virginia Agricultural and Experiment Station (the acronym 'VATES' gives the variety its name) specifically for compact size, dark color, and improved cold tolerance compared to the taller, more open Georgia types. Vates produces distinctly compact plants (18–24 inches tall vs. the 36–48 inches of Georgia Southern), with upright, heavy, dark blue-green leaves that are more tightly held on the stem than the open habit of older types. The compact habit makes Vates practical for smaller garden spaces and easier to manage in the fall garden without the sprawling character of the traditional large types. The dark blue-green color is visually attractive and indicates high chlorophyll content. Vates shows better cold hardiness than Georgia types — surviving temperatures to 15–18°F rather than the 20–23°F limit of less cold-hardy types — and is notably slow to bolt in spring. This slow-bolting character extends the productive leaf harvest into late spring, 2–4 weeks beyond when other varieties have bolted and become bitter. Vates is consistently recommended by eastern U.S. extension services as one of the most reliable all-purpose collard varieties. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Vates Kale (Dwarf Blue Curled Scotch Kale)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart. Vates is a classic dwarf selection of curly Scotch kale, bred at Virginia's Truck Experiment Station for a compact, low, uniform habit that resists bolting and lodging better than taller curly kales, with tightly ruffled blue-green leaves. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating hard freezes and actually improving in flavor as cool weather converts starches to sugars, making it a mainstay of fall and winter kale plantings across a wide range of climates. Harvest outer leaves regularly as needed, leaving the growing center intact for continued production over a long harvest season. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Vatican White Clary Sage
description: Sow seed indoors and transplant after danger of frost, or sow directly in mid-summer where plants are to bloom the following year, into lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil. Vatican White is a compact seed-strain selection of clary sage bred for a shorter, more uniform habit than the wild species, producing tall spikes of pure white flowers held in showy pale bracts over large, wrinkled, felted gray-green leaves in early to midsummer of the second year. Like the species, its flowering stems and leaves are used in aromatherapy and traditional herbal preparations, and the strong-scented foliage is a striking foil for blue- and purple-flowered clary sage selections in an herb or cutting garden. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy plants once bloom finishes; self-sown seedlings often appear the following spring. Matures in 120–365 days from seed.

name: Vedrantais Melon (French Charentais Heirloom)
description: Vedrantais is a classic, open-pollinated French Charentais heirloom that many chefs and growers regard as the truest expression of the Charentais type, distinct from generic Charentais seed blends sold under that name alone. Fruit is small and round with a smooth, gray-green rind lightly ribbed toward the blossom end, enclosing deep-orange flesh with an intensely honeyed, floral aroma prized in French markets. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily as harvest approaches and watch for a faint crack or softening at the stem end rather than waiting for the fruit to fall free on its own. A hot, relatively dry growing season brings out the fullest sugar and fragrance this variety is known for. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Veestar Strawberry
description: Veestar is an Ontario-bred June-bearer prized across the Canadian prairies and northern U.S. Midwest for combining very early ripening with exceptional winter hardiness. The first flush of berries is notably large and firm with bright red color and good flavor, though fruit size drops off quickly as the harvest continues, so the earliest picks give the best quality. Its vigor and productivity have kept it a standard recommendation for short-season, cold-winter gardens for decades. Apply a thick winter mulch and remove it gradually in spring to protect crowns from late freezes without delaying growth. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Vegetable Amaranth (Chinese Spinach)
description: Scatter seeds on the surface of fertile, moist soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing, using thinnings as baby greens. Vegetable amaranth thrives in conditions that defeat spinach, lettuce, and other cool-season greens, making it the premier summer leafy vegetable for hot, humid climates. Harvest entire young plants thinly, or cut growing tips regularly from larger plants to stimulate bushy regrowth; the tricolor varieties also produce striking ornamental foliage in red, yellow, and green. Young leaves and tips are cooked as a spinach substitute in Asian, Caribbean, and West African cuisines — they cook down dramatically and benefit from high heat in a wok. Remove plants before seed heads shatter if naturalizing is not desired. Matures in 25–45 days from seed.

name: Vegetable Fern (Paku)
description: Plant divided crowns in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; vegetable fern is a fast-spreading tropical fern of Southeast Asia and the Pacific whose tightly coiled young fiddleheads and tender upper fronds are harvested every few days as a mild, slightly mucilaginous green, stir-fried, added to soups, or blanched for salads. It thrives in soggy, even seasonally flooded ground along ditches, pond edges, and rice-paddy margins, making it a useful crop for the wet, shaded corners of a warm-climate garden where few other vegetables perform. Keep the crown constantly wet and cut fronds regularly to encourage a steady flush of new, tender growth; plants die back completely at the first frost and must be grown as an annual or protected in pots outside zone 9b. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Vegetable Hummingbird (Agati, Scarlet Wisteria Tree)
description: Sow seeds (scarify or nick seed coat to improve germination) directly in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun after last frost; plants grow very rapidly and begin producing edible flowers within 3–6 months. Sesbania grandiflora (vegetable hummingbird or agati) is a fast-growing tropical tree or large shrub grown throughout South and Southeast Asia as one of the most productive edible-flowering plants — producing spectacular, orchid-like flowers 2–4 inches long in white (the typical form) or red, that are harvested and cooked as a vegetable throughout Southeast Asian and Indian cuisines. The flowers are slightly bitter, nutritious (high in calcium, iron, and vitamin C), and used stir-fried, in curries, in salads, and in soups; they are a common street food ingredient in Thailand, India, and the Philippines. All parts of the plant are edible: young leaves are used like spinach, young seed pods like string beans, and the flowers are the most prized part. Sesbania fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, improving soil fertility. The tree is native to tropical Asia and grows with such speed that it can produce harvestable crops within its first growing season as an annual in temperate climates. Matures in 60–180 days from seed.

name: Vegetable Spaghetti Winter Squash
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, giving the vines plenty of room to spread. This heirloom is unique among winter squashes: when cooked, the flesh separates into spaghetti-like strands that stay tender yet al dente. Let fruits fully ripen to a hard, golden rind and cure them before storing; the mild, low-calorie flesh is delicious with a bit of butter or a favorite sauce. Matures in 88–100 days from seed.

name: Veinte Cohol Banana (Twenty Cohol, Short-Cycle Cold-Hardy Fruiting Banana)
description: Veinte Cohol is a short-statured, fast-fruiting banana that has drawn interest from coastal Georgia growers as a specialty crop because it reaches flowering and produces a mature bunch much faster than typical dessert bananas, sometimes within a single frost-free season from a spring-planted pup. The rhizome tolerates cooler conditions than tender Cavendish types, dying back at freezing but regrowing from the root system the following spring in zone 8b-9 gardens. Bunches are smaller than commercial Cavendish bunches, with plump, soft-textured fruit that trials have described as having a mild lemony note. Its compact height and shortened cropping cycle make it a practical choice for growers wanting homegrown bananas outside true tropical zones. Matures in 270–425 days from transplant.

name: Veitchberry
description: Plant rooted cane tips in spring and train onto a wire trellis, cutting out fruited canes after harvest and tying in new primocanes for the following season. Veitchberry is an English hybrid bramble raised in the early twentieth century by the Veitch nursery dynasty, one of several blackberry-raspberry crosses developed in Britain around the same era as the loganberry. It produces large, dark purple-black, conical berries with an aromatic flavor closer to blackberry than raspberry, borne on long, vigorous, thorny trailing canes. It survives mainly in heritage fruit collections and specialist nurseries today, having been largely superseded by more disease-resistant modern hybrids. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Veldt Grape (Harjora, Winged Treebine)
description: Plant stem section cuttings in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to part shade; water sparingly — Cissus quadrangularis is drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Cissus quadrangularis (veldt grape or harjora) is a tropical African and Asian succulent vine that looks unlike any typical grape-family plant (Vitaceae) — it produces thick, fleshy, distinctly four-winged-square (quadrangular = four-cornered) green stems segmented at intervals like bamboo nodes, with small, deciduous, kidney-shaped leaves and tiny clusters of red berries at the nodes. The plant is primarily known not as a food or ornamental but as one of the most important plants in Ayurvedic medicine — it is called 'harjora' in Sanskrit (literally 'bone-joiner') and is used for more than 2,000 years to accelerate fracture healing, treat osteoporosis, joint pain, and as a bone-strengthening tonic. Scientific studies have confirmed that extracts of C. quadrangularis stimulate osteoblast (bone cell) activity and accelerate bone mineralization. It is widely sold as a supplement in India and, increasingly, in Western natural health markets. In the garden in zone 9–12, Veldt grape is an ornamental curiosity — the square, succulent, bright-green stems and climbing or trailing habit make it an unusual specimen for a succulent or tropical garden. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Velvet Apple (Mabolo, Butter Fruit, Kamagong Fruit Tree)
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Velvet Apple grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates and often benefits from afternoon shade protection in the intense heat of zone 9-10 summers. Diospyros blancoi is an evergreen fruit tree from the Philippines in the family Ebenaceae (the ebony and persimmon family), producing one of the most striking and unusual fruits in the tropical fruit world. The ripe fruits are perfectly round (3–4 inches in diameter), covered in a dense coat of fine reddish-brown to coppery velvet-soft hairs — like an incredibly large, round, red-brown cherry with velvet skin — from which the common name 'Velvet Apple' derives. Beneath the velvety skin is a firm, creamy-white to pink flesh with a sweet, mild flavor combining banana, cream, and mango notes and a dry, slightly astringent texture similar to some persimmons. The fruits have a striking, pungent odor when freshly harvested that many people find unpleasant (sometimes compared to ripe cheese or onion), but this odor dissipates with ventilation and does not affect the pleasant flavor of the flesh. In the Philippines, the tree is doubly valued: for its edible fruit and for its heartwood (called 'kamagong' — Philippine ebony), one of the hardest and heaviest woods in Southeast Asia, used for fine furniture and tool handles. The tree is also an ornamental specimen with glossy, dark-green foliage. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Velvet Mesquite
description: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep, well-aerated soil in full sun; velvet mesquite is the dominant mesquite of Arizona desert grasslands and saguaro cactus country, nearly identical to honey mesquite (P. glandulosa) but more densely hairy (velutinous) on the leaves and pods, tolerating the extreme heat and seasonal drought of the Sonoran Desert. The long, flat, tan seed pods mature in late summer and are very high in sugar and protein — edible by humans (ground into mesquite flour), consumed by coyotes, javelinas, deer, and dozens of bird species. The fragrant, cream-colored flower spikes in spring attract swarms of native bees. Deep taproots (up to 60 feet) access groundwater far below the surface. An important nitrogen-fixing tree that improves soil fertility. The aromatic wood produces some of the finest barbecue smoke in the world — prized for smoked meats throughout the Southwest. Matures in 1095–2190 days from seed.

name: Velvetleaf Blueberry (Sourtop Blueberry, Canada Blueberry)
description: Plant in strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), well-drained and sandy or peaty, in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a low, colony-forming native shrub of the boreal forest and northern Great Lakes and New England barrens, distinguished from the closely related lowbush blueberry by the fine, dense, velvety hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its light blue-green leaves — a texture you can feel by running a leaf between your fingers. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into loose colonies and, like other lowbush blueberries, is fire-adapted, resprouting vigorously from its roots after burning or hard mowing; commercial growers of Maine's wild blueberry barrens manage mixed stands of this species and Vaccinium angustifolium on a two-year burn-and-harvest cycle for the same reason. The small, powder-blue, sweet berries ripen in mid- to late summer and are borne most heavily on wood that grew the previous year, so avoid heavy pruning right before a harvest season. Foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall. Plant at least two genetically distinct plants for reliable cross-pollination and best fruit set. This is strictly a cold-climate plant, thriving where winters are long and cold; it struggles and rarely fruits well south of its native range. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Ventana Strawberry (Early-Fruiting UC Davis Day-Neutral Strawberry)
description: Set plugs or bare-root crowns at soil level, crown neither buried nor exposed, in fertile, well-drained beds in full sun; in zone 8-9 plant in fall for a winter-through-spring harvest. Ventana is a day-neutral strawberry from the University of California, Davis breeding program, selected for producing an unusually large, early flush of fruit soon after planting compared with older day-neutral types, followed by steady production through the cooler months. Because it flowers on new growth regardless of day length rather than requiring the short days that trigger June-bearing types, Ventana keeps fruiting through a Gulf Coast winter whenever temperatures stay in the 35-85°F range. Feed lightly but regularly through the season to sustain the heavy, near-continuous fruit set, and plan to replace plantings after one to two years as yields decline. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Ventura Celery
description: Ventura is a vigorous, disease-resistant green stalk celery bred for reliable performance in home gardens and market rows alike, producing thick, crisp, well-filled ribs without the fussiness of older heirloom types. Its heat tolerance and slow-to-bolt habit make it more forgiving than many stalk celeries during warm spells, and it needs no blanching to stay pale and mild. Feed heavily and keep the root zone consistently moist, since any drought stress produces stringy, hollow stalks. Gardeners choose Ventura when they want a dependable, all-purpose green celery that performs well from spring through fall without special handling. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Ventura Lemon (Cold-Hardy Meyer-Type Lemon)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun, watering deeply and regularly during the growing season. Ventura lemon produces medium-sized, thin-skinned, juicy fruit with a mild, less acidic flavor similar to Meyer lemon, borne nearly year-round on a compact, thornless tree well suited to patio containers. Mature trees tolerate brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s F better than standard Eureka or Lisbon lemon, though young trees should still be protected with frost cloth during hard freezes. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually and watch for iron and zinc deficiencies in alkaline soils. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Ventura Strawberry Fig (Adriatic-Type Red-Fleshed California Fig)
description: Ventura Strawberry is a California selection within the Adriatic group of fig cultivars, named for the deep red, berry-like color and flavor of its flesh rather than for any trait of its skin. Fruits are medium-sized with dark purple-black skin and a thick, juicy, red interior that carries a distinct strawberry-like sweetness; as with other Adriatic types it sets a dependable main crop without needing pollination. The tree performs well in hot, sunny conditions and has become a sought-after specialty selection among Southern fig collectors for its rich flavor and productivity. Grow it as you would other common-type figs, in full sun with excellent drainage, and expect the first fruit within two to three years of planting a rooted cutting. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Venus Grape (Seedless Blue University of Arkansas Table Grape)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy to help manage humidity-related fungal disease. Venus was bred by the University of Arkansas grape breeding program and produces genuinely seedless, blue-black berries with a slip-skin texture and sweet, richly fruity flavor reminiscent of Concord grapes, on a vine with good resistance to the common grape diseases that plague less resilient cultivars in humid climates. Its early to midseason ripening and reliable disease tolerance have made it a popular home-garden choice for gardeners wanting a seedless table grape without a heavy spray program. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Verde Puebla Tomatillo
description: A traditional Mexican tomatillo landrace from the state of Puebla, producing large, round, golden-green fruit that fills and splits its papery husk with a firmer texture and a sweeter, more lemony tang than many standard green tomatillo selections. The vigorous, sprawling plants bear over a long season and hold up better than most tomatillos to cool weather at the end of the season, continuing to set fruit as temperatures drop and tolerating a light frost without a sharp decline in production. Use the ripe golden-green fruit for a milder, less acidic salsa verde, or harvest slightly underripe for the sharper tartness preferred in some traditional recipes. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two for reliable cross-pollination and stake or cage the sprawling vines to keep fruit off the ground. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Vermentino Wine Grape (Heat-Tolerant Mediterranean White)
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Vermentino is a Mediterranean white grape most closely associated with Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, prized for producing crisp, refreshing wines with bright citrus and herbal notes and a characteristic faint saline minerality, made in a style well suited to warm-climate coastal cuisine. The vine is naturally heat- and drought-tolerant, retaining useful acidity even in hot growing conditions better than many other white varieties, which has made it an increasingly popular choice for warm-climate plantings outside its traditional Mediterranean range. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor through canopy work since the variety can be quite vigorous, and pick based on acid retention rather than sugar alone, since Vermentino's appeal rests heavily on preserving its signature freshness. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Vermillion Sweet Potato (Early Red-Skinned Louisiana Release)
description: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy to sandy soil after the danger of frost has passed and the ground has warmed; Vermillion is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (formerly trial line LA13-81) bred to combine the deep orange flesh of established Gulf South varieties with a distinctive red-purple skin that stands out on the market table and holds its color well through months of storage. It was developed to mature roughly ten days faster than Covington, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a shorter window between transplanting and harvest and a bit more flexibility for late plantings or short-season sites. Roots size up reliably in both sandy and heavier garden soils, though as with any sweet potato, deep, loose ground produces the straightest, most uniform tubers. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skin wounds and convert starches to the sugars that give sweet potatoes their flavor. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Vermont Beauty Pear (Small Richly Flavored New England Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Introduced from Vermont in the 1890s, this heirloom bears small, yellow, red-blushed pears that punch well above their size in flavor, with rich, sweet, aromatic flesh that made it a favorite dessert pear in New England home orchards despite never achieving wide commercial distribution. The compact fruit size and hardy constitution suited it well to the shorter growing seasons and colder winters of its home region. Harvest while still firm in early fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vermont Cranberry Bean (New England Heirloom Shell Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; can be harvested as a shell bean at 55–65 days (when pods are plump and mottled red-cream) or allowed to dry fully for 75–90 days for a dry-bean crop; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous shell bean harvest. Vermont Cranberry is a heirloom bush bean with deep New England roots — the speckled red-and-cream oval seeds are the traditional 'cranberry bean' of Vermont and New Hampshire, where they have been grown for baked beans since at least the 1700s. The name 'cranberry bean' (also applied to other speckled beans throughout New England) refers to the red cranberry-like speckled coloration of the pods and seeds at the shell bean stage, not to any relationship with cranberries. The shell beans have a rich, creamy, full flavor that is considered by many cooks superior to navy beans or Great Northern beans for traditional New England baked beans — the beans hold their shape well under long, slow baking while developing a creamy, dense interior texture that absorbs the sweet-savory baked bean flavors. At the dry bean stage the seeds turn darker and lose their red mottling; still excellent for winter cooking. Adapted to short New England growing seasons; performs equally well in Gulf Coast fall gardens. Matures in 55–90 days from seed.

name: Vernon Rabbiteye Blueberry (Mid-Season Vigorous Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Vernon is a mid-season rabbiteye blueberry bred for the Gulf South, producing an upright, vigorous, productive bush with firm, well-flavored, medium-to-large berries that hold well on the bush without excessive splitting in humid weather. It fills the harvest gap between early cultivars like Climax and later ones like Tifblue or Ochlockonee, giving home orchards a steadier, more extended supply of fresh fruit. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid high-nitrogen feeding late in the season, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vernon White Sapote
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind; Vernon is a California-bred white sapote selection prized for consistent, heavy production and self-fertility, removing the need to plant a second tree for pollination as some white sapote cultivars require. The medium-sized, thin-skinned, green-to-yellow fruit has smooth, custard-textured flesh with a sweet flavor often compared to a blend of banana, peach, and vanilla pudding. Trees grow fast and can reach substantial size, so plan for eventual shade and root spread; prune after harvest to maintain a manageable height and encourage branching for next season's crop. Fruit is ready to pick when it softens slightly and yields to gentle pressure, then finishes ripening at room temperature over several days. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Veronica Romanesco (Fractal Chartreuse Romanesco Broccoli)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to give the large outer leaves room to develop. Veronica is an early-maturing, reliable Romanesco selection known for its striking, spiraling, fractal-patterned chartreuse-green heads made up of pointed, pyramidal spirals, a strikingly geometric vegetable with a mild, nutty flavor closer to cauliflower than broccoli. It matures notably faster and more dependably than older Romanesco varieties, an important advantage in regions with a shorter cool season for heading brassicas to develop properly. Harvest the central head while the spirals are still tight before it begins to loosen and flower; in the Gulf South, a fall planting timed to head in cool weather generally outperforms a spring crop, which can bolt as temperatures rise. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: Vert de Massy Cornichon (French Gherkin)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive, picking at 1–3 inches long. Vert de Massy (Green of Massy) is the traditional French cornichon gherkin, a small, bumpy-skinned pickling cucumber prized in France for the production of cornichons — the tiny, intensely flavored pickles that accompany pâté, charcuterie, and raclette throughout French cuisine. The fruits are small, cylindrical to slightly tapered, dark green with small warts and spines, and have firm, crisp flesh with excellent flavor even when very small (1–2 inches). Harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive — if fruits are allowed to mature they divert energy from new production. Pickled in white wine vinegar with tarragon, chervil, and pearl onions in the traditional French method; also excellent as fresh gherkins. The vines are compact and productive. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Verte de Bordeaux Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — figs produce best in lean conditions and can become overly vegetative in rich, heavily fertilized soil; Verte de Bordeaux is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of southwestern France, producing small to medium, pear-shaped fruits with green to greenish-yellow skin that remains green even when fully ripe — a distinctive appearance that surprises consumers expecting a ripe fig to be darker. The deep burgundy-red interior flesh has an intensely rich, wine-like, complex sweetness that fig connoisseurs often rate among the finest flavors in the Ficus carica species. The petite size (1–2 inches) and striking green skin with deeply colored interior make it a specialty market favorite. In zone 9 Verte de Bordeaux produces consistently and handles the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers well. The green skin can be confusing to novice growers who may pick the fruit too early — harvest when the neck of the fig bends and the fruit softens. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vertissimo Chervil (Vigorous Slow-Bolt Curled Chervil)
description: Vertissimo is a dense, clump-forming chervil selected for vigor and slow bolting, producing more leaf over a longer harvest window than older curled types before running up to flower. Its dark green, tightly curled foliage regrows quickly after cutting, making it well suited to repeated harvests from the same planting rather than a single cut-and-done crop. Like all chervil it carries a mild anise-parsley flavor best used fresh, since drying or prolonged cooking destroys the delicate flavor. Give it partial shade and consistently moist soil in zone 9, where the cool months from fall through spring are its only realistic growing window. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Vetiver Grass (Khus Grass)
description: Plant divisions 6–12 inches apart in well-drained or heavy clay soil in full sun; Vetiver is one of the most useful multipurpose plants for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. Its roots grow extraordinarily deep (10–15 feet), anchoring slopes and roadsides against severe erosion even in the heavy subtropical rains of the Gulf South — making it the preferred bioengineering plant for slope stabilization in zone 9–12. The roots contain vetiverol and vetivone compounds that are among the most valuable fixatives in high-end perfumery (Chanel No. 5 uses vetiver root) and aromatherapy — dried roots can be used in sachets, potpourri, and natural insect repellents. The tall, upright, blue-green clumps are ornamentally attractive and exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Vetiver is non-invasive — unlike many ornamental grasses, it does not self-seed prolifically and spreads only by clump expansion. The Vetiver Network International promotes its use for sustainable soil and water conservation throughout tropical and subtropical regions. Harvest roots after 2–3 years for fragrance; divide clumps every 3 years to maintain vigor. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Vic Secret Hops
description: Vic Secret is an Australian aroma cultivar developed by Hop Products Australia in Victoria state, producing cones with pronounced pineapple, pine, and passionfruit notes that pair well with Galaxy in modern hazy and Australian-style IPAs. It shares Galaxy's preference for a long, warm growing season and full sun exposure to fully express its aromatic oils. The bine is moderately vigorous and appreciates a tall trellis and well-drained, fertile soil. Harvest when cones are dry and lupulin-rich, since underripe cones give a noticeably weaker fruit character. Matures in 150–200 days from transplant.

name: Vicks Plant (Camphor Plant, Succulent Coleus)
description: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in spring; established plants prefer well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun and are drought-tolerant once established. Vicks Plant is a succulent, aromatic tropical Plectranthus with rounded, thick, velvety, grey-green leaves that release a strong, unmistakable mentholated camphor scent when touched or bruised — the exact aroma of Vicks VapoRub, from which it takes its common name. It is grown primarily as an aromatic novelty and sensory herb for children's gardens, therapy gardens, and container collections, but has traditional use as a steam inhalant for colds and congestion in South African folk medicine. The stems are succulent and snap easily in frost; treat as a houseplant or tender annual north of zone 10, or grow in containers that overwinter indoors. Propagates extremely easily from stem cuttings placed in water or moist soil. Matures in 60–120 days from transplant.

name: Victor Roselle (Florida Cranberry Heirloom)
description: Victor is one of the oldest named roselle selections grown in the United States, introduced in Florida in the early twentieth century and still favored by south Florida home gardeners for large, bright-red, exceptionally plump calyces. The tall, vigorous plants yield a heavier calyx crop per bush than many seed-strain roselles sold today, and the reddish stems and lobed foliage make an attractive hedge-like screen through the season. Grow it in full sun, fertile well-drained soil, and generous spacing, harvesting calyces about a week after the petals drop while still firm and before the inner seed pod toughens. Use the tart calyces fresh or dried for tea, syrup, and jelly. Matures in 100–130 days from seed.

name: Victoria Blue Sage
description: Victoria Blue, or mealycup sage, is a drought-tolerant salvia grown for its deep blue-purple flower spikes dusted with a powdery texture. Surface sow the seed indoors under light about eight weeks before the last frost, since it needs light and warmth to germinate. Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants about a foot apart. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong the long bloom season, which supports bees and makes excellent cut and dried flowers. Matures in 90–110 days from seed.

name: Victoria Elderberry (Kentville Nova Scotia Research Station American Elderberry)
description: Victoria was released in 1957 from the Kentville Research Station in Nova Scotia as a seedling of Adams No. 2, part of the same Canadian breeding program that produced Kent, Nova, Scotia, and Johns. It ripens mid-season, later than Nova but around the same time as Kent, with medium-sized purple-black berries whose skin is lighter than Kent's or Nova's while the juice inside remains intensely dark purple. Victoria tolerates the shorter, cooler growing seasons of higher latitudes better than many American cultivars and performs well in the partial shade of a woodland-edge planting. It is a proven cross-pollinator for Ranch, and interplanting with any second cultivar improves fruit set and cluster size over a solid block planting. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Victoria Plum
description: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Victoria is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a pollinator improves yield. The single most widely grown plum in England and one of the best-known European dessert plums in the world, it bears heavy crops of large, oval, red-blushed yellow fruit with juicy, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, and its reliable, self-fertile heavy bearing has made it a standard first-choice plum for a home orchard with room for only one tree. Its very heavy crops often require significant hand thinning of young fruit to prevent limb breakage and to improve the size and quality of the remaining plums. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, thin crowded fruit clusters, and support heavily laden branches in a good fruiting year. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Victoria Red Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Table Grape)
description: Train on a trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Victoria Red is a seeded red table grape that has survived over 25 years of extreme Pierce's disease pressure at the Tarkington Vineyards test site near Victoria, Texas, making it one of the few table grapes with genuinely sustained tolerance to the disease that otherwise makes grape growing across the Gulf Coast so difficult. It produces large, sweet clusters with sugar levels reaching up to 25 brix, eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or made into juice. Because it was bred specifically for hot, humid Texas and Gulf Coast conditions, it needs none of the intensive spray programs required to keep Pierce's-disease-susceptible European grapes alive in the region. Harvest clusters once berries have colored fully and taste sweet, since grapes do not continue ripening after picking. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Victoria Rhubarb
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with high organic matter content; Victoria is the oldest and most widely grown named rhubarb variety, introduced in the 1830s in Britain and remaining the standard variety against which others are compared — it has an exceptionally long cultivation record of nearly 200 years as a garden and commercial vegetable. The thick, large, greenish-pink to light red stalks are produced in large quantities and have the classic, sharp, tart-sour rhubarb flavor used in pies, crumbles, jams, and sauces — the pairing of rhubarb's tartness with strawberry sweetness in strawberry-rhubarb pie is one of the iconic spring desserts of North American and British cooking. Victoria produces primarily green to light pink stalks rather than the deep red of ornamental varieties like Crimson Red; the color is purely cosmetic with no effect on flavor. As a cool-climate perennial, Victoria thrives best where winters are cold and long (zones 3–6) but performs adequately through zone 8 with attention to soil improvement and consistent watering. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Victoria Rhubarb
description: Start Victoria rhubarb seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before setting plants into a permanent, fertile bed spaced 3 to 4 feet apart. This cold-hardy heirloom perennial develops deep crimson-tinged stalks with a rich sweet-tart flavor and returns for many years. Do not harvest the first year and take only a few stalks the second, letting the crown establish. Never eat the leaves, which are toxic, and remove flower stalks to keep energy in the roots. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Victory Loquat (Vigorous Productive Orange Loquat)
description: Victory loquat is grown for its vigorous habit and heavy, dependable fruit set, producing orange-fleshed fruit of good size and pleasant sweet-tart flavor over a long harvest window in late winter to spring. Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and allow ample spacing for its larger-than-average mature canopy. Because Victory tends to set fruit prolifically, thin clusters after fruit set to prevent overcropping, which can lead to smaller fruit and biennial bearing. Protect the fall bloom from hard freezes, and mulch well to conserve soil moisture through the humid Gulf Coast growing season. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Victory Onion (Alpine Leek)
description: Unlike most culinary alliums, this broad-leafed perennial of the subalpine forests of Europe and northeastern Asia thrives in partial shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil rather than open, sun-baked beds, making it a good companion for a woodland or shade herb garden. It is a slow starter, typically taking two to three years from seed to reach a harvestable clump size, so most gardeners begin with nursery divisions instead. Both the broad garlicky leaves and small bulbs are edible and are prized in Japan (gyoja-ninniku) and Korea (myeongi), where young spring leaves are harvested sparingly, leaving most of the clump intact so it can bulk up for future seasons. Established clumps are long-lived and can be divided every several years to propagate new plantings. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Vidal Blanc Grape (Vidal 256, Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)
description: Vidal Blanc, officially Vidal 256, is a French-American hybrid bred from Ugni Blanc and Seibel 4986 that has become one of the most widely planted white wine grapes in the eastern and southern United States for its combination of productivity, cold hardiness, and good fungal-disease tolerance. It produces heavy clusters of thick-skinned, golden berries late in the season, valued both for crisp dry table wines and for late-harvest or ice-wine-style dessert wines where hard freezes concentrate the sugars. Train it on a high-wire cordon or Geneva double-curtain system in full sun, and prune to manage its vigorous, fruitful growth, which can overcrop and require cluster thinning for best wine quality. Like most French-American hybrids, Vidal Blanc carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance, so southern extension programs generally recommend it for the upper and middle South rather than the most Pierce's-disease-prone Gulf Coast counties. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vidanga (False Black Pepper)
description: Vidanga is a sprawling, woody, scandent shrub native to the forest margins of India's Western Ghats, valued in Ayurvedic tradition for its small peppercorn-like berries. Its hard seed coat is dormant and benefits from mechanical scarification before sowing to achieve reliable germination. In cultivation it needs a host tree, fence, or trellis to scramble over as it matures, along with dappled light and consistently moist, well-drained soil typical of a humid subtropical or tropical understory. Berries are harvested once fully ripe and dried for use in traditional preparations, though overharvesting from the wild has made cultivated sources increasingly important. Matures in 730–1460 days from seed.

name: Vierling Dill (Tall Blue-Leaved Heirloom Dill)
description: Vierling is a European heirloom dill grown for its steel-blue, finely cut foliage and thick, sturdy stems that hold up well in cut-flower arrangements once the chartreuse seed umbels open. It is notably slow to bolt compared with older dill strains, keeping tender leaf production going longer into warm weather before the plant switches over to flowering and seed. In zone 9, fall sowing lets plants establish through the cool months and reach their full 3-to-5-foot height by spring, when the wide seed heads attract beneficial insects and pollinators. Harvest leaves continuously for fresh dill weed, and let a few plants flower and seed to collect dill seed for pickling or to let the planting self-sow. Matures in 45–95 days from seed.

name: Vietnamese Balm (Kinh Gioi)
description: Direct sow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost; Vietnamese balm (kinh gioi) is one of the most important and distinctive aromatic herbs in Vietnamese cuisine, with a complex flavor profile that combines lemon, mint, and slightly pungent herbal notes in a fresh, cooling combination that is essential in classic Vietnamese dishes. The leaves are used fresh as a raw herb garnish in pho, spring rolls, banh mi, and grilled meat dishes, added at the last moment so the volatile aromatics are preserved. It looks similar to lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) but has a completely different and more complex fragrance. In Vietnam it is used both as a culinary herb and medicinally for digestive and respiratory complaints. It grows rapidly in warm weather and is highly productive with regular harvesting from the growing tips, which also keeps the plant compact and delays flowering. Self-sows freely in warm climates; treat as an annual in zones 7 and colder. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Vietnamese Cilantro (Rau Ram Heat-Tolerant Cilantro Substitute)
description: Root 4-inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; transplant to partial shade after last frost. Vietnamese Cilantro (Persicaria odorata, Rau Răm in Vietnamese) is a Southeast Asian tropical herb that produces an aroma remarkably similar to cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) combined with a slightly peppery, more complex note — making it the primary heat-tolerant substitute for cilantro in Gulf South gardens, where true cilantro bolts and becomes bitter in temperatures above 75°F. Vietnamese cilantro is a creeping, semi-aquatic perennial that grows vigorously in warm, moist conditions — it is widely grown in Vietnam and Southeast Asia where it is used fresh in spring rolls (gỏi cuốn), rice paper wraps, laksa (the spicy Southeast Asian noodle soup that uses rau răm as a key garnish), and various dipping sauce accompaniments. The narrow, pointed leaves with distinctive dark V-shaped markings are the visual identifier. In the Gulf South, Vietnamese cilantro solves the common problem of wanting fresh cilantro-flavored herbs in July through September when true cilantro is impossible to grow — it grows vigorously in the summer heat and provides a suitable (though not identical) flavor substitute. Matures in 30–45 days from transplant.

name: Vietnamese Coriander (Rau Ram, Hot Mint, Laksa Leaf)
description: Root stem cuttings in water and transplant to moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 9, partial shade is strongly preferred to prevent leaf scorch in summer heat. Persicaria odorata (Vietnamese coriander or rau ram) is the tropical herb that resolves the gardener's dilemma of having fresh coriander flavor through the heat of summer — it produces pointed, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with distinctive chocolate-brown chevron markings that taste intensely of fresh cilantro with a spicy, peppery undertone; the flavor is actually considered more complex and intense than true coriander by many Southeast Asian cooks. Rau ram is indispensable in Vietnamese cuisine — it is the canonical garnish for pho, rice noodle salads, and laksa soups and is used extensively in Cambodian and Malaysian cooking. In zone 9, it thrives year-round (dying back in rare hard freezes but resprouting from roots), making it far more practical than annual cilantro for consistent harvest. Plants root from stem cuttings placed in water within days — the easiest possible propagation; overwintered plants in pots can be brought indoors when frost threatens. Matures in 45–75 days from transplant.

name: Vietnamese Jaina Dragon Fruit (White-Fleshed Pitaya)
description: Grow on a strong post-and-collar or trellis in full sun with excellent drainage; Vietnamese Jaina is a widely grown selection of the classic white-fleshed pitaya, valued for oval fruit that commonly reach a pound or more with mild, refreshing sweetness. It is self-fertile, unlike many white-flesh types that need a pollinator partner, so a single plant can set fruit reliably once mature. Flowers open for a single night and are best hand-pollinated near dusk for heavier fruit set. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-30s but suffer scale damage below that; wrap or move containers during hard freezes. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Vietnamese Perilla
description: Direct sow or transplant into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Vietnamese perilla (rau tia to) is the large-leafed, flat-surfaced green strain of perilla used extensively in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cooking, distinctly different in appearance and flavor from the ruffled Japanese shiso cultivars. The broad, flat, dark green leaves with a slightly purple reverse are used as a table herb in pho, bún bò Huế, spring rolls, and salad plates — leaves are torn and added raw at the table rather than cooked. The flavor is more robust and less refined than Japanese shiso, with strong anise, mint, and basil notes that pair well with the bold flavors of Vietnamese broths. In zone 9 the plant performs best in the cool seasons of spring and fall; it tends to bolt and become bitter in peak summer. It tolerates partial shade and is ideal for the edge of a vegetable garden or under taller plants where it can capture filtered light. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Vietnamese Pomegranate (Vietnam Pink Pomegranate)
description: Vietnamese pomegranate is a large-fruited, thin-skinned selection prized among Gulf Coast and Florida growers for tolerating humidity and damp soils far better than most pomegranate cultivars, with reports of good fruiting even in muggy coastal conditions that cause fruit splitting and skin disease in Mediterranean-bred types. Arils are juicy and mildly sweet with distinctly soft, easy-to-chew seeds, making the fruit pleasant for fresh eating without the seed-spitting typical of hard-seeded cultivars. In areas with mild winters the tree tends to stay evergreen and can flower and set fruit in more than one flush per year rather than concentrating into a single fall harvest. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect it to shrug off the humid-summer disease pressure that limits some classic dry-climate cultivars in the Deep South. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Vietnamese Red Garlic (Purple Stripe Hardneck)
description: Vietnamese Red is a purple-striped hardneck garlic prized for a creamy, buttery texture and a sweetness that intensifies with roasting, distinguishing it from sharper rocambole types. Bulbs typically hold 9 to 12 large cloves wrapped in skins streaked with rose and purple. Grow it as a standard hardneck: plant cloves pointed end up in fall, cut the scape once it curls to push more energy into the bulb, and cure the harvested bulbs in a shaded, airy spot for a few weeks before storage. It has become a favorite among cooks who want sweetness without excessive heat. Matures in 240–270 days from transplant.

name: Vignoles Grape (French-American Hybrid White Wine Grape)
description: Vignoles produces small, tightly packed clusters of golden berries that build high sugar levels while retaining sharp acidity, making it a favorite for late-harvest and dessert-style white wines as well as crisp dry versions. Its thin skins are prone to bunch rot in humid weather, so growers should prioritize cluster thinning and canopy airflow, and consider netting against birds drawn to its concentrated sweetness. The vine is more cold-hardy than vinifera types and tolerates the shorter growing seasons of the upper Midwest and Northeast. Expect full production by the third or fourth growing season. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Viking Aronia
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist or periodically wet soil; Viking is a Scandinavian-selected cultivar of black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) developed for maximum berry production, selected in Sweden for its very heavy crop load of large, dark purple-black berries on an upright, vigorous shrub. The berries ripen in late August–September and are among the most tannin-rich, astringent fruits in cultivation when eaten raw — the name 'chokeberry' derives from this mouth-puckering astringency. Processed into juice, syrup, wine, jam, or dried, the astringency mellows and the extraordinarily high anthocyanin and polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown fruit — makes aronia products popular as nutritional supplements and functional foods. Viking is one of the highest-yielding aronia cultivars per area, producing 10–20 pounds per mature shrub. The shrub also provides excellent ornamental value with white flower clusters in spring and brilliant orange-to-red fall foliage. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Viking KB3 Asparagus (Canadian Open-Pollinated Hybrid)
description: Viking KB3 is an open-pollinated strain developed in Canada and long favored in short-season, cold-winter growing regions for its exceptional hardiness and reliable rust tolerance. Unlike the all-male Rutgers hybrids, Viking KB3 produces both male and female plants, so expect some volunteer seedlings to appear around the bed over time and thin them out to avoid overcrowding. Its spears are medium-thick with tight, purple-tinged tips and hold up well to the freeze-thaw cycles of prairie and northern climates. Because it is open-pollinated, saved seed from a healthy stand will grow true enough for home use, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sustaining asparagus patch. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Villafranca Lemon (Thornless Florida Heirloom Lemon)
description: Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil, allowing space for a nearly thornless, densely foliaged canopy. Provide even moisture throughout the year and protect young trees from hard freezes with covers or trunk wraps. Villafranca bears Eureka-type lemons that are medium-sized, juicy, and nearly seedless, produced almost continuously in warm climates with a heavier main crop in winter. Long grown in Florida and the Gulf Coast as a dooryard favorite, it is valued for producing well even under humid, subtropical conditions that can trouble other lemon cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Villard Blanc Grape (Seyve-Villard 12-375, French-American Hybrid White Wine Grape)
description: Villard Blanc, registered as Seyve-Villard 12-375, is one of the classic French-American hybrid wine grapes bred in the early 20th century by Bertille Seyve and Victor Villard to combine vinifera-quality fruit with the fungal-disease resistance of American parentage. It produces large clusters of greenish-white berries that ripen into a crisp, aromatic dry white wine and has historically been planted across the humid eastern and southern United States, where straight vinifera varieties struggle with black rot, downy mildew, and powdery mildew. Train vines on a cordon or high-wire trellis in full sun with good air movement, and prune hard each winter, since Villard Blanc is a vigorous grower that needs canopy management to ripen fruit well and avoid disease pressure in wet years. It carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance compared with purpose-bred Gulf Coast hybrids, so it performs best in the upper and middle South rather than the most humid Gulf Coast counties. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vina Walnut (Early-Harvest Heirloom California Persian Walnut)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Vina benefits from a compatible pollenizer for best nut set; the nuts mature and are ready for harvest roughly two weeks earlier than the widely planted 'Chandler,' making it useful where an earlier harvest window is desirable. Vina is an older, unpatented California-bred Persian walnut cultivar that predates modern UC Davis releases such as 'Chandler,' 'Howard,' 'Sunland,' 'Tulare,' and 'Solano.' It was historically grown in California's Central Valley walnut industry and has served as a reference cultivar in University of California walnut research, and remains of interest to heirloom orchardists for its earlier ripening and long production history. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Vincent Kiwi (Low-Chill Fuzzy Kiwifruit for Warm Winters)
description: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and train the vine onto a sturdy arbor or trellis capable of supporting many years of heavy growth. Vincent is a female fuzzy kiwi cultivar developed for areas with mild winters that do not reliably provide the roughly 800 chilling hours Hayward needs, which is why California Rare Fruit Growers lists it alongside Elmwood, Dexter, and Abbott as suitable options for southern California, the Gulf Coast, and Florida rather than the traditional cool-winter kiwi belt. Fruit is large and egg-shaped with good flavor, but because kiwi vines are dioecious, Vincent must be planted near a compatible male vine to set a crop, as it will not produce fruit on its own. Prune hard during dormancy to control the vine's naturally rampant growth and to keep fruiting wood within easy reach for harvest. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Vinson Watts Tomato
description: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed and stake or cage firmly from the start. Vinson Watts is a West Virginia Appalachian family heirloom that arrived at Seed Savers Exchange through Vinson Watts, who grew it for many years before contributing it to the seed exchange; it produces very large, 1–2 pound orange beefsteak fruits with deep, meaty, mostly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that rivals the better-known Kellogg's Breakfast and Dr. Wyche's Orange. The vigorous indeterminate vines are productive and the fruits have a pleasing globe shape and smooth skin that resists cracking better than some large heirlooms. An excellent choice for anyone building a collection of orange heirloom beefsteak tomatoes. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Viognier Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Viognier is a white wine grape native to the Rhône Valley of France, historically centered on the tiny appellation of Condrieu, where it came perilously close to disappearing entirely in the mid-20th century before a revival brought it back to prominence in France, California, and beyond. The grape produces full-bodied, richly aromatic white wines with pronounced notes of peach, apricot, and honeysuckle, a distinctive perfumed character that sets it apart from crisper, more neutral white varieties. The vine can be inconsistent in fruit set, sometimes producing loose, uneven clusters in cool or wet spring weather, so site selection and bloom-time weather matter more for Viognier than for many other varieties. Train to a permanent trellis, thin fruit if clusters set unevenly, and pick based on aromatic ripeness, since Viognier can lose its signature perfume if left to hang too long. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Violet de Gournay Radish
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart once true leaves appear. Violet de Gournay is a French market-garden heirloom named for the Normandy town of Gournay, producing round to slightly oval roots with smooth deep violet-black skin surrounding crisp white flesh. It matures faster than the larger Black Spanish winter radishes it is sometimes confused with, and its flavor is notably milder, making it suited to fresh eating rather than storage. Keep soil evenly moist during root sizing to prevent the skin from cracking or turning woody. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Violet de Provence Artichoke (Small French Purple Artichoke)
aliases: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Violet de Provence'
description: Violet de Provence is a classic French heirloom prized for its slender, pointed buds flushed deep violet-purple over green bracts, picked small and young before any fibrous choke develops so the whole bud can be trimmed and eaten. It produces earlier and more heavily than many of the large-headed globe types, throwing numerous side shoots that extend the harvest over several weeks. Cutting the entire plant back hard after the first flush encourages a second smaller crop of buds within a couple of months. It is a true perennial in mild-winter climates but needs a thick mulch or overwinter protection anywhere winter temperatures drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Violet Mustard (Purple Orychophragmus)
description: Direct sow in fall in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; violet mustard is a Chinese brassica grown both as a winter vegetable and as a spring ornamental — the young leaves through winter have a mild, pleasant flavor used fresh in salads or cooked, and the plant concludes its season with a spectacular display of pale to bright violet flowers in spring that are edible as garnish and highly attractive to early pollinators. The winter foliage often develops attractive purple-violet tints in cold weather. In zone 9, it self-sows to naturalize, returning each fall for a winter vegetable and spring flower display with no replanting. An excellent edible-ornamental for the winter garden. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Violet Queen Cauliflower (Open-Pollinated Purple Cauliflower)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart, and keep soil evenly moist since curds can lose color and flavor if plants are stressed by drought as they mature. Violet Queen is an open-pollinated cauliflower whose deep purple curds come from anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple carrots, and the color contrasts strikingly with its dark green wrapper leaves in the garden. Because it is not a hybrid, seed can be saved from year to year, and the curds hold their purple color raw but fade to green when cooked, so it is best featured in salads, slaws, or briefly steamed dishes where the color matters. Harvest promptly once curds are full-sized, since heads left too long in warm or bright conditions can dull from vivid violet toward a duller, greener tone. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Violet Wood Sorrel
description: Plant small bulbs 1–2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; violet wood sorrel tolerates drier soil and more sun than O. acetosella and is better suited to most eastern US garden conditions, naturalizing in open woodlands, dry meadows, and thin lawns. Oxalis violacea is a native eastern North American spring wildflower producing small clusters of violet to rose-pink, 5-petaled flowers with a yellow throat above clover-like, trifoliate, green to purple-tinged leaves in mid-spring, and often reblooming again in fall; the bulbs multiply slowly to form colonies in well-drained soils. The leaves and flowers are edible with the characteristic sour, lemony oxalis flavor and can be used as a garnish or in salads; consume in moderation due to oxalic acid content. It is a charming, low-growing native for rock gardens, shaded borders, and naturalizing under deciduous trees. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Violet's Multicolored Butterbeans (Multicolor Speckled Pole Lima Bean)
description: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous semi-bush vines, which will readily top a 7-foot support and can reach 10 feet. This Georgia family heirloom, preserved for four generations by Violet Brady Westbrook's family in Banks County, produces 3-5 inch pods filled with small, richly flavored seeds displaying a striking rainbow of colors — cream, beige, red-brown, and violet-purple, swirled and speckled so that no two beans look quite alike. Plants show good disease and drought resistance, useful traits for humid Gulf Coast summers. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh butterbeans or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage; the colorful seed coats fade somewhat with cooking but the flavor remains excellent fresh or dried. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Violetta Artichoke (Italian Purple Baby Artichoke)
description: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after vernalization. Violetta is a classic Italian heirloom artichoke producing smaller, tender, purple-tinged buds traditionally harvested young and eaten whole, including the tender inner leaves and heart, either braised, fried, or grilled in traditional Italian preparations like carciofi alla romana. The striking violet-purple coloring on the bud scales, especially pronounced in cooler weather, makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Like other seed-grown artichokes it can flower and produce a harvest the first year if properly vernalized as a young seedling, and in mild-winter zones it may persist as a short-lived perennial for a second season of harvest. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Violetta di Firenze Eggplant (Florentine Purple-White Striped Italian Heirloom)
description: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; Violetta di Firenze produces fewer, larger fruits than Asian types — typically 2–4 fruits per plant at a time — harvest when fruits reach 4–6 inches across and the skin is still glossy; do not allow to over-ripen (seeds enlarge and flesh becomes bitter). Violetta di Firenze (Florentine Violet) is a traditional Italian heirloom eggplant from the Florence area of Tuscany, where it has been grown for generations as the quintessential garden eggplant of the region — so important locally that it appears in Florentine recipe traditions and Renaissance-era botanical descriptions of the kitchen garden. The variety is immediately recognized by its dramatic appearance: very large (6–10 inches across), round to pear-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with beautiful vertical striping in shades of lavender-violet and white; no other commonly grown eggplant has the same combination of large round shape, deep ribbing, and purple-white striping. The flesh is creamy-white with a mild, sweet, slightly nutty flavor with less bitterness than many eggplant varieties — the large cavity and abundant flesh make it particularly suited for stuffing (ripieno), slicing and grilling, or layering in the classic Italian Parmigiana di Melanzane. The plant is robust and tall (30–48 inches) and requires staking; it is adapted to long, warm Mediterranean summers and performs well in Gulf Coast zone 8b–10 conditions with the hot summers they provide. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Violette de Bordeaux Fig (Negronne Fig, Petite Negri Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Violette de Bordeaux (called Negronne in California and known as Petite Negri in some American nurseries) is a small-statured French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of France — one of the most beloved fig varieties among connoisseurs because of its extraordinary flavor. The small (1.5–2 inch), deep purple-violet to nearly black berries have blood-red interior flesh with a rich, complex, intense sweetness with strawberry-raspberry undertones — a flavor profile significantly deeper and more complex than larger, milder figs. The tree's compact size (6–8 feet tall and wide) makes it an ideal container specimen for patios, balconies, and small urban gardens where a standard fig would overwhelm the space. Violette de Bordeaux is the go-to container fig recommended by specialty nurseries. The skin is quite thin and fruits bruise easily, limiting its commercial shipping potential but making it perfect for eating fresh off the tree. In zone 9, it fruits reliably August–October and can be moved into protected areas during cold snaps in zone 9a. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Violette de Sollies Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Violette de Sollies has Protected Designation of Origin (AOP) status as the primary fig of Sollies-Pont commune in Var, Provence — the most commercially important fig production area in France. It accounts for approximately 80% of French commercial fig production and is the fig you encounter in French supermarkets and on French cheese boards. The large, round to pear-shaped fruits have dark violet to nearly black skin and deep red to garnet flesh with an exceptionally creamy, melt-in-the-mouth texture and rich, complex sweetness. The PDO designation reflects the specific microclimate of the Var region and the care taken to produce the variety at optimal quality. Violette de Sollies is a fall-ripening variety, producing its main crop in September–October in zone 9 — later than most other figs and extending the fresh fig season into autumn. The exceptional flavor quality and French culinary prestige make it a premium choice for zone 9 gardens where the warm fall provides ideal ripening conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Violette di Firenze Eggplant
description: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Violette di Firenze (Violet of Florence) is a striking Italian heirloom eggplant from the Tuscany region, producing large, squat, round to pear-shaped fruits with distinctive lavender-to-violet skin streaked with white — a bicolor pattern that is dramatically different from the solid-purple standard eggplant. The large fruits (6–8 inches across, up to 2 pounds) have flesh that is notably sweeter, milder, and less bitter than standard globe eggplant types, with fewer seeds and a creamier texture when cooked. The Italian tradition of grilling, broiling, or pan-frying Violette di Firenze without salting (a technique used to reduce bitterness in standard eggplant) reflects the naturally mild, sweet character of this variety.
