The striking bicolor appearance makes it a showstopper in the garden and at market. Cut fruits at their most beautiful stage — when lavender-violet with white streaks and still firm — rather than allowing them to develop the dull, fully-mature purple that indicates over-ripeness. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Violetto Artichoke
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Violetto is an Italian artichoke type producing elongated, conical to teardrop-shaped heads with striking purple-green bracts that deepen to rich violet as the buds develop — the ornamental purple coloration makes Violetto one of the most attractive artichokes for kitchen garden displays and edible landscape design. The heads are smaller than American Green Globe types (typically 2–3 inches across) but considerably more tender in the bract meat and heart, with a milder, slightly more nutty flavor that is less assertive than the large green varieties. Smaller Violetto heads can be eaten raw when very young and tender — an important distinction from large artichokes that require cooking. In Italian cooking, Violetto di Romagna and similar purple artichoke types are specifically selected for preparations requiring tenderness: carciofi alla giudea (deep-fried), carciofi sott'olio (preserved in olive oil), and raw shaved artichoke salads. The purple color is heat-sensitive and fades during cooking, but the ornamental value in the growing plant is substantial. Matures in 90–150 days from transplant.

name: Virginia Beauty Apple (Spicy Russeted Virginia Heirloom)
description: Plant in a sheltered but sunny site and prune to an open canopy to help the fruit color and to control the tree's tendency toward biennial bearing. Virginia Beauty is a late-19th-century Virginia heirloom noted for its striped red skin, patches of russet, and distinctively spicy, aromatic flesh that improves in flavor during a few weeks of storage. It has long been a favorite among Southern heritage orchardists for fresh eating and cider, prized as much for its complex flavor as for its keeping ability into winter. Matures in 165–185 days from transplant.

name: Virginia Jumbo Peanut (Large-Seeded Southern Boiling Peanut)
description: Plant shelled seed about an inch and a half deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since peanuts push their flower stalks ('pegs') down into the soil to form pods underground and need friable soil for those pegs to penetrate easily. Virginia Jumbo is the classic large-seeded Virginia-type peanut behind most of the boiled and roasted-in-shell peanuts sold across the South, prized for producing the biggest pods and kernels of any common peanut type, typically two large seeds per pod. Hill soil slightly around the base of plants as they grow to give pegs an easier path into the ground, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and peg development, since drought stress at that stage sharply reduces yield. Dig the whole plant once leaves begin yellowing in fall, and cure pods in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before shelling or storing. Matures in 130–150 days from seed.

name: Virginia Mountain Mint (Native Perennial Aromatic Pollinator Mint)
description: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil; thin rhizome spread by division every 2–3 years if needed. Harvest fresh stems for herbal use any time before flowering. Virginia Mountain Mint (Pycnanthemum virginianum) is a native perennial herb of the mint family (Lamiaceae) native to eastern and central North America from the Atlantic coast west to the Great Plains — one of approximately 20 native Pycnanthemum species in North America, all of which share the common characteristic of intense, spearmint-like aroma from leaves and stems. Pycnanthemum species are among the most scientifically documented pollinator plants in eastern North American native plant research: the dense flat-topped clusters of small, two-lipped white flowers with purple markings attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees, with studies recording 200+ native bee species visiting Pycnanthemum in bloom. This extraordinary pollinator attraction makes Virginia Mountain Mint one of the highest-value native plants for residential pollinator gardens and meadow plantings. The aromatic leaves have culinary and traditional medicinal uses — dried leaves make a spearmint-character tea, fresh leaves can be used as a mint herb substitute, and the strong fragrance deters deer browsing. Virginia Mountain Mint is a robust, reliable native for moist meadow and garden borders where the spreading habit can be accommodated. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Virginia Mountain Mint (Southern Mountain Mint)
description: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia mountain mint is the most heat-tolerant and southeastern species of the mountain mints, thriving through the summer of zone 8–9 where its more northerly relatives like P. virginianum begin to decline. Pycnanthemum pycnanthemoides produces erect, branching stems with lance-shaped, strongly mint-scented leaves and the flat-topped clusters of tiny, white, purple-dotted flowers that are the genus hallmark, blooming July through September and attracting an astonishing diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, butterflies, and skippers. Mountain mints are among the most comprehensively documented native pollinator plants in eastern North America, with studies recording over 100 insect species on a single planting. The plant spreads by rhizomes into a colony but is not aggressive; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and share with other gardeners. Excellent in naturalistic meadow plantings, rain gardens, and native border plantings from Virginia through the Gulf Coast. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Virginia Peppergrass
description: Virginia Peppergrass is a native annual or biennial of open, disturbed ground, roadsides, and garden edges throughout eastern North America, producing a basal rosette of toothed, peppery-flavored leaves followed by upright racemes of tiny white flowers and distinctive round, notched, flattened seed pods that rattle pleasingly in the breeze. The young basal leaves are edible raw in salads, contributing a sharp, peppery, radish-like heat, and the ripe seed pods can be ground or crushed as a mild pepper substitute in cooking. Sow directly in fall in thin, well-drained, even nutrient-poor soil in full sun; it germinates readily in disturbed or compacted ground where other plants struggle. Once established it self-sows freely, naturalizing open areas with minimal effort. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Virginia Sweet Tomato
description: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, deeply prepared soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem and staking firmly to support the large fruits. Virginia Sweet is a stunning American heirloom bicolor beefsteak tomato with large, 1–2 pound fruits that are golden-yellow with dramatic red streaking on the skin and brilliant pink-red and golden-yellow marbled flesh that is as beautiful to look at as it is flavorful — sweet, rich, and low-acid. It is related to other bicolor heirlooms like Big Rainbow and striped varieties that are prized both for taste and visual appeal; the swirling interior color pattern is most pronounced in cool weather. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the yellow shoulder transitions fully from green. Matures in 78–90 days from transplant.

name: Virginia Wild Ginger (Little Brown Jug Ginger)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; Virginia wild ginger is a native evergreen groundcover of Appalachian and Piedmont forests, closely related to the little-brown-jug (Hexastylis arifolia) and sometimes confused with it. The heart-shaped to arrowhead-shaped, leathery, dark evergreen leaves are ornamental year-round, providing low, dense coverage under deciduous trees. The odd, reddish-brown, jug-shaped flowers are hidden under the leaves at ground level, pollinated by ground beetles and ants. Like all Hexastylis species, it spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeds modestly to naturalize in appropriate shade conditions. Distinguished from H. arifolia by its broader distribution extending into Virginia and Maryland and subtle leaf differences. More cold-hardy than H. arifolia. An excellent, low-maintenance evergreen groundcover for Appalachian native woodland gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Viroflay Spinach
description: Sow Viroflay seeds half an inch deep in cool soil, thinning to 4 to 6 inches apart for full-size plants. This vigorous French heirloom produces large, tender leaves up to 10 inches long with a mild, sweet taste. Harvest baby leaves early or let plants mature for hearty cooking greens, and keep the soil evenly moist. Grow it in the cool weather of spring, fall, or winter, since heat and long days trigger bolting. Matures in 45–55 days from seed.

name: Vista White Loquat (White-Fleshed Sherbet-Flavored Loquat)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; loquats tolerate poor soils and short dry spells once established but size and flavor improve with regular moisture during fruit development; thin heavy clusters for larger fruit and harvest when fully colored and slightly soft, since loquats do not continue ripening after picking. Vista White is a California-selected loquat grown mainly by home orchardists and specialty growers for its distinctive creamy white to pale-yellow flesh, a marked contrast to the orange flesh of widely grown cultivars like Premier and Big Jim. The round, light-yellow fruits hang in grape-like clusters of fifteen to twenty and have a delicate, very sweet, almost sherbet-like flavor with mild tang, making them popular for fresh eating. Trees bloom in fall and ripen fruit in late winter to spring, ahead of most other tree fruit, and tolerate periods of drought and a range of soil types once established as long as drainage is good and soil salinity is low. As with all loquats, the open flowers and developing fruit are more cold-sensitive than the tree itself, so a sheltered, south-facing planting site improves crop reliability in zone 8-9 gardens near the cooler edge of the loquat's range. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Vit Mâche (Corn Salad)
description: Sow seed thinly at a shallow depth in cool soil, since mâche germinates poorly once temperatures climb into summer range. Vit is a widely grown European strain prized for producing larger, rounder, more upright rosettes than generic corn salad, giving a better yield of tender leaves per plant. The mild, faintly nutty flavor and buttery texture make it a classic addition to winter salads, often paired with beets or walnuts in French cuisine. Rosettes tolerate hard frost and light snow cover, so plantings can be harvested through much of the winter with minimal protection. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Vitamin Green
description: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Vitamin Green is a non-heading Asian brassica green selected for extremely rapid growth, mild flavor, and excellent nutritional value — the name reflects its high vitamin content (particularly vitamins A, C, and K) relative to other leafy greens. The smooth, round to slightly oval, bright medium-green leaves are strikingly mild in flavor — among the mildest of all Asian brassica types, with a clean, grassy-vegetable taste more like spinach or mild bok choy than the mustardy pungency of standard Asian mustard greens. This mildness makes Vitamin Green accessible to people who find other Asian greens too strongly flavored. In the kitchen it is interchangeable with bok choy or baby spinach in virtually any preparation — stir-fries, soups, braising, steaming, and raw use in salads and baby green mixes. The combination of very rapid growth (30–45 days to full size, 20–25 days to baby green stage), mild flavor, and excellent nutritional content makes it one of the most practical cool-season greens for zone 9. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Vitaverde Cauliflower
description: Vitaverde produces a pale apple-green curd with the domed, tightly beaded texture of a classic cauliflower rather than the looser florets of broccoli, giving it a hybrid appearance often marketed as broccoflower. The lime-green color comes from chlorophyll in the curd tissue and carries a milder, slightly sweeter flavor than white cauliflower with no need for blanching or leaf-tying. It holds its curd quality in the field longer than many white types before the curd begins to open or discolor, giving a wider harvest window. Grow Vitaverde for a striking, easy-care alternative to white cauliflower that performs reliably without extra fussing. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Vitelotte Noire Potato (French Purple-Fleshed Fingerling)
description: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil; as a late-maturing fingerling it needs a full season to size up its knobby tubers. Vitelotte Noire is a classic French heirloom potato with deep purple skin and equally deep purple flesh throughout, nicknamed 'Truffe de Chine' (Chinese truffle) for its dark, irregular tuber shape, and prized by chefs for the striking color it brings to gratins, chips, and purées without losing much pigment when cooked. Its dense, nutty flavor and firm texture hold up well in roasted and sautéed preparations. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, and cure tubers in a cool, dark spot before storage. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Viva Italia Tomato (Hybrid Roma Paste Tomato)
description: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Viva Italia is an improved hybrid roma-type paste tomato that addresses the main weakness of heirloom Roma — its susceptibility to disease. An AAS (All-America Selections) winner, Viva Italia combines the thick-walled, low-moisture flesh and rich, concentrated paste-tomato flavor of traditional Roma with VFFNTA disease resistance (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Alternaria), making it far more reliable in humid climates and typical garden soils than open-pollinated Roma varieties. The determinate, compact (3–3.5 foot) plants produce large, concentrated sets of uniform, thick-skinned, 2–4 oz, elongated-oval, bright red fruits with very low moisture content and dense, meaty flesh — exactly what's needed for sauce, paste, sun-dried tomatoes, and canning. Because of the dense flesh and concentrated flavor, Viva Italia produces much higher yields of usable sauce per pound of fruit than wet, beefsteak-type tomatoes. An outstanding choice for serious sauce-makers who want disease resistance and reliability. Matures in 68–75 days from transplant.

name: Vivax Bamboo
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, contained within a rhizome barrier; vivax bamboo is one of the tallest, fastest-growing temperate bamboos, with culms reaching 25–45 feet and diameters of 2–3.5 inches — making it among the most productive timber bamboos available in zones 5–10. The spring shoots are edible and moderately sweet; the culms are strong and used for construction, fencing, and crafts. Its extreme cold hardiness (to about –10°F / USDA zone 5) makes it one of the few large-statured bamboos reliable in cold climates. CAUTION: Like all Phyllostachys species, vivax is a spreading 'running' bamboo with invasive potential — rhizome barriers are mandatory in all garden settings. The cultivar 'Aureocaulis' has yellow culms with green stripes. Matures in 365–1825 days from transplant.

name: Vivian Romaine Lettuce
description: Sow seed shallowly in cool weather, keeping the soil moist and cool for good germination, and make succession sowings for continuous salads. This emerald-green romaine forms tight heads that reach a striking 12 to 16 inches tall and 4 to 6 inches across, giving large, sturdy leaves ideal for salads and lettuce wraps. Its bolt resistance and vigorous growth let it hold longer into warm weather than many romaines. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Volkamer Lemon Rootstock
description: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Volkamer lemon is a vigorous, cold-hardy understock widely used in Gulf Coast home citrus production. A vigorous, cold-hardy lemon relative of uncertain hybrid origin, its own fruit is coarse and of little culinary value, but it is highly valued as a rootstock for producing large, fast-growing, precocious, and productive trees with notably better cold tolerance than many other citrus rootstocks, making it a common choice for home citrus trees in the marginal-climate Gulf South. Its vigor and cold hardiness have made it especially popular for backyard citrus in Texas, Louisiana, and coastal areas of the Gulf Coast where winter cold snaps threaten less hardy rootstocks. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and expect a large, fast-growing, heavily-bearing tree that will need ample permanent space. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Von Blackberry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Von is a trailing (dewberry-type) blackberry selected by the University of Georgia specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, with exceptional heat tolerance and disease resistance suited to the humid conditions of the lower South. Unlike the erect University of Arkansas varieties that were developed for upland conditions, Von was selected specifically for performance in the hot, humid, rainy conditions of coastal Georgia, the Florida panhandle, and Gulf Coast zone 9. The large, sweet, flavorful berries ripen in May–June in zone 9, earlier than most erect varieties. Von requires a trellis or fence to support its trailing, vining habit, but the trailing type has the advantage of naturally positioning the fruiting lateral branches where they receive maximum sun exposure. Disease resistance to orange rust and rosette disease is an important selection criterion in zone 9 where these diseases can be serious problems for susceptible trailing blackberry varieties. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Voodoo Child Dragon Fruit
description: Grow from cuttings taken from a healthy mother plant and support the vining stems on a post or arbor in full sun with fast-draining, cactus-style soil. This deep magenta-red-fleshed selection is grown by home collectors specifically for its intensely colored, richly flavored fruit, which stands out from the milder white-fleshed types. Because the succulent stems are damaged by hard freezes, Gulf Coast growers generally keep it container-grown so it can be moved to a garage or greenhouse whenever a freeze warning is issued. Fruit set improves with hand pollination shortly after the night-blooming flowers open, since many dragon fruit types are only partially self-fertile. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Vorlon Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy cage or stake support; Vorlon is a large beefsteak tomato bred by Tom Wagner, the Washington State plant breeder also responsible for Green Zebra, known for developing novel tomato colors and flavors. Vorlon produces large (often 12–20 ounce) fruits with a distinctive deep purple-to-near-black exterior that develops from sun exposure on the skin — the dark color comes from anthocyanin pigments (the same blue-purple compounds in blueberries and purple cabbage) that accumulate in the skin when exposed to sunlight. When sliced, Vorlon reveals a complex interior with dark-streaked red flesh and a rich, full-bodied, complex tomato flavor with earthy, wine-like undertones that distinguish dark tomato varieties from standard red types. The anthocyanin content in dark tomatoes like Vorlon represents significantly higher antioxidant levels than red-only tomatoes — a characteristic that has made dark-skinned tomatoes of interest in nutritional research. The dramatic appearance of the purple-black exterior with rich red interior when sliced makes Vorlon outstanding in salads and fresh presentations. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Vostorg Honeyberry (High-Vitamin C Siberian Haskap)
description: Vostorg is a Siberian-bred haskap released in the early 2010s and known for consistently large, heavily wax-coated blue-violet fruit — often over an inch long — and for carrying some of the highest vitamin C content measured among haskap cultivars in comparative trials. The sweet-tart flavor with a pronounced sour edge makes it popular fresh as well as processed. Like other haskap, it flowers very early in spring, often weeks before other fruiting shrubs, so choose a planting site that avoids frost pockets even though open blooms tolerate light freezes. Vostorg's Siberian origin gives it outstanding cold hardiness but, as with other haskap, it struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is best reserved for short-season northern gardens. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Vranja Quince (Fragrant Serbian Heirloom Quince)
description: Vranja is a Balkan quince selection that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in British and northern European gardens for its large, downy, pear-shaped fruit and unusually showy spring bloom of pale pink flowers up to two inches across. The species is native to mountain slopes and tolerates real winter cold, but flowers open early enough to need a sheltered, sun-baked spot so fruit has a long enough warm season to swell and perfume the air before frost. Trees are self-fertile and productive without a second cultivar nearby, though yields are typically moderate rather than heavy. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit turns deep golden-yellow and releases its strong floral aroma, then store briefly before cooking into jelly, paste, or preserves, since the raw flesh stays hard and astringent. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Vulcan Swiss Chard (Brilliant Red-Stemmed French Heirloom)
description: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to their final spacing, watering consistently to keep stalks tender and prevent bitterness. This French heirloom is grown chiefly for its glossy, deep crimson stalks and veins that hold their vivid color even after cooking, contrasting with dark green, slightly savoyed leaves. It is a dependable cut-and-come-again green that keeps producing new leaves from the crown for months. Matures in 55–60 days from seed.

name: VX211 Walnut Rootstock
description: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; VX211 is a vigorous clonal understock with improved crown gall tolerance, not grown for its own nuts. Another clonally propagated hybrid rootstock selection from the University of California walnut breeding program, it combines strong vigor and good tolerance of a range of soil conditions with improved resistance to crown gall compared to traditional seedling Paradox rootstock, while offering the propagation uniformity that clonal selections provide over genetically variable seedling stock. It has become a favored alternative to RX1 on sites where crown gall rather than Phytophthora or nematode pressure is the primary soil-borne concern. Graft a desired named English walnut variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect vigorous, uniform growth with improved resilience against crown gall infection. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Vydubetsky Cornelian Cherry (Red Star, Ukrainian Long-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Vydubetsky, sometimes marketed as Red Star, is a Ukrainian cornelian cherry cultivar released in 1990 by breeder Svitlana Klymenko at the M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden in Kyiv, selected for its unusually long, elongated dark-red fruit that can reach over an inch in length. It is one of the most productive named Cornus mas selections, with mature specimens reported to bear well over 100 pounds of fruit in a good year, and the flesh is tender yet firm with a sweet-tart, refreshing flavor suited to fresh eating once fully ripe as well as jams, syrups, and cordials. Like other cornelian cherries it opens small yellow flowers on bare branches in late winter, is extremely cold-hardy, and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban pollution once established. Harvest when fruit is deep red and slightly soft for the best flavor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: W. Murcott Afourer Mandarin (Late-Season Seedy Parent of Tango Mandarin)
description: Afourer, marketed in the US as W. Murcott, is a late-winter Moroccan-origin mandarin valued for deep orange color, intensely sweet flavor, and easy-peel skin, ripening after most other mandarins have finished. Unlike its seedless sport Tango, Afourer readily develops seeds when planted near other citrus, so growers wanting guaranteed seedless fruit should isolate it or choose Tango instead; those without nearby citrus can grow Afourer itself for a slightly richer, more complex flavor some tasters prefer. It is a vigorous, productive tree that bears heavily once established and benefits from fruit thinning in on years. Water deeply but infrequently and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for best fruit quality. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wabash American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)
description: Wabash is a historic Midwestern selection of native American persimmon valued for its large fruit size relative to wild trees and its vigorous, dependable growth. Orange-fleshed fruit ripens in fall and turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich once fully soft, but stays mouth-puckeringly astringent if eaten too early, so wait until fruit yields to gentle pressure or drops naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established, and its deep taproot makes it a long-lived, low-maintenance choice for food-forest or wildlife plantings. Provide a second genetically distinct native persimmon nearby for best fruit set unless a known self-fertile selection is planted, and remove root suckers regularly to keep it from forming a thicket. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wabash Pawpaw (Vigorous Large-Fruited Peterson Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Wabash is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected from Neal Peterson's long-running breeding program for its combination of large fruit size and notably vigorous, healthy tree growth. Fruit has the classic rich, tropical pawpaw flavor — often described as a cross between banana, mango, and custard — with good flesh-to-seed ratio. As with all pawpaws, Wabash is self-incompatible and requires a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination; hand-pollinating between two different cultivars' open flowers with a small brush improves fruit set in home gardens where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce. Mulch young trees well and keep soil consistently moist through the first two seasons, since pawpaw's shallow, fleshy root system is intolerant of drought while establishing; mature trees are considerably more drought-tolerant. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wacissa Mulberry (Florida Heirloom Deep-Purple Sweet Mulberry)
description: Wacissa was selected from a long-lived tree found in the small town of Wacissa in the Florida panhandle, and the original tree was still cropping heavily at nearly seventy years old. It bears abundant 1.5-inch, deep purple-black fruit with a rich, sweet flavor often compared to blackberry, on a fast-growing tree that tolerates poor soil and drought once established as well as periods of wet ground. A useful trait for Gulf Coast gardeners is its later, more conservative bud break compared with some other mulberry selections, which helps the spring flush avoid damage from a late frost. Trees can be kept large as shade trees or pruned hard and repeatedly to form a dense hedge, screen, or windbreak. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wagener Apple (Late-Keeping New York Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Wagener originated in New York State in 1791 and became a widely respected 19th-century American apple, valued for its crisp, juicy, well-balanced tart-sweet flesh and, notably, its long storage life, holding good eating quality well into winter under proper cold storage conditions long before mechanical refrigeration was common. The medium, red-striped fruit is a genuine dual-purpose apple, good for fresh eating as well as cooking, and it holds a place in apple breeding history as a parent of the modern cold-hardy Idared. The precocious, productive tree bears young and reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the longest keeping quality. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Waido Mizuna (Large-Leaf Mizuna)
description: Waido, meaning wide leaf in Japanese, is a larger-statured mizuna selection bred for bunching markets, with broader, less deeply cut leaves than standard mizuna and thicker, crisp petioles. Direct sow into fertile soil and keep evenly moist to encourage tender, mild-flavored growth. Whole heads can be cut for bunching or leaves picked individually for stir-fries and hot pot greens. Cold-hardy and slow to bolt compared to smaller mizuna types, making it a good choice for extended fall harvest. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Waimanalo Papaya
description: Waimanalo was developed by the University of Hawaii as a low-branching, compact papaya bred to resist mechanical damage and reduce losses from fruit fly infestation compared to older Hawaiian selections. The medium-large, round-to-oval fruit has thick orange flesh with good sugar content, and the short, sturdy trunk starts fruiting closer to the ground than many other papaya types, easing harvest. It performs best in a warm, sheltered spot with fast-draining soil, since papayas are highly susceptible to root rot in wet ground. Gulf Coast growers usually treat it as a fast-fruiting annual or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Waingaro Feijoa
description: Waingaro takes its name from the Waingaro district in New Zealand's Waikato region, an area associated with feijoa selection work outside the better-known Golden Bay breeding grounds, and produces medium to large oval fruit with sweet, aromatic flesh typical of the newer New Zealand dessert-type cultivars. The shrub grows with a sturdy upright habit and thick, leathery, silver-backed evergreen foliage that holds up well to wind and salt-tinged Gulf Coast breezes near the coast. Its heavy spring flush of white-and-crimson blossoms draws pollinating insects and produces the fleshy, sweet, edible petals feijoa growers often snack on before the fall fruit crop arrives. Full sun, well-drained slightly acidic soil, and even summer moisture bring out this cultivar's best fruit size, and mature plants need only an occasional shaping prune to stay productive and attractive as a hedge or specimen. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wakegi Onion (Japanese Bunching-Shallot Hybrid)
description: Plant divided bulb clusters in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wakegi onion is a sterile hybrid grown only from bulb divisions, never from seed, and multiplies quickly into a clump that can be split every year. A traditional Japanese hybrid between bulb onion and bunching onion, it produces slender, mild-flavored, scallion-like stalks from a clustering base of small bulbs, combining the easy perennial habit of a bunching onion with a slightly stronger, more onion-like flavor. Harvest by pulling whole young stalks as needed through fall, winter, and spring in mild climates, leaving several bulbs in place to keep the clump multiplying, or dig and divide the whole clump every one to two years to maintain vigor and share starts. It is far less prone to bolting than seed-grown bunching onions and provides a reliable, low-effort source of fresh green onions for most of the year. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Waldin Avocado
description: Waldin is one of the oldest named Florida dooryard avocados still commonly planted, valued for its early-to-midseason harvest and reliable heavy bearing on a vigorous, wind-tolerant tree. Fruit is medium to large, smooth-skinned, and pear-shaped with pale green, watery-textured flesh typical of the West Indian race, which lends good tolerance of Florida's hot, humid lowland conditions but less cold tolerance than Mexican-race cultivars. As a Type A flowering cultivar it benefits from a nearby Type B pollinator for heavier fruit set. Choose Waldin where summer heat and salt-air exposure near the coast are bigger concerns than winter cold, since it lacks the frost hardiness of Mexican-race selections. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Waldo Blackberry (First Thornless Trailing Bramble)
description: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, thornless trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since like other trailing types they will not support themselves. Waldo was released by the USDA-ARS breeding program in Oregon in 1989 as the first thornless trailing blackberry ever introduced, a milestone that made hand-harvesting far safer than with the thorny trailing types that preceded it. The berries are medium-sized with a notably high drupelet count, ripening late in the trailing-blackberry season, and the canes show good resistance to common foliar diseases. Waldo's flavor is considered milder and less aromatic than the thorny standard 'Marion', so it has mainly been used as a parent in later thornless breeding programs rather than planted widely on its own. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Walking Stick Cabbage (Jersey Cabbage, Jersey Kale)
description: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking young plants in windy sites and stripping lower leaves as they yellow to encourage the tall, straight stalk this heirloom is famous for. Walking Stick Cabbage, also called Jersey cabbage or Jersey kale, is a historic giant kale from the Channel Islands traditionally grown for two purposes at once: the young leaves are edible and used as livestock fodder or cooked greens, while the plant is left to grow over a full season into a remarkably tall, woody stalk that was traditionally dried, straightened, and varnished into walking sticks and canes, a cottage tradition dating back centuries on Jersey. In the vegetable garden it makes an unusual, dramatic vertical accent as well as a productive source of greens over many months, tolerating poor soil and coastal conditions well. Harvest lower leaves continuously through the growing season for eating, and let a stalk mature untouched at season's end if canes are wanted. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Walking Stick Collard (Tall Perennial Heirloom Collard from the Carolina and Gulf South Tradition)
description: Start seeds indoors; transplant to permanent location and allow to develop over multiple seasons. Harvest outer lower leaves as needed year-round. Walking Stick Collard is one of the most historically distinctive vegetables of the American South — a tall, perennial collard type that was maintained for generations in family gardens across the Carolinas, Georgia, and the Gulf South as a semi-permanent garden plant rather than an annual crop. The 'walking stick' in the name refers to the thick, woody stems that develop as the plant grows upward over multiple years: historical accounts describe Southern farmers and homesteaders harvesting old Walking Stick Collard stems, drying them, and using them as walking sticks, canes, and tool handles — a practical byproduct of a plant grown primarily for its edible leaves. The leaves are classic collard — large, blue-green, thick, and of the rich, mild-bitter flavor that defines Southern greens cuisine — harvested continuously from the lower stem as the plant elongates upward. A well-established Walking Stick Collard plant can produce leaves continuously for 3–5 years in zone 9's mild climate, making it a true perennial food plant for gardens where winter rarely kills brassicas completely. The variety is maintained by seed savers and small heirloom seed companies as a Southern heritage vegetable; it is not available in commercial mass-market seed catalogs but has been preserved through the living tradition of Southern kitchen gardens and organizations like Seed Savers Exchange and Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Walking Stick Collard's extraordinary height (sometimes reaching 6–8 feet) and its multi-year productive life make it one of the most distinctive and visually arresting vegetables possible in zone 9 gardens, forming a structural element with year-round productivity that no annual collard variety can match. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Walking Stick Kale (Jersey Kale)
description: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost, transplant after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; walking stick kale (Jersey kale) is a traditional biennial brassica of the Channel Islands and Cornwall, where it was grown for the extraordinary height its main stem achieves in the second year — up to 6–10 feet tall — with stems so strong and straight that they were traditionally dried, lacquered, and sold as walking sticks, canes, and umbrella handles, a traditional cottage industry on the Isle of Jersey. The large, dark green, curled leaves produced at the top of the tall stem are edible (though tough) throughout the growing season, and the plant is also fed to livestock. Primarily a curiosity and heritage vegetable today, prized by collectors of unusual brassicas. Requires staking as it grows taller. Harvest leaves from the base upward as needed, leaving the growing tip intact for continued height. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: Wall Germander
description: Surface-sow seeds or take 3 in softwood cuttings in late spring; cuttings are generally more reliable as germination can be slow. Wall germander is an ancient medicinal herb used historically as a bitter digestive tonic; it has glossy, dark-green, oak-like leaves and rosy-pink summer flowers that attract bees. Plant in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is extremely drought-tolerant once established and makes an excellent low edging or clipped knot-garden hedge. Trim after flowering to maintain a tidy, compact form; harvest small quantities of fresh foliage for occasional medicinal use. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Wall Rocket (Sand Rocket)
description: Broadcast seeds lightly over prepared soil and press in gently without covering, as the tiny seeds need light to germinate well; thin to 4-6 inches apart once seedlings are established and harvest the outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production. Wall rocket is a wilder, more pungent relative of common arugula, with deeply lobed, almost dandelion-like leaves that carry a sharper, more sulfurous edge and pair especially well with cured meats, strong cheeses, and dressed lentils. It thrives in poor, dry, even gravelly soils where most salad greens would fail, making it useful for difficult spots in the garden. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed each season and they will self-sow prolifically, often producing volunteers in cracks in paving, at wall bases, and in disturbed soil across the garden. Matures in 21–40 days from seed.

name: Walla Walla Bulb Onion
description: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out once the soil is workable, or sow in fall to overwinter in mild-winter regions. This famous long-day onion traveled from Italy to Walla Walla, Washington, and produces enormous, juicy, sweet bulbs that are one of the best for eating fresh. It matures early enough to grow as an intermediate-day type; these sweet onions do not store long, so enjoy them soon after harvest. Matures in 110–130 days from transplant.

name: Walla Walla Onion
description: Start Walla Walla seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and transplant seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This long-day heirloom produces exceptionally sweet, crisp, juicy yellow bulbs and performs best in northern gardens. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and keep the bed weeded while the large bulbs form. These onions are sweet but do not store long, so use them fresh soon after the tops fall and dry. Matures in 110–125 days from transplant.

name: Walter Tomato
description: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set determinate plants 2–3 feet apart in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Walter tomato was released by the University of Florida in 1963, the same year as Tropic, and quickly became a commercial and home garden staple in the Southeast for its reliable production, disease resistance, and compact determinate growth habit. It produces medium-large (6–8 oz), red, round fruits with smooth skin, firm flesh, and good canning and fresh-eating quality, with resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. Walter's determinate habit (which concentrates flowering and ripening into a defined period rather than producing continuously like indeterminate types) makes it efficient for gardeners who want a single large harvest for preserving and canning. Once the standard commercial processing tomato in Florida, it remains an important heirloom for Gulf Coast gardeners who need a reliably productive, disease-resistant, compact-season tomato. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Waltham 29 Broccoli
description: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after hardening off when temperatures are consistently below 80°F during the day. Waltham 29 broccoli was developed by the Waltham Field Station of the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 as an improvement over earlier open-pollinated varieties; for decades before hybrid broccoli varieties became dominant in the 1970s and 80s, Waltham 29 was the standard home garden and market broccoli. It produces a large, domed, blue-green to grey-green central head of excellent flavor and tight bead formation, followed by adequate sideshot production; it is notably more tolerant of fall frost than many varieties and holds well in the field without yellowing. Still widely grown for its reliable open-pollinated nature (seed-saveable), cold tolerance, and classic blue-green broccoli flavor. Excellent for fall production in zones 5–11. Matures in 74–85 days from transplant.

name: Waltham 29 Broccoli
description: Start Waltham 29 seeds indoors 5 to 6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants 18 to 24 inches apart in rich soil. This cold-tolerant heirloom is bred for fall harvests, producing large blue-green central heads followed by side shoots. Keep the plants well watered and feed with nitrogen to encourage big, tight heads. Cut the central head while the buds are still firm and closed, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Waltham 29 Broccoli
description: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. This heirloom is specially adapted to fall growing and produces 4 to 6 inch blue-green central heads followed by a prolific flush of side shoots. Cut the central head while the buds are still tight, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks; the plants tolerate frost well. Matures in 70–85 days from transplant.

name: Waltham Butternut Squash (Classic Long-Storing Winter Squash Heirloom)
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Waltham Butternut is the standard commercial and home garden butternut squash — developed by Robert Young at the Waltham Experiment Station in Massachusetts and recognized with an All-America Selections award for its exceptional production, uniformity, and storage quality. The classic cylindrical fruits with tan skin, small seed cavity, and large neck of deep-orange flesh represent the butternut ideal: consistent shape, excellent flavor, and long storage life (3–6 months at cool room temperature). The Cucurbita moschata species provides better heat and humidity tolerance than C. pepo winter squash types — allowing Waltham Butternut to succeed in Gulf South conditions where pepo types (acorn, Delicata) often struggle with disease and heat in late-season production. In zone 9, the most reliable production method is a late-summer planting (July–August direct sow) for a fall harvest (October–November) — the fall planting avoids peak summer heat during vulnerable early growth and produces during the cooler fall weather that improves storage quality. Cure harvested fruits for 10 days at 80–85°F to harden the skin and develop the characteristic butterscotch sweetness that distinguishes fully cured butternut from freshly harvested green fruit. Waltham Butternut vines spread extensively (6–10 feet) and require substantial garden space. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Waltham Butternut Winter Squash
description: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the long vines room to spread. This classic butternut yields four to five tan, richly sweet fruits per plant, and its solid stems help resist squash vine borers. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind and cure it in a warm, dry spot; properly cured butternut stores for months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup. Matures in 90–105 days from seed.

name: Waltham Washington Asparagus (Rust-Resistant Mary Washington Strain)
description: Waltham Washington was selected at the University of Massachusetts's Waltham Field Station from Mary Washington lines for improved cold hardiness and stronger resistance to asparagus rust, making it a reliable choice for shorter, colder growing seasons than the original Mary Washington tolerates well. Spears emerge thick and green with a light purple blush at the tightly closed tip, in the classic heirloom shape home gardeners expect. As an open-pollinated strain it produces both sexes, so female plants will drop red berries in late summer that can self-sow into the row if not managed. Allow two full seasons of unharvested fern growth before cutting begins, then harvest for six to eight weeks each spring once the bed is mature. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wampee (Wampi)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-protected conditions; wampee (wampi) is a Chinese subtropical fruit tree in the citrus family (Rutaceae) producing large drooping clusters of small, round, yellowish-white to golden fruits about the size of a large grape, with a thin, slightly oily skin and aromatic, translucent flesh that ranges from sweet to pleasantly acid-sweet, with a distinctive, complex, resinous-floral fragrance from essential oils in the skin. The flavor profile has notes of citrus, lychee, and a slight bitterness that makes it uniquely refreshing. Native to South China and widely grown in southern China, Vietnam, and Thailand, it has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and is a significant regional fruit crop in Guangdong. The fruits are eaten fresh, made into preserves and wine, and the essential oil from the rind is used in Chinese medicine and as a fragrance. It grows well in the humid subtropics of zones 9–11 and is more compact and manageable than many tropical fruit trees. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wando Pea (Heat-Tolerant Shelling Pea)
description: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep 2–6 weeks before last frost; Wando tolerates both cool and moderately warm conditions and is particularly valuable for later-season spring planting in Southern zones. Wando pea was developed by USDA and named for the Wando River in the Charleston, South Carolina area, reflecting its adaptation to warm Southern conditions. Unlike most shelling peas that drop flowers and fail to set pods when temperatures rise above 75°F, Wando continues producing pods at temperatures 5–10°F warmer than other varieties, extending the harvest window in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 24–30 inch plants produce smooth-seeded peas (less sweet than wrinkled but better adapted to warm-soil planting) in pods with 6–8 peas; the flavor is good. Exceptionally valuable for fall pea production in zones 7–10 when planted in late August–September. Matures in 68–75 days from seed.

name: Wando Shelling Pea
description: Direct sow seed as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, since peas germinate and grow best in cool soil. Introduced in 1943 as a cross between Laxton's Progress and Perfection, this heirloom is both cold tolerant for early sowing and more heat tolerant than most peas, extending the season on both ends. The sturdy 24 to 30 inch plants carry seven to nine medium peas per pod; provide light support and pick regularly to keep them producing. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Wani Mango (Binjai, Jack Mango)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; requires consistent rainfall or irrigation during fruit development. Mangifera caesia (wani mango or binjai) is a large Mangifera species native to the humid lowland rainforests of Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Sarawak and Sabah (Malaysian Borneo), where it is planted around villages and sometimes bears enormous quantities of fruits. The fruits are remarkable: large (4–6 inches long), elongated-oblong to kidney-shaped, pale green to yellowish-white when ripe — larger on average than common mangoes — with white to pale-yellow flesh. The flavor is more distinctly turpentine-acidic than common mango, with a sweetness that varies considerably by seedling; selected clones can be mild and pleasant. The flesh is rather fibrous and the skin is not eaten. In Sarawak, wani fruits are sold fresh in markets and eaten as a fresh fruit, in rujak (spicy fruit salads), and processed into pickles. The bark and young leaves have traditional medicinal uses in Malaysian herbal medicine. Wani requires a genuinely tropical, hot, humid, low-frost-risk climate and is suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental United States (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). A collectors' fruit tree for the most dedicated tropical fruit enthusiast. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wapsie Valley Corn (Iowa Heirloom Dent-Flint Corn)
description: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; its relatively short season and dent-flint hybrid vigor make it forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt. Wapsie Valley is an Iowa heirloom named for the Wapsipinicon River valley and preserved by Sand Hill Preservation Farm, combining dent and flint characteristics in the same ears along with striking orange, red, and multicolor kernels. It is valued both for its ornamental appeal on the stalk and for producing flavorful cornmeal, and it has become a favorite among small-scale growers seeking a productive, easy-to-grow open-pollinated corn with real regional history. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato (Iowa Heirloom Peach-Yellow Sweet Cherry Tomato)
description: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield gently to pressure and separate easily from the calyx. Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato is an Iowa heritage cherry tomato distinguished by its pale peach-yellow coloration and the exceptionally sweet, low-acid flavor that develops as fruits ripen fully. The name refers to both the peach-like appearance of the ripe fruit (the pale skin with a subtle blushed tinge on the sunny side closely resembles a small yellow peach) and the Wapsipinicon River region of northeastern Iowa where the variety was grown and saved by farm families through the twentieth century. The variety reached national seed-saver networks through the Seed Savers Exchange network and has been grown in trial gardens across the country where it consistently earns high marks for flavor complexity — a balance of sweetness with sufficient acid to provide depth, rather than the flat sweetness of some low-acid cherry types. As an indeterminate variety, Wapsipinicon Peach continues to grow and produce throughout a long warm season, which is particularly advantageous in zone 9 where the long frost-free period extends production well into fall. Fruits cluster in modest-sized trusses and are best harvested when fully colored and just soft; they have a thinner skin than many modern cherry types, which is prized for fresh eating but means they are more susceptible to cracking after rain or irrigation following dry periods. Cage or stake firmly and prune suckers selectively to manage plant size and improve air circulation in humid conditions. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Warba Potato
description: Warba was developed at the University of Minnesota and released in the 1930s, valued ever since as an exceptionally early, reliable red-skinned potato for gardeners who want new potatoes as soon as possible after planting. The round tubers have light red skin and white flesh with good flavor, best eaten fresh since Warba does not store as well as later-season varieties. Its very short season makes it a practical option for a Gulf Coast spring potato crop planted in late winter, since it can be dug well before summer heat and humidity set in. Hill soil around the base of the plants as they grow to protect the shallow tubers and increase yield. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Warren 346 Pecan (Early-Ripening Scab-Resistant Northern Native Pecan)
description: Warren 346 was selected from a grove of native pecan trees owned by Dale Warren near Chillicothe, Missouri, and has become a benchmark early-ripening cultivar for northern pecan growing regions. Its defining trait is very early ripening, with shuck split beginning as early as the last week of August and nuts starting to fall free by mid-September, well ahead of most Gulf South cultivars. Nuts are small, about 92 per pound, but well filled at 51% kernel. The tree is notably scab resistant, though it is more susceptible to powdery mildew than many Gulf South cultivars, so watch for that disease instead. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it with a Type II pollinator nearby. Matures in 1825–2920 days from transplant.

name: Warren Pear (Mississippi Heirloom Pear)
description: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Warren is an outstanding southern heirloom pear discovered in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, by T.O. Warren around 1960 — a chance seedling that produces buttery, very sweet, nearly grit-free fruit with the silky texture of a fine European dessert pear. This exceptional fruit quality, combined with good fire blight resistance (the most devastating pear disease in humid southern climates), has made Warren one of the most highly regarded pear varieties for the Gulf South in recent decades. Most European pears are highly susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), the bacterial disease that kills branches and causes heavy losses in hot, humid climates — Warren's relative resistance makes it a practical choice where standard European pears like Bartlett routinely fail. The medium-to-large, greenish-yellow fruits ripen in August in zone 9 and require off-tree ripening (store at room temperature after harvest) to reach their full, buttery sweetness. Plant with Hood or Kieffer for cross-pollination. Warren is not always easy to find at nurseries but is available from regional southern specialty nurseries and bare-root mail-order sources. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Warrior Bunching Onion
description: Direct sow seed in spring for summer harvests, thinning to about an inch apart, or leave clumps to overwinter. This 2016 All-America Selections winner is a cold-hardy bunching onion with crisp texture and a strong, pungent flavor, and it resists pink root rot. Harvest by pulling whole clusters of upright green stalks, or cut individual stems and let the plants regrow for repeated cut-and-come-again picking. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Warsaw Pasta Squash (Polish Bush Spaghetti Squash)
description: Warsaw Pasta is a spaghetti-type squash from Poland, offered in the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Compact, disease-resistant bush plants bear pale yellow, elongated-oval fruits weighing about 2-5 lbs. When cooked, the fine-grained flesh separates into tender, mild-flavored strands like traditional spaghetti squash, and the bush habit makes it a good choice for gardeners with limited vine space. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Warted Hubbard Squash (True Hubbard)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, in hills enriched with compost, spacing 5–7 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill and provide consistent moisture through the long growing season. True Hubbard is the heavily warted, dark blue-green Hubbard squash that was a staple of 19th-century New England kitchens; fruits weigh 10–20 pounds and have extremely hard, deeply ribbed and warted blue-green skin and dense, dry, bright orange flesh with outstanding sweet, nutty flavor. The exceptional storage quality — fruits in good condition can last 6 months or more at cool temperatures — made it the premier cellar squash before canning became widespread. Harvest only after the vine has fully died back and the rind cannot be dented with a thumbnail; cure for 2 weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to cold storage. Matures in 100–115 days from seed.

name: Warty Goblin Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, giving vines 6 feet of room to sprawl. Warty Goblin is a novelty hybrid pumpkin bred purely for eerie ornamental appeal, producing 8-20 pound fruit with a hard orange rind studded in dense, gnarled green warts that persist for weeks after harvest before slowly fading. The plants show useful intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, helping the vines stay productive later into the season than many older open-pollinated types. Because the flesh is stringy and thin compared to culinary pumpkins, Warty Goblin is grown strictly for Halloween decorating rather than cooking; harvest once the rind has fully hardened and cure briefly before display. Matures in 100–105 days from seed.

name: Wasabi (Japanese Horseradish)
description: Plant in constantly moist, cool, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; wasabi is among the most challenging and most coveted of culinary herbs — the genuine pungent root condiment used in Japanese cuisine is irreplaceable by the horseradish-and-green-dye substitute sold widely as 'wasabi paste.' It grows naturally along cool, shaded mountain stream banks in Japan, where it is cultivated in channels of continuously flowing, mineral-rich spring water under dense forest canopy. The combination of strict cool-temperature requirements (above 68°F it declines, above 80°F it may die), full shade, and consistently high, reliable moisture makes it one of the most exacting herbs to grow in most American gardens. It produces handsome, heart-shaped, glossy leaves on long petioles that are attractive in a shaded, moist position, and after 18–24 months the thick, knobby, pale-green rhizome is ready to harvest and freshly grate — releasing the volatile, sinus-clearing, horseradish-like compounds far more nuanced and complex than anything in a tube. In zones 8–10 it can succeed in deeply shaded, constantly moist, cool microclimates such as the north-facing side of a house or under dense tree canopy near water. Matures in 540–730 days from transplant.

name: Wasabi (Japanese Horseradish)
description: Plant in consistently moist, cool, well-oxygenated, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial to full shade; wasabi is one of the most challenging and rewarding edible plants a gardener can grow, requiring very cool temperatures (46–70°F) and near-constant moisture. In Japan it grows along cold mountain streams in deep shade where water temperature remains near 55°F year-round. The thick rhizome (the 'root') takes 12–18 months to reach harvest size, grated fresh at the table in a circular motion on a sharkskin grater to produce the intensely pungent, clean-heat paste. The authentic flavor is entirely different from the horseradish-and-dye paste sold as 'wasabi' in most restaurants. In zone 7–8, wasabi can be grown in a deeply shaded, cool, constantly moist garden bed or container with refrigerated-water irrigation; in zone 9 it requires careful site selection, mulching to keep roots cool, and may struggle in summer heat. The large, heart-shaped leaves are also edible and pungent. Matures in 365–540 days from transplant.

name: Wasabi Arugula (Wasabi Rocket)
description: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks. This selection of salad arugula is bred for an intense, sinus-clearing heat reminiscent of true wasabi, with deeply lobed, dark green leaves that pack noticeably more pungency than standard arugula, especially as plants mature or experience heat or drought stress. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in mixed salads, or let plants grow larger for a bold, spicy addition to sandwiches and cooked greens where its heat mellows somewhat with cooking. Partial shade in warm climates helps delay bolting and keeps the intense flavor from becoming overwhelming; keep soil consistently moist to slow premature flowering. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Wasabina (Wasabi Mustard Green)
description: Wasabina is a mizuna-type mustard green selected for a sharp, wasabi-like bite that adds punch to salad mixes without needing actual wasabi root. Direct sow shallowly into rich soil and grow as a cut-and-come-again crop, snipping the glossy, deeply serrated leaves at baby size for the mildest, most versatile flavor. It thrives in cool spring and fall conditions and tends to bolt in summer heat, so succession sow every few weeks for continuous harvest. Use sparingly as a spicy accent in mesclun mixes, sandwiches, or sushi-style garnishes. Matures in 21–35 days from seed.

name: Washday Southern Pea (Quick-Cooking Tennessee Heirloom Cowpea)
description: Washday is an old-time Tennessee heirloom southern pea, so named because its small cream-colored seeds with dark hilums cooked up quickly enough to fit into a busy laundry day. Half-runner vines set clusters of 3-4 pods, each 5-6 inches long, for relatively easy picking despite the vining habit. It is now a rare, at-risk heirloom, listed among threatened Place-Based Foods of Appalachia varieties, making it a good conservation choice for gardeners wanting to keep an old regional pea in circulation. Matures in 75–80 days from seed.

name: Washington Navel Orange (Classic Seedless Navel Orange)
description: Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil, keeping the graft union above the soil line, and water deeply and regularly while the tree establishes its root system. Washington Navel traces to a bud sport discovered in Bahia, Brazil in the early 1800s and became the foundation of the California citrus industry after Eliza Tibbets planted budwood from it in Riverside in 1873; it remains the standard by which other navel oranges are judged, prized for its large, easy-peeling, essentially seedless fruit with sweet, richly flavored flesh and the small secondary "navel" fruit embedded at the blossom end. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree for weeks without losing quality, but the tree itself is notably more cold-sensitive than many other sweet oranges, so gulf coast growers outside the mildest coastal pockets should plant it in a warm microclimate or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Fertilize lightly but regularly through the growing season and thin out crossing or dead wood in late winter to keep the canopy open. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Water Apple (Watery Rose Apple, Bell Fruit)
description: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple tolerates periodic waterlogging and is well-suited to wet, low-lying areas. Syzygium aqueum (water apple or watery rose apple) is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia that produces the most 'watery' of all the rose apple relatives — distinctive, bell-shaped to pear-shaped fruits (1.5–2 inches long) in white, pale pink, or red, with an extremely high water content (as the name suggests), a thin, glossy skin, crisp texture, and a very mild, barely-sweet, cucumber-like flavor. The fruit is refreshing rather than richly flavored — in tropical heat, the high water content makes water apple a thirst-quenching fruit eaten fresh as a hydrating snack, cut into slices and served with salt and chili, or made into a light agua fresca. The tree is notably tolerant of wet soils and periodic flooding compared to other Syzygium species — it grows naturally along stream banks and in seasonal swamps in its native habitat. It is distinctly different from the rose apple (S. jambos) in its smaller, lighter, more watery fruit, smaller tree size, and tolerance of wet conditions. Widely grown in home gardens throughout Southeast Asia and the Philippines. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Water Caltrop (Bat Nut, Water Chestnut of Europe)
description: Place fresh nuts in shallow, still water in full sun after last frost; water caltrop is a floating aquatic annual with attractive diamond-shaped floating leaves and distinctive 4-horned nut fruits (resembling a bat or medieval caltrop weapon) that have been consumed in Asia and Europe since the Neolithic period. The large starchy nuts are boiled, roasted, or eaten raw and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor; they are still commonly sold in Chinese, Japanese, and South Asian markets. Listed as invasive in many US states due to rapid spread and choking of natural waterways — only cultivate in well-contained, sealed garden ponds from which fruits are thoroughly collected to prevent seed escape. Historically important in China, where it is among the most ancient cultivated aquatic crops. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Water Celery
description: Plant divisions in consistently wet soil, shallow water, or at pond margins in partial shade to full sun; water celery (water parsley, minari, Japanese parsley) is an East Asian aquatic edible herb widely consumed in Korean, Japanese, and Chinese cuisines — fresh young stems and leaves have a crisp texture and fresh, parsley-celery flavor that makes them excellent in Korean naengmyeon (cold noodles), doenjang-jjigae (soybean paste soup), japchae, salads, and as a garnish. It grows naturally in shallow streams, rice paddies, and wet meadows, making it an excellent functional plant for rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and ornamental pond margins where few edible plants thrive. The lacy, finely divided, bright-green foliage creates an ornamental effect at the water's edge, and the plant spreads steadily by stolons in ideal wet conditions to create dense, productive colonies. A variegated cultivar ('Flamingo') with pink, white, and green foliage is grown as an ornamental. Harvest the young stem tips continuously for kitchen use. Avoid consuming the related O. crocata (hemlock water dropwort), which is highly toxic. Matures in 45–75 days from transplant.

name: Water Chestnut
description: Sprout small corms in a tray of moist soil indoors a few weeks before transplanting; plant sprouted corms 1–2 inches deep in the mud bottom of containers, tubs, or shallow water features kept filled to 2–4 inches above the soil surface. Water chestnuts are tropical grass-like sedges grown for their crunchy, sweet corms that form in the mud at the base of the rush-like stems. Drain the growing container in early fall before frost and allow the foliage to die back completely, then harvest corms by sifting through the mud; the crisp, mild corms can be eaten raw or cooked and retain their crunch even after stir-frying. In frost-prone climates store harvested corms in moist sand in a cool (40°F) location and re-plant the following spring. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Water Hickory
description: Water Hickory is the hickory of the riverine swamps, bottomland hardwood forests, and floodplain edges of the southeastern coastal plain, native from Virginia to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas, where it grows alongside bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp chestnut oak in the seasonally flooded alluvial soils of river terraces and floodplain edges. Its small, thin-shelled nuts are very bitter and not generally eaten by people, but they are an important food for wood ducks, squirrels, and wild turkeys in bottomland habitat — waterfowl consume large quantities of the nuts that fall into flooded bottomland pools in fall. Like all hickories, Water Hickory is slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with the deep taproot making transplanting nearly impossible after the first year of growth; direct-seed into the permanent planting site in fall for best results. Grow in moist to periodically flooded, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil in full sun — the only hickory species reliably tolerant of extended seasonal flooding. Matures in 3650–7300 days from seed.

name: Water Hyssop (Brahmi, Bacopa)
description: Plant in saturated to moist, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; water hyssop is an aquatic or semi-aquatic plant that thrives in shallow water, at pond margins, and in consistently wet garden beds — it will not thrive in dry or even moderately dry conditions. Bacopa monnieri (water hyssop or brahmi) is a creeping, aquatic to semi-aquatic herb native to wetlands across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, including the southeastern United States; in Ayurvedic medicine, brahmi is one of the most revered medicinal herbs, used for centuries as a cognitive enhancer and adaptogen to support memory, concentration, and anxiety reduction — modern pharmacological research has partially supported these traditional uses, identifying bacosides as the active compounds. The fleshy, succulent, oblong leaves and small, white to pale-blue 4-petaled flowers identify the plant in the wild; in cultivation it is grown in water gardens, at pond margins, and in constantly moist beds. In zone 9 gardens it grows as a year-round perennial in moist areas and may naturalize. The botanical Bacopa monnieri is completely different from the ornamental Sutera cordata (also marketed as 'Bacopa' — see separate entry). Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Water Mimosa (Sensitive Neptunia, Floating Neptunia)
description: Root stem cuttings in shallow water or wet mud in full sun; water mimosa (Neptunia oleracea) is an aquatic legume of tropical Asia, Africa, and the Americas, floating on the surface of ponds, ditches, and slow-moving water with spongy, air-filled white stems that provide buoyancy. The young shoots, leaves, and flower buds are widely eaten as a vegetable in Thai, Vietnamese, and Southeast Asian cuisine — blanched or stir-fried with a mild, crisp texture and slightly mucilaginous character similar to water spinach. The leaves also fold up when touched, like the related sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica). Caution: it is listed as invasive in Florida and should be grown only in contained water features in that state; elsewhere it is an interesting aquatic edible for warm-climate water gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Water Mint
description: Plant in moist to wet soil or at the margin of a pond or stream in partial shade; water mint is the wild European native mint from which the widely planted peppermint (Mentha x piperita) was bred as a hybrid with spearmint, and it retains a strong, cool menthol fragrance in its leaves and stems. It is one of the most shade- and moisture-tolerant of all mints, making it uniquely valuable for the shaded bog garden, rain garden, or pond margin where other herbs struggle. The strongly scented leaves are used exactly like other culinary mints — in teas, as a culinary herb, in drinks, and for fragrance. Dense clusters of lilac-mauve flowers in summer and fall attract an outstanding variety of pollinators, particularly hoverflies, bumblebees, and small native bees. Like all mints, it spreads by underground stolons and should be contained with buried barriers or grown in sunken pots where spread is unwanted. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Water Pepper (Smartweed, Tade, Marsh Pepper Knotweed)
description: Sow seed shallowly into wet, rich soil or shallow standing water in full sun, thinning seedlings once established; the plant self-sows readily, so many gardeners simply let a small patch persist year to year. Young leaves and sprouts carry a sharp, peppery bite from a compound related to capsaicin and are used fresh in Japanese cuisine, most famously as benitade, the tiny red-leaved sprouts served with sashimi, and historically as a pungent seasoning across Europe before black pepper became widely available. Harvest leaves continually through summer for the strongest heat and pinch flower spikes to keep foliage production going. Because it spreads by seed in wet ground, site it where naturalizing is welcome rather than near sensitive wetlands. Matures in 45–60 days from seed.

name: Water Rose Apple (Water Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; water rose apple is a tropical Asian Syzygium closely related to the wax jambu (S. samarangense) and produces similar bell-shaped, hollow fruits that are crunchy, mildly sweet, and extremely refreshing with a high water content — as the name suggests. The fruits range from white to pale pink and are eaten fresh as a cooling fruit, particularly popular in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines where they are sold by street vendors. The tree is medium-sized and can be kept more compact than many tropical fruit trees. It bears fruit prolifically in the tropics and is beginning to appear in specialty tropical fruit nurseries in Florida. In zone 9a, grow in a large container and move indoors in winter; the fruits are produced year-round in frost-free conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from seed.

name: Water Spinach (Kangkong, Morning Glory Vine)
description: Direct sow or root stem cuttings after frost in rich, moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; water spinach (kangkong in Filipino/Malaysian, rau muống in Vietnamese, ong choy in Cantonese) is one of the most important leafy green vegetables in Southeast, South, and East Asian cuisines, prized for its mild flavor, tender texture, and extremely rapid growth in warm, humid weather — it can be harvested in as little as 30 days from planting and can produce multiple harvests per season. The hollow stems and young leaf tips are stir-fried in garlic and oyster sauce in countless Southeast Asian dishes. It grows prolifically in the heat and humidity of zone 9–12 and is one of the most productive warm-season greens available. Important regulatory note: Ipomoea aquatica is classified as a federal noxious weed in the US and cultivation may require a state permit in some states — verify local regulations before growing. In Florida and other Gulf states it should be grown in contained beds well away from natural waterways. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Watercress
description: Sow seed on the surface of consistently moist, fertile soil near a stream, pond edge, or other reliably wet site; watercress requires more water than almost any other salad green. In garden beds without standing water, water deeply every day and mulch heavily to retain moisture. Harvest stem tips of 4–6 in regularly to encourage bushy growth; the plant becomes bitter and coarse after flowering. Succession plantings from rooted stem cuttings placed in shallow water provide a continuous supply through the cool season. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: Watergate Muscadine Grape
description: Watergate is a bronze-fruited muscadine grown mainly for fresh eating, producing large berries with a good, sweet flavor. The skin runs a bit tougher than some fresh-market bronze selections, which makes the fruit resist splitting and hold well after picking, though individual berries within a cluster tend to color and ripen unevenly rather than all at once. Because it is female-flowered, Watergate needs a nearby self-fertile or male vine to set a crop and is best used as a companion selection alongside a perfect-flowered variety rather than as a stand-alone planting. Site it on a sturdy arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, and pick clusters over several passes as berries finish coloring. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Waterleaf (Gbure, West African Talinum Leaf Vegetable)
description: Sow seed shallowly or root stem cuttings directly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the bed consistently damp since this succulent-leaved green wilts quickly in dry conditions. Waterleaf, known as gbure in Yoruba and grown widely across West Africa, is a fast-growing, heat-loving leafy green with thick, glossy, mildly mucilaginous leaves used much like spinach in soups and stews, most famously in Nigerian edikang ikong soup. The plant grows as a spreading, succulent-stemmed perennial in frost-free climates but is easily grown as a warm-season annual elsewhere, tolerating both the intense heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer that stresses many temperate greens. Harvest by pinching young stem tips and leaves regularly, which encourages new branching and keeps a steady supply of tender growth; plants regrow quickly after cutting. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: Waterleaf (Philippine Spinach, Lagos Spinach)
description: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in full sun to part shade in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production.
