Talinum fruticosum (waterleaf, Philippine spinach, or Lagos spinach) is a widespread tropical leafy vegetable native to South America but naturalized and cultivated throughout the tropics of Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean — it is one of the most important leafy green vegetables in West African cuisines (especially Nigerian cooking, where it is called 'waterleaf' or 'gbure') and is increasingly grown in Southeast Asian communities across the United States. The thick, succulent, slightly mucilaginous leaves are highly nutritious (rich in protein, iron, calcium, and vitamins) and are cooked in soups, stews, and stir-fries much like spinach — they have a mild, pleasant flavor that intensifies slightly when cooked. The plant produces cheerful, tiny, bright-pink, five-petaled flowers continuously through the growing season. It is extremely heat-tolerant and productive during Gulf Coast summers when cool-season greens have long expired, filling the important summer greens gap in zone 9 gardens. Self-seeds readily in warm climates. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Watermelon
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, sandy loam hills with generous compost worked in; watermelons thrive with long, hot summers. Avoid overhead irrigation once fruits are sizing up, as uneven moisture causes cracking. Ripeness indicators include a dull surface sheen replacing the glossy skin, a cream or yellow ground spot on the underside, and a dry tendril nearest the fruit. Thump the fruit and listen for a deep, hollow resonance to confirm ripeness. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Watermelon Beefsteak Tomato (West Virginia Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the very heavy fruit. Watermelon Beefsteak is a West Virginia heirloom dating to the 1800s, later listed in a 1958 seed catalog, that produces huge, pink-skinned beefsteak fruit with purplish-red flesh reminiscent of watermelon coloring, weighing up to 1-2 pounds at maturity. The flavor is mild, juicy, and sweet, and the large flattened fruit is prized for slicing into broad rounds for sandwiches and salads. Matures in 75–85 days from transplant.

name: Watermelon Radish
description: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and compaction; Watermelon Radish is a Chinese heirloom daikon-type radish producing large (golf ball to small apple sized), round roots with an unremarkable white-green exterior that opens to reveal a dramatically vivid magenta-pink interior — when sliced crosswise the cross-section closely resembles a miniature watermelon, with the pale green rind and pink-red interior creating the watermelon pattern that gives this radish its common name. The visual reveal of slicing a Watermelon Radish is one of the most surprising in the vegetable garden — the dramatic interior color makes it the most visually striking vegetable for salads, garnishes, and decorative vegetable presentations. The flavor is milder, sweeter, and less pungent than small red radishes, with only moderate spiciness and a crisp, juicy texture. The large size provides substantial raw radish slices for salads, vegetable platters, and pickled preparations. Fall-grown roots develop the most vivid pink color. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: Watermelon Radish
description: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in loose, deeply prepared, stone-free soil in late summer or early fall; thin seedlings to 4–6 inches for proper root development. Watermelon radish is a Chinese heirloom daikon type with a pale green exterior that conceals a vivid magenta-to-pink interior resembling watermelon flesh. Fall planting is strongly preferred over spring — cool nights concentrate sugars and deepen the interior color while reducing pungency. Harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter; slice thinly for salads, pickle in rice vinegar, or roast where the color intensifies to brilliant crimson. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: Wattleseed (Elegant Wattle, Bramble Wattle)
description: Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free; this arid-zone Australian shrub tolerates drought, poor soil, and salinity once established. The ripe, dried seed pods are harvested, roasted, and ground into wattleseed, an Aboriginal bushfood staple with a nutty, roasted-coffee, caramel flavor used to season breads, ice cream, and native spice blends. Prune lightly after seed harvest to maintain a manageable shrub form and encourage a fuller next season's pod set. Matures in 730–1095 days from seed.

name: Wavy Bay Laurel (Pie Crust Bay)
description: Site 'Crispa' in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; once established it needs little supplemental water and tolerates the same dry-summer conditions as the species. This dense, pyramidal cultivar is grown for its tightly undulating, crimped leaf margins — the wavy 'pie crust' edge is most pronounced on container-grown plants and gives the foliage a distinctive ruffled texture that stands out in wreaths and holiday arrangements. Small inconspicuous yellow flowers appear in spring, and the aromatic leaves can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like ordinary bay laurel. Give it room to grow, since it is a vigorous, fast-growing selection with an assertive root system best kept away from foundations or hardscaping, and protect container specimens when temperatures drop much below 12°F. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wavyleaf Oregon Grape (Undulata Mahonia)
description: Grow in ordinary, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Undulata tolerates more direct sun and dry spells than most other Oregon grape selections once its roots are established. Its glossy, spiny-toothed leaflets are distinctively crimped and wavy along the margins, giving the foliage a rippled, more refined texture than the flat-leaved species, and it holds a good deep green through winter with less bronzing. Dense clusters of fragrant yellow flowers open in early to mid spring, followed by dusty blue-black berries. It suckers modestly to form a tight, uniform mass, which combined with its density has made it a popular choice for informal flowering hedges and mixed shrub borders; prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wax Apple (Java Apple, Rose Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax apple thrives in tropical lowland conditions with high humidity and warm temperatures year-round. Syzygium samarangense (wax apple or Java apple) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Andaman Islands, widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia for its distinctive, pear-shaped to bell-shaped fruit with thin, waxy, translucent red to deep-red (or white, green, or pink depending on variety) skin, crispy, spongy, mildly sweet flesh, and a hollow, air-filled core with a rose-water scent — the fresh eating experience is unlike any other fruit, refreshingly crisp and very mildly sweet. The tree is evergreen with large, oval, glossy leaves and produces clusters of showy white to pale-pink, brush-like flowers (typical of the Myrtaceae family) followed by fruits in clusters. In the United States, wax apple cultivation is primarily limited to southern Florida and Hawaii; in zone 9, container culture or greenhouse growing is required. Named varieties include 'Jambu Air' (very dark red, sweet) and 'Pearl' (white-green, milder flavor). Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wax Currant
description: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; wax currant is a compact, twiggy shrub with small, rounded, waxy-textured leaves and tubular, pale pink to whitish spring flowers that are visited by early-season bees and occasional hummingbirds. Small, bright red, glossy berries ripen in summer and are edible, though quite tart and seedy, generally best used cooked into jelly or syrup rather than eaten fresh out of hand. It is markedly more drought tolerant than most cultivated currants and gooseberries, thriving in the same dry, rocky, low-fertility soils found on sagebrush foothills and canyon slopes throughout its native range. Prune out the oldest stems periodically to renew productive wood, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, both of which encourage lush, mildew-prone growth in this otherwise tough, low-maintenance native shrub. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wax Jambu (Java Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax jambu tolerates brief flooding better than most tropical fruits and grows well near water features. Trees are self-fertile and fruit heavily along the branches — a single mature tree produces hundreds of bell-shaped, crisp, mildly sweet fruits per season. Fertilize three times per year with a balanced fertilizer; maintain a regular irrigation schedule during flowering and fruiting to prevent premature fruit drop. Harvest when fruits reach their full color (pink, red, or white depending on variety) and the waxy skin is firm and glossy; the spongy flesh has a very short shelf life and is best eaten within a day or two of picking. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wax Myrtle
description: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils and thrives in coastal and inland settings alike. Myrica cerifera is a fast-growing, aromatic, nitrogen-fixing native evergreen shrub or small tree of the Southeast, valued for its densely branched form that provides excellent year-round cover, nesting habitat, and foraging sites for wildlife; the distinctive blue-gray, waxy-coated berries produced in dense clusters along the stems attract over 40 bird species including yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and bluebirds. Plant in groupings to form evergreen screens or wildlife hedgerows, and allow the plant to grow to its natural multi-stemmed form for maximum habitat value. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wax Myrtle (Southern Wax Myrtle, Bayberry)
description: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; minimal care once established. Morella cerifera (southern wax myrtle or bayberry) is one of the most ecologically important and garden-useful native shrubs of the Gulf Coastal Plain, native from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma. The aromatic, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (crushed, they release a distinctive bayberry-bay-spice fragrance) are used dried in wreaths, sachets, and as a flavoring herb similar to bay laurel in coastal Southern cooking. The small, silvery-waxy, blue-gray berries produced on female plants are the basis of bayberry candle wax — melted from the berries and cast into candles with the distinctive bayberry fragrance beloved in New England and Colonial American tradition. Wax myrtle is among the most adaptable native plants for Gulf Coast gardens: it tolerates salt spray, wet conditions, drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions equally well, making it outstanding for beach landscapes, rain gardens, wet corners, and dry banks alike. The plant fixes nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria (actinorrhizal nitrogen fixation), improving soil fertility. As a screening shrub, hedge, or small tree, it grows rapidly (2–3 feet per year when young) to 10–15 feet. Native birds eat the waxy berries and nest in the dense foliage. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wax Rose Pereskia (Bleo)
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 10–12; wax rose pereskia is a leaf-bearing cactus from Central America and the Caribbean — one of the few cacti that retains broad, true leaves and tolerates partial shade, making it appear almost non-cactus-like in growth form. The large, waxy, orange-pink flowers are strikingly beautiful and ornamental. Throughout Southeast Asia and tropical America, the tender young leaves are consumed as a nutritious leafy vegetable — boiled briefly and eaten as a pot herb or raw in salads. The leaves are high in antioxidants and have been studied for anti-inflammatory properties in traditional Malay medicine. Unlike most cacti, it grows in humid tropical conditions with partial shade, making it a unique edible cactus suitable for shaded, moist positions in tropical gardens. The leaves have a slightly mucilaginous texture when cooked, similar to okra. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Wayne Southern Highbush Blueberry (Firm Early-Maturing North-Central Florida Blueberry)
description: Wayne is a 2017 University of Florida southern highbush release bred for consistent early maturity and firmer fruit than the older standard Jewel, making it a good hand-harvest option for north-central Florida and comparable Gulf Coast growing areas. Its chill requirement runs higher than many UF releases, so it is best matched to sites with cooler winters within the region rather than the mildest coastal strip. Plant in sulfur-acidified, well-drained beds and provide a second early-season southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination. Renewal-prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wealthy Apple (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Pioneer Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Wealthy was bred by Minnesota horticulturist Peter Gideon in 1868 from a seedling grown from Siberian crabapple stock, and its success proved for the first time that quality apples could be reliably grown in Minnesota's harsh climate, making it foundational to the entire Northern apple-breeding tradition and a direct or indirect parent of many later cold-hardy varieties. The medium-sized fruit has red-striped skin over a pale yellow-green background and crisp, juicy white flesh, sometimes streaked with red, carrying a bright, tangy-sweet flavor good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. As one of the hardiest widely available apple varieties, Wealthy is an excellent choice for northern growers, though it also performs reliably across a broad range of climates; fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is best used within a few months, since it is not a particularly long-keeping variety. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Webbs Wonderful Lettuce
description: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season, since it matures more slowly than modern hybrid icebergs. Introduced by the Webbs seed company of Stourbridge, England, in the early twentieth century, this crisphead forms large, dense, frilly-edged pale green heads with a satisfying crunch and is long considered one of England's finest garden icebergs. It remains a staple of British allotments, valued for standing in the garden without premature bolting. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Weber American Persimmon (Early-Ripening Alabama Native Persimmon)
description: Weber is a named selection of native American persimmon that came out of Alabama and stands out among American persimmon cultivars for its early ripening, finishing its crop well ahead of frost in a region where the growing season is long and hot. Fruit is larger than typical wild-seedling persimmons, with deep orange, almost red flesh and an enjoyable, richly sweet flavor once fully soft; like all American persimmons it is intensely astringent while firm and must ripen completely before eating. The tree shares the species' deep taproot and excellent tolerance of heat, drought, and humid conditions, along with good general disease resistance, making Weber a strong choice for Gulf Coast and Deep South food-forest and dooryard orchard plantings. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon nearby for best pollination and fruit set, and remove root suckers to control spread. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wee-B-Little Pumpkin (Miniature Bush Pumpkin)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Wee-B-Little's compact bush habit and short 6-8 foot vines mean it needs far less garden space than standard pumpkins and grows well in large containers. This 1999 All-America Selections winner produces three to four miniature, deep-orange pumpkins per plant, each weighing only 8 ounces to a pound, with smooth skin that takes paint and carving detail beautifully. The uniform bush habit and heavy fruit set make it a favorite for classroom gardens and children's plots where kids can grow and claim their own small pumpkin. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, leaving 3-4 inches of stem attached to extend shelf life. Matures in 90–95 days from seed.

name: Weeping Forsythia (Lian Qiao)
description: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or layer low branches, then plant out in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Distinct from the common ornamental hybrid forsythia, this species is grown for its fruit capsules, harvested green or ripe and used in traditional Chinese medicine formulas said to clear heat and support the body during colds and sore throats. Prune right after spring flowering so next year's fruiting wood has time to develop. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wega Parsley (Disease-Resistant Curled)
description: Wega is a European market-garden curled parsley bred with better field tolerance of Septoria leaf spot than many older curly strains, so foliage tends to stay cleaner and greener through the humid stretches of a long growing season. Leaves are tightly and evenly curled with a rich medium-green color that holds its quality well after cutting. Vigorous regrowth after each harvest makes it a dependable choice for gardeners who want several cuttings from one planting. It is grown the same way as other curly parsleys, with regular outer-leaf harvest to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Wehani Rice (Aromatic Reddish-Brown Basmati-Type Rice)
description: Wehani was developed over roughly a decade by a California rice-growing family, working from basmati-type parent stock, and its name is drawn from the initials of five family members. It is grown as a whole-grain (brown) rice with a reddish-brown bran layer left intact, and it is one of the longer-season aromatic rices, needing a generous warm summer to fill and ripen its large, basmati-shaped grains. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or lined stock tank, keeping standing water over the root zone through most of the season and drawing it down as the heads dry and color darkens toward harvest. When cooked it releases a toasty, peanut-like aroma that has made it a favorite in home rice blends and pilafs. Matures in 120–140 days from seed.

name: Weiki Kiwi (Self-Fertile Hardy Kiwiberry)
description: Weiki is a German-bred self-fertile hardy kiwiberry, prized alongside Issai as one of the few Actinidia arguta selections that reliably fruits from a single vine, though yields improve when a male vine is nearby. Fruit is small, smooth-skinned, and sweet with a mild kiwi flavor, ripening in early fall slightly ahead of many standard dioecious cultivars. Vines are vigorous twining climbers needing a permanent trellis or pergola and hard annual pruning to manage growth and keep fruiting spurs productive. Weiki tends to begin bearing at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, making it a practical choice where trellis space is limited. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Welcome Gooseberry (Mildew-Resistant Canadian Red Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Welcome was developed in Canada from American gooseberry (Ribes hirtellum) stock, valued for combining good resistance to American gooseberry mildew — the disease that plagues many older European-type varieties — with reliable production of medium red berries carrying a pleasant, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. The upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and harvest than more sprawling heirloom types, and its cold hardiness suits it well to northern home gardens. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for fresh eating, or pick a bit earlier and firmer for pies, jams, and other cooked preparations where tartness is desired. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Weld (Dyer's Rocket)
description: Surface sow seeds in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; weld is a Mediterranean native biennial that was, for two millennia before the development of synthetic dyes, the primary source of the most important yellow dye in European textile history — yielding from the whole plant at flower a brilliant, pure, fast, golden-yellow color from the flavonoid luteolin (the plant's specific epithet) that was far more color-fast than the yellow of many competing dye plants and combined with blue woad or indigo to produce the green used in many historical tapestries and textiles. Archaeological evidence of weld cultivation dates to Neolithic Europe. As a garden plant it is ornamental in a quiet way — producing tall, narrow, spike-like racemes of small, four-petaled, pale-yellow-green flowers in summer. The self-sowing habit maintains naturalized colonies in disturbed, lean, sunny situations. A meaningful plant for natural dyers, herb gardens, and historical plant collections, and an important species for the sustainable textile and craft revival of plant-based natural dyeing. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Welder Muscadine Grape (Heritage Texas Muscadine)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Welder is a heritage Texas muscadine selection, originally found growing wild along the Texas Gulf Coast, long valued by home growers for its vigorous, reliably productive vines and dark bronze-to-purple berries with the strong, musky-sweet, classic muscadine flavor favored for fresh eating, jelly, and homemade wine. Its Gulf Coast origins give it excellent heat and humidity tolerance, and it has a long track record of thriving with minimal care in Texas and Louisiana home gardens where more refined modern cultivars can sometimes struggle. Welder is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinizer, though yields benefit from having other muscadine vines nearby. Like other muscadines, it shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make bunch grapes difficult in the humid South. Harvest as berries darken fully and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure, and train the vigorous vine to a sturdy two-wire trellis with annual winter pruning. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wellington Mulberry (Wellington Black Mulberry)
description: Wellington is a historic black mulberry selection traced to a tree on the New York property of pomologist Richard Wellington and long grown through the New York State Fruit Testing Cooperative at Geneva, valued as one of the hardiest true black-fruited mulberries available for northern gardens. The medium, cylindrical fruit ripens over several weeks in mid-to-late summer, extending the harvest window, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor well suited to fresh eating and preserves. Trees tolerate temperatures well below 0°F and adapt to a range of soils as long as drainage is adequate. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wellington XXX Black Currant
description: Wellington XXX is a heritage English black currant cultivar dating to the early 20th century, still grown for its heavy, reliable yields of large, richly flavored, dark berries well suited to jams, syrups, and cordials. It is a vigorous, spreading bush that produces well even in cooler, shorter-season climates, and its mid-season ripening helps spread the harvest when grown with earlier or later black currant selections. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune out about a quarter of the oldest wood each winter to stimulate new fruiting canes, since black currants fruit best on one- and two-year-old growth. Watch for reduced vigor and yield in hot-summer regions, as this cultivar performs best where summers stay relatively cool. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wells Pawpaw (Large Sweet Maryland Pawpaw)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Wells is a named pawpaw cultivar selected from a wild tree in Maryland — valued for its exceptionally large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with classic banana-custard character, and good productivity. Wells produces some of the largest pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with individual fruits commonly weighing 6–12 ounces and occasionally larger — a significant attribute for a species where fruit size varies enormously between seedling selections. The large, heavy fruits have creamy-yellow flesh with minimal fiber, full banana-vanilla custard flavor, and a smooth texture that makes them outstanding for fresh eating and pawpaw-based recipes (ice cream, smoothies, bread, beer). Wells ripens mid-to-late season (late September to early October in zone 7–8, slightly earlier in zone 9) and requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar such as Shenandoah or Susquehanna for maximum fruit set. The very short shelf life inherent to all pawpaw fruit (2–4 days at room temperature, up to 2 weeks refrigerated) limits commercial distribution but is not a problem for home gardeners harvesting on demand. Hand-pollination with a small brush during the brief flowering window significantly improves fruit set in home orchard settings where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Welsh Onion (Bunching Onion)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 4–6 inches, or start in trays and transplant in clusters of 3–5 seedlings. Welsh onion does not form a bulb but produces clumps of hollow, cylindrical green stalks that are harvested like scallions; the entire green top and white base are edible. Harvest outer stalks from established clumps as needed, leaving the center to continue growing; clumps also divide easily and can be split every 2–3 years. Extremely cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free once established, it serves as a permanent perennial scallion in most temperate gardens. Matures in 65–120 days from seed.

name: Wenatchee Moorpark Apricot (Pacific Northwest Large-Fruited Self-Fruitful Apricot)
description: Wenatchee Moorpark takes its name from Washington's Wenatchee Valley fruit-growing district, where it was selected as a more reliably productive, self-fruitful alternative to the old English Moorpark type it resembles in fruit quality. Fruit is large with golden-orange skin and a red blush, and richly flavored flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and drying. It has become a favorite home-orchard apricot in the Pacific Northwest because its moderate chill requirement suits the region's maritime winters while its bloom holds up reasonably well against the area's variable, wet springs. As with most apricots grown in the Northwest, watch for brown rot in wet spring weather and prune to an open form for good air circulation through the canopy. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wentworth American Highbush Cranberry (Early-Ripening Fruit Selection)
description: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun, since this selection tolerates woodland-edge conditions better than many fruiting shrubs. Wentworth was selected for producing earlier-ripening, larger, better-flavored clusters of tart red berries than typical seedling highbush cranberries, though a second unrelated seedling nearby improves pollination and fruit set. The berries soften and mellow after a frost and cook down into a bright, tart preserve or sauce reminiscent of true cranberry, a useful substitute in regions where cranberry bogs are not practical. Its tolerance of part shade and reliable fruit set make Wentworth a good choice for a hedgerow or forest-garden edge planting where full sun is not available all day. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: Wepster Hazelnut (Filbert)
description: Wepster is one of the Oregon State University hazelnut releases bred to withstand Eastern Filbert Blight, functioning primarily as a reliable pollenizer for later-blooming EFB-resistant varieties like Jefferson and Yamhill. It forms a moderately vigorous, well-branched bush that begins bearing within a few years of planting. Because hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible, always plant it alongside a compatible bloom-overlap partner rather than as a stand-alone tree. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Weschcke Black Walnut (Cold-Hardy Northern Selection)
description: Weschcke traces to the pioneering cold-climate nut breeding work of Carl Weschcke in Minnesota and is grown for producing large kernel pieces that crack out more easily than typical wild black walnut seedlings while retaining strong winter hardiness. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and plenty of room, since mature black walnuts become large shade trees; roots and leaf litter release juglone, so keep tomatoes, potatoes, and other juglone-sensitive plants at a distance. Black walnut is wind-pollinated and self-fertile, but nut set and size improve with a second seedling or grafted tree nearby for cross-pollination. It is best suited to northern growers seeking a hardier, better-cracking alternative to wild-type black walnut rather than to Gulf South plantings, which favor Persian or heartnut types instead. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: West Indian Lemongrass (Classic Culinary Lemongrass)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay warm. West Indian lemongrass is the standard culinary lemongrass of Southeast Asian and Caribbean cooking, forming a large, dense, fountain-like clump of long, narrow, intensely citrus-scented leaves surrounding thickened, tender stalk bases that are harvested, crushed, and used to flavor soups, curries, teas, and marinades. Unlike East Indian lemongrass, which is grown mainly for essential oil production and has a somewhat harsher aroma, West Indian lemongrass has the milder, sweeter citrus fragrance preferred for cooking. In zone 9 the clump usually dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in spring if mulched heavily; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter or replanted annually. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: West Indian Locust
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hymenaea courbaril is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods once established — water regularly in establishment years, then rely primarily on rainfall in tropical conditions. Hymenaea courbaril (West Indian Locust, Jatobá, or South American Locust) is a massive, long-lived, evergreen to semi-deciduous tree native to the Caribbean islands, Central America, and tropical South America from Mexico through the Amazon Basin, where it is one of the dominant canopy trees of seasonally dry and humid tropical forests. The tree produces large, hard, oblong, woody, dark-brown pods enclosing a dry, starchy, sweet-sour, floury pulp around the seeds — an important traditional food of indigenous peoples throughout its range, eaten directly, ground into flour for bread and porridge, or fermented into beverages. The pulp is nutritionally dense, rich in carbohydrates, protein, and calcium. Hymenaea courbaril is also one of the primary historical sources of Jutahy (or jatobá) copal resin, exuded from the trunk and roots as a hard amber-colored substance used in traditional varnishes, incense, and folk medicine for respiratory conditions and skin ailments. The extremely dense, hard, durable heartwood — among the hardest commercial timbers of the Americas — has been used for heavy construction, flooring, furniture, and tool handles for centuries. A very slow-growing, exceptionally long-lived tree requiring 10+ years to first fruit. Matures in 3650–7300 days from transplant.

name: West Indian Vanilla (Pompona Vanilla, Vanillón, Big-Leaved Vanilla)
description: Plant in partial shade to bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, organic-rich medium — West Indian Vanilla climbs most vigorously on rough-textured supports in conditions that approximate its native tropical forest habitat: bright, filtered light, consistent warmth, and humid air with good drainage at the roots. Vanilla pompona is a hemi-epiphytic climbing orchid vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean islands, and northern South America in the Orchidaceae family, closely related to the commercially dominant Vanilla planifolia but producing shorter, thicker, more barrel-shaped vanilla pods with a distinctly different, somewhat sweeter aromatic profile. As with all Vanilla species, the vine climbs by clasping aerial roots to tree bark or other rough surfaces, can reach impressive lengths (30+ feet), and produces axillary clusters of the characteristic large (2-inch), greenish-yellow to pale yellow vanilla orchid flowers — each lasting only a single day, requiring prompt hand pollination in cultivation to set the pods. The pods (the 'vanilla beans' of commerce) take 9–12 months to mature after pollination, then must be cured through a weeks-long process of sweating, drying, and conditioning to develop the characteristic vanilla aroma. Vanilla pompona has been used as an alternative and supplement to V. planifolia in commercial vanilla production, particularly in the Caribbean, and is more resistant to the Fusarium root rot disease that threatens V. planifolia plantations. An interesting food plant for zone 10-12 tropical gardens with appropriate climbing structures. Matures in 730–2190 days from transplant.

name: Westcot Apricot (Extremely Cold-Hardy Prairie Apricot)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Westcot was bred on the Canadian Prairies from Manchurian apricot stock specifically to survive the extreme winter cold of Saskatchewan and similar climates, extending apricot growing into regions far too harsh for standard European apricot varieties. The small, orange-yellow fruit is smaller and slightly tarter than familiar supermarket apricots but is genuinely good for fresh eating, drying, and preserves, and represents one of the few reliable ways prairie and northern growers can produce apricots at all. As with other extreme-hardy apricots, the tree itself easily survives severe winter cold, but early spring bloom remains vulnerable to late frost, so choose a planting site that avoids frost pockets and drains cold air away from the tree during bloom. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Western Sandcherry
description: Plant in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; western sandcherry is a low, spreading Great Plains native shrub prized for extreme cold hardiness and drought tolerance well beyond that of most cultivated cherries or plums. White flowers cover the branches in early spring ahead of the leaves, followed by dark purple-black, cherry-plum-flavored fruit that ripens in mid- to late summer and is excellent fresh, dried, or made into jam and wine, though astringency varies by seedling. It is widely used as a dwarfing rootstock and as a parent in cold-hardy plum-cherry hybrids for northern climates where standard stone fruits fail to overwinter reliably. Prune out old, unproductive stems at the base every few years to renew vigor, and expect strong drought tolerance once established, needing supplemental water only during the driest stretches. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Western Schley Pecan (Widely Planted Southwestern Irrigated Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety, and provide consistent irrigation during nut fill, since this cultivar was developed for and performs best under the irrigated growing conditions of the arid Southwest. Often simply called Western in the trade, it produces a thin-shelled, well-filled nut with good flavor and has become one of the most heavily planted commercial pecan cultivars in New Mexico, Arizona, and West Texas orchards. It shows somewhat better tolerance of drier climates than many Southeastern-bred cultivars but still performs acceptably in the more humid Gulf South when given good air circulation and disease management. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Western Wild Ginger (British Columbia Wild Ginger)
description: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; western wild ginger is the native groundcover wild ginger of Pacific Northwest moist forests, producing large, glossy, dark evergreen, heart-shaped leaves and the characteristic small, brownish-maroon, three-pointed, urn-shaped flowers hidden at the base of the plant and pollinated by ground beetles and ants. The leaves have a pleasant ginger scent when crushed. Western wild ginger spreads more vigorously than eastern wild ginger by horizontal rhizomes, eventually forming dense, weed-suppressing mats under conifers and deciduous trees. An exceptional shade groundcover for the Pacific Northwest, competing effectively with English ivy and other invasives while providing excellent, low-maintenance native coverage. The rhizomes have been used as a ginger substitute by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples, though in small quantities only — large amounts of Asarum species may be toxic. Evergreen foliage persists through Pacific Northwest winters. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Westfield Seek-No-Further Apple (Prized Massachusetts Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Westfield Seek-No-Further originated in Westfield, Massachusetts in the 1700s and earned its confident name from admirers who felt that once you had tasted it, there was no need to look any further for a finer apple — high praise reflected in the variety's long-standing reputation among heirloom apple enthusiasts as one of the best-flavored New England apples. The dull red, faintly striped skin covers crisp, tender, aromatic flesh with a rich, nutty sweetness balanced by mild tartness, considered by many connoisseurs to rank among the finest dessert apples of the colonial American tradition. The tree bears reliably though the fruit's somewhat delicate skin bruises more easily than tougher modern varieties, so handle harvested fruit gently; ripens in fall and keeps reasonably well in cool storage. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Westland Winter Kale (Classic Hardy British Curly Kale)
description: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Westland Winter is a classic, cold-hardy curly kale long grown in Britain for reliable winter harvests, producing dense, tightly ruffled, blue-green leaves on sturdy, productive plants that stand up well to cold, wind, and less-than-ideal soil. Its exceptional cold hardiness makes it a strong choice for extending the harvest deep into winter in colder climates, and like other kale it becomes noticeably sweeter and more tender after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the central rosette to continue producing new growth over the season. Matures in 55–65 days from transplant.

name: Whale Spinach (Large-Leaf Heat-Tolerant Summer Hybrid)
description: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to final spacing, watering deeply to sustain the plant's large leaf size through warm weather. Named for its oversized, smooth blue-green leaves, this hybrid was selected specifically to resist bolting under longer days and warmer temperatures than most spinach can tolerate. It gives Gulf Coast growers a wider sowing window on either end of the cool season, holding productive quality later into spring and earlier into fall. Matures in 35–42 days from seed.

name: Whaley Cherimoya
description: Grow Whaley cherimoya the way you would other named Annona cherimola selections: plant a grafted tree in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and hand-pollinate the flowers with a small brush each morning, since cherimoya blossoms open female before shifting to male and rarely pollinate themselves. Dating to 1920s Hollywood, California, Whaley produces medium-to-large, elongated, conical fruit with light green, gently bumpy (tuberculate) skin and sweet, aromatic, custard-textured flesh with the classic pineapple-banana-vanilla flavor of good cherimoya. The tree tolerates cool nights better than most tropical fruit trees but is killed by hard freezes, so young plantings need winter protection in marginal zones. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within two to four years and benefit from consistent moisture through flowering and fruit set. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Whaley's Favorite Cabbage Collard (South Carolina Family Heirloom)
description: Kept for generations by a South Carolina family as a home-garden seed-saving tradition, this variety is part of the same cabbage-collard lineage as White Mountain and Yellow Cabbage Collard. Its broad, smooth, light-to-medium green leaves have slightly crinkled edges and gather into a loose, rounded, cabbage-like head rather than growing fully open like a typical collard. The texture is markedly more tender than standard collards, and the flavor is milder and sweeter, especially after a frost, which suits it to quick sautes as well as the long, slow-simmered pots traditional to Southern cooking. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Whangkeumbae Asian Pear (Korean Gold Pear)
description: Whangkeumbae was released to Korean orchards by the national horticultural research institute and has since become a widely grown commercial cultivar valued for its high sugar content and attractive yellowish-green skin at harvest. The flesh is crisp and juicy, eaten fresh at full ripeness rather than softened in storage the way European pears are. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and, as with most nashi cultivars, offers limited natural resistance to fire blight. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wheatgrass
description: Soak the hard red winter wheat seed overnight, then spread it densely over a tray of moist growing mix and keep it evenly moist and bright. The seed sprouts rapidly into lush green blades that are ready to cut in about eight to twelve days, when they reach 6 to 9 inches tall. Snip the grass at the base for juicing, which yields a drink rich in vitamins, minerals, and chlorophyll; sow fresh trays in succession for a continuous supply. Matures in 8–12 days from seed.

name: Wheatland Heirloom Grain Sorghum
description: Wheatland is an open-pollinated heirloom grain sorghum, sometimes marketed as milo, that produces large, well-filled heads of round, off-white seed on stalks 6 to 7 feet tall. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same hot, dry conditions that stress corn, making it a reliable backup grain crop in areas prone to summer dry spells. The dried grain can be ground into a gluten-free flour or cracked for cereal, and the mature stalks and leftover heads make useful livestock and poultry feed. Harvest whole heads once the seed has hardened and the plant has begun to dry down, then thresh and winnow before storage. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Whiddon Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Cape Fear and Desirable Replacement Pecan)
description: Whiddon was released by the University of Georgia in 2015 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Pawnee and Desirable, developed as a replacement for Desirable and Cape Fear in Georgia orchards. It produces a large, slightly oblong nut, about 40 per pound, with 52-54% kernel matching Desirable's color, and its scab resistance is good in well-managed orchards and superior to Desirable's. Whiddon shows a clear alternate bearing pattern, with off-year crops running roughly 50% lighter than on-year crops, so growers should plan for crop thinning in heavy years. As a Type I pollen shedder, pair it with a Type II cultivar for reliable pollination. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Whinham's Industry Gooseberry
description: Plant dormant bushes in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, in full sun or light shade, and prune to an open vase shape each winter to ease harvesting among the thorny stems. A very old English cultivar dating to the mid-1800s, Whinham's Industry remains popular for its notable tolerance of poor, heavy, or shaded conditions where many other gooseberries struggle, along with strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew. Its medium-to-large, hairy-skinned berries ripen from green to a deep dusky red with a rich, sweet-tart flavor good for both dessert use and cooking. The vigorous, spreading habit and dependable heavy cropping have kept it a garden favorite for over a century. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Whippoorwill Cowpea (Historic Speckled Southern Heirloom Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, and avoid rich, heavily fertilized ground, which pushes vine growth at the expense of pod production in this vigorous heirloom. Whippoorwill is one of the oldest documented Southern cowpea varieties, grown since before the Civil War and named for its speckled brown-and-tan seed coat, which resembles the mottled plumage of the whippoorwill bird. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant, it was historically valued as a dual-purpose crop, grown both for its rich, earthy-flavored dried and fresh peas and as a soil-building, nitrogen-fixing cover crop plowed under to enrich depleted fields, a role it still serves well in a home garden rotation. Its tough constitution and long history make it a genuine piece of Southern agricultural heritage as well as a reliable, low-input summer crop. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage. Matures in 65–80 days from seed.

name: Whippoorwill Southern Pea
description: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil and allow vines to sprawl freely; Whippoorwill is a pre-Civil War Southern heirloom with a sprawling, semi-vining habit that naturalizes well in field conditions. The speckled brown-and-cream seeds are distinctive and historically used both as a fresh shell pea and a dry bean, with a rich, slightly nutty flavor preferred by many Southern gardeners over modern varieties. It is particularly favored for field cultivation as a dual-purpose food and cover crop in the South, where it fixes substantial nitrogen and suppresses summer weeds. Seeds are saved easily — allow selected pods to dry fully on the vine. Matures in 70–85 days from seed.

name: White Acre Pea (Sweet Small-Seeded Gulf South Cream Pea)
description: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Acre pea is one of the most distinctive and prized southern pea varieties of the Texas and Gulf Coast tradition — a small-seeded cream pea producing petite, white to cream-white seeds with exceptionally sweet, buttery, delicate flavor that differs meaningfully from the larger-seeded, more robust flavor of standard cream peas and blackeye peas. The small seed size of White Acre is characteristic — the peas are notably smaller than regular cream peas, more compact in the shelled bowl, and cook to a sweeter, creamier texture with a refined flavor profile that has made White Acre the preference of many Gulf South cooks for fresh summer pea dishes. In zone 9, White Acre produces abundantly from its first harvest through summer and into fall — planting succession crops every 3–4 weeks from April through August provides continuous fresh pea production throughout the longest part of the growing season. White Acre is a semi-bush to vining type reaching 18–24 inches and performs well without staking in most garden conditions. The vines fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for subsequent crops. Harvest when hulls are well-filled but still green for fresh-shelled use; allow to dry completely for storage. White Acre is particularly important in Gulf Coast cuisine and is a foundational variety of the traditional summer pea dishes of Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. Matures in 60–70 days from seed.

name: White Adriatic Fig (Classic Italian Green-Skinned Honey-Flavored Jam Fig)
description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Adriatic is a classic Italian fig cultivar grown commercially in California (it is the primary variety used for dried figs and fig paste in California production) and traditionally cultivated in Gulf South kitchen gardens for its exceptional fresh-eating quality. The medium-to-large fruits have green-to-yellow-green skin at full ripeness with amber to light strawberry-rose interior flesh of unusually high sweetness and a clean, honey-like flavor that ranks among the most highly regarded of all common fig varieties for fresh use. The flavor of fully ripe White Adriatic fresh from the tree — warm, sweet, delicate — is the benchmark against which many other figs are judged. The thin skin is part of what makes the fresh flavor exceptional; it also means ripe fruits are delicate and should be harvested promptly before rain or excess humidity causes splitting. White Adriatic is a vigorous, productive fig tree that typically begins bearing in its second year from planting and reaches full production by year 3–5. In Gulf South zone 9, the main crop ripens in late July through September; a breba (early) crop may develop on previous year's wood in June in years when the wood survives winter undamaged. Self-fertile, requiring no pollinators. Best eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest; or made into fig preserves and jam where the delicate honey flavor is retained. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Anniversary Oregano (Variegated Shade-Tolerant Culinary Oregano)
description: Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most Mediterranean oreganos that demand baking sun, White Anniversary holds its dense, creamy-white-edged foliage and low mounding habit even in a partly shaded border or woodland-edge herb bed. The flavor is milder and sweeter than Greek oregano, so use it more generously in salads, dressings, and light sauces where its delicate, edged leaves also serve as an attractive garnish. Shear the plant back by about a third after its small white summer flowers fade to keep the mound tight and to encourage a flush of fresh, well-variegated new growth. It spreads gradually into a tidy groundcover rather than aggressively, so division every two to three years is usually enough to keep it vigorous. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: White Bee Balm (Basil Bee Balm)
description: White bee balm is the most shade-tolerant of all native bee balms — the only species that thrives in partial shade under deciduous trees rather than requiring full sun — and produces whorls of pure white to pale lavender flowers on upright stems from June through August, providing a critical nectar source for native bumble bees, hummingbird moths, and butterflies in shaded garden areas where most pollinator plants fail. Its strong basil-like fragrance (the 'clinopodia' means 'resembling basil') makes it useful as a culinary herb and potpourri ingredient; leaves dried at peak bloom make an aromatic tea with a floral, oregano-like character. Unlike red bee balm (Monarda didyma) and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa), white bee balm is less aggressive and more restrained in its spread, forming tidy clumps rather than rampaging colonies; it is also more resistant to the powdery mildew that plagues its relatives in humid conditions. An excellent choice for native shade gardens under mature hardwoods where its white flowers provide elegant, fragrant bloom from early to midsummer. Matures in 180–365 days from seed.

name: White Bermuda Onion (Classic Mild Flat Short-Day Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this classic short-day onion needs the shorter daylight of a southern winter to bulb properly. Long grown in Texas, Louisiana, and other Gulf Coast states before more modern hybrid sweet onions became common, White Bermuda produces flattened, disc-shaped bulbs with thin, pure white skin and mild, tender flesh with relatively low pungency. Because the papery skin is thin, cured bulbs do not store as long as pungent storage onions and are best used within a few months of harvest. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: White Bitter Melon
description: Direct sow White Bitter Melon seeds in warm soil in full sun after last frost; provide a sturdy trellis or fence and train vines upward for maximum production; water consistently at the base and fertilize every 3–4 weeks with a balanced vegetable fertilizer; harvest fruits when they are pale cream to white and firm, before they begin to yellow. White Bitter Melon is the pale-fruited form of the familiar bitter melon vine (Momordica charantia), grown throughout Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and diaspora communities worldwide for its distinctive culinary role in curries, stir-fries, and stuffed preparations. The white-skinned variety differs from the standard warty green variety in bearing longer, smoother, paler-green to creamy-white fruits that are generally considered less intensely bitter — making it a better entry point for cooks unfamiliar with the characteristic bitterness, while retaining the distinctive gourd flavor that defines dishes like Kerala's Bitter Melon Thoran and Chinese stir-fried bitter melon with eggs. In zone 9–12, the vine grows vigorously and produces heavily from midsummer through fall; in zone 9, it may return from the root if the crown is protected from frost. Like the standard green bitter melon, the unripe fruits are the primary culinary use; ripe, yellow fruits split to reveal bright-red seed arils that are sweet and edible but the pulp becomes very bitter. Matures in 55–75 days from seed.

name: White Borage
description: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in its permanent spot in any well-drained soil, including poor or dry ground, in full sun to light partial shade. 'Alba' is a true-breeding white-flowered strain of common borage, differing from the species only in flower color — pure white, star-shaped blooms replace the usual vivid blue — while retaining the same fuzzy gray-green leaves and mild cucumber flavor. The white flowers show up beautifully against the foliage and are prized by cooks for garnishing pale dishes, drinks, and desserts where a blue flower would clash. Deadhead spent flower stalks to extend bloom and limit volunteer seedlings, since it crosses readily with blue-flowered borage if both are grown nearby. Matures in 50–70 days from seed.

name: White Chayote
description: Plant a whole, slightly sprouted White Chayote fruit on its side with the sprouting end just above the soil level in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a very sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vine; water deeply once or twice weekly during active growth; harvest fruits when they are 3–5 inches long for the most tender, mild-flavored results. White Chayote is a traditional variety of the widely grown Mesoamerican perennial vine vegetable, distinguished by its smooth to very lightly furrowed, cream-white to pale-green skin compared to the spiny, dark-green skin of the more common commercial variety. Like all chayote, it is planted by burying the entire fruit — the seed is inside and too large to separate without harm — and the vine emerges from the fruit and climbs vigorously. In zone 10–12, the vine grows as a long-lived perennial with a massive tuberous root system; a well-established vine can produce hundreds of fruits per season. White Chayote fruits are notably smoother and many cooks consider the flavor slightly milder and sweeter than spiny green varieties; they are used in all the same ways — raw in salads, steamed, boiled, stuffed, or pickled. The young leaves and shoot tips, tuberous roots, and seeds are all edible as with all chayote. An excellent year-round producer in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens, dying back to the ground in mild frost and re-emerging in spring. Matures in 120–150 days from transplant.

name: White Chia (Pale-Seeded Chia Variant)
description: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. White Chia produces pale cream-to-white seed rather than the typical dark brown-to-black coloring of standard chia, an attractive variant for gardeners wanting visual variety in a home-grown chia harvest, with the same nutritional profile and whorled purple flower spikes appearing in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris. Matures in 120–160 days from seed.

name: White Cross Berry
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, average to poor soil; Grewia bicolor is highly drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry and semi-arid conditions — once established it requires little or no supplemental water in warm arid and semi-arid climates. Grewia bicolor (White Cross Berry or Crossberry) is a thorny, much-branched shrub or small tree native to the dry, open savannas, bushveld, and semi-arid woodland of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to South Africa and Mozambique — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important shrubs of African savanna ecosystems. The distinctive bicolor leaves — deep green and glossy above, densely silver-white hairy and felted beneath — give the plant a shimmering two-tone appearance in the breeze. Small, 5-petaled, yellow or cream star-shaped flowers are borne prolifically from the leaf axils in summer, followed by round to oblong, 2–4-lobed berries — ripening from green through reddish-orange to dark brown or black — that are sweet-mucilaginous, edible raw or dried, and important bush food across the plant's range. The berries are browsed by elephants, giraffes, and many antelope species, and are eaten by indigenous peoples dried as a sweetener or fermented into beer. The roots and bark carry extensive traditional medicinal uses across sub-Saharan Africa for fevers, diarrhea, and sexually transmitted infections. An excellent drought-tolerant, wildlife-attracting shrub for hot, dry, sunny gardens in zone 8–11. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Currant
description: White currant is a yellow-fruited mutation of red currant sharing identical cultivation requirements: it fruits most heavily on spurs of two-year-old and older wood. The translucent, ivory-white berries are sweeter and milder than red currants and are prized for elegant fresh-eating and jellies. Prune each late winter to maintain 8–12 canes of mixed ages, removing canes older than 5 years. Harvest entire strigs when berries have turned fully translucent white-golden and taste sweet; check local Ribes restrictions before purchasing. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: White Currant (Pale Currant)
description: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white currant fruits best with some afternoon shade in warm climates and benefits from a cross-pollinator though it is largely self-fertile. Ribes sativum in its white-fruited forms (often grouped with R. rubrum) produces distinctive, translucent, pearl-white to pale-pink berries with a milder, less tart flavor than red currants, making them more suitable for fresh eating and elegant as a garnish on desserts; they are excellent for jelly, wine, and as a decoration for cakes and pastries. White currant is one of the most attractive of all fruiting shrubs when in fruit — the translucent clusters catch the light beautifully. 'Blanka', 'Primus', and 'White Versailles' are classic cultivars available from specialty nurseries. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Deadnettle
description: Plant in moist to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; white deadnettle is a European mint-family herb with nettlecreeper-shaped leaves (which it resembles but it does not sting — hence 'deadnettle') and conspicuous white hooded flowers throughout spring and early summer. The white flowers, with their distinctive hood and nectar guides, are exclusively pollinated by long-tongued bumblebees that can reach the nectar at the base of the long corolla tube — shorter-tongued bees cannot access it. The plant has a long history of use in European herbal medicine, with the flowers and leaves used as an anti-inflammatory herb, wound herb, and menstrual regulator. Young leaves and flowers are edible in salads. Spreads moderately by rhizomes and self-sows to form a semi-wild presence in the shade garden. Matures in 60–120 days from seed.

name: White Doyenne Pear (Virgalieu)
description: Plant bare-root trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinizer for best fruit set. White Doyenne was, for generations before Bartlett rose to dominance, the standard dessert pear of American and European gardens, prized for smooth, melting, richly flavored flesh on a small to medium yellow fruit often blushed with red. It is more susceptible to fire blight and pear scab than modern resistant releases, so it suits growers more interested in preserving a genuinely historic variety than in low-maintenance production. Pick the fruit while still firm in early to mid fall and ripen it indoors at room temperature for the best flavor and texture. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: White Egg Turnip (Fast-Maturing Egg-Shaped Heirloom)
description: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and thin young seedlings to a few inches apart; White Egg is a classic 19th-century American heirloom prized for its smooth, pure-white, egg-shaped roots that sit mostly above the soil line, making them easy to spot and pull. Flesh is exceptionally fine-grained, crisp, and mild for a turnip, holding its quality raw in slaws as well as cooked, and the roots reach usable size faster than almost any other turnip variety. Because it matures so quickly it is an excellent choice for a fast catch crop between other plantings or for gardeners who want an early fall harvest well before frost; roots left in the ground too long lose their fine texture and become woody, so check size regularly and harvest promptly once roots reach 2–3 inches across. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: White Gem Parsnip (Smooth-Skinned Canker-Tolerant Variety)
description: White Gem is an English garden parsnip selected for very pale, smooth skin, a bluntly wedge-shaped root, and good field tolerance to canker, making it a reliable choice where older heirloom types tend to scar and rot at the shoulder. Keep the bed consistently moist through slow, patchy germination and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding, which encourages forked roots. Its clean, uniform appearance and sweet, fine-grained flesh have made it a popular choice for both kitchen use and vegetable show competitions in the UK. Leave roots in the ground until after several hard frosts, since the cold converts starches to sugar and produces the variety's characteristic sweetness. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: White Genoa Fig
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; White Genoa is an Italian light-skinned fig producing medium to large, greenish-yellow to pale gold fruits with amber to pink-tinged flesh and a mild, sweet, delicate flavor — one of the milder-flavored fig varieties, with a honey-sweet taste that lacks the robust winey complexity of dark-skinned varieties but is exceptionally appealing for fresh eating by people who find strong fig flavor too intense. The pale skin and light flesh of White Genoa produce an elegant presentation as fresh fruit or in light-colored preserves; it makes an outstanding pale-gold fig jam. It is widely grown in Australia and California where it performs well in Mediterranean-type climates and is considered one of the best light-skinned figs for fresh eating. In zone 9 and the Gulf Coast, White Genoa performs comparably to its reputation in warm Mediterranean climates. The light-colored fruits are prone to souring and cracking if they crack near the eye in wet weather; plant in locations with good air circulation. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: White Grano Onion
description: Start White Grano seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before transplanting, setting seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This short-day heirloom forms smooth white bulbs about 3 inches across with mild, low-pungency flavor and does best in southern regions. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and keep the bed free of weeds while bulbs develop. Harvest when the tops fall over, then cure in a dry, airy place before short-term storage. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: White Guava Tree
description: This evergreen tropical bears fragrant white-fleshed guavas with a flavor blending passion fruit and sweet melon, rich in vitamin C. Give it full sun and warm, humid conditions in rich, well-drained soil. Water regularly and feed with a balanced fertilizer during active growth for the heaviest fruiting. In climates that dip below freezing, grow it in a large pot and shelter it indoors during cold snaps. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Half Long Parsnip
description: Sow White Half Long seeds half an inch deep in deep, loose soil and keep the surface consistently moist, since parsnips germinate slowly and unevenly. Use fresh seed each year and thin seedlings to 3 to 6 inches apart. This heirloom develops smooth, creamy-white roots with a sweet, nutty flavor that deepens after frost. Leave the roots in the ground through cold weather and harvest as needed, since freezing converts starches to sugars. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: White Half Runner Bean (Mountaineer Half Runner)
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing 2–3 feet of support for the semi-vining plants; white half runner is the most popular snap bean in the home gardens and farmers markets of the Appalachian mountains and Southern uplands, occupying the productive middle ground between bush beans (no support needed, shorter production) and full pole beans (requires tall trellis, longer season). The semi-vining plants produce abundantly over a concentrated 2–3 week period, making them excellent for canning and freezing in large batches as well as fresh table use. The pods are round, stringless when young, and have excellent fresh-eating flavor. White seeds make it useful as a dry bean after pods mature fully. The Mountaineer White Half Runner was bred at the West Virginia Extension station specifically for the cool-summer Appalachian region but is equally productive in the Gulf South when planted in spring or fall. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: White Horehound
description: White horehound is a hardy, wooly-leaved perennial in the mint family, long used for herbal candies and traditional remedies. Surface sow the seed on well-drained soil and keep it cool and lightly moist, as germination can be slow and uneven. It thrives in full sun and lean, dry ground, tolerating drought once established, and its bitter foliage tends to be deer resistant. Harvest leaves as flowering begins and cut plants back to prevent excessive self-seeding. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: White Hyssop
description: Sow White Hyssop indoors in a warm, well-drained starting mix; transplant after hardening off into lean, dry to moderately moist, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun. Prune back hard after the first flush of bloom to keep plants dense and bushy and to encourage a second round of flowers. The crisp white flower spikes make a striking contrast when planted alongside the standard blue-flowered species or the pink 'Roseus' strain in an herb or pollinator border, and the strongly camphor-scented leaves are harvested the same way as standard hyssop for bittering liqueurs, savory rubs, and traditional teas. Being a seed strain, some plants may show faint blush tones; rogue out off-color seedlings if pure white bloom is desired. Matures in 75–100 days from transplant.

name: White Icicle Radish (Long White Radish, Lady Finger Radish)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep and thin to 2–3 inches apart; White Icicle is faster-maturing than daikon (25–35 days vs. 60+ days) and milder than Chinese black radish, fitting into the cool-season rotation between spring planting and summer heat; harvest before roots reach maximum size for finest quality. White Icicle is a classic heirloom radish that has been grown in American gardens since the 19th century and appears in Victorian-era seed catalogs as one of the standard garden radish varieties. Unlike the small, round, red radishes (Cherry Belle, Champion, Sparkler) that dominate modern radish offerings, White Icicle produces elongated, cylindrical, all-white roots 4–6 inches long with a gentle taper — resembling a large, smooth, pale daikon in miniature. The flavor is milder and less pungent than round red varieties at the same stage of maturity, and the texture is firm and crisp without the slight woodiness that can develop in large round varieties. White Icicle is excellent for fresh eating in salads (the white color is elegant against greens), for cutting into sticks for crudités platters, for Japanese-style pickles, for cooking in stir-fries (where it holds its shape better than rounder types), and for the traditional French preparation of radishes served with butter and salt. The elongated shape also makes White Icicle more practical for slicing in certain applications where round radishes are inconvenient. Matures in 25–35 days from seed.

name: White Imperial Currant
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall into fertile soil in full sun to light shade, removing the oldest third of stems each winter to keep productive new wood coming. White Imperial is a long-cultivated heirloom white currant prized as one of the sweetest and mildest of all currant varieties, with translucent, creamy-white berries pleasant enough to eat straight off the strig rather than only cooked into preserves. The upright, productive bush ripens long clusters in midsummer and is self-fertile, so a single bush sets a full crop. Its mild flavor and pale, attractive fruit make it popular for fresh eating, garnishing, and pale jellies where a less tart currant is wanted. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Indian Guava
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil — guavas tolerate a wide range of soil types including sandy and slightly alkaline soils; White Indian Guava is a white-to-cream-fleshed cultivar of common guava producing round to oval fruits with yellow skin when ripe, white to pale-cream flesh, and a sweeter, milder, less musky flavor than pink-fleshed guava varieties — the gentler flavor makes White Indian more approachable for people who find the distinctive strong fragrance of pink guava overpowering. The fruits have very few, soft seeds and a texture similar to a ripe pear. White-fleshed guavas are preferred in some Asian cuisines where they are eaten fresh with salt and chili or blended into drinks; they also make exceptional guava paste, jelly, and guava cheese when cooked. The trees are prolific once established and produce two or more crops annually in zone 9 and 10. Thin fruits to 4–6 inches apart to encourage larger fruit development. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Ivory Mulberry
description: White Ivory, a Whitman Farms selection, produces unusually large white berries with a light crimson blush and an intensely sweet, complex flavor that fans describe as among the best-tasting mulberries available. It grows into a substantial shade tree if left unpruned, so gardeners with smaller lots should plan on regular heading cuts to keep it at a manageable height. Its pale, non-staining fruit is especially good dried, and the extended ripening period spreads the harvest out over several weeks. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and expect a tough, low-maintenance tree once established. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Jaboticaba (Yellow Jaboticaba)
description: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; white jaboticaba (also called yellow jaboticaba) is a Brazilian species of jaboticaba producing smaller fruits than the common jaboticaba (Plinia cauliflora), with the distinctive yellow-green to white skin of the ripe grape-like fruits distinguishing it from the deep purple-black common jaboticaba. Like all jaboticabas, the fruits grow caulifloresly — directly on the trunk and main branches of the tree rather than on the branch tips — creating the remarkable, otherworldly spectacle of hundreds of fruits clustering directly on the bark. The flavor of white jaboticaba is sweeter and less astringent than the more common purple types, with a delicate, pleasant muscat-like sweetness. Used for fresh eating, jams, and fruit wines. Rare and highly prized even in Brazil, much rarer outside its native range than the common jaboticaba. A prized collector's fruit for zone 9–11 gardens where unusual tropical fruits are cultivated. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: White Jersey Sweet Potato (Dry-Type White Heirloom)
description: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in well-prepared, loose, well-drained, sandy loam soil after soil warms above 65°F; White Jersey produces best in sandy or light soils. White Jersey is an American heirloom sweet potato representing the 'dry' type that was dominant in American cooking before the mid-20th century when moist orange-fleshed varieties became the standard; grown in New Jersey's sweet potato tradition since at least the 1850s, it produces pale buff to tan-skinned roots with cream-white flesh that cooks to a dry, fluffy, mealy texture resembling an Irish potato more than a modern sweet potato. The flavor is mild, subtle, and lightly sweet without the intense caramel sweetness of orange varieties. This dry, starchy texture was highly prized in traditional American cooking for sweet potato pie (which sets firmer), sweet potato biscuits, and baked goods where a drier texture improved the final product. Now maintained by seed savers as a historical artifact of early American sweet potato culture; an excellent educational variety for understanding the dramatic change in American sweet potato preferences over 150 years. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: White Jute (Fiber & Potherb Jute)
description: Broadcast seed thickly into warm, fertile, consistently moist soil, since dense stands both suppress weeds and are the standard method for fiber production; thin or transplant survivors to a few inches apart for leaf harvest instead. Pinch or cut young shoots and the topmost tender leaves regularly starting around 5–6 weeks to keep plants leafy and to delay the tough, fibrous stem growth that signals the shift toward fiber-stage maturity; cooked leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to okra. If left unharvested for fiber, stalks are cut at the base once the lower leaves yellow, then retted in water to separate the bast fiber. White jute tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic flooding far better than most leaf greens, making it a reliable warm-season crop through the Gulf Coast summer. Matures in 40–60 days from seed.

name: White Lady Turnip
description: Direct sow seed in cool weather for spring and fall crops, thinning seedlings to two to four inches apart. This premium Japanese salad turnip forms pure white, smooth-textured roots that are mild and sweet, delicious raw in salads and crudite trays as well as pickled or cooked. Grow it quickly with steady moisture and harvest young as a baby turnip for the best crisp, tender quality. Matures in 30–45 days from seed.

name: White Lisbon Bunching Onion
description: Direct sow seed in succession from spring through summer, thinning to about an inch apart for a steady supply of scallions. Popular since the 1700s, this dependable heirloom green onion thrives in a wide range of soils and tolerates both heat and cold. Blanch the stems by hilling soil around the bases for longer white shanks, and harvest young for mild flavor before any bulb forms. Matures in 55–70 days from seed.

name: White Malabar Spinach
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; White Malabar Spinach (Basella alba 'Alba') is the green-stemmed, white-flowered form of Malabar spinach — distinct from the red-stemmed Basella rubra (Ceylon Spinach) in having entirely green stems, greener foliage, and smaller white berries. The large, thick, glossy, heart-shaped to oval leaves have the same mild, slightly mucilaginous spinach substitute quality as the red form, used raw in salads when young and tender or cooked in the same manner as spinach — sautéed, in soups, curries, and braised dishes throughout Southeast Asian, Indian, and West African cooking. The white form is favored in some cuisines where the red pigment of the red form is undesirable in finished dishes; the green stems and white berries also make it slightly more attractive as an ornamental vine for trellises and fences. In zone 9 White Malabar Spinach is the premier summer leafy green — a vigorous, heat-loving vining plant that fills the summer gap when all cool-season greens have finished and heat prevents new sowings. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: White Marseille Fig (White Fig of Marseille)
