description: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor, dry soils better than most fruit trees and perform well in raised beds and large containers where root pruning encourages fruiting. White Marseille (also spelled 'Marseilles') is one of the oldest fig varieties in documented cultivation, known in European gardens since at least the 16th century and praised in early horticultural literature for its sweet, honey-like flavor; the medium to large, turbinate fruits have pale greenish-yellow to creamy-white skin and translucent white to pale amber interior flesh with a mild, delicate sweetness and gentle fig fragrance unlike the darker, richer intensity of dark figs. A common fig type that requires no pollinator; produces a reliable main crop (August–September) and often a smaller breba crop in early summer. Excellent container and espalier candidate; protect from frost below 15°F as a large container specimen that can be moved indoors. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: White Marseilles Fig (Lattarula Italian Honey Fig, Sweet Golden-Fleshed Mediterranean Fig)
description: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to shape. White Marseilles is one of the oldest documented fig varieties in European cultivation — referenced in 17th-century English garden literature and grown continuously in Mediterranean European gardens for centuries under various local names including Lattarula (Italian, meaning little bottle), Blanche (French), and White Marseilles (English, after the port city of Marseilles from which it was widely distributed). The fruit is medium to large, turbinate (pear-shaped) to round, with pale green to yellowish-green skin that becomes translucent amber-green at full ripeness — visually distinctive from the dark-skinned black and brown figs that are the most common fig types sold in American nurseries. The flesh is pale amber, extremely sweet and rich with a honey-like quality — the Lattarula name acknowledges the syrupy honey character of the ripe fruit — and the flavor is described as one of the finest among common fig varieties, with a complex sweetness that surpasses the simpler flavor of standard commercial brown turkey types. White Marseilles performs well in the warm, long growing seasons of zone 8–10, where the extended summer gives the main crop time to fully develop the honey concentration that distinguishes it. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Micromeria (White Za'atar, Zuta Levanit)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; trim lightly after flowering to maintain compact form. Micromeria fruticosa (white micromeria, white za'atar, or zuta levanit) is a small aromatic subshrub native to the dry rocky hillsides, terra rossa soils, and limestone outcrops of the Eastern Mediterranean — particularly Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, and the Palestinian territories. The plant has distinctive small, oval, white-hairy (tomentose) leaves with a soft, felted texture, giving the plant an overall white-gray appearance; hence 'white' za'atar or zuta levanit. The fragrance and flavor are unique: a gentle, warm, herbal-thyme character with a subtle mint and tea-like undertone — softer and more delicate than either thyme or savory. In Israel and the Levant, M. fruticosa is one of the most beloved traditional herbal teas, prepared by infusing fresh or dried leaves in hot water; it is believed to be calming, digestive, and to relieve cold symptoms. It is also one of the plants historically used in za'atar spice blends in the Levant, where different communities have distinct formulations using various combinations of Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, Satureja thymbra, and M. fruticosa. A delightful low-growing groundcover for sunny, dry, Mediterranean-climate gardens. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: White Mountain Cabbage Collard (South Carolina Heading Heirloom)
description: This South Carolina family heirloom was donated to Seed Savers Exchange along with a family memory of the leaves being used for homemade sauerkraut. Unlike open-leaf collards, White Mountain is compact with short stems, and when spring-sown it draws its yellow-green-blue leaves into a fairly tight cabbage-like head by fall rather than staying loose and upright. It represents the cabbage-collard branch of Southern collard breeding, alongside Yellow Cabbage Collard and Whaley's Favorite, where growers selected for a heading habit combined with collard-style leaf texture. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: White Mulberry
description: White mulberry is a fast-growing, exceptionally hardy tree bearing sweet, mild fruit and historically grown to feed silkworms. It tolerates drought, heat, and poor soils, thriving in full sun in a very wide range of conditions. Plant a fruiting cultivar rather than a fruitless ornamental, and site away from walks since the ripe fruit drops freely. Prune in winter to control size, and expect abundant crops within a few years. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: White Pakistan Mulberry
description: White Pakistan produces strikingly long, creamy white berries that commonly stretch three to five inches, with a rich, honey-like sweetness and very little acidity that makes them excellent for fresh eating straight off the tree. It is a distinct, alba-type selection from the better-known Morus macroura 'Pakistan' shahtoot, and is noted for being more cold-hardy than black-fruited mulberry cultivars while retaining strong heat tolerance for Gulf Coast summers. The tree grows vigorously into an ornamental, productive landscape specimen with a long harvest window. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune as needed to keep the long fruit clusters within easy reach. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Pearl Bitter Melon
description: This Taiwanese-type bitter melon produces oblong fruit that opens pale green and ripens to a smooth, ivory-white skin, a milder-tasting and visually striking alternative to the typical dark green Chinese and Indian types. Fruits run 6-9 inches long and about 3 inches across, with noticeably less bitterness than most bitter melon selections, making it a good introduction to the crop for first-time growers. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun with consistent moisture, and harvest while the skin is still firm and pale rather than letting it soften and yellow. It has become popular in West Coast Asian markets, commanding a premium price over standard green types. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: White Pearl Currant (Sweet Pale-Fruited Ornamental Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. White Pearl is a white currant cultivar, a translucent, pale ivory-colored color form of the red currant species that lacks the anthocyanin pigment giving red currants their color, resulting in a noticeably milder, sweeter flavor with less tartness — a trait that makes white currants especially good for fresh eating out of hand rather than only for jelly and cooking. The long, drooping strigs of pearly, translucent berries are also strikingly ornamental against the green foliage. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on spurs of older wood like other red-type currants, so prune to an open framework in winter and remove the oldest wood to maintain vigor. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Peppermint (Mild Peppermint)
description: White peppermint is the paler-stemmed botanical form of Mentha x piperita, lacking the purple-red pigmentation of black peppermint and carrying a lighter green leaf and a milder, less pungent menthol flavor. It is favored where a softer peppermint note is wanted, such as in delicate teas and light confections, and was historically grown alongside black peppermint in commercial oil fields as a distinct strain. Contain its spreading rhizomes with a buried barrier or a sunken pot, and keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season for the best leaf quality. Cut plants back hard after flowering to renew tender growth for a second harvest before frost. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: White Portugal Onion (Mild White Heirloom Spring Onion)
description: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; pull at any size from scallion stage through full bulb maturity. White Portugal (also called White Silver Queen, Italian White, or White Silverskin in some seed catalogs) is a traditional open-pollinated white-skinned onion with a long history in American and European kitchen gardens — one of the primary heirloom white onions before the development of modern F1 hybrid white types. The bulbs are medium-large, somewhat flattened to globe-shaped, with silvery-white papery skin and white flesh. The flavor is notably milder than yellow storage onions — White Portugal has lower pungency than standard yellow types, making it well-suited for fresh eating, pickling, and preparations where mild onion character is preferred. White Portugal is the traditional pickling onion for pearl onion preparations and for cocktail onions; the white color remains clean through pickling without the discoloration that sometimes occurs with yellow-skinned types. The variety is also excellent harvested young as a green/bunching onion (scallion), where the white sheath and mild flavor make it among the most attractive bunching onions. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved year to year from the best-formed bulbs. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: White Proso Millet
description: Drill or broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep into warm, weed-free soil and thin stands to 4-6 inches apart; white proso is the pale-hulled market class grown for birdseed and human food rather than wildlife plots, and buyers pay a premium for clean, unmixed white seed lots. The plant tillers moderately and produces a loose, drooping panicle that ripens unevenly from the top down, so watch for shattering once the lower seeds harden. Cut whole stalks when most of the panicle has turned from green to straw color, then finish drying the bundles under cover for 10-14 days before threshing and winnowing. Because proso millet is one of the shortest-season grains available, a second planting is often possible in zones with a long enough frost-free window. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: White Runner Bean
description: White-flowered runner bean prized for its large white seeds and vigorous ornamental vines. Sow seeds 1.5 inches deep at the base of a tall trellis or teepee once soil warms to 60 F. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering to ensure good pod set, as heat above 90 F can cause blossom drop. Harvest young pods for snap use or allow to dry on the vine for shell beans. In mild climates the fleshy roots may overwinter and resprout the following spring. Matures in 70–100 days from seed.

name: White Russian Kale
description: Direct sow or transplant this kale in spring or late summer, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart. Introduced in 1994, White Russian is a white-ribbed cross between Red Russian and Siberian kale that grows especially sweet in cool weather and stands up well to frost. Harvest young leaves for tender baby greens or let plants mature for full-sized leaves; a hard frost only improves the sweet flavor. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: White Sage
description: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in lean, fast-draining mix; refrigerate seeds for 2 weeks before sowing to improve germination rates. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun — white sage is a California chaparral native that is highly drought-tolerant once established but will rot quickly in wet, heavy soil. Avoid supplemental irrigation once plants are established in their second season; overwatering is the most common cause of death. Harvest mature leaves and small branches by cutting, and dry in bundles in a warm, well-ventilated space for aromatic and ceremonial use. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: White Sapote
description: White sapote is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen tree that bears creamy, custard-flavored fruit often compared to a blend of peach and vanilla. Grafted cultivars (Vernon, Suebelle, Cuccio) fruit in 3–5 years and produce more reliably than seedlings, which can take a decade or more and show highly variable fruit quality. Trees are self-fertile, though two cultivars nearby increase set. Harvest when fruit is light green to yellowish, yields slightly to palm pressure, and separates easily from the stem; it ripens to soft within 3–5 days at room temperature and has very short shelf life. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: White Satin Carrot
description: A creamy white carrot with crisp, sweet, mild flesh and no pigment, popular in mixed rainbow bunches. Sow shallowly in deeply worked sandy loam and maintain constant surface moisture until emergence. Thin carefully to prevent crowding, which causes twisted or stunted roots. Keep beds weeded early since carrot seedlings are easily overtaken. Harvest at full size, wash gently, and store in cold, humid conditions to retain crispness. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: White Scallop Squash
description: Sow White Scallop seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to one strong plant every 24 to 36 inches. This heirloom patty pan squash produces flat, scalloped-edge fruits with tender white flesh on productive bush plants. Harvest the fruits young at 2 to 4 inches across for the best flavor and texture, picking often to keep new ones forming. Keep the soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs during warm weather. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: White Spear Bunching Onion (Heat-Resistant Scallion)
description: White Spear produces tall, straight, blue-green tops over long, cylindrical white shanks that stay uniform and resist the splitting and curling that plague many bunching onions during peak summer heat. It is less winter-hardy than overwintering types such as Evergreen Hardy White, so it performs best sown for a spring-through-fall harvest window rather than left to stand through hard freezes. Its clean, uniform stalks and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for a continuous summer scallion supply. Harvest at pencil thickness for the mildest flavor and most tender texture, or let shanks thicken slightly for a stronger bite. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: White Sprouting Broccoli (Hardy English Heirloom Overwintering Broccoli)
description: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer or early fall, spacing plants wide to accommodate a full season of growth before the harvest of edible flower shoots the following late winter. White Sprouting is a classic English heirloom broccoli grown as a hardy biennial: plants spend fall and winter building a large rosette of foliage, then in late winter to early spring send up a profusion of small, tender, cream-white flowering shoots that are harvested continually over several weeks, much like purple sprouting broccoli but ivory-headed and typically a touch earlier. Regular picking of the central and side shoots before flowers open encourages continued production, and the long harvest window makes it valuable for filling the late-winter garden gap when little else is producing. It needs a long, cool growing season to perform well and is best suited to mild-winter climates like the Gulf South where it can overwinter in the open ground without protection. Matures in 220–260 days from transplant.

name: White Stinkwood
description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Celtis africana is drought tolerant once established, growing well in a wide range of soils including clay, rocky, and alkaline soils typical of the South African highveld and bushveld — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Celtis africana (White Stinkwood, Witstinkhout) is a large, graceful, fast-growing deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the forests, river margins, and bush-margins of South Africa (particularly the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga) and extending north through East Africa. The English common name 'stinkwood' refers to the smell of freshly cut wood — the dried wood does not smell strongly and is actually a fine-grained, attractive timber used for furniture and flooring in South Africa (though far less valuable than the true 'Black Stinkwood,' Ocotea bullata). Celtis africana is one of South Africa's most popular garden shade trees: fast-growing, with an elegant, slightly weeping branch structure, fine-textured, lime-green foliage that provides deep shade, and outstanding wildlife value — the small, round, yellow-orange to red-black fruits are eagerly eaten by many fruit-eating birds including barbets, mousebirds, bulbuls, and starlings. The tree supports many butterfly species and is larval host plant for the Charaxes butterfly group. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: White Sweet Spanish Onion (Classic Long-Day Mild White Onion)
description: Start seeds indoors in late winter and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last hard frost. This long-established long-day onion produces large, globe-shaped bulbs with clean white skin and mild, juicy, sweet flesh with a milder bite than most storage onions, making it a popular choice for fresh eating, salads, and onion rings. Because long-day onions need the extended summer daylight of higher latitudes to bulb properly, it performs best north of about zone 7 and tends to produce poorly or bolt in the short-day Deep South. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development and cure bulbs in a warm, airy spot after the tops fall over, though sweet types like this one store for a shorter time than pungent storage onions. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: White Transparent Sugarcane (Heirloom Pale-Stalked Chewing Cane)
description: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. White Transparent is an old chewing-cane heirloom with pale, whitish-yellow-green stalks, distinct from the purple, red, and striped canes traditionally grown alongside it in the same dooryard patch. Like other chewing types it has a soft rind and high juice content, with fibers that cling together in a wad rather than shredding when gnawed, making it a favorite for fresh peeling and eating rather than crushing for syrup, though the juice can be pressed like any cane. It is maintained today mainly through small heirloom cane collections and informal seed-saver networks in Florida and Louisiana rather than commercial nurseries. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy, disease-free stalks before the first hard freeze, bed them horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and cover heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic to keep them dormant without freezing until replanting the following spring once soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh chewing from October through December after cool nights have sweetened the stalks. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: White Triana Fig (Andalusian Heirloom)
description: White Triana is an old-world Spanish heirloom associated with the Triana district of Seville in Andalusia, distinct from the White Adriatic, White Genoa, and White Marseilles already grown here. Fruit is medium-sized, ripening to a pale yellow-green-to-creamy-gold skin with translucent amber, lightly strawberry-tinged flesh that carries a syrupy, low-acid sweetness. It is self-fruitful and produces both a breba and a main crop, and growers report it holds up especially well through long, hot, humid summers rather than favoring the drier Mediterranean climates that stress some other Spanish and Italian heirlooms. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Triumph Sweet Potato (Vintage Dry-Type Southern Heirloom)
description: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy-loam soil hilled into ridges, and hold off on nitrogen-rich fertilizer since it pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation. White Triumph is a vintage dry-type sweet potato with tan to yellowish-white skin and snow-white flesh that cooks up firm and mealy rather than moist, closer in texture to a baking potato than to a modern orange-fleshed variety, with a mild, only lightly sweet flavor. Vines are vigorous and the roots are known to resist soil rot and scurf better than many old white-fleshed types, giving reliable mid-season yields around 90-105 days. Dig before the first frost once vines start to yellow, then cure in a warm, humid spot for a week or two to firm the skin and improve keeping quality. Matures in 90–105 days from transplant.

name: White Turmeric (Zedoary, Wild Turmeric, Gajutphal)
description: Plant in loose, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; white turmeric (zedoary) has white to pale yellow flesh with a complex camphoraceous, ginger-mango-like aroma and a peppery-bitter flavor quite different from yellow turmeric. An ancient spice from India and Southeast Asia, it was an important medieval European import and remains in use in Indonesian, Sri Lankan, and Japanese cuisines as well as Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese medicine. Fresh rhizomes are sliced thin and eaten in salads, pickled, or used to flavor rice and curries; the dried powder gives a pale cream-yellow color to foods. The showy cone-like flower bracts are also used in tropical landscaping. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: White Velvet Okra (Smooth Round-Pod Heirloom Okra with Velvety Texture)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms to 70°F; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest pods at 2–3 inches for most tender pods. White Velvet Okra is an heirloom okra variety distinguished from the standard elongated ridged types by its round, smooth pods — the 'velvet' texture of the surface, which lacks the prominent longitudinal ridges of varieties like Clemson Spineless, and the pale green to cream-white color at harvest maturity (before fully ripening to cream-white and drying). The round-pod okra group, of which White Velvet is one of the best-known American heirloom examples, represents a different selection from the standard commercial okra breeding that prioritized uniformly ridged, elongated pods for mechanical harvesting and packing. Round-pod types have thinner, more tender pod walls and a slightly different texture and mucilage content than ridged types — attributes that some cooks prefer, particularly for preparations where the 'sliminess' of okra is considered a negative quality. White Velvet's pods harvested at 2–3 inches have a tender, delicate texture and mild flavor appropriate for sautéing, grilling, pickling, and use in gumbo where the mucilaginous properties of okra serve as a natural thickener. The plant is vigorous and heat-tolerant — essential qualities for zone 9 summer production — and produces prolifically throughout the summer if harvested regularly. The cream-white color at harvest maturity (before pods fully dry and tan) makes White Velvet visually distinctive from the dark green and burgundy okra varieties and attractive for fresh-market presentation. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: White Versailles Currant (Classic French White Currant)
description: White Versailles is a long-cultivated French white currant, dating to the nineteenth century, valued for its vigorous growth and long, well-filled strigs of large, pale golden-pink berries with a mild, honeyed flavor milder than most red currants. Ribes species are restricted or banned in some states and counties as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust, so verify local rules before ordering plants. The vigorous, upright bush establishes quickly and tolerates a wider range of soils than many currant cultivars, though it still fruits best with consistent moisture and a mulched, cool root zone. Because fruit forms on older spurwood, prune out only the oldest third of stems each winter rather than cutting hard, and net ripening clusters against birds, which find the pale, glowing fruit just as attractive as red currants. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: White Vienna Kohlrabi
description: Sow White Vienna seeds half an inch deep and thin to 4 to 6 inches apart for well-formed bulbs. This heirloom cole crop develops smooth, pale green globes with crisp, mild, slightly sweet flesh where the stem swells above the soil. Keep growth fast and steady with even moisture, and harvest the bulbs while they are 2 to 3 inches across before they turn woody. Both the swollen stem and the young leaves are edible raw or cooked. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: White Wing Onion (F1 Early Sweet White Onion)
description: Start seed indoors under lights and transplant hardened seedlings into rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to let bulbs expand freely. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development, since this fast-maturing type sizes up quickly and does not tolerate drought well during that stage. White Wing is a widely grown hybrid valued for its early maturity, glossy white globe-shaped bulbs, and mild sweet flavor best used fresh, as short-season sweet onions like this one are not bred for long winter storage. Matures in 85–95 days from transplant.

name: White Winter Pearmain Apple (Griffin's Pearmain, Historic Low-Chill Heirloom)
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This old American heirloom likely originated as a chance seedling in the central-eastern United States in the late 1700s or early 1800s and was carried west by settlers, becoming known in Texas orchards under the local name Griffin's Pearmain. Its chill requirement of about 400 hours puts it comfortably within reach of most zone 8-9 Gulf Coast winters, unusual for a variety with such deep heirloom roots. The translucent, waxy yellow skin surrounds firm, aromatic flesh often described as honeyed with tropical notes, and the tree is vigorous, precocious, and a reliable pollenizer for other apple varieties planted nearby. It ripens later than the Israeli and Florida-bred selections, giving Gulf South growers a late-season, better-keeping option. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: White Wonder Cucumber
description: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; White Wonder is an heirloom slicing cucumber producing large, 7–8 inch fruits with ivory-to-cream-white skin, crisp white flesh, and an exceptionally mild, cool, lightly sweet flavor with virtually no bitterness — the mildest of all cucumber types. The white color results from the absence of chlorophyll in the skin rather than from immaturity; properly ripe White Wonder fruits are uniformly ivory-white and are never green. The skin is thin and does not require peeling, and the flesh is juicier and more tender than standard green cucumbers with the same thin-skinned type. White Wonder cucumbers are a curiosity and conversation piece in the garden and at farmers' markets, attracting attention precisely because the white color is unexpected. The heat tolerance is comparable to standard cucumber types, and the vigorous vines produce well through zone 9 spring and fall seasons. Pick every 2–3 days to maintain production. Matures in 58–65 days from seed.

name: White Wonder Feverfew (Double Pompom Feverfew)
description: White Wonder produces fully double, all-white pompom flowers rather than the single daisy blooms of the species, giving it a look closer to a miniature chrysanthemum and making it a favorite for cutting gardens and dried arrangements. Culturally it behaves like the species: it tolerates poor soil and drought once established but flowers best with regular moisture and a sunny spot. Deadhead spent blooms frequently to extend flowering and to prevent the plant from setting seed, since double-flowered selections often produce a mix of double and single offspring when they self-sow. Cut stems for indoor arrangements just as the pompoms fully open, and divide or replace clumps every few years as vigor declines. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: White Wood Betony (Alba Wood Betony)
description: Alba is the white-flowered selection of wood betony, forming the same neat rosettes of deeply veined, scallop-edged, dark-green foliage as the species but topped in early summer by upright spikes of clean white tubular flowers instead of the typical rose-pink to magenta of the type plant. It brightens a partly shaded herb garden or woodland-edge planting and combines especially well with darker-flowered companions, where its pale spikes read as a cooling accent rather than competing with the species' hot pink tones. Grow exactly as the species: moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, undemanding once established, and long-lived without division. Bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators visit the white form as readily as the pink, making it a useful addition to a wildlife or medicinal herb border without sacrificing pollinator value for color variety. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: White Yam
description: Plant sett pieces 4–6 inches deep in loose, deeply dug, well-drained soil — white yam tubers grow straight down and require at least 18 inches of loose, stone-free soil. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence for the twining vines, which can reach 15–20 feet. The large, starchy white or cream-fleshed tubers (distinctly different from sweet potatoes, which are Ipomoea) are the most important traditional food crop in West Africa, where yam is eaten pounded into fufu, roasted, boiled, or fried as chips. Unlike the common yam varieties in Western grocery stores (which are often actually sweet potatoes), true white yam has a dry, starchy texture and neutral flavor that complements bold sauces and stews. Harvest when vines yellow in fall, dig carefully to avoid breaking tubers. Matures in 210–270 days from transplant.

name: White-seed Melon
description: Direct sow Cucumeropsis mannii seeds in hills in full sun in rich, deep, well-drained soil after temperatures are consistently warm; train vines on a trellis or allow to sprawl on the ground; harvest mature fruits when the skin yellows and stems cork; dry seeds thoroughly before storage or use. White-seed Melon is one of two major 'egusi' cucurbits of West Africa (the other being the egusi watermelon, Citrullus lanatus var. citroides), distinguished by its round, smooth, cream-green fruits and large, flat, distinctly white seeds. The plant is a trailing or climbing annual vine with lobed, cucumber-like leaves and small yellow flowers — grown entirely for its seeds, which are the primary ingredient in Egusi Soup, the beloved national dish of Nigeria and a staple across much of West and Central Africa. The seeds are dried, then ground into a paste or coarse meal and fried in palm oil with onions and tomatoes before adding stock and leafy greens (typically bitter leaf or pumpkin leaf) to create the rich, deeply savory egusi soup. Seeds can also be pressed to produce egusi oil, a golden cooking oil with a mild, nutty flavor. The flesh of the fruits is not eaten (bitter and unpalatable) — the crop is exclusively a seed crop. An important protein and fat source in West African diets where meat is expensive. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Whitebeam
description: Sow cleaned seeds directly into a nursery bed in autumn, covering lightly with 1/4 inch of soil; the distinctive white-felted leaves of seedlings make them easy to identify and separate from weeds in spring. Whitebeam is notably tolerant of shallow, alkaline, and chalky soils, making it one of the few ornamental fruiting trees suited to difficult chalk downland conditions. Grow in full sun for the most compact habit and the best berry production; established trees are drought-tolerant and require little supplemental watering except during prolonged dry spells. Allow five or more years from seed for the tree to reach flowering size and begin producing its scarlet autumn berries. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Whitebrush (Beebrush)
description: Whitebrush is a wiry, semi-deciduous native shrub of Texas, the Gulf Coast, and northern Mexico in the same genus as lemon verbena, and it shares that cousin's fragrant foliage; the tiny tubular white flowers appear in dense spikes in flushes after rain and are so attractive to bees that ranchers and beekeepers prize the resulting honey. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer, since seed germination is slow and unreliable, and root them in a well-drained mix before transplanting. Plant in full sun in lean, alkaline, or caliche soils and avoid heavy fertile ground or overwatering, which encourages lank growth and reduces flowering; once established the shrub shrugs off drought and heat with ease. Dry the aromatic leaves for a mild, lemony-anise tisane much as one would with lemon verbena, and prune lightly after bloom flushes to keep the naturally airy, twiggy form tidy. Matures in 545–1095 days from transplant.

name: Whitesmith Gooseberry (Classic English Dessert Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant, thorny bushes in cool, fertile, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open framework for good air movement and easier picking. Whitesmith is a long-established English dessert gooseberry prized for its smooth-skinned, pale greenish-white to creamy fruit that turns genuinely sweet once fully ripe, making it one of the better gooseberry cultivars for eating fresh rather than only cooking. The vigorous, slightly arching bush crops heavily but can be prone to mildew in humid conditions, so good spacing and airflow matter more than with some mildew-resistant modern hybrids. Harvest in stages, picking some berries green and firm for pies and preserves and leaving the rest to ripen fully for fresh eating. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Whopper Improved Tomato (Large-Fruited Hybrid Beefsteak)
description: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vigorous vine to support the heavy fruit. Whopper Improved is a Park Seed hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for large, meaty, flavorful fruit and broad resistance to common tomato diseases, making it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting big slicing tomatoes without the disease susceptibility of many open-pollinated beefsteak heirlooms. It produces well over a long season in the Gulf South's extended warm months. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking, and feed regularly to sustain the large fruit size through the harvest season. Matures in 70–75 days from transplant.

name: Wichita Pecan (Western High-Quality Pecan, Type II Commercial Pecan)
description: Plant in deep (4+ feet), well-drained loam or sandy loam in full sun; Wichita is very productive and precocious, bearing significant crops at 5–6 years after planting, earlier than most other varieties; supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring to prevent zinc deficiency; in humid southeastern conditions, Wichita is susceptible to pecan scab and may require fungicide protection. Wichita pecan is one of the most widely planted commercial pecan varieties in the southwestern United States — the dominant variety in the major commercial pecan production areas of western Texas and New Mexico where supplemental irrigation is available and the dry summer climate limits scab disease pressure. The variety was released by the USDA in 1959 and quickly achieved widespread planting in the irrigated orchards of the West Texas Pecan Belt (around San Saba, San Angelo, and the Pecos River region) and New Mexico's Mesilla Valley, where the combination of hot days, cool nights, low humidity, and fertile alluvial soils creates ideal pecan-growing conditions. Wichita produces large to very large nuts (40–45 per pound) with excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and an exceptional, rich buttery flavor — consistently rated among the highest-quality pecans for flavor by tasting panels. The kernels are plump and well-filled, bright golden-yellow in color, and have the mild, sweet, buttery flavor characteristic of high-quality western-grown pecans. Wichita is a Type II protogynous variety — meaning the pistillate (female) flowers become receptive before the pollen is shed — so it requires pairing with a Type I variety for reliable pollination. Early-bearing, high-quality, and widely available — Wichita is an excellent choice for zone 8–9 home orchard plantings where summer humidity is not extreme. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Wickson Crab (High-Sugar Cider Crabapple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, watering deeply while the young tree establishes and pruning in late winter to maintain an open canopy. Wickson was bred by Albert Etter in Northern California from a cross involving 'Newtown Pippin', selected for a tiny, cherry-sized golden-red crabapple with an extraordinarily high sugar and acid content rather than for fresh eating. Modern craft cider makers seek it out specifically because a small addition of Wickson juice to a blend adds concentrated sweetness, sharp acidity, and aromatic complexity that balance out blander cider apples. The heavy annual crop of small fruit ripens in early to mid fall and the tree also produces a good spring bloom, making it useful as a multi-purpose pollinizer, cider component, and ornamental in a home orchard. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wickson Plum (Luther Burbank's Sweet Crisp Yellow Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Wickson was bred by legendary plant breeder Luther Burbank in the early 1900s and named for a friend, producing translucent yellow-skinned fruit with an exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, dense flesh that has made it a favorite among chefs and farmers-market growers seeking intensely sweet, distinctive stone fruit. The plum's crisp texture, closer to an apple's crunch than the soft, juicy give of most plums, sets it apart texturally as well as in flavor, and it has enjoyed a revival of interest among specialty growers rediscovering Burbank's historic introductions. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, and harvest once fruit turns translucent gold and yields slightly to pressure for the sweetest flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wiki Tu Feijoa
description: Wiki Tu is a New Zealand-bred feijoa cultivar developed as part of the modern wave of Kiwi selections aimed at improving on the older American-market standards like Mammoth and Triumph, prized both for good fruit quality and for its reliability as a cross-pollinator. Fruit is medium-large, oval, and smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic flesh and a moderate seed count, ripening in the mid-season window typical of New Zealand feijoa breeding lines. The shrub is vigorous and heavy-flowering, and its abundant, well-timed pollen makes it a favored partner cultivar for other New Zealand-origin feijoas in mixed plantings, improving yields across the whole hedgerow rather than just its own fruit set. Like other feijoas it thrives on Gulf Coast heat and humidity once established, tolerating brief winter cold snaps and needing only routine watering and an annual light prune to keep its evergreen form tidy. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wild Achocha (Slipper Gourd Relative)
description: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; wild achocha grows and fruits quickly through a single warm season. A fast-growing Andean relative of the more widely grown achocha (Cyclanthera pedata), it produces smaller, spiny, hollow, cucumber-flavored fruit on vigorous tendril-climbing vines, harvested young and cooked or pickled much like its better-known relative, with a similarly mild, crunchy texture. Extremely productive and easy from seed, it thrives in ordinary garden soil with a support to climb and can produce a heavy crop of small fruit within two to three months of sowing in warm weather. Harvest fruit young, while still tender and before seeds mature and harden, for the best eating quality, and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive through the season. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wild African Cucumber / African Horned Cucumber (wild)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun after soil temperatures reach at least 65°F. This drought-tolerant scrambling vine needs little supplemental water once established but appreciates a deep soak at planting. Harvest the very young, pale-green fruits before they develop their characteristic spines and bitterness, as mature fruits require prolonged cooking or are best reserved for medicinal use. In cooler climates, start seeds indoors 3–4 weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather settles. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wild Angelica
description: Angelica sylvestris is a tall, statuesque biennial or short-lived monocarpic perennial native to moist woodland margins, riverbanks, and damp meadows throughout Europe and temperate Asia, closely related to garden angelica (A. archangelica) but more tolerant of shade and with a wilder, more ornamental character; it produces large, pinnate, bright-green leaves, hollow, purplish-tinged stems, and showy, rounded umbels of white to pink-flushed flowers in summer that are exceptionally attractive to a wide range of pollinators including native bees, hoverflies, and butterflies. Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained to moisture-retentive, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade of a woodland edge, damp border, or streamside planting; seed viability is very short-lived and must be sown as fresh as possible — refrigerator storage can extend viability for a few weeks. The plant dies after flowering and setting seed (monocarpic) but self-sows prolifically in suitable moist, partially shaded conditions, maintaining a garden colony once established; remove spent flower heads promptly if self-sowing is not desired. The ornamental purple-dark cultivar 'Purpurea' ('Vicar's Mead') has become popular in naturalistic garden design for its striking, deep-purple stems and foliage, particularly effective in damp, partly shaded wild gardens. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Wild Banana (Balbis Banana, Saging na Saba)
description: Plant suckers in deeply cultivated, rich, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Musa balbisiana is more drought-tolerant than Musa acuminata and can tolerate brief dry spells once established, but performs best with regular moisture. Musa balbisiana (wild banana) is one of the two ancestral wild banana species from which virtually all cultivated banana and plantain varieties worldwide derive — along with Musa acuminata, it contributed the 'B' genome to many banana cultivars (Cavendish bananas are triploid AAA; plantains are typically AAB or ABB — the B refers to M. balbisiana's genetic contribution). The species produces seedy, starchy fruits that require cooking and are eaten in Asia, but its primary horticultural significance in Western gardens is as an ornamental banana and as an ancestor of cultivated types. It produces striking, large, paddle-shaped leaves on a 10-to-15-foot pseudostem — similar in appearance to the plantain but slightly smaller — and is among the most cold-hardy Musa species, surviving temperatures to 22–25°F when well-mulched, making it more reliable as a zone 8 ornamental landscape plant than most banana species. In zone 9, it grows as a near-permanent perennial specimen. Matures in 270–480 days from transplant.

name: Wild Basil
description: Surface-sow seed in fall directly in the garden, or press it lightly into a moist seedbed in early spring, as the fine seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate well. This minty-aromatic native of Europe and western Asia thrives in lean, well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade, where it forms upright clumps bearing dense whorls of small purplish-pink flowers from June through September that are magnets for bumblebees and butterflies. The leaves can be used fresh or dried as a thyme-like culinary herb in soups, stuffings, and savory dishes. Cut plants back by half after the main flush of bloom to encourage a second flush and keep growth compact. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Wild Bergamot
description: Surface-sow seeds onto moist starting mix and keep at 65–70°F; wild bergamot germinates in 10–21 days and is more drought-tolerant than the cultivated red bee balm. Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun for the most aromatic foliage and best disease resistance. Harvest leaves and flowers throughout summer for oregano-scented teas with a mild thymol character, used traditionally by many Indigenous nations for cold and fever support. Divide established clumps every 2–3 years as the center tends to die out. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Wild Betel Leaf (La Lot, Cha Plu)
description: Set rooted cuttings or rhizome divisions in humus-rich, constantly moist soil in full to partial shade; a thin bark or leaf mulch keeps the shallow, creeping stems from drying out between waterings. Piper sarmentosum spreads as a low groundcover of heart-shaped, glossy, peppery-aromatic leaves used fresh as a wrap for Thai miang kham and grilled in Vietnamese cha la lot, so keep harvesting young leaves to encourage bushy new growth rather than flowering spikes. It dies back hard below about 40°F, so gardeners outside zone 9–11 grow it in containers that overwinter indoors near a bright, humid window. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to renew vigor and generate new plants for sharing. Matures in 75–120 days from transplant.

name: Wild Ceylon Cardamom (Greater Cardamom, Long Cardamom)
description: This is the wild, indigenous form of cardamom found in the rainforests of southwestern Sri Lanka, distinguished from the cultivated Malabar and Mysore types (var. minor) by its notably taller stature, larger elongated seed pods, and inflorescences that stand more erect above the foliage rather than trailing along the ground. It is only rarely brought into cultivation today, valued mostly by collectors and gene banks preserving cardamom's genetic diversity, since commercial growers favor the higher-yielding cultivated types. Give it the same deep, humid shade, constant soil moisture, and rich organic mulch that true cardamom requires, and expect a slower, more forest-like clump that takes several years to flower. Because seed-grown wild stock is variable and difficult to source, propagation is almost always by division of established rhizome clumps. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wild Chervil, Cow Parsley
description: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild chervil self-seeds prolifically and can become invasive in disturbed sites — thin seedlings to prevent overcrowding. NOTE: Anthriscus sylvestris closely resembles Conium maculatum (poison hemlock) and Oenanthe crocata (hemlock water dropwort), both deadly poisonous; always positively identify by the red-flushed hollow stems and distinctive aroma before handling. Anthriscus sylvestris is a widespread European biennial or short-lived perennial that produces large, finely cut, fern-like, bright-green leaves from spring through early summer and frothy, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers on tall stems that are spectacular bee and hoverfly forage in May and June; the ornamental dark-leafed cultivar 'Ravenswing' has deep, chocolate-burgundy foliage that is one of the most striking dark-leaved plants for partial shade in cool-climate gardens. The young leaves and stems have a mild anise-parsley flavor and are edible as a salad herb before flowering, though positive plant ID is essential. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wild Cinnamon (Cinnamon Bark)
description: Native to the Florida Keys, the Caribbean, and the Bahamas, this slow-growing evergreen shrub yields an aromatic cinnamon- and pepper-scented inner bark that was historically dried and used as a cinnamon substitute and pungent seasoning, and is still an ingredient in some Caribbean bay-rum style preparations. The glossy leathery leaves also release a peppery cinnamon scent when crushed and can be used sparingly as a seasoning. Grow in full sun to light shade in sharply drained, sandy or limestone soil; established plants are highly drought- and salt-tolerant coastal hammock natives. Clusters of small dark purple-red flowers give way to bright red pea-sized berries that ripen over winter. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Wild Crapemyrtle (Texas Barbados Cherry, Manzanita)
description: Malpighia glabra, sometimes sold as wild crapemyrtle for its crinkled, crape-myrtle-like pink flowers, is a smaller and notably more drought- and cold-tolerant relative of the commercially grown acerola (Malpighia emarginata), native to the thornscrub and caliche soils of South Texas and Mexico. It produces small, tart, bright red fruit high in vitamin C, borne in flushes after rain through the warm season, though the fruit is smaller and less abundant than named acerola cultivars. Grow in full sun in well-drained, even rocky or alkaline soil; established plants tolerate significant drought and brief cold snaps better than true acerola, making it a good xeric hedge or specimen shrub in South Texas and similar Gulf Coast landscapes. Prune lightly to shape after flowering flushes; it needs minimal supplemental fertilizer once established. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wild Garlic (Ramsons)
description: Plant bulbs in autumn in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade beneath deciduous trees; wild garlic is a spring ephemeral of European and Asian deciduous forests that completes its entire growing cycle from late winter through late spring before going fully dormant. The broad, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive garlic aroma can be harvested as soon as they emerge in late winter for salads, pesto, and compound butters; they are milder and more versatile than cultivated garlic leaves. White star-shaped flowers in spring are also edible and edible. The plant naturalizes freely by self-seeding to form large carpets — plant densely from the start for a showy spring display under trees. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Wild Ginger
description: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in deep shade to partial shade; wild ginger is one of the finest native groundcovers for dense shade, forming a low, tight carpet of large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves that suppresses weeds effectively under mature trees where even grass fails. The small, maroon-brown, jug-shaped flowers bloom at soil level in early spring, hidden beneath the foliage and pollinated by early ground beetles. The rhizomes have a spicy, ginger-like fragrance and have been used as a ginger substitute in traditional cooking, though they are not botanically related to culinary ginger (Zingiber officinale). An outstanding native groundcover for moist, deeply shaded sites under deciduous canopy. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Wild Goose Plum
description: Plant pits in fall in a sunny, well-drained spot with slightly acidic to neutral soil; this heat-tolerant native plum performs exceptionally well in the southeastern and south-central United States where many other plums fail. Thin seedlings to the strongest individual and allow it to develop naturally; wild goose plum will begin producing fruit within three to six years from a strong seedling and often spreads via root suckers to form a productive thicket. Cross-pollination with another wild plum or a compatible named variety will significantly improve fruit set and yields of the flavorful red-yellow fruits. This species is an important parent of many named southern plum varieties and provides early spring blooms that are a critical food source for native pollinators emerging from winter. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wild Magic Basil (Herbalea Sterile Ornamental-Culinary Basil)
description: Plant started cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, or grow in containers and overwinter indoors in cold climates. Wild Magic, part of the Herbalea breeding series, is a sterile interspecific basil hybrid that flowers continuously all season with showy magenta-purple bracts and blooms, resembling an ornamental ageratum as much as a culinary herb, while never setting viable seed. Because the flowers never mature to seed, the plant channels its energy into nonstop bloom and fresh leaf production rather than bolting and turning bitter the way seed-grown basils do once they flower. The bright green leaves carry a mild, sweet, faintly Thai-basil-like flavor and can be harvested continuously alongside the edible flower spikes, which make an attractive, mildly spicy garnish. It also tolerates cooler nights better than most seed-grown sweet basils, extending the usable season at both ends. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Wild Medlar (African Medlar, Vangueria)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — a true bushveld species. Vangueria infausta (wild medlar or African medlar) is a deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savanna and bushveld regions of eastern and southern Africa — common across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique, and Kenya in seasonally dry habitats. The plant produces round to slightly flattened, 1–2 inch fruits that ripen from green to yellowish-brown, with soft, sweet-acid, mealy flesh and 4–5 large seeds. The flavor when fully ripe is pleasant — sweet with fruity-acid notes somewhat reminiscent of a tart apple-medlar — and the fruits are eaten fresh throughout rural sub-Saharan Africa, as well as dried into a concentrated fruit leather, fermented into traditional beer, or made into jams and sauces. The tree is highly drought-resistant, adapted to seasonally dry and poor soils of the African bushveld, making it a candidate for water-wise agroforestry in dry subtropical climates. The leaves, bark, and roots have extensive use in southern African traditional medicine. As an ornamental and food plant in zone 9–11 dry climates, wild medlar is a low-maintenance, wildlife-friendly tree that produces an edible crop under difficult conditions. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wild Mint (American Wild Mint)
description: Plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; wild mint is North America's only native mint species and has the widest natural range of any mint in the world — native from the Atlantic Coast to Asia across the boreal zone. It grows naturally at stream banks, pond margins, moist meadows, and woodland edges, forming spreading mats of intensely aromatic leaves with a clean mint-spearmint fragrance used exactly like cultivated spearmint for teas, cooking, and flavoring. The small lavender-purple flower whorls in summer attract numerous native bees including specialized pollen bees in the genus Cleptes. Unlike garden mints, it is fully native and supports native insects while providing the same culinary utility. It tolerates partial shade and moist soil conditions that are inhospitable to most culinary herbs. Contain with underground barriers or allow to naturalize in appropriate wet areas. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Wild Opium Lettuce
description: Lactuca virosa is a tall, coarse European biennial that has naturalized widely in North America; it produces a milky latex called lactucarium that was historically used as a mild sedative and opium substitute, though its effects are weak and its safety profile is poorly established. Surface-sow the light-dependent seeds in autumn or early spring into open, disturbed soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 12–18 inches apart; plants form a basal rosette in the first year before bolting to flower in the second. This plant is NOT recommended for eating raw — the sap is intensely bitter, and the plant's medicinal alkaloids should be treated with caution; consult qualified herbalists and current literature before any medicinal use. Grow primarily as a botanical curiosity or living link to historical apothecary gardens, where it was once a staple of the physician's herb patch. Matures in 90–150 days from seed.

name: Wild Oregano (Common Marjoram)
description: Sow direct after last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; avoid rich, fertile soil which produces lush but relatively flavorless plants — oregano's essential oils are most concentrated when the plant is slightly stressed by poor soil and minimal water. Origanum vulgare is the common wild oregano of Europe and the source of dried Italian-style oregano; the species varies enormously in flavor intensity depending on climate and selection, with Mediterranean-climate plants (especially Greek 'Hirtum') being the most pungent, while cool-climate plants can be nearly flavorless. The species naturalizes easily in dry, sunny banks and rock gardens and produces masses of tiny, pink to white flowers in summer that are excellent nectar sources for bees and butterflies. Subsp. hirtum (Greek oregano) is the pungent, strongly flavored selection recommended for culinary use. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wild Oregano / Bolivian Oregano
description: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost date; this tropical shrub grows vigorously in heat and humidity that would stress common oregano, making it an excellent substitute in warm-climate gardens. Water deeply but infrequently once established, allowing the soil to dry out between sessions, as the plant is highly drought-adapted and prone to root rot in soggy ground. Harvest stem tips regularly throughout the warm season, as frequent cutting promotes dense branching and keeps the intensely oregano-scented leaves at peak potency for culinary use. In zone 8, mulch heavily around the base before the first frost and cut plants back to a few inches in late winter; they will resprout vigorously from the woody base as temperatures climb. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Wild Rice (Annual Wild Rice)
description: Sow fresh, never-dried seeds in fall directly into waterlogged mud or 6–24 inches of still water at the margins of ponds, lakes, or slow-moving rivers; wild rice is one of the most ecologically and culturally important native grains of North America, forming dense stands in the Great Lakes region that have sustained Ojibwe and other Indigenous peoples for millennia and providing critical food for migrating waterfowl. The tall, feathery annual grass germinates in spring when water warms, forms a floating seedling stage, then rockets upward to 4–10 feet by midsummer, bearing separate male and female florets on a large open panicle. Grain shatters and falls into the water when ripe in late summer — harvest by canoe, bending stalks over the gunwale and knocking seeds loose. Because viability is lost within days of drying, only purchase or plant seeds stored in water. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Wild Rice (Northern Wild Rice)
description: Sow wet-stored seeds in 6–24 inches of clean, still or slow-moving fresh water in full sun over a muddy bottom — wild rice requires specific aquatic conditions and will not grow in conventional garden beds. It is an annual grass of northern North American lakes that produces one of the most prized indigenous food grains in its season, with a distinctively nutty, earthy, chewy character that is incomparably superior to the paddy-cultivated product sold commercially. The tall plants emerge from submerged seeds in spring, grow through summer, and produce loose, open grain heads above the water in late summer — traditionally harvested by canoe, knocking the ripe seeds into the hull. Because the seeds ripen unevenly and shatter easily when ripe, harvesting requires repeat passes or netting under the heads. An outstanding wildlife food for ducks, geese, and marsh birds. Best grown in a controlled pond, large rain garden, or constructed wetland. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Wild Rocket (Sand Rocket, Annual Wall Rocket)
description: Direct sow thinly in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 4–6 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously. Diplotaxis muralis (wild rocket or sand rocket) is a European native annual brassica closely related to but distinct from common cultivated arugula (Eruca sativa) — it is the species known in Italy as 'rucola selvatica' (wild rocket) and is considered by Italian chefs to produce a more authentic, intensely peppery-bitter arugula flavor than the cultivated form. Wild rocket has smaller, more deeply pinnately-lobed leaves, a more intensely pungent, sharp, mustardy-bitter flavor, and tiny, four-petaled yellow flowers (compared to arugula's cream-white flowers) — the flowers are also edible, mildly peppery and attractive as a salad garnish. This species tends to self-seed prolifically once established, naturalizing in disturbed, lean, dry soils where it forms self-perpetuating patches. In Italian cuisine, rucola selvatica is the traditional garnish for authentic Neapolitan pizza (layered fresh on the hot pizza immediately before serving), served with bresaola, aged cheeses, and in traditional Campanian and Pugliese salads. More bitter and pungent than cultivated arugula — use in smaller quantities or mix with milder greens. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Wild Sarsaparilla
description: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; this low-growing woodland native has a single compound leaf rising on an upright stem from the underground rhizome, giving it a distinctive appearance among shade plants. The fragrant root has long been used as a flavoring agent and sarsaparilla-like tonic, and the small dark berries are edible though not particularly flavorful. It spreads slowly by horizontal rhizome to form colonies and is excellent for naturalizing a dry shade area under conifers. Division is necessary for propagation as seed requires a double dormancy period of warm-then-cold stratification. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Wild Service Tree
description: Harvest fruits in late autumn and clean the seeds free of pulp before sowing 1/4 inch deep in a nursery bed; expect germination to be slow and potentially staggered over one to two springs, as wild service tree seeds are notoriously variable in their dormancy. Grow in well-drained loamy or clay soil in full sun to light shade, as this species thrives on the woodland edge in its native European habitat. The russet-brown berries are astringent when first ripe but become sweet and date-like after frost or bletting; harvest after the first hard frost for the best flavor. This rare woodland indicator species is long-lived and slow-growing, rewarding patience with outstanding maple-like autumn foliage and excellent value for pollinators and wildlife. Matures in 2555–4380 days from transplant.

name: Wild Spanish Thyme / Iberian Thyme
description: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun and gritty, low-fertility soil to replicate the rocky Iberian slopes where this thyme naturally carpets the landscape. Harvest small-leaved stems frequently throughout the growing season to encourage branching and to capture the delicate, slightly floral thyme flavor before the plant flowers. After blooming, shear plants back by about half to prevent woodiness and to stimulate a flush of fresh growth for late-season harvesting. This species forms a tidy, low mat suitable for edging herb beds or tucking into gaps in stone walls. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Wild Strawberry (Virginia Strawberry)
description: Plant rooted runners in moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this native species is one parent of the cultivated strawberry and produces intensely flavorful small red fruits that surpass commercial strawberries in taste, though not in size. The plant spreads vigorously by runners to form a dense groundcover that suppresses weeds and tolerates moderate foot traffic. Fruits are borne in late spring through early summer; birds, chipmunks, and turtles compete for the harvest so a loose barrier net may be needed. Divide or thin the planting every 2–3 years by removing older central crowns and retaining the vigorous outer runners. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Wild Sweet Potato (Man of the Earth, Manroot)
description: Ipomoea pandurata is a native perennial vine of eastern North America that grows from a massive, starchy taproot — sometimes exceeding 20 pounds — which stores energy through winter cold and summer drought alike. The vine climbs or sprawls vigorously from late spring through fall, bearing large white morning-glory flowers with deep magenta-purple centers that open each morning from June through September. Scarify seeds by nicking the seed coat with a file or sandpaper and soak overnight before direct sowing after last frost in well-drained soil; established plants from the taproot need little supplemental water once settled. The root is edible and was used historically by Indigenous peoples across eastern North America, though it is starchy and bitter raw, requiring long cooking to be palatable. Matures in 365–730 days from seed.

name: Wild Thyme (Creeping Thyme)
description: Sow seed in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; wild thyme is variable from seed — for specific flower color or mat habit, use vegetatively propagated plants. Thymus serpyllum is the low, mat-forming wild thyme of European heaths and rocky hillsides, spreading to form dense, fragrant carpets 2–6 inches tall bearing tiny, deep rose-pink to purple flowers in early summer that are covered with honeybees and butterflies; it is equally valuable as a culinary herb (leaves have a pleasant, mild thyme flavor) and as a ground cover, lawn substitute, and rock garden plant. It tolerates light foot traffic, making it excellent for planting between stepping stones and in paths; it is more cold-hardy and mat-forming than common thyme (T. vulgaris) and significantly more ornamental in flower. Shear lightly after blooming to keep compact. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Wild Treasure Blackberry (Thornless Wild-Flavor Trailing Cultivar)
description: Wild Treasure is a thornless trailing blackberry released in 2010 by the USDA-ARS breeding program, bred from a cross between a selection of the wild Pacific dewberry (Rubus ursinus) and the thornless trailing cultivar 'Waldo'. It was specifically developed to recapture the small, intensely flavored, wild-blackberry character of native R. ursinus in a plant that is thornless and machine-harvestable, unlike the prickly wild species itself. The long, trailing canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and wide row spacing typical of trailing types. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest, tie in the new primocanes for next year's crop, and favor a cool-summer, well-drained, full-sun site, since trailing blackberries of this parentage are best suited to Pacific Northwest-like growing conditions. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Wild Turmeric
description: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curcuma aromatica is dormant in winter and emerges in spring — mulch heavily to protect rhizomes from frost below zone 9, lift and store indoors in colder climates. Curcuma aromatica (Wild Turmeric, Kasturi Manjal, or Cochin Haldi) is a clumping rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to the subtropical forests of northeast India, Bhutan, and Myanmar, now cultivated across South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China. The rhizomes are bright orange-yellow internally — richly aromatic with a floral rose-camphor-turmeric scent — and are the primary ingredient in traditional South Asian skin-care and cosmetic preparations: traditional face packs (ubtan), skin-brightening pastes, and bath scrubs used in Hindu ritual bathing ceremonies, wedding preparations, and daily skin care, particularly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal. The curcumin content is lower than common turmeric (C. longa) so it is rarely used as a food spice. The ornamental value is exceptional: stunning pink to rose-purple, cone-shaped flower spikes emerge directly from the ground on separate stems before the large paddle-shaped leaves in spring — among the most beautiful of all Curcuma flowers. Excellent partial-shade ornamental spice plant for zone 8–11 gardens. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Wild Yam (American Wild Yam, Colic Root)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to dappled shade, giving the twining vine a fence, shrub, or trellis to climb. Wild Yam is a native North American woodland vine long used in traditional herbal medicine, historically valued for its knotty rhizome, which contains diosgenin, a plant steroid compound that served as an early industrial source for synthesizing progesterone and other steroid hormones; despite folk claims, the raw rhizome is not directly hormonally active when eaten and is not a food crop like true cultivated yams. In the garden it is grown chiefly as a native woodland vine for naturalized shade plantings, valued for its heart-shaped leaves, twining habit, and small, inconspicuous summer flowers followed by distinctive three-winged seed capsules in fall. It spreads slowly by rhizome once established and tolerates a range of shaded conditions, making it a good choice for a low-maintenance native groundcover vine at a woodland edge. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wildcat Cayenne Pepper (AAS-Winning Extra-Large Straight Cayenne)
description: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after frost danger has passed. Wildcat is an AAS regional winner selected for extra-large cayenne pods, roughly 8 inches long and straighter than typical cayenne fruit, with thicker, fleshier walls than older varieties. Heat is notably mild for a cayenne, in the 500-1500 Scoville range, giving a smoky, peppery sweetness that works well fresh, dried, or ground. The strong, compact, evenly branching plant sets fruit heavily and holds up well through the growing season with routine picking to encourage continued production. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Wilder Currant (Historic American Red Currant)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Wilder is an older American red currant cultivar long grown for its productivity and long, evenly filled clusters (strigs) of bright red, tart-sweet berries. It is self-fertile and bears reliably without a second bush for pollination, making it a practical single-plant choice for a small garden. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, with the classic bright, tart currant flavor that mellows only somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit mainly on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework each winter and remove any wood older than three years to keep the bush vigorous and productive. Net the bushes as fruit ripens, since birds are strongly drawn to currants. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wilder Red Currant
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, renewal-pruning the oldest canes each winter to keep yields high. Wilder is a vigorous early twentieth-century American red currant selected for its long, well-filled clusters of large, bright red berries and reliably heavy cropping. It is a workhorse jelly and juice currant, valued more for productivity and fruit size than for fresh eating, since the flavor stays tart even at full ripeness. Like other red currants it fruits on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood, and it is best grown in regions with cool summers and consistent moisture. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wilhelmsburger Rutabaga (Austrian Heirloom Purple-Top Swede)
description: Sow seed directly and thin to a final spacing of six to eight inches, since this Central European heirloom needs room for its globe-shaped root to bulk up. Wilhelmsburger produces a purple-topped, pale yellow-fleshed root known for dense texture and a mild, almost nutty sweetness that intensifies after a light frost. Leave roots in the ground into cool fall weather before harvesting for the best flavor and longest storage life, and use the tender young tops as cooked greens if thinning early plantings. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Wilking Mandarin (King-Willowleaf Heirloom Tangerine)
description: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil, since this older California cultivar performs best with reliable summer heat. Water deeply and regularly, and thin heavy fruit set to reduce the tree's tendency toward alternate bearing. Wilking produces deep orange, richly flavored fruit with a loose peel late in the mandarin season, and its flowers are notably fragrant. Though largely superseded commercially, it survives in heritage collections and backyard orchards as a parent of several modern mandarin hybrids, including Kinnow. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Willamette Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Hybrid, Large-Nutted Southern Selection)
description: Willamette was bred in North Carolina in 1953 by crossing a blight-tolerant native American chestnut seedling from Ohio with a composite Chinese chestnut parent combining the Kuling, Meiling, and Nanking selections, giving it strong genetic resistance to chestnut blight along with much larger nuts than a typical Chinese chestnut. The medium-sized, upright, widely spreading tree flowers late and profusely after full leaf-out, which helps it dodge late spring frosts, and bears heavy, regular crops of extremely large, glossy chocolate-brown nuts that are notably sweet and release freely from the burs at ripening in mid-September. It has long been favored for orchard and food-forest plantings in the southeastern United States, where it tolerates summer heat and humidity better than European or American chestnut. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and mulch to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity through the growing season. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Willamette Hazelnut (Historic Oregon Standard Filbert)
description: Released by Oregon State University in the mid-1970s, Willamette was for decades the dominant commercial hazelnut in the Willamette Valley before newer blight-resistant releases like Jefferson and Yamhill took over much of the acreage. It bears medium-sized, good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous, upright tree and ripens in mid-season, ahead of many older varieties. Like most pre-1990s Pacific Northwest cultivars it carries only limited resistance to eastern filbert blight, so orchard sanitation and, where needed, fungicide timing matter more than with modern resistant selections. Plant with a distinct, cross-compatible pollenizer within about 100 feet for reliable nut set. Matures in 1460–1825 days from transplant.

name: Willamette Hops (Mild English-Type Aroma Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Willamette, named for Oregon's Willamette Valley where it is extensively grown, is a widely planted English-type aroma hop bred as a Fuggle-derivative, valued for its mild, pleasant, slightly floral and spicy character well suited to English-style ales, brown ales, and other beer styles calling for a gentler hop presence than the assertive citrus hops popular in American IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a lighter harvest than in the Pacific Northwest. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Willamette Raspberry (Pacific Northwest Processing Standard)
description: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and support the upright canes with a simple wire trellis to keep the heavy midseason crop off the ground. Willamette was released by Oregon State University and for much of the twentieth century was the standard red raspberry of the Pacific Northwest processing industry, valued for firm, richly flavored, deep-red berries that hold together well for freezing and canning as well as fresh eating. The floricanes bear a single concentrated crop in early-to-mid summer, and the plant's moderate vigor and reasonable disease tolerance made it a dependable choice for both commercial fields and home gardens for generations. It prefers the cooler summers of its native range and, like most red raspberries, is a more marginal performer in hot, humid climates, so give it the coolest, best-drained spot available outside the Pacific Northwest. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes each spring to the sturdiest four or five per foot of row. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: William's Pride Apple (Very Early Disease-Resistant Dark Red Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also a product of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding effort, William's Pride carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and powdery mildew. The dark red, medium fruit ripens unusually early, often before the Fourth of July in warmer growing areas, with crisp, aromatic, mildly tart flesh. Because it softens fast after ripening, plan to harvest over a short window and use the fruit fresh rather than storing it. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Williams Banana (Williams Hybrid Cavendish)
