description: Williams is the Cavendish subgroup clone that built much of the modern export banana industry in Australia, California, and the Canary Islands, valued for reliable yields and classic sweet dessert fruit. It runs slightly shorter and stockier than Grand Nain but shares the same thin-leafed, cold-sensitive constitution, so a hard freeze can kill the pseudostem to the ground and set fruiting back a full season. In the Gulf South, grow it in a warm, wind-sheltered microclimate or large container, feed heavily through the growing season, and wrap or mulch the base deeply before winter. Expect one bunch per stalk before that stalk is cut back and replaced by a sucker. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Willits Citrange (Historic Cold-Hardy Swingle Orange-Trifoliate Hybrid)
description: Willits was among the first citrange hybrids Walter Swingle produced in his original 1897 trifoliate orange x sweet orange crosses, made in response to the catastrophic Florida freezes of the 1890s that wiped out groves as far south as Orlando. It later proved important as a parent of the Telfair and Thomasville citrangequats, lending its cold hardiness to those kumquat hybrids as breeders continued pushing citrus culture northward. The tart, seedy, orange-like fruit carries more acid than a true sweet orange and suits marmalade or ade far better than fresh eating, but the tree's trifoliate-influenced hardiness lets it survive freezes near 0°F that would kill standard oranges outright. Site it in full sun with sharp drainage and expect a semi-deciduous, lightly thorny habit typical of citrange hybrids, especially in colder Gulf Coast winters. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Willoughby Gooseberry (Cold-Hardy Canadian Red Gooseberry)
description: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Willoughby was bred in Canada for genuine cold hardiness and good resistance to American gooseberry mildew, producing medium, deep red berries with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and cooking alike. The productive, reliable bush handles harsh northern winters better than many European-type gooseberries, making it a solid choice for cold-climate home orchards wanting good disease resistance without sacrificing fruit quality. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften, and pick regularly through the ripening window, since gooseberries can be used both underripe and tart for cooking or fully ripe and sweet for fresh eating depending on preference. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Willow Leaf Lima Bean (Heat-Tolerant Heirloom Pole Lima)
description: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines. Willow Leaf lima bean is a Southern heirloom named for its distinctively narrow, willow-shaped leaflets, quite different from the broader foliage of most lima beans, and is prized for continuing to flower and set pods through the intense heat of a Gulf South summer that causes many other lima varieties to drop blossoms and stall production. Harvest pods once well-filled but still bright green for fresh shelling, or let them dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Regular picking of mature pods encourages the vine to keep flowering and setting new pods through the long growing season. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Willow-Leaf Bay Laurel
description: Grow willow-leaf bay in full sun to light shade in fertile, well-drained soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind in the colder part of its range. This RHS Award of Garden Merit form of common bay is prized for slender, willow-like leaves with a gently undulating edge that give the whole shrub a finer, more feathery texture than plain bay laurel. New leaves emerge with a coppery flush before settling into deep matte green, and small clusters of pale yellow-green flowers appear along the stems in spring. The narrow leaves are just as pungent as the species and can be picked and dried for the kitchen at any time once the plant is established; clip lightly through the growing season to maintain a dense, formal shape or leave it looser as a specimen tree. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Willow-leaved Sea Buckthorn
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil — willow-leaved sea buckthorn tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony ground and is highly drought-tolerant once established, making it a superb windbreak tree for cold, exposed sites. Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days before sowing in early spring, or sow fresh seed in fall for natural stratification. Because the species is dioecious, include at least one male tree for every five to six female trees to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set; the dense orange berry clusters ripen in late summer to autumn and are extraordinarily rich in vitamin C, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids. Larger and more tree-like than common sea buckthorn (H. rhamnoides), it can reach 30 feet, providing significant shade and windbreak value while producing a heavy fruit crop. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Wilma Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Type Avocado)
description: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and shield young trees for their first few winters with frost cloth or a temporary cold frame. Wilma is one of the Mexican-race cold-hardy avocado selections identified and propagated by Texas dooryard growers for in-ground planting where standard Florida and California avocado varieties would not survive winter. Fruit is small to medium, dark-skinned, and rich-flavored with the characteristic anise-scented leaves of the Mexican race, ripening over a late-summer to fall window typical of these cold-hardy types. Plant with a complementary flowering-type cultivar nearby for the best fruit set, since cross-pollination between Type A and Type B avocados generally improves yield over a single tree alone. Mature trees tolerate brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit; young trees remain the most vulnerable and should be protected through at least their first two winters. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wilson Pawpaw
description: Wilson was propagated from a wild seedling tree found growing near Cumberland, Kentucky, and was carried forward into the University of Kentucky and Kentucky State University regional pawpaw variety trials, where it scored well against both older named selections and newer breeding-program releases. The tree itself is notably strong-growing and long-lived, and it produces medium-to-large fruit with good, sweet flavor typical of the better wild Kentucky selections rather than the very largest fruit sizes bred into recent commercial cultivars. Its Appalachian Kentucky origin makes it a useful genetic contributor for growers wanting regionally adapted stock, and it remains available through a handful of specialty native-fruit nurseries. Give young trees consistent moisture and partial shade, moving them into fuller sun as they approach bearing age around year five or six. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Wilson White Sapote
description: Plant Wilson in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind; it is a dependably heavy-bearing tree, one of the earlier California white sapote selections still grown today. The fruit is somewhat flattened rather than round, with good, rich, custardy flavor typical of the species, but it softens and turns quickly once picked and does not hold in storage as well as newer cultivars like Reinecke Commercial. For that reason, Wilson suits growers who plan to eat, share, or process fruit soon after harvest rather than store or ship it. Pick as soon as the fruit softens slightly at the stem end and use within a few days for best quality. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Win-Win Choi (Miniature White-Stem Bok Choy)
description: Direct sow in early spring after danger of hard frost has passed, or in late summer for a fall harvest, spacing seedlings close together for the miniature form Win-Win Choi is bred to produce. Win-Win Choi is a compact, white-stemmed hybrid pac choi that forms a bulky, uniform, vase-shaped head only about a foot tall at full size, making it well suited to close spacing, containers, and gardeners who prefer a smaller-format bok choy to the larger green-stemmed types. Its improved heat tolerance compared to many pac choi varieties allows for a longer planting window into warmer weather before bolting becomes a concern. Harvest whole plants at the baby stage for tender salad use or let them fill out for a heartier stir-fry green. Matures in 35–45 days from seed.

name: Window Box Roma Tomato (Compact Paste Tomato)
description: Transplant into a sunny window box or small container after the last frost; the plant stays extremely compact, so it needs no staking or cage even when loaded with fruit. Window Box Roma is an All-America Selections winner bred to bring true plum-shaped paste tomatoes to the smallest growing spaces, producing 1.5-2 ounce oblong red fruit with meaty, low-moisture flesh well suited to sauces despite the plant's diminutive 12-18 inch stature. It offers one of the few genuinely dwarf paste-tomato options for balconies and windowsills. Matures in 60–68 days from transplant.

name: Windowbox Basil (Compact Dwarf Container Basil)
description: Start seed indoors or direct sow after the last frost, and grow in a container or small bed in full sun. This compact, naturally mounding basil was selected specifically for small spaces, staying dense and tidy in a windowsill pot or patio container rather than stretching tall and leggy like standard Genovese basil. The small, aromatic leaves have classic sweet basil flavor and are well suited to snipping a few at a time for garnish and light cooking use. Regular light pinching keeps the plant full and encourages continuous new growth through the season. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Windsor Blueberry
description: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Windsor is a southern highbush blueberry requiring 500–600 chill hours — more than the ultra-low-chill varieties like Flordablue and Biloxi, but still significantly less than northern varieties that require 800–1,200 hours. This intermediate chill requirement makes Windsor suitable for zone 9a where winters typically provide 500–700 chill hours but unsuitable for the warmer zone 9b areas. The advantage of Windsor's higher chill requirement is higher fruit quality — the berries are larger, firmer, darker, and more flavorful than very-low-chill varieties, with the rich, complex blueberry flavor that intensifies with more winter dormancy. Windsor was developed to provide the best possible fruit quality while still meeting the reduced chill requirements of the upper Gulf Coast. The midseason ripening (May–June in zone 9) follows the earliest varieties and provides an extended blueberry harvest season when planted alongside Biloxi or Flordablue. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Windsor Fava Bean
description: Direct sow seed very early in spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in fall where winters are mild, since fava beans need cool weather to set pods. The sturdy, upright plants bear ornamental white-and-black flowers and reach several feet tall. Eat the young pods like snap beans, pinch the tender growing tips as a spring green, or shell the beans and cook them while still green for a sweet, buttery treat. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Windy Rabbiteye Blueberry
description: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Windy was bred from a Florida 79-19 x Florida 79-27 cross specifically for its unusually low chilling requirement among rabbiteyes, giving it early flowering and early ripening well suited to mild-winter zone 8-10 Gulf South gardens where higher-chill rabbiteyes bloom unevenly. The vigorous, upright plants sucker freely from rhizome buds at the base, so annual mowing or pruning of basal sprouts keeps the crown narrow and manageable. Fruit has a notably shallow calyx scar and firm texture suited to fresh eating; because Windy sets poorly alone, plant with another early rabbiteye cultivar within about 50 feet for full-sized berries. Mulch with pine bark to keep the shallow root system cool through hot, humid summers. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wine Grape
description: Wine grapes thrive in lean, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.5–6.5 and perform best on slopes with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Establish a vertical shoot positioning (VSP) trellis with catch wires at 4 and 5 ft above the cordon wire. Rigorous dormant pruning — leaving only 30–60 buds per vine depending on vigor — is essential for fruit quality. Harvest timing is cultivar- and use-specific; measure Brix (sugar) with a refractometer and monitor seed color and berry flavor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wineberry
description: Wineberry, native to Japan and China, produces small, brilliant red, jewel-like drupes with a sweet, delicate flavor; it is grown for fruit production in Asia and has naturalized extensively in the eastern U.S. and should be grown only in contained settings or where legal. The canes are covered in red glandular hairs and tip-root readily, so remove spent canes promptly and clear any rooted tips. Harvest when berries are uniformly bright red and detach easily from the sticky calyx — they do not ripen after picking and must be used within 1–2 days. Pruning follows the same floricane/primocane cycle as standard raspberries. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Winecrisp Apple (Scab-Resistant PRI Apple)
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Winecrisp was bred through the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistance breeding program and carries genetic resistance to apple scab along with good resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray home orchards. Fruit is medium-sized with dark red skin over crisp, dense, wine-tinted flesh with a tangy-sweet flavor that improves in storage, and the tree stores exceptionally well into winter. Harvest in mid to late fall once background color shifts from green to yellow, and thin fruit clusters to one apple each in late spring to encourage consistent annual bearing and better fruit size. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winesap Apple (Virginia Heirloom Keeper Apple, Self-Fertile Cider Apple)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Winesap is self-fruitful but yields improve with a cross-pollinator; harvest in October–November when deep red and firm; Winesap is an outstanding storage apple — sound fruits keep 3–6 months in a cool root cellar (32–40°F) while maintaining flavor and crispness far longer than most modern varieties. Winesap is one of the great classic American apple varieties, documented in Virginia since at least 1817 and possibly earlier, with origins that suggest development in New Jersey in the late 1700s before spread throughout the Shenandoah Valley and Appalachian apple-growing regions that became its primary production territory. The variety has a characteristic that made it enormously valuable before refrigeration: extraordinary keeping quality — Winesap apples stored in a cool root cellar or spring house could remain crisp, tart, and flavorful from harvest in October through March or April of the following year, making Winesap the standard winter apple of Appalachian farmsteads for generations. The fruits are medium-sized, deep red to almost black-red with yellow-green patches, with firm, dense, creamy-yellow flesh and a distinctive spicy-winy flavor with pronounced tartness and aromatic quality — unlike the mild sweetness of most modern commercial apples. Winesap is excellent for fresh eating (for those who appreciate tart, complex flavor), cider making, cooking, and drying. Its self-fruitfulness and cold-hardiness make it a practical single-tree orchard choice for zones 5–7. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winged Bean (Asparagus Pea)
description: Scarify or soak seeds 12–24 hours before sowing 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, low-fertility soil; inoculate with cowpea rhizobium to promote nitrogen fixation. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence at least 6 feet tall as soon as plants emerge, as vines climb rapidly and are very productive when vertical. Virtually every part of the winged bean is edible — harvest young pods at 3–4 inches with frilly wings still tender, leaves and shoot tips as greens, flowers as a colorful salad garnish, and mature dried seeds as high-protein pulses. In the tropics, tuberous roots also form and can be harvested and eaten like yam. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Winged Passion Fruit (Fragrant Granadilla, Sweet Calabash, Red Passion Fruit)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and provide a sturdy trellis or fence; established plants fruit more reliably than recently transplanted ones, so patience through the first season is required. Passiflora alata (winged passion fruit) is a Brazilian passion fruit species that stands out from the more commonly grown P. edulis for two extraordinary qualities: its flowers and its fruit fragrance. The flowers are among the most beautiful of any Passiflora — large (3–4 inches across), deeply colored in crimson-red sepals with purple-and-white banded corona filaments, strongly fragrant, and produced in profusion from summer through fall. The aroma alone makes this an exceptional garden plant. The large, oval to oblong fruits (3–5 inches long) are distinctly fragrant when ripe, with a sweet, aromatic, tropical scent often described as more complex and perfumed than standard purple passion fruit (P. edulis); the golden-orange interior pulp is sweet and aromatic with a flavor that is mellower and less acidic than standard passion fruit, more approachable for fresh eating. The vine grows vigorously in zone 9–10, covering trellises and fences rapidly with glossy dark green leaves that have distinctly winged (four-angled) petioles — the characteristic that gives the species its common name. Pollination by large bees (especially carpenter bees) or hand-pollination improves fruit set. One of the most rewarding edible passion fruits for Gulf Coast gardens where it performs as a true perennial. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Winged Sumac (Shining Sumac, Flameleaf Sumac)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil in spring; winged sumac (Rhus copallinum) is the most widely distributed sumac in the eastern United States, recognizable by the distinctive 'wing' of tissue along the central leaf stem, and producing brilliant, glossy clusters of small red berries that can be used to make sumac-ade (sumac lemonade) or dried and ground as a tart, tangy spice similar to Middle Eastern sumac (Rhus coriaria). The fall foliage color of winged sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub — blazing scarlet, orange, and crimson in October — making it a superb ornamental as well as a food plant and wildlife species. High-value wildlife shrub providing critical late-season fruit for birds (songbirds, turkeys, quail) and dense thicket cover. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Winged Yam (Water Yam)
description: Plant tuber sections with at least one dormant eye in fertile, loose, deeply dug soil (tubers can reach 18 inches long) in full sun to partial shade; provide a strong trellis as vines grow vigorously to 15–20 feet. The large, starchy tubers are harvested after the vines die back in fall; a single tuber can weigh 20–50 pounds in good conditions. The most widely cultivated true yam in the world, Dioscorea alata is eaten boiled, baked, fried, or pounded into fufu and is a dietary staple across the tropics. In zone 8 the tubers may survive mild winters if mulched deeply; in zones 9–11 the plant can become invasive — check local regulations and avoid planting near natural areas. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Winkler American Hazelnut (Blight-Resistant Native Hazelnut Selection)
description: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winkler is a long-cultivated named selection of the native American hazelnut, valued in nut-breeding circles for its strong natural resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that devastates the larger-nutted European hazelnut (Corylus avellana) across much of its Eastern US range. Because of this resistance, Winkler has been widely used as breeding stock for filbert-blight-tolerant hybrid hazelnuts, and it can also be grown directly as a small, multi-stemmed shrub for a reliable, low-input nut crop. Nuts are smaller than European hazelnut but flavorful, ripening in late summer to fall and often eaten by wildlife if not netted or harvested promptly. Like other hazelnuts, Winkler is not self-fertile and needs a second, genetically distinct hazelnut planted nearby for pollination and nut set — wind, not insects, carries the pollen, so plant within about 20 feet for reliable results. The shrub suckers over time to form a multi-stemmed thicket; thin out old wood periodically to keep the planting productive and easy to harvest. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winona Strawberry
description: Winona is an early-twentieth-century strawberry cultivar developed in Minnesota and grown for generations in northern home gardens for its exceptional cold hardiness and reliable annual June crop. The medium-sized berries are dark red, aromatic, and well suited to preserving, with a rich, old-fashioned strawberry flavor prized by heirloom growers. Vigorous runnering fills in matted rows quickly, making it well suited to the traditional matted-row growing system used across the northern Plains and upper Midwest. Because it predates most modern disease-resistant breeding, rotate planting sites and use certified disease-free stock to avoid buildup of soilborne pathogens. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Winter Banana Apple (Aromatic Banana-Scented Indiana Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with two different compatible pollinizer varieties nearby. Winter Banana was discovered in Indiana in 1876 and takes its name from a genuinely distinctive banana-like aroma and subtle fruity flavor note unlike any other common apple, carried in pale waxy-yellow skin blushed with soft pink to rose-red. The tender, crisp, aromatic flesh is best for fresh eating, where its unusual fragrance and flavor are most appreciated, and it also has a long history of use as a pollinizer tree for other apple varieties despite producing little viable pollen itself, thanks to its extended, reliable bloom period. Fruit ripens in fall and keeps reasonably well in cool storage, though its main appeal remains the striking aroma that makes it a memorable, conversation-starting addition to a home orchard. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winter Bloomsdale Spinach (Cold-Hardy Overwintering Savoy Spinach)
description: Sow directly in late summer or early fall so seedlings size up before short days and cold arrive, then protect with a low tunnel or thick mulch through the coldest months for an early spring harvest. This vigorous savoy-leaf hybrid was bred specifically for exceptional cold tolerance and holds its dark, crinkled foliage through hard freezes better than standard Bloomsdale types. Many growers value it as one of the most reliable spinach selections for season extension in cold climates. Matures in 40–45 days from seed.

name: Winter Cress (Yellow Rocket)
description: Direct sow in late summer or fall for winter harvest, or very early spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; winter cress is a naturalized European biennial widely established along roadsides, stream banks, and disturbed areas throughout North America, producing dark green, deeply lobed, pungent leaves throughout cold weather — an important wild food and forage vegetable in lean months. The young rosette leaves harvested in fall through early spring are pungent and slightly bitter, excellent as cooked greens (boiling twice mellows the bitterness) or raw in small amounts as a peppery salad green. The early spring flower buds (harvested before they open) are excellent steamed or sautéed like broccoli raab and milder than the leaves. Traditionally gathered as a spring tonic green throughout Europe and Appalachia. Self-sows prolifically to establish permanent patches in moist, disturbed, sunny to partially shaded sites. Matures in 45–75 days from seed.

name: Winter Delight Jujube
description: Winter Delight is one of several jujube selections imported from northern China by Oregon nurseryman Jim Gilbert, valued for its compact, naturally tidy tree and crisp, egg-shaped fruit that ripens toward the tail end of the jujube season. Because a major nursery mislabeled Autumn Beauty as Winter Delight years ago, some plants sold under the name actually ripen earlier than expected, so confirm fruiting time with the source nursery if season length matters for your planting plan. The tree is markedly cold-hardy and tolerates the poor, dry soils typical of the species, needing little more than an occasional deep watering during establishment. Fruit is best harvested at the crisp green-to-tan stage for fresh eating, or left to fully brown and wrinkle for a chewier, date-like texture. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Winter Density Lettuce (British Cold-Hardy Romaine-Butterhead Cross)
description: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; Winter Density tolerates more cold than most lettuces and can be direct-sown in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) or late summer for fall harvest; thin to 8–10 inches apart; harvest as baby lettuce at 3–4 weeks or allow heads to mature fully; the heads hold in the garden well without bolting even in warm spring weather. Winter Density is a British heirloom lettuce representing a distinct type: a cross between the upright, crisp Romaine (Cos) type and the loose, buttery Butterhead type, producing compact, upright heads with the outer leaf structure and dark green color of Romaine but the soft, buttery, pale interior leaves and gentle flavor of Butterhead. The flavor is excellent — sweet, slightly nutty, and mild — while the cold tolerance (to around 22°F without protection) and slow-bolting behavior make it one of the most productive lettuces for extended spring seasons and for winter harvests in mild climates (zones 7–10). It is notably more shade-tolerant than most lettuces, performing well under tall vegetables in summer where direct-sun types would bolt. Winter Density was widely grown in English kitchen gardens throughout the 19th and 20th centuries as a reliable, all-conditions lettuce, and has been preserved through seed-saving networks and specialty seed companies. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Winter Grape (Chicken Grape)
description: Plant against a fence, arbor, or large tree in moist, fertile bottomland soil in full sun to light shade; winter grape is a wide-ranging native liana of eastern floodplains and stream banks, historically confused with the closely related riverbank grape but distinguished by glossier, less deeply cut leaves and a smooth (not cobwebby) leaf underside. Its small, intensely fragrant spring flowers draw bees and other pollinating insects in large numbers, and the tart, blue-black grapes hang on the vine into late fall, sweetening after frost and feeding songbirds, foxes, and raccoons through the lean months. Because it climbs by tendril into the tree canopy rather than mounding as a shrub, give it a tall, sturdy support and prune hard each dormant season to keep growth manageable near structures. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Winter Grape (Graybark Grape, Sweet Mountain Grape)
description: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines against a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Winter grape is a vigorous, high-climbing native vine of river bottoms, thickets, and woodland edges across the Gulf South, bearing small, tart black grapes that ripen unusually late, often persisting on the vine into fall, which gives the plant its common name. Its dense, gray, felted young growth and strong disease and heat tolerance have made native populations valuable in grape breeding programs seeking rootstock resilient to Gulf Coast humidity and pests. In the home landscape it is best used as a screening or wildlife vine on a large arbor, since it grows quickly and needs annual pruning to control its size. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Winter King and Queen Watermelon (Mennonite Heirloom Winter Keeper)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills spaced 6–8 feet apart. Winter King and Queen is a rare American keeper melon, offered as early as 1923 by the Aggeler and Musser Seed Company and later documented by Amy Goldman in Melons for the Passionate Grower; it produces smaller, tough-rinded fruit (roughly 9 pounds on average) with a nearly white, exceptionally hard rind striped in dark green and firm, crunchy red flesh. Unlike most watermelons it is picked and set aside to store for weeks after harvest, continuing to ripen in a cool, dry spot into the winter months, which earned it the nickname Christmas watermelon in some regions. Midwestern Mennonite communities kept the variety alive largely for its pickled rind, and the resulting vinegar pickle is now listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste; fresh flavor is good but secondary to its unmatched keeping ability among heirloom watermelons. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Winter Luxury Pie Pumpkin (Heirloom Netted-Skin Pie Pumpkin)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun in well-drained, rich, well-amended soil; harvest when rind is fully orange and the characteristic netting pattern covers the surface. Winter Luxury is a heirloom pie pumpkin dating to before 1893 that is distinguished from all other pumpkins by its striking surface appearance: the orange rind is covered with a delicate pattern of raised, interlacing cream-colored corky netting that gives each fruit a lacy, elaborately textured surface unlike any other pumpkin variety. Beyond the striking visual character, Winter Luxury is widely regarded as one of the finest pie pumpkins ever developed — the smooth-grained, dense, deep-orange flesh is finely textured, very sweet, and has a silky quality when cooked that produces exceptionally smooth pumpkin puree without the stringiness or wateriness of field-type pumpkins. The 5–9 lb fruits are the ideal size for fresh pie production, yielding enough puree for two large pies per fruit while remaining manageable to handle. Seed Savers Exchange and heirloom seed preservationists have long championed Winter Luxury as an example of what specialty breeding for cooking quality can achieve, and it consistently wins pie pumpkin taste tests among gardeners who grow multiple varieties side by side. A beautiful and genuinely outstanding baking pumpkin with over 130 years of cultivation history. Matures in 95–105 days from seed.

name: Winter Melon (Wax Gourd, Ash Gourd, White Gourd)
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, deeply cultivated, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a very sturdy trellis or along the ground; keep evenly moist. Benincasa hispida (winter melon or wax gourd) produces the largest cultivated gourd after pumpkins and bottle gourds — round to oblong fruits 8–32 inches long weighing 10–50 pounds, with a white, waxy powder coating the mature skin (which gives it the 'wax gourd' name) and very mild, white, watery flesh that absorbs surrounding flavors in cooking. Winter melon is a cornerstone ingredient in Chinese cuisine — the thick rind is scooped out and the hollowed gourd is used as a serving vessel for delicate winter melon soup garnished with carved decorations; the flesh is added to stir-fries, soups, and dim sum. It is called 'winter melon' despite being a summer crop because the mature fruits store exceptionally well at room temperature for months through winter (up to a year if undamaged), providing a critical source of fresh vegetable during historically difficult winters in Asia. In zone 9, it produces very well in summer heat; the large fruits are harvested in fall when the waxy bloom has fully developed. Matures in 70–110 days from seed.

name: Winter Mexican Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mexican-Race Avocado)
description: This Mexican-race avocado is grown less for fruit size than for cold hardiness, tolerating brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit once established, which puts it within reach of gardeners at the cooler northern edge of avocado country. Fruit is small, six to ten ounces, with thin, dark purple-black skin and rich, high-oil flesh carrying the anise-scented foliage and fruit typical of Mexican-race types. Harvest runs fall into early winter; because the tree tends toward biennial bearing, thinning a heavy crop can help even out production year to year. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winter Nelis Pear
description: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Winter Nelis ripens very late and needs a period of cold storage before it develops its best flavor. An old Belgian variety introduced in the early nineteenth century, it bears small, unassuming, dull green-russeted fruit that belies exceptionally rich, sweet, aromatic flesh once properly ripened, and it was among the most widely planted winter dessert pears in nineteenth-century American orchards for its outstanding flavor and long storage life. Unlike fall-ripening pears such as Bartlett, it needs weeks of cool storage after harvest before the flesh softens and the rich flavor fully develops, rewarding patience with one of the best-flavored of all winter pears. Harvest while still hard and green in mid-to-late fall, store cool for several weeks to a few months, then finish ripening at room temperature for a few days before eating. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winter Savory
description: Sow direct around last frost date in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; winter savory requires excellent drainage and performs poorly in heavy clay or moist soil. Satureja montana is a woody-based, semi-evergreen perennial herb with narrow, glossy, dark-green, very aromatic leaves and masses of tiny, lilac-white flowers in late summer; it has a more robust, resinous, slightly bitter-peppery flavor compared to the more delicate annual summer savory (S. hortensis) and is the traditional seasoning for beans and lentils in many European countries, particularly in the south of France (where it is called poivre d'âne — donkey pepper). The semi-evergreen foliage can be harvested year-round in mild climates; it is an attractive, low, mounded, shrubby herb for the front of sunny borders and herb gardens. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Winter Sun Mahonia (Early-Flowering Glossy-Leaf Winter Shrub)
description: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Winter Sun, a sister seedling to Charity, bears upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers that open earlier in the fall-to-winter season than most Mahonia x media selections, held above glossy, dark green, holly-like evergreen foliage. Its earlier bloom timing extends the winter flowering window in the shade garden, providing an early nectar source before other Mahonia hybrids open. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Winter Tarragon
description: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, covering lightly and keeping flats warm. This anise-flavored marigold thrives in heat and humidity where true tarragon struggles. Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil once nights stay warm, and pinch to encourage branching. Harvest leaves through the season for culinary use in place of French tarragon. In frost-free zones it behaves as a perennial, blooming golden flowers in fall. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Winter's Bark
description: Native to the temperate rainforests of Chile and Argentina, this evergreen tree is named for the English navigator Captain William Winter, whose crew used its pungent, cinnamon-and-pepper-flavored bark as an antiscorbutic and spice in the 1570s. The aromatic bark, stripped in strips from branches, was historically dried and used as a pepper substitute, and is still occasionally used this way by foragers today. Unlike most tropical spice trees, it prefers cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil and part shade, tolerating more cold than true cinnamon or nutmeg but disliking hot, dry summers. Clusters of small ivory-white, jasmine-scented flowers appear in spring on mature specimens, followed by small blue-black berries. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Winterbor Kale
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Winterbor is an F1 hybrid curly kale developed for exceptional vigor, uniformity, and extraordinary cold hardiness — the 'Winter' in the name reflects its ability to withstand severe freezes that damage most other kale varieties, making it the standard commercial and home garden curly kale in northern climates. The very densely curled, heavily blistered, blue-green leaves are the archetypal kale-chip and sautéed-kale leaf — the extreme surface area created by tight curling traps oil and seasonings, making Winterbor the variety most frequently used in kale chip recipes where maximum crispiness requires maximum surface contact with the baking sheet. Unlike flat-leaf or lacinato kale varieties, the heavy curl structure of Winterbor makes the raw leaves quite firm and fibrous — they benefit from massage with oil and salt to soften before use in salads, making it primarily a cooking kale rather than a fresh salad variety. Repeated hard freezes dramatically improve the flavor of all kale, but particularly Winterbor: cold temperatures convert accumulated starches to sugars, making late-winter harvested Winterbor among the sweetest and most palatable versions of this species. Matures in 55–65 days from seed.

name: Winterbor Kale (Blue-Green Curly Hybrid Kale)
description: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before fall transplanting or direct sow in late summer for fall production; Winterbor is a Dutch hybrid kale developed by Royal Sluis that became one of the most popular commercial and home garden kale varieties worldwide, valued for its combination of highly productive, tight, attractive blue-green curly leaves, exceptional cold hardiness, and distinctively superior flavor after frost. The tightly ruffled, heavily curled leaves are more tender and less tough than some older kale varieties, making Winterbor more pleasant to eat both raw in salads and cooked. The blue-green color is attractive and the upright habit (plants grow upward rather than sprawling) makes garden management easy. Winterbor is exceptionally cold-hardy — tolerating temperatures to 15°F without damage — and the cold-sweetening effect that makes kale improve after frost is particularly pronounced in Winterbor, making late-season harvested plants dramatically sweeter and more tender than those harvested before cold weather. In zone 9, Winterbor is primarily grown as a fall-through-winter crop (September–February) when temperatures allow proper kale production; it tolerates Gulf Coast mild winters better than more tender greens. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Wintergreen
description: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil under deciduous or evergreen shade; wintergreen is a native North American woodland plant that thrives in conditions hostile to most herbs, particularly under conifers or in acidic woodland gardens. Established plants slowly spread into a glossy evergreen mat bearing small white flowers in summer and bright red berries through winter. Harvest the thick, aromatic leaves at any season for wintergreen tea; crush a leaf to confirm the characteristic methyl salicylate fragrance before using. Both berries and leaves are edible and safe in culinary quantities; the essential oil is very concentrated and should not be used internally. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Winterstar Strawberry (UF/IFAS Early-Season Gulf-Latitude Hybrid)
description: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Winterstar was released in 2011 from a 2005 cross of 'Florida Radiance' and 'Earlibrite' by the UF/IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center in Balm, Florida, and was positioned to complement rather than replace the two industry-standard cultivars of the era, Festival and Florida Radiance. As with other short-day cultivars grown in the Deep South annual plasticulture system, set out fresh crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds and treat the planting strictly as a winter annual, since plants decline rapidly once summer heat arrives. Fruit ripens on a schedule comparable to Radiance, with good early-season production valuable for growers and home gardeners who want fruit on the table before the main winter flush. Matures in 100–160 days from transplant.

name: Winterthur Viburnum (Compact Possumhaw with Multi-Season Berry Color)
description: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites, including rain gardens and pond margins. Winterthur is a compact selection of native possumhaw viburnum producing showy clusters of berries that pass through a striking sequence of pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen in late summer and fall, often displaying several colors on the same cluster at once, in addition to attractive burgundy-red fall foliage. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits typical residential borders better, and planting a second unrelated clone nearby improves the reliability and abundance of berry set. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wintertime Chilean Pernettya (White-Berried Prickly Heath)
description: Wintertime is a female Chilean pernettya selection grown for its pure white berries, a striking contrast to the pinks, reds, and purples of most other Gaultheria mucronata cultivars, and it holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit for garden performance. As a female clone of a dioecious species it needs a male G. mucronata planted nearby to pollinate its flowers, but once fertilized the berries are notably long-persisting, often holding their color and firmness on the plant well past midwinter. The dense, low, prickly-leaved evergreen mound works well as underplanting beneath rhododendrons, camellias, or other acid-loving shrubs, where its winter fruit display stands out against darker foliage. Provide the same moist, humus-rich, lime-free soil and part-shade woodland conditions required by the species. Matures in 545–730 days from transplant.

name: Wiri Wiri Pepper (Guyanese Berry Pepper)
description: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. This heirloom from Guyana produces marble-sized, perfectly round fruit that dangle upright like tiny berries, ripening from pale green through orange to bright red on a compact, heavily branched bush. Heat runs fierce and fruity, typically well into habanero territory, and the little pods are the signature ingredient in Guyanese pepper sauce as well as a favorite for pickling whole. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Wisconsin 55 Tomato (Crack-Resistant Heirloom Slicer)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking or caging the vines for support. Wisconsin 55 was developed by plant pathologist J.C. Walker at the University of Wisconsin in the 1940s to resist early blight and leaf spot, and it went on to become one of the most popular home garden tomatoes in the upper Midwest through the mid-20th century. The round, deep red, six- to eight-ounce fruit is notably resistant to cracking and holds firm texture for slicing, canning, and cooking. Matures in 72–80 days from transplant.

name: Wisconsin SMR 58 Cucumber (Scab-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
description: Direct sow an inch deep after the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil with room for vines to spread or climb a trellis. Wisconsin SMR 58, standing for Smooth or Spot Mosaic Resistant, descends from a University of Wisconsin breeding program that improved disease resistance in the older Wisconsin SMR line, becoming a standard pickling cucumber for home gardeners and small-scale growers because of its reliable yields, disease tolerance, and dependable performance across varied soils. Fruit is straight, blocky, and medium green with light spines, best picked young at 2-4 inches for pickles or left a bit larger for fresh slicing. Because it remains true from seed, it can be maintained by home seed savers who isolate it from other cucumber varieties. Matures in 50–58 days from seed.

name: Witherod (Wild Raisin, Possumhaw Viburnum)
description: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; witherod is a multi-season native shrub of wet woodland edges, swamp margins, and boggy thickets from Newfoundland to Florida, producing flat-topped clusters of small, white flowers in spring, followed by berries that go through an extraordinary color sequence as they ripen from early summer through fall: green, then pink-salmon, then red, then blue, and finally blue-black, with the multiple colors sometimes present simultaneously on a single cluster. The fully ripe blue-black berries are edible and have been eaten by Indigenous peoples and settlers — they have a sweet, raisin-like flavor, giving rise to the name 'wild raisin.' The fall foliage turns brilliant red to burgundy-red, often among the best fall color of any viburnum. Outstanding for moist sites, rain gardens, and naturalistic plantings where its tolerance of consistently wet soil is invaluable. The fruit is an important wildlife food for migrating birds in fall. Matures in 730–1825 days from transplant.

name: Witherod Viburnum (Wild Raisin)
description: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; witherod viburnum is a native shrub of moist, acidic habitats across eastern North America — bog edges, streambanks, moist meadows, and pond margins from Newfoundland to Alabama. The berries pass through an extraordinary sequential progression of colors as they ripen — starting green, then turning through pink, blue-pink, and finally blue-black — so that clusters simultaneously display three or four colors. The fully ripe blue-black berries, called 'wild raisin,' are edible and sweet enough to eat raw or dried. Spectacular scarlet to burgundy fall foliage adds further season-long interest. Plant 2 or more plants of different clones for improved berry set. An exceptional wildlife shrub offering berries for over 30 bird species and the flowers feed numerous native bees and pollinators. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Witloof Chicory (Belgian Endive)
description: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in deep, loose, fertile soil; witloof chicory develops a long taproot like a parsnip that must be carefully dug in fall. To produce authentic Belgian endive chicons, lift the roots after tops die back, trim leaves to 1 inch, and force the roots upright in moist sand or potting mix in a dark, cool location (50–60°F) for 3–4 weeks until compact, pale yellow-white chicons 4–6 inches long emerge. The chicons have a pleasantly bitter flavor that mellows when cooked — they are traditionally braised, grilled, or wrapped in ham and baked with béchamel. In zone 9 the summer heat makes root development challenging; the fall-sow schedule is critical to success. Matures in 100–120 days from seed.

name: Wojtek Honeyberry (Polish-Bred Pollinator Haskap)
description: Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, spacing plants so their early flowers overlap with the bloom window of the main fruiting cultivars they are meant to pollinate. Wojtek is a Polish-bred haskap selection valued in North American plantings less for its own medium-sized, tangy berries than for its reliable early flowering, which makes it a favored cross-pollination partner for several popular Saskatchewan-bred honeyberry cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter lows well below -30F, but performs poorly in hot, humid summer climates. Limit pruning in the first several years to dead or crossing wood, since haskaps fruit on second-year and older canes, then thin out the oldest stems periodically to maintain vigor. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wolf Plum (Historic Iowa Native American Plum)
description: Site in full sun on well-drained soil and pair with a second American plum seedling or named cultivar, since Wolf will not set a useful crop on its own. Wolf was selected from wild stock in Iowa during the late 19th-century prairie plum boom and was carried on USDA horticulturist W.A. Kerr's influential list of over a hundred promising native plum selections gathered from Midwest farms and nurseries. Its round, thick-skinned red fruit ripens in mid- to late summer and holds up well for cooking into jams, butters, and preserves. Like most native plum selections of its era, it suckers from the root to form a spreading thicket unless suckers are removed, and it tolerates the cold, drought, and heavy clay soils of the northern plains far better than introduced plum species. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wolf River Apple (Giant Wisconsin Heirloom Baking Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating near the Wolf River in Fremont, Wisconsin in the mid-1800s, this heirloom is famous chiefly for the sheer size of its fruit, with individual apples sometimes weighing over a pound and reportedly large enough that a single apple can fill a whole pie. The pale yellow-green skin blushed with red covers soft, mild, mellow flesh that is better suited to baking and sauce than fresh eating, since the flavor is pleasant but unremarkable on its own. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and vigorous, and its dramatic fruit size has kept it a curiosity and conversation piece in heirloom orchards for generations. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wolfe Loquat (Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Florida Loquat)
description: Grow Wolfe on well-drained soil in full sun and thin the fruit clusters in late winter to encourage larger individual loquats. This Florida-origin selection produces heavy clusters of large, sweet-tart orange fruit slightly earlier than many older loquat varieties, and the tree shows better resistance to fire blight than some standard selections. Gardeners along the Gulf Coast plant Wolfe for its dependable, showy late-winter to early-spring harvest, which arrives when almost no other tree fruit is ripe, and for its evergreen, ornamental year-round foliage. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Womack Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Thorny Blackberry)
description: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Womack is an erect, thorny blackberry released from the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program and bred specifically to withstand the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Texas and the western Gulf South. It produces medium to large, firm, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and holds up well to summer heat that causes softer varieties to decline in quality. As an older Texas A&M release, it is a dependable, disease-tolerant option where more modern thornless varieties struggle with heat stress. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select vigorous new primocanes to tie in for next year's crop; wear heavy gloves when working the thorny canes. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Wonderberry (Garden Huckleberry)
description: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; wonderberry (also sold as 'garden huckleberry') is a Solanum species grown for its small, jet-black berries — promoted by plant breeder Luther Burbank in the early 1900s as 'the most delicious berry in the world' but received with disappointment because fresh berries have a bland, somewhat bitter, black-nightshade flavor. Cooked into pies, jams, and sauces (with generous sugar) the flavor improves considerably and is quite pleasant. An annual bush producing enormous quantities of marble-sized black berries through the growing season, making it productive even if the flavor is underwhelming fresh. Distinguished from black nightshade (S. nigrum) by its larger plant size, larger berries, and slightly different botanical characteristics. Like all black-berried Solanum, only fully ripe (jet-black) berries should be eaten; all green parts and unripe berries are potentially toxic. An easy-to-grow novelty edible for those interested in unusual fruits. Matures in 70–90 days from seed.

name: Wonderful Pomegranate
description: Pomegranate 'Wonderful' is the most popular home-garden variety, forming a large shrub or small tree that produces glossy red fruit filled with tangy-sweet, ruby-colored seeds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fertile, so a single plant will fruit. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then reduce as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In climates colder than zone 8, grow it in a large container and move it to a protected spot over winter. Prune in late winter to shape and remove suckers, and harvest fruit in fall when it colors up and sounds metallic when tapped. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Wonderful Pomegranate (Classic Large Deep-Red Gulf South Pomegranate)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Wonderful is the dominant commercial pomegranate variety of California and the standard against which all other pomegranate varieties are evaluated — producing very large (10–16 oz), round, deep-red to scarlet-red fruits with a thin, hard rind enclosing hundreds of ruby-red arils (the juicy, seed-containing sacs) with a complex tart-sweet, deeply flavored, astringent juice that defines the classic pomegranate flavor profile. The ornamental quality of pomegranate is exceptional — showy orange-red flowers (May–July in zone 9), then large, jewel-colored fruits that ripen to deep red-purple by October–November. Pomegranate is an ancient cultivated fruit (documented cultivation for 4,000+ years) that is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, long-lived fruit trees available for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, pomegranate thrives in the hot summers and mild winters — requiring only 150–200 chill hours — and established trees are remarkably long-lived, with historic specimens surviving 50–100+ years with minimal care. The ornamental summer flowers and autumn fruit make pomegranate as valuable as a landscape specimen tree as it is as a fruit producer. Self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator) and resistant to most pests and diseases common in Gulf South gardens. Harvest fruit when the exterior skin has fully colored and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Wood Apple (Elephant Apple)
description: Wood apple is a deciduous tree from South and Southeast Asia related to bael; it tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soils and drought conditions that defeat most fruit trees, making it valuable for arid-zone agroforestry. The spherical, gray-shelled fruits have a hard woody shell that must be cracked open with a hammer; the dark, pungent, sticky flesh inside is strongly acidic and astringent and is usually mixed with sugar, coconut, and spices or blended into drinks rather than eaten plain. It is self-fertile and pollinated by insects; a single tree crops reliably after the first 5–7 years. Harvest when fallen fruit has fully ripened on the ground, or remove from the tree when the gray shell turns slightly yellowish and sounds hollow when struck. Matures in 2190–3650 days from transplant.

name: Wood Avens
description: Direct-sow seeds in fall or early spring in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees or shrubs; wood avens is a versatile woodland herb long used in traditional European herbal medicine and as a flavoring, with roots that carry a mild clove-like fragrance and were historically used to flavor ale and preserve linens. The small, five-petaled yellow flowers appear from late spring through summer and are followed by burr-like seedheads that cling to clothing and fur, dispersing the plant throughout the woodland garden. Both the young leaves and roots are edible — add young leaves to salads and use the dried roots as a mild clove substitute in cooking or herbal infusions. Establishes readily under deciduous canopy and self-seeds to form a low, naturalistic groundcover that tolerates root competition. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Wood Betony
description: Cold-stratify seed for 2–4 weeks in the refrigerator, then surface-sow onto moist, peat-based starting mix in a warm location; germination can be slow and erratic. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade or dappled light, where wood betony colonizes the herbaceous layer of meadow and woodland edge. The square stems bear whorls of rosy-purple flowers in early to midsummer and are ornamental as well as useful. Harvest aerial parts — stems, leaves, and flowers — in full bloom, drying for use in traditional headache and digestive bitters teas, where the herb is valued for its mild nervine and astringent properties. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Wood Betony (Common Betony)
description: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; wood betony is a European native wildflower of woodland edges, meadows, and hedgerow banks that was for centuries one of the most widely used and highly valued medicinal herbs of the Western herbal tradition — credited with such broad healing powers in medieval Europe that the Saxon physicians listed 29 distinct ailments it was believed to cure, and the advice 'sell your coat and buy betony' circulated as a proverb for its all-encompassing virtue. As a garden ornamental it forms neat rosettes of deeply veined, scallop-edged, dark-green, softly hairy leaves and in early summer produces upright, square-stemmed spikes of densely clustered, bright rose-pink to magenta-purple tubular flowers that are magnets for bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators. The rich flower color is clear and cheerful in the summer border, and the plant is undemanding in well-drained to average soils. Excellent for the cottage herb garden, medicinal garden, or wildlife border. White ('Alba') and pink cultivars are available alongside the species. Matures in 90–180 days from seed.

name: Wood Calamint (Basil Thyme, Woodland Calamint)
description: Sow seeds or plant divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; harvest leaves as needed before flowering for best flavor. Calamintha sylvatica (wood calamint or basil thyme) is a European woodland herb in the mint family (Lamiaceae), native to the forests, hedgerows, and shaded rocky slopes of southern and central Europe — with a particularly close association with Italian cuisine. The leaves have a distinctive aroma and flavor that has been aptly described as a synthesis of fresh basil and thyme with additional minty notes — more complex and interesting than either herb alone. In Italian cooking, this herb is known as 'nepitella' (or 'mentuccia' in Lazio) — an important and distinctly Italian culinary herb with a long tradition in Roman and Umbrian cooking. It is a classic pairing for artichokes (in Roman-style carciofi alla romana), porcini mushrooms, tripe (trippa alla Romana), and game dishes; the herb adds a fresh, aromatic complexity that is genuinely distinct from standard basil or thyme. Wood calamint is notably more shade-tolerant than most herbs — it grows well at the edge of light shade under trees, making it useful for herb gardens with limited full-sun space. The small, white to pale-lavender flowers attract bees prolifically and the plant is excellent for pollinator gardens. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wood Nettle (Canada Wood Nettle)
description: Sow seed in early spring in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in dappled shade to full shade — the natural habitat is rich woodland floodplains and stream banks; wood nettle bears stinging hairs on both stems and leaves that are completely deactivated by cooking, making the young leaves and stem tips harvested before flowering excellent when boiled, steamed, or sautéed, with a flavor comparable to stinging nettle but perhaps more delicate. Rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins. An important larval host plant for the red admiral butterfly (Vanessa atalanta). Always handle with gloves to avoid stinging; once wilted by heat or drying, all sting is gone. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Wood Sage (Woodland Germander, Garlic Sage)
description: Plant divisions or transplants in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; wood sage (Teucrium scorodonia) is a European woodland perennial with wrinkled, sage-like leaves with a distinctive garlicky-sage aroma, producing graceful spikes of small yellow-green flowers in summer that are excellent for bees and hoverflies. Despite the name it is a germander (Teucrium genus), not a true sage, and has been used historically as a bittering agent in ale before hops became standard and as a medicinal herb in European folk medicine. Naturalizes beautifully under oak trees and at woodland edges, spreading slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding; tolerates dry shade well once established. A valuable shade-tolerant herb for the woodland garden. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Wood Sorrel
description: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) in partial to full shade; wood sorrel requires cool, consistently moist conditions and performs poorly in heat and drought, making it a plant for zones 3–7 and cool, moist microclimates. Oxalis acetosella is a delicate, low-growing European and Asian native found in cool, moist woodland floors; it has characteristic shamrock-like, trifoliate, bright-green leaves that fold down at night and in bright light, and bears small, white flowers with pink veins in spring. The leaves have a distinctive, sharp, lemony-sour taste from oxalic acid and are used as a garnish, in salads, and to make refreshing cold drinks in Scandinavian and European folk traditions; the flavor is best when the plant is growing in cool shade. Consume in moderation as oxalic acid can be problematic in large quantities, especially for those prone to kidney stones. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Woodard Rabbiteye Blueberry (Classic Large-Berried Southern Blueberry)
description: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. One of the older, longer-established rabbiteye blueberry cultivars, Woodard is valued for its unusually large, soft-textured, mild-flavored berries that ripen in early-to-mid season, a bit ahead of many later rabbiteye types. The bushes are moderately vigorous and productive, though the soft fruit texture makes it better suited to fresh home use and processing than commercial shipping. Keep soil consistently moist through bloom and fruit development, and mulch well to conserve moisture and maintain the acidic soil conditions blueberries require. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Woodcote Sage (Cream-Purple Variegated Culinary Sage)
description: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a touch of afternoon shade in hot climates helps the leaf variegation stay crisp rather than scorching. Woodcote is a compact culinary sage cultivar whose new growth emerges cream and soft pink before maturing to gray-green, giving a softer, pastel-toned variegation pattern than the older, bolder Tricolor sage. The leaves carry the same savory culinary sage flavor as green cultivars and can be used interchangeably in cooking. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound tidy and encourage the flush of freshly colored new leaves that make this cultivar distinctive. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Woodman Pecan (Low-Input Scab-Resistant South Louisiana Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and pair with a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Kanza for cross-pollination. Woodman originated in south Louisiana, where it was identified by grower Hilary Langlois on land once owned by his uncle, and it has earned a following among LSU AgCenter-recommended cultivars for outstanding resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that limits pecan production across the humid Gulf Coast. The tree is notably vigorous and productive even under low-input management, bearing a crop most years with minimal fertilizer or spray, which makes it a practical choice for home orchardists who do not want to run an intensive spray program. Because it is a relatively new introduction from a single grower's selection rather than a formally released breeding-program cultivar, published nut-size and kernel-percentage data are limited; growers should expect the vigorous growth and disease resistance typical of other South Louisiana scab-resistant selections. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer and correct zinc deficiency with an annual spring foliar spray. Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Woolbright American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Early-Ripening Native Persimmon)
description: Woolbright is a long-documented named selection of American persimmon, cataloged alongside classic cultivars such as Early Golden, John Rick, and Miller in pomological surveys of the species. It produces large fruit, typically carrying two to eight seeds, with excellent rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. Fruit ripens comparatively early, around the start of October, but the flesh is notably soft and splits easily once it falls, so it is best gathered promptly rather than left to accumulate on the ground. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, unripe fruit is strongly astringent and must be allowed to fully soften before eating. Woolbright is a productive, reliable bearer and tolerates the heat, drought, and marginal soils typical of native persimmon growing conditions once established. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Woolly Blue Curls
description: Trichostema lanatum is a stunning California native evergreen shrub in the mint family, prized for its intensely aromatic narrow leaves and dramatic spikes of electric-blue flowers wrapped in showy woolly purple-violet calyxes that bloom from spring through summer and draw hummingbirds and native bumblebees in abundance. Propagate by softwood cuttings rather than seed, and plant out in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun — this plant will not tolerate clay, wet soils, or summer irrigation once it is established. It is native to the dry chaparral and coastal sage scrub of southern California and performs best in California-style dry gardens in zones 8-10. Excellent drainage is the single most important factor for long-term success; plants sited correctly are long-lived and largely care-free. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Woolly Huckleberry
description: Native to the pine flatwoods and sandy, moist savannas of the southeastern Coastal Plain, this low, colony-forming shrub takes its common name from the fine, soft hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its leaves. It tolerates the dappled, partial shade found beneath open longleaf pine canopy far better than open-sun blueberry species, making it a useful native groundcover for acidic, humid Southeastern gardens. Small black berries ripen in summer and are sweet and edible, though lightly borne compared to cultivated blueberries, and are best gathered for fresh snacking or preserves rather than large-scale harvest. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) and avoid disturbing the shallow, spreading rhizome mat once the colony is established. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Woolly Thyme
description: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; woolly thyme forms one of the lowest, densest, most carpet-like groundcovers available, producing a silvery-gray, velvet-textured mat of tiny, densely woolly leaves only 1–3 inches tall that spreads steadily without becoming aggressive. Pale pink flowers cover the mat in early summer, attracting bees. The plant is one of very few groundcovers that tolerates moderate foot traffic and thrives between flagstones, along dry stone paths, and in gravel gardens. It is primarily ornamental — the woolly leaves are not as flavorful for cooking as other thymes — and is grown for its exceptional textural effect. Excellent in rock gardens, as an alternative to lawn in dry, sunny spots, and in Mediterranean-style plantings. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Wooly-leaf White Sapote
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Casimiroa tetrameria tolerates brief light frost once established — provide winter irrigation in dry climates and mulch the root zone against cold. Casimiroa tetrameria (Wooly-leaf White Sapote or Matasano) is an evergreen to briefly deciduous tree native to the highlands of central Mexico and Guatemala, closely related to the more widely cultivated White Sapote (Casimiroa edulis) and distinguished by its distinctively velvety-woolly leaf undersides (the species name 'tetrameria' references the 4-merous flowers, while the woolly leaves differentiate it visually from C. edulis). The smooth, round to oval, 2–3 inch, green-skinned fruits contain creamy-white to cream-yellow, smooth, dense, rich, sweet flesh with a buttery-custard flavor and soft, satiny texture — eaten fresh, chilled, or pureed into smoothies and ice cream. Casimiroa tetrameria is considered by some tropical fruit enthusiasts to produce sweeter, richer fruit than the common white sapote, and the tree shows somewhat improved cold tolerance, performing well in zone 9 with good drainage. Graft onto Casimiroa edulis rootstock for earlier fruiting and better uniformity. The seeds contain mildly sedative alkaloids (casimiroin) and should not be eaten; wash hands after seed handling. Matures in 1095–2555 days from transplant.

name: Worcester Pearmain Apple
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Worcester Pearmain ripens in late summer and is best eaten promptly, since it does not store for long. Bred in Worcestershire, England in the nineteenth century, it bears bright crimson-red, medium apples with crisp, white flesh carrying a distinctive light strawberry-like aroma and flavor that sets it apart from most other dessert apples, ripening in late summer as one of the more colorful and distinctively flavored early-season varieties. Its attractive bright color and unusual, well-loved fruity flavor have made it a longstanding favorite for fresh eating straight from the tree, though the fruit softens and loses its best texture within just a few weeks of harvest. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up fully and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and distinctive flavor. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Worcesterberry
description: The worcesterberry is a North American species of gooseberry (Ribes divaricatum) sometimes grown as a productive alternative to European gooseberries because it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and American gooseberry mildew. The small, dark purple-black berries resemble currants more than typical gooseberries and ripen in midsummer with a tart, rich flavor excellent for jams and pies. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, keeping 8–10 canes of mixed ages. Verify state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering, as some states still restrict the genus. Matures in 548–730 days from transplant.

name: World Beater Pepper (Ruby Giant)
description: World Beater, also sold as Ruby Giant, is a pre-1912 heirloom sweet pepper bred from a cross of Chinese Giant and Ruby King, combining the size of one parent with the productivity of the other. Fruits are exceptionally large and blocky with thick, sweet flesh that ripens from green to red, making it a favorite for stuffing or roasting whole. The sturdy, three-foot plants carry a heavy fruit load, so working in compost at planting and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers properly. Choose this variety when garden space allows for a true old-fashioned giant bell rather than a modern hybrid. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Wormwood
description: Artemisia absinthium is a silver-white, intensely aromatic shrubby perennial with silky, deeply dissected, ghostly pale foliage that makes it one of the most striking foliage plants in the dry garden; the bitter compounds (including thujone) were historically used medicinally as an anthelmintic (worm expeller), digestive bitter, and febrifuge, and are the source of the bitterness in vermouth and historically in absinthe. The foliage is strongly allelopathic — plant away from edible crops. The silver-gray foliage is an outstanding foil for purple-flowered companions like salvias and catmints. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Wren's Egg Pole Bean
description: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; provide trellis or poles 5–7 feet tall for support; vines twine naturally. Wren's Egg (also called 'Bird Egg', 'Speckled Bird Egg', or 'Speckled Cranberry Pole') is one of the oldest heirloom pole beans in continuous American cultivation, documented in seed catalogs and garden records since at least the early 1800s and traditionally maintained in New England and mid-Atlantic home gardens; it is named for the distinctive speckled coloring of both the pods and the dried seeds, which closely resemble the delicate speckled pattern of a wren's egg — a mix of cream or buff background with irregular red-brown, maroon, or rose speckles. The flat pods can be harvested young (45–60 days) as a snap bean or left to mature fully (75–90 days) for dry bean use. As a dry bean, Wren's Egg produces plump, oval seeds with excellent, rich flavor for baked beans and soups. The pods become increasingly stringy as they mature; harvest snap pods at 4–6 inches for best eating quality. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Wright Heartnut
description: Wright is a named heartnut cultivar recognized in nut grower circles for ripening earlier in the season than many other heartnut selections, along with good cracking quality and a clean kernel release. Early ripening makes it a useful choice in shorter-season northern locations where later heartnut selections may not fully mature before fall frosts. Provide the same deep, well-drained soil and full sun that other heartnuts and walnuts require, and expect grafted trees to begin bearing within four to seven years. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Wrinkled Crinkled Crumpled Cress
description: This cress was bred by Oregon seedsman Frank Morton as a cross between 'Persian' and 'Curly' garden cress, combining the deeply savoyed, ruffled leaf texture of curly types with a sturdier, more upright habit that lifts leaves clear of soil splash for cleaner cutting. It germinates and grows fast enough to be treated almost like a microgreen, ready for its first cutting in under three weeks, and is notably slower to bolt than most other cress selections, giving several extra cuttings per sowing. Use it as a peppery, tangy addition to salad mixes, sandwiches, and garnishes wherever a sharper bite than lettuce is wanted. Matures in 20–30 days from seed.

name: Wush Wush Coffee
description: Named for the forested district of Wushwush in southwestern Ethiopia where it grew as an untamed local landrace, this heirloom Arabica was carried to South America in the 1990s and has since found a following among growers in Colombia and Panama chasing its unusually floral, fruit-driven cup, often compared to Geisha's. As with most Ethiopian landraces it is genetically variable rather than a single fixed clone, so performance and flavor can differ from planting to planting, and yields tend to run lower than modern commercial cultivars. Grow it at higher elevations under filtered shade in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and treat it as a connoisseur's planting rather than a high-volume producer. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wyken Pippin Apple (Old English Dessert and Cider Heirloom)
description: Wyken Pippin is an old English dessert apple that originated in the eighteenth century at Wyken, near Coventry in Warwickshire, and it has stayed relevant largely through its role as a parent of later English apples, including Laxton's Superb. The medium, yellow-green fruit is lightly russeted and carries a firm, mild, sweet flavor considerably less sharp than many old English apples, making it a pleasant fresh-eating variety as well as a useful cider component. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well into winter in cool storage, a trait valued long before mechanical refrigeration existed. The tree is a dependable, moderately vigorous grower; provide a compatible pollinator and well-drained soil, since like most old heirloom apples it was never bred for scab or fire blight resistance in humid growing regions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Wyldewood Elderberry
