description: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil; Wyldewood is a named American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) cultivar developed from wild selections in Oklahoma by the Oklahoma State University extension program, selected for extraordinary production of large, dense berry clusters — corymbs up to 10–14 inches across with hundreds of small, dark purple-black berries per cluster. Wyldewood is considered one of the highest-yielding American elderberry cultivars, with mature plants producing 12–20 pounds or more of fruit clusters annually. The berries are used for elderberry syrup (widely used as an immune-support supplement), elderflower and elderberry liqueurs and wines, jams, pies, and lemonade. Raw elderberries contain very small amounts of cyanogenic compounds and should not be eaten raw in large quantities; cooking neutralizes these compounds. Wyldewood is specifically bred for Oklahoma and surrounding regions and performs excellently throughout zone 9 conditions. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Wynyabbie Gem Australian Rosemary (Lavender-Mauve Flowering Hybrid)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Wynyabbie Gem is a vigorous natural hybrid between coastal rosemary (Westringia fruticosa) and the inland species W. eremicola, combining a denser, more upright habit with more consistently produced lavender-mauve flowers than the straight species, which typically blooms white to very pale lavender. It grows into a substantial rounded shrub, useful as an informal hedge, screen, or freestanding specimen in hot, dry, coastal or inland landscapes, and like its parent species tolerates salt spray, poor soil, and extended drought once established. Flowers appear nearly year-round in mild climates, providing a steady nectar source for bees. Lightly shear after flowering flushes to maintain a dense, compact form. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Xie Shan Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Chinese Satsuma Mandarin)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and protect young trees with frost cloth for their first several winters until they gain size and cold hardiness. Xie Shan is a satsuma mandarin selection out of China favored by cold-hardy citrus enthusiasts and Gulf South growers for beginning to bear at a young age and setting unusually heavy crops of small to medium, easy-peel, seedless, sweet fruit that ripen early in the fall citrus season. The compact, naturally dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be given winter protection in the coldest zone 8 locations. As with other satsumas, fruit quality and cold tolerance improve once the tree is well established, so give young trees consistent water and a balanced citrus fertilizer through their first few growing seasons. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Xtra-Tender 277A Sweet Corn (Warm-Soil Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep only once soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet corn germinates poorly in cool, wet soil; plant in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination, and keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular bicolor supersweet hybrid known for exceptionally tender, high-sugar kernels that hold their sweetness well after picking, and it is widely grown by both market farmers and home gardeners across warm Southern regions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks have browned and kernels release a milky juice when pressed. Matures in 77–84 days from seed.

name: Y-Star Squash (Golden Yellow Star-Shaped Heirloom Pattypan)
description: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Y-Star is an heirloom pattypan type distinguished by its pointed, star-like scalloped edges and rich golden-yellow color, giving it a more angular silhouette than the rounded scallop shape of other pattypan squash. Harvest small, at about 2-3 inches across, for the sweetest flavor and most tender skin; larger fruit can be left to mature for seed saving or ornamental use. Matures in 50–55 days from seed.

name: Ya Li Asian Pear (Duck Pear)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires a different Asian pear variety nearby for pollination, since it is not self-fruitful. Ya Li, meaning "duck pear" for its elongated, bottle-like shape, is one of the oldest and most widely grown Chinese Asian pear cultivars, producing medium to large fruit with thin, smooth, pale greenish-yellow skin quite unlike the golden-russeted surface of Japanese-type Asian pears. The white flesh is crisp, exceptionally juicy, and mildly sweet with a refreshing, delicate flavor, best enjoyed fresh at harvest since, like all Asian pears, it does not ripen further or improve in storage after picking. It is a vigorous, productive, and widely adaptable tree, valued in Chinese cuisine both fresh and cooked into sweet soups and simmered dessert preparations. Thin heavy fruit clusters to one fruit per spur for larger, better-quality pears, and watch for fire blight susceptibility common to the Asian pear group. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Ya Shi Xiang Tea (Duck Shit Aroma Dan Cong)
description: Ya Shi Xiang is a named Phoenix (Feng Huang) Dan Cong cultivar from Ping Keng Tou village in the Guangdong highlands, whose deliberately unappealing name, Chinese for 'duck droppings aroma,' was reportedly chosen by the farmer who first propagated it to discourage others from taking cuttings, despite the tea itself having a delicate, floral, honeysuckle-and-almond character. Like other Dan Cong selections it is a large-leaved arbor type suited to warm, humid highland conditions and traditional oolong processing, withering, bruising, partial oxidation, and roasting, rather than green tea methods. It is considered one of the most important and widely grown of the classic Dan Cong aroma cultivars. Cultivate with the acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil standard to all tea camellias. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yabukita Tea
description: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yabukita tea is a cold-hardy cultivar bred in Japan and tolerates more winter cold than many other tea cultivars. Developed in Shizuoka Prefecture in the early twentieth century and released commercially in 1953, this cultivar became so dominant in Japanese tea production that it now accounts for the large majority of all tea grown in Japan, prized for its balanced, clean, slightly sweet flavor well suited to sencha and other steamed green tea styles. Its relatively good cold hardiness compared to many tea cultivars, combined with reliable yields and disease resistance, made it the standard choice for Japanese tea farmers for decades and a natural benchmark against which newer Japanese tea cultivars are still compared. Harvest the youngest leaves and unopened buds by hand in spring for the highest-quality tea, and prune the shrub into a rounded hedge form typical of commercial tea cultivation to encourage dense, flush new growth. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yacon
description: Plant rhizome crown divisions (not the large storage roots) in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun around the time of last frost; yacon grows into a large, sunflower-relative plant 4–8 feet tall and requires a long warm season of 5–7 months for best root development. Smallanthus sonchifolius is an Andean perennial grown for its large, sweet, crisp, apple-pear-textured storage tubers, which are uniquely high in fructooligosaccharides (FOS) — prebiotics that the human body cannot fully metabolize — making yacon one of the very few vegetables with a negligible glycemic impact despite its sweet flavor. Roots are harvested after the first frost kills the tops, then cured in sunlight for 1–2 weeks (which converts some FOS to fructose and sweetens the flavor considerably); they are eaten raw like jicama in salads, pickled, juiced, or roasted. Propagate exclusively from the knobby, reddish-purple rhizome crowns attached to the base of the stalks, not from the large tan storage roots, which will not sprout. Matures in 180–240 days from transplant.

name: Yadkin Southern Highbush Blueberry (Large-Fruited NC State Release)
description: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Yadkin, released by North Carolina State University in 1997, needs a moderate 500 to 600 chill hours and ripens in the late-mid part of the season, bearing unusually large, flavorful berries on a bush noted for excellent adaptability across a range of soil types, from heavier clay-influenced ground to sandier sites, more forgiving than some southern highbush selections that demand near-perfect drainage. It suits the cooler edge of the Gulf South and areas just north of it where winter chill runs a bit higher than the mildest coastal zones. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yamhill Hazelnut (OSU EFB-Resistant Compact Hazelnut, Eastern-Adapted Filbert)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yamhill requires a cross-pollinator (Jefferson, Wepster, or another EFB-resistant OSU variety); it is semi-compact and tends to produce a shorter, multi-stemmed bush form; nuts ripen September and fall naturally — harvest promptly from the ground; Yamhill typically begins bearing in year 3–4, earlier than some older varieties. Yamhill hazelnut is an Oregon State University variety released in 2009 from the OSU hazelnut breeding program — one of the first wave of EFB-resistant named hazelnut varieties developed specifically to allow hazelnut production throughout the eastern United States, where Eastern Filbert Blight (Anisogramma anomala) has prevented the success of standard European varieties including Barcelona. The OSU breeding program incorporated EFB resistance from the wild Turkish hazelnut (Corylus colurna) and other resistant species into productive, quality-fruited cultivars adapted to commercial and home hazelnut production. Yamhill's EFB resistance is now documented in variety trials throughout the mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states where EFB pressure is severe, showing dramatically better survival and production than Barcelona and other susceptible varieties. Yamhill tends to have a compact, bushy habit (shorter than Barcelona) and produces medium-sized, round nuts with good flavor and moderate kernel percentage — suitable for home fresh use, roasting, and processing. The combination of EFB resistance, compact habit, and earlier bearing age than older varieties makes Yamhill one of the most important hazelnut releases for home orchardists east of the Cascades. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yan Hu Suo
description: Should be avoided during pregnancy. Plant dormant tubers in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil, ideally under deciduous trees, since this spring ephemeral emerges and flowers before the canopy leafs out, then dies back and stays dormant through summer heat. The tuber is a well-known TCM analgesic, traditionally decocted to invigorate blood circulation and relieve menstrual, abdominal, and musculoskeletal pain, and is distinct from ornamental Corydalis grown for foliage. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Yangambi Km5 Banana (Nematode-Resistant Ibota Dessert Banana)
description: Yangambi Km5 is a traditional AAA-genome dessert banana of the Ibota subgroup, originally collected in the Democratic Republic of Congo, that has been widely studied by tropical agriculture researchers as a rare natural source of resistance to burrowing nematode and other root-damaging pests that plague most commercial banana cultivars. This underlying disease and pest tolerance can translate into a sturdier, lower-maintenance plant for home gardeners, though it remains fully cold-tender like other AAA dessert types and must be grown in a warm, frost-free season. The fruit is a sweet dessert banana suitable for fresh eating. Grow it in full sun with rich, consistently moist soil and heavy feeding through the warm months. Matures in 365–545 days from transplant.

name: Yantarnyi Cornelian Cherry (Amber, Ukrainian Yellow-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
description: Yantarnyi, meaning "amber" and sometimes sold under that translated name, is a Ukrainian cornelian cherry cultivar introduced in 1982 by breeder Svitlana Klymenko at the M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden in Kyiv. It bears an abundant crop of oval, translucent amber-yellow fruit around an inch long, with a more delicate, fragrant, and less astringent flavor than red-fruited seedlings, making it especially pleasant eaten fresh in addition to preserves, syrups, and light-colored cornelian cherry jelly. Like the species it flowers on bare stems in late winter, is extremely cold-hardy, and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban conditions once established. Its bright fruit color makes it a striking companion planting alongside red-fruited cultivars such as Vydubetsky or Pioneer. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yard-Long Bean
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the soil reaches 65°F and all frost danger has passed, spacing 6–12 inches apart along a sturdy trellis or fence at least 5 feet tall; yard-long beans (also called asparagus beans or Chinese long beans) are vigorous tropical vines that thrive in hot, humid summers and outperform standard snap beans in zones 8–11, producing slender pods that can reach 18–24 inches long and should be harvested when they reach pencil thickness, typically at 12–18 inches, before seeds bulge. Harvest every 2–3 days to keep vines productive through the season. Unlike common beans, these plants are drought-tolerant once established but perform best with consistent moisture and do not require staking if pods are kept picked. Matures in 55–80 days from seed.

name: Yardlong Bean (Asparagus Bean)
description: Sow seeds 1 in deep once soil is reliably warm; yardlong beans are vigorous climbers that need a sturdy trellis or fence at least 6 feet tall. Unlike common beans, they thrive in high heat and set pods prolifically during summer weather that causes snap beans to drop their blossoms. Harvest when pods are pencil-thin and roughly 12–18 in long, well before they reach their potential 36 in — longer pods become fibrous and bitter. Check daily once pods begin forming, as they move from prime to over-mature in just 2–3 days. Matures in 60–80 days from seed.

name: Yarlington Mill Apple (Bittersweet Cider Apple)
description: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Yarlington Mill blooms early, so avoid frost pockets that could damage the spring flowers. Named for a mill in Somerset, England, near which the original seedling tree was found, this attractive pink-blushed apple is a classic bittersweet cider variety producing soft, mellow tannin and good juice volume, widely planted both in traditional West Country English cider orchards and in newer American craft cider plantings. Its early, showy pink spring bloom makes it ornamentally attractive as well as productive, and it is a consistent, moderately vigorous bearer that combines well with sharper or bittersharp varieties in a cider blend. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yates American Persimmon (Heavy-Bearing Virginia Persimmon, Wildlife Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Yates American persimmon is drought-tolerant and productive in a wide range of conditions including poor and clay soils; harvest fruits from the ground after frost softening in October–November; the heavy fruit production of Yates makes it particularly attractive for wildlife plantings, permaculture food forests, and home orchards where a sustained fall crop of native fruit is valued. Yates is a named American persimmon cultivar known primarily for its exceptional productivity — consistently producing heavy crops of medium-sized fruits that ripen and drop over an extended period in October and November, making it valuable for both human harvest and as a wildlife-attracting planting throughout the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states. The extended fruit-drop period provides a sustained food source for deer, raccoons, foxes, opossums, and many songbirds rather than a brief burst of fruit, making Yates a popular choice in wildlife habitat plantings and food forest designs where the ecological role of the persimmon is as important as human harvest. For human use, the fruits are medium-sized (1–1.5 inch), deep orange to reddish-orange at maturity, with the intensely sweet, slightly grainy, honey-apricot flesh characteristic of excellent American persimmon after frost softening — a quality that exceeds most commercial fruit in richness when fully ripe. The trees are extremely adaptable across the range of Virginia and mid-Atlantic climates from zone 4 through 9. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yates Apple (Small Long-Storing Southern Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Yates is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early-to-mid 1800s, prized by Southern orchardists for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and other diseases that plague apple growing in the humid South, along with dependable annual production even in years when other varieties bear poorly. The fruit is small, red-striped over yellow, with firm, crisp, tart-sweet flesh better suited to cider, preserves, and cooking than fresh eating, though many old-time growers enjoy it fresh once it mellows in storage. Its most celebrated trait is exceptional keeping quality — properly stored fruit holds firm and flavorful for months longer than most apples, historically making it a reliable source of fresh fruit through winter before refrigeration was common. Because it requires a moderate chill accumulation, it performs best in zone 6-8 and is marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yatsubusa Sansho (Dwarf Japanese Pepper)
description: Yatsubusa is a naturally dwarf, densely branched selection of Japanese sansho pepper that tops out at only a few feet tall, in contrast to the much larger habit of standard sansho, while still producing the same aromatic kinome leaves and numbing, citrusy green peppercorns used in Japanese cooking. Its small stature and slow growth rate make it well suited to a large patio container or a compact bed near the kitchen, where both male and female plants should be grown together if a berry harvest is wanted alongside the leaf crop. Give it some afternoon shade and steady moisture, since the shallow root system in a pot dries out faster than an in-ground shrub. Prune lightly to maintain shape rather than to control size, since this cultivar is naturally restrained compared to its parent species. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yaw Weed (Wild Indian Mulberry, Cheese Shrub)
description: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; drought and salt-spray tolerant once established. Morinda royoc (yaw weed or wild Indian mulberry) is a native North American coastal shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — related to noni (Morinda citrifolia) and producing very similar compound, syncarpous white fruits (multiple small flowers fuse into a single fleshy structure), though much smaller and with a less objectionable odor than commercial noni. It is native to the coastal hammocks, shell middens, sandy beaches, and disturbed coastal areas of South Florida, the Florida Keys, the Caribbean islands, and the coastal Gulf of Mexico. The plant has a distinctly scrambling or climbing growth habit, with the stems leaning on and scrambling through other shrubs. The roots yield a traditional reddish-orange dye used by Caribbean indigenous peoples; the leaves and bark have traditional medicinal uses in Caribbean herbal medicine for skin conditions and fevers — the 'yaw weed' name refers to use for yaws (a tropical bacterial infection). As a native coastal landscape plant, yaw weed is exceptionally salt, drought, and wind tolerant — suitable for difficult coastal conditions where little else grows. The fruits are edible but not palatable fresh; birds eat them readily, providing wildlife habitat value. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Yaya Carrot (Early Nantes-Type Hybrid Bunching Carrot)
description: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in loose, deeply tilled, stone-free soil; keep consistently moist through germination (7–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches apart. Yaya is a Bejo Seeds hybrid Nantes-type carrot that has become one of the most popular fresh-market and home garden bunching carrots in North America — selected specifically for its early maturity, exceptional sweetness, and consistent cylindrical uniformity that makes bunches visually attractive and professionally presentable. The roots are the classic Nantes shape: blunt-tipped, 6–7 inches long, uniform diameter, with smooth, bright orange skin and minimal core differentiation from the phloem to the xylem — the internal uniformity of color contributing to the sweet, mild, candy-sweet flavor that Yaya is known for. Yaya matures 10–14 days earlier than most mid-season Nantes types, allowing early-season bunching carrot production or an additional succession planting late in the season. It holds well in the ground after reaching maturity without rapid overgrowth or cracking, giving a flexible harvest window. Market gardeners consistently rate Yaya among the highest for customer satisfaction — the exceptional sweetness and uniformity of color and shape are immediately apparent to buyers. One of the best-performing bunching carrots for both farm market sales and home garden fresh eating. Matures in 56–65 days from seed.

name: Yehuda Loquat (Israeli Large-Fruited Mango-Flavored Loquat)
description: Yehuda, also spelled Jehuda, is an Israeli loquat cultivar prized for large, light-orange, apricot-shaped fruit with a thick skin that peels away to reveal richly sweet flesh some growers describe as mango-like when fully ripe. It is self-fertile and typically begins bearing three to five years after transplanting, with flowers opening from December through February. Loquat blossoms and young fruit are cold-tender, so a hard freeze during this winter bloom window can reduce or eliminate the following spring's crop even though the tree itself tolerates considerable cold. Yehuda is a vigorous grower that reaches medium size at maturity. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Baby Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Fleshed Icebox Watermelon)
description: An All-America Selections winner from the 1970s, Yellow Baby was one of the first widely available yellow-fleshed watermelons bred for home gardens, packing bright lemon-yellow flesh and thin, tender rind into a round 7-pound icebox-size fruit. The novel flesh color and honeyed flavor make it a conversation piece at the table, and its fast maturity suits shorter growing seasons better than full-size Southern types. Grow it exactly as you would any bush-type icebox watermelon: full sun, consistent moisture until fruit begins to ripen, then reduced watering to concentrate sugars. Because the pale flesh makes the usual red-ripeness cues useless, rely on the drying tendril and yellowing ground spot to judge harvest timing. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Yellow Bell Pepper
description: Start Yellow Bell seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in warm soil, then transplant 12 to 18 inches apart once nights stay warm. This heirloom ripens from green to a bright golden yellow with sweet, crisp, thick-walled flesh. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and stake plants carrying a heavy fruit load. Harvest peppers green for firmness or leave them to color up fully for maximum sweetness. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Bell Tomato (Appalachian Heirloom Yellow Paste Tomato)
description: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking or caging to support heavy clusters of fruit. Yellow Bell is a Roma-shaped yellow paste tomato that is a family heirloom from Tennessee, introduced commercially in 1986 by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange; the vigorous plants set 5-12 fruits per cluster and bear heavily until frost, ripening from green through creamy yellow to a rich golden-yellow with a sweet, full flavor well suited to yellow sauces, salsas, preserves, and catsup. Matures in 60–70 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Bellflower Apple (Bell-Shaped Colonial-Era Heirloom)
description: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Yellow Bellflower originated in New Jersey in the 1700s and takes its name from its distinctive elongated, bell-like shape, tapering from a broad base to a narrower crown, unlike the more rounded shape of most common apples. The pale yellow skin, often blushed with a soft pink flush on the sun-exposed side, covers crisp, juicy, tart flesh that mellows somewhat in storage, making it a genuinely versatile apple good for fresh eating once fully ripe, excellent in pies and sauce for its bright acidity, and historically valued for cider as well. The tree is a reliable, long-lived bearer; harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for good keeping quality through much of the winter. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Bhut Jolokia Pepper (Yellow Ghost Pepper)
description: Yellow Bhut Jolokia is a bright lemon-to-gold-podded phenotype of the classic Northeast Indian ghost pepper, with the same characteristically wrinkled, thin-walled fruit and searing heat as the red strain. Some growers report a slightly fruitier, less smoky flavor than red bhut jolokia, making it popular for hot sauces where a lighter color is desired. Provide full sun, rich well-drained soil, and even watering, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under moisture stress. Wear gloves when handling ripe pods, as the oils cling stubbornly to skin. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Bourbon Coffee (Amarelo de Botucatu)
description: First noticed in the São Paulo town of Pederneiras around 1930, Yellow Bourbon arose from a natural cross or mutation involving red Bourbon coffee, and it ripens to a golden-yellow rather than the usual red, a trait that also seems to slow the fruit's sugar breakdown and lets growers pick over a longer harvest window. Brazilian growers quickly embraced it for combining Bourbon's celebrated sweetness and balance with noticeably heavier yields, and it remains a staple parent behind many later Brazilian cultivars. Grow it exactly as you would red Bourbon, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade, with steady warmth and moisture and protection from frost. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Brandywine Tomato
description: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost in rich soil, staking or caging immediately. Yellow Brandywine is a yellow-fruited version of the legendary Brandywine heirloom (or a closely related strain), producing the same large, potato-leaved plants and big, meaty, irregular fruits but ripening to a beautiful golden-yellow with a noticeably sweeter, milder, lower-acid flavor than either the pink or red Brandywine strains — many tomato connoisseurs actually prefer it for its tropical sweetness and lack of sharpness. Fruits reach 12–24 oz and are outstanding for slicing, caprese preparations, and tomato salads where the golden color provides visual contrast; the low acid level means less canning stability so use for fresh eating. Shares the Brandywine family's potato-leaved foliage (a dominant genetic marker that distinguishes true Brandywines from impostors) and late, slow maturity that rewards patient gardeners with exceptional fruit. Matures in 80–100 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Cabbage Collard (Virginia Heading Heirloom Collard)
description: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants ample room to form their characteristic loose head. Yellow Cabbage Collard is a distinctive Virginia heirloom, unusual among collards for forming a semi-blanched, cabbage-like heart of pale yellow-green leaves at the plant's center rather than staying fully open-leaved, giving it a milder, sweeter flavor and more tender texture than typical collards, especially in the blanched inner leaves. Outer leaves can still be harvested cut-and-come-again style through the season, while the forming head is left to mature for a more tender harvest later. Cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, and the plant tolerates hard freezes well. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best head development. Matures in 75–90 days from seed.

name: Yellow Cabbage Collards (Loose-Heading Heirloom Collard)
description: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Cabbage Collards are a distinctive Southern heirloom type that blurs the line between collards and cabbage, forming a loose, blanched, pale yellow-green head at the center of the plant rather than the fully open rosette of leaves typical of most collard varieties. The blanched inner leaves are notably tender and mild, sweeter and less assertively cabbage-flavored than standard collards, making this variety popular for gardeners who find ordinary collards too strong. Like other collards it tolerates considerable cold and its flavor improves after light fall frosts. Because the plant's value lies partly in the self-blanched head, avoid stripping too many outer leaves early in the season and let the center fill in before beginning regular harvest, then continue picking outer leaves as the plant keeps producing from the growing point. Matures in 75–90 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Catuaí Coffee (Catuaí Amarelo)
description: Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas bred Catuaí from a Mundo Novo x Caturra cross in 1949, and the resulting breeding population segregated into both red- and yellow-fruited forms, with the yellow color tracing back to a Bourbon ancestor's recessive gene. Catuaí Amarelo keeps the same compact, sturdy, early-bearing habit as its red sibling, but growers and cuppers often note a slightly sweeter, more delicate flavor along with a somewhat later, more even ripening window, since yellow cherries soften less obviously than red ones and are easier to leave on the branch a bit longer. Its dwarf stature and strong branch attachment keep it manageable in a large container and resistant to fruit drop in wind. Breeders have since used it as a parent of other compact yellow-fruited cultivars, including Obatã. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Crookneck Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, rich, well-drained soil; Yellow Crookneck is one of the fastest-producing and most heat-tolerant summer squashes, making it particularly well-suited to warm and humid Gulf Coast gardens where it produces heavily in spring and again in fall. Yellow Crookneck squash has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1700s — it was listed in American seed catalogs before the Civil War — producing curved, club-shaped yellow fruits with bumpy skin and mild, buttery, slightly nutty flesh that is the quintessential taste of Southern summer gardens; harvest at 4–6 inches when the skin is still tender and seeds are small. In hot climates, a fall planting (direct sow in late summer) often outperforms spring; the plants are relatively short-lived under heat stress but can be succession-planted. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Yellow Crookneck Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, warm soil after last frost; yellow crookneck is one of the oldest continuously grown summer squash types in North American gardens, with its distinctive curved neck and bumpy, golden-yellow skin being immediately recognizable. Harvest when 6–8 inches long for the best texture; fully mature fruits become tough-skinned and seedy. The sweet, mild flavor is excellent sautéed in butter with onions, grilled, or added to casseroles. Bush types have largely replaced the older spreading vine types; they produce heavily over a long season if harvested regularly. In humid climates, powdery mildew is common in midsummer — select modern disease-resistant cultivars like 'Supersett' or 'Gentry' for best results. Matures in 50–65 days from seed.

name: Yellow Doll Watermelon (Early Icebox Yellow-Fleshed Watermelon)
description: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; fertilize at planting and again when vines begin to run. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit turns brown and dry and the underside spot (where the melon touches the ground) turns from white to cream-yellow. Yellow Doll is an early-maturing, icebox-sized watermelon notable for its yellow flesh — a less common flesh color that surprises many people used to only red-fleshed watermelons. The small (5–8 lb), round to oval fruits have light green skin with subtle darker green stripes and the distinctive bright yellow to golden-yellow interior flesh that gives the variety its name. The yellow flesh is very sweet and mild, with a slightly different flavor character than red-fleshed types — some tasters describe it as cleaner, less assertive, and honey-sweet rather than the more complex sweetness of red watermelon flesh. This mild quality makes Yellow Doll particularly popular with children and those who find standard watermelon's flavor too strong. Yellow Doll's early maturity (65–75 days vs. the 80–95 days of standard large varieties) is a practical advantage for short-season gardeners, as is the small fruit size — a single 6-lb fruit is the right amount for 2–4 people without waste, compared to the 25+ lb fruits of standard varieties that require multiple meals to consume. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Yellow Dragon Fruit (Yellow Pitahaya, Cactus Pear Pitaya)
description: Root stem cuttings in gritty, well-drained cactus mix and grow on a strong post or trellis in full sun; yellow pitahaya is considered by many tasters to be the sweetest and most flavorful dragon fruit — its white interior flesh with tiny edible black seeds is measurably higher in sugar than red or white-flesh types, with a rich, tropical, almost honey-like sweetness and no bitterness. The fruits have yellow, spiny (not scaly) skin without the prominent pink 'scales' of other types. A significant advantage over other dragon fruits: yellow pitahaya is self-fertile and does not require hand pollination or a second plant to set abundant crops. Grows slower than Selenicereus undatus but the superior flavor makes it the most prized of the dragon fruit species. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Egg Plum (Large Egg-Shaped Heirloom Canning Plum)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Yellow Egg is an old heirloom plum grown for its large, distinctive, genuinely egg-shaped fruit, which ripens to a bright, waxy yellow and can rival a small chicken egg in both size and shape, an unmistakable variety in the orchard. The firm, meaty flesh holds up exceptionally well to canning and cooking, historically making it one of the preferred varieties for home preserving even though the somewhat tart, thick skin makes it less popular for fresh eating than sweeter dessert plums. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the firm fruit tolerates handling well, making Yellow Egg a practical choice for home orchardists focused on putting up jams, canned plums, and baked goods rather than fresh snacking. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Eye Bean (Maine Yellow Eye, Steuben Yellow Eye, New England Heirloom)
description: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; allow pods to dry fully on the vine before harvesting, then shell and continue drying beans before storage. Yellow Eye bean (also called Maine Yellow Eye, Steuben Yellow Eye, or Molasses Face bean) is one of the defining heirloom dry beans of New England — a white bean with a distinctive yellow-to-orange eye mark on one end (the hilum area) that resembles a yellow eye, giving the variety its evocative name. The bean has an extraordinarily long history in New England agriculture, where it has been the traditional baked bean variety for generations in Maine — the characteristic bean in the famous Maine Saturday Night bean suppers and baked bean tradition that stretches back centuries to Native American cooking and early colonial adaptation. The large, creamy-white beans cook to a silky, tender texture without becoming mushy, holding their shape while absorbing surrounding flavors; they have a mild, rich, nutty flavor that makes them outstanding for slow-baked preparations, bean soups, and any dish where bean quality is the focus. Yellow Eye is considered by many New England cooks to be the finest baked bean, superior in flavor and texture to navy beans or pinto beans for this application. An outstanding heirloom that connects culinary tradition, regional identity, and genuine eating quality. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Yellow Finn Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Finn is a Finnish heirloom predating the modern yellow-flesh varieties it helped inspire, producing round to oval tubers with tan skin and dense, buttery-yellow flesh. The flavor is rich and naturally buttery even without added fat, and the moderately waxy texture holds together well for potato salad while still mashing smoothly. It stores well for a fingerling-adjacent heirloom and tends to be more drought-tolerant than many modern hybrids once established. Choose it over Yukon Gold when a true heirloom lineage and slightly denser, more old-fashioned texture are preferred. Matures in 85–100 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Gentian (Great Yellow Gentian, Bitterwort)
description: Sow stratified seed in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil, since this long-lived alpine meadow perennial forms a substantial taproot and resents being moved once established. Broad ribbed leaves form a large basal clump for the first several years before the plant sends up tall stalks of striking whorled yellow flowers, usually not before its third or fourth season. The intensely bitter root, harvested only after many years of growth, is a classic European digestive bitter used in traditional tonics and liqueurs; commercial harvest generally waits until plants are at least four to ten years old. Give it cool summers, good winter drainage, and full sun to light shade, as it struggles in hot, humid climates. Matures in 1460–1825 days from seed.

name: Yellow Globe Danvers Onion
description: Yellow Globe Danvers is a classic American heirloom onion developed near Danvers, Massachusetts, in the 1850s and grown for generations as a reliable, well-storing globe onion. The medium-sized bulbs form tight round globes with papery yellow-brown skin over firm, pungent flesh well suited to cooking rather than fresh eating. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin or space plants so bulbs can round out fully without crowding. Lift once the tops have fallen over and dried, cure in a warm, airy location for a couple of weeks, and expect this variety to store as well as any classic long-day storage onion. Matures in 100–110 days from seed.

name: Yellow Granadilla (Water Lemon, Jamaica Honeysuckle)
description: Named for its glossy, laurel-like leaves, this vigorous tropical vine bears fragrant lavender-and-white flowers followed by egg-shaped, orange-yellow fruit filled with juicy, translucent, sweet-tart arils prized fresh or blended into drinks throughout the Caribbean and northern South America. It requires a strong, permanent trellis or arbor since mature vines are heavy and long-lived, and it is intolerant of any frost, making it best suited to true tropical or protected coastal conditions. Provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during fruit development, and hand-pollinate where natural pollinators are scarce to improve fruit set. Harvest fruit as it colors fully and begins to soften near the stem end. Matures in 180–270 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Granex Onion (Classic Vidalia-Type Short-Day Sweet Onion)
description: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Yellow Granex needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly and will not perform well planted in spring in most of the country. Yellow Granex is the classic variety behind Georgia's famous Vidalia sweet onion, prized for large, flattened, golden-skinned bulbs with exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pungency flesh that develops from the low-sulfur soils and mild winters of the Deep South. It is one of the best-suited onion types for Gulf Coast gardens specifically because the region's short winter day length and mild temperatures match its bulbing requirements closely. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, then cure carefully in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot, since sweet onions like Yellow Granex have thinner skins and shorter storage life than pungent long-day storage onions. Matures in 150–175 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Granex PRR Bulb Onion
description: Start seed indoors in winter and transplant to the garden while still cool, since this is a short-day onion that bulbs best in southern regions. For really sweet, mild bulbs, grow it in soil that is low in sulfur; this pink-root-resistant type is among the few approved to be sold as a Vidalia onion. Keep plants weed-free and evenly watered, and cure the harvested bulbs before use, as sweet onions do not store long. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Groove Bamboo
description: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, contained within a deep rhizome barrier; yellow groove bamboo is distinguished by its attractive yellow sulcus — a distinctive yellow groove running along one side of each otherwise green culm — making it one of the more ornamental of the hardy Phyllostachys species. The spring shoots are edible, milder than many bamboo species, and are considered among the better-tasting shoots of temperate bamboos; harvest them while still below knee height before sheaths open. Culms reach 15–25 feet at maturity and tolerate temperatures to –10°F (–23°C), rivaling Phyllostachys bissetii for cold hardiness. Containment with a rhizome barrier is mandatory, as this running bamboo spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes. Matures in 1095–2190 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Habanero Pepper
description: Start Yellow Habanero seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil around 85F since this species germinates slowly. Transplant the plants 18 to 24 inches apart into a warm, sunny bed. The lantern-shaped fruits ripen golden-yellow with intense heat around 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units and a sweet, tropical, fruity flavor. Handle the ripe pods with gloves, and harvest steadily to keep the productive plants setting fruit through the warm season. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Haw
description: Plant in dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun along the Coastal Plain; yellow haw is a rare and botanically distinctive native hawthorn prized for its fall display of attractive yellow to greenish-yellow, pear-shaped to rounded haws that are notably sweeter and more palatable than those of most other hawthorns. Its spring flowers provide nectar for early native bees, and the fruit is consumed by mockingbirds, brown thrashers, and other birds that frequent the dry, sandy-woods habitats where this species thrives. It performs best in lean, well-drained soils and is intolerant of heavy clay, standing water, or overly enriched garden beds. Yellow haw's rarity in the wild makes cultivating it from locally sourced seed a valuable contribution to the conservation of Coastal Plain plant diversity. Matures in 1460–2920 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Huffcap Perry Pear
description: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. A popular traditional English perry pear valued for producing consistently excellent, low-tannin, medium-acid perry, it bears small, fiddly fruit that yields an extremely sweet, sharp, fruity, and intense juice when milled at just the right moment of ripeness. Its low-tannin profile makes it a favorite for blending into lighter, more approachable perries, in contrast to the harsh bittersharp varieties that need long aging to soften. Harvest the fruit once it begins to drop and blett in early fall, then mill and press promptly for perry. Matures in 1460–2555 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Indian Woman Bean (Buckskin Montana Heirloom Soup Bean)
description: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after danger of frost has passed, spacing bush plants 4-6 inches apart in rows. Also known as Buckskin or Buckskin Girl, Yellow Indian Woman is a Montana heirloom that reached Native American communities through European settlers and is prized for producing heavy yields of small, milky-yellow seeds in under 75 days, among the fastest-maturing dry beans available. The mild, creamy flavor resembles a pinto bean and the seeds hold their shape well in slow-cooked soups and stews, while also cooking noticeably faster than most other dry beans. Water regularly through bloom and pod fill, then let pods dry completely on the plant before shelling and storing. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Yellow Jersey Sweet Potato (Dry-Fleshed Southern Heirloom)
description: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun. Yellow Jersey is an old-fashioned Southern heirloom with pale yellow-tan skin and light yellow, dry, mealy flesh, a texture closer to a baking potato than the moist, syrupy sweetness of modern orange-fleshed varieties, and it was once among the most widely grown sweet potatoes in the South before moister types like Beauregard became dominant. Vines are moderately vigorous and productive, and the drier flesh makes the roots well suited to baking and frying rather than the candied dishes moist types are typically used for. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and before the first frost, and cure the roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts, firm the skin, and develop full sweetness before storing. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Long Neck Fig (Distinctive Elongated Bottleneck-Shaped Heirloom)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Yellow Long Neck is a heirloom fig grown as much for its unmistakable, unusual shape as for eating quality, producing fruit with a dramatically elongated, narrow neck tapering to a rounded body, a form so distinctive that a single glance identifies the variety among any collection of figs. Beneath the pale yellow-green skin, the amber-honey flesh is sweet and richly flavored, good for fresh eating, drying, and preserves once the tree is established and producing reliably. The vigorous tree performs well in fig-collector gardens seeking novelty forms alongside more standard varieties, and general fig culture practices — full sun, well-drained soil, and winter root protection in colder zones — apply equally here. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Mangosteen (Mysore Gamboge, Yellow Gamboge, Egg Tree)
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Yellow Mangosteen grows best in the filtered light and moist, rich conditions of its native South Asian forest habitat and benefits from shade protection during establishment. Garcinia xanthochymus is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen tree native to the Western Ghats and Mysore region of India and adjacent Burma (Myanmar) in the family Clusiaceae — the same family as the famous Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana). The tree has a naturally elegant form: a pyramidal to columnar crown of large, glossy, deep-green, lance-shaped leaves that hang in graceful, slightly pendant arrays from the branches. In summer, the tree produces smooth, round to slightly oval fruits 2–4 inches in diameter with bright golden-yellow skin when ripe, containing 1–4 large seeds surrounded by soft, translucent, sweet-sour, juicy pulp. The flavor is distinctive — a complex sweet-sour combination reminiscent of both apricot and tamarind, refreshing as a fresh fruit and excellent in juices, jams, and chutneys. Yellow Mangosteen is considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts to be more adaptable to cultivation outside the tropics than the famously difficult Purple Mangosteen — it tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil conditions and performs in zone 10 where G. mangostana struggles. Also grown as an ornamental specimen tree for its attractive form and handsome foliage. Matures in 730–2190 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Mombin (Hog Plum, Jocote Amarillo)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; yellow mombin (hog plum) is a large deciduous tropical tree of Central and South America and the Caribbean producing clusters of small, oval, golden-yellow fruits, 1–2 inches long, with a distinctive sweet-tart, highly aromatic tropical flavor that combines elements of mango, plum, and passionfruit with a resinous, citrus-like quality. The thick, waxy skin encloses a small amount of translucent yellow flesh surrounding a large seed. In the Caribbean, Central America, and tropical Brazil, the fruit is eaten fresh, made into juice, agua fresca, ice cream, wine, and vinegar — Spondias mombin juice is a major street beverage in countries like Colombia, Costa Rica, and Brazil. The tree is fast-growing, highly drought-tolerant once established, and tolerates a range of soil conditions from light sandy to heavy clay. It is distinct from the ambarella (S. dulcis) and red mombin/jocote (S. purpurea). Matures in 1825–3650 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Moruga Scorpion Pepper
description: This is a yellow-fruited selection of the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, sharing the same bumpy, tailed pod shape and ferocious heat as the original red strain but ripening to a bright golden-yellow instead. Growers often note the yellow form carries a slightly more citrusy, less smoky flavor than red Moruga types, making it popular for hot sauces where color as well as heat matters. Give plants the same long, warm growing season and rich soil that other Trinidad superhots require, and expect a later, more compact fruit set than milder chinense varieties. Because pod color can be the only visible way to distinguish it from other Moruga strains, keep seed-saved plants isolated from red-fruited relatives to preserve the true-to-type yellow trait. Matures in 100–125 days from transplant.

name: Yellow of Parma Onion (Italian Heirloom Storage Onion)
description: Sow seed indoors under lights in late winter, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, spacing plants a few inches apart to allow bulbs to swell. Keep soil evenly moist through bulbing, then stop watering and let tops fall over naturally before harvest to cure for storage. Yellow of Parma is a classic Italian heirloom valued for its large, globe-shaped, straw-colored bulbs, mild sweet flavor, and notably good keeping quality compared to other sweet onion types, making it a long-standing favorite in northern Italian kitchen gardens. Matures in 100–115 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Onion
description: Start seeds or transplant pencil-thick seedlings in full sun in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil early in spring; yellow onions are the most versatile and widely grown culinary onion, with their characteristic balance of sulfurous pungency and underlying sweetness that mellows to a rich sweetness when cooked, making them essential in virtually every cuisine worldwide. Long-day varieties (required for zone 3–6 where summer days exceed 14 hours) include 'Copra' and 'Patterson'; short-day varieties (zone 7–10) include 'Texas 1015', 'Candy', and 'Georgia Sweet'. Harvest when most tops have fallen over naturally; cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for 2–4 weeks. Well-cured yellow onions store for 3–6 months. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Oxheart Tomato (Heirloom Heart-Shaped Low-Seed Slicer)
description: Yellow Oxheart is a heirloom slicing tomato that produces large, pointed, heart-shaped fruit in golden yellow, with the dense, meaty, low-seed flesh typical of oxheart-type tomatoes and a mild, sweet flavor with less acidity than most red varieties. The heavy 8-16 ounce fruit and sprawling indeterminate vine both need substantial support, so use a heavy-duty cage or stake set at transplanting. Because oxheart types can be prone to blossom end rot on their first large fruit, keep watering consistent and avoid letting the soil dry out and then rewetting heavily. Matures in 80–85 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Passion Fruit (Golden Passion Fruit, Maracujá Amarelo)
description: Sow seed just below the surface in warm starting mix and maintain 75–85°F for germination; yellow passion fruit is the world's most commercially cultivated passion fruit, producing golf-ball- to lemon-sized yellow-skinned fruits with intensely fragrant, tart orange-yellow pulp that is the basis of most commercial passion fruit juice. A rampant perennial vine to 30 feet, it needs a very sturdy trellis or fence and frost-free conditions; train two or three main canes horizontally along wires and allow laterals to cascade. Flowers require cross-pollination between two genetically distinct plants, or hand-pollination outside the tropics where native bee pollinators are absent. Harvest when fruit begins to show yellow color and drops easily from the vine. Matures in 150–210 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Pear Tomato
description: This indeterminate heirloom produces heavy clusters of small, bright yellow pear-shaped fruits with a mild, tangy flavor. Provide sturdy caging or staking, since vines sprawl vigorously all season. Pinch suckers if you want a more manageable plant and pick fruit regularly to keep production going. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking and blossom-end rot. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Pear Tomato (Heirloom Yellow Cherry Tomato)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cherry tomato with a history extending back to at least the 1800s — producing clusters of small, bright-yellow, pear-shaped fruits with a distinctive teardrop shape and mild, low-acid, sweet flavor. The fruit shape and bright yellow color make Yellow Pear one of the most visually distinctive tomatoes in the garden, and it is a consistent favorite at farmers markets and in mixed salads where its cheerful yellow color and unusual shape create visual interest. The low-acid flavor profile makes it approachable for children and adults who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The indeterminate vine grows vigorously to 5–8 feet and sets fruit prolifically throughout the growing season — an established Yellow Pear plant produces hundreds of fruits over the course of the season. Seed can be saved from non-hybrid heirloom Yellow Pear true-to-type for future seasons — select fruit from the most vigorous and productive plants. In zone 9, Yellow Pear performs well in the spring window (February–June) and fall window (September–frost) but stalls during the peak summer heat above 95°F. The low-acid taste makes it excellent for children's snacking, fresh salads, and pasta dishes where a mild tomato flavor is preferred. Matures in 70–78 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Persimmon
description: Plant Diospyros decandra in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly throughout the year; protect from temperatures below 40°F; harvest fruits when they reach full yellow color and have a slight give to finger pressure — they should be non-astringent even when firm, unlike temperate persimmons. Yellow Persimmon is an underappreciated tropical fruit tree that deserves far wider cultivation than it currently receives outside Southeast Asia. Unlike the more widely known Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) which is astringent when underripe, Yellow Persimmon (madan in Thai, 'ten stamen' in English — referring to its ten stamens vs. 16 in D. kaki) produces small, round, bright-yellow fruits that are sweet and non-astringent even when firm, and have a honey-sweet, mildly vanilla-flavored flesh. The fruits are eaten fresh in Thailand and throughout Indochina as a dessert fruit, and the tree is planted as both an ornamental (handsome, glossy-leaved, with fragrant, cream-white flowers) and a fruit tree in village gardens. The tree grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shade tree in the tropics, producing fruits that ripen over an extended season from late summer through winter. An excellent rare fruit tree for zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical gardens seeking both ornamental beauty and unusual fresh fruit. Matures in 1825–5475 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Petite Watermelon
description: This compact, early-maturing heirloom yields round 5 to 7 pound melons with sweet yellow flesh, ideal for small gardens and containers. Sow in warm soil and give vines room to run along the ground or a low trellis with fruit support. Water deeply but reduce moisture as fruits ripen to concentrate sweetness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy. Matures in 70–80 days from seed.

name: Yellow Potato Onion (Heirloom Multiplier Onion)
aliases: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Yellow Potato Onion'
description: Yellow Potato Onion is a true heirloom multiplier onion documented in American gardens since before 1790, grown from small saved bulbs rather than seed. Each planted bulb divides underground into a cluster of new bulbs ranging from an inch to several inches across, so a gardener can keep a perpetual supply going year after year without buying sets or seed again. It tolerates drought better than seed-grown onions and is widely adapted across the country, with fall planting generally producing larger bulbs than spring planting. Set bulbs about 2 inches deep with the tip just at the soil surface, and harvest once the tops die back, saving the largest bulbs to replant and the rest for the kitchen. Matures in 110–130 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Santol (Sweet Santol)
description: Yellow santol is the sweeter of the two long-recognized forms of santol, formerly classified as a separate species (Sandoricum indicum) before both were merged into Sandoricum koetjape as varieties distinguished mainly by leaf color in fall and fruit character. Its thinner-skinned fruit has a comparatively thick, mild, sweet layer of cottony pulp around the seeds, making it the preferred type for fresh eating rather than processing. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with steady moisture, giving the large canopy plenty of room to develop; grafted trees fruit within a few years while seedlings take considerably longer. Harvest when the smooth skin turns fully yellow and use fresh, or in preserves and candies as with the more common red type. Matures in 1460–2190 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Sarson (Yellow Seed Mustard)
description: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow sarson is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season crop for both its greens and oilseed. This South Asian mustard type produces bright yellow flowers on branching stems, and its distinctive yellow, rather than brown or black, seed is the traditional source of high-quality mustard oil used across northern India and pressed for cooking, along with young leaves harvested for the classic dish sarson ka saag. Fast-growing and adapted to cool weather, it bolts and sets seed quickly once days lengthen and warm, so plant it early enough to establish good leaf growth before it flowers if greens are the primary goal. Harvest leaves young and often for eating, or allow plants to flower and set seed pods for a home-scale oilseed or seed-saving crop, threshing dried pods once they turn brown and brittle. Matures in 90–120 days from seed.

name: Yellow Sweet Spanish Onion
description: This heirloom long-day variety forms large, golden globe bulbs with a mild, sweet flavor, best suited to northern gardens with long summer days. Start seed early indoors and transplant seedlings while cool weather encourages leafy growth before bulbing. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist, then taper off water as tops fall over. Cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storage. Matures in 110–120 days from seed.

name: Yellow Sweet Spanish Utah Bulb Onion
description: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants four to six inches apart. This long-day heirloom, grown in the U.S. since at least 1916, forms large 3 to 6 inch globe-shaped bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and grows best in states north of the 37th parallel. Keep the soil evenly moist during bulbing, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place before storing. Matures in 110–130 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Tea Camellia (Large Variegated-Leaf Selection)
description: Yellow Tea is grown chiefly as an ornamental tea camellia, valued for leaves that can reach nearly 8 inches long and are heavily marked with yellow variegation, a striking departure from the uniform dark green of most tea selections. The oversized foliage also gives it novelty appeal for home tea processing, though the name refers to its leaf color rather than to Chinese "yellow tea" processing methods. Grow it as you would any China-type tea camellia, in evenly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with some afternoon shade to protect the variegated leaves from scorch. Expect a full-sized shrub similar in stature to standard tea camellias. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Tomatillo (Sweet Yellow-Ripening Tomatillo, Fruitier and Milder Alternative to Green)
description: Start indoors; plant two or more for cross-pollination. Harvest when husk just fills completely and turns yellow-gold. Yellow Tomatillo (sometimes called 'miltomate amarillo' in its native Mexican context) is a color variant of the tomatillo (Physalis ixocarpa) that ripens to golden-yellow rather than the standard green, with a fundamentally different flavor profile: sweeter, less acidic, more fruity, and less pungent than the standard green tomatillo. The standard green tomatillo has an assertive, somewhat tart flavor with herbaceous, citrus-like notes that characterize the classic salsa verde (green sauce) of Mexican cuisine; the tartness and acidity are fundamental to the sauce's role of cutting through rich meats and cheeses. Yellow tomatillo has less of this characteristic tartness and more fruit-forward sweetness — a flavor profile that lends itself to milder, sweeter sauces and preparations where the aggressive acid of green tomatillo would be too dominant. Yellow tomatillo salsas tend to be used in different culinary contexts than green tomatillo salsas: they pair well with fish, light meats, and as a condiment where a sweeter, less assertive sauce is preferred. The plants grow identically to standard green tomatillo varieties — vigorous, spreading, 3–5 feet tall, requiring two plants for pollination — and have the same growing requirements. The papery husk that encloses the developing fruit is similar in color to green tomatillo husks (tan-brown with green veining) and turns slightly yellow-tan as the fruit inside ripens; the fully ripe fruit inside is a clear lemon-yellow to golden color. Matures in 65–80 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Transparent Apple (Very Early Translucent-Skinned Russian Apple)
description: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Introduced from Russia in the 1870s, Yellow Transparent is one of the earliest-ripening apples grown in North America, producing pale, almost translucent yellow-green skin over soft, tart, juicy flesh that cooks down quickly into a smooth sauce. Because the thin skin bruises easily and the fruit does not store, it is best picked directly for immediate use in pies, sauce, and fresh eating rather than for the fruit bowl. The tree is notably cold-hardy and productive, and its extremely early ripening has long made it a favorite for the first homemade applesauce of the year. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Velvetleaf (Sawah Lettuce)
description: Plant divisions after last frost into rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water in full sun; yellow velvetleaf spreads readily by seed and runners in warm, wet conditions and is best grown in a contained bog bed or submerged container. Broad, glossy, velvety-textured leaves rise on long stalks from the shallow water of rice paddies and wetlands across Southeast Asia, where the young leaves and flower stalks are harvested as a popular cooked vegetable, and cheerful three-petaled yellow flowers add ornamental value above the foliage. It grows and spreads quickly in warm, wet, nutrient-rich conditions, making it a fast-establishing addition to a pond margin or paddy-style bed, but its vigorous self-seeding habit means it can become weedy in the very rice paddies it is sometimes intentionally grown alongside. Harvest young leaves and flower stalks regularly for the best eating quality, and confine plantings to a contained wet bed to prevent unwanted spread. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Wonder Alpine Strawberry (Pale-Fruited Bird-Resistant Woodland Strawberry)
description: Yellow Wonder is a day-neutral alpine strawberry that ripens to a pale lemon-gold rather than red, a trait many gardeners value because birds are less likely to spot and peck the fruit before it can be picked. Plants form compact, runnerless clumps and flower and fruit continuously from summer into fall once established. Surface-sow seed indoors, keep evenly moist, and transplant seedlings into rich, well-drained soil in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates. The soft, sweet, low-acid berries have a pineapple-tinged wild-strawberry flavor and bruise easily, so pick and use them promptly rather than storing. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Wood Sorrel (Common Wood Sorrel)
description: Yellow wood sorrel is a native perennial that self-sows throughout gardens and lawns without cultivation; it is included here as a wild edible and forager's herb rather than a planted crop. Oxalis stricta produces the classic shamrock-shaped, clover-like trifoliate leaves and tiny yellow five-petaled flowers that are familiar to any gardener as a common weed; the young leaves and stems have a pleasant, sour, lemon-like flavor from oxalic acid that is refreshing in small quantities in salads, garnishes, and herb butters. Children particularly enjoy the tangy flavor of the raw leaves. Foragers note: consume in moderation as large quantities of oxalic acid can irritate the kidneys; avoid if prone to kidney stones. The small seed pods explode when ripe, launching seeds several feet — the primary reason it spreads so freely. Matures in 30–60 days from seed.

name: Yellow Yam (Twelve-Month Yam, Yellow Guinea Yam)
description: Plant tuber pieces with at least one eye 4–6 inches deep in loose, deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the yellow guinea yam is a major food staple in West and Central Africa, producing large (up to 10 lb) elongated tubers with yellow-orange flesh and a pleasant earthy flavor quite different from sweet potato — the starchy tubers are boiled, roasted, fried, or pounded into fufu and other traditional preparations. Grows as a perennial tropical vine requiring sturdy staking; in frost-free zones it can remain in the ground year-round, multiplying year after year. Requires a long frost-free growing season of 8–9 months for full tuber development. Harvest when vine begins to die back. Matures in 240–365 days from transplant.

name: Yellow Yam (Yellow Guinea Yam, Cayenne Yam, Yellow Cocoyam)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, loamy to sandy soil with a tall climbing support — Yellow Yam vines climb vigorously (10–20 feet) and require sturdy support throughout the growing season; deep, loose, well-worked soil allows the tubers to expand to their full size without impediment. Dioscorea cayennensis is a tuberous, annual to perennial twining vine native to West Africa and naturalized throughout the tropical world in the Dioscoreaceae family, one of the most important yam species in West African cuisine — the principal yam of the 'yam belt' that stretches across Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, and Togo where yams are a dietary staple, ceremonially important, and economically critical. The distinctive feature of D. cayennensis is the yellow to deep orange-yellow flesh of the tubers — in contrast to the white-fleshed D. rotundata (white guinea yam), D. cayennensis tubers have the appearance of cooked sweet potato inside after cooking. The large (5–15 pound per tuber), cylindrical to irregularly shaped tubers are smooth-skinned and store well after curing. In zone 9-12 gardens, the vine grows vigorously through the warm months before dying back as days shorten, signaling tuber maturity. Raw tubers contain dioscorine and other toxic alkaloids — always cook before eating. One of the finest true yam species for Gulf Coast tropical food gardens. Matures in 240–300 days from transplant.

name: Yellowfin Zucchini (Bright Yellow Straight-Fruited Hybrid Squash)
description: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants about 30 inches apart. Yellowfin produces glossy, bright golden-yellow, straight cylindrical fruit on a compact, open bush plant, offering a color and shape alternative to more common golden zucchini types. Pick regularly at 6-7 inches long, since yellow-skinned summer squash can develop a tougher skin if left to oversize. The bright color makes Yellowfin easy to spot at harvest time and an attractive addition to mixed squash displays. Matures in 45–50 days from seed.

name: Yellowhorn (Chinese Flowering Chestnut)
description: Plant in full sun in deep, fast-draining, even poor or rocky soil; yellowhorn is a small deciduous tree native to northern China where it grows on dry hillsides, and it is notably drought tolerant once established but intolerant of wet feet or heavy, poorly drained clay. In spring it puts on a striking floral display of white, horse-chestnut-like flower panicles marked with red-to-yellow throats, followed in late summer by leathery green seed capsules that split open to release large, dark, chestnut-flavored seeds edible raw or roasted. Trees need several years of establishment before producing a meaningful nut crop, and while broadly self-fertile, planting more than one seedling improves pollination and yield. Give it a full-sun, well-drained site away from irrigation runoff or low spots where water collects. Matures in 1460–2190 days from seed.

name: Yellowstone Carrot (Yellow Carrot)
description: Sow seed thinly 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, friable, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Yellowstone is one of the top-performing yellow carrots for home gardens, producing uniform, 7–9 inch, Nantes-type cylindrical roots with vivid yellow skin and flesh throughout and a notably mild, sweet, slightly fruity flavor that some tasters prefer to standard orange carrots; it lacks the beta-carotene of orange types but is rich in lutein, a carotenoid beneficial to eye health. Excellent for fresh eating, roasting (where it holds its color beautifully), and for adding visual variety to rainbow carrot mixes. The flavor improves after mild frost. Direct sow works best as the taproot does not transplant well. Matures in 70–75 days from seed.

name: Yerba Buena
description: Propagate from stem-tip cuttings or layered runners, as nursery plants are more reliable than seed-grown starts, and set into cool, shaded beds in spring with consistent moisture. This low, mat-forming evergreen herb of Pacific Coast forests produces an intensely sweet mintlike fragrance that made it the aromatic plant of choice for tea among Indigenous peoples of California and the Pacific Northwest. Plant it beneath conifers or deciduous trees where it can sprawl freely as a fragrant groundcover in dappled shade with moderate, even moisture. Harvest young stems and leaves throughout the growing season to steep as a refreshing herbal tea, and divide established mats every few years to keep growth vigorous. Matures in 90–180 days from transplant.

name: Yerba Buena
description: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yerba buena is a trailing California and Pacific Coast native mint relative that forms a loose, low groundcover of small, rounded, glossy leaves with a refreshing, minty fragrance released when brushed or crushed. Historically brewed as a mild, pleasant herbal tea by Native Californians and early Spanish settlers (the plant lent its name to the original Spanish name for the settlement that became San Francisco), it remains valued today mostly as a fragrant, shade-tolerant groundcover rather than a major culinary herb. Small, inconspicuous white to pale lavender flowers appear in the leaf axils in summer, largely incidental to the plant's soft-textured foliage display. It spreads gently by trailing, rooting stems under open tree canopy, tolerating dry shade better than many groundcovers once established, making it a good low-maintenance choice for woodland garden paths and understory plantings. Matures in 180–365 days from transplant.

name: Yerba Mansa (Lizard Tail, Swamp Root)
description: Plant rhizome divisions into saturated, mineral-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a pond edge, rain garden low point, or irrigated bed that never fully dries out. The thick, spicy-scented roots have long been used by Southwestern Indigenous peoples and traditional herbalists as an antimicrobial wash and poultice, and the plant is equally valued as a striking wetland groundcover with white, cone-centered spring flowers reminiscent of anemones. It spreads steadily by rhizome once established, so give it room or a contained wet bed. Divide congested clumps in early spring to renew vigor and share starts. Matures in 90–120 days from transplant.

name: Yerba Mate
description: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Yerba Mate is the holly-family tree whose dried, roasted leaves produce the traditional caffeinated infusion consumed throughout South America — Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Brazil — where it is estimated that hundreds of millions of people drink it daily. The dried leaf contains caffeine, theobromine, and theophylline at levels between tea and coffee, producing an alert, focused energy without the jitteriness of coffee. The flavor is distinctly grassy, herbaceous, slightly bitter, and smoky from the traditional drying process, though home-dried leaf from fresh garden plants is milder and greener. In zone 9 the plant grows as a large, handsome evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy, dark green, oval leaves. Harvest young leaves in spring for the most delicate flavor; leaves harvested throughout the growing season become progressively stronger. The plant tolerates the moist, acidic, sandy loam soils of the Gulf Coast better than many ornamentals, thriving where high rainfall and humidity prevail. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yerba Santa (Mountain Balm, Consumption Weed)
description: Yerba santa is a drought-adapted evergreen shrub native to the dry chaparral and foothill slopes of California and southern Oregon, where it forms colonies from spreading underground rhizomes. Establish new plantings from rooted stem cuttings or transplanted rhizome divisions set into fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun, since the resinous, sticky, lance-shaped leaves and seed have a notoriously low, fire-cued germination rate in cultivation. Once established, the deep root system needs little to no summer irrigation and resents heavy clay or regular watering, which promotes root rot. Harvest mature leaves any time after the second year; it has a long history of use brewed into a bittersweet tea for coughs and colds, and the dried leaf was historically used to mask the bitterness of other medicines. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yezberry Maxie Honeyberry (Large-Fruited Japanese Haskap)
description: Maxie is a Japanese-type haskap bred by Oregon State University's Dr. Maxine Thompson and released under the Yezberry name for its unusually large, olive-shaped fruit, among the biggest of any honeyberry selection. It blooms later than Russian-derived haskaps, which lets it dodge most late-spring frosts and lines its flowering up with the other Yezberry cultivars it needs for cross-pollination. Give it well-drained, slightly acidic soil and afternoon shade in hot summer areas, since intense heat can scald the ripening fruit. Established plants tolerate winter cold to roughly -40F but need consistent moisture through fruit set to size up properly. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Yi Zhi (Sharpleaf Galangal)
description: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alpinia oxyphylla prefers high humidity and consistent moisture — mulch deeply, water regularly during the growing season, and cut back dead stems after dormancy; mulch root zone in zone 8 to protect from hard freezes.
