Alpinia oxyphylla (Yi Zhi or Sharpleaf Galangal) is a large, clumping, rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to the tropical forest understory of Hainan Island, Guangdong, and Guangxi provinces in southern China. It is one of the 'Four Southern Chinese Herbs' (Nan Yao Sì Hua) — Hainan-native plants of highest importance in Traditional Chinese Medicine — commercially cultivated at scale on Hainan as one of the most economically significant medicinal crops of the island. The aromatic, cone-shaped seed pods (harvested before full ripeness and dried) are used in TCM preparations for digestive complaints, frequent urination, and cold-deficiency conditions of the spleen and kidney. The spicy, warming, aromatic seeds taste of a combination of cardamom, pepper, and ginger. The plant is also ornamentally beautiful — tall, graceful, lanceolate leaves and elegant, arching inflorescences bearing white flowers with bright-pink suffused lips. Excellent partial-shade specimen for Southern gardens (zone 8–11) where the tall, tropical-looking foliage provides substantial presence even when not in bloom. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Yin Yang Bean
description: Also called orca or calypso bean, this dry bush bean bears striking black-and-white seeds resembling the yin-yang symbol. Direct sow 1 inch deep after frost danger passes, spacing 4 inches apart in rows. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant until they rattle before harvesting. Pull whole plants and cure them in a dry, airy spot if wet weather threatens the maturing crop. Reduce watering as pods fill to encourage even drying and prevent mold. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Yoder #68 Shagbark Hickory
description: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance. A named selection prized among nut tree enthusiasts for producing thinner-shelled, easier-to-crack nuts with excellent sweet flavor compared to typical wild shagbark hickory seedlings, which often have very thick, difficult shells that discourage home processing despite the excellent nut quality. Like all shagbark hickories it is a large, long-lived forest tree distinguished by its shaggy, peeling bark and needs considerable time, often a decade or more, before reaching significant nut-bearing maturity, making it a true multi-generational planting. Provide deep, well-drained soil and full sun, protect the young tree's long taproot from damage during transplanting, and be prepared for a long wait before the improved, easier-cracking nuts this selection is known for become available in quantity. Matures in 2555–3650 days from transplant.

name: Yoinashi Asian Pear
description: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yoinashi (Japanese for 'good pear') is a compact, rounded Asian pear reaching only 8–15 feet at maturity, making it one of the more manageable choices for a smaller Gulf Coast home orchard. The medium-sized fruit has lightly russeted gold-to-bronze skin and crisp, aromatic flesh with butterscotch and floral notes, ripening from mid-August into September and storing several months longer than many other Asian pear cultivars. Its early bloom period and good fire blight resistance are both useful traits in the humid South, though a late freeze during an unusually early bloom year can still reduce fruit set. Because it is self-fruitful, a single tree will produce a crop, but pairing it with another early-flowering Asian pear improves yields further. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: Yokohama Squash (Japanese Heirloom Moschata Squash)
description: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season. This dark-green, deeply ribbed Japanese heirloom shares Cucurbita moschata's excellent resistance to vine borers and squash bugs with better-known Gulf-adapted moschata types, making it a strong performer where humidity and pests knock out C. maxima and C. pepo squash. The dense, sweet orange flesh stores for months after curing in a warm, dry spot. Its heat tolerance and disease resistance make it a good companion or alternative to Seminole pumpkin for zone 8-10 gardeners wanting variety in their moschata winter squash. Matures in 95–110 days from seed.

name: Yolo Wonder Bell Pepper (Virus-Resistant Open-Pollinated Sweet Pepper)
description: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yolo Wonder is one of the most important open-pollinated bell pepper varieties in American horticulture — developed at the University of California, Davis, from California Wonder breeding stock specifically to incorporate resistance to tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), a common disease that devastates susceptible bell pepper varieties throughout warm-season gardens. Yolo Wonder produces large, four-lobed, blocky, thick-walled fruits in the classic California Wonder mold — essentially identical in fruit character to California Wonder but with the added practical advantage of TMV resistance that makes it significantly more reliable in gardens where the virus is endemic in the soil. The fruits ripen from green to red and have full, sweet bell pepper flavor at both stages. Yolo Wonder is the virus-resistant standard for open-pollinated bell pepper production that replaced California Wonder in many commercial plantings when TMV was recognized as a major production challenge. As an open-pollinated variety, seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The practical combination of virus resistance, large fruit size, thick walls, and excellent flavor has kept Yolo Wonder among the most commonly recommended open-pollinated bell peppers for home gardeners in disease-prone environments throughout the Gulf South. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Yomogi (Japanese Mugwort)
description: Grow yomogi in loose, humus-rich soil in the light shade beneath deciduous trees, where its silvery-backed leaves stay tender and less coarse than plants grown in full sun. Cut the youngest leaf tips repeatedly through spring and early summer before flowering begins, since older leaves turn tough and bitter. The finely chopped, blanched leaves give kusa mochi and other Japanese rice sweets their deep green color and a distinctive herbal, slightly resinous flavor, and the dried leaf is also steeped as tea. It spreads by rhizome, so give it a bounded bed or a large container if you want to keep its cheerful colonizing habit in check. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: York Elderberry (Largest-Cluster American Elderberry, New York Station Release)
description: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun; York elderberry is drought-tolerant once established but produces better with consistent moisture; prune back to 6–12 inch stubs in late winter every 2–3 years to rejuvenate; harvest berry clusters in August–September when fully ripe and deep purple-black; process or cook berries within days of harvest as raw elderberries contain cyanogenic compounds and must be cooked for safe consumption. York elderberry was released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in the mid-20th century as part of an American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) improvement program aimed at developing varieties with larger, more consistently sized berries and heavier individual clusters compared to wild-harvested elderberries. York is noted for producing some of the largest individual berry clusters of any named American elderberry variety — the flat-topped cymes (berry clusters) of York regularly reach 10–12 inches across and bear very heavy loads of ripe berries at the dark purple-black ripening stage. The individual berries are also somewhat larger than those of Adams and many other named varieties. This large cluster size and individual berry size make York an excellent choice for home elderberry production where maximum yield per plant and ease of harvest (larger clusters are faster to pick) are priorities. York ripens approximately 2 weeks after Adams, making the York + Adams combination the standard planting recommendation for home elderberry operations wanting to extend the harvest window and ensure reliable cross-pollination between the two varieties. All elderberry processing requires cooking — raw elderberries contain sambunigrin, a cyanogenic glycoside that is destroyed by heat; cooked elderberries are used for syrup, juice, jam, jelly, and elderberry wine. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: York Hazelnut (Late-Blooming Blight-Resistant Pollinizer)
description: York is an Oregon State University-released hazelnut selected mainly as a compatible pollinizer for eastern-filbert-blight-resistant orchard cultivars, shedding pollen over a long, late window that overlaps well with modern main-crop bloom times. It also carries strong blight resistance itself and produces a respectable crop of good-quality, medium-sized kernels in its own right, not just pollen. Grow it exactly as other hazelnuts, in deep, well-drained soil and full sun, and prune out root suckers each year to keep the tree in a single-trunk or multi-stem form rather than a thicket. Harvest as nuts drop free of the husk in early fall. Matures in 1095–1460 days from transplant.

name: York Imperial Apple (Pennsylvania Heirloom Keeping and Cider Apple)
description: Discovered near York, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, this apple built the Mid-Atlantic processing and cider industry for over a century thanks to its exceptional storage life and steady yields. The fruit has a distinctive lopsided, flattened shape and firm yellow flesh with a red blush, making it easy to pick out among other apples in the bin. Flavor is mild and sweet-tart, better suited to pies, cider blends, and long winter storage than fresh eating off the tree. Choose York Imperial where a long-keeping, reliable dual-purpose apple with real regional history matters more than dessert-apple looks. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Youngberry
aliases: Rubus caesius x idaeus x ursinus hybrid
description: The youngberry is a dewberry hybrid developed in Louisiana in the early 1900s by B.M. Young, producing very large, dark maroon-purple berries with a high juice content and sweet-tart flavor excellent for wine, juice, and pies. Culture is similar to boysenberry: train long, trailing canes on a T-trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; after harvest, cut all fruited canes to the ground and tie new primocanes in their place. The plants are less cold-hardy than standard blackberries and benefit from cane protection or mulching in zone 6 winters. Harvest when berries turn uniformly dark purple-black and release easily from the plug. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Yu Choy
description: Grown for its tender flowering stems, yu choy is a fast staple of Cantonese cooking with a mild, sweet flavor. Direct sow and thin to about 4 inches, keeping the soil consistently moist for quick, succulent growth. Harvest the main stem with a few leaves and a cluster of yellow buds when the first flowers just begin to open. Cutting the central stalk encourages tender side shoots for a second picking. Grow in cool weather to avoid the bitterness and toughness that come with heat. Matures in 40–50 days from seed.

name: Yuan Zhi (Chinese Senega Root)
description: May interact with sedative medications and is not a substitute for treating depression or cognitive decline. Start seed indoors in a sandy, gritty mix and transplant into lean, well-drained soil once the ground can be worked, since this steppe native resents wet, heavy conditions and is slow and seldom available outside specialty herb nurseries in the US. The pencil-thin roots are dried and aged for three to four years before use in TCM formulas traditionally taken to calm the mind, ease coughs with phlegm, and support memory. Matures in 1095–1460 days from seed.

name: Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce
description: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce is a large-headed butterhead type from the former Yugoslavia, producing open, loose heads of deeply wine-red outer leaves that contrast dramatically with the pale green-to-yellow interior heart — one of the most visually striking red butterhead lettuce varieties. The large heads weigh 8–12 ounces at maturity with a buttery, tender, mild flavor characteristic of the butterhead type. Yugoslavian Red maintains its deep red color even during the warmer stretches of fall in zone 9, when most red lettuces revert to green with heat — this color stability is a primary reason it is favored for warm-climate fall gardens. The loose, open head structure forms quickly and is ready for harvest at 50–60 days. The deep red outer leaves are high in anthocyanin antioxidants; the green interior provides visual contrast when the head is split or leaves are separated in a salad. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Yukina Savoy
description: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yukina Savoy is a distinctive Asian brassica with dark green, heavily blistered (savoy-textured), crinkled leaves on upright rosette plants — a texture entirely unlike the smooth leaves of tatsoi, pak choi, or komatsuna. The savoy-type leaf surface catches dressings and sauces in cooking and stands up to heat and wilting better than smooth-leaved types. The flavor is mild and slightly mustardy, similar to komatsuna but with a hint of sweetness, making it suitable for stir-fries, soups, steaming, and raw use as a baby green. Yukina Savoy is notably cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures below 20°F with light mulch) and heat-tolerant for a brassica, making it one of the most adaptable fall-through-spring greens for zone 9 gardens. Cut outer leaves for continuous harvest or cut the whole head at once for cooking. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Yukina Savoy Brassica (Japanese Savoyed Brassica Green, Gulf South Winter Leafy Green)
description: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 40 days or cut whole plant. Yukina Savoy (Brassica rapa var. narinosa 'Yukina Savoy') is a Japanese brassica green that occupies an unusual position in the Asian brassica spectrum: it is not clearly tatsoi (which is also var. narinosa but with very different flat-rosette form), not bok choy, not komatsuna, and not napa cabbage, but shares characteristics with all of these while maintaining its own distinctive identity primarily defined by the heavily savoyed (puckered, crinkled, blistered) texture of the leaves. The savoy texture in Yukina produces a leaf that is visually striking — deep green, heavily textured, with bold surface relief — and practically advantageous in cooking because the crinkled surface texture holds oils, sauces, and seasonings in a way that smooth-leaved brassicas cannot. The flavor is mild and versatile, somewhat between spinach and bok choy — appealing to gardeners who find other Asian brassicas too strongly flavored but want more character than spinach. Yukina Savoy is extremely productive in cool weather, producing large rosettes of leaves over an extended harvest season. It is widely used in restaurant and specialty market salad mixes in the American Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, where its striking appearance makes it a valuable visual element in mixed greens. Matures in 40–55 days from seed.

name: Yukon Gold Potato
description: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun; Yukon Gold is a Canadian-bred variety introduced in 1980 that transformed the North American potato market by demonstrating that consumers would pay a premium for a potato with inherently golden flesh and superior flavor. The medium-large, round to oval tubers have smooth, thin, slightly golden skin and deep butter-yellow flesh with a naturally buttery, slightly sweet flavor that requires no added butter to taste rich and satisfying. Yukon Gold is equally excellent baked, mashed, roasted, and sautéed — its lower starch content than russets makes it a smooth masher that doesn't become gluey. It is now the most widely planted 'specialty' potato in North America and has spawned an entire category of yellow-flesh varieties. In zone 9, plant January–February in loose, well-drained soil; hill soil around stems as they emerge. Harvest new potatoes when plants flower (60–70 days); for cured storage, harvest after vines die back. Cure at 60–70°F for one week before storing in a cool, dark location. Matures in 70–90 days from transplant.

name: Yutakamidori Tea
description: Developed in Japan and now the dominant tea cultivar in Kagoshima Prefecture, second nationally only to Yabukita, Yutakamidori is distinguished by notably late budbreak, a trait that helps the tender new growth escape the late spring frosts that can damage earlier-budding cultivars. Its leaves yield a rich, full-bodied, slightly sweeter sencha than Yabukita, making it a popular complement grown alongside Yabukita to spread out harvest timing and add flavor diversity to blended green teas. It tolerates the warmer growing conditions of southern Japan's Kagoshima region well. Cultivate it with the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and partial shade as other tea cultivars, hand-plucking young flushes for the best quality. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yuzu (Japanese Citrus)
description: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; yuzu is self-fruitful and produces better with cross-pollination, though single-tree production is adequate. Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a Japanese and Chinese citrus species of great antiquity, prized throughout East Asian cuisine — particularly in Japanese cuisine — for its extraordinary aromatic zest and juice that has a flavor profile unlike any other citrus: intensely fragrant, complex, floral-tart with notes of grapefruit, mandarin, and pine. The rough, bumpy, medium-sized (2–3 inch diameter) yellow fruits are rarely eaten whole but their zest and juice are foundational in ponzu sauce, yuzu kosho, miso soup, hot pots (nabe), cakes, and flavoring sake. Yuzu trees are extremely thorny (the thorns can be 3–4 inches long) and slow to begin fruiting (5–8 years from seed; 3–5 years from grafted trees) but among the most cold-hardy of all citrus, surviving to 14–17°F. Now widely available as grafted plants and grown by American chefs and home gardeners. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Yuzu Ichandrin (Cold-Hardy Ichang Papeda-Type Yuzu)
description: Yuzu Ichandrin is a naturally occurring hybrid of Ichang papeda and mandarin, grown for its intensely fragrant, lemon-lime-flavored, seedy 3-inch fruit used for zest, juice, and preserves rather than fresh eating. It is exceptionally cold-tolerant for citrus, with mature wood reported to survive brief exposure near 0F, making it one of the few citrus relatives worth trying in marginal zone 7b-8 gardens with a sheltered microclimate. The tree is notably thorny and vigorous, so allow generous space and prune to keep fruit within reach. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, mulch the root zone for winter, and expect fruit to ripen in late fall. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Yuzuquat (Cold-Hardy Lemon-Flavored Yuzu-Kumquat Hybrid)
description: Yuzuquat is a tri-generic hybrid, developed by Texas citrus breeder John Brown, combining hardy yuzu with 'Nagami' kumquat to produce a small tree far tougher than any true lemon. It carries fragrant spring flowers followed by egg-sized, sour, aromatic fruit that substitutes well for lemon in cooking and drinks, with juice and zest both usable in the kitchen. The compact, glossy-leaved evergreen tree suits a sheltered full-sun spot in the ground in zone 9a, or a large container that can be moved to cover on the rare hard-freeze night. Reduce watering during winter dormancy and keep soil sharply drained year-round to avoid root problems in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Za'atar Oregano (Biblical Hyssop, Lebanese Oregano)
description: Propagate from stem cuttings (seeds are slow and variable) and plant in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky soil in full sun; Origanum syriacum is native to rocky limestone hills of the eastern Mediterranean and requires excellent drainage — it declines in heavy or wet soil. Origanum syriacum is the 'true za'atar' plant of the Middle East — the primary ingredient in the za'atar spice blend that is ubiquitous in Levantine cuisine (the blend also includes sesame seeds, sumac, and salt). It is sometimes called Biblical hyssop because many scholars believe it is the ezov/aizov of the Hebrew Bible. The flavor is more intense, pungent, and earthy than Italian oregano with a distinctive mineral-herb complexity that makes it unique among Mediterranean herbs; harvest by cutting stems before full flowering for maximum flavor. Hardy only to zone 7; treat as an annual or pot plant in colder climates. In warm zones 8–11 it can be grown as a perennial hedge-shrub. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Za'atar Savory (Pink Savory, Thyme-Leaved Savory)
description: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; avoid overwatering — this plant demands dry conditions. Satureja thymbra (za'atar savory, pink savory, or thyme-leaved savory) is a compact, woody-based perennial from the dry limestone hillsides, macchia scrub, and garrigue of the Eastern Mediterranean — native to Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Lebanon, and Israel. It is one of several specific plants that go into the za'atar herb blend of the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean — alongside Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, and Micromeria fruticosa — and is also used independently as a culinary and medicinal herb. The flavor of S. thymbra is warm, complex, and intense: more resinous and thyme-like than common summer savory (S. hortensis), with oregano notes and a subtle bitterness that adds depth to za'atar blends, grilled meats, and herb breads. The plant forms a neat, mounding, evergreen (in mild winters) subshrub with small, deep-green, aromatic leaves and pink to light-purple flowers that attract bees abundantly in early summer. It performs well in Mediterranean-climate gardens (zone 8–10) with excellent drainage and lean soil — exactly the conditions found on Greek island hillsides. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: Za'atar Thyme
description: Surface-sow the tiny seed and press in without covering, as light aids germination. Grow in lean, gritty soil in full sun where it forms a low aromatic mound prized in Middle Eastern spice blends. Water sparingly once established, since the plant resents soggy roots and rots in wet clay. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the habit compact and encourage fresh flavorful leaves. In cold zones, mulch the crown or overwinter a potted plant under cover. Matures in 80–110 days from seed.

name: Zabala Fruit
description: Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil, since it is less cold-hardy than its Asian Lardizabalaceae relatives and appreciates protection from harsh winter wind. Deep maroon-purple flowers appear in winter, and because plants are typically dioecious, both a male and female specimen are needed to set the dark purple, sausage-shaped fruits filled with sweet white pulp. Its thick, glossy, evergreen trifoliate leaves make an unusual dense screen for shaded courtyards in mild coastal climates. Water regularly during establishment, then allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings once mature. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Zahter (Spiked Thyme, Za'atar Zahter)
description: Plant in well-drained, dry, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or stony soil in full sun; never plant in heavy, wet, or fertile soil, which causes rot and premature death. Thymbra spicata (zahter) is a small, woody, drought-tolerant perennial herb native to rocky limestone hillsides in Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon, and Israel — a close relative of thyme (Thymus) with a similar but distinctly more savory, spicy-bitter, oregano-like aroma and flavor profile. It is one of the traditional species used to make the Middle Eastern spice blend 'za'atar' (which includes multiple wild herb species depending on region), and the fresh or dried leaves and flowering tops are used to season meats, breads, cheese, and olive oil throughout Turkey and the Levant. In Turkish cuisine, zahter (za'atar in Arabic/Hebrew) is a primary herb for the spice blend used with olive oil and flatbread. The plant produces dense, spike-like inflorescences of pink to purple flowers in summer that are excellent for pollinators. In zone 9, it thrives in dry, alkaline, well-drained conditions and is highly drought-resistant once established. Matures in 60–90 days from transplant.

name: Zapallito Squash (Zapallito de Tronco)
description: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, since this compact bush type needs less room than typical maxima squash and tolerates close spacing well. A traditional South American variety popular in Argentina and Uruguay, it produces small, pale-green, round to slightly ribbed fruit best picked young and tender at 3-4 inches for use in stuffed-squash dishes and stews. Frequent picking every couple of days encourages continued production through the season, much like a zucchini. Its compact habit and rapid maturity make it well suited to smaller garden beds and container growing. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.

name: Zapotec Pleated Tomato
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and stake or cage the indeterminate vines; Zapotec Pleated is a Mexican heirloom tomato from the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, producing large (8–16 ounce), deeply ridged and pleated, hollow, orange-red fruits unlike any standard tomato — the characteristic heavy ribbing creates a natural cavity in the hollow center that makes Zapotec Pleated the ideal stuffing tomato for chiles-rellenos-style preparations, baked stuffed tomatoes, and presentations where the natural hollow serves as an edible container. The thick, meaty, sweet-acidic flesh has excellent flavor and the hollow structure minimizes the gel and seeds that make most large tomatoes watery when sliced. The unusual appearance — rustic, ridged, and slightly irregular — reflects the traditional Mesoamerican approach to tomato selection where utility (hollow stuffing structure, thick walls) was prioritized alongside flavor. In zone 9 the fall planting often produces the most attractive, well-colored fruits as cooler October temperatures enhance both color development and flavor concentration. Matures in 80–90 days from transplant.

name: Zavory Pepper
description: Zavory was bred to deliver the full fruity, floral aroma of a habanero with almost none of the heat, registering only around 100 Scoville units compared to 30,000 or more for a standard habanero. Glossy, bullet-shaped fruit ripens through green, yellow, orange, and finally red on prolific, heat-loving plants, and any single stage can be harvested for eating. Because it needs a long, warm season to size up and ripen fully, start seed early indoors and grow it in the hottest, sunniest spot available. It suits cooks who want habanero flavor in salsas, chutneys, or fresh salads without the burn. Matures in 90–100 days from transplant.

name: Zebrina Mallow (French Hollyhock, Striped-Flower Ornamental Mallow)
description: Zebrina bears the same edible young leaves, stems, and 'cheeses' (round seed pods) as ordinary common mallow, but is grown chiefly for its striking flowers — pale lilac-white petals boldly veined and streaked with deep violet-purple, giving each bloom a distinctive candy-striped appearance that has made it a fixture of English cottage borders for generations and earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Direct-sow into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; like the species, Zebrina tolerates poor soil and drought once established but produces the most abundant bloom with regular moisture through summer. Plants form an upright, branching clump 3-4 feet tall that flowers continuously from early summer into fall, and readily self-seeds true to type in favorable conditions, though scattered seedlings sometimes revert toward plain pink species flowers. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and reduce unwanted self-sowing where a tidier planting is wanted. Matures in 60–90 days from seed.

name: Zebrune Shallot
description: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out in early spring, spacing them several inches apart. This eschalion, or banana-type shallot, produces large, elongated, easy-to-peel bulbs with coppery-pink skin and a sweet, mild flavor prized by chefs. Grow it much like an onion with steady moisture and weed control, then cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot; they store well for months. Matures in 100–120 days from transplant.

name: Zedoary
description: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curcuma zedoaria is dormant in winter — cut back dead stems after frost and mulch heavily in zone 8–9, then lift and store rhizomes in colder climates. Curcuma zedoaria (Zedoary or White Turmeric) is a large, ornamental, clumping ginger-family perennial native to northeast India (Assam), Bangladesh, and the Malay Archipelago, cultivated throughout South and Southeast Asia for its fat, fleshy, grayish-white rhizomes with a distinctive camphor-lemon-pepper-bitter aroma and flavor profile entirely different from common turmeric (C. longa). The rhizomes are used fresh, dried and ground, or steam-distilled for essential oil in Indonesian, Thai, and Indian cuisines for curries, pickles, and medicinal preparations; zedoary was also an important European medieval spice — traded under the name 'zedoary' in Arab and European commerce as early as the 6th century CE. Medicinally, the rhizomes are used in Ayurvedic and Unani medicine as a digestive tonic, carminative, and anti-inflammatory. The plant is also ornamentally attractive — large, paddle-shaped leaves with a distinctive purple midrib stripe, and showy, cone-shaped pink-and-white flower spikes emerge from the ground before the main foliage in spring. Excellent food garden spice for partial-shade positions in zones 8–11. Matures in 270–365 days from transplant.

name: Zefa Fino Fennel (Bolt-Resistant Swiss Florence Fennel)
description: Direct sow into rich, evenly moist soil since fennel forms a taproot and transplants poorly; Zefa Fino is the Swiss-bred workhorse behind much of the modern Florence fennel seed trade, prized for holding in the ground and resisting bolting far longer than older open-pollinated types even under fluctuating spring temperatures. Plants form large, dense, rounded white bulbs with a sweet, mild anise flavor and crisp texture that stays tender rather than turning pithy as the season progresses. Mound soil around the swelling base as the bulb develops to keep it pale and tender, and harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball to a fist before the plant sends up a flowering stalk. Matures in 80–90 days from seed.

name: Zenjimaru Persimmon (Ancient Japanese Sweet Persimmon)
description: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Zenjimaru is among the oldest named persimmon cultivars in cultivation, traced to a temple orchard in Japan roughly 800 years ago, and is historically important as the earliest documented source of the naturally sweet, non-astringent trait later bred into many modern kaki cultivars. It is a pollination-variant type: fruit that develops seeds from cross-pollination loses its astringency and becomes sweet and edible while still firm, while unpollinated, seedless fruit stays astringent until it softens fully. The tree bears small to medium, round, orange-red fruit with a thin glossy skin and rich, sugary flavor, and is notably vigorous, disease-resistant, and productive across a range of soils and climates. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to reduce limb strain, and harvest in mid to late fall once fruit colors fully. Matures in 730–1460 days from transplant.

name: Zenmai (Japanese Royal Fern)
description: Close relative of the ornamental royal fern, this East Asian species is grown specifically for its edible spring fiddleheads, which emerge wrapped in distinctive rusty-brown wool and are harvested young, then parboiled and soaked to remove bitterness before use in Japanese and Korean cooking as zenmai. Leave most fronds on the plant to mature into tall, upright fertile and sterile fronds that provide good textural contrast through summer and clean yellow fall color. It thrives in the same moist, humus-rich, part-to-full-shade conditions as other Osmunda species and resents drying out, making it a good fit for rain gardens or pond edges. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Zephyr Summer Squash
description: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost; Zephyr is a bush-type summer squash that requires no staking and produces heavily from a compact plant. Zephyr is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid summer squash with a visually striking bicolor pattern — straight, yellow upper portion with a distinctive lime-green tip — and very nutty, firm flesh with a noticeably drier texture than standard yellow squash that holds up well to sautéing, grilling, and roasting without becoming waterlogged. Harvest at 4–6 inches for peak tenderness and flavor; the compact bush plants are excellent for small gardens where the large rambling vines of traditional squash would be impractical. Powdery mildew tolerance and prolific production make it a reliable summer standby. Matures in 54–65 days from seed.

name: Zeppelin Delicata Squash
description: Zeppelin is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by organic seed growers to improve on older delicata strains, selected specifically for better disease tolerance and more uniform, elongated cream-and-green striped fruit. Like other delicata types the thin, edible skin means the whole squash can be roasted without peeling, and the dense, sweet, corn-and-chestnut-like flesh has made delicata squash increasingly popular at farmers markets. Vines run further than bush delicata types, so give them room to sprawl or train them up a sturdy trellis to save garden space. Because it is a stable open-pollinated variety rather than a hybrid, seed can be saved from isolated plantings for a true-breeding crop. Matures in 90–100 days from seed.

name: Zermatt Leek (Swiss Giant Early Leek)
description: Zermatt, also sold as Swiss Giant Zermatt, is an early European leek that reaches harvest size faster than most fall or winter types, making it a good lead-in variety ahead of longer-season leeks like Tadorna in a succession planting. It grows tall with a sweeter, more delicate flavor than onion, well suited to creamy soups and light braises. Grow in well-drained soil with consistent moisture and harvest before hard freezes arrive, since it lacks the deep winter hardiness of true storage leeks. Matures in 70–80 days from transplant.

name: Zespri SunGold Kiwi (Zesy002 Gold Kiwifruit)
description: Zespri SunGold, registered under the cultivar name 'Zesy002', was selected by the Zespri and Plant & Food Research breeding program in New Zealand from a cross made around 2000 at Te Puke and released to growers in the early 2010s as a hardier, more disease-tolerant replacement for the original gold kiwifruit variety, 'Hort16A', which had been devastated by bacterial canker (Psa). The smooth, hairless, bronze-gold skin lacks the pointed beak of its predecessor and often shows a faint pink to red blush around the stem end, surrounding sweet, golden-yellow flesh that is markedly less acidic than green kiwifruit and notably high in vitamin C. Because Zespri holds exclusive commercial rights and licenses SunGold vines only to contracted growers within its marketing system, home gardeners generally cannot legally obtain true 'Zesy002' vines outside that licensed network, unlike most other gold kiwi cultivars. Where it is grown commercially, it follows standard golden kiwifruit culture: a sturdy overhead trellis, a compatible male pollinator vine, and open pruning to maximize airflow and reduce Psa pressure. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Zestar! Apple (Minnewashta)
description: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1999 out of the same breeding program that later produced Honeycrisp, Zestar! ripens in late summer, weeks ahead of most main-season apples, filling a gap for gardeners wanting a crisp fresh apple early in the season. The flavor pairs bright tartness with a distinctive brown-sugar sweetness and a notably crunchy texture for such an early apple. Winter hardiness is excellent, letting it succeed in cold northern gardens where many early apples struggle. Grow it for the first crisp, flavorful apple of the year, but plan to eat or process the crop quickly since it does not store as long as later-season cultivars. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Zeus Hops (High-Alpha American Bittering Hop)
description: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Zeus (also sold as Columbus/Tomahawk/Zeus, or CTZ) is a high-alpha-acid American bittering hop developed for efficient, potent bitterness in a wide range of beer styles, with a pungent, slightly herbal and resinous aroma alongside its primary role as a bittering rather than aroma hop. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges vigorously each spring, climbing 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; because its high alpha-acid content delivers strong bitterness from a relatively small harvest, even a modest home planting can supply a meaningful amount of bittering hops for brewing. Harvest cones in late summer when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dry promptly. Like other hops, Zeus prefers a cool, long-day growing season and performs poorly through the sustained heat and humidity of Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, most open site available and expect a lighter yield than in traditional hop-growing regions. Matures in 120–180 days from transplant.

name: ZigZag Jujube
description: ZigZag is grown as much for its winter silhouette as for its fruit, with branches that kink sharply at each node to create a strikingly angular, sculptural form once the leaves drop in fall. Fruit is large for the species and turns a deep chocolate-brown at full ripeness, with a sweet, apple-like flavor typical of well-ripened jujube. The tree stays naturally compact and is partially self-fertile, though planting a second cultivar such as Autumn Beauty nearby improves both fruit set and size. Like other jujube selections, ZigZag develops a deep taproot early on and becomes strongly drought-tolerant once past its first year or two in the ground. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Zill Mango (Early-Bearing Florida Dooryard Mango)
description: Zill was developed by the well-known Zill nursery family of Boynton Beach, Florida, and is valued for its compact tree size, precocious and consistent bearing, and early ripening relative to most other Florida cultivars. The small to medium fruit has deep red skin and mild, sweet, moderately fibrous flesh. Its smaller, more manageable stature makes it a practical choice for home gardens with limited space or for container growing in cooler parts of zone 9. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is damaged by even brief cold snaps. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Zimmerman Pawpaw
description: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Zimmerman is an Ohio-origin pawpaw selection known for very sweet, richly flavored flesh with a notably low seed count for the species, making the fruit easier to eat fresh than many wild seedlings. It ripens in the midseason window and produces medium to large fruit on a vigorous, cold-hardy tree with the classic pyramidal pawpaw form and large, tropical-looking drooping leaves. Because pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen, interplant Zimmerman with an unrelated cultivar such as Susquehanna or Taytwo, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief spring bloom to improve fruit set in home orchard settings. Matures in 1825–2190 days from transplant.

name: Zinfandel Wine Grape
description: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Zinfandel thrives in warm climates and is prone to uneven ripening within a single cluster, requiring careful harvest timing. Genetically identical to the Croatian variety Crljenak Kaštelanski and Italy's Primitivo, this vigorous red wine grape produces loose clusters of thin-skinned, sweet grapes that ripen unevenly on the same bunch, with green, pink, and fully ripe purple-black berries sometimes present simultaneously, a quirk growers must manage carefully to avoid overripe, raisined fruit alongside underripe berries at harvest. Vigorous and productive in warm, sunny climates, it also produces the pink blush wine known as White Zinfandel when pressed with minimal skin contact, making a single variety the source of two very different wine styles. Manage canopy density to promote even ripening, monitor clusters closely as harvest approaches given the variety's uneven ripening tendency, and provide full sun and heat for the best sugar development. Matures in 730–1095 days from transplant.

name: Zinner Pecan (Scab-Resistant Thin-Shelled Type-2 Pecan)
description: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible Type-1 pollinator such as Gafford nearby, since pecans are wind-pollinated and cross-pollination between a Type-1 and Type-2 cultivar produces much better nut set than a single cultivar alone. Zinner is a Type-2 pecan valued for combining good resistance to pecan scab with a notably thin, easy-cracking shell that yields plump, high-quality kernels, making it appealing for home growers who want good disease resistance without sacrificing nut quality. As with other scab-resistant cultivars, it is a lower-maintenance choice for Gulf South home orchards without a regular commercial fungicide program. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches consistent bearing age. Matures in 1825–2555 days from transplant.

name: Zipper Cream Cowpea (Easy-Shelling Cream Southern Pea)
description: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they turn from green to a pale cream-tan color and feel plump. Zipper Cream is a beloved Southern heirloom cowpea named for its distinctive, easy-shelling pods — the seam splits open with a simple pinch or tug, quickly releasing rows of smooth, cream-white peas without the tedious shelling required by many other cowpea types. The mild, sweet, creamy flavor and tender texture of the peas make Zipper Cream one of the most popular fresh-shelling Southern peas for the table, while its productive, heat-loving vines perform reliably through the hottest stretch of summer when many other vegetables falter. As with all cowpeas, the roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods regularly at the cream stage for the best fresh-eating quality, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for shelf-stable dried peas. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Zipper Cream Pea (Cream 40 Pea)
description: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Zipper Cream is one of the most popular Southern peas in home gardens and small farms of the Gulf Coast for its exceptionally easy shelling — the pods split along a natural 'zipper' seam that allows the cream-colored peas to fall out with almost no effort, a practical advantage that makes large harvests much faster to process. The peas themselves are plump, cream-white, and have a mild, sweet, buttery flavor prized in Southern pea dishes, boiled fresh with ham or bacon, or frozen for winter use. A bush-type plant that produces heavily over a long season; heat and drought tolerant once established. One of the most recommended varieties for first-time Southern pea growers because of the easy harvest and reliable production. Matures in 65–75 days from seed.

name: Zlata Radish (Golden-Skinned Yellow Radish)
description: Sow seed directly half an inch deep in cool, moist soil and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. Zlata is a round, golden-yellow-skinned radish with crisp white flesh and a mild flavor, notably slower to turn pithy or overly hot than many red radishes when the weather warms, which extends its harvest window into the edge of the cool season. The bright yellow skin adds welcome color contrast to salads, radish plates, and pickles alongside standard red and white types. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across, and keep soil consistently moist through growth, since inconsistent watering causes cracked or overly pungent roots. Matures in 25–30 days from seed.

name: Zloty Lan German Chamomile
description: Zloty Lan is a vigorous Polish-bred tetraploid selection of German chamomile prized for larger flower heads and a notably higher essential-oil content than common seed strains, making it a favorite among growers who dry the blooms for tea. Sow directly where plants are to grow after the soil has warmed, pressing seed onto the surface without covering, and keep the bed evenly moist until germination. Harvest flower heads by hand every few days once petals reflex downward, which keeps the plant blooming for weeks and yields the most concentrated oil. Deadheading spent flowers or letting a few go to seed will both extend bloom and allow this self-seeding annual to return the following year. Matures in 60–75 days from seed.

name: Zodiac Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Machine-Harvest Processing Cultivar)
description: Zodiac is a thornless trailing blackberry from the USDA-ARS/Oregon State cooperative breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, bred from two thornless selections, ORDS 2707-1 and ORDS 2785-2. It produces high, early-to-midseason yields of small-to-medium, glossy, conical berries with firm texture and a strong, aromatic, well-balanced sugar-acid flavor, and is bred primarily for machine harvest in commercial processing fields. Like other trailing types it needs vigorous training onto a multi-wire trellis and generous row spacing. Its Pacific Northwest breeding background means it is best suited to cooler-summer climates and will need trialing for heat and disease tolerance before relying on it in hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens. Matures in 365–548 days from transplant.

name: Zolfino Bean (Italian Pratomagno Yellow Heirloom Bean)
description: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Zolfino beans are bush type and do not require staking; harvest when pods are dry and papery. Zolfino is an Italian heirloom bean from the Pratomagno hills of Arezzo province in Tuscany, where it has been grown for centuries at elevations between 1,300 and 2,600 feet on the slopes of the Pratomagno massif — the specific local environment (poor, well-drained, slightly acidic volcanic soil with cool nights) contributes to the bean's exceptional quality. Zolfino (the name likely derives from 'zolfo,' Italian for sulfur, referring to the pale yellow color) is a Slow Food Presidium product, meaning it is recognized as an endangered, culturally important food requiring preservation support; only farmers in the Pratomagno area using traditional methods are technically authorized to use the Zolfino denomination. The small (thumbnail-sized), round, pale yellow beans have extraordinarily thin skins — almost imperceptible when eaten — and cook to a dense, creamy, buttery texture entirely different from the grainy or mealy texture of common dried beans; the flavor is rich, earthy, and complex with sweet undertones. Outstanding in simple Italian preparations: olio e fagioli (beans with olive oil), in ribollita soup, or simply simmered with sage, garlic, and good olive oil. Matures in 75–95 days from seed.

name: Zoom Witloof Chicory (Forcing Belgian Endive)
description: 'Zoom' is a widely grown F1 witloof chicory selected for producing homegrown Belgian endive, valued for uniform, blemish-free, torpedo-shaped roots that size up reliably even without the deep, stone-free soil older open-pollinated witloof strains prefer. Sow directly in late spring to early summer and grow through the season to develop a taproot roughly 1.5 to 2 inches across; in fall, cut the foliage back to an inch above the crown, lift the roots, and hold them cold until ready to force. To produce chicons, replant the trimmed roots upright and closely spaced in a deep container of moist sand or soil, cover completely to exclude all light, and hold at 50-60F; pale, tightly furled chicons are ready to cut in three to four weeks. Because the roots bulk up more evenly than many older varieties, this hybrid tends to give a higher yield of usable chicons per planting. Matures in 105–115 days from seed.

name: Zucchini Elite (AAS-Winning Compact Dark-Green Hybrid Zucchini)
description: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed, spacing plants about 30 inches apart in full sun. Elite is an All-America Selections-winning hybrid valued for uniform, glossy dark-green fruit, strong yields, and improved tolerance to common summer squash viruses. Its tidy, semi-compact bush habit performs well in raised beds and smaller gardens where sprawling squash would be impractical. Harvest fruit at 6-7 inches for the sweetest flavor and most tender skin, checking plants every day or two during peak production. Matures in 47–50 days from seed.

name: Zumi Crabapple (Calocarpa)
description: Calocarpa is a naturally occurring selection of the Zumi crabapple, a hybrid found in Japan, chosen for its especially abundant crop of small, bright red, long-persisting fruit. Fragrant white flowers open from soft pink buds in mid-spring against fine-textured, lobed foliage, followed by pea-sized fruits that ripen red in fall and typically hang on well after leaf drop, providing months of winter interest and a reliable food source for birds in the lean months. The broadly pyramidal, densely branched tree eventually grows quite large, so site it with plenty of room away from walkways where dropped fruit could become a nuisance. It is a dependable, cold-hardy choice for a specimen tree where winter fruit display is a priority. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Zuni Gold Bean (Pueblo Heirloom Golden Dry Bean)
description: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 4-6 inches apart in rows. Zuni Gold is a Native American heirloom bush dry bean traditionally grown at Zuni Pueblo in the arid high desert of New Mexico, its smooth, golden-yellow seeds cooking up creamy with a mild, buttery flavor prized in traditional Zuni and Southwestern cooking. Adapted over generations to the low rainfall and short growing season of the Southwest, it tolerates dry conditions better than many bean varieties bred for wetter climates. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before harvesting for storage as a dry bean. Matures in 85–100 days from seed.

name: Zutano Avocado (Low-Chill Type B Avocado, Early Season Pale Green Avocado)
description: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Zutano performs best with a Type A companion (Hass, Mexicola) for cross-pollination; harvest September through November when fruits are full-sized and soften slightly over 5–7 days after picking; Zutano fruits stay green at ripeness and have a watery, mild flavor — better for cooking than fresh eating but valuable for early-season harvest timing. Zutano avocado is a California-developed variety from the Mexican race lineage with one of the lowest chill requirements of any commercial avocado, performing well in the warmest avocado-growing regions and ripening its crop earlier in the season (September–November) than the dominant Hass variety (January–June harvest). The variety was developed by R.J. Hazzard in Fallbrook, California in the 1920s and entered the California nursery trade where it became valued primarily as a cross-pollinator for Hass and other Type A varieties due to its abundant, reliable Type B pollen production and good overlap with Hass bloom times. Zutano's fruit quality is frankly mild and somewhat watery compared to Hass, Fuerte, or Reed — the flesh is pale yellow-green, less rich in oil, and more watery in texture — making it less valued for fresh eating than the richer varieties. However, Zutano provides practical value as: (1) the best early-season fresh avocado available from your own tree in September when Hass season hasn't started; (2) a reliable Type B pollinator that ensures good fruit set on Hass and other Type A trees in the same garden; and (3) a lower-chill, cold-somewhat-tolerant variety for zone 9 margins where Hass reliability is borderline. Matures in 1095–1825 days from transplant.

name: Zwolle Seedling Rhubarb
description: Zwolle Seedling is a long-established Dutch rhubarb valued for its heavy early flush of thick, bright red-pink stalks and its tolerance of forcing under a pot or dark cover for an extra-early crop. Compared with slower-establishing cultivars it comes into full production quickly, making it a favorite where growers want an early, dependable harvest without a long wait after planting. Flavor is well balanced between tart and sweet, with tender flesh that cooks down smoothly. As with all rhubarb, satisfy its winter chilling requirement for strong spring growth, harvest by pulling rather than cutting, and never eat the leaves, which are toxic. Matures in 365–730 days from transplant.

name: Zydeco Twist Okra (AAS-Winning Spineless Spiral-Podded Okra)
description: Zydeco Twist was an All-America Selections regional winner recognized for pods that spiral and twist rather than growing straight, a shape that lets the pods stay tender and stringless a few days longer than most straight-podded types before they turn woody. The plant is compact and spineless, with no itchy prickles on the pods or foliage, making harvest far more comfortable than on older bristly okra varieties. Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost in full sun, and pick pods every day or two once production starts, since okra quickly overshoots the tender stage in hot weather. Its shorter, well-branched habit fits into smaller garden beds better than tall heirloom okra varieties while still producing heavily through the heat of summer. Matures in 50–60 days from seed.
